## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margins of the individual pages and indicating the material treated; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any of the Fathers wrote on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture.

This is the most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reissued works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection itself: a single, methodical, chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now assembled for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# Exposition on the Catholic Epistles

## Prologue on the Seven Canonical Epistles

(Cave, *Literary History*, under the year 700.)

[Col. 0009A] James, Peter, John, and Jude published seven Epistles, which ecclesiastical usage calls “Catholic,” that is, universal. The Epistle of James is placed first because he undertook the governance of the Church of Jerusalem. In the catalogue of the apostles, Peter and John are ordinarily named first. Yet the fountain and origin of evangelical preaching, beginning [“from Jerusalem” is absent] spread throughout the whole world. The apostle Paul also honored the dignity of that see by naming him when he said: “James, Cephas, and John, who were regarded as pillars of the Church” (Gal. 2). Or certainly, because he sent his Epistle to the twelve tribes of Israel, who were the first to believe, it rightly had to be placed first.

Peter’s Epistle is rightly second, because he wrote to the “elect resident foreigners,” who in Greek are called *proselytes*—that is, to those who had been converted from paganism to Judaism and from Judaism to the grace of the evangelical election. John’s Epistles are rightly placed third, because he wrote to those who believed from among the Gentiles, although they had previously belonged neither by nature nor by profession to the chosen people. Finally, many ecclesiastical writers—including Saint Athanasius, bishop of the Church of Alexandria—affirm that his first Epistle was written to the Parthians.

Jude’s Epistle is rightly placed last because, although he too is great, he is nevertheless inferior to the three preceding apostles; or because the Epistle of James was written first, then Peter’s, and afterward John’s, and for that reason they still retain the order in which they were written. For it is established that blessed James completed his martyrdom in the thirtieth year after the Lord’s Passion. Peter suffered in the thirty-eighth year, that is, in the last year of Nero, and in his second Epistle he himself wrote: “I know that the putting off of my tabernacle will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ also made clear to me by revelation.” Hence it is evident that he wrote this Epistle when his Passion was approaching, whereas James had departed to Christ much earlier.

Nor would it have been fitting to separate Peter’s Epistles from one another, since he wrote them to the same Churches. John, moreover, wrote his Epistles and Gospel together much later. After the Lord’s death he returned from exile and found that, in his absence, the Church had been disturbed by heretics, whom he attacks in his Epistles, frequently calling them Antichrists.

# On the Epistle of the Blessed James

[Col. 0009]

## Chapter One

[Col. 0009B] “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes that are scattered abroad: greeting.”

The apostle Paul said of this James: “James, and Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should preach among the Gentiles, and they among the circumcision” (Gal. 2). Therefore, since he had been appointed an apostle to the circumcision, he took care to teach those who belonged to the circumcision by speaking with them when present, and to console, instruct, rebuke, and correct them by his Epistle when absent.

“To the twelve tribes,” he says, “that are scattered abroad: greeting.” We read that, after blessed Stephen had been killed by the Jews, “on that day there arose a great persecution against the Church which was at Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles.” To those, then, who had been scattered and had suffered persecution for righteousness’ sake, he sends the Epistle.

But he sent it not only to them [Col. 0010B], but also to those who, having received the faith of Christ, had not yet taken care to become perfect in works, as the following parts of the Epistle testify; and likewise to those who continued entirely without faith and even endeavored, as far as they could, to persecute and disturb the faith itself in believers [Col. 0010C]. All of them, however, were exiles from their homeland, scattered by various circumstances, and wherever they were they were oppressed by enemies through innumerable massacres, deaths, and afflictions, as ecclesiastical history sufficiently explains.

We also read in the Acts of the Apostles that, at the time of the Lord’s Passion, they had already been scattered far and wide, as Luke says: “There were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under heaven” (Acts 2). Many of those nations are also named individually when he continues: “Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the inhabitants of Mesopotamia,” and so forth (ibid.).

Thus James encourages the righteous not to fall away from the faith amid temptations; he chastises sinners and admonishes them to abstain from sins and to advance in virtues [Col. 0011A], lest those who had received the mysteries of faith prove fruitless—or even liable to condemnation. He admonishes unbelievers to do penance for the killing of the Savior and for the other crimes in which they were entangled, before heavenly vengeance should destroy them piecemeal, whether invisibly or visibly.

“Count it all joy, my brethren, when you fall into various temptations.”

He begins with the more perfect, so that his word may proceed in order to those whom he saw as dead and in need of correction and elevation to the summit of perfection. It should be noted that he does not simply say, “Rejoice,” or “Count it joy,” but “Count it all joy when you fall into various temptations”: consider yourselves worthy of complete joy if it should happen that you endure temptations on account of Christ’s faith [Col. 0011B].

“This is thankworthy,” Peter says, “if, because of conscience toward God, a person endures grief, suffering unjustly” (1 Pet. 2). His fellow apostle Paul likewise says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come, which shall be revealed in us.” All the apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been deemed worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus. Therefore we ought not to be sorrowful when we are tempted, but when we have been overcome by temptations.

“Knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience. But let patience have its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.”

“For this reason,” he says, “you are tested by adversities: so that you may learn the virtue of patience, and through it demonstrate and prove that you carry in your heart a firm faith in the future reward.” This passage should not be considered contrary, but rather understood as agreeing, with what the apostle Paul says: “Knowing that tribulation produces patience, and patience testing” (Rom. 5).

Patience produces testing because the person whose patience cannot be overcome is thereby proved to be perfect. This too is taught below, when he says: “Let patience have its perfect work.” And again: “The testing of your faith produces patience.” That process causes the faithful to be exercised through patience, so that by it their faith may be proved to be as perfect as possible.

“But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all generously and does not reproach anyone, and it shall be given him.”

All saving wisdom must indeed be requested from the Lord, because, as the wise man says [Col. 0011D], “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and it has always been with him” (Sir. 1). Nor can anyone understand or possess wisdom through free choice without the help of divine grace, however strongly the Pelagians contend otherwise.

Here, however, he seems specifically to be speaking of the wisdom we need to use amid temptations. “If any of you,” he says, “cannot understand the benefit of the temptations that come upon the faithful for the purpose of testing them, let him ask God to grant him understanding, so that he may recognize with how much fatherly affection the Father chastises his children, whom he is preparing to make worthy of an eternal inheritance.”

He wisely says, “who gives to all generously,” so that no one, conscious of his own weakness, should distrust his ability to receive when he asks, but rather everyone should remember [Col. 0012A] that “the Lord has heard the desire of the poor.” As the same writer says elsewhere: “The Lord has blessed all who fear him, both small and great” (Ps. 113).

But because many ask the Lord for many things without deserving to receive them, he adds how they ought to ask if they wish to obtain what they request.

“But let him ask in faith, without doubting.”

That is, let him conduct himself by living well in such a way that he is worthy to be heard when he asks. For whoever remembers that he has not obeyed the Lord’s commands rightly despairs of the Lord attending to his prayers. It is written: “The prayer of one who turns away his ear from hearing the law shall be an abomination” (Prov. 28).

“For he who doubts is like a wave of the sea driven and tossed by the wind.”

A person whose conscience is gnawed by sin and who doubts his reception of heavenly rewards easily abandons the state of faith, in which he seemed to serve God in tranquility, at the impulse of temptations. At the will of the invisible enemy, like a gust of wind, he is carried into various errors of vice.

“A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.”

“In all his ways,” he says, both in adversity and prosperity. A person is double-minded who kneels to pray to the Lord and utters words of prayer, yet, while his conscience accuses him within, doubts that he can obtain what he asks.

A person is double-minded who wishes both to rejoice here with the world and to reign there with God. Again, a person is double-minded who, in the good deeds he performs, seeks not inwardly the reward but outwardly the approval of others.

Hence a certain wise man rightly says: “Woe to the sinner who enters the earth by two paths” (Sir. 2) [Col. 0012C]. The sinner enters the earth by two paths when what he displays in his actions belongs to God, while what he seeks in his thoughts belongs to the world. All such people are unstable in all their ways, because they are very easily discouraged by the adversities of the world and entangled by its prosperities, so that they turn aside from the way of truth.

“Let the lowly brother glory in his exaltation.”

“For this reason,” he says, “you ought to count it all joy when you fall into various temptations: because everyone who humbly suffers adversity for the Lord will receive from him the exalted rewards of the kingdom.”

“But the rich in his humiliation.”

The verb “let him glory” is understood from the preceding verse. It is clear that this was said by way of mockery, which in Greek is called *irony*. “Let him,” he says [Col. 0012D], remember that the glory in which he boasts of his riches and despises—or even oppresses—the poor must come to an end, so that, humbled, he may perish eternally with that purple-clad rich man who despised Lazarus in his poverty.

“For as the flower of the grass he shall pass away.”

The flower of grass delights both smell and sight, but it very quickly loses the grace of its beauty and fragrance. The present prosperity of the ungodly is therefore most fittingly compared with it, since it cannot possibly endure for long.

“For the sun rises with its burning heat and dries up the grass, and its flower falls.”

He calls the sun’s burning heat the sentence of the strict Judge, by which the temporal splendor of the reprobate is consumed at the end.

The elect also flourish, but not like grass. “The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree” [Col. 0013A] (Ps. 91). The unrighteous flourish temporarily; like grass, they will quickly wither, and like garden plants they will soon fall. The righteous flourish like trees, because their flower—that is, their most certain hope—awaits an enduring fruit. Their root also, namely charity, remains fixed and immovable.

For this reason the wise man says: “I have produced fruit like a vine, with the sweetness of fragrance” (Sir. 24). Finally, the righteous Naboth preferred to die rather than transfer his ancestral vineyard into a garden of vegetables. To transform the ancestral vineyard into a garden of vegetables is to exchange the strong works of virtue that we received from the teaching of our fathers for the fragile delight of vices.

The righteous prefer to lay down their life rather than choose earthly goods over heavenly ones. Hence the psalm is almost speaking of them when it says [Col. 0013B] that “they shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall yield its fruit in its season” (Ps. 1), and so forth.

But what of the unrighteous? “The beauty,” he says, “of his countenance shall perish.” So also the rich man shall wither in his ways. He does not mean every rich man, but the one who trusts in the uncertainty of riches.

By setting the rich man in contrast with the humble brother, he shows that he is speaking of the rich man who is not humble. Abraham too was rich in this world, yet after death he received the poor man into his bosom and left the rich man in torments. He did not leave him in torments because he was rich—for Abraham himself had been rich—but because he had refused to be merciful and humble, qualities that Abraham possessed.

Conversely, Abraham received the beggar Lazarus, not because he was poor in possessions—for Abraham himself had been poor in that respect—but because he was humble and innocent, qualities that Abraham himself possessed.

Such a rich man, therefore—that is, the proud and impious man who places earthly joys before heavenly ones—shall wither in his ways. That is, he shall perish in his wicked actions because he neglected to walk in the Lord’s straight path.

But while he falls like grass before the sun’s heat, the righteous person, by contrast, like a fruitful tree, both endures wholly the heat of that same sun—that is, the Judge’s severity—and brings forth the fruits of good works, for which he will be rewarded eternally. Hence it is rightly added:

“Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.”

A similar saying occurs in the Apocalypse: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life,” which, he says, “God has promised to those who love him” (Rev. 2) [Col. 0013D].

He openly admonishes us that we ought to rejoice all the more in temptations, the more certainly it is clear that God often lays a greater burden of temptations upon those whom he loves, so that through the exercise of temptations they may be proved perfect in faith. When they have truly been proved faithful—that is, perfect and complete, lacking in nothing—they rightly receive the promised crown of eternal life.

“Let no one, when he is tempted, say: ‘I am tempted by God.’”

Up to this point he has discussed the temptations that we suffer externally, by the Lord’s permission, for the sake of being tested. He now begins to speak of those that we endure inwardly, at the instigation of the devil or through the persuasion of the weakness of our nature.

He first destroys the error of those who think that, just as good thoughts are admittedly inspired in us by God, so evil thoughts are also generated in our minds at his instigation. Therefore no one, when he is tempted, should say that he is tempted by God—namely, by the temptation through which the rich man, walking in his ways, withers.

That is, no one who commits robbery, theft, false witness, murder, adultery, or other such acts should say that he had to commit them because God compelled him, and therefore could not in any way avoid carrying them out.

“For God is not a tempter of evils.”

The word “temptations” is understood. He himself tempts no one—namely, with the temptation that deceives the merciful into sinning.

There are two kinds of temptation: one that deceives and another that tests. In the first sense, God tempted no one; in the second, God tested Abraham. Concerning this the prophet also asks: “Prove me, O Lord, and try me” (Ps. 25).

“But each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire,” and so forth.

He is drawn away from the right path and enticed toward evil. Jerome says of this verse in *Against Jovinianus*:

“Just as God is perfect in good works—for it is not of the one who wills or the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy and assists, that we are able to reach the goal—so in evils and sins our seeds are the incitements, but completion belongs to the devil. When he sees that we have built hay, wood, and stubble upon the foundation of Christ, he sets fire beneath it. Let us build gold, silver, and precious stones, and he will not dare to tempt us, although even in this our possession is not certain or secure: for the lion lies in ambush in secret places in order to kill the innocent. The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, but temptation through tribulation tests righteous people.”

“Then, when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is completed, brings forth death.”

Temptation operates in three ways: suggestion, delight, and consent. Suggestion belongs to the enemy, while delight and consent belong to our weakness.

If, when the enemy suggests sin, we do not wish to take delight in or consent to it, the temptation itself becomes an occasion of victory for us, through which we may deserve to receive the crown of life. But if, through the enemy’s suggestion, we are gradually drawn away from a right intention and begin to be enticed by vice, we offend by taking delight in it, but have not yet incurred the fall of death [Col. 0014D].

If, however, the action of sin conceived in the heart follows the delight, then the enemy departs victorious, and we, already guilty of death, remain behind. To establish this by examples:

Joseph was tempted by the words of his mistress. But because he had no lustful desire, he could be tempted only by suggestion, not by delight or consent; therefore he escaped victorious.

David was tempted by the sight of another man’s wife. Because he had not yet overcome the appetite of the flesh, he was drawn away and enticed by his own desire. When he completed the crime he had conceived, he incurred the guilt of death and was condemned by his own mouth, although he escaped it through repentance.

Judas was tempted by love of money. Because he was avaricious, he was drawn away and enticed by his own desire and fell into destruction by consenting [Col. 0015A].

Job was tempted in many ways. But because he had not placed either his possessions or the health of his body before divine love, he could indeed be tempted by the enemy’s suggestion, but was entirely unable to consent to or even delight in sin.

When it is said, “Sin, when it is completed, brings forth death,” this points in the opposite direction to what was said above concerning the one who endures temptation: “When he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life.” Just as the person who overcomes temptation deserves the rewards of life, so the person who is enticed by his desires and overcome by temptation deservedly incurs the ruin of death.

“Do not err, my beloved brethren.”

He means: do not suppose that the temptations of vices originate from God [Col. 0015B]. We know, of course, that some people, because of the merits of their preceding crimes, have been permitted by the just severity of the Judge to fall into further crimes. Hence the apostle says: “Because they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not fitting, being filled with all iniquity” (Rom. 1).

“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights.”

After teaching that the vices by which we are tempted do not come from God but are present in us through ourselves, he shows conversely that whatever good we do, we receive through God’s gift. Hence he calls him the Father of lights, knowing him to be the author of spiritual gifts. This agrees with the apostle Paul’s statement: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4).

“With whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration.”

Because there is no mutability in God’s nature, and because his light, like the light of this world, is not interrupted by any shadow of change, it is clear that he sends us only gifts of light and not also the darkness of errors.

“Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth.”

The Lord also says in the Gospel: “You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you” (John 15). And through the prophet Hosea: “I will love them freely” (Hos. 14).

What he had said—that every good and perfect gift descends from God—he confirms by adding that it was not through our merits but through the gift of his will that, by the water of regeneration, he changed us from children of darkness into [Col. 0015D] children of light.

“That we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.”

Lest we think that, when he says he brought us forth, we have become what he himself is, he shows that by this adoption a certain primacy among creatures has been granted to us.

Some have translated these verses as follows: “Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, so that we should be the firstfruits of his creatures.” That is, so that we might be better than the other creatures that we see.

The Law commanded the firstfruits of crops and animals to be consecrated to the Lord; it also ordered the firstfruits of gold and silver to be brought for the work of the tabernacle—that is, the finest things among metals. And the prophet Jeremiah said of God’s ancient people: “Israel was holiness to the Lord, the firstfruits of his harvest” (Jer. 2).

[Col. 0016A] “You know, my beloved brethren.”

“It is well known to you,” he says, “that you have had the means of falling to the depths from yourselves, while your illumination by the Lord has occurred not through your own foresight but through heavenly grace going before you.”

“Let every person be swift to hear, but slow to speak.”

Here he instructs the hearer in moral precepts. He rightly first admonishes him to apply his ear to the teacher as quickly as possible, but to open his mouth for teaching only slowly, because it is foolish for anyone to wish to preach to others what he himself has not learned.

Whoever loves wisdom should first, as he admonished above, ask it from God. Then, as a humble hearer, he should seek a teacher of truth. In the course of his activity, he should carefully restrain his tongue not only from idle speech, but also from proclaiming the very truth he has recently learned [Col. 0016B].

Solomon, writing about the distinction between times, says: “A time to keep silence, and a time to speak” (Eccl. 3). For this reason the Pythagoreans, trained in the discipline of natural knowledge, ordered their pupils to remain silent for five years, and only then permitted them to preach.

For it is safer for truth to be heard than preached. When it is heard, humility is preserved; but when it is preached, it is scarcely possible for a little boasting not to creep into anyone, however slightly. Jeremiah, describing the life of a well-trained young man, therefore rightly counts the modesty of silence among the first exercises of virtue. “It is good,” he says, “when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He shall sit alone and keep silence” (Lam. 3).

“And slow to anger.”

The maturity of wisdom is perceived only with a tranquil mind. For it is written that “anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Eccl. 7).

He does not turn the speed of anger into such slowness as to approve it; rather, he admonishes us to beware lest anger creep upon us in the hour of disturbance and quarrels. Or, if it should creep upon us, we should restrain its force within the barriers of the mouth and, when the critical hour has passed, purge it more freely and completely from our heart in due time.

Alternatively, he commands us to be slow to anger so that we do not turn the serenity of our countenance into sternness for arbitrary reasons, but only when a definite reason exists. For example, if we see that those close to us—especially those entrusted to our care—cannot otherwise be corrected, then we should show them severity in word or even in stricter judgment, while maintaining, insofar as human nature permits, a serene state of mind [Col. 0016D].

For, I believe, Phinehas, Samuel, Elijah, and Peter were slow to anger, yet they put sinners to death either by the sword or by the word. Moses too, although he was a very meek man, left Pharaoh, whom he saw to be incorrigible, in great anger and threatened him with punishment, which he also carried out.

“For the anger of man does not work the righteousness of God.”

The meaning is straightforward: whoever carelessly subjects himself to the vice of anger, even if he appears righteous to human beings, is not yet perfectly righteous in the divine judgment.

But the passage can be understood more profoundly because it is said of the Lord: “But you, O Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility” (Wis. 12). Whatever human judge, having lost tranquility of mind, judges a delinquent—even if he judges justly—cannot imitate the righteousness of the divine judgment, into which no disturbance can fall.

“Therefore, putting away all filthiness and abundance of wickedness, receive with meekness the implanted word.”

First he commands both body and mind to be cleansed from vices, so that people may become worthy to receive the word of salvation. Whoever does not first turn away from evil cannot do good.

He calls all filthiness that of both flesh and soul. “Receive,” he says, “the implanted word”: that is, receive by learning the word that we place in your hearts through preaching.

Or the meaning should be understood in this way: the word implanted in you on the day of redemption, when God freely brought you forth, you should now receive more perfectly, fulfilling in works what you already hold in teaching [Col. 0017B].

“Which is able to save your souls.”

Even if you suffer temptations in the body or are consumed by death at the hands of the faithless.

“But be doers of the word, and not hearers only,” and so forth.

Paul says the same concerning those who observe the Law: “It is not the hearers of the Law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the Law shall be justified” (Rom. 2).

And in the Apocalypse, after John had said, “Blessed is he who reads, and those who hear the words of the prophecy of this book,” he immediately added: “and keeps the things written in it” (Rev. 1).

“But whoever looks into the law of perfect liberty and continues in it.”

He calls the grace of the Gospel “the law of perfect liberty.” For “the law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7). And elsewhere: “You have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons” (Rom. 8). Again: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Cor. 3). The Lord himself says: “If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed” (John 8).

“Not becoming a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this person shall be blessed in his deed.”

Blessedness is prepared not by the fruitless hearing of the word but by carrying out the work. Thus the Lord also says to his disciples: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” (John 13).

“If anyone thinks himself religious but does not bridle his tongue, deceiving his own heart, this person’s religion is worthless.”

Above he had admonished us not only to hear the word of God but also to do it. Now he adds that even if someone appears to practice by his deeds the commandments of the Lord that he has learned, he nevertheless boasts in vain of the righteousness of his works if he does not also restrain his tongue from slander, lies, blasphemies, foolish talk, excessive speech itself, and the other things by which he is accustomed to sin.

As Paul, affirming the saying of a pagan poet, says: “Evil communications corrupt good manners” (1 Cor. 15).

“Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this.”

He beautifully adds “before God and the Father,” because there are people who appear religious to human beings but are regarded as profane by God. Hence Solomon says: “There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end leads to death” (Prov. 14).

[Col. 0018A] “To visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself undefiled from the world.”

Because he had said that the doer of the work would be blessed in his deed, he now states which deeds especially please God: namely, mercy and innocence.

By commanding us to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, he signifies everything that we ought to do mercifully toward our neighbor. The extent of its value will be revealed at the very time of judgment, when the Judge will say: “As long as you did it to one of the least of these my brethren, you did it to me” (Matt. 25).

By commanding us to keep ourselves undefiled from the world, he shows all the things in which it is fitting for us to preserve our purity. Among them are the matters he had instructed us above to observe: that we should be slow to speak and slow to anger.

# Chapter Two

“My brethren, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glory, with partiality.”

He shows that those to whom he was writing had indeed been imbued with evangelical faith, but were empty of works. Because he had taught that the Lord’s commandments were to be fulfilled through almsgiving to the poor, he saw that they had acted in the opposite way: what ought to have been done for the poor on account of eternal rewards, they had instead done for the rich on account of earthly advantages. He therefore rebukes them as they deserved.

At the beginning of this statement he appropriately calls our Lord Jesus Christ “the glory,” so that we may remember that obedience is owed rather to his commands. Although he is “the brightness of glory” (Heb. 1), he rewards with eternal glory whatever is given to the poor for love of him, rather than any human dignity being honored—of human beings it has generally been said: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass,” and so forth (Isa. 40).

“For if a man wearing a gold ring and splendid clothing enters your assembly, and a poor man in dirty clothing also enters, and you pay attention to the one wearing the splendid clothing and say to him, ‘You sit here in a good place,’ while you say to the poor man, ‘You stand there,’ or, ‘Sit here beneath my footstool’—”

In explaining this statement, let us use the words of blessed Augustine:

“If we refer this distinction between sitting and standing to ecclesiastical honors,” he says, “we must not think it a small sin to hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glory, with partiality. For who could tolerate a rich man being chosen for a seat of honor in the Church while a poorer man, more learned and holier, is despised?

“But if he is speaking of ordinary places at which people sit, who sins here—if indeed anyone sins—unless he judges inwardly within himself in such a way that the richer man appears better to him precisely because he is richer?”

This is what he seems to have indicated by adding:

“Have you not judged among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?”

He continues:

“Listen, my beloved brethren.”

“Observe more carefully,” he says, “because those who are richer in the world are not therefore better in the divine judgment.”

Does not God choose the poor in this world, rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom that he promised to those who love him? He calls poor those who are humble and who, through contempt for visible things [Col. 0019A] but faith in invisible riches, appear despicable to this world. For our Lord Jesus Christ chose such people when he said: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom.” He chose such people when he created poor parents for himself, by whose service he would be nourished when he came into the world. Yet he made them illustrious and noble through the expectation of the kingdom to come.

But you have dishonored the poor man—namely, the one to whom it was said, “You stand there,” while the man wearing the gold ring was told, “You sit here comfortably.”

Do not the rich oppress you by their power, and do they not themselves drag you before the courts? Do they not blaspheme the good name that has been invoked over you? Here he shows more plainly who the rich are, concerning whose humiliation [Col. 0019B] and destruction he had spoken above: namely, those who put their riches before Christ and are wholly alienated from his faith. Moreover, by their power they oppress those who believe, dragging them before the courts of more powerful men and blaspheming the name of Christ, which is above every name. That many Gentiles, and especially the leading men among the Jews, did this in the time of the apostles is shown clearly enough both in the Acts of those same apostles and in the Epistles of the apostle Paul.

If, however, you fulfill the royal law according to the Scriptures, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you do well. But if you show partiality, you commit sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors. See how he calls them transgressors, because the rich man is told, “Sit here,” and the poor man, “Stand there.” Therefore, lest they think that transgressing the law in this single matter was a contemptible [Col. 0019C] sin, he immediately added:

“Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all. For he who said, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ also said, ‘You shall not kill.’ Now if you do not commit adultery but do kill, you have become a transgressor of the law.”

This refers to what he had said: “Convicted by the law as transgressors.” Since this is so, it seems to follow—unless it is shown that the passage must be understood in another way—that anyone who says to the rich man, “Sit here,” and to the poor man, “Stand there,” giving the former greater honor than the latter, must be judged guilty of every crime: of idolatry, blasphemy, adultery, murder, and, since it would be tedious to list them all, of every offense. For by stumbling in one point, [Col. 0019D] he has become guilty of all.

It must therefore be asked how one becomes guilty of all by stumbling in one point, if he has kept the whole law. Or is it perhaps because love is the fullness of the law, by which God and one’s neighbor are loved, and upon these commandments the whole law and the prophets depend? Thus, rightly, the one who acts against that on which everything depends becomes guilty of all. No one sins except by acting against it. For “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,” and whatever other commandment there may be, are summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Love does no evil to one’s neighbor. “Love, therefore, is the fullness of the law” (Rom. XIII). He thus becomes guilty of all by acting against that on which everything depends.

Why, then, are sins not said to be equal? Or is it perhaps because the one who sins more gravely [Col. 0020A] acts more seriously against love, while the one who sins more lightly acts against it less seriously? Nevertheless, even if he stumbles in one point, he is guilty of all, because he acts against that on which everything depends.

So speak, and so act, as those who are beginning to be judged by the law of freedom. The law of freedom is the law of love, concerning which it is said: “If, however, you fulfill the royal law according to the Scriptures, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself,’ you do well.” Therefore, he says, by speaking and acting in this way, take care that, by loving your neighbors, you may deserve to be loved by God, and that, by showing mercy to your neighbors, you may await mercy at the divine judgment.

Alternatively: just as the law given through Moses is the law of servitude, so the grace of the Gospel, which came through Jesus Christ, is the law of freedom, as the Apostle testifies when he says: [Col. 0020B] “For you did not receive the spirit of servitude again in fear, but you received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Hebr. VII). And again: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (II Cor. III). If, therefore, you speak, he says, and act in this way, as those who are to be judged by the law of freedom, this is what it means to begin to be judged.

For the one who despises the law of Moses will be judged more severely than the one who despises the natural law. Likewise, the one who knowingly despises the grace of the Gospel will be judged more severely than the one who disregards the decrees of the Mosaic law. “For from everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required; and from the one to whom they have entrusted much, they will demand more” (Luke XII). Hence the Apostle also says: “For if the word spoken through angels was confirmed, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of [Col. 0020C] reward, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? It first began to be proclaimed through the Lord and was confirmed to us by those who heard” (Hebr. II). And again: “Anyone who invalidates the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded as common the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” (Hebr. X).

Both interpretations, however, look toward one end: namely, that by responding to divine grace with righteous deeds, we may be kind to one another, compassionate, and forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave us.

For judgment will be without mercy for the one who has not shown [Col. 0020D] mercy. The one who could have shown mercy but did not do so before being judged will be judged without mercy. Although this is rightly understood of all the merciless, it is nevertheless entirely clear that the greater the mercy someone has received from the Lord, the more unjustly he has denied mercy to his needy neighbor, and the more justly he will pay the penalty for his impiety. Therefore the Lord wisely warns: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven. Give, and it will be given to you” (Luke VI). Judgment, therefore, will be without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy.

But mercy triumphs over judgment. For just as the one who [Col. 0021A] did not show mercy will grieve when condemned at God’s judgment, so the one who did show mercy will rejoice and be glad when rewarded.

Alternatively: mercy triumphs over judgment. It is not said, “Mercy defeats judgment.” For it is not opposed to judgment; rather, it triumphs over it because more people are gathered through mercy—though only those who have shown mercy. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V). Again, “Mercy triumphs over judgment,” that is, mercy is placed above judgment. Wherever an act of mercy is found, even if there happens to be something deserving punishment at the judgment, the fire of sin is extinguished as though by a wave of mercy.

What good is it, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but has no works? And so forth. From this point he discusses the works of mercy at greater length, so that he may console those whom he had previously terrified greatly [Col. 0021B] by his teaching, while admonishing them how even daily sins—without which no one lives here—may be expiated by daily remedies. Otherwise, the person who, by stumbling in one point, becomes guilty of all, since “we all stumble in many ways” (James III), would carry to the tribunal of so great a Judge a great mound of guilt gathered little by little and would not find the mercy he had failed to show. Rather, by forgiving and giving, he may deserve to have his debts forgiven and the promises fulfilled for him.

But if a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, “Go in peace, keep warm and eat your fill,” but does not give them what the body needs, what good is that? So also faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself, and so forth. [Col. 0021C] It is clear that just as mere words of piety do not restore a naked or hungry person if food and clothing are not also provided, so faith preserved only in words does not save. For without the works of love by which it may revive and be animated, it is dead in itself.

Nor is the Lord’s statement contrary to this: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI). It must be understood there that only the one who truly believes is meant—namely, the one who practices through his actions what he believes. And since faith and love cannot be separated from one another, as the Apostle Paul testifies when he says, “There is faith that works through love” (Gal. V), the apostle John appropriately offers concerning love a statement like the one James gives concerning faith: “Whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his [Col. 0021D] heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (I John III).

You believe that there is one God; you do well. The demons also believe—and tremble. Do not think that you accomplish something great by believing that there is one God. The demons do this too; they believe not only in God the Father but also in the Son. Hence Luke says: “Demons also came out of many, crying aloud and saying, ‘You are the Son of God.’ And rebuking them, he would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ” (Luke IV).

They not only believe but also tremble. Hence the legion that possessed the man cried out to him in a supplicating voice: “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me” (Mark V). Those, therefore, who [Col. 0022A] do not believe that God exists, or who do not fear the God in whom they believe, must surely be judged more sluggish and more insolent than the demons.

But neither is believing that God exists and trembling before him a great thing if one does not also believe in him—that is, if one does not retain love for him in one’s heart. For it is one thing to believe someone, another to believe that he exists, and another to believe in him. To believe someone means to believe that what he says is true. To believe that he exists means to believe that he is God. To believe in him means to love him.

Many, even wicked people, can believe that what he says is true. They believe it is true but do not wish to do it, because they are lazy when it comes to action. To believe that he himself is God, the demons too have been able to do. But to believe in God is known only by those who love God—those who are Christians not merely in name but also in deeds and life. For without love, [Col. 0022B] faith is empty; with love, it is the faith of a Christian; without love, the faith of a demon.

Therefore, whoever does not wish to believe in Christ does not yet even imitate the demons. And if he already believes in Christ but hates Christ, he possesses a confession of faith in fear of punishment, not in love of the crown. For the demons too feared being punished. Finally, when blessed Peter confessed the Lord, saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI), he seems to have uttered from his mouth almost the same words that the demons also uttered. But their confession, because it was spoken with hatred, was rightly condemned by Christ; Peter’s, because it proceeded from inward love, was rewarded with eternal blessedness.

But do you wish to know, O empty man, that faith without works is idle? The apostle Paul, preaching that a person is justified by faith without works, [Col. 0022C] was not properly understood by those who took his statement to mean that, once they had believed in Christ, they would be saved by faith even if they acted wickedly and lived criminally and shamefully. This passage of the present Epistle explains how the same meaning of the apostle Paul is to be understood.

Therefore James makes greater use of the example of Abraham, showing that faith is empty if it does not act well, because Paul too used Abraham’s example to prove that a person can be justified without works. When Paul recalls Abraham’s good works, which accompanied his faith, he clearly shows that the apostle Paul does not teach through Abraham that a person is justified by faith without works in such a way that, if someone believes, good works are no concern of his. [Col. 0022D] Rather, he teaches this that, if someone believes, good works are no concern of his. Rather, he teaches this so that no one may think that he reached the gift of justification, which is found in faith, through the merits of earlier good works.

The Jews wanted to place themselves above the Gentiles who believed in Christ because they said that they had reached evangelical grace through the merits of the good works contained in the law. For this reason many of them who believed were scandalized that Christ’s grace was extended to uncircumcised Gentiles. Hence the apostle Paul says that a person can be justified by faith without works—that is, without preceding works. For once justified by faith, how can a person fail to act justly?

When James therefore says:

“Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered his son Isaac upon the altar?”

he elegantly urged that an example of good action should be learned [Col. 0023A] from the patriarch himself, encouraging those who had believed from among the Jews to follow the deeds of their first and greatest ancestor, as worthy descendants.

And because he was urging them not to fail in temptations and to prove their faith through works, he aptly set forth the patriarch’s example, by which he could instruct them in both virtues. For what greater temptation, apart from those involving wounds to one’s own body, can befall someone than that an old man should be compelled to kill his only and most beloved son? How, then, would he delay giving his tunics or food to the poor for the love of God, when the old man did not delay giving to death, at the Lord’s command, the son whom he had received as his heir?

Thus what the blessed Paul says agrees with this statement of blessed James: “By faith [Col. 0023B] Abraham offered Isaac with this statement of blessed James: “By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, and he was offering his only-begotten son, he who had received the promises, to whom it had been said, ‘In Isaac shall your offspring be called,’ considering that God was able even to raise the dead” (Hebr. XI).

In one and the same deed, then, James praised the magnificence of blessed Abraham’s works, while Paul praised the steadfastness of his faith. Yet Paul did not put forward a statement different from or contrary to James. Both knew that Abraham was perfect in faith and works; therefore each of them praised in him especially the virtue that he saw his own hearers needed more.

Because James was writing to people who held faith without works to be idle, he appropriately brought forward an example in which Abraham’s principal faith—faith that had previously been praised by the testimony of Scripture [Col. 0023C]—might be seen—might be seen not to have lain sluggishly idle in his heart, but to have burned, already proved, for obedience to divine commands.

Paul, however, was instructing people who exalted themselves in their works without the grace of faith. He showed that “without faith it is impossible to please God” (ibid.). To rebuke and correct their presumption, he gathered examples of all the patriarchs and plainly taught that all had been approved by the testimony of faith.

Hence, speaking specifically of Abraham, he added that he offered Isaac by faith, “considering,” he says, “that God was able even to raise the dead” (ibid.). He therefore joined the deed to faith: Abraham wished to offer his son immediately because he believed that God would raise him at once. He believed that God would raise him after [Col. 0023D] death because he believed it was true what he had heard: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called.”

The blessed James likewise subsequently explains this union of both virtues, saying: “You see that faith was working together with his works, and by works faith was brought to completion, and the Scripture was fulfilled that says: ‘Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God.’”

The apostle Paul argued most firmly from this testimony in his Epistle to the Romans, plainly teaching that the power of faith is so great that, once its mysteries have been received, it can immediately make a person righteous who had been ungodly. Because Abraham believed God with such great and fervent faith that he was ready in spirit to do everything God commanded, his faith was rightly counted as righteousness by God, [Col. 0024A] who knew Abraham’s faith, who knew Abraham’s faith.

And so that we too might know the faith by which he was justified, God tested him by commanding him to offer his son. Through works faith was brought to completion—that is, it was shown to be perfect in his heart by the carrying out of the works.

Even today, if someone who has recently come to the faith receives baptism, proposes to serve God’s commandments with his whole heart, and immediately departs this life, he departs justified by faith without works, because, by God’s providence, he did not have time in which to act and prove his faith. But those who survive for a long time after receiving the sacraments of faith and do not take care to persist in good works must be reminded of what blessed James, having set forth the example of Abraham’s faith and works, immediately added:

[Col. 0024B] “You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.”

When he says “by works,” he means by works of faith. For no one can possess perfect works without faith, whereas many may possess faith without works if they do not have time for action. Concerning such people it is said: “He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding or deceit should mislead his soul” (Wis. IV).

Likewise, was not Rahab the prostitute also justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way? Lest they make the excuse that they were unable to imitate the works of so great a father as Abraham—especially since no one now compelled them to offer and kill their children, and since God himself instead prohibits this through the Scriptures—he adds the example of a criminal woman, a foreign woman, who nevertheless, through works of mercy [Col. 0024C] and the duty of hospitality shown to God’s servants even at the peril of her life, deserved to be justified from her sins, enrolled as a citizen of the Israelite people, counted in the catalogue of their royal lineage, inserted into the genealogies of our Lord and Savior himself, which descend from the stock of the patriarchs, and rescued from the destruction of her perishing homeland, whose faithlessness she had abandoned.

By these examples of the woman converted to better things, he urges his hearers to avoid entering the homeland that is perishing and to remember that, having withdrawn from its crimes by believing, they must also separate themselves from it through fruitful works, so that they may deserve to be joined to the assemblies of the saints and attain fellowship with their Redeemer.

He therefore urges them to receive the messengers of Jesus—that is, to listen gladly to the preachers of the word of the Gospel [Col. 0024D]. And when they learn that these preachers have been rejected by their fellow citizens or indeed sought for execution, as the Acts of the Apostles often records, they themselves should instead, having received from them counsel for their salvation, send them back in peace to the Lord Jesus.

The foregoing book of the Acts of the Apostles indicates that this was done at Jerusalem by Gamaliel, the teacher of the blessed apostle Paul, who had once been held in honor by the entire Jewish people and is now more greatly honored by the whole Church of Christ through the revelation of the relics of the protomartyr Stephen. When the Jewish council was planning to kill the apostles, Gamaliel by wiser counsel frustrated their designs and sent the apostles, rescued from their ambushes, back unharmed to preach Jesus.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0025A]

### Do not become many teachers, my brothers.

The Acts of the Apostles makes clear how great a zeal there was among believers in apostolic times to spread the word more widely. Thus Apollos, a man highly learned in the Scriptures, knowing only the baptism of John, preached Christ boldly. Yet because he was wise, as soon as a teacher came to him, he very easily supplied what he lacked and returned fully equipped to the task of preaching.

Others, departing from Judea for Antioch in greater ignorance, taught believers from among the Gentiles that they could not be saved unless they were circumcised according to the law of Moses. They imposed no small burden of controversy upon the chaste preachers. Blessed James therefore removes these and similar teachers from the ministry of the word, lest they obstruct those who were able to fulfill it properly.

Knowing that you will receive the greater [Col. 0025B] judgment. For just as the one who has ministered well acquires for himself an honorable rank, so the one who, being unlearned, attempts to usurp the office of teaching, and who does not announce Christ sincerely, will deserve a greater judgment of condemnation than if he perished alone in his own crime.

For we all offend in many ways. He did not say, “You offend,” when he was reproving those whom he saw to be less perfect both in knowledge and in conduct, and was removing such people from the teacher’s chair. He feared that they might either harm the little ones by preaching in error and turn their ears away from hearing teachers by getting there first, [Col. 0025C], or else defile the things they preached correctly with the filth of incorrect action, thereby darkening the path of evangelical perfection with a false opinion.

Rather, he says, “We offend,” since we are Christ’s; so the Apostle speaks. He prefaced the statement with “in many ways” and added “all,” so that all the imperfect might look around themselves more cautiously in action and speech, recognizing with greater certainty that not even the perfect good—those who walk under the guidance of the Holy Spirit’s grace—can pass through the way of this life without some offense of sin, according to what is written elsewhere: “The heavens are not clean in his sight” (Job XV). And as Solomon says: “For there is no just person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccl. VII).

[Col. 0025D] If anyone does not offend in speech, he is a perfect man. How does he say that the man who does not offend in speech is perfect, when he had already said, “We all offend in many ways”? Is it because the elect can offend in many ways and yet remain perfect through perseverance?

Rather, it must be understood in this way. For there are different kinds of offenses. The elect offend in one way, the reprobate in another, as Solomon testifies when he says: “For the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble into evil.” Even if the righteous person happens to offend through the weakness of the flesh or ignorance, he nevertheless does not cease to be righteous. For just as this kind of offense is daily and unavoidable, so there is also a daily remedy of prayers and good works, which quickly raises the righteous person who has stumbled, lest he fall to the ground and soil the wedding garment of love and faith with the dust of vices.

If anyone, then, does not offend [Col. 0026A] in speech, he is a perfect man—in that speech whose offense human frailty can avoid: deceitful speech, slander, cursing, pride, boasting, excuses for sins, rivalry, dissension, heresy, lying, perjury, and also idle speech, as well as excessive speech about matters that seem necessary. Whoever guards himself from offense in such speech is a perfect man. “The one who guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from distress” (Prov. XXI).

He is also able to guide the whole body with a bridle. This verse depends on what precedes. “If anyone,” he says, “does not offend in speech, he is a perfect man, and he is also able to guide the whole body with a bridle.” This plainly means: if anyone avoids the slip of the tongue, which is almost [Col. 0026B] unavoidable, he learns, through a firmly established habit of the same restraint, to keep watch over the other members of the body—which can more easily be disciplined—so that they do not turn aside from the right path.

If we put bridles into horses’ mouths so that they may obey us, and we direct their whole bodies. The unspoken sense is: how much more ought we to put the bridle of restraint into our own mouths so that we may obey our Creator, seeking through the guarding of the tongue to attain uprightness also in our actions?

If, however, we read, as some manuscripts have it, “Just as we put bridles into horses’ mouths,” there will be no difficulty, because it is joined to what follows: “So also the tongue is a small member,” and so forth.

Behold, even ships, although they are large and are threatened by strong [Col. 0026C] winds, are turned by a very small rudder wherever the impulse of the one directing them wishes. The large ships on the sea are human minds in this life, whether good or bad. The strong winds by which they are driven are the desires of the mind, by which they are naturally compelled to do something through which they reach either a good or an evil end.

The rudder by which such ships are turned wherever the impulse of the one directing them wishes is the intention of the heart. Through it the elect, after crossing the waves of this world, reach the happy harbor of their heavenly homeland; but the reprobate, as though destroyed by Scylla or Charybdis amid the stormy errors of this life—which they did not know how to abandon—perish.

And because “the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart,” it is rightly added:

[Col. 0026D] So also the tongue is a small member, and it makes great boasts. It certainly raises up great rewards if the impulse of the directing mind governs it well, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “The one who understands will possess the helm.” But if it governs badly, it raises up great destruction, to itself and its own, in the opposite direction. Hence Solomon also says: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII).

It therefore raises up life when it teaches the Church well; but, on the contrary, death when it does something grave. For he says this against those who, deprived both of life and of knowledge, presumed to teach and therefore injured the Church all the more.

If it is read as it is found in certain manuscripts, “And it boasts greatly,” the kind of boasting intended here is the one mentioned later, when, after listing several vices of the tongue, he added: “But now you exult in your pride” [Col. 0027A]. Every such boasting is evil. The mother of blessed Samuel also restrains us from it with pious exhortation, saying: “Do not multiply lofty speeches, boasting” (I Sam. II). Thus the tongue boasts greatly when, despising the thoughts and words of others, it vaunts itself as uniquely wise and eloquent.

Behold how great a fire sets alight how great a forest. “How great” means “how small.” Indeed, the manuscripts also read: “Behold, a small fire.” For just as a fire growing from a small spark often sets a great forest ablaze, so the lack of restraint of the tongue, nourished by its frivolities, destroys wherever it reaches a great abundance of good works and many fruits of the spiritual life; it also generally consumes countless leaves of speech [Col. 0027B] that had seemed excellent.

And the tongue is a fire, the universe of iniquity. The tongue is a fire because, by speaking wickedly, it devours the forest of virtues. Hence the wise man says of the fool: “The opening of his mouth is a conflagration.” Opposed to this fire of destruction is that salutary fire which, consuming the hay and straw of vices with the tongue, illuminates the hidden places of the heart. By it holy teachers are inflamed, so that they themselves burn with love and kindle others, as it were with fiery tongues, by preaching.

Concerning them it is rightly written: “There appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and it rested upon each one of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts II).

It is rightly said of the undisciplined tongue that it is the universe of iniquity, because nearly all crimes are either contrived through it, such as robberies and fornications; committed through it, such as perjuries and false testimonies; or defended through it, when an impure person, excusing the crime he has committed, pretends by display to possess the good he has not done.

And it sets on fire [Col. 0027C] the wheel of our birth, being set on fire by Gehenna. By “Gehenna” he means the devil and his angels, for whom Gehenna was made. Wherever they may be—whether flying through the air or wandering on earth or beneath the earth, whether roaming or confined—they always carry with them the torments of their flames, like a feverish person who, whether placed in ivory beds or in sunny places, cannot escape the heat or chill of the illness implanted in him.

Thus the demons, whether they are worshiped in gilded temples or rush through the air, always burn with the fire [Col. 0027D] of Gehenna. Warned by their own punishment, they suggest to deceived human beings, out of envy, the fuel of vices by which those humans too may perish.

In contrast, the holy city of God, the new Jerusalem, is said to descend from heaven from God, because whatever heavenly thing we do on earth, we have certainly received as a heavenly gift in order to do it.

By “the wheel of our birth” he means the unceasing course of temporal life, by which, from the day of our birth until death, we are incessantly driven along as though on a constantly turning wheel. Hence Solomon, after saying, “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of affliction come” (Eccl. XII), added shortly afterward: “And the wheel is broken over the cistern, and the dust returns to the earth from which it came.”

The tongue therefore sets the wheel [Col. 0028A] of our birth on fire when, by wicked speech, it contaminates the whole state of our conduct. Again, he calls it the wheel of our birth because, cast away from inward stability through the merit of our first transgression, we are snatched here and there with wandering minds, rushing uncertainly through everything and not knowing where danger or salvation lies.

This wheel of our birth is set on fire by the fire of the tongue that stains it when the vice of our innate disturbance is compounded by foolish and harmful speech.

For every kind of beasts, birds, serpents, and other creatures is tamed and has been tamed by human nature. We read in Pliny that the most savage serpent, the asp, was tamed in Egypt by a head of household and that, every day, after emerging from its cave, it was accustomed to receive its food [Col. 0028B] at his table. We also read, in the account of Marcellinus Comes, that a tiger was tamed and sent from India to the emperor Anastasius.

He therefore wishes it to be understood that the tongue of the wicked surpasses beasts in ferocity, birds in lightness or exultation, and serpents in poisonousness. For there are beastlike people who “sharpened their tongues like a sword” (Ps. LXIII); there are birdlike people who “set their mouth against heaven” (Ps. LXXII) and whose “mouth spoke vanity” (Ps. CXLIII); and there are serpentlike people, concerning whom it is said: “The poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. XIII).

But no human being can tame the tongue. This statement can rightly be understood in two ways: no good teacher can tame the tongues of those who neglect to restrain [Col. 0028C] themselves from foolish loquacity, and no speaker exists who does not at some time offend with his tongue.

Finally, concerning the perfect man placed in the midst of the greatest temptation, it is truthfully said: “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips” (Job I). Yet afterward, having heard God’s words, he reproved himself for the foolishness of his speech, saying: “I have spoken once; would that I had not spoken, and a second time, to which I will add no more” (Job XXXIX).

An unsettled evil, full of deadly poison, and so forth. He adds “unsettled” because he had said that the tongue could not be tamed, although beasts and birds are tamed. But he says that it is “full of deadly poison” in order to explain why he called it untamable, since it is agreed that even serpents can be tamed. He goes on to add more concerning the cruelty [Col. 0028D] of its poison.

From the same mouth proceed blessing and cursing. This ought not to be so, my brothers. Does a spring pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening? Just as sweet and bitter water cannot simultaneously bubble forth together from a single spring, and even if they are mixed in a vessel or cistern, the sweet water is immediately made bitter by the bitter, while the bitter is not changed into sweetness by the addition of the sweet, so blessing and cursing cannot in any way coexist in one mouth.

Whoever has made a habit of blessing God in prayer or preaching his word, while also not ceasing to curse human beings, clearly destroys the sweetness of his blessing by the bitterness of his cursing. “A little leaven [Col. 0029A] corrupts the whole lump” (I Cor. V). And “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV).

Finally, if you make a tube with two openings through which water enters and one through which it exits, and pour bitter water into one opening and sweet water into the other, there is no doubt that, when the two reach the single outlet, they will be mixed and the water will appear bitter. For surely sweet water is much more easily changed into bitter when the two are mixed than bitter water is changed into sweet.

From this example it is gathered that evil conversations corrupt not only good character, as the Apostle testifies, but also good speech.

Let's ensure no accidental omission: all paragraphs through end. Good. Markdown only.

Could a fig tree, my brothers, produce olives, or a vine figs? [And so forth.] It is evident that, just as a tree cannot, after losing its natural fruit, produce from itself the fruit of another tree, so a person who curses, even if he seems for a time to speak something good, can in no way possess the fruit of blessing. But if someone wishes to examine these matters more deeply, the fig tree whose leaves our first parents used to cover their nakedness after recognizing their transgression may be understood as a covering of excuse. By means of it they then tried both to fend off the Creator’s rebuke from themselves and to cast it back upon the Creator himself; and now many fools incline their hearts toward an evil word, “to excuse their excuses in sins” (Ps. 140).

In the olives the fruit of mercy may be understood, and in the vine the fervor of love. “But I,” he says, “like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord, have hoped in the mercy of my God” (Ps. 52)—that is, like one who produces the fruit of mercy, I myself have hoped for mercy from the Lord. Likewise: “And your cup,” he says, “how splendidly it intoxicates!” (Ps. 23). This is plainly said of the love of God, which “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5).

A fig tree therefore cannot produce olives, because whoever strives to excuse himself in sins rather than accuse himself gives the works of mercy performed for his neighbors not with a perfect heart, but rather with a proud one. Nor can a vine produce figs, because the one who is perfectly intoxicated with divine love now accuses no one for his errors except himself.

## [Col. 0029B]

“Who among you is wise and disciplined? Let him show his works by good conduct, in the gentleness of wisdom.”

Because he had imposed silence upon wicked teachers and forbidden those whom he saw to possess neither perfection of life nor restraint of speech to occupy the office of teaching, he consequently admonishes them that, if anyone among them is—or thinks himself to be—wise and disciplined, he should demonstrate his learning more by living wisely and in a disciplined manner himself than by teaching others. For the one who performs whatever good he can with a gentle heart and serene speech plainly gives clear evidence of a wise +person. “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 111).

But whoever is more eager to preach the word than to practice it generally incurs the guilt of foolishness through love of self-display, zeal for contention, ease of eloquence, envy of other teachers, and ignorance of Catholic truth. To such a person Solomon’s saying aptly applies: “Where there are many words, there is often want” (Prov. 14). Hence here too it is rightly added:

## [Col. 0029D]

“But if you have bitter jealousy and there are contentions in your hearts, do not boast,” and so forth.

He says “bitter jealousy” because there is also a sweet jealousy, from which the apostle Simon rightly received the name of a perfect heart. Elijah also possessed it when he said: “With jealousy I have been jealous for the Lord God of hosts, because the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant” (3 Kings 19). And the apostle Paul says: “For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God” (2 Cor. 11).

There is also a good contention, which the Lord commanded us to have, saying: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke 13). “Do not boast,” he says, “and be liars against the truth.” For Truth itself proves that those who bring forth words of wisdom from their mouths, while carrying bitter jealousy and a zeal for unfruitful contention in their hearts, are not worthy of glory.

## [Col. 0030B]

“This is not the wisdom descending from above, but earthly, natural, demonic.”

And Paul says that “the natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God.” It should be noted, however, that “natural person,” or “natural wisdom,” derives not from *animal* but from *soul*, as the Apostle testifies: “The first man Adam was made a living soul, the last Adam a life-giving Spirit” (1 Cor. 15). “But not first that which is spiritual, but that which is natural.”

That this word is derived from *soul* is confirmed by Greek usage, in which language “soul” is **ψυχή** (*psychē*), while “natural” is **ψυχικόν** (*psychikon*). The Latin word *animalia* may indeed appear to have received its name from *anima*, “soul,” but in Greek it has a wholly different and dissimilar etymology. For among the Greeks animals receive their name from the fact that they live: since **ζωή** (*zōē*) means “life,” they call animals **ζῷα** (*zōa*).

When, therefore, the Apostle very often names in his Epistles the carnal person, the natural person, and the spiritual person, by “spiritual” he means either the Lord himself, who appeared in flesh and soul and was full of the Holy Spirit, or every elect person, who naturally consists in flesh and soul and has also received, according to the measure of Christ’s gift by which he is enlightened, the grace of the Holy Spirit.

He calls a person “carnal” or “natural” when, possessing no spiritual grace, he knows how to think or do only those things naturally implanted in the senses of flesh or soul. Rightly, therefore, contentious and proud wisdom is described as earthly, natural, and demonic: while the soul seeks earthly glory, and, deprived of spiritual grace, remains alone and thinks about those things naturally implanted in it after the guilt of the first transgression, it is justly deceived by an evil spirit and turns itself toward deeds that are irrational and harmful.

## [Col. 0030D]

“For where jealousy and contention are, there are instability and every evil work.”

“With all vigilance,” he says, “guard your heart, because from it life proceeds.” For as the root of the heart is, so, in the sight of the inner judgment, is the whole fruit of one’s action. Whoever conceals wickedness in his heart through envy or contention has every evil work, however upright it may appear to human beings—namely, because of the instability of a mind wavering here and there, which has neglected to fix itself upon the single anchor of heavenly contemplation.

## [Col. 0031A]

“But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, persuadable, consenting to what is good.”

This is the gentleness of wisdom, which above he commanded them to possess: opposed to the bitter jealousy and contention of fools; through it, the virtue and teaching of holy preachers are joined together in the peace of love and concord.

“First,” he says, “it is pure, then peaceable.” Pure, namely, because it understands chastely; peaceable, because it does not, through arrogance, separate itself at all from the fellowship of its neighbors. It is gentle, persuadable, and consenting to what is good because it belongs to the wise to give assent to the persuasion of good people—just as Peter promptly assented to the one reproving him—while rejecting the teaching of the wicked with complete resolve, whether by teaching or by living.

## [Col. 0031B]

“Full of mercy and good fruits.”

This is also the good conduct which above he instructed the wise and disciplined person to display: namely, to be merciful in spirit and to show outwardly, through works of piety, the fruits of that same mercy.

“Judging without pretence.”

To the extent that pure wisdom properly employs this virtue, contentious and blasphemous wisdom entirely lacks it. For whoever desires to appear more learned and more perfect than others must work very hard both to learnedly attack his neighbor as though he were less discerning, and to pretend that he has done or said good things even among those from whom he is estranged.

## [Col. 0031C]

“The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.”

Everything we do in this life is seed for future recompense; the recompense itself is the fruit of present works, as the Apostle testifies: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. For the one who sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but the one who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit” (Gal. 6).

Therefore it is rightly said that the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace. For the fruit of righteousness is eternal life, which is repaid for righteous works: those who seek peace and pursue it sprinkle the soil of their hearts with that peace to which they devote themselves, as with the finest seed, so that through the daily growth of good works they may reach the fruit of heavenly life.

Concerning this it is written elsewhere: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Ps. 126), and so forth to the end of the psalm. The reprobate also sow and reap, because in judgment they will receive according to their merits. Yet they are recognized as reaping not fruit but corruption, because they do not enjoy eternal goods—for *fruit* is so called from *enjoyment*—but will pay everlasting penalties for the corruption in which they lived.

## [Col. 0031D]

# CHAPTER IV

“From where are wars and quarrels among you? Is it not from this?” That is, from jealousy and contention, which he had forbidden above. Hence here too, explaining the same matter more fully, he adds:

“And from your desires which wage war in your members,” and so forth.

Desires wage war in the members when the hands, tongue, or consent of the other members intemperately obeys what the wicked mind perversely suggests. Concerning this he also said near the beginning of this Epistle: “Each person is tempted by his own desire, being drawn away and enticed,” and so forth.

The desires mentioned here may also be understood as desires for earthly goods—namely, the pursuit of kingdoms, wealth, honors, and dignities. For the sake of these and countless similar things, quarrels and wars are frequently undertaken among the wicked.

## [Col. 0032A]

“You quarrel and wage war, and you do not have because you do not ask.”
