“You quarrel and wage war,” he says, plainly for temporal glory; yet you cannot obtain it, because you have not taken care to ask the Lord to grant you whatever is beneficial. For if you asked him with devout intention, he would give you both the earthly things necessary for temporary use and the heavenly goods for eternal enjoyment.

“You ask and do not receive, because you ask badly,” and so forth.

He had already said that they did not ask, and now he says that they ask badly, because whoever asks badly appears, in the sight of the inner witness, to ask for nothing at all. A person asks badly when, disregarding the Lord’s commands, he desires heavenly benefits from the Lord. He also asks badly who, having lost love for heavenly things, seeks only to obtain earthly goods, and seeks them not to sustain human weakness but to satisfy unrestrained pleasure. This is what he says: “So that you may spend it on your desires.”

## [Col. 0032B]

“Adulterers, do you not know that friendship with this world is the enemy of God?”

He rightly calls adulterers those whom he rebukes for having turned away from love of heavenly wisdom toward an embrace of worldly friendship, whom he saw, having despised the Creator, serving mammon instead. Above he had spoken of God’s open enemies: “Do not the rich oppress you by their power, and do they themselves not drag you before the courts? Do they not blaspheme the good name that has been invoked over you?” (James 2).

But lest you think that only those who openly blaspheme him, persecute his faith in the saints, and condemn them by an unjust judgment are God’s enemies, he shows that those too are God’s enemies who, under the faith and confession of Christ’s name, serve the allurements and love of the world—who, faithful in name only, prefer earthly things to heavenly ones.

He presses this home in the following verse, adding: “Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God.” All lovers of the world, all seekers of trifles, are therefore God’s enemies—all who belong to those of whom it is said: “For behold, your enemies, Lord, will perish” (Ps. 92). Whether they enter churches or do not enter churches, they are God’s enemies. For a time they may flourish like grass, but when the heat of judgment appears, they will perish, and the beauty of their countenance will fall away.

## [Col. 0032D]

“Or do you think that Scripture speaks in vain?”

He means the Scripture which, restraining the faithful from association with the wicked, speaks through Moses in this way: “You shall not make a covenant with them, nor with their gods. They shall not dwell in your land, lest perhaps they make you sin against me if you serve their gods; this will certainly be a stumbling block to you” (Exod. 23). And again: “You shall not do their works, but you shall destroy them and shatter their statues” (ibid.).

## [Col. 0033A]

“Does the spirit that dwells in you desire jealousy?”

This should be read interrogatively, as a rebuke, as though he were saying: Does the Spirit of grace, by whom you were marked on the day of redemption, desire this—that you envy one another? Certainly it is not the good spirit that works the vice of envy in you, but the evil one.

A similar form of expression occurs in the psalm: “A brother does not redeem; a human being will redeem” (Ps. 49). For it is understood in this way: If Christ did not redeem us—he who deigned to become our brother through his humanity—could some mere human being possibly suffice to redeem us?

Some explain this sentence as follows: “The spirit that dwells in you desires jealousy.” It desires [something] against jealousy—that is, it desires the disease of envy to be conquered and uprooted from your minds.

Others understand it as referring to the human spirit, so that the meaning is: Do not desire; do not cling to the friendships of this world, because the spirit of your mind, while it desires earthly things, desires jealousy—since you envy others for possessing the things you yourselves desire to acquire.

## [Col. 0033B]

“But he gives greater grace.”

The Lord gives greater grace than the friendship of the world, because the latter grants earthly goods for a time, and goods that must be lost with sorrow, whereas he bestows eternal joy. He next explains to whom he grants this grace.

“Therefore he says: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

God punishes thieves, perjurers, the lustful, and other sinners as despisers of his commandments; but he is said especially to resist the proud, because those who trust in their own strength suffer greater punishment—those who neglect, through repentance, to submit to divine power, and who, as though sufficient to save themselves, refuse to seek the help of heavenly grace.

On the other hand, he gives grace to the humble, because those who humbly submit themselves, in the wounds of their vices, to the hands of the true physician rightly receive the gifts of the health they desire.

It should be noted that blessed James placed this saying about the proud and humble in his Epistle from the parables of Solomon according to the ancient Translation, just as Peter did in his Epistle. In our edition, however, which descends from the Hebrew truth, it is expressed thus: “He will mock the mockers, and will give grace to the gentle.”

The Lord will mock the mockers in accordance with what Paul says about those who, refusing to receive him when he comes in the name of his Father, will receive the Antichrist when he comes in his own name (John 5): “Because,” he says, “they did not receive the love of truth so as to be saved, therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie” (2 Thess. 2).

He mocked the mockers when, at the Jews’ words, “If he is the king of Israel, let him come down from the cross and we will believe him” (Matt. 27), he patiently endured until, dead and buried, he overcame both their insults and death itself by a swift resurrection.

“But he will give grace to the gentle,” because he bestows upon those who humbly follow him both perfection in good works and the gifts of blessed everlastingness.

## [Col. 0034A]

“Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.”

Draw near to the Lord by following his footsteps in humility, and he will draw near to you through mercy, freeing you from distress. No one is far from God because of geographical distance, but because of affections. For, though dwelling in the same earthly place, the one who pursues virtue and the one who sinks into the filth of vices are far apart from God, while the other has God near.

Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 145). And again: “Salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 119)—that salvation of which we sing: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. 27).

And the Lord himself, when he urged us to draw near to him, saying, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11), immediately showed that this was to be fulfilled not by the feet but by deeds, when he added: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (ibid.).

## [Col. 0034B]

“Cleanse your hands, sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.”

This is truly to draw near to the Lord: to possess purity of action and simplicity of heart. “The innocent in hands and pure in heart,” he says, “will receive blessing from the Lord and mercy” (Ps. 25). And this is truly for the Lord to draw near to us: to give us the gifts of his mercy when we seek them with sincerity. “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. 1).

## [Col. 0034C]

“Be miserable, and mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned into mourning, and your joy into sorrow. Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.”

“Do not,” he says, “love becoming rich and rejoicing in this world; but, mindful of the crimes you have committed, take greater care that through the brief miseries and passing poverty and lamentation of this life you may reach the everlasting joys of the heavenly kingdom, so that, instead of temporal delight in the riches you acquired through wicked labor, you may not beg forever, mourn, and pay the penalty.”

## [Col. 0034D]

“Do not slander one another, my brothers.”

This vice of slander also pertains to the deadly poison of the tongue, concerning which he said: “You quarrel and wage war.”

“Whoever slanders his brother, or whoever judges his brother, slanders the law and judges the law.”

He slanders the law who slanders his brother, as though the law itself had not acted rightly when it forbade slander, saying through the Prophet: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Ps. 101). And in Leviticus: “You shall not be an accuser, nor a whisperer among the peoples” (Lev. 19).

It may also be understood in this way: Whoever slanders his brother who is obeying the commands of the law slanders the law and judges the law that gave such commands. For example, the law commanded: “You shall not remember the injury done by your fellow citizens.” Therefore whoever slanders his brother, and whoever judges the brother whom he sees willingly bearing injuries for the love of God, certainly slanders the law and judges the law that commanded us to forget injuries.

## [Col. 0035A]

“But who are you that you judge your neighbor?”

He censures the rashness of the person who takes pleasure in judging his neighbor and does not care to consider the condition of his own weakness and the uncertainty of this temporal life. And because sometimes, through a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, those who judged their neighbor are subjected to the power of the person they judged, and sometimes are snatched from the world while that person still lives, he next censures the rashness of those who, possessing no certainty about the length of their own lives, extend their minds into the future as though they possessed many years of profit. For he continues:

## [Col. 0035B]

“Behold, now, you who say: Today or tomorrow we will go into that city, and spend a year there, and trade, and make a profit—you who do not know what will happen tomorrow.”

He points out that such a plan contains folly in many respects: they deliberate about increasing their profit, suppose that they will live for a long time, assert that it lies within their power where they will spend a year, and in all these matters refuse to recall to mind the examination of the heavenly Judge.

## [Col. 0035C]

“For what is your life? It is a vapor, appearing for a little while and then vanishing.”

He does not say, “What is our life?” but “What is your life?” For the righteous truly begin to live when they have reached the end of this life. But the enemies of the Lord, once they have been honored and exalted, will fail; “like smoke they will fail” (Ps. 37).

It should not be thought that this is the same opinion which the impious are said, in the Book of Wisdom, to have expressed among themselves: “For we were born from nothing, and afterward we shall be as though we had not been” (Wis. 2). “For smoke is the breath in our nostrils, and speech a spark to move our heart. When it is extinguished, the body will be ashes, and the spirit will be dispersed like soft air.”

They reasoned in this way because they believed there was no life except this one, saying with Epicurus: “After death there is nothing, and death itself is nothing.” Blessed James, however, introduced the present saying to teach that the life of the wicked is brief in the present, yet is followed in the future by eternal death, in accordance with blessed Job’s words: “They spend their days in good things, and in an instant they descend to the underworld” (Job 21).

## [Col. 0035D]

“Therefore, for one who knows how to do good and does not do it, it is sin.”

Throughout the text of this Epistle blessed James shows that those to whom he wrote possessed knowledge of how to do good and had likewise learned the right faith, so that they even presumed that they could become teachers of others; yet they had not attained perfection of works, humility of mind, or restraint of speech.

Accordingly, among his other words of rebuke and exhortation, he now greatly frightens them by declaring that the one who knows how to do good and does not do what he knows has a greater sin than the one who sins in ignorance. Yet even the one who errs unknowingly cannot be entirely free from guilt, since ignorance of the good itself is no small evil.

For this reason the Lord says: “The servant who knew his master’s will and did not act according to his will will be beaten many times. But the one who did not know and did things worthy of blows will be beaten few times” (Luke 12).

# CHAPTER V

## [Col. 0036A]

“Come now, rich people, weep, howling over the miseries that will come upon you.”

Now, while it is an acceptable time, while it is “the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6), he says: avoid future punishments by weeping and giving alms.

“Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you, and will eat your flesh like fire.”

Not only does the visible fire of Gehenna torment impious and merciless rich people, but the very memory of their decayed and empty riches—which could most easily have redeemed them from their wickedness—will burn their souls no less before the judgment and even their flesh after the resurrection. For then they will begin to be gravely angry with themselves because they were unwilling to wash away their crimes through almsgiving.

Finally, the rust of money was allowed to remain for that man clothed in purple as a testimony of wickedness and was turned into an increase of punishment when, at Abraham’s rebuke, he heard: “Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke 16).

The flesh may also be understood as the bodily pleasures themselves, which the rust of money eats like fire, while an external flame rages against the luxurious soul and torments it, and the pain of its own greed, piercing no less inwardly, accuses it.

This also often happens in the present life: some people lose the riches they had used badly, and, after losing their possessions, begin too late to grieve that they had possessed them without fruit. Then they lament that they did not give their goods to the needy, when, overtaken by need themselves, they are forced to beg.

## [Col. 0036C]

“You have stored up anger for yourselves in the last days.”

Because you neglected the nakedness and hunger of the poor and rejoiced in storing up treasuries of money for yourselves, you have accumulated for yourselves the anger of the inner Judge, without making provision for your own future. Although it has not yet appeared, it remains fully certain in the last days—that is, when the end of temporal days arrives.

“Behold, the wages of the laborers who harvested your fields, which has been defrauded by you, cries out.”

What great wickedness there is in the proud! Although they have sufficient wealth, they disdain not only to receive and refresh the poor who come from every direction, but also refuse to pay their own hired workers or servants the wages due for their labor.

Blessed Job indicates that he took great care to avoid this impious vice when he says: “If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep with it; if I have eaten its fruits without payment and afflicted the soul of its farmers, let thistle grow for me instead of wheat, and thorn instead of barley” (Job 31).

“And their cry has entered into the ears of the Lord Sabaoth.”

He calls him “Lord Sabaoth,” that is, “Lord of hosts,” to terrify those who think that the poor have no protector. The Psalmist’s saying suits this passage: “For to you the poor person is abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Ps. 10 according to the Hebrew). And what is written in the Book of blessed Job: “For God will not hear in vain, and the Almighty will regard the causes of individuals” (Job 35).

“You have feasted upon the earth.”

Neglecting the heavenly joys to which you could have come through afflictions and fasts, you love only bodily feasts, which in the future will be followed by such great hunger and thirst that not even a single drop of water will then be obtainable from elsewhere to cool your burning tongue.

## [Col. 0037A]

“And you have nourished your hearts in luxuries.”

They nourish their hearts in luxuries who, in accordance with that saying of Ecclesiastes, do not restrain their hearts from enjoying every pleasure and delighting in the things they have prepared. They regard this as their portion if they themselves use the fruits of their labors, taking no care for the nourishment or enjoyment of the poor (Eccl. 2).

“You have led away and killed the Righteous One on the day of slaughter, and he did not resist you.”

He calls the Lord and Savior “the righteous,” concerning whom blessed Stephen, the first martyr, also speaks to those same Jews: “Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced the coming of the Righteous One, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become” (Acts 7).

It is therefore apparent that blessed James addresses those rich people concerning whom he says: “Come now, rich people, weep, howling”—those who had conspired to kill the Lord and had not yet received the faith in his name by which they would be saved.

He also speaks of them above to believers: “Do not the rich oppress you by their power, and do they themselves not drag you before the courts? Do they not blaspheme the good name that has been invoked over you?” (James 2).

And because he writes to the twelve tribes that are in the dispersion, he admonishes the faithful to perform works of faith in such a way that he also urges those who had not yet believed to turn both to the Lord’s faith and to the works of faith. He recalls to them that they killed the Son of God and, as though they had accomplished no evil, gave themselves over to luxury and greed, taking no care to amend so great a crime through repentance and almsgiving.

The words “greed will eat their flesh like fire” apply especially to them, as does the declaration that they had stored up anger for themselves in the last days. This was plainly fulfilled in them after James’s killing, when the city of Jerusalem—or rather the whole province of Judea—was conquered and devastated by the Romans, and [because of] the other crimes they had committed [the construction is defective in the supplied text].

## [Col. 0037C]

“Therefore be patient, brothers, until the coming of the Lord.”

After rebuking the proud and unbelieving, he turns again to those who had been oppressed by such wickedness, exhorting them to patience and indicating that the end of such afflictions is near—either because they themselves will be snatched away to the Lord and receive the fruit of their patience, or because their persecutors will be deprived of the power to persecute.

## [Col. 0037D]

“Behold, the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the earth, patiently enduring until he receives the early and the late rain,” and so forth.

If the farmer works so patiently for the fruit of the earth that he awaits and hopes will come in time, how much more ought you to endure all present adversities for the fruit of the heavenly reward, which you can possess forever?

For you will receive a temporal fruit, namely, the life of the soul after death. You will also receive the late fruit, the incorruption of the flesh at the judgment. Or certainly, the temporal fruit is in works of righteousness, and the late fruit in the recompense of labors, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “You have your fruit in sanctification, and the end is eternal life” (Rom. 6).

## [Col. 0038A]

“Do not groan against one another, brothers, so that you may not be judged.”

It is as though you were suffering adversities greater than your merits, while your persecutors, despite having committed the greatest crimes, appear to suffer no adversity at all. “So that you may not be judged”—namely, by the judgment of condemnation, because you criticize this Judge as though he were judging unjustly.

## [Col. 0038B]

“Behold, the Judge stands before the door.”

He will repay both the rewards of patience to you and the punishment your adversaries deserve to them. He stands before the door because he is either near to knowing everything you do or will soon come to repay both you and your persecutors what each of you has deserved.

“Take, brothers, as an example of an evil outcome, and of long-suffering, labor, and patience, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.”

See, he says, that the prophets, though so holy and so free from sins that the Spirit of God spoke his mysteries to human beings through them, had an evil outcome in that they suffered death at the hands of unbelievers—such as Zechariah, Uriah, and the Maccabean martyrs. In the New Testament there were John, Stephen, James the son of Zebedee, and many others.

Yet they did not wish to groan over such an outcome, but rather to endure it with long-suffering. Others endured prolonged labors, but bore them patiently and without murmuring: Noah in the building of the ark for a hundred years; Moses in the rescue and leadership of the people for forty years; David in enduring exile without guilt; Joseph in the servitude imposed upon him through his brothers’ treachery.

## [Col. 0038C]

For both matters he added a firm and unchanging example, saying: “You have heard of Job’s endurance, and you have seen the Lord’s end.”

“You have learned through reading of Job’s labor and patience, and how, through the Lord’s mercy, he received double all that the enemy had taken from him by deceit. You yourselves also saw the Lord’s outcome on the cross, which he accepted with long-suffering; and through the preaching of the Gospel you have learned of the glory of his resurrection and ascension into heaven.”

“For the Lord is merciful and compassionate.”

He is so either that in the present he may free his own from temptations and glorify before human beings those who live steadfastly in the faith, or that after death he may crown them in secret and yet not remove from human beings the memory of the praise they have deserved.

## [Col. 0038D]

“Above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth, or by any other oath. Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; No, no.’”

He desires to drain the deadly poison of the tongue completely from his hearers. He had forbidden them to slander one another, prohibited judging one’s neighbor, and forbidden them to groan against one another in adversities—all of which are manifest sins. He adds this practice, which seems light to some, in order to abolish the custom of swearing oaths as well.

That this too should by no means be considered insignificant is plainly evident to those who carefully consider the Lord’s saying: “Every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12), so that you may not fall under judgment.

“Therefore,” he says, “I restrain you from the guilt of swearing, lest, by frequently swearing to what is true, you should at some point fall even into perjury. Rather, keep farther from the vice of perjury by being unwilling to swear even to the truth except in the most immediate necessity.”

But the one who, although never committing perjury, swears more often than truth requires also falls under the guilt of judgment. For by the very idleness of excessive speech he sins and offends the Judge, who forbade both every useless word and every oath.

## [Col. 0039A]

“Is anyone among you sad?” and so forth.

Having earlier forbidden the brothers to groan against one another in afflictions, he now shows what should be done instead. “If,” he says, “a burden of sorrow has fallen upon any one of you, whether some injury inflicted by other people, an accidental fault, an unexpected domestic loss, or any other circumstance has caused you distress, do not at that hour come together to murmur against one another and lodge complaints against God’s judgments. Rather, hasten to the church and pray to the Lord on bended knees, asking him to send the grace of his consolation, lest the sorrow of the world, which produces death, swallow you up” (2 Cor. 7).

By the frequent sweetness of psalmody, drive the harmful plague of sadness from your heart as well.

## [Col. 0039B]

“Is anyone among you sick?” and so forth.

Just as he gave advice to the sorrowful, so he gives counsel to the sick concerning how to guard himself against the folly of murmuring. Corresponding to the manner of the wound, he also prescribes the manner of the remedy: commanding the sorrowful person to pray and sing psalms for himself, while directing the one who is sick either in body or in faith—because he has suffered the greater wound—to remember to seek healing through the assistance of many, and specifically of the elders. He should not entrust the cause of his weakness to younger and less learned men, lest perhaps he receive from them some harmful exhortation or counsel.

## [Col. 0039C]

“And let them pray over him, anointing him,” and so forth.

We read that the apostles also did this in the Gospel, and the practice of the Church now maintains that the sick are anointed by presbyters with consecrated oil and are healed with prayer accompanying it.

Nor is it permitted only to presbyters to use this oil; as Pope Innocent writes, all Christians may likewise use it by anointing themselves or their own in a time of need. Nevertheless, this oil may be prepared only by bishops.

For when he says, “with oil in the name of the Lord,” he means oil consecrated in the name of the Lord. Or certainly, because when they anoint the sick person they must also invoke the Lord’s name over him.

## [Col. 0039D]

And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him. Many are punished with bodily illness or even death because of sins committed in the soul. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians, who were accustomed to receive the Lord’s Body unworthily: “That is why many among you are weak and sick, and many are asleep” (1 Cor. XI). If, therefore, the sick are in sins, and have confessed these to the priests of the Church, and have earnestly sought to abandon and amend them with a perfect heart, they will be forgiven. For sins cannot be forgiven without a confession of amendment. Hence it is rightly added:

“Therefore confess your sins to one another,” etc. In this statement, however, the following distinction should be observed: we ought to confess our daily and lesser sins to one another, to those equal to us, and believe that we are saved through their daily prayer. But we should disclose the uncleanness of a more serious leprosy according to the law concerning the priesthood, and take care to be purified according to his judgment, in whatever manner and for whatever length of time he commands.

“For the continual prayer of a righteous person has great power,” etc. He fittingly demonstrates by an example how much the continual prayer of a righteous person avails, since Elijah, by praying only once, held back the heavens for so long, withheld rain from the earth, and denied its fruits to mortals; and again, when he wished, when he recognized that the time had come, and when he saw that the heart of the proud king and of the idolatrous people had been bent toward repentance by the long wasting of famine, he prayed only once and restored to the earth the fruits and waters that he had withheld. Thus it follows:

“And again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain,” etc. Elijah therefore prayed once both before and afterward, and this one Elijah obtained such great things; how much, then, is accomplished by the frequent prayer of many righteous people? Yet lest our weakness should tremble, thinking that it could not do similar things to so great a prophet, who deserved to be carried up to heaven in a chariot of fire, blessed James, intending to speak of his prayer, wisely began as follows: “Elijah was a man like us, subject to suffering.” He was indeed a man, although inferior in virtue to no human being; he was like us in the origin of his flesh, and subject to suffering, as we are, both in the frailty of mind and of flesh. He showed that he was fragile in the flesh when he sought food from the widow of Sarepta. He also showed that he had been subject to suffering in mind when, after restoring the waters to the earth and destroying the prophets and priests of the idols, he was terrified by the threats of a single woman and fled through the wilderness.

How great a merit it is before the Lord to pray for the sick and, when they confess their sins, to restore them to the health they have lost is made clear by what follows:

“My brothers, if any one of you should wander from the truth,” etc. Since, in the earlier parts of this Epistle, our tongue is restrained from malicious or idle speech, it is appropriately shown at the end what above all we ought to say. We are therefore commanded to pray and sing psalms to the Lord whenever we are struck by adversity. Likewise, we are to confess our sins to one another and pray for one another, devoting as much care as we can to the salvation and health of our neighbors—not merely temporal health, but rather eternal health. For if it is a great reward to rescue from death flesh that will one day die, how great is the merit of freeing from death a soul that will live without end in the heavenly homeland?

It should certainly be noted that some manuscripts read: “He will save his own soul from death.” Because of the ambiguity of the Greek, this too can rightly be interpreted in that way. Indeed, whoever corrects one who is wandering thereby acquires for himself greater joys of heavenly life. “He will save his own soul,” he says, “from death, and will cover a multitude of sins.” Whoever turns a sinner back from error, and by this conversion hides his sins from the sight of the inner Judge beneath the superimposition of a better life, also conceals from the gaze of Him who sees all his own offenses, whatever they may be, by caring for his neighbor, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI).

In this exhortation blessed James does not forget what he said earlier: “Do not become teachers in great numbers, my brothers” (Jas. III). There he removes the imperfect from the office of teaching in their own conduct, an office they sought through boastfulness. Here, however, he teaches those who are instructed in every respect what they ought to do for the salvation of their neighbors out of fraternal love. For what the teacher is said to do here is elsewhere attributed to charity, as blessed Peter the Apostle says: “Because charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. IV). Nor should it be passed over that this conversion of the one who has gone astray is accomplished not only by speaking, but very often also by good conduct. If someone, even while his tongue remains silent, shows his neighbors examples of good action and turns them toward imitating the works of almsgiving, hospitality, or other virtues that they had neglected, he is certainly carrying out the office of a teacher; and for the salvation of the brother whom he has corrected, he will receive a sure reward from the merciful Judge.

## INTO THE FIRST EPISTLE OF PETER

[Col. 0041]

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0041B]

“Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ,” etc. In Latin, *advenae*—“newcomers” or “sojourners”—are called *proselyti* in Greek. The Jews used this name for those who, born among the nations, chose to believe in God, accept circumcision, and lead their lives according to Jewish custom and the law of God. Some of those who believed in Christ at their preaching belonged to this group on the holy day of Pentecost, when the apostles received the Holy Spirit in the appearance of fire, since Scripture says that Jews and proselytes were also present.

He therefore calls them “chosen newcomers,” because they had come from paganism to the knowledge and acceptance of the divine law and, having received the legal sacraments, had deserved to attain the reception of the grace of faith. Hence the holy presbyter Jerome, speaking of them, says:

“Because Peter, after his episcopate of the Church of Antioch and his preaching to those of the dispersion who had believed from the circumcision in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, went to Rome in the second year of Claudius to defeat Simon Magus.”

But if we too can truthfully say to God with the prophet, “For we are sojourners with you on the earth, and pilgrims, like all our fathers” (Ps. XXXVIII), then we ought also to believe that the Epistles of blessed Peter were written to us and to read them as having been sent to us. Indeed, in those very Epistles he warns us, as though we had our homeland elsewhere, saying: “Beloved, I beseech you, as newcomers and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires” (1 Pet. II).

The addition “of the dispersion” signifies that they had been scattered from Jerusalem in the persecution that took place under Stephen, or certainly that, in other manifold persecutions, they had suffered for the faith at the hands either of Jews or of the nations and had often been driven from their own dwellings, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles. Paul also says to the Galatians: “You have suffered so many things in vain, if indeed in vain.”

“Of the dispersion of Pontus, Galatia,” etc. All these provinces are Greek regions in Asia. There is also another Bithynia in Europe, from which those who are Bithynians in Asia are said to derive their origin. The Bithynia that is in Asia is also called Greater Phrygia, and it is separated from Galatia by the river Hierus.

“According to the foreknowledge of God the Father,” etc. These verses are connected with what he had said earlier: “To the chosen newcomers.” They were chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father. Hence the Apostle also says: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.” And elsewhere: “Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world.”

They were chosen so that, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, they might be sanctified, cleansed from all sins, and begin to obey the Lord Jesus Christ. They had perished through the disobedience of the first-formed man, so that, sprinkled with Christ’s blood, they might avoid the power of Satan, just as Israel escaped the domination of the Egyptians through the blood of the lamb. He speaks of “sprinkling” according to the custom of the ancient Scripture, in which things that were to be sanctified were ordinarily sprinkled with the blood of sacrifices. Moreover, the Lord himself plainly says of this: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI).

“May grace and peace be multiplied.” May you perfectly complete what you have begun well. He rightly names grace first and peace afterward, because without the grace of Christ we cannot attain the peace of reconciliation; indeed, we can possess nothing peaceful except through his grace.

“Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He renders praises of blessing to God the Father in such a way as to demonstrate that the Lord our Savior is both God and man. When he says, “God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” he calls him the God of the Lord Jesus Christ because he remembers that the Lord Christ himself became man; but he calls him “the Father of our Lord” because he does not doubt that this same Lord of ours has always existed as the Son of God.

“Who according to his great mercy regenerated us,” etc. God is rightly blessed by us: although by our merits we had been born for death, by his mercy he regenerated us for life. He did this through the resurrection of his Son, since he loved our life so greatly that he ordained that Christ should die for it; and, having destroyed that same death through the resurrection, he displayed to us the hope and example of rising again. He died so that we would not fear dying. He rose from the dead so that we might hope that we too would rise through him.

[Col. 0043A]

“Into an incorruptible inheritance,” etc. He says “incorruptible” because of the heavenly life, which is touched neither by old age, illness, death, nor any sadness. “Undefiled,” because no unclean person can enter it. “Unfading,” because even in the minds of blessed human beings that heavenly way of life can never grow worthless through long familiarity, as the luxuries and delights of the present age sometimes become distasteful through prolonged habit and use.

“Kept in heaven in you.” He says “kept in you” as though he had said “kept for you,” that is, kept now for the purpose of being given back to you in heaven at the appointed time. Or certainly, “kept in heaven in you,” because he who gave believers the power to become children of God (John I) also gave them the power to receive an inheritance in heaven by persevering to the end, so that they may be saved. Therefore he says that the inheritance is kept for those whose merits, with the Lord’s help, he knows will bring them to it, because those who do not preserve the Father’s discipline do not deserve to receive an inheritance from him.

“Who are guarded by the power of God through faith,” etc. The Lord also says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John XIV). And again: “It is not mine to give to you, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father” (Mark X). Seats in the kingdom of God, dwelling places in the Father’s house, and salvation in heaven have therefore been prepared; let only the one who desires to receive them make himself worthy. But since no one can become worthy by his own effort alone or arrive at eternal salvation by his own strength, it is rightly stated beforehand: “Who are guarded by the power of God through faith.” No one can be preserved in good by the power of his own freedom; rather, the help of Him from whom we received the beginning of good action must be sought in everything, so that we may be brought to perfection.

“In which you will exult,” etc. The words “in which” signify that salvation will be revealed and given to the worthy at the last time. Concerning this the Lord also says: “But I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John XVI).

“Now for a little while, if it is necessary, to be grieved.” He says that it is necessary to be grieved because one cannot attain eternal joys except through the sadness of the passing age and its afflictions. He says “for a little while” because, when the eternal reward is bestowed, everything that seemed grave and bitter amid the tribulations of this age will appear brief and light.

“So that the tested quality of your faith may be much more precious than gold,” etc. The Book of Wisdom also compares the sufferings of the saints with gold tested by fire, saying of the Lord: “As gold in the furnace he tested them, and as the victim of a whole burnt offering he accepted them” (Wis. III). For those whom he has proved faithful in the furnace of tribulation he will receive in the joy of recompense as an offering pleasing to himself. The patience of the saints is rightly compared with gold, because just as nothing among metals is more precious than gold, so nothing is more worthy of all praise before God.

For this is written: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV). Just as gold enclosed in a furnace is tested by the flames, but once brought out its brilliance becomes evident, so the steadfastness of the faithful appears contemptible and foolish amid the pressures of unbelievers; but when the time of recompense arrives, after the contest of tribulations has ended, their virtue will show how great its glory was and how greatly it advanced through the flames of suffering. Hence it is appropriately added:

“It is found for praise and glory,” etc. The testing of faith is found to result in praise when the Judge, praising it, says: “I was hungry, and you gave me food,” etc. (Matt. XXV). It is found to result in glory when he precedes it by glorifying it: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid.). It is found to result in honor when, while the impious fall into eternal punishment, “the righteous will go into eternal life” (ibid.). Concerning this he himself says: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him” (John XII).

“Although you do not see him, you love him,” etc. Paul also says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. II).

“Concerning this salvation the prophets searched and examined,” etc. They searched and examined, in secret, from the Lord or from the angels, concerning the future grace of the Gospel: when, and in what order, eternal salvation would come to the world. This is found in their books. Hence one of them, out of his great love for saving knowledge, deserved to be called by the angel “a man of desires.” They prophesied by speaking openly to human beings and by explaining what they themselves had learned in the hidden depths of contemplation.

“Searching into what time or what kind of time the Spirit of Christ signified in them,” etc. The evangelist signified these glories when he said: “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII). There are two glorifications of the Lord according to the form of the man he assumed: one, when he rose from the dead; the other, when he ascended into heaven before the eyes of his disciples. A third remains, also before human eyes, when he comes in his own majesty and that of the Father and of the holy angels, to render to each according to his works.

“To whom it was revealed that they were serving not themselves,” etc. Among the many mysteries revealed to the prophets, when they diligently searched and examined the future salvation, this too was revealed to them: that this salvation would not come in their days, but rather in yours, who are born at the end of the ages. He says this to urge them to care for the salvation that has been offered—salvation that the prophets and the righteous of earlier times loved so greatly that they desired to live in the world at the time when, once the world had been stripped away, they might immediately be permitted to ascend to the heavenly kingdoms.

“Through those who preached the Gospel to you,” etc. He had said above that the prophets, through the Spirit of Christ, foretold his sufferings and subsequent glories; now he says that the apostles announce these same things to them through the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. Hence it is clear that the same Spirit of Christ was formerly in the prophets and afterward in the apostles. For this reason both proclaimed to the peoples the same faith in Christ’s sufferings and subsequent glories: the former as still to come, the latter as already having come. Thus there is one Church, whose one part preceded the Lord’s bodily advent and whose other part followed it.

“Into whom the angels desire to look.” It is certainly evident that such great subsequent glory followed for Jesus Christ, the man who suffered for us, that even the heavenly angelic powers, although perfected in eternal blessedness, rejoiced continually to behold not only the immortal magnificence of his divinity but also the splendor of his assumed humanity.

Yet we must examine more carefully how he says that the angels desire to look into him, since desire is not usually spoken of regarding something we possess, but regarding something we wish to possess—for no one desires what he has. How, then, do they desire to look upon Christ, whose face they never cease to behold? Perhaps divine contemplation so blesses the citizens of the heavenly homeland that, in a manner ineffable to us, they are always satisfied by the sight of his glory and yet always insatiably hunger for his sweetness as though it were new.

For, as blessed Pope Gregory says, wonderfully distinguishing bodily and spiritual delights: bodily delights, when they are not possessed, kindle within themselves a grievous desire; but when they have been obtained and consumed, they immediately turn the one eating them toward disgust through satiety. Spiritual delights, by contrast, are distasteful when they are not possessed, but when they are possessed they are desired; and the more abundantly they are eaten, the more abundantly they are hungered for by the one eating them. In bodily delights, appetite produces satiety, and satiety produces disgust; in spiritual delights, appetite produces satiety, and satiety produces appetite. Spiritual delights increase desire in the mind even while satisfying it, because the more their flavor is perceived, the more one recognizes what is to be loved more greatly.

The statement, “Into whom the angels desire to look,” can also rightly be understood of the Holy Spirit, of whom he had promised: “Those who preached the Gospel to you through the Holy Spirit sent from heaven.” Blessed Peter wished to attribute this to the grace of divine mercy: He who possesses such majesty and glory that his vision—like that of the Father and the Son, since it is indeed one and the same—is desired by the angels in heaven sent the Spirit to earth for the sake of human salvation and poured him into the minds of believers for their illumination.

“Therefore, having girded the loins of your mind,” etc. Since this has been promised to you, he says, that after this life you will see the revelation of Jesus Christ, whom the angels now see, take greater care to make yourselves worthy of receiving it, since the grace promised to you is so much greater. He “girds the loins of the mind” who restrains it from thought. He rightly says, “Hope in the grace offered to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ,” because whoever awaits the Lord’s coming with the loins of the mind girded—that is, chaste in mind and body—rightly hopes when he is revealed. But whoever does not know how to please the Lord rightly fears, in the hope of good things, lest he come too quickly.

“As children of obedience,” etc. He rightly wishes them to be children of obedience, whom in the preface he had called chosen for obedience and for the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ.

“But according to him who called you, the Holy One,” etc. This resembles what is said in the Gospel: “Therefore you also must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. V).

“And if you invoke him as Father.” This means saying in prayer: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. VI).

“Who judges without partiality,” etc. He is not like a human father, who ordinarily spares sinful children more indulgently than servants. God the Father, however, possesses such justice and mercy that he both changes humble and obedient servants—and even enemies who stretch out their hands to him—into adopted children, and in turn makes those who appear more honored under the name of children completely excluded from the perpetual inheritance because of the fault of disobedience.

“Conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourn.” This is so that through laziness and negligence you may not prove unworthy of such a Father, and, while secure during the time of your present sojourn, become unable to attain the promised blessedness of your homeland.

“Knowing that you were redeemed not with perishable things, gold or silver,” etc. The greater the price by which you were redeemed from the corruption of carnal life, the more you ought to fear offending the mind of your Redeemer by returning to the corruption of vices.

“Born again not from corruptible seed,” etc. There is a similar statement in the Gospel of John: “To those who believe in his name, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John I). Just as the price of the Lord’s Passion by which we were redeemed is incorruptible, so too the sacrament of the sacred font through which we are reborn is incorruptible. These are so connected with one another that one cannot confer salvation upon us without the other. For the Lord, at the time of his Incarnation, redeemed us all together by his sacred blood; therefore, in our own time, each of us must also attain participation in that same regeneration through the regeneration of baptism.

Regarding this regeneration it is rightly said that it occurs not from corruptible seed, but through the word of the living God, which endures forever. From this it may be understood that, just as corruptible flesh is born from corruptible seed, so through water consecrated by the word of God a life is granted to us in flesh and soul alike—a life that knows no end. He aptly supports this with prophetic testimony, adding:

“For all flesh is like grass,” etc. Just as corruptible flesh generates corruptible flesh, so the word of the Lord, which remains forever, gives eternal life in flesh and soul alike to those whom it restores through water.

Saint Cyprian, in his book *On the Conduct of Virgins*, recalls this testimony as follows:

“Isaiah’s God cries out,” he says: “All flesh is grass, and all its splendor is like the flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell, but the word of the Lord remains forever.”

It is fitting for no Christian, and especially not for a virgin, to value any splendor or honor of the flesh, but only to desire the word of God and to embrace good things that will remain forever. Or, if there is to be glory in the flesh, it is plainly then, when one is tortured in the confession of the Name; when a woman is found stronger than the men who torture her; when she endures fires, crosses, iron, or wild beasts so that she may be crowned. Those are the precious necklaces of the flesh; those are the body’s better ornaments.

The reader should not be troubled that in this prophetic statement one translation has “splendor,” while our Translation has “glory,” for both are customarily translated into Latin from the one Greek word δόξα (*doxa*).

## CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0047B]

“Therefore, laying aside all malice and all deceit,” etc. Since you have recently been reborn, he says, and have become children of God through baptism, now become through the pursuit of good conduct what newborn infants are by the nature of their innocent age: wholly ignorant, that is, of malice and deceit, of pretense, envy, slander, and enslavement to other vices of this kind.

Just as infants naturally desire their mother’s milk so that they may grow toward salvation and reach the point of eating bread, so you should seek the simple beginnings of faith first from the breasts of Mother Church—that is, from the teachers of both Testaments, who either wrote the divine utterances or preach them to you with the living voice—so that, by learning well, you may arrive at the nourishment of the living Bread that descended from heaven. This is accomplished through the sacraments of the Lord’s Incarnation, by which you were reborn and nourished, until you arrive at the contemplation of the divine majesty.

“Desire rational and guileless milk,” etc. By the command to desire milk he touches upon those who come unwillingly and reluctantly to hear sacred readings, ignorant of the thirst and hunger of which the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. V). Consequently they reach the perfect growth of salvation more slowly, by which they could be nourished with solid food of the word—that is, come to know divine mysteries and perform greater good works.

“If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet.” Once, he says, you have put away and amended the malice and filth of your heart, desire Christ’s life-giving nourishment, if you have some perception of how abundant the sweetness of God is. For one who tastes nothing of heavenly sweetness in the mind will hardly avoid defiling himself with earthly enticements.

The Psalmist rightly urges us to taste how sweet the Lord is, because there are some who understand God not as something that tastes sweet inwardly, but as something that sounds impressive outwardly. Although they grasp certain hidden things by understanding them, they cannot experience their sweetness. They know what such things are, but, as I have said, they do not know how they taste.

And since in the very psalm from which he took this verse it is written beforehand, “Approach him and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII), blessed Peter rightly adds:

[Col. 0048A]

“To whom you draw near, a living stone,” etc. He also takes this testimony concerning the stone from the psalm, where it is written: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. CXVII). Lest anyone, in a Jewish interpretation, think that the prophet was singing about a material stone that, contrary to human arrangement, would be placed in the construction of some earthly house by divine judgment, he wisely added “living”: “To whom you draw near,” he says, “a living stone,” so that he might signify that this was spoken of Christ.

He is rightly called a stone: coming in the flesh, he deigned to insert himself into the building of the holy Church in order to strengthen it. He is “living,” since he could say: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). He was rejected by human beings when they said: “We have no king except Caesar” (John XIX). He was chosen by God when he himself said: “But I have been established as king by him” (Ps. II), and so forth. He was honored when, after the death of the cross, God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name (Phil. II), and so forth.

“And you yourselves, like living stones,” etc. He says that they are to be built upon it because no spiritual building can stand without our Lord Jesus Christ, the living stone. “No one can lay another foundation besides him” (1 Cor. III). Through participation in him the faithful become living stones, although through unbelief they had been dead stones—that is, hard and insensible stones—to whom it is rightly said: “I will take from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. XXXVI).

But they are fitted as living stones for the spiritual building when, through the discernment of a learned teacher, their superfluous actions and thoughts are cut away and they are squared as though by the blow of an axe. Just as courses of stones in a wall are carried by one another, so each of the faithful is carried by the righteous who preceded them in the Church, and they in turn carry the righteous who follow, through teaching and endurance, up to the final righteous person. The one who is carried by those before him will not have someone after him whom he must carry. But the one who carries the entire building and is himself carried by no one is Christ the Lord. Hence the prophet also calls him a precious stone, laid as a foundation.

He also calls the elect “living stones” to indicate the effort of their good intention or action, which, with the grace of God going before and accompanying it, must always be exercised. For dead stones—that is, material stones—when they are prepared or placed in a building, can neither assist the labor of the worker nor do anything by themselves except fall; wherever and however the builder places them, they remain there insensibly or slip away and fall.

Blessed Peter does not wish us to imitate the hardness and insensibility of such stones, but to be built as living stones upon Christ the foundation, so that, with grace helping us, we may cooperate by living soberly, justly, and devoutly, according to the example of the one who said: “And his grace toward me was not empty, but I labored more than all of them” (1 Cor. XV). He was a living stone in the building of the holy Church, striving diligently to labor lest he appear to have received God’s grace in vain. And lest he seem to have attributed any part of that labor to himself, he added watchfully: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (ibid.).

Thus, whoever, with Christ granting and helping him, strives tirelessly in good works is built by Christ as a living stone in his house. But whoever, after being incorporated into the holy Church through the grace of regeneration, makes no effort to do anything further for his salvation is, like a dead stone, wholly unworthy of the heavenly building. He must therefore be rejected by divine examination, and another who is worthy must be substituted in his place, according to the precept of Leviticus, in which the stones of leprous houses are ordered to be inspected by the priest and, if they cannot be purified, to be counted among the unclean and removed from the arrangement of clean stones.

“Be built up,” he says, “as spiritual houses.” He says that those houses are to be made spiritual, although the one house of Christ is formed from all the elect, angels and human beings alike. Similarly, although there is one Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, it is often called “churches” in the plural because of the many gatherings of the faithful, distinguished by different tribes, languages, and peoples. Hence he himself says: “I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify these things to you in the churches.”

Nor should it be passed over that some manuscripts have, in the singular number: “Be built up, a spiritual house”; others: “Be built upward into a spiritual house.” In this the unity of the whole holy Church is commended more openly. When he had said, “Be built up as spiritual houses,” or “as a spiritual house,” he added:

“A holy priesthood.” By this he very clearly exhorts us to become a holy priesthood ourselves and to be built upon the foundation of Christ. He calls the whole Church a holy priesthood, although under the law only the house of Aaron possessed that name and office. For we are all members of the High Priest, and we are all marked with the oil of gladness. What follows applies to all alike:

“To offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.” He calls our works, almsgiving, and prayers spiritual sacrifices, in distinction from the fleshly victims of the law. The concluding words, “through Jesus Christ,” apply to everything he had said beforehand, because through his grace we are built upon him by wise architects—that is, the ministers of the New Testament—and through his Spirit we become spiritual houses, fortified against the rains, winds, lightning, and temptations.

We are able to share in the holy priesthood and to perform anything good that is acceptable to God only through him. Just as branches cannot bear fruit by themselves unless they remain in the vine, so neither can you, he says, unless you remain in me.

“Therefore Scripture contains: ‘Behold, I place in Zion a stone,’” etc. He presents this testimony from Isaiah to confirm what he had said earlier: “To whom you draw near, a living stone,” asserting and affirming that the Lord our Savior is called a stone by the prophets because of his firmness. He adds:

“And everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.” He says this because of what he had stated: “And you, like living stones, are being built up.” The apostle’s words beautifully correspond both to this prophecy—“drawing near to the living stone,” or “believing in him,” you will not be put to shame—and to the verse of that psalm in which, after saying, “Approach him and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII), it immediately adds: “And your faces will not blush” (ibid.). John says something similar: “And now, little children, remain in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not be put to shame by him at his coming” (1 John II).

“To you, therefore, who believe, there is honor.” That honor, namely, that you will not be put to shame by him at his coming, but, as he himself says: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him” (John XII).

“But for those who do not believe, ‘the stone which the builders rejected,’” etc. Just as they rejected him while building their own deeds, refusing to place him in the foundation of their hearts, so they themselves will be rejected by him at his coming, when he will refuse to receive into the building of his house, which is in heaven, those who rejected him. This distinction between the honor of believers and the rejection of unbelievers extends thus far. He then continues concerning believers:

“This has become the head of the corner.” Just as a cornerstone joins two walls, so the Lord united the people of the Jews and the nations in one fellowship of faith. Immediately afterward he adds concerning unbelievers:

“And a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.” Hence Paul also says: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, but to the nations foolishness” (1 Cor. I).

“To those who stumble at the word,” etc. They stumble at the word simply because they have happened to hear the word of God. They stumble in mind when they refuse to believe what they hear. To heighten their foolishness, he adds: “Nor do they believe in that for which they were appointed.” For they were appointed for this—that is, by nature they were made human beings for this purpose: to believe God and obey his will. Solomon bears witness to this when he says: “Fear God and keep his commandments; this is every human being” (Eccles. XII). That is, every human being was naturally made for this: to fear God and obey his commandments.

Some manuscripts read: “In which they were also appointed,” which may be understood according to what Paul says when speaking of God: “For in him we live and move and exist” (Acts XVII).

You, however, are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, etc. This testimony of praise was once given through Moses to the ancient people of God; now the apostle Peter rightly gives it to the Gentiles, because they have believed in Christ, who, like a cornerstone, united the Gentiles to the salvation that Israel had in him. He calls them a chosen race on account of their faith, distinguishing them from those who, by rejecting the living stone, have themselves become rejected. He calls them a royal priesthood because they have been united to the body of him who is both supreme King and true Priest—granting his own people a kingdom as King, and, as High Priest, cleansing their sins through the sacrifice of his blood. He names them a royal priesthood so that they may remember both to hope for an everlasting kingdom and [Col. 0051A] always to offer God sacrifices of blameless conduct. They are also called a holy nation and a people of acquisition, in accordance with what the apostle Paul says when explaining the prophet’s judgment: “But my righteous one lives by faith; and if he withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with him. But we,” he says, “are not of withdrawal unto perdition, but of faith unto the acquisition of the soul” (Heb. 10). And in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops to govern the Church of the Lord, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts 20). We have therefore become a people of acquisition through the blood of our Redeemer, just as formerly the people of Israel was redeemed from Egypt by the blood of the lamb. Hence, in the following verse also, he mystically recalls the ancient history and teaches that it must likewise be fulfilled spiritually for the new people of God, saying:

[Col. 0051B]

So that you may proclaim his mighty deeds, etc. For just as those who were freed from Egyptian slavery through Moses sang a song of triumph to the Lord after crossing the Red Sea and the drowning of Pharaoh’s army, so we too ought, after receiving the remission of sins in baptism, to render thanks worthy of heavenly benefits. For the Egyptians who afflicted the people of God—and whose name is also interpreted as “darkness” or “tribulations”—aptly signify, through what follows, our sins, which are erased in baptism. The liberation of the children of Israel and their leading into the land long ago promised to their fathers also corresponds to the mystery of our redemption, by which, with the grace of Christ enlightening and guiding us, we make our way toward the light of our heavenly dwelling. [Col. 0051C]

That light of grace was also displayed by the pillar of cloud and fire, which both protected them from the darkness of night throughout that journey and led them by an ineffable path to the promised dwelling places of their homeland.

Who once were not the people of God but now are the people of God, etc. These verses clearly indicate that he wrote this Epistle to those who had come to faith from the Gentiles. Once alienated from the way of life of the people of God, they have now been united to his people through the grace of faith and have obtained the mercy they had not known how to hope for (Eph. 2). He takes this from the prophet Hosea, who, foretelling the calling of the Gentiles, says: “I will call ‘my people’ the one who was not my people, and ‘having obtained mercy’ the one who had not obtained mercy. And it shall be that in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God” (Hos. 1–2).

[Col. 0051D]

Beloved, I urge you as strangers and pilgrims, etc. Up to this point blessed Peter has instructed the Church in general, explaining either the benefits by which divine mercy calls us to salvation or the gifts by which God formerly deigned to honor the Jews and now honors us. From here he carefully exhorts the various classes of the faithful not to make themselves unworthy of so great a grace of the Holy Spirit by living carnally. He warns those distinguished by the title of royal and priestly dignity not to degenerate, overcome by the wickedness of their vices, from the glory of the nobility once bestowed or promised to them. Thus he addresses first free persons and slaves, then women and men in particular; afterward, following a general exhortation, he shows elders and young men how they ought to conduct themselves.

[Col. 0052A]

He appropriately teaches free persons to abstain from carnal desires, because a freer way of life is accustomed to tolerate greater dangers from enticing pleasures, which wage war against the soul. For when the flesh is feebly subjected to flattering desires, the army of vices is already firmly armed against the soul. He suitably calls them strangers and pilgrims, so that they may submit their souls less to earthly things insofar as they remember that their homeland is in heaven. In this life the distinction between the elect and the rejected is ordinarily this: the elect, now pilgrims and exiles, await their homeland in the future; consequently, they take less delight in present and perishable joys, the more they hope to receive future joys without end and to reign with Christ forever. The rejected, however, have their homeland here; they know only how to yearn for the desires of this life. Therefore, after this life they will be banished into perpetual exile, where, deprived of every pleasure, they will suffer only adversity amid torments.

[Col. 0052B]

So that, in what they malign you, etc. It often happened that pagans who disparaged the faith of Christians because they had abandoned their gods later, observing their chaste conduct and unconquered spirit in Christ, ceased to slander them and began instead to glorify and praise God, who was proved good and just by the goodness and justice of his worshipers. “Let them glorify” God, he says, “on the day of visitation”—that is, at the time of recompense—“and let the unbelievers already recognize how much glory is to be granted you by God,” when they see you steadfastly following him amid the dangers that oppose you.

Therefore be subject to every human institution for God’s sake. By “every human institution” he means every human dignity, every person, every authority to which divine providence has willed that we be subject. This is the meaning of what he says, “for God’s sake,” because “there is no authority except from God. And whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13). He subsequently explains which institution he means, adding:

[Col. 0052C]

Whether to the king as supreme, etc. He mentions only the king and governors, and not masters, because here he is specifically instructing those who, as we have said, are masters of slaves. Subsequently he also admonishes slaves concerning how they should serve their masters. He therefore teaches the faithful—who are servants of the eternal King—to be subject even to the authorities of the world, lest it be possible to disparage faith and Christian religion on the grounds that they disrupt the rights of human society. What was said, “to every human institution,” can also properly be understood in this way: it signifies both faithful and unbelieving masters of worldly affairs.

[Col. 0052D]

For the punishment of evildoers but the praise of those who do good. He does not mean that all kings or governors know how either to punish evildoers or to praise the good. Rather, he simply describes what the conduct of a good judge ought to be: that he restrain those who do evil and reward those who act well. Even if he acts unjustly when he condemns the good, nevertheless what he does contributes to their praise if they patiently endure his wickedness and patiently resist his folly. “Do you wish,” he says, “not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it” (ibid.). He does not say “by it” but “from it,” because even if human authority does not praise you—or even if it persecutes you, or kills you with the sword as it did Paul, or crucifies you as it did Peter—you will have praise from it, since, through what it does wrong against you, who are just and innocent, the patience of your virtue earns the crown of praise. The words that follow show that this too was the intention of blessed Peter in this statement, for he says:

Because this is the will of God, that by doing good, etc. This, then, is the praise of the good, to which he says governors were sent by the king: when the good, despite the ignorance of foolish governors, use their conduct of goodness to win their own everlasting praise.

[Col. 0053A]

As free persons, and not as having freedom as a covering for wickedness, etc. Those do good as free persons who, the greater the freedom they enjoy among human beings, bind themselves all the more closely—or rather, more freely—to divine service. But those too do good as free persons who, following the example of the patriarch Joseph, although oppressed by human servitude, are compelled by no device to become servants of vices. By contrast, those turn their freedom into a covering for wickedness who, the less they are restrained by the yoke of human service, the more broadly they are enslaved to the dominion of sins; and when they serve vices with impunity, they call it freedom, using this name to conceal their guilt.

This can also be understood generally in accordance with the apostle Paul’s statement: “You were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh” (Gal. 5). We are rightly called free because through baptism we have been released from the bonds of sins. [Col. 0053C]

Having been redeemed from demonic slavery and made children of God, we have not received, along with so great a gift of freedom, a greater opportunity or license to sin. On the contrary, if we sin, having immediately lost our freedom, we become slaves of sin. Whoever thinks that the Lord freed him for the purpose of sinning more freely changes his freedom into a covering for wickedness. Blessed Peter wishes us to be free from the service of sins, so that we may remain good and faithful servants of our Creator. Hence he adds:

[Col. 0053B]

But as servants of God. Honor everyone, etc. He urges us to show fitting honor to all and, in accordance with the Lord’s command, to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and to God the things that are God’s (Luke 20). Appropriately, among other things, he commands free persons to love the brotherhood, so that they may remember that even those who are subject to them by temporal condition have been made their brothers in Christ, invoking with them the Father who judges without partiality.

[Col. 0053D]

Slaves, be subject in all fear to your masters, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the difficult, etc. By “difficult” he means undisciplined, deriving the term from the Greek language. In Greek, schola (σχολή) is the name for a place where young men ordinarily devote themselves to literary studies and attend to their teachers; hence schola is interpreted as “leisure” or “free time.” Indeed, in the psalm where we sing, “Be at leisure and see that I am God” (Ps. 45), the Greek has σχολάζετε (*scholazete*) for what we say “be at leisure.” [Col. 0054A]

In Greek, scholastici are the educated; dyscoli are the uneducated and uncultivated. Yet he wishes subjects to obey both kinds, explaining more clearly how above he commanded us to be subject to every human institution. Another Translation has “difficult” instead of “dyscolis.” And the holy bishop Fulgentius gives the passage in his little works as follows: “Serving with fear not only the good and gentle, but also the more difficult.”

But if, while doing good, you patiently endure, etc. We must observe more attentively how greatly he glorifies the condition of slaves. He declares that those who do good and, without guilt, are beaten by cruel and wicked masters are imitators of the Lord’s Passion. You hear that he suffered for us, and you rejoice because he died for you; attend to what follows:

[Col. 0054B]

Leaving you an example so that you may follow his footsteps. An example of tribulations, not pleasures; of insults, scourges, pains, reproaches, thorns, the cross, wounds, and death. It is written in the psalm: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult ways” (Ps. 16). What words of God’s lips could these be except those by which he promises eternal life?

He himself bore our sins, etc. Having addressed slaves specifically above, he now admonishes everyone generally, so that masters too may recall what God and the Lord endured for them. Indeed, he instructs the whole Church concerning what its author endured for its liberation. For he does not say “your sins,” but adds himself as well: “He himself,” he says, “bore our sins in his body upon the wood.”

[Col. 0054C]

For you were like sheep going astray. How can he call them both sheep and straying, since those who live their lives in error are reckoned by the name of goats rather than sheep? It is because the Lord knows those who are his, and he also endures many who live badly for a long time, although he foresees that they will be saved among the number of his sheep.

But now you have returned to the shepherd and overseer of your souls. He touches upon the Gospel parable in which the merciful Shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the desert, comes to visit the one that had gone astray. For what is said there—that after finding it he placed it joyfully upon his shoulders—blessed Peter has anticipated here by saying: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood.” For he plainly wished to redeem us in such a way that, hanging upon the wood where he would remove our sins, he carried it upon his shoulders.

[Col. 0054D]

“To the shepherd,” he says, “and overseer of your souls.” He is the shepherd, plainly, because he gives us the pastures of eternal life and supplies, in the present, the pastures of temporal graces. He is the overseer of your souls because “the Rising One from on high has visited us, to give light to those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1). Each day he visits that light which he has given us, preserving it so that it does not fail—or rather, helping it to grow. Some manuscripts have the Greek: “To the shepherd and bishop of your souls.” In Latin, *episcopus* means “overseer.” For truly, “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers,” so that he may deliver them from all their tribulations (Ps. 33).

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0055A]

Likewise, let women be subject to their own husbands, etc. It should be noted that blessed Peter wishes good and honorable women to be subject to unbelieving husbands on this condition: that they not only do nothing evil at their command, but also persist in such chaste conduct, unconquerable in its steadfastness, that they may serve as examples of chastity and faith even to their husbands.

Whose adornment should not be outward, etc. For, as Cyprian says: “Those who put on silk and purple cannot put on Christ. Adorned with gold, pearls, and necklaces, they have lost the adornments of the heart and breast. If Peter also warns women that they must be restrained and governed by religious observance according to ecclesiastical discipline—women who commonly excuse their adornment on the grounds of their husbands—how much more is it proper for a virgin to observe this, for whom no indulgence for adornment is appropriate, nor can the guilt of falsehood be transferred to another, but she alone remains in the offense?”

[Col. 0055B]

But the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and gentle spirit, etc. He preaches chastity and the adornment of the inner person in the incorruptibility of a quiet and gentle spirit, saying in a sense: “Your outward person has been corrupted, and you have ceased to possess the blessed integrity that properly belongs to virgins; imitate the incorruption of the spirit through strict abstinence, and provide by the mind what you cannot provide in the body. For Christ seeks these riches and this adornment of your union.” It is remarkable that this opinion is also found in Pythagoras, dictated by the law of natural knowledge: that the true adornments of married women are modesty, not clothing.

[Col. 0055C]

Husbands, likewise, living together according to knowledge, etc. He says “likewise,” calling husbands to imitation, because above he had already commanded wives, saying: “Let husbands observe your chaste conduct in the fear of God.” “According to knowledge” means that they should know what God desires and give honor to the womanly vessel. If we abstain from intercourse, we give honor. If we do not abstain, it is clear that intercourse is contrary to honor.

So that your prayers may not be hindered. Paul also says: “Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7). He therefore states that prayers are hindered by marital duty, because whenever I render the marital debt to my wife, I cannot pray. But if, according to another statement of the apostle, we must pray without ceasing, then I must never serve marriage, lest I be hindered for even an hour from the prayer to which I am commanded always to devote myself.

[Col. 0055D]
