In faith, all of one mind, showing compassion. Since above he had taught various persons, conditions, and sexes with appropriate distinction, he now admonishes everyone together to have, in the cause of the Lord’s faith, one heart and one soul.

For you have been called to this, that you may possess the blessing as an inheritance. This refers, plainly, to the Judge’s saying: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25). The blessing of inheritance may also be understood as that by which the Church is blessed perpetually in the future life. Hence, rejoicing now in hope of future things, it says: “I will exalt you, my God and King, and I will bless your name forever and ever” (Ps. 144). Whatever, therefore, each person desires to find in the future, let him strive to meditate upon and practice in the present: namely, to bless the Creator and his neighbor with a sincere voice, and also to make himself worthy of both divine and fraternal blessing.

[Col. 0056A]

For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, etc. Since blessed Peter had forbidden us to return evil for evil and had rather commanded us to bless those who curse, he rightly establishes by prophetic testimony that both the good and the wicked are always seen by the heavenly scrutiny. Thus we may remember that our patience in enduring the wicked and our benevolence in wishing good for our persecutors will be rewarded with an eternal prize, while our persecutors, if they refuse to repent, will be punished with a fitting penalty. If, however, they repent, we too, on account of the salvation of those for whom we prayed to the Lord, will receive the crown of righteous rejoicing.

[Col. 0056B]

And who is there who will harm you, etc. He is speaking of what comes upon us from adversaries through insulting words, losses of temporal possessions, and bodily torments. When these and similar things are inflicted upon the faithful, they can in no way harm those who are zealous for what is good and are so according to knowledge. Rather, they bring the palm of patience to those who bear them with equanimity and patience; conversely, they greatly harm those who inflict them by increasing their eternal punishment.

If someone is overcome by such adversities and falls away, it is not the person who inflicted the evil who harmed him, but he harmed himself by refusing to bear it patiently. The house built by the wise man did not fall, not because it had not endured the violence of storms, but because it was founded upon rock. Nor did the house foolishly built by the foolish man fall merely because it was battered by storms, but because it had been set upon sand. Adversity struck and tested both equally, but the firmness of the foundation gave one the crown of perseverance, while the folly of the fragile structure overthrew the other.

[Col. 0056C]

No misfortune brought by the devil, by an evil person, or by the general whirl of perishable things can harm a perfect lover of what is good. Nevertheless, it is clear that many lovers of what is good have been harmed by others when they were badly instructed in the knowledge of the truth they love. How many who desired to believe rightly in God according to Catholic teaching and to live rightly in the Church were unknowingly led astray by the madness of Arius, by the wickedness of Sabellius, or by that of other heretics? Read the book of John Chrysostom that he wrote on the subject: “No one can be harmed by another except by himself.”

But even if you suffer anything for the sake of righteousness, you will be blessed. He says: Not only does the one who inflicts evil upon those doing good do you no harm, but when the enemy persecutes you because of the good things he hates, he provides you with the cause of greater blessedness by exercising the strength of your patience, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness.”

[Col. 0057A]

But sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts. What is it to sanctify the Lord in our hearts except to contemplate, with the innermost affection of the heart, how great is his holiness and how incomprehensible his glory? How much strength to conquer can he give to those who hope in him, whose immeasurable holiness shines forth?

Always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason, etc. We ought to give an account of our hope and faith to those who ask in two ways: we should make known to everyone the just reasons for our hope and faith, whether they ask faithfully or unbelievingly, and we should always keep our profession of faith and hope undefiled, even amid the pressures of our adversaries. Through patience we show how reasonably we have learned to preserve it, since for its love we neither fear to suffer adversity nor to undergo death.

[Col. 0057B]

With gentleness and fear, having a good conscience. He urges us to observe a quality in the very knowledge of teaching, namely, that humility—which is the teacher and mother of all virtues—be expressed both in speech and displayed in conduct.

So that, in what they malign you as evildoers, etc. Those who ridicule in you the faith and hope of heavenly things, which they cannot see, should see your good works and through them be put to shame, since they cannot openly deny that these works are good. Or certainly the passage should be understood in this way: “Take care, by doing good, that those who malign your good conduct may, when the time of future recompense arrives, be put to shame when they see you crowned with Christ and themselves condemned with the devil.”

[Col. 0057C]

For it is better, if the will of God should will it, to suffer while doing good than while doing evil. This statement elegantly exposes the folly of those who, when rebuked by their brothers for their faults or even restrained by punishments, endure it with complete patience; but when they suffer without guilt either verbal insults, losses of possessions, or any other adversity from their neighbors, immediately burst into anger. Those who until then appeared innocent make themselves guilty through impatience and murmuring.

To make clear how greatly the scourges differ according to the disparity of merits, let us consider that Tobias, Saul, and Elymas were struck by one and the same affliction of blindness. Tobias was struck so that the virtue of his patience might shine more widely as an example to all; Saul was struck so that he might be changed from the persecutor Saul into the apostle Paul; Elymas, however, was struck so that, enduring the punishment deserved by his faithlessness, he might cease to lead astray those who were going to believe.

[Col. 0057D]

And if I were given the choice, I would rather, together with so great a Father, be subjected to just scourges, whether divine or human, than be driven toward the pursuit of righteousness by the force of unjust blows. Again, I would rather be drawn away from sins by a scourge than be subjected to eternal punishment because of the incurable burden of sins.

[Col. 0058A]

For Christ also died once for our sins, etc. Therefore, whoever suffers as a just person imitates Christ. Whoever is corrected by scourges imitates the thief who recognized Christ on the cross and entered Paradise with Christ from the cross. Whoever does not cease from his sins even amid scourges imitates the thief on the left, who went up onto the cross because of his sins and after the cross fell into Tartarus. He mentions that Christ died once precisely to recall to us that eternal reward is given in return for our temporary sufferings.

So that he might offer us to God, put to death indeed in the flesh, etc. Concerning this putting to death of the flesh and making alive of the spirit, which those who labor patiently for the Lord possess, the apostle Paul also says: “Although our outward person is being corrupted, yet the one within is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4). Christ therefore offers us to God the Father when, through the putting to death of the flesh, we rejoice to be sacrificed for him—that is, he displays our laudable life in the sight of the Father.

[Col. 0058B]

Or certainly he offers us to God when, freed from the flesh, he introduces us into the eternal kingdom. Indeed, concerning what is said, “but made alive in the Spirit,” Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, refers this not to the human spirit—which is made more fully alive when the flesh is put to death, in accordance with the prophet’s statement about the Lord, “to make alive the spirit of the humble and to make alive the heart of the contrite” (Isa. 57)—but rather to the grace of the Holy Spirit, who gives eternal life to those who put their flesh to death.

He also uses this testimony against the Arians, who contradict the equality of the Holy Trinity, asserting that, through the indivisible unity of divine operation by which the Father gives life, the Son gives life and the Holy Spirit gives life. The Father and the Son do so because it is written: “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those whom he wishes.” The Holy Spirit does so, as this testimony declares, where it is said of the Son: “that he might offer us to God, put to death indeed in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit.” Therefore, since their operation is one, their substance or essence cannot be different.

[Col. 0058C]

In which also he came and preached to those who were confined in the flesh, etc. He who came into the world in the flesh in our own times and preached the way of life also preached, coming in the Spirit, to those who before the Flood were unbelieving and living carnally. For he was present through the Holy Spirit in Noah and the other saints who lived at that time, and through their good conduct he preached to the wicked people of that age, so that they might turn to better things.

[Col. 0058D]

He calls those “confined in the flesh” who were weighed down heavily by carnal desires. Hence Scripture says of them: “All flesh had corrupted its way” (Gen. 6). When he says “in which,” he signifies “in that which he had previously mentioned,” namely, “that he might offer us to God.” For even then, if anyone had wished to believe the Lord’s preaching—which he displayed through the life of the faithful—he rejoiced to offer them also to God the Father. But if any maligned the good as evildoers, they were put to shame when the Flood came.

What he says, “in which,” can also be understood of both groups: that is, he came in the Spirit and preached both to those who were confined in the flesh, so that through that same preaching a crown of praise might arise for those who believed and shame for those who persisted in unbelief.

Some manuscripts have: “In which also he came and preached in the Spirit to those who were in prison.” This refers to the same intention concerning the wicked and unbelieving: because their understanding is darkened, they are rightly said even in this life to be confined in prison. In that prison, namely, they are still weighed down by inner darkness—that is, by blindness of mind and unjust works—until, released from the flesh, they are cast into outer darkness and into the prison of eternal condemnation. Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “And the judge will hand you over to the officer, and you will be thrown into prison” (Matt. 5).

[Col. 0059A]

The saints, too, may rightly proclaim themselves placed in a prison in this life when they thirst for the joy of their heavenly homeland, in accordance with the Psalmist’s saying: “Lead my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Ps. 141). There is, however, a great difference between the two prisons. The rejected are in the prison of sins and ignorance; the righteous, although placed in the prison of tribulations, enjoy the light of righteousness with hearts always expanded toward God. The apostles Paul and Silas prefigured them when, at midnight, in the innermost horror of the prison, bound and scourged though they were, they sang a hymn of praise to God with the most joyful voice.

One interpreter understood this passage as follows: the saints resting in the underworld desired that consolation of which the Lord says to the apostles, “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Matt. 13); and of which the Psalmist says, “My eyes have failed in expectation of your word, saying, ‘When will you comfort me?’” (Ps. 118). [Col. 0059C]

He held that, when the Lord descended into the underworld, this consolation or exhortation was preached even to those who were in prison and had once been unbelieving in the days of Noah.

[Col. 0059B]

That interpreter may have said this, but the Catholic faith holds that, when the Lord descended into the underworld, he led out from there not the unbelievers but only his faithful, bringing them with him to the heavenly kingdoms. Nor does he demonstrate the way of life to souls stripped of the body and confined in the prison of hell for their crimes; rather, in this life, either through himself or through the examples and words of his faithful, he daily demonstrates the way of life. Concerning these people it is aptly said:

Who formerly were unbelieving, etc. The patience of God itself was also his preaching, since Noah, devoting himself for a hundred years to the work of building the ark, showed by the daily execution of his work what was going to happen to the world. Hence Paul says: “Or do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. 2), etc.

Another Translation has this passage as follows: “Christ died once for our sins, the just for the unjust, so that he might bring us to God, put to death in the body but made alive in the spirit. In that spirit he also preached to those who were in prison, who formerly had not believed in those days when they were awaiting the patience of God, in the days of Noah,” etc.

[Col. 0059D]

In which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water, etc. He says that the form of baptism is likened to the ark and the waters of the Flood. This is entirely appropriate, because the construction of the ark from smoothed timbers signifies the building of the Church, which is formed from the gathering of faithful souls by the architects of the word. The fact that, while the whole world perished, a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water signifies that, compared with the Gentiles, Jews, heretics, and false believers who perish, the number of the elect is much smaller.

[Col. 0060A]

Hence it is said of the narrow gate and confined way that leads to life: “And few are those who find it” (Matt. 7). And again: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12). Concerning this little flock the following is also aptly added:

Not the removal of the filth of the flesh, etc. For where is there a good conscience unless there is also an unfeigned faith? The apostle Paul teaches that “the goal of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1).

The fact that the water of the Flood did not save those outside the ark but killed them undoubtedly prefigured every heretic who, although possessing the sacrament of baptism, is plunged into hell by those very waters by which the ark is lifted toward heaven.

The number eight itself—the number of souls saved through water—signifies that the holy Church received the washing of baptism as a sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection, so that just as he rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we, cleansed from sins through the water of regeneration, might walk in newness of life (Rom. 6). On the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day, the Sabbath—the Lord rose from the dead and displayed both an example to us of the future resurrection and the mystery of a new way of life, by which, though placed on earth, we might live a heavenly life. Peter himself explains this by adding:

[Col. 0060B]

Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, etc.

[Col. 0060C]

For just as, rising from the dead, he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God, so also he signified that through baptism the way of salvation and entry into the heavenly kingdom is opened to us.

He rightly says, “swallowing up death.” For what we swallow we cause, through the power of our body, never again to appear after it has been taken in. The Lord swallowed up death, utterly consuming it when he rose from the dead, so that it could no longer prevail against him through the touch of any corruption. While the appearance of a true body remained, every stain of its former frailty was entirely absent.

The same thing is promised to us at the end, as the Apostle says when speaking of our resurrection: “Then will come to pass the saying that is written: Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor. 15). It is rightly said “swallowed up,” because when we too have become participants in eternal life, the power of an immortal body will remove every fault of former corruption, just as a flame ordinarily consumes a drop of water cast into it by the force of its heat.

[Col. 0060D]

Having gone into heaven, he says, etc. There is no doubt that the angels and all the powers and authorities of the heavenly homeland have always been subject to the Son of God, whom they praise, fear, and adore together with the Father and the Holy Spirit as one God without beginning. But blessed Peter necessarily judged that it should be emphasized that the humanity he assumed was raised through resurrection to such glory that, by incomparable exaltation, it was placed above every angelic dignity and power.

Accordingly, the Psalmist, when he said to the Father concerning him, “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8), [Col. 0061A] immediately added: “You crowned him with glory and honor and appointed him over the works of your hands; you subjected all things beneath his feet” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, since Christ suffered in the flesh, etc. After establishing, through the mystery of the ark and the Flood, the example of the Lord’s resurrection and of our cleansing that takes place in baptism, he returns to what he had begun to say: that, imitating the work of our Redeemer, we should patiently endure the wickedness of evil people amid the good deeds we perform.

It should be noted that he speaks distinctly when he says, “since Christ suffered in the flesh.” For, as blessed Ambrose says: “His flesh suffered, but the Divinity was free from death; according to the law of human nature, he subjected his body to suffering.” But can the Divinity die when the soul cannot? “Do not fear,” he says, “those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10). If, therefore, the soul cannot be killed, how can the Divinity?

Because the one who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sins, etc. Whoever among the saints has surrendered his body to the violence of persecutors for martyrdom—there is no doubt that, to the extent human nature permits, he has abstained from sins until the end of his life. For what could one who was fastened to wood, surrounded by blows from stones, subdued by the bites of beasts, placed upon flames of fire, pierced by the lashes of scorpions, or afflicted by any other kind of punishment think about the perpetration of sin or carnal desires, except that he could turn his mind only to the will of God, compelled to desire nothing but that, when the struggle was ended, he might receive the crown of life?

Blessed Peter therefore desires us always to imitate the mind of such people when, setting before us the example of the Lord’s Passion, he commands us to arm ourselves with the same thought against the wickedness of the evil and against the allurements of vices. He wishes us to understand that even we, resting in the peace of the Church, if we put on the character of one who suffers, can easily, with the Lord’s help, avoid every fall into sin and subject all desires to the commands of the divine will.

Hence the Psalmist also entreats the Lord, saying: “Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Psalm 118). And the Apostle says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians 5). Whoever therefore extinguishes carnal desires in his mind through fear of heavenly judgments is already like one crucified and suffering for Christ; existing as though dead to sins, he lives only for the service of God.

[Col. 0061C–D]

In this they are astonished, since you do not run with them, etc. Because, he says, you have crucified your flesh with its vices and desires, it follows that, although on account of their faithlessness they blaspheme you, as people separated from their fellowship, they nevertheless continually see in your conduct works of righteousness and piety, which they rightly admire, and on account of which they rightly praise and venerate the Christian faith.

Who will give an account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. Therefore, he says, care less and grieve less if, while doing good, you are blasphemed by the reprobate. For even if you remain silent, God the judge—who is certainly just—will not remain silent or be restrained; he will repay them with the fitting rewards for their blasphemy and you with the fitting rewards for your patience.

For this reason the Gospel was preached even to the dead, etc. Such is God’s care, such his love, such his desire that we be put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit, that he commanded the word of faith to be preached even to those who are entangled in greater crimes and rightly numbered among the dead—namely, in lusts, desires, drunkenness, revelries, drinking bouts, and unlawful worship of idols—so that they too, their carnal desires having been judged—that is, despised and cast off—might live spiritually and, together with those whom the grace of the Gospel found living innocently, await eternal life.

[Col. 0062A–B]

But the end of all things will draw near. So that no one might flatter himself about the remoteness of the future judgment, in which he had said that the living and the dead would be judged, he prudently warns that, although the arrival of the final crisis is uncertain, it is nevertheless certain to all that they cannot remain long in this mortal life.

Therefore be prudent, etc. The Lord likewise commanded us in the Gospel always to pray and keep watch in view of the uncertain end. Speaking about the day of judgment, he says: “Keep watch, praying at all times, so that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke 21).

We are rightly commanded to keep watch in our prayers, so that when we stand at prayer every carnal and worldly thought may withdraw, and the mind may then think of nothing except that for which it prays. For the enemy frequently slips in and, deceiving us subtly, distracts our prayers so completely that we have one thing in our heart and utter another with our voice, although God ought to be prayed to by sincere intention—not by the sound of the voice, but by the meaning of the soul.

Above all, maintain continual mutual charity among yourselves. He rightly added “continual,” because we are always able to love, but we cannot always remain watchful in prayer, since the weakness of the flesh obstructs us; nor can we always devote ourselves fully to the virtues he next mentions, namely, hospitality, teaching, the administration of gifts—whether common or particular—for our neighbors, and other things of this kind. These must necessarily be performed through the service of the body and at suitable times. Charity itself, however, by whose impulse these outward actions are performed, because it presides over the inner person, can always be possessed within, even though it cannot always be displayed publicly.

[Col. 0062C–D]

Because charity covers a multitude of sins. This is especially evident when one says truthfully to God: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6). It is certainly established that all the good works we perform cleanse and cover the faults we have committed. But this is said particularly of charity, by which we forgive our neighbors what they owe us, because it is most just in God’s sight that it be repaid to us according to the measure of mercy with which we have measured.

Conversely, the wise man terrifyingly rebukes the hard-hearted, saying: “A man harbors anger against a man, and seeks healing from God” (Ecclesiasticus 28). Nor should we doubt that, even in the person who through charity does whatever he can for the correction of his neighbor—by admonishing, rebuking, or chastising—charity itself covers a multitude of sins. James bears witness to this when he says: “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James 5).

[Col. 0063A–B]

If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God. He fears, that is, lest he say or command anything contrary to God’s will, or contrary to what is clearly commanded in the holy Scriptures, and be found to be like a false witness of God, or sacrilegious, or introducing something foreign to the Lord’s teaching, or indeed suppressing and passing over something that pleases God. For God himself most explicitly commands preachers of the truth concerning those whom they instruct for life, saying: “Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28). He commands us to hand on to our hearers everything that he himself commanded—not other things, and not merely some of these things, but all of them, for observance.

If anyone ministers, etc. Let each person offer every good thing he can to his neighbor with all the greater humility, the more certainly he knows that he cannot possess from himself what he offers.

[Col. 0063C]

So that God may be honored in all things through Jesus Christ, etc. This accords with the command of Jesus Christ himself, where he says: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5). God is therefore honored in our actions when, whatever we do well and according to his will, we attribute not to our own merits but to his grace. Conversely, the evil we do we attribute solely to our own wickedness or ignorance.

Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial, etc. Some manuscripts read: “Do not regard yourselves as strangers in the fiery trial.” The meaning of both expressions is evident. No faithful person ought to be surprised that he suffers the heat of tribulations in this life, since for a definite reason he is now tested by tribulations so that, when he has been proved, he may be judged worthy to receive the crown of the future life. Nor should anyone consider himself, for this reason, a stranger and foreigner to the members of Christ, because he is struck by the adversities of the present age, since neither the Lord’s departure in death (Psalm 67), nor the persecution of unbelievers in his Church, has ever ceased—from the first martyr Abel to the last elect who will be born at the end of the age. Therefore, after saying well, “Do not be surprised at the fiery trial,” he added:

As though something strange were happening to you. For it is a very ancient and frequent occurrence that God’s elect endure the adversities of the present life for the sake of eternal salvation.

[Col. 0063D–64A]

Let none of you suffer as a murderer, etc. For one suffers as a reviler when, at the time of his own suffering, he becomes unrestrainedly enraged against his persecutor to his own injury.

For it is time for judgment to begin from the household of God. Scripture makes known two judgments of God: one hidden, the other manifest. The hidden judgment is the punishment by which each human being is now either exercised for purification, admonished toward conversion, or, if he has despised God’s calling and discipline, blinded for condemnation. The manifest judgment is that by which the Lord will come to judge the living and the dead.

The present passage says that the time has come for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord, that is, from the Church, which through the exercise of present afflictions is prepared for future joys. For the reprobate now lead their transitory life so much more securely and without any stroke of vengeance, the more nothing but vengeance remains for them in the future, according to the saying of blessed Job: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld.”

[Col. 0064B]

And if it begins with us, what will be the end of those, etc.? From this it is gathered with what severity the strict Judge will strike those whom he condemns there, if here he thus torments those whom he loves. For if sons are scourged, what should the most wicked servants expect?

And if the righteous will scarcely be saved, etc. The Pelagians refuse to believe that the whole mass of the human race has been corrupted and condemned in one man, and that the grace of Christ alone heals and frees it from the fault and condemnation of that one man. Why, then, will the righteous scarcely be saved? Is it difficult for God to free the righteous? Certainly not. But in order to show that nature was justly condemned, even the Almighty does not wish to free it easily from so great an evil. For this reason sins are easy, while righteousness is laborious—except for those who love it. But the charity that makes them lovers comes from God.

It should be noted that blessed Peter took this sentence from the Proverbs of Solomon according to the Old Edition alone. In our version, however, which descends from the source of the Hebrew truth, it is written: “If the righteous is repaid on earth, how much more the impious and the sinner?” (Proverbs 11). This plainly means: If the fragility of mortal life is so great that not even the righteous, who are to be crowned in heaven, pass through it without tribulation because of the countless stain of corrupted nature, how much more do those who are deprived of heavenly grace await the certain outcome of their perpetual condemnation?

CHAPTER V

[Col. 0064D]

Therefore I appeal to the elders among you, etc. He calls himself a witness because he stood present with Christ while he suffered and saw everything as it happened. Or certainly because he too suffered imprisonment, chains, and scourging for the name of Christ, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles.

And a sharer in the glory that is to be revealed in the future. This was so when on the holy mountain he saw the heavenly glory of Christ’s face with James and John, or when with the other disciples who were present he saw the power of his resurrection and ascension.

Feed the flock of God that is among you. Just as the Lord commanded blessed Peter to take care of his entire flock, that is, the Church, so Peter himself rightly charges the succeeding pastors of the Church to protect, with watchful governance, each member of the flock of God who is with him.

[Col. 0065A]

Exercising oversight, not under compulsion but willingly, etc. He feeds and oversees God’s flock under compulsion who, because of poverty in temporal goods and having no means by which to live, preaches the Gospel so that he may be able to live from the Gospel. He does so willingly and according to God who preaches the word of God with regard not to any earthly possession but only to the heavenly reward.

The Apostle Paul distinguishes these two from one another, saying: “If I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship.” A stewardship is said to be entrusted to one who is ordered to take charge of an external matter for a time. For example, the person who is commanded to distribute his master’s grain to his fellow servants at the proper time resembles one who evangelizes not willingly but unwillingly.

[Col. 0065B]

Not for the sake of shameful gain, but willingly. He oversees God’s flock for the sake of shameful gain who preaches for profit and earthly advantages, although all religious works ought to be done willingly. This accords with the example of the construction of the tabernacle, which prefigured the present construction of the Church. There the whole multitude of the children of Israel offered the firstfruits to the Lord with the readiest and most devoted mind for the work of the tabernacle, giving everything of their own accord; and the craftsmen themselves likewise offered themselves willingly for the work.

Nor as domineering over those allotted to you, etc. You should first demonstrate in your actions and preserve in an undivided heart the humility that you desire your subjects to have toward you and toward one another, according to the Lord’s saying: “You know that those who appear to rule the nations lord it over them, and their leaders exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you; whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your minister, and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be the servant of all” (Matthew 23).

Paul carefully observing this command says: “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord, and ourselves as your servants through Jesus.”

[Col. 0065C–D]

Likewise, you younger men, submit yourselves to the elders. After teaching the elders how they should preside, it was necessary also to instruct the younger in obedience to their paternal oversight. There was no need to say more to them, but only to give the command of submission. For he had commanded the elders to become an example to their subjects, and it was enough for the younger to look to the examples of their elders when they acted well and to imitate them devotedly.

But so that the leaders, hearing this, might not think that the rights of due humility were to be observed only toward their subjects and not also by themselves, he immediately added a general admonition:

All of you, practice humility toward one another. For he says “all,” both elders and younger, who are commanded to practice the virtue of humility toward one another—some by governing, the others by obeying humbly. We read that this was both exemplified and enacted in Peter himself when, as he entered Caesarea, Cornelius came to meet him and humbly fell at his feet; Peter lifted him up still more humbly, saying: “Rise, I too am a man, just as you are” (Acts 10).

Cornelius, moreover, had not yet been reborn in Christ and had not yet been incorporated into the members of the Church. Thus he teaches all to have humility toward one another both by example and by word, because he knew that everyone must beware the vice of pride, which cast the angels down from heaven. With the accompanying saying of Solomon he salutarily terrifies and consoles all, saying:

For God resists the proud, etc. He next explains what that same grace is which God confers upon the humble, adding by way of admonition:

[Col. 0066A–B]

Therefore humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, etc. He grants this grace to the humble: the more they have been humbled for his sake in the time of struggle, the more gloriously they will be exalted by him at the time of recompense.

Humiliation in this passage can be understood in many ways: the humiliation by which a beginner on the way of virtue is salutarily worn down for the cleansing of the sins he has committed; that which, through voluntary devotion of mind, the more perfect offer to God or to their neighbors in times of peace regarding the circumstances of life; and that by which, when storms of persecution assail, the unconquered mind is armed through the virtue of patience. Every form of humility devoted to God is followed by its reward: those who humble themselves during their time of pilgrimage will be exalted at the time of his visitation.

Be sober and watchful, etc. In explaining this sentence, let us set down not our own words but those of blessed Cyprian:

“He goes around each of us, and, like an enemy besieging enclosed walls, examines and tests whether some part of the members is less steadfast and less faithful, through whose entrance he might penetrate within. He presents alluring and easily obtained pleasures to the eyes, so that by sight he may destroy chastity. He tests the ears with melodious music, so that by hearing a sweeter sound he may loosen and soften Christian vigor. He provokes the tongue with abuse; with injurious taunts he incites the hand to wanton violence and slaughter. To make a person fraudulent, he sets unjust profits before him; to capture the soul with money, he introduces ruinous bargains. He promises earthly honors so that he may take away heavenly ones. He offers falsehoods so that he may steal away the truth.

“And when he cannot deceive secretly, he threatens openly, directing the terror of raging persecution against the servants of God, always restless and always hostile. In peace he is crafty; in persecution, violent. Therefore the mind must stand prepared and armed against all the devil’s deceptive snares and open threats, always as ready to resist as the enemy is always ready to attack.”

[Col. 0066D–67A]

Resist him, strong in faith, etc. Be all the stronger in faith, he says, and have all the greater confidence for overcoming the devil’s cunning, because you know that you are not being tested alone. The very suffering that wears you down is common also to the Church of Christ throughout the whole world, namely, to your brotherhood. And since the righteous have always suffered from the foundation of the world, you should be ashamed to be unable to endure this alone among all others.

Through Silvanus, your faithful brother, etc. The expression “appealing” may be referred to what precedes, since he may have written briefly, not commanding but appealing to them to remain strong in faith. It may also be properly joined to what follows, so that he is understood not only to testify that this is their true grace, which he proclaims in writing—for “there is salvation in no one else, in whom it is necessary for us to be saved” (Acts 4)—but also to appeal to them to make this the reality of their own grace, with which they have been imbued in Christ.

For the grace of Christ becomes the grace of those who receive it with a pure heart. Whoever despises God’s grace does not diminish the grace itself; rather, he makes it not his own—that is, he makes it of no benefit to himself.

[Col. 0067B–C]

The Church gathered in Babylon greets you, etc. He calls Rome “Babylon” figuratively, because of the confusion of its manifold idolatry. In its midst the holy Church, still young and very small, was already shining, according to the example of the Israelite people, who once, few in number and held captive, sat beside the rivers of Babylon and mourned the absence of the holy land, unable to sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land (Psalm 136).

Blessed Peter appropriately says, while exhorting his hearers to endure present adversities, that the Church which is with him is established in Babylon—that is, in the confusion of tribulations. Yet he confirms that it is gathered there, to show that the holy city of God cannot in this life be free from the mingling with and oppression of the city of the devil, which Babylon signifies.

He calls Mark his son, because Mark is said to have become his son in baptism. Hence it is clear that Peter wrote this Epistle before he sent Mark from Rome to Alexandria to evangelize. During the reign of the emperor Claudius, both Peter and Mark came to Rome; and Mark himself, having written his Gospel at Rome, was sent to Alexandria. It follows that, when one asks where or when Peter wrote this Epistle, the place was Rome and the time was that of Caesar Claudius.

[Col. 0068A]

Greet one another with a holy kiss. A holy kiss, a true kiss, a peaceful kiss, a dove-like kiss—not a deceitful or polluted one, such as Joab used in killing Amasa, or Judas in handing over the Savior, or such as those use who speak peace with their neighbor while evil is in their hearts (Psalm 27). Those greet one another with a holy kiss who do not love in word or with the tongue, but in deed and in truth.

[Col. 0068B–C]

Grace to all of you who are in Christ Jesus. He began the Epistle with grace, completed it in grace, and suffused its middle with grace, so that in every part of his speech he might condemn the Pelagian error and teach that the Church of Christ can be saved only through his grace.

And when he said deliberately, “Grace to you,” he added, “to all who are in Christ Jesus,” so that he might indicate that, although he had written these things to a few Churches—those of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia—he was writing to all the Churches of Christ throughout the world.

So also John, when he admonished individually the seven Churches of Asia as was appropriate, added each time the conclusion: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches” (Revelation 2). He thereby plainly indicated that everything he wrote to any one Church was written to all who possessed a healthy hearing and to all the Churches of the faithful.

ON THE SECOND EPISTLE OF PETER

[Col. 0067]

CHAPTER I

[Col. 0067C]

Simon Peter, servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, etc. It is written later in this Epistle: “Behold, beloved, I am writing this second Epistle to you.” Hence it is evident that he wrote this Epistle to the same people to whom he had sent the first: to the elect proselytes of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.

He recognizes them as his equals, not because they had received circumcision according to the Law, which he himself possessed by nature as a Jew, but because they had obtained the same faith that he himself had received through the illumination of Christ’s grace. For it is not legal circumcision but only evangelical faith that joins the peoples of the nations to God’s ancient people.

But because the same faith cannot save without works, the text rightly adds:

In the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ. To these, then, he writes the Epistle; these are the people whom the apostle Peter greets: those who have received a faith equal to his and exercise it through works of righteousness. This is the righteousness that human prudence did not discover and legal instruction does not teach, but that our Lord and Savior, speaking through the Gospel, revealed when he said: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). And again: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill.’ But I say to you,” etc. (ibid.).

[Col. 0068C–69A]

May grace and peace be fulfilled for you, etc. In the first Epistle he wrote: “May grace and peace be multiplied for you” (1 Peter 1). In this one: “May grace and peace be fulfilled for you,” because he wrote the former Epistle to beginners and this one to the more perfect. Peace and grace are multiplied for those who make good progress in this life through faith, but they will be fulfilled for those who arrive in the other life through sight.

Thus, when he said, “May grace and peace be fulfilled for you,” he rightly added, “in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.” For “this is eternal life,” he says, “that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). And again: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8).

How his divine power has granted us everything, etc. This sentence depends upon what precedes. Its meaning is: May grace and peace be fulfilled for you in this, that you perfectly know our Lord Jesus Christ. And through him may you also know how, by his grace, everything belonging to his divine power has been granted to us—everything sufficient for obtaining life and preserving piety.

Hence he says: “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15). And elsewhere: “The glory that you gave me I have given them” (John 17).

If one reads the passage as certain manuscripts have it—“which has been granted for life and piety”—the meaning will be this: You should know how our Lord has bestowed upon us, according to the measure of our capacity, all the gifts of his divine power, which power has been granted to us for attaining life and piety.

This manner of expression is exceedingly common in Scripture and is called by grammarians an ellipsis, that is, an omission of a necessary word. An example occurs in the Psalm: “For neither from the east nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains.” The implied words are: “The way of escape is evident,” because God is judge everywhere (Psalm 74).

[Col. 0069B–C]

Through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and virtue. This too depends upon what precedes, because through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior we have recognized all the mysteries of his divinity by which we would be saved.

He called us by his own glory and virtue because he sent neither an angel nor an archangel for our salvation, nor did he find in us any good merit for which we should be saved. Rather, seeing us weak and inglorious, he restored us by his own virtue and glory. Hence he says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15).

Through which he has granted us the greatest and precious promises. “Through which,” he says, means through the knowledge of him, because the more perfectly anyone knows God, the more deeply he perceives the greatness of his promises.

[Col. 0069D]

So that through these you may become sharers in the divine nature. He suddenly changes person. Having first said of himself and his own people, “He has granted us precious promises,” he immediately turns to those to whom he is speaking: “So that through these,” he says, “you may become sharers in the divine nature.”

He does this not accidentally but providentially. The Lord, he says, revealed all the secrets of his divine power to us—who are Jews by nature, born under the Law, and instructed by his own bodily teaching—and granted to us, his disciples, the greatest and precious promises of his Spirit, so that through these he might also grant you, who are from the nations and were unable to see him bodily, a share in his divine nature. We teach you what we heard from him, and through his mysteries we consecrate you.

Accordingly, what he said above—“May grace and peace be fulfilled for you in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ, how everything belonging to his divine power that leads to life and piety has been granted to us”—can most rightly be understood as follows: May grace and peace be fulfilled for you in this, that you too know our Lord Jesus Christ in such a way that, just as through him all the promises or gifts of his divine power that lead to life and piety have been granted to us, so also they have been granted to you.

Just as we have received gifts promised by him, or confidently trust without any doubt that we will receive them, so you too, believing in his gifts, should not be doubtful.

[Col. 0070A–B]

Escaping the corruption of the desire that exists in the world. He rightly says that the world’s desire possesses corruption and therefore must be fled, in accordance with the one who said: “Flee from sins as from the face of a serpent” (Ecclesiasticus 21). For there is also an incorruptible desire, of which it is sung: “My soul has desired and languished for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm 83).

Concerning this desire, the Book of Wisdom beautifully speaks through a figure of speech called in Greek κλῖμαξ, in Latin gradatio (“gradation”): “The beginning of wisdom,” it says, “is the truest desire for discipline” (Wisdom 6). Care for discipline, then, is love; love is the keeping of its laws; the keeping of its laws is the perfection of incorruption; incorruption makes one near to God. Thus the desire for wisdom leads to the everlasting kingdom.

[Col. 0070C]

Applying every care, supply virtue in your faith. Here he uses “virtue” not for courage or miracles but for good conduct. This must rightly be joined to faith, lest faith be idle and dead without works. He therefore rightly commands that every care be applied, because “whoever is slack and negligent in his work is a brother to one who destroys his own work.”

And in virtue, knowledge. In accordance with Isaiah’s saying: “Learn to do good; seek judgment.”

And in knowledge, self-restraint. Once they have learned to do good, they should immediately abstain from evil, lest their knowledge of heavenly things fall into emptiness if anyone neglects to restrain himself from earthly allurements.

And in self-restraint, patience. Self-restraint must always be accompanied by patience, so that whoever has learned to contain himself from the pleasures of the world may also endure its adversities with a steadfast heart, armed on the right and on the left with the weapons of righteousness (2 Corinthians 6).

[Col. 0070D]

And in patience, piety. Toward those whom he patiently endures, he should also be compassionate, in accordance with the Apostle Paul’s saying: “Charity is patient; it is kind” (1 Corinthians 13).

And in piety, brotherly love. Each person should perform works of piety toward his opponents with no other aim than brotherly love. In every temptation, he should seek this above all: to convert by prayer or good deeds those whom he cannot win merely by teaching or rebuking, so that they may come to an affection of piety.

[Col. 0071A]

And in brotherly love, charity. Here he calls “charity” especially that love by which we love the Creator. As the stages of virtue advance, it is rightly joined to brotherly love, because neither can God be perfectly loved without one’s neighbor, nor one’s neighbor without God.

The love of God is indeed superior to love of one’s neighbors, because we are commanded to love them as ourselves, but God “with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength” (Mark 12). Nevertheless, through the practice of brotherly love we ought to ascend to love of the Creator. “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4).

For if all these things are present and abound among you, they will not leave you idle, etc. By “abound” he means that they prevail against the battles of vices through superior virtue.

[Col. 0071B]

For whoever does not possess these things is blind, etc. The eye signifies knowledge; the hand signifies action. The blind person who gropes with his hand is one who, lacking knowledge of right action, does whatever appears right to him. Ignorant of the light of truth, he stretches out his hand toward a work he cannot see and raises his steps onto a path he has not foreseen. Thus, suddenly and miserably, he falls into the ruin of perdition, which he could not foresee.

Such is everyone who does not possess the things Peter describes, because we ought to reach participation in divinity through the successive stages of spiritual virtues. Solomon, on the other hand, admonishing his wise hearer, says: “Let your eyelids go before your steps” (Proverbs 4). This plainly urges us to take diligent care in all our actions to foresee what end will follow us, and carefully to examine what is done according to God’s will and what is done otherwise.

[Col. 0071C]

Therefore, brothers, strive all the more to make your calling and election sure through good works. “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20, 22). The calling of all who come to faith is sure. But those who steadfastly join good works to the sacraments of faith they have received make their calling and election sure in the eyes of those who observe them. Conversely, those who return to crimes after their calling, when they depart this life in such a state, make it certain to all that they are reprobate.

For if you do these things, you will never fall into sin. He speaks of the greater sins, which whoever commits has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God, and from which everyone who devotes himself to the virtues mentioned above remains free before the Lord. Otherwise, there are lesser sins, concerning which it is written: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good” (Ecclesiastes 7); and “no living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142).

[Col. 0071D–72A]

For in this way entrance into the eternal kingdom will be richly supplied to you, etc. The saying of the prophet Ezekiel concerning the building situated on the mountain is suitable to this passage, where he says: “And its ascent has eight steps” (Ezekiel 40).

Here too blessed Peter enumerates eight stages of virtue by which, fleeing the corruption of worldly desire, we ought to ascend to the dwelling of the heavenly kingdom: faith, virtue, knowledge, self-restraint, patience, piety, brotherly love, and charity. Concerning these stages the Psalmist says: “He has arranged ascents in his heart” (Psalm 83), and so forth, until he says: “They will go from virtue to virtue; their God will be seen in Zion” (ibid.).

[Col. 0072A–B]

For this reason I will always remind you of these things, etc. Why does he wish always to remind of good works those whom he says possess knowledge and have been confirmed in the presence of the truth? Perhaps for this reason: so that they may exercise the knowledge they possess through works and firmly preserve the truth in whose presence they have been confirmed, lest at some time, through teachers of error, they fall away from the simplicity and purity of faith. He speaks at greater length about such teachers later in the Epistle.

This agrees with the statement of blessed John, who says: “I have not written to you as though you did not know the truth, but as those who know it” (1 John 2). The apostles therefore write and remind those who know the truth so that they may observe what they know. Hence John, speaking shortly afterward, adds: “Let what you heard from the beginning remain in you” (ibid.).

[Col. 0072C]

But I consider it right, as long as I am in this tabernacle, etc. We commonly use a tabernacle on a journey or in war. Therefore the faithful rightly testify that, as long as they are in the body and are pilgrims away from the Lord, they are in tabernacles, in which they complete the journey of this life and wage battle against the adversaries of truth.

Certain that the putting off of my tabernacle is swift. Blessed Peter most beautifully calls his death not “death” but “the putting off of his tabernacle,” because for God’s perfect servants to remove the restraints of the flesh is plainly like travelers, when their journey is completed, entering their own home in place of a tent; or like those who have been on campaign, when the enemy has been routed or struck down, returning to their homeland. For they know that their only proper home, their only citizenship, their only homeland, is in heaven. Concerning this the apostle Paul likewise says: “We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have an edifice from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (II Cor. V).

For we did not follow unintelligent fables, etc. Here he touches upon pagans and heretics alike. The former did not hesitate to call whatever pleased them “gods”; the latter, after receiving the mysteries of the true God, thereafter strove not to attend to the divine Scriptures but rather to twist them, by misinterpreting them, toward their own erroneous understanding.

And we heard this voice brought from heaven, etc. Some deny that this Epistle was written by the blessed apostle Peter. If they had considered this verse more carefully, as well as what follows—“when we were with him on the holy mountain”—they would by no means have doubted the author of this Epistle. For it is established, in accordance with the testimony of the Gospels, that Peter himself heard the aforesaid voice from above on the mountain where the Lord was glorified, together with his fellow apostles James and John.

And we have the prophetic word made more certain. Namely, that word which is spoken concerning the Mediator between God and human beings: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II). “For,” he says, “if anyone should think that our testimony is not to be believed—that we saw the divine glory of our Redeemer in secret and heard the Father’s voice addressed to him—certainly no one will dare contradict the prophetic word, nor will anyone doubt this word, which was long ago inserted into the divine Scriptures and which all attest to be true.”

To which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, etc. The order of the sense is: “You do well to attend to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place.” For in the night of this present age, full of dark temptations, where scarcely anyone is found who does not stumble, what would become of us if we did not have the lamp of the prophetic word? But will the lamp always be necessary? Certainly not. “Until,” he says, “the day dawns.” “In the morning I shall stand and contemplate” (Ps. V). For the present, it belongs to the night-lamp that we are children of God, and “it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (I John III). In comparison with the wicked, indeed, we are day, as Paul says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V). But if we are compared with that life in which we shall be, we are still night and need a lamp.

And the morning star may rise in your hearts. Who is this morning star? If you say “the Lord,” that is too little. The morning star itself is our enlightened understanding. It is this that rises in our hearts; it is this that will be illuminated and made manifest. Love will be what we now desire and, because it is absent, long for; and what it will be, each of us will see in the other, as now we see one another’s faces.

Understanding this first, that every prophecy of Scripture, etc. This verse depends upon what he said above: “To which you do well to attend.” For those who attend to the words of the prophets do well, so that through them they may possess the light of knowledge. They must first understand that none of the holy prophets preached doctrines of life to the people by his own interpretation; rather, what they had learned from the Lord, they commended to their hearers as things to be practiced. What heavenly mysteries they had received in secret, they simply handed on to God’s people, whether by speaking or by writing. They did not act like the divine interpreters of the nations, who brought before the crowds of the deceived whatever they themselves had fabricated in their own hearts, as though it were the pronouncement of a divine oracle. Therefore, just as the prophets wrote not their own words but God’s, so their reader cannot use his own interpretation, lest he deviate from the meaning of the truth; rather, he must attend in every way to how the one who wrote wished his words to be understood.

For prophecy was not at any time brought forth by human will, etc. To be able always to foretell future things (sic); rather, the Spirit himself filled their hearts whenever he wished. Likewise, it was not within their power to teach whatever they wanted, but they spoke only what they had learned after being enlightened by the Spirit. We say this so that no one may dare to explain the Scriptures according to his own desire.

Someone once interpreted these words of the blessed Peter absurdly, saying that, just as a pipe receives the breath of human [*aeris*; the printed reading is uncertain, perhaps “air”] so that it may resound, yet cannot understand the sound it produces because of its insensible nature, so the prophets, inspired by the Spirit of God, uttered with their mouths whatever that same Spirit wished, while they themselves did not retain in their minds what they said, in accordance with Maro’s words: “He gives forth sound without understanding.” It is plainly evident that this is the most shameless error. For how could they give such sound counsel for right living to their hearers if, being like madmen, they themselves did not know what they were saying? Why are they called “seers,” if they were prophets? Why is it written, “The word which Isaiah saw” (Isa. II), or “which some other prophet saw,” unless because, in the hidden realm of heavenly visions, they recognized mysteries with the clearest insight of the mind, and then openly expressed them to their hearers in whatever words they wished?

## CHAPTER II

But there were also false prophets among the people, etc. A *secta* in Latin is called *haeresis* in Greek when someone, with foolish obstinacy, never ceases to follow the errors he once began to pursue. Who could fail to know that this is characteristic of heretics?

And they deny the Lord who bought them, etc. Concerning this purchaser Paul also says: “You were bought with a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (I Cor. 6). It is therefore deservedly that they bring swift destruction upon themselves: they deny their Redeemer and refuse rightly to glorify him by confessing him and to bear him in their body by doing good. All heretics do this. Arius says that our Redeemer is inferior to the Father in divinity; Photinus says, “Christ is a human being, not God”; Manichaeus says, “Christ is God alone; he is not truly human”; Ebion says, “Christ did not exist before Mary but took his origin from her”; Apollinaris says, “Christ is only God and flesh; he never assumed a rational soul”; Pelagius says, “Christ is not the Redeemer of little children in baptism, because, conceived without iniquities and born from their mother without sins, they have absolutely no sin that ought to be forgiven them; therefore Christ is not the Savior of all the elect.” These and the other heretics with them plainly deny the Lord who bought them with the price of his blood, because they preach him not as the truth reveals him but as they themselves invent him. Consequently, having been alienated from the Redeemer, they await nothing more certainly than the pit of destruction.

And many will follow their debaucheries, etc. The way of truth will be blasphemed by heretics not only in those whom they draw out into their heresy and associate with themselves, but also in those whom, through their most impure deeds and sacrifices, or through the accursed mysteries they perform, they stir up to hatred of the Christian name. The uninstructed then suppose that all Christians are enslaved to such crimes. Of such people Scripture says: “Through you my name is blasphemed among the nations” (Isa. LII).

For whom judgment from long ago does not cease. Since “from long ago” signifies past time, while “does not cease” is a verb in the present tense [as printed], nothing else seems to be meant except that the judgment of destruction against the wicked began long ago; it continually torments them in the present and will never cease at any time.

For if God did not spare the angels who sinned. Many verses here are brought to a close with the same conclusion: “The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation.” For if, he says, God did not spare the angels who sinned, but handed them over to the punishments of hell and keeps them for greater torments on the day of judgment; if, destroying the original world through the Flood because of its crimes, he preserved righteous Noah; if, punishing the crimes of Sodom, he rescued Lot, a worshiper of righteousness, from among the unrighteous—it is certainly established that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, but to reserve the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment. It should also be noted that, when he says that God did not spare the angels who sinned, he indicates that these evil angels were not created evil by God but became evil by sinning.

But, having dragged them down by the cords of hell, he delivered them to Tartarus, etc. Another translation has the verse as follows: “But thrusting them back into the prisons of the darkness of the lower world, he delivered them to be kept for punishment at the judgment.” He therefore shows that punishment at the final judgment is still owed to the apostate angels, concerning which the Lord says: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV), although they have already received this hell as a punishment—that is, the lower, darkened air—as a prison. For in relation to the height of heaven, this expanse of air can already be called hell; and in relation to the height of that same air, the earth lying below can be understood as hell and as the deep.

He calls the “cords of hell” the very arrogance of pride by which their spirit swelled up against the Creator. Cords are ropes by which sailors suspend sails, so that, when the breeze blows, they leave the calm of the harbor and entrust themselves always to the uncertain waves of the sea. The efforts of unclean spirits are suitably compared to such cords: as soon as, driven by the breath of pride, they raised themselves against the Creator, they were dragged by those very efforts of their exaltation into the depths of the abyss.

Some manuscripts read: “But, having dragged them down by the roaring of hell, he delivered them to Tartarus.” This signifies either the sound of their heavenly exaltation or their wailing in punishment. For beasts roar when they suffer hunger or some other affliction; so these spirits, unable to endure anything that opposes them because of the excess of their pride, roar whenever adversity comes upon them.

And he did not spare the original world. It is this same world in which the human race now dwells, and which those who lived before the Flood inhabited. Yet that world is rightly called “the original world,” as though it were another, because, as is written later in this Epistle, that world then perished, inundated by water. The heavens that existed previously also perished—that is, all the turbulent expanses of this air were consumed by the rising height of the waters—and the earth too was changed into another form as the waters exceeded their bounds.

For although certain mountains and valleys are believed to have been made from the beginning, they were not as great as those now seen throughout the whole world. This might perhaps have been denied if we did not even now see the face of the earth changed every year by the overturning of waters. It is believed that this happened then to a far greater extent, because a stronger and more prolonged assault of waters besieged and washed over the earth.

But he preserved Noah, the eighth preacher of righteousness, etc. Everyone knows that Noah was born in the tenth generation from Adam, but he calls him “the eighth” because eight people escaped the Flood, and he was one of them. He mentions the number eight in order to suggest secretly that the time of the Flood signifies the ordeal of the final judgment, when, with all the reprobate condemned, all the righteous will receive the glory of perpetual life.

There are six ages of the present world; the seventh age is now also being lived, in that life where the souls of the saints enjoy a blessed Sabbath—that is, eternal rest. The eighth is to come at the time of the resurrection of all and the universal judgment.

He calls Noah “a preacher of righteousness” because, by practicing works of righteousness before the eyes of all, he showed how one ought to live before the Lord. He is not found to have taught anyone by word—for not even one speech of his is recorded as addressed to God or to a human being—but, in what is the mark of the greatest virtue, throughout the building of the ark, the arrival of the Flood, and the beginnings of the age that followed, he obeyed the heavenly commands, silent in mouth but most ready in the devotion of his heart.

And the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, etc. Since he asserts that the cities of the ungodly were reduced to ashes, this must be understood in two ways. First, he reduced them and the neighboring lands to ashes by fire; and afterward, when he covered the places of the conflagration with the waters of the Dead Sea, he wished to preserve the surrounding region as an image of its ancient punishment.

For exceedingly beautiful fruits grow there, which arouse in those who see them a desire to eat them. If you pluck them, they split open and dissolve into ash, raising smoke as though they were still burning. Hence it is said in the Book of Wisdom: “This delivered the righteous man from the ungodly who were perishing, when he fled from the fire descending upon the Pentapolis. As a testimony to their wickedness, the desolate land smokes, and trees bear fruit at a fixed time” (Wis. X). The implied words are: “And the desolate land itself continues to smoke.” This too is what is added here:

Setting them forth as an example of those who would act impiously. For the fire that once punished the Sodomites clearly demonstrates that the wicked will suffer without end. The fact that their land continues to smoke, and that its exceedingly beautiful fruits contain ash and stench within, openly indicates throughout all ages that carnal pleasure, even if it smiles upon the minds of fools for the present, reserves nothing for itself in the invisible world except burning, except that the smoke of its torments may rise for ever and ever.

And righteous Lot, oppressed, etc. The unjust deeds and words of his neighbors tormented the holy man alike. He saw them daily and was utterly unable to correct them. Yet he conducted himself so watchfully that neither the sight nor the sound of their crimes clouded the gaze of his chaste mind in any respect; rather, with unwearied concentration, he persisted in the works of righteousness he had begun.

Or certainly he was righteous in sight and hearing because those present saw in him nothing except works of righteousness and heard nothing except words of righteousness; and those absent heard nothing reported about him except what pertained to righteousness. This was like the example of blessed Job, who says: “The ear that heard me blessed me, and the eye that saw me bore witness for me” (Job XXIX).

It should be noted that the blessed Peter follows here the example of the Lord’s teaching. For the Lord himself, speaking in the Gospel about the day of judgment, recalls the sudden coming of both the Flood and the Sodomite fire, in which the righteous are delivered while the reprobate are seized by the snare of unexpected destruction. Elsewhere too, when he sought to restrain the minds of his disciples from the arrogance of pride, he set before them the example of the angelic fall: “I was watching Satan,” he said, “falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke X).

The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, etc. He says that the unrighteous are reserved for punishment on the day of judgment, not because, even before the day of judgment, once separated from the body, they do not suffer punishments according to their merits, but because more severe torments await them at the judgment, when they will also be punished in the body they have received again. For now they are tormented in the soul alone. Hence, reproaching the cities that refused to receive the word of the Gospel, the Lord concluded as follows: “It will be more bearable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.”

Especially those who, after the flesh, walk in the desire of impurity. He means fornicators, who because of the guilt of their corruption will suffer greater torments at the judgment than the unrighteous in general.

And they despise authority, being audacious and self-pleasing. He means the proud and arrogant, who themselves too will pay heavier punishments than those generally imposed.

They are not afraid to introduce sects, blaspheming. He means heretics, who, blaspheming the faith or life of the orthodox, introduce sects bearing their own name—that is, heresies. They too will hear the same judgment as those mentioned earlier, since a stronger torment awaits the stronger offenders.

Where angels, although greater in strength and power, do not bring a blasphemous judgment against them. The word “where” signifies “in the fact that they despise authority, that they are audacious, that they are self-pleasing, that they make heresies—that is, sects—and that they blaspheme.” By doing these things, they deserved to become demons and to pay the penalties of their pride. Their spiritual nature could not be polluted by the obscenity of carnal desire. Unless perhaps, when they entice human beings into this desire, he means that they too are to be judged for it, just as for the other evils that they persuade human beings to commit.

But these people, like irrational animals by nature, etc. Just as it is natural for irrational animals, in pursuit of food, repeatedly to fall unknowingly into capture and destruction, so heretics, compared with foolish beasts, blaspheme the uncorrupted and sound teaching—and the life—of the Catholic Church in order to satisfy their appetite for corruption, and by impious recklessness weave for themselves the snares of eternal destruction.

Ecclesiastical history reports that heretics of this kind existed even in the times of the apostles: the Simonians, Menandrians, Basilidians, Nicolaitans, Ebionites, Marcionites, Cerdonians, and many others. After rightly saying of them, “Blaspheming, they will perish in their corruption,” he added:

Receiving the reward of injustice. He calls the punishment that their works of injustice deserve the “reward of injustice,” especially in those who, although they themselves serve corruption of the flesh, nevertheless blaspheme the conduct of those who live chastely. Held fast by insane errors, they do not cease to disparage those who think soundly.

Considering the pleasures of the day delights of corruption and defilement. Pleasure is understood both in a good and in a bad sense. In the good sense, as when paradise is called “the paradise of pleasure,” and as the Psalm sings: “You will give them drink from the torrent of your pleasure” (Ps. XXXV). In the bad sense, as Solomon says: “Youth and pleasure are vanity” (Eccl. XI). It is also understood indifferently, as when Sarah said: “After I have grown old and my lord is elderly, shall I give myself to pleasure?” (Gen. XVIII).

Pleasure is therefore rightly called “of the day” when the saints delight in the Lord. But evil pleasure belongs to the night, when the reprobate perversely delight in completing the works of darkness. He therefore rightly says of the unrighteous that they consider the pleasure of the day to be delights of corruption and defilement, because many are so sluggish, perverse, and shameless that, although they indulge in the most impure and accursed pleasures, they nevertheless judge these to be the best and, as it were, full of light.

Some join the first word of this verse to the preceding verse, reading: “Receiving as the reward of injustice pleasure,” and explain it according to the words of the apostle Paul: “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves” (Rom. I). A little later: “Practicing shameful acts, they received in themselves the reward that was fitting for their error. And since they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a depraved mind, to do what is unfitting” (ibid.). But we have thought that the distinction we found in the works of blessed Pope Gregory should be followed.

Alluring unstable souls. Prostitutes are commonly called *pellices*, a term derived either from pollution or from the beauty of their skin by which they entice the unwary. Thus those who, by teaching evil, subject unstable souls to erroneous sects of various doctrines, as though to the pleasures of adulterers, allure them.

Following the way of Balaam from Bosor, etc. Heretics often put forward doctrines so foolish and sacraments so accursed that even dull minds—whether pagan or wholly lacking the understanding of divine knowledge—detest their madness; and, by thinking more sanely, rebuke their twisted ways, which oppose God.

What is worse, and more frequent, is that sometimes many Catholics love the reward of injustice so greatly that, even though taught by the unlearned, clerics are deservedly torn apart by laypeople. They are rightly compared with the prophet who was rebuked by the words of a she-ass speaking contrary to nature, yet was not restrained from his intended wicked journey.

The name of the city from which Balaam is said to have come also most aptly suits such people. For *Bosor* is said to mean “fleshly” or “in tribulation.” There is no other reason why people devoted to lust adulterate the word of truth out of love of money or desire for temporal things than that they have enslaved themselves to the desire of the flesh. They are plainly unworthy of the apostolic praise with which he glorifies true believers: “But you, brothers, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit” (I Thess. V).

Hence they are placed in tribulation—not, indeed, the tribulation they themselves endure for the Lord, but rather that in which they oppress the minds of the weak through the perverse examples of their works, so that the weak cannot rise to salvation or come to their senses.

The name of Balaam himself, which is interpreted as “vain people” or “one who casts them down,” also suits such men. For those who voluntarily abandon the way of truth they have recognized—what are they but vain people? What do they do but cast their hearers into destruction, preaching to them not what would heal them but what pleases them, namely, erroneous things? Concerning them he rightly adds:

These are waterless springs, etc. Saint Jerome, setting these verses forth in his book against Jovinian, explains them as follows:

“Does it not seem to you that the apostle has painted a new faction of ignorance? For they open up, as it were, springs of knowledge, since they promise a shower of doctrines that they do not possess, like clouds of prophecy to which the truth of God might reach; yet they are driven about by the whirlwinds of demons and vices. They speak grandly, and all their speech is pride. Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean; and those who have withdrawn a little from sins return to their own error and devote themselves to the luxury of food and the delights of the flesh. Who would not gladly hear: ‘Let us eat and drink, and we shall reign for ever’ (Wis. II; Isa. XXII; I Cor. XV)? Those who are sweet in speech call the wise and prudent perverse.”

For the true proverb happened to them: “The dog has returned to its vomit,” etc. He calls this a true proverb because he takes his testimony from Solomon’s Proverbs, where it is given with its interpretation: “As a dog,” he says, “returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly” (Prov. XXVI). He added on his own: “And a washed sow in the wallowing-place of mud.”

When a dog vomits, it certainly casts out the food that was weighing down its chest. But when it returns to its vomit, it is again burdened by what had relieved it.
