Likewise, those who mourn their sins certainly cast out by confession the wickedness with which they had been badly filled and which weighed upon the inmost parts of their minds. But when they repeat it after confession, they take it up again.

A sow, while being washed in a wallowing-place of mud, becomes dirtier. And one who mourns a sin but does not abandon it subjects himself to a heavier punishment, because he both despises the forgiveness he might have obtained through weeping and, as though wallowing in muddy water, soils himself: by withdrawing purity of life from his tears, he makes even those tears themselves filthy in the sight of God.

## CHAPTER III

Behold, beloved, I am writing this second Epistle to you, in which, etc. By “in which” he means “in the Epistles,” or “in those to whom he writes the Epistles.”

In the last days scoffers will come, etc. They mock the faith and hope of Christians, who vainly promise themselves that the time of the resurrection will come.

Walking according to their own desires, etc. The apostle Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, says: “I beseech you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, not to be quickly shaken from your understanding or terrified, whether by spirit, word, or letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were imminent” (II Thess. II).

The blessed Peter therefore reproves and calls “scoffers” those who assert that the Lord’s coming and promises are delayed; Paul restrains those who suppose that the day of the Lord is imminent. It is therefore clear to all who love his coming that their minds must be restrained with moderation in this speculation, so that we neither suppose that the day of the Lord is near and about to arrive quickly, nor, conversely, that it will come only later. We should diligently concern ourselves with this alone: whether he comes sooner or later, that when he comes he may find us ready.

For they willingly remain ignorant of this: that the heavens existed previously, and the earth was formed from water, etc. The earth consists of water, concerning which God said at the beginning of creation: “Let the waters be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear”; and it happened so (Gen. I). The earth is likewise sustained by water through the word of God, because by divine arrangement its interior is wholly filled with channels of water, just as we see the bodies of living creatures overflowing with channels of blood, lest they fail through dryness if the irrigation of water ceased. Indeed, we see lands become parched when their moisture has been consumed by the heat of summer, and soon turned into dust that the wind scatters.

Another edition has: “The heavens were formerly constituted from water and through water.” This signifies the moist and turbulent air. Scripture is accustomed to call this “heaven,” and sometimes “the heavens.” Hence it is written: “The kite in heaven knows its time” (Jer. VIII).

Through which the world that then existed, inundated by water, perished. By “through which,” he means the heavens and the earth that he had mentioned earlier. Through these, the world that consisted in them perished when they were destroyed. For the higher parts of the world were scarcely touched by the Flood.

The earth therefore perished because, submerged and covered by the waters, it not only lost for so long a time the fruit-bearing condition implanted in it, but also, as we have explained above, received in many places a form unlike that which it had first received. The heavens too perished, insofar as the extent and spaces of this air were concerned. “For,” as Saint Augustine says, “the water rose and occupied the whole expanse in which birds fly.” Thus the heavens near the earth certainly perished, in accordance with the expression “the birds of heaven.”

“There are also,” he says, “the heavens of heavens above in the firmament; but whether they too will perish by fire, or only those that also perished in the Flood, is a somewhat more difficult question among learned people.”

But the heavens that now exist and the earth, etc. The meaning of the blessed Peter is therefore clear: he asserts that the earth and heavens that perished in the Flood and were restored after the Flood are to be destroyed by the final fire.

But let this one thing not escape your notice, beloved: that one day with the Lord is as a thousand years, etc. Some think this statement should be understood as though the day of judgment had the length of a thousand years. They do not consider that he does not simply say, “One day will be as a thousand years,” but rather: “One day,” he says, “with the Lord is as a thousand years.” For in the knowledge of divine power, past, future, and present things stand equally. The periods of time that seem long or short to us are, with the Creator of times, certainly intervals of equal extent, according to the Psalmist: “For a thousand years in your sight are as yesterday, which has passed, and as a watch in the night” (Ps. LXXXIX), which are reckoned as nothing; “their years shall be.”

For it is clear that the Psalmist compares a thousand years not with the future day of judgment but with yesterday, which has passed, before the eyes of the Creator. Indeed, he compares all our years—that is, the whole time of this age—to a single watch of the night, which is one quarter of the night. So the blessed Peter, as though comparing each day of the present age with a thousand years and a thousand years with each day before the Lord, asserts that they are equal—that is, of the same measure. For he sees all things, small and great alike.

Moreover, if Peter had wished this to be understood only of the day of judgment, namely, that it would truly be as long as our thousand years, he could have indicated his meaning more plainly, and there would have been no need to add “with the Lord.” For if that final day were so long, it would also become apparent to all human beings when it arrived.

The Apostle recalls these things in order to refute those whom he had previously said were asking: “Where is the promise or his coming?” He shows that the Lord has by no means forgotten his promise or his coming to judge the living and the dead. But since he embraces each day of our age in his eternal memory in such a way that he surveys a thousand-year cycle as easily as the space of one day, and a thousand years as easily as the span of a single day, it must plainly be understood that he also knows with complete certainty the end of all those days and years, and has foreknown without any doubt when the glory of his coming will be revealed and when the promised rewards will be given to the saints. Hence it is rightly added:

The Lord is not delaying his promise, etc. He who knows all times, the last and the earliest, does not delay his promise; rather, he reveals it at the time that he predestined before all future times. Therefore he still delays, so that the full number of the elect may first be completed, a number which he decreed with the Father before the ages.

Hence in the Apocalypse the souls of the martyrs, who longed for the day of judgment and his resurrection to come, were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be fulfilled.

Those who understand the blessed Peter’s statement as though he were saying that the day of judgment would last as long as a thousand years refer this to the fact that those who leave the body with some sins, yet have been predestined to share in the lot of the elect, must be purified through fire for that length of time and only then, after all their sins have been forgiven, come to life.

But they do not see how shameless it is to believe that so great a company of the perfect and righteous, having received in the twinkling of an eye blessed and immortal bodies, must wait in the air or on earth for the judgment to end throughout a thousand-year period, and only then, when their companions have been fully prepared, hear the long-desired sentence: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV).

But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, etc. Without doubt he means those heavens that passed away in the Flood—that is, this air nearest to the earth, which is destined to be destroyed by fire and which, as is rightly believed, occupies as much space as the waters of the Flood occupied.

Otherwise, if someone asserts that the higher heavens, where the sun, moon, and stars are placed, will pass away, how does he wish to understand the Lord’s statement: “Then the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven” (Matt. XXIV)? For if the place of the stars, that is, heaven, passes away, how can it be said that on that same day of the Lord the stars will either be darkened or fall, while the fire consumes the place of the stars in which they are fixed and causes it to pass away?

But the elements will be dissolved by heat. There are four elements from which this world consists: fire, air, water, and earth. That immense fire will consume them all. Yet it will not consume them all so completely that they cease to exist altogether. Rather, it will consume two of them to a certain extent and restore the other two to a better form. Hence it is said later:

But new heavens and a new earth. He did not say “other heavens and another earth,” but that the old and ancient ones would be changed for the better, in accordance with David’s words: “In the beginning you founded the earth, O Lord, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and all things will grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed” (Ps. CI).

Whatever therefore will perish, grow old, and be changed will certainly, after being consumed by fire, resume a more pleasing appearance when the fire has departed. “The form of this world has passed away,” not its substance, just as the substance of our flesh does not perish, but its form will be changed when “what is sown as an animal body will rise as a spiritual body” (I Cor. XV).

Concerning fire and water we read nothing of this kind; rather, we have in the Apocalypse: “And the sea is no more” (Apoc. XXI). We have in the prophets: “And the light of the lamp will no longer shine for you” (Apoc. XVIII).

And we await his promise, in which righteousness dwells. Righteousness dwells in the age to come, because then each of the faithful will receive the crown of righteousness according to the measure of his struggle—something that cannot at all take place in this life, in accordance with Solomon’s words: “I saw under the sun wickedness in the place of judgment, and in the place of righteousness iniquity. And I said in my heart: God will judge the righteous and the wicked, and there will then be a time for every matter” (Ecclesiastes III). And again: “I saw,” he says, “the oppressions that are carried out under the sun, and the tears of the innocent, with no one to comfort them, and that they, abandoned by all help, could not resist their violence; and I praised the dead more than the living” (Ecclesiastes IV). He therefore praised innocent dead people more than the living because the former, having completed their struggle, had been rewarded with everlasting blessedness, whereas the latter were still placed in the contest. He complained that he had seen oppressions under the sun because he knew that above the sun there is a just Judge, who dwells on high and regards the lowly (Psalm CXII), and above the sun there are dwelling places in which the righteous receive the rewards due to their righteousness. What he says, “in which righteousness dwells,” can also be understood in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Psalm CXVII). And in the Apocalypse John says of the heavenly city: “Nothing defiled, or that practices abomination and falsehood, shall enter it, except those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life” (Apocalypse XXI).

Therefore, beloved, as you await these things, strive to be found spotless, and so forth. These are the holy vigils of which the Lord says: “Blessed are those servants whom, when the lord comes, he finds watching” (Luke XII). The person who keeps watch is one who preserves himself free from the stains of vices; who, insofar as it lies within him, maintains peace with all people; and who, enjoying the happiest peace within himself, subjects every enticement of the flesh to the rule of the spirit. And when he said, “Strive to be found spotless and blameless,” he rightly added, “before him,” that is, before the Lord, because only the one whom divine judgment declares clean is perfectly clean. Hence it is said in praise of good spouses: “They were both righteous before God” (Luke I). “Before God” is rightly added, because human judgments often deceive.

And regard the patience of our Lord as salvation. Do not think that the Lord is delaying the promise; rather, understand that he patiently waits for this reason: so that more may be saved.

As also our most beloved brother Paul wrote to you according to the wisdom given to him. He recalls that Paul wrote to them because, although Paul wrote specifically to certain Churches, he is nevertheless shown to have written generally to all the Churches throughout the world that constitute the one Catholic Church. It should also be noted that here Peter praises Paul’s wisdom, whereas Paul himself says of himself: “For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (I Corinthians XV). Behold, Paul humbles himself by remembering his former unbelief and places the innocence of the other apostles before himself. Behold the first of the apostles, as though forgetting his own precedence and the keys of the kingdom given to him, marvels at the wisdom given to Paul. For it is plainly the custom of the elect to admire the virtues of others more than their own, and through those virtues to stir themselves toward progress.

It should likewise be noted that Paul says in his Letters: “When Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he was blameworthy” (Galatians II). Paul therefore reproves Peter in his Letters, yet Peter himself, reading those same letters again, judges them worthy of praise. For when he found himself rightly reproved in them, he did not disdain it as an insult, but gratefully accepted it as an act of devotion. Such mutual conduct is known not by every mortal, but only by those who have learned from the Lord to be gentle and humble of heart, and who know how to anticipate one another in showing honor.

In which there are certain things difficult to understand, and so forth. Heretics corrupt all the Scriptures. For there is no book of either the New or the Old Testament in which they have not understood many things perversely. They have also often distorted the Scriptures themselves from their proper state, either by removing, adding, or changing whatever their treachery dictated. It is established, for example, that the Arians erased from the Gospel the statement that the Savior made: “Because God is spirit” (II Corinthians III), since they did not wish to believe that the Holy Spirit was God almighty. He rightly calls them unlearned and unstable, because they possess neither the light of knowledge nor the firmness of mind by which they might remain among the learned until they were instructed. For the one remedy for the unlearned is humbly and steadfastly to lend an ear to the words of the learned. Since heretics do not possess this grace of steadfastness, they are swept even out of the Church by the wind of pride, like light chaff. Concerning them he appropriately adds:

To their own destruction. For those who attempt to corrupt the holy Scriptures and to disturb and pervert the Catholic faith condemn no one else in doing this than themselves. But the Church of Christ, after the darkness of error has been dispelled, enjoys its true light. Hence, appropriately, at the end of the Apocalypse—which is the conclusion and, as it were, the seal of the whole divine Scripture—it is said: “If anyone adds to these things, God will add upon him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share from the book of life and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book” (Apocalypse XXII).

The things difficult to understand in Paul’s Letters, which he says are corrupted by the unlearned and unstable, are chiefly those in which he speaks of the grace of God that justifies the ungodly (Romans IV), that is, makes the ungodly righteous. For he himself says: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans V). Not understanding this, they thought that he was saying: “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Romans III). But far be it from Paul to teach his hearers to do evil in order to obtain good; his entire purpose is to restrain everyone he can from evil and summon them to do good. When he says, “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans V), he commends the gift of grace all the more strongly, for grace is accustomed both to forgive great sins in those who have been converted and to forgive lesser ones. The greater the sins someone committed before conversion, the greater the indulgence of the giving grace he received after conversion. The Apostle is therefore speaking of sins that we have already committed, so that no one may perish in despair of forgiveness because of the magnitude of his crimes. He was not, as his enemies interpreted him, urging people to commit more sins so that through them they might receive greater good. Hence blessed Peter rightly adds by way of admonition:

You therefore, beloved, knowing these things beforehand, keep watch, and so forth. Knowing beforehand that foolish people will introduce various errors—some denying the future judgment, some falsifying the divine utterances, some interpreting them wrongly, some loosening the reins of lust, and others rendering the hearts of the wretched senseless through other and different deceptions—keep watch, lest by any trickery of those who lead you astray you fall away from the steadfastness of your faith.

But grow in grace, and so forth. In accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “They shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Psalm LXXXIII).

To him be glory both now and unto the day of eternity. Glory always belongs to God our Savior and Lord: now, while we remain in the flesh amid the pressures of daily adversities and journey as pilgrims away from him; and especially then, when he comes, long desired by all nations, and deigns to illumine us with the presence of his vision. Meanwhile, sighing for that vision, we rightly sing diligently: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Psalm LXXXIII).

# ON THE FIRST LETTER OF SAINT JOHN

[Col. 0085]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0085B]

That which was from the beginning, and so forth. Blessed John the Apostle composed this Letter concerning the perfection of faith and charity, praising the devotion of those who persevered in the unity of the Church, while refuting the impiety of those who disturbed the peace of the Church with their insane teaching—especially Cerinthus and Marcion, who maintained that Christ did not exist before Mary. For their sake also he wrote his Gospel: there, indeed, affirming in his own words and in those of the Lord that the Son is consubstantial with the Father; here, drawing out in his own words what he had learned from the Lord and refuting the folly of the heretics by apostolic authority. Hence, at once, at the beginning of the Letter, he indicates both the true divinity and the true humanity of that same God and our Lord Jesus Christ, saying: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard.” For the Son of God existed from the beginning; but the disciples heard that same Son of God appearing in a human being, and they saw him with their eyes, as he explained more fully in the Gospel.

For what he says here, “That which was from the beginning,” is what he says in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John I). And what he adds here, “which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes,” is what he adds there more fully: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John I). And lest he seem to say too little in stating, “which we have seen with our eyes,” he adds:

Which we have looked upon, and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life. For they not only saw the Lord with bodily eyes, as the others did, but also looked upon him attentively, perceiving his divine power with spiritual eyes as well—especially those who saw him transfigured on the mountain, one of whom was John himself. When he says, “And our hands have touched concerning the Word of life,” he overcomes the madness of the Manichaeans, who deny that the Lord assumed true flesh. The apostles could not doubt that it was true, since they proved its reality not only by seeing but also by touching it—especially John himself, who was accustomed to recline at his breast during the supper and therefore touched his limbs with all the greater freedom, the nearer he was to him.

After his resurrection from the dead, their hands also touched the Word of life, when they learned without any doubt that he had truly received flesh, although now incorruptible, hearing from him himself: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have” (Luke XXIV). It is rightly said, “And our hands have touched concerning the Word of life,” because when they also proved by touching with their hands the reality of his flesh resurrected from the dead, they came to know more certainly that he was the Word of life, that is, the true God. Hence Thomas, who was more specially commanded to touch him, immediately after touching his flesh confessed him to be God, saying: “My Lord and my God” (John XX).

And the life was manifested, and so forth. He speaks of that life which says in the Gospel: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John XI). It was manifested when it was revealed through divine miracles in the flesh, and the disciples who were present saw what they might bear witness to later with unquestionable truth—when, performing signs, he manifested his glory, as the same John writes, “and his disciples believed in him” (John II). Since the Apostle John testifies with his fellow apostles that he saw the life manifested, let the heretic Apelles, with his followers, be confounded. He maintained that this same life—that is, the Lord and Savior—appeared to the world not truly as God, but as a human being in appearance.

And we announce to you the eternal life, and so forth. He existed with the Father eternally in divinity; in time he appeared to the world in humanity.

What we have seen and heard we announce to you, and so forth. Blessed John plainly shows that all who desire to have fellowship with God must first be joined to the fellowship of the Church, and must learn that faith and be instructed in those sacraments which the disciples received from the Truth itself dwelling in the flesh. Those who believe through the teaching of the apostles are not in any respect less related to God than those who believed through the Lord himself preaching in the world, except insofar as the quality of their faith or works distinguishes them.

Hence, concerning this fellowship of the saints which they have with the Father and the Son, the Son himself, pleading with the Father, says: “Holy Father, keep them in your name whom you have given me, so that they may be one as we are” (John XVII). And shortly afterward: “But I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, so that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us” (John XVII).

And we write these things to you so that your joy may be full. The joy of teachers becomes full when, by preaching, they lead many to the fellowship of the holy Church and to fellowship with the God and Father and his Son Jesus Christ, through whom the Church is strengthened and grows. Hence Paul also says to those whom he was instructing in the faith: “Make my joy complete by thinking the same thing, having the same charity, being united in soul and thinking the same thing” (Philippians II).

And this is the message that we have heard from him, and so forth. In this statement blessed John both demonstrates the excellence of divine purity, which we too are commanded to imitate, since he himself says: “Be holy, for I am holy, the Lord your God” (Leviticus XIX), and refutes the insane doctrine of the Manichaeans, who claimed that God’s nature had been defeated in battle by the prince of darkness and had become corrupted.

If we say that we have fellowship with him, and so forth. He calls sins, heresies, and hatreds “darkness.” Mere confession of faith therefore by no means suffices for salvation when the testimony of good works is absent. Nor does uprightness of works profit without the simplicity of faith and love. Whoever is besieged by darkness in any respect cannot have fellowship with him in whom there is no iniquity. “For what fellowship has light with darkness?” (II Corinthians VI).

[Col. 0087C]

But if we walk in the light, and so forth. The distinction in the wording should be noted: he says that God is in the light, whereas we ought to walk in the light. The righteous walk in the light when, serving through works of virtue, they advance toward better things. Divine holiness, however, to which it is said, “But you are the same” (Psalm CI), is rightly said to be in the light, because complete goodness, always existing, finds nothing in which it can make progress. It is said to the faithful: “Walk as children of light” (Ephesians V). “For the fruit of light consists in all goodness and righteousness and truth.” God, however, always exists as good, just, and true, without any progress. If, therefore, we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another. For it is clear evidence that we advance by walking on the way of light if we rejoice in the bond of brotherly fellowship, with which we may reach the true light together.

Even if we are found to perform works of light and seem to preserve inviolate the obligations of mutual love, we must nevertheless not think that by our own progress or diligence we can be completely cleansed from sins. For what follows is:

And the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from every sin. The sacrament of the Lord’s Passion both released all our former sins in baptism and, by the grace of that same Redeemer, forgives whatever we have committed through daily weakness after baptism. This is especially so when, amid the works of light that we perform, we humbly confess our errors to him each day; when we receive the sacraments of his blood; when, forgiving our debtors, we pray that our debts may be forgiven us; and when, mindful of his Passion, we willingly endure every adversity.

It is remarkable that, when speaking of the Lord, he says: “And the blood of Jesus his Son.” The Son of God, according to the nature of his divinity, could not have blood. But because that same Son of God also became the Son of man, he rightly calls it the blood of the Son of God on account of the unity of his person, in order to demonstrate that he assumed a true body and truly poured out his blood for us. He also refutes the heretics who deny either that true flesh was assumed by the Son of God or that the Lord Jesus truly suffered in the flesh he assumed. Paul says something similar: “The Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his blood” (Acts XX).

[Col. 0088B]

If we say that we have no sin, and so forth. This statement is directed against the heresy of Pelagius, who both claimed that all infants are born without sin and said that the elect could progress so far in this life that they might exist without sin. Since the prophet also says, “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Psalm L), we cannot be without guilt in the world, since we entered the world with guilt. But the blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from every sin, so that our debts do not hold us under the power of our enemy because the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, freely paid on our behalf what he did not owe. For by undergoing on our behalf the undeserved death of the flesh, he freed us from the deserved death of the soul.

If we confess our sins, he is faithful, and so forth. Since we cannot be without sin in this life, the first hope of salvation is confession; no one should think himself righteous and raise his neck before God’s eyes. Next comes love, because “charity covers a multitude of sins” (I Peter IV), which is therefore commended to us with repeated praise in what follows in this Letter.

He beautifully intimates both things together: that we ought to ask for our sins and that we obtain God’s indulgence when we ask. He therefore calls God faithful in forgiving sins, because he who taught us to pray for our sins and debts promised paternal mercy and forgiveness to follow. He also asserts that God is just, because he justly forgives true confession: “that he may forgive us our sins,” he says, “and cleanse us from every iniquity.” In this life he forgives the elect their daily and minor sins, without which they cannot live on earth; after the dissolution of the flesh he cleanses them from every iniquity, bringing them into that life in which they will neither wish nor be able to sin any longer. Now he remits greater temptations for those who pray, so that they may not be overcome; he remits lesser ones, so that they may not be wounded. Then he cleanses them from all things, so that no iniquity at all may remain among the blessed in the everlasting kingdom.

If we say that we have not sinned, and so forth. He himself, through a human being filled with his Spirit, said: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Ecclesiastes VII). Through himself also he taught that we cannot be free from offenses, when he commanded us to pray: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew VI). Therefore, taught by Pelagius, no one should believe that he can live free from sins and debts when he sees the apostles, at the Lord’s command, praying for their own offenses.

It is also written elsewhere: “The righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Proverbs XXIV). It is impossible for any of the saints not sometimes to fall into minor sins—committed through speech, thought, ignorance, forgetfulness, necessity, will, or sudden attack—and yet they do not cease to be righteous, because, with the Lord’s help, they quickly rise from guilt.

## CHAPTER TWO

My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. He is not contradicting himself when, after declaring above that we cannot live without sin, he now says that he writes to us for the purpose of preventing us from sinning. There he necessarily, prudently, and beneficially warned us of our weakness, lest anyone please himself as though innocent and perish all the more by exalting himself on account of his merits. Here, correspondingly, he exhorts us that, if we cannot be free from every fault, we should nevertheless make every effort within our power not to live negligently by disregarding the weakness of our condition, but to fight vigorously and watchfully against every vice—especially the greater and more obvious ones, which, with the Lord’s help, we can more easily overcome or avoid—so that, in accordance with Paul’s statement, “temptation may not seize us except what is human” (I Corinthians X), that is, only what human weakness cannot completely avoid.

But if anyone should sin, we have an advocate, and so forth. Observe how John himself preserves the humility that he teaches. Certainly he was a righteous and great man, who drank the secrets of the mysteries from the Lord’s breast. Yet he did not say, “You have me as an advocate with the Father,” but, “We have an advocate,” he says. He said “we have,” not “you have.” He preferred to place himself among sinners, so that he might have Christ as an advocate, rather than place himself forward as an advocate in Christ’s place and be found among the proud who are condemned.

Nor should it be said that bishops or superiors do not pray for the people. The Apostle prays for the people, and the people pray for the Apostle, who says: “Praying together for us and for you, that God may open to us a door for the word” (Colossians IV). The Church prayed for Peter when Peter was in chains, and its prayer was heard; likewise Peter prayed for the Church, because all the members pray for one another. The Head intercedes for all, of whom it is written: “Who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Romans VIII).

For the Only-Begotten Son to intercede for humanity means that he shows himself human before the coeternal Father. To have prayed for human nature means that he assumed that same nature in the height of his divinity. The Lord therefore intercedes for us, not by voice but by mercy, because by assuming what he did not wish to condemn in the elect, he preserved it. And when he said that we have Jesus Christ as an advocate with the Father, he rightly added “the righteous.” A righteous advocate does not undertake unjust causes. He will defend us as righteous in the judgment if we now recognize and accuse ourselves as unjust. For how could the one who now rages against his own injustice through tears not be righteous?

And he himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins. He who in his humanity intercedes for us with the Father is the same one who in his divinity is our propitiation with the Father.

Not for ours only, and so forth. The Lord is not the atoning sacrifice only for those to whom John was writing while they were living in the flesh, but also for the whole Church spread throughout the breadth of the world, extending from the first chosen person to the last who will be born at the end of the world. With these words he condemns the schism of the Donatists, who claimed that the Church of Christ was confined solely within the borders of Africa.

The Lord therefore intercedes for the sins of the whole world, because throughout the whole world there is the Church that he purchased with his blood. Nor does what he says here conflict with what he says later: “The whole world lies in the evil one,” because throughout the whole world there are also those who serve the evil one, that is, the ancient enemy.

And by this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments. What commandments he means he reveals in what follows: namely, charity.

Whoever says that he knows him and does not keep his commandments, and so forth. Christ is called the Truth: “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). In vain, therefore, do we applaud ourselves in him whose commandments we do not perform. Nor should we consider it a great thing merely to know the one God, since even the demons believe and tremble. What it truly means to know God he next demonstrates, saying:

But whoever keeps his word, and so forth. Therefore, the person who truly knows God is the one who, by keeping his commandments, proves that he has love for him. For this is what it means to know God: to love him. Whoever does not love him plainly shows that he does not know how lovable he is. He has not learned to taste and see how gracious and sweet the Lord is if he does not continually strive to please him.

By this we know that we are in him, and so forth. That is, through an exceedingly great love, to pray even for enemies, as he himself did when he said, “Father, forgive them” (Luke XXIII). It also means to despise all the prosperity of the world with a courageous spirit, and willingly to endure mockery and reproach, as he himself said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX).

Beloved, I am not writing a new commandment to you, and so forth. The same love is both an old commandment, because it was commended from the beginning, and a new commandment, because, after darkness has been cast out, it infuses the desire for new light. Hence what follows is rightly added:

What is true both in him and in you, and so forth. Behold why it is new: darkness belongs to the old person, whereas light belongs to the new person. Finally, the Apostle Paul says: “Strip off the old person and put on the new” (Ephesians IV); and again: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians V).

Whoever says that he is in the light and hates his brother, and so forth. The Lord commanded us to love our enemies. Therefore, whoever says that he is a Christian and hates his brother remains in sins until now. He rightly added “until now,” because all human beings are born in the darkness of vices, and everyone remains in darkness until they are illumined through Christ by the grace of baptism. Even the person who approaches the font of life to be reborn, and the drink of precious blood by which to be redeemed, while hating his brother—even if he considers himself illumined by the Lord—remains in darkness until now. He could not in any way cast off the shadows of sins who did not take care to put on the inward parts of charity.

For this reason Simon, recently washed with the water of baptism, heard from the one who possessed the keys of heaven: “You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity” (Acts VIII). For, disregarding the fellowship of brotherhood, he desired to buy with money the gift of the Spirit, by which the unity of the Church is preserved, and to possess it privately.

Whoever loves . . . and there is no scandal in him. That is, no offense. For whoever loves his brother endures all things for the sake of the unity of unity. “Great peace belongs to those who love your name” (Psalm CXVIII), that is, charity, “and there is no scandal for them” (ibid.). Paul also says: “Bearing with one another in charity, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians IV).

But whoever hates his brother is in darkness, and so forth. Unaware, he goes into Gehenna; ignorant and blind, he is hurled into punishment, departing from the light of Christ, who warns and says: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII).

I write to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake. He glorifies all his hearers, whom he had himself preceded in Christ, by calling them children, because they had been reborn from water and the Spirit and had received forgiveness of sins. And lest you doubt that the faithful can rightly be called children of the earlier fathers, hear the prophet singing of the Church: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm XLIV); and again, to the same Church: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (ibid.).

[Col. 0091D]

I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. He calls them fathers not because of age, but because they are greater and mature in wisdom. For old age is venerable, not when it is long-lasting or reckoned by a number of years. “The understanding of a person is gray hairs, and an undefiled life is the age of old age” (Wisdom IV). It is the mark of fathers to remember and know ancient things and to reveal them to those who are younger. Hence it is written: “Ask your fathers, and they will announce it to you” (Deuteronomy XXXII). He therefore rightly calls fathers those who have learned to know the one who is from the beginning—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit—and faithfully to preach him to their hearers.

I write to you, adolescents, because you have conquered the evil one. The period of adolescence is slippery because of the incitements of the flesh, but suitable for combat because of the strength of age. Hence John writes to adolescents who have conquered the temptations of carnal pleasures through love of God’s word. He also writes to those who, with greater perfection, have bravely despised all the devices of the wicked enemy when persecutions were inflicted on account of God’s word.

I write to you, infants, because you have known the Father. By infants he means those who are humble in spirit. The more they consent to humble themselves under the powerful hand of God, the more sublimely they come to know the mysteries of his eternity, as the Son says of such people to the same Father: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Luke X).

I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. He commends and repeats this: Remember that you are fathers. If you forget him who is from the beginning, you lose your fatherhood.

I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and so forth. Consider again and again that you are young men. Fight so that you may conquer; conquer so that you may be crowned. Be humble, lest you fall in the battle.

Do not love the world, and so forth. He writes these things generally to all the children of the Church: to those who are fathers through the maturity of prudence and teaching; to those who are infants through the devotion of humility; and to those who are adolescents or young men because they have conquered the struggles of temptation. To all of them alike he commands that they use this world for necessity, but not love it for superfluous desires, as Paul also says: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans XIII).

If anyone loves the world, and so forth. Let no one deceive himself. One heart cannot contain two loves so opposed to one another. Hence the Lord also says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew VI); and again: “You cannot serve God and mammon” (ibid.). For just as love of the Father is the fountain and origin of all virtues, so love of the world is the root and fuel of every vice. Hence what follows:

Because everything that is in the world, and so forth. By “everything that is in the world,” he means all who dwell in the world in their minds, who inhabit the world through love—just as those whose manner of life is in heaven inhabit heaven, whose heart is above even though they walk in the flesh on earth. Everything, therefore, that is in the world—that is, all lovers of the world—possesses nothing except the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life.

Under these names of vices he includes every kind of vice. The desire of the flesh is everything that pertains to bodily pleasure and luxury, among which food, drink, and sexual intercourse are the chief. Concerning these Solomon says: “The leech has two daughters saying, ‘Give, give’” (Proverbs XXX). The desire of the eyes is every curiosity involved in learning wicked arts, watching shameful or useless spectacles, acquiring temporal possessions, and even discerning and criticizing the vices of one’s neighbors. The pride of life exists when someone boasts of his honors.

Human desire is tempted only through these three things. Through them Adam was tempted and overcome: through the desire of the flesh, when the enemy showed him the food of the forbidden tree and persuaded him to eat it; through the desire of the eyes, when he said, “Knowing good and evil, your eyes will be opened” (Genesis III); and through the pride of life, when he said, “You will be like gods” (ibid.).

Christ was tempted through these things and conquered. Through the desire of the flesh—that is, food—when it was suggested: “Tell these stones to become loaves of bread” (Matthew IV); through the desire of the eyes—that is, curiosity—when he was urged from the pinnacle of the temple to throw himself down, in order to test whether angels would receive him; and through the pride of life—that is, empty boasting—when, after he had been set upon a mountain, all the kingdoms of this world were shown to him and promised to him if he would worship.

[Col. 0093B]

Which is not from the Father but is from the world. The struggle of vices was not naturally implanted in us by God the Father and Creator; rather, it is shown to have come upon us from love of this world, which we preferred to the Creator. For God made human beings upright, and they themselves became entangled in countless questions, as Solomon testifies. Hence James also says: “Let no one, when he is tempted, say, ‘I am tempted by God.’ For God is not a tempter of evils; he himself tempts no one” (James I). Each person, however, is tempted when drawn away and enticed by his own desire.

And the world will pass away, and its desire, and so forth. The world will pass away when, on the day of judgment, it is changed through fire into a better form, so that there may be a new heaven and a new earth. Its desire will also pass away, because then there will no longer be time for practicing lust or any sin. “On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Psalm CXLV)—those, certainly, that they directed toward the desires of this world.

But the thoughts of the one who does the will of the Lord do not perish when the world passes away. Because he desired heavenly and eternal things, they remain unchangeable forever, since he will attain the heavenly rewards that he desired. Hence the Lord says of the devout woman—or rather, of every soul that has perfectly followed his will: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke X). Whoever therefore desires to remain unshaken and at rest forever should embrace the things that cannot pass away and follow the will of him who is eternal: God.

My little children, it is the last hour. By “the last hour” he means the final period of the age, which is now taking place, in accordance with the Lord’s parable in which he relates that laborers were hired for the vineyard at the first, third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours. From the first hour, indeed, those cultivated the Lord’s vineyard who, from the beginning of the world, served the will of their Creator either by teaching or by living rightly. From the third hour, those from the time of Noah. From the sixth hour, those from the time of Abraham. From the ninth hour, those from the time when the Law was given. From the eleventh hour, those from the time of the Lord’s Incarnation until the end of the age, who serve the heavenly commands. At this hour, moreover, both the future coming of the Savior in the flesh and the subsequent plague of Antichrist, who would attack the proclamations of salvation, were marked beforehand by the prophetic foretelling. Hence it follows:

And just as you heard that Antichrist is coming, etc. By “Antichrists” he means heretics; but those also who destroy by perverse actions the Catholic faith that they profess are rightly called Antichrists—that is, opponents of Christ. All of these bear witness to that great Antichrist who will come at the end of the age, as to their own head. Hence Paul also says of him: “The mystery of iniquity is already at work” (II Thess. II).

By this we know that it is the last hour. By what? Because many Antichrists have arisen. What he says can also be understood in this way: that even then it was the last hour, because the persecution of that time, inflicted by heretics, bore a great resemblance to that final persecution which will come as the day of judgment approaches—although the former afflicted the Church only with mad words, while the latter will also afflict it with savage swords.

They went out from us, but they were not of us. It seemed that we ought to mourn as over a loss when we heard, “They went out from us”; but consolation is immediately supplied when he adds, “But they were not of us.” For it is clear that none can go out except Antichrists, while those who are not opposed to Christ can in no way go out. Whoever is not opposed to Christ clings to his body.

Yet there are some who are inwardly in the Lord’s body, since his body is still being healed, and perfect health will not come until the resurrection of the dead. They are in Christ’s body as bad humors: when they are vomited out, the body is relieved. So also, when the wicked go out, the Church is relieved. “They went out from us,” he says; “but do not be sad: they were not of us.” How do you prove this?

For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us. From this, then, it must be understood that many who are not of us receive Christ’s sacraments with us. But temptation proves that they are not of us, because when temptation comes upon them, they fly out as though carried away by a gust of wind, since they were not grain. All, however, will fly away when the Lord’s threshing floor begins to be winnowed on the day of judgment. If some have gone out by sinning but return through repentance, they are shown to be not Antichrists but to be in Christ, provided that the end of their present life finds them remaining in the Church.

But that they may be made manifest, because not all are of us. Therefore, by the Lord’s permission, some leave the Church even before the final shaking, showing that they were not members of the Church and did not belong to Christ’s body. In this way it becomes plainly clear that not all who are placed inwardly with us and receive Christ’s sacraments are of us, but only those who perform works worthy of those sacraments within the unity of Christ’s Church.

But you have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things. The spiritual anointing is the Holy Spirit himself, whose sacrament is represented in visible anointing. He says that all who have the ability to recognize good and evil possess this anointing, and that those whom the anointing itself teaches have no need to be taught.

And well, when he had been speaking about heretics, he suddenly turns to his hearers and says that they have an anointing from the Holy One, thereby showing them, by contrast, that heretics and all Antichrists are deprived of the gift of spiritual grace. They do not belong to the Lord, who is accustomed to being called “Holy” by the prophets; rather, among the ministers of Satan, who possess no holiness, they occupy the place of perdition.

I have not written to you as though you were ignorant of the truth, etc. For you know the truth of faith and life, having been taught by the anointing of the Spirit, and you have no need to be taught except to persist in what you have begun.

[Col. 0095B] And because every lie is not from the truth. This verse depends on what precedes, and its meaning is: “We have not written to you as though you were ignorant of the truth, but as though you knew it—and also knew this: that every lie is not from the truth.” Here, moreover, we have been taught how to recognize Antichrist. Christ says, “I am the truth” (John XIV). Every lie, however, is not from the truth. Therefore all who lie are not from Christ. He does not say that some particular lie is not from the truth: every lie is not from the truth. Let no one deceive himself; let no one delude himself.

Who is the liar except the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? He had said beforehand that every lie is not from the truth; but because there are many kinds of lies, differing greatly among themselves, he now presents, as it were, the singular lie of denying Christ, since this lie is so wicked and detestable that, by comparison with it, other lies appear either small or nothing at all. Accordingly, it was said to sinful Jerusalem: “Sodom has been justified in comparison with you” (Ezek. XVI).

This denial properly belongs to the Jews, who say that Jesus is not the Christ. But heretics also, who hold wrong beliefs about Christ, deny that Jesus is the Christ, because they do not think rightly about Christ. They do not confess him to be as divine truth teaches, but as their own vanity invents. Bad Catholics, too, who disdain to obey Christ’s commandments, deny that Jesus is the Christ: they do not render him, as Christ and Son of God, the service of fear or love that is due, but, as though he were a man of no power, they do not fear to contradict him at will. Thus all these are proved to be liars and Antichrists—that is, opponents of Christ—as the Apostle testifies when he says: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. I).

This is the Antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son. By this statement he strikes both heretics and, above all, the Jews, who, while denying that Jesus is Christ the Son of God, nevertheless claimed to have God as their Father. He shows that those who deny the Son confess God the Father in vain. Hence the Lord himself, denouncing them, says: “If God were your Father, you would certainly love me; for I proceeded from God and came” (John VIII).

[Col. 0096A] Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father, etc. Here he seeks confession of the heart, voice, and deed, such as Paul sought when he said: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” This means plainly: no one can serve Christ the Lord with perfect confession and action unless the grace of the Holy Spirit grants it.

Let what you heard from the beginning remain in you, etc. Follow with your whole heart, he says, that faith and those teachings which you received through the voice of the apostles from the earliest days of the Church’s birth. These alone make you participants in divine grace. And if someone says to you, “Behold, here is the Christ; behold, there,” do not believe it. “For false prophets will arise,” as the Lord foretold (Mark XIII).

“And you,” he says, “will remain in the Son and in the Father.” He places the Son first because, as the Son himself says, “No one comes to the Father except through the Son” (John XIV). No one will see the glory of divine exaltation unless he has been reborn through the sacraments of the humanity that the Son assumed. Or perhaps he named the Son first and then the Father so that the Arians would not say that the Son must be believed inferior to the Father because he is never found named before the Father.

And this is the promise that he himself made to us: eternal life. It is as though you were asking about your reward and saying: “Behold, I guard and obey what I heard from the beginning. For this persistence I endure dangers, labors, and temptations. With what result, with what reward? What will be given to me afterward?” “This,” he says, “is the promise that he made to us: eternal life.” Let the memory of the promised reward make you persevere in your work.

I have written these things to you concerning those who lead you astray. The deceivers whom he names are to be understood not only as heretics, who seek by perverse teaching to turn people away from the faith, but also as those who, by the allurements or adversities of this age, wickedly draw the minds of the weak away from the promise of eternal life, either by soothing them or by frightening them.

And as for you, let the anointing that you received from him remain in you, etc. With the Lord’s help, he says, see to it that you preserve whole in heart and body the grace of the Holy Spirit that you received in baptism, in accordance with the saying of the Apostle Paul: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (I Thess. V). Thus, when the Spirit teaches you inwardly, you have less need to be instructed outwardly by human teaching.

The anointing of which he speaks may also be understood as the love of God, which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. V), and which very swiftly inflames the heart it fills to observe God’s commandments.

But just as his anointing teaches you about everything. He rightly added “about everything,” just as in the Gospel the Lord, speaking of the same Spirit, says to the disciples: “He will teach you all things” (John XIV). For unless that same Spirit is present in the heart of the hearer, the teacher’s speech is useless. Therefore, let no one attribute to the human teacher what he understands from the teacher’s mouth, because unless the one who teaches is within, the teacher’s tongue labors outwardly in vain.

Yet the teacher must not cease doing what he can, in accordance with what Paul says: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (I Cor. III).

And it is true, and it is not a lie. By frequent repetition he carefully impresses upon them that what he proclaims is true and entirely free from every stain of falsehood, so that he may restrain those who presume to preach otherwise and may also diligently warn us that eternal life cannot be found in any other way than by following that purity of faith and conduct which was given through the apostles to the primitive Church, and by remaining until the end of this life in its observance and preservation.

A similar saying is that of the Apostle Paul: “Let no one deceive you with empty words; for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience” (Eph. V). But what is said in another Translation—“And it is truthful, and it is not lying”—refers back to the preceding verse, where it says, “But just as his anointing teaches us about everything,” signifying that this same anointing is truthful: that is, the Spirit himself, who teaches human beings, cannot lie.

And just as it taught you, remain in him. Do not allow yourselves to be led away by various and foreign teachings. Remain in him with the faith and the observance that he himself taught. “For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. XXIV).

And now, little children, remain in him, so that when he appears, etc. Whoever remains in the Lord amid the persecutions of unbelievers and the mockery of carnal neighbors has confidence at his coming, knowing that “the patience of the poor will not perish forever.” But whoever is ashamed either to offer the other cheek to one who strikes him, or patiently to endure an insult inflicted by a neighbor, or to observe other such things that the Lord commanded—or, certainly, fears publicly to profess himself a Christian in a time of persecution—cannot have confidence at the Lord’s coming, because he neglected to preserve in this life the confidence of his profession. Rather, he will be put to shame by him at his coming. Hence he says: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty and that of his Father and of the holy angels” (Luke IX).

If you know that he is righteous, know also, etc. Our righteousness at present comes from faith. Perfect righteousness belongs only to the angels—and scarcely even to the angels, if they are compared with God. Nevertheless, if there is some perfect righteousness among the souls and spirits whom God created as angels and saints, righteous and good, turned away by no fall and brought down by no pride, but always remaining in contemplation of God’s Word and finding nothing else sweet except the one by whom they were created, perfect righteousness is found in them.

In us, however, righteousness has begun to exist according to the Spirit through faith. Hence the Psalmist says: “Begin to the Lord with confession” (Ps. CXLVI). “Begin,” he says. The beginning of our righteousness is confession of sins. Once you have begun not to defend your sin, you have already begun righteousness. It will be perfected in you when nothing else delights you to do. When death is swallowed up in victory, when no desire will prick you, when there will be no struggle with flesh and blood, when there will be the crown of victory and triumph over the enemy—then righteousness will be perfect.

Therefore, if you know that he is righteous, he says, know that everyone who practices righteousness has been born from him—that is, from Christ. And because he said, “has been born from him,” he exhorts us, now that we have been born from him, to become perfect. Hear, finally, what follows.

## CHAPTER III

See what kind of love the Father has given us, etc. Great is the grace of our Creator, who has granted us both to know him and to be able to love him, and to love him as children love a father. It would already be a great thing if we could love him as faithful servants love their masters, or as devoted hired laborers love their employers.

The same John bears witness in the Gospel to how we ought to become children of God: “He came to his own,” he says, “and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John I). When these two testimonies are joined together, it is clear that we become children of God through faith and love.

Through this, too, the doctrines of Pelagius and Arius are condemned. The heresy of Pelagius—who dared to say that human beings could be saved without God’s grace—is condemned by the statement that love or power is given to us by God, through which we receive adoption as children. Arius, moreover, who said that the Son was inferior and unlike the Father, is refuted by the fact that John says here that the Father gives us love by which we are called and are children of God, and in the Gospel, through the Lord and Savior, says that power is given to believers to become children of God. For it is clear that those who bestow heavenly gifts equally and without distinction upon human beings are of one substance and possess the same power.

For this reason the world does not know us, because it did not know him. Here he calls “the world” the lovers of the world. It is not surprising that those who love the world cannot love a brother separated from the love of the world and devoted solely to heavenly desires. “Religion is an abomination to the sinner,” as Scripture testifies.

Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. Paul also says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Coloss. III). The faithful person is dead through the extinguishing of the former life that was in sins, and possesses a new life in Christ through faith, whose greatness has not yet appeared visibly to us.

We know that when he appears, we shall be like him. Paul explains this also in other words: “When Christ,” he says, “your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Coloss. III). “We shall be like him,” he says, because when we enjoy the contemplation of the immutable and eternal divinity, we too shall be immortal.

We shall indeed be like him because we shall be blessed; yet we shall be like the Creator as creatures. For who among the children of God will be like God? This may, however, also be understood as referring to the immortality of the body. In this respect, too, we shall be like God—but only like the Son, who alone in the Trinity assumed a body, in which he died and rose again, and carried it up to heavenly things.

Because we shall see him just as he is. God’s being consists in remaining eternal and unchangeable. Hence he says to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. III); and, “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (ibid.). We shall therefore see him just as he is when we contemplate him in the very substance of his divinity. In this life this is granted absolutely to none of the elect, since even the lawgiver himself, who was accustomed to contemplate the Lord in angelic form, pleaded with him, saying: “Lord, show me yourself, so that I may see you” (Exod. XXXIII), and heard from the same Lord: “No one shall see my face and live” (ibid.). Yet, because of his great holiness, he was told: “I will show you every good thing” (ibid.).

Hence Paul also says: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII). Thus what was answered to Moses is true: no one can see God’s face and live (Exod. XXXIII)—that is, no one living in this life can see him just as he is. Many have seen him, but they saw the form that God’s will chose, not the form that nature fashioned. The statement of John is rightly understood in this way: “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him just as he is.”

Not as people saw him when he willed, in the form in which he willed, and not in the nature that remained hidden in him even when he was seen; but as he is—that which Moses asked of him when he said, “Show me yourself” (Exod. XXXIII), to the one who spoke with him face to face.

This does not mean that anyone has ever comprehended the fullness of God, not only with the eyes of the body but even with the mind itself. For it is one thing to see and another to comprehend the whole by seeing. What is present is perceived in some manner by sight, but the whole is comprehended by seeing that which is so seen that nothing of it is hidden from the one who sees, or whose boundaries can be surveyed—just as nothing is hidden from you concerning your present will. You can, however, survey the boundaries of your ring.

For example, I have posited two things, one pertaining to the vision of the mind and the other to bodily eyes. Sight must be referred to both—that is, both to the eyes and to the mind.

And everyone who has this hope in him sanctifies himself, etc. Many say that they have the hope of heavenly life in Christ, but by living carelessly they nullify this confession. The person who strives to devote himself to good works clearly gives evidence of heavenly hope, certain that no one will attain the likeness of God in the future except by imitating God’s holiness in the present, sanctifying himself—that is, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, and living soberly, justly, and devoutly.

We are commanded to imitate the purity of divine holiness according to the measure of our capacity, just as we are instructed to hope for the glory of divine likeness according to our measure—that is, the measure of a creature.

Nor should we think that the Pelagian doctrine is aided by the statement that a person “sanctifies himself,” as though someone could sanctify himself by free will without divine assistance. Rather, whoever has hope in the Lord sanctifies himself by striving as much as he can and by beseeching in all things the grace of the one who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV), and by saying to him: “Be my helper; do not forsake me” (Ps. XXVI).

Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity. Let no one say, “Sin is one thing and iniquity another.” Let no one say, “I am a sinner, but I am not unrighteous.” For everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, because sin is iniquity.

The force of this statement is more easily grasped in the language of the Greeks, in which the Epistle was composed. Among them, iniquity is called ἀνομία (*anomia*), signifying something done as though against the law or without law, since law is called νόμος (*nomos*) in Greek.

When John therefore says that everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity—that is, ἀνομία—and that sin is iniquity, he plainly indicates that everything we sin, we do against God’s law, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “I have counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors” (Ps. CXVIII). All who sin are guilty of transgression. This means not only those who despise the knowledge of the written law given to them, but also those who, through weakness, negligence, or even ignorance, corrupt the innocence of the natural law that we all received in the first-created human being.

The Latin term also accords with the same reasoning: *iniquitas* (“iniquity”) is so called as being opposed to *aequitas* (“equity”). Whoever commits sin also commits iniquity, and sin is iniquity, because whoever sins shows himself to be opposed to the equity of the divine law by sinning.

But, lest we who cannot be wholly free from sins and iniquities despair altogether of salvation, let us consider what follows concerning the Lord:

And you know that he appeared in order to take away sins, etc. John the Baptist also gave this testimony concerning the Lord: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” The Lord was able to take away sins because there is no sin in him. So many and such great people came into the world perfect, but none of them could take away the sins of the world, because none could be without sin in the world.

Therefore let Pelagius not boast, and let Julian, his follower, not exalt himself, when he hears that everyone who has hope in the Lord sanctifies himself. No one takes away sins—not even the Law, although it is holy, just, and good—except the one in whom there is no sin. He takes them away both by forgiving what has been committed, by helping so that they may not be committed, and by bringing us to the life where they cannot be committed at all.

Everyone who remains in him does not sin. To the extent that he remains in him, to that extent he does not sin.

And everyone who sins has neither seen him nor known him. By “seeing” and “knowing” he means the vision and knowledge of faith, through which the righteous rejoice even in this life to see God, until in the future they reach the very appearance of his open vision, of which it was said above: “Because we shall see him just as he is.”

Therefore everyone who sins has neither seen him nor known him. For if he had tasted and seen how gracious the Lord is (Ps. XXXIII), he would certainly not separate himself by sinning from the vision of his glory. And to the extent that the righteous pour forth the memory of the abundance of his goodness and rejoice in his righteousness (Ps. CXLIV), to that extent they strive, by abstaining from sins, to conform to his unchangeable and incomparable righteousness.

Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, etc. And above he says: “He sanctifies himself, just as he is holy.” This does not mean that our righteousness or holiness can equal divine righteousness or holiness, since it is written: “There is none holy like the Lord” (I Sam. II).

There is as much difference between a human face and its image in a mirror as there is between imitation and reality. Yet just as there are eyes here, so there are eyes there. The thing itself is different, but just as the image refers to likeness, so we too possess the image of God—not, however, the image that the Son possesses, who is equal to the Father. For if we were not, in our own measure, as he is, we would not be called like him in any respect.

Therefore he sanctifies us just as he himself is holy. But he is holy in eternity, while we are holy through faith. We are righteous just as he is righteous. But he is righteous in his own unchangeable perpetuity, while we are righteous by believing in the one whom we do not see, so that one day we may see him.

Whoever commits sin is from the devil. This does not mean deriving the origin of the flesh from the devil, as the impious Manichaeus believes concerning all human beings, but taking from him the imitation or suggestion of sinning—just as we have become children of Abraham by imitating Abraham’s faith. Conversely, the Jews, who were children of Abraham, abandoned Abraham’s faith and became children of the devil, as the Lord says to them: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII).

Because the devil sins from the beginning. After prefacing “from the beginning,” he added the present-tense verb “sins,” because from the time when the devil began to sin at the beginning, he has never ceased—restrained neither by the enormity of present punishments nor by fear of future ones. Hence anyone who neglects to restrain himself from sinning is rightly said to be from him.

The devil sins from the beginning—that is, from the time when he himself was made, when the origin of all creatures also began. For there is no doubt that angels were created among the first creatures. While the rest referred the glory of their creation to the praise of the Creator, the one who was created first, as soon as he saw the height of his own brightness, swelled with pride against the Creator along with his followers. Through that same pride, sinning from the beginning, he was changed from an archangel into the devil.

For this the Son of God appeared, to destroy the works of the devil. All sinners are born from the devil insofar as they are sinners. Adam was made by God; but when he consented to the devil, he was born from the devil, and he begot all those who were like himself. That birth cast them down to death; the second birth, namely baptism, raised them to life. The former birth dragged sin along with it; the second birth frees from sin.

For this reason Christ came as a human being, to undo human sins. Concerning this undoing, what follows is rightly added:

Everyone who has been born from God does not commit sin, etc. [Col. 0102A] He is not speaking here about every kind of sin. For “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (I John I). Rather, he speaks of violating love, which the person who possesses within himself the seed of God—that is, the word of God through which he was reborn—cannot commit. He makes this clear by continuing:

By this the children of God and the children of the devil are manifest, etc. Love alone, therefore, distinguishes between the children of God and the children of the devil. Those who possess love have been born from God. Those who do not possess it have not been born from God. Whatever else you wish, have it; but if you do not have this one thing, nothing benefits you. If you lack other things, have this, and you have fulfilled the law. For whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law, and love is the fullness of the law.

Because this is the message that you heard from the beginning: that you should love one another. The Lord said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John XV).

Not like Cain, who was from the evil one, etc. He explains how Cain was from the evil one: namely, because he himself had evil works. Therefore, where envy is present, fraternal love cannot exist. The sin of the evil one—that is, the devil—is in such a breast, because the devil also cast the human being out through envy.

Thus he names Abel’s righteous works only as love, and Cain’s evil works only as hatred of his brother. It is not a small matter that he hates his brother and envies his brother’s good works (so). This is how people are distinguished. Let no one pay attention to words, but to deeds. Why, if he does not do good to his brothers, does he reveal what he possesses within himself? People are tested by temptations.

Do not marvel, brothers, if the world hates you. By “the world” he means lovers of the world. It is not surprising that those who love the world cannot love a brother who has been separated from love of the world and is devoted solely to heavenly desires. For religion is an abomination to the sinner, as Scripture testifies.

We know that we have been transferred from death to life because we love the brothers. Let no one falsely exalt himself over his virtues, and let no one measure the poverty of his strength beyond measure. Whoever is full of fraternal love gives clear evidence that he belongs to the lot of the elect, because he has deserved to have a portion in the land of the living.

Whoever does not love remains in death. He means the death of the soul. “The soul that sins shall itself die.” The life of the flesh is the soul; the life of the soul is God. The death of the body is the loss of the spirit; the death of the soul is the loss of God.

It is therefore clear that all who are dead in soul are born into this light, carrying original sin from Adam. But through Christ’s grace, the faithful are regenerated so that they may live in soul. Yet the mystery of baptism and faith benefits only those whom it draws from death to life—those who love their brothers with sincere hearts.

For this reason it must be noted that he does not say, “Whoever does not love will come into death,” as though he were speaking of the everlasting punishment that awaits sinners in the future. Rather, he says, “Whoever does not love remains in death”—in that death from which he could rise even in this life if he loved his brothers perfectly. Hence it is said in the Apocalypse: “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection” (Apoc. XX); “over these the second death has no power.”

Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. If anyone regarded hatred of a brother as insignificant, would he not also regard murder in his heart as insignificant? He does not move his hands to kill a person, yet he is already held by God as a murderer. The other is alive, and this one is already judged a killer.

And you know that every murderer does not have eternal life remaining in him. Even if he is seen here living among the saints through faith, he does not have within himself life that remains forever. For when the time of retribution arrives, the one held by this kind of murder—so that he disagrees, quarrels, and has no peace with his brothers—will be condemned along with Cain, who was from the evil one.

It must be noted that he does not say simply, “A murderer does not have life remaining in him,” but, “Every murderer,” he says. That is, not only the one who attacks his brother with a sword, but also the one who pursues him with hatred.

By this we have recognized the love of God, etc. We have learned what perfect love ought to be in us from the example of the Lord’s Passion. “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV). Hence Paul also says: “God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. V).

The blessed Peter was admonished to have this love when the Lord said, “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John XXI). He replied that he loved him, and immediately heard: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish” (ibid.). The evangelist says that he spoke this to signify by what death Peter would glorify God.

To the one who confessed his love, the Lord entrusted his sheep, teaching him to lay down his life for those same sheep as a testimony of perfect love. “He laid down his life for us,” he says, “and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.”

But perhaps someone will say: “How can I have this love?” Do not quickly despair of yourself. Perhaps it has been born in you, but it is not yet perfect. Nourish it, lest it be stifled. “And how,” you ask, “do I know that love has been born in me, so that I may nourish it?” Hear what follows:

Whoever has the substance of this world and sees his brother in need, etc. Behold where love begins.
