If you are not yet capable of dying for your brother, already make yourself capable of giving your possessions to your brother. For if you do not have compassion on a brother who is suffering distress, the love of the Father from whom you were both regenerated certainly does not remain in you.

My little children, let us not love in word or with the tongue, etc. That is, in deed: when a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, let us give them what the body needs. Likewise, when we see them lacking spiritual gifts, let us provide what we can for their need.

And in truth: let us bestow these same benefits upon them with a sincere intention—not for human praise, not through boasting, and not to the injury of others who, though endowed with greater possessions, have done nothing of the kind. For whatever mind is contaminated by such wickedness cannot have the purity of truth dwelling in it, even if it appears to bestow the work of love upon its neighbors.

By this we know that we are from the truth. That is, when we perform works of mercy in truth, it is evident that we are from the truth, which is God, since we imitate his perfection according to our measure.

And in his presence we shall persuade our hearts. This sentence depends on what precedes. Because we love our neighbors in deed and in truth, we clearly know that, in the presence of supreme truth, we persuade our hearts.

For whenever people intend to do something, they turn and persuade their hearts to consider that very action. But those who think evil thoughts would, if they could, hide them from God, as the one who says testifies: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be reproved” (John III).

Those, however, who meditate on doing good easily persuade their hearts that they desire to be revealed in the presence of the divinity. This is usually a sign of supreme perfection, when each person rejoices that his deeds or thoughts are seen by God. Hence he says immediately afterward: “But whoever practices the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be manifested, because they have been done in God” (ibid.).

Through true love, therefore, we know that we are from the truth, and that in the presence of this same truth we persuade our hearts—that is, we persuade our hearts to have thoughts worthy of the divine presence.

Because if our heart condemns us, etc. If our conscience itself accuses us inwardly because we do not perform our good works with the intention with which they ought to be performed, how can we remain hidden from the knowledge of the one to whom it is sung: “Behold, you, Lord, have known all things,” and, “Because darkness will not be darkened from you, and night will be illuminated like day” (Ps. CXXXVIII)?

Dearest ones, if our heart does not condemn us, etc. If it answers us truthfully that we love, and that the love within us is genuine—not feigned but sincere, seeking our brother’s salvation and expecting no advantage from him except his salvation—then, if our heart does not condemn us, namely when in prayer we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6), we have confidence before God, not in the sight of human beings, but where God himself sees into the heart.

And whatever we ask, we shall receive from him, etc. This is a great and desirable promise given to the faithful. But if anyone is so foolish and senseless that he takes no pleasure in heavenly promises, let him at least fear what Wisdom thunders in opposition, saying: “Whoever turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. 28). Nor should what the blessed John says appear contrary to this: that Paul asked the Lord three times that Satan’s angel depart from him, and could not obtain this (2 Cor. 12); rather, it was said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (ibid.). For although, when we pray, we do not always receive what we want, we nevertheless receive the reward of our devotion for salvation. Thus Paul himself, when asking the Lord, received not what he sought but what was useful. On the other hand, the reprobate are often heard according to their wishes, though not for their salvation. Hence even their head, the devil, was heard according to his wish when he sought to test blessed Job, but to his own condemnation. He was permitted to test Job so that, once Job had been proved, the devil might be punished. Therefore, when John had said that whatever we ask we shall receive from him if we keep his commandments, as though you were asking which commandments, he immediately added:

And this is his commandment: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, etc. He first used the singular, “commandment,” and then subsequently added the commandments, namely faith and love, because these plainly cannot be separated from one another. For without faith in Christ we cannot rightly love one another, nor can we truly believe in the name of Jesus Christ without brotherly love. “And let us love one another,” he says, “as he gave us commandment.” That is, with pure love—not as thieves or perpetrators of any other crimes love one another, for they too love one another, but not chastely. Rather, he gave us this commandment when he said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 15). For what is “as I have loved you” except “Love to the end for which I loved you”—namely, so that you may reach the heavenly kingdoms? And by what reward are these commandments of faith and love kept? He continues:

And whoever keeps his commandments remains in him, and he himself in him. Let God therefore be your house, and be God’s house; remain in God, and let God remain in you. God remains in you to contain you; you remain in God so that you do not fall. Keep his commandments; hold fast to love. Do not tear yourself away from his faith, so that you may glory in his presence, and you will remain secure in him—now through faith, then through sight. He too will remain eternally in you, as the Psalmist sings to him: “They will rejoice forever, and you will dwell in them” (Ps. 5).

And by this we know that he remains in us, from the Spirit whom he gave us. In the earliest times, the Holy Spirit fell upon believers, and they spoke in tongues they had not learned. Now, however, because the holy Church has no need of external signs, every believer in the name of Jesus Christ who possesses brotherly love bears witness to the Holy Spirit dwelling within him. For this is what the Holy Spirit produces in a person: that love may be in him. “Because God’s love,” Paul says, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). But since many who do not have love, and who divide the unity of the Church by perverse doctrine, nevertheless insist that the Holy Spirit is within them, it is rightly added:

CHAPTER IV

Dearest ones, do not believe every spirit, etc. And who tests the spirits, or by what means they can be tested, the Lord teaches in the Gospel, where he foretold that such things would come, as John proves had already come in his own time. “Beware,” he says, “of false prophets who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits. Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” (Mark 7). These, then, are the fruits by which the evil spirits speaking through false prophets can be recognized: namely, the thorns of schisms and the harsh thistles of heresies, by which they defile those who approach them carelessly, tearing apart their faith. Conversely, the fruits of the good—love, joy, and peace in the Holy Spirit—are aptly represented by the fragrance of grapes and the sweetness of figs.

By this the Spirit of God is recognized, etc. Here “confession” means not only confession of the Catholic faith but also the good work accomplished through love. Otherwise, some heretics, many schismatics, and many false Catholics confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, but deny their confession by their deeds, since they do not have love. For it was God’s love that brought the Son of God into the flesh. Therefore, whoever does not have love denies that he came in the flesh, and is proved not to have the Spirit from God. But the Spirit of God is the one who says that Jesus Christ came in the flesh—the one who says it not with the tongue but by deeds, not by uttering it but by loving.

And every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God. He dissolves Jesus who denies either his divinity, his soul, or his flesh, which the Catholic faith teaches that he truly possessed. He too dissolves Jesus who corrupts Jesus’ commandments and words, either by seeing them perversely or by interpreting them perversely. And the one who disturbs the unity of the holy Church, which Jesus came to gather, strives, insofar as he can, to dissolve Jesus. It is no wonder that such people are not from God, since they cut apart God’s works, words, or sacraments. Indeed, they are so far from being from God that some of those who wished by their perverse doctrine to separate Christ’s divinity from the dispensation of his humanity even erased from this Epistle the verse that says, “And every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God,” lest their error be convicted by the authority of blessed John. Finally, Nestorius showed that he was unaware that this sentence had been included in authoritative copies, and therefore did not fear dissolving Jesus and thereby making himself a stranger to God. He claimed that the blessed virgin Mary was the mother not of God but only of a human being, thereby making one person belong to humanity and another to divinity; nor did he believe that there was one Christ in the Word of God, the flesh, and the soul, but proclaimed separately one Son of God and another of man.

And this is the Antichrist, of whom you have heard that he is coming, etc. He will come as the day of judgment approaches, when that supremely wicked human being, the son of iniquity, is born into the world. And now he is already in the world, dwelling in the minds of those who oppose Christ, whether in profession or in conduct, without remedy through repentance.

You are from God, little children, and you have conquered him. You have conquered the Antichrist by confessing that Jesus Christ came in the flesh—that is, by possessing the love taught by Jesus Christ when he came in the flesh, which he himself also commends in the Gospel, saying: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). For how could the Son of God lay down his life for us unless he assumed flesh, in which he could die? Therefore, whoever violates love, whatever he may say with his tongue, denies by his life that Christ came in the flesh, and he himself is the Antichrist. “And you have conquered him,” he says. But by what means did they conquer? By the power of free choice? Certainly not. Let Pelagius be silent; let John himself speak:

Because the one who is in you is greater, etc. Thus he teaches them to preserve humility, lest they attribute victory to their own strength and be overcome by arrogant pride. Amid adversities he teaches them always to have confidence and hope of victory, remembering that the Lord is greater in protecting than the devil is in attacking.

They are from the world, etc. The Antichrists—that is, the heretics—even though they invoke Christ’s name and mark themselves with Christ’s sign, are nevertheless from the world: that is, they belong to the number of those who savor worldly things, seek weak things (*infirma*; perhaps *infima*, “lowest things”), and are ignorant of heavenly things. Therefore they speak from the world, opposing the Christian faith by the reasoning of worldly wisdom. They say that the Son of God cannot be coeternal with the Father; that a virgin cannot give birth while remaining undefiled; that flesh cannot rise from the dust immortal; that a human being made from earth cannot receive a dwelling in heaven; and that a newborn infant cannot be held bound by the guilt of the first human being unless, reborn in Christ through the water of baptism, he is saved.

And the world listens to them. For they cannot recall spiritual hearts from the simplicity of faith to worldly and carnal perceptions. But any Catholics who, hearing the Lord’s sentence, “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5), and again, “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses; but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6), say that they cannot possibly leave their own injuries unavenged—these are plainly proved to be from the world, and therefore to speak from the world. And because they do not have the inner organs of love, they preserve the undefiled mysteries of faith in vain. Nor can they be free of the name Antichrist, since they are proved to oppose Christ’s commandments.

We are from God. Whoever knows God, etc. For the carnal person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God; they are foolishness to him. Whoever, therefore, refuses to hear the preachers of love is clearly recognized as not knowing God and not being from God, because he has neglected to imitate the love that God exercised toward human beings.

By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error. Namely, by this: whoever hears us has the Spirit of truth; whoever does not hear us has the spirit of error. This is the discernment of spirits about which he warned above, saying: “Test the spirits, whether they are from God.” But let us see what he is about to command, and in what we ought to hear him:

Dearest ones, let us love one another, etc. He has strongly commended love, which he said is from God; he is about to say even more, so let us listen attentively:

And everyone who loves is born from God, etc. What more could be said? God is love. To act against love, therefore, is to act against God. Let no one say, “When I do not love my brother, I sin against a human being; it is easy to sin against a human being, provided I do not sin against God alone.” How do you not sin against God when you sin against love? God is love.

By this the love of God was revealed among us, etc. As the Lord himself says: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). Thus Christ’s love for us was proved, because he died for us. The Father’s love for us was proved by this: that he sent his only Son to die for us. So the apostle Paul also says: “He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, how did he not also, along with him, give us all things?” (Rom. 8).

In this is love, etc. We did not love him first. For he loved us for this purpose: that we might love him. Grace precedes a human being so that he may love God, and through that love perform good works. Hence the Psalmist says: “My God, his mercy will precede me” (Ps. 58).

And he sent his Son as an expiation, etc. This too is the greatest sign of divine love toward us: before we even knew to ask him for our sins, he sent his Son to us, so that he might freely grant forgiveness to those who believe in him and call us to share in the glory of the Father. In some manuscripts this verse is read as follows: “And he sent his Son as the sacrificer for our sins.” A sacrificer (*litator*) is one who offers sacrifice. For the Son of God sacrificed for our sins, not by offering victims of animals but by offering himself. Thus Paul rightly exhorts us, saying: “Therefore be imitators of God, as dearly beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and handed himself over for us, an offering and sacrifice to God as a pleasing aroma” (Eph. 5). This agrees with what John too added here in exhortation, saying:

Dearest ones, if God loved us, etc. But what follows—

No one has ever seen God—requires a more extensive discussion, since the Lord promises that God will be seen by the pure in heart, and says of the saints that their angels always see the face of the Father in heaven. The same John also sets down this statement in his Gospel, where he immediately explains how God can be seen, saying: “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known” (John 1).

The blessed Father Ambrose explained this as follows:

“And therefore no one has ever seen God, because no one has perceived, no one has grasped with mind or eyes, that fullness of divinity which dwells in God. For ‘seen’ must be referred to both. Finally, when it is added, ‘The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known,’ the vision of minds rather than of eyes is declared. Appearance is seen; power is made known. The former is grasped by the eyes, the latter by the mind.”

Likewise, blessed Augustine, discussing the same question in his book *On Seeing God*, says:

“Therefore, when the Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, makes him known by an ineffable revelation, the rational, pure, and holy creature is filled with an ineffable vision of God. We shall attain this when we have been made equal to the angels, because we shall see face to face (1 Cor. 13). Just as these visible things are recognized by the bodily senses, no one has ever seen God; for if he has ever been seen in some manner, he was not seen as this nature is seen, but was seen by his will, appearing in whatever form he wished while his nature remained hidden and unchanged in itself. In the manner in which he is seen as he is (1 Cor. 13), he is perhaps now seen by certain of his holy angels. By us, however, he will then be seen in this way, when we have been made equal to them.”

And later, explaining the sentence of Saint Ambrose, he says:

“No one has ever seen God, either in this life as he is, or even in the life of the angels as these visible things are seen by bodily vision, because the Only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has made him known. Hence what he reveals is said to pertain not to the sight of bodily eyes but to the vision of minds.”

Again, after much else:

“But he has admonished pure hearts concerning that vision by which we shall see God as he is (1 Cor. 13). Since bodies are called ‘visible’ according to ordinary usage, God is therefore called invisible, lest he be believed to be a body. This is not because he will deprive pure hearts of the contemplation of his substance, since this great and supreme reward is promised to those who worship and love God. The Lord himself said this when he visibly appeared to bodily eyes and promised that the invisible one would be contemplated by pure hearts: ‘Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him’ (John 14). For his nature is invisible, equally with the Father, just as it is equally incorruptible. The apostle placed these together when he said: ‘To the King of ages, invisible and incorruptible,’ commending the divine substance to human beings by whatever preaching he could.”

God, therefore, is an invisible reality, and he must be sought not with the eye but with the mind. But just as, if we wished to see the sun, we would purify the bodily eye, through which light can be seen, so, if we wish to see God, let us purify the eye of the heart, through which God can be seen: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). But since this vision is hoped for in the future, what must we do while, still dwelling in the body, we are away from the Lord? What consolation should we use when we are not yet permitted to enjoy the divine vision?

If we love one another, God remains in us. But no one should suppose that this love, in which God remains, is preserved by some lowly and idle gentleness—or rather, not gentleness but indulgence and negligence. That is not love but weakness. Let love burn for correcting and reforming. If conduct is good, let it delight us; if bad, let it be amended and corrected. If, therefore, we love one another with sincere and disciplined love, God remains in us, made manifest indeed through the works of love, although he does not yet appear visibly.

And his love is perfected in us. We must ask how he can say that the perfection of divine love consists in mutual love, when the Lord declares in the Gospel that it is not a great thing if we love those who love us, unless that same love also reaches our enemies, about whom he seems here to say nothing at all. Perhaps we must love our enemies too out of regard for fraternal love—namely, so that they may not always remain enemies, but may recover from the devil’s snares and be joined to us in a brotherly bond. “If we love,” he says, “one another, God remains in us, and his love is perfected in us.” Begin to love, and you will be perfected. You have begun to love; God has begun to dwell in you, so that by dwelling ever more perfectly he may make you perfect.

By this we know that we remain in him, etc. You know this very thing—that he has given you of his Spirit—by what means? Question your inward parts. If they are full of love, you have the Spirit of God, as Paul bears witness, saying: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5).

And we have seen and testify, etc. Let no one despair of salvation. Though the diseases of wickedness that weigh us down are great, the almighty physician has come to save. Yet let each person remember that the same Son of God who came meekly to save will come in severity to judge.

Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, etc. He speaks of a perfect confession of the heart, one that cannot be corrupted by the deceit of heretics who give evil counsel, shaken by the torments of persecuting pagans, undermined by the example of carnal brothers, or made to falter by the sluggishness of one’s own weakness. There are indeed people who even in words deny that Jesus is the Son of God, as many are reported to have done at the very time when John wrote this. There are also those who confess it in words but deny it in deeds. Thus it is appropriate that he now says: “Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he himself in God.” Just above he said: “If we love one another, God remains in us,” clearly indicating that whoever has love for his brothers truly bears witness that Jesus is the Son of God.

And we have known and believed the love that God has for us. We have known that Jesus is the Son of God and that the Father sent him as the Savior of the world. And we have believed the love that God has for us, because, although he had one only Son, he did not wish him to remain alone, but, so that he might have brothers, adopted us to possess eternal life with him.

God is love. He said this above; behold, he says it again. Love could not have been commended to you more fully than by saying that God is love. Perhaps you were about to despise God’s gift; surely you do not despise God as well?

And whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him. The one who contains and the one who is contained dwell reciprocally in one another. You dwell in God, but so that you may be contained; God dwells in you, but so that he may contain you and prevent you from falling. For the Apostle says of love itself: “Love never falls.” How does one fall whom God contains?

By this love is perfected with us, etc. He explains how each person may prove how far he has advanced in it. Whoever has confidence on the day of judgment has perfected love within him. What does it mean to have confidence on the day of judgment? It means not to fear the coming of the day of judgment. When someone first turns from evil deeds through repentance, he begins to fear the day of judgment, lest, when the just Judge appears, he himself, being unjust, be condemned. But as he progresses and is encouraged by a good way of life, he learns not to fear what he feared, but rather to desire the coming of him who is desired by all nations, hoping that through the merit of good action he will be crowned with the saints. From where we may have confidence on the day of judgment, he makes clearer by adding:

Because as he is, so are we in this world. But can a human being be like God? We must remember what was said above: “as” does not always indicate equality, but may indicate a certain likeness. When you say, “As I have ears, so does an image,” do you mean that it is exactly so? Nevertheless, you say “as.” If, then, we have been made in the image of God, why should we not be like God—not in equality, but according to our measure? We therefore have confidence on the day of judgment because, as he is, so are we in this world: namely, by imitating in this world the perfection of love whose example he gives us daily from heaven. Of this the Savior says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5).

There is no fear in love. Namely, in that kind of love which, in imitation of divine goodness, knows how to do good to enemies and love them.

But perfect love casts out fear. Specifically, that fear of which it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110). By this fear, every beginner in works of justice fears that the severe Judge may come and, finding him insufficiently disciplined, condemn him. That fear is driven out by the love that, on account of the merit of justice, has confidence on the day of judgment. Perfect love also expels from the mind fear of present adversities. This was the love sought by the one who pleaded with the Lord: “Deliver my soul from fear of the enemy” (Ps. 63). It was possessed by the one who said: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” etc. (Rom. 8).

Because fear has punishment. The conscience of sins torments the heart, since justification has not yet been accomplished. Therefore the Psalmist speaks of that perfection of righteousness: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced” (Ps. 29)—that is, so that there may be nothing to prick my conscience. Fear pricks, but do not fear: love enters, and heals what fear wounds.

But whoever fears is not perfect in love. For fear has punishment, just as a physician’s operation has pain, although, just as desired health follows the physician’s operation, so the desired love follows fear. Nor should it be thought contrary to these words of blessed John that the Psalmist says: “The holy fear of the Lord endures forever and ever” (Ps. 18). There are two fears. One is the fear by which people fear God lest they be sent into hell. That is the fear that introduces love, but it comes in order to depart. For if you still fear God because of punishments, you do not yet love the one whom you fear in this way; you do not desire good things but avoid evil ones. Yet by avoiding evil you correct yourself and begin to desire good. Once you have begun to desire good, there will be in you that holy fear—namely, fear of losing those very good things—not fear of being sent into hell, but fear that the presence of the Lord whom you embrace, and whom you desire to enjoy forever, may depart from you.

Let us therefore love God, etc. Let us love him because he first loved us. For how would we love him unless he had first loved us? Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15). We shall be perfect in love if, just as he loved us first for no reason other than our salvation, so we too love him for no purpose other than love itself. But since there are people who love God in words only, the text appropriately adds:

If anyone says, “Because I love God,” etc. How do you prove that he is a liar? Listen:

For whoever does not love his brother, etc. Whoever loves his brother loves God. He must love God in order to love love itself. For God is love. And lest anyone dare say, “What prevents me from loving God even if I do not love my brother?” the text rightly adds:

And we have this commandment from God, etc. How do you love the one whose commandment you hate? Who would say, “I love the emperor, but I hate his laws”? The true lover of God does not speak in this way, but says: “See that I have loved your commandments, Lord” (Ps. 118). And therefore he confidently adds: “In your mercy give me life” (ibid.).

CHAPTER V

Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ, etc. Who is the one who believes that Jesus is the Christ? The one who lives as Christ commanded. Let no heretic or schismatic say, “We too believe that Jesus is the Christ.” For even the demons believe and tremble, and, as we read in the Gospel, they confessed and knew that he himself was the Christ. But because they do not have love and works of truth, they are not from God.

And everyone who loves the one who begot loves also the one who has been begotten by him, etc. With wondrous skill in preaching, blessed John sought to kindle us to love of our neighbor. First he recalled that everyone who believes perfectly is born from God; then he indicated how just it is that whoever loves God should love the one who has been born from God. If someone is so slow to understand that he has neglected to love a human being because he is human and because he endures with him the same earthly pilgrimage, he must at least be admonished to love him for this reason: that he has been born from God, that he has become with him a participant in divine grace, and that he awaits with him the same rewards of heavenly life. This exhortation applies especially to those who have become our brothers not only through sharing human nature but also through profession of the faith. Yet because there are some who love their neighbors on account of kinship or some temporal advantage, the holy Evangelist rightly reveals by what he adds what true love of neighbor is:

By this we know that we love the children of God, etc. Therefore, only the one who is also recognized as burning with love of the Creator is proved to love his neighbor rightly. And lest anyone deceive himself about love of the Creator by professing to love him in words only, after saying, “By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God,” he rightly added, “and do his commandments.”

For this is the love of God: that we keep his commandments. The Lord himself also says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14). The proof of love, therefore, is the performance of the work. We truly love if we restrain ourselves from our own desires in order to obey his commandments. For whoever still gives way to unlawful desires plainly does not love God, because in following his own will he contradicts God.

And his commandments are not burdensome. The Lord himself also says: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11). Nor should this seem contrary to the words either of the Lord or of blessed John: that the Lord elsewhere says that narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life (Matt. 7); and the prophet says to him: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept difficult ways” (Ps. 16); and the Apostle says: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14). What is hard and rough by nature is made light by hope of heavenly rewards and love of Christ. It is hard to suffer persecutions for the sake of righteousness, but this too is made pleasant by the fact that the kingdom of heaven belongs to those who suffer in this way. Hence it is rightly added:

For everything that is born from God conquers the world. The divine commandments are not burdensome for this reason: all who devote themselves to them with true devotion, and with an equal mind despise both the world’s adversities and its allurements, even loving death as an entrance into their heavenly homeland. And lest anyone confidently believe that by his own strength he can overcome either the world’s pleasures or its hardships, the text appropriately adds:

And this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith. Namely, that faith which works through love; that faith by which we humbly implore the help of the one who says: “In the world you will have affliction, but take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16).

Who is the one who conquers the world, etc. He conquers the world who, believing that Jesus is the Son of God, joins to that faith works worthy of it. But is faith and confession of his divinity alone sufficient for salvation? Consider what follows.

This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ. He who was the eternal Son of God became human in time, so that he who had created us through the power of his divinity might recreate us through the weakness of his humanity. He came through water and blood—water, namely, of the washing, and the blood of his passion. Not only did he graciously consent to be baptized for our cleansing, thereby consecrating and handing over to us the sacrament of baptism; he also gave his blood for us, redeeming us through his passion, so that, continually nourished by its sacraments, we might be sustained for salvation.

And it is the Spirit who testifies that Christ is truth. When the Lord was baptized in the Jordan, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove, bearing witness that he is truth—that is, the true Son of God, the true mediator between God and human beings, the true Redeemer and reconciler of the human race, truly himself pure from every stain of sin, truly sufficient to take away the sins of the world. The Baptist too, understanding this when he saw the arrival of that same Spirit, said: “The one who sent me to baptize in water said to me, ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1). Since, therefore, the Spirit testifies that Jesus Christ is truth, he himself calls himself truth, the Baptist proclaims him truth, and the Son of Thunder preaches the truth, let the blasphemers who teach that he is a phantom be silent; let the memory of those who deny that he is truly God or truly human perish from the earth.

For there are three who bear witness on earth, etc. The Spirit bore witness that Jesus is truth when he descended upon him after his baptism. For if he were not the true Son of God, the Holy Spirit would certainly not have come upon him with such a manifestation. Water and blood also bore witness that Jesus is truth when they flowed from his side as he hung dead upon the cross. This could in no way have happened if he had not possessed the true nature of flesh. Nor should it be left unmentioned that, before his passion, when he was praying, his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground (Luke 22); this too bears witness to the truth of the flesh he assumed. In this matter also, blood and water bore witness to him: they flowed vigorously from the side of the dead man, contrary to the nature of dead bodies, and for that reason were fitting for the mysteries and appropriate as a testimony to the truth. They indicated that the Lord’s own body would live more fully after death, raised in glory, and that his death itself would give us life. The fact too that his sweat ran down to the ground like drops of blood bore witness to the sacred mystery that he would wash the Church throughout the whole world with his blood. There are therefore three who bear witness to the truth.

And the three, he says, are one. These remain undivided, and none of them is separated from its connection with the others, because divinity cannot be believed without true humanity, nor humanity without true divinity. In us too these three are one—not by the nature of the same substance, but through the same operation of the mystery. For, as blessed Ambrose says: “The Spirit renews the one who remains; the water contributes to the washing; the blood pertains to the price.” The Spirit made us sons of God by adoption, the water of the sacred font washed us, and the Lord’s blood redeemed us. One testimony is therefore invisible, the other visible; both accompany the spiritual sacrament.

If we receive human testimony, the testimony of God is greater, etc. Great is the testimony of a human being that he bears concerning the Son of God, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109). And, speaking in the person of the Son himself: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son” (Ps. 2). Likewise, speaking in the person of the Father about the Son: “He will call upon me, ‘You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation’” (Ps. 88). “My Father,” because I am the Son of God; “my God,” because I am human; “the protector of my salvation,” because I am destined to suffer and to be saved from death. And “I shall make him my firstborn,” he says, “highest among the kings of the earth” (ibid.).

This is a great and true testimony, and a testimony of a human being concerning the Son of God worthy of all acceptance; but much greater is the testimony of God, who himself bore witness concerning his Son when, addressing him from heaven, he said: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Luke 3). Great is the testimony of the Forerunner, who, bearing witness concerning the Son of God, said: “I baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 3). Greater is the testimony of the Father, by which he sent the Holy Spirit upon him, visibly as well, although he had always been full of the Spirit.

Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God within himself (1 John 5:10). Whoever believes in the Son of God in such a way that he practices by his actions what he believes has the testimony of God within himself. This testimony, certainly, is that he too may rightly be counted among the children of God, since the only Son of God himself promises this to his faithful: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him” (John 12).

But if you have deserved to possess the testimony of God, if you have God as witness to your undefiled faith, what harm can the disgrace inflicted by human beings do you? What harm even can persecution do? For if God is for us, who can be against us?

Whoever does not believe the Son makes him a liar, etc. In vain do Jews and heretics think that they believe in and venerate the Father, so long as they despise Christ and refuse to believe in him. For whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.

Those who do not believe the Son—who says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), and who, when Caiaphas asked, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?” (Mark 14), answered, “I am” (ibid.)—but maintain that he either is not the Christ, or is not the Son of God, or is not like the Father, plainly make the Father a liar, because they do not believe the testimony that he bore concerning his Son—namely, the testimony I mentioned above: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Luke 3). They also reject the testimony he gave him when the hour of his passion was approaching. As he prayed and said, “Father, save me from this hour. But it was for this reason that I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name” (John 12), the Father answered, even with the crowd listening, from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (ibid.), thereby indicating that he truly was the God and Father in heaven of the one who, as true man, was destined to suffer death on earth.

And this is the testimony: that God gave us eternal life. “He gave us,” he says, “eternal life.” Yet the one who speaks was still living in the flesh a temporal life subject to death. But he gave us eternal life in the same way as he gave us the power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name. And, so that you may know that the power to possess eternal life was given by God, hear the prophet: “Who is the person who desires life and longs to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit,” and so forth, through to the end of the psalm (Ps. 33). Thus he gave us eternal life, but to us who are still pilgrims on earth he gave it in hope; to those who reach him in heaven he will give it in reality.

And this life is in his Son. That is, in faith in and confession of his name, in receiving his sacraments, and in observing his commandments. Hence he himself also says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). And Peter says of him: “For there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4).

Whoever has the Son has life, etc. So that it would not seem that he had said too little by stating that life is in the Son, he added that the Son himself is life. The same Son also demonstrated this while glorifying the Father, when he said: “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5). But how that same life, which belongs equally to the Son and the Father, also enlightens believers, the Son himself indicates elsewhere while praying to the Father: “Just as you gave him authority over all flesh, so that he might give eternal life to all whom you have given him. And this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17).

I have written these things to you so that you may know that you have eternal life, etc. “So that you may know,” he says—that is, so that you may be certain of your future blessedness—you who believe in Christ, and so that you may not be led astray by the deceit of those who deny that Jesus is the Son of God and therefore assert that those who have believed in his name will gain no benefit from him.

What astonishing madness in the heretics! Throughout this Epistle the Son of God is repeatedly named, yet they themselves insist that Christ is not the Son but a creature of God. They find grounds for this nowhere at all except where his humanity is mentioned.

And this is the confidence that we have toward him, etc. He gives us great confidence that we may hope for heavenly blessings from the Lord, since in this life as well we obtain whatever we ask of him beneficially, in accordance with what he himself promises believers in the Gospel: “I say to you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it will be done for you” (Mark 11).

It must be observed, however, that the Lord hears us when we pray in this way only if we ask for what he himself commanded. He says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness” (Matt. 6). Accordingly, when John had said, “Whatever we ask, he hears us,” he rightly inserted: “According to his will.”

Therefore, he commanded us to have full and unwavering confidence of being heard only concerning those things that correspond not to our own interests or temporal consolations, but to the Lord’s will. We are also commanded to include this in the Lord’s Prayer: “Your will be done” (ibid.), that is, not ours. For if we also remember the Apostle’s statement, “We do not know what we ought to pray for as we should” (Rom. 8), we understand that sometimes we ask for things contrary to our salvation, and that it is most beneficial for us to be denied what we request by the one who sees our welfare more clearly than we do. There is no doubt that this also happened to the teacher of the Gentiles himself.

And we know that he hears us, whatever we ask, etc. He repeats in various ways what he had already said, in order to stir us more vigorously to pray. Yet the qualification he stated remains: that we should ask according to the will of our Creator. This can be understood in two ways: namely, that we should ask for what he wills, and that we should come to ask him as the sort of people he desires us to be. This means possessing the faith that works through love (Gal. 5), and above all remembering that evangelical command: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins” (Mark 11).

Whoever knows that his brother is committing a sin that is not unto death, etc. These and similar requests are made according to the Lord’s will, since they concern the duty of fraternal love. He is speaking of daily and lesser sins, which are as easily cured as they are difficult to avoid. But James explains more clearly the order in which this mutual petition on behalf of sins should be carried out, saying: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5).

Therefore, if you have perhaps sinned by word, thought, forgetfulness, or ignorance, go to your brother, confess to him, and ask for his intercession. If he makes you aware of his own frailty by confessing sincerely, then you too should wipe away his errors through devout intercession. But let this be understood of lesser sins. If, however, you have committed something more serious, bring in the presbyters of the Church and chastise yourself under their examination.

There is a sin unto death, etc. A serious question arises here, because blessed John plainly shows that there are certain brothers for whom we are not commanded to pray, although the Lord commands us to pray even for our persecutors. This cannot be resolved in any other way than by acknowledging that some sins committed by brothers are more grievous than the persecution of enemies.

A brother’s sin unto death, then, occurs when, after the knowledge of God that was given through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, someone attacks brotherhood and is inflamed by the fires of envy against the very grace by which he was reconciled to God. A sin not unto death occurs when someone has not withdrawn love from his brother, but through some weakness of spirit has failed to show the duties owed to brotherhood.

Accordingly, the Lord says on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” [Luke 23; printed reference: “Luc. XXV”]. For they had not yet entered into the fellowship of holy brotherhood, having not yet become participants in the grace of the Holy Spirit. Blessed Stephen also prays for those by whom he was being stoned, because they had not yet believed in Christ and were not fighting against that common grace.

For this reason, I believe, the Apostle Paul does not pray for Alexander, because he was already a brother; and he had sinned unto death—that is, by attacking brotherhood through envy. But for those who had not severed love and had instead succumbed through fear, he prays that they may be forgiven. For he says: “Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm; the Lord will repay him according to his works. You also avoid him, for he strongly resisted our words” (2 Tim. 4). Then he adds for whom he prays, saying: “At my first defense no one came to my assistance, but everyone deserted me; may it not be held against them” (ibid.).

Sin unto death can also be understood as the sin concerning which he forbids anyone to make a request, namely because forgiveness for a sin that is not corrected in this life is sought in vain after death. Yet if we examine what follows carefully, the former interpretation seems more consistent with the tenor of this passage. For he adds:

Every injustice is sin, etc. “So great,” he says, “is the diversity of sins that everything which departs from the rule of equity is counted among sins,” although lesser sins cannot in any way take away or diminish the merit of the just person’s righteousness—those, that is, without which they cannot pass through this life at all. On the other hand, certain sins depart so far from every share in righteousness and are committed with such great iniquity that, unless they are corrected, they plunge their perpetrator into eternal punishment without any dispute. Concerning such sins it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18).

By this statement of blessed John, the foolish argument of the Stoics is plainly rejected. They dared to say, against all human understanding, and to assert that all sins are equal, claiming that it makes no difference whether someone has stolen a human being, an ox, or a chicken, because it is not the animal but the mind that commits the crime.

The heretic Jovinian followed them, asserting that there is no difference between marriage and virginity, and that those who abstain are not in any way to be preferred in the privilege of reward to those who simply feast. Everything, therefore, that is committed or conceived unjustly must be referred to sin. But some sins are unto death, of which the Apostle says: “Those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5).

We know that everyone who is born of God does not sin. That is, he does not commit sin unto death. This can also be understood of every capital crime, and specifically of that by which brotherhood is violated, as we explained above. But we also said that sin unto death can rightly be understood as a sin prolonged until the time of death, in accordance with the statement that everyone who is born of God does not sin.

In fact, King David committed a mortal crime. For who does not know that adultery and murder deserve everlasting death? Nevertheless, because David was born of God, because he belonged to the fellowship of the children of God, he did not sin unto death: he soon obtained pardon for his guilt through repentance.

But the generation of God preserves him, etc. The grace of Christ, through which the faithful have been reborn, preserves those who have been called saints according to the divine purpose, so that they do not commit sin unto death; and, if they should fall through the frailty of the human condition, it protects them so that they cannot be touched by the wicked enemy.

It should also be said that we remain in the generation of God as long as we do not sin; indeed, those who persevere in the generation of God cannot sin or be touched by the wicked one. For “what fellowship has light with darkness, or Christ with Belial?” (2 Cor. 6). As he says, “just as day and night cannot be mingled, so righteousness and iniquity, sin and good works, Christ and Antichrist, the wicked one and the generation of God cannot be mingled.”

We know that we are born of God, etc. We are of God because we have been regenerated by his grace and baptism through faith, and preserved so that we may remain in faith. Lovers of the world, however, are subject to the enemy, either because they were never released from his dominion by the water of regeneration, or because after the grace of regeneration they have been returned to his dominion by sinning again.

Not only lovers of the world, but also those who have recently been born and do not yet possess discernment of good and evil, belong, because of the guilt of the first transgression, to the kingdom of the wicked enemy—unless, through the grace of the benevolent Creator, they are rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Col. 1).

Thus he does not simply say that the world is placed in the wicked one, but adds a qualification: “And the whole world,” he says, “is placed in the wicked one.” For, as blessed Ambrose says: “We are all born under sin, and our very birth is in fault.”

Pelagius vainly strives to assert that newly born infants do not need to be reborn by the grace of baptism, because they are born as free from every stain of sin as Adam was when he was created pure in paradise; that they draw no stain of original guilt from him and are in no way guilty until they begin to sin of their own will.

But, setting aside the poisons of the Antichrists—which throughout this Epistle the one who drank from the fountain of life at the Lord’s breast condemns and expels from the Church—let us hear, at its close, the good word of salvation that he pours forth for us. Let us attend to the works of the highest King that he describes. It follows:

And we know that the Son of God has come, etc. What could be clearer in these words? What could be sweeter? What stronger statement could have been made against all heresies?

Christ is the true Son of God. The Father of Christ Jesus our Lord is the true God. The eternal Son of God came temporally into the world—the one who was in the world and through whom the world was made. He came for no other reason than our salvation, that is, to give us understanding so that we might know the true God.

No one could come to life without knowledge of God, and no one could know God except by his teaching, as he himself says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Luke 10). The meaning understood is: “the Father and the Son.” For the Son reveals both, since, appearing visibly in the flesh, he deigned through his Gospel to disclose the mysteries of his divinity.

This is the true God and eternal life. He had said that the Son was the true God, and he repeats many times that this one is true God. He says that this one is eternal life. Not in the way that eternal life is promised to us—as something that receives us in time and never again sets an end to our living well—but the Son is life without a beginning in time, always remaining, and always destined to remain without end.

Little children, keep yourselves from idols. You who have come to know the true God, in whom you have eternal life, keep yourselves from the teachings of heretics, which lead perpetually to death, because, like those who make idols in place of God, they exchange the glory of the incorruptible God through perverse doctrines for the likeness of corruptible things (Rom. 1).

Keep yourselves from love of money, which is the service of idols. Take care not to place any allurements of the world before love of the Creator. This too will be counted among idols, so that, devoting yourselves to the care and pursuit of truth alone, you may deserve to rejoice endlessly in its vision. For “the world is passing away, and its desire; but whoever does the will of the Lord remains forever” (1 John 2).

# ON THE SECOND EPISTLE OF JOHN

[Col. 0119]

The elder to the elect lady and her children, etc. Some think that this Epistle and the following one were not written by John the Apostle but by a certain presbyter John, whose tomb is still shown today at Ephesus. Papias, a hearer of the apostles and bishop of Hierapolis, also frequently mentions him in his little works. But the general consensus of the Church now holds that these Epistles too were written by John the Apostle, because they plainly display great similarity of language and faith with his first Epistle, and likewise detest heretics with zeal.

John calls himself “the elder” either because he was already advanced in age when he wrote these Epistles, or because the name “elder,” that is, presbyter, is also fitting for a pontiff on account of the maturity of his wisdom and gravity. Hence Peter says: “Therefore I appeal to the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ” (1 Pet. 5).

“The elder,” he says, “to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth”—that is, I love with true love, namely the love that is according to God. Or certainly, I love them because I see that they persevere in the truth.

And not I alone, but also all, etc. Since he is beginning to write against heretics, because they have fallen away from the truth of the faith, he rightly recalls that there is one love in the Holy Spirit among all who have known the truth. In this way, by the unanimity and multitude of Catholics together, he terrifies those who, though few, have separated themselves from their fellowship.

Indeed, all Catholics throughout the world follow one rule of truth. Heretics and unbelievers, however, do not all agree in a unanimous error; rather, they attack one another no less than they attack the way of truth itself.

Because of the truth that remains in you, etc. “We love you and your people,” he says, “for no other reason than because of the truth of the faith, which remains forever unconquerable in us, since we have found that you too guard the same truth invincibly.”

Grace, mercy, and peace be with you from God the Father, etc. Because the heretics of that time—Marcion and Cerinthus in particular—denied that our Lord Jesus Christ was truly the Son of God and assigned him a beginning through human birth, John rightly recalls, in order to refute these blasphemers, that he is the Son of God the Father.

He also testifies that grace, mercy, and peace are given to the faithful by him just as by God the Father, in order to demonstrate that he is equal and coeternal with the Father, and he indicates that his gifts are the same as the Father’s, just as the Lord himself, speaking of his own consubstantiality with the Father, says: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5).

And now I ask you, lady, not as though writing a new commandment to you, etc. By this statement he rebukes the heretics who, abandoning what they had heard from the apostles, were attempting to introduce new doctrines and thereby to shatter the bonds of fraternal love. He therefore says that he is writing no new commandment at all, but merely urging that the ancient faith and unblemished charity remain in everything.

For many deceivers have gone out into the world, etc. This may be understood of heretics who indeed confess that Jesus Christ has become incarnate, but do not think correctly about some aspect of his faith—denying either his true flesh, his true soul, his true divinity, his true Father, God, his true Holy Spirit, God Almighty, or something else that the right faith confesses.

It may also be understood of the Jews, who entirely deny Jesus Christ, falsely swearing that Christ has not yet come in the flesh for the salvation of the world, but awaiting the Antichrist, who will come for their destruction.

Everyone who goes beyond and does not remain in the doctrine, etc. Note the difference in the words, and embrace the truth of the faith. He says that the one who does not remain in the doctrine of Christ does not have God, while the one who remains in his doctrine has both the Son and the Father. In this way he shows that the Father and the Son are one true God, and he refutes as liars those who assert either that the Son is not God or that he is later than, or lesser than, the Father.

If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, etc. What John taught in words concerning the detestation of schismatics or heretics, he also practiced in deeds. For his hearer, the most holy and most steadfast martyr Polycarp, bishop of the Smyrnaeans, relates that once, when John had entered a bathhouse at Ephesus in order to bathe and saw Cerinthus there, he immediately leapt up and left without bathing, saying: “Let us flee from here, lest the bathhouse itself collapse—the bathhouse in which Cerinthus, the enemy of truth, is washing.”

On another occasion, when Polycarp encountered Marcion, and Marcion said to him, “Recognize us,” Polycarp replied: “I recognize you, I recognize the firstborn of Satan.”

Such caution did the apostle and his disciples then exercise in matters of religion that they would not tolerate even verbal fellowship with anyone who had strayed from the truth, just as Paul says: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition, knowing that such a one is perverted and sins, being self-condemned” (Titus 3).

The children of your elect sister greet you. Just as he forbids greeting the adversaries of truth, so, conversely, he sends greetings in the name of the elect to the elect, so that unbelievers may be detested by all good people—if perhaps they might be willing to be corrected even in this way—and so that peace and charity among the faithful may continually increase.

# ON THE THIRD EPISTLE OF JOHN

[Col. 0121]

The elder to the most beloved Gaius, etc. Who this Gaius was, and what sort of man he was, is shown in the course of the Epistle. For he increased the faith in Christ that he had received with good works; and although he himself was scarcely able to preach the word, he nevertheless rejoiced to support from his own resources those who preached it.

We think that this was the Gaius whom Paul mentions in his Epistle to the Romans, saying: “Gaius, my host and host of the whole Church, greets you” (Rom. 16). Since “host” is customarily used both of one who receives and of one who is received, he was the host of the whole Church because he kindly received all who came to him, both preachers and hearers of the word, as the following parts of this Epistle plainly show.

Hence John loves him “in truth”—that is, he appears to love him not for the sake of temporal advantages, but solely with regard to everlasting goods. Gaius appears to have been from Corinth, since Paul, while staying in that city, wrote the Epistle to the Romans and sends greetings from him by name. In the Epistle to the Corinthians as well, Paul mentions Gaius as apparently a citizen of Corinth, saying: “I thank my God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name” (1 Cor. 1).

My most beloved, I pray concerning all things, etc. “I repeatedly ask this of the Lord in my prayers,” he says, “that you may bring to completion what you are doing well. And just as your soul now—that is, the inner intention of your mind—is prospering, that is, progressing in abundant works of almsgiving, in the generosity of a bountiful spirit, and in the financial resources that you distribute to those in need, so may you always, with the Lord’s help, lead a life full of virtues.”

I have no greater joy than this, etc. That is, that I may know that those whom I have begotten for God by preaching or baptizing are observing both the truth of the right faith and good works.

My most beloved, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brothers, etc. “You act faithfully” means, as though he had said: “Just as you are truly faithful, so you act,” showing your faith by your works.

For they have gone out for the sake of the Name, receiving nothing from the Gentiles. When he says “for the sake of the Name,” “of the Lord Jesus Christ” is understood. The ancients spoke in this way. They went out for the sake of the Lord’s name for two reasons: either they came of their own accord to preach his name, or they had been expelled from their homeland by their fellow citizens or countrymen because of faith in and confession of the holy Name.

Therefore, we ought to welcome such people, etc. Blessed John, who had abandoned everything for Christ, joins himself to the company of wealthy believers in order to make them more eager to show mercy to the poor and to strangers. Nor should we doubt that he could truly have said what we read that Paul said: “You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my needs and to those who were with me. In everything I showed you that by laboring in this way we must support the weak and remember the word of the Lord, as he said: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive’” (Acts 20).

He calls them “co-workers in the truth,” because one who gives temporal support to those who possess spiritual gifts becomes a co-worker in those spiritual gifts. For since few have received spiritual gifts, while many abound in temporal possessions, the wealthy thereby join themselves to the virtues of the poor when they share their wealth with those holy poor.

Hence the Lord says: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matt. 10).

I would perhaps have written to the Church, but the one who loves to have first place among them, etc. Diotrephes appears to have been some proud and insolent heresiarch of that time, preferring to usurp for himself the primacy of knowledge by teaching new things rather than humbly listening to the ancient commands of the holy Church that John preached. Accordingly, Diotrephes is interpreted aptly as “beautifully foolish” or “beauty gone mad,” so that the name itself marks the treachery of his heart.

For this reason, if I come, I will call attention to his deeds. That is, by rebuking him, I will bring them more openly to everyone’s notice. This accords with the Apostle Paul’s statement: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?”

What he does, babbling malicious words against us. It must be observed that, just as we ought not to provoke the tongues of slanderers through our own fault, lest they perish, so we ought to endure with equanimity those provoked by their own malice, so that our merit may increase. At times, however, we must also restrain them, lest, while they spread evil about us, they corrupt the hearts of innocent people who might otherwise have been able to hear what is good.

This is why John rebukes the tongue of his slanderer: so that those who could have listened might not fail to hear his preaching and remain in depraved ways.

My beloved, do not imitate evil, but what is good. He explains what good he wants him to imitate by adding:

Demetrius is commended by everyone. For he himself received the weak and supported the needy for the sake of the truth. He therefore presents him to Gaius as an example to imitate, so that Gaius too may likewise be found worthy of everyone’s praise.

Peace to you. The friends greet you, etc. He sends the friends a greeting of peace and salvation, thereby showing that Diotrephes and the other enemies of truth are strangers to your salvation and peace.

# ON THE EPISTLE OF JUDE

[Col. 0123]

Jude, servant of Jesus Christ, etc. The Apostle Jude, whom Matthew and Mark call Thaddaeus in the Gospel, writes against the same corrupters of the faith whom Peter and John also condemn in their Epistles.

Beloved, while making every effort to write to you, etc. He speaks of their common salvation, of that salvation which was common to him and to them. For all the elect have one common salvation, faith, and love of Christ.

Appealing to you to contend for the faith once delivered to the saints. He appeals to you not to learn any faith other than the one once delivered to you by the apostles, but always to fight for this faith, even unto death.

For certain people have slipped in, etc. He says “for this judgment,” that is, for this condemnation, which the ungodly deserve by their actions. Hence the Lord says: “Those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5)—that is, of condemnation.

Turning the grace of our Lord into licentiousness. The grace of our Lord softened the harshness of the Law. For while the Law said, “If anyone does this or that, let him be overwhelmed with stones; if anyone does this or that, let him be burned with fire,” the Lord, relaxing the strictness of the Law, granted through the grace of the Gospel the opportunity to cleanse committed crimes through repentance and the fruits of almsgiving.

But those turn his grace into licentiousness who now sin with greater license and freedom because they do not see themselves immediately subjected to the severity of the Law for the crimes they have committed.

And denying the only Ruler and our Lord Jesus Christ. Our Lord Jesus Christ is the only Ruler with the Father and the Holy Spirit, just as the Father alone is Ruler with the Son and the Holy Spirit, and just as the Holy Spirit alone is Ruler with the Father and the Son. The whole Trinity itself—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is the sole female ruler (*dominatrix*).

For whatever person you name within that holy and undivided Trinity, he is the one God alone. And when you name the whole Trinity together, you name the one true God.

Thus it must rightly be understood that all heretics who deny that the Father of Christ is the true, good, and just God deny the only Ruler and our Lord. All who deny that Jesus Christ is truly the Son of God likewise deny the only Ruler and our Lord. All who diminish the power of the Holy Spirit also contradict the majesty of the only Ruler and our Lord, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together are the one Ruler and our Lord.

But I wish to remind you, although you know all things once for all, etc. That is, since you know all the mysteries of the faith and have no need to hear from new teachers anything recent as though it were holier.

Because Jesus, saving the people from the land of Egypt, etc. By “Jesus” he does not mean Joshua the son of Nun, but our Lord, showing first that he did not have his beginning from the birth of the holy Virgin, as the heretics claim, but that, according to the mystery of his name, the eternal God existed for the salvation of believers.

He then indicates that he saves believers in his mercy in such a way that he also justly condemns unbelievers. Thus, when they cried to him in their Egyptian affliction, he first saved the humble, and then struck down in the wilderness those who murmured against him, the proud.

He repeats this so that we too may now remember that, through the waters of baptism, which the Red Sea signified, he saves believers while also requiring from us after baptism a humble life, separated from the filth of vices, such as the secluded life of the wilderness appropriately represented.

If anyone violates this life, whether by departing from the faith or by doing evil, then, as though returning in heart to Egypt, he will deserve not to reach the promised homeland of the kingdom but to perish among the ungodly.

Alternatively: “He destroyed a second time those who did not believe,” because the just Judge, when their guilt demands it, strikes some both now and hereafter. For punishment frees from torment only those whom it changes. For those whom present evils do not correct are brought on to what follows.

And the angels who did not preserve their own principality, etc. Here too, as in the preceding statement, we must first remember that Jesus our Lord punished the transgressing angels.

The one who, at the end of the ages, was born from a Virgin and received the name Jesus at the angel’s direction was himself, before all ages, born God from the Father. Together with the Father, he ordered every creature as he willed, and from the beginning condemned the angels who grew proud beneath the darkness of this air, reserving those same angels for more severe punishments on the day of judgment.

Therefore those deserve condemnation who contend that Christ Jesus was not the true God but merely a human being, and that he was born from both sexes [i.e., from human parentage]. It must then be inferred that he who did not spare sinning angels will not spare proud human beings either.

He will condemn these also, when they have not preserved their own principality—that is, the one by which they were made children of God through the grace of adoption—but have abandoned their dwelling. Their dwelling is the unity of the Church, in which they were reborn to God; or, certainly, the seats of the heavenly kingdom that they were to receive if they preserved the faith. He will condemn them severely before the judgment, and more severely at the universal judgment.

As Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighboring cities, etc. Because he had supplied an example of condemnation for those who deny the only Ruler and our Lord Jesus Christ—having recalled either the destruction of the murmuring and unbelieving people in the wilderness or that of the angels who rose up wickedly against their Creator—he now supplies an example of the punishment of those who turn the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ into licentiousness by recalling the burning of Sodom.

Likewise, these people defile the flesh, etc. The sense understood is: these too are to be condemned like the Sodomites, who defiled the flesh; like the unbelieving people, who blasphemed the majesty of divine power; and like the angels, who despised the dominion of their Creator.

When Michael the archangel, disputing with the devil, etc. It is not readily apparent from which Scriptures Jude took this testimony. Nevertheless, it should be known that we find something similar in the prophet Zechariah. For he says:

“For the Lord showed me Jesus the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan was standing at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to Satan: ‘May the Lord rebuke you, Satan; may the Lord rebuke you, who chose Jerusalem’” (Zech. III).

But in this passage it is very easily understood that Jesus the priest desired to free the people of Israel from Babylonian captivity and to return them to their native land. Satan, however, resisted him, unwilling for God’s people to be liberated and desiring rather that they be enslaved to their enemies and the nations. Therefore the angel who was the people’s helper rebuked him and removed him from injuring that same people.

But when Michael contended with the devil over Moses’ body, we do not know. Nevertheless, there are some who say that the same people of God were called “Moses’ body,” because Moses himself was a part of that people; and therefore Jude could rightly say that what he had read was done concerning Moses’ body, when in fact it had been done concerning the people. But wherever and whenever this dispute between the angel and the devil took place, it must be carefully observed that, if Michael the archangel did not wish to speak blasphemy against the devil who opposed him, but restrained him with measured speech, how much more must human beings avoid every blasphemy—and especially avoid offending the majesty of the Creator with undisciplined speech. [Col. 0126C–D]

Woe to them, who have gone in the way of Cain, etc. Those go in Cain’s way who, out of envy of better men, assume for themselves the name of teachers, by which they may be honored. They have been poured out in the error of Balaam who, for love of earthly advantages, oppose the truth they themselves know. They perish in the rebellion of Korah, who descended alive into the underworld: all who, through desire for an unwarranted primacy, separate themselves from the unity of the holy Church, and, although knowing and foreseeing how great an evil they are committing, nevertheless descend into the hell of crimes. Indeed, the Lord rebuked Cain when he was contemplating fratricide, but envy did not allow him to be saved. The Lord forbade Balaam, as he was journeying against the people of God, but love of money prevented him from obeying. Moses tried to restrain Korah in his pride, while the Lord spoke through him; but the arrogance with which Korah burned made him incurable.

So, indeed, so do heretics act: they disdain being corrected by the rebuke of the holy Church. Rather, like Cain, they strive to kill their brothers with the sword of evil doctrine; like Balaam, to deceive them with wicked counsel; and like Korah, to rise up against Catholic teachers—all to their own destruction. [Col. 0126D–0127A]

These are blemishes at their feasts, etc. Someone who sins is stained; the stain is the crime itself, which contaminates the person who commits it. Therefore he calls the heretics whom he rebukes “blemishes,” because they perish and pollute not only themselves in their banquets and drunkenness—whether carnal or spiritual—but also destroy and defile others. [Col. 0127A–B]

Clouds without water, etc. Clouds are the holy preachers who, having their manner of life in heaven, flash with miracles and rain down words. Of them it is said to God: “And your truth reaches to the clouds.” But heretics are clouds without water. They have set their mouths in heaven through words of pride, but they do not irrigate the hearts of their hearers with the water of wisdom. They are carried about by winds—as if at the prompting of invisible spirits—and are swept into diverse errors of vice. [Col. 0127B]

Autumn trees, fruitless, twice dead, uprooted. A tree that does not produce good fruit is dead; but a tree that has also produced the fruit of an evil deed is called twice dead. If the one who refused to bear the fruit of good works is said, because of his barrenness, to deserve being cut down and thrown into the fire, what punishments do you think he deserves who has borne the worst fruits either by acting perversely or by perverting others?

Nor is it surprising that trees proven to have been uprooted are called fruitless and twice dead. For it is said of the saints: “Rooted and founded in charity” (Eph. III). Those who are not afraid to uproot themselves from the firmness of charity rightly lose whatever good fruit they appear to possess. Such people are rightly compared with autumn trees, so that the hopelessness of their salvation may be shown. For in autumn not only do no fruits grow, but even those that had grown and ripened usually fall.

Those who themselves neglect to bear the fruits of faith, and who strive to uproot the good works they see faithful people performing and turn them into perishable pursuits, are likened to that season. [Col. 0127C–D]

Wild waves of the sea, foaming out their own confusion. The wild waves of the sea are perverse teachers, who are always restless, swollen with pride, dark, and bitter in themselves; and they never cease attacking the peace of the Church, as though it were a barrier of stability and firmness. Such people are rightly said to foam out their own confusion, because, like swelling waves, the higher they raise themselves in pride, the more completely they dissolve, confused, into the lightest foam and perish. [Col. 0127D–0128A]

Wandering stars, for whom the storm of darkness has been reserved forever. The wandering stars, which are seven, never rise or set in the same place where they did the day before. Sometimes they descend to the lowest regions of the winter zone; sometimes they ascend to the heights of the summer zone; sometimes they return to the middle line of the equinoctial zone.

So, indeed, so are heretics. Although they promise the light of truth, they never persist in the same condition of teaching. Rather, shaping their doctrine now one way and now another, they themselves reveal how contemptible is the display of light they proclaim.

Among the planets—that is, the wandering stars—the best known are the moon and Lucifer, who is also called Vesper. These are sometimes understood in a good sense: the Lord is the sun; the Church is the moon; and Lucifer is John the Baptist, who preceded the Lord by being born before him in the flesh and by bearing witness to his light.

But we also read of the sun in a bad sense, when the Lord speaks of the seeds sown on rocky ground: “But when the sun rose, they immediately withered” (Matt. XIII). Explaining this, he adds: “But when persecution arose because of the word, they were immediately scandalized” (ibid.). The heat of the sun therefore indicates the fervor of persecution.
