We read of the moon in a bad sense: “A fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. XXVII). Of Lucifer in a bad sense: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer!” (Isa. XIV). This may be understood not only of the devil’s first fall but also of his members who fall from the Church through heresy.

Of Vesper in a bad sense: “And you cause Vesper to rise over the sons of the earth” (Job XXXVIII). For Antichrist and his ministers, although they transform themselves into angels of light, do not bear witness to the divine light as Lucifer does to the sun. Rather, they display works of darkness to their followers, like the star called Vesper, which appears in the west in the evening and stands as the forerunner of the coming night.

“Wandering stars,” he says, “for whom the storm of darkness has been reserved forever.” They will rightly be sent into the eternal darkness of torments, because under the name of light they were bringing the darkness of errors into the Church of God. They deservedly will be struck by a storm of punishments, because, like maritime tempests, they disturbed the peace of the faithful. [Col. 0128A–C]

But Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied concerning these, etc. He does not speak against all human beings, but against all the ungodly, leaving none of them unpunished. Of these he continues:

And to convict all the ungodly. He expressly calls Enoch the seventh from Adam, the one who prophesied these things, in order to confirm by an example what he said above: that long ago ungodly people had been marked out for such judgment—people who in their own time secretly entered in to subvert the faith of the godly. [Col. 0128C–D]

And to convict, he says, all the ungodly concerning all the works of their ungodliness, etc. This statement is indeed true, because when the Lord comes in judgment, he will convict the ungodly and judge the wicked not only for their deeds but also for their words.

Nevertheless, it must be known that the Book of Enoch, from which he took this passage, is classified by the Church among the apocryphal Scriptures—not because the sayings of so great a patriarch can in any way be rejected or ought to be regarded as false, but because the book offered under his name does not appear truly to have been written by him; rather, it seems to have been published by someone else under his name.

For if it truly belonged to him, it would not contradict sound faith. But since it contains many incredible things—including the claim concerning the giants that their fathers were not human beings but angels—it is rightly clear to learned people that writings sullied by falsehood are not the work of a truthful man.

Hence this same Epistle of Jude, because it bears testimony from an apocryphal book, was rejected by many in the earliest times. Nevertheless, by authority, antiquity, and usage it has now deserved to be counted among the holy Scriptures, especially because Jude took from the apocryphal book a testimony that was not apocryphal or doubtful, but was manifestly radiant with the true brightness of the light. [Col. 0128D–0129A]

These are murmurers, complainers, etc. The less someone has extinguished the desires of the flesh within himself, the more he murmurs and complains about the present hardships of the Church. In contrast, holy Daniel and the other men who desired heavenly things despise all transitory things that appear adverse in proportion to the intensity with which they ardently desire heavenly things alone. [Col. 0129B]

These are those who separate themselves, etc. The wicked separate themselves from the lot of the just because they are carnal—that is, because they follow the desires of their own soul—and because they have not deserved to possess the Spirit of unity by whom the Church is gathered and made spiritual. They therefore drift apart because they do not possess the bond of charity. [Col. 0129B]

But you, beloved, building yourselves up upon your most holy faith, etc. We pray in the Holy Spirit when, pierced by divine inspiration, we seek heavenly help in order to receive the good things that we cannot possess from ourselves.

Thus blessed Jude admonishes us to build ourselves upon the foundation of holy faith; thus he commands us to join living stones to the house of God, which is the Church; thus he instructs us to keep ourselves in the love of God, so that we never presume upon our own strength but hope in the help of divine protection.

No one should therefore declare, according to the doctrine of Pelagius, that he can save himself by himself. Rather, we should all ask for the coming of the Holy Spirit into us, so that, inspired by him, we may be able to pray more fervently; otherwise, together with those who do not possess the Spirit and therefore remain carnal, we might be separated from the fellowship of the holy Church. [Col. 0129C–0130A]

And some indeed convict as already judged, but others save by snatching them from the fire, etc. The phrase “in fear” must be joined to all three things he has proposed. Whoever rebukes apostates and shows them to be worthy of condemnation must act in fear, lest something of the same kind happen to himself or to those he loves. The person who rescues another by correcting him from the burning of vices must consider that he himself may also be tempted. And the person who compassionately shows mercy to a repentant neighbor must likewise act cautiously, lest he prove either more severe or more indulgent than is right. [Col. 0130A–B]

Hating even the tunic stained by the flesh. He calls our body the carnal tunic. We must not hate our body, but we must hate this stain in every way and, as far as we are able, act so as to render it unstained, so that from being carnal it may deserve to become spiritual. Since this must be accomplished not by the power of our own will but by the grace of God, he rightly adds:

But to him who is able to preserve you without sin, etc. He rightly says here that we are to be placed in exultation before the presence of God’s glory, after earlier warning us to serve God in fear. For the more anxiously we are concerned about our actions in the present, the more greatly we will rejoice in the future over the reward we have received. [Col. 0130B]

To the only God our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory and majesty. This conclusion attributes in every respect, and before all ages, equal and coeternal glory and kingdom to the Father and the Son. It also refutes the error of those who believe that the Son is lesser than or later than the Father, when it says that glory, majesty, dominion, and power belong to God the Father through Jesus Christ our Lord.

And this is not from the beginning of some period of time, but before every age, and now, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 0130B–C]

[Col. 0129]

# EXPLANATION OF THE APOCALYPSE (C)

## LETTER TO EUSEBIUS

[Col. 0129D]

### BEDA GREETS HIS DEAREST BROTHER EUSEBIUS

The Apocalypse of Saint John, in which God has deigned to reveal in words and figures the internal wars and conflagrations of his Church, appears to me, brother Eusebius, to be divided into seven sections.

In the first of these, after an extensive preface and an enumeration of the Lord’s sufferings and subsequent glories in order to strengthen the faith of the weak, the Church sees one like the Son of Man clothed. After mentioning what has been done or is to be done specifically in the seven churches of Asia, it describes the general struggles and triumphs of the whole Church.

There, in the sixth place, the Jews are deliberately placed beneath the Church, and the future temptation of the whole world is announced; he also promises that he himself will come quickly. In the seventh place he presents Laodicea as lukewarm. For when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose that he will find faith on earth (Luke XVIII)? [Col. 0129D–0130D]

In the second section, after describing the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders at God’s throne, he sees the Lamb, when the seven seals of the sealed book have been opened, reveal the future conflicts and triumphs of the Church.

Here, in accordance with the custom of this book, he preserves the order through the sixth number, omits the seventh, and then recapitulates; following the order as it were, he concludes two narratives with the seventh. But the recapitulation itself must be understood according to the passages concerned. Sometimes he recapitulates from the beginning of the Passion, sometimes from the middle of time, sometimes from the final distress alone or from a time not long before it. He nevertheless preserves this fixed principle: he recapitulates from the sixth. [Col. 0130D–0131A]

The third section, under the figure of seven angels sounding trumpets, describes various events of the Church.

The fourth, under the figure of a woman giving birth and a dragon persecuting her, discloses the struggles and victories of that same Church and bestows worthy rewards upon both armies. Here too the words and deeds of the seven angels are recalled, though not in the same manner as above. For with mystical skill he preserves this number almost everywhere, since it is also characteristic of that same John, in the Gospels and Epistles as well, to say nothing half-heartedly or briefly. [Col. 0131A–B]

The fifth section pours out upon the earth, through seven angels, the seven final plagues.

The sixth presents the condemnation of the great prostitute, that is, the impious city.

The seventh shows the adornment of the Lamb’s wife, namely, holy Jerusalem descending from heaven from God.

I have also thought it worthwhile to recall briefly the seven rules of Tychonius, a man highly learned among his own people, by which students are greatly assisted in understanding the Scriptures.

The first of these concerns the Lord and his body: the movement from the head to the body, or from the body to the head, while nevertheless remaining within one and the same person. One person speaks, saying: “As a bridegroom he placed a headdress upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with an ornament.” Yet it must be understood which of these statements applies to the head and which to the body—that is, which to Christ and which to the Church. [Col. 0131B–C]

The second concerns the Lord’s divided body, or rather the Lord’s true and simulated body, as Saint Augustine preferred to call it. The Church says: “I am dark and beautiful, like the tents of Kedar and like Solomon’s curtains” (Song I). She does not say, “I was dark and I am beautiful,” but says that she is both, because of the communion of the sacraments and because of the temporal mingling, within one net, of good and evil fish. The tents of Kedar belong to Ishmael, because he will not be heir with the son of the free woman. [Col. 0131C–D]

The third concerns promises and the Law, which may also be called, in another way, the Spirit and the letter, or grace and commandment. For Saint Augustine this appears to be a great question rather than a rule to be applied in solving questions. It is this very matter that the Pelagians, because they did not understand it, either established as their heresy or enlarged. [Col. 0131D]

The fourth concerns species and genus. A species is a part; a genus, however, is the whole of which it is a part. Thus each city is a part of the whole province, and each province a part of the whole world.

Hence these terms have entered common knowledge, so that even uneducated people understand what has been established specifically and what generally in any imperial command.

This also occurs with human beings. For statements made about Solomon exceed his individual measure and become clear when referred instead to Christ and the Church, of which Solomon was a part. The species is not always exceeded, however. Often statements are made that clearly apply either to the species as well or perhaps to it alone. But when Scripture passes from species to genus, as though it were still speaking about the species, the reader’s attention must remain vigilant. [Col. 0131D–0132A]

He places fifth the rule that he calls “concerning times.” It may also, as I think, be called “concerning numbers.” He says that it operates by the figure of synecdoche or by legitimate numbers.

Synecdoche is either from the part to the whole or from the whole to the part. This manner of expression also resolves the question concerning Christ’s resurrection. The final part of the day on which he suffered cannot amount to one day unless it is taken for the whole day, including the preceding night; and the night during whose final part he rose cannot amount to another day unless the whole day is taken, including the dawning Sunday. Otherwise there cannot be three days and three nights during which he foretold that he would be in the heart of the earth. [Col. 0132A–B]

By “legitimate numbers” he means those which divine Scripture commends with particular prominence, such as seven, ten, or twelve. These generally signify either the totality of time or the perfection of some matter.

Thus, “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Ps. CXVIII), means nothing other than, “His praise is always in my mouth” (Ps. XXXIII).

The same values apply when these numbers are multiplied either by ten—for example, seventy and seven hundred—or by themselves, as ten times ten produces one hundred and twelve times twelve produces one hundred forty-four. In the Apocalypse this number signifies the universality of the saints. [Col. 0132B–C]

Tychonius calls the sixth rule “recapitulation.” In the Scriptures certain things are said as though they followed in temporal order or were narrated in a continuous sequence, when the narrative secretly returns to earlier matters that had been omitted.

Thus in Genesis it says: “These are the sons of Noah according to their tribes and languages. From these the nations were divided over the earth” (Gen. X). Immediately afterward it says: “Now the whole earth had one language and the same words” (Gen. XI). This appears to be said as though, at the time when they were dispersed, they had all possessed one language; rather, by recapitulating, it secretly adds: “How the languages were divided.” [Col. 0132C–D]

His seventh rule concerns the devil and his body. Sometimes something is said of the devil that can be recognized not in him personally but in his body. Thus the Lord, explaining to blessed Job the deceptions and powers of that enemy, says among other things: “Will he multiply prayers to you, or speak soft words to you?” The devil himself is nowhere read to undertake repentance, but his body, condemned at the end, will say: “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Luke XIII).

These rules are therefore found not only in the Apocalypse—that is, in the Revelation of the holy apostle John—which Tychonius both understood vigorously and expounded with sufficient truthfulness and catholic orthodoxy, except only in those passages where, attempting to defend the schism of his own party, that is, the Donatists, he laments the persecutions which they suffered as heretics from the religious emperor Valentinian: their churches, peoples, houses, and possessions being handed over to the control of Catholics, and their priests being thrust into exile. He calls these events martyrdoms and boasts that they were foretold in the same Apocalypse.

Rather, anyone who observes attentively will find that these same rules operate throughout all canonical Scripture, and especially in the prophets. In this work we too have followed the sense of that author. For the sake of brevity we have omitted some things that he supplied from outside; but we have taken care to add more on points which, to him—as an ingenious man and, as was said of him, one who “blossomed like a rose among thorns”—seemed clear and unworthy of investigation, insofar as we could attain them through the tradition of teachers, the memory of our reading, or even the grasp of our own understanding. [Col. 0132D–0133B]

For we also have this commandment: to return to the Lord the talents we have received with interest. And since it had seemed desirable to divide the work in question into three books for the relief of the mind, for, as blessed Augustine says, “the reader’s attention is refreshed by the end of a book just as a traveler’s weariness is refreshed by an inn,” nevertheless, so that those seeking particular passages might find them more easily, it seemed necessary to preserve throughout the same uninterrupted sequence of chapters, according to the brief divisions I had once placed at the beginning of the individual books.

I judged that the sluggishness of our people—that is, the English—should be taken into account. Our nation received the seed of faith only recently, namely in the time of blessed Pope Gregory, and has cultivated it rather indifferently as far as reading is concerned. I therefore resolved not only to clarify the meanings but also to condense the statements. For clear brevity is usually more firmly fixed in the memory than lengthy disputation. [Col. 0133B–0134B]

May you prosper in Christ, dearest brother, and may you always deign to remember your Bede.

## EPIGRAM ON BLESSED JOHN AND HIS APOCALYPSE

[Col. 0133]

While John is driven as an exile from the human world,

And forbidden to behold the realms of the Coic soil,

The beloved of the Lord enters joyfully the court of heaven,

The palace of the high-throned King, and rejoices to stand among its choirs.

Here, when he turns his sacred eyes upon the world below,

He sees ships wandering across the waves everywhere,

And Babylon and Jerusalem fighting with mingled armies,

Now one side, now the other, taking up weapons and flight.

But the white-clad soldier follows the gentle Lamb,

That with his Leader he may receive the blessed kingdoms of heaven.

A scaly serpent plunges his battalions through blind Tartarus,

And overwhelms his own with flames, plague, and famine. [Col. 0134B]

While I desired to unfold what his appearance, purpose, and order of battle were,

What art, what phalanx, what victory, or what weapons he possessed,

I traversed the broad fields sown by the ancients

And gathered a few shoots from the sacred fields,

Lest a greater abundance produce disgust at the meal,

Or prevent me from preparing such a feast for a humble guest.

Therefore, if my dishes taste pleasing to your lips,

Give praise beyond the stars to God who reigns.

If not, nevertheless embracing a friendly spirit,

I ask you, correcting what I sing, to scrape it with the pumice stone.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0133]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0133C]

The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ, which he gave to him, etc. Once the Church had been founded through the apostles, it was necessary to reveal by what course it would be extended and by what end it would be completed, in order to strengthen the faith of preachers against the adversities of the world. John testifies that Jesus Christ received this revelation of the mystery from God, referring, in his customary manner, the glory of the Son to the Father.

Which must happen soon. That is, the things that are to come upon the Church in the present age.

And he signified it. He intertwined the same Apocalypse with mysterious statements, lest it become commonplace by being manifest to everyone.

Sending it through his angel. The angel appeared to John in the figure of Christ, as will become clearer in what follows.

To his servant John. Through John, who by the singular privilege of chastity deserved to see these things before others, he made the same things publicly known to all his servants. [Col. 0133C–D]

Who bore witness to the Word of God and to the testimony of Jesus, etc. So that you may not doubt John’s identity, he is the one who bore witness, as he saw it, to the eternal Word of God and to that same Word incarnate, saying: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father” (John I). [Col. 0133D–0134C]

Blessed is the one who reads, etc. Teachers and hearers are blessed because eternal joys follow the brief period of labor for those who keep the word of God. [Col. 0134C]

John to the seven, etc. Through these seven churches he writes to the whole Church. Universality is customarily signified by the number seven, since the whole period of this world unfolds through seven days.

Grace to you, etc. He wishes us grace and peace from God the eternal Father, from the sevenfold Spirit, and from Jesus Christ, who, having assumed humanity, bore witness to the Father. He names the Son in the third place, since he was about to speak more fully about him. He also names him last because he himself is the first and the last, having already named him in connection with the Father when he said, “who is to come.” [Col. 0134C–D]

The firstborn of the dead, etc. This is what the Apostle says: “We saw Jesus Christ crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death.” And elsewhere, explaining the shame of the cross, he adds: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.” [Col. 0134D]

And he made us a kingdom, etc. Because the King of kings and heavenly Priest, by offering himself for us, united us to his body, there is no saint who lacks spiritually the office of priesthood, since he is a member of the eternal Priest. [Col. 0134D–0135A]

Behold, he is coming with the clouds, etc. He who first came secretly to be judged will then come openly to judge. He recalls these things in order to strengthen the Church, now oppressed by enemies, to endure sufferings, since then she will reign with Christ. [Col. 0135A]

And those who fought against him, etc. Seeing him as the powerful Judge in the very form in which they judged him as one of the least, they will lament themselves in belated repentance.

Even so, Amen. What he knows with complete certainty, through God’s revelation, is destined to happen, he confirms by inserting “Amen,” assuring that it will come without doubt.

I am α and ω, the beginning and the end, etc. The beginning, whom no one precedes; the end, whom no one succeeds in the kingdom. [Col. 0135A–B]

Who is, and who was, etc. He had said the same thing about the Father. For God the Father both came and is to come in the Son.

I, John, etc. He discloses the person, place, time, and cause of the vision. He also testifies that he saw it in the Spirit, lest anyone think he had been deceived by a carnal apparition.

I was on the island, etc. The history is well known: Emperor Domitian exiled John to this island because of the Gospel. It was fitting that he should then be granted access to the secrets of heaven, when he was forbidden to go beyond the fixed boundaries of the earth. [Col. 0135B]

I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day. He also indicates the fitting time for a spiritual vision. Scripture customarily expresses the appointed limits of causes, just as it often expresses those of places or of the body or air, and likewise those of time. Angels visit Abraham at midday and Sodom in the evening. Adam became afraid after midday at the voice of the Lord walking. Solomon received wisdom at night, though he did not preserve it. [Col. 0135B–C]

And I heard behind me, etc. He is first warned by a voice so that he may turn his gaze toward the vision.

And send it to the seven churches, etc. At that time Christ’s Church was not located only in these places, but the whole fullness is contained in the number seven. Asia, which is interpreted as “elevation,” signifies the proud height of the world in which the Church is an exile; and, as is customary in divine mystery, the genus is represented in the species.

The Apostle Paul also writes to seven churches, though not to the same ones as John. Although these seven places are a figure of the entire sevenfold Church, nevertheless the things which he rebukes or praises took place specifically in them. [Col. 0135C–D]

And having turned, etc. Here the form of the Church is beautifully described: she bears before her the light of divine love in the radiance of a pure heart, in accordance with what the Lord says: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke XII).

He signifies her inner and outer perfection through two groups of the number seven, while the individual members of her body, possessing the four bodily qualities, love the Lord their God with all their heart, all their soul, and all their strength. [Col. 0135D]

And in the midst of the seven lampstands one like the Son of Man. He says “like the Son of Man” when, having conquered death, he had ascended into heaven. Although we had known Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him in that way.

He rightly says, “IN THE MIDST.” For, as it says: “All who surround him will offer gifts.” [Col. 0135D–0136A]

Clothed in a long robe. Poderis, which in Latin is called a tunica talaris, “an ankle-length tunic,” is a priestly garment. It displays Christ’s priesthood, by which he offered himself for us as a sacrifice to the Father on the altar of the cross.

And girded around the breasts with a golden belt. By the breasts he means the two Testaments, with which the body of the saints, joined to him, is nourished. The golden belt is the choir of the saints, clinging to the Lord in harmonious charity and embracing the Testaments, preserving—as the Apostle says—“the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV). [Col. 0136A–B]

Now his head and his hair were white, etc. The antiquity and immortality of his majesty are shown by the whiteness of the head. The foremost among the saints, clinging to him like hairs, shine like wool because of the sheep who will be at his right hand, and like snow because of the innumerable throng that has been whitened and the elect given from heaven.

And his eyes were like a flame of fire. The Lord’s eyes are the preachers, who offer spiritual fire: light to the faithful and burning to unbelievers.

And his feet were like burnished bronze, as though burning in a furnace. By the feet of fire he means the Church of the final age, which must be tested and proved through intense pressures. Orichalcum is bronze brought to a golden color by much fire and treatment.

Another translation, which says “like the orichalcum of Lebanon,” signifies that the Church is to be persecuted in Judea, whose mountain is Lebanon, especially at the end. The Temple too often received the name Lebanon; to it it is said: “Open your doors, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars” (Zech. XI). [Col. 0136B–C]

And his voice was like the voice of many waters. The voice of confession, preaching, and praise resounds not only in Judea but among many peoples.

And he held seven stars in his right hand. In Christ’s right hand is the spiritual Church. “The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing” (Ps. XLIV). To her, standing at his right hand, he says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV). [Col. 0136C]

And from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword. He who judges visible and invisible things, after killing, has authority to cast into the fiery Gehenna. [Col. 0136D]

And his face was like the sun shining in its strength. As the Lord appeared to the disciples on the mountain, so he will appear to all the saints after judgment. For the ungodly will see in the judgment the one whom they pierced (John XIX).

This entire appearance of the Son of Man also applies to the Church, with whom Christ himself was made one in nature, granting her priestly honor and judicial authority, so that she may shine like the sun in the kingdom of her Father (Matt. XIII). [Col. 0136D]

And when I had seen him, I fell at his feet. Like a human being, he trembles before a spiritual vision, but the Lord’s mercy drives away human fear. [Col. 0136D–0137A]

Do not fear; I am the first and the last. The first, because all things were made through him. The last, because all things are restored in him.

And I have the keys of death and hell. “I not only conquered death by the resurrection,” he says, “but I also possess dominion over that same death.” He also granted this to the Church by breathing the Holy Spirit upon her, saying: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them,” and so forth. [Col. 0137A]

Write therefore what you have seen, etc. Make known to all what you alone have seen: namely, the various struggles of the Church, and the evil people within her who will remain mingled with the good until the end of the age. [Col. 0137A]

The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches. That is, the rulers of the churches. For the priest, as Malachi says, is “the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II). [Col. 0137B]

## CHAPTER TWO

And to the angel of the church of Ephesus write. In accordance with the character of its name, he both rebukes and praises part of this church. Ephesus is said to be interpreted as both “great falling” and “my will in her.”

Thus says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand. That is, he holds you in his hand and governs and sustains you by his power.

Who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands. He moves about in your midst, examining the hearts and searching the inmost thoughts of each person. [Col. 0137B–C]

I know your works and your labor, etc. “I see,” he says, “that you diligently perform good works and patiently endure the intolerable injuries of the wicked. You carefully examine the words and deeds of the false apostles and have been unwilling in any way to yield to them.”

But I have this against you, that you have abandoned your first charity, etc. In some respects you have abandoned the love with which you began; unless you recover it, I will deprive you of the promised reward of light. In other respects, however, you have hated the examples of the wicked—namely, idolatry and fornication. For these are the deeds of the Nicolaitans, as will be explained below. [Col. 0137C]

Whoever has an ear to hear, let him hear, etc. What he writes to individuals he shows that he is saying to all the churches. For it was not only the church of the Ephesians, if it did not repent, that was to be moved from its place; nor is the seat of Satan found only at Pergamum, and not everywhere. So too the other matters concerning individual churches are common to the whole Church. [Col. 0137C–D]

To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise. The tree of life is Christ. Through the vision of him in the heavenly paradise, and through his presence in the present body of the Church, holy souls are refreshed.

Write to the angel of the church in Smyrna. He suggests to this church that persecution must be endured, which also accords with its name. For Smyrna means “myrrh,” which signifies the mortification of the flesh.

“These things says the first and the last, who was dead and came to life.” He who created all things also restored all things by dying. An apt preface for one who is about to urge patience.

“I know your tribulation and your poverty—but you are rich.” For “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Fortunatus aptly explained this in a brief verse:

> The poor man reigns in want, possessing God.

“Those who say that they are Jews and are not.” They confess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him. For “Jew” is the name of a religion. Hence the Apostle also says: “He is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter.”

“Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison, that you may be tested.” These words apply to the universal Church, against which the devil continually wages inextricable enmity.

“And you will have tribulation for ten days.” He signifies the whole period during which the commandments of the Decalogue are necessary. For as long as you follow the light of the divine word, you must suffer the prison of the hostile enemy. Some understand the ten persecutions of the nations—from Nero Caesar to Diocletian—to be signified.

“Be faithful unto death,” etc. He shows how far the ten days extend when he urges that faith be preserved unto death.

“Whoever conquers will not be harmed by the second death.” Whoever remains faithful unto the death of the flesh will not fear the eternal death of the soul.

And write to the angel of the church in Pergamum. Pergamum is interpreted as “dividing their horns”: he who, by judging, distinguished between the virtue of the faithful and the faithlessness of the Nicolaitans, so that the horns of sinners might be broken and the horns of the righteous exalted.

“These things says he who has the sword sharp on both sides.” He appropriately announced judicial power in advance, since he was to bestow rewards on the victors and render punishment to those who went astray.

“I know where you dwell, where the throne of Satan is,” etc. I approve your patience: you have dwelt among the reprobate, who are the devil’s throne, and you worship me not merely in name, by which you are called Christian, but with an undivided faith even during a bloody persecution. Yet I condemn the fact that I also see deceptive teachers among you.

“And in those days Antipas was my faithful witness,” etc. Some understand this as a martyr who suffered at Pergamum; others understand the Lord Christ, who is even now, insofar as it lies within the power of unbelievers, killed by them.

“To eat and to fornicate.” These are the two principal practices by which all the carnal contend, whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame. But every evil work is also idolatry and spiritual fornication.

“Those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.” They were called Nicolaitans after Nicolas the deacon. Clement reports that, when rebuked for jealousy concerning his beautiful wife, he replied that anyone who wished might take her as his wife, and that, for this reason, he taught unbelievers that the apostles permitted everyone indiscriminately to share in women and to have them in common. The Nicolaitans are also said to have preached certain fanciful and almost pagan ideas about the beginning of the world, and not to have separated their food from things sacrificed.

“To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna.” Whoever, though hypocrites urge him otherwise, despises the allurements of the flesh will rightly be satisfied with the sweetness of the invisible bread that came down from heaven.

“And I will give him a white stone.” That is, the body now made white by baptism, then shining with the glory of incorruption.

“And on the stone a new name written.” So that we may be called—and be—children of God.

“Which no one knows except the one who receives it.” For whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar. The hypocrite does not taste how sweet the Lord is.

And write to the angel of the church in Thyatira. Thyatira is translated “into a sacrifice.” The saints, however, present their bodies as a living sacrifice.

“These things says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire.” He explains below what the fiery eyes are, saying: “I am he who searches the kidneys and hearts, and I will give to each of you according to your works.”

“And his feet were like aurichalcum.” He explains this also by saying that the final works of this church are more numerous than its earlier ones.

“But I have this against you: you permit the woman Jezebel,” etc. In your work and faith you are indeed worthy of praise, but in this you are blameworthy: you do not rebuke with a fitting denunciation the synagogue of the false apostles, which pretends to be Christian. The name Jezebel, which signifies a flow of blood, suits heretics. It is conjectured specifically that a woman in the aforesaid church taught the crimes mentioned, and that she was a figure of the whole Jezebel spread throughout the world; against her he also openly threatens punishment.

“And to seduce my servants to fornicate,” etc. She certainly taught fornication and spiritual idolatry under the name of Christ. For how could she openly teach the worship of idols when she claimed in the Church to be a prophet?

“Behold, I cast her into a bed.” By the just judgment of God, she who laid the wretched low in the bed of lust is made to lie in the bed of eternal punishment.

“And her children into death.” Here he calls the woman’s posterity and works her “children”; against them he threatens not the momentary death of the body but the eternal death of the soul.

“And all the churches will know that I am he who searches the kidneys and hearts.” In the kidneys he signifies pleasures; in the heart, thoughts.

“And I will give to each of you according to your works.” Our works and words can therefore be known to human beings, but only he who sees what each person thinks and what pleases each person knows how souls are formed and toward what they desire to arrive through those works. But why is he said to be the knower of hidden things when he punishes fornication and idolatry, crimes that are manifest, unless it is because these too can be called offenses even in the smallest matters? “You will destroy,” he says, “all who fornicate away from you” (Ps. 62). And the same Apostle John, who hears these words, concluded in this way when discussing false brothers: “Little children,” he said, “keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5).

“But I say to you and to the rest who are in Thyatira.” Just as he urges the impious to repentance and threatens punishment, so he encourages the godly to patience with eternal rewards.

“Those who have not known the depths of Satan,” etc. Likewise, those who practice iniquity do not know God, even though they preach him. In this sense God too, although he knows everyone, has not known the workers of iniquity.

“I will not lay upon you any other burden,” etc. “I will not allow you to be tested beyond what you can bear.” Alternatively: “Beware,” he says, “of false prophets” (Matt. 7). For I am not sending you a new doctrine, but preserve what you have received to the end.

“For the one who conquers falsehood and keeps my commands,” etc. In Christ the Church possesses this power, as the body does in the head. In him, according to the Apostle, God has given us all things (Rom. 8).

“And he will rule them with an iron rod.” With inflexible justice he rules the gentle, so that they may bear more fruit; but he destroys the stubborn, so that either they may perish eternally or their earthly desires and the filthy affairs of the old humanity may be crushed within them—whatever has been acquired and implanted from the mire of sins.

“And I will give him the morning star.” Christ is the morning star: when the night of the world has passed, he promises and reveals to the saints the eternal light of life.

## CHAPTER III

And write to the angel of the church in Sardis. He rebukes this angel—that is, the priest—for being insufficiently diligent in correcting evils. Yet he praises some who walk in white garments, to whom the name of Sardis, certainly a precious stone, is appropriate.

“I know your works: you have a name that you are alive, but you are dead.” You appear to yourself to be alive, but if you do not keep watch in correcting the wicked, you will already be counted among the dead.

“For I have not found your works complete before my God.” The works of a ruler are not complete before God if he has not also striven to rouse the others, even though he may seem harmless to human beings.

“I will come to you like a thief.” As in the evangelical parable, so here too, by the example of a thief against whom one must guard, he warns us beforehand to keep watch.

“But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments.” He did not say “a few,” but “a few names.” For he calls his own sheep by name—he who knew Moses by name and writes the names of his own in the heaven of the saints.

“The one who conquers will thus be clothed in white garments.” He calls everyone to imitate the attire of those who have preserved the pure-silk garment of baptism inviolate.

And write to the angel of the church in Philadelphia. Philadelphia is interpreted as “brotherly love.” Through it the door of the kingdom is opened, and it is promised that the Lord loves it.

“These things says the holy and true one, who has the key of David.” That is, royal power, whether because he was born from David’s line or because David’s prophecy was disclosed through Christ’s dispensation.

“He who opens, and no one shuts,” etc. The secrets of the divine law are disclosed to the faithful by Christ’s sole authority and closed to unbelievers.

“Behold, I have set before you an open door,” etc. The door of heavenly knowledge, which Christ opened for his Church, is never shut by anyone’s force or effort.

“Because you have little strength,” etc. He shows the reason why the Church deserves these gifts: it trusts not in its own powers but in the grace of Christ the King. It is both the praise of the protecting God and of the Church’s devotion that the door of conquest is opened to one of little faith, and that little strength is strengthened by faith.

“Behold, I will give some from the synagogue of Satan, who say that they are Jews and are not.” He then promised this to the whole Church, because not only in Philadelphia did some believe from the synagogue of the Jews, as we find in the Acts of the Apostles.

“Because you have kept the word of my patience,” etc. Because you have preserved my example in enduring adversity, I in turn will preserve you from the pressures that threaten. Not so that you will not be tested, but so that you will not be overcome by adversity. And although the Church is always exercised by adversities, here the hour of testing and the humiliation of the Jews under the time of Antichrist may nevertheless be signified, so that, just as in what follows the sixth sequence repeatedly does, here too, in the sixth angel, the final persecution may be indicated. In that persecution the wicked among the Jews are believed to be deceived and to deceive others, while others, understanding the law spiritually through the admonitions of the great prophet Elijah and incorporated into the members of the Church, are believed to overcome the enemy bravely.

“Behold, I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have,” etc. Do not grow weary through enduring. For I will soon help you, lest, if you fail, someone else receive the reward decreed for you. Thus the number of the saints, which is fixed with God, cannot be diminished by the faithlessness of the growing weeds. For if the crown lost by one is handed to another, the place of the one who lost what he held does not remain empty.

“The one who conquers I will make a pillar in the temple of my God,” etc. Whoever overcomes adversities for my sake, glorified in the temple of the Church, will no longer fear any loss through adversity. These pillars—that is, holy men—now fortify the Church by supporting it; then they will adorn it by standing out, like the two pillars at the entrance of Solomon’s temple.

“And I will write upon him the name of my God.” For, evidently, we are called children of God by adoption.

“And the name of the city of my God, the New Jerusalem.” He will be joined to the unity of the Church, which has been begotten into a new life by heavenly grace.

“And my new name.” That is, the name “Christian.” It is not new for the Son of God, who possessed this glory before the world existed, but it is new for the Son of Man, who died and rose again and sits at the right hand of God.

And write to the angel of the church in Laodicea. Laodicea is said to mean “the beloved tribe of the Lord,” or “they were in the vomit.” For there were also people to whom he would say: “I am about to vomit you out of my mouth”; and likewise: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and discipline.” From the Greek, however, it is interpreted as “righteous people.”

“These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness,” etc. “Amen” is interpreted as “truly” or “faithfully.” Christ, therefore, who is truth in the essence of his divinity, recalls that through the mystery of the Incarnation he became the beginning of God’s creation, so that by these words he might conform the Church to the endurance of sufferings.

“I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot,” etc. You are neither fervent in faith nor wholly unbelieving. If you were still unbelieving, hope of conversion would still remain for you; but now, because you do not do the will of the Lord that you have come to know, you will be cast out from the entrails of my Church.

“Because you say, ‘I am rich and have grown wealthy,’” etc. Content with faith alone, you vainly claim the riches of righteousness for yourself. But if you truly desire to be rich, purchase the fervor of charity, tested by the flame of afflictions, after abandoning everything; and anoint the eyes of your mind not with the antimony (*stibium*) of deceptive boasting but with the collyrium of divine knowledge. To anoint the eyes with collyrium is to obtain an understanding of Holy Scripture through the execution of good works.

“Those whom I love, I rebuke and discipline.” Do not refuse to suffer adversity, since this is a special sign of being loved by the Lord.

“Therefore be zealous and repent.” He shows that there were people there whom others ought to imitate and follow.

“Behold, I stand at the door and knock,” etc. I knock at the door of your heart with the right hand of exhortation. If you willingly receive it, you will be considered worthy to have me as your inhabitant and coheir.

“The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne.” He calls the confessor a participant in power and judgment. “He made us sit,” he says, “in the heavenly places in Christ.”

“As I also conquered and sat with my Father on his throne.” The conquering Lord sat on the throne with the Father because, after the contests of his passion and after the palm of his resurrection, he showed more clearly to everyone that he was equal to the Father in power.

Observe that in each church the Lord first indicates his power; then, intermingled always with admonition, he sets out the Church’s works, whether they are to be praised or censured; finally, he repays each side with the reward due to it, a reward that can be understood both in the present and in the future. When he adds, “Whoever has ears, let him hear,” it is undoubtedly fitting to understand “ears” as the heart’s ears, directed toward obedience to the commandments.

## CHAPTER IV

After this I saw, and behold, a door opened in heaven. Having described the Church’s works and what it would be like, he recapitulates from Christ’s birth, intending to say the same things in another way. Throughout this book he repeats the entire period of the Church under various figures. “Behold,” he says, “a door opened in heaven.” Appropriately, he who is about to ascend looks upon the heavenly door, since he is promised that lofty mysteries will be disclosed to him. Or because Christ is the door: whoever believes that he was born and suffered ascends into heaven—that is, into the height of the Church—and sees the future, having become spiritual, as he says.

And immediately I was in the Spirit. And the first voice that I heard—clearly resembling the earlier voice that had said: “What you see, write in a book” (Rev. 1).

And behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one seated upon the throne. The Lord inhabits the Church, which has been established in a heavenly manner of life. Pope Gregory interprets the throne of God in Micah’s vision as the angelic powers. Presiding more deeply over their minds, he arranges all things below.

And the one seated there was like the appearance of a jasper stone and a sardius. Jasper signifies the color of water; sardius signifies fire. We know that judgment is celebrated through these two. For, as he says, “as it was in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. 24).

And a rainbow surrounded the throne, resembling an emerald in appearance. The rainbow, produced when the sun illumines the clouds and first made after the flood as a sign of propitiation, signifies that the Church is fortified through the intercession of the saints whom the Lord illumines. They are rightly compared with the emerald stone, whose greenness is exceedingly intense: the more perfectly they hope for the imperishable inheritance, the more powerfully they protect the others through prayer.

And around the throne were twenty-four seats, etc. The Church, which he had seen on one throne because of the fellowship of faith, he now sees seated on twenty-four seats, generated through the two Testaments from the patriarchs and apostles, and seated because of its judicial dignity in Christ. For all the members will sit and judge, but in one head and through one head. For how could the saints sit in judgment while standing at the Judge’s right hand? The twenty-four elders may also be understood as those who complete the perfection of work, commended by the number six, through the clear preaching of the Gospel. For four times six makes twenty-four.

Clothed all around in white garments, and with golden crowns on their heads. That is, clothed in good works and seeking the joys above through the unceasing remembrance of the mind. For the word “head” often signifies the mind.

And from the throne proceed flashes of lightning, voices, and thunderclaps. This is what Mark says: “But they went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word through the signs that followed” (Mark 16).

And seven burning lamps before the throne, etc. He speaks of one Spirit in sevenfold form, for the Spirit is one. Sevenfoldness, however, is perfection and fullness. Having mentioned the Holy Spirit, he appropriately follows with the water of baptism, in which that same Spirit is believed to be received.

And before the throne there was something like a glassy sea, resembling crystal. Because of the faith of true baptism, it is compared with glass, in which nothing appears externally other than what it contains internally. It is also figured by crystal, which is formed from water into ice and a precious stone: thus the grace of baptism is signified.

And in the midst of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures, full of eyes before and behind. He fills all the parts of God’s throne—that is, of the Church—with the light of the Gospel, through knowledge of past and future things.

And the first living creature was like a lion, etc. These living creatures are interpreted in many ways. Blessed Augustine, following the order of this book, says that Matthew is understood in the lion, since he narrates Christ’s royal lineage; Christ also conquered as the Lion from the tribe of Judah. “A lion’s cub is Judah” (Gen. 49). In Matthew Christ is feared as king by a king, worshiped by the Magi, and is the king who settles accounts with his servants, the king who makes a wedding for his son, and finally the king who separates the sheep from the goats.

Luke is understood in the calf, which was the great sacrifice in the Law. Not only do the beginnings of Luke’s Gospel vary around the temple and sacrifices, but it also concludes in this way: “And they were always in the temple, praising and blessing God” (Luke 24).

The face of a human being signifies Mark, who, saying nothing about the Lord’s royal or priestly power, simply narrates the deeds of Christ as a human being. The eagle, however, is John, who keenly beholds the birth of the Word as though it were the rising of the sun.

The living creatures sometimes signify the evangelists and sometimes the whole Church. Its fortitude is displayed in the lion, its offering in the calf, its humility in the human being, and its sublimity in the flying eagle.

Each of them had six wings. Through the perfection of its teaching, the Church raises people to the heights. The number six is called perfect because it is completed by its own parts: one, which is one-sixth of six; two, which is one-third; and three, which is one-half, together make six.

Alternatively: the six wings of the four living creatures, which amount to twenty-four, indicate the same number of books of the Old Testament. These support the authority of the evangelists and confirm the truth.

And all around and within they are full of eyes, etc. The holy Church watches over itself diligently both before God and before human beings. The Psalmist had looked upon its inner eyes when he said: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44). Its external eyes he indicates when he immediately adds: “Clothed in variety, with golden fringes” (ibid.).

Alternatively: whether you attend to the literal sense or seek an allegory, you will always find light from the Gospel. Another translation reads: “Full of eyes before and behind.” For the light of the Gospel shines upon the enigmas of the Law and pours the radiance of the new grace into the world.

And they had no rest day or night, etc. The holy living creatures throughout the whole time of the world affirm the one dominion of the Godhead, the omnipotence, and the eternity of the Holy Trinity, while the perpetual praise of intellectual creation remains in the heavens.

The twenty-four elders fell before the one seated on the throne and worshiped. When the living creatures resound with praise—that is, when the evangelists preach Christ’s dispensation—the whole Church, which consists of rulers and peoples (for this is what the doubled number twelve signifies), immediately falls on its face and worships the one who lives for ever and ever.

And they cast their crowns before the throne. In this way they ascribe whatever virtue and whatever dignity they possess to him who created all things from nothing.

## CHAPTER V

And I saw in the right hand of the one seated on the throne a book written within and on the outside. This vision shows us the mysteries of Holy Scripture disclosed through the Lord’s Incarnation. Its harmonious unity contains the Old Testament as though on the outside and the New Testament within.

Sealed with seven seals. That is, either covered with the entire fullness of hidden mysteries, or written according to the arrangement of the sevenfold Spirit.

And I heard a strong angel proclaiming with a loud voice: “Who is worthy to open the book?” He indicates the preaching of the Law. For many prophets and righteous people desired to see what the apostles saw (Matt. 13). And concerning this salvation, as Peter says, the prophets “searched and investigated” (1 Pet. 1).

This is the book that in Isaiah is impossible to open both for one who knows letters and for one who does not. Yet even there its opening is proclaimed in this way: “On that day the deaf will hear the words of the book” (Isa. 29). Concerning it Ezekiel also says: “I saw, and behold, a hand extended toward me, in which was a rolled-up book; and he spread it out before me. It was written within and on the outside” (Ezek. 2). There he also added what John omitted—what was written in the book—saying: “Written in it were lamentations, a song, and woe” (ibid.). For the whole sequence of the Old and New Testaments warns that repentance must be undertaken for sins, that the heavenly kingdom must be sought, and that the infernal weeping must be avoided.

And no one in heaven or on earth was able, etc. Neither an angel nor any of the righteous, even one released from the bonds of the flesh, was able to reveal or investigate the mysteries of the divine Law, or to look upon it—that is, to contemplate the splendor of the grace of the New Testament. Thus the children of Israel could not look upon the face of the bearer of the Old Testament, which contained the New.

And I wept greatly. Recognizing the common misery of the human race, he grieved.

And one of the elders said to me: “Do not weep,” etc. He is forbidden to weep because what had long been hidden had already been fulfilled in Christ’s passion: when Christ gave up the Spirit, the veil of the temple was torn (Mark 15). He is told: “Judah, a lion’s cub, you have gone up to the prey, my son” (Gen. 49), etc. What follows describes how and where the Lion from the tribe of Judah conquered.

And I saw in the midst of the throne . . . [lacuna] . . . and a Lamb standing as though slain. The same Lord who is a Lamb by dying innocently also became a lion by conquering death bravely. Tychonius says that the lamb is the Church, which received all power in Christ.

Having seven horns and seven eyes. The Spirit is sevenfold in Christ because of the eminence of his power: he is compared to horns because of power and to eyes because of the illumination of grace.

And he came and took the book from the right hand of the one seated on the throne. The Son of Man is said to have received from the right hand of God the book—that is, the dispensation of the Incarnation itself, arranged by the Father and by himself according to what he is as God—because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit dwell upon the throne together. For Christ, who in his humanity is the Lamb, is himself, in his divinity, the right hand of the Father.

And when he had opened the book, etc. When the Lord proved through his passion that the proclamations of both Testaments were fulfilled in him, the Church, giving thanks, also offers itself to sufferings, so that, according to the Apostle, it may “fill up what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in its flesh” (Col. 1). The harps, on which strings are stretched over wood, signify bodies prepared to die; the bowls signify hearts opened wide by the breadth of charity.

And they sang a new song, etc. They celebrate the sacraments of the New Testament, which have been completed in Christ, following with praises that very dispensation of his which they confess belongs to Christ alone.

“And you redeemed us for God by your blood,” etc. Here it is made still clearer that the living creatures and the elders are the Church, which was redeemed by Christ’s blood and gathered from the nations. He also shows what heaven they are in when he says: “And they will reign upon the earth.” And I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne, and of the living creatures and the elders.

And their number was thousands of thousands. Innumerable thousands of peoples flowing into the Church praise God.

“To whom all power was given in heaven and on earth.” For if the righteous are called children of God, why not also the angels? The heavenly host too may fittingly sing this in congratulation at our redemption. Thus holy Pope Gregory also explained it, adding: “For the voice of the angels is in praise of the Creator, namely, the innermost wonder of contemplation.”

And the four living creatures said, “Amen,” etc. While the peoples in the Lord’s Church resound with praises, the teachers confirm the same thing and, by way of example, worship the Lord together.

## CHAPTER VI

And I saw that the Lamb had opened one of the seals. Since the seals are first broken and the book is afterward opened, he reverses the customary order for a definite reason. For the suffering and rising Lord taught that he himself was the end of the Law. Then, ascending into heaven and sending the Holy Spirit, he strengthened the Church with the gift of a more secret mystery. At that time, therefore, he opened the book; now he breaks its seals.

In the first seal, therefore, he sees the glory of the primitive Church; in the following three, a threefold war against it; in the fifth, the glory of those who triumph amid this war; in the sixth, the events that will come in the time of Antichrist, together with a brief recapitulation of what preceded; and in the seventh, he sees the beginning of eternal rest.

And I heard one of the four living creatures saying: “Come and see.” We too are admonished by the great voices of the Gospel to behold the glory of the Church.

And behold, a white horse, etc. The Lord presides over the Church, which has been whitened by grace beyond snow; bearing the weapons of spiritual teaching against the impious, he conquers and receives a crown in his own people. Concerning him it is said: “He received gifts among human beings” (Ps. 67). While presiding over them also from heaven, he was persecuted by Saul.

And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature, etc. He is carefully instructed to observe the opposing cavalry as well, so that, just as he draws joy from the Church’s prosperity, he may also derive caution from foreknowledge of its adversities.

And another horse went out, a red one. Against the victorious and conquering Church went out a red horse—that is, a sinister people, bloodstained by its rider, the devil. Although we have read in Zechariah of the Lord’s red horse, that one is red with his own blood, whereas this one is red with another’s.

And to its rider it was granted to take peace from the earth. Clearly, its own peace. The Church, however, received the eternal peace that Christ left to it.

And a great sword was given to him. Either he makes some into transgressors against the faith, or he makes others martyrs. Concerning this it is said to blessed Job: “He who made him applied his sword” (Job 40)—that is, either so that he would not test the saints as much as the impious wished, or because vengeance for his rage would return upon himself.

And behold, a black horse, etc. The black horse is the crowd of false brothers, who possess the scales of right confession but harm their companions through works of darkness. Since it is said among the living creatures, “Do not harm,” it is shown that there is one there who harms. Concerning this preceding horse the Apostle says: “Fights without, fears within.”

“A two-pound measure of wheat for one denarius,” etc. “Beware,” he says, “lest by a most evil example you scandalize your brother, for whom Christ died, and who bears the marks of the sacred blood and chrism.” For whether perfect in merits or among the least, all in the Church who have nevertheless been imbued with faith in the Holy Trinity have been redeemed by the same perfect price of the Lord’s blood. Nor is it without reason that a double measure, rather than a single measure, expresses the perfection of faith or work, both of which rest upon the twofold root of charity.

And behold, a pale horse, etc. Heretics who disguise themselves as Catholics, deserving of death as their inhabitant, drag after themselves an army of the lost. For the devil and his ministers are called, by metonymy (*metonymicōs*), “death” and “hell,” because they are the cause of death and hell for many. It may also be understood simply: those who are spiritually dead here will be followed there by eternal punishment.

And authority was given to him over a fourth part of the earth. Behold, the madness of Arius, arising from Alexandria, reached as far as the Gallic Ocean, savagely pursuing the godly not only through hunger for the word of God but also with the bodily sword. Another edition translated it as “a fourth part,” because three evil horses, trusting in the devil as their ruler, kick against the fourth cavalry, that of the Church.

And when he had opened the fifth seal, etc. Since he had said that the Church is presently afflicted in many ways, he also speaks of the glory of souls after the suffering of their bodies. “I saw them,” he says, “under the altar”—that is, in the inner sanctuary of eternal praise. For the golden altar, placed farther within and near the ark of the Lord’s body, offers the Lord not flesh and blood, as the outer altar does, but only the incense of praise. Those who now present their bodies as a living sacrifice will then, when the bonds of the flesh have been broken, offer him a sacrifice of praise (Ps. 115).

It may also be understood as a hyperbaton, so that he did not see them beneath the altar, but saw those who had been killed beneath the altar—that is, beneath the testimony of Christ’s name, as it is said of the Maccabees: “They fell under the covenant of God” (2 Macc. 7).

And they cried out with a loud voice, saying. The great cry of the souls is the great desire for those things that they know the Lord intends to do. For it is not right to believe that they desire anything contrary to God’s will, since their desires depend upon his will.

“How long, O holy and true Lord, will you refrain from judging and avenging,” etc.? They do not pray these things out of hatred for the enemies on whose behalf they prayed in this world, but out of love for equity, by which they are in agreement with the Judge, since they are placed near him. They pray for the day of judgment, when the reign of sin will be destroyed, and for the resurrection of the bodies of the dead. For even now, when we are commanded to pray for our enemies, we nevertheless say to the Lord in prayer: “Your kingdom come” (Matt. 6).

And individual white robes were given to them. For now the souls of the saints possess individual robes, rejoicing in their blessed immortality. But when the bodies rise, according to Isaiah, they will possess double things in their own land.

And they were told to rest for a little while longer, etc. The desire for resurrection is not rejected; it is deferred because of the increase in the number of brothers to be gathered. The joy of the souls themselves may also be represented by white robes, since, when the Lord reveals to them that the impious will be condemned at the end and that many will be joined to their number through martyrdom until the end of the world, they, filled with inward charity, may prefer to be content with this consolation and to have their joys deferred for this period, until the number of their brothers is completed.

And I saw when he had opened the sixth seal, etc. When the sixth seal is disclosed, the final persecution is announced; and just as the Lord was crucified on the sixth day, the world is shaken by darkness and terror.

And the sun became black like sackcloth. As though Christ’s power were either covered over or his teaching temporarily obscured, or as though he were veiled from protection, when the ministers of Antichrist begin to rage against Christ’s servants.

And the whole moon became like blood. The Church will shed blood for Christ more abundantly than usual. He said “the whole,” because the final earthquake of the earth will occur throughout the entire world; previously, as it is written, it occurred in particular places.

And the stars fell upon the earth, etc. Those who outwardly shine as heavenly beings in the Church, driven by the wind of the final persecution, will be proved to have been earthly. Their works are aptly compared with unripe figs—that is, useless and falling figs.

And the sky receded like a scroll being rolled up. Just as a rolled-up book contains mysteries within but does not display them outwardly, so then the Church, known only to its own members, will withdraw while cautiously avoiding the persecution, so that it will not be seen by outsiders, from whom it is hidden.

And every mountain and island was removed from its place. By mentioning the Church’s members according to the varying quality of their offices or powers, he predicts that none will be free from this storm. Yet their movements will differ: the good will flee in precaution, while the evil will give way by following.

And the kings of the earth, the princes, and the tribunes. We understand “kings” as powerful people. For he wishes it to be understood as referring to every rank and condition. Otherwise, who will be kings then except the one persecutor?

They hid themselves in caves and among the rocks of the mountains, etc. When the weaker members then seek to be strengthened by the examples of the lofty in the Church, fortified by their counsels, protected by their warnings, and sheltered by their prayers, they ask, as it were, that the mountains themselves fall upon them through compassionate affection. For “the high mountains are for the deer, and the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs” (Ps. 113).

“And hide us from the face of the one seated on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb.” Thus they ask that, when he comes, he may find us not reprobate but steadfast in faith, with our sins covered by the intercession of the saints and by the mercy of God.

And who will be able to stand? Certainly the one who has taken care to keep watch, stand firm in faith, and act courageously. But if you refer this earthquake, in its literal sense, to the very day of judgment, it is not surprising if earthly kings and princes, terrified, seek refuge in the mountains of the saints, as we already read has happened with the rich man dressed in purple and poor Lazarus.

## CHAPTER VII

**After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth.** That is, the four principal kingdoms—namely, those of the Assyrians, the Persians, the Greeks, and the Romans. For just as in the preceding seals, after the Church’s manifold conflicts, he saw the joys of the triumphant souls, so now also he is going to demonstrate by examples what victory will follow the kingdom of Antichrist: the preceding kingdoms of the world, which have already yielded to the authority of Christ’s Church. Great causes must necessarily be confirmed by still greater arguments.

**Holding the four winds of the earth, etc.** By a certain exercise of their power, they suffocated everything, allowing nothing to breathe freely according to its own will. By the earth, the diversity of provinces is signified; by the sea, that of islands; and by the trees, the different ranks and conditions of human beings. Alternatively: the four angels are to be understood as the same four winds, in accordance with the prophecy of Daniel, which says: “Behold, four winds of heaven were fighting upon the great sea, and four beasts were coming up from the sea” (Dan. VII).

**And I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, [Col. 0149D] etc.** The Lord, born in the flesh, who is the angel of the great counsel—that is, the messenger of the Father’s will—visited us, “the Dawn from on high” (Luke I), bringing the standard of the cross with which he would mark the foreheads of his own.

**And he cried out with a loud voice to the four angels.** The Lord’s loud voice is exalted preaching: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

**Do not harm the earth or the sea, or the trees.** From the time when the Lord suffered, not only the dominion of the hostile enemy but also the power of worldly rule has been crushed, as we see with our own eyes and read in the statue that the stone cut from the mountain shattered.

**Until we mark the servants of our God on their foreheads?** The dominion of the nations was broken for this purpose: so that the faces of the saints [Col. 0150A] might freely be marked with the sign of the faith against which they had resisted. Indeed, the very figure of the cross signifies that the Lord’s kingdom has been extended everywhere, as the ancient saying confirms:

> Look upon the world, square in its ordered parts,  
> that you may know the kingdom of faith holds all things.

For it was not without reason that the Lord’s name, the Tetragrammaton, was written on the forehead of the high priest, unless because this is the sign on the foreheads of the faithful, concerning which the Psalm “For the winepresses” sings: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth” (Ps. VIII), and so forth, until it says: “that you may destroy the enemy and the defender” (ibid.).

**And I heard the number of those who were marked, etc.** Once this number has been completed, the innumerable multitude of the whole Church is signified. It has sprung from the patriarchs—whether by descent of the flesh or by imitation of faith. For, he says, “if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring” (Gal. III). The multiplication of twelve by twelve itself pertains to the increase of perfection, and its completion into the sum of one thousand signifies the square, solid number of ten, indicating the Church’s stable life. It is often represented by the number twelve for this reason: it stands throughout the square world in the faith of the Holy Trinity. For three times four is the excellence of the double denarius. Finally, twelve apostles were chosen to preach this same faith to the world, figuratively representing by their number the mystery of their work.

**From the tribe of Judah twelve thousand were marked, etc.** Appropriately he begins with Judah, from whose tribe our Lord arose; and he omits Dan, from whom Antichrist is said to be destined to be born, as it is written: “Let Dan be a serpent on the way, a horned snake on the path, biting the horse’s hooves, so that its rider may fall” (Gen. XLIX). He has determined to expound not the order of earthly generation but, according to the interpretation of the names, the virtues of the Church, which hastens from present confession and praise toward the right hand of eternal life.

This is what the name of Judah, who is placed first, and Benjamin, who is placed last, conveys. Judah, therefore, whose name is interpreted as “confession” or “praise,” is placed first, because no one attains the summit of good works without the beginnings of confession. Unless through confession we renounce evil deeds, we are not formed in righteousness.

Second comes Reuben, whose name is interpreted as “seeing a son.” That works are signified by sons is attested by the Psalmist, who says among the blessings of the blessed man: “Your sons are like olive shoots” (Ps. CXXVII). And below: “that you may see your sons’ sons” (ibid.). He does not mean that one who fears the Lord cannot be blessed unless he has begotten sons and received grandchildren, since a greater reward awaits faithful virgins; rather, by sons he signifies works, and by sons’ sons the fruits of works—that is, the eternal reward.

After Judah, therefore, comes Reuben: after the beginnings of divine confession and praise follows the perfection of action. But because “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV), Gad follows Reuben; Gad is interpreted as “temptation” or “girded.” After beginning a good work, a person must necessarily be tested by greater temptations and girded for heavier battles, so that the strength of his faith [Col. 0151A] may be proved. Solomon says: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II). Likewise the Psalmist: “You girded me with strength for battle” (Ps. XVII).

And because “we call blessed those who endured,” therefore Asher, that is, “Blessed,” follows Gad in a sufficiently fitting order. Blessed is the one who endures temptation; when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life (James I).

Since those who are secure in the faithful promise of this blessedness are not constricted but rejoice in hope and are patient in tribulation, they sing with the Psalmist: “In tribulation you enlarged me”; and again: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. CXVIII). Rejoicing with the mother of blessed Samuel, they say: “My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies, because I have rejoiced in your salvation” (1 Sam. II). Therefore Naphtali follows, whose name means “breadth.”

Manasseh follows him; Manasseh is interpreted as “forgotten” or “necessity.” Through the mystery of this name we are warned that, instructed by the anguish of present temptations and forgetting what lies behind, we should press forward, according to the Apostle, toward what lies ahead, so that we may attend to the flesh not in desires but only as necessity imposed by the human condition (Phil. III). Concerning this, the Psalmist, sighing for better things, prayed: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. XXIV).

Simeon is placed beneath him, that is, “he heard sorrow,” or “the name of a dwelling place,” so that by the significance of this name too he might impress more clearly what must be possessed here and what must salutarily be awaited. The joy of the heavenly dwelling will be given to those whose spirit here is saddened by fruitful repentance. To them it is said: “Your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John XVI).

Therefore Levi is joined next, that is, “added.” By this we understand either those who purchase eternal things with temporal goods, as Solomon says: “The ransom of a man’s soul is his own wealth” (Prov. XIII), or those who, following God’s counsel, receive in this world a hundredfold with tribulations, and in the world to come eternal life (Mark X). The saying also applies to them: “He who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccles. I). The bitterness of tribulations was added even to blessed Job for this purpose, so that, once he had been tested, the reward of his merits might be made greater.

Hence Issachar, whose name means “reward,” rightly follows him. For, as the Apostle teaches, “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII). The battle is fought more fruitfully when a certain reward is hoped for.

God brings about and perfects this in the dwelling place of strength, which is called Zebulun, when strength is perfected in weakness (2 Cor. XII). Thus the body, which enemies consider weak and through whose substance they also strive to inflict destruction upon the soul, experiences itself to be unconquered when God strengthens it, as blessed increase follows.

The name Joseph indicates this, signifying gifts of grace that are to be added. You may understand this either as the spiritual profit gained from the doubled return of talents, or as referring to those things that are rendered to God the Redeemer through the devoted worship of the faithful.

And so that you may understand that all those whom both the order and the interpretation of their names show to have been placed here symbolically will stand at the right hand of Christ, the eternal King, in the future judgment, Benjamin is placed last, as I said: “son of the right hand.” He is as it were the end of the sequence, when, after the last enemy, death, has been destroyed (1 Cor. XV), the blessedness of an eternal inheritance will be given to the elect. This may refer either to each individual believer, who is called a son of the right hand, or to the whole assembly of the Church, of which it is sung: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a golden garment and surrounded by variety” (Ps. XLIV).

Therefore twelve thousand are marked from each tribe, because whatever virtues individual believers may attain, they must always be strengthened by the faith of the ancient fathers and formed by their examples. It is entirely certain that the number twelve often designates, on account of the total number of the apostles or patriarchs, the form of the teachers and often the form of the whole Church.
