And another angel came out of the temple, crying, etc. The angels whom we read of in the Gospel as reapers of the earth, and who have all been sent for service on behalf of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation (Hebrews I), weigh the merits of the Church individually and report them daily to the Lord.

Send your sickle and reap, etc. “Behold,” he says, “because iniquity has abounded, the love of many has grown cold” (Matthew XXIV); and as the heat of evils presses upon it, the harvest of the world has almost ceased to live. Therefore, lest the already ripe grains fall, “for the sake of the elect those days are shortened” (ibid.); consign the weeds and the chaff to the flames, but store the heavenly fruit in blessed barns (Matthew XIII).

And another angel, etc., himself also having a sharp sickle. If Christ was seen as the reaper in the white cloud, who is the vintager except the same one, elegantly repeated on account of the Church’s twofold fruit? For the one who sowed good seed in his field (Matthew XIII) also planted a vineyard in a fertile place, but each cultivation degenerated through the negligence of its guardians.

And another angel came out from the altar, who has authority over the fire, etc. There is, as Jerome says, a twofold office of angels: some bestow rewards on the righteous, while others preside over the torments of individuals. As it is said: “Who makes his angels spirits,” etc. The two angels who proclaim the dry harvest and the ripe vineyard may be understood as the prayers of the Church, which, with a loud voice—that is, with great daily longing—prays for the Lord’s kingdom to come, saying:

Send your sharp sickle, etc. The harvest, like the vintage, is partly earthly and partly heavenly. The ripeness of both, however, indicates the end of the age.

For its grapes are ripe. That is, the sins have reached completion. Yet the perfection of the good can also be called ripeness. For, as holy Pope Gregory says: “Although the end of the world depends upon its own order, nevertheless, when it finds the more perverse, it becomes known that they are deservedly to be overwhelmed by its ruins.”

And the angel cast his sickle into the earth, etc. The one who has the reaping sickle also has the vintage sickle. For there is one judgment, and it will take place at one time. But in the harvest and the vintage he indicates the beginning and the end of that same oppression.

And he cast it into the great vat of God’s wrath, etc. If this harvest and vintage concern only the wicked, the winepress signifies punishment. But if they concern the good as well, the treading of the winepress and the threshing of the threshing floor crush what is useless and test what is useful. As the Apostle says, precious metals are tested by fire, while wood, hay, and straw are consumed (1 Corinthians III). Both take place outside heavenly Jerusalem. The vat is called the vat of wrath in the manner of speech by which it is said: “On the evil day the Lord delivered him” (Psalm XL).

And blood came out of the vat, etc. Vengeance went forth as far as the rulers of the peoples. For in the final struggle vengeance for the blood of the saints that had been shed went forth even as far as the devil and his angels. As it is written: “You sinned in blood, and blood pursues you.” Above, it was said concerning the horses:

For one thousand six hundred stadia. That is, through all four parts of the world. For the quaternity is arranged in fours, as in the four faces of the fourfold creatures and in the wheels. Four times four hundred is one thousand six hundred.

Tychonius interprets the reaper and vintager as the Church, becoming radiant after the flames of persecutions and holding the power to bind and loose. He says that the angel from the temple or altar, declaring the command of the Red One—that is, the Lord—not with an audible voice but by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, who works in his body, teaches that the time has come for the wicked to be anathematized. He has authority over the fire, namely, the fire that came out of the mouths of the witnesses and consumed their enemies.

Thus far concerning the Church’s conflict and the mature end of each side’s struggle.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0177]

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0177B]

And I saw another sign in heaven, great and wondrous. Having restored the order once more, and about to narrate the same plagues of the final persecution, he wished to make the hearer attentive by saying: “A great and wondrous sign.”

[Col. 0177C] Seven angels. That is, the Church full of a sevenfold grace.

Having seven final plagues. Because God’s wrath is completed in them, he called them “final.” For God’s wrath continually strikes the disobedient people with seven plagues—that is, perfect ones—as is frequently stated in Leviticus: “I will strike you with seven plagues” (Leviticus XXVI). These will be the final ones when the Church has departed from their midst.

And I saw something like a glassy sea mixed with fire. Namely, the clear fountain of baptism, consecrated by the fire of the Holy Spirit; or, in what pertains to the quality of fire, reddened by martyrdom.

And those who conquered the beast and its image, etc. Those who conquer the beast’s frauds consequently appear to stand above the fiery baptism, striving, according to the Apostle, to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints (Jude III).

Having the harps of God and singing, etc. That is, carrying hearts dedicated to God in praise, tuneful with the truth of both Testaments; or, flesh stretched out upon the wood of the Passion. Here not merely the sound of the voice but also the effect of good works is signified.

Great and wondrous are your works, Lord God Almighty, etc. This song is found in both Testaments, in which the Lord, both truthful and merciful, is sung by all ages as the Judge to be worshiped. He repeats what he had begun, saying:

And behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened. The vision accords with the song. For, so that the Lord might be worshiped by all nations, that temple of God’s mysteries, once enclosed within the walls of a single city, has now begun to be opened spiritually to the whole world.

And seven angels came out of the temple, having seven plagues. This is what Mark says: “But they went out and preached everywhere.”

Clothed in a clean, shining stone. “As many of you as were baptized in Christ,” says the Apostle, “have put on Christ” (Galatians III). For he himself is the supreme chosen cornerstone. Or, if you understand the singular number as used for the plural, it signifies various ornaments of virtues. Another translation has “white linen,” enjoining mortification of the heart upon teachers, in accordance with: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, having preached to others, I myself should be found disqualified” (1 Corinthians IX).

And girded around their breasts with golden bands. Whoever wishes to preach mighty things should not only mortify his body, but also bind his breast with the gold of wisdom. Or certainly, to bind the breasts with golden bands means to restrain all the movements of mutable thoughts by the bonds of the love of God alone.

[Col. 0178D] And one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels, etc. These are the bowls that the living creatures and the elders carry with the incense; they are the Church, which is also the seven angels. For these same bowls are said to contain both the sweetness of supplications and the anger of punishments, when they are poured out by the saints for the coming of God’s kingdom. Then God’s judgments, no longer hidden like the abyss but open like bowls, are foretold as bringing salvation to the righteous and destruction to the wicked, as the Apostle says: “For we are the good odor of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (2 Corinthians II).

And the temple was filled with smoke, etc. The Church, about to preach to the nations, first grows warm itself with the fire of love and emits the smoke of devout confession, giving thanks to God for his indescribable gift.

[Col. 0179A] And no one could enter the temple, etc. No one can be incorporated into the members of the Church unless, hearing the mysteries of the faith, he learns from the preachers that Jesus has been appointed by God as Judge of the living and the dead. But if you interpret the smoke as the hidden mysteries of God’s judgments, these remain impenetrable and closed to mortals until, when the plagues of the present age have ended, the Lord comes—he who both illuminates the hidden things of darkness (1 Corinthians IV) and reveals how much either usefulness, for testing the faith of the Church, or justice, for blinding the Jews who did not receive the love of truth so that they might be saved, the coming of the Antichrist will bring about.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0179B]

And I heard a loud voice: Go and pour out the seven bowls, etc. Authority has been given to the Church to inflict judgment upon those condemned and mercifully to grant absolution to those who have turned back. The command was indeed given to all the angels to pour them out upon the earth; but these earthly people receive different names according to the variety of their sins, so that the fullness of preaching, vengeance, and guilt alike might be reckoned by the number seven.

And the first went and poured out his bowl upon the earth. Preachers pour out the bowls of God’s wrath in two ways: when they spiritually impose the punishments of the wicked upon the wicked themselves by judging them, as Peter said to Simon: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts VIII); or when they make them known to the holy Church through preaching, as the same Apostle said: “For whom judgment from long ago is not idle, and their destruction does not sleep” (2 Peter II). A third way can also be understood: when some sinner, having heard the preaching of truth, is corrupted by the more serious wound of contradiction. Concerning this the Lord says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John XV).

And a grievous wound occurred, etc. Those who, having abandoned the Lord, venerate the devil will spiritually perish from the worst wound of that same impiety.

And the second poured out his bowl upon the sea, etc. Those who are marked not only by the character of the Antichrist but also persecute the stability of Christ’s servants with the waves of bitter persecution will now be punished by spiritual vengeance, which he calls blood; and those who boasted that they were alive will be proved to have served the author of death.

And the third poured out his bowl upon the rivers, etc. These too—those who pretend to offer sweet things in order to pour their venom into the unwary—will be punished with a vengeance worthy of an everlasting plague.

And I heard the angel of the waters saying: You are just, etc. By the angel of the waters he means all the angels of the peoples, joining in divine praises with inward devotion because, in taking vengeance for the blood of his servants, he has made the murderers drink death.

And I heard another saying from the altar: Yes, Lord God Almighty, your judgments are true and just. What the angels are, the altar also is: giving thanks to God, that is, the inward devotion of the saints, whether angels or human beings, who preside over the peoples by teaching them.

And the fourth poured out his bowl upon the sun, etc. The persecutors of the Church, who, like a burning sun, attempt to dry up the seed of God’s word, are destined to be burned by the future heat of Gehenna. Or, if you interpret the sun as the splendor of the wise, it was not the angel, as he poured his bowl upon the sun, but that sun itself that was given power to afflict people with heat and fire. For when wise men, overcome by torments, are touched by the error of evil conduct, all the weak, persuaded by their example, burn with temporal desires. Yet “heat,” as we said, may also be understood to mean that the devil’s body is irreparably tormented by the steadfastness of the saints and is stirred up to blasphemy. Concerning this the prophet says: “Zeal has seized an unlearned people; and now fire consumes the adversaries.” Here “now” is excepted, namely, the fire of that final judgment.

And the people were scorched by great heat. At present, insofar as he is permitted, the devil makes his own people bright. The Holy Spirit has defined that brightness and joy as plagues and pains. For above too we read that the devil’s army killed people with fire, smoke, and sulphur—not that it visibly killed them, but that it destined those who consented to these punishments.

And the fifth poured out his bowl, etc. The throne of the beast—that is, his kingdom, like judicial authority—is darkened by these plagues, namely, by the false joy of earthly happiness, and is deprived of light, as the Psalm says: “You cast them down while they were being raised up” (Psalm LXXII). For he did not say, “after they had been raised up.”

And they chewed their tongues because of the pain. Just as the righteous will eat the fruits of their labors, so too the wicked, exposed to punishments worthy of his blasphemy, is, as it were, filled with his own tongue. Therefore, blaspheming under God’s wrath, they harmed themselves, imagining that their joys had been pierced through.

And they blasphemed the God of heaven, etc. He does not attribute this to their hardness, but to the just indignation of God, who inflicted such a kind of plague in which they do not come to their senses. For who, physically afflicted, would not perceive the hand of God, like Antiochus? He said that they blasphemed—not openly, but while luxuriating in sins.

And the sixth angel poured out his bowl upon that great river, the Euphrates, etc. As the people perish, Babylon’s abundance will perish, and nothing living, nothing green, that is not suited to fire will remain. This is what he said above: “The harvest of the earth dried up” (Revelation XIV), while the saints hasten to meet the Sun of righteousness. Alternatively: just as, while the wicked man grows proud, the poor man is set ablaze, so, when the pestilent man is scourged, the wise man will become more astute. But, passing over the customary order, he briefly recapitulates from the beginning with the seventh angel.

And I saw from the mouth of the dragon and from the mouth of the beast, etc. The spirit of the devil, of the Antichrist, and of the rulers of his body—called threefold according to the number of the parts of one body—is likened to frogs, living creatures horrible in their place, appearance, and troublesome croaking. Although these appear to inhabit the waters, they nevertheless roll about in filth and mud. Hypocrites, promising the water of life to their own people, lie hidden in the filth which those who believe lay aside in the water when they are dead. Thus Pharaoh, who dared to enter after the people in order to destroy them in baptism, was killed there himself.

For they are demonic spirits performing signs. In this way, they too must be believed capable of performing signs, just as Pharaoh’s magicians did. Nor is mention of them in connection with frogs made without reason, except to foretell that Satan’s ministers would at that time also perform similar signs. For the magicians were permitted by their incantations to have power as far as the sign of the frogs.

And they will go out to the kings of the whole earth, to gather them for battle, etc. Just as there are holy kings for whom, once the Euphrates has dried up, the way from the East is opened, so too the wicked kings of the earth are mentioned: not gathered from the whole world into one place, but with each nation attacking the saints in its own place. By the great day of the Lord he means the entire period beginning with the Lord’s Passion. The day of judgment can also be understood: the devil’s army, gathered throughout the whole period of the present life, will come to be overthrown before the Lord the King.

Behold, I am coming like a thief. Another edition more appropriately has: “For the great day of God Almighty. Behold, he comes like a thief.”

Blessed is the one who keeps watch and guards his garments, etc. Blessed are those whose sins are covered (Psalm XXXI), who veil the shamefulness of a blameworthy life before the eyes of the righteous at the judgment with the covering of subsequent good works. And in the Gospel, the Lord, using the example of a thief who must be guarded against, commands the servants to keep watch.

And he will gather them into the place called in Hebrew Hermagedon. Elsewhere he explains this place by saying: “He gathered them for battle, and they surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city” (Revelation XX), that is, the Church. Conversely, the place of the wicked may be understood as the devil, who will rejoice to recover, in a lost human being inflated by the swelling of usurped divinity, the former ambushes—that is, those once forbidden by the Lord. For Hermagedon is interpreted as “resurrection into former things,” or “a rounded mountain.”

And the seventh poured out his bowl upon the air, etc. Just as above the blood of vengeance went out as far as the horses’ bridles—that is, toward the unclean spirits—so here, when the final vengeance is poured over the same aerial powers, it is said to have happened, meaning that the end is at hand, when, as the Apostle says, “the last enemy, death, will be destroyed” (1 Corinthians XV). Thus far, the final persecution has been described under the name of plagues, all of which Tychonius wishes to be understood in the contrary sense. “A plague,” he says, “is to receive an incurable wound and great wrath: to receive the power to sin, especially against the saints, without yet being chastised by a greater wrath of God.” For the outcome of the wicked’s blessedness is death, just as, conversely, the Church’s torments and humiliation are its glory. For at that very time the whole impious people will be unharmed by every bodily plague, as though it had received the entire power of raging. Nor will there then be any need for one of the wicked to be scourged by the fulfillment of sins and the completion of wrath, or to be restrained from fury.

[Col. 0182A] He recapitulates from that same persecution, describing the ruin of the impious city.

And there were flashes of lightning and voices, etc. When at the end of the age there is such tribulation as has not been since the beginning (Matthew XXIV), the greatest signs will also shine forth together. But whether they arise from the side of the good, from the side of the wicked, or come together against one another from both sides, is not sufficiently clear here—as happened between Moses and the magicians of Pharaoh.

And the great city was made into three parts. The impious city wages a threefold war against the Church of Christ. Gentiles and Jews assail it in open conflict, heretics by stealthy defection, and false brothers by wicked examples. This was also represented above by the three evil horses, the red, black, and pale.

And the cities of the nations fell. That is, all the strength and confidence of the nations. For the ruin of the wicked is great delight, and the destruction of the unjust is joy.

And Babylon the great came into remembrance before God, etc. Babylon falls, or drinks the wrath of God, when it receives power against Jerusalem, especially against the final Jerusalem. For this reason he said that it had fallen through the earthquake which he makes for the Church. But if you refer this to the day of judgment, then the wicked man will come into remembrance before God—he who now says in his heart: “God has forgotten.”

And every island fled, and the mountains were not found. The Church, which, because of the eminence of its steadfastness, is compared with islands and mountains, prudently hides itself from the waves of its persecutors.

And great hail, like a talent, descended from heaven upon the people. The hail of God’s wrath is likened to a talent: heavy in weight and inflicted upon each person according to a just judgment, in proportion to the diversity of their faults. All the plagues of Egypt were also figures of spiritual plagues.

And the people blasphemed God, etc. Some sins are the cause of sin, some are the punishment of sin, and some are both. As Isaiah says: “Behold, you were angry, and we sinned” (Isaiah LXIV). Here blaspheming God because of the hail is recognized both as sin and as the punishment of sin.

## CHAPTER XVII

Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great prostitute, etc. The multitude of the lost, who, having abandoned the Creator, prostrated themselves to be defiled by demons, is said to sit upon the waters—that is, upon the discord of the peoples.

[Col. 0182D] By contrast, the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. The Apostle betrothed these to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ.

With whom the kings of the earth committed fornication, etc. The whole takes precedence over its parts. For the kings and inhabitants of the earth are the individual people who proudly seek earthly things; the enticement of the world defiles them with the lust of vices, and madness of mind intoxicates them.

And he carried me away into a desert in the spirit. He uses “desert” to signify the absence of divinity, whose presence is paradise.

And I saw a woman sitting upon a scarlet beast, etc. The devil, bloodstained with impiety, blasphemous, and inflated, elevates the corruption of the wicked by the arrogance of presumption.

[Col. 0183A] Having seven heads and ten horns. That is, possessing the kings and kingdoms of the world, whose glory he also displayed to the Lord on the mountain. For, as we said above, the universality is often indicated by the numbers seven and ten.

And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet. In the purple, the deception of simulated rule is shown; in the scarlet, the bloodstained appearance of impiety.

And gilded with gold and precious stone and pearls. That is, with all the enticements of simulated truth. Finally, he explains what lies within this beauty, saying:

Having a golden cup, etc. The golden cup [Col. 0183B] full of impurities is hypocrisy, because hypocrites outwardly appear righteous to human beings, but inwardly are full of every kind of filth. For what the poison is in gold, that is the beast lurking beneath the guise of a harlot.

And on her forehead a name was written: Mystery, etc. This corruption is immediately shown in her very face to be the nurse of vices; but because it is discerned only by prudent judgment, the fact that she is adorned with the utmost splendor indicates that this name is mystical.

And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints, etc. It is one body, hostile both within and without: although it may appear separated in place, it nevertheless acts in common through the unity of the Spirit. Thus the descendants of the wicked are accused of stoning Zechariah in intention, although they themselves did not do it.

And I was astonished when I saw her, with great astonishment. And the angel said to me: Why are you astonished? etc. That is, the devil once ruled in the world, but when the Lord was crucified he was cast out; at the end of the world, however, he will be released from the prison of his confinement, and “by the breath of the Lord’s mouth he will perish forever” (II Thess. II). Tychonius refers the beast to the devil’s entire body, which is completed through the succession of generations, one replacing another. This is especially so because the woman whom he had promised to show seated upon many waters—that is, upon peoples—he showed seated upon the beast.

The seven heads are seven mountains, etc. The heads, he says, of the beast are the kings of the world, made equal to lofty mountains because of the swelling of their pride. Upon these wanton impiety rests, so that they may oppress by force and deceive by fraud.

Five have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come. Having described the fullness of worldly rule by the number seven—whose final part, namely the kingdom of Antichrist, had not yet come—he consequently testifies that five kings have passed away, that the sixth is present, and that the seventh is to come.

And when he comes, he must remain for a short time. Because the Lord sees that we are both proud and weak, he mercifully says that the days which he has brought upon us as especially evil have been shortened. Certainly, he does this both to terrify pride through the adversity of the time and to sustain weakness through its brevity.

And the beast that was, and is not, is itself the eighth, etc. Antichrist, who will reign at the end of the age, belongs to the number of the kingdoms of the world because of the unity of that same body of the impious, of which he is the head; but because of the singular power of his wickedness, he is also included in the order of his own particular place.

And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings, etc. The kingdoms of the world have not yet fully displayed their power in persecuting the Church. Although even now they rule over very many, the power of their insane boasting was more violent when they also deceived many by signs. Some interpret this as referring to ten future kings, when the final persecution draws near, who will divide the world among themselves, also in accordance with Daniel’s prophecy, where he said of the fourth beast: “And it had ten horns; and behold, another little horn arose in the midst of them; and three of the first horns were plucked up before it” (Dan. VII). They also say that Antichrist, born in Babylon, will overcome the kings of Egypt, Africa, and Ethiopia; after these have been killed, seven other kings as well will submit their necks to the victor. Others, however, say that Antichrist is placed in the number eleven to signify transgression. For eleven signifies the transgression of the perfection represented by ten.

But they will receive authority as kings for one hour after the beast. He said “as kings,” because those who oppose Christ’s kingdom reign as though in a dream.

These have one purpose, etc. That is, with equal agreement and complete devotion they serve the devil—for this is what it means to receive a kingdom after the beast: to oppose Christ by imitating the devil.

These will wage war against the Lamb, etc. So that human weakness might not fear the savagery of the ancient enemy, he describes the seven-headed beast, armed with the horns of worldly rule, as being conquered by the triumphing Christ. Indicating that Christ triumphs in his own members, he adds:

And those who are with him, called, chosen, and faithful. He rightly placed “chosen” first, for many are called, but few are chosen.

And the ten horns that you saw, etc. The glory of the world, which they now embrace with wanton love, they will then begin to detest with the greatest hatred, when they see themselves condemned at the end as the Lamb conquers. This may also be understood otherwise: either because among the proud there are always quarrels, or because “whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X).

And they will make her desolate and naked. Through the wrath of God they themselves make the world desolate, while they are devoted to it and use it unjustly.

And they will eat her flesh, etc. Having stripped her of her customary luxuries, they will burn her in the fires of Gehenna.

For God has put it into their hearts, etc. God, he says, the just and mighty judge, to whom justice has always been pleasing, permitted the impious to perform such deeds as punishment for their former sin—deeds for which he would deservedly bring the end of the entire world, as the Gospels testify happened at Sodom and in the Flood.

[Col. 0185A] So that they may give their kingdom to the beast, etc. That is, so that they may obey the devil until the Scriptures are fulfilled, through which God said that the fourth kingdom would bring the earth to an end, as we read in Daniel: “The fourth will be a kingdom upon the earth, which will prevail over all those kingdoms. It will devour the whole earth, overthrow it, and destroy it” (Dan. VII).

And the woman whom you saw is the great city, etc. Thus also below, when he was commanded to contemplate the bride of the Lamb, he saw the holy city descending from heaven. When he described it, he said: “And the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it” (Apoc. XXI). For there are two cities in the world: one arising from the abyss, the other from the heavenly regions. Hence he now compares that same impiety—which he had described under the guise of a stripped and burned harlot—to the ruins of a deserted city.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0185B]

And after these things I saw another angel descending from heaven, having great authority, etc. This strong angel, who illuminates the earth, may be understood both as the Lord incarnate and as the teachers of the Church. Endowed with heavenly light, they proclaim the world’s downfall, saying: “The kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. III, IV).

Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, etc. “Do not fear,” he says, “O Jerusalem, the power of the earthly city,” which falls spiritually by the very fact that it prevails over you through the assault of its wicked citizens. Isaiah likewise describes Babylon as inhabited by unclean monsters. For it is nothing other than the city of the devil, which receives every unclean soul and in which every impurity dwells throughout the world.

And the merchants of the earth became rich through the power of her luxuries. Those who exchange their souls in an unhappy trade for temporal abundance are called rich in sins. For excessive luxury makes people poor rather than rich.

Come out of her, my people, etc. Thus also Isaiah says: “Come out from their midst, and do not touch anything unclean. Purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII). Having foretold Babylon’s ruin, he introduces the departure that constitutes Babylon’s ruin. For when Lot has departed from Sodom, they will be utterly destroyed.

Repay her as she herself repaid you. For visible and invisible afflictions come out from the Church into the world.

And double the double according to her works. So that she who enjoyed temporal luxuries may be tormented by eternal punishments.

Because in her heart she says: I sit as queen, and I am not a widow, etc. Because she delighted in present luxuries and refused to guard against future vengeance, she will therefore be punished in a short time by both spiritual and bodily destruction. By contrast, the citizens of the heavenly homeland, who set Jerusalem at the beginning of their joy, do not wish to make the Lord’s song resound in a foreign land (Ps. CXXXVI)—that is, to receive in the present the joy owed to the future age.

And the kings of the earth will weep and mourn over her, etc. This weeping of Babylon’s kings, merchants, and sailors may be understood in two ways: either when, on the day of judgment, all the glory of the world has perished and only the memory of their former life remains to the impious, who say, “What did our pride profit us? Or what did the boasting of our wealth bring us? All these things have passed like a shadow” (Wis. V); or when, in the present, the abundance of possessions ceases and the distress of various nations approaches, so that the opportunity for the outpouring of carnal delights—through which the desires of the wicked were being fulfilled—is taken away.

When they see the smoke of her burning. That is, the sign of destruction, since smoke precedes fire. For what else are this devastation and collapse of the world than the smoke of impending Gehenna?

Standing far away because of fear of her torments. They stand far away not in body but in spirit, while each fears for himself what he sees another suffering through accusations and power.

[Col. 0186B] Saying: Woe, woe, that great city, Babylon, etc. The Spirit names the city, but they mourn the world, whose punishment has cut short its existence after a very brief time and caused all its industry, corrupted by defilement, to cease.

And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her, etc. They mourn the failure of all the world’s splendors and of those things that are either pleasant to the bodily senses or useful for external purposes. The appearance of metals pertains to sight; spices, to smell; ointments, to touch; wine, wheat, and oil, to taste. By the mention of beasts of burden and slaves, the remaining aids of human life are understood to perish. This is meant in the two ways I have mentioned: either that these things fail when the world dies, or that the miserable survivors lament as the ruins of their own city the destruction of those who, by death, have left behind the joys of the world. They are also said to stand far away because they fear a similar punishment.

Those who became rich through her will stand far away. Wherever the Spirit says that people were enriched by her, he signifies the riches of sins. Below, however, where the voice of the unjust is heard saying, “Woe, woe, that great city, in which all who have ships at sea became rich,” riches of possessions are understood. They think that they have been enriched by the cleverness of their faction.

She who was clothed in fine linen, purple, and scarlet. Is a city clothed in fine linen or purple, and not human beings? Thus they lament themselves, while they are stripped of the things mentioned above.

And every helmsman and all who sail, stood far away, etc. Could everyone who sails the sea be present to see the burning of the city? Rather, he says that all the devotees and workers of the age fear for themselves when they see the ruin of their hope.

Saying: What is like this great city? That is, the world cannot be restored to wholeness.

And they threw dust upon their heads. That is, reproaching the face of their rulers, by whom they had been deceived and were perishing; or, in late repentance, accusing the madness of their own heart, which is the governing part of the human being.

Because in one hour she has been laid waste. Note that each of the mourners laments not only the loss of riches but also the sudden and unforeseen ruin of the deceptive age.

Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints, apostles, and prophets. [Col. 0187A] Thus also the Lord, predicting the world’s ruin in the Gospel, added: “When you see these things happening, look up and lift up your heads” (Luke XXI)—that is, make your hearts glad.

Because God has judged your judgment concerning her. This is what the souls of the saints sought with a great cry: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you refrain from judging and avenging our blood?” (Apoc. VI).

And one strong angel lifted up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying: With such force Babylon will be thrown down. Or, as another edition reads: “Thus with force the great city Babylon will be cast down.” The city of the age, because of the weight and error of sinners, is compared to an unstable millstone. For the impious walk in circles. It is rightly swallowed by the waves of vengeance, because it oppressed the citizens of Jerusalem with the waves of unbelief, when, sitting by the rivers of Babylon, they wept over the absence of heavenly Zion. The Lord says that the authors of scandal will be punished by such a penalty. The Church, indeed, is also compared to a stone, but to one stable and firm, which scorns the assaults of storms. The millstone may also be understood as the crushing of punishments. For blessed Ignatius is said to have spoken thus when he was about to suffer: “I am God’s grain; I am ground by the teeth of beasts so that I may become pure bread.”

The voice of harpists and musicians, etc. He had postponed the sound belonging to the five senses, which he now says, among other things, will be removed from the world. It is as though he said: Whatever is beautiful to sight, harmonious to hearing, smooth to touch, pleasant to smell, and delightful to taste will pass away from the age.

[Col. 0187C] And every craftsman of every craft will no longer be found in you, etc. Everything, he says, that belongs to the use or enjoyment of human life is removed from the impious. And he added the reason, saying:

Because your merchants were the rulers of the earth. That is, because “in your lifetime you received good things” (Luke XVI).

And in her was found the blood of prophets and saints, etc. Was it the same city that killed the apostles, the prophets, and all the saints? Rather, this is the city that Cain founded with the blood of his brother and named after his son Enoch—that is, after all his posterity. For seven generations of Cain are recorded. Into the building of this city all righteous blood is poured, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah (Matt. XXIII)—that is, of the people and the priest.

## CHAPTER XIX

After these things I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven saying: Alleluia, etc. The Church now says this in part, but then she will say it perfectly, when the separation has taken place and she has been vindicated more openly.

She who corrupted the earth through her prostitution, etc. He mentions two deeds of the harlot: that she corrupted herself through evil and persecuted the good. By these two things, I think, he encompasses all the crimes of the wicked.

And again they said: Alleluia. The Church praises the Lord over his judgments with unceasing devotion. For Alleluia means “Praise the Lord.” Indeed, the psalms that begin with “Praise the Lord” begin among the Hebrews with Alleluia.

And her smoke rises forever and ever. He said “has risen,” not “will rise.” Babylon is always proceeding toward destruction, and is already being burned in part, just as Jerusalem passes into paradise, as the Lord made clear in the account of the poor man and the rich man.

And the twenty-four elders fell down, and the four living creatures worshiped God. The Church venerates God not merely with the service of her lips but with the supreme sweetness of devotion.

Saying: Amen, alleluia. Although these words can be translated—for, as I said, they are rendered as “faith” or “truth” and “the praise of the Lord”—nevertheless, out of reverence, authority is preserved for them in their first language. The Church also continually sings Alleluia on Sundays and throughout the entire period of Pentecost, because of the hope of the resurrection that will come in the Lord’s praise.

And a voice came from the throne, saying: Give praise to our God, etc. When he commands this to be done and recalls that it has been done, he indicates that the praise of his servants, the elect, has been approved. “The small and the great,” he says, because lack of intellectual ability does not hinder one whose heart and tongue are filled with the praise of the Lord.

And I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude and what seemed to be the voice of many waters, etc. The great voice of the singers is the great devotion of the heart. Through manifold repetition of praise, it celebrates both the ruin of the impious and the eternal glory of the Lord and of his own people.

[Col. 0188C] And let us give him glory, because the marriage-feast of the Lamb has come. The marriage-feast of the Lamb takes place when the Church is joined to the Lord in the bridal chamber of the heavenly kingdom.

And his wife has prepared herself. By constantly devoting herself to works of righteousness, she has shown herself worthy of the spiritual banquet and the everlasting kingdom. This may also be understood according to the Gospel parable, which tells of virgins rising when the bridegroom comes and trimming their lamps—that is, counting the works they carry with them, for which they await the reception of eternal blessedness.

And it was granted to her that she should clothe herself in shining, bright fine linen. It was granted to her to be clothed in her deeds. By contrast, the impious, who, according to Isaiah, weave spiders’ webs, will not be covered by their works. For their works are useless works.

And he says to me: Write: Blessed are those who have been invited to the marriage-feast of the Lamb. He says that they are invited not to a midday meal but to a supper, because the banquet at the end of the day is supper. Therefore those who come, when the time of the present life has ended, to the refreshment of heavenly contemplation are certainly invited to the supper of the Lamb.

These are the true words of God. That is, what I have foretold will truly happen.

See that you do not do this. I am your fellow servant and one of your brothers. Above he had said: “I am the first and the last” (Apoc. I). Thus he shows that the angel was sent as a figure of the Lord and the Church. For at the end he also says: “I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify these things to you in the churches” (Apoc. XXII).

[Col. 0189A] Those who have the testimony of Jesus. After the Lord Jesus had raised the assumed human being above the heavens, the angel feared being worshiped by a human being—namely, worshiping above himself the human being who was God. We read that this had been done by human beings before the Lord’s Incarnation and had by no means been prohibited by angels.

The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy. Whatever the spirit of prophecy has said is the testimony of Jesus, who has testimony from the Law and the Prophets. “Do not worship me, therefore,” he says, “as God, since I have come to bear testimony to his powers.” Thus far he has spoken of Babylon’s ruin; from this point onward, of the future glory of Jerusalem.

And I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse, etc. The Lord, who is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV), and to whom it is said through the prophet, “For you have done marvelous things, ancient purposes, faithful, amen” (Isa. XXV), mounted the seat of a white body—that is, of an immaculate body—to overthrow the aerial powers.

And in righteousness he judges and fights. He judges as the King of the ages. He fights because, always suffering together with his members, he battles in them.

And his eyes were like a flame of fire. At times he calls God’s commandments “eyes,” and at times the Spirit. “Your word,” he says, “is a lamp to my feet, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII). And concerning the Spirit: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII).

And upon his head were many diadems. In him we shall perform valorous deeds; in him the multitude of the saints is said to possess a crowned splendor.

He had a name written that no one knows except himself. [Col. 0189C] “Except himself,” he says, because the whole Church is in him. For the perfect knowledge of the Word of God is revealed to those who have been worthy to be the body and members of Christ. In the same way the Lord also says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III).

And he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood. Christ’s garment should be understood according to its various aspects. Here, therefore, he appears to indicate the very work of the Passion: the incorrupt birth is signified in the white horse, and the innocent death in the bloodstained garment.

And his name was called the Word of God. Because the same one who appeared for a time as a human being destined to suffer was, in the beginning, God with God (John I). He is called the Word either because nothing visible or corporeal exists in the substance of his nature, or because through him the Father created all things. The complete knowledge of his nature, as he said above, is known only to himself and the Father. For “the peace of God surpasses all understanding” (Phil. IV)—that is, the peace by which God himself is at peace with himself transcends the understanding of every creature, whether human or angelic. For “there is no numbering of his wisdom.” When it is said, “and to whomever the Son wishes to reveal” (Matt. XI)—namely, that he knows the Son and the Father—this refers to the capacity of the creature.

And the armies that are in heaven followed him on white horses. That is, the Church in shining bodies imitated him. Because of the struggle of her contest, she rightly receives the name “army.”

Clothed in white, clean fine linen. This he explained above as the righteous deeds of the saints, in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “Let your priests be clothed in righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI).

And from his mouth proceeds a sharp sword. Thus also Isaiah says: “He made my mouth like a sharp sword” (Isa. XLIX). And the Apostle says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI).

And he himself treads the winepress of the wine of the fury and wrath of God Almighty. For even now he treads it, until he treads outside the city.

And on his garment and on his thigh he has written: King of kings and Lord of lords. This is the name that none of the proud know. In the Church, however, it is inscribed not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, on the tablets, that is, of the heart (II Cor. III). The thigh signifies the posterity of the seed. Hence Abraham, lest his posterity be mingled with foreigners, used his thigh as a third witness between himself and his servant. Concerning this, the Apostle, raising up seed for the dead brother, says: “For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (I Cor. IV). It may also be understood in this way: the Church reigns by serving in Christ and rules over rulers. The same name is also written on the garment, because through the mystery of his birth and the work of his Passion his majesty and kingdom are disclosed to us. In what follows he explains what this attire of the king and the army signifies: namely, the labor of the final contest and the glory of the kingdom that follows.

And I saw an angel standing in the sun, etc. That is, preaching in the Church, which shines more brightly the more it is oppressed and cries out more freely.

Saying to all the birds, etc. He calls the saints birds, living the life of heaven: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. XXIV). Gathering them into one body, he had said that an eagle was flying in mid-heaven.

Come, gather for the great supper of God, etc. “Come,” he says, “you who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. V), to the banquets of the kingdom to come, where, once the fury of the proud has been restrained, you will be filled with the light of divine justice.

And the flesh of horses and of those seated upon them. I think these are the horsemen whom he had described as coming against the Lord’s white horse at the opening of the seals.

And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth . . . to make war, etc. He explains how that supper of God has been prepared: namely, with the devil attacking the Church but being defeated.

The two were cast alive into the lake of burning fire and sulfur, etc. This seems to signify that the devil and Antichrist will be punished with a punishment far greater than that of other human beings or demons, just as it is more grievous to be burned alive in flames of sulfur than to die quickly by the sword. Unless perhaps it signifies that divine aversion has overtaken them in advance. For “whoever has not believed has already been judged” (John III). Whether you understand by this Antichrist called the false prophet or heretics, no mortal sins more grievously than heretics, who, after they have come to know Christ, deny him.

[Col. 0191A] And all the birds were filled with their flesh. If the righteous now rejoice when they see the vengeance of the impious, how much more then, when they are present with the Judge himself and become one spirit with him. The birds may also be understood as unclean spirits, who will be satisfied by the destruction of their own kind. Tychonius explains this supper as follows: “At all times the Church eats the flesh of her enemies, while she is eaten by them; but in the resurrection she will be satisfied, having been avenged of their carnal work.”

## CHAPTER XX

And I saw an angel . . . holding the key of the abyss, etc. Recapitulating from the beginning, he explains more fully how he said above: “The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the abyss, and it will go into destruction” (Apoc. [Col. 0191B] XVII). The Lord, therefore, endowed with the Father’s authority, descended into the flesh to wage war against the prince of the world and, after binding him, to seize his vessels.

And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, etc. The devil is interpreted as “flowing downward.” In Greek he is called *diabolos*, “the accuser.” Satan means “adversary” or “transgressor.” He is called dragon because of his harmful wickedness; serpent because of his skill in deception; devil because of the fall of his status; Satan because of his obstinacy in opposing the Lord.

And he bound him for a thousand years. That is, restraining his power from deceiving the human beings who were destined to be liberated, he curbed it. If he had been permitted to exercise it fully by force or fraud, over so long a time he would have deceived very many of the weak. He said “a thousand years,” meaning a part: the remainder of the thousand years of the sixth day, on which the Lord was born and suffered.

And he cast him into the abyss. That is, into the hearts of the persecuting people. Not because the devil had not previously been there, but because, excluded from believers, he began to possess the impious more fully—those who are not only alienated from God but hate God’s servants all the more intensely. The Lord visibly demonstrated this when he drove him out of human beings into pigs.

And he shut it and sealed it over him so that he might no longer deceive the nations. He forbade him and, as though closing him with a royal seal, prevented him from deceiving the nations—those, namely, who are destined for life and whom he had previously deceived so that they might not be reconciled to God.

[Col. 0191D] After these things he must be released for a short time. Then he will be released, as Saint Augustine says, when the time will also be short—for he is read to rage with all his strength and that of his followers for three and a half years—and when those with whom he must wage war will be such that they cannot be conquered by the force and snares of his assault. If he were never released, his malignant power would be less evident, the most faithful endurance of the holy city would be less tested, and, finally, it would be less apparent how greatly the almighty God had made such good use of his great evil.

And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, etc. He indicates what is done during these thousand years in which the devil is bound. For the Church, which will sit with Christ upon twelve thrones to judge, is already seated and judging. She has deserved to hear from her King: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

And the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus, etc. The words to be supplied are what he will say shortly afterward: “They reigned with Christ for a thousand years.” The Church therefore reigns with Christ among the living and the dead. For this reason, as the Apostle says, Christ died so that he might rule over both the living and the dead (Rom. XIV). But he mentioned only the souls of the martyrs because those who fought for the truth unto death reign especially after death. As for what follows:

And those who did not worship the beast, etc. We should understand this together of the living and the dead: whether they are still living in this mortal flesh or, having died, they reign with Christ, already now in a certain manner appropriate to this age, throughout the entire interval signified by the number of a thousand years.

The rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years were completed. Whoever throughout this entire period, during which the first resurrection—that is, of souls—is taking place, has not heard the voice of the Son of God and passed from death to life will certainly, in the second resurrection, which is that of the flesh, pass with that very flesh into the second death—that is, eternal torments.

This, he says, is the first resurrection. Namely, the resurrection by which we rise through baptism, as the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Col. III). For just as the first death in this life occurs through sins, when the soul that sins itself dies, so the first resurrection in this life occurs through the forgiveness of sins.

Blessed and holy, etc. That is, the one who has preserved what he has become by rebirth.

But they will be saints of God and of Christ. Another edition reads: “Priests of God and of Christ.” This is not said only of bishops and presbyters, who are properly called priests in the Church; rather, just as we are all called “Christs” because of the mystical anointing, so we are all priests, because we are members of the one Priest. Concerning these the Apostle Peter says: “A holy people, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II).

And they will reign with Christ for a thousand years. When the Spirit wrote these things, he said that the Church would reign for a thousand years—that is, until the end of the world—and hence there might be doubt. For it is clear that the reign is perpetual.

And when the thousand years have been completed, etc. He called them completed as a whole although only a part had passed, for he will be released with three years and six months of the final contest still remaining. But apart from this figure, the time is rightly said to have ended. Those very small remnants should not be counted, since seven hundred years—and as many as God wills—are called an hour by the Apostle.

And he will go out and deceive the nations, etc. He will then deceive them for the purpose of gathering them for this battle. Previously also he deceived them in whatever ways he could through many and varied evils. “He will go out” means that he will burst forth from the hiding places of hatred into open persecution. Moreover, Gog and Magog either signify the whole by a part or, according to the interpretation of their names—which mean “covering” and “from the covering” (*tectum* and *de tecto*)—indicate hidden and open enemies. They themselves are the covering, because the enemy is now enclosed and ruled in them; and they themselves will be from the covering when they are about to burst forth into open hatred.

And they went up over the breadth of the earth, etc. This does not mean that they came or will come to one place, as though the beloved city—that is, the Church—were to be confined in some single location. Rather, by the expression “the breadth of the earth,” he preferred to indicate that she would then be persecuted among all nations and would not abandon her military service, using the language of a camp.

And fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them. This should not be thought to be the final punishment, but rather the fire of envy by which the adversary will be tormented because of the steadfastness of the saints. For heaven is a firmament. This is the fire that went out from the mouths of God’s witnesses and will devour their enemies. For on the last day he will not rain fire upon them; rather, he will send those gathered and judged before him into eternal fire, concerning which he adds here:

And the devil who deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and sulfur, etc. That is, at the final judgment the devil will be cast into eternal fire, where all those whom he brought forward beforehand—that is, the greater part of the impious city—will also be. The beast must be understood according to its various contexts: now as the devil, now as Antichrist, now as the impious city itself. The name of the fire descending from heaven may also signify the sudden destruction of the impious, when the Lord comes and kills Antichrist by the breath of his mouth (II Thess. II). He explains at greater length how, when Christ judges, the devil and his followers will be sent into the fire.

And I saw a great white throne, etc. He said that he saw one seated upon the throne, from whose presence earth and heaven fled. For after the judgment has been completed, he indicates that heaven and earth will exist when heaven and a new earth begin to be—through a transformation of things, not their total destruction. For “the form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. VII); he did not say its substance. The same things, it is believed, will be changed for the better.

And I saw the dead, great and small, standing in the presence of the throne. For when the Son of Man has sat upon the throne of his majesty, then all the nations will be gathered before him.

[Col. 0193D] And the books were opened, etc. Another edition reads: “Which is the life of each person.” By the books opened, therefore, he means God’s Testaments. For the world will be judged according to both Testaments. The book of each person’s life he calls the record of our deeds—not that the Knower of hidden things possesses a commemorative book.

And the dead were judged from these things, etc. That is, they were judged from the Testaments according to what they did or did not do from them. The books may also be understood as the deeds of the righteous, since, when the reprobate are condemned by comparison with them, they read, as though in an opened book, the good that they themselves refused to do.

And the sea gave up its dead, etc. This certainly happened before the dead were judged. Therefore he recapitulated what he had omitted and follows the sequence, saying:

And judgment was given concerning each one, etc. He signifies that the bodies are to be gathered from the earth and the souls from their respective places. He designates the good by the name of death, since they have suffered only the dissolution of the flesh and not punishment as well. He designates the evil by the term “hell.” This may also be taken literally: all bodies, including those swallowed by the waves or devoured by a beast, will rise again. Tychonius explains it as follows: “The nations whom he will find alive here are the dead of the sea. And death and hell gave up their dead: these are the nations buried.” Having said, “And each was judged according to his works,” he briefly added how death and hell were also cast into the lake of fire. He means the devil and his followers, whom hell will follow, seated above on the pale horse. For he repeats what he had already said more clearly by anticipating it: “And the devil who deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and sulfur.” What he had added there more obscurely—namely, that the beast and the false prophet were also cast there—he explains more openly here.

And whoever was not found written in the book of life. That is, whoever was not judged by God to be alive. Hence those seem to me to speak more correctly who interpret the books opened above as the consciences of individuals and their disclosed deeds. The book of life, however, they interpret as God’s foreknowledge—which cannot be deceived—concerning those to whom eternal life will be given, in which they are written, that is, known beforehand. Having finished the judgment in which he saw that the wicked were to be condemned, it remains for him also to speak of the good.

## CHAPTER XXI

And I saw a new heaven and a new earth, etc. This will happen in the order that he already stated above by anticipation: that he saw one seated upon the throne, before whose face heaven and earth fled, once the impious had been judged. Then the form of this world will pass away through the conflagration of heavenly fires, so that, with heaven and earth changed for the better, the quality of both transformations may correspond to the incorruption and immortality of the saints’ bodies. But when he says:

And the sea was no more. Whether it will be dried up by that immense heat, or whether it too will be transformed into something better, I would not readily say. For we read that there will be a new heaven and a new earth, but not that there will also be a new sea. Unless perhaps, as prophetic speech is accustomed to do, it has mingled figurative expressions with literal words and represented by the name “sea” the turbulent life of this age, which will then cease.

And the holy city, the new Jerusalem, etc. This city is said to descend from heaven because it is heavenly grace by which God made it. Made ready like a bride adorned for her husband; for there is another Jerusalem that is adorned not for her husband but for an adulterer.

Behold, the dwelling of God with human beings, etc. God himself will be the reward of eternal blessedness for the elect, and those whom he possesses will possess him forever.

And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Such great and exalted splendor of that city will appear through God’s gift that no traces of antiquity will remain. [Col. 0195A] For heavenly incorruption will raise their bodies up, and the contemplation of the eternal King will nourish their minds.

And death will be no more, etc. For he had foretold that death would be cast into the lake of fire. The same statement may also be understood in this way: once the holy city has been glorified at the final judgment, pain, mourning, and mortality will remain only in Gehenna.

And he said to me, “Write,” etc. And he said to me, “It is done.” These things ought to be believed, not explained, especially since he says that they have been done in the past, so that he leaves no one room to doubt the future.

I am Alpha, etc. Just as at the beginning of the book he testified that he was this, so it was fitting that it be repeated a third time, so that no other God might be believed to exist either before him, as Isaiah says, or after him (Isa. XLIII). And because the subject is the end of the world, he himself may be understood as the one who brings the age to completion, who is said to be its Creator.

I will give to the thirsty, etc. From this fountain he now sprinkles believers on the way, while in the homeland he provides it abundantly for the conquerors to drink. Both are given freely. For “the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” And “from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace” (John I).

But for the cowardly, the unbelieving, and the abominable, etc. To encourage vigilance, he always mingles harsh statements with gentle ones. Thus also Psalm 144, while abundantly proclaiming the grace of the Lord’s mercies, suddenly introduces his strict judgment, saying: “The Lord guards all who love him, but he will destroy all sinners” (Ps. CXLIV). He joins the cowardly to the unbelieving because the one who doubts the victor’s reward fears to undergo the danger of the contest.

And the portion of all liars will be in the burning lake. He shows that there are many kinds of lying, but the most dangerous and most detestable is the lie by which one sins against religion; concerning this he said above: “They say that they are Jews, and they are not, but they are lying; for they are the synagogue of Satan.”

And one of the seven angels came, etc. The same preachers who inflict the sevenfold, that is, universal, plague upon the wicked also disclose to the Church its future joys.

“Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.” He calls the Church both bride and wife: remaining undefiled, she continually gives birth to spiritual children for God. Or because, now betrothed to God, she is then to be brought to an immortal marriage.

And he carried me away in the spirit onto a great and high mountain, etc. After Babylon’s downfall, the holy city, which is the Lamb’s bride, is seen placed upon a mountain. For the stone cut from the mountain without hands crushed the statue of worldly glory, grew into a great mountain, and filled the whole world (Dan. II).

Descending from heaven from God, possessing the glory of God. For then she will appear more splendid, when, through the Spirit by whom her bridegroom is believed to have been conceived and born, she has fully deserved to bear the heavenly image.

Its light was like a precious stone. The precious stone is Christ, who says: “The glory that you gave me, I have given them” (John XVII).

Like a jasper stone, like crystal. Jasper signifies the brightness of virtues; crystal, the inward purity of the mind and unfeigned faith (I Tim. I).

And it had a great and high wall. That is, an unconquerable firmness of faith, hope, and love. The Lord himself, protecting the Church on every side, may also be understood as the great wall, concerning which Isaiah says: “A wall and a rampart will be placed in it” (Isa. XXVI)—that is, the Lord’s protection and the intercession of the saints, who prepare a way for him by teaching the hearts of believers.

Having twelve gates. These gates are the apostles, who, initially for all the nations, opened the entrance to the Church by their writings and their works.

[Col. 0196B] And on the gates twelve angels. That is, teachers who follow the apostles’ footsteps in the mystery of faith and the word.

And names written, etc. He signifies the memory of the ancient fathers implanted in the hearts of preachers. Hence the high priest, when he was to enter the tabernacle, was also commanded to carry the memorial of the fathers upon the breastpiece of his chest.

Three gates on the east, etc. I think that by such careful description of the gates he wished to indicate the mystery of the number twelve. Through it the fullness of the apostles, or the perfection of the Church, is represented, because through the Church the faith of the holy Trinity was to be proclaimed to the four-square world.

And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, etc. What the gates are, the foundations are; what the city is, the wall is. The patriarchs too may be designated by the term “foundations,” since they held within themselves the names of the apostles—that is, their figure. Through them this city became established, although through the apostles, as through gates, it was opened more widely to the nations who would believe. It should also be noted that when “foundations” is expressed in the plural, it signifies the teachers or virtues of the Church; when expressed in the singular, it signifies the Lord himself, who is the foundation of foundations.

And the one who was speaking with me, etc. Christ, who is the wisdom of God (I Cor. I), “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII), measures the holy city. For, establishing all things according to number, measure, and weight, he distributes gifts of grace to each of the faithful according to their spiritual capacity. [Col. 0196D] The teachers of the Church may also be understood here: frail in body but heavenly in mind, they carefully examine the merits of individuals.

And the city is set out as a square. The city is therefore said to be set out as a square and placed with equal dimensions on every side because it is not permitted to show any inequality. To be perfect, according to the apostle—that is, to have understanding and to possess peace—is truly to stand firm in square solidity.

And he measured the city by twelve stadia. That is, he saw, or granted, the Church to be perfect in faith and works. For the perfection of the four chief virtues, raised up by faith in the holy Trinity, as though by the number twelve, constitutes the Church’s dignity.

[Col. 0197A] Its length and width and height are equal. This is that solidity of unconquered truth by which the Church, supported by the length of faith, the breadth of love, and the height of hope, is not allowed to be carried about by every wind of teaching (Eph. IV). If it possesses any one of these to a lesser degree, the Church’s perfect stability will not exist.

And he measured its wall, one hundred forty-four cubits. This sum contains the squareness of the number twelve—for twelve times twelve makes one hundred forty-four—and itself signifies the stable perfection of the holy city.

The measure of a human being, which is that of an angel. For the Church consists of human beings gathered together, and, exalted by Christ’s promises, hopes for equality with the angels. As far as the literal sense is concerned, he indicated that the angel appeared to him in human form.

[Col. 0197B] And the structure of the wall was of jasper stone. This is what the apostle Peter urges: “And you, like living stones, are being built into spiritual houses” (I Pet. II).

But the city itself was pure gold, like pure glass. The Church is represented by gold; it is often described as adorned with golden lampstands and bowls because of its devotion to wisdom. He referred the glass to faith in the truth, because what is seen outside is also within, and in the saints of the Church nothing is feigned or opaque. This may also refer to the time when thoughts are perceptively disclosed to one another.

The foundations of the city wall were adorned with every precious stone. By the names of various stones, either the forms of the virtues, or their order, or their diversity, is indicated; by these the whole heavenly Jerusalem is built. It is difficult for individuals to flourish in every virtue. Accordingly, when Isaiah was describing the adornment of this same city, saying, “Behold, I will arrange your stones in order, and I will found you upon sapphires” (Isa. LIV), and so forth, he immediately added, as though explaining it: “All your children will be taught by the Lord” (ibid.).

The first foundation was jasper. There are many kinds of jasper. One is green in color and appears tinged as though with flowers. Another resembles emerald, but has a thick color; they say that it drives away all phantoms. Another gleams with a color as though white snow and the foam of sea waves were mixed together. Jasper therefore indicates the unfading greenness of faith, which is steeped in the sacrament of the Lord’s passion through the water of baptism and, as its merits advance, is furnished with every flower of spiritual grace. Whoever possesses this faith drives away empty fears, as the blessed apostle Peter warns: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (I Pet. V). Such a person can say with the bride: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song V). Hence, appropriately, from this stone the wall’s structure is both fortified and adorned here and, in Isaiah, the battlements of the same city are likewise fortified and adorned.

The second was sapphire. Moses explained both the color and the mystery of this stone when, describing God’s appearance, he said: “Under his feet was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear” (Exod. XXIV). Ezekiel likewise says that the place where God’s throne is has the likeness of sapphire; and the Lord’s glory consists in this color, which bears the image of the one who is above heaven, so that whoever is such may say with the apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). Struck by the sun’s rays, it emits a fiery radiance from itself. Because the mind of the saints, always intent upon heavenly things and renewed daily by the rays of divine light, seeks eternal things with a kind of increasing contrition and ardor, and urges others to seek them. Its reputed discovery in the Red Sea signifies that through the Lord’s passion and the washing of holy baptism the minds of mortals are exalted toward the presumption of heavenly things.

[Col. 0198B] The third was chalcedony. Chalcedony shines like the pale appearance of a lamp’s fire, and it has a luster under the open sky, not inside a house. It represents those who, supported by heavenly desire, nevertheless remain hidden from human beings and, as though in secret, carry out their fasts, almsgiving, and prayers. But when they are commanded to come into public service, whether for teaching or for other needs of the saints, they immediately reveal what radiance they have carried within. It is said to resist engraving, but when heated by the sun’s rays or by rubbing with the fingers, to attract straw to itself. This aptly suits those who allow no one to overcome their strength, but rather by the fire of their own light and ardor bring the weaker together with them until they are joined to its authority. Of one of these it is said: “He was the burning and shining lamp” (John V)—burning in love, shining in speech. They continually revive the light of their virtues with the oil of inward love, so that it does not fail. And the fact that it is born among the Nasamones, which is a province of Ethiopia, indicates those who, beneath the burning heat of love, nevertheless remain obscure, as though soiled by dark skin.

The fourth was emerald. Emerald is of such intense greenness that it surpasses all green herbs, leaves, and gems, dyeing the air around it green with reflected color; it rightly prospers through green oil, although it is imbued with this by nature. It has many varieties, but the Scythian are the noblest. The Bactrian hold second place; the Egyptian, third. It signifies souls ever green with faith. The more they are tested by the adversity of the world, represented by the cold of Scythia, [Col. 0198D] the more they hope to conceive in their minds the imperishable inheritance preserved in heaven, and strive to spread it among their neighbors by preaching. They also advance toward contempt for the world through the cup of the Lord’s passion and through the inward richness of love given by the Holy Spirit.

The homeland of this same stone also aptly corresponds to them in a beautiful manner: a rich but uninhabitable land. For although it abounds in gold and gems, griffins possess the whole region—most savage winged creatures, or rather flying beasts. They are four-footed, with bodies resembling lions but heads and wings like eagles. The Arimaspians fight with them; these are said to be distinguished by one eye in the middle of their forehead, so that they may obtain the stones, which the savage creatures seize and the Arimaspians guard, with marvelous eagerness.

For the Psalmist had approached this land, rich in the treasures of virtues, when he said: “Behold, I have fled far away, and remained in the wilderness” (Ps. LIV)—that is, by distancing and withdrawing my mind from the enticements of the world. In it he had encountered hostile beasts when, in his imprecation, he said: “May deceitful lips that speak iniquity against the righteous with pride and contempt be struck dumb” (Ps. XXX). In it too he declares that he has found desirable treasures when, with delighted wonder, he continued: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (ibid.), and the rest through the end of the psalm.

Against these winged creatures, eager to snatch away from us the seed of the divine word, all the saints keep watch with the single-minded attention of heavenly desire, as though with one eye, so that they may seek out and unearth the jewel of faith and the other virtues. For the higher any virtue is, the fewer cultivators it has and the more severe a persecution it endures from unclean spirits. Like dreadful griffins, earthly through the abasement of their merits but winged through the height of their proud minds, these spirits struggle tirelessly not to possess spiritual riches for their own use, but to take them away from human beings. And because such sublimity of faith became known to the world through the Gospel, emerald is appropriately placed fourth, on account of the four books of the Gospel.

The fifth was sardonyx. Drawing whiteness from onyx and redness from sardius, it received the name sardonyx from both. There are many varieties. One resembles red earth. Another appears two-colored, as though blood were shining through a human fingernail. Another consists of three colors: black beneath, white in the middle, and vermilion above. Human beings are compared to it: ruddy through bodily suffering, white through purity of spirit, yet despised in themselves through humility of mind, protesting with the apostle: “Although our outer self is being corrupted, nevertheless our inner self is renewed day by day” (II Cor. IV). And again: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but by this I am not justified” (I Cor. IV). Likewise the Psalmist: “Although a human being walks in the image of God” (Ps. XXXVIII)—that is, in the virtue of the mind—“yet he will be troubled in vain” (ibid.)—that is, through the weakness of the flesh. Since suffering is also involved in bodily weakness—“For those who kill the body cannot kill the soul” (Luke XII)—and humility descends from the frailty of that same body, as it is said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII), sardonyx is rightly inserted as the fifth foundation, since it is certain that our body subsists through the five senses.

The sixth was sardius. Sardius, which is wholly blood-red in color, signifies the glory of the martyrs, concerning which it is said: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV). It is rightly placed sixth, since our Lord was both incarnate in the sixth age of the world and crucified on the sixth day of the week for the salvation of the whole world.

The seventh was chrysolite. Chrysolite gleams like gold and has fiery sparks. By its appearance are represented those who, shining with the understanding of heavenly and true wisdom, pour forth words of exhortation upon their neighbors, or even signs of virtues, like sparks of fire. Of them, as Arator says:

> Love presses upon their minds; ardor boils over in their speech.

Since this is accomplished solely through the gift of spiritual grace, chrysolite most appropriately occurs as the seventh foundation. For the grace of the Holy Spirit is often represented by the number seven; concerning it he says above: “And from the seven spirits who are before his throne” (Rev. I). This interpretation is also supported by the fact that a kind of this same stone is found in blue and green colors. Hence among the Hebrews it is called *tharsis*, from its resemblance to the color of the sea. Green signifies the integrity of faith, which is called the beginning of wisdom; water, figuratively, pertains to the Holy Spirit, as the Lord attests when he says: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” This he said concerning the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive (John VII).

[Col. 0200B] The eighth was beryl. Beryl is like water struck by the sun’s radiance and made reddish and beautiful in color. But it does not shine unless it is polished and shaped into a six-sided form. For the reflected brilliance of its angles is sharpened. It signifies people who are indeed perceptive in intellect, but shine even more brightly through the light of heavenly grace. That water designates the depth of understanding is attested by Solomon, who says: “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth” (Prov. XVIII). But neither human nor even divine wisdom has perfect radiance unless the completion of works is also joined to it.
