For perfection of action is very often represented by the number six, especially since the work of this world was completed in that number. And because it is said to burn the hand that holds it, the meaning is undoubtedly clear: whoever is joined to a holy man is refreshed by the fire of his good conduct.

The ninth was topaz. Topaz is as rare in discovery as it is precious in the quantity of its commercial value. It is said to have two colors: one of the purest gold, the other shining with an ethereal brightness. It has a rosy richness and a modest purity, resembling chrysoprase in size or color; when struck by the sun’s splendor it is especially brilliant, surpassing the most precious radiances of all gems and uniquely summoning the eye’s eager delight to its appearance. If you wish to polish it, you darken it; if you leave it to its own nature, it radiates. It is said to be marvelous even to kings, so that they recognize that they possess nothing like it among their riches.

Its exceptionally beautiful natural quality is most appropriately compared with the excellence of the contemplative life. Holy kings, whose heart is in God’s hand, rightly prefer this life to all the riches of good works and every jewel of the virtues, directing toward it the gaze and attention of their pure mind above all. The more often they have been struck by the splendor of heavenly grace, the more ardently they embrace in their spirit the sweetness of heavenly life. Holy men therefore possess a golden color from the inward flame of love, and an ethereal color from contemplation of heavenly sweetness. The latter is often diminished by the turmoil of the present age, as though by the rubbing of a file. For the mind cannot easily, at one and the same moment, be distressed by earthly labors, troubles, cares, and pains while also contemplating, in a tranquil state, the joys of heavenly life; rather, sighing, it cries out: “My eye is troubled because of anger; I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. VI).

That it is said to be found on the island in the Thebaid called Topazion, from which it also received its name, is to be understood in two ways: first, because that region in particular—that is, the regions of Egypt—abounds in flocks of monks; and second, because whoever dwells near the Sun of righteousness is colored, so to speak, by the radiance of ethereal light. And fittingly, just as the perfection of the active life is placed in the eighth order, so the jewel of contemplative sweetness is placed in the ninth. This is either because Holy Scripture speaks of nine orders of angels, whose life it imitates, or because it is separated from the ten of perfect blessedness by only one degree, so to speak—that of death. Sighing with the highest desire for this, the prophet said: “Therefore I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz” (Ps. CXVIII)—that is, above all the splendor of tested action and above all the height of contemplative joy that can be achieved in this age. He delighted in the exceedingly sweet love of your commandments. Their first and greatest is: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matt. XXII). It is absolutely certain that this cannot be perfectly fulfilled except at the summit of that heavenly kingdom.

The tenth was chrysoprase. Chrysoprase is a mixture of green and gold, also drawing from it a kind of purple radiance, with golden drops interspersed. It is born in India. It signifies those who, earning the greenness of the eternal homeland through the splendor of perfect love, also reveal it to others through the purple light of their martyrdom. When, despising the present life and preferring eternal glory, they follow the examples of the Lord appearing in the flesh, they already display the radiance of their merits as though in India—that is, near the rising of the sun. And because they await, desiring to shine like the Sun in the Father’s kingdom and then to reign with their King, with whom they now suffer, they are rightly placed in the tenth position. For by the denarius with which the workers in the Lord’s vineyard are rewarded, the image of the eternal King to be received is represented. There, what could not be achieved in the ninth degree will be fulfilled in every respect: the Decalogue will be completed in perfect love of God and neighbor.

The eleventh was hyacinth. Hyacinth is found in Ethiopia and has a blue color. The finest kind is neither sparse nor dulled by density, but shines through a mixture of both and draws forth a gently purified bloom. It does not glow uniformly; rather, it changes with the appearance of the sky. In clear weather it is transparent and pleasing, but under cloudy skies it vanishes and withers before the eyes. It indicates souls always devoted to heavenly contemplation and drawing near, insofar as is permitted to mortals, to an angelic way of life.

[Col. 0202A] They are commanded to guard their hearts with every form of discretion, lest, being clever through excessive subtlety of understanding, they dare to seek things higher than themselves and investigate matters too difficult for them (Ecclus. III). For “it is the glory of God to conceal a word”—that is, to reason cautiously about God or about Christ as a human being—or lest, conversely, through sluggish indifference, they slide back to the weak beginnings of faith and the elementary stages of God’s words. Rather, walking along the royal road, protected on the right and on the left by the weapons of righteousness, let them proceed (II Cor. VI), and, changing their expression suitably with the sky according to the observance appropriate to the time, let them say to those who observe them: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (II Cor. V).

Like a hyacinth surrounded by clouds, it says: “You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own inward parts” (II Cor. VI). And again: “For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II). And, as though seen in clear light, it says: “But among the mature we speak wisdom” (ibid.).

The twelfth was amethyst. Amethyst is purple, mixed with a violet color, and, like the radiance of a rose, pours forth certain gentle flames. Yet in its purple there also appears something not wholly fiery, but like reddening wine. Its purple beauty therefore signifies the attire of the heavenly kingdom; its rosy and violet hues signify the humble modesty and precious death of the saints. Their mind is raised chiefly toward what is above, even when they are seen outwardly suffering disgrace, always remembering the Lord’s promise amid adversity: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke XII). They spread the flame of love not only among one another but also toward their persecutors, and, kneeling, implore: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” While drinking the cup of passion, they are rather made drunk by constant remembrance of that wine which gladdens the human heart (Ps. CIII), which the Lord promised he would drink anew with his disciples in the Father’s kingdom (Matt. XXVI).

In jasper, therefore, the greenness of faith is represented. In sapphire, the height of heavenly hope. In chalcedony, the flame of inward love. In emerald, the strong confession of that same faith amid adversity. In sardonyx, the humility of the saints amid their virtues. In sardius, the revered blood of the martyrs is expressed. In chrysolite, spiritual preaching amid miracles. In beryl, the perfected action of preachers. In topaz, their ardent contemplation is shown. In chrysoprase, both the work and the reward of blessed martyrs. In hyacinth, the heavenly lifting-up of teachers toward what is above and, for the sake of the weak, their humble descent toward human things. In amethyst, the continual remembrance of the heavenly kingdom in the minds of the humble is represented.

Each precious stone is assigned to its own foundation. For although all the perfect—those by whom the city of our God is adorned and founded on his holy mountain—shine with the light of spiritual grace, “to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge, to another gifts of healings, to another kinds of tongues, to another faith in the same Spirit,” and so forth (I Cor. XII). Its craftsman and founder is God, who is the foundation of foundations [Col. 0203A] and who also deigned to become high priest for us, so that by the sacrifice of his own blood he might both cleanse and consecrate the walls of the same city. Everything that the Father possesses, he possesses as his own.

Hence the same stones, inscribed with the names of the patriarchs, were commanded to be placed upon the breast of the high priest, so that through this most beautiful mystery it might be revealed that all the spiritual anointings which each of the saints received individually and in part were completed together and perfectly in the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ.

I seem perhaps to have explained these precious stones at greater length than the concise manner of interpretation warranted. It was necessary to explain carefully their natures and homeland, then to investigate their mystery more diligently, and also to follow their order and numbers. [Col. 0203B] But as far as the depth of the subject itself is concerned, I seem to have said very little, and that briefly and in summary. I earnestly beg the reader: if he sees that I have proceeded along the right path, let him give thanks to God. But if he discovers that matters have turned out otherwise than I wished, let him join me in asking the Lord to forgive my error. But enough of this; let us consider what remains.

And the twelve gates are twelve pearls, each one a single pearl. All the glory of the head is referred to the body. And just as the true light, which enlightens every human being (John I), granted the saints to be the light of the world, so he himself, although he is the one incomparable pearl, which the wise merchant buys after selling everything (Matt. XIII), nevertheless compares his own people to the radiance of pearls.

And the street of the city was pure gold, etc. He constructs the streets from the same metals with which he had already said that the city was adorned. For there are also many people of a broader and lower way of life, surrounded by the highest virtues in the Church, who shine with purity of mind and the radiance of their works.

And he saw no temple in it, etc. Although, he says, I have said that the city was built of stones, I did not thereby signify, in a material structure, the resting-place of the saints, for God himself is their one house, light, and rest.

And the city has no need of the sun or the moon to shine upon it. For the Church is not governed by light or by the elements of the world; rather, Christ, the eternal sun, leads it through the darkness of the world.

For the glory of God will illuminate it. In the homeland we will enjoy that very light by which we are now guided as we walk on the way. By the same light, while we are being formed, we distinguish between good and evil; then, when blessed, we will see only what is good.

And the nations will walk by its light. This signifies that the same Lamb is now the way for those journeying as strangers, and then will be the life of the citizens.

And the kings of the earth will bring their glory and honor into it. Here he calls spiritual kings those who bring all the riches of their virtues to the praises of the Church.

And its gates will not be shut by day, for there will be no night there. He declares that the Lamb’s light—or rather, that the Lamb himself as everlasting light—will be perpetual in that city, once the time of night has been removed. That the gates will not be shut is an indication of complete security. For there it will no longer be said, “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI), but rather: “Be still and know that I am God” (Ps. XLV).

[Col. 0204A] And they will bring the glory and honor of the nations into it. Because it is to be gathered from all the nations.

And nothing unclean will enter it, etc. He describes the Church of that time when, after the wicked have already been separated from among them, only the good will reign with Christ. Yet even now every unclean and lying person is not in the Church, nor does the one who hates the city of God see its light, because darkness has blinded his eyes.

## CHAPTER XXII

And he showed me the river of the water of life, etc. In the river of life flowing through the middle of the city, the celebration of baptism is not being announced as still future; rather, the fruit of that sacrament is already being revealed. For now the Church sows in the Spirit, so that then it may reap eternal life from the Spirit (Gal. VI).

And on both sides of the river, the tree of life. The tree of life is seen beside the fountain of life. Whether you interpret it as the glory of the holy cross or as the Lord Christ, it was already revealed before baptism in the Old Testament, and now, as the mystery of baptism shines forth, it nourishes the saints with heavenly fruit. For “there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts IV). The same tree which John described as flowering in the golden Jerusalem, and Moses in paradise, Solomon said was the tree of life for those who embrace it. I think this river prefigured the Jordan, beyond which Moses gave the peoples teachings of salvation, and within which Joshua opened the promised land.

Producing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit each month. By the twelve months he signifies the whole duration of life—namely, that life of which it is said: “And your years will not fail” (Ps. CI). And again: “From month to month, and from Sabbath to Sabbath” (Isa. LXVI). There the Lord’s present face, eternal health, is the eternal food of life. It may also be understood simply that through the teaching of the twelve apostles the cross of Christ bears fruit.

And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations. If the fruit is understood as the reward of blessed immortality, the leaves are rightly understood as perpetual song, which falls to the healing of those who now sing in a fortunate condition. For there the healing of the nations is true, redemption is complete, and happiness everlasting.

And they will see his face. The vision of God is reserved for us as the reward of faith. Understanding this to be the highest good, Philip said: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV). For it had to be carefully commended [Col. 0204D] that the saints would see and possess in actual form what, while living by faith, they believe.

And his name will be on their foreheads. The confession of the holy name, preserved now among enemies, will then glorify the victors in the homeland.

And night will be no more, etc. There the weakness of bodies will need neither the rest of night nor the light of fire, when God will be all in all (I Cor. XV)—he who is the true light (John I) and the eternal rest of the saints. If you refer these words to allegory, there the exhortation of the prophets and the preaching of the law will not be necessary; these are now called a lamp in a dark place, because, when all things have been fulfilled in the contemplation of God, the promise will be held in perfection.

And he said to me, “These words are most trustworthy and true.” [Col. 0205A] He was not doubting John’s lack of confidence; rather, he was commending the true vision to the whole Church, in which he knew that even little ones would be present.

And the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets sent his angel. “Do not doubt,” he says, “the identity of the one giving the warning. For the very God who is accustomed to imbue the spirits of the prophets with heavenly vision sent me to show you these future things in advance.”

To show his servants what must soon take place. He taught that, as I have said, he had foreseen what was generally useful to all.

Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book, etc. “I am blessed” is understood. For the blessed bishop Dionysius of Alexandria connects these verses in this way, while refuting the error of certain heresies that arose on the occasion of this little book and transferring the meaning of the same prophecy, cleansed of every cloud of carnal interpretation, to eternal and heavenly promises.

I fell down to worship at the angel’s feet, etc. Either he repeated something that had happened once, which, having been restrained, he did not dare to repeat; or, struck by the great astonishment of the visions, he confesses that he wished to worship a second time.

I am your fellow servant, etc. Note how often he calls both John the prophet and this book a prophecy; for it has much in common with the prophets, not only in its meanings but also in its words. How many verses of Isaiah, how many of Zechariah and the other prophets, will you find here!

Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, etc. As the judgment approached, the divine commands, judgments, and promises had to be revealed, so that by observing them the gentle might obtain a reward, while the defiant, by neglecting them, might incur punishment.

[Col. 0205C] “Let the one who does harm continue to do harm, and let the one who is filthy continue to be filthy.” Here he reveals God’s hidden but just judgments, by which wicked people are permitted to advance toward worse things—that is, to reach the summit of wickedness—so that a just judgment may be found. This resembles the saying: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matt. 12).

“I am Α and Ω,” and so forth. In Α he signifies the divinity of the Word, and in Ω the humanity he assumed. The Beginning without end—a point repeatedly confirmed throughout this book—whether because the divinity and humanity of the one Christ are often indicated, or so that the whole Trinity, which is of one nature, may be signified. Through the prophet it says: “Before me [Col. 0205D] no God was formed, and after me there will be none” (Isa. 43).

“That they may have authority over the tree of life.” He promises a worthy reward for the white robes—that is, for an unstained life—namely, that one may enjoy the sight of the Lord, who is eternal life. For “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

“And may enter the city through the gates.” Those who keep the commandments of the Lord, who says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out, and will find pasture” (John 10)—that pasture, naturally, which is also promised [Col. 0206A] here, namely, the tree of life—these unquestionably enter the Church through the gates. The gates, that is, of righteousness, which the Psalmist asks to have opened for him (Ps. 117). But the one who tries to climb in by another way is “a thief and a robber” (John 10); concerning such people it is also added here:

“But outside are dogs, sorcerers, and the sexually immoral,” and so forth. For all the fury of the wicked now also assails the Church from within; but when the master of the household enters, and, when the saints have entered the marriage feast with him, shuts the door, then they will begin to stand outside and knock at the door (Luke 13).

“I am the root and offspring of David.” Here he expresses the twofold nature of his person: he is the same one who made David according to his divinity, and who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh. In the Gospel the Lord puts this question to the Jews: how, namely, [Col. 0206B] can Christ be David’s son, when David in the Spirit calls him his Lord? (Matt. 22).

“Bright and morning star.” After the night of the Passion, by appearing as the light of resurrection, he showed the ages the light of resurrection and life through both word and example. Concerning him it is said to blessed Job: “Do you bring forth the morning star in its time?” (Job 38).

“And the bridegroom and the bride say: Come.” The Head and body of the Church exhort the individual members to faith.

“And let the one who hears say: Come.” Whoever has perceived within his mind the inner light of faith or charity should summon others to it as well.

“Let the one who wishes take the water of life freely.” Thus free choice is summoned by the words “Let the one who wishes take,” so that grace may immediately be proclaimed in what follows: [Col. 0206C] “the water of life freely”—without any preceding merits. For even the desire itself is a gift of God.

“If anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues written in this book.” He said this concerning falsifiers, not concerning those who simply state what they think, without mutilating the prophecy in any respect.

“The one who bears witness to these things says: Yes, I am coming soon.” It is Christ himself who bears witness, announcing that he will come to the Church. To him the Church devoutly responds, in the manner of the Song of Songs:

“Amen, come, Lord Jesus Christ.” She cries this out daily in prayer: “May your kingdom come” (Matt. 6). And in the Psalm: “I shall sing and understand in the blameless way; when will you come to me?” (Ps. 100).

[Col. 0206D] “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.” Let the Pelagians go and, trusting in their own power, deprive themselves of the Lord’s grace. But when the Apostle Paul seeks protection and says, “Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7), let John, mindful of his own name, answer and say: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid.). And lest the Donatists flatter themselves over God’s singular gift, let them hear that, when he commended God’s grace as his final farewell, he added: “with you all.” Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0205] Let the reader by no means be surprised not to find here an Exposition on the Epistles of Saint Paul, which older editions of the Venerable Father contain. We shall publish this exegesis—less rightly attributed to Bede than to Florus the deacon—under this name, among the writers of the following century, at the year 860. EDITOR.]

THE EXEGETICAL WORKS OF BEDE THE VENERABLE, ANGLO-SAXON PRIEST, OR PART II OF ALL HIS WORKS. SECTION TWO.—DOUBTFUL AND SPURIOUS WORKS.

[Col. 0207]

A BOOK OF SENTENCES ON THE SIX DAYS OF CREATION, COLLECTED FROM THE FATHERS. (C)

ON THE FIRST DAY.

[Col. 0207A]

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” This chapter is the head of all books. For all divine Scripture is divided into two parts, the Old Testament and the New. Some passages disclose inward realities, as in: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). Others narrate things that happened, as in: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Others announce future events, as it is said: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty” (Matt. 25). Others prescribe what must be done, as in: “You shall love your neighbor” (Matt. 5).

How, then, is it divided into two parts? Because some passages are spoken according to figure, as in the Song of Songs, and: “Adam heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden” (Gen. 3). Others are according to the factual truth of events, such as the people’s departure from Egypt and their walking through the sea on foot. Still others are spoken in both ways, such as the crossing of the Red Sea, and those miracles that the Lord performed [Col. 0207B] in the Gospel.

It says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” We must inquire in what beginning God created heaven and earth: whether in the beginning of time, or in the beginning in the sense that this was the beginning of his creation, from which other things began to exist. For they were not coeternal with God.

Let us say: In the Beginning who is coeternal with himself, God made heaven and earth—that is, in the only-begotten Son, who is the Wisdom of the Father. Concerning him the Apostle says: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1); and in the Psalm he says: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103). Again the Apostle says: “Because in him all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible” (Col. 1). For the Evangelist also says of Christ: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John 1).

Nevertheless, we must ask whether God first made heaven and earth in the beginning, or the light. And if the light was created first, why did he not say: “In the beginning God created light”? We must understand that he created heaven, earth, and light simultaneously. For there is no difference except one of origin. Just as a person cannot narrate two familiar [Col. 0208A] parables simultaneously, so the Lord acted here: he first narrated what had its origin, and afterward what was made from it, although he made both simultaneously. Thus what is prior only in origin during the act of making is prior in time during the narration.

Therefore, since Holy Scripture had to narrate both the events and the things narrated, it was reasonable for it first to narrate that from which something was made, and only afterward what was made from it. This was for the sake of those slower in understanding, so that they might grasp that bodily things were made from something. For there is no difference between the creation of heaven and earth and that of light, except the difference between a word and a voice.

Why did he not say, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” but said “created”? It was because of the formlessness of matter, and also because of the spiritual sense.

Again, a Recapitulation.

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” The Beginning is Christ, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you.” In this Beginning, therefore, [Col. 0208B] God made heaven—that is, the spiritual beings who contemplate and seek heavenly things. In him he also made the carnal, who have not yet laid aside what is earthly.

“But the earth was formless and empty”—that is, because it had not yet been separated from the sea. “And empty”—that is, because it had not been enclosed by shores or adorned with vines, that is, with trees or animals.

Again, a Recapitulation.

“But the earth was formless and empty.” The earth of our flesh, namely, was formless and empty before it received the form of instruction. “And darkness was over the face of the abyss,” because there was no light to pour over it; if there had been, it would certainly have been above it. But what was it? That is, air thickened and deprived of daylight.

Again, a Recapitulation.

“And darkness was over the face of the abyss,” because the blindness of sins and the deep darkness of ignorance covered our hearts. “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” [Col. 0209A] Hence the blessed Apostle says: “Above the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ” (Eph. 3). Elsewhere he says: “It surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4).

He therefore indicates something begun, over which the Spirit of God was said to be borne—not spatially, but by a power surpassing and exceeding all things. For there are two reasons why God loves his creation: so that it may exist and remain. It must be formed in order to exist, and remain in the commandment of the Creator.

Therefore the Spirit of God was borne over the waters, so that there might be something that would remain. For this reason he first named the things that were formless, and afterward the Holy Spirit, because every slight love is placed beneath the things it loves.

Recapitulation.

“And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” That is, the Spirit of God the Father. Concerning this same Holy Spirit the Apostle says: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8).

If, then, there is no difference between the person of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, why does he not say, “Whoever does not have the Spirit of the Spirit,” or, as he says, [Col. 0209B] “the Spirit of the Father” or “the Spirit of the Son”? Why does he not say “Father of the Spirit” or “Son of the Spirit”? Because there is no relational construction by which this could be expressed, as one says “the servant of the Lord,” or “the Lord’s servant,” or “the Son of the Father,” and “the Father of the Son.”

For if he had said “Father of the Spirit,” he would have shown God to be the Father of the Spirit. Or if he had said “Son of the Spirit,” he would have demonstrated that the Holy Spirit was the Father of the Son, since the Spirit is neither Father nor Son, but proceeded from the divine substance.

For this reason he does not say that the Holy Spirit was born from the Father or the Son, because he was not born as the Only-Begotten was, nor made as we were, so that he might be called a son by the adoption of grace.

And how is the Holy Spirit said to be coeternal with the Father and the Son? Because he said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and is coeternal with them. For he always proceeded; he was not always given, since he can always become a gift without having always been given. The Holy Spirit always proceeded, and it was prepared by the Father that he should be given. At that time, however, there was no one to receive him—neither angels [Col. 0209C] nor human beings—except the Creator of all things.

And if the three are one—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (1 John 5)—why, then, is the Father not said to have been sent by the Son or by the Holy Spirit? The order of paternal reverence is preserved.

Recapitulation.

“Now the Spirit of God was already being borne over our dark and unstable heart, as over the waters.” In him we might find rest by abiding, be given life by his breath, and be washed by his wave.

ON THE CREATION OF LIGHT.

“God also said: Let there be light.” Is this light visible or invisible? It is called invisible because it is the angelic creation, which our eyes are unable to behold. For it was reasonable that on the fourth day he should fashion the stars in heaven, which our eyes could see.

Is this angelic creation temporal or timeless? It was temporal in the angels, timeless [Col. 0209D] in God. It was temporal in the sense that what was spoken was expressed by the eternal God through the coeternal Word in the spiritual creature that he had already made when it was said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

But this speech was not merely without any sound; it was also without any bodily movement. The spiritual creature was, in a certain manner, implanted in his mind and reason through the coeternal Word of the Father. Yet it is exceedingly difficult to grasp how this can be said: God did not command temporally, nor did the creature hear temporally, since he surpasses all times by contemplation of the truth. Rather, the things were intellectually expressed to themselves, as the Wisdom coeternal with the Father transmits speech, as to beings capable of understanding, toward those things that are below, so that a temporal movement might occur in temporal things, whether in their formation or their administration.

“And light was made.” That is, the angelic creation, because at that time they came to know and understand their Creator.

Why does he not repeat: “And God made the light,” [Col. 0210A] as he repeats this concerning the other creatures that he created? In the case of the firmament he says: “Let there be a firmament,” and again: “God made the firmament.” The reason is that it was unnecessary to say, “God made the light,” because it was an intellectual creature—that is, the angels.

When he says “Let there be a firmament,” or similar words concerning the other creatures, he says this in reference to angelic knowledge. For it is not surprising if God first wished to show his holy angels, who had turned toward him at the original creation of light, what he would subsequently do.

But when he says “And God made,” that is, in the proper nature of things, it was no longer necessary to repeat this concerning the angels, because at that time, as we have said, they had turned to acknowledge their Creator.

For when that eternal and unchangeable Wisdom—which was not made but begotten—transfers itself into a spiritual and rational creature, as into holy souls, so that, once illuminated, they may shine, a certain luminous affection of reason comes to be in them. This can be understood as the light that was made when God said, “Let there be light.”

[Col. 0210B] The spiritual creation already existed, signified by the name “heaven,” when it was written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”—not the bodily heaven, but the incorporeal heaven, in which all the holy angels are understood.

“And God saw that the light was good.” Why did he praise only the light and not the night? That is because neither night nor day had yet been made, but only the angelic light. It would have been unworthy of God to praise something formless, which had not yet been formed; he praised instead the thing that had been formed, namely, the angelic light.

“And he divided the light from the darkness.” What is the division of light from darkness except the distinction between what has been formed and what is formless?

“And he called the light day.” Why did he call the light day? Because day had not yet been formed. The same day was named in relation to the appearance of the thing that had been made.

“And the darkness he called night.” Why did he likewise call it night, although it had not yet been formed at all? This night, which is well known to us, is the absence of the sun over the earth. When the sun sets, we call it evening; when morning begins, we call it day.

But [Col. 0210C] here night is the deprivation of work, or night itself is called a possibility that exists in created things, from which something can come to be even when those things are not changed. And again according to the spiritual sense.

Recapitulation.

“God also said: Let there be light.” That is, let the illumination of faith appear. On the first day he gave the light of faith, because faith is first in conversion. Hence the first commandment itself is: “The Lord your God is one God.”

Because of this faith the Lord himself also wished to appear invisibly in the world. Even then, according to the grace of his presence, God divided the righteous—that is, the sons of God and of light—from sinners, as from darkness, calling the former day and the latter night.

For since the righteous are called by the name of light in the Church, hear the Apostle: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

“And evening came and morning came, one day.” What is evening [Col. 0210D] except the completion of each individual work? And morning—that is, the beginning of what follows.

ON THE SECOND DAY.

“God also said: Let there be a firmament.” This was either because of the firmament of stability, or because of the impossibility of crossing between the waters above and the waters below.

We nevertheless judge that the nature of the waters there is suspended not in vaporous thinness but in icy solidity, to moderate the nature of the stars, lest they condense the creatures placed beneath them through excessive heat.

But whatever kind of waters they may be there, we have not the least doubt that they are there. The authority of this Scripture is greater than the capacity of every human mind.

As for the consistency of the heavens, an explanation must be sought. Here the Lord mentions that one firmament was made, but the Apostle testifies that he was caught up to the third heaven. What, then, are we to say except that the smallest drops, gathered together into one, form a single collection, and that because of the weight of their mass the air [Col. 0211A] cannot support them, but gives way by pouring that weight downward? This is rain.

Therefore they understand the heaven to be between water and water: the air between the moist vapors from which clouds gather above and the seas spread out below.

The second heaven is that which we see with the spirit, from which that disk filled with animals descended to Peter in the ecstasy of his mind. The third heaven is that which we know with the mind, so secret and remote that those who are either wholly purified or snatched away from the senses of the flesh may be able ineffably to behold, in the love of the Holy Spirit, the things that are in that heaven: the very substance of God, the Word through whom all things were made.

“And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.” The Spirit of God was therefore present to be written down, as though someone might ask him how it had rightly been made and he might answer:

“God said: Let there be”—that is, what was in the eternal Word of God to be made. Then he begins to narrate each thing that was made.

When we hear, “And so it was made,” we understand that the creature made [Col. 0211B] did not exceed the limits of its kind prescribed in the Word of God. But when we hear, “God saw that it was good,” we understand that it pleased him in his benevolent Spirit—not as though something unknown had pleased him after it was made, but rather that it pleased him in that goodness in which it remained made, since it had pleased him to make it.

Concerning the form of heaven, we should say briefly that our authorities knew what the truth contains, but that the Spirit of God, who spoke through them, did not wish to reveal matters that would provide no useful benefit for salvation.

As for the dispute that commonly arises among many concerning the form of heaven—whether it exists in the shape of an extended skin, a sphere, or a vaulted chamber—we do not see what would prevent a skin extended in the manner of a vaulted chamber from being curved, or from being stretched around into a rounded hollow, like a sphere.

Again, a Recapitulation.

Then, on the second day, God arranged the firmament—that is, the solid foundation of the holy Scriptures. For in the Church the firmament is understood as the divine Scriptures, [Col. 0211C] because heaven will be folded up like a book.

“And he separated the waters above this firmament.” That is, the heavenly peoples of the angels, who do not need to receive this firmament so that, by reading, they may hear the word of God (Matt. 24). They always see him and love him.

But he placed this firmament of his law above the weakness of the lower peoples, so that the spiritual, receiving it, might learn how to distinguish between carnal and spiritual things, as between the waters above and the waters below.

ON THE THIRD DAY.

“Then God said: Let the waters that are under heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.” Why, then, did he not say, “Let the dry land become visible,” or “Let the waters be gathered,” except because these things are closer to formlessness than the heavenly bodies, so that from them, through the numbering of the days, the weaker things might be formed?

For this reason he did not command it to be introduced in the same way as the things above [Col. 0211D], but ordered the gathered waters to appear by themselves as the weaker elements of creation.

Where, then, were the waters gathered if they had previously occupied the whole earth? There, clearly, where they were drawn back so that the earth might be uncovered.

And if some part had previously appeared dry, where could the waters have been gathered? Therefore the abyss did not occupy everything. Rather, we should understand either that water had first covered the earth in the manner of a mist, or that, surrounding the earth far and wide, it had left a hollow place capable of receiving the waters as they flowed together, so that the dry land might appear.

Again, a Recapitulation.

After this, on the third day, he gathered together the salty lower waters. This means unbelieving human beings, who are shaken by the storm of desires and the waves of carnal temptations, and who contain within themselves something like bitterness.

He separated the dry land from them—that is, the spring of peoples thirsting for faith. Then he fixed the boundaries of the proud and restrained them, so that they might not disturb the dry land, that is, the soul thirsting [Col. 0212A] for God, with the turbulent waves of their iniquities.

He allowed it to bring forth the fruit of good works according to its kind. “You shall love your neighbor” in the provision of carnal necessities, possessing within itself seed according to likeness, so that from its own weakness people may be moved to compassion and to assist those in need, producing also a tree of strong timber.

“And fruitful”—that is, a benefaction by which the one suffering injustice may be snatched from the hand of the powerful, and by which the shelter of protection may be provided through the strong timber of just judgment.

“And God saw that it was good, and said: Let the earth bring forth green grass, producing seed, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit according to their kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth. And so it was made. And the earth brought forth green grass bearing seed according to its kind, and trees producing fruit, each having its seed according to its species. And God saw that it was good; and evening came and morning came, the third day.”

Why does he say that all these things were commanded to be made together—to make the earth sprout [Col. 0212B] and to gather the waters—except because all these things are fixed in the earth by their root? For this reason they are said to belong to the same day: although they spread far and wide through their growth, they are nevertheless not moved from their proper places by their own bonds.

Trees live, yet they do not live by means of a soul but by greenness. For that sap is poured into the root; then it is transformed into the quality of the tree, and afterward into the spreading of the branches, and from there into the greenness of the leaves.

Hence he says, “And fruit-bearing tree,” because not all trees produce fruit. The fruit is understood here because every tree has its own use, and every plant likewise has its own utility, both openly and secretly.

ON THE FOURTH DAY.

“Then God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, to divide the day and the night, and let them be for signs and seasons and days and years, and let them shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth. And so it was made. And God made [Col. 0212C] two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars; and he placed them in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth, to rule the day and the night, and to divide the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good; and evening came and morning came, the fourth day.”

What was in the Word of God according to the begotten Wisdom was then made in the spiritual creature, that is, in the angels. Then the lights themselves were made in their proper kind, to serve as signs and seasons.

Who does not see how obscurely it has been stated that the seasons began on the fourth day, as though those preceding three days could have passed without time? Yet they had the time of their own creation, because the creature received its name from their mutual relation, although those three days did not have the distinction of the stars.

“The greater light to rule the day,” because we understand that the day cannot become bright unless it is assisted by the light of the sun, nor the night by the appearance of the stars if the moon is absent, in the manner in which the moon’s presence illuminates it.

They nevertheless ask whether these principal lights of heaven [Col. 0212D] are equal in power, but appear larger or smaller to our earthly eyes because of their different distances from the earth. For just as heaven was made first, so it had to be adorned first.

On the fourth day the stars were made, by whose shining the lower dwelling place upon the earth is illuminated, lest its inhabitants be brought into a dark habitation. Therefore, through successive movements, the weak bodies of those below are restored by rest. As the sun revolves, the alternation of day and night came to be, because of the alternation between sleeping and keeping watch.

And lest that night remain without adornment, it was decorated with the light of the moon or of the stars, so that it might console human beings themselves, who, while traveling or working, are compelled by the necessity of the night to continue their journey or labor; and so that animals, which cannot endure the light of the sun, might likewise be consoled with equanimity.

When he says, “God said: Let there be,” we understand Scripture’s intention as returning to the eternity of the Word of God. For he did not find anything requiring recreation that he had not found already created in the Word of God.

Therefore [Col. 0213A] God did not say “Let this be made” or “Let that be made” as many times as this is written in the book. For he begot one Word, in which he spoke all things before the individual things were made.

“And let them be for signs and seasons”—not according to heretics or philosophers, who pursue empty signs, but according to the truth of signs. Signs and seasons are said to pertain to the moon or to the stars of heaven.

It must be asked whether heaven revolves in a circle, or whether the stars move around. We should understand that the stars move around, while heaven itself stands firm.

“And evening came and morning came, the fourth day.” Why did he mention evening and morning but say nothing about night? What else, then, should we call night except the absence of light, which seemed to remain between evening and morning?

Or was it because the first light signified the angelic creation? By contemplating their Creator, the angels, with the most harmonious love and without the blindness of ignorance, never cease to praise their Creator forever. Nevertheless, at the beginning and end of the work they clearly understood what [Col. 0213B] is called evening and morning.

And again according to the spiritual sense.

Again, a Recapitulation.

Then, on the fourth day, the lights shone forth, fixed in the firmament of the law—that is, the Evangelists, teachers, and Holy Scriptures, cohering through disputation, demonstrating the light of wisdom to all below.

At the same time the rest of the multitude of shining stars also appeared: that is, the multitude of different virtues in the Church. Shining in the obscurity of this life, as in night, they divide within this firmament of Scripture sensible things from intelligible things, as it were between the light of the perfect and the darkness of the immature, and they serve as signs of virtues and miracles.

They also serve as seasons and years, because preachers live and pass away in their appointed times. But the word of the Lord remains forever.

Why did the earth first sprout and the lights then come to be, except because illumination for contemplating the appearance of heavenly [Col. 0213C] power comes after good works?

ON THE FIFTH DAY.

“God also said: Let the waters bring forth creeping creatures with living souls, and birds over the earth under the firmament of heaven. And God created the great sea creatures and every living and moving creature that the waters had brought forth according to its kind, and every bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good, and he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let the birds multiply upon the earth. And evening came and morning came, the fifth day.”

What, then, is the reason that he first adorned the waters with creeping creatures, before adorning the earth with animals? The reason was that the visible realm appeared first, so that it might first receive its adornment; or because, in the beginning, heaven received its adornment—that is, from the angels, when they were created. Likewise, the earth was clothed with herbs and trees. The reason, then, was that the waters [Col. 0213D] should receive their adornment from creeping creatures, or the air from flying creatures.

For what is the reason that we often read similarly about the creation of heaven, earth, and sea—how they were created—while nothing was indicated about the air? We must not suppose that Scripture overlooked that element here, unless it is because divine Scripture customarily calls heaven and earth the whole world. And therefore we should understand the air as belonging to heaven and earth.

Whatever is moist or spread out in the manner of vapor belongs to the earth; whatever is tranquil and quiet is said to belong to heaven. The air, moreover, is so like water that it is shown to become enriched from its exhalations; it produces the breath of the storm—that is, wind—and, conversely, clouds, and is able to support the flight of birds. For he did not say, “Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature of living soul, and let the air bring forth flying creatures over the earth,” but said, “Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature of living soul, and the flying creature over the earth,” because air is made from water.

Whatever is wave-like [Col. 0214A] or fluid was given to the fish. Whatever is moist or suspended in the manner of vapor was plainly entrusted to flying creatures, because just as the fish of the sea swim in the waters with their little fins, so the birds of heaven appear to fly through the air with their wings as though through water. And for this reason they are said to fly beneath the firmament of heaven, not within the firmament of heaven, because there is a contiguous space there in which birds cannot fly.

This air extends from the luminous boundary of heaven down to the fluid waters and the bare earth. Yet not all of it belongs to the earth, but only that region from which fire, hail, snow, ice, and the spirit of the storm begin to descend. Whatever is higher is said to belong to heaven because of its tranquility.

Demons are said to dwell in the air. Therefore the air tolerates their presence because they use an aerial form, and from there they attack the human race. Immediately after they were created, they were cast out from the presence of God. Hence the Savior says to his disciples in the Gospel [Col. 0214B]: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10).

How, indeed, is he said to have fallen if he did not stand? He did not remain in the company of the holy angels, but as soon as he saw himself in the splendor of God, he raised himself in pride against his Creator. And he said: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High.” Immediately he was cast down from the height of heaven into the air, together with all his attendants who followed him. They did not persist in divine love as did those who were established so firmly that, even if they wished to sin, they could not, because at the beginning they possessed their own free choice, just as the human race now appears to possess it.

Those beings fell through their own free choice and received God’s sentence, so that, even if they wished to recover, they could not. Again the Lord said: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth” (John 8).

How, however, was he a murderer from the beginning? He first slew Adam in paradise when he persuaded him to eat the fruit, and Adam was made mortal from immortal; afterward he slew the human [Col. 0214C] race down to the coming of the Savior.

How did he not stand in the truth? Because he did not merit to receive what had been promised to him: that he should remain forever with his Creator, together with the other angels. Instead, he was cast down to the earth with his companions. There, without doubt, they suffer punishment, because the sidereal fire in the air holds power over them; and, according to their kind, it has been assigned to them as a sort of prison until the time of the day of judgment comes, when they will be cast into eternal fire, “where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Luke 13).

The air, moreover, is often stirred up and severely frozen, producing snow; sometimes it is compressed more intensely and becomes a storm; sometimes there are flashes of lightning and thunder. And when it pours down to the lowest regions, it gives way, because the air cannot endure to sustain these things. Yet all these events occur through divine providence and by the hidden judgment of God.

Some, however, refer these four elements of the world to the five bodily senses [Col. 0214D]: fire to the eyes, air to hearing, moisture to smell and taste, and touch to the earth. They also say that nothing can be seen without fire and nothing touched without earth, and that consequently all the elements are present in human beings; but that each element received its name from the one it possesses in greater measure.

When the body becomes excessively cold through the deprivation of heat, it dulls the sense, because the movement that heat supplies to the body grows cold. Fire affects air, air affects moisture, and moisture affects the earthly element, with the subtler penetrating the denser. The more subtle anything is in bodily nature, the closer it is to spiritual nature, although it is far removed from it in kind, since one is bodily and the other is not.

Accordingly, since sensation belongs not to the body but to the soul through the body, although it may be argued precisely, according to the diversity of bodily elements, that the senses are distributed through the body, nevertheless the soul, in which the power of sensation resides, though it is not bodily, stirs the power of sensation through the subtler body.

Movement therefore begins in all the senses with the subtlety of fire, but it does not proceed to the same point in all of them [Col. 0215A]. In sight, the heat is restrained until it reaches light; in hearing, the heat of fire penetrates as far as the more fluid air; in smell, pure air passes through and reaches the moist exhalation from which this denser breath arises; in taste, it passes through even this and reaches the more substantial moisture. Once that too has been penetrated and traversed, when it reaches the earth’s heaviness, it activates the final sense, that of touch.

It must also be investigated when the smallest fish, animals, or worms—which Scripture does not mention—were created, since the question must be addressed of how all creatures, from the largest elephant to the smallest worm, were created.

We must therefore understand by reason where this smallest creature came from, since Scripture gives no indication of it here. It must be understood that, when God separated waters from waters, the smallest animals, which are formed from water, had their nature within those very waters.

And those worms that arise from the bodies [Col. 0215B] of the dead—where do they come from? We must understand that they possess within those bodies the power by which they are born.

Did the water cover the earth, or the earth the water? [The text reads: “the water covered the earth,” as though some part of the earth had slipped over the water; immediately the water burst forth into its place, and the earth returned.] [sic]

How, then, does he say elsewhere: “For he founded it upon the seas, and prepared it upon the rivers” (Psalm 23)? If here the water covered the earth, either he is speaking of higher ground, where the mountains appear to be, or the statement refers to islands, where the earth is higher than the water.

But this should rather be understood according to the spiritual sense, because the simple in the Church are founded upon the wise. Thus they are called living waters, because they support those whom they perceive to be weaker. For as much as there is between the moon and the stars of heaven, so much is there between holy rusticity and holy simplicity.

From where are fish generated—from water or from themselves? This must be understood from water, since he says: “Let the waters bring forth [Col. 0215C] the creeping creature of living soul.”

“And he blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply.’” Why did these animals deserve to receive a blessing like that of human beings? This is to teach us that this blessing remains in the other animals.

## Recapitulation

Again, during this fifth day, creeping creatures of living souls were made in the waters—that is, human beings renewed to life through the sacrament of baptism. Flying creatures were also made, namely, holy souls flying toward the things above.

## On the Sixth Day

“God also said: ‘Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its kind: cattle, creeping creatures, and beasts of the earth according to their species; cattle also, and every creeping creature of the earth according to its kind, a living soul.’”

And there are the simple animals that were given for the use of the human race. Creeping creatures, however, are those that crawl upon the earth: snakes and the rest. The beasts of the earth are [Col. 0215D] bears, lions, leopards, and others. Whatever fights with teeth or claws is called a beast.

The question must be asked whether these venomous animals, at the beginning, when they were created, possessed venom as they do now. We should understand that, just as they were created then, so they remain. Nevertheless, at the beginning they did not possess the power to harm, as we can demonstrate from snakes: when a viper attacked Paul’s hand, it did him no harm, because it had the power to attack but did not have the power to injure. The same is true of the beasts, when Daniel was thrown into the lions’ den. They did not harm him but licked his feet.

Or perhaps these venomous animals were created to terrify human beings, because God foresaw that humanity would sin, so that people might understand the punishments of hell. For elsewhere he says: “Their worms shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isaiah 66).

Why, then, do beasts harm one another, since they have no original sin from which punishment could be exacted from them [Col. 0216A]? As blessed Augustine says, “Beasts are fellow citizens within their own kind.” When they see a beast belonging to another civic group, they immediately quarrel among themselves, because animals live and perceive; trees, as we have said, live but do not perceive. Human beings, however, live, perceive, and understand, because they possess the discernment by which they distinguish good from evil.

## On the Creation of Human Beings

“And God saw that it was good, and said: ‘Let us make the human being in our image and likeness.’”

He says this to signify the plurality of persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Immediately he adds: “And God created the human being,” to show the unity of the divine majesty.

“In his image”—that is, so that he might remain immortal. “And likeness”—that is, so that he might possess understanding of mind, unlike animals, which do not know how to distinguish good from evil.

He did not clothe him with bodily features, but with understanding of mind, so that he might understand his Creator [Col. 0216B] and praise him forever without mortality. Yet “when he was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Psalm 48).

Because he did not wish to observe the commands of his Creator, in accordance with the command given to him, he was made mortal in body like an animal, but not in soul, because he remained immortal.

Why does he not repeat: “And he made the human being,” as he did with the other creatures that he created? This was unnecessary, because the human being was an intellectual creature, like the angels. For his being made is his understanding the Word of God the Father, through whom all things were made (John 1).

Why does he not say “according to its kind,” when the propagation of humanity is perfectly evident? This too was unnecessary, since Adam was created in such a way that he would remain immortal, and the ages would pass while he remained immortal; or because the human race was destined to proceed from him, not from different creatures, as there are different kinds of animals, fish, and birds.

[Col. 0216C] It was not so with humanity that different human kinds existed upon the earth. Rather, the human race proceeded from one human being, because the human being surpasses the animals: his mind is raised toward heaven, and he understands that he should seek his Creator in heaven, the one who created him.

“And let him rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of heaven, and the beasts, and every creature.” That is, let him understand that he was made in the image of God, since he surpasses so many animals through the understanding of his mind.

“And God created the human being in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.”

What does it mean that he says he created the female together with the male, when she had not yet been formed, but was to proceed from Adam? It is like the fact that many things are hidden in a tree’s seed: first it is fixed in the root, then expressed in the nature of the tree, and afterward in the spreading of the branches, and thereafter in the greenness of the leaves, and so on. Thus the woman was hidden in Adam’s body [Col. 0216D], because she was fashioned from Adam’s rib.

“And he blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and all living creatures that move upon the earth.’”

Why did the human being deserve to receive this blessing? It was so that God would not appear to condemn the procreation of children, as though people might say that having children was sinful. Thus the Lord blessed human beings in the procreation of children, to make clear that there is no sin in it if they marry lawfully.

If, then, Adam was created in such a way that he would remain immortal, what does “Increase and multiply” mean? This must be understood to mean that they were not to beget children according to the lust of the flesh or any evil desire, nor as they now bear children in pain. Rather, just as each person commands his limbs to perform some action—his hand in working or his foot in walking—so they ought to have begotten [Col. 0217A] offspring in paradise.

But if they were supposed to beget offspring in this way, why did they not come together in paradise and beget children before they had been cast out? Because as soon as the woman was created, she transgressed and was cast down from the height of immortality into the lowest depths.

How, then, would their bodies have had to change if they had remained immortal? This must be understood as follows: if they had not sinned, they could not have died at all. But once that number had been fulfilled—the number corresponding to the angels—their bodies would have been changed for the better, without mortality.

“And God said: ‘Behold, I have given you every plant bearing seed, and every fruit-bearing tree, that you may have it for food.’”

Was Adam immortal or mortal? And if mortal, how was he immortal? And if animal, how was he spiritual? And if spiritual, why did he take food in common with the other animals?

He was mortal and immortal: mortal because he was able to die, immortal because he was able not to die. If he had not sinned, he could not have died at all [Col. 0217B]; but after he sinned, he became mortal.

He was mortal and immortal. He was mortal by his condition, immortal by God’s gift, which God provided for him through the tree of life. From that tree he was cast out after he sinned, so that he could die.

If this voice was something striking the air, how is this speech to be understood? That very Word of his, before every sound of air and before every flesh and voice of cloud, was in that highest Wisdom through which all things were made; it did not resound as though in human ears.

Why, then, is it that, though we have been reborn through Christ, we do not receive the very immortality that Adam possessed before sin? We did not receive what we lost in Adam, namely, an animal body; rather, we receive something so much better as the spiritual is superior to the bodily. Hence the Apostle says: “The animal body is sown; the spiritual body rises” (1 Corinthians 15).

We did not receive the immortality of a spiritual body. Instead, we received righteousness, from which Adam fell through sin. Of this the blessed Apostle says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind,” [Col. 0217C] and what follows (Ephesians 4).

How, then, are we to be renewed? We shall be renewed from the oldness of sin, not into the former animal body in which Adam existed, but into something better—that is, a spiritual body—when we become equal to the angels through heavenly dwelling.

We shall also be renewed in the spirit of our mind, according to the image of the one who created us, which Adam lost through sin. We shall also be renewed in the flesh, when this corruptible body puts on incorruption and this mortal body puts on immortality, so that it may be a spiritual body.

Adam had not yet been changed into this body, but he was destined to be changed, because in our body we bear the image of the earthly human being, while in our mind we bear the image of the heavenly human being.

Again the Apostle says: “If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one, as it is written: ‘The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit.’ But the spiritual was not first; rather, the animal, and afterward the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. Such as the earthly man is, such also are the earthly [Col. 0217D]” (1 Corinthians 15).

“Let us put on the image of the one who is from heaven.” From the very beginning of the human race we have put on the image of the earthly human being. We now bear the image of the heavenly human being by faith, believing that we shall dwell in the resurrection.

“And God saw all that he had made, and they were very good. And evening came and morning came: the sixth day.”

If God created all things very good, from where, then, did evil increase? Evil would not have existed if we had not produced it. Nor would it have been something beyond nature; rather, the loss of the good received that name.

Why did he not bless the trees or the herbs, but human beings and animals? He blessed these either because of the propagation of offspring, or because of the distinction of the male and female sexes, or because trees have no faculty of perception or understanding. Animals live and perceive but do not understand. The human being both perceives and understands. Therefore he did not say to the trees, “Increase and multiply.”

## On the Seventh Day

[Col. 0218A]

“Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their adornment. And God completed on the seventh day his work that he had made. And he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work that God created in order to make.”

That is, he completed the creation of heaven and earth: heaven with all its adornment, and earth with all its works.

“And he completed his work on the seventh day.” On the sixth day, when he said, “It is finished,” and, bowing his head, gave up his spirit (John 19). On the seventh day he rested in the tomb, and then everything that had been written about him was completed.

The Jews observed this day as a shadow, as it had been commanded to them by God through Moses. For us, however, that day signified rest: if we complete our works in good works, we shall rest with Christ forever. For *sabbatus* is interpreted as “rest,” because Christ is our rest, in whom we rest, since through [Col. 0218B] his death he transferred us from death to life.

“And he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it.” Why did he bless the seventh day, on which he created nothing? Perhaps it might otherwise appear that he was in need, as a human being becomes weary after labor and says, “I give thanks to my God because I have completed my work.”

The Lord did not act in this way. Rather, he blessed the day on which he created nothing to demonstrate that creating all things involved no labor for our God, because he merely said, “Let it be,” and they were made. Therefore he himself rested on the seventh day, so that he might make us rest in it.

Wherein did he bless the seventh day? In nothing except himself, because he is blessed by no one except himself and sanctified by no one except himself. Although he had not made everything, he was not thereby diminished, because nothing changeable is perceived in God—neither in eternity, nor in truth, nor in will. Rather, all things remain fixed and unchangeable with him.

What, then, is this day? It is the first, the second, and the last, because it is the repetition of the seventh day.

Do those three days that [Col. 0218C] preceded the placing of the stars in heaven belong to the days, or not? This must be understood affirmatively: they belong to the days, because there was no light that our eyes could have perceived before then, since the authority of this Scripture is greater than the capacity of every human intellect.

Just as Christ is light in one sense and stone in another—light literally, stone figuratively—so there was one angelic light and another light belonging to the stars.

Why did he not bless the first day, on which he created the angelic light, or the day on which he completed everything? He did not sanctify the day on which he began to do this, nor the day on which he completed it, lest his action in making or completing these things appear to have been a source of joy to him. Instead, he sanctified the day on which he rested from them in himself.

Yet he was never without that rest. He displayed it to us through the seventh day, signifying that we do not attain his rest except after the completion of our work.

And therefore it is understood that evening did not follow upon this day, because our rest after the completion of our work will be an endless joy. For on it he had ceased [Col. 0218D] from all his work—that is, from fashioning new and previously unknown things of the world, which God created in order to make. He continues to govern the world until its end; hence he himself said in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5).

Why did he not place morning on the first day, nor evening on the last? He did not place morning there because it has no beginning, nor evening because it has no end and is enclosed by no boundary.

And again, according to the spiritual sense.

## Recapitulation of the Six Days

After these events, on the sixth day the earth brings forth a living soul, when our flesh, abstaining from dead works, bears living sprouts of virtues: “according to its kind,” that is, living by imitating the saints, as the Apostle says: “Be imitators of me” (1 Corinthians 4).

We live according to our kind when, in good works, we imitate holy men as those near to us.

Then the earth brought forth beasts: human beings powerful in [Col. 0219A] worldly affairs or savage through the ferocity of pride. Likewise it brought forth cattle: faithful people living in simplicity. It also brought forth serpents: harmless holy men who, through the alertness of their intelligence, distinguish good from evil and, insofar as is permitted, investigate earthly things by crawling upon them, so that they may understand eternal things. These are not the venomous serpents who place themselves in the earthly desires of this world.

After this God made the human being in his own image: the perfect man, who does not act by imitating just any holy man, but by contemplating and beholding truth itself, and who practices righteousness so that he may understand and follow that truth in whose image he was made.

He also received authority over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, cattle, wild beasts, and creeping creatures, because everyone who has become spiritual and has likewise been made like God, according to the Apostle, “judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 15).

What follows—“Male and female he made them”—indicates spiritual people in the Church and those who obey. For just as woman is subject [Col. 0219B] to man, so the less perfect person obeys the spiritual and perfect man, as the Apostle says: “We ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you and preside over you in the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 5).

They are told: “Increase and multiply,” whether in languages or in the spiritual degrees of understanding, so that through the understanding of reason they may rule over all carnal disturbances, as over irrational living creatures.

Every seed-bearing plant and every fruit-bearing tree, which was given to human beings as food, signifies the faithful, who share their offerings with the saints. Hence the Apostle says: “If the Gentiles have become sharers in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things” (Romans 15).

These are the fruit-bearing trees.

In these stages, then, as in days upon which there is evening, the evening signifies the completion of each individual work, and the morning the beginning of what follows on the seventh day. After the good works of these, so to speak, six days, a person established in the spiritual paradise hopes for rest of mind. This signifies the blessed life, where the fountain of wisdom is divided [Col. 0219C] into four streams of virtues, where one may eat the grace of the tree of life, and where one may gather useful disciplines of conduct as the fruits of the trees.

Paradise is the life of the blessed; the four rivers are the four virtues; its trees are all useful disciplines; the fruits of the trees are the conduct of the devout; and the tree of life is wisdom itself, the mother of all good things. Of it Solomon says: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her, and blessed is the one who holds her” (Proverbs 3).

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the transgression of the commandment.

Thus far the work of the six days has been explained: how it is to be understood spiritually in the Church. Next it must be set forth what these things signify as a figure of the world.

“Over six days God completed all his works, and on the seventh he rested.”

The works of God, through the succession of times, make known the human race in this world in six ages. The first of these extends from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to [Col. 0219D] David; the fourth, from David to the deportation to Babylon; the fifth, from the Babylonian deportation to the humble coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sixth, which is now in progress, until the world comes to an end, until the Most High comes for judgment. The seventh is understood as the rest of the saints, which has no evening, since no limit now closes it.

Let us therefore proceed briefly through these ages of the world and, retracing the order of their times, distinguish their mystical differences. In the first age, something like light was made: man in paradise. In that age God divided the sons of God, under the name of “light,” from the sons of men, as from darkness; and the evening of this day was the Flood.

The second age was made like the firmament between water and water: namely, that ark which floated amid rain and seas. Its evening was the confusion of languages.

The third age was made when, through Abraham, He separated His people from the nations, distinguishing them like dry land from the waters, so that it might [Col. 0220A] bring forth the growth of herbs and trees—that is, spiritual saints and the fruit of the Holy Scriptures. Its evening was the sin and wickedness of the most evil king Saul.

From David the fourth age began, when God placed lights in the firmament of heaven: that is, the splendor of the kingdom, like the excellence of the sun; and, in the likeness of the moon, a light obedient to it, like the synagogue; and its princes as stars. This age has its evening in the sins of the kings, because of which that people deserved to be taken captive to Babylon.

In the fifth age, namely, in the Babylonian deportation, creatures in the waters and birds of the air were made, as it were, because at that time the Jews began to live among the nations as in the sea. They had no stable place, like flying birds. The evening, as it were, of this day is the multiplication of sins among the Jewish people, when they were so blinded that they could not even recognize their own Lord.

The sixth age now takes place in the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. For just as on that sixth day the first man, Adam, was formed from the clay [Col. 0220B] of the earth in the image of God, so in this sixth age of the world the second Adam, that is, Christ, was born from the Virgin Mary. The former was made a living soul, the latter a life-giving spirit. And just as on that day a living soul was made, so in this age those who desire eternal life are made. And just as on that sixth day the earth produced kinds of serpents and beasts, so in this sixth age of the world the Church brought forth nations desiring eternal life.

This same meaning was made clear by the vessel shown to Peter. And just as on that day male and female were created, so in this sixth age of the world Christ and the Church are revealed. And just as on that day man was placed over cattle, serpents, and the birds of heaven, so in this age Christ is placed over peoples and nations, so that they may be ruled by Him—whether they are devoted to carnal desire like cattle, darkened by earthly curiosity like serpents, or lifted up by pride like birds.

And just as on that day man and the animals with him were fed with seed-bearing herbs, fruit-bearing trees, and green plants, so in this age the spiritual man, [Col. 0220C] who is a good minister of Jesus Christ, is spiritually fed with the elements of the Holy Scriptures and with divine law, in order to conceive the fruitfulness of reasoning and speech. These are like seed-bearing herbs, partly for the usefulness of moral conduct in human life, like fruit-bearing trees, and partly for the strengthening of faith, hope, and charity unto eternal life, like green plants that do not wither from any heat of tribulations. By these spiritual foods he is fed in such a way that he understands many things.

The carnal man, however—that is, the little one in Christ, like God’s cattle—is fed so that he may believe many things which he is not yet able to understand; nevertheless, both have all the same foods.

Would that the evening, as it were, of this age not find us! For it is of this that the Lord says: “Do you suppose that when the Son of Man comes, He will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke XVIII). After this evening there will be morning, when the Lord Himself comes in glory. Then those will rest with Christ from all their works to whom it was said: “Be perfect, as your Father [Col. 0220D] who is in heaven is perfect” (Matthew V). Such people do works that are very good indeed. After such works, rest is to be hoped for on the seventh day, which has no evening.
