These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created on the day on which the Lord God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it appeared on the earth, and every plant of the countryside before it sprouted. It must be investigated whether all these things were made in one day or over six days, as Scripture here recalls. And if they were made over six days, how then does Holy Scripture say: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus XVIII)? He created all things together according to the substance of things; but according to the appearance of their form He did not create all things together.

For just as a mother nourishing an infant in her womb waits for it to grow strong, so the Lord waited for the slowness of human understanding. In the beginning all things were created with Him, but they did not immediately appear in their visible form, when He said: “In the beginning God created [Col. 0221A] heaven and earth” (Genesis I). Then, as we have said, all things that arose from heaven and earth were made with Him, although He wished to divide them according to their visible form over six days.

Thus, although He says that on the fourth day He placed the stars in heaven, they were already made with Him in heaven on the first day; on the fourth day they came into visible form. For just as in a seed many things are hidden—the root, bark, leaves, fruit, and many other things that come from the tree—so with God all these things were previously hidden and later appeared in visible form.

Thus all things were made together, as the Lord said: “My Father is working even now, and I am working” (John V). For although He created all things together then, He nevertheless governs them daily—in watering, planting, building, and in other matters. Just as a man who cultivates a field, if he abandons it, leaves it uncultivated, so the world created by God cannot exist without God’s governance, according to the apostle Paul: “Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives [Col. 0221B] the growth” (I Corinthians III).

There are also others who wish to understand these seven days as the seven gifts of the grace of the Holy Spirit: namely, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isaiah XI).

They say that God made heaven and earth through the spirit of wisdom; through the spirit of understanding He made the firmament, and separated waters from waters; through the spirit of counsel He separated the waters from the dry land and caused the earth to sprout; through the spirit of fortitude He placed the lights in the firmament of heaven, so that they might divide day from night; through the spirit of knowledge He adorned the waters with creeping creatures and the air with flying creatures; through the spirit of piety He clothed the earth with animals and created man, together with the other things that follow; and through the spirit of the fear of the Lord, on the seventh day, He sanctified His work.

So we too must imitate these seven gifts of the grace of the Holy Spirit in ourselves. Through the spirit of wisdom we must make heaven and earth—that is, meditate on heavenly things and abandon earthly [Col. 0221C] things—or separate light from darkness, that is, our perfected works from the darkness of evil deeds.

Through the spirit of understanding we must make a firmament between the upper and lower waters—that is, holy discipline between vices and virtues—so that we do not incline toward vices.

Through the spirit of counsel we must separate the waters from the dry land—that is, reject wicked people from the soul that knows the words of God.

Through the spirit of fortitude we must place lights in the firmament of heaven—that is, love of God and of neighbor, because Saint John said: “He who hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III).

Through the spirit of knowledge we must adorn the waters with creeping creatures and, in other respects, send a voice from the secret places of our heart toward heaven, just as fish give a high leap with their fins and birds fly through the air. So we too must always raise our understanding toward higher things.

Through the spirit of piety we must make cattle, serpents, and the rest—that is, we must possess simplicity and prudence for discerning good and evil, and produce the fruit of good works, [Col. 0221D] so that we may be able to imitate the examples of the saints and Truth itself, in whose image we were made.

Through the spirit of the fear of the Lord we must rest in the rest of eternal life, because it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm CX).

Why did He not place morning on the first day, or evening on the seventh day? He did not place morning on the first day because He foresaw man sinning in paradise, and the night of ignorance followed him. He did not place evening on the seventh day because He foresaw that man would return to forgiveness through the coming of the Savior.

And in the beginning, if night followed day, or day followed night—which followed which? Night followed day. But now, after the coming of the Savior, day follows night. This signified fallen man: when he transgressed, night followed him, that is, sin. After the coming of the Savior, however, day follows night, because He restored us to forgiveness and through His death transferred us from death to life, which we had lost through the fault of our first parent Adam.

Night followed him [Col. 0222A] because holy people entered the prison of hell until the coming of the Lord. Now day follows us, because after His resurrection all the saints, departing from the body, go to Christ. What we lost in Adam, we received through Jesus Christ.

### Recapitulation

These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created on the day on which the Lord God made heaven and earth. Although seven days were counted above, one day is now mentioned, on which God made heaven and earth, every shrub of the field, and every plant of the countryside.

By the name of this day, according to the prophet, the whole time of this life is signified—the time in which heaven and earth were made, that is, in which visible creatures are distributed, administered, and exist.

But what does it mean that, after naming heaven and earth, He now added “the shrub of the field” and “the plant of the countryside,” while saying nothing of the other things that are in heaven and earth, or even in the sea? It means that [Col. 0222B] by “the shrub of the field” an invisible creature is signified, such as the soul. It is called a shrub because of the vigor of life, and a plant because of that same life, which never withers.

Then, when He added: “Before it was upon the earth,” this is understood as “before the soul sinned.” Stained by earthly desires, it is rightly said to have been born upon the earth or to be upon the earth.

“For the Lord God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no man to till the earth.” Therefore the earth had not sprouted, because the Lord had not rained upon the earth; and there was no man to till the earth, because the earth sprouts and produces fruit especially through the rain and through the man who tills it.

Thus He added: “For the Lord God had not yet rained upon the earth,” as though He were saying openly: Before the soul sinned, the Lord had not yet granted the rain of instruction from the clouds of the Scriptures to water the soul.

For the sake of man, who is earth, our Lord had not yet assumed the cloud of our flesh, [Col. 0222C] through which He poured out the most abundant rain of the Holy Gospel.

But when He adds: “And there was no man to till the earth,” this is because no man worked in the Virgin from whom Christ was born. He is the stone cut from the mountain without hands—that is, without intercourse or human seed—cut from the virgin womb as from the mountain of human nature and the substance of flesh (Daniel II).

## ON THE ASCENT OF THE SPRING AND THE IRRIGATION OF THE EARTH

But a spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth. What is this spring that watered the entire face of the earth? It was not like the Nile, which waters Egypt alone; rather, this spring is said to have watered the whole world.

Perhaps one spring was named before paradise was planted, and, having received the assistance of moisture, it watered the whole surface of the earth. Or, after paradise had been [planted] and the rushing outflow of the waters had been checked [Col. 0222D], that spring was divided through its channels to water the whole face of the earth.

Just as we now see waters flowing through the beds of rivers and the courses of streams, and by their overflow flooding the neighboring region, so then many streams proceeded, as it were, from one spring.

Or one spring was named, hidden in some hollow of the earth, and from it all the great and small springs proceeded.

But why is this spring not plainly found, when it appears to have watered the whole face of the earth? Perhaps because of the sin of our first parent Adam this spring was withdrawn, so that it might remove the earth’s fertility and impose greater labor upon the human race.

And how could one spring water the entire earth? And if it watered the earth, how could it water the mountains, since some of them are said to have great height?

This must be understood: at that time, in the newness of the earth, it is credible that not everything, but many things, were full. Or just as the Nile waters the whole land of Egypt, so then that [Col. 0223A] river could have watered the entire face of the earth through God’s command and power.

Or the singular number was used for the plural. For Scripture does not say “one spring,” but simply: “A spring rose,” and: “Watering the whole face of the earth.” Thus it says: “The frog and the locust came up over the land of Egypt” (Exodus VIII), while many frogs and locusts are understood. So perhaps one spring was named, while many springs are understood.

### Recapitulation

“A spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.” The virgin earth of the Lord, Mary, is most rightly understood here, of whom it is written: “Let the earth open, and bring forth the Savior” (Isaiah XLV). This earth was watered by the Holy Spirit, who is signified in the Gospel under the name of spring and water.

Then God formed man from the clay of the earth—that is, Adam from the dust of the earth.

Some wish to say that man was created in the image of God because the Lord Himself [Col. 0223B] created him with His own hands. But this must not be accepted at all, as though the Lord had created any bodily thing bodily, as it says: “In the beginning You, O Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of Your hands” (Psalm CI).

For God did not fashion these things bodily through works of hands; rather, by His command and power He ordered everything to be made as He wished.

Why did He make him from the clay of the earth, and why not from the clay of paradise? The reason was that He created from the earth the man who was destined to return to the earth, as it is written: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis III).

Here it must be asked whether Adam was made immediately in an imperfect age, or in childhood. It should be judged that he was formed immediately at a mature age because of the miracle, just as He made wine from water, along with many other things that would take too long to recount.

And again:

### Recapitulation

“Then the Lord God formed man from the clay of the [Col. 0223C] earth” (Genesis II). Christ was made in the same way, according to what the Apostle says: “From the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans I), as though from the clay of the earth, from the breathing of man [reading uncertain].

“And He breathed into his face the breath of life.” What is “the breath of life”? It means to make a breath—that is, to make a soul. As the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “The spirit proceeds from Me, and I have made every breath” (Isaiah LVII).

And again: “He breathed into his face,” and the rest—namely, the infusion of the Holy Spirit, through which He made the man Christ.

“And man became a living soul,” that is, he began to feel in the body, as a living being.

### Recapitulation here

And he now narrates everything in order, explaining how the things that he passed over above were created.

Others, however, say that the soul proceeded from the Divinity, since it says: “And He breathed into his face the breath of life.” But this must not be accepted at all: that the soul proceeds from the Divinity. Those who say this speak against the Catholic faith, [Col. 0223D] because the Divinity is never changed, whereas the soul is made better when it does good.

They say this because, just as the Lord came to His disciples in the Gospel, breathed upon them, and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit,” and the Holy Spirit was then given from the Divinity to the holy apostles, so the soul too might have been given from the Divinity.

But this must not be accepted at all, because breathing is the breath of the body. The holy apostles received the Holy Spirit from the Divinity; the soul, however, is not from the Divinity, but was born from God and made from nothing.

It must be investigated when the soul was created: whether it was created on the sixth day, when He formed man from the clay of the earth. Would this not then contradict divine Scripture, which says: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus XVIII)?

If the soul was created then, where was it hidden until man received it? Perhaps it was hidden among God’s creatures until it [entered] man. But how could the soul, created innocent, enter a body [Col. 0224A] which God foresaw would sin?

Far be it from us to accept that the soul was created for this reason and kept in reserve so that it might enter a body which God foresaw would sin; for if this were so, God would appear to have been the author of sin.

But far be this from us, because it is not so. Rather, it must be understood and accepted that the soul itself entered voluntarily in order to administer the body, because the body is perceived through the soul. For if the soul is absent, the body is dead.

And why did He breathe the spirit of life into no other member—neither the crown of the head, nor the forehead, nor the chest—but only into the face?

Because the fire whose principal location is in the liver ascends into the brain, as into the heaven of our body. From there three parts are produced.

The anterior part is that through which every sensation rises from the brain into the forehead, from the forehead into the face; from the face it is distributed through minute channels, as through organs, into the four bodily senses: sight, hearing, smell, and taste.

The posterior part, [Col. 0224B] through which all movement operates, makes its way upward from that same anterior part into the crown of the head. From the crown it proceeds to the marrow of the spine, and from there distributes every movement into the limbs.

The anterior part is rightly placed before the posterior, because movement follows deliberation.

There is also a third part, in which memory is fixed, because whatever you wish to do, or have previously done, is established in memory. Where there is no memory, there is no voluntary movement.

From this voluntary movement, that is, from the anterior part, hair and nails are produced. Everything is understood through the senses, because man possesses a sense that animals do not have, and from this voluntary movement is produced the power by which the mind is administered.

This is understood through air and light. Air enters the lungs as into organs, then into the veins, and reaches the heart, which we call the arteries.

And does the soul, or the body, perceive—or not? It must be understood that the body is administered through the senses [Col. 0224C]: through the eyes it sees, through the ears it hears, and through taste and smell it perceives.

What is sweet or bitter? And is the soul made from the five senses of the body? [Col. 0224C] It must be understood that we have no means by which we can prove this. For when the soul of a human being wishes to consider something secret, it closes its eyes or its ears and considers what it has done, what it will do, or its Creator, who created it.

What, then, is the soul? If there is some substance from which souls are made, what is that substance itself? What is its name? What is its form? What function does it have among created things? Does it live or not? If it lives, what does it contribute to the affections of the universe? Does it lead a blessed life or a wretched one?

What, then, is the soul? It is not heaven, nor earth, nor air, nor fire, nor water, nor God, nor the stars, nor sight, nor hearing, nor smell, nor taste, nor the other things that would take too long to enumerate, whether in heaven or on earth. The soul is none of these.

Where, then, is the soul from? If it was given from God and made from nothing—for man, who was made from earth, will return to earth.

Likewise, snow or a storm is made from water and is air; it takes from the earth and returns to water and to earth. Air too is taken [Col. 0224D] from water. But the soul has no element to which it may return, except its Creator, who created it, after it has departed from the body, if it has acted rightly.

And how do those who are blind, who do not possess sight, see dreams just as those who possess sight do? This must be understood as follows: they are overcome by sleep in the brain, and their images cannot break out into the external world; then they see those images within themselves. Their mind never sleeps.

The origin of the soul must be investigated: where does it come from when a human being is born?

Some say that just as flesh is born from flesh, so the soul is born from soul. But Scripture nowhere relates where the soul comes from when a human being is born, nor does it explain how the soul of the woman came to be, as it explains how her flesh was made.

Others say that each person’s soul is given by God when he is born. Thus it is said in Isaiah: “I have made every breath” (Isaiah LVII)—that is, every soul. And similarly it is written in the Psalm: “He fashioned their hearts one by one” [Col. 0225A] (Psalm XXXII).

Others say that the soul is given from the parents, just as flesh comes from flesh.

They seem to contradict Scripture, which says: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus XVIII), as though He appeared always to be creating new souls.

Others say that all souls were created when He made everything together, and that they are hidden in a certain place until a human being is born; then the soul is given to him by God.

But this is not something that can be established from our own considerations—whether it should or should not be so, or how the soul is given to man—because Scripture nowhere relates it.

We cannot discern what Truth has left unsaid. It says nothing even about the woman’s soul, how it was made; it only relates how Adam’s soul was given.

From where, then, did our Savior Jesus Christ receive His soul? Not from Adam, but from the same source as Adam, that is, from God. For although He descended from the line of sin, He was not conceived from the line of sin; nor was it flesh of sin, but the likeness of sinful flesh.

For from that source [Col. 0225B] He did not receive the liability of dying.

And when the soul departs from this body, is it bodily or incorporeal? How, then, is it spoken of, if it is incorporeal? An incorporeal thing is simultaneously among bodies. And where is it carried—to a bodily place or an incorporeal one? It is carried to an incorporeal place, though such places are described by comparison with bodies.

It is therefore asked whether the soul can exist without the body among the angels in perpetual blessedness, without defect.

Why, then, is it necessary that the body rise again, so that it may then put on the immortality which it now lays aside in its mortal state? It is because the administration of the body is indeed present, and the mind is delayed by it, so that it does not proceed to the highest state until the body rises again. What is now a burden to it will then be in glory.

And why is it necessary that little children who have Christian parents, a father and mother, be born again through the water of baptism? It is because each person is born in original sin, and unless he is born again through the water of baptism, he cannot enter the kingdom of God, as the Savior shows in the Gospel, saying: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” [Col. 0225C] (John III).

### Again, according to the spiritual meaning

“And man became a living soul,” namely, so that the one who was perfect might be believed to be both perfect God and man.

## ON THE PLANTING OF PARADISE

The Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which He placed the man whom He had formed. Paradise is called a place of delights, or a place flourishing with an abundance of graces.

Saint Augustine said that this paradise was planted in a certain place where earthly man could dwell. But paradise is understood spiritually as the place to which the souls of the saints now go when they depart from the body. This paradise was planted as its figure, in accordance with the truth of historical events.

“And the Lord God brought forth from the soil every tree [Col. 0225D] beautiful to look upon and pleasant to eat, and also the tree of life in the midst of paradise.”

He did not produce other trees than those which He had earlier said He created on the third day; now He relates how He brought them forth into visible form in paradise.

And this tree of life was such that whoever tasted of it would remain immortal. At that time, however, it appeared in paradise to be like earthly food—not like other food, which tends to produce distaste, but food by which one might be made steadfast in complete health.

Yet what did this tree contain? The other trees contained nourishment, but this one contained a sacrament.

Although this was historically enacted, just as it is said of paradise that it prefigured the Church—and just as what happened with Hagar and Sarah, and many other things that took place historically, also prefigured something else—so this tree prefigured the tree of the cross.

### Again: Recapitulation

“The Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, [Col. 0226A]” and so forth. Paradise is the Church. For it is written of her in the Song of Songs: “My sister is a garden enclosed” (Song of Songs IV).

Paradise is planted from the beginning because the Catholic Church is known to have been founded by Christ, who is the beginning of all things.

The river flowing out from paradise bears the image of Christ flowing from the Father’s fountain. He waters His Church with the word of preaching and with the gift of baptism. Of this the prophet rightly says: “The Lord our God is a glorious river, leaping upon thirsty ground.”

The four rivers of paradise are the four Gospels, sent forth for preaching among all the nations.

The fruit-bearing trees are all the saints; their fruits are their works; the tree of life is the Holy of Holies, namely Christ. Whoever stretches out his hand toward Him will live forever.

## ON THE TREE OF THE KNOWLEDGE OF GOOD AND EVIL

“The tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” Why did it receive this name? [Col. 0226B] Because God created all things very good.

By recognizing good and evil, one recognizes how great the difference would have been between obedience, which is good, and disobedience, which is evil. If he had transgressed, it would have been evil for him; if he had not transgressed, it would have been good for him, because he would not have learned the experience of punishment.

## ON THE GOING FORTH OF THE RIVER

“A river went forth from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there it is divided into four heads. The name of the first is Phison; it is the one that surrounds the whole land of Evilath, where gold is born. The gold of that land is excellent; there too bdellium and the onyx stone are found. The name of the second river is Gehon; it is the one that surrounds the whole land of Ethiopia. The name of the third river is the Tigris; it flows opposite Assyria. The fourth river is the Euphrates.”

As was indicated above concerning the river itself, four rivers flow out from paradise, two of which have proper names. The Tigris itself is the Nile, which [Col. 0226C] surrounds the whole land of Egypt. Phison itself is the Ganges.

### Recapitulation

Again, according to the spiritual meaning, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil properly signifies free choice of the will, which has been placed in the midst of us for recognizing good or evil. Whoever, abandoning God’s grace, tastes from it will die by death.

“Then the Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight, so that he might work it and guard it.”

Whenever Scripture speaks of the person of man, it names both God and Lord, in order to show how advantageous it is for him to possess the Lord God as his own: that is, to live obediently under His dominion.

How was he to work it? Not with servile labor, but with the honorable will of the soul. And he was to guard it so that he might commit nothing for which he would deserve to be expelled from it.

Thus anyone is rightly said not to have guarded his own property if he acts in such a way that he loses it. It was not necessary to guard paradise on account of beasts, or to work it through servile labor on account of anything else, because [Col. 0226D] He said: “Behold, I have given you every plant,” and so forth.

Rather, the Lord was to work righteousness, piety, and the other good things in him. God grants this to man, because man can do nothing without God’s help.

God was to work him so that he might be righteous, and guard him so that he might be safe. For if God were to abandon him and withdraw His support, he would remain empty, since God has no need of any good thing from him.

But we all need His dominion. For it is written: “I have said to the Lord, You are my God, for You have no need of my goods” (Psalm XV). And in another place it is written: “But for me, it is good to cling to God” (Psalm LXXII).

## ON THE COMMANDMENT CONCERNING THE TREE

“And He commanded him, saying: ‘Eat from every tree of paradise, but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat. For on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.’”

[Col. 0227A] Why did the Lord prohibit him from eating from that tree? Because He knew that he would be condemned if he transgressed.

For it was necessary that man, placed under the Lord God, be prohibited from something, so that obedience itself might be his virtue in pleasing his Lord. If he had kept the commandments of his Creator, obedience itself would have been a virtue for him, which he lost after the transgression.

### Recapitulation

“Then the Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight.” God assumed flesh and became the head of the Church.

“So that he might work it and guard it”: that is, so that from all the nations He might fulfill the Father’s will concerning the Church, and so that the word spoken by the Lord might be fulfilled: “I was keeping them in Your name; those whom You gave Me I guarded” (John XVII).

And God said: “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself.”

Here He plainly shows that they were to produce offspring, when [Col. 0227B] a helper like himself was given to Adam—that is, Eve, fashioned from his side.

They were not to produce offspring in the way they do now, so that children might succeed their dead parents in their place, but so that they might remain immortal and, after the appointed number had been completed, be changed into better things.

Then the Lord God formed from the soil all the animals of the earth and all the birds of heaven, and brought them to Adam to see what he would call them. “Whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name.”

How did He bring them, since God is unchangeable? Was it through an angel, or through Himself? This must not be accepted at all as though God had carried these things out bodily. Rather, it was to show that all things live and perceive for Him, just as the she-ass spoke with Balaam, along with many other examples. For man received this power from the Lord, so that he might have dominion over the beasts to the present day.

### Recapitulation

[Col. 0227C] “And God said: ‘It is not good for man to be alone.’”

Let the heretics be refuted who think that Christ was man alone and not also God.

“Let us make him a helper like himself.” For in the man He assumed, the Church was joined to God.

And Adam gave names to all the animals, all the birds of heaven, and all the beasts of the earth; but for Adam no helper like himself was found. [Col. 0227D]

When, then, did the fish receive names, since he does not mention this here, but speaks only of the animals? Names were gradually assigned as the kinds of fish became known—that is, when they were created.

### Again: Recapitulation

“Adam gave them their names,” and so forth. This signifies the nations that would be saved in the Church and would receive names through Christ, which they had not previously possessed. As it is written: “I will call My servants by another name” (Isaiah LXV).

“But for Adam no helper like himself was found.” This is because, although each person may be faithful or just, no one can be made equal to Christ.

“For who,” says Moses, “is like You among the gods, O Lord?” And David too says: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm XLIV).

No one could have freed the human race from death and overcome death itself except Christ, as the Apocalypse says: “No one was found worthy, either in heaven or on earth or under the earth, to open the book” (Apocalypse V).

## ON THE INFUSION OF SLEEP AND THE CREATION OF WOMAN

“Then the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam. And when he had fallen asleep, He took one of his ribs and filled in flesh in its place.”

How, then, did the Lord God cast such sleep upon Adam that he did not at all feel the rib being taken from him?

This is to be understood as meaning that he became a participant in the care of the angels, [Col. 0228A] entering into the sanctuary and understanding the final things among them. There he immediately awoke and burst forth, saying:

This now is bone from my bones, etc. “And the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam.” And Adam said: “This now is bone from my bones, and flesh from my flesh.” Why did he make the woman from a rib? He did so to show that Christ would be born from a woman. Just as the woman was then made from the man, so Christ was born from a woman, because power proceeded from a woman into the world. Although at that time death had entered the world through a woman, this was either to demonstrate that chaste members ought not to be opposed by God, or—because of the force of the commendation—to declare that the woman had been fashioned from a rib.

## Recapitulation

“Therefore God cast Adam into a sleep,” etc. Adam slept, and a woman was made for him from his side; Christ suffered and slept upon the cross, his side was pierced by a lance, and the sacraments flowed forth, from which the Church was to be formed. [Col. 0228B] The prophet sings of this sleep, saying: “I slept, and took rest, and rose again, because the Lord raised me up” (Psalm 5). It continues:

“And he placed flesh in its stead.” So also Christ, by dying, placed his flesh upon the gibbet of the cross for the Church.

And Adam said: “This now is bone from my bones, and flesh from my flesh.” For whether they are holy, spiritual, and most steadfast in temptations, or less perfect, both belong to one body of Christ and to one Church. “She shall be called woman” (*virago*), “because she was taken from man”; therefore she is called Eve, because she is the mother of all living beings.

“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” Now both were naked, Adam namely and his wife, and they were not ashamed. They were not ashamed because they no longer felt within their members a law resisting the law of their mind, nor the violent enticements of the flesh within the body of death (Romans 7). Hence the Apostle [Col. 0228C] does not say, “Let there be no sin in your members,” but says, “Let it not reign” (Romans 6). For it does not reign when we do not obey its desires.

And again, according to the spiritual sense, a recapitulation.

“She shall be called woman, because she was taken from man.” So also the name of the Church was given from Christ: *Christian*, since the Church was taken from his side. All these things, therefore, were made as figures of what would benefit the Church.

“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother,” etc. Interpreting this, the Apostle says: “But I am speaking of Christ and of the Church” (Ephesians 5). Therefore what was completed historically in Adam is signified prophetically in Christ. He leaves the Father when he says: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world” (John 16). He also left his mother, that is, the synagogue adhering carnally to the Old Testament, which was his mother according to the seed of David in the flesh. [Col. 0228D] And he clung to his wife, that is, to the Church, so that through the peace of the New Testament the two might be one flesh. Although he is God with the Father, through whom we were made, he became through the flesh a participant in what is ours, so that we might be the body of that head.

After this she is called Eve, life and mother of the living, because she was made from the side of her husband; and the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone does not eat my flesh and drink my blood, he does not have life in himself” (John 6). From this point onward, the command that Christ received figuratively we have received in him, because every Christian appropriately bears the person of Christ, as the Lord himself says: “Whatever you did for one of these least ones, you did for me” (Matthew 10). Thus it is said to him: “Eat from every tree of paradise,” by which spiritual delights are signified. “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, gentleness, self-control,” as the Apostle says (Galatians 5).

And let us not touch the tree planted in the middle of paradise, [Col. 0229A] the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. That is, let us not wish to grow proud of the nature of our free choice, which is in the middle, lest, deceived after acquiring knowledge, we experience evil as well.

## Concerning the Serpent’s Cunning

“But the serpent was more cunning than all the animals of the earth that the Lord God had made.” This serpent was not more cunning by its own nature—that is, more prudent or wiser—but because of the devil, who was speaking through the serpent. Hence the Lord Christ said in the Gospel: “The sons of this age are more prudent than the sons of light” (Luke 16).

How did the serpent speak to the woman: by itself or through the devil? This must be understood as follows: the devil entered into the serpent, and thus spoke to the woman. Just as he now customarily enters his vessel and speaks through it, so then he spoke through the serpent. For just as a man commonly treads upon an organ, and the organ feels nothing from it, so then the serpent felt nothing of what was spoken.

Why did he permit her to be tempted through this animal? [Col. 0229B] It is not surprising that he permitted the temptation through the serpent, through which the devil had been permitted to act, since that ancient enemy has a most wicked will and a most evil power: he always has the will to do evil, but has no power to harm without God’s permission.

Why did he permit him to tempt one whom he foresaw would consent? What is surprising if he permitted this to happen, since they possessed free choice to do evil or good? It does not seem to me that it would have been a great praise for the future human being if he could live well merely because no one persuaded him to live badly. That is, there would have been no praise if he had lived well for the reason that he had no temptation in his members.

Why, then, did he permit him to tempt one whom he foresaw would consent? Because he was going to do it by his own will through guilt, and by God’s justice was to be ordered through punishment. And how would he have been blameworthy if God had not permitted him to be tempted, since he possessed free choice and, with God’s help, could resist the temptation—he who resists the proud [Col. 0229C] and gives grace to the humble (James 4)? Resistance would have been a great praise, just as the saints now endure many temptations and, with God’s aid, overcome them; therefore they receive a greater reward with Christ.

And if this temptation could cast them out of paradise, it must be understood that it could not have done so had they not lifted themselves up in empty glory, which their hostile enemy promised them, saying: “If you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods.” In this they were lifted up; hence it is written: “Before destruction the heart is exalted,” and so forth (Proverbs 16).

Why did God, who foreknew that human beings would be sinners and condemned, permit them to be born? And why would he not leave them to themselves, since they possessed free choice? If they did not wish to preserve what they had been made, they would receive condemnation and serve as an example to others who behold their punishment and become good through the sight of evil. For they consider what happened to them on account of their sins. There is one nature that cannot sin, and there is a nature that can sin. One [Col. 0229D] is found in angels, the other in human beings.

It was fitting that they should have praised God on account of both natures; nevertheless, in both natures iniquity was found, because an evil will corrupted a good nature, while the good nature had been created by God. A perverse will makes it evil. And if someone should say, “Why did God create evil human beings?” the proper answer would be: It would not have been better, for by mercifully making good use of another’s evil he would be crowned, rather than himself being evil and justly punished according to his deserts.

Why cannot the devil be restored, while the human being can? So that he might demonstrate both power and mercy, and so that they might have something to fear and something to hope for. And what is surprising if the devil entered into the serpent, when the Lord permitted him to enter into swine?

Others wish to say that the devil was envious of the human being because he had been created in the image of God; and for this reason he persuaded him to eat the fruits in paradise, which had been forbidden so that he would not eat them. Hence the Apostle says: “The root of all evils is greed” [Col. 0230A] (1 Timothy 6), that is, love of money. At that time he did not desire money, but wished to deceive the human being. And since it is written elsewhere, “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Eccl. 10), this must be understood thus: pride did not proceed from the devil’s envy; rather, envy proceeded from pride. Both were found together at the beginning, because through pride he was cast down from heaven, and through envy he deceived the human being.

## Concerning the Serpent’s Suggestion to the Woman

The serpent said to the woman: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” The woman replied: “We eat from the fruit of the trees that are in paradise; but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise, God commanded us not to eat from it and not to touch it, lest perhaps we die.”

Why did the serpent first question the woman, and why did she herself indicate from which tree they had received the command not to eat, so that the transgression might become inexcusable? [Col. 0230B] Because she had no means by which to excuse herself, since she plainly understood which tree they had been forbidden to eat from.

The serpent then said: “You shall certainly not die. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.” This is how the devil has acted up to the present day. He always persuades people to despise God’s commands; and what God threatens, he makes seem mild, easy, and safe. Therefore many are deceived by his seduction.

That serpent, wiser than all the beasts, signifies the devil; he is called a serpent because he moves with winding cunning. But why did he deceive through the woman and not through the man? Because our reason cannot be seduced into sin unless it is preceded by the delight of a carnal inclination of weakness, which ought rather to obey reason as a ruling man. This takes place secretly within every human being, [Col. 0230C] in a certain hidden marriage.

We receive the suggestion through the woman, meaning the animal sense of the body; reason is the man. Therefore, when an evil suggestion arises, the serpent seems to speak. But if thought alone takes pleasure in it, while reason restrains that suggestion, and consent to carrying out the act does not follow, only the woman appears to have eaten what was forbidden. If the mind itself also decides that the sin should be committed, then the man has been deceived; then the woman seems to have given food to the man.

To consent to the enticement from the forbidden tree is to eat. Then the human being is rightly expelled from blessed life as from paradise, and the sin is imputed to him even if the deed does not follow; for although guilt is not present in the actions, the conscience is nevertheless held guilty in its consent.

This is according to the anagogical sense (*anagoge*). According to metaphor, however, this cunning serpent could signify the craftiness of heretics. Some of them, with excessive fluency and subtlety, promise the opening of hidden matters through illicit curiosity [Col. 0230D] and knowledge of good and evil; they even claim to demonstrate this in the human being himself, as in the tree planted in the middle of paradise.

Against this serpent the Apostle cries out when he says: “I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted” (2 Corinthians 11). Our carnal desire is seduced by the words of this serpent, and through it Adam is deceived—not Christ, but the Christian.

Thus the serpent says to the woman: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” So the curious desire of heretics, and so wicked preachers, inflame the hearts of carnal hearers to love the deception of error, saying: “Why do you avoid possessing hidden knowledge? Always seek out new things; penetrate the knowledge of good and evil.” Hence, in Solomon, that woman who holds the opinion of the heretics says: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant” (Proverbs 9).

Then the same serpent added: “On whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will immediately [Col. 0231A] be opened, and you will know good and evil like gods.” So all heretics profess the privilege of divine generation and deceive people by promising knowledge; they criticize those whom they find believing simply. And because they persuade people entirely of carnal things, they try to bring about the opening of carnal eyes, so that the inner eye may be darkened.

## Concerning the Woman’s Consent

The woman therefore saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful to behold; she took its fruit and ate, and gave some to her husband, who ate. Let each of us learn an example from this. One should never look upon what is not permitted to occur, lest one be deceived through desire and pleasure, as Eve was: she first looked at the tree, then took pleasure in it, and ate.

Why did he make his suggestion to the woman and not to the man? Because of the woman’s softness or weakness. [Col. 0231B] As the Apostle Paul said: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived” (1 Timothy 2). How was this said, when blessed Paul says elsewhere: “In the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come” (Romans 5)?

He said this because Adam was not deceived by the serpent, but through the woman: the woman first ate through the serpent’s suggestion and then gave it to her husband. For “the man is the image and glory of God, but the woman is the glory of the man” (1 Corinthians 11). Therefore he did not first persuade the man, but the woman, in whom softness was contained.

And why did Adam eat from the forbidden tree, concerning which he had been commanded not to eat, when he knew that, if he did so, God’s sentence would be fulfilled—the sentence previously spoken to him: “If you eat from it, you shall die”? He ate because of his love for the woman, since he did not wish to offend or grieve her, just as we read that Solomon acted: because of his love for women, he provoked his God against himself.

So Adam acted: while he loved the woman, he despised the commands of his Creator and was cast down [Col. 0231C] from lofty immortality into the depths of the earth.

And the eyes of both were opened. They were opened for no other reason than that they should desire one another, as the punishment for sin. When they had been cast away from the tree of life, their bodies immediately assumed a diseased and mortal condition, because before they sinned they felt no law in their members resisting the law of their mind. Afterwards, however, they immediately felt in their members another law resisting the law of their mind and taking them captive under the law of sin (Romans 7).

And again, according to the spiritual sense.

The woman therefore saw that the tree was good, etc. The woman ate first, not the man, because carnal people are more easily persuaded into sin, whereas spiritual people are not deceived so quickly.

## Concerning the Man’s Consent

[Col. 0231D] And she gave it to her husband, and he ate. This happened because, after the delight of our carnal desire, our reason too is subjected to sin.

When they realized that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together. Those cover themselves with a fig leaf who embrace the harshness of the world, who burn with the itch of carnal pleasure, and who, deceived by heretical perversity and stripped of God’s grace, gather coverings of lies like fig leaves, making themselves girdles of perversity when they lie about the Lord or the Church.

And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise at the evening breeze after midday. God walks in such people, and does not stand, because they do not remain steadfast in his command. It is rightly “at the breeze after midday,” because that more fervent light of charity is already being taken away from them as the darkness of errors approaches. Hence it is written: “They follow the shadow, and not the light.”

Adam and his wife hid themselves from the face [Col. 0232A] of the Lord God in the midst of the tree of paradise. But how could they hide themselves from God’s face? Can anything be hidden from God? This must be understood as meaning that everyone who commits sin or despises the Lord’s command hides himself from God, because God regards him as unknown on account of his sin. As he said in the Gospel: “I do not know you” (Luke 13).

For it is impossible that anything should be hidden from God, since it is written: “The eyes of the Lord observe good and evil” (Proverbs 15). But each person hides himself among the trees of paradise, because, turned away from the command of the Creator, he lives in error and in the pleasures of his own free choice.

## The Voice That Rebukes or Calls Back

The Lord God called Adam and said to him: “Where are you?” He replied: “I heard your voice in paradise, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.” He said: “Who told you that you were naked, unless you ate from the tree concerning which I commanded you not to eat?”

This is not the voice of one who is ignorant, but of one who rebukes. [Col. 0232B] In calling him, he recalls him to repentance; in asking him, he shows that God rightly regards sinners whom he condemns as unknown.

And if Adam was such that he could understand God’s speech, like the angels, did he still need to possess perfection of understanding? How would he have been able to comprehend God’s speech? From this it must be understood that God spoke to him through an angel, just as he spoke to the fathers; for Adam did not know through understanding what God wished to say, as the angels do.

Concerning his being naked, this is understood to mean that they were already feeling in their bodies the law of sin, which they had not possessed before they sinned. If they had not eaten from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, they could not have died at all, as was indicated above.

And again.

God called Adam and said to him: “Where are you?” Here he shows that, if some who have fallen away from faith or good works into their lies [Col. 0232C] and desires, God does not despise them, but still calls them to return through repentance, because he does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live. Therefore no sinners whatsoever should despair, since even the ungodly are summoned to hope for pardon.

## Concerning the Man’s Excuse

Adam said: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate.” And the Lord God said to the woman: “Why did you do this?” She replied: “The serpent deceived me.”

Where humility ought to have appeared, pride came first. They had been questioned so that they might confess their sin; instead, both offered an excuse, each excusing his guilt through another: Adam through the woman, and the woman through the serpent. They increased the guilt they ought to have confessed and seemed, as it were, to accuse God—Adam for having given him the woman as a companion, and the woman likewise for having placed the serpent in paradise [Col. 0232D]. They received vengeance where they ought to have found mercy, and were cast down from lofty immortality into the depths of the earth.

## Concerning the Serpent’s Curse

After this he says to the serpent: “Because you have done this, you are cursed above all the animals and beasts of the earth. You shall walk upon your breast.” By the name “breast” the pride of the mind is signified; by the name “belly,” the desires of the flesh. Through these two things the devil creeps into those whom he wishes to deceive: either through earthly desire and lust, or through pride and irrational ruin.

“And you shall eat earth,” that is, those whom you have deceived through earthly desire shall belong to you. “All the days of your life,” that is, throughout the whole time in which you exercise this power, before the final punishment of judgment.

“I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.” The devil’s seed is perverse suggestion; the woman’s seed is the fruit of a good [Col. 0233A] work by which perverse suggestion is resisted. She will crush his head if the mind excludes him at the very beginning of an evil suggestion; he lies in wait for her heel because he strives to deceive the mind that he did not deceive through the first suggestion at the end.

Some have understood the words, “I will put enmity between you and the woman,” as referring to the betrothed virgin from whom the Lord was born. At that time the Lord was promised as destined to be born from her in order to conquer the enemy and destroy death, of which the enemy was the author, as it is written concerning David: “From the fruit of your womb I will place upon your throne” (Psalm 131).

They also understand the following words, “She will crush your head, and you will lie in wait for her heel,” as referring to the fruit of Mary’s womb, which is Christ: “You will trip him so that he may die; but after conquering you, he will rise again and crush your head, which is death.” So David also said, speaking in the person of the Father to the Son: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample upon the lion [Col. 0233B] and the dragon” (Psalm 90). He called the asp death, the basilisk sin, the lion the Antichrist, and the dragon the devil.

## Concerning the Woman’s Curse

God also said to the woman: “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions. In pain you shall bear children, and you shall be under the power of the man; he shall rule over you.”

What does it signify, concerning the woman’s punishment, that he says to her, “In pain you shall bear children,” except that carnal pleasure seeks to prevail through some evil habit? At the beginning it suffers pain, and through a better habit gives birth to a good work, as to children.

What he added—“Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you”—signifies that the carnal will which had struggled painfully to form a good habit, now instructed by those very pains, becomes more cautious; and, so that it may not fall, obeys reason and willingly serves it as a woman serves a commanding husband.

## Concerning the Man’s Curse

[Col. 0233C] But he said to Adam: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the earth in your work. In toil you shall eat from it all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the plants of the earth. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

And Adam called his wife’s name Eve, because she was the mother of all the living. From then on she is called the mother of the living—that is, of those who do right—to whom sins are opposed, which are signified by the name of the dead.

Now, through the sentence imposed upon the man, our reason is convicted. Having been seduced above by the desire for sin, it bears the curses of earthly labor and the pains of temporal cares, like thorns and thistles—provided that it is dismissed from the paradise of blessedness so that it may work the earth, that is, labor in this body and lay up for itself the merit of returning to eternal life, which is signified by the name of paradise. [Col. 0233D]

## Concerning the Garment of Mortality

The Lord God also made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife [Col. 0234A], clothed them, and said: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now therefore, lest he perhaps stretch out his hand and take also from the tree of life, eat, and live forever.”

This is the voice of the Trinity—of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—as if he had said: “Just as we know the difference between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience, so now Adam understands that he not only had not been made what he wished to become, but did not even preserve what he had been made.”

He also received a tunic of skins by divine judgment, by which name the mortality of the body is signified in the historical account. In the allegorical sense, however, those who are withdrawn from carnal perceptions and live according to carnal pleasures receive and cover themselves with the consequences of divine law, so that, if they should at some time turn to God, they might stretch out their hand to the tree of life and live forever. The stretching out of the hand properly signifies the cross, or the anguish of repentance, through which eternal life is recovered.

## Concerning Their Expulsion from Paradise and the Fiery, Turning Sword

[Col. 0234B]

The Lord God sent him out from the paradise of pleasure, so that he might work the earth from which he had been taken. He expelled Adam and placed before the paradise of pleasure the Cherubim and a fiery, turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life.

This sword was placed so that the human being would not enter paradise and eat from the tree of life, lest he remain immortal and become irreparable, like the demons, who cannot be restored. For this reason the turning sword was placed, so that when the time of mercy arrived through the coming of our Savior, it could again be removed.

For before his coming all the just and elect penetrated the barriers of hell; now, however, all the saints, departing from the body, go to Christ, as the Savior says in the Gospel: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there [Col. 0234C] my servant will be also.”

And again, this is the path for those returning.

“Through the fiery turning sword”: that is, by recognizing and lamenting their sins through temporal tribulations; and through the Cherubim—that is, through the fullness of knowledge, which is love—he will reach the tree of life, Christ, and live forever.

For *Cherubim* is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” The fiery turning sword, placed to guard the way to the tree of life, signifies temporal punishments. No one can reach the tree of life except through these two things: endurance of afflictions and fullness of knowledge, that is, through love of God and neighbor. “Love is the fullness of the law” (Romans 13); it is the mother of virtues, which the saints, imitating God’s footsteps, strive with all their strength to fulfill also in others.

Let us pursue this love and strive to exercise it in our works, so that we may be able to reach the tree of life, which is Christ, and, refreshed and satisfied by its sweet and pleasant fruit, may deserve to rejoice forever with him and his saints without end. [Col. 0234D] Amen.

[Col. 0233]

# A Dialogue of Questions on Genesis from the Sayings of the Fathers

[Col. 0233D] **DISCIPLE.**

First of all, my teacher, I need to inquire who is held to be the author of this book that among us is called Genesis.

[Col. 0234D] **MASTER.**

As our predecessors have indicated and handed down, they assert that Moses was the author of this work—that is, of the five books which, according to the Greeks, are called the Pentateuch—even though the title does not say this, but he himself reports it as though concerning another person: “The Lord said to Moses.”

An example of this occurs in the New Testament, where the apostle John, whenever he wished to report something about himself, carefully concealed his name, saying: “Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following,” etc. (John 21).

**DISCIPLE.**

From where did Genesis receive this name?

**MASTER.**

The Seventy translators, Symmachus, and Theodotion rendered it “In the beginning”; and in Hebrew it is written *Bresith*, which Aquila interprets as “in the heading.” Therefore, according to the sense more than according to the translation of the word, it can be understood of Christ, who is acknowledged as the creator of heaven and earth both at the very beginning of Genesis, which is the head of all the books, and at the beginning of the Gospel of John the Evangelist.

Hence, in the Psalter, he himself says concerning himself: “In the heading of the book it is written concerning me” (Psalm 39), that is, at the beginning of Genesis. And in the Gospel: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1).

Therefore it must be known that this book is called *Bresith* among the Hebrews, [Col. 0235B] who have the custom of giving volumes their names from their beginnings.

**DISCIPLE.**

In the Book of Prefaces to Genesis, what is described according to the reliability of the historical account?

**MASTER.**

It describes the structure of the world and the creation of the human being, the Flood, the division of the earth, the confusion of languages, and the deeds of all the patriarchs, [Col. 0235C] up to Israel’s entry into Egypt.

**DISCIPLE.**

I wish to know what this Scripture signifies when it speaks about the present age.

**MASTER.**

Five things: either its generation, that is, its creation; or its governance; or what happens to natures; or what occurs through wills; or the consequences that follow from the results of the will.

**DISCIPLE.**

In what ways has this Scripture signified the generation of the age?

**MASTER.**

In three ways. Sometimes something is written as having been made by God’s will alone, as in: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1). Sometimes it is written as made by will together with speech—either speech of command, as in: “Let there be light,” and “Let there be a firmament” [Col. 0235D] (ibid.); or deliberative speech, as in: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness” (ibid.).

Or it is made by will, speech, and decree, as in: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (ibid.). And again: “Let the earth bring forth green vegetation, producing seed according to its kind, and a fruit-bearing tree making fruit, whose seed is in itself,” and so forth (ibid.). This continues to operate in stages after the seventh day, until the end of the age. For these things proceed from that decree.

**DISCIPLE.**

Is there any difference among these three?

**MASTER.**

There is. Those things that were made by will alone, or also by speech, were newly made; but those made by decree are similar to the things that, as we have said, were newly made. Moreover, the former occurred during the first six days, while the latter continue as long as the age endures.

[Col. 0236A] **DISCIPLE.**

Give the order of the things made during the six days.

**MASTER.**

At the very beginning of creation, heaven, earth, angels, air, and water were made.

**DISCIPLE.**

Prove that the angels, waters, and air were made.

**MASTER.**

They are shown to have been made from other passages of Scripture, as in: “He makes his angels spirits” (Hebrews 1). And: “Praise him, all his angels” (Psalm 148). And: “Waters that are above the heavens, praise the name of the Lord, because he himself spoke, and they were made” (ibid.). And: “For the sea is his, and he himself made it” (Psalm 94).

Air is customarily indicated in the holy Scriptures by the name “heaven,” as in: “The birds of heaven” (Luke 8), although it is certain that birds fly through the air. We have shown that heaven was made. [Col. 0236B]

That these things preceded the other creatures is demonstrated by Scripture, since in praises and blessings they are placed before the other creatures. There is also a reason: the heavenly creature ought to have preceded the earthly. Concerning the waters, Scripture itself says that the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.

**DISCIPLE.**

Follow the order of generation.

**MASTER.**

At the beginning of the first day, light was made; on the second, the firmament; on the third, the sea and the growths of the earth; on the fourth, the lights of heaven; on the fifth, the swimming creatures and birds; on the sixth, the remaining animals and the human being.

**DISCIPLE.**

What difference is there in the manner of these creatures’ production?

[Col. 0236C] **MASTER.**

Some were made from nothing, such as heaven, earth, and the other things made up to the completion of the first day, as we have said; others were made from things already made on the first day.

**DISCIPLE.**

Give proofs of these things.

**MASTER.**

Whenever Scripture wishes to show that things were made from something else, it either signifies this openly, as in: “Let the earth bring forth,” and “Let the waters bring forth” (Genesis 1), and similar passages; or it indicates it through the subtle meaning of its words.

Thus, when it says, “Let there be a firmament” (ibid.), it clearly signifies that something fluid and liquid already existed—that is, the waters—which, when they were shown to have been solidified, was called the firmament that was being made.

Again, it called the lights “derivative,” since they were made on the fourth day, to show that they were made from the light produced on the first day. But among the things made on the first day, nothing is declared to have been made from something else, either by an explicit or by a subtle word.

[Col. 0236D] **DISCIPLE.**

Nothing after the first day is shown to have been made from things that did not exist.

**MASTER.**

Only the soul of the human being—and here too something must be noted—for although some things were made either from nothing or from things already made, the human being alone is composed from both.

**DISCIPLE.**

What other differences do we assign to the creatures?

**MASTER.**

The things made during the first six days did not come into being naturally or through generation from something similar. The remaining things that are produced naturally arise from the divine decree, except, of course, for miracles.

[Col. 0237A] **DISCIPLE.**

Give the third difference.

**MASTER.**

Some creatures—that is, rational creatures—were made for their own sake, such as angels and human beings. The rest are understood to have been made not for their own sake, but for the sake of the aforementioned angels or human beings. The human being, however, must be understood to have been made principally for his own sake according to the soul, but secondarily according to the body.

**DISCIPLE.**

What creatures besides angels and human beings did not need one another for their own sake?

**MASTER.**

They did need one another, though not for utility, but for ornament. For useful things are useful not to themselves, but to angels and human beings, for whose sake they are also understood to have been made.

They do, however, provide ornament for one another. [Col. 0237B] Heaven was unadorned without the heavenly lights; the lights themselves, lest they have been made superfluously, needed the eyes of those who see them; the sea was unadorned until it either received its proper place or was filled with animals; and the earth was unformed apart from the use of its inhabitants or of things growing upon it. Irrational animals were useless without human governance, and useless plants were superfluous in the absence of animals’ use.

Thus all things needed one another, or needed the things that are made each day. But, as we have already said, being unformed is one thing, and being useful another: something unformed is shown to be useful in itself for another.

**DISCIPLE.**

Is there any difference in ornament itself?

**MASTER.**

There is. Some things are adorned during the six days: heaven with lights, earth with plants, and the sea with fish. Others are adorned as long as the world lives: [Col. 0237C] the sea with ships, the earth with buildings and the other things constructed by human skill, and the human being himself with knowledge.

Still others will receive their beauty in the future: the body, incorruption; mortal things, immortality; and the heavenly kingdom, the dwelling of the saints.

It should also be noted concerning ornaments that, for things made among human beings either by skill or by the arts, the cause is found in human beings; but for the rest, the cause is in God.

**DISCIPLE.**

Give the fourth difference.

**MASTER.**
What emerged simultaneously and as if suddenly created were the plants, the luminaries, the creatures that swim, and the flying creatures, as well as the terrestrial animals and quadrupeds. Some things, however, did not emerge simultaneously, but as if with a certain delay: the sea, the earth, and the human being—for he too is described as having been made gradually, just like the rest.

**DISCIPLE.**

Give the fifth distinction among creatures.

**MASTER.**

Some creatures rule over the others by reason, such as rational beings; others are made for use, such as the heavenly luminaries; still others obey by the necessity of nature, such as birds, quadrupeds, and things similar to them.

**DISCIPLE.**

Give the sixth distinction.

**MASTER.**

Those that rule over the others—that is, rational beings—are moved by will and reason; those that obey for the sake of use or necessity are moved by nature.

**DISCIPLE.**

How many materials did those things that were made from something have?

**[Col. 0238A] MASTER.**

Six: earth, waters, air, fire, light, and the rib.

**DISCIPLE.**

Give the origins of each.

**MASTER.**

From earth came the green plants, vegetation, and animals. From the waters came the firmament, the sea, the swimming creatures, and the flying creatures. Simultaneously from earth, waters, fire, and air came all things that are renewed through the succession of time. From light came the luminaries; from the rib, Eve.

**DISCIPLE.**

How is it proved that fire was made, or from what, or when?

**MASTER.**

We can establish from the general testimony of Scripture that it was made, when it says of God: “Who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them” (Psalm 145). For fire is certainly among them. It is also indicated by a specific prophecy, where it says: “Praise the Lord, dragons and all deeps, fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy wind” (Psalm 148); and before this it had said: “For he spoke, and they were made” (Psalm 32); and again: “Bless all the works of the Lord, bless the Lord” (Psalm 102); and it added: “Bless the Lord, fire and heat” (Daniel 3).

Whether, however, fire was made from nothing, like the other things, or from something else, is uncertain. For many maintain that it is a particle of the heavenly luminaries. Indeed, even now we have often seen people transform fire in a particular way from the rays of the sun; and if this is so, it was made on the first day. But Scripture more wisely called this “light” rather than “fire,” so that it might receive its name from its better use.

**DISCIPLE.**

Give the seventh distinction among creatures.

**[Col. 0238C] MASTER.**

All things that were made from something are bodies; incorporeal things, however, were made neither from something else nor were other things made from them. These incorporeal things must not be understood in the same way as God is called incorporeal. In comparison with him, nothing is corporeal—just as nothing is immortal or invisible. There is one manner in which these words apply exclusively to the Divinity, and another in which we speak of creatures, such as animals or angels.

**DISCIPLE.**

Can we ask how God made the world?

**MASTER.**

This question is pursued more rashly than cautiously. For it is not permitted to human beings to know the manner in which any divine creature was made. If anyone knew how some things were made from nothing, he would, in knowledge and power, be equal to the Creator.

**DISCIPLE.**

Augustine.—If God ordered all things “in number, measure, and weight,” where did he order number, measure, and weight themselves?

**MASTER.**

Number, measure, and weight are God himself. He is number without number, from whom every number comes; he is measure without measure, from whom every measure comes; he is weight without weight, from whom every weight comes. For the whole of creation is not outside him, as though he saw it somewhere else, in the way that human memory retains something and then produces it. Thus all creation is the will of the Creator. The will of the Creator is not outside the nature of the Creator: where there is will, there is nature. Yet nature is eternal in the same way as will is eternal.

No new thought arises in God for the formation of a creature. Therefore the Trinity, God, ordered all things in himself, because he held within himself all that he made. The statement can also be understood in another way: “He ordered all things in number, measure, and weight”—that is, he made all the things he created possess number, measure, and weight.

Augustine, in his book Against the Manichaeans, began as follows:

Many ignorant, uncultivated, and, so to speak, presumptuous people, following the manner of the Manichaeans, are accustomed to inquire and object: “If God made heaven and earth at some point in time, what was he doing before he made heaven and earth? Or where was he, and what suddenly moved him to make something that he had never before made throughout eternal ages?” We answer them:

“God created heaven and earth in the beginning”—not in the beginning of time, but in Christ, when the Word was with the Father, through whom and in whom all things were made. But if we believe that God made heaven and earth in the beginning of time, we must certainly understand that before the beginning of time there was no time. For God made time as well; and therefore, before he made time, there was no time. We cannot say, then, that there was some time when God had not yet made something. For how could there have been time that God had not made, since he himself is the maker of all times?

And if time began together with heaven and earth, no time can be found in which God had not yet made heaven and earth. When it is asked, “What suddenly moved him?” this is said as though some periods of time had passed during which God did nothing. But time could not pass before God had made it, because no one can be the maker of times except one who exists before times.

Certainly the Manichaeans themselves read the Apostle Paul, praise and honor him, and yet deceive many by wrongly interpreting his Epistles. Let them tell us, then, what the Apostle Paul said about “the acknowledgment of the truth that accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the eternal times.” What could “eternal times” have had before them? Let them be compelled to explain this, so that they may understand that they do not understand, since they rashly seek to criticize what they ought carefully to have investigated.

If they do not say, “What suddenly moved God to make heaven and earth?” but remove the word “suddenly” and say only, “What moved God to make heaven and earth?” we answer that we do not say that this world is coeternal with God, because this world does not possess the eternity that God possesses. God made the world, even though time began together with the creature that God made. Thus time is called eternal, but it is not eternal in the same way that God is eternal, because God exists before time and is the maker of time.

Just as everything God made is very good, but is not good in the same way as God, who made it, so these things were made; they were not begotten from him so as to be what he is. Rather, he made them from nothing, so that they would be equal neither to him, by whom they were made, nor to his Son, through whom they were made.

If these people say, “What moved God to make heaven and earth?” they should be answered by first learning the power of the human will, since they desire to know the will of God. They seek to know the causes of God’s will, although God’s will itself is the cause of everything that exists. If God’s will has a cause, is there something that precedes God’s will? It is impious to believe this.

Therefore, when someone asks, “Why did God make heaven and earth?” the answer is: “Because he willed it.” The will of God is the cause of heaven and earth, and therefore God’s will is greater than heaven and earth. But the person who asks, “Why did he will to make heaven and earth?” or “Where was he before they were made?” is seeking something greater than the will of God. Nothing greater can be found.

Let human rashness therefore restrain itself, and let it not seek what does not exist, lest it fail to find what does exist. If anyone desires to know the will of God, let him become God’s friend. Certainly, if someone wished to know the will of a human being with whom he was not a friend, everyone would laugh at his shamelessness or folly. No one becomes God’s friend except through the purest conduct and through that fulfillment of the commandment of which the Apostle says: “The fulfillment of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5). If these people possessed this, they would not be heretics.

## Recapitulation

What follows in the book of Genesis—“But the earth was invisible and unformed”—the Manichaeans criticize in this way: “How did God make heaven and earth in the beginning, if the earth already existed, invisible and unformed?”

Thus, because they wish to criticize the divine Scriptures before knowing them, they fail to understand even the clearest statements. For what could have been said more plainly than this: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth; but the earth was invisible and unformed”? That is: In the beginning God made heaven and earth, but the earth itself, which God made, was invisible and unformed before God arranged all things, with ordered distinction, in their proper places and stations; before he said, “Let there be light,” “Let there be a firmament,” “Let the waters be gathered,” “Let the dry land appear,” and the other things that are set forth in order in the same book, in a manner that children can grasp.

All these things contain such great mysteries that whoever learns them will either grieve over the emptiness of all heretics, because they are human beings, or laugh at it, because they are proud. The book continues:

“And darkness was over the abyss.” The Manichaeans and their followers criticize this by saying: “Was God therefore in darkness before he made light?” They themselves are truly in the darkness of ignorance, and therefore do not understand the light in which God was before he made this light.

They know no light except the light perceived by bodily eyes. Therefore they worship this sun—which we see not only together with the larger animals but also with flies and little worms—as though it were a particle of that light in which God dwells. But let us understand that God dwells in another light. This is the light of which we read in the Gospel: “The true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world.”

The light of this sun does enlighten a human being, but it enlightens the human body and mortal eyes—eyes in which we are surpassed by eagles, which are said to look upon this sun much better than we do. That other light, however, does not nourish the eyes of irrational birds; it nourishes the pure hearts of those who believe in God and turn away from love of visible and temporal things toward the fulfillment of his commandments. All people can do this if they wish, because that light enlightens every person coming into this world.

Thus darkness was over the abyss before this light came to be. Immediately afterward it is said: “And God said, Let there be light.” Where light is absent, there is darkness—not because darkness is something in itself, but because the absence of light is called darkness.

Silence is not some thing in itself; where sound is absent, the condition is called silence. Nakedness is not some thing in itself; where a covering is absent from a body, the condition is called nakedness. Emptiness is not something; a place where there is no body is called empty. So, as we have already said, darkness is not something; where light is absent, the condition is called darkness.
