We have said this because they are accustomed to ask: “Where did that darkness over the abyss come from before God made light? Who made or begot it? Or, if no one made or begot it, was darkness eternal?” They speak as though darkness were something. But, as has been said, it received this name from the absence of light.

Because these people, deceived by their fables, believed that there was a race of darkness in which bodies, forms, and souls existed, they think that darkness is something and do not understand that darkness is perceived only when we do not see—just as silence is perceived only when we do not hear. As silence is nothing, so darkness is nothing.

They say that the race of darkness fought against the light of God, just as another equally foolish person might say that a race of silences fought against the voice of God. But for the present we undertake to refute and disprove these follies. Now we have resolved to defend, insofar as the Lord grants us strength, the things they criticize in the Old Testament, and to show that human blindness is powerless against the truth of God. The text continues:

What is written—“And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters”—the Manichaeans commonly criticize in this way: “The water, then, was the dwelling place of the Spirit of God, and it contained the Spirit of God.” In their perverse minds they attempt to pervert everything, and they are blinded by their own wickedness.

When we say, “The sun is borne over the earth,” do we mean that it dwells in the earth and that the earth contains the sun? Yet the Spirit of God was not borne over the water in the same way that the sun is borne over the earth, but in another way, which few understand. The Spirit was not borne over the water through spatial extension, as the sun is borne over the earth, but through the power of his invisible majesty.

Let them tell us, then, how the will of a craftsman is borne over the things that are to be made. If they do not understand these human and everyday matters, let them fear God and believe with a simple heart what they do not understand, lest, when they attempt with sacrilegious words to strike down the truth they cannot see, the axe return upon their own legs.

The truth cannot be cut down, because it remains unchangeable. Whatever blows are aimed against it rebound and return with greater force upon those who dare to strike what they ought to believe, so that they might deserve to understand.

Next they ask, mockingly: “Where did the water itself come from, over which the Spirit of God was borne? Is it written above that God made the water?” If they asked this piously, they would discover how it should be understood.

The word “water” is not used here to signify what we can now see and touch. Nor was the earth called invisible and unformed such as the earth now is, which can be seen and handled. Rather, by the words “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” the whole of creation that God made and established is signified under the names “heaven” and “earth.”

These names of visible things were used because of the weakness of children, who are less capable of grasping invisible things. First, therefore, a confused and formless matter was made, from which all the things that were distinguished and formed would come. I believe that the Greeks call this *chaos*. For elsewhere we read this said in praise of God: “You who made the world from formless matter,” and so forth.

Some manuscripts read, “from unseen matter.” Thus God is rightly believed to have made all things from nothing. For even if all formed things were made from this matter, this matter itself was nevertheless made entirely from nothing.

We must not resemble those who do not believe that almighty God could make something from nothing, because they observe that craftsmen and all sorts of artisans cannot make anything unless they have material from which to make it. Wood assists the carpenter, silver assists the silversmith, gold assists the goldsmith, and earth assists the potter, enabling each to complete his work.

If the material from which they make something did not assist them, they could make nothing, since they themselves do not make the material. The carpenter does not make wood; he makes something from wood. The same is true of all other artisans.

Almighty God, however, needed no assistance from anything that he himself had not made in order to accomplish what he willed. If some thing that he had not made assisted him in making the things he wished to make, he would not be almighty—which it is sacrilegious to believe.

That formless matter, then, which God made from nothing, was at first called “heaven and earth,” not because it already was heaven and earth, but because it could become them. Consider the seed of a tree: we might say that it contains roots, a trunk, branches, fruit, and leaves—not because they already exist there, but because they will come from it.

So it was said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” as though it were the seed of heaven and earth, while the matter of heaven and earth was still confused. But because it was certain that heaven and earth would come from it, the matter itself was already called “heaven and earth,” according to the manner of speech used by the Lord when he says: “I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15).

This was not because it had already been done, but because it was absolutely certain to happen. Shortly afterward he says: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.” Why, then, had he said, “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you,” unless he knew that he would do this?

In the same way, the matter from which heaven and earth had not yet been made could be called “heaven and earth,” although they had to be made from nowhere else. Countless such expressions are found in the divine Scriptures, just as in our ordinary speech we say of something that we confidently hope will happen, “Consider it already done.”

This still formless matter, already called the invisible and unformed earth, was so named because among all the elements of the world the earth appears less beautiful than the others. It was called invisible because of its obscurity and unformed because of its lack of form. This same matter was also called water, over which the Spirit of God was borne, just as the will of an artisan is borne over the thing he is making.

Although only a few may be able to grasp this, I do not know whether even a few human beings can explain it in human words. This matter was not improperly called “water,” because everything that grows on earth—animals, plants, trees, and similar things—begins to be formed and nourished from moisture.

All these names, therefore—heaven and earth; invisible and unformed earth; the abyss with darkness; and water over which the Spirit was borne—are names for formless matter. An unknown reality was thus suggested to the less experienced by familiar terms, and by many terms rather than one, so that, if it had been given only one name, it would not be taken to be precisely what people were accustomed to understand by that name.

It was called “heaven and earth” because heaven and earth would come from it. It was called “invisible and unformed earth,” and “darkness over the abyss,” because it was formless and could not be perceived or handled in any shape, even if there were a human being who could see and handle it. It was called “water” because it was pliable and yielding to the one working upon it, so that all things could be formed from it.

Under all these names, then, there was unseen and formless matter, from which God established the world.

## In the beginning God created heaven and earth

This chapter is the head of all books. For all divine Scripture is divided into two parts, the Old Testament and the New.

Some passages reveal eternal things, such as: “In the beginning was the Word.” Others narrate things that have been made, such as: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Others announce future things, such as: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty” (Luke 9:26). Still others prescribe what must be done, as when it says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 19:19), and so forth.

It is divided in another way because some passages are spoken figuratively, such as the Song of Songs and the statement, “Adam heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden.” Other passages are according to the truth of events, such as the people’s departure from Egypt and their walking through the sea on foot. Still others are spoken in both ways, such as the crossing of the Red Sea and those miracles that the Lord performed in the Gospel.

**DISCIPLE.**

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” We must inquire with the greatest care which beginning is meant: whether the beginning of time, or the beginning that was the beginning of his creation, from which other things began to exist. For they were not always coeternal with God.

**MASTER.**

Let us say that God made heaven and earth in a beginning coeternal with himself—in the only-begotten Son, who is the Father’s wisdom. Of him the Apostle says, “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and the Psalm says, “You made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103:24). The Apostle says again: “For in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible” (Colossians 1:16).

**DISCIPLE.**

Genesis is the beginning. “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”; the angels were made afterward. If the angels were made before, God did not create heaven and earth first of all.

**MASTER.**

When the stars were made together, Scripture says: “My angels praised me with a loud voice.” The stars were made on the fourth day, and the angels already existed; for they were not made on the third or second day.

The things that were made appear in this order. On the third day, the earth was separated from the waters. On the second day, the firmament was made, where the sun, moon, and stars move. The first day itself, however, is the angelic nature, which was first called by the name “heaven.”

This clearly shows that the first day was spiritual—that is, the angelic nature—and that this heaven, which we perceive with our eyes, was made afterward. For when it says, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” it does not mean “first of all,” as you claim. Rather, “in the beginning,” that is, in the Son—or rather, through the Son—God made every spiritual and bodily creature, which was called by the name “heaven and earth.”

When the Jews asked him who he was, he answered that he was the Beginning: “The Beginning, who is also speaking to you.” First, therefore, he wished to speak of heaven and earth as a kind of spiritual and bodily matter, and then to weave the sequence of how each thing was made individually.

By “heaven,” he seems to me to have meant the abyss of waters, the dark and, in a certain sense, fluctuating life of Adam, unless it turns toward the Creator and becomes light and contemplates that the Trinity is God in God.

We do not say this as though the matter preceded its form in time, as wood precedes a chest and a voice precedes a word, but only in origin. The first creature, therefore, was light—not the light made on the fourth day, but spiritual light, that is, the angelic nature.

Yet it must be understood that heaven, earth, and light were created simultaneously. The only distinction is one of origin. Just as a person cannot recount two familiar stories at the same time, so the Lord narrated first what had priority in origin and afterward what had been made from it, although he had made both simultaneously. That which is prior only in the order of making is therefore narrated first in time.

Since Holy Scripture had to narrate both the events and the things narrated, the proper order was to narrate first that from which something had been made, and afterward the thing made from it, so that those slower in understanding could grasp it. Bodily things were made from something; there is no difference between the creation of heaven, earth, and light except the difference between a word and a voice.

**[Col. 0243D] DISCIPLE.**

Why did he not say, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” but “created”?

**MASTER.**

Because of the formlessness of the matter.

**DISCIPLE.**

Give the spiritual meaning.

**MASTER.**

Christ is the Beginning, as he himself says in the Gospel: “The Beginning, who is also speaking to you.” In this Beginning, therefore, God made heaven—that is, those who meditate upon and seek heavenly things. In him he also made the carnal, who have not yet put off the earthly human being.

**DISCIPLE.**

“But the earth was empty and void.” Why empty and void?

**[Col. 0244A] MASTER.**

It was empty because it had not been separated from the sea; it was void, he says, because it was not enclosed by shores or adorned with its proper alternations—that is, with trees and animals.

Spiritually understood: the earth of our flesh was empty and void before it received the form of teaching.

**DISCIPLE.**

Why is it said that darkness was over the face of the abyss?

**MASTER.**

Because there was no light to be poured over it; if there had been, it would certainly have been present. Alternatively, it was because the air was dense and lacked enduring light.

In another sense, darkness was over the face of the abyss because the blindness of sins and the profound darkness of ignorance covered our hearts.

**DISCIPLE.**

Jerome.—Explain how the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.

**MASTER.**

Where our books have *ferebatur*, “was borne,” the Hebrew has *merahefeth*, which we may render “was brooding” or “was cherishing,” after the likeness of a bird brooding over eggs with its warmth.

From this we understand that the passage does not speak of the spirit of the world, as some think, but of the Holy Spirit, who is himself also called the giver of life to all things from the beginning. If he is the giver of life, he is, as it were, the Creator and God: “You send forth your Spirit,” it says, “and they are created.”

**DISCIPLE.**

Augustine.—“The Spirit of God was borne over the waters”: was he borne locally, like the sun and the stars, or in another way?

**MASTER.**

The Holy Spirit is God. He is not contained or extended by place, nor is he subject to changes of time; rather, he is wholly present everywhere.

How, then, did he name the creature over which the Holy Spirit was said to be borne? Not locally, but in power. The Lord made his works not from need but from generosity, and he has no need of the things he made. Love that is needy and impoverished is subject to the things it loves. The Holy Spirit was therefore said to be borne over the creature because he did not work upon that creature from need.

**DISCIPLE.**

Ambrose.—How was the Spirit of God borne over the waters?

**MASTER.**

As the Apostle says: “The love of Christ surpasses knowledge” (Ephesians 3:19), and elsewhere: “It surpasses every understanding” (2 Corinthians 10:5). Thus he indicates something begun, over which the Spirit of God was said to be borne—not spatially, but by a power surpassing and excelling all things.

There are two reasons why God loves his creature: that it may exist and that it may remain; that it may be formed and remain in obedience to its Creator’s command.

Therefore, so that it might exist, the Spirit of God was borne over the water. So that it might remain, God saw that it was good. For this reason he first named the things formless and afterward named the Holy Spirit, because every lesser love is placed beneath the things it loves.

**DISCIPLE.**

Again, Augustine in the *Hexameron*.—I ask you to explain more fully and abundantly the formlessness of matter.

**MASTER.**

It is true and evident that everything mutable is formed from some formless condition. At the same time, the clearest reasoning teaches that the matter of no nature could have existed except from God, although Scripture says: “You who made the world from formless matter.”

Formless matter is not prior in time to formed things, since both were created together: both the thing made and that from which it was made. The voice is the matter of words, while words indicate a formed voice. Likewise, God the Creator did not first make formless matter in time and afterward, in a second act of consideration, form it according to the order of the various natures.

Scripture could not avoid dividing by the times of its speech what God did not divide according to the times of his making. When we speak of matter and form, we understand both simultaneously, although we cannot express both simultaneously.

If spiritual light was made when God said, “Let there be light,” this must not be understood as that true light coeternal with the Father through which all things were made. Rather, it is the light of which it could be said, “Wisdom was created before all things,” because light was made through uncreated wisdom.

How both the thing that was illuminated and the illumination itself could have been made simultaneously, yet narrated at different times, we explained shortly before when we discussed matter.

**[Col. 0245B] DISCIPLE.**

Augustine.—“And God said, Let there be light.” Did he speak during the day, or before every day? If he spoke during the day, he spoke temporally; if he spoke temporally, he spoke through some creature. Therefore light is not the first creature.

**MASTER.**

He spoke neither during the day nor temporally; rather, before every creature he begot his Word. God’s speech, therefore, is the Word.

But divine Scripture, accommodating itself to children and in a certain sense suckling them so that they may advance and receive spiritual nourishment, chose to call the formation of every creature “speech.” Thus, if we ask how light was made, we hear: “It was in the Word of God that it should be made.” If we ask how the other things were made in order, the answer is: “They were in the Word of God to be made.” Hence the statement: “God said, Let there be light.”

The divine nature does not speak in bodily ways, nor, whenever it is said “he spoke,” does it form a word. He begot one Word, coeternal and consubstantial with himself, in which he spoke all things ineffably.

**DISCIPLE.**

Again.—“And God said, Let there be light.” Is this light visible or invisible?

**MASTER.**

It is called invisible because it is the angelic creation, which our eyes cannot behold. It was appropriate that on the fourth day he should fashion the stars in heaven, which our eyes could behold.

**DISCIPLE.**

Is this angelic creation temporal or timeless?

**MASTER.**

It was temporal in the angels but timeless in God. It was temporal in the sense that we understand what was expressed by the eternal God through the coeternal Word in the spiritual creature that he had already made when it was said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

This speech, however, was impressed upon the mind and reason of the spiritual creature in a certain manner—not only without any sound, but also without any bodily movement of the spiritual creature—through the coeternal Word of the Father.

It is extremely difficult to grasp how God, who commands neither temporally nor with a creature hearing temporally, and who by contemplation of the truth surpasses all times, transmits to things below, through an intellectual expression impressed upon the creature and coeternal with the substance of the Father, what is like an intelligible utterance, so that temporal movement might occur in temporal things, whether they were being formed or governed.

Again, it says: “And the light was made”—that is, the angelic creation, because at that time they began to recognize or understand their Creator.

**DISCIPLE.**

Why does he not repeat, “And God made the light,” as he repeats this with the other creatures that he created? For with the firmament he says: “Let there be a firmament,” and again: “And God made the firmament.”

**MASTER.**

It was necessary that he say, “God made the light,” because it was an intellectual creature—that is, an angelic one.

When he says, “Let there be a firmament,” or the corresponding words concerning the other creatures, he spoke this in the knowledge of the angels. It is not surprising if God, in the first creation of light, wished first to show his holy angels, who had turned toward him, what he would subsequently do.

When he says, “And God made,” that is, in the proper nature of things, it was no longer necessary to repeat this concerning the angels, because they had then, as we said, turned toward the knowledge of their Creator.

When that eternal and unchangeable wisdom—which was not made but begotten—transfers itself into a spiritual and rational creature, as into holy souls, so that, having been enlightened, they may shine, a luminous affection of reason arises in them. This can be understood as “light made,” when God says, “Let there be light.”

The spiritual creation already existed, signified by the name “heaven,” when it was written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” This does not mean bodily heaven, but incorporeal heaven, in whose nature all the holy angels are understood to exist.

**Gregory.—**The angels were created in such a way that, if they wished, they could remain in the light of blessedness; but if they did not wish to, they could also fall. Thus Satan fell with his legions of followers. After his fall, however, the angels who remained were so confirmed that they can no longer fall at all.

This was well signified at the very beginning of Genesis, in the historical account of the present book, because God created heaven and later called it the firmament. Those who were first created well were therefore, as we said, called “heavens,” but afterward were called “the firmament,” because they received the power of unchangeability so that they would no longer fall at all.

**Gregory again.—**“God said, Let there be light, and there was light,” and shortly afterward: “And evening came to be.”

In this life, sin is not abandoned through the practice of righteousness in such a way that one remains unshaken in that same righteousness. For rectitude expels guilt from the dwelling place of the heart, yet the guilt that is driven out sits at the doors of our thoughts and knocks, asking to be admitted.

Moses indicated this spiritually when he narrated bodily the moments of time: “There was light,” and shortly afterward added: “And evening came to be.”

The Creator, who foreknew all human guilt, then expressed in time what is now enacted in the mind. Light is brought toward evening because the light of rectitude is followed by the shadow of temptation.

But because the light of the elect is not extinguished by temptation, it is said not that night came to be, but evening. For temptation often conceals the light of righteousness in the hearts of the upright, but does not destroy it: it may draw them into the pallor of trembling, but it does not extinguish it completely.

[Col. 0246D] **Ambrose.**—“And God said, ‘Let there be light.’” That is, let the illumination of faith appear. On the first day he gave the light of faith, because faith is first in conversion. Hence the first commandment itself is: “The Lord your God is one God.” For the sake of this faith the Lord himself desired to appear visibly in the world. Already then, in accordance with the grace of his foreknowledge, God divided the righteous—that is, the children of God and of light—from sinners, as from darkness, calling the former “day” and the latter “night.” For since the righteous are called by the name of light, hear the Apostle: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

**DISCIPLE.**

**Augustine.**—“And God saw that the light was good.” If God suddenly saw that the light was good, did he not know this beforehand, and did the seeing impart knowledge to him?

**MASTER.**

Every work is preceded by the will. For when we consider what we ought to do—for no one does anything while ignorant of it—and consider how the things that we have decided to do after reflection are to be accomplished, then, since it cannot happen to a human being that he does something while ignorant, how much less can it happen to God, who made all things according to his eternal and unchanging counsel, in whatever manner he willed? For he did not see things after they had been made in one way and things yet to be made in another; rather, he saw things made in the same manner in which he had seen them to be made.

**DISCIPLE.**

“And God saw that the light was good.” Why did he praise only the light and not the night?

**MASTER.**

That is because night and day had not yet been made; there was only angelic light. For it was unworthy of God to praise an unformed thing that had not yet been formed. He praised instead that thing which had been formed—that is, the angelic light.

**DISCIPLE.**

[Col. 0247B] **Augustine.**—“And he divided the light from the darkness.” Scripture says, “He divided the light from the darkness.” For everything that is divided can also exist. Therefore, just as light has being, so darkness has being. Why does Scripture not say, “God saw that the darkness was good,” as it says this concerning the light?

**MASTER.**

God created all the angels good, with a good and unchangeable will. But because he foreknew that some of them would fall through pride, by the unchangeability of his foreknowledge he divided the good from the evil. Thus he called the evil “darkness” and the good “light”: of the latter he said that they were good, but of the former he said nothing at all, lest he seem to approve the sins that were darkness.

**DISCIPLE.**

**Elsewhere.**—“He divided the light from the darkness.” What is it to divide the light from the darkness?

**MASTER.**

It means the distinction between a formed thing and an unformed thing.

**DISCIPLE.**

“He called the light day, and the darkness night” (Genesis 1). Why did he call the light day and the darkness night, when they had not yet been formed?

**MASTER.**

He called the light “day” because “day” was named with reference to the appearance of the thing that had been made; and he called the darkness “night” because this night, which is most familiar to us, consists in the sun’s absence over the earth. When the sun declines, we call it evening; when morning begins, we call it day. Here, however, night is the privation of work; or night itself has been called possibility, which exists in created things and from which they can come to be, even if they are not changed.

[Col. 0247D] **DISCIPLE.**

“And evening came and morning came, one day” (ibid.). How is this to be understood?

**MASTER.**

What is meant by evening except the completion of the individual works, and by morning except the beginning of those that follow?

**DISCIPLE.**

**Augustine.**—You will establish that the first day was a spiritual creature; how, then, did it have evening and morning?

**MASTER.**

Before every creature came to be in its own time, it first had to be known by the angels in the very Word of God, and then made in its own time. Therefore the creature’s knowledge of itself was evening, whereas its knowledge in God was morning, because the creature is seen more fully in the Lord than it is seen in itself—more precisely, the things that have been made are seen more fully in the art by which they were made than in the thing itself that was made. Hence the evangelist John says: “What was made, in him was life” (John 1).

Therefore all things that have been made, and that do not possess life, are life in the Word of God, but are not life in themselves. Heaven, earth, and a stone do not possess life, yet in the Lord they are life. Thus all the principles of creatures live in God without beginning, yet changeably. Consequently, they are seen more fully by the holy angels in the Word of God, where they are life, than in themselves, because the angels’ knowledge grows, so to speak, toward evening in comparison with God.

Thus the first day was the angels’ knowledge of the firmament; the second, their knowledge of the separation of earth and sea; the third, their knowledge of the sun, moon, and stars; the fourth, their knowledge of reptiles and animals; the fifth, their knowledge of domestic animals and wild beasts, and of humanity itself. For the sixth day does not mean that the spiritual creature—that is, the angelic creature—was given knowledge six times over in a single day. “Six times” refers to the perfection of the number six.

But concerning the number and the perfection of the number six I shall gather something for you from the holy Scriptures. Listen willingly and prepare yourself wholly to hear. One cannot be divided among numbers, for every number rises from one. Therefore numbers can be divided if one is a part of them. What else, then, does the division of two into one, and of three into one, show here except the Trinity, which is God? For although there are three persons, they are believed to exist in the unity of one nature.

Four has two parts: its fourth is one, and its middle is two. One and two make three. Behold its parts: it neither increases beyond them nor is completed by them, and therefore it is an imperfect number.

Five has only one part, namely its fifth.

The number six, therefore, is perfect, because it is completed by its parts. It has one, which is its sixth; two, which is its third; and three, which is its half. Thus one, two, and three make six.

For this reason, because of the perfection of this number, he worked all creation in six days. These three parts of the number six show us that the triune God made all creation in the Trinity of number, measure, and weight. We frequently find the perfection of the number six to be of great importance in the holy Scriptures, especially in the Lord’s single death and his single resurrection.

The death of our Lord Jesus Christ was not in the soul, but in the flesh alone; our death, however, is not only in the flesh but also in the soul: in the soul because of sin, and in the flesh because of sin’s punishment. But since he had no sin, he did not die in the soul, but only in the flesh. This was because of the likeness of sinful flesh, which he had drawn from Adam.

Thus his simple death was twofold, and his resurrection single. The resurrection benefited [us; the reading is compressed]. The death of his flesh and its resurrection are twofold: the death of our soul and its resurrection. We have two deaths and two resurrections. Two and two make four. Add to the one death of the Lord and his one resurrection our four, and they make six.

[Col. 0248D] Thus the Lord’s single element and our double element make three, and they have three parts, according to what we said above concerning the number six. The thirty-six hours during which the Lord was in the underworld also correspond to this single and double division. Twelve, therefore, were daylight hours and twenty-four nighttime hours. The twenty-four correspond to our twofold death, while those twelve hours correspond to the Lord’s single death.

Indeed, his birth also has the number six: the Temple was built over forty-six years.

**DISCIPLE.**

The Jews assert in the Gospel, where the saying is understood of the Lord’s body, that “forty-six years” stand for days. They say that an infant is formed in the womb over forty-six days and thereafter grows until the day of birth. Forty-six times six makes 276, which amounts to nine months and ten days. Count, therefore, from the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when the Lord suffered—since he is also believed to have been conceived then—to the eighth day before the Kalends of January, and you will find 276 days, which are constituted by the number six.

What are we to say about the woman in the Gospel whom Satan had afflicted for eighteen years and whom the Lord healed? We say that those years too have the number six: three times six is eighteen.

That woman signifies the human race, which, in the sixth age of the world, he freed from the devil’s captivity. The first age extends from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to David; the fourth, from David to the transmigration to Babylon; the fifth, from the transmigration to Babylon to John the Baptist and the coming of the Lord and Savior; the sixth is the age now in progress, until the Most High comes for judgment.

In the sixth age, therefore, the human race is restored to the image of God. Eighteen years clearly demonstrate not only the six ages but also three periods: one before the law, another under the law, and a third under grace.

The year itself, therefore, is also contained in the number six. It has 365 and a quarter days. Six times sixty makes 360. Five and a quarter days remain. Five days belong to the sixth month; and yet, if you reckon that quarter as a day, the whole makes six plainly.

Behold how much the Lord has deigned to help me. Concerning the perfection of the number six, I have given an account—not as much as I wished, but as much as I could.

## The disputation concerning the second day begins

“And God said: ‘Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters’” (Genesis 1).

**Augustine.**—The order and weight of the elements do not permit there to be a substance of water above the heavens. Water yields to earth, air yields to water, and fire yields to air. It is wholly impossible for the second element, which is water, to be above the fourth, which is fire. How, then, is it said: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters” (ibid.)?

**MASTER.**

I have no doubt that those waters, which Scripture says are above the heavens, exist there, whatever their nature and form may be. For just as these clouds, which are certainly carried above the air, are so carried, so I think it possible that thin and subtle waters may be carried above the heavens.

On the basis of this weight of the elements, many philosophers mock the resurrection of the flesh and say that it cannot happen that a human being, who was certainly made from earth, should be in heaven. But Truth refutes them: it causes many earthly animals to fly through the air, and fire, which is certainly the fourth element, to exist in the earth. Therefore God’s power, which is shown capable of doing these things, causes both human beings and water to be above the heavens.

But yielding to such arguments from adversaries, one man made a praiseworthy attempt to demonstrate the waters above the heavens, so as to establish the credibility of Scripture from visible and perceptible natures. First he showed what was easiest: that this air is called heaven, since we speak of a clear or cloudy heaven, and since the birds are called “the birds of heaven.”

When he had thus proved that this air is called heaven, he wished it to be thought that it was called “firmament” for no other reason than that its interval divides between the water-vapors and those waters that float more heavily upon the earth. Thus, from the air that lies between the moist vapors from which the clouds above are gathered into a mass and the seas spread out below, he wished to show that heaven exists between water and water.

Nevertheless, it may be held that the elements’ own weights do not prevent waters from existing even above that lofty heaven: just as waters were able to exist above this expanse of air in tiny particles, so they could exist above it. For they persuade us, by a very subtle argument, that there is no body, however small, in which division comes to an end. Therefore, if water can—as we see it can—be reduced to drops so tiny that they are carried vaporously above this air, why could it not also hang above that lighter heaven in tinier drops and lighter vapors?

Some of our own people also attempt to refute them by arguments concerning the qualities and courses of the stars. They assert that the star they call Saturn is extremely cold and completes the zodiacal circle in thirty years. They are therefore asked how that star can be cold, when it ought to be hotter in proportion as it is carried higher in the heavens.

For undoubtedly, when a rounded mass is moved in a circular motion, its inner parts move more slowly and its outer parts more quickly; and whatever moves more quickly is certainly hotter. Consequently, the star mentioned ought to have been hot rather than cold. Surely, then, its proximity to the waters established above the heavens makes it cold.

It is also customary to ask what shape and figure heaven should be thought to have: whether heaven, like a sphere, encloses the earth on every side, with the earth balanced at the center of the world’s mass; or whether it covers the earth from above over a considerable portion, like a disk.

But someone may say: How is it not contrary to those who attribute the shape of a sphere to heaven that our Scriptures say: “He stretches out heaven like a skin” (Psalm 103)?

It can be answered that a skin is stretched not only flat but also into a rounded hollow; for both a wineskin and a bladder are skins.

**Ambrose.**—Some brothers also raise a question concerning the movement of heaven: whether it stands still or moves. For if it moves, they say, how can it be called “firmament”? Yet the name “firmament” does not compel us to think that heaven stands still. It may be understood to have been called firmament not because of standing, but because of firmness, or because it is an impassable boundary between the waters above and below.

This, however, should be understood: the stars travel around, while heaven itself stands firm, as the poet says:

> “For the substance of heaven remains undefiled throughout its age.”

We judge that the nature of the waters there is suspended not in vaporous thinness but in icy solidity, to temper the natures of the stars, lest they consume the creatures placed beneath them with excessive heat.

We therefore say of those waters that, when the smallest drops are gathered together into one mass, they form a single collection; and because of the heaviness of their weight, the air cannot support them, but, spreading their weight downward, gives them passage to the lowest place. This is rain.

Thus they wish the air that lies between the moist vapors from which the clouds above are gathered into a mass and the seas spread out below to be understood as heaven between water and water.

The second heaven is that which we perceive through the spirit: from it the disk filled with animals, sent down to Peter, descended during the ecstasy of his mind.

The third heaven is that which we know with the mind. It is so hidden and remote—either wholly purified or carried away from the senses of the flesh—that those things which are in that heaven are able, in the ineffable love of the Holy Spirit, to see the very substance of God, the Word through whom all things were made (John 1).

**Isidore.**—At last let the heretics cease to rave, [Col. 0250D] and, confounded, acknowledge that he who was able to create all things from nothing was also able to establish that nature of water in heaven with icy solidity. For since they themselves say that the sphere revolves, shining with fiery stars, did not divine Providence necessarily ensure that water would overflow within and above the sphere of heaven, to temper those burning fires among the stars?

Again: “On the second day,” he says, “God arranged the firmament”—that is, the solidity of the holy Scriptures. For in the Church the divine Scriptures are understood as the firmament, because heaven will be folded up like a book. He separated waters above this firmament—that is, the heavenly peoples of the angels, who have no need to receive this firmament so that, by reading, they may hear the word of God. They always see him and love him.

But he placed the firmament of his law above the weakness of the lower peoples, so that, by receiving it, they might learn how to distinguish between carnal and spiritual things, as between the waters above and the waters below.

[Col. 0251A] “And evening came and morning came, the second day.” A question arises concerning the third day.

**DISCIPLE.**

“But God said: ‘Let the waters that are beneath the heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.’”

**Augustine.**—Here a question arises: If water covered the whole earth, there was no place where the waters could be gathered, since water covered the whole earth. How, then, does Scripture say: “Let the waters that are beneath the heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear”?

**MASTER.**

Water covered the whole earth like a very thin mist, which afterward was brought together and gathered into one, so that the appearance of the earth could become visible. Nevertheless, the earth, which lay depressed over a great extent, could also have provided hollow places to receive the waters as they flowed together, so that the dry land might appear.

**Ambrose.**—We should briefly point out that anyone who is not moved to ask when the forms of the waters and the earth were created should understand that on this day nothing was done except that these two were separated.

For when, before the enumeration of the days, it was said, “The earth was invisible and unformed,” Scripture was indicating what sort of earth God had made, since it had already said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1). Nothing else should be understood by these words except that he wished to suggest the formlessness of bodily matter—provided that a slow understanding does not slip into the error of trying to separate matter and form in time as well, because Scripture separates the two in its wording.

**DISCIPLE.**

**As above.**—“Let the waters that are beneath the heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear” (Genesis 1). Why, then, does it not say, “Let the dry land become visible,” or, “Let the gathered water become visible”?

[Col. 0251C] **MASTER.**

Because these things are closer to formlessness than the heavenly bodies are, or because weaker things are created from them through the enumeration of the days, he did not wish it to be stated in the same manner as what was made previously.

Hence, in the spiritual sense, he says above: “On the third day he gathers the lower waters, which are salty, into one place” (ibid.). These are unbelieving human beings, who are shaken by the storm of desires and the waves of carnal temptations, and who contain bitterness within themselves, as it were.

He separated from them the dry land, namely the people thirsting for the fountain of life. Thereafter he fixed the boundaries of the proud and restrained them, lest they disturb the dry land—that is, the soul that knows God—with the turbulent waves of their iniquities. Thus the soul may be permitted to bring forth, according to its kind, the fruit of good works: loving its neighbor by providing assistance in bodily needs and possessing within itself seed according to the likeness of that love, so that, out of awareness of its own weakness, it may be moved to compassion and help those in need.

It also brings forth a tree of strong timber and one that bears fruit (ibid.)—that is, a benefit by which the person suffering injustice is rescued from the hand of the powerful, through the shelter of protection provided by the strong timber of righteous judgment.

It follows:

“And God called the dry land earth, and he called the gatherings of waters seas” (ibid.).

**Jerome, in the Book of Hebrew Questions.**—It should be noted that every gathering of waters, whether salty or fresh, is called “seas” according to the idiom of the Hebrew language. Porphyry therefore attacks in vain the miracle that the Lord walked upon the sea, because the Lake of Gennesaret is called a sea, since every lake and every gathering of waters is called “seas.”

It follows:

“And God saw that the light was good, and said: ‘Let the earth bring forth green grass,’” and so forth, “and it was so. And the earth brought forth green grass producing seed according to its kind” (ibid.).

**Gregory.**—What is represented in this passage by grass except good action? Although we hold that this historically took place in the world’s creation, we may nevertheless appropriately understand the earth as prefiguring the Church. She brought forth green grass in him, in whom she produced, in response to the word of God, works of fruitful mercy.

It follows:

“And a tree bearing fruit according to its kind, each having seed according to its species.”

**Gregory.**—A tree produces seed according to its own species when our mind gathers from itself a consideration of another person and gives birth to the sprout of a righteous deed. Hence a certain wise man says: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4). Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Whatever you want people to do to you, you also do to them” (Matthew 7).

It is as though he were saying openly: Look upon your own species in another person, and from yourselves recognize what you ought to offer to others. And as we said above, the earth signifies the Church, which both refreshes us with the nourishment of the word and guards us with the shelter of her protection; she feeds by speaking and protects by helping, so that she brings forth not only grass for refreshment but also, with the fruit of action, a tree of protection.

**DISCIPLE.**

**Augustine.**—When God said, “Let the earth bring forth green grass producing seed and fruit-bearing trees” (Genesis 1), when did he make fruitless trees, or thorns and thistles?

**MASTER.**

God made everything simultaneously, as Scripture says: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus 18). Therefore fruitless trees should in no way be called fruitless if they provide human beings with assistance in some way. For even if we do not find something in them to eat, we find something for medicine, and something for use.

Consider how many benefits they provide. Fruit-bearing trees are so called from enjoyment (*frui*), and from every tree we can obtain some assistance. We rightly call no tree fruitless.

As for thistles and thorns, although they grow for human toil after the sin of humanity, as Scripture says, “Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you” (Genesis 3), it should nevertheless not be said that they first sprang from the earth at that time. They already existed, certainly, for the food of cattle and birds; they were not produced to increase the punishment of humanity.

“And God saw that it was good, and evening came and morning came, the third day.”

Whenever this statement occurs to you, remember the sentence concerning the first day that we set forth: “If God suddenly saw that the light was good,” and so forth (Genesis 1).

## The fourth day begins

**DISCIPLE.**

“God also said: ‘Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide the day from the night, and let them be for signs and seasons, and for days and years, so that they may shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth.’” Did times not exist before this? (Genesis 1).

**MASTER.**

**In the Hexameron.**—Who does not see how obscurely it is stated that the seasons began on the fourth day, as though the preceding three days could have passed without time, although they too had the time of their own creation? Yet those three days did not have the divisions established by the stars.

Many also inquire at great length what sort of moon was made, whether a new moon or a full moon. But I shall say plainly that, whether God made a first-quarter moon or a full moon, he made it perfect.

Everything that, through the progress of nature and at the appropriate times, in some way emerges and unfolds already existed hidden within it beforehand—not in the appearance or bodily mass of the thing, perhaps, but in the power and principle of its nature. Otherwise, perhaps, a tree that is empty of fruit and bare of leaves during winter would have to be called imperfect at that time.

Some even dare to say that many stars are equal to the sun or larger than it, but appear small because they are farther away. If that is so, why do they venerate these stars, which move through the constellations, all the more? Why do they claim that they are the lords of the constellations?

For if someone should argue that those retrograde motions of the stars—or perhaps their slowness—are caused by a new sun, while attributing this power to the sun alone for other, more hidden reasons, it is certainly clear from their books that, in their delusions, they suspect that the force of created things has deviated from the truth.

Since those bodies are not more powerful than earthly and bodily things in the matters they themselves discuss, they may at least recognize this from the following: when many bodies of different kinds—animals, herbs, and shrubs—are sown at one and the same moment of time, and innumerable things are born at one and the same moment, even in different places and in the same places on earth, such are the variations in their development, actions, and affections that, if these people considered them, they would truly, as the saying goes, lose sight of the stars.

We must therefore admit that, whenever they say something true, they say it under the influence of some exceedingly hidden impulse, which human minds undergo without knowing it. Since this occurs for the deception of human beings, it is the work of seductive spirits. They are permitted to know certain truths about temporal matters through the sharpness of a more subtle sense.

Some of this knowledge arises from their more cunning experience, owing to their very great length of life; some comes from the holy angels, who learn these things from almighty God and reveal them to the spirits at his command. He distributes human merits with the most hidden integrity of justice. At times those wicked spirits even predict, as though by divination, things that they themselves are going to do.

**DISCIPLE.**

It follows: “And God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night; and the stars. And he placed them in the firmament of heaven, so that they might shine over the earth, rule the day and the night, and divide the light from the darkness” (Genesis 1).

[Col. 0253C] How, I ask, are these things to be understood according to the spiritual sense? Please explain.

**MASTER.**

**Isidore.**—On the fourth day the lights appeared, fixed in the firmament of the law—that is, the evangelists and teachers of the holy Scriptures, joined together through disputation and displaying the light of wisdom to all those below.

At the same time there also emerged the multitude of the other shining stars—that is, the multitude of different virtues in the Church. Shining in the obscurity of this life as in night, they divide within this firmament of Scripture things perceptible from things intelligible, as between the light of the perfect and the darkness of the little ones.

They are signs of virtues and miracles. They also serve for seasons, days, and years, because preachers live and pass away at their appointed times, while “the word of the Lord remains forever” (1 Peter 1).

**DISCIPLE.**

[Col. 0253D] Why did the earth sprout first, and the lights come into being afterward?

**MASTER.**

Because illumination by the light comes after good works, for contemplating the beauty of divine power.

**DISCIPLE.**

“And God saw that it was good, and evening came and morning came, the fourth day” (Genesis 1). Why did he mention evening and morning, but indicate nothing about night?

**MASTER.**

What else, then, should we call night except the absence of light, which seemed to remain between evening and morning? Or is it because the first light signifies the angels’ creation: by contemplating their Creator, they do not cease to praise him forever in the most harmonious love, without the blindness of ignorance? Yet at the beginning and completion of the work they clearly understood what is called evening and morning.

## The fifth day begins

“God also said: ‘Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living creatures, and birds upon the earth beneath the firmament of heaven’” (ibid.).

**DISCIPLE.**

Why, then, did he first adorn the waters with reptiles before adorning the earth with animals?

**MASTER.**

**Ambrose, in the Hexameron.**—The reason was that what first appeared visibly should also first receive its adornment. Or it was because, at the beginning, heaven received its adornment—that is, the angels—when they were created.

Similarly, the earth received its adornment when he clothed it with grasses and trees. It was therefore fitting that the waters should receive their adornment from reptiles, and the air from birds.

[Col. 0254B] **DISCIPLE.**

Why do we so often read similarly about the creation of heaven, earth, and sea—when they were created or how they were created—while Scripture says nothing about the air?

**MASTER.**
It should not be supposed that he omitted any element in this Scripture, unless because it is customary for divine Scripture to call heaven and earth the whole world. Therefore it must be judged that air belongs to heaven and earth; and whatever is moist or stretched out in vaporous form belongs to earth, whereas whatever is calm and still is said to belong to heaven. That air is like water, and is shown to become enriched by its exhalations, is evident from the fact that the breath of a storm makes it mist. For the ether is so near the heaven in which the luminaries are found that it too receives the name “heaven.” When it is said in the Psalm, “Praise him, heavens of heavens” (Ps. 148), it is sufficiently clear that this air is called not only heaven but also “heavens,” just as “earths” are spoken of, although there is one earth.

We also read in one of those Epistles called canonical that the aerial heavens once perished in the Flood. I do not know how this can be understood unless the denser quality of this air was changed into the nature of water. Therefore, in creating inhabitants for the lower parts of this world—which are often mentioned in their entirety under the name “earth”—it was fitting that animals should first be produced from the waters. Afterwards they were produced from the earth, and likewise, as we have already said, air is similar to water and is shown to become enriched from its exhalations.

For this reason it is not written, “Let the waters produce reptiles possessing living souls, and let the air produce flying creatures that fly over the earth”; rather, both kinds of living creatures are related to have been produced from the waters. Whatever, therefore, is water—whether it flows and is wave-like and fluid, or whether it is thinned and suspended in vaporous form—so that the former appears assigned to reptiles and the latter to flying creatures, both are nevertheless attributed to moist nature.

And so there are those who, with the most subtle consideration, distinguish the five bodily senses according to the four customary elements. They say that the eyes belong to fire, the ears to pure air, the sense of smell to moist air, taste to corporeal humors, and touch to the earthly element. Thus all the elements are in all things, but each is called by what it possesses in greater measure.

The reason that sensation is dulled by the deprivation of heat, when the body becomes excessively cold, is that the motion which heat supplies to the body grows sluggish. Fire affects air, air affects moist matter, and moisture affects earthly things; in other words, the subtler penetrate the coarser. The subtler anything is in corporeal nature, the nearer it is to spiritual nature. Yet the soul, in which the power of sensation resides, although it is not corporeal, exercises the vigor of sensation through the subtler body.

In this way motion reaches all the senses through the subtlety of fire, though it does not reach the same point in all of them. In sight it reaches, through restrained heat, as far as light; in hearing, as far as the more fluid air; in smell, it passes through pure air and reaches the moist exhalation from which this denser atmosphere subsists; in taste, it passes through even this and reaches the denser humor. Once it has penetrated and traversed that, when it reaches earthly heaviness, it activates the final sense, touch.

He therefore did not fail to understand the natures of the elements when he first related the heavenly luminaries, then the animals of the waters, and lastly those of the earth—not because he omitted air, but because he named its purer part after heaven and its denser part after earth. The fact that we also perceive waters and winds by touch is due to this: earth alone is mingled with all the elements.

Birds therefore fly in heaven—but in that heaven which the Psalm includes under the name “earth,” not in the firmament, but according to the firmament.

Nor am I unaware that certain philosophers assigned animals to their respective elements. They said that earthly animals included not only those that creep and walk upon the earth, but also birds, since birds too rest on the earth when fatigued by flying; that aerial animals were demons; and that heavenly animals were gods, some of whom we call luminaries and others angels. To the waters, however, they assigned fish and beasts of their own kind, so that no element might be without its animals.

Two elements are assigned to undergoing action—moisture and soil—and two to acting—air and fire. Air extends from the boundary of the luminous heaven down to the flowing waters and exposed earth. Yet moist exhalations do not darken its entire expanse, but only as far as the point where earth already begins to be called earth, as in the Psalm: “Praise the Lord from the earth” (Ps. 148). The upper part of the air, because of its pure tranquility, is joined in common peace to the heaven beside which it lies, and is called by its name.

Perhaps it was in this region that the transgressing angels, with their prince—now the devil, but then an archangel—were before their transgression. For none of our people doubts that they were heavenly or superheavenly angels. It is therefore not surprising that, after their sin, they were thrust into this darkness, where there is nevertheless air, thinly overlaid with moisture. Through it God’s work administers, from the highest to the lowest, all that he created by hidden commands: it stirs winds and drives them with greater force; it kindles and gathers fires; it forms clouds; it thickens them with rain; it makes snow from freezing clouds; and, when the clouds freeze more turbulently and densely, it makes hail; or, when the air is spread out, it makes clear weather.

But, as we have already said, air is made from water. Flying creatures of heaven exist in the air; hence we call birds “birds of heaven,” and demons are said to dwell in the air. The air therefore tolerates and supports them because they use an aerial form. From there they attack the human race, since, as soon as they were created, they were cast out of the sight of God. Thus the Savior says in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10).

Here one rightly asks how he is said to have fallen if he did not stand. But it must be understood that he did not persevere in the fellowship of the holy angels. As soon as he looked upon himself in the brightness of God, he raised himself up in pride and said: “I will ascend into heaven, and I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven; I will sit on the mountain of the Covenant, on the sides of the North. I will ascend above the heights of the clouds of heaven; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). At once he was cast down from the height of heaven into the air, together with all his attendants, because they did not remain in divine love like those who were established so firmly that, even if they should wish to sin, they could not. At the beginning they had possessed free choice, as the human race appears to possess it.

Those, however, who fell through their own choice received God’s sentence, so that, even if they should wish to be restored, they cannot. The Lord said something else: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth” (John 8).

## DISCIPLE

Why a murderer?

## MASTER

Because he first slew Adam in paradise, when he persuaded him to eat the fruit; and from immortality Adam became mortal. For this reason he slew the human race until the coming of the Savior.

## DISCIPLE

How did he not stand in the truth?

## MASTER

Because he did not deserve to receive what had been promised him: that he might remain forever with his Creator together with the other angels. Instead, he was cast down to earth with his followers. There, without doubt, they suffer punishment, because in the air the starry fire rules over them; and the air has been assigned to them as a kind of prison according to their nature, until the time of the Day of Judgment comes, when they will be cast into eternal fire.

The text continues:

“God created the great sea creatures and every living and moving soul, which the waters had produced according to their kinds, and every flying creature according to its kind” (Gen. 1).

## DISCIPLE

I wish to know when the smallest fish, animals, and worms—which Scripture does not mention—were created. Since an explanation is required, where did they come from, from the greatest elephant down to the smallest worm, when Scripture has said nothing here?

## MASTER

It must be understood that, when God separated the waters from the waters, the smallest animals that are formed from water already had their nature within the waters themselves. The worms that are found in the bodies of the dead have their power of generation within those very bodies. Fish, too, are produced from the waters, since it says: “Let the waters produce reptiles possessing living souls” (ibid.).

## DISCIPLE

If water covered the earth—or, I ask you, did the earth cover the water?—please tell me.

## MASTER

Water covered the earth. For if some portion of earth had slipped onto the water, the water would immediately have burst out, and the earth would have returned to its place.

## DISCIPLE

How then does the Psalm say, “For he founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers” (Ps. 23), if water covered the earth?

## MASTER

He says this of higher land, where mountains appear to be, or it was said of islands, where the land is higher than the water. But it is better understood according to its spiritual meaning: in the Church, the simple are founded upon the wise. They are therefore called “living waters,” because they support those whom they perceive to be lower or weaker than themselves. For the distance between holy rusticity and holy simplicity is as great as that between the moon and the stars of heaven.

The text continues:

“And he blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea’” (Gen. 1).

## DISCIPLE

Why did these animals deserve to receive a blessing, as man did?

## MASTER

We should understand this blessing as continuing in the other animals as well, so that the birds may multiply upon the earth.

“And evening and morning came: the fifth day” (ibid.).

## Questions concerning the sixth day

“And God said: ‘Let the earth produce a living soul according to its kind: cattle, reptiles, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds.’ And it was so” (Gen. 1).

## DISCIPLE

Ambrose.—We must ask whether these poisonous animals, at the beginning when they were created, possessed poison as they do now.

## MASTER

This must certainly be understood: just as they were then created, so they remain. Yet at the beginning they did not possess the power to cause harm, as we can prove from snakes. When a viper attacked Paul’s hand, it did him no harm, because it had the power to attack but did not have the power to injure.

The same may be understood of beasts. When Daniel was thrown into the lions’ den, those lions did him no harm. Or perhaps these poisonous animals were created to frighten man, whom God knew would sin, so that he might understand the infernal punishments. For elsewhere it says: “Their worms do not die, and their fire is not extinguished.”

Why, then, do beasts harm one another, when they have no original sin for which punishment could be inflicted upon them?

## On the Creation of Man

## DISCIPLE

Ambrose.—“And God saw that it was good, and said: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness’; and God made man in the image of God” (Gen. 1). First, we learn briefly that it should not be understood indifferently that, in the other works, it is said, “God said, ‘Let it be made,’” whereas here God said, “Let us make.”

## MASTER

This was to suggest, so to speak, the plurality of persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—while he immediately instructed us to understand the unity of the Godhead by saying: “And God made man in the image of God” (ibid.). This is as though he had said: “God made man in his own image.”

Nor should this be passed over: when he had said, “In our image,” he immediately added, “And let him have dominion over the fish of the sea and the other animals devoid of reason,” so that we may understand man to have been made in the image of God in that respect in which he surpasses irrational animals. That respect is reason itself, or the mind, or understanding.

Although it may be argued with the utmost subtlety that the human mind, in which man was made in the image of God, is a certain rational life divided between contemplation of eternal truth and administration of temporal affairs—and that in this way it becomes, as it were, male and female, with one part giving counsel and the other obeying—nevertheless, the image of God is not properly said to consist in this except in that which adheres to the contemplation of unchangeable Truth. As a figure of this, the Apostle Paul says that only the man is the image and glory of God.

Isidore.—“And God made man in his own image” (ibid.), that is, for eternity and immortality; and in his likeness, so that he might possess understanding of mind, unlike animals, which do not know how to distinguish between good and evil.

## DISCIPLE

Augustine.—What are we to understand by what is read in Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (ibid.)?

## MASTER

In the mind, that is, in reason and understanding. The mind itself, when it thinks about eternal things, is to be called the image of God. In thinking about eternal things, it is a man, as the Apostle Paul says: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (1 Cor. 7)—that is, the more fully he extends himself toward what is eternal, the more he is formed in the image of God. Therefore he must not be restrained from holding himself there and moderating himself accordingly.

But when he does or thinks what belongs to temporal things, he is called a woman. Then he is not to be called the image of God, and for that reason he ought to cover his head, lest his advance toward lower things become excessive, lest, while doing what is permitted, he desire what is forbidden.

“And the Lord God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Gen. 1).

## DISCIPLE

What does it mean that he says he created the female together with the male, when she had not yet been formed?

## MASTER

Because she was destined to proceed from Adam. Thus, in the seed of a tree, many things are hidden. First it is fixed in the root; then it appears in the character of the tree; afterwards in the spreading of the branches; then in the greenness of the leaves; and so forth. In the same way, the woman was hidden in Adam’s body, because she was fashioned from his rib.

The text continues:

“And he blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth; subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and all living creatures that move upon the earth’” (ibid.).

## DISCIPLE

Why did man deserve to receive this blessing?

## MASTER

So that he might not appear blameworthy in begetting children, and so that it might be declared that they incurred no sin thereby if they married lawfully.

## DISCIPLE

If Adam was therefore created in such a way that he would remain immortal, why were they told, “Increase and multiply”?

## MASTER

This must be understood to mean that they were not to beget children according to the lust of the flesh or by any evil will. Nor were they to give birth to children in pain, as they do now. Rather, just as each person commands his limbs to perform some action—his hand in working or his foot in walking—so they ought to have begotten offspring in paradise.

## DISCIPLE

But if they were to beget offspring in this way, why did they not join together in paradise, before they had been cast out, in order to beget children?

## MASTER

Because as soon as the woman had been created, she transgressed and was cast down from the lofty height of immortality into the depths below.

## DISCIPLE

How, then, would their bodies have had to change if they were to remain immortal?

## MASTER

This must be understood as follows: if they had not sinned, they could not have died at all. But, once that number had been completed according to the number of angels, their bodies would have been changed for the better, without mortality.

## DISCIPLE

Augustine.—Was the first man made mortal or immortal?

## MASTER

He was mortal in some respects and immortal in others. The first man therefore had a body like ours, but without sin. He did not have a law in his members opposing the law of his mind (Rom. 7), which he certainly deserved after his transgression.

Adam therefore had an animal body, but through the power of that tree by which he was sustained he did not grow old or fail; in paradise that tree had received the name “tree of life.” Consequently, if he had kept God’s commandment, by the merit of obedience he would afterwards have been changed into that spiritual body which is promised to the saints in the resurrection.

Thus he could have avoided death if he had adhered to pious obedience toward God. For he was not made in such a way that he could not die, like those other natures that cannot die at all; rather, he was made so that obedience would make him immortal and disobedience mortal.

## DISCIPLE

If Adam was immortal or mortal—and if mortal, how was he immortal; and if animal, how was he spiritual? Or why did he share food in common with the other animals?

## MASTER

He was mortal and immortal. He was mortal because he could die; immortal because he could avoid dying. If he had not sinned, he could not have died at all; but after he sinned, he became mortal.

Again: he was mortal and immortal. He was mortal by his condition; immortal by God’s gift, which was supplied to him through the tree of life. When he sinned, he was cast away from that tree, so that he could die.

## DISCIPLE

What, then, is the reason that we, who have been reborn through Christ, have not received the immortality that Adam possessed before sin?

## MASTER

We did not receive what we lost in Adam, namely, an animal body. Rather, we received something much better, inasmuch as the spiritual is superior to the bodily. Hence the Apostle says: “The animal body is sown; the spiritual body rises” (1 Cor. 15).

We did not receive the immortality of a spiritual body, but we received the righteousness from which Adam fell through sin. Concerning this the Apostle also says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth” (Eph. 4).

He will therefore be renewed from the oldness of sin—not into the former animal body in which Adam existed, but into something better, namely, a spiritual body, when we become equal to the angels of God through heavenly dwelling.

We will also be renewed in the spirit of our mind according to the image of him who created us, which Adam lost through sin. We are renewed also in the flesh, when this corruptible body puts on incorruption and this mortal body puts on immortality, so that it becomes a spiritual body. Adam had not yet been changed into this body, but was destined to be changed, because in our body we bear the image of the earthly man, while in the mind we bear the image of the heavenly (1 Cor. 15).

The Apostle says again: “If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one, as it is written: ‘The first man, Adam, became a living soul; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.’ But the spiritual was not first; rather, the animal, and afterwards the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so also are the earthly” (ibid.).

Let us put on the image of him who is from heaven. The image of the earthly man we put on from the very beginning of the human race; but now we bear by faith the image of the heavenly man, which we believe we shall possess in the resurrection.

## DISCIPLE

Why did he not bless trees and herbs, but man and animals?

## MASTER

He blessed these because they propagate offspring, or because of the male and female sexes; and also because trees have no faculty of sensation or understanding, whereas animals feel but do not understand, while man both feels and understands. Therefore he did not say to the trees, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1).

## DISCIPLE

“And God said to them: ‘Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed upon the earth,’” up to, “And it was so. And God saw everything that he had made, and they were very good” (ibid.). Since God created everything good, and since nothing exists that was not created by him, where does evil come from?

## MASTER

Augustine.—Evil is not a nature; it has received this name from the privation of good. In the end, good can exist without evil, but evil cannot exist without good. There can be no evil where there is no good. Thus we speak of a good angel and an evil angel, a good man and an evil man.

But the angel is good, while the vicious quality is evil; the man is good, while the vicious quality is evil. Therefore, when we say “good,” we praise the nature; when we say “evil,” we censure not the nature but the vice that belongs to a good nature.

The text continues:

“And evening and morning came: the sixth day. Thus the heavens and the earth and all their adornment were completed” (Gen. 1–2).

## The beginning concerning the seventh day

Jerome.—“And God completed on the sixth day the works that he had made” (Gen. 2). In the Hebrew, instead of “the sixth day,” it has “the seventh day.” We shall therefore press the Jews, who glory in the leisure of the Sabbath, with the argument that already at the beginning the Sabbath was dissolved, since God worked on the Sabbath, completing his works on it and blessing the day itself because on it he completed everything.

## DISCIPLE

It says, “He blessed the seventh day and sanctified it.” Why did he bless the seventh day, on which he created nothing?

## MASTER

It was so that he might not appear needy, as when a man, tired after work, says, “Thanks be to God, I have finished my work.” The Lord did not act in this way. Rather, he blessed the day on which he created nothing in order to show that the creation of all things involved no labor for him. God merely said, “Let it be,” and they were made (Ps. 32). Therefore he rested on the seventh day, so that he might make us rest in him.

## DISCIPLE

Augustine.—Since rest comes only after labor, why is God said to rest? Was he also wearied by his work, so that he is said to have rested?

## MASTER

God did not rest in any creature, as though he needed its good, but in himself. In fact, he is not read to have rested on any one of the days, but after the works of the sixth day. From this it clearly appears that God made no creature out of need, but solely by his good will. If he rested in any creature, he would have made some creature out of need. Therefore, because he made no creature out of need, he rested in no creature.

For when Scripture says that God rested on the seventh day from all his works that he had made, I think this can be understood to mean not that he rested because he needed those good things in order to be happier, but that he brought the seventh day itself—that is, the angelic nature—into his rest. Thus they might see in God that, just as every creature was to be formed, so too it was evident that he had made no creature out of need but solely from goodness. I think this can be understood as God’s rest.

God’s rest may also be understood in another way: he rests when he causes us to rest through good works, according to the manner in which God says to Abraham, “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22), that is, “I have caused you to be known.” So here too God is understood to rest when he grants rest to his saints.

Again, it may be understood in another way. God is said to rest from creating new creatures, because after bringing forth the works of the six days he created no creature thereafter. For when he says, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5), this is understood not as creating a new creature, but as administering the creature he created, as Junilius says.

God is said to have rested on the seventh day not from creating, since every creature is renewed daily through his ordering and providence, as is evident; rather, this was signified: after those six days he created no substantial kind or nature that was unknown to the world, new and untested. For this day is the first, it is the second, it is the last, because it is a repetition of the seventh day.

## DISCIPLE

Why did he not bless the day on which he created the angelic light, or the day on which he completed everything?

## MASTER

He did not sanctify the day on which he began this work, nor the day on which he completed it, lest his action appear to have been a source of joy either in making those things or in having made them. Rather, he sanctified the day on which he rested from them in himself and showed us that rest through the seventh day.

Nevertheless, he was never without that rest; he signified that his rest is not perceived until after the completion of the work. For this reason it is understood that evening did not follow upon this day, because our rest will be in the perfection of the work, without end and in joy.

The text continues:

“These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created, on the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it arose upon the earth, and every herb of the region before it sprouted.”

## DISCIPLE

An explanation must be sought as to whether all these things were made in one day or over six days, as Scripture relates. And if they were made over six days, how is the holy Scripture true when it says, “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18)?

## MASTER
