He created all things together according to the substance of things; but he did not create all things together according to the appearance of their form. Just as a mother, nourishing an infant in her lap, waits for it to grow strong, so the Lord accommodated the slowness of human understanding.

In the beginning, everything was created with him, but it did not immediately come forth into visible form. When it says, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1), then, as we have said, all things that were destined to arise from heaven and earth were made with him, although he wished to divide them according to their visible form over six days.

For example, Scripture says that he placed the stars in heaven on the fourth day; yet on the first day they were made with him in heaven, and on the fourth day they came forth into visible form. Just as many things are hidden in a grain of seed—the root, bark, leaves, fruit, and many other things that come from the tree—so all these things were first hidden with God and afterwards came forth into visible form.

## DISCIPLE

If, then, he created all things together, how is it true that we read, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5)?

## MASTER

Let your expertise understand that, although he then created everything together, he nevertheless governs it daily by watering, planting, building, and by his activity in all other things. For just as a man who cultivates a field, if he abandons it, leaves it uncultivated, so the world, created by God, cannot exist without God’s governance, according to the Apostle Paul: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3).

Others wish to understand these seven days as the seven gifts of the grace of the Holy Spirit: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of fear of the Lord (Isa. 11).

They say that through the Spirit of wisdom God made heaven and earth; through the Spirit of understanding he made the firmament and separated the waters from the waters; through the Spirit of counsel he separated the waters from the dry land and caused the earth to sprout; through the Spirit of fortitude he placed the luminaries in the firmament of heaven to divide day and night; through the Spirit of knowledge he adorned the waters with reptiles and the air with flying creatures; through the Spirit of piety he clothed the earth with animals, created man, and made all the other things that are born; and through the Spirit of the fear of the Lord he sanctified his work on the seventh day.

In the same way, we ought to imitate these seven gifts of the Holy Spirit within ourselves. Through the Spirit of wisdom we should make heaven and earth—that is, meditate on heavenly things and abandon earthly things—or separate light from darkness, that is, our perfected works from the darkness of wicked works.

Through the Spirit of understanding we should make a firmament between the lower and upper waters, that is, holy discipline between vices and virtues, so that we do not incline toward vices.

Through the Spirit of counsel we should separate the waters from the dry land, that is, reprobate people from the soul thirsting for the word of God.

Through the Spirit of fortitude we should place luminaries in the firmament of heaven, that is, love of neighbor, because Saint John said: “He who hates his brother is in darkness” (1 John 2).

Through the Spirit of knowledge we should adorn the waters with reptiles, and so forth—that is, send a voice from the ark of our heart toward heaven. Just as fish give themselves an upward leap with their little fins, and the birds of heaven fly about in the air, so we ought to raise our understanding toward higher things.

Through the Spirit of piety we should make serpents and cattle, and so forth—that is, possess simplicity and prudence for discerning between good and evil; and, producing the fruit of good works, learn how we may imitate the examples of the saints and Truth itself, in whose image we were made.

Through the Spirit of the fear of the Lord we should rest in the rest of eternal life, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110).

## DISCIPLE

“These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created on the day when the Lord made heaven and earth”—above, seven days were counted; now one day is named, on which God made heaven and earth, every shrub of the field, and every herb of the region (Gen. 2).

## MASTER

By the name of this day, according to prophecy, the whole time of this life is signified: the time in which heaven and earth were made, that is, the time in which visible creatures are ordered, governed, and exist.

Hence Moses both related distinctly, day by day, everything that was created, and nevertheless added that all things were created together, saying: “These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, on the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it arose upon the earth, and every herb of the region” (ibid.).

He who had related that heaven and earth, shrubs and herbs, were created on different days now reveals that they were made in one day, so that he might clearly show that every creature came into existence together according to substance, although it did not come forth together according to visible form.

The text continues:

“For the Lord had not rained upon the earth; and there was no man to work the earth; and a spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth” (ibid.).

## DISCIPLE

Augustine.—If it watered the whole earth, then it also watered the mountains, since mountains are certainly earth. If it watered the mountains, there was a flood. And how had the earth brought forth green grass producing seed? Or how did man dwell on the earth if water covered the whole earth?

## MASTER

The singular “spring” is used in place of the plural. If you examine this carefully, you will frequently find it in the holy Scriptures. In the Psalm you have: “He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them, and the frog, and it destroyed them” (Ps. 77), although there was certainly neither one dog-fly nor one frog. Elsewhere: “The locust came” (Ps. 104). It does not say “locusts,” but “the locust.” Here too the singular is used for the plural, according to what the most renowned of poets said: “They fill both with armed soldiery.”

Moreover, “spring” was said on account of the unity of nature, so that in it we understand all the springs that are on the earth, because in some way they all flow from the nature of one abyss.

When it says, “It watered the whole surface of the earth,” it does not mean that it watered the entire earth, but a part. For a part is signified by the whole, just as we say, “Christ died; Christ rose again,” although he died and rose again only according to the flesh.

Or, as Ambrose says: “A spring was named which, having received the assistance of moisture, watered the entire surface of the earth.” Or, after paradise had been planted, that disruption of the waters was dammed up. The spring was divided into channels to water the entire surface of the earth, just as we now see waters flow through riverbeds and channels of streams, and, overflowing from them, flood the neighboring places.

So then, as if from one spring, many flowed forth; or one spring was named, hidden in a certain hollow of the earth, from which all springs, small and great, proceed.

## DISCIPLE

What is the reason that this spring is not plainly found, although it appears to have watered the whole surface of the earth?

## MASTER

Perhaps, because of the sin of our first parent Adam, this spring was withdrawn, so that abundance might be taken away from the earth and the human race might undergo greater labor.

Isidore, elsewhere.—“A spring rose from the earth, watering the entire surface of the earth” (Gen. 2). The earth, the mother of the Lord, is rightly called the Virgin Mary, concerning whom it is written: “Let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Savior” (Isa. 45). The Holy Spirit watered this earth; in the Gospels he is signified under the name of “spring” and “water.”

## On the Breathing of Life into Man

## DISCIPLE

“Then the Lord formed man from the mud of the earth” (Gen. 2). The first point that commonly raises a question is what kind of mud this was, or what material is signified by the name “mud.” Please explain this to me as well.

## MASTER
They are accustomed to reproach this sharply: enemies of the ancient Books, who view everything in a carnal manner and therefore are always in error, object that God fashioned man from clay. They say: “Why did God make man from clay? Was better and heavenly material lacking to him from which he might make man, so that he formed a fragile and mortal nature from the filth of the earth?” They do not understand, first, how many meanings the terms “earth” and “water” have in Scripture. Clay is a mixture of water and earth.

We have said that the human body began, after sin, to be corruptible, fragile, and destined for death. For what horrifies them in our body is nothing except mortality, which we deserved by condemnation. But what is difficult or surprising for God—even if he made man from the clay of this earth—to make his body such that it would not be subject to corruption, if man, keeping the Lord’s commandment, had been unwilling to sin? If we say that heaven itself was made from nothing, or from formless matter, believing in an omnipotent craftsman, what is surprising if the body that was made from whatever kind of clay could by an omnipotent craftsman be made such that, before sin, no trouble or want would torment man and no corruption would cause him to decay?

Thus it is asked superfluously from what God made man’s body, if what is now being discussed is the formation of the body. For I have learned that some of our people understand it in this way. They say: “After it was said, ‘God fashioned man from the clay of the earth,’ the words ‘in his own image and likeness’ were therefore not added, as they are now when the formation of the body is being discussed.” At that earlier point, they say, the inner man was signified, when it was said, “God made man in the image of God.” But even if here too we understand man as made from body and soul, so that this speech is not the beginning of some new work but a fuller reconsideration of what was first briefly indicated, the mixture itself may not improperly have received the name “clay.” For just as water gathers, glues, and holds earth together when clay is produced by their mixture, so the soul, vivifying the body’s material, shapes it into harmonious unity and does not allow it to slip away and dissolve.

## DISCIPLE

Augustine.—It may rightly be asked how those causal principles which he implanted in the world when he first created all things together were established: whether, as we have seen all things being born, shrubs and animals in their formation and growth pass through periods of time differing according to the diversity of their kinds; or whether Adam, as is believed, was formed without any gradual increase, being immediately fashioned at mature manhood, like water changed into wine and a staff into a serpent.

## MASTER

Why should we not believe that they possessed both possibilities, so that from them would come whatever he who was to make it had determined? For many things are going to occur according to lower causes; yet, if they occur in this manner, they are truly going to occur in God’s foreknowledge. But if, in that foreknowledge, they are otherwise destined to occur—rather, just as they exist there, where the one who foreknows cannot be deceived—then that is how they will occur.

Old age is said to be future in a young man; yet it is not future if he is destined to die beforehand. This will happen according to the disposition of other causes, whether woven into the world or reserved in the present. For according to certain causes of future events, Hezekiah was destined to die; yet God added fifteen years to his life, doing precisely what he had foreknown before the foundation of the world that he would do and had preserved within his will.

There it was determined not only that Adam could be made in this way, but also that it was necessary for him to be made in this way. Yet God does not act against the cause which he undoubtedly established willingly; he does not act against his own will. But if he did not fix all causes in the creature originally created, and reserved some within his own will, those which he reserved in his will certainly do not depend necessarily upon those which he created. Nevertheless, they cannot be contrary to the causes he reserved in his will, because God’s will cannot be contrary to itself.

He therefore established these causes in such a way that what they are causes of could arise from them, but need not necessarily do so. The others he concealed in such a way that it was necessary for that to arise from them which he had made possible through these causes.

It follows:

## Augustine

“And he breathed into his face the breath of life” (Genesis 2).

## DISCIPLE

How are we to understand this breathing, if God is incorporeal?

## MASTER

This must be understood clearly: just as he did not fashion man with bodily hands, so he did not breathe with throat or lips. Nevertheless, we must believe and understand—and in no way doubt what right faith holds—that the soul exists from God as something he made, not as part of the nature that he himself is, whether he generated it or produced it in some other manner.

As for the philosophers’ opinion concerning the transmigration of souls, whatever its truth or falsity may be, it is not compatible with the Catholic faith to believe that the souls of animals pass into human beings, or those of human beings into animals. As for the stories that are told of people seeming to remember the bodies of animals in which they had existed, these are either false reports, or something of this kind has been produced in their minds by demonic deceptions. For if it has happened in a dream that a person, through a deceptive memory, seemed to remember having been something he was not or having done something he did not do, what is surprising if, by some just and hidden judgment of God, demons are permitted to produce something similar even in the minds of those who are awake?

The Manichaeans, however, who either think themselves Christians or wish to be thought so, are worse and more detestable in this doctrine of the transmigration or revolution of souls than those pagan philosophers—or any other foolish people—who hold such a belief. For the latter distinguish the nature of the soul from the nature of God. The former, however, claiming that the soul is nothing other than God’s own substance, indeed precisely what God is, do not hesitate to describe it as so shamefully changeable that they insanely suppose there is no kind of grass or worm with which it is not mixed, or into which it cannot be transmigrated.

Accordingly, since the anterior part of the brain, from which all the senses are distributed, is situated toward the forehead, and since the face contains, as it were, the organs of sensation, I think it was therefore written that God breathed the breath of life into man’s face. The anterior part is rightly placed before the posterior, because the former also directs the latter.

It follows: “From the one comes sensation, from the other movement,” just as deliberation precedes action; and just as bodily movement, which follows sensation, does not exist without temporal intervals. We cannot perform such intervals of time through voluntary movement except with the aid of memory. Therefore three chambers, as it were, of the brain are identified: one anterior, toward the face, from which all sensation proceeds; another posterior, toward the neck, from which all movement proceeds; and a third between the two, in which they show memory to be active, so that, when movement follows sensation, a person does not fail to connect what ought to be done if he has forgotten what he is doing.

But when we ask where the soul itself comes from—that is, from what sort of material God made this breath, which is called the soul—nothing corporeal ought to present itself. For just as God surpasses every bodily creature, so the soul surpasses every corporeal creature in the dignity of its nature. Through light and air—which, even within this world, are pre-eminent bodies and possess greater capacity for acting than for suffering corporeal density—just as through things more akin to spirit, moisture and earth administer the body.

Corporeal light announces something; but that to which it announces is not the same as the light itself. This is the soul, to which it announces, not the thing that announces. When the soul painfully senses the body’s affections, it is disturbed because its own activity—by which it is present to govern the body—is impeded by the body’s disordered condition. This disturbance is called pain. The air infused into the nerves obeys the will and moves the limbs, but it is not itself the will.

For the soul is one thing, and these bodily services, vessels, or organs of the soul are another—whatever the more suitable terms may be. This is plainly evident from the fact that, when the soul turns away from everything through intense thought and concentration, it may fail to notice many things placed before its open and healthy eyes. At times it even forgets where it comes from and where it is going, and passes unconsciously through a village toward which it had been heading, while the nature of its body remains sound but its attention has been diverted elsewhere.

It is credible that every body can be changed into every other body; but it is absurd to believe that any body can be changed into a soul. Let us therefore consider whether it may perhaps be true—and it seems to me more tolerable to human opinion—that God, in those first works when he created all things together, also created the soul, which he would inspire in its own time into the limbs of the body formed from clay, and that in those things created together he causally established the body’s principle, according to which it would be made when the human body was to be formed.

For we rightly understand neither “in his own image” except of the soul, nor “male and female” except of the body. Let it therefore be believed—if no authority or truth of Scripture contradicts it—that man was made on the sixth day in such a way that the causal principle of the body was already present in the elements of the world, while the soul itself was created already and lay hidden in God’s works, until, in its own time, God breathed it—that is, inspired it—into the body formed from clay.

If this is so, we shall acknowledge that the soul was not originally created among those things so that it might be prescient of its future work, whether just or wicked. For God is not to be praised only for those creatures to which he gave foreknowledge, since he is rightly praised also because he created animals, whose nature is inferior to human nature even in sinful human beings. The nature of man is from God; the iniquity by which man entangles himself through the misuse of his freer will is not. Yet if man did not possess free will within the nature of things, he would be less excellent.

We must conceive of a man living justly without foreknowledge of future events; and one must live in such a way that the excellence of a good will is not impeded in right living, and that he who lives without knowledge of the future nevertheless seeks to please God by faith. Whoever is unwilling for such a creature to exist among created things contradicts God’s goodness; whoever does not want it to suffer punishment for its sins is an enemy of justice.

We have been led to this conclusion by all these testimonies of divine Scripture, whose truthfulness no one doubts except an unbeliever and an impious person: namely, that God, from the beginning of the world, first created all things together. Some things he made through the natures already established, and some through pre-established causes; thus the Almighty made not only present things but also future ones, and then rested from those works, so that thereafter, through their administration and governance, he might also create the orders of times and temporal things.

Nevertheless, concerning what God inspired into man by breathing into his image, I affirm nothing except that it is from God in such a way that it is not God’s substance, and that it is incorporeal—that is, not a body but a spirit. It was not generated from God’s substance, nor did it proceed from God’s substance; it was made by God, but not in such a way that any bodily nature or irrational soul was transformed into its nature.

## Remaining Questions Concerning the Nature of the Soul

## DISCIPLE

“He breathed into his face the breath of life” (Genesis 2). What are we to understand by “the breath of life”?

## MASTER

This means “to make the soul,” as Isaiah says: “The form proceeds from me, and I made every breath” (Isaiah 57)—that is, every soul.

## DISCIPLE

What are we to make of the fact that the soul, created innocent, entered a body which God foreknew would sin?

## MASTER

Far be it from us to accept that the soul was created for the purpose of entering a body which God foreknew would sin, and was reserved for that purpose; for if this were so, God would be the author of sin. But it is not so. Rather, we should understand and accept that, with God inspiring it, the soul voluntarily entered the body in order to govern it, because the body is perceived through the soul; for if there is no soul, the body is dead.

## DISCIPLE

What, then, is the soul? Or, if there is some reality from which souls are made, what is that reality? What is its name? What is its form? What function does it possess among created things? Does it live, or not? If it lives, what does it contribute to the affections of the universe? Does it lead a blessed life or a wretched one? What, then, is the soul? It is neither heaven, nor earth, nor air, nor fire, nor water, nor God, nor the stars, nor sight, nor hearing, nor taste, nor the other things—which would take too long to enumerate—that are in heaven and on earth. From where, then, does the soul come?

## MASTER

The soul is given by God and made from nothing. For man, who was made from earth, returns to earth. Likewise, snow and storms, which are formed from water, and air, which takes its substance from earth, return to water; and again they return to earth, from which they were taken, through the air. The soul, however, has no element to which it can return, except its Creator, after it has departed from the body, so that, under his governance, it may receive what it deserves.

## DISCIPLE

We must therefore investigate how the soul comes to man when he is born.

## MASTER

Some say that, just as flesh is born from flesh, so soul is born from soul. But Scripture nowhere states where the soul comes from for a person when he is born, nor how it was brought forth from the woman’s soul itself, as it states concerning flesh how it was made.

Others, however, hold the better view: that each person’s soul is given by God when he is born, as it is written in Isaiah: “The spirit proceeds from me, and I made every breath”—that is, every soul. And as it is written in the Psalm: “He fashioned their hearts one by one.”

Still others rashly say that all souls were created when God made all things together, and that they are hidden in some place until a person is born; then the soul is given to him by God. But in considering our own affairs, we must not determine what God either permits or does not permit concerning how the soul is given to man, since Scripture nowhere states this. We cannot distinguish what the truth has left unsaid; and Scripture says nothing else about this matter except how the soul was given by God.

## DISCIPLE

From where, then, did our Savior receive his soul?

## MASTER

Not from Adam, but from the source of Adam—that is, from God. For although he descended from the lineage of sin, he did not conceive from the lineage of sin, since he himself was not sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh. He did not therefore receive from it the guilt of dying.

## DISCIPLE

When the soul departs from this body, is it corporeal or incorporeal?

## MASTER

It is certainly incorporeal.

## DISCIPLE

How, then, is it carried, if it is incorporeal?

## MASTER

It is incorporeal, yet similar to bodies.

## DISCIPLE

And where is it carried—to a corporeal place or to an incorporeal one?

## MASTER

To incorporeal places similar to corporeal ones.

## DISCIPLE

It is therefore asked whether the soul can exist without the body among the angels in perpetual blessedness, without any deficiency. What need is there, then, for the body to rise again, so that the soul may put it on as immortal then, though it now lays it aside as mortal?

## MASTER

The administration of the body is indeed present, and through it the mind is delayed from proceeding to that highest state until the body rises, so that what is now a burden to it may then be its glory.

## DISCIPLE

What need is there, then, for infants whose parents—a Christian father and mother—are Christians to be born again through the water of baptism?

## MASTER

Because everyone is born in original sin, and unless he is born again through the water of baptism, he cannot enter the kingdom of God (John 3:5).

## On the Planting of Paradise

Jerome, in the Book of Hebrew Questions, says as follows:

“And the Lord God planted a paradise in Eden, toward the east.” For “paradise” he has “garden,” that is, *gan*. Moreover, *Eden* is interpreted as “delights.” Accordingly, Symmachus translated it as “a flourishing paradise.” Likewise, the word that follows, “toward the east,” is written in Hebrew as *miqqedem*, which Aquila rendered ἀπὸ ἀρχῆς, “from the beginning.” We too can say “from the beginning.” Symmachus has ἐκ πρώτης, “from the first,” and Theodotion likewise ἐκ πρώτης. This too signifies not the east but the beginning.

From this it is demonstrated most clearly that, before he made heaven and earth, he had already established paradise. For it is read in Hebrew: “The Lord God had planted paradise in Eden from the beginning.”

Augustine, in the *Hexameron*:

“And God planted a paradise in Eden, toward the east, and placed there the man whom he had fashioned.” I am not unaware that many people have said many things about paradise; nevertheless, there are, as it were, three general opinions on the matter. One belongs to those who wish paradise to be understood only corporeally; another to those who understand it only spiritually; and a third to those who understand it in both ways, corporeally and spiritually. I shall therefore say briefly that I acknowledge the third opinion to be pleasing to me.

God therefore had planted a paradise of delights, that is, toward the east, and placed there the man whom he had fashioned. For it is written that it was made—as a certain wise man said—in a particular place where this earthly man could dwell. Spiritually, paradise is understood as the place to which the souls of the saints now go when they depart from the body; this earthly paradise was planted as its figure, in accordance with the historical truth of the events.

But what follows—“and the tree of life in the midst of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil”—must be considered more carefully, lest it force us into an allegorical interpretation in which these were not actual trees, but the name “tree” signified something else. For it is said of Wisdom: “She is a tree of life to those who embrace her.”

Nevertheless, although there is an eternal Jerusalem in heaven, a city was also established on earth to signify it. Likewise, although Sarah and Hagar signify the two Testaments, they were nevertheless also two actual women. And although Christ irrigates us through the suffering of the tree with a spiritual stream, there was also a rock from which water flowed for the thirsty people when it was struck with a rod. Of this it is said: “The rock was Christ.”

This is not like the fatted calf that was slaughtered for a feast when the younger son returned. There the narrative itself is a figure, rather than a figurative interpretation of historical events; here, however, the event also took place in history, while that other matter had only been foretold in figures.

So too Wisdom—that is, Christ himself—is the tree of life in the spiritual paradise, to which he sent the robber from the cross. But a created tree existed in the bodily paradise to signify that tree of life. Nor did God wish man to live in paradise corporeally without the mysteries of spiritual realities being presented bodily.

There was therefore nourishment in the other trees; but in that tree there was a sacrament. What did it signify, except Wisdom, of whom it was said: “She is a tree of life to those who embrace her”—just as it might be said of Christ: “He is a rock flowing with water for those who thirst for him”?

I add this as well: although that tree supplied bodily food, it supplied such food as to strengthen the human body with stable health—not as other food does, but through some hidden inspiration of health-giving power. Indeed, ordinary bread too possessed something greater, by which God rescued one man from the need for food for a period of forty days with a single *collirida*.

It follows:

Now let us consider the tree of the knowledge of good and evil: why did it receive this name, since God created all things exceedingly good? We must recognize how great the distinction was between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience. If he transgressed by eating from it, it would be evil for him; but if he kept the commandment of his Creator, it would be good for him, since, had he not transgressed, he would not have learned through experience what punishment was.

## DISCIPLE

“And a fountain rose from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there it divides into four heads,” or into four parts. How is this to be understood?

## MASTER

Augustine.—Let no one be troubled by the fact that, concerning these rivers, some are said to have new sources and others entirely unknown ones, since what ought rather to be believed is that the place of paradise itself is far removed from human knowledge, and that four divisions of waters proceed from it, as the most trustworthy Scripture testifies.

But those rivers whose sources are said to be known may themselves have passed beneath the earth somewhere and, after traversing extensive regions, emerged elsewhere, where they were said not to be at their own sources. For who does not know that some waters commonly behave in this way?

Augustine likewise:

The river that proceeded from Eden—that is, from delights, pleasure, and feasting—is signified by the Prophet in the Psalm, where he says: “You will give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Psalm 35:9).

“It is divided,” he says, “into four parts,” and signifies the four virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.

It is called the Pishon; this is the Ganges. The Gihon is the Nile, as can also be observed in the prophet Jeremiah. Today these rivers are called by other names, just as the river now called the Tiber was formerly called the Albula. The Tigris and Euphrates, however, still retain the same names. Yet, as I have said, these names signify spiritual virtues, as the interpretation of the names themselves also shows, if one considers the Hebrew or Syrian language.

Thus Jerusalem, although it is a visible and earthly place, nevertheless signifies spiritually the city of peace. And Zion, although it is a mountain on earth, signifies contemplation; this name is frequently transferred in the allegories of Scripture to spiritual understanding. Likewise, the man who descended from Jerusalem to Jericho, as the Lord says, was wounded on the road and left by robbers injured and half-dead (Luke 10:30). Although these places are found on earth according to the historical account, the passage necessarily compels us to understand them spiritually.

Prudence, therefore, which signifies contemplation of truth itself, is beyond every human mouth, because it is inexpressible. If you wish to speak it, you give birth to it—or rather, you labor in childbirth more than you bring it forth—for the Apostle also heard there “inexpressible words which a human being is not permitted to speak.”

This prudence circles the land, which possesses gold, carbuncle, and *prasinus* stone: that is, it possesses the discipline of living, which, as though refined away from all earthly filth, shines like the finest gold; and truth, which no falsehood overcomes, just as the radiance of the carbuncle is not overcome by night; and eternal life, signified by the greenness of the *prasinus* stone, because of its verdure, which does not wither.

The river that circles the land of Ethiopia, exceedingly hot and burning, signifies fortitude, lively and tireless through the heat of action.

The third river, the Tigris, goes toward the Assyrians and signifies temperance, which resists lust, a powerful adversary of the counsels of prudence. Hence the Assyrians are often placed in Scripture as a symbol of adversaries.

The fourth river is not said to travel against anything or to circle any particular land. For justice pertains to every part of the soul, since it is the soul’s order and equity, through which these three virtues are harmoniously joined to one another: first prudence, second fortitude, third temperance—and justice is the established joining and ordering of them.

## Recapitulation Concerning Paradise, the Fountain, the Rivers, and the Tree of Life

Isidore:

“The Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning.” Paradise is the Church. For this is how it is read concerning her in the *Song of Songs*: “My sister is a garden enclosed.” Paradise is planted “from the beginning” because the Catholic Church is known to have been founded by Christ, the prince of all.

The river flowing out of paradise bears the image of Christ flowing from the Father’s fountain. He waters his Church with the word of preaching and the gift of baptism. Of this the Prophet fittingly says: “The Lord our God is a glorious river leaping forth upon thirsty ground.”

The four rivers of paradise are the four Gospels, sent out for preaching among all nations. The fruit-bearing trees are all the saints; their fruits are their works.

The tree of life is the Holy of Holies—namely Christ. Whoever stretches out his hand toward him will live forever.

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is free choice itself, placed in the middle for distinguishing good and evil. Whoever, having abandoned God’s grace, tastes from it shall die the death.

It follows:

“Therefore the Lord God brought the man and placed him in the paradise of delight, so that he might work it and guard it.”

## DISCIPLE

What, I ask, was he to work, and what was he to guard? Paradise, and nothing else?

## MASTER

This passage gives rise to a twofold interpretation. If man was to work paradise—that is, work at something in paradise—he worked not from the necessity of obtaining food but for pleasure. He had not yet sinned, and the earth had not yet brought forth thorns and thistles for him, so that he would eat his bread in the sweat of his face. This is what he deserved after sin.

Before sin, therefore, he worked paradise through cultivation not from want or necessity, but solely, as we have said, by his will; and he guarded it through discipline. He did not guard paradise against beasts or any animals, but guarded himself, lest through sinning he lose what he could have preserved by obeying.

Alternatively, God placed the man himself in paradise so that he might work and guard it: he was to work so that he might be good, and guard so that he might be safe. Whichever interpretation is adopted—whether man worked paradise through cultivation and guarded it through discipline, or God worked upon the man himself so that he might be good and safe—the passage has a reasonable meaning under either interpretation.

It follows:

“And the Lord God commanded him, saying: ‘You may eat from every tree of paradise, but you shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death.’”

## DISCIPLE

Augustine.—Since God threatened man with death on the day he touched the forbidden food, why did he not die on that same day, as Scripture says: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death”?

## MASTER

Holy Scripture very clearly shows that there are four deaths.

The first death is that of the soul, which abandons its Creator; for when it abandons him, it sins. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22). Here you have the dead, according to the soul, burying the dead, who are dead according to the flesh.

This statement therefore very clearly reveals two deaths: one of the soul and another of the body. The third belongs to the soul alone, which suffers it when it departs from this body. We read of this in the Gospel concerning the rich man: “Father Abraham,” said the rich man, “send Lazarus to me, so that he may cool my tongue with his finger, for I am being tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24).

The fourth death occurs when the soul receives the body again so that it may be cast into eternal fire. This accords with what the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the future judgment: “Go into the eternal fire,” and so forth (Matthew 25:11).

On the day, therefore, when Adam sinned, he died in his soul. For just as the body lives through the soul, so the soul, if it is to live blessedly, lives through God. Adam’s soul having died, he is rightly said to have died; from this first death three others subsequently followed. For the latter were to follow because the first had preceded: on the day Adam sinned, he died in his soul.

## DISCIPLE

How could Adam fear death, when he had no knowledge of it at all?

## MASTER

Just as we know the resurrection, although we have never experienced or seen it, so he knew death. He knew that when the soul leaves the body it produces death, and that when it returns to its body it produces resurrection. We know resurrection, although we have never experienced it; so too he knew death—not yet through experience, but through knowledge.

He knew what it meant to live, and through the deprivation of life he certainly knew what death was. Darkness is known through the deprivation of light, and silence is known through the deprivation of sound; so Adam knew death through the deprivation of life.

It follows:

“God also said: ‘It is not good for man to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself.’”

## DISCIPLE

Augustine.—How is this to be understood?

## MASTER

Certainly, if I am asked for what purpose this helper ought to have been made, nothing else plausibly occurs to me except the procreation of children. The seed, for example, has a helper in the earth, so that a shoot may arise from both.

Nor do I see what could have prevented their having honorable marriage even in paradise, so that offspring might be generated from their seed without any restless ardor of lust and without any labor or pain of childbirth. This would not have been so that children might succeed their dying parents, but so that, while those who had begotten them remained in a certain stable condition of bodily form and drew bodily vigor from the tree of life planted there, those who were born might also be brought forth into the same condition. Then, when the appointed number had been completed, if all lived justly and obediently, they would be transformed into eternal life.

This may also be considered in the case of Enoch, who, having begotten children and pleasing God, did not die but was translated. Why, then, if Adam and Eve had lived justly and chastely begotten children, could the children not have succeeded them through translation rather than death?

Since this is so, why should we not believe that, before sin, they could have commanded their generative limbs for the procreation of children just as the soul, without any trouble and as though in accordance with the law of pleasure, moves the other limbs in any work? They could have commanded the limbs from which offspring arise by the same motion by which the feet are commanded when walking, so that conception would occur without ardor and childbirth without pain.

But by transgressing the commandment they deserved to have in their limbs the movement of that law of death, which opposes the law of the mind. What punishment could be more just than that the body—the soul’s servant—should not obey every command, since the soul itself had refused to serve its Lord?

Therefore, after the Lord God had formed from the earth all the living creatures of the land and all the birds of heaven, he brought them to Adam, and so forth.

## DISCIPLE

Did God bring all the animals and all the birds of heaven to Adam in the same way that bird-catchers or hunters bring them to their nets? Or perhaps a voice of command came from a cloud, which they understood as though they possessed rational souls, and, having heard it, nevertheless listened?

## MASTER

The animals and birds did not receive this capacity so as to be capable of reason, by which they could obey their Creator. Yet within their own kind they obey God—not through the rational judgment of the will, but because he moves all things at suitable times without himself being moved temporally.

He moves himself without time and place; he moves created spirit without place but temporally; he moves bodily creation temporally and locally. Substance precedes that which is moved only temporally; judgment, therefore, precedes that which is moved neither temporally nor locally.

That which is moved temporally—that is, created spirit—moves itself through time without place; the body is moved through time and place. The creating Spirit, however, moves himself without time and place.

Thus the rational spirit in human beings—and likewise the irrational spirit—and sight are moved. But the rational spirit possesses understanding, by which it can judge whether sight consents or does not consent. Animals and birds, however, did not receive this judgment; nevertheless, according to their kind and nature, they are impelled when touched by some visual stimulus.

Thus the angelic nature, fulfilling God’s command, moves the perceptions of every kind of living creature, leading each where it does not know. If human beings can tame certain kinds of animals so that they seem to carry out some human wishes, how much more can angels do so?

## DISCIPLE

What causes God, whom you assert to be moved, not to be moved in time? And what causes created spirit, which is moved in time, not also to be moved in place?

## MASTER

The Lord, who established time and exists before time, has nothing in him that is past or future, no new plan and no new thought. For if something new and additional were present in him, then something would have been added to God, and he would no longer be immutable.

God is therefore unchangeable: nothing is added to him, there is no new thought and no new plan. For this reason he is not moved in time.

Created spirit, such as that of the angels, although it contemplates God’s eternity and glory without time, is rightly believed to be moved in time because it fulfills God’s commands in lower things within time. Their bodies descend from heaven to be moved into a place and ascend into heaven.

The spirit of human beings is moved in time by remembering the past, awaiting the future, and learning certain new things. For when I recall some reading or some city, my spirit is moved by thinking in such a way that it remembers these things in time; but it is not thereby moved in place.

If it is moved in place, is it moved in heaven or on earth? For there is no place apart from heaven and earth. Where, then, was the spirit itself—in heaven or on earth—when it saw that reading or that city?

Therefore, if it saw it in no place in order to remember it, it saw it within itself. And because it has a beginning, thought is everything that has a beginning and time.

Accordingly, according to the reasoning stated above, created spirit can be moved through time but not through place; the creating Spirit moves without time or place; the body moves through both time and place.

It follows:

“Therefore the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam and took one of his ribs,” up to: “She shall be called Woman, because she was taken from her man.”

### Jerome

“And the Lord God sent an ecstasy upon Adam”—for *ecstasy*, that is, an excess or departure of mind, the Hebrew has *thardema*, which Aquila interpreted as καταφοράν (*kataphoran*), and Symmachus as κάρον (*karon*), that is, a heavy and profound sleep. Accordingly, it follows: “And he slept.” The same verb is used of the sleep of Jonah when he was snoring. It follows:

“This now is bone from my bones, and flesh from my flesh.” [Col. 0272D] “She shall be called woman, because she was taken from man.” It does not appear in Greek or Latin why she should be called *woman* because she was taken from *man*; but the etymology is preserved in the Hebrew language. For a man is called *’îš* (*Is*), and a woman *’iššāh* (*Issa*). Hence Symmachus wished beautifully to preserve the etymology even in Greek, saying: “She shall be called *andris* [ἀνδρίς], because she was taken from her man [ἀνήρ].” In Latin we can say: “She shall be called *virago*, because she was taken from man.” Theodotion, however, suspected another etymology, saying: “She shall be called *assumption*, because she was taken from man.” For *Issa*, according to the variation of the accent, can also be understood to mean “assumption.”

### Augustine

But if one asks about the woman who had previously been made, what that causal condition was like—whether she already possessed this feature, so that it was necessary according to it for a female to be made from the man’s side, or whether she possessed only the possibility of being made in this way, while the necessity that she should be made so was not already established in creation but was hidden in God—let me say what seems to me the case. All these natures have their customary courses: from certain natural laws of their own, existing as it were in the beginnings of things, everything that is generated takes its rise and development at its proper time, together with the ends and declines proper to each kind. Thus wheat does not grow from a grain of bean, nor an animal from a human being.

Above this natural movement and course of things, the Creator’s power retains within itself the ability to make something other than what their quasi-seed principles contain. The principles of these and similar modes exist not only in God but were also implanted and consolidated by him in created things. Thus, for a piece of wood cut from the earth—dry, polished, without any root, soil, or water—to blossom suddenly and produce fruit: God indeed gave natures, which he created, the capacity for even such things to arise from them. Yet he also gave it in another manner, so that they would not possess these things in their natural process, but in the process by which they had been created in such a way that their nature would thereafter be more fully subject to his will.

God therefore has hidden within himself the causes of certain acts of creation, which he did not insert into created things. [Col. 0273B] There too is grace, through which sinners are saved. For as regards an evil nature corrupted by its own will, it has no means of returning by itself, but only through God’s grace. For this reason the Apostle called the mystery of this grace hidden not in the world but in God, who created all things.

Consequently, whatever was done to signify this grace—not by the natural movement of things but miraculously—also had its causes hidden in God. If one such thing was that the woman was made from the man’s side, and from the side of a sleeping man, then the original condition of things, when on the sixth day it was said, “He made them male and female,” did not contain that the female must be made in precisely this way, but only that it could happen in this way. Otherwise God would be doing something contrary to the causes he had established by his will, through a changeable will. That it would happen, and that something entirely different would not happen instead, was hidden in God, who created all things. [Col. 0273C]

### Augustine, On the Soul of Woman

Scripture has related how the woman was made from flesh. But it was silent about the soul, making us all the more attentive, so that by this fact those who believe that the soul comes from the soul of man—just as flesh is made from flesh by parents for their children, through the seeds of both things being transmitted—might be refuted, or might not.

For from this they are first moved to say that God made one soul, which he breathed into the face of the man whom he had formed from dust, and that from it the remaining souls of human beings are then created, just as all human flesh also comes from that man’s flesh. This suspicion is easily met. If they think that the woman’s soul was made from the man’s soul because it is not written that God breathed into the woman’s face, why do they believe that the female soul likewise came from the man, when not even that is written?

Let us first hold most firmly that the nature of the soul is not transformed into the nature of the body, so that what was already a soul becomes a body; nor into the nature of an irrational soul, so that what was the soul of a human being becomes that of an animal; nor into the nature of God, so that what was a soul becomes what God is. It should also be no less certain that the soul is nothing other than a creature of God.

Let us now consider whether the following passage confirms one position alone, or whether what is written can be accommodated to both: “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12).

For from these words of the Apostle those who defend the propagation of souls attempt to establish their position in this way. “If,” they say, “sin, or the sinner, can be understood as referring only to the flesh, we are not compelled by these words to believe that the soul comes from parents. But if, through whatever enticement of the flesh, it is nevertheless only the soul that sins, how should we understand the words ‘in whom all sinned,’ unless the soul too was propagated from Adam, just as the flesh was?”

It is indeed written most truly and most faithfully: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V, 17). Yet I think no one, learned or unlearned, doubts that the flesh cannot desire without the soul. Therefore the cause of carnal desire is not in the soul alone, but still less is it in the flesh alone. It arises from both: from the soul, because without it no pleasure is perceived; from the flesh, because without it the pleasure of the flesh is not perceived.

When the Apostle says that the flesh desires against the spirit, he unquestionably means the carnal pleasure which the spirit experiences from and with the flesh, opposed to the pleasure which it experiences by itself. For when the spirit commands the bodily members to serve a desire with which it alone is inflamed—as when a book is taken up for writing, reading, discussing, or listening—or when bread is broken for a hungry person, the flesh displays obedience; it does not arouse desire.

When something opposes those and similar desires by which the soul alone desires, and which nevertheless gives that same soul pleasure according to the flesh, then the flesh is said to desire against the spirit. Those who have been placed under grace struggle against this sin, not so that it may not exist in their body—for it belongs to mortal life, and is judged as something dead—but so that it may not reign. It does not reign when its desires are not obeyed.

According to this view, we neither say the utterly absurd thing that the flesh desires without the soul, nor agree with the Manichaeans, who, seeing that the flesh cannot desire without the soul, supposed that the flesh possessed another soul from another nature opposed to God. Nor are we compelled to say that Christ’s grace is unnecessary for any soul.

### DISCIPLE

When it is said to us, “What has the soul of an infant deserved, so that it is harmful for it to depart from the body without receiving baptism?”

### TEACHER

The reply is that God gives new souls individually to human bodies so that, by living rightly from flesh that comes from sinful flesh and original sin, and by subduing carnal desires under God’s grace, they may acquire merit by which they may be transferred, together with the body itself, to a better state at the time of the resurrection.

Yet it is necessary that, when they are joined in a remarkable way to earthly and mortal members—especially members propagated from sinful flesh—they should first give them life and later, as age advances, govern them, as though they were weighed down by forgetfulness. If this forgetfulness were in some manner indigestible, it would be attributed to the Creator. But when the soul gradually recovers from the period of this forgetfulness, what harm is there in its being, as it were, briefly immersed in sleep, from which it may gradually awaken and emerge into the light of understanding?

Before it can live according to the spirit through maturity of age, however, it needs the sacrament of the Mediator, so that what it cannot yet accomplish through his sacrament and faith may be accomplished through those who love it.

“What, then,” someone says, “if its family does not take care of this, whether through unbelief or negligence—will that perhaps do no harm? What benefit, then, is there for the one who is assisted?”

I confess that I have not yet heard, or read anywhere, what those who attempt to assert, according to the Holy Scriptures—or according to what is found in them, or what is not contrary to them—that new souls are given to bodies not drawn from their parents, could answer on their own behalf. But even if those who affirm the transmission of souls should prevail—not by disputing but by proving their case—it still would not follow that Christ’s soul should also be believed to have come through the transmission of that transgressor.

For although Christ’s body was taken from the flesh of a woman who had been conceived from that propagation of sinful flesh, nevertheless he was not conceived from her in the same way in which she had been conceived. Nor was he himself sinful flesh, but the likeness of sinful flesh.

Finally, if I am asked from where Christ Jesus received his soul, I would certainly prefer to hear better and more learned men on the matter; yet, according to my own capacity, I would more willingly answer: not from Adam, but from where Adam came—that is, from God.

There is a passage in the Epistle written to the Hebrews that deserves careful consideration. When the priesthood of Christ was distinguished from the priesthood of Levi through Melchizedek, in whom a figure of this matter had gone before, the text says: “See how great this man is, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth from the first fruits” (Heb. VII, 4).

Christ was not tithed there in the person of him whose flesh derived from that source not the heat of a wound but the material for a remedy. For since that tithing belonged to the prefiguring of the remedy, what was being tithed in Abraham’s flesh was what was being healed, not what effected the healing.

The same flesh belonged not only to Abraham but also to the first earth-born man himself; it contained both the wound of transgression and the medicine for the wound. The wound of transgression was in the law of the members; the medicine for the wound was in that which was taken from there, without the act of desiring, from the Virgin, for the sake of sharing death without sin and providing an example of resurrection without falsehood.

At this point they may perhaps say: “Just as he could be present there according to the flesh and yet not be tithed, why could he not also be present according to the soul without being tithed, since in bodily seed there can be an invisible power that arranges numbers incorporeally, to be distinguished not by the eyes but by the understanding from that corporeal mass which is perceived by sight and touch?”

But why should I labor over a matter that cannot be persuaded by words to anyone unless he possesses an intellect of such a kind and extent that he can anticipate the effort of the reader without even waiting for the whole argument? I shall therefore briefly gather the point: if what we said could happen with the flesh could also happen with the soul, then perhaps Christ’s soul has been understood, and is transmitted, in such a way that it did not draw the stain of transgression along with it.

But if it could come from that source without this guilt, then the question of the arrival of the other souls—whether they come from parents or from above—does not thereby receive an answer. Let those who can prevail do so. I still waver between both positions, and at one time am moved in one direction, at another in the other, provided only that I do not accept that the soul is either a body or some bodily quality or conjunction—if it should be called that—which the Greeks call *harmonia* (ἁρμονία).

I earnestly admonish you to consider, with the Lord helping my mind as far as I can, that I would not believe anyone who chatters about these matters. If some have been preoccupied by the opinion that souls are propagated from parents, let them consider themselves as best they can, and meanwhile understand that their bodies are not their souls. For no nature is closer by which God can be conceived incorporeally than the nature made in his own image; and nothing is nearer than that one who believes the soul to be a body should also believe God to be a body.

### DISCIPLE

Was it necessary for Adam, since he needed a wife, that she could not be made in any other way than by removing a rib from him while he slept, from which his wife would be built?

### TEACHER

She could have been made in another way, but he judged it more fitting that she should be made in this way, so that something might be signified by it. For just as a rib is removed from the sleeping Adam and made into a wife, so also, when Christ dies, blood is poured from his side so that the Church may be built. By sharing in the body and blood of Christ, the Church becomes Christ’s wife.

### DISCIPLE

It follows. What does Adam’s statement mean: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh”? And blessed Paul the Apostle, when he cited this passage, explained it by saying: “This mystery is great; but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church” (Eph. V, 32). But how did he leave the Father, since he is of one substance with the Father? Or where could the Father be without the Son, since the Son himself is called Wisdom, who “reaches mightily from end to end and disposes all things sweetly”?

### TEACHER

If the Son is there where the Father is, then the Father cannot be without the Son, nor the Son without the Father; for just as they are inseparable in nature, so they are separable in persons. Thus the Son himself says of the Father in the Gospel: “He who sent me is with me” (John VIII, 29).

How, then, does he leave the Father and cling to his wife, that is, to his Church, except in the manner described by the Apostle: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 6)?

That form, therefore, is the taking of servile condition, or the emptying of himself, although it is not an abolition of divinity or a loss of nature. Nevertheless, because of the form of a servant in which he is recognized to have appeared, he is rightly said to have left the Father.

He also left his mother, namely, the Synagogue, which clung carnally to the Old Testament; and he clung to his wife, that is, to the Church, so that through the peace of the New Testament the two might be one flesh. It follows.

### Ambrose

“And Adam and his wife were naked, and they were not ashamed.” It is entirely true: the bodies of the two human beings living in paradise were naked, and they were not ashamed. For what would have caused shame when they had felt no law in their members resisting the law of their mind—the law that followed them as a punishment for sin after their transgression, when disobedience seized what had been forbidden and justice punished what had been committed?

Before this occurred, they were naked, as has been said, and they were not confused; there was no movement in the body to which shame was due. They thought nothing needed to be covered because they had felt nothing that needed to be restrained. How they were going to propagate children has already been discussed. Yet it must not be believed that they would propagate them in the same way after the crime had been committed and the aforementioned punishment had followed, when, even before they died, death had already been conceived and was moving through the bodies of disobedient human beings in the most just reciprocal action of disobedient members.

“But the serpent was more cunning than all the living creatures of the earth that the Lord God had made. He said to the woman: ‘Why did God command you?’” and so forth.

### DISCIPLE

### Augustine

How could the serpent speak in paradise, when it is evident to some that it is an irrational animal?

### TEACHER

The serpent could not speak by itself, nor did it assume this ability because it had received it from the Creator. Rather, the devil used it, as though it were an instrument through which he might emit articulate sound. Through it he spoke the words, although even the serpent itself did not know this.

Thus a nature lacking reason is subjected to a rational nature; yet the latter does not do everything it wishes with or through it, but only as much as it has received from God.

### DISCIPLE

And if serpents do not understand, how do they hear the words of the Marsi, so that they come out of their caves at their incantations?

### TEACHER

Although they lack understanding, they are by no means without bodily sensation. They possess sight, hearing, taste, and smell; and therefore, although they hear the words of the Marsi, they certainly do not understand them. They do not obey through understanding; rather, so that they may come out of their caves at the words of the Marsi, they are compelled by the devil, with God’s permission. Hence testimony is given concerning that first event: the devil deceived the first human being through a serpent in paradise.

### DISCIPLE

### Ambrose

Why did he permit him to be tempted through this animal?

### TEACHER

It is not surprising that he was tempted through the serpent, through which the devil was prefigured, since that ancient enemy possesses a most wicked will but a most justly limited power. He always has the will to do harm, but he has no power to inflict harm without God’s permission.

### DISCIPLE

Why did he permit him to tempt the one whom he foreknew would consent?

### TEACHER

### Ambrose

I shall say what he grants me to understand or permits me to say. It does not seem to me that the human being would have deserved great praise if he could live rightly for the reason that no one persuaded him to live wrongly, since he had both the natural capacity and the power of willing not to consent to the one who persuaded him.

Why, then, would he not permit the one whom he foreknew would consent to be tempted, since he would do so by his own will and through guilt, and would be ordered by God’s justice through punishment?

Some are nevertheless troubled by this temptation of the first human being, because God permitted it to occur, as though they did not now see the entire human race being ceaselessly tempted by the devil’s ambushes. Why does God permit this also? Is it not because virtue is tested and exercised, and because the palm is more glorious when one does not consent after being tempted than when one cannot be tempted?

### DISCIPLE

Again, the same as above. “He should have made,” they say, “a human being who would not wish to sin at all.”

### TEACHER

We grant that the nature which would not wish to sin at all is better. Let them also grant that the nature which was made able not to sin if it wished is not evil. The former is found in the holy angels, the latter in holy human beings.

Those who chose the side of wickedness and corrupted an admirable nature by a blameworthy will ought not, merely because they were foreknown, to have been left uncreated. For God does not need the righteousness of any upright person, much less the wickedness of a perverse one.

When sound reasoning demonstrates two goods that are not equal—one higher, the other lower—those dull of heart do not understand that by saying both must be of the same kind they are saying nothing exists except the one. Thus, when they wish to make kinds of goods equal, they diminish their number.

Who would listen to them if they said: “Since the sense of sight is more excellent than that of hearing, there should be four eyes and no ears”? Yet they might say, “If God had wished it, these too would have been good.” How much better did God will that they should be what they wished to be: good without fruitlessness, but evil without impunity.

“But he foreknew that their will would be evil.” Certainly he foreknew it; and because his foreknowledge cannot be deceived, the evil will is not his but theirs.

### DISCIPLE

Why, then, did he create those whom he foreknew would become such?

### TEACHER

Because just as he foresaw that they would become evil, so also he foresaw what good he himself would bring about from their evil deeds. He made them in such a way that they would be an instrument of training for others and an example of fear.

“Then,” they say, “there is something in God’s works that needs another’s evil in order to advance toward good.”

Have human beings become so hardened and blinded—by I know not what zeal for contention—that they neither hear nor see that when some are punished, very many are corrected? What pagan, what Jew, what heretic does not daily prove in his own household the discipline imposed upon them through the work of divine providence?

“Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills.” He foresaw that some would be good, and he created them; he foresaw that some would be evil, and he created them. Offering himself to the good for their enjoyment, and bestowing many of his gifts even upon the evil, he seeks nothing for himself; nor does he derive advantage from the works of the good, while benefiting the good even through the punishments of the evil.

### Again

If it is asked why the devil was permitted to tempt through the serpent, it should not be surprising, since Christ himself permitted demons to enter the pigs.

The nature of the devil itself is more often examined with anxious scruple. Certain heretics, offended by the trouble caused by his evil will, attempt to remove it from the creation of the highest and true God and to assign to it another beginning opposed to God.

They cannot understand that everything which exists, insofar as it is some substance, is good, and cannot exist unless it comes from that true God from whom every good comes. Evil, however, consists in the will’s moving disorderly, preferring lower goods to higher ones. Thus it came about that the spirit of a rational creature, delighted by its own excellence and exercising its own power, swelled with pride; through pride it fell from the blessedness of the spiritual paradise and wasted away through envy.

Nevertheless, there is a good in the very fact that it lives and gives life to a body—whether an aerial body, as in the spirit of the devil himself or of demons, or the soul of a human being, even one who is malicious and perverse.

Some say that the devil himself fell from the heavenly abodes because he envied the human being made in God’s image. But envy follows pride; it does not precede it. Envy is not the cause of pride; pride is the cause of envy.

Since pride is love of one’s own excellence, while envy is hatred of another’s happiness, it is sufficiently clear which arises from which. By loving his own excellence, a person envies either those who are equal to him, because they become his equals, or those who are superior, because he does not become their equal. A person is therefore envious by being proud, not proud by being envious.

The prophet called him “the beginning of the Lord’s creation,” because God made him to be mocked by his angels—not because he created him first, but because, knowing that by his own will he would become one who harmed the good, he created him so that through him he might benefit the good.

For this is what “to be mocked by his angels” means: he is mocked when temptations, by which he tries to corrupt the saints, become beneficial to them. He was therefore the beginning of creation for the sake of mockery.

That the devil spoke through the serpent is taught by ordinary experience. For serpents, as was said above, are more moved by human songs than any other kind of living creature. This is no small testimony that human nature was first led astray through conversation with a serpent.

Demons are permitted to do this in order to preserve the memory of the first event, by which they acquire a certain familiarity with the human race.

### DISCIPLE

Could that temptation drive them out of paradise, or not?

### TEACHER

It must be understood that it could not have done so if they had not been lifted up into empty glory when their hostile enemy promised them, saying: “If you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods.” For it is written: “The heart is exalted before destruction” (Prov. XVI, 18).

### Isidore’s Recapitulation

That serpent, wiser than all the beasts, signifies the devil. He is called a serpent because he moves about with winding cunning.

But why was it through the woman that he deceived the man, and not through the man? Because our reason cannot be seduced into sin unless pleasure comes first, in the carnal affection of weakness, which ought rather to obey reason, as a woman obeys a husband who rules her. This is enacted in each human being within a certain hidden and secret marriage.

Let us understand the serpent as suggestion, the woman as the animal sense of the body, and the man as reason. Therefore, when an evil suggestion occurs, the serpent speaks, as it were. But if thought alone takes pleasure in it, and, with reason restraining it, consent to carrying out the act does not follow, the woman alone is seen to have eaten what was forbidden.

But if the mind itself also decides that the sin should be committed, then the man has been deceived, and the woman is seen to have given food to the man. To consent to enticement is to eat from the forbidden tree.

Then a person is rightly expelled from blessed life, as from paradise, and sin is imputed to him even if the act does not follow. For although guilt is not present in deeds, the conscience nevertheless retains it in consent.

This is according to the anagogical sense. According to metaphor, however, this cunning serpent can signify the craftiness of heretics. Some, with excessive and subtle talk, promise the opening and knowledge of hidden things through illicit curiosity, and in the human being himself—as in a tree planted in the middle of paradise—display that ignorance.

Against this serpent the Apostle cries out when he says: “I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted” (II Cor. XI, 3).

Our carnal desire is seduced by the words of this serpent, and through it the Christian Adam is deceived—not Christ. Thus this serpent says to the woman: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?”

So too the curious desire of heretics, and so too wicked preachers, inflame the carnal hearts of credulous hearers toward the pursuit of error, saying: “Why do you flee from possessing hidden knowledge? Always seek new things; penetrate the knowledge of good and evil.”

Hence the woman in Solomon, representing the type of heretics, says: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant” (Prov. IX, 17).

Then the same serpent added: “On whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will immediately be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

So too all heretics generally profess the attainment of divinity and are deceived by the promise of knowledge. They criticize those whom they find believing simply. And because they persuade people to carnal things, they try, as it were, to produce the opening of carnal eyes as well, so that the inner eye may be obscured.

It follows:

“Then the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and she took of its fruit” [Col. 0279C] “and ate.”

### Isidore

The woman ate first, not the man, because carnal people are more easily persuaded to sin, and spiritual people are not deceived so quickly.

It follows:

“And she gave it to her husband, and he ate.” This is because, after the pleasure of our carnal desire, our reason also is subjected to sin.

“And when they realized that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together and covered themselves.” Likewise, those who burn with the itching of carnal pleasure embrace the harshness of the world. Those who have been deceived by heretical perversity and stripped of God’s grace gather coverings of falsehood, like fig leaves, making themselves belts of perversity when they lie about the Lord or the Church.

As Gregory says: “After the sin of disobedience, Adam immediately covered his private parts, because after insulting God in spirit he immediately found an insult in the flesh. And because he did not wish to be subject to his Creator, he experienced the laws of the flesh that he governed, so that the confusion of his disobedience might rebound upon him, and, having been overcome, he might learn what he had lost by being elated.”

It follows:

### DISCIPLE

### Augustine

God brought all the animals and birds to Adam, and when he saw them, he gave them names. A little later it is said of the woman:

“Then the woman saw that the tree was good for food.” Behold, Scripture most clearly shows that the eyes of both were open. For it is not permissible to say that the first human beings had been made blind. Why, then, does the same Scripture shortly after touching the forbidden tree say: “The eyes of both were opened”?

### TEACHER

If their eyes had not been open, he would not have given names to the animals, nor would she have seen the beauty of the tree. It is true that their eyes were open; yet, unless they had been closed with respect to something, Scripture would never have said, “The eyes of both were opened.”

They were opened, namely, to nothing other than recognizing one another, so that there might be a law in their members resisting the law of the mind, and so that even in their members there might be a movement not subject to the will—a just vengeance, certainly, from God: the human being who had refused to be subject to God would not have a body subject to him.

Their eyes were therefore opened to this: that their members might be moved by desire.

It follows:

“And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise at the breeze.”

### DISCIPLE

### Augustine

“Adam and Eve his wife then hid themselves from the face of the Lord among the trees of paradise.” I ask you, therefore, explain what that walking of God means.

### TEACHER

Far be it from us to believe that the Trinity became corporeal or local because it is said to walk. Everything local is certainly a body, and every body is local. God, however, is incorporeal; he does not move bodily, is not confined by place, and is not transferred from one place to another.

His walking must be understood as having taken place through some creature. From the surrounding circumstances of Scripture, I recall that our predecessors understood this creature to have been a human being.

### Gregory

“When Adam heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise at the evening breeze, he hid himself among the trees of paradise.” Sometimes God speaks through angels both by words and by events, intimating through certain movements what he narrates in speech. For after his sin Adam could not see God in his divinity; rather, he heard words of rebuke through an angel.

### DISCIPLE

But we must ask what it means that, after the human being’s sin, the Lord no longer stands in paradise but walks.

### TEACHER

This plainly signifies that, when guilt invaded, he showed that he had moved away from the human heart. What does “at the evening breeze” mean, except that the warmer light of truth had departed and the coldness of guilt was constricting the sinful soul?

The first human being is found hiding after his sin at the evening breeze because he had lost the midday heat of charity. Now, under the shadow of sin, he languished as though in the coldness of a breeze. Of this same sinful human being it is written: “For he followed the shadow.”

He had lost the warmth of charity; the human being had abandoned the true sun and hidden himself under the shadow of inward cold. Hence the voice of that same Truth says: “Iniquity will abound, and the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV, 12).

Therefore he rebuked Adam while walking, so that he might reveal his wickedness to blind minds not only through words but also through events. Thus the sinful human being might hear through words what he had done; through the walking he might perceive, having lost the state of eternity, the instability of his mutability; through the breeze he might recognize his torpor after the heat of charity had been driven out; and through the sun’s decline he might understand that he was drawing near to darkness.

### DISCIPLE

The Lord called Adam and said: “Where are you?” What does it mean that after the fall the Lord asks Adam, “Where are you?” Did divine power not know to what hiding places the servant whom nothing escapes had fled after his sin?

### TEACHER

We must unquestionably believe that “all things are naked and open to his eyes.” Yet because he saw that Adam had fallen through guilt and was hidden under sin, as it were, from the eyes of Truth, and because he approves the darkness of Adam’s error, he acts as though he did not know where the sinner was, and calls and asks him, saying: “Adam, where are you?”
