By calling him, he gives a sign that he is recalling him to repentance; by asking him, he plainly indicates that he does not acknowledge sinners as those who are justly to be condemned. In this passage, therefore, let the despairing return to hope, since even the impious are summoned to hope for forgiveness.

Adam says: “I heard your voice, Lord, in paradise, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.”

The Lord says: “Who told you that you were naked, unless you ate from the tree from which I had commanded you not to eat?”

And Adam said: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate.”

### Gregory

It must be understood with the utmost care that sin is committed in the heart in four ways and completed in action in four ways.

In the heart it is committed through suggestion, pleasure, consent, and the boldness of self-defense. Suggestion comes through the adversary, pleasure through the flesh, consent through the spirit, and the boldness of self-defense through pride. Guilt, which ought to terrify the mind, lifts it up; and while casting it down, it raises it, but by raising it more grievously overthrows it.

Thus the ancient enemy broke the uprightness of the first human being with these four blows. As we said above, the serpent suggested, Eve took pleasure, Adam consented, and, when questioned, he refused through boldness to confess his guilt.

What happened in our first parent is also enacted daily in the human race. The serpent suggested, because the hidden enemy secretly proposes evil to human hearts. Eve took pleasure, because the carnal sense immediately submits itself with delight to the serpent’s words.

Adam, placed over the woman, gave his assent, because while the flesh is carried away into pleasure, the spirit too, weakened, is bent from its uprightness. When questioned, Adam refused to confess his guilt, because the spirit, separated from truth through sin, is hardened all the more wickedly in the boldness of its ruin.

Adam had fled in fear, intending to hide himself; yet when questioned he revealed how much he still swelled with pride even while afraid. For when present punishment is feared because of sin, while the lost presence of God is not loved, that fear arises from swelling pride, not from humility. [Col. 0281C]

Sin is likewise completed in action in four ways. First, hidden guilt is committed; afterward the offense is openly revealed before human eyes without shame; then it is made habitual; and finally it is nourished either by the seductions of false hope or by the wretched stubbornness of despair.

It follows:

And the Lord said to the woman: “Why have you done this?” She replied: “The serpent deceived me.”

**Gregory.**—They were questioned for this purpose: that, by confessing, they might erase the sin they had committed by transgression. Hence that serpent, the tempter who was not to be recalled to forgiveness, was not questioned about his guilt. The man was therefore asked where he was, so that after committing the offense he might come to his senses and, by confessing, acknowledge how far he had withdrawn from the face of his Creator. But both chose to provide themselves with the defenses of excuse rather than of confession. When the man wished to excuse his sin through the woman, and the woman through the serpent, they increased the guilt which they had attempted to defend. Adam indirectly blamed the Lord, since he himself had made the woman, while Eve referred the guilt back to the Lord, who had placed the serpent in paradise. For they had heard from the mouth of the deceiving devil, “You shall be as gods”; and because they could not become like God in divinity, they attempted, to complete their error, to make God like themselves in guilt.

Thus, while they tried to defend their guilt, they added to it, so that when examined their sin became more atrocious than it had been when committed. Hence even now the branches of the human race draw bitterness from this root. When someone is reproved for his conduct, he hides himself beneath words of defense as beneath the leaves of a tree, and, like someone seeking the shadowy recesses of an excuse, flees from the face of the Creator, unwilling that what he has done should be known. In this concealment he hides not himself from the Lord, but the Lord from himself. He acts so that he may not see the One who sees everything, not so that he himself may not be seen; for every sinner, the beginning of illumination is the humility of confession.

God also said to the serpent: “Because you have done this, you are cursed among all the living creatures and beasts of the earth. You shall walk upon your breast, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life. I shall put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel.”

**Jerome, in the Hebrew Questions.**—In Hebrew it is written thus: “You shall walk upon your breast,” that is, so that he might disclose the craftiness and deceitfulness of its thoughts, since all its steps would be wickedness and fraud. Further, where it follows, “You shall eat earth,” the Hebrew has *aphar* in place of “earth,” which we may render “ash” or “dust.” “She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel,” because our steps too are hindered by the serpent, and the Lord will swiftly crush Satan beneath our feet.

**Recapitulation.**—It is subsequently said to the serpent: “You shall be cursed among all living creatures; you shall walk upon your breast [Col. 0282B] and belly.” By the term “breast,” the pride of the mind is signified; by the term “belly,” as the Seventy translated it, the desires of the flesh are signified. By these two things the devil creeps upon those whom he wishes to deceive: either by earthly desire and lust, or by pride and senseless ruin.

“And you shall eat earth”—that is, those whom you deceive through earthly desire shall belong to you.

“All the days of your life”—that is, for the whole period during which you exercise this power, before that final punishment of judgment.

“I shall put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.” The devil’s seed is perverse suggestion; the woman’s seed is the fruit of a good work by which perverse suggestion is resisted. “She shall crush his head” if the mind excludes him at the very beginning of an evil suggestion. He lies in wait for her heel because he strives to deceive at the end the mind which he did not deceive by his first suggestion.

Some, however, understood the words “I shall put enmity between you and the woman” as referring to the Virgin from whom the Lord was born, since at that time the Lord was promised as one who would be born from her to conquer the enemy and destroy death, whose author he was. For what follows—“She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel”—is understood of the fruit of Mary’s womb, which is Christ: “You shall trip him up so that he may die; but he, rising victorious, shall crush your head,” which is death.

So David too had said, speaking in the person of the Father to the Son: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample upon the lion and the dragon.” By “asp” he meant death, by “basilisk” sin, by “lion” Antichrist, and by “dragon” the devil.

**Jerome, in the same book.**—“Multiplying, I shall multiply your sorrows and your groanings, and your turning shall be toward your husband.” In place of “sorrow” and “groaning,” the Hebrew has “pangs of conception”; and, “your association shall be with your husband.” In place of “turning,” Aquila translated “association,” while Symmachus translated “desire” or “impulse.”

**Elsewhere, Isidore.**—As for the punishment of the woman, what does the statement “In pain you shall bear children” signify, except that when carnal pleasure wishes to overcome some evil habit, it suffers pains at the beginning and thus, through a better habit, gives birth to a good work as to children? What he added—“Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you”—signifies that the carnal will which, amid pain, had struggled in order to form a good habit now, instructed by those very pains, becomes more cautious lest it fall; it obeys reason and willingly serves it as a wife serves a commanding husband. Thereafter she is called the mother of the living—that is, of rightly performed deeds—to which sins are opposed, since sins are signified by the name “the dead.”

But to Adam he said: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife more than to me,” and the rest. Then: “Cursed is the earth in your work; with labors you shall eat it all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the plants of the earth,” and the rest, up to: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go.”

**Jerome.**—“Cursed is the earth in your works.” Here “works” signifies not the cultivation of the soil, as many suppose, but sins. In Hebrew it reads so, and Aquila does not differ when he says: “Cursed is the ground because of you.” Theodotion likewise has: “Cursed is Adama in your transgression.”

**DISCIPLE.**

**Gregory.**—“Cursed is the earth in your work.” When the divine voice sets forth the dart of a curse, to be punished by a grave vengeance, so that it even closes the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, what does it mean that now, for the sinning man, the divine voice brings upon the earth the very thing that man is forbidden to do?

**MASTER.**

It must be understood that Holy Scripture speaks of a curse in two ways: one that it approves, and another that it condemns. One curse is pronounced by the judgment of justice, the other by the spite of vengeance. A curse pronounced by the judgment of justice was spoken against the first man when he sinned, as he heard: “Cursed is the earth in your work.” A curse by the judgment of justice is pronounced when God says to Abraham: “I shall curse those who curse you” (Gen. XII, 3).

Conversely, because a curse not pronounced by the judgment of justice but uttered in the spite of vengeance is condemned, we are admonished by Paul’s preaching voice, which says: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. XII, 14), and again: “Nor shall the cursers possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 10).

God, then, is said to curse, while man is forbidden to curse, because what man does out of the malice of vengeance God does only with the scrutiny and power of justice. Even holy men, when they pronounce a sentence of cursing, do not bring it forth from a desire for vengeance, but from the scrutiny of justice. Within themselves they perceive the subtle judgment of God and recognize which evils rising outwardly deserve to be struck by a curse; and they do not sin in that curse because they do not disagree with the inward judgment.

Hence Peter hurled a sentence of cursing against Simon, who offered him money, saying: “May your money be with you for destruction” (Acts VIII, 20). For by saying not “It is,” but “May it be,” he used not the indicative but the optative mood, thereby indicating what he meant. Hence Elijah said to the two captains of fifty who came to him: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you” (IV Kings I, 10). The outcome of the matter showed with what truth and reason each sentence was confirmed. Simon perished in eternal destruction, and the flame coming down from above consumed the two captains of fifty.

The subsequent power testifies that the mind was pressed by a sentence of cursing. For when the innocence of the one who curses remains intact, yet the curse consumes the one who is cursed even unto destruction, it is inferred from the end of both parties that the sentence was hurled against the guilty by one and inward judge.

**Isidore, as above.**—Now, through the sentence imposed upon the man, our reason is reproved. Seduced beforehand by the desire of sin and removed from the paradise of blessedness, it has the earthly works of the curse; it also has the pains of temporal cares, like thorns and thistles. Yet it is dismissed from the paradise of blessedness so that it may work the earth—that is, labor in this body—and establish for itself the merit of returning to the blessed life signified by the name “paradise.” Thus he may at some time stretch out his hand toward the tree of life and live forever.

The stretching out of the hand aptly signifies the cross or the torment of penitence, through which eternal life is recovered.

**Gregory.**—“You are earth, and into earth you shall go.” The first man was created in such a way that, while he remained, time would pass away, lest he himself pass away with time. He therefore stood amid moments as they ran onward, since he was in no way moving toward the end of life through the increasing succession of days. He stood more firmly the more ardently he clung to the One who stood above him.

But when he touched what had been forbidden, he immediately began, after offending the Creator, to pass away with time. Hence it was said to him: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go,” having lost the condition of immortality. The course of mortality swallowed him up; and as he was drawn from youth to old age, and from old age to death, by passing away he learned what it had meant to stand.

Because we are born from his stock, we retain the bitterness of the root as though in a young shoot. Since we derive our origin from him, we receive his course by being born, so that in the very daily moment in which we live we continually pass away from life, and the span of life which is thought to increase for us diminishes from the same source. Infancy passes into childhood, childhood into adolescence, adolescence into youth, youth into old age, and old age into death. In the course of the present life, through these very increases, we are driven toward decline, and we continually fail in the very direction in which we believe ourselves to be advancing through the extension of life.

We cannot have a fixed condition here, where we have come only to pass away. Nor could the first man have possessed this very daily passing from life before his guilt, because while he stood, time passed by; but after he sinned, he immediately found himself in a kind of collapse of his former state.

**Jerome.**—“And Adam called the name of his wife Eve, because she was to be the mother of all the living.” Eve is interpreted as “life,” or as “calamity.” Concerning her the poet sang:

> Eve was then a shining white dove, but afterward black,  
> Made poisonous by the serpent’s deceitful fraud;  
> She stained innocent Adam with filthy spots,  
> And the victorious dragon soon gave coverings of fig leaves to the naked.

The Lord God also made leather tunics for Adam and his wife, clothed them, and said: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now, therefore, see to it that he does not perhaps stretch out his hand and also take from the tree of life, eat, and live forever.”

**DISCIPLE.**

**Augustine.**—Since God is one, as Scripture says, “Hear, Israel: your God is one God” (Deut. VI, 4), how does he say here: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us”? For “us” indicates plurality.

**MASTER.**

Although God is one, he is nevertheless a Trinity: namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. “One of us” is said not because of a plurality of gods, but because of a plurality of persons. “Knowing good and evil” is as though he said: “Just as we know the difference between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience, so Adam now understands that he was not only made what he ought to become, but did not preserve even what he had been made.”

He also received a leather tunic by divine ordinance. In the historical sense, this commonly signifies the mortality of the body. In the allegorical sense, it signifies the pleasures withdrawn from carnal senses, which follow and cover the person living carnally under divine law, so that he might at some time be converted to God and might at some time stretch out his hand toward the tree of life—that is, toward Christ—and live forever.

And the Lord God expelled Adam from paradise so that he might work the earth from which he had been taken. Before the paradise of pleasure he placed the Cherubim and a flaming, turning sword to guard the way to the tree of life.

**Jerome.**—Not, as others suppose, that God made Adam himself, whom he had expelled, dwell opposite the paradise of pleasure; rather, after expelling him, he placed the Cherubim and the flaming sword before the gates of paradise to guard its entrance, so that no one might be able to enter.

**Isidore.**—Through the flaming sword—that is, through temporal tribulations—by acknowledging and mourning his sins; and through the Cherubim, that is, through the fullness of knowledge, which is charity, let him reach the tree of life, Christ, and live forever.

Again: “Cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge”; the turning sword placed to guard the way of the tree of life signifies, as we said above, temporal punishments. No one can reach the tree of life except through these two things: endurance of troubles and fullness of knowledge—that is, through love of God and neighbor. “The fullness of the law is love” (Rom. XIII).

Adam knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain; and again she bore his brother Abel (Gen. IV).

**Isidore.**—The birth of Adam’s two sons bears the likeness of two peoples who, at different times, were to come to the faith, equal in their works but unequal in their love before God. Abel was a shepherd of sheep, while Cain was a farmer. Concerning them the poet sang:

> God, by a distinct command, judges the sacred offerings of the two brothers,  
> Accepting the living and rejecting the earthly;  
> The farmer, driven by envy, strikes down the shepherd.

Our flesh is expressed in Cain’s offering as the image of the soul. Abel was a shepherd of sheep, as we have already said, and Cain a farmer.

After many days Cain offered gifts to the Lord from the fruits of the earth. Abel also offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat portions. The Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts, but he did not look upon Cain and his gifts. Cain became very angry, and his face fell (ibid.).

**DISCIPLE.**

**Jerome.**—How could Cain have known that God had accepted his brother’s gifts and rejected his own?

**MASTER.**

The interpretation given by Theodotion is therefore correct: “The Lord kindled fire upon Abel and upon his sacrifice, but upon Cain and upon his sacrifice he did not kindle it.” We read that fire customarily came from heaven to consume a sacrifice both at the dedication of the temple under Solomon and when Elijah built an altar on Mount Carmel.

**DISCIPLE.**

**Augustine.**—Why are Cain’s gifts from the fruits of the earth rejected, while Abel’s gifts from the fat portions of his flock are accepted?

**MASTER.**

Cain bore the type of the Jews, because they practiced bodily sacraments according to the Old Testament. With the arrival of faith in the New Testament, their sacrifices were rejected, while God accepted offerings from the sheep in innocence, which Abel signified. Hence in the psalm concerning the offerings of former times it is said: “You did not desire offerings and burnt offerings” (Ps. XXXIX).

**DISCIPLE.**

**Jerome.**—What does the Lord’s statement to Cain mean: “Why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be quiet; his turning is toward you, and you shall rule him” (Gen. IV)?

**MASTER.**

We are compelled by necessity to linger somewhat longer over individual points. For the sense in Hebrew is very different from that found in the translators of the Septuagint. God said to Cain: “Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? If you do well, is not every offense forgiven you? But if you do not do well, sin will sit before the doors, and its association will be toward you, and you shall rule it.”

This means: “Why are you angry, and, tormented by the bitterness of envy toward your brother, do you let your face fall toward the earth? If you do well, every offense will be forgiven you”—or, as Theodotion says, “It will be acceptable,” that is, “I shall accept your gift, just as I accepted your brother’s.”

“But if you do evil, sin will immediately sit before your entrance, and you will be accompanied by such a doorkeeper. Yet because you possess free choice, I warn you that sin must not rule you, but you must rule sin.”

The error in the translators of the Septuagint arose because “sin”—*athath* in Hebrew—is masculine gender, whereas in Greek it is feminine; and those who translated it rendered it in the masculine gender, as it was in Hebrew.

**DISCIPLE.**

**Gregory.**—How is the statement understood: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned”?

**MASTER.**

We offer rightly when we do something with a right intention. But we do not divide rightly if we do not carefully discern it. To divide rightly what has been offered is to weigh all our good efforts by discerning them carefully. Whoever neglects to do this sins even while offering rightly.

We therefore offer rightly when we perform a good work with good zeal; but we do not divide rightly if we postpone exercising discernment in a good work. Nor do we divide rightly if we neglect to distribute to our neighbors what we receive through God’s gift.

**DISCIPLE.**

**Augustine.**—“And Cain said to Abel: ‘Let us go outside.’ And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him” (Gen. IV). What does it signify that Cain killed his brother Abel in the field?

**MASTER.**

We have already said above that Cain signifies the Jews, who killed Christ, while Abel signifies Christ. Abel, the younger, is killed; Christ, the head of the younger people, is killed by the Jewish people, the elder. The former was killed in a field, the latter at the place of Calvary.

**Interpretation of Names.**—Cain is interpreted as “possession” or “lamentation”; Abel as “mourning” or “vanity,” or “vapor,” or “wretched.”

**Isidore.**—Then God asks Cain, not as one ignorant, but as a judge questioning the guilty whom he is about to punish, and says where his brother is. He replied that he did not know and that he was not his brother’s keeper. Even now, what do the Jews reply when we question them about Christ with the voice of these holy Scriptures? They answer that they do not know Christ.

Cain’s deceitful ignorance is the Jews’ false denial. They would in a certain sense be keepers of Christ if they had wished to accept and preserve the Christian faith. And he said to him: “What have you done? Behold, the voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth. Now, therefore, you shall be cursed upon the earth, which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand” (ibid.).

**DISCIPLE.**

How is it understood that Abel’s blood cried from the earth to the Lord?

**MASTER.**

Abel’s blood signifies the blood of Christ, which the whole Church receives and says: “Amen.” Consider for yourself what kind of cry the whole Church makes while it drinks Christ’s blood and says “Amen.”

The Jews, therefore, who are understood in the person of Cain because they do not believe in Christ and do not drink Christ’s blood, are cursed upon the earth—upon that earth, namely, which opened its mouth after confession and drank the blood of its brother, that is, of its Christ. Because the Jews do not drink it, they are cursed.

“Now, therefore, you shall be cursed upon the earth,” and the rest, up to: “Everyone who kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold” (ibid.).

**DISCIPLE.**

**Damasus to Jerome.**—What does the statement written in Genesis mean: “Everyone who kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance” (ibid.)?

**MASTER**

**Jerome to Damasus.**—Before we speak about the question, it seems appropriate to set out the editions of each translator alongside the Hebrew itself, so that the meaning of Scripture may be understood more easily:

*Vaiomer lo adonai lachen col horeg Cain, sibathaim iucam.*

Aquila: “And the Lord said to him: Therefore everyone who kills Cain shall be avenged sevenfold.”

Symmachus: “And the Lord said to him: Not so; but everyone who kills Cain shall be avenged in a hebdomad, or seven times.”

The Septuagint and Theodotion: “And the Lord said to him: Not so; but everyone who kills Cain shall pay seven acts of vengeance.”

After Cain had killed his brother, the Lord asked him, “Where is Abel your brother?” He replied insultingly, “I do not know; am I my brother’s keeper?” (ibid.) Therefore, condemned by the curse to live groaning and trembling, he did not wish to beg forgiveness. Instead, adding sins to sins, he thought the offense so great that the Lord could not forgive it.

Finally, he replied to the Lord: “My guilt is greater than that I should be forgiven” (ibid.), that is, “I have sinned more than I can suppose myself to be absolved.”

“Behold, you drive me out today from the face of the earth, and from your face I shall be hidden, and I shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth; and everyone who finds me will kill me” (ibid.).

“I am expelled,” he says, “from your sight. Trembling under the consciousness of my crime and unable to bear the light itself, I shall hide so as to remain concealed. Everyone who finds me will kill me.” This is according to the Septuagint edition.

This seems to us to be the meaning. As for what Aquila rendered “sevenfold,” and Symmachus “in a hebdomad,” or “seven times,” our predecessors hold the following opinion: they think that Cain was killed by Lamech in the seventh generation. Adam begot Cain; Cain begot Enoch; Enoch begot Irad; Irad begot Maviael; Maviael begot Mathusael; Mathusael begot Lamech, who was the seventh from Adam. According to what is written in a certain Hebrew volume, Lamech killed Cain unintentionally, as he himself later confesses:

> “For I killed a man for my wound,  
> and a young man for my bruise;  
> for vengeance shall be taken sevenfold from Cain,  
> but from Lamech seventy-sevenfold” (ibid.).

Some think that Cain was killed by Lamech in the seventh generation and, according to another interpretation, paid the penalty for his crime by living upon the earth groaning and trembling through all those generations.

I think nothing obscure remains, once he understands himself to have been agitated by bodily trembling and a maddened mind, as though the Lord were saying: “Everyone who kills you will release you from great torment.” It is not that the one who struck Cain would be subjected to seven acts of vengeance, but that the killer, by killing the one who had been left alive for punishment, would pay the seven acts of vengeance that had continued in Cain for so long.

It is as though the Lord were speaking to Cain: “You shall not die as you wish; rather, you shall be preserved alive for a long period. You shall live so unhappily in this light that whoever kills you will confer a benefit upon the one killed, by freeing you from so many tortures.”

Now, while we are engaged in another matter, something you had not asked about has entered our discussion: what are the seventy-seven acts of vengeance that must be paid in Lamech? They say that there are seventy-seven generations from Adam to Christ. Read Luke the Evangelist again, and you will find that what we say is so.

Thus, just as Cain’s sin was dissolved in the seventh generation—for the Lord will not avenge the same thing twice, and one who has received his evils once during life will not suffer in death the same torments he suffered in life—so Lamech’s sin, that is, the sin of the whole world and of the blood that was shed, is dissolved by the coming of Christ. He takes away the sins of the world (John I); he washed his garment in the blood of the grape (Gen. XLIX); and he alone trod the winepress (Isa. LXIII). Ascending red from Edom to heaven (ibid.), he offered the angels a spectacle as they cried:

> “Lift up your gates, O princes,  
> and the King of glory shall enter.  
> Who is this King of glory?  
> The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory” (Ps. XXIII).

A certain Hebrew told me that in their apocryphal books seventy-seven souls are found among Lamech’s descendants, and that they were destroyed by the Flood. In this number, he said, vengeance was exacted from Lamech, because his race endured until the cataclysm of the waters.

Elsewhere they speculate in various ways about Cain’s seven acts of vengeance. They assert that his first sin was that he did not divide rightly; the second, that he envied his brother; the third, that he acted deceitfully when he said, “Let us cross over into the field”; the fourth, that he killed his brother; the fifth, that he brazenly denied it, saying, “I do not know; am I my brother’s keeper?” (ibid.); the sixth, that he condemned himself, saying, “My iniquity is greater than that I should be forgiven” (ibid.); and the seventh, that even after being condemned he did not repent, unlike the Ninevites and King Hezekiah, who postponed the death hanging over them with tears, so that those who had been condemned might not perish but might obtain God’s mercy by practicing repentance.

They also say that the most merciful God prolonged his life until the seventh generation for this reason: so that, compelled at least by his very misfortunes and the sorrow of his long life, he might repent and deserve absolution.

Some interpret the number seven as full and perfect, gathering testimonies from many passages of Scripture. They say this is the meaning which we touched upon above: that whoever killed Cain would free him from an immense punishment extending through all his sufferings.

There are also those who repeat Peter’s question from the Gospel: “Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him—up to seven times?” (Matt. XVIII). Jesus says to him: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy-seven times” (ibid.). They think that death and sin kept sabbath in the seventh generation, when Enoch was taken up and was not found, because God translated him.

As for the seventy-seven, they follow the interpretation that at Christ’s coming the sting of death and sin was broken.

I shall add another opinion, lest I seem to have omitted anything. Some interpret the seventh year of remission, the fiftieth year of the jubilee, and the four hundred and ninetieth year—which they wish to be understood as seventy times seven—in many ways. They assert that for this reason the debtor of the Gospel is set in relation to the sacred numbers fifty and five hundred, and also the fiftieth psalm of repentance, which is completed in seven weeks and breaks forth at the beginning of the eighth.

But lest the discussion proceed too far, let it suffice to have spoken this far on the subject. From what we have found, you will be able to construct for yourself a vast forest of discussion, knowing that Origen composed his twelfth and thirteenth books on Genesis entirely about this question.

“Cain went out from the face of the Lord and dwelt in the land of Naid” (Gen. IV). The land is therefore not called Naid, as our common people suppose; rather, the sentence of God is fulfilled, that he wandered here and there as a fugitive and exile. In Hebrew it is called *Nod*, and it is interpreted as σαλευόμενος (*saleuomenos*), that is, “shaken,” “unstable,” and “of uncertain dwelling.”

**Recapitulation.**—God also said to Cain: “You shall be cursed upon the earth” (Gen. IV). There is no doubt that this passage clearly signifies the Jews, who, unwilling to be under grace but wishing to be under the law, were to be cursed and excluded from the Church, as the Apostle testifies: “For all who are of the works of the law are under a curse” (Gal. III).

It follows: “When you work the earth, it shall not give you its fruits” (Gen. IV). For in that very earth which Christ bore—that is, in his flesh—they worked our salvation by crucifying Christ, who died for our sins. Yet that same earth did not give them its power, because they were not justified by the power of his resurrection, who rose for our justification (Rom. IV). Although he was crucified in weakness according to our condition, he lives by the power of God (II Cor. XIII).

This, then, is the power of that earth which he did not reveal to the impious and unbelieving. Hence, when he rose, he did not appear to those by whom he had been crucified, as he did not appear to Cain working the earth, so that that grain might be sown.

“You shall be a wanderer and a fugitive” (Gen. IV), or, as it is written in the Septuagint, “You shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth.”

Now surely who would not see, who would not recognize, throughout the whole earth wherever that people has been scattered, how it is wandering among the nations and exiled from Jerusalem, how it groans after losing its kingdom and trembles in fear among innumerable Christian peoples?

Therefore he replied, saying: “My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve forgiveness. Behold, you drive me out today from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face; and I shall be a wanderer and a fugitive upon the earth. Everyone who finds me will kill me” (ibid.).

Truly, as a wanderer and fugitive, he groans and trembles lest, having lost his earthly kingdom, he also be killed by bodily death. He calls this a greater concern than the fact that our earth does not give its power, lest he die spiritually. For he has a carnal understanding and hides himself from the face of God; that is, he does not regard it as serious to have God angry with him. What he fears is that he may be found and killed.

He has a carnal understanding, like one who works the earth, although he has not received its power. “To set the mind on the flesh is death” (Rom. VIII), which he does not understand. Having lost his kingdom, he groans and fears bodily death.

But what did God answer him? “By no means will this happen; rather, everyone who kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold” (Gen. IV). Or, as the Septuagint translated it: “He shall pay seven acts of vengeance.” That is, he shall remove from them the seven acts of vengeance to which they are bound because of the guilt of Christ’s death, throughout this whole period which is more fully represented by the seven-day cycle. For it is sufficiently evident to faithful Christians that the Jewish nation has not perished, but has deserved dispersion alone, according to what Scripture says:

> “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law;  
> scatter them by your power, and bring them down” (Ps. LVIII).

**Recapitulation.**—The Lord placed a mark upon Cain, so that everyone who found him would not kill him (Gen. IV). This is truly marvelous: all the nations subjected by the Romans passed over into the rites of Roman sacrifices and accepted those sacrilegious practices for observance and celebration; but the Jewish nation, whether under pagan rulers or under Christian ones, did not lose the mark of its law and circumcision by which it is distinguished from the other nations and peoples. Rather, every emperor or king who found them in his kingdom found them with that same mark of theirs and did not kill them.

Cain therefore went out from the face of the Lord and dwelt in the land of Naid (ibid.). Thus Jews and all who are stubborn in various errors, resisting the truth, go forth as slaves from the face of God—that is, from the mercy of his love, or from participation in his light—and dwell as fugitives in the land of turmoil, that is, in carnal disturbance opposed to God’s joy, and therefore opposed to Eden, which is interpreted as “feasting,” where paradise was planted.

It follows:

“Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch; and Cain built a city, named after his son Enoch” (ibid.).

**DISCIPLE.**

What, then, does it signify figuratively that the offspring of the impious built a city at the very beginning of the world?

**MASTER.**

May your Charity know beforehand that you see the impious established in this life, while the saints are guests and pilgrims. Hence Abel, as a pilgrim on earth—that is, the Christian people—did not found a city. The city of the saints is above, although here it appears among those in whom it sojourns, until the time of its kingdom arrives.

**Repetition follows.**—This son, in whose name the city of Enoch was founded, signifies earthly Jerusalem; Enoch is interpreted as “possession.” This city has both a beginning and an end that are earthly, where nothing more than what is seen is hoped for.

It follows:

“Enoch begot Irad. Irad begot Maviael. Maviael begot Mathusael. Mathusael begot Lamech” (Gen. IV).

**Interpretation of Names.**—Enoch: dedication. Irad: descending, or strengthening. Maviael: “Who is the Lord God?” or “God from life.” Mathusael: the sending forth of death, or “he is dead,” and “he asked.” Lamech: humbled, or striking, or struck.

This Lamech took two wives. The name of one was Ada, and the name of the second was Stella. Ada is said to mean “testimony”; Stella, “her shadow.” Ada bore Jabel, who was the father of those dwelling in tents and of shepherds. Jabel means “departing,” or “changed,” or “flows away.” His brother’s name was Jubal. He was the father of those who play the cithara and the organ. His name is also interpreted as “carried away” or “departing.”

It follows:

**[Col. 0290A]** Lamech said to his wives Ada and Stella: “Hear my words, and listen to my speech. For I have killed a man by my wound, and a young man by my bruise. For vengeance shall be taken sevenfold from Cain, but from Lamech seventy-sevenfold” (ibid.).

It has already been said elsewhere according to the historical sense that seventy-seven generations are found from Adam to Christ, in which Lamech’s sin—that is, the sin of the whole world—was dissolved by the shedding of Christ’s blood.

Indeed, seventy-seven acts of vengeance were also established against the Jewish people because of Christ’s killing, in accordance with that Gospel passage in which the apostle Peter was told that forgiveness should be granted not merely seven times but seventy-seven times, if the brother repents (Matt. XVIII)—that is, that the returning Jew, after the seventy-seven established acts of vengeance, should be received into Christ’s forgiveness.

It follows:

“Again Adam knew his wife, and she conceived and bore a son; and she called his name Seth, saying: ‘God has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed’” (Gen. IV).

Hieronymus.—Seth is properly called *θέσις* (*thesis*), that is, “placing,” because God placed him in the place of Abel; therefore he is called Seth, that is, “placing.” Accordingly Aquila says: “And he called his name Seth, saying: ‘Because God has placed for me another seed.’”

Hieronymus continues.—“And Seth also had a son, whom he called Enos. He began to invoke the name of the Lord God” (Gen. IV). Just as Adam is interpreted as “man,” so Enos, according to the variations of the Hebrew language, means “man” or “male.” And fittingly he bore this name, since it is written of him: “Then there was a beginning of invoking the name of the Lord.” Although many think otherwise, namely, that at that time idols were first fashioned in the name and likeness of the Lord.

Recapitulation.—Seth is interpreted as “possession,” or “resurrection,” and he is Christ. His son Enos is interpreted as “man,” and he began to invoke the name of the Lord. What is this understood to mean? Because every human being who is a child of the resurrection lives in confession, as long as he journeys on earth, the matter of those two men, Abel and Seth, should not be passed over lightly: Abel is interpreted as “mourning,” while his brother Seth is “resurrection,” because in them the death of Christ and his life from the dead are prefigured. Therefore, to put it briefly: Abel is mourning, Seth resurrection, and Enos man, because after mourning comes resurrection, and from resurrection comes the human being who invokes God.

“Enos also fathered Cainan. Cainan fathered Malaleel. Malaleel fathered Jared. Jared fathered Enoch” (Gen. V). This Enoch, the seventh from Adam, who pleased God and was translated, signifies the seventh rest, to which everyone is transferred who, as on the sixth day—that is, in the sixth age of the world—is formed through the coming of Christ. For when six thousand years and the remaining periods that follow have passed, and judgment has taken place, heaven and earth having been renewed, the saints are transferred to the life of perpetual immortality.

This too should be noted: in the genealogy of Seth no woman born there is expressly named, whereas a woman is mentioned only in the genealogy of Cain. This signifies the earthly city, which until its end will possess a carnal generation arising from the union of husbands and wives.

**DISCIPLE.**

What, then, is the significance of the fact that through Seth the number ten, or rather twelve, is found from Adam to Noah, while in Cain the number eleven is found? I ask you to explain.

**MASTER.**

That number ten through Seth, from Adam to Noah, indicates the fulfillment in the Church of the commandments and of works according to the Law. When Noah’s three sons are added to this number, with the rejected one placed in the middle, the number twelve is completed. This number is distinguished in the figures of the patriarchs and apostles because of the parts of seven, one multiplied by the other. For three times four, or four times three, produces it.

But the fact that Adam’s genealogy through Cain ends with the number eleven reveals the transgression of the commandments, or sin. Since Lamech is found written as the seventh from Adam, three sons and one daughter are added to him so that the number eleven may be completed, thereby signifying sin. The number itself is closed by a female, and from that sex the beginning of sin was committed, through which we all die—namely, so that the pleasure of the flesh, which had resisted the spirit, might follow. Hence Lamech’s daughter herself is called Noema, that is, “pleasure.”

“This is the book of the generation of Adam. On the day when God created man, he made him in the likeness of God; male and female he created them, and he blessed them; and he called their name Adam, on the day when they were created” (ibid.). Here too, and where Matthew’s Gospel says, “The book of the generation of Jesus” (Matt. I), it should be noted that this corruptible beginning looks toward the incorruptible beginning, where it says, “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ.” For he sets book against book and beginning against beginning, because it is written: “In the first *mari* [the reading is uncertain] you will crush his head, and in the last *mari* [likewise uncertain] his hind parts.”

**Hieronymus in the Hebrew Questions.**—“And he called their name Adam,” that is, “man.” The name “man” applies both to male and female. “Adam lived two hundred and twenty years and fathered one according to his likeness and image, and he called his name Seth.” It should be known that, down to the Flood, wherever our books say that someone fathered after two hundred years or more, the Hebrew has one hundred years, followed by the remaining years.

“But the days of Adam after he fathered Seth were seven hundred years” (Gen. V), because they had erred in the two hundred. Consequently, seven hundred is given here, whereas in the Hebrew it has eight hundred, in addition to the one hundred above.

“And Mathusala lived one hundred and seventy-seven years and fathered Lamech. And Mathusala lived, after he fathered Lamech, eight hundred and two years. And he fathered sons and daughters. And all the days of Mathusala that he lived were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died” (ibid.).

**DISCIPLE.**

There is a famous question, debated throughout all the Churches: according to careful calculation, Mathusala is reported to have lived fourteen years after the Flood. For when Mathusala was one hundred and sixty-seven years old, he fathered Lamech. Again, when Lamech was one hundred and eighty-eight years old, he fathered Noah. Thus, up to the day of Noah’s birth, Mathusala’s years of life total three hundred and fifty-five. But the Flood occurred in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life. Consequently, when the calculation is made in its parts, the Flood is proved to have occurred in the nine hundred and fifty-fifth year of Mathusala’s life. Since he is said above to have lived more than nine hundred and sixty-nine years, there is no doubt that he lived fourteen years after the Flood. How, then, is it true that only eight persons were saved in the ark?

**MASTER.**

It remains, then, that here too, as in many other passages, there is an error in the number. For I find it written thus in the Hebrew and Samaritan books:

“Mathusala lived one hundred and eighty-seven years and fathered Lamech. And Mathusala lived, after he fathered Lamech, seven hundred and eighty-two years, and fathered sons and daughters. And all the days of Mathusala were nine hundred and sixty-nine years. And he died. And Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years and fathered Noah.”

From the day of Mathusala’s birth, therefore, to the day of Noah’s birth, there are three hundred and sixty-nine years. Add Noah’s years to these, since the Flood occurred in the six hundredth year of his life. Thus it follows that Mathusala died in the nine hundred and sixty-ninth year of his life, in the very year when the Flood began.

This Mathusala is the son of Enoch, who is seventh from Adam in the genealogy of Seth, who walked with God and was not seen, because God took him. Concerning this Enoch the poet also sang:

> Enoch first, even unto chaos, by his vigorous merits,  
> Through many ages already attained innumerable years;  
> Nature losing her bounds, whom the earth rightly bore  
> As one begotten, but whom death marvels to have taken away.

Mathusala fathered Lamech, whom we have already mentioned above. This Lamech represented the figure of this world, whose sin Christ absolved through the shedding of his blood after seventy-seven generations of the world, as the evangelist Luke writes.

This Lamech fathered a son and called his name Noah, saying: “This one will give us rest from our works” (ibid.). Noah is interpreted as “rest.” Because through the Flood all the works that had previously been performed under him came to rest, he was called “rest.”

When Noah was five hundred years old, he fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth. And when human beings had begun to multiply upon the earth and had fathered daughters, the sons of God, seeing the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.

**Hieronymus.**—“The sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were good” (Gen. VI). The Hebrew word *Elohim* is common in number, and “God” and “gods” are likewise called by it. Therefore Aquila, understanding “holy ones” or “angels” as gods, ventured to say in the plural: “the sons of gods.” “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst God judges” (Ps. LXXXI). Symmachus, following this interpretation, likewise says: “The sons of the powerful saw the daughters of men,” and so forth.

Many maintain that those born from the lineage of Seth were called sons of God because he began to invoke the name of the Lord. For just as the prophet, prophesying, called John the Baptist an angel: “Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Mal. III), and so forth, so in this passage we understand the sons of God, or angels, to be righteous men, born of a righteous stock but having fallen into sin. Another prophet likewise calls priests angels.

**DISCIPLE.**

**Hieronymus.**—“The Lord God said: ‘My spirit shall not remain in these men forever, because they are flesh’” (Gen. VI). In Hebrew it is written: “My spirit shall not judge these men forever, because they are flesh.” How is this to be understood?

**MASTER.**

It means that the human condition is frail: “I will not preserve them for eternal punishments, but here I will repay them according to what they deserve.” Therefore the passage expresses not severity, as it is read in our books, but God’s clemency, since the sinner is visited here for his crime.

Hence, in anger, God also says to certain people: “I will not visit their daughters when they have committed fornication, nor their brides when they have committed adultery” (Hos. IV). And in another place: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges; nevertheless I will not remove my mercy from them.”

It continues: “And their days shall be one hundred and twenty years” (Gen. VI).

**DISCIPLE.**

If human life was shortened to one hundred and twenty years from that day, what is the meaning of the fact that many of the fathers are remembered as having lived two hundred, three hundred, or more years after the Flood?

**MASTER.**

Human life, then, was not shortened to one hundred and twenty years, as many mistakenly think; rather, that period was given to that generation for repentance. And lest God appear cruel because he had not granted sinners a place for repentance, he added: “Their days shall be one hundred and twenty years”—that is, for the performance of repentance (ibid.).

For we find that Abraham lived one hundred and seventy-five years after the Flood, and others lived longer. But because they disdained to repent, God did not wish to await the appointed time. Instead, shortening the period by twenty years, he brought on the Flood in the one-hundredth year designated for repentance.

Consider that Noah lived three hundred years after the Flood. From this it is clear that the one hundred and twenty years were given to that generation for repentance, and were not established as the limit of mortal life.

It continues:

“Now giants were upon the earth in those days. And afterward, when the sons of God went in to the daughters of men and they bore children for them, these were the giants, men renowned from of old” (ibid.).

In Hebrew it reads: “Fallen ones were upon the earth in those days,” that is, *Niphilim*. “And afterward, when the sons of gods went in to the daughters of men and they bore children for them, these were the mighty men, men renowned from the beginning.”

Instead of “fallen ones” or “giants,” Symmachus interpreted them as “violent men.” The name “fallen ones” is applicable to angels and to the children of the holy, as we said above.

It continues:

“And the Lord saw that the wickedness of men was great upon the earth, and that every thought of their heart was directed toward evil at all times; and it repented him that he had made man upon the earth,” and so forth, up to: “For I repent that I made them” (ibid.).

**DISCIPLE.**

**Gregory.**—What does it mean that the omnipotent God, who is bound by no mutability of human condition, and for whom being cannot cease to be, is described as having repented in time of his creation?

**MASTER.**

Very often in sacred language, just as the wise draw their speech from the wise men of the world, so now, for the benefit of humanity, God, the creator of human beings, assumes in himself the language of human emotion. Thus it is said: “It repented him that he had made man upon the earth,” although it is entirely certain that he who sees all things before they come to pass neither did anything in repentance nor repents.

Therefore, just as it is not surprising that spiritual beings often use the words of the flesh, so it is not surprising that the ineffable Spirit, the Creator of all things, should, in order to draw flesh toward understanding him, form within himself the language of the flesh.

It continues in the Book of Hebrew Questions:

“These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a just and perfect man in his generation; he walked with God” (Gen. VI). Jerome expressly says “in his generation,” to show that he was just not according to perfect justice, but according to the justice of his generation. “He walked with God,” that is, he followed his footsteps.

It continues:

“And the Lord said to Noah: ‘The end of all flesh has come before me. The earth is filled with iniquity because of them, and I will destroy them along with the earth. Make for yourself an ark of smoothed wood’” (ibid.).

And Jerome says: “Make for yourself an ark of squared wood.” Instead of “squared, bituminized wood,” we read in Hebrew: “Gathering, you shall make the ark, and you shall finish it above with a cubit.”

For “Gathering, you shall make the ark,” the Hebrew has: “You shall make the south side of the ark.” Symmachus interpreted this more clearly, saying *διαφανές*, that is, “transparent” or “lucid,” you shall make the ark, intending a window.

It continues:

“You shall make compartments in the ark,” and so forth, up to: “And the water subsided, and the fountains of the abyss and the floodgates of heaven were revealed” (Gen. VI–VIII).

Instead of “the fountains were revealed,” all the interpreters translated “were closed and stopped up.” And instead of what follows, “The water ceased upon the earth,” and so forth, it is written: “The waters returned from the earth, going and returning.”

Note, according to Ecclesiastes, that all waters and streams return through hidden channels to the womb of the abyss.

“After forty days Noah opened the door of the ark that he had made and sent out a raven; and it went out and did not return to him until the waters had dried up from the earth” (Gen. VIII).

Instead of “door,” “window” is written in Hebrew. Concerning the raven, the passage is otherwise expressed: “He sent out the raven, and it went out, going forth and not returning, until the waters had dried up from the earth.”

This is according to Jerome.

Recapitulation of the foregoing.—Noah, in all things and in all his actions, signifies Christ. Noah is interpreted as “rest,” and the Lord says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI).

Noah alone is found righteous among that people, and seven persons are granted to him on account of his righteousness. Christ alone is righteous and perfect, and the seven Churches are granted to him, because of the sevenfold Spirit illuminating them, as one Church.

The fact that Noah is saved through water and wood signifies the cross and baptism. For just as he and his household were saved through water and wood, so the household of Christ is healed through baptism and the passion of the cross.

Noah constructed the ark from imperishable wood; Christ builds the Church from human beings who will live forever. For that ark signified the Church, which floats upon the waves of this world.

The command that the same ark be made from squared wood sanctifies the stable life of the saints, prepared for every good work. For whichever way you turn it, a square stands firmly.

The fact that the ark’s timbers are joined with bitumen inside and outside signifies, in the structure of unity, the endurance of charity, so that the fraternal bond may not yield to scandals assailing the Church, whether from those who are inside or from those who are outside, and so that the bond of peace may not be dissolved.

Bitumen is an exceedingly hot adhesive. It signifies the ardor of love, which, through the great strength of fortitude, endures everything in order to preserve spiritual fellowship.

The ark is three hundred cubits long, so that six times fifty may be completed, just as the whole period of this world extends through six ages. In all of these Christ has never ceased to be preached: in the fifth age he was foretold through prophecy; in the sixth he was proclaimed through the Gospel.

The three hundred cubits may also signify the wood of the passion. For the numerical value of those letters displays the sign of the cross, through which those who become companions in Christ’s passion by baptism obtain the length of eternal life.

Its breadth extends to fifty cubits, as the Apostle says: “Our heart has been enlarged.” By what, unless by spiritual charity? Therefore he says again: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

On the fiftieth day after his resurrection Christ sent the Holy Spirit, by whom he enlarged the hearts of believers.

Its height rises to thirty cubits. This number is contained ten times in the three hundred cubits of its length, because Christ is our height. At the age of thirty he consecrated evangelical teaching, testifying that he had not come to destroy the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. V).

The Law is recognized in the ten commandments; therefore the ark’s length is completed by ten times thirty.

Noah himself is counted as the tenth from Adam. The ark, being six times as long as it is wide and ten times as long as it is high, displays the form of the human body, in which Christ appeared.

The length of the body, from the crown to the feet, is six times its breadth, which extends from one side to the other, and ten times its height. Its breadth is measured from the back to the belly, as when one measures a person lying on his back or face down. Thus the distance from the head to the feet is six times the distance from right to left, or from left to right, and ten times the height from the ground.

Thus the ark was made three hundred cubits in length, fifty in breadth, and thirty in height (Gen. VI).

Again, the fact that the same ark is gathered together and completed above in one cubit (ibid.) signifies that the Church, the body of Christ, is exalted and perfected when gathered into unity. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters.”

The fact that an entrance is made for it at the side signifies that no one enters the Church except through the sacrament of the remission of sins, which flowed from Christ’s opened side.

The fact that the lower parts of the ark are constructed with two and three chambers signifies that the Church gathers from all nations a twofold multitude, because of circumcision and uncircumcision, or a threefold multitude, because of the sons of Noah, whose descendants filled the world.

Therefore these lower parts of the ark are so called because in this earthly life there is a diversity of nations. But at the top we are all perfected into one, and this diversity is no longer present, because Christ is all things to all people, completing us in one cubit of heavenly unity.

The fact that every kind of animal is enclosed in the ark signifies that from all peoples and nations a congregation is formed in the Church. The sheet shown to Peter also signifies this: that clean and unclean animals are there, just as in the Church good and evil are present in the sacraments.

The fact that the clean animals are sevenfold and the unclean twofold does not mean that there are fewer evil people than good, but that the good preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Holy Scripture commends the Holy Spirit in a sevenfold operation: wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, and fear of the Lord (Isa. XII).

Hence the number of fifty days pertaining to the coming of the Holy Spirit is completed in seven times seven, which make forty-nine, with one added, because it is said: “Eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”

The wicked are represented by the number two because they are prone to schism and, in a certain way, are divisible.

The fact that Noah himself is counted as the eighth together with his household signifies that in Christ the hope of our resurrection appeared, because on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day of the Sabbath—he first rose from the dead. This day is the third from the Passion, but in the number of days that continually turns throughout all time, it is both the eighth and the first.

The fact that the Flood occurred seven days after Noah entered the ark signifies that we are baptized in the hope of future rest, which was signified by the seventh day.

The fact that, apart from the ark, all flesh that the earth sustained was destroyed by the Flood signifies that outside the fellowship of the Church, the water of baptism, although it is the same water, not only does not avail for salvation but rather avails for destruction.

The fact that it rained for forty days and forty nights signifies that every guilt of sins admitted against the ten commandments of the Law throughout the whole world—which is contained in four regions—is washed away through the sacrament of heavenly baptism.

Ten commandments multiplied by four make forty. Or the guilt pertaining to the days, contracted from prosperity in worldly affairs, and that pertaining to the nights, contracted from adversity in worldly affairs, is washed away through the sacrament of baptism.

Noah was five hundred years old when the Lord spoke to him and commanded him to make an ark, and he was six hundred years old when he entered it. From this it is understood that the ark was built over one hundred years. What else do those one hundred years seem to signify here except the individual ages of the world?

Thus the sixth age, from the completion of five hundred years to six hundred, signifies the building of the evangelical Church in its manifestation.

Therefore, whoever takes thought for his life should be like squared wood, prepared for every good work, and should enter the holy construction. The second month of the six-hundredth year, in which Noah entered the ark, likewise signifies that same sixth age.

Two months are concluded by the number sixty. From the number six, therefore, come sixty, six hundred, six thousand, sixty thousand, six hundred thousand, six hundred times, and whatever thereafter rises in infinite increase through the same numerical progression.

The fact that the twenty-seventh day of the month is mentioned also pertains to the significance of squaring, which has already been explained through the squared wood. Here it is clearer, because the Trinity perfects us, prepared for every good work—that is, squared in a certain manner—in memory, by which we remember God; in understanding, by which we know him; and in will, by which we love him.

For three times three, and this again three times, makes twenty-seven, which is the square of the number three.

The fact that in the seventh month the ark came to rest, that is, rested, refers back to the significance of that seventh rest. And because the perfected find rest, there too the number of that square is repeated. For on the twenty-seventh day of the second month this mystery was commended, and again on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month the same commendation was confirmed when the ark rested.

For what is promised in hope is exhibited in reality. Moreover, because that seventh rest is joined to the eighth resurrection, the rest that awaits the saints after this life does not end when the body is restored. Rather, the whole human being—no longer in hope but already in reality, renewed on every side by perfect and immortal salvation of spirit and body—receives the gift of eternal life.

Because the seventh rest is joined to the eighth resurrection, and because this is contained in the sacrament of our regeneration, that is, in baptism, there is a profound and deep mystery in the fact that the water rose fifteen cubits above the mountains, exceeding their height.

Eight and seven, therefore, make fifteen. Eight signifies resurrection, and seven signifies rest. This sacrament of resurrection and rest transcends all the wisdom of the proud, so that they can in no way investigate the height of the resurrection and rest through the depth of their knowledge.

And because seventy is counted from seven, and eighty from eight, when the two numbers are joined, the water was raised for one hundred and fifty days. This commends and confirms to us the same height of baptism, in which the new human being is consecrated to hold the faith of rest and resurrection.

The fact that the raven sent out after forty days did not return—either because it was intercepted by the waters or because it was enticed by some floating body—signifies people made exceedingly foul by the impurity of desire and therefore held fast to the things outside, in this world.

Or it signifies that those rebaptized by people outside the ark—that is, outside the Church—are killed by baptism, being led astray and held fast [*sic*].

The fact that the dove, having been sent out and finding no rest, returned shows that through the New Testament rest was not promised to the saints in this world. For it was sent out after forty days, and that number signifies the life lived in this world.

Finally, after seven days the dove was sent out and brought back a fruitful olive branch, because of that sevenfold spiritual operation. This signified that some who have been baptized even outside the Church, if the richness of charity has not failed in them, may at a later time, as at evening, like the dove, be led into the fellowship of unity as though by a kiss of peace.

When it was sent out after another seven days and did not return, this signifies the end of the world, when the saints will have rest—not still in the sacrament of hope, which is joined to us in this present age as long as we live and which flowed from Christ’s side, but in the very perfection of eternal salvation, when the kingdom will be handed over to God the Father, so that in the clear contemplation of unchangeable truth we will need no bodily ministries.

**DISCIPLE.**

Why, in the six hundred and first year of Noah’s life—that is, when six hundred years had been completed—is the roof of the ark said to have been opened?

**MASTER.**

When the sixth age of the world has ended, the hidden sacrament and promise will be revealed.

**DISCIPLE.**

Why is the earth said to have dried on the twenty-seventh day of the second month, as though the necessity of baptism had already ended?

**MASTER.**

In the number of days, it is the fifty-seventh day—for it is the twenty-seventh day of the second month. This number, arising from the joining of spirit and body, contains seven times eight, with one added because of the bond of unity.

**DISCIPLE.**

Why do those who entered separately leave the ark joined together? For it had been said: “Noah and his sons, his wife, and the wives of his sons entered the ark” (Gen. VII); the men were mentioned separately and the women separately.

**MASTER.**

Because in this present age the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. V), they entered separately as a type of that division. But afterward Noah and his wife, his sons and the wives of his sons, leave together.

This means that males and females are joined together because at the end of the world, in the resurrection of the righteous, the body will cling to the spirit in complete and perfect peace, with the resistance of mortality’s need or desire removed.

The fact that all the animals are given to them for food corresponds to what is said to Peter concerning the sheet: “Kill and eat” (Acts X). The command that they eat after the blood has been poured out means that their former life should not remain in their conscience as though suffocated, but should have the character of an outpouring through confession.

God established a covenant between himself and human beings and every living soul, promising not to destroy it again by a Flood—the bow, namely, that appears in the clouds, which never shines except from the sun.

Those do not perish in the Flood who recognize Christ’s glory in the prophets and in all the divine Scriptures, as in the clouds of God, and do not seek their own glory.

Jerome said in the Book of Places: “Ararat is in Armenia, in the mountains.” The ark is said to have come to rest on Ararat after the Flood, and it is said that traces of it remain there to this day. Jeremiah also mentions these mountains in his vision against Babylon.

Josephus too, in the first book of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, presenting accounts from secular literature, says: “When Noah perceived that the land had been freed from the Flood, he allowed seven further days to pass. Then, releasing all the animals and beasts through the open enclosures, he himself went out with his offspring, sacrificing victims to God and rejoicing with his children.”

The Armenians call this place “the exit” or “the going forth,” since the inhabitants of those regions testify that the ark first came to rest there, and that certain remains of its timbers still survive.

All who have written barbarian histories remember this ark and the Flood. One of them is Berossus the Chaldean, who, reporting concerning the Flood, spoke as follows:

> It is said that part of this ship remains in Armenia near the mountain of the Cordyaeans, and that some people tear off bitumen from it and carry it about; they use it especially for cleansing and purification.

There is also the Egyptian Jerome, who composed the antiquities of the Phoenicians in an elegant style, as well as Mnaseas and many others.

Nicolaus of Damascus, in the ninety-sixth book, also reports:

> In Armenia, above the region of the Minyas, there is a mountain called Baris. Many are said to have fled to it during the Flood and to have been saved there. Others, floating in the ark’s vessel, are said to have reached its summit, and for many generations afterward the timbers of the ark were customarily displayed.

I think these are none other than those whom Moses, the lawgiver of the Hebrews, set forth in his books.

The poet also sang of the ark as follows:

> The dove brings to the ark news of the receding Flood  
> In its beak, a branch of flourishing olive.  
> The raven, caught by gluttony among foul corpses,  
> Had clung there; but she brings back the new joys of peace.

**Hieronymus.**—“And these were the sons of Noah who went out from the ark: Shem, Ham, and Japheth” (Gen. IX). The translators of the Septuagint, often unable to render the letter *heth*, which has a double aspiration, into Greek, added the Greek letter *chi*, to teach us that such words should be aspirated.

Thus in the present passage they translated “Cham” for what is properly “Ham.” For Egypt too is called *Ham* in the language of the Egyptians to this day.

“And Noah planted a vineyard, and drinking wine he became drunk,” and so forth, up to: “Their faces were turned away, and they did not see their father’s nakedness” (ibid.).

Now, as for the fact that after the Flood Noah became drunk from the vineyard he had planted and was uncovered in his house, who could fail to see here a figure of Christ? He became drunk when he suffered; he was uncovered when he was crucified—in his own house, that is, among his own people, namely, the Jews, who were of his blood.

Then the mortality of his flesh was exposed. Seeing this nakedness, that is, the passion of Christ, Ham mocked it, and the Jews, seeing Christ’s death, derided it.

Shem and Japheth, like two peoples believing from circumcision and uncircumcision, having recognized their father’s nakedness, by which the Savior’s passion was signified, took a garment, placed it upon their backs, entered with their faces turned away, and covered their father’s nakedness; they did not see what they covered with the garment (ibid.).

In a certain manner we cover Christ’s passion with a veil—that is, we honor it as a sacrament—and, explaining the reason for its mystery, we cover the Jews’ disparagement.

The garment signifies the sacrament; the backs signify remembrance of past events, because the Church celebrates Christ’s accomplished passion and does not yet look toward one still to come.

Their brother Ham, who was in the middle (ibid.), signifies the impious Jewish people. He was in the middle because he held neither the primacy of the apostles nor the last place among the Gentiles who believed.

He saw his father’s nakedness because he consented to the death of the Lord and Savior. “Afterward he announced it outside to his brothers” (ibid.). Through him what had been hidden in the prophet was made manifest, and therefore he became the servant of his brothers.

For what else is that people even today than a kind of book chest for Christians, carrying the Law and the Prophets as testimony to the Church’s affirmation, so that we may honor through the sacrament what they announce to us through the letter?

When Noah awoke and learned what his younger son had done to him, he said: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers. Blessed be the Lord God of Shem; let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem” (ibid.). How is this to be understood?

**Hieronymus.**—From Shem the Hebrews arise; from Japheth, the people of the Gentiles. Since the multitude of believers is broad, it received its name of breadth from the breadth signified by Japheth.

When he says, “And may he dwell in the tents of Shem,” this is prophesied concerning us, who, after Israel has been cast out, dwell in the instruction and knowledge of the Scriptures.

### Spiritual Exposition

After this, therefore, those two are blessed who honored their father’s nakedness [Col. 0298C]:

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of Shem; let Canaan be his servant. May Japheth be enlarged, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem.”

This Shem is the elder by birth, from whom the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles were born and descended. Japheth, however, is the father of the nations; his name is also interpreted as “enlargement.” For the people from the nations, having been enlarged into a vast multitude, were destined to dwell with the prophets and apostles.

Indeed, in accordance with Noah’s prophetic blessing, we see Japheth’s dwelling has passed into the tent of Shem—that is, into the house of the Law and the Prophets: the Church is rather justified, younger in time indeed, but greater than the Law in grace.

Cham, moreover, whose name is interpreted as “crafty,” is the middle son, as though separated from both: he neither remains among the first beginnings of the Israelites nor in the fullness of the nations. He signifies not only the crafty class of the Jews but also that of heretics—not crafty through the spirit of wisdom, but through impatience, by which the beginnings of heretical movements are accustomed to seethe and disturb the peace of the saints [Col. 0298D]. Yet all who glory in the Christian name and live ruinously also seem to bear his figure.

For they both proclaim Christ’s Passion, which was signified by that man’s nakedness, through their good confession, and dishonor it through their evil conduct. Of such people it was said: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7). Therefore Cham is also cursed in his son, as in his fruit—that is, in his work. Hence appropriately his son is called Canaan, which is interpreted as “their movement.” What else is this than their work?

Again, the fact that Cham’s descendants are condemned when Cham sins signifies that the reprobate commit offenses in the present, but in the future—that is, afterward—receive the sentence of condemnation. The Jewish people also, which crucified the Lord, transmitted the punishment of its condemnation to its children. For they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

After Noah’s two sons had therefore been blessed and the one in their midst had been cursed, their generations are subsequently set out [Col. 0299A]. From these arose seventy-two nations: fifteen from Japheth, thirty from Cham, and twenty-seven from Shem.

### On the Building of the Tower, etc., up to the Division of Languages

The first among human beings after the Flood, Nemrod, son of Cush, seized tyranny through a new desire for power. He reigned in Babylonia, which was called Babel because languages were confused there; the name is interpreted as “confusion.” The same Nemrod became the author of the tower’s construction. Because he attempted to penetrate the heights of heaven beyond the limits of his nature, he is not unsuitably compared with the devil, who, swelling with the thought of his heart, wished to exalt himself above the stars—that is, intending to make himself equal to God above every angelic power—when he says: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14).

What, however, is signified by the title “hunter,” except the deceiver of earthly souls, who captures human beings for death? His tower is the pride of this world, or the impious doctrines of heretics. After they have moved away from the East—that is, withdrawn from the true light—and have come to the plain of Shinar, which is interpreted as “shaking off of teeth,” they immediately build a tower of their impiety against God and, with wicked daring, break through the pride of their doctrines. They wish, through unlawful curiosity, to penetrate the heights of heaven.

But just as those people were divided through pride from one language into many, so heretics, separated from the unity of faith by their confession, are divided among themselves by the diversity of their error, as though by the discord of language. The destructive agreement of their arrogant conspiracy arms them against God; then the disagreement of their doctrines divides them, when sudden confusion arises. The Trinity itself condemns them—the Trinity against which they offend—and disperses them when it says: “Come, let us confuse their language there” (Gen. 11), namely, in the variety of error or schisms.

At the time when the diversity of languages occurred, the language that had previously existed remained in the house of Heber alone. So now also, in the Church alone, which is the house of Christ, there remains the unity of confession and the peace of faith, while all the reprobate are divided.

### Let Us Now Consider the Division of the Nations According to Jerome

The sons of Japheth were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. Japheth, Noah’s son, had seven sons. They possessed the land in Asia from Mount Amanus and the mountains of Taurus, through Coele-Syria and Cilicia, as far as the river Tanais; in Europe, they extended as far as Gadeira, leaving their names to places and peoples. Many of these names were later altered, while the rest remain as they were.

They are: Homer, the Galatians; Magog, the Scythians; Madai, the Medes; Savan, the Ionians, who are also the Greeks—hence the Ionian Sea; Tubal, the Iberians, who are also the Spaniards, from whom the Celtiberians derive, although some suspect that they were Italians; Meshech, the Cappadocians, whose city is still called Mazaca; and Tiras, the Thracians, whose name has not been greatly altered.

I know that someone has recently related Gog and Magog, both from the present passage and from Ezekiel, to the history of the Goths wandering in our land. Whether this is true will be shown by the outcome of the war itself. Certainly, educated people of earlier times have generally called all Goths Getae rather than Gog and Magog.

These seven nations, which I have said came from the stock of Japheth, dwell toward the north. The sons of Gomer were Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The Greeks call the Ashkenazim the Rheginians; Riphath refers to the Paphlagonians; Togarmah to the Phrygians.
