The sons of Javan were Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. From these the nations of the islands were divided among their own lands: “Each according to his language, his families, and his nation.”

From the Ionians—that is, the Greeks—descended the Elishans, who are called Aeolians. Hence the fifth language of Greece is called Aeolic, which they call πέμπτη διάλεκτος, “the fifth dialect.”

Josephus considers Tarshish to be the Cilicians. He says that the aspirated letter θ was corrupted by later generations into τ through faulty pronunciation; hence their metropolis is called Tarsus [Col. 0300A], a city made famous by the apostle Paul.

The Kittim are the Citians, from whom the city of Cyprus is still called Citium. The Dodanim are the Rhodians; this is how the translators of the Septuagint rendered the name.

Let us read the books of Varro on antiquities, those of Sisinnius Capito, and the Greek Phlegon, together with the other highly learned men. We shall see that almost all the islands, and the shores of the entire world and the lands near the sea, were occupied by Greek settlers. As we said above, they possessed all the coastal regions from the mountains of Amanus and Taurus as far as the British Ocean.

The sons of Cham were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan. Cush is called Ethiopia by the Hebrews to the present day; Mizraim is Egypt; Put refers to Libya. From him the river of Mauretania is still called Put, as is the entire surrounding region, the land of Put. Many Greek and Latin writers testify to this. Why, however, the ancient name of Libya remained only in one part of that climate, while the rest of the land was called Africa, is not a matter for this place or time.

Canaan, moreover, possessed the land that the Jews afterward occupied after expelling the Canaanites.

The sons of Cush were Sheba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. Sheba was the ancestor of the Sabaeans, of whom Virgil writes:

“Only among the Sabaeans is the branch of frankincense,”

and elsewhere:

“A hundred altars glow with Sabaean incense.”

Havilah refers to the Gaetuli, in the more remote part of Africa, adjoining the desert. Sabtah was the ancestor of the Sabatheni, who are now called Astabari. Raamah and Sabteca gradually lost their ancient names, and it is unknown what names they now bear in place of the old ones.

The sons of Raamah were Sheba and Dedan. This Sheba is written with the letter shin; the earlier Sheba, from whom we said the Sabaeans were named, is written with samekh. The name is now interpreted as referring to Arabia. For in Psalm 71, where we have, “The kings of the Arabians and Sheba will offer gifts,” the Hebrew reads, “The kings of Saba”: the first name is written with shin, the second with samekh.

Dedan is a nation of Ethiopia in the western region. Cush fathered Nemrod, whom we have already mentioned above. “He began to be powerful upon the earth,” and shortly afterward: “The beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar” (Gen. 10).

Nemrod, son of Cush, seized, as we explained above, a tyranny previously unknown among the people. He reigned in Babylon, which was called Babel because the languages of those building the tower were confused there. Babel is interpreted as “confusion.”

He also reigned in Erech, that is, Edessa; in Accad, now called Nisibis; and in Calneh, which later, its name having been changed, was called Seleucia by King Seleucus—or, indeed, is the place now called Κτησιφών, Ctesiphon.

From that land Asshur went out and built Nineveh and the city of Rehoboth. From this land the empire of the Assyrians grew. They founded, from the name of Ninus, son of Bel, the great city called Ninum, which the Hebrews call Nineveh. The whole prophecy of Jonah concerns its destruction or repentance.

When it says, “Nineveh and the city of Rehoboth” (ibid.), we should not think that these are two cities. Since Rehoboth is interpreted as “broad places” or “streets,” it should be read in this way: “And he built Nineveh and the streets of the city” [Col. 0300D].

It follows: “Mizraim fathered Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, and Casluhim, from whom came the Philistines and the Caphtorim” (ibid.).

Except for the Lehabim, from whom the Libyans later received their name—they were previously called Putites—and the Casluhim, who afterward were called Philistines, whom we improperly call Palestinians, the other six nations are unknown to us. They were destroyed in the Ethiopian war and disappeared, together with their former names, into oblivion. They occupied the land from Gaza to the farthest borders of Egypt.

It follows: “Canaan fathered Sidon, his firstborn, and the Hittites, the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites” (ibid.).

The firstborn of Canaan was Sidon, from whom the city in Phoenicia is called Sidon. Next came the Arkite, who founded the town of Arca, situated opposite Tripoli at the foot of Lebanon. Not far from it there was another city called Sim, which, later destroyed by the varied fortunes of war, preserved only its former name for the place.

The Arvadites are those who possessed the island of Aradus, separated from the Phoenician coast by a narrow strait. The Samareans are associated with Edessa, the famous city of Coele-Syria, which both Syrians and Hebrews call Amath even to our day, as it was called among the ancients. The Macedonians who reigned after Alexander’s death called it Epiphaneia. Some think that Antioch was so called; others, though not correctly, seek to support their opinion with a name that seems plausible and think that Emath was the first station after Antioch for those traveling to Edessa, and that it was the same place that the ancients called Emach.

“The boundary of the Canaanites extended from Sidon, as one travels toward Gerar, as far as Gaza, and toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.” The other cities—Sidon, Gerar, Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim—are known to everyone.

This, however, should be noted: Lasha itself is the place now called Callirhoe, where hot waters burst forth and flow into the Dead Sea.

The sons of Shem were Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram. They occupied the part of Asia extending from the Euphrates River to the Indian Ocean. Elam was the ancestor of the Elamites, the princes of Persia. Asshur has already been discussed: he founded the city of Ninus. Arpachshad was the ancestor of the Chaldaeans; Lud of the Lydians; Aram of the Syrians, whose metropolis is Damascus.

The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash. Uz, founder of Trachonitis and Damascus, held dominion between Palestine and Coele-Syria. Hence the translators of the Septuagint, in the Book of Job, where the Hebrew reads “the land of Uz,” translated the region as Ausitis, or, as though from “Hus,” Husitis.

Hul was the ancestor of the Armenians; Gether of the Acarnanians or Carians. Mash, for whom the translators of the Septuagint rendered Mosoch, refers to those now called Maeonians.

“Arpachshad fathered Shelah, and Shelah fathered Eber” (Gen. 10). Eber had two sons. One was named Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided; his brother was named Joktan.

Eber, from whom the Hebrews descend, gave his son Peleg a name through a kind of prophecy. Peleg is interpreted as “division,” because in his days the languages were divided at Babylon.

Joktan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab (ibid.). I have been unable to discover the later names of these nations. Since they are far from us, either they are still called by their original names, or it is unknown what changes they have undergone. They possessed the entire region of India from the river Kabul, the land called Ieria.

It follows.

Peleg, son of Eber, fathered Reu. Reu fathered Serug; Serug fathered Nahor; Nahor fathered Terah. These are the generations of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran fathered Lot, and Haran died before Terah his father in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldaeans (Gen. 11).

Let us also report what Jerome understood concerning this chapter in his book of Hebrew Questions. It follows:

“And Haran died before his father in the land in which he was born, in the region of the Chaldaeans.” Instead of what we read, “in the region of the Chaldaeans,” the Hebrew has ur Chasdim, that is, “in the fire of the Chaldaeans.”

The Hebrews relate that the following story arose from this occasion: Abraham was thrown into a fire because he refused to worship the fire honored by the Chaldaeans. He was rescued by God’s help and escaped from the fire of idolatry. This is indicated by the later statement that Terah went out with his offspring from the region of the Chaldaeans; the Hebrew has, “from the fire of the Chaldaeans.”

This is also the meaning of the statement now under discussion: “Haran died before Terah his father in the land of his birth, in the fire of the Chaldaeans”—that is, because he refused to worship the fire, he was consumed by fire.

The Lord later says to Abraham: “I am the one who brought you out from the fire of the Chaldaeans” (Gen. 15).

It follows.

[Col. 0302A] “Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran. The father of Milcah was also the father of Iscah.”

Haran, son of Terah and brother of Abram and Nahor, fathered two daughters, Milcah and Sarai, also called Iscah, διώνυμον, “having a double name.” Nahor took Milcah as his wife, and Abram took Sarai. At that time, marriage between uncles and their brothers’ daughters had not yet been prohibited by law, just as, among the earliest human beings, marriages between brothers and sisters had been contracted.

### Disciple

### Jerome

“Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran” (Gen. 12).

An insoluble question arises. If Terah, Abram’s father, fathered Abram at the age of seventy while he was still in the region of Chaldaea, and later died at the age of 205 in Harran, how is Abram now said to have departed from Harran after Terah’s death at the age of seventy-five, when it is demonstrated that 135 years elapsed from Abram’s birth to his father’s death?

### Master

The Hebrew tradition we mentioned above is therefore true: Terah went out from the fire of the Chaldaeans with his sons, and Abram, surrounded by the Babylonian conflagration because he refused to worship it, was rescued by God’s help. From that time, the days of his life and the period of his age are reckoned—from the time when he confessed the Lord and rejected the idols of the Chaldaeans.

It may be, however, since Scripture has left the matter uncertain, that Terah departed from Chaldaea a few years before his death and came to Harran; or else that he came to Harran immediately after the persecution and remained there for a longer period. If anyone therefore disagrees with this explanation, let him seek another solution; then he will rightly disprove what we have said.

### Isidore

The Lord spoke to Abraham, saying: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land that I will show you. I will make you into a great nation,” etc., up to: “In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.”

Who else went out in Abraham from his land and from his kindred, in order to become wealthy among foreigners and to be made into a great nation, except Christ? Having left the land and kindred of the Jews, he now prevails, as we see, among the peoples of the nations.

But we too must go out, following Christ’s example, from our own land—that is, from the resources of this world and earthly works—and from our kindred, that is, from our former way of life, customs, and vices, which cling to us from our birth and are joined to us as though by a kind of affinity and blood relationship.

Or we must go out from our father’s house—that is, from every remembrance of the world—so that, renouncing it, we may be enlarged among God’s people and, when the time comes, be brought into the land of the heavenly promise.

Two promises, however, are given to Abraham. One is that his offspring will possess the land of Canaan, when God says: “Go into the land that I will show you, and I will make you into a great nation.” The other is far more excellent: it concerns not a carnal but a spiritual offspring, through which he is father not of one Israelite nation but of all the nations that follow the traces of his faith. This began to be promised in the words: “All the families of the earth shall be blessed in you.”

It follows.

“The Lord appeared to Abram and said: ‘To your offspring I will give this land,’” etc., up to: “He came to Shechem and to the illustrious valley,” and further: “He continued on his way, advancing still farther toward the south.”

Having received a second oracle concerning the promise of that land, he built an altar there to the Lord who had appeared to him. From there he departed and dwelt in the wilderness. Driven from there by the scarcity of famine, he descended into Egypt, where he said that his wife was his sister. He was not lying, because she was related to him by blood.

When Pharaoh, king of Egypt, wished to take her as his wife, he was terrified by extremely great portents. Afflicted with many evils on her account, once he learned by divine revelation that she was Abram’s wife, he immediately restored her unharmed and with honor. When we begin to speak of Abimelech, we shall explain this matter.

### Jerome

“And Abraham departed and went into the desert, and famine arose over the land.”

It should be noted that in the present passage and in many others, where “desert” is written, the Hebrew has “toward the south.”

### Disciple

We must therefore observe what follows:

“The princes of Pharaoh saw her and praised her to Pharaoh; they brought her into his house, and he treated Abram well on her account. He acquired sheep, cattle, donkeys, male and female servants, mules, and camels.”

### Master

Although the bodies of holy women are not defiled by violence but by the will, and although Sarai can be excused on the ground that, during a time of famine, in a foreign land she could not resist the king alone in a manner appropriate to her husband, the shameful necessity may nevertheless be excused in another way.

According to the Book of Esther, among the ancients any woman who pleased the king was anointed for six months with myrrh oil, and for six months was treated with various perfumes and women’s preparations. Only then did she enter the king’s presence.

It may therefore be that, after Sarai had pleased the king, while her entrance to the king was being prepared for a year, Pharaoh gave Abram many gifts, and Pharaoh was afterward struck by the Lord, while she nevertheless remained untouched by intercourse with him.

It follows.

“Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and all that belonged to him, and Lot with him, into the desert. Abram was very rich in livestock, silver, and gold. He went from where he had come, through the desert as far as Bethel.”

He is beautifully said to have gone up after being liberated from Egypt. Yet the following presents a difficulty: how could he have been very rich when he departed from Egypt?

This is resolved by the Hebrew truth, where it is written that Abram was “very heavy” or “exceedingly burdened”—that is, βαρὺς σφόδρα, “exceedingly heavy.” He was weighed down by the burden of Egypt. Although his wealth of livestock, gold, and silver may be apparent, if these things are Egyptian, they are nevertheless heavy for a holy man.

Finally, the Hebrew does not read, as we find in the Septuagint, “He went from where he had come through the desert as far as Bethel,” but rather: “He went on his journey toward the south as far as Bethel.”

For this reason he departed from Egypt: not to enter the desert when he left Egypt, but to come by way of the south, which is opposite the north, to the house of God, where his tabernacle had been between Bethel and Ai, at the place of the altar that he had previously built. There he invoked the name of the Lord.

When Abram returned from Egypt, from where he had come, Lot then departed from his uncle Abram into the land of Sodom, without abandoning their affection. He avoided discord because they had become wealthy and their shepherds were quarreling with one another.

Abram remained in the land of Canaan and dwelt near the oak of Mamre, which is Hebron. Mamre was the name of one of Abraham’s friends.

It follows.

“The men of Sodom were evil and sinners exceedingly in the sight of God.”

The words “in the sight of God” have been added unnecessarily here by the translators of the Septuagint. The inhabitants of Sodom were evil and sinners in the eyes of human beings. But a person is called a sinner “in the sight of God” when he can appear righteous to human beings.

Thus, in the praise of Zechariah and Elizabeth, it is said that both were righteous in the sight of God; and in the psalm it is said: “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2).

The Lord spoke to Abram after Lot had separated from him:

“Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you now are, toward the north, the south, the east, and the sea, for I will give you all the land that you see, to you and to your offspring.”

He set out the four regions of the world: east and west, north and south. Since it is read throughout the Scriptures, it is enough to say here once that “the sea” is always placed for the west, because the region of Palestine is situated so that it has the sea on its western side.

It follows.

[Col. 0304A] “At that time Amraphel, king of Shinar; Arioch, king of Pontus; Chedorlaomer, king of the Elamites; and Tidal, king of the nations, entered into battle against the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar.

“All these gathered at the Valley of Salt, that is, the Salt Sea. Bela is called in the Hebrew language κατάποσις, that is, ‘devouring.’ The Hebrews therefore relate that this same place is called Salissa elsewhere in Scripture, and is again described as μόσχον τριετίζουσαν, that is, ‘a three-year-old heifer,’ because it was swallowed up by a third movement of the earth.

“From the time when Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim were overthrown by divine fire, that place was called ‘the little one.’ For Segor is interpreted as ‘little,’ and in the Syrian language is called Zoara. The valley of the salt marshes, as is written in this same book, where there had previously been wells of bitumen, was changed after God’s anger and the rain of sulphur into the Dead Sea. The Greeks call it λίμνη ἀσφαλτῖτις, that is, ‘the bitumen lake.’”

It follows.

“These kings took all the property of Sodom and Gomorrah, as well as Lot and his property, since he was Abram’s nephew and lived in Sodom. One of those who escaped came and reported to Abram the Hebrew.

“When he heard that Lot had been captured, Abram counted 318 of his household servants. Taking them with him, he pursued the enemy. He recovered everything that they had seized, and also Lot. He pursued them as far as Dan, a town of Phoenicia now called Paneas.

“Dan is one of the sources of the Jordan. The other is called Jor, which is interpreted as ῥεῖθρον, that is, ‘stream.’ When these two springs, which are not far from one another, join into a single rivulet, it is thereafter called the Jordan.”

### Isidore

Afterward Abram rescued Lot, who had been captured by the five kings who had attacked Sodom, taking with him into battle 318 household servants.

But what did this victory of Abram over the five kings signify? The father of faith conquered them mystically. It signified that, when our faith has been confirmed in the ruling spirit, it subdues by the word of God the corresponding senses of our body.

For just as he was victorious over the kings through his immediate action, so faith, victorious through the soul, will triumph over the outward person. The fact that he defeated hostile kings not through a multitude or the strength of armies, but with only 318 companions, already prefigured the mystery of the cross. The letter tau expresses the number three hundred, and thus this sign foreshadowed that Christ’s Passion would free us from the dominion of the five bodily senses, which had previously taken us captive through various vices.

When Abram was returning from the slaughter of his enemies, Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God, immediately came to meet him. He blessed Abram, the circumcised man, offering bread and wine.

### Jerome

Because my little work is once and for all a collection of Hebrew Questions and traditions, I shall insert what the Hebrews think about this matter.

They say that this man was Shem, Noah’s son. By reckoning the years of his life, they demonstrate that he lived as far as the time of Isaac. They also say that all the firstborn sons of Noah were high priests until Aaron exercised the priesthood.

Salem, moreover, is said to be Jerusalem, which was previously called Salem.

The blessed Apostle, in the Letter to the Hebrews, speaks of Melchizedek as being “without father and mother” and refers him to Christ, and through Christ to the Church of the nations. For the glory of the whole body is referred to its members, because Abram, who possessed the foreskin, blessed the circumcised man; and in Abram were Levi and, through Levi, Aaron, from whom the priesthood later came.

From this he wishes it to be inferred that the priesthood of the Church, which possesses the foreskin, blessed in circumcised Abraham the priesthood of the synagogue.

When it says, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4), our mystery is signified in the word of reconciliation or order—not through Aaron’s offering of rational victims, but through the offering of bread and wine, that is, the body and blood of the Lord Jesus.

As we stated above, the fact that Paul the Apostle speaks of him as being without father and mother refers figuratively to Christ, as we have already shown. He alone is born from a father without a mother, according to his divinity; and he alone is born from a mother without a father, according to his humanity.

Because the great patriarch gave Melchizedek the priest all the tithes of his property after receiving the blessing, he understood spiritually that a future priesthood among the nations would be better than the Levitical priesthood, which was destined to arise from him in Israel. It was also destined that the priesthood of the Church, which possesses the foreskin, would bless in circumcised Abraham the priesthood of the synagogue.

For the one who blesses is greater than the one who is blessed. Hence the priests born from Abraham’s seed received tithes, according to the command of the Law, from their brothers—that is, the people of Israel—whom they blessed; these were truly given to their greater and more eminent men.

The name itself, Melchizedek, is interpreted as “king of peace” or “king of righteousness,” and this is then referred to Christ. He is the King of peace, because through him we are reconciled to God. He is likewise the King of righteousness, because he will come to distinguish the holy from the impious.

He alone is both priest and king, because, for the redemption of all, he offered himself to God the Father as a sacrifice. He is the true King: in the present age he rules his people, and in the future he will judge them.

### Jerome to the Presbyter Evagrius on Melchizedek

You sent me a volume that was **anonymous and without an owner** (*ἀνώνυμον καὶ ἀδέσποτον*), and I do not know whether you removed the name from the title, or whether the writer, wishing to avoid the danger of having to defend his position, declined to acknowledge its author. When I had read it, I understood that the very famous question concerning the priest Melchizedek had been pursued there through numerous arguments, with the writer attempting to teach that the one who blessed so great a patriarch was of a more divine nature, and ought not to be reckoned among human beings. Finally, he dared to say that the Holy Spirit had appeared to Abraham, and that it was the Holy Spirit himself who had been seen in human form.

How, however, the Holy Spirit brought forth bread and wine, and received the tithes of the spoil which Abraham carried back after conquering the four kings, he was entirely unwilling to address. You ask me to reply concerning what I think either of the writer or of the question. I confess that I wished to conceal my opinion and not involve myself in a dangerous and contentious (*φιλεγκλήμων*) treatise, in which whatever I might have said would have earned me critics. But then, when I read the letter again and found on the last page that I had been adjured by extraordinary entreaties not to reject the petitioner, I went back through the books of the ancients, so that I might see what each of them said and answer you, as it were, on the advice of many.

At once, at the beginning of Genesis, in Origen’s first homily, I found a passage written about Melchizedek. In a lengthy discussion he proceeded to the point of calling him an angel. He spoke with nearly the same arguments with which your writer spoke of the Holy Spirit, whereas Origen spoke of the heavenly powers. I passed on to Didymus, his disciple, and saw that he had followed his teacher’s opinion step by step. I turned to Hippolytus, Irenaeus, Eusebius of Caesarea, Eusebius of Emesa, and also to our Apollinarius and Eustathius, who was the first bishop of the Church of Antioch and who, against Arius, sounded a most renowned trumpet of war. I discovered that all of them, by different arguments and side paths, had arrived at one crossroads: they said that Melchizedek had been a human being, a Canaanite king of the city of Jerusalem, which was first called Salem, afterward Jebus, and finally Jerusalem.

Nor is it surprising that he is described as a priest of God Most High without circumcision, the ceremonies of the Law, or descent from Aaron. Abel, Enoch, and Noah also pleased God and offered sacrifices; and in the Book of Job we read that he was both a presenter of gifts and a priest, and that he sacrificed victims daily for his sons. They also say that Job himself was not of the tribe of Levi but of the stock of Esau, although the Hebrews maintain otherwise.

In what way Noah, having become drunk in his house, lying naked, and being mocked by his middle son, provided a type of the Savior, and Ham a type of the Jewish people; in what way Samson, the lover of the prostitute and impoverished Delilah, killed many more of his enemies in death than he had killed while alive, thereby expressing the passion of Christ—all this shows that nearly all the holy patriarchs and prophets expressed, in some respect, a figure of the Savior.

So too Melchizedek, because he was a Canaanite and not of the Jewish race, went before as a type of the priest, the Son of God, of whom it is said in the hundred and ninth Psalm: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

They interpret his “order” in many ways: he alone was both king and priest; he exercised the priesthood before circumcision, so that the Gentiles might not receive the priesthood from the Jews, but the Jews from the Gentiles; he was not anointed with priestly oil, as the commands of Moses prescribe, but with the oil of exultation and the purity of faith; he did not sacrifice victims of flesh and blood or receive the entrails of brute animals—that is, whatever lies above the food—but consecrated the sacrament of Christ through simple bread and pure sacrifice. There are many other matters which the brevity of a letter cannot contain, and they have been treated more fully in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which all the Greeks accept, as do some of the Latins.

In that Epistle this Melchizedek—that is, the righteous king, the king of Salem, that is, the king of peace—is said to be “without father and without mother.” How this is to be understood, the text immediately explained in one word: *ἀγενεαλόγητος*, “without genealogy.” This does not mean that he existed without father and mother, since Christ too, according to both natures, had both a father and a mother; rather, it means that he is suddenly introduced in Genesis as appearing to Abraham when Abraham was returning from the slaughter of his enemies. Neither before nor afterward is his name recorded.

The Apostle declares that the priesthood of Aaron—that is, the priesthood of the Jewish people—had both a beginning and an end. But Melchizedek—that is, Christ and the Church—exists eternally, both in the past and in the future, and has no author. When the priesthood is transferred, the Law too is changed, so that the word of the Lord proceeds no longer from Hagar the slave-woman and Mount Sinai, but from Sarah the free woman and the citadel of Zion, and the Law of God from Jerusalem.

He heightens the difficulty of the matter at the beginning, saying: “Concerning whom we have much to say, and it is difficult to interpret.” This is not because the Apostle was unable to interpret it, but because his hearers at that time were not ready. He was persuading Hebrews—that is, Jews—not those who were already believers, to whom he would have indiscriminately disclosed the mystery.

Yet if the Chosen Vessel is astonished at the mystery and confesses that the subject of his discussion is ineffable, how much more ought we, little worms and gnats, to confess that the only knowledge we possess is ignorance, and to point out a very great house through a small opening, saying that two priesthoods—the priesthoods of the former and the later people—have been compared with one another by the Apostle.

His whole argument makes this point: before Levi and Aaron there was a priest, Melchizedek, from the Gentiles. His merit is praised to such a degree that he blessed Abraham, in whose loins were the future priests of the Jews; and everything that follows in praise of Melchizedek is referred to the type of Christ, whose progress consists in the mysteries of the Church.

I read these things in the books of the Greeks, and, as though displaying very broad regions of the earth on a small tablet, I wished to indicate them—not by extending the spaces of the arguments and discussions, but by signifying infinite matters through certain points and summaries—so that in a short letter you might learn at once the opinions of many.

But because you ask affectionately, and everything I have learned ought to be poured into faithful ears, I shall also set forth the opinion of the Hebrews; and, so that nothing may be lacking to your curiosity, I shall append the very words:

“And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine; and he was priest of God Most High. And he blessed him and said: ‘Blessed be Abram by God Most High, who created heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, who delivered your enemies into your hand!’ And he gave him tithes of everything.”

They report that this man was Shem, the first son of Noah, and that at the time when Abraham was born he was 390 years old. Their calculation is as follows. In the second year after the Flood, when Shem was one hundred years old, he fathered Arphaxad. After Arphaxad’s birth he lived five hundred years, making six hundred in all. Arphaxad, at the age of thirty-five, fathered Shelah; Shelah, himself thirty years old, fathered Eber, whom we read fathered Peleg at the age of thirty-four. Again, Peleg, after completing thirty years, fathered Reu; and Reu, after thirty-two years, fathered Serug. When Serug had reached thirty years, Nahor was born. Nahor, at the age of thirty-nine, fathered Terah. We read that Terah, at the age of seventy, fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

Add the years of each generation individually, and you will find 360 years from the birth of Shem to the birth of Abram. Abram died in the 175th year of his life. Thus, after the calculation has been made, it is found that Shem outlived his tenth-generation descendant Abram by thirty-five years.

They also report that, until the priesthood of Aaron, all the firstborn of Noah’s stock—whose succession and order are described—were priests and sacrificed victims to God. These were the birthright privileges which Esau sold to his brother Jacob. It is therefore not surprising if Melchizedek came out to meet the victorious Abram, brought bread and wine for the refreshment of Abram and his warriors, and blessed him, since he owed this right to his great-grandson, and received from him tithes of the spoil and victory.

Or, since the matter is regarded as uncertain, he may have displayed his own tithes of his property and his ancestral generosity toward his descendant. Both interpretations are possible, both according to the Hebrew text and according to the Septuagint translators: that Melchizedek himself received tithes of the spoils and gave Abram tithes of his property. Nevertheless, the Apostle in his Epistle to the Hebrews defines the matter most clearly: it was not Abraham who received tithes of Melchizedek’s wealth, but the priest who received a portion of the enemies’ spoils.

Salem, however, is not—as Josephus and all our writers think—the name Jerusalem, composed from Greek and Hebrew, which the mixture of a foreign language proves to be absurd. Rather, it is a town near Scythopolis, still called Salem today. There, the palace of Melchizedek is shown; the magnitude of its ancient ruins displays the grandeur of the former structure.

Concerning this place it is also written in the latter part of Genesis: “Jacob came to Succoth,” that is, “to tents,” “and made houses and shelters for himself there; and he crossed over to Salem, a city of the region of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan.”

It must also be considered that, when Abraham was returning from the slaughter of the enemies whom he pursued as far as Dan, which is now called Paneas, it was not the road from Jerusalem, but the town of Shechem, the metropolis, that lay on his route. Concerning this place we also read in the Gospel: “John was baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there were many waters there” (John I).

It makes no difference whether it is called Salem or Salim, since the Hebrews very rarely use medial vowels, and since, according to the variety of places and regions, the same words are pronounced with different sounds and accents.

These things we learned from the most learned men of that nation. They so firmly reject the idea that Melchizedek was the Holy Spirit or an angel that they even assign him the most certain name of a human being.

And indeed it is foolish to say, in the interpretation of the type, that Christ’s priesthood has no end, while Christ himself, both King and Priest, has bestowed both upon us, so that we may be a royal and priestly race, and, like a cornerstone, join the two walls together, making one flock from two herds under one good shepherd.

Thus certain people refer these matters to *ἀναγωγή*, the higher or spiritual interpretation, and remove their historical truth, saying that Melchizedek was not a king but an angel shown in human likeness. The Hebrews, however, strive so earnestly to show that Melchizedek, king of Salem, was Shem, the son of Noah, that they connect the preceding passage in this way:

“The king of Sodom went out to meet him”—clearly meaning that Abraham, after returning from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, met him in the Valley of Shaveh, which is the King’s Valley. Immediately afterward it says: “And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine,” and so forth.

If, therefore, this was the King’s city and the King’s Valley—or, as the Septuagint translated it, the plain, which the Palestinians today call Aulon—it is clear that the man who reigned in the earthly valley and city was a human being.

You have what I heard and what I read concerning Melchizedek. My task was to cite witnesses; yours is to judge the credibility of the witnesses. But if you reject them all, you will certainly not accept your spiritual interpreter, who, ignorant in speech and knowledge, pronounced Melchizedek to be the Holy Spirit with such arrogance and authority that he proved the truth of what is sung among the Greeks:

“Ignorance produces confidence; learning produces fear.”

After a long illness I was scarcely able, during the days of Lent, to compose this work. While preparing myself for another task, I spent the few remaining days on the exposition of Matthew. I resumed my abandoned studies with such eagerness that what benefited the exercise of my tongue harmed the health of my body.

### “After this victory Abram said to the Lord: ‘Lord God, what will you give me, since I shall go childless, and Masek, the slave-woman of my household—this Damascus Eliezer—will be my heir?’”

### Jerome

“And Abraham said: ‘Behold, you have not given me offspring, and the son of my slave-woman will be my heir.’”

Where we have, “And the son of Masek, my slave-woman, will be my heir,” the Hebrew has written *uben Mesek bethi*. Aquila translated this as *ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ποτίζοντος οἰκίαν μου*, that is, “the son of the one who gives drink to my household.” Theodotion, however, has *καὶ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἐπὶ οἰκίας μου*, that is, “and the son of the one who is over my household.”

The meaning is this: “I am dying without children, and the son of my steward or household manager, who administers everything and distributes provisions to the members of the household, and whose name is Damascus Eliezer, will be my heir.”

Eliezer is interpreted as “My God is my helper.” For this reason, they say, Damascus was founded and received its name. The text continues.

“And the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision, while he was anxious about his descendants, seeing that no son was being born to him, yet holding to the promise that had been made to his offspring.” Immediately there is presented to him a twofold figure of his promised seed: its future likeness to the sand of the sea and its future multitude like the stars of heaven.

“Therefore God brought Abram outside and showed him the stars of heaven, saying: ‘So shall I make your seed’”—that is, the Christian people, whose father you are by remaining steadfast in faith—“so shall I make it shine with the light of the resurrection.”

Then he showed him the sand of the sea and said: “So shall your seed be in multitude.” That is, the Jewish people will indeed be a numerous nation, but will remain barren and unfruitful like sand.

After this, when God promised him that he would be the possessor of the promise, he asked for a sign by which he might recognize it—not as though he doubted that it would happen, but asking how it would happen.

The Lord said to him: “Take for yourself a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram, a turtledove, and a pigeon.” Abram took all these, divided them down the middle, and placed the two parts opposite one another. He did not divide the birds.

Birds of prey descended upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away. When the sun had set, fear fell upon Abram, and a great, dark terror seized him. A smoking furnace and a flaming torch appeared, passing between the divided pieces.

And it was said to him: “Know with certainty that your seed will be a stranger in a land that is not its own; it will serve and be afflicted,” and the rest.

Thus the measure of the promised seed of Abraham was established, and this is the figure. By the young heifer is signified the people placed under the yoke of the Law; by the she-goat, the same people, also destined to be sinful; by the ram, the same people, also destined to reign.

The animals are called three-year-old because, through the divisions of time—from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, and from Abraham to David—the people grew as though passing through a third age.

By the turtledove and the pigeon are signified spiritual peoples, undivided sons of the promise and heirs of the future kingdom. Their temporal age is not mentioned because, contemplating eternal things, they have passed beyond temporal desires.

But what does it mean that those three animals are divided, with their parts set opposite one another, except that carnal people, both in the former people and now, are divided among themselves? The birds, however, are not divided, because spiritual people are undivided. They do not contemplate schism and are not led astray by heretics; peace is always among them, whether they withdraw from the crowds, like the turtledove, or live among them, like the pigeon. Yet each bird possesses simplicity and innocence.

The birds of prey descending upon the divided carcasses signify unclean spirits seeking some food for themselves from the division of carnal people. The fact that Abram sat there and drove them away signifies that, at the end of the world, many carnal people will be freed from their afflictions through the merits of the saints.

The fear and great dark terror that fell upon Abram around sunset signify the great disturbance that will come upon the saints from Antichrist near the end of this age. Concerning it the Lord says in the Gospel: “For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning,” and so forth (Matthew XXIV.21).

When it is added that, after the sun had set, a dark gloom appeared, and a smoking furnace and a flaming lamp passed between the divided pieces, this signifies the day of judgment that will follow the end of the world, when the peoples of the saints and of the wicked will be separated by fire.

What was said to Abram—“Know with certainty that your seed will be a stranger in a land that is not its own; they will reduce them to servitude, humble them, and oppress them for four hundred years”—was plainly prophesied concerning the people of Israel, who were destined to serve in Egypt. It does not mean that they served under the Egyptians for four hundred years, but that this number was completed within that affliction, because the reckoning begins from the time when these things were promised to Abraham.

Then, on account of the future wandering, so that his seed might not mingle among the nations, circumcision was given to him as a sign, in these words:

“Every male among you shall be circumcised. An infant of eight days shall be circumcised among you, whether born in the household or purchased. The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant.”

Why should the soul of a tiny, crying child perish, a child who knows neither good nor evil and is uncircumcised, when the child itself has not broken God’s covenant, but those who neglected to circumcise it have done so? It is to signify that children have broken God’s covenant in the sin of the first human being, not according to their own action but according to their origin, in whom all sinned.

All are born sinners—not personally, but by origin. Unless regeneration frees a person, his soul perishes from his people, because he has broken God’s covenant when, in Adam, he too sinned originally. The text continues.

### “In the fourth generation they shall return here.”

Pope Damasus asked blessed Jerome how this statement agrees with what is written in Exodus: “In the fifth generation the children of Israel went out from the land of Egypt.” Let us therefore set down what he answered.

### Damasus

Why does God say to Abram that the children of Israel would return from Egypt in the fourth generation, while Moses afterward writes in Exodus: “In the fifth generation the children of Israel went out from the land of Egypt”? Unless this is explained, it certainly appears contradictory.

### Jerome

When I read this problem, I began to wrestle with it silently. Immediately running through Genesis and Exodus, I found the passages that seemed to create the difficulty. At first, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things, I thought they were irreconcilable, as many other matters also are.

It is written that Methuselah lived fourteen years after the Flood, yet he did not enter the ark with Noah. Again, although the Lord himself said to Abram, “Know with certainty that your seed will be a stranger in a land that is not its own; they will reduce them to servitude, oppress them, and humble them for four hundred years,” Moses afterward writes in Exodus: “And it came to pass after four hundred and thirty years that all the power of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt.”

Hagar also carries Ishmael on her shoulders as though he were a nursing infant and tender child, although he is found to have been about eighteen years old or more, so that it is ridiculous for so large a young man to have sat upon his mother’s neck.

Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, began his reign in the forty-first year of his age and reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years, although his father, who began to reign in his eleventh year and reigned for forty years, could not have fathered a son in the eleventh year of his own reign.

While I anxiously turned over these and many similar oracles within myself, he who holds the key of David opened a door for me. He led me into his chamber and placed me in the cleft of the rock, so that, after the raging wind, after the earthquake of my land, after the fire of ignorance in which I was burning, the voice of a gentler breeze might come to me, and I might say: “I found him whom my soul sought; I shall hold him and not let him go” (Song of Songs III.4).

For although Scripture appears to contradict itself, both statements are true, though they differ.

The children of Israel went out from the land of Egypt in the fourth generation. Review the genealogy of Levi:

Levi fathered Kohath. Kohath fathered Amram. Amram fathered Aaron. Aaron fathered Eleazar. Eleazar fathered Phinehas.

Kohath entered Egypt with his father Levi. Again, Eleazar went out of Egypt with his father Aaron. Review the genealogy from Kohath to Eleazar, and four generations are counted.

Some wish to begin with Abram and continue to Phinehas, as we have done with Eleazar. But if you wish to demonstrate a different number—how, according to Exodus, the children of Israel went out from the land of Egypt in the fifth generation—then let the tribe and genealogy of Judah be counted.

Judah fathered Perez. Perez fathered Hezron. Hezron fathered Amram. Amram fathered Amminadab. Amminadab fathered Nahshon. Nahshon fathered Salmon.

Perez entered Egypt with his father Judah. Nahshon is described as the prince of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness; his son Salmon entered the promised land. Count, therefore, from Perez to Nahshon, and you will find only five generations. Some, however, just as we began with Levi at Kohath, begin here with Hezron and continue to Salmon.

These matters, most holy pontiff, I have explained to you from the resources of my study as best I could. According to the question proposed and according to both editions, so that no one may think the accounts contradictory, I believe the problem has been more fully resolved through both genealogies, namely those of Levi and Judah.

If any of our rivals and detractors dislike this, I shall come to a shorter answer and say that there is no difference in the matter: according to each genealogy, both statements are true and each has a complete meaning.

Aquila too, who interprets the word not, as some think, more contentiously but more diligently, translated the passage literally where the Septuagint has, “In the fifth generation the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt.” He translated it: “Armed, the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt.”

Although, instead of “armed,” we have explained it according to the ambiguity of the Greek expression as “equipped” or “instructed and warned,” we have explained it as best we could, and I do not wish this to be burdensome to the reader.

When discussing the Hebrew books, it is not fitting to hunt for Aristotle’s arguments, nor should a little stream be drawn from Cicero’s river of eloquence. Quintilian’s ears should not be soothed with fine-spun phrases and schoolroom declamation.

What is needed is a plain style, resembling everyday speech and smelling of no nocturnal labor—a style that explains the matter, unfolds the meaning, and makes obscure things clear, not one that grows leafy through the arrangement of words.

Let others be eloquent and be praised, as they wish, with puffed cheeks; let them weigh frothing words. For me it is enough to speak so that I may be understood. When discussing the Holy Scriptures, I seek to understand the simplicity of the Scriptures.

Although Jerome, interpreter of the divine Law, had judged the questions concerning the death of Methuselah, the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt after 430 years, Hagar and Ishmael, and Rehoboam to be insoluble, nevertheless we find elsewhere in his writings that all of them have been resolved, as the style of the present book partly reveals.

### “Sarai said to Abram: ‘Behold, God has closed me off so that I cannot bear children. Go in to my slave-woman, so that I may have children by her.’”

### Jerome

Carefully note that in Hebrew the procreation of children is written as “building.” For it is read there: “Go in to my slave-woman, if perhaps I may be built up through her.” Perhaps this is also what is written in Exodus: “God blessed the midwives, and they built houses for themselves.” The text continues.

“Sarai afflicted her slave-woman Hagar because she held her in contempt. She fled, and the angel of the Lord found her beside a spring of water in the wilderness, beside the spring on the road to Shur.”

She was naturally wishing to go by the road to Shur, an Egyptian road that leads through the wilderness to Egypt.

“And he said to her: ‘Return to your mistress and humble yourself under her hand.’ She returned and gave birth to a son, and called his name Ishmael, because God heard my humiliation.”

Ishmael is interpreted as “hearing of God.” “He will be a rustic man; his hand will be against everyone, and everyone’s hand against him; he will dwell opposite all his brothers.”

For “rustic” the Hebrew has *phere*, which is interpreted as “wild ass.” This signifies that his descendants will dwell in the wilderness—that is, the wandering Saracens, whose settlements are uncertain. They attack all the nations adjoining the wilderness on their side, and are themselves attacked by everyone.

“And the Lord spoke to Abraham, saying: ‘Behold, my covenant is with you, and you shall be the father of a multitude of nations. Your name shall no longer be called Abram, but Abraham, because I have appointed you the father of many nations.’”

### Jerome

It must be noted that wherever we read “covenant” in the Greek Testament, the Hebrew has *foedus* or *pactum*, “treaty” or “agreement,” namely *berith*.

The Hebrews say that God added the letter *he* to Abraham and Sarah from his own name, which among them is the tetragrammaton. At first he was called Abram, which is interpreted “exalted father.” Later he was called Abraham, which is translated “father of a multitude”; the word “nations,” which follows in the meaning, is not present in the name but is understood.

Nor is it surprising that, although in Greek and in our language a letter appears to have been added, we say that the Hebrew letter *he* was added. It is a characteristic of that language to write with *he* but read it as *a*; conversely, they often pronounce the letter *a* as *he*.

The text continues: “And God said to Abraham: ‘As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her Sarai, but Sarah shall be her name.’”

### Jerome

Those who think that Sarah was first written with one *r* and afterward had another *r* added are mistaken. Since *r* is the number one hundred among the Greeks, they imagine many absurd things about her name. However one may wish to change her name, one must employ a Hebrew, not a Greek, explanation, since the name itself is Hebrew.

No one, when calling someone by a name in one language, derives the etymology of the name from another language.

Sarai, therefore, was first called with the letters *sin*, *resh*, and *yod*. When the *yod*, that is, the element *i*, was removed, the letter *he* was added, which is read as *a*, and she was called Saraa.

The reason for this change of name is as follows. Previously she was called “my princess,” the mistress of one household alone. Later she is called simply “princess,” that is, *ἄρχουσα*, “ruler.”

For the text continues: “I shall give you a son by her, and I shall bless him, and he shall become nations, and kings of peoples shall come from him.”

Significantly, where in Greek we read, “God said to Abraham: ‘Sarai your wife shall not be called Sarai by name,’” the Hebrew has: “You shall not call her name Sarai,” that is, “You shall not say to her, ‘You are my princess.’” She is already destined to be the princess of all nations.

Some make the very foolish suggestion that she had previously been called “leprous” and afterward “princess,” although leprosy is called *zaraath*. In our language the words may appear somewhat similar, but in Hebrew they are completely different. *Zaraath* is written with *tsade*, *ayin*, *resh*, and *tav*, and it is plainly very different from the three letters—*sin*, *resh*, and *he*—with which Sarah is written.

### Recapitulation

Here the promise concerning the calling of the Gentiles in Isaac, the son of promise, is already explained—that is, by grace and not by nature. For since he was to come from an aged father and a barren mother, and since this was to occur through regeneration rather than through the natural generation represented by Ishmael, circumcision was commanded at the same time, when a son was promised through Sarah as a type of the Church, not when Ishmael was born, who represented the Jews.

But what else does circumcision signify except renewed nature through baptism, after the stripping off of the old human being? And who is the eighth day except Christ, who, after the week was completed—that is, after the Sabbath—rose again?

The command that not only sons but also household servants, whether born in the household or purchased, should be circumcised testifies that the grace of redemption pertains to everyone.

Hence even the names of the parents are changed, so that everything may resound with newness. Abram, as he was previously called, is interpreted “exalted father”; Abraham means “father of nations.” By this name it was foretold that many nations would follow the traces of his faith. The text continues.

### “Then the Lord appeared to Abraham in the valley of Mamre, as he was sitting at the door of his tent. When he lifted his eyes, three men appeared standing near him. When he saw them, he worshiped and said: ‘Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes, let your feet be washed, and rest beneath the tree.’ And Abraham went to Sarah and said: ‘Hurry; mix three measures of fine flour.’”

### Jerome

Because the three measures are stated here without qualification, and the measure is uncertain, I added that the Hebrew has “three *seahs* of fine flour,” that is, three amphorae, so that we may recognize the same mystery here and in the Gospel, where the woman is said to leaven three measures. The text continues.

“Sarah made cakes baked under the ashes, while Abraham ran to the flock and prepared a fattened calf after it had been slaughtered. He also brought milk and butter and stood beside them beneath the tree. When they had eaten, they said to him: ‘Where is Sarah your wife?’ He answered: ‘Behold, she is in the tent.’”

“‘I shall return to you at this time, and Sarah shall have a son.’”

Instead of “at this time,” we read in Hebrew “the time of life,” so that the order or meaning is: “I shall return to you at the time of life.” It is as though he had said, “If I live, if life accompanies me.”

“And Abraham fell upon his face, and laughed, and said in his heart: ‘If a son is born to a hundred-year-old man, and if Sarah, at ninety, gives birth.’” And shortly afterward: “And you shall call his name Isaac.”

### Jerome

The opinion differs, but the etymology is one, as to why he was called Isaac. Isaac is interpreted as “laughter.”

Some say that he was called “laughter” because Sarah laughed, but this is false. Others say that he was called so because Abraham laughed, and this we approve. For after his son Isaac was named after Abraham’s laughter, we then read that Sarah laughed also.

She laughed within herself, saying: “Nothing like this has yet happened to me, even though my lord is old.”

The Hebrew reads very differently: “And Sarah laughed within herself, saying: ‘After I have grown worn out, pleasure has come to me.’”

At the same time, note that where we have “pleasure,” the Hebrew has *Eden*. Symmachus translated the passage in this way:

“After I had grown old and wasted away, youth came to me.”

Concerning this the poet also sang:

> Already the wounded entrails of aged Sarah were withering,  
>   
> Consumed by the wasting of old age, and denying offspring;  
>   
> The cold blood was dying in her aged body;  
>   
> When, in the aged husband, the cold depths of the womb  
>   
> Swelled toward a new birth, and the trembling mother,  
>   
> Gave birth to the hope of a mighty nation,  
>   
> And laid her late-born child at her breast.  
>   
> The father offered him to God for slaughter; but the sacred ram  
>   
> Was slaughtered at the altar in place of the boy.  
>   
> O holy mind of the righteous man, set beyond ordinary piety,  
>   
> Possessing a greater piety, he despised the wounds of his son.  
>   
> Embracing God’s commands, and by the help of the typical blood,  
>   
> He teaches what was to come: that by the blood of Christ  
>   
> The gracious Lamb would die for the human race.

It must also be known that in the Old Testament four people were called by their own names before they were born, without any veil or concealment: Ishmael, Isaac, Solomon, and Josiah. Read the Scriptures.

## Recapitulation

It must be noted that Abraham bears within himself a threefold figure: first, that of the Savior, when, having left his kindred, he came into this world; secondly, that of the Father, when he sacrificed his only Son; and thirdly—the figure he bears in this passage—that of the saints, who received Christ’s coming with joy.

That tent of Abraham prefigured Jerusalem, where at the beginning the prophets and apostles dwelt, and where, when the Lord first came, he was received by believers but hung upon the wood by unbelievers. In the three men who came to him, the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ was foretold. Two angels accompanied him; most understand these as Moses and Elijah: one the giver of the ancient Law, who indicated the Lord’s coming through that same Law; the other, who is to come at the end of the world, to announce Christ’s second coming and preach his Gospel to the Jews. Hence, on the mountain, when the Lord had been transfigured, these two—Moses and Elijah—were seen with him by the apostles.

But the fact that Abraham saw three and worshiped one—thereby indicating the Lord and Savior, whose coming he had already awaited—corresponds to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Abraham longed to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8:56). For then he beheld the mystery of the sacrament that was to come. Thus also he washes their feet, to signify the purification of the washing that was to come at the end of the world; for feet signify the final things.

Indeed, he also prepares a meal, namely a fattened calf. This young, fattened calf is the body of the Lord Jesus Christ. This is also the Lord’s calf, sacrificed upon the tree of the cross for the salvation of believers. This is the calf of the Lord’s body, which in the Gospel is killed for the sinful son.

[Col. 0313B] But he also set out milk and butter with the calf’s flesh. Our Apostle announces that milk represented the ancient Law when he says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (2 Cor. 3:2). “For you were not yet able to receive it, nor indeed are you able even now.” He had delivered to them the commandment of the Law, as though milk pressed from the breasts of the two tablets—that is, the covenant of faith. Because of the infancy of their understanding, they were not yet able to receive the solid and substantial food of evangelical teaching.

Butter, however, exceedingly rich and fat, is the testimony of the Gospels, which is given to believers like oil as a sign. Abraham therefore set out the calf with milk and butter to eat, because neither can the body of the Lord, which is the calf, exist without the milk of the Law, nor the milk of the Law without butter—that is, without the testimony of the Gospel.

The three measures from which Sarah made ash-baked loaves indicated the image of Noah’s three sons, from whom the whole human race was born. Believing in the divine Trinity, they were to be moistened with the water of baptism through the Church, of which Sarah was an image, and brought together into one bread, the body of Christ. These are the three measures that the woman in the Gospel is known to have leavened.

The believers’ unity must consist of unleavened loaves because it is to be without the leaven of malice, without the anguish of wickedness, and without the fervor of perverse teaching. They were ash-baked so that, through repentance for past sins, they might be cooked by the vapor of the Holy Spirit and become, like acceptable food, pleasing and welcome to God.

Their sitting beneath the tree was a sign of the Lord’s Passion, whose preachers they are. But when God promised a son to barren Sarah, saying, “At this time I will come,” he did not indicate a date but the character of his coming, when a faithful people was to be born through the promised Son. For this is the barren Sarah to whom the Lord says through the Prophet: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband” [Col. 0313D] (Isa. 54:1).

Sarah’s laughter is not doubt but prophecy. That laughter has a twofold meaning: either that Christ would become laughter to unbelievers, or that he would mock all his enemies in his judgment, as it is written: “I also will laugh at your destruction and mock,” and so forth (Prov. 1:26). Hence he who was born from Sarah was himself called Laughter. For Isaac, translated from Hebrew into Latin, means “laughter.”

Then, again, a future son is promised to that same Isaac, who will become a great nation. “And in him,” he says, “all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.” By these words two things were historically promised to him: the Jewish nation according to the flesh, and all nations according to faith.

The text continues:

> And Abraham said, “Please do not be angry, Lord, if I speak,” and so forth, up to the overthrow of the cities.

### Jerome

Because the Lord seemed, by questioning, to press him for an answer, he softens what he asks by his introductory words.

The text continues:

[Col. 0314A]

> The Lord said, “Can we hide from our friend Abraham?” up to “Shall I not destroy it for the sake of ten?” and so forth. And Lot spoke to his sons-in-law, who had taken his daughters.

### Jerome

Since Lot’s two daughters are later said to have been virgins—indeed, he himself had earlier said to the men of Sodom, “Behold, I have two daughters who have not known a man”—and Scripture now mentions that he had sons-in-law, some think that those who had husbands remained in Sodom, while the virgins went out with their father.

But since Scripture does not say this, the Hebrew truth must be explained. It reads: “Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, who were going to take his daughters.” They had therefore not yet been joined to their husbands in marriage.

The text continues:

> And he said to him, “Behold, I have admired your face.”

In Hebrew it has: “Behold, I have accepted your face,” that is, “I yield to your requests.” Symmachus, interpreting according to the sense, says: **ὁράσει ἐδυσωπήθην τὸ πρόσωπόν σου**—“I have been moved by the sight of your face.”

> Behold, a flame was rising from the earth like the vapor of a furnace.

In Hebrew we read instead: “Behold, **Kitor** was rising from the furnace,” which is like **ἀναπνεύμασις**; we can render it “vapor,” “smoke,” or “ash.”

> And Lot went up from Segor and settled in the mountain, he and his two daughters with him, for he was afraid to settle in Segor.

### DISCIPLE

### Jerome

The question is why he first preferred Segor to the mountain as a place of refuge and wanted it to be spared for his dwelling, yet now migrates again from Segor to the mountain.

### MASTER

We shall answer that the Hebrews’ conjecture concerning Segor is true: because it was frequently destroyed by earthquakes, it was first called Bale and afterward Salissa. Lot was afraid, saying: “If, while the other cities still stood, this one was often overthrown, how much less will it now be able to escape the general ruin?” This occasion of unbelief also provided the beginning for intercourse with his daughters.

Since he had seen the other cities destroyed while this one remained standing, and since he himself had been rescued by God’s help, he certainly ought not to have doubted what he had heard had been granted to him. But what is said in excuse for the daughters—that they thought the human race had perished and therefore slept with their father—does not excuse the father.

Finally, the Hebrews place a mark above what follows: “And he did not know when she lay down with him, nor when she rose from him,” as though it were incredible and contrary to nature that anyone could have intercourse without knowing it. The text continues:

> And Lot’s two daughters conceived by their father. The firstborn bore a son and called his name Moab. He is the father of the Moabites to this day. The younger also bore a son and called his name Ammon. He is the father of the Ammonites.

Moab means “from the father,” and the entire name is an etymology. Ammon, however, for whom the reason for the name is given as “son of my kindred,” or, more accurately in Hebrew, “son of my people,” is formed so that part of the name’s sense is conveyed by derivation, while in part it is itself the word. For **Ammi**, from which the Ammonites are named, means “my people.”

## Recapitulation of the Same Matter

Sodom was therefore turned into ashes, while Lot was delivered with his daughters. But what does it signify that the Lord said the city would be spared if fifty righteous persons, down to ten, were found in Sodom?

He established the number fifty as a sign of repentance, in case they might perhaps turn and be saved. For the number fifty is always referred to repentance. Hence David also wrote a psalm of repentance under that number. Accordingly, when God sees that the life of sinners has no desire to return to repentance, which the number fifty prefigures, he immediately restrains the burning heat of immoderate lust with the fire of Gehenna.

He said that Sodom would not perish if as many as ten righteous persons were found there, because if Christ’s name is found in anyone through the observance of the Ten Commandments, that person does not perish. The figure of the number ten demonstrates the cross of Christ.

The fact that there are five cities consumed by fiery rains signifies, unless I am mistaken, that all who have treated the five senses of their body lustfully will be burned in that future conflagration.

Lot himself, Abraham’s righteous and hospitable brother in Sodom, who deserved to escape safely from that fire—which was a likeness of the future judgment—bore the type of Christ’s body. This body now groans among all the saints amid the wicked and impious, whose deeds it has not shared, and at the end of the world it will be delivered through the mingling of waters, while those others are condemned to the punishment of eternal fire.

His wife, however, represented the kind of people who, though called by God’s grace, look back and strive to return to what they had left behind. Concerning them the Lord himself says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62). Hence she too is forbidden to look back, so that he might show by this that those who have been regenerated by God’s grace and desire to escape the final punishment must not return to their former life.

The text continues.

But the fact that she looked back and remained behind, being changed into salt, provides an example for seasoning believers, so that others may be salted by her. Christ himself did not pass over her, saying: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17:32)—that is, so that he might season us, as it were, with salt, so that we would not neglect these matters like fools but guard against them wisely. For she also gave this warning when she was changed into a statue of salt.

The text continues.

But the fact that Lot himself, fleeing burning Sodom, came to Segor and did not climb into the mountains signifies the following. To flee burning Sodom is to avoid the fires of unlawful flesh or the desires of the world. The height of the mountains is the contemplation of the perfect. But because there are many righteous people who flee the world’s enticements yet, being occupied in active life, cannot ascend to the summit of contemplation, this is what is meant by Lot’s leaving Sodom but not reaching the mountains: a condemnable life is abandoned, but the height of contemplation is not yet grasped with subtle understanding.

Hence Lot says to the angel:

> This city is near; we can flee there. Is it not a small one? And my soul will live in it?

It is therefore called “near,” yet it is said to be safe for salvation, because the active life is neither entirely separated from the cares of the world nor wholly alienated from the joy of eternal salvation.

The text continues.

In Lot himself, when his daughters slept with him, something else was figured—not what was signified when he was delivered from Sodom. At that time he seemed to bear the person of the future Law, from which certain people, propagated from it and placed under the Law, become drunk, in a manner of speaking, through misunderstanding, and bring forth works of unbelief by failing to use it lawfully.

“For the Law is good,” he says, “if anyone uses it lawfully,” as the Apostle says (1 Tim. 1:8).

Let us also hear what the poet sang about Lot and his wife:

> While Lot’s wife, as Lot fled the chaos of Sodom, looked back,  
> She remained astonished, changed into a statue of salt.  
> Turned into the punishment she deserved: for no one,  
> Avoiding the guilty dangers of a despised world,  
> Will be saved by looking backward; nor should the plowman,  
> Performing a worthy task, turn his face toward what lies behind him.

Why did the patriarch Abraham declare to King Abimelech that Sarah was his sister, when she was his wife? It therefore seems improper that he should have lied.

### Jerome

He did not, as many think, lie when he said, “She is my sister.” She was indeed his sister by his father, though not by his mother: she was the daughter of his brother Aran, not of his sister.

But since Hebrew has: “She is truly my sister,” that is, “the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother,” and since this sounds more strongly as though Sarah had been Abraham’s sister, we say in his defense that at that time such marriages had not yet been prohibited by law.

The narrative about Abimelech follows: Abraham concealed that Sarah was his wife and called her his sister, lest, after killing him, foreigners should take her captive. He was confident that God would not permit her to be violated, just as previously he had not permitted Pharaoh to violate her. Thus Abimelech, warned in a dream, did not defile her by intercourse but restored her untouched to her husband.

Nevertheless, I wish to know who was represented in that man, and whose wife she is who, in this pilgrimage and among foreigners, is not permitted to be polluted and defiled, so that she may be without stain or wrinkle for her husband.

The Church lives rightly for the glory of Christ, so that her beauty may be an honor to her husband, just as Abraham was honored among foreigners because of Sarah’s beauty. When she is told in the Song of Songs, “O beautiful among women,” kings rightly offer gifts to her beauty, just as King Abimelech offered gifts to Sarah, marveling in her at a beauty he could love but could not violate.

For the holy Church of the Lord Jesus Christ is a wife in secret. In hiddenness and in spiritual secrecy, the human soul cleaves to the Word of God, so that “the two may be one flesh” (Matt. 19:5). By this the Apostle commends the mystery of the great marriage in Christ and the Church.

Therefore the earthly kingdom of this age—the figure of which was borne by the kings who were not permitted to pollute Sarah—did not know or discover the Church as Christ’s spouse except when it attempted to violate her. By the divine testimony given through the faith of the martyrs, that kingdom yielded; and in its later kings it honored her with gifts, though in its earlier kings it had been unable to subject her to corruption. What was then represented first and afterward in the same king was fulfilled over time in the earlier and later kings of this kingdom.

When it is said that Christ’s Church is his sister by the father, not by the mother, the kinship being commended is not that of earthly generation, which will be abolished, but of heavenly grace, which will remain forever. Through that grace we, the mortal race, have received the power to be called and to be children of God.

We did not receive this grace from the Synagogue, the mother of Christ according to the flesh, but from God the Father. But, calling this kinship earthly in view of the other life, where no one dies, Christ taught us to deny it rather than acknowledge it, when the disciple says: “Do not call anyone on earth your father; for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. 23:9).

The fact that the Church’s husband is concealed from foreigners, while whose sister she is is not concealed, has an immediately apparent explanation: it is hidden and difficult to understand how the human soul is joined or united to the Word of God—or, as it is better and more aptly said, how the one is God and the other a creature. In this respect Christ and the Church are called bridegroom and bride, or husband and wife.

But because Jesus Christ and all the saints are brothers by kinship of divine grace, not by earthly blood, this is more expressively and intelligibly said to be by the father, not by the mother. All the saints are brothers among themselves through the same grace, but no one of them is the bridegroom of the rest by their fellowship.

## On Isaac’s Play with Ishmael

I wish to know how the play of Abraham’s two sons should be understood according to the literal sense.

### Jerome

Let us follow, according to the historical account, the opinions of earlier interpreters.

“Sarah,” it says, “saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, playing.” What follows—“with Isaac his son”—is not present in the Hebrew.

The Hebrews therefore explain the matter in two ways: either Ishmael made idols out of clay, in accordance with what is written elsewhere, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play”; or, because he was older, he claimed for himself the place and privileges of the firstborn in opposition to Isaac, as though in play.

When Sarah heard this, she could not tolerate it. This is confirmed by her own words:

> Cast out this slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.

> And he took bread and a skin of water and gave it to Hagar, placing the child upon her shoulder, and sent her away.

Here a question arises: what does this expulsion of Ishmael with his mother mean? When Isaac was born, Ishmael was thirteen years old, and after Isaac’s weaning he was expelled from the house with his mother. Many offer different opinions about this passage: some assign the time of weaning to the fifth year, while others claim the twelfth year. But, choosing the shorter age, we calculated that Ishmael was expelled with his mother after eighteen years. It would not be fitting for so large a youth to have been seated upon his mother’s neck. I ask you to explain this more accurately.

It is indeed a Hebrew idiom that every son, in comparison with his parents, is called an infant and a child. Nor should we be surprised that a barbarous language has its own peculiarities, since even today at Rome all sons are called infants.

Abraham therefore placed the bread and the skin upon Hagar’s shoulder. Having done this, he gave the boy to his mother—that is, he handed him over to her care and entrusted him to her—and so sent him out of the house.

What follows—

> And she cast the boy beneath a fir tree, and went away and sat opposite him at a distance, about a bowshot,

should be understood in this way:

> For she said, “I shall not see the death of my child.”

And she sat opposite him. Then the text adds:

> And the boy cried and wept, and the Lord heard the boy’s voice from the place where he was. And the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven, and so forth.

Let no one be troubled by this. In Hebrew, after the words “I shall not see the death of my child,” the text reads that Hagar herself sat opposite the boy, raised her voice, and wept, and that God heard the child.

As the mother wept and sorrowfully awaited her son’s death, God heard the child, concerning whom he had promised Abraham, saying: “I will also make the son of your slave woman into a great nation.” Otherwise, the mother too was lamenting not her own death but that of her son. God therefore spared the one for whom the weeping had taken place.

Finally, what follows says:

> Rise, take the boy, and hold his hand.

From this it is clear that the one being held was not a burden to his mother but a companion. The fact that he is held by a parent’s hand shows the solicitude of affection.

The question is why Sarah earlier wanted her husband to receive a son from the slave woman, and afterward orders him expelled from the house with his mother.

### Isidore

There is no doubt that she did this not because she was inflamed by jealousy, but because she was compelled by the mystery of prophecy.

For Hagar, as the Apostle says, bore a people into slavery, the carnal people; but Sarah, the free woman, bore a people who are not according to the flesh but have been called into freedom—and Christ freed them by that freedom.

This mystery therefore prefigured that the former people, generated in the slavery of sins within the house of Israel—that is, within the Church—would not remain forever, nor be heirs or companions of the worshipers of Christ, nor possess the kingdom of heavenly glory with the noble Son, that is, with the faithful people.

Let us now examine what follows.
