What does it signify that, as Hagar went out, she placed the infant upon her shoulders, except that the sinful and foolish people weighed upon the neck of their mother, the Synagogue, when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25)?

The bread indicated that the former priesthood would carry with it the bread of the Presence, as it is written, and would eat it.

The skin of water, which failed, signified the Jewish purification that was destined to fail—or their carnal doctrine enclosed in dead skin, that is, in the dead flesh of the old man, condemned by the sentence of transgression. It neither provides refreshment nor satisfies thirst, but, warm with fever, provokes vomiting.

The fact that Hagar wandered in the wilderness with her son signifies that the Synagogue, together with its people, expelled from its land without priesthood and sacrifice, wanders throughout the whole world and utterly ignores the Way, who is Christ.

The fact that her son perished from thirst shows a people possessing no spiritual purification. But when she cast her son, dying of thirst, beneath the tree, and, as the angel pointed it out, saw a spring, this signified that some among that people would seek refuge beneath the shadow of the wood of the cross.

When the boy cried out weeping, and God heard him, and, as the angel pointed it out, he saw the spring, this is spoken concerning those who turn from the Jews to Christ, and who, weeping over their past errors, are heard.

With the eyes of their hearts opened, they see the spring of living water, that is, Christ, the Son of the living God, who says: “I am the fountain of living water; let the one who thirsts come and drink” (John 7:37). Hence Ishmael is interpreted as “hearing” or “exaudition.”

This angel is an image of Elijah, through whom that people will come to believe, as it is said through Malachi: “Behold, I send you Elijah, who will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children” (Mal. 4:5), and so forth.

But when the angel of the Lord immediately called Hagar, saying, “Rise, take the boy, for I will make him into a great nation,” this signified either that the numerous Jewish people would reign in this age, or that those who among the Jews would believe in Christ would attain the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

As for the same angel who speaks to Hagar: Scripture first calls him an angel, and afterward the Lord. We must believe that he was the Son of God, who has always spoken through the Law and the Prophets. He is called an angel because of his obedience to the Father’s will, but God according to the Father’s nature, because he himself is truly God, just as the Father is.

## On the Well of the Oath

### Jerome

Abraham said to Abimelech:

> You will accept these seven ewe-lambs from me, so that they may be a testimony for me that I dug this well.

Therefore he called the name of that place “Well of the Oath,” because the two of them had sworn there.

Where the text here reads “Well of the Oath,” Hebrew has **Beersheba**. I do not hesitate to explain what this is intended to mean.

There are two reasons why it was so called: either because Abimelech received seven ewe-lambs from Abraham’s hand—for seven is called **šebaʿ**—or because they swore there, since an oath is likewise called **šebaʿ**.

If we have read this name earlier, before the event that gave rise to it, we should know that it has been spoken by prolepsis, as with Bethel and Gilgal. Until the time when they were so called, those places certainly had other names.

It must also be noted from both the earlier passages and the present one that Isaac was not born beside the oak of Mamre, or in the valley of Mamre, as it is found in Hebrew, but in Gerar, where Beersheba is still a town. That province, not long ago, was called Salutaris after the division of the provinces of Palestine among the governors.

Scripture bears witness to this when it says:

> And Abraham dwelt in the land of the Philistines for many days.

The text continues:

> And God said to Abraham, “Take your son, your beloved Isaac, and go to the land of vision,” and so forth.

I wish to know what this land of vision is.

It is difficult to translate the idiom of the Hebrew language into Latin where the text now says, “Go to the high land.” Hebrew has **Moriah**, which Aquila translated as **τὴν καταφανῆ**, that is, “the manifest” or “conspicuous” land. Symmachus has **τῆς ὀπτασίας**, that is, “of vision.”

The Hebrews therefore say that this is the mountain on which the Temple was later built, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, just as it is written in Chronicles:

> And they began to build the Temple in the second month, on the second day of the month, on Mount Moriah.

It is therefore interpreted as “illuminating” and “shining” because there is the **Dabir**, that is, the oracle of God, as well as the Law and the Holy Spirit, who teaches human beings the truth and inspires the prophets.

The text continues:

> And he went to the place that God had appointed for him on the third day.

It must be noted that the journey from Gerar to Mount Moriah, that is, to the site of the Temple, takes three days, and consequently the text says that he arrived there on the third day.

Some therefore judge incorrectly when they think that Abraham was living at that time beside the oak of Mamre, since from there to Mount Moriah is scarcely a full day’s journey.

The text continues:

> And Abraham lifted up his eyes, and behold, a ram behind him was held by its horns in the thicket of Sabech.

How is this to be understood?

Eusebius of Emesa has said something ridiculous here:

> “Sabech,” he says, “means a he-goat which, with upright horns, rises high so that it may pluck the leaves of a tree.”

Aquila, again, translated it as **συχνεών**, which we may call “a thicket” or “a place of brambles,” or, if we explain the force of the word, dense branches intertwined with one another. Symmachus, led to the same opinion, says:

> And a ram appeared, afterward held by its horns in a net.

But in this passage alone, some seem to have translated more accurately—the Septuagint and Theodotion—who retained the name **Sabech**, saying:

> In the thicket of Sabech by its horns.

For **συχνεών**, or “net,” which Aquila rendered, and which Symmachus writes with the letter sigma, has here the letter samekh. From this it is clear that **Sabech** does not mean a mass of densely growing plants or branches woven together like a net, but is the name of the thicket, which is called so in Hebrew.

I myself, investigating carefully, have frequently found **συχνεών** written with the letter samekh.

The text continues:

> And Abraham called the name of that place, “The Lord saw.”

Why did it receive this name?

Where the text here has “saw,” Hebrew has “will see.” Among the Hebrews this has become a proverb, so that whenever they are in distress and desire to be lifted up by the Lord’s help, they say: “On the mountain the Lord will be seen”—that is, “Just as he had mercy on Abraham, so he will have mercy on us.”

For this reason, even now they are accustomed to blow a horn as a sign of the ram that was given.

## Recapitulation

Abraham is commanded to sacrifice his only son, but he obeys God and fulfills his vow. He saddles the donkey, places the wood upon it, sends the servants away at a distance, and ascends alone with his son. He reaches the place in three days. Before the son arrives at the place of sacrifice, he himself carries the wood on which he is to be sacrificed.

Then Abraham arms himself with a sword, and when he is already almost striking, he is instructed to spare him. Yet he does not abandon his fervor without sacrifice and blood. A ram appears in the thicket, caught by its horns. It is sacrificed, and the sacrifice is completed. After the sacrifice, Abraham is told:

> I will bless you and multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea. Your offspring shall possess the gates of their enemies, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your offspring, because you obeyed my voice.

## Spiritual Explanation

Let us now see what mystery lies hidden beneath this sacrament.

When this Abraham brought his only son to be sacrificed, he bore the person of God the Father. But what does it mean that he received him as an old man? God does not grow old. The very proclamation concerning Christ had, in a certain sense, already grown old when Christ was born. It began from Adam, where it was said, “The two shall be one flesh” (Matt. 19:5). That great mystery—the mystery of Christ and the Church—was completed in the sixth age of the world, which signifies Abraham’s old age. For that mystery of God was ancient and long-lived.

Sarah’s old age, in the people of God—that is, in the multitude of the prophets—signifies the same thing, because at the end of the ages Christ was born from that people of holy souls.

Her barrenness indicates that in this age we have been saved in hope, and that in Christ, as in Isaac, we have all been born. She prophetically announced the Church’s birth at the end of the ages through the wondrous grace of God, not through natural fertility.

Now the sacramental meaning of the subsequent history, which was figuratively foreshadowed, must be examined.

Who, then, was represented in Abraham, as was said above, through that sacrifice, except the exalted Father? And who in Isaac except Christ?

For just as Abraham offered his only and beloved son to God as a victim, so the Lord gave his only Son for us all. And just as Isaac himself carried the wood upon which he was to be laid, so Christ bore upon his shoulders the wood of the cross on which he was to be crucified.

The two servants who were left behind and not brought to the place of sacrifice represented the Jews. Living servilely and understanding carnally, they did not understand Christ’s humanity or his Passion; therefore they did not reach the place of sacrifice.

Why were there two servants? Because the people itself was to be divided into two parts. This happened when Solomon sinned, when that same people was divided with respect to the kingdom—not through an error of impiety. To these two parts the Prophet often says: “Israel the apostate and Judah the treacherous,” and so forth (Jer. 3:8).

The donkey was the senseless foolishness of the Jews. This senseless foolishness carried all the sacraments, but did not know what it was carrying.

As for what was said to them, “Wait here with the donkey,” up to “We will return to you,” hear the Apostle: “A partial hardening has come upon Israel” (Rom. 11:25). This partial hardening is here with the donkey, “until the fullness of the nations,” he says, “should enter.”

That is, after we have worshiped, when the sacrifice of the Lord’s cross has been fulfilled and has been preached among the nations—this is what is meant by “until the fullness of the nations should enter.”

What is meant by “We will return to you”? “And so all Israel will be saved.”

The three days in which they came to the place of sacrifice signify the three ages of the world: one before the Law, another under the Law, and a third under grace.

Before the Law extends from Abraham to Moses; under the Law, from Moses to John; thereafter begins the age of the Lord and whatever remains. The third day is the age of grace, in which, in the third age, as though after three days, the mystery of Christ’s sacrifice was completed.

Then Isaac is placed upon the altar with his feet bound, and the Lord is suspended upon the wood and fastened to the cross.

But what was figured in Isaac passed over to the ram. Why? Because Christ is the sheep: he is both Son and Lamb; Son because he was born, ram because he was sacrificed.

But what does it mean that the ram was caught in the thicket? The cross has horns. For when two pieces of wood are joined together, they form the appearance of a cross. Hence it is written concerning him: “Horns are in his hands.”

The ram caught by its horns therefore signifies the crucified Lord. The thicket consists of thorns. Thorns signify the wicked and sinners who hung the Lord upon the cross. The Lord was therefore suspended among the thorns of the Jewish sinners, just as he says through Jeremiah: “This people has surrounded me with the thorns of its sins.”

Others have understood this ram, bound by its horns in the thicket, as the same Christ crowned with thorns by the Jews before he was sacrificed.

After the sacrifice was completed, Abraham was told:

> In your offspring all the nations shall be blessed.

When did this happen except when the ram says:

> They dug my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones (Ps. 21:17–18)?

When that sacrifice was completed in the Psalms, then the same Psalm said:

> All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations (ibid. 28–29).

After Abraham sacrificed the ram in place of his son Isaac, he called the name of that place “The Lord saw,” because it means “The Lord caused [it] to be seen,” namely through the incarnation.

The text continues:

> I wish to be instructed concerning Job and his lineage, so that the truth may be clearly revealed.

### Jerome

> And they announced to Abraham, saying: “Behold, Milcah has also borne sons to Nahor your brother: Uz his firstborn, and Buz his brother, and Kemuel, the father of the Syrians, and Chesed.”

Nahor, Abraham’s brother, had his firstborn, Uz, from Milcah, his wife, the daughter of Aram. From Uz descended Job’s lineage, as it is written at the beginning of his book:

> There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job (Job 1:1).

Some therefore judge incorrectly that Job was of Esau’s lineage. For what is found at the end of his book—because it was translated from the Syriac language, and because he is said to be the fourth after Esau, along with the other material contained there—is not found in the Hebrew books.

The second son born to Milcah was Buz, whom the Septuagint wished to render as Bauz. According to the Hebrews, that Balaam, the diviner, was descended from his line. In the Book of Job he is first called Helius, a holy man and prophet of God; afterward, through disobedience and desire for gifts, when he wished to curse Israel, he was called by the name “diviner.”

“Then the anger of Helui, son of Barachiel the Buzite, was kindled”—that is, he descended from the root of this Buz.

Kemuel was the father of Damascus. Damascus itself is called Aram, which is written here for Syria and is read under that name in Isaiah.

Caseth is also the fourth, from whom the Chaldeans, that is, the Caldeans, were afterward named.

## On Sarah’s Death
### Jerome

What are we to understand by the place Arboc, where Sarah is said to have died? “Sarah died,” he says, “in the city of Arboc, which is in the valley; this is Hebron in the land of Canaan.” But the words “which is in the valley,” placed here, are not found in the authoritative manuscripts. The name of the city, too, has gradually been corrupted by copyists and readers. For we must not suppose that the Seventy Translators rendered the Hebrew name of the city barbarously, corruptly, and otherwise than it is pronounced in their own language. Arboc means absolutely nothing; rather, it is called Arbec—that is, “four”—because Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were buried there, as was Adam himself, the original prince of the human race, as is shown more clearly in the Book of Joshua. It continues:

“And Ephron said to Abraham: ‘Hear us, my lord; you are a prince from God among us. Bury your dead in the chosen tomb of ours.’” In place of *king* he has *prince* or *duke*. For *nasin* means not “king” but “duke.” It continues:

“And Abraham weighed out to Ephron the silver that he had spoken in the hearing of the sons of Heth.” In Hebrew, as we have written it here, his name is written *Ephron* the first time and *Ephran* the second. After he had been overcome by the price so that he would sell the tomb and receive the silver—although Abraham compelled him—the letter *waw*, which among them is pronounced like *a*, was removed from his name; in its place he was called *Ephran*. Scripture thus indicates that he was not a man of complete and perfect virtue, since he was able to sell the memorial places of the dead.

Therefore let those who sell tombs know that their name is changed and something of their merit perishes—not only when they are compelled to accept a price, but even when they extort it from those who are unwilling to pay; for even that man is secretly reproved because he accepted the money unwillingly.

### Recapitulation

Sarah dies in the hundred and twentieth year of her life, and, after purchasing the field from Ephron, they bury her. But I wish to know what is meant by Sarah’s being buried in a double tomb. This at least must be understood: the soul that dies to the world in order to live for God is received into a twofold rest of life—that is, in the practice of good works and in the contemplation of the Divinity.

### On the oath of the servant at Abraham’s thigh

[Col. 0321C] **Jerome.**—“Abraham was old and advanced in age. He said to his servant, the elder who was over all that he possessed: ‘Place your hand under my thigh, so that I may bind you by oath before the God of heaven and earth: you shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, but you shall go to my land and my kindred, and from there take a wife for my son Isaac.’ The servant placed his hand under Abraham’s thigh and swore to him.”

Why does he swear at Abraham’s thigh, as though at a holy place? Concerning this word the Hebrews relate that he swore by the sanctification—that is, by circumcision. We, however, say that he swore by the offspring of Abraham, that is, by Christ, who was to be born from him, in accordance with the words of the evangelist Matthew: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.”

It continues:

“And the servant went into Mesopotamia of Syria, and stood beside the well; and behold, Rebecca came to draw water for the flocks. And the servant said: ‘Behold, I stand beside the spring of water, and the daughters of the men of the city will come out to draw water. Let the maiden who comes out to draw water be the one to whom I say, “Give me water from your jar to drink,”’” and so forth up to: “She is the one whom the Lord has prepared for the son of my master,” and what follows.

“And the man took a golden earring, weighing a didrachm.” *Baca*, which is written here for “didrachm,” is half an ounce. A *shekel*, which in Latin speech is corruptly called a *siclus*, weighs an ounce.

What does it mean that this passage is found in such varied forms in the translations? In some copies, I find that Abraham’s servant said: “And behold, the maiden who comes out to draw water,” and so forth. In others, however, instead of “maiden” we read “young woman.” Explain how these versions agree with one another.

In Hebrew we read there also “young woman,” which in Greek is called *neanis* (νεανὶς): *Alma*. This same name occurs in Isaiah, where in our manuscripts it is written: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive.” Aquila translated: “Behold, the young woman shall conceive and bear.” In Hebrew: “Behold, the *alma* shall conceive.”

It must therefore be noted that the name *Alma* is never written except of a virgin, and that it has the etymology *apokryphos* (ἀπόκρυφος), that is, “hidden.” For it is written in Job: “But wisdom—where is it found, and where is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of every living being.” Where we have now said “it is hidden,” the Hebrew, because of the inflection of the verb, has a different form: *Naalma*. Something similar occurs, although it is inflected in the masculine gender. And in the Books of Kings it is written in the words of Elisha to Gehazi: “The Lord has hidden it from me.”

Therefore *alma*, which is interpreted as “hidden”—that is, a virgin guarded with the greatest care—seems to me to express greater praise than merely “virgin.” A virgin, according to the Apostle, can be so in body and not in spirit; but a hidden woman who is a virgin possesses an intensification (*epitasin*, ἐπίτασιν) of virginity, so that she is both virgin and hidden. And one who is hidden is, according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, consequently also a virgin; whereas from the fact that someone is a virgin it does not immediately follow that she is hidden.

We read this same word in Exodus of Mary, the virgin sister of Moses. Let the Jews therefore show it written somewhere in the Scriptures that *alma* signifies only a young woman and not a virgin; then we shall concede to them that the words found in Isaiah among us—“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear”—mean not a hidden virgin but a young woman who is already married.

It continues:

“And they sent away Rebecca their sister, and her possessions, and Abraham’s servant and the men who were with him.” In Hebrew it reads: “And they sent away Rebecca their sister, and her nurse, and Abraham’s servant, and his men.” For it was fitting that a virgin going to her wedding without her parents should be comforted by the companionship of her nurse.

It continues:

“For Isaac lived in the land of the South, and he went out to meditate in the field toward evening.” I desire to know what this going out of Isaac into the field toward evening signifies. It seems to me to indicate the place from which he had once been led away by his Father for sacrifice.

As for the words “he went out to meditate in the field,” which in Greek is called *adoleschesai* (ἀδολεσχῆσαι), Hebrew has: “Isaac went out to speak in the field, as evening was already declining.” This signifies, in accordance with the fact that the Lord alone prayed on the mountain, that Isaac also—who was a type of the Lord—went out from his house to pray as a righteous man and offered spiritual sacrifices either at the ninth hour or before sunset.

It continues.

### Disciple

“And Rebecca saw Isaac, and she took her *theristrum* and covered herself.” Explain what a *theristrum* is.

### Master

A *theristrum* is called a cloak; it is also a kind of Arabian garment still worn by the women of that province.

It continues.

“And Abraham added another wife and took one named Keturah, and she bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. Jokshan fathered Sheba and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim. The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Sheba, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the sons of Keturah. Abraham gave everything he possessed to Isaac; but to the sons of his concubines he gave gifts, and while he was still alive he sent them away from Isaac his son toward the east, to the eastern land” (Gen. XXV).

### Disciple

Who is this Keturah, or from what family was she, and what is the interpretation of her name? I ask you to explain.

### Master

In Hebrew, Keturah is interpreted as “joined” or “conquered.” For this reason the Hebrews suspect that, although her name was changed, she was the same person as Hagar the Egyptian, who, after Sarah’s death, became Abraham’s wife. In this way they seem to excuse the age of the already decrepit Abraham, so that an old man may not be accused of indulging in new marriages after the death of his aged wife.

Leaving aside what is uncertain, we say this: according to the historians among the Hebrews, the sons born to Abraham from Keturah occupied Troglodytis (Τρωγλοδύτις) and Arabia, now called Eudaimon (Εὐδαίμων), as far as the Red Sea. It is said that one of Abraham’s descendants, named Epher, led an army against Libya, settled there after defeating its inhabitants, and that his descendants named Africa after their forefather.

Alexander, called Polyhistor, and Cleodemus, surnamed Malchus, are witnesses to this matter; in Greek they unravel a barbarian history.

As for the statement that the sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim, they think that *Asshurim* is to be translated “merchants,” *Letushim* “workers who forge bronze and iron,” and *Leummim* *philarchos* (φίλαρχος), that is, “a ruler of many tribes and peoples.” Others contend that the Asshurim were so called because they were Syrians, and that many regions of India were occupied by Abraham’s sons from Keturah.

### Recapitulation from the oath of the servant at the thigh to the sons of Keturah

We must observe why Abraham, asking his servant for fidelity under oath, said: “Place your hand under my thigh, and I bind you by oath before the God of heaven” (Gen. XXIV). What does “the God of heaven” in relation to Abraham’s thigh mean except that a sacrament is being indicated? For by the thigh offspring is understood.

What, then, was that oath except that it signified that the God of heaven would come in the flesh from Abraham’s lineage? This servant, moreover, bore the image of the Law, through which the bride—that is, the Church of Christ—was betrothed.

The young man therefore went to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor, and stood beside the well, seeking a bride for his master’s son (ibid.). So also the Law, which comes after faith, came to the font of baptism; there, while praying, it encountered the virgin Rebecca, that is, the Church.

Rebecca saw the young man—that is, the prophetic word—and lowered the jar from her shoulder (ibid.), namely, the elevated eloquence of the world, bending herself toward the humble prophetic word. She received from the young man a golden earring—that is, she accepted the ornaments of faith or conduct, and also the golden meanings of the Scriptures and the clear eloquence of silver—and so Rebecca followed the young man and came to Isaac.

The Church, following the prophetic word, came to Christ. Yet she is led upon the back of a camel, because the Church, hastening to Christ from the Gentiles, is found to have been turned away from the twisted and vicious ways of its former life. When she saw Isaac, she descended from the camel, because, once the Lord was recognized, the Gentiles abandoned their vices and, turning away from lofty pride, sought the path of humility. She was also covered with a cloak in modesty, because in his presence she is ashamed of the errors of her former life.

As for Isaac’s going out into the field when the day was already declining, this signified that at the end of the world, as though at the close of the day, Christ would come. He went out, as it were, into a field, because although he is invisible, he showed himself visible in this world when the needs of the Church required it.

The Church found him at the well of vision—that is, in the contemplation and understanding of truth, where she might receive a higher understanding—or at the washing of water, where she might be purified. Thereafter she was joined to her bridegroom Christ, cleaving to him in the glory of eternity and the kingdom.

It continues.

What is meant by Abraham’s taking Keturah as his wife after Sarah’s death? Was it perhaps because of incontinence, when he was already advanced in age? Far from it. It was for the procreation of children, since seed like the stars of heaven had been promised to him through his son Isaac.

Let us therefore see what this Keturah signifies. Just as Hagar and Ishmael signified the carnal people of the Old Testament, so Keturah and her sons signified heretics, who consider themselves to belong to the New Testament but are called the sons of a concubine. Sarah alone is always called a wife, as it is written: “My dove is one, my perfect one is one” (Song VI).

It continues.

What are we to understand from the fact that Abraham gave everything he possessed to his son Isaac, but gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and separated them from him? Some gifts are indeed given to the sons of concubines—that is, to carnal people—but neither heretics nor Jews, because they pursue material gains, attain the promised kingdom. There is no heir except Isaac, because those counted as offspring are not the children of the flesh but the children of the promise.

### On the death of Abraham

**Jerome.**—“And Abraham died in a good old age, old and full of days, and was gathered to his people.” The addition found in the Seventy Translators is incorrect: “Abraham died failing,” because it is unfitting for Abraham to fail and diminish.

Moreover, what we have rendered “in a good old age, old and full,” is written in the Greek manuscripts as “full of days.” Although this seems to explain the meaning—that he died full of light and of the works of the day—

### Likewise, the names of the sons of Ishmael in their generations and names

**Jerome.**—“The firstborn of Ishmael was Nebaioth and Kedar,” and the rest, up to the place where it says: “And they dwelt from Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt as one goes toward Assyria; he fell before all his brothers” (Gen. XXV).

Twelve sons were born to Ishmael. The firstborn was Nebaioth, from whom the entire region extending from the Euphrates to the Red Sea is called Nabataea to this day; it is part of Arabia. Even the towns, villages, fortified settlements, and tribes of those regions are known by the names of these men: Kedar is in the desert; Duma is another region; Teman is toward the South; and Kedemah is said to lie toward the East.

But at the end of this chapter, where according to the Seventy we read, “He shall dwell opposite all his brothers,” the reading we have given is more accurate: “He fell before all his brothers”—that is, he died in the hands of all his sons, with his children surviving him, and no one having been taken by death before him.

That “brothers” can be used for “sons” is shown by Jacob’s words to Laban: “What is my sin, that you pursued me, and that you searched through all my vessels? What have you found among all the vessels of your house? Let it be placed before my brothers and your brothers, and let them judge between us” (Gen. XXXI). For we cannot believe that, as Scripture relates, Jacob had any brothers with him apart from his children.

It continues, concerning Rebecca’s conception.

“And Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren, and he heard him and granted conception to Rebecca” (Gen. XXV).

**Jerome.**—“And Rebecca conceived, and her children struggled within her.” For “struggled,” the Seventy Translators placed *eskirtōn* (ἐσκίρτων), that is, “they played”; or, as Aquila translated it, “the children were being crushed in her womb.” Symmachus, however, used *diepleon* (διέπλεον), that is, “they were carried along on the surface like a ship.”

It continues: “And the first came out red, entirely hairy like a skin” (ibid.). Where we have written “hairy,” the Hebrew has *Se‘ir*. Hence Esau also, as we read elsewhere, was called Seir—that is, “hairy.”

[Col. 0324D] **Disciple.**

**Gregory.**—God promised Abraham, saying: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. XXI). He also said to him: “I have made you the father of many nations” (Gen. XVII). Again he promised him, saying: “Blessing I will bless you, and I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore” (Gen. XXII).

It is therefore plainly evident that almighty God had predestined Abraham’s offspring to be multiplied through Isaac. Yet it is written: “Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren; and he heard him and granted conception to Rebecca” (Gen. XXV). If, then, the multiplication of Abraham’s race through Isaac was predestined, why did he receive a barren wife?

### Master

Those things that holy men accomplish by praying are predestined in such a way that they are obtained through prayers. Even the predestination of the eternal kingdom has been arranged by almighty God in such a way that the elect reach it through labor, so that by asking they may merit to receive what almighty God determined before the ages to give them.

Consider whether this is true in relation to what you have proposed, and you will be able to prove it readily: predestination is fulfilled through prayers when the man through whom God had predestined Abraham’s offspring to be multiplied obtained by prayer the ability to have children.

### Recapitulation

Isaac, then, while asking the Lord that his barren wife might give birth, received what he requested. Twins struggled within her, confined by the narrowness of the womb. While these things were occurring, she inquired of the Lord and received the answer: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your body; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger” (ibid.).

The figurative meaning of this event is known even to the Jews, though they do not believe it: the people of the Church would overcome the people of the Synagogue, and the Jewish nation, once greater in time, would serve the lesser people of Christians.

The same can also be said of each one of us: two nations and two peoples are within us, namely, those of vices and virtues. One is lesser, the other greater. For the wicked are always more numerous than the good, and vices outnumber virtues; nevertheless, in us too, by the grace of God, one people overcomes the other, and the greater serves the lesser. The flesh serves the spirit, and vices yield to virtues.

Esau comes forth first, red and entirely like a hairy skin. Then his brother Jacob comes out, and his hand had grasped Esau’s heel (ibid.). But why is he entirely red and hairy, except because the former people was defiled by the blood of the prophets and of Christ and was surrounded by the filth of sin and wickedness? For this reason the younger held his heel: mystically, the lesser people was to overcome the greater.

It continues.

“Esau became a man skilled in hunting and an agricultural man. But Jacob was simple and dwelt in tents” (ibid.). Another translation has: “He dwelt at home.”

[Col. 0325C] **Gregory.**—What is signified by Esau’s hunting except the life of those who, spread out among external pleasures, follow the flesh? He is also described as an agricultural man because lovers of this world inhabit external things all the more intensely as they leave their inner selves uncultivated.

Jacob, however, is said to dwell simply in tents, because all who avoid scattering themselves in external cares remain simple in the dwelling of their thought and conscience. To dwell in tents or in a house means to confine oneself within the secrets of the mind and not to disperse oneself outwardly through desires; rather, those who gape after many external things withdraw from thoughts that have alienated them from themselves.

**Jerome.**—“And Esau said to Jacob: ‘Give me a taste of this red stew, because I am fainting’” (ibid.). Therefore his name was called Edom. “Red,” or “ruddy,” is called *Edom* in the Hebrew language. Thus, because he sold his birthright for red food, he received the name of Ruddy—that is, Edom.

[Col. 0325D] **Gregory.**—Concerning Esau, who sold his birthright to his brother for a dish of lentils, he says as follows:

We must know that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways. Sometimes it anticipates the time of need; sometimes it does not anticipate the time, but seeks more luxurious foods. Sometimes any food would suffice, yet it demands that it be prepared with excessive care. Sometimes the kind and time of the food are appropriate, but the mind exceeds the measure of nourishment in the quantity consumed. At other times, what it desires is more contemptible, yet it sins more gravely in the heat of its immense longing.

We can show these forms of vice more clearly if we establish them through more evident examples. Jonathan incurred the sentence of death from his father because he anticipated the appointed time for eating by tasting honey. The people led out of Egypt died in the wilderness because, scorning manna, they desired meat, which they considered more luxurious. The first sin of the sons of Eli arose because, at their request, the priest’s servant wanted to receive from the sacrifice not meat cooked according to ancient custom but raw meat, which he could prepare more carefully.

And when it is said to Jerusalem, “This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, and abundance of water” (Ezek. XVI), it is plainly shown that she lost salvation because, together with the fault of pride, she exceeded the measure of immoderate indulgence.

For this reason he lost the glory of the firstborn: he intensely desired a desirable food, namely, lentils. By preferring them to his birthright when he sold it, he showed how he panted after that appetite. It is not the food but the appetite that is at fault. Thus we often consume more luxurious foods without guilt, while we taste more contemptible foods only with the guilt of desire.

This Esau, whom we have mentioned, lost his primacy for lentils, whereas Elijah preserved the strength of his body by eating meat in the wilderness. Therefore the ancient enemy, understanding that the cause of condemnation is not food but the desire for food, subjected the first man to himself not through meat but through a fruit, and tempted the second not through meat but through bread.

Hence Adam’s sin is often repeated even when what is consumed is lowly and worthless. For Adam alone did not receive the command forbidding him to eat the prohibited fruit. When God points out that certain foods are harmful to our health, he forbids them to us, as it were, by a sentence. When we touch harmful things in desire, what else are we doing but tasting what is forbidden?

We must therefore consume what the necessity of nature seeks, not what the appetite for eating suggests, lest, if this moderate discernment does not watch carefully enough, someone plunge himself into the abyss of unlawful desire.

**Isidore.**—The fact that this Esau sold his birthright to his younger brother for food and afterward was deprived of the paternal blessing promised to him signifies the same Israelite people. As the Book of Exodus indicates, it was called the firstborn son; yet it not only lost the honor of its primacy, but also did not merit to obtain the prepared reward of the heavenly kingdom. The Lord reproaches it in a certain manner when he says: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation doing his will” (Matt. XXI).

The birthright itself was the priestly garment, which the firstborn, clothed in it together with their father’s blessing, wore when they offered sacrifices to God like high priests, before Aaron was chosen for the priesthood.

Thus the Jews lost, through their desire for earthly love, both the glory of the future kingdom and what belonged to it.

It continues.

### On the generations of Isaac’s sons

A famine then arose in the land, and Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar (Gen. XXVI).

**Jerome.**—“Isaac sowed in that land and found a hundredfold barley in that year” (ibid.). Although Isaac sowed in a foreign land, I do not think that the yield of barley was so great for him. I therefore consider the Hebrew reading better, which Aquila also translated: “And he found a hundredfold estimate”—that is, *hekaton eikasménon* (ἑκατὸν εἰκασμένον).

Although “estimate” and “barley” are written with the same letters, the forms *se‘arim* mean “estimates,” whereas *se‘orim* mean “barleys.” Since Scripture does not specify the kind of crop that yielded a hundredfold, it seems to me to indicate the multiplication of all his virtues.

Accordingly, it follows: “And the Lord blessed him, and the man became great, and he went on, growing greater, until he became exceedingly great” (ibid.). But I do not know whether the multiplication of barley could make anyone glorious.

It continues.

“And Isaac departed from there and came to the valley of Gerar, and dwelt there” (ibid.). In Hebrew, instead of “valley,” it has “torrent.” For once Isaac had become great, he could not have dwelt in a valley. He dwelt beside the torrent of which it is written: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way” (Ps. CIX). Elijah also drank from it in the time of famine.

But because Elijah was not like Christ, that torrent dried up for him. Our Lord, however, was also handed over in the torrent, dedicating our regeneration and the sacrament of baptism.

It continues.

“And Isaac dug a well in the valley of Gerar, and found there a well of living water” (ibid.). Here too, instead of “valley,” it has “torrent.” A well of living water is never found in a valley.

It continues.

“And they dug another well, and they quarreled over it also, and he called its name Hostility” (ibid.). For “hostilities,” Aquila translated *ten antikeimenēn* (τὴν ἀντικειμένην), and Symmachus *enaktíōsin* (ἐνακτίωσιν), that is, “adversarial” and “opposing.” In Hebrew it has *Satan*. From this we understand that *Satan* is interpreted as “opponent.”

“And they dug another well, and they did not quarrel with them, and he called its name Broad Places” (ibid.). For “broadness,” Hebrew has *Rehoboth*, confirming what we said above: “He built Nineveh the city, and Rehoboth”—that is, “its streets” (Gen. X).

It continues.

“And Abimelech came to him from Gerar, with Ahuzzath his friend and Phicol the commander of his army” (Gen. XXVI).

In Hebrew, instead of *Ahuzzath*, it has “the company of his friends,” so that the word signifies not so much a single man as a crowd of friends who had come with the king, among whom was Phicol, commander of the army.

It continues:

“And Isaac’s servants came and reported to him concerning the well which they had dug, and said to him: ‘We have found water.’ And he called its name Abundance” (ibid.).

I do not know how the Seventy Translators have: “And Isaac’s servants came and reported concerning the well which they had dug; and they said to him: ‘We have not found water.’ And he called its name Oath.” What etymology could justify calling it “Oath” because he had not found water?

On the contrary, in Hebrew—which Aquila and Symmachus also follow—the meaning is that he found water, and for that reason the well itself was called “Abundance.” “And the city was called Beersheba” (ibid.), that is, “well of abundance.”

Although above we asserted that Beersheba was named either from the word of the oath or from the number of the seven sheep, since *sabe* means “seven,” Isaac now, because water had been found, slightly altered the letter in the name of that city, which had already been so called. Instead of the Hebrew *sin*, with which *sabe* begins, he used the Greek sigma—that is, the Hebrew *samekh*.

Otherwise, according to the rule of allegory, after so many wells it would in no way be fitting for Isaac to have found no water at the end of his virtues.

### Recapitulation from the preceding section

At the Lord’s command and blessing, Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines. There, out of fear, he pretended that his wife Rebecca was his sister. The foreign king discovered that she was Isaac’s wife when he saw him playing with her.

What does it mean, in the sacrament of Christ and the Church, that so great a patriarch played with his wife, and that the marriage was recognized in this way? Whoever carefully examines the mystery of her husband in the holy Scriptures surely sees how not to fall into error by sinning in the Church. He discovers that Christ temporarily concealed his majesty, by which in the form of God he is equal to the Father, in the form of a servant, so that human weakness might be able to receive him; and in this way he fittingly adapted himself to his bride.

For what is absurd—or rather, what is not suitably adapted to the prediction of future events—if God’s prophet played in a bodily manner so as to win the affection of his wife, when the Word of God himself became flesh in order to dwell among us (John I)?

After this Scripture relates that, after the Lord had blessed Isaac and he had become exceedingly great, he undertook the work of digging the wells that the servants of his father Abraham had dug. But the Philistines, envying him, stopped them up by filling them with earth, and so forth (Gen. XXVI).

Who is this Isaac except our Savior? When he descended into this torrent of Gerar, he first of all wished to dig again those wells that the servants of his father had dug. Moses had dug the well of the Law; David, Solomon, and the prophets had written the books of the Old Testament. Yet the Jews’ and heretics’ earthly and sordid understanding had filled these wells.

When Isaac wished to cleanse them, to show that everything said by the Law and the prophets had been said about him, the Philistines—that is, the Jews, alienated from the kingdom of God—quarreled with him. But he departed from them. He cannot be with those who do not want the wells to contain water but earth. He says to them: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

Isaac therefore dug a new well—or rather, Isaac’s servants dug it. Isaac’s servants are Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Peter, James, Jude, Paul, and the others, all of whom dug the well of the New Testament and found living water, which is a spring of water leaping up into eternal life (John IV).

But those who think in earthly terms still quarrel over these things. They can endure neither the establishment of what is new nor the cleansing of what is old; they oppose the evangelical wells and resist the apostles. Because they contradict everything and quarrel, it is said to them: “Since you have judged yourselves unworthy of the grace of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

After this Isaac dug a third well and called its name Broad Places, saying: “Now God has enlarged us and made us fruitful upon the earth” (Gen. XXVI). Truly Isaac—that is, Christ—was enlarged. He filled the whole earth with the knowledge of the Trinity and established the Church’s breadth throughout the world.

Previously God was known only in Judea and was named in Israel (Ps. LXXV); now “their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII). For Isaac’s servants went out through the whole world, dug wells, and showed water to everyone, while the apostles baptized all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. XXVIII).

### Disciple

But what does it mean that Isaac called the wells opened by Abraham by the same names as his father had called them?

### Master

It must certainly be understood that Moses is also called Moses among us, just as every prophet is called by his own name; the names of the wells are not changed, as though they were the designations of different wells. These matters are mystical.

[Col. 0328C] **Gregory.**—In the moral sense, Isaac is described as digging wells among a foreign people. By this example we learn that, placed in the hardship of this pilgrimage, we should penetrate the depths of our thoughts, and that, until the water of true understanding answers us, the hand of our inquiry must never grow sluggish in drawing out the earthly things of the heart.

Yet the Allophyli lying in wait fill these wells, because unclean spirits, when they see us carefully confessing our sins, pour troublesome thoughts of temptation into us. And because, if we often attend to sacred speech, we endure the snares of wicked spirits more grievously: they scatter the dust of earthly thoughts over our minds in order to obscure the eyes of our attention from the light of inner vision.

The mind must therefore always be emptied and incessantly dug out, lest, if it is left unexamined, the earth of thoughts accumulate over us until it swells into perverse works. Hence it is said to Ezekiel: “Son of man, dig through the wall” (Ezek. VIII)—that is, break the hardness of the heart with repeated blows of examination.

### On the generations of Isaac’s sons

**Jerome, in the Book of Questions.**—“And Jacob said: ‘Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man, but I am a smooth man’” (Gen. XXVII). Where we read “hairy,” Hebrew has *se‘ir*. Hence the mountain Seir and the region in which he lived were afterward so called. We have spoken of this above as well.

“And Rebecca took the desirable garments of her elder son, which she had with her at home” (ibid.). Here too, as we have already mentioned, the Hebrews relate that the firstborn performed the office of priests and possessed a priestly garment. Clothed in it, they offered sacrifices before Aaron was chosen for the priesthood.

It continues.

“And Esau said: ‘He was rightly named Jacob, for behold, he has supplanted me twice.’” Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter.” Because he deceived his brother by cunning, he alluded to his name—just as Jacob was first called this because he had grasped the heel of his dead brother.

It continues:

“And Isaac said to Esau: ‘You shall serve Jacob your brother after the blessing has been made firm, and there will come a time when you will remove his yoke from your neck’” (ibid.).

This signifies that the Idumeans would serve the Jews, and that a time would come when they would cast off the yoke of servitude from their neck and oppose their rule.

According to the Seventy Translators, however, it reads: “There will be a time when you remove and loosen the yoke from your neck.” The sentence seems to trail off and not to be complete.

### Disciple

**Jerome to Damasus.**—Why did Isaac, a just man dear to God, bless not the one he wished but the one he did not wish, deceived by error?

### Master
[Col. 0329B] I shall postpone for a little while the types, and pass over what our predecessors interpreted concerning this passage—not because I do not assent to their opinion, but because you are asking only why a just man should have been ignorant of something and should have acted contrary to his own will. To this the strict answer must be that no human being, except him who, for our salvation, deigned to assume flesh, possessed complete knowledge or drank from the most certain streams of teaching. Hence it is not surprising if the exalted patriarch was nevertheless ignorant of something. For “we know in part and we prophesy in part,” and now “we see through a mirror in an enigma” (I Cor. XIII); and, according to what we ought to pray, Scripture says that we do not know (Rom. VIII). For “when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be destroyed” (I Cor. XIII). But “what man sees, he sees in the face, whereas God looks into the heart” (I Reg. XVI). Similarly, Samuel did not know which of Jesse’s sons he ought to bless until, after the Lord had revealed it, he learned that David, who was among the flocks, was to be anointed king (Ibid.). [Col. 0329C] Or again, when his servant Gehazi forbade the Shunammite woman to approach, the prophet Elisha said: “Let her alone, for her soul is in anguish, and the Lord has concealed it from me and has not told me,” and so forth (IV Reg. IV).

Therefore it is not surprising that the patriarch Isaac, for his greatest benefit, did not know what he was doing, since at that time he was all the more in error when he wished to delay at home the son devoted to bloodthirsty pleasure—and one who could later kill his brother—while overlooking the one who lived innocently, and to establish his own will rather than God’s (Rom. X). I think it belonged to the divine dispensation that his eyes should be blinded; and although he said, “The voice indeed is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands” (Gen. XXVII), he nevertheless did not understand that the younger son stood before him as the instructor of his brother concerning the blessing.

Junilius.

## DISCIPLE

What is the “type” which you said above that you would postpone?

## TEACHER

[Col. 0329D] What we call a figure or form, as the Apostle says: “All these things happened to them in figure” (I Cor. X); and again: “Adam, who is the form of the one to come” (Rom. V). For it is not without reason that one thing signifies many things.

## DISCIPLE

What, then, is a type or figure?

## TEACHER

The signification of present, past, or future things through works, insofar as works are a manifestation.

## DISCIPLE

Give examples of types of past things.

## TEACHER

Such as the humility of catechumens. They bear a type of those who were excluded from paradise, and, [Col. 0330A] fearing the divine gaze because of the consciousness of their sins, they therefore walk in public with their heads covered.

## DISCIPLE

Give an example from present things.

## TEACHER

Such as Aaron’s vestment, which bore the names of the twelve tribes engraved upon its stones, showing that he was, in a certain sense, interceding for the whole people.

## DISCIPLE

Give an example of future things.

## TEACHER

There is no difficulty in these matters; nevertheless, by way of excess, consider how the two covenants were displayed in Isaac’s two sons.

## DISCIPLE

Since we have given almost the same definition of prophecy, what is the difference?

## TEACHER

[Col. 0330B] In prophecy, future things are signified by words, insofar as they are words. In types, things are made manifest through things. Yet these two can be combined in a single definition, so that we may say that prophecy is a type in words, insofar as they are words; and, conversely, that a type is prophecy in things, insofar as they are recognized as things. Let what has been said here about types, figures, or forms suffice.

## DISCIPLE

Also, as Gregory says above: What does the action of Esau and Jacob signify—that one is sent out to hunt so that he may be blessed, while the other is blessed by his father through his mother’s substitution?

## TEACHER

It is perfectly clear, if one follows the history of sacred reading; nevertheless, within that history the matter is drawn somewhat more subtly toward its meaning. [Col. 0330C] Observe that Jacob did not steal the blessing of the firstborn through fraud, but received it as something owed to him, having purchased it from his consenting brother at the price of the latter’s relinquishment. But if someone, understanding more deeply, wishes to examine both events through the mysteries of allegory, let him rise immediately from history to mystery.

## DISCIPLE

What does it mean that Isaac desires to eat from the hunt of his elder son?

## TEACHER

For almighty God desired to be nourished by the good work of the Jewish people. But when that people delayed, Rebecca substituted the younger son, because, while the Jewish people seeks good works outside, the grace of the mother brought in the gentile people, so that it might offer the almighty Father the food of good works and receive the blessing of the elder brother. It offered those same foods from domestic animals, because the gentile people does not seek to please God through external sacrifices. Through the voice of the prophet it says: “[Col. 0330D] In me are your vows, O God, which I shall repay to you—praises” (Ps. LV).

## DISCIPLE

What does it mean that Jacob covered his hands, arms, and neck with the skins of young goats?

## TEACHER

A young goat was often accustomed to being offered for sin; and the gentile people, not being ashamed to confess itself sinful, slaughtered within itself the sins of the flesh.

## DISCIPLE

What is signified by Jacob’s being clothed in the garments of his elder brother?

## TEACHER

He was clothed in the precepts of sacred Scripture, which had been given to the elder people, through good works. The younger one uses at home the garments that the elder, going out, [Col. 0331A] left inside; the gentile people could not possess them while it attended only to the letter within them.

## DISCIPLE

What does it indicate that Isaac does not recognize the same son whom he blesses?

## TEACHER

Concerning the gentile people, the Lord says through the Psalmist: “A people whom I did not know served me” (Ps. XVII), and so forth.

## DISCIPLE

What does it mean that he did not see him in the present son, yet foresaw many things for him in the future?

## TEACHER

[Col. 0331B] When almighty God, through his prophets, foretold that grace would be granted preferentially to the gentile people, he did not see it in the present through grace, since he had then left that people in error; yet, because he was one day going to gather it, he foresaw it through the grace of the blessing. Thus the same Jacob, who bears the figure of the gentile people, is told in the blessing: “Behold, the odor of my son is like the odor of a full field, which the Lord God has blessed” (Gen. XXVII).

For, as Truth says in the Gospel, “The field is this world” (Matt. XIII). And because the people of the elect gives off the fragrance of virtues throughout the whole world, the odor of faith is the odor of a full field. The flower of the vine has one fragrance, because great is the virtue and renown of preachers, who intoxicate the minds of believers. The flower of the olive has another, because sweet is the work of mercy, which, like oil, warms and shines. The flower of the rose has another, because wondrous is the fragrance that glows and smells sweet from the blood of martyrs. The flower of the lily has another, because the life of the flesh is white with the incorruption of virginity. The flower of the violet has another, because great is the virtue of the humble, who, holding the lowest places out of desire, do not raise themselves from the earth above their humility, and preserve in their minds the purple of the heavenly kingdom. The ear of grain has another fragrance when it is brought to maturity, because the perfection of good works is prepared to satisfy those who hunger for righteousness.

[Col. 0331C] Since, therefore, the gentile people is scattered throughout the world in its elect, and through the virtues it performs fills all who understand with the fragrance of a good reputation, it is rightly said: “Behold, the odor of my son is like the odor of a full field” (Gen. XXVII). But because it does not possess these virtues from itself, he adds: “Which the Lord God has blessed.” And because the people of the elect rises through some of its members to contemplation, while through others it grows rich solely in the work of the active life, the following is rightly added: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth an abundance” (Ibid.).

For dew falls gently from above, and we receive the dew of heaven whenever, through the infusion of inward contemplation, we perceive something subtly. But when we also perform good works through the body, we are enriched by the richness of the earth.

## DISCIPLE

What does it mean that Esau returns late to his father?

## TEACHER

[Col. 0331D] There is no doubt that the Jewish people returns late to appease the Lord. To it also this is said in the blessing: “There will be a time when the yoke is loosed from your neck” (Ibid.), because the Jewish people will be freed from the slavery of sin at the end. As it is written: “Until the fullness of the gentiles has entered, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI).

Also, from the same author cited above: It is perfectly clear that no Jew who had fully learned the Law was ignorant of the coming of our Redeemer. Hence King Herod, terrified by the arrival of the Magi, diligently sought out the priests and rulers to learn where Christ was to be born. They immediately answered him: “In Bethlehem of Judea.” They therefore knew beforehand the one whom, at the time of his Passion, they ignored while they despised him. Their prior knowledge and subsequent ignorance are well and briefly signified by Isaac’s blindness: while [Col. 0332A] blessing Jacob, he foresaw what would happen in the future, but did not know who was standing before him in the present. Thus the people of the Israelites, who received the mysteries of prophecy but nevertheless kept their eyes blind in contemplation, did not see him when he was present, although they had foreseen so much about him in the future. They were entirely unable to see placed before them the one whose coming they had announced long beforehand.

## Recapitulation from the same author cited above

What the blessing of Jacob indicated figurally. The words of the martyr Hippolytus, as Jerome, a man of outstanding knowledge and learning, explained them, ought to be set down here.

“Isaac,” he says, “bears the image of God the Father; Rebecca, of the Holy Spirit; Esau, of the former people and of the devil; Jacob, of the Church and of Christ. Isaac’s old age shows the consummation of the world. His eyes becoming dim declares that faith has perished from the world and that the light of religion has been neglected before him.

“That the elder son is named signifies the Jews’ reception of the Law. That the father loved his food and his catch signifies human beings saved from error, whom every righteous person [Col. 0332B] hunts through teaching. The blessing is the word of God’s promise and the hope of the future kingdom, in which the saints will reign with Christ and celebrate the true Sabbath.

“Rebecca, full of the Holy Spirit, knowing what she had heard before she gave birth—that the elder would serve the younger—represents here the form of the Holy Spirit, who knew what would be future in Christ and first contemplated it in Jacob. She speaks to the younger son: ‘Go to the flock and bring me two young goats from there’ (Gen. XXVII), prefiguring the Savior’s coming in the flesh, in which he would especially free those who were held liable to sins. Indeed, throughout all the Scriptures, young goats are understood as sinners.

“That he is commanded to bring two signifies the taking up of the two peoples; their being young and good shows souls that are teachable and innocent. Esau’s robe is the faith and Scripture of the Hebrews, which were first given to them and afterward put on by the gentile people. The skins wrapped around his arms are [Col. 0332C] the sins of both peoples, which Christ, in the extension of his hands, fastened together with himself to the cross. For in his body he bore not his own sins but those of others.

“That Isaac asks Jacob why he has come so quickly expresses his wonder at the swift faith of believers in the churches. That pleasing foods are offered signifies a sacrifice pleasing to God and the salvation of sinners. That the blessing follows and he delights in its fragrance openly proclaims the power of the resurrection and the kingdom. For he is blessed in this manner: ‘Behold, the odor of my son is like the odor of a full field’ (Ibid.).

“The world is filled with the fragrance of Christ’s name, like a field; his blessing is from the dew of heaven, that is, from the rain of divine words, and from the richness of the earth, that is, from the gathering of the peoples. The multitude of grain and wine signifies the multitude whom he gathers through the sacrament of his body and blood. The peoples from the gentiles who have been converted to him serve him. Tribes worship him—that is, the peoples believing from the circumcision. He is the lord of his brothers, because he rules over the Jewish people. [Col. 0332D] The sons of his mother worship him, because he himself was born from her according to the flesh.

“He who curses him is accursed, and he who blesses him will be filled with blessings. Our Christ, I say, is blessed from the mouth of the ignorant people—that is, he is truly proclaimed. But another is thought by the Jews to be blessed, the one whom they, in their error, await.

“After the blessing had been given, Isaac suddenly trembled with an even greater astonishment and realized that he had blessed one person in place of another. Yet he was not angry when the mystery had been revealed to him; rather, he confirmed the blessing in his son, saying: ‘I have blessed him, and he is blessed.’ This is Isaac’s first blessing, given to the younger people of the Christians.

“Nevertheless, the elder son was not wholly despised, because when the fullness of the gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved. [Col. 0333A] The prophecy of this second blessing is as follows: ‘In the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven shall your blessing be’ (Ibid.). In the richness of the earth, certainly—that is, in the fertility of possessions and the power of the kingdom that existed in that people. ‘And in the dew of heaven shall your blessing be’—that is, in the utterances of God; for to them were entrusted the utterances of God and the covenants of the Law.

“But when he says, ‘You shall live by the sword’ (Ibid.), this means that the people devoted to bloodshed carried out murders against Christ and the prophets. ‘And you shall serve your younger brother’ (Ibid.)—that is, the Christian people. ‘There will come a time when you will shake off and loosen the yoke from your necks,’ when, converted to the grace of Christ through acknowledgment of the faith, you lay down the burden of the Law; then you will no longer serve the younger people but, through faith, will be called a brother.”

Accordingly, after his father’s blessing, Esau, stirred by the goads of envy, deceitfully plots the murder of his brother Jacob. The Jewish people likewise premeditated this against Christ: it not only handed the Lord over to the cross, but also persecuted those who believed in him to the shedding of blood.

But Jacob, fleeing his brother’s treachery, leaves his ancestral home and his parents [Col. 0333B] and goes to a distant region to take a wife for himself. In the same way Christ, leaving his parents according to the flesh—that is, the people of Israel—and his homeland—that is, Jerusalem and all the regions of Judea—went among the gentiles, taking the Church from them, so that what was said might be fulfilled: “I will call the one who was not my people, my people, and the one who was not beloved, beloved; and in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God” (Rom. IX).

## Jacob’s journey into Mesopotamia of Syria

“Proceeding into Mesopotamia,” and so forth, up to: “This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. XXVIII).

## Jerome

“And Jacob called the name of that place Bethel, whereas Luz was formerly the name of the city” (Ibid.). This follows what he had said above: “How terrible is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.” Now he gives the place a name and calls it Bethel, that is, “house of God.” The place had previously been called Luza, which is interpreted as “nut” or “almond.” [Col. 0333C] Hence certain people absurdly suppose that the Hebrew word *Ulam* is the name of a city, although *Ulam* means “formerly” or “previously.” The order of the expression is therefore this: “And he called the name of that place Bethel, and Luza was formerly the name of the city.” All the ancient Scriptures are full of the word *Ulam*, or *Elem*, which means nothing other than “before” or “previously,” or “vestibule,” or “above the threshold,” or “doorposts.”

## Recapitulation

Jacob came to the place that was then called Bethel, placed a large stone beneath his head, and, while sleeping, saw a ladder set up and resting upon heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending. After seeing this, he awoke and anointed the stone, saying: “Truly this is the house of God and the gate of heaven”; and after saying these things he departed (Ibid.).

Jacob’s sleep is the death or Passion of Christ. The stone at his head, which is named in a certain sense, signifies Christ, already anointed. “The head of a man is Christ” (I Cor. XI). For who does not know that Christ is named from anointing? [Col. 0333D] It is the house of God because Christ was born there, in Bethlehem; it is the gate of heaven because there he descended to earth and there again ascended to heaven. The raising up of the stone is Christ’s resurrection.

Moreover, the ladder is Christ, who said: “I am the way” (John XIV). Upon it the angels ascended and descended; these signify the evangelists and preachers of Christ. They ascend when, in order to understand his supremely exalted divinity, they rise above every creature to find him: “In the beginning was the Word with God, through whom all things were made” (John I). They descend when they find him “made of a woman, made under the Law, in order to redeem those who were under the Law” (Gal. IV).

For in that ladder, from earth to heaven, from flesh to spirit, carnal people become spiritual through progress, as though by ascending; and the spiritual themselves descend in a certain way to nourish them with milk, since they cannot speak to them as spiritual people but as carnal people (I Cor. III). He himself is above in his head and below in his body, which is the Church.

[Col. 0334A] We therefore understand him to be the ladder, because he said: “I am the way” (John XIV). One ascends to him so that he may be understood in the heights; one descends to him so that the little one may be nourished in his members; and through him alone people raise themselves up so that they may await him sublimely. Through him they also humble themselves so that they may proclaim him with sublimity and moderation.

After this vision, as Jacob traveled from that place, he saw sheep and shepherds, a well of living water, and a large stone placed over the well. Figuratively, the peoples of the righteous are signified by the sheep, as in the Gospel passage: “He will place the sheep at his right hand” (Matt. XXV). The shepherds are the prophets, who, filled with the Holy Spirit until the Lord’s coming, governed the people of the Israelites. The stone placed over the well bore the figure of the Lord. The well signified the grace of the Holy Spirit, which was to come to the Church from the gentiles through Christ’s preaching; it was covered because Christ had not yet come and become human.

## Jacob’s marriage

## Jerome

[Col. 0334B] “Laban therefore said to Jacob: ‘Complete the week of this one, and I shall give you this one also’” (Gen. XXIX). After Jacob, deceived by fraud, had taken Leah as his wife instead of Rachel, his father-in-law Laban told him to complete seven days after the first sister’s wedding and then take Rachel, for whom he would serve another seven years. Thus, contrary to the mistaken opinion of many, he did not take Rachel as his wife after another seven years, but after the seven days of the first wedding. For it follows:

“And he went in to Rachel, and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and served him another seven years. And Leah conceived and bore a son, and called his name Reuben” (Ibid.).

For the sake of brevity in the reading, I wish to give together the etymologies of the names of all the patriarchs. “And she called,” he says, “his name Reuben,” saying: “Because the Lord has seen my humiliation” (Ibid.). [Col. 0334C] *Reuben* is interpreted as “son of vision.”

“And she conceived,” he says, “another son, and called his name Simeon,” saying: “Because the Lord has heard me, since my husband hated me, and he has given me this one also” (Ibid.). *Simeon* is interpreted as “hearing.”

Concerning the third it follows: “And she conceived again and bore a son, and said: ‘Now my husband will be with me, because I have borne him three sons.’ Therefore she called his name Levi” (Ibid.). Where we read, “My husband will be with me,” Aquila translated: “My husband will be attached to me.” In Hebrew this is said as *Ilaue*, and the Hebrew teachers translate it differently, saying: “My husband will pursue me,” that is, “I have no doubt about my husband’s love for me. He will be my companion in this life, and his love will lead and pursue me even unto death, for I have borne him three sons.”

“And she conceived and bore and gave birth to a son, and said: ‘Now for this I shall confess to the Lord’; and therefore she called his name Judah” (Ibid.). *Judah* means “confession”; the name is therefore derived from the confession of the one confessing. Here, however, “confession” is understood as thanksgiving or praise, as frequently in the Psalms and in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI), that is, “I give you thanks” or “I glorify you.”

“And Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son, and Rachel said: ‘God has judged me, and has heard my voice, and has given me a son’; therefore she called his name Dan” (Gen. XXX).

[Col. 0334D] She expressed the reason for the name, so that because the Lord had judged her through the son of the maidservant, she might give him the name of judgment. *Dan* is interpreted as “judgment.”

“And Bilhah conceived again and bore a son, and Rachel said: ‘God has made me dwell with my sister, and I have prevailed’; and she called his name Naphtali” (Ibid.). Here the reason for the name *Naphtali* is explained quite differently from the explanation written in the book of Hebrew names. Hence Aquila says: “[Col. 0335A] God has caused me to associate, and I have associated” (*Synanestrepsen me ho theos, kai synanestrephen*), whereas in Hebrew it is written: *Naphthale Elohim, Naphthaleti*. Therefore she gave the name *Naphtali* from companionship or comparison, since the word can signify either.

But what follows is: “And Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, bore Jacob a son; and Leah said: ‘In fortune,’ and called his name Gad” (Ibid.). Where we have rendered “in fortune,” and where it is said in Greek, *en tychē*—which can be rendered “in outcome”—the Hebrew has *Bagdad*, which Aquila interprets as “girding has come”; we may also say “in girding.” For *ba* can sound like the preposition “in,” and *Gad* means “has come.” Thus, from the outcome—or from the girding, which is called *Gad*—Zilpah’s son was named Gad.

It follows:

“And Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, bore a second son to Jacob, and Leah said: ‘Therefore blessed, because women call me blessed’; and she called his name Asher, ‘riches’” (Ibid.).

“Riches,” that is, *ploutos*, has been wrongly added, since the etymology of the name *Asher* is made clear by the authority of Scripture, which says: “I am blessed, and women call me blessed.” Because she is called blessed by all, she called her son “blessed.” [Col. 0335B] Therefore *Asher* does not mean “riches,” but only “blessed” in this passage. Elsewhere, according to the ambiguity of the word, “riches” can also be so called.

“And God heard Leah, and she conceived and bore a fifth son, and Leah said: ‘God has given me my wages to my husband’; and she called his name Issachar” (Ibid.).

The Septuagint interpreters rendered the etymology of this name as “There is a reward.” It should not therefore be thought, as many read incorrectly by adding a pronoun, that the text says “which is a reward”; the whole name means “there is a reward.” For *yesh* means “there is,” and *sachar*, “reward.” This was because, through the mandrakes of her son Reuben, she had diverted to herself the marital intercourse owed to Rachel.

“And Leah conceived again and bore a sixth son to Jacob. And she said: ‘God has endowed me with a good endowment at this time. My husband will dwell with me, because I have borne him six sons’; and she called his name Zebulun” (Ibid.).

[Col. 0335C] Where we have “My husband will dwell with me,” the Septuagint translated, “He will love me.” In Hebrew it is *Izboleni*, and the sense is: “Because I have borne six sons to Jacob, I am now secure. My husband will dwell with me, and my son shall be called a dwelling place.” Therefore the interpretation in the book of names, “Zebulun, the flow of night,” is wrong and forced.

“After this she bore a daughter, and called her name Dinah.” This is translated as “cause,” which the Greeks more significantly call *dikē*. For she became the cause of the quarrel at Shechem.

After the sons, the names of the parents should also be set down. *Leah* is interpreted as “laboring”; *Rachel*, as “sheep.” Her son Joseph, because his mother desired that another be added to her, is called “increase.”

## Spiritual recapitulation

Jacob, therefore, proceeding into Mesopotamia, took as wives the two daughters of Laban, Rebecca’s brother (Gen. XXVIII–XXX).

That is, first Leah, second Rachel; then he took for himself Leah’s maidservant, named Zilpah, and Rachel’s maidservant, Bilhah. From these four he fathered twelve sons and one daughter. From Leah, namely, he fathered Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun; from Rachel, Joseph and Benjamin; from Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, Dan and Naphtali; from Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, Gad and Asher. These are the twelve sons of Israel.

Now we must observe what the four wives of Jacob—two free women and two maidservants—prefigured. We know that the Apostle understands by the free woman and the maidservant whom Abraham had the two covenants; but there, because there is one of each, what is said appears more readily. Here, however, there are two and two. Furthermore, there the son of the maidservant is disinherited, whereas here the sons of the maidservants receive the promised land together with the sons of the free women. Therefore something else is undoubtedly signified here.

Although Jacob’s two free wives are thought to pertain to the New Testament, to which we have been called in freedom, they are not two without reason, except because two lives are proclaimed to us in the body of Christ: one temporal, in which we labor; the other eternal, in which they will contemplate the delight of God.

For Leah, as we have said, is interpreted as “laboring”; Rachel, however, as “ewe,” and according to the opinions of others, “the beginning that is seen,” or “the Word.” The activity of this life, then, in which we live by faith, is laborious in its works and uncertain as to what outcome it will produce for the benefit of those whom we wish to assist. She is Leah, Jacob’s first wife, and for this reason she is said to have been weak-eyed. The thoughts of mortal human beings and our foresight are timid and uncertain; but the hope of eternal contemplation of God possesses a sure understanding of the truth. She is Rachel, and therefore she is also said to be beautiful in face and appearance.

Every devoutly zealous person loves her, and for her sake serves the grace of God, because our sins, even if they have been like scarlet, will be whitened like snow (Isa. I). Laban, indeed, is interpreted as “whitening,” and Jacob serves him for Rachel’s sake. No one turns under the grace of the remission of sins to serve righteousness except in order to live peacefully in the Word, from whom is seen the Beginning, who is God. Therefore one serves for Rachel’s sake, not for Leah’s.

For who would ultimately have loved the labor of actions and sufferings in works of righteousness? Who would have sought that life for its own sake, just as Jacob did not love Leah? Yet, once she had been placed under him for the purpose of begetting, he embraced her and experienced her fruitfulness. The Lord, because she could not be loved for her own sake, first made her bearable so that one might reach Rachel; afterward he commended her on account of her children.

Thus every useful servant of God, established under the grace of the whitening of his sins, meditates on what else in his conduct he loves except the teaching of wisdom.
