Most people, thinking that they will receive it as soon as they have exercised themselves in the seven commandments of the Law, seek love of neighbor, so that no one may be harmed: “Honor your father and your mother; you shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet your neighbor’s property, you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Deut. V).

After these commandments have been observed, once the endurance of labor—through various temptations, as through the night of this world—has attached itself to a person for the sake of the desired delight of doctrine, Leah is unexpectedly joined to him in place of Rachel. He endures her so that he may reach Rachel, if he loves perseveringly, after receiving seven other commandments, as though it were said to him: “Serve another seven years for Rachel, so that you may be poor in spirit, meek, mourning, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, and peacemaking” (Matt. V).

A person would wish, if it were possible, to reach at once the delights of beautiful contemplation without any endurance of labor, which must be embraced in doing and suffering. But this cannot happen in the land of the dying. This seems to be signified by what was said to Jacob: “It is not customary in this place for the younger to be given before the elder,” because the elder may reasonably be called that which is earlier in time; and labor in good works is earlier in human activity than the rest of contemplation.

One thing, then, is to be pursued, but many things must be endured for its sake. Thus Jacob’s two wives are both free, since they are daughters of the remission of sins—that is, of Laban, which means “whitening.” Nevertheless, one is loved and the other endured; but the one who is endured is first and more abundantly fruitful, so that, if not for her own sake, at least for the sake of her children, she may be loved.

For the labors of the righteous bear their greatest fruit in those whom they beget for the kingdom of God amid many temptations and tribulations, preaching the Gospel to those for whose sake they have “more abundant labors, beatings beyond measure, and more frequent deaths” (2 Cor. XI), for whose sake they have “conflicts outside and fears within” (2 Cor. VII), and whom they call their joy and crown (Phil. IV). Children are born to them more easily and more abundantly from that word of faith by which they preach Christ crucified (1 Cor. I).

Rachel, however, clear of sight, is transported toward God (2 Cor. V), and sees “in the beginning” the Word of God with God (John I); she wishes to give birth but cannot, because “who will recount his generation?” (Isa. LIII). Therefore, when the contemplative life longs to behold the ineffable divinity, it wishes to be free from every occupation, and for this reason it is barren, since it does not come to the aid of those under various pressures.

But because she too sometimes burns with the desire to beget—for she wishes to teach what she knows—she sees her sister abounding in children through the labor of action, and grieves that people run rather toward that virtue by which their needs are served than toward the one from which something divine is learned. This grief seems to be represented in what is written: “And Rachel envied her sister” (Gen. XXX).

Accordingly, because the pure understanding of a spiritual substance cannot be expressed in words clothed in flesh, she chose to convey the teaching of wisdom through every kind of bodily likeness, just as Rachel chose to receive children from her husband through her maidservant rather than remain altogether without children.

Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, is interpreted as “aged.” From the old life, devoted to bodily senses, bodily images are aroused even when something is heard about the spiritual and unchangeable substance of divinity.

Leah also received children through her maidservant, inflamed by the love of possessing a more numerous offspring. We find, however, that Zilpah, her maidservant, is interpreted as “gaping mouth.” Therefore this maidservant represents those whose mouths gape in preaching the evangelical faith while their hearts do not gape. Of such people it is written: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Mark VII). And concerning them the Apostle says: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?” (Rom. I).

Nevertheless, so that through this conditional wife the free wife Jacob—she who labors—might receive sons as heirs of the kingdom, the Lord says: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII). Hence the Apostle says: “Whether from pretense or from truth Christ is proclaimed, in this I rejoice, and I will continue to rejoice” (Phil. I), as though the maidservant rejoices when she gives birth to a more numerous offspring.

There is, however, a certain fruit of Leah that comes through Rachel’s benefit. Rachel, in order to lie with her husband on the night owed to her, accepts mandrakes from Leah’s son and permits him to lie with her sister.

What should be said about the mandrake? I have found it to be a beautiful and sweet-smelling plant, but its taste is insipid. Therefore I understand the mandrake fruit to represent popular good reputation. Hence the Apostle says: “He must also have a good testimony from those outside” (1 Tim. III). Although such people have little discernment, they nevertheless often return a reward for the labor of those who will provide assistance to them, namely, the splendor of praise and the fragrance of a good reputation.

Nor do those who are first in the Church attain this popular glory unless they are involved in the dangers and labor of action. Therefore Leah’s son found the mandrakes by going out into the field—that is, by walking honorably among those outside (1 Thess. IV). But that teaching of wisdom, which is most remote from the noise of the crowd, fixes the mind in the contemplation of truth with sweet delight.

She would not attain even a little of this popular glory except through those who, acting amid the crowds and directing the activities of the people, preside over them. For when these active and busy men, through whom the welfare of the multitude is administered and whose authority is dear to the people, bear witness, then the life devoted to leisure for the pursuit and contemplation of truth is also, in a certain sense, given mandrakes through Leah.

To Leah herself, however, they come through her firstborn son—that is, through the honor of fruitfulness, in which lies all the fruit of an active life laboring amid the struggles of temptations.

Many who burn with good intelligence and zeal, although they might be capable of governing peoples, nevertheless avoid going out into turbulent occupations because they are wholly devoted to the leisure of doctrine, embracing it with all their heart as though it were beautiful Rachel. Yet because it is good that this life too, as it becomes more widely known, should earn popular glory, it is unjust for it to attain that glory if someone keeps at leisure his love, suited and capable of administering ecclesiastical responsibilities, and does not undertake the governance of the common good.

Therefore Leah says to her sister: “Is it a small thing that you have taken my husband, unless you also want the mandrakes of my son?” (Gen. XXX). By “one husband” she signifies all those who, although capable through the virtue of action and worthy of having the governance of the Church entrusted to them for the administration of the sacrament of faith, are inflamed by zeal for teaching and for investigating and contemplating wisdom, and withdraw from all the troubles of action, wishing to remain at leisure for learning or teaching.

Thus the words mean: “Is it a small thing that you have taken my husband, and do you also want the mandrakes of my son?”—as though it were said: “Is it not enough that the life of study keeps at leisure men necessary for the labor of practical affairs, but it also seeks popular glory?”

Therefore, in order to acquire it justly, Rachel gives her husband to her sister that night, so that those who are suited by strenuous virtue to the governance of peoples, even if they love to devote themselves to knowledge, may accept the burden of experiencing temptations and cares for the common good, lest the teaching of wisdom to which they had decided to devote themselves be blasphemed, and so that it may gain from the less instructed peoples the good reputation—signified by those fruits—that is necessary for the exhortation of learners.

But that these men are compelled to undertake this care is clearly signified as well. When Jacob came from the field, Leah met him, detained him, and said: “You shall come in to me, for I have hired you with the mandrakes of my son.” As though she were saying: “You wish to confer a good reputation upon the teaching that you love; do not flee from dutiful labor.”

Anyone who observes these things being done in the Church sees and experiences in actual examples what we understand from the books. Who does not see this happening throughout the whole world: people coming from the works of the world and going into the leisure of knowing and contemplating truth, as though into Rachel’s embrace, and then being intercepted and drawn into ecclesiastical necessity, being appointed to labor as though Leah were saying: “You shall come in to me”? Through those who administer this mystery of God, begetting sons of faith in the night of this world, even that life is praised by the peoples—a life whose love caused them to convert and abandon the hope of the world, and from whose profession they were taken up to the merciful governance of the flock.

In all their works and labors they act so that the profession from which they converted—because it has produced such rulers of the people—will not be disgraced but glorified more brightly, as Jacob did not refuse Leah’s night in order that Rachel might enjoy the sweet-smelling and shining fruits.

At times Rachel herself also, through God’s mercy, gives birth by herself, although only after great difficulty, since it is exceedingly rare that one may grasp: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John I). Whatever is said about this may be received piously and wisely, without the phantasm of carnal thought, and beneficially, at least in part.

In another interpretation, Victorinus the martyr and the others understood Leah and Rachel as likenesses of the Church or the Synagogue. They thought that Leah, the elder, represented the Synagogue, because she first gave birth to God’s people; and she is said to be weak-eyed, because the Law given through Moses is veiled and sealed.

Rachel, however, younger and beautiful, first barren and afterward fruitful, is a likeness of the Church. She is younger because she came later in time; beautiful because her eyes, in body and in the Holy Spirit, are lovely—the eyes that were deemed worthy to perceive the Gospel. She too was barren for as long as the Synagogue was giving birth to its people.

But why did Jacob serve for Rachel, and why was Leah, the elder, substituted for her, unless because the Lord, in order to take up the Church, first joined the Synagogue to himself?

Jacob’s service of seven years for the two wives therefore signifies the time of the present life, because it turns through seven days. In this life the Lord took the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father’s will unto death (Phil. II).

Jacob served for sheep, and our Lord says: “I did not come to be served, but to serve” (Matt. XX). Jacob fed sheep, and the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd” (John XIV). Jacob took for himself, as the profit of his wages, a varied flock; Christ gathered to himself the diversity of the nations.

Jacob placed three rods, with their bark cut away, in the watering troughs, so that his sheep might multiply by looking at them. Our Lord, in the water of baptism, set before the faithful people the names of the three Persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—so that whoever fully perceives this may become a sheep of God.

### Jerome

“Jacob said to Laban: ‘I will pass through your entire flock today. Separate from it every speckled and variegated animal, and every single-colored animal among the lambs, and the variegated and speckled among the goats; and this shall be my wage. And my righteousness will answer for me tomorrow, when my wage comes before you. Everything that is not speckled or variegated among the goats and lambs shall belong to me,’ and so forth” (Gen. XXX).

Among the translators of the Septuagint the sense is greatly confused, and to the present day I have been unable to find any of our people who explained clearly what is being said in this passage.

“Do you wish,” Jacob says, “that I should serve you for another seven years? Do what I ask. Separate for me all the speckled and variegated animals, both sheep and goats, and deliver them into the hands of your sons. Again, from both flocks give me the white and black animals—that is, those of a single color. If, then, anything variegated is born from the white and black animals, which are single-colored, it will be mine; but if anything single-colored is born, it will be yours. I am not asking for anything difficult. The nature of the animals works in your favor, so that white are born from white and black from black. My righteousness works in my favor, while God regards my humility and labor.”

Laban gladly seized the option he had been given. He did as Jacob requested and traveled a three days’ journey, separating the flocks between Jacob and his sons, so that no deceit might arise from the proximity of the animals.

Jacob therefore devised a new stratagem and opposed natural art to the nature of white and black animals. He took three rods—of poplar, almond, and pomegranate—although the Septuagint has rods of storax, walnut, and plane. Stripping the bark in places, he made the color of the rods variegated, so that wherever he left the bark on the rod, the original color remained; but wherever he removed the bark, the white color was exposed.

He watched the time when the animals were being mounted and, after mating, eagerly went to drink. He placed the variegated rods in the channels. He brought the rams and he-goats to the sheep and goats in the very eagerness of drinking, so that, from their twofold desire—as they eagerly drank and were mounted by the males—the females might conceive offspring such as the shadows of the rams and he-goats mounting above them appeared in the mirror of the water. For the color of the images was also variegated because of the rods placed in the channels.

Nor is it surprising that this should be the nature of women at conception: whatever they have seen or conceived in their minds, in the final heat of pleasure when conception occurs, such offspring they produce.

The same thing is also said to happen among herds of mares in Spain. Quintilian, in the case in which a matron was accused because she had given birth to an Ethiopian, argues in her defense that this is the nature of conceptions, as we have described above. It is also found written in the books of Hippocrates that a woman was about to be punished on suspicion of adultery because she had given birth to an exceedingly beautiful child unlike either parent and unlike the family, unless the aforementioned physician had solved the question by advising them to investigate whether perhaps such a painting was in the bedroom. When it was found, the woman was freed from suspicion.

“After the young goats and lambs had been born variegated and speckled from the white and single-colored flocks, Jacob separated them and kept them far from the original flock. Whenever anything single-colored—that is, white or black—was born, he delivered it into the hands of Laban’s sons. He placed the rods he had stripped in the channels where the waters were poured out and where the animals came to drink, opposite the animals, so that they might conceive when they came to drink. The animals conceived opposite Jacob’s rods, the rods he had placed before the animals in the channels for them to conceive from. But with the late-born sheep he did not place them, and the late-born were Laban’s, while the early-born were Jacob’s.”

This is not found in the Septuagint translators. Instead of “late-born” and “early-born,” they translated something else that I do not understand and that has no bearing on the sense.

What Scripture says is this: “Jacob, prudent and shrewd, maintained justice and fairness even in his new stratagem.” For if all the animals had produced variegated lambs and young goats, there would have been some suspicion of deceit, and Laban would openly have become hostile to the matter. Therefore he regulated everything in such a way that he himself received the fruit of his labor while Laban was not completely despoiled.

Whenever the sheep and goats were mounted in the early season, because the spring offspring are better, he placed the rods before them so that variegated offspring would be born. But whenever the sheep and goats sought a male late, he did not place the rods before their eyes, so that single-colored animals would be born. Whatever was born first was his, because it was variegated and speckled; whatever came afterward was Laban’s. Animals of a single color were born, both black and white.

In the passage where it is written that they conceived from the rods, the Hebrew has *Yehammenna*. I cannot express the force of the Hebrew word except by circumlocution. *Yehammenna* properly denotes the final heat in intercourse, by which the whole body is shaken and which is near the end of the act of pleasure.

### The same author as above

“Your father has deceived me and changed my wage ten times, and God did not allow him to harm me. If he said, ‘The speckled animals shall be your wage,’ every animal was born speckled; and if he said, ‘The single-colored animals shall be your wage,’ every animal was born single-colored” (Gen. XXXI).

Where we have translated “He changed my wage ten times,” the translators of the Septuagint have “ten lambs.” I do not know what opinion led them to this, since the Hebrew word *Monim* sounds more like “number” than “lambs.” Indeed, the following context proves this sense more strongly, since Laban continually changed the agreement with each successive birth.

If he saw that variegated animals were being born, after the birth he would say: “I want variegated ones to be born for me in the future.” Again, when he saw single-colored animals being born—for when Jacob heard this, he did not place the rods in the channels—he would say that the future offspring should produce single-colored animals for him.

And what more need be said? Up to ten times Laban’s arrangement concerning his own flock, or Jacob’s, was changed. Whatever he had proposed should be born was turned into the opposite color.

But so that no one may think ten births in six years incredible, read Virgil, where it is said: “Twice pregnant are the flocks.” The nature of the Italian and Mesopotamian sheep is said to be the same.

### The following, by the same author

“And Rachel stole her father’s idols” (Gen. XXXI). Where we now read “idols,” the Hebrew has *Teraphim*. Aquila translates this as *μορφώματα* (*morphōmata*)—that is, “figures” or “images.” This is mentioned so that we may know what *Teraphim* means in the Book of Judges.

It continues:

“And he crossed the river and came to Mount Gilead” (ibid.). It is not that the mountain was called Gilead at that time, but, by anticipation—as we have often said—it is called by the name by which it was afterward to be known.

### Again, above

“And you changed my wage ten lambs” (ibid.). The same error as above: “number” should be read instead of “lambs.”

It continues:

“And Jacob said to his brothers: ‘Gather stones.’ And when they had gathered stones, they made a heap and ate. And Laban called it the Heap of Testimony, while Jacob called it the Heap of the Witness.”

A heap is called *Gal* in the Hebrew language, while “testimony” is *ed*. Again, in the Syriac language a heap is called *igar*, while testimony is *Saadutha*. Jacob therefore called it “Heap of Testimony,” *Galaad*, in the Hebrew language. Laban called the same thing—that is, “Heap of Testimony,” *igar Saadutha*—in the language of his people. For he was a Syrian and had changed the ancient language of his ancestors for the language of the province in which he lived.

### Recapitulation

“After the long servitude that Jacob endured with his father-in-law for his wives, as though they were his wages, the Lord also commanded him to return to his native land. Then, without his father-in-law’s knowledge, he hurried away with his wives and company. But Laban pursued him in Mount Gilead with fury and searched for the idols that Rachel had stolen, though he did not find them” (Gen. XXXI).

What, then, does this itself signify figuratively? Although Laban previously played another role, he now represents the type of the devil. Laban, indeed, is interpreted as “whitening.” “Whitening” may not inappropriately be understood as the devil, who, although dark by merit, transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. XI).

Jacob serves him—that is, in part, the Jewish people among the reprobate—from whose flesh the incarnate Lord came. Laban may also express the world in this way: it pursues Jacob with fury because it attempts to oppress by persecution the elect, who are members of our Redeemer.

Jacob took away Laban’s daughter—that is, the daughter of the world or of the devil—when Christ joined the Church from among the Gentiles to himself. He also draws her away from her father’s house, since through the prophet he says to her: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. XLIV).

What, moreover, is designated by the idols except greed? Hence Paul says: “Greed, which is the service of idols” (Eph. V).

Laban came to Jacob but did not find the idol, because, after displaying the world’s treasures, the devil found in our Redeemer traces of no earthly desire (Matt. IV); but because Jacob did not have them, Rachel covered them by sitting upon them.

Through Rachel, who is called “ewe,” the Church is represented. To sit is to seek the humility of repentance, as it is written: “Rise after you have sat” (Ps. CXXVI). Rachel therefore covered the idols by sitting upon them, because the holy Church, following Christ, has covered the vice of earthly desire through the humility of repentance.

Concerning this covering of vices the prophet says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI). Rachel therefore signified us, because we press down the idols by sitting upon them if, through repentance, we condemn the faults of greed.

This impurity of greed does not impede those who run courageously, to whom it is said: “Act courageously, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. XXVI); rather, it especially overtakes those who, walking as though with an effeminate step, are weakened by the flatteries of the world. Hence Rachel’s words there are also: “According to the custom of women, it has now happened to me” (Gen. XXXI), that is, she revealed that she was experiencing something like a woman’s condition.

“But after Laban had pursued Jacob and found him, and after they had spoken with one another and entered into a covenant, Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar. He said to his brothers: ‘Bring stones.’ And they gathered them and made a mound. Laban called it the Mound of the Witness, and Jacob called it the Heap of Testimony.”

Among the faithful, both Jews and Gentiles, the prominent stone is a witness in the likeness of Christ; the heap of stones is the multitude of believers.

It continues:

### Jerome

“And the angels of God met him, and Jacob, when he saw them, said: ‘These are the camps of God’; and he called the name of that place Camps” (Gen. XXXII).

Where we have “camps,” the Hebrew has *Mahanaim*, so that we may know which place is meant whenever the word is interpreted elsewhere. And beautifully, as he goes to his hostile brother, he is received by choirs of accompanying angels.

“And Jacob said: ‘God of my father Isaac, Lord, who said to me, “Return to your land, and I will bless you,” I am less than all your mercies and all the truth that you have shown to your servant’” (ibid.).

Where we have “I am less,” something else that disturbs the sense is contained in the Greek and Latin codices.

It continues:

“And he said to him: ‘What is your name?’ He answered: ‘Jacob.’ And he said to him: ‘Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but your name shall be Israel, because you have prevailed with God, and you will be strong with men’” (ibid.).

Josephus, in the first book of the *Antiquities*, thinks that Israel was so called because he stood against the angel; but, examining this carefully, I could not find it at all in the Hebrew. And why must I seek the opinions of individuals, when the one who gave the name himself explains its etymology? “Your name,” he says, “shall not be called Jacob, but your name shall be Israel.”

Therefore Aquila interprets it: *Ὅτι ἤρξας μετὰ Θεοῦ*—“Because you have ruled with God”; Symmachus: *Ὅτι ἤρξω ἰσχύι πρὸς Θεόν*—“Because you have prevailed by strength against God”; the Septuagint and Theodotion: *Ὅτι ἐνίσχυσας μετὰ Θεοῦ*—“Because you have grown strong with God.”

For *Sarith*, from which the name Israel is derived, signifies “prince.” The sense, therefore, is this: “Your name shall not be called Supplanter,” that is, Jacob, “but your name shall be Prince with God,” that is, Israel. For just as I am a prince, so you too, who were able to wrestle with me, shall be called a prince. And if you were able to fight with me, who am God—or with an angel, since many interpret the passage differently—how much more will you prevail with men, that is, with Esau, whom you need not fear?

But the interpretation later given in the *Book of Names*—“Israel, a man seeing God,” or “a mind seeing God”—which has been worn smooth by almost everyone’s usage, seems to me to have been interpreted not so much truthfully as forcibly. Here *Israel* is written with these letters: *iod, sin, res, aleph, lamech*, which is interpreted as “prince of God,” or “directed by God,” that is, *εὐθύπατος Θεοῦ*.

But “a man seeing God” is written with these letters: for “man,” from three letters—*aleph, iod, sin*—and pronounced *ais*; “seeing,” from three—*res, aleph, he*—and pronounced *rahe*. Moreover, *El*, from *aleph* and *lamech*, is interpreted as “God,” or “strong.”

Although, therefore, those who translated Israel as “a man” or “a mind seeing God” possess great authority and eloquence, and their shadow overawes us, we are guided more by the authority of Scripture and of the angel or God who himself called him Israel than by that of any secular eloquence.

The following passage likewise says: “And he blessed him there, and Jacob called the name of that place ‘Face of God,’ for I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved” (ibid.). In Hebrew it says *Phanuel*, so that we may know that this is the very place which, in the other books of Holy Scripture, is read in Greek as *Phanuel*, just as it is written in Hebrew.

### Again, from the preceding book

“And he divided the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two maidservants, and placed the maidservants and their children first; Leah and her children next; Rachel and Joseph last; and he himself went before them” (Gen. XXXIII).

He did not, as many suppose, make three groups, but two. Indeed, where we have “divided,” Aquila has *ἡμίσευσε*, that is, “divided in half,” so that he made one company of the maidservants with their little ones, and another of Leah and Rachel, who were free, with their children. He made the maidservants go first and the free women second; he himself went before both groups to meet his brother and worship him.

It continues:

“And Jacob built a house there, and for his animals he built tents or tabernacles. Therefore he called the name of that place Tabernacles” (ibid.).

Where we have “tabernacles,” the Hebrew reads *Succoth*. To this day there is a city across the Jordan bearing this name, interpreted as Scythopolis, about which we wrote in the *Book of Places*.

It continues:

“And Jacob came to Salem, a city of Shechem in the land of Canaan, when he had come from Mesopotamia of Syria” (ibid.).

An error arises concerning how Salem may be called the city of Shechem, since Jerusalem, where Melchizedek reigned, had previously been called Salem. Either both cities bore the same name—which we can also find in the case of several places in Judea, so that the name of a city and place is the same in different tribes—or else we say that this *Salem*, which is now named for Shechem, is interpreted as “completed” and “perfect,” while the one that was later called Jerusalem is translated in our language as “peaceful.”

Both meanings are expressed by this word with a slight change of accent. The Hebrews relate that Jacob’s dislocated thigh was restored and healed there; for this reason the same city received the name meaning “healed” and “perfect.”

### Repetition

“After these things had occurred, Jacob sent messengers and gifts to his brother Esau. Afterward, when he had led all his people across the torrent, he himself remained alone, and behold, a man wrestled with him. Jacob prevailed over him and did not release him until he had extorted a blessing and received the sacred name Israel” (Gen. XXXII).

In this event the image of the Lord’s mystery was principally prefigured. That man evidently bore the type of Christ; Jacob prevailed over him only because he wished it, so that he might signify the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, in which Jacob appeared in the type of the Jews—that is, in the offspring of his body, he appeared to prevail over God and, as though wrestling with a weak man, to enter into combat with his flesh and grow strong in his Passion, as it is written when they said: “Crucify him” (Mark XV).

Yet Jacob obtained a blessing from that same angel whom he had overcome in victory; the imposition of his name was certainly itself a blessing. Israel is interpreted as “seeing God,” which will be the final reward of all the saints.

“That same angel touched the breadth of his thigh and made him lame” (ibid.); thus Jacob was at once blessed and lame. He was blessed in those of the same people who believed in Christ, and lame in the unbelievers.

The sinew or breadth of the thigh is the multitude of the offspring or of the race. There are many in the Church who, degenerating from the faith of their fathers and straying from the precepts of their author, limp along the paths of their error. Of them it was prophetically foretold: “And they limped from their paths” (Ps. XVII). Yet that people, after its strength had been touched, not only limps but also grows numb, so that it can no longer beget children.

Finally, when the same patriarch added that he had seen God face to face, although he had previously said that a man had wrestled with him, this signifies that the same God was destined to become man, the one who would wrestle with the people of Jacob.

### Jerome continues

“And Hamor and his son Shechem came to the gate of the city, and they spoke to the men of the city, saying: ‘These men are peaceful toward us’” (Gen. XXXIV).

Where the Septuagint translators have rendered “peaceful,” Aquila translated *ἀπηρτισμένους*, that is, “completed” or “perfect”; in place of this, the Hebrew reads *Salamin*. From this it is clear that what we said above about Salem is true.

It continues:

“And they entered the city carefully and killed every male” (ibid.).

Where the Greek reads *ἀσφαλῶς*, that is, “carefully” or “securely,” the Hebrew has *Beta*, that is, “boldly and confidently.”

## Recapitulation

“Then Hemor, the son of Sichem, violated Dinah, the daughter of Jacob. After intercourse with her, he wished to join himself and his household to the family of Israel; but Simeon and Levi, her brothers and avengers of her virginity, killed him by treachery together with all his people.”

But what does the statement mean: “Dinah went out to see the women of that region; and when Sichem, the son of Hemor the Hivite, the ruler of that land, saw her, he loved her and seized her, slept with her, and overpowered the virgin by force; and his soul was joined to her, and he soothed her grief with flatteries” (ibid.)?

Dinah goes out to see the women of a foreign region whenever a mind, neglecting its own pursuits and attending to the affairs of others, wanders outside its proper character and order. Sichem, the ruler of the land, overpowers her because the devil corrupts a mind found occupied with external concerns. “His soul was joined to her,” because he sees her united to himself through iniquity. And because, when the mind recovers from its fault and tries to mourn what it has done, the corrupter calls empty hopes and assurances before its eyes in order to deprive sorrow of its usefulness, the text rightly adds: “And he soothed her grief with flatteries.” Sometimes he speaks of the more serious deeds of others; sometimes that what was done is nothing; sometimes of God’s mercy; sometimes he promises that there will still be time for repentance. Thus, while the deceived mind is led on by these things, it is held back from its intention to repent, so that it perceives no good at that time because no evil now troubles it; and then it is more fully beset by punishments, since at that time it even rejoices in its sins.

## Jerome

“And Jacob came to Luz, in the land of Canaan, which is Bethel” (Gen. 35). Here it is most clearly proved that Bethel was not Ulam Luz, as was said above, but Luza, that is, formerly called “the almond tree.”

## Recapitulation

“After this God spoke to Jacob, that he should dwell in Bethel; there Rachel died while giving birth to Benjamin.”

But what does it mean that, when Rachel gave birth to this same Benjamin, she called his name “Son of my sorrow,” except that she was prophetically foretelling the future Paul, who would arise from the tribe of Benjamin and afflict the children of the Church during the time of his persecution? Alternatively, through Benjamin the heavenly Jerusalem was represented, which is in the territory of that same Benjamin. Its people inflict great grief upon their mother by shedding the blood of the prophets, and also by crying out with impious voices for Christ’s death: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

## Jerome again

“And Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died, and she was buried beneath Bethel” (Gen. 35). If Rebekah’s nurse, named Deborah, died—as the Septuagint translators also rendered it here—and the Hebrew word itself is *Meneket*, we cannot know why they rendered it “substance” there and “nurse” here.

It follows:

“And God said to him: Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name; and he called his name Israel” (ibid.). Earlier, no name is imposed upon him by the angel; rather, it is declared that one is to be imposed by God. What is therefore promised there as future is here shown to have been fulfilled.

It follows:

“And it happened, when they were approaching Cabratha in the land of Canaan, in order to come to Ephrata, that Rachel gave birth” (ibid.). The Hebrew word *Cabratha* occurs again later, where Jacob says to Joseph: “But when I had come from Mesopotamia of Syria, your mother Rachel died in the land of Canaan, on the road to Hippodrome, as I was coming to Ephrata” (Gen. 48). I do not know what the Septuagint translators intended when they rendered it “Hippodrome.” Immediately afterward, where the Hebrew says, “And they buried her on the road to Ephrata, that is, Bethlehem,” the Septuagint translators again put “Hippodrome” for *Ephrata*, although, if *Cabratha* is “Hippodrome,” *Ephrata* certainly cannot also be “Hippodrome.”

Aquila translated the passage as follows: “And it happened, ‘on the way of the land’ (καθ’ ὁδὸν τῆς γῆς), entering Ephrata.” But it is better translated: “at the chosen season of the land, when he entered Ephrata.” This signifies the spring season, when everything bursts into flower and the season of the year is chosen; or when travelers, passing along the road, pluck and choose from the neighboring fields whatever comes to hand, with their various flowers.

*Ephrata* and *Bethlehem* are names for the same city, with a similar interpretation. For *Bethlehem* is rendered “house of the father,” on account of that bread which is said to have descended from heaven.

It follows:

“And it happened, when she was giving up her soul—for she was dying—that she called his name Son of my scent. But his father called his name Benjamin.”

In Hebrew the similarity of the names is audible. “Son of my sorrow,” the name imposed by the dying mother, is called *Benoni*. “Son of the right hand,” that is, of strength—the name Jacob changed it to—is called *Benjamin*. Hence those who think that *Benjamin* means “son of days” are mistaken. The right hand is called *jamin*, ending in the letter *n*; days, however, are also called *jamin*, but end in the letter *m*.

It follows:

“And Israel departed and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Ader.” The Hebrews wish this to be the place where the Temple was later built, and they understand the tower of Ader to mean “the tower of the flock,” that is, of gathering and assembly. The prophet Micah also bears witness to this when he says: “And you, tower of the flock, misty daughter of Zion,” and so forth.

At that time Jacob had his tents beyond the place where the Temple was later built. But if we follow the order of the road, it is the place of the shepherds near Bethlehem, where either the flock of angels sang at the Lord’s birth, or Jacob pastured his own sheep and gave the place its name, or—what is more likely—some future mystery was even then being shown by a certain prophecy.

## Jerome

“And Jacob came to Isaac his father at Mambre, in the city of Arbec; this is Chebron.” For *Arbec*, the Septuagint has “a plain,” although Chebron is situated on a mountain. The same city is also called Mambre, having been so named in ancient times after Abraham’s friend.

## These are the generations of Esau

“And Adesa gave birth to Eliphaz for Esau.” This is the Eliphaz whose memory is preserved in the Book of Job.

“These are the sons of Esau, and these are their rulers: he is Edom, and these are the sons of Seir.” Esau, Edom, and Seir are names of one man; why he is called by different names was stated above.

As for what follows—“and the Horites inhabiting the land,” and so forth—after enumerating the sons of Esau, the text goes back further and explains who had been rulers in the land of Edom before Esau, from the race of the Horites, who in our language are interpreted as “free men.” Let us read Deuteronomy carefully, where it is written more clearly how the sons of Esau came and killed the Horites and possessed their land as an inheritance.

“And the sons of Lotan were Hori and Aeman, and Lotan’s sister was Tamna.” This is the Tamna mentioned above: “And Tamna was the concubine of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn son, and she bore Amalek.” The Horites are mentioned because Esau’s firstborn son took a concubine from among their daughters.

As for Theman, Kenaz, Amalek, and the rest, we should know that names were later given to regions of Idumea from these persons.

It follows:

“This is Anah, who found Jamin in the wilderness while he was pasturing the asses of Zibeon his father.” Much and varied discussion of this passage occurs among the Hebrews; among the Greeks and among our people there is silence concerning it.

Some think that *Jamin* refers to waters, for the same letters are used to write “waters” as are written in this word. They maintain that, while pasturing his father’s asses in the wilderness, he discovered collections of water which, according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, are called “seas”—that is, that he discovered a pool, something difficult to find in the desert.

Some think that the word signifies hot springs, in proximity to the Punic language, which borders on Hebrew. Others suppose that he brought wild asses to female asses and discovered such a mating, from which extraordinarily swift asses were born, called *Jamin*. Most think that he was the first to cause herds of mares to be mounted by asses in the wilderness, so that new animals, mules, might be born from them contrary to nature.

Aquila translated the passage as follows: “This is Anas, who found ‘with the *simeim*’ (σὺν τοῦ σιμεὶμ).” Symmachus likewise has “the *simeim*” (τοὺς σιμεὶμ), an interpretation indicating the plural number. The Septuagint and Theodotion, however, translated it alike, saying “the *iamein*” (τὴν ἰαμεὶν), which indicates the singular number.

It follows:

“And Jobab, son of Zare of Bosra, reigned in his place.” Some suspect that this was Job, as is added at the end of his book. The Hebrews, however, assert that he was descended from Nahor, as was stated above.

Meanwhile, Reuben, moved by lustful desire, rushed passionately upon his father’s concubine. This crime of incest would not be recorded unless the future perversity of the people were being proclaimed. Nevertheless, the outrage of the man who committed it is also considered; in the Scriptures, however, it is a prophecy of future events.

For through Reuben, the firstborn, the firstborn people of Israel, the people of circumcision, is signified. It pollutes the bed of the concubine—that is, it repeatedly defiles the law of the Old Testament by transgression.

The Apostle Paul teaches that the law of the Old Testament is represented in the concubine when he says: “Abraham had two sons: one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. These two are the two Testaments.” Hagar, who was a concubine, is therefore placed in the figure of the Old Testament.

There is therefore one dove of her mother, who, as a chaste virgin, queen, and bride, is joined through the Gospel to Christ, the King of the Church.

There are therefore two kinds of useless people in the human race: one consisting of those who harm, the other of those unwilling to benefit; and whatever good they possess in this earthly life they waste, as though pouring seed upon the ground. The one who is first in evil is the one who harms, rather than the one who does no good. Therefore the elder is called “evil,” while the younger and later one is the one who poured his seed upon the ground.

The name of the elder, who is called *Her*, is interpreted as “skin-clad,” such as the tunics in which the first human beings were clothed in the punishment of their condemnation after being dismissed from paradise. The name of the younger, who is called *Onan*, is interpreted as “their sorrow”—the sorrow of those who are of no benefit, although they have the means to benefit, and lose it upon the ground.

The greater evil is the taking away of life, signified by the skin, than the failure to give life, signified by the sorrow of those who have no benefit. Yet God is said to have killed both, signifying that he removed the kingdom from such men.

The third son of Judah, who is not joined to that woman, signifies the time from which kings from the tribe of Judah ceased to arise for the Jewish people. He was indeed a son of Judah, but Tamar no longer received him as a husband: he belonged to the same tribe of Judah, but no one any longer reigned among the Jewish people. Hence his name, *Sela*, is interpreted as “his dismissal.”

Holy and righteous men do not belong to this interpretation. Although they existed at that time, they belong to the New Testament, since by prophesying they were knowingly useful. Such was David, who lived at precisely the time when Judea had begun to have no kings from the tribe of Judah.

The elder Herod should not be counted among its kings as Tamar’s husband. He was a foreigner and was not joined to her by that sacramental mystical anointing which would have been like a marriage bond. He ruled as an outsider, having received his power from the Romans and from Caesar. The same applies to his sons, the tetrarchs, one of whom was called Herod after his father and who agreed with Pilate in the Lord’s Passion.

These foreigners were not counted as belonging to that mystical kingdom of the Jews, to such an extent that the Jews themselves publicly cried out, gnashing their teeth against Christ: “We have no king but Caesar.” This was not true except in relation to the universal dominion of the Romans—for Caesar too was a king, though not properly of the Jews—but, in order to deny Christ and refuse to worship him, they condemned themselves by that utterance.

At the time when the kingdom had already failed from the tribe of Judah, the kingdom of Christ, our true Savior and Lord, had to come—one who would not harm but would greatly benefit. For this had been prophesied: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations.”

At that time, all Jewish teaching and the mystical anointing from which they were called “Christs” had also failed, according to the prophecy of Daniel: “Then he came for whom the expectation of the nations had been reserved; and the Holy of Holies was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.” For he was born in the time of the elder Herod, but he suffered under Herod the younger, the tetrarch.

Judah himself therefore bore the figure of this one who was coming to the sheep that had perished, the house of Israel, when he went to shear his sheep at Thamna, which is interpreted as “failing.” For the ruler had already failed from Judah, as had all Jewish teaching and anointing, until he came for whom it had been reserved.

He came with his shepherd, the Odollamite, whose name was Hiras, interpreted as “the vision of my brother.” The Odollamite means “testimony in water,” since the Lord came with precisely this testimony, possessing a testimony greater than John’s, yet using testimony in water on account of the weak sheep.

For Hiras himself, as we have already said, is interpreted as “the vision of my brother.” John truly saw his brother—his brother according to the seed of Abraham, according to the kinship of Mary his mother and Elizabeth John’s mother—and he saw him as his God and Lord, because, as John himself says, “from his fullness he received.”

He truly saw him, and for this reason no one born of women arose greater than he: of all who foretold Christ, he alone saw what many righteous men and prophets desired to see and did not see. He greeted him from the womb and recognized him more perfectly through the dove; therefore, as an Odollamite, he truly bears witness in water.

The Lord came to shear the sheep—that is, to unload them from the burdens of sins—of which, in the Church’s praise in the Song of Songs, it is said: “His teeth are like a flock of sheep that have been shorn.”

Then Tamar changes her appearance. For *Tamar* is also interpreted as “changing”; she changes her appearance and her name, and from the synagogue becomes the Church. Yet the name of bitterness remains in her—not the bitterness in which she gave the Lord gall, but that in which Peter wept bitterly.

Judah in Latin means “confession.” Therefore bitterness must be mingled with confession, so that true repentance may be foreshadowed. Through this repentance the Church, established among all the nations, is made fruitful. For it was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name throughout all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

Even the appearance of a prostitute signifies the confession of sins, for it bears the figure of the Church. Tamar, called from the nations, sits in this appearance at the gate of Neman, or Enahin, which is interpreted as “springs.” Like a stag, she hastens to the springs of water, desiring to reach the seed of Abraham.

She conceives without his knowing her, because this was foretold concerning him: “The people whom I did not know served me.” In secret she receives the ring, necklace, and staff: she is marked by calling, adorned by justification, and exalted by glorification. “Those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:30).

But, as I said, all this is still in secret, where the conception of holy fruitfulness also takes place. The promised kid is sent to her as to a prostitute. The kid signifies the reproach of sin, sent through the same Odollamite as one rebuking and saying, “Brood of vipers.” But the reproach of sin does not find her, because the bitterness of confession has transformed her.

Afterward, by the public signs of the ring, necklace, and staff, she overcame the Jews who judged rashly. Judah himself already represented them, for even today they say: “This people is not Christ’s, nor do we possess the seed of Abraham.” But when the certain proofs of our calling, justification, and glorification are brought forth, they will undoubtedly blush and be confounded, and will confess that we have been justified more than they.

For the Church, when accused by the Jews as an adulteress of the law, brings forward the pledges that she possesses. She displays the staff, that is, the sign of the Passion; the necklace, the lawful bond of the law; and the ring, the pledge of immortality.

The Scripture then presents Tamar giving birth and carrying twins in her womb. The first, called Zara, put out his hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread around it; then, when he drew his hand back inside, the second, called Phares, put out his hand and came forth first at birth.

Figurally, this corresponds to Israel extending its hand into the works of the law and drawing it back stained with the blood of the prophets and of the Savior himself. Afterward the people of the nations burst forth, so that “the last would be first, and the first last.”

## Jerome

“And Israel loved Joseph above all his sons, because he was the son of his old age, and he made him a variegated tunic.” For “variegated tunic” Aquila translated “an ankle-length tunic” (ἀστραγάλειον), that is, a tunic reaching to the ankles; Symmachus, “a sleeved tunic,” whether because it descended to the ankles and was distinguished by the marvelous variety of the craftsman’s handiwork, or because it had sleeves. For the ancients used tunics without sleeves more often.

And it adds: “Judah’s wife bore him a son, and he called his name Shelah; and she was in Ghazbi when she bore him.” The Hebrew word here has been put for a place-name, which Aquila translated as a thing, saying: “And she called his name Selom; and it came to pass that she deceived in the childbirth after she had borne him.” After she bore him Selom, her childbearing ceased. *Chazbi*, therefore, is not the name of a place, but means “deceit”; hence elsewhere it is written: “The work of the olive tree will deceive,” that is, the olive will not produce fruit.

It follows:

“And Judah, having been comforted, went up to those who were shearing his sheep, he and Hiras his Odollamite shepherd.” In place of “shepherd,” “friend” is read; but the word is ambiguous, because both names are written with the same letters. Yet “friend” is read *re*, “shepherd” *ro*.

“And she sat at the gate of Enan, which is on the road to Thamna.” The Hebrew word *Enaim* is rendered “eyes.” It is therefore not the name of a place, but the sense is: “She sat at the fork or crossroads, where the traveler must carefully look which road he should take.”

It follows:

“Judah recognized her and said: ‘She is more justified than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah.’” The Hebrew has, “She has been justified from me,” not because she was righteous, but because, in comparison with him, she had acted less badly: she had not wandered into disgrace, but sought children.

It follows:

“Behold, his brother came out, and she said: ‘Why has the breach been made for your sake?’ And she called his name Phares.” In place of “breach,” Aquila and Symmachus translated “division,” which in Hebrew is called *Phares*. Thus he received the name of division because he divided the membrane of the afterbirth. Hence the Pharisees, who separated themselves from the people of God as though righteous, are called “divided.”

After this his brother came out, in whose hand was the scarlet thread, and she called his name Zara. This name means “rising” or “east”; whether because he appeared first, or because very many righteous persons were born from him, as is contained in the Book of Chronicles, he was called Zara, that is, “rising.”

## Concerning Joseph

## Jerome

“And they sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty gold pieces.” In the Hebrew it has “silver pieces,” not “gold.” Nor should the Lord have been sold for a cheaper metal than Joseph.

The Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Putiphar, a eunuch, Pharaoh’s chief cook. In many passages Scripture mentions chief cooks—that is, chiefs of cooks—in place of commanders of the army. For the Greek *mageireuein* means “to kill.” Joseph was therefore sold to the commander of the army and warriors, not to Petephre, as it is written in the Latin, but to Putiphar the eunuch.

## Student

How can he later be said to have had a wife, if he was a eunuch?

## Teacher

The Hebrews report that Joseph was bought by this man because of his exceptional beauty for a shameful service; and after his master had caused his male organs to wither, he was later chosen, according to the custom of performing sacred rites (*hierophantein*, ἱεροφαντεῖν), for the priesthood of Heliopolis. Aseneth, whom Joseph later took as his wife, was this man’s daughter.

It follows:

“After these things, the chief cupbearer of the king of Egypt sinned.” Where we have “chief cupbearer,” the Hebrew has *Maskeh*: the same word that we previously read in the name of Abraham’s servant, whom we may call, in common usage, a cupbearer.

The office should not be considered insignificant, since among barbarian kings even to the present day it has been one of the greatest dignities to present the king with his cup. The poets too write about Ganymede and Jupiter, saying that he assigned his beloved to this office.

It follows:

“And behold, a vine was before me, and on the vine were three branches, and it itself was budding with three branches.” In Hebrew this signifies three shoots, and three branches or tendrils; they are called *Sarigim*.

“And I seemed to myself to be carrying three baskets of *chondrites* on my head.” In place of “three baskets of *chondrites*,” the Hebrew has “three baskets of fine flour.”

“And behold, seven cattle came up from the river, beautiful in appearance and choice in flesh, and they were feeding in Ahu.” *Ahu* is written twice in Genesis; it is neither a Greek nor a Latin word. But the Hebrew itself is corrupt. It is written *Ahu*, that is, “in the marsh.”

Since among the Hebrews the letters *vau* and *yod* are similar and differ only in size, the Septuagint translators rendered *Ahu* as *Achi*. According to their custom, to express the doubled aspiration, they joined the Hebrew letter *heth* to the Greek letter χ.

It follows:

“And Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying: Without God there shall be no answer bringing salvation to Pharaoh.” The Hebrew has it differently: “Without me, God will answer peace to Pharaoh.” Symmachus, translating more explicitly in his customary manner, rendered it: “Not I, but God will answer peace to Pharaoh.”

It follows:

“And behold, seven years of great abundance will come throughout all the land of Egypt.” I am surprised that the Hebrew word *Saba*, which above we interpreted as “abundance” or “satiety” in connection with the well that Isaac’s servants dug last, the Septuagint now very correctly interpreted there as “oath.” Yet “oath,” “seven,” “satiety,” and “abundance” can all be understood according to what the passage and its order require. In the subsequent passages as well, wherever “abundance” is read, the same Hebrew word is written.

It follows:

“And he cried out before him as a herald, and appointed him over all the land of Egypt.” Aquila translated this: “And he cried out in his presence for genuflection.” Symmachus, interpreting the Hebrew word itself, says: “And he called him, Abrech.”

It therefore seems to me that what should be understood is not so much “herald” or “genuflection”—which can be taken as occurring in greeting or worshiping Joseph—as what the Hebrews relate, saying that the phrase means “tender father.” *Ab* means “father,” while *rech* means “delicate” or “very tender.” Scripture thus indicates that, in wisdom, he was indeed the father of all, but in age he was a very tender young man and boy.

It follows:

“And Pharaoh called Joseph’s name Zaphanath-Phaaneah, and gave him Aseneth, the daughter of Putiphar, priest of Heliopolis, as a wife.” Although in Hebrew this name sounds like “discoverer of hidden things,” since it is an Egyptian name it must be interpreted according to that language.

In the Egyptian language, therefore, Zaphanath-Phaaneah is interpreted—or, as the Septuagint translators wished to render it, ψομθοφανήχ—as “savior of the world,” because he delivered the world from the imminent destruction of famine.

It should be noted that he took as his wife the daughter of his former master and purchaser, because by that time he was the priest of Heliopolis. For it would not have been lawful for the priests of that idol to exist without being eunuchs, so that the true suspicion of the Hebrews concerning him, which we mentioned earlier, is confirmed.

It follows:

“And two sons were born to Joseph before the years of famine came, whom Aseneth, daughter of Putiphar, priest of Heliopolis, bore to him.”

Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh, because he said: “God has made me forget all my labors and all my father’s household.” He called the name of the second Ephraim, because he said: “God has made me grow in the land of my humiliation.”

Observe, in view of the question about Joseph’s sons that will shortly be raised, that before the time of famine, when Jacob entered Egypt, Joseph had only two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.

He called the first Manasseh because he had forgotten his labors—for that is how “forgetfulness” is called in Hebrew. He called the second Ephraim because God had increased him; from this name “increase” is translated into our language.

It follows:

“And bring gifts to the man: some resin, honey, incense, storax, terebinth, and nuts”—or, as Aquila and Symmachus translated it, “almonds.”

We have included this passage so that we may know that where our copies have “incense,” the Hebrew has *nechota*, which Aquila translated as “storax.” Thus the “house of Nechota” read in Isaiah is most clearly understood as a chamber of incense or storax, because various spices were stored there.

It follows:

“And they drank and became drunk with him.” This is an idiom of the Hebrew language, which uses “drunkenness” for “satiety,” as in the passage: “In his showers it will rejoice as it sprouts”—clearly referring to land watered by rains.

It follows:

“And place each man’s silver in the mouth of his sack, and put my silver cup into the sack of the younger.” For “sack,” the Hebrew has *peron* or “bag”; for *condy*, that is, “cup,” which we also read in Isaiah, Aquila translated “goblet,” and Symmachus “vial.”

“Come down to me, do not delay, and you shall dwell in the land of Gosen of Arabia.” “Of Arabia” has been added here; it is not found in the Hebrew books. Hence the error became widespread that the land of Gosen was in Arabia.

Moreover, if, as it appears in our copies, Gosen is written with a final *m*—which I by no means approve—it signifies “a land watered by rain,” for *Gosen* is rendered “into rain.”

It follows:

“And Pharaoh said to Joseph: Say to your brothers, ‘Do this: load your wagons and go to the land of Canaan.’” For “wagons,” which the Septuagint and Theodotion translated as “conveyances” (τὰ φορεῖα), the other translators have “beasts of burden.”

“And he gave them provisions for the journey.” The word *zeda*, which all the translators here rendered with one voice as “provisions” (ὑθισιτισμός), that is, “provisions” or “rations,” also occurs in the Psalter. Where our copies read, “Blessing his widow, I will bless her,” although in many copies some read *theran* (θήραν) instead of *viduam*, that is, instead of χήραν, the Hebrew has *zeda*: “Blessing his provisions, I will bless them.”

*Theran* can more readily mean “hunting” than “grain,” although it is customary among the Egyptians also to call flour *theran*, which they now corruptly call *atheram*.

## Spiritual Recapitulation

From this point the history of Joseph follows: he is sold by his brothers, brought into Egypt, and there exalted. Joseph, one of Jacob’s twelve sons, whom his father loved more than the other sons, prefigured Christ the Lord, whom God the Father, born according to the flesh, preferred to the other brothers descended from Abraham’s stock. Hence it is also said there: “Jacob loved him because he had begotten him in his old age.” For as the world was growing old, the Son of God, dawning through the birth of the Virgin Mary, came late, as the son of old age according to the mystery of the body he assumed—he who was before and, as now, is forever with the Father.

The multicolored tunic that his father made for him signified the diversity of peoples gathered from all nations into the body of Christ. That dream, in which his brothers’ sheaves bowed down to his sheaf, is what was fulfilled in Christ. All the kings of the earth worshiped him; all nations serve him, offering, through faith, the fruit of good works. He is the one whom the sun, moon, and stars worship. Concerning the sun it is said: “Praise him, sun and moon, and all the stars.” For the excellence of the saints worships him under the name of the sun, the splendor of the Church under the image of the moon, and the multitude of all peoples under the figure of the stars.

Therefore his father rebuked him, saying: “Shall I, your mother, and your brothers worship you?” This rebuke signifies the hardness of the people of Israel, because they recognize that Christ was born from them, yet disdain to worship him.

Jacob sends his son Joseph to look after his brothers; God the Father sent his only-begotten Son to visit the human race, weakened by sins. He was sent by that Father of whom it is written: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh,” to see whether the sheep were in a right condition; and Christ says in the Gospel: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

Joseph therefore found his brothers at Dothaim, which is interpreted as “choice” [Latin: *delectio*]. Truly they were in a great defection, since they were plotting parricide. When Joseph’s brothers saw him from a distance, they plotted to kill him; and the Jews, seeing the true Joseph, the Lord Jesus Christ, all resolved with one accord to crucify him, saying: “Crucify him” (John XIX, 6).

An exceedingly savage beast devoured him—that is, Judas and the Jewish beast killed him. Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, I am sending you among wolves.” They stripped Joseph their brother of his multicolored and ankle-length tunic, and the Jews, through the death of the cross, stripped Christ of his bodily garment. The multicolored tunic signified a garment adorned with the diversity of all virtues.

They sprinkled the tunic with the blood of a kid, because, accusing him with false testimonies, they brought into hatred the one who forgave everyone’s sins. Then he was cast into a cistern, that is, into a pit; and Christ, stripped of human flesh, descended into hell. Joseph was lifted from the cistern and sold to the Ishmaelites, that is, to the nations; and Christ, after emerging from hell, was bought by all nations through the commerce of faith.

Joseph was sold for thirty pieces of silver through Judah’s advice, and Christ was sold for the same number through the counsel of Judas Iscariot.

Then Jacob, lamenting the loss of his posterity, mourned his son as a father mourns one who has been lost, and as a prophet he wept over the purpose of the Jews. Finally, he tore his garment, as we read that the high priest did during the Lord’s passion. The veil of the temple was also torn, prophesying that his people had been stripped and showing that the kingdom had been divided.

Joseph therefore descended into Egypt, and Christ into the world. A eunuch bought him—that is, a chaste people disciplined by the Gospel. Joseph was beautiful in appearance; likewise David says concerning Christ: “You are more beautiful in form than the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips.”

But, he says, a woman cast her eyes upon him, intending to commit adultery with him. This woman was a figure of the Synagogue, which, as it is written, often prostituted itself after foreign gods. Likewise, she wanted to hold Christ in the crime of her adultery, so that he would deny himself to be God and observe the commandments of the Pharisees and scribes rather than those of the Law, which was like her husband.

But Christ, refusing the unlawful doctrine, was seized by the hand of the adulterous Synagogue through the garment of his body; he stripped himself of mortal flesh and, free from death, ascended into heaven. When the prostitute could not hold him, she slandered him, saying that he blasphemed the Lord’s temple and was said to be a transgressor of the Law.

Yet neither prison terrified him, nor did the realms below retain him; even when he had descended there as though to be punished, he freed others from it.

Finally, Joseph found two eunuchs, bound in prison from the household of the king. They signified the figure of two peoples, believers and unbelievers, who, enclosed under sin and held liable to Adam’s transgression, were kept in bondage. They are called eunuchs because they had received the rule of a chaste discipline. “The utterances of the Lord,” it says, “are chaste.”

Then, after the Lord rose from the dead following the threefold light, and after the obscurity of the Law had been revealed as Joseph revealed the dreams, the people of believers were released from sins and freed from the prison of hell. It is restored to the ministry of divine Law; but the unbelieving and impious people of the Jews, because they did not believe in the wood of conversion, is hung upon the wood of transgression, as happened to that other eunuch who represented the image of the Jews.

Furthermore, Pharaoh relates a dream, and Joseph interprets it. But what do the seven years, displayed in seven full ears of grain or in seven fat cows, signify except the gifts of the seven spiritual charisms, through which the abundance of faith overflows in generous devotion? By contrast, the seven barren and fasting years signified, in the last times, hunger for truth and justice.

Joseph gathered all the abundance of grain during the seven years—that is, he stored the grain of the saints’ faith in granaries through those seven charisms, as through seven years—so that when the seven years of scarcity begin, that is, when the iniquity of the seven capital crimes arises under Antichrist, when there will be a famine of faith and salvation, the saints and believers together may possess an abundant harvest of righteousness, lest their faith fail through the thinness of words during the scarcity.

Then Joseph, who had assumed the type of Christ, was given a royal chariot, and a herald proclaimed before him; Pharaoh appointed him over the whole land of Egypt. Likewise, after our Lord had been sold by Judas, as Joseph was sold by his brothers, and had risen from the prison of the underworld, he ascended the chariot of the heavenly kingdom, concerning which it is said: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold.” He received from the Father the authority to preach and judge, as the apostle Paul says: “He gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians II, 10).

He also received a ring, namely the priesthood of faith, by which the souls of believers are marked with the sign of salvation, and on our foreheads and hearts the figure of the eternal king is expressed through the sign of the cross. He is clothed in a linen robe—that is, in holy flesh brighter than fine linen, and in the robe of immortality. He also received a golden chain, that is, good understanding.

A herald goes before him—that is, John the Baptist, who preceded him and proclaimed: “Prepare the way of the Lord” (Luke III, 4). He will also have another herald, the trumpet of the angel, because he himself said: “He will come with the trumpet of an angel.”

Joseph is called “Savior of the world” in the Egyptian language. What could be clearer concerning Christ? When the Savior is shown under the figure of Joseph, it is not only the Savior of one land, Egypt, but of the whole world.

Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before King Pharaoh; and Christ is read to have been the same age when, under the type of Pharaoh, he appeared revealed before the king. He therefore received a wife from the nations, that is, the Church, from whom he fathered two sons, that is, two peoples gathered from Jews and nations.

After the years of abundance, famine rightly prevailed throughout the whole world, because there was no one who did good. After this, Joseph saves Egypt from the scarcity of grain; and Christ frees the world from hunger for the word of God. For Christ opened his granaries throughout the whole world, and by distributing his grain subjected everything.

Unless Joseph’s brothers had sold him, Egypt would have perished; unless the Jews had crucified Christ, the world would have perished.

Joseph is interpreted as “increase” or “enlargement.” But in that Joseph only Egypt had enlargement; in our Joseph, the whole world deserved to have increase. He distributed wheat; our Joseph distributed the word of God. “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Romans X, 18).

Jacob says to his sons: “Is there grain in Egypt?” God the Father also says: “Out of Egypt I called my Son.”

Ten of the more perfect therefore descend—that is, the Jews, constituted according to the number of the Law’s Decalogue. Though Joseph recognized them, he was not recognized by them; so too the Hebrews are known by Christ, but they themselves do not recognize him. They gave him money, but Joseph—that is, Christ—gave them grain and returned the silver, because Christ is not bought with money but with grace.

Joseph saw Benjamin, his little brother; mystically, Jesus also saw Paul when light shone around him. He is called little because he did not yet bear the mature age of faith in the flesh. Hence he is also read to have been a young man when he guarded the garments of those who stoned Stephen.

Joseph wept; and Christ weeps over Paul’s blindness. He then washed his face in order to restore to him the light he had lost. Christ washes his face when Paul was baptized, through whom the Lord Jesus was seen by many.

Then a silver cup was placed in the sack of the younger brother alone. But what does it mean that Joseph’s cup was found in Benjamin’s sack, except that in Paul’s body the eloquence of heavenly doctrine was already shining, since he was learned in the Law, but was not yet subject to it? The cup of doctrine was within the sack, a lamp beneath a bushel.

Nevertheless, Ananias was sent and laid on him his hand; he untied the purse. When the purse was untied, the silver shone forth, and when the scales fell away like little pieces of sackcloth, the sack—that is, the veil of the Law—being removed, he obtained the grace of freedom. With unveiled face he preached the word of the Gospel.

He was given thirty pieces of silver together with five excellent robes. Whoever preaches the Trinity or the cross of Christ receives thirty pieces of silver from Christ. Therefore Paul says: “For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians II, 2).

He received five robes, that is, the disciplines of wisdom and the manifold forms of every kind of understanding. Paul therefore excels, and his share of merits overflows; nevertheless, the brothers—that is, the other preachers—also have their own grace: two robes, namely, that they confess Christ to be both God and man, according to what is read in Proverbs: “All her household are clothed with double garments”—that is, with mystical or moral understanding.

Gifts are also sent to the father; the son honors the father. Christ invites his people to promised gifts. Donkeys carry these gifts: those useless and laborious Gentiles now carry useful gifts in the type of Christ. In the Gospel they carry the giver of gifts.

Joseph dismissed his brothers, who announced to their father, saying: “Joseph lives, and he himself is lord over all the land of Egypt.” Jacob was terrified—that is, the unbelieving people—but after recognizing Christ’s deeds, his spirit revives; and he who seemed dead in faith is brought to life by the resurrection of Christ.

He is therefore summoned by his sons, that is, by Peter, Paul, and John: the Jewish people are invited to grace.

Judah meets them; his name is interpreted as “confession,” because confession now precedes those whom unbelief formerly possessed, and thus the true Joseph, Christ, meets them.

For who at the end of the age will receive the Jewish people? Not according to their merits, but according to the election of his grace. He lays his hand upon their eyes and removes their blindness—he whose blindness he delayed, so that the one who previously did not think that he should believe might believe last.

Hence the Apostle also says: “A partial blindness has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Romans XI, 25).

## Jerome

All the souls who entered Egypt with Jacob, and who came forth from his loins apart from the wives of Jacob’s sons, were sixty-six souls. But the sons of Joseph who were born to him in Egypt were nine souls. Thus all the souls who entered Egypt with Jacob numbered seventy-five.

There is no doubt that, apart from Joseph and his sons, the sixty-six souls who came forth from Jacob’s loins entered Egypt. The number is confirmed by counting them one by one, and it is found in the Hebrew volumes.

But concerning what we read in the Septuagint: “The sons of Joseph who were born to him in Egypt were nine souls,” let us know that in Hebrew, instead of “nine,” there are two. Ephraim and Manasseh were born to Aseneth, the daughter of Potiphera, in Egypt before Jacob entered Egypt and before the time of famine began.

The following passage, which we read above—“The sons of Manasseh whom his Syrian concubine bore to him were Machir; and Machir fathered Gilead. The sons of Ephraim, Manasseh’s brother, were Shuthelah and Tahan. The sons of Shuthelah were Edem”—has been added, since it describes as having happened earlier something that occurred later. For at the time when Jacob entered Egypt, Ephraim and Manasseh were not of such an age that they could have fathered children. It is therefore clear that all the souls who entered Egypt from Jacob’s loins were seventy, although sixty-six entered first and three souls were born in Egypt—namely Joseph with his sons—and Jacob himself was the seventieth.

Lest we seem to speak against the authority of Scripture, the Seventy Translators also translated in Deuteronomy that seventy souls entered Egypt. If anyone therefore supports our position, he will make Scripture contradict itself. For the Seventy Translators themselves, because here they said that seventy-five souls entered Egypt by *prolepsis*—that is, including Joseph and his descendants—record in Deuteronomy that only seventy entered.

But if, conversely, this is brought against us: how is it that in the Acts of the Apostles, in Stephen’s dispute, it is said to the people that seventy-five souls entered Egypt? The answer is easy. Saint Luke, who was the historian himself, when sending the volume of the Acts of the Apostles to the nations, ought not to write anything contrary to the Scripture that had already been disseminated among the nations. Certainly, at that time the authority of the Seventy Translators was held in greater esteem than that of Luke, who was regarded among the nations as unknown, insignificant, and not of great credibility.

This general principle should be observed: whenever the holy apostles or apostolic men speak to peoples, they generally make use of testimonies that had already been disseminated among the nations, although many report that Luke the evangelist, as a proselyte, was ignorant of Hebrew letters.

The text continues:

“Judah he sent ahead of him to Joseph, into the land of Rameses.”

In Hebrew there is neither the city of Heroes nor the land of Rameses, but only Gosen. Some Jews assert that Gosen is now called the Thebaid, and that the passage which follows—“He gave them the land of Egypt to possess, Rameses”—refers to a village. They think that it was formerly called Arsinoë.

The text continues: “And he said to him, ‘Swear to me.’ And he swore to him, and he worshiped toward the top of his staff.”

Here, too, some people falsely pretend that Jacob worshiped the top of Joseph’s scepter, supposedly worshiping his son’s authority in honoring him, whereas in Hebrew it is read quite differently. “And Israel worshiped,” it says, “at the head of the bed.” That is, after he had sworn, and after the son had become secure concerning the request he had made, he worshiped God toward the head of his bed.

For that holy and God-devoted man, weighed down by old age, had his bed positioned in such a way that the posture of his reclining body was readily prepared for worship without any difficulty.

“And it was announced to Joseph: ‘Behold, your father is ill.’ And he took his two sons with him, Manasseh and Ephraim.”

This demonstrates what was stated above: at that time Joseph had only two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh. For if, many years later, when his father Jacob was dying, he brought only two sons to receive the blessing, then certainly, at the time when his brothers entered Egypt, his sons could not have been old enough to beget children; and consequently Jacob could not have had grandsons through them.

## [Col. 0354C]

“And Israel strengthened himself and sat upon his bed.”

I do not know why the Seventy Translators rendered the same word differently in different places. I state this boldly: the very word *mitta*, which they translated here as “bed,” they named above when we said that Jacob worshiped the staff rather than the bed.

The text continues:

“Now, your two sons who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you into Egypt are mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are. But those whom you beget after them shall be yours; they shall be called by the names of their brothers.”
