If anyone doubted that seventy souls of the sons of Israel entered Egypt, and that Joseph at the time when Jacob entered had not nine sons but only two, the present chapter confirms it. Jacob himself says that he had two sons, not nine.

When he says that Ephraim and Manasseh shall be to him as Simeon and Reuben, this signifies: just as Reuben and Simeon will be two tribes and will be called by their own names, so Ephraim and Manasseh will be two tribes, will beget two peoples, and will inherit the land of promise as my sons also do.

But the remaining sons, he says, whom you will beget after my death—showing that they had not yet been born at that time—shall be yours. They shall be called by the names of their brothers for their inheritance. They shall not receive land separately, nor shall they have their own allotments like the other tribes; rather, they shall be mingled with the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh as appendages of the people.

The text continues:

“Jacob said to Joseph: ‘I have given you Shechem, a distinguished portion, above your brothers, more than to your brothers, which I took from the hands of the Amorites by my sword and bow.’”

“Shechem” has been declined according to Greek and Latin usage; in Hebrew it is called *Shechem*, as the evangelist John testifies. Although it is read incorrectly as “Sychar,” the error has become established; it is now Neapolis, the city of the Samaritans.

Since *Shechem* is translated in Hebrew as “shoulder,” he made a fitting allusion to the name when he said: “I will give you one shoulder.” For instead of “distinguished,” that is, *exaireton*—“chosen” or “exceptional”—the Hebrew reads “one.”

When he says that he possessed it by bow and sword, he calls the bow and sword justice, by which he, a pilgrim and foreigner, deserved to be delivered from danger after Shechem and Hamor had been killed. For, as we read above, he feared that the neighboring towns and fortified places would rise against him because of the destruction of the allied city.

And the Lord did not allow them to harm him. Or it may certainly be understood in this way: “I will give you Shechem, which I acquired by my strength”—that is, with the money I obtained through much labor and sweat.

When he says “above his brothers,” he shows that he gave it to Joseph’s tribe without death, and a mausoleum is still visible there today.

## Recapitulation

Joseph therefore gave his father and brothers the best land, Gosen, supplying them with food because famine had oppressed the land. So too the Lord, choosing the best land for his parents—that is, for the patriarchs and prophets, from whom Christ was descended according to the flesh—or for all the saints, of whom he says in the Gospel: “These are my brothers, who do the will of my Father” (Matthew VII, 21)—gives them the land, namely, the promised kingdom of God. Concerning it the Prophet says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm XXVI, 13).

## Another Recapitulation

After this Joseph hastened to receive his father’s blessing and presented his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. In them, just as it happened with Esau and Jacob, when the Lord said, “The elder shall serve the younger,” so it also happened with these two sons of Joseph.

The elder, Manasseh, whose name is interpreted as “forgetfulness,” bore the type of the Jewish people, which forgot its Lord who made it. The younger, representing Christians, signifies fruitfulness, which is proper to the younger people: it is the body of Christ, which has been made fruitful throughout the breadth of the world.

When Jacob wished to bless them, he placed Ephraim at his left and Manasseh at his right. But he crossed his hands, prefiguring the mystery of the cross: transferring the right hand to the younger and the left to the elder, he placed them symbolically upon their heads. Thus the likeness of the cross marked upon their heads foretold scandal for the Jews and future glory for Christians. Through the mystery of the cross, the elder was made left from right, and the younger right from left, because, while the Jews were falling into our deserts, we attained their glory.

By this sacrament the younger people of the nations was placed above the elder people of the Jews. Hence the same patriarch said: “This one shall indeed become a people, but his younger brother shall be greater than he.”

## Concerning Jacob’s Blessings upon His Sons

### Jerome

Jacob therefore called his twelve sons and, blessing them, said:

“Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sons, hard to bear and hard in insolence and injury; do not boil over like water. For you went up upon your father’s bed; then you violated the couch when you went up.”

In Hebrew it is written as follows:

“Reuben, my firstborn, my strength and the beginning of my children, greater in bearing strength; you were poured out like water; do not increase. For you went up upon your father’s couch and defiled the bed in your ascent.”

The meaning is this: You are my firstborn, greater among my children; you sat according to the order of your birth, and the inheritance that by right was due to the firstborn—to receive the priesthood and the kingdom. This is shown by bearing the burden and by great strength. But because you sinned, and like water that cannot be contained in a vessel you were poured out in the rush of desire, I therefore command you not to sin any longer. Remain among your brothers, mourning the punishment of your sin, because you lost the rank of the firstborn.

## Repetition

Jacob called his sons in order to bless them. Speaking mystically and in sequence, he spoke truly as one who knew what was to come. He told them what would happen in the last times, beginning in this way:

“Reuben, my firstborn.”

According to the mystical understanding, Reuben appears to represent the person of the former people. To him the Lord also says through the Prophet: “Israel is my firstborn.”

For, according to what was owed to the firstborn, it belonged to him to receive the priesthood and the kingdom. It is added: “You are my strength,” because from that people came the foundation of faith; from that people came the strength that is Christ.

But how is he himself “the beginning of sorrows,” except because he was always inflicting injury upon God the Father, turning his back toward him and not his face? He was first in gifts, because the utterances of God were given first to them. The legislation and the covenant, or promise, were given first to them.

He was greater in authority, certainly because of the greatness of his strength, since that same people reigned more abundantly than the others in this age. But he was poured out like water by sinning against Christ: like water that cannot be contained in a vessel, he was poured out in the rush of desire.

Therefore he added: “Do not increase any further,” because after that people had been scattered throughout the whole world, it was greatly weakened and diminished.

But why did he deserve such things? He explained as follows: “Because you went up upon your father’s couch.”

This does not mean, as the Jews understand it, that it was said because he had intercourse with his father’s concubine Bilhah. The prophecy was announcing future events, not those that had already happened, since the patriarch himself said: “I will announce to you what will happen in the last days.” Therefore what he foretold as future must not be referred to the past.

He was proclaiming the Lord’s passion and the audacity of the firstborn people. That people went up upon the couch of God its Father and stained his bed when it seized the Lord’s body, in which the fullness of divinity rested, hung it upon the cross, and defiled it with iron.

## Jerome

“Simeon and Levi are brothers; they have completed the iniquity of their scheme. Let my soul not enter into their counsel, and let my heart not be joined to their assembly, because in their fury they killed men, and in their desire they hamstrung a bull.”

Necessity compels us, in accordance with the purpose of this work, to repeat at greater length what differs from the Hebrew truth. For there it is read:

“Simeon and Levi are brothers; vessels of the iniquity of the Amorites. Let my soul not enter into their secret, and let my glory not be desolated in their assembly, because in their fury they killed a man, and in their lust they undermined a wall.”

It signifies that he did not share their plan when they killed Shechem and Hamor, men joined to them by treaty, and shed innocent blood against the peace and friendship that had been established. They were carried away by a kind of fury and, in their cruelty, destroyed the walls of the city that had received them as guests.

Hence he continues and says:

“Cursed be their fury, because it was insolent; and their anger, because it was harsh. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.”

Levi did not receive a separate inheritance, but throughout all the tribes he had only a few cities for habitation. Concerning Simeon it is written in the Book of Joshua that he too did not obtain his own allotment, but received something from the tribe of Judah. In Chronicles it is written more clearly that, after he had multiplied and had no place for a possession, he went out into the desert.

Some interpret prophetically the men who were killed as the apostles, and the bull that was hamstrung as Christ, by the Pharisees.

## Recapitulation

Jacob turned to Simeon and Levi and said:

“Simeon and Levi are brothers, warring vessels of iniquity.”

By Simeon and Levi the scribes and priests of the Jewish people are understood. The scribes of the Jews came from Simeon, while the chief priests came from the tribe of Levi. Concerning them it is written: “They took counsel to hand Jesus over to death” (Matthew XXVI, 4).

Regarding that counsel, the patriarch who already saw God in his mind says: “Let my soul not enter into their counsel, and the rest” (Genesis XLIX).

For even at that time the holy patriarch shuddered to behold such great crimes as the Jews would commit in the last days.

The text continues:

“Because in their fury they killed a man” (ibid.), that is, Christ, according to what is written: “Woe to their souls, because they have devised an evil plan against themselves, saying: ‘Let us bind the righteous, because he is useless to us’” (Wisdom II).

“And in their pain they undermined a wall” (Genesis XLIX), when they pierced with a lance that spiritual and strongest bulwark which guards Israel.

“Cursed be their fury, because it was obstinate”—that is, obstinate in perpetrating so great a crime—when, inflamed with fury and anger, they delivered Christ to Pontius Pilate the governor, saying: “Crucify him, crucify him” (Mark XI), and, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John XIX).

“And their indignation, because it was harsh,” when they asked for the robber Barabbas and demanded that the prince of life be crucified.

“I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis XLIX). Two things are named here: division and scattering. This is because some of them believed in God, while others remained in unbelief. Those who separate from them and come to faith are called divided; those whose homeland and temple have been overthrown, and whose unbelieving race is scattered throughout the world, are called scattered.

## Jerome

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (ibid.).

Because Judah is interpreted as “confession” or “praise,” it is accordingly written: “Judah, your brothers shall confess to you,” or, “Your brothers shall praise you.”

“Your father’s sons shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub; from the seed, my son, you have risen; lying down like a lion, and like a lion’s cub, who will rouse him?” (ibid.)

Although this contains a great mystery concerning Christ, nevertheless, according to the literal sense, kings would be generated from David’s stock, and all the tribes would worship him. For he does not say, “The sons of your mother,” but “The sons of your father.”

What follows—“From the seed, my son”—has in Hebrew: “From captivity, my son, you have risen,” to show that he would lead captive peoples. According to the more sacred understanding, his ascent on high and his leading captivity captive (Ephesians IV) signify—or, as I think better, captivity signifies the passion and ascent signifies the resurrection.

“Binding his colt to the vine, and the cord to the foal of his she-ass” has in Hebrew:

“Binding his colt to the vine, and to Sorek, my son, his she-ass” (Genesis XLIX).

This means that he joined the foal of the she-ass, upon which Jesus sat—that is, the people of the Gentiles—to the vineyard of the apostles, because they are from the Jews; and he bound the she-ass to Sorek, that is, to the chosen vine, upon which the Church gathered from the nations sits.

When he says, “My son,” he turns directly to Judah, indicating that Christ would accomplish all these things. It must also be known that where we read, “Binding his colt to the vine,” the Hebrew may read, instead of “colt,” “your city,” according to the same meaning, with the Church represented in different words.

Of this it is written elsewhere: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew V), and, “The river’s rushing waters make glad the city of God” (Psalm XLV).

## Recapitulation

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Genesis XLIX).

Through this Judah the true confessor, Christ, is expressed, who was born according to the flesh from his tribe. His brothers praise him—namely, the apostles and all his coheirs, who through adoption have been made sons of God the Father and, through grace, brothers of Christ, whose Lord he is by nature.

“Your hands shall be upon the necks of your enemies” (ibid.).

By those same hands and by the same trophy of the cross he both protected his own and healed his enemies and opposing powers. As the Father also promises him, saying: “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet” (Psalm CIX).

“Your father’s sons shall worship you” (Genesis XLIX), because many of Jacob’s sons worship him and have been saved through the election of grace.

“Judah is a lion’s cub” (ibid.), because in being born he became little, as it is written: “A little child is born to us” (Isaiah IX).

“To the prey, my son, you have risen” (Genesis XLIX)—that is, by ascending the cross, you redeemed captive peoples. Those whom the opposing lion had seized, you rescued by dying.

Finally, returning from the underworld, you ascended on high and led captivity captive (Ephesians IV); resting, you lay down like a lion (Genesis XLIX).

Most clearly Christ lay down in his passion when, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John XIX), or when in the tomb he rested securely, as though in a kind of sleep of the body.

But why “like a lion” and “like a lion’s cub”? In his sleep he was a lion because he fulfilled this not by necessity but by power, according to what he himself had said: “I have authority to lay down my life, and no one takes it from me, but I lay it down myself” (John X).

What he added—“And like a lion’s cub” (Genesis XLIX)—means that he died from the same source from which he was born. Natural philosophers write concerning a lion’s cub that, when it is born, it sleeps for three days and three nights. Then, shaken, as it were, by its father’s growl or roar, it is said to awaken from its sleep in the den.

This is very appropriately applied to Christ’s death in the passion: lying for three days and three nights in the chamber of the tomb, he fulfilled the sleep of death. Christ therefore rested well like a lion, since he conquered not only the bitterness of death but also death’s dominion itself.

Again, he is rightly called a lion’s cub because he rose on the third day. Hence the passage about his resurrection is joined to this:

“Who will rouse him?” (ibid.)

That is, no human being will do so, except himself, according to what he said concerning his body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II).

The text continues:

> “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis XLIX).

This passage most clearly refers to Judah. For so long, an unbroken succession of kings from his seed remained among the Jews, until Christ was born of the Virgin for the redemption of the world. The histories of the Jews prove this, showing that the first foreign king among the Jewish people was Herod, in whose time Christ was born. If the Jews think that Christ has not come, then the kingship of the Jews has not remained from the tribe of Judah to this day. Thus, a king did not fail from the people of Judah until he came for whom it had been reserved.

But because he who was to be sent benefited not the Jews alone, it follows: “And he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.” “Binding his foal to the vine” (ibid.). The foals are the people from the nations, upon whom the burden of the Law had never yet been imposed. He joined this foal to the vine of the apostles, because the apostles are from the Jews. For “the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. VI), and “to the vine, O my son, he binds his she-ass” (Gen. XLIX). He himself said: “I am the true vine” (John XV). To this vine, therefore, he binds his she-ass, upon which the Church, gathered from the nations, rides. He therefore bound her to the vine of his body by the bond of charity, and fastens her with the ties of evangelical discipline, so that, living in imitation of him, she may become “an heir of God and a joint-heir with Christ” (Rom. VIII).

Others understand this she-ass to be the Synagogue, slow-footed, that is, and weighed down by the heavy burden of the Law. “He shall wash his robe in wine” (Gen. XLIX), whether this means his flesh in the blood of his Passion, or the holy Church in that wine which “shall be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. XXVI), “and his cloak in the blood of the grape” (Gen. XLIX). The cloak consists of the nations whom he joined to his body, as it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, unless I clothe all these as with a garment” (Isa. XLIX). Christ cleansed us in the blood of the grape when, like a cluster of grapes, he hung upon the wood of the cross. Then blood and water flowed from his side (John XIX); the water washed us, but the blood redeemed us.

“His eyes are more beautiful than wine” (Gen. XLIX). The eyes of Christ are the apostles and evangelists, who provide the light of knowledge to the entire body of the Church. They are shown to be more beautiful than wine because their teaching surpasses the austerity of old wine: that is, the evangelical precepts are far clearer than the tradition of the ancient Law and than the commandments of the Old Testament.

“And his teeth are whiter than milk” (ibid.). The teeth are the holy preachers, who cut people away from errors and, as though chewing them, transfer them into the body of Christ. By the name “milk” is signified the teaching of the Law, which nourished the carnal people, like little children, with a cup of milk. The teachers of the Church have become whiter than this milk; they chew and distribute the strong and substantial food of the word. Of them the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Solid food is for the mature” (Heb. V). And rightly does he say that his teeth are whiter than milk. For all who are mature, and who, by explaining the nourishment of Scripture, supply the Church’s body with the subtle and refined understanding called spiritual, ought to be bright and pure, free from every stain.

**Jerome.**—“Issachar desired what was good, resting between the boundaries and seeing that rest was good, and the land, that it was rich. He placed his shoulder under labor, and became a farming man” (Gen. XLIX).

In Hebrew it is written thus: “Issachar is a bony ass, lying between the boundaries, and seeing that rest is good, and the land, that it is beautiful. He bent his shoulder to bear, and became one serving for tribute.” Because he had said above that Zebulun would possess the shores of the great sea and would also touch Sidon and the other cities of Phoenicia, he now returns to the inland province. Issachar, who was to possess the most beautiful territory near Naphtali in the region of Galilee, is made by his blessing its inhabitant.

He calls him a bony ass, and speaks of his shoulder as bearing, because he would labor greatly in cultivating the land and transporting to the sea the things that grew within his borders, while also carrying tribute to the kings. The Hebrews say that, metaphorically, this signifies that, meditating on the holy Scriptures day and night, he devoted his attention to labor; and therefore all the tribes serve him, carrying gifts to him as to a teacher.

**Recapitulation.**—“Issachar is a strong ass” (ibid.). Issachar, whose name means “reward,” refers to the people of the nations, whom the Lord purchased at the price of his blood. This Issachar is written to be a strong ass because formerly the gentile people were like a brutish and lustful animal, existing without any reason; but now it is strong, submitting its neck to the dominion of the Redeemer and bearing the yoke of the Lord’s discipline and of the Gospel.

Lying between the boundaries, he saw that rest was good and the land that it was excellent. To lie between the boundaries means to rest while awaiting the end of the world, seeking nothing of the things that are now taking place in the intervening time, but desiring the final things. The strong ass saw rest and an excellent land when the simple gentile people raised themselves to the strength of good works because they were advancing toward the homeland of eternal life. Hence he also places his shoulder under the burden, because, desiring to reach the promised rest, he willingly bears all the burdens of the commandments. Therefore he became one serving for tribute: that is, he offers gifts of faith and offerings of good works to his King and Christ.

**Jerome.**—“Dan shall judge his people like one of the scepters of Israel. Let Dan be a serpent on the road, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s heels, and let his rider fall backward. I shall await your salvation, O Lord” (ibid.).

Samson, judge of Israel, was from the tribe of Dan. Thus Jacob, seeing in the spirit Samson the Nazirite growing his hair and then triumphing over his enemies after slaughtering them, says that he will not allow anyone to pass through the land of Israel, in the likeness of a serpent or horned serpent lying in wait along the roads. Even if some reckless man, trusting in his own strength as in the speed of a horse, should wish to pass through the land like a plunderer, he would not be able to escape.

He speaks throughout by the metaphor of the serpent and the rider. Seeing, therefore, your Nazirite so strong—who died because of a prostitute, and by dying killed our enemies—I thought, O God, that he himself was your true Christ, your Son, because he died and did not rise again, and once more Israel was captured and led away. Another Savior of the world and of my race must be awaited, that he may come for whom it has been reserved, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations (ibid.).

**Recapitulation.**—“Dan shall judge his people like another tribe of Israel. Let Dan be a serpent on the road, a horned serpent on the path,” and so forth (ibid.).

Some say that the Antichrist is foretold in these words and that he will come from this tribe; others say that they refer to Judah, by whom Christ was betrayed. They declare that these writings designate both a rider and the Lord assumed in flesh. They wish “fall backward” to mean that he would return to the earth from which he had been taken. But because he rose on the third day, he says: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord” (ibid.). So also he says through David: “You will not abandon my soul to the underworld” (Ps. XV).

This is how some explain the passage. Others, however, transfer this prophecy to the Antichrist, because in this place Dan is asserted to be a serpent and a biter. Accordingly, not without reason, when the Israelite people had received their lands in the division of the camps, Dan first encamped toward the north, signifying him who had said in his heart: “I shall sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I shall ascend above the heights of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV).

Of him the prophet says: “From Dan the snorting of his horses was heard” (Jer. VIII). He is called not only a serpent but also a horned serpent. For *cerasta* in Greek—κέρατα—means “horns,” and this serpent is said to be horned. Through it the coming of the Antichrist is rightly asserted, because he will arm himself against the way of the faithful with the poisonous bite of his preaching, and also with the horns of power.

Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? Thus he becomes a serpent on the road (Gen. XLIX), because he urges those whom he flatters as though sparing them to walk in the broad expanse of the present life; but he bites on the road, because he destroys with the poison of his error those to whom he grants liberty.

Again he becomes a horned serpent on the path (ibid.), because those whom he finds faithful and constraining themselves to the narrow ways of the heavenly commandment, he attacks not only with the wickedness of crafty persuasion but also presses with the terror of power; and, in the anguish of persecution, after the benefits of feigned sweetness, he exercises the horns of his power.

In this passage the horse signifies the world, which through its pride foams as it runs along the course of passing time; and because the Antichrist strives to seize the end of the world, this horned serpent is said to bite the horse’s heels. To bite the horse’s heel means to strike the final period of the age, so that its rider may fall backward.

The rider of the horse is anyone who is exalted by the indignation of the world. He is said to fall backward, and not on his face, as Saul is said to have fallen. To fall on one’s face means to recognize one’s sins in this life and to mourn them through repentance. To fall backward, where one cannot see, means to fall suddenly from this life and not to know to what punishments one is being led.

And because Judea, seized by the snares of its error, awaits the Antichrist instead of Christ, Jacob, turned in the same passage into the voice of the elect, rightly says: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord” (ibid.). That is: I do not faithfully believe in the Antichrist as the unbelievers do, but in the true Christ, who will come for our redemption.

It follows:

[Col. 0360D] “Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships” (ibid.). Zebulun is interpreted as “dwelling-place of strength.” It signifies the Church, most strong for enduring every kind of suffering. She is on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships so that she may be a refuge for believers and show the harbor of faith to those in danger.

Established with immovable and unshaken firmness against all the storms of the world, she awaits the shipwreck of the Jews and the storms of the heretics, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. IV). Though she is struck by their waves, she is not broken by the waves; she does not yield to any storms of heresies, nor does she collapse when shaken by any wind of schisms.

She extends as far as Sidon; that is, she reaches the nations. It is also read in the Gospel that some of the apostles were taken from there, and that the Lord often taught in those places, as it is written: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: the people sitting in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. IX).

**Jerome.**—“Gad shall plunder like a band of raiders, and he himself shall plunder the heel” (Gen. XLIX). We have translated this according to the Hebrews. But where we have placed “band of raiders,” the text has *Gedud*, alluding to the name Gad. This may be expressed more significantly by the Greek word εὔζωνος, that is, “girded” or “equipped.”

The whole passage refers to the fact that, when Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh returned to their sons whom they had left in possession beyond the Jordan, after thirteen years they found that a great war had arisen against them from the neighboring nations and fought bravely after defeating their enemies. Read the book of Jesus son of Nave and Chronicles. I do not deny that there are many mysteries in the blessings of the patriarchs, but they do not belong to the present little work.

**Recapitulation.**—“Gad, girded, shall fight before him” (Gen. XLIX). This Gad, girded, indicates the person of the Lord, who at his first coming, in the humility of his own [Col. 0361B] state, advances to fight before the coming of the Antichrist, girded most powerfully with the sword of his word around his thigh (Ps. XLIV). With this sword he divided his enemies—that is, son from father, daughter from mother, daughter-in-law from mother-in-law.

According to what is read in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X). But when he says, “He himself shall be girded afterward” (Gen. XLIX), the glory of our Lord at his second coming is shown. For when the Antichrist comes, Christ will confront him afterward, that is, following in his tracks, advancing with swift coming, so that he may kill him with the sword of his mouth.

Hence Gad is also appropriately interpreted as “a band of raiders,” because afterward, that is, close behind his feet, he will spring against the Antichrist’s prepared assault like a bandit, with a swift and unexpected coming. Thus the evangelist cries out, saying: “For the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (I Thess. V).

Christ, therefore, is written as fighting against the Antichrist both before and afterward. He fights before him, for, in the hiddenness of humility, Moses openly shows that this prophecy of the patriarch specifically pertains to Christ. Thus he says: “Blessed is Gad in breadth; he rested like a lion, and he seized the arm and the crown of the head, and he saw his principality” (Deut. XXXIII).

Let them recognize, then, who rested like a lion except Christ in his tomb; who broke the crown and arms of the powerful except our Redeemer, who humbled the strength and pride of the exalted; who saw his principality except the one to whom principality, honor, and kingship were given.

It follows:

“Aser is a rich bread; he shall provide delicacies for kings” (Gen. XLIX). Aser, whose name means “delicacies,” is Christ himself, whose height is the riches of wisdom and knowledge (Rom. XI), who for our sake became poor although he was rich (II Cor. VIII). His bread became rich—namely, his flesh, which is the holy of holies; whoever eats it shall not die forever (John VI).

He also provides the delicacies of wisdom to kings, that is, to those who rule their own thoughts well, who are masters of their vices, who chastise their bodies and bring them into subjection (I Cor. IX).

**Jerome.**—“Naphtali is a released shoot, giving beautiful words in its offspring” (Gen. XLIX).

In Hebrew it is written thus: “Naphtali is a watered field, giving beautiful utterances.” This signifies either that hot springs arise in that tribe or that it is watered by Lake Gennesaret and by the flow of the Jordan. The Hebrews, however, wish “watered field” and “beautiful utterances” to be prophesied because of Tiberias, which seemed to possess knowledge of the Law.

Moreover, where we and the Septuagint have placed “watered field” and “released shoot”—στέλεχος ἀνειμένον, that is, “a loosened shoot”—the Hebrew reads *Aiala seluha*, which may also be translated “a released deer,” referring to the early crops and indicating the speed of a more fertile land. But it is better if we refer everything to the teaching of the Savior, since he taught especially in that region, as is also written in the Gospel.

[Col. 0362A] **Recapitulation.**—Naphtali, which is interpreted as “expanse,” signifies the apostles and holy preachers, whose teaching has spread throughout the breadth of the entire world. From this tribe came the apostles, who are the leaders of the churches: “the leaders of Zebulun and the leaders of Naphtali.” Without doubt these refer to the persons of the apostles. They are the “sons of those shot forth” (Ps. CXXVI), that is, of the prophets, who, placed in the hands of the mighty God and shot forth like arrows, reached to the ends of the earth (Ps. XVIII).

Hence Naphtali is rightly written here as a released deer, because the apostles and preachers, springing forth with the swift leap of deer, transcend the entanglements of this world. Meditating on what is lofty and sublime, they give beautiful utterances: that is, they preach the teaching of the Lord and Savior to all the nations.

**Jerome.**—“Joseph is a son who has increased, a son who has increased beside the spring; the daughters proceed in orderly fashion upon the wall. They embittered him, contended with him, and were hostile to him, having arrows against him. His bow rested in the strong one, and the arms of his hands were broken by the hands of the strong one of Jacob; from there the stone of Israel shall be shepherded by the God of your father,” and the rest (Gen. XLIX).

Because the Seventy translators disagree in many places, we have expressed the interpretation of the remainder as it is found in Hebrew. The sense of the chapter is this:

“O Joseph, who are so called because the Lord increased you for me, or because you are destined to become greater than your brothers—the very strong tribe of Ephraim, as we read in the books of Kings and Chronicles: ‘O,’ I say, ‘son of Joseph, you are so beautiful that the whole crowd of the girls of Egypt looks upon you from walls, towers, and windows. For your brothers envied you and provoked you to anger; they had arrows of jealousy and were wounded by darts of rivalry. But you placed your bow and your weapons of war in God, who is a strong defender. Your bonds, with which your brothers had bound you, were loosened and broken by him, so that from your seed the tribe of Ephraim might arise, strong and stable, harder than a stone, and ruling, unconquered, over the twelve tribes of Israel.’”

**Recapitulation.**—“Joseph is a son who increases” (ibid.). This prophecy, after the Lord’s Passion, assumed the image of the Father’s voice, by which, upon his return to heaven after victory, the Father addresses him, saying: “Joseph is a son who increases”—a son who increases among the nations. For when the Synagogue had abandoned the people because of unbelief, he enlarged for himself an innumerable people of the Church from all the nations. David also sang this, saying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord,” and the rest (Ps. XXI).

He is a son who increases and is beautiful; for his beauty surpasses everyone in appearance, according to what is sung of him in the Psalms: “You are beautiful above the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV).

“The daughters ran along the wall” (Gen. XLIX): that is, the nations, or the churches, which believed in Christ. Through the firmness of faith, they run along as though upon a wall, having climbed it through love of Christ’s beauty, so that they may behold the true bridegroom in contemplation, be joined to him by the kiss of charity, and remain attached to him.

But “they rebuked him” when the peoples of the Synagogue attempted to oppress the holy Lord by slandering him with false testimonies; they envied him, having arrows. No one, indeed, shot arrows at Joseph or cast any weapon of injury at him, but this came specifically upon Christ.

“His bow rested in the strong one” (ibid.). For Christ placed his bow and his weapons of war in God, who is a strong defender. By his power all the wickedness of the faithless is struck down, and the bonds of his arms were broken—the bonds with which his brothers bound him and led him to Pilate, or by which they hung him upon the wood of the cross. They were cut apart by the hand of almighty God.

Jacob, from whose mouth the Lord himself, the good shepherd, came forth, is the stone and firmness of those who believe in Israel.

“The God of your father shall be your helper” (ibid.). Who could help the Son except the Father, God alone, who said: “Jacob is my servant; my soul shall receive him.”

“And the Almighty shall bless you with the blessings of heaven above, with the blessings of the abyss lying below” (ibid.).

For he subjected all things heavenly to him through the blessing of heaven, and all things earthly through the blessing of the abyss lying below, so that he might rule over angels and human beings in all things.

“With the blessings of the breasts”—that is, either of the two Testaments, one of which announced him and the other displayed him; or the blessings of Mary’s breasts, which were truly blessed because, by them, the holy Virgin gave the Lord the drink of milk. Hence the woman in the Gospel says: “Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that you sucked” (Luke XI).

“With the blessings of the breasts and of the womb” (Gen. XLIX). Here also the womb of that same mother is blessed—namely, the virginal womb that brought forth Christ the Lord for us. Of it Jeremiah says: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. I).

“The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of your fathers” (Gen. XLIX).

“The blessings of your heavenly Father,” he says, “which were given to you from the height of heaven and of the abyss, have been strengthened,” that is, they have prevailed over the blessings of your fathers. For the Father’s blessing in the Son grew stronger beyond the merit of all the saints, whether patriarchs or prophets, so that no saint could be compared with him, until he came.

“The desire of the eternal hills” (ibid.). These hills are the saints who, prophesying Christ’s coming, awaited his Incarnation with great longing. Of them the Lord says: “Many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see,” and the rest (Matt. XIII). These saints are called hills because of the excellence of their holiness. They are also called eternal because they attain eternal life and do not perish with the world, but are believed to be eternal.

“Let all the blessings come upon the head of Joseph” (Gen. XLIX). These blessings are placed upon the head of Christ, who received them when he became incarnate.

“And upon the crown of Nazareth.” Of him it is written: “For he shall be called a Nazirite” (Matt. II), that is, the holy one of God among his brothers, because he is the exalted head of all the saints. He also calls them his brothers in the Psalms, saying: “I shall declare your name to my brothers,” and so forth.

**Jerome.**—“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he eats the prey, and in the evening he gives food” (Gen. XLIX).

Because this is most clearly a prophecy concerning the apostle Paul, it is evident to everyone that in his youth he persecuted the Church, while in his old age he became a preacher of the Gospel. Nevertheless, in Hebrew it is read thus: “Benjamin is a ravenous or capturing wolf; in the morning he eats the prey, and in the evening he divides the spoils.” The Hebrews explain this as follows:

The altar upon which sacrifices were offered, and at the base of which the blood of the victims was poured out, was in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. This, they say, signifies that the priests offer sacrifices in the morning and in the evening divide among themselves what has been granted to them by the people according to the Law. They place the bloodthirsty and voracious wolf over the interpretation of the altar, and the division of the spoils over the priests who serve the altar and live from the altar.

**Isidore.**—We read that one of the teachers, when speaking in the city of Jerusalem, referred to the things written about Benjamin. “Benjamin,” he says, “is interpreted as ‘son of sorrow.’ By lot he received the place in which earthly Jerusalem is situated, which has now been rejected and cast away because of unbelief. For this Jerusalem is designated in her children under the person of Benjamin.

“For just as Benjamin receives the final blessing, so the same people will be saved last, after the fullness of the nations has entered” (Rom. XI). For it is said: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf.” He is called a wolf because that people shed the blood of the prophets and the righteous; he is called ravenous because of his greed. From great hunger for the word of God and famine, he became ravenous, because they themselves also violently seize the kingdom of God.

“But this one eats the prey in the morning.” The morning is understood as the time when he received the Law. Then the first illumination of knowledge was given to the world. He eats in the morning because he consumes and continues to meditate upon the Law that he received in the morning, although, by following the law of righteousness, he did not reach the law of faith.

“But in the evening he shall divide the spoils” (Gen. XLIX). The evening is the final time, when he will be converted. Then he will divide the food; then he will understand that the letter must be divided from the spirit; and then he will recognize that ‘the letter kills, but the spirit gives life’ (II Cor. III).

Therefore, because he has now been enlightened by the grace of the Lord and begins in the Law to divide and separate spiritual things from bodily things, he is said to divide the food in the evening—something he did not previously do, although he had meditated on the Law throughout the day.

But it is asked why Jacob made all those whom he begot of free women and maidservants equal in honor, sons and heirs, unless it was to show that Christ the Lord grants heavenly rewards to all the nations who are reconciled to his body through faith, with all possessing equal honor and glory. There is no distinction whether one is Jew or Greek, Barbarian or Scythian, slave or free, because Christ is all and in all.

For this reason our Savior and Lord assumed the form of a servant, and served both the free and the slave, so that in all who believe in him he might bestow an equal gift of heavenly blessings. He does not prefer one who is nobler according to the flesh. Whoever earns the Lord’s approval by faith is not darkened by any stains of carnal birth. For the prophet also indicates that this will happen, when the Lord says: “In the last days I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Acts II).

[Col. 0363]

# QUESTIONS ON EXODUS, FROM THE SAYINGS OF THE FATHERS: A DIALOGUE

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0363D]

We have briefly excerpted and touched upon certain mysteries from the book of Genesis, together with the more obscure matters of history that are covered by allegorical figures, drawing them from the books of the ancients. We now append, one by one, some of the typical and figurative mysteries of the succeeding Law, taken from the writings of holy men, bringing forth only a few passages from their style.

For who could investigate all the things of the Law? They are so immense that they cannot easily be explained even according to the text of the history. Nevertheless, we have followed the subject as far as we thought sufficient for the connected work, so that neither the little book might exceed due measure nor the reader incur weariness.

## CHAPTER ONE. What Exodus contains

[Col. 0365A]

**DISCIPLE.**

What does Exodus describe, according to the historical faith?

**TEACHER.**

Exodus contains the slavery and slaughter of the Hebrews, the plagues of Egypt, the departure of the people, and the protecting cloud. It also contains the crossing of the Red Sea, Pharaoh’s drowning with his chariots, and the singing of glory; likewise the encounter with the wilderness, the food of manna, and waters changed into sweetness; the battle with Amalek, the commandments of the Decalogue, and the ark of the covenant; and also the dedication of the tabernacle and of the offerings.

## CHAPTER TWO. Concerning the seventy souls

First of all, seventy souls entered Egypt with Jacob; seventy disciples are sent throughout the whole world to preach the word of God. In another sense, these seventy souls who entered Egypt are mystically understood according to the number of remission: namely, so that remission of sins might be granted to this age, which was represented by Egypt, after so many sins and sacrileges. For Egypt is shown by many prophetic utterances to figurally signify this world.

## CHAPTER THREE. Concerning the death of Joseph

After Joseph and his brothers died, the children of Israel multiplied and grew exceedingly strong. So also, after our true Joseph had tasted death for all—a death by which he destroyed the devil, who held the power of death—the people of the faithful multiplied. For unless, as he himself says, the grain of wheat had fallen into the earth and died, the Church of the world would certainly not now have produced such abundant fruit (John XII).

## CHAPTER FOUR. Concerning the affliction of the people

[Col. 0365C] Pharaoh afflicts the children of Israel with mud and brick. Israel is an image of our people, while Pharaoh is an image of the devil, who imposed upon them the heaviest yoke of slavery: to work with mud and brick, that is, to toil at muddy and earthly works, mixed also with straw—that is, with trivial and irrational deeds—so that by these acts of vice he might crush the people of God and shut them in behind the wall of all sins, the wall of unbelief, so that no one might destroy or overcome his kingdom.

## CHAPTER FIVE. Concerning the killing of the males

Pharaoh also commands the males to be killed and the females to live. Thus afterward he tried to prevent the strength of faith from prevailing, seeking that, once the virtues had been killed, vices might remain. He sought to kill in a person the strongest and manly thoughts of the soul, by which we understand heavenly and divine things—that is, reason, prudence, steadfastness, innocence, and faith—and to let live in him what appears feminine, weak, fragile, and inclined to vices: ambition, drunkenness, lust, anger, credulity, fury, and other things of this kind, which are represented under the figure of women.

## CHAPTER SIX. Concerning the discovery of Moses

Then Moses is found exposed on the bank of the river, and the Lord, whose type Moses bore, is found by believers at the river of the washing and at the water of baptism. The infant wept because Christ was mourning the sins of the old man whom he had assumed. Hence, when he raised Lazarus, he wept, lamenting the faithlessness of the Jews.

Pharaoh’s daughter, descending to the washing of the river, gathered up the infant. She is the Church among the nations, desiring the sanctification of the saving washing; she received Christ, expelled from the Synagogue, his carnal mother, as an infant, because he then appeared to be little when he was seen in human form.

She found Moses enclosed in a little basket of papyrus, which is made from many wild reeds. The Church found Christ hidden in the hearts of the saints, who, woven together into unity from the members of many brothers, have all become one body in Christ; and, receiving him with religious observance, they protect him.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. Concerning the Egyptian who was killed

Meanwhile Moses delivered a foreign brother from an Egyptian. He could not endure that his brother, who was suffering injury from an Egyptian, should remain unavenged; he defended his brother and killed the same Egyptian. His figure is readily apparent: in this pilgrimage the devil, who wrongfully attacks us, is killed by the Lord Christ, who defends us.

But the fact that he buried the slain man in the sand makes clear that the death-dealing presence of the devil already lies hidden in those who have no stable foundation. Hence the Lord builds the Church upon a rock, and compares those who hear his word and do it to a prudent man who builds his house upon a rock, so that it may not yield to temptations and collapse.

But those who hear and do not act he compares to a foolish man building upon sand, whose house, when tested, brings about a great ruin (Luke VI).

## CHAPTER EIGHT. Concerning the manifestation of the Lord in the bush

Then, while Moses was tending the sheep of Jethro his father-in-law, he saw a bush burning and not being consumed. The Lord appeared to Moses in the bush, sending him to a nation that he knew would become wicked.

There was a flame in the bush—that is, among thorns—and the bush was not burned up. The bush signifies the thorns of Jewish sins; the flame in the bush signifies the word of God. Thus, when the Law was given to them, there was a flame in the bush: although the Law was given, the sins were not consumed, nor was the bush burned beneath the fire.

Others understand the burning but unconsumed bush as the Church, which is set aflame by persecutions but does not perish when the Lord speaks in her.

The fact that the Lord is read to have appeared to Moses in that same bush shows that he appears to believers nowhere except in the Church, because no one can worthily stand or see God unless he has laid aside all earthly and mortal vices.

What did those sandals signify that Moses was commanded to remove? The command that Moses be unshod also has another figure. It was the custom of the ancients that, if a bride wished to reject her bridegroom, he would be unshod, and this was a sign of rejection. Therefore Moses is commanded to remove his sandals, so that he might not approach the Church, which was signified by the bush, as a bridegroom wearing shoes.

This was reserved for Christ, who was the true bridegroom. Of him John says: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (Mark I). The same was said, of course, concerning Joshua and Moses.

The Hebrews, however, say that God appeared to Moses in the bush and not in another kind of wood so that the Jews might not perhaps carve an idol from that same wood, for he always removed the opportunity for idolatry.

## CHAPTER NINE. Concerning the rod changed into a serpent

[Col. 0366D]

Moses is then sent to deliver the people of Israel, and he says to the Lord: “What sign shall I have, so that they may believe me, because you have sent me?” And the Lord said to him: “Throw upon the ground the rod that you carry in your hand.” He threw it down, and it became a serpent. Moses was terrified and fled. The Lord said to him: “Take hold of its tail.” He took hold of it, and it again became a rod (Exod. III, IV).

What does this signify? The serpent persuaded the human being to death; therefore death came from the serpent. The rod, therefore, in the serpent signifies Christ in death. Yet Moses was terrified and fled. What does Moses’ fleeing from that serpent mean except what is read as having happened in the Gospel: Christ died, and the disciples were terrified and withdrew from the hope in which they had been?

But what does the command “Take hold of its tail” mean? What is the tail except its rear part? This signified: “You shall see my rear parts.” First it became a serpent, but when its tail was seized, it became a rod again. For first he was killed; afterward, when everything had been accomplished, he returned by rising again to what he had been. Once death had been destroyed through the restoration of life, nothing of the serpent appeared in him.

The tail of the serpent also signifies the end of the age, because the mortality of the Church winds along through the slippery course of time. Some depart and others come through death; death was sown, as it were, through the serpent. But at the final end, like the tail of the age, we return to the hand of God; once seized, we shall be restored, and, when death, the last enemy, has been destroyed, we shall rise and become a rod in the right hand of God (I Cor. XV).

## CHAPTER TEN. Concerning Moses’ hand put into his bosom
Again another sign is given to Moses: “Put your hand into your bosom,” he says, “and he put it in. Draw it out,” he says, “and he drew it out, and it was found white” (Exod. IV)—that is, unclean. For whiteness on the skin is leprosy, not a healthy brightness. [Col. 0367B] Indeed, God’s own inheritance, that is, his people, was sent forth from him and became unclean, as it is written concerning it: “Why do you turn your face away, and your right hand from the midst of your bosom?” (Ps. LXXIII). But when he says to him, “Put it back into your bosom” (Exod. IV), he put it back, and it returned to its own color. So too the Jewish people is now alienated from God’s bosom and remains unclean outside; but he will call it back, and it will return to its former color when it recognizes the Lord Savior. For now a partial blindness has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel may be saved (Rom. XI).

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the waters changed into blood

Then the waters cast upon the earth by Moses are changed into blood—that is, the peoples are changed into faith in the blood of Christ. For the Apocalypse says: “The waters that you saw are peoples and nations” (Rev. XVII).

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Moses’ entrance to Pharaoh

[Col. 0367C]

After this Moses and Aaron enter before Pharaoh, requesting that the people of Israel be allowed to travel a three-day journey into the desert and there sacrifice to the Lord God. What is this three-day journey that we must travel, so that, coming out of Egypt, we may reach the place where we ought to offer sacrifice? This journey is Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV); and we must travel this way for three days. For whoever confesses the Lord Jesus with his mouth and believes in his heart that God raised him from the dead on the third day will be saved (Rom. X). This, then, is the three-day journey by which one reaches the place where sacrifice is offered to the Lord and a sacrifice of praise is rendered.

“We shall sacrifice to the Lord our God,” they say, “the abominations of the Egyptians” (Exod. VIII); for the Egyptians disdain eating sheep. But what the Egyptians abhor, the Israelites offer to God, because the simplicity of conscience—which the wise men of this age, that is, the citizens of Egypt, regard as foolishness—[Col. 0367D] the righteous offer to God as a sacrifice, and they seek to please God by that which they recognize as rejected and contemptible to the age and to the world, according to the Apostle who says: “For God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (I Cor. I).

But from the moment Moses began to speak to Pharaoh, the people of God are afflicted—that is, from the moment the word of God has been brought into a human soul, the crafty enemy rises up more fiercely and sends greater vices by which it may be overcome. Before the word that would rebuke vices arrived, they remained at peace; but once the word of God begins to expose and distinguish each person’s conduct, then great disturbance arises.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the rod changed into a dragon

Moses then threw down his rod before Pharaoh, [Col. 0368A] and it became a serpent and swallowed the serpent of the Egyptians, signifying that the Word would become flesh and empty the venom of the dreadful serpent through the remission and forgiveness of sins. For the rod is the direct, royal word, full of power, which is the insignia of sovereignty.

The rod became a serpent because he who was the Son of God, born from God the Father, became the Son of Man, born from a Virgin; and, like a serpent raised up on the cross, he poured medicine into the wounds of humanity. Hence the Lord himself also says: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John III).

For Moses’ rod, changed into a dragon, swallowed the rods of the magicians; and Christ, after the dignity of his glory, became obedient even to death (Phil. II), and through that very death of the flesh consumed the sting of death, as the prophet testifies: “I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O underworld” (Hos. XIII).

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Pharaoh’s hardening

[Col. 0368B]

“The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart,” namely because after sin he hardened the devil in such a way that he would never be softened by the compunction of repentance, as it is written of him in Job: “He will be hardened like a stone” (Job XLI).

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the ten plagues

Then plagues are inflicted upon Egypt. Although those events happened bodily in Egypt, they are nevertheless now enacted spiritually in us. For Egypt is an image of the world.

The first plague is that in which the waters are first changed into blood. The Egyptian waters are the wandering and slippery doctrines of the philosophers, which are rightly changed into blood because they think carnally about the causes of things. But when the cross of Christ has shown the light of truth to this world, it will rebuke such doctrines with chastisements, so that from the character of the punishments it may recognize its own errors.

In the second plague frogs are produced. These are thought [Col. 0368C] figuratively to signify the songs of the poets, who through a certain empty and inflated melody, like the croaking and songs of frogs, brought tales of deception into this world. For the frog is exceedingly talkative vanity; the animal itself is useful for nothing else than returning the sound of its voice in shameless and importunate cries.

After this gnats are produced. This animal is indeed suspended by wings, flying through the air, but it is so subtle and tiny that it escapes the sight of the eyes unless they are sharply observant. When it settles on the body, however, it pierces it with a most painful sting, so that one who cannot see it flying immediately feels it when it has flown upon him. This kind of animal is therefore compared with heretical subtlety, which pierces souls with the subtle stings of words and surrounds them with such great cunning that each deceived person neither sees nor understands from where the deception comes.

But when, at the third sign, the magicians ceased, saying, “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII), those magicians represented heretics and shared their obstinacy. [Col. 0368D] The Apostle makes this clear when he says: “Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so also these resist the truth, men corrupted in mind and rejected with regard to the faith; but they will not progress further, for their folly will be manifest to all, as theirs also was” (II Tim. III).

These men, who through that corruption of mind were exceedingly restless, failed at the third sign, making the Holy Spirit who was in Moses their adversary. For the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God, is placed third. Hence, failing at the third sign, they said: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII). Just as the Holy Spirit, when reconciled and appeased, grants rest to the meek and humble of heart, so, contrariwise, against the harsh and proud he stirs up restlessness. That restlessness was signified by those very small flies, at which Pharaoh’s magicians failed, saying: “This is the finger of God.”

In the fourth place Egypt is struck with flies. For the fly is an exceedingly insolent and restless animal; and what else can it signify but the insolent cares [Col. 0369A] of carnal desires? Egypt is struck with flies because the hearts of those who love this world are driven about by the restlessness of their desires.

Moreover, the Seventy translators rendered this as *cynomyia*, that is, “dog-fly.” By this, canine behavior is signified, in which the will and lust of the flesh are reproved in human minds. This passage may also signify, through the dog-fly, the forensic eloquence of men, by which, like dogs, they tear one another apart.

Then, in the fifth place, Egypt is struck by the death of animals, or cattle. Here the senselessness and folly of mortals are reproved: like irrational beasts, they have bestowed the worship and name of God upon images impressed not only in wood and stone in the form of human beings but also in the form of cattle. They venerate Ammon-Jupiter in a ram, Anubis in a dog, and Apis in a bull; and the other monstrosities by which Egypt marvels at its god, and in which they believed divine worship to reside, [Col. 0369B] were the very things in which they saw pitiable punishments.

After this, in the sixth plague, ulcers and swollen blisters appear. In the ulcers the deceitful and suppurating wickedness of this age is reproved; in the blisters, swelling and inflated pride; in the fever of anger and rage, madness. Up to this point such punishments are measured out to the world through figures of its errors.

After this, however, punishments come from above: voices, namely thunder and hail, and fire running about. In the thunder, rebukes and divine corrections are understood, because God does not strike in silence but gives forth voices; he also sends instruction from heaven, through which the chastised world can recognize its guilt. He gives hail as well, by which the tender growths of vices that are still emerging may be destroyed. He gives fire, knowing that there are thorns and thistles for that fire to consume. Concerning this the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII). Through this fire the incentives of pleasure and lust are consumed.

As for the mention of locusts in the eighth place, [Col. 0369C] some think that by this kind of plague the fickleness of the human race—divided and discordant within itself—is refuted. In another sense, locusts are to be understood as the mobility of frivolity, like souls that wander and leap toward the pleasures of the world.

In the ninth plague darkness was made, either to reprove the blindness of their minds or so that they might understand how exceedingly obscure are the reasons of divine dispensation and providence. For “God made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII). Those who rashly and boldly sought to distort these things, asserting one claim after another, fell into thick and tangible darkness of ignorance.

Finally, the firstborn of the Egyptians are destroyed: either the principalities, powers, and rulers of this darkness of the world, or the authors and inventors of the false religions that existed in this world—which the truth of Christ extinguished and destroyed together with their authors.

Moreover, concerning what follows, “In their gods he executed judgment” (Exod. XII), the Hebrews maintain that on the night when the people departed, all the temples in Egypt were destroyed, either by an earthquake [Col. 0369D] or by the impact of lightning. Spiritually, however, we say that when we depart from Egypt, the idols of error fall, and every worship of perverse doctrines is shaken.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning Passover

Meanwhile Passover takes place in the slaughter of the lamb. Christ is slain, of whom it is said in the Gospel: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John II). The lamb is sacrificed in the evening; at the evening of the world the Lord suffered. Those who celebrate Passover are forbidden to break the bones; the Lord’s bones are not broken on the cross, as the evangelist testifies when he says: “You shall not break his bone” (John XIX).

The doorposts of the Israelites are smeared with the lamb’s blood, so that the destroying Angel would not dare to inflict ruin. The faithful people are marked on their foreheads with the sign of the Lord’s Passion for the protection of salvation, so that only those who are marked in heart and [Col. 0370A] forehead with the blood of the Lord’s Passion may be freed from destruction. These also proclaim in their works: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV).

Hence the solemnity itself is called Passover, which we may call a passage, because, proceeding from worse things to better, we leave behind dark Egypt.

But when he says that no foreigner may eat of that lamb, that it must be eaten in one house, and that they must not carry any of its flesh outside, this is properly understood as written concerning the sacrament of Christ’s body, of which that lamb was a figure. His body and blood are commanded to be eaten in one house—that is, in one Church—and not to be carried outside, namely among the communities of heretics, which wander outside the unity of that Church.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the silver and gold taken from the Egyptians

Afterward God commanded the people through Moses to ask the Egyptians for articles that they might take away; [Col. 0370B] and so Moses and the departing people, by command of the Lord God who commands nothing unjustly, despoiled the Egyptians of their gold and silver.

What else could these things have prefigured except that certain teachings are signified by the gold, silver, and clothing of the Egyptians—teachings learned from the customs of the nations through no useless diligence? But whether this is what it signifies, or whether it signifies that precious souls from among the Gentiles, like golden and silver vessels, are joined to the people of God together with their own bodies, which the clothing signifies, so that they may be liberated together from this wicked age—

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the Unleavened Bread

When Scripture says, then, that the children of Israel departed from Egypt after the leaven had been removed, we too must strive in every way, if possible, to depart from the enticements of this age and not walk in the leaven of former malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. [Col. 0370C] This means living as the new person after abandoning the former person with his vices.

They ate unleavened bread for seven days; we, however, should conduct ourselves simply and purely throughout these seven days in which this world is carried through, days that continually revolve in their appointed order. Every day the Lamb is slain for us, and Passover is celebrated every day, if we do not possess the leaven of malice and wickedness, and if, having been renewed, we take no pleasure in anything belonging to the corruption of the former self (I Cor. V).

For what else is leaven except corruption of nature, which, first departing from its natural sweetness, has itself been corrupted through distress? In this dwelling-place we are commanded always to remember our departure from Egypt, to celebrate Passover—that is, our passage from worse things to better—and to consecrate to the Lord the firstborn of our womb, that is, the beginning of all our works and virtues.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the pillar of fire and cloud

[Col. 0370D]

Even then the Lord is seen by night in a pillar of fire and by day in a pillar of cloud, going before the people and becoming their guide on the journey. This preceding cloud is Christ; he is likewise the pillar, because he is upright and firm and supports our weakness. He shines by night, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind (John IX).

It may also appropriately be understood in this way: the mystery of Christ is manifest as in the day, in the flesh as in a cloud; but in judgment it will be like the terror of night, because then there will be great tribulation in the world like fire. It will shine for the righteous and burn for the unrighteous.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the division of the sea

When the Egyptians were following, Moses struck the waters with his rod, and the children of Israel passed through the midst of the Red Sea. What is the Red Sea except baptism, consecrated by the blood of Christ? The enemies who follow with their [Col. 0371A] king and die behind them are past sins, which are destroyed, and the devil, who is drowned in spiritual baptism. The Egyptians do press upon us; sins urge and pursue us, but only as far as the water.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the song of glorification

After crossing the Red Sea, the people sing a song to God, with the Egyptians and Pharaoh drowned. Likewise the faithful, after they have descended from the laver, when their sins have been extinguished, send forth a hymn in a voice of thanksgiving, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. XXV). Yet he says this better and more worthily who has a tambourine in his hand like Miriam—that is, who has crucified his flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. V) and put to death his members that are upon the earth (Col. III).

After the crossing of the sea the people are led through the desert: [Col. 0371B] all the baptized, that is, throughout the world, are in the desert, since they do not yet enjoy the promised homeland but, hoping for what they do not see and awaiting it with patience (Rom. VIII). There, tested laboriously and dangerously, they must not return in heart to Egypt. Nor does Christ finally abandon them there, for that pillar too does not depart.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the waters of the sea

After leaving the Red Sea, the people encounter a wilderness. Entering it for three days, they had no water; then they came to a bitter spring, which received its name from its bitterness. When the people see the waters, they murmur and cannot endure drinking. Moses throws a piece of wood into the waters, and they become sweet.

Understand the bitter waters as representing the deadly letter of the Law. If the confession of the cross is cast into them and the mystery of the Lord’s Passion is mingled with them, then the bitter water becomes sweet, and the bitterness of the letter is changed into the sweetness [Col. 0371C] of spiritual understanding. Hence it is also written: “The Lord appointed for his people law and judgments, and tested him” (Exod. XV).

In another sense, the fact that the bitter waters become sweet by receiving wood within them was an indication that the bitterness of the nations would one day be changed into the uses of sweetness through the wood of Christ’s cross.

According to the preceding interpretation, it must be understood that Israel was first led to false and bitter waters; and after these had been made sweet when the Lord displayed the wood, the people came afterward to springs. First the people are led to the letter of the Law, and as long as they remain in it, they cannot depart from bitterness.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the twelve springs and the seventy palm trees

When, therefore, the water has been made sweet through the wood of life, and the Law has begun to be understood spiritually, one passes from the Old Testament to the New and comes to the twelve apostolic springs. There the trees of the seventy palms are found. [Col. 0371D]

For it was not only the twelve apostles who preached the faith of Christ; the other seventy who were sent to preach the word of God are also mentioned. Through them the world was to recognize the palms of Christ’s victory. Indeed, these twelve springs watering the seventy palm trees prefigure apostolic grace, watering the peoples in a sevenfold number multiplied by ten, so that through the sevenfold gift of the Spirit the Decalogue of the Law may be fulfilled.

Meanwhile the people murmur in the desert because of hunger. Then they turned and looked from afar upon the glory of God in the cloud, and in the evening they saw quail, and in the morning of the following day, manna. What else are birds and food to be understood as signifying except divinely sent proclamations, which pass through resonant words like winged creatures flying through the air, by which those who strive to reach the homeland of the heavenly kingdom are nourished through faith?

The food of the birds may also signify the sayings of the ancient Law, which nourished the carnal people as with flesh through divinely sent words, as through winged creatures. [Col. 0372A] Hence they are given in the evening, because all the things granted to them in a carnal manner were destined to have an end. But when the light of faith had been revealed, manna is given to the people.

Manna, certainly, is Christ, who descended from heaven like living bread (John VI), who is rained upon the whole world through the evangelical clouds—not upon the murmuring and testing Synagogue, but upon the believing Church that places its hope in him. This is unfailing manna; this is the true bread and the heavenly food of angels, by which the Word of God nourishes the corruptible incorruptibly. So that man might eat it, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John I); those who feed upon it live spiritually.

For those who received the ancient figure carnally died. It is not unfitting, then, that heavenly sayings are also signified by manna. Hence the interpretation of the name has this meaning: *manna* is interpreted as “What is this?” When we hear the Law of God being read in the Church, we ask the teachers, saying: “What is this?”

This manna was small, like coriander seed, and sweet. What is smaller or more subtle than the word of God, [Col. 0372B] or what is sweeter and more pleasing than the sayings of God, which are above honey and the honeycomb?

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the flesh of birds and manna

But what does it mean that on the sixth day twice as much is commanded to be gathered, enough also for the Sabbath? This sixth day is the sixth age of the world, in which we now live. In this age, therefore, the person gathers twice as much who, because of his hope of eternal life, both hears and does the word of God.

In this age the person stores up twice as much who both lives well and shows mercy to others. This was stored up for the Sabbath and did not decay. For good works done for the sake of future rest remain in the future age.

But those who were unbelieving and kept manna beyond what was required for the Sabbath had worms boil out of it, and it rotted. Those who hoard for the sake of the present life and love of the world have worms boil out of their hoards—worms that will not [Col. 0372C] die. These are the worms generated by greed and blind desire for riches. These are the people who possess money and, seeing their brothers in need, close their hearts against them.

Moreover, the person who sins after receiving the word of God finds that the word of God itself becomes a worm for him, continually digging into his conscience and gnawing at the secrets of his heart, like a worm gnawing wood, which is the cross of Christ. Yet Christ is also a worm, as he himself says: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI).

For just as he is a stumbling-block to some and a resurrection to others, so in the manna he becomes, for believers, the sweetness of honey, but for unbelievers, a worm.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the rock struck with the rod

After the manna, the people seek relief from the heat of thirst, and a spring bursts forth from the rock. The rock that, when struck, poured out water bore the figure of Christ’s Passion, through which, once opened, all things flowed. The wood [Col. 0372D] of the Passion approached him like a rod, so that grace might flow forth for believers. When the rock was struck, the spring flowed; when Christ was struck on the cross, he poured forth upon the thirsty the grace of the laver and the gift of the Holy Spirit.

The Apostle proves that this rock bore the figure of Christ when he says: “They drank,” he says, “from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X).

But what does it mean that the thirsty people murmur against Moses because of the water, and that for this reason God commands him to show them the rock from which they should drink? It means that if someone opposes the Law of Moses, murmurs against him, and dislikes the Law written according to the letter, Moses shows him the rock, which is Christ, and leads him to it so that he may drink from it and refresh his thirst.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning the battle against Amalek

After this Moses ascends the mountain, and Joshua [Col. 0373A] wages war against Amalek. Moses holds the rod and stretches out his arms in the form of a cross; thus the enemy—that is, the devil, who strives to block the way to the heavenly homeland—is overcome by the sign of the Lord’s cross.

While Moses lifted up his hands, Israel prevailed; but if he lowered them again, Amalek prevailed. For when we raise our actions toward heaven, the rulers of darkness are subjected; but, on the contrary, when we pray with lowered hands—that is, when we pursue an earthly way of life—the victorious enemy follows after us.

Moses sat upon the stone that had seven eyes in Zechariah and is called the stone of help in the book of Samuel. Aaron and Hur, like the people or the two Testaments, supported both his hands.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning Moses’ kinsman

After Amalek was defeated, Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, came. He brought Zipporah, that is, the Church, and the two [Col. 0373B] sons, each begotten from one of the two peoples, and advised Moses concerning the seventy elders.

Moses listened to him and did everything he said. Here it is a matter of great wonder that Moses, a prophet full of God, who spoke with the Lord face to face, should receive counsel from a Gentile and do everything he told him—unless it was to give the rulers of the peoples an example of humility and to indicate an image of the future sacrament.

For he knew that one day what was lacking in the Law would be completed through the people gathered from the Gentiles at his suggestion, and that it would bring a good and spiritual understanding to the Law of God. He knew that the Law would listen to this same people and do everything it said, and that the deficiency of the Law would be completed through the suggestion of the Gospel.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning Moses’ ascent of the mountain

After this, on the forty-[Col. 0373C]seventh day after the departure from Egypt, the people came to Mount Sinai. There Moses ascended to the Lord, and the Lord descended to him.

But what does it mean morally that Moses ascended the mountain and the Lord descended upon the mountain? The mountain is the height of our contemplation, to which we ascend so that we may be lifted up to behold the things that lie beyond our weakness. But the Lord descends to this mountain because, when the saints have made great progress, he reveals a little of himself to their understanding.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning Mount Sinai and the thunder

Then, on the fiftieth day after Passover had been celebrated, the Law was given to Moses. Thus, on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s Passion, which that Passover prefigured, the Holy Spirit, the promised Paraclete, was given, descending upon the apostles and those who were with them, numbering one hundred and twenty according to the number of the Mosaic age. [Col. 0373D] When the tongues of believers were divided, the whole world was filled with evangelical preaching.
