The Law is said there to have been written by the finger of God, and the Lord says concerning the Holy Spirit: “By the finger of God I cast out demons” (Luke XI).

There the whole people sees voices and lamps, the smoking mountain, thunder and lightning, and the sound of a trumpet resounding. In the voices and thunder the cry of the preachers is understood; in the lamps, the brightness of miracles; in the sound of the trumpet, the powerful preaching of the saints. All these things were fulfilled at the coming of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, when all Christ’s disciples thundered through the diversity of languages with commandments and signs.

*Sinai* is interpreted as “bush,” which signifies the Church, in which the Lord also speaks to Moses. But the fact that the Lord descended to give the Law in fire and smoke signifies that he illuminates the faithful by displaying his brightness, while through the smoke of error he obscures the eyes of unbelievers.

The fact that he appears in darkness signifies that the impious, [Col. 0374A] who set their minds on earthly things, did not recognize him descending in the darkness of wickedness—that is, being born in humility. To others he appeared in darkness and gave the Law, because, as though through darkness, he said to unbelievers who would not follow the truth of his Law: “Though seeing, they may not see; and though hearing, they may not hear” (Luke VIII).

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the ten words

The Lord therefore gives Moses the Law of our innocence and of the knowledge of himself, establishes it in ten words, and writes it with his finger on tablets of stone. These commandments are distributed in such a way that three concern love of the divine Trinity, while seven concern love of one’s brother, through which human society is not harmed.

The first commandment of the Decalogue pertains to God the Father, when it says: “The Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI), so that, hearing this, you may worship the one [Col. 0374B] God the Father and not pour out your fornication upon many fabricated gods.

The second commandment pertains to the Son, when it says: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exod. XX). That is, do not suppose that the Son of God is a creature, since every creature is subject to vanity; rather, believe that he is equal to the Father, God of gods, the Word with God, through whom all things were made (John I).

The third commandment, concerning the Sabbath, pertains to the Holy Spirit, whose gift promises us eternal rest. Since he is called the Holy Spirit, the seventh day was therefore also sanctified. For on the other days the sanctification of works is not named, except on the Sabbath, where it says: “God rested” (Gen. II).

This commandment therefore pertains to the Holy Spirit both because of the name of sanctification and because of eternal rest, which pertains to the gift of the Holy Spirit. For it says there: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day. Six days you shall labor and do [Col. 0374C] all your work; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. You shall do no work on it” (Exod. XX).

The work of six days contains the work of six thousand years; but in the seventh the rest of that blessed time of the kingdom is shown. The Jews sin when they celebrate it carnally, and we do not adapt ourselves to the faith of a deceiving falsehood. God cries out through the prophet: “My soul hates your new moons and Sabbaths” (Isa. I). How, then, were those Sabbaths sanctified which the Lord hated?

That Sabbath, therefore, is sanctified in which eternal rest is promised to us after the good works of this life. Thus, whatever we do, if we do it for the sake of the rest of the future age, we truly observe the Sabbath.

After these three commandments, the sevenfold number of commandments follows, pertaining to love of one’s neighbor. It begins with the honor of parents, which is nevertheless fourth in order: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. XX). For a person [Col. 0374D] opens his eyes through his parents, and this life begins from their love. Hence this commandment is first among the seven, just as the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Honor your father and your mother” (Matt. XV), which is the first commandment.

But how is it first, since it is fourth? It is because it is first in the sevenfold number, since it pertains to love of one’s neighbor; it is first on the other tablet. For this reason the two tablets of the Law were given.

In this commandment, therefore, children are ordered to honor their parents, not to be insulting toward them, but to show them the reverence owed through the duty of devotion. For whoever does not know how to honor his parents—whom will he be able to spare, when he hates his own?

Fifth: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX), that is, no one may join himself to other women outside the bonds of marriage in order to satisfy lust. For the man who approaches another woman besides his own specifically commits adultery.

Sixth: “You shall not kill” (ibid.). For not only does the person who commits murder by [Col. 0375A] deed become a murderer; so too does the person who encounters someone hungry or naked, who might die unless he comes to his aid by offering clothing and food. He too will be held to be a murderer.

Seventh: “You shall not steal” (ibid.), which is the vice of rapacity.

Eighth: “You shall not bear false witness” (ibid.), which is the crime of lying and falsehood.

Ninth: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (ibid.). In this commandment he forbids the intention of adulterous thought. For it is one thing to do such a thing with someone other than one’s wife, and another not to desire another man’s wife. Therefore there are two commandments: “You shall not commit adultery,” and, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.”

Tenth: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (ibid.). In this commandment he condemns worldly ambition and restrains the desire for possessions.

Thus the first forbids surreptitious deception, the second error, the third destroys love of the world, the fourth impiety, [Col. 0375B] the fifth crushes fornication, the sixth cruelty, the seventh rapacity, the eighth destroys falsehood, the ninth adulterous thought, and the tenth desire for the world.

And it should be noted that just as the Egyptians are struck by ten plagues, so the tablets are inscribed with ten commandments by which the people of God may be governed, so that demons may be put to death.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the two tablets

Why was the Law written on two tablets, unless either to signify the two Testaments or because of those two commandments concerning love of one’s neighbor, on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. XXII)? These commandments are explained on the individual tablets. On one there are three commandments pertaining to love of God; on the other, seven pertaining to fellowship with one’s neighbor.

But why were the tablets themselves made of stone, unless to signify the stony heart of the Jews? Through the stones he demonstrated insensibility; through their hardness, the stupidity of their [Col. 0375C] minds. Concerning this the prophet says: “I will take away from them their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh” (Ezek. XI). Hence the Apostle also says: “Not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshy hearts” (II Cor. III).

The term “fleshy tablets” does not mean that we should think carnally. Rather, because flesh feels in comparison with stone, which is without sensation, the hardness of stone signifies a heart that does not understand, while the sensitivity of flesh signifies a heart that understands.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the command: “You shall make an altar of earth” (Exod. XX)

The Lord also adds there: “You shall not make for yourselves gods of gold or silver; you shall make an altar of earth for me” (ibid.).

To make an altar of earth is to hope in the Incarnation of the Mediator. For our gift is then accepted by God when humility—that is, whatever good a person does—has been placed upon this altar, upon faith in the Lord’s Incarnation. [Col. 0375D] On an altar of earth, therefore, we offer the gift of our offerings if we establish our actions firmly upon faith in the Lord’s Incarnation.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning what he says: “You shall not build it of hewn stones” (ibid.)

Then he adds: “If you make an altar of stone for me, you shall not build it of hewn stones. If you lift a knife over it, it will be defiled” (ibid.).

The hewn stones are those who tear apart unity and separate themselves from the fellowship of their brothers through hatred or schisms. Christ does not receive such people in his body, whose figure is foreshadowed by the construction of that altar.

The unhewn stones, from which the altar is commanded to be built, are those who are made solid by unity of faith and conduct. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “You are living stones, built together into a spiritual house” (I Pet. II). No iron was applied to them, because they are incorrupt; [Col. 0376A] they have not received the flaming darts of the evil one, because they form one altar through the unity of faith and the harmony of love.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning what he says: “You shall not approach it by steps” (Exod. XX)

“You shall not approach my altar by steps.” That is, you will not come to me by gradually preferring one person to another, nor will you distinguish between an earlier and a later one in time, because you will not have the Lord, who has been divided and separated from unity, as your gracious protector.

This is what the Arians do: they divide the inseparable substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

After this, many more precepts of the Law are given; passing over them, we shall discuss the matters that are more necessary.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning the Hebrew serving for six years
It is prescribed afterward in the Law that if a Hebrew [Col. 0376B] boy should happen to fall into servitude, he is to serve for six years, but in the seventh he is to be released free. But if he does not wish to leave servitude on account of his wife and children, his ear shall be pierced, and he shall be a slave forever. This is not said of the present age, but of the future: for after serving through the six ages of this world, on the seventh day—that is, in the eternal Sabbath—we shall be freed, provided that we wish to be free while we are still serving sin in this world. But if we do not wish it, our ear will be pierced as a testimony to our disobedience, and with our wife and children, whom we have preferred to freedom—that is, with the flesh and the habitual works of sin—we shall be slaves forever.

### CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Law of Retaliation

What, then, does it signify that in this law one is commanded to give an eye for an eye? The eye is each teacher, as it were, showing the way of life. But if such a teacher [Col. 0376C] attempts to extinguish the hearer’s intention through some pernicious doctrine, if he injures the eye of the soul and disturbs its understanding, he must necessarily be removed from the governance of the Church; and his turbulent and savage understanding, which generates a stumbling block to the faith, must be cast out.

Likewise, if someone injures the hearer’s tooth, by which he was grinding the food of the Scriptures and, dividing it, distinguishing it spiritually so as to convey from it a subtle meaning into the inner parts of the soul, whoever therefore, by pulling out such a tooth, tries to cut it away from the body of Christ, let that tooth be removed. For it is said of such men: “You have crushed the teeth of sinners” (Psalm 3).

Indeed, a hand is also demanded for a hand, and a foot for a foot. The hand is the action of the one who works, by which one proceeds toward good or evil. Therefore let the one who causes scandal be cut off, not only in faith but also in actions, which are signified by the hand; or let him be cut off if he provides an occasion of stumbling, signified by the feet. Let him also receive burning, because he has burned and handed over a brother’s soul to Gehenna. [Col. 0376D] By these marks it is shown that this attacker, with all his members cut off, is to be severed from the body of the Church, so that the others, seeing it, may have fear and not act in the same way.

### CHAPTER XXXVII. On Offering Tithes and Firstfruits

Among these matters, the Israelite people are also commanded to offer to God tithes of all crops and the firstfruits of all things. Spiritually, the firstfruits of crops or of the firstborn signify the beginnings of good works, or the good will itself, which precedes the work—something the Pelagians offend against by claiming it for themselves. But when God commands us to offer these things to him, he indicates that they belong to his grace.

In offering tithes to the Lord, the number ten signifies perfection, because the number increases up to it. Therefore, just as in the firstfruits we are commanded to refer the beginnings of our intentions to God, so in the tithes we are commanded to refer [Col. 0377A] the completion of our works to him, from whom both the beginning of a good work and the fulfillment of its perfection are designated.

But what he said—“You shall exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep” (Exodus 13)—signifies this: by the donkey, uncleanness is represented in this passage; by the sheep, innocence. To exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep, therefore, is to convert the beginnings of an unclean life to the simplicity of innocence, so that after the sinner has done those things which, as unclean, the Lord rejects, he may now, by doing them, bring forth those things which he may present to God’s sacrifice as clean. What follows—“If you do not redeem it, it shall be killed”—means that an unclean mind, subject to sins, will be killed by everlasting death if it is not changed for the better.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Calf Burned with Fire

Moses, then, descended from the mountain with the tablets. When he heard that the people had consecrated themselves to the idol, he judged them unworthy to receive the Law and threw the tablets from his hands. After breaking them, he burned [Col. 0377B] the calf which they had celebrated in song.

But what does this calf, which the children of Israel made in the wilderness, signify? Or what does it mean that Moses burned the calf itself with fire, crushed it into small pieces, sprinkled it into water, and gave it to the people to drink? If he broke the tablets which he had received written by the finger of God—that is, by the operation of the Holy Spirit—because he judged them unworthy to read them; and if, finally, so that the calf might be entirely abolished by them, he burned it, crushed it, sprinkled it into water, and submerged it, why did he give this water to the people to drink? Who would not be stirred by this deed to seek and understand its prophetic significance?

Let attentive minds recognize, then, that the calf signified the body of the devil—that is, human beings among all the nations, for whom the devil is the head, that is, the author, of these sacrileges. It was golden because the rites of idolatry appear to have been instituted by wise men. Concerning them the Apostle says:

“Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; [Col. 0377C] but they became futile in their thoughts, and their senseless heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents” (Romans 1).

From this supposed wisdom came the golden calf—such as even the leading men of the Egyptians, like learned men, were accustomed to worship as images.

This calf, therefore, signified the entire body, that is, the whole society of the Gentiles devoted to idolatry. The Lord Jesus will burn this sacrilegious society with that fire of which he says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12). Since no one can hide from its heat, when the nations believe in him, the devil’s form in them will be dissolved by the fire of his power.

Then that whole body is crushed—that is, torn away from the fusion of its evil conspiracy, humbled by the word of truth—and, after being crushed, is thrown into water, so that the Israelites, that is, preachers of the Gospel, [Col. 0377D] may transfer them through baptism into their own members, that is, into the Lord’s body. To one of these Israelites, namely Peter, it was said concerning those very Gentiles: “Kill and eat” (Acts 11).

Why also was it not said, “Cut up and drink”? Thus that calf, through the fire of zeal, the sharp edge of the word, and the water of baptism, was swallowed up by those whom it had attempted to swallow.

### CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Three Thousand Men Who Were Killed

Now we must inquire what prophetic significance there was in the fact that Moses ordered many of those who, in his absence, had made an idol for themselves to be killed, without any regard for family relationship.

It is easy to understand that the killing of such vices is signified by the intention directed against those men, who had fallen into such vices and thus into the same idolatry. The Apostle commands us to rage against such vices when he says:

“Put to death, therefore, what is earthly in you: fornication, uncleanness, [Col. 0378A] lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3).

To go from gate to gate means to run with the sword of rebuke from vice to vice, through which death enters the mind. Moreover, the number twenty-three thousand of those slain indicates a threefold form of sins. For every sin is committed either by deed, by word, or by thought.

### CHAPTER XL. On the Breaking of the Tablets

Moses therefore went up into the mountain again, and God once more gave him the Law on other tablets, cut in the likeness of the earlier ones.

But what did those same tablets signify, which Moses first received from the Lord and immediately broke? The tablets displayed the image of the ancient Law, which, after not much time, was brought to an end on account of the people’s sin. The others, cut again in the likeness of the former, bore the figure of the New Testament. These [Col. 0378B] are not broken, so that it might be shown that the words of the New Testament would remain.

For this reason they are rightly marked as to be read in ten words, so that through the same number the figure of the cross might be expressed. Its form is found in the letter X. For one straight stroke runs from top to bottom; again, another, not unlike it, is joined across by the arms. Hence he himself also says: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” (Luke 12)—certainly through the passion of the cross, whose image was present in the tablets.

### CHAPTER XLI. On the Forty Days During Which Moses Fasted

What does it mean that Moses fasted for forty days? His action has a certain figure in the consideration of this number. For Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted for a period of forty.

We are therefore instructed from the Law [Col. 0378C], from the Prophets, and from the Gospel itself, which bears witness from the Law and the Prophets. Hence also, on the mountain, the Savior shone forth between the two figures, so that we might restrain our appetite from all the enticements of the world, as by a fast of self-control, for as long as the perfection of the tenfold Law is preached throughout the four parts of the same world—that is, throughout the whole earth—since ten multiplied by four marks the number forty.

### CHAPTER XLII. On the Lord’s Saying to Moses: “You Shall See My Back” (Exodus 33)

**DISCIPLE.**

What is the vision described as having appeared to Moses in the wilderness, which is sometimes called an angel and sometimes the Lord?

**TEACHER.**

He is called an angel because he served by speaking outwardly; but he is called the Lord because, presiding inwardly, he supplied the effectiveness of speech. Thus, when the speaker is governed from within, he is named both an angel because of his service and the Lord because of his inspiration.

**DISCIPLE.**

How are we to understand the Lord’s saying to Moses: “Leave me, so that my anger may burn against them, and I will make you into a great nation” (Exodus 32)? How could a servant allow the omnipotent Lord [Col. 0378D] to do whatever he wished?

**TEACHER.**

It can be understood as granting the servant the boldness to intercede, as though he were openly told: “Consider how greatly you are valued by me, and recognize that you will be able to obtain whatever you ask for on behalf of the people.”

For whenever the saints oppose God’s anger, they receive from him the role of being placed against the force of the blow. So, if I may put it this way, they rise up with him against him. Divine power sets them against itself, because when they perhaps oppose themselves to the anger raging against them, the grace of the one who is angry inwardly cherishes them, and inwardly raises up those who serve him, while he tolerates as though opposing him those whom he inwardly supports. [Col. 0379A]

He therefore bears the contradiction of those who intercede, a contradiction which he himself inspires; and, as though imposed upon one who wills it, that is commanded to be done by him.

**DISCIPLE.**

When I consider the fathers of the Old Testament, I recognize that many of them, as the history of sacred Scripture attests, saw God. Jacob saw God, for he said: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my life has been preserved” (Genesis 32). Moses saw God, concerning whom it is written: “The Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Exodus 33). Job saw God, for he said: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you” (Job 42). Isaiah saw God, for he said: “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne” (Isaiah 6), and so forth, up to what he says: “I have seen the King, the Lord of hosts, with my eyes.” Micaiah saw God, who says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left” (2 Chronicles 18).

What, then, is the meaning of the fact that so many fathers [Col. 0379B] of the Old Testament testified that they had seen God, while he himself says: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exodus 33), and John says: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1)?

**TEACHER.**

This is plainly understood to mean that, as long as one lives in mortality, God can be seen through certain images, but the appearance of his very nature cannot be seen. The soul, breathed upon by grace through the Spirit, sees God through certain figures, but does not reach the very power of his essence.

This is why Jacob, who testifies that he saw God, saw him only in an angel. This is why Moses, who spoke with God face to face, as a man speaks with his friend, says in the very words of his conversation: “If I have found favor in your sight, show yourself to me openly, so that I may see you” [Col. 0379C] (Exodus 33).

Certainly, if the one with whom he was speaking was not God, he would have said, “Show me God,” and not, “Show yourself to me.” But if he was God with whom he was speaking face to face, why did Moses ask to see the one whom he was seeing?

From this request of his it is gathered that he thirsted to behold him in the radiance of his unbounded nature—the one whom he had already begun to see through certain images—so that heavenly knowledge might be present to the eyes of his mind, in such a way that no temporally created image would intervene between those eyes and the vision of eternity.

Thus the fathers of the Old Testament saw God, and yet, in accordance with John’s statement, “No one has ever seen God” (John 1), and in accordance with the same Lord’s statement, “No human being shall see me and live” (Exodus 33). For those who remain in mortal flesh can see him through the unbounded light of eternity.

But if by some people, while they still live [Col. 0379D] in this corruptible flesh and yet grow through immeasurable virtue, the eternal glory of God can be seen through a certain sharpness of contemplation, this too does not conflict with the judgment of the same Truth, which says: “No human being shall see me and live” (ibid.). For whoever sees Wisdom, which is God, dies completely to this life, so that he may no longer be held by love of it.

No one who still lives carnally has seen him, because no one can embrace God and the world at the same time. Whoever has seen God dies to this world, being wholly separated from its pleasures either by the intention of the heart or by the effect of his works. No one, therefore, has seen God and lived—as though it were openly said: No one has ever seen God spiritually and lived carnally in the world.

**DISCIPLE.**

What does Moses’ statement to God mean: “You repay the iniquity of the fathers upon the children and grandchildren, to the third and fourth generation” (Exodus 20), when it is written:

“What is this proverb that you repeat as a saying in the land of Israel? ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.’ As I live, says the Lord God, this proverb shall no longer be used among you. Behold, all souls are mine; [Col. 0380A] the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins shall die. The father shall not bear the iniquity of the son, nor shall the son bear the iniquity of the father. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him,” and the rest (Jeremiah 31).

These statements do not seem to sound equally and harmoniously. I ask you to strive to resolve this difficulty.

**TEACHER.**

In both statements, since a different sense of the author is found, the mind is instructed to seek carefully the path of discernment.

We inherit original sin from our parents, and unless we are saved by the grace of baptism, we also bear our parents’ sins, because we are, so to speak, one with them. He therefore repays the iniquity of the fathers upon the children when the soul of the offspring is polluted by original sin on account of the parents’ guilt.

And again, he does not repay the iniquity of the parents upon the children, because when we are freed from original guilt through baptism, we possess not the sins of our parents but those [Col. 0380B] which we ourselves commit.

This can nevertheless be understood in another way: whoever imitates the iniquity of an evil parent is also bound by that parent’s offense. But whoever does not imitate the parent’s iniquity is not burdened by the parent’s sin. Thus an unrighteous son of an unrighteous father pays not only his own sins, which he has added, but also his father’s, when he does not fear to add his own wickedness to the ways of his father, by which he knows that the Lord was angered.

It is just that one who, under the judgment of a strict judge, does not fear to imitate the ways of an unrighteous parent should be compelled in the present life also to pay the penalties for that unrighteous parent’s guilt.

Hence it is also said there: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins shall die” (ibid.), because sometimes children are killed in the flesh even because of their father’s sin. But once original sin has been removed, it is not retained in the soul on account of the parents’ wickedness.

**DISCIPLE.**

What does it mean that young children are often seized by demons?

**TEACHER.**

This can be understood to mean that the child’s flesh is punished on account of the father’s punishment. The unrighteous father is struck in himself, but often does not feel the force of the blow except through his children, so that the pain of the father’s flesh may burn more fiercely and the father’s wicked mind may be punished through the sufferings of his children.

But when not little children, but even more mature children, are struck because of their parents’ guilt, what else is plainly indicated than that they suffer the penalties of those whose deeds they have followed?

Hence it is rightly said: “To the third and fourth generation” (Exodus 20). The children can see the life of their parents which they imitate; vengeance extends as far as those who have seen what they would follow in evil.

### Recapitulation

What, then, did Moses ask when he said that he wished to see the Lord’s glory [Col. 0380C]: “If I have found favor with you, show yourself to me openly” (Exodus 33)? He received a fitting answer for the present life: that he could not see the Lord’s face, which no human being could see and live.

What, then, does “You cannot see my face” mean, except that although human nature—even after the resurrection—may advance to angelic equality and rise tireless to contemplate God, it still cannot fully prevail to see his essence? Not even the perfection of the angels reaches or comprehends it wholly, according to the Apostle, who says: “The peace of God, which surpasses every understanding” (Philippians 4)—with “understanding” understood to include that of the angels.

For the Trinity alone knows itself completely, together with the assumed humanity, which is the third person in the Trinity.

Then, in the words that follow, the future Church of Christ is signified by God; it is a mystery represented in figure. Moses bore the type of the Jewish people, who would afterward believe in Christ. Therefore he was told: “When I have passed by, you shall see my back” [Col. 0380D] (Exodus 33).

Some say that this meaning was fulfilled in the Gospel when Jesus ascended [Col. 0381A] the mountain, where Moses appeared speaking with Jesus. They therefore say that the promise which he received on Mount Sinai was fulfilled there, when it was said: “You shall see my back.”

He saw his back, therefore; that is, he saw the things that were done later and at the end.

When the Lord says to Moses: “There is a place beside me; you shall stand upon the rock” (ibid.), and shortly afterward, “I will remove my hand, and you shall see my back” (ibid.), this means that Christ is seen only through the Catholic Church. The Lord therefore declares that there is a place beside him from which he may be seen.

Moses is placed upon the rock so that he may contemplate God’s appearance, because unless someone holds firmly to the solidity of faith, he does not recognize the divine presence. Concerning this solidity the Lord says: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16).

### CHAPTER XLIII. On the Glorification of Moses

When Moses descended again with the tablets, [Col. 0381B] his face appeared glorified, but was nevertheless covered with a veil. This signified that the Law is covered and concealed by a mystical veil, hidden from unbelievers.

The word of the Law possesses the glory of knowledge, but it is secret. It also has the horns of the two Testaments, with which it advances armed against false doctrines.

When Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts; and plainly, because of the excessive hardness of their hearts, unbelievers receive the Scriptures of the Law and the Prophets in a carnal manner. Moses’ entire face is covered by a kind of veil, so that they cannot endure the glory of the Law as it speaks.

But if they turn to God, the veil is removed: “the letter that kills will die, and the Spirit that gives life will be made alive” (2 Corinthians 3). “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118).

### CHAPTER XLIV. On the Construction of the Ark

Let us now examine the ark of the Lord’s covenant [Col. 0381C], in which the tablets of the Law had been placed.

This ark, which Moses made from imperishable wood, signifies the Church of Christ, built from all the saints, incorrupt in mind and body, and possessing within it the two tablets of the covenant—that is, observance of the Law and of the Gospel.

The ark is gilded within and without; so also the Church ought to shine like gold, both inwardly through the splendor of its life and outwardly through the brightness of its teaching and wisdom.

The golden crowns around it, and the golden rings which are commanded to be attached at its four corners, signify this: as the Church extends throughout the four parts of the world, it is undoubtedly girded with the four books of the holy Gospel. Yet it is enclosed within the circumference of a single crown—that is, within the unity of the same faith.

The poles are also made from acacia wood and inserted into the same rings for carrying it, because strong and steadfast teachers are to be sought as imperishable wood, instructed by the study of sacred books. They should always cling to the unity of the holy Church, proclaim it, and, as though inserted into the rings, carry the ark. They are also commanded to be covered with gold, so that when they sound forth their teaching to others, they themselves may also shine with the splendor of their life.

### CHAPTER XLV. On the Golden Urn, the Tablets, and the Rod

In this ark of the covenant [Col. 0381D] there was a golden urn, as well as the tablets and Aaron’s rod.

As stated above, this ark is the Church, possessing two stone tablets—that is, the enduring firmness of the two Testaments. We also understand the golden urn as the pure and undefiled flesh of Christ, which preserves within itself the hidden manna of perpetual divinity and bears the enduring, heavenly sweetness of that angelic bread.

Aaron’s rod, moreover, expresses the saving standard of our same supreme and true high priest, Jesus Christ, [Col. 0382A] ever flourishing with the verdure of immortal remembrance.

### CHAPTER XLVI. On the Mercy Seat and the Cherubim

The mercy seat placed above the ark of the covenant signifies Christ himself, who intervenes as mediator and propitiator between God and humanity. Concerning him the Apostle says: “Whom God put forward as a propitiation through faith in his blood” (Romans 3).

This mercy seat is placed above the ark, just as Christ is the head of the Church. On its right and left stand two cherubim, signifying the fullness of knowledge—that is, love of God and of neighbor—through which the Lord is revealed. No one can reach God except through love, for “the fullness of the Law is love” (Romans 13).

Others understand these same two cherubim as the two Testaments, which overshadow the mercy seat of God—that is, the mysteries of Christ—according to the prophet’s testimony: [Col. 0382B] “You shall be known in the midst of the two living creatures.”

They look toward one another with turned faces as they are brought together in spiritual meaning. Then each agrees with the other for the better, and they harmonize more correctly in all things. Indeed, they cover the oracle, or mercy seat, on either side, because the Old and New Testaments, like Christ, cover the mysteries of the Church beneath figures of enigmas.

### CHAPTER XLVII. On the Altar

That altar signified the body of Christ, or all the saints, in whom the divine fire always burns and the flesh is always consumed.

### CHAPTER XLVIII. On the Table

The table, set forth as a table of peace and faith, bore the type of the Church. At it we are nourished by the food of the Scriptures. To its unity, from the whole world, the people of God are gathered by apostolic voices, as Solomon says:

“Wisdom has built herself a house; she has prepared her table, she has mixed her wine in the mixing bowl,” and the rest (Proverbs 9), saying: “Come and eat of my breads” (ibid.).

### CHAPTER XLIX. On the Lampstand and the Oil

That lampstand with seven branches bore the image of the Holy Spirit, who through his sevenfold grace enlightens the whole Church, established in the unity of faith.

Others understand the same lampstand as Christ, bearing the seven churches, in which he shines with the sevenfold splendor of the Holy Spirit.

For this lampstand the snuffers are made, which in Isaiah are called tongs. Some have interpreted these as the two Testaments, by which sins are cleansed and which are joined to one another through the unity of the Holy Spirit.

The lampstand is commanded to burn outside the veil of the testimony, which has been hung across it, because the truth of the Holy Spirit now shines without any veil of the Old Testament.

The oil, which God commanded to be taken from olive trees, likewise displays the grace of the Holy Spirit, possessing peace and mercy through the coming of the Savior. From it the light of truth is kindled in our hearts.

### CHAPTER L. On the Tabernacle

The figure of the tabernacle [Col. 0382D] now follows, which Moses is commanded by the Lord to construct.

Allegorically, this tabernacle is the Church, established in the wilderness of this life. Concerning it the Psalmist says: “For he hid me in his tabernacle in the day of evils” (Psalm 26).

The tabernacle is therefore furnished with various kinds of materials, some precious and some less valuable. This shows that some in the Church are saints and others sinners. All the faithful are situated within the body of the Church, whereas unbelievers are placed outside its embrace.

When the tabernacle itself was made as a type of the Church, [Col. 0383A], the Lord commanded that its four columns be founded on silver bases.

These four columns are the four evangelists, made solid by the holy firmness of faith. They are called silver because of the brightness of the divine word.

The bases of these columns are the prophets, who by their support bear the structure of the Church. For the evangelists place the Church upon the firm foundation of the prophets, and by their authority confirm the faith of the Gospel.

The golden head of the columns is the one of whom the Apostle says: “The head of a man is Christ” (1 Corinthians 11).

### CHAPTER LI. On the Columns, Bases, and Capitals

Meanwhile, he commands gilded boards to be erected [Col. 0383B] and their silver bases to be cast.

What are signified by the boards, except teachers and apostles, spread throughout the world by the extension of their preaching? What are signified by the silver bases, except, as stated above, the prophets, who are set beneath the boards and support them, firm and cast in place? For the life of the apostles and teachers, while it is instructed by their preaching, is strengthened by their authority.

Hence two joined bases are placed beneath each board, because when the holy prophets agree in their words concerning the Incarnation of the Mediator, the preachers who follow build the Church without doubt; and when the prophets do not differ among themselves, they fasten those later preachers more firmly within themselves.

Thus he rightly placed the skins of rams beneath them, so that by the rams he might indicate the leaders and superiors of the Churches. Because they do not fear to devote themselves to temporal cares, they ought to bear the winds of temptations and the rains of the world’s adversities, so that those who within the Church shine spiritually like fine linen, hyacinth, and purple may shine securely within, while their superiors and rulers labor outside against the storms and whirlwinds of the age.

### CHAPTER LII. On the Veil Hung in the Middle of the Tabernacle

When the veil is stretched across the middle of the tabernacle [Col. 0383C] and the outer part is separated from the inner, it signifies that the people of the Church are not yet permitted to see the things that have been promised, as though screened off, until they come.

Thus the Apostle also says: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13).

As long, therefore, as we are in this world, we see the truth as through a mirror, placed as though in the holy place but not yet reaching the Holy of Holies.

The holy place can signify those things in the present age through which one can maintain a holy way of life. The Holy of Holies, however, which is entered only once, requires passage to heaven, where the mercy seat and the cherubim are, and where God can appear to the pure in heart.

Yet while established in this way of life, we do not remain without the help of the Holy Spirit. From the one fountain of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0383D] we have seven lamps to illuminate the people of God—that is, the Lord’s sevenfold grace, sent throughout the whole world—which enlightens the peoples of the Church with the radiance of the Holy Spirit and the diverse brightness of spiritual gifts.

This hung veil, which concealed the inner part of the tabernacle so that the things stored there could not be seen, can indeed signify the time that existed under the Law, because what the Law and the Prophets had sung was hidden. With the veil interposed, those things could not be seen.

But afterward, when Christ came and, at the time of his passion, tore that veil from top to bottom, all those things that had previously been hidden were revealed to our faith through the Lord’s passion. The Apostle says: “But to us God has revealed them through his Spirit, for the Spirit searches everything, even the deep things of God” (1 Corinthians 2).

### CHAPTER LIII. On the Various Gifts for the Construction of the Tabernacle
Offerings are presented with a single purpose, yet they are diverse, for the construction of the tabernacle, as it is written: “Gold and silver, bronze, precious stones” (Exod. XXV). In addition, there were fine linen, scarlet, violet, and purple; also rams’ skins dyed red and violet skins; as well as imperishable wood and goats’ hair for the construction of the tabernacle (ibid.). Whatever else was necessary for worship and for the sacred vestments, men and women alike supplied: bracelets, earrings, rings, and every golden vessel set apart as offerings to the Lord. “If anyone had violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, fine linen, and goats’ hair” (Exod. XXXV).

The form of the former tabernacle, therefore, is a type of the Church. These gifts signify the gifts of merits with which the Church is adorned. Her faith is compared with gold, and the word of preaching with silver. The fact that men and women supply what is necessary for the ornament or tabernacle signifies that within the Church the virtues of the strong, represented by men, and the modest works of the weak, represented by women, all find their place, because they are accepted for the uses of holy edification.

The contribution itself, however, is not made under compulsion but willingly, because faith is voluntary. The bracelets, which bind the arms, signify the works of those set over others who labor greatly. The earrings express the obedience of subjects. The rings display the seal of hidden things. Thus teachers conceal certain matters from those of lesser understanding and hide them, as it were, beneath a seal, lest the mysteries of God be entrusted to the unworthy. Hence the righteous person rejoices and says: “I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I may not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII).

The ornaments of the right hand signify good works and the right hand. By the golden vessel set apart as an offering to the Lord, the understanding of divinity is meant. This is separated from the love of the weak to the extent that the command lifts it toward those things alone that are earthly. Violet signifies hope for heavenly rewards; purple declares blood and the endurance of sufferings offered out of love for the everlasting kingdom. Twice-dyed scarlet signifies charity, which is dyed twice in its perfection, since one is adorned by love of God and of one’s neighbor. Fine linen signifies the spotless incorruption of the flesh and the most radiant brightness of holiness. For fine linen is white linen. The goats’ hair, from which the roughness of hair-cloth is woven, signifies the harsh affliction of repentance.

While some are disciplined through the bracelets and rings by strong instruction, others display devoted obedience in hearing through the earrings and bracelets on the right hand, together with upright action; some possess, through the golden vessel, a splendid and more subtle understanding of God; others, through violet, purple, and scarlet, do not cease to hope for, believe in, and love the heavenly things they have heard, even those they do not yet know through a more refined understanding. Some offer the incorruption of the flesh through fine linen. Others, through goats’ hair, harshly lament what they willingly admitted.

Behold: from such great diversity of works one tabernacle is made, just as from diverse dust one globe of earth is formed, watered by the infusion of the Holy Spirit. The imperishable wood of Sethim signifies all the saints, incorrupt in mind and body; for they do not perish with the world but remain eternal.

The precious stones signify confessors, apostles, priests, and all the righteous, whom the blessed Apostle Peter also calls living stones: “You are living stones, being built together into the temple of God” (I Pet. II).

All these things, therefore, are brought into the tabernacle of God, so that no one may despair of salvation. One offers gold, that is, understanding; another silver, that is, eloquence; another the voice of bronze, and thus many things come to be in the tabernacle: the table, the lampstand, the altar, the columns, the bases, the boards, the bowls, the cups, the censers, the vessels, the mortars, and the snuffers; the pegs and the tents. Through these diversities the whole beauty of the tabernacle—that is, of the Church—is distinguished.

For the tabernacle is the Church, in which there is the table, that is, the unity of faith; or certainly sacred Scripture, by which all the faithful are nourished with spiritual food. The lampstand with its seven lamps is Christ together with the seven Churches. Its snuffers signify the two Testaments. The columns are the holy teachers, strengthened by the solidity of faith. The bases are the prophets, who bear the structure of the Church upon their foundation. There too are the boards, the apostles, expanded through the preaching of faith.

The tents are the overseers and preachers, who labor more intensely against the storms of this age. There are also the bowls, that is, the distributions among human beings. There are the pegs, namely, the leaders of the Church, upon whom all kinds of peoples hang, like vessels. The cups are the words, or meanings, of doctrine. The censers are the virtues of works, or the prayers of the saints, by which an aroma of sweetness rises to the Lord. The vessels are the apostles and teachers, full of life-giving waters. There are lilies, the brightness of virginity; or mortars, the endurance of labors and sufferings by which the members of penitents are put to death.

These forms and distributions of gifts have been divided by the Holy Spirit among the faithful, so that in each distribution the perfect tabernacle of Christ may be constructed—in them God dwells in the midst of the saints.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the ointment with which the tabernacle is anointed

The ointment with which the tabernacle is anointed is chrism, with which the faithful people are anointed in the Church, in whom divinity dwells as in a tabernacle. This ointment may also be understood as the virtues of the saints, or the fragrance of righteousness spread far and wide. Concerning it the Apostle says: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of his righteousness” (II Cor. II).

## CHAPTER LV. On the compound incense

The incense is composed of four very fragrant substances ground into the finest powder: stacte, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense. The Apocalypse of the blessed John shows that these have been established as a figure of the prayers of the faithful: “Then the twenty-four elders fell before the Lamb, each holding a harp and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints” (Apoc. V).

Although the nature of these four fragrances also seems to signify the form of the four elements: frankincense, which is transparent, may be compared with air; stacte with water; galbanum and onycha with earth and fire. Thus, through these, the incense pleasing to God may be the prayer of praise offered by creation for all things that are in heaven and beneath heaven, on earth and in the waters.

The blood with which Moses sprinkled and purified the people, the tabernacle of the covenant, and everything that was in it, saying, “This blood is the blood of the covenant” (Exod. XXIV), is shown wonderfully to proclaim the blood of the Lord Jesus. By it the hearts of all believers are purified; by it the faith of the Church is sealed; by it the whole people—that is, the body of Christ—and the entire tabernacle are sanctified. The Lord said to his disciples: “This is my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many” (Mark XIV), thereby fulfilling in truth what had been shown figuratively through Moses.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the vestment of the high priest

It must now be demonstrated what the vestments of the high priest are and what they signify. Aaron the priest signifies the one to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). The vestment of this priest is the Church, concerning which the Apostle says: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V).

The four colors from which his vestment is woven signify the diversity of merits that shines within the holy Church, in the body of Christ. The *poderis*, that is, the priestly linen garment, signifies the Incarnation of Christ, which is from the earth and is represented in the feet. Linen arises from the earth. The turban on his head and the golden plate signify the splendor of divinity, so that we may appear to be adorned with the *poderis* according to the human nature and with the turban according to the divine nature.

The undergarments that he puts on display the chastity and integrity of Christ’s body. The belt with which the priestly breast is bound signifies the choir of the saints, or concord, who embrace Christ in the unity of faith. The long tunic, extending from the head to the feet, is the same Church of Christ, destined to remain until the end of time.

This whole vestment is violet. Violet shines with an airy color, signifying that the whole Church should set its mind on the things above and rise wholly toward the love of heavenly things. The pomegranates placed below declare the unity of that same Church. For just as many seeds within a single pomegranate are protected by its outer rind, so within the number of the holy Church the unity of faith covers the peoples, whom the diversity of merits shelters within.

The bells among the pomegranates signify harmonious testimonies, namely, prophecies, and the holy teachers placed in the midst of the Church, whose tongues resound with the knowledge of doctrine. The bell touches both edges, that is, the parts of the Law and the Gospel. These bells are placed at the lower edge of the garment so that those who discuss both the end of the world and the future life may never be silent.

The shoulder-piece indicates the power and kingdom of the Savior, as it is written: “The principality is upon his shoulders” (Isa. IX). The two emerald stones placed on the shoulder-piece, one on the right and one on the left, are the two peoples: the Gentile, who is on the right, and the Jew, who was once on the right but is now on the left. Engraved upon them are the names of the twelve patriarchs, that is, for the imitation of the examples of the lives of the holy apostles.

Others have said that these same two stones are the two Testaments, or the letter and the spirit, in which all the mysteries of the Law are held: the spirit on the right, the letter on the left.

The breastpiece placed upon the chest, distinguished by a fourfold arrangement of stones, figures the evangelical word, which through its fourfold order sets forth for us the truth of faith and the doctrine of the Trinity. The apostolic word agrees with it both in the power and in the number of the gems. This breastpiece is twofold, because the knowledge of evangelical doctrine is both covered and hidden, simple and mystical.

Likewise, the same priest, Christ, is not improperly interpreted in his members, and especially in the high priest, who dwells among holy things and offers a sacrifice for the people, preparing through sacred rite the sacrifice of the spotless Lamb.

First, the fact that the breastpiece of judgment is fastened upon Aaron’s chest by binding cords signifies that the priestly heart must not be possessed by wandering thoughts, but must be restrained by reason alone. This is also vigilantly joined to the breastpiece, so that the names of the twelve patriarchs may be inscribed. For the holy Fathers, whose examples he must never cease to imitate, must always be carried upon his breast.

The fact that the priest is bound by the covering of the shoulder-piece on both shoulders signifies that he must always be fortified by the ornament of the virtues against adversity and prosperity alike. The fact that the shoulder-piece is commanded to be made of gold, violet, twice-dyed purple-red scarlet, and twisted fine linen demonstrates how greatly the priest ought to shine through the diversity of his virtues.

Gold gleams in the priest’s attire when he excels in the understanding of wisdom. Violet, which shines with an airy color, is joined to it, signifying that everything he handles should rise toward the love of heavenly things. Royal purple is mingled with it so that he may suppress the suggestions of vices as though by royal authority.

Twice-dyed scarlet is also joined to the shoulder-piece, so that in the sight of the internal Judge the good of all the virtues may be adorned by charity. Charity, which depends upon love of God and neighbor, shines as though from a twofold dye. To this twice-dyed scarlet is joined twisted fine linen. Fine linen arises from the earth with a shining appearance; through it the glowing beauty of bodily purity is signified. This twisted beauty is fastened to the shoulder-piece because chastity is brought to the perfect brightness of purity when the flesh is afflicted through abstinence.

It is also girded with a belt, by which the provocations of possessions and the luxury of lust are restrained. When the priest enters the tabernacle, he is surrounded by bells on his tunic, so that he may have the voices of preaching and not offend the judgment of the heavenly Observer through silence. The pomegranates are joined to the bells so that through his teaching the unity of faith may be signified.

The fact that the priest entered the first part of the tabernacle every day to offer sacrifices prescribes daily perseverance for us: we must never depart from this place where the people of God are instructed by heavenly voices, but must offer every day the spiritual sacrifice of confession and praise—that is, the humility of our souls, which are the true sacrifices—as it is written: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Ps. L).

The fact that once a year the high priest, leaving the people, entered the Holy of Holies, where the mercy seat was, signifies our High Priest, the Lord Jesus Christ. While he was in the flesh, he was with the people throughout that entire year—the year of which he himself says: “He sent me to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of propitiation” (Luke IV).

Thus, once a year, on the day of propitiation, he enters the Holy of Holies; that is, having completed his dispensation, he penetrated the heavens and entered to the Father, to make him propitious toward the human race and to intercede for all who believe in him.

[Col. 0387]

# QUESTIONS ON LEVITICUS

## CHAPTER I. On the four kinds of principal offerings

[Col. 0387B]

At the beginning of Leviticus four kinds of principal offerings are described, which are commanded to be offered to the Lord as a sweet fragrance: first, a calf from the herd without blemish; second, a lamb from the sheep; third, a turtledove and a dove; fourth, fine flour, unleavened, anointed with oil, and baked in an oven. The remaining sacrifices were offered according to the character of the circumstances and the person of the people.

The first sacrifice, the calf from the herd, demonstrates Christ descended from the line of the patriarchs. With the plow of his cross he subdued the earth of our flesh and enriched it with the seed of the Holy Spirit, bearing the fruit of virtues. This calf is without blemish because he is led to suffering without sin. He is offered not in the tabernacle but at its entrance, because Christ suffered outside the camp.

His blood is offered through the sons of Aaron the priest; this is understood of Annas and Caiaphas, because, having made their plan, they shed Christ’s blood.

The second victim, the lamb offered from the sheep, signifies the same Christ on account of his innocence. He is the Lamb who is led to sacrifice in Isaiah and is shown by John to all: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John I). The lamb is therefore rightly offered in sacrifice, so that the figure of Christ’s innocence and passion might be displayed.

The kid is also appropriate, because through his death the author of sin, the devil, is recognized as slain.

The third sacrifice is called the turtledove and the dove. It is clear that the turtledove is the flesh of Christ, since Solomon says: “Your cheeks are beautiful like a turtledove” (Song I). John the Baptist declares that the dove bears the figure of the Holy Spirit when he says: “Upon whom you see the Holy Spirit descending like a dove, he is my Son” (Matt. III). Accordingly, the turtledove and the dove—that is, Christ’s flesh joined to the Holy Spirit—are, through the mystery of the passion, a sacrifice to God as a sweet fragrance.

These three sacrifices are offered by a human being, that is, by Christ Jesus.

The fourth sacrifice is offered by the soul, that is, the Church offers a sacrifice of fine flour. It proclaims the figure of the Catholic Church, which is gathered from many grains of believers, like fine flour from many grains, and which, through the millstone of the Law and the Gospels, separates the letter from the spirit; united through the water of baptism, anointed with the oil of chrism, and made firm by the fire of the Holy Spirit, it is made pleasing to God through humility of spirit.

These are the four offerings, displaying the fourfold condition of Christ and the Church.

## CHAPTER II. On the figures of the victims

The diversities of the victims are set forth, whose type bore the image of Christ’s passion. For after he himself had been offered, all the victims ceased—those that had preceded in type or shadow of him and had figured that sacrifice which the one true Priest, the Mediator between God and human beings, offered.

It had previously been necessary to enact the promised figures of that sacrifice in the victims of animals, on account of the future cleansing of flesh and blood. Through that one victim there would be forgiveness of sins contracted from flesh and blood, which did not possess the kingdom of God (I Cor. XV), because that same bodily substance would be changed into a heavenly quality.

He himself was offered in the calf because of the power of the cross; in the lamb because of innocence; in the ram because of sovereignty; in the goat because of the likeness of sinful flesh, so that he might condemn sin concerning sin (Rom. VIII); in the turtledove and dove because of God becoming human, since the Mediator between God and humanity was shown in the conjunction of two substances.

Moreover, in the mixing of fine flour he clearly demonstrated the Church, gathered through the water of baptism, which is the body of Christ.

Morally, we offer a calf as a gift to God when we overcome the pride of the flesh; a lamb when we correct irrational and foolish impulses; a kid when we overcome wantonness; a dove when we display simplicity of mind; a turtledove when we preserve the chastity of the flesh; unleavened bread when we walk not in the leaven of malice but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (I Cor. V).

## CHAPTER III. On the fire of the sacrifice

The fire in the sacrifice signified that which is like victory absorbing death (I Cor. XV). These rites were properly celebrated among that people whose kingdom and priesthood were a prophecy of the king and priest who was to come, in order to rule and gather the faithful from all nations, bring them into the kingdom of heaven, to the sanctuary of the angels, and to eternal life.

Just as the Hebrews celebrated the sacred rites of this true sacrifice, so the pagans celebrated sacrilegious imitations—imitations of what the nations sacrifice, as the Apostle says: “They sacrifice to demons and not to God.” For the sacrifice of blood is an ancient and prophetic reality, testifying from the beginning of the human race to the future passion of the Mediator. The sacred writings show that Abel was the first to offer it.

## CHAPTER IV. That honey is not offered in God’s sacrifice

The fact that honey is not offered as a sacrifice to God indicates that nothing pleasurable or sweet belonging to this world is pleasing to God, and that nothing lacking some sharpness will be acceptable to truth. Hence the Passover is also eaten with bitter things.

## CHAPTER V. That salt is mixed into all sacrifices

[Col. 0389A]

By contrast, salt is commanded to be mixed into all sacrifices, so that everything we offer for the honor of Christ may always receive the salt of reason and discernment.

## CHAPTER VI. That oil is offered in sacrifices

The fact that oil was offered in the sacrifice signifies that whatever we devote to the worship of Christ and the devotion of the saints, we should do entirely with cheerfulness: “God loves,” as the Apostle says, “a cheerful giver,” and nothing should be done “from sorrow or compulsion” (II Cor. IX). Oil signifies cheerfulness, as it is written: “That he may gladden his face with oil” (Ps. CIII).

## CHAPTER VII. On the sacrifice of one who uttered an oath and on cleansing

[Col. 0389B]

Concerning one who made an oath that he would do something, whether good or evil, and then allowed the matter to pass into forgetfulness, it is said: “He shall offer a lamb from the flocks, or a she-goat, and the priest shall pray for him and for his sin. But if he cannot offer a sheep, let him offer two turtledoves or two young doves: one for sin and the other as a burnt offering” (Lev. V).

To utter an oath is to bind oneself by a vow to divine service; and when we promise good works, we pledge that we will do good. But when we vow abstinence and the mortification of our flesh, we swear that for the present we will do ourselves harm.

Since no one in this life is perfect, however devoted to God he may be, the lamb from the flocks or the she-goat is commanded to be offered for sin amid these pious vows, however slight. For what is signified by the lamb if not the innocence of the active life? What is signified by the she-goat, which often feeds while hanging upon the highest and most remote cliffs, if not the contemplative life?

Therefore, whoever sees that he has not fulfilled these promises and resolutions ought to gird himself more diligently for God’s sacrifice, either with the innocence of good works or with the lofty pasture of contemplation.

The lamb is rightly commanded to be offered from the flocks, but the she-goat is not commanded to be offered from the flocks, because the active life belongs to many, whereas the contemplative life belongs to few. When we do what we see many doing and having done, we give, as it were, a lamb from the flocks. But when the virtue of the one offering is insufficient for either a lamb or a she-goat, two young doves or turtledoves are added as a remedy for the penitent.

We know that young doves or turtledoves are associated with the song of lamentation. What, then, is signified by two young doves or two turtledoves if not the twofold lamentation of our repentance? When we do not rise to offer good works, we should mourn ourselves in two ways, because we have neither done what is right nor ceased from doing what is wrong.

Hence one turtledove is commanded to be offered for sin and the other as a burnt offering. A burnt offering is called that which is wholly consumed by fire. We therefore offer one turtledove for sin when we give a groan for our fault; from the other we make a burnt offering when, because we have neglected good things, we burn ourselves completely and blaze with the fire of grief.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the sons of Aaron who were destroyed

The sons of Aaron, who placed strange fire upon the altar and were consumed by divine fire, signified those who, having despised God’s tradition, seek foreign doctrines and introduce teachings based on human action. The Lord rebukes and reproves them in the Gospel, saying: “You reject the commandment of God in order to establish your own tradition” (Matt. XV).

Anyone who lights a strange fire may also be seen as one who, kindling in the sanctuary of his heart the fire of some bodily or worldly desire, dares to approach the altar of the Lord, which accepts only the kindling of that fire. Concerning it the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII). With this fire the Lord Jesus will always kindle us, so that we may be enlightened in our understanding and not burn in our vices.

## CHAPTER IX. On the distinction of foods

Now concerning the distinction of foods: the Law allowed certain animals for eating as clean and prohibited others as unclean. First, it must be understood that whatever has been established by God is clean and purified by the authority of its very establishment.

What, then, is meant by the animals? Human morals, acts, and desires are painted through them, and through these people themselves become clean or unclean.

Thus it says that these are clean: “Whatever has a divided hoof and chews the cud among the cattle, you shall eat” (Lev. XI). In saying this, it was distinguishing not cattle but human conduct.

Finally, those people are clean who chew the cud, who always carry the divine commandments in their mouths as food. They also divide the hoof, because, believing the two Testaments—the Law and the Gospels—they complete their life with the firm step of innocence and righteousness.

The Jews, likewise, do chew the words of the Law, but they do not divide the hoof; that is, they neither receive the two Testaments nor establish the steps of their faith in the Father and the Son. For this reason they are considered unclean.

Heretics too, although they divide the hoof by believing in the Father and the Son and receiving the two Testaments, are nevertheless unclean, because they do not chew the doctrine of truth in their mouths.

For Scripture adds: “Of all that are produced in the waters, whatever has fins and scales, these you shall eat; but whatever does not have fins and scales shall be an abomination to you” (ibid.).

Thus, among fish, those with scales and a rough surface are considered clean; rough, shaggy, firm, and serious human conduct is approved. Those without these qualities are called unclean; they signify conduct that is fickle, slippery, treacherous, and effeminate.

What does the Law mean when it says, “You shall not eat the camel,” if not that, by the example of the animal, it condemns a shapeless life, twisted by crimes? When it prohibits the pig as food, it surely censures a life that is muddy and filthy and delights in the squalor of vices. When it condemns the hare, it condemns men who have been transformed into women.

Who would make the body of a weasel into food? Rather, it censures theft. Who would eat a lizard? Rather, it hates the uncertain variability of life. Who, finally, could eat a gecko, so that the Law would prohibit it so emphatically? Rather, it execrates the stains of minds.

Who would eat a hawk, a kite, or an eagle? Rather, it hates those who live by violent crime and robbery. Who would eat a vulture? Rather, it curses those who seek prey through another’s death. Likewise, when it prohibits the raven, it condemns black desires.

When it prohibits the sparrow, it rebukes intemperance. When it prohibits the owl, it hates vanities that flee the light. When it prohibits the *caradrius*—the lapwing or plover-like bird—it condemns excessive looseness of speech. When it prohibits the swan, it denotes pride of the lofty neck. When it prohibits the bat, it signifies those who seek errors resembling the darkness of night.

Thus the Law also execrates in animals things that are not criminal in them, because they were born with them, but which, contrary to nature, have been sought not from their creation but from error.

There was once an ancient period when these shadows or figures had to be practiced or observed by the people, so that they had to abstain from foods that creation had indeed commended but the Law had prohibited.

But now Christ, the end of the Law, has come (Rom. X), opening all the Law’s contents, unlocking what was obscure, and revealing with unveiled truth all the mysteries that antiquity had covered from us—the distinguished teacher, heavenly instructor, and revealer. Under him it is said: “Now all things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean; rather, their mind and conscience are defiled” (Tit. I).

## CHAPTER X. On the uncleanness of women who give birth

The question of the uncleanness of childbirth and the contagion of leprosy follows. For it says: “A woman who has conceived seed and given birth to a male shall be unclean for seven days and shall be purified on the eighth. But she who has given birth to a female is written to remain in uncleanness for twice seven days” (Lev. XII).

There is no doubt that certain mysteries of a hidden secret are contained in these tablets. The week may signify the period of the present life, because the world was completed in a week of days. As long as we are placed in the flesh, we cannot be perfectly pure, unless the eighth day has come—that is, the time of the future age. Yet on that day the one who has acted manfully must be purified.

Immediately the mother who has given birth to him becomes clean. For the one who has been purified from vices will receive his flesh through the resurrection. But whoever has had nothing manly in himself against sin and has remained slack and effeminate in his actions will be purified from his uncleanness neither in the week of the present age nor in the future one.

## CHAPTER XI. On leprosies

[Col. 0391B]

The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: “A man whose flesh and skin has developed a different coloration, whether a patch or something resembling a shining mark—that is, a lesion of leprosy—shall be brought to Aaron the priest, or to one of his sons. When he sees the leprosy on the skin and the hairs changed to a white color, it is a lesion of leprosy, and he shall be separated according to his judgment” (Leviticus 13).

Leprosy signifies false doctrine. Therefore lepers are rightly understood as heretics who, lacking the unity of true faith, profess various doctrines of error and mix truths with falsehoods, just as leprosy stains human bodies by producing variation in both sound and diseased places.

Concerning this leprosy, we find that the lawgiver established six kinds in human beings: first, that of the head and beard; second, that of baldness and receding hair; third, that of flesh and skin; fourth, that of the skin of the body and white scars with redness; fifth, that of sores and scars; sixth, that of burns.

He bears leprosy on his head who sins against the divinity of the Father or against the Head himself [Col. 0391C], who is Christ. For “the head of a man is Christ” (1 Corinthians 11). This leprosy is found among the Jews, Valentinians, Marcionites, Photinians, Manichaeans, Arians, Sabellians, Macedonians, Anthropomorphites, Priscillianists, Donatists, Nestorians, Eutychians, and all who bear leprosy on the scalp, because they openly defend the faithlessness of their error through manifest perversity.

They bear leprosy on the beard who form a perverse opinion about the apostles and saints of Christ, and falsely allege that they preached some error. For just as a beard is an adornment of a man, so the holy apostles and teachers are adornments of Christ’s body.

They have leprosy on the body who disparage the Church, such as the Carpocratians, who deny the resurrection of the flesh; the Novatians, who condemn marriage and deny repentance to sinners; the Heraclites, who, among their other errors, do not believe that little children possess the kingdom of heaven; and the Arians, who forbid offerings to be made for the dead.

They bear leprosy on flesh and skin who endeavor to advocate carnal or external things, such as the Corinthians, who believe that the future resurrection consists in the desire of the flesh; or the Arians, who say that, even if those who remain in the faith live carnally, their sins cannot be counted. [Col. 0391D]

They bear leprosy on the scar of a healed sore who, after knowing God and receiving his healing, and after the manifestation of the faith received from Christ, once again display on the scar itself some indication of error or the faithlessness of an earlier doctrine.

He bears leprosy on living flesh who holds some false opinion about the soul, which is the life of the flesh, such as the Luciferians, who say that the soul is propagated from the substance of the flesh, and the Arabians, who believe that the soul dies together with the body.

The Manichaeans have leprosy on the scar of a burn: by the futile torture of abstinence they burn their bodies, and through unbelief produce from it not purity but leprosy. Concerning such people the Apostle preached:

> “Some will depart from the faith,” he says, “paying attention to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, and having their conscience branded, forbidding marriage and abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful” (1 Timothy 4). [Col. 0392A]

He further added the colors of leprosy: pale, red, white, livid, black, and flowering. Thus, when he speaks of pale leprosy, he denotes a weak and fragile faith of the soul, which, having lost the color of complete health, languishes in the weakness of error.

When he displays red leprosy, he denotes a mind stained by the blood of homicide and injury. When he speaks of white leprosy, he refers to those heretics who call themselves pure, or to others who glory in a false merit, such as Pelagius and Novatian.

When he mentions black or livid leprosy, he condemns the marks of envy and spite. When he indicates black leprosy, he detests a conscience blackened by the smoke of sacrifices and the pyre of idolatry.

When he speaks of leprosy flowering over the whole body and covering the entire skin of the body from head to foot, he points to the crime of avarice, because now it is considered splendid and pleasing for a person to be happy in this world and to appear rich in the present age. [Col. 0392B] For this pest of avarice stains every class of human beings, as though the whole body, with the frequent contagion of this error.

When he speaks of leprosy having redness mixed with paleness, he denotes a person who, although weak-minded and deceitful, easily bursts into rage and, because of the fickleness of his character, quickly commits perjury. Pallor signifies a lying tongue; redness reveals anger.

There is therefore a leprosy of sin which is cleansed by sacrificial offerings—that is, by a contrite and humbled heart. For “a sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Psalm 50).

The water by which leprosy is washed away is baptism. It is also kept outside the camp for a purification of seven days—that is, it is purified through recognition of the sevenfold Spirit.

There is also a kind of leprosy that is removed at the priest’s command, namely, through teaching. But the kind of leprosy that cannot be cleansed at all belongs to those who sin against the Holy Spirit and do not say that penitents can obtain forgiveness. Concerning them Truth says: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matthew 12) [Col. 0392C].

As for the command that lepers leave the camp and remain outside until their leprosy is cleansed, this means that heretics must be cast out from the Church until they are purified from their own error and thus return to the Lord.

Such a person is commanded to remain unclean, with his garments torn, his head uncovered, and his mouth veiled, while awaiting the cleansing of his leprosy. In the same way impenitence ought to remain unclean: with garments torn, that is, with every secret thing exposed; with the head uncovered, so that his denunciation may be seen by all; and with the mouth closed, so that he may no longer teach or speak impiously.

But Scripture further added that leprosy may be found in vessels, on the walls of a house, in clothing, in the warp, and in the woof. Leprosy on the walls of a house signifies the assembly of heretics, which must be cleansed by the priest. Leprosy in vessels signifies each person’s sins of the body. Leprosy in the warp or in clothing signifies sins committed outside the body or perpetrated within the body itself. The warp signifies the human soul, and the woof the sensations of the softest body. [Col. 0392D]

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the High Priest and His Worship

The Lord said to Moses: “The high priest—that is, the greatest priest among his brothers—upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured and whose hands have been consecrated for the priesthood, and who has been clothed in holy garments, shall not uncover his head, shall not tear his clothing, and shall not enter at all upon any dead person. He shall not defile himself even for his father or mother, nor leave the sanctuary, lest he pollute the sanctuary of his God, because the oil of the holy anointing of his God is upon him. I am the Lord. He shall marry a virgin; he shall not take a widow, a divorced woman, a defiled woman, or a prostitute, but a maiden from his own people, lest he defile his offspring” (Leviticus 21).

The great priest among his brothers [Col. 0393A] is the one of whom it is written: “Go to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20).

Upon whose head the oil of anointing was poured, as the prophet David says: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44).

His hands were consecrated: he possesses consecrated hands because he extended them in his Passion for the expiation of the whole world.

His clothing is not torn—that is, he does not permit his Church, which clings to him and is his own garment, to be divided into heresies and schisms.
