The figure of this garment was that seamless tunic of Jesus, woven throughout, which was not torn during his Passion but was preserved undivided by its possessor.

He must not approach death, because “he committed no sin” (1 Peter 2). For death is understood as sin, as it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die.”

He is not defiled in father or mother. [Col. 0393B] In his mother Christ was not defiled, since before the ages he was born from the Father; likewise, in his Father he was not defiled when he was born in this world from his mother. For he alone entered this world pure, proceeding from a virgin’s womb without human contamination.

All of us, when we sin, are defiled in our father, from whom we were created, if we fall into heresy. Likewise, we are defiled in our mother if, while believing in God, we injure the Church in some respect or stain the freedom of our heavenly mother with the unworthy slavery of sin.

He shall not depart from the holy places, because Christ, by assuming flesh, descended into the world in such a way that he never abandoned heaven.

He shall not marry a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute, but a virgin. The widow and divorced woman is the Synagogue, concerning whom the Lord speaks through Isaiah, saying: “Where is the bill of divorce of your mother, by which I dismissed her?” (Isaiah 50).

The prostitute is heresy, which lies open to the error or lust of many. Such women are not joined to Christ; only the virgin Church is, for she has neither stain nor wrinkle. [Col. 0393C] Concerning her the Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2).

The soul, too, is said to be a bride, but only the soul that is proved incorrupt through the simplicity of faith and purity of conduct. The soul that departs from the yoke of the Law and does not observe the precepts of the Gospel is both virgin and widow. It is divorced because, by sinning, it is separated from Christ’s body, even if it is not cast out by a bishop. It is a prostitute when it receives lovers—namely, hostile powers and demons who desire its beauty. For the soul was created beautiful by God, and exceedingly fair, since it bears the image and likeness of God.

Next it says: “He shall take a wife from his own people”—that is, the soul which is joined to him by faith—“and he shall not defile his offspring,” that is, the word of God preached in the Church. As it is written in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet” (Matthew 7:6).

Up to this point, the things spoken about the high [Col. 0393D] priest have referred mystically to Christ. From here onward, they are interpreted as applying to his members, especially to priests, to whom the spiritual sacraments belong. Their many privileges must also be briefly reviewed.

Concerning him it says: “He shall not uncover his head,” that is, he should honor the sacraments of Christ, who is the Head, through the veil of mysteries. “He shall not tear his garments,” lest he pass into heresy and schisms. “He shall not enter upon any soul that is dead,” that is, he shall not approach any sin that leads to death.

“He shall not be defiled for his father or his mother”: he must not indulge the love of his parents with such excessive affection that he offends his Lord and Creator, nor pity his relatives so greatly that he appears guilty before God. How many bishops, how many monks, while caring for their parents, have lost their souls.

“He shall not leave the holy places,” so that he may always remain in holy work and thought. For whoever speaks what is [Col. 0394A] idle and worthy of reproach departs from the holy places and pollutes God’s sanctification, because he does not walk as a servant of Christ.

“He shall not marry a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute, but a virgin”: he must embrace nothing of the old man or of his former will, but possess a life flourishing in complete purity.

“He shall take a wife from his own people”: that is, he should embrace the life of the saints, to whom he is made near through faith.

Among these instructions, the same priests are commanded not to drink wine or strong drink while ministering in the temple, lest their hearts be weighed down by drunkenness, gluttony, and the cares of this life. Nor are they to have any portion in the earth except God alone, lest, while thinking about earthly things, they forget heavenly things.

They are also commanded to exclude from this banquet neighbors and hired laborers, and to give the leftovers of the food only to servants. The neighbor is the heretic, who claims the title of Christian name as one who is near. The hired laborer represents the Jew, who seeks the fruit of observing the Law in a carnal manner.

With such people, therefore, the priest of God does not [Col. 0394B] share the nourishment of the Gospel, which is given for the refreshment of souls. It is given only with the servants of Christ. From these offerings, the breast and right arm are placed upon the altar for the priest: in the breast, pure thoughts and knowledge of doctrine; in the right arm, good works for battle against the devil, so that with an armed hand he may complete by the example of his works what he has conceived in his heart.

He is also given the jaw from the private portions, so that he may possess eloquence. From the victims he is given the stomach, so that by its indication he may learn to extinguish luxury and despise gluttony.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Priests Who Are Not to Offer Sacrifice

Among these instructions the priests are also commanded not to be marked by any bodily defect [Col. 0394C]: not blind, not lame, neither small nor large, nor with a crooked nose; not with a broken foot or hand, nor hunchbacked; not bleary-eyed, nor having a white spot in the eye; not suffering from a persistent itch, nor from an eruption on the body, nor being burdened. All these things refer to a defect of the soul. For it is the character of the soul, not nature, that is condemned.

A blind priest is one who does not understand the Scripture of knowledge and, through ignorance, does not know where to direct the step of his teaching or conduct. Concerning such people it is written: “All his watchmen are blind.”

A lame priest is one who indeed understands what he ought to teach, but does not fulfill the precepts that he teaches.

He has a small nose who is not capable of maintaining the proper measure of discernment.

He has a large and crooked nose who is furious and threatening, with the arrogance of pride or with excessive discernment.

He has a broken foot or hand who does not strive to follow the way of God that he teaches.

A hunchbacked priest is one who is weighed down by the burden of earthly desire and turns his attention only slowly toward heavenly things.

A bleary-eyed priest is one whose intellect flashes toward knowledge of the truth but obscures it by living carnally.

He has a white spot in his eye who is blinded by the arrogance of wisdom or righteousness.

He has a persistent itch who is continually dominated by the wantonness of the flesh.

He has an eruption on his body who is mentally devastated by avarice. Unless avarice is restrained while still small, it inevitably spreads without measure.

A burdened priest is one who, even if he does not practice disgraceful behavior in deed, is weighed down in mind without restraint by such thoughts.

Such a person can neither enter the holy places nor possess the title of bishop, because he is burdened by earthly desires and deprived of knowledge of the truth. [Col. 0394D]

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the Washing of Aaron and His Sons

Furthermore, what is meant by the fact that, according to God’s command, Moses is read to have washed Aaron and his sons? [Col. 0395A] Even then they signified, through the sacrament of baptism, the purification of the world and the holiness of all things.

They do not receive the garments until their filth has first been washed away, nor are they appointed to sacred service unless they are reborn as new men in Christ.

That Moses washes them signifies the Law. For we must be washed by God’s commandments. When, prepared to put on Christ, we have removed our leather tunics, then we shall be clothed in linen garments, containing nothing of death but being entirely white. Thus, rising from baptism, we shall gird our loins in truth, and the whole disgrace of our former sins shall be concealed.

Therefore David also says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Psalm 31:1).

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the Offering for the Priest’s Sin

What is meant by the figurative law that commands a calf to be sacrificed for the priest’s sin and the people to be sprinkled seven times with its blood by the priest’s finger? It then commands that two goats be offered: one, on which the Lord’s lot has fallen, is to be killed, and the people are likewise to be sprinkled with its blood by the priest’s finger, as with the blood of the calf. The other, upon which all the sins and curses of the whole people are to be placed, is to be led into a deserted place and left there. [Col. 0395B]

But first it is necessary to explain the sacrifice of the calf, and then to recount the causes and mysteries of the goats.

This calf, which is commanded to be killed for the cleansing of the priest and the whole people from sin, bore in itself a figure of our Lord and Savior. He was sacrificed not only for the sins of the priestly people but also for the entire human race, for all nations, with God the Father permitting it.

As the Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

It is fitting, therefore, that in this passage the people are commanded to be sprinkled seven times with the blood of this calf by the priest’s finger, so that it might be shown that our redemption and purification are effected in Christ’s blood through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit.

The two goats plainly demonstrated the figure of two peoples, because of the original transgression of sin. They bear the form of goats whose likeness appears in the Gospel: goats, that is, sinners who are to be on the left, but among those who would believe in Christ and wholeheartedly repent of their sins [Col. 0395C] and receive the grace of baptism.

These receive, in the likeness of the goat upon which the Lord’s lot fell, a figure whose blood is commanded to be mixed with the blood of the calf, so that, made sharers in Christ’s Passion, they may become participants in his glory.

But what does it mean for the goat to fall to the Lord’s lot, unless it means that the believing people, whose figure that goat bore, are regarded as the Lord’s companion and co-heir in the kingdom? As the Apostle says: “We are heirs of God, but fellow-heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17).

The other goat, which does not fall to the Lord’s lot, bears the likeness of unbelievers who never wished to believe in Christ. They receive the curse of the whole people and all the iniquities of the human race, and they are cast into a deserted place.

But what does it mean to receive all iniquities and curses, unless it means that all the sins committed by the human race from Adam until Christ will be received by those alone who neither wished to believe in Christ nor to be purified by Christ’s blood? Thus, burdened and weighed down by the iniquities and curses of the whole human race, they will be cast into a deserted place—that is, into the outer darkness. [Col. 0396A]

There is weeping and gnashing of teeth there; and in the lake of fire, which is Gehenna, their fire will not be extinguished and their worm will not die.

## CHAPTER XVI. Which Animals Are Not to Be Offered in Sacrifice

The diversity of victims, and which are or are not to be offered, is enumerated in this book of Leviticus. But through comparison with animals, the conduct of human beings is being demonstrated.

If someone offers a sacrifice of peace offerings to the Lord, whether in fulfillment of a vow or as a voluntary offering, from cattle or sheep, he shall offer an unblemished animal, so that it may be acceptable; there shall be no defect in it.

If it is blind, broken, scarred, has a rash, an itch, or an eruption, you shall not offer it to the Lord, nor shall you burn any of it upon the altar of the Lord.

An ox or sheep with an ear or tail cut off may be offered voluntarily, but a vow may not be made from such an animal. [Col. 0396B]

Any animal whose testicles have been crushed, shorn, cut, or removed you shall not offer to the Lord, and you shall not do this at all in your land.

You shall not offer to your God bread from the hand of a foreigner. Whatever else they may wish to give, you shall not accept, because everything is corrupt and blemished.

First, a spotted or variegated animal is rejected from the sacrifice, that is, one in which there is a diversity of sins and which shifts now into lust and greed, now into various crimes.

A blind animal is also rejected: one who neither sees God nor does his works.

A broken animal is likewise rejected: one tormented and crushed by carnal vices.

An animal bearing a scar is rejected: one who does not lament the wounds of his sins with worthy repentance, but inwardly continues to carry the sign of his former disease through the desires of his will.

An animal with its tongue cut off is also rejected: one who does not confess God or meditate upon the divine law.

An animal with a rash is rejected: one who boils with the itch of lust and the heat of desires. [Col. 0396C]

Likewise, one with an itch is rejected: one who completes the sin of the flesh through the deed of his thought.

An animal with an eruption represents the gathering of heretics, which frequently plunges itself into the body of the Church; an eruption produces a livid discoloration.

Those with a cut-off ear represent people who do not obey the word of God, because they do not do what has been commanded.

The one with a cut-off tail is the person who does not complete the good he has begun with the end of perseverance.

An animal that is mutilated or has its testicles removed indicates those who, although possessing a man’s body, are feminized by the practice of disgraceful conduct.

Those entangled in these crimes are rejected from the Lord’s sacrifice. They neither become sharers in Christ’s Passion nor participants in heavenly sanctification. [Col. 0396D]

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the Remaining Ceremonies

Nor are the loaves of a foreigner offered to the Lord—that is, the superstitious doctrine of heretics or the superstitious studies of secular literature, which are outside the faith and are considered foreign.

Such offerings are rejected by the Lord, and this kind of sacrifice is cast out by the Catholic Church.

[Col. 0395]

# QUESTIONS ON NUMBERS

## CHAPTER I. The Catalogue of the Stations

[Col. 0395D]

**DISCIPLE.** Our first question is this: why did this book receive the name Numbers?

**TEACHER.** This book, one of the five books of Moses, was called Numbers because in it the census and number of the perfected men among the multitude of Israel that went out from Egypt are recorded. [Col. 0396D] Their journeys and stations are also numbered, from the borders of Egypt to the place and time at which Moses died.

The day of the tabernacle’s dedication and the manner of the offerings are likewise reckoned there, not without the mystery and significance of a sacred number.

The catalogue of the stations of the children of Israel, which are numbered from the first to the last, contains forty-two [Col. 0397A] in all. Concerning these Matthew speaks: “From Abraham to David, fourteen generations; and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ, fourteen generations”—that is, forty-two generations altogether.

Through these the Hebrew journeys, hastening to pass from earth to heaven, and, having left behind the Egypt of the world, enters the promised land.

Nor is it surprising that through this mystery of number we should arrive at the kingdom of heaven, under which the Lord and Savior proceeded from the first patriarch to the Virgin, as to the Jordan, which, flowing in a full stream, overflowed with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

The first station is the city of Rameses, which was at the farthest borders of Egypt. There the people assembled and went out into the desert on the day after Passover, in the sight of the Egyptians.

Some have thought that Rameses may be interpreted as “commotion” or “thunder,” because, when we have been stirred by the evangelical trumpet, awakened like thunder, we go out with joy in the first month, when winter has passed, when spring begins, and when all things are renewed.

We go out on the fifteenth day of the first month, on the day after Passover, in the full light of the month, after eating the spotless Lamb, with our feet shod according to the Apostle, our loins girded in chastity, and staffs prepared in our hands. [Col. 0397B]

## CHAPTER II. The Passover of the Second Month

The second station is at Succoth, where they bake unleavened bread and first pitch their tents. Hence the place received its name. For Succoth is interpreted as “tents” or “tabernacles.”

When, therefore, we have gone out from Egypt—that is, from the world—we first pitch our tents, knowing that we must proceed inward and hasten on our heavenly journey toward the holy land.

The third station is Etham, which is at the edge of the wilderness. [Col. 0397C] There the Lord is first seen going before the people in a pillar of fire.

Etham signifies “strength” or “profession.” Let us therefore prepare strength for ourselves, taking up perfect vigor, so that amid the darkness of errors and the confusion of night the light of the knowledge of Christ may appear.

Let our day also possess a protecting cloud, so that under these guides we may be able to reach the land of holy promise.

The fourth station is Pi-hahiroth, which is opposite Baal-zephon. Pi-hahiroth is interpreted as “the mouth of nobles.” Therefore, having assumed strength, let us become noble in the Lord, despising Baal-zephon as well—for Baal-zephon is interpreted as “lord of the north”—and avoiding his pride.

Departing from this station, the children of Israel crossed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness. They saw Pharaoh perish with his army, while Miriam led the song with tambourines.

The fifth station is Marah, to which the children of Israel came after crossing the sea, after three days. Marah is interpreted as “bitterness.”

After the preaching of the Gospel, after the tents of those who are migrating, after assuming the strength of faith, and after baptism and victory, [Col. 0397D] one comes again to bitterness, so that pleasure and luxury may be brought to an end through the bitterness of life, and sweetness may again be restored through the wood of the cross, as through torment.

The sixth station is Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, as a figure of the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples of the second rank.

From their springs we draw the drink of doctrine, and we pluck the sweet fruits of victory. Therefore Elim is rightly rendered “strong rams”: for they are the robust leaders, the shepherds of the flock of sheep, the teachers of the nations.

The seventh station is again at the Red Sea. Here the question arises: how, after crossing the Red Sea and passing the springs and Elim [F. “and Marah and the springs of Elim”], did they come again to the Red Sea? Perhaps, as they proceeded on their journey, some gulf of the sea came before them, beside which they pitched camp.

For it is one thing to cross the sea and another to pitch tents nearby. From this we are taught that, even after the discipline of evangelical doctrine and the sweetest foods of triumphs, the sea may sometimes open before us, and former dangers may be placed before our eyes. [Col. 0398A]

The eighth station is in the wilderness of Sin, which extends as far as Mount Sinai. Sin is interpreted as “bush” or “hatred,” because after we have come to the place of the Church, about which the Lord will speak to us, we should deserve the great hatred of the enemy.

The ninth station is Dophkah, which is called “knocking,” in accordance with what the Lord says: “Knock, and it will be opened to you.”

The meaning is clear: after we have come to the place of the Church, we begin to knock at the sacraments.

The tenth station is at Alush, which is interpreted as “leaven.” A woman takes leaven and mixes it into three measures of flour until the whole is leavened.

In this wilderness the people murmur because of hunger. In the evening they receive quail, and in the morning of the next day manna. Note that manna is given at the tenth station—that is, after the perfection of the Decalogue, they eat the bread of angels. [Col. 0398B]

The eleventh station is at Rephidim, which is interpreted as “the dissolution of the strong” or “the relaxation of hands.”

There, when the people were thirsty, water burst forth from the rock of Horeb in the likeness of Christ. There Jesus, as a type of the Savior, wages war against Amalek; and through the sign of the cross the assaults of demons rising against us are overcome.

There Jethro came to Moses, giving the counsel of the seventy elders; and, as a type of the Church to be gathered from the nations, the diminution of the Law is completed at the prompting of the Gospel.

Rephidim is beautifully called “the dissolution and healing of the strong,” either because Amalek was dispersed or because Israel was healed.

The twelfth station is in the wilderness of Sinai, where the apostolic number immediately comes to mind. Sinai is interpreted as “bush,” and it signifies the Church in which the apostles preach to us.

At this station Moses ascended to the Lord, and there the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, giving the Law to his people. There the tabernacle is constructed; there the truth of sacrifices, the variety of vessels, the garments of the high priest, and the ceremonies of priests and Levites are prescribed. [Col. 0398C]

There the number of the people and Levites is given, together with the distribution of the people among the individual tribes. The offerings of the leaders are also described at this station.

Two silver trumpets are likewise commanded to be made there for moving the camps.

There too it is commanded that those who could not attend Passover in the first month because they were unclean should assemble in the second month.

But what does it mean that those who lived far away, or who were unclean in soul, were commanded to celebrate Passover in the second month? This is plainly understood as a type of the people of the nations, who, having fornicated with all the demons, appeared unclean in soul. Yet, cleansed through a saving confession, they are commanded to pass over into a second birth, as it were into the second month.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the Nazirites

[Col. 0398D]

At this station the Nazirites are commanded not to drink wine, strong drink, or anything derived from grapes, nor to eat it—not even dried grapes, and not even vinegar made from wine.

But in Proverbs it is commanded: “Let those in power who are prone to anger not drink wine, lest, when they have drunk, they forget wisdom.”

What, then, is signified by the name of Nazirites, except a life of abstinence and self-restraint?

Here luxury is forbidden in wine, and every earthly pleasure in strong drink. Strong drink is made from various ingredients, just as pleasure arises from the diverse passions of vices.

Those do not drink wine but drink strong drink who, in order to deceive people, pretend to possess certain shadows and images of virtues.

Those eat dried grapes who, for the sake of human eyes, are discolored by the pallor of abstinence so that they may gain glory from people.

Those drink vinegar who, after a holy life, fall back into the oldness of former vices and take pleasure in the corruption of their former wickedness.

God therefore commands that those who have assumed the title of holiness [Col. 0399A] be free from all these vices, and that those who turn back from so lofty a state of mind desire no such disturbance.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning Lepers, Those with Discharges, and the Unclean

At this station lepers, those with discharges, and the unclean are cast out of the camps.

The lepers are heretics; those with discharges are unstable in thought; the unclean are unclean in conduct. Thus, as though infected and diseased, they are separated from the camp of the Church, lest by the contagion of their behavior they pollute the life of the innocent.

## CHAPTER V. The Age of Those Fit for Battle

There the people chosen for battle are counted from the age of twenty.

But why from the age of twenty, unless because from this age battles against each of the vices arise? Therefore they are chosen for combat, so that they may struggle against lust and not be overcome by luxury.

## CHAPTER VI. The Levites and the Keepers of the Vessels

[Col. 0399B]

There the Levites are also commanded to serve the tabernacle from the age of twenty-five, and from the age of fifty they become keepers of the vessels.

What is signified by the twenty-fifth year, in which the flower of youth begins to appear, except the very battles against the vices that arise against each person?

And what is expressed by the fiftieth year, in which the jubilees also rest forever, except inward rest after the battle of the mind has been subdued?

What, moreover, are signified by the vessels of the tabernacle except the souls of the faithful?

The Levites therefore serve the tabernacle in their twenty-fifth year and become keepers of the vessels in their fiftieth, so that those who still endure the struggles of attacking vices through the consent of pleasure may not presume to take charge of others.

But when they have subdued the battles of temptation, when they are already secure in themselves concerning inward tranquility, let them undertake the guardianship of souls. [Col. 0399C]

But who can completely subdue these battles, when Paul says: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin”?

Yet it is one thing to endure battles bravely and another to be weakened and conquered by battles. In the former, virtue is aroused so that people may not become exalted; in the latter, virtue is utterly extinguished so that they may not remain standing.

Then the Law commands that all the Levites shave all the hair of their flesh, because those who are taken up for divine service ought to appear pure before God’s eyes from every thought of the flesh, lest the mind bring forth something illicit in thought and make the beautiful appearance of the soul deformed, as though by hairs that bear fruit.

## CHAPTER VII. The Two Trumpets

After this, two trumpets are commanded to be made, at whose blast the people are moved to battle.

For this is written concerning them to Moses: “Make for yourself two silver trumpets, beaten out.” Shortly afterward: “When the short, interrupted blast sounds an alarm, the camps shall move.”

The army is led by two trumpets [Col. 0399D] because through the two Testaments, or through the two commandments of charity, the people are summoned to the battle line of faith.

They are commanded to be made of silver so that the words of the preachers may shine with the brilliance of eloquence and not confuse the minds of their hearers through any obscurity of their own.

They are beaten out because those who preach the life to come must grow through the blows of present tribulations.

It is rightly said: “When the short, interrupted blast sounds an alarm, the camps shall move,” because whenever a subtler and more finely articulated discourse of preaching is expounded, the minds of the hearers are stirred more ardently to the battles of temptation.

From here onward the children of Israel move on from Mount Sinai and pass into the graves of desire.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Graves of Desire
The thirteenth station is at the Graves of Lust, where the people, growing weary of the heavenly bread, desired Egyptian meats [Col. 0400A], and a sudden fire consumed many of them. From this we learn that those who abandon worldly conduct and have rejected the Egyptian pots—that is, the ardors of carnal desires—must not murmur against the heavenly bread or desire the poisonous things of the Egyptians, which are great meats, but must endure the simple food of manna, that is, a pure and heavenly life. Otherwise, if, after receiving the angelic manna, which is heavenly life or doctrine, we again desire the Egyptian meats, which are the carnal pleasures of this world, and the lusts of our former ways, we shall be consumed by nausea and immediately tormented by the Lord’s fire; and our desire will be turned into burial mounds, so that we become whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every kind of uncleanness.

## CHAPTER IX. The Seventy Chosen Men

[Col. 0400B] At this station the Spirit descends upon seventy chosen men. Then the Lord descends in a cloud, withdraws from the spirit that was upon Moses, and places it upon the seventy men. For when Christ, in the flesh, descends in the cloud, the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured out through faith upon the peoples; and upon the chosen in the languages of the seventy nations comes that gift of heavenly power which had once been in Moses and the prophets.

## CHAPTER X. Miriam’s Reproach

The fourteenth station is in the wilderness of Hazeroth. At this place Aaron the priest, together with his sister Miriam, incurs the occasion of offense: both reproach their brother because he had taken a foreign woman as his wife. Immediately Miriam breaks out with the contagion of leprosy. Here the figure of the mystery was evident: that priestly people of the fathers disparaged Christ the Savior against the Church gathered from the nations. Therefore she is covered with the filth of leprosy [Col. 0400C] and does not return to God’s tabernacle until the time appointed for the fullness of the nations is fulfilled. Then that same people will be able to recover its former health, when a sevenfold spiritual recognition has pleaded for its pardon.

The fifteenth station is at Rithmah, which is translated “sound” or “juniper.” They say that this wood preserves fire for a long time, so that, if its embers are covered with ashes, they last until the following year. From this we learn that, after the Graves of Lust, or the caves, we must pass to wood that remains hot for a long time, so that we may be fervent in spirit and proclaim the Lord’s Gospel with a clear sound and a voice raised on high. From this station to the thirty-second, the following histories are contained. Since they are not distributed among the individual stations, we too shall relate them together.

## CHAPTER XI. The Twelve Spies

[Col. 0400D]

Twelve spies are sent to the holy land; a cluster of grapes is brought back on a piece of wood, and Christ’s Passion is briefly revealed. The Jewish people murmur, fearing the attack of the giants; against God’s will they fight Amalek and the Canaanite, are defeated, and learn what sacrifices they ought to perform in the holy land. Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Korah, rise up against Moses and Aaron, and are swallowed by a chasm in the earth. The high priest, armed with a censer, enters between the dead and the living, and the wrath of God is halted by the priest’s voice. Aaron’s staff produces a flower and a leaf, and its greenness, preserved after drying, is consecrated as an eternal memorial. The red heifer is burned as a whole burnt offering, and its ashes serve for a special sprinkling. Briefly noting the figures of these events, we shall begin with the twelve spies.

The spies were sent to explore the fruitful land, but they terrified the people so that they would not believe they could receive the land promised by the Lord. They displayed the example of the scribes [Col. 0401A] and Pharisees. For just as those men were sent by Moses to examine only the land’s fertility with careful attention, so these others were commanded through the Law and the Prophets to contemplate the Lord’s advent through searching the Scriptures. That land was the holy flesh in which they could attain the kingdom of God, the abundance of spiritual fruits, and eternal life.

But just as the former spies frightened the people through despair, so that they would not trust God’s promise, so these scribes and Pharisees persuaded the Jewish people not to believe in Christ, desiring to return to the Egypt of this age. They rejected the manna of faith and sought the black pots of sins, the rotten onions of blasphemers, and the melons withered by the corruption of vices and lusts.

The cluster of grapes that two bearers brought from the promised land on a piece of wood—the cluster hanging from the wood—is plainly Christ, promised to the nations through the wood of the cross and poured forth according to the flesh from the womb of his mother Mary, from an earthly [Col. 0401B] lineage. The two bearers who walked beneath the burden of that cluster represent the two peoples. The first is the blind and wayward Jewish people, ignorant of the grace that hung there and weighed down by the burden of the One suspended, to whom it will be subjected in judgment. Of them it is said: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see; and bend their backs continually” (Ps. 68:23).

The one who came behind represented the people of the nations. Believing and having Christ before its eyes, it sees him while always carrying him, and follows him as a servant follows his lord and a disciple his teacher, just as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me” (Luke 9:25).

This is the cluster poured out for our salvation, which shed the wine of its blood through the crushing of the cross and offered the Church the cup pressed from his Passion.

This is the cluster accompanied by the pomegranate, as a gift of grace follows it: namely, our mother the Church, containing within herself, in the number of the seeds, a multitude of peoples glittering with the sign of Christ’s blood in its redness. Within herself she also possesses a differentiated [Col. 0401C] grace, as the Apostle says: “Charisms are divided, and gifts are distributed by the grace of the Holy Spirit.” The unbelievers, judging themselves unworthy of all these things, did not deserve to receive the land of Christ’s flesh flowing with milk and honey. Through faith, his servants—that is, the Christian people—attained it; and concerning his teaching the Church says daily: “How sweet are your utterances to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103).

We are taught by evangelical examples that the fig which they brought with the cluster from the promised land also bore the image of the Law. Just as the cluster is acknowledged to display the figure of the Savior, so in the Song of Songs the Church says of Christ: “My brother is like a cluster of Cyprus” (Song 1:13), because neither can Christ exist without the Law, nor the Law without Christ.

## CHAPTER XII. The Man Gathering Wood

[Col. 0401D]

After this, a certain man gathering wood on the Sabbath is put to death by the people. What does it signify that, by God’s command, he was slaughtered so atrociously by the whole people? This is easily brought forward by unbelievers. Let them understand, then, that all these things happened to them in figure. They were written for our correction.

That former carnal man, who dared to violate the Sabbath day while gathering wood, and was therefore punished, signified the form of the one who is now found marked with the sign of Christ yet performs a carnal work—that is, gathers wood, hay, and stubble suitable for the food of eternal fire (1 Cor. 3). While he gathers these things to his own destruction, if he is discovered, he is driven out by everyone and immediately killed, when he is judged by spiritual people. Thus everything that happened to those Jews through the Law is to be understood figuratively.

## CHAPTER XIII. Korah, Dathan, and Abiram

[Col. 0402A]

The destruction of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram now follows. They judged themselves entitled to the authority to offer sacrifice against Moses and Aaron the priest, and paid the penalties for their attempts.

They signify those who attempt to create heresies and schisms and deceive many by drawing them along with themselves; who despise Christ’s priests, separate themselves from the fellowship of his people and clergy, and dare to establish churches and another altar, uttering another prayer in illicit words and profaning the truth of the Lord’s sacrifice through false offerings. Those who strive against God’s ordinance will, because of the audacity of their presumption, be plunged alive into the depths when the joints of the earth are torn apart. Not only those who are leaders of error, but also those who, by consenting, have become participants in them, will perish in the vengeance prepared for the fire of eternal judgment.

## CHAPTER XIV. Aaron with the Censer

[Col. 0402B]

Then holy Aaron began to draw the people away from the destruction of death. Taking the censer, he ran to meet the devastation, and, standing in the midst of the survivors and the slain, he blocked the deadly plague by placing himself before it like a wall.

This priest is the Lord Jesus Christ, the beginning. Seeing the ruin of death in the world, this priest came from the height of heaven and met it like a giant running his course (Ps. 18:6). He stood between the living and the dead, because he was born and died. Thus, taking the censer of his Passion and presenting it as an aroma of sweetness, he suspended the destruction of eternal fire and endured the hostile death.

## CHAPTER XV. The Flowering Staff

Aaron’s staff, which flowered after being dry, signifies [Col. 0402C] the flesh of Christ. After it was cut from the root of Jesse, it revives, having been put to death in a more vigorous manner. Thus the staff greening after dryness is Christ rising after death.

We understand the staff and the flower to be one and the same, so that in the staff the power of the ruler, and in its flower its beauty, may be displayed. Hence he says in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.”

Others think that this staff, which produced a flower without moisture, is the virgin Mary, who without sexual union gave birth to the Word of God. Of her it is written: “A staff shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root”—namely Christ, who, bearing the type of the future Passion, is the flower of virgins, the crown of martyrs, and the grace of those who practice continence, purple with the bright light of faith and the blood of the Passion.

## CHAPTER XVI. The Red Heifer

Meanwhile the red heifer remains, burned as a whole burnt offering, whose ashes were the purification of the people. For this is what is said concerning it to Moses and Aaron [Col. 0402D]:

“Command the children of Israel to bring you a red cow of full age, in which there is no blemish and which has not borne a yoke. You shall hand it over to Eleazar the priest. It shall be led outside the camp and slaughtered in the sight of everyone. Eleazar shall dip his finger in its blood and sprinkle it seven times toward the entrance of the tabernacle. He shall burn it while all look on; he shall commit to the flames its hide, flesh, blood, and dung. The priest shall also cast cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet twice-dyed into the flame that consumes the cow. Only then, after washing his clothes and body, shall he enter the camp; and he shall be unclean until evening. The one who burned it shall also wash his clothes and body and shall be unclean until evening. A clean man shall gather the ashes of the cow and pour them outside the camp in a very clean place, so that they may be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel and used for the water of sprinkling, because the cow was burned for sin.

“[Col. 0403A] The children of Israel and the resident aliens shall have this as a holy ordinance in perpetuity. Whoever touches a dead person and is thereby unclean for seven days shall be sprinkled with this water on the third day and shall be clean on the seventh day. If he is not sprinkled on the third day or on the seventh, he cannot be cleansed.”

The red heifer is the flesh of the Savior, rosy with the blood of the Passion, of full age because he accepted the Passion at the fullness of his age. The fact that no yoke was placed upon it shows that Christ’s flesh was not subjected to sin or overcome by any sin.

The fact that the children of Israel seized it and led it outside the camp, with the priest Eleazar standing by, signifies the Jewish people and the priestly consent to the Lord’s death: they cast him outside Jerusalem and crucified him. Therefore, just as those who offer the heifer are unclean, so those who seized the Lord are regarded as sinners. And just as the one who gathers the ashes of the sprinkling is clean, so all are clean who proclaimed Christ’s Passion to the nations and sprinkled his teaching throughout the whole world, gathering peoples for the Lord.

We think that the wood and the hyssop [Col. 0403B] signify the cross and baptism. For by a bundle of hyssop the lambs were sprinkled with blood, and those who were to be cleansed were customarily sprinkled with it; this figuratively represented the washing of baptism and the cleansing of the eternal fountain.

By the scarlet twice-dyed, we understand the figure of the sacred blood by which sinners are washed. It is twice-dyed because through it we are cleansed both in body and in heart. These three things were handed down for the purification of sins: first, through the cedar, faith in the wood of the cross; second, through the hyssop, martyrdom; third, through the scarlet, the sacrament of the Lord’s blood.

Just as they are commanded to be purified there on the third day, so every soul is purified from all the filth of its offenses if it believes that Christ the Lord was raised from the dead on the third day. Such a person will also be clean on the seventh day, that is, when the kingdom of the saints arrives with the Lord, and blessed and joyful will receive a share in that heavenly kingdom.

But whoever has not been sprinkled—that is, whoever has not been fortified by faith in this grace—will perish from the kingdom of the Holy of Holies [Col. 0403C] and from the people of the faithful.

The tabernacle is commanded to be sprinkled seven times with the blood of this heifer because there are seven charisms of the Holy Spirit, distributed through Christ’s blood among the peoples of the Church, through which they are cleansed from every offense, as the Apostle says: “You have now been washed in the blood of Christ and in his Passion.”

The fact that the heifer is burned with its hide and bones, and that the paschal lamb is likewise burned so that its bones are not broken, shows that the legs of the body of the Lord Jesus Christ were not to be broken in the Passion, as the Evangelist testifies.

Morally, however, the red cow, whose ashes are the purification of the people, cannot be slain and offered at the Lord’s altar except by one who has not performed earthly works, has not drawn the yoke of sin, and has not been bound by the chains of sins.

Now, after the spies and the cluster, after the destruction of the proud and the priestly censer, and after the flowering staff and the sprinkling of the burned heifer, let us return to the stations.

[Col. 0403D] The sixteenth station is at Ramoth, which in Latin is translated “division of the pomegranate.” It signifies the Church, which, like a pomegranate, covers many seeds with a single rind, enclosing the whole multitude of believers in the unity of faith.

The seventeenth station is at Libnah, which in Latin is translated “brick.” We read that the Egyptian people groaned while making bricks. From this we learn that on the journey of this life we now grow and now diminish as we pass from one state to another, and that, after the ecclesiastical order, we often migrate back to brick—that is, to carnal works.

The eighteenth station is at Rissah, which is translated “bridles.” For if, after making progress, we again descend to muddy works, we must be bridled and directed by the restraints of the Scriptures, lest we run astray and headlong.

The nineteenth station is at Kehelathah, which is interpreted as “Church,” so that the wandering steps of those who run may be drawn back by bridles to the Church [Col. 0404A] and may hasten to enter again through the gates they had previously left.

The twentieth station is at Mount Shepher, which is interpreted as “beauty,” that is, Christ. See what bridles accomplish: they draw us away from vices, introduce us to the choirs of virtues, and make us dwell on Christ, the most beautiful mountain. Concerning it, it is written: “Come, let us ascend the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. 2:3).

The twenty-first station is at Arad, which is translated “miracle.” See how beautiful is the order of virtues: after the bridles, they are admitted into the Church. After dwelling there, we ascend to Christ’s mountain, where, being placed, we marvel at what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2:9).

The twenty-second station is at Makheloth, which is translated “assembly,” that is, Church. In it the multitude of believers is gathered, according to what is written: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1).

[Col. 0404B] The twenty-third station is at Tahath, which is interpreted as “terror.” When someone comes to the Church, ascends Christ the most beautiful mountain, and confesses Christ’s greatness in astonishment and wonder, let him then add fear, which is the guardian of blessedness, so that he does not think arrogantly, because “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6).

The twenty-fourth station is at Tarah, which some translate as “malice” or “pasture.” This is appropriately referred either to the overseers of the Churches or to the guardianship of the soul, so that each person who possesses fear may be vigilant lest the devil attempt to enter the sheepfolds—that is, the Churches—through the various openings of vices.

The twenty-fifth station is at Methca, which is translated as “sweetness.” You have ascended to the heights of the Father, admired the choirs of virtues, feared ruin, and cast down those lying in wait. Immediately the sweet fruit of your labor follows, so that you may rightly say: “How sweet are your utterances to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103).

The twenty-sixth station is at Heshmonah, which in Latin signifies “haste,” namely, so that, after tasting the sweet fruits of labor, we may not be content with rest and idleness, but hasten again toward higher things, forget what lies behind, and stretch ourselves toward what is ahead (Phil. 3:13).

The twenty-seventh station is at Moseroth, which is interpreted as “bonds” or “discipline,” namely, so that we may proceed with hurried step to teachers, wear down their thresholds, and consider their precepts, virtue, and the mysteries of the Scriptures to be eternal bonds.

These are Christ’s bonds, concerning which one reads in the Church, or in Isaiah: “Exalted men shall pass over to you and shall be your servants; they shall walk behind you, bound with bonds” (Isa. 45:14). There are also the devil’s bonds, which Samson broke and thereby conquered his enemies. Of such bonds the Prophet says: “You have broken my bonds; to you I shall sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115:7).

[Col. 0404D] The twenty-eighth station is at Bene-jaakan, which by interpretation is translated “sons of necessity” or “sons of gnashing.” Who are these sons of necessity? The psalm itself teaches us: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 28:1). What necessity is so great that it is imposed upon the unwilling?

When you have been instructed in the divine Scriptures and have learned their laws and testimonies, which are the bonds of truth, you will contend with adversaries, bind them, and lead them captive in chains. From former enemies and captives you will make them children of God, so that you may suddenly say with Zion: “I was barren and did not give birth; I was exiled and captive—who raised these? I was abandoned and alone. And where were these?” (Isa. 49:21).

The interpretation “sons of gnashing” refers to this meaning: out of fear of punishment and of that place where there is “weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 13:42), the crowds of believers submit their necks to Christ the Lord and abandon the devil’s bonds.

[Col. 0405A] The twenty-ninth station is at Mount Gadgad. Gadgad is interpreted as “messenger,” or “girding,” or indeed “cutting.” For we cannot otherwise make disciples and believers the sons of necessity of their teachers unless we kill their most savage instructors. In their slaughter, let our hand not spare in drawing a shoulder or the tip of an ear from the lion’s mouth.

Concerning “messenger” and “girding,” this may briefly be said: we should propose great incentives to virtue to the sons of necessity when we announce to them the rewards of the future and teach those who are girded how to rebel. Whatever a teacher does concerning these three things, he stands upon the mountain.

The thirtieth station is at Jotbathah, which is interpreted as “goodness,” and this is Christ.

The thirty-first station is at Hebronah, which is interpreted as “passage,” that is, the world, concerning which the Apostle says: “The form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7:31). Coming here, God’s saints desire to pass on to better things. [Col. 0405B] Of them the Psalmist sings: “Nor did those who passed by say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’” (Ps. 128:8).

The thirty-second station is at Ezion-geber, which is translated “on the wood of a man.” These woods of a man may signify the multitude of the nations, represented by groves and all kinds of trees. Up to this point, the wilderness of Paran contains eighteen stations, which are set out in the catalogue of the preceding journey.

The thirty-third station is in the wilderness of Zin. This is Kadesh (Num. 33:36). Zin is interpreted as “holy” by antiphrasis, like a grove when it gives no light, or “war,” though it is in fact dreadful.

## CHAPTER XVII. Miriam’s Death

At this station Miriam dies and is buried. In Miriam, prophecy appears to have died; in Moses and Aaron, the end is imposed upon the Law and the Jewish priesthood [Col. 0405C]. They cannot themselves cross over into the promised land, nor lead the believing people out of the wilderness of this world, unless it is Jesus alone, God—that is, the true Savior, the Son of God.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Moses’ Hesitation at the Rock

At this place Moses offends the Lord on account of the waters of contradiction and is forbidden to cross the Jordan. Disturbed by the people’s murmuring, he strikes the rock with his staff in hesitation, as though God could not cause water to flow from the rock, although he had already done so before.

What, then, does Moses’ faith signify here, since he hesitated to bring water forth from the rock? We rightly understand this to have been a prophecy concerning Christ. Although Moses in the holy Scriptures assumes one person or another in order to signify different matters, here he was assuming the person of the Jewish people placed under the Law, and he represented it in a prophetic utterance.

[Col. 0405D] For just as Moses, striking the rock with his staff, doubted God’s power, so that people held under the Law given through Moses, fastening Christ to the wood, did not believe that he was the power of God. But just as the struck rock poured out water for the thirsty, so the wound of the Lord’s Passion became life for believers.

We have, concerning this matter, the most splendid and faithful apostolic utterance, when he spoke about it and said: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4).

Therefore God commands that this carnal apprehension concerning Christ’s divinity should die in the very height of Christ, when he commands the death of the flesh to occur through Moses’ death. For just as Christ is the rock, so Christ is also the mountain. The rock is humble strength; the mountain is lofty greatness. For just as the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ,” so God himself says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14), asserting that he himself is the mountain and that his faithful, founded in the glory of his name, are the city.

For the wisdom of the flesh lives when [Col. 0406A] Christ’s humility is despised on the cross, as though the rock had been struck. “Christ crucified is a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the nations” (1 Cor. 1:23). But the wisdom of the flesh dies when Christ the Exalted One is recognized as the height of the mountain. “To those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24).

The thirty-fourth station is at Mount Hor, in the farthest borders of Edom. There Aaron ascended at the Lord’s command and died in the fortieth year after the exodus from Egypt, in that very year when the new people was about to enter the promised land. Although on the mountain he left the priesthood to his son Eleazar, and although the Law leads those who fulfill it to the summit, that very elevation is not beyond the waters of the Jordan, but at the farthest boundaries of earthly works.

The people mourn him for thirty days. Aaron is mourned; Jesus is not mourned. In the Law there is a descent to the underworld; in the Gospel, a passage to paradise.

The Canaanite also hears that Israel has arrived [Col. 0406B] and, at the place of the spies, where they knew that the people had formerly offended, enters battle and takes Israel captive. Again a battle is fought in the same place: the victor by vow is defeated, and the defeated prevail. By this we understand that, when enemies attack us after we have been deprived of God’s help and lead us captive, we must not despair of salvation, but arm ourselves again for battle. It can happen that we conquer where we were conquered and triumph in the very place where we had previously been captives.

## CHAPTER XIX. Aaron’s Death and the Wounding by Serpents

The thirty-fifth station is at Zalmonah. The thirty-sixth station is at Punon. These two stations are not found in the historical sequence.

At them, after Aaron’s death, the Israelite people murmur against God and Moses, grow weary of the manna, and are wounded by serpents. But what does it signify that the deadly bites [Col. 0406C] of the serpents were healed when the bronze serpent was raised and looked upon, except that now, in the type of the Savior—who triumphed over the ancient iron serpent on the gallows—the poisons of the devil are overcome, so that whoever truly and plainly gazes upon the image of the Son of God and his Passion is preserved?

The Lord’s own words also signify this when he says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:14–15).

The serpent itself, which was hung on the wood, is bronze because bronze is generally more durable than the other metals. The bronze serpent was suitably hung on the wood, so that the Lord might be signified as mortal in the serpent and eternal in the bronze: thus he was shown to have died according to his humanity, yet to be like bronze according to his divinity.

Beautifully, the first station, Zalmonah, is interpreted as “little image,” because there the image of the Savior was expressed through the bronze serpent that hung on the wood. [Col. 0406D] Beautifully also, the second, Punon, is interpreted as “mouth,” because after we come to know the Passion of the Son of God, what we believe in our heart we pronounce with our mouth, reading the Apostle’s words: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

The thirty-seventh station is at Oboth, which is translated “magicians” or “python spirits.” This shows that, after the image of God displayed in the reasoning of the heart and the confession of faith uttered by the mouth, serpents and magical arts rise up to provoke us to battle. But we, surrounding our heart with vigilance, harden our ears so that we do not hear the voices of enchanters, and disregard the songs of the Sirens (Ps. 58:5–6).

The thirty-eighth station is at Iye-abarim, on the borders of Moab, which signifies “heaps of stones of those passing over,” that is, the saints hastening through this age to pass over to other stations.

## CHAPTER XX. Sihon King of the Amorites and Og King of Bashan

[Col. 0407A]

The thirty-ninth station is at Dibon-gad. At this place war is waged against Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan. Although the historical event concerning these kings is known, a spiritual meaning is also attached through the interpretations and qualities of their names.

Sihon is interpreted as “temptation of the eyes,” by which the devil is signified, for he transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14) and, through heresy and schism, falsely presents what resembles truth in order to deceive the unwary. The Amorites—that is, those who make bitter—have him as their king. For unless some imitation of truth precedes, there are no heresies that make bitter and no schisms that embitter the Church.

This king is therefore killed in each person when each one condemns imitation and loves truth.

Og, however, is interpreted as “conclusion,” while Bashan means “confusion.” For the devil always works to close the way to the Lord by setting up his idols [Col. 0407B], so that people will not believe in Christ. “Conclusion” comes first, so that the king may be followed by “confusion” as by a people: those whom he now shuts away from belief in Christ will all be confounded when Christ appears.

This station, Dibon-gad, is interpreted as “strongly understood temptation,” because, if the imitation that embitters the Church through schism or heresy is overcome, and the conclusion that closes the way of faith through sacrilege is defeated, temptation is nevertheless understood and then strongly overcome.

The fortieth station is from Dibon in Gad, at Almon-diblathaim, which is translated “contempt of cakes” or “of reproaches.” From this we learn that all the sweetness and enticements of passing pleasures in the world are to be despised and reproaches loved. If reproaches are falsely brought against us, they produce blessedness, as the Savior teaches most fully when he says: “When people reproach you, you will be blessed” (Luke 6:22).

## CHAPTER XXI. Moses’ Death

[Col. 0407C]

The forty-first station is on Mount Abarim, opposite Mount Nebo, where Moses dies and is buried after seeing the promised land. Nebo is interpreted as “conclusion,” in which the Law ends and its memory is no longer found. The grace of the Gospel, however, extends without any end: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5).

At the same time, we must consider that the dwelling of those who pass onward is situated in the mountains and still requires progress. For after many mountains we descend to the plains of Moab and the waters of the Jordan, a descent signified by their name. Nothing is more dangerous than the glory of desire, boasting, and a mind swollen with the consciousness of virtues.

## CHAPTER XXII. Balaam and Balak

[Col. 0407D]

The forty-second station is in the plains of Moab beside the Jordan, near Jericho, where they pitched their tents from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim in the plains of Moab. Since this is the forty-second and final station, let us relate how certain events took place there.

The people, sitting there, are blessed at God’s command by Balaam the diviner, whom Balak had hired, and the curse is changed into praises.

But what does it mean that this Balaam, while striving to reach his intended destination, is spoken to by the she-donkey he was riding after she saw the angel? For what is this she-donkey except the brutish Gentile people, which Balaam—that is, the seducer of idolatry—once subjected to whatever error he wished, as though it were a brute animal offering no rational resistance to repentance?

Yet this beast saw the angel of God, whom the man could not see. It both saw and reported what it saw, and it spoke, so that we might recognize that in later times, at the advent of the great angel of God, that Gentile people would, after its hardness of stupidity had been changed and its tongues released for God, speak out. [Col. 0408A] Though formerly subject to unbelief, it would burst forth into the voice of faith and confession.

This may also be understood of our flesh. Often the flesh, touched by affliction and scourged, points out God to its own mind, whom the mind itself, presiding over the flesh, did not see. In this way it impedes the anxiety of the spirit that desires to make progress in this world, as though traveling on a road, until the invisible one who meets it becomes known.

Hence Peter rightly says: “The mute beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s madness” (2 Pet. 2:16). A madman is rebuked by the mute beast of burden when an exalted mind is reminded by afflicted flesh of the good of humility, which it ought to retain.

But Balaam did not obtain the gift of this rebuke because, proceeding to curse, he changed his voice, not his mind. He gave Balak the advice that he should place women in a house of prostitution and altars before their doors, so that when the children of Israel came, they would first sacrifice to idols and then enter to the women. [Col. 0408B] Hence Israel commits fornication with the daughters of Midian.

But what does it mean that this Balaam concludes by sound reasoning that the people of God could be deceived, giving counsel that, on the side where he knew the children of Israel were weak, destructive snares should be laid for them? He did not doubt that, once women were offered to them in abundance, they would immediately fall into the ruin of fornication, because he knew that their desires were corrupt.

Thus spiritual wickedness, in the figure of Balaam, tests each of us with crafty malignity, laying insidious snares especially through those affections of the soul in which it perceives that we are diseased. For example, when it sees that the rational faculties of our soul have been corrupted, it attempts to deceive us by that very means.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Phinehas the Priest

But Phinehas the priest, moved by zeal in order to appease the Lord’s fury, seized Zimri, who had entered in to the prostitute, and pierced them both with a dagger. He signified [Col. 0408C] through the cross of Christ not only idolatry but also every carnal affection or lust of the first age, and showed that God is then appeased when the desire of the flesh is extinguished.

After this the people are again counted, and the Levites are counted as well, so that, after the first carnal people have been killed, a new people of God may be enrolled, one that will cross the Jordan through baptism and receive the promise of the heavenly inheritance.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Number of the People

The fact that six hundred thousand armed men are counted as having gone out from Egypt, yet of these only two entered the promised land, demonstrates figuratively that many pass through baptism to faith, but very few reach the heavenly homeland. This corresponds to the figure in the Gospel in which many are called but few are found chosen (Matt. 20:16).

The fact that only two enter may refer either to those who receive the promises of the heavenly kingdom from both peoples, or to those who are predestined to eternal blessedness through the two ways of action and contemplation.

[Col. 0408D]

## CHAPTER XXV. The Five Sons of Zelophehad
The five daughters of Zelophehad then appeal, and by God’s judgment receive an inheritance among their brothers; nor is the people of the Law excluded from possession of the Gospel. Then Jesus succeeds Moses on the mountain and learns what ought to be offered spiritually in the Church; for the Gospel succeeds the Law, and there the Law admonishes that its commandments must be carried out, while grace fulfills them.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The kinds of offerings.

First, what ought to be offered on each individual day; then what is offered on the Sabbath, on account of the hope of eternal rest; what is offered at the new moons, for the renewal of life; what is offered at Passover, when through baptism we are buried with Christ, as though passing from the dead into newness of life; and what is offered at Pentecost, on account of the grace of the Holy Spirit and the forgiveness of the remission of sins; what is offered at the new moon of the seventh month; and what is offered on the fast of the tenth day of that same month. What is offered at the Feast of Booths, when the tabernacles are erected, on the fifteenth day of the aforesaid month.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The death of Balaam.

Thereafter war is waged against the Midianites, and Balaam the diviner dies; in his death the error of faithlessness is slain by the wood of the cross. Then the spoil taken from Amalek is divided, and an offering from it is made of souls in the tabernacle of God.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The sons of Reuben and Gad.

[Col. 0410A]

After this the sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh receive their possession near the Jordan, and do not wish to have an inheritance in the land of promise. They signify that those whom the many entanglements of the world occupy have no desire whatsoever for the dwelling of the heavenly homeland.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The destruction of idols.

Thereafter it is commanded that the people destroy the idols in the holy land and that none of the former inhabitants be spared, signifying that, when through faith we enter the holy land of promise, we should extinguish every vice along with idolatry.

[Col. 0409]

# QUESTIONS ON DEUTERONOMY

[Col. 0409B]

**DISCIPLE.**—What does Deuteronomy write, according to the truth of the history?

**TEACHER.**—In Deuteronomy, which is the second Law, there are recounted the things that Moses spoke to the people at Pharan, Oboth, Laban, and Aseroth, up to Kadesh-barnea: namely, commands and promises, curses for sins, and promises of blessedness. There Moses sings his song; there he gives a blessing to the children of Israel; and there, having seen the land of promise, he dies and is buried.

Some of the Hebrews, however, count only four books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, or Numbers. They say that Deuteronomy is a repetition of those same books, and, as it were, a kind of exercise in the Law, for this reason alone: the other four contain the particular causes of the events that happened, whereas this one contains them all.

## CHAPTER I. What is signified by the statement that Deuteronomy was written by Moses in eleven days.

[Col. 0409C]

The book of Deuteronomy is a repetition of the preceding four books of the Law. For while those books contain their particular subjects, this one nevertheless repeats everything. It too contains countless mysteries of its own, from which I have woven together a few things to be committed to memory as an exercise for the reader.

Deuteronomy is called the second giving of the Law, which signifies the Gospel. At its beginning, therefore, we must note what is indicated by the statement that Deuteronomy was written by Moses in eleven days: namely, the fall of the Jewish people in the Gospel through transgression of the commandments of the Decalogue.

## CHAPTER II. On the forty years laboriously completed by the children of Israel.

What, then, did the forty years signify, after which the children of Israel, having completed their labor, entered the land of promise? Through these forty years the whole period of the world is signified, during which the Church lives amid labors and dangerous temptations, hoping through patience for what it does not see, until it reaches the promised homeland of eternal happiness.

For this reason the Lord also fasted for forty days and was tempted for forty nights in the wilderness. His body, which is the Church, must necessarily endure temptations and labors in this world, until that time comes when, after the temptations, it receives consolations.

Moreover, the fact that Israel’s clothing was not corrupted by any wear during all those years in the wilderness, and that the dead skin of their sandals lasted so long without blemish, can symbolize the incorruptibility of bodies, where what is corruptible will remain without corruption.

[Col. 0410B]

## CHAPTER III. On not planting a tree beside the altar of God.

“You shall not plant any tree beside the altar of God, nor plant a grove in the land.” It is said, accordingly, that a grove must not be planted in the temple. Groves consist of leafy and fruitless trees, planted solely for the delight of the eyes.

Such also are the Gentiles, who arrange their reasoning with verbal ornament, do not turn themselves away from vices, but delight others and persuade them through this kind of seduction. We, however, in accordance with God’s command, do not plant a grove beside the altar of God if, around the faith of the Lord, we compose nothing fruitless in words and nothing alluring to secular ears, but hold solely to the knowledge of preaching in the purity of truth.

The Apostle avoided planting this grove in his preaching when he said: “We speak not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit and of power” (1 Cor. II, 13).

[Col. 0410C]

## CHAPTER IV. On removing the foreskin of fruit-bearing trees.

“When you have entered the land and planted fruit-bearing trees in it, you shall remove their foreskins; their fruit-buds shall be unclean for you, and you shall not eat from them.”

Fruit-bearing trees, then, are works fruitful in virtues. We remove the foreskins of the trees when, suspicious of the weakness of our very beginning, we do not approve the beginnings of our works.

We regard the fruits that bud forth as unclean and do not adapt them to our food, because when the beginnings of a good work are praised, it is fitting that this should not nourish the mind of the one performing it, lest, while the praise received is pleasantly enjoyed, the fruit of the good work be eaten before its proper time.

## CHAPTER V. On not working with the firstborn of an ox and not shearing the firstborn of sheep.

[Col. 0410D]

“You shall not work with the firstborn of an ox, and you shall not shear the firstborn of sheep.”

To work with the firstborn of an ox means to display the beginnings of a good way of life in public activity. To shear the firstborn of sheep means to strip our good beginnings from the covering of their concealment and expose them to human eyes.

We are therefore forbidden to work with the firstborn of an ox and restrained from shearing the firstborn of sheep, because, even if we begin to practice something vigorous, we ought not to display it openly too soon. Rather, when our simple life begins whatever is innocent, it should not abandon it to the coverings of its secrecy, as is fitting, nor display it to human eyes as though its fleece had been removed.

Let the firstborn of oxen and sheep therefore be useful only for divine sacrifices, so that, if we happen to begin something innocent, we may sacrifice it in honor of the innermost Judge upon the altar of the heart. Without doubt, he receives it all the more willingly the more it is hidden from human beings and is not stained by any desire for praise.

Often, however, the beginnings of a way of life are still mixed with carnal living. Therefore they ought not to become known too quickly, lest, when the good things that please are praised, the mind, deceived by its praise, be unable to detect the evils hidden within them.

[Col. 0411A]

## CHAPTER VI. On not plowing with an ox and an ass together.

“You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together.”

By the name of the ox is understood the people established through circumcision and placed under the yoke of the Law; by the ass, the people of the Gentiles, belonging to the Gospel.

He plows with an ox and an ass together who receives the Gospel in such a way that he does not abandon the ceremonies of Jewish superstitions, which preceded it in shadow and image.

Again, sometimes the life of those who work well is signified by the ox, and the senseless folly of fools by the ass. What, then, does “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together” mean? It is as though he said: Do not join a fool with a wise person in preaching, lest, through the one who cannot fulfill the task, you hinder the one who is capable.

If necessary, anyone can yoke an ox and an ass together without damaging the work. But a wise person and a fool should not become companions so that one commands and the other obeys, nor so that they proclaim the word of God together with equal authority; this cannot occur without scandal.

## CHAPTER VII. On not muzzling the ox that treads out the grain.

“You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading.”

It has been said that by the name of the ox the life of each person who works is expressed.

[Col. 0411C]

The Apostle Paul says in one place, reproaching and grieving that no one had shared with him in the matter of giving and receiving, except that elsewhere he openly explained the matter, saying: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things?” (1 Cor. IX, 11). This signifies: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading.”

Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (1 Tim. V, 18). Scripture therefore wishes material things to be supplied to teachers, from whom spiritual things are received, since whoever occupies preachers [with preaching] prevents them from providing the necessities of life for themselves.

## CHAPTER VIII. On not boiling a kid in its mother’s milk.

“You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.”

Here the kid is introduced as a figure of the sinner. Therefore the sinner must not be boiled in his mother’s milk—that is, he must not be cleansed by the moderate and tender disciplines of the Church. Rather, his sins must be boiled away by harsher commands, since his crimes are great, so that the one who has destroyed himself through the allurements of wantonness may redeem himself through stronger discipline.

[Col. 0411D]

## CHAPTER IX. On not wearing a garment woven of wool and linen.

“You shall not wear a garment woven of wool and linen.”

By wool simplicity is signified; by linen, subtlety. Indeed, a garment made from linen and wool conceals the linen within and displays the wool on the surface.

Therefore one wears a garment woven of wool and linen who, under the language of innocence, conceals within a subtlety of malice.

This is according to the moral sense. In the higher allegory, however, we are forbidden to mix wool or purple with linen garments—that is, to live disorderly and to wish to combine different kinds of profession: for example, for a religious woman to possess the ornament of marriage, or for one who married because she could not remain continent to display the appearance of virginity. This is sin in every respect.

And so it is whenever something inappropriate from a different kind or religious state is woven into anyone’s life. What was then figured in garments is now made manifest in conduct.

## CHAPTER X. On not taking the upper or lower millstone as a pledge.

“You shall not take the upper or lower millstone as a pledge.”

Sometimes we use “take” to mean “carry off.” Hence birds eager to seize are called *accipitres*, “hawks.” The Apostle Paul likewise says: “For you endure it if someone devours you, if someone takes” (2 Cor. XI, 20), as though he were saying: “If someone seizes.”

The pledge is the debtor’s confession. A pledge is taken from a debtor when the confession of sin is already obtained from the sinner.

The upper and lower millstone are hope and fear. Hope lifts upward, while fear presses the heart downward. Yet the upper and lower millstones are necessarily joined to one another, so that one is useless without the other.

Therefore hope and fear must continually be joined in the sinner’s mind, because repentance hopes for mercy in vain if it does not also fear justice; and it fears justice in vain if it does not also trust in mercy.

The taking of the upper millstone as a pledge is therefore forbidden, because the preacher must arrange his preaching to the sinner with such care that, neither by abandoning hope does he remove fear, nor by removing hope does he leave the sinner in fear alone.

He removes the upper millstone if he says to a weeping sinner, “You will not receive forgiveness for what you have done.” He removes the lower one if he flatters the sinner through deception and says: “Do evil as much as you wish without fear, for God is merciful and ready to forgive.”

The two millstones are held properly, however, when hope is furnished with fear and fear is accompanied by hope.

## CHAPTER XI. On not rejecting the Egyptian.

[Col. 0412C]

“You shall not reject the Egyptian, because you were an immigrant in his land.”

Although, when renouncing the world, we avoid the Egyptian land—that is, our former worldly way of life or desire—nevertheless, while we remain subject to the necessities of the present world, we do not utterly destroy the Egyptian nation.

Although we separate ourselves from it through discernment, we do not think about superfluities, but, according to the Apostle, are content with daily food and clothing. This is what was figuratively commanded in the Law: “You shall not reject the Egyptian.”

## CHAPTER XII. On not having different weights in one’s bag.

“You shall not have different weights in your bag, a greater and a lesser; you shall not have in your house a larger and a smaller measure. You shall have a just and true weight, and your measure shall be equal and true, so that you may live for a long time upon the land.”

The same legislator also forbids this in Leviticus, and Solomon likewise gives a corresponding judgment on the matter: “A large weight and a small one, and double measures, both are unclean before God; and whoever uses them will be fettered by his own devices” (Prov. XX, 10).

Therefore we must strive not only in the bodily but also in the spiritual sense, so that we have neither different weights in our hearts nor double measures in the house of our conscience.
