That is, we must not ourselves undertake those things that are weighed by a stricter rule with a more relaxed indulgence, while burdening those to whom we preach the word of the Lord with stricter and heavier commands than we are able to bear.

When we do this, we are, as it were, weighing or measuring the reward and fruit of the Lord’s commands with a different weight and measure. For if we administer them in one way to ourselves and in another way to our brothers, the Lord rightly reproves us because we have different balances or double measures, in accordance with Solomon’s judgment: “A double weight is an abomination to the Lord, and a deceitful balance is not good in his sight” (ibid., 23).

[Col. 0413A]

## CHAPTER XIII. On the testimony of three being valid.

“One witness shall not stand against another, but every word shall stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses.”

Although historically this divine judgment must be observed, nevertheless, when we contend against any impious persons or heretics, we must call the holy Scriptures to witness. Our opinions and testimony have no credibility without these witnesses.

Accordingly, for proof and for a firm statement, I bring forward two witnesses: the New and the Old Testament. I also bring forward three: the Gospel, the Prophet, and the Apostle. Thus every word will stand.

## CHAPTER XIV. On taking the wife of one’s brother.

[Col. 0413B]

The command that a brother should take his brother’s wife in order to raise up offspring not for himself but for his brother, and that he should call whatever was born from her by his brother’s name—what else does this prefigure in a figure except that every preacher of the Gospel ought to work in the Church in such a way that he raises up seed for his deceased brother, that is, for Christ, because Christ died for us, and that what is raised up should bear his name?

Finally, the Apostle fulfills this—not carnally in the preceding signification, but spiritually in its completed truth—when he recalls that he begot through the Gospel those whom he raised up in Christ Jesus, and reproves them because they wished to belong to Paul. “Was Paul,” he says, “crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. I, 13). It is as though he were saying: “I begot you for your deceased brother; you are called Christians, not Paulians.”

But whoever, having been chosen by the Church, refuses the ministry of evangelizing is deservedly and rightly despised by the Church herself. This is what is meant when he is commanded to spit in his face—not, certainly, without the sign of this disgrace: he is deprived of one shoe, so that he may not belong to those to whom the Apostle himself says: “And having your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. VI, 18).

And concerning these he says through the Prophet: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things!” (Isa. LII, 7).

For whoever holds the evangelical faith in such a way that he can benefit both himself and the Church, yet refuses to do so, is rightly understood to be barefoot in both feet. But whoever thinks that, because he believes, he has taken sufficient care of himself, while avoiding concern for winning others, loses, as though in disgrace, the shoe of one foot.

[Col. 0413C]

## CHAPTER XV. On the fearful and timid man who is not to enter battle.

“A fearful man and one fainthearted shall not go forth to battle. Let him go and return to his house, lest he make the hearts of his brothers fearful, just as he himself has been terrified by fear.”

By these words he teaches that no one who still fears stripping himself of earthly works can undertake the practice of the profession of contemplation or spiritual warfare, lest he return again to weakness of mind and, by his example, turn others back from evangelical perfection and establish them unfaithfully in error.

Such men are therefore commanded to withdraw from the battle and return to their houses, because no one can fight the Lord’s battles with a divided heart. A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.

Such persons ought not even to undertake the beginning of renunciation; it is better for them to remain in the active life than, by timidly following contemplation, to involve themselves in greater danger. For it is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill.

Likewise, the one who has taken a wife, or who has planted a vineyard, as though they were the propagation of children, is excluded from such military service. A servant of a wife cannot serve in the divine army.

As the Apostle says: “He who is with a wife is concerned with how he may please his wife, and is divided” (1 Cor. VII, 33). Nor can anyone devote himself to contemplation who is still fixed upon the delight of the flesh. “No one,” says the Apostle, “who serves as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Tim. II, 4).

## CHAPTER XVI. On the destruction of the seven nations that the Lord delivered to Israel.

“When the Lord your God has brought you into the land that you are entering to possess, and has destroyed before you many nations—the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite—seven nations much greater in number than you and stronger, and the Lord has delivered them to you, you shall strike them down to complete destruction.”

These seven nations are the seven principal vices, which every spiritual soldier is admonished to overcome and utterly destroy through the grace of God.

The reason they are said to be greater in number is that there are more vices than virtues. Yet they are counted as seven nations in the catalogue; in the account of their conquest, however, they are mentioned without a number. Thus it is said: “And you have destroyed many nations before you.”

The people of carnal passions that proceeds from the tinder and root of this sevenfold source of vices is more numerous than Israel. From gluttony arise feasting and drunkenness; from fornication, obscene speech, buffoonery, mockery, and foolish talk; from avarice, lying, deceit, thefts, perjuries, the pursuit of shameful gain, false testimony, violence, inhumanity, and rapacity; from anger, murders, shouting, and indignation; from sadness, resentment, faintheartedness, bitterness, and despair; from acedia, idleness, drowsiness, intrusiveness, restlessness, wandering, instability of mind and body, talkativeness, and curiosity; from vainglory, contentions, heresies, boasting, and presumptuous innovations; from pride, contempt, envy, disobedience, blasphemy, murmuring, detraction, and many other similar things.

Although these are far greater in number than the virtues, when those seven principal vices from whose nature these things proceed have been conquered, all the others immediately subside and, together with them, are destroyed in perpetual annihilation.

That these pestilences are also stronger, we plainly perceive from the very struggle against our nature. The pleasure of carnal passions fights more forcefully in our members than the pursuit of virtues, which are acquired only through the greatest contrition of heart and body.

We are commanded, however, to possess the territories of these destructive nations in a salutary manner. This is understood as follows. Every vice has its own station in our heart. But if the vices are overcome by the spiritual peoples—that is, by the virtues fighting against them—the place that the spirit of lust or fornication had occupied in our heart will thereafter be possessed by chastity; the place that fury had seized will be reclaimed by patience; the place that sadness, working death, had occupied, salutary strength will begin to exclude [or cultivate, *excolere*], and joy filled with gladness will possess it; the place that acedia had devastated, strength begins to cultivate; the place that pride had trampled, humility begins to cultivate.

Thus, when each vice has been expelled, the children of Israel—that is, souls who see God—will possess their places, meaning their contrary effects.

## CHAPTER XVII. What is signified by the fact that, when the Lord spoke with Abraham about future events, he is read to have counted not seven but ten nations.

When the Lord spoke with Abraham about future events, he is read to have counted not seven nations but ten, whose land was promised to be given to his offspring. This number is most clearly completed by adding the idolatry of the Gentiles, the blasphemy of the Jews, and the error of heretics.

Before the knowledge of God and the grace of baptism, either the impious multitude of the Gentiles or the blasphemous multitude of the Jews is subjected to these powers, as long as one dwells in intellectual Egypt.

But if someone renounces it, leaves it, and through the grace of God reaches the spiritual wilderness, then, freed from the assault of three nations, he undertakes battle only against the seven counted by Moses.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the woman captured in war.

“If,” he says, “you go out to war against your enemies and see a woman beautiful in appearance and desire her, shave all the hair of her head, cut her nails, clothe her in mourning garments, and she shall sit in her house mourning her father and mother and her paternal household; after thirty days she shall be your wife.”

Let the Jews say how these practices are observed among them. What is the reason, what is the meaning, of shaving the woman and cutting her nails? Let us suppose, for the sake of argument, that the man said to have found her came upon her in such a condition that she had neither hair nor nails. What would he have that, according to the Law, could be removed?

For us, however, whose warfare is spiritual and whose weapons are not carnal but powerful through God: if we find a beautiful woman—that is, a soul created beautiful by God—in a Gentile way of life, and wish to join her to the body of Christ, then, having laid aside the worship of idolatry, she is clothed in the mourning garments of repentance and mourns her father and mother—that is, every memory of the world and its carnal allurements.

Then, with the razor of the word of God and instruction, all the sin of her unbelief, which is dead and empty, is shaved away. This is what the hair of the woman’s head and her nails signify.

Only then, purified by the water of the saving bath, is she joined to the holy people of God: when she has nothing dead upon her head and nothing upon her hands from those things that are regarded as dead through unbelief, so that she carries nothing unclean or dead in either her understanding or her actions.

The command that she be taken as a wife after thirty days signifies faith and works through the numbers three and ten. She is therefore rightly joined through faith in the Trinity and through the work of the Law.

But whatever Israelite soul—namely, one adhering to the body of Christ—to him without blemish, in sincerity of faith and purity of actions. [The sentence is incomplete in the source.]

Others have thought that this woman beautiful in appearance signifies some rational discipline, found wisely expressed among the Gentiles. When we discover such a discipline, we must first remove and cut away from it all the uncleanness of its superstition, and then take it up in the pursuit of truth.

For none of the disciplines of the Gentiles is wholly clean, since among unbelievers there is no wisdom to which some uncleanness or superstition is not joined.

## CHAPTER XIX. What is signified by the axe falling from its handle.

What does it signify that the Lord commanded through Moses, saying: “If someone goes with his friend simply into the forest to cut wood, and the wood of the axe escapes his hand, and the iron, having slipped from the handle, strikes and kills his friend, he shall flee to one of the cities mentioned above and live, lest perhaps the near kinsman of the one whose blood has been shed pursue him, driven by grief, and overtake him and strike his life”?

We go into the forest with a friend whenever we turn our attention to observing the faults of our subjects. We cut wood innocently when we remove the vices of sinners with a pious intention.

But the axe escapes the hand when correction extends itself into harshness beyond what is necessary. The iron springs from the handle when a harsher word than the correction requires goes beyond its proper limit. It strikes and kills the friend when, through an insult that has been uttered, it kills the hearer’s spirit of love.

The mind of the person corrected suddenly collapses into hatred if immoderate reproof subjects it to more than it should.

But the one who strikes the wood carelessly and destroys his neighbor must flee to three cities, so that, defended in one of them, he may live. If he turns to the laments of repentance and hides himself within the unity of the sacrament under hope, faith, and charity, he is not held guilty of the murder he committed.

When the near kinsman of the slain finds him, he does not kill him, because when the strict Judge comes—the one who joined himself to us through the fellowship of nature—he will certainly not demand guilt from the one whom hope, faith, and charity have hidden beneath his pardon.

## CHAPTER XX. On pollution in a nocturnal dream.

“If there is among you a man who has been polluted by a nocturnal dream, he shall go outside the camp and shall not return until he has washed himself with water at evening; after sunset he shall return to the camp.”

A nocturnal dream is a hidden temptation through which something shameful is conceived in the heart by a dark thought, although it is not completed through bodily action.

The man polluted by a nocturnal dream is therefore commanded to go outside the camp, because it is fitting that one who has been polluted by an unclean thought should consider himself unworthy of the fellowship of all the faithful. He should place the merit of his fault before his eyes and despise himself in comparison with the reputation of the good.

To go outside the camp after being polluted is for one struggling with a shameful assault to despise himself when compared with the continent.

He is washed with water at evening when, seeing his failing, he turns to the lamentation of repentance, so that by his tears he may wash away everything that hidden pollution accuses as hostile.

But he should return to the camp after sunset: when the heat of temptation has cooled, it is necessary that he again take confidence concerning the good of fellowship.

After water, when the sun has set, he returns to the camp, because after the laments of repentance, when the flame of illicit thought has grown cold, the mind is restored to presume upon the merits of the faithful, so that he no longer considers himself far removed from the others, rejoicing that he has been cleansed through the affection of his innermost ardor.

## CHAPTER XXI. On carrying a stake.

Moreover, Moses commands the Israelite people that, when they go out for the necessities of nature, they should carry a stake on their belt and, after digging the earth, cover what has been done.

For, weighed down by the burden of corruptible nature, certain superfluous thoughts erupt from the womb of our mind like the burdens of the belly.

But we must carry a stake beneath our belt, so that, always girded for reproving ourselves, we may have a sharp goad close at hand. It should continually pierce the soil of our mind with the pain of repentance and conceal what bursts forth from us with a foul odor.

## CHAPTER XXII. On applying forty lashes to those who offend.

[Col. 0416D]

The fact that he commanded offenders to be reproved with forty lashes in proportion to the measure of their sin has already been explained: through the number forty, the figure of the present age is signified, in which the Church, spread throughout the four quarters of the world, lives under the Decalogue of the Law.

We are beaten with the number forty when, in this present age, we are scourged by the lashes of repentance. Therefore every sinner ought to be worn down by temporal lashes, so that he may be found purified at the judgment.

“Blessed is the man whom the Lord corrects.” No eternal punishment will be able to afflict those whom the discipline of repentance has struck here. For if we are beaten here on account of our sins, there we are found without sin.

[Col. 0417]

# QUESTIONS ON THE BOOK OF JESUS SON OF NUN

## CHAPTER I. On the death of Moses and the leadership of Jesus son of Nun.

[Col. 0417A]

After the death of Moses, therefore, the Lord speaks to Joshua, saying: “Moses my servant is dead. Rise and cross the Jordan, you and all the people, into the land that I will give to the children of Israel.”

Moses is therefore dead; the Law is dead. The legal commandments have now ceased, and Jesus—that is, Christ the Savior, the Son of God—holds the leadership. He introduces the people into the land concerning which the Lord says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. V, 5).

## CHAPTER II. On the two spies and the prostitute Rahab.

This Jesus, son of Nun, sends two spies to the city of Jericho, and they are received by the prostitute Rahab.

This Jesus, leader of the people, reveals the Lord Christ both by his name and by his deed. Jericho, however, is the world, to which the Lord Christ sent the two Testaments to examine the conduct of human beings.

For, before the arrival of his judgment, in order to test more fully the faith of believers or the obstinacy of rebels, he sent the Law and the Gospel as two spies.

Rahab holds the type of the Church, which has been gathered from foreign and alien nations and which formerly prostituted itself in the desires of the flesh through idols.

Concerning such people the Lord says: “They go before you into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XXI).

She alone therefore receives the Lord’s Testaments and faithfully preserves them. She does not betray her guests at all; rather, she chooses to endanger herself, provided that she may preserve them unharmed and safe.

She firmly believes that the world will fall just as that city did. For herself and for the salvation of all her people, she makes a covenant with the Lord’s Testaments. In her house she places scarlet, that is, the sign of blood.

If anyone is found outside her, he will in no way escape the world’s ruin and the conflagration of the age.

## CHAPTER III. On the crossing of the ark and the division of the Jordan.

[Col. 0417C]

The people cross the Jordan with the ark of the covenant. But what does it mean that, while the same ark of the covenant is being led across the Jordan by the priests and Levites, the crowd follows, and, while the river’s water stands piled up, the people proceed along a harmless path?

All these things are fulfilled through a mystical operation among the peoples of the Church.

When someone comes to the font of baptism and, with the priestly and Levitical order standing by, is initiated into the mystical sacraments, then through baptism, as through the streams of the Jordan, he enters by the ministry of the priests and obtains the land of the heavenly promise.

The fact that part of the river’s waters, which recoiled backward, remains in sweetness, while another part flowed into the sea’s bitter whirlpool, signifies the variety among those who are baptized. For among all who are baptized, some preserve the sweetness of heavenly grace that they have received, while others are changed into the bitterness of sins.

[Col. 0417D]

The fact that the priestly and Levitical order shows the way to the people of God signifies priestly teaching. They teach the people to go out from Egypt—that is, from the errors of the world—and to cross through the vast wilderness—that is, through the temptations of the age.

The fact that the priestly and Levitical order attends the ark of the covenant, in which the Law is carried, plainly indicates that they themselves are to enlighten the people.

## CHAPTER IV. On the two half-tribes armed and preceding Israel.

The two half-tribes that received land from Moses beyond the Jordan, leaving their wives and children behind, crossed over with their brothers and offered them assistance in fighting until they themselves also obtained their inheritance.

Those who receive an inheritance beyond the Jordan through Moses and advance armed and girded with their brothers are understood here as those from the former people who first obtained the inheritance of the Law. Hence they are all understood to be firstborn.

Reuben is the firstborn of Jacob by Leah. Gad is the firstborn of the same man by Zilpah. Manasseh is the firstborn of Joseph, born of the Egyptian daughter of the priest Potiphera.

In these firstborn, therefore, those from the earlier people are figuratively signified who pleased God through the Law. They do not rest, but rise ready to aid their brothers.

When we labor in the contest of this life and have a struggle against hostile powers, those who were justified through the Law before Christ’s coming come to our aid.

For we have seen Isaiah and Jeremiah, girded and ready, wounding the fiercest enemies of our heart with the arrows of their books.

Daniel too girds himself for our aid when he instructs and warns us about the kingdom of Christ and the future deception of Antichrist.

Ezekiel is also present, marking out heavenly mysteries for us in the fourfold circles of the wheels.

Hosea also teaches the companies of the army in pairs, and they precede us with their loins girded in the truth that they preach, for our assistance.

These strong men therefore fight together with us until we attain the homeland of the heavenly promise.

## CHAPTER V. On the twelve stones.

«Accordingly, when the children of Israel crossed the Jordan, they took twelve stones from the middle of the river and set them up as a testimony.»

Immediately afterward follows the type of the second circumcision, to signify to us that, when we rise from the bath, we ought to gather for ourselves the most steadfast examples of apostolic life, whose testimony we may always behold for the imitation of virtue.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Second Circumcision

«After crossing the Jordan, Jesus came to Gilgal, and there he was commanded to make flint knives for himself and to circumcise the children of Israel a second time.»

Let the Jews inquire how anyone can be circumcised a second time with a fleshly circumcision. For one who has been circumcised once has nothing left that can be removed a second time. But for us, for whom the law is spiritual, these matters are appropriately explained.

We say, then, that the first circumcision took place through the law in Egypt. But if someone passes from the law through the baptism of the Jordan to the Gospel, then he receives a second, spiritual circumcision through the Rock, who is Christ. Thus, cleansed by such a circumcision, he is free from the reproaches of Egypt—that is, from the enticements of bodily vices.

The name of the place, Gilgal, which is interpreted as “revelation,” shows that, while anyone walks through the desert of this life in the foreskin of unbelief, his eyes are blinded.

Let us consider what follows as well. After the circumcision of the Gospel, the Passover is immediately celebrated in the place of revelation, and that Lamb who was slain for the salvation of the world is sacrificed. When the manna of the figurative law had ceased, the people first ate the bread of Christ’s body, which the incorruptible land of promise—that is, the Virgin Mary, the mother of the Lord—brought forth; its grain, falling into the earth, produced abundant fruit.

And observe the order. After we have passed through the waters of the bath under Jesus son of Nave—that is, under Jesus Christ our leader—and have been marked by faith with spiritual circumcision, then, arriving by these stages, we celebrate the Passover: that is, believing in Christ sacrificed for the salvation of the world, we are immediately nourished by that bread of the Lord’s body.

Next Christ, the prince of the army of the heavenly virtues, meets us, holding the sword of the Gospel for cutting away the pollution of our flesh. Joshua’s question to the angel—“Are you for us or for our adversaries?” (Joshua 5)—indicates the discernment of his followers, who distinguish between good and evil by discernment, lest the adversary deceive them under the appearance of good.

Hence it is also said to Jeremiah: “If you separate the precious from the vile, you will be as my mouth, surrounded” (Jeremiah 15).

## CHAPTER VII. On the Destruction of Jericho and the Salvation of Rahab

«After this, Jericho is surrounded and conquered. Against it no sword is drawn, no battering ram is directed, nor are weapons hurled; only priestly trumpets are employed continuously for seven days. Thus, when the ark has gone around it, the walls of Jericho are brought down.»

Jericho, by interpretation, means “moon.” The moon, however, represents the appearance of this world, because, just as the moon wanes through its monthly completions, so this world, hastening toward the completion of the ages, falls through its daily declines.

The Church is represented in the ark, while the strong preachers are signified by the bronze trumpets. Thus the Israelites carry the ark around this city of Jericho for seven days while the bronze trumpets sound; and its walls fall through the presence of the ark and the sound of the bronze trumpets. For in this age, which revolves through the succession of seven days, while the ark is carried—that is, while the Church moves around the whole earth—the walls of Jericho, meaning the exaltation of the world, and the obstacles of unbelieving pride, collapse at the voices of the preachers, as at the sound of trumpets.

This continues until, at the end of the ages, “the last enemy, death,” is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15), and, through the destruction of the ungodly, the one house of Rahab, like the one Church, is delivered from the disgrace of the world’s fornication through the window of confession in the blood of remission.

This prostitute dwells in Jericho, as in this mortal age. In order that she may be saved, she sends scarlet through the window of her house, as through the mouth of her body: this signifies confessing for salvation the blood of Christ for the remission of sins.

Those who were found in her house were saved from the city; and all who are found within the Church are likewise saved. Outside this house, however—that is, outside the Church—no one is saved.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Achan’s Theft

«Meanwhile Achan steals from the devoted things of the city of Jericho a cloak and a golden bar, on account of which, when God became angry, certain people from the nation perished by the hand of the enemy.»

Jericho, as has been said, represents the world. The person who defrauds it of its devoted things and hides them in his tent is the one who inserts worldly customs into the Church’s secret places; who, while remaining under the worship of God, loves the festivals or spectacles of the world; who consults sorcerers, haruspices, and augurs; or who persuades others to observe the other rites formerly practiced in Jericho—that is, in this world.

Because he secretly introduces worldly ways of life after putting on the garment of faith, he is like one who takes a cloak from the devoted things. But the person also defrauds Jericho of its devoted things who introduces into the Church the doctrine of heretics or the superstitious studies of secular literature.

Arius, Marcion, and Basilides stole this golden rule, fitted out in eloquent speech. These men stole golden rules from Jericho, attempted to introduce into the Church the false sect of the philosophers, and tried to defile the whole Church of the Lord, so that many others perished through them. Therefore they were cast out as devoted things; oppressed and destroyed, as though by a heap of stones, by the multitude of their sins. Their author and destroyer was, among others, the devil, who through their impiety had overcome certain of the faithful.

Again he is overcome and defeated, and, hanged by the people of God, is killed through the power of the wood of the cross.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Construction of the Altar

«After defeating the enemies, Jesus built an altar to the Most High God from whole stones, into which no iron had been inserted, as Moses had commanded; he offered a sacrifice and wrote the Deuteronomy of Moses’ law on the stones.»

Let us therefore see who these stones are from which the altar was built. All who believe in Christ Jesus are called living stones. Concerning them the Apostle says: “You are living stones, built into a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2).

No iron was inserted into these stones, because they are incorrupt and undefiled in flesh and spirit, and have not received the flaming darts of the Evil One. They form one altar through the unity of faith and the harmony of charity.

In these stones Jesus our Lord also wrote Deuteronomy—that is, the law according to the Gospel. Let us hear him saying: “It was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery’; but I say to you, whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5).

Jesus therefore wrote this new law in the hearts and minds of believers who are worthy of the construction of the altar.

## CHAPTER X. On Curses and Blessings

«After this, all the people, the elders, the leaders, and the judges went on either side of the ark. They stood, as Moses had commanded in Deuteronomy, with six tribes on Mount Gerizim, to bless the people; these were the more noble tribes: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin. The other six, the less noble, stood opposite on Mount Ebal, to curse; among them were Reuben, who had defiled his father’s bed, and Zebulun, the last son of Leah, and the sons of the maidservants.»

The ancient histories indeed report these events; but we must examine what belongs to the narrative’s mystical meaning.

Who, then, are those who walk beside Mount Gerizim, and who are those who walk beside Mount Ebal?

Those who walk here beside Mount Gerizim, chosen for blessing, figuratively indicate those who come to salvation, inflamed not by fear of punishment but by love of the heavenly promise.

The other half, who walk beside Mount Ebal, where the curses were pronounced, indicate those who fulfill what is written in the law not out of love for blessings or promises, but from fear of future punishments, so that they may attain salvation.

All walk around the ark who do not depart from the bosom of the Church. Yet we call those more noble who act rightly from desire for goodness itself and from love of eternal blessing, rather than those who pursue good out of fear of evil.

Therefore Jesus alone can cut down and shape such minds and spirits from all peoples: he establishes some on Mount Gerizim for blessing, and others on Mount Ebal for cursing—not so that they may receive curses, but so that, contemplating the prescribed curses and the punishments appointed for sinners, they may beware of incurring them and correct themselves through the punishment of fear.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Gibeonites

«Meanwhile the Gibeonites, terrified by fear of destruction, came to Jesus with deceit and cunning, dressed in old garments and worn-out sandals, begging to be saved. At once they received salvation from Jesus. When he nevertheless recognized their deception, he appointed them cutters of wood and carriers of water.»

In their figure are shown those who come from the world to the Church, who have faith in God and bow their heads to the priests, and who minister and serve the saints, in order to provide some useful service. They are also ready to contribute to the adornment or ministry of the Church.

Yet in their morals and former way of life they remain unchanged. They put on the old person with his deeds and are wrapped in ancient vices, just as the Gibeonites were covered with old garments and worn-out sandals. Beyond believing in God and appearing devoted in their reverence toward the servants of God and the Church, they possess no amendment or renewal of character.

Such people therefore carry within the Church, for a time only, something like a sign of salvation; but among the spiritual—that is, among the saints of God—they do not attain eternal kingdom or freedom.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Battle at Gibeon

It is reported that at Gibeon, while Jesus son of Nave was fighting, the sun and moon stood still until Israel destroyed its enemies. Scripture says: “The sun stood still over Gibeon, and the moon over the valley of Elom” (Joshua 10). Scripture adds: “For God had never so listened to a human being” (ibid.).

Our Jesus therefore caused the sun to stand still not only then, but much more now, at his coming, while we wage war against the nations of vices and wrestle against rulers and authorities, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Ephesians 6).

The Sun of righteousness continually stands beside us. He never abandons us and does not hasten to set, because he himself said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

The five kings signify the five bodily senses, which conquer the Gibeonites—that is, carnal human beings. These kings flee to a cave when, while situated in the body, they plunge themselves into earthly actions. Yet when Jesus fights—that is, when the evangelical preaching fights—they are overcome; and when the Word of God enters into us, that is, into the cave of our body, all of them are killed together.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Extinction of the Nations and the Division of the Land

«After the nations had been extinguished or destroyed, Joshua divided the promised land among the peoples by lot.»

Thus Christ in a certain manner drove out from the face of his faithful the nations—that is, the evil spirits of pagan errors—and divided the land by lot, with one and the same Spirit working all things in us and distributing his gifts to each person as he wills.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Division of the Land among Two and Nine Half-Tribes

These divine utterances report that a first and a second division of the inheritance took place. The first was made through Moses; the second, which is the stronger, through Jesus.

Moses determined to give possession beyond the Jordan to only two and a half tribes—namely, Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. All the others received their inheritance through Jesus.

This indicates that more people would receive the heavenly promises through faith in Jesus Christ than had obtained them through the law. For those two and a half tribes undoubtedly foreshadowed the earlier people. They are called two and a half, however, because those who lived under the law attained knowledge of the Trinity but did not possess perfect understanding of it.

Thus the book of Ecclesiasticus also says: “He did not first complete the knowing of wisdom, and the weaker one did not investigate it” (Ecclesiasticus 24).

The nine and a half tribes, however, which receive the promise of the holy land through Jesus, as has been said, held the figure of the new people. Through faith and grace, after the bath—as through the crossing of the Jordan—they received the inheritance of the eternal promise from Jesus our Lord.

But for this reason these are also called nine and a half tribes: those who possess the inheritance under Jesus are not said to complete the number ten in its entirety, as a perfect number, because neither at the Lord’s coming nor in his incarnation was everything announced to us perfectly through him alone.

Hence he himself says to the disciples: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But the Spirit of truth will come, who proceeds from the Father; he will take from what is mine and announce it all to you” (John 16).

Perfection, therefore, in the sum of all good things consists in the Holy Spirit. Otherwise nothing will be considered perfect in one who lacks the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XV. That the Levites Did Not Receive an Inheritance of Land

The Levites did not receive an inheritance of land because Jesus our Lord himself is their inheritance. As it is written: “I am their inheritance, and no possession shall be given to them in Israel. For I am their possession” (Ezekiel 44).

God wished himself to be called the possession and lot of the clergy because they had become ministers of his altar. For this reason *cleros* is interpreted as “lot.”

Therefore one rightly possesses God as an inheritance who strives to be poor in spirit, so that he may serve God without any impediment and may appropriately say with the Psalmist: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Psalm 15).

## CHAPTER XVI. That the Dwelling Places of the Levites Were Distributed among All the Tribes

The fact that Jesus assigned dwelling places to the Levites throughout all the tribes signifies that those in the Church of God who devote themselves to knowledge and administer the grace of teaching should in turn receive from all those to whom they dispense divine things the earthly support that they themselves do not possess.

Thus what the Apostle commands may be fulfilled: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Corinthians 9).

These men are rightly said to be divided among all the tribes, because they live through the provision of all.

## CHAPTER XVII. That the Levites Received Forty-Two Cities as Their Possession

The fact that they also received forty-two cities undoubtedly signifies the preaching of the saints. They possess the teaching that consists of the Decalogue of the law and the fourfold number of the Gospel, as though they possessed four tens of cities; two are added to these because they proclaim everything they preach in both a moral and a mystical sense.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Extinguished People of Canaan

It is said that, after the Israelite people had received the promised land and divided it, the whole Canaanite population—that is, the gentile people—was not killed in the territory of the tribe of Ephraim but was made tributary, as it is written in the book of Judges: “The Canaanite dwelt in the midst of Ephraim as a tributary” (Judges 4).

What, then, does the tributary and the Canaanite—namely, the gentile people—signify, except vice?

Often we enter the promised land through great virtues, because we are strengthened by deep hope in eternity. But while we destroy exalted vices, we nevertheless retain certain small ones, as though allowing a Canaanite to live in our land.

Yet that Canaanite is made tributary, because we humbly turn to our own advantage the very vice that we cannot subdue, so that the mind may recognize itself as lowly even in its own affairs: by its own strength it cannot conquer even the small things it assails.

Hence it is well written again: “These are the nations that the Lord left, in order to educate Israel through them” (Judges 3).

For some of our smallest vices are still retained, so that the mind’s attention may always exercise itself anxiously in the struggle and may not grow proud of victory when it sees enemies living within itself—enemies by whom it still fears to be conquered.

Israel, therefore, is educated by the nations left behind when the exaltation of our virtue is restrained by certain small vices, and when, through those that resist it in small matters, it learns that it cannot subdue greater things by its own strength.

# QUESTIONS ON THE BOOK OF JUDGES

## CHAPTER I. On the Enslavement of the People and Their Deliverance

The history of Judges indicates no small number of mysteries. First, judges succeed Joshua, just as after Christ the Apostles and rulers of the churches succeeded him, to govern and direct the faithful whom he himself leads to the hope of the eternal promise.

Throughout this book, the offenses of the Jewish people, their enslavement, their cry, and God’s compassion are recorded. For many years they were servants of numerous kings because of their offenses, and, when they turned again, they were set free.

But what does it mean that, whenever they sin, they are often handed over to the power of the enemy, except that our sins, when we transgress, furnish strength to our enemies? When we do evil in the sight of the Lord, then our adversaries are strengthened—that is, the powers of the demons, the spiritual forces of wickedness.

But again, when we turn back, the Lord raises up saviors and judges—that is, rulers and teachers—which God sends to the aid of those who cry out to him with their whole heart. Thus he sent Othniel, who defeated Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia; he sent Ehud, who killed Eglon, king of Moab; he sent Jael and Deborah, who killed Sisera.

Their history must be briefly recalled because of its mysteries.

## CHAPTER II. On Deborah and Jael

At that time Deborah the prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, judged the people. She sat beneath the palm tree between Ramah and Bethel, on Mount Ephraim, and the children of Israel went up to her for every judgment (Judges 4).

Deborah, whose name is interpreted as “bee, without speech,” must be understood figuratively, in the form of prophecy. Concerning her it is said: “How sweet are your words to my throat” (Psalm 118).

Let us consider where the place of prophecy is described. “Under the palm tree,” he says. Prophecy has its seat under the palm tree because it leads those whom it instructs through its teachings to the palm of the heavenly calling.

Prophecy is said to sit between Ramah and Bethel. Ramah is interpreted as “height,” and Bethel as “house of God”—for it teaches us, placed within the house of God, to seek not the things that are on earth but the things that are in heaven (Colossians 3).

She sent for Barak and summoned him to herself (Judges 4). Barak is interpreted as “flashing” or “lightning.” A flash has light, but not lasting light; it shines for a short time and then ceases.

Barak therefore bears the form of the earlier people, who, first of all, were called and invited through prophecy to hear the words of God. They indeed shone in the splendor of the law and flashed for a brief time, but did not remain long.

When Deborah said to Barak—that is, when prophecy said to the earlier people—“The Lord God of Israel has commanded you: Go up Mount Tabor and take ten thousand men” (ibid.), Barak replied to prophecy in the person of the earlier people: “I will not go unless you go up with me.”

Deborah said to him: “I will go with you, but the primacy will not be yours on the road by which you go; Sisera will be delivered into the hand of a woman” (ibid.).

This appears to show that primacy is not with that people, nor does the palm of victory remain with it, but with Jael, the woman—that is, with the Church.

For this Jael, a foreign woman in whose hand the victory was achieved, bears the figure of the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Jael is interpreted as “ascent,” because through the Church one ascends to heaven.

«With a tent-peg this woman killed Sisera the enemy»—that is, by the point and power of the wood of the cross she killed the devil. Barak, that is, the earlier people, could not do this through the commandments of the law.

For she alone, through the wood in which, by spiritual mysteries, the salvation of believers afflicts the enemy of faith, strikes him. Then she covers his dead body with coverings—that is, she leaves him enclosed in the hearts of carnal people.

His deadly works are hidden only among those living in the corruption of life and committing mortal sins. When, by living wickedly, they are separated from the body of Christ, they become members of the devil.

## CHAPTER III. On the Angel’s Oracle to Gideon

Afterward the people of Israel are handed over to Midian, and for their deliverance the angel of the Lord speaks to Gideon. What his deeds signify mystically must now be demonstrated.

«While Gideon was beating the wheat harvest with a rod beneath an oak tree and threshing the grain from the chaff, he saw an angel and received an oracle from him: he was to bring the Lord’s people out from the power of their enemies into poverty.»

This Gideon evidently presented a figure of Christ. Under the shadow of the sacred cross, established in the foreordained mystery of the future Incarnation, he separated the elect of the saints from the chaff of vices by the uprightness of judgment, as though by a rod.

«When this Gideon heard from the angel that, although the thousands of the peoples would fail, the Lord would free his people from their enemies through one man, he immediately cooked a kid. In accordance with the angel’s command, he placed its flesh, together with unleavened bread, upon a rock, and poured the broth of the meat over it. When the angel touched it with the tip of his rod, fire immediately burst forth from the rock, and thus the sacrifice offered to God was consumed.»

By this sign it appears to have been declared that the rock prefigured the body of Christ, as Paul testifies: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10).

Already then, in the ministry, it was declared that the Lord Jesus, crucified in his flesh, would remove the sins of the whole world. He would cleanse not only the sins of actions but also the desires of souls.

The flesh of the kid refers to the guilt of deeds, while the broth refers to the enticements of desires, as it is written: “The people desired an evil desire, and they said, ‘Who will feed us with meat?’” (Numbers 11).

The angel therefore stretched out the rod and touched the rock, from which fire came forth. This showed that the Lord’s flesh, filled with the divine Spirit, burns away all the sins of human nature. Hence the Lord also says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12).

The learned man, foreseeing the future, therefore perceived the heavenly mysteries. Accordingly, following the oracles, he killed the bull-calf dedicated by his father to idols, and he himself sacrificed another seven-year-old bull-calf to God.

This deed most clearly revealed that after the Lord’s coming all sacrifices belonging to paganism were to be abolished, and that the one sacrifice of the Lord’s passion was to be reverently offered by the peoples to God for our redemption.

Indeed, that bull-calf was a type of Christ, in whom, as Isaiah said, the sevenfold fullness of spiritual virtues dwelt (Isaiah 11).

## CHAPTER IV. On the Mystery of the Fleece and the Threshing Floor

«Gideon therefore foresaw the mystery of victory. Yet, although strong and faithful, he still sought fuller evidence from the Lord concerning the future victory. He placed a fleece of wool on the threshing floor for one night, so that dew might be only upon it and there might be dryness over all the earth. Then again he placed the fleece in the same manner, so that dew might fall over the whole earth and there might be dryness in the fleece.»

Perhaps someone might ask whether he seems unbelieving in asking both things, since he had already been instructed by frequent signs. Far from it. He was not doubtful; rather, he foresaw future mysteries and, being prudent, examined them most carefully, so that he might believe the mystery more fully when he understood the oracle.

What, then, is the fleece drenched with dew and the threshing floor dry, and afterward the threshing floor drenched and the fleece dry, except that at first the one Hebrew nation possessed the mystery of grace while the whole world was empty of it?

For the threshing floor signified the whole world. Indeed, when the whole world was dry through the fruitless worship of pagan superstition, that heavenly dew of visitation was on the fleece.

Afterward, however, because the sheep of the house of Israel that had perished—represented under the figure of the fleece—rejected the fountain of living water, the dew of faith dried up in the breasts of the Jews, and that divine rain transferred its grace into the hearts of the Gentiles.

Hence the whole world is now moistened with the dew of faith, while the Jews lack the prophecies and all the charisms.

Nor is it surprising that those who have been deprived by the Lord of the abundance of prophetic rain should suffer the dryness of faithlessness, since he says: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it” (Isaiah 5).

He represented that nation under the name of the fleece either because, in obedience, it retained the same rain that he wished, according to his purpose, to be preached—that is, to be revealed to the uncircumcised nations.

## CHAPTER V. On the Battle with the Three Hundred

After this most careful explanation of the mystery, «when Gideon was preparing to fight against the Midianites and was bringing out the multitude of his army for battle, he was instructed by divine warning that, when he came to the river, all whom he saw drawing water on bended knees were to be removed from the battle. It happened that only three hundred men remained, those who had drawn water standing with their hands. With these Gideon went to battle and armed them not with weapons but with trumpets, torches, and jars.»

For, as it is written there, «they placed their burning torches inside the little jars, held the trumpets in their right hands and the jars in their left, and, coming close to their enemies, blew the trumpets and smashed the little jars. The torches appeared, and the enemies, terrified on one side by the sound of the trumpets and on the other by the flashing of the torches, were put to flight.»

Why is such a battle brought forward by the prophet in this way? Did the prophet intend to indicate that the victory of battle under Gideon’s leadership signified the coming of our Redeemer against the devil?

Such things were indeed done that, the more they surpass ordinary military practice, the more they do not depart from the mystery of prophecy. For who ever came to battle with jars and torches? Who, coming against weapons, abandoned weapons? These things would certainly have seemed ridiculous to us if they had not been terrifying to the enemy.

But by the testimony of this victory we have learned not to regard lightly the smallness of what was done.

Gideon, therefore, coming to battle, signifies the coming of our Redeemer, of whom it is written: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Psalm 23).

He prophesied our Redeemer not only by his deed but also by his name. For Gideon is interpreted as “going around in the womb.”

Our Lord, through the power of his majesty, fills and surrounds all things; yet through the grace of his dispensation he entered the womb of the Virgin.

What, then, is “going around in the womb” except that Christ, almighty God, lives within the womb through the substance of weakness, and outside the world through the power of his majesty?

Midian, however, is interpreted as “from judgment.” This was not judgment arising from the fault of one who repels, but the judgment of one who judges justly. They are therefore called “from judgment” because they are alienated from grace.

Since they were to be repelled and destroyed as enemies, they bear even in the meaning of their name the merit of the Redeemer’s just condemnation. Against them Gideon goes to battle with three hundred men.

The number three hundred is commonly understood to signify the fullness of perfection. What, then, is indicated by the number three hundred, except perfect knowledge of the Trinity?

With these men our Lord destroys the adversaries of faith; with these he enters the battle of preaching—those who are able to know divine things and who know how to understand perfectly what God is in the Trinity.

It should also be noted that this number of three hundred is contained in the letter tau, which bears the form of the cross. If the upright stroke that projects above the transverse line were added, it would no longer be merely the form of a cross but the cross itself.

Since, therefore, the number three hundred is contained in the letter tau, and since, as we have said, the form of the cross is shown by the letter tau, it is not without reason that those who are represented by the three hundred following Gideon are those to whom it was said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16).

Those who follow the Lord take up the cross more truly the more vigorously they subdue themselves and are afflicted by the compassion of charity toward their neighbors.

Hence it is said through the prophet Ezekiel: “Mark a tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve” (Ezekiel 9).

Or certainly, in these three hundred, who are contained in the letter tau, it is expressed that the iron of the enemies is overcome by the wood of the cross.

«They were therefore led to the river to drink water. Those who drank on bended knees were removed from military service.»

Water signifies the teaching of wisdom. The standing knee signifies upright action.

Those who are said to have bent the knee while drinking water and then withdrew, forbidden to take part in the battle, are those who do not absorb teaching together with upright works.

Those, however, who drink the streams of teaching in such a way that they are not bent carnally toward wicked works proceed under Christ’s leadership to battle against the enemies of faith.

«They therefore go with trumpets, torches, and jars.» As we have said, this was the order of battle: «They blew the trumpets; the torches were placed inside the jars; when the jars were broken, the torches were revealed; and when their light flashed, the enemies were terrified and turned to flight.»

The cry of the preachers is therefore signified by the trumpets, the brightness of miracles by the torches, and the frailty of bodies by the jars.

The commander brought with him to the battle of preaching men of this kind, who, scorning the preservation of their bodies, would strike down their enemies by dying and overcome their swords not with weapons but with patience.

Our martyrs came armed under their leader into battle—but with trumpets, jars, and torches.

They sounded the trumpets when they preached. They broke the jars when they offered their bodies, destined to be dissolved in suffering, to the swords of their enemies. They shone as torches when, after the dissolution of the body, they flashed forth through miracles.

Immediately the enemies were put to flight, because, when they saw the bodies of the martyrs flashing with miracles, they were shattered by the light of truth and believed what they had attacked.

They blew the trumpets so that the jars might be broken. The jars were broken so that the torches might appear. The torches appeared so that the enemies might be put to flight.

That is, the martyrs preached until their bodies were dissolved in death. Their bodies were dissolved in death so that they might flash forth through miracles. They flashed forth through miracles so that, by the divine light, they might strike down their enemies.

It should also be noted that the enemies stood before the jars but fled before the torches. For the persecutors of the holy faith resisted the preachers while they were still in the body. After the dissolution of their bodies, however, when miracles appeared, they were put to flight, because, terrified by fear, they ceased persecuting the faithful.

We must also consider what is written there: they held the trumpets in their right hands and the jars in their left.

We call whatever we esteem greatly “the right hand,” and whatever we regard as worthless “the left hand.” It was therefore rightly written there that they held trumpets in their right hands and jars in their left, because the martyrs of Christ esteem the grace of preaching highly but regard the usefulness of their bodies as of little importance.

Whoever values the usefulness of the body more than the grace of preaching holds the trumpet in the left hand and the jar in the right.

If the grace of preaching is kindled in the first place and the usefulness of the body placed second, it is certain that the trumpets are held in the right hands and the jars in the left.

## CHAPTER VI. On Abimelech
“Gideon dies and leaves seventy sons; and one named Abimelech, born of a concubine, who hired wandering men for himself, and they followed him. He entered his father’s house and killed his seventy brothers upon one stone, and only Jonathan, the youngest, remained, because he had been hidden,” and so forth.

If this event indicated nothing prophetic, why would it have been written at such length that Gideon had seventy sons and many wives, but also a concubine from whom he had begotten one evil son? And since the deed was shameful, it would have been still more shameful if such things appeared in the divine writings as examples for posterity—unless the events, through types and figures, displayed the image of some great reality.

Gideon, therefore, as was said above, prefigured the Lord. His very many wives are the many nations that adhered to Christ through faith. [Col. 0427B] His seventy sons are the seventy languages spread throughout this world, among which he was destined to beget sons for himself through faith. In this passage he calls the concubine the Synagogue, which in the last times will believe in Antichrist. Of her John says in the Apocalypse: “They say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan” (Apoc. II). From her, in the last times, the most wicked son—that is, Antichrist—is to be born. He will be the son of the slave woman, that is, of that sinful Synagogue, because, as it is written, “the one who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII). This son, I say, after gathering the impious to himself, will wickedly seize the kingdom, as Abimelech did. Having killed the noble sons—that is, those who, believing in Christ from different nations and languages, have been begotten by God—he will bring about a persecution so that he may kill nearly all the saints.

“But above the seventy,” he says, “there was a younger son, born of a noble marriage, who had hidden himself. He went up to the summit of Mount Gerizim and cried out in a loud voice to the people of Shechem, setting forth a parable for them.” This younger son, therefore, who flees in order to escape the enemy’s sword, is a figure of the remnant of the people of Israel who, with Elijah preaching in the last times, will believe and escape the sword of Antichrist.

“He went up,” he says, “to the summit of Mount Gerizim.” But why did he go up the mountain? Because no one can either prophesy or escape the persecution of Antichrist unless he has first ascended the mountain of blessing—that is, the height of faith and virtues. This is Mount Gerizim, which Moses assigns to blessing.

“After he had gone up, he raised his voice, cried out, and said: ‘Hear me, men of Shechem. The trees went to anoint a king over themselves, and they said to the olive tree: “Reign over us.” It answered them: “Can I abandon my richness, which gods and men use, and go to be promoted among the trees?” The trees said to the fig tree: “Come and receive kingship over us.” It answered them: “Can I abandon my sweetness and my exceedingly fine fruit, and go to be moved about among the other trees?” The trees also spoke to the vine: “Come and reign over us.” It answered them: “Can I abandon my wine, which gladdens God and men, and be moved about among the other trees?”’” (Judg. IX).

When the forest trees had been rejected by the olive, the fig tree, and the vine, they came to the bramble to make him their king.

But first let us see why the olive, the fig tree, and the vine were unwilling to reign over the trees. The forest trees signify vain and wandering men, prepared for eternal fire. Therefore the olive, the fig tree, and the vine rightly refused to reign over them, since they were wholly unworthy.

The olive signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit and the anointing of peace. The fig tree bears the image of the sacred law, as it is written in the Gospel: “A certain householder planted a fig tree in his vineyard” (Luke XIII). Who is the householder except God, who is the Father of his household—that is, of all believers? He planted a vineyard, that is, a people, because “you brought a vine out of Egypt” (Ps. LXXIX). In this vineyard he planted [Col. 0428A] a fig tree—that is, he placed the law in his people. This law cast the primitive people down upon the earth like large, dry, useless figs, and afterward produced other fruits: namely, the Christian people, whom it brought, with glory and honor, to the proper maturity of evangelical discipline and to the most pleasant richness of Christ.

“But the vine,” he says, “was unwilling to reign over them.” It is clear that the vine bears the type of our Savior, as he says in the Gospel: “I am the true vine” (John XV). Since, therefore, that people who is destined to serve Antichrist will already have been given over to a reprobate mind, as the Apostle says (Rom. I)—the people whom he calls the forest trees—and since it must believe the lie, that is, Antichrist, because it refused to believe the truth, Christ, it is therefore rejected from the kingdom of the vine, that is, of Christ; from the olive, that is, from the grace of the Holy Spirit; and from the fig tree, that is, from the sweetness of divine law. It comes to the bramble.

The bramble is a kind of thornbush, commonly called the bear’s thorn, exceedingly rough and thorny. Through it the type of Antichrist is rightly signified, [Col. 0428B] for he will ravage the human race with every kind of harshness and savagery.

“But fire,” he says, “will come out of the bramble—that is, iniquity from Antichrist—and will devour together with him all who trust in him.”

## CHAPTER VII. Jephthah and His Daughter

“Then the children of Israel again began to serve the Baals and foreign gods, and they were delivered into the hands of the children of Ammon. Then Jephthah the Gileadite, fleeing from the presence of his brothers, was appointed leader in the war against the children of Ammon. After returning from his victory, he sacrificed his daughter, who was the first to meet him after the victory. For he had made this vow: whatever should meet him on his return, he would sacrifice to the Lord.”

Who, then, was foretold in Jephthah except the Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior? Fleeing from the presence of his brothers—that is, the Jews—he received authority among the Gentiles, because he fulfilled all the mysteries of human salvation that he had sworn to accomplish. Like a daughter, he offered his own flesh to the Lord for the salvation of Israel. We read that the Father swore and vowed the Only-Begotten, as the Psalmist says: “As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob” (Ps. CXXXI)—namely, that he would fulfill the oath of religious devotion in the passion of his flesh, for the salvation of the human race.

According to the history of the Testaments, these things thus appear to have been accomplished through Christ, in accordance with the religious promise that he had sworn would be fulfilled. After Jephthah’s death he was delivered into the hands of the Philistines, and Samson was born to deliver Israel.

## CHAPTER VIII. Samson and His Deeds

Samson, once the Lord’s Nazirite, certainly bears the type of Christ: first, because his birth was announced by an angel; next, because he is called a Nazirite and himself delivered Israel from its enemies; finally, because he overturned their temple, and many thousands of men who had mocked him perished.

The birth of Samson, announced through an angel, first resembles the prophets who announced the Lord’s birth according to the flesh; and then also the angel who spoke to Mary, saying: “Mary, you have found favor before the Lord, and you have conceived in your womb and will bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel. He will save his people from their sins” (Luke I).

Samson is interpreted as “sun.” Since our Redeemer is also called the sun, hear the Lord Jesus himself being called by that name through the prophet: “The sun of righteousness shall rise for you, and healing is in his wings” (Mal. IV). Truly he is the sun of righteousness, who illumines the minds of all believers with heavenly protection. He is truly a Nazirite and holy of God, after whose likeness that Nazirite was so called.

As Samson was proceeding toward the mystery of marriage, a roaring lion met him. But who was represented by Samson when he first encountered and killed the lion while going among foreigners to seek a wife, except Christ, [Col. 0429A] who, intending to call the Church from the Gentiles and conquering the devil, says: “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world” (John XVI)?

What does the honeycomb extracted from the mouth of that slain lion signify, except that, as we observe, the laws themselves of the earthly kingdom—which roared against Christ—now, their ferocity having been destroyed, even offer protection for the preaching of evangelical sweetness?

Again, what did he represent in himself by killing a few while he lived, but many enemies when he died after destroying the temple? Surely this: while he lived, the Lord destroyed a few who were lifted up by the pride of unbelief; but when the temple of his body was dissolved, he destroyed many more, and by dying cast down all those among the Gentiles whom he had endured while living.

The remaining events—how the treacherous woman shaved his head and handed him over to the Philistines to be mocked; how he was captured, blinded, and assigned to the mill—do not represent Christ. Rather, they portray those who glory only in the name of Christ in the Church and are continually entangled in evil deeds. The man signifies rational understanding, while the flesh is received typologically as the woman.

If we consent to the woman—that is, to our flesh—when lust flatters us, or if we consent to other evil works, we are stripped and deprived of the grace of the Spirit, which is signified by the hair of the Nazirite, and we are deceived. Thus the devil mocks proud and sinful people when Christ’s grace has been violated, just as Samson was mocked when his hair was cut.

But what does it mean that Samson, captured by the Philistines, was assigned to the mill after he lost his eyes? Surely this: after evil spirits have gouged out the eye of contemplation within a person by the goads of temptation, they send the person outside to circle endlessly through labor. If that person should someday return through repentance, the hair is restored to him, as it were: that is, when grace flourishes again, he is restored to salvation.

Then, after overthrowing the pillars of desire and lust, he casts down his victorious enemies; and, with the battle renewed, he will finally triumph most courageously over the demons.

[Col. 0429]

# QUESTIONS ON THE BOOK OF RUTH

[Col. 0429B]

Let us now consider Ruth, for she bears the type of the Church. First, she is a foreigner from the Gentile people; having left her homeland and everything that belonged to it, she goes into the land of Israel. When her mother-in-law tried to prevent her from going with her, she persevered, saying: “Wherever you go, I will go. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. The land that receives you when you die shall receive me; in it I will die.”

That she was a wife undoubtedly reveals that the Church was typified in her. For thus the Church, called from the Gentiles to the Lord, leaves her homeland, which is idolatry, and abandons every earthly manner of life. She confesses that the Lord is her God, in whom the saints believed; that she will go to the place where the flesh of Christ ascended after the Passion; that for his name she will suffer in this world even unto death; and that she will be joined to the people of the saints, namely, the patriarchs and prophets.

Moses showed in his song that she would be joined to the company of those holy people who came from the stock of Abraham, saying: “Rejoice, Gentiles, with his people.” That is: you who are to believe from the Gentiles, rejoice with eternal joy together with those who were chosen first.

After Ruth entered the land of Israel with her mother-in-law, the merits of her service brought it about that she was joined to a man descended from Abraham. First she was offered to the one whom she herself believed to be the nearer relative. He denied that he could marry her. When he withdrew, as witnessed by the ten elders, Boaz was joined to her and blessed by those same ten elders, because the first of the relatives confessed that he could marry her.

Here we believe that the figure of John the Baptist is displayed. For when he was thought to be the Christ and was asked who he was, he did not deny, but confessed, saying that he was not the Christ (John I, 20). When those who had been sent continued asking who he was, [Col. 0430B] he answered: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (ibid. 23). Finally, he himself confesses concerning the Lord, saying: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (ibid. III, 29). He shows himself to be the friend of the bridegroom when he adds: “The friend of the bridegroom is the one who stands and hears him, and rejoices because of the bridegroom’s voice” (ibid.).

They therefore thought that he was the Christ, because they did not understand that Christ had come at the time of his visitation. He is the Bridegroom of the Church, who had been promised beforehand through the prophetic voices. But just as that relative denied his claim, and afterward Ruth was joined to Boaz, so Christ—who is truly the Bridegroom of the Church, whom the oracles of all the prophets had proclaimed—deigned to take the Church as his own and to offer to God the Father, from all the nations throughout the whole world, countless peoples.

As for the relative removing his sandal, it was the ancient custom that if a bridegroom wished to repudiate a bride, he removed his sandal, and this was the sign of repudiation. Accordingly, he is ordered to remove his sandal, so that he would not approach the Church as a bridegroom wearing a sandal. This was reserved for Christ, who was the true Bridegroom.

The blessing of the ten elders shows that all nations were to be saved and blessed in the name of Jesus. For among the Greeks, iota signifies ten. It is the first letter with which the name of the Lord Jesus is written. This, as we have said, demonstrates that all nations are to be saved and blessed through him.

Let no one, therefore, hesitate to believe these things as they have been stated, when he sees that all things both preceded from the beginning in earlier figures and have been manifestly fulfilled through the Lord’s coming, while what remains is to be accomplished in truth in the same manner—all the voices and figures of the sacred Scriptures agreeing. These things have been fulfilled by the one who promised them through his Son Jesus Christ, our Lord, King, and Savior, with whom glory and honor belong to him forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0429]

# QUESTIONS ON THE BOOKS OF KINGS

## BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER I. The Birth of Samuel

[Col. 0429D]

After the Book of Judges comes the Book of Kings. Observe the sequence of the times: first judges, afterward kings; so there will first be judgment and then a kingdom. In these times, through many and varied means, the mysteries of Christ and the Church are revealed.

For from the very beginning of the kingship, when the priesthood was changed through the rejection of Eli in Samuel, and the kingdom was changed through the rejection of Saul in David, it was proclaimed beforehand that a new priesthood and a new kingdom would come in the Lord Jesus Christ, after the old had been rejected—the old being a shadow of what was to come.

Did not David himself, when he ate the bread of the Presence, which no one was permitted to eat except priests, foreshadow in one person the future union of both kingdom and priesthood, that is, in the one Jesus Christ? Thus the succession of Samuel the priest prefigured the new and, as foretold, everlasting priesthood, which is Christ Jesus, with Eli the priest rejected—that is, with the Jewish priesthood cast aside.

Samuel’s own mother, who had previously been barren and afterward rejoiced in fertility, and whose name, Anna, is interpreted as “his grace,” signifies the Christian religion itself, and finally the grace of God through which Christ is born for us. She also signifies the Church, once barren but now fruitful and rejoicing in the praise of God.

In her song she appears to prophesy nothing other than the transformation of the Old Testament or priesthood into the New Testament or priesthood, which is Christ. Unless perhaps someone should say that Anna prophesied nothing, but merely praised God with exultant proclamation because a son had been granted to her.

What, then, does she mean when she says: “He has made the bow of the mighty weak, and the weak have been girded with strength. Those who were full of bread have become diminished, and the hungry have crossed the land; because the barren woman has borne seven, while she who had many children has grown weak in her sons”? Did she herself bear seven, although she had been barren? She had only one when she said these things. Nor did she afterward bear seven, or six with Samuel as the seventh, but three sons and two daughters.

Furthermore, in that people, when no one yet reigned, why did she place at the end: “He gives strength to our kings and exalts the horn of his Christ”? From where did she say these things, unless she was prophesying?

The Church of Christ, the city of the great King, full of grace and fruitful in offspring, therefore says what she recognizes to have been prophesied about herself long beforehand through the devotion of this pious mother: “My heart has been established in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God my Savior,” and so forth.

Meanwhile Samuel was serving in the temple of God, girded with an ephod. But the sons of Eli, ignorant of the divine sacrifices, sinned before the Lord, and through them many mocked God’s sacrifice. Thus Eli the priest was condemned because of their iniquity, since he punished the miserable men who were sinning with insufficient severity. He did restrain and rebuke them, but with the gentleness and mildness of a father, not with the severity and authority of a high priest.

From this judgment priests should learn how they themselves are punished because of the sins of their sons, that is, because of their crimes. Even if they are holy, the guilt of their subjects is nevertheless charged to them if it is not restrained.

### CHAPTER II. The Prophet Sent to Eli

A certain prophet of God came to Eli the priest and said to him:

“Thus says the Lord: Was I not openly revealed to the house of your father when it was in Egypt, in Pharaoh’s house? And did I not choose him from all the tribes of Israel for myself as priest, so that he might go up to my altar, burn incense for me, and wear the ephod before me? And did I not give to you and to your father’s house all the offerings from the sacrifices of the children of Israel?

“Why, then, have you kicked aside my victim and my offerings, which I commanded to be offered in the temple, and honored your sons more than me, so that you might eat the first portions of every sacrifice of my people Israel?

“Therefore thus says the Lord God of Israel: I plainly declared that your house and your father’s house would minister in my presence forever. But now, says the Lord, far be this from me. For whoever honors me, I will honor; but those who despise me will be held in contempt.

“Behold, the days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there will be no old man in your house; and you will see your rival in the temple amid all the prosperity of Israel.”

This prophecy concerning the change of the priesthood was not fulfilled in Samuel, but was foreshadowed in the Lord Jesus Christ. After the prophet Samuel there were still priests from the line of Aaron, such as Zadok and Abiathar in the reign of David, and others afterward, before the time came when this change of the priesthood had to be accomplished through Christ.

For when he said, “I plainly declared that your house and your father’s house would minister in my presence forever; but now, says the Lord, far be this from me. Whoever honors me, I will honor; but those who despise me will be held in contempt”—behold, these are the days that were foretold; they have already come. There is no priest according to the order of Aaron.

For what follows there—“I will raise up for myself a faithful priest”—is spoken of Christ Jesus, the true priest of the New Testament.

What is added—“And whoever remains in your house will come to be prayed for”—is not properly spoken of the house of this Eli, but of that Aaron from whose line people remained until the coming of Christ. Even to this day there are not lacking people from that family who are converted. Concerning them another prophet said: “The remnant shall be saved.” Hence the Apostle also says: “So therefore at this present time also there is a remnant saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. XI, 5).

This statement is properly understood of such remnants: “Whoever remains in your house will come to be prayed for.” Clearly, the one who believes in Christ is such a person, just as in the time of the apostles the first believers came from that very people and believed. Even now there are some—although very rarely—who believe, so that what this man of God said may be fulfilled in them.

What he immediately adds—“And he will offer a silver coin and a round loaf of bread”—what is signified by the silver coin except the confession of the mouth, which is made by believers for salvation? Silver is commonly used to signify speech, as the Psalmist testifies where it is sung: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, proved on the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. XI, 7).

Therefore this one who comes says: “Let me go, I beg you, to one priestly portion, that I may eat a morsel of bread.” By the priestly portion he means the body of Christ, that is, the Church, whose priest and mediator between God and humanity is the man Christ Jesus. To this people the Apostle Peter says: “A holy people, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. I, 9).

In this priestly portion he asks to eat a morsel of bread. In these words the sacrifice of Christians is elegantly expressed, concerning which the Priest himself says: “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John VI, 52). This is the sacrifice—not according to the order of Aaron, but according to the order of Melchizedek.

### CHAPTER III. The Captivity of the Ark
