After these things had been foretold by that prophet to Eli as a figure of the change from the Old Testament, the Philistines, because the Lord was angry with Israel, drew up their battle line against them. The Israelites brought the ark to their camp, but the ark was captured by the enemies.

They themselves were not only defeated and put to flight; there was also a great slaughter of those who were killed. Nevertheless, this event signifies something of the future.

Prophetically, the ark being captured by foreigners indicated that God’s covenant would pass to the Gentiles. When Eli the priest was told that the ark of the Lord had been captured, he fell from his seat and died. As the ark of the Lord passed to the Gentiles, the Jewish priesthood perished and came to an end.

Eli’s two sons also fell, and the wife of one of them was widowed and soon died in childbirth because of the same upheaval. By this clear sign it was prefigured that, after the Jewish priesthood had been extinguished, the carnal synagogue, which adhered to it carnally, would perish. When Eli was cast down from the priestly seat, the seat of the Jews was shown to be vacant, and the glory of the priesthood and kingdom extinguished.

But what does it mean that, after the Philistines had placed the ark of the Lord in the temple of their god Dagon, they entered the temple and found their god fallen and broken, with his head and both hands cut off?

As soon as the Lord’s Testament reached the Gentiles, the idols that possessed the deceived world were immediately destroyed, and every error of images collapsed, unable to endure the presence of God. In Dagon’s severed hands the work of idolatry is cut off; in his severed head the pride of the devil is signified, from which sin had its beginning.

That it was found on the threshold also bears a great meaning, so that it might recognize the definite and predetermined end of its idolatry. The threshold signifies the end of a journey.

The same event also has great symbolic significance in the fact that, in the ruin and destruction of their god Dagon, they found only his back, with all his limbs broken. The back signifies flight, for those who flee from their pursuers turn their backs. Hence it is written concerning the enemies: “You will make them turn their backs.”

Where are the idols? They have perished. And if some remnants are hidden by certain people, they have fled.

As for those who captured the ark of God being struck in their hindquarters, this punishment appears to signify that if anyone receives the Testament of God but loves the things behind him, he will justly be tormented by those very things. They ought, as the Apostle says, to regard them as dung (Phil. III, 8).

Those who take up the divine Testament while looking backward and failing to strip themselves of their former vanity are like those enemies who placed the ark of the covenant beside their idols. The old things fall even against their will, because “all flesh is grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell; but the ark of the Lord remains forever,” the hidden covenant of the kingdom of heaven, where the eternal word of God is (I Pet. I, 24–25).

Those cows of the Philistines that carried the ark of God signified the figure of saints who renounce the world and have not taken upon themselves the yoke of any offense. Just as those cows, because of their affection for their calves, nevertheless did not turn aside from the straight path, so the saints who renounce the world ought not, out of regard for family ties, to be hindered from their good purpose.

As Moses says: “Those who say to their father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to their brothers, ‘I do not recognize them,’ and who have not known their sons: these have kept your covenant, and observed your commandments, your judgments, Jacob, and your law, Israel” (Deut. XXXIII, 9–10).

The one who eagerly desires to know God as a servant is the one who, out of love for his devotion, wishes not to know what he once knew carnally.

### CHAPTER IV. Samuel’s Sacrifice and the Stone of Help

After Eli’s death, Samuel ruled Israel. When all the people had gathered, he cried out to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord heard him. While he was offering a burnt offering, the foreigners approached to fight against the people of God. The Lord thundered against them; they were thrown into confusion, stumbled before Israel, and were defeated.

Then Samuel took one stone and placed it between Masphat and Sicelech. As the translators of the Septuagint rendered it, he placed it between New Mizpah and Old Mizpah. He called its name Stone of Help and said: “Thus far the Lord has helped us.”

Masphat is interpreted as “intention.” That Stone of Help is the majesty of the Savior, through whom one must pass from the old Mizpah to the new—that is, from the expectation placed in the carnal kingdom, which was a false carnal happiness, to the expectation placed through the New Testament in the kingdom of heaven, where there is the truest spiritual happiness, than which nothing is better.

“Thus far God helps us.”

This Samuel invoked the name of the Lord, and God heard him; and at harvest time he obtained rain. In the sacred Scriptures, rain signifies the words of the Gospel or of the law, as Moses also says: “Let my speech be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew” (Deut. XXXII).

Christ therefore gave this rain to the world at harvest time—that is, when the Gentiles were to be gathered—“so that, like grain in granaries, they might be gathered into the bosom of the Church.”

Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life. Until his time there had been judges and leaders over Israel. But Samuel’s sons turned aside after avarice, accepted gifts, and became such unjust judges [Col. 0434A] that the people, unable to endure them, asked for a king like the other nations.

### CHAPTER V. The Anointing of Saul as King

For this reason God gave them Saul as king, and at the Lord’s command he was first anointed to the kingship by the prophet. In the fact that he was anointed, he too bore an image of Christ.

Hence blessed David, who himself was also called “Christ,” said to the man who claimed to have killed Saul: “How were you not afraid to stretch out your hand against the Lord’s Christ?” (I Sam. XXVI, 9).

This is why Saul towered above everyone from the shoulders upward: our head is above, and it is Christ.

But in the fact that he was afterward rejected and cast aside when David succeeded him in the kingdom, he represented the people of Israel, who, as foretold, were destined to lose the kingdom they had acquired when Christ our Lord would reign through the New Testament—not carnally, but spiritually. [Col. 0434B]

### CHAPTER VI. The Fast Ordered by Saul

As Saul was going to fight against the Philistines, he imposed a fast on the whole army until he returned from the battle. But his son Jonathan, seeing honey on the surface of the field, extended the tip of his staff, dipped it into the honeycomb, and tasted it; and his eyes were enlightened.

They were not enlightened so that he could see—for he had already been seeing—but so that he might discern, because he had touched what was forbidden. That fall, like Adam’s, made him attentive and rendered him ashamed.

By this event the one who strives to serve God is warned that he must despise all the enticements of worldly pleasures. For he cannot fight against the spiritual Philistines—that is, against the rulers of this darkness—with strength and weapons if he still refuses to avoid the sweetness of this world.

“Honey drips from the lips of the prostitute” (Prov. V, 3), and this signifies the delight of carnal pleasure. According to mystical interpretations, Jonathan is thought to have borne this meaning and, being discovered by lot, to have been delivered only with difficulty through the prayers of the people.

### CHAPTER VII. King Agag Spared and Killed by Samuel

Saul again entered into battle against Amalek. After killing all the enemies, he spared Agag the king and refused to destroy everything according to the Lord’s command; and the Lord became angry with him.

Samuel came, took a sword, and cut Agag into pieces.

When some people read in the Scriptures that the saints spare none of their enemies, they become cruel and, thirsting for human blood, say that the righteous struck their enemies so completely that none was left alive. They do not understand that mysteries are foreshadowed in these words, and that we are thereby instructed that, when fighting against vices, we must leave none of them behind but kill them all.

For if we spare them, this can be counted as guilt against us, just as it was counted against Saul, who kept alive the king of Amalek. No one will remain righteous if he preserves any sin within himself, as Saul did. But the saints, represented by Samuel, rage against their enemies—that is, against the vices of sinners—in such a way that they do not allow any sin to remain unpunished.

### CHAPTER VIII. Saul Seized by an Evil Spirit

When Saul therefore withdrew from the Lord because of his disobedience, he was seized by an evil spirit from the Lord. For an evil spirit of the Lord rushed upon him.

If it was the Lord’s, why was it evil? If it was evil, why was it the Lord’s?

This sentence is contained in two expressions: in the Lord there was just authority, and in the devil an unjust will. The same spirit was evil through its most wicked will, and the Lord’s through his most just authority.

The devil was therefore called the Lord’s spirit because of the mystery: God makes good use even of evil spirits, either for the condemnation of some, or for correction, or for testing. Although the malignity is not from the Lord, the authority is nevertheless from God alone.

So elsewhere the “sleep of the Lord” is mentioned, which had overcome Saul’s soldiers when David took the spear and cup from beside the head of the sleeping man. The sleep that had then seized the men had been infused at God’s command, so that David, his servant, would not be perceived as present in that place.

The evil spirit is therefore called the Lord’s—that is, God’s minister for doing in Saul what the most just Judge deemed that he should suffer. In the will by which that spirit was evil, it was not God’s; but as a creature created by God, and in the authority it had received—not from itself, but through the justice of the Lord of all—it belonged to the Lord.

### CHAPTER IX. David’s Anointing
[Col. 0435B] Accordingly, when Saul had been rejected because of his disobedience, the Lord sent Samuel to Jesse; and, taking a horn of oil, he anointed David king. But let us see how this same David prophetically signified Christ. For David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable”; and what is stronger than that Lion of the tribe of Judah, who conquered the world? And what is more desirable than the one of whom it is said, “The DESIRED ONE of all nations will come” (Hag. 2:8)? This David is anointed for a future kingdom, announcing Christ through that anointing—for Christ is named from *chrism*, that is, anointing oil.

David, then, is transferred from the pastoral office of tending sheep to the kingship of human beings. David himself, that is, Jesus, is said to have been taken away from the sheep of the Jewish people and transferred to the kingdom of the nations. For Christ is no longer among the Jewish people: he was taken away from there and now tends the flocks of the nations.

David was also trained in musical songs. For by the rational and measured harmonies of diverse sounds, joined together in concordant variety, he indicates the unity of the Church, composed and ordered as one body; the Church [Col. 0435C] resounds daily in various ways and modulates with mystical sweetness.

While still a boy, this David, singing sweetly—or rather, powerfully—on the lyre, restrained the evil spirit that was at work in Saul. This was not because such power belonged to that lyre, but because the figure of Christ’s cross, mystically represented by wood and the stretching of the strings, and the passion itself that was being sung, already then oppressed the demon’s spirit.

David also killed a lion and a bear: the bear, namely, the devil; the lion, Antichrist—one secretly lying in wait for human beings at that time, the other raging most openly in the future.

This David overcame a giant in battle, when foreigners were fighting against the Lord’s people. Pride challenged humility; the devil challenged Christ. Holy David took weapons of war in order to go out against Goliath, but because of his age and the small stature of his body he could not carry those weapons. He cast off the burdensome arms, took five stones from the stream, and placed them in a shepherd’s pouch. Armed with these, [Col. 0435D] he went forth and conquered. This is what happened with that David.

But if we search out the mysteries, Christ is understood in David. Foreseeing the time when the revelation of the New Testament and the commendation of grace would be made known, he laid down his weapons and took five stones. He therefore laid down the bodily sacraments of the Law, which were not imposed upon the nations. He laid down what we do not observe, although we understand that it was set forth and established for some signification.

Finally, he laid down these weapons as though they were the works of the sacraments of the Old Law, and took up the Law itself. For the five stones signify the five books of Moses. He therefore took those five from the stream—that is, from the world. The mortal world flows onward and passes away; everything that comes into the world flows past.

They were in the stream as though in that people. At first the stones were useless there and lay idle; they were of no benefit, and passed along upon the currents. But what did David do? To make that Law useful, he received grace. For the Law cannot be fulfilled without grace. The fullness of the Law is love.

[Col. 0436A] Because grace therefore brought about the fulfillment of the Law—and grace is signified by milk, for milk is gratuitous in the flesh, where the mother does not seek to receive but strives to give; the mother gives this freely and is distressed if there is no one to receive it—how did David show that the Law cannot operate without grace? He took those five stones, by which the Law was signified in the five books, and, wishing to join them to grace, placed them in the shepherd’s pouch with which he used to milk the sheep.

Armed with these, he went out against the proud Goliath, who boasted and placed his confidence in himself. He took one stone and cast down the devil. He struck him on the forehead, and he fell, in that part of the body where he did not bear the sign of Christ. You may also note this: he placed five stones but sent forth one. The five books were read, but unity conquered. For the fullness of the Law is love, as the Apostle says: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:3).

Then, after he had cast him down and struck him, he took away his sword and cut off his head with it. And our David does this: [Col. 0436B] he casts down the devil from his own possessions when those whom the devil held in his power, and through whom he slaughtered other souls, come to believe in Christ. They turn their tongues against the devil, and thus Goliath’s head is cut off with his own sword.

## CHAPTER X. On David’s contest with Goliath the Philistine, in which Saul promises David marriage to his daughter in exchange for one hundred Philistine foreskins

Meanwhile, David’s victory offended King Saul, who was indignant that the voices of public congratulation resounded with acclamation for him in thousands but for David in ten thousands. Hence arose Saul’s envy, and the seed of hatred against David.

That cunning dissembler, so that he might expose David to danger without openly laying a trap for him, decided to bind him to marriage with his daughter Michal if David, as victor, brought him one hundred foreskins of the Allophyles. David brought him two hundred in exchange for the hundred; and from the very point at which, by royal design, he was thought likely to perish, he gained a more glorious trophy. [Col. 0436C]

So also, while the Jews tried to kill Christ against the will of God, through the very act by which they believed they were extinguishing him they brought about the salvation of the nations.

But the fact that David first brought the foreskins of foreigners and then became attached to Saul’s daughter in marriage signified that Christ would not first promise himself in marriage to the Synagogue unless he had previously become glorious among the nations. For first he circumcised the pollution of the flesh among the nations, and afterward he was joined to the Synagogue. For, as it is written, “After the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).

He brought twice as many—namely, two hundred foreskins—either because the acquisition consisted of Jews and nations together, or because the number of the people acquired from the nations is greater than that of the Jews who believe.

## CHAPTER XI. David, singing, drives the unclean spirit from Saul

[Col. 0436D] Saul then increased his hatred against David to such an extent that, while David was accustomed to play the lyre for the relief of his spirit, the king attempted to transfix him with a spear.

But what does it mean that, when an adversarial spirit invaded Saul, David’s lyre, once taken up, calmed his madness? Saul signifies the exaltation of the Jews, while David signifies the humility of Christ. When Saul is seized by an unclean spirit, his madness is tempered by David’s singing. Thus, when the understanding of the Jews is turned into madness through blasphemy, it is fitting that the salvation of their minds should be recalled, as though by the sweetness of a lyre, through the tranquility of evangelical speech.

## CHAPTER XII. Saul sends guards to David’s house to kill him

Saul sent guards to David’s house to watch him and kill him. David, however, withdrew in the proper manner, fled, and was saved. When Saul’s messengers came, [Col. 0437A] they found a statue placed in David’s bed, with a goatskin at its head.

Let us therefore hear what it signifies that Saul sent men to guard David’s house in order to kill him. This does not refer to the Lord’s cross, but nevertheless pertains to his passion. Christ was crucified, died, and was buried. That burial was therefore like a house, to guard which the kingdom of the Jews sent men when guards were stationed at Christ’s tomb.

How, then, was the house guarded, if David represented Christ, so that Christ was to be killed, whereas Christ was killed not in the tomb but on the cross? This is referred to the body of Christ, because to kill Christ meant to remove the name of Christ. For no one would have believed in Christ if the lie of the guards had prevailed—the guards who were bribed to say, “While we were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him” (Matt. 28:13).

To wish to kill Christ, then, is to extinguish the name of his resurrection, so that the lie might be preferred to the Gospel. But just as Saul could not kill David, so the kingdom of the Jews could not erase the memory of Christ.

Those who wished, through Saul’s power—that is, through the kingdom of the Jews—to presume against Christ stumbled upon the stone of stumbling as upon a statue. His kid appeared to be a lamb, because they persecuted him as a sinner in whom they had found no sin.

David therefore avoided the blow of the royal hand and escaped Saul’s persecution by fleeing to Samuel. Saul sent messengers to seize David. Samuel, however, was among the prophets and the company of prophets who were prophesying at that time. The messengers who were sent received the same spirit and prophesied. When others were sent, the same thing happened to them, and likewise to a third group.

Afterward, when Saul himself had come, [Col. 0437C] the Spirit of God came upon him; he walked along, entered, and prophesied.

It is asked how those men, when they had been sent to seize a man and lead him to death, could have been considered worthy to be made such by the Spirit; and how Saul himself, who had sent them and who came seeking to shed innocent blood, could have been worthy to receive that Spirit and prophesy.

As far as the literal sense is concerned, it is not surprising that a reprobate person prophesied transiently for a moment, since many others are also recorded as having possessed a similar gift of prophecy. Such was that reprobate Balaam, whom Scripture does not fail to declare condemned by divine judgment, yet who nevertheless possessed prophecy.

Nor do those words written in the Gospel bear little witness to this view: many will say on that day, “Lord, Lord, in your name we ate and drank, and in your name we performed many mighty works.” To them he will say, “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matt. 25:41).

Mystically, however, the example of this Saul and his messengers represents in this statement certain heretics who possess something good from the gifts of the Holy Spirit—for example, the Testaments of the Law and the Gospel, and the sacrament of baptism.

When such people come to the Catholic Church, [Col. 0437D] what they possess must not in any way be violated or treated as though it were not something they have received and ought to hand on. Yet they should not for that reason be thought to possess salvation, simply because we do not reject what we believe they received. Rather, they must come to recognize unity and fellowship in the bond of love. Without this, whatever they may possess—even if it is holy and worthy of reverence—is of no benefit to them. They become all the less worthy of the reward of eternal life because they have not used well the gifts they received in this life, which is transitory.

Likewise, the example and image of this Saul and his messengers appropriately represent the Jews in this passage. While they desire to oppose Christ, they have the sacraments of the Law and the Prophets in their mouths, as a testimony to Christ; and with the Church, as with the prophets, they dispute from the Scriptures, just as those men prophesied with the prophets.

## CHAPTER XIII. Those sent against David begin to prophesy

[Col. 0438A]

David therefore rose and again fled from Saul’s presence. He came to the priest Abimelech, from whom he took Goliath’s sword and received the bread of the Presence. This event brought death upon the priest and punishment upon a religious city.

Such is the factual account of what happened. But as far as the mystery of prophecy is concerned, it was fulfilled in Christ our Lord. While he was present in the flesh and avoiding Jewish persecution, he passed over to the apostles, with whom he partook of the food he desired; for he had earnestly desired to eat the Passover.

From them he took Goliath’s weapons, that is, the devil’s weapons; for he himself, being strong, plundered the strong man’s goods. Against those by whom Christ was received, the devil brought tribulations and death. For, as the Apostle says, “All who desire to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12). And the Lord says, “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:20).

[Col. 0438B] In Doeg the Idumean, the person of Judas the betrayer is represented. Through him the devil acted in such a way that, after his betrayal had been carried out against Christ, the Church afterward suffered persecution; very many of Christ’s disciples and priests were killed, and they endured the gravest persecutions for the name of Christ.

## CHAPTER XIV. David comes to Abimelech the priest

Meanwhile, while David was fleeing from Saul, he wished to hide with a certain king of Gath named Achish. But when his glory had been reported to him, fearing that the same king to whom he had fled might, through envy, plot some harm against him, David feigned madness. As though seized by frenzy, he altered his behavior: saliva flowed down his beard, he collapsed in their hands, and he went out toward the doors of the gate.

King Achish said, “Why have you brought this man to me? Do we lack madmen?” And so he dismissed him.

Achish is interpreted as “How is it?” This signifies the ignorance of one who marvels at the Word but does not recognize it. [Col. 0438C] This was fulfilled among the Jewish people, who saw Christ but did not recognize him.

Before them he altered his mouth and departed. For there were carnal commandments of the Law, and there were sacrifices according to the order of Aaron. Later he himself instituted a sacrifice from his body and blood according to the order of Melchizedek.

He therefore altered his mouth in respect of the priesthood; he altered it in the commandments, giving another covenant and nullifying carnal observance. He then collapsed in their hands when they seized him and crucified him.

He went out toward the door of the gate—that is, he humbled himself even to the door of our faith. For the door of the gate is the beginning of faith. From there the Church begins and reaches toward vision. When it believes what it now sees, it will deserve to enjoy it when it begins to see him face to face.

As for the saliva that, in that apparent madness, flowed down his beard, the Apostle explains it by saying: “Jews demand signs, [Col. 0438D] and Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to the nations; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. For the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1:23–25).

Saliva signifies weakness. But when it says that the foolishness of God is stronger than human beings, do not attend merely to the saliva; attend to the fact that it flows over the beard. Just as weakness is shown in the saliva, so strength is shown in the beard. He therefore concealed his strength beneath the body of his weakness. What was weak outwardly appeared as saliva, but inwardly divine power was hidden as though beneath the beard.

## CHAPTER XV. David flees to King Lachis

Afterward, in the wilderness of Engaddi, when Saul was intent on pursuing David, David entered a cave and hid there. [Col. 0439A] But the king, unexpectedly caught in the trap, fell into what he had plotted against an innocent man. For it is written: “Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it himself” (Ecclus. 27:20).

David, however, repaying good for evil, did not kill his enemy; instead, as testimony to what had happened, he cut off the edge of the royal cloak. It would have been easier to destroy an adversary caught in a trap than merely to outwit him.

What, then, does it mean that this man, fleeing from Saul’s presence, hid in a cave? Why did he hide except to be concealed and not found? What is it to be covered by a cave except to be covered by earth? Whoever flees into a cave is covered by earth so that he cannot be seen.

Jesus carried earth—that is, flesh—which he had received from the earth, and concealed himself in it so that he would not be found by the Jews. “For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

Why, then, did they not find the Lord of glory? Because he had hidden himself in a cave: that is, he presented the weakness of his flesh to their eyes and concealed the majesty of his divinity beneath the covering of his body, as in the hidden recess of a cave.

They therefore, not recognizing God, persecuted a human being. [Col. 0439B] He could die only in a human being, and he could be crucified only in a human being, because he could not be held except as a human being.

He therefore placed earth before those who sought evil, but preserved life for those who sought good. According to the flesh, he fled from Saul’s presence into a cave, because he suffered, concealing himself from the Jews even to the point of death.

But why did he wish to remain patient even unto death, so that he might flee from Saul’s presence into a cave? A cave may be understood as the lower part of the earth. And certainly, as is manifest and known to all, his body was placed in a tomb that had been hewn from rock. That tomb was therefore a cave. Our David fled there from Saul’s presence. For the Jews pursued him until he was placed in the cave.

But what does it mean that Saul the persecutor entered the cave to relieve his bowels? It signifies that the Jews expelled, like a foul odor, the malice conceived in their minds against Christ; [Col. 0439C] and by their worse deeds, when they killed Christ, they displayed the harmful thoughts they had harbored within themselves.

Yet David did not wish to kill Saul. Although he had the persecutor in his power while hidden in the secret cave, he preferred to spare him rather than kill him. So also Christ, while he was in the cave of the flesh, had the persecuting people in his power, but did not kill them.

For it was written concerning them through the prophet: “Do not kill them.”

David therefore silently cut off only the edge of Saul’s cloak, to show prophetically that Christ did not kill the Jews but merely took away their royal glory, leaving them empty of throne and rule.

The cutting off of the cloak signifies the cutting off of the kingdom. Saul himself demonstrated this elsewhere when he sinned through disobedience. When he begged forgiveness and asked Samuel to return with him to appease God, Samuel refused. As he turned his face away and departed, Saul seized the corner of his garment and tore it. Samuel then said to him: “Today the Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand and will give it to your neighbor, and [Col. 0439D] Israel will be divided into two peoples.”

Thus this king figuratively bore the role of Israel, the people that was destined to lose its kingdom while it persecuted Christ.

## CHAPTER XVI. David takes the spear while Saul is sleeping

[Col. 0439D] This was demonstrated again shortly afterward, when the same David, fleeing from Saul’s presence, entered the king’s camp. Finding Saul asleep, he did not strike him or kill him, but took only the spear that was beside his head and the water jar, while everyone was sleeping. Then he left the camp and crossed over to the summit of the mountain.

What does this mean? The Jews were pursuing Christ, but in their pursuit they were sleeping, because they were not watchful in their hearts. Hardness of heart is a kind of sleep. They sleep in the old life and do not awaken to the new.

Christ came and did not kill them, but took from them the water jar—that is, the grace of the Law. He took away the royal insignia of kingship, the power in which they placed great value, by which they protected themselves temporally, and [Col. 0440A] which through unbelief they exercised against God.

Then our victorious David, having entered their camp and afterward departed, ascended to the height of the heavenly mountain.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Amalekites are overcome by David

Meanwhile, while David was fleeing and traveling with Achish king of the Philistines to battle against Israel, the Amalekites rose up, attacked Ziklag, destroyed it, and took captive everything that belonged to David and his men.

David therefore returned to pursue the Amalekites. He found an Egyptian boy exhausted; the Amalekites had abandoned him on the road when he had fallen ill. When David found him, he restored him with food and made him the guide of his journey. Thus he pursued the Amalekites, found them feasting, and utterly destroyed them.

What does it mean that the Egyptian boy, an Amalekite, became exhausted on the road, except that the lover of the present age, covered by the blackness of his sin, is often left behind by that same age, weak and despised? [Col. 0440B] He cannot run along with it, but, broken by adversity, grows sluggish.

David found him because our Redeemer, truly strong of hand, sometimes converts to his love those whom he finds despised by the world’s glory. He feeds him with food because he refreshes him with knowledge of the word. He chooses him as a guide for the journey because he also makes him a preacher.

The one who could not follow the Amalekites becomes David’s guide, because the person whom the world abandoned as unworthy not only receives God into his converted mind but also, by preaching, leads him even into the hearts of others.

With this guide, David finds and destroys the Amalekite while he is feasting, because those whom the world disdained to have as companions, by preaching Christ destroy the world’s pleasure.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Saul consults the witch

After Samuel’s death, when the Philistines had gathered [Col. 0440C] against Israel, Saul consulted the Lord, but he did not answer him. Saul then sought a witch who would raise Samuel for him. When Samuel was immediately raised, he said to Saul, “Why have you disturbed me so that I should be raised?”

Historically, it is asked whether the witch summoned the prophet himself from the underworld, or whether it was some imaginary apparition produced by the deceit of demons.

On this question, [Col. 0440D] Bishop Augustine of blessed memory wrote the following to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan:

“You ask, then, whether an evil spirit could raise the soul of a righteous person and, as though summoning it from the hidden repositories of the dead, call it forth so that it might be seen and speak with Saul. Is it not more astonishing that Satan himself took up the Lord and placed him upon the pinnacle of the temple? Whatever the manner in which he did it, it happened. In the same way, it remains hidden how Samuel was raised.

“Unless perhaps someone should say that the devil had easier permission to take up the living Lord wherever he wished and place him wherever he wished than to raise the spirit of the dead Samuel from its dwelling place. If the Gospel account does not disturb us in that case because the Lord willed and permitted it to happen, without any diminution of his power and divinity—for he allowed himself to be seized, bound, mocked, crucified, and killed by the Jews themselves, although they were perverse and unclean and were doing the works of the devil—then it is not absurd to believe that, by some dispensation of the divine will, it was permitted that the spirit of the holy prophet should appear before the king’s eyes, not unwillingly or under the domination of magical power, but willingly and obediently to God’s hidden dispensation, which was concealed from that witch and from Saul. Through this appearance the prophet’s spirit would pronounce the divine sentence by which Saul was to be struck.

“Nevertheless, there may be another and easier interpretation of this event: that we should not believe that Samuel’s spirit was truly raised from its rest, but rather that some phantom and imaginary apparition was produced by the devil’s machinations.

“For this reason Scripture calls it by the name of Samuel, because images are customarily called by the names of the things of which they are images. Thus everything that is painted or fashioned [Col. 0441A] is called by the names of the things of which it is an image. When a picture of a human being is made, each proper name is used without hesitation, and one says, ‘That is Cicero; that is Sallust; that is Achilles; that is Hector; this is the river Simois; that is Rome,’ although they are nothing other than painted images.

“Thus, although the cherubim are heavenly powers, the figures fashioned from metal, which God commanded to be placed above the ark of the covenant for the sake of signifying a great reality, were nevertheless called ‘cherubim.’ Likewise, when someone sees a dream, he does not say, ‘I saw an image of Augustine,’ but, ‘I saw Augustine,’ even though at the time when someone saw such a thing Augustine knew nothing about it. It is therefore perfectly clear that people see not the persons themselves but their images.

“Pharaoh likewise said that in his dream he had seen ears of grain and cattle, not images of ears of grain or cattle. If, then, it is clearly established that images are called by the names of the things of which they are images, it is not surprising [Col. 0441B] that Scripture says that Samuel was seen, even if perhaps an image of Samuel appeared, fashioned by the agency of him who transforms himself into an angel of light and equips his ministers as ministers of righteousness.

“Now, if it troubles you that true predictions were made to Saul by an evil spirit, it may also seem surprising how demons recognized Christ, whom the Jews did not recognize. When God wishes even weak spirits to know certain temporal truths—provided that they pertain to this mortal existence—it is easy and not incongruous for the omnipotent and just God, for the punishment of those to whom such things are foretold, so that they may suffer in advance through foreknowledge of the evil that threatens them, to impart some form of divination even to such spirits through the hidden arrangement of his mysteries. What they have heard from the angels, they may then announce to human beings.

“They hear only as much as the Lord and governor of all either commands or permits. Thus also, in the Acts of the Apostles, the spirit of the python bears witness to the Apostle Paul and attempts to act as an evangelist. [Col. 0441C] Yet these spirits mix deceit with the truth they have been able to know, and they proclaim it not so much to instruct as to deceive.

“Perhaps this is why, when that image of Samuel foretold to Saul that he would die, it also said that he would be with him. This is certainly false. [Col. 0442A] For in the Gospel we read that the good are separated from the wicked by a great interval after death, when it testifies that a great chasm had been placed between the proud rich man, already suffering torments in the underworld, and the one who had lain covered with sores at his gate but was now established in rest.

“Or, if Samuel said to him, ‘You will be with me,’ because this referred not to equality of blessedness but to a common condition of death—that both were human beings and both could die, and that the dead man was foretelling death to the living—then, according to either interpretation, this passage may be understood in a way that does not conflict with the faith.

“This is so unless, through a deeper investigation, it should be determined with certainty whether the human soul, after departing this life, can be summoned by magical incantations and appear to the sight of the living while bearing the features of a body, so that it can not only be seen but also recognized.

“And if this is possible, it must further be asked whether even the soul of a righteous person might be willing to appear—not compelled by magical rites, but consenting through more hidden mysteries and obeying the supreme law. If it should become clear that this cannot happen, [Col. 0442B] then both interpretations cannot be admitted in the exposition of this Scripture; once one has been excluded, the imagined likeness of Samuel, produced by a demonic rite, must be understood.

“Since, however, whether such a thing can happen or cannot happen, Satan’s deceit and his cunning operation in fabricating images remains multifaceted and constantly watchful for the deception of human senses, let us not hastily prescribe limits to more careful inquiry. Rather, let us suppose that something of this kind was done through the ministry of that witch’s evil spirit, so long as we are not granted the ability to devise or explain anything further.”

These are the things that blessed Augustine then wrote concerning the witch and Samuel.

## CHAPTER XIX. Saul and Jonathan are killed

When battle had therefore broken out, the Philistines struck Israel with a great blow, and Saul and Jonathan fell in the battle. The pious prophet then lamented them figuratively. Although they had been powerful and had always prevailed over their enemies, they were wounded and injured and immediately fell in the midst of battle.

“How have the mighty fallen in the midst of the battle?” he says.

In this way also the devout Christian people mourn those who, while fighting against demons, slip and fall in the world, which is slippery. For the mountains of Gilboa are interpreted as “slippery mountains.”

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0441]

## CHAPTER I. David is warned through the prophet not to build the temple

[Col. 0441C]

After Saul’s death, David was anointed and reigned; and he transferred the ark of the covenant to his own city. When he wished to build a temple for God, he was warned by the Lord through the prophet in these words: “You will not build a temple for me, because you are a man of blood.”

What, then, does it mean that David, who labored in external wars, was forbidden to build God’s house? We are God’s temple, because we are built for true life as his dwelling, as Paul bears witness when he says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple.”

But a man of blood is forbidden to build a temple for God because one who is still occupied with carnal deeds must not presume to build up the Church spiritually. For an eye burdened by dust cannot look clearly upon a blemish in a limb, and a hand holding mud cannot wipe away dirt that has been thrown upon it.

## CHAPTER II. On David’s sin with Bathsheba

I shall now touch briefly, as far as I can, upon what David’s sin signified prophetically. The names themselves, when interpreted, sufficiently show what this event also [Col. 0442C] prefigured.

David, as we have said, is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable.” Bathsheba means “well of satiety” or “seventh well.” Whichever of these interpretations of her name we adopt for the point we intend to make, it fits well enough.

For in the Song of Songs the bride, who is the Church for him, is called a well of living water; and the name of the number seven is joined to this well as a sign of the Holy Spirit, because of the significance of Pentecost, on which day the Holy Spirit came from heaven.

To forty-nine, which is seven times seven, one is added, by which unity is commended. In this interpretation lives that apostolic statement: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”

By the spiritual gift—that is, the gift of seven—the Church became a well of satiety, because in her there was made a spring of water leaping up into eternal life; whoever possesses it will never thirst.

Now, if we ask who her husband was, what else is signified by the interpretation of his name except the devil? To him, through a most evil marriage, all those had been assigned whom the grace of God frees, so that the Church, without spot or wrinkle, might be joined to her own Savior.

For Uriah is interpreted as “my light is God,” while Hittite means “cut off.” He was either cut off, on account of pride, from the heavenly light that he had from God because he did not stand in the truth, or, having fallen and lost his true powers, he transformed himself into an angel of light, daring to say to God, “My light is God.”

This David, then, sinned gravely and wickedly. God also reproved his crime through the prophet by rebuking him, and David himself washed it away through repentance.

Nevertheless, that desirable one of all nations, walking as though on a roof terrace—for he placed his tabernacle in the sun—loved the Church as she washed herself upon the roof, that is, as she cleansed herself from the filth of the world and transcended and trampled upon the earthly house through spiritual contemplation.

Having begun with her the first acquaintance of their union, he afterward killed the devil, who had been completely separated from her, and joined her to himself in an everlasting marriage.

Let us therefore hate sin, but let us not extinguish the prophecy. Let us love that David as much as he ought to be loved who, through mercy, freed us from the devil. Let us also love this David, who healed in himself so grave a wound of iniquity through the confession of repentance and humility.

But perhaps someone may say: If David bore the image of Christ, how is it written that he had many wives and concubines, when Christ both detests and condemns such things?

This happened for the sake of the figure. David’s many wives indicated the image of the many peoples and nations who would be joined through faith to the fellowship of Christ. His concubines, however, signify the churches of heretics, which boast that they remain under the title of Christ’s name; but because they pursue Christ for carnal profit, they are called not wives but concubines.

Accordingly, if kings today have several wives or concubines, it is a crime, because the figures for which pardon was granted in the case of wives or concubines have now passed away. But now that the figures have passed away, no pardon is granted.

## CHAPTER III. On Absalom

What does it signify that Absalom, the parricidal son, pursued his father, while his father at first withdrew and fled from before him, confident of victory because he knew that the impious man would perish? Yet he also mourned him with great grief and lamented the death of the parricide.

For it is written that David fled from the presence of his son who was waging war against him. And because it is written concerning the people of Jerusalem, “I nourished and exalted children, but they rejected me,” that same Jewish people, which betrayed Christ, was figuratively signified by his impious son.

Absalom, as some interpret it, is understood as “the father’s peace.” This seems strange in the historical account: how can “the father’s peace” be understood of one who pursued his father in war?

But those who attend carefully to the allegory recognize that Absalom is Jerusalem, whose name is also interpreted as “peace.” From Jerusalem’s presence Christ fled when, abandoning it through his suffering, he withdrew in faith among the nations.

Others understand Absalom as Judas the betrayer, whom Christ endured with such great and astonishing patience as though he were good, even though he knew his thoughts; Christ admitted him to the meal at which he commended and handed on to the disciples the figure of his body and blood.

Finally, at the very moment of the betrayal, Judas received a kiss. It is rightly understood that Christ offered peace to his betrayer, although Judas was being ravaged by the inward war of such a wicked thought. Absalom is therefore called “the father’s peace” because the father possessed the peace that Absalom did not possess.

## CHAPTER IV. On the fact that David orders water to be brought to him from the cistern at Bethlehem
David himself, too, during the battle with the Philistines, when he was thirsty and searching for water, said: “Who will give me a drink from the cistern that is in Bethlehem?” The cistern was near the gate, while David was surrounded by enemies, and the enemy forces had encircled the camp. Three men broke through the mass of their adversaries, drew water from the cistern that was in Bethlehem, and brought it to the king to drink. But the king refused to drink it; instead, he poured it out to the Lord and said: “Far be it from me to do this—to drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives.” Thus he conquered nature: though thirsty, he did not drink, and he gave an example of himself, [Col. 0444B] by which the whole army might learn to endure thirst. But if you wish to look more deeply and peer into the mystery, David knew not the water that is in Bethlehem, but Christ, born in that same Bethlehem from a virgin, whom he foresaw in the spirit. Therefore he wished to drink not the water of a stream, but the cleansing that flowed from Christ’s side. That is, he was not thirsting for the element of water, but for the blood of Christ. Hence he did not drink the water offered to him, but poured it out to the Lord, signifying that he thirsted for Christ’s sacrifice—not for a natural stream, but for that sacrifice in which there would be forgiveness of sins; he thirsted for the eternal fountain, not one sought through the dangers of others, but one that would remove the dangers of others.

## CHAPTER V. Why the seventeenth Psalm alone is found in the Books of Kings

It is asked why only the seventeenth Psalm is found written in the Books of Kings. And rightly this Psalm alone is found in the Books of Kings, [Col. 0444C] because it signifies that kingdom in which we shall have no adversary. Its title is: “On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.” For who is represented in David except the one who came in the flesh from David’s seed? In his body, which is the Church, he still suffers enemies. Hence, concerning that persecutor whom he slew by his voice and, as it were, consumed by incorporating him into his own body, there sounded from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” But when does he deserve to seize this body of his from the hand of all its enemies, except when that last enemy, death, is also destroyed, so that he may attain the kingdom of God?

## CHAPTER VI. The catalogue of David’s mighty men as a type of the saints

Next is woven the catalogue of mighty men, as a figure of the saints. Although they advance in the greatness of their virtues, they nevertheless do not reach the excellence of the divine [Col. 0444D] Trinity. Hence it is written there: “He did not reach the three.” For who can be compared with the Lord, or who can be like God among the sons of God?

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0443]

## CHAPTER I. Solomon

[Col. 0443D]

Solomon follows, in whom a certain image of what was to come was made—in that he built the temple and had peace, in accordance with his name. For Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful.” And [Col. 0444D] this name most truly suits the one through whom, having received the remission of sins from our enemies, we are reconciled to God as mediator. Indeed, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son. He himself is that peaceful one who made both one, breaking down the dividing wall of hostility in his flesh and abolishing the law of commandments by decrees, so that he might create [Col. 0445A] the two in himself as one new man, making peace; and coming, he proclaimed peace to those far away and peace to those near. In the Gospel he himself says: “I leave you peace; my peace I give you” (John XIV, 27). By these and many other testimonies the Lord Christ is shown to be the peaceful one.

## CHAPTER II. The building of the temple

In that he built a most excellent temple for the Lord, he also signifies Christ, because Christ built a dwelling for God in the heavens—not from wood and stones, but from holy people, that is, from believers. To them the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (II Cor. XVI, 16).

But the fact that this same house was built with stones hewn and finished, and that neither hammer nor axe nor any iron tool was heard in the temple of God while it was being built—what did that house signify, as was said above, [Col. 0445B] except the holy Church, which the Lord inhabits in the heavens? For its construction the souls of the elect are brought forward like polished stones. When it is built in heaven, no hammer of discipline resounds there, because we are brought there as stones already hewn and finished, so that we may be arranged in places suited to our merit. We are struck outside for this reason: so that we may be found there without reproach.

The multitude [F. *altitudo*, “height”] of this temple of the Lord refers to faith, its length to hope, and its breadth to charity. Through these three virtues, as through the lines of the holy Church, its heavenly structure rises.

Moreover, the fact that the inner walls of the temple were covered with wood was fashioned as a mystery of the Lord’s cross, under whose protection all the saints are sheltered. Like living stones, through perseverance in unbroken peace, they are established in the structure of the Church by the unity of faith. The temple is rightly clothed inwardly with wood, because one believes with the heart unto righteousness.

The fact that, at the time of the dedication, the glory of the Lord filled [Col. 0445C] the house means that the glory of the Lord is Christ, with whose faith Moses was filled so that he might spare the sinful people. The Lord answered: “I will be merciful to them. Nevertheless, as I live, and as my name lives, the whole earth shall be filled with my glory.” The seventy-first Psalm likewise sings: “The whole earth shall be filled with my glory.” Hence the angels cried out to the shepherds: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14).

But the fact that a cloud filled the house of God, and that the priests could not minister because of the cloud, indicates the proud Jewish chief priests and teachers. While they disdain to investigate the mysteries of Christ’s birth, they lost the ministry owed by their faith through the cloud of error. The darkness of unbelief filled their minds so completely that, as their own merits demanded, they did not recognize the worship of faith.

Again, the fact that Solomon made twelve bronze oxen in the same temple and set them in a bronze basin, facing in [Col. 0445D] different directions but joined together in one place at the rear—what else do we believe is signified by the twelve oxen except the twelve Apostles? They look toward different directions with their faces, but they are placed in the basin so that they are united from behind. In the present life they are divided among different parts of the world for the duty of preaching; but in the life that follows this one, they come together in the unity of eternal glory.

Thus they look out over the diverse world while preaching, but stand together in unity. They are bronze because the sound of their preaching resounded throughout the whole world, as it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Psalm XVIII, 5). By the basin we understand the circle of the earth, whose circumference the Apostles traversed while teaching the nations to be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER III. Solomon’s wisdom

[Col. 0446A]

Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered five thousand. What else is signified by the three thousand proverbs except the fullness of faith in the Law and in the Gospels, handed down by Christ? Since this fullness is described in many ways through allegorical meaning under the mystery of the Trinity, it is called “three thousand proverbs.”

His five thousand songs are understood through the five bodily senses. Whoever governs them well through various virtues is blessed, and through them he sings to the Lord, as it were, five thousand songs.

Solomon also discoursed from the cedar to the hyssop. By the cedar is understood the height of heavenly glory, as the Prophet also testifies: “The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree, and shall multiply like the cedar that is in Lebanon” (Psalm XCI, 13). Hyssop, however, is a lowly plant clinging to rock, by which Christ’s humility is signified.

Our Redeemer therefore discoursed from the cedar to the hyssop, because he descended from the lofty excellence of heavenly [Col. 0446B] glory until he reached the humility of the flesh. Indeed, by the name of cedar the proud arrogance of the wicked is also signified, as David says: “The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars” (Psalm XXVIII). Thus Christ discourses from the cedar to the hyssop, because he judges the hearts of the wicked and of the humble (Eccles. III).

He also discoursed over wood when he hung upon the cross. For then he bent down the arrogance of the world’s cedar, since he brought it down even to the humility of hyssop—that is, to the foolishness of the cross and to faith despised by the world.

## CHAPTER IV. Solomon’s judgment

It is also read that this most wise man first rendered judgment between two women contending over affection. In one of them love was burning; in the other, pretense was stealing what did not belong to it.

In that judgment, therefore, Solomon [Col. 0446C] was a figure of Christ. There the wicked woman represented the impious people—namely, the synagogue or the heretics—who desired the son of the true mother, that is, the Church, not in order to preserve him, but truly in order to kill him.

But just as, when Solomon’s sword divided them, the groaning of the true mother revealed the genuine child, so also, when the Spirit of Jesus Christ teaches, those who have been seduced by their mother and caught in the error of heretics sometimes deserve to recognize the Church, their mother, groaning on their behalf.

Thus it appears sufficiently and appropriately that this woman represented the impiety of the heretics or of the Synagogue. They wickedly kill their own children by nurturing them, and by enticing others they invade them until they destroy them.

## CHAPTER V. The queen of the South

The queen of the South, who, stirred from the remotest regions, came desiring to hear Solomon’s wisdom, [Col. 0446D] already then represented the future queen from the Gentiles who would desire Christ.

According to the prophetic word, she was “surrounded with variety, clothed in golden garments” (Psalm XLVI); she had forgotten her own people and her father’s house. She hastened, barbarian in nation but not in mind: outwardly she was a foreigner, yet inwardly she desired to become a citizen of the saints.

Therefore she is considered worthy not only of the heavenly reward of resurrection, but also of apostolic authority to judge adulterous Jews, in the very mouth of the Judge. Having marveled at Christ in Solomon, she had fulfilled, in the mystical image of the Church, the true longing of the heavenly queen.

## CHAPTER VI. Solomon’s other works

What, then, shall I say about Solomon’s other works, since Holy Scripture severely reproves and condemns him? It records nothing about his repentance or about God’s indulgence toward him. Nor does anything at all [Col. 0447A] occur that signifies something good in allegory through this lamentable downfall of his—unless perhaps someone should say that the foreign women, with love for whom he burned, signify the elect churches from the Gentiles.

This could perhaps be understood without absurdity if, for Solomon’s sake, they had abandoned their gods and worshiped his God. But since he offended his God on their account and worshiped their gods, nothing good can be inferred from it.

Nevertheless, I do not think that it signifies nothing; rather, it signifies evil, as we said concerning Lot’s wife and daughters. In the person of this Solomon there appears both extraordinary excellence and extraordinary overthrow.

Therefore, what existed in him at different times—first good, then evil—is displayed in the Church in this present age both together and at one time. For I think that by his good are signified the good members of the Church, and by his evil the evil members of the Church, as within the unity of one threshing floor the good are in the grain and the evil in the chaff, or within the unity of one field the good are in the wheat and the evil in the weeds.

## CHAPTER VII. The division of the ten tribes

[Col. 0447B]

The fact that after Solomon’s death ten tribes were separated from the temple, while two remained, sufficiently indicates what the Apostle says concerning that whole people: “A remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. IX).

## CHAPTER VIII. Elijah and Elisha

What did those great and distinguished [Col. 0448A] prophets signify, who also performed many miracles—Elijah and Elisha, his disciple?

Elijah is fed during a time of famine, with ravens bringing bread in the morning and meat in the evening, so that Christ may be understood: sinners confess faith to him, as it were hungering for our salvation, now having the first fruits of the Spirit (Rom. VIII), but at the end, as it were at the evening of the world, also the resurrection of the flesh.

Elijah is sent to be fed by a foreign widow, who wished to gather two pieces of wood before she died. Here the sign of the cross is expressed not only by the name of wood but also by the number of pieces of wood.

The flour and oil are blessed: the fruit and joy of charity, which, when expended, is said not to fail. “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX).

By blessing his widow, I think, the Church is signified, whom Christ fed not with grain but with the bread of the word. Concerning her David says: “Blessing his widow, I will bless” (Psalm CXXXI)—that widow, namely, whom the Apostle says, once her husband has died, [Col. 0448B] is free to marry whom she wishes (I Cor. VII).

When the Law came to an end, whose end is Christ (Rom. X), the Church, passing over into the liberty of grace, married Christ as though she were the widow of the Law.

Now in her vessels the oil of grace and the flour of blessing do not fail, while hunger remains throughout the foreign nations. Their lack of food for life and of faith in the Trinity was aptly prefigured by that former three-year famine.

The fact that, during the time of drought, that cloud appeared through Elijah and that, as a sign of the rain to come, the trace of a human being was later seen, signified that, when Christ was born in the likeness of a human being, rain would descend from heaven upon the earth and cleanse us from sin.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0447]

## CHAPTER I. The two companies of fifty, burned with their soldiers by fire

[Col. 0447C]

“The impious king sends two companies of fifty with the soldiers subject to them to bring Elijah before him; they are consumed by divine fire. But the third who is sent is saved.”

The number fifty is a confession of repentance, which declares the remission of sins. Therefore the Jews, unwilling to acknowledge the Lord Christ as perfect, or as the prince of repentance, say to him: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” (John VIII).

These are to be extinguished in the future by divine fire. But the third company of fifty, because it was converted to the faith and recognized the mysteries of the Trinity, obtained pardon.

## CHAPTER II. Elisha heals the barren and bitter waters of Jericho

[Col. 0447D]

“Elisha is asked by the people to heal the barren and bitter waters of Jericho. He takes a rough vessel, puts salt into it, and casts it into the river; immediately the waters are healed.”

By this deed the prophet proclaimed that “the Word would become flesh and dwell among us” (John I). Therefore, in the likeness of the Word, he “put salt—that is, wisdom—into an earthen vessel, into this human body, and cast it into the water.”

This signified that all the peoples, represented under the figure of waters, who were barren throughout the world, would receive fruitfulness and blessing through Christ’s incarnation.

## CHAPTER III. The children cursed by Elisha and devoured by beasts

The prophet Elisha himself also bore the figure of Christ. Indeed, his very name is interpreted as “salvation of God.” And who is the salvation of God [Col. 0448C] except his Son, who is everywhere also called the Savior?

The children who mocked the salvation of God—that is, Elisha—represented the Jews, who mocked the Lord the Savior on the way to the cross. They said: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead,” because Christ was to ascend the cross at the place of Calvary.

But when “Elisha turned and cursed them, and two bears came out of the forest and killed forty-two of the boys who were blaspheming,” so also Christ, after his passion and resurrection from the dead, after he had ascended into heaven—as Elisha ascended to Bethel, that is, to the house of God—turned and cursed the Jews. In the forty-second year after his ascension, he sent against them two bears from the forests of the Gentiles, namely Vespasian and Titus, and they struck them down in a cruel slaughter.

## CHAPTER IV. The staff sent by the servant, and the dead man who was not raised

[Col. 0448D]

“Elisha sends a staff by a servant upon the dead man, but he does not revive. He comes himself, joins himself to the dead man, fits himself to him, and the dead man revives.”

The Word of God sent the Law through his servant, but it did not benefit the human race, which was dead in sins. He himself came, descending from the heights of heaven as though from the summit of a mountain; he humbled himself (Philipp. II), conformed himself to us, joined his limbs to our dead limbs, and applied medicine for our mortality from his own body.

Then he breathes seven times over the dead man and gives the sevenfold Spirit to the human race, through whom the person brought to life rises from the death of sins.

## CHAPTER V. The iron and wood that leap into the depths and return to the wood

“When wood was being cut with axes, the iron leaped from the wood, sank into the depths of the river, and, when Elisha threw wood upon it from above, returned to the wood” (Col. 0449A).

Thus, when the presence of Christ operating through his body was cutting down the impious Jews as fruitless trees—for John had said concerning him: “Behold, the axe is laid at the root of the trees” (Matt. III)—the body itself departed from them when the passion intervened and descended into the depths of hell. After it had been laid in the tomb, it rose again, as though returning to its handle when the spirit came back.

## CHAPTER VI. Hezekiah’s illness and the fifteen years added to his life

“When Hezekiah was lying on his bed and suffering from a severe illness, the prophet Isaiah approached him in the name of the Lord, announcing that he would die. But he prayed to the Lord at the very appointed time of death; immediately God heard his voice and granted the one who prayed fifteen additional years of life.”

What mystery does this number of fifteen years contain? For, as the Apostle says: “As a person has acted, so shall he receive” (Eph. VI; Coloss. [Col. 0449B] III).

Therefore, because this king had completed the Decalogue of the Law together with the five books of Moses through complete observance, he received fifteen years added to his life according to the number of the Law that he had kept.

Through this we are to understand figuratively that all who preserve the fullness of the entire Law through the mystery of this number attain the reward of eternal salvation and, through the consummation of the Law, pass over into the fullness of eternal life.

As a sign of the salvation to be granted to this king, it is written that the sun turned backward over the ten steps of his house, on which the shadow customarily descended, and returned toward the rising point from which it had ascended. Let us see what mystery this number contains.

These steps are the sequences of time through which the shadow of the figures of Christ descended; through them, in turn, Christ, the sun of righteousness, ascended after the resurrection.

The first step of descent—from God into the angel—was in the angel who was the messenger of the great counsel. Hence Jacob also speaks in this way: “And the angel of God said: I am the one to whom you anointed the title and vowed the vow” (Gen. XXXI), [Col. 0449C] so that he might show both an angel and God.

The second step of descent—from the angel into the patriarchs—was in the patriarchs, “because, as the Apostle says, he himself worked in all things” (I Cor. XII).

The third was in the giving of the Law, “because he himself also spoke in the Law.”

The fourth step was in Joshua, “so that he might lead the people into the land of promise.”

The fifth was in the judges, “because through them he himself ruled the same people.”

The sixth was in the kings of the Jews, “because in them he himself reigned.”

The seventh was in the prophets, “because through them he was proclaimed.”

The eighth was in the chief priests, “because he himself is the great Priest of the Father.”

The ninth was in the human being.

The tenth was in the passion.

Through these ten steps, by which Christ himself descended as the shadow of the ancient Law, Christ the sun of righteousness again ascended through the same steps into heaven after his resurrection and illuminated that entire shadow of the Law with the rays of truth, revealing obscure things, opening what was closed, and uncovering everything that was hidden.

## CHAPTER VII. Hezekiah’s riches displayed to the Chaldeans through the disease of boastfulness

[Col. 0449D]

The fact that King Hezekiah lost his riches by displaying them boastfully to the Chaldeans, and therefore heard through the prophet that they would be carried away, signifies the servant of God who, after losing his virtues through empty glory, soon loses them altogether. The treasures of good works are thereby shown to pass, through an unhappy exchange, into the dominion of demons, just as Hezekiah, through his desire for display, caused his treasures to pass under the dominion of the Chaldeans.

## CHAPTER VIII. The transmigration to Babylon under King Nebuchadnezzar

As for the transmigration itself to Babylon—when the Spirit of God, through the prophet Jeremiah, commands them to go there and pray for those in whose kingdom they are living as foreigners, because their peace would also be their peace, and [Col. 0450A] to build houses, renew vineyards, and plant gardens—who would fail to recognize what this prefigured, if he considered that the Israelite men “in whom there is no deceit” were transferred, through apostolic administration, together with the mystery of the Gospel, to the kingdom of the Gentiles?

Therefore the Apostle, as though repeating Jeremiah, says to us: “I desire, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and charity. For this is good and acceptable before our Savior God, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II).

For from this, even for those who believed, dwellings of peace were built: the basilicas of Christian assemblies; renewed vineyards, the peoples of the faithful; and planted gardens, where, among all the vegetables, that grain of mustard also reigns. Beneath its far-reaching [Col. 0450B] shade even the lofty arrogance of the nations rests, like the birds of heaven.

## CHAPTER IX. The seventy years of captivity and Jesus the priest

The fact that after seventy years, according to the prophecy of the same Jeremiah, the people return from captivity and the temple is renewed—what believer would not understand that, after the periods of time have passed which run their course through the repetition of the number seven in the days, we too, that is, the Church of God, must return from our pilgrimage in this world to that heavenly Jerusalem, through Jesus Christ the great Priest?

That Jesus, the great priest of that time, through whom the temple was built after the captivity, bore the figure of Christ. The prophet Zechariah saw him in filthy clothing, while the devil stood accusing him. The filthy garment was removed from him [Col. 0450C] and a garment of honor and glory was given to him.

So the body of Jesus Christ, which is the Church, after the adversary has been overcome in the judgment at the end of time, is taken from the mourning of pilgrimage into the glory of eternal salvation.

This is also sung most clearly in the Psalm of the dedication of the house: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with sorrow” (Psalm XXIX).

## CHAPTER X. The vessels of the Lord carried away to Babylon, and the Babylonian king as a type of the devil

The fact that a former king of Babylon carried away from Jerusalem the vessels of the Lord, appointed for sacrifices or mystical sacraments, and likewise led away captives and assigned them to his own uses; but that, after the captivity had been dissolved through God’s mercy, those vessels were brought back—not melted down—and again devoted to divine worship: the Babylonian king is the devil.

[Col. 0450D]

He led the unhappy people away from Jerusalem—that is, the Church—through the captivity of their bodies into Babylon, that is, into the confusion of heretical perversity.

But the portion of the vessels also signifies the sacraments themselves, through which the perfection of divine worship is fulfilled. Some of our heretics have carried away these things with them: first, the very name—they are called Christians; they have carried away the Law, the Gospel, the Apostle, the Psalter, baptism, “Amen,” and “Alleluia.”

## CHAPTER XI. The people’s return to Jerusalem

When, under the Lord’s regard, the people hasten to return to Jerusalem—that is, to the vision of peace, which is the Church of the living God—having abandoned ignorance through confession and being led by the Lord, they carry these vessels, that is, the sacraments, with them. They do not alter them but bring them back intact.

They do not break them as though they needed to be renewed for the better; rather, they restore them to the old temple and adapt them there to divine uses, rejoicing that they were not lost among the impious but preserved even among them and restored to the people.

[Col. 0451A]

We do not erase the Gospel; we do not obliterate the Apostle; we do not change “Amen” or “Alleluia”; we do not repeat baptism.

## CHAPTER XII. The Maccabees

[Col. 0451B]

What shall I say about the Maccabean brothers, who under King Antiochus endured dreadful tortures for the sacred laws?

Their devout mother, while she was being subjected to various punishments, not only did not weep but, rejoicing, encouraged them toward the glory of martyrdom. So also the mother Church rejoices and struggles in her martyrs, attaining greater glory through the martyrdoms of her children while she celebrates that they have overcome the devil through the sevenfold Spirit.

Who could touch upon, with whatever brevity, all that is announced figuratively in those ancient books of the Law and the Prophets? Unless perhaps someone thinks that it is merely a product of ingenuity to turn into mystical meanings, through interpretation, those things that unfolded in the order of events over their appointed times. Perhaps the Jews—or the pagans—dared to say this.

But apostolic authority presses down the necks of those who wish to call themselves Christians. Instructing certain people, the Apostle says: “All these things happened to them in figure” (I Cor. X); “and all these things were figures for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.”

And all things have been brought to completion in mysteries through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor, glory, kingdom, and power, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER XIII. How many years are reckoned from the departure of Simon Maccabee to the birth of Christ

From the departure of Simon Maccabee, 128 years are reckoned up to the birth of Christ.

His son John, who was also called Hyrcanus, held the high priesthood for twenty-seven years after his father. After him, Aristobulus, the son of John, held it for one year. After him, Alexander Jannaeus was king and high priest for twenty-seven years.

Then his wife Alexandra, who was [Col. 0451C] also called Salissa, ruled the kingdom of the Jews for nine years. After her, her son Hyrcanus ruled for thirty-four years. After him the foreigner Herod succeeded to the kingdom, and in the thirty-second year of his reign Christ was born.

## CHAPTER XIV. David kills the lion and the bear

David said to Saul: “Your servant was tending his father’s flock, and a lion and a bear came and carried off a ram from the midst of the flock. I pursued them, struck them, and tore it from their mouths; and they rose up against me. I seized their jaws, strangled them, and killed them. For I, your servant, killed both the lion and the bear” (I Reg. XVII).

David signifies Christ. By the lion and the bear, the persecutors of the holy Church are signified. By the lion, the emperors and other rulers of the earth; by the bear, the Jews, who persecuted the Church of God. By the ram, the martyrs are signified.

The lion and the bear therefore came [Col. 0451D] and carried off the ram from the midst of the flock, because the persecutors took certain faithful people from the Church and killed them under the name of their neighbor.

And just as David pursued the lion and the bear, struck them, and rescued the ram from their mouths, so our Redeemer pursued certain persecutors when he inflicted on them, in the present age, the punishment they deserved—as first upon Herod, and then upon others, a second and a third time, and upon many others.

He struck them when he condemned them to eternal death. He rescued the ram from their mouths because he freed the people of the faithful from being torn apart by them.

They rose up again against David because, during the times of persecution, when some were being punished, others rose up against Christ in order to extinguish his name and worship completely.

But David seized their jaws, strangled them, and killed them. By the jaw, which is close to the mouth, the blasphemies of the Jews and pagans are signified.

Christ [Col. 0452A] seized the jaws of the persecutors, strangled them, and killed them when, after the emperors believed in Christ, all the worship and error of the Gentiles was so suffocated that none of the persecutors dared open his mouth to blaspheme Christ. All were extinguished when the nations believed in Christ.

The same David, when he went to battle against the Philistine, took with him his staff, which he always held in his hands. He chose five very smooth stones from the stream, put them into the bag that he had with him, took a sling in his hand, and advanced against the Philistine (ibid.).

By the staff, by which a person is supported, the Apostles are signified. They supported Christ, as it were, when they completed the work for which he had come into the world, as the Apostle says: “For we are God’s fellow workers” (I Cor. III).

By his bag, his humanity is signified. By the five stones, the five books of Moses are signified, which he put into the bag because he gave the human being whom he assumed knowledge of the five books.

By the sling we may understand his tongue.

David’s advance [Col. 0452B] against the Philistine can be understood allegorically in two ways.

Our Savior advanced against the Philistine when he was led by the Holy Spirit into the desert to be tempted by the devil (Matt. IV) and to conquer the devil. David put five stones into his bag but struck down Goliath with one, because our Savior possessed equally the knowledge of the five books, but from one book—that is, Deuteronomy—he drew three testimonies, by which he conquered the devil’s three temptations.
