And just as David hurled the stone with the sling and killed Goliath, so also our Lord brought forth the testimonies of sacred Scripture with his tongue and overcame the devil.

Alternatively: David proceeded to battle against the Philistine; likewise Christ hastened toward his passion in order to conquer the devil. David struck down Goliath with a stone; likewise Christ destroyed the devil by his death.

Although David had no sword in his hand, he took the Philistine’s sword, killed him with his own sword, and cut off his head (I Reg. XVII).

[Col. 0452C]

The devil’s sword is death. “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. II). This is the sword by which he killed the first human being, and then the human race, until it was redeemed by Christ. We incur this sword when we sin.

But Christ did not possess this sword, because he committed no sin, and “no deceit was found in his mouth” (I Peter II). Nor was he liable to original sin, because he had not been born from a man’s intercourse, which cannot be without sin.

Thus Christ, who did not owe death, borrowed death from the devil, who was its author, and through death killed that very prince of death.

By the head of the Philistine, the human race is signified in this passage. David cut off the Philistine’s head because Christ separated the multitude of the elect from the devil’s body. He carried it to Jerusalem (I Reg. XVII) because he placed the multitude of the elect in the heavenly blessedness called Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XV. Ahab persecutes Elijah

[Col. 0452D]

In the Book of Kings it is written: “When King Ahab of Israel had begun to persecute Elijah, at the Lord’s command he went into the wilderness and sat beside the torrent of Cherith. Ravens also brought him bread and meat morning and evening, and he drank from the torrent” (III Kings 17).

Elijah prefigured Christ; by the torrent of Cherith we ought to understand the Law. *Cherith* is interpreted as “falsehood”—not because the Law is false. For wise men commonly set parables before their hearers so that what they wish to convey may be understood more clearly, and they introduce speaking beasts and birds. If you attend only to the words of the parables, you will see that they are falsehood; but if you attend to their meaning, you will recognize the truth.

Likewise, certain legal precepts, if you attend only to the letter, will seem useless to you; but if you attend to their spiritual meaning, great truth shines forth for you in the letter. Thus certain legal precepts are falsehoods to the Jews, because they understand them carnally; but to us they are truth, since we take care to understand them spiritually.

By the ravens, however, the priests of the Jews are signified, darkened by the veil over their hearts. By the meat, the perpetual sacrifice is signified, which was offered both morning and evening. The loaves signify the bread of the Presence, which was continually placed before the Lord. He drank from the torrent (ibid.) because Christ took delight in the observances of the Law.

After many days the torrent dried up (ibid.), because, when Christ came in the flesh and preached the Gospel, observance of the Law ceased and from that time achieved nothing, as the Lord says: “The Law and the prophets lasted until John” (Luke 16). And again he says to Israel through the prophet: “Do not continue to offer sacrifice in vain; incense is an abomination to me. I will not endure your new moons and Sabbaths; your assemblies are wicked” (Isa. 1).

And the Lord said to Elijah: “Go to Sarephath of the Sidonians, and remain there. For I have commanded a widow there to feed you.” He arose and went to Sarephath (III Kings 17).

Elijah went to Sarephath because Christ, abandoning the faithless Jews, passed through his apostles to the Gentiles. *Sarephath* is interpreted as “burned” or “bread-distress.” For the Gentiles, who were the city of the devil and are signified by Sarephath, were burned by the fire of their vices. Concerning this fire Scripture says: “All of you who kindle a fire, girded with flames, walk in the light of your fire and in the flames which you have kindled for yourselves” (Isa. 50). They are girded with flames who are burned on every side by the fire of their vices. They are also called “bread-distress,” because no preacher had ever approached them to impart to them the nourishment of God’s word.

When he came to the gate of the city, a widow appeared to him gathering sticks (III Kings 17). The woman has the same signification as the city: they signify the Church gathered from the Gentiles. She was a widow because, through the demands of her sins, she had lost God as her husband.

And he called her and said to her: “Bring me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink” (ibid.). He asked for lesser things in order to arrive at greater ones. By “a little water,” which refreshes the soul of the thirsty, we may understand the willingness of the hearers, because just as water refreshes the tongue of the thirsty, so the ready disposition of hearers refreshes the minds of preachers.

When she was going to bring it, he called after her, saying: “Bring me also a morsel of bread in your hand” (ibid.). What we do not know is, as it were, behind our backs. Elijah therefore called out behind the woman because holy preachers proclaimed to the Gentiles the God whom they did not know. By the morsel of bread we may understand the beginnings of faith. And because those who first take care to confess their sins come appropriately to faith, it is rightly added:

The woman said: “As the Lord your God lives, I have no bread, except as much as a handful of flour can hold in a jar, and a little oil in a small vessel” (ibid.). The *lecythus* was a vessel in which oil was kept.

By the flour, we may understand reason; by the oil, works of mercy. Thus the Gentile people, recognizing that they had grievously gone astray, confessed that there was nothing good in them except only that they seemed to possess a little reason and a little from works of mercy. For the Gentiles had little reason: they were rational in part, but for the greater part irrational. What is more irrational than saying to wood or stone, “You are my god”? They also had little mercy, because nature itself often impelled them to help the wretched.

By the vessels containing the flour and oil, their hearts are signified.

“I am gathering two sticks,” she said, “that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son, so that we may eat and die” (ibid.).

The sticks gathered in the city are useful for nothing except to be burned in the fire. By the sticks, therefore, the errors of the Gentiles, devised through diabolical fraud, are signified. The woman gathered two sticks because the Gentile people gathered various errors from the teaching of philosophers and poets, for which they would be thrust into everlasting fire.

But what does she mean by saying, “So that we may eat and die”? We eat in order to preserve life in the body; but she says that she will eat in order to die because the teaching of the Gentiles brings death rather than life.

To her Elijah said: “Go, and do as you have said. Nevertheless, first make me from that little flour a small cake baked in ashes, and bring it to me; afterward you shall make one for yourself and your son.”

By bread, faith is signified; by ashes, repentance is often signified, as blessed Job says to the Lord: “Therefore I rebuke myself, and I do penance in dust and ashes.” The bread is therefore covered with ashes when an unbeliever comes to faith and first takes care to mourn the evils he has committed, so that he may approach more suitably to receive the faith of Christ, which is given in baptism.

Elijah therefore commanded the woman to make bread from the flour and bring it to him because holy preachers urged the Gentiles to prepare from the good of reason, which they had received from God, the food of faith for God and to bring it to him. Each person brings faith to the preacher when, in response to the priest’s question about how he believes, he confesses his faith.

Elijah ate the bread which the woman made because the progress of the children is the reward of preachers. Therefore Elijah commanded the woman to prepare for him first, and afterward for herself and her son, because the conversion of the sinner is first credited to the preacher; afterward the converted person prepares bread for himself when, exercising himself in good works, he obtains the result that he may become heir of the heavenly homeland.

When Elijah says, “The jar of flour shall not fail, nor shall the small vessel of oil diminish, until the day on which the Lord gives rain upon the earth,” this signifies that faith and good works will not fail from the hearts of the elect until the Lord comes to judgment with all his saints.

## CHAPTER XVI. Elisha Cleanses Naaman the Syrian from Leprosy

Elisha prefigured Christ, while Naaman signified the people of the Gentiles. There were many lepers in Israel, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian (Luke 4), because when Christ came in the flesh, both Jews and Gentiles were surrounded by the leprosy of their sins.

But while the Jews remained in their iniquity, the Gentiles were cleansed from the leprosy of their sins. Therefore Elisha commanded Naaman, saying: “Go and wash seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh shall be restored, and you shall be clean.” He went and washed, and his flesh became like the flesh of a little child, and he was cleansed from his leprosy (IV Kings 5).

The water of the Jordan prefigured baptism, because Christ was baptized in it. Naaman was washed in the waters of the Jordan and cleansed from leprosy because the people of the Gentiles have been cleansed from the leprosy of their sins by the water of holy baptism.

His sevenfold washing prefigured the sevenfold Spirit, through whose operation the remission of sins is granted in baptism. For just as the body is visibly cleansed by the waters of baptism, so the soul is invisibly cleansed from all sins through the operation of the Holy Spirit.

Gehazi, however, who received the price of healing from Naaman and inherited his leprosy, signifies those who sell their teaching to people—those whom the Lord in the Gospel calls not shepherds but hirelings. Elisha therefore bestowed health, while Gehazi received the price, because perverse teachers demand the price of healing from those whom divine mercy saves. They therefore become heirs of their leprosy because, remaining in the evils which those teachers despised through God’s grace, they acquire everlasting condemnation for themselves.

This Naaman the Syrian, whose name is interpreted as “the faithful strength of them,” represents the heart of the nations, once stained by the leprosy of faithlessness and wickedness but cleansed through the sacrament of baptism from every defilement of mind and body.

Having been advised by the captive girl—that is, by the grace of heavenly inspiration—which the Gentiles seized because the Jews were unable to preserve it, he was urged to hope for salvation and commanded to wash seven times, because only the baptism that regenerates through the Holy Spirit saves.

Hence his flesh is rightly remembered as having appeared after the washing like the flesh of a little child—either because grace, the mother of all who are baptized in Christ, gives birth to them all into one infancy, or rather because that child should be understood of whom it was said: “A child is born to us; a son is given to us” (Isa. 9). To his body the whole offspring of believers is joined through baptism.

And, so that all the sacraments of baptism might here be shown to you, in which we are commanded to renounce Satan and confess the faith, Naaman denies that he will henceforth sacrifice to foreign gods and declares that he will serve the Lord alone in all things.

He is also glad to take a portion of the holy land with him, because those who have been baptized ought likewise to be strengthened by participation in the Lord’s body.

Naaman is therefore rightly preferred to the Jews, since while water washes his body, faith soaks his breast—that is, the people of the Gentiles are preferred to the Jews, who are filthy with the leprosy of obstinacy.

## BOOK OF VARIOUS QUESTIONS (C, G)*

## QUESTION ONE. Concerning the Star and the Magi

Some think that the Magi who came from the East to the Lord born in the flesh and worshiped him after offering gifts did not at all understand in those gifts those most exalted mysteries which the holy Church now understands: namely, the king in the gold, God in the frankincense, and the man who in due time would die and be buried in the myrrh. They think that the Magi, conveying in these mysteries more than they understood in their own minds, simply offered as a gift to the king whom they had come to worship those things that were more precious in their homeland.

But if we carefully weigh their own words, which they spoke when they came to Jerusalem—“Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East, and we have come to worship him” (Matt. 2)—we find that the matter was quite otherwise.

It is clear that they understood him to be a man, since they say: “Where is he who has been born?” It is also clear that they understood him to be a king, which they themselves declare by the word. And it is clear that they believed him to be God, since they add: “And we have come to worship him.” For highly learned men would not have come from so far away to worship one whom they believed to be merely a man and a king, and not also God.

They also formed this most noble and divine judgment concerning him: although he was King of the Jews, he was capable of saving even the Gentiles who wished to believe in him and come to him. They proved this above all by their own coming and action.

Some who look less carefully at Scripture have also said that the star which appeared to them served as their guide on the journey from the East to the vicinity of Bethlehem and went before them on the road. But when, leaving the road to Bethlehem, they turned their journey and eyes toward Jerusalem, the star that guided them disappeared, until they again turned their steps from Jerusalem back toward Bethlehem.

Yet an investigation of the truth of the Gospel itself shows that this did not happen at all. Rather, they saw the star only in the East and immediately understood that it signified the rising of the king born in Judea, of whom Balaam had prophesied: “A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a scepter shall arise out of Israel, and shall strike the leaders of Moab” (Num. 24).

For they themselves were astrologers and had carefully committed to memory what had been said concerning the star. Therefore, as soon as they saw it, they came to Judea, where they knew that the king had been born, and especially to the royal city, thinking that they would find his birth more widely known there.

When they learned from the prophetic testimonies that he had been born in Bethlehem, they immediately journeyed there and were granted the star they had seen in the East as their guide.

Thus the Gospel has it. First the Magi themselves say: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East.” They did not say, “Because it led us from the East to these regions.” Then the evangelist himself testifies concerning them: “When they had heard the king, they departed, and behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them.” Nor did he write that elsewhere they had seen the star, which they had seen only in the East, until, after hearing about the king, they directed their journey toward Bethlehem.

Concerning this star it should be noted that, when they came to Bethlehem, it was not seen high in the heavens among the other stars, but near the earth. For when the evangelist says, “It went before them until, coming, it stood over where the child was,” he plainly indicates that it stood near the house in which the child was. For the heavenly bodies situated at the highest point of the sky, when they have reached the center of the heavens, appear to stand above the crown of every house, however large the city may be.

## QUESTION TWO. Concerning the Apostle’s Statement: “From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one” (II Cor. 11)

When the Apostle says, “From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one,” he means that he was scourged by them five times, but in such a way that he was never struck forty times, but always thirty-nine times.

For the Law commanded that, when judges flogged an offender, they should regulate the measure of punishment so that the number of blows would not exceed forty, lest, as it says, “your brother be horribly lacerated before you” (Deut. 25).

That this is how the passage should be understood, and that the ancients understood it so, is also attested by a painting of this same book, which the most reverend and learned Cudum, bishop of the East Angles, brought with him from Rome to Britain. In that book nearly all the sufferings or labors of the Apostle himself had been depicted in their appropriate places.

There this passage was depicted as though the Apostle lay naked, lacerated by scourges and drenched with tears. A torturer stood above him holding a four-thonged whip in his hand, but retaining one of the thongs in his hand; he had the other three extended solely for striking.

The painter’s meaning is readily apparent: he made the Apostle be beaten with three thongs so that by this means he might not complete the number of forty blows.

[Note: The negating particle is missing.]

For if he struck with four thongs, striking ten times would produce forty blows.

[Note: “Forty” must unquestionably be read.]

But if he struck thirteen times with three thongs, how would he complete forty blows? Thus the Jews were indeed permitted to strike the offender forty times, but, granting him something from their own allowance and showing mercy, they struck the Apostle forty times.

What the same Apostle says in the feminine plural, that he received *quadragenas plagas*—forty blows—signifies, of course, that he suffered them five times, each time one less than forty. In Greek this is expressed simply as **τεσσαράκοντα παρὰ μίαν**, that is, “forty less one.”

## QUESTION THREE. Concerning the Apostle’s Statement in the Same Place: “Night and day I was in the depths of the sea” (II Cor. 11)

When the same Apostle says, “Night and day I was in the depths of the sea,” I have heard some assert that Theodore of blessed memory, a most learned man and formerly archbishop of the English nation, explained it in this way: that at Zizicus there had been a very deep pit prepared for the punishment of criminals, which, because of its immense depth, was accustomed to be called “the depths of the sea,” and that Paul endured its filth and darkness, among countless other sufferings, for Christ.

But if we review the venerable writings of the Fathers, it is plainly evident that in these words they usually understood nothing other than what they literally say: namely, that the Apostle, having by some accident fallen into the depths of the sea and having been surrounded by the waves for both day and night, afterward returned, under God’s guidance, to the open air and the land.

Hence they also count among the divine miracles the fact that a man held beneath the waves for so long could neither be suffocated by the waters surrounding him nor devoured by the beasts of the sea. Indeed, they declare that Peter’s walking upon the waves without being submerged is no more wondrous than Paul’s being held beneath the waves without being killed.

But if we wish to understand something mystical in the very different miracles of the two apostles, it is readily available. Paul, not only shipwrecked three times but also placed night and day in the depths of the sea and everywhere protected and delivered by the Lord, signifies that the just will be rescued by the Lord from every danger.

They are to be saved not only from temptations assaulting them externally, but also, even if they seem to have been overwhelmed by the flood of death itself and hidden from human affairs, they will nevertheless be recalled to life by the power of their Creator.

Peter, moreover, walking with free steps upon waves stirred by the wind, but, when he began to sink through fear, raised up by Christ’s right hand, signifies that the same elect overcome with unconquered faith all the temptations and persecutions of the wicked inflicted upon them at the devil’s instigation, and despise them as though they were nothing.

Those who always embrace the help of their Creator cannot be submerged altogether in the waves of the world. If at times they begin to be disturbed as human beings, they are immediately rescued by him whom they habitually invoke without ceasing, saying: “And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”

## QUESTION FOUR. Concerning the Same Apostle’s Statement: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord,” etc. (Heb. 10)

When the Apostle says, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord,” this is the meaning: What need have you to avenge your own injuries, when you are unable either to know the hearts of human beings or to judge their acknowledged crimes with a tranquil mind?

Rather, whatever is done against you, forgive it from the heart as you would to brothers and neighbors, so that God may also forgive you your sins, knowing that, if they wish to be corrected, you will have them as companions in good things. Otherwise, they will be condemned more rightly by divine judgment—which cannot err, just as it cannot be subject to anger—than by yours.

“Reserve vengeance for me,” he says, “and I will repay.”

And because we must not only patiently endure the evils of the wicked but also willingly bestow our own good things upon them, so that, overcome, they may return to love us, and, admiring the power of our gentleness and patience, may begin to imitate it and, abandoning their former ways, turn to works of virtue, he added this exhortation:

“If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (Rom. 12).

By his head he means his mind, which holds the place of a citadel and command in all our actions and thoughts. By the burning coals he calls the flame of love, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12).

Far be it from us to believe that the Apostle—or Solomon, from whose Proverbs he took this statement—wished to teach us to do good to our adversaries with the intention and purpose that, by persisting ungratefully in these benefits, they might suffer greater and everlasting fires of torment.

Rather, they command us to show mercy to needy enemies, to soften by the soothing application of good deeds the swelling and hardness of their hearts, and to strive, by applying the fire of love, to rouse them to love us again in the Lord.

## QUESTION FIVE. Concerning the Same Apostle’s Statement: “Let each person abound in his own judgment” (Rom. 14)

When the Apostle says, “Let each person abound in his own judgment,” some think that he means: “It is sufficient for each person, for righteousness, to do what seems best to him.”

This is by no means to be understood in that way. For what if someone is a heretic who thinks himself Catholic? Or if someone lives wickedly and thinks that the path he follows is the right way of truth? Would such conduct be sufficient for him as an act of righteousness by which he might attain salvation—especially since the Apostle does not say in the indicative mood, “He abounds,” but in the imperative: “Let each person abound in his own judgment”?

He therefore commands that, if we are unable to grasp the higher mysteries of the divine sacraments, we should nevertheless serve the Lord humbly and devotedly in those matters which we understand and judge truly ought to be believed and confessed.

In this way what he commanded will also be fulfilled: that each person should abound in his own judgment, when we take care to devote ourselves abundantly to good works in those matters which we have learned from great teachers ought to be believed or done, so that through carrying out what we know we may also deserve to attain to the knowledge of higher things which we do not yet know.

Hence he rightly adds: “If you think otherwise about anything, God will reveal this also to you” (ibid.). That is: If you practice the good things you know through charity, divine grace will grant you that, if you think anything otherwise than you ought, you will at some time understand it.

This is plainly evident in the case of blessed Cyprian. With his fellow bishops in Africa, he decreed that heretics should be rebaptized, contrary to the custom of the Church. But because he diligently abounded in good works according to his own judgment, which seemed right to him, he soon deserved to be corrected and, through the instruction of spiritual men, to be brought back to the universal norm of the holy Church.

## QUESTION SIX. Concerning the Words of David with Which He Mourned Saul and Jonathan His Son after Their Death

You asked about the words of David in which he mourned Saul and Jonathan his son after their death, and in that mourning seems also to curse Mount Gilboa, where they were killed. You ask how these words agree with the time or mystery of the Lord’s Passion, so that, as you write, they are spoken in all the churches in responsories on Holy Saturday of Easter as a commemoration of that same Passion—as though an impious king, killed by his enemies on account of his crime, could prefigure the innocent King Christ, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found (I Pet. 2).

You should know that Saul truly does signify the death of the true Christ, which Christ deigned to undergo without guilt. After receiving the anointing of sacred chrism, from which Christ is also called the Lord’s Anointed, Saul deserved to be killed by his enemies.

Hence *Gilboa* is rightly interpreted as “rolling” or “descent.” For they were rolling in the filth of sins, according to the saying in Proverbs: “A sow washed returns to wallowing in the mire” (II Pet. 2). Having strayed from the straightness of the way of salvation, they were already rushing downward, that is, toward the desires of this age. On account of those desires they did not hesitate to hand over the King of heaven and earth to death.

For this reason it is rightly wished for them that they receive neither dew from heaven nor rain—a wish whose fulfillment we see today in the facts themselves, since heavenly grace departed from them and was transferred to the people of the Gentiles.

Isaiah also threatened that this would happen to them under the figure of a vineyard, speaking in the person of the Lord: “And I will command the clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. 5).

This means plainly: “I will command the apostles and all apostolic men not to preach the word of life to them any longer, but to leave them empty in their barrenness and destined to be burned by everlasting fire, unworthy of the watering of the heavenly word which they arrogantly rejected.”

Nor should it seem absurd to you that the deeds of the wicked may signify something good, or that, conversely, the good works of the righteous may be placed in an opposite signification.

Read the *Moralia* of holy Pope Gregory, where he explains how blessed Job cursed his own day, saying: “Let the day perish on which I was born,” and so forth (Job 3). You will see that it is most customary in Scripture for both good things to be understood in the signification of evil things and the evil deeds of human beings in the signification of good things.

Indeed, he interprets Uriah, the most faithful soldier of King David, and his most pious and innocent deeds and words, in an evil signification; and, conversely, he interprets David himself, in his greatest crime, in a good signification.

Otherwise, if good could not be signified through evil and evil through good, it would never be permissible to write in black ink, but everything would always have to be written in shining gold, because “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (I John 1). Nor, again, should the names Absalom and Doeg, wicked men, be written in the bright red of the titles of the Psalms, but only in black.

Therefore, just as on the pages of books we may depict both evil and good in any color without reproach, so also in the realm of signification good and evil may quite properly be expressed through all kinds of human deeds.

Although it happens much more often, and is heard much more sweetly, that good is figured through good and evil through evil.

But just as in the painting of walls it is not fitting to depict a dark-skinned Ethiopian in white or a Saxon with a white body or hair in dark color, so in the recompense of merits each person will receive according to his own work. In the judgment, each will appear in countenance as he was in deed. It will not matter at all what each person figured, but what he did.

## QUESTION SEVEN. What Is Meant in the Psalm: “Your Word Is Exceedingly Refined by Fire” (Ps. 118)

Meanwhile you asked what is meant in the Psalm by: “Your word is exceedingly refined by fire.” The same expression also occurs in Proverbs: “Every word of God is refined by fire” (Prov. 30).

Know, therefore, that this expression must be understood quite differently from how it appears to sound. Something is usually called *ignitum*—“fired” or “fire-filled”—when it is wholly suffused and filled with fire; for example, iron or bronze melted in the midst of flames, indeed something completely full of fire.

In this sense it is said of Joseph: “The word of the Lord set him on fire” (Ps. 104), that is, it filled him so completely with the heat and flame of divine power that he himself seemed wholly kindled by the Spirit of God and, as it were, suffused with fire.

Such were those who said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24).

But when the Lord’s word is declared to be *ignitum*, or the word of God to be *ignitus*, it should be understood as tested by fire, like gold or any other metal which, having been melted by fire, contains no foreign or useless dross, and in which everything that remains is true and perfect and cleansed from every taint of vice.

For in this way the words of the Lord, containing within themselves faith in eternal goods, are entirely true and established neither idly nor uselessly. Hence the Lord says: “Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things are accomplished” (Matt. 5), so that nothing there may be judged to exist which is not perfect and proper.

Understand, therefore, *ignitum* as “tested by fire” or “purified by fire” (II Kings 22). The one Greek word **πεπυρωμένον** has thus been translated into Latin according to the translators’ preference both as *ignitum* (“fired”) and as *igne examinatum* (“tested by fire”).

For where it is said, “The words of the Lord are tested by fire,” the same single word, **πεπυρωμένα**, is used in Greek. From this word is also derived: “You have tested us by fire” (Ps. 65), which some have rendered, “You have set us on fire.”

Every word of God is *ignitus*, or tested by fire, because through the illumination of the Holy Spirit it is supported by sincere and steadfast truth.

## QUESTION EIGHT. Concerning the Re-transporting of the Lord’s Ark from the House of Aminadab by King David
David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand, and so forth (2 Samuel 6).

In the account of the blessed king and prophet David, in which he is said to have brought back the ark of God, approved humility, condemned pride, and punished rashness are displayed. For David himself, who was not ashamed humbly to dance before the ark of the Lord, soon merited to receive the promise that the Son of God would be born from his lineage. His wife, moreover, who despised that same humility of his, was not found worthy to be made fruitful by his seed, but paid the penalty of perpetual barrenness. The priest, too, who touched the ark of God with heedless rashness, atoned for the guilt of his presumption by an untimely death. Here one must consider how greatly he sins who approaches the body of the Lord while guilty, if that devout priest was punished by death because he handled the ark—which clearly prefigured the Lord’s body—with less reverence than he ought.

According to the allegory, however, David signifies Christ, and the ark signifies the Church. David sought to bring the ark into his own city, but because an opposing circumstance intervened, he diverted it elsewhere for a time, and thereafter completed what he had greatly desired. For the Lord, appearing in the flesh, preached the Gospel to the children of Israel, that is, to his own people; but a partial blindness occurred in Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles entered, and thus all Israel might be saved.

But in order to examine these matters more precisely one by one: David gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand, because the Lord established the primitive Church from Israel—not from all Israel, but by associating with himself those who were chosen. For not all who are from Israel are Israelites, but the children of the promise are counted as the seed.

They are reported to have numbered thirty thousand—that is, those perfected in the firmness of faith, works, and hope. Three pertains to faith because of the confession of the Holy Trinity; ten pertains to works because of the Decalogue of the Law; a thousand pertains to their perfection and to hope for eternal life, above which there is nothing, just as no number is greater than a thousand. For even if you say ten thousand, thirty thousand, or even a thousand thousand, you do not go beyond the number one thousand by counting it, but multiply it either by itself or repeatedly by lesser numbers.

Multiply three by ten, therefore, lest faith without works be dead. Likewise multiply thirty by a thousand, so that faith, which works through love, may hope for its reward nowhere other than in heaven. Thus the chosen from Israel signify peoples who rightly believe, work, and hope. The men of Judah who were with David signify the apostles and teachers who clung more familiarly to Christ’s side.

Strengthened by both armies, the Lord rejoices to bring forward the ark—that is, to enlarge the Church—and to implant it in the hearts of those who had not believed. The ark is placed upon a new cart, so that the grace of the New Testament may be poured into minds renewed in baptism, and so that new wine may be ordered to be preserved in new wineskins.

Previously the ark had been in the house of Aminadab, who was in Gabaa, because the faith of the Church now preached also flourished before the time of the Lord’s Incarnation in those who followed the devotion of the patriarchs and prophets. Aminadab, whose name is interpreted as “my voluntary father,” signifies either Abraham, the father of faith, or Moses, the lawgiver. Each of them guards the ark in Gabaa, because by the lofty example of virtue he fortifies the hearts of believers. Hence Gabaa is interpreted as “hill”; it is a place in the city of Cariathiarim.

When the ark had been brought out, David danced, and all Israel before the Lord danced to various kinds of music, because, as soon as the proclamation of the new grace began, the Lord invited everyone to offer praises to God the Father in humility, saying: “Whoever serves me must follow me” (John 12). Some received through the Spirit a message of wisdom, others a message of knowledge, others various kinds of tongues, others the gift of healing, and so forth.

As the ark proceeded with these and similar kinds of charisms—that is, as the primitive Church grew—they came to the threshing floor of Nachor, meaning a prepared threshing floor, namely the Church of the Gentiles, to be consecrated by the truth of faith. Of it John says: “He will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matthew 3).

There the priest, who touched the ark too carelessly, as though correcting it, was immediately struck down by the Lord and died. This happened because the Jewish people, while envying the Gentiles, deprived themselves of the gift of salvation; and while seeking to mix the Law with the Gospel, removed from themselves the grace of both.

“And he held it,” it says, “because the oxen had kicked” (2 Samuel 6). For the oxen’s kicking signifies that the preachers of the Gospel acted more freely concerning the faith, not entering according to the custom of the Law, but interpreting spiritually the Sabbaths, new moons, circumcision, and sacrifices. Those who came down from Judea to teach the brothers attempted to correct them as though they were straying: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts 15). James also said to Paul concerning them: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the Law” (Acts 21).

Therefore, because the priest had been killed, David was unwilling to divert the ark of the Lord to himself, into the city of David, but diverted it to the house of Obededom the Gittite. This signifies that, when the Jews rejected the word, the apostles were taken away from them and sent to instruct the Gentiles, lest preaching that was heard but not received should harm them further.

Hence the place of the threshing floor of Nachor, which demonstrates the faith of the Gentiles prepared for the Lord’s grace, is called “the striking down of Uzzah,” namely because through the offense of those men salvation came to the Gentiles.

Obededom, whose name is interpreted as “serving man,” is surely the one of whom the Lord says to the Father: “You will appoint me as head of the nations; a people whom I did not know served me” (Psalm 17). Having first mentioned the rejection of the Jews, as though the death of Uzzah, he says: “You will rescue me from the disputes of the people” (ibid.).

The name of the city also fits. Geth means “winepress,” signifying the cross on which the true vine was destined to be trodden and pressed. The entire people of the Gentiles may rightly be called Gittite, when it says: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6).

The three months during which the ark remains there signify faith, hope, and charity. For just as a month is completed by its days, so each virtue reaches perfection by its own stages. These months continue until the fullness of the Gentiles enters.

At last David returns and brings the ark into the city of David, because, when Enoch and Elijah preach, the Lord will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children. He sacrifices oxen and rams—that is, he crowns with the blood of martyrdom those who thresh the Lord’s threshing floor and lead his sheep—and he himself openly manifests the example of his Incarnation and Passion, which the Jews had hitherto not believed.

This is signified by the fact that David himself was girded with a linen ephod. For linen, produced by the earth and brought to the whiteness of a garment through manifold labor, displays the truth of human flesh triumphing amid scourges.

While everyone rejoices and hymns resound at the entrance of the heavenly ark, Michal alone, the daughter of Saul, is absent from those leading the ark. Indeed, she looks through a window at David humbled, because, when the Jews believe at the end of the world, there will be some who follow Christ in profession but follow the Antichrist in their works.

It is fitting that the same Michal—whose name, on account of the instability it symbolizes in carnal people, is interpreted as “all water”—is called not David’s wife but Saul’s daughter. For those who serve Christ in faith only are not to be crowned with his kingdom, but are to be condemned by the anathema of his persecutors, whom they imitated.

Let the wicked rage and despise the humility of the Church; nevertheless, the ark of the Lord enters its appointed place. It is placed in the midst of the tabernacle that David had pitched for it—that is, the faith of the Church is preached, advances, and is implanted in the hearts of all whom the Lord had predestined to eternal life.

David offers holocausts and peace offerings before the Lord. Christ, who is at the right hand of God and intercedes for us (Romans 8), commends the faith and devotion of the Church to the Father. Following David’s example, he blesses the faithful and humble and nourishes them with the food of the mystery of salvation.

He distributes to each person one bread-cake, namely of the one who descended from heaven and gives life to this world; one portion of roasted beef, namely of the fattened calf that was slaughtered for the younger son returning to his father and roasted in the fire of passion, saying: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd”; and fried semolina in oil, namely flesh utterly cleansed from the stain of sin, but toasted in the frying-pan of the cross because of its most abundant love for human salvation.

And rightly one bread-cake and one portion of meat are given, because there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.

The faithful receive these gifts in another sense as well: when we are one bread and all one body in Christ, and when each person chastises the wantonness of his flesh, subjects it to servitude, and cooks it in the fire of the Holy Spirit; and when, through compassion, they make the fruits of good works exceedingly rich with the oil of mercy and bring them to fervent heat.

But Saul’s daughter, having entered the king’s chamber in vain, produces no fruits of conceived seed, because those who receive the word of God only through the ear, without the offspring of good works, await the day of everlasting death.

## QUESTION IX. On the angels

[Col. 0462B]

What is the nature, creation, and status of the angels? The angels were created before the creation of the world; and before the creation of all the angels, the devil was formed, as it is written: “He is the beginning of the ways of God.” Hence, in comparison with the angels, he was also called an archangel.

He was created first in rank of precedence, not in length of time. That the devil held primacy among the angels, from which confidence he fell so that he might fall without restoration, the prophet announces by these words: “The cedars were not higher than he in the paradise of God; the fir trees did not equal his summit. No tree of paradise was compared with him in beauty; how God made him beautiful.”

The condition of an angel differs from the condition of a human being. For humanity was created in the likeness of God; but the archangel who fell was called “the seal of God’s likeness,” as the Lord testifies through Ezekiel: “You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God.”

For the more subtle his nature is, the more fully was it formed in the likeness of divine truth.

The devil fell from heaven before humanity was created. For as soon as he was made, he burst into pride and was cast down from heaven. Indeed, according to the testimony of Truth, he was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because immediately after he was made he fell. He was created in truth, but because he did not stand, he immediately fell from the truth.

By a single fall of pride, when they compare themselves with God in arrogance, the devil too fell. But the human being returned to repentance, recognizing that he was inferior. The devil, however, was not content merely to have fallen by thinking himself equal to God; he even claimed to be superior to God, according to the Apostle’s words concerning the Antichrist: “Who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped.”

The devil no longer seeks forgiveness because he is not moved to repentance. His members, however, often ask forgiveness through hypocrisy, although because of their evil conscience they do not deserve to obtain it.

Let human misery learn that God is more quickly moved to grant forgiveness because he has compassion on weak humanity. Humanity itself drew a weakness for sin from its lower part, namely from the flesh, by whose exclusion the soul is held confined.

The apostate angels have no forgiveness because they were not burdened by any weakness of bodily frailty when they sinned. Human beings, however, return to forgiveness after sin because they drew from their earthy material the weight of weakness. Therefore, because of the weak condition of the flesh, a return to salvation lies open to humanity, just as the Psalm says: “He knows our formation. Remember, Lord, that we are dust” (2 Thessalonians 2:4). And again: “Remember,” it says, “what our substance is.”

After the apostate angels fell, the rest were established through perseverance in eternal blessedness. Hence, after the creation of heaven, we find at the beginning: “Let there be a firmament.” And the firmament was called heaven, indicating by the number that, after the angels’ ruin, those who remained earned the firmness of eternal perseverance and blessedness that they had previously lacked: after the devil’s expulsion, the holy angels were granted the perseverance in holiness and the blessedness that they had previously lacked.

It must therefore be understood that the wickedness of the evil serves the humility of the saints, because from the place where the wicked fall, the good advance.

The number of the good angels, diminished after the fall of the evil angels, will be completed from the number of all the elect, whose number is known to God alone.

Among the angels there are distinctions of powers, and ministries have been distributed among them according to the dignity of their ranks. Some are set above others both in the height of their power and in the knowledge of virtue. Thus some serve the commands of others and obey their orders. Hence an angel sends an angel to the prophet Zechariah and commands him what he must announce.

Holy Scripture testifies that there are nine distinctions or orders of angels: angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, principalities, powers, cherubim, and seraphim.

The prophet Ezekiel also describes the number of these orders under the same number of names of stones when he speaks of the primacy of the apostate angel: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, and jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (Ezekiel 28:13).

By this number of stones the angelic orders themselves are designated. Before his fall, the apostate angel possessed them as though attached to his garment of adornment. When he saw himself brighter than all in comparison with them, he immediately became swollen with pride and raised his heart to arrogance.

The angels always rejoice in the Lord, not in themselves. The devil, however, rejoiced in himself, because he sought not the things of God but his own.

There is no greater wickedness than for anyone to wish to glory not in God but in himself. The angels of God, however, know everything before it comes to pass in reality, and what is still future among human beings the angels already know because God reveals it.

The transgressing angels, although they lost holiness, did not lose the living intelligence of their angelic nature. For the keenness of their foreknowledge arises in three ways: through the subtlety of their nature, through experience of times, and through revelation by higher powers.

Whenever God grows angry with this world through some scourge, angels are sent to carry out vengeance. Yet they are restrained by divine power, so that they do not inflict as much harm as they desire.

The good angels, however, are appointed to the ministry of human salvation, to administer the affairs of the world and govern all things at God’s command, as the Apostle testifies: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14).

The angels assume the bodies in which they appear to human beings from the upper air, and they take on a solid appearance from the heavenly element, through which they may be displayed more clearly to human eyes.

It is believed that individual nations have angels appointed over them. This is shown by the testimony of the angel speaking to Daniel: “I came,” he says, “to announce it to you, but the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me” (Daniel 10:13). And afterward: “There is no one who helps me except Michael, your prince” (ibid., 21).

It is likewise proved that all human beings have angels, when the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “Truly I tell you, their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10).

Hence, when Peter was knocking at the door in the Acts of the Apostles, the apostles inside said: “It is not Peter, but his angel” (Acts 12:3).

If the angels contemplate and see God, why does the apostle Peter say: “Into whom the angels of God desire to look” (1 Peter 1:12)? And if they do not then contemplate and see him, how, according to the Lord’s statement, do “their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven”?

Both statements are rightly understood. For we truly believe that the angels both see God and desire to see him; they possess him and hasten to possess him; they love him and strive to love him.

If they desire to see him in such a way that they do not enjoy the fulfillment of their desire, that desire would involve necessity. But that necessity is not punitive, and every kind of punishment is far removed from the blessed angels, since punishment and blessedness never coexist.

Again, if we say that they are satisfied by the vision of God, satisfaction ordinarily gives rise to weariness; yet we know that they cannot grow weary of the vision of God, which they both desire and possess.

What, then, remains except that we believe both simultaneously in a wondrous way: they desire and are satisfied; they desire without labor and are satisfied without weariness. So that desire may not involve necessity, those who desire are satisfied. And again, so that satisfaction may not involve weariness, those who are satisfied desire.

The angels see the face of the Father through satisfaction; but because this satisfaction knows no weariness, the angels desire always to gaze upon him.

Whenever an angel is placed in the Holy Scriptures in the place of God, it is not the Father or the Holy Spirit who is meant; rather, in the dispensation of the Incarnation, the Son alone is understood.

Before the coming of the Lord’s Incarnation, there was discord between angels and human beings. But when Christ came, he made peace in himself between angels and human beings. At his birth the angels cried out: “Peace on earth to people of good will.”

Through Christ’s Incarnation, therefore, humanity was reconciled not only to God, but peace between angels and human beings was also restored.

That there had been discord between angels and human beings before Christ’s coming is recognized especially from the fact that, when angels were greeted by human beings in the Old Testament, they disdained to return their greeting. In the New Testament, however, when this was done by John, it is not only received reverently, but he is forbidden to do it: “See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant and one of your brothers.” In the Old Testament a human being is despised by the angel and his greeting is not returned, because humanity had not yet passed over into God. But humanity is regarded with favor by God and reverently greeted by the angel; for we read that the angel greeted Mary.

By this it is understood that, through the Lord’s Incarnation, peace was given and restored to human beings and angels.

## QUESTION X. On the sins of human beings and their punishment

[Col. 0464C]

I would like to know how it is just that a fault committed within a finite span should be punished without end. This would rightly be said if the strict judge weighed not the hearts of human beings but their actions.

The wicked sinned within a finite span because they lived within a finite span. For surely, if they could have done so, they would have wished to live without end so that they could sin without end. Those who never cease sinning while they live show that they always desire to live in sin.

It therefore belongs to the great justice of the Judge that those should never be without punishment who in this life never wished to be without sin.

God is compassionate and does not feed upon the suffering of the miserable; but he is just, and therefore he is not forever appeased without avenging the wicked. No just person feeds upon cruelty, and a delinquent servant is ordered to be beaten by a just master so that he may be corrected from his wickedness. He is beaten for this purpose: that he may be reformed.

But when the wicked are handed over to the fire of Gehenna, if they never come to correction, for what purpose will they burn forever? Almighty God, because he is compassionate, does not feed upon the torment of the miserable; but because he is just, he is not forever appeased without avenging the wicked.

All the wicked, however, assigned to eternal punishment, are punished for their own wickedness, yet they will burn for a further purpose: so that all the righteous may see in God the joys they receive, and in the wicked may behold the punishments from which they escaped. Thus they will recognize themselves as debtors to divine grace forever, all the more deeply because they see forever the evils being punished that they overcame through God’s help.

## QUESTION XI. On the dwelling of souls until the restoration

I would like to know whether, before the restoration of their bodies, the souls of the righteous can now be received into heaven. We cannot affirm this concerning all the righteous, nor can we deny it concerning all.

For there are souls of certain righteous people that are delayed from the heavenly kingdom in certain dwelling-places by the penalty of an unjust allotment [Latin *dicationis* uncertain]. What else is suggested by this except that they possessed something lacking in perfect righteousness?

Nevertheless, it is clearer than daylight that the souls of the perfectly righteous, as soon as they leave the prison of this flesh, are received into heavenly dwellings.

The Truth itself also testifies to this, saying: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matthew 24:28). Since our Redeemer is bodily there, undoubtedly the souls of the righteous are gathered there as well. Paul desires “to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). Whoever therefore does not doubt that Christ is in heaven cannot deny that Paul’s soul is in heaven.

He also says concerning the dissolution of his body and the dwelling of the heavenly homeland: “We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands but eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1).

If, then, the souls of the righteous are now in heaven, what is it that they receive on the day of judgment as the reward of their righteousness? In them there surely increases at the judgment this distinction: now they enjoy only the blessedness of their souls, but afterward they will enjoy the blessedness of their bodies as well, so that they may rejoice in the very flesh in which they endured sufferings and torments for the Lord.

For this doubled glory it is written: “The righteous shall possess double.” Hence, before the day of the resurrection, it is written concerning the souls of the saints: “They were given each a white robe, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be fulfilled” (Revelation 6:11).

Those who have now received one robe each will therefore have two robes at the judgment, because now the matter concerns the souls alone, but then they will rejoice in the glory of souls and bodies together.

## QUESTION XII. Whether the good recognize the good in the heavenly kingdom, and the wicked recognize the wicked in punishment

[Col. 0465C]

I would like to know whether the good recognize the good in the kingdom, and the wicked recognize the wicked in punishment. The answer to this matter is demonstrated more clearly than daylight in the Lord’s words, which we have already cited above.

There it was said: “There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and he feasted splendidly every day” (Luke 16:19), and the passage continues until he says: “Son, remember that you received good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (ibid.).

The rich man, having no hope of salvation for himself, turns to seek the salvation of his own, saying: “Therefore I ask you, father, to send him to my father’s house,” and so forth (ibid.).

These words clearly declare that the good recognize the good and the wicked recognize the wicked. For if Abraham had not recognized Lazarus at all, he would never have spoken to the rich man placed in torment about Lazarus’s former affliction, saying that he had received evil things during his life.

How could he fail to recognize those present when he even took care to pray for the memory of those absent?

This also demonstrates that the good recognize the wicked, and the wicked recognize the good. For Abraham recognizes the rich man when he says: “Remember that you received good things during your life.” And the chosen Lazarus is recognized by the condemned rich man, who asks that he be sent by name: “Send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue.”

In this recognition of both parties, the fullness of their retribution increases: the good rejoice more because they see those whom they loved rejoicing with them; and the wicked, while suffering with those whom they loved in this world while despising God, are consumed not only by their own punishment but also by that of the others.

Something even more marvelous occurs among the elect: they recognize not only those whom they knew in this world, but recognize the good whom they never saw as though they had seen and known them.

For when they see the ancient fathers in that eternal inheritance, those whom they always knew through their works will not be unknown to them through vision. Since all there behold God in a common radiance, what could they not know there, where they see the one who knows all things?

A certain man of our own time, venerable in life, deeply religious, and worthy of praise, died three years ago. As other religious people who were present testified, at the hour of his departure he began to look upon the prophet Jonah, and also Ezekiel and Daniel.

While he said that they had come to him and, lowering his eyes, offered them the service of reverence, he was taken from the flesh.

From this it is plainly understood what knowledge there will be in that incorruptible life, if this man, still placed in corruptible flesh, recognized the holy prophets whom he had certainly never seen.

It often happens that the departing soul also recognizes those with whom it is to be assigned to one dwelling because of equality either of sins or of rewards. Many see at their departure those whom they will have as equals either in the kingdom or in punishment.

## QUESTION XIII. On free will

[Col. 0466B]

God made humanity perfect, namely, such that a person could both will the good and not will it. This is free will: to will and not to will, freely and without constraint.

This willing belongs to humanity by nature, as it is said in Wisdom: “To us belongs willing, but to God belongs accomplishing”—to us, that is, by nature. And the Apostle says: “To will is present with me by nature” (Romans 7:18).

But by sinning, humanity corrupted this willing and this good and, as it were, extinguished it, though not completely, because some spark of good always remained in it. When the Apostle said, “God works willing,” we do not understand him to mean that God now first places willing in a person, but that he raises up and makes live again the will that exists in a person by nature, though corrupted and almost extinguished.

Thus we reconcile these two statements: what Scripture says, “To us belongs willing,” and what the Apostle says, “God works willing,” together with free will.

God—or rather, what he necessarily does—made humanity such that it could will the good and not will the good. For if he had made it such that it could never do anything except will the good, he would have made it unchangeable.

Nothing is unchangeable except God, because he cannot do anything except will the good. God, however, can beget what he is, but cannot make what he is. We can say something similar about humanity. A human being can beget what he is, but cannot make what he is, although he can paint his own image on a wall or form it in wood.

Since there had to be some distinction between the Creator and the creature, God could make something that he was not, but not something that he was: he could make a human being capable of willing the good and not willing the good, which God himself is not; but he could not make a human being incapable of willing and not willing the good, which is what God himself is.

God gave rational creation an effective power of good nature by which to know him. This good natural power of knowing him may be called grace. The Roman Gentiles took great confidence in it, attributing to themselves the fact that they had believed so well after hearing the truth of the Gospel.

They did not consider that the same nature, left to itself by God, was sufficient for salvation in neither angel nor human being. Indeed, if it had been sufficient, neither angel nor human being would have needed God, since each would have possessed sufficiency in himself and would thus have been his own god, as though equal to the true God. There would be neither one God nor one Almighty.

Thus God alone remained wholly sufficient; neither angelic nor human nature can ever perform anything good, and even when grace is added to it, it can fall back.

**Response.** Why, then, did God add himself to it, if through that addition it would not advance? Clearly, so that, when it falls, it may recognize itself as without excuse through the aid added to it, and, when it perseveres, may give thanks to God for the addition of grace.

Therefore the good nature of rational creation can indeed cooperate in good when grace is added to it. But if, left to itself, it accomplishes nothing good and instead plunges itself into evil, it is clear that sin is the efficient cause of death, while death is the necessary effect of sin, as the Lord testifies when he says to Adam: “On whatever day you eat from the forbidden tree, you shall surely die” (Genesis 2).

Therefore whoever dies by a necessary death is powerless to rise again by himself. But Christ, who was without sin, was without the necessity of death, as he himself testifies when he says: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10).

Christ’s death, therefore, was voluntary, not necessary. For this reason he could rise again by himself, so that his resurrection might be the common resurrection of those who had died, or have died, or will die in Christ under the necessity of death.

God is said to foreknow all things that occur through the power of nature or through the power of freedom. He is also said to know that the things which are done as good things will be good through the addition of grace.

God’s predestination, therefore, is the addition of divine grace. Consequently, whoever denies that Christ was predestined denies that he is the Son of Man. For the human nature that had been in Adam’s loins and was subject to Adam’s sin became free from every fault through the addition of grace in the very union with the Word of God, although it retained the punishment of sin, so that in his resurrection Christ might destroy it. The destruction of that punishment is the destruction, or cleansing, of our corruptions.

All evil thoughts are not always stirred up by the prompting of the devil, but sometimes arise from the movement of our own free will; good thoughts, however, are always from God. It should be understood that the first human being is said to have possessed free will before tasting the fruit, but after tasting it became a slave of sin.

But since he had possessed free will, we must consider what freedom that will had. Certainly, the will was free so long as it remained in its own power, so that, compelled by no force—neither God’s nor the devil’s—it could do whatever good or evil it wished. Yet although it was free in this respect, namely, that no master or force could compel it to will or not will something, it was nevertheless weak in itself, so that, because of its weakness, it could do the same thing if it did not consent to the devil—not one in need, but one who was persuading. [Col. 0467C] But it could in no way stand by its own strength; and if it wished to accomplish something, it could do so through God’s assistance, provided that it did not believe, contrary to God’s counsel, that it should will the good.

Since Adam therefore possessed free will and had a possibility belonging to himself, he also had one belonging to another, so that there might be in a human being something which God could justly reward: namely, a free will serving God without compulsion, so that there might be in God something for which he could be glorified when he strengthened the human being by his own power. Because Adam was therefore free and weak, after he trusted in himself alone, consented to the enemy through his free will, and fell through his own fragility. If he had trusted in the Lord alone, he certainly would not have fallen at all with the Lord’s assistance.

But after the fall of our first parent the whole world had become a slave of sin. The Lord came, therefore, restoring us to our former condition and returning to us the free will of our father: free, as before, from an external force, but subject to a new weakness of its own, so that no one might presume upon himself, but might always trust in God alone.

Yet this free will appears to be contradicted by the fact that the Lord predestined his saints from eternity to eternal life, and likewise predestined for his saints the cause of eternal life, namely, their merit, while he predestined eternal death for the rejected—but not the cause of eternal death, since God predestined the sins of no one. For it is not part of God’s disposition how a sinner sins; nevertheless, since he knows that the person will sin, he ordains death for him as a true judge.

But if he ordains and predestines life for the good and death for the evil, he seems to impose force upon free will. Since his predestination cannot fail, it would necessarily follow that the one whom he predestined to death is evil and the one whom he predestined to life is good. And if it is necessary that this one be good and that one evil, then free will has perished, since it is compelled by necessity.

If the will is not free but is compelled by necessity, then the person who sins whether he wishes to or not should not be blamed, nor should the one who does good whether he wishes to or not be praised; praise and blame ought instead to be attributed solely to the one who compels. Why, then, is there punishment for the wicked and glory [Col. 0468A] for the just? In that case the reward received by the just would not be a reward, but merely God’s grace; nor would the punishment of the unjust be vengeance, but an injustice—which God forbid.

God’s predestination therefore compels us by no force toward good or evil. Rather, God, in whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning, possessed from eternity in his sight as present the things that would be future for us. He presented us to himself as the kind of people we would be, whether through our own wickedness or through righteousness, and judged us as though we were present.

For what is past or future in our experience never passes from God’s sight, but is always present. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24). If words which pass away in an instant for us remain forever with God, who could doubt that things which are transient for us remain permanent in God’s sight?

Since, therefore, we have always been present in his sight, and he sees us presently as the kind of people we would become—whether for good through him, or for evil not through him but through ourselves—he did nothing inappropriate if, seeing different merits, he also repays us with different rewards. Our wickedness presented itself from eternity as evil in God’s sight through its own depravity, and God destined it for death.

What, then? Did God compel us to appear evil to him from eternity? Certainly not. Rather, we compelled him to see us as evil. For example, if I see someone lying down, it is necessary either that the person whom I see lying down is lying down, or that it is false that I see him lying down. Is that necessity imposed by the one lying down or by the one seeing? Certainly, the necessity that he lie down is not imposed by the one who sees, but by the one who placed himself there in order to lie down.

God, therefore, for whom nothing is future or past, sees us always present to him as evil—not in order to impose upon the just a necessity of wickedness, but because that wickedness cannot remain hidden from the presence of the judge.

Did Peter deny God because the Lord said, “You will deny me” (Matthew 26)? Or did Judas betray him because the Lord said, “You will betray me” (ibid.)? Or did Lazarus die because God said, “Lazarus sleeps” (Luke 11)? Judas had already arranged with the Jews concerning the betrayal; Peter alone, when he heard about the denial, swore that he would not deny him. Yet Peter was more compelled by the Lord’s words to do what he did not wish than Judas was compelled to accomplish what he wished.

Nevertheless, it was impossible for the one who knew all things not to know what was going to happen to these men. Thus, just as predestination to death does not compel the wicked to perish, so predestination to life does not compel the good to be saved. But when the Lord predestined the good to life, he predestined them in such a way that this very predestination is obtained through our merits and prayers.

Did the Lord not say to Abraham, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Genesis 21)? Although the Lord had promised fertility of offspring in Isaac, his wife Rebecca was nevertheless barren. Isaac prayed, and the Lord granted conception to Rebecca (Genesis 25). If God promised fertility and gave barrenness, while Isaac prayed, what else does this mean but that prayer obtained what had been predestined?

It can therefore be inferred that God promises us his good things in such a way that they are nevertheless acquired through our labor. And if we are willing, he will cooperate with us in the labor involved in everything we do well.

## QUESTION XIV. On Original Sin

It is asked why the transmission of original sin and the entrance of death into the world are attributed to the first man, Adam, and not to the woman or to the serpent, since both had sinned first: the serpent by suggesting, and Eve by consenting.

The answer is that we unjustly received from the devil the inheritance of sin, with whose origin and nature we have no communion. Therefore, through suggestion or imitation we could be like him, but by transmission we were not conformed to him.

We do not receive the suggestion of sin from Eve, our mother, because we received the origin of our seed not from the mother but from the father. [Col. 0469A] Therefore, from the source’s mass from which we are principally transmitted, guilt is also transmitted to us originally. Adam also sinned more gravely because Eve was deceived, whereas Adam was neither seduced nor deceived, but sinned knowingly.

It is asked by what weight Adam’s sin was so great that it could destroy not only him but the whole human race. The answer is: because he did not sin through necessity, ignorance, or weakness. Not through necessity, because he was compelled neither by the devil’s violence nor by lack of food to eat the fruit; not through ignorance, because, although he had been created most wise, he had been warned by the Lord about that very matter; and not through weakness, because, while he had God present as his helper, he could in no way have fallen if he had wished to ask him about it or trust in him.

It is asked why, since the Lord removed all sins from us by redeeming us, he did not also remove the punishment of sin, so that even in this life we might be incapable of suffering and immortal. [Col. 0469B] He did this with the greatest reason. For if he had made us immortal after his redemption, everyone would hasten to the faith not because of love for God and eternal blessedness, but solely to attain the immortality of this bodily life. Thus the fruit of faith would perish, since it would not be sought out of love for God.

He left us subject to suffering, lest it appear desirable for us to cling to this life; rather, we should hasten toward that rest which is unending with the Lord. For what would have happened if he had completely removed our capacity for suffering, while this life—with its many and great tribulations—were loved so much that scarcely anyone would remember eternal blessedness?

It should be noted that if someone baptizing says, “I baptize you in Christ Jesus,” and does not say, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” as the Lord instituted, it is not true baptism. Therefore one must take care not to misunderstand the Apostle’s words when he says, “Now I baptize in Christ Jesus,” interpreting them otherwise than they were spoken.

“So that we may no longer serve sin” (Romans 6): [Col. 0469C] certain heretics wanted to assert that if a sinner returned to sin after baptism, he could in no way again be received into repentance, since after baptism he ought not to return to sin. But this is false, as the Lord testifies: “The sinner, at whatever hour he groans, will be saved. Death will no longer rule over him” (Romans 6)—that is, some participation in death, such as weeping and thirsting, and so forth.

The fact that he ate after the resurrection he did not do from hunger; rather, he did it as a kind of sign by which to reveal himself. Similarly, when we have died to sins, we ought not to return to them, so that they may rule over us.

It should also be noted that it is not said, “Christ re-surrected,” as one says *rehabuit*, “he had again,” for the Lord did not rise twice or three times, but once. “Christ, having been raised from the dead, dies no more.” He died only once, not twice; one death was sufficient, because he died in relation to sin—that is, for the destruction of sin. Since he destroyed sin, one death was sufficient. [Col. 0469D]

Indeed, he does not die again. For the fact that he died—namely, that he died in relation to sin, that is, in order to destroy sin—occurred once, not twice. It is as though he said: This is what “once” means: that he himself died in order to destroy sin.

He therefore disproves those who say that the Lord died in the air for the devil in the same way as he died for us in the world.

On the first day on which Adam was created, he was old—not in age, but by an appropriate likeness. For just as an old thing declines and is drawn toward sunset, so Adam, at the very hour when he sinned, descended toward the sunset of death as though he were old; and every sinner after him did likewise.

But Christ was a new human being both in a spiritual sense and because, although he became human, he was nevertheless king of angels and human beings. There is also another general sense: just as a new thing grows and is strengthened, so Christ grew from strength to strength, as Scripture testifies: “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom before God and human beings.” In imitation of him, we too must become new, ascending from strength to strength. [Col. 0470A]

Adam had one condition when he had been created in Paradise, while he still ate and drank and performed the other functions of the body. The incarnate Son assumed this condition for himself.

His second condition was after the fall and after his departure from Paradise, when he was subject to the condition of death. The Lord took this from him so that he could die.

His third condition was not what he actually possessed, but what he ought to have possessed if he had remained obedient: namely, that he could neither have sinned nor have wished to sin. In this way Christ could neither sin nor wish to sin.

There are two callings: one general and the other special. The general calling is expressed in the words, “Many are called” (Matthew 22), because all of us are generally called to the faith. The special calling is expressed in the words, “But few are chosen” (ibid.). This indicates that all are generally called to life through faith, but that few are predestined to life through the election of good merits.

It should be understood that before the Law the fathers were saved by the same faith by which we are saved now. Why, then, did God add circumcision, if faith was sufficient for salvation at that time?

The answer is that our Lord always devises and establishes such things by which our merits can be increased. [Col. 0470B] Thus, in order to exalt our father Abraham through greater merits, he commanded him to observe circumcision, just as he imposed obedience upon Adam when he had been placed in the earthly Paradise, so that afterward, through those merits—if he had remained obedient—he might transfer him to the heavenly kingdom.

Or the Lord wished that, just as the Jews differed from the gentiles in faith, so they might also differ in outward appearance. Alternatively, outward circumcision was a sign of inward circumcision.

Again it is asked: If circumcision was good, why was it changed, since no good thing ought to be changed, and does this not make God appear changeable? It is false that no good thing ought to be changed, because we see that times and ages change, and yet they are good.

Again it is asked why that particular member is circumcised and not another. This is done because that member is more inclined toward sin. Why, then, are all the members not circumcised, since all continually offend? Certainly because it would either be disgraceful if the nose or eye were circumcised, or it would be intolerable.

Again it is asked why women were not circumcised. [Col. 0470C] The mystery is understood in this: the man signifies rationality, which can always be purer than sensuality; sensuality must be restrained and governed by reason, just as a woman is governed by a man.
