For example, the eye can never take care not to see unlawful things, and the other external senses are likewise unable to do so.

It should be noted why the Apostle says, “Through one man death entered into the world” (Romans 5), since it entered rather through the devil’s persuasion, Eve’s consent, and Adam’s knowledge.

It is not attributed to the devil because humanity received no origin in transmission from the devil. Nor is it attributed to Eve, because the man is not from the woman, but the woman from the man; and after receiving the male seed, she adds her own contribution secondarily. We see something similar in the earth: it first receives the seed, then supplies its own moisture and causes it to sprout.

Guilt is therefore imposed upon the man alone, because he sinned knowingly and with his eyes open, and preferred not to offend his wife for the moment rather than persevere in obedience to God. [Col. 0470D]

It is asked why original sin is imputed to a child still in its mother’s womb, and why a baptized person does not produce a baptized child. The answer is that from what is corrupted nothing but what is corrupted can be born.

Again: insofar as a human being is concerned, he is cleansed in baptism; but because he cannot procreate without concupiscence, that corruption is also imputed to his offspring. It is like the earth receiving seed purified from chaff, while the seed nevertheless does not arise without chaff.

But why is original sin imputed to the soul, since it is created new and clean by God? The answer is that the soul is united with the body in the same person, and through this customary union it is corrupted by the body.

For example, someone may cast good seed into the earth, and afterward the earth’s mixture may produce not good fruit but weeds. But why does the better part, namely the soul, not draw the more impure part, namely the body, along with it and transform it into its own condition? This must be left to divine judgment. [Col. 0471A]

Since the Lord removed original sin, it is asked why he did not also remove the punishment of that sin. The answer is that the Lord mercifully provided for us in this matter: we are able to die, because we cannot ascend to heaven without some merits, just as Adam, while placed in Paradise, could not do so either.

The Lord therefore wished to compel us by every necessity to strive toward that place. If the fear of death were removed, no one would advance, since now, amid so many imminent dangers and so many troubles and hardships of the world, only very few, compelled by them, attain eternal life. Indeed, humanity would become incorrigible like the devil, without fear.

## QUESTION XV. On Human Redemption

The first question is why the Lord did not redeem humanity by a word alone. The answer is as follows: if he had commanded that humanity be saved by a word alone, the devil could have complained that he had used the Lord’s power rather than the equity of justice. [Col. 0471B]

The second question is by what right equity accomplished this. The answer is that the devil had made the Lord’s human being captive—possessing human nature but not human guilt—and how rightly he crucified Christ, in whom he had no right arising from sin. Therefore, by right and according to the law of nations, the devil deserved to lose what he possessed through wicked fraud.

The third question is why this suffering is called redemption. The answer follows: just as Esau sold his birthright for a dish of lentils, so Adam, when he rashly tasted the fruit, subjected himself as a slave to the devil. The Lord Jesus, returning like for like, intoxicated him with a similar drink by which that deadly enemy had killed the first parent.

For just as the devil gave Adam death to drink through the taste of the fruit, so the Lord offered him a certain sweet cup when he allowed the devil to take pleasure in the many insults which he inflicted upon him.

The fourth question is why salvation could be accomplished neither through an angel nor through a human being. The answer is that it could not be accomplished through a human being because it was impossible for the lost to redeem the lost or for the captive to free the captive. [Col. 0471C]

Nor could it be accomplished through an angel, because even if an angel granted salvation, he could not confer divinity, which he did not possess from himself.

The fifth question is why he did not assume an angelic nature for the redemption of humanity. The answer is that the devil would again have complained that his contest with the Lord had not been fairly matched, since the Lord would have brought a sword against one holding a staff.

The sixth question is why he delayed for so long. The answer is that the Lord was going to accomplish something new, unheard-of, and marvelous, which first had to be promised and confirmed by many witnesses. If it had happened suddenly, no one would have believed something so extraordinary; even with so many and such certain signs, very few were found who placed their faith in Christ when he came.

Moreover, if the Lord had come to save the world before the Law was given, someone could have said that his coming was unnecessary, since he could have given certain commandments that would have brought salvation. The Lord therefore wished us first to experience everything, so that it might be demonstrated that we could be saved by no other way except through him, and so that everything might be attributed solely to his grace. [Col. 0471D]

The seventh question is why he did not redeem the devil as he redeemed humanity. The answer is certainly that, although the devil was situated amid the most abundant and perfect delights of his Lord, he fell through his own fault, with no one inspiring or persuading him, but because he was lifted up by pride. Humanity, however, was deceived and fell through another’s prompting—namely, through the devil’s persuasion.

The Apostle wrote fourteen Epistles, showing by their very number that they correspond with the Decalogue of the Law and with the four Gospels, from whose faith and truth they differed in no respect.

Yet they seem to have been added unnecessarily after the Gospels, since the Gospels contain the perfect teaching of faith, instruction in virtues, and correction of vices. Nevertheless, the Epistles were necessary after the Gospel. Although everything is written in the Gospel, what is there stated only in broad outline is taught here fully and sufficiently.

Moreover, when new vices arose in the Church, [Col. 0472A] new situations and new remedies were required: commandments that flowed from the Gospels, yet were not superfluous because of their particular novelty and necessity. In this respect the Apostle relies upon the authority of the prophets, who, after the Law of Moses had been given, under the Lord’s inspiration and command, provided spiritual correction against vices that had returned.

When the Lord, exhorting us to humility in the Gospel, warned that no one invited to the wedding feast should recline in the first place, he was admonishing against pride, showing that no one should prefer himself to others or boast of his own merits.

“Through the Law I came to know that sin must be avoided.” Sin—that is, the devil, who caused me to sin—worked concupiscence in me through the commandment of the Law. This did not happen because the Law gave me a necessity of sinning, but by way of opportunity.

Before the Law, the devil was as though asleep, not taking care to drive those to death whom he saw going there voluntarily. But when he saw that the Law had been given, contradicting the way of sin, [Col. 0472B] he understood that he would either lose them completely or compel them to go along the way of death that had been forbidden to them.

In this way, when the good of the Law had awakened him, he began to strive and labor more intensely, so that he might compel them unwillingly to go where previously they had gone willingly. Thus, taking an opportunity from the Law, he began to incite them to sin.

But because they did not trust in God and trusted in themselves, they could not resist. Therefore they sinned more because of the opportunity provided by the Law: they were disobedient to God and committed greater sins.

It is like an enemy rising against a weak opponent. He would not exercise all his strength against him; but if he saw him fortified and strengthened, he would rise against him with greater force because of that circumstance, since then either he would be defeated or he would conquer.

We ordinarily call an opportunity—not a true cause—the advantage which the devil has against us when he sees us striving toward good.

It should be noted that the Apostle identified three laws: the law of the flesh, which is the law of sin; the Law of Moses; and the law of the mind, which is also the law of the spirit.

He said that in Christ Jesus they had been freed from death, and truly they had been freed in Christ from its cause. [Col. 0472C] For God the Father, sending his Son not in sinful flesh but in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned our sin “concerning sin” (Romans 8)—that is, concerning his Son, who was sin, meaning a sacrifice for sin.

God the Father is said, improperly speaking, to send the Son, because he does not send him in such a way as to remove him locally from himself, since the Son is everywhere present with him. Nevertheless, he is said to send him by a certain likeness: just as we separate from ourselves the person whom we send, so the Father sent the Son when, in assuming flesh, he separated him from himself to some degree.

Although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cooperated in the conception of the blessed Virgin Mary, only the person of the Son assumed flesh. Thus he appears to send him, as it were, away from himself, because he did not assume flesh from the Virgin together with the Son.

It must be understood that the Son was sent not to a virgin in the abstract, but in the likeness of a virgin; and not in flesh simply, but in the likeness of sinful flesh.

For if he had said that Christ possessed an image of flesh, [Col. 0472D] he would already seem to agree with that heretic who asserted that Christ had an imaginary and phantasmal body—like the man who says, “If a virgin gave birth, it was a phantom.”

Therefore Christ must be said to have been sent not in an image but in the likeness of flesh, and not of flesh simply but of sinful flesh. Christ did not possess merely similar flesh, but real flesh and a real body. Since this flesh was entirely without sin—most clean, pure, and real—it was nevertheless like our sinful flesh in its capacity for suffering and its mortality. Thus he had our flesh, not the flesh of sin, but flesh like sinful flesh.

If the Father, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and concerning sin—that is, concerning the Son who was a sacrifice for sin, as has been said—condemned sin, then he condemned in our flesh the sin that was his concern: original and actual sin, destroying it completely in the death of the Son. He also weakened the tinder of sin that remained in the flesh, from which sin arises, so that carnal titillation no longer attacks the faithful as it used to, if they trust in the Lord and remember his Passion. [Col. 0473A]

It should be understood that although he suggests that the Jews served through fear, this must not be understood of the true Jews. They were holy men who belonged to our faith and our covenant; just as we now serve under grace, so they served through love. He is speaking of false Jews.

It must be considered how the Holy Spirit was given to false Jews, so that through that Spirit they might serve God, and yet not in fear, since wherever the Holy Spirit is given, he produces love rather than fear.

The answer is that in what they did well they had the Spirit as its worker; but in what they did out of fear alone, they had not the Spirit but themselves as its source. Thus the Holy Spirit was the author of good service, not of wicked fear; and so the Spirit gave them service, while their service was exposed through fear. For no reward is earned by those who do something out of fear.

Thus we have received the Spirit of service, not one that exists in fear but in love. [Col. 0473B] Why was the more perfect Spirit given to us than to them? Because he makes us adopted children, and we truly are children as a matter of cause.

For the Spirit himself gives testimony in many ways—that is, through many signs—to our spirit that we are children of God, because we served God with filial love, not servile fear.

Our spirit makes itself a child of God when it serves God himself out of love. The Holy Spirit testifies and approves that it is his child: it does not withdraw from God, but rather cooperates with him in everything from day to day, advancing it toward greater things. It would not do this if our spirit served in fear.

Christ was sacrificed once in himself, yet in the sacrament he is sacrificed for the people not only throughout all the solemnities of Easter but every day. The person who, when asked, answers that he is sacrificed has certainly lied.

The Lord invited servants and prepared food for them—himself. [Col. 0473C] Who would dare to eat his Lord? Yet he says: “Whoever eats me lives because of me” (John 6).

When Christ is eaten, life is eaten; he is not killed in order to be eaten, but gives life to the dead. When he is eaten, he restores, but he is not diminished.

Therefore, brothers, let us not fear eating that bread, lest perhaps we allow him to pass by and afterward, when we wish to eat him, fail to find him. Let Christ be eaten: when eaten, he lives, because he rose after being killed. Nor, when we eat him, do we divide him into parts.

Since this is what takes place in the sacrament, the faithful know how they eat Christ’s flesh. Each person receives his own portion; hence the portions themselves are called “parts.” He is eaten in portions, yet the whole remains intact in heaven, and the whole remains intact in your heart.

The whole was with the Father when he came into the Virgin; he filled her, yet did not depart from him. He came in the flesh so that human beings might eat him, and he remained with the Father so that he might feed the angels.

What you know, brothers—and what you do not know—you ought to know: when Christ became human, a human being ate the bread of angels. How, then, by what means, by what way, through what merits, and with what dignity did a human being eat the bread of angels, unless the Creator of angels became human? [Col. 0473D]

But faith justifies, as it is written: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1). Through faith, original and actual sins are then forgiven, and, in addition, merits are increased.

Hence it is rightly asked why it pleased divine providence to superimpose circumcision, or what benefit its imposition brought.

The answer is that God’s mercy always desires us to ascend from strength to strength and desires nothing more than our progress. Therefore, just as he gave the first human being a law by which, if it were observed, he could attain the glory of freedom from suffering and immortality, so he gave Abraham and his descendants the commandment of circumcision, through whose completion their merit in obedience would greatly increase.

Alternatively, carnal circumcision signified spiritual circumcision, which is purity of heart and the cutting away of the mind’s vices. Thus, just as the Jews differed from the other nations in the inner human being, so they might also be distinguished in the outer human being by circumcision. [Col. 0474A]

The Lord also wished them to carry this sign on their bodies and, as it were, to have it before their eyes, so that they might attend to its meaning through frequent meditation and devote themselves to works of faith.

Again it is asked: If circumcision was holy and useful, why should it have been changed, and baptism substituted for it?

The answer is this. After God, because of his love with which he loved us, sent his Son so that he might become human and appear to human beings (Ephesians 2), the gifts of his grace began to flow to us more abundantly: stronger and greater innocence, and more plentiful righteousness.

Therefore, in place of circumcision, the baptismal washing of salvation was instituted, so that through the cleansing of the outward human being the more splendid adornment of the inward human being might be shown.

Water was specifically chosen as the element for this sacrament because it restores brightness to dirty things, refreshes the thirsty, irrigates the earth and makes it fertile, and extinguishes fire. It signifies spiritual grace, which cleanses the soul, refreshes it inwardly, extinguishes the tinder of sin, and grants the soul progress in virtue. [Col. 0474B]

It is asked by what right of equity he set him free. [Col. 0474B] The answer is this: The Son of God became human, assuming from his Virgin Mother the nature of the human race without sin—a nature which sins did not hold captive under that providential arrangement [reading uncertain].

But the wicked enemy saw him crying, weeping, and doing the other things required by human nature. Not believing that he was not subject to him or free from transgression, since he had learned from so many signs that he was mortal, the enemy attacked him, inflicted insults, and multiplied injuries.

When the enemy laid an unoffending hand upon him, the bond and written indictment on which he relied fell away from him as he demanded punishment from one in whom he found no guilt.

Thus the bond of our condemnation and written charge was dissolved. The wicked enemy, while seeking more, lost what belonged to him, because this is the most just law: whoever lays claim to another’s property loses his own.

It is asked why circumcision was imposed only upon males, since now we see both sexes hasten equally to the grace of baptism. [Col. 0474C]

The answer is that it secretly contained within itself the mystery of its meaning. The name “woman” signifies sensuality, while the name “man” signifies rationality, as the Apostle says: “The man is the head of the woman” (1 Corinthians 11). The rational spirit of the man governs animal affection as a husband governs his wife.

Thus, to signify that this animal nature cannot be entirely free from vices, nor through its own purity be made equal to its husband—that is, to the rational spirit—circumcision was imposed upon males but not upon females.

In baptism, however, this meaning is not observed. Since sins are forgiven equally to both sexes through grace, both equally hasten to the grace of baptism.

It is asked why this suffering is called redemption. [Col. 0474D] The answer is this: Just as Esau sold his birthright for a dish of lentils, so the wretched first parent, through the sweetness of the fruit which he tasted, bound himself under sin and the devil’s service.

For the sweetness of the forbidden thing by which the wretched human being had been sold, the Lord offered the devil the sweetness of insulting and striking him, and finally crucifying him, patiently enduring everything they wished to inflict upon him.

Thus, by a forbidden sweetness the devil deceitfully bought him, and by a forbidden sweetness the Lord redeemed him for himself.

Again it is asked what reason there was for his assuming human nature to accomplish this human redemption, rather than the more noble angelic nature, as the Apostle says: “For he never took hold of angels, but once took hold of the seed of Abraham” (Hebrews 5).

The answer is that it was fitting and proper that we should be redeemed through the nature by which we had committed sin; and perhaps the devil could have complained that he was unjustly losing the servitude of the human race unless he were conquered by the very thing he had subjected.

Moreover, just as the Son of God could not bring a remedy unless he were God, so, unless he were truly human, he would not provide an example. [Col. 0475A]

It is also asked why he delayed his coming and this redemption for so long. [Col. 0475A] The answer is that something new and marvelous was going to happen, and therefore it had to be proclaimed through a long succession of times.

If it had happened suddenly and been unknown to everyone, no one could have believed it. Even after so many revelations, so many signs, so many prophecies, and so long a delay, scarcely any were found who offered their faith.

There is another answer as well, which you will find earlier.

Since sin began with a woman, and before the woman with the devil—of whom the Gospel says that he was a murderer from the beginning—and since the devil sinned first by persuading, the woman by consenting, and the man through the woman’s persuasion, it is asked why, when the Apostle speaks of the sin that had passed into everyone through the succession and transmission of descendants, it is not attributed to the serpent or to the devil.

**Answer.** Because no human generation came from him at all. [Col. 0475B] Nor is it attributed to the woman, because posterity is named not from the woman but from the man. The male sex is more noble, as the Apostle says elsewhere: “The man is not from the woman, but the woman from the man.”

It is therefore attributed to the man because procreation proceeds principally from male seed, which is corrupted by original sin, and secondarily from the female contribution. For example, seed proceeds principally from grain, while it increases secondarily through the moisture of the earth.

From corrupted matter nothing whole or incorrupt can be born, in accordance with the saying of holy Job: “Who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed?” (Job 14:4).

If anyone seeks more deeply why the worse part prevailed against the better, this must be left to God’s judgment. We affirm only this truth: unless the soul and body of the human being were together subject to original sin, both would not need to be freed from it, nor would the Son of God, truly human, have assumed both personally for himself.

Again, it is consequently asked: if original sin is remitted to human beings through baptism, what prevents the punishment of that same sin from being immediately discharged, so that one no longer fears death or is subject to any suffering?

The answer is that the gracious and merciful Lord has also provided for us in this matter. In heaven, indeed, he has prepared for us a kingdom and a life better and more joyous than anything that could exist in this world. But who would direct his mind toward it, knowing that in this world he would live forever without any suffering, when even the fear of death, our flesh so full of miseries, and the world itself, almost destroyed by its own afflictions, scarcely drive us toward God? Therefore he willed this life to become bitter to us, so that the other might become sweeter. Hence, after the transgression of the first parent, the Lord said: “See that he does not take from the tree of life and live forever” (Gen. 3:22).

The foreskin is that skin which the Jews circumcised. Because the Gentiles retained it, they were reproached by the Jews as uncircumcised—not merely as those who possessed a foreskin, but as the foreskin itself, that is, as the uncleanness it represented. God commanded Abraham to cut away this skin, which is the seat of lust, so that he and the others might understand, through that voluptuous part separated from the body, that all pleasures must be removed from the mind. It was fitting that original sin should be punished especially in that member from which it was also propagated.

A man, rather than a woman, was therefore circumcised, so that there might be an indication of the two states of the soul, masculine and feminine, which the Apostle subsequently calls flesh and spirit. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mark 14:38). It is shown that the incentive to sin was not removed from the flesh of the righteous, for their testing, but that through grace it was removed from the spirit, together with the consent to delight in it and its contagion, so that they might renounce it.

Thus, when the Apostle perceived the opposition of the incentive to sin in the members of the flesh and of the good will in the spirit, he cried out: “Who will deliver me from this body of death, since I am weak in myself against these things?” (Rom. 7:24). And he adds: “The grace of God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid. 7:25), thereby showing that he failed in confidence in his own strength but trusted in divine strength.

Nevertheless, although the woman was not circumcised, she was cleansed from original sin through solemn rites, sacrifices, and offerings. The cutting away of sin ought to have been shown especially in that member because it was more subject than all the others to sin, both through the original propagation of sin into children and through its actual perpetration in the individual. Thus, what Adam covered on the first day for cutting in all his children, God caused to be circumcised on the eighth day of each person’s birth for the remission of sin. Those who were infected by sin at the beginning of the world were also to be more severely punished in this life by the law in the members of origin and pleasure; and in the eighth age, at the end of the world after the day of judgment, they were to be marked as flayed of every contagion of sin.

It is also asked why circumcision was completed in the man and not in the woman, and in the male member rather than in the other members.

**Answer.** In the man alone, and not in the woman, because immediately after the sin the woman received a twofold sentence: one, together with the man, of mortality and susceptibility to suffering on account of the transgression; the other, in that same original member of propagation, that she alone should bear her children in pain because of the serpent’s disobedience and the man’s deception.

It was therefore fitting that the man likewise, who had sinned knowingly and more gravely, should receive a twofold sentence: one of mortality for the transgression, and the other of circumcision in the original member, because he had consented to the enemy and to his wife.

Circumcision was completed in the male member and not in the others both because it would have been excessively cruel and intolerable to circumcise every member, and to show that there was not yet a complete circumcision of the mind in outward form. Circumcision punished original sin in the original member, and, by its temporal punishment anticipating eternal punishment, removed guilt. The rest of the law likewise removed sin from the other members by punishing it, since it could not remit it through grace—as in “tooth for tooth” and “eye for eye.” It gave neither advancement in the virtues, nor remission of actual offenses, nor assisting grace.

But the one who knew that sin could not pass unpunished, and who wished to make the remedy more complete and more gracious, commanded in his baptism that the whole human being be washed without any punishment, by the single and complete grace of the water of regeneration. Thus the entire inner person, in every part, might be seen to be cleansed from every sin, both original and actual, and moreover to be reshaped, freely and made radiant, into the new splendor of the virtues.

In accomplishing this great mystery, he took care to choose a suitable element—namely, water, rather than wine, oil, or any costly liquid. Since water is nowhere sold but is freely available to all nations, its lack of preciousness would not dishonor so great a sacrament. Rather, because it is not costly but freely available, it would show itself suitable equally to the poor and the rich, and thus display the gratuitous grace of God, since it is free. It is also necessary, because it is necessary to everyone, and its outward effect expresses its inward efficacy.

For just as water, more than all other liquids, not only washes away filth but also restores whiteness, so the grace of baptism not only washes away all the filth of vices but, extinguishing the fires of lust, restores the whiteness of every virtue.

Hence baptism was rightly placed after circumcision: because the law could not make the servant of the flesh perfect, grace might make him perfect and preserve him. Since water also causes the earth to germinate, it announces the fruitfulness of good works; and as it has many uses, so it signifies many mysteries of its own.

If, as some object, the angelic nature had become incarnate, then, since both angel and human being are capable of sinning according to their nature, our fragility, united to it, would very easily have fallen, since it is evident that both natures had sinned in themselves. It is likewise evident that human nature cannot exist without sin unless divinity comes to its aid.

It is asked why the Lord gave his disciples his body and blood not before but after the supper, when no one dares to receive the Lord’s body and blood except while fasting.

The answer is that he ought not to begin the New Testament until the Old Testament had first been completed. This is shown where he says: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15); and again: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another, just as the Lord God loved you” (John 13:34).

The devil strikes a human being in three ways: in the forehead, in the side, and in the back. In the forehead, when, to one who wishes to begin some good work, he suggests pride in the very intention, while that person thinks he will act well and then inwardly boasts. In the side, when, while he is acting, his mind is exalted. In the back, when, after recognizing and examining himself before the deed has been done, he finally makes confession at the end of his life.

[Col. 0477]

## EXEGESIS OF THE BOOK OF THE PSALMS (C)*

### FIRST PREFACE

[Col. 0477]

In the First Book of Chronicles it is read that, when the prophet David had grown old in devoted service to the Lord, he selected four thousand young men from the Israelite people to perform with their own voices, to the great delight of heavenly grace, the Psalms that he himself had produced under the Lord’s inspiration, using organs, lyres, nablas, tambourines, cymbals, and trumpets.

From this number we frequently find names inserted in the titles, such as Jeduthun, Asaph, the sons of Korah, and similar names—not because they themselves, as some wish to maintain, were the authors of the Psalms, but because they were placed over the musicians and proved to be trustworthy administrators of those matters. By such commemoration they received honor, since they served the sacred office with devoted minds; especially because their names are also known to indicate meanings appropriate to the matters concerned.

Thus Cassiodorus.

Jerome likewise says:

> “I know,” he says, “that some think the Psalter is divided into five books, so that wherever it is written among the Septuagint interpreters, *γένοιτο γένοιτο*—that is, ‘Let it be, let it be’—there the end of the books occurs; in Hebrew, instead, it reads ‘Amen, amen.’ But we, following the authority of the Hebrews, and especially that of the apostles, who always call it the book of Psalms in the New Testament, maintain that it is one volume. We also affirm that all the Psalms belong to those authors who are placed in the titles: namely, David, Asaph, the sons of Korah, Heman the Ezrahite, Moses and Solomon, and the others whom Ezra gathered into one volume. For the Hebrew title itself, which is interpreted as ‘the volume of hymns,’ in agreement with apostolic authority, shows not several books but one volume.”

Hilary likewise says:

> “Concerning those Psalms which, under various superscriptions, are found without the names of their authors, this is the tradition of the men of ancient times: those that follow without an author’s superscription are to be considered the work of the author named in the superscription of the Psalm preceding them.”

It must not be overlooked that among the Hebrews the Psalms do not have a differentiated numbering, but were written without notation of sequence. They are not marked there as first, second, third, fiftieth, or hundredth; rather, their sequences and numbers are mingled without any distinction.

For, as the ancient transmitters relate, Ezra gathered them—unarranged and scattered according to the diversity of their authors and times—into one volume and collected them there. But the seventy elders, following the tradition of Moses, remained in the synagogue for the preservation and teaching of the law. After King Ptolemy entrusted them with the task of translating the whole law from Hebrew into Greek, they understood through spiritual and heavenly knowledge the power of numbers and arranged the Psalms into number and sequence. Assigning each number according to its efficacy and completion, they allotted to the Psalms an order that was itself complete and efficacious.

Thus the third Psalm, according to its historical position, is later than the fiftieth, but it was placed before it because of a certain sacramental significance. The fiftieth Psalm, according to its historical position, is also later than the fifty-first. But the power and perfection of the number fifty-one required that the impenitent Doeg the Idumean, because of his prior hatred of David, should be placed later, while the later Psalm should be placed earlier, so that the remission of sins might be located at number fifty; whereas the punishment of treachery, exceeding the appointed number of remission, would lack pardon, since it had lost both the time and the number of repentance.

For since the remission of sins was established at fifty, the number in which there is the sabbath of sabbaths, according to the prefiguration of the year of Jubilee, this Psalm, in which repentance is placed first and remission of sins is requested, is consistently placed in the order of that number.

The book of Psalms is contained in three groups of fifty, and this arises from the reason and number of that blessed expectation of ours. Whoever carefully considers the completion of each group of fifty and the providential arrangement of the Psalms in this order will find that it corresponds to the dispensation of our salvation.

First, through the remission of sins we are reborn as a new human being. Then, after the remission granted through repentance, we await the future kingdom of the Lord in the age of that holy city, Jerusalem. Finally, when heavenly glory has been completed in us, the whole company of spirits proclaims the praises due to God. Amen.

## ACCOUNT OF HOW THE HOLY SPIRIT DICTATED THE PSALTER

[Col. 0477]

David, the son of Jesse, while he was in his kingdom, chose four men to compose the Psalms: Asaph, Heman, Ethan, and Jeduthun. Nine are by David himself; seventy-two are attributed to David; thirty-two are without superscription; twelve are attributed to Asaph; twelve to Jeduthun; and nine to the sons of Korah. Two belong to Haggai and Zechariah; one to Moses; and one to Solomon.

Thus eighty-eight recited the Psalms, while Abiud struck the *synpsalma* and the lyre, when David had brought the ark of God into Jerusalem after it had been recalled from Azotus forty years later and had remained in the house of Aminadab. He placed it upon a new cart and brought it to Jerusalem, together with seventy chosen men from every tribe of the children of Israel.

From the tribe of Levi he selected two hundred and eighty men, among whom he appointed four leaders to preside over the singing: Asaph, Ethan, Heman, and Jeduthun. Dividing among each of them seventy men who responded with praise to the Lord in song, he assigned one to strike the cymbals, another the *cynira* [the reading is uncertain], another the lyre, and another to raise the horn trumpet. David stood among them, himself holding the Psalter.

Seven choirs preceded the ark, together with sacrifices of calves. The entire people followed the ark.

There are therefore one hundred and fifty Psalms. Of these, as we said above, David himself composed nine; seventy-two are attributed to David; thirty-two are without superscription; twelve are attributed to Asaph; twelve to Jeduthun; nine to the sons of Korah; two to Haggai and Zechariah; one to Moses; and one to Solomon.

Thus all the Psalms of David, son of Jesse, king of Israel, amount to one hundred and fifty, with two hundred and one *diapsalmata* [musical or liturgical divisions], one beyond the number—that is, a Psalm of David written specifically for him.

### SECOND PREFACE

[Col. 0479]

Since, with the help of him without whom every action and intention is fruitless, we are about to begin the Psalter, let us briefly preview, as far as we can, the few matters that we know ought to be stated beforehand.

It must therefore be understood that all divine Scripture either pertains to history, to morals, or to mystery. This division, however, must not be understood in such a way that its parts are never mingled. For moral teaching and mystery are often found in history, as in Genesis and in many books of the Old Testament, of which it is said that no word is free from mystery.

History and mystery are also found in moral teaching, as in many sermons of Augustine and of the other holy Fathers, in which many things are spoken historically and according to mystery—that is, according to the spiritual meaning.

Moral teaching and history are likewise found in mystical Scripture, as in the very Psalter toward which we are proceeding and in many of the prophets.

Nevertheless, this is said in different ways according to the abilities of different people who use the Scriptures in different ways. Some proceed according to history alone, such as inexperienced priests when they explain only the Gospels simply to the people according to the letter. Others proceed according to morals alone, such as priests more advanced in knowledge when dealing with those same Gospels. Still others proceed according to mystery, such as those who have advanced through God’s gift so that the secrets of the divine Scriptures, hidden from others, may be disclosed to them.

Thus the previously stated division is valid: divine Scripture is either historical, as Genesis; or moral, as sermons; or concerned with mystery. This last part pertains especially to prophecy.

Prophecy is defined as follows: prophecy is divine inspiration that demonstrates, with unchangeable truth, the events of things either through visions, through actions, or through the sayings of certain persons.

It occurs through visions, as in Ezekiel, Daniel, and blessed John. When they were in ecstasy, divine inspiration foreshowed future things through certain images.

It occurs through actions, as in the sacrifice of Abraham. Warned by God to sacrifice his own son, Abraham did not doubt that the one who had given him a son in his old age, contrary to the course of human generation, could also raise him from the dead. As he hastened to carry out the command, a heavenly messenger again ordered him to spare the boy. Abraham looked behind him and saw a ram offered to him; he took it and sacrificed it in place of his son.

Through this sacrifice divine inspiration foreshowed that, in our Savior Jesus Christ, who would come in the unity of true flesh and divinity, humanity alone should suffer for the salvation of the world, while divinity, together with it, should remain undefiled and unharmed. This is rightly understood through Isaac, whose name is interpreted as “laughter” or “joy,” because through the humanity he assumed he brought peace and joy to angels and human beings.

The humanity of Christ is also rightly understood through the ram, concerning which it is written elsewhere: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter,” and so forth.

Prophecy may also be understood through the actions of Jacob, who, by crossing his hands, blessed Joseph’s sons Manasseh and Ephraim, placing his right hand upon the younger Ephraim and his left upon the elder Manasseh. Through this, divine inspiration foreshadowed the character of two peoples who would arise from different seed—that is, what sort of people they would be. One, understood through Manasseh, whose name is interpreted as “forgetfulness,” was rejected; the other, understood through Ephraim, whose name is interpreted as “fruitful,” was chosen.

Prophecy occurs through sayings, as in what is read in Moses concerning Christ: “I will raise up a prophet from among your brothers; hear him as myself,” and as in the Psalter and in the sayings of certain prophets.

The inspiration described above occurs in two ways: either through grace or through permission. Through grace, as in Moses and the other good men; through permission, as in the prophetic Sibyl and in unbelieving philosophers, who foretold many things about Christ under divine inspiration.

Their utterances are understood through the silver and golden vessels that the Israelite people borrowed from the black Egyptians. For by their sayings and opinions the divine page is adorned by Israel—that is, by the faithful—as with silver and gold.

Prophecy through sayings is divided into the past, the present, and the future.

It concerns the past, as in the book of Genesis. The mind of a human being born so long afterward could not, without divine inspiration, have been sufficient by itself to remember or narrate the order of the first creation of things, as Moses does there.

It concerns the present, as in the blessed John’s statement about Christ: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” For this reason Elizabeth, when the glorious Virgin came to her, says: “And how has this happened to me, that the mother of my God should come to me?”

It concerns the future, as in the Psalter and in whatever has been foretold concerning Christ’s first and second coming and the condition of the Church.

With regard to the present subject, prophecy through sayings is further divided as follows. Prophecy speaking about Christ sometimes speaks of his divinity, as where it says: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you,’” and, “With you is the beginning,” and in similar passages.

At other times it speaks of his body—that is, of the faithful, who are said by analogy to be his members, because they are governed by him as members are governed by the head.

At other times it speaks of his humanity, as when it says: “The kings of the earth stood by,” and in similar passages.

When this prophecy speaks of the body, it sometimes introduces a perfect person praying, as in “To you praise is fitting,” and so forth; Moses introduced this. At other times it introduces someone of lesser status, such as a penitent soul. At other times it introduces the head himself, with that affection by which he gave himself for us in order to make us a pleasing sacrifice to God the Father.

It often speaks of the members as though it were speaking of the head itself, as where it says: “My God, my God, why…” Just as the tongue sometimes speaks on behalf of the mind, as when it says, “I have been torn apart,” so sometimes, through the union and affection of the members, it speaks of them as though of itself, as when it says on behalf of the foot: “Why do you trample upon me?”

It must be understood that when prophecy speaks of Christ’s humanity, it is rightly said to speak of God. For what else is it to speak of that flesh which was conceived without carnal pleasure, born without pain, and lived without sin amid sin, than to speak of divinity?

Likewise, when prophecy that speaks of the body assigns certain Psalms to David himself, this magnificent name—interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable in appearance”—is attributed to the members because of their close union with the head, to whom the name David properly belongs. Is it not therefore rightly said that, when it speaks of such things, it speaks of divinity? Certainly it can be.

Now let us proceed to the title.

Among Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins alike, this book is entitled, with reference to the whole, “The Book of Hymns, Soliloquies concerning Christ.”

A hymn is properly the praise of God written in meter. The entire Psalter is composed metrically in Hebrew. Hence it is properly called in Hebrew “the book of hymns.” Among us, and perhaps among the Greeks, it does not preserve the meter, because of the hindrance caused by translation. Nevertheless, it is rightly called among us the book of hymns, because although it does not retain the meter, it does retain what is most important: namely, that in every part, among us as among the Hebrews, the praise of God is conspicuous.

It is not called the book of Soliloquies concerning Christ because the Psalter speaks only of Christ in every part, since at times, as we showed above, it also speaks of the body—that is, of the Church. Rather, because it speaks chiefly and above all of his divinity or humanity, we may say that it is given this name emphatically.

So, in the Gospel, the Jews call Abraham their father, not because he is the father in faith of the many nations that believe, but because they especially gloried in his fatherhood, since he was their father according to the flesh.

If anyone examines the matter more deeply, the Psalter may also be said to speak only of Christ because, even when it speaks of the body, it speaks of Christ himself through his members, by reason of the great union between body and head, as we said above.

It must be understood that two translations of the Psalter are in use and held in honor among the Latins: the Roman and the Gallican.

The Roman is the one used by the Romans and by most Italians. It was taken from the Greek into Latin from Symmachus and Aquila, according to the Seventy Interpreters of King Ptolemy.

The Gallican is the one used especially by the Gauls. This is the more important one, produced at the request of Pope Damasus by blessed Jerome, who translated it from Hebrew into Latin according to the sense. Jerome had previously made another translation, likewise taken from Hebrew but literal, transferring word for word in a simple manner. That version was less complete because of the difference between the languages.

Several other translations were also made among the Latins, but none of them is in use.

With reference to the whole, this book is entitled among the Hebrews *Nablat*, and among the Greeks and Latins *Psalterium*.

A *psalterium* is properly a musical instrument shaped like the letter delta, which is triangular, with a hollow belly above. Ten strings are stretched regularly across its upper exterior surface. When they are touched with the fingers or struck with a plectrum, they produce from the upper part a harmonious melody and a sweet sound.

This book is called the Psalter by analogy with that instrument. Just as the musical instrument produces sound from its upper part, so this book sounds forth from above: that is, it reveals heavenly and divine things to us, because it teaches us what the faithful ought to know concerning Christ’s humanity and divine nature.

It also teaches the ten principal commandments, signified by the ten strings of the musical instrument, in which the whole New and Old Testament is contained.

Of these ten commandments, three pertain to love of God and seven to love of human beings. They were distinguished on two tablets and given to Moses.

The three that pertain to love of God are these:

“Your Lord God is one.” This is explained as follows: “Do not go whoring after foreign and changeable gods”; that is, do not worship mutable and diverse idols, because your God, whom you ought to worship, is one—that is, he remains forever. He cannot be changed into Jupiter or Apollo or any other such demon.

The second commandment is: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain.” That is, do not believe that the Word, incarnate for your sake, is merely a creature and not the Creator. To take the name “Christ” in vain would be to do this, for, as Ecclesiastes testifies, every creature that is under the sun is vanity.

The third commandment is: “Observe the Sabbath”; that is, keep a spiritual Sabbath.

The person who keeps a spiritual Sabbath is one who, inspired by God, does everything he does during this life for the attainment of the future rest. The present life is signified by the seven days in which the Lord worked all that exists in the world.

The seventh day, the Sabbath, after he had seen that the things he had made were good and had rested, signifies the future rest. Therefore each person ought to work during the six days—that is, during this present life—in such a way that he does not fear being expelled from eternal rest.

For this reason the book of Genesis appropriately describes morning and evening during the six days, saying, “And morning was made, one day,” and similarly in the others. But on the seventh day, that is, the Sabbath, it is silent about night, by which adversity is signified. In the future rest, which is understood through the Sabbath, eternal joy is possessed without any adversity or sadness.

Carnally, however, the person keeps a Sabbath who, whether he works or rests, hastens only toward earthly pleasure and repose.

The seven commandments that pertain to human beings are these: “Honor your father and mother”; “You shall not kill”; “You shall not commit adultery”; “You shall not steal”; “You shall not bear false witness”; “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife”; “You shall not covet his property.”

The whole of these commandments may be summed up as follows: no one should do to another what he does not wish to be done to himself.

In the first commandment, impiety toward parents is removed. It was placed first among these seven because it is the beginning of love of one’s neighbor. In one’s own family, if one truly loves one’s parents, one learns to love one’s neighbor.

The three commandments concerning God signify the holy Trinity; the seven signify our conduct in the world, which is marked by the number seven.

Concerning these ten commandments it is said: “Agree with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way, lest perhaps, when he has overcome you, he hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the torturer.”

Our adversary is these ten commandments, which contradict the things we continually do. In this life, signified by the way, we must agree with them by ceasing from the things they command us to cease from, if we wish to avoid future torments.

Since we have explained above what the Psalter is, let us also say what a Psalm is.

A Psalm is properly that harmonious melody which is produced by the strings of a musical instrument, namely the Psalter, when they are set in motion by the fingers or struck by a plectrum.

The parts of this book are called Psalms because they teach us to hymn or to sing psalms—that is, by the skill of the heart, striking the ten commandments as though they were strings with our fingers, we may, through their execution and practice, render ourselves sweet melodies to our Creator.

In divine Scripture, “Psalm” is used for a sweet and pleasing work.

It must be understood that the cithara is the opposite of the musical instrument called the Psalter. The cithara has below the hollow space that the Psalter has above. In divine Scripture, the cithara is usually understood as the mortification of the flesh, since it sounds from below.

The Psalter, which sounds from above, signifies the vivification of the spirit. If we wish to be made alive in the spirit, we must first produce a sweet sound for God from below by mortifying our flesh, withdrawing its pleasures, and giving to the poor what we withdraw from ourselves. Then, from above, we must adorn the mind—that is, having put vices to death, we must adorn it with virtues and place it in contemplation.

It should also be noted that, except for the first Psalm, each Psalm bears its own title, added by Ezra the scribe.

When Ezra the scribe returned with the Israelite people from the captivity of the Chaldeans to Judea and found the royal city of Jerusalem burned and completely stripped of the temple’s ornaments and books, he repeated this prophecy—that is, the Psalter—as well as many other things, from memory and in full. He arranged the Psalms as they now stand and added titles both to the book as a whole and to each Psalm individually.

Blessed Augustine admits that the reason and knowledge of this arrangement must be left to the Holy Spirit alone. It seems that David, who composed them, did not arrange them in this way, because of the transposition of historical events found in certain Psalms according to this arrangement.

Some say that Ezra arranged the Psalms differently from the historical sequence so that they might be understood not historically but mystically. For this reason he added historical titles to some and not to others.

He also entitled certain Psalms with the names of the four leaders of the singers whom David placed in charge of the psalmody before the Lord’s ark. For it is read in the book of Chronicles, in the Hebrew, that when David brought back the Lord’s ark, which had been returned by the Philistines, from the house of Aminadab in Gibeah to Jerusalem, so that he might place it in the tabernacle he had prepared, he selected four thousand singers from Israel. With their own voices and every musical instrument, they were to rejoice with him before the advancing ark in sweet melody in these Psalms to the Lord.

To lead these singers, he appointed one hundred and fifty leaders, so that the melody might be harmonious. Then he assigned four masters to all of them in singing: Asaph, Ethan, Heman, and Jeduthun.

The Holy Spirit already signified through this that, with the cooperation of the one about whom the Psalms had been composed—that is, Christ—the Catholic Church, gathered from every part of the world and from nations differing in language and customs, would render a harmonious melody to God in the unity of faith and Christian religion.

Through the number four, both among the singers and among the masters, the four regions of the world are signified; through the thousand, those perfected and gathered into the Church are signified.

Ezra entitled certain Psalms with the names of these four leaders of the singers, either because they themselves assisted in their melody or, better, because their names, according to their interpretation and mystery, suit the Psalms themselves.

For the same reason certain Psalms were entitled with other names, such as those of Haggai, Zechariah, and Moses—not because, as some say, those men composed the Psalms, for David alone composed them all.

It must be understood that this prophecy—that is, the Psalter—is used more frequently than all the others in the Church because it contains more mysteries concerning Christ and the Christian religion, and because it was used in a similar manner by the fathers of the Old Testament.

It must not be passed over that in this prophecy, as in the others, certain future things are spoken of in the present or the past tense. This occurs because nothing is future to the Holy Spirit, who reveals them, and because among us nothing is as certain as what is present or past.

If anyone asks about the purpose and intention of this work, let him briefly summarize both as follows: because of that most grievous death which the first father, through the transmission of sin, had brought upon the whole world in common, and from which neither an angel, nor a philosopher, nor any creature could rescue the perishing, God the Father, through the Holy Spirit, showed blessed Patriarch David—more fully and more openly than to anyone else—that Christ would assume flesh and establish the Church through the sacrament of his body and blood, and that the end would one day come.

Therefore that most holy man composed this book under the prophecy of that future salvation, with the intention of consoling the human race and instructing the Christian religion.

Now let us proceed to the book.

## EXEGESIS BEGINS

[Col. 0483]

## ON THE FIRST PSALM

[Col. 0483B]

### ARGUMENT

It generally urges everyone to pursue the virtues, adding at the same time what good reward follows good deeds and what evil consequences follow evil deeds. Tertullian, in his book *On the Spectacles*, asserts that this Psalm may also be understood of Joseph, who buried the Lord’s body, and of those who do not gather for the spectacles of the nations.

### EXPLANATION

The first Psalm does not have a title because nothing ought to be placed before our head, the Lord and Savior, about whom it is going to speak plainly. Although other Psalms also say many things about him, none speaks in this way about his life among human beings on earth. Since everything that is to be said here looks toward him, it is rightly placed at the head of the sacred work.

Some have said that it occupies the place of a title, others that of a preface.

The prophet is said to recount the text of this entire Psalm. In the first part he sets forth the life of the holy Incarnation; in the second he recalls that the wickedness of sinners will receive its deserved punishments at the future judgment.

### COMMENTARY
The first psalm lacks a title for two reasons: either because it is itself the title and beginning of the others, or because, more closely and openly, in accordance with the way he lived among human beings, it speaks of him—that is, of Christ—who [Col. 0483D], according to his divine essence, is without any beginning, and from whom all things take their beginning.

The purpose of the first psalm is to exhort the faithful, following the example of the Head, to hasten to rise again from the soul’s threefold death: that is, insofar as they can, to strive to return from the region of unlikeness into which they were led through their first parent, and to join themselves to their Head in freedom from sin.

Every death of the soul occurs in three ways: either through pleasure alone, or through pleasure and consent, or through the accomplishment of sin. Pleasure is the will to sin, which arises in the soul from stimulation and incitement, from the inclination to sin that exists in us, and from suggestion—that is, from the incitement of the instigator, the devil, when it comes upon us. This is the soul’s first death.

The second is consent, when we apply ourselves outwardly to carrying the matter out as far as we can. The third is the act of sin itself. This is divided into two kinds: simple action and habitual action, just as the two preceding kinds are also divided. What has been said concerns voluntary sins.

These three things are called the soul’s death because through them the soul withdraws from him who is its life and husband—that is, from God—and joins itself to death, that is, to the devil.

These three deaths of the soul are signified by the three dead persons whom the Lord raised. The daughter of Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, is raised in the house by the lifting of the hand; by her pleasure is signified, since it is still, as it were, modest, because it has not yet appeared outwardly [Col. 0484C] and gives no example. Therefore she is raised while remaining in the house, when one comes to make satisfaction for it, and it is cleansed by light remedies, namely almsgiving and similar works.

By the lascivious young man, carried out of his mother’s house before he was raised, consent is understood. Consent is situated in outward application and gives an example to those who see it. Therefore, unless this sin is erased by serious repentance—indicated by the fact that the Lord does not extend a hand to him—he is addressed with something like a blow and a grave command: “Young man, I say to you, arise.”

By Lazarus, four days in the tomb and stinking, are understood both the simple act and the habit of sinning. Concerning habit it is said: “The beasts have rotted in their dung.” This is absolved only by upright and weighty satisfaction, signified by the loud cry and the stirring of the Lord’s spirit at his raising.

Through these three deaths, Adam, the propagator of sin, withdrew from God by dying; the Prophet hints at this in the first verse of this psalm [Col. 0484D].

The whole psalm may be read either as spoken by the voice of the Head, speaking about himself and his members, or as spoken by the voice of the Prophet in the person of the Head. It is as though he said:

Formerly there went before us in the human race a wretched and unhappy man, to be imitated by no one—namely, Adam, the propagator of sin. He went away from his Creator into the region of unlikeness, taking delight in many sins; he stood by giving consent to pleasure; he sat by carrying out his sins and becoming an example to his descendants.

But there was to come a blessed man, that is, one endowed with every good, to whom the grace of the Holy Spirit was given without measure, and therefore one truly to be imitated—namely, Christ, existing as a man, that is, strong and yielding to no temptation. He will not go away from his God by straying even in the will toward sin; he will not stand by consenting; he will not sit by teaching others to sin through his example.

Observe the order of the words. Once going away from Christ—even in the will—is removed, standing and sitting are likewise understood to have been removed. Therefore, so that nothing be superfluous, let us refer these matters to his members, just as what we affirmed about Adam can be understood of his descendants who resemble him [Col. 0485A].

Thus, if it is said: “The man who is to come, that is, Christ, did not go away, even in the will, insofar as he himself is concerned”; or, if he should go away in the will of one of his own—that is, in pleasure—he will not stand, that is, consent, but by his help he will return, putting pleasure to death. Or, if one of his own should stand by consenting, he will not sit by carrying out sin and providing an example, as Adam went away both in himself and in his descendants by taking pleasure, consenting, and giving an example of sin.

Note that he says, “the counsel of the ungodly.” He calls the deceiving serpent and the deceived Eve “the ungodly.” He calls it “counsel” because Eve believed the serpent, who said that as soon as she and her husband ate of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, they would be like gods. Because Adam was placed in their counsel—that is, because he yielded to them—he became disobedient to the Creator and incurred the soul’s threefold death mentioned above.

We may also understand “the way of sinners” as their evil works, namely those of Eve and the serpent: acting and speaking against God [Col. 0485B]. Adam was their equal in this. Or by “the way of sinners” we may understand the evil works of all those who became sinners by Adam’s example.

By “the seat of pestilence” the example of sin is rightly understood. A seat signifies teaching authority. Those who are teachers easily draw others by their example toward evil or toward good. Pestilence, however, is a disease widely spread, involving all or nearly all. In the same way, sin exemplified by Adam, involving many, leaves no one free except the one whom he frees who himself does not even agree to go away in the will.

It should be known that Adam was not deceived as Eve was, as though he believed that he would ever become like God. Rather, as we read, he preferred not to trouble his wife by resisting her persuasion instead of obeying the Creator’s commands. He was also deceived in this: he refused to confess his sin, but shifted the blame onto its author, saying: “The wife whom you gave me as a companion gave me to eat.” Eve likewise tried to excuse herself through the serpent, saying: “The serpent persuaded me” [Col. 0485C].

The verse may also be expounded in another way, so that each thing we deny of Christ is compared with each thing first attributed to the earthly man, in accordance with the purpose of this psalm: to exhort us that, just as we have borne the image of the earthly man, so we should bear the image of the heavenly one.

It may accordingly be spoken in the voice of the Prophet as follows:

Formerly there went before us a wretched and unhappy man who went away—that is, withdrew from the Creator’s commands by apostasy through disobedience. Therefore he stood in the way of sinners, that is, afterward repeatedly carried out the acts of a wicked habit; and he sat in the seat of pestilence, that is, taught wicked doctrine and became ambitious for earthly things.

But another was to come who would neither stray from any commandment, nor carry out wicked deeds, nor teach wicked doctrine, nor be ambitious as that man was.

In this interpretation, “the counsel of the ungodly” and “the way of sinners” are understood with reference to Adam, as was said above. With reference to Christ, however, both here and above “the counsel of the ungodly” are called evil works, from which he was free although he lived among them [Col. 0485D].

As for “the way of sinners,” we may understand either this world or the way of sinners, into which way Christ came by being born—that is, by living among sinners. But he did not stand there, because no worldly allure detained him. Rather, as is read elsewhere, like a strong and swift giant he ran along this way.

Adam is said to have given wicked doctrine because he showed his descendants not only how to do evil by example but also how to curse by his word. Christ, on the contrary, brought saving doctrine to the world.

Adam was ambitious; Christ refused to accept the kingdom offered to him. For it is read that when he had satisfied five thousand men in the desert with five loaves and two fish, those thousands wanted to appoint him king for themselves in the flesh, so that they would no longer experience any need for earthly food. Rejecting this and exhorting them to seek a spiritual kingdom, he said: “Work for the food that does not perish but endures” [Col. 0486A].

Royal power, through which domination is acquired, and evil doctrine are rightly called pestilence, since both involve many. For no one truly exists who lacks the love of ruling. The Apostle also speaks of the persuasion of wicked doctrine: “Whose word spreads like a cancer.”

The ungodly are properly called idolaters and unbelievers; sinners are called transgressors of the written law, although the word may also be understood otherwise.

**But in the law of the Lord.** Since it is not enough for anyone’s blessedness to abstain from evil without doing good, he therefore adds, in order to prove that the man who is perfect and truly blessed is to come: “But in the law of the Lord.”

This may be understood of the members as well as of the Head; and, with respect to the final interpretation, opposites are here set against opposites. With respect to going away from the commandment, he is said to be “in the law”; with respect to standing and sitting, “meditating in the law.”

According to the first interpretation, the statement is simply made. It should be understood that being “in the law” is one thing and being “under the law” another. To be in the law is to act voluntarily according to the law; to be under the law is to be driven and weighed down by the law. In the latter there is servitude; in the former, freedom. In the latter there is servile fear; in the former, filial love.

It is therefore rightly said of Christ that his will—that is, his affection—will be in the law of the Lord the Father, which he says: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it”; and, “My food is to do the will of the Father,” and so forth.

Being in the law may also be attributed to the members, who fulfill the law not through fear but through love, in accordance with the saying: “The law is not laid down for the righteous,” and so forth. To meditate in the law is to persevere in the law through filial love.

By “day” and “night” we may understand either all time, or prosperity by day and adversity by night. In Christ we shall call the whole period from his birth to his Passion prosperity; the Passion itself we shall call adversity. In the members, the time of persecution is adversity, and the time of rest from persecution prosperity. In both periods, neither the Head nor the members departed from the law of the Lord.

Thus, from this passage: “Whoever …” [the following *pro* is uncertain in the supplied text]. And likewise from this: “Whoever contends lawfully will be crowned.”

Of Christ’s day of prosperity it is said: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced.” Of the night of adversity it is said: “And until night they rebuked,” and so forth.

**And he shall be like a tree.** This verse may be read of the Head alone, or of the members together with the Head, if we adhere to the straightforward interpretation.

It may be understood as follows: Because this great man will be such in himself and such in his own, as has been said, therefore he and his own will be like a tree—that is, comparable to a tree planted in a well-watered place, which in the season of ripe fruit sends forth leaves and flowers earlier and yields more abundant fruit.

This applies particularly to the Head, of whom it is said that, while still a boy, he sat among the teachers and expounded the Scriptures to them. It also applies to the members, such as the apostles, who did not learn what they knew through lengthy practice in doctrine, but, as soon as they had been breathed upon by the divine fire, immediately sent forth leaves—that is, words of preaching. No one’s words ever produced as much fruit as those of the Head and his members [Col. 0486D].

If the verse refers only to the Head, it may be continued in this way: It is no wonder that this man who is to come will be such, since he will not go away but will rather be in the law of the Lord; for he will be, deservedly, that true tree of life, placed in the midst of the Church and signified by the material tree placed in the midst of paradise.

That tree, according to his humanity, was planted beside—that is, near—the streams of water: that is, it was joined and united to the wisdom of God the Father, namely, the Word. This wisdom is the streams of water because from it there flow into the various members subject to it waters—that is, spiritual gifts. For since the wisdom of the Father, the Son, is consubstantial with the Father, spiritual gifts must flow from the Son just as from the Father, of whom it is said: “Every perfect gift,” and so forth.

Or it may be understood differently, as referring to the united human and divine nature. That tree—that is, the united nature—was planted, that is, prepared through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0487A], so that it might be beside—that is, near—the streams of water: that is, so that it might fully receive the streams of water, meaning the irrigation of spiritual gifts. For the fullness of every grace of the Spirit was in that man, of whom it is written: “In whom dwells,” and so forth; and again: “God does not give the Spirit by measure.”

Or otherwise: the tree was planted—that is, born and placed—beside, that is, near, the streams of water, meaning among peoples drifting away through vices, like a physician among the sick. Hence it is said: “I have not come to call the righteous,” and so forth.

Or otherwise: the tree of his humanity was planted—that is, conceived—in the Virgin’s womb beside the streams of water, that is, under the complete overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, which destroyed in her every incentive to vice. Hence it was said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” and so forth.

It should be known that in Holy Scripture “water” is understood in three ways: either as spiritual gifts, in accordance with the saying, “The rushing of the river,” and, “The water that I shall give”; or as peoples, as in the Song of Songs: “Many waters,” and so forth; or as flatteries, whence it is said: “Let not the storm overwhelm me,” and so forth.

Spiritual gifts are called water for this reason: just as our exterior—that is, our body—is washed by these material waters, so by those spiritual gifts our interior—that is, our soul—is washed.

Peoples are called waters because they are always in flux, both with respect to the instability of their own life, which is always passing away, and with respect to the vices through which they flow downward.

Flatteries are also called waters because, just as water softens something, so flatteries often soften and break the spirit of many.

Note that it says: “Which shall give its fruit in its season.” The season of that tree—that is, of Christ—for bearing fruit is said to have been after Christ himself was glorified through the resurrection and ascension. Its season for bearing fruit had not yet come, of which it is said: “The Holy Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”

This is not said because Christ had borne no fruit before his glorification—raising the dead, healing the sick, and converting many through his preaching—but because that fruit was small in comparison with the fruit he gave after his glorification through the apostles, when the Holy Spirit was sent down from above and illuminated and strengthened their hearts. Through those apostles he established the Church throughout the whole world, when the sound of their preaching went out into all the earth and to the ends of the world [Col. 0487C].

Christ is called the tree of life by this comparison: just as Adam and Eve, had they not sinned, would have become immortal by tasting the fruit of the material tree of life planted in paradise, so whoever spiritually and worthily tastes Christ is immortal in soul. He himself bears witness to this when he says: “Whoever worthily eats my flesh and drinks my blood shall never taste death,” and so forth.

**And its leaf shall not …** He calls Christ’s words of preaching “a leaf” by this comparison: just as on a tree the leaf comes first and the fruit follows, so the fruit of Christ’s preaching followed his words, namely, the salvation of many [Col. 0487D].

That leaf—that is, those words—will not wither, meaning that they will not be ineffective, because they will always bear fruit somewhere.

Of these words it is said: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell, but the word of the Lord remains forever.” And again: “Heaven and earth will pass away,” and so forth. And again: “My word will not return to me empty, but it will bear fruit wherever I send it.”

**And all things …** By “all things” he understands both the words and the deeds that Christ will do in himself and in his members. Just as these things will be good in him, so they will prosper in the faithful themselves—that is, they will be brought to a successful outcome.

We may also say, if we press the point, that even the things Christ will do—that is, will permit the devil to do—in his members, insofar as human beings judge them, will occur for their prosperity. Although it may seem to have harmed Peter that he denied the Lord, it nevertheless benefited him greatly, since, once corrected, he learned in himself how he ought to have mercy on the weakness of others [Col. 0488A]. The same may be said of the rest.

**Not so the ungodly, not so.** What has been said thus far pertains to the warning and terror of the wicked. Here he understands the ungodly as both false Christians and unbelievers.

It is as though he said: The godly will prosper in every word and deed that takes place in them; but the ungodly will not be so, that is, they will prosper neither in words nor in deeds. He repeats the statement to confirm that the wicked will truly be punished, a point that seemed true to few. Hence it is said: “The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him, says the Lord.”

The ungodly will not prosper but will be like dust, that is, comparable to dust. Just as a material wind separates from solid earth and casts away the loose earth without moisture or weight that is called dust, so the wind—that is, their pride—casts away those who are dust, meaning those who lack the affection of charity, that is, love of God and neighbor, and who are therefore disobedient to God’s commands. It casts them from the face—that is, from the presence—of the true promised land, namely, the heavenly Jerusalem, where only the good will be.

Of that land it is said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord.” And again: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit,” and so forth.

Or they are cast from the face of the earth, that is, from its representation—meaning from stability in God. In them the commands of God, which are the stability of the good, will neither be represented nor seen, because those commands make them stable against hostile temptations.

Or they are cast from the face of the earth, that is, from the beauty and glorification of their own flesh. For although the ungodly will rise again, they will not receive their flesh glorified, because their resurrection will not be to glory but to disgrace.

Of this earth it is said: “Wait for the Lord,” and so forth, “that you may inherit the land.” Whoever in this life patiently awaits the Lord’s coming, enduring scourges and not straying from the way—that is, from his commands—will finally, in the resurrection, receive the earth, that is, his flesh, as an inheritance. It cannot then be taken from him or troubled; he will receive it glorified, so that he will neither lose it again nor be disturbed in it [Col. 0488C].

Because all the ungodly will be like dust, the truly ungodly—that is, idolaters—will not rise so as to be present at the judgment, for they will not come to judgment. Of them it is said: “The ungodly has already been judged”; and, “Those who sinned without the law will also perish without the law.”

Nor will sinners—that is, transgressors of the written law, namely false Christians—be in the counsel of the righteous, that is, in either judgment of the righteous: either to judge, as certain righteous persons do, namely the apostles and martyrs, and so forth, or to be judged for salvation, as certain of the righteous will be, to whom it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father,” and so forth.

This was added to humble false Christians, so that, when they heard that unbelievers would not come to judgment because they had not received the law, they would not think that they themselves, because of the sacraments of Christianity, would come for judgment and, although they had received them unworthily, would nevertheless either judge or at least be judged in such a way as to be saved.

Here “the ungodly” and “sinners” are understood in their proper senses. “Counsel” is used for judgment because every judgment conducted rationally is carried out through counsel.

It should be known that there will be many distinctions among those who rise again. Some will rise so as to come to judgment; others so as not to come to judgment, because they have already been judged. Among those who come, some will judge and others will be judged. Among those who are judged, some will be saved and others will not. This distinction may be noted in the verse mentioned above.
