**For the Lord knows.** Since it has been said that the wicked will either not come to judgment or, if they come, will not be in the counsel of the righteous, it is understood by contrast that the good are granted what is denied to them. He adds the reason for both.

It is as though he said: The good will have these things, and the wicked will lack them, because he who is absolutely Lord, and whose office it is to reward, knows the way of the righteous—that is, he approves their works. Hence it is said: “The Lord knows those who are his.”

Since he ought to have said that he does not know the way of the ungodly—that is, that he rejects the works of the wicked, which they habitually perform, as is indicated at the same time—he instead uses what is clearer and what necessarily follows: it will perish [Col. 0489A].

For just as God’s knowing pertains to being and salvation, so his not knowing pertains to nonbeing and perdition. The Lord’s not knowing is used for rejecting, in accordance with the saying: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.” For it cannot be said that God, who knows all things, does not know something as though he were ignorant. Rather, his not knowing is rejecting: not defending whatever is worthy of perishing.

We may also call “the way of the righteous” the Head of the righteous, that is, Christ, whom God the Father approves, since he has given all judgment to the Son. Just as he approves him, so he approves those who imitate him. Hence it is said: “I will, Father, that where I am, there …,” and again: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.”

The way of the ungodly is likewise their head, that is, the devil, whom all his own will accompany into perdition and into that fire of which it is said: “Which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

This final verse may also be read first, and the preceding verse may be supplied as its cause. The continuation would then be:

Therefore the godly will prosper, but the ungodly will not so prosper, because the Lord knows their way, whereas he does not know the way of the ungodly, which will perish; and the preceding verse shows why it will perish.

It is as though he said: The way of the ungodly will perish because the ungodly—both idolaters and false Christians—do not rise in this first resurrection, that is, by placing themselves in judgment, so that they might condemn in themselves what ought to be condemned and approve what ought to be approved. And because they will not rise in this first resurrection, therefore those sinners—that is, the ungodly—will not be in the counsel of the righteous, that is, in the assembly of the righteous, at the future resurrection.

For there are two resurrections, one first and the other second. The first is in the present, when someone rises in soul from the death of vices through repentance. The second will be on the day of judgment, when the good rise in the flesh through the unchangeability and impassibility of the body, so that they can no longer suffer anything in the flesh itself.

No one will possess this second resurrection unless he has possessed the first. For it is necessary that whoever has been deprived of the first also be deprived of the second.

## IN PSALM II

### ARGUMENT

David makes a general complaint to God that, although the kingdom was given to him from above, both the nations and the people of Israel envied him, directing his common complaint toward the correction of all. Alternatively, Christ speaks about his Passion and power. Read this in Luke.

### EXPLANATION

David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable.” This applies to no one more suitably than to Christ almighty, who is truly most strong and is to be sought with the greatest desire.

The Prophet speaks of his Passion, and the Lord himself will speak his own words. Among the Hebrews, however, this psalm also has no title, but, joined to the preceding psalm, forms one psalm that begins with blessedness and is brought to completion in blessedness.

This psalm is divided into four parts. In the first, the Prophet speaks about the Jews because of Christ’s Passion. In the second, the words concern the lie of the judges. In the third, the words are those of the Lord and Savior concerning his almighty kingdom and his ineffable generation, insofar as human weakness can leave the matter unspoken. In the fourth, the Prophet is left exhorting the peoples to come to the Christian faith once they have recognized the Lord’s majesty.

### COMMENTARY

**Why did the nations rage?** Here the Head is introduced through prophecy rebuking the Jews and the nations because, failing to recognize the physician of salvation, they were about to make an irrational raging and assault against him in his Passion.

He speaks here of his Passion and that of his own, and of the acquisition of his kingdom, in this manner:

The Jews thought that the strongest possible reason for them not to lose their place and nation, and for the world not to follow him, was his death. But this became the strongest possible reason why they themselves lost their place and nation, when, destroyed by Titus and Vespasian, they were scattered throughout the world into captivity—and why the whole world followed him.

For if the Jews had not thought that he would fail to rise again, they would not have crucified him. But because he died, he rose again; because he rose again, he ascended; and because he ascended, he sent the Holy Spirit, who so enlightened the hearts of the apostles that, when their teaching had been spread everywhere, it caused nearly the whole world to follow him.

This whole matter is well indicated by the saying: “There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord.”

This psalm appears to be the same as the preceding one because it refers to the same thing, namely, the Head, and in a certain way both deal with the same subject. Yet it is clearly different from that psalm, both because of the title attached to it and because of the different purpose assigned to it.

The purpose of this psalm is to exhort the faithful, following the example of the Head, to share in suffering in the present so that at last they may reign together in the future. For the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him.”

This purpose differs completely from the preceding purpose: exhorting us to rise from the soul’s threefold death, and exhorting us that, just as we have borne the image of the earthly man, so we should bear the image of the heavenly man.

Nor does it hinder this distinction that Peter is said to call this psalm first in the Acts of the Apostles. It is called first not in relation to the preceding psalm, which is, as it were, the title of all the others and therefore lacks a title, but in relation to the following titled psalms, among which it is the first to be titled in this manner: “A Psalm of David.”

A psalm, according to the meaning of the word, is defined as follows: a psalm is a hymn composed according to the rule of some meter, which, in the likeness of an instrumental device, is known to indicate heavenly power to us.

This definition rightly applies to the words of this psalm. For they were composed both metrically and in Hebrew, and they indicate heavenly power [Col. 0490C], because they indicate to us Christ’s Passion and resurrection, through which he obtained the kingdom that is above every kingdom.

The same applies in the other cases.

“Psalm” is also understood as an action, by this comparison: the sound of a musical instrument, which is properly called a psalm, is produced through our action when we strike the strings with our fingers or with a plectrum. In accordance with this, both meanings can be expounded here in the title.

“Psalm”—that is, the following words, which indicate heavenly power—or the action noted in those words, namely acting in such a way as to speak of the Passion and the acquisition of the kingdom—is attributed not to the historical David but to the true David, that is, to Christ.

He is truly strong of hand because he bound the devil and took away his spoils—that is, Peter, Paul, and others like them, whom the devil had held captive in the first parent—and distributed them as ornaments of his house, when, after transferring them into the Church, he gave one the grace of languages, another the grace of healings, and another something of the kind.

Christ is also truly desirable to behold. At the sight of him the angels are refreshed, and of him it is said: “Whose face the whole earth desires,” and, “Beautiful in form above the sons of men.”

This may also be said of his humanity. For in him, even according to the flesh, there was nothing that would not truly refresh and nothing that ought not truly to be embraced, because he was entirely free from sins and abounded in every virtue. This cannot be said of anyone else.

This psalm is connected with the preceding one if that psalm is read in the voice of the Head, with a change from the third person to the first, as often happens, in this way:

I, through whom all my imitators will prosper both in words and deeds, am present, calling, justifying, glorifying, and doing every good thing. Why, then, will the nations rage against me?

But if the preceding psalm is read in the voice of the Prophet, the continuation is as follows:

I, of whom my prophet foretold so many and such great things—namely, that I would not go away even in thought, but would be wholly in his law, and so forth—am present, ready to confer every good upon everyone.

Why, then, will the nations—that is, the Gentiles—rage against me in my Passion, and why will the peoples—that is, the Jews—meditate vain things against me [Col. 0491A]?

It is as though he said: They did this for a base cause—or rather, for no cause at all.

By “the nations” he means the soldiers of Pilate, who were both Romans and Gentiles, and who crucified the Lord with their tongue, while the Jews did so with their hands.

They had no other cause against him except that the Jews, accusing Christ because he said that he was a king, said: “Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.” This was no cause at all. For both Jews and Gentiles had heard enough from him to understand what kind of king Christ meant himself to be, when he said: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

He says that the peoples—that is, the Jews—meditate vain things in two ways. Either because they did not recognize how saving his coming was, but still expected the Messiah to come, which was vain because he had already come. This is clearly confirmed in the Gospel by someone who, seeing him, said: “Truly, either there are two, or this is he.”

Or because they thought that they would not lose their place and nation if they killed him, and that the world would not follow him. This was vain, as has been said above.

Or because they thought that they would not crucify Jesus when they said: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone.” This too was vain, for their tongue was a sharp sword.

**The kings of the earth stood by.** Not only will the lesser rage against me and mine—so will the greater—because the kings of the earth, that is, those who pant after earthly things and do not attend to heavenly things, will stand, that is, stand for themselves, and will consent to the persecution of me—that is, of mine.

And the princes, that is, tyrants inferior to kings, will gather together for this one purpose: to be against the Lord, that is, God the Father. They will do this because they will be against me, Christ, persecuting me and mine.

Hence it is said: “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father.”

I say that all of them, both lesser and greater, will say against me and mine:

**Let us break their bonds.** That is, their institutions, so that the Christian religion may not bind us; and let us cast away from us the yoke, that is, the dominion and authority of Christ and his own.

For those placed in authority over the Church seem to exercise a kind of yoke and dominion over their subjects, whom they instruct. Of this yoke it is said: “For my yoke is easy,” and so forth.

With respect to Christ’s Passion, understand by the kings of the nations first Herod, who wanted to kill Jesus among the children, and Herod the second, his nephew, who also consented to the killing. Concerning this it is read in Christ’s Passion: “And Herod and Pilate became friends on that day.”

With respect to Christ, understand by the princes the leaders of the Jews—Pilate, Annas, and Caiaphas. At that time the Jews lacked a king, in accordance with the saying: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah,” and so forth.

With respect to the members of Christ, understand by the kings Nero and those like him; by the princes, any tyrants inferior to kings, persecutors of the saints.

The words “Let us break their bonds” may also be read in another way, as an exhortation from Christ to his members against persecutors [Col. 0491D]. It is as though he said:

Both the greater and the lesser will join together against us through their deceptions and persecutions, attempting to draw us to themselves. But let us break their bonds—that is, let us despise the flatteries by which they sought to bend us—and cast away their yoke, that is, disregard the threats and tribulations they will inflict upon us.

**He who dwells in the heavens.** According to the interpretation just given, continue as follows: Therefore let us cast away their yoke, refusing to consent to their drawing us away from the faith, because the Lord will laugh at them—that is, at some time he will bring them to the same faith.

According to the first interpretation, the continuation is as follows:

The kings and princes will indeed stand against us, but they will accomplish nothing, because he who dwells in the heavens—that is, in righteous souls—the Lord, namely the Father, will laugh at them. That is, with respect to their former condition, he will make them objects of derision, when he will even take some of them to himself during the Passion: the thief, the man who said, “Truly this was the Son of God,” and the centurion [Col. 0492A], of whom it is read in the Passion, together with many others.

He will make those who formerly seemed to rule rejoice afterward in submitting, and those who had been enemies become friends. With respect to their former foolishness, this will be like mockery.

And those whom he will laugh at here, taking them to himself, he will mock—that is, he will make them worthy of mockery and contempt—in the future.

Or the repetition may refer to the present, to intensify their ignorance, in accordance with which “mockery” and “derision” may properly be understood. Derision properly consists in disgraceful words; mockery is the contempt expressed by wrinkling the nose.

Thus it will be as though he said: He will make them do something that will be laughable both in word and in bodily gesture.

The heavens are appropriately called the souls of the righteous. Solomon says that the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom. It is also established that wisdom is God. Since, therefore, God’s seat is heaven, in accordance with what he himself says, “Heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet,” it is entirely fitting that, if the soul is the seat of God, as Solomon proves, the soul should also be called a temple.

Then he will speak. Truly, he will mock them in the future, because he will speak to them in his anger—that is, in anger that cannot be reconsidered or revoked—then, when his anger, now hidden, will be manifest, namely when he reproaches them, saying: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and so forth. And he will trouble them—that is, he will make them troubled and confused—in his fury, when he says in his most severe judgment: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.”

It should be understood that anger is not to be taken in God as some movement, as it is in a human being. In a human being, anger properly is the movement of a soul that loves the law against a soul that does not love the law. The remaining irrational movements should be called fury, not anger. Through this anger, many things are often judged rightly among human beings. Hence, by analogy with it, anger is attributed to God: that power by which he most justly punishes the creature subject to him—not with agitation, but with tranquility. Solomon therefore says of God: “Lord God of hosts, you judge all things with tranquility and dispose them most justly.” Yet this power is called anger in God with tranquility in relation to those who suffer, because to them God appears to be agitated.

God’s anger is twofold: one present and hidden, the other manifest and future. It is hidden and present when the wicked human mind in this life is given over to inner darkness—that is, is oppressed by blindness. Of this it has been said: “The wicked man does not know that he is being punished until, unwillingly, he suffers what he willingly perpetrated.” It will be manifest in the future when the wicked are openly and irrecoverably given over to outer darkness—that is, to the hell of fire. Both of these are noted in the book. Through “then” manifest anger is indicated; through “his own” it is said to be irrevocable. For whatever is once condemned by God is condemned eternally. Hence it is rightly said that in the present there is only a place for mercy. No one will obtain mercy in the future except one who has earned it here.

## “But I have been appointed”

[Col. 0492D] Here he openly begins to speak about obtaining the kingdom. It is as though he said: The nations, peoples, and rulers will stand against the Father and against me, wishing to crush and destroy me, and through me the Father. But I will be exalted, because I am so certain that I will be appointed king by him—that is, by the Lord—as though I had already been appointed king. And this will be upon his holy mountain, which is Zion—that is, upon the Church—in order that I may proclaim to Zion his command and will, that is, the Father’s.

Zion is a certain high mountain, once situated within Jerusalem. From there they used to observe from afar and foresee enemies or any newcomers, and its name is interpreted as “watchtower.” Thus, both because of its significance and because of its interpretation, the name Zion rightly suits the Church, that is, the faithful: for they are lofty through the eminence of their virtues and firm in their foundation, that is, in the stability of faith, just as a mountain is both high and firm. They ought to look toward what is far away—that is, toward future things, not present things; toward what lies ahead, not what lies behind—just as things situated far away were observed from Zion. Concerning these things the Apostle says: “For we, with unveiled face, behold the grace of God.”

## “The Lord said to me: You are my Son”

It is as though he said: Why do I say that I have been appointed king? I say this because the Lord Father commanded me to become incarnate, and he himself would hand the nations over to me, so that I might cultivate them as an inheritance. The matter is stated in the book as follows: “The Lord Father said to me, his Word”—inasmuch as I was his equal, I could ask nothing from him.

## “Ask of me”

That is: Make yourself such that you can ask—that is, assume human nature. “I will give you the nations as an inheritance,” that is, so that you may cultivate them by your teaching and they may nourish you through good morals. For just as someone cultivates an inheritance and the inheritance nourishes him, so the nations are called Christ’s inheritance: he cultivates them through preaching, and he is nourished by their good works, that is, takes delight in them. Hence elsewhere he says: “My food is to do the will of my Father.”

And I will give you not only a few nations, [Col. 0493B] but also the ends of the earth—that is, I will give you as a possession the nations situated at the farthest ends of the earth. I call the possession and inheritance yours—that is, belonging to you—because you are my Son, not adopted but proper, because I begot you, not temporally but today, that is, in eternity.

Although we cannot properly speak about God through any words available to us, nevertheless expressions that signify the present time, such as “today,” approach more closely to speech about the divine essence, to which all things are present. For this reason “today” has been placed here to signify his eternity, which is wholly present all at once.

We may understand “the ends of the earth” in another way: as referring only to the perfect, who are called God’s true possession because they have distanced themselves so far from earthly things that they retain nothing in themselves except what barely suffices to meet necessity.

## “You will rule them with an iron rod”

For this reason I will give you the nations as your inheritance: because you will be a worthy heir, namely because you will rule them with a rod—that is, with justice—which is signified by an iron rod because of its straightness, that is, its irrevocability. For whatever is once just or unjust before God remains forever just or unjust. Therefore his justice is irrevocable, not changeable like human justice.

“And you will shatter them like a potter’s vessel,” that is, you will crush in them carnal desires, the muddy affairs of the old man, and whatever has been soiled and contracted from the old clay.

God is like our potter, because he made us; and we are like pottery because, just as a potter breaks a vessel when something has happened in it contrary to his intention, so that he may change it for the better, God breaks by his correction and admonition whatever has clung to us through vices contrary to his creation, and restores us to something better.

## “And now, kings, understand”

Here the exhortation of the Head to the faithful begins. He addresses them sympathetically, with great familiarity and kindly affection. It is as though he said: God the Father will subject you to me and give you as an inheritance; and through this subjection and service you have now become kings, ruling yourselves and others. Hence it is said elsewhere that to serve God is to reign.

“Understand,” that is, act intelligently: consider what you, who are servants, owe the Lord. For what understanding is more worthy than knowing what a creature owes the Creator, what a servant owes the Lord, and what a human being owes God? No one knows anything more worthy.

And you who judge the earth—that is, who have the power to judge earthly-mindedness, meaning to condemn in yourselves and in others whatever ought to be condemned—be instructed. That is, accept instruction, namely the chastisements of God, concerning which it has been said: “The father chastises the son whom he loves.”

## “Serve the Lord”

He explains what he means by “understand.” Therefore he added “Serve,” so that they would not become proud because he had called them kings. It is as though he said: Although I have called you kings, nevertheless serve the Lord as servants. To understand means to act in this way—not in exaltation, but in fear; and not in servile fear, but rejoice, that is, do this joyfully.

And so that they would not turn this rejoicing toward an outpouring of rashness rather than toward the guarding of holiness, he adds: “with trembling.” Fear pertains to the soul, trembling to the body.

## “Take hold of his discipline”

Again he explains what it means to be instructed. It is as though he said: If you wish to know what it means to be instructed, take hold of discipline—that is, desire to grasp even what is fleeing from you: the chastisements of your Father, by which you will be disciplined and approved.

You ought to take hold of these not only so that you may escape future punishments, which are greatly to be feared, but also out of love of justice. He expresses this as follows: “Lest at some time”—that is, so that the Lord Father may not at some time become angry with you, by that power through which he most justly punishes the creature subject to him, and give you over to inner darkness, that is, to blindness of mind. Thus you may perish from the just way, that is, through blindness of mind withdraw from justice. How grave this is, the one who has experienced the sweetness of justice knows.

## “When his anger has been kindled”

He adds this so that perishing from justice might not seem a small matter. It is as though he said: It is exceedingly grave to perish or fall away from the Lord’s justice, because when his anger—that is, the power through which he most justly avenges himself—which now burns secretly in those whom he presently gives over to inner darkness, that is, to blindness of mind, when that anger, I say, has been kindled—that is, has burned openly—by giving them over to outer darkness, that is, to Gehenna, he ought to have said: “They have been condemned eternally,” or something worse, if anything worse were possible.

But to intensify the matter he sets down the opposite, namely: “For all will be blessed who trust in him,” that is, in the Lord. It follows from this that those who do not trust in him are wretched. Those are said to trust in the Lord who have already done, or will still do, such things that it is right for the Lord to reward them.

# PSALM III

**A Psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son.**

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0494C] This may apply to Hezekiah, who, surrounded by the Assyrian army, called upon the Lord. Alternatively: the voice of Christ to the Father concerning the Jews.

## EXPLANATION

Understand David as Christ and Absalom as Judas Iscariot, from whose face Christ fled, either bodily by withdrawing to the Mount of Olives or spiritually by concealing the light of his knowledge and love. And, appropriately for the concordance of the sacrament, each persecutor perished by the same punishment of hanging.

It should be noted that this psalm was sung after the fiftieth psalm, as were many others relating to Saul’s plots; but it was placed first for the sake of the mystery. The one that recalls the three-day resurrection is placed third, while the one that ought to have been fiftieth displays the fruit of remission and repentance.

This entire psalm is adapted to the person of Christ. First, he speaks to the Father, reproaching the persecutors who spoke irreligious words against him; second, the faithful people are instructed not to fear death, when he consoles them most certainly by the example of their author through the hope of resurrection.

## COMMENTARY

### “Lord, why have they multiplied?”

This psalm is entitled as follows: “A Psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son.”

It is read in the historical account, in the Book of Kings, that after David had committed adultery and murdered Uriah, while David did not yet reign over all Israel but only in Judea, his son Absalom lost the favor of his father David because he killed his brother Amnon on account of his sister Tamar, whom Amnon had violated.

Afterward, having been restored to his father’s favor through Joab, he acquired chariots and horsemen for himself from every quarter and gradually began to aspire to his father’s kingdom. At last he openly had himself proclaimed king and drove his father from the kingdom.

After this had happened, the men of Judah who were with David were eventually gathered to fight against Israel, whom Absalom had assembled. As they went out to battle, the father, standing at the city gate, carefully asked each man to preserve for him the boy Absalom, whom he loved.

After the armies had engaged, Absalom’s army soon fled. As Absalom himself was fleeing, he leaped upon a leafy oak. Because he was long-haired, his hair caught among the dense branches, and he hung there from the mule he had been riding, which continued on in flight.

When one of the king’s soldiers saw this, he reported it to Joab, the commander of the army. At Joab’s command, he returned and struck Absalom with a fatal wound. When David heard this, he mourned his death with unbelievable weeping, as the history relates.

This psalm was taken from that history and composed by David in the same persecution—not because it deals historically with the persecution of the historical David, but because mystically it deals with the persecution inflicted upon the spiritual David by his son Judas.

Through that historical David, the spiritual David, that is, Christ, is to be understood. Through his son Absalom, Judas, the spiritual son of this one, is to be understood. Judas can rightly be called a son, in accordance with the saying: “The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them.” This was said concerning the apostles.

By the fact that the historical David, driven away by his son, fled from his face, the flight of this spiritual David is to be understood: he fled from the face of his son Judas, who was persecuting him, both historically and mystically.

Historically, he fled when, on the night on which he was handed over, Judas went away to the Jews and Christ withdrew with his disciples to the mountain, where he prayed alone. Mystically, he fled from Judas when the power and wisdom of God abandoned Judas’s mind. He fled when he ceased to enlighten his mind, and when, after Judas had unworthily received the morsel of bread at the supper, Satan invaded his mind.

Through Absalom’s hanging, Judas’s hanging is likewise to be understood. Hated by heaven and earth, he was retained by neither heaven nor earth; suspended between the two, he suffered an end worthy of his deeds through his own hanging.

By the fact that the historical David escaped his son’s persecution after the son’s death, it is understood that Christ, once his betrayer Judas had been lost, escaped all tribulation and anguish when, after his passion, he was glorified by his resurrection, ascension, and sitting at the right hand of the Father.

The name Absalom is interpreted as “peace of the father.” This may seem very astonishing, both according to the history and according to the mystery, since the historical Absalom persecuted his father with such determination, and the mystical Absalom, that is, Judas, enraged the spiritual Father with such savagery.

But to one who examines the matter more carefully it will not seem astonishing. “Peace of the father” does not refer to sons but to fathers. And just as the historical father David is read to have had such peace toward his son Absalom, although Absalom was persecuting him, that David asked each individual member of the army going out to battle to take care of him and mourned his death with such affection that he said, “Absalom, my son,” and so forth, so the spiritual David is found to have had immense peace toward Judas the betrayer.

Although Christ knew Judas’s wicked plans, he endured his presence. He did not exclude him from the most sacred supper, in which he gave his disciples the figure of his most holy body and blood, nor did he refuse him the kiss of peace when Judas was handing him over, even though that wicked man was being inwardly ravaged by an internal war with the speed of a thought.

The aforesaid title is explained as follows:

“Psalm”—that is, the following words called a psalm, because they reveal to us heavenly power in the likeness of a musical instrument—those words, I say, together with their meaning and proper significance, are attributed to David, not the historical David but the true one.

I mean words that, through their events and significations, possess among us an understanding such as they possessed then, insofar as the Holy Spirit is concerned, to whom all things are present: namely, concerning the persecution that Christ was going to suffer from Judas, his son.

The events signified were present then, when the historical David fled from the face of his son who was persecuting him historically.

It should be understood that this psalm ought to be continued from the preceding one, both because it is the voice of the Head, just as the preceding psalm is, and because it speaks about the same matter. For it treats of Christ’s persecution and glorification, which amounts to the same thing as Christ’s passion and the attainment of the kingdom, concerning which the preceding psalm spoke. It also has the same intention as the greater part of that psalm.

For just as the intention of the preceding psalm was to exhort us to compassion so that we might also attain co-glorification, so this psalm has the same intention. Nevertheless, it differs in this respect: there he simply exhorted us to compassion of whatever kind; here he intensifies the matter, exhorting us not to fail in passion, however great the persecution threatening us, even if many thousands of persecutors surround us.

This is also presented as an example of our Head, against whom persecution became so violent and so great that among the number of his disciples there was not lacking one—or even many—who were added to the number of his persecutors.

For it may be conjectured that not only Judas the betrayer fell away from Christ’s disciples in his persecution of him, but that certain others who had previously followed the Lord and believed in him may likewise have consented to the same persecution. Concerning them it is read: “And nearly all of those seventy-two were scandalized and went back.”

The continuation is as follows:

I, concerning whom so many and such great things have been foretold, am present, prepared to bestow every good upon all and willing to heal everyone. Therefore I ought to be received kindly by all and persecuted by no one.

Yet the persecutors, both from the Jews and from the nations, both great and small, both mine and strangers, will rage against me with such determination that among the number of the disciples there will not be lacking one who is added to the number of the persecutors.

But, O Lord Father, why will those who trouble me be multiplied so greatly? It is as though he said: I endure this for my great glory and for their immense confusion.

All these things, insofar as they concern the prophet, are to be understood of the future, as are the preceding matters.

Truly, many will trouble me. For many rise up—not to defend me, as they ought, but against me, that is, opposed to me, and for themselves, that is, for their own place and nation.

### “Many say to my soul”

Truly, many will be against me, because many will speak against me for the condemnation of my soul—that is, of my life—in order to kill me. Speaking about me, they will say: “There is no salvation for him in his God.”

It is as though they said: This Christ will not be saved by that God in whom he trusts, so that he may raise him up. Before his passion Christ had said in many discourses that God the Father would raise him from the dead. Speaking about himself, he also said: “He will be handed over to the nations to be mocked.” And again: “Destroy this temple,” and so forth, along with many similar statements.

The Jews did not believe these things. Therefore, thinking that they could utterly condemn him to death—which they truly would have done if he had not risen—they crucified him. For if they had hoped that he would rise, they would never have led him through crucifixion to the glory of resurrection.

### “But you, Lord”

They will say that you will not save me by raising me up, but you, Lord Father, plainly know that they are lying. For just as you received me as a human being, born without pain and conceived without carnal desire, joined to me from a virgin’s womb through your Word, so you will receive me from the tomb by raising me.

I am therefore as certain that you will truly receive me as though you were already my receiver. I trust this because, although I am my own disgrace, possessing in myself nothing but the reproach of sin, you are my glory, making me free from sins.

And you will be the one who exalts my head—that is, my mind or spirit—in the passion, so that it will not recoil from it in any way but receive it gladly and eagerly. Hence it has been said: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”

“Head” is taken to mean “mind” in many places in Sacred Scripture, as where it says: “Let the oil of the sinner not anoint my head”; and again: “When you do this, you will heap burning coals upon his head.”

What is read in the Apostle may also be applied here: “The head of the woman is the man, but the head of the man is Christ.” By “woman” vitality, or sensuality, is understood; by “man,” the more worthy part of the mind, namely reason, which is the head of vitality, because, like a head, it governs the other members when reason itself is so governed by its own head, that is, by Christ, that it does not deviate in anything.

“My glory” and “the one who exalts my head” may also be read differently, so that the meaning is: You will receive me from the tomb in such a way that you will be my glory—that is, you will glorify me through immortality and impassibility—and after my glorification you will be the one who exalts my head, that is, you will exalt me, who am the head of my people, through my sitting at your right hand.

“My receiver” can also be explained in this way: You are my receiver, that is, my defender; you have undertaken my cause in order to act against my enemies. You, I say, are my glory—that is, the one in whom alone I ought to glory, and not in myself.

Hence it has been said: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord.” And again: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him glory only in knowing and recognizing me, says the Lord.”

In this interpretation, “the one who exalts my head” remains unchanged.

### “With my voice I cried to the Lord”

You will rightly receive me by glorifying and exalting me, because I will make myself fit to be received, insofar as I am able.

For I will cry not to gold, not to silver, but to you, Lord, so that I may be received by you and have you as my reward. I will cry, I say, with this voice—not an exterior voice, which is produced by the noise of beaten air, but the voice of the heart.

Although this voice is silent to human beings, it is nevertheless a cry to God. Through it no less is obtained by prayer, even though no sound comes from the body, provided that no earthly thoughts intervene in the affection of prayer and the whole affection of the mind is directed toward him.

Such a voice—that is, this kind of application of the mind—is called a cry to the Lord because of the force of the affection itself. It is by no means frustrated but is always heard.

The one who cries with this voice is the person who, with a heart closed to every earthly affection, directs the entire affection of the mind not toward anything earthly but toward God, so that he may receive God himself as his reward.

The one who desires earthly things more than God does not cry with this voice. Therefore he does not ask God for God’s own sake, so that he may have God as his reward, but asks for God on behalf of those earthly things. Such a person is more wretched when he is heard than if he were not heard. For the more he receives here the harmful benefits he desires, the more grievous disadvantages will press upon him in the future.

Hence it is rightly said concerning the voice described above: “When you pray, enter your room, and after shutting the door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

For what else is entering a room through prayer and closing the door than withdrawing into the mind, removing the door—that is, the senses—from attention to earthly things, and devoting oneself wholly and intentionally to divine contemplation alone?

### “And he heard me”

Because I will cry in this way, the Lord Father will therefore hear me by raising me up. He will hear me from his holy mountain—that is, from myself, who am his holy mountain.

This is said of Christ according to the fact that there are two natures in him. In him there is both that to whom it is fitting to ask, namely the human nature, and that to whom it is fitting to hear, namely the divine nature. It belongs to a human being to ask, but to God to hear.

Christ himself is called a mountain because of the eminence of his virtues, in accordance with what was said of him through the prophet: “And in the last days the mountain of the Lord will be prepared at the top of the mountains.”

Or alternatively: “He heard me in the resurrection from his holy mountain.”

Or again: “He heard me from his holy mountain,” that is, on account of his justice—or mine—which is called a mountain because of its eminence, in accordance with the saying: “Your justice is like the mountains of God.”

For it was just, both with respect to the Father, who is truly just, and with respect to his Son Christ, who was handed over to death without cause, that he should raise up the Son who had been condemned innocently.

Or: He heard me in the resurrection from his holy mountain—that is, on account of the humility of the flesh assumed. For, obedient to his command and will, I assumed flesh from the Jews, who were once called the mountain of God because of the eminence of the Law and the many sacraments granted uniquely to them, by distinction.

### “I slept and was overcome by sleep, and I rose again, because the Lord received me”

He shows by what hearing God the Father heard him: namely, by giving him the power to lay down his life and to take it up again.

It is as though he said: I slept. Pay attention to the force of the pronoun “I.” It was not the Jews, who were persecuting me, who compelled me to undergo the passion; rather, I slept of my own will, that is, I underwent the passion.

Properly speaking, to sleep is the rest that precedes sleep; and properly speaking, to awaken is the state after sleep, when someone is neither entirely awake nor entirely asleep. Therefore he uses “sleeping” for the passion that preceded death, and “sleep” for death itself, when he says: “I slept,” that is, I endured the passion of my own will, “and I was overcome by sleep,” that is, after the passion I entered the sleep of death.

Nevertheless, after three days I rose from the dead, because the Lord Father—or the divine nature—returned from the underworld after destroying it in order to take up its own flesh; he received me by raising me from the tomb.

Or, because the Lord received my cause in order to act on my behalf, as stated above.

### “I will not fear thousands of people surrounding me”

Because the Lord Father will either receive me from the tomb or undertake my cause, I will not fear the thousands of the tumultuous people surrounding me in my passion—not to imitate me, but to insult me.

For it is read that when the Lord had been crucified, many thousands of people who had gathered in Jerusalem for the Passover festival went out to him merely as spectators, or even for the purpose of insulting or mocking him. Few went out of compassion—namely, the good, who were few and hidden.

Hence it has been said: “I looked around, and there was no one to help me.” And again: “I trod the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me.”

### “Rise up, Lord; save me, my God”

For you have struck all those who oppose me without cause; you have crushed the teeth of sinners.

Here the Head prays on behalf of the members, that is, on behalf of the faithful, in order to exhort them all the more to share in his suffering here and at last to be glorified with him.

It is as though he said: You, Lord Father, who make me unafraid of my innumerable persecutors, rise up also in my people—that is, make my people rise up—for then they will be saved. Hence it has been said: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

And you ought to rise up in my people because you, who are God of all by your power, are my God—that is, the God of my people—by their will. They do not wish Jupiter or Apollo, but you alone, to be their God.

The Lord is said to rise up not because he is sleeping or reclining, but because he makes us, who are sluggish through the weakness of the flesh, rise up through the strengthening of the soul.

It is the custom of Sacred Scripture to attribute to God what he does in us. Hence the Apostle says: “Do you want proof that Christ is speaking in me?” He says “speaking” instead of “making me speak”; and elsewhere it is said: “The Spirit asks on our behalf,” that is, “makes us ask.”

### “The Lord’s is salvation, and upon your people is your blessing”

You ought therefore to save those who make you their God, O Father, because they are your servants and you are their Lord; and it belongs to a master to save a servant who cannot save himself.

Hence it has been said: “The hardship of poverty is burdensome not to the servant but to the master.”

And because saving them is your work, therefore may not just any blessing, but your blessing—that is, one belonging to you, namely the increase of virtues, which is received from you alone—be upon your people, that is, upon those who make themselves not their own people but your people, seeking not what belongs to them.

God’s blessing is properly understood as an increase of virtues, in accordance with the saying: “May the Lord our God bless us,” and so forth. Conversely, his curse is understood as a diminution of virtues.

### “For you have struck all those who oppose me”

This is a proof of what was said above by contrast: God will truly bless his people because, conversely, he will curse the people who are not his.

He says it in this way: You, Lord Father, will not only strike all those who oppose me, both in me and in my people, by giving them with their prince, the devil, to Gehenna on the day of judgment; you have already struck them with an interior blow, namely by giving them blindness of mind.

And rightly so, because they oppose both me and my people without cause. And because they oppose me without cause, you have crushed—that is, weakened and rendered ineffective—their teeth, because they were sinners. Conversely, you have sharpened the teeth of the good—or not only of theirs, but also of all sinners.

This interpretation will apply if we understand those who specifically oppose Christ as the persecutors who persecuted him in his passion.

Some teeth belong to the good and others to the wicked. The teeth of the wicked are persuasive words that disparage Christ and the faithful. Through these words, something is often diminished or cut away from the body of Christ—that is, from the Church—like a piece cut off by real teeth from those who are less cautious; and they make such people their own members in the body of the devil.

The leaders of iniquity are also called the teeth of the wicked. By their threats and by the authority of their example they often draw certain people away from Christ and join them to the devil.

The Apostle recalls these evil teeth when he says: “See that you do not bite one another, lest you consume one another.”

The teeth of the good, on the other hand, are persuasive words and the sweet teaching of good people. Through these, they take various parts away from the body of the devil when they convert unbelievers. They are also the holy leaders of the Church who, fulfilling in their works what they teach in words, withdraw many from the devil and join them to Christ both through teaching and through the example of a good life.

Concerning them it was said in the Song of Songs, in Christ’s voice to the Church: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep ascending from the washing, all of which bear twins, and none among them is barren.”

This is explained as follows: The perfect in the Church, who are called teeth and who crush the body of the devil through sound teaching and the example of a good life, take away many and transfer them into the inward parts of the Church. They are like flocks of shorn sheep because, just as shorn sheep lay aside the burden of their fleece, so they have cast off the burden of earthly cares.

They are ascending from the washing because they have been cleansed from the filth of sins in baptism. And they all bear twin offspring because, by carrying out the two commandments in which the whole Law and the Prophets are contained, they bring forth their fruit in such a way that none among them is barren—that is, devoid of the fruit of good works.

This psalm may also be read entirely in the person of the Head, in the voice of the Church. The Church speaks to the Lord its God amid the raging storms of tribulations, showing that it ought not to fail in tribulations, since these have been given to it both to increase its glorification and because it has him as its consoler and helper, who will free it from all its anguish.

Through this, it intends to exhort its members to possess steadfast patience in tribulations.

It is as though it said: Lord, why have those who trouble me multiplied throughout the world? Has this not happened by your permission for the great increase of my perfection?

It has indeed happened. Therefore they ought not to frighten me.

### “Many rise up”

Truly, those who trouble me are numerous, because many rise up against me, wishing to destroy the Christian name. Those many say, for the condemnation of my soul—that is, so that they may draw me away from the faith: “Let us persecute this Church, because it has no salvation placed in its God,” that is, the God whom it trusts as its helper will not save it by defending it.

For the persecutors would never strive to destroy the Church they were ravaging if they thought that God cared about its progress and salvation.

### “But you, Lord”

My persecutors say, O Lord, that you will not save me; but they are lying. For you are my receiver: through your incarnate Word you received my nature in order to save me, or you received my cause in order to act on my behalf.

You, I say, are my glory—that is, the one in whom alone, and not in me, who am my own disgrace, I ought to glory—or you will be my future glory, because you will glorify me through confession.

I know this because you have already exalted the one who is my head, that is, Christ, through confession. He will draw me to the same glory where he is.

### “With my voice to the Lord”

This does not change. “To cry” is understood here as we explained above. Here too Christ is called the holy mountain, concerning whom it was said: “It will be in the last days,” and so forth.

### “I slept”

Truly, the Lord heard me, because I rose. I rose from the death of vices—not by myself, but because the Lord, namely the Father’s Word, received me, that is, my nature, or received my cause in order to act on my behalf.

It was necessary that I rise, because I slept, oppressed by lesser sins, namely venial sins.

### “And I was overcome by sleep”

That is, I suffered the sleep of criminal sins, from which I could in no way rise by myself.

Concerning this rising it has been said: “Rise, you who sleep; rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.”

### “I will not fear thousands of people”

Because the Lord, by receiving me, made me rise from the death of vices, I will not fear the thousands of my persecutors.

And so that I may [perhaps: “may not”] fear, rise up, God—that is, you who until now have been known only to a few. Hence it has been said: “God is known in Judah.”

Rise now in the knowledge of many, so that my persecutors may also come to know you. And thus save me, by making them cease from persecution. This belongs to you to do, because you are my God and there is no other.

### “For you have struck them all”

Truly, you will rise up in the knowledge of my persecutors, because you have already struck all those who oppose me—that is, you have struck some from every class of those who persecute me with a good blow, striking and mortifying the vices in them.

And you have crushed the teeth of sinners, that is, the malicious words and wicked life through which they were cutting away the less cautious from the body of Christ. You have destroyed these things in many sinners by making some who had been persecutors into good preachers.

The Lord’s is salvation, and upon the people. Neither its continuation nor its exposition is altered. The psalm mentioned above may also be read in a third way, namely, as spoken in the person of some member of the Church—that is, some believer surrounded by innumerable throngs of vices and earthly attachments. Since the accumulation of vices and harmful pleasures, under the assault of the devil and his angels, attempts through evil suggestions to lead the believer’s resisting mind into the law of sin and death—that is, into despair—the believer speaks in prayer to God his Creator, lamenting his misery in order to move God to pity him and come to his aid, saying:

“Lord Father, why have the enemies who trouble and afflict my soul multiplied so greatly that they are trying to lead me altogether into death?” As though he were saying: “Because of my great sin and my misery”—that is, “for this reason you must come to my aid.” And truly many trouble me, because many things—that is, many vices and evil desires—rise up against me, namely, in order to overwhelm my soul. They speak not in words but in the effect of the matter, just as good bread, although it does not speak in words, nevertheless speaks to you, declaring that its baker is good. So these things speak, I say, toward the condemnation of my soul, namely, to force it into despair, so that it believes there is no salvation for it in its God—that is, that you, who are its God and Creator, no longer care to save it or are no longer able to do so.

The remaining words that follow are understood in the same way as those spoken above concerning the body, that is, the Church, with this one qualification: as there they are understood collectively, here they are understood partially. Moreover, the “thousands of people” pursuing him, mentioned below, are referred in this interpretation not to external enemies but to internal ones—that is, to vices and evil desires. They are rightly called a people, because they produce great disturbance and strife in the soul.

# ON PSALM IV. To the End. A Song of David.

[Col. 0501A]

## Argument.

Hezekiah glories against his rivals in the help of the Lord, reproving them so that they may not trust in falsehood; rather, abandoning evil thoughts, they should serve God always. Alternatively, the Prophet rebukes the Jews. Arnobius gives another interpretation: the God of justice heard his Son when he was placed upon the cross; the Jews, who became angry against him, sin against him even to this day.

## Exposition.

“The end of the law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes” [Rom. 10:4], who is the glorious perfection of all good things; or, as some prefer, this was said for us, upon whom the end of the ages has come.

A psalm is a sound-producing musical instrument by which divine praises were sung; a song is something that resounded with heavenly praises through human voices. These terms appear to have been joined together because the words were sung with instruments and with choirs of psalm-singers, in a consonant cry accompanying the heavenly sacrifices. Thus, by all these words, we are reminded that this song is spoken concerning the Lord Christ.

Throughout the psalm, the words are those of holy Mother Church. In the first section she asks that her prayer be heard, rebuking unbelievers who, while worshiping false gods, neglected the worship of the true Lord. In the second she admonishes the whole community that, having abandoned deceptive superstition, it ought to offer a sacrifice of righteousness; and, in order to turn the minds of the Gentiles through the promise that had been made, she recalls the great benefits that the Lord has bestowed upon Christians.

## Commentary.

### When I called, he heard me, the God of my righteousness.

This psalm is entitled as follows: “To the End: A Psalm, a Song of David.” In Scripture, “end” is understood in two ways: either as consumption or as completion—that is, perfection.

It means consumption when we say, “The bread is finished,” that is, consumed. It means perfection when we say, “The cloth is finished,” that is, completed. In this latter sense, as perfection, the word “end” is fittingly applied to Christ, who is the true end and perfection of the shadow of the old law. Hence it is said: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.”

The designation “To the End” is added to the titles of certain psalms in order to indicate the final David, that is, Christ, who is the end of the law. He may also be called the end in relation to the historical David, who was his shadow and figure.

Christ is signified by the titles bearing this designation sometimes on his own account, when the psalm properly concerns the head, as here. Sometimes he is signified on account of the whole body, that is, the Church, or on account of some member of the Church, that is, some believer, if the psalm bearing that title is either the voice of the whole Church or only of one member—that is, of the soul of some believer—as many examples will be found below.

The Church and every member may nevertheless also be called “the end” in relation to the people who were under the law, just as Christ is called the end in relation to that David. For that whole people was a shadow of the people of the Church, and its parts were figures of the parts of the Church.

A psalm, as stated above, properly means the harmonious melody produced on a musical instrument—that is, the psalter—when its strings are struck from above. A song properly means when someone uses his free voice joyfully in the praises of God, without the sound of a musical instrument accompanying it. Such a voice is more pleasing than the sound of an instrument, because it contains both the melody supplied by the sound and articulated words.

A psalm of a song occurs when, after the sound of a musical instrument has begun, the free voice follows and joins it in melody. Conversely, a song of a psalm is said to occur when, after a choir has begun, the instrument follows to soften the melody of the singing, as is customary in certain churches.

It is exceedingly sweet when both—namely, words and free voice together with the sound of the instrument—are joined in whatever order, and much sweeter than when either is taken by itself. In accordance with the likeness of that arrangement in which the psalm precedes and the song follows, the words of this psalm are called “A psalm of a song.” For they indicate to us the power from above, which is signified by “psalm,” and the things they indicate belong to great joy and delight, which is signified by “song.”

They speak of Christ’s glorification, accomplished in his resurrection, ascension, and confession. These things should be regarded by us as exceedingly joyful and delightful, because through his resurrection and glorification we have been given certainty that we too shall rise and be glorified with him, if only we imitate Christ.

If one considers the matter carefully, the order of the words may also be perceived here. In the words that follow, Christ’s invocation of God the Father before his glorification comes first; this may be understood through “psalm.” What follows concerns the glorification itself, which is much more joyful than invocation, and is therefore understood through “song,” since, as stated above, a song is a more joyful voice than a psalm.

In brief, the title mentioned above may be explained as follows: the words that follow, which are called “A psalm of a song,” as explained, are attributed to David—not the historical David, but David referred to “the end,” that is, the final David, namely Christ, who is the end of the law.

The whole psalm is the voice of the head, attributed to him after the resurrection. In this psalm he intends to exhort believers that, for the present, they should pray and labor to attain the first resurrection—that is, that they should rise here from their vices—so that at last they may be heard concerning the second resurrection and reach it. He presents himself to us as an example of this hearing: because he invoked worthily, he was heard, so that we too might strive to invoke worthily and thus be heard.

If someone asks whether Christ experienced the first resurrection, he should know that he did not experience it at all. There can be no rising unless there has first been a fall; but Christ did not fall in any way, either actually or originally.

That he did not fall actually is clear. It is equally clear that he did not fall originally. Only those suffer the fall of original sin who are generated through the punishment of that original sin, namely, through concupiscence. Christ, however, was not generated through concupiscence, because he was conceived by the Holy Spirit without carnal pleasure. Christ, therefore, must rightly be said to have been entirely free from original sin.

Some nevertheless say that Christ’s flesh touched the original fall in a certain way—materially, that is, but not personally. For all flesh commonly suffered the fall in Adam. Yet although that flesh which was joined to the Word touched the fall with respect to its material nature, because it was born from sinful flesh, with respect to the person of Christ it must be judged entirely free from every fall.

Such people say that Christ’s immunity from sin should be understood as the first resurrection. The former opinion, however, is the more probable.

The psalm is continued in this manner:

“I, concerning whom the prophets foretold so many and such great things, am present, calling, justifying those called to faith, and invoking God the Father for the glorification of the resurrection. And you, believers, invoke him by my example, because if you invoke him, you will be heard, just as I was heard.” This is what he says:

“The God of my righteousness heard me by glorifying me through the resurrection. When I called”—that is, because I called him into myself, not gold or anything else, remaining in his will and deviating in nothing from his commandments.

For it is one thing to call God and another to invoke God. The one who invokes God calls God himself into himself, calling him for his own sake and not for the sake of anything else, and because he fulfills what is commanded. The one who merely calls says, “Lord, Lord,” but does not do what is commanded; he calls God not for God’s sake but for the sake of something else.

He says, “God of my righteousness,” in order to blunt our pride, since we presume upon ourselves. The one who was coequal with the Father in the divine nature judged it rash to act presumptuously concerning himself.

[Col. 0503A]

### In tribulation.

The head himself turns familiarly to God the Father, as though saying: “Truly you have heard me, because you enlarged me when I was placed in tribulation”—that is, you led me from the narrowness of tribulations into the broad expanse of joys.

This may be understood in two ways. Either, after the tribulation of his passion, he led him into the breadth of joys—that is, to the heavenly goods, which are both vast and eternal. Or God the Father led him, placed amid the tribulation of sinners—that is, born among sinners and living among them—into the breadth of joys, that is, into the fullness of the grace of the virtues, because he was free from sin and possessed every virtue in himself.

Hence it is said: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity.” And again: “God, your God, has blessed you above your companions,” and many similar passages.

Narrowness pertains to tribulation just as breadth pertains to joy. For just as joy enlarges the mind, so tribulation makes it narrow. Hence it is said: “Tribulation and anguish upon every soul of one who works evil” [Rom. 2:9]. Anguish follows tribulation.

Alternatively: “You enlarged me”—that is, you gave me an enlarged and expansive heart in charity—“in tribulation,” that is, in the passion, so that the charity of my heart would extend not only to all my friends but also to my enemies. For our Lord prayed for his enemies in his passion, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

Of this enlargement it is said: “Narrow is the way that leads to life” [Matt. 7:14]. No one travels this way unless he has an enlarged heart. For only to those who possess this enlargement—and thus true love of neighbor, without which divine love cannot be possessed—is the way of life, which is narrow to others, spacious and passable, because they are free from every impediment.

Alternatively: “You enlarged me”—that is, you gave me a broad and expansive heart—so that I might glory in the tribulation itself, knowing that through it I would obtain a great good. Hence the Apostle says: “Not only do we suffer, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance character, character hope, and hope does not disappoint” [Rom. 5:3–5].

### Have mercy on me.

Here the head prays for the members, so that God the Father may hear those who are now praying for the first resurrection, in order that they may finally reach the second. He speaks of them as though of himself, as if saying:

“You, Father, who heard me, have mercy also on me”—that is, on those who are mine—and show such mercy that you hear my prayer, that is, the prayer of those who are mine, now offered for the first resurrection.

### Sons of men.

Now he turns to the members, that is, to the believers themselves, exhorting them to prepare themselves in such a way that they may be worthy to be heard. As though he were saying:

“O you sons not of one man—that is, of Christ, whom you ought to imitate—but you who until now have been sons of men, or of earthly parents, bearing their image and doing their evil works: put aside, so that you may be heard, the heaviness of heart caused by desires for earthly things. These are a burden, not a support; they withdraw the mind from the worship of the true God and make it serve idols.

“For how long—that is, how long do you wish to be heavy of heart, to have a heart weighed down by these vanities, and to leave no room within you for divine propitiation, with hearts not raised upward but cast down toward the lowest things?”

As though he were saying: “If until now you have wandered from the truth with no one coming to your aid, at least recognize me as your physician.”

### Why do you love vanity?

Truly you have a heavy heart, for you love vanity and seek falsehood—that is, you seek to be blessed in vain and false things, pursuing these later and false goods as though they were good and true, and neglecting the former goods, namely, the heavenly ones.

But why—that is, for what benefit—do you do this pointlessly? As though he were saying: “You seek blessedness in vain and false things, although only truth can give it.”

Earthly things are called vain because they are transitory and unstable like a shadow. Hence Ecclesiastes says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity, whatever man does under the sun” [Eccl. 1:2, 14].

They are also called false because they do not give what they promise—namely, sufficiency and abundance. From this it is evident that they do not bring blessedness.

### And know that—

As though he were saying: “So that you may no longer seek blessedness in vain things, know me”—that is, consider me—not now as mortal and fragile, but as immortal, incorruptible, and exalted above all the heavens, because I did not care for vain things.

Know me, I say, because I have been set before you as an example. For the Lord Father has glorified his Holy One—that is, the one whom he made free from sins and unconcerned with vain things, namely, the Holy of holies and God of gods—and has presented him to you as something marvelous and desirable, so that, seeing me glorified through the resurrection and co-reigning, you might strive to imitate me, laboring here for the first resurrection, so that he might finally receive you in the second.

He appropriately says “he has made marvelous.” For what could be more marvelous or desirable to a mortal, suffering, and transitory being than to appear immortal, impassible, and eternal? Nothing.

[Col. 0504B]

### The Lord will hear me.

Again he transfers himself to them, speaking of them as though of himself. As though he were saying:

“Just as the Lord Father made me marvelous, so he will make you marvelous if you imitate me. For he will hear you with respect to the glorification of the second resurrection, when I cry out”—that is, when I cause you to cry out with the voice of the heart—for the first resurrection, striving toward him and asking for nothing except him, just as I did.

He rightly says that he cries out in those whom he makes cry out. For that cry is his, in accordance with what he says elsewhere: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” [Matt. 10:20].

### Be angry and do not—

As though he were saying:

“So that you may deserve to be heard, be angry with yourselves concerning the past.” That is, you who judge the sins of others should be your own judges, punishing yourselves for past evils. “And thereafter do not sin”—that is, exercise caution against sinning in the future.

“If you say anything deserving correction in the thought of your mind, let those things be only in your hearts”—that is, let them remain within your hearts and not also burst forth in speech. Yet for these same things be pierced with remorse toward repentance and tears in your beds—that is, in your hearts.

He fittingly says “in your beds.” For bedrooms are properly the resting places of beasts. So our hearts are not seats of reason but, as it were, wild-animal lairs when they receive thoughts of this kind, which are worthy of correction in themselves even if they do not burst forth into speech.

### Offer the sacrifice.

As though he were saying:

“I tell you to be angry with your past sins so that you may offer a sacrifice”—that is, put your own vices to death by producing worthy fruits of repentance, afflicting yourselves for each sin to the extent that worthy repentance requires. This will be a sacrifice of righteousness, that is, a righteous sacrifice.

For nothing is more just than that one who punishes the sins of others should punish his own, and that each person should afflict himself as much as his defiled conscience deserves, thereby making himself a pleasing sacrifice to God.

This may also be read differently together with the preceding verse, if “be angry” is referred not to past vices but to unlawful impulses, which we cannot prevent from arising within us. For it is a punishment of original sin that unlawful impulses are not under our control; rather, they rise up within us especially when we least wish them to, through the suggestions of the devil and through the tinder of sin that is present in our flesh.

Therefore we must restrain them so that they do not reach action. Blessed Paul speaks of these impulses: “There is sin in your mortal body, but let it not reign”—that is, let it not be carried into action. Unlawful impulses reign when they are carried into action.

Our head, Christ, commands us to guard against this. As though he were saying:

“So that you, sons of men, may be heard by God the Father concerning the second resurrection, be angry and do not sin”—that is, if anger or some other unlawful impulse begins to rise within you through the devil’s suggestion, do not sin.

He places anger for all the other impulses. “Do not sin”—that is, do not carry those impulses, which are not in themselves sin, into grave sin by carrying them through to action.

“And whatever belongs to goodness that you speak outwardly, let it be in your hearts”—that is, speak it from the heart, so that you are not that people of whom it is said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” [Matt. 15:8].

“And be pierced with remorse in your beds”—that is, always have remorse in your hearts as a safeguard of holiness, so that “the one who stands may take heed lest he fall” [1 Cor. 10:12].

Moreover, so that you may be perfect, “offer the sacrifice of righteousness”—that is, do good works and take up the virtues, which you ought justly to do and through which you will render God favorable to you, as though through a sacrifice. And after you have sacrificed, hope in the Lord.

Note that there can be no hoping unless sacrificing comes first. Unless someone offers himself as a sacrifice by willingly putting himself to death, as the former interpretation held, he has no basis for hoping in the Lord.

To hope in the Lord is to await confidently from the Lord the reward of true and future goods, with a genuine consciousness of good works. Hope concerns only future and true goods. It concerns future things because no one hopes for what is past or present, but only for what is future.

It concerns true goods alone because the Apostle says: “Hope does not disappoint” [Rom. 5:5]. This would be false if hope could concern either false goods or evils.

Sometimes “to hope” is used improperly in the sense of “to fear.” Future and true goods are truly to be loved and desired because they do not deceive. Earthly things, however, because they deceive and are vain, are to be sought only for the sake of necessity.

But because many doubt whether true goods exist, or what they are—namely, all those who desire earthly things—he adds their question concerning true goods, in order to show them irrational by proving that these goods truly are good. Their question is as follows:

### Who will show us true goods?

As though they were saying:

“We do not wish to believe that those are true goods which no one returning either from hell or from heaven has shown us.”

### It is marked.

He proves that those who ask in this way are irrational, and here the head himself speaks in the person of one member, that is, of a believer. As though he were saying:

“They say that no one has shown those goods, and they lie, because by nature they have been shown to everyone by God.

“For, O Lord Father, the light—that is, the brightness—of your countenance, namely, reason and understanding, through which your will is clearly shown to us, specifically what goods you wish us to seek, has been marked upon us”—that is, impressed upon our higher part, namely, upon my soul.

“Through this you gave”—that is, showed—“joy to me in my heart,” namely, that I ought to rejoice only in the goods of my soul and not in bodily goods.

Alternatively: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us”—that is, your luminous countenance has been impressed upon our soul. This is said by way of likeness, as though the face of God were represented in our soul as clearly as the image of a face is clearly represented in a statue.

In accordance with this it is said: “God formed man in his own image and likeness” [Gen. 1:27]. The image of God in our soul is reason and understanding. His likeness is piety, justice, humility, and the other virtues, which he implanted naturally in our soul so that we might be good. The rest remains unchanged.

### From the fruit of grain—

You, Lord, have naturally shown human beings what true goods are, but the wicked do not perceive this, because they have been multiplied—that is, scattered—and divided into many directions by their thoughts.

“From the fruit”—that is, because of the abundance—“of grain,” not your grain but that of the one who says: “I am the bread of life, who came down from heaven” [John 6:35, 41]. Rather, it is from the fruit of their own—that is, earthly—grain.

And from the fruit of their own wine, that is, earthly wine, which dulls and intoxicates the body—not from your wine, which dulls the soul—and from the fruit of their own oil, not yours.

Christ’s wine is the cup of Christ’s passion, that is, imitation of him. It drives the soul mad, because it makes the soul thirst for death and not feel its torments.

The illustrious martyr Lawrence had drunk deeply of this wine. When he had already been roasted, he nevertheless mocked the tyrant who was torturing him, saying: “I am roasted,” and the rest.

The Apostle also drank from the same wine when he said: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” [Phil. 1:23].

Christ’s oil consists likewise in spiritual gifts, with which he soothes and relieves those to whom he grants them. Concerning this it is said: “God has blessed you with the oil of exultation,” and “you have made my head rich with oil” [Ps. 44:8; 22:5].

The oil of the wicked may be understood both as material oil, by which they seek to become rich, and as flattery, by which they are soothed and in which they take pleasure. Concerning this oil it is said: “Let the oil of the sinner not make my head rich” [Ps. 140:5].

### In peace in the same place.

Those wicked people do not perceive true goods because they have been scattered. But I, to whom you have shown them, will sleep—that is, I will withdraw myself from the care and misery of this anxious worldly life—and in the present and in the future I will rest eternally, existing in peace, never able to receive its opposite, but always advancing into the same peace, continuing in peace and admitting no war.

### For you, Lord—

Truly I shall rest in the future in eternal peace, because then, Lord Father, you will give me true goods. Here and now you have wished and commanded me not to exist in actuality, without hope, as the wicked do, but to exist here in hope alone, so that in the future I might exist in actuality.

# ON PSALM V. To the End, for Her Who Receives the Inheritance. A Psalm of David.

## Argument.

After his illness, Hezekiah gives thanks to the Lord and worships in the temple. Alternatively: the voice of Christ to the Father.

## Exposition.

“To the End”—that is, for the Church, which, when Christ rose, received the gifts of spiritual goods. The Church herself is sometimes called the Lord’s inheritance, having been purchased with his precious blood. Hence it is said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” [Ps. 2:8].

This entire psalm is spoken by the person of the Catholic Church. In the first section she asks that her prayer be heard, proclaiming that heretics and schismatics must be excluded from the Lord’s gifts. In the second section she prays that, through understanding the divine Scriptures, she may be directed along the straight path to that blessed homeland, declaring that the faithless are completely alien to it. Finally, she recalls the rewards of the blessed, so that through one proclamation she may turn the wicked by the punishment foretold and stir the righteous by the rewards promised.

## Commentary.

### My words.

The title of this psalm is as follows: “To the End, for Her Who Receives the Inheritance.”

The inheritance of the Church is Christ, who will feed her in the future, when he will be all in all. He is also her eternal life, signified by that land of which it is said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord,” and: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” [Ps. 26:13; Matt. 5:5].
