The Church herself is also Christ’s inheritance, because he cultivates her through his teaching, and she feeds him through her good works, in which he takes delight as in good food. Hence he says elsewhere: “My food is to do the will of my Father” [John 4:34].

She who receives the inheritance is the Church which, called to that inheritance described above, labors through prayer and manifold devotion to attain it, so that she herself may also become an inheritance. Or, as some books read, she has already received that inheritance, if not in reality, at least in hope. Hence the Apostle says: “For we have been saved in hope, awaiting the redemption of our body” [cf. Rom. 8:23].

The following psalm was composed for this Church—that is, in her person.

In brief, the title mentioned above may be explained as follows: the words that follow, which are called a psalm because they indicate power from above, composed by the prophet David, are referred to the end—that is, to Christ, who is both the end of that David and the end of the law, as stated above. They are referred to Christ “for her who receives the inheritance,” that is, these words are referred to Christ because they were spoken for her, in whose place they are spoken—she who, called to the inheritance, receives that inheritance; that is, they are spoken in the voice of the Church, which is his body.

For in Christ the head, the body, and the individual members are contained. Therefore, as we said above, in the preceding title some things are expressed through the body, as in the present psalm, which is the voice of the body, that is, the Church; and some things through one member, as in the psalm that follows this one, spoken in the voice of any penitent soul.

The intention of this psalm is as follows: the Church, placed amid the various entanglements of the present life that seek to draw her back so that she may not reach the inheritance to which she hastens after being called, persists in prayer and repeatedly entreats her God, so that by his aid and guidance she may avoid the entanglements of this world and reach her inheritance—that is, reach him himself.

She says:

“Lord, whose inheritance I desire to possess and whose inheritance I wish to be, receive with your ears my words”—that is, show toward me, who await your help, such an effect of assistance that you may appear to have received my words with your ears.

This is said by way of likeness, because when someone does what he is asked to do, he appears to have received the words of those asking him with his ears.

It does not mean that God the Father, who is wholly eye and wholly ear, has ears like a creature. Since the expression had been used improperly, he determines how it should rightly be understood. He adds “to the words, a cry,” which pertains to the vivid intention of the soul, in which the soul strains itself as the body does in an outward cry. Thus he indicates that he previously received the words—not those produced by the noise of beaten air, but those produced by the voice of the heart.

As for “receive,” he says “understand,” because understanding properly pertains to the cry of the soul, just as ears pertain to bodily words.

### Attend to the voice of my prayer.

That is, make me attentive to the voice of my prayer, so that I may not pray less fervently; or, make yourself attentive to my prayer by fulfilling it.

You ought to do this because you are my king and my God—that is, because I wish you to be both my king and my God, and I establish you as such.

Christ is called our king according to his humanity, according to which, living among human beings, he ruled us through the innocence of his teaching and example of life, and through the other virtues. Hence it is said: “He fed them in the innocence of his heart, and guided them by the understanding of his hands” [Ps. 77:72].

He is called our God according to creation, for it belongs to God to create.

### For to you I shall pray.

For this reason I ask you to understand my cry: I shall ask only for what is fitting. I shall pray not to gold, not to silver, and not to obtain anything else, but to you alone, so that I may have you as my inheritance.

Therefore you will hear my words, so that you may deliver me in the morning—that is, when, with the darkness of vices and unbelief driven away, the light of the true sun shines forth.

Or you will hear my voice, made in me—that is, in diligence. “Morning” is used for diligence because those who are diligent in their duties customarily rise in the morning for their work.

Or you will hear my voice, and if you do so it will be manifest in the morning—that is, in your holy advent, in which it will be morning, because there the brightness that will begin for the good will have no end, and darkness will never be joined to it.

### In the morning I shall stand before you.

Since you will hear my voice, I shall therefore stand before you—that is, I shall stand beside you and be present to you in the morning, namely, at your second advent, as though I were your intimate companion.

Or you will find me standing and watchful, not lying down and sleeping, in that morning—that is, at your second advent. Hence it is said: “Watch, because you do not know at what hour” [Matt. 24:42], and again: “Stand, righteous ones; watch, pray, be strengthened in the Lord, and let all your affairs be in charity.”

And again: “I shall see”—that is, I shall understand—what I cannot now see clearly because I am hindered by bodily things: namely, that although you appear in the present to will iniquity, because you permit the wicked to be mixed with the good, you do not in fact will iniquity. You will show this openly then, when you separate the sheep from the goats.

This may also be understood of the present, in accordance with the other interpretations of “morning.” Thus “morning” may mean the night of vices driven away and the light of the true sun shining forth; or, existing in the morning—that is, in perseverance in prayer—I shall stand before you.

The more clearly someone beholds the truth, or the more diligently he attends to it, the more he stands before it, even in the present. Thus I shall stand before you, and I shall also see here in the present what it is not granted to everyone to see: namely, that although you appear to will iniquity because you permit the wicked bodily to dwell among the righteous, you do not will iniquity. For just as in the future you will separate them bodily and mentally, so here also you divide them from one another mentally: you blind the minds of the wicked but illuminate the minds of the good.

### He shall not dwell.

Truly you do not will iniquity, because neither will the evil one—that is, the slanderer—dwell beside you in the future rest, nor will any unjust people remain before your eyes.

Although certain unjust people, namely transgressors of the law, will come before you in judgment, none of them will remain before your eyes—that is, in glory. Hence it is said: “Let the ungodly be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God” [cf. Isa. 26:10].

### You hate all—

Truly the unjust will not remain before you, because you hate—that is, reject—all workers of sin.

He proves this both from the lesser and from the greater, saying that you will destroy all who speak falsehood. For speaking falsehood is less than committing sin, while destroying is greater than hating.

Solomon says concerning falsehood: “Every mouth that lies kills the soul” [Wis. 1:11].

Nevertheless, it must be understood that there are two kinds of lies which, although not entirely free from fault, involve little fault at such times.

One is told for the sake of joking, as when we say to a child, concerning his absent teacher, “The teacher has come,” in order to frighten him.

The other is an officious lie—that is, one told for the sake of benevolence. For example, if someone is pursuing a person with a drawn sword, and we know that person to be hiding, we deny having seen him because we wish to save him.

Although this may appear good, it is nevertheless a sin, because it is a lie. Therefore it must be avoided, because falsehood is the death of the soul. The person whom God wishes to save can be saved by God, while we can avoid the death of the soul by remaining silent about the truth.

For it is not a sin to keep silent about the truth. This is evident from Christ, who alone was without sin and nevertheless kept silent about the truth when he said: “I have many things to say” [cf. John 16:12].

Some wish to include among lies those cases in which there is a double intention. For example, if someone entrusted a sword to another and made a promise to return it as soon as he asked for it, but later, when he asked for the sword in order to kill himself or someone else, refused to return it in order to restrain his fury.

Here there would be a double intention, because, while the first intention remained, another had been added. Yet this should not be called a lie, because what had been promised was not denied in this case: if the one who had entrusted the sword had asked for it with a good intention, the person to whom it had been entrusted would have returned it to him immediately.

The same applies in other cases.

“Man of bloodshed.” He clearly proves that God hates workers of iniquity, because he hates the man of bloodshed, that is, the murderer. He likewise proves, from an equality and from a part, that he will destroy liars, because he will cast out—that is, disinherit—the deceitful person. Deceitful is one who has one thing ready on his tongue and carries another concealed in his heart; such a person is equivalent to a liar. For every deceitful person is a liar, and every liar is deceitful, if both are understood in relation to their words.

“To abhor,” that is, to disinherit, relates to “to destroy” as a part, and is derived from abominable sons, that is, disinherited sons. Because they have in some way committed an abomination—whether by beating their own parents or by doing something similar against human law—they are customarily disinherited. Thus God also will disinherit the deceitful person and the man of bloodshed: that is, he will make them deprived of the heavenly inheritance. A true murderer, who knowingly and willingly kills someone, is called a man not merely of blood but of bloodshed, because he has poured out the blood of two persons: that of the one whom he killed and his own. He first kills himself by shedding his own blood, that is, by losing the life of his soul. For Augustine says that every person sins against himself before sinning against another.

## “But I”

They will indeed be disinherited, but I shall receive an inheritance, because, O Lord, I shall enter your house, that is, the heavenly rest, which is the heavenly Jerusalem, constructed of living and firm stones. I shall enter in order to become a stone in its building and possess you as my inheritance.

Or, “I shall enter your house,” that is, the ecclesiastical institutions, which are your house—that is, established by you. I shall enter by observing them, and this not through myself but “in the abundance of your mercy,” that is, through Christ your Son, through whom you have displayed great mercy, because through him both heavenly and earthly things have been reconciled.

Or, “in the abundance of your mercy,” that is, through your great mercy—namely, through your calling and justification. Or, “in the abundance of your mercy,” through the many whom you have mercifully saved. For the Church enters the house of God through its many faithful, as through its members; and these faithful, however just they may be, are saved by divine mercy. No one will ever be so just that he is saved by his merits alone.

“I shall enter,” I say, “your house, and afterward I shall worship you”—with the voice, namely, of the heart; that is, I shall make myself fit for you. Approaching your holy temple, that is, striving in innocence, I shall conform myself to Christ, who through you was made a holy temple, namely, one in which the fullness of divinity might dwell.

Or, “I shall worship, turning toward your holy temple,” in which you deign to dwell. For God dwells in the hearts of the faithful. Hence Solomon says: “The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom.” I shall worship, I say, not in arrogance but in fear—not servile fear, but yours, that is, filial fear, belonging to the guarding of holiness.

I note that he says, “I shall worship toward the temple.” Formerly the Israelite people were commanded to assemble at Jerusalem at least once a year, in order to worship there in the temple of the Lord. Jerusalem is situated in the mountains. By this it was signified that a certain man would come, in whose veneration and faith many nations would assemble: namely, Christ. He was rightly signified by the temple at Jerusalem, which was on the mountains, because it is written concerning him: “In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountain.”

## “O Lord, lead me”

The connection is as follows: “So that I may be able to enter your house and worship toward the temple; therefore, O Lord, lead”—that is, lead me gradually from virtue to virtue—the Church, established in righteousness. This is not human righteousness, which is not straight because it returns evil for evil, but yours, which is straight because you command us not only to return good for good but also good for evil. Hence it is said: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you.” And likewise: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him,” and so forth.

“Lead me,” I say, and do this in such a way that you direct my way—that is, make my works straight, so that they may be in your sight, that is, so that they may please you. You must do this because of my enemies: that is, because I am surrounded by many enemies who wish to draw me away from the straight way and from the truth.

## “For there is not”

Truly, because of my enemies you must direct me, for they are such that there is no truth in their mouth; and therefore whatever they persuade me of is false. Nor is it surprising that there is no truth in their mouth, because in their heart there is nothing but vanity—that is, whatever they think is vain: things belonging to earthly matters, which are vain, and not to true goods.

## “Their throat is an open grave”

Truly, there is no truth in their mouth, because their throat—that is, their voice—is like an open grave. Follow the comparison. Just as every open grave is open either in order to receive a corpse or, if it has already received one, to emit stench, so whatever evil is said to the good is said either so that, through their perverse persuasions, they may conform the good to themselves and thus bury them in death, or so that through their poisonous or mocking words they may inflict upon them a stench—that is, disturbance and annoyance.

Hence the Church rightly says: “Because their throat”—that is, because the speech of its enemies—is before him like an open grave: either so that it may bury her in death, or so that through disturbance it may inflict reproaches and curses upon her.” “Throat” is used for “voice” because the air that emerges from the throat through the movement of the lungs becomes voice through the striking of the tongue, like a plectrum, and the impact against the palate.

## “With their tongues”

Not only now is the throat of my enemies open like a grave, but they have always acted deceitfully against me, in order to drag me away from the truth. “With tongues” not yours but theirs—that is, poisonous tongues.

And therefore, O Lord, judge them—that is, punish them with a just punishment—namely, so that those who wish to remain in filth may become still filthier, and thus incur a greater condemnation. You must do this because you are God; hence it is necessary that you be a just judge.

## “Let them fall by their own counsels”

He explains how he understands that they ought to be judged. As though he were saying: “Thus, O Lord, judge them”—that is, let them suffer a heavier fall into greater vices because of their counsels, that is, because of their wicked thoughts, from which they do not wish to recover.

And those who have expelled you from themselves, unwilling to have you as their inheritance, expel them from yourself more and more, taking away from them the knowledge of truth and thrusting them into the blindness of ignorance. Do this according to the multitude of their ungodliness—that is, in proportion to what their great ungodliness has deserved. For it is just that those who have expelled you greatly should themselves be greatly expelled.

And they ought to be expelled because, O Lord, though they have eyes dimmed by disease with which to see your light, and though they refuse to taste in their fevered palate how sweet you are, they have rejected you as though you were bitter food and sour drink, and have provoked you—that is, have provoked you to anger. Another translation has: “For they have embittered you, O Lord,” which agrees very well with this meaning.

“Judge” above can also be understood in a good sense, and the whole passage can thus be read for the good of those enemies, as though the Church were praying for them and offering an example of praying for enemies:

Since, O Lord, the enemies are so lost that there is neither truth in their mouth nor in their heart, deliver me from them and judge them with a good judgment: destroy in them what they are—that is, evil—and make them what they are not—that is, good—so that those who are ungodly may become godly, and enemies may become friends. Hence it is said: “Turn the ungodly, and they shall not be.”

“Judge,” I say, for you can do this because you are God. Judge them in such a way that they fall away from their wicked thoughts; and do not merely expel them from those thoughts, but, O Lord, expel them according to the multitude of their ungodliness—that is, as much as their great ungodliness requires. For those who have sinned greatly require much correction.

And you ought to expel them because they have provoked you: that is, because, wishing to place themselves above others and to rule, they have provoked you to this anger, so that you may make them subject.

## “And let all who hope”

Therefore I ask you to convert my enemies, O Father, so that they too, after they have been converted, and all who hope in you with confidence—that is, who at present seek to be only in hope and not in possession—may rejoice with you in eternal rest.

According to another interpretation, the connection is as follows: “The enemies are indeed condemned, but all who hope in you shall rejoice.” And truly they shall rejoice, because they shall exult with an exultation that continues forever—that is, eternal exultation in the future. Meanwhile, in the present, you shall dwell in their minds for their protection and consolation.

And because you will dwell in them, they will glory in you—that is, in the future, as a repetition—or even in the present they will have glory and joy of mind in you: all who love your name, not their own, as Adam did, who desired for himself the name “God.” Rather, they love your name: that is, they wish you to be judged their lord and themselves to be your servants.

For the one who loves the name of God is the one who does not wish to withdraw himself from the service of the Lord and who prefers to depend upon the Lord rather than to exist from himself. Because Adam did not wish this, he incurred condemnation.

## “For you bless”

Truly they will glory in you, because you bless—that is, in the present you give increase in virtues to the just person, by which he may attain eternal glory. For you command what you will, and you yourself accomplish what you command. Hence it is clear that you remember that commandment of which it is said: “Without me you can do nothing.”

## “O Lord, with a shield”

He demonstrates by its effect that the Lord truly blesses the just. As though he were saying: “There is no doubt, O Lord, that you will bless the just; for you have already crowned us”—that is, just as a crown surrounding someone protects him, so you, O Lord, have already protected us—that is, me, the Church, with all my members—in baptism from the assaults of the devil.

“And you will crown us,” that is, you will protect us in the future from eternal condemnation, by your good will—that is, with your grace and mercy, which are present to us here and hereafter as a shield.

# ON PSALM VI

For the end: a hymn of David concerning the Eighth.

## ARGUMENT

Hezekiah, weakened by illness, invokes the Lord, lamenting the frailty of human nature.

Alternatively: the voice of Christ to the Father.

Read this with reference to the resurrection of Lazarus.

Note the order of the mystical arrangement: in the fifth psalm the inheritance to be given in the morning is promised; in the sixth, the resurrection at the judgment is feared.

## EXPLANATION

“Concerning the end” is already known. A hymn is praise of the Divinity, composed according to the rules of some meter.

“Concerning the Eighth” signifies the Lord’s coming, when, after the week of the world has ended, he will come to judge the world. Hence this psalm begins with the greatest trembling.

In this psalm the confident man proceeds in four ways. At the beginning he makes the judge favorable to himself, soothing his mind by appealing to the power of judgment, to his own weakness, and to the judge’s custom of sparing. In the second division he recounts his own sufferings, by which he is afflicted and saddened and groans. In the third he separates himself from the wicked, knowing that this is most pleasing to the good judge, so that the mind may be rendered estranged from those to whom justice itself was known to be opposed. Finally he disturbs and rejects all the wicked, because he did not wish in any way to have a share with them.

## COMMENTARY

### “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger”

This psalm is entitled as follows: “For the end, with songs concerning the Eighth: a psalm of David.”

Certain mistaken people called the day of judgment “the Eighth,” with reference to the seven thousand years that began from Adam. They said that, after those years had ended as though they were seven days, the day of judgment would certainly follow, and thus they made themselves and others certain about that day.

Yet an inconsistency arises: Scripture is falsified, for it says: “It is not yours to know the times,” and so forth; and again: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief”; and once more: “Of that hour and of that day no one knows, except the Father alone; neither the angel, nor the power, nor does the Son himself know.”

But since no hidden things of the Father are concealed from the Son, we must understand that he does not fail to know that day with respect to himself; nevertheless, he is said not to know it because he kept it unknown from his disciples, to whom he revealed many other things. Thus it is said: “The Lord tempts you, that he may know”—that is, that he may make you know.

Once that rash calculation has been removed, the day of judgment can very appropriately be called “the Eighth” for this reason: after these temporal things, which revolve according to the number seven of the days and are therefore taken as seven days, that eighth day follows—the day of judgment. On it, the souls, having attained eternity, will no longer owe anything to time or change.

The day may also be called “the Eighth” in another way: with reference to the six days by which the labor of this life is understood, and during which the Lord is read to have labored; and with reference to the sixth day—that is, the rest in which the souls of the just who have died have been placed while awaiting the common resurrection, so that there they may receive the double robe of immortality. When this waiting has ended, then, together with the six aforementioned days—that is, with the labor of this world—the eighth day, undoubtedly, follows: the day of judgment.

The day may also be called “the Eighth” with reference to carnal and spiritual generation. Carnal generation belongs to the number four; spiritual generation to the number three.

Carnal generation belongs to four not because of the body, which is composed of four elements or four qualities—for the body is dry, hot, cold, and moist—or because of the four humors that are in every human being. Spiritual generation belongs to the number three because three powers pertain to the spirit, that is, to the soul: reason, irascibility, and concupiscibility. Two further things are added to these: virtue and instruction. Instruction is for illuminating reason, while virtue is for restraining irascibility and concupiscibility.

Carnal generation began from Adam and lasted until Moses—that is, until the Law—and also under Moses, that is, under the Law, until Christ. For although certain religious men subject to the world lived under the Law, nevertheless, because they prefigured spiritual things to come through carnal things, that is, through certain carnal observances, they are called a carnal generation.

Spiritual generation began with Christ, when the transition was made from carnal circumcision, or passage was made to spiritual circumcision, when the passage was made from shadow to reality.

After the carnal observances that pertain to the flesh and the Old Testament, and the spiritual observances that pertain to the spirit and the New Testament, have been completed—and in all these things we must consider the number seven, referring the number four to the flesh and the number three to the spirit—the eighth day follows. On that day each person will receive what is owed according to his merits. That day transfers the saints to eternal salvation, but the wicked to eternal condemnation.

Fearing that condemnation, every faithful soul, desiring eternal salvation and therefore recalling its past sins and groaning over them, presses upon and deals with the Lord its God as will be found in the psalm.

But first let the title be explained. This psalm, a historical psalm of David, reported in songs—that is, in divine praises—is referred to the end, that is, to Christ. It was made for the Eighth, that is, in the voice of a certain faithful soul fearing the eighth day, the day of judgment; that soul is his member. In this world that soul prays to be healed, so that it may not fear being rebuked or corrected on that day.

From this the intention can easily be grasped. It speaks in this way: “O Lord, burn and cut me in this world, so that you may not rebuke me”—that is, condemn me—in your fury, that is, in the anger you will show to the wicked on the day of judgment.

“Rebuke” is used for “prove,” for “accuse,” and for “condemn,” as here. “Nor correct me”: that is, find no sin in me on account of which you might show me worthy of correction in purgatorial fire. For every sin a person commits is punished either by the person himself or by God.

### “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for”

So that you may neither rebuke nor correct me, have mercy on me in this world—that is, place your healing hand upon me, because I am weak, that is, because I need medicine on account of the weakness of my mind.

What follows has the same meaning as what came before: “Heal me,” that is, have mercy on me, because my bones are troubled—that is, because the powers and strengths of my mind have been diminished on account of sins weighing it down.

This refers back to “I am weak”; or alternatively: “Have mercy on me, for I am weak in my flesh.” For many movements of the flesh rise up against me. “Heal me, for my bones are troubled”: that is, because I am weak in mind.

### “And my soul is greatly troubled”

And lest “bones” be understood as the body, he adds what makes clear what we ought to understand by bones: “My soul is greatly troubled”—that is, weakened in its bones, that is, in its strength.

And because it is troubled, you, O Lord, how long will you delay? That is, why do you not burn me here? Why do you not cut me, so that on the eighth day you may neither rebuke nor correct me?

Do not delay, but just as you turned away when I turned away from you, so turn toward me—that is, make yourself turned toward me by making me turn toward you.

Or alternatively: “Because my bones are troubled,” that is, my soul is troubled within itself. For the higher power of the soul, namely reason, resists the lower power, namely sensuality.

And because my soul is troubled within itself, “how long will you be troubled in me?” That is, how far will your disturbance in me rise? Will it rise to the point that you either rebuke or correct me, although you do not become troubled by a person who troubles himself—that is, corrects himself—in this world, while you become troubled by one who does not trouble himself here?

And because my soul is troubled within itself, that is, because it corrects itself, “turn, O Lord,” that is, be turned toward the one who has turned toward you. Turn toward me, who have turned toward you, as it is written: “Turn to me, and I will return to you.”

And not only turn, but also rescue my soul, which clings to the perplexities of this life, and save me by granting perseverance—not because of my merit but because of your mercy. For since I have often transgressed your commandments, nothing is owed me on account of my merit except just condemnation. As it is written: “To the sinner who has been given a commandment and does not keep it, nothing is owed except just condemnation.”

In this verse the difficulty of salvation is shown, and in the next the place of conversion. For when it says, “Turn, O Lord,” and not merely “turn,” but also “rescue my soul,” and not merely “rescue me,” but also “save me,” and not because of my merit but because of your mercy, since I can do nothing through myself, a great difficulty is shown to exist in the one who is saved.

And the more difficult the matter is, and the greater the labor by which it is attained, the greater the vigilance that must be applied. Thus it is proved by the contrary: if there is great difficulty for the one who is saved, great punishment is owed to the one who is not saved.

### “For in death there is no one”

Turn toward me in this world, O Lord, because in death there is no one who remembers you—that is, after the separation of body and soul no one becomes mindful of you with benefit to himself. No one who has not repented of his sins in this world repents profitably after he has died, because this world alone is the place of mercy, while after this world there is only the place of justice.

Therefore rescue my soul and save me here, because who will make confession to you in hell?

This does not mean that confession cannot occur in hell, nor should the rich man be brought forward as an objection, since he is read to have confessed in hell when he said in his heart to Abraham: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water to cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.”

But by hell let those deepest darknesses be understood into which the wicked, together with their head, the devil, will be cast after the day of judgment, when there will no longer be a place for confession.

Or alternatively: “O Lord, turn toward me who have turned, so that I may not be in death”—that is, in some criminal sin, which truly is the death of the soul—and thus be forgetful of you, because “there is no one who remembers you in death”: that is, no one remembers you profitably while impeded by criminal sin. Even if such a person is sometimes pierced with remorse, he will not thereby be saved unless he is completely removed from criminal sin.

Therefore rescue my soul and save me, so that, not being in hell, I may confess to you: “For who will make confession to you in hell?” That is, who could make a praiseworthy confession to you if he were in hell—that is, in the depth of vices? No one.

As it is written: “When the sinner comes into the depth of vices, he will despise.”

There is one confession that is praiseworthy and another that is penal. Confession is praiseworthy when someone offers praises to God for good deeds, as in: “I confess to you, O Lord the King,” and so forth. It is penal when someone confesses his sins, condemns them, and consequently asks for punishment. In this verse, according to the earlier interpretation, the place of conversion is shown.

### “I have labored in my groaning”

“O Lord, heal me; and, insofar as I was able, I have made myself fit to receive healing, because I have labored in my groaning”—that is, I have groaned continually because of my sins.

“And I shall wash my bed every night”—that is, I shall cleanse my conscience through each lapse into sin, with my tears, that is, with the tears of my heart.

And not only shall I wash it, but I shall also water my couch—that is, I shall water that same conscience, pouring tears into its interior. To wash means to moisten something externally; to water means to soak it internally.

The conscience is rightly called a bed. Just as one rests and labors in a bed—one rests there when healthy and labors there when sick—so one rests and labors in the conscience: one rests in a good conscience and labors in a bad one.

We may also understand pleasure by “bed,” because in pleasure one rests and labors as in a bed: one rests in good pleasure and labors in bad pleasure.

We may also understand something different by “couch” than by “bed.” For the body is rightly understood by “couch.” Just as a couch is a bed made of straw, which can easily be destroyed by the wind, so the body can easily be harmed and torn.

Thus the passage should be explained: “I shall not only wash my bed”—that is, my conscience—“but I shall also water my couch,” that is, I shall soak my body with tears.

It should be understood that the use of different tenses, such as “I have labored” and “I shall wash,” is not caused by the necessity of the narrator but by the emotion of the one praying. The Psalmist could have said “I labored” or “I washed.” Or “I have labored and I shall wash” may be understood as though he were saying: “I served you in one matter, but because I was not sufficient for you through that, I shall do this other thing, so that I may be sufficient for you.”

### “My eye is troubled by fury”

Therefore I shall wash my bed, because my eye—that is, my inner person—is troubled, that is, stunned by your fury, by contemplating the fury you will show to the wicked on the day of judgment and by remembering my sins.

Or, “my inner person is troubled,” that is, blinded by fury—that is, by the sin of the first parent.

And therefore my eye is also troubled, because I have grown old among all my enemies, whether carnal or spiritual. Carnal enemies may appear either as friends or as enemies. For no greater enemy of the soul exists than a temporal friend, for whose sake one often labors so greatly only for earthly things that God is postponed.

He says, “I have grown old,” because such a person has become a member of the first and old human being, or because he is comparable to an old garment, which is useful neither for use nor for adornment.

Or alternatively: “My eye,” that is, my inner person, “is troubled by fury,” that is, by its own anger, which blinded it and did not allow it to be patient. And it is not only troubled by its own anger, but also: “I have grown old among all my enemies,” whether carnal or spiritual.

### “Depart from me, all of you”

The faithful soul, recalling its past sins and groaning over them, shows that it has been heard by the Lord. Offering itself to us as an example—that if we groan over our sins, we shall be heard by the Lord—it says:

“I have grown old among all my enemies. But you, my enemies, whether spiritual or carnal, who work iniquity—in me through wicked persuasions and in yourselves through evil deeds—depart from me, now spiritually, and one day locally, namely when it is said to you: ‘Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire,’ because the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping”—that is, the voice of me who weeps.

### “The Lord has heard my supplication”

It is proved from its parts that God truly has heard my voice, because he has heard my supplication made for my sins and has received my prayer made for perseverance. For supplication is properly made for the removal of sins, while prayer is made for perseverance in the good.

### “Let them be ashamed and greatly troubled”

And because the Lord has received my prayer, “let them be ashamed.”

Or alternatively: Let my enemies depart from me in such a way that they are ashamed on the day of judgment in their own conscience, saying: “We fools regarded their life as madness and their death as dishonorable. Look how they have been placed among the sons of God!”

And let them be greatly troubled, fearing their punishments, and let them turn from evil to worse when they are cast into the deepest darkness; and let them be greatly ashamed of that turning—indeed, quickly. This will happen soon: the time is short.

It should be understood that this statement—“Let them be ashamed,” when they say, “We fools regarded their life as madness”—refers only to carnal enemies and not to spiritual ones, that is, not to demons, because they will not say this.

Or alternatively: “You carnal enemies, who now work iniquity both in me and in yourselves, depart from me according to an evil disposition and draw near according to a good one.” You ought justly to do this because God has heard the voice of my weeping—that is, my God has heard me weeping over my sins. Likewise he will hear you when you weep over your sins.

Therefore let my enemies be ashamed of their past sins. Or let them depart from me in such a way that they are ashamed of their sins and are greatly troubled because of them—that is, very greatly. Let them be pierced in their hearts and thus turn to repentance. And let them be greatly ashamed of what they previously gloried in—their sins—and let them do this quickly, that is, without delay.

For the one who promises salvation to the penitent does not promise tomorrow to the one who postpones it.

These three verses can also be read with the order changed, beginning with “The Lord has heard my supplication,” but it is better to read them in their proper order.

# ON PSALM VII

A psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Chusi, son of Jemini.

## ARGUMENT

Hezekiah, accused by his enemies and betrayed by his own people, beseeches the Lord, invoking his judgment against those who falsely accused the innocent.

## EXPLANATION

Chusi is interpreted as “Ethiopian.” By this name Saul is represented because of his bloodthirsty and cruel ways, and he is called the son of Jemini because he descended from that stock, as the history of the Kings relates.

Allegorically, understand David as Christ and the Ethiopian as the persecuting Jewish people.

I have explained the meaning of this title by following Jerome, because, as he himself testifies, there are some who think that this psalm was sung against Absalom, when Chusai, David’s friend, destroyed the counsel of Achitophel.

They should be understood to be seriously mistaken, first because the name Chusai is written with the letter samekh, whereas here it is written with sin; second, because David, who had commanded the leaders of his army, “Spare the boy Absalom,” would never have spoken of his death in the words, “He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity; he opened a pit,” and so forth—especially since he mourned that man’s death with his head uncovered; finally, because that man is written to be David’s friend, the son of Arachi, whereas this one is written to be the son of Jemini.

Therefore the prophet, extending his own case into the future mystery of the Lord the Savior, in the first division, speaking in his own person, beseeches the Lord that he may be freed by his power from all his persecutors.

In the second section the same prophet asks that the glory of his resurrection, once manifested, may come to his aid.

In the third he introduces him speaking, inasmuch as he was made humble, so that he might be judged according to his righteousness and truth; terrifying the wicked with vengeance and promising the good gratuitous rewards.

In the fourth part the prophet speaks again, warning the Jews to depart from the iniquity they have undertaken through fear of the future judgment, lest they should have to suffer the punishments they deserve.

This psalm can also be understood as spoken in the person of the Lord’s human nature, if what is humbly said there is referred to our weakness, which he bore.

## COMMENTARY
Lord my God, in you I have hoped.

This psalm is entitled: “A Psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord because of the words of Cush the son of Jemini.” It is read in the Second Book of Kings that Absalom, cruelly persecuting his father David, drove him from the kingdom. When a certain intimate of his, Cush, wished to accompany David in his flight, David earnestly begged him to return, to take Absalom’s side, and carefully observe and secretly report to him the counsels which Absalom, at the instigation of his counselor Ahithophel, was devising against him. Therefore Cush returned to Absalom and faithfully carried out what David had requested.

This psalm took its occasion from that historical account. But since the history itself is not contained in the psalm, let us dwell on the interpretations of the names, so that through them we may reach the mystery of the psalm. They are as follows: Cush is interpreted as “silence,” Jemini as “right hand,” and Ahithophel as “ruin of a brother.”

From these interpretations Judas the traitor again comes before us, bearing the figure of Absalom, according to the meaning of the name Absalom, “peace of the father,” because his father—that is, Christ—had peace toward him, although Judas was waging war in his heart through his deceptions. And just as we find in the Gospel that the disciples are called “sons,” as in the passage, “The sons of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them,” so we also find them called “brothers,” as when it is said, “Go, announce to my brothers.” In this prophecy too it is said, “I shall declare your name to my brothers.” And in the Apostle: “The firstborn among many brothers.”

Therefore that disciple who through criminal deceit betrayed the Lord to the Jews is rightly called “the ruin of a brother,” which is the meaning of Ahithophel. But Cush, whose name means “silence,” is rightly understood as our Lord Jesus Christ having fought against those treacheries in silence—that is, in the deepest secrecy. This silence was the partial blindness that happened to Israel when it was persecuting the Lord, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter and thus all Israel might be saved.

By this silence our Lord Jesus Christ, concealing the mysteries of his venerable passion, turned the voluntary ruin of his brother—that is, the criminal deed of the betrayer—into an element of the order of his mercy and providence. What Judas did with a perverse mind for the destruction of one man, Christ himself, by his provident governance, turned toward the salvation of all.

A perfected soul, worthy to know that silence, therefore sings the psalm to the Lord; it sings “because of the words of Cush,” that is, because of the revelation of that silence. Among unbelievers and persecutors there is silence and secrecy; among believers, however, there is not silence, but the words of silence—that is, the reason of that secret, manifested and explained.

This secret is called “Cush the son of Jemini,” that is, “of the right hand.” For what was accomplished for the saints was not to be hidden from the saints. A perfected soul therefore sings prophetically to the Lord, to whom the secret was revealed, “because of the words of Cush”—that is, because of the manifestation of that silence which God the Father, by his right hand—that is, favorably and mercifully—wrought for our salvation. Thus this silence is called the son of the right hand, that is, Cush, the son of Jemini.

It should be known that the words spoken thus far are those of blessed Augustine. If they seem difficult to anyone, let him gather their substance from the following, clearer exposition.

In this psalm every perfected soul praises God the Father because he has revealed to it the mystery of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, which had been hidden from the wicked. Our Lord Jesus Christ endured, with such silence—that is, with such patience and humility—the ferocity of the persecution of the impious Jews and of Judas the betrayer, as an example of humility, that they, not recognizing his divinity, plotted for the destruction of that one man what God the Father, merciful and favorable, turned by a wonderful ordering toward the salvation of all believers. For “if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

This silence by which our Lord Jesus Christ fought against the plots of his persecutors was that blindness which happened in Israel so that light might enter all the nations. This was the provident governance that, by an ineffable power, turned the wickedness of the persecutors toward the salvation of all. For this revelation the perfected soul sings to the Lord in this prophecy.

According to this interpretation, the title given above is explained as follows. This psalm is attributed either to the prophet David himself, of whom it was said, “I have found David, the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart,” or to any soul perfected in this way. That perfected soul sang the psalm—that is, proclaimed it joyfully, not so much with its voice as by good works—to the praise of the Lord, “because of the words of Cush,” that is, because of the manifestation of the silence described above, which the Holy Spirit made known to it. Cush, that is, “silence,” is the son of Jemini, that is, “of the right hand,” because God the Father, by his right hand—that is, mercifully—ordained it for the salvation of all.

Blessed Jerome opposes this interpretation and, in a certain sense, attacks blessed Augustine, saying that the Cush after whom the psalm is entitled was not Cush the Archite, who frustrated Ahithophel’s counsels, but another Cush. Accordingly, the title is explained in this way.

Cush is interpreted as “Ethiopian.” All those blackened by sins are called Ethiopians. Here, however, by the Ethiopian—that is, Cush—Saul is understood above all, since he persecuted holy David. Through Saul all deadly persecutors who persecute the one signified by David—that is, Christ—both in themselves and in his members, are rightly understood.

Saul is interpreted as “petition.” As an interpretation, this name sends us toward death, of which it is written: “God did not make death, but the impious summoned it to themselves with hands and feet.” The words of Cush, that is, of the Ethiopian, are understood as the attempts by which persecutors draw the saints away. Some of these words are visible and others invisible. Visible words are called deeds; invisible words are the utterances that are spoken.

At times persecutors strive to draw the saints away by deeds—that is, by inflicted torments—and at times by threats. From these words every perfected soul, already partly liberated by the Lord who has shown it how wicked and harmful those words are, gives him thanks and praise in the following psalm, and entreats him to free it completely.

Following blessed Jerome, therefore, we explain the aforementioned title as follows. This psalm is attributed to David—that is, to every perfected soul—which sang it to the praise of the Lord because of the words of Cush: because it deserved to know the words of Cush, that is, of the Ethiopian, and to be partly liberated. Cush, I say, the son of Jemini, that is, of the exceedingly grievous persecutor Saul.

“Jemini” is added here not for the interpretation of the name, but to intensify the persecutors, so that it may indicate how grievous are the persecutors understood here: namely, those who even descended from the persecutor’s stock and whose sins enter into the offspring of their fathers. A certain most wicked man named Jeminus was from the tribe of Benjamin. From that same tribe came Saul, the most grievous persecutor of holy David, and also Saul the ravening wolf, together with nearly all the most grievous sinners.

It should be known that, according to both of the interpretations of the title given above, the following psalm may be read in the voice of any perfected soul—whether David, or any perfect person from that earlier people who existed before Christ’s birth, or from the later people. This must be understood according to the variation of the interpretations given below.

In the voice of a perfected soul of the earlier people it will be read as follows.

As though it said: “Lord, I have hoped in you, not in myself, as Adam did, who wished to depend not on you but on himself; nor in the flesh, because everyone who makes flesh his arm is accursed. But I have hoped in you—that is, I have cast all my hope upon you—and rightly in you, because you, who are God of all by power, are my God by your will.

“Therefore save me—that is, preserve me by rescuing me through perseverance—from all who persecute me, that is, from all the members of the devil who wish to revile me: from all of them, both invisible and visible, both those who confront me and those who pursue me. Moreover, free me from the very head, that is, from the prince of darkness, the devil, lest he, who is like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour, at some time—that is, at any time—snatch my soul away to earthly pleasures.

“For the soul is snatched away when it is drawn back from the Lord and entangled in earthly pleasures. Truly he will snatch it, since there is no one to redeem me from the devil himself if you do not free me, and no one to heal me from his members unless you save me.”

Visible persecutors are wicked people who seek to draw us away by their evil persuasions. Invisible persecutors are the vices themselves, or evil spirits, who incite us to sins through wicked suggestions.

Just as the Israelite people, returning from Egypt, had persecutors who pursued them, such as Pharaoh and his army, and others who confronted them, namely Amalek and the other peoples who came against them to resist and repel them, so a perfected soul, withdrawing from the power of darkness, has enemies who pursue it: its former vices and whatever people or demons have already persuaded it to commit any sin. It also has enemies who confront it, namely future vices and whatever persuaders may lead it toward them.

This is indicated when it says, “from all who persecute me.” And because, as long as we are in the flesh, the place of death is always within us, and therefore an enemy always threatens even the most perfect—the author of death, the devil—the perfected soul, after asking to be saved from his members, also asks to be freed from the head himself. Anyone who considers the title carefully can plainly adapt this interpretation to it.

[Col. 0518B] Lord my God.

Here the same name that he placed above is resumed, and what is said here clearly pertains to the earlier title. The perfected soul, whose voice is heard in this psalm, shows that the mystery and secret of the Lord’s passion have been revealed to it—namely, the patience and humility that our Lord Jesus Christ displayed in his passion. When those who repaid him with evil for good, he repaid them with good for evil, praying to the Father for them.

The soul shows this, I say, when it declares that it can imitate that secret as far as it is able, in order to encourage others by its example. It is as though the Lord, explaining the silence, had used this admonition: “For your sake, an impious and sinful person, I endured my persecutors with such humility; I bore my betrayer with such patience. What, then, will you do? Will you not imitate me?”

As though the Lord had spoken in this way, the perfected soul answers him, saying:

“Lord, who redeemed me at the price of your blood, and my God, who created me, if I have done what I ought not to have done”—and it explains what this is—“if that iniquity which is considered equity among human beings is in my hands, that is, in my works; namely, if I have repaid evil for evil, rather than imitating you, when those who repaid me evil for good did so, and I did not repay good for evil.”

Here he notes great patience. For it is greater patience not to repay evil for evil to those who, after receiving benefits, inflict evil upon us, than it would be if they had wished to harm us without having first received any benefit.

The whole passage is therefore as though it said: “Lord, if I have not done what I ought to have done—that is, if I have not imitated what you taught me to do by doing it yourself, but have repaid evil for evil—I shall incur this evil: I shall fall—that is, be defeated—before my invisible enemies, empty, that is, made unable to conquer in my soul, although outwardly I wished to be victorious by repaying evil for evil.”

This will happen deservedly, that is, justly, because I preferred to do what is worse rather than what is good. Concerning this emptiness it is said: “He boasts vainly who, being a human being, desires to avenge himself upon another human being.” While he seeks openly to overcome a human being, he is secretly overcome by the devil, becoming empty through a vain and proud joy because he could not be defeated.

He does not know how much more glorious a triumph it is to overcome one’s own spirit than to conquer another person. Hence Solomon says: “The one who conquers his own spirit is stronger than the one who conquers a city.”

[Col. 0518D] Let the enemy pursue my soul.

“Let me fall” means that the enemy—that is, the devil—should pursue my soul inwardly, because it is always his task to pursue it, lest it be at rest. He adds, “and seize it,” that is, deceive it. For one who always pursues does not always seize, since he does not always deceive. And let him seize it so that he may trample it—that is, make my life, my soul, trampled beneath earthly desires, to such an extent that he may reduce it to earth, that is, make it his food.

The devil is called not only a lion but also a serpent. To the serpent it was said from the beginning: “Upon your breast you shall crawl, and you shall eat earth.” The devil therefore has as food those souls that are earth—that is, those wholly entangled in earthly desires and evil pleasures—because he delights in them and refreshes himself in them.

And let him trample my life—that is, my soul—in such a way that he brings my glory, that is, my glorious conscience, down into dust, that is, destroys it. The Apostle says: “Our glory is the testimony of our conscience.”

This glory is true, solid, and perfect when it is possessed inwardly, where God alone sees it. But when it is sought outwardly in human praise as a cause of exaltation, then it is brought down from its former solidity into dust—that is, into dissolution. Hence Boethius says: “For in a certain way it diminishes the good of a conscience that approves itself.” And Macrobius says: “The wise person places his fruit in conscience, but the foolish person in praise.”

Here he warns all the perfect especially to beware of pride or exaltation. This vice is of such a kind that it must be feared even in right actions. It is the first vice to confront those withdrawing from the Lord, as in Adam, and the last to confront all those returning to him, even after the other vices have been overcome.

It should be known that such statements in sacred Scripture as “May I fall deservedly,” and “May the enemy pursue me,” and the like, should not be called curses, as they appear to be, but prophecy within the prophets, agreeing with the divine judgment. In general, wherever they can be understood as rejoicing in God’s just judgment, they are spoken in that sense.

Here, however, these words are not placed so that the prophet or the perfected soul should incur these evils, but so that by them he may show what will happen to those in whom the things that he indicates ought to be removed from himself are present—namely, those who do what they ought not to do or fail to do what they ought to do.

He presents it as the consequence corresponding to the opposite of the preceding condition. As though he said: “If I have done what I ought not to have done, or have not done what I ought to have done, then I shall incur the evils mentioned above. But if I have done what I ought to have done, or have not done what I ought not to have done—that is, if I have imitated you—then you, Lord, do for me what you ought to do: rise up against my persecutors in your anger.”

That is: Make known to them how unavoidable and terrible your future anger will be against the wicked, so that they may be converted and cease persecuting me.

“And be exalted in the boundaries of my enemies,” that is, obtain power and dominion over the impious. Those who were previously the boundaries of my enemies—that is, the possession of the demons—make pious from the impious, so that through these enemies, by whom you were formerly blasphemed, your name may be glorified.

“And that you may be exalted, rise up in the commandment that you gave.” As though he said: “You commanded the first human being obedience and humility, which he lost through pride at the devil’s instigation. To overcome that pride, rise up, Lord my God, in the commandment that you gave; appear in the humility and obedience of the flesh that you assumed, through which you will rise against the enemies to conquer them.”

And you ought to rise, because in this way the synagogue—that is, the congregation of the many believing peoples—will surround you in imitation. He rightly says “will surround.” For concerning these people it was said: “As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament.”

And for the strengthening of this synagogue, that is, the multitude of believers, after completing the obedience of the assumed flesh, you, Lord, to whom alone it is proper to ascend into heaven by your own power—for it was said, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven”—return on high, that is, into heaven, from which you descended, so that from there you may send the Holy Spirit to strengthen the hearts of believers.

These interpretations properly suit a soul from the earlier people. For it is not fitting for anyone from the later people to desire things that preceded them, namely Christ’s incarnation and his ascension.

[Col. 0519D] The Lord judges the peoples.

The perfected soul from the earlier people, turning its discourse toward us, proves that the Lord will truly return on high after completing his obedience. For he who returns is the true Lord, who will sit at the Father’s right hand and to whom the Father has given all judgment. He will judge the unbelieving peoples, condemning rather than saving them: now by a hidden judgment, giving them over to inner darkness, and finally manifestly giving them over to outer darkness.

[Col. 0520A] Judge me, Lord, according to my righteousness.

The faithful soul, which before perfection feared being accused or corrected in judgment, now that it has been perfected and made secure through reflection on the silence described above, no longer fears judgment and says:

“You, Lord, who judge the wicked according to their merits, judge me also here according to my righteousness—that is, according to what is appropriate to that righteousness, since I imitate your silence by returning good for evil—and according to what is appropriate to my innocence, by which I harm neither myself nor another.

“I call this righteousness and innocence ‘above me,’ because I have them not from myself but from you, who are above me. For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, given by the Father of lights.”

Here “to judge” is understood in a good sense, namely, of the temporal scourges that God grants perfect people in the present life for the preservation of holiness and as an example of his just judgment. For if he does not spare beloved sons here, he will much less spare fugitive servants in the future.

It should be known that medicine has two functions: one by which sickness is driven away, and another by which health is preserved. The faithful soul, therefore, which earlier asked to be healed in another psalm, saying, “Have mercy on me, Lord; heal me,” and so forth, having already obtained health, here asks that the remaining function of medicine—the preservation of health—be given to it by the Lord when it says, “Judge me, Lord,” and so forth.

[Col. 0520B] Let the wickedness of sinners be consumed.

The connection is as follows: “So that you, Lord, may judge me according to what I ask, permit the wickedness of sinners to be consumed”—that is, completed—against me. Permit the impious to fulfill against me what they have planned, so that they may scourge and persecute me. In this way you will direct me as a righteous person, because those scourges will be the guardianship of my health.

For the persecution of the wicked is always the salvation of the good. Hence it was said: “The impious lives for the pious.” What a furnace is to gold or straw, and what a file is to iron, the impious is to the pious. For just as straw is reduced to ash while gold is purified, so in persecution the righteous become more righteous, and the filthy become filthier.

[Col. 0520C] Searching.

He shows that God truly directs the righteous because he searches the hearts—that is, their thoughts—and the kidneys—that is, the delights of the righteous—not merely by knowledge, as in the case of sinners, but also by his favor. This is itself a form of his direction.

It is proper to God to search hearts and kidneys. A human being judges according only to deeds or words and does not discern with what intention each person acts or what delights each person. God, however, discerns where each person’s mind is directed and what delights each person.

And because he sees that the whole intention of the wicked is directed toward the desire of the eyes and of the flesh, while the good are delighted not by things below but by things above, he judges both justly: he permits the wicked to err, but directs the good.

“Kidneys” are properly used for carnal pleasures because the kidneys and the lower part of the human being are in that region where the pleasure of human generation especially dwells, through which human nature is transmitted by the succession of offspring into the miserable and sorrowful joy of this world. Here, however, “kidneys” is understood of good pleasures.

We may also understand “hearts” here as cares, and “kidneys” as the outcomes of cares. For each person desires to reach that which delights him.

[Col. 0520D] My just help is from the Lord.

Therefore you, Lord, will direct me, the righteous one, through my scourges, because what is truly my help—namely, that I may be directed by you—is justly given to me by you, the Lord, who make those upright in heart be saved by persevering in uprightness (sic). The text is as though it said: “It is just, Lord, that to me, who am infirm, you should give the medicine of restored health.”

Hence the Apostle says: “If Christ died for us when we were impious, much more shall we be saved from wrath through him.” Those are called upright in heart who join heavenly delights to pure thoughts.

[Col. 0521A] The Lord is a just and strong judge.

After the perfected soul, which is now receiving health from the Lord, has taken occasion from the hidden judgment that is presently exercised upon the impious for the preservation of health, and has prayed by inserting this petition, it returns to the judgment concerning the impious.

As though turning toward the impious, it says: “Since the Lord already judges you, impious people, by a hidden judgment—that is, through blindness of mind—what will happen to you at the end? He will then give you manifestly to outer darkness.”

Since you have not denied this, grant also the medicine by which health may be strengthened. He says:

“God the Father is a just judge, rendering to each according to his merits; and he is strong, that is, no one will be able to resist him. Yet he is patient in the present, because he does not grow angry”—that is, he does not gather the ministers of his wrath, the devils, to avenge himself each day. Those ministers delight in human punishment not because of justice but because of their own wickedness, and therefore they are always ready to do harm.

“God, I say, who is judge, unless you impious people are converted in the meantime by doing penance while he judges you secretly, will finally judge you manifestly. For he will brandish the sword—that is, his Son—whom at his first coming he sent humbly, concealed in the sheath of humanity. At his second coming for judgment he will brandish him, that is, send him forth in such manifest anger that, now revealed, he will flash light for the pious and terror for the impious; he will appear gentle to the just and terrible to the unjust.”

He will do this not without providence, because he has already stretched out his bow—that is, the Scripture of the New and Old Testaments—in which he has established and threatened that judgment.

It is compared to a bow because, just as in a bow the rigidity of the wood is bent by the string, so in Scripture the hardness of the Old Testament is bent and softened by the strength of the New Testament, as by a string; and the shadow of the Old Testament is explained through its truth.

He has therefore stretched the bow and prepared it as if for shooting: that is, he promises in it the utterly certain death of the impious. Moreover, in that bow he prepared the vessels of death—that is, the apostles—by instructing and equipping them in the divine Scripture. From themselves, as from vessels, they poured out such a liquid—that is, such statements—as were for believers unto life, but for unbelievers unto death.

Hence the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God, for some unto life, but for others unto death.”

He also made his arrows in that bow—that is, his divine and penetrating judgments—or he instructed the saints and apostles there, as his arrows, for those who burn with love, so that they might derive benefit from it.

The apostles are called arrows because, penetrating cold hearts with divine judgments, they kindled those of believers with the fire of which it was said: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” That is, the love of God and neighbor.

Heretics may also be called vessels of death. Because they approach the divine Scriptures with perverse desires and out of arrogance, God permits them both to understand them perversely and to expound them perversely, for their own death and that of many others. They are therefore rightly called vessels of death. Yet this is permitted, with respect to the faithful, not without benefit. The true Catholics are compelled through them to search out and understand the truth in the divine judgments.

Hence the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest.”

Christ is called a sword because through his humility God the Father overcame his enemies, and because through him, as through a sword, there will be a cutting and separation between the good and the wicked on the day of judgment.

[Col. 0521D] Behold, he travails with iniquity.

He shows for whom the apostles are vessels of death. As though he said: “Behold, it can be seen that they truly are vessels of death for certain people.”

Someone travails with iniquity—that is, labors through consent to fulfill iniquity, meaning any deception. This is because he has conceived pain—that is, has derived pleasure from pain, meaning from some earthly thing. And because he has conceived and travailed, he afterward gives birth to iniquity—that is, completes the deception itself.

Notice that he says “pain.” Earthly things are called anxiety and labor: labor in acquiring them, anxiety in retaining them, and pain in losing them. To travail means the labor before childbirth, while to give birth means to bring forth the child.

Someone therefore conceives from pain when he derives a perverse pleasure from some earthly thing. He travails when he gives his consent to the pleasure and strives to complete what delighted him. He gives birth when he brings it to completion in others.

If, however, as was said above, we understand the vessels of death as heretics, the connection will remain the same, but the meaning will change. It will then show not for whom they are vessels of death, as it did concerning the apostles, but how they are vessels of death. A heretic takes pleasure in a perverse persuasion, gives it his consent, and joins action to his consent.

[Col. 0522A] He opened and dug out a pit.

He repeats what the preceding verse said, in other words, adding greater force. A pit is a place containing water whose bottom lies hidden. To this the hidden pleasure involved in fraud concerning earthly things is compared.

To open a pit is to widen it; to dig out a pit is to carry it downward into depth. To make a pit, therefore, is to prepare some fraud concerning earthly things. To open it is to add consent to the pleasure itself. To dig it out is to persist in carrying out the fraud.

And because someone has made, opened, and dug out a pit, he falls into the pit that he made—that is, he suffers in fraud a prior and heavier fall than the one he prepared for another.

Blessed Augustine says that no one first sins against another without first sinning against himself. It therefore appears that whoever wishes to defraud another in earthly matters deceives himself before deceiving the other. The other suffers loss of money; this person suffers loss of innocence. The other is punished outwardly with the lighter loss; this person is inwardly grievously wounded by the sword of greed.

He added this to show God’s just judgment, because God inflicts punishment upon the wicked not from his own anger but from their own wickedness, so that what served as enticements for a person sinning become instruments for God when he punishes.

It should also not be passed over that, just as in a womb, once conception has occurred, one thing is conceived and another is generated—the seed is conceived, while the human being is generated—so also in the preceding comparison, pain, that is, some thing, is conceived through pleasure, while iniquity is generated.

[Col. 0522B] His pain shall be turned back.

He shows how someone falls into his own pit: his pain—that is, his wickedness—will be turned back upon his head, that is, upon his soul. It will make subject what ought to have been superior, and make serve what ought to have ruled.

For everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. His iniquity will also descend upon his crown, that is, it will become superior to reason, which is like the crown of the head—that is, in the soul, since reason is the nobler power of the soul. Wherever desire rules, reason is oppressed and brought into subjection.

The two preceding verses can also be read merely as a comparison. It is as though he said: “What should you think about someone who conceives pain, travails, and gives birth to iniquity?” The same as about someone who spends his whole life preparing a pit for someone and is finally thrown into it; then his pain—that is, whatever earth he had painfully removed from the pit—is heaped back upon his head.

It is also the same as with someone who had wickedly prepared a gallows or some punishment for another, and afterward his iniquity descended upon his own crown, so that the unjust punishment was turned back upon himself. This happened to Haman in the case of the punishment he had prepared for Mordecai, and to many others.

For just as labor would be the consequence for each of those two, so all who persist in earthly frauds will have all their labor directed toward condemnation.

[Col. 0522D] I will confess to the Lord.

After the soul has considered the just judgment in the case of the good and the wicked—how God protects the just by illuminating them from himself, and punishes the unjust by condemning them not from his own anger but from their own wickedness—it makes a praiseworthy confession to God concerning such great justice, saying:

“I will confess to the Lord according to his righteousness,” that is, I will praise the Lord because of his just judgment in a confession of the voice. “And I will sing psalms,” that is, I will perform good and pleasing works for the name of the Lord—not for the glorification of my own name but of his. And rightly so, because he is the Most High and therefore worthy of all praise.

To this belongs the saying: “So that, seeing your works, they may glorify God who is in heaven.”

This confession is not without purpose. There were some who attributed the condemnation of the wicked and the salvation of the good not to God’s just judgment but to fate, astrology, or other such things.

It should be known that if this psalm is read in the person of a perfected soul from the later people, nothing in the interpretation given above needs to be changed, except perhaps where it says, “Rise up, Lord, in the commandment that you gave.” In accordance with this, the preceding “Rise up” may also be varied in any interpretation, without changing the connection, as follows.

As though the perfected soul from either the later or the earlier people said: “If I have done what I ought to have done by imitating you, now you, Lord, do for me what you ought to do: rise up in your anger,” that is, increase your grave and unyielding anger against my enemies; permit them to scourge and persecute me.

“For I know that while I am scourged by them, you do not neglect me, but rise up in anger against them. And be exalted in the boundaries of my enemies,” that is, obtain dominion for yourself over my enemies, who are boundaries—that is, the borderland of the devil—using those very enemies for their condemnation: permitting them, after the light of truth has been withdrawn, to do the things by which they will be condemned.

Hence it was said: “For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do.”

## “Rise up, Lord God”

As though he were saying: “Rise up in anger against enemies, but toward friends—that is, toward us—you who are our Lord by your power and our God by creation, rise up in the commandment that you have given,” that is, make us advance in this commandment of yours—[the intervening abbreviated phrase is uncertain]—namely, that our love extend even to our enemies; or make us rise up in the commandment of humility and obedience that you have given, so that even toward our persecutors we may be obedient and humble. Thus, by our example and imitation, the synagogue of the peoples—that is, the multitude of believers—will surround you. And for its illumination return on high, that is, make your return to heaven appear by implanting in their minds the light of truth and the other things that are spoken of you. For Christ is born, suffers, rises again, and ascends daily, according to the understanding of those who come to the faith.

Or otherwise: “Rise up, Lord, in your anger, and be exalted at the boundaries of my enemies,” [Col. 0523C] that is, become high above my enemies, so that they cannot attain to the contemplation of you but lose knowledge of you. That is, rise up against the Jews and also against any other persecutors: make yourself lofty in the commandment that you have given, in the obedience and humility of your humanity, so that they may not recognize that you were truly humbled by incarnation, passion, and the other things, but may think the things said about you false. Thus, through the blindness of these people, the synagogue of the peoples will surround you—that is, a multitude of the faithful or of the unfaithful. For the expulsion of the Jews became the reception of the nations.

And because among these many will not be truly faithful—namely, those who bear the Christian name but do not observe the commandment, like hypocrites and heretics—you, Lord, return on high on account of this synagogue, which is to be blinded in part: that is, withdraw yourself from them, going on high and removing from them the sight and knowledge of you, so that “the filthy may become still filthier.” And indeed he will return, for in this way the Lord now judges the peoples secretly, although eventually he will judge them openly. [Col. 0523D]

This psalm may be read entirely as spoken in the person of the Head, according to which the title prefixed above is explained in the following manner. This psalm is attributed truly to David, that is, to Christ, whom David sang—that is, whom he joyfully proclaimed in his praise—“for the words of Cush,” that is, because what was Cush among persecutors and unbelievers, namely silence—the reconciliation accomplished through Christ’s mediation, because the lowest things have been joined to the highest and heavenly things to earthly things—this silence, I say, became words among the faithful, that is, the manifest reason of Christ.

Hence it came about that many attained to the perfection of his body, that is, of Christ, through knowledge of that Cush. Cush was the son of Jemini, that is, of the right hand, because God the Father, in his mercy toward the world and for the salvation of all, brought about that silence through Christ the Mediator; and, in order that it might bear fruit, he also deigned to reveal him. For this revelation our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God the Father and exhorting us to conformity with himself, [Col. 0524A] prays in this psalm for himself and for his members, saying:

“Lord my God, I have hoped not in myself but in you. Therefore save me,” that is, save my people from all those who persecute them, as explained above, “and deliver me in myself,” lest he who is like a lion—that is, the Jewish people, which truly gave a grievous roar in its persecution of Christ when it said, “Crucify him, crucify him”—lest he, I say, at some time seize me, that is, take away my soul, so that I have no power to take it up again.

And you ought to deliver and save me, because there is no one who can redeem—that is, deliver me in myself—if you do not deliver me; nor is there anyone who can save me in my members if you do not save me.

## “Lord my God”

He resumes the same name, as though saying: “For this reason also you ought to deliver and save me, Lord my God, because I have done neither in myself nor in my members what I ought not to have done.”

For if I have done that which I ought not to have done, and he specifies it as above, then I [Col. 0524B] do not refuse to fall—that is, to be cast down from my enemies, the Jews—empty, that is, without victory, so that I cannot take up my soul again. This would justly happen, because I, who ought to have been the Head in glory, would have become an example in disgrace.
