And so I would fall, so that the enemy—that is, the Jewish people—would pursue my soul in the tribulation of the passion, seize it by compelling me to death, and trample my life—that is, my soul—into the earth after death, shutting me in the tomb as someone earthly and no longer capable of rising again, and placing a seal on the tomb with guards. Thus he would bring my glory—that is, the glory of my resurrection—down into dust, that is, into nothingness.

But if I have done what I ought to have done, then you, Lord, rise up in anger against my enemies and be exalted at the boundaries of my enemies, as was explained above in the preceding exposition; and rise up in my friends in the commandment that you have given, that is, make those who cling to me rise up in your commandment, whether of love or of obedience and humility. Thus, through their teaching [Col. 0524C] and example of life, as through that of the apostles, the synagogue of believing peoples will surround you in me. And to confirm this through the sending of the Spirit, return on high, with me as a human being returning on high, since through my humanity you descended from above.

It should be noted that ascent is not attributed to God according to local movement, since he fills all things. God’s descent is rather this: that the highest majesty of divinity became known to us through the humility of human nature united to the Word. His ascent is that through the same humanity, glorified after death, the great power of God was declared by resurrection, ascension, and the great confession of faith.

Or otherwise: The synagogue of persecuting peoples, because of the zeal of those who advance in the commandment, will surround you in the persecution of me and my members. And to blind this synagogue, return on high through my return, withdrawing knowledge from them, as was said above. The remaining words are unchanged.

But when he says, “Judge me, Lord, according to [Col. 0524D] my righteousness, and according to my innocence upon me,” such words in this reading are to be referred to the members.

# ON PSALM VIII

**To the end, for the winepresses. A psalm of David.**

## ARGUMENT

The Prophet marvels at God’s power, by which he governs the entire mass of the world, and gives thanks that so great a Creator has deigned to remember humanity. Alternatively, the Church offers praise to Christ concerning the faith of all believers. Read in connection with the Gospel of Mark.

## EXPLANATION

“For the winepresses” refers to the members of the Church. For just as grapes pressed in winepresses, with their very hard seeds crushed and their skins emptied, pour forth the sweetest wines, so in the Church the pressure of repentance healthfully draws forth sweet tears from obstinate habits and swollen pride.

The Church, therefore, of ancient times—in which [Col. 0525A] there is truly a winepress of bodies but the salvific fruit of souls—at its first entrance joyfully sings the praises of Christ the Lord, proclaiming his majesty and his exalted works. In the second part it comes more openly to human nature, which, from the most depraved condition into which Adam’s sin had corrupted it, it declares to have grown to the heights of great things. Thus the one person of the Lord Christ, existing from two natures and in two natures, unconfused and distinct, is recognized salvifically and without doubt.

## COMMENTARY

“Lord, our Lord, how …”

This psalm is entitled: “To the end, for the winepresses, to David.” It is explained as follows: These words are referred to the end, that is, to perfection. They are a psalm, that is, praise of God, attributed to David himself, or to the prophet himself, or to someone so perfect among the earlier people as David was, through whom the Holy Spirit both acted and spoke.

I say that this psalm is spoken to the praise of God “for the winepresses,” [Col. 0525B] that is, for the churches, whose future existence the Prophet, or any similarly perfect person, foresaw through the Holy Spirit.

Sacred Scripture often signifies not merely one thing but several things through comparisons. Thus it sometimes signifies the Church by a threshing floor or a winepress, and at other times by nets or by Noah’s ark, in which good and evil, clean and unclean things, were contained.

The Church is compared to a winepress or threshing floor because, just as in a winepress and on a threshing floor the purpose is to separate the fruit from its coverings—although those coverings were necessary, since they were born together with the fruit, grew with it, and brought it to maturity—so the Church, through the activity of God’s ministers, works to separate the good from the evil, and lovers of the world from lovers of Christ: now at least in mind, and at some future time to be separated in body.

Yet it is necessary that these wicked people now be locally mixed with the good, so that they may bring the good toward a certain maturity, that is, toward perfection. But the time will come when [Col. 0525C] they will store the grain in the granary and burn the chaff in unquenchable fire; they will store the wines in cellars, but throw the grape-skins outside, where the beasts of the earth may fill their bellies.

There is also another interpretation of the winepresses, though it does not depart from the meaning of the churches. The grape is the divine word. When, because it must be spoken, the word assumes the sound of a voice by which it may be conveyed to the ears of hearers, its meaning is enclosed within that very sound as the grape is enclosed in grape-skins.

Thus that grape reaches the ears of hearers as though it were the tread-floor of the winepress, and there it is separated, so that the sound of the voice reaches only as far as the ears, while the meaning is received into the memory of those who hear, as though into a certain vat of the winepress. From there it flows into moral discipline and the disposition of the mind like wine from the vat into cellars. If negligence does not make it sour, it will be strengthened by age; but if negligence makes it sour, it will become the vinegar with which the Jews gave the Lord drink—that is, they turned it into corrupt morals and evil deeds.

For with this vinegar the Jews embittered the Lord by wrongly understanding the divine Scriptures.

Martyrdoms may also be compared to winepresses. [Col. 0525D] For what takes place amid such great persecution of the wicked and tribulation of the good—when the good are scourged and afflicted in every way—but that their mortal bodies are thrown to the beasts of the earth like food, while their souls are stored in the storehouses of eternal blessedness?

Now let us approach the literal meaning. The Prophet David—or anyone so perfect, filled with the Holy Spirit, who acted and spoke in him—foresaw that, at the time of Christ’s and the apostles’ preaching, congregations of believers would come into existence, that is, churches. Yet these cannot exist without a mixture of the wicked. In them, through the activity of God’s ministers, the good would be separated from the wicked, now in mind and eventually also in body.

Foreseeing this, I say, he bursts forth in admiration into the praise of God, [Col. 0526A] for the consolation and instruction of those who would come later and also for the instruction of his contemporaries, saying:

“Lord,” the Lord of all by power, but specially our Lord by grace—for “we worship what we know, while others worship what they do not know”—“your name,” that is, your praise and fame, “how marvelous,” that is, how venerable and praiseworthy, it will be through the establishment of the churches, not only in Judea but throughout the whole earth.

Formerly the Lord’s name was known only in Judea; afterward, as the Church spread through the preaching of the apostles, it went forth into every part of the earth.

## “For your magnificence has been exalted”

Therefore your name will be marvelous, because your magnificence—that is, your magnificent Son, who is to be called Magnificence because he will make many magnificent—will be exalted above the heavens for the increase of your praise. This is so certain that it can already be said as though it were past: “Your magnificence has been exalted above the heavens.”

Here “heavens” means the books of the Old and New Testaments. [Col. 0526B] They are called heavens because they are engraved, that is, sculpted, with various figures. Just as in a work of art some sculpted things appear outwardly while others lie hidden within, so many mysteries lie hidden in these books.

Christ has been exalted above these heavens by surpassing them, because in both his words and his deeds he surpassed all the scriptural proclamations made concerning him.

Or otherwise: “He will be exalted above the heavens,” that is, he will surpass the apostles and the other heralds of truth in the fullness of the grace of the Holy Spirit. Hence it is said to him through the Prophet: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.” Or he will be greater in both words and deeds than what they proclaim about him.

Of his deeds it is said: “No one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him”; and again: “From the beginning of the world it has not been heard.” Of his words it is also said: “No one has ever spoken as this man speaks.”

Or otherwise: “He will be exalted above the material heavens,” when, having taken up his flesh from the dead, he ascends into that highest heaven of which he himself is the light, to sit at the right hand of the Father.

The apostles and other heralds of truth are called heavens [Col. 0526C] because they rain upon us the words of teaching and flash upon us through miracles. Of them it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God,” and many similar things.

## “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise”

Truly your name will be marvelous through your Magnificent One, because through him you will perfect praise for yourself—that is, you will cause perfect praise to arise from the mouth of infants and nursing children, that is, from the preaching of untrained apostles.

“For God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; he chose the weak to shame the strong; he chose the things that are as though they were not, to destroy the things that are.” All this was said concerning the apostles. Though previously foolish in knowledge, weak in power, and as though nonexistent in reputation, they overcame philosophers and powerful men by divine teachings, having been taken up by the Lord and sent to preach.

This was done with great foresight by the Lord, lest, if he had chosen the philosophers of the world as ministers of his preaching, it should be thought that, if they accomplished anything great, it came not from the dignity of the subject they preached but from their worldly wisdom or power.

The order of the words may also be noted here. [Col. 0526D] An infant is less than a nursing child. Let us therefore understand by “infants” the other apostles, who knew nothing beforehand; and by the “nursing child,” Paul, who, although he had previously known something, was nevertheless still like a nursing child before he was chosen, in comparison with Plato and the other philosophers.

From their mouth God perfected praise for himself when he bent the heavens—that is, the lofty and hidden Scriptures—to their capacity and opened them to them. Through the humility of historical faith, concerning events accomplished in time, he raised their minds, instructed and strengthened, to the height of spiritual understanding.

“You perfect praise for yourself,” I say, and this “because of your enemies,” so that you may destroy the enemy of your sect and the avenger—that is, the defender—of his own sect, whether Jew, false prophet, or heretic. For the Jews and false apostles were greatly scandalized by the sound teaching of such men.

He calls anyone an enemy of God [Col. 0527A] who wickedly opposes the divine dispensation of power and wisdom administered through Jesus Christ for the salvation of all.

Or otherwise: “From the mouth of infants,” that is, of the simple Hebrew children instructed by no one, “you will perfect praise for yourself,” confounding your enemies, the Jews. For the Jews were greatly confounded and disturbed when, as the Lord approached his passion and came to Jerusalem on the sixth day before Passover, their uninstructed children—taught by no one except the Holy Spirit—went out to meet him, crying aloud with the greatest pomp: “Hosanna to the Son of David.”

## “For I shall see the heavens”

Truly your Magnificent One will be exalted above the heavens, whether the books or the apostles, because there will be many heavens. For I shall see—not in myself but in my descendants. Thus it is said: “The Lord brought them into the mountain of his sanctification.”

The Lord did not personally bring the children of Israel whom he led out of Egypt into the promised land, since all but two of them died before reaching it. Yet he is said to have brought them in through their descendants, whom he did bring in.

Similarly, it is said here: “I shall see in my descendants, [Col. 0527B] in the time of your Magnificent One, your heavens,” that is, your books, engraved and composed by them, in which the Holy Spirit will speak and act. Therefore they will be called “the work of your fingers,” that is, of the Holy Spirit.

For more books were made after the truth became manifest at Christ’s coming than had existed before. Hence it is rightly said: “I shall see your heavens,” and so forth.

The finger is understood as the Holy Spirit because of the diversity of gifts. No member of our body manifests as many different movements as the hands do through the fingers. To this belongs the fact that the tablets on which the Law was given to Moses are said to have been written by the finger of God, that is, by the Holy Spirit; and that in the Gospel it is said: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God,” and many similar things.

Or otherwise: “I shall see in my descendants your heavens,” that is, your apostles, so renewed and filled with spiritual gifts that they can be called “the work of your fingers,” that is, the work of the Holy Spirit. “And I shall also see the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars”: the moon, that is, the universal Church; and the stars, that is, the individual lesser churches, such as the seven churches of Asia. [Col. 0527C] You will establish both of these through your apostles.

Or, according to the first interpretation, it will be said: “I shall see the heavens,” that is, the books, “and the moon and the stars,” which you will establish through those heavens, that is, through the books. For the commandments of the divine books are the foundation of both the universal Church and the individual churches; through them those churches are strengthened and supported like a building by its foundation.

The whole Church is signified by the moon because of the waning it undergoes. No one of such perfection lives in the Church that he does not often fall and rise again. Hence it is said: “The righteous falls seven times and rises again.”

The individual churches are compared to stars because, just as one star differs from another in brightness, so the various churches differ among themselves in the expression of diverse spiritual gifts. One excels in generosity, another in chastity, and so forth.

## “What is man?”

Because it was noted above that some imitators of the old man are to be regenerated [Col. 0527D] into the new man—a point suggested in the following verse and in the first verse, where mention was made of the establishment of churches through the name to be glorified throughout the earth—and because it was said that God’s Magnificent One, that is, the Son of Man, would be exalted above all the heavens, the Prophet resumes his earlier wonder.

As though he were saying: “Lord, our Lord, what is man?” That is, of what dignity is man simply considered in himself—the old man, and everyone who bears his image—that you deign to remember him, though he has been separated from you by sin, preparing for him the aid of healing?

Or also: “What is the Son of Man,” that is, the man born of the Virgin, the Lord’s man, “that you visit him” through the presence of your Word joined to him?

As though he were saying: “In himself the simple man and the Son of Man are nothing, insofar as he is born from sinful flesh; but in relation to you—who remember the one and visit the other—he is something great.”

It should be known that every Son of Man is man, but not every man is the Son of Man. “Man” in the simple sense [Col. 0528A] refers to the first transgressor and to all who follow in his footsteps. “Son of Man,” however, refers to the Lord’s man, that is, Christ, as here.

All who have been regenerated from the old man are also called sons of men. But because many are not regenerated, not every man is the Son of Man. The man in the simple sense is the beginning of every Son of Man. For repentance and the washing away of the old man are always the generation of the Son of Man, that is, of newness. Animality precedes spirituality. Hence the Apostle says: “Not first the spiritual, but the animal,” and so forth.

## “You made him a little lower”

Although you visit the Son of Man, you make him a little lower than the angels, “a little” that is, in a small matter: in the weakness of the flesh and in the tribulation of passion and death.

But this will do no harm, because you will immediately crown him—that is, adorn him with the glory of resurrection and the honor of confession. Through both you will establish him above the works of your hands, [Col. 0528B] that is, you will make him superior to every good rational creature, both higher and lower, which may more nobly than other things be called your work.

For you will subject all rational things beneath his feet, that is, beneath his power, in the manner of a figure of speech; or beneath his feet, that is, you will subject all things even to his humanity.

For by the feet, which are the lower part of the body, Christ’s humanity is signified, since it is lower than his divinity. He demonstrates this by parts, because all things are included.

## “Sheep and oxen”

Among human beings, “sheep” means rational people who bear the fruit of simplicity and innocence. Angels are also called sheep, according to the Gospel saying: “If anyone has one hundred sheep and loses one of them,” and so forth.

The number one hundred, which is perfect, signifies perfection in the supercelestial rational creature. By the ninety-nine, which is an imperfect number, is understood the imperfection and diminution of reason that occurred in that creature through the first man, who through disobedience [Col. 0528C] fell from the glory of knowledge of God.

Among human beings, “oxen” means heralds of truth who bear fruit and beget others in the faith. For this reason he also used the feminine plural: “all oxen.” Among angels, those may be called oxen who proclaim some salvation to human beings, through which they make them fruitful for God, as Gabriel did when he proclaimed the most holy incarnation of the Lord to blessed Mary, and in other such cases.

In addition he places here “cattle,” referring to the subjection of the wicked among human beings, in order to display the complete constitution of the Church. He also secretly notes here what was said above in the title concerning the winepresses: that in the Church the good are mixed with the wicked.

They are now separated in mind through the activity of God’s ministers, and eventually they will also be separated in body. And lest, if he simply said “and the cattle of the field,” we refer it to the same group, he adds this expression to indicate that others are to be understood here.

Those who are irrational human beings, desiring and rejoicing only in earthly pleasures, are called “the field.” They walk through the field—that is, through the broad way that leads to destruction—where nothing difficult is climbed and no hardship is overcome. A level plain appears everywhere [Col. 0528D] until they arrive at unavoidable destruction.

Of them it has truly been said: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame.”

“Birds” in the simple sense means elevated people who exceed the common measure. “Birds of heaven,” that is, of the air, means those who are more elevated, such as those of whom it is said: “We will magnify our law,” and the rest; just as there are many material birds of heaven because they move about in the air.

Those, however, are specifically called birds of heaven who frequent the higher air.

By “fish of the sea,” which have a broader space in which to move than river fish, are signified the curious among earthly things, such as merchants who search through the broad depths of the sea—that is, of this world—in pursuit of troublesome profits.

Their business dealings are compared to those paths made in the true sea by the course of ships or other things, because just as quickly as those paths are destroyed, so quickly all the labor of these people is brought to nothing.

Having displayed the perfect future constitution of the Church, consisting of the Head and the members, [Col. 0529A] both good and wicked, he resumes again, for confirmation, his first wonder, saying:

“Lord, our Lord.”

# ON PSALM IX

**To the end, for the hidden things of the Son. A psalm of David.**

## ARGUMENT

David prays to the Lord concerning the deceitful designs of his son, giving thanks that their outcome did not follow them. It may also fit Hezekiah, giving thanks after the destruction of the Assyrian army. Alternatively, the Church offers praise to Christ concerning the Jews and the prince of demons.

## EXPLANATION

The name “Son” signifies the person of the Lord and Savior. [Col. 0529B] For when a name is given without stating to whom it belongs, it must be understood as referring to some supreme person.

“For the hidden things,” which he placed in the plural, indicates not one but both of his comings. It should nevertheless be known that the Hebrew has “for the death of the Son.” But the Seventy Interpreters preferred to conceal Christ’s passion and resurrection, previously unknown to the world, under the word “concealment,” lest they be easily recognized by the nations at that time.

Symmachus likewise translated it, “For victory over the death of the Son.” He had the custom of translating the Hebrew word *Lamanasse*, which the Seventy rendered “to the end” and Aquila rendered *Imnicopoim*, that is, “to him who gives victory,” as *Epinicion*, a word that properly signifies a triumph and a triumphal psalm.

This entire psalm is drawn from the person of the Prophet. In the first statement he says that he will joyfully sing to the Lord because he has confounded the devil, whose worship he destroyed through the loving dispensation of his coming.

Second, he encourages the faithful to sing to the Lord, who avenges the blood of the poor and exalts them from the gates of death.

Third, he tells sinners that, together with Antichrist, the end of the wicked will come. [Col. 0529C]

Fourth, moved by the excessive wickedness of the wicked themselves, he turns to the Lord and, as though he had withdrawn from defending the poor, says that the Lord has given the wicked permission to exercise their presumption.

Fifth, he prays that the time of that dreadful judgment may come, so that all these things may quickly reach their end and the wickedness of no human being may prevail any longer.

## COMMENTARY

“I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart.”

This psalm is entitled: “To the end, for the hidden things of the Son. A psalm of David.” It is explained as follows: This psalm was composed by the historical David, but it is to be referred not to some historical event but to the end, that is, to perfection, namely, to the fullness of time, when God sent his Son, made under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law, and when the imperfection of time passed away, during which the truth had previously lain hidden beneath a shadow. [Col. 0529D]

I say that this is a psalm spoken for the understanding of, or attention to, the hidden things of the Son of God.

One might ask whose son’s hidden things are meant here, since no specification is added, unless the title of the preceding psalm removes this uncertainty. That title, dealing with Absalom, the historical son of David, includes the specification “of his son”; moreover, when that wicked man waged war against his father, he stirred up not foreign nations but Israel alone against him.

In this psalm, however, many things are understood of the nations. This clearly leads us to understand here not the hidden things of some historical son of David, but rather those of the only-begotten Son of God the Father, who, by excellence and without qualification, calls himself the Son, saying: “If the Son makes you free, you will truly be free.”

The distinction placed here—“for the hidden things”—leads us, by opposition, to understand that certain things belonging to the Son are manifest; in contrast with them, these things are called hidden.

To see these hidden things more perfectly, let us consider both kinds, [Col. 0530A] namely, the hidden and the manifest things of the Son.

Two comings of Christ are most certainly believed to exist. One is past: humble and hidden, when he appeared in the flesh. The Jews did not believe in him, but he benefited the nations, because “a partial blindness has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the nations enters.”

The other coming is manifest, namely, his coming on the day of judgment. The Jews themselves await it, as do we. In it even the wicked will openly confess that Christ is the one who rightly grants rewards to the just and inflicts punishments upon the wicked, although that confession will not be for their salvation but for the accumulation of their condemnation.

These two comings are followed by two judgments. The humble coming is followed by a hidden judgment; the manifest coming is followed by a manifest judgment.

The hidden judgment is taking place in the present, as Peter testifies in his Epistle, saying: “It is necessary that the scourge now begin from the house of God.”

He calls “scourging” the just judgment that is exercised in the present [Col. 0530B] for purification in the house of God, that is, among the faithful.

The hidden judgment is that punishment secretly administered in the present, so that it may either exercise converts for purification, admonish the wicked to conversion, or prepare the hardened, through present blindness, for eternal damnation.

The Lord also makes these two judgments clear in the Gospel, speaking in this way about the manifest judgment: “Whoever believes in me does not come into judgment but passes from death to life.”

This is to be understood as follows: Every true believer is so purified in the present judgment by a temporary affliction, with which God the Father scourges every son whom he receives, that there is no need for him to come to judgment as one requiring purification; instead, he immediately passes into glory.

Concerning the hidden judgment he says: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged,” that is, through the blindness of the hidden judgment he has already been prepared for the eternal condemnation of the just judgment.

These are the hidden and manifest things of the Son. [Col. 0530C] For the understanding and recognition of these hidden and manifest things, each according to its proper manner and time, this psalm was composed by David the Prophet in the voice of the Head, or also by some perfect person from the earlier people.

We may also indicate the hidden and manifest things here without the foregoing prolixity of words. By the hidden things we may understand the prosperity now permitted to the wicked and the sparing of them, so that eventually they may be rejected; while the good are now scourged so that eventually they may be received into glory.

This is hidden to people who see the matter in the opposite way. By these hidden things we may understand the manifest things that will follow later, when the good will openly be received and the wicked rejected.

Now let us approach the literal meaning. In this psalm the voice is that of the Head, exhorting us to rejoice at his humble coming and to conform ourselves through imitation of his passion, so that here we may embrace the hidden and passing discipline of the Father and in the future escape the manifest punishment that devastates the wicked.

He says:

“Lord Father, I will confess to you,” that is, I will praise you in myself and in my members through good works, not falsely, like the people who honor with their lips, but “with my whole heart,” that is, with complete affection. [Col. 0530D]

The person who praises the Lord with his whole heart reserves no corner of his heart for himself in which he possesses anything earthly, but hastens to praise God with every affection of his heart through good works.

He also praises God with his whole heart who in no way resists the divine disposition, attributing nothing to fate, constellation, or anything of that kind, as certain foolish people do. Such a person understands that one ought to rejoice in tribulations, because he knows that every present punishment is given either to exercise converts who have already turned toward purification, to admonish the unconverted to conversion, or to prepare those unwilling to convert for eternal damnation.

“Confess” is therefore used for “praise,” because after a true confession of sins there follows a praiseworthy confession: the change of an evil life into a good life, by which God is truly praised.

“I will confess to you,” I say, “and likewise I will recount in myself and in my members, through good works, your wonderful works”—all your works that can be recounted. [Col. 0531A]

This qualification is added because the Head did not recount certain things either in himself or in his members, concerning which it was said: “It is not for you to know the times,” and so forth; and again: “I have many things to say to you”; and again: “Concerning that day or hour no one knows except the Father alone,” and the rest.

Or otherwise: “I will recount all your wonderful works,” not only those that you perform openly in the body, but also those that you accomplish invisibly, which is far more worthy and excellent.

For it was more excellent to raise Saul the persecutor invisibly in his mind than to raise Lazarus visibly in his body. Visible miracles summon the soul to illumination, but invisible miracles illuminate the soul that has been summoned. Thus I will recount everything by passing, in myself and in my members, through invisible miracles to the understanding and belief of invisible things.

That is to recount perfectly all the wonders of God.

## “I will rejoice and exult in you”

In this way I will recount and confess, because [Col. 0531B] I will rejoice in mind and exult in body—that is, I will rejoice perfectly. This is indicated by both expressions.

And I will do this not in myself or in any worldly acquisition, but in you, from whom my being will depend, and I will also sing, that is, I will work well, not for my own glory but to glorify your name, because you are the Most High.

This properly applies to the Head himself, that is, to Christ, who says: “I have not come to do my own will”; and again: “My glory is not my own.”

It also applies to the members in their own way, according to what was said: “That they may see your good works and glorify God who is in heaven.”

“In turning my enemy backward.” I shall rightly sing praise to you, because whatever I shall please you by, or whatever I shall become, will be through you; for you will turn my enemy backward—not I: that is, the devil tempting me, both by himself and through his members, and by himself and through his members wishing to place himself and his members first. Through victory you will make him, both in himself and in his own, be backward—that is, defeated and put last. For what is less worthy is always behind what is more worthy, not in time but in dignity.

This is what John understood when he said, “He who comes after me was made before me.” This was fulfilled in Christ when, being tempted by the devil, he said to the one who wished to be pre-eminent, “Go behind me, Satan.” It is also fulfilled daily in his members when, being tempted by the devil through suggestions or by his ministers through incitements, they do not succumb to them but, conquering them, go before them.

Or otherwise: “Turning my enemy backward,” that is, the prince of the world, the devil, who, before he was expelled by you, went ahead outwardly; you will make him follow your people, both in himself and in his members, while he vainly persecutes them. And truly the devil and his members go backward, whether tempting or persecuting, because they will grow weak—that is, they will be ineffective in both—and will finally perish, removed from your presence, when it is said to them, “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.”

And truly the devil and his ministers, while tempting, will grow weak, because you will not merely make—but have already made—judgment: that is, you have established a disposition in me and in my members which they, by tempting, wished to make their own. They wished to make it obedient to themselves; but you, by strengthening it against temptations, will make it ours—that is, you will make it serve rather the advantage of me and my members. And the cause—that is, the devil’s suggestion and the incitement of his ministers—which they thought was theirs, meaning that it would attain their glory, you will make mine: that is, you will make it advance my glory and that of my members. In this you will sit upon the throne worthily—that is, you will judge justly—in this, you who judge all justice and no injustice.

A throne is a judicial seat, and he alone is said to sit upon it because he judges rightly. For he does not sit upon a royal seat; indeed, it should not even be said that he is there, since he does not rule there. Hence “to sit upon the throne” is rightly used here for just judgment.

According to another interpretation, it will be understood as follows: “Truly the devil and his ministers, while persecuting me and my members, will grow weak, because you will make judgment”—that is, their judicial power—and the cause—that is, the accusation—which they will exercise in condemning me and my members, for their own glory. That judicial power and accusation you will make mine—that is, you will turn it toward the glory of me and my members and toward their disgrace. “And in this he will sit upon the throne”: that is, you will prepare for yourself my soul and the souls of my members as a throne, a judicial seat—you who judge all justice through me. For the Father has given all judgment to the Son. Hence it is said, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.”

These two verses may also be read otherwise, so that they are understood as follows: “Therefore I shall sing praise to your name, because you will turn my enemy”—that is, the Jewish people, who previously failed to recognize their weakness and therefore despised and passed by me as physician. Just as a madman, while failing to understand his illness, does not honor the physician by following him but despises him by going ahead of him: so, I say, you will turn that enemy backward. That is, through the preaching of your apostles you will make him recognize his illness and humbly follow and honor me as physician.

Or truly they will be turned backward, for they will grow weak in themselves—that is, they will recognize their weakness. Thus their face will perish in them: that is, the deformity of sin by which they had darkened themselves before your face, when your virtues came upon them. So Saul’s face had perished when he said, “I live now not I, but Christ lives in me.”

Or their face will perish from before your face—that is, through those in whom your face will be openly represented, namely through the apostles’ teaching. And it will perish because my condemnation will save them. This is what he says: “For you, Lord Father, have already made, in your ordinance, judgment”—that is, the condemnation by which I shall be condemned—and the cause—that is, the accusation by which I shall be accused—“to be mine,” that is, to be that of my members, beneficial to my members. And in this you have sat upon the throne: that is, you have judged justly in this. For it was just that the judge of human beings, who had come to confer salvation, should be sacrificed for the salvation of human beings. Hence the Apostle says: “For it was fitting to perfect through death the author of the salvation of those many sons whom he was to lead into glory.” What we have now said about the Jews can also be said about any Gentiles who persecute the members of Christ.

“In order to rebuke the nations.” It is as though he said: You made my judgment and my cause fruitful, because through this you rebuked, through me, the nations—that is, all who live in a Gentile manner. This does not mean that Christ himself personally rebuked the nations, since no one among them is said to have come to him except a certain Canaanite woman and a certain centurion of great faith; for he himself says, “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.” Rather, this happened when the apostles, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, openly reproved the vices of all evil people.

And because you rebuked the nations, therefore the impious perished: that is, the one who had previously been impious, being justified, became pious. Hence it is said, “Turn the impious, and they shall be no more.” And he perished in this respect because you erased their name—that is, the name of impiety within them—not only in the present age but forever.

And because “forever” is ordinarily understood as a duration so long that nothing longer can be conceived by the human mind, as in “The Lord will reign forever, and beyond,” he adds, “and into the age succeeding this present age”: that is, into true eternity, which follows this age. For just as this age proceeds through days, months, and years passing away and succeeding one another, so eternity itself proceeds, as it were, through infinite ages passing away and succeeding one another.

Blessed Augustine says that another translation has, “into the age and into the age of the age.” But because in the Greek from which this translation was made there is a certain noun, αἰῶνα, which is equivocal between “age” and “eternal,” “eternal” has here been placed according to that reading.

“The enemies have failed.” Through this you erased their name, because not only will the weapons of the enemy—that is, of the devil—not be sufficient, but they have already failed by your ordinance. He calls the various opinions of errors by which the devil, as with a sword, slaughtered the souls of those whom he deceived through those errors “weapons.” That sword destroyed all these weapons: the sword which God the Father sent, hidden in its sheath at Christ’s humble coming, but brandished in manifest majesty at his glorious coming. For after Christ’s coming, although those weapons remained in some people, they had little effectiveness.

This is what he says: “The weapons have failed,” that is, they have been destroyed, having reached the end—that is, the perfection and fullness of time, when Christ came. Or they have failed, going to the end: that is, you destroyed them through complete failure and crushing.

The soul of every impious person is a city in which the prince of Babylon—that is, the devil—reigns. In this deceitful and fraudulent city, deceptive and treacherous counsels occupy the place of a court. The functions of the various members provide an escort for this principality in carrying out wickedness: through the eyes we are deceived into carnal desire, through the ears into sensuality, through the hands into rapacity, and so likewise through the other members.

The pleasures of the flesh are also the populace of this city, along with the turbulent movements of the soul that stir up daily rebellions within a person. These kingdoms are destroyed by the divine word when, through holy preaching, fraudulent counsels are quieted, unlawful pleasures subdued, and the functions of the members taken captive, so that what the Apostle urges may be fulfilled in us when he says, “You presented your members to serve iniquity unto iniquity,” and so forth.

Hence he says: “You destroyed the cities”—that is, the souls of the impious, insofar as the devil’s kingdom existed in them—“through the word of preaching.” And it must be understood that these things, namely fraudulent counsels and the rest, would in no way be said to exist in evil cities unless they had first existed in individual human beings.

Or otherwise: “The weapons of the enemy” are the open contradictions which the devil formerly produced through his members against the Christian name. They are designated as weapons because whoever fights with a weapon—that is, with a sword—fights openly. These, I say, “failed at the end,” as was said above, and not in a few cases. But “you destroyed the cities”—that is, the conspiracies and gatherings of those contradictors—by transferring them into the Church.

And I rightly say that you have already destroyed them, because already with you their memory has perished: that is, their reputation and glory, which they wished to acquire for themselves through the persecution of the Christian name. And rightly it perished, because this will happen “with a sound”—that is, irrationally, just as there is no rational understanding where there is only undifferentiated sound without words. This irrationality is sufficiently expressed when they are compared to oxen, as the Lord said to Saul: “It is foolish for you to kick against the goad.”

Or otherwise: “Their memory perished with a sound,” that is, amid the clamor of impiety: memory perished in them, and impiety, which makes a clamor in the soul.

Or otherwise: “Their memory perished with a sound,” that is, with great labor and effort in denying oneself. For great labor is required for someone to deny himself and take up his cross.

Or otherwise: “Their memory perished with the sound of preaching,” that is, through the thunder and terror which the apostles, in their preaching, inflicted on them by threats of the future judgment.

“And the Lord remains forever”: that is, I, whom they wished to disinherit and drive out as a slave, having been made Lord, remain in the house—that is, I dwell in the faithful—not for an hour but forever. Hence it is said, “The slave does not remain in the house forever, but the son remains forever.” And again: “Of his kingdom there will be no end.” Here the Head speaks about himself as though about a third person.

“He prepared his throne for judgment.” The Lord rightly remains forever in the house, because he prepared his throne for judgment. That is, I, through the condemnation of my passion, prepared a throne for myself: I acquired judicial power for myself from God the Father, who, because I was judged for human beings, appointed me judge of human beings.

Hence it is said: “Christ became obedient to the Father unto death; therefore God the Father exalted him,” and so forth.

“And he”—that is, I, who previously, placed in humility, did not appear to be myself, who was not yet made myself, namely Lord and judge of all—“will judge the world with manifest judgment at the end of the age”: that is, I will judge those who, although previously they were earth—that is, earthly—will become, through good works, the world—that is, perfect.

I will judge them “in equity,” that is, in equality, conforming them to myself in glory there, because here they conformed themselves to me through good works. And I will judge the peoples—that is, those who stir up evil tumults and rebellions—“in justice,” that is, in comparison with the justice of the perfect, because here they did not conform themselves to the perfect and will not be associated with them there in glory.

For there will be no judgment there except in the conscience, by which each person will join himself there either to the good or to the evil to which he conformed himself here.

“And the Lord became.” The same Creator of all, who will then be judged openly, became—that is, was created through the humility joined to him—and was therefore constituted Lord. For the present, meanwhile, he is a refuge—that is, a shelter—in which he is defended and received who had previously fled into a far country through the first transmission of sin.

He is, I say, a refuge for the poor, not outwardly but inwardly: that is, for the truly poor person who has so impoverished himself in mind that he loves nothing which either abandons him while he lives or will be abandoned by him at death, but desires only eternal things, which are stable.

And he is a refuge because he is a helper in times of need—that is, where it is fitting, namely in inward virtues—even if he does not help outwardly, because he places virtues in his own people so that they may not be diverted or fail. And this happens when it is necessary, namely in tribulation, when they are afflicted outwardly.

Or otherwise: He is a helper of his own in tribulation—that is, through tribulation—and through certain bitter things given amid times of opportunity, that is, amid prosperity. For when God permits certain bitter and harsh things to be mixed into the worldly prosperity of his own people, he truly helps them in this. For at once the perfect soul perceives what fragile things worldly goods are, despises them, and fixes its desire upon heavenly things.

These two verses may also rightly be read in the third person, that is, referred to the Father, so that they are understood as follows: “The righteous Lord, the Son, remains forever in the house.” That is, I, because the Lord Father, in judgment—that is, in my condemnation—prepared for himself his throne: he made me a judicial seat, so that through me he might judge others.

Or otherwise: “In judgment,” that is, in the endurance and steadfastness of my condemnation, he prepared for himself, through the example of imitation, his throne—that is, the apostles in whom he would sit and through whom he would judge others. And the Lord himself will finally judge the world openly through me, and so forth. Meanwhile, through me he has become a refuge for the poor, as was explained above.

“And let those who know your name hope in you.” Here he turns toward the Father himself. It is as though he said: Because I, the Lord, am a refuge for the poor—or because you are one in me—therefore, O Lord, let those who know your name hope in you.

Or it may be connected according to the later interpretation concerning the Helper in times of opportunity. Because they recognize, through the tribulation mixed with prosperity, that earthly things are contemptible, let them hope not in themselves, so that they presume something about themselves, as Adam did; nor let them hope in earthly things, but let them cast their hope upon you, knowing that without you they can do nothing.

Let those hope in you, I say, who truly know your name. It is written concerning this name that “the Lord is his name.” That name—that is, that Lord—truly knows only the one who voluntarily subjected himself to him as a servant.

It is also written, “He who is has sent me to you,” and, “I am who I am.” This too is a name, and only the one who does not desire things that flow through “was” and “will be”—that is, transitory things—truly knows it. For just as such things are awaited with great longing before they are acquired, which is signified by “will be,” so they are lost with great sorrow, which is signified by “was.” He desires only the things that are: that is, eternal things alone.

And rightly they ought to hope in you, because you are not merely one who abandons them, but you have already, in your purpose, not abandoned those who seek you and deny themselves.

“Sing praise to the Lord who dwells.” Here he turns to the members, as though he said: And in order that you may be able to hope, sing praise to the Lord—that is, work well for the glory of God.

Note that there is no hoping unless singing praise to the Lord precedes it. I mean the Lord who dwells in Zion, or who now, through his indwelling, makes you Zion—that is, watchmen—so that at last you may attain the true vision.

For just as Zion is the first place encountered by someone ascending to Jerusalem, so in the present life the good practice contemplation, in order finally to arrive at Jerusalem—that is, at the true vision of peace.

“Sing praise,” I say, “to the Lord,” and so that whoever loves God may also love his brother: “Declare among the nations”—that is, to the Gentiles—“his concerns,” that is, his intense affections, for he wished his Word to be humbled through incarnation and passion for the salvation of all, and wished this to be announced.

“Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul,” because a time will come when the punishment of those who kill and the glory of those who are killed will be made manifest.

This is what he says: “The Lord will not merely remember, but has already remembered,” so that eventually he may require, through the manifest punishment of those who kill and the manifest glory of those who are killed, their blood—that is, the devotion of those who proclaim him—which will be poured out by persecutors.

It must be noted that he does not say “remembered” in order to suggest that any forgetfulness falls upon God. Rather, because to those who yearn with their whole affection for that glory, and for the wicked to be separated from them, God appears, on account of the delay, almost to have forgotten, he uses “remembered” according to their perception.

And because forgetfulness is ordinarily understood to precede remembrance, he adds: “Indeed, he has not forgotten the cry”—that is, the desire of the mind—“of the poor,” who cry daily, “Avenge, O Lord, the blood of your saints.”

Of the poor, I say, who speak through me, the truly poor one who, though I was rich, became poor for all: who thus cry to the Father for them, “Lord Father, have mercy on me”—that is, have mercy on my members—“and look upon my humility”—that is, keep before your eyes the affliction of my members, inflicted on them by my enemies, namely by the persecutors of the Christian name. Granting my members steadfastness so that they do not fail, but granting those enemies blindness of mind.

Or otherwise: “Lord, have mercy on my members; and in order that you may have mercy, look upon my humility”: that is, my humiliation in my members, in whom I have been cast down not only through their own sins but also through the sin of the first parent. I mean the humility inflicted upon me in my members by my enemies—that is, by the serpent and Eve.

Or otherwise: “Lord Father, have mercy on me in my members, and look upon my humility”: that is, consider my humble satisfaction in my members, by which I, recognizing that through pride I have wandered far from my homeland, labor to return home through obedience.

“Look,” I say, “so that, by looking, you may rescue me from my external or internal enemies, lest I fail because of them.”

“Who lifts me up from the gates of death.” I ask you to have mercy, and truly you will do so, because you have already begun: for you lift me up in my members, rescued from the gates of death—that is, from carnal desires. Although these are the first death, they are nevertheless called the gates of death because they are entrances to two other, more serious deaths, namely consent to sin and the performance of sin.

You lift me, I say, from those gates, so that, if they arise in my members through the punishment of the first parent, they may not reign through consent and action. Hence it is said, “Let sin not reign in your mortal body.”

Or otherwise: “Who lifts me up from the gates of death,” that is, from the five bodily senses, which are the gates of death—that is, approaches to sin: the eyes to curiosity, the ears to sensuality, the hands to rapacity, and likewise the others. From those gates, I say, you lift me and my members up, so that we do not attend to things below but to things above.

Or “from the gates of death,” that is, from human judgments, which in ancient times were customarily held before the gates of cities, so that those going out and coming in, seeing the condemnation of the wicked and the reward of the good, might avoid what ought to be avoided and desire what ought to be done.

These human judgments are called the gates of death because they cannot be exercised without injustice. From those gates, I say, you lift me—that is, my members—so that we judge not according to human beings but according to you, who are not a respecter of persons.

These three interpretations of “the gates of death” chiefly refer to the members. With regard to the Head, however, it may be understood as follows: “You lift me up from the gates of death,” that is, from the humility and passibility of humanity, which are approaches to death; you lift me up in the resurrection through immortality and impassibility.

Or, more simply: “You lift me up from the gates of death,” that is, from the power of death by which all who are born carnally are commonly held; you lift me up so that I am not held by it.

Or: “You lift me up from the gates of death,” that is, from Tartarus, as though from material gates by which those who are thrust there are held enclosed.

This happened when the very divinity, which had cooperated in the human soul while it rested in the tomb, descended to the underworld of death, broke the gates, chained the prince of darkness, and rescued his own in supreme triumph. It did not return in that same soul, but on the third day it raised up its own flesh by divine right.

Therefore, I say, you lift me up so that I may announce, both in myself and in my members, all your praises—that is, everything pertaining to your praise, whether you perform it openly in the body or secretly. But, because what is done in the mind is far more worthy, I shall announce these things not to dogs, who prefer to bark obstinately rather than hear and understand humbly, nor to pigs, who neither care to understand nor trouble themselves to contradict, but lie sunk and wallow in the mire of carnal pleasures.

Hence it is said, “Do not cast pearls before pigs, nor give what is holy to dogs.” Rather, let me announce these things to Zion—that is, to those who watch and have already been converted.

Zion, I say, is made a daughter if she maintains vigilant custody of her salvation, so that she does not look back at the things she has left behind. This is rightly signified by “daughter,” for parents ordinarily exercise greater vigilance over daughters than over others in the household.

And let me announce it to her “in the gates,” that is, in public, where many gather, as at gates, without shame. Hence it is said, “Whoever is ashamed of me before human beings, I also shall be ashamed of him before my Father.”

Or “in the gates,” that is, through ecclesiastical institutions or sacraments, namely baptism and other such things, which are gates—that is, approaches to salvation.

Or let me announce it to her while I myself exist “in the gates,” that is, in virtues and good works, which are gates leading to blessedness. For the preacher’s tongue is rightly despised if it does not arise from the substance of his preaching—that is, if he teaches one thing by his words and another by his deeds.

The preceding verse, “For you require their blood,” can also be read otherwise than has been stated, so that it is an exhortation by the Head to love of neighbor.

It is as though he said: You who are more perfect ought therefore to announce the Lord’s concerns to the nations—that is, to those living in sins—because, if you do not announce them and do not correct their impiety, the Lord is one who requires their blood—that is, he will require their condemnation from you. And if he delays for the present, he will nevertheless remember it in the manifest judgment.

Nor is it surprising that he will remember, because he has not forgotten the cry of the poor—that is, their manifest iniquity, the poor who are deprived of every virtue, which is signified by “cry,” as in, “The cry of Sodom has come to me,” and in the Apostle, “Let all clamor be removed from your midst, together with every wickedness.”

That cry, I say, does not allow the Lord to forget, but compels him to require their blood from you, because you did not announce him to them. Hence it is said: “If you announce his iniquity to the wicked, and the wicked does not turn, the wicked shall perish in his iniquity, but you shall deliver your soul. But if you do not announce it, the wicked shall indeed perish, but I shall require his blood from your hand.” Again, in the Apocalypse it is written: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come.’”

According to this interpretation, the following verse, “Have mercy on me, Lord,” is connected not with what immediately precedes, as earlier, but with what was said above: “For you have not abandoned those who seek you, Lord.”

It is as though he said: “You, Lord, who have not abandoned those who seek you”—that is, who always have mercy on those who seek you—“have mercy on me,” that is, on my members, and so forth. The meaning does not change.

“I shall rejoice in your salvation.” Because you, Lord, lift me and my members up, therefore I shall rejoice, in myself and in my members, in your salvation.

This verse can also be connected with “Let them hope in you” as with its principal clause. From “Sing praise to the Lord” up to this point, an interpolation seems to have occurred.

It is as though he said: I say that those who know your name should hope in you, and they will do this by my example, since I truly hope in you. For I do not merely rejoice now, but I and my members shall always rejoice—that is, I shall rejoice perfectly, inwardly and outwardly, however much I may be troubled and afflicted.

And this joy is not in my own presumption, as Adam’s was, but in your salvation—that is, in your saving work, namely in your Word joined to me as a human being. “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

But the nations that persecute us will not rejoice, because they have been fixed—that is, immutably condemned—by God’s hidden judgment. And this is not because of your anger, but because of their own guilt, namely in that destruction which they inflicted upon us: that is, in the tribulation which they prepared for us.

For while they prepare to kill the body outwardly, they themselves are first killed inwardly. Hence it is said, “No one sins against another without first sinning against himself”; and, “The one who dug a pit first fell into it.”

Here he touches upon God’s just judgment, by which he does not punish the wicked out of his own anger but because of their own wickedness.

“In this snare which they hid.” He explains how the nations have been fixed: their foot—that is, the affection of those who bring about destruction—will not merely be caught when they are openly handed over to the outer darkness, but has already been caught through inner darkness in this snare which they themselves hid—that is, secretly prepared for the destruction of others.

The foot is the soul’s affection, that is, the soul’s love. This affection is called a foot because, just as the body is carried by the feet, so the soul is carried by its affections.

This affection is sometimes good and sometimes evil. If it is evil, it is called desire; if good, it is called charity. Pernicious pleasure follows the evil affection, while fruitful pleasure follows the good.

The snare here is also a fraudulent and hidden thought intended to deceive another. Therefore, the foot of the one whose affection is so entangled in a deceitful thought that he applies both pleasure and consent to carry out that wicked thought is caught in the snare.

And he rightly says “is caught,” for a fraudulent thought is like a certain bond and impediment of the soul, preventing it from attending to the truth.

“The Lord is known.” Now they are secretly caught; but eventually the Lord, who here and now performs hidden judgments, will reveal the one—that is, the fact—that the sinner has been caught in the works of his own hands: that the transgressor of the commandments is condemned by his own guilt, not by the Lord’s anger.

That Lord, I say, who now is not known, will eventually be known truly to be Lord, when they are openly handed over to the outer darkness. Hence it is said: “The impious does not know that he is being punished except when he openly pays the penalty for what he willingly committed.”

“Let sinners be turned in hell.” This can be read in two ways: either as rejoicing over the divine judgment or as compassion.

According to the interpretation of rejoicing, it will be understood as follows: Let the sinner who is unwilling to know the Lord, now caught through inner darkness—let this happen, namely, let condemned sinners be turned in inner blindness. That is, let them pass from the sins in which they now are into hell, that is, into the depth of vices, so that they may be completely deprived of the knowledge of God.

Hence it is said, “When the sinner has fallen into the depth, he will despise iniquities.” And because sinners are called transgressors of the law written for them, lest this be referred only to the Jews who possess the law, he adds: “Let all the nations be turned”—that is, all who live in a Gentile manner, who forget the God whom they know naturally through the reason given to them, because they do not wish to hear his commandments; or, if they hear them, neglect them.

And the whole meaning is this: Let it happen that those who are filthy become still filthier. For the more they become filthy—that is, the more they are handed over to inner darkness—the more wicked they will be against the just; and if anyone is just, he will become more just.

“For the poor man will not be forgotten to the end.” Therefore, I say, let sinners be turned into darkness, and let the one who is just become more just.

For the oblivion of the true poor man, who has impoverished himself in mind, although it now appears to exist—when the wicked flourish in worldly things while he, by contrast, withers—this oblivion, I say, will not extend to the end: that is, it will not be complete.

Or it will not exist “because the end will come”: that is, it will not appear when the final separation arrives, when the sheep will be separated from the goats and he himself will be placed at God’s right hand.

And truly there will not be oblivion to the end, because “the patience of the poor”—that is, the reward of the patience of the truly poor—although it now appears to have perished, will nevertheless not perish to the end: either completely, or when the end arrives, as was said above.

Hence it is said elsewhere, “Patience is necessary, so that we may receive the fruit.”

And so that it may not perish, rise up, Lord, in them: that is, make them rise through constancy and perseverance, so that they do not fail.

And let the human being—that is, some earthly person bearing the old human being, who wishes to make them fail—not be strengthened: that is, let him not prevail against them in the effectiveness of his small undertaking or purpose.

But let the nations—that is, those living irrationally and not attending to their sins—be judged: that is, let them be secretly condemned through blindness in your sight, not outwardly but inwardly in the heart, where you alone are permitted to see. This is so that, because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, as the Apostle says, they may be handed over to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting.

“Appoint, Lord.” It is as though he said: Once they have been judged, because they did not wish to have me, the bearer of your law, as their Head, appoint over them—that is, give them, for greater condemnation—a bearer of the law, an advocate and defender of his own law, not yours: the devil, or Antichrist, his messenger.

This is said concerning those who will obey his command in persecuting the Christian name when he comes, or even concerning any member of the devil among human beings who will make himself a head and give his own commands against the Christian name, as Nero, Diocletian, and other powerful persecutors of the Church did. Many people, consenting to their commands, subjected themselves to them.

For it is necessary, as though he said, that they be under some head. And because they did not wish to be under me, whom you made their Head, make them have the kind of head they deserved.

And therefore do this so that the nations—that is, those themselves who live in a Gentile manner without the law—when at last they withdraw from your presence into the outer darkness with their head, may know—that is, experience—“because [in place of ‘that’] they are human beings here, not sons of human beings.”

That is, they live according to the old human being, not the new.

Or, if “because” is understood causally, it will be said as follows: Let the nations at last know what it is fitting for nations to know. This will rightly happen because they are human beings here.

This has been said according to the interpretation in which the bearer of the law is understood as any member of the devil.

According to the interpretation concerning Antichrist, it will be understood as follows: Let the nations know that through that Antichrist they have become not gods but human beings: that is, they have not been exalted in virtues but plunged into vices, although he himself is exalted above everything called God or worshiped as God.

“Why, Lord?” Let the nations know in the future, when they withdraw from you, what they already knew beforehand: that they did not belong to you as those who reign in you, but remained human beings. You have truly withdrawn from them, although, because of their present prosperity, you appeared to have drawn near.

But let your own people, from whom you appear to have withdrawn because they wither in the present, know that you have not withdrawn from them. For that withdrawal was rather an approach, because through it you look toward their advantage.

For “why”—that is, for what other reason, if not for their advantage—have you withdrawn far away, that is, appeared to withdraw far from them? Truly it was for their advantage.

For although, when they are scourged, you appear to despise them, you do not truly despise them. You despise them only in tribulation, in times of opportunity—that is, where it is fitting—outwardly, as they are scourged, in appearance; yet inwardly you regard them through the constancy which you supply.

He says “in times of opportunity” in the plural because of the many outward attacks which the saints suffer, such as confiscation of property, scourging, burning, and other things of this kind.

While the wicked man exalts himself. Truly you do not despise them, because the more the wicked man—that is, any persecutor—exalts himself in the savagery of persecution, the more the true poor man whom the wicked persecutes is inflamed to love of the faith and to right living. Here blessed Augustine says: “It is remarkable, and yet true, with what zeal, by comparison with sinners, the poor man is inflamed toward right living.” The poor man, I say, is inflamed. But the wicked man, both head and members—for both are taken collectively in “the wicked man”—because they do not wish to make themselves poor, are seized, that is, condemned, by an interior blinding, not only in their deeds but also in the deceitful counsels which they contemplate carrying out.

These statements have been made according to the interpretation given above, in which any member of the devil is understood. But if the reference above is taken to be to the Antichrist, then “Why, O Lord,” which has just been read simply, will be an exhortation of the head, preparing and fortifying his members so that at the time of the Antichrist—of whom it is said, “And there will come a time such as there has not been,” and so forth—they may not fail because of his exceedingly severe persecution, but may remain steadfast and persevering, knowing that they have not then been abandoned by the Lord, although this may seem so because of the savagery of the tribulations.

For since two severe persecutions have already preceded in the Church, the first of which is signified by the lion, because it was violent—namely, because it was carried out by powerful tyrants who first attempted to destroy the Christian name—the second is signified by the serpent, because it was deceitful, having been carried out by heretics. Concerning them John says: “They went out from us, because they were not from us. For if they had been from us, they would not have gone out from us.” The persecution that will occur at the time of the Antichrist will be more severe, because it will be both deceitful and violent: violent because of his kingdom, since he will be a king; deceitful because of his miracles, and therefore exceedingly dangerous.

The continuation does not change in this interpretation. For it will be said as follows: “Let the nations subject to the Antichrist know that through him they have become not gods but human beings; but let your people know that you, who will seem at that time to have withdrawn from them because of the severity of the tribulation, have not withdrawn but rather have drawn near, as was said above. For while that wicked man, the Antichrist, exalts himself more by persecuting, the more the true poor man will be inflamed by patiently suffering for the good. But the Antichrist himself and his members will be seized, that is, condemned, in the counsels which they contemplate.”

All these things have now been read according to the rejoicing of God’s judgment. But the same words from “Let sinners be converted” may also be read up to this point as an expression of compassion, as was said above, so that it may be understood as follows:

Since wretched sinners, because here they do not attend to God’s hidden judgments, are seized by an interior blindness and are not converted, let them at least be converted by the activity of their minds as they go to hell—that is, by considering the outer darkness into which they will plainly be thrust. It is as though he said: If they do not fear the hidden judgment because they do not perceive it, let them at least fear the manifest judgment, which has truly been announced to them, and in this way let them be converted.

And rightly they ought to be converted on account of hell. For hell will truly be theirs, because a time will come when vengeance upon the wicked will be made manifest for the good. He says this as follows: “For the forgetfulness of the true poor man, who now, when he is persecuted by sinners, seems to have been forgotten, will not endure forever; nor will patience”—that is, the reward of the patience of those poor—“perish forever. Rather, they will truly be rewarded, and thus the savagery of those others will be condemned.”

Therefore, O Lord, so that they may be converted before they are condemned, rise up within them—that is, make your anger known to them—and let the old man—that is, sensuality—not be strengthened, that is, not prevail in them, but let the flesh be weakened and reason prevail. Thus let the nations—that is, those who previously lived irrationally—be judged by themselves, that is, let them become angry with themselves through remorse and repentance, and let this occur not carelessly outwardly but diligently inwardly, namely, in your sight, in the heart where you see.

And so that they may truly be judged, O Lord Father, appoint me as the bearer of your law over them—that is, subject them to me—so that those who previously departed from you through pride may return to you through obedience. Appoint me, I say, so that those who were previously nations may know from my example that they are human beings—that is, rational beings—and may perceive for what they were created: namely, to serve as servants, not to exalt themselves as lords; and so that they may not claim to depend upon themselves, but may recognize that they are your creature.

Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away? As though he said: Since you, O Lord, were going to draw near to them by rising up within them and appointing me over them, why—that is, for what reason—did you previously withdraw far away, allowing them to fall into sins? As though he said: You did this for their benefit. Hence it is said: “For those who love God all things work together for good,” and so forth.

And truly you departed for their benefit, because you often despise those whom you have purposed to save in tribulation—that is, when the soul is afflicted by vices. For just as the body is afflicted by scourges, so the soul is afflicted by vices. Hence it is said: “Tribulation and distress upon every soul of man who works evil.” And you do this in opportunities—that is, for the sake of the many benefits which they gain from it. For often the fall of one becomes the cause of the resurrection of many sinners.

So it was with David, because after he had fallen into adultery and murder, once he recognized himself and was led by profound repentance, he rose perfectly from the fall into many vices. It was also greatly beneficial to Peter that he denied the Lord at the voice of a single maidservant, because through this he rose perfectly, if there had been any fall in him, and afterward became more steadfast. So it is with the others.

While the wicked man exalts himself. Truly you appropriately despise him in tribulation, because to the extent that someone, remaining wicked, exalts himself by sinning, to that same extent, once he has become poor—that is, after his conversion—he is inflamed by a good life in humbling himself. This is plainly evident in Paul. Although he was foremost among the apostles, nevertheless, recalling his innumerable previous falls, he said: “For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle.”

The poor man is indeed inflamed; but those who do not become poor and remain wicked are seized more and more by an interior blindness, not only in their deeds but also in their counsels, by which—that is, through which—they contemplate deceiving others. Nor is it surprising that they are seized, since, for the greater accumulation of their condemnation, flatterers are present with them. When these men praise the evil things which the others desire in their hearts, they bind them in their sins. Hence it is said: “The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins.”

The passage is found in the book as follows: “For the sinner is praised by flatterers in the evil desires of his soul.” And not only the sinner—that is, the transgressor of the written law—but also every unrighteous man “will be blessed,” that is, praised by his flatterers in his evil desires, in which he ought not to be congratulated.

Blessed Augustine says: “Let no one congratulate a man who prospers in his evil way, whose sin lacks an avenger but has a flatterer present. For by this God becomes even more angry with him.”

The book says this as follows: “While the sinner is praised by the flatterer, he embittered”—that is, made the Lord exceedingly bitter and harsh toward himself—to such an extent that he cannot taste his sweetness. Hence blessed Augustine says: “He makes the Lord bitter toward himself who, by sinning, falls into such weakness that he cannot taste the food of truth in which healthy souls rejoice.”

And because he has embittered the Lord—that is, he will not seek him—or the sinner himself will not seek him, that is, will neglect the Lord—“according to the multitude of his anger”: either the Lord’s anger, because the Lord has become angry with him in many ways, or the sinner’s anger, because the sinner himself has acquired great anger from the Lord.

God is not in his sight. Therefore the sinner will not seek the Lord, because he does not attend to the fact that there is a judge in the affairs of the world. Or the Lord will not seek him because he is not regarded by him. For he is not present in his sight through attention—that is, in the heart of that sinner, where God sees what he reveals through its effect—because his ways, that is, the works of that sinner, are polluted, that is, ineffective, not merely for a time but throughout the whole period of his life. This would not be so if he attended to the presence of a just judge in the affairs of the world. Since he does not attend to him, it is evident that the Lord has truly become embittered against him.

Your judgments are removed. Therefore God is not in his sight because your judgments, O Lord—both those which you now carry out secretly and those which you will finally carry out openly—are removed from his face, that is, from his knowledge. He neither attends to the present hidden judgment nor fears the future manifest judgment. And this is because he will be condemned here among all his external enemies. As though he said: He prospers in all external matters.

For he said in his heart. He shows by effect, from particular instances, that the sinner truly does not attend to God’s judgments, because he thinks evil, speaks vainly, and acts perversely. From his thought he begins by saying this:

“The sinner said in his heart”—that is, while thinking—“I shall not be moved from my evil purpose,” that is, “I shall always act wickedly, because just as I am in this generation without misfortune, so I shall also pass from this generation into the future generation without misfortune,” that is, “I shall suffer no punishment for my sins in the future.”

Or otherwise: The wicked man said in his heart—understand, “I shall act wickedly with perseverance”—“I shall not be moved,” that is, “I shall not be advanced by reputation from this generation into a later generation without misfortune,” that is, “unless I commit some grave evil through which I may acquire fame.”

An example of this may be Herod, the slaughterer of the innocents. When he was near death and knew that he was hated by everyone, he had fifty of the best men in all Israel imprisoned and ordered them to be killed at his death, so that when many people wept over their slaughter, they might appear to be weeping over his death.

His mouth is full of cursing. That is, the mouth of the man who thinks such evil also speaks evil, because it is full of cursing—that is, blasphemy and detraction against God and the saints. Therefore it is full of bitterness, that is, he makes God wholly bitter and harsh toward himself. It is also full of deceit against his neighbor, because he always strives to deal deceitfully with his neighbor. This is because labor and pain are only beneath his tongue—that is, because he deals only with earthly things, which are labor in acquiring and pain in losing—so that in these matters he may act deceitfully toward his neighbor beneath his tongue, that is, in his thought, which is beneath the tongue because it precedes words.

Hence Horace:
