> Afterwards he brings forth other emotions through the tongue as interpreter.

He not only thinks and speaks evil but also acts evil, as though he said—or as though he were saying it in this way:

“He sits in ambush,” that is, with delay and painstaking cunning he occupies himself with deceptions, “with the rich,” that is, with lovers of this age who have not made themselves poor in mind. He does this first in secret, deceiving them by flatteries, in order to kill the innocent—that is, to draw the innocent away from his innocence and, by conforming him to himself, make him guilty.

I say “the innocent” because his eyes, that is, all his affections, look toward the poor man—that is, toward the innocent man who has made himself poor in soul—in order to deceive him.

Or this may have been said by way of comparison, because a person who passes by and looks toward him seems to be moved by compassion for him. Accordingly it may be understood as follows: “He truly strives to kill the innocent, because his eyes look toward him as toward a poor man,” that is, he displays a kind of deceptive compassion in order to deceive him.

So one reads in the passions of the saints about certain tyrants who, as though moved by compassion, said to those whom they wished to draw away: “My son, consider your nobility; consider your youth,” and other such things, so that they might deceive them secretly.

He repeats what he said above, “He sits in ambush,” equivalently, in order to add another aspect of deception. For those who draw others away sometimes use deceitful deception, which has already been mentioned; at other times they use violent means inflicted through tortures. Concerning this he adds, saying:

“He lies in wait for the poor man, looking secretly toward him if he can,” that is, in concealment. But if he cannot do so secretly, “he becomes like a lion,” that is, he inflicts violence openly. And again, “If he cannot do this, he becomes like a serpent in its cave,” that is, he returns to deceiving secretly.

He lies in wait, I say, “to seize the poor man,” that is, to draw the poor man away. By “seizing the poor man” I mean that he attracts him into his own sect by conforming him to himself. And he truly attracts him because he humiliates him, that is, turns the poor man aside toward his own party, “in his snare,” that is, through his secret or violent deception.

This harms him more than it benefits him, because by humiliating the other he inclines himself, that is, prepares himself for destruction. “And he will fall,” that is, he will suffer a grievous fall: he will incur irremediable eternal death in his soul when he has gained dominion over the poor, that is, when he thinks himself victorious because he has completely subjected some poor men to himself by imposing his sect upon them.

For he said in his heart. He sets forth the manner of his fall. As though he said: He will truly fall. For he will fall in this way, because he will deny the true judge in the affairs of the world. I do not say that he will say it later; he has already said it in his heart, as is shown by his effect, since he acts wickedly in every way:

“God has forgotten earthly things, and he has turned his face away forever,” that is, altogether, so as not to see these things.

Or otherwise: “He has turned his face away so that he may not see,” with this as the purpose. There are two ends of God’s kingdom, the higher and the lower. Hence it is said: “Reaching from end to end mightily.” The higher end is where the celestial creatures are above; the lower end is where the earth is the lowest element, together with the things that are of the earth.

Some erroneous thinkers held that God, because he possessed such great majesty, would never deign to bend down to inspect or govern this lower end. This is plainly false, because otherwise all things would drift about at random by chance.

Rise up, O Lord. Up to this point he has dealt chiefly with the hidden judgment; now he begins to deal with the manifest judgment, so that through its opposite we may see the hidden judgment more clearly. Nevertheless, the whole psalm is entitled as concerning hidden things because of the greater and more worthy portion, in which he chiefly treats of those hidden things.

The continuation is as follows: Many say that God has forgotten earthly things. But you, O Lord God, who now lie low before them because they do not consider your hidden disposition and your judgment, rise up—that is, appear exalted to them in your manifest judgment—and let your hand be exalted. That is, let me, whom you sent to defeat the powers of the air, first sent in humility, be exalted when sent to judge in majesty, with a multitude of angels and saints.

Let this be done so that you may not forget the poor—that is, so that you may then show that you have not forgotten the poor, as the wicked assert, by taking the poor into glory and sending the wicked into Gehenna.

And you ought to rise up, for they have provoked you without cause. For what reason—that is, for what cause—did the wicked man provoke God? As though he said: He had rather a reason not to provoke than to provoke, since he saw that all things were arranged in a certain order.

He repeats the provocation itself in order to destroy it, saying: “For the wicked man said in his heart, ‘God will not inquire into the things we do.’” But he lies, because you see—that is, you will inquire—since even now, in the present, you consider the labor, that is, the zeal of those who inflict evils upon your poor, and the pain of those who endure them. Yet you delay vengeance so that at last you may deliver them—that is, the wicked—into your hands, in order to exercise manifest power over them at the final separation, when those whom the delay of their deserved punishment does not move to repentance will be delivered over.

Hence the Apostle says to the unrepentant wicked man: “Do you not know that God’s patience is calling you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart you are storing up wrath for yourself.”

The poor man is abandoned to you. Rightly you consider the poor man’s cause, since he does not consider himself. For the poor man himself has been abandoned by himself to you—that is, he has renounced himself and the world for your sake—and therefore you will be his helper, since for your sake he has been made an orphan.

Properly speaking, an orphan is one who lacks a father during the years of childhood. Nevertheless, by analogy anyone who renounces himself for God is called an orphan, because he has now been stripped of his former father: the world, according to which he was begotten carnally, and the devil, who begot him in carnal desires. Hence it is said: “You are from your father the devil.”

And just as it is especially the duty of a judge to undertake the case of those who lack their own advocate, namely, orphans and widows, so it belongs to God, who is the true judge, to undertake the case of his orphans.

Break the arm. Because you are the arm of the sinner, therefore, O Lord, destroy the arm—that is, the power—of the sinner, that is, of the transgressor and every wicked person, so that he may not be able to afflict or draw away the poor man.

And you will truly break it, because his sin will be sought in the manifest judgment, to see what place it has, and its place will not be found. As though he said: Let it now be supposed that someone passes over through the activity of his mind to consider the manifest judgment and inquires whether sin still has its former place. He will find that it lacks a place.

In the present, while the wicked are mixed with the good, sin has a place, because the wicked man lives alongside the devout. But just as a file has no place once iron has been smoothed, and a furnace has no place once gold has been purified, so at the final separation there will be no place for sin. For when perfect and unchangeable righteousness has come to exist in all the good, nothing will remain in them that requires further purification.

Sin will nevertheless exist in another way. For just as the patience of the poor will not perish with respect to its reward, so the sins of the wicked will not perish with respect to eternal condemnation.

The Lord will reign forever. There truly will be no place for sin, because the Lord, who now reigns in those who are changeable in some way—for no one is so perfect that he does not sometimes fall in the smallest matter—will then reign forever.

Hence Horace:

> That one is best  
> Who is burdened by the smallest things.

The Lord, I say, will then reign forever, that is, in those who will truly be eternal and will no longer fear any change. And he defines “forever,” saying: “And for age upon age.”

But you who now live in vices like the nations will then perish, eternally separated from his earth—that is, from those who, although previously earth, have become his worthy possession. And you will truly perish, because then that will be fulfilled for which the poor sigh with their whole desire. There will be an eternal division between the good and the wicked.

He says this as follows: “The Lord has heard,” that is, he will then show that he has heard the desire of the poor here, fulfilling it. And because “desire” may also be understood as words of prayer, he adds more by turning himself toward the Lord when he says:

“Your ear”—that is, the power of hearing which is in you, O Lord, who are wholly ear and wholly eye, and other such things—“that ear, I say, has heard,” that is, it will then show that it has heard “the preparation of their heart,” that is, their good affection, which makes their heart very prepared and attentive.

And what that desire is, he makes clear: “To judge the orphan and the humble,” that is, so that you may make a judgment—that is, a separation—between the good and the wicked, for the benefit of the one who, by putting to death for himself the father that is the world or the devil, has made himself an orphan.

And he did this not out of arrogance, as Diogenes renounced the world in order to be seen by human beings, but for the sake of benefit, namely, so that he might obey your commandments.

And to this end, so that the one who is merely a man, still imbued with the old dregs, who in this life first set himself to iniquity and then added the same iniquity along with others, persuaded others so to magnify himself—that is, to make a great name for himself—may no longer be able to add to that former position in order to magnify himself over the earth—that is, over your people, who will then be stable and solid like earth.

## INTO PSALM X  
A Psalm of David, “For the End.”

### ARGUMENT

The words of David when, fleeing from Saul, he was compelled to live in the deserts. Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ. Read in Genesis: the destruction of Sodom.

### EXPLANATION

The end always directs attention toward Christ, but sometimes it signifies his passion and sometimes his resurrection. Now it declares the holy faith, in which heretics fight against the most faithful Christians. It must therefore be understood that this psalm was uttered for the destruction of heretics.

This entire psalm is to be referred to the person of the prophet. In the first section he speaks of the heretical plotters who strive to convert Catholics to their own depravity. In the second he threatens the Lord’s judgment and clearly shows what they may suffer in that retribution, so that, fearing the Lord’s justice, they may abandon their superstitious falsehoods.

### COMMENTARY

“In the Lord I trust”—how is this said to my soul? This psalm is entitled as follows: “For the End, a Psalm belonging to David.” This is explained in this way: The following words, which are a psalm because they instruct toward the praise of God, are attributed to David himself, or to the prophet himself, or to some more perfect person from the earlier people, or to someone from the later people exhorting others to beware of the leaven of heretics.

These words are referred to the end because they were spoken concerning things that were going to happen at the end of time, that is, in the fullness of time, namely, in the time of the Church.

This psalm speaks against heretics because the prophet—or any perfect person whose voice is heard in this psalm—foresaw that certain pestilential men would arise from the body of Christ, that is, from the Church, asserting that they alone were righteous and true worshipers of Christ. “They went out from us, because they were not from us.” They will strive to separate many from the breasts of holy mother Church and draw them into their sect, saying that they themselves are on the mountain, that is, in the eminence of virtues, while others are in the valley, that is, in the lowliness of vices.

Therefore they confidently admonish them as follows: “Come over to us, who are in higher places; adhere to us. Behold, Christ is with us.”

Sacred Scripture calls this Christ by various names: at one time a lion, at another a mountain, and so forth. Foreseeing this, he instructs us in this psalm what answer we should give when they deceive us and how we ought to remain in purity and sincerity of faith.

It is as though he said: Certain stiff-necked bulls are going to appear—that is, heretics—asserting their error through arrogance, not through ignorance. For arrogance makes a heretic, not ignorance. They will say to us: “Come over to us, to the mountain. Behold, Christ is with us.”

You will answer them in this way, each one for himself: “I hold to one mountain. I trust in the Lord, who is the mountain of mountains. How then do you say”—that is, with what confidence do you dare to say—“to my soul, ‘Move over to the mountain’”? That is, “Leave the valley of humility in which you are and add our eminence,” when you are rather the lowest of all.

I speak to my soul which is like a sparrow—that is, cautious of snares and winged with virtues and divine commandments—and which has already found for itself a secure dwelling, that is, ecclesiastical institutions. Your efforts are therefore in vain.

Or it may also be said in this way: When you say such things, you suppose that my soul is fickle and unstable like a sparrow. It certainly is not.

I speak to you who, in order to persuade others of your error and commend yourselves, exaggerate the sins of others and accuse true teachers, saying to me: “You truly ought to come over to us, because the sinners”—that is, transgressors of the written law—“whom you follow have bent the bow,” that is, have strained divine Scripture greatly through their perverse temptations.

“Behold”—that is, it is manifest—“they have prepared their arrows by bending them,” that is, deceitful and deceptive opinions, “in the quiver,” that is, secretly in their hearts, “so that they may shoot,” that is, secretly deceive “the upright in heart,” that is, good people who are not cautious and prudent, such as we are, but who are still placed in darkness—that is, not yet exalted—as you, in your simplicity, are.

For they destroyed what you established. Therefore, you most wicked heretics, impose this upon the good because you yourselves have done it: through your perverse interpretations you have corrupted holy Scripture.

He says this by turning toward the Lord: “O Lord, the heretics have wickedly destroyed what you established by interpreting it falsely,” that is, the Scriptures which you brought forth through your men filled with the Holy Spirit.

Then he turns again to the heretics, as though saying: “You heretics have destroyed the work of the Lord, but you ought not to have done so, because the righteous”—that is, Christ, who is to be called simply “the righteous”—“who left unity and concord to his own, said: ‘My peace I leave you; my peace I give you.’”

He also endured his betrayer with such patience that he gave him, together with the other disciples, the first Eucharist, prepared by his own hands and commended by his own mouth. He even sent him with the others to preach the kingdom of heaven, to demonstrate that the gifts of God reach those who receive them with faith, even if the one through whom they are received is such as Judas himself was.

That righteous one, I say, did this for you—that is, earned this from you—and because of it you, by corrupting the Scriptures, have destroyed the unity which he himself left.

The Lord is in his holy temple. The righteous man did nothing against you, but he himself does this: he mercifully saves his own, and he not only permits the wicked, because of their evil intention to ascend to the Scriptures so that they may be condemned from them, to understand them perversely; he also permits their perverse teaching to advance toward the condemnation of many.

He indicates this where he says: “He rains snares upon sinners.” The nominative placed here, namely “the Lord,” governs this expression.

He first inserts a statement about the salvation of the good, and then one about the condemnation of the wicked in themselves, saying:

“The Lord”—he says simply “the Lord”—that is, Christ, the true Lord, “is in his temple,” that is, in the faithful who are his temple through the unity of faith. Concerning this temple it is said: “The temple of God is holy, which you are.” And again: “Whoever violates the temple of the Lord, God will destroy him.”

He violates the temple of God—that is, violates unity—who, for the sake of his own primacy, separates himself from Catholic unity, as do those who, out of arrogance, strive to establish against the common faith what they understand perversely: namely, heretics.

He defines which temple he means, saying: “His seat is in heaven,” that is, in those who have been made heaven from earthly beings. Hence it is said: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” And again: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet.” They are heaven not through their own merits but through the regard of his mercy.

He says this as follows: “His eyes look toward the poor man.” Just as someone who, after passing by a poor man, turns his eyes back toward him seems to be moved by compassion for him, so God shows the regard of his mercy toward his poor man whom he is going to save.

He looks toward the poor man in this way because “his eyelids question the sons of men.” Although “sons” may be understood of both the good and the wicked, here, according to blessed Augustine, since the reference is to the poor, we shall understand “sons of men” as those whom the old man brings forth, with groaning and pain, into the new man—that is, those who through repentance of the old man have been regenerated into the new man.

These sons of men are exercised by certain obscure passages of Scripture, as though God’s eyes were closed, so that they may seek; but by certain manifest passages of Scripture they are illuminated so that they may see.

This frequent opening and closing in the Scriptures is like God’s eyelids, closing and opening the Scriptures, just as eyelids close and open the eyes. Concerning these Scriptures it is said elsewhere: “For this reason they are covered, lest they become worthless; for this purpose they are opened, that they may nourish.”

These eyelids—that is, the obscurities and openings of the Scriptures—question, that is, test, those sons of men whom we have mentioned. They test them in this way: they are not worn out by the obscurities of Scripture and rejected, but are exercised so that they may seek; nor are they puffed up by knowledge of the Scriptures, but are strengthened.

By contrast, the wicked are rejected by the obscurities and are not exercised; they are puffed up by knowledge and are not strengthened. In this both groups are rightly tested.

For just as a master, excluding his servants from his secret counsel, tests those whom he later wishes to admit—namely, those who bear their rejection patiently—and also tests those whom he will reject, namely, those who do not bear it patiently but become indignant, and who attribute the fact that they were once admitted not to the master’s grace but to their own arrogance, so the Lord, through his eyelids—that is, through the obscurities of his Scriptures—tests his own and also tests those who are not his.

The Lord questions the righteous and the wicked. He shows which sons of men he has understood here, and this is a proof from equals: that the Lord truly questions the sons of men through his eyelids. For he questions—that is, tests—the righteous, that is, the poor man, as was said above; and he also questions—that is, tests—the wicked. Here he adds something concerning the evil.

Here we shall understand as poor those who, after receiving the faith, have become corrupt—that is, heretics. The Lord tests them for their condemnation through his eyelids, because, worn out by obscurities, they are rejected; puffed up by knowledge, they are not strengthened.

Therefore they are blinded by the Lord, so that they both understand the Scriptures perversely and are condemned, and, by interpreting them perversely for others who deserve it, condemn those others along with themselves.

But he who loves iniquity. We must understand, beyond what is stated, that the righteous man, when questioned by the Lord, answers more justly according to his capacity. But the man who loves iniquity—that is, the corrupt man—hates his own soul. He gives such an answer, if not in words, at least in action, in which he shows that he hates his own soul: he is rejected by obscurity and puffed up by ambition.

Therefore the Lord condemns not only him but also others through him. He says this, now at last introducing the person of the higher nominative:

“The Lord rains,” that is, through the rain of the wicked’s evil teaching, “upon sinners,” who have evidently deserved it. He sends snares, that is, many impediments of falsehood, so that they cannot attend to the truth.

He shows what those snares are through the following: “The portion of their cup.” That is, what those sinners receive, in a certain measure, from the wicked’s perverse teaching. Division is made through a cup, and therefore the cup is placed here as a measure whose quantity is known, so that they may know that nothing occurs without order or measure, even in the condemnation of the wicked.

For although God did not create darkness, he nevertheless ordered it. Hence it is said: “God divided the light from the darkness.”

That portion, I say, is “fire,” by which they are first devastated through the incitements of carnal desires. From that fire proceeds “brimstone,” that is, the stench of evil works, by which the good themselves are separated from the wicked. And thus follows “the spirit of storms,” that is, a grievous swallowing up in destruction, when at the end they will be thrust into ineffable punishments.

It must be known that all interpreters of the Scriptures, whether good or evil, may be called clouds—that is, rainers together—because they rain upon others, as it were, through their good or evil teaching.

Hence the Lord says to the righteous heralds of truth: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon that prostitute,” which was said concerning Judea and Jerusalem.

And from the same Scripture the Lord rains through good teachers the latter rain—that is, timely and fruitful teaching—upon good earth, that is, upon the good; and through heretics he rains harmful rain, that is, pestilential teaching, upon the wicked. From the same material rain, wheat is produced for fine flour, and darnel for burning.

For the Lord is righteous. Above he said, “And the Lord saves the righteous,” where he stated that he sits in them; and he said that he condemns the wicked, where he stated: “The unrighteous man hates his own soul,” and, “He rains upon sinners,” and so forth.

Now he gives the reason for both. As though he said: The Lord saves the righteous because he himself, who is truly righteous, loves righteousnesses—that is, each of the righteous. But he condemns the wicked because his face—that is, the expression and severity of his countenance—saw this to be equity, that is, just.

## INTO PSALM XI  
A Psalm of David, “For the End, for the Eighth Day.”

### ARGUMENT

It is sung from the person of David that in his time every holy person had failed and the truths among the sons of men had been diminished. Alternatively, Christ speaks on behalf of his suffering people about the Jews. Read in Luke.

Alternatively, this psalm is written for the eighth day, that is, for the Lord’s Day of Christ’s resurrection, when faith failed and the truths were diminished, so that they even offered money to the guards of the body; but the Lord destroyed their deceitful lips.

### EXPLANATION
The eighth, as has already been said in the sixth psalm, pertains to eternal rest. For this world does not receive the eighth day; rather, when the seventh has ended, it always returns to the first. The prophet therefore asks that the wickedness of this world be destroyed, so that one may attain that truth of the future promise. And rightly is the eighth day fitted to this psalm, in which the vicious custom of this age is abandoned and the coming of that innocence is requested.

In the first part, the prophet asks to be rescued from the perversity of this world, since the deceitful and proud were denying the Lord’s power through criminal slanders. In the second, he proclaims that the Father’s promise is to be fulfilled through the almighty Son, praising the Lord’s utterances in concise form, just as earlier he had rebuked impious speeches.

## COMMENTARY

### Save me, O Lord

[Col. 0547C] This psalm is the voice of the prophet David—or of any of the perfected from the earlier people who awaited and worked for the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ—through whom they understood that true salvation would come to the world. It had indeed been prefigured in carnal things, but was to come in the time of fulfillment, that is, at Christ’s coming, when the shadow withdrew and the truth succeeded it.

Because these faithful, through the Holy Spirit and within the carnal institutions, truly recognized that future reality, they intend in this psalm to exhort and console their contemporaries, so that they may believe with them that it would truly come and may long for its arrival with every desire. They also intend to exhort those who would come after his advent, as we do, so that they may understand and embrace it with complete devotion as something already past.

For blessed Augustine says: “Those were signs, and these too are signs: those of future things, these of past things.” Therefore, just as they understood salvation as coming through carnal things, so we must understand it through the mystical spiritual realities now taking place among us as though it had already come.

[Col. 0547D] Accordingly, this psalm is entitled: “For the end, a psalm for the eighth, to David,” whether to the prophet or to some more perfect person from the earlier people who, through carnal institutions, understood the spiritual things that were to come—that is, those striving toward the end, desiring the end to come, namely, the fullness of time.

I say that the psalm is “for the eighth,” that is, for the true salvation and rest that was bestowed at Christ’s coming and is to be desired. It is called the eighth because, after the changing variety of temporal things—which are represented by the number seven, since they revolve through seven days—the eighth day will begin. Night will never interrupt it. That is, then that true salvation, by which we now rest in hope through the Lord’s coming, will openly appear in truth. Hence the Apostle says: “For in hope we have been saved.”

Let us now approach the literal meaning. The prophet—or any perfected person from the earlier people, whose voice is heard in this psalm—desiring the coming of true salvation, prays as follows:

[Col. 0548A] “Lord Father, because I am awaiting the medicine I need and desiring it, save me”—that is, send the one whom you are going to send, the Holy of holies, the God of gods—“through whom true salvation may come to me, and through whom health that has been destroyed may be restored.”

I truly need this salvation, because “the holy one has failed,” that is, holiness has perished in the first holy one whom you sent, namely Adam, whom God placed before the fall in the fullness of virtues, and through him in me. Holiness therefore failed because the first human beings and their descendants withdrew from your commandments. Thus he says: “For the truths have been diminished among the children of men.”

Here he speaks of “truths,” just as above he spoke of “justices,” with respect to individual persons, although there is one true justice and truth from which all are illumined. For God is the one truth, who says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” His commandments too are truth, making those who fulfill them true. When the first parents withdrew from these commandments, and afterward their children through the guilt of their parents, truths were diminished in each individual.

### They have spoken vanity

[Col. 0548B] The truths have truly been diminished because vanities have multiplied. For each person—that is, individual human beings—has spoken vanity within himself, placing confidence in earthly things through his actions. They made those things, which are vanity of vanities, their reliance and neglected God.

And they spoke vanity not only within themselves but also to their neighbor—namely, so that whoever hates God might also hate his neighbor, just as, conversely, whoever loves God also loves his neighbor. To speak vanity to one’s neighbor is to persuade him to pursue earthly things, which are truly vanity, and to love and desire them.

They did this by example and by speech. They had “deceitful lips,” that is, deception in their words for the purpose of misleading their neighbor, because “they spoke with heart and heart,” that is, not with a simple heart but with a divided one. He does not say that they spoke with “heart and heart” because they had several material hearts—for each person has only one heart—but because of their different intentions: they displayed one intention in their words and held another in their minds. Thus acts everyone who has one thing ready on his tongue and another hidden [Col. 0548C] in his breast.

### May the Lord destroy them

This is not a curse but rejoicing in divine judgment. It is as though he said: “Because they destroy truth and act deceitfully with their neighbor, let what they deserve happen to them—namely, may the Lord destroy by eternal condemnation those who may emphatically be called deceitful lips themselves because of their excessive deceit.”

And may he destroy them not in part but entirely, so that you may think nothing excepted. May he also destroy “the boastful tongue,” that is, the proud-speaking tongue.

He likewise calls heretics and their imitators “the boastful tongue” emphatically. They attempt to establish, to the ruin of others, the cause of primacy, which they have perversely understood. He identifies them by saying that they do not merely say, but have always said, whether in their hearts or in their actions:

“Our tongue”—that is, the opinions that we possess by our own interpretation, with no one revealing them to us, neither God nor human being—“we shall magnify,” that is, we shall assert them for our own glorification; “because our lips”—that is, our eloquence—“are from us,” that is, on our side [Col. 0548D], since it defends and commends us.

Or, “our lips are from us,” that is, we ourselves possess them, and no one else has taught them to us. “Who, then, is our lord? What, therefore, did Jerome, Augustine, or any teacher contribute to us, when we have everything from ourselves?”

The perfected soul from the earlier people says this prophetically, as though placing itself in the time of the heretics. With reference to earlier times, it may also be applied to the scribes and Pharisees, who attributed nothing to Moses or to the other prophets but arrogated everything to themselves.

The earlier “may he destroy” may also be read in a good sense as an expression of rejoicing, as we have already explained in other similar passages.

### Because of the misery

The perfected soul, which earlier desired salvation, now shows itself certain of the coming of that true salvation, so that it may exhort its contemporaries to desire and truly hope for it, and later people [Col. 0549A] to receive with joy the salvation that truly came.

It is as though it said: “The Lord will truly save me, because the Lord Father says”—that is, he has ordained—“Now I shall arise.” For God’s saying is his ordaining.

“I”—who earlier rose humbly in the servants sent to the vineyard, namely, in the patriarchs and prophets, one of whom they stoned, another scourged, another killed, and so on—“shall now arise openly in the Son.” For “they will reverence the Son.”

“And I shall do this because of the misery of the poor,” that is, because of the misery that the needy suffer in body or soul through the punishment of the first sin, which is to be taken away; “and because of the groaning of the poor,” that is, the groaning which the poor utter on account of that misery and which is to be consoled. Hence it is said: “I have seen the affliction of my people,” and so forth.

Here he calls “the needy” those who do not regard themselves as sufficient for true salvation through carnal observances or through free will, without the true salvation bestowed through our Lord Jesus Christ. This applies to the earlier people.

With reference to us, the needy may be said to be those [Col. 0549B] who consider themselves sufficient neither through free will nor through any merits of their own, but place all their hope in that salvation.

The poor, however, are all those who, recognizing this neediness, relate themselves to the one through whom need is driven away with the kind of affection with which certain worldly poor relate themselves to the rich: they kiss their hands, follow them humbly, and do other such things.

### I will place him in your salvation

“I shall truly arise now, because I shall place”—in my salvation, through which I shall arise, namely, in the Son—“that which must be placed in salvation,” so that he may take away misery and console groaning.

And I, who earlier acted uncertainly in the servants, shall act confidently in him, both in words and in deeds.

He truly acted confidently in words. Hence it is said: “Never has anyone spoken as this man speaks.” And again: “He was speaking as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees.”

He also acted sufficiently confidently in deeds when, having made a whip of cords, he drove the large crowd, together with the rulers and priests, out of the temple. [Col. 0549C]

He also acted confidently through him with respect to others, when through him he established people such as the Apostle describes when he says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” and so forth.

### The Lord’s utterances are pure

The two preceding verses are read as spoken in the Father’s voice. The words that follow, however, are read as spoken in the voice of the prophet or of the perfected soul.

It is as though he said: “God the Father will truly act confidently in him, because the utterances of that Lord”—that is, of Christ—“will be pure utterances,” that is, unchanging. What they approve once, they will never disapprove; what they deny once, they will never affirm. In this they will be comparable to a chaste woman, who presents herself the same way in her husband’s presence and absence.

Or they will be “pure,” that is, free from the reproach of pretense and not unchaste, because they will proclaim nothing for earthly profit, as certain hypocrites do. The Apostle speaks of them: “Some preach Christ not purely.” Those preach not purely who preach not for spiritual benefit [Col. 0549D] but for earthly profit, pretending that piety is a source of gain.

They will therefore be pure in such a way that they will be “silver tested by fire,” that is, bright like silver reheated by fire; “tested for the earth,” that is, entirely free from earthly dross; and “purified sevenfold,” that is, purified in many ways.

Or otherwise: the Lord’s utterances will not be uncertain—that is, they will not produce impurity—as were the utterances of the servant, Moses, who, because of their hardness, permitted the Jews to divorce their wives whenever they wished or to marry others. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Moses permitted you, because of the hardness of your hearts, to divorce your wives and to send a writ of dismissal. But I say to you: Whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another commits adultery.”

The Lord’s utterances, I say, will not be unchaste but pure—that is, making people chaste—and making them so chaste that, like silver tested by fire, they will be comparable to silver thoroughly purified by fire. Thus, just as silver, when beaten, does not split—that is, does not break apart [Col. 0550A]—but grows in length and breadth, so those purified by fire, by tribulation, beaten by scourges and other extraordinary means, will not split—that is, will not fail—but will grow in length through firm perseverance and in breadth by extending their love even to their enemies.

Thus acted the one who said on behalf of those stoning him: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”

And they will be “tested for the earth,” that is, through confession of the Trinity; and “repurified,” that is, perfectly purified; “sevenfold,” that is, through the grace of the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit.

The needy and the poor—those who understand these utterances spiritually and do not cling to the letter alone—will adhere to such utterances.

The impious, however—that is, the prosperous and rich, who believe themselves sufficient for true salvation through both free will and their own merits—will not adhere to these utterances. For they “walk in a circuit,” that is, they cling only to the letter and recoil from grace, namely, from spiritual understanding.

They therefore “walk in a circuit,” [Col. 0550B] that is, they delight and prosper in earthly things, which are a circuit because they continually revolve through the sevenfold number of the ages. Those who delight only in these things do not attain true goods.

And from this wayward generation—that is, from those who walk in a circuit—you, Lord Father, will save us, so that they may not conform us to themselves. You will preserve us by leading us through perseverance into eternity, that is, into true and eternal salvation, which was called the eighth in the title.

And you will truly preserve us, because just as those who walk in a circuit have multiplied from the fruit of their grain and oil—that is, in earthly things—so you have multiplied, that is, enriched in many ways, the true children of human beings, namely those regenerated into the new human being.

And you have done this according to your height, that is, in accordance with what befits your majesty: you have enlarged them not in vanities but in virtues, so that they may ascend from virtue to virtue until the God of gods is seen in Zion, and thus they may receive the eighth, that is, true salvation.

Or otherwise, as though someone were to say: “If this generation is impious and walks in a circuit [Col. 0550C], why, then, are they born? Why, then, do they survive?”

To this the prophet, or the perfected soul, responds: “O Lord, you have multiplied the number of the earthly children of human beings, that is, of earthly parents, according to the height of your incomprehensible plan.” Hence it is said: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God,” and so forth.

# PSALM XII

*For the end, a psalm of David*

## ARGUMENT

The prayers of Hezekiah, besieged by the Assyrians. Alternatively, the voice of Christ to the Father; in Mark he speaks about the devil.

## EXPLANATION

The whole psalm speaks about the love of the Lord Christ, as the prophet looks upon nearly the entire world enslaved to idolatry.

In the first part, he asks that his faith be fulfilled through the coming of the holy Incarnation, so that in this way at least the Gentiles, brought to confusion [Col. 0550D], might recognize their Creator.

In the second, he urgently asks that the Lord’s face be illumined in order effectively to instruct our petitions, lest he succumb through any deception of the enemy, although he always says that he has trusted in the Lord’s mercy.

## COMMENTARY

### How long, O Lord?

The voice in this psalm is that of the prophet, or of any perfected soul, whether from the earlier or the later people, longing and groaning to come to that true contemplation and perfect knowledge which will exist only when Christ is all in all; when, seeing face to face, we shall know perfectly even as we have been known; and when the last death will be destroyed and its sting—that is, sin—will perish.

In this psalm the perfected soul presents itself to others as an example through its longing, so that it may instruct them how greatly and with what desire they ought to groan and sigh, in order that, removed from this mire [Col. 0551A], they may reach that true vision which knows no darkness.

In this sense the psalm properly concerns those who say with the Apostle: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ.” And just as the preceding psalm treated the first coming, so this one treats the second.

It may also be understood in another way. The perfected soul—or the prophet—placed in the tribulation and turmoil of this life, where it is shaken as though by surrounding winds amid storms of vices, fears that, just as through the first parent it has already partly incurred the loss of understanding truth, so amid so many impediments it may also incur the condemnation of eternal blindness.

It therefore prays and desires that the Lord restore in the present the knowledge of truth, insofar as it can be possessed here. It presents itself as an example to others and urges them to seek with the whole ardor of their minds the knowledge of truth, insofar as it can be possessed in this life, so that through it they may finally attain the true knowledge described above.

[Col. 0551B] This psalm is entitled: “For the end, a psalm of David.” This is explained as follows: The psalm is attributed to the prophet David, or to any soul striving toward the end—that is, toward perfection—which desires either the true knowledge that will exist without end or as much of it as can be possessed in the present, so that it may finally arrive at that perfect knowledge.

And it says:

“Lord Father, you appear to have forgotten me while I am delayed away from my homeland”—that is, from true knowledge—or at least while I do not possess as much present knowledge as can be possessed here.

“But how long will you forget me?” That is, how long will this forgetfulness of me last? Will it extend to the end of the world, that is, will it be complete?

Or otherwise, so that the response is this: This forgetfulness will tend toward the end—that is, it will be delayed until the limit that you have ordained—whether the true knowledge or the present one. For just as it has been ordained when the wickedness of the evil will be consumed, so also the virtue of each good person will eventually be perfected.

Or in a third way: “How long will you forget me, not bringing me to the end,” that is, to the knowledge of perfection, whether future or present? “And how long will you turn away”—that is, permit your face, your knowledge, whether final or present, to be turned away [Col. 0551C] from me?

### How long shall I place plans?

This may be understood interrogatively or responsively, but the responsive interpretation is better.

It is as though he said: “You will forget me and turn your face away for as long as I place plans in my soul,” that is, for as long as the law that fights against the law of my mind will dominate in my members.

Thus, placed amid adversities, I shall necessarily devise plans in my soul by which I may escape adverse sins—that is, so that I may not commit sins.

I serve, and, as a wretched person, I shall necessarily place the pain of compunction in my heart. This will be “by day,” that is, throughout the whole of the present life, which revolves from day to day. For as long as we are in this life, there is always something remaining against which we must struggle.

Those, however, who have already been placed at such a height of contemplation as can be attained here, higher than all else, have been freed, as it were, from struggles. Such are said to have been certain brothers in Egypt who, through the long duration [Col. 0551D] of solitary life and the mortification of the flesh, no longer experienced any carnal impulses.

Here “soul” and “heart” have the same meaning. Yet because “heart” is usually applied to inner affection, he assigns the pain to the heart. The soul’s plan, which is lighter because it is easier to avoid a fall than to rise after falling, is related here to the saying: “Let the one who stands beware lest he fall”; and likewise: “If we say that we have no sin,” and so forth.

Or otherwise, “by day” may mean: “Although you turn your face away from me, nevertheless the plan that I place in my soul and the pain in my heart are by day,” that is, through your illumination.

### How long will he be exalted?

This is phrased as a question, but because a question does not alter the meaning, let us state it thus:

“I shall place plans and pain for as long as”—that is, until—the enemy, whether the devil or carnal habit, is exalted over me, that is, strives through unlawful impulses to oppress me.

And so that he may not truly be exalted, Lord God of all by power [Col. 0552A] and my Lord by will: you who earlier turned your face away, look upon me; you who earlier had forgotten, hear me.

By such looking and such hearing, illumine through the thought of truth the eyes—not of the body, but those whom I regard as mine, namely, the eyes of the soul’s reason and understanding.

“Give light,” I say, “lest I ever sleep in death,” that is, lest I consent against your commandments by going into death, namely, into some deadly criminal sin.

And let this be so that my enemy may never say—that is, so that he may at some time be unable to say through the effect of things—“I have prevailed against him.” This must be guarded against very carefully, because he will rejoice greatly if he can say it.

He expresses this as follows: “Those who afflict me”—that is, invisible enemies who afflict both the soul through temptation and the body through penal suffering—“who did not rejoice over blessed Job when he was afflicted yet victorious, will rejoice over me if I am moved either from a good purpose or from steadfastness in faith.”

But so that they may not rejoice, I shall not be moved. This will not come from me, but [Col. 0552B] because I have hoped not in myself but in your mercy, so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord.”

And because I have hoped in you, my heart has rejoiced, that is, perfect joy will be in my mind, “in your salvation,” that is, through true salvation, namely Christ. For either at the end you will make me know perfectly, or even in the present insofar as possible, and thus perfectly at the end.

And because I shall rejoice in God, I shall sing to the Lord, that is, praise the Lord with voice and heart. He has granted me these spiritual goods, which do not belong to the human day, namely hope and perfection.

And I shall also sing psalms by doing good through the body, as through an instrument, not for my own glory but to glorify the Lord’s name, so that “they may see your good works,” and so forth.

# PSALM XIII

*For the end, a psalm of David*

## ARGUMENT

In place of “fool,” the Hebrew has *Nabal*, from which [Col. 0552C] Abigail also said of her husband Nabal: “Truly, according to his name, he is a fool.”

Hezekiah speaks these words against Rabshakeh. Alternatively, they are the words of Christ to the rich man who questioned him in Matthew, and concern the Jewish people.

## EXPLANATION

The Church of Christ condemns the madness of the Jews. That face of the Lord which was sought in the twelfth psalm is now said to have arrived.

Therefore, in the first interpretation, the Church rebukes the Jews, who did not believe after seeing Christ. In the second, it says that those who refused to recognize the fruitful fear of the Lord are thrown into confusion by empty terror. Finally, their conversion at the end of the age is foretold.

## COMMENTARY

### The fool has said

The voice in this psalm is that of the Head, reproaching and rebuking the hardness of the Jews. They refused to recognize the physician who was present and sent to heal them [Col. 0552D], although they saw his works and failed to perceive the signs. Yet one of the Jews said: “No one can do the things you do unless God is with him.”

By reproaching them, he urges them to recognize—even if they neglected him in bodily form, lest they perish entirely—the one who, though absent bodily, is present in divinity through the heralds of truth.

It may also be said that this is the voice of the prophet before Christ’s coming, likewise reproaching the hardness of the Jews and the Gentiles’ long unbelief. He exhorts both groups: the Jews, so that when the Holy of holies comes to take away their iniquity, they may receive him with joy and recognize the time of his visitation; and the Gentiles, so that they may kindly receive him whom they were not worthy to see in bodily presence, since he said: “I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel,” but whom the apostles announced to them.

This psalm is entitled: “For the end, a psalm to David.” This is explained as follows: The psalm is attributed to David himself, the true Head—that is, [Col. 0553A] to Christ—or also to the prophet. It is a psalm, I say, striving toward the end, that is, toward perfection, because it exhorts both Jews and Gentiles toward perfection, namely, toward Christ.

It should be understood that, insofar as the voice is that of the Head, the Head here speaks about the Jews alone by means of a certain comparison: a powerful king or emperor, having gathered his army, might look from some high tower or watchtower to see who was behaving bravely there and who was sluggish.

He compares God the Father to the emperor, himself to the tower, and the Jewish people to the army. In the third verse he says:

“The Lord Father looked down from heaven,” that is, from me, whom he made his heaven, in which he might sit. For “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself,” as though from some lofty watchtower and elevated vantage point.

He “looked upon the children of men,” that is, upon the Jews, who were the children of true human beings—namely, the patriarchs and prophets—according to the flesh, not spiritually.

[Col. 0553B] He looked in order to see—not because anything is hidden from him, but so that he might enable others to see—whether there was among them anyone understanding God in mind or seeking him in action, since I had lived among them.

But no one understanding or seeking was found among them, because that people, truly foolish, who did not recognize the physician and did not attend to the time of visitation, said—both by their attitude of despising me and by thinking in their hearts—“This man is not God.”

They truly affirmed this when they said: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath”; and again: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?”—and many similar things.

They themselves, not their Creator, are blameworthy for this foolishness. For although their Creator had made them according to his likeness and image through reason and understanding, they corrupted themselves by departing from their good nature through their own vice.

Therefore they became abominable to God, that is, contemptible and disinherited, “in their pursuits,” that is, because of their pursuits: because they made the Lord’s command void on account of their traditions, or because they loved [Col. 0553C] the world more than God, the creature more than the Creator.

Nor is this surprising, because “there is no one among them who does good,” that is, anything directed toward salvation—“there is not even one.”

This is not to be understood as though there were no one among them doing good, since there were many disciples of the Lord and many prophets. Rather, it is said by comparison, as though he said: So many are doing evil that, even if some are good, they may be regarded as not even one in comparison with the wicked.

The same is true of the saying concerning the primitive Church: “Rejoice, barren woman, who do not bear,” and likewise: “Olive and Samaria, you justified your two sisters, Sodom and Gomorrah,” together with many similar passages.

Or otherwise: “There is no one among them who does good, not even one,” except the one who was made one with me—that is, the one of whom I am the Head and who is my member.

### They have all turned aside

For this reason there is no one among them doing good: because all have turned aside. Again, this is said because of the multitude of the wicked.

[Col. 0553D] “All,” I say, “have turned aside,” that is, have deviated from the truth—the learned and the unlearned, the higher and the lower alike. By turning aside they became useless both to themselves and to God.

This does not mean that God seeks some benefit from us, since he is himself the good, content in himself. Rather, because goodness is naturally implanted in him, he seeks our benefit in us and counts it as his own.

### There is no one who does good

This repetition shows by what means they became useless.

### Their throat is an open tomb

They truly do not do good because they do evil instead. Their throat is like an open tomb.

Just as a tomb is open either to receive a corpse or, if it has received one, to emit a stench, so their throat is open either to greed, so that they may exercise excessive gluttony, or so that they may tear away from Christ’s body as many people as they can and bury them in themselves, as though they had swallowed them, through conformity to themselves.

Or it is open for deceit, so that those whom they cannot devour they may at least corrupt in some way. [Col. 0554A] “Bad conversations corrupt good morals.” Their mouth is an open tomb in this respect, because they always acted deceitfully with their tongues—that is, with poisoned tongues—pretending to offer words of instruction while possessing the poison of harm.

This is because “the venom of asps,” that is, deadly thoughts, is under their lips, that is, in their hearts.

The statement may also have been made by way of this comparison. Just as an asp presses one ear firmly against the earth and blocks the other by curling its tail over it, lest it hear the voice of the wise enchanter, so those Jews applied one ear, as it were, to earthly affections, to which they clung firmly, and blocked the other as though with a curved tail.

The memory of past evils blinded them so that they would not hear the voice of the wise enchanters, that is, the heralds of truth. In this interpretation we shall call earthly affections and the memory of sins “poison,” through which they are compared to asps.

### Their mouth is full of cursing

[Col. 0554B] Not only is their throat a tomb, but their mouth also—that is, the mouth of the Jews—is full of cursing, namely, blasphemy against God, calling me demon-possessed, the son of a carpenter, a destroyer of the law, and other such things.

It is also full of bitterness, that is, bitter words, when they said to Pilate: “Take this man away, and release Barabbas; crucify him,” and similar things.

Or this and the preceding passage may be understood as in another psalm: their mouth is full of cursing, that is, of bitterness, because they made the Lord bitter to themselves.

“Their feet,” that is, their affections, “are swift,” not only to kill by word—hence it is said: “Their tongue is a sharp sword”—but also to shed the blood of the good by the sword.

Therefore “there is misery in their ways”: in the present, when they are handed over to inner darkness; and in the future, when they are handed over to outward destruction.

Hence it is said: “Whoever falls upon that stone will be broken, but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.”

The one who stumbles over Christ’s commandment, that is, over the cornerstone, will fall upon the stone and be broken here in the present, when he is condemned to inner blindness. But if [Col. 0554C], once broken, he does not repent, then, when the stone falls upon him—that is, at the manifest judgment—he will be utterly crushed, that is, handed over to eternal punishments.

Therefore destruction will come upon them because they did not know “the way of peace,” that is, me, who am the way to true peace, ever proceeding into unity. And because I wished to be their true peace, it is said: “He is our peace, who made both one.”

They did not know me—that is, they did not honor me as the physician they needed, but despised me as useless and harmful. This was because “the fear of God is not before their eyes,” that is, because they do not fear God’s judgment, either present or future.

They are deceived in this, because eventually they will also experience the manifest judgment.

He says this as follows: “Will they not at last truly know that God is to be feared—all those who now work iniquity?” He speaks emphatically of those Jews who did not know the physician but instead killed him; who drove the heir out of the vineyard; who, after killing the servants, [Col. 0554D] showed no reverence even to the son; and who also devour my people, that is, my saints and apostles, or strive to devour them and conform them to themselves.

They devour them, I say, “as bread for food,” that is, so continually that they take pleasure in it, just as bread is a person’s regular food, in which he continually delights.

The devourers of the Lord’s people may also be understood more broadly: all those who, whatever their nation, devour God’s saints by trying to conform them to themselves. Hence it was said to Peter concerning the wicked: “Kill and eat.”

Those in authority who exercise their offices not for the salvation of their subjects but for earthly profit are also rightly called devourers of the people. Of them it is said: “Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel,” because they punish even lesser sins when they can extract nothing from them, but, induced by payment, consent to greater sins both in themselves and in others.

### They have not called upon the Lord

[Col. 0555A] For this reason they work iniquity and devour my people: because they have not called upon the Lord.

This is equivalent to saying: They were handed over to a reprobate mind, so that they might do what is unfitting, because they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge.

The one who does not call upon God is the person who places something else before himself and makes it his god. This is what the Jews did, clinging only to earthly things.

He says this as follows: “The Jews trembled there,” that is, in the loss of their earthly kingdom, “where there was no need to fear,” that is, no useful reason to fear. For they lost the heavenly kingdom while fearing the loss of the earthly one.

### For the Lord

He shows how the Jews will eventually know that the Lord is judge and is to be feared: namely, because the Lord, who now is “in the righteous generation”—that is, who dwells in those who have been made righteous through him—will then be its rewarder.

He turns to the Jews themselves, as though saying:

“But among you Jews he will not be,” because you have “confounded”—that is, insofar as you could do so by will and action—“the counsel of the poor,” that is, his humble coming. Though he was rich, he became poor [Col. 0555B] for your sake.

You did this without cause, for the only reason was that the Lord alone was his hope: you saw no worldly pomp in him, and therefore he was contrary to your works.

Christ’s humble coming is rightly called “counsel,” because while everything else held complete silence, he alone brought a remedy to the perishing world and became the completion of supreme blessedness—of the ancient plan, the new restoration, and eternal happiness.

The Jews confounded this counsel, if not in reality, then at least in desire and estimation, when through his death they thought they had removed his name from the earth.

## Concerning Psalm 13

“Who will give from Zion?” You indeed confounded the counsel of the poor, O Jews, but you ought not to have done so, since this is the one of whom he truly foretold: “He will come from Zion, who will turn away the captivity of Jacob,” since no other can be meant. For who else will come from Zion—that is, being born from the Jews, who on account of the worship of the true God and the many outstanding benefits of God, the Law, and the prophets granted to them were called Zion, that is, “watchers,” and Israel, that is, “those who see God”? [Col. 0555C] Who, I say, coming from Zion will give salvation to Israel—that is, the salvation promised by the prophet to the Jews—if this one does not give it? Certainly no one. Hence someone says in the Gospel: “Either there are two, or this is he.” Hence also it was said to David: “Let one out of a thousand be your counselor.”

And truly this one will give salvation. For he will give it when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father—namely, when the Lord the Father, because he has already in hope turned away captivity, will completely turn away from his people the captivity into which it fell through its first parent, when this mortal person puts on immortality. Then Jacob will rejoice perfectly—that is, everyone who is progressing toward that salvation, who here was Jacob, that is, “supplanter,” the supplanter of his invisible supplanters. And Israel will rejoice—that is, everyone who reaches it—and thus he will have become Israel, that is, a man truly seeing God.

Jacob is therefore understood as the one who is progressing, and Israel as the one who has arrived, because when Jacob was returning to his own land, [Col. 0555D] while still journeying he was still Jacob; but when he had nearly reached his homeland, he was called Israel by the angel.

As we said above, this psalm can also be read as spoken in the person of the prophet, in a mixture of Gentiles and Jews. Accordingly, the Prophet will begin in this order, first rebuking the Gentiles’ prolonged unbelief:

“The fool”—that is, the Gentile people, truly foolish, who preferred manifest idols to the Creator—said, if not with his voice, at least in his heart, and demonstrated by his actions, that the true God is not to be worshiped and feared by all. From this error they themselves are blameworthy, not the God who created them, because it arose from their corruption—that is, not from an imperfect creation—and the judgment is not thereby changed.

“All have turned aside.” Here he treats Jews and Gentiles together, as the similar wording indicates. Nothing is changed except that what was previously referred to the Jews alone we now refer to both; and what was previously said under examples in the mouth of particular persons is now said simply: [Col. 0556A] “They have not known the way of peace.” This is stated only in the third person.

“Will they not all know?” Here too we shall understand Jews and Gentiles together. We shall refer “they work iniquity” to the Jews, as before, but “they devour my people” to the Gentiles, on account of their superiority. The Prophet says in this sentence, “my people,” that is, the people of which I am a part, just as each person commonly says of the people or nation of his own homeland, “my people” or “my nation”—that is, the people of which I am a part.

“They have not called upon the Lord.” We shall refer this also to both groups. We shall understand “fear” with respect to the Jews as fear concerning place and nation, but with respect to the Gentiles as the loss of some earthly advantage.

“You have confounded the counsel of the poor.” We can also refer this to the Gentiles. Even if they did not confound it in the head, they nevertheless confounded it in the members. The remainder is unchanged, except that we shall understand Israel and Jacob more broadly of the Gentiles.

# PSALM XIV

*A Psalm of David.*

[Col. 0556B]

## Argument

The words of a people in Babylonian captivity, desiring to return to its homeland and enumerating by what merits someone might reach it. Alternatively: because the whole Law is contained in the Decalogue, it expressed ten forms modeled on Christ, by which he is shown to have taught what he is shown to have done.

## Explanation

The Lord responds to the prophetic question by the example of the Decalogue: one reaches the courts of his blessedness through ten virtues. The entire division of this psalm is contained in a question and an answer; but the question comprises one verse, whereas the answer extends through six verses.

## Commentary

### “Lord, who will dwell?”

This psalm is entitled “A Psalm of David,” and is therefore to be attributed to the Prophet. [Col. 0556C] The Prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit, foresaw that the Church would be multiplied beyond the number of the perfect—namely, that there would be many who were Christians in name but not in reality, rejoicing only in the Christian name and not in the Christian religion. To show that the name alone has no value unless each person strives to walk as Christ walked, he proceeds under the likeness of a perfect king, military commander, or emperor who, when war had broken out and many brave and cowardly men had gathered, asked his own lord which of them he wished to serve with him in the tent and afterward reward in the palace.

It is as though he were briefly saying: Let no one congratulate himself on the Christian name alone, without the reality, for the name without the reality will not benefit him, whether so that he may serve in the tent or reign together with the king in the palace.

Tents are temporary campaign dwellings in which soldiers of this world labor for a time, so that afterward they may enjoy their rewards for a longer period. These tents signify [Col. 0556D] the present Church, in which battle is waged against the devil and the flesh, because whoever serves honorably in this tent will rejoice eternally in the heavenly palace. Hence the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him.”

It should also be noted that, following the likeness mentioned above, the Prophet proceeds in such a way that he first describes the noble soldiers and then the ordinary soldiers, who both serve honorably in the tent and will reign in the palace. Thus, by contrast, we may recognize who are unworthy of the tent and the palace.

He begins in this way with the Lord:

“Lord,” that is, King of all, to whose service so many have gathered, “who will dwell in your tent?” That is: whom have you chosen from so great a number, who will both serve honorably here in the tent and at last rest with you on the mountain—that is, in the height of your heavenly glory?

Another translation has: “Who will make pilgrimage?” This is quite fitting. For the present life is nothing other than a pilgrimage. Hence the Apostle says: “While we are in this life, we are pilgrims away from the Lord.”

[Col. 0557A]

### “He who enters without blemish”

Here the noble soldiers are described. It may be read either as the Lord’s response or as the Prophet himself answering his own question:

He, namely, will dwell honorably in the tent and at last rest honorably on the mountain who “enters”—that is, who in this life has entered into the heavenly life together with those who live well—and “conducts himself without blemish,” that is, without the crime of sin.

And because it is not enough to turn away from evil unless good is added, he continues:

“And he who practices righteousness,” that is, whatever he can rightly do, he does.

He explains this righteousness in parts, saying:

“He who speaks the truth,” that is, true things, and in such a way that what he says is in his heart—that is, that it proceeds from a good disposition.

We can also speak the truth with an evil disposition, as when someone asks which of two roads is straighter and I point out the straighter one—not because it is straighter, but so that he may fall among robbers or encounter some other evil. What I said would indeed be true, but it would proceed from an evil disposition. [Col. 0557B]

“And who has not acted deceitfully with his tongue,” that is, who has not sinned against his neighbor even with his tongue, which is the height of perfection. For it is not without reason that the tongue is placed in a moist place; rather, just as someone easily slips on a wet surface, so we easily sin with the tongue. Hence it is said: “The man is perfect who does not stumble in speech.”

And he not only does not offend his neighbor by word, but also does not harm his neighbor by doing evil. If someone else has brought reproach upon his neighbor, he himself has not accepted it—that is, he has not wanted it to happen. Moreover, the wicked person—that is, the slanderer of his neighbor—has been reduced to nothing in his sight: that is, he has been despised and counted as nothing.

But those who fear the Lord with chaste fear he glorifies—that is, he values highly and exalts.

At this point blessed Augustine says something noteworthy, namely this:

“No wicked person knows what a wicked person is unless he turns from the immutable eternal reality, under the appearance of the Creator, toward the appearance of the creature, which was made from nothing.”

This should be understood as follows: a human being is wicked—that is, acts wickedly—only when he neglects the Creator [Col. 0557C] in whose likeness he was made and desires earthly things, which were made by him from nothing.

### “He who swears to his neighbor”

Here the ordinary soldiers are described, which is indicated by swearing. For the perfect it was said: “Let your word be Yes, yes; No, no.” Whatever is more than this is from evil—namely, from the evil of the person who demands that something be believed about him, because he has often deceived others, and from the evil of the person from whom he demands it, who again believes his brother wrongly.

Because of this evil, it is often necessary to swear in human agreements, although, as is said here, if someone swears, he must not deceive. Nevertheless, the perfect are forbidden to swear, lest through the habit of swearing they eventually happen to commit perjury.

“He who has not given his money at interest,” that is, who has not lent his money to anyone in order to receive more in return, but has distributed it mercifully to the poor—or distributed it in such a way that he did not want it to remain with the borrower and demanded back no more than he had given.

“And who has not accepted gifts against the innocent,” [Col. 0557D] so as to make the case of the guilty superior to the case of the innocent, as corrupt judges often do.

### “He who does these things”

Here he plainly adapts the psalm to its purpose. It is as though he were saying:

Whoever does these things mentioned above, whether concerning the more perfect or the less perfect soldiers, that person alone will dwell honorably here in the tent and will not be moved, having completed his service, from the palace forever.

Therefore, whoever does not do these things should not applaud himself because of the Christian name.

# PSALM XV

*The inscription of the title: To David himself.*

## Argument

Hezekiah, in sickness, beseeches the Lord and gives thanks for the restoration of his life; and it is explained that he has no need of human things. Alternatively: the voice of Christ to the Father.

## Explanation

[Col. 0558A]

Although all the inscriptions of the titles affixed to the beginnings of the psalms are said to have some meaning, this psalm alone, contains some unknown mystical significance which this first psalm specifically contains through its title. Since the title written above the crucified Lord was: “This is the King of the Jews,” it is not inappropriate that, in the psalm in which the same King is about to speak of his passion and resurrection, a commemoration of this inscription should come first.

The addition “to David himself” is likewise shown to refer not to any other person but to the Lord the Savior himself, of whom the psalm is sung.

Throughout the psalm the person of the Lord the Savior is introduced. In the first section, speaking from the humanity he assumed, he addresses the Father and asks to be preserved, because he has always placed his hope in him. He also explains how his saints are chosen not according to carnal desires but according to spiritual virtues, asserting that everything he endured was brought to the glory of his inheritance.

In the second section, the same person gives thanks to the Father, who, appearing at his right hand, overcomes the iniquity of this world by the power of his omnipotence. [Col. 0558B] Hence he declares that his soul has been delivered from hell, and after the glory of the resurrection he recalls that it has been placed amid the delights of the Father’s right hand.

## Commentary

### “Preserve me, Lord”

In this psalm our King speaks according to the particular reality of the humanity he assumed. Here he treats of his passion, praying to the Father for the steadfastness of the obedience for which he was sent—not because anything was lacking to him who possessed such power that he could say, “I have power to lay down my life and power to take it up again,” and, “No one takes my life from me,” and, “After three days I will rise again,” so that he needed to pray in order to obtain something; rather, he did this in order to give, in himself, to us, for whose salvation he had come, a model of prayer for endurance and steadfast obedience. Through these, what we lost through the disobedience of our first parent might be restored to us.

He also shows that his endurance and obedience are followed by a sure reward, namely, the incorruption of the flesh in the tomb and the glorification of the resurrection, so that he might [*carnificaret*: “torture or execute us”; the reading is materially uncertain]. If we become partners in his endurance and obedience, we shall also share in his reward.

The psalm is entitled in this way: “The inscription of the title: A Psalm to David himself.” This is explained as follows:

This psalm is attributed to David himself, the true head [Col. 0558C]—that is, to Christ—not to the historical David. It is an inscription of a title because it treats of that affair, namely, the obedience of the passion, through which our Lord Jesus Christ obtained for himself the kingdom concerning which this title was written by divine ordinance. It was placed above his head by Pilate while he slept upon the cross:

“This is Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.”

Let us now approach the literal sense.

It is the voice of the Lord’s man, as we said above, praying for the completion of his obedience. It is as though he were saying:

Long ago there was one whom you, Lord, did not preserve because he did not hope in you. But me, O Lord Father, preserve—that is, [Col. 0558D] just as you have already preserved me in my soul through freedom from sin, so also preserve my body from corruption—because I have hoped in you, that is, I have placed my entire hope in you.

And truly I have hoped, because I rightly said to you, Lord: “You are my God.” No one can rightly say this unless divinely inspired, since no one can even say “Lord Jesus” except through the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle testifies.

He rightly says to the Lord, “My God,” who both subjects himself entirely to him and places nothing before himself except him. And truly, for the reasons mentioned above, you will preserve me, because the objection that is made to earthly lords cannot be made to you. Since you are the good that is self-sufficient, you do not need my goods—namely, either that I serve you or that I give something to you, as earthly lords do.

### “To the saints who are in the land”

Truly I said to the Lord, “You are my God,” because I did what I ought, since I “made wondrous” all my desires—that is, the desires given to me by him, for I did not come to do my own will—for [Col. 0559A] those who are his, that is, who are in the land of the living.

“I made them wondrous,” I say: I did wondrous things for them, so that their own desires would appear foul and contemptible to them, while mine would appear wondrous—that is, desirable.

I call them saints because they are perfected in the virtue of good works. I made these desires wondrous for them in such a way that they possess them not only in their affection, but that they also appear manifestly in them through their works. For they understand both what the humanity of my divinity benefits them and what the divinity of my humanity benefits them.

This means that those who were dead in sins have already received eternal life through the hope of the resurrection. The humanity of Christ benefited us in this respect: lest we die in sins, it died. His divinity benefited us in this respect: when it raised the flesh from death, it bestowed the immortality of life through the hope of the resurrection. Hence it was said that by dying he destroyed our death, and by rising again he restored our life.

“The land of the living,” that is, the heavenly homeland, is emphatically said [Col. 0559B] to belong to the Lord, although the land of the dying—the present dwelling place—also belongs to him. Those are said to be in the land of the living, if not in the present reality, at least in hope, whose bodies alone are on earth while their minds dwell in heaven. Hence the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven.”

This same verse can also be continued in another way. It is as though he were saying:

For what benefit do I ask to be preserved? This benefit: that I will both make my desires wondrous and have made them wondrous for his saints.

If “he made wondrous” is understood according to a certain transposition, it may be stated thus:

Truly the Lord Father will preserve me, because through me he has already made his desires wondrous.

The meaning is changed in neither interpretation.

### “Their infirmities have been multiplied”

Truly I, or the Lord Father through me, have made his desires wondrous for others, because through me their infirmities have been multiplied—that is, they have recognized their many infirmities through my teaching and the example of my life, not so as to seek destruction, but so as to seek a physician for salvation.

“And afterward they hastened,” that is, hurrying to me as physician, [Col. 0559C] they approached with concern—not carnally, as before, but spiritually, because I will no longer ask blood from them in the form of goats, but calves of the lips.

He says this as follows:

“I will no longer gather their assemblies,” that is, their gatherings, which have become little assemblies—small gatherings—after they became mine.
