For good people, however numerous they may be in virtue, are always fewer in number as human beings. Conversely, although the wicked may be more numerous in terms of human number, they are nevertheless few, because they are destined for perdition.

“I will not gather them from blood,” that is, for the sake of shedding blood in sacrifice. “Nor will I remember their names,” that is, I will not distinguish them by names, as they were previously distinguished toward a certain excellence when it was said: “Say to the house of Judah; say to the house of Levi.” This was on account of their dignity: kings were chosen from the tribe of Judah, and priests from the tribe of Levi.

Alternatively, by “names” here we can understand that the Jews were formerly called righteous [Col. 0559D] and worshipers of the true God in comparison with the Gentiles, while the Gentiles were called unclean and sinners. These names do not remain now, because God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him. Likewise: “There is neither Jew,” and so forth.

“I will not remember them,” I say, “and this through my lips”—that is, through the peace promised before the ages of the world and completed through me.

Here “peace” may be understood either as the reconciliation through him of things below with things above. This is rightly signified by “lips,” when it is proclaimed concerning it: “Let him kiss me with the kiss,” and so forth; or as the peace he established between the Gentile and Jewish peoples, abolishing enmity in the flesh and destroying the middle wall of partition by which they were separated.

Hence it was said: “He is our peace, who made both one.”

We may also understand by “lips,” which are instruments of speech and preaching, the heralds of truth, so that it may be stated thus:

This fact—that they will not be separated—will come about through lips, [Col. 0560A] that is, through preachers who place them in harmony of faith.

### “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance”

For this reason I will not distinguish them by names, because they themselves will not distinguish themselves. For all will choose one inheritance, namely, God.

He says this as follows:

“The Lord Father will be the portion of my inheritance,” that is, of those whom he gave me as an inheritance, “and of my cup”—that is, of those same people who are my cup, meaning the portion of humanity given to me.

For through a cup a portion is distributed. That is, mine will not choose for themselves any other portion among earthly things except the Lord.

Or alternatively:

“The Lord will be the portion of my inheritance,” that is, of my people; “and of my cup,” that is, the Lord will be the inheritance of the things allotted to my people, and the cup—the portion—given to my people.

It is as though he were saying:

Let others choose the world as their inheritance; mine will choose no inheritance for themselves except the Lord. Let others drink the deadly pleasures of the world; mine will drink only the life-giving drink, because they will have the Lord as their cup.

### “You are,” and so forth

According to the first interpretation, the Gentiles are understood as the inheritance [Col. 0560B] given to Christ as an inheritance. The passage may therefore be continued as follows:

When I say that this inheritance is mine, I do not attribute it to myself but to you, Father, because you are the one who will restore to me my inheritance, given to me from eternity. Hence the Apostle says: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world.”

This inheritance, lost in Adam’s transgression, you will restore to me through the obedience completed in me.

### “The cords have fallen”

Here he speaks by way of analogy. Heirs customarily divide their estates by measuring rods or cords, and sometimes a rod or cord falls to one person in a beautiful place, while another receives a shameful place.

Thus, in the division of humanity, those upon whom the cords have fallen for Christ are beautiful with the adornment of virtue; but those who have fallen to the devil are utterly shameful.

The literal sense is continued as follows:

Therefore, when I say that you will restore the inheritance, I add “mine,” for mine is glorious. For “the cords”—that is, the divisions—“have fallen,” that is, you do not cast them, but by the grace that saves them they have come to me in glorious places, that is, among those who are greatly adorned with virtues.

And truly in glorious places, [Col. 0560C] because my inheritance—that is, those who have been given to me as an inheritance—although they are ragged and despised and have become like the refuse of all things, are nevertheless glorious to me.

Therefore I will bless the Lord Father by obeying him in all things, because he has granted me understanding concerning my people—namely, reason and discernment of such a kind that they might imitate the endurance of my obedience, through which he restored them to me as an inheritance.

This can be read otherwise, according to the interpretation in which we call the Lord the inheritance:

It is as though he were saying:

For this reason, Lord, you will be the inheritance of my people, because you are the one who will restore to me my inheritance—that is, the glory of co-eternity and of the majesty that I possessed, like yours, with you before the world existed.

This does not mean that I ever lost it, but that they lost its mercy, understanding, and hope through the first fall; [Col. 0560D] and with them you will restore its understanding and hope through my obedience and resurrection. For I am in them, and through them you will restore it to me.

He then specifies what that inheritance is. It is as though he were saying:

I call your glory my inheritance because, just as the boundaries of the priests’ and Levites’ possessions once fell, in the division of the promised land, in the more excellent and beautiful places, so the cords—that is, the boundaries—of my inheritance are in glorious places, that is, in your eternity and majesty.

This has been said merely by way of analogy. And I rightly say “in glorious places,” for the effect demonstrates that they are glorious: my inheritance itself—that is, your co-eternity and co-majesty—is glorious to me in my people, that is, my people, to whom it has been revealed, regard it as exceedingly glorious and precious.

Or for this reason I will bless the Lord Father: he has granted me understanding in my people, that is, he has so enlightened my people that they both understand that great glory and already possess it in hope according to their condition.

For whoever truly eats here—that is, imitates Christ—will in the future live the same life as Christ, becoming co-eternal with him and glorified together with him according to his measure.

[Col. 0561A]

### “Moreover, even to and [un…]”

He adds “moreover” because what follows does not pertain to that glory but to the humanity.

It is as though he were saying:

I will also bless the Lord for this reason: my kidneys—that is, my carnal kinsmen, from whose kidneys I came—rebuked me, that is, by harsh rebuke they disciplined me, into obedience extending to the night—that is, to the experience of death.

Alternatively, by “kidneys,” which are the lower part of the body, we can understand Christ’s lower nature. Thus he might be saying:

My kidneys—that is, the mortality and passibility of my humanity—brought me, when rebuked, all the way to the night, as above.

But, certain of my reward, and therefore paying no attention to the pain but to the prize, I kept the Lord the rewarder before me, always having him inwardly in my sight. And rightly so, since when those persecutors were on my left, provoking me to impatience by their insults and saying, “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross,” and similar things, [Col. 0561B] the Lord himself was at my right hand, in the better part, supplying me with strength, so that I would in no way be moved from the steadfastness and patience required to complete my obedience.

For this reason my heart rejoiced—that is, there was joy in my heart and in my thought—and my tongue brought forth expressions of exultation, namely: “No one will take my life from me,” and so forth.

Moreover, my flesh will rest in hope. He explains in what hope:

In this hope, namely, that although my soul will descend into hell, nevertheless you will not abandon it to be possessed by hell. Nor will you allow my enemies, who desire to see—or rather, to experience—your holy one, the one who sanctifies others, to see corruption of the flesh in the tomb.

And truly you will not allow this, because you will not only accomplish it in reality, but you have already made known to me in your plan “the ways of life,” that is, the resurrection, which is called a way to life. Through it the hope of recovering the life we had lost has been given to us, and at last life itself will be given in reality.

Then you will fill me—that is, fill me greatly—with joy in your presence. You will glorify me through confession. And there will be delights for me at your right hand, that is, in your more excellent goods—in your glory and majesty, or in eternal life, which is also signified by the right hand. [Col. 0561C]

According to the saying: “His left hand is under my head,” and so forth, I call these delights those that continue to the end of delights—that is, to such perfection that they cannot be more perfect.

This verse can also be read otherwise and connected in part, so that it is stated thus:

For this reason you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor allow it to see corruption in the tomb, because you have made known to me, and through me to others, the ways of life—that is, patience and obedience, which are ways leading back to life through the obedience that was lost.

And because they have followed those ways to completion—when, following my example, they have perfected patience and obedience—you will then fill me, that is, my people perfectly, with joy abiding in your presence. This means that they will always be in your presence, and then there will be delights for them at your right hand, that is, in eternal life, continuing to the end, as stated above.

[Col. 0561D]

# PSALM XVI

*The Prayer of David.*

## Argument

David beseeches the Lord to make him, as one possessing a devoted heart, worthy to be heard, since his enemies attacked him without cause. Alternatively: Christ speaks to the Father concerning the Jews.

## Explanation

Since many psalms contain prayers within their text, it may be asked why this one bears such an inscription. Although other psalms contain brief prayers interwoven with various matters, this one is almost entirely a supplication in its composition.

David, as is well known, signifies our Lord, from whose person this whole psalm was uttered for the instruction of the human race.

A threefold prayer is drawn from Christ’s humanity in this psalm.

The first is where, according to his righteousness, he asks that what is owed to him be restored.

The second is that he be delivered from the plots of the Jews. [Col. 0562A]

In the third he beseeches the swiftest resurrection, so that the perverse Jewish people may not be permitted to insult him any longer and so that the crowd of believers may have no uncertainty concerning his majesty: he declares that he will remain in eternal blessedness.

## Commentary

### “Hear, Lord, my righteousness”

This psalm is entitled “The Prayer of David himself.” It is explained as follows:

This psalm is attributed to the true David, that is, to Christ. It is a prayer. It should be understood, however, that although almost all psalms can be called prayers because they contain some prayer within them, this one is specifically prayed and specifically entitled because it is for the greater part a prayer.

In this psalm our Lord Jesus Christ prays in the very struggle of his passion, from that affection for his own by which he wished to suffer for them. He asks that the Lord Father manifest to his own the judgment by which his persecutors thought they were condemning him through judicial authority, and make them recognize that this judgment proceeded not from the counsel of those who were plotting the destruction of one person alone, but from his ineffable goodness and his plan for the salvation of all. [Col. 0562B]

Once they have clearly recognized this, they will in no way be able to turn away, since they will both rejoice in his birth and be conformed to his passion.

He speaks in this way:

Lord Father, because you treated Adam according to his injustice, so as not to hear him, hear my righteousness. That is, show in the outcome that you have heard me, whom you made righteous through freedom from sins.

“ hear my righteousness” says more than if he had said “hear me as righteous,” because he presents the cause for being heard. Almsgiving also prays, and righteousness prays.

“And attend to my supplication,” that is, make yourself attentive to hearing, or make me attentive, so that I may not act half-heartedly in my supplication—that is, the supplication made by me for my own.

“And perceive with your ears,” that is, hear through the power of hearing that exists in you, “my prayer,” that is, the prayer made for my own.

As blessed Jerome says, supplication is for sins, while prayer is for perseverance.

I call it a prayer made [Col. 0562C] “not with deceitful lips.” A person prays with deceitful lips when the voice of his mouth does not agree with the voice of his heart.

### “From your presence”

He explains from where he asks to be heard so fully. It is as though he were saying:

For this I pray and beseech, Lord Father: let that judgment by which the Jews thought they were exercising judicial authority against me, for their own glory and advantage, turn out to their glory and advantage and to their disgrace—that is, let it become manifest, or let it clearly appear to have proceeded from your presence, that is, from your will and plan, for the advantage of all who desire it.

For may your eyes—that is, the most diligent and penetrating discernment that is in you—see in this matter the just arrangements, both in my glorification and in the condemnation of my people.

Nothing is more just than that those who condemned the innocent without cause should themselves be condemned, and that the innocent should be glorified.

You have tested my heart. Truly you will now do what I ask, [Col. 0562D] because earlier you did what was useful for me: the presentation of past events is the certainty of future ones. This is equivalently what is said here, and the order is reversed, so that it should first be understood in this way: You, Lord Father, visited me in the night. “Night” may be called any tribulation that causes disturbance. “Fire,” however, signifies severe tribulation, which seems to burn. We may therefore understand “night” in our Lord Jesus Christ as his arrest, binding, spitting, blows, and the other insults; and “fire” as the crucifixion itself.

A visitation is also a physician’s approach to advise the sick. All the scourges by which God the Father chastises every son whom he receives may be called a visitation, because through them he provides for their salvation. As far as Christ is concerned, however, tribulation is called a visitation for no other reason than that he himself healed our illnesses and bore our pains. There was no weakness in him.

The text is therefore understood as follows: “You visited me,” that is, you provided me with visitation as a physician, and through me with others, in the night, in the earlier tribulation; [Col. 0563A] “and you examined me,” that is, you made me pure from every stain; likewise, as regards those others, in the fire, that is, in the fiery tribulation of the crucifixion. Through both of these you tested my heart, that is, you made my heart—tested through the patience preserved even to the experience of death—remain steadfast. And because you tested me, that is, because no iniquity was found in me, every evil was removed from me to such an extent that even my mouth would not speak of these deeds, that is, I would not utter an evil word because of so great a persecution. To do that is the work of human beings: when people cannot avenge themselves by striking back, at least they speak evil words when they are afflicted. But I rather guarded the ways of the Lord.

Or otherwise, the statement may be understood thus: When I say that there is no iniquity in me, I do not say this so that my mouth may speak of human deeds, that is, so that I may boast in the manner of human beings; rather, I say it because this is in fact the case. For I guarded, and so forth.

Or otherwise: Iniquity was removed from me to such an extent that my mouth did not even speak of human deeds—understand, deeds to be glorified—so that I not only did not do anything, but did not even say anything pertaining to human praise; instead, I both did and said everything for your praise. This is evident from the fact that I guarded the difficult ways, that is, your commandments, which seem difficult to others. Another translation has “the ways of the robber.”

Accordingly, it may be understood in this way: I guarded the difficult ways, that is, the ways of the robber. For just as a robber, who dares not appear on the public and broad road, always travels by thorny and difficult paths, so I endured everything difficult and everything harsh. In accordance with that saying of Cato: “I have never spared either myself or my spirit in any offense.”

Or otherwise: I guarded the ways of the robber, that is, I avoided the works of evil people, so that I would not fall into them. Although these ways may seem pleasant, in the end they are hard, because at their conclusion they are narrow and rough. I did this because of the words of the lips, that is, because of the permission of peace and reconciliation between the highest and the lowest, ordained by you, Father, before the ages and fulfilled through me.

Or otherwise: I did this because of the words of the lips, [Col. 0563C] that is, because of the sayings of the prophets, so that the proclamations of Scripture concerning me might be fulfilled.

What was read above in one way—“not with deceitful lips”—may also be read in this manner and joined to the following verse, so that it is understood as follows: By this prayer I ask you, Lord Father, to hear and attend, so that my judgment, that is, every sentence issued by me and by my people concerning any matter, may proceed from your face, that is, proceed from sincere reason and true understanding derived from you, and may not be on deceitful lips, that is, may not proceed from fraud or any pretense. And may not outward eyes, but my eyes, that is, my inward eyes, which above all I ought to use, see equity both in me and in my people—equity, namely, in the rewarding of the good and the condemning of the wicked, and in approving what ought to be approved and rejecting what ought to be rejected. One translation indeed has this wording: “my eyes and equity.”

What follows is not changed, except that in the following verse we may understand “night” as inward and hidden persecution, namely, the devil’s temptation. This happened secretly to Christ on the mountain, from the devil—that is, when he was alone with him—and it happens daily to those who are perfect. It is called “night” because it causes disturbance; yet it is a visitation because it is beneficial. By “fire,” on the other hand, we may understand every outward persecution, whether in the Head or in the members.

Perfect my steps. It is as though he said: I took care to fulfill the words of the lips and guarded the difficult ways; I did this to perfect my steps. Therefore, Lord Father, perfect my steps in your paths, that is, make my steps—my apostles and the others through whom I shall enter into human knowledge, those whom you gave me—perfect in your narrower commandments. It is as though he said: They were yours, Father, and you gave them to me; therefore preserve them. I say, perfect them, so that my footsteps, that is, the signs of my life, namely, good works, may not be moved away from them.

I cried out. You will truly perfect them, because I alone, being free from sin, was fit for this and cried out to you, that is, I directed toward you the free and powerful intention of prayer. And I truly cried out, because you, who are God [Col. 0564A] and therefore hear the prayers of the good, have already heard me in many things.

Therefore incline your ear, that is, let the power of hearing which is in you not abandon me because of my humility—I am so weak that I cannot be raised up except by you—and hear my words, that is, my prayer made for my people. By this hearing, namely, make your mercies wondrous to them: make it appear wondrous and desirable to them that you chose them before they existed, called them when they were lost, restored them, justified them, and glorified them. These are your mercies. Make them wondrous, I say, so that they may hope in you, and thus be saved, because you save all who hope in you.

From those who resist your right hand. After praying that weakness might be driven away from his people, he also prays that their health may be preserved. It is as though he said: After you have driven weakness away from my people by making your mercies wondrous to them, preserve health in them. Namely, guard me from those who resist your right hand, that is, from the contradictors of the truth who resist me, who am the right hand for defeating your enemies. Guard them, I say, as the apple of the eye, that is, as you guarded me, who am the apple of your eye.

The pupil is the smallest part of the eye, yet through it the whole body is directed. Thus Christ is called the pupil of the eye, that is, of the Church, which is the true light that enlightens everyone coming into this world.

Or otherwise: Guard my people as those are to be guarded who are the pupil of the eye—that is, through whom, although they are few, the light of truth is poured into the whole body of the Church.

And protect me. That is, my people, under the shadow, that is, under the protection of your wings, namely, charity and mercy, with which you overshadow us as with wings. Here “charity” is understood as the love with which he himself first loved us, even before we existed. “Mercy,” however, is the proper affection of the humanity assumed by the Word. Or by “wings” we may understand love of God and love of neighbor. They are called wings because, as blessed Augustine testifies, without these two virtues one does not fly to heavenly glory.

Protect my people, I say, from the face of the wicked, [Col. 0564C] that is, lest the wicked, conforming them to themselves, imprint their own face upon them. The wicked truly afflict them, because they first afflicted me. It is as though he said: If they did not spare me, the green wood, neither will they spare those who are dry wood.

They afflicted them in this manner: My enemies, that is, my persecutors, the Jews, surrounded my soul—not for imitation, but for condemnation. They shut themselves in by their fat, that is, in their fat tongue they hardened their pride. Fat animals, such as bulls, are usually thick-necked and proud; so the Jews, because of the prosperity of temporal things, grew proud against the Lord. For their mouth spoke pride against him, that is, many proud statements, such as: “We have no king but Caesar,” and similar things.

Now casting me out. They truly grew proud against me, because, after I had first been cast out of the synagogue, they cast me out even to crucify me outside the city, so that it would not be polluted—now, when the opportunity was given to them. Previously no one had laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.

Or: the one whom long ago they cast out in the persons of the servants sent to them, now they cast out in my own person. They surrounded me for insult and mockery. This was because they set their eyes on turning toward the earth, that is, they clung wholly to earthly things and in no way looked toward heavenly things.

Or otherwise: They set their eyes on turning toward the earth, that is, while crucifying me they considered only the affliction of the flesh; they did not attend to the glorification of the resurrection that was to come.

They received me like a lion ready for prey. They truly turned their eyes downward, because they received me—that is, they brought it about through the disciple that he should hand me over to them; they received me with the chief priests so that they might seize me, and with the governor so that they might crucify me. In all these ways they received me: the leaders like a lion ready for prey, and the lesser ones like a lion’s cub dwelling in hiding, pretending that they were innocent of his condemnation.

The lesser ones acted thus when they said, “It is not lawful for us to crucify anyone”; [Col. 0565A] while the governor acted thus when he said, “I am innocent of the blood of this Just Man,” and so forth.

Rise up, Lord. They received me, but you, Lord, who now lie as though prostrate before that people because it does not recognize that you care for and govern worldly affairs, rise up against it—that is, appear manifestly powerful to it. Anticipate it, namely, in your vengeance. Let the blindness of its mind anticipate its sin, so that what it maliciously believes it is doing to destroy me may instead be accomplished by your provident disposition for the salvation of many.

It is as though he said: Let blindness come upon them, so that the fullness of the Gentiles may enter; and supplant it, so that it may lose—through my death—the place and the nation, while it thinks that through my death it will retain them.

And deliver my soul by raising me from that impious people. Deliver your sword from the enemies of your hand, that is, deliver my soul, by which your hand—that is, your divine power, namely the Word—armed itself to drive away the aerial powers. Deliver it by the resurrection from the enemies of that hand of yours.

Lord, from the few. It is as though he said: So that that wicked people may be supplanted, Lord, divide them—already separated from the few, that is, from the good, who, although they are greater in virtue, are few in number. Divide them, I say, morally from the few, that is, exclude them from their land also in a local sense, and do this during their lifetime, that is, while my persecutors are still alive: let them lose their place and nation.

Many of them were still alive when they were destroyed by Titus and Vespasian. Or “during their lifetime” may mean: in the present, divide them from their earthly dwelling, those whom you will divide from the heavenly homeland.

It is worthy that this should happen, because their belly, that is, their memory or their carnal will, has been filled, that is, filled to overflowing, with your hidden things, that is, with wicked crimes—namely, my deception, arrest, binding, and similar acts—which are hidden from you not in knowledge but in gracious regard.

It is as though he said: They satisfied their carnal heart against me in matters in which they ought not to have done so.

The belly is called the memory because, just as of the things received by the belly one part is expelled and another part is transferred into the limbs, so the memory receives various judgments or understandings. After reason examines them, it rejects false and useless things as though by digestion; the remainder it transfers into moral discipline and the disposition of the mind.

The expression “your hidden things” may also be understood otherwise, with the distinction made as follows: Divide them from the earth, as above, and divide them also from your hidden things, that is, from the mysteries of the sacraments, so that they may not perceive the sacrament of your incarnation and passion, and similar mysteries.

They deserved this well, because their belly was filled with things by which it ought not to have been filled. For they were sated with sons, that is, with evil works—namely, when they demanded that the disciple hand me over to them, and demanded from Pilate that he crucify me, and so forth. Our works, both good and evil, are called our sons, as though generated by us.

One translation has: “They were sated with swine’s flesh.” This fits well on account of the uncleanness of their works. Among the Jews the pig is an exceedingly unclean creature, [Col. 0565D] and they were so completely sated that their sins overflowed upon their descendants. For they divided their remnants, that is, their excessive sins, among their little ones, that is, their children. This happened when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

Or otherwise, the statement may be understood thus: The fact that their belly was filled did not benefit them, but their children. They themselves were sated, as with coarse food, by satisfying their carnal heart in my death. This did not benefit them but their children, because they left behind remnants which they ought to have made their own—that is, the understanding of the glory of the resurrection and ascension and of other such things. These were like delicate and subtle food, just as remnants are in relation to coarse food, and by them they truly would have been refreshed.

They did not perceive these remnants and left them to their little ones, that is, to their descendants, who had become little, that is, humble.

Or otherwise, so that the same meaning may be understood here equivalently: blindness happened in part to Israel so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter. If someone should ask, “Why, Lord, did this happen, so that some of Israel were so blinded that their belly was filled with your hidden things?” the answer may be given as follows: You should not be surprised that this happened, because in this they became like those birds that are filled not for themselves but to nourish their chicks, such as doves and certain other birds.

This is what is meant: They were sated, as we have said above, not for themselves but for their children, that is, for the benefit of their children. This happened because they left to their descendants the remnants which they ought to have made their own, namely, so that they might be among those of whom it is said: “the remnant shall be saved.” Those remnants, I say, they left to their descendants, who were little ones, that is, humble. For in them, at the end, that salvation which was promised to the remnants will truly be fulfilled.

But I. It is as though he said: You will anticipate and supplant my enemies, Lord; but I, who was regarded by them as guilty, will appear in righteousness, that is, as righteous in your sight—that is, before those who are worthy for you to behold them, namely, the good. And I shall not be satisfied with a few, but shall be satisfied, that is, shall become known to many, when your glory appears, that is, the glory of the resurrection given to me by you—when I have risen, ascended, and sent the Holy Spirit.

Or otherwise: They will indeed be divided from the earth; but I, who did not appear to them, will appear in righteousness, that is, in perfect obedience, so that I may be worthy to be in your sight—that is, worthy for you to behold and raise me—and I shall be satisfied with eternal delights when your glory appears to me, that is, when I have been exalted through enthronement.

# PSALM XVII

For the end; for David, the servant of the Lord, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul; and he said.

## ARGUMENT

David sang this psalm near the end of his life, as the title itself indicates, in thanksgiving. Alternatively, David speaks in the likeness of Christ, who in the Passion was established in the underworld, addressing the Father in John.

## EXPLANATION

The title signifies the servant of the Lord, Christ the Savior, of whom it is said: “For a child is born to us.” The historical account narrates how David was rescued from the plots of all his enemies; in accordance with his likeness, the resurrection of the Lord and the release of his members from the devil’s power are declared.

This psalm cannot apply to only one person. First, in its historical order, the Prophet speaks, giving thanks that divine mercy deigned to rescue him from grave dangers. Second, the Church speaks: before the Lord’s coming she endured countless calamities, and afterward, when he had mercy on her, he granted her the medicine of the holy Incarnation and, through the benefit of baptism, gathered the Christian people from throughout the world. Third, the voice of Christ the Savior enters into the subject of mercy, [Col. 0566D] where his virtue and power are described through the most beautiful allusions. Fourth, the words of the Catholic Church are again set forth, and with great exultation the gifts granted by the Divinity are praised.

## COMMENTARY

I will love you, Lord. This psalm is called a song, or “the words of a song,” that is, an exultant voice, because in it our Lord Jesus Christ, our Head, namely Christ, gives thanks and praise to God the Father for the victory of his Passion, in which he was delivered from his enemies, that is, from the Jews who persecuted him; for the glory of the resurrection, through which he also seized dominion over death; for the glory of the ascension and enthronement; for the sending of spiritual grace; and for the perfection of his body, that is, the Church.

Having sent the Holy Spirit through the preaching of the apostles, he gathered the Church into the unity of faith from many waters, that is, from many peoples, and took it as a glorious inheritance, without wrinkle or stain.

For all these things, I say, he gives thanks in order to exhort and instruct us, so that, just as we are his members, so far as lies within us and with his help we may strive both to be delivered in the present from all our enemies, inward and outward, and meanwhile to give whatever thanks we are now able to give; and in the future also to be delivered from the hand of Saul, that is, from the power of death, when this mortal puts on immortality and the last enemy, death, is destroyed. Then we may eternally offer full and worthy thanks to Christ our Lord, who will then be all in all, and to the Father through him.

This psalm is entitled as follows: “For the end; for the servant of the Lord David, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul; and he said.”

This is explained in the following way: “The words of this song,” that is, of this psalm, which is a song, namely, a voice of joy, as we said above, are referred not to history but to the end, that is, to perfection in Christ; or “to the end” means to the fullness of the time of grace. Thus the title removes us from a carnal understanding.

The words are said to be attributed to the prophet David, spoken by him when historically he was delivered from Saul and his other enemies—not for his own sake but for the servant of the Lord, that is, in the person of Christ, who was truly called a servant on account of his purity. Or, according to certain books, we may simply say that they are attributed to David, the servant of the Lord, that is, to Christ.

The servant himself spoke these words to the Lord, that is, to the praise of the Lord, so long beforehand through his Prophet, on the day, that is, in contemplation of the time when the Lord Father had already delivered him in his plan, though he was to deliver him in reality, in himself and in his members.

We may also say that he had already delivered him in certain of his members who had gone before. He delivered him, I say, from the hand, that is, from the power, of all his enemies. The Head he delivered from the hand of the persecuting Jews, and the members from the hand of every persecutor, inward or outward. He also delivered him [Col. 0567C] from the hand of Saul, that is, from the dominion of death: the Head in the first resurrection from the dead, and the members in the future common resurrection.

And that servant, namely Christ, spoke in this way to the praise of the Father: Lord Father, Adam was moved to love himself; the world moves certain people to love themselves. But I shall love you alone, not myself, so that I may do your will, not mine.

Because he speaks for our instruction, he turns to us, showing the fruit of his love for him. It is as though he said: I shall rightly love him, because he himself is my strength, that is, whatever good there was by way of strength in me and in my people comes from him. He is therefore my strength because he is my deliverer, that is, because through his Word he delivered me as a human being. This is to be understood with respect to the matter, not the person. He delivered my people from the fetters and bonds of death.

For, as the Apostle says, we were all held under the law of sin and death, and all would have been sold eternally under sin, unless God the Father had freed us through his Word as purchased slaves. Since he is my deliverer, therefore he is my refuge: I, who materially fled from him in myself and in my people through the first man who led us into death, shall flee back to him in order to live.

And rightly shall I flee to him, because he himself is my firmament, that is, he made me, who flee to him, firm and steadfast in his commandments. He is, I say, in all things my God, that is, worthy to be made my God.

He explains how he is the deliverer: He is my God because he is my helper, that is, because he provides me and my people with the help of his calling. He does this so that I may hope in him; therefore I shall hope in him alone. And rightly so, because he is my protector, that is, my shield against the vices that attack, lest, presuming upon myself, I raise against him the horn of pride.

He is also the horn of my salvation, that is, he has become for me the firm height of my salvation. This may be understood by analogy: just as a horn projects beyond the flesh and becomes hard, so the Lord raises the perfect above carnal desires and, as it were, makes them hard by strengthening them in spiritual things.

Therefore he is my protector and my horn because he is my supporter, that is, because he took up my cause to be conducted against all. Hence, praising him, I shall call upon the Lord.

The statement “my supporter” may also be understood more simply, and connected with what follows much later: “He admitted me from on high.” Accordingly it may be explained thus: The Lord is my protector and the horn of my salvation because he is my supporter, that is, because he assumed me as a human being. He assumed me in this way because God the Father sent his Word from on high, that is, from his bosom, and through that Word, personally united to me, assumed me as a human being.

This is the voice of the Lord’s humanity. He assumed me, that is, my body, the Church, from many waters, that is, from many peoples—not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles.

Therefore I shall call upon the Lord alone with the strong intention of my heart, and not upon anything else, praising him through good works. Thus I shall be saved, in myself and in my people, through steadfastness, delivered from my enemies and those of my people, both carnal and spiritual.

I greatly need this salvation, since I am weak in myself and in my people. This is said equivalently in the words: The pains of death, that is, mortality and vulnerability leading to death, surrounded me and my people. They troubled me, that is, they brought upon me and my people sadness and agitation for a time, which is what “trouble” signifies.

The torrents of iniquity, that is, the violent assaults of those who are themselves called iniquity, troubled me. They are comparable to a torrent because, just as torrent water is not natural but suddenly rises from an inundation of rain, then quickly subsides and dries up, so the attacks of the wicked, however fiercely they rage now, will soon fail. For the time is short.

This is said for our exhortation and instruction, so that if it ever happens that we suffer something—which truly is necessary—we may bear it willingly and patiently. Patience is necessary for us to receive the promise, knowing that all present tribulations will quickly come to an end.

The pains of hell. This shows which torrents of iniquity he means. It is explained as follows: “The pains of hell,” that is, of the lower regions, are those who grieved over the loss of lower things or rejoiced in their acquisition. Thus they became “inferior,” that is, lowest of all, grieving when they heard from me and from my people: “The world is passing away, and its desire,” through which the hopes of earthly things that they desired were taken away from them.

They surrounded me and my people. This may also be understood together with the preceding verse in another way, with the preceding verse continued as follows: They are truly my enemies, because the pains of death—that is, the Jews who grieved that I was alive, which became death, that is, condemnation, for them—surrounded me, not for imitation but for condemnation; and the torrents of iniquity troubled me, as before.

The pains of hell surrounded me, I say: those who, out of envy, grieved that I was alive, which became death for them, because through it they were led into the hell of vices. This is repeated so that the cause of their grief might be stated.

Now he adds the purpose for which they surrounded him, saying: The snares of death overtook me. He calls “snares of death” the deceitful and hidden counsels by which the Jews and every wicked persecutor plotted to deliver him to death.

The snares of death, inspired by them, overtook me, that is, they fraudulently prepared condemnation for me, as though I were unaware, according to their reckoning. Or their deceits overtook me in this sense: when they first wished to harm me or my people, they themselves were first harmed. For everyone sins against himself before sinning against another.

But in the tribulation inflicted upon me by them I did not strive to repay them evil for evil; instead, through patience I called upon the Lord alone. And I cried out, that is, I directed a strong intention of prayer toward God my God alone, in order to win his favor.

Therefore the Lord heard my voice, that is, the intention of my heart, from his holy temple, that is, from me myself, whom he made his holy temple by the fullness of spiritual grace, so that he might dwell in me. For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.

He says this for our instruction, to show that whoever calls upon the Lord worthily is heard from nearby, since God is within him. For the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.

And he truly heard me, because my cry, that is, the intense voice of my heart, entered his ears, that is, it was heard by the power of hearing that is in him. This happened because that cry was in his sight: it was not produced with the noise of struck air, but proceeded from the heart, where he himself sees.

The earth was shaken and trembled. He shows by its effect that the Lord truly heard him, because he caused him to rise again. Yet he does not state the resurrection itself, but something joined to it, namely, the earthquake that occurred at it, saying: The earth was shaken, that is, it was moved simultaneously in every part; and because of that shaking the earth trembled, that is, earthly people were stupefied.

Then, through the preaching of the apostles, the foundations of the mountains, that is, the firm hopes in earthly things held by proud rulers who had placed all their confidence in earthly matters, were disturbed, that is, they were troubled together with them. For those mountains themselves, that is, the rulers, began to distrust their hope in earthly things when they heard the apostles saying: “The world is passing away, and its desire,” and “Do not place your hope in the uncertainty of riches.”

After the disturbance, those foundations were completely shaken when, at the exhortation of the same apostles, many who had previously trusted in earthly things despised them. This happened because the Lord was angry with them, that is, because the coming wrath of the Lord against every soul that works evil was revealed to them.

And smoke—that is, a tearful prayer of supplication—rose up in his wrath, that is, in the awareness of his wrath, namely of the Lord himself; it rose up in repentance, that is, was multiplied. The flame followed that smoke, because fire, that is, the ardor of charity and divine love, blazed in their hearts from his face, that is, through knowledge of the Lord himself.

And by that fire the coals, that is, those who, although they had been burning according to their first creation in the first man, had become coals in that same man—extinguished in the ardor of good desire and darkened, lacking knowledge of the truth—were kindled again by that fire, that is, they received the ardor of good desire.

He speaks as though answering the question of how this happened and in what order: The Lord inclined the heavens, that is, the apostles, in whom he himself sat, according to the saying: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” He inclined them, that is, humbled them to endure every bodily affliction, for love of him and for the salvation of their brothers. In this he gave others an example, so that they might love God and not hesitate to give their souls for their brothers.

This was beneficial so that the coals might be kindled. And in inclining the heavens, he himself descended in them to endure the same afflictions. For the one who said, “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again,” was crucified in Peter, stoned in Stephen, and treated similarly in the others.

And in descending, darkness—that is, the lovers of earthly things, who in the darkness of their wickedness did not know God—was under his feet and those of his people, by analogy. Although those people seemed to be more exalted, they themselves were darkened, while he and his people were lower and humbled because they were afflicted by them. Yet in the truth of the matter, he and his people trampled them as though under their feet, because they despised and mocked them, like that famous martyr who mocked the tyrant in his suffering, saying: “I am roasted; turn me over now and eat.”

And he mounted upon the cherubim. The Lord descended in the heavens that had been inclined, yet in that descent he mounted upon the cherubim. “Cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” Accordingly, those who possess love of God and neighbor are rightly understood as cherubim, since this twofold love is the fullness of knowledge: the whole Law and the Prophets are contained in these two commandments.

The meaning is this: However greatly the Lord humbled himself in the affliction of his people before the wicked, he nevertheless mounted upon the cherubim, that is, he appeared exalted and as inaccessible light to the saints who possessed the fullness of knowledge. And “above” means that he surpassed even their vision by a great distance.

He shows how he is said to have mounted: And he flew, that is, he was swiftly exalted. He flew, I say, above the wings of the winds, that is, he ascended higher than the wings of the winds are able to rise.

The winds are called the souls of the saints because of their lightness, since they are not weighed down by earthly things, which are a burden rather than a support. The wings of the holy souls are their virtues, by which they raise themselves into the air of freedom, that is, with whose help they are freed from the servitude that belongs to earthly things.

The meaning is this: The Lord was exalted beyond the capacity of the holy souls, however much they might be winged with virtues.

And he made darkness. As if he were saying: However greatly the Lord ascended, he nevertheless did not abandon his own, because he made darkness—that is, he established the obscurity of the Church’s sacraments as his hiding place, that is, as the place in which he might be hidden from the wicked. For the wicked do not perceive the divine power in his sacraments. But his tabernacle—that is, those who serve him, whom he himself inhabits for a time in the present as a tabernacle, but will inhabit eternally in the future—they are around him; that is, they visibly see and know him in those very sacraments, just as those who are around someone see the person around whom they are.

Or alternatively: He made darkness his hiding place—that is, he made the hidden hope in the hearts of the faithful his hiding place, in which he might be hidden without abandoning them, even amid those worldly darknesses in which we walk by hope and not by sight. This is the present condition, when we do not see what we hope for but await it with patience. It is equivalent to saying that the Lord did not abandon his own because he is present in some through hidden hope, which has just been discussed; and in others through manifest activity, which follows when he says: “His tabernacle,” that is, those who openly serve him and who are, as stated above, his tabernacle, “are around him,” that is, they are seen to surround him and know him openly, because they manifestly perform his works.

Yet no one among those who serve him should suppose that, through this knowledge, he is already in the future light, in the manifestation of God himself, when they will see him face to face. For all the prophecies and apostolic Scriptures through which they have received that tiny measure of knowledge which they possess are dark in comparison with the brilliance of that light. This is what he says:

“Water”—that is, doctrine—“watering the hearts as water waters the earth”; “being in the clouds,” that is, in the prophets, who, from above—that is, from afar—have drenched us with their doctrine like clouds; “and the water of this air which is beneath the clouds,” that is, the doctrine of the apostles, who are beneath the prophets because they explain their sayings. They are signified by the air, which is nearer to the earth than the clouds, because they are nearer to us in time and explain the truth more openly than the prophets. Both, I say, this doctrine is dark in comparison with the radiance of that shining and bright light which will be in his presence—that is, in the manifestation of the Lord himself—when “we shall know even as we are known.”  
[Col. 0570B–D]

The preceding verse can also be read quite suitably in another way. The passage, “He inclined the heavens and came down,” may be understood as explaining in what order it happened that “fire was kindled in the knowledge of the Lord’s anger, and the coals were burned.” It happened in this way: the Lord the Father inclined the heavens—that is, he humbled his apostles—so that they might be intelligible to us and adapt their doctrine to our capacity.

These heavens are also raised up when, in mind, they surpass God, namely when they speak about the divine essence of things to which the common understanding of human beings cannot attain; as when one says, “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth. They are inclined, however, when in their teaching they reason soberly, condescending to human weakness. The Lord himself descended in this inclination, since it was not they but rather he himself who spoke in them.

In this way the darkness—that is, the lovers of the world, who had previously been dark—came to be beneath his feet, that is, beneath the affections of the Lord himself which were in the apostles. Such people laid aside their earthly affections and subjected themselves to spiritual ones.

And he ascended upon the cherubim. This verse is not changed. The following verse, however, according to that interpretation in which we understand the darkness beneath his feet in a bad sense, may be read as follows: The Lord indeed flew upon the wings of the winds, yet he did not abandon his own, because he also secretly made use of the wicked for their benefit, and openly made use of certain more perfect good people for the instruction of other, less perfect good people.

This is what he says: The Lord made darkness his hiding place—that is, he appointed darkened men as his hiding place, that is, men through whom he might secretly work for the benefit of his own. For by divine arrangement the wicked person lives for the benefit of the righteous, although the wicked person himself does not know it. This accords with the saying: “Assyria is the rod of my anger,” but “he himself did not understand.”

But “his tabernacle around him” means that the good openly show in their works that they know God, and thus the Lord offers an example to others through them.

With the same continuity of thought, this may also be said in the following way: The Lord made darkness his hiding place; that is, he made my body, joined to the Word, his hiding place, so that he might be hidden from the wicked. But “his tabernacle”—that is, the apostles and the others whom he manifestly inhabits through good activity—“is around him”; that is, they know him openly, and thus what they say about him they say openly. This was necessary for opening the prophetic Scriptures.

For “water,” that is, doctrine, existing “in the clouds of this air”—that is, in the prophets, who contain within themselves the air, that is, the apostles who explain them—is dark in comparison with the radiance of the light that shines in his presence, that is, in those apostles who are now the Lord’s presence because they were his companions and he taught them by word and example.

I say that it is in the clouds of the air—clouds that passed through the air itself, that is, made a passage through it. For the prophets, who had previously belonged only to the Jews, were transferred through the apostles from the Jews themselves to the Gentiles, in accordance with the saying: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you,” and so forth.

These clouds were first hail and afterward coals of fire. They were hail through rebuke. Rebuke is rightly compared with hail, because, just as hail falling upon cold and hard earth beats it while remaining hard, but falling upon moist and warm earth melts and turns into a nourishing rain, so rebuke accomplishes nothing in the hearts of the wicked, whereas in the hearts of the good it bears fruit like a satisfying rain upon good soil.

And because fervent love followed that rebuke in the good, therefore after the hail there were also coals of fire. Thus those clouds were both hail and coals of fire.

For the Lord entered those clouds through threats, from each heaven—that is, from each of the apostles. And “the Most High,” that is, the same Lord, gave his voice, namely the voice of exhortation, in those same clouds, from each heaven. This was the thunder; and the voice consisted of hail and coals of fire, as stated above.

Moreover, the Lord sent his arrows—that is, his evangelists, winged with virtues like arrows and piercing human hearts—and through those arrows he scattered those to whom he sent them, with a beneficial scattering, namely by destroying what they were insofar as they were wicked.

Or he scattered them, that is, divided them, so that to some they might be “the fragrance of life unto life,” and to others “the fragrance of death unto death.” He did this in the following way: he multiplied his lightnings, that is, through the apostles and evangelists he increased miracles that terrified human hearts like lightning. Thus he troubled them, that is, caused those to whom he sent them to be stunned with amazement.

Through those same lightnings the true fountains of waters springing up into eternal life appeared; that is, the false apostles were distinguished from the true apostles. Through those fountains the foundations of the world were uncovered; that is, the writings of the prophets, which were the foundation of the Church, were explained.

And this revelation, Lord, was made through your rebuke—that is, through the rebuke which you gave through them when they said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near.” It was also made through the inspiration of the spirit of your anger—that is, because through them you inspired the spirit of your anger, namely your stormy and grievous anger, when they said: “Unless you repent, you will perish.”  
[Col. 0571A–D; Col. 0572A]

He sent from on high. The discourse turns toward us, as if he were saying: How was this brought about through the rebuke and through the inspiration of the Lord’s anger? It happened in this way: the Lord the Father sent the Holy Spirit from on high—that is, from the heavenly dwelling where he himself remains—upon the apostles, strengthening them.

And so that they might rebuke and announce the spirit of the coming anger, he received me through those apostles—that is, my body, namely the Church. He received me in such a way that he took me from many waters—that is, he chose the Church itself, which is my body, from many peoples as a splendid inheritance, without spot or wrinkle.

Or alternatively: The Lord sent his Word from on high—that is, from his bosom—and thus took me as a human being, because he united that Word to me; and through me he chose the apostles, to whom he eventually sent the Holy Spirit. Thus through them he took me by taking up the Church from many waters, as stated above.

He took me up in this way because, when many persecuted me after I had turned toward him in my own people, he delivered me—that is, my people—from my enemies, enemies whom I call exceedingly strong, that is, those who prevailed not only to afflict, disturb, and crush this miserable life.

This refers to the external persecutors of bodies, who not only afflicted some but also took away their bodily life. He delivered me also from those who hated me inwardly, that is, from the destroyers of souls, who bear a more grievous hatred than the persecutors of bodies.

And they truly hated me, because they were strengthened; and they were so strengthened that they prevailed over me—that is, over my people—namely, to destroy some who did not yet possess a perfect knowledge of God, although afterward they came to their senses.

Observe that immediately after “he took me up” he places “he delivered me.” For it is written that after the children of Israel drank from the water that flowed from the rock, the Amalekites immediately rose up against them. The Amalekites, however, are interpreted as “those who lick the earth.”

This therefore indicates that after someone approaches the teaching of Christ, who is truly the rock, receives his grace, and thus resists carnal desires, the pursuing Amalekites immediately confront him, inwardly and outwardly. Hence Solomon says: “My son, when you approach the service of God, prepare your soul for battle.”  
[Col. 0572B–C]

They came before me. They were truly strengthened against me because they came before me in my own people, that is, they oppressed my people, although in this they themselves were forestalled: when they wished to injure first, they were first injured by inward punishment.

They came before me, I say, “in the day of my affliction,” that is, in the present life, which is a time of affliction, followed by exaltation. For whoever is afflicted in this life for Christ will be exalted in the future.

This affliction benefited me in my own people because the Lord the Father became my protector—that is, the protector of my people—by disturbing the foundation of earthly pleasure through the bitterness mingled with their sufferings.

He became protector in this way because he led me—that is, my people—from bodily narrowness into spiritual breadth, so that they might even rejoice in tribulations, knowing that “tribulation produces patience,” and so forth.

Thus he saved me—that is, my people—through steadfastness. This was not because of merits, but because he himself first willed me, that is, had good will toward my people before they had it toward him. And because he willed me, he also caused me to will him in my people.

Nevertheless, the Lord will repay me in my people according to my righteousness, that is, according to the righteousness of good will given to me by him in my people. For the one who gave me the will to do good will also give me the ability to do good, and he will repay me again for my good works.

This is what he says: “According to the purity of my hands,” that is, according to the pure works in my people—pure, that is, clean, and not done for human approval—the Lord will repay me in my people. He will give both the crown of righteousness in the future and, in the present, lead me into the breadth of faith, which works through love.  
[Col. 0572D–Col. 0573A]

What has been said is shown more fully in the book. As if he were saying: He led me into the breadth of faith in this way: I kept the ways of the Lord in my people, that is, all the commandments and all the works of the Lord, which are the way to him.

And he added long-suffering to this breadth, because I never acted wickedly in my people by departing from my God, that is, from the Lord himself, whom I made my Lord. This was because I always have before my eyes—that is, set before the eyes of my heart—all his judgments, whether in the present or in the future.

In the present: the chastisements of those being corrected, the temptations of those being tested, and the blinding of those being hardened. In the future: both the punishments of the wicked and the rewards of the good.

Because I know these judgments, I did not cast away from me, in my people, his righteousnesses—that is, the chastisements of the Lord the Father, which justify my people and are given here as an example of the future judgment.

This is what those do who collapse beneath the burden, unwilling to bear the weight of the day and the heat. Concerning these chastisements it is said: “My son, do not neglect your father’s discipline, nor become weary when you are reproved by him,” and so forth.

And thereafter I will not cast it away, but I will be blameless in my people, that is, existing without a capital crime while remaining with him—that is, adhering to him. Moreover, I will observe myself, that is, my people will observe themselves, from every iniquity, not merely from a stain.

I call this iniquity “mine” because of excessive affection. This should not be understood as though iniquity could fall upon God; it is said according to the statement that he himself bore our sins and healed our sicknesses.

In this verse also perseverance is signified.

And the Lord will repay me. As if he were saying: The Lord indeed led me into the breadth of faith so that I might work through love, and he gave me perseverance in my people; and from this the Lord himself will repay me in my people according to my righteousness, that is, according to the righteousness of my people given by him—namely, according to the breadth of faith, according to long-suffering, and also according to the good works proceeding from them.

This is what he says: “And he will repay me,” that is, my people, “according to the purity of their hands,” that is, also according to their clean works, which they perform both through love and with long-suffering.

He does this because those works are before his eyes, that is, they were not done hypocritically to win human approval, but from the heart so that they might please him alone.

Observe this order. In the preceding words he first placed the will to do good, and from the will to do good he said that a recompense of doing good follows, which is already something greater. From doing good he said that a recompense of working through love and perseverance follows, which is more perfect still.

From these two he also says that a recompense follows: namely, that the one who is righteous becomes more and more righteous until at last he receives the crown of righteousness.  
[Col. 0573B–D]

The preceding sequence can also be read in another way. According to the interpretation in which we referred “he sent from on high” to the sending of the Word, we may also refer what follows to the head itself.

In this interpretation, “he took me from many waters and delivered me from my exceedingly strong enemies” refers to the body, that is, to the Church, as before. What follows, however, refers to the head.

As if he were saying: The Lord delivered me in my people, and he also delivered me, the head, through the resurrection, from those who hated me—that is, from the Jews, who truly hated me with the greatest hatred.

“For they were strengthened against me,” that is, they prevailed against me in the Passion. They were strengthened in this way because “they came before me,” that is, they afflicted me, although they themselves had been forestalled by inward punishment, namely blindness of heart, in the day of affliction—that is, at the time of the Passion—when they were permitted to afflict me. Yet this did me no harm, because the Lord became my protector, that is, he protected me from them by raising me.

Moreover, he led me from the narrow prison of the Jewish people into the breadth of the Gentiles through the apostolic preachers, whom he transferred from the Jews to the Gentiles, in accordance with the saying: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you,” and so forth.

He made me safe among those Gentiles by saving them through me. This was not because of their merits, but because he first willed me, that is, his good will toward them preceded, so that they might be saved through me.

Or it was not anyone’s merit but his will alone that accomplished this: he took me, the human being, through his Word, so that through me he might save them.

Nevertheless, the same Lord the Father will repay me because he took me up solely by his grace, according to my righteousness—that is, according to my perfect obedience—glorifying me, namely through the resurrection and ascension. According to the purity of my hands—that is, according to my works—he will also repay me.

Nor is this surprising, because I kept all the ways of the Lord himself: I did not apostatize from his commandments in anything, nor did I ever act wickedly in a way that would make me depart from the Lord himself into a distant region, as Adam did.

This was because I set all his judgments before my eyes, that is, before the eyes of my heart, as stated above. Therefore I did not cast away his righteousnesses—that is, his chastisements—from myself, but willingly received them.

And thereafter I will always be blameless, that is, I will transgress none of his commandments, remaining with him—that is, adhering to his will. And so I will be blameless; likewise, I will observe myself, that is, my people will observe themselves, from every iniquity, which I call mine because of excessive affection.

Therefore the Lord the Father will repay me, that is, he will repay my people, just as he will repay me according to their capacity, according to the righteousness of my works and according to the obedience of my people, by which they will imitate me.

And according to the purity of my hands—that is, he will repay them according to their good works proceeding from obedience—which will be before his eyes, as before.  
[Col. 0574A–B]

With the holy you will be holy. This is connected in the same way according to both interpretations. Here the head turns familiarly toward God the Father by addressing him in the second person.

As if he were saying: Truly, Lord, you will repay me according to their righteousness and according to the purity of their hands, because you will make this recompense: the one who is righteous will become more righteous, and thus they will attain true salvation, just as, conversely, you permit the one who is perverse to become more perverse.

The wording is explained as follows: You, Lord, who are truly holy and sanctify others, will be with each holy person so as to sanctify him more and more, and thus make him innocent. And with each person made innocent by you, you will be present so that he may become more innocent.

I say “truly innocent” because he harms no one, although you may seem to inflict punishment upon some. Rather, each wicked person is bound by the cords of his own sins.

And you, who are truly chosen before all others, chosen, that is, in virtue, will be with the chosen person so that he may become more chosen.

Observe the order of the words. Someone first becomes holy when he is cleansed from uncleanness; afterward he becomes innocent through the pursuit of virtue; and finally he becomes chosen, as though by perfection he had already been separated from the others.

It may also be said in this way: You, Lord, will be holy with the holy, that is, the holy person will regard you as holy; the innocent person, as innocent; and the chosen person, as chosen. And “with the perverse you will be perverted,” that is, the perverse person will regard you as perverse, saying: “The way of the Lord is not equitable.”

Another translation has: “With the perverse you will be perverted.” This is to be understood as follows: When someone is perverted from the good in which he was created into evil, and neglects to repent, then you turn yourself before him from mercy into judgment.

Similarly, the passive expression found in this translation can be explained in this way: “With the perverse you will be perverted,” that is, you will become perverse from mercy into justice, handing him over to a more grievous blindness of mind so that he may continually become more perverse.  
[Col. 0574C–D]

For you enlighten. Here he speaks openly, for the completion of the Church. He prays here to the Father for those other sheep of whom it was said: “I have other sheep,” and so forth—namely, for the Gentiles—so that they too may be converted to the perfection of his body, that is, the Church, together with the elect from the Jews, into one flock, that is, into one concord of faith, and be brought under one head.

The passage is connected as follows: The perverse, Lord, who save the humble and condemn the proud, regard you as perverse. But however much you may appear perverse to them in this respect, do not on that account cease saving those of them who are worthy of salvation.

Rather, O Lord, my God—that is, the one whom I make my God—“enlighten my darkness,” that is, those among the Gentiles who, although they are now dark, will in the future be mine, having been made light by you, Lord.

You ought to enlighten them because you already enlighten—that is, have enlightened—my lamp, that is, the apostles and certain people from the Jews, through whose teaching and activity I shine upon others.  
[Col. 0575A]

For in you I will be delivered. You will truly enlighten them, because I, placed in you, will be delivered—that is, my people, placing their hope in you and receiving your faith, will be delivered through you from temptation, so that they may not succumb to any temptation or be carried about by every wind of doctrine.

And, persevering in you, my God, whom they too will make their God, they will cross that wall—that is, the obstacle which sins have built. They will be reconciled with the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, with the citizens above—through virtues and good works, from whom they had been removed and separated by sins, and they will become one Church with them.  
[Col. 0575B]

My God. They will truly be delivered through you, Lord, and cross the wall, because you, who are my Lord—that is, the one whom I make my Lord—will deliver me from the contradictions of the Jewish people and establish me as head of the Gentiles, so that they may be subject to me and imitate me.

This verse occurs much later. The reason so many things have been inserted between them is that the head might demonstrate in several ways that he rightly makes his God his Lord, and thus exhort the Gentiles themselves to make him their God as well and to set aside their empty idols.

Since these Gentiles had gone astray in idolatry in many ways, they had to be recalled to the worship of the true God. Therefore it is not without reason that he inserts so many arguments in commendation of this truth, and then turns to the Gentiles themselves.

As if he were saying: I rightly make him my Lord and God because his way—or his commandments and works, by which one comes to him—is not polluted, that is, it does not belong to that uncleanness which is found in the sacrifices of idols, whose altars were often polluted even with human blood. Rather, it is unpolluted, that is, it belongs to true purity.

Or we may say this: The way of the Lord by which he himself approaches us—that is, virtues and good works—is unpolluted, that is, truly clean. For he does not dwell in a body subjected to sins.

And the sayings of the Lord himself are tested by fire, that is, the Lord’s commandments make people such that they can be compared with silver tested by fire, as stated above.

The same Lord is the protector of all who hope in him, but the rejecter and despiser of those who presume upon themselves. For this reason you are rightly my God.

And therefore also: “Who is God besides the Lord?” That is, who among all those whom you Gentiles worship as gods is Lord besides that Lord whom we serve in spirit? Or who among those other gods is truly God besides our God—that is, the one whom, after the good service has been completed, we will receive as an inheritance on which we may feed eternally? Certainly, no one.  
[Col. 0575C–D]

God who girded me with strength. He is also my God for this reason: he is the God who girded me—that is, my people—with strength, namely so that their works would not be dissipated by desire.

And he made my way—that is, the way of my people—blameless, that is, he established for my people such things as would lead them to him, namely sincere faith, firm hope, and perfect charity, which are blameless, that is, clean and holy.

Who perfected my feet. He is also my God for this reason: he perfected my feet—that is, the affections of my people—like the feet of deer, that is, he made them resemble the feet of deer, so that they might be agile in leaping over these earthly, shadowy, and muddy things and in climbing to the heights, as deer do.

And he establishes me—that is, my people—upon high places, that is, he fixes the intention of my people upon the heavenly dwelling, so that even while still in the flesh they may conduct themselves in heavenly things.

Therefore he is also my God who teaches my hands for battle, that is, who teaches me to perform such good works as will overcome the enemies and destroyers who wish to bar my people from the kingdom of heaven.  
[Col. 0576A]

And you made my arms like a bronze bow, and so forth. Here he turns familiarly toward the Lord the Father, so that by this he may encourage them more strongly to make him their God as well and thus become his intimates.

As if he were saying: Justly, Lord Father, do I make you my God, because you also made my arms—that is, the arms of my people—like a bronze bow. That is, you made my people embrace, as with arms, the tireless pursuit of good works, which is rightly signified by a bronze bow. For if a bronze bow could be made, it would be tireless.

This is an analogy drawn from the impossible. You also gave me—that is, my people—the protection of your salvation, that is, such protection from vices as is deserved by those whom you save.

This protection consists in the fact that your right hand—that is, the favor of your grace—received me to defend me.

Therefore your discipline—that is, your fatherly chastisements, by which you correct every son whom you love—your discipline, I say, not permitting me to go astray, corrected me to the end. That is, it directed me so in my people that whatever I did I referred to that end by which one adheres to you.

And that same discipline of yours, which directed me to the end, will teach me, by preserving me in good works, to reach that end.

Therefore you are rightly my God, and for this reason also: you enlarged my steps, that is, you gave a broadened heart to my steps—that is, to the apostles and other heralds through whom I walk into the knowledge of human beings.

You gave them an enlarged heart so that the sadness of the Passion would not constrict them, but they would rejoice in tribulations and extend the affection of their hearts even to praying for their persecutors.

And you enlarged their hearts so that they would be beneath me, that is, so that they would act not according to their own will but according to mine and obey my commandments. They would not be above me or give me commandments, as Peter did.

When the Lord said, “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem,” and so forth, as though wishing to take precedence in teaching, Peter said: “Be favorable to yourself, Lord; this shall not happen.” For this he received a severe answer from the Lord, who said: “Get behind me, Satan.”

As if he were saying: Do not give commandments to me, whom it is rather fitting to occupy the lower place and obey my commandments. For Satan is interpreted as “flowing downward.”

And because you enlarged my steps, the footprints—that is, the signs which I impressed upon others by deeds and words for imitation of me—were not weakened in them, that is, they were not rendered feeble, but were preserved with manly strength.

Through such steps I will pursue my enemies and those of my people with a beneficial persecution, and I will overtake them for good. I will not turn back from this persecution until they cease to be what they are as enemies.

They will cease in this way: I will break them in the place where they must be broken through those steps of mine. Nor will my enemies be able to stand, that is, resist the spirit of wisdom speaking in them. Rather, they will fall beneath my feet—that is, beneath the feet of my people—which means that they will change their carnal affections into the spiritual affections of my people.

Therefore the enemies will be broken and fall through those steps because my people are virtuous for this purpose. For you, Lord, girded me—that is, crowned and fortified me—with strength, that is, with virtuous men, namely the apostles and others, for the purpose of waging this battle, namely pursuing the enemies, and so forth.

And you brought low those who rose up against me—that is, my destroyers and persecutors—through those virtuous men, so that they might come to be beneath me. Those who wished to be superior to my people became inferior to them in two ways: either they were converted and accompanied those whom they had previously persecuted, or, when they thought they had overcome them through tortures and destructions, they were instead despised by those whom they had persecuted.  
[Col. 0576B–D]

And my enemies. This refers specifically to the head and is spoken about the Jews; it is connected with the principal passage above.

As if he were saying: I rightly make you my God because you gave me the backs of certain enemies of mine—that is, my persecutors from among the Jews, who formerly went before me as though I were God—making them my imitators, so that they would not precede but follow.
