This is to be understood of those who were converted and repented.

But those who hated me—that is, those who remained in hatred and were not converted—you have already destroyed in your plan, because you will destroy them throughout the earth in captivity, taking away from them their place and nation.

You will destroy them for this reason: they will indeed cry out to you while still awaiting the Messiah, but they will not cry out worthily.

He says this by speaking of the future as though it had already occurred: “They have cried out and will still cry out, and there was not, nor will there be, anyone to save them.” They cried out, I say, even to the Lord the Father; but because they did not cry out through the Mediator, and therefore cried out unworthily, the Lord himself did not hear them, nor will he hear them.

Therefore I will crush them—that is, divide them—throughout the nations, as dust is crushed, that is, divided and destroyed, before the face of the wind, that is, in the presence of a powerful wind. And, once diminished, I will erase them, that is, I will trample them everywhere among all the nations like mud that is trampled in the streets, that is, in the broad and public roads where it is trampled everywhere.

This was said as a simple comparison. But if someone considers it inwardly, it may be understood as follows: “I will crush them like dust before the face of the wind,” that is, they will be dry and fruitless like dust, not receiving the rain of the divine word. Inflated by pride, they will be carried away through that very pride from firm hope, just as the wind carries dust away from the stability of the earth.

And I will erase them as those must be erased who are the mud of the streets, that is, those who, slipping along the broad roads of perdition, walk through the lusts of the flesh.

This concerns the contradictions of that people, which is like the mud of the streets, the people who said: “We do not want this man to reign over us,” and many other such things in which they contradicted me.

You will deliver me, Lord Father, by raising me, and you will enlarge my name, which had previously been confined among them, because you will establish me as head of the Gentiles.

Thus this verse will be connected with what precedes if it is read in its proper order.

According to this reading, “My God,” to which the preceding passage was connected, will be understood differently. The preceding verse—“For in you I will be delivered from temptation”—will be understood not only of the Gentiles, as before, but commonly of all believers.

It will then be connected as follows: “My God,” as if he were saying: Truly, Father, in you, my Lord, they will be delivered and will cross the wall, because you will be my God—that is, the God of my people. That is, they will make you their God, just as I made you my God, so that they may act not according to their own will but according to yours.

He then turns toward them, as if saying: You will rightly make him your God, because “his way,” and so forth.

In this reading also, everything up to “You will deliver me” is inserted so that God may be commended through these things generally to all believers, not only to the Gentiles as before.

Nor is it necessary to refer everything to “My God,” as before. Some statements stand independently; others are connected with one another. The meaning, however, does not change up to “You enlarged my steps.”

According to blessed Augustine, this is understood of the affections, and is connected with what follows.

As if he were saying: Through this your discipline will teach me to reach the end, because you enlarged the steps in my people—that is, you gave my people enlarged affections, so that they would not be obstructed by carnal constraints, but would work cheerfully even with regard to those mortal things and members that are beneath them.

You enlarged them in such a way that they would be beneath me—that is, beneath my people. This means that these affections would not dominate them, but they would dominate their affections.

And my footprints were not weakened in them, as stated above. Through such things I will pursue my enemies, that is, the carnal affections that pursue inwardly. I will overtake them, subduing them so that they themselves are not overtaken by those affections; that is, the carnal affections will not prevail over them.

And I will not turn back from pursuing them until those who bark at me cease, that is, until the carnal affections themselves cease—those affections which stand at the sides of my people like attackers, as though to tear them apart.

And they will truly cease because I will break them. Thus they will not be able to stand, that is, endure, but will fall beneath my feet—that is, the carnal affections will be converted into spiritual ones.

This will happen because you girded me with strength for battle, that is, you restrained the flowing desires of the flesh in my people so that they would not impede them in such a battle.

Through this you brought low those who rose up against me, that is, the carnal pleasures which previously strove to extinguish spiritual desire in my people. You brought them so low that they came to be beneath me, that is, they were changed into spiritual affections.

According to this interpretation, “And they will fall beneath my feet” means the same thing here as it did earlier; but it is repeated after the proof, as a conclusion.

What follows is referred in the same way to the head and to the Jews as before.

The people whom I did not know. He concludes: Therefore you will deservedly appoint me head of the nations, because that Gentile people—namely, the people whom I did not know in bodily presence—will serve me. And they were more easily brought to this because they obeyed me at the hearing of the ear, that is, as soon as they heard through the apostles the preaching of the words; hence they will be blessed. For blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.

But those who ought to have been sons, namely the Jews, having become alienated—who alienated themselves from the inheritance—lied; that is, they became liars before you, Father, who had raised them as sons. This happened to me, that is, for my glory and benefit. Of these sons it is said: “I have begotten and nourished sons, but they have despised me.” And again: “You are of your father the devil.” And: “The sons of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness,” and many similar passages.

They were liars in many ways. For they often said to Moses: “Whatever the Lord commands us, we will do.” But because they did not say this from the heart, they soon forgot it. Again, concerning Christ they said: “This man said, ‘I can destroy this temple,’” and so forth. And: “We found this man subverting our nation.” And: “His disciples came and stole him away,” [Col. 0578C] and countless similar statements.

Truly they became alienated sons. For they were alienated to such an extent that, although I had brought them a new grace by which they might be renewed, nevertheless they became old—that is, they remained in the oldness of their error—and they limped, that is, they lacked the New Testament as though it were their right foot. They limped away from their paths, that is, because of their paths, namely their traditions, by which they had already nullified the Lord’s commandments in the former Testament.

For, as the Gospel says, they took care of outward things pertaining to bodily cleanness, while neglecting true purity. The Lord himself showed them that this was frivolous when, being reproached concerning the apostles’ unwashed hands, he replied: “To eat with unwashed hands,” and in many similar passages.

The Lord lives. As if he were saying: Those men, like wicked servants, have become strangers, excluded from the household. But the Lord, whom they wished completely to eradicate, lives; that is, I, whose name they also tried to erase, live and remain in the household forever. And I live because my God—that is, the Father who sent me, whom I truly know to be God—lives forever.

I say that he is blessed, that is, exalted and lifted up through me. By this he indicates that, just as he lives through the Father, so also whoever clings to him will live through him. In accordance with the saying: “As the living Father sent me,” and so forth.

And let God be exalted. As if he were saying: Just as he is blessed through me, so let my people always exalt through me God the Father, the author of my salvation. He is deservedly to be exalted by my people because he has been magnified, namely, because he always magnifies in virtue those saved by me, whom he appointed king.

And truly he is the author of my salvation, because in raising me he shows mercy to me, the true David, his Christ. And he will show mercy to his seed on account of him, that is, on my account: you will raise up spiritually all those whom I beget. In the present you will raise them from the death of the soul; finally, from the corruption of the flesh. And he will do this forever, that is, eternally. [Col. 0579A]

Although this verse can be read in its own order, it is joined to the preceding verse in this way because that arrangement is more convenient.

God, who gives me vengeance. He turns familiarly to the Father, as if saying: You, I say, are exalted, O God, who avenge me and mine against my enemies. This is specifically because you subdue the formerly proud Jewish peoples after they have been converted, that is, you humble them, so that they may be beneath me, above whom they previously wished to be.

And you will subdue them in this manner because you will be my deliverer through resurrection from my enemies, those who crucified me in true anger, when they said: “Take this man away and crucify him.” For after Christ’s resurrection had been glorified through the apostles, many of the Jews who had previously doubted him believed, and they said to the apostles: “Men, brothers, what shall we do?” They replied to them: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord.”

And from those who rise up against me—that is, truly you will deliver me—because you will exalt me above those who rise up against me. You will do this through the glory of the resurrection, so that the very resurrection of my enemies against me, by which they wished to crush me, may become my exaltation.

You will also rescue me, or mine, from the unrighteous man, that is, from every class of the unrighteous, so that they may not be led astray by them. And for this reason—namely, because you will both exalt me and rescue mine—I will confess to you among the nations in my people, that is, I will make a laudable confession to you in my people throughout all nations, namely in faith and innocence.

I will also sing a psalm to you by doing good through them for your name, that is, not for their glory but for the glory of your name.

# PSALM XVIII  
## A psalm of David, for the end.

## ARGUMENT

In this psalm the providence of God is commended. By this very fact he showed that he exercises great care for human beings, when he so composes the elements created by him that he can afterwards be known through them. The prophet also speaks here about the coming of Christ [Col. 0579C] in relation to Matthew.

## EXPLANATION

This inscription is very well known. It refers the words of the psalm to the Lord Christ, concerning whose first coming the prophet is going to speak. This is the first psalm on that subject; four others follow, namely the seventy-ninth, the eighty-eighth, the ninety-sixth, and the one hundred sixteenth.

Throughout the psalm the words are those of the prophet. His first account praises the Lord’s preachers, and he himself adds words concerning the Lord’s Incarnation through the most beautiful comparisons. The second praises the commandments of the New and Old Testaments. The third begs the Lord to cleanse him from hidden vices, so that the Lord may make him a worthy Psalmist.

## COMMENTARY

The heavens declare. Foreseeing through the Holy Spirit that, in the future, the people contemporary with Christ’s coming would display such hardness and madness of heart [Col. 0579D] that they would not recognize even the physician sent for the salvation of all, nor notice the time of their visitation, the prophet openly reproves and rebukes them in this psalm. He demonstrates that Christ’s coming would be certain and indubitable through manifest signs and through the proclamations of the holy apostles. In addition, he commends Christ’s spotless law.

He does all this to exhort them, so that eventually they may lay aside their madness, recognize the physician together with the time of their visitation, and, having formerly received the law of a servant, rejoice to receive the law of God. This law is so much more worthy of embrace as the Lord is worthier than the servant.

It should be understood that, according to the saints, this psalm together with the two following psalms constitutes one psalm. Since they deal with the same matter, merely in different sections, and pursue the same aim—namely, to rebuke the hardness of the Jews—they also have the same title: “A psalm of David, for the end.”

This is explained as follows: This psalm is attributed to David the prophet, and it is referred to the end, that is, to Christ, because this psalm concerns the glory of the Incarnation, the preaching of the apostles, and the holiness of Christ’s new law. The other psalms are each referred to their own subject in their own way.

The prophet begins in this psalm by rebuking the blindness of the Jews through the manifest preaching of the apostles. He speaks of the future, because of its certainty, almost as though it were present or past.

It should be understood that the apostles and the other holy preachers are called “heavens” because they are raised far above earthly things, bearing God, thundering through their proclamations, and flashing through miracles. Thus he says:

The heavens—that is, the holy apostles and other preachers—declare, that is, will openly declare to others, the glory of God, that is, the glorious Son of God the Father, through whom he accomplished his glorious work in the world. For although we were all sinners, through him he made us righteous from sinners, sons from servants, devout from ungodly people, and those condemned he took up into the kingdom. This truly was the glory of God, not our merit, because although we had deserved nothing good, we received so great a good, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “The kindness of God our Savior appeared, who did not save us because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy,” and so forth. [Col. 0580B]

And the firmament—that is, those same holy preachers, whose heart has been raised from earth to heaven and strengthened by the Holy Spirit—announces the works of his hands, that is, the works of the power of God.

He says the same thing as before, but somewhat more explicitly. Although by “firmament” we understand the same persons as by “heavens,” “firmament” more closely signifies the steadfastness that is in them, whereas “heaven” does not do so to the same degree.

It should be understood that he does not say “the works of his hands” because God the Father has hands and works with hands. He is not confined by human limbs. Rather, he is said to do whatever he does by word, that is, by wisdom, or by hand, that is, by power. The Son is his wisdom and power. Therefore what he accomplished through the Son is rightly called “the work of his hands,” that is, of his power.

And because that work which we first understand through glory is more worthy than all the works that the Son performed in the flesh, it is therefore emphatically called the work of God’s hand.

This may also be distinguished from the preceding interpretation in the following way: “The heavens declare the glory of God” outwardly in words, while “the firmament,” that is, their heart strengthened by the Holy Spirit, announces inwardly within itself the works of his hands. Through the fact that their heart is made steadfast by God—and even if the world rages against them, it accomplishes nothing—they represent in themselves the work of God’s hand, that is, of his power: a steadfastness so great that they could possess it from nowhere except God.

Day to day. As if he were saying: They announce the glory of God in such a way that spiritual persons speak spiritual things to spiritual persons, and carnal persons speak carnal things to carnal persons.

By “day” we understand those who possess an extremely clear and luminous intellect for contemplating divine things, as John possessed when he said: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth.

“Night,” by comparison, refers to those who consider and teach things comprehensible to human beings, such as those who speak about Christ’s humanity and about mortal things.

And just as the one who is a day does not merely indicate the word—that is, divinity—to another day, but pours it forth, as it were, bringing from the depths of his heart what he preaches, so the one who is a night to other nights indicates not “word” but knowledge—that is, humble and human things—readily.

The same preachers can indeed be day and night at different times and in relation to different people. Paul suggests this when he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober-minded, it is for you that we are sober-minded.”

Again, in the same Epistle, he says to the Corinthians: “We speak wisdom, that is, divine things, among the mature.” Wisdom properly concerns divine things, while knowledge concerns human things.

And again, in the same Epistle: “We testified that we knew nothing among you except Christ, and him crucified.” As if he were saying: I did not preach higher things to you, but humble things according to Christ’s humanity.

This verse can also be explained and connected in another way, as follows:

The heavens will indeed announce the glory of God, and this announcement will not last for a short time but will embrace the entire course of the ages, because day will always be joined to day in this proclamation, and night to night, and thus it will exist at every time. For every time is either day or night.

Nor will this announcement be made in only one kind of language, but in every kind, because there are no languages—that is, complete discourses—nor even individual utterances within discourses, voices—that is, distinct expressions—whose sounds are not heard from the apostles as though they were their own.

Therefore the sound of their preaching went forth from Judea, reaching the whole earth, that is, every part of the earth, and even all the corners of its regions, because their words reached all the ends of the world. For no inhabited corner of the earth exists where apostolic teaching, either through the apostles themselves or through their disciples and successors, has not become known.

In this interpretation “sound” and “words” are understood as equivalent.

It may also be said in another way, with each term taken in its proper sense:

The sound of the apostles—that is, the simple voice of their preaching—went forth commonly into the whole earth, but it did not prosper everywhere. Their words, that is, their voice when it reaches understanding—which is properly called “word”—reached only the ends of the world, that is, only those who have ended their earthliness within themselves and are saints perfected in the world.

Their words, I say, belonged to those who declared in this way that glory of God, that is, the Son of God, coming to wage war against the kingdoms of darkness. He placed his tent, that is, his military dwelling, namely his human body, in which for a time he served God the Father as in a tent, in the sun, that is, in time.

This is signified by the sun because times are chiefly distinguished by the sun. He who was with the Father without time was born from his mother within time.

Or otherwise: He placed his tent in the sun, that is, in the labor of the present life. For he did not come to enjoy some earthly pleasure, but to labor at fulfilling the obedience imposed upon him. Hence he himself also says: “I did not come to be served, but to serve.”

Labor is signified by the sun because one who works in the sun labors more heavily than one who works outside the sun.

Or otherwise: He placed it in the sun, that is, in an openly visible place. For many splendid signs, both preceding and accompanying and following his coming, made it sufficiently manifest to rational beings. Scripture even testifies that certain irrational creatures recognized him in the manger.

Thus, however the phrase is understood, he placed it in the sun because, proceeding from his bridal chamber—that is, from the virginal womb, which is rightly called a bridal chamber because, having assumed humanity in it, he joined the Church to himself as a bride—he proceeded as a bridegroom. He was adorned inwardly with the fullness of divinity and with virtues, just as bridegrooms usually proceed from their bridal chambers adorned outwardly.

He himself, that is, the notable one. For although many adorned persons had entered this world, such as John the Baptist and others of that kind, he surpassed them all, because he alone was truly free among the dead.

He, I say, proceeding, rejoiced, that is, came joyfully into this world, not to remain there but to run a course, that is, to complete the course of this life. For he was born, grew, taught, and so forth.

And in rejoicing he was like a giant. A giant is both swift and strong. He too was swift, because no enticement held him back; and he was strong, because death could not overcome him but was itself conquered by him.

It is also said that giants had serpent-like feet; by this they are shown to be strong, although clinging to the earth and humble. Christ likewise was humble in mercy beneath all, but strong in majesty above all.

Again, a giant is tall in body, and Christ was truly tall in dignity, because his going forth is from the highest heaven, that is, his going forth from the bosom of the Father. The Father is the highest heaven because he is the first heaven—not in dignity or power, but in order, since he is from no other and is light in himself.

The Son is called the heaven of heaven because he is light from the Father, who is light. The Holy Spirit is called the heaven of heavens because he is light from lights. Concerning this going forth it is said: “His going forth is from the Father, and his return is to the Father,” and so forth. [Col. 0582A]

And his encounter. He calls his “encounter” his equality. For one thing is properly said to meet another when it is equal to it.

It is as if he were saying: When he had gone forth from the Father and had come into the world, he found nothing equal or comparable to himself until he returned again to the Father. For his encounter—that is, his equality—reaches to his summit, that is, to the highest heaven from which he proceeded.

And because he is so high, there is no one who can or ought to hide himself from his heat, that is, from knowledge of him.

This is said by way of comparison. If a great fire were burning in some house, its heat and brightness would penetrate every corner of the house and reach everyone dwelling there. Similarly, when Christ was placed in the middle of the world—that is, in Judea, which was enclosed by the nations—he shone forth like a burning fire.

He shone through miracles, and his knowledge grew hot in the word of preaching; through himself and through his preachers it reached everyone. We may also call his “heat” that love by which he handed himself over for us, which was announced to all through the preachers. Therefore no one can excuse himself through ignorance.

The preceding verse—namely, “He placed his tent in the sun”—can be connected and partly explained in another way, as having been spoken against heretics who said that Christ was present only among themselves. Thus the Africans affected by heresy in the time of blessed Augustine took their opportunity from that verse in the Song of Songs which says: “Where do you pasture at noon?” For they understood this literally and thought that it referred exclusively to themselves because of the location of their land.

We shall therefore say:

Because the sound of the apostles reached everyone, the glory of God placed its tent—that is, the Church, which is compared to a tent, as stated above—not merely in some corner of the earth, as the heretics say, but in the sun, that is, in an openly visible place, spreading it among all.

And it is in an openly visible place because he himself rejoiced like a giant, that is, his coming was exalted and manifest. [Col. 0582C]

Or he placed the Church itself through the apostles in the sun, that is, in labor. For the apostles did not teach bodily pleasure but labor, namely, that whoever followed Christ should walk as he himself walked.

And he placed it in labor because he too came to labor, not to pleasure. For he proceeded from his bridal chamber and rejoiced like a giant, as was said above. He came to run the course, that is, to complete the course of the obedience imposed upon him.

He completed it in this manner: he went forth from the highest heaven, that is, from the Father; he descended incarnate, was born, grew, taught, died, was buried, and rose again. And his encounter reached to his summit, that is, he ascended and sat at the Father’s right hand.

From there he sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, in fire to burn up the hay of the flesh, but to test and purify the gold of virtues. Thus they were strengthened and boldly announced his glory everywhere.

Therefore there is no one who can or ought to hide himself from his heat, that is, excuse himself from having received knowledge of him in the ordinary sense mentioned earlier, or from having felt the fervor both of the teaching and of the love that his Spirit bestowed upon the apostles and, through them, upon others. [Col. 0582D]

The law of the Lord is spotless. Truly no one ought to excuse himself from knowledge of him, but should willingly know him and, having received his law, accept the law of a servant.

For although the law of the servant was blemished with respect to the letter, since it said: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy,” and because it permitted a writ of divorce to be issued to wives, and other such things, through which it made many people blemished, the law of the Lord—that is, the new law of Christ—is spotless. It commands the opposite: both that one should love an enemy, and that “if anyone divorces his wife except on account of fornication and marries another, he has committed adultery,” and so forth.

And whereas the former law restrained the hand without instructing the mind, so as to restrain the affection, this law instructs souls, not by fear of punishment, but by turning them freely toward imitation of itself.

And whereas the testimony of the servant was unreliable, because it promised many things that did not occur according to the letter, the testimony of the Lord, that is, of Christ, concerning the Father is reliable, because whatever he testified concerning him is true. Hence it is said: “No one knows the Father except the Son, or the one to whom he wishes to reveal him.”

The Lord, I say, bestows wisdom, that is, true goods, and pure understanding upon little ones, that is, upon the humble. Hence it is said: “You have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones.” And again: “He resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

It should be understood that law and testimony are the same thing. It is called “law” insofar as it prohibits; “testimony,” insofar as it testifies to and affirms something.

The righteousness of the servant was also not straight, as when it commands that a woman caught in adultery be stoned, and so forth. The righteousness of the Lord—that is, the works that the Lord declares and commands to be righteous—is straight. For he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.

And he taught nothing except what he did. Whereas the former commandments saddened hearts, saying “an eye for an eye” and similar things, these gladden the hearts of his people, so that they rejoice in the things they imitate cheerfully and with love, not slavishly and with fear.

Every commandment of the Lord is also clear, that is, without the veil of carnal observances; it enlightens the eyes rather than dulling them, unlike the commandment of the servant, which outwardly sounded one way while inwardly concealing another.

The fear of the Lord is also holy—not that legal fear, which was punitive and dreaded the loss of temporal goods, the desire for which often causes the soul to commit fornication, but the chaste fear by which the Church, his bride, is more careful to avoid offending the bridegroom whom she loves, the more fervently she loves him.

Therefore perfect love does not cast out this fear, because it is not servile like the former but filial. For this reason it remains forever and ever, that is, eternally.

The judgments of the Lord are also not false like the judgments of the servant, which deceived people in confirming and promising according to the letter. Rather, they are true. Whether he threatens or promises something in the present, he does not deceive, since whatever he says must happen. Nor will anyone in the future be able to take away either rewards from the good or punishments from the wicked. All of this belongs to the judgments of the Lord.

These judgments are not made righteous by human opinion or favor, as were the judgments of the servant, but are justified in themselves, that is, they possess within themselves the quality by which they are righteous.

They are more desirable than gold and precious stone, that is, more desirable than everything pleasing to the sight and delightful among earthly things. The desire for such earthly things causes the judgments of God not to be desired: the guilty fear them, the arrogant and proud despise them, and fools do not believe them.

He sets down these two things as more precious than everything else, and he does so for the wise, not the foolish; for the faithful, not the unfaithful.

This may also be understood inwardly: a person may be “gold” through pure understanding and a “precious stone” through steadfastness of faith, so that he is not consumed by fire but is taken up into God’s treasury.

Such a person will desire the judgments of God above himself, that is, more than himself, because he has placed God’s will before his own.

The judgments of God are also sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, that is, sweeter than everything delightful to taste, or pleasant to a sound mind, not one afflicted by fever.

“Honey” is someone who, already freed from the bonds of this life, as though pressed out from the honeycomb, awaits the day on which he may enter God’s banquets.

The “honeycomb” is one who is still wrapped in this life—not hardened against it, but filling it. Such a person needs a certain pressure from the hand of God, not one that crushes but one that presses out, by which he may be strained from the present life into the eternal one.

For such people the judgments of the Lord are sweeter than all else, because they have placed his will before their own.

Indeed, your servant. The judgments of the Lord are so desirable because there is great reward in keeping them.

When every outward advantage has ceased, the reward is great: for the person who keeps them through true understanding, which they themselves give, they are pleasant in the present and health-giving in the future; for the person who does not keep them, they are harsh in the present and harmful in the future.

That there is a great reward in keeping them should be believed on the testimony of one who has experienced it. For your servant keeps them, that is, I, who wish to be my own freedman or your freedman, as Adam wished. Yet, being your servant in spirit, I keep them—not by speaking but by doing.

For to speak well and live badly is nothing other than to condemn oneself by one’s own voice. The prophet says this after turning to the Lord.

Who understands sins? Truly, understanding is found in keeping the judgments of God. In sins there is no understanding, but rather blindness.

He says this in the form of a question: Who, implicitly, while remaining in sins, understands sins? Certainly no one. Therefore, Lord, my Redeemer from evil and my helper in good—Redeemer so that I may begin, helper so that I may be perfected and arrive—cleanse me first from hidden things, that is, from evil thoughts and desires that secretly exist within me.

Then spare your servant from the sins of others, that is, remove from me the evil persuader. For a person must first be cleansed from his own sins before he can be spared from the sins of others.

Every sin is committed by someone either by himself or because another persuades him. Both kinds of fault became clear at the very beginning. The evil angel fell through what was hidden within himself, whereas Adam sinned through another’s persuasion.

Or we may say that he calls original sins “hidden,” because they descend secretly into everyone through the transmission of sin, and therefore he rightly says “my” sins. This is something hereditary.

He calls actual sins “others’,” as though they came from outside rather than by inheritance.

Or, conversely, we may call actual sins “hidden,” because the greater part of them is concealed from each person by his own conscience; and we may call original sins “others’,” because they came from elsewhere, that is, from the first father.

If they do not rule over me. The reference here is not to the words but to their meaning. As if he were saying: Therefore, Lord, I ask to be cleansed from hidden sins and from others’ sins, because if these enemies—namely, hidden vices and others’ sins—do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless, that is, without a capital crime.

And I shall also be cleansed from the greatest sin, that is, pride. It is called the greatest sin because it is the beginning of every sin; because it cast down the angel and made a devil from an angel; and because it shut him out from the kingdom of heaven.

It is also the greatest because, just as it is the first thing encountered by those departing, so it is the last thing encountered by those returning. This vice must also be avoided in good deeds.

And after I have been cleansed in this way, then not only my deeds but also the words of my mouth will be such as to please you, Lord; that is, they will be humble, not pompous.

And not only my words but also the meditation—that is, the thought—of my heart will always be such as is worthy to be in your sight, that is, pleasing to you. It will not be arrogant but humble.

# PSALM XIX  
## A psalm of David, for the end.

## ARGUMENT

The people, besieged by the Assyrians, pray for Hezekiah, their king. Alternatively, the prophet exhorts one who is working. The Church also speaks to Christ as he goes to the cross, as Arnobius holds.

## EXPLANATION

Now that the words of the title are known, let us discuss something from the text of the psalm.

The prophet, therefore, filled with illumination concerning future events, prays that prosperity may come to the holy Church, which he knew with certainty would come to it through the Lord’s coming.

At the first entrance, the prophet asks that Christ the Lord hear and receive the Church, wearied by the varied turmoil of the world.

Second, he prays that the Lord, in his mercy, confirm all its counsel and its right faith, promising that the faithful people will be magnified not by worldly piety but by divine power.

## COMMENTARY

May the Lord hear you. As stated above, this psalm is the same as the preceding one, because, although it deals with the same matter, it has not only the same title but also the same purpose.

For just as in the preceding psalm the prophet rebukes the hardness of the Jews, who did not recognize the time of their visitation, by speaking of the Lord’s manifest Incarnation and of the preaching of the apostles, so in this psalm also he openly rebukes them by speaking of his manifest resurrection and of the glory that followed the resurrection—namely, that many were saved and that all, by rising again and being glorified together, received salvation.

Here he speaks under the form of a wish, in order to express greater affection and to exhort those whom he rebukes. Thus, when they eventually come to their senses and recognize the time of their visitation, they may wish to be saved and to be conformed here to Christ, so that at last they may be glorified together with him: “If we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him.”

This psalm is connected with the preceding one. As if he were saying:

Lord, whom the heavens will announce, who will place your tent in the sun, and who are my helper and Redeemer: may the Lord the Father hear you, that is, raise you up as you cry out for glorification, in the day of tribulation, that is, at the time of the Passion, since the wicked will be permitted to afflict you.

This hearing was made manifest when, as he said, “Father, glorify me with the glory that I had before the world existed,” a voice descended from heaven saying: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again.”

And may he protect you, that is, your people. The name—that is, the praise and fame—of God, who, although he is God of all by power, is God by will of Jacob, that is, of the later and humble people, understood through the younger Jacob. They labor to glorify that name because they are Jacob, that is, the supplanters of the blessing promised to the former people, who are understood through Esau.

They purchase the birthright by food, that is, they acquire primacy and dignity, which had belonged, as it were, to the former people through their contempt for earthly things. For they direct their eyes not toward what is behind but toward what is within, that is, toward future goods.

And this is the glorification of such a name of God—as if he were saying: Let this be their protection.

May the Lord the Father also send help to you, that is, to your people, from the holy place, that is, from your holiness. In other words: May your holiness be help to your people.

And may he protect you, that is, your people, from Zion, that is, from contemplation, because they do not devote themselves to present things but contemplate future things from afar.

Or otherwise: May he send help to you from the holy place, that is, may he make a sanctified body for you, so that help may come from that holy place—that is, from the multiplication of the saints—through teaching and example, one saint from another.

And from Zion may he protect you, that is, may contemplation be protection for your people, as above.

May the Lord the Father also remember every sacrifice. That is, may he make your people mindful so that they imitate you in all your sufferings and tribulations, which you will endure before the cross and through which, as through sacrifices, you will reconcile God the Father to the human race.

And the burnt offering, that is, your entire sacrifice, when on the altar of the cross you will offer yourself wholly for us as a sacrificial victim of reconciliation—which is rightly understood through the burnt offering.

For “burnt offering” is interpreted as “wholly burned.” In former times there were sacrifices in which only part was burned for the gods, while the rest was retained for the feasts of those who offered the sacrifices. Other sacrifices, however, were wholly burned on the altar of the gods. These were called burnt offerings and were considered holier.

Similarly, here by “every sacrifice” we understand all the hardships that preceded the Passion, such as his capture, binding, and similar events, in which he sacrificed certain portions, so to speak, in relation to the burnt offering that followed, when he offered himself entirely on the altar of the cross.

Let that burnt offering, I say, be made fat, that is, pleasing to God the Father, so that it may be turned into joy—[the source reads: “revertantur”]. For fat victims were more acceptable than others, and therefore they were also commanded to be offered in the law.

And may the Lord grant you not according to the desire of your enemies, who wished to erase your name through death, but may he grant you the effect of your death according to your own desire. For you truly foresaw both what the humanity of divinity would accomplish and what the divinity of humanity would accomplish.

The dead humanity brought about the death of vices; the divinity, raising it again, brought about justification.

And may the Lord the Father confirm all your counsel in your death, namely, both concerning the blinding of the Jews and concerning the salvation of the Gentiles.

We shall rejoice in your salvation. So that the prophet, who lived so long beforehand, might not seem to have made this wish without cause, he adds the reason for it. As if he were saying:

Therefore, Lord, my Helper and Redeemer, I wish that the Lord the Father hear you in the glorification of the resurrection, because in your salvation—that is, in this salvation brought about by your resurrection—we shall rejoice.

That is, it is not only I, living so long beforehand, who rejoice, but all those like me will rejoice forever, up to that salvation which has already been given to us in him through hope. For we have been saved in hope, and finally we shall be magnified in the very glory of the resurrection, if in this life we have glorified the name of our God through humility and good works. [Col. 0586B]

May the Lord fulfill. He returns to the form of a wish, as if saying: Since we shall also rejoice, may the Lord fulfill, that is, complete, all your petitions—not only those that you will make on earth for glorification, but also those by which, exalted at the right hand of the Father, you will daily intercede for us.

For the very presence of Christ’s humanity continually prays to the Father for his own.

## Now I have known

Here he shows, for the greater reproach of the Jews’ hardness, that he was certain, so long beforehand, of Christ’s future resurrection. As though he were saying: Truly, the Lord will fulfill your petitions, both in you and in your members, because I have now known, so long beforehand, that the Lord God the Father will not merely save his Christ, but has already saved him in his ordering—wholly, that is, both in the Head and in the members. For he will raise up the Head and fit to him a suitable body. For the perfect Christ is the Head together with the body.

## He will hear

That is: truly he will save Christ in the body, [Col. 0586C] because he who heard him from the earth, when he was still mortal and passible, for his glorification, will hear him from heaven—that is, from the sublimity of impassibility and immortality—crying out for the body. Or heaven and earth may both be taken literally and materially.

And truly he will hear him for the body, because the salvation of the right hand—that is, of his favor and propitiation—will be in powers (*potentatibus*), that is, those saved through his grace will be saved potentially, because eternally. But the salvation of the left hand—that is, through present prosperity, of which it is said, “You will save humans and beasts, Lord”—is called “of the left hand,” not because there is anything sinister in God, but because it does not proceed from his worthy propitiation, since it is transitory and even deadly. That salvation, I say, will be in weaknesses, and this because those who are saved through it do not call upon God as they ought: they come to call upon him in chariots, that is, trusting in the revolving succession of temporal things. And they come in horses, [Col. 0586D] that is, in worldly pomp and arrogance, not, of course, to glorify the Lord’s name. For this is what the Jewish people did, placing their hope not in God but in earthly things; it was their custom, at least at Passover, to assemble at Jerusalem every year, to offer sacrifice and pray.

But we, who have been saved through the right hand, will call upon him—not in arrogance, but in glorifying the name of him whom, through voluntary servitude, we make both our Lord and our God, because, as creatures, we obey him as our Creator. Another Translation has here, instead of “We will call upon him,” “We will exult,” which fits quite well.

## They are bound

Therefore those saved through the left hand call upon him in this manner, because they are bound by earthly desires, rushing through excessive love of place and nation against the stone of stumbling and rock of offense; and because they love earthly things, they have fallen away from the face of heavenly things.

But we, on the contrary, have risen from earthly things into hope of heavenly things through faith, and have been raised upright by a good uplifting. Or: we have risen through invocation, and have been raised upright through faith.

And, that we may rise and be raised upright perfectly, O Lord Father, save this king of yours, in whom we will rejoice and through whom we will be powerfully saved, who will give us in his Passion an example of fighting, which pertains to a king; save him through the glorification of resurrection and ascension, so that, having become a priest at your right hand, he may constantly intercede for us. For it belongs to kings to fight, and to priests to pray and sacrifice.

And hear us, crying out through this Mediator in the day—that is, in purity of mind—in which we shall call upon you, whenever we call upon you.

# PSALM XX

**To the end. A Psalm of David.**

## ARGUMENT

A song concerning Hezekiah, after the Assyrians had been slain and his illness cured.

## EXPLANATION

[Col. 0587B]

This psalm first sings of the Lord Savior’s Incarnation, and afterward of the deeds of his divinity, so that you may plainly recognize that he is the Son both of the Virgin Mother and of God the Father. In the psalm’s first account, the prophet speaks to the Father about the Lord’s Incarnation; in the second, he describes his various virtues and his glory, declaring from the condition in which he suffered to what summit and pinnacle of affairs he attained. In the third, turning toward the Lord in the manner of those who desire, he prays that those things which he knows will come to pass may be accomplished at his judgment.

## COMMENTARY

### O Lord, in your strength

In this psalm also, as in the two preceding ones, the prophet rebukes the Jews’ hardness by commending Christ’s humility, which they refused to recognize, and by showing that they will one day experience him as harsh who now do not recognize him as humble. He thus urges them, when they come to their senses, to prefer recognizing him here as humble rather than finally encountering him as a severe judge coming in majesty.

The title is the same as in the two preceding psalms: “To the end. A Psalm of David.” This is explained as follows: This psalm is attributed to the prophet David and is to be referred to the end, that is, to Christ, whose humility, as we have said, it commends.

It is connected with what precedes in this way, as though he were saying: I have said, Lord, that you should save the king, and you ought to save him, because this king will presume nothing of himself and attribute nothing to himself, but will rejoice only in your strength—that is, in your Word joined to him—through which alone he will regard himself as strong. And he will greatly exult in your salvation, that is, in your salvation being over him, that is, in its being entrusted to him: namely, that through him you have determined both to reconcile the lowest things with the highest and to give life and salvation to all things.

### You have granted the desire of his heart

He will rightly rejoice in your strength, because through him you have already granted him strength by your predestination, since in reality you will grant him the desire of his heart, [Col. 0587D] that is, whatever his heart will desire, having already made him such that he desires nothing except what ought to be desired—namely, both to lay down his life for his own and to take it up again for his own. For he died because of our sins and rose because of our justification.

And you will not deprive him—that is, you will not deny him anything in the desire of his lips, that is, in his words—because whatever he asks of you, whether for his own salvation or that of his members, you will not deny him.

Or otherwise: You will not deprive him in the desire of his lips, that is, of the twofold peace which they wished to establish. Namely, you will grant his desire both that they leave peace and that they give peace. In accordance with this: “I leave peace with you; I give you my peace.” For he left peace to those who would follow him only in their interior, but to those who come to him he will give his peace, namely, so that they may have peace not only inwardly but in both respects. This twofold peace is understood as belonging to the lips, which is put in the plural. For we give a kiss with the lips, and a kiss is a sign of peace; thus peace is signified by the lip.

[Col. 0588A]

And otherwise: You will not deprive him by denying him the desire not only of himself but also of his lips, that is, of his heralds, who are rightly understood through the lips, since these are instruments of speech. Namely, you will grant his heralds what they desired: that where he is, they too may be. He asked this of the Father, saying: “Father, I will that where I am, there my own also may be.”

### For you have gone before him

Therefore you will grant him his desire and fulfill the desire of his lips, because you will make him such that he is worthy for his desire and will to be fulfilled. For he will not have been anticipated by the bitterness of gall with which we were all anticipated in Adam—that is, by original sin. Rather, in his very conception you will go before him, that is, fortify him, so that that sin may not reach him: in blessings, that is, in multiplied sweetness—namely, that he will be conceived without sin and born without pain.

And you will not give him the Spirit according to measure, and that he will be free from sin, and other such things.

And already you have placed—that is, you will place—upon his head, that is, either upon him who is the Head or at the beginning of his preaching, a crown: the multitude of apostles and other perfect people surrounding him. A crown, I say, made of every precious stone, that is, adorned with twelve precious gems, namely, the apostles, who rightly are gems because they shine both with virtues, proclamations, and signs.

### He asked for life

Truly you will grant him his desire, because he will ask life of you—that is, resurrection and eternity for himself and his own. And you have granted it to him—that is, you will truly grant him life—not just any life, but length of days, that is, eternal life; and not only to himself but to his own, because you will grant his own length of days through inner resurrection in the present and through outer resurrection in the future.

Length of days, I say, to be prolonged through the present age and through the age following this age—that is, into eternity.

### Great is his glory

You will indeed grant him life, and in this salvation of yours—that is, through this salvation of yours—his glory will be great: that is, his life and that of his own will be glorious and eternal, and you will make it magnificent. For through this you will place upon him, as upon a foundation, glory and great beauty: glorious men in virtues and very beautiful in miracles—or glorious in conscience, or very beautiful in virtues—not a few but many.

### For you will make him a blessing forever

That is, a multitude. “Forever and ever,” that is, eternally, because there will never be lacking perfect people who are joined to him as Head. And at last you will make him and his own joyful with complete and eternal joy before your face, that is, in their sitting at your right hand.

And rightly so, because this king does not presume upon himself, but hopes—that is, places his hope in you alone, Lord. And he will not be shaken through pride, placed in the mercy of the Most High, that is, established in the riches given him by you, who are Most High: namely, in freedom from sins and in the fullness of divinity singularly granted to him, just as the first man became proud in his riches, namely, in freedom of will and abundance of virtues.

### Let your hand be found

Here the prophet turns to the king himself, whose humility he has thus far commended while pitying the Jews’ hardness, since they did not perceive his humility.

As though he were saying: O Lord King, who will possess such great patience, may your hand—that is, your humble power, while it is not yet raised up to strike like the right hand—be found, that is, recognized in humility in the present by all your enemies, that is, by the Jews who oppose you.

But let your right hand—that is, your power—finally find all those who hate you, that is, those who in the present refused to recognize your humble hand for salvation, when it will already have been raised to strike in judgment, like the right hand.

This, however, is rejoicing in the divine sentence, not an imprecation.

### You will place them like a furnace

Truly your right hand will find those who hate you, because you will make them such that they are like a burning furnace. For just as the interior of a burning furnace is consumed, so they will be consumed by their own conscience in the time of your face, that is, of your manifestation and severity, namely, on the day of judgment.

And then the Lord will trouble them in his anger, that is: You, whom they previously refused to have as Lord in humility, will trouble them in your anger, that is, in anger appropriate to you, before which no servant will dare resist, when you say to them: “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire.”

And then that perpetual fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels, will devour them.

And truly they will be troubled, because you, Lord King, will destroy their fruit, that is, their evil works—not by consigning them to eternal oblivion so that they are not punished, but you will destroy them in this respect: because they separated themselves from the land of the living, they will lack the good reward.

And you will destroy their seed, that is, their imitators, separated from the children of true human beings, that is, from the good, who will imitate the patriarchs, apostles, and the other true human beings. For that very separation will be their destruction.

And rightly you will destroy their fruit, because those evils which they thought they would suffer while you reigned—namely, the loss of their place and nation—they have now avoided; that is, in their own estimation they will most certainly turn them back upon you in your death. And they will devise plans, namely, so that the world may not follow you and so that they themselves may obtain the kingdom.

These plans they could not establish, because “there is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord.”

### For you will place them

Therefore you will finally place them like a furnace of fire and trouble them, because they will not be participants in the first resurrection, so that they may then be participants in the second. Rather, they will be given over to a reprobate mind, because you will make them the back—that is, you will make them as contemptible as those who are the back, that is, whom you despise and do not regard.

But their face—that is, your knowledge, which ought to have been theirs through the law given to them—you will prepare for them after it has been taken away, that is, you will place it among the remnants, that is, among their descendants, who through humility will become your remnants, those remnants, namely, of which it was said: “And let the remnants be saved.”

Or otherwise: Their face—that is, what their will is like—you will prepare, that is, manifest, in your remnants, that is, in your lower member, namely, in your body, which they will crucify.

Or in your remnants, that is, in your apostles and saints, whom they will persecute. They will be remnants because of you, that is, the refuse and rejection of all.

Or otherwise: Their face—that is, what they most desire and seek—you will prepare, that is, manifest, in your remnants, that is, in their desire for place, nation, and the other temporal things for whose sake they will crucify you. These are your remnants, that is, the remnants of your people, whom they despise.

Or otherwise: Their face—that is, the knowledge which ought to have been theirs—you will prepare in their last descendants, those who will exist in the time of Antichrist; and you will do this through your remnants, that is, through Elijah and Enoch, whom you preserve alive for this purpose.

### Be exalted, O Lord

You will indeed place them, for the present, among the back, and at last destroy them because they refused to recognize your humility. But you, Lord, whose strength they considered weakness when they said, “God has abandoned him,” be exalted—that is, appear exalted and great in your strength—by rising again, ascending, and sending the Holy Spirit.

And then we, who recognized you beforehand in your humility, will sing and chant your powers, that is, we will celebrate your powers with our mouths and celebrate them also in our deeds.

# PSALM XXI

**To the end, for the morning reception. A Psalm of David.**

## ARGUMENT

David, suffering under Absalom’s faction, entreats the Lord.

Alternatively, the Jews think that this psalm was sung concerning Esther, namely, because through her danger and intercession with the king the people of Israel were released from death.

## EXPLANATION

Whether “to the end” or “David” is understood as referring to Christ is known. The morning reception indicates the time of the resurrection, when he took up his mortal body, having laid aside the condition of the old man, glorified in great glory.

In Hebrew, however, it is written: “For the morning hind,” by which the same Lord is undoubtedly signified—he who killed serpents and consumed poisons, and who, while the Jews persecuted him with canine rage, sought the heights of heaven.

Throughout the psalm the Lord Christ speaks, but in the first part he cries out that he has been abandoned by the Father, showing that he received the Passion as a dispensation and commending his most powerful humility through the rejection of human beings. In the second part he prophesies the sacred Passion through various comparisons, praying that, while his enemies rage in this way, he may be delivered by divine protection. In the third he admonishes Christians to praise the Lord, who through his resurrection has regarded his catholic Church, lest, hearing only of the Passion, the hearts of mortals should be afraid.

## COMMENTARY

### My God, my God, look upon me

This psalm is titled as follows: “To the end, for the morning reception. A Psalm of David.” This is explained in the following way: This psalm is attributed to David—not to the historical David, but to David “to the end,” that is, to Christ, toward whom, as toward the end, that is, perfection, all things tend.

I say that the psalm was spoken or sung by him for the morning reception. Some books have “for the morning assumption,” which amounts to the same thing. The morning reception or assumption is itself called the resurrection.

For when the Lord was assumed into eternal life, he received the flesh that he had laid aside—mortal, passible, and corruptible—made immortal, impassible, and incorruptible. This reception is called “morning,” either because historically it took place in the morning of the first day of the Sabbaths, or because it is called morning even if it took place not in the morning but beforehand, since, just as the morning time, which is called morning, like the first dawn, drives away the darkness of night and introduces the first light of day, so in the Lord’s resurrection the cloud of preceding sins departed from us and the sun of justice shone upon us.

For just as Christ died for sins, so he also rose for our justification.

This psalm, then, was called “for the morning reception,” that is, for the resurrection, because in it our Lord prays to God the Father not to delay his resurrection until the common resurrection of all. And he did not delay it, because he raised him on the third day.

It should be understood, however, that although this psalm is titled as concerning the resurrection, it first speaks at length about the Passion, which is the cause of the resurrection. Hence, once the Passion has been made clear, what is said about the resurrection is more suitably understood.

And in this psalm our Lord explains his Passion to us more carefully than in any other, because he sets before us both what he suffered and why he suffered, to exhort us to imitate both as far as we can: namely, both to rejoice in his Incarnation and to be conformed to his Passion, so that we may also rejoice in his resurrection, and so that whoever hears may say, “Come.”

It should also be noted that in Hebrew the title reads, “For the morning hind,” which is understood quite appropriately. For it is said that the nature of hinds is, when the darkness of night has been driven away and the light of day rises, to seek the heights from the depths with a certain natural joy.

Thus Christ’s flesh is rightly compared to a hind: in the resurrection, freed from the darkness of former tribulations, it sought, as it were, the depths from the heights [read: the heights from the depths], with joy and great gladness, when it rose from the corruption of mortality into the incorruption of eternity. He used the feminine form, “hind,” because he compared it to flesh, which is of the same gender.

Now let us come to the literal meaning.

The first six verses of this psalm can be read in two ways: either so that the Head speaks for himself in them, in the person of the old man who was crucified with him—that is, in the person of his members, whose oldness, that is, sins, he himself, who did not commit sin, crucified in himself.

For by his death he destroyed our weaknesses and healed our wounds by his wounds.

According to this interpretation, the meaning is as follows: Lord Father, God of all by nature but my God uniquely by grace granted to me above others, look upon me, that is, upon my members, whom long ago you saw in the first parent when he was placed in an abundance of virtues, but who lost that sight through his disobedience. Look upon them, I say, through my obedience, for this regard is necessary, because you abandoned them in this respect: the oldness of sin has prevailed.

And why did you abandon me, that is, my members? Because their sins have made you far from my salvation, that is, from the salvation of my members. For salvation is far from sinners.

These words clearly imply that the Head is not speaking here in his own person. For how could the one who, since he is the Son of God, is God, and of whom it was said, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself,” be abandoned or made far from salvation? And again: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” This Word, incarnate, hung upon the cross and spoke such words. Certainly this could not be.

[Col. 0591B]

And because, although he spoke these things in the person of his members, the words nevertheless seem to sound as though they concern what he himself did, it is added, after this has been determined: “the words of my sins.”

As though he were saying: The words I have now spoken—“Look upon me,” “You have abandoned me,” and the rest—are not words of justice spoken in my own person, but are “words of sins,” that is, they are utterances spoken in the person of the members on account of their sins. I made those sins mine because I transferred their punishment to myself, so that they might also make my justice theirs.

For otherwise it is impious to understand this of him who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found.

### My God, I will cry out by day

He shows that his members have truly been abandoned, because they are not heard either in prosperity or in adversity.

As though he were saying: Truly you have abandoned my members. For I, that is, my members, will cry out to you by day, that is, in temporal prosperity, so that it may not be changed. And they will cry out in the night, that is, in adversity, so that it may be changed for the better.

And yet, because they will cry out with the impure words of sins, you will not hear them. And that you do not hear them I do not regard as happening to me, that is, to my members, for folly, that is, so that they become foolish, but for wisdom: so that they may understand that you wish them to cry out not with the impure words of sins, seeking temporal things to their condemnation, but with words of a new conversion to you for eternal life.

It should be understood that God’s failure to hear his own in tribulation is for their great benefit: namely, so that they may understand that he is the physician and tribulation is medicine for salvation, not punishment for condemnation. It is as when someone placed under a treatment cries out while being cut or burned: the physician does not hear him according to his desire, but according to his health.

It greatly benefited Paul that he was not heard concerning the thorn of the flesh, because his virtue shone forth more greatly in weakness; and because he cried out with the words of sins, that is, for temporal health, he ought not to have been heard. For whoever asks for temporal advantage cries out with the words of sins.

If someone asks why God does not hear his own in tribulation when they cry out with the impure words of sins, while he has heard certain people who seem to have cried out in this way—such as the three youths, whom he delivered from the furnace of fire; Daniel, from the pit; and Susanna, from the false accusation—let him know that they did not cry out with the words of sins, and that they were delivered bodily for this sole reason: so that their salvation might serve as an example to others.

Nor should it be passed over that, just as some are not heard outwardly while they are nevertheless heard most fully inwardly for salvation, so some are heard to their condemnation. Thus the devil was heard in the persecution of blessed Job, but he was heard to condemnation.

### But you dwell in the holy one

That you do not hear my members in tribulation is not indeed for folly, but it is for wisdom.

You who dwell in the holy one—that is, in the one whom, because you do not hear him, you make holier—do so so that he may understand that he has not been heard for salvation. For those in whom you dwell are certainly made better by tribulation.

Or it is as gold will be tested by fire: if at some time an enemy seeks to touch one of them, either through bodily suffering, some external loss, or even the death of his loved ones, and he is permitted to do so, may the one who is touched keep a firm heart in him who does not withdraw himself—that is, in God. For even if he withdraws his ear from one who weeps outwardly, he nevertheless applies mercy to one who prays inwardly.

For he knows how to refresh us, who made us—you, I say, who are the praise of Israel, that is, who make everyone who is Israel praiseworthy: one who fixes his attention upon you and does not presume upon himself, so as to stretch his hand, contrary to what is forbidden, toward illicit things, as Adam did.

### In you they hoped

Here he removes the notion that it is through God’s injustice that he does not hear his own when they cry out. Rather, it is through their fault, because they cry out with the impure words of sins.

For if they cried out worthily, he would hear them, as he often heard the earlier fathers—the patriarchs—and those whom he led out of Egypt, because they cried out worthily, that is, with words of justice.

He says this as follows: Our fathers, that is, our predecessors [Col. 0592B] from the earlier people, hoped, that is, placed their hope in you, Lord, and not in themselves. They hoped worthily, I say, and you delivered them. They also cried out not with words of sins but to you, that is, they cried out with words of justice, and therefore they were truly saved by you, because they hoped in you and not in themselves; and they were not confounded, that is, their hope did not deceive them.

The repetition of “they hoped” so many times is not pointless, but is repetition for confirmation.

### But I

The fathers, crying out with words of justice, were heard. But I—now no longer speaking in the person of the old man, but speaking as myself, that is, with words of justice—say according to what I am that I am a worm, because I am both mortal and born from a virgin without the joining of a man, just as a worm is born from matter without a father. And I am not merely a human being, because of the Word joined to me.

As though he were saying: I, who was made in a human being beyond a human being, so that human pride might at least thereby deign to imitate my humility, and in whom I surpass the justice of the fathers and of all human beings, am nevertheless as one not heard by you, Lord, while I transfer the weakness of my members into myself and, as one weak, pray as their example.

In this respect I am not heard: I have been made the reproach of human beings, to such an extent that they even impute me to others as a reproach. For the Jews regarded it as the greatest reproach when they said to the blind man concerning him: “You are his disciple,” and so forth.

And I have not been made the reproach of just any human beings, but I am the rejection of the people, that is, I have been despised by all the common people.

This is as though he were saying: It was not for this reason, Lord, that I was made—that you should not hear me, although I am in a human being above a human being—but because you determined to complete through my death the salvation promised to the human race.

At this point blessed Augustine says something that fits this interpretation quite well, namely:

> Did the one who heard the fathers when they cried out to him fail when it came to the Son? Certainly he did not fail, but truly heard him, because through him he fulfilled the salvation promised before the ages. Nor should it be believed that Christ said for himself, as though fearing death, “Father, if it is possible, take this cup from me,” and similar words. Rather, he said this from our weakness, so that he might strengthen us, though fearful, to imitate his Passion. For Paul did not fear death, who said, “I desire to depart.” Lawrence did not fear it, nor Stephen, nor the others of this kind. How, then, would it be fitting that what a soldier could do, a commander could not? Certainly, in no way.

Now let us repeat from the beginning, so that in the verses mentioned above the Head may speak in his own person. According to this, the usual text may be read quite suitably: “Look upon me.” The meaning is as follows:

Lord God of all by nature, but my God by grace, do not look upon those who insult me by saying, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross,” but look upon me in my humility, so that your regard may appear in me—namely, so that you may make me rise from the tomb, not descend from the cross.

For it was far more glorious and fitting that the Lord, having completed his obedience, should rise from the dead against their expectation than that, as though unable to endure, he should descend from the cross at the voice of those who insulted him. Moreover, if he had descended, he would have seemed to obey their request and thus to strengthen their wickedness.

Look upon me, I say, because you have abandoned me—that is, you seem to have abandoned me outwardly, since you allow me to suffer the most shameful death at the hands of my enemies.

And why have you abandoned me in this way? Because the words of my sins—that is, the manifest sins of my members—make you far from my salvation, namely, my outward salvation. For they seek this: that you should not save me outwardly in the body, but allow me then to die outwardly on the cross, so that through my death those sins may be destroyed.

### My God, I will cry out

Therefore I seem to have been abandoned by you, because I will cry out both in myself and in my members, and you will not hear me.

Here we should understand the cry as one that he did not make for himself but for our weakness, so that when he says, “Father, if it is possible,” and similar words—where, according to the literal sense, he seems outwardly not to have been heard—he was nevertheless truly heard according to what he intended in his heart, not only in these matters but wherever he wished.

In this interpretation “day” means his flesh, freed from the darkness of sins. “Night” means Paul and the other faithful, who, however perfect they may be, are nevertheless not free from sin, in accordance with the saying: “If we say that we have no sin,” and so forth.

They are rightly called “night” in comparison with the Lord’s humanity.

The text will therefore be understood as follows: I will cry out by day, that is, through my own body, which is day. And I will cry out in the night, that is, in my members, who in comparison with me will be night. And yet you will not hear me, that is, I will seem not to have been heard, nor will my members seem to have been heard. And this failure to be heard will not be for me or my members unto folly, but rather unto wisdom, as was said above.

### But you

This is added lest the Father seem to have despised the Son because he was not heard.

As though he were saying: I seem indeed not to have been heard, and in this I seem to have been despised. But you do not despise me, because you dwell in your holy one within me. For “God was in Christ,” and so forth. You, I say, are the praise of Israel, as above.

### In you they hoped

This is connected with the first verse as follows: It is no wonder if I seem to have been abandoned by you, Lord, because, although you formerly heard the fathers even when they cried out for earthly things, you seem not to hear me when I cry out worthily.

The text is explained in the same way as before, except that hoping, crying out, being delivered, and being saved are here referred to earthly things. Earthly things here mean victory over enemies, the water that flowed from the rock in the desert, and other such matters, for which the fathers were heard.

### But I

The fathers were indeed heard, but I seem not to have been heard because I am a worm: my enemies neglect to condemn me, just as a worm is disregarded by one who tramples it; and I am as though I were not a human being, that is, as though no regard for humanity were shown toward me.

This is truly thought of me, because I have been made the reproach of human beings and the rejection of the people, as stated above.

[Col. 0593D]

### All who see me

As though he were saying: I have been made the reproach and rejection in this way because all who see me have mocked me and spoken about me, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews,” and similar things.

With their lips alone and not with their hearts, and they moved the head of their body, insulting me outwardly, because earlier they had moved their head—that is, their mind—inwardly away from true contemplation, so that they would not understand me as one who is over the needy and poor.

They, I say, spoke to one another about me: “He hoped,” that is, he says that he placed his hope in the Lord; therefore let the Lord rescue him, so that he may not be afflicted by us, and let him save him, so that he may not suffer death.

He truly will do this, for, they say, “the Lord himself desires him,” that is, loves him. This is said ironically.

### For you are he

Therefore they despise me in this way because they pay attention to nothing in me except human weakness. And this is because you drew me from my mother’s womb, that is, made me a human being. For this is the common law of all who are born: they are drawn from the womb.

[Col. 0594A]

Or: “You are he who drew me,” and so forth, that is: You alone are holy by grace; you were the way by which I was born from the Virgin, not a human father. Through this I seem to be contrary to them, because I am unlike them.

And you are my hope, that is, I made you my hope from my mother’s breasts, that is, because of the human weakness which I took from my mother. For according to you, you are not my hope, but my Father before all ages. And from the womb—that is, from my humanity—I have this: that I have been cast upon you in hope. From grace I have this: that, because you freed me from sins, I have been cast—that is, cast far forth—upon you, because I trust in you more than others do.

And this is because you are my God, that is, you have become my Creator—not according to the Word, which is coeternal and consubstantial with you, but from my mother’s womb, that is, according to the humanity assumed from my mother.

These two verses can also be understood in another way and connected as follows:

The Jews say such shameful things against me because I do not agree with their carnal law. For you, Lord, drew me from the womb of my mother, the Synagogue, that is, you made me not be enclosed in the darkness of carnal observances, placing salvation for me in them, though they are like the womb of the Synagogue, consuming many.

Whoever has not yet been reborn into the light of Christ is enclosed in the darkness of that womb if he places a firm hope of salvation in the carnal observance of the Sabbath, circumcision, and other such things.

And you have become my hope, that is, the hope of me, removed through you from the breasts of my mother, the Synagogue, so that I would not suck, as though from breasts, carnal observances, taking delight in them as they do.

And from the womb I have been cast upon the earth, that is, the womb of my mother, the Synagogue, which did not carry me, cast me out from itself. Yet I did not fall, because, having been cast out, I was placed in you: you did not permit me to slip into sins, but raised me up in spiritual things.

And you are my God from my mother’s womb, that is, the womb of my mother, the Synagogue, could not bring it about that, like a little child, I should forget you. Rather, I established you as my God, that is, my defender and helper.

Therefore, Lord, do not depart from me, [Col. 0594C] that is, do not withdraw your help from me, or do not delay my resurrection until the common resurrection of all.

Because tribulation is near. Therefore, do not depart, because tribulation is near—that is, the weakness of mortality and susceptibility to suffering, through which I am subject to tribulation, is near me because it is within me. Or, “tribulation is near” means that those who will trouble me are already around me. And there is no one to help me; therefore I especially need your help.
