Nor is this without cause, for many calves have surrounded me—that is, a multitude of the wanton people has surrounded me for my condemnation—and fat bulls, that is, their rulers, proud in earthly prosperity, have besieged me as one accused and destined for condemnation.

And they have opened their mouth against me, not yours: that is, they condemned me not on the basis of the judgments of Scripture, but according to their own desires. They, I say, were like a lion ready to devour, one that seizes and roars. The Jews were a seizing lion when they seized and bound the Lord and brought him to the chief priests; they were a roaring lion when with one voice they said to Pilate, “Crucify him, crucify him.”

Like water poured out. They opened their mouth, I say, and in this way I was poured out—that is, I was condemned by them contemptuously, without any caution or care—just as water is poured out more carelessly than other liquids. Therefore all my bones, that is, all the stronger among my people, were scattered. Hence it is said: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.” And because the bones were scattered, therefore my heart—that is, the teaching of Scripture, which is my heart because it deals especially with what is within me, namely, with divinity, and which had previously been firm—became melting, that is, pliable, and weak, in the midst of my belly, that is, in the heart of my people, who were more tender and weaker, just as the belly is softer than the other parts of the body.

In brief, the meaning is this: The proclamations of Scripture, which testified that salvation would come to the world through me and which had previously been firmly believed by my people, became doubtful among the less perfect when they saw me condemned to death. Hence two of them, as he went with them on the road to the resurrection, became almost doubtful and said: “We had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel.” And because the heart became melting—that is, my power, which had previously seemed solid and firm, dried up, that is, became contemptible like earthenware, being made fragile—therefore my tongue, that is, the tongue of my people, clung to their jaws, that is, all my heralds fell silent.

And this happened because you brought me, in their estimation, into the dust of death: that is, they thought that I, like any ordinary dead man, would be reduced to dust and would not be raised by you.

These three verses just mentioned can also be explained otherwise, if in “I was poured out like water” a different comparison is understood. Water that is poured out both prepares a fall, washes away filth, and irrigates the earth upon which it is poured. So also the death of Christ prepared a fall for his persecutors, the Jews—if not outwardly, at least inwardly, through blindness of mind, for blindness happened in part to Israel—and washed away the filth of sins in believers, and watered the hearts of the faithful with the rain of teaching. Hence it is said of him: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel.”

According to these different comparisons, what follows is also differentiated accordingly. “I was poured out like water,” that is, by my condemnation I prepared for certain people the ruin of their minds. Therefore, while those people were persecuting me, all my bones—that is, the apostles and all my stronger members—were scattered, that is, disturbed and driven everywhere. And because the bones were scattered, my heart, and so forth, also came to be disturbed—that is, the weaker were also thrown into confusion.

The wording in the following reading does not change. According to the other comparison, it will be said as follows: “I was poured out like water,” because I both washed and irrigated; and I washed and irrigated in this way because all my bones—that is, all my apostles and heralds—were scattered to preach throughout the whole world. In this way my heart—that is, the teaching of Scripture, which had previously been difficult to understand—became through them melting like wax, that is, soft and intelligible, even in the midst of my belly, that is, in the heart of the weak.

And through this my power, which had previously been thought soft and weak, dried up—that is, became hard and strong—in the hearts of my people, like earthenware refired in a furnace. And my tongue, that is, the tongue of my people, clung to their jaws: that is, it spoke so incessantly and rapidly in preaching that it seemed unable to remain still even for a moment, but rather, as it were, to cling to the jaws and continually bring forth words. And because the preaching of my people increased through this, you, Lord, brought me into the dust of death—that is, into the knowledge of the Gentiles, who had previously been mortal dust because they had not received the rain of the divine word, or who had been covered and defiled with the dust of sins even unto death.

Because they have surrounded me. Therefore you brought me into the knowledge of the nations, because those to whom you had first sent me—that is, the Jews—rejected me, since they surrounded me like dogs.

According to the other interpretation of “the dust of death,” this verse will be connected more remotely as follows: Therefore I ask, Lord, that you not depart from me, because dogs—that is, the Jews, barking more from habit than from truth—not a few but many, have surrounded me, not in order to imitate me but to condemn me.

And truly they were many, because the council—that is, the entire assembly of the malignant Jews—besieged me in the court of condemnation, so that I might not escape. And while besieging me, they pierced my hands and my feet, fastening them with nails to the cross. They counted all my bones, that is, they stretched me out on the cross so that they could count all my bones.

And yet those who above all ought to have honored me—the ones whose dead I had raised, whose sick I had healed, and to whom I had been sent—those very people truly, that is, in reality, regarded me. They saw me together, great and small alike, fixing their eyes upon my flesh but not reaching my divinity. And they looked upon me, that is, they made themselves a spectacle in me in which they could rejoice.

And as they crucified me, they divided my remaining garments among themselves. But my better garment, namely the seamless tunic, they did not divide, because it was precious; instead, they cast lots over it to determine who would receive it whole. This was done not by their will but by divine providence.

These two verses, which we have interpreted historically, can also be understood spiritually, so that the meaning is as follows: Not only did the Jews, who besieged me, rise up against me, who was the green wood, but also against the dry wood, that is, against my members, and inflicted many evils upon them. For they pierced—that is, mangled—my hands, meaning the greater ones among my people, in whom I worked not only through speech but also through the wondrous signs of miracles, namely the apostles who preached while the Lord worked with them, and so forth.

And they pierced my feet, that is, my lesser heralds, who, although they did not shine with miracles to the same extent, were nevertheless my feet, carrying me into the knowledge of human beings. And they counted all my bones, that is, all those in whom some strength of virtue appeared, not in order to imitate them but to condemn them.

And those who ought to have honored them rather than persecuted them, because they too, like me, were principally sent to them, looked upon them in their tribulations and treated them as a spectacle. And some of them divided my garments among themselves, that is, my imitators, both apostles and others, concerning whom it is said: “I live, says the Lord, because you will clothe yourselves with all these as with a garment.” So did the Corinthians, who thought that the grace of baptism varied according to the merits of those who baptized, saying: “I am of Cephas,” “I am of Paul,” “I am of Apollos,” and similar things.

Or we may understand the garments as the sacraments of the Church, with which Christ himself is covered and, as it were, clothed. These sacraments too they received in different ways. Some said that in baptism only actual sins were remitted, not original sin; others said that only original sin was remitted, and so forth. Here a fraudulent persecution carried out by heretics is indicated; above, a violent one.

And over my garment. This should be referred not to evil, as the preceding passages were, but to good. Yet it is spoken of the same people mentioned above in connection with those evils, who were eventually converted. Nor is this surprising, since no one has been saved except from among sinners.

Here the seamless garment of the Lord, woven from above, is understood as the unity of faith and charity. It was woven from above because it first proceeded from God, who loved us first, so that he gave his only-begotten Son for us. This garment is not torn, because the unity of faith is given to each person—not divided, but whole—and a lot is cast over it because it is given to no one through the exaltation of merits, but solely through grace, which is signified by the lot. Therefore the lot is rightly placed over it, because grace precedes.

The meaning is this: “They cast lots over my garments,” that is, whoever among them received my garment—the unity of faith—cast a lot over it, that is, understood that they had received it not from merits but from grace.

But you, Lord. They persecute both me and my people in this way; but you, Lord Father, do not withdraw your help from me and from my people. Rather, look upon me for the defense of me and mine, in this manner: Rescue my soul through the resurrection from the sword, that is, from the sentence of my enemies, which kills like a sword, since they say of me: “God has abandoned him.”

And rescue my only one, my bride, the Church whom I love uniquely, from the hand of the dog, that is, from the power of every hostile adversary who contradicts her. And save me from the mouth of the lion, that is, grant perseverance to my people, so that they may not be devoured by the mouth of a people prepared to consume them like a lion.

And save my humility, that is, save me in my humility from the horns of the unicorns, that is, from the pride and arrogance of the Jews, who exalt themselves through the singular pride of their righteousness. The unicorn is an animal with one horn. The Jews are compared to it because they seemed to have one horn: they trusted only in one covenant and in earthly promises, not in heavenly ones.

I will tell of your name. Up to this point he has shown that he suffered; he also inserted material concerning the resurrection, both in these two preceding verses and above, where he said, “Do not depart from me.” Now he begins to show why he suffered.

It is as though he said: I ask that I and my people be saved for this reason: I and my people will tell of your name, that is, of your glory and praise—namely, that from sinners you make righteous people, and from those condemned you take people into the kingdom—to my brothers, that is, to others reborn from the same spiritual fruit from which I was born.

And I and my people will praise you in the midst of the Church, that is, not merely in a Church consisting of Jews, but in the catholic Church, that is, in the universal Church, whose one wall came from the Jews and the other from the Gentiles, joined together through the cornerstone.

Or, because each individual believer is also called a church, we can say: “I will praise you in the midst of the Church,” that is, in the heart of each believer, who is a member of the Church.

I will praise you, then, saying this: All who fear the Lord with chaste fear, not servile fear, praise him with true praise—that is, by their works, not by their mouths.

By those who fear the Lord I understand the seed of Jacob and the seed of Israel, and therefore the whole seed: all of you who are imitators of the later Jacob, to whom the elder will serve, because you are true supplanters of vices. You, I say, glorify the Lord not only with your mouths but also with your works.

And all the seed of Israel, that is, all those who, although previously the seed of Jacob—that is, reborn in faith, which is understood through Jacob—have become the seed of Israel, that is, restored to vision and true contemplation, just as the same person formerly called Jacob deserved to be called Israel.

All these, I say, fear the Lord with true and chaste fear, for he is rightly feared and praised both by me and by them.

For he did not despise the condition of the poor in me, nor did he disdain the supplication made by me for the sins of my people, such as this: “Father, preserve those whom you have given me,” and similar prayers.

And truly he did not disdain it, because he did not turn his face away from me or from my people—that is, his presence and goodwill—for he heard me on behalf of myself and my people when I cried to him.

With you is my praise. Here he turns to the Lord. It is as though he said: You heard me for this reason, because my praise is with you, that is, I seek praise from no one except you. Or I desire that you also be praised in me, and that I be praised in you, in a Church that is not small but great.

The Church was small when Peter, who represented it, became afraid at the voice of a servant girl and denied Christ. But it was great when that same Peter, after the grace of the Holy Spirit had been sent from heaven in fire upon the apostles, said before tyrants and rulers: “We must obey God rather than you.”

This can also be distinguished otherwise, so that it is read independently: “My praise is with you, and my vows”—that is, the vows I made when I offered myself upon the altar of the cross—“I will repay in the great Church,” that is, I will offer myself again through the daily sacrifices of my people in the sacraments.

I say that I will truly repay the same vows in the presence of those who fear him, that is, insofar as good people understand them; they are not the same in the presence of the wicked, who understand nothing in the sacraments except what appears outwardly.

Or otherwise: “I will repay the vows that I offered upon the altar of the cross,” that is, I will give myself again in my people, who will offer themselves just as I offered myself.

I say that I will repay them in the presence of—that is, in the soul of—those who fear the Lord. In that soul they see the truth, because even if they do not suffer outwardly, they will nevertheless always be prepared in soul, so that, if the occasion arises, just as I laid down my soul for all, they too will not hesitate to lay down their souls for their brothers.

The poor shall eat. I will repay the vows of which the poor shall eat. That is, those who despise the world will truly eat them, if the reference is to the sacraments; and they will be eternally satisfied, because in the bread and wine visibly set before them they will understand another, invisible reality, namely the true body and true blood of the Lord. These are true food and true drink, by which the belly is not distended but the mind is fattened.

But if the passage is referred to the Passion, it will be understood as follows: “The poor shall eat my vows,” that is, they will take delight in my Passion as someone takes delight in a pleasant dish; but they will be satisfied, that is, they will imitate me. Imitation itself is the true eruption of satiety: once satisfied, they will neither fear the poverty of this world nor desire its abundance.

Then they will praise the Lord with true praise—those who, although they had sought him in Adam before he sinned and had lost him in that same Adam through disobedience, now seek him through faith and good works. They will praise him because, although their bodies die on account of sins, their hearts will nevertheless live through faith and good works for ever and ever, that is, eternally.

And through this they will live. They will remember God in thought and deed, as though previously forgetful of him. Thus those who had formerly turned away will be wholly converted to the Lord, so that they may fulfill his will—namely, all the ends of the earth, that is, all who have now brought all earthly-mindedness within themselves to an end.

And when converted they will worship the Lord, revere him, and praise him—not hypocritically, but in his presence, that is, in the heart, where he sees. This will not be done by many only, but by all the families of the nations: no family among the Gentiles will remain that does not worship God.

He uses “families” for the various nations, such as the Scots, Britons, and others. Hence in another translation we also find: “all the nations of the Gentiles.”

And rightly all the nations will worship the Lord, because they are the Lord’s kingdom; therefore he will rule in them.

All the fat ones have eaten. Not only will the poor eat of my vows, but also all the fat ones of the earth, that is, every kind of wealthy person concerned with earthly things—those who have alienated nothing earthly from themselves. They will eat my vows with the poor in reality, insofar as the reference is to the sacraments.

And they will worship, because they will approach with a certain outward reverence. Or “they will eat” means that they will take pleasure in my Passion. And they will worship while pretending to possess my true reverence; but they will not be satisfied, because all who descend into the earth—that is, those who take pleasure only in earthly things, or who attend to nothing in the sacraments except what is earthly and visible—will fall, that is, they will suffer the fall of eternal condemnation, in his presence, that is, in the soul where he sees, whom they thought they could deceive.

And my soul. They indeed will fall, but my soul, that is, the soul of my people, will not fall here; rather, it will stand, because it will live not for itself but for him, and will do not its own will but God’s.

Hence the Apostle says: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

And my seed, that is, the imitators of my people, will serve him, namely the Lord, the Father, whose purchased servants they are.

And rightly they will live and serve him, because the true generation that is to come—a spiritual generation, not a carnal one—will be announced, that is, attributed, not to Peter, or Paul, or any other person, but to the Lord alone.

Observe the parallel. In the Law it was commanded that if a man who had taken a wife died without children, his brother should marry the same woman in order to raise up offspring for his deceased brother, and that the children born should be called not by the name of the living man but by the name of the deceased.

So Christ also took his bride, namely the Church, which was almost barren while he was alive, because she bore few children. But after Christ died upon the altar of the cross, his brothers, namely the apostles, took up his bride, the Church, and begot many children in her through the word of preaching. All of them are called by the name of the deceased, not by their own names. They are called Christians and children of God, not Petrines or Paulines.

Hence it is rightly said: “A generation to come shall be announced to the Lord.” And it is to come for this reason: The heavens, that is, the apostles and other holy heralds, will announce his righteousness, that is, his perfect obedience. It will belong to the people who will be born—not carnally, but whom the Lord will cause to be born through the Holy Spirit in faith and good works—whose workmanship and creation, as the Apostle says, we are.

# ON PSALM XXII

Psalm of David.

## ARGUMENT

He foretells the people’s return from Babylon, recounting with how many consolations from God those returning were sustained on the journey and with what abundance of goods they were endowed after their return. Likewise, it is the voice of the Church after baptism, addressed to Esther. Alternatively: since in the twenty-first psalm we had the tribulation of the Passion, in the twenty-second we receive the joy of the resurrection.

## EXPLANATION

The Christian reborn in baptism speaks throughout the whole psalm, giving thanks because he has been led from the aridity of sin to pastures and to the water of refreshment.

It should be noted that just as previously he received the Decalogue of the Law, so here he rejoices that he has been enriched with ten benefits. Because this psalm has no division according to persons but according to subject matter, we have attached not divisions, as in other psalms, but the numerical letters to each individual section.

## COMMENTARY

The Lord governs me. The psalm is attributed to David, that is, to every perfect soul.

In this psalm there is the voice either of each perfect member of the Church or of the whole Church, contemplating the great and innumerable benefits bestowed upon it by Christ, the true shepherd, and rejoicing in them while commending them to its companions, that is, to its descendants. Those who have not yet experienced how sweet these benefits are should hasten to experience them and not delay turning to God. Those who have experienced them should strive to be refreshed for the better by those most abundant pastures by which the belly is not distended but the mind is fattened.

The meaning is therefore as follows: It is as though he said, “Adam, the perverter, distorted me, but the Lord—that is, Christ, who is the true shepherd—governs me, so that I may not stray from the true pastures.” Or, according to another Translation, “He feeds me,” so that, with him governing me, I will lack nothing necessary.

For even if the good suffer some want outwardly, nevertheless nothing is lacking to them when that want benefits the soul more than it harms it, because it is the soul’s nourishment. Hence it is said: “Those who fear God lack nothing.” And truly I will lack nothing, because he has placed me in a place where I may both feed and drink.

This is drawn from the likeness of rich pastures. He says it in this way: “He placed me,” that is, he established me, the Church from both Gentiles and Jews, “beside the water of refreshment,” that is, beside the waters of baptism, which refreshed us because they restored us from oldness to newness.

We are placed beside the waters because the grace of baptism is the foundation of a new way of life. I say that he placed me in a pasture, that is, in ecclesiastical institutions, where there are many pastures, namely many teachings of Scripture that feed the soul. And it was not placed in just any location, but in one where it is exceedingly pleasant and delightful.

It should be known that although the rule of grammarians uses *pascua* only in the plural, with the genitive *pascuorum*, divine Scripture, which is not subject to that rule, uses *haec pascua*, *huius pascuae*, and plural *pascuae*.

“He placed me,” I say, “beside the water of refreshment,” and then he led me out into those pastures—not destructive waters but nourishing ones—by adding the moral interpretation to the historical, and afterward the spiritual interpretation.

In this way he wholly turned my soul back to himself, without spot or wrinkle. And he led me, that is, he brought me from virtue to virtue, having placed me upon the paths of righteousness, that is, in the deeds commanded by his righteousness, along which few walk.

The one who is upon these paths is the person who, because he is willing and not compelled, has subjected them to himself. He does not have them over him, because he is not oppressed by them. And he did not do this through my merit, but for the sake of glorifying his name through me.

For even if I walk. Here he turns to the Lord, rejoicing in and commending his benefits. The passage continues as follows: Truly I am upon the paths, because I will no longer fear evils—that is, capital crimes leading to the mountain.

And if I walk—that is, even if I conduct myself—in the midst of the shadow of death, that is, among those who are the shadow of the eternal death that awaits them, since they represent its hope in themselves by being shadowy and dark in heart, just as a shadow represents the shape of the body whose shadow it is.

Or, “in the midst of the shadow of death” means in ignorance, which is the middle—that is, common to all—as the Apostle testifies when he says: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part,” and so forth.

This ignorance is the shadow of death, that is, the likeness of mortal ignorance that will eventually exist in the outer darkness.

Or, “in the midst of the shadow of death” means in the present and common life, which, through the daily falls that everyone suffers in it, is a shadow—that is, a figure—of death, meaning the mortal fall that those thrust into Gehenna will suffer.

Therefore I will not fear evils, because you are with me now through faith and will one day be with me through sight.

I will not fear evils for this reason also: your rod, that is, your fatherly correction, and your staff, that is, your help, by which I am supported as by a staff. Or the rod means your lesser correction, by which, while I was a child, you rescued me; and your staff means your heavier correction, by which, when I had become mature, you urged me from an animal life into a spiritual one, so that I might advance in it.

For we customarily threaten lesser animals with a rod, but urge greater ones with a staff. These two, I say, did not disturb me; rather, these very things consoled me.

And this happened because you prepared a table for me, that is, you made them a pleasant refreshment, in my presence—that is, in my soul, which is my true sight—against those who trouble me. What they thought would bring me sadness, you made bring me joy.

Or otherwise: You prepared a table in my presence, that is, you set before me the patience of the Lord’s Passion as an example, so that I might be refreshed by it as by a table and rejoice against those who trouble me, namely so that I might not believe them, however fiercely they raged.

Or: You prepared a table for me, that is, divine Scripture, which refreshes and consoles me when it says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul,” and many similar things. Blessed Peter also said: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials.”

You have fattened. Because you prepared a table, in preparing it you fattened my head, that is, you gladdened my mind with oil, that is, with spiritual joy.

Priests and kings are anointed with oil, and through that anointing they are gladdened; hence oil is used as a symbol of joy. It signifies spiritual joy because that joy surpasses every other joy, just as oil floats above other liquids.

“Fatten” can also be understood as “soothe,” because spiritual joy soothes hearts amid outward hardships, just as something anointed with oil is soothed externally.

And he should have said, “You have made me drunk with your cup.” But in order to give the statement greater force through wonder, he says the same thing in this way: “Your cup,” that is, the imitation of your Passion—a cup, I say, not merely drinking but intoxicating, that is, making drunk, not the body but the soul, just as it made drunk the one who, not even feeling the heat of the fire, said: “I have been roasted.”

That cup, I say, how splendid it is! How sweet and admirable it is!

And your mercy. Your mercy indeed preceded me in all these things, and that same mercy will follow me, assisting me, all the days of my life—that is, of this mortal life.

And it will do this for as long as I dwell in the house of the Lord, that is, in the superheavenly rest, in which one dwells for length of days, that is, eternally.

Equivalently, one may say: Your mercy will accompany my life until it brings me into your life.

# ON PSALM XXIII

Psalm of David, for the First Sabbath.

## ARGUMENT

He foretells to the people—or rather commands them—by what resources of life they may be released from Babylonian captivity.

## EXPLANATION

“The First Sabbath” signifies the Lord’s Day, which is the first day after the Sabbath, on which the Lord rose from the dead. Because the whole psalm is sung after the resurrection, this title was placed before it, so that it might fittingly admonish the hearts of the faithful.

After the Lord’s resurrection, the prophet, made more joyful, addresses the human race, which was laboring under various kinds of resurrection. In the first part he defines that the whole world belongs to the Lord, so that just as no one would prove himself excluded from his dominion, so no one should believe himself alienated from the faith.

In the second place he determines by what virtues those established in his Church are endowed. In the third he addresses the most foolish superstitious people, so that, while serving the true Lord, they may depart from the perversity that harms them.

## COMMENTARY

The earth is the Lord’s. A psalm of David, for the First Sabbath.

The First Sabbath is customarily called the Lord’s Day, at whose dawn our Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead. And fittingly, on the day on which he had made the world, he also renewed it.

The Lord’s Day was the first day on which the Lord established the world, according to the words of Genesis: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

By “heaven” here we do not understand our heaven, but that heaven whose light is the Lamb himself. By “earth” we understand the composition of the remaining elements and that whole mass which the Lord ordered during the other five days before the Sabbath, on which he rested.

Here, however, “the First Sabbath” is understood differently. The Sabbath, that is, rest, was for us the Lord’s resurrection, by which, rising again, he caused us to rise with him. Ascending also and sitting at the right hand of the Father, he caused us to ascend and sit with him—now in hope, and one day in reality. For we have been saved in hope.

Therefore the First Sabbath means the first period after the Sabbath, that is, the period of the apostles’ preaching, during which that Sabbath—that is, the resurrection—first became known.

The Second Sabbath may be called the period of the preaching of those who succeeded the apostles. In the same way the Third, Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Sabbaths can readily be marked in the succession of preachers, up to that true Sabbath when eternal rest will receive the souls of the saints.

Or, just as divine Scripture calls the whole week “Sabbath” from its more excellent part, according to the Gospel passage, “I fast twice on the Sabbath,” so the entire period between the Sabbath of the resurrection and the true future Sabbath may also be called Sabbath. Within this Sabbath the First Sabbath, the Second, and the rest may be marked as above.

Thus the prophet, foreseeing through the Holy Spirit that future period in which the apostles would preach with such constancy and clarity, composed this psalm while contemplating that period with special attention, in the person of the apostolic trumpet or voice.

Accordingly, the title mentioned above is explained as follows: This psalm is attributed to David, either to the prophet himself or to any of the apostles, who are truly strong of hand and desirable in vision.

The psalm, I say, was possessed or sung at the First Sabbath—that is, in contemplation of the future period of apostolic preaching, insofar as the prophet is concerned; but insofar as the apostles themselves are concerned, this hymn was truly celebrated in their own time.

In this psalm the apostles exhort us through a certain comparison: just as the people of ancient times received their victorious leaders returning from their enemies with a triumph and with every joy, so we too should receive with complete gladness and joy the Lord Jesus Christ, the victor over death and destroyer of the body of sin, who returned from the underworld in triumph, and we should strive to be conformed to him.

It is as though the apostles said: Let all rejoice in subjecting themselves to Christ, because he is truly Lord and the true victor.

For the earth, previously occupied by the prince of darkness, now belongs to the Lord. “Earth” here means what contains for what is contained: earthly people, who were formerly held captive under the yoke of the devil, have passed into the right of their Lord once death was destroyed and its prince bound.

And because the earth, considered simply as earth, is not the Lord’s through habitation, he adds: “And its fullness,” or, “the earth is the Lord’s.”

He determines what its fullness is when he says: “The inhabited world belongs to the Lord.” By “the inhabited world” and “fullness” we understand the perfect, namely the apostles and those like them. For the inhabited world signifies perfection, according to Horace:

> Entirely smooth and rounded,  
> against whom Fortune always rushes powerless.

And complete numbers are called perfect numbers.

And all of them are the Lord’s from among those who are called the inhabited world: they do not apostatize but dwell, that is, persevere, in that inhabited world—in perfection.

“The earth is the Lord’s” can also be explained in this way: the earth, that is, human flesh, which previously was not the Lord’s because it could be taken away from him, since it was mortal and subject to suffering, has now been received through incorruption in the resurrection and made the Lord’s own. It has now escaped every change, and in this the victory mentioned above is again signified.

The following passages do not change under this interpretation.

For he. The inhabited world, that is, the perfect, rightly belongs to the Lord because the Lord himself founded that inhabited world, that is, made himself its foundation for others through good example and teaching.

He founded the inhabited world, I say, upon the seas, that is, planted it among those who had previously been like seas. For just as the sea is bitter and always tossed about, so those whom the Lord made—and still makes—the inhabited world, that is, the perfect, formerly fluctuated and were troubled amid the bitterness of the cares and anxieties of this world.

This is also evident in the apostles themselves. Matthew truly fluctuated, for the Lord took him from the tax booth. The others did so in their own manner.

And he prepared the inhabited world even upon the rivers, that is, upon the rulers of the age who are greedy. Just as rivers continually flow into the sea, so, always growing bitter through the ardor of possession, they plunged more and more deeply into the waves of this life. One of these was Paul, along with many others. That is, he established the Church upon the seas and upon the rivers as well.

Who will ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who will stand in his holy place, and so forth? Since the Lord has placed his inhabited world at such a height, who, having lain until now in the lower region of sins and death, will ascend the mountain of the Lord—that is, to the exalted height of the Church, which the Lord prepared and which is called a mountain both because of the excellence of its virtues and because of its steadfastness?

Or who, having ascended, will stand—that is, remain—in his holy place, that is, in this great eminence of the Church, which the Lord established? For many ascend who do not remain.

Innocent in hands. As if he were saying: He will truly ascend the mountain, and stand upon it, who is innocent in hands, that is, clean in works; and who is clean of heart, that is, clean also in thoughts. That man too will ascend who has not accepted his soul occupied with vanity, or with vain affections and pleasures—that is, who has not regarded it as precious and dear, but rather has considered it wretched and corrected it severely. For it is a punishment of sin that vain affections, although they are never brought into action, trouble our mind; and perfect men do not allow these to rise up within them with impunity.

Or, “has not accepted,” that is, has not considered his soul to be in vanity, that is, within transitory things, which are vain, according to the saying: “Vanity of vanities,” and so forth. This is as many fools do, who despair of the soul’s life after death and of their own resurrection, and therefore neglect their souls. Rather, he understands his soul to be truly eternal, and therefore labors as much as he can to prepare for it an eternal dwelling.

“Nor has he sworn”: that is, he too will ascend the mountain who has sworn to his neighbor—which often has to be done in human contracts—but has not sworn deceitfully, that is, has not deceived him. And such a person will receive blessing, that is, multiplication, from the Lord: namely, that in the present he may merit well, and in the future be well rewarded. This does not come from merits, but from grace alone, because he will receive mercy from God—that is, because God’s good will and his grace will precede in him, and this is not from merits but from God.

I say, from God his Savior, that is, from him who, according to the preceding mercy, will save him through the blessing mentioned above. And he will save him because this is the generation of those who seek him; that is: such people belong to those who seek the Lord himself in the present through faith and good works, and finally find him. This is what he says: “Of those who seek,” I say, and finally find “the face” and presence—not of a new God, but of the God of Jacob, that is, of him who gave primacy to the one born later. This will happen when they see him face to face.

“Lift up the gates.” Since the earth belongs to the Lord, and no one ascends his mountain except the innocent in hands and heart, and so forth, therefore, O princes who have hitherto unjustly held primacy among human beings, lift up the gates—that is, lift them toward yourselves and remove greed and fear, through which you have hitherto shut human beings beneath the yoke of your domination as though behind gates. For whoever is subject to an earthly lord is subject either through hope of acquiring something from him or through fear of losing what he has already acquired.

Thus Sallustius too says that hope and fear are parts of the commonwealth, and the sense is: Desist, earthly princes, from unjust condemnation, because there will no longer be any place for your supremacy. No one will be desirous of earthly things or afraid of losing them. And you, eternal gates, set against those gates—that is, renunciation of the world and its pomp, and conversion to the Lord, leading those who enter through you into eternity—you, I say, be lifted up, that is, be enlarged and exalted, so that those other gates may be brought low. And thus there will enter into human minds not the king of disgrace but the King of glory, that is, Christ. He will be shown, in his appointed time, namely on the day of judgment, by the blessed and only powerful King of kings and Lord of lords, God the Father.

For it is glorious to be under God as king, but disgraceful to be under a human king. Our disgrace—namely, that we did not rule ourselves—caused us to be placed under a human king.

“Who is this?” Human nature, which previously had known no kings except those of disgrace and had sought them, asks in wonder who should be called the King of glory, and says by way of interrogation: Do you wish to know who this King of glory is? He, namely, who is truly Lord, because by the price of his blood he made us purchased slaves for himself; who is strong, though you thought him weak; and powerful, though you believed him oppressed.

Or he is strong because he destroyed the gates of death, and powerful because he cast out and chained the prince of the world. This Lord is truly powerful in this battle: when the gates of death have been broken and the heavenly gates opened, he will finally say: “Rejoice, perfect ones, because I have conquered the world.”

“Lift up the gates.” Here he addresses the aerial powers, that is, the demons, saying: O princes, that is, O aerial powers, you too lift up your gates—that is, remove your vices and evil suggestions, through which you have hitherto obtained primacy over those who worshipped the army of heaven, that is, the sun, moon, and similar things.

And you, eternal gates—that is, you who lead to eternity—be lifted up, that is, be enlarged; and thus the King of glory will enter, as was said above. The eternal gates set against the gates of the demons, who ruled over those worshipping the army of heaven, are charity and chastity. Charity is that by which the one God is loved above all things; chastity is that by which the soul, after his love, fornicates among the many who are called gods but are not (sic). All who worship idols do this.

“Who is this?” Since many—as the blessed Augustine and Ambrose also testify—among the good angels were ignorant of the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation until they saw him exalted above all things, therefore, as though the demons were wondering, he calls this one the King of glory by way of interrogation, just as above. Do you wish to know who this King of glory is? He, namely, who is Lord not only over you apostate demons but also over the powers, that is, the heavenly armies; or he is the Lord of powers, that is, one whose possession and gifts are not earthly things but powers alone. And he who is such is truly the King of glory.

It should be known that these last four verses, according to the interpretation we have now given them, are customarily placed first by some, and the beginning of the psalm is then connected to them in this way: Therefore you, earthly princes and aerial powers, ought to lift up your gates, and you, eternal gates, ought to be raised up, so that the King of glory may enter, because the earth belongs to the Lord—that is, because he is the Lord who claimed for himself the earth overrun by the enemy, and so forth.

The first “Lift up the gates” can also be read in another way than has been said above: namely, by “princes” we may understand the good angels appointed to guard human beings. Of them it is said in the Gospel: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” Thus it may be said: Since the earth belongs to the Lord, therefore you, princes—that is, angelic powers appointed over human beings for their protection—do what is yours to do in meeting the Lord: lift up your gates, that is, enlarge the virtues in those subject to you, so that the Lord, the author, may be able to enter with the entire pomp of triumph.

And you, eternal gates—that is, you virtues leading to eternity—be lifted up. This means: You human beings, in whom the virtues reside, obey as you ought; namely, enlarge the virtues within yourselves, and thus he will enter. What follows remains unchanged.

## ON PSALM XXIV

[Col. 0604B] To the end, a psalm of David.

### ARGUMENT

A prayer is formed from the person of the people dwelling in Babylon.

### EXPLANATION

Since the words of the title are already known, and this psalm is the first of the Hebrews to lack an alphabetic letter, let us recognize that it does not contain the sixth and nineteenth letters. Throughout the psalm the Church pleads not to appear contemptible before the Lord’s sight and before her enemies.

In the first section she asks to know the Lord’s institutions and ways. In the second she requests his benefits, which he granted to the holy fathers from the beginning of the world. In the third she says that those who keep the Lord’s commandments deserve eternal rewards, declaring that she continually remains in the same will. Thus the first portion contains five letters, the second six, and the third nine.

### COMMENTARY

[Col. 0604C] To you, Lord, I lifted up. This psalm is entitled “A psalm of David,” that is, it is to be attributed to every more perfect person, whether among the Apostles or among others. For in this psalm it is the voice of every perfect soul, hymning the Lord in him, so that by its example it may exhort and instruct us concerning how we ought to be disposed toward our Lord, and what we can obtain from him—or ought to seek from him—through such devotion. It says:

Lord, Father, my soul, once cast down from you in Adam and trampled, as though into the earth, by carnal desires and lusts, was then not mine; now, however, I not only lift it up but have long since lifted it up through a spiritual vow and desire toward you. Therefore I shall not be put to shame, that is, I shall suffer no further shame, because I trust in you.

As if he were saying: Formerly I presumed upon myself, and, mocked because of my pride, I was ashamed, because I was cast down into such weakness that I fear death even from the smallest things. But I shall no longer be put to shame, because now I do not presume upon myself but trust in you; and rightly in you, because you are my God, that is, my Creator and re-creator. Or because I am no longer, as before, my own god according to my will, but have made you my God.

“Nor let them mock me.” I trust in you, I say, and therefore let neither my external nor my internal enemies—who try to drag me down through their serpent-like and hidden persuasions—mock me, that is, let them not make me ineffective by dragging me down. If that happens, they will mock me, saying: “This man began to build and was unable to finish.”

Therefore he says that they should not mock me. For all who wait for you will not be confounded: that is, none who patiently wait for you as their rewarder will be confounded. Hence it is said: “If he delays, wait for him, because he will come and will not be late.” Nor will those be confounded who bear the weight of your commandments, carrying the burden of the day and the heat. None of them, I say, will be confounded by their enemies, because they will neither be dragged down nor mocked by them.

[Col. 0605A] Let all who act unjustly be confounded. This is not a curse but a prophecy of divine judgment, or a rejoicing in advance. As if he were saying: Those who wait for you will not be confounded, but let all who act unjustly—that is, those who prefer earthly things to heavenly things, laboring for earthly matters and despising heavenly ones—be confounded. They do this “in vain,” that is, uselessly and to no purpose, because through those things they are impeded rather than helped. This expression is taken from irrational animals, which, the more they move, the more they become entangled.

Let all such people, I say, be confounded with eternal confusion. But so that I may not be confounded or act unjustly, Lord, show me your ways, that is, your commandments. I call them your ways because they lead no one to destruction, as the broad ways do, along which the beasts of the field walk. And teach me your paths—not merely to possess them in words, but also in works—your stricter commandments, known to few.

Direct me in your truth. This is a separate statement. As if he were saying: Lord, I have gone astray in my falsity; but direct me, so that I may no longer wander from the way of justice, in truth—that is, in your true commandments. I speak of truth that is yours. You are truth itself, and all truth is from you; from me there is nothing but falsity.

For every human being is a liar. And so that I may be directed in truth, teach me truth itself—not merely to hold it in words but to practice it in reality. This belongs to you to do, because you are my Savior, not I, who am a traitor. For when I had been expelled from paradise and had wandered as an exile into a distant region, I could not return by myself, because it is written concerning the way of iniquity: “Everyone who walks in it will not return.” But I was freed by you, who were rightly able to do this, because you are my God and Savior.

Therefore I waited for you—that is, I patiently awaited you as my rewarder—or I bore the weight of your commandments throughout the day, that is, throughout the whole time of my conversion; or throughout the day, that is, with complete sincerity of mind. And because I waited, therefore, Lord, forget my transgressions and remember your compassions and mercies.

Compassion is the performance of works of mercy; mercy, however, is the devout affection of the heart that precedes compassion. This is said by analogy. As if he were saying: Remember, Lord, the good things that you have already bestowed upon many, so that you may bestow them upon me in the same way.

The text is expounded as follows: “Remember, Lord, your compassions,” that is, the works of mercy displayed from the beginning of the world. You even showed such compassion to sinful humanity that you did not abandon it despite so many and such great consolations of your creation, and did not allow the necessities of life to be lacking for it.

And remember your mercies, that is, your devout affections, which have existed from eternity—that is, which were in you from the beginning of the world and even before it. For mercies have always existed in God, whereas compassions have been displayed temporally, one by one, as in Abel, Abraham, and the others.

“Do not remember the sins of youth.” Remember your compassions, indeed, so that you may have mercy; but do not remember—that is, do not reserve for punishment, but let them be as though erased from your memory through mercy—the manifest sins of my youth, that is, those which I knowingly committed after renewal in the water of baptism, through which I blossomed again from the old age of sin into the condition of virtue, as into youth.

Or, because young people are usually reckless, we may say simply: Do not remember them by reserving them for punishment—the manifest sins of my youth, that is, of my recklessness, which I knowingly and rashly committed. And do not remember my ignorances, that is, my hidden sins, which I committed unknowingly, whether through recklessness or after the renewal of baptism.

“According to your mercy.” Do not remember my sins, I say, but rather remember me, Lord, so that you may have mercy according to your mercy—that is, according to what befits you, not according to what befits my anger. I speak of you, to whom it belongs alone to have mercy, alone to heal, and alone to forgive sins. And do this not because of my merits but because of your goodness, that is, your sweetness.

“Sweet and upright.” So that no one might presume upon the Lord’s goodness without considering that the uprightness of justice is also in him, and thus wish to sin freely, he turns to us and shows that both qualities are in him when he says: The Lord is sweet and upright.

He is sweet in this respect: that he forgives sinners and ungodly people their former sins if they convert. He is upright in this respect: that the mercy of calling and forgiveness, which possesses grace without merits, ultimately requires merits in due and just order according to a righteous judgment.

And truly he is sweet and upright, because he postpones mercy for those who are straying outside the way, so that they may be brought into the way. This letter says the equivalent: “For this reason he will give a law,” that is, correction, “to those who stray outside the way,” so that he may place them in the way.

Or otherwise: The Lord is truly upright because he also inflicts paternal scourges upon the sons whom he receives as an example of judgment, so that through this we may understand what will happen to fugitive servants. This is what he says: For this reason—namely, because he is upright—he will give a law, that is, the restraint of paternal words, to sinning sons who, although they sin, are nevertheless in the way, that is, they walk in the commandments and commit only venial sins.

He will do this so that those who sin outside the way—namely, those who, not subject to God’s commandments, freely commit serious and every kind of illicit act—may know what awaits them. And in this judgment, that is, in this paternal correction, he will not disturb those to whom he gives the law, but will direct them into the way of justice, having made them gentle: namely, so that they do not resist his scourges like wild and untamed creatures, but become more restrained when they are goaded and return to the way. Just as well-tamed animals return to the way when they are goaded and move more calmly, so will these.

And he will teach them, having made them meek: namely, so that they contradict God’s will in nothing, but obey in all things and subordinate their own will to his. These, I say, he will teach and enable to know, for an increase in perfection, his ways, by which he himself comes to us and we come to him.

He shows what those ways are when he says: All the ways of the Lord by which either we come to him or he comes to us are mercy and truth. Mercy, because he is appeasable; truth, because he is an incorruptible judge. He has already displayed one of these two ways by forgiving sins; he will display the other in the future by examining merits. Thus all God’s ways may be called his two advents: one as the merciful one, the other as the judge.

Whoever holds to these ways will reach him—anyone who, recognizing that he was freed without any merits of his own, lays aside pride and thereafter guards against the severity of the judge, because he has already experienced the clemency of the one who comes to his aid.

All these ways are ways of mercy, not for just anyone, but for those who seek his covenant: that is, for those who, having become gentle and meek, recognize that his first coming was as the merciful one and that his second will be as the judge. For this reason they seek his affection and seek his covenant in works, that is, the eternal inheritance promised by him, to receive which he redeemed us by his blood.

They also seek the testimonies of his covenant, that is, the testimonies made about him in the prophets and evangelists, so that they may become all the more certain through them. Or they seek his testimonies, that is, those commandments which the Lord testified to, so that those who observe them may reach that covenant.

“Because of your name.” Since the three verses just mentioned were inserted to show that no one ought to presume upon the Lord’s goodness, he now returns to the main point, changing the person. As if he were saying:

Truly you will remember me, Lord, because you will be favorable to my sin by not reserving it for punishment. And do this not because of my merit but because of your name, that is, because of your glory and praise, so that those who understand may glorify you as God.

Do this also because I make room within myself for your favor, in that my sin is very great to me—that is, it seems to me exceedingly great and difficult. For anyone whose sin seems small to him has a great sin before God; conversely, whenever a person’s sin seems great to him, it is small before God.

Hence the blessed Augustine says: “God forgives sins to the extent that each person recognizes them.” And it was said to Saul: “When you were little in your own eyes, you were great in my eyes; but when you began to be great in your own eyes, you became little in my eyes.”

So that no one might err by saying that the Lord would be favorable to him because his sin was very great to him, he wishes to show by clear signs who it is whose sin truly seems great, first asking: “Who is the person who fears the Lord?” This is equivalent to saying: Who is the one to whom his sin truly seems great? For fear of the Lord—which is filial, not servile—makes sin seem great, however small it may be.

He immediately adds the sign of one who fears the Lord, saying that the Lord himself establishes a law for the one who fears him, a lasting law, not an hourly one; he has established for him a rule on the way which that person freely chose, so that he might not sin with impunity. For it is not fitting for the Lord’s soldiers to be temporary or merely occasional. Here “way” is understood either broadly as the rule of Christianity, or as any stricter form of life within it, such as the monastic or eremitical life, or something similar.

“His soul will dwell among good things.” Here again he gives another sign of one who fears the Lord: his soul will dwell—that is, will dwell for a very long time and will always remain—in good desires and thoughts.

“And his seed will inherit the land,” that is, his works will cultivate his flesh as diligently as someone cultivates an inheritance, uprooting from it the thorns and thistles which it previously produced for him—that is, vices—so that in the future he may receive it as a glorified inheritance.

Again he gives a sign of one who fears the Lord when he says: “The Lord is the strength of those who fear him,” that is, the Lord makes those who fear him have the Lord himself as their strength. He does not make them have the world as their strength; rather, he makes them strong in himself and weak in the world.

“And his covenant,” that is, the promise of eternal inheritance made by him, is also a strength for those who fear him: that is, it is the reason why those who fear him cling to him so firmly. The Lord and his covenant are their strength, so that in the end either the covenant itself may be revealed to them when they receive it, or the Lord himself may be revealed to them face to face. In accordance with this he says in the Gospel: “I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him.”

“My eyes are always toward the Lord.” Since the Lord establishes a law for those who fear him and strengthens them, therefore my inner eyes—that is, all my affections—are always directed toward the Lord, not toward anything earthly. I ought rightly to look toward him, because he will draw out my feet—that is, my affections—from the snare, that is, from every earthly perplexity by which we are entangled.

“Look upon me and have mercy on me.” Here again, after an insertion, he returns to the main point, and the passage is connected as follows:

Because my sin is very great to me, therefore, Lord, who despised me in Adam, look upon me—that is, attend to my weakness—and have mercy on me by making me persevere. You ought to have mercy because I am alone—that is, I have toward you the affection of an only child, who, just as he is loved uniquely by his mother, so uniquely loves her.

And because I am poor—that is, I attribute nothing to myself and presume upon nothing in myself—it is very necessary that you have mercy, because the tribulations of my heart have multiplied. That is, I recognize that the tribulations of my heart are manifold in adversity and prosperity alike, because I fear the fall of prosperity as much as the fall of adversity. Therefore deliver me from my necessities, that is, from the tribulations of my heart, which means from my vices.

[Col. 0608A] “See my humility.” You ought to deliver me because I am humble and labor. And, so that you may deliver me, see my humility—that is, attend to the abasement of my weakness—and my labor, which I endure while striving to make satisfaction.

Or, “I see my humility,” that is, I consider it, because I humble myself without cutting myself off through any boastfulness about my righteousness from the unity of my body, as heretics do. And see my labor, because I endure the undisciplined and wicked who are mixed in with me. For just as straw and grain are together on the threshing floor, so the wicked are mixed with the good in the Church.

And forgive me all my sins, which I commit, namely, through the necessity of the way. For although the perfect soul that speaks here is free from greater crimes, it still needs the washing of the feet, that is, the forgiveness of venial sins. Just as, if someone walks through dust, it is necessary that at least his feet become dusty and must be washed, so whoever lives in this life—which is compared to a dusty road—however perfect he may be, is nevertheless not entirely free from every sin, and therefore at least needs the washing of his feet. Hence it is said: “The one who has been washed all over needs only to wash his feet.”

“Look upon my enemies.” This is connected to the same point as the preceding verse. As if he were saying: In order to deliver me, look upon my enemies, who wish to drag me down, and drive them back. This is necessary because they have multiplied: they are not only external but also internal, like the heretics who, although they exist within the Church, nevertheless try through deceptive persecution to drag down the others who are in it. Concerning them it is said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.”

Therefore you must drive back my enemies, who hate me without cause. For they hate me with unjust hatred. It is unjust hatred to hate one who labors for his own salvation. Every perfect and good person labors for the benefit of all, because he prays for all; therefore whoever hates a good person exercises unjust hatred.

“Guard my soul.” Since my enemies have multiplied and have hated me unjustly, therefore, Lord, guard my soul, so that it may not decline into conformity with them. Deliver me from every perplexity of living together with them, lest I secretly incur hatred against them. And do not let me be put to shame, that is, do not allow me to be turned toward the shame of weakness, because I have hoped in you and not in myself, as before, when I presumed upon myself and, mocked because of my pride, was put to shame.

“Innocent ones, and so forth.” As if he were saying: What fruit do I seek in asking you, Lord, to guard and deliver me? This is the fruit: the innocent and upright—that is, the good, who neither harm their neighbor and who practice upright works—will cling to me through conformity and imitation of good works, because they have already clung to me as well.

They will do this not because of me but because I have waited for you: that is, because I have patiently awaited you as my rewarder and have borne the weight of your commandments. This means: They will not imitate me because of anything that I possess or do from myself, but solely in that by which I imitate you.

Hence Paul also says: “Be imitators of me, beloved, just as I am of Christ.” As if he were saying openly: Follow me, not according to the works that I do from myself, but according to what Christ works in me.

“Deliver, God of Israel.” As if he were saying: Because the innocent and upright will cling to me, therefore, Lord, deliver Israel—that is, protect all those whom you prepare for the true vision, namely, the vision that will be face to face—so that among them you may also deliver me, to whom they cling. Deliver them, I say, from all their tribulations, both external and internal, so that they may not be dragged down by them.

## ON PSALM XXV

To the end, a psalm of David.

### ARGUMENT

From the person of the captives in Babylon, a true prophetic song of the saints is composed, as they confidently seek release from captivity because of the goodness of their conscience. Alternatively, the prophet bears witness concerning himself.

### EXPLANATION

The entire text of the psalm is to be applied to the perfect Christian, who, persevering in the Church through the praise of various merits, consoles himself with divine benefits.

The holy person whom we have described, in the first interpretation of the psalm, begs that his innocence be regarded, because he has had no share with wicked people. Secondly, he asks not to be mixed with heretics or schismatics in the Lord’s judgment, because he has declared that he loved the Lord’s house.

### COMMENTARY

“Judge me, Lord.” The title is as follows: “A psalm for David,” that is, to be attributed to every perfect soul. In this psalm the perfect faithful soul speaks, exhorting us that, if anyone is good, he should not think himself good alone, and that he should not fear the present mixture of the wicked, knowing that the time of separation will come, when what is light will be carried away by the wind, while what is heavy will remain on the threshing floor.

Rather, he should desire, pray for, and long for this: that the Lord may not allow those whom he now permits to live together to perish together in the future. The soul says:

Lord and Father, you have already morally separated me from the wicked; judge me, Lord—that is, separate me from them also in place in the future, so that you may not allow me to perish there with them, just as here you allow me to live together with them.

These petitions might appear troubling and dangerous—namely, that the faithful soul seems presumptuously to ask to be separated from the wicked—unless this consideration came to its aid: it is not the pride of one who is arrogant, but the confession of one who is not ungrateful. He shows this in what follows.

As if he were saying: I do not say this—that you should judge me—out of proud arrogance, but because, after the mercy you have granted me in advance, I possess some merit of innocence, whose ways I have guarded. This is what he says:

“I have walked in innocence,” that is, I have lived innocently in the present life, which is an entrance into eternal life. Yet this innocence of mine was given by you. I have walked in innocence, I say, and I shall walk further, because I shall not grow weak as I proceed. And I attribute this entirely to you alone, because I am one who hopes—not in myself or in anyone else, but in you, Lord, in whom alone one ought to hope, and not in a human being.

For whoever hopes in a human being, when the human being falters, his hope also falters; and because the human being falls, his hope falls. But whoever hopes in the Lord has firm hope; and just as the Lord is eternal, so his hope will also be eternal.

“Test me and try me.” I say, “Judge me”; and so that you, Lord, may judge me in the future, test me and prove me now. There are two kinds of testing: one by which God trains the good for salvation, and another by which the devil, when permitted, deceives the wicked to condemnation.

Concerning the good kind of testing it is said: “God tests you so that he may know”—that is, so that he may make you know—and: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tested beyond what you can bear, but will provide a way with the testing,” and: “God tested Abraham,” and many similar passages.

Concerning the evil kind of testing, it was instituted that in our daily prayers we should say: “And do not lead us into testing.” Of both kinds it is said: “Let no testing overtake you except what is human.”

Here, however, the good kind of testing is intended: Test me, Lord—that is, scourge me, burn me, cut me—in the present, so that I may be tested, not for you, who know everything, but for me, who do not know myself, and for others who are ignorant of me.

And by testing me, prove me, that is, lead me to a complete experience and knowledge of my weakness, so that I may be proved not to you, from whom nothing is hidden, but to myself and to others, from whom I conceal myself just as I do from myself.

Peter did not know himself when he said: “Lord, even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” But when he was tested by the Lord and denied him at the voice of a servant girl, he recognized his weakness, because he went outside and wept bitterly.

That other disciple, Thomas, likewise did not know himself. After he had said with great confidence, “Let us also go and die with him,” when he saw the Lord being seized, he was the first to run away. So it happens every day when wicked priests, as though they had raised the banner of the cross, are the first to exhort others, saying: “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord,” and are the first to run away.

Prove me, I say, and, in order to prove me, burn my kidneys and my heart. By the kidneys are understood pleasures; by the heart, thoughts. The meaning is: Apply a medicinal purgative, as though by fire, to my pleasures and thoughts, so that nothing evil may delight me and nothing evil may enter my thoughts. If anything evil is in them, let it be burned up and destroyed by that fire which, when you send it into the earth, you wish to burn—that is, by the fervor of love of God and neighbor.

“Because your mercy.” Therefore I ask you to prove, test, and burn me, because in all these things your mercy is before my eyes. That is, your mercy is manifest to me, because I clearly recognize that through all these things you have mercy upon me.

Therefore I displeased myself in my former falsity and applied myself to your truth, so that I might approve only what ought to be approved and reject what ought to be rejected. Existing in that truth of yours, I became pleasing—that is, pleasing to myself and to you.

And in this way I remained in your truth, because I did not sit with the council of vanity, that is, I did not choose to set my heart upon those who try to devise how they may become blessed through presumption upon transitory things. This is impossible. Their assembly is properly a council of vanity.

The text is expounded as follows: I did not sit—that is, I did not consent—with the council of vanity, that is, with those who devote themselves entirely to the vanity of temporal things. For even if I were physically present among them, I was nevertheless far from them in mind.

Thus, if some holy man approached a theater physically in order to intercede for someone, he would indeed be physically present, but his mind would nevertheless be far from theatrical matters. Conversely, someone whose entire intention was to come to the theater might be physically absent because prevented by some serious business, yet mentally present in theatrical matters.

Here “I did not sit” is understood to mean that he did not consent openly. For one who sits acts through lingering and deliberate consideration, and therefore what he does is manifest. I not only did not sit by consenting openly, but I also shall not enter with those who practice iniquity, that is, I do not even give the hidden consent of conscience, as one who enters conceals himself outwardly after entering.

“With those who practice iniquity” means those who prefer vanity to truth; or it may refer to any who seek what is unjust, that is, what is not equitable—those who transgress the law naturally written in the hearts of all, namely, that they should not do to others what they do not want done to themselves.

“I hated the assembly of the wicked.” I did not sit, I say, with the council of vanity; rather, I hated the assembly of the wicked, that is, the congregation of all who act evilly. Understand “hate” here as perfect hatred: namely, that he should hate not the people themselves but the evils they commit.

Hence the blessed Augustine says: “People must be loved in such a way,” and so forth.

Because I hated them, therefore I shall not sit—that is, I shall not chatter—with those ungodly people, because what they approve will not be my chattering. This conclusion follows from what contradicts the preceding statement, in order to confirm it.

[Col. 0610D] I will wash my hands among the innocent. I will not sit, I say, with the impious, but rather I will wash my hands, that is, I will make my works clean, O Lord, so that I may be placed among the innocent; and with these washed hands I will surround your altar, that is, I will embrace and touch—now by hope, but eventually in reality—that exalted state of yours, namely eternity and impassibility, in which you, the immortal priest, daily offer yourself as a sweet offering to God the Father for us. This sublimity may be called an altar, that is, *altara*, “high altar,” in comparison with that lowliness in which you, previously mortal and passible, offered yourself temporally upon the altar of the cross. No one will reach that altar except with washed hands, that is, with clean works, even though many embrace this present altar with unwashed and unclean hands.

It may also be understood by analogy with the fact that priests and Levites customarily surround the altar with coverings and various ornaments, according to the saying: “Surround the altar of the Lord, O Levites of Zion, and clothe yourselves in white garments,” and so forth. [Col. 0611A] Accordingly, it may be said: “I will surround your altar with washed hands,” that is, by these clean works and virtues I will adorn your faith in me as with coverings. Since faith is the foundation of good works, if those good works are absent, it is idle and dead, according to the saying: “Faith without works is dead.” This faith is therefore called an altar, because without it nothing acceptable is sacrificed. For there is no place of true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church, that is, outside the unity of faith.

In order that I may hear the voice of praise. I will wash my hands, I say, and surround your altar in both ways and in such a manner—that is, I will act—so that I do not refer this to my own praise, but so that in all these things I may hear, that is, recognize through the truth presiding within me, which naturally dwells in each person through reason, that every voice of praise belongs only to your praise and not to mine. You alone are worthy of praise in my good works, not I, because if there is anything praiseworthy in me, it comes from you; but whatever is blameworthy in me comes from me.

Or otherwise: I will therefore surround the altar, that is, faith, with good works, so that I may hear from the truth, as above, the voice of your praise—that is, by what voice you are to be praised—not only by an outward voice, but also by the intention of the heart and by good action. And I will not merely hear this in myself, but will also proclaim to others all your wonders: namely, that from servants you have made sons, from the impious pious, and from the condemned you have taken up men into your kingdom as your own—not through my merits or those of others, but as proceeding solely from your grace.

O Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house. The passage is connected as follows: For this reason, O Lord, I will surround your altar, that is, I will adorn your faith with good works, because I have always loved making my soul a beautiful house and a glorious dwelling-place for you.

According to the other interpretation, in which we said “I will surround your altar,” the passage may be connected and arranged in this way: I will wash my hands, and with washed hands I will surround your altar, that is, I will touch your sublimity. Therefore, O Lord, do not destroy my soul in future eternal condemnation [Col. 0611C] with the impious, that is, with the irreligious who hate you and worship idols. Do not destroy my life, that is, my very soul, with men of blood, that is, with those who hate their neighbor, who are rightly called men of blood, that is, murderers, according to the saying: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer.” This is equivalent to saying: “Do not permit me, O Lord, to perish with those with whom here you permit me to live.”

This accords well with the intention; therefore you should not destroy me with such wicked people, because I have always tried, as far as I could, to associate myself with the good. For I have always loved the beauty of your house, that is, I have loved holy men, who are the beauty, that is, the ornament, of your house, that is, of your Church in which you dwell, so that I might conform myself to them. And I have loved the place of the dwelling of your glory, that is, the place in which your glorified ones dwell, so that I might share that place with them.

Here “place” signifies what “house” signified earlier, namely, the Church. By “glory” likewise we understand what we previously understood by “beauty,” namely, perfect and holy men; yet “glory” signifies perfection more explicitly. For those are called “the glory of God,” that is, “glorious,” who have already attained such perfection that they attribute no good to themselves but to the Lord, and glory not in themselves but only in the Lord.

In whose hands. For this reason, O Lord, I ask that you not finally destroy me with the impious and with men of blood, because their works are evil and therefore deserve great destruction. He says this as follows: “Iniquities are in their hands,” that is, their works are iniquitous in many ways. What was given to them for attaining the heavenly homeland they turn toward acquiring worldly gifts, thinking that piety ought to be a source of gain where they should instead be pious, as in judging and similar matters. He suggests this when he says: “Their right hand is filled with gifts.”

If they do anything that appears right, that is, good, they do it not for the sake of goodness but [Col. 0612A] because they have been overcome by gifts. Understand “gifts” broadly: a gift from the hand, a gift arising from office, and a gift arising from the tongue. In all these there is grave guilt.

A gift from the hand occurs when money is given for something illicit. Wicked bishops do this: they give money at the curia and receive the staff of disgrace. A gift arising from office occurs when some bodily service is demanded or rendered in exchange for spiritual glory. This is evident in the curial chaplains. A gift arising from the tongue is received when something that ought to be done solely out of piety is instead done for favor and human praise. For example, if a dispute arose between a poor man and a rich man, and a judge, wishing to be praised for simulated piety, defended the poor man’s unjust cause against the rich man, he would not have entirely withdrawn his hands from an illicit gift.

But I have walked in innocence. Those with whom I ask that you not destroy me are indeed such and so wicked. Yet although I may seem to have presumptuously and dangerously made troublesome requests above, when I said, “Judge me, O Lord; test me; try me; burn me; do not destroy me with the impious,” nevertheless I am unlike them because of their evil works. For I have entered upon—that is, I have ordered my life in—my innocence, as was explained above.

Therefore, O Lord, redeem me from those impious men. Let the price of so splendid a redemption benefit me, that is, the price of your blood, so that I may not be conformed to those impious men who trample upon your blood, disregarding the mystery of your Passion. And always have mercy on me in all the dangers of this age, so that I may not fall in any way.

For this reason I ask you to redeem me and have mercy on me, because my foot, that is, all my affection, has stood and will now stand upright—that is, it will not depart from the uprightness of your justice. Therefore I will bless you, that is, I will not conceal you but will make you manifest through the preservation of my life in the world and through good works to those who are in the Church, so that, seeing me, they may glorify you.

Or, “I will bless you” means: I will multiply your body, that is, the Church, adding some to it through my conformity to it—not a few, but many, because I will do this in many churches.

## IN PSALM XXVI. A psalm of David before he was anointed.

### ARGUMENT.

Hezekiah, made more joyful by the death of the Assyrians, renders to God the duties and vows of thanksgiving. It is also to be read concerning those who first enter the Lord’s house, and concerning Isaiah: “Behold, those who serve you shall eat good things.”

### EXPLANATION.
