David was anointed three times: once in Bethlehem, in the presence of his father, by Samuel; a second time in Hebron by the tribe of Judah, after Saul’s death; and a third time there by all Israel after the killing of Saul’s son.

Since no psalm is recorded as having been composed before the first anointing, it remains to understand that the second anointing is designated by this inscription. Before its occurrence, while he was still an exile because of Saul’s plots, he is shown to have sung this psalm. It should be noted that the words “before he was anointed” are not found in the Hebrew books.

Because he was frequently delivered from his fiercest enemies before he became king, the Prophet speaks throughout the psalm. In the first section he says that he fears the Lord and fears no one else, and he testifies that amid the adversities of the world he has one refuge: although he struggles against bodily dangers, he himself dwells in the house of the Lord with the firmest devotion of mind. In the second section, delivered from many disasters, he gives thanks in various ways and, by the spirit of prophecy, promises himself hope of future blessedness.

### COMMENTARY.

The Lord is my illumination. This psalm is entitled “A psalm of David before he was anointed,” that is, before he was anointed with the third anointing. It is recorded in the Book of Kings that the blessed David was anointed three times.

First, while he was still a boy, when Saul, having greatly transgressed, had been rejected by the Lord, he was anointed by the Prophet Samuel in his father’s house, with the Lord simply commanding that he be king. Second, he was anointed by the Prophet Nathan as king over Judah alone, in Hebron. Third, he was anointed king over Jerusalem and all Israel.

Before this third anointing, he is said historically to have composed this psalm—not with the intention of pursuing the historical narrative, but mystically speaking in the voice of those who are now initiated to the Lord in the Church through the twofold anointing of oil and chrism and who await the third, perfect anointing, which will occur when we see face to face.

It is also recorded that in ancient times only two classes of persons were anointed: kings and priests. In these two persons one future king and priest was prefigured, namely Christ, so called from *chrisma*, “chrism.” He is king because he rules and guides us, and priest because he intercedes for us with the Father. He was likewise both priest and sacrifice.

He was a sacrifice because, since that priest found nothing worthy to offer to God the Father, he offered himself for us, cleansing and washing us—he, the spotless lamb, with his own blood—and incorporating us into himself and making us his members, so that in Christ himself we might be christs. For the whole Christ is head and members.

Thus the anointing pertains not only to him but also to us. Hence it is said: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood,” and so forth. This third anointing, of which the title speaks, will be completed spiritually in us in the life promised to us, namely when we shall know as we are known.

Therefore we may say that this psalm is the voice of a faithful soul desiring to come to that life in which it will receive the perfect anointing, and meanwhile desiring that grace which will be perfected in us at the end, when the Lord will be all in all. Hence the title rightly says, “Before he was anointed,” because it is the voice of a perfect soul desiring the true anointing that will be perfected in us at the end.

Now we are anointed in the sacrament of oil and chrism. Through this sacrament something wonderful and ineffable is signified—what we shall be in the end—which we ought to desire with our whole purpose. Therefore now, in the sacrament, we sigh and groan, so that at last we may rejoice in the reality signified by the sacrament.

Let us now approach the literal sense. This is the voice of any faithful person, as we said above, desiring that the final anointing be perfected in him. Since he intends to instruct us, through the anointing he turns to us and says:

The Lord is my illumination, that is, the Lord has enlightened my soul, which was previously in the darkness of unbelief, through the knowledge of faith given to me: in the first anointing of oil, when I renounced Satan and his pomp; and in the second anointing of chrism, when I openly became a confessor of his name.

Let the darkness therefore depart. Hence the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”

And the Lord is my salvation, that is, the Lord has saved me, who was previously in the weakness of mortality and corruption, and has already removed me, as it were, from every weakness through the sure hope of rising into the glory of immortality and impassibility, which he has given me. Let weakness therefore depart. Hence the Apostle says again: “For by hope we were saved,” and so forth.

Whom then shall I fear? As if he said: Since I belong in such a way to the Almighty that he enlightens me and saves me, whom else shall I fear besides him? No one, certainly. For salvation comes from him, and it is such salvation that no one can take away; and his light is such that no one can darken it. What the Almighty gives, no one takes away except the one who gives it.

If anyone wishes, “illumination” may also be referred solely to the first anointing, in which we simply renounce Satan, while “salvation” may be referred to the second, in which we are strengthened more firmly, since in it we profess the name of Christ. From him we also receive the name by which we are called Christians.

The faithful soul appropriately speaks here of the first two anointings, so that, by showing itself grateful for them, it may deserve to be brought to the third, which it desires. It should also be known that the anointing performed through the laying on of hands by bishops, called Confirmation in popular usage as though it were distinct from the two mentioned above, is the same as the second. Because of arrogance, however, it was not granted to individual priests, just as many other things were not.

This verse may also be understood simply in this way: “The Lord is my illumination,” that is, through knowledge of his faith he enlightens me, and this is directed toward salvation. For faith itself is the approach to true salvation.

The Lord is my protector. The Lord, I say, is my illumination and salvation, and the Lord is also the protector of my life, that is, of my soul. For just as a shield protects someone from external weapons, so the Lord protects the soul from the fiery darts of the hidden enemy, that is, the devil. And while the Lord protects me, from whom else shall I tremble? From no one, certainly.

As if he said: Let my enemies rage as much as they wish and devour my flesh; nevertheless, while the Lord protects me, I shall not tremble. For neither does the soul, which he inhabits, tremble, nor will the flesh, even though it may be entirely consumed by enemies, tremble at anything, since at the end it will be clothed with immortality and impassibility. If a mortal protects a mortal, he makes him secure; much more, then, will the eternal Lord, protecting me, a mortal, make me secure.

When the harmful approach. Since the Lord enlightens, saves, and protects me, I shall not tremble. For when those who cause harm—that is, enemies wishing to injure me with their cursing teeth—approach me, although they prevail against me externally insofar as they tear me apart, they do not harm me but rather benefit me.

They approach not so as to injure me inwardly by bringing me down, but only to devour my flesh, that is, to afflict me externally, and thus consume my carnal desires within me. Therefore I shall not tremble at them, because they can kill the body but cannot kill the soul.

Those who trouble me. He explains what he said, as if he were saying: I say that when those who cause harm approach me, they do not injure me but merely devour my flesh. For while they intend to weaken me and bring me down, they themselves have instead been weakened, because they have been made ineffective in their purpose; and while they prepare my fall, they themselves have rather fallen inwardly in their soul.

But I have risen. He first indicates whom he means by saying: My enemies, namely, those who wish to bring me down. I call them enemies because they trouble me both externally and inwardly.

If armies encamp against me. Since those who persecute me are weakened and fall, while I rise, therefore, even if armies should encamp against me—that is, if a multitude of those conspiring to oppose me should gather against me—still I shall not fear.

Or, because soldiers customarily consult their commanders after setting up camp about how they should conduct themselves in battle, we may also understand it this way: “If armies encamp against me,” that is, if all the counsels of my enemies are directed against me, even though those enemies are fortified by their multitude and worldly power like armies, nevertheless, although the flesh fears them externally, my heart—that is, my inward self—will not fear.

For what is more secure than the Lord enlightening, saving, and protecting me? Nothing, certainly.

If battle should arise. Not only, if armies are against me, shall I not fear; even if battle should arise against me—that is, if persecution itself and the scourges of my enemies should rise against me—I shall nevertheless not fear.

For what can battle do to me? Will it take away my reward from me? Certainly not. For the reward I have chosen is of such a kind, and placed in such a location, namely in heaven, that none of my enemies can take it away. Unless the one who gives it is conquered, no one will take away what he gives.

I shall not fear battle, I say, but rather I shall hope, that is, I possess a fixed hope of obtaining the reward, because I have asked one thing—understand, one petition—from the Lord, and I shall never cease to ask for it but shall always seek it. It is this: that I, who now dwell temporarily in a tent, may finally dwell, that is, remain steadfastly, in the house of the Lord, that is, in the heavenly homeland, which is inhabited forever.

A house is a permanent dwelling, whereas tents belong to travelers and soldiers and are inhabited temporarily. Therefore the house of the Lord rightly signifies the heavenly dwelling, which is eternal; the tents signify the present life, which is lived temporarily in the Church.

I asked to dwell in the house of the Lord, where I shall dwell not temporarily but for all the days—not of my death but of my true life—that is, eternally. The days of the present life are called not days of life but days of death, because while we are in the present life we sin continually, and by sinning we die; for sin is the death of the soul.

The days of the future life, when the last death and its sting, that is, sin, will already have been destroyed, are rightly called days of life, because no night of adversity will interrupt them. Indeed, one day without night would be the better expression than many days; but divine authority has wished to signify eternity not only by one day, one month, and one year, but also by many days and many years.

That I may see the will of the Lord and visit his temple. For he hid me in his tent; on the day of troubles he protected me in the secret place of his tent.

Therefore I wish to dwell in the house of the Lord, so that there I may see the will of the Lord in its entirety. The will of the Lord is that we should not do what we ourselves desire, but that we should constrain our will according to his will. Even those who are most perfect now see this will only in part, since there is no one whose own will does not often steal upon him.

It will then be seen when the Lord himself is all in all, because then we shall not apostatize from him even in thought. Then, I say, I shall see the will of the Lord, and I shall also visit him, that is, with desire and continual attention I shall see the Lord himself face to face, having truly become his temple, in which he may dwell worthily and continually.

Or, “I shall visit his temple” means: I shall see in his presence the Lord’s human being, namely Christ, who is the temple of the Lord himself. According to the saying: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.” And again: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity,” and so forth.

For he hid me. The sense is as follows: Someone might say to him: “Dare you, an unclean sinner, to ask for such things? Dare you, wicked sinner, to hope for such things?” And he himself replies: “I certainly dare—not through presumption of my own, but through God’s pledge.”

He displays and explains that pledge, so as clearly to show that if, while placed far away—that is, in this life, which is an exile—he has not denied such things to him, then, when he is near, he will much less deny him the things he has just mentioned. As the Apostle says: “While we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord.”

The passage is connected as follows: With this confidence I shall always seek the aforesaid petition from the Lord, because the Lord has already given me the pledge of that petition. For, placed in his tent—that is, in his Church, which is rightly compared to a tent because throughout this life it wages war against vices and carnal desires—he has hidden me, that is, he has placed me in a hidden place, because he has armed me with faith, hope, and charity.

These are rightly called hidden, because what they are is not yet manifest. Faith is “the expectation of future things, the proof of things not seen.” Hope likewise concerns future things; for what a person sees, he does not hope for. Perfect charity also is not yet present but is future.

He hid me, I say, and he did this on the day of troubles, that is, in the present age, which is called the day of troubles because of the evils—that is, the afflictions and temptations—to which mortal life is subject. Concerning this day we pray continually in the Church: “But deliver us from evil.”

In the future there will be days of good, because then every temptation and persecution will cease. He not only hid me but also protected me, that is, he gave me protection against every attack in the secret place of his tent, that is, in that part of his tent, the Church, which is hidden.

The secret place of the tent is also called that priest who entered once into the holy of holies, hidden from us, that is, removed from our eyes and placed at the right hand of the Father, where he intercedes daily for us. Hence the Apostle says: “The true life is hidden with Christ in God,” and we are above there with him through faith, hope, and charity.

He himself is also here below with us through goodness, defense, and the unity of his body, according to what he promised when he said: “Behold, I am with you all the days of your life, until the consummation of the age.” And truly he is with us, since otherwise it would not have been said to Paul, who was persecuting the Church: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

He exalted me upon a rock. Truly he protected me in the secret place of his tent, because although according to the body I am still humbled in the dust, he has already exalted me upon an exalted rock, that is, in Christ, who is a rock because of the solidity of the Church, concerning which it is said: “The rock was Christ.”

For through him he has made us sit by hope at his right hand, and he has exalted me in such a way that now, while I am still far away because I bear a mortal body, he has exalted my head, that is, he has raised my mind, even though he has subjected my flesh, so that it may be above my enemies and despise my persecutors, who kill only the body but cannot kill the soul.

He has exalted me upon the rock, that is, in Christ, because he has already exalted my head, that is, Christ himself, who is my head. He has exalted him through the Ascension, confession, and eternity, so that he is above my enemies, that is, so that he no longer fears death; for death will no longer rule over him.

I went around and offered sacrifice. The Lord hid me, protected me, and exalted me. But what did I do? I did what I ought to have done, insofar as I was able.

For I went around—not bodily, but in mind. I surveyed the entire world believing in the Lord, and, placed in his tent, that is, in the Church, outside which there is no place of true sacrifice, I offered to the Lord a sacrifice of shouting, that is, I sacrificed to him and poured out in his praise an immense and ineffable joy of mind.

I rejoiced that he had been humbled temporally, through which he chose so many thousands. By such a sacrifice God is appeased. Since speech cannot express this joy, it remains for the mind to rejoice aloud. For *jubilation* is the name given to such joy conceived in the mind that words are insufficient to explain it.

Therefore this great joy is rightly called a sacrifice of jubilation or shouting, because just as some people, when singing praises, burst forth when words fail into a certain intense and inarticulate sound, which is properly called jubilation or shouting, so this great joy cannot be adequately explained in words. When speech fails, it must be completed by the whole affection of the mind.

Or otherwise: “I went around,” that is, I surveyed every creature in my mind, and its various species were like different voices praising God. In this contemplation I offered a sacrifice of shouting, that is, with such great joy of mind I praised the Lord with thanksgiving that words could not suffice to express it.

I will sing and make melody. Thus far he has explained the pledge given by the Lord, and from it he draws the conclusion, as if he were saying: Since the Lord, while I was still far away, gave me this pledge—namely, that he hid me in his tent, and so forth—I am therefore confident that at last in the house of the Lord I shall sing and make melody to the Lord, that is, I shall praise the Lord with every affection and intention.

There every work will cease except the praise of the Lord. Whether that praise will be expressed only through affection or also through the voice is unknown. Through “I will sing” and “I will make melody,” every affection is therefore indicated in the future, because now, in the present, all our affection is gathered into voice and heart, to which singing pertains; or into action, to which making melody pertains.

The preceding sequence may also be read in another way, namely as follows: I asked one thing from the Lord, which I shall never cease to ask but shall always seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord. That is, that I may not be excluded by any adversities from the number of those who maintain the truth and unity of the Lord’s faith throughout the whole world, but rather that I may persevere in ecclesiastical institutions and be a member of the Church, which is called not only a tent but also the house of the Lord, although improperly with respect to the explanation given above.

And this I ask for all the days of my life, that is, as long as I live in this life of mine, which is fleeting and fragile. In this interpretation the plural number of days is taken properly.

Therefore I now desire to dwell in the house of the Lord so that I may see, that is, recognize in the present, the will of the Lord, with this purpose: that at the end, after persevering, the pleasing beauty may appear to me, so that I may contemplate it face to face.

This is to say: I now wish to see in hope so that afterward I may see in reality, and thus finally visit the Lord, having become his temple, namely when death has been swallowed up in victory and I have been clothed with immortality, having become his temple.

For he hid me. Therefore I shall always ask such a petition from the Lord with such confidence, because I have this pledge from him: the Lord, in his tent—that is, in the dispensation of his incarnate Word, which was his tent, in which he fought against the prince of the world, and through which he arranged to become incarnate for the salvation of all believers, whom he chose in him before the foundation of the world—hid me.

That is, he ordained that I should belong to him as a member belongs to its head. This is hidden because we are indeed sons, but what we shall be has not yet appeared.

He did this on the day of troubles, that is, in the present age, which is the day or respite of troubles, as was said above. And he protected me in the secret place of his tent, that is, he gave me protection and security in the believing heart directed toward righteousness. This heart is the secret place of his tent, that is, of me, who am his tent.

And upon the rock—that is, in his firmness and constancy placed within me—he exalted me, that is, he made me conspicuous, so that through my works this constancy itself might be known to others. Through that constancy he exalted my head, that is, my mind, even now, while I still bear a mortal body, above my enemies, so that I might despise them.

But what did I do? I did what I ought to have done, because I went around and offered sacrifice, and so forth. The sense does not change. And because the Lord exalted me upon the rock, exalted my head, and so forth, therefore I shall sing and make melody to the Lord, that is, I shall praise the Lord continually with mouth, heart, and deed, saying:

Hear, O Lord, my voice, and so forth. According to the first reading, the continuation will be as follows: In the future I shall sing and make melody in the house of the Lord. But what shall happen in the meantime? As if he were saying: One must groan and pray. For while we are in this exile, we are wretched and needy; it belongs to the wretched to groan and to the needy to pray.

Therefore, so that others may do the same by my example, I shall groan and pray, saying: O Lord, hear my voice, that is, the voice of my heart, with which I cried out to you, that is, which with a determined intention I directed to you in petition of the one thing. And have mercy on me by giving me that petition; hear me crying out for it.

This is repetition, which the faithful soul makes in order to indicate that what it asks is great, and therefore that great affection is needed by each person to ask for it.

To you my heart has said. You ought therefore to hear me, because my heart—which does not speak to a human being and which I have not displayed to a human being—has spoken to you, O Lord, who alone understand its hidden things.

“My face has sought you,” that is, the presence of my heart has sought you, because beyond all things it has always sought your presence, since among all things it has found nothing so precious as you.

And afterward I shall seek your face, that is, I shall always strive to see you face to face. Therefore, O Lord, do not turn your face away from me; that is, do not let me fail to find what I seek, namely your presence.

Do not turn away from your servant in anger, that is, you who in anger turn away from those who are free and who do not worship you willingly but for the sake of something else, so that they may find something other than you—the thing for whose sake they worshiped you. Do not turn away from me, your servant, who willingly subject myself to you, in anger, so that I may find something other than you. No anger is more grievous to one who loves and seeks the truth of your countenance.

[Col. 0618A] Be my helper. Do not turn away from me, I say, but rather be my helper and do not abandon me. As if he were saying: You have already placed me on the way, because you gave me free will and reason; therefore do not abandon me but help me. For if you abandon me, behold, I shall go astray; behold, I shall remain behind; behold, I shall fail, and I shall make no progress at all.

Do not despise me, that is, do not scorn me, a mortal seeking you, the eternal; me, the lowly, seeking you, the Most High—you who are my salvation, that is, you who alone save me and all who are saved. You can do this because you are God.

For my father and my mother. Therefore you ought not to abandon or despise me, because my father, the old man—namely Adam—and my mother, that is, Eve, abandoned me through their transgression, that is, exposed and disinherited me.

Or my father was the one whom I formerly had, namely the devil, who is the father of those concerning whom it is said: “You are from your father the devil,” and who works in the sons of unbelief. And my mother was the society of unbelievers. These two begot me temporally and morally.

They, I say, abandoned me while I was seeking you. For as soon as someone is transferred into the kingdom of light, he is abandoned by the kingdom of darkness. But when they abandoned me, the Lord took me up to cherish, nourish, and console me with temporal goods, and to make me blessed with eternal goods.

Set a law for me, O Lord, in your way, and direct me in the right path because of my enemies. Here he makes an apostrophe to the Lord, as if saying: Since you, O Lord, have taken me up, set a law for me, that is, a stable and firm law.

Make it for me in your way, that is, in the one whom you have appointed as my way, namely in the new man, Christ, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” For the new man gave new commandments to the world.

This is to say: Make me persist in the rule of the New Testament; and, leaving aside the common law, direct me also individually through mercy in the right path, that is, in the uprightness of your strict commandments, which are hidden and known to few. Do this because of my enemies, so that they may be avoided.

Do not hand me over to the desires of those who trouble me, for unjust witnesses have risen against me, and iniquity has lied to itself. Therefore I ask you to set a law for me and direct me in the path because of my enemies, so that you may not hand me over—that is, my mind.

For each person’s mind is what the person is. Do not hand me over to the desires, that is, to the conformity, of those who trouble me, which their souls desire. We refer this only to the mind because the body has been granted to the enemies, according to what is said in Job: “The earth has been given into the hands of sinners.”

You should not hand me over to their desires, because unjust witnesses—that is, those themselves who testify unjustly, attempting to persuade people that one can be blessed in earthly things, which cannot be—have risen against me so that their conformity might appear in me.

Nevertheless, with your grace coming to my aid, iniquity has not yet lied to me, that is, those wicked men have not yet persuaded me of their lie. Therefore they have lied only to themselves and not to me.

[Col. 0618D] I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. Iniquity has therefore lied only to itself and not to me, because I believe, that is, I have hope of seeing the good things of the Lord—namely, ineffable, unchangeable, and eternal good things.

I say this while placed in the land of the living, that is, in heavenly rest, which truly is the land of the living, because the one who for my sake deigned to assume the land of the dying and to die among the hands of the dying—that is, Christ—will rescue me from the land of the dying.

Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and endure the Lord. Here he turns to exhorting others, as though he were saying: So that each of you may hope to see the Lord’s goodness, as I do, wait for the Lord. That is, although the Lord delays, do not—though you bear the burden of the day and its heat—lose confidence, since confidence has great merit, as the Apostle testifies. He shows how the Lord is to be awaited when he says: Act manfully. For the Lord is not to be awaited with hands hanging idle—that is, so that anyone should be inactive—nor with weakened knees, namely, so that one who stands should take care not to fall. Rather, act manfully and determine manfully to act, lest the phrase be referred to some bodily presumption. He says: Let your heart be strengthened; that is, do not rashly perform something outwardly, but let your heart—that is, your inward self—be strengthened through confidence. And in this way endure the Lord, that is, await the Lord patiently, bearing the burden of his commandments.

# ON PSALM XXVII  
*Of David.*

## ARGUMENT

Hezekiah, at the time of his illness, entreats the Lord. It is also to be read with reference to Daniel. Christ speaks to the Father concerning the Jews. It should be known, moreover, that this psalm too, except for one letter, is written in the Hebrew volumes according to the order of the letters.

## EXPLANATION

[Col. 0619B] It is evident that David in the titles always signifies Christ: “strong of hand” in the struggle of the Passion, and “desirable” in the splendor of the Resurrection; but sometimes he signifies Christ in himself, sometimes in his members. When *to this David* is prefixed, no other person may be understood, but the mediator himself between God and human beings, who speaks throughout this psalm, praying from the humility of the flesh he assumed concerning the punishments due to his persecutors—not out of a desire for malice, but in witness to vengeance.

In the first section, the Lord Christ prays in respect of what he is as a human being, that his prayer may be heard at the future time of his Passion. In the second, he gives thanks because he has been heard in what he requested. At the end of the psalm he joins this petition: that, just as he himself was raised by the power of his divinity, so his people, who are to believe in his name, may be saved.

## COMMENTARY

“To you, O Lord, I will cry.” The title is as follows: “A psalm belonging to this David.” Whoever wishes to expound it should pay attention to the pronoun. For nouns signify substance together with quality, whereas pronouns signify substance alone. Therefore this title is explained in this way: This psalm is attributed to David—not to the historical David, nor to anyone to whom the name David happens accidentally to apply—if it belongs to *this* David, that is, to him who is substantially David: “strong of hand” and “desirable in appearance.”

For in this psalm there is the voice of the Mediator, truly strong of hand, praying to the Father in the very conflict of the Passion for his own resurrection, so that it may not be postponed until the common resurrection of all, and meanwhile for the inner resurrection of his own, and eventually also for their outward resurrection. No one should be surprised that he prays for this so repeatedly and so earnestly, because what he prays for is so great and so important that it deserves repeated attention and petition. Through this he admonishes us how earnestly and desirously, according to our measure, we ought to seek the same thing.

If it were temporary and so delightful, it ought truly to be embraced by everyone; how much more, then, when it is an unending blessedness whose joys are enclosed by no end and disturbed by no bitterness. Finally, knowing that the Father has given all things into his hands and has heard him in all things, he gives thanks to the Father, because he has heard him both for himself and for his own. He exhorts us also to give thanks, as far as we can, following his example, so that we too may deserve to be heard in our petitions.

But when he seems in this psalm to wish things against his enemies, this is not a wish of malice, but an enumeration of their punishment. Thus, in the Gospel, when certain cities refused to believe in his miracles, he does not maliciously wish what he says for them, but announces what threatens them, saying: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida,” and so forth.

We shall now approach the text itself. It is the voice of the Head, as we said above, acting before the Father both for himself and for his own:

“Lord Father, I who have already cried and am crying will cry to you”—that is, I shall direct a strong intention of heart, both in myself and in my own, toward you without interruption—because you are God of all by nature, but my God and the God of my own by grace. “And I will cry for this: that you may not be silent toward me,” that is, so that, though angry, you may never be silent—not consenting to the question of my own, that is, to their petition for the first resurrection, being turned away from me, that is, from those who are mine.

For it belongs to angry teachers to be silent in answer to their disciples’ questions and to turn their faces away. “Do not at any time be silent toward me”—that is, I will cry also for this: that you may not be silent toward me personally, turned away from me, so that you may not separate the unity of your Word from me. “At any time” means “at some time,” namely, in my death, which would then seem to be the case if you postponed my resurrection until the common resurrection of all.

And therefore, so that you may neither be silent toward my own nor keep silent toward me: if you are silent toward my own, they will be like those who descend into the pit—that is, into the depth of vices—where they despise what has been established and are not here partakers of the first resurrection, so that at last they may become partakers of the second. And if you keep silent toward me by separating the unity of your Word from me, I shall be like those who descend into the pit—that is, I shall undergo the corruption of the flesh.

For we become like the others born into the deep misery of this age, which is a pit of confusion, in which lovers of the world are entangled in the mire of sensuality and carnal desires, and therefore tend only toward corruption. For, because the eternity of your Word does not cease to unite itself to me, I am not such as the others who are born into the deep misery of this age, where your Word is not recognized, as though you were silent.

“Hear, O Lord, the voice of my prayer.” As though he were saying: So that neither I nor my own may be made like those who descend into the pit, hear the voice of my supplication; that is, hear the strong intention of heart with which I supplicate you for myself, and hear the voice with which I pray to you for my own.

“And when I lift up my hands”—that is, when I am also crucified, lifting my hands on the cross—“toward your holy temple”: that is, so that through me many may be made your sanctified temple. Or, “I lift up my hands” means: I perform manifest works and signs “toward your holy temple,” that is, so that others, seeing my works, may imitate them and conform themselves to me, and thus become your sanctified temple. For “the temple of God is what you are.”

“Do not hand me over together with sinners.” Therefore, Lord, do not be silent toward my own, so that you may not hand them over to the death of the depth of vices together with other sinners. And therefore do not keep silent toward me, lest you destroy me—that is, so that you may not give me over to the destruction of corruption together with those who work iniquity, namely, with the Jews who work iniquity against me.

He shows what iniquity this is: they speak peace outwardly with me, their neighbor, both according to the flesh and with regard to the mercy that I wished to show them, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth,” and many similar things. But in their hearts, although they speak peace outwardly, there are evil things, because they are plotting my betrayal and my death.

“And therefore, Lord, give them according to their works”—that is, let them receive what they deserve. “And give them according to the wickedness of their devices”—that is, because through their wickedness they devise and desire evil, let them not find good, but evil. “And repay them according to the works of their hands”—that is, although what they do may benefit others, repay them according to what they intend.

For the Jews, in crucifying God, intended by his death nothing other than the destruction of that one person, although the Father turned this, through his provident ordering, toward the salvation of many.

“And repay them their recompense.” As though he were saying: In place of the truth that I preached to them, they repaid me with sheer falsehood, because they lied about me in many things, as when they said: “We found this man subverting our nation,” and: “This man said, ‘I can destroy the temple of God,’” and many such things. Therefore repay them with falsehood, so that, blinded, they may remain in it.

And this is as though he were saying: It is not malice, but an announcement of their deserved punishment. “For they did not understand”—that is, they did not proceed intelligently in the works of God the Father, because they did not consider for what purpose God the Father had ordained that his Word should be united to me and that I should be born, die, and rise again.

And therefore, “because they did not understand the works of his hands”—that is, they did not attend to the works performed by me, who am his hand, works so great that they could openly be called his, that is, the works of the Lord Father. Hence one of them said: “No one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.”

Or, “they did not understand the works of the Lord,” that is, of me: they did not attend to the manifest signs and works that I myself performed for them. Or, “they did not understand the works of the hands of the Lord”: they did not even consider the works that the Lord’s Apostles performed among them. They were his hands, through whom he worked.

And therefore, Lord, “destroy them”—that is, make them ineffective, so that they may not harm me. And if at some time they harm me—that is, if at any time they rise up against my own—let them not prevail against them.

And because destruction is sometimes carried out for the sake of building, as it is said, “Overturn the wicked, and they shall be no more,” he adds: “And you shall not build them.” As though he were saying: You will destroy them, not so that they may be built up into something better, but so that they may be utterly consumed.

“Blessed is the Lord, for he has heard the voice of my supplication.” Here he gives thanks to the Father, knowing that he has placed all things in his hands. And because in every supplication he made, both for himself and for his own, the Father heard him, he exhorts us also to give thanks.

This passage may be connected with what precedes in the following way: I said, “Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication.” And because the Lord truly heard the voice of my supplication, both for me and for my own, “blessed is the Lord”—that is, may the Lord be multiplied and increased; may the number of those through whom the Lord’s name is not blasphemed but glorified among the nations increase.

“The Lord is my helper and my protector; in him my heart has hoped, and I have been helped.” Truly the Lord heard me when I supplicated, because he helps me as I endure tribulation. He is my protector because he will protect me when I rise again through immortality.

And rightly he is my helper and protector, because however greatly my body is afflicted, my heart has always hoped in him—that is, it has always held firm hope in him—and therefore I have been helped by him.

And truly I have been helped, because my flesh, which first flourished in Adam while he remained in the fullness of virtues, and which withered in him through his transgression—this must be understood with respect to the whole mass of humanity—this same flesh, I say, has now blossomed again through the immortality received from the Lord.

And therefore I will confess to him—that is, I will offer him a praiseworthy confession through good works in my own—not now under compulsion, but by my own will. For those who believe in me will confess to him not under the necessity of fear beneath the law, but by free will within the law. Since I am in them, I will confess to him.

“The Lord is the strength of his people and the protector of the salvations of his Christ.”

My own will rightly confess to the Lord, because the Lord himself is the strength of the people that makes itself his—that is, of the people who do not wish to establish their own righteousness, but to be subject to the Lord’s righteousness; who claim nothing for themselves on the basis of their merits and do not consider themselves strong from themselves.

To that people, I say, the Lord gives strength—that is, steadfastness to fight amid the dangers of this age. And the Lord is the protector of the salvations of his Christ: he protects those saved through me, his Christ, after the strength and labor of battle, through immortality.

Here we should understand by those saved through Christ only the Apostles and their immediate successors in the primitive Church, so that what follows may be distinguished from them.

“Save your people.” Here he turns in apostrophe to the Lord, as though saying: You, Lord Father, who will protect those saved in the primitive Church, save, through perseverance in goodness, the whole future people who will not make themselves their own, so that they may not act according to their own will but according to yours, namely, so that they may wholly subordinate their will to yours.

“And bless your inheritance”—that is, multiply in number and virtue those who make themselves your inheritance, so that you may exalt and possess them. Rule them temporally in the present, restraining them from evil and directing them toward good; and in the future raise them up, bringing them even to eternity, that is, to eternal glory.

# ON PSALM XXVIII  
*A psalm of David, at the consummation of the tabernacle.*

## ARGUMENT

The exhortation of Hezekiah, which, after being delivered from the Assyrians and from death, he was to use toward the Jews, so that thanksgiving and vows might be rendered to God for such great benefits. It is also to be read with reference to the superstition concerning the day of the Sabbath of Passover, and with reference to Noah and the Flood.

Alternatively, “the consummation of the tabernacle” means the end of the world, at which the sons of God offer the sons of rams, to be placed at the right hand.

## EXPLANATION

The consummation of the tabernacle signifies the perfection of the Church, which, because it wages war against carnal vices, rightly received the name of a tabernacle of warfare. The Prophet, foreseeing that the ends of the world would be brought to faith, first addresses the whole human race, so that it may offer devout sacrifices. Second, in a sevenfold account, through various allusions, he enumerates the virtues of the Holy Spirit, so that you may recognize one power belonging to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Third, he says that the Trinity dwells in holy baptism and that the Lord gives virtue and blessing to the one who has been reborn from it into the Christian people.

## COMMENTARY

“Bring offerings to the Lord, sons of God.” The title is as follows: “A psalm of David at the consummation of the tabernacle.”

The tabernacle is the present Church, which is rightly called a tabernacle because tabernacles properly belong to travelers or soldiers. The Church is a traveler in the present age, according to the Apostle: “For as long as we are in this mortal body, we are away from the Lord.” The Church is also now engaged in warfare, because it continually wages battle against carnal vices.

The consummation of the tabernacle means the perfection or fullness of the Church, according to all the members that it will attain until the end. For the prophet David, foreseeing through divine revelation that the Church would be brought to completion throughout the whole world by the blessed preaching of the patriarchs and prophets, and especially of the Apostles and their successors, and that the Holy Spirit would cooperate and preach together with them, sings this psalm in praise of that same Holy Spirit.

No praise can be offered to him except what he himself causes to be spoken concerning him. He enumerates the sevenfold grace of his gifts, which he wishes to be understood by the expression “the voice of the Lord,” placed seven times in this psalm, since the whole consummation will be completed through these seven gifts.

Everything went before in the Head, since the Holy Spirit was not given to him by measure. Everything may also have been present in Peter. Or, if not everything, there is no doubt that many gifts were present in him and in the other Apostles. Likewise, whoever labors in this consummation does not act from himself, but on account of some gift received from the Holy Spirit—for example, knowledge of different languages, discernment of spirits, or some other gift, or several gifts.

The Prophet’s purpose in this psalm is to exhort us to strive to insert stones or certain parts into the consummation of this tabernacle, and never to cease praising so great a craftsman, from whose gift proceeds whatever good anyone does or whatever good anyone says about him.

He speaks in this way, principally exhorting the Apostles to the consummation of the tabernacle:

“O you sons of God”—that is, Apostles, whom God dwelling in Christ called especially through himself and begot in faith—“bring offerings,” that is, sacrifice yourselves to the Lord. The one who wholly orders himself according to God’s will offers himself to the Lord, and, imitating Christ, eats his humble body. Hence it has been said: “Whoever considers what he ought worthily to vow to God should slay and offer himself.” This is what is required; this is what is owed.

“Bring yourselves,” I say, “and bring also to the Lord the sons of rams”—that is, those whom you, being rams, will beget in faith through evangelical teaching. The Apostles are called rams both because they are principally the leaders of all, because they begot others in faith through evangelical preaching, and because they strike with both horns—that is, they confirm their judgments through both Testaments and shatter the sayings of their enemies.

He shows how they ought to bring both themselves and their sons when he says: “Bring glory and honor to the Lord”—that is, bring yourselves as glorious, honorable through virtues and good works. And lest they ascribe that glory to themselves, he adds: “Bring glory to the Lord,” so that you attribute it not to your own name but to the glorification of his name.

“And so worship”—that is, venerate—the Lord “in his holy court,” that is, in the Church, which is his holy court. For just as a court is usually called the vestibule before a house, in which the master of the house often takes pleasure, so the Church is like a court before the heavenly house, because through it one enters that house, in which the Lord takes pleasure in good morals and works.

Or, “in his holy court” means in the heart expanded through charity and sanctified and adorned by good works and virtues. Both features are usually found there: it is spacious and adorned.

“The voice of the Lord is over the waters.” Truly you ought now to bring yourselves to the Lord and worship him. For now is the time when the one whom the Prophets foretold as the future Savior is present, through whom you can offer yourselves as an acceptable sacrifice.

This is what the verse says: “The voice of the Lord”—that is, the voice of the only-begotten Son of God—“thundered,” that is, spoke terribly from the cloud of flesh, “over the waters,” that is, over the Jewish peoples, saying: “Unless you repent, you will die.”

The Jewish people is called “waters” in the plural either because of the twelve tribes, which were like distinct peoples, or because of the two principal divisions, namely Judah and Israel.

He determines whose voice had thundered when he says: “The God of majesty,” that is, of omnipotence, truly existing as Lord—he himself thundered, not only over the Jews directly, but also through you, his Apostles, over many waters, that is, not only over the Jews but also over the nations.

He explains how the voice of the Lord thundered both in himself and in his own when he says: “The voice of the Lord thundered in himself with power,” that is, with supreme might, not weakness. Hence it is said: “He was teaching them not as their scribes and Pharisees, but as one having authority.”

But in his own, the voice of the Lord thundered “in magnificence,” that is, in magnificent glory, so that they would not merely preach but also confirm by signs what they preached. Hence it is said: “God cooperating and confirming the word by the signs that followed.”

He shows how the Lord thundered through his own in magnificent glory: “The voice of the Lord thundered over the cedars of Lebanon”—that is, over the lofty people, elevated by wealth, power, and even nobility, from every nation whom he was compelling to the humility of repentance.

And truly the Lord will break every cedar through them, because he will also break the cedars of Lebanon, which is an argument from the greater. For *Lebanon* is interpreted as “whitened” or “whitening.” Lebanon therefore signifies the Jewish people, who, among other peoples, darkened, as it were, by the worship of idols and the baseness of the flesh, appeared white because of their nobility of descent, worldly power, and the fact that they alone received the ceremonies of the law.

By the cedars of Lebanon, then, are understood the proud among the Jewish people, who, because of the singular wickedness they claimed for themselves, always contradicted the truth more vehemently. The Lord broke some of them through himself and through his Apostles; and there is no doubt that he broke many others who contradicted less and more readily recognized their error.

For the nations, who had placed the creature before the Creator, easily recognized that they had gone astray and therefore repented immediately at the sound of the apostolic voice.

But if this is referred to the Lord himself, then we shall first refer the cedars to the Jews alone; and what follows—“And the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon”—will merely specify which cedars he broke.

“And he will shatter them.” I say that the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and this is how they will be broken: the Lord God’s Word—or the Lord Father acting through the Word—will shatter those cedars, or the people signified by the cedars, “as a calf of Lebanon is shattered.”

For the calf born and raised in Lebanon—namely, Christ, led from that Lebanon to sacrifice—was humbled even unto death. Following his example, the Lord will shatter the cedars, because he will make those who were previously cedars imitate his humility.

Therefore I say that he will shatter them like a calf, because “the beloved”—that is, the only-begotten Son of God, chosen above all and uniquely beloved—“will be like one of the sons of the unicorns,” that is, he will be a human being such as I am.

Hence it is also said in Moses: “The Lord will raise up a prophet from among your brothers, like me”—that is, a human being as I am. “Listen to him.” For Christ came in the likeness of sinful flesh, because he was born from sinners, but not in sinful flesh, because he committed no sin, and deceit was not found in his mouth.

The unicorns are the Jews, either because they raise themselves up through the pride of their singular righteousness, or because they place their confidence in only one Testament, or only in earthly things and not in heavenly ones.

Or otherwise: Truly the Lord will shatter them like a calf of Lebanon, because “the beloved”—that is, each person chosen in faith—and therefore beloved, will be humble, just as the son of the unicorns, that is, Christ, was humble.

Or “the beloved,” that is, the only-begotten Son of God, will be shattered in the manner in which he will be the son of the unicorns: he will be humbled outwardly only according to the flesh, not inwardly according to his divinity.

“The voice of the Lord dividing the flame of fire.” Truly the voice of the Lord will break the cedars, because it will divide the flame of fire, shake the desert, and so forth.

This is what the verse says: “The voice of the Lord will thunder”—the Lord, I say, who divides, that is, separates and divides the flames of fire, or the raging anger of the persecutors. This happened when, through the preaching of the Apostles, he transferred some who had previously been persecutors into his charity, while leaving others in their wickedness.

“The voice of the Lord thundered, shaking the desert”—that is, the Gentile people, previously abandoned by the patriarchs, prophets, and other worshipers of God. Therefore he will shake the desert, that is, through the preaching of the Apostles he will cultivate it and make it arable land.

And this will happen in the following way: the Lord will move—that is, he will cause the desert of Kadesh to be celebrated by moving it toward their knowledge through the Apostles. Kadesh means “holy” in the language of the law; it was previously a desert among the Jews with respect to spiritual understanding and, in the literal sense, simply as well.

He explains how that desert is shaken when he says: “The voice of the Lord will thunder, preparing the stags”—that is, he will prepare Apostles who surpass and repel the poisonous teaching and persuasion of those who thought true blessedness could be possessed in earthly things and taught this to others. In this they are comparable to stags.

For it is the nature of stags each year to cast off their antlers and renew them, while swallowing a poisonous serpent without any injury. Through these stags—that is, through these Apostles—the Lord will reveal the thickets.

This is said by way of comparison. Stags, when entering dense woodland, customarily separate the branches with their antlers and open a field where they and the other animals may feed. In the same way, the holy Apostles opened the shadowy and hidden mysteries of Scripture, in which they themselves might feed and feed others.

As these thickets are revealed through the Apostles and their successors, everyone—that is, some from each nation—will declare glory: they will proclaim the glory of the Lord in his temple, that is, in the Church, which is called not only God’s tabernacle but also his house and temple.

Each will do this according to the gift received from the Holy Spirit. Some will do so through words and deeds; others through good works alone; and thus in different ways.

This will happen because, while the Lord wanders in his ark—that is, in ecclesiastical institutions, in which the eight souls, that is, all the perfect, will be saved—here and there through the Flood, that is, through human beings who had previously been like a flood, placed in the depth of vices and in the storms of carnal desires, he will cause his saints to dwell in that flood.

That is, he will make those who were previously a flood into habitable and fertile land. And thus the Lord will sit—that is, dwell—in them, so that he may be their King forever, that is, rule them eternally.

And this is how he will rule them: the Lord will give strength—that is, steadfastness in goodness—to his people. The Lord will also bless them, that is, give increase to that same people both in number and in virtue, so that at last he may place them in peace, going into unity—that is, into eternal rest.

Thus he will bless the people who are placed here in peace, that is, in the observance of a good life. The observance of a good life consists in having conflict with vices and peace with excellent morals.

# ON PSALM XXIX  
*A psalm of a song at the dedication of the house of David.*

## ARGUMENT

Hezekiah, exalted by the outcome of so glorious a victory, was struck by illness so that, reminded of his frailty, he might lay aside his arrogance. In his person, therefore, thanksgiving is proclaimed for those struck down by error, saved from illness, and rescued from enemies; and it is sung for the way of life of the temple, as though for its dedication.

Alternatively, the Church prays with praise.

## EXPLANATION

“A psalm of a song” means that, with a chorus leading the human song, the art of the organ’s harmonious sound is joined to a hymn. Wherever this expression occurs, it shows that, through knowledge of divine understanding, the practice of good work must be undertaken, insofar as prior knowledge acquired from God precedes the desired effectiveness of the faithful deeds.

The house of David signifies the body of the Lord as a temple; its dedication signifies his resurrection, through which he was brought into eternal glory and power.

In the first account, after the glory of the Resurrection, the Lord gives thanks to the Father because he delivered him from the adversity of this world, commanding the saints to sing praise to the Lord, since all things have been placed under his power.

Second, he says that he must not be moved from his steadfastness, adding that praises of divinity ought to be offered by the living rather than the dead.

Third, he returns joyfully and exultantly to his resurrection, because, having laid aside the frailty of the flesh, he continues in the eternal glory of his majesty.

## COMMENTARY

“I will exalt you, O Lord.” The title is as follows: “A psalm of a song at the dedication of the house of David.”

The house of David is the Church, which in the present age is built through the highest labor and through various tribulations, both universally and in each individual. This house will finally be dedicated in the common resurrection, when this mortal existence is swallowed up by immortality and the glory of God’s people appears.

That people is now greatly troubled and hindered in its building by the sons of Edom, that is, Esau. Then, truly in amazement at that glory, it will say: “Behold, these are the ones whom we once held in derision and as an example of the reproach of death. How have they been counted among the sons of God, and how is their lot among his saints?”

For to dedicate properly means to assign a new building to a solemn use. Truly this house will be assigned to solemn use when God himself eternally dwells in each person, being all things in all.

Now, although he dwells in us, he often departs from us because of our bad merit. That change will then be entirely excluded. This dedication, however, has already partly occurred in reality and partly in hope.

The foundation has already been dedicated in reality: Christ, who has now risen and has again been placed at the right hand of God the Father, and who truly is the foundation. According to the Apostle: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ.”

But the dedication of the walls and roof of this building has already occurred in hope. For whatever preceded in the Head must follow in the members. Hence it is said: “God the Father, who raised Christ from the dead, will also raise us in him.”

The title is therefore explained as follows: This psalm—that is, this hymn—which is “of a song,” that is, of exultation, because it pertains to that true joy which no sadness will interrupt, is “of the dedication of the house of David,” that is, it concerns the dedication of the house of the true David.

For in this psalm there is the voice of the Head, giving thanks to God the Father because he turned the sadness of his Passion into the joy of the Resurrection. Through this he also gave his house the hope of future dedication and, for the present, the righteousness of inward resurrection. In this he exhorts us that, however greatly we may be afflicted, we must not fail in the building, so that at last we may truly rejoice in the dedication.

In this psalm our Head, Christ, prays from human weakness, according to which it is appropriate for him to pray.

For if you consider that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God,” he has no one to whom he may pray, nor anyone for whom he may pray. But if you consider that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” then he has one to whom he may pray and someone for whom he may pray.

He prays for you, a human being, because he became mediator between supreme righteousness and the lowest iniquity. I say, he is a human being not iniquitous but weak: so that, by being not iniquitous, he might be joined to supreme righteousness, and, by being weak, he might be joined to our weakness.

The sense is as follows: Lord Father, the first human being, Adam, exalted himself and as though depressed you, since it could appear either that you were weak, having made a human being whose conduct you did not know, or that you were not perfectly good, since your own associate so quickly abandoned you.

But by humbling myself I will exalt you, because my glorification will be your exaltation. And rightly I will exalt you, because you have received me—that is, you have undertaken my cause against wicked advocates, namely, against the Jews.

Therefore you have not delighted my enemies—that is, the teacher of iniquity, the devil, and the Jews. And even if he became exalted over me outwardly, although they rejoiced in my death, their joy lasted only for a time and was turned for them into eternal sadness.

“O Lord my God, I cried to you.” Therefore you did not delight my enemies, Lord, because I cried—that is, I directed a strong intention of heart toward you—considering that you are my God. I am not my own god, as wretched Adam thought himself his own god and wished to depend on his own will.

And because I cried to you, you healed me—that is, you restored through immortality the body that I carried wounded by passibility. He explains how he healed me when he says:

“O Lord, you brought my soul out of the underworld.” You did not permit my soul to remain in the underworld like the others, but brought it back in triumph, and thus glorified me with the second resurrection, since you had previously glorified me through the first resurrection.

For you saved me—that is, you raised me first inwardly through freedom from sins—me, I say, separated from those who descend into the pit, that is, from those who dwell in the depth of vices.

There is indeed a pit into which nearly the whole mortal race descends: the abyss of sensuality and every kind of wickedness. He did not descend into it, for he committed no sin, and deceit was not found in his mouth.

“Sing praises to the Lord, his saints.” Behold, the dedication of the Head has already been indicated where it was said: “You brought my soul out of the underworld.” And because what preceded in the Head must necessarily follow in the body, the old and true proverb is fulfilled: “Where the head is, there are the other members.”

Therefore, as though he were saying: Since you have in me, your Head, such certainty of your glorification and resurrection, you, his saints—that is, you whom the Lord Father has already sanctified through the righteousness given in my resurrection—sing praises to the Lord Father.

As though he were saying: Lament over the present; sing praises concerning the future; pray concerning the reality; rejoice in hope.

He expresses the last point as follows: “Give thanks”—that is, offer praise—“for the remembrance of his holiness,” that is, to the Lord himself. Although you had forgotten him by transgressing his commandments, he did not forget you. Rather, he remembered your holiness—that is, he remembered me, raising me through whom he sanctified you after justifying you.

Because his wrath is in his indignation.

Truly you ought to sing psalms to the Lord and give thanks, because he avenged in you the sin of your first parent through wrath, and restored life to you in me through mercy. He expresses this as follows: “Wrath is in his indignation,” and so forth. Indignation properly means that, when we are moved against someone, we turn our face away from him. Thus, when Adam transgressed and chose to obey his wife and the serpent rather than observe the Lord’s command—who had said to him, “You shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil”—the Lord turned his face away from him. For he withdrew from him the light of his grace, and then evening came upon him, because the true sun set for him.

In accordance with that passage from the book of Genesis: “When the Lord was walking in the garden at the afternoon breeze.” For it was, as it were, midday while the fervor of observance of God’s commandments persisted in Adam; [Col. 0627B] but after midday the sun inclines toward setting. So too in Adam the sun, as it were, declined toward its setting, when after the transgression of the commandment the knowledge and light of truth failed in his mind and the night of ignorance entered in. Hence he who had previously lived in an abundance of virtues and habitually rejoiced at the Lord’s presence was then compelled by ignorance of him to fear and hide himself, when the Lord said to him: “Adam, where are you?” Not that he was ignorant of the place, but as if he were saying: “Behold, wretched man, you who wished to exalt yourself beyond what was permitted—into what weakness you have cast yourself.”

In this evening weeping arose, because that wretched offshoot of sin was punished with death inwardly and outwardly. Through him the whole human race incurred this misery of mortality, so that it continually falls inwardly and outwardly. And this weeping, that is, this misery, will remain even in the most perfect until the morning of rejoicing, that is, until the universal resurrection, when we shall be dedicated anew in the joy previously lost and crowned with the robe of immortality.

[Col. 0627C]

This morning was already prefigured by the Lord’s morning resurrection, which took place on the first day of the week. The literal sense of these two verses, whose meaning we have set forth above, is explained as follows. Wrath, that is, mortality and every misery of human weakness, came upon us in his indignation, that is, when the Lord was indignant with transgressing Adam. And the life of immortality—which you were unable to recover by any of your merits—was restored to you in his will, that is, through his mercy and goodwill alone, not through your merits, since you had deserved nothing except wrath; it has been restored now in hope, so that it may finally be restored in reality.

Or, if we wish to take the expression emphatically, we may call Christ himself the will of the Father, because he did not deviate from his will even in thought. Adam, however, may be called the indignation, since he deserved nothing but wrath. You may also read it in this inverted order: You ought therefore rightly to give thanks to the Lord, because life has been restored to you in his will, that is, through me, who am [Col. 0627D] his will. For this reason he ordained that I should be born and die: so that you might die in sins; and for this reason he caused me to rise again: so that you too might rise to true life. And truly life was given to you through my will, because wrath was given in indignation, that is, through the one who alone deserved indignation.

And this weeping, that is, this wrath which arose at evening, as was said above, will remain—that is, it will long abide—in human beings, outwardly and inwardly. It will truly remain, because the joy of dedication, although it is already possessed in hope, will nevertheless be deferred in reality until the morning of the universal resurrection, when the light of the true sun will appear.

Or we may understand “weeping” as sin itself, from which wrath came beforehand, and explain it thus: “Wrath was indeed in indignation. And because of it weeping will remain always among those who turn toward evening,” that is, among those who retain the traces of the old condition and conform themselves to evening. But the joy now, meanwhile, of the inner resurrection, and eventually also of the outward resurrection, will belong to those who turn toward morning, that is, to those who conform themselves to Christ, who is the morning of true light. [Col. 0628A]

It must also be understood that evening came through Adam in the human race, and that our morning may be compared with the evening of the Head and with his morning. For the Head, that is, Christ, was buried at evening, lay in the tomb for three days, and rose on the morning of the third day. We too were buried in the evening—that is, when, after Adam’s transgression, the sun of truth set for him—in the darkness of sin and ignorance. If we consider the ages of the world, we lay in that tomb for three days. The whole period before the Law is reckoned as one day; likewise, the whole period under the Law is called the second. When the third day arrived, that is, the time of grace, we rose already through an inner resurrection in the morning, when the sun of righteousness drove away the night of sins; and in this same time we shall finally rise also through an outward resurrection.

I said in my prosperity: “I shall not be moved forever.”

For this reason wrath was given: because the first man, placed [Col. 0628B] by the Lord in an abundance of virtues, said, if not in words, then in deed: “I shall not be moved,” that is, “I shall not stand by the Lord’s command, which said that I must not eat; rather, I shall stretch out my hand, take the fruit, and be like God.”

But life was restored in me, the second man, because I existed in my prosperity—that is, in an abundance far greater and more excellent than his. For it is of me alone that it was said that God does not give the Spirit by measure. The abundance of this one was also greater than that of the other in this respect: the other could only avoid death if he did not sin, whereas this one could in no way die by sinning.

I, then, existing in abundance, said: “I shall not be moved,” that is, “I shall not apostatize from the Lord’s commandments, persevering forever.” And I do not ascribe this perseverance to myself, but to the Lord. For you, O Lord, supplied strength—that is, steadfastness—so that I could not fall away from my beauty, that is, from the freedom from sins which you gave me. And you did not do this because of my merits, but by your will, that is, solely through your good pleasure and mercy.

[Col. 0628C]

You turned your face from me.

Truly you supplied me with strength through mercy alone, because in wrath you had taken it away. For in transgressing Adam you turned your face—that is, the light of your truth—away from my people and from me, insofar as I am considered with respect to the human mass. In this way my people were troubled by sin and by the weakness of mortality which they received from him; and I myself, with respect to the punishment of sin, was troubled, though not with respect to sin itself.

For Christ hungered, suffered cold, and thirsted because of the punishment of sin; but he did not know sin. And because of this distress I shall cry out, that is, I shall direct a strong intention of heart toward you, O Lord. In this way I shall plead with you, both for myself and for my people, addressing you as Lord of all by nature and my Lord by grace, saying:

“O Lord, what profit will there be in my blood,” that is, in the shedding of my blood? What fruit will follow from my passion if I descend into corruption? That is, if I do not rise again for the consolation and justification of others, but my flesh is given [Col. 0628D] over to the corruption of decay?

Truly there will be no profit, because the dust—that is, sinners worn down by sins and light like dust, who are to be converted and justified through my resurrection—will otherwise not give thanks to you, that is, they will make no praiseworthy confession to you. And will they give thanks to you? Certainly not.

Or, if I do not rise again, who among the Apostles or others will announce to that dust your truth, that is, that the true life promised has been restored through me? Certainly no one will announce it, because no one will hope for it.

The Lord heard and had mercy on me.

I said to the Lord, “What profit is there in my blood?” and so forth, pleading with him. And the Lord heard my prayer, and the Lord had mercy on me by raising me up, justifying my people inwardly, giving them the sure hope of perfect salvation; and the Lord became my helper, taking up my cause against my enemies.

He shows how he had mercy and turns directly to him, saying: “You have changed, O Lord, my mourning,” that is, [Col. 0629A] you have changed the sorrow of my passion and of my people into joy for me and for them. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “The world indeed will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful; yet your sorrow will be turned into joy.”

And you changed it in this way because you tore my sackcloth, that is, you allowed my mortal flesh to be torn and pierced on the cross. A sackcloth is properly a certain thick garment, once suitable for military use, woven from the hair of goats and young goats. By young goats and goats, sinners are rightly understood, because of their stench.

The mortal flesh of Christ, therefore, which you assumed from sinners, is rightly understood as a sackcloth. For he was born from sinners and came in the likeness of sinful flesh, but not in sinful flesh; for he put on the sackcloth, but did not assume the merit of the sackcloth, that is, sin, because he alone emerged free from sin.

You tore the sackcloth, I say, in the passion, and surrounded me with joy, that is, with the joyful and triumphant robe [Col. 0629B] of immortality and incorruption in the resurrection—me in reality, but my people in hope. And you did this so that my mortality might no longer groan to you, but my glory might sing to you, that is, praise you in the manifestation of the reality: my immortality and impassibility.

And my glory, already given to them in hope, means that I shall no longer be pierced by mortality. Hence it is said: “And death shall no longer rule over him.” Nor shall my people any longer be pierced by the goads of sins, especially capital sins. Hence the Apostle also says: “So that we may no longer serve sin.”

And so, O Lord my God, I shall give thanks to you forever, that is, I shall make an eternal praiseworthy confession to you in myself and also in my people. For if we confess here what we have done against him, he will be merciful to us and forgive us. And eternally we shall confess to him what he himself has done for us: that he made the impious pious, sinners righteous, slaves sons, and those condemned received into the kingdom.

## ON PSALM XXX

*To the end. A Psalm of David, for ecstasy.*

[Col. 0629C]

## ARGUMENT

It is foretold in what words the people held captive in Babylon supplicate God for their return, what evils they suffered, and what return will take place in the future, if God grants it. Alternatively, it is the confession of those who believe in God.

## EXPLANATION

The title is familiar and pertains to the Lord Christ, whose passion and resurrection are the subject of the entire psalm. Throughout the psalm the words are those of the Lord and Savior.

At the outset he prays to the Father that he may be delivered from the evils threatening him, and then, having undoubtedly been heard, he rejoices. Secondly, he returns to his passion and describes the event in a marvelous narrative through various allusions. Thirdly, he gives general thanks for himself and for the faithful people, because he has bestowed the gifts of his mercy upon the universal Church. He also exhorts the saints [Col. 0629D] to persevere in the love of the Lord, since above they heard both the rewards of the good and the retributions of the wicked.

This psalm may, according to its historical sense, be understood of him himself.

## COMMENTARY

In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me not be put to shame forever; in your righteousness deliver me.

The title is as follows: “To the end. A Psalm of David, for ecstasy.” *Ecstasy*, as Augustine says, is a Greek word, interpreted as “excess”; strictly speaking, however, ecstasy means an excess or departure of the mind from itself.

There are two forms of this excess: fear, namely, and attention directed toward higher things. It is such that the mind already slips away from its inward memory. For when divine secrets are revealed to the saints, their customary inward memory truly departs from them, because they think of nothing human but attend solely to heavenly and spiritual things.

Paul was in this heavenly attentiveness when he said: “Whether we are beside ourselves in mind, it is for God; or whether we are sober-minded, it is for you.” As if he were saying: “If we were always considering only lofty and sublime things, [Col. 0630A] when could you, who are weak, ascend to us? But so that you may be able to reach us, the love of God—who humbled and emptied himself for us—compels us to think soberly and to condescend to you.”

This aspect of ecstasy, namely attention directed toward higher things, pertains to this psalm in the following way: the holy man who speaks in this psalm is placed in this heavenly attentiveness and exhorts us, by his example, to direct our attention toward higher things in such a way that we slip away from our inward memory—that is, that we no longer think about or desire earthly things, but only heavenly ones.

The other aspect of ecstasy, which is considered in fear, is not separate from the structure of this psalm. For this psalm deals in various ways with the tribulation suffered by the holy man who speaks here, not only outwardly from sinners but also inwardly from false brothers. Because of this he is in a certain sense afraid, having been carried outside himself: he fears that he may succumb, and therefore he prays to be delivered from it, exhorting us that, whenever we are afflicted, we too should pray [Col. 0630B] not to fail.

And if we fear, we should fear in such a way that we also hope, since the one who acts in this psalm not only fears but also hopes. Fear without hope is despair, whereas hope without fear is presumption. Therefore we must both hope and fear: fear because of human weakness, so that “the one who stands may take heed lest he fall”; hope because of the divine promise, since, even if there is some disturbance in the human heart, divine consolation nevertheless does not abandon us.

Hence someone aptly says of this psalm: “Let us attend to the psalm: if he prays, let us pray; if he groans, let us groan; if he rejoices, let us rejoice; if he hopes, let us hope; if he is afraid, let us be afraid.”

The title is explained as follows: These words are referred not to history, but “to the end,” that is, to Christ through his member; they are a psalm, that is, praise attributed to David, the perfect man—truly “strong of hand”—one alone and without plurality. For this one person speaks, through his affinity with unity, in the person of many.

It is a psalm, I say, which is ecstasy, because in it the perfect man, whose voice corresponds to both forms of ecstasy [Col. 0630C] mentioned above, acts and perseveres in this manner with the Lord his God:

“Lord, unhappy Adam hoped in himself and therefore was put to shame. But I have hoped in you alone, not in myself, and therefore I shall not be put to shame forever,” that is, I shall not incur eternal shame, nor shall I dread temporal shame here rather than eternal shame.
