There is a certain temporal shame which is a useful disturbance of the soul when it considers its sins: by looking upon them it blushes, and by abhorring them it corrects itself. The Christian soul ought not to fear this shame but to seek it in every way, because if it loves this shame, it avoids eternal shame; but if it does not seek it, it incurs divine shame.

Eternal shame will come when their iniquities lead the wicked in the opposite direction, that is, to the left. To them it will be said: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire.” Then they will blush when it is reproached to them: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and so forth.

“I shall not be put to shame,” I say, because I have hoped in you; and in your righteousness deliver me from the danger of death. If you turn back [Col. 0630D] to my righteousness—which deserved wrath alone—you will condemn me; but in your righteousness you will save me.

This righteousness is mine, that is, given to me by you. Yet it is called yours, lest human pride presume upon itself, as those did who established their own righteousness and refused to be subject to the righteousness of God. Therefore they did not attend to the grace of God, that is, to true salvation. It is rightly called grace, that is, freely given. For freely he called us, and freely he called us, justified us, and glorified us.

Therefore, O Lord, deliver me in your righteousness, that is, in your grace, and rescue me. As if he were saying: “Deliver me by that which justifies me, namely, that which makes the impious pious, the blind seeing, the fallen rise, and the weeping rejoice. Thus, finally, it may free me from eternal shame; meanwhile, let it rescue me from conformity with the wicked.” Another translation has both expressions, namely, “Deliver me” and “Rescue me.”

Incline your ear to me.

“Deliver me,” I say, “and incline”—you, who are exalted, toward the humble; the physician toward [Col. 0631A] the sick; God toward the human being—“your ear,” that is, direct toward me, who am crying out, the power of hearing which is in you; that is, dispose your mercy over me.

For what greater mercy could there be than that God ordained that his only-begotten Son should become incarnate for us—not to live for us, but to die for us? Incline, I say, and hasten to rescue me, that is, finally to separate me from the fellowship of the wicked. And you will indeed hasten, because the time is short, and nothing possessing an end ought to seem long.

Be for me a protecting God.

I say that you should finally rescue me. But meanwhile, be for me a protecting God, that is, protecting me against every assault and ambush of the enemy; and be for me a house of refuge. For I fled from you and lost myself; I shall take refuge in you so that I may find myself. For if I withdraw from you, wherever I flee, I shall find you: if you are angry, as my punisher; if you are reconciled, as my helper.

Therefore be for me a house to which I, who have already fallen away by withdrawing from you in the field, may retreat, so that I may make [Col. 0631B] myself safe—that is, so that I, who previously lost myself, may find myself.

For you are my strength.

Therefore, O Lord, I ask you to be my house of refuge and my protector, because you are my strength, giving me patience so that I may be strong enough to endure the tribulations and persecutions of my enemies.

And you are my refuge, enabling me to leave them, so that I may not conform to them. For your name, which is to be glorified through me, you will lead me—that is, you will make me persist in and love your will, while utterly despising my own.

And in this way you will lead me, that is, you will exalt me from virtue to virtue. And in this way you will nourish me, that is, for now you will feed me with milk, so that afterward I may be fit to eat solid food, by which the angels are nourished.

Note the comparison. As a mother’s tenderness takes the solid food on which a little child cannot be nourished and transforms it within her own flesh so that it becomes milk, and thus offers it to her child until he becomes capable of being nourished by solid food, so the clemency of the highest Father transformed the solid food of the angels—[Col. 0631C] that is, his wisdom, for receiving which our perversity was not fit—into flesh, clothing it in flesh, and offered us its humility as though in the food of milk.

By eating it, that is, imitating it, may we finally become fit to be nourished by the true bread on which the angels feed. For in order that man might eat the bread of angels, the King of heaven became man.

You will lead me out of the snare.

“You will nourish me,” I say, “and in nourishing me you will lead me out,” that is, release me from the snare which the devil and his ministers have hidden—that is, secretly prepared—for me.

He calls the snare every deception and ambush of the devil. In this snare he prepares and conceals two entanglements for us: error and terror. Error is present in allurements, by which he deceives us; terror in tribulations, by which he breaks us.

But let us imitate the example of our Emperor, who not only deigned to become incarnate for us, but also deigned to be tempted for us. First he was tempted by error on the mountain [Col. 0631D] by the devil, when, displaying to him all the world’s allurements, he said: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.”

But he could not be deceived, because he closed the door of desire against error, saying: “Go away, Satan; you shall not tempt the Lord your God.” Then, as the Evangelist testifies, he withdrew from him for a time, intending to return. Since he could not deceive him by error, he wished to break him by terror, preparing passion for him.

But he accomplished nothing in this way either, because Christ likewise closed the door of fear against terror. Therefore, when we too are tempted by the devil or his ministers, let us close the door against the error of desire and block the gate against the terror of fear; thus we shall be led out of this snare.

For you are—

Therefore, I say, you will lead me out of the snare, because I chose you alone to be my protector against the ambushes and assaults of the enemy.

And because I have you as my protector, therefore, O Lord, I commend my spirit—that is, my soul—to be defended from the snare of error and terror [Col. 0632A]— not to my weakness but into your hands, that is, into your omnipotence.

And rightly do I do this, because you will most certainly redeem it from there, since you have already redeemed it through the sacrament of faith. You, I say, who are the God of truth, that is, who deceive no one in your promises.

You hate those who observe vanities.

Truly you are the God of truth. For you are not the God of falsehood, because you hate those who observe vanity. They observe vanity who, while fearing to die, die. For by fearing to die they lie, and by lying they die. They lied in order to live. For falsehood is the death of the soul.

Thus, while they flee from one death, they incur a double death. To flee from death in this way is superfluous and futile, because although they may appear able to delay death, they cannot remove it. And all this happens because they love this life and these temporal goods, which are vain.

Or understand it in this way: If you hope in money, nobility, or some special dignity, [Col. 0632B] you are observing vanity. For while you hope, you breathe your last; and while you breathe your last, you lose that in which you hoped. This too is futile, that is, harmful.

Let us therefore love those things which neither abandon us while we breathe nor are abandoned by us while we breathe.

But I have hoped in God.

You indeed hate, O Lord, those who observe vanity, but you do not hate me, because I did not look toward vanity but toward truth. For I have always hoped, and I shall hope, in you, O Lord.

And I shall hope in this way: I shall rejoice outwardly and be glad inwardly, that is, I shall rejoice fully—not in my righteousness but in mercy, that is, in your grace. In it I rightly ought to rejoice, since, just as earlier you looked with contempt upon me when I was exalted in Adam, giving me over to distress, so now you have looked upon me when humbled, because you have already saved my soul in hope from distress, that is, from all sins and miseries.

They are called distresses because, when we fell away from the light of truth in our first parent, we necessarily fell into these miseries, [Col. 0632C] from which we can in no way be perfectly saved until the end; nevertheless, we have been saved in hope.

Augustine speaks of these distresses as follows:

“Who could enumerate the distresses of the soul, or adequately commend the things that must be avoided? Certainly no one. For it is a great distress not to know another’s heart. Hence it happens that we often think badly of a faithful friend, but think well of a faithful enemy. From this comes the saying: ‘Do not judge before the time,’” and so forth.

It is also a great distress not to know one’s own heart, as Peter did not know his when he said: “Lord, even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.”

Moreover, mortality itself is a great distress, because everyone must die, yet no one wishes to die. To struggle against old habits and detest evil, and yet to do evil, are also grave distresses; and there are many other countless distresses of the soul which no one can explain.

Nor did you enclose me in the hands of the enemy.

“You saved me,” I say, “from distresses, and in this way you enclosed”—that is, you did not permit and will not permit [Col. 0632D]—“me,” that is, my soul, “in the hands,” that is, in the power, “of the enemy.”

Here understand “enemy” not as some familiar person or your neighbor, but as the worst enemy, the ancient serpent, in whose hands everyone who dies in his sins is enclosed. But whoever turns away from his impiety and does righteousness will not die and will not be enclosed in his hands.

You did not enclose me, I say, in the hands of the enemy; rather, you set my feet—that is, my affections—in a spacious place, that is, in the breadth of love. In other words, you made your righteousness easy for me, so that with an enlarged heart I might run through it. Just as it is difficult for one who is unwilling, so it is easy for one who loves.

For narrow is the way that leads to life, since no one runs along it except with an enlarged heart.

Have mercy on me, O Lord.

Up to this point there has been, as it were, the rejoicing of the perfect man that he has been delivered from tribulations and saved from distresses, and that his feet are in a spacious place. Why, then, does he now say, as if danger were again threatening, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, because [Col. 0633A] I am afflicted”?

For if he is afflicted, he is constrained; but if he is constrained, how are his feet in a spacious place? Perhaps he says this because those who are one body have one voice. In that body some members experience the ease of righteousness, while others still labor under tribulation; and if one member suffers, the others suffer with it; if one member is glorified, the others are glorified with it.

Therefore the former are saddened by the tribulation of the latter, and the latter are consoled by the glorification of the former. This happens because love creates a bond; the bond embraces unity; unity preserves love; and love leads to glory.

Accordingly, this perfect man who speaks here, although delivered from tribulations, speaks on behalf of his companions or of any weak persons with whom he sympathizes:

“Have mercy on me, O Lord, and it is necessary that you have mercy, because I am afflicted.”

But why does the grain, which previously rejoiced amid so great a multitude of chaff, now suffer tribulation? Because the love of many has already grown cold. And because those whom he formerly saw in the temple of the Lord he now sees in the theater. And now he hears those whom he formerly heard singing ecclesiastical hymns singing theatrical songs.

And I am not only afflicted but also angry. Why is he angry? [Col. 0633B] Because he sees people confessing God with their mouths but blaspheming him in their conduct; renouncing the world in words but clinging to it in deeds. He sees many such things, at which the body of Christ is angry, that body which inwardly lives by the Spirit of Christ.

The literal sense is expressed as follows: “My eye,” that is, my understanding, “is in anger,” that is, it is angry with false brothers. The eye, I say, is disturbed only by reasonable anger, not extinguished by hatred. For it is permissible to be angry at the evils which the wicked do, but it is not permissible to hate the wicked themselves.

And not only the eye, that is, the understanding, is troubled; my soul also, that is, my reason, and my belly, that is, my sensual faculty, are troubled. Understand by these two groups of three all the inward parts.

As if he were saying: “All my inward parts are troubled, but not my outward parts.” [Col. 0633C] For when we see such great perversity and wickedness prevailing among the wicked that we can neither rebuke nor correct it, then we may be angry, but we may not cry out; for if we cried out, we would accomplish nothing and would instead create a great stumbling block for ourselves.

When this happens, the inward parts alone are troubled, not the outward parts. Sensuality is that power of the soul which desires from outward things only as much as suffices for the body’s need. As long as it preserves this measure, it is subject to its husband, that is, to reason. But when it exceeds the yoke of its husband, it casts it off and, agreeing with the devil, stretches out its hand toward unlawful things, like Eve toward the fruit; thus it also seduces her husband.

For my life has failed in sorrow.

My inward parts are rightly troubled, because my life, which ought to have progressed in joy, has failed in sorrow. It must be understood that the life of a holy man perfected in the Gospel of Christ is not necessary for himself but for the ordering of others. Nor does he live for his own sake, but so that his life [Col. 0633D] may provide an example to others.

When by his example he wins some people and joins them to the body of Christ, then his life progresses in joy. Conversely, if he cannot bring anyone into conformity with himself, his life fails in sorrow.

Hence this perfect man complains, saying: “My life has failed in sorrow, and not a short life, but my years,” that is, my long life, which I have spent so as to benefit others. “I have failed in groanings,” not in clear voices, because I see such great perversity that the pain of the heart may be expressed only through groaning, not through the voice of correction.

My strength has weakened in poverty.

Therefore my life has failed in sorrow, and my years in groanings, because my strength—that is, the vigor of love toward my neighbors, who were to be saved through my example—has been weakened, not in me but, with respect to its effectiveness, in poverty, as though through a lack of food.

For since I hungered for nothing other than to save some people, I found no one through whom, by conforming himself to me, he might refresh me. [Col. 0634A] And it is no wonder that my strength has weakened, because even my bones—that is, the stronger members among my companions, who were my support—have been inwardly troubled, as was said above, not so much by the persecution of enemies as by the impiety of false brothers.

More than all my enemies.

Therefore my strength has weakened and my bones have been troubled, because I have become a reproach above all my enemies, that is, I have been held in greater contempt than all my enemies—namely, the Jews and pagans who contradict the truth.

Yet this comes about, as if he were saying, because false Christians are found who live worse within the sacraments of the Church than either Jews or pagans live according to their own rule.

This should be referred to the enemies themselves. For another translation has: “Among all my enemies I have become a reproach, and I have become exceedingly a reproach to my neighbors.”

He calls “neighbors” those who previously wished to approach the ecclesiastical rule and enter the Church but were repelled because of the private life of the false brothers, [Col. 0634B] among whom he became a reproach. Either they themselves commonly reviled him along with the others, or they even say: “Why should we approach you, when you lead a much more shameful life than we do?”

And to my acquaintances—that is, even to those who were known either to me or by me in the ecclesiastical institutions, because they had already become accustomed to living in them—I am, I say, a terror, because they are afraid to approach me and even doubt me.

As if he were saying: “Because of certain people we have fallen into doubt.”

Those also who knew me not only in the ecclesiastical institutions but saw me in the Holy Scriptures—because they had read there many things foretold, both about one perfect person individually and about all perfect people collectively—those, I say, although they seemed very wise and perfect, fled from me outside, that is, they left the Church and became heretics.

Of them it is said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.”

And among these I was given over to oblivion, removed from their hearts [Col. 0634C] as though I were someone dead in sins; or as though dead from the heart, that is, utterly dead in the innermost part itself.

I have become like a ruined vessel.

Because my life has failed in sorrow, my strength has weakened, and I have become a reproach above all my enemies, and so forth, I have become like a discarded vessel, that is, a broken vessel fit for no use.

For just as a broken vessel uselessly spills the liquid poured into it, which was intended to be poured through it into others, so I have labored. I prepared myself to benefit others, but my labor and my preparation flowed away uselessly, because there was no one willing to follow me.

And this happened especially because I heard the reproach of many, that is, I became a reproach to many—enemies, neighbors, and acquaintances alike. I became a reproach also to those who had previously seen me and fled from me, to many, I say, who dwell all around, that is, who merely go around and do not enter.

They go around and do not enter because they love [Col. 0634D] the wheel of time. They do not enter into the truth because they do not love eternity; devoted to temporal things, they are bound to the wheel, as it were.

While they dwell in that circuit—since they were in it but I did not consent to it—they conspired against me, that is, they took counsel together against me, to seize my soul, that is, to thrust me, who was within the truth, outside it and place me with themselves in the circuit.

The enemies did this through threats and persecutions; the false brothers through seductive flatteries.

But I—

They indeed conspired to devour me, but they did not accomplish their plan, because, placed amid so many reproaches and so many scandals—persecutions outside, seditions or seductions within—I hoped in you, O Lord, not in man, for in you it is firm and certain to hope.

Whoever hopes in man, when man totters, totters himself, and so does his hope. When man falls, his hope also falls. But in the Lord there is no progression and no failure; he neither increases nor diminishes but always remains the same. Therefore his hope is fixed and certain.

I hoped, I say, in you. [Col. 0635A] And I showed this in deed, because I said to you—not with the noise of the mouth’s voice but with the silent voice of the heart:

“Deliver me, O Lord, from the hands of my enemies,” and so forth.

And rightly did I say this to you, because you alone are my God—not Donatus, not Marcion, nor even Paul himself is my God. “Were you baptized in the name of Paul?” Certainly not, but in the name of Christ.

And rightly do I make you my God, because my lots, that is, my portions, to which I belong—that is, the portions of the saints—are not in human hands but in your hands, that is, in your power alone. For the fact that they are portions of the saints does not depend on their merits but on your grace.

The grace of God is called a lot because, just as something obtained by lot does not come through a selection based on merits, so those chosen by lot are chosen not because of merits but by chance.

Or: “My lots are in your hands,” that is, let others choose whatever portions in the world they wish, but my lots will be in your hands. That is, I shall choose nothing except what properly belongs to your power. [Col. 0635B]

And therefore let Donatus, or Marcion, or any such person not assign to me Africa or some particular portion of the earth.

Rescue me from the hands of my enemies. This must always be prayed for, this must be desired with every wish: that we may be rescued by the Lord from the hands, that is, from the power, of our enemies. It should be noted, however, that some are enemies against whom we ought to pray, and others for whom we ought to pray. Against the devil and his angels we ought to pray, lest we be deceived by them, because they envy us the kingdom of heaven. They grieve that we are ascending to the place from which they fell; but for human enemies, in whom there is some hope of conversion, we ought to pray. Nevertheless, it must be understood that enemies, whatever sort of people they may be, are not to be hated, lest, when an evil person hates the evil he suffers, there be two evil persons. The good person, therefore, should love the evil that he suffers, so that there may be only one evil person.

“Rescue me,” I say, and so forth. “Rescue me,” I say, “from those who persecute me,” that is, from false brothers who persecute deceitfully. He therefore prays for them even in a particular way, because their persecution is nearer and more dangerous. For such people, when they are not tolerated by the good and are not permitted to live according to their own way, immediately seek a means of breaking away from unity and of causing some disturbance. We ought to pray for such people, that they may be converted and recover their senses. And if they have already departed, let them return; but if they are still within, though in a perverse manner, let them be changed for the better and become steadfast.

Make your face shine. “I say, Rescue me”; and, in order that you may rescue me, “make your face shine upon me”—make me not a freedman, either of myself or of you, but your servant. That is: make me such that, in my words and deeds, it may appear that I belong to your inheritance and possession. And in order that you may illumine me, “save me, O Lord,” that is, make me persevering; and do this not on account of my merits, but in your mercy—that is, not because I am worthy, but because you are merciful. Therefore I ask you to save me, lest I be put to shame, that is, lest I incur eternal shame; for I ought not to be put to shame, since I have called upon you. The reason he gives may indeed seem easy and slight, but it is nevertheless sufficiently weighty. For the wicked call upon God, but do not truly invoke him, because they do not call upon him freely—that is, for his own sake alone—but in order to make him the servant of their wickedness: namely, so that through him they may acquire gold, silver, or other things which they could in no way possess by themselves. Those alone call upon God rightly who call upon him freely and, by calling upon him, prepare in their hearts a disposition worthy of him.

Let the wicked be put to shame. “As for me, I shall not be put to shame”; but let the wicked, in contrast, be put to shame—that is, let them incur eternal shame. And, in order that they may finally be put to shame, let them in the present be brought down to hell, that is, into the depths of vices; let them now be given over to inner darkness, so that finally they may be given over to outer darkness. This is not a wish of malevolence, but a declaration of their punishment. Or it may simply be expressed in this way: Let the wicked be put to shame in the future, and let them be put to shame in such a way that they are brought down to hell, that is, into eternal shame.

And let deceitful lips become mute. This cannot happen in the present life, because here they continually tear others apart and blaspheme, and with poisoned tongues they always contradict. But at last they will truly become silent—namely, when their iniquities will expose the wicked in contrast to them, and there will no longer be any place for sin.

Which speak against the righteous. Those, I say, are deceitful lips which speak iniquity against the very head of the righteous and against each individual righteous person, in the arrogance of their words and in the abuse of created things. Their arrogant words against the righteous are such as these: “What do you believe? What do you hope for? It is certain that you labor, but uncertain that what you hope for will come. When, then, will what you hope for arrive?” These words too are truly very wicked. For it is the height of iniquity to take away the righteous person’s hope.

In the abuse of created things, however, those speak iniquity who desire and love earthly things, which the Lord did not wish to love and possess, so as to teach that they should be despised—not because they were not within his power to possess. By doing this they contradict Christ himself, whom they do not wish to imitate. And because he is the head of all the righteous, they also contradict the righteous in him; in both respects they act wickedly.

How great is the abundance. They speak, I say, in arrogance and in abuse. But they do not consider how great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord. According to blessed Augustine, the passage may also be connected, with the insertion of certain words, in this way. The perfect man, who earlier rejoiced as though freed from tribulations, and who shortly before groaned on account of the fellowship of his companions in tribulation, now considers the goods of God which he saw inwardly in spirit. These goods are seen secretly by the faithful alone; the wicked do not know them, because the wicked know how to see only the goods of this age, while they neither know how to consider nor even how to conceive the goods of the age to come. Hence they speak against the righteous in arrogance and abuse. Considering those goods, I say, and commending them to people whom he wishes to tolerate here but not to love as present realities, he says, as though in admiration of those goods: “O Lord, how great is the abundance of your sweetness!”

He calls the immortal and true wisdom of God the Father, which he made known through his incarnate Word and which he gives partly to the faithful in the present, while in the future he will give it perfectly, “sweetness.” By the two expressions he uses—namely, “how great” and “abundance”—he indicates that it is so vast that it can be comprehended neither in number nor in measure, according to the saying: “Of his wisdom there is no number.”

“Great,” I say, “and abundant is your sweetness, O Lord. Although you have concealed it from the wicked, you have nevertheless hidden it,” that is, reserved it, “for those who fear you” with chaste fear, not fear of human beings, and who strive toward you. It is as though one of those who speak iniquity were to say: “Where is that sweetness of which you speak? Show it to me.” And he would reply: “I cannot show it to you, because it is not for you to say, ‘Taste and see that the Lord is sweet,’ since you have lost the palate of your heart through the fever of iniquity. It can be shown only to those who fear the Lord, because the Lord has reserved it for them alone.”

You have perfected it for those who hope in you. To those who strive toward you and fear you, you have indeed concealed your sweetness; but you have “perfected” it—that is, you have already made it as perfect as it can be here—and at last you will perfect it completely for those who hope in you in such a way that they are not afraid to confess their hope in the sight of the children of men. That is, they do not yet blush to profess your faith before rulers and whatever persecutors are not children of the new human being but children of human beings—that is, those who remain in the old condition.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever is ashamed of me before human beings, I also shall be ashamed of him before my Father; but whoever is not ashamed of me, neither shall I be ashamed of him.” Therefore, whoever you are, do not be ashamed of your hope. Rather, let it dwell upon your lips just as it lives in your heart.

You will hide them in the hidden place of your face. You have truly perfected your sweetness for those who openly hope in you, because at last you will “hide” them—that is, you will fortify them, separated from the turmoil of human beings, by whom they must necessarily be disturbed so long as they are still grain together with chaff on the threshing floor.

And you will place them in the hidden place of your face. Notice that the Lord does not promise his people a place in paradise, or in Abraham’s bosom, or in heaven, but in himself. Let God dwell in you here, and at last he will make you dwell in himself. Receive him here in your heart, and he himself will receive you in his countenance. For he who now secretly protects his own in the place of this present life will at last protect them in himself as their place.

“How, however, can God be a place?” Blessed Augustine says that even if he had a voice with which to explain it, there would be no ear capable of hearing it. Nevertheless, by a certain suitable comparison this may be understood as follows: by “the hidden place of his face” we may understand the brightness of his countenance, in which the Lord will finally place the good as in a fortified stronghold, hidden from the wicked, according to the saying: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.”

You will protect them. At last you will hide those who hope in you; but in the meantime you will protect them, placed in your tabernacle—that is, in the present Church, which is the place of warfare and pilgrimage.

From the contradiction of tongues. Here heretical and schismatic tongues continually cling to us, tear us apart, and blaspheme. What, then, must we do? Let each person withdraw into the holy Church and hold fast to the rule of truth and unity. In this way he will remain secure from the contradiction of tongues.

The words “You will hide them,” which we read as referring to the future, may also be spoken of the present in this way: “At last, O Lord, you will perfect your sweetness for those who openly hope in you. But in the meantime you will hide them,” that is, fortify them against the turmoil of human beings, “in the hidden place of your face,” that is, in the secret place of their hearts, in the righteousness of the believer, where they behold your hidden face. Thus you will protect them in your tabernacle, and so forth.

For holy and perfect men, when they are mocked by the wicked and many insults are spoken against them, commonly withdraw into the secret place of the heart, where they take delight in the sweetness of the Lord’s countenance. There they speak familiarly with the Lord himself, as it were, and are strengthened by him against every disturbance.

Benedictus Dominus. After the perfect man had considered so many benefits of the Lord—namely, that he would not permit the one who hoped in him to be put to shame forever; that he would lead him out of the snare and save his soul from distress; and especially that, as he had just said, he had reserved for those who feared him the abundance of sweetness which he hides from the wicked, and would at last perfect it for those who openly hoped in him, whom he now again protects in his tabernacle—for all these things, I say, he says: “Blessed be the Lord,” that is, may the Lord be exalted and increased in his members.

And because the preceding matters had been stated at length, he gathers them together briefly, saying: “For he has shown wonder,” and so forth. It is as though he said: “Rightly I say, ‘Blessed be the Lord,’ because he has made this mercy of his, spoken of above, wondrous”—that is, wondrous and desirable—“for me, the perfect man, both in me and in my companions, in whose person I speak.” For this perfect man is understood here as representing the whole body of the Church.

And he did not make it wondrous for me in a few people, but “in a fortified city,” that is, in the multitude of the Church, which is fortified; or because it is populous, just as populous cities are fortified; or because it is protected by faith, hope, and charity as by bulwarks.

Another translation has: “In a city of encirclement.” Blessed Augustine explains this as follows. He says that the city of the surrounding region was formerly Jerusalem, which the nations surrounded on every side, where there were the priesthood and the temple, where sacrifices were offered and prophecies were proclaimed; where also the Lord preached, taught, performed miracles, suffered, rose again, and ascended.

But after all these things he did something far more exalted: he did not permit the mercy of his Christ to be confined within that people as in a vessel, but, as though the vessel had been broken, he poured out his name like oil among all the nations. He did this by sending the Holy Spirit from heaven, by whom he kindled the hearts of the apostles like pieces of wood and, through them, set the forest of the nations ablaze on every side. Hence it is rightly said here that the Lord made his mercy wondrous “in a fortified city,” that is, in a populous city.

But I said in ecstasy. “I say: Blessed be the Lord, because he has made his mercy wondrous in a fortified city.” Yet I, placed in this manifestation of wonder “in ecstasy”—that is, in an ecstasy of my mind, because of fear of the tribulations which I saw about to rage against me, so that this manifestation of wonder might take place through me and my companions—not only from persecutors outwardly but also from false brothers inwardly, and therefore fearing that I might hinder it, said: “Lord, I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.”

It is as though he said: “The evils raging against me show that I have lost the regard of your mercy. For if you looked upon me, you would not permit me to suffer so much.”

Blessed Augustine says that the title of the psalm took its occasion from this passage, because “ecstasy” is mentioned here. The remaining aspect of ecstasy may also be noted here, namely, an intention directed toward higher things, if the passage is understood in this way: “I, placed in the ecstasy of my mind”—that is, transcending my human condition in order to contemplate the sublimity of your mercy—“said: ‘Lord, I have been cast away from the sight,’” and so forth; “I am not worthy of such great mercy from you as I formerly was.”

Ideo exaudisti. I did not exalt myself, but humbled and accused myself, saying: “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.” Amid such great tribulations I did not cease to cry out to you on account of this tribulation, and therefore you heard the voice of my prayer and of my companions when I cried out to you—that is, because I cried out not with my mouth but with the intention of my heart, to you alone, the Lord, and to nothing else.

Love the Lord, all his saints. The perfect man, having experienced humility in tribulation and having experienced that God heard him when he cried out to him, urges us to imitate him and cry out to the Lord, saying: “Love not yourselves or the world, but love the Lord,” that is, cry out to the Lord. For the one who despises the world and denies himself truly cries out to the Lord.

“Love him,” I say, “all you who will in this way be his future saints.” You ought to love him because “the Lord will require truth,” that is, he will seek this true love wherever it may be found. For what is more true than for the creature, which cannot subsist by itself and from whom it receives its being, to love the Creator on whom it depends?

He will, I say, require truth, and he will abundantly repay falsehood, because the Lord will recompense those who practice pride—that is, every kind of sin, since pride is the beginning of every sin—abundantly, that is, persistently, according to their merits.

This truth may also be understood in contrast to the falsehood of those of whom he said above: “Those who saw me fled outside,” whom he called acquaintances or neighbors. Pride is plainly to be noted in those same people who despise unity. For the Lord will finally examine both their falsehood and the truth of those who preserve unity, and he will recompense each according to its character.

And lest waiting for this seem too long to the weak—because he did not say “he repays” but “he will repay”—he urges them to wait patiently, saying: “Act manfully.” And I do not mean in the body, but “let your heart be strengthened” in perseverance, so that you may not have weakened hands and feeble knees.

I address all of you who hope in the Lord, because you truly love him.

It should be understood that this psalm is read, following Augustine and Cassiodorus, in the person of any perfect man. It is also read by some in the person of the Head, speaking partly on his own behalf and partly on behalf of his members. According to this interpretation, the title is explained as follows: “This psalm refers not to history but to the end,” that is, to perfection, “and is attributed to David,” that is, to the Head.

The psalm, I say, was spoken by him in the very struggle of the Passion, in ecstasy—that is, in fear of death—not because it is in any way permissible to understand that he feared death from himself, but only from the weakness belonging to us, which he transformed in himself, as has been said elsewhere.

It is as though he said: “Lord Father, Adam hoped in himself, and therefore he was put to shame; but I hoped in you. Therefore, although I may appear for a time to have been put to shame by my enemies, this shame will not be eternal. And, so that I may not be put to shame forever, rescue me, O Lord”—that is, raise me from the dead, not in my righteousness but in your righteousness, by which you made me free from sins.

“And you, who are exalted, incline your ear to me, who am humble”—that is, extend your favor toward me. “Hasten to rescue me,” that is, do not delay my resurrection until the common resurrection. And in order that you may finally rescue me, in the meantime be the God who protects me. Be for me a house of refuge against those same enemies, so that you may save me—that is, make me persevere—lest I be broken by them.

And rightly do I ask this of you, because you alone are my strength: whatever strength I possess against them I have not from myself, but from you. You are also my refuge: I am not a refuge for myself, as Adam was a refuge for himself, because he fled back to himself and destroyed himself. I, however, will flee to you in order to find myself.

And you will lead me back—that is, you will lead my knowledge from the confinement of the Jewish people into the breadth of the nations. Thus you will nourish me—that is, you will join many members to me, the Head, and make me grow.

You will do this by leading me out through the resurrection from the snare which they concealed for me—that is, from the death which my enemies, the Jews, secretly prepared for me. Rightly will you do this, because you alone are my protection, whereas I am my own downfall.

And because you truly will lead me out, I confidently commend my spirit into the hands of your power. Properly speaking, something is “commended” when it is given to someone with such confidence that the one who entrusted it may receive it back whenever he wishes.

And rightly do I commend it to you, because you will return it to me; you will redeem me from death, just as you have already redeemed me through freedom from sin, since you are the God of truth and do not deceive in your promises. Therefore what you promised through the prophets concerning my resurrection you will truly fulfill.

You have hated all. You are indeed the God of truth, but you are not the God of falsehood, because you hate all who observe vanity—namely, the Jews—that is, who prefer to lose their innocence through my death rather than, while I remain alive, lose their place and nation. They act uselessly, since they will nevertheless lose their place and nation.

Or it may be said that the Jews practiced vanity when they stationed soldiers to guard the tomb, fearing that the disciples might steal the Lord’s body and say to the people: “He has risen from the dead.” This was useless, because, against their will and without their knowledge, he rose on the third day.

Ego autem in Domino speravi. They observe vanity; I, however, do not observe vanity, because I cling to truth. For I have hoped in you, O Lord, and therefore I shall exult and rejoice—that is, I shall rejoice fully, not in my righteousness but in your mercy, as before.

And rightly shall I rejoice in you, because just as you despised Adam when he exalted himself and condemned him to many necessities, so you looked upon me when I was humbled to such a degree that I did not depart from you even in my will.

And you saved my soul from necessities—that is, from all sins—by the true innocence given to me. And you did not shut me in, nor will you permit me to be shut in, in the hands of the enemy—that is, of the Jewish people—so that they might utterly remove my name. Rather, you have established, and will establish, my feet—that is, my apostles, through whom I walk—in a spacious place, that is, in the widespread multitude of both Jews and Gentiles who will hear the word of truth from them.

Have mercy on me, O God. Up to this point the Head has spoken on his own behalf; here he speaks on behalf of his members. It is as though he said: “Join good conclusions to good beginnings. Just as you have had mercy on me in myself, so also have mercy on me in my members.”

And there is need of this, because “I am troubled,” that is, my members are troubled inwardly and outwardly; and because I am in them, I too am troubled.

This is because “my eye”—that is, the reason of my members—has been disturbed from the pure contemplation of truth which it previously possessed, in that anger which Adam, the transgressor, merited. And “my soul”—that is, my sensibility—has also been disturbed. And “my belly”—that is, what is more tender in my members, namely the flesh itself—has been disturbed.

Neither my sensibility nor ours would desire unlawful things, nor would the flesh be so fragile, if Adam had not sinned. And surely all these things have been disturbed in them because the very life of my members, which ought to have been eternal, suffered decline in pain—that is, in that anger for which they must always grieve. Since what follows from anger makes the matter seem more serious, he has used “anger” itself in place of its consequence.

And “the years of my members,” which ought to have been eternal, “have failed in groaning”—that is, in the same anger, for which there must always be lamentation. This is more grievous still.

And “the strength”—that is, the steadfastness—“of my members has been weakened” by that same anger, so that it is “in poverty,” that is, in complete need. And “my bones”—that is, my intellectual faculty, which was the chief strength of my members—“have been disturbed.”

And for the restoration of all these things which that anger disturbed, “I have become a reproach,” that is, I have been condemned with manly severity, without any consideration, before all my enemies.

According to another translation: “I have become a reproach above all my enemies,” that is, I have been held in greater contempt than all my enemies, both Jews and Gentiles—namely, Pilate’s soldiers, who crucified him. And among my enemies I have become especially a great reproach to my neighbors, that is, the Jews, from whose loins I came.

Therefore I have become a terror to my acquaintances, that is, to those who had previously known me perfectly, namely the apostles, who, when they saw him being seized, left him and fled.

And those other disciples too who saw me—that is, who had seen me as exceedingly needy and poor, because they had previously seen me performing miracles as God and teaching—then fled away from me. They judged me, God in human form, to be merely an ordinary man, and I was given over to oblivion among them, removed from their hearts like any dead person.

For they thought that I was subject to the law of those who die. Or they were those who said: “We had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel.” Thus I became for them like a discarded vessel—that is, a broken vessel. In other words, whatever I had taught them became worthless to them, just as liquid flowing out of a discarded, that is, broken, vessel is considered worthless.

This happened because I “heard”—that is, patiently endured—the reproach of many, namely of the Jews and of the Gentile soldiers dwelling in the surrounding region, that is, of those who loved place and nation and the other earthly things which revolve in the wheel of time.

This was because I did not come down from the cross when those who insulted me said: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days”; and, “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross”; and similar things.

Thus, while those who dwelt in that surrounding region thought me merely a man, they gathered together against me and took counsel to seize my soul—that is, to kill me and utterly erase my name.

But they could not, because I hoped in you, O Lord. And I said: “Rescue me from the hands of my enemies, the Jews, and from the nations that persecute me.” You ought to do this because you are my God and the God of my members.

My lots and those of my members are in your hands, because we will choose nothing for ourselves except what pertains to me. And in order that you may rescue me, make your face shine upon me, who do not wish to be your freedman, as Adam was, but am your servant. That is: glorify me through resurrection and ascension, so that it may be evident that I belong to you.

And save me—that is, make my members persevere—not in their own righteousness but in your mercy, lest they be put to eternal shame. You ought to do this because they have called upon you in themselves, and not upon anything else.

Because I am in them, I have called upon you; but let the wicked who do not make you their God—namely, the Jews who persecute me—be put to eternal shame, and in the present let them be brought down to hell, and let their deceitful lips finally become silent.

Their lips now speak iniquity against me, the righteous, in arrogance, when they say: “We have no king but Caesar.” They speak iniquity also in their abuse of created things, because they prefer to retain their place and nation rather than innocence. They do not consider the abundance of your sweetness, promised through me to the world and destined to be bestowed upon it.

“Which you have hidden,” and so forth. The meaning of these four verses remains the same as in the preceding interpretation.

[Col. 0641A] Benedictus Dominus. From everything stated above, as before, he says: “Blessed be the Lord.” And because the matters were stated in scattered form, he gathers them together briefly, saying: “For through his apostles he made wondrous all his mercy displayed to the world through me,” that is, to my members, “in a fortified city,” as above.

[Col. 0641A] Ego autem. The Lord indeed made his mercy wondrous. But in order that this manifestation of wonder might take place, I said in the evident reality of the event: “Lord, I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.” “Why have you forsaken me?” It is as though he said: “I humbled myself and permitted myself to be afflicted to such a degree that I seemed unworthy of your regard.” I said this, he continues, “in the ecstasy of my mind,” that is, as though placed in ecstasy by fear of death. He endured this fear not from himself, but from the weakness of our nature which he bore.

And because I humbled myself so greatly, therefore you heard, O Lord, the voice of my prayer—that is, the intention of my heart—when I cried out to you on behalf of my members.

And so that you may hear them, “love the Lord, all his saints,” and so forth. Here too, toward the end, the meaning of the preceding interpretation remains unchanged.

# Psalm XXXI  
## Of David: Understanding

### Argument

The prayer of Hezekiah, because he fell into illness on account of pride; it also applies to other saints living in a similar condition.

### Explanation

Since this is a psalm of repentance, David is mentioned first because of the titles, referring to the Lord Christ, since whatever this penitent is about to say looks toward him. Then “understanding” follows, because no one mourns sin unless he has understood it; and rightly has such a psalm been prefaced by this inscription.

The sinner understood too late that he had become worse, because he confessed that he had remained silent too long about sins which ought immediately to have been disclosed to the Lord, hearing from the Lord: “I will give you understanding, and I will instruct you.”

In the first part of the psalm the penitent speaks, clearly acknowledging his sin and declaring the punishment he deserved on account of strict judgment. He had believed that his guilty deeds ought to be concealed; here, briefly, the beginning and account of the matter are contained.

In the second part there is only correction. For after condemning himself by his own confession, he believed that the Lord ought to spare him.

In the third part, commending the blessings of repentance, he also asserts that the saints in this world entreat the Lord, in whom he rightly declares that he has his refuge.

In the fourth part the Lord, responding to his words, promises to surround those who hope in him with mercy.

These four parts are divided by the insertion of *diapsalmata*, except where it is clear that the arrangement follows the form customary in prophetic utterances.

### Commentary

Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates. This psalm commends to us divine grace and our justification, dependent on none of our preceding merits but solely on prevenient grace.

Its title is “Understanding of David,” not because others do not possess understanding, but because this psalm especially discloses a particular understanding of the greatest necessity to all. It teaches, namely, that no one should believe that free choice or his own merits are sufficient for blessedness, but should understand that he can be saved only by the grace of God.

In this psalm the prophet speaks against that arrogant people of stiff neck, who wished to establish their own righteousness and refused to be subject to the righteousness of God. Because they believed that they could be saved by themselves, they despised the grace of God.

This is rightly called grace freely given, because preceding merits do not confer it. Therefore this psalm is rightly entitled “Understanding of David.”

Concerning this understanding blessed Augustine says:

> “It is plainly and manifestly understanding. Let no one boast of his works before faith. Let no one become lazy in good works after receiving faith, because grace alone brings it about that God does not repay the punishment that is owed, but gives the grace that is not owed. He owes vengeance, yet grants forgiveness. Begin, therefore, to be in faith through forgiveness.”

Again, in order to add more concerning the same understanding, he says that understanding, or intelligence itself, is this. Let no one presume upon his own righteousness in order to reign; nor let anyone presume upon divine mercy in order to sin. Rather, let each person, according to what he is conscious of in himself, either grieve and be corrected or rejoice and be approved.

If he finds that he has gone astray, let him return so that he may walk on the road. If he stands on the road, let him walk so that he may arrive. Thus no one should become proud outside the road, and no one should be lazy on the road.

The first understanding is to know that you are a sinner. The consequence of this understanding is that, once you have begun to work well in faith through love, you should not ascribe this to your merits but attribute it to divine grace.

Then there will be no deceit in you: you will not have one thing in your heart and another on your lips, as do those whom the Lord in the Gospel compares to whitened tombs, saying that outwardly they appear righteous to human beings, but inwardly they are full of deceit and iniquity.

For the person who, although wicked, presents himself as righteous by defending his iniquity is truly deceitful.

And because everything by which we are saved must be ascribed solely to grace, those are not blessed in whom the Lord finds no sins. For he finds sins in everyone, because all have sinned and all lack the glory of God.

If, then, only those are blessed whose iniquities, increased before grace, have been remitted—that is, forgiven—when grace comes upon them, we may understand “iniquities” here as both original and actual sins, in accordance with what follows: “And whose sins are covered.”

This may be repetition, not because the narrator requires it, but so that the remission of the Church’s iniquities may be displayed more explicitly.

Or, if we wish to distinguish the terms, we may understand “iniquities” as original sins and “sins” as actual sins, which are ours through our own transgression. On this interpretation the meaning is simple: those are blessed whose iniquities, in their original condition, have been remitted—that is, forgiven—and whose actual sins have been covered, that is, abolished by grace.

God covers sins because he does not wish to punish them. He does not wish to know them because he prefers to forgive them. Therefore sins are covered.

They are covered not so that they may live, but so that they may not be seen. For God turns his face away from sins, not so that he may turn it toward us. Again, sins are covered not so that they may be unknown, but so that they may not be counted against us. This immediately follows.

It is as though he said: “Rightly I affirm that those are blessed whose iniquities and sins are covered. For that man is truly blessed to whom the Lord will not impute sin”—that is, against whom the Lord will not exact punishment for any sin before grace, whether original or actual, nor for any sin after grace.

For if he has sinned after receiving grace, there is no deceit in his spirit—that is, in his heart—because he does not defend his sin but humbly confesses it.

Deceit is truly found in the spirit of those who defend their sins by boasting of their merits. For while righteousness sounds outwardly, iniquity lies hidden inwardly.

They labor in vain to defend their sins, because they refuse to humble themselves so as to recognize their iniquity and instead seek to exalt themselves by defending it. Their strength is therefore destroyed, because no one is strong in himself, but only in the Lord.

As it is written: “For strength is made perfect in weakness.”

The phrase “nor is there deceit in his spirit” may also be understood independently and of another person, so that it reads as follows: “That man is blessed to whom sin will not be imputed. And that man too is blessed in whose spirit there is no deceit.”

Another translation has: “In his mouth,” according to which “spirit” is understood as “voice,” as may appropriately be taken here.

Quoniam tacui, inveteraverunt. The prophet says this not on his own behalf but in the person of that proud people against whom he speaks in this psalm.

It is as though he said: “In the spirit of the one who is blessed there is no deceit, but in my spirit there is deceit, because I was silent about what ought to have been proclaimed, and I proclaimed what ought to have been kept silent, all day long,” that is, continually.

I was silent about what would have advanced me; I cried out about what would have caused me to fail. I was silent about confession; I cried out in presumption. I was silent about sins; I cried out about merits.

Therefore “my bones grew old.” For if I had been silent about merits and cried out about sins, then my bones would have been renewed—that is, my strength would have been strong in the Lord—because in this way I would have been found weak in myself.

But because I was silent about sins and cried out about merits, my bones grew old—that is, they remained in their old condition—because by confessing sins I refused to love newness. Those who are restored from sins are restored through mercy.

Quoniam die ac nocte. Therefore my bones grew old, because your hand—that is, your chastisement—was made heavy upon me, who was proud through presumption and not humbled through confession, day and night—that is, continually.

Or “day and night” may mean in prosperity and adversity. The expression is like that of a teacher who scourges a proud child and does not spare him. The Lord humbles one who exalts himself; that is, he lays his hand heavily upon him.

And because this person refused to be humbled by confessing his iniquity, he suffered under the weight of divinity—that is, he was made too weak to restrain any movement—so that he might return to his heart and recognize himself as a sinner.

But when he endured the heavy hand of the Lord humbling him, he immediately perceived how gentle was the hand of the Lord lifting him up, because he considered his sins and rejected, or recovered from, them.

He indicates this in what follows when he says: “I have turned in my misery.”

It is as though he said: “Your hand, O Lord, was made heavy upon me, and in this misery of mine”—that is, in this continual wretchedness and affliction which I suffered from the weight of your hand—“I turned to you.”

This happened when the thorn was fastened, that is, when my conscience was pierced through the law. For the law fixed the thorn—that is, it caused the conscience to be pierced—because the law warned each person to acknowledge himself guilty when he saw that he could not fulfill it.

One translation has: “While the thorn is fastened.” This truly agrees well with the meaning. For bodies that are straight and upright are borne by the spine. Thus “spine” rightly signifies pride in one’s own righteousness, a pride which was also humbled through the law, since the law confined all things under sin.

It should be understood that here he speaks only in the person of those from that proud people for whom he said, “Because I was silent,” and so forth, who were converted.

Or perhaps he speaks in his own person, according to his former condition.

[Col. 0643C] My transgression. I have truly turned back. For your hand was made heavy upon me, and the thorn was fixed in me; I recognized the transgression that I had committed against the commandments, and the iniquity—that is, whatever other sin there was—as my own, namely, as having proceeded from my fault. And I made both known to you: the transgression and the fact that it was mine, not yours, nor fate’s, nor that of anything of the kind. And I did not hide it—that is, I openly acknowledged that it was iniquity, humbly through confession, so that you might mercifully hide it by not punishing it. For when someone opens his sins to the Lord by confessing them, the Lord himself hides them by not punishing them. And the converse is also true: if he hides them by not confessing them, the Lord reveals them by punishing them.

“I said, ‘I will confess.’” I truly made my transgression and my iniquity known. For I said—that is, I resolved in my heart—this: “I will confess my iniquity to the Lord,” that is, my every sin. Thus it was against me, not against the Lord himself. For many confess their own righteousness, like the man who says, “I have certainly committed no sin,” or, “I did indeed do this, but it is not a sin.” [Col. 0643D] Many others, even if they confess their iniquity, nevertheless confess it not against themselves but against the Lord, like the man who says, “I have indeed sinned, but it is not my fault, because God made me such that I would easily sin.” Or, “Fate caused this,” or, “The stars caused it,” or, “The hostile race of darkness, which rebels against God, causes human beings to sin,” or something of that kind. All who say such things go around the Lord from a distance in order to accuse him, because they do not wish to come to him by the direct route in order to appease him. For if they were to say briefly, “Lord, it is we who have sinned; neither you, nor fate, nor the stars, nor anything of that kind is to be accused, but we alone, because, although you had given us free choice, we knowingly and willingly consented to the devil”—if, I say, they were to say such things, they would come by the direct route to appease the Lord. I said that I would confess to the Lord in my resolve; and while there was not yet a word in my mouth, the Lord’s ear was already in my heart, because, as soon as I resolved, you, Lord, forgave me not only the sin [Col. 0644A] but also the impiety of the sin. For “sin” is called the evil that he committed; but “the impiety of sin” is what he referred not to himself but to the Lord.

“For this reason every holy person will pray.” He says this again against that proud people who, presuming on their own righteousness, did not seek the grace by which sins are forgiven. The sense is connected in this way: “You, Lord, have indeed granted me the forgiveness of sin. And for this forgiveness every future holy person will pray to you, so that he may come to you when it is fitting to pray, since there will be one who hears—namely, in the opportune time, that is, in the time of grace.” Of this it is said: “Behold, now is the acceptable time,” and so forth. And because he foresaw that many heresies would arise in that acceptable time, he foretells them to us, so that he may fortify us beforehand against them. Then he turns to us. It is as though he said: “Certainly everyone sanctified by grace will pray to the Lord; nevertheless, not everyone will reach him, because, placed amid the flood of many waters—that is, in the depths of many heretical doctrines [Col. 0644B]—they will not draw near to him.”

By “many waters” understand the various and foreign doctrines of the heretics. One kind of water—that is, doctrine—taught that human beings sinned because they were made to sin; another blamed the stars; a third blamed the hostile race of darkness that rebels against God; and there were many other such doctrines, against which it is said: “Drink water from your own cistern and from the stream of your own well.” For the wells are the apostles, whose doctrine we ought to drink, that is, to follow closely. Opposed to these many waters is that one water which comes from the innermost source of pure truth—namely, the water of humility of heart. What else does it teach than that a person should humble himself, deny himself, and utterly despise himself? This water is found neither in Aristotelian nor Platonic teachings, nor in any philosophical sayings, although many wondrous things are contained there; but it was handed down by the one who, though rich, became poor for our sake, and though innocent, wished to be washed and sacrificed for our sake.

“You are my refuge.” He addresses God directly. It is as though he said: “Against these many waters—which roar and press upon me but do not overwhelm me, which drive me on but do not drown me—you, Lord, are my refuge, delivering me from the tribulation that these roaring waters have already surrounded and will continue to surround me. [Col. 0644C] You are, I say, God, my joy in hope; and, so that at last you may be my joy in reality, rescue me from all my enemies who surround me.”

“I will give you understanding.” The connection above with the principal sense is as follows: “I said in my heart, ‘I will confess,’” and so forth. And while I was saying this, you were already at the door and were coming to meet the one who wished to enter to you. For you said: “Come near, son; I will give you good understanding for life”—namely, so that you may recognize sin and thus not presume upon yourself, but, by confessing your sins and doing good, rejoice in me until you reach the place where you are not in hope but in reality. “I will give,” I say, “understanding; and on this way, on which you will walk after receiving understanding—that is, in doing good—I will instruct you, not so that you may cling to yourself, but so that you may not stray from it and may advance upon it.” I will instruct you in this manner because I will establish my eyes upon you—that is, I will direct the light of my understanding toward you, fixing the eyes of my mercy upon you, so that you do not turn your eyes away from me. [Col. 0644D]

“Do not become like a horse and a mule, which have no understanding.” Up to this point he has spoken about those who cry out their sins and keep silent about their merits. Here, however, he turns principally to those who keep silent about their sins and cry out their merits, exhorting them, like the people mentioned above, to repent. It is as though he said: “Since it is evident from my case that the Lord forgives sin only in those who trust in him alone, and promises understanding and instruction on the way, and so forth, therefore you who until now have boasted of your merits and kept silent about your crimes, do not henceforth become like a horse and a mule—that is, irrational and untamed—so that you do not obey your own rider, namely the Lord, but throw him off and fail to recognize him, as the most untamed horses and mules do.”

[Col. 0645A] Or this may be understood because a horse submits itself to any rider, while a mule, being a beast of burden, allows itself to be loaded by anyone. According to this comparison, the passage may also be understood as follows: “Do not become like a horse and a mule”—that is, do not submit yourselves to just anyone, nor allow yourselves to be loaded by just anyone with various and foreign doctrines, so that by this you become like horses and mules. You ought not to do this, because horses and mules have no understanding—that is, no reason as you have.

“With bit and bridle restrain their jaws, those who do not draw near to you.” He addresses the Lord directly. It is as though he said: “I exhort those who are proud of their righteousness not to become like a horse and a mule. But those who wish to become like a horse and a mule, and therefore do not draw near to you by humbling themselves—restrain their jaws, that is, their boasting, you, Lord, with bit and bridle, which are one thing and are here understood as the same: any divine scourging in the present life.” For the wicked are often condemned by a twofold crushing, here and in the future. The jaws, by which the mouth is moved for speaking, rightly signify boasting about merits. But because jaws are mandibles, Cassiodorus [Col. 0645B] understands “bit and bridle” here as referring only to the removal of temporal goods. This is not a desire for ill-will, but a declaration of their punishment.

“Many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord.” Truly, Lord, you will restrain those who do not draw near to you, because there will be many scourges for the sinner who does not confess but defends his sins, since he will be scourged both here and in the future. And because it might be objected that the good, too, are scourged, he removes the implication that these are scourges, calling them mercy instead. For the Lord scourges a servant whom he intends to drive away in one way, and a son whom he intends to receive into the inheritance in another. It is as though he said: “Sinners will indeed be scourged, but those who hope in the Lord will not be scourged; rather, mercy—that is, loving and fatherly correction—will surround them,” that is, will protect them.

“Rejoice in the Lord.” Since the Lord’s mercy will so greatly surround those who hope in him, therefore you, the righteous—that is, those restored and made righteous by the Lord’s mercy—rejoice in heart and exult in body, [Col. 0645C] that is, possess complete joy in the Lord. “And glory,” that is, do not merely endure willingly the scourges of mercy, but also glory in them, all of you who are not crooked but upright in heart.

Those are called upright in heart who direct and smooth their hearts according to God’s will in such a way that nothing done by him displeases them; and whatever they suffer, they consider themselves to suffer justly. Those crooked in heart, however, are those who prefer their own will to God’s will, who are displeased by what he does, and who think that they suffer any evils unjustly. Hence they fall into one of these perverse opinions: either they say that God does not exist, or that he is unjust; or, diminishing his governance, they say that he does not administer earthly affairs.

## ON PSALM XXXII

A Psalm of David, to the end.

### ARGUMENT

After the victory over the Assyrians, a triumphal song is composed, in which it is taught that all the things in which mortals rejoice apart from God are objects of futile hope. [Col. 0645D]

### EXPLANATION

In this psalm the prophet exhorts the faithful Church to psalmody, enumerating the power and works of the Creator, so that, recognizing his virtue and goodness, it may hasten more eagerly to praise him. Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks, but in the first section he urges the righteous to rejoice in the Lord, who sustains his creatures by wondrous power; in the second he declares blessed the one who has been found worthy to belong to his worship, signifying the Christian times in which a multitude of nations was to believe.

### COMMENTARY

“Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord.” The title is: “A Psalm attributed to David,” namely, to the prophet, or to any perfect person. The holy commentators say that this psalm is connected with the preceding one. [Col. 0646A] This seems quite fitting, because just as in the preceding psalm he exhorted no one to presume upon his merits before seeing that no one is saved except by grace, so here he exhorts the faithful who have already been made—that is, the righteous—not to have an idle faith. For faith without works is dead.

Thus, in the preceding psalm, the first part of the meaning of the title may be discerned: let no one boast of his good works before faith. In this psalm, the remaining part may be discerned: once faith has been received, let no one be sluggish in good works. It is as though he said: “Let the unrighteous—that is, the unbelieving—rejoice in the world, so that, when the world passes away, their rejoicing may also pass away. But you, the righteous—that is, the faithful who believe in him who justifies the ungodly—rejoice in the Lord, not in the world, so that, just as the Lord is eternal, your rejoicing may also be eternal.”

And because it is fitting to rejoice in such a way as to praise the one in whom there is nothing that displeases the good, and to whom everyone is pleasing who is not himself displeasing to him, he suitably adds: “Praise is fitting for the upright.” He calls the righteous “upright.” As was said above, the upright are those who do not distort God’s will, but direct their hearts [Col. 0646B] according to it, grateful to him for everything that is done by him. For even if human frailty disturbs them in some respect, divine equity consoles them. Therefore they praise God both in adversity and in prosperity, because such praise befits the upright alone, that is, the righteous.

The unrighteous and crooked do not praise the Lord in this way. Hence it is said: “If he does good to you, he will bless you; but if evil befalls him, he will not bless you.” Rather, he will reproach you, saying that you are unjust because you afflict him while you do not punish others who are more wicked than he.

“Confess to the Lord.” Since it belongs to the upright to praise God, therefore you, the righteous, confess to the Lord—that is, praise the Lord on the lyre, and sing psalms on the psaltery. When he says, “Confess on the lyre, and sing psalms,” do not turn your mind toward theatrical instruments, but toward spiritual ones.

For the lyre sounds from its lower part, and from our lower condition we have two ways of praising God: from prosperity and from adversity. There is an earthly prosperity [Col. 0646C] when we live in bodily health and when the things by which we live abound, and when fruits are produced in plenty. Since these things belong to earthly life, whoever does not praise the Lord because of them proves ungrateful. There is likewise an earthly adversity when we labor in illnesses and various tribulations. From these things, too, we ought to praise God, knowing that they occur only through his gracious ordering, whose wisdom reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly.

Again, if the things by which we live are lacking, if fruits are not produced abundantly, or if these things are violently taken away from us, let us praise the Lord even for that, playing the lyre for him with that pre-eminent lyre-player who said: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord.” For even if what he gave is taken away, he who gave it is not taken away.

The psaltery, however, resounds from its upper part. And you, attending to God’s heavenly gifts [Col. 0646D]—namely, what commandments he has given you, with what heavenly teaching he has imbued you, and what he has granted you above others from the innermost source of pure truth—praise the Lord, singing to him on a ten-stringed psaltery.

For the ten strings are the Ten Commandments: three concern love of God, while seven concern love of neighbor. These matters were sufficiently explained at the beginning of this treatise. Touch the psaltery by fulfilling the law, which the Lord your God did not come to abolish but to fulfill. Whoever praises the Lord by good works in the fulfillment of the law contained in the Ten Commandments sings to the Lord on a ten-stringed psaltery.

“Sing to him a new song.” Since the law pertains both to oldness and to newness, this has been added for clarification. It is as though he said: “I exhort you to confess and sing psalms to the Lord on the ten-stringed psaltery in this manner: sing to him not with your tongue but with your life a song [Col. 0647A] that is not old but new.”

No one sings a new song unless he has been renewed by grace. The new song is the new charity by which a person loves not only a friend but also an enemy as himself, whereas the old song is the old hostility. “Sing,” I say, “to the Lord, and sing psalms well to your teacher,” namely, so that you displease him in nothing. This will happen if you sing psalms to him with a shout—that is, with immense and ineffable exultation of mind.

A shout, or jubilation, is a certain sound signifying that the heart is giving birth to what it cannot express. Since such praise is ineffable, it befits only the Ineffable. The Ineffable is one whom speech cannot express. And if you cannot speak, yet ought not to remain silent, what remains except that you should rejoice—that is, let your heart rejoice without words, and let the immense breadth of your joys exceed the limits of syllables?

“For the word of the Lord is upright.” Therefore you ought to sing psalms to the Lord with a shout, because the Word of the Lord who was in the beginning—that is, the Son of God the Father—is upright [Col. 0647B], since he deceives no one. He promises nothing without fulfilling it. If he did so, he would be not upright but crooked.

And all his works—that is, the Lord’s works—are in faith, that is, they are to be done by us faithfully, not deceitfully. Let our works therefore be in faith, so that we may become faithful, believing in him. For “the righteous person lives by faith.”

We find that the Lord is faithful in the Apostle’s words, where he says: “God is faithful, who will not allow it,” and so forth. And again: “If we endure, we shall also reign. If we deny him, he will also deny us. But if we do not believe him, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself.”

God is called faithful in one way, and a human being in another. A human being is faithful when he believes God who makes a promise; God is faithful when he fulfills for a human being what he has promised. He himself has become our faithful debtor; you should be a demanding creditor. Let us therefore hold fast to the most faithful debtor, since we already hold fast to the most merciful promiser.

“He loves mercy.” Another reason for the same conclusion. We ought therefore to sing and praise the Lord because he loves [Col. 0647C] mercy, both to show it and to have it shown by us, and because he loves to exercise judgment and to have it exercised by us. Let mercy not pass us by, then, because judgment follows.

For now is the time of mercy, both of the mercy that the Lord shows and of that which he wishes us to show. God’s mercy is displayed in this: he calls those who are opposed; to those who turn back he grants forgiveness; he patiently awaits sinners so that they may turn. And as soon as they turn, he forgets the past and promises the future. He exhorts the sluggish, consoles the afflicted, teaches the diligent, and helps those who struggle. He abandons no one who labors and cries out to him. He himself gives the means by which sacrifice may be offered to him; he himself grants the means by which he may be pleased.

This mercy does not exclude judgment from him, because just as he is merciful toward those who turn, so he is just toward those who do not turn; just as he is merciful toward the humble, so he will be just toward the proud; and just as he is merciful toward those who confess, so he will be just toward liars.

He himself, who loves to show this mercy and this judgment, also wishes [Col. 0647D] us, insofar as we can, as needy people, to show mercy and to judge all equally—that is, not to accept the person of the poor in judgment. For one who, by sparing the poor man’s little purse, wounds the poor man’s own heart is more unjust than just.

The Lord loves mercy, I say; this is evident because “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord,” that is, full of those restored by the Lord’s mercy. But what of the heavens? It is as though he said: “The heavens do not need mercy, because there is no misery in the heavens; but on earth misery abounds, so let mercy abound. The earth is full of misery; let it also be full of mercy.”

And lest anyone think that the heavens stand firm by themselves and have no need of the Lord, he says: “The heavens were established by the word of the Lord.” That is, the fact that the heavenly host—such as the cherubim and seraphim—stood firm when the devil transgressed was not from themselves, but they received it from the Lord the Father and his Word.
