And not merely part of their strength, but all their strength, is from the Spirit of his mouth—that is, from the Lord’s Spirit, the Holy Spirit. Observe here the order of the Holy Trinity. First he placed the Lord the Father and the Word; now he places the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0648A]

This verse may also be read in another way. It is as though he said: “Whence did it come about that the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord? From this, namely, that the Lord sent certain heavens—that is, the apostles—throughout the whole world, so that everywhere they might sow and spread his mercy.” For no mercy is greater than the forgiveness of sins, and this forgiveness they proclaimed throughout the whole world in the name of the Trinity.

And as though someone might ask how they dared to go, since they were sheep among wolves, he replies that they dared to go because those sheep were strengthened so that they would not fear wolves; indeed, one sheep would consume many wolves. They were strengthened by the Word of the Lord, by whom they had been chosen. For God chose the foolish and weak things of the world to confound the wise and the strong.

They were strengthened above all by this: all their strength was from the Holy Spirit. When he was sent upon them from heaven, their hearts were so confirmed that they did not tremble at all amid raging wolves. [Col. 0648B] Their strength, I say, “gathers the waters of the sea,” that is, the bitter and false thoughts of their persecutors, which previously lay in the open; it compresses them, as into a wineskin within the limits of a skin, so that they might rage only within themselves and not outwardly as before.

For while the apostles were preaching, the word of God was multiplying, and the multitude of believers was increasing. Although the wicked were not absent—for in the threshing floor there are both chaff and grain, and in the winepress both wine and grape-skins, and both oil and dregs—those wicked people nevertheless did not dare to exercise their wickedness openly as before, being pressed down by so great a multitude of the faithful.

The waters of the sea were gathered, I say, into a wineskin. This was not done uselessly, because the Lord—or that strength—placed the abysses, that is, the worst people sunk into the depths of vices, among his treasures, that is, in the Church, as in treasuries, so that from them he might bring forth gifts for his own whenever he wished, just as a lord can bring forth something from his treasure.

For the Lord knows how to bring forth his gifts for his soldiers, what to bring forth, when, and in what measure; [Col. 0648C] he gives the wicked power over the good for the instruction of the latter and the condemnation of the former. The wicked person lives for the sake of the devout person, because he is to him what a file is to iron and what a furnace is to gold.

This verse can also be connected with the preceding interpretation concerning the word of the Lord. It is as though he said: “The Lord loves mercy, as we said above. He also loves judgment, as is evident from this: he gathers the waters of the sea as into a wineskin,” and so forth. The meaning does not change, except that some understand “as into a wineskin” as a mere comparison. For just as someone who gathers something into a wineskin retains as much as he wishes and pours out as much as he wishes, so, at the Lord’s command, the wicked are granted as much power to rage as they are not granted. This pertains to the present judgment.

“Let all the earth fear the Lord.” Since the Lord has placed the abysses in treasuries, therefore let all the earth—that is, the well-cultivated earth, namely the faithful—fear the Lord, not the abysses themselves. It is as though he said: “When it hears such things, [Col. 0648D] let the earth not exult with empty and arrogant joy, as though fearing nothing, but let it fear the Lord.”

Let it rejoice because the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy; but let it fear because the Lord has placed the abysses in treasuries, so that through them he may instruct his own for the heavenly treasures. Therefore, let the one who previously promised himself security on the basis of hope return to fear. For to hope without fear is presumption.

“Let all the earth fear the Lord,” I say, “and let all who inhabit the world be moved to fear by him alone, not by another.” By those who inhabit the world he means those who love perfection, or those who so inhabit and cultivate themselves that they become a world—that is, perfect.

The lion rages: fear the Lord. The serpent lies in wait; the devil lies in wait: fear the Lord alone.

“For he spoke.” Therefore the Lord alone is to be feared, because all things were made by him, and they can do nothing except what he permits. For “he spoke, and they were made,” that is, in the first creation all things were made by him through his Word and wisdom, and they were also restored by him. For he commanded—that is, he gave commandments—and [Col. 0649A] through those commandments they were created in good works, although previously they had simply been created.

They were created in this way because the Lord scattered the plans of the nations against the faithful. What were these plans? “Let them be seized, torn apart, imprisoned,” and other such things—the plans that the Lord scattered with a good scattering. For many fierce persecutors became good believers.

And he was rightly able to scatter the plans of the nations against the members, because he also rejected—that is, destroyed—the thoughts of the peoples, the Jews, against the head. And not only the thoughts of the lower peoples, but he also rejected the plans of the rulers, that is, of Pilate, Annas, and Caiaphas. This is an argument from the greater: it was a greater thing to rise against the head than against the members.

“But the plan of the Lord.” Their plan, I say, was scattered. But the plan of the Lord—namely, the ancient plan of ordering, the new plan of restoration, and eternal happiness—was not scattered through his Word, but remains forever.

And he repeats the same thing in clearer words, saying: “The thoughts of his heart will remain [Col. 0649B] in the present generation and in the future generation.” Here he speaks of the Lord God according to our manner of understanding, as though he sometimes sat and deliberated, then took counsel with his intimates—not because such things exist in God, but so that through what we know in ourselves we may approach divine and invisible realities.

“Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord.” Since the Lord is so powerful that through him all things were made and restored, and since he makes foolish and scatters the plans of the wicked, while no one scatters his own plan, therefore that nation is truly blessed whose Lord is himself, who necessarily is the God of all but is their Lord by their will.

Or the passage may be connected more simply in this way. It is as though he said: “What is that plan of the Lord which remains forever? This, namely: that the nation whose wealth is not silver or gold or anything earthly, but whose God is its Lord, alone is truly blessed.” That is, it is the nation that chooses for itself, as its inheritance, the one whom it has by necessity as Lord according to his lordship; and which the Lord himself, in turn, chooses for himself as an inheritance, [Col. 0649C] to cultivate through himself and through his own. He is filled and rejoices in its fruits—that is, its good works and virtues.

For all the good are both the Lord’s inheritance and possess him as their inheritance, as was said above in the fifth psalm, whose title is “For her who receives the inheritance.” And it was the Lord’s plan that such people should be blessed.

“The Lord looked down from heaven.” It is as though he said: “How does the Lord choose that inheritance? In this way: the Lord sent the first heaven, namely Adam, placed in the sublimity of virtues. In that heaven he looked upon us while Adam remained obedient, and in that same heaven he looked away from us when Adam became disobedient.”

Then he sent another heaven, more stable than that one: the second Adam, that is, the Lord’s man, to whom the Spirit was not given by measure, and of whom it was said: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.”

From this heaven he looked upon that inheritance through the effect of mercy; [Col. 0649D] and then he saw the effect of that mercy, displaying it in the calling of all the sons of true human beings—that is, imitators of the patriarchs and prophets, who were true human beings—not dehumanizing themselves—were in hell [reading uncertain]. For the Lord sees those who see him. By “sons of human beings,” understand the same people previously signified by “the blessed nation.”

“From his prepared dwelling place.” This is a repetition intended to specify which sons of human beings are meant: those understood through the prepared dwelling place, that is, through the heaven. But if by “the prepared dwelling place” we understand the apostles themselves, whom the Lord truly prepared because he himself called, taught, and sent them, then the passage is properly differentiated.

For through them also the Lord looked upon all who inhabit the earth, according to the saying: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth,” and so forth, because through them and their successors he called and converted many to the faith.

Those who inhabit the earth are properly called inhabitants because they cultivate their own earth—that is, their flesh—in such a way that it does not sprout thorns and thistles [Col. 0650A] for them, but various flowers of virtues, so that at last they may receive it glorified.

“He who fashioned them individually.” It is as though he said: “He looked upon the inhabitants of the earth both from heaven and from the prepared dwelling place, calling those whom he made fit to be called.” He fashioned them—that is, by the hand of his omnipotence and mercy he formed their hearts, that is, their souls, individually—that is, giving individual gifts to individuals: to some kinds of tongues, to others the word of knowledge and wisdom, and so forth, though these gifts do not divide unity through pride.

For just as in our body there are both members and diverse functions of the members, but health is one, so in Christ’s body there are many members and diverse functions of the members, and diverse gifts are granted to those individuals, but charity is one.

The one who is an eye among Christ’s members ought not to despise the one who is a foot; rather, the eye ought to foresee for the foot, and the foot ought to walk for the eye, as happens in good monastic communities.

He, I say, looked upon them who fashioned them. And because he fashioned them, [Col. 0650B] he alone perfectly understands all human works, since he penetrated intelligently to the end of their intentions. For he who made the human being knows what is in the human being; a human being sees the face, but God sees the heart.

“A king is not saved by great power.” Since the Lord’s looking upon, seeing, and choosing for an inheritance truly constitute salvation, it was noted above that the Lord saves. He proves this, as though saying: “Truly the Lord alone saves, because no one else does.”

No one else saves, because neither a king—that is, anyone powerful—nor a giant—that is, anyone strong—saves, although one might expect it more of them. The king and the giant do not save because they cannot even save themselves; this is an argument from the greater.

He expresses it as follows: “A king will not be saved by great power,” that is, by great might; “and a giant will not be saved by his great strength.” This is because the horse—that is, all earthly pomp, whether in strength or in power—is deceptive with respect to true salvation.

I say this because the horse—that is, anyone who trusts in such pomp, [Col. 0650C] in the abundance of strength—however much he abounds in it, will not be saved.

These two verses may also be read in another way, if by “king” we understand anyone who governs his illicit impulses well, and by “giant,” according to another characteristic of the term, anyone who not only governs himself but is also swift, so that no worldly allure delays him. The sense would then be: “Truly the Lord alone saves, not merits; for even the one who is a king, governing his impulses well, and, still more, the one who is a giant—that is, swift, not delayed by any worldly allure—will not be saved by his own strength, although they might most of all appear likely to be saved.”

This is because the horse on which the flesh—that is, human nature—is carried deceives them, that is, makes those striving toward salvation slip. For falling according to the flesh is easy, so that whoever stands should always beware lest he fall.

I say this so that they may know that a king or a giant will not be saved, however great their virtue or however abundant that virtue may be, if they make it their own rather than giving thanks for it and assigning it wholly to divine [Col. 0650D] grace.

And as though someone might say, “What, then? From where will salvation come?” he says: “Behold from where salvation will come: the eyes of the Lord”—that is, the regard of the Lord’s mercy—“will be upon those who fear him with chaste and filial fear, not servile fear.”

And because fear without hope is despair, lest we understand these fearful people as despairing, he says: “And upon them”—that is, over them—“will be the eyes of the Lord, who, although they fear, nevertheless hope in his mercy,” which comes only from above and does not proceed from merits. Therefore they hope in him so that at last he may rescue their souls from eternal death. And meanwhile he nourishes them with the sustenance of Sacred Scripture in famine—that is, in this present life, which is a time of famine, because here the good always hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied.

“Our soul.” Since the Lord will finally rescue us from death and meanwhile nourish us, our soul rightly endures the burden of the Lord’s commandments, patiently bearing the burden of the day and the heat, according to the saying: “The Lord will come, [Col. 0651A] and he will not delay; if he tarries, wait for him.”

Our soul also rightly endures the Lord because he is our helper in good and our protector from evil—or our helper so that we may be perfected, and our protector so that we may not fail. And because at last our heart, although now sorrowful, will truly rejoice in him, when he will be all in all, we rightly not only hope but have hoped—that is, we have fixed the anchor of our hope not in the world but in his name, which is holy.

He rightly hopes in this name, “Lord,” who willingly and truly subjects himself to its service. And in the Lord this name, “Lord God,” is holy and chaste because he is not served to our disgrace but to our glory, not to death but to life.

Among human beings, however, those whom people serve for robbery, plunder, murder, and other iniquities do not bear the name “lord” in a chaste or holy manner.

“Let your mercy be upon us.” Since our heart will rejoice in you, therefore, Lord, let your mercy—that is, the justification of your grace—be upon us [Col. 0651B] in the present. Let it be according to the measure by which we have hoped, that is, in proportion to the hope we have placed in you. For the more fully each person casts himself upon the Lord, the more abundantly the Lord will have mercy on him. Hence it is said elsewhere: “He forgives to the extent that each person recognizes himself.”

## ON PSALM XXXIII

A Psalm of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, who dismissed him, and he departed.

### ARGUMENT

Hezekiah, having defeated the Assyrian, promises always to bless the Lord and prays that an angel helper be sent to him; then, following his own example, he calls everyone to the praise of God.

Likewise, the voice of faith through fasting.

Likewise Arnobius: “Unless you change your countenance before the prince of vices, dismiss him, and devote whatever time of life remains to you to the Lord of the virtues, you do not truly say: ‘I will bless the Lord at all times.’”

### EXPLANATION
When Saul was pursuing David, he fled to King Achish, where he was regarded with suspicion through envy. He deliberately changed his appearance, filling his mouth with saliva, so that he might be judged possessed and, through the resulting pity, be released unharmed. David, therefore, is Christ; Achish is the Jewish people, among whom Christ was incarnate but appeared unrecognizable to those who envied him. Hence Achish is said to be interpreted as “How is he?” This is the expression of one who wonders and does not recognize: for although the Jews admired Christ’s miracles, they did not at all recognize that he was God. And David rightly, with his appearance changed, let his saliva fall upon his beard; saliva signifies weakness, while the beard signifies strength, because Christ, “though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” Nor is there any error in the king’s name, since, having been regenerated from a father, he could also be called Abimelech, which is interpreted as “my father is king,” or “the kingdom of my father.” But the sense of the mystery also fits, because the Jews had a father who was king, concerning whom it is said: “But the sons of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness.” “He released him and went away”: he released the Jews and went away to be believed among the Gentiles.

It can also be said that he changed his appearance before Abimelech the priest when he pretended that Saul had sent him to obtain weapons and loaves for himself and his companions. Throughout the psalm the prophet’s words are arranged in such a way that the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, except the sixth, are placed in order at the beginnings of the verses. In the first part he promises that he will bless the Lord, urging the meek to persevere with him in his praise. In the second, the conversion of the faithful, which consists in the rewards of those who have merited well, is not left unmentioned. In the third, he admonishes them as though they were sons, telling them from what sins they ought to abstain. In the fourth, he says that the righteous will be rescued from all tribulations and that the wicked will suffer the punishments they deserve. The first of these parts contains four letters, the second six, the third four, and the fourth the remaining seven.

## Commentary

[Col. 0652A]

**I will bless the Lord at all times.** The title is as follows: “A psalm of David, when he changed his appearance before Abimelech, released him, and went away.” The historical account in the Book of Kings relates that, after the killing of Goliath, when David, the Lord’s young servant, had attained such glory that even the women in their choruses preferred him to Saul, saying, “Saul has struck down a thousand, and David ten thousand,” Saul was greatly angered and began to envy him; he also began devising how he might kill him. When that holy man understood this, he fled from him into the kingdom of Achish, king of Gath, in order to hide there. But when his glory became known there as well, the soldiers brought him to King Achish and told him what kind of man he was and how great he was. Fearing that Achish too might, out of envy, plot his death, he changed his appearance before him, pretending in his madness to be possessed. He behaved in these ways: he beat a drum at the gate of the city, was carried along by his own hands, fell forward at the doors of the gate, and saliva ran down his beard. When Achish saw this, he said: “Why have you brought me this possessed man? Do we have need of possessed people?” Thinking the madness genuine, he released him. Thus he went away unharmed.

It should be noted, however, that the title calls this Achish “Abimelech” for two reasons: either because Achish was also called by this other name, or so that, by changing the name, it might draw us away from the historical account and lead us into the mystery. For Abimelech is interpreted as “the kingdom of my father.” The mystical David, namely Christ, whom all these events prefigured, was the son, according to the flesh, of that historical David, whose kingdom was the Jews. Before that kingdom—that is, in the presence of the Jews—Christ himself changed his appearance, that is, his will, because he converted the legal sacrifices instituted according to the order of Aaron into sacrifices of bread and wine according to the order of Melchizedek, who first offered them after they had been instituted. In this respect his will could appear to have been changed, although it was the same, because those former sacrifices were only a shadow, that is, signs of these.

[Col. 0652C]

How did he do this? In this way: he behaved as follows. Just as the historical David behaved—that is, he acted toward people in the manner of the insane and threw himself upon each of them—so the Word of the Father behaved when he displayed toward us an attitude of mercy, taking upon himself the weakness of our flesh and bearing our infirmities, even to the point of laying down his life for us and destroying our death by his own death. Nothing was greater or better than this attitude. Hence the Apostle rebukes those who are without affection and mercy.

He also beat a drum. A drum is made from dry hide stretched over wood. The historical David beat a drum when, while pretending madness, he stretched himself out lengthwise and breadthwise. Christ, however, beat a drum when he stretched his body, like dry hide—that is, without the moisture of carnal desires—upon the wood of the cross, so completely that even his bones could be counted, according to the words: “They counted all my bones,” and what follows. The historical David did this at the doors of the city in a literal sense; Christ did it mystically. For the city is the society of the angels and of the citizens above; its doors are the hearts of believers, because through faith we have access to it. These doors, that is, our hearts, had previously been closed to the truth, whose knowledge we had lost in our first parent. But Christ beat a drum at the doors of the city—that is, to open our hearts to the truth—so that in him, whom we had previously thought to be merely a man, we might understand and recognize that Word which was in the beginning with God, and at whose sight the angels rejoice, because it is personally united to him. This was manifested both through his genuine suffering, by which he patiently endured all things, and because he did not come down from the cross, but rose powerfully from the tomb and ascended into heaven.

And he was carried in his own hands. In the case of the historical David this can perhaps be understood only in a playful way. Christ, however, was carried in a certain manner in his own hands when, at the Last Supper, he offered his disciples the blessed bread, commended by his own mouth, saying: “This is my blood.” In this way he commended his humility to us: that we should eat his humble body in joyful participation in his birth, and drink his blood by conforming ourselves to his passion.

[Col. 0653A]

The historical David also fell forward at the doors of the gate in a literal sense; Christ humbled himself under every tribulation, even to the point of enduring the most shameful death of the cross, and this at the doors of the gate. These are the approaches and beginnings of our faith: Christ’s birth, his passion, and his death. For if Christ had not been born, he would not have been mortal; if he had not been mortal, he would not have died; if he had not died, he would not have risen again; if he had not risen again, he would not have ascended, and so forth.

Saliva also ran over his beard: in David’s case historically, but in Christ’s case mystically. Saliva belongs to children, whereas the beard belongs to adults. The words by which the Lord commended his humility, saying, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves,” seemed childish and impossible; but great power was hidden in them, because through them he spiritually admonished us to imitate his humility, so that we might ascend to his exalted state.

Thus Christ changed his appearance before Abimelech, that is, in the presence of the Jewish people. But because they did not understand the change in his appearance—that is, the conversion of the legal observances into the new sacrifice—they despised him and released him; he, however, through the preaching of the apostles, went away to the Gentiles. Among them the new sacrifice and his humility are celebrated everywhere at his command.

Abimelech or Achish, together with his kingdom, can plainly be understood as referring to those about whom we read that, when Christ commended his humility by saying, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves,” about seventy-two were scandalized and went away. For Achish is interpreted as “How is he?” But “how” is the word of someone astonished and ignorant. And they, like astonished and ignorant people, said: “How can these things happen? Is he going to cut off pieces from his flesh and give them to us to drink?” The Gentiles, however, to whom he rightly went after departing from the Jews, can be understood as those of whom it is subsequently said: “And turning to the twelve, he said, ‘Do you also wish to go away?’” And Peter, answering on behalf of all, said: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life; for the flesh profits nothing, but the spirit gives life.” It is as though he were saying: “Your words, understood carnally, profit nothing; but, received spiritually, they give life.”

The title may be explained in another way. This psalm—that is, the action signified by the words that follow, namely, the commendation or praise of humility—is the subsequent praise of the true David, namely Christ, signified at the time when the historical David changed his appearance before Achish, as stated above. That event was a sign of the action of this true David.

Or the entire title can be explained allegorically, so that it may be said: This psalm belongs to the true David, uttered by him when he changed his appearance before Abimelech, converting the sacrifice into that of Melchizedek, as stated above. For in this psalm the voice of the head commends his true humility to us. Therefore the psalm corresponds well to the title. For in the title it is said: “When he changed his appearance.” Through this change of appearance the commendation of humility was accomplished, and this is what the psalm discusses.

[Col. 0653D]

It is as though he were saying: “I who blessed the Lord for a time in the legal sacrifices instituted according to Aaron will bless the Lord at all times—that is, eternally—through the sacrifices instituted according to Melchizedek.” Hence it is said: “According to the order of Melchizedek: you are a priest forever.”

Or otherwise: The first Adam blessed the Lord for an hour, namely, while he remained in humility; but I, the second Adam, will bless the Lord by preserving humility at all times, both before the passion and in the passion itself, without deviating from his will even in thought. Christ says this as a commendation of humility in himself; every Christian must also take care of this, so that the human being who through pride became a devil may through humility become an angel. For Christ became human so that the human being might become an angel.

But whoever is to become an angel must remain in humility of heart, so that he may always bless the Lord, whether the things by which we live prosper or are disturbed, whether he grants or takes away. For even if these things are taken away, he himself is not taken away.

And what it means to bless the Lord at all times he shows when he says: “His praise will always be in my mouth”—not the mouth of the body, but mine, that is, in the mouth proper to me, the mouth of the heart. This is a repetition if it refers to the same thing; but it can be made different if it is referred to the members in this way: “I will bless the Lord at all times in myself and also in my members, because his praise will always be in my mouth,” that is, in the mouth of my members, as stated above.

He subsequently shows how one should bless the Lord at all times, in order to instruct us. It is as though he were saying: “I will bless the Lord at all times in this way: my soul will claim nothing for itself and presume nothing about itself, but it will be praised—that is, it will consider itself worthy of praise—not in itself, since it would be blameworthy, but in the Lord, because of this one thing only: that it has fixed its hope in the Lord.” And you, he says, should seek to be praised and to glory not in yourselves but in the Lord. “So that you may always bless the Lord, my soul will be praised in the Lord.”

Let those hear this with the ear of hearing—not just anyone, but the meek, that is, those who wish to be tame animals rather than untamed ones, wishing to have the Lord as their rider and guide, lest they be thrown headlong. Let them hear, he says, and rejoice, that is, imitate, and not be saddened. For the untamed, who wish to presume upon themselves and glory in themselves rather than in the Lord, do not rejoice when they hear that each person should rejoice only in the Lord; instead, they are saddened.

**Magnify the Lord with me.** Here he turns directly to the meek. It is as though he were saying: “You meek ones, hearing and rejoicing at this, magnify—that is, venerate and exult in—the Lord by humbling yourselves, not separately through pride, as the heretics do, but with me, that is, not in separation but in unity.”

This is spoken by Christ, the lover of true wisdom. He does not envy those who share his love, but wishes to draw everyone in so that they may share his love. For this love is not like the vicious and shameful love of this world, in which each person wishes to see and love alone. True wisdom, however, is common to all who love it and yet remains whole for each individual. Therefore we too ought, by whatever means we can, to draw all whom we can into this love with us: by exhorting, pleading, and giving reasons.

He says how the Lord is to be magnified: “Let us exult in his name,” preserving the humility he commanded and striving toward the same thing—that is, not toward the destruction but toward the concord of unity—so that, just as Christ’s body remained whole in the hands of his persecutors, so it may also remain whole in the hands of those who profess him.

[Col. 0654D]

For we read that, during the Lord’s passion, toward evening on the day of Preparation, the legs of those who had been crucified with him were broken so that they might be freed more quickly from this misery; but his legs were not broken, because when they came to him they found that he had already died peacefully. His body remained whole so that this might signify that no division was to be made in his body, that is, the Church, but that unity was to be preserved.

**I sought the Lord.** I say, “Magnify the Lord,” and in this take me as an example, because I sought nothing else from the Lord. Rather, I sought him—that is, setting aside all other rewards, I sought God alone as my reward—and therefore the Lord heard me, not outwardly but inwardly. Such seeking takes place outwardly rather than inwardly, and so does the hearing.

Let each person therefore enter his own heart, drive avarice and every perverse desire from it, and thus seek the Lord in order to be heard. “He heard me,” I say, and he heard me in this way: he rescued me, the head, from all inward tribulations by freeing me from sins; and from outward tribulations by resurrection. Likewise, the voice says that he will hear and rescue from all tribulations, in the present from inward ones, and eventually from outward ones.

**Draw near to him and be enlightened.** It is as though he were saying: “I sought the Lord, and therefore I was heard and rescued. You too should seek the Lord through humility, and thus draw near to him.” For the more each person humbles himself, the more he approaches God; and the more he exalts himself, the farther he withdraws from him. Therefore he says: “Draw near to him through humility.”

Draw near in heart, not in body—not with the foot, but with affection. Draw near by following in faith, yearning in heart, and running in charity, without limping—that is, by adhering to the two commandments, namely love of God and love of neighbor, through which one runs toward him.

Draw near, I say, and be enlightened by the light of true knowledge, so that you may understand that by following humility you will attain immense exaltation. It is as though he were saying: “If you draw near, you will be enlightened, to such an extent that your faces will not be confounded by any injuries or insults,” that is, they will not be saddened but will rejoice.

For the faces of the proud are confounded by every injury, because they grieve that there are people superior to them who inflict these things upon them. But the faces of those who follow Christ’s humility are not confounded in tribulations; rather, they glory, because they know that through these very things they are superior to those who inflict them.

This may also be understood with reference to the future. When, at the end, we are all invited to the wedding feast of the true bridegroom, Christ, those who possess the wedding garment will not have their faces confounded; but those who lack that garment will have confounded faces and will not dare to appear. Concerning them it is said: “Let the wicked be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God.”

**This poor man cried out.** He shows in himself how one should draw near to the Lord. It is as though he were saying: “I say, ‘Draw near,’ and take me as an example for this, because this poor man—that is, I, who, although I was rich, humbled myself into poverty for the sake of all—this poor man, I say, cried out,” that is, he directed an unremitting action and intention toward God.

Therefore the Lord heard him, because he will save him from all his tribulations, inward or outward, as stated above. And you too, he says, should be poor—that is, humble, not exalted—and cry out by acting without remission. Then the Lord will hear you and save you. For no one is heard except the poor.

**The angel of the Lord encamps.** Up to this point he has said: “Take me as an example.” But here he says: “Take me as your helper,” speaking for the moment about his own person. It is as though he were saying: “I say, ‘Magnify and draw near to the Lord.’ And so that you may be able to do this, help will not be lacking, because the angel of the Lord—the angel, namely, of the great counsel, that is, of the ancient plan, the new restoration, and eternal happiness—he, I say, will encamp,” that is, will establish an army, whether as a guard of angels or as steadfastness of the virtues.

He will encamp in such a way that this encampment will protect on every side those who fear him, and thus he will rescue them both in the present and in the future. Understand this as having been spoken by way of comparison, like the line:

“Pompey’s standards shut the accused Milo in.”

**Taste and see.** This plainly pertains to the change of appearance mentioned in the title, because here he openly commends his humility. It is as though he were saying: “Because the Lord will hear you when you cry out to him, and the angel of the Lord will encamp and rescue you, therefore taste—not the legal sacrifices now, but my humility—according to the manner in which it should be tasted by the palate of the heart. That is, eat my body and drink my blood, and by tasting see what ought to be seen: understand the Lord’s sweetness here through contemplation, and in the future through direct vision. This is truly to be understood, because the Lord himself is truly sweet—that is, pleasant—to the one who understands him.”

Note, however, that there is no seeing unless tasting has come first. By following humility we will attain the sublimity of divinity.

“Taste,” I say, “and you ought to taste, because the one who hopes in him—that is, in the Lord, the one who accustoms himself to tasting the truth, presuming nothing about himself but hoping in the Lord—is blessed,” not in the world, but because his virtue, that is, his blessedness, consists in virtue.

And because hope without fear is presumption, he adds: “Fear the Lord, all you his saints,” as the punisher of every wickedness—that is, all who hope in him. And do not hesitate to fear him, nor do anything evil out of fear of poverty, as many do, because there is no poverty for those who fear him. As far as the literal sense is concerned, this seems false, since they often suffer poverty in outward things; yet it is true insofar as it concerns that poverty in which true poverty consists, namely, spiritual things.

**The rich have grown poor.** There is no poverty for those who fear him; but the rich and proud, who presume upon themselves and for whom there seems to be no poverty at all, naturally hunger for the true and supreme good. For every concern of mortals, pursued through different forms of activity, strives to reach the one end of blessedness, as Boethius says. They hunger, I say, and yet, because they have gone astray, they have grown poor—that is, they suffer a complete deprivation and have not been filled with that food.

But those who seek the Lord will lack no good thing—that is, they will suffer no lack of any true good. This is repeated: those who seek and those who fear are the same.

**Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord.** Consider what this man, beating the drum and displaying affection, says in such a gentle way. It is as though he were saying: “I spoke more harshly to you when I said, ‘Fear the Lord.’ But in order to address you more gently, I say: Come, children in heart, even if not in body, to me your father, and hear me with the ear of hearing, because I will teach you how you ought to fear the Lord.”

No one should arrogate this to himself or claim it rashly, because only the person who does what follows fears the Lord. He expresses this equivalently in the form of a question: “Who is the man who desires life, and who loves to see good days?” This is to say: “Who is the one who fears the Lord?”

For the person who truly fears the Lord strives toward eternal life and loves good days. These good days are removed from every necessity of tribulations and temptations. They are not the days of this region, the land of the dying, but belong to the land of the living. Abraham did not see these days, nor Paul, nor Christ himself, for they hungered, suffered cold, and endured various tribulations—unless perhaps they possessed them inwardly here through hope, though they were ultimately to possess them in reality.

**Keep your tongue from evil.** It is as though he were saying: “Only the one who does the following desires life and loves good days.” Therefore, whoever you are, keep your tongue from evil—that is, from slander against your neighbor, blasphemy against God, every foolish utterance, and falsehood.

And because we sometimes act deceitfully even when speaking the truth, he says: “And your lips,” so that they may not speak deceit in order to deceive your neighbor.

Turn also from every evil, so that you may not sin only in speech, but neither in action nor in thought. And because it is not enough not to strip the poor man unless we also wish to clothe him, nor is it enough not to take what belongs to another unless we also give what belongs to us, he says: “And do every good thing that you can.”

And in doing these things, seek peace here, so that at last you may pursue the true peace, which no war will disturb. This peace cannot be possessed here. For from there Christ, our true peace, rose and ascended. He left peace to those who follow him, and he will give peace to those who reach him.

This is the peace he left: that we should, insofar as it lies within us, maintain concord with all people. If we preserve this peace, we will eventually rise and ascend, and thus, when we reach him, we will obtain the true peace, when he will be all in all.

Here, however, there is no true peace. For although here we have peace—a bread—against the war of hunger, we are never so satisfied that the war is not renewed again. Therefore pursue it.

**The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.** I say, “Seek peace and pursue it,” and you truly can do this because the Lord’s mercy will help you. Or, when I say, “Seek peace and pursue it,” do not attribute this to yourself, but to divine mercy alone, because the eyes of the Lord—that is, the Lord’s merciful regard—will be upon you, protecting you.

For they will be upon all the righteous, that is, those who seek peace and fear him. And his ears—that is, the power and benevolence of his hearing—will attend their prayers, that is, the prayers of the righteous.

Yet if, when they see that he sometimes does not immediately hear them, they suppose that he is cruel, he is not cruel in this, but rather merciful. By not hearing, he hears, because he is a physician: he cuts away and removes what is rotten in them. He does not spare the wound; for if he spared it, he would be more cruel than merciful.

And lest the wicked, taking an opportunity from this, say: “Since the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, we will do whatever we please with impunity, because he will not see us,” the Holy Spirit confronts them through the mouth of his prophet. It is as though he were saying: “The Lord’s gracious regard will indeed be upon the righteous; but his face—that is, the regard of his angry indignation—will be upon all who do evil,” not for good but for evil, namely, so that he may destroy from the land of the living the memory they prepared for themselves in the land of the dying, consigning it to oblivion—not with respect to punishment, but with respect to a favorable reward.

For just as the Lord regards the righteous from near at hand for salvation, so he regards the unrighteous from afar for condemnation, according to the words: “For the Lord is exalted, and he regards the humble,” and so forth. And truly he will destroy their memory, to whom he says: “I do not know you.”

**The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them.** He said that the Lord regards both the righteous and the unrighteous, and here he first demonstrates this concerning the righteous. It is as though he were saying: “Truly the eyes of God are upon the righteous, because the Lord heard them.” And this was because the righteous cried out through unremitting action. He heard them in this way: he freed them from all their tribulations—that is, from the more serious ones, namely, from the inward tribulations through which one proceeds to outward ones unless one is freed from them.

He freed them, I say, but some in one way and others in another. For was the God of the three young men not also the God of the seven Maccabees? Did he rescue the former from the fire but abandon the latter in the fire? The former sang hymns in the furnace; the latter breathed their last in the fire. Yet he rescued both, though differently: the former bodily, for the confession of their enemies; the latter spiritually, for the greater blinding of their enemies. The same applies to the others.

**The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart.** The Lord heard the righteous because he is a God near to them, just as he is a God far away from the unrighteous. He expresses this as follows: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart,” that is, those who have raised up their heart but then crushed it by humbling it. He is near to the righteous.

Therefore he will save the humble in spirit from tribulations, as stated above—that is, those same people who do not grow proud and presume nothing about themselves. It is necessary that he save them, because the tribulations of the righteous are many: in the present they are afflicted in many ways, inwardly and outwardly, so that after many tribulations they may reach infinite rewards. Conversely, after a few present tribulations the unrighteous reach innumerable miseries.

The tribulations of the righteous are many, I say, and the Lord has already freed them from all these tribulations in hope; eventually he will free them in reality. They have been freed in this way because the Lord guards all their bones, so that not one of them will be crushed—that is, completely broken.

This seems false according to the literal sense. For we find that the bone of the robber crucified with the Lord, who confessed him, was broken just as the bone of the one who did not confess him was broken. But here “bones” must be understood as the supports of the soul, that is, the virtues. In their case it is true that, with the Lord guarding them, the bones remain whole—that is, they are not crushed by the blows that break outward bones.

In that robber, faith could not be crushed, even if his legs were broken. When the other robber blasphemed against the Lord, he said: “Remember me when you come into your kingdom.”

**The death of sinners is most evil, and those who hate the righteous will offend.** Having shown that the eyes of the Lord are truly upon the righteous, he returns to the other side, namely, the unrighteous. It is as though he were saying: “Truly the face of the Lord’s anger will be upon the wicked, so that he may destroy them, because the death of sinners—that is, of those who do evil—which will destroy them, will be most evil.”

Here “death” must not be understood as the dissolution of the body, but as the death of inward things, namely, the separation of the soul from God, who is its bridegroom and true life. This death is truly most evil, because just as living in charity is the greatest good, so dying to charity is the greatest evil.

From this death the other death also results. Even if the dissolution of the body seems good to fools, because they see the funeral of such people carried along with great pomp, it is nevertheless evil, because the soul of the one whose body is placed here and carried on an ivory bed is buried in hell.

The death of sinners is most evil, I say, and it is most evil because “those who hate the righteous will offend.” That is, these sinners commit a serious offense in this matter, because they hate the righteous absolutely—that is, Christ, whom they ought to love—since they trample upon his blood, refusing to imitate his humility.

Here the sin is identified, and from it follows the fact that their death is most evil. From this kind of death, even if the Lord does not redeem the souls of the freed, he will redeem the souls of his servants, that is, the righteous.

And truly he will redeem them from death, because the cause of that death will be absent from them. For all who hope in him—that is, who do not presume upon themselves but humble themselves—do not offend by hating the righteous. They will not trample upon his blood but will imitate his humility.

Here we may understand “the righteous” to mean not Christ alone but also Paul, who said: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.”

## ON PSALM XXXIV

A psalm for David himself.

## Argument

[Col. 0658C]

On the occasion of his troubles David composed this psalm in the time of Jeremiah, and explains what he endured and how he prayed. Alternatively, the entire psalm is spoken in the person of Christ, and through Christ it can be referred to all the psalms.

## Explanation

The entire psalm is spoken in the person of Christ, who asks to be delivered from the persecution of his enemies. For David is rightly understood as Christ, and when the psalm is assigned to David himself, it does not indicate any one of his members but Christ himself, the Mediator.

Throughout this psalm the words are those of the Lord Christ, beginning with the dispensation in which he suffered. In the first section he asks that a recompense be returned for the persecutions, praying for things opposed to them which nevertheless will be beneficial to their conduct. In the second he rejoices in his resurrection and sharply reproaches the wickedness of the Jews. In the third he promises that, through his members, he will be present throughout the whole world to confess the Father’s power, which delivered him from his enemies through the benefit of the resurrection. He prays that the persecutors may be confounded and that the faithful may exult in great glory.

## Commentary

**Judge, Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me.** In this psalm the voice of the head speaks now for itself, now for its members, invoking the Lord God amid the tribulation of this world, with the body now afflicted just as the head was then.

The title is as follows: “A psalm for David himself,” that is, to be attributed to the head itself, who is the true David. As stated above, David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable in appearance.” Christ is truly strong of hand because he conquered our death; and he is desirable in appearance because he promised eternal life.

He is also desirable in appearance and strong of hand because what is stronger than the hand that touched the bier and raised the dead man? What is stronger than that hand which conquered the world, not armed with iron but pierced upon the wood? And what is more desirable in appearance than the one whom the holy martyrs did not see, yet strove to come to see by dying?

Therefore let our soul sing to him, let our body sing to him, and let our heart also sing to him.

Here our head first speaks for itself, saying—not out of the malevolence of wishing, but with the foreknowledge of prophecy:

“Lord Father, judge those who harm me,” that is, the Jews who wished to harm me, the head, and who by their judicial power judge me guilty, failing to distinguish me from the impious through punishment. Judge them by your judicial power, according to their cause, as guilty; but judge me as innocent. Give them over to a debased mind because of their wickedness, but raise me up because of my innocence.

“And those who fight against me,” that is, my members, “and do not overcome me: fight against the Gentiles, or against any others, making them powerless and ineffective, so that they may not conquer but be conquered and converted.” For just as “judge” above is understood in an evil sense, so “fight” here is understood in a good sense. This is referred to the body, just as the former was referred to the head.

[Col. 0659B]

**Take up armor and shield, and rise to my aid.** I say, “Fight,” and in order to fight, take up your armor. Behold the great spectacle: to see God armed.

The principal armor of God is the soul of the Lord’s human being acting here, which he used to overthrow the powers of the air, like a powerful sword. The Lord’s armor is also the souls of the righteous, and our souls as well, provided that we have made good progress—that is, provided that he has first armed us with the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

With these spiritual and invisible weapons the Lord arms our souls against spiritual and invisible enemies, so that they may become his weapons. He then takes them up, since in themselves they were like immobile weapons, incapable of fighting. He uses them as swords both to overthrow enemies and to defend us.

When he adds, “and shield,” this is not added as something different. For spiritual weapons are not like bodily weapons, in which the sword is not the shield, nor the shield the breastplate or helmet, because in these spiritual weapons there is identity. The same faith is found verbally as breastplate and shield: shield because it repels the flaming darts of the evil one; breastplate because it protects our inward being from diabolical temptations.

Or, because weapons are called from the arms they protect, the description of the weapons may be understood by way of excellence, since the shield protects the arms most especially.

“Take up,” I say, “the weapons.” And in this way, you who previously seemed to lie prostrate under evils, rise into the knowledge of many by defending your own with those weapons and overthrowing your enemies. And do this “for my aid,” that is, for the aid of my members.

Pour forth the sword, and conclude against those who persecute me; say to my soul: “I am your salvation.” Arise, I say, so that you may arise; pour forth the sword—that is, let the number of the righteous be multiplied, so that they may be spread everywhere, whose life is your sword for the crushing of enemies and the protection of your own. And through their multitude conclude—that is, make a conclusion and fortification—against those who persecute me, that is, [Col. 0659D] my people, persuading them that his salvation lies in Jove and the other demons, or in earthly things, and thus wishing to lead them astray. It is as though he were saying: “Let the number of the good become so great that the adversaries are stupefied and afraid, having nothing with which to contradict us.” Conclude, I say, and say this plainly, so that I and my people may understand: say, I repeat, “I am your salvation,” and no other; that is, whether an angel or a human being comes to my aid, I shall always say of you: “You are my salvation.” And even if these earthly things provide me with some comfort, I shall say that you are my salvation, because you console me through them in this life, which is like a road, where all these things ought to be a lodging for the traveler, not a house for the inhabitant.

“Let those who seek my soul be confounded and afraid. Let those who devise evil against me be turned back and confounded.” I therefore ask you to conclude against them and say such things to my soul that those who seek my soul and that of my people—not for imitation but for condemnation, [Col. 0660A] not for salvation but for leading astray—may be confounded with a salutary confusion. For one confusion is salutary and another is not. Those are confounded with a salutary confusion who pass from the number of unbelievers into the number of the faithful, or from the number of persecutors into the number of the members, as Paul did. It should be understood that some of the wicked are joined together in such a way that they are separated from the Lord and condemned; others in such a way that they are converted to the Lord. Here he first speaks of those who are converted; afterward he will speak of the others.

“Let those who seek my soul be confounded,” I say, “and let them be so confounded that they are afraid”—that is, that they dread their sins—and let them fear the righteous, having nothing with which to contradict them. Let them be turned away from persecuting, so that those who were previously ahead may now be behind, beside the Lord’s feet; that is, those who were formerly in front may become followers, and persecutors may become preachers. “Let them be turned away,” I say, “and confounded,” so that those who now devise evil against me and mine may become those who desire good for me. [Col. 0660B] But those who do not wish this should become like dust, and so forth.

Here he begins to speak of those wicked people who are joined together in such a way that they are condemned. What precedes—namely, “Let those who devise evil against me be confounded”—may also be referred to the same people in this way: Let those people indeed be turned back; but, by contrast, let not only those who persistently do evil to me and mine, but also those who persistently devise it, receive what they deserve: let them be confounded with an eternal confusion. Meanwhile, let them become like dust before the face of the wind. Dust of the earth is easily carried away by the wind; here, however, “wind” means every carnal impulse and temptation, or diabolical suggestion. Sinners are called dust because they lack the moisture of affection and mercy, and are easily overthrown by the wind of pride and temptation. It is as though he were saying: “Let them become such that they do not withstand any evil impulse, but yield to them all.” Or, alternatively, let them be easily overturned or driven about by every wind of heretical teaching. And for this purpose let an evil angel of the Lord constrain them—that is, compel them, so that they may be cast down more violently—through whom the Lord also works. [Col. 0660C] According to the saying: “The Lord sent an incursion through evil angels.”

Let their way also—that is, their entire present life—be darkness, that is, ignorance of the truth, and slippery ground, that is, a falling into every carnal desire. For this purpose, again, let an evil angel of the Lord pursue them—that is, compel them. This entire verse may also be understood solely by way of comparison, as follows: Let their life be like that of a person who suffers a persecutor in a dark and slippery place. Such a person is in the greatest distress, because he is not even allowed to wait for the light.

“For without cause they hid from me the destruction of their snare; they reproached my soul in vain.” I say that such things should happen to them because they deserve them: for without cause—that is, although I had deserved no evil from them, but rather had done them much good by raising their dead and healing their sick—they nevertheless hid, that is, secretly prepared, the destruction of the snare. I say “their” snare, not mine: they wove together many means, as a snare is woven, by which they wished to ensnare [Col. 0660D] me for destruction, so that the world would not follow after me. But that snare was theirs, because they themselves were rather ensnared for inward destruction. I, however, rose again, and the world followed after me.

“They hid,” I say, “the destruction.” But from whom did they hide it? They hid it from me, who knew the hearts of those who were hiding it, although I was among them as though ignorant. And they reproached my soul—that is, they brought many reproaches against my life—and this in vain. Their accusations were empty with regard to the fact that they brought charges which they had not securely understood, or, as he himself had said, had not received rightly. For example: “This man said, ‘I can destroy the temple of God,’” and so forth. With regard to him, this saying was solid and complete, because he rose again on the third day. But with regard to those who understood it of Solomon’s temple, it was not solid but empty. For something is properly called empty when it is not solid but hollow within.

“Let the snare come upon him which he does not know, and let the trap which he has hidden [Col. 0661A] seize him, and let him fall into that very snare.” Behold a fitting punishment and a deserved retribution. For it is entirely just that every sinner should be bound by the cords of his own sins, and that each person should be condemned by his own wickedness. It is as though he were saying: “They secretly prepared for me the destruction of a snare; let them secretly fall into that same snare.”

The passage may be explained literally as follows: the snare is their wickedness, by which they wished to ensnare me for destruction, and which they do not know will harm them. According to the saying: “Moreover, the wicked man does not know that he is being punished, except when he openly pays the penalty for what he unwillingly committed willingly.” Let that snare, I say, come upon that people—that is, let it be poured back upon them—so that they may be harmed by the very thing through which they wished to harm me.

He explains this by saying: “And let the trap which he has hidden seize him,” that is, let that iniquity which he secretly prepared for me, as though I were ignorant, in order to capture me, seize him; and let it seize him in such a way that he falls into the snare—not another snare, but the very one which he hid for me—that is, when I rise again, let his own iniquity become for him an everlasting fall and condemnation. [Col. 0661B] This is said by way of comparison. Such is the wickedness of everyone: it is as if someone prepared a cup of poison for another and later, having forgotten, drank it himself; or as if he prepared a pit for someone else and fell into it. For whatever corrupts another necessarily corrupts most of all that from which it proceeds and in which it principally exists.

“Capture” may also be understood independently, so that it does not explain the preceding phrase, and the sense may be stated thus: let a capture like that capture which that people prepared for me seize them; that is, just as at the feast of Passover, when they had gathered from everywhere, they secretly deliberated in order to seize me, so on a similar day, when they have gathered from everywhere, may they be seized by Titus and Vespasian. The rest remains unchanged.

“But my soul shall exult in the Lord, and shall rejoice over my salvation.” Let the trap indeed seize them, and let them fall into the snare; but of my soul I shall not speak as one making a wish in uncertainty, saying that it may exult. Rather, I shall state that it shall exult—not presuming upon itself, but in the Lord. It shall also rejoice, that is, it shall possess complete [Col. 0661C] gladness. He indicates this through these two expressions, since exultation belongs to the body, whereas rejoicing belongs to the soul.

“It shall exult,” I say, “and rejoice,” not in itself but in its salvation—that is, in the resurrection granted to it from above by the Word personally united to it. Nor shall my soul alone exult; my body also shall, because all my bones—that is, all the stronger members among my people—even if the flesh does not say so, since “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak”—all my bones, I say, because of their joy at the hope of resurrection given to them in me, shall say: “Lord, who among the angels, or archangels, or patriarchs, or prophets, or the gods of the nations, is like you?” No one, certainly.

And rightly shall they say this, because you both rescue them from the temptations of demons and rescue me from the hands of enemies. He says this as follows: “You are the one who rescues your needy people from themselves,” that is, people who presume nothing upon themselves, “from the hand of those stronger than they,” that is, from the power of the devil and his angels, who are stronger because formerly they prevailed over the whole human race in Adam [Col. 0661D] when he was deceived, and even now prevail over some whom they deceive through their flattering suggestions.

And you truly rescue the needy, who attributes absolutely nothing to himself, and the genuinely poor man, who, although he was rich, became poor for the sake of all: from those who plunder him—that is, from the power of those who tried to plunder him from you, that is, to separate him from you—saying: “God has abandoned him,” and “This man is not from God,” and other such things.

Here he speaks about himself in the third person and shows how they plundered him, saying: “Unrighteous witnesses”—that is, those who bore false testimony against me—rising against me, questioned me through punishment, namely by striking and spitting upon me, about things which I did not know. But what did he not know? Did he know nothing, when he even saw the hearts of his persecutors and foresaw their deceits? Certainly he was ignorant of nothing with regard to vengeance, but he did not know such things by committing them.

“They repaid me.” They questioned me, I say, and while questioning me repaid me evil only for good: [Col. 0662A] for the life which I had come to bestow, death; for honor, blasphemies; for healing, wounds. They also repaid barrenness to my soul in place of fruitfulness, because my soul had come for this purpose and labored to make them, sprinkled with the rain of God’s word, bear good fruit and become fertile. They, however, displayed in themselves only barrenness, because they did not allow themselves to be regenerated through me, but remained like that fig tree in which the hungry Lord found no fruit, but only leaves: for there was abundance in their words but scarcity in their deeds.

“But I…” They indeed questioned me about things I did not know and repaid evil for good; but I, although they were so troublesome to me and raged against me in every way, merely clothed myself in sackcloth. That is, I concealed my divine power and exposed to them only the sackcloth—that is, the mortal flesh with which I was clothed—as an object against which they might rage. For if the one who, by a single word, struck to the ground those seeking to seize him had wished to exercise his divine power against his persecutors, there is no doubt that he could have [Col. 0662B] killed them all by a mere nod.

It should be known, however, that sackcloth is made from the hair of goats and kids, and through the goat and kid sin is signified because of its stench. Christ’s flesh is therefore called sackcloth because it bore the punishment of sin, although it did not commit sin. His flesh was mortal, and mortal only in punishment, because, being without sin, it is like our flesh. According to the Apostle’s saying: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, in order to condemn sin in the flesh through sin”—that is, in order to destroy our death through his death. For both Christ’s death and our death are called sin, because his death is the effect and punishment of the sin which Adam committed.

“I humbled my soul with fasting.” Although they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth. From this it is evident that my soul, which hungered and thirsted for nothing except their conversion, was fasting. Yet in this fasting I humbled my soul—that is, I did not become angry, as powerful people commonly become angry when food is taken from them at a fixed time.

[Col. 0662C] This fasting was so great that amid such a crowd of persecutors he found no one with whom he could refresh himself except the thief hanging beside him, while even the disciples had fled after abandoning him and were hiding in the crowd. Peter also—the one who had earlier cried out so rashly, “Lord, even if I must die with you, I will not deny you”—was hiding in the crowd and trembled at the voice of a little servant girl. “I humbled myself,” I say, “in fasting, and I prayed for them, saying: ‘Father, forgive them.’”

And I shall pray not to someone far away but to someone near, because my prayer would be turned into my bosom—that is, into what is hidden within me—since my humanity would pray for them to the Word personally united to it.

These two verses may also be read in another way, so that the sense is: “They repaid me evil; but I, although they were troublesome, nevertheless clothed myself in sackcloth”—that is, I converted some of them who had previously been like sackcloth, thorny and fruitless, and made them like a soft garment with which I might be clothed. According to the saying: “As I live, says the Lord, [Col. 0662D] you shall be clothed with all these things as with a garment.”

And I do this because in that grievous fasting which I suffered on account of their lack of conversion, I humbled my soul—that is, my life—by eating with publicans and sinners and associating with them, so that I might draw some of them to myself and thus bring that fasting of mine to an end in them. “I humbled myself,” I say, “and prayed for them.” And although my prayer does not benefit all of them, it will nevertheless be turned—that is, it will become visible—in my bosom among those who are converted; that is, in those signified by Moses’ hand being returned to his bosom.

Here we are sent back to the history in which it is said that, when the Lord commanded Moses to return to Egypt and lead his people out from there, Moses asked the Lord for a sign, saying: “Lord, what sign will there be for me, so that they may heed me?” And the Lord said to him: “Bring your hand out of your bosom.” He brought it out, and behold, it had become entirely leprous. Again he said to him: “Put your hand back into your bosom.” He put it back, and it had become like the rest of his flesh.

Moses’ bosom [Col. 0663A] signifies the bosom of the Lord. And the bosom of the Lord is faith, hope, charity, and ecclesiastical institutions. Whoever is brought out from this bosom—such as heretics who have gone out from us—becomes leprous in sins. If it happens that he returns, he becomes like the others who are healed from the leprosy of sins within the bosom. And whoever is in this bosom is converted into the same state, because naturally, when Adam was placed in the fullness of virtues, we were in this bosom; but through that same transgressor we went out from it.

“Like a neighbor and like our brother, I was pleasing; like one mourning and sorrowful, I humbled myself.” In his passion I prayed for them, and beforehand, when I admonished them, I was pleasing to them as though I were admonishing a neighbor—that is, some disciple—or as though I were admonishing our brother, that is, some apostle, because they obeyed me easily, as a brother or neighbor would.

But by the greater part of those who despised sound doctrine I was humbled in such a way that outwardly I was like one mourning and inwardly like one sorrowful—that is, as though I possessed complete sadness. [Col. 0663B] Good prelates commonly rejoice in the progress of their subjects and grieve over their failure as over their own. Hence the Apostle says: “I live now, if you are in the Lord.”

“And against me they rejoiced and gathered together; scourges were gathered against me, and I did not know.” I was humbled by them, I say, and this because they rejoiced and gathered together—that is, they gathered together joyfully against me. When they assembled, innumerable scourges were gathered against me by them; yet I did not know the cause, not with regard to judgment but to the deed, because I was conscious of no evil.

“They gathered together,” I say, and in that assembly they were divided among themselves, because some said, “He is good,” while others said otherwise. Yet neither one group nor the other was moved to compassion, because they tempted me, and so forth.

This may also be understood as follows: the effect indicates that they came against me without cause, because they were scattered throughout all the nations and yet still were not moved to repentance. In accordance with the temptation they attempted, the continuation will proceed.

[Col. 0663C] In this way scourges were gathered against me, because they tempted me, saying: “Teacher, we know that you have come from God”; and, “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?” and other such things. “They also mocked me,” that is, they derided me with mockery, with a base and contemptible derision. “And they gnashed their teeth against me,” that is, with their biting words, saying: “Crucify him, crucify him.”

But you, Lord Father, when will you look upon me, the head, so that I may be freed from them? When will you also look upon my body? At the appointed time you will look upon me, the head, by raising me again, and also upon the body. You do not delay with regard to the head out of inability, but for a reason; nor do you delay with regard to the body out of weariness, but out of love.

The Lord did not delay Christ’s resurrection until the third day because he was unable to raise him even at the first moment, but for a reason, because it is written in the Gospel: “Today and tomorrow I perform healings, but on the third day I am perfected.” On the first day—that is, before the Law—the Lord performed healings in certain people, such as blessed Abel and Abraham, [Col. 0663D] and the other patriarchs. On the following day—that is, under the Law—many were saved, such as Moses and Aaron and all who observed the Law spiritually. On the third day, in the time of grace, through the Word sent to earth, salvation was completed and perfected. This is why Christ rose not on the first or second day, but rather on the third.

With regard to the body also, although the Lord could, whenever he wished, raise either individuals separately or many together, he does not delay the resurrection out of weariness but out of love—because, since he himself is perfect, he loves the perfection for which humanity was first created to be completed in the body also before that resurrection. According to the saying: “Wait a little while for God,” and so forth.

Let us now return to the literal sense. “Look,” I say, “upon me and the body at the appointed time. Therefore do not delay my resurrection until the general resurrection, but quickly restore my soul by freeing it through resurrection from the wickedness—that is, from the evil—[Col. 0664A] of those who gnash their teeth against me. And at the time appointed by you restore also my only one—that is, the Church, my bride—freed from lions, that is, from the savage rulers who persecute her.

“Shall I confess to you in the great Church, and shall I praise you among a weighty people?” It is as though he were saying: “For what benefit do I ask you to restore both me and my only one? For this reason: I shall confess to you in myself and in my people, in the great Church.”

The Church is truly great because it is spread throughout the whole world. But because chaff and grain—that is, the evil and the good—are together in it, when the wind of winnowing and temptation comes, the chaff, which is light, is driven away, while the grain, which is heavy, remains among the weighty people.

It is as though he were saying: “I shall confess to you in the Church generally, among both the good and the evil; but I shall truly and especially praise you among a weighty people,” that is, among holy men whom ancient adversity does not drive away.

“Let those who oppose me unjustly not rejoice over me, [Col. 0664B] those who hate me without cause and wink with their eyes.” I also ask you to restore me, the head, and the body, so that if they rejoiced over my death and over the imprisonment of my people, they may not rejoice over me—that is, to the depression of me and mine—because I was not raised again and because mine were led astray.

They are those who oppose me and mine unjustly, in that they hated me, the head, without cause, since I had done them no evil but much good. And they wink with their eyes in fraudulent persecution—that is, they outwardly assent to me with their eyes, though they inwardly hate me. They assent with their voice to what they contradict in their heart; they assent with their face to what they deny in their will.

And what wonder if they do this with dry wood, when they did it with green wood—that is, with me? For outwardly they spoke peacefully to me, saying: “We know that you have come from God, teacher,” and other such things. Yet while speaking in this way they were devising deceit in their hearts against me, namely, the wrath of the earth: they were angry with me on account of earthly things, fearing that through me they would lose their place and nation.

And they not only devised these things but also did what they had devised, because they opened their mouths [Col. 0664C] against me, roaring before Pilate: “Crucify him.” And after they had accomplished against me what they wished, they rejoiced and said: “Good, good!” That is: “It has gone well for our soul, because our eyes have seen what we always desired to see and what we wished for in every way.”

“You have seen, Lord; do not be silent, Lord; do not depart from me.” It is as though he were saying: “They, I say, saw the punishment, but you, Lord, saw my cause and innocence. Therefore, Lord, if you were silent concerning the punishment, do not be silent concerning vengeance. Or, just as you were not silent concerning the command—namely, so that through me you might command what you wished—so also do not be silent concerning judgment, so that you may avenge my condemnation upon them. And do not depart from me,” that is, from mine, in persecution; rather, as you promised through me, be with them until the consummation of the age, so that you may protect them from their enemies.

“Arise and attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord, to my cause.” Do not be silent, I say, but [Col. 0664D] rather arise in vengeance, you who appeared to lie inactive in punishment. And attend—that is, make yourself attentive—to the public manifestation of the judgment which they made concerning me, judging according to my deed, not according to theirs, so that what they thought would be to their glory and my disgrace may instead be turned to my glory and their disgrace.

I call you “my God” by creation and power, and “my Lord” by submission and will. In this he instructs us to make him, who is our God by necessity, our Lord also through submission and will.

He explains how he asks him to attend when he adds: “Attend, I say, to discerning my cause.” It is as though he were saying: “I do not ask you to attend to what I have in common with thieves, namely punishment, but to the cause—that is, because blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.” This cause distinguishes them among the good alone, although the punishment is common. Therefore it is the cause, not the punishment, that makes a martyr. For if punishment made a martyr, every wicked person who was beheaded or [Col. 0665A] killed in some other way would be crowned—which is an unfitting conclusion.

“Judge me according to your justice, Lord my God, and let them not rejoice over me. Let them not say in their hearts: ‘Good, good for our soul,’ nor let them say: ‘We shall devour him.’”

Attend, I say, to the cause, and judge me—that is, distinguish me from the wicked in punishment—according to justice, that is, according to my true obedience, which is nevertheless yours, since it was given to me by you, Lord my God.

And you ought to judge in such a way that the enemies who rejoiced over my death may not rejoice over me as one not raised again. They formerly said at my death, “Good, good for our soul.” Let them no longer say this when they see me risen again in their hearts; and if they pretend outwardly with their lips, let them rather say: “Woe, woe to our soul.”

For the Jews experienced infinite sadness when they heard that Christ had risen, and they would have preferred by every means not to have crucified him rather than to have crucified him and seen him rise again. Let them not say, I repeat, “Good, good,” nor let them say, “We have devoured him,” thinking that they had previously entirely erased my name from the earth. Rather, let me devour them, and let mine also devour their persecutors, both Gentiles and Jews.

Here he sends us back to the history [Col. 0665B] in which it is contained that, when Moses remained on Mount Sinai for forty days in order to receive the Law from the Lord, the Israelite people murmured against Aaron, demanding idols. Since Aaron could not correct them by reason, he wished to turn them back through loss. He therefore commanded them to bring their golden and silver ornaments, and from them he made a molten calf.

Afterward, when Moses returned from the mountain and was greatly distressed by this, he had it ground into powder and gave them the mixture to swallow.
