This signified that the true Israelites who would become apostles, and the other holy heralds, were understood to swallow up not only certain Jews but also Gentiles who had been idolaters, through that idol, namely the molten calf: by conforming them to themselves, they were to devour them in evil and transfer them into the body of Christ. [Col. 0665C]

The things said above, beginning with “Arise and attend,” may also, in their own manner, be referred to the members and their persecutors, both from the Gentiles and from the Jews.

“Let those who rejoice over my evils be ashamed and afraid together. Let those who speak wickedly against me be clothed with confusion and fear.” Let them not say, I repeat, “We have devoured him,” whether this refers to me or, with regard to my people, to them. Rather, let them be ashamed of their sins and at the same time be afraid—that is, let them dread them—or let them be ashamed of me and mine, recognizing that they are sinners and more unworthy.

These are the people who now rejoice over my evils and those of my people. Let them be so ashamed and afraid that they are clothed with confusion and fear—that is, let their confusion and fear be so complete that it surrounds them like a garment. Let those who now speak evil—not only do evil against me, but speak about me and mine—be clothed in this way.

And let them truly be ashamed and afraid, because all those who previously wished to establish their own righteousness will exult and rejoice when they now wish to establish my righteousness. [Col. 0665D] May they indeed exult and rejoice, and so forth.

The two verses just mentioned may also be understood in a bad sense as follows: Let my persecutors and those of my people not say, “We shall devour”; rather, let them be ashamed and at the same time be afraid—that is, let them incur outward shame and inward harmless fear because of their wickedness in the present—those who rejoice over my evils and those of my people. In the future, however, let all who speak wickedly about me—that is, about me and mine—be clothed with complete confusion and fear. This will truly happen when they say: “We fools considered their life madness,” and so forth.

“Let those who desire my righteousness exult and rejoice, and let them always say: ‘May the Lord be magnified’—those who desire the peace of his servant.”

It is as though he were saying: “Let the wicked and persecutors suffer both here and in the future.” By contrast, let all those who [Col. 0666A] previously wished to establish their own righteousness but now wish only for my righteousness exult and rejoice inwardly—that is, possess complete joy—both here and in the future.

And let them always say: “May the Lord be magnified,” that is, exalted, and never the servant. Let them presume nothing more upon themselves, but ascribe everything to the Lord. These are those who desire the peace given through me, his servant—that is, to humanity. This peace consists in conflict with vices and concord with the best moral qualities.

And they will truly say, “May the Lord be magnified,” because my tongue—that is, my heart, which is called a tongue because it speaks to God—will always meditate, O Lord, that your justice exists. Hence it is written in the Gospel that the Lord Jesus answered the evil thoughts of his adversaries. That is, it will presume nothing upon itself but will ascribe all righteousness to you.

It will meditate your true and perfect praise on that day, which will be the whole day—that is, in the future life, where there will be perpetual day without night—and throughout the whole day, that is, with complete purity of mind. Or “throughout the whole day” means that it will meditate on God’s praise continually.

For if you sing a hymn in the Church, you praise the Lord; but if you do not sing, [Col. 0666B] you restore the body with food or sleep. And this is not for the pleasure of the flesh, but so that you may not fail in God’s service. If, whatever you do, you always set the Lord before your mind, the complete innocence of your works continually praises God.

## ON PSALM XXXV

“To the end, for the servant of the Lord, a psalm of David.”

### ARGUMENT

When he was being pressed by Saul’s ambushes, he sang this psalm, especially at the time when, though Saul wished to kill him, he took only the cup as a sign of fidelity and carried off the spear. Alternatively, the Prophet is said to speak this psalm with praise concerning the deeds of Judas himself.

### EXPLANATION

By “the servant of the Lord,” understand no one other than him who, although he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant, becoming obedient [Col. 0666C] unto death. The whole psalm is spoken from the person of the Prophet.

In the first section he strongly accuses the despisers of the Law, declaring that they do not dwell with the Lord because of their ungodly desires. In the second, under the praise of the Lord, he describes the gifts of rewards bestowed, and says that they are filled with the abundance of the Lord’s house. In brief, this psalm concludes with the ruin of the wicked.

### COMMENTARY

“The unrighteous man said that he should sin.” The title is as follows: “To the end, for the servant of the Lord, David,” according to Cassiodorus, who explains it in this way.

These words do not refer to history but “to the end,” that is, to perfection, namely to Christ. This is because they are attributed to David—that is, to someone more perfect among his members. I say “David,” not understood historically, even if one looks to the Prophet, but “the servant of the Lord,” that is, one who is truly the Lord’s servant, serving not carnally but spiritually.

This servant of the Lord rebukes in this psalm his unjust fellow servants, who propose to themselves that they should sin, [Col. 0666D] not because they are unable to understand, but because they are unwilling—and who unjustly transfer the blame for their sins to their author. He reminds them that they sin not through any fault of their creator, nor because of difficulty or necessity, but because of their perverse will: they are unwilling to understand in order to act well. Thus he says:

“The unrighteous man said”—that is, proposed and resolved—“that he should sin,” that is, sin continually. He does not say this openly before human beings, because he fears being rebuked or condemned by them, but “within himself,” that is, in his guilty heart.

Here “the unrighteous man” does not mean one individual, but the entire race of the wicked, which opposes itself in understanding so that it may act well—not because it cannot, but because it does not wish to. For it is one thing when someone tries to understand something but cannot because of human weakness, since “the corruptible body weighs down the soul.” For example, human weakness cannot grasp what is said about the equality of the Trinity or about “the Word which was in the beginning with God,” and other matters concerning divinity. [Col. 0667A] In such things ignorance is not a sin.

But it is another thing when the human heart acts more perniciously against itself, namely by refusing to understand what it could understand if the will were willing. This is not because the matter is difficult, but because the will is perverse and turned away. This occurs when people love their sins and hate divine commandments, because the divine word is your adversary if you love your iniquity, but your friend if you hate it.

Thus there are two forces against your iniquity: you and the divine word. You cannot overcome it by yourself; therefore, if you hate that iniquity and God forgives it, you will be free. But if you love it, everything said against it is opposed to you—not because you cannot understand, but because you do not wish to.

For that commandment is exceedingly plain and clear to every human being: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another,” because everyone can recognize this within himself. Therefore, whoever does not understand this will not be blamed on account of difficulty but rather on account of the will. [Col. 0667B]

And because this is what the unrighteous person is like, he said—not from difficulty but from his will—that he should sin. And because he did not dare to do so openly, he fled to the hidden consciousness of his heart. But if he fears the sight of a human being, he ought much more to fear the sight of God, who sees what is in the heart just as a human being sees what is on the face. He could understand this if he wished to pay attention.

But he does not pay attention because the fear of the Lord is not before his eyes—that is, because he does not consider God as judge in his affairs. If he did consider this, he would certainly fear him.

“For he acted deceitfully in his sight, so that his iniquity might be found out for hatred,” and so forth. He proves this from the disposition of the unrighteous person, because he does not fear God: he does what he would not do if he feared him.

He acts deceitfully in his sight—that is, in his heart, where God himself sees. And he acts deceitfully for this purpose: so that his iniquity may be found out for hatred, that is, because he does not truly wish to find his iniquity in order to hate it once found.

There are many who seem to try to investigate their iniquity, [Col. 0667C] yet fear to find it, lest it be said to them: “Until now you sinned in ignorance; but now that you know your iniquity, cease to sin.” Such people act deceitfully rather than sincerely, fearing to find the iniquity which they pretend to seek.

There are also others who act deceitfully in order to find iniquity, because they do not sincerely seek to investigate and hate it. And because there is deceit in the search, there is defense in the discovery. If they sought it sincerely, they would truly hate it once found and would not defend it by saying: “What have we done? Does not everyone do this? Is God going to destroy everyone who does such things?” Defending iniquity, they say many similar things. From this it is apparent that they act deceitfully, not sincerely.

“**The words of his mouth.**” He proves this only with respect to the other part, namely those who, as it were, discover iniquity and defend it. For the unjust man truly acts deceitfully, since the words of his mouth are not merely iniquitous but are themselves iniquity, because he defends the iniquity he has discovered. His words are therefore iniquitous in their defense because deceit preceded them in the investigation. Deceit was indeed present there, because he did not wish to do what he could have done—namely, genuinely to investigate and understand iniquity, so that he might set it aside and thus act well.

He proves this from the contrary. It is as though he said: He truly did not wish to understand in order to act well, because instead he both conceived iniquity and brought iniquity to completion. Thus he says: “The unjust man meditated iniquity persistently,” that is, sinning in his bedchamber, namely in his heart; and he also brought into effect what he had wickedly conceived, because “he stood by every way that was not good”: he persevered in every evil deed.

The ways of the wicked are called their perverse works. Our heart, however, is figuratively called our bedchamber, because the healthy—that is, the good—rest there, while the sick—that is, the wicked—labor there. Good people habitually withdraw from outward noise into the secrecy of the heart, and there rest and rejoice, provided that they find there a good wife, namely delight in immortal wisdom [Col. 0668A]. Yet one must be very careful lest an evil wife drive someone out from there, namely the smoke of an evil conscience.

How wretched, then, is this unjust man, who, where he ought most to rest—in the heart—labors to have tumult rather than rest. “He stood,” I say, “by every way that was not good.” This happened because he did not truly investigate and hate the malice that was in him, namely the tinder of sin; rather, he consented to it in every respect. For in the present life we cannot be without malice, but we can hate it.

Thus the Apostle says: “There is sin in your mortal body, but let it not reign so as to make you obey the desire of the flesh.” There will, however, be a time when we shall not have malice—namely, when this mortal nature puts on immortality and the last enemy, death, is destroyed. Before that time, the delight of iniquity will always be in us. Therefore, on the contrary, let the delight of obedience to God’s commandments be present in us, so that we may fight against iniquity and overcome it. For it is one thing not to fight but to be in perpetual peace; that will occur when we are clothed with immortality [Col. 0668B]. It is another thing to fight and be defeated; this occurs in those who first devote themselves to good works and divine commandments, then become proud and presume upon themselves. It is yet another thing to fight and conquer; this belongs to the good, who presume nothing about themselves and say with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God!” Another condition is not to fight at all, but rather to be dragged along by iniquity. It is of this kind that he speaks here when he says: “He did not hate malice.”

**“Lord, your mercy is in heaven.”** The passage is connected in this way: The unjust man does not speak because he cannot act well, but because he does not wish to act well; nevertheless, your mercy, Lord, will not abandon him, by which you save such men “as beasts,” as is stated below. Yet your mercy—that is, mercy worthy of you—is found only in heaven, namely in holy men who, lifted above earthly things, have become heaven.

One must understand that the mercy of God consists of many kinds of gifts. Some of his gifts are earthly and temporal, and through them he saves bodily [Col. 0668C]—the unjust man mentioned above, like the beasts, and other merely human beings, that is, those who bear the image of the old man and not of the new. They regard this salvation as a great thing and rejoice in it exceedingly.

Other gifts of God are heavenly and eternal. These are partly common already to holy men, but ultimately they will be possessed in full together with the angels. These are the mercies of which he says: “Lord, your mercy is in heaven.” It is as though he said: That mercy of yours is known to us, because “your truth”—that is, the truth of your commandments—“has reached the clouds,” that is, has established certain clouds. The knowledge of your commandments caused certain men to rise upward from those heavens and become clouds, namely the apostles and preachers, through whom that mercy became known to us.

Holy preachers are called clouds because of their flesh: through their flesh the divine power hidden within it thundered to us through threats, flashed through miracles, and rained upon us through words.

**“Your justice is like the mountains.”** He shows that certain men truly have been lifted upward from heaven and made clouds. It is as though he said: They truly are clouds, because they are like mountains, that is, resemble mountains in many ways—both because of the steadfastness of their faith and because of the eminence of their virtues.

And just as the rising sun first illuminates the mountains and from there shines into the valleys, so the true sun of justice, namely Christ, having risen, first opened the hearts of those mountains so that they might understand the Scriptures; from there he shone upon us, because through them he opened to us the hidden mysteries of the Scriptures.

They are, I say, like mountains—mountains, moreover, of God, from whom help comes, according to the saying: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which my help will come.” There are, however, other mountains that are not God’s, such as Donatus, Marcion, and the other heretics who usurp for themselves the primacy of teaching. These mountains are not mountains of help but of shipwreck, because those who look toward them are not lifted up but suffer shipwreck.

They are, I say, like mountains, and this is not by their own merits [Col. 0669A], Lord, but by your justice, that is, by your grace alone, which justifies them. He demonstrates this by a likeness in reverse. It is as though he said: These men are mountains through your justice, just as, conversely, the fact that the unjust are “a great abyss”—not merely in two criminal acts but in many, that is, in many crimes—comes about through judgments that are not unjust but just, because they are yours.

For it is not, as some suppose, unjust that the wicked are given over to a depraved mind; rather, it is God’s most just judgment. According to the Apostle: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God; therefore they became futile in their thoughts. For while claiming to be wise, they became fools.”

He uses the plural “judgments” because each individual crime has its own judgment. It should also be known that Saint Augustine takes “your justice,” as we said above, as an ablative, and “judgments” as an accusative. They may, however, also be taken as nominatives, if the passage is understood in this way: “One truth made certain of your people clouds.”

Such men are not merely to be called your just men, but even your justice itself; by their excellence they are like the mountains of God. Conversely, “your judgments”—that is, the unjust men judged and condemned by you—are “a great abyss.” And it might be asked: Since they are an abyss, why do they live? Why do they survive?

He answers: They live not because they have deserved it, but because you, Lord, save—and will save—men of this kind with a temporal salvation, which they regard as a great thing, like the beasts. You will do this in accordance with the way in which you have multiplied your mercy, so that it might exist not only in heaven but also among those others who are like earth. You, I say, are God, and therefore it is fitting that you should bestow abundant mercy upon your creatures.

This psalm may also be read differently from the beginning up to this point, so that its sense is as follows, as though it said: “It is falsely claimed d. n. r. g. h. that rain a. b. e. f. p. r. [occurs] by necessity rather than by power” [the abbreviated words in the source are uncertain].

Accordingly, it may be understood in this way: “The unjust man said”—that is, determined and affirmed—“that he sins by necessity,” as though shifting the blame onto nature and its author. Yet the fact that he sins is in himself, that is, in his free will. The author or nature is therefore not to be accused; rather, the man himself is to be blamed, because through his free will he disposed himself to sin.

Some, however, read the words as “so that he does not sin.” This may also be understood in the following way: “The unjust man said that he does not sin in himself,” that is, by his own free will, but rather because he was created in such a way that he would necessarily sin.

Why does he say such things? Because “the fear of the Lord is not before his eyes”: he does not believe that God will judge earthly matters. And he truly does not fear God, because “he acted deceitfully in his sight,” namely in his heart, where God himself sees. He acts deceitfully in this respect: although from the commandments of Scripture and from its threats he could understand what ought to be held and what ought to be avoided, he pretends that he cannot understand it. He does this with respect to so many things that his iniquity may be found by all—that is, that it may be evident to everyone that his iniquity is worthy of hatred, and ought to be hateful to all.

**“The words of his mouth.”** He truly acts deceitfully, because the words of his mouth are iniquitous, that is, false; and they are iniquitous because they are deceit. This is so because he says that he cannot understand, not because he truly cannot, but because he did not wish to understand in order to act well.

And not only are the words of his mouth iniquitous; he also conceives and performs iniquity, as he says: “He meditated iniquity,” and so forth. The interpretation remains unchanged.

**“Lord, your mercy is in heaven.”** It is as though he said: Among these unjust men who act in such ways, Lord, there is your wrath; but in heaven there is your mercy, as before. These judgments of yours—namely, that your wrath is in the former and your mercy in the latter—are not a small abyss but a great one; that is, they are inexhaustible and inscrutable. According to the saying: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God,” and the rest.

**“Men and beasts.”** The passage is connected in this way: In those men there is indeed your wrath, yet even such men are not abandoned by your mercy, Lord, because you save such human beings as beasts, as above.

The words **“Lord, in heaven”** may also be connected in another way and partly explained as follows. The unjust man said, I grant, that he sins by necessity, but he lies. For if this were so, why would the Lord and Father have sent us in the heaven of heavens—that is, in Christ—his book, according to whose model we should be written and to whom we should be conformed? It would have been sent in vain.

But because that is not the case, therefore, Lord and Father, your mercy—by which you called and justified us—has been manifested to us by you in the heaven of heavens, namely in Christ. The truth of the promises of eternal blessedness has likewise been manifested there. Both this mercy and this truth have served to establish certain clouds.

The remaining points are unchanged, as they were explained in the preceding interpretation.

**“The sons of men.”** The men mentioned above will be saved for a time, namely by temporal goods that they share with the beasts. But “the sons of men” are those who are distinguished not only from the beasts but also from those men, because just as the latter bear the image of the earthly, so the former bear the image of the heavenly. They are imitators of true men, namely the patriarchs and prophets [Col. 0670B].

Such men, I say, “will hope”—that is, they will not possess the object of their hope here in the present reality, but nevertheless in hope—because they will not pursue the temporal goods shared with the beasts; rather, they will hope for eternal goods with the angels. They will do so “under the shelter of your wings,” that is, under the defense of your protection.

This is said by way of mere likeness, since a hen also protects her chicks beneath her wings. Or we may understand his wings as charity and mercy: charity, by which he descended to us; mercy, by which he called and justified us. We may also understand them as the promises of both Testaments—one concerning temporal things, the other concerning spiritual things. In the Old Testament, insofar as the literal sense is concerned, the promise was made concerning temporal goods; in the New, spiritual and eternal things are promised.

The Lord comforts those who hope in him for the present with temporal goods, but in the end he will make them blessed with eternal goods.

The sons of men, I say, “will hope,” and such men “will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house.” He wished to promise this, but could not state it directly, because he had no words with which to explain it. Yet because he saw men drinking immoderately and filling themselves so thoroughly with wine that they completely exceeded the bounds of human understanding and seemed to put on another nature, he wished through this likeness to explain the abundance of heavenly joy and grace.

Even in the present life, God’s saints, when filled with grace, become so transformed that they pass from a human mind into a divine one, to such an extent that they fear no torments and do not even look upon their fathers standing nearby, or their weeping wives or children.

He says: “They will be intoxicated,” that is, they will be so filled that, like drunkards, they will surpass their own minds, through “the abundance”—that is, the overflowing richness—“of spiritual grace, which is your house, Lord,” namely, which descends from your house, that is, from the heavenly dwelling. “For every good gift is from above.”

And they will truly be intoxicated, because “you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight,” Lord, that is, from the rush of the abundant grace of your gifts. These gifts are your delight, that is, things that give pleasure [Col. 0670D]. A torrent is properly a quantity of rainwater that abounds and usually runs down from the mountains with force.

**“For with you is the fountain of life.”** He rightly says, “You will give them drink,” because this is yours to do. The fountain of life—that is, your Word, from whom true life proceeds—is called a fountain because it gives drink to the thirsty; it is called bread because it refreshes the hungry; it is called light because it illuminates the blind; and it receives many similar names.

That fountain, I say, is with you: it is consubstantial and coeternal with you. Therefore we shall see you, the Father, who are light—not light from light, but light in your light—through that Word which is your light, namely light proceeding from you. Let us see you through him.

**“Send forth, Lord”—** that is, send him whom you are going to send; “stretch forth as a defense your mercy,” namely your Son, who is not merely merciful but must himself be called Mercy. Stretch forth, I say, your mercy “to those who know you,” that is, to those who wish to know you through him. And also stretch forth your justice, that is, your faith which justifies us [Col. 0671A]. This faith will be given through him to those who, by means of it, will become upright of heart—those who do not twist your heart toward their own heart but direct their own heart toward yours.

This is the prayer of the faithful from the later people, not with respect to the sending of the Word, which has already occurred, but with respect to knowledge of him.

**“Let not the foot of pride come to me.”** Therefore, Lord, I ask that you stretch forth your mercy, so that I may be taught humility by him and by eating his humble body.

“Let not the foot of pride come to me,” that is, let the exalted affection of pride no longer creep upon me. Pride is called a foot because by it we withdrew from the Lord into the land of unlikeness; and just as through the exalted Adam we fell, so through the humbled Christ we rose again. Christ was the example of true humility.

When the Jews insulted him by saying, “You have a demon,” he did not curse them, but humbly denied what was not true; what was true he accepted by keeping silent, lest he seem to return a curse, and so that he might preach the truth and teach humility [Col. 0671B].

“Let not,” I say, “the foot of pride come to me, and let not the hand of the sinner”—that is, the evil action of a wicked persuader—“move me to act wrongly.” Here he asks for two things: to be freed from a perverse affection and from evil persuasion. These two vices became evident at the beginning, because the devil fell through a hidden affection, and Adam through another’s persuasion.

Nevertheless, whoever you are, preserve what is within you, and you will not fear what is outside. Therefore, lest you fall into arrogance within yourself, avoid in this way the perverse persuasion that comes from outside.

**“There they fell.”** I ask that you drive away from me the foot of pride because “there,” that is, in that foot, they fell at the beginning. All who now practice iniquity suffered a grave fall—both the devil and human beings.

He explains how they fell: they were expelled from the inner paradise, that is, from the inward joy of the soul in which they were created. And because they were expelled from the inner paradise, they could not remain in the outer paradise: Adam in the earthly one, and the devil in the heavenly one.

# ON PSALM XXXVI

A Psalm of David himself.

[Col. 0671C]

## ARGUMENT

In this psalm the faith of those people is built up who, disturbed by the temporal prosperity of the wicked, interrupt their own virtues. Read in the Wisdom of Solomon.

## EXPLANATION

“Of David himself,” as is to be understood above. This psalm exhorts us to faith and demonstrates the salvation of the Church. It admonishes believers, since many mortals are disturbed by the affliction of the good and the prosperity of the wicked, to such an extent that they both desire virtues that are not rewarded in this life and pursue vices.

This psalm is composed to drive away such an error, repeatedly warning that the end of both groups should be considered. Throughout the psalm the voice of the Church is introduced. It is arranged according to the Hebrew alphabetical order, though it lacks the sixteenth letter [Col. 0671D].

In its first division it warns that no one ought to imitate those who do evil, but should ask the Lord for whatever good is to be hoped for, since he knows how to grant what will be beneficial and to bestow what will endure forever. In the second it says that sinners are tormented here by the greatest anguish of envy, because they recognize that they possess nothing in their actions comparable to the good. In the third it declares that it has never seen the just man abandoned, interweaving the punishments of the wicked and the rewards of the blessed in a useful admonition. The first division contains six letters, the second seven, and the third eight.

## COMMENTARY

**“Do not envy those who do evil.”** The title is “A Psalm of David himself,” that is, to be attributed to one or many who are more perfect within the body of Christ. There are indeed two kinds within the body of Christ: the more perfect, who are good, and the less perfect.

Those who see the wicked living happily and flourishing in every earthly prosperity, and who are indignant at their flourishing and desire it for themselves, are truly still less perfect. Against such people the more perfect act in this psalm, instructing them not to grumble about the flourishing of the wicked or desire it, lest they become like them. Rather, they should place their hope in the Lord and prefer to rejoice in him eternally to flourishing here with the wicked for an hour.

There may also be a very suitable approach to this psalm in the following way. Our Lord, speaking to us through his elect, wishes and causes us to be cautious in all things, since he has a time for speaking and not yet for judging, while we have a time for hearing and not yet for repenting in vain. For then there will indeed be repentance, but it will be fruitless. Divine justice will restore to them what they lost through their own injustice.

It is just before God that he now bestow mercy and then exercise judgment. Therefore, Christian man, do not be disturbed because you see the wicked living happily, overflowing with abundant possessions, rising in dignity, and flourishing in every kind of glory [Col. 0672B]. Nor should your heart say that there is no divine judgment, but that everything is driven by chance and shaken by fortuitous movements.

Perhaps you will say: If God regarded human affairs, why would his iniquity flourish while my innocence suffers? Whoever thinks this, whoever is sick with this illness, drink in your heart the healing antidote of this psalm against such a disease. For every illness of the soul finds its medicine in the Holy Scriptures.

Do not therefore murmur; do not envy, that is, do not imitate those who do evil when considering those who do evil—namely, do not wish to imitate their flourishing. For since no one flourishes here except by acting wickedly, as robbing and stealing, if you desire to flourish, you will have to be wicked in the same way.

Nor should you be jealous—that is, love—those who commit iniquity, so as to desire their flourishing. “Jealousy” is sometimes used for anger and indignation, as in: “The zeal of your house has consumed me”; sometimes for love, as in: “The Lord has been zealous for his people.” Likewise, “to envy” may mean either to be jealous, to imitate, or to desire, as the Apostle says: “Be zealous for the better spiritual gifts” [Col. 0672C].

**“For they will wither quickly like grass.”** You ought not to desire the flourishing of the wicked because they will quickly wither—that is, both they and their flourishing will fail—like grass, which is in flower today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven. They will quickly fall, like garden vegetables, that is, they will quickly fall; “vegetables” is the proper name for certain plants among herbs.

What is properly called a vegetable among herbs creeps along the ground; because it has no deep root, it remains green in winter and withers in summer. Trees, however, because they have deep roots, even if they appear dry in winter, put forth leaves, blossom, and bear fruit when summer comes.

The wicked are compared to vegetables because they do not have the deep root of charity. They flourish in winter, that is, in the present age, which is called winter because of the storms of tribulation and the waves of bitterness. When summer comes—when the true sun rises at midday and appears in the majesty of the Father of angels—then they will wither, because they will be handed over to eternal flames [Col. 0672D].

The just, however, are comparable to trees because they have the deep root of charity. Now, in winter, they wither, according to the saying: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” But in the summer mentioned above they will be adorned with the ornaments of leaves, that is, of good works, and enriched with the abundance of fruits, that is, with a multitude of rewards.

**“Hope in the Lord.”** Since the flourishing of the wicked will vanish so quickly, it is as though he said: Do not envy that flourishing, but hope only in the Lord and not in the world; and do whatever good you can, not the iniquity of those who do evil.

Doing this, “dwell in the land,” that is, in the Church, which is called well-cultivated land. Do not abandon ecclesiastical institutions but observe them, because outside the Catholic Church there is no place for the true sacrifice.

Or understand it in this way: By doing good, dwell in the land, that is, cultivate your own flesh, so that eventually you may receive it glorified; and thus you will be nourished by the riches of that land [Col. 0673A]. If you consider the Church, the riches of this land are its Lord and its God. If you consider our flesh, its riches will be immortality and freedom from suffering.

**“Delight in the Lord.”** If by “land” you understood the Church, then this is an explanation of what its riches are, namely the Lord; therefore delight only in the Lord.

But if by “land” you understand human flesh, the passage is connected in this way: Hope in the Lord and, by hoping, delight in the Lord. Whatever you do, do it for the Lord with joy, not with sadness, because “God loves a cheerful giver.”

Then the Lord will give you your requests—not necessarily those of the flesh, but those of your heart; that is, he will fulfill all your spiritual petitions.

For this to happen, “reveal your way to the Lord,” that is, devote yourself to works that are worthy of being revealed to the Lord. Whether we wish it or not, our good and evil works are revealed to the Lord with respect to his knowledge; but only good works are revealed to him with respect to his approval.

For this reason it is said: “Reveal your way to the Lord,” that is, your life—what you suffer, why you groan, and what you desire [Col. 0673B]. You suffer because you see that the flesh desires against the spirit. You desire the same thing expressed in the words: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ.”

Reveal this to the Lord through the affection of your heart, and hope firmly, because through him you will be freed. He himself, and no other, will do for you what follows: he will bring forth your justice, that is, your faith, which hopes for what is not seen and is now hidden. According to the saying: “Beloved, we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be.”

That faith, I say, he will bring forth through reward as into the light, that is, into manifest knowledge—when you receive what you believed without seeing. And “your judgment,” that is, your discernment—namely, that you preferred to follow poor Christ rather than the rich world—he will bring forth not simply into light but as into the light of midday, that is, into the clearest possible knowledge [Col. 0673C], through reward.

This judgment is a greater merit than faith by itself, because there are some who are faithful and will be saved but do not possess this judgment, namely the judgment by which they abandon the world and follow Christ.

He will indeed bring it forth at last. But what will happen in the meantime? It is necessary, as he says, to suffer and be saddened. However greatly you may suffer, be subject to the Lord; that is, let your entire being and your life consist in submitting to the Lord’s commandments. In submitting, pray to him that you may not fail in the vineyard, so that you may rejoice when you receive the coin at evening.

**“Do not envy.”** It is as though he said: Since such great hope will be given to you in the future, do not envy here—that is, do not become angry and indignant at him, namely at the wicked man who prospers in his way, in this present life. You suffer on the journey, but you will rejoice when you arrive. He has prosperity on the journey, but at his arrival there will be every kind of hardship.

Do not, I say, envy him, namely the man who commits injustices, that is, sins, as though by necessity—not by nature, but because “the prosperity of fools destroys them.” It is as though he said: If you wish to prosper with him, you will act unjustly as he does.

Therefore do not envy him, but cease from anger, so that you do not become angry at the flourishing of that man who commits injustices. “Abandon wrath,” that is, indignation and murmuring against the same man. Wrath gives rise to fury. The meaning is: Let anger or fury over that man’s flourishing not trouble your eye; instead, consult the eye of your faith.

If he had promised you temporal goods, you would have reason to be angry. But if he promised you only heavenly and eternal things, you ought not to be angry; you should await them patiently. Thus I say: Do not envy, lest you become wicked, that is, lest you become one of those who do evil. Otherwise, as it were, he says, I make no such assertion.

You must be exceedingly careful not to become wicked, because all who do evil will be destroyed persistently—that is, they will be placed outside the boundaries of heavenly Jerusalem, or outside the boundaries of their own land, namely their flesh, so that they will not cultivate it well [Col. 0674A].

Conversely, those who do not murmur but endure—that is, patiently await the Lord, not as though he were some deceiver but as the truth itself, not as though he were weak but as the Almighty—will inherit the land, or Jerusalem, which is the land of the living, or their own flesh glorified with immortality and freedom from suffering.

Therefore the Lord must still be awaited, but let no one think the wait long, because it will be brief. The time is short. For if we run through all the chronicles, we shall find that Adam was expelled from paradise, as it were, yesterday. If what has preceded us is so short, what follows will be much shorter.

It will be brief, I say, and after that brief time the sinner will no longer exist—not because he will utterly cease to be, but because he will have no usefulness. Now the wicked man is useful to the pious; but just as a file has no place on smoothed iron, so after the completion of the just there will be no place for the wicked.

In the meantime, the Lord makes a scourge of him by which the wicked may fail and the pious advance. Why, then, does the wicked man applaud himself? Is God not making a scourge for himself out of him? He assigns him to a task for me, but trains me for an inheritance.

The sinner will not exist, I say, because if you seek his place—that is, the use he will have then—you will not find it.

Conversely, the meek, who do not murmur but patiently await the Lord, will inherit the land, as was said above. Then they will “delight in the abundance of peace,” because although now they possess whatever peace they have only inwardly, then they will have peace both inwardly and outwardly.

Or understand it in this way: Just as the unmeek—that is, those who do evil—now delight in much gold, much silver, and many such things, so then the Lord himself will be whatever delight can be imagined for his people, because he will be all things in all.

Since he himself is true peace, everything will be peace for them. Thus they will delight in the abundance of peace, that is, in peace multiplied in many ways.

But what will happen in the meantime? It will be necessary to endure much tribulation in order to reach that peace. In the meantime, “the sinner,” that is, any persecutor, “will watch the just man,” that is, will act treacherously against him through deceitful persecution. He will also gnash his teeth at him, that is, pronounce manifest sentences of condemnation in order to crush him.

But what concern is this? None, of course, because “the Lord will laugh at him,” that is, will make him laughable—the sinful man. This truly is mockery: while his iniquity destroys your body, it corrupts his own soul. It makes you approved and him a sinner. Indeed, this truly is mockery: while his iniquity destroys your body, it corrupts his own soul. It makes you approved and him a sinner; and the one whose spirit is always devastated is condemned ever more severely.

The Lord, I say, will laugh at him, because it belongs to him to do so, since the Lord sees that his day will come—the day of reckoning. This reckoning will be twofold: good or evil. He who foresaw the day of Judas the betrayer also foresaw the day of Saul the persecutor: the former’s day for punishment, the latter’s for glory. Judgment was executed upon both: one was destined for the fires of Gehenna, the other was struck down into eternal life.

**“Sinners have unsheathed the sword.”** He appears to explain both things that he said above: the sinner’s hidden and manifest persecution of the just. He first explains the manifest kind in this way: Sinners “unsheathed the sword,” that is, they exercised manifest condemnation against the just. For whoever fights with a sword fights openly.

Here blessed Augustine says: The sinner unsheathes the sword against your body, but does his own heart remain unharmed? He attempts to kill you in the body, but he himself is killed in his mind. He is like someone who thrusts a sword through your body in order to cut another person’s garment.

Sinners, I say, unsheathed the sword, and they also “bent their bow,” that is, prepared hidden snares for the just. With a bow one fights secretly and from a distance.

**“To deceive the poor man.”** He assigns each phrase to its corresponding object [Col. 0675A]. They bent the bow in order secretly to deceive “the poor and needy,” that is, the just man who presumes nothing about himself—by dragging him away and conforming him to themselves.

They unsheathed the sword in order openly to slaughter, that is, to kill, those who are upright of heart, namely the just.

What will happen to them? It is as though he said: Let them receive what they deserve. Let their sword enter their own hearts; that is, let their iniquity rebound upon them. “Let their bow be broken,” that is, let their snares become ineffective.

The meaning is: Let them not wound you inwardly in your mind; rather, let them kill themselves in their souls. If they take away external things, what concern is that? None. For it is better for you, the just man—and for anyone else—to possess that little which they cannot take away, namely faith, hope, and the other virtues, which they regard as little, than to possess the great riches of sinners.

Or, better, it is preferable for you to have only the little that is necessary for food and clothing rather than the many riches of sinners.

This verse may also be connected in another way, if we insert the intervening verse, “Do not envy,” as follows: Since sinners kill themselves, do not envy those who do evil, so as to desire their flourishing.

You ought not to do so, because it is better—that is, more useful—for you, the just man, to follow the little one, namely the humble Christ, than to possess the great riches of sinners.

I say this because “the arms”—that is, the riches, all power, and strength—“of sinners will quickly be broken.” In the meantime, however, the Lord strengthens the just. It is as though he said: Let sinners rage as much as they wish, and as much as they are permitted; nevertheless, nothing will harm you, because the Lord strengthens the just by the example of patience.

For a little while they will suffer, and without faith they will rejoice. And so that you may not fail in this brief time, consider what he endured for you, who had nothing of his own for which he would have had to suffer.

Even if you suffered many things, would you reach such insults and so many temptations? Would you reach those reproaches and injuries? Would you finally reach that insulting garment or crown of thorns? Would you reach the cross? The cross is no longer punishment but glory, because it has passed from the place of tortures to the foreheads of emperors [Col. 0675C]. And since he transformed such great glory into his sufferings, what does he reserve for his faithful? Certainly, something great.

**“The Lord knows the days of the blameless.”** The Lord strengthens the just because he knows—that is, approves—the days of the blameless, namely the times of the just men’s tribulation and affliction, however much the wicked reject and disparage them.

And because the Lord knows their days, their inheritance—whether the heavenly Jerusalem or their glorified flesh—will be their inheritance forever, that is, eternally.

**“They will not be confounded in the evil time.”** Their inheritance will truly be eternal because they will not be confounded, that is, they will not suffer eternal confusion, “in the evil time,” namely on the day of examination and distress so far as the wicked are concerned. Rather, they will receive that inheritance when it is said: “Come, blessed of my Father.”

In the meantime, even now, they will be filled inwardly with heavenly joy, as much as is possible in “the days of famine,” that is, in the present life, where the fullness perceived by the just, for which they hunger, cannot yet be fully attained.

And truly the just will not be confounded in the future, because only sinners will perish—not because they will cease to exist, but because they will be deprived of their inheritance.

The enemies of the Lord. The sinners will truly perish, because all the enemies of the Lord will utterly fail, that is, they will suffer eternal failure—which I say truly, that is, in reality. This will not be long delayed, but will happen immediately, as soon as they have been honored, that is, raised and exalted by honors and wealth; at once they will fail like smoke. For the higher smoke rises, the more it dissipates; likewise, the greater the exaltation of the wicked now, the heavier their future downfall will be. Their exultation will indeed be brief, but their condemnation will be eternal.

The sinner will borrow. Sinners will deservedly perish, because the sinner will borrow, that is, he receives a loan from the Lord—not only that he exists, but also that he is a human being, that he is sound in his faculties and healthy in body, and that he is wealthy, and that he possesses reason by which he can praise God and give thanks. Yet he will not repay this loan, because he praises God neither inwardly nor outwardly, and therefore he will deservedly perish. The righteous, however, will not be put to shame but will deservedly be saved, because the righteous continually shows mercy to his own soul by doing good. Hence Solomon says: “Have mercy on your soul, and you will be pleasing to the Lord.” But he shows mercy to his own soul who does not receive his soul in vain, that is, who does not indulge his soul in vanities; rather, he is angry with his own soul and is thereby even moved to repentance. This is the first mercy that each person ought first to show his own soul; afterward, it remains to help others as well.

The righteous, I say, shows mercy and will repay, that is, he will repay to the utmost of his ability the loan that he received from the Lord, giving thanks inwardly and outwardly. The Gallican translation has “He lends at interest,” which is explained as follows: “He shows mercy, I say, and lends at interest,” that is, he gives whatever he can, inwardly and outwardly, for God. This is to lend at interest, because he will receive a hundredfold of what he gives once over.

Let moneylenders not rejoice, however. For the Lord does not want you to be a moneylender; through his prophet he describes among his own soldiers the man who did not give his money at interest; and yet that same Lord commands you to be a moneylender, because he says in the Gospel: “If you lend at interest, you will have no hope”; and again: “Unless you lend at interest, you will have no hope.” He forbids being a moneylender and wants one to be a moneylender. He forbids you to lend money to human beings, or anything else in order to receive more by giving it, because if you do this, you will be a moneylender who is not to be praised but condemned. He therefore commands you to lend to God: give earthly things and receive heavenly things; give little and receive much; give earth and receive heaven. If you do this, you will be a moneylender who is not to be blamed but praised.

Because those who bless will inherit the earth. The righteous will truly repay, that is, he will repay to the Lord the loan he received, because the righteous will bless him, that is, they will magnify and exalt him by giving him thanks and offering themselves as an example to others. Therefore those who bless him will inherit the earth, as was said above; but sinners do not repay the loan to the Lord, because they curse him. Hence those who curse him will perish utterly, that is, they will perish, separated from that inheritance.

With the Lord. The righteous do indeed bless the Lord, but they do not possess this from themselves; they possess it from the Lord himself, because the steps—that is, the affections and works—of a human being are directed entirely by the Lord, as another translation has it. Or, according to this translation, we may say: The fact that a person’s steps are directed belongs to God, not to the person. It is not always within a person’s power to direct his own steps; for human steps would be crooked and our paths bent if the Lord had not directed us. But he directed our steps in this way: he came, called us, justified us, redeemed us, poured out his own blood, and gave this price.

For it was little that he had made you a human being, unless he himself became human for your sake. Having become human, he endured every kind of temporal hardship to instruct you, so that you too might endure these sorrows and hardships and thereby reach eternal joys. Endure labor in order to receive your reward, because truly eternal labor would have to be endured for eternal rest. But if you were to labor eternally, when would you reach eternal rest? Surely never. Therefore our labor is temporal, and for that reason it must be endured.

The steps, I say, are directed by the Lord; therefore whoever is truly human will wish to follow his way, that is, the Lord’s way. Whoever is truly a Christian ought to keep the way of Christ, because otherwise he will not be able to reach the destination toward which he is traveling.

When he falls, he will not be shattered. The Lord will truly direct his steps, because the one directed by him will not be inwardly shattered when he falls, that is, when the same thing is seen outwardly. No fall will be for his destruction, but rather for his exaltation, according to the saying: “The righteous falls seven times,” that is, the righteous is afflicted by tribulation in every way. For the number seven is perfect, and therefore “seven times” signifies complete tribulation. Yet he rises again, because tribulation is not for his depression but for his raising up. He will therefore not be shattered, because the Lord places his hand beneath him and strengthens him by the example of his own endurance.

I was young, and indeed I have grown old. Just as in the preceding psalm you understood “the wicked” as referring to the whole race of evildoers about which he was speaking, so understand “the righteous” as the one who speaks here on behalf of the body of the righteous. The verse itself requires this, and it may be connected as follows: Truly the Lord places his hand beneath the one whom he directs—that is, the righteous—because he does not abandon the righteous now, nor has he abandoned him from the time when he first became righteous.

Neither in my youth nor in my old age have I seen the righteous abandoned, because I was young. This is evident from the words: “Indeed I have grown old,” meaning “because I have grown old.” This righteous person, who speaks here on behalf of others, was young in relation to the earlier righteous, who were as if in their youth because they first came to faith; he has now become old in relation to those who come in this later age. The meaning is that neither among the earlier righteous nor among the later righteous can anyone be found whom the Lord has abandoned rather than strengthened.

“I have not seen,” he says, “the righteous abandoned, nor have I seen his offspring seeking bread,” that is, I have never seen the imitators of that righteous person seeking bread or lacking bread—not bread for the stomach, but the bread of the word, of which it is said: “Man does not live by bread alone,” and what follows. The righteous truly does not lack that bread, because he always has it in his heart or on his lips, according to the saying: “He will meditate on his law day and night.”

He eats this bread when he reads or hears one of God’s commandments; he chews it again when he reflects on what he has read or heard, so as to make it fruitful for himself. Hence Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise, but a fool swallows it.” Fools do this. Therefore they are comparable to animals that do not chew the cud, and for this reason are unclean. The righteous, however, will not forget what he has read and heard but will chew it again; therefore he is a clean animal. Solomon says the same thing about this: “And holy thought will save you.”

All day long he shows mercy and lends. The offspring of the righteous truly does not lack bread, because all day long, that is, continually, he shows mercy to his own soul while either eating or chewing that bread. He also lends, that is, he does whatever good he can for others by word and deed; and thus, even if he is poor, he is nevertheless rich. One must not look at an empty chest but at a conscience full of God; not at outward resources but at inward charity, that is, good will, which is never idle. For if it does not give money, it gives counsel, assistance, and itself—or at least a good intention.

He shows mercy, I say, and lends; therefore his offspring, that is, his works, will be in blessing, that is, in multiplication with respect to reward, because he will receive a hundredfold for each thing. Do not, then, envy those who do evil, whoever you are, so that your offspring may be in blessing; rather, turn away from evil. Or the passage may be connected simply in this way: Since the offspring of the righteous will nevertheless be in blessing, therefore, whoever desires that blessing, turn away from every evil and do whatever good you can, and do it without murmuring—that is, do not think there is loss in giving, but rather in keeping. What you have given you have not lost; what you have kept, you have lost.

Pay attention, then, to God saying: “Make for yourselves purses that do not decay and treasures that do not fail in heaven, where no thief approaches.” And dwell forever and ever. As if he said: If you turn away from evil and do good, then you will dwell in the heavenly inheritance forever and ever, that is, eternally.

Because the Lord loves judgment. I therefore say that this must be done without murmuring, because the Lord loves to make judgment, that is, he will be a careful examiner. This is indicated by the word “loves,” distinguishing between those who murmur while doing good and those who do not murmur. In that judgment he will not abandon his saints, namely, those who do good from the heart and not with murmuring, because they will be preserved forever.

This verse may also be connected in the following manner: I therefore say, “Turn away from evil and do good,” because the Lord loves such judgment, that is, such discernment—namely, that each person should turn away from evil and do good—and he will not abandon his saints who discern in this way forever.

It may be connected in a third way as well: “Turn away from evil and do good,” but in doing these things you will suffer many adversities. Do not be concerned or grieved, however, because the Lord loves such judgment to be exercised upon his own. He chastises every son whom he receives, and he did not spare even his own Son, in whom he found nothing blameworthy.

Although he may seem to abandon his saints, he does not thereby abandon them; rather, they will be preserved forever. The unrighteous, however, will not be preserved, because they will be punished eternally. This is because the offspring of the wicked will perish, that is, the works of those unrighteous people will perish—not with respect to punishment, but with respect to good reward.

The righteous, however, will not be punished but will be preserved, as was said above, because they will inherit—that is, they will receive as an inheritance—the earth, whether the heavenly Jerusalem or their glorified flesh. And lest he open the breast of greed to the avaricious person, who would immediately suppose that an earthly inheritance is promised here and would thereby strive toward righteousness, he explains what earth they will receive.

As if he said: I say that they will inherit the earth, but not for an hour, as they might possess some earthly property; rather, they will dwell in it forever and ever, that is, eternally. And they will be above it, that is, they will be its possessors. This concerns the heavenly homeland. With respect to the flesh, the meaning is as follows: They will dwell in such a way that they will be above it, that is, the spirit will always be superior to the flesh. For here, although the spirit is naturally superior to the flesh, it is often subject to the flesh, namely, when it is deceived by carnal pleasure.

[Col. 0678C] The mouth of the righteous will meditate on wisdom. The righteous will deservedly inherit the earth, because they continually meditate on wisdom, speak it, and retain God’s law in their hearts. This is expressed as follows: “The mouth of the righteous will meditate on wisdom,” that is, he continually speaks to himself what pertains to wisdom, that is, to a good life—a life that contends with vices and maintains peace with excellent conduct.

And his tongue, that is, the tongue of the righteous, will speak of every judgment to others, that is, everything that truly ought to be judged and held fast. Such a person does not belong to those of whom it is said: “This people honors me with their lips,” because God’s law is not merely in his mouth but in his heart, as in the saying: “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another.” Since he is such a person, his steps, that is, his affections, will not be overcome, because he will not sin even in thought.

The sinner watches the righteous. As if he said: Therefore let the righteous remain secure among the ungodly and the unrighteous. What harm can the ungodly do to him? None at all. The sinner does indeed watch the righteous, but the Lord does not abandon him.

This verse may also be connected in another way, so that, just as what preceded was a reason concerning the righteous, this too may be a reason concerning the unrighteous. As if he said: The unrighteous will deservedly be punished, because the sinner watches the righteous in order to ambush him; and he does this because he seeks to kill him, that is, to devour him completely, sometimes deceitfully and sometimes violently.

But what concern is this? None, I say, because the Lord will not abandon him, namely, the righteous, even if he is outwardly delivered into the hands of the sinner. For although the enemy may rule over the righteous person’s flesh, according to the blessed Job: “The earth has been handed over to the hands of sinners,” nevertheless his spirit will be saved.

The Lord will not abandon the righteous, I say, nor will he condemn him; rather, he will exalt him when judgment takes place in the future, that is, when a judgment of condemnation is rendered against the ungodly, for the honor of the righteous. Conversely, the Lord will not condemn the righteous even when he is judged in the present by that ungodly person concerning the godly person, and when the godly person suffers punishment according to the will of the ungodly. For even if the godly person then seems to be condemned, he is not truly condemned: if he receives a sentence from an inferior judge, he will receive a crown from the superior one.

Therefore do not envy those who do evil, but rather wait for the Lord and keep his ways. This continuation may also be made: I said that the Lord will not abandon the righteous but will save him. Yet let none of you seek this salvation in the present, because this is still the time of labor, not yet of reward. Therefore patiently await the Lord, who will finally appear as the one who pays what he owes, the one whom you already hold as your debtor.

Do not wait with slack hands and weakened knees, but keep his way, that is, his works or commandments. Thus, when he comes, he will exalt you—not with some temporal dignity, but so that you may receive the land of the living as an inheritance, that is, for an eternal inheritance. You will see this land when the sinners have perished. While they stand far away on the left, you will be with the other righteous on the right, to whom it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father”; but to them: “Go, accursed,” and so forth.

I saw the ungodly. The sinners will truly perish, because I have already foreseen their destruction. For he is as if saying: I have already entered in thought into the sanctuary of God and considered their final destiny.

This is how it appears in the book: “I saw,” that is, I considered, “the ungodly in this world, exalted above many and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon,” that is, raised in the manner of the highest in all worldly glory, who are signified by the cedars of Lebanon. Having seen this, I passed beyond these temporal things in my mind, in order to see his final destiny. And behold, the ungodly was no more—not that he did not exist at all, but because he was as though he did not exist.

Therefore I say that he was no more, because he had no place. For I sought him, and his place was not found, that is, no use or purpose belonging to him was found. Therefore do not envy, but keep innocence.

Or the passage may simply be connected as follows: Since the ungodly will have no place in the future, therefore, in order that you may have a place, keep innocence. Do not steal; do not act unjustly in order to acquire money and thereby lose innocence. Rather, lose money in order to acquire innocence.

[Col. 0679C] And behold equity, that is, what it is equitable for you to see in yourself—namely, understand that whatever you suffer, you suffer justly. Or “behold equity” may mean: understand that you must labor now in the vineyard so that you may receive your reward in the evening. For no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully.

You ought both to keep and to behold these things, because the peaceful person—that is, the person who does not murmur but keeps innocence and beholds equity—has a remainder, that is, things to come and later things. And although his earlier circumstances seem dry, his later circumstances will be rich.

But the unrighteous. There will truly be no place for the ungodly, because the unrighteous will perish utterly, that is, they will perish exceedingly. Together, that is, both in body and in soul. They will perish because the remainder of the ungodly, that is, the future state of those unrighteous people, will not merely fail to exist; it will perish, that is, it will be as though it did not exist. For however rich their former state may be, their later state will nevertheless be exceedingly dry.

But the salvation of the righteous. The unrighteous will indeed perish, but the righteous will not perish, because salvation from the Lord will continually belong to the righteous. He proves this by its several aspects: even in the time of tribulation—that is, in the present life, which is full of distress and tribulation—the Lord will be their protector, that is, the protector of the righteous, because he will be a shield for them against the fiery darts of the evil one.

He will help them in perfecting good works; he will free them from hindrance, so that they do not fail; and he will free them in such a way that he will completely rescue them from sinners, that is, from every perplexity and conformity to sinners. Thus at last he will save them with true and eternal salvation. This is because they hoped in him, that is, because they did not murmur about the prosperity of the wicked, but preferred to be with the Lord in hope rather than with them in possession.

## ON PSALM XXXVII

A Psalm of David, for the commemoration of the Sabbath day.

### ARGUMENT

Hezekiah, being ill, implores the Lord. Alternatively, a confession of patience and a virtue leading to salvation. Read Job.

### EXPLANATION

[Col. 0680A]

By saying “for the commemoration,” this title declares to us that, since we are entirely unable to avoid sin, we should at least restrain ourselves from frequent sin by always keeping this before the eyes of our mind, as he says elsewhere: “And my sin is always before me.”

As for its explanation in relation to the Sabbath: every penitent person, amid the wounds of his sins, ought always to retain the memory of eternal rest. Some apply this psalm to the history of the blessed Job, but Jerome thinks that it was sung by some penitent person, or mystically from the person of the Lord the Savior, at the time of his Passion.

This psalm of the penitent is divided into four sections. In the first, a penitential life moves the mercy of the gracious Judge. In the second, he says that his body has been furrowed by blows and his soul wounded by the reproaches of his friends. In the third, healing medicine is added, when he testifies that he has entrusted his entire hope to the Lord amid adversities, and declares himself ready for scourges and deserving more than he suffers. In the fourth, [Col. 0680B] delivered from every danger, he professes God to be the author of his salvation.

### COMMENTARY

Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger. The title is as follows: “A psalm for David himself, in remembrance of the Sabbath.” The Sabbath is rest, and it is understood as rest because the Sabbath is said to be the time when we cease from bodily labor. Our rest signifies that true rest which we had in the first Adam and lost through him, and which we received through the second Adam, that is, Christ—if not yet in reality, at least in hope. For we have been saved in hope, awaiting the redemption of our body.

A certain person, therefore, grieving and mourning in this psalm remembers this Sabbath, that is, this rest. The title calls him not simply David but “David himself.” This is because nowhere do we read that the blessed prophet David remembered the Sabbath according to the observance of the Jews. They observed the Sabbath because it was not something to be remembered but something to be observed; it necessarily came among the seven days. No one remembers anything except what is absent.

What, then, does this remembrance of the Sabbath mean, which takes place with such great pain, such great sorrow, such great groaning, and such great weeping? Or what benefit does it bring? A great one, I say, because blessed is whoever is so miserable. Hence in the Gospel the Lord calls certain people who groan and weep blessed.

Let us therefore understand here as well someone remembering such a Sabbath, some unknown person mourning—and would that we were he! Here indeed is someone grieving, mourning, remembering the Sabbath. For the Sabbath is rest. Without doubt, the person who remembers the Sabbath in this way was in a certain state of unrest. He therefore narrates the unrest he was suffering and commends it to God, fearing something more serious than the condition in which he found himself.

That he is in an evil state he says openly, and there is no need for an interpreter, suspicion, or conjecture. What evil he is in cannot be doubted from his words; there is no need to investigate, but only to understand what he says. Indeed, unless he feared an evil more serious than the one in which he was, he would never have begun in this way: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,” and so forth.

It must be understood that some will be rebuked by the Lord in the future, while others will be chastised in anger. Those will be rebuked in fury who either did not have Christ as their foundation—concerning which the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ”—or, if they had him, built nothing good upon him.

To rebuke is to convict someone by accusing him. Such people will, as it were, be rebuked when the Lord reproaches them: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and other things of this kind. Condemnation normally follows accusation. Likewise, having been convicted by such an accusation, he will condemn them in his fury, that is, by a terrifying and strict divine sentence, when it is said to them: “Go, accursed,” and so forth.

Fearing these more serious things, the person speaking here in this psalm—apart from the present life, whose countless evils he laments—groans and prays in this way. As if he said: It is destined, Lord, that you will rebuke some people in your fury. Therefore I ask you: do not rebuke me in your fury, that is, do not allow me to be among those who will be rebuked in your fury, as was said above.

It is also destined that some will be chastised in your anger. Therefore, Lord, scourge me, cut me, burn me, purify me here, so that you may not then chastise me in your anger. Those are chastised in God’s anger who have Christ as their foundation but build upon it not only gold, silver, and precious stones, but also mix in wood, hay, and straw, that is, commit certain venial sins, some more serious and others lighter.

It is therefore necessary that such people be chastised in anger, that is, that they be placed for the time being in the fire of purgatory before the day of judgment, so that whatever is unclean in them may be burned away by it, and so that at last they may be found worthy to be among those who will be crowned on the right.

Nor does this person fear that correction without reason, because he considers it more grievous than anything ever suffered by robbers, holy martyrs, or anything more severe that a human being could imagine. But if those whom we mentioned above were to build upon the foundation only gold, silver, and precious stones, that is, good works, then they would fear neither the fire that will burn the ungodly eternally nor the fire that will chastise the godly.

It must also be understood that some of the saints—as the Gospel testifies—do not come into judgment but pass from death to life. For even if they build some straw, that is, commit minor sins, these are so slight that the fire of tribulation which they suffer here, or even the punishment of death, completely burns them away. Since such people contain nothing in which the fire can find its own material, as soon as they are separated from the body they pass into eternal life. Conversely, some of the wicked immediately incur eternal punishments.

For your arrows. Therefore, Lord, I ask you not to rebuke or chastise me in the future, because there are many and great things that I suffer in the present. Therefore, I ask that it be enough for you to have inflicted punishments upon me here. He begins to enumerate these things, satisfying the Lord and offering up what he suffers so that he may not suffer more grievous things, saying:

“For your arrows are fastened in me.” He calls the arrows God’s punishments, that is, all the penalties and miseries that we suffer inwardly or outwardly. We contracted all these miseries through the transgression of our first parent, Adam. Hence we bear a mortal body full of temptations and anxieties, subject to bodily pains and bound to necessities. Even when it is healthy, it is changeable and weak.

Why else would this person say, “There is no health in my flesh,” unless health—as the health of this life is called—were not true health to those who understand rightly and remember the Sabbath, but rather a great infirmity? For if it were health, it would not be corrupted so easily by natural illness, hunger, thirst, and other things of this kind. These things are called natural because what was the punishment of sin in Adam is nature in us. Hence the Apostle says: “For you were once by nature children of wrath.”

Let us now return to the literal sense. “Your arrows,” I say, “not one but many, are fastened in me.” And with these arrows you have strengthened your hand upon me, that is, you have displayed a firm and continual power over me, because I suffer and have suffered punishment for sin without interruption. This is said by analogy with some master who beats someone and, as it were, keeps his hand upon the person whom he holds beneath a continual rod.

There is no health in my flesh. You truly fastened arrows in me, because you did so inwardly and outwardly. There is no true health in my flesh, as was said above, and this proceeds from the face, that is, from the presence of your anger, because by this the anger you held against Adam, the transgressor of the law, is represented.

There is also no peace in my bones, that is, there is no firmness in the virtues, which are the bones, or supports, of my soul. This too proceeds from the face, that is, from the presence of my sins, because by this the sin of disobedience is also represented, which Adam committed principally and which all his posterity committed in him.

This one sin is spoken of in the plural as “sins,” because it made Adam himself guilty of many crimes. It must also be understood that the voice of the head speaks in the psalm sometimes for itself and sometimes for its members. Although there is no distinction of persons here, there is nevertheless a distinction of dignities.

Here is the head that saves and the body that is saved; the head displaying mercy and the body, as it were, lamenting misery; the head for cleansing and the body for confessing. How, then, does the one in whom there was no sin say, “because of the presence of my sins”? He says this because he speaks these words, as well as the others mentioned above, in the person of his members.

Nor is it surprising that those have one voice whose flesh is one. Hence the Apostle says: “The two will be one flesh. This mystery is great, but I am speaking with reference to Christ and the Church.” Therefore, because of their great closeness, the head does not separate the body from itself, making the sins of the members its own, since he himself also shared in their punishment. He does this so that the body may not separate the head from itself in suffering, but rather make his suffering its own.

[Col. 0682B] For my iniquities. I rightly said “my sins,” because I am at fault—not you, Lord, nor anything that was made, nor anything else—because my iniquities, that is, my disobedience and transgressions, which I committed in Adam, have risen above my head, that is, have prevailed over my head and enveloped it.

For I raised my head against you, while iniquity cast it down. Hence it is said elsewhere: “His pain will return upon his head, and his iniquity will descend upon his crown.” Here “head” is understood as the more noble part, namely the soul, which was truly depressed through disobedience because it lost the knowledge of the true light.

“My iniquities,” I say, “have risen above me, and they have grown heavy upon me,” that is, they have oppressed my mind as a heavy burden oppresses someone. Just as that person cannot raise himself up, so my mind cannot raise itself to the pure contemplation of truth. All these things refer to the members, as do what follows.

My scars have become foul and have rotted. My iniquities, I say, have grown heavy upon me; my iniquities have risen above my head. Therefore my scars have also become corrupt, and so corrupt that they have even rotted, that is, become rotten. Or “they have rotted” means “they have emitted a stench,” according to another translation.

Scars arise from healed wounds. In us there were wounds from Adam’s transgression and from our own actual sins. These wounds were healed and, as it were, formed scars through faith and the grace of baptism. But because of our weakness it happens that no one is so perfect that at some time he does not slip into sin through another actual offense.

Therefore the scars that were previously healthy become corrupt and foul, or rot. For even if the things committed by perfect people who remember the delightful fragrance of the Sabbath are very slight, they nevertheless seem foul and abominable to them. No one understands how delightful the fragrance of the Sabbath is unless the stench of sin is abominable to him.

“My scars,” I say, “have become corrupt,” and this proceeds from the face, that is, from the presence of my foolishness, because by this my foolishness is represented. You wanted me to be wise, and you taught me true wisdom, saying: “You may eat from every tree of paradise, but you shall not eat from the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil.” I, however, made myself foolish, because I consented to the serpent rather than to you.

I have become miserable. As if he said: Because even my scars have become corrupt, therefore I have become miserable, that is, full of many miseries. And I who raised myself up through pride have been bent down, that is, humbled through punishment—and this to the end of my bending, that is, with complete abasement.

Or I have been bent down in such a way that my bending will last until the end, that is, until one reaches the Sabbath.
