Hence I became miserable and bent down: all day long, that is, continually, I entered and went out, that is, I lived in this present life, which is an entrance into the future life, being saddened—that is, saddened inwardly and outwardly at once—remembering the Sabbath but not yet possessing it.

For my loins, and so forth. I am rightly not merely sad but saddened, because there is nothing good for me inwardly or outwardly. My loins are filled with illusions, that is, my soul is filled with vanities. “Loins” are understood as pleasures; pleasures, however, are inward. Therefore the soul, which is inward, is signified by the loins.

He calls those vanities and phantasms “illusions” that continually intrude upon us both when we are thinking and when we are praying. “My loins,” I say, “are full of illusions,” and there is no true health in my flesh, as was said above.

The meaning is: It is no wonder that this person is saddened, because he has no joy from any side. Since the whole human being consists only of flesh and soul, there is vanity in his soul and infirmity in his flesh. Therefore, saddened, he rightly proceeds until the soul strips off vanity and the flesh puts on health.

The soul will not strip off vanity until it finally apprehends truth; nor will the flesh put on health until it strips off infirmity. This will finally happen when mortality puts on immortality and corruption puts on incorruption.

I am afflicted and humbled. He repeats what he said above, namely, that he has become miserable, as though this had been established by the causes he has added. As if he said: Because there is vanity in my soul and infirmity in my flesh, therefore I am afflicted, that is, full of miseries; and I am exceedingly humbled, because I have been humbled not for an hour but until the end, as was said above.

No one understands this excessive humiliation except the person who considers the immeasurable height of the Sabbath. “I am afflicted,” I say, “and exceedingly humbled”; therefore I was always roaring, that is, I uttered toward the Lord the roar of the strongest earnestness, proceeding from the groaning of my heart.

One groaning belongs to the flesh, another to the heart. The groaning of the flesh is produced by temporal things, and it is known to human beings because it makes itself known outwardly. The groaning of the heart, however, is that by which holy men appeal inwardly; it is hidden from human beings, but manifest to God alone, to whom every intention of the soul is open and every heart speaks.

Because it is known to God alone, he therefore adds: “Lord, all my desire,” that is, what I desire while groaning in this way, “is before you,” not before human beings, who do not see the heart. Therefore you know my desire, because my groaning, which is hidden from human beings, is not hidden from you; rather, it is manifest to you.

Our desire is our prayer. If continual desire is continual prayer, then if you do not cease desiring, you do not cease praying; for continual desire is a continual voice. You will be silent if you cease to love. Hence the Lord says of certain silent people: “Because iniquity will abound, charity will grow cold.” The coldness of charity is the silence of the heart; the fervor of charity is the cry of the heart.

If charity always remains, you always cry out; if you always cry out, you always desire; if you always desire, you remember the Sabbath; and if you remember the Sabbath, your groaning is not hidden from the Lord.

[Col. 0683D] My heart is troubled. As though someone were asking, “Where does this groaning come from?”—from this, namely, that my heart is troubled, that is, entirely disturbed. How many and how insignificant are the things that trouble the human heart! A lion roars, a robber attacks, the earth trembles, and the heart is thrown into confusion, because anxiety is inflicted from every side. This happens because the strength—that is, the steadfastness—which we possessed in our first parent while he remained in the fullness of virtues, abandoned us when he transgressed. For if strength had not abandoned us, whatever unusual event occurred, our heart would not fear it. Hence it is rightly said here: “My heart is troubled,” because my strength abandons me.

And because the light of my eyes—namely, of my inner eyes—is not with me, I say “is not with me” because that light itself, the true and worthy light, is not with me. For God himself is our light, and he is the wisdom of God in which Adam used to rejoice while he remained obedient; but by offending, he withdrew into the shadow and hid among the trees of paradise, because he no longer possessed the light in which he had previously rejoiced.

But the one for whom the head speaks here, already redeemed, confessing, and placed within the body of Christ, says that the light is not with him. Nevertheless, he possesses the light of faith, in accordance with the saying: “Beloved, we are children of God.” But that light of which it is subsequently said, “But it has not yet appeared what we shall be; when it appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is”—that light, I say, he does not yet possess, because this is the voice of those journeying abroad, not yet established in their homeland. For while we are in the body, we are away from the Lord, and for as long as this continues we do not possess that true light. Yet at last, if we love Christ here, we shall truly possess it. For he himself says: “If anyone loves me, he will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”

My friends and my neighbors. Up to this point the head has spoken on behalf of the members; now, however, he speaks on his own behalf. What he has said so far is something each person suffers from himself, through the punishment of sin; but what follows he suffers from those among whom he lives. And just as the head did not separate himself from the members in what he suffered within himself, so neither should the members separate themselves from the head in what he suffers externally from persecutors. Rather, just as he made our sins his own, so let us make his suffering our own.

The passage is connected in this way: “I said that the light of the inner eyes is not with me in my members. And in order that this light might be restored, I became obedient to the Father unto death. In this obedience, my friends—not true friends, but those who pretended at first to be friends, saying, ‘Good Teacher, we know that you have come from God’—and my neighbors, namely the Jews, from whose loins I came, did the following. What did they do? The friends indeed stood against me in my condemnation, while the neighbors approached bodily, though they were far away in mind. They came sufficiently near when they lifted him up upon the cross.

“And not only did the friends and neighbors stand against me, but those who had previously been beside me—that is, those whom I had previously taught and kept around me, namely the apostles—stood far away, because they abandoned him and fled. In the midst of these things, those who sought my life used force against me—not according to the truth, but according to their opinion—when they seized and bound me.

“Elsewhere the Lord rebukes those who do not seek his life, when he says, ‘There is no one who seeks my life’; here, however, he rebukes those who do seek it, which no one who offers resistance can fail to understand. There he rebukes those who do not seek it for imitation; here he rebukes those who seek it for condemnation.

“And those who sought evil. They used force against me, I say; and, in order that they might do so opportunely, those who sought evils to bring against me—that is, for my condemnation—did so because they could not find any. Many spoke of death while tempting him, saying, ‘We know that you have come from God, Teacher’; and even in that death, when they bribed the soldiers so that they might conceal and falsify his resurrection.”

But I. They, I say, spoke vanity against me; but I, as though I were deaf, did not hear—not because he truly did not hear, but because he answered them nothing, as though he did not hear. And I was like a mute man who does not open his mouth, saying nothing in reply. Hence it is said: “Like a sheep led to the slaughter,” and so forth.

And I became like a man. This has been repeated because of what is added, namely, “and I became like one who has no rebukes in his mouth.” This does not mean that he had many things with which to contradict them or in which to rebuke them—he who had previously rebuked them so sharply and so often—but that he did not wish to contradict or rebuke them because he had come in great humility to be judged, though he was to come in great majesty to judge.

And as though someone were to say, “Why did he not contradict them? Why did he not rebuke them?” he adds the reason, as though saying: “I did not wish to rebuke them because, O Lord, I hoped,” that is, I placed all my hope in you, choosing you alone as avenger and rewarder, in accordance with the saying: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord.”

And because I hoped in you, therefore you, Lord my God, by your will—for you possess power over all things—will hear me by blinding my enemies and raising me from the dead.

Here your head, Christian, admonishes and instructs you: if tribulation ever overtakes you and you seek a defense but no one accepts it, do not be disturbed, nor abandon your case. Instead, preserve patience within, where no one suppresses your cause. For even if false testimony prevails against you among human beings, it has no power with God, before whom your case must be pleaded. Therefore preserve a pure conscience, so that you may worthily say: “For I have hoped in you, O Lord.” Do not fear false witnesses; do not refute wicked accusers.

Because I said. Therefore, Lord, you will hear me because I resolved always both to have patience and to teach patience. For I said—that is, I determined in my heart—that I would preserve patience and, by my example, strengthen my members in patience, lest my enemies—that is, the enemies of my members—should at some time rejoice, that is, should be able to rejoice in their impatience, and, having become superior to me, should greatly rejoice over me—that is, having become superior to my members because an opportunity had been offered them to reproach them.

And lest at some time they should speak great things against me—that is, against my members—when my feet, that is, the affections of my members, have been moved by impatience, just as they once spoke great things when the very feet of my members were moved. This occurred when Peter denied him at the voice of a maidservant, although previously they had often spoken great things.

Behold, here again the head returns to the weakness of the present age and looks toward his feet when he says: “Let them not rejoice over me,” and so forth. For sometimes, as is the condition of our life, our feet are moved and we slip into some sin; then evil tongues rise up against us and rejoice in taunting us on that account. Hence, if they were good, they ought rather to suffer with us; but they belong to those of whom it is said: “Those who afflict,” and so forth.

For I am ready for scourges. I say, “Let them not rejoice exceedingly,” and “Let them not speak great things.” And truly they will not rejoice exceedingly, nor will they speak great things, because I, both in myself and in my members, am ready for scourges—that is, I and my members have been born to endure scourges.

For those for whom eternal life is being prepared must be scourged here. The divine sentence in Solomon is true: “My son, do not despise the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are reproved by him. For whom the Lord loves, he chastises. He scourges every son whom he receives.” Therefore, let them not rejoice exceedingly, nor speak great things. If the son is scourged, an inheritance is being prepared for him.

Indeed, each son must be scourged here to such an extent that he did not spare even his own Son, in whom he found no cause for scourging. I am ready, I say, for scourges, both in myself and in my members.

And my pain—that is, the pain of my members—is always in my sight, that is, in the heart of my members, where they themselves perceive the truth. It is pain not over the medicine, but over the wound; that is, not over the scourge, but over the cause of the scourge, namely sin, because every scourge is medicine for sin.

Human beings grieve over the scourge, not over the cause of the scourge. But the one who speaks here, and those on whose behalf he speaks, are not such people, as he shows below by adding:

For I will declare my iniquity. As though someone were asking, “From where does your pain come?”—not from the scourge, but from the wound, that is, from iniquity. This is evident from the disposition by which I will declare that the iniquity is mine—that is, my members will declare that the iniquity is theirs, by confessing their sin.

And I will not merely declare it by confessing; I will also be solicitous in my members, repenting worthily for sin. For I will consider my sin—that is, I will do whatever must be done to abolish sin. Here he teaches that no one should be secure merely because he confesses his sins, unless he also repents worthily.

These things must be done for sin: let tears flow, let litanies be made, let the hand of the needy be filled. Let the recipient rejoice in what you have given, so that you may rejoice in God’s gift.

But my enemies live. I and my members will indeed consider sin; but my enemies and the enemies of my members neither consider nor will consider sin, because they live—that is, they flourish and rejoice in earthly things, in which they regard their true life as consisting. And because they flourish in this way, they have been strengthened and made powerful to oppress me and my members.

They have multiplied with an evil multiplication—not like the stars of heaven, which pertains only to the good, who increase in glory, but they have multiplied like the sand of the sea, so that they may be barren and fruitless like the sand of the sea.

They are those who hate me and my members unjustly—that is, who have held an unjust hatred against me and against my members. Unjust hatred is to wish evil to one who wishes good for oneself. One who does not return good for good is ungrateful. One who returns evil for evil is not good. But one who returns evil for good is unjust.

Those who repaid evil. He explains unjust hatred. As though he were saying: “They hated me unjustly in this way: they repaid me and my members with evil for good, disparaging us as though stripping away the wings by which we were carried upward. They disparaged me with respect to the unity of divinity, when they said, ‘This man is not from God,’ and similar things; but they disparaged my members with respect to their virtues, calling them evildoers and magicians.

“And they did this for no other reason than that I followed goodness in myself and in my members—that is, I persisted in true obedience—so that I would not apostatize from the Lord even in my will. For this reason they regarded me as opposed to their works.”

Do not abandon me. My enemies hate me and my members; but you, Lord my God, by your will, do not abandon me, the head—that is, do not allow your holy one to see corruption. Nor depart from me—that is, from my members—by permitting them to be corrupted. Rather, attend to my help and to the help of my members, namely, that you may raise me up and bring them to the Sabbath. You, I say, O Lord, who are the God and author of my salvation and of the salvation of my members.

## Psalm XXXVIII

“To the end, for Jeduthun, a song of David.”

## Argument

[Col. 0686C]

Amid the sorrows pressing upon him under Saul, he sang this psalm, which contained more exhortation for the benefit of his hearers than supplication for himself. Alternatively: the prophet rebukes those who possess riches and do not know for whom they will leave them.

## Explanation

The name Jeduthun signifies that this song was sung by his choir. And because Jeduthun is interpreted as “leaping over them,” it signifies one who transcends earthly things in mind and leaps over those who cling to the ground and, bent toward the earth, think about what is below. Dwelling on high in his mind, he philosophizes in a free song about the vanity of the age.

And lest you suppose that this too is a psalm of repentance because it mentions afflictions, he added “a song of David.” Singing belongs to one who rejoices, and sometimes also to one who grieves, but never to one who is repenting. It should be noted that psalms which have “song” in their title always sing out the joy of victory amid adversities.

A song, insofar as it pertains to the art of music, is produced when a choir, exercising its freedom, does not merely sing to the accompaniment of the organ, but exults in the abundance of its voice. A psalm, however, is produced when the human voice ceases and only the striking of the accompanying organ is heard. Hence, mystically, a psalm signifies the act of work, while a song signifies the joy of the mind.

This Jeduthun, a leaper over vices, offers us the form of a just man. In the first part of the psalm he testifies that, for the greatest benefit, he kept silent against enemies lying in wait; he asks to know the end of his life, so that perhaps he may deserve to behold the Lord’s Incarnation even with the eyes of the flesh.

Second, he proves that mortal fear is vain, since all things have been established under the Lord’s power. Third, he asks that harmful sins be forgiven him, so that his life may be brought to a prosperous conclusion.

## Commentary

I said: I will guard my ways. The title is as follows: “To the end, for Jeduthun, a song, to David himself.” As was said at the beginning of the book, Jeduthun was one of the four leaders of song whom David chose to sing before the ark of the Lord when it was brought back.

His name is not placed in the title because this psalm was composed by him, but because the interpretation of his name properly suits this psalm. The title is explained in this way: these words are referred to the end, that is, to Christ, who is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes; they are attributed to David himself, that is, to each more perfect member of the body of Christ.

These words constitute a song, that is, they pertain to joy and gladness, because the person who has truly leaped over all earthly things and laid aside the cause of sadness truly rejoices. His is the voice of this song, I say, sung for Jeduthun—that is, so that we might become Jeduthun—or in the person of each one who is truly Jeduthun.

Blessed Augustine seems to approve this understanding of the psalm’s intention when he says: “Here the voices of one who is called Jeduthun are to be expected and heard, teaching and exhorting us to despise what is below and to disdain all earthly joys. And if each one of us can become Jeduthun, in what he sings he finds himself and hears himself.

“Let us therefore hear the interpretation of this name and seek the understanding of the truth. Jeduthun is interpreted as ‘leaping over them.’ Over whom? Over those who remain below, namely, those who rejoice in all these earthly things. Therefore, if someone has sung while leaping over these things, let him strive to be what he has sung; let him rejoice in being what he has sung.

“This man, who is called ‘leaping over them,’ has leaped over certain people bent toward the earth, clinging to the ground, thinking about what is below, and placing their hope in transitory things. But this leaping is not to be done with feet, wings, or ladders, but only by affection and good will. By these let us walk, ascend, and fly. By these let us leap over all earthly things, setting spiritual joy and sacred delights before us in the divine utterances and the holy Scriptures.

“Let us therefore hear him leaping as he sings, and leaping by singing, saying: ‘When the sinner stood against me, I said: I will guard my ways,’” and so forth.

This Jeduthun, while living among human beings, preaching, exhorting, and rebuking, had said certain things that he ought to repent of and that he could not recall, since it is difficult for anyone not to stumble in speech. The perfect person is one who does not sin in speech.

When this had happened to him, he resolved to keep silent and determined to say nothing. His words show this when he says: “When the sinner,” that is, the unjust slanderer, the contradictor and perverter of words, “stood against me,” contradicting and distorting what I said, “fearing that scandal might arise, I said”—that is, I determined this within myself—“I will guard my ways.” That is, I will apply diligence to my works so that I may not act rashly, in such a way that I do not sin with my tongue—not even sinning in speech.

I placed a guard over my mouth. I resolved this, I say, and carried it out, because I placed guards over my mouth by remaining completely silent. I placed this guard in this way because I became mute, that is, I stood before that sinner as though mute.

And therefore I was humbled, that is, I was regarded as worthless by him. I became so completely silent that I kept entirely silent even about all the good things that ought to have been said. Therefore my pain, which I had previously experienced in speaking and keeping silent, and to which I had applied silence as a remedy, was renewed. For I began to regret more that I had not said what ought to have been said than I had previously regretted saying what ought not to have been said.

My heart grew hot. My pain was renewed, I say, and thus my heart grew hot within me; that is, within myself my heart became fervent and restless. It grew hot for two reasons: because of keeping silent and because of speaking.

For when I saw transgressors, I was wasting away, yet I did not rebuke them. Hence I feared that divine sentence: “You wicked and lazy servant, you did not put my money out at interest, so that when I came I might certainly have demanded it with interest.” And what follows: “May the Lord turn this away from his stewards.”

For behold, with hands and feet bound, the servant is cast into outer darkness—not as one who overturns things in order to destroy, but as one who is lazy in distributing. What, then, will happen to those who have squandered their possessions through luxury, if those who preserved them in laziness are condemned in this way? Much worse, therefore.

My heart grew hot, I say, and in this meditation of mine—that is, in my wavering between the concern to speak and to remain silent—when I was placed among people prepared to slander and desiring to be instructed, fearing that I might scatter pearls before swine and anxious lest I distribute food to fellow servants, the fire within me began to blaze—that is, apart from those earlier alternatives, speaking and keeping silent, a certain desire for higher things began to burn within me, so that I might sigh for that end which, once attained, leaves nothing further to seek, where I might find a remedy for my former anxiety.

I spoke with my tongue. The fire blazed, I say, and in the heat of that fire I spoke with my tongue—that is, with the tongue of one who leaps over earthly things—not with the intention of instructing a hearer, but with the intention of being instructed by one from whom I wished to hear, and from whom inwardly I hear whatever good I hear.

I spoke, I say, this: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end,” the end to which I shall finally come, beyond which nothing further is to be sought. “My end,” that is, an end suitable to me as one who leaps over earthly things—namely, the end that is lacking to me, not the course that is already present.

The Apostle, while running, looked toward this end; that is, he confessed his imperfection, observing one thing in himself and seeking another elsewhere. For he says: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect, brothers; I do not consider myself to have apprehended it. But one thing”—understand, “I will do”—forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead. That is, I follow the intention of my heart toward the prize of the heavenly calling, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. For this is the end.

He said “according to intention,” not according to arrival or attainment. Let us therefore run, let us direct our minds, let us seize it. While he was here, this Jeduthun asked that this end be made known to him, so that he might know what was lacking to him and so that, as leapers over earthly things, they might not remain on the way but might hasten upward with their whole intention. (Thus.)

And the number of my days. “Make my end known to me,” I say, “and also the number of my days”—that is, the number of those days which belonged to me according to my original constitution. Make known to me the number, I say, not the number that does not exist, but the one that does.

For these days are as though they do not exist, since they depart almost before they arrive. And when they arrive, they do not remain, because they immediately pass away. But those days—or rather, that one day—which is without end and without night does not pass away but always remains, because it is preceded by no yesterday and driven forward by no tomorrow.

He calls this day the “number of days,” not because there are many days, but because it contains the span of many days. Make known to me, I say, both my end and the number of my days, so that I may know what is lacking to me—that is, so that I may recognize my imperfection and thus attend more carefully to true perfection.

It is as though he were saying: “Something is still lacking to me as I labor; and as long as I do not receive what is lacking, I continually pursue, according to my intention, the prize of the heavenly calling.” For there is a certain dwelling-place at the end of the race, in which there is a homeland without exile and life without temptation.

I am not yet there; this is what is lacking to me. Therefore I am humbled more by what is lacking than I rejoice over what is present. For those who believe that they possess something while they are here do not receive what is lacking, because they consider what is present to be great. Whoever thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself.

Behold, you have made my days measurable, and so forth. I rightly say what is lacking to me. For behold what is lacking to me: you, Lord, have made those days that ought to have been mine—namely, immeasurable and unfailing days—because of my evil merit and by your just judgment, measurable; that is, short and failing.

And my substance—this mutable and changeable essence in which I now exist, which I brought about through my evil merit—is as nothing before you; that is, in comparison with that substance of mine which was and has been made a praise before you. For you truly are, and therefore what is before you truly exists.

Yet all things are vanity. The passage is connected in this way, as though he were saying: “I have despised what is below, trampled upon all earthly things, leaped over everything mortal, fixed my mind on what is above, and desired the number of days that truly exists to be made known to me. Yet I, who have already transcended so much, while I still bear a mortal body and labor in this corruption, and while what I desire remains uncertain to me, am subject to every vanity.

“For every living human being”—that is, every mortal and suffering person, whether one who clings to earthly things or one who leaps over them—and even I myself, Jeduthun, am all vanity. That is, I belong to complete vanity, both inwardly and outwardly: inwardly in one respect and outwardly in another. For Solomon says: ‘Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.’ What abundance does a person have from all his labor with which he labors under the sun?

“For all things under the sun are visible, and therefore they are vain. The things above the sun are invisible, and therefore they are true. But this Jeduthun, while still living, possesses some things under the sun and some above the sun.

“Under the sun he possesses things both inwardly and outwardly. Outwardly: sleeping, waking, growing young, growing old, and other things of this kind. Inwardly: becoming angry, grieving, being uncertain about the things he desires, and similar things. In this respect he belongs to complete vanity.

“Above the sun, however, he possesses that desire of which we spoke earlier, as well as faith, hope, love, and the other virtues. And just as he possesses vanity from the things under the sun, so from these he possesses truth. Therefore he groans because of the former and burns with desire for the latter.”

Yet the human being is in an image. Humanity, I say, belongs to vanity, and yet the human being is in the image of God, because he was made according to the image and likeness of God—namely, through reason, understanding, and innate goodness.

But the human being himself passes away; that is, he often falls inwardly and outwardly, disfiguring himself from that image. And he does not pass away only through himself, but also because of others, because he is troubled—that is, anxious—on account of others in these earthly matters. This is a source of disturbance for him both here and in the future, and he is troubled in vain—that is, uselessly and without cause.

Let us therefore hear of this vain disturbance, so that we may trample upon it and leap over it, to where there is no disturbance.

He hoards. Truly disturbed is the person who hoards—that is, who plows, sails, acquires from every business, steals, and plunders so that coin may be placed upon coin—and yet all in vain, because he does not know for whom he will gather these things.

But perhaps you will judge that he gathers them for his children—this too was observed by that same Jeduthun—but he received this in vanity, because it is a voice of piety and an excuse for iniquity. For is anything hoarded for the dying from the dying, for those who pass away from those who pass away—indeed, for the dying from those who are dying, for those who pass away from those who pass away? Is it even hoarded for those not yet born? For how does he know that they will be born or that, once born, they will possess these things?

Therefore, “hoard up treasures for yourselves in heaven.” Let them be placed, that is, in the hand of the poor, so that they may be found in the hand of the rich; let them be placed in the hand of the needy, so that they may be found in the hand of the Almighty.

What has been read from “My heart grew hot” up to this point may also be read differently, so that it runs as follows: Because my pain was renewed through excessive silence, my heart therefore grew hot with a love of speaking. And in that meditation of mine the fire—that is, the fervor of love for God and neighbor—burns in the tongue of the one who leaps over earthly things, praying in this way:

“Lord, make my end known to me,” that is, the end of the one who leaps over earthly things—namely, so that I may know at what point I ought to keep silent and at what point I ought to speak. “And also make known to me the number of my days,” not the number that does not exist, but the one that does exist, so that in speaking and keeping silent I may possess a proper balance regarding those days. Thus I may neither keep silent out of hatred nor say anything out of rashness, and may know what is lacking to me.

This interpretation is not changed by the following verse.

Yet all is vanity. My substance, I say, is as nothing; how much more, then, is the substance of others? But miserable humanity does not attend to this, because every human being, whether one who clings to earthly things or one who leaps over them—that is, Jeduthun himself—is all vanity, striving in every way after vanity in these earthly matters.

And this is true to such an extent that the human being himself may even be called “all vanity,” although he ought not to be. For, making his vanity still less tolerable, the miserable man does not remain long in this vanity but quickly passes away.

Observe this in the image: as quickly as the image of some body, represented in a mirror, disappears, so quickly the human being himself passes away. Yet this unhappy person strives after vanity, not only for his own sake but also for the sake of others, being troubled in vain, as was said in another reading.

And now what is my expectation? The passage is connected as follows: “My substance is as nothing.” And when I have been placed in such great weakness—now, that is, when I have already become somewhat one who leaps over earthly things—what is my expectation? That is, what should I await, in what should I hope?

Should I hope in the things that are under the sun, which I now despise, or rather in the things that are above the sun, toward which I direct myself? Certainly, in those above the sun.

He confirms this choice by a question: “Is not the Lord my expectation?” As though he were saying: “Truly, the Lord alone is to be awaited by me, from whom all things proceed, who made all these things, and by whom I myself was made among all these things.”

Then he turns familiarly to the Lord himself, whom he has resolved to await. As though he were saying: “Rightly, Lord, you are to be awaited by me, because my substance, now fragile and not incorruptible, truly exists only when it is with you—that is, when, made immortal and incapable of suffering, it comes into your presence face to face.”

From all my iniquities. As though he were saying: “So that I may belong, Lord, to that true substance, rescue me”—that is, cleanse me in the present from all my iniquities.

Why does this one who leaps over earthly things, who has already transcended so much, ask to be freed, and from what iniquities? For this reason: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.”

What he says by “all” has this meaning: “Rescue me not only so that I may not fall back into the things from which I leaped—that is, into more serious sins—but also so that I may be freed from those for which it is necessary to wash the feet, namely, from venial sins, for which we pray daily, saying: ‘Forgive us our debts.’”

This man teaches us that although he has transcended so much, he still asks to be rescued, because true perfection cannot be possessed in this life. Our only perfection here is that, if we are able to leap over certain things, we understand that others remain, toward which we must hasten.

The Apostle shows both points. After saying, “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect, brothers; I do not consider myself to have apprehended it,” thereby showing that he is not yet perfect, he immediately adds that he is perfect, and shows in what respect he is perfect, saying: “Whatever we are perfect in, let us think this way.”

As though he were saying openly: “This is the true perfection of all of us who are perfect: that we understand this—that we are not yet able to possess true perfection.”

Rescue me, I say, and I ask you to rescue me because you have allowed me for so long to be a reproach to the foolish. This means: “For so long you have willed me to live and preach the truth among foolish people who love vanity, from whom we cannot avoid being mocked, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to human beings, and to angels”—angels both praising and blaming us, and human beings likewise.

I became mute. He explains how he became a reproach. As though he were saying: “Because, while I was preaching the truth, I was despised by foolish people, I became mute,” that is, I became mute before them. And to such an extent that I never opened my mouth.

But you, Lord, remove these blows from me—namely, reproach and the other miseries that I suffer. They are yours, I say, because by your just judgment you made them.

By the strength of your hand. Truly, you made them, because I failed—that is, I fell into this condition of mortal misery—through the strength of your hand, that is, through your unconquerable power. Yet this was not unjust, because it happened through rebukes that I deserved. For rebuke follows sin.

He shows how it happened through rebukes, saying: “For you chastised”—through the punishment mentioned above, namely, “You shall surely die.” You did not utterly condemn the first human being, and in him all humanity, out of your severity, but because of his iniquity—that is, because of his disobedience and presumption.

As though he were saying: “In myself I recognize iniquity; in you, equity.”

And you chastised to such an extent that you made not only his flesh but also his soul wither—that is, become so lukewarm and fragile as a withered and fragile spider, which dissolves even when touched lightly.

Or alternatively: A spider labors so greatly in weaving a useless web that it tears out its own entrails, and at last hangs there dry and dead. Similarly, from that first failure we suffer this evil: we devote ourselves so intensely to these useless worldly things that not only our flesh but also our soul fails, casting away its inner parts—namely reason and understanding—in accordance with the way the text may be read: “You made his soul wither,” that is, fail through useless labor, just as a spider fails in its useless weaving.

Yet in vain. According to the earlier interpretation, the passage is connected as follows: “You indeed made his soul withered and liable to perish, yet every human being”—that is, whoever among human beings lives—is troubled, that is, anxious, about earthly things, and this in vain, as was said above.

According to the later interpretation, this is connected with what precedes, namely, “You chastised,” in the same way.

Hear my prayer. As though he were saying: “So that I, Lord, may not be troubled, hear my prayer for perseverance in the good, and my supplication for cleansing from venial sins. Receive,” I say, “my tears”—that is, my tearful supplication—“with your ears,” that is, hear it through the power of hearing that resides in you.

Why does one who leaps over earthly things shed such tears? For this reason: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves”; and because “whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow.” It is as though he were saying: “The more I desire what is absent, the more I groan until it comes.”

[Col. 0691C] Do not be silent. Thus, Lord, I ask you to hear my prayer and receive my supplication. Do not, turned away from me in anger, remain silent; rather, speak to me so that I may perceive it: “I am your salvation.”

And you ought not to be silent because we seek—not a lasting city here, but one that is to come. For I am with you already by hope, though not yet naturally a citizen, but a resident alien, that is, a temporary inhabitant.

And I am with you as a pilgrim still, namely, placed in pilgrimage, not as a citizen of your household. A pilgrim is more distant than a resident alien. A resident alien is one who already dwells among others but does not yet possess the rights of a citizen; a pilgrim is one who has not yet arrived but is still journeying.

There are many who are pilgrims but are not with the Lord. All lovers of the world are indeed pilgrims in the region of dissimilarity, removed from that heavenly homeland, and they are not with God but rather with the devil, their father.

I am, I say, with you as a resident alien and a pilgrim, and this in the same condition as all the fathers—that is, in the condition in which my spiritual fathers, namely the patriarchs and prophets, were with you. For just as they were first with you in hope and then departed to you, so I am now with you in hope, where at last I shall be in reality.

Forgive me. As though he were saying: “I am now with you, Lord, in hope; but so that I may be with you in reality, forgive me”—that is, in the meantime grant me forgiveness and cleansing from the venial sins that I commit through the necessity of the journey—“so that I may be refreshed,” that is, so that I may possess a conscience refreshed and quiet from every disturbance of sin, “before I depart from here,” that is, before I die.

And it is necessary, Lord, that you forgive, because if you do not forgive and I depart, I shall no longer be. This does not mean that I shall not exist at all, but that whoever departs from true being—that is, from God—is as though he does not exist, because he loses true being.

## Psalm XXXIX

“To the end, a psalm of David.”

[Col. 0692A]

## Argument
The people returned from Babylon give thanks to the Lord. Alternatively, he who in Psalm 38 said, “What is my expectation? Is it not God?” now says in Psalm 39, “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he regarded me.” And he who there had said, “Hear my prayer,” here says, “He heard my prayer.” Likewise, concerning Paul’s patience, where he announces Christ beforehand. Read this in the Acts of the Apostles.

## EXPLANATION

It is often said that David signifies Christ and the end, whose members begin the psalm while he himself, the head, brings it to completion. In the first interpretation, the Church of the Gentiles gives thanks because, freed from the world’s long-standing sorrow, she has deserved to attain the joys of the New Testament. In the second, the Lord himself speaks, explaining the holy Incarnation and the righteousness of his [Col. 0692B] preaching. For this reason he implores the Father’s help, so that he may overcome the dangers inflicted by the Jews; he asks that his enemies be confounded and that all who hope in him rejoice.

## COMMENTARY

### “Waiting, I waited”

The title is as follows: “For the end, a psalm of David,” truly attributed to David. For it is the voice of the head speaking in this psalm, now for himself, now for his members, exhorting us to remain steadfast in faith and good works and to await the promised inheritance with patience. He sets himself before us as an example when he says, “Waiting, I waited for the Lord,” and shows that no one can attain that blessedness through free choice or through legal sacrifice, but only through grace.

At the end also he prays that the grace promised to the earlier people of the Jews, and partly bestowed upon them, may likewise be granted to that other people, namely, the people of the Gentiles, so that “there may be one fold, just as there is one shepherd.” [Col. 0692C] It is as though he said: Adam waited for the Lord, but he did not wait while waiting, because he remained obedient only for a time. But I waited while waiting—that is, I waited with complete patience and perseverance—not for a human consoler, who might fail in his own weakness before he could restore me, but for the Lord, the true consoler. And I waited not for a human promiser, who could be deceived and deceive, but for the Lord, who is a faithful promiser and a reliable debtor.

So be an avaricious exactor. And because I waited in this way, the Lord not only attended to me but also attended to my interests—that is, he applied himself so as to benefit me. And truly he benefited me, because he heard my prayers, made on behalf of my people. The effect demonstrates this: “He brought me out,” that is, my people, “from the pit of misery,” that is, from the depth of iniquity. Many are in that pit who do not realize that they are there, because they do not consider their sins or cry out to the Lord. Therefore they are not rescued from it. Of them it is said: “When the sinner has fallen into the depth of iniquity, [Col. 0692D] he will despise it.”

There are others also in the same pit who, because they recognize themselves and lift their heads upward, saying, “From the depths I cried to you, Lord,” are rescued from it. These are devout petitioners and tearful criers. “He brought me out,” I say, “from the pit,” and also “from the mud of dregs.” Mud mixed with dregs is both filthy and slippery. By “the mud of dregs,” therefore, we may understand either carnal desires, such as lust, which both defiles and overthrows many; or ambition, which overturned the first human being and creeps in like a cancer into almost everyone; or even the wicked mingled with the good in the Church, just as pure liquid and dregs are mixed together in the same vessel. For the wicked defile and overthrow others by their conformity to them.

And he not only brought me out, but also “set my feet”—that is, those by whom I was to enter into the knowledge of the Gentiles, namely, the heralds; or “my feet,” that is, the affections of my people, which previously were carried about by every doctrine. After they had received one sound doctrine, [Col. 0693A] he established them—that is, made them stable and firm—setting them upon a rock, that is, in a firm and safe place, namely, in ecclesiastical institutions. Or, “upon me, the rock.” For the rock was Christ. He strengthened them because through me he made them steadfast, and thus he directed “my steps,” that is, the works of my people, or those by whom I was to go forth into the knowledge of the Gentiles.

### “And he put into my mouth”

He established, I say, the feet of my people and directed their steps. In this way he put into my mouth—that is, into the mouth of my people—a new song, both in the mouth of the heart and in the mouth of the body: a new song, that is, new charity and new humility. For just as the old song is old hostility and pride, so the new song is new charity and new humility.

I call it a new song, and it is a hymn—that is, praise to God. Although by nature he is the God of all, he is ours—that is, mine and my people’s—by grace. These are the things for which God chiefly descended to us, namely, charity and humility; and for this reason he is chiefly praised through them.

### “Many shall see”

[Col. 0693B] It is as though he said: For what benefit was this done—that you brought my people out of the pit of misery and put a new song into their mouths? This benefit: so that many might see it and fear, as indeed many will see and fear.

There are two orders in the Church: some who go before and others who follow. Those who go before are examples to those who follow, so that the latter may imitate them; those who follow are imitators of those who went before. Therefore he says: Many will see those who went before and who persist along the narrow way; and, seeing them, they will fear, because they themselves proceed along the broad way, which is narrow at the end, and do not rather imitate those others.

And therefore they will hope—that is, they will place their hope, by imitating them, not in them but in the Lord, whom they will imitate in them. As it is written: “Be imitators of me, beloved, as I also am of Christ.” And therefore they will hope not in them but in the Lord, because all their virtue and help will principally come from the Lord, according to the saying: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, [Col. 0693C] from where help will come.” The principal help, namely, comes from the Lord.

### “Blessed is the man”

They will rightly hope in God, because from him they will obtain blessedness. For every man whose hope is the name of his Lord is blessed—that is, the man who makes this name, “Lord,” his hope. Everyone does this who presents himself as a faithful and willing servant of the Lord.

And so I say that he is blessed if he does not look toward vanities—that is, toward worldly things—by pursuing them. For no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back will be fit for the kingdom of God.

And because there are many who give little attention to vanities, such as gold, silver, and things of that kind, because they do not care about them, yet who are not truly steadfast because they take pleasure in amusing entertainments, such as charioteers, tightrope-walkers, dogs, and birds, he adds: “And if he does not look toward false insanities,” that is, toward amusements and games. These are indeed insanities because they render a person deranged; but because they do not entirely take away his mind, they are called false insanities. True insanities, however, are anger, rage, and similar things, which completely derange a person. [Col. 0693D]

### “You have done many wonderful things, Lord”

I say: if he does not look toward false insanities, toward which one ought not to look, since no poverty compels him to do so, because you, Lord my God and my people’s God through grace, have done many wonderful things—that is, your spectacles, things pertaining to you—then one ought to look toward these rather than toward false insanities.

If someone delights in watching a charioteer, let him rather delight in seeing a person restrain lust, anger, and similar passions. For the one who properly restrains the horses of lust or avarice as they rush toward destruction acts far more nobly than the one who drives horses around in circles or rides them.

Likewise, if someone admires a tightrope-walker, let him rather admire Peter, who walked upon the sea, and imitate him by treading upon the sea that Peter trod. For the sea is the world, as divine Scripture testifies. In it are the harmful bitterness of pleasures, [Col. 0694A] the waves of tribulations, the storms of temptations, and human beings devouring one another through slander, like fish in the sea.

Everyone ought to despise and tread upon this sea—that is, the world—and walk upon it. Yet you will not tread upon it, nor will you overcome it, unless the one who first trod upon it commands you. For if he commands you to come to him, he will not allow you to perish.

You, I say, Lord, have done wonderful things, and this solely in your thoughts—that is, through yourself, without the counsel or assistance of anyone, according to the saying: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” and so forth.

Therefore, because you did this through yourself alone, there is no one who can be compared with you, much less preferred to you. Yet this is what those do who prefer other things to you: they abandon the Church and run after amusements. Above all, this is done by idolaters, who worship the creature and put the Creator second.

### “I have proclaimed and spoken”

The connection is as follows: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord.” And while waiting, I proclaimed [Col. 0694B] what had to be proclaimed by deed; and I spoke what had to be spoken by mouth.

It may also be connected with what immediately precedes in this way: You, Lord, have done wonderful things, and I and my people have proclaimed those wonderful things by our deeds and spoken of them with our mouths. For not only Christ, but also the apostles and holy heralds, taught by word and example that the world must be trodden underfoot and carnal desires restrained.

Christ acted first and then spoke, according to the saying: “The first account I composed, O Theophilus, concerning all the things that Jesus began to do and to teach.” Doctrine is then truly sound when the teacher’s deeds and words do not disagree.

I proclaimed, I say, and I spoke; and as I and my people proclaimed and spoke, those who believed were multiplied beyond number—that is, more came than belonged to the Lord. There is a fixed number of the faithful who belong to the heavenly Jerusalem. These are the lovers and observers of God’s commandments, of whom it is said: “The Lord knows those who are his.”

But those who build the walls of the Church and disregard God’s [Col. 0694C] commandments belong to the Church’s sacraments only by calling; they are not among that number of whom it is said: “Many are called,” and so forth.

### “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire”

I proclaimed, I say, and I spoke, and it was necessary for me to come and proclaim because you, Lord, established legal sacrifices only for a time and no longer wished them to exist.

This may also be connected in the following way: You, Lord, did wonderful things in your thoughts, and among those thoughts this was one: that you no longer wished legal sacrifice and legal offering to exist.

For while the time of that true sacrifice known to the faithful had not yet arrived—namely, before Christ, the true Lamb, offered himself for us upon the altar of the cross—it was prefigured through various figures and mysteries, by some who already foresaw it through the Holy Spirit and by others who did not know it.

But after the time of that true sacrifice arrived, the words of fulfillment came, [Col. 0694D] and the words of promise were taken away. The signs that promised withdrew after the promised reality had been presented. This is what he says: After the true sacrifice was present, you did not desire sacrifice and offering, which had been signs of promise.

What, then, did you desire? Ears—that is, you desired that there be perfect obeyers. Therefore you prepared ears for me—that is, you bestowed perfect obedience upon me as an example for others, and also upon my people in their own way.

Nor is it inappropriate that he calls obedience “ears.” Through the ears, commandments enter the soul and teach it obedience. Thus the instrument of obedience is placed here for obedience itself.

### “But a burnt offering”

I say that you desired obedience. But that legal sacrifice which was called a burnt offering—that is, something wholly burned, of which nothing was kept back but which was entirely consumed upon the altar—and that other offering called a sin offering, you did not require; that is, you no longer wished them to be made. For all these things differed within the legal system. [Col. 0695A]

Then, when you no longer desired sacrifice and burnt offering and did not require them, I said in the presence of the reality: “Behold, I come.” It is as though he said: Behold, now is the time for the things that were promised to come and for the things that promised them to be taken away.

Therefore I come, Lord, to do your will—that is, to offer you true obedience. This is what I ought to do, because although you are God of all by nature, you are my God by grace. I ought also to do your will because I have always willed—that is, loved—to do your will, not mine.

And because I have also willed your law—that is, your will, which is the written law—I have willed it in the midst of my heart, that is, with a firm and complete will. For what is in the middle of anything is firmer and more certain. Therefore, if we refer this to the head himself, by “the midst of my heart” we shall understand the firm will of the heart.

We may also understand by Christ’s heart all who are in concord and incorporated into him, [Col. 0695B] and by “the midst” those who are firmer among them. Accordingly, it may be said: Not only did I will your will and your law in myself, but also in my people; and if not in all, at least in the midst of my heart—that is, in those who are firmer and more perfect.

Another Translation has: “In the midst of my belly.” According to this reading, the argument proceeds from the lesser: he truly willed his will in his own people. It is read: “For he also willed it in the midst of his belly,” that is, in the heart of the weak. For by the belly, which is soft, the soft and weak are signified.

I come, I say, to do your will, and I have willed your law. And rightly so, because “in the heading of the book it is written concerning me, that I should do your will.”

The Apostle says: “The head of the woman is man, the head of man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God.” The Word of the Father incarnate was the book promised and set before us as an example, according to which we were to be inscribed and conformed to it.

And in the heading of this book—that is, in God the Father—it was written—that is, firmly ordained before all ages—concerning Christ that he should offer true obedience to God [Col. 0695C] the Father for our redemption, according to the saying: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world.” Hence he says: “In the heading of the book,” and so forth.

### “I have proclaimed your righteousness”

I said, “I come to offer true obedience.” And when I came, suffering, dying, and rising again, I proclaimed in the presence of the reality your righteousness—that is, your faith which justifies. For from this our faith, by which we are justified, began, according to the saying: “He died for our sins and rose for our justification.”

I proclaimed, I say, through myself and my people, your righteousness in the Church—not a small Church, but a great one, spread throughout the world; or not a weak Church, but a great one, strong and firm.

Previously, while they still doubted the resurrection, the Church was weak. Peter represented its form when, at the voice of a servant girl, he denied the Lord. But after the Lord rose and they became certain of the future resurrection, then the Church first became strong. Peter also represented its type in himself [Col. 0695D] when he said before the rulers: “We must obey God rather than you.”

I proclaimed, I say, and I shall proclaim.

### “Behold, my lips”

It is as though he said: Behold, consider that I shall truly proclaim, because I shall not restrain—that is, I shall not allow to be restrained—my lips, that is, my heralds, through whom I shall speak as through lips, from proclamation.

Or by “lips,” which are soft, we may understand only the softer and weaker among the heralds. Thus the argument proceeds from the greater, according to the saying of blessed Job: “The lips around my teeth have been left.”

By “teeth,” which are the firmer part of the mouth and body, we should understand Christ’s strong steadfastness in the Passion. The bones—that is, the apostles, who were stronger than the others—did not stand around him in the Passion, because they abandoned him and fled. Only the lips—that is, the women, who are signified by the lips because of the softness and fragility of their sex—stood around him.

Accordingly, it is read in the Passion: I shall not allow the lips to be restrained; therefore they shall not be restrained, [Col. 0696A] because you, Lord, knew—that is, chose and made—them to be such that they could not easily be restrained. For you know that they have in their hearts what they sound forth with their mouths. Whoever has the truth in his heart cannot easily be prevented from speaking it with his mouth.

### “Your righteousness”

Truly I shall not restrain my lips, because I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart—that is, in the heart of my people. I shall not allow my people to hide your justifying faith in their hearts; rather, they shall proclaim it for the benefit of their neighbors.

The righteousness of God is both to be hidden in the heart and not to be hidden. It is to be hidden in the heart—that is, retained in memory—so that no one may sin rashly. Hence it is said elsewhere: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you.”

But it is not to be hidden—that is, it is to be proclaimed for the benefit of one’s neighbor. Hence it is said here: “I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart.”

And the statement is repeated because of what he adds: “I said,” that is, I shall make my people [Col. 0696B] say and proclaim your truths, which follow from those commandments.

### “I have not hidden your truth”

That is, your true commandments, and your salvation—that is, salvation given by you through me, who am your salvation, giving salvation to the human race.

And truly my people will speak your truth and salvation, because I have not hidden—that is, I shall not allow my people to hide—your mercy and your truth.

Your mercy is that by which you call and forgive sins; your truth is that by which you reward merits and fulfill promises. Even in the presence of a great council—that is, even if a great multitude of adversaries assembles—my people will not, through fear of them, cease proclaiming mercy and truth, according to the saying: “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus.”

### “But you, Lord”

Here he begins to pray that the grace promised and likewise bestowed upon the earlier people may also be bestowed upon those other sheep, namely, those from the Gentiles.

The connection is therefore this: My people will do what belongs to them. But you, [Col. 0696C] Lord, who are God of those far away and God of those near—far away from sinners and the proud, such as the Pharisee boasting of his merits, but near to the good and humble, such as the Publican confessing his sins—you, I say, do what belongs to you: do not keep your mercies far from me—that is, from those who are to come from the other sheep.

Grant that my heralds may find ready obeyers among those other sheep. And truly do not keep them far away, because your mercy and your truth—your mercy by which you forgive sins, your truth by which you reward merits—have always received me, that is, my people.

This means that they have never been absent from my people of the earlier community, but have always consoled them. For, as he says, they would not dare to convert unless they were secure of forgiveness, nor would they persevere unless they were secure of reward.

And just as they have always received me in those people, so they will receive me in these others. The manifestation of past things is a guarantee of future things.

### “For evils have surrounded me”

[Col. 0696D] It is necessary that you not keep your mercies far away, because evils have surrounded me on every side—that is, they have surrounded my people in those sheep—so many sins that they cannot be numbered.

For who is sufficient to know the number of those evils for which the one who says, “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from the sins of others,” groans?

And not only lighter sins, such as venial sins, have surrounded me in my people, but “my iniquities”—that is, the more serious sins, namely, idolatry and every kind of criminal sin belonging to those who are to become mine among the other sheep—have seized me.

Because of my excessive affection, I call these sins “mine”; they have seized me—that is, those who will become mine. And they have done so to such an extent that I could not see—that is, my people are powerless to see what must be seen.

Their eye, blinded by pleasures and darkened by sins, cannot see the light of truth unless it is first cleansed; and only the pure in heart see that light.

### “They have multiplied”

[Col. 0697A] Truly the iniquities have seized my people, because they have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head—that is, of my people—since although the hairs of some people can be counted, these iniquities are countless.

Even if someone guards himself against the mass of sins—that is, against criminal sins—there are nevertheless so many venial sins that he commits even in a single day that they exceed all number.

Or by “the hairs of his head” we may understand his heralds of the Word, who is the head, adhering to him and adorning him as hairs adhere to and adorn the head. Accordingly, it may be said: The iniquities of my people have multiplied to such an extent that they are beyond the hairs—that is, they surpass those who adhere to me as hairs adhere to the head, namely, they surpass all my heralds, so that they cannot be washed away and erased through them without your great and manifest help.

Therefore it is necessary that you not keep your mercies far away. Their iniquities have multiplied to such an extent because their heart—that is, the heart of my people—has abandoned me, that is, has abandoned my people.

Nor is it surprising that it abandoned them, [Col. 0697B] because it first abandoned you. If they knew you, they would know themselves; and if they knew themselves, you would forgive them.

A person’s heart abandons him when he presumes upon himself, does not recognize his weakness, and does not consider his sins. Peter’s heart abandoned him when he presumed upon himself, saying: “Lord, even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” The result made this sufficiently clear.

### “May it please you, Lord”

And because the iniquities of my people have multiplied so greatly, it has pleased me, Lord, that they should be rescued. And I ask that it also please you, Lord, to rescue me—that is, my people—from iniquities.

Or, “May it please you”: just as it pleased you to rescue the heralds, so may it please you to rescue these people also. Lord, look toward helping me—that is, my people.

It is as though he said: Previously you despised my people, and free choice has been weakened in them; but a spark still remains in them by which they can somehow see you. To help that spark, so that they may see you fully, you, Lord, who previously looked away, now look toward them.

### “Let them be confounded”

[Col. 0697C] It is as though he said: I say that you should look toward them so that those who now seek my life and the life of my people, in order to take it away—that is, to condemn it—may be confounded, recognizing that they deserve confusion, and may at the same time be reverent—that is, may fear their sins, or my heralds.

Let them be converted, I say, from evil to good, so that they may be behind—that is, not go before but follow—and thus may be reverent, that is, may fear fully. This applies not only to those who commit evil but also to those who now wish evil upon me and my people, so that afterward they may wish good upon me.

### “Let them bear it immediately”

This is said concerning the deceitful and the flatterers. It is not a wish for malevolence but a declaration of their punishment.

It is as though he said: Let those who wish evil upon me, once they recognize themselves, be converted. But let them bear their confusion, which they have deserved, not only in the future but immediately—that is, without delay, even in the present—so that those who say to me and my people, “Well done, well done,” may suffer a double crushing.

They say this to me while rejoicing in my [Col. 0697D] death; and they say it also to my people when they are doing evil: “Well done, well done,” that is, “It is good, it is good that you are acting as you do,” in order to deceive them. For the tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins.

By contrast, let those who seek you rejoice outwardly and be glad inwardly—that is, let them possess complete joy, here and in the future—having you as their foundation, seeking you, the Lord, through me, the Mediator, and not themselves.

And in order that they may be worthy of such great joy, let them presume nothing upon themselves, but always say: “Let the Lord be magnified, never the servant.”

For if the Lord makes a righteous person from an impious person, a son from a servant, and thus calls him to glory, let the Lord be magnified. If he calls a sinner to forgiveness, let the Lord be magnified. Again, if he calls a righteous person to the crown, let the Lord be magnified. Thus let the Lord always be magnified.

Those who love your salvation say this—not their own salvation, but yours—that is, those who expect to be saved not through their own merits but through your grace.

### “But I”

Let them say this concerning you; but concerning himself let each one speak for himself: “I am a beggar and poor.”

[Col. 0698A] That is, I am comparable to a beggar. Even if he possesses something from himself, it is nevertheless little, and therefore he asks from others what he lacks.

And I am comparable to a poor man, who possesses absolutely nothing through himself, because I presume nothing upon myself and think that I possess nothing from myself. Therefore the Lord is concerned for me—that is, he cares for me.

For if he cared for you when you did not exist, so that you might exist, will he not care for you now that you are what he willed you to be? Certainly he will, because “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.”

### “My helper”

This humbled man turns familiarly to the Lord. It is as though he said: Truly they say that you care for me, because you, God of all by nature, are my helper in perfecting what is good and my protector in avoiding evil. Therefore do not delay—that is, do not postpone—the promised blessedness and inheritance.

These two verses may also be read in another way, as though the head speaks here in his own person. Accordingly, it may be said: I desire that they say, “Let the Lord be magnified,” and that they humble themselves. [Col. 0698B] In order that they may do this, I have given myself to them as an example.

Although I was rich with the Father, I am a beggar and poor—that is, I presented myself in the guise of a beggar and a poor man as an example of humility.

And because I humbled myself, the Lord the Father is concerned for me, because he will restore my poverty with his riches, giving me immortality and impassibility.

And truly you, Lord, are concerned for me, because you, my God and my people’s God through grace, are my helper in perfecting obedience and my protector from the sentence of the enemies who wish to erase my name.

Therefore, Lord, do not delay—that is, do not postpone me until the general resurrection.

# PSALM XL

“For the end, a psalm of David himself.”

## ARGUMENT

The illness and healing of Hezekiah are foretold, and how, on the occasion of his sickness, hidden enemies were exposed by their attacks, and how the illness itself benefited his devotion. [Col. 0698C] Likewise, the voice of Christ concerning his Passion and Judas the betrayer. It should be read with Isaiah.

Alternatively, any Christian may speak against the unclean spirit and against the man of his own dregs—that is, against the flesh.

## EXPLANATION

These words ought by now to be very familiar to us through frequent use. But, to touch briefly upon what has been said, everything is directed toward the Lord Christ.

The fact that this psalm is placed in the number forty magnifies it; that number is frequently applied to cleansing and purification. At the first entrance, the Prophet speaks, declaring blessed the giver of alms and celebrating him with manifold blessing. Second, the Lord recalls his glorious Passion. Third, to strengthen the hope of the faithful, he likewise foretells his resurrection.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0698D]

### “Blessed is he who understands”

The title in this psalm is the same as in the preceding psalm, namely: “For the end, a psalm of David.” The intention of the speaking person and the subject matter are also the same here as above.

It is connected with the sentence just stated in the preceding psalm as follows. It is as though he said: I am indeed a physician and a poor man, but something else must be understood in me besides the form of a beggar and a poor man, because blessed is he who understands something about me beyond my being needy and poor.

A distinctive intention may also be assigned to this psalm, namely this: it is the voice of the head exhorting us that, just as we understand him to be truly human, so we should also understand him to be truly God.

This is because such understanding is that grace by which we are justified and the true faith through which the righteous person lives eternally.

According to this interpretation, the verse is not connected with the preceding psalm, but is as though he said: I, who was promised by the patriarchs and foretold by the prophets, have come in the form of poverty and humility. Blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me.

This is what he says: The one who understands in me not merely a needy and poor man, but something beyond one who is needy and poor—that is, more than needy and poor—is truly blessed [Col. 0699A], truly holy in justifying grace and life-giving faith.

He understands Christ as more than needy and poor when he understands him to be poor among human beings but rich with the Father, needy on earth but powerful in heaven. While weakness was being shown to us, divinity lay hidden within. For his poverty was our fullness, and his weakness was our strength, because, so that man might eat the bread of angels, the King of angels became man.

He explains how the one who understands in this way is blessed, saying: “The Lord will deliver him from all tribulations on the evil day,” that is, on the day of examination and tribulation. It will be evil for many because on it the things now hidden will be made manifest, according to the saying: “He will bring forth your righteousness like the light.”

### “May the Lord preserve him”

This appears to be a wish, but it is a certain promise concerning the future. He explains how he says that the Lord will deliver him: he will preserve him. [Col. 0699B] Just as he has already preserved him through the inner resurrection, so then he will preserve him in the body through the outward resurrection.

And so may it happen, namely, that the Lord preserve him. And may he preserve him in such a way that the one whom he has already quickened in the soul through faith—for “the righteous lives by faith”—he will then quicken in the body through immortality and incorruption.

And lest he think that he has been neglected here because it was said only that he would be delivered in the future, he adds that in the meantime the Lord should make him blessed on earth, where everything is misery and where it is therefore difficult to become blessed.

And I say that he should make him blessed on earth in such a way that, although he hands over the earth—that is, the flesh—to the hands of enemies, he does not hand him over in soul—that is, in their will and conformity.

And so that he may not be handed over in soul to his enemies:

### “May the Lord help him upon the bed of his pain”

That is, may he make him lord of his own bed.

The bed of pain is the weakness of the flesh. When the soul consents to it and accommodates itself to its desires, it is carried by the flesh itself. [Col. 0699C] But when the soul prevails over it and rules it, then the bed—that is, the flesh—which previously carried the soul, is itself carried by the soul.

This was signified in the case of the paralytic man who, having been lowered through the roof into the house, was told by the Lord: “Rise, take up your bed, and walk into your house.”

The weakness of the flesh is called a bed of pain because every weakness of the soul—that is, every soul that has not yet attained the fullness of perfection—chooses some earthly thing in which it may rest and recline with a kind of repose. For it can hardly endure forever the exertion of labor and the mind stretched toward God.

Therefore it chooses something in which it may rest, such as the innocent pleasures of good men: a well-cultivated garden, an orchard, and things of that kind.

But because God wishes us to love only heavenly and eternal things, he mixes bitterness even into these innocent pleasures: he often troubles us, and we suffer tribulations and temptations. He does this so that through the bitterness of lower things we may be raised to love higher things.

He suggests this when he adds:

### “You have turned his entire bed”

[Col. 0699D] It is as though he said: For this reason I call it a bed of pain, because “his bed in his sickness”—that is, what he himself, while in the sickness of the flesh, chose to serve as his bed, as rest and delight—you have turned entirely, that is, you have disturbed it completely by the bitterness mixed into it.

But because these same bitternesses are imposed upon us not unjustly but by the Lord on account of our evil merits—a matter that everyone ought to consider—he adds:

### “I said: Lord”

It is as though he said: Truly, Lord, you have turned his entire bed, because I considered this and knew that it had been done justly, and in my people I said this so that I might make others understand the same thing.

For they did not say it themselves, but I said it, because I was the cause of their saying: “Lord, have mercy on me,” that is, burn, cut, and scourge me in every way; turn the bed, provided only that you heal my soul, which has deserved evil and has therefore become sick.

For it was not fate, fortune, a star, [Col. 0700A] or anything else, but I myself who sinned against you; you alone can heal and alone can forgive sins.

### “My enemies”

I made my people say and understand this. But my enemies did not understand it, because they spoke evil to me, and so forth.

These words may also be explained in another way: “You have turned his entire bed,” and what follows may be connected with this interpretation.

Thus it may be said: I call it a bed of pain because in his sickness—that is, in the inconstancy and impatience of the first man, which became his because it descended upon him—you turned his entire bed. You made it comparable to the bed of a sick person who turns his entire bed—that is, disturbs it.

For just as a sick person, twisting himself here and there because of pain, disturbs the very thing in which he ought to rest, so everything that ought to have been firm in this man has been disturbed by that sickness—that is, by that inconstancy.

To restore this weakness, I alone among human beings was suited for the task, and alone possessed such affection toward the wretched. I said, transferring their misery to myself [Col. 0700B] so that you might erase it: “Lord, have mercy on me.”

And by transferring their weakness and sins to myself so that you might heal them, I said: “Lord, heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.”

Yet he himself did not sin in anything, for he alone existed without sin. But he bore the punishment for our sins as though he himself had sinned.

My enemies. I came to restore human infirmity, but my enemies did not understand this, nor did they receive me as a physician. Rather, they said—or resolved and declared—things evil against me, indeed for the sake of their own reputation, whereas it would have been more truly to their advantage to say these things: “When will he die, and when will his name perish?” That is: “When shall we be able to bring about the death of this man, who opposes us in everything? And when shall his name perish,” that is, be blotted out from the earth, “before we lose our place and nation?” For if, as he seems to say, “we let him remain like this, the Romans will come and take away our place and nation.”

And if he entered. I rightly call them enemies, since even those who pretended to be friends were the greatest enemies. For if one of them entered, that is, wished to be with me familiarly while pretending to be a friend—which applies especially to Judas, but also to the others who said, “Teacher, we know that you have come from God,” and to their like—he entered, I say, “to see,” that is, to investigate our freedom, not so that he might find something worthy of belief, but so that he might discover some evil to denounce. The Apostle speaks of such men: “Certain false brothers slipped in to spy out our freedom.”

When that man entered, then, and saw nothing but what was true, his heart nevertheless spoke nothing but vanity, because he distorted everything. And therefore he “gathered,” that is, stored up iniquity for himself, in accordance with the saying: “For those murderers have stored up evils for themselves,” and so forth.
