He went out. He did indeed enter and speak vanity; afterward he went outside, that is, the man who had previously pretended to be a friend openly showed himself to be an enemy. And as he went out, he spoke, directing everything toward the same end, namely, vanity as before.

[Col. 0700D] They whispered against me. It is as though he said: Because both the false friends and the open enemies were therefore all enemies, they all whispered evil things against me secretly among themselves; and each of them considered evil things against me in his own mind, according to their opinion. Yet this was for me, that is, in reality for my glory. They also openly discussed those same evils with others, because they “established,” that is, jointly resolved, an evil word against me.

The evil word was spoken when they wished to kill the physician, saying, “Crucify him, crucify him.” But what remedy was there? None, certainly, because I shall rise again as easily as anyone sleeping rises from sleep. From this it is clear that he truly rises if he becomes healthy. For is there anyone who sleeps who will not rise again? Certainly he does rise.

And indeed the man of my peace. They truly established an evil word against me, because even the man of my peace—namely Judas, one of the twelve, in whom I had always had peace; to whom, even when he betrayed me, I did not refuse a kiss; in whom I had also placed my hope—did so.

But how could the one who knows his heart have hoped in him? In this way: Judas was sent with the other apostles to preach the kingdom of God. Therefore many who had been instructed by him placed their hope in him; and the Lord was in those who hoped, as also in those who hungered.

And the man who ate my bread, whether historically or spiritually: he ate not only the carnal ordinances but also the spiritual things he had received from me. This man, I say, of whom one would have thought least of such conduct, “magnified treachery,” that is, increased the overthrow against me, because he incited others to it.

But you, Lord. They indeed established an evil word against me, but you, Lord, have mercy on me and on my people. And so I say, “Have mercy”: raise me up, namely, outwardly, and my people as well. Now raise me up inwardly, so that at last you may raise them up inwardly; and thus I shall repay them—that is, my enemies—with the evil that they established against me, and my people will repay them also.

[Col. 0701B] Christ himself repaid them in this respect, because by his permission they lost their place and nation. And, because he willed it, the Church was planted there, from which the synagogue was uprooted. His own people repaid them in this respect because they caused some of them, after conversion, to become subject who had previously wished to rule.

In this I have known. You will truly have mercy on me and on my people, because my enemy, who rejoiced over me when I was dead, will not rejoice over me when I have not been raised. Foreseeing this, I knew that you had desired me, that is, that my sacrifice and obedience were pleasing to you.

But me. You rejected the enemies on account of their iniquity, and therefore they will not rejoice. But I shall rejoice, because you received me into your favor on account of my innocence. This innocence is the integrity of a life without sin, payment without debt, and punishment without merit.

You received me, I say; and therefore, although for a time you seemed to weaken me before human beings because of the scourges, you nevertheless established me [Col. 0701C] forever, that is, placed me eternally in your sight, making me immortal and incapable of suffering by your ordinance. For “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more,” and so forth. This is because you received me and established me.

Blessed. That is, may the Lord be increased and exalted. Although by nature he is the God of all, he is “the God of Israel,” that is, of the later people, to whom the elder people serves by grace. Blessed, I say, with a blessing beginning in the present age and continuing into the age to come. Let there be blessing among those sheep, and let there be blessing for him among these sheep.

## Psalm XLI

For the end; an understanding for the sons of Korah.

### Argument

The people, captive in Babylon and mindful of their homeland, pray. Alternatively, before baptism, the voice of Christ speaks to those who are to attain the faith. Read in Isaiah.

### Explanation

The sons of Korah, like Heman, Ethan, Asaph, and Jeduthun, were not psalmists but singers. David chose them for psalmody; yet, because of the significance of their names, they were fittingly attached to the titles.

Korah is said to mean “Calvary,” at the place signified by whose name the Lord was crucified. Therefore those who serve the banner of his Passion with complete devotion are rightly called the sons of Korah.

This psalm also suits every Christian who is girded with the flame of the Lord’s charity. We should remember what blessed Jerome says: “Surveying the whole Psalter with an attentive mind, I nowhere find that the sons of Korah sang anything sorrowful. For their psalms are always joyful and pleasant; having despised worldly things, they desire heavenly and eternal things, in agreement with the interpretation of their name.”

The son of Korah, whom we have said is marked by the honor of the cross, declares at the beginning of this psalm that every desire of his mind has been transferred to the Lord. In the second part he speaks to his soul, saying that it ought not to be troubled in this age, because God is its refuge, fixed by firm deliberation.

### Commentary

As the deer longs. The title is as follows: “For the end; for understanding; a psalm for the sons of Korah.” Korah was one of the singers whom David chose when bringing back the ark of the Lord. He had several sons, but they are not meant here. The name Korah is not placed here historically but mystically.

Let us therefore investigate the mystery. It is a matter of great sacramental significance that Christians, that is, the sons of Christ, are called the sons of Korah. For Korah is interpreted as “bald” or “calvary.”

Christ, too, is called Korah, that is, “bald,” either because he alone possessed perfection without excess. Nothing seems less likely to impede perfection in the human body than hair being cut off; similarly, a human being established in an abundance of virtues was perfect. Vices, however, are excessive, because they are added beyond perfection. Christ was free from this excess of vices, and therefore he is rightly called bald.

Or he is also called bald because he was prefigured by the bald Elisha, whom the boys mocked as he ascended the mountain, saying, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.” He turned and cursed them, and immediately two bears came out of the forest and devoured forty-two of them.

Likewise, when Christ was ascending the mountain—that is, the cross—the boys, namely, the foolish Jews, mocked him in many ways, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews,” and other such things. For this sin, after forty years had passed, the two bears—namely Titus and Vespasian—devoured them, the forty-two boys having already prefigured the number.

They came from the forest, that is, from the Gentile world, which was uncultivated like a forest because it had not yet felt the plowshare of apostolic teaching. They came forth, I say, and consumed them.

Christ is also called bald because he was crucified at the place of Calvary. Thus those who are the sons of his Passion, redeemed by his blood and bearing on their foreheads what his enemies fixed at the place of Calvary, are rightly called the sons of Korah.

This psalm is sung for these sons “for understanding.” Let us therefore awaken our understanding. Since it is sung for us, and since we wish to be sons of Korah, let us understand what we are to understand.

I venture to say in what understanding this psalm is sung: “His invisible things are perceived and understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made.” Let us therefore love together, burn together with thirst, and run together toward the fountain of understanding.

Let us long like the deer for that fountain of which Scripture says elsewhere: “For with you is the fountain of life.” He himself is fountain, light, and understanding. He is fountain because he gives drink to the thirsty; light because he enlightens the blind; and understanding because he illumines the soul eager for knowledge. Everyone who understands is illumined not by an outward but by an inward light.

Run, therefore, to the fountain; desire the water of the fountain—not casually, but like a deer. Run eagerly; desire eagerly. In the deer, speed is a distinguishing mark.

Divine Scripture also notes another feature of the deer. The deer consumes the serpent, and after killing the serpent burns with an even greater thirst and runs more eagerly to the fountain. Serpents are vices. Therefore consume the serpents of iniquity, and you will desire the fountain of truth more intensely.

There is also another thing that is said about deer and seen in them. Because they seek distant regions, either by swimming across the sea or by traveling in a herd, one places the burden of its head upon the haunches of another. In this way they carry one another and do not abandon one another, but complete the journey they have undertaken.

The Apostle addresses such deer when he says: “Bear one another’s burdens.” These deer, established in faith but not yet seeing what they have believed, desiring to understand what they love, long for the fountain of waters—not in order to wash, but in order to be refreshed.

The voice of these deer—or rather, of the deer of deer, that is, of Christ—is heard in this psalm. By his example he exhorts us, established in this mortality, this capacity for suffering, and this corruption, to desire, groan, and sigh with our whole purpose to reach that fountain where mortality will put on immortality and corruption will put on incorruption.

The title is therefore explained in this way: This psalm is directed “to the end,” that is, to Christ, whose voice it is. It is sung for the sons of Korah, that is, for imitators of Christ’s Passion; and it is sung “for understanding,” that is, so that they may understand what must be understood—namely, with what desire and ardor one must run to the fountain of understanding.

Now let us approach the literal meaning. It is the voice of the Head, as we have said, speaking before the Father for our exhortation:

“O God, my soul,” that is, the lowliness of my humanity, “desires to come to you, the fountain of life and understanding.” That is: “Just as, and with as great an ardor and speed as, the deer, by consuming serpents, longs to come to the fountains—not merely to certain failing springs, but to the fountains of waters where it may have complete refreshment—so shall I have refreshment with you.”

He wished to express something great, but had no words with which to declare it in his own way; therefore he applied himself to this comparison with the deer. Two things are noted here in the deer: desire and speed.

But how does he desire to come to God the Father, from whom he could never depart? “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself.” Yet he says this according to our condition. As long as he was in our infirmity, he seemed distant from God; but after he put on immortality and incorruption, he then first appeared to belong to God.

My soul thirsted. He repeats what he said in stronger words, as though he said: “I therefore say, Lord, that my soul desires you because my soul thirsted”—that is, it burned with the thirst of great desire—to reach you, to see and understand you, the God whom I call the fountain because you conquered our death, and from whom all our strength comes to me and to my people.

As I live because of the Father, so everyone who eats me lives because of me. Why did it thirst? In order that I might come and appear before your face, because you are God.

Out of his great affection he says: “And when shall I come and appear before your face?” I shall come at the appointed time, because in perfect obedience I shall ascend, destined to sit eternally at your right hand. This is not the voice of one who doubts, but of one who desires.

When he says, “I shall come and appear,” he again speaks from our infirmity. The Lord is immortal and incapable of suffering. Therefore only that which is immortal and incapable of suffering can properly be said to come before him.

My tears have been my bread. It is as though he said: “I shall truly come and appear before the face of God, because, in my desire to come, my tears”—that is, human misery, which must always be mourned by human beings because it came upon them through their sin—“have been my bread.”

They are “my” tears because I received them into myself out of an affection of mercy, so that through my misery—or rather, through my mercy—their misery might be destroyed.

Those tears, I say, were bread for me, that is, for refreshment, not for exhaustion. They were pleasing to me, not objects of lamentation; a source of joy, not bitterness, day and night, that is, continually, although I suffer great bitterness in them, because it is said to me daily—that is, continually, as a reproach: “Where is your God?”

Why, he says, has God abandoned you, though you make him your intimate, since he gives you neither counsel nor help?

These things I remembered. They despised me in this way, but I did not forget; rather, I remembered these things firmly—that I had been born, according to your fixed and established plan, not from them but from you, in order to suffer such things.

Therefore I first poured out my soul within me, that is, I humbled and weakened my soul by considering myself, attending to what I, a creature, owed the Creator; what the lesser owed the greater; what a servant owed the Lord.

Then I poured it out, that is, I extended my soul beyond myself by considering higher things, attending to the future glory destined for me through perfect obedience.

And rightly I not only poured it out but poured it forth, because I shall truly reach great glory. For I shall pass onward to the house of God, either the heavenly house, in which I shall be crowned with immortality and incapacity for suffering, or the Church, which is to be established and is called the house of God.

Just as Eve was born from the side of the sleeping Adam, so from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross came forth the sacraments—namely blood and water—from which the Church was established.

I say that I first existed in, or came to, the place of the tabernacle, that is, into observance of the legal ordinances. For he first fulfilled the legal requirements: he was circumcised, presented in the Temple, and purified according to the Law.

He had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it; afterward he brought the spiritual realities. The legal ordinances are called a tabernacle because tabernacles are not permanent dwellings but are set up only for a time. Ecclesiastical ordinances, however, are called a house because a house is a permanent dwelling, and they too endure.

I speak of the tabernacle as admirable, not in itself but because of the things signified through it.

In a voice of exultation and confession. I say, “I shall pass onward,” but this will not occur through sadness or compulsion, because “no one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down.” Since I have authority to lay down my soul, I do not lay it down in sadness or under compulsion, but with gladness and willingness.

This passage will take place in a voice of exultation and confession, that is, of exultant confession and praise, as great as the sound of banqueters’ exultation and praise. For among some people, banqueters customarily utter exultant words and praise their host.

Why are you sad, my soul? Since you are destined to come to such great glory, my soul, and through you the house of God will be established, why are you therefore sad, as you appear to be, and why do you trouble me?

It is as though he said: “This happens for the great benefit of my people.” He truly was sad, for he says in the Gospel: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” Nothing in him was feigned. Yet he did not have that sadness from himself—that is, from fear of death—but transformed into himself the infirmity of his members, of whom it was said: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak,” in order to console and exhort them not to despair, even if they approached death fearfully.

Hope in God. Do not be sad or troubled, but hope in the Lord. Hope that the purpose for which he wished you to be assumed by his Word will be accomplished.

Hence it is said elsewhere: “That they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent”; and again: “That they may bear witness to the truth.” These are the reasons for which he came.

He indicates this equivalently when he says: “You ought therefore to hope in the Lord, because, although I do not yet confess him, what I shall confess to him in the future is destined to come.” That is, I shall make a full confession of him in my people, who will recognize both that he is the true God and that I was sent by him, and who will say:

“The salvation of my countenance”—that is, Christ the Savior—is human, is a man like me.

Hence another Prophet says: “The breath of our nostrils is the Lord.” Through a part he signifies the whole; and again: “The Spirit is before our face.” The Word, who was spirit—that is, invisible—appeared to us through the humanity he assumed.

He is, I say, “the salvation of my countenance,” and yet he is my God. Insofar as he was made man, he is Savior; insofar as he is the Word, he is God the Creator.

To myself, my soul. I say that my soul is sad and troubled. But the fact that it is troubled must be referred to myself. It is as though he said: “Let no one think that this trouble is common to me and to others, namely, that I am troubled by fear of death. This trouble must be referred to myself, because it does not arise from compulsion or natural necessity, but from my own will.”

Another translation has, “Within myself.” This should be understood as follows: “This trouble is within myself,” that is, within me, not according to the Word but according to the fact that I am human. The solution is therefore the same as before.

And because you, Lord, gave me this steadfastness—namely, that no one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down—which was equivalently expressed in this way:

“For this reason I shall give you these thanks: I shall remember you from the land of the Jordan and of Hermoniim, from the little mountain.”

Or the passage can be connected in this way: “For what benefit is my soul troubled? For this reason, namely, so that remembrance of you may be established among both peoples, Jews and Gentiles.”

He says it as follows: “I shall remember you,” that is, “I shall cause you to be remembered,” both among those from the land of the Jordan—which can be taken historically as referring to those who inhabited the land of promise around the Jordan—and also mystically.

Jordan is interpreted as “descent.” Only those among that people remember God who descend, that is, humble themselves for the grace of baptism and for the mortification signified there, according to the saying: “As many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were buried with him in death.”

And I shall remember you, that is, I shall cause you to be remembered, among those from the land of Hermoniim. Hermon is interpreted as “anathema.” Since they worshiped not the Creator but the creature, and even the work of the creature, such as handmade idols, they needed not only humiliation but also to anathematize themselves most fully in their former condition and renounce the devil.

“I shall remember you,” I say, “from the land of Hermoniim,” with remembrance proceeding from the little mountain—that is, from those among the Gentiles who will be converted. They will be a mountain through the excellence of their virtues and yet little, that is, humble.

The abyss calls to the abyss. They and these will truly remember you, because “the abyss,” that is, the profound thinkers among the Jews, “calls,” that is, calls into itself, the abyss—that is, the profound thinkers among the Gentiles—because they strive to incorporate and form them within themselves in faith.

This occurs “at the voice,” that is, in the manifestation and exposition, of your cataracts.

Alternatively, the statement “the abyss calls to the abyss” was foretold “at the voice of the cataracts,” that is, of the prophets. Cataracts are properly hidden channels through which water runs. Therefore the prophets are rightly understood by cataracts: they are hidden in their Scriptures, through whose coverings and veils they reveal heavenly things.

All your heights. The abyss therefore calls to the abyss, or this can therefore happen, because by my death I destroyed the death of my people. He says equivalently:

“All your heights”—that is, every eternal condemnation that you inflicted upon human beings on account of their sins—and “your waves,” that is, the punishments of sin, which indeed came and remained upon Adam, but, coming upon me through the judgment of my enemies who thought me impure and eternally condemned, passed over—that is, perished—in my death.

They have already perished partly in reality, namely with respect to sins, and partly in hope, namely with respect to the punishments of sin.

He calls eternal condemnation and sins “heights” because they are heavy, just as something falling from a height causes more serious injury.

But so that wicked people, hearing that sins and the punishments of sin have passed away, might not promise themselves hope whatever evil they might do, he adds:

By day the Lord commanded. It is as though he said: “I say that they have passed away.” By what means, and in exchange for what, have they passed away? By this, namely, if they attend to the fact that the Lord’s mercy is present by day and his song by night, which the Lord himself commanded through me.

Or the passage can be connected simply in this way: “The heights and waves have indeed passed away; and, in order that they might pass away, the Lord the Father commanded through me.” That is, I perform this embassy among human beings, and the Lord made this known through me: his mercy is by day.

That is, whatever one possesses in the day—whether progress in virtue or prosperity in this life—is not from one’s own merit but from his sole mercy. Therefore no one should presume upon himself but should humble himself before him alone.

He also made this known through me: his song must be sung in the night, that is, in adversity. The person who sings the Lord’s song in the night is the one who does not fail but glories in tribulation.

Prayer with me. Since the Lord’s song must be sung in the night, therefore the song is with me, not departing from me, sung to God the Father, the author of my life—that is, the one who makes me perfect in such charity that I even pray for my enemies, and thus truly live.

For just as hating an enemy is death—because “whoever hates his brother is a murderer,” that is, kills himself—so loving an enemy and praying for him is life.

He says what that song is: prayer made by me for my future enemies, when I said, “Father, forgive them.”

Prayer is truly with me, because in praying I say to God concerning my people: “Lord, you are the protector.” I do not say “of my people,” but, out of my great affection for them, I say “my protector.” This means: “Lord, it is your task to protect my people; therefore let your mercy and truth protect them.”

Why have you forgotten me? Since you are the protector of my people, why have you forgotten—as it appears—because of the tribulation they suffer? I do not say “of my people,” but, because of my excessive affection, I say “of me.”

And why do I go about sad among my people while my enemy afflicts me, because of sin, according to what Isaiah says in the person of the Lord: “I made every breath,” that is, every soul; “but because of sin I troubled him somewhat,” and did not condemn him utterly.

He has now become sad and has gone away sorrowful in his ways. When he says, “while my enemy afflicts me,” understand it in this way: The enemy afflicts, and the wretched human being often fails because he is overcome.

Or, even if he does not fail, nevertheless, under the pressure of persistent tribulations, persecutions, and oppressive temptations, he fears continual danger on account of sin; he fears a fall, so that the one who stands may take care not to fall.

Why am I sad?

While my bones are broken. I am therefore rightly sad among my people, because my enemies—that is, the enemies of my people—not those who lie in wait but those who trouble me, that is, my people, reproached me outwardly and inflicted many insults upon me among my people.

This happened while my bones were being broken, that is, those among my people who are firmer and stronger in tribulation.

Some are broken through sin, like Peter, who denied Christ at the voice of a maidservant. Others, even though they are not broken through sin, nevertheless seem to be broken because of the tribulation they suffer.

While they say to me every day. I am truly reproached in this way: they say to me—that is, to my people—for contempt, every day, that is, continually:

“Where is your God?” That is, what counsel or help does your God, whom you are always boasting about, provide for you? None, certainly.

Why are you sad, my soul? Here he returns to what was said above, as though he said: Since such great things are destined to occur through you, my soul—namely, that both Jews and Gentiles will remember the Lord, that some will bodily lead others to goodness, and the other things already mentioned—why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?

This is for the benefit of my people, as was said above. Do not be sad, I say; do not be troubled. Hope only in God, attributing nothing to yourself and presuming nothing concerning yourself, because “I shall yet confess to him,” and so forth.

He says this for the exhortation of his people, as though he said: “You who are mine, imitate me by hoping in the Lord. Do not presume upon yourselves, because nothing is in you or from you; rather, hope in God for what you truly ought to hope.”

For it remains that you will confess to him, both through yourselves and through others who say to him: “The salvation of my countenance, and my God,” as explained above.

## Psalm XLII

A psalm of David.

### Argument

The people, as above. Alternatively, the voice of the Church speaks to those who have received the faith from Christ.

### Explanation

David signifies Christ, to whom this psalm is directed from the person of the most faithful Christian. Just as the preceding psalm teaches that everything must be despised out of love for the Lord, so this one warns that, lest the world’s tribulation overwhelm us, we should rejoice in the courts of the Lord.

This psalm suits every believer who, in its first part, entreats the Lord to free him from the company of unbelievers at the coming of the final judgment. In the second part he confidently declares that he will enter the Lord’s altar, where there is ascent only for the blessed. Therefore he says that his soul must not be troubled by the afflictions of this world, because he already glories in the heavenly gift.

### Commentary

Judge me, God. The title is as follows: “For the end; a psalm of David.” It is explained in this way: These words do not refer to history but “to the end,” because this is a psalm of David “for the end,” that is, the psalm is attributed to those things that pertain to the end, namely Christ.

The seed of Abraham, the holy seed, has been placed in the midst of evils: grain still pressed by chaff, wheat by weeds, wine by grape-skins. Considering what it still shares with the wicked—to live, hunger, thirst, keep watch, possess bodily health, enjoy the abundance of crops, and similar things—from which it must eventually be separated, it bursts into this utterance, wishing and sighing to be separated from them soon in place, from whom it has already been separated in cause.

“God, who will eventually judge me, judge me,” that is, do not delay judging; do not delay separating me from the wicked, among whom I am now mixed in place.

For I do not fear your judgment, as though he said, because I have known your mercy. Therefore I dare to say, “Judge me.” In the meantime, if you do not yet distinguish them in place, at least distinguish my cause from that of an unholy people, that is, from the wicked.

Let there be a difference, as though he said, between you who believe and those who do not believe; between you who hope and those who do not hope; between you who persevere and those who fail.

Their infirmity and ours are alike, but their conscience is different. Their labor is alike, but their desire is unequal, because “the desire of the wicked shall perish.” The desire of the good, however, is Christ, who remains forever, because just as he will show himself mortal to mortals, so he will show himself immortal to immortals.

Distinguish the cause now, I say, and at last rescue me also in place from the wicked man—that is, from every kind of wicked person who persuades others to love wicked things, namely earthly things—and from the deceitful man, who has the appearance of giving counsel but conceals poison for harm.

Since this rescue requires patience and perseverance, according to the saying, “Patience is necessary, so that we may receive the promise,” he adds:

For you are God my strength. It is as though he said: “Rescue me at last by giving me inward patience and perseverance now.”

I ask patience and perseverance from you because you, who are God and therefore alone strong, are my strength, not I. I am weakness to myself; you are health. I am weakness to myself; you are strength.

And since you are my strength, why have you rejected me, as you seem to have done through the tribulations I suffer? And why do I go about sad while my enemy afflicts me—that is, while I fear the enemy? Because of sin, for which you have troubled me somewhat. Hence I fear danger and fear falling, as was said above.

Send out your light and your truth. It is as though he said: “Lord, so that I may not be rejected, so that I may not go about sad, and so that I may not be afflicted by the enemy, send out your light and your truth,” that is, your Christ.

He is life and light according to the Word, because all things are illumined by him; and he is truth according to the man, because that man is nothing other than what had to be proclaimed. He said: “The one whom you have now hidden,” according to the saying: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”

Send him out, I say, without delay to judgment, so that he may separate me from the wicked; and thus I shall enter the altar of God.

Formerly the altar was in the more secret part of the Temple, into which only the high priest entered once a year, as the Apostle says. Here, however, the altar signifies that sublimity of divinity to which we shall then attain when we see God as he is.

Christ our high priest has already entered this altar bodily, having become a priest and continually interceding for us, so that we too may enter. That sublimity is called an altar because whoever enters there is taken up as a whole burnt offering, and there finds life if here he has had his cause distinguished.

He determines what this altar is. It is as though he said: “I shall enter the altar,” namely, God, that is, the presence of God, who makes my youth rejoice—that is, makes me renewed and changed from suffering to incapacity for suffering, from corruption and death to incorruption—and will make it rejoice eternally.

It is as though he said: “Let us hope for this reward, because we have already received its pledge.” He shows what the pledge is when he says:

They themselves have led me. The passage is connected in this way: “If you send out your light and your truth, I shall enter the altar,” because your light and truth have already led me—that is, led me from the kingdom of darkness into the kingdom of light.

They have led me, the seed of Abraham, that is, the body of the righteous, and from every direction—from the Gentiles and from the Jews—they have brought me into one thing, namely, your holy mountain, that is, the holy Church, which is called a mountain because of the excellence of its virtues and the steadfastness of its faith.

He defines what he calls the mountain: “They have brought me into your tabernacles,” that is, into the ecclesiastical ordinances. In them we must serve for a time as in a tabernacle, so that afterward we may rejoice eternally.

I will confess to you on the lyre. I say, “I will enter the altar of God,” but I will not enter unless I first play the lyre for him. Therefore, in order that I may enter, I will confess to you—that is, I will praise you on the lyre, namely, by rejoicing in tribulation and by doing good works—which I ought to do, because you are my God.

There are two musical instruments that signify our works, differing from one another in this respect: the psalterium and the lyre. One gives its sound from above, the other from below. The psalterium, which sounds from above, signifies those works of ours that we perform without vexation and tribulation, such as those performed by people engaged in contemplation—for example, the praise of the holy angels, who continually say: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.” The lyre, however, which sounds from below, signifies the good works that we perform while we are still placed in active life and tribulation, which proceeds from what is inferior in us [Col. 0708C]. If we persevere patiently there, that very patience is like a sweet melody to God.

Therefore we must take care not to break our lyre through impatience. For if we fail through our impatience, behold, we break our lyre and cease from divine praise.

Why are you sad, my soul? Since, my soul, you are destined to come to such dignity that you will enter the altar of God and rejoice eternally, why are you sad, and why do you trouble me? Because of sin, certainly, on account of which you fear danger and fear falling. But who speaks here, and to whom? The superior speaks to the inferior—that is, reason to sensuality—not soul to flesh. For sadness belongs to the soul, whereas pain belongs to the flesh.

Hope in God. “Do not,” I say, “become sad; do not become troubled, but hope in God”—that is, presume nothing from yourself, since nothing exists from you or in you; rather, be willing to hope in God, through whom you are whatever you are. Therefore I say, “Hope in God,” because, even if I do not now confess to him, there will nevertheless come a time when I shall confess to him fully—that is, praise him—namely, when I enter his altar.

And truly I shall confess to him, because he who is my God is also my physician. He says this as follows: “He is the salvation”—that is, the Savior—“of my countenance.” For if there is any perverse will or affection in me, he himself saves and purifies it. And he can rightly do this, because he is my God—that is, the one whom I make mine through submission and will.

This psalm can also be read in another way, so that the title is understood as follows: “These words are referred to the end,” because they are the psalm of the true David, that is, of Christ. For Christ speaks in this psalm, praying to the Lord the Father that he whom the Father does not distinguish in punishment, he may distinguish through the glorification of resurrection in the matter of his cause; and that he whom his enemies judge guilty, he himself may judge innocent.

He exhorts us, following his example, not to fear the unjust judgments of human beings, but to await the just judgment of God, and to strive at last to attain his sublimity, and to be seen innocent by him, while meanwhile we play the lyre for him.

He says as follows: “God the Father, my enemies judge what is unjust and what pleases them concerning me; but you, by your just judgment and according to what pleases you, judge me. They judge me guilty; judge me innocent. And if you do not distinguish me in punishment, at least distinguish my cause from an unholy nation”—that is, glorify me through resurrection. For through the resurrection it became evident that he had a just cause.

“Judge me,” I say, “and deliver me”—that is, my people—“from a wicked and deceitful man,” as above, so that they may not be led astray by them. Therefore I say that you should judge me and deliver me, because you are the God of my strength and of my people. Why, then, have you rejected me?”—as it appears, because of the tribulations that I suffer. “And why do I walk sorrowfully while the enemy afflicts me?” For the great benefit of my people. For this reason you rejected me, and for this reason I walk sorrowfully: so that you may send forth your light and your truth.

And you, Lord, send me forth from the enclosure of the Jewish people [Col. 0709B], and make me known to the nations, me who am your light and your truth. I am light because of the Word; truth because I commanded nothing except what ought to be commanded—namely, the truth.

Therefore I say that you should send forth your light and your truth, because that light of divinity which is in me, and the truth of the commandments given through me, will lead me—“led” being used prophetically in place of “will lead,” according to prophetic usage—that is, they will lead me from the sheep of the earlier people to the sheep of the later people, namely, to the nations. And thus they will bring me together from every direction to establish one thing, namely, to establish your holy mountain—that is, the Church. And they will bring me into your tabernacles—that is, to the knowledge of those perfected people who are to serve you as soldiers from both peoples.

And I will enter the altar of God. “I shall be led,” I say, “and I shall be brought in.” And this will happen because I shall ascend and send the Holy Spirit. He intimates this when he says: “I will enter the altar”—that is, I shall ascend and enter into the sublimity of the presence of God the Father. I shall enter to God the Father in order to sit at his right hand, and he will make glad my youth—that is, the freedom from sin that is in me—by granting immortality and incorruption. After this, as though he were saying, “I shall send the Holy Spirit,” and thus I shall be led and brought in.

Nevertheless, before I enter, I must play the lyre. Therefore, O God, I will confess to you—that is, I will praise you—because you are my God; on the lyre—that is, in the mortification of the flesh.

And you also—as though he were saying this to us—if you wish to enter, play the lyre.

Why are you sad, my soul? As though he were saying: “Since such great glory is destined for me, that I shall both be led and brought into the holy mountain, and that I shall enter the altar of God, why then are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” On account of my people, certainly, not on my own account.

Therefore do not become sad, but hope in God—hope, namely, that the effect for which he willed you to be assumed by his Word may be brought about. “For I shall yet confess to him,” and so forth. This is to be explained in the same way as in the preceding psalm.

# ON PSALM XLIII

*To the end; for the sons of Korah; for understanding.*

[Col. 0709D]

## ARGUMENT

The prophet recalls the afflictions and supplications of the Maccabees. It is also to be read as a confession (*exomologesis*) in connection with Paul’s Epistle to the Romans.

## EXPLANATION

As was said above, the sons of Korah are the sons of the cross—that is, martyrs or confessors—who in this psalm complain to the Lord that the ancient saints easily dominated their enemies, whereas they themselves acquired victories through the most grievous punishments of martyrdom.

“For understanding” is rightly added, because a higher understanding is needed to discern that, by the dispensation of one and the same Creator, formerly the uneducated peoples were summoned to faith by earthly gifts, and the land of Canaan was given to them as an inheritance. Now, however, as faith has increased and the gate of the heavenly kingdom has been opened, Christ’s soldiers must be approved through a greater struggle, lest they wish to remain longer in this life and seek heavenly goods with insufficient zeal.

Whether you receive these as the words of martyrs or of confessors, in the first part they say that they heard that their fathers were victorious over many nations, whereas they themselves will see vengeance upon their enemies at the future judgment. These enemies will be conquered not by bow or sword, but by the Lord’s own judgment.

In the second part they enumerate the torments of the various necessities that they suffer in the world, and they remember that amid these things they persevere in God.

In the third, they pray for assistance, so that those who are now grievously afflicted may be helped at the time of the resurrection.

## COMMENTARY

We have heard, O God, with our ears. The title is as follows: “A psalm for the end, for the sons of Korah, for understanding.” That is: This psalm is referred to the end because it is sung by certain sons of Korah—that is, by certain imitators of Christ’s passion, namely, by the holy martyrs, earlier sons of Korah, for the understanding of other future sons of Korah.

For the counsel of God is a matter of great consideration and profundity: namely, why, when he led our fathers, the sons of Israel, out of Egypt with such a powerful hand and an outstretched arm through manifest signs, and destroyed all their pursuing enemies in the Red Sea, and granted them great and incredible victories despite their small number of soldiers, he treats the later people—namely, the true Israelites—as though they had offended him, as though he had despised them, as though he had forgotten them, as though he were not the same God.

But because this does not happen without a reason, the title does not simply say, “For the sons of Korah”; it adds, “for understanding”—namely, so that they may understand that they have not been abandoned or forgotten. God therefore takes away from them what they wrongly desired, in order to teach them what they ought rightly to desire.

For if he were always present with them and favorable to them amid the prosperity of this life, and never mixed any adversities into it, they would think that these things were the highest goods and would not ask him for better things. Therefore bitterness is mixed into this falsely sweet life, so that what is truly sweet may be sought.

Let us therefore hear the psalm, so that we may understand these same things in the psalm [Col. 0710C].

This son of Korah, who speaks in this psalm, wondering why God seems to have abandoned those whom he willed to test through tribulations in these times, recalls past times and announces future ones. He speaks as though saying: “Lord, we have heard such things from our fathers about the past, and such things about the future; but in the meantime we suffer things very different.” He begins as follows:

“Lord God, we have heard with our ears”—that is, attentively—“because our fathers announced to us in their Scriptures your work, which you performed not by them but by yourself, in their days”—namely, in the days of our immediate fathers—“and in ancient days”—that is, in the time of the ancient and earlier fathers.

And what was that work? This: “Your hand”—that is, your power—“destroyed the nations. And you planted them”—namely, our fathers—“in the place of the nations.”

And truly you destroyed the nations, because you afflicted many peoples with slaughter—namely, the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, and the others. Those whom you did not afflict by slaughter, you expelled from their land, and you brought our fathers in [Col. 0710D].

For not by their own sword. As though he were saying: “Did you do this for our fathers because they were more numerous and stronger than we?” Certainly not. For they possessed that land—the land of promise—not by their sword, that is, by their own power. And their arm—that is, their strength—did not save them, but your right hand—that is, your favor and graciousness.

And your arm—that is, your Son—and the light of your countenance—that is, the fact that you were present with them through such manifest signs that you were understood to be present with them—this, I say, saved them. And this was because you took pleasure in them—that is, because it pleased you to do so in them.

Thus, in many things, you chose to act toward them in such a way that it could be said: “The Lord acts on behalf of these people; the Lord governs these people.”

You are the same. As though he were saying: “The times have indeed changed, but you have not changed, because you are the same. You are my king”—that is, you rule me—“and you are my God”—that is, my Creator.

You, I say, who command—“commanded” is intended—salvation for Jacob: for the earlier people you commanded bodily salvation, not through your own proper substance, by which you are whatever you are, hidden, but through a creature subject to you—namely, through angels and prophets.

For this later Jacob, however, the spiritual Jacob, you command spiritual salvation through your Wisdom—that is, through your Son—according to the words: “In many parts and in many ways God formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son.”

In you we shall scatter our enemies. As though he were saying: “The things stated above were spoken to us by our fathers concerning the past. The things that follow were spoken to us by those same fathers concerning the future: that we shall scatter”—that is, separate from ourselves at the final winnowing—“our enemies in you, the horn”—that is, through our protector.

For certain animals customarily protect themselves with horns; therefore “horn” is used for defense. Or “in you, the horn” means through the one by whom we also are a horn. For a horn is born from flesh, grows above the flesh, and hardens into something other than flesh. Therefore holy men are signified by the horn: they surpass carnality and harden into spiritual strength.

“We shall scatter,” I say, “our enemies, and we shall utterly despise those who rise up against us”—that is, those who now rise up against us, striving to impose their own form upon us. “And I shall glorify in your name.”

And truly, it is in your name, not in our merits. “For”—used in place of “because”—“I shall not hope in my bow” any more than the father hoped in his sword. And “my sword will not save me,” which means: I shall not be saved through any merits of my own. By the bow, which strikes less powerfully than the sword, lesser merits are signified; by the sword, greater ones.

For you saved us. Truly my sword will not save me, because you alone saved us—“will save us” is intended—from those who afflict us. Conversely, you confounded—“will confound” is intended—those who hate us, saying to them: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.”

In God we shall be praised. As though he were saying: “You will save us in this way, because we shall be praised”—that is, we shall appear praiseworthy—not in our merits, but in you, God, all day long, namely, where there will be an entire day, a day without night, because it will be without end.

“And we shall confess to you”—that is, praise you—“forever,” that is, eternally; and this by glorifying your name.

But now, as though he were saying: “These things concerning the past have been told to us, and future things have been announced. In the time between them, however, we suffer things very different, because you have rejected us”—that is, you seem to have rejected us—“and confounded us”—that is, made us objects of confusion. And this is because you do not go forth with our armies.”

As though he were saying: “We go out to battle against heretics and persecutors, and you do not appear to go out with us, because you allow us to be overcome in the body. But you went out with our fathers, because you granted them such manifest victories that you truly appeared to go out with them.”

You turned us back. I say that you go out with us for this reason: you turned us back—that is, you permitted some of us to be turned backward—to such an extent that they are behind our enemies; that is, the enemies go ahead and they follow, because they have been led astray and conformed to their enemies.

Therefore those who hate us plundered us—that is, they seized certain of us like prey in order to conform us to themselves. Nor is this surprising, because you gave us—or permitted us to be given—to our enemies for devouring like sheep, not reserved for fertility but destined for food and slaughter.

And you scattered us among the nations—that is, you permitted us to be scattered, some through being led astray, others through persecution, with the nations serving as the occasion of it.

And you sold your people for no price. That is, you were comparable to someone who proposes to sell something and receives nothing in return. For we have seen those whom you gave; we have not seen those whom you received. And if you received any, there was no multitude in this exchange, because those whom you received were few. You gave the precious martyr Stephen and received no one.

In this way you made us a reproach to our neighbors—namely, to the false Christians who are called fellow believers with us. And you made us a mockery and, what is more, a derision to those who are around us—that is, to the nations that surround us on every side [Col. 0712A].

You made us a likeness. Truly you made us a derision, because you made us a likeness to the nations—that is, you caused us to appear among the nations accursed and abominable. For those who curse customarily bring forward as a likeness those whom they regard as abominable, saying to someone: “May you perish as that wicked man perished.”

And you made us a shaking of the head among the peoples—that is, so that those who insult us may shake their heads against us just as they did against Christ, our head.

All day long there is shame. As though he were saying: “Because of all the things mentioned above, my shame is against me”—that is, in their estimation, before me—all day long, that is, continually.

And the confusion of my face covered me—that is, it appears to them that I am covered with great confusion. It comes from the voice”—that is, on account of the voice—“of one reproaching me with the crimes of him through whom I believe all my sins are erased.”

For he reproaches me with Christ crucified, mocked, and despised. And it comes from the voice of one speaking abusively—that is, contradicting the truth. It comes, I say, from the face of an enemy who not only contradicts—that is, contradicts the truth—but also persecutes—that is, stretches out his hand against me.

All these things have come. He has narrated what was spoken concerning the past, what was announced concerning the future, and what he suffers in the intervening time. Now he shows what he suffers being done to him “for understanding,” saying as follows:

“All the things that were foretold for these intervening times have come upon us. Nevertheless, we have not forgotten you, Lord, despite the many things we suffer, knowing—as was said in the title—that what we wrongly desired is being taken away from us so that we may understand what we ought rightly to desire.

And truly we have not forgotten you, because we have not acted wickedly”—that is, unfaithfully—“in your covenant”—that is, in your pact. For a rational creature has a pact with the Creator, and a faithful servant with the Lord: namely, to deny himself as far as he can, renounce the devil, despise earthly things, and love heavenly things.

And it did not turn back. Truly we have not acted wickedly in the covenant, because our heart did not turn away from you so as to go backward. For it does not look back at what is behind, but is always stretched toward what lies ahead.

And this is because you turned our paths away from your way—that is, you caused our paths to be cut off from and diverted away from your way. For our paths were in the pleasures of the flesh and the desires for earthly things. Therefore we were walking along the broad way that leads to destruction and by which many go.

But you taught us to walk along the narrow way that leads to life. As though he were saying: “Where are you going? That way leads to death. Therefore do not go there; go this way, because this way leads to life.”

Some books read: “You did not turn aside,” which is understood as follows: “You did not twist our paths away from your way; rather, you directed them according to your way.”

And truly you directed our paths according to your way, because you humbled us—that is, you taught us to be humble—as you too were humbled in the place of affliction, that is, in the pilgrimage of this life, in which there is a time of affliction, after which a time of exaltation follows.

You humbled us, I say, to such an extent that you even willed us to be killed, because the shadow of death covered us—that is, the present death, which is a shadow, that is, a likeness, of eternal death. For the separation of the body from this life represents for us the separation of the wicked from true life, that is, from God.

Or it may be understood simply as follows: “The shadow of death covered us”—that is, the wicked, wishing to overshadow us, oppressed us unto death [Col. 0712D].

If we have forgotten. This is connected with what precedes as follows: We have not forgotten God because, if we had done so, he would rightly take vengeance upon us. He says this as follows:

“If we have forgotten the name of our God, and to such an extent that we have spread out our hands to a strange god”—that is, if we worship idols—“will not God investigate this with just vengeance against us?” Certainly he will investigate it, because he knows the hidden things of the heart—that is, he knows all hidden things—to such an extent that he is also the scrutinizer of the marrow and thoughts.

But it is evident from this that we have not forgotten him, because we are being put to death for you all day long.

The preceding verse, “If we have forgotten,” can also be read through aposiopesis as follows: “Truly, Lord, we have not forgotten you. For if we have forgotten the name of our God, and if we have spread out our hands to a strange god”—as though he were saying: “Let all evils come upon us.”

And as though someone might say: “Is God therefore unjust, since he does not avenge us, who remember him in this way, upon our enemies?” He replies: “Certainly he is not unjust, because he will exact from our enemies, by a fitting vengeance, those things that they inflict upon us. And will he not exact them?” Certainly he will, because he knows all the hidden things of the heart.

From this he also knows our intention: we suffer this not for an empty name, but for his sake. It is as though he were saying: “There have not been lacking, Lord, those who underwent death for the sake of the glorious name of this world. But you know that we are put to death all day long for no other reason than you. And we have been regarded by our enemies as so worthless that we are to be killed like sheep not reserved for fertility but for slaughter” [Col. 0713B].

Rise up; why do you sleep, Lord? As though he were saying: “Since we are put to death for your sake, rise up, Lord, so that you may become known to the nations.” This means: “You slept, Lord, on the cross; you slept, Lord, in death. But for us who believe in your resurrection, you have already risen; for the unbelieving nations who persecute us, however, you are still sleeping.

Therefore rise up for them so that you may become known—that is, so that they may believe that you have risen. For if you rise up for them, our being put to death will cease.

Why do you sleep for the nations? Rise up, I say, so that you who now appear to have rejected us through the tribulation we suffer may not also reject us forever—that is, with complete rejection.

A person is rejected with complete rejection when, fearing bodily punishments, he is led astray and joined to the wicked.

Why [your] face? I say, “Do not reject us forever,” because you turn away—that is, appear to have turned away—your face from us. And why do you turn away? He shows how you turn away: “You forget”—that is, you appear to have forgotten—“our poverty,” that is, our lowliness, by which we make ourselves altogether poor, presuming nothing from ourselves.

Therefore you forget our poverty—that is, you forget our tribulation, which always threatens us with tribulation [Col. 0713C].

Because our soul has been humbled in the dust. Truly you forget our poverty, because our soul—that is, our life—has been humbled in the dust, that is, among those who are that dust of which it is said: “Which the wind drives away from the face of the earth.”

And it has been greatly humbled, because our belly has been glued to the earth. This is said by way of likeness. For someone who is humbled so as to kneel still has some further degree to which he can be humbled. But someone whose belly is so humbled that it is glued to the earth—that is, joined to it—has no further degree to which he can be humbled. Therefore the phrase is used here for extreme humility or humiliation [Col. 0713D].

These two verses can also be read in another way, so that they mean: “Truly you turn your face away, because you forget our poverty”—that is, our poor people.

For just as in the body of Christ the perfect men are called abundance and riches, so, conversely, in that same body those who are liable to be led astray and overcome are called poverty. God forgets these people when they are led astray. But because the perfect men grieve and are distressed on their behalf, he adds:

“And you forget our tribulation”—that is, you also forget those perfect people among us who grieve for them. I say this because our soul—that is, those who are animal and more imperfect—has been humbled, so that they are already in the dust, among those who are that dust which the wind drives away from the face of the earth.

And this is why our belly—that is, the softer among us—has been glued, that is, joined, to the earth, because they have been conformed to the wicked, who are that earth which is the food of the serpent, that is, of the devil. Therefore those who are perfect rightly suffer tribulation on their behalf.

Rise up, then, Lord, and make our innocence known to the nations, because by rising up you will help us. Therefore help and redeem us, whether we are still placed in prosperity—that is, not yet led astray—or afflicted in adversity—that is, already led astray. And do this now not for the sake of our merits, but for the glorification of your name.

# ON PSALM XLIV

*To the end; for those who will be changed; for the sons of Korah; for understanding; a song for the beloved.*

## ARGUMENT

The prophet speaks about Christ to the Church. It is to be read in connection with the Gospel of Matthew concerning the Queen of the South.

## EXPLANATION

“To the end” designates the Lord the Savior; “for those who will be changed” refers to those who will be changed from error to faith, from paganism to the Church, from the struggle of martyrdom to the palm of victory, and from the sadness of the world to everlasting joy.

“For the sons of Korah, for understanding” means: for the sons of the cross, so that they may understand the psalm spiritually and not think that it is to be interpreted of Solomon, although Solomon too is beloved and has taken up a song for the beloved Son to whom it is said: “This is my beloved Son.”

Having been filled with heavenly banquets, the prophet promises to pour forth the praises of the Lord’s Incarnation, so that others may share in what has satisfied him.

The first part of this epithalamium contains praises of the bridegroom—that is, of the Lord the Savior—in four ways. In the second, the Church, the bride, is praised through a similar number of mystical virtues.

## COMMENTARY

My heart has poured forth a good word. This psalm is sung of a holy wedding: of bridegroom and bride, of king and people, of the Savior and those who are to be saved.

It is sung for the sons of Korah—that is, for the bald. This nevertheless must not be understood mockingly, lest we be found to possess a childish sense, like those children who, foolishly chattering and cursing to their own destruction, shouted after the holy man Elisha: “Go up, baldhead!” Two bears came out of the forest and devoured them.

These children signify people who possess a mind ignorant of understanding, such as the Apostle also wishes us to be when he says: “Do not become children in your understanding; in evil be children, so that in understanding you may be perfect.”

Nevertheless, the Lord exhorts us to imitate children, saying in the Gospel: “Unless you become like this little child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” Whoever therefore delights in imitating a child should not delight in ignorance, but in innocence.

Through their ignorance those children shouted after the holy man and were devoured by beasts. They prefigured foolish people, children in the same state of mind, who mocked someone bald, crucified in the place of the skull; and therefore they were devoured by beasts—that is, by the devil and his angels, who work in the sons of disobedience.

Such children were those who stood before the sacred wood of the cross, shook their heads, and said: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God”; and: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross,” and similar things.

We are the sons of this mocked man, because we are the sons of Christ—that is, the sons of the crucified one.

This psalm is sung for us. Its title is: “To the end, for the sons of Korah, for those who will be changed, for understanding; a song for the beloved.”

Each son of Korah understands this change of which the psalm sings if he recognizes what he was formerly and what he is now. First, let him see the whole world changed: formerly worshiping idols, now worshiping the Creator; formerly serving creatures, now serving the Creator. Then let him see himself made new from old, chaste from unchaste, pious from impious, faithful from unbelieving, generous from a robber.

In this way he understands that this psalm is sung for the sons of Korah, for those who will be changed, for understanding. And it is a song for the beloved.

Here he now determines through whom this change takes place: through the beloved, that is, the bridegroom, whom this psalm specially presents as beloved by the Father.

When they crucified this beloved, they saw him, but without understanding, because, fevered and delirious, they did not recognize the physician. For if they had known him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

Let us therefore rejoice in this wedding, because we are the ones who are marrying, we are invited to this wedding, and we belong to it. For we are those who are being changed and have been changed. The Church, which is the bride, is present at this wedding.

The psalm is called a song because in ancient times certain songs used to be sung for those who led a bride to marriage and for those who married. Whatever praise, honor, and glory such songs contained belonged to the bridegroom and the bride.

Such a song was called an epithalamium, because it was “over the bridal chamber”—that is, concerning a wedding. Similarly, this psalm is called a song and an epithalamium, a song over the bridal chamber. For here are the bridegroom, the bride, and the bridal chamber.

The bridegroom who comes to the wedding is the Word who “in the beginning was with God, and the Word was God.”

The bride who marries is the Church, whom that Word joined to himself through the humanity he assumed. The bridal chamber of this marital union is the virgin’s womb, in which, as has been said, through the human nature he assumed, the Word of God joined the Church to himself and loved her when she was ugly, in order to make her beautiful.

Let the bridegroom therefore come forth, described by one of his praisers: “Beautiful everywhere, just everywhere.” And if we find anything ugly in him, let us not love him, even though he himself loved us when we were ugly, in order to make us beautiful.

The title is to be constructed as follows: “This song is to be referred to the end,” because it deals with the end; it was sung for the beloved—that is, for the honor and praise of the bridegroom who is specially beloved; it was proposed to the sons of Korah, for those who will be changed—that is, on account of the change made in themselves—for understanding, namely, so that they may understand both that they have been changed and that this change did not come from themselves or from elsewhere, but through the beloved.

Now let us approach the literal meaning.

It is asked whose voice is speaking in this psalm. Some say it is the voice of the prophet; others understand it as the voice of the Father saying: “My heart has poured forth,” and so forth. Through these words the Father commends to us a certain ineffable birth and an indescribable generation, lest we think that something was taken from outside so that the Word might be generated from it.

Human beings customarily take wives in marriage and beget children from them. Therefore, lest we think that God the Father took a wife for himself or needed some external assistance in generating the Word, he says: “My heart has poured forth a good word.”

And since he did not have words by which he could properly explain this ineffable reality to us—for sacred Scripture, when it speaks of the highest and most excellent things, customarily draws likenesses from lowly things, through which our mind may be drawn from visible things to invisible things—God the Father, speaking by means of a likeness, begins profoundly by saying: “My heart pours forth a good word.”

For those who pour forth breath emit it from below. The heart, however, is something truly inward and hidden. Hence the sense is as though he were saying: “My heart”—that is, my innermost substance, by which I am whatever I am while remaining hidden—“has poured forth”—that is, has ineffably generated from itself—“a good word.”

Nor is it surprising that the Father speaks of the Word as poured forth from the innermost heart, since each of us also generates counsel from his heart without needing a wife or external assistance.

For when you are about to build something, you generate counsel from your heart. And the structure that does not yet exist in the building already stands in the plan. What you are going to make is already present in that by which you will make it.

You already praise a building that does not yet exist, in hope of the building but in approval of the plan. Yet no one else praises your building until your plan has either been explained or seen through its execution.

Therefore, if all things were made through the Word, and if the Word is from God, look upon the structure made through the Word, and in this work of craftsmanship marvel at the plan—that is, at the Word.

For what sort of Word is it through which earth, sea, heaven, and all their adornment were made? “All things were made through him,” as the Gospels testify. And they were made good because he himself is good.

The Father, therefore, speaks of his good and beneficent Word, through which alone we can in any way be good: “My heart has poured forth a good Word.” By adding “good” he shows that the Word is substantial, coequal, and coeternal with him. For “no one is good except God alone.”

Therefore, if the Word is good and the Word is God, I say: “I speak my works to the king.” This is a repetition of what came before. For to speak is to generate a word from the heart.

Blessed Augustine says in this passage:

“I fear that this will not be understood by those who are slower of understanding; nevertheless, I shall speak. Let whoever can follow, lest what has been said remain without a follower, and let whoever can follow. Attend, then, to how speaking itself is to generate the Word from the heart. For what is ‘I speak’? I bring forth a word. And when the Father says of himself, ‘I speak this,’ ‘I speak’ means: ‘I bring forth the Word.’ And if the Father brings forth the Word from the heart—that is, from the understanding—when he himself is entirely that understanding, he brings it forth, just as we bring forth our word from our heart, though our word is light and fleeting.”

Nevertheless, there is a great difference between our speaking and the Father’s speaking. Our speaking begins and quickly passes away; the speaking of God the Father has no beginning and lacks an end, because it never comes to an end.

Therefore it is not called a second word, but God spoke only once. For if both what is spoken and the one by whom it is spoken always remain, it must not be called a second word, because it is always the first.

Therefore there is only one Word, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father.

Why, then, does he say: “I speak my works to the king”? For this reason: all the works of the Father were in the Word. Whatever he was going to make in the creature had entirely preceded it in the Word.

For if it were not in the Word, it would not exist in the creature, just as nothing exists in your building that was not first in the plan.

Hence the Evangelist says: “What was made in him was life.” Therefore what was made existed, but it existed in the Word.

All the works of the Father were in the Word; yet they were not still works—they were the Word. And the Word was God, and the same Word was God with the Father, in whom are the things that have been made for us. The things that have passed away from us have not passed away from him.

In this interpretation the text is understood as follows: “I speak my works to the king”—that is, from the innermost heart I pour forth a good word. Through “I speak” we have “I pour forth from the heart”; through “works,” the Word, because all the works of the Father have existed eternally in the Word; through “king,” the good one. Thus it is plainly a repetition of what came before.

**My tongue.** Since someone had explained the depth through inappropriate comparisons, he therefore introduces another comparison to explain the same matter, one somewhat clearer, saying: “My tongue,” etc. He takes the cause for the effect—namely, the tongue for the word that has been uttered, and the pen of a scribe for the word that has been written. But what similarity does the Father’s Word have to a scribe’s word? What similarity does a rock have to Christ, a lamb to God’s simplicity, or a lion to God’s strength? Very little, certainly. Yet it is the custom of Sacred Scripture, because it cannot properly explain things of the greatest height, to introduce comparisons from lowly things in order to explain them—comparisons indeed slight, but not to be despised. For unless this were done, our mind would never be restored through visible things and raised toward invisible things. Therefore, when God the Father explains his Word through this comparison, he did not wish to compare it with a spoken but with a written word. In this he has two, though improper, points of similarity: just as a written word neither sounds nor passes away, so the Word of God neither sounds through struck air nor passes away, but always remains, as was said above.

The wording is explained and connected in the Father’s voice as follows: “My heart,” I say, “has poured forth a good Word. And my tongue”—that is, my Word—“is the pen of a scribe”; that is, it can be compared to the written word of a writer, and not of just any scribe, but of one who writes swiftly. For the Word of God is swifter than all things, because “his word runs swiftly,” reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly. No scribe, however swift, is so fast that he does not have to write letter after letter, syllable after syllable, and word after word. The Word of God, however, comprehends everything simultaneously. Therefore, if there were a writer so swift that he could grasp in the briefest instant whatever he was going to write, God’s Word could in some measure be compared with his written word. [Col. 0716D]

What we said above may also be read as repeated with reference to God, but without repetition, as though the Father, the Lord, were saying: “My heart has poured forth a good Word, and to this king”—that is, to this Word poured forth from my heart—“I declare all my works,” because through him I order and accomplish them temporally. Thus we shall not now understand the Father’s works in the Word with reference to providence, as in the preceding exposition, but with reference to temporal ordering.

**My tongue.** For this reason I say to this king, “my works,” because my tongue—that is, this Word—is to me what the pen is to a scribe. I use this Word as an instrument for governing what I accomplish temporally, just as a scribe records and arranges with a pen the word that he hears or discovers by thinking. It is, I say, the pen of a scribe—not of just any scribe, but of one who writes swiftly; that is, if there were such a scribe that he could write many things simultaneously in several places, my Word could be compared to that pen, since it orders many things at once. Whatever comes to pass, however disordered it may seem to us, nevertheless receives its order from that Word—that is, from God’s providence.

If someone should ask how the Father’s saying this about the Word pertains to the epithalamium, let him know that it pertains very greatly. For just as fathers commonly commend their sons whom they are giving in marriage, so God the Father, before presenting his Word to us as bridegroom, first commends him by his lineage, showing that he is consubstantial with himself, coeternal, and equal in power.

**Fair in form.** Here he is already treating him as bridegroom. It is as though he were saying: “You, Lord, the Word, proven by me, God the Father, to be God, and shown by me, who am coeternal with you, to be coeternal: fair Bridegroom, most powerful King, gird yourself with the sword, go forth prosperously, and reign.”

The two verses just mentioned can also be read in another way, since there were some who understood and expounded them as spoken in the person of the prophet, in accordance with what is plainly an epithalamium, which the prophet sings to the honor of the bridegroom and bride. It is as though he were saying: “My heart”—that is, the inmost intention of my whole heart and mind—“has poured forth,” that is, brought forth from above, “a good word,” that is, a hymn to God. For what is better than praising God? Certainly nothing. And although a hymn to God pertains to the whole of the good life, here it must be referred above all to the words of this epithalamium, which already serves for the praise of God by intention, even if not yet in reality, when he says, “has poured forth”: “My heart,” I say, “has poured forth a good word.”

In pouring it forth, I dedicate it—*dico* being used for *dedico*, “I dedicate”—to my king, that is, to God who governs me, so that my works may be changed from oldness into newness; that is, so that what I accomplish through this transformation may arise from human nature and not from corruption. This is to say: Whatever good I do, I attribute entirely to God and nothing to myself, which everyone ought to do. For the highest work is to presume nothing on one’s own behalf, but to ascribe everything to the Lord. [Col. 0717C]

**My tongue.** It is as though he were saying: “I arrange to speak a good word in my heart and bring it forth; and my tongue”—that is, my word—“is the pen of a scribe”; that is, it is written by me. This means: I bring forth a word so that it may remain and be made known, and I also write it. And this word is not only the word of my own scribe, but also the word of another scribe, namely, God the Father, who writes swiftly—that is, quickly fulfills what I, by bringing it forth and writing it, promise.

This means: Whatever I promise concerning the Incarnation, the ordering of his Son, and the transformation that is to be accomplished, God the Father does not delay fulfilling through him. For what is recognized as accomplished is perceived to have unfolded swiftly. Nor should anything that has an appointed end be thought slow.

**Fair in form above the sons of men.** It is as though he were saying: “I declare and write something good.” And this is that thing: “Fair in form,” and so forth.

**Gird yourself with the sword, and go forth, and the rest.** What follows does not differ whether it is read in the Father’s voice or in the prophet’s voice. But why does he say “above the sons of men” only, when he is also fair above the angels? The reason is that he wishes to specify what the coming bridegroom assumed. He did not assume an angelic creature—some of whom had perished without regard to salvation, while others persevered in truth without regard to deception—but he assumed human nature, because the human being had indeed perished, yet with the prospect of salvation.

Therefore God the Father, or the prophet, says: “Lord Word, although you are fair in the form of your divinity, you are also fair in the assumed form of your humanity, among the sons of men and above the sons of men.” For he was born among the sons of men and lived among the sons of men. He surpassed all the sons of men in beauty because he alone was free from sin. And because he did not receive the Spirit by measure, he ought immediately to add: “Gird yourself with your sword.” But he inserts certain remarks in praise of him.

It is as though he were saying: “You are rightly fair above the sons of men, because through you other human beings have been saved. For grace has been poured out broadly over all, upon your lips”—that is, through your words. Here the cause is taken for the effect. Or “upon your lips,” that is, through the presence of your humanity, according to which a part is placed for the whole. Or “upon your lips,” that is, through your heralds, through whom you speak to others as through lips.

This is to say: Harshness was given through Moses, your servant, who said, “An eye for an eye,” and so forth; but through you grace was given—that is, every sweetness and delight. For he came with the kiss of peace and the word of peace. What is sweeter than that grace by which our sins have been forgiven? In accordance with the saying: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven.” He forgave debts and paid what was not owed, because he suffered not for his own sin but for ours.

Here again is grace: he created you freely; when you had perished, he sought you; when he had found you, he recalled you. He did not count past things against you; he promised future things.
