And so that this grace might be spread through you, God the Father therefore blessed you—that is, increased you in the growth of virtues—“forever,” that is, eternally, so that you might never fall as wretched Adam did. God also blessed Adam, placing him in the fullness of virtue, but the unhappy man endured in it only for a time. [Col. 0718C]

**Gird yourself with your sword.** It is as though he were saying: “You, Lord Word, who are so fair, gird yourself, as the most powerful King, with your sword.” This sword is the word of divine preaching, with which the soul of the Lord’s man has been armed for defeating the aerial powers and shaking out the ruler of the world. This sword also separates son from father, daughter from mother, and daughter-in-law from mother-in-law, in accordance with the saying: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to separate a son against his father,” and so forth. Understood historically, this is clear. For often, through the admonition of the Word of God, a son abandons the world against his father’s will and becomes a monk.

It can also be understood spiritually in this way. Through this Word of God many believers have been made and separated from that father of whom it is said: “You are of your father the devil,” and they have renounced him. They have also been separated from that father and mother of whom it is said elsewhere: “For my father and my mother have forsaken me.” The daughter too is spiritually separated from her mother, because the daughter is the believing people born from the Synagogue, which resists its mother, the Synagogue, through faith.

The daughter-in-law, however, is the Church from the Gentiles, which resists its mother-in-law, the Synagogue, whose son is Christ the bridegroom according to the flesh. Of him it is said: “A man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife.” Hence the Apostle says: “This is a great sacrament, but I speak of Christ and the Church.” For Christ left God the Father through humility; he also left the Synagogue, his mother, which clung to the ancient sacraments; and he cleaved to his wife, that is, to the Church. “And the two are one flesh,” namely, Christ and the Church, suffering the same things and desiring the same things.

The wording is as follows: “Lord Word, gird yourself”—that is, arm yourself—“with your sword, so that it may be upon your thigh,” that is, upon your humility, to protect it. “That which is your thigh,” that is, your humanity; for above and more exalted than human nature is the Word. “You,” I say, “most powerful in that sword.” Hence it is said: “He was speaking not as the scribes and Pharisees, but as one having authority.”

It can also be constructed otherwise, so that it reads: “Gird yourself with your sword, you who are most powerful above your thigh,” that is, above your flesh. For no one is so powerful in the flesh that his own Eve does not at some time deceive him. Therefore he alone was most powerful over the flesh whom no carnal enticement could hold.

That the thigh, which is a part, may be understood as human flesh is established by the authority of the saying: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh,” that is, from his flesh. The holy father Abraham also, holding by faith the greatness of the name in the humility of his offspring, neither fearing shame nor failing to recognize the truth, commanded his servant, with his hand placed beneath his thigh, to swear—as though upon the Gospel—understanding by the thigh him who would be born carnally from his seed, in whom all the nations would be blessed. [Col. 0719B]

**In your appearance and beauty.** “Gird yourself,” I say, “and be intent”; that is, be intent in your appearance according to divinity, and in beauty according to humanity free from sin. Do not be negligent or have slack hands, as Adam was in his beauty—that is, in the fullness of virtue granted to him—and therefore lost it.

“And go forth from virtue to virtue,” not adversely but prosperously. Adam went forth when he reached out his hand toward the apple and wished to become like God; but he went forth adversely, because when he wished to be lord, he became a servant. Christ, however, went forth: he was born, grew, taught, suffered, rose again, ascended, and was placed at the right hand of God the Father. In this progress there was great prosperity, because instead of mortality he became immortal, and instead of corruption incorruptible.

**Reign.** It is as though he were saying: “Having defeated the enemies in your progress, recover the kingdom seized by them; and thus reign,” that is, be King everywhere. And it is just that you should reign because of the truth announced by you and by your people in the Gospel, and because of the meekness and patience displayed by you and by your people in tribulation.

For what greater patience is there than that Christ himself prayed for his enemies in his Passion and did not even open his mouth to curse, in accordance with the saying: “Like a sheep,” and so forth? Stephen likewise prayed for those who were stoning him, saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Many others did the same.

Hence it is said: “Because of your meekness and that of your people, and because of the righteousness already partly displayed by you and by your people and partly still to be displayed.” Righteousness follows judgment, in accordance with the saying: “I waited for him to perform judgment and righteousness.” Judgment is to separate what must be approved from what must be rejected; righteousness is to fulfill the former and omit the latter after the separation.

And while the Lord lived among human beings, what else did he do except both speak righteousness and perform righteousness? What else did his people do? Certainly nothing. They too will still perform righteousness when he separates the sheep from the goats, placing the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left. His people too will perform this righteousness—not because they themselves will separate them, but because they will judge them by comparison with themselves, and thus will be the cause of the separation, in accordance with the saying: “The saints will judge the nations,” and so forth. [Col. 0719D]

**And he will lead you.** “It is just,” I say, “that you should reign, and truly you will reign, because your right hand”—that is, your power and divinity—“will lead you.” It will lead you from those former sheep to other sheep. And this will happen wonderfully: doing divine things and enduring human things. He did divine things because he raised the dead, gave sight to the blind, and healed lepers. He suffered human things because he was crucified, died, and was buried.

**Your arrows are sharp.** “Your right hand,” I say, “will lead you, and it will lead you in this way, because your arrows will be sharp.” By arrows he means the divine commandments, given principally by him and sent through the Apostles, evangelists, and other heralds of the truth. These arrows are sharp because they pierce hearts and strip away charity. Saul was struck by these arrows, and Paul arose. The most cruel persecutor was struck, and the most faithful preacher arose. [Col. 0720A]

All those who are made friends of Christ from being his enemies are likewise struck by these arrows. “Your arrows,” I say, “will be sharp, and by these arrows the peoples who are struck will fall, not away from you but beneath you,” so that they may submit themselves to you—and this in the heart. In their hearts they raised themselves against you, and in their hearts, humbled, they will fall before you. And they will fall not in just any heart, but in that heart which belonged to the enemies of the king, so that they may become the friends of the king; thus enemies become friends.

**Your throne, O God.** Because your arrows will be sharp and the peoples will fall beneath you, therefore your throne—that is, your kingdom—will not be temporal, like the kingdom of the Jews. It will sit through the age that follows this age; that is, it will be eternal. This is because you are God. It is not fitting that God, who is eternal, should have a temporal throne.

Of this throne it is said: “The Lord will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” His throne is also called the souls of the righteous, in whom he will reign eternally.

And rightly your throne will be eternal, because the scepter of your kingdom—that is, its rule—is a scepter of uprightness. The scepter of his kingdom is that of which it is said elsewhere: “You will rule them with an iron scepter,” that is, with unbending justice, by which he crushes some and rules others. He crushes the carnal, but rules the spiritual.

This scepter is a scepter of uprightness because it straightens those who were previously bent and crooked—namely, those who loved themselves, desired to rule themselves, and refused to submit their will to God, striving instead to bend his upright will according to their own perverse will. He straightens them so that they now love not their own will but God’s will.

**You have loved righteousness.** Truly your scepter is a scepter of uprightness, because you have loved every righteousness. He proves this from the opposite, namely, because you have hated iniquity.

Thanks be to God, because he hates iniquity, not us: he hates guilt, not nature. The term “unrighteous” identifies the guilt in us, while “human being” identifies nature. We made the guilt, but he made the nature. He does not hate in us what he himself made, in accordance with the saying: “You have mercy on all, O Lord, and hate nothing that you have made”; rather, he hates in us what we made—that is, sin.

Let us therefore also hate what we have made in ourselves, and so we shall be his friends. For if we hate what he hates, then we love what he loves.

But how ought we to hate it? By punishing it, certainly, because no sin will remain unpunished. Either you will punish it, or he will punish it. But if you acknowledge it, he will forgive it. Let us therefore anticipate him by punishing sin now, while he still spares us; for he still threatens with the bow and has not yet brandished the sword.

Let us take notice of sin, so that we may be with the one who says: “For I acknowledge my iniquity,” and so forth. For if we take notice of it, God will not take notice of it; but if we do not take notice of it, then he will take notice of it and punish it.

“You have loved righteousness,” I say, “and hated iniquity.” And so that you, O God the Word, might do these things, “your God”—that is, God the Father—“anointed you,” with reference to the prophet. With reference, however, to the Father’s voice, it will be said in this way: “I, the Father, anointed you,” that is, perfected you in the grace of spiritual gifts.

To receive this anointing, God became human, yet in such a way that he remained true God. For God, who was entirely anointing oil, could not be anointed through himself. Jacob the patriarch prefigured this anointing of Christ’s human nature. He took the stone that he had placed beneath his head at night, set it up as a pillar in the morning, and poured oil over it, saying: “Truly this place is holy.”

The stone placed beneath the head signifies Christ’s humanity, since Christ is the head, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “The head of a man is Christ.” The anointing of the stone signifies the anointing of spiritual grace in Christ.

The angels whom Jacob saw ascending and descending upon the anointed stone signify Christ’s heralds, ascending at one time and descending at another. They ascend when they explain his divinity, as does the one who said: “In the beginning was the Word.” They descend when they speak of his humanity, as does the same evangelist when he said: “And the Word became flesh.” [Col. 0721A]

They ascend in order to raise up the mature; they descend in order to nourish the little ones. And these say that this place is holy because they recognize that they have been sanctified through him.

There was also a ladder there by which the angels descended and ascended, because Christ’s humanity was like a ladder by which we ascend into heaven, since he has already made us sit at the right hand of God the Father.

“I have anointed you,” I say, “O God the Son, God the Father—not with the oil of sorrow, with which others were previously anointed through disobedience, but with the oil of gladness,” that is, with spiritual, not bodily, oil. For there is one spiritual oil and another bodily oil. Bodily oil exists in the sign; spiritual oil exists in the sacrament. The former has outward effect; the latter inward effect.

**And has anointed you above your companions.** Christ’s companions are all who share human nature. He himself became a companion of our mortality so that we might become companions of his divinity. Yet above all these companions he himself was anointed with the oil of gladness—that is, with spiritual grace—because it was said of him: “For God does not give his Spirit by measure.” [Col. 0721B]

**Myrrh, and drop, and cassia.** Because God the Father anointed you so perfectly that you both loved righteousness and hated iniquity, you therefore chose such garments for yourself that myrrh and drop would breathe forth from your garments.

Christ’s garments are holy men, in accordance with the saying: “As I live, says the Lord, you will be clothed with all these things as with a garment.” The whole Church is also Christ’s garment, which he joined to himself without spot or wrinkle. To make it without spot, he washed it in his own blood. To make it without wrinkle—that is, without deceit and hypocrisy—he stretched it out upon the cross.

He himself was in the Church through his humanity. That stretching signified nothing other than the breadth of charity which the Church ought to possess toward the love of God and neighbor.

By myrrh, drop, and cassia—which are names of perfumes—all the fragrances of virtues are to be understood, by which the saints delight God, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “We are the good odor of Christ to God in every place, both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing.”

Therefore he says: “From your garments”—that is, from the saints surrounding and adorning you, as a body is surrounded by garments—“myrrh, drop, and cassia will breathe forth,” that is, the fragrances of all virtues. By these fragrances “the daughters of kings”—that is, holy men—“have delighted you.”

They are called daughters rather than sons because, just as greater care and attention are owed to daughters than to sons, so greater caution must be exercised toward those whom holy men have begotten in faith. They are “kings,” that is, Apostles who rightly govern themselves and others. One of them truly was such as he said: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become rejected.”

The daughters, I say, were generated by those kings not in their own honor but in yours. They are not reckoned by their names, so that they are called “Petrinians” or “Paulinians,” but by your name, because they are called Christians.

From these fragrances, I say, they delighted you, issuing “from ivory houses”—that is, from their most innocent and chaste hearts. Ivory possesses whiteness, and whiteness signifies innocence, because where there is whiteness there is no stain. Likewise, true innocence is without stain before God, so that it harms neither itself nor another.

Furthermore, the animal whose mouth is ivory is exceedingly chaste, because it knows only one mate, and that with the greatest restraint; once the mate is dead, it never knows another. Therefore ivory rightly signifies chastity and innocence, and ivory houses signify chaste and innocent hearts. [Col. 0721D]

**The queen stood.** Up to this point the epithalamium seems to have pertained to the honor of the bridegroom, although in the preceding verse some mention was also made, in a certain sense, of the bride. Now, however, the epithalamium of the bride clearly begins.

It is as though he were saying: “While such fragrances continually delight you, the daughters of kings, the queen”—that is, the Church—“has stood,” already in intention, and “will stand” in reality, at your right hand, that is, in your more honored place, both here and in the future: here through good works, and in the future through eternal rewards.

But the one who, so to speak, will stand at the left will not be queen; rather, she will be concubine and servant, the one of whom it is said: “Cast out the servant woman and her son.” For the son of the servant woman will not be heir with the son of the free woman.

The queen, I say, will stand at your right hand, “in a gilded garment,” that is, in all the garments of virtues with which she is clothed. The ornaments are “gilded,” that is, having gold placed above them, or shining with charity. Just as gold is placed above the other metals so that it may shine more brightly, so our works are more acceptable and splendid if they have charity joined to them.

Hence the Apostle says: “Let all your things be done in charity.” And charity is superior to the other virtues. Thus, after speaking about spiritual gifts, the Apostle adds concerning charity: “I show you a still more excellent way.”

The queen, I say, is surrounded by a variety of virtues. It is as though he were saying: Although those virtues are one in charity, in themselves they are many.

Or it may be understood otherwise: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a gilded garment,” that is, in the sacraments of doctrine with which she is clothed. These garments are gilded because everything tends toward gold—that is, toward the acquisition of good morals. Gold is used for wisdom, that is, for good morals.

The queen, I say, is surrounded by a variety of tongues, because the same doctrine is expressed in various languages, in accordance with the saying: “The Apostles spoke in various tongues the mighty works of God.” Yet all these tongues tend toward the same gold and toward instructing people in the same faith. Just as different parts of a single garment exist for the same purpose, so they all work together to compose the garment. [Col. 0722B]

**Hear, daughter, and see.** Behold, he has brought forth the bride, and now addresses her directly, just as earlier he addressed the bridegroom when he said: “Fair in form.”

It is as though he were saying: “Since you will stand at the right hand and will have a gilded garment, therefore, queen, daughter of the king and bride of the king, hear the promises and see them fulfilled. Hear in order to believe; by believing, see; by seeing, live. And in hearing, incline your ear,” that is, hear in humility.

“And, in order to incline your ear, forget your people”—namely, the people of Babylon, from whom this King took you, ugly, in order to make you beautiful. “And forget the house,” that is, the household of your father, namely, the devil, who made you ugly because he made you sinful and unjust.

If you do this, then the King who loved you when you were ugly in order to make you beautiful will desire your beauty—that is, you, now made beautiful. Let this not seem a small thing to you, for he himself is your Lord, who redeemed you, and he is your God, because he made you. It ought therefore to seem very great to you: he both makes you free and also takes you into marriage.

For this reason you must also hear him and forget your people and your mother, because then, following your example, “the daughters of Tyre”—that is, the Church from the Gentiles—will worship him also.

Tyre and Sidon are cities near Judaea, as is recorded in the Gospel, where it says: “Jesus departed from Judaea and withdrew into the regions of Tyre and Sidon, and behold, a Canaanite woman.” From there came that unclean dog which, by confessing herself to have become a dog, signifies the Gentiles, who were previously confined in earthly things.

The sons of Tyre are therefore called those converted from the Gentiles and now brought out of confinement. “The daughters of Tyre,” I say, “will worship,” and not in a simple manner, but “with gifts,” offering themselves and also distributing their possessions to the poor. For there is no place for true sacrifice outside the Church.

And just as in ancient times no one came to Jerusalem empty-handed, so one must not come empty-handed to this temple of the Church, which was represented by that former temple, because the Lord wishes his treasures to be increased. Let whoever can offer gold and silver; whoever cannot do this should at least offer himself.

And not only will the daughters of Tyre worship, but also “the rich of the people”—that is, secular and powerful men from that people understood through Tyre, namely, converts from the Gentiles—will entreat, that is, venerate and desire, your face, O daughter!

Here “face” refers to the service and fervor of the charity of the primitive Church, whose members sold all their possessions and placed them at the feet of the Apostles, so that they might be distributed to each according to his need.

Understand “the rich” as men like those of whom the Apostle says to Timothy: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living and true God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment.”

He has said that they will worship with gifts; but because many make these gifts more for human display than before God, he describes for us the face of that primitive Church, so that we may imitate it.

It is as though he were saying: Those who worship with gifts and entreat the face of the Church ought to consider that this face is such that “all the glory of the king’s daughter”—the primitive Church, that is—is not outwardly before human beings, but inwardly, in the conscience before God’s sight.

Hence the Apostle says: “For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience.” Its glory is also “in golden borders,” that is, in perseverance in good works. Borders are at the end of a garment, and therefore borders signify final perseverance. Gold, as was said above, signifies good morals and good works.

Although her glory is hidden inwardly, nevertheless she is “surrounded with varieties,” that is, she has a manifold outward adornment of virtues.

The Lord commands both things. For while in one place he says: “Beware of practicing your righteousness before men, in order to be seen by them,” elsewhere he says: “Let your light shine before men, so that, seeing your works, they may glorify God who is in heaven.”

These statements seem contrary, but they are not. The hand should be visible, while the intention remains hidden. [Col. 0723B]

**Virgins will be brought to the king.** The passage is connected in this way: Not only will the daughters of Tyre worship, but other new virgins will also be brought to this king, the aged David, to warm him afterward—that is, after the first one.

For just as young women were brought to King David when he was already old, to cherish and warm him, so new virgins will be brought daily to the true David, Christ, now almost old, because it has been a long time since the Church, which is his kingdom, began. This happens whenever some unbelievers are converted; they warm him with the fervor of faith and good works.

And not just any virgins will be brought, but such as are near—that is, related to his former bride, or imitators of her in faith. “O king, they will be brought to you.” They will be brought not in any manner, but in gladness of heart and exultation of body—that is, in complete joy, not sadness—for God loves a cheerful giver.

And rightly in joy, because they will be brought into the temple—that is, into the king’s secret place—for this purpose: that they themselves may become a temple and living stones. Some foolish virgins were brought into the temple, but did not become a temple; rather, they went out from the temple, like apostate heretics. [Col. 0723C]

**In place of your fathers sons have been born.** As though someone were asking from whom these virgins would be brought, since there are no fathers from whom they ought to be brought, he answers that they will be brought by sons.

And he turns to the king in this way: “O Lord King, sons—not according to the flesh but according to faith—have been born to you,” such as Martin, Hilary, and others like them, who take the place of the holy Apostles, who were especially fathers to others begotten in faith.

“Your fathers,” I say, that is, appointed by you; and you will appoint these sons as princes, just as the fathers were appointed not only over Judaea but over the whole earth—that is, in every part of the earth.

Therefore these sons will remember not their own name but yours. They will beget many sons not in their own name but in yours, because they are not called Martinian or Hilarian, but Christian. This will occur in every generation that passes away and in the generation that follows.

This is to say: Throughout the present life they will always remember you. Therefore they will confess—that is, render true and fitting praise—to you also forever. He defines what “forever” means: extending into the age that follows this age.

# ON PSALM 45

*For the end, for the sons of Korah, a psalm concerning hidden things.*

[Col. 0724A]

## ARGUMENT

It is sung in the person of the two tribes, giving thanks for their deliverance when Pekah son of Remaliah and Rezin, king of Syria, wished to attack Ahaz, king of Jerusalem, but were unable to do so; rather, they themselves were crushed by the king of the Assyrians.

It should also be read in connection with the reading from the Acts of the Apostles.

## EXPLANATION

“The end” signifies Christ; “the sons of Korah” signifies Christians, in whose person this psalm is sung. “Concerning hidden things” signifies the coming of the Lord the Savior, which he arranged through the wondrous mystery of his divinity for the salvation of human beings.

The sons of Korah, who are to be understood as the faithful—that is, Christians—first declare in the opening part of the psalm that they do not fear the disturbances of the world, because God is shown to be their refuge and strength.

Second, they say that Christ appears in the midst of his Church, which he built in himself as upon the most solid rock.

Third, the multitude of believers speaks generally while contemplating the divine miracles, saying that almighty God breaks the weapons of wickedness, removes wars, and changes the sadness of the faithful into eternal joys.

## COMMENTARY
God our refuge and strength. The title is as follows: “For the end; a psalm of the sons of Korah concerning hidden things.” This means that this psalm refers not to history but to the end of time. It is assigned to the sons of Korah, or sung by certain sons of Korah; “by other sons of Korah concerning hidden things” is to be understood as meaning “so that they may understand hidden things.” Here, “hidden things” are called those things that were concealed from ages and generations and have been made manifest in the fullness of time, namely: either the hidden coming of Christ, that is, his incarnation, or the incorporation of Gentiles and Jews. The latter occurred because the natural branches of the olive tree were broken off and the wild olive was grafted in—that is, in part the Jews were expelled and the Gentiles received. In accordance with the passage: “A partial blindness has happened in Israel,” and so forth.

[Col. 0724C]

In this psalm there is the voice either generally of all those of the early Church, apart from the apostles, or only of those who, seeing uneducated men become so wise after the sending of the Holy Spirit that no one could resist their wisdom, and seeing them perform miracles, and hearing that this was done by the gift of the one whom they themselves had crucified and whose death they had plotted, were cut to the heart and came to the apostles saying: “What shall we do, men and brothers?” Peter answered: “Repent,” and so forth. The voice, I say, either of all these together or only of the latter, is the voice of those exhorting us, in every tribulation, to choose as our only refuge and help him who alone has mercy and alone can forgive sins; for it is not proper to a Christian to seek refuge and help from anyone but his God and Savior. Thus they say:

“Our God, who are a refuge—and not a worthless one—but strength,” that is, powerful, because reliable and secure.

[Col. 0724D]

For there are refuges among human beings that are weak and hardly safe. Our God, I say, is a helper in all tribulations, whether common or particular. Here, however, tribulation must chiefly be understood as consciousness of sins, which is more grievous the more inward it is. For if something is rotten within, it will never truly be sound outwardly. And if a debt to the treasury is burdensome, the debt of sin is much more burdensome. Its repayment will itself be destruction.

The consciousness of sins is therefore the more grievous tribulation, because if someone is troubled outwardly, he has somewhere to flee and seek rest—namely, a city, a house, a bedroom. Finally, if he is disturbed in that very bedroom by a wicked wife, it remains for him to flee to his own mind. But if the smoke of an evil conscience drives him from there, the wretched man has nowhere further to flee.

He is a helper, I say, in tribulations which, when recognized at the apostles’ admonition, found us—not we them. For he finds sin who, by searching himself, recognizes his sin. Hence it is said: “Return, transgressors, to your heart.” But sins find those who, when another admonishes them, recognize those very sins.

[Col. 0725A]

And tribulations have found us exceedingly, because nothing is more unjust than for a sick person to kill the physician—which, indeed, we acknowledge that we have done. This statement is made according to the interpretation that the voice belongs only to those who, cut to the heart, came to the apostles. But according to the interpretation that it is generally the voice of the primitive Church, it will be understood: “They have found us exceedingly.”

For through obedience we remained in paradise, and were in a place of health and rest. But when through disobedience we withdrew into the region of unlikeness, then we came, as it were, into places of tribulation and unrest. Thus tribulations found us in their own places. And they found us exceedingly, because they entered even into the soul.

Therefore we will not fear. Since our God is a refuge and helper in tribulations, therefore we will not fear the future judgment, namely, while the Jewish land is surrounded on every side by the bitterness of the Gentiles. And that land which appeared habitable because of the Law and the Prophets will be shaken—that is, it will suffer disturbance.

This happened when the Jews, after the apostles had been strengthened by the Spirit and were proclaiming the resurrection and ascension of Christ, were so disturbed that they drove them away from themselves and forbade anyone to speak in the apostles’ name.

And we will not fear even while the mountains—that is, the apostles, distinguished in faith and virtues—are transferred from the Jews into the heart of the sea, that is, to the Gentiles. The Gentiles are represented by the sea both because of the bitterness of their morals and because they surrounded Judea.

But lest we think that this people is the one of whom it was said, “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me,” rather than the people of whom Isaiah said, “I will place my law in their hearts,” he adds: “Into the heart of the sea.”

Paul makes this transfer of the mountains clear when he said: “The word of salvation has been sent to you, but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.”

[Col. 0725C]

Through these mountains the mountain of mountains was also transferred, of which it was said: “And it shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared at the top of the mountains.”

And he who says of himself to the apostles, “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain”—that is, to me—“Move from here and cast yourself into the sea,” and so it will happen.

This is to be understood as follows: the more a mustard seed is crushed, the sharper it becomes. Therefore the meaning is: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed,” that is, strong and steadfast in tribulation, then you will say to me, the mountain: “Remove yourself from Judea and cast yourself into the sea,” that is, “Cross over to the Gentiles.”

For through the apostles the Lord was preached, known, and glorified among the Gentiles.

The meaning of the whole verse is this: those who speak here, confident that they have God as their refuge and help, say: “We will not fear the punishment to come while the Jewish land is shaken and while the mountains—and through the mountains the mountain of mountains—is transferred into the heart of the sea, because we will cling to the mountains.”

But those who will be shaken, or who abandon the mountains because of the disturbance, will rightly fear.

The waters roared and were troubled. He shows how the mountains—that is, the apostles—were transferred to the Gentiles: namely, because they roared, that is, made their sound heard among the Gentiles. For the Lord thundered threats through them, flashed through miracles, and poured down commandments. Therefore the waters—that is, the teachings and practices of those who are understood by the sea, namely, the Gentiles—were first troubled with an evil disturbance.

Hence some of them said about Paul: “Who is this man, a new preacher of demons?”

And the mountains also—that is, the philosophers and their powerful men—were troubled in the strength of our God, who is refuge and strength; that is, they were troubled because of the steadfastness and endurance given by him to the apostles.

This verse may also be read in the following way, as though he were saying: “While the mountains are transferred into the sea, the waters”—that is, the apostles, or their teachings, who are understood by the sea—“roared”; that is, they opposed those mountains.

[Col. 0725D]

And this was because they were first troubled within themselves. Hence, because the waters roared and were troubled, the mountains themselves—that is, the apostles—were troubled, that is, saddened, because they endured scourges and feared for those who were lesser or weaker, in the strength—that is, in the perseverance and harshness—of that roar.

The river’s flood. The waters, I say, were troubled, and the mountains were troubled. But what concern is that? None, namely, because however great the disturbance may be outwardly, it will harm none of the faithful, since the river’s flood—that is, the abundance of spiritual gifts—makes glad inwardly the city, that is, the people of God.

For there is one river of which it was said: “For with you is the fountain of life.” This one river produces many floods, because it flows into Peter and Paul and their equals, according to the passage: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

The flood, I say, makes glad the city of God. And it makes it glad in this way: because the Most High God sanctified—that is, strengthened by that flood—his tabernacle, that is, his soldiers.

And truly the tabernacle has been sanctified, because it will not be moved by any tribulations from the steadfastness of faith. This is because God is in its midst, since he favors all equally and is present to all, like something situated in the middle and relating equally to those around it.

And he is in its midst in this way: God has already helped it, and will help it—that is, the city—by granting steadfastness, and this in the morning, that is, diligently. For those who rise in the morning appear diligent in their work.

And “at dawn,” that is, through the illumination produced by that flood. Or, “he will help it in the morning,” that is, through his resurrection, which took place in the morning of the first day of the Sabbath and was for us a dawn, that is, an illumination.

Through the Lord’s resurrection, those who had previously feared death became so steadfast that they not only ceased to fear death but even desired it.

Another translation has: “God will help it with his countenance.” If this is explained, it means: “He will be present to it through such signs that he will be understood to be present.”

The nations were troubled. Because the city of God had become steadfast in tribulation, the nations were therefore troubled with a good disturbance. For whereas they had previously been troubled in order to destroy, they were now troubled in order to build.

And the kingdoms also—that is, the kings who had previously been aroused to oppose—were now humbled in order to worship.

Nor is this surprising, because the Lord is not only Lord of human beings but also of powers, that is, of the heavenly armies. He previously spoke through the creature subject to him; now, being with us, he is Emmanuel, which means “with us,” that is, God of our nature.

And he is the one who receives us, that is, our physician, who took upon himself our weakness in order to heal it; and he is the God of Jacob, that is, of all those who wrestle and those who are supplanted.

He, I say, now gave his voice principally through himself and through the apostles. Therefore the earth—that is, the Gentile people, which had previously been dust but has now become cultivated soil—has been moved in order to bear fruit.

Come and see. Since the Lord of hosts, being with us and having become our receiver, gave his voice, therefore all of you, come with the steps of faith so that you may believe, and by believing see so that you may live.

See, I say, the works of the Lord, which the Lord—who is not only Lord of human beings but also of powers, being with us, our receiver, the God of Jacob, a repetition made for emphasis—has established as wonders, that is, things to be marveled at, and which are seen over the earth, that is, over those who have been made cultivated soil from dust.

He explains those works, as though saying: “These, I say, are the works that the Lord established, namely, that the Lord removes wars,” that is, takes away all opposition and resistance to holy doctrine, if not from the chaff, at least from the grain, to the end of the earth, that is, in every part of the earth.

The sound of the apostles has gone out into all the earth, or “to the end of the earth,” that is, to such an extent that they made those who had previously rebelled become the end of the earth, namely, so that they would bring all earthly-mindedness in themselves to an end.

The Lord, I say, will shatter the bow, that is, hidden opposition; and he will break the weapons, that is, manifest opposition; and the shields, that is, the defense of evil presumption. He will burn the defense of sin.

[Col. 0727A]

And he will destroy them with fire—not just any fire, but the fire that he himself came to cast upon the earth and wills to burn, namely, through love of God and neighbor.

He himself, I say, declares: “Be vacant,” that is, empty yourselves of the vices with which you were full, so that you may be filled with virtues.

And “see,” that is, recognize that I am God. You ought to recognize this, because I truly am God, who will be exalted—that is, glorified—in you Gentiles.

And finally I will also be exalted in the Jewish land, because it was foretold of it: “And the remnant will be saved.”

Here he clearly notes the incorporation of Jews and Gentiles, which was foretold in the title.

This psalm may also be ordered and construed differently from the beginning, so that it reads as follows: “Our God the Lord, namely, the Lord of hosts with us, our receiver, the God of Jacob, gave his voice, and therefore the earth was moved.”

And how it was moved has already been stated: namely, because the nations were troubled and the kingdoms were humbled.

He, I say, is the one who is refuge and strength and helper in tribulations, which have found us exceedingly.

The rest remains unchanged.

## PSALM XLVI

“For the end; a psalm for the sons of Korah.”

[Col. 0727B]

### ARGUMENT

This song is sung in a manner resembling a triumphal hymn from the perspective of the Maccabees, because, after the Gentiles or the transgressing Jews had been defeated, the Temple was restored together with its sacred rites. It is also to be read in connection with the reading from the Acts of the Apostles, after Christ ascended to the Father.

### EXPLANATION

The title is familiar, signifying Christ and Christians, although the entire hymn was sung from the perspective of the sons of Korah, yet divided by the insertion of a diapsalm.

First, the Gentiles are urged to sing praises to the Lord, because he subjected all things to the people of his possession and placed them in his inheritance.

Second, the Lord’s ascension and kingdom are described, because his saints will enjoy him without end.

### COMMENTARY

All nations, clap your hands. Our Lord God revealed to us in many different ways throughout the sacred Scriptures the faith in which we stand, from which we live, and through which we are also saved.

Although he varies the mysteries of his words, he commends the same faith, so that while the order of expression varies and an ancient matter is renewed, a person may be prepared in heart to retain it, and afterward may not be lazy about reflecting on the same things and continually ruminating what he has eaten—that is, what he has heard—lest we be found unclean animals rather than clean ones.

Thus in this psalm the same matter, already often foretold in other psalms, is repeated. Its title is: “For the end; for the sons of Korah; a psalm to David himself.”

This is explained as follows: this psalm refers to the end, sung by certain sons of Korah, that is, so that other sons of Korah may become imitators of Christ and of his passion.

The psalm, I say, is attributed to David himself, that is, to those more perfect in the body of Christ.

It is the voice of the holy apostles exhorting us to return thanks, as far as we can, to God, who descended for us and endured death: namely, to clap our hands to him with mouth and deed; to recognize as exalted the one against whom the Jews stumbled as against a little child; and to fear as terrifying, though with chaste fear, the one whom they regarded as contemptible.

According to some who make this psalm one with the preceding psalm, it may be connected with what was said above as follows, as though he were saying: “Since the Lord will be exalted not only among the Gentiles but also in the Jewish land, therefore all nations, clap your hands to God,” that is, praise God in good works, “and shout to him,” not with just any voice, but with a voice of exultation, that is, in exultant praise.

For whether we merely do good works without praising him with our voice, or do the opposite, we would be sluggish; therefore both are commanded.

For the Lord is Most High. Therefore you ought, all nations, to clap your hands to God and shout with your voice, because the Lord—that is, Christ—who was previously little has now become exalted; who was previously an object of ridicule has now become terrifying; and who is now a great king not only over Judea but over the whole earth.

He, I say, subjected the Jewish peoples to us apostles and heralds, and not only the peoples but also the nations—that is, the Gentiles—he placed under our feet, that is, under our affections, so that we, who were previously killed by our own people, might be honored by these, and because we were expelled by the former, we might be received by the latter.

And because he subjected both peoples and nations to us in this way, he chose—by taking up what he had chosen before the ages and arranging it—his inheritance, associating with us both Jews and Gentiles.

He explains what that inheritance is: he chose the beauty of Jacob, that is, the beautiful men signified by Jacob, because Jacob he loved, but Esau he hated.

For there were two brothers in their mother’s womb, fighting and striking one another. God chose one and rejected the other. One is understood as Jacob in all good things, and the other as Esau in all evil things.

God ascended with a shout. As though someone might say, “How did God choose this inheritance?” he answers: “In this way,” namely, because he ascended into heaven and from there sent the Holy Spirit, who strengthened our hearts so that peoples and nations might be subjected to us.

It may also be connected as follows: “Truly the Lord is Most High, because he has now ascended to the place that those who crucified him could not follow.”

And this occurred with a shout, that is, amid the immense joy and amazement of the apostles; and the Lord ascended with the voice of an angelic trumpet.

For the angels comforted the apostles, who were stupefied and in a certain sense alienated from themselves, as the Lord ascended, as though saying: “The body is indeed taken from your eyes, but God is not separated from your hearts. See him ascending; believe in him who is absent; hope for him who comes through hidden mercy; always feel him to be present.”

Sing praises to our God. Since the Lord has become Most High and terrifying, and a great King over the whole earth, therefore all nations, sing praises both by deed and by voice.

He explains to whom they should sing: “Sing praises to God,” namely, to God the Father, our God, that is, favorable to us.

“Sing praises to our King,” that is, to the Son; sing praises also to the Holy Spirit.

And you ought to sing praises because God has become King through the knowledge not only of the Jews but of the whole earth.

God is always, whether he wishes it or not, the King of the whole earth; nevertheless, he is called King only when he is known to reign.

Hence Isaiah says: “The God who redeemed you will be called the God of the whole earth.”

God is King, I say; therefore sing praises not foolishly but wisely. For they sang foolishly while they worshiped idols, but now they sing wisely, because they worship the Creator.

God will reign. He must therefore be praised wisely, because God will reign—that is, he will be recognized as reigning—over all nations, if not in the chaff, at least in the grain.

He indicates this when he says that God already sits by his plan and will also sit in reality upon his holy throne, that is, upon the souls of the righteous.

Prepare yourselves, therefore, for the Lord, and he will sit in us, because Solomon says: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.”

Princes of the peoples. Truly the Lord has reigned over the nations, because he will raise up nations from stones and make them children of Abraham.

He says this in the manner of a prophet, speaking of the future in the present tense: the princes of the peoples of the Gentiles, who, as long as they had hearts of stone, were separated from God, have now been gathered with the God of Abraham, namely, having become his children—not bearing his flesh, but possessing his faith.

This happened because the gods of the earth—that is, the apostles, who were regarded as gods on earth—strong, that is, persevering in tribulation and preaching, were greatly lifted up, that is, honored and exalted, with the Lord cooperating and confirming the word through the accompanying signs.

Peter was indeed greatly exalted when even the sick were raised by the touch of his shadow.

Therefore their princes readily believed and received faith through them.

Or it may be understood otherwise, as though he were saying: “The Gentiles were received because the Jews were expelled.”

He indicates this by saying: “Because the gods”—that is, the Jews, who because of the Law and the Prophets were, by comparison with others, like gods—“the strong ones of the earth,” that is, those presuming upon their earthly nature, namely, upon worldly power and glory, “have been greatly lifted up,” that is, they became so proud that they did not consider the physician who had come to them necessary for them, and therefore they killed him.

Thus this was fulfilled: “Because a partial blindness has happened in Israel, so that the fullness …”

## PSALM XLVII

“A psalm of song for the sons of Korah, for the second day of the Sabbath.”

### ARGUMENT

In the estimation of people who do not know God, he appeared great because of the things he accomplished in the city. It is also to be read in connection with the Apocalypse of John, as a figure of the future Church in Jerusalem.

### EXPLANATION

The second day of the Sabbath is the second day after the Sabbath, which is now called the second feria. On that day, as Genesis relates, God made the firmament in the midst of the waters and called it heaven.

There the elevation of the holy Church is prefigured. Suspended, as it were, between the lower and upper waters, it is lower than the angelic sublimity but higher in its worldly manner of life.

Therefore, just as in Psalm XXIII, the first day of the Sabbath, on which light was made, shows beforehand that the Lord’s resurrection is to be sung, so in the present psalm the second day of the Sabbath, on which the firmament was made, displays the summit of the Church.

The sons of Korah—that is, those of the Lord’s passion—make the psalm of this song resound for it.

In the first section they praise the Lord because, enlarging his Church, he displayed his power to all the kings of the earth.

In the second they give thanks for the coming of the Savior, exhorting future bishops to distribute ranks in the Church through which the Savior may be recognized, he who guards his servants with eternal protection.

### COMMENTARY

Great is the Lord and worthy of praise. Our Lord God made something other than the works themselves known to us through the distinction of his works.

For it is written in the book of Genesis that he distinguished his works over six days.

On the first day he made light and divided it from darkness. Through this he wished us to understand something other than merely what was made.

By the light made on the first day, we are to understand that through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ a light was made for us, because a return was granted to us from darkness to light and from death to life.

By that same light, divided from darkness, the separation of the faithful and the unfaithful is to be understood.

Those who believe in Christ’s death and resurrection, and in things like these, are the light separated from darkness. Of these the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”

Those who remain in unbelief are darkness.

We dealt with this matter of the first day above in a certain psalm concerning the first day of the Sabbath: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it.”

On the second day of the Sabbath, that is, on the second day, God made the firmament and established it in the midst of the waters.

By this firmament the Church is signified, the body of that head of whom the preceding psalm, concerning the first day of the Sabbath, speaks.

The Church is properly understood as consisting in the saints, who do not easily yield to the temptations of this age.

For only those strengthened in faith and founded in charity are rightly called by the name “firmament.”

Of them the Apostle says: “We who are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak.”

Elsewhere he also says of the Church: “The Church of the living God, the pillar and firmament of the truth.”

The entire period from the Lord’s ascension until the common resurrection of all may be called the second day of the Sabbath.

During this period, through the apostles and holy heralds, this firmament—that is, the Church—is established and consolidated in the midst of the waters, that is, of evils, whose bitterness surrounds it on every side.

This psalm deals not with the firmament as signifying, but with what is signified by it.

Its title is: “A song of praise for the second day of the Sabbath, for the sons of Korah.”

This is understood as follows: this song of praise, that is, this hymn of exultation, is sung concerning the second day of the Sabbath, that is, concerning the things signified by the created things of the second day of the Sabbath.

It is assigned to future sons of Korah, that is, to all who may wish to be imitators of Christ’s passion, so that they may progress more and more.

It is the voice of a prophet—or of any perfect person from the earlier people—who recognizes through the Spirit that the Church is to be established and exhorts us not to withdraw ourselves from it but, as far as we can, to strive to enter this building, so that we may become living stones in it, if not squared, at least of some kind.

Therefore he begins to commend this building, saying:

“The Lord the Father will become great,” that is, magnificent through good works, not in Babylon but in the city of our God.

Here he understands “city” as the assembly of the faithful, that is, the Church, which is the city of our God, who was made ours by assuming our nature, because it pertains to the incarnate Word.

And the Lord will also become exceedingly—that is, greatly—worthy of praise, since he will not depart even in thought from his holy mountain, that is, Christ, who is the head of this city.

This mountain is hewn from a mountain, that is, born from the Jewish people without the hands of those who cut him—that is, without the hands of human embraces.

For Mary, from whom he was born, did not know a man.

This mountain, however, grew and became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.

Therefore do not be slow to ascend this mountain, because it was not slow to come to you while you slept.

You do not need to labor or travel in order to find this mountain. But if you do not ascend this mountain and make progress upon it, then you will truly be a stranger.

It is founded in exultation. He mentioned two things: the city and its holy mountain.

Now he first treats of the city, and afterward will treat of the mountain, saying:

“The city of the great King.”

Since a great city is fitting for a great king, it is founded in exultation, that is, in the exultations of the whole earth.

No one truly exults except one who exults in God.

He shows this in its parts: Mount Zion—that is, certain Jews who are called Mount Zion, or “mountain of contemplation,” because of their observance of the legal rites—is the city of the great King, because it is one wall.

And the sides of the north are also the city of the great King, because they are the other wall.

The sides of the north are the most despairing people among the Gentiles, who clung most closely to that north which said: “I will set my throne in the north and will be like the Most High.”

Because in them iniquity abounded, charity grew cold; this is rightly understood through the north.

For the north wind is opposed to the southern region, the warm quarter, because it is cold.

Therefore the devil and all those cold in charity are understood by the north. They are opposed to holy men, who always have the true sun of justice present.

One of these was also the son who, after devouring his substance with prostitutes, went away into the region of unlikeness and clung to one of the rulers of that region, namely, the north.

But at last he returned to himself, because the Church was also to be constituted from the most despairing and ruined people, and said: “I will arise and go to my father,” and so forth.

Behold, with this man’s return, there are two peoples; behold, the two walls of the Church.

Through the one who returns, the Gentile people are understood, who had withdrawn so far from their father that they even worshiped idols.

Through the one who remained with his father, the Jewish people are signified, persevering in the legal institutions.

From these two the Church is constituted, and Mount Zion and the sides of the north are the city of the great King.

Some books have “of Mount Zion,” which is construed as follows: “The city is founded in the exultation of the whole earth, of Mount Zion,” that is, by those converts from the Jews who exult.

For this reason he says “of the whole earth,” although he is dealing only with Jews, because among the Jews themselves there were certain very despairing tribes, such as the tribe of Benjamin, from which Saul and all the rulers of that people came.

God in her houses. Mount Zion, I say, and the sides of the north are the city of the great King.

And this is how it happens: he will be known—that is, he will be recognized as present through evident signs—not only in one house but also in the houses of that city, that is, both in the people from the Gentiles and in the people from the Jews.

This was said against the arrogance of the Jews, who boasted of their father Abraham and thought that they alone would be saved.

And the Lord will rightly be known in her houses, since he will receive her, as a good physician, in order to heal and protect her weakness.

This receiving may refer either to his hidden and continuous mercy or to the incarnation of the Word.

For behold. As though someone might say, “Against whom is it necessary for him to protect her?” he answers: “It is truly necessary, because kings”—that is, not only common people but also savage rulers, such as Diocletian and Maximian—“have gathered together to attack her.”

“And behold”—consider what I say to be true—“because the kings themselves, however different in religious practice, came together for this one purpose: to destroy the Church and erase the Christian name.”

But those same kings, seeing this city thus founded, were amazed, and so forth.

The preceding verse may also be read in a good sense and connected with what was said above as follows:

“I say, therefore, that the sides of the north are the city of the great King, because not only the common people of the Gentiles but also kings, such as Constantine and many others, are included.”

Or generally we may understand “kings” as all those who rule their unlawful impulses well; all of them have been gathered into this city.

“Behold”—consider what I say to be true—“because, although unlike in morals and language, they came together into one,” that is, into the same harmony of faith.

But how did this happen? In this way: the kings themselves, seeing this city founded in this manner, that is, through such evident signs and miracles, and seeing that one wall was from the uncircumcision and the other from the circumcision, were amazed at the display of miracles, were troubled in conscience by their sins, and thus were moved to repentance.

This happened because trembling—the trembling of the future judgment—seized them through the threats of the heralds.

There, that is, in trembling, there will be pains in them like the pains of a woman giving birth, that is, of one repenting.

I say, pains not barren but fruitful, for giving birth is followed by offspring.

Therefore observe here the conception and recognize the labor.

Isaiah says: “Because of your fear, Lord, we conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation.”

Thus these kings, through fear of the Lord, conceived fear and afterward gave birth to the spirit of salvation, because by believing in the one whom they feared they were saved.

And truly they will have pains like those of a woman giving birth, because you, Lord, will crush the ships of Tarshish, that is, you will humble the pride of the Gentiles, who formerly swelled in spirit because of the uncertain riches of this age.

This occurred in a vehement spirit, that is, in great fear, because of the threat of the future judgment.

Or “in a vehement spirit,” that is, in a fire consuming vices, namely, in the burning ardor of love of God and neighbor.

Observe that he says “the ships of Tarshish.”

There were those who said that Cilicia was signified by Tarshish, a very wealthy and powerful region, because Tarshish is its metropolitan city.

Others also said that the city now called Carthage was once called Tarshish.

This ought to seem surprising to no one, since it was also called Byrsa, from the hide of a bull.

Its beginnings flourished so greatly through voyages and commerce that the pride of the Gentiles—who presumed upon the uncertainty of riches just as sailors presume upon the uncertain blowing of the winds—is not improperly signified by “the ships of the Tarshishites.”

Likewise, if Cilicia is signified by Tarshish, the pride of the Gentiles is not improperly signified through Cilicia as a wealthy and glorious homeland.

This may also appropriately be understood according to the interpretation of the name.

For Tarshish is interpreted as “exploration of joy.” By this the Gentiles are rightly signified, because formerly they sought joy in earthly and transitory things, thinking that blessedness truly existed in them.

The Lord crushed and humbled their ships—that is, their pride and glory—in a vehement spirit.

As we have heard. This may be connected as follows: “Trembling seized the kings,” the same kings, I say, saying: “As we have heard,” and so forth.

Or it may simply be connected in this way: because the Lord will crush the ships of Tarshish, that is, because he humbled the pride of the nations, “as we have heard promised, so we have seen fulfilled”; as we heard in the promises, so we saw in the manifestations.

Where did we see it? In the city of the Lord, who is also called the Lord of hosts, that is, of the heavenly armies.

In the city, I say, of our God, that is, belonging by right to the Word, who is our God, that is, a participant in our nature.

This happened because God the Word founded it in himself.

For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ. His foundation is not temporal; rather, its establishment remains forever.

We have received, O God. Here he clearly treats of the holy mountain, just as above he treated of the city.

As though he were saying: “In this way our God founded the city, because, O God the Father, we have received him who should not merely be called merciful but, emphatically, Mercy itself.”

[Col. 0732B]

And if not in everyone, at least in the midst of your temple, that is, in the perfect.

For all who have received the sacraments of faith are the temple of God.

But those who have the appearance of godliness among us because they have received the sacraments, yet deny its power because they do not observe works of godliness, are, I say, like the circuit of this temple.

Those who both have the appearance of godliness and hold its power, because they practice the works of faith, are the middle of this temple.

They receive the Lord into themselves, because he dwells in them through faith and action.

The others both receive him and do not receive him: they receive him through the sacraments, but do not receive him through their works.

According to your name, O God. It is as though he said: We, I say, who are in the middle of the temple, have received him; but are there perhaps only a few because they are in the middle of the temple? No, rather many. For, O God, according to your name—that is, according to the fact that your name has been spread abroad and proclaimed—so, that is, to the same degree, your praise has been extended. It is as though he said: Just as you are named everywhere by your heralds, so you are praised everywhere.

[Col. 0732C] Or otherwise: Your praise has been so extended and so magnified that it corresponds to your name—that is, to what befits your name, namely, the majesty of your name. For it has reached to the ends of the earth, because it is in every region of the earth; or it is in those who have made themselves the ends of the earth, retaining nothing except what is strictly necessary—and scarcely even that.

And lest some misguided person say, “Then only a few will be placed on the right, while many will be on the left; and therefore God, taking pity on the small number of those on the right, transfers some from the left to their company,” the prophet, through the Holy Spirit, counters this error by saying: Your right hand, Lord, is full not of goats but of lambs, because it is full of righteousness—that is, of such persons as may themselves be called righteousness. This amounts to saying: No wicked persons, but only the righteous, will be placed at God’s right hand. And the righteous will be many, while the wicked will be few, because nothing is so subject to scarcity as what is destined for perdition.

Let Mount Zion rejoice. Since only the righteous will be placed on the right, and these will not be few but many, let those who are to be placed on the right rejoice; while those who have been placed on the left should strive to be transferred to the right. He says this as follows: Let Mount Zion rejoice—that is, let those who are to be placed on the right from the circumcision rejoice; and let the daughters of Judah also exult, that is, the sons of confession—namely, those who from the nations have become your sons through confession—for they too are to be placed on the right.

[Col. 0732D] Let them exult, I say, Lord, not on account of themselves but on account of your judgments—that is, because your just commandments have been kept. Or, on account of your judgments, namely, because it pleased you to judge, so that partial blindness might come upon Israel and thus the fullness of the nations might enter. Hence the daughters of Judah also ought to exult—that is, the sons of confession who have been received—as well as the faithful among the Jews who have not been blinded.

Or on account of your future judgments, already partly escaped, namely, in hope. For we have been saved in hope, though in the end they will be wholly escaped—namely, because not one grain will fall among the multitude of chaff destined to be burned.

[Col. 0733A] Surround Zion. Until now he has spoken as though about those who are in the middle of the temple; now he turns to those who are around the temple, exhorting them to become the middle, as though he said: Let those who are to be placed on the right exult; but you who are placed on the left, who are still around the temple, surround Zion in the middle—and not with an evil surrounding, namely, to lie in ambush for it, but embrace it through love, so that you may imitate it. And narrate what you narrate not in your own rashness, but in its towers—that is, relying upon the authority of its towers, namely, upon the authority of the holy apostles, who are the towers of that city, concerning which he says elsewhere: “Love is strong as death.”

For just as the devil was powerful for destruction, so Christ—whom love alone caused to come to us—was powerful for restoration; and just as the former was powerful for casting down, so the latter is powerful for raising up. Set your hearts, I say, upon strength; and in this strength distribute—that is, receive distributively—the houses of Zion. It is as though he said: There are two houses of this city: those who are around the temple and those who are in its middle. [Col. 0733B] Every believer ought to receive them separately: those in the middle for imitation, and those around it for avoidance.

Or by “houses” we may understand different families. One family, as it were, consists of those eminent in chastity, another of those eminent in generosity; and thus, according to the particular gifts of the Holy Spirit, there are different families. These they ought to distribute, so that in some they may imitate one virtue, in others another, and thus in each whatever is good.

I say this so that you may do these things and become a good example to others—namely, so that you may narrate them not only in the present to your children, but also narrate them to your descendants in another future generation: namely, that this God who has been received in the middle of the temple is our God—that is, the God of our nature, both true God and true man—remaining forever and unto ages of ages. And he himself, by himself, not through a creature subject to him, will govern us here in good works and thus lead us into eternal ages.

# ON PSALM XLVIII

*For the end; a psalm of the sons of Korah.*

[Col. 0733C]

## ARGUMENT

A common exhortation is directed to all people, so that they may not value highly the riches of the world, but rather, if riches should happen to abound, give thanks to God for them and distribute them for eternal rest. Likewise, this is the voice of the Church concerning Lazarus and the rich man clothed in purple.

## EXPLANATION

All the words of this title draw attention to the Lord and to those redeemed by his blood. Throughout the psalm the words are those of the omnipotent Son. In the first section he tells what he will say or give to the faithful at the time of his incarnation; in the second, what will come upon fools; in the third, what will follow for the righteous and the impious. In the fourth he admonishes his own not to fear the rich of the world, who will leave all their goods along with the light.

## COMMENTARY

Hear this, all nations. The title is as follows: “A psalm of David, for the end, for the sons of Korah.” [Col. 0733D] This means that this psalm of the prophet David—or of any faithful and perfect soul, whether from the former people or from the later one—is set forth for the end to the sons of Korah, specifically so that they may avoid the customary perversion.

For the customary perversion among human beings is that, although they ought to live according to God’s will, they prefer God to live according to their will. And while they themselves do not wish to be corrected, they want God to be corrupted, judging that what he wills is not just, but that what they will is just. Those who love him for the sake of earthly advantages and temporal goods murmur against him when they see the good afflicted and the wicked prospering, as though he did not deign to govern human affairs or did not care for these lower matters.

The divine word speaks against such people also in this psalm. We need not make you attentive to it, since the prophet himself makes you sufficiently attentive—not only you, but all people, whether righteous or unrighteous—by saying: “All nations,” that is, you who still live as gentiles, hear these things that I shall say, so that you may be corrected.

[Col. 0734A] Why does he say “all nations”? Was his voice so loud that everyone could hear it? Certainly not. Rather, through the Holy Spirit he foresaw that what had been written and read within that one Jewish people would be revealed and read again among all nations. Therefore he said: “Hear, all nations”; and you also, all who inhabit the world, receive these things with your ears.

This appears to be a repetition, unless perhaps we say that earlier he addresses the wicked, while here he addresses the righteous. And he seeks those ears that the Lord requires in the Gospel when he says: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

For only those possess ears for hearing who inhabit the earth—that is, their own flesh—not those whom the earth inhabits; that is, not those who are subject to their flesh, but those who rule it by governing all its unlawful impulses well. They are not carried by the bed of sorrow; rather, they carry it themselves.

Therefore he says: “All who inhabit the world”—that is, all who, by inhabiting and cultivating the earth of your flesh, make it a world, that is, rounded and perfected—receive, I say, these things that I shall say. [Col. 0734B] And do not receive them in an ordinary way, but with ears—that is, with ears for hearing.

It is as though he said: For the present, let good and evil hear together; but when the time of separation comes, then it will appear who heard with a reason and who without a reason. Those hear without a reason who remain in gentility; those hear with a reason who inhabit the world.

Let all the earthborn hear these things—that is, all who bear the image of the earthly and seek an inheritance for themselves on earth, like giants striding upon their own breasts, who had serpent-like feet because they could not raise themselves from the earth. And let all the sons of men hear—that is, those who bear the image of the Son of Man, namely, Christ. And therefore let them hear as sons—that is, as imitators of true men, namely, the patriarchs and prophets.

Let the earthborn hear on account of judgment; let the sons of men hear on account of reward. It is a repetition, though with weightier and more explicit terms. For the name “earthborn” indicates wickedness more explicitly than “nations.”

[Col. 0734C] Let rich and poor, gathered together into one, hear at present the one who teaches, lest in the future they hear God separately as judge. For then the rich will hear: “Go, accursed ones, into the fire”; while the poor will hear: “Come, blessed ones,” and so forth.

A person is called rich either because he possesses riches and is puffed up by them, or because he does not possess them but wishes to possess them in order to be exalted by them. Likewise, people are called poor who neither possess nor care to possess; or, if they possess, are as though they did not possess.

God does not inspect the chest or the wine-cellar, but the conscience. In this way many who are not rich in body are ruinously rich in heart, while many who are rich in body are healthfully poor in heart. Such poor rich people were those concerning whom the Apostle said to Timothy: “Command the rich of this world,” and so forth.

[Col. 0734D] My mouth shall speak wisdom. You ought to hear what I shall say because certain great things will be spoken. For my mouth shall speak true wisdom. And because many speak wisdom with their mouth but not from their heart, like that people concerning whom it was said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me”—and because meditation properly belongs to the heart—he adds: “And the meditation of my heart,” that is, my meditating heart, not neglecting, shall speak prudence, so that each person may foresee why there is fear on the evil day and may labor in such a way that he will not fear there.

This amounts to saying: What I shall say, I shall not say merely with my mouth, but shall bring forth from my heart. And lest we suppose that he speaks from his own mouth and from his own heart, and therefore despise him, he says that what he will speak he first hears with the ear of hearing from the Truth presiding within him.

For many speak without hearing what they say. Such are all those who say and do not do. Concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat; whatever they tell you, do and observe, but do not act according to their works.”

Therefore he says that he will first hear and then open. And when he says: “I will incline my ear to a parable,” he means: Before I speak, I will humble the power of hearing within me, so that, with the Truth presiding inwardly, I may hear.

“I will humble it,” he says, “to a parable,” because it is necessary that I still hear in a parabolic manner. For as long as we are in this body, we are exiles from the Lord and see only in part. Hence the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma.”

[Col. 0735A] However much anyone may carve out and cultivate his heart, however much he may withdraw into the inner regions in order to see inward things, nevertheless, while we remain in this corruption, the vision we possess is like an enigma or a parable—that is, an obscure likeness—compared with the vision that only the good will possess after this corruption.

There will nevertheless be there a bodily vision of Christ common to all, just as here it was common to the good and the wicked, since it was said: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced.” But that vision of which the Lord says, “If anyone loves me, he will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him,” is reserved for those who love him alone.

And concerning this vision it was said: “Let the impious be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.” Nor will this vision be capable of being seen with outward eyes, but only with inward eyes.

[Col. 0735B] I will incline my ear, I say, in order to hear; and afterward I will open my proposition—that is, what I have set forth as something to be displayed in the psalter, that is, in the body through action.

For just as a musician uses a psalter as an instrument for producing a particular sound, so the soul uses the instrument of the body to open what it has heard inwardly from the Truth. It is understood more clearly when it is opened in words and deeds.

Why shall I fear on the evil day? The iniquity of my heel shall surround me. The connection is as follows: I say that I shall open my proposition. This, then, is that proposition: Why shall I—or anyone else—fear on the evil day? Namely, because the iniquity of the heel will surround us.

It is as though he said: This cause of fear lies within the power of my free choice, so that I can either admit it or avoid it. I shall avoid it, and thus on the evil day I shall not fear but rejoice.

The evil day is the day of calamity and misery, which will be evil for many but good for many others. For just as it is evil for those who perish, so it is good for those who are saved.

[Col. 0735C] The perfect person who speaks here says that he fears on this day not on his own account, but by transferring others into himself. What he says—“The iniquity of my heel shall surround me”—may be understood in this way: through the heel, which is a part of the foot, the whole foot is understood; and afterward, through what produces something, the thing produced is understood—namely, the foot for the way.

Even so, our heels will be our ways, namely, crooked ways. For whatever we possess from ourselves will be crooked; whatever is from God is good. The meaning, then, will be: “The iniquity of my heel,” that is, of my ways, which are crooked, “shall surround me,” that is, shall oppress me on the evil day. And this will be the cause of my fear, or of anyone’s fear.

But since it lies within the power of our free choice either to persist in crooked ways or not to avoid crooked ways and to persist in the straight way—the way that says of itself, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”—we shall not fear but rather rejoice.

Or otherwise: We are easily overthrown through the heel because we rely upon it more firmly. Therefore the heel signifies those sins by which we are more easily overthrown into destruction, namely, mortal sins. According to this interpretation the meaning will be: “The iniquity of my heel,” that is, my wicked overthrow, namely, my mortal sins, “shall surround me on the evil day”; and therefore I shall fear.

[Col. 0735D] Or otherwise: The heel is the extremity of the foot; therefore the heel signifies the final state of works, against which the devil lies in wait for us most intensely, because if the end is evil, the preceding life will be of no value.
