Or, to put it differently: Through the heel, on which we stand more firmly, our state is signified—namely, humility and love, which the devil continually strives to destroy in us through their opposites. For blessed Gregory says: “He does not care to take away what belongs to us, but to strike love in us.”

The meaning, then, is this: On the evil day I shall fear because “the iniquity of my heel”—that is, its wicked overthrow, namely, of the humility and love in which I ought to have stood more firmly—“shall surround me,” that is, shall oppress me there.

Or otherwise: Since the heel clings to the earth, carnal desires are signified by it; and when we cling to these, we easily slip. Therefore we suffer the tempter’s snares more intensely in this matter, although we ought to crush his head.

[Col. 0736A] Hence it was said to Eve and the serpent: “He shall lie in wait for your heel, and you shall crush his head.” For the serpent—that is, the devil—will always lie in wait for the heel, that is, for the fall of our flesh, so that through the very thing in which we are weak he may deceive us.

But we ought to crush his head—that is, the beginning of his suggestion—against the rock, namely Christ, so that it may not be carried through into action. For blessed is the one who will seize him and dash him against the rock.

But since, as he says, all these things lie within my power, I shall avoid them completely and thus fear nothing.

Those who trust. He describes who those are who fear on the evil day, or whom the iniquity of the heel will surround: all those who trust in their own strength.

[Col. 0736B] The preceding verse may also be understood entirely as a question, if one does not wish to say that the perfect person who speaks here fears by transferring others into himself. It would then be as though he said: Why shall I, or any perfect person, fear on the evil day? Surely the iniquity of my heel will not surround me? Certainly not, for it will surround only those who trust in their own strength—that is, those who presume upon themselves and do not hope in the Lord—and who glory in the abundance of their own riches, that is, earthly riches, rather than in the Lord, who promises exaltation to the humble and threatens condemnation to the proud.

A brother does not redeem, and so forth. They glory, I say, in riches, although one ought not to glory in them; nor ought one to glory in friends, although friendship is the most precious kind of wealth.

And truly one ought not to glory in friends, because a human being, however much he may be a friend, will not redeem anyone from the coming wrath. And truly a human being will not redeem, because even a human brother will not redeem.

This brother-man is the one who is true God and true man, who said: “Go, announce it to my brothers,” and with whom we have God the Father in common. Hence whoever calls him Father must also call this one brother.

[Col. 0736C] Although this human brother redeemed all alike if they approached him, nevertheless he did not redeem those who trample upon the blood of the righteous and do not drink their price—that is, those who do not delight in his Passion but receive God’s grace in vain. Hence the Apostle says: “We urge you not to receive the grace of God in vain.”

The brother-man, I say, does not redeem him, and this because he will not give God—that is, to that human brother—his own propitiation, namely, what properly belongs to him. In other words, he does not display true humility and true obedience, through which he might make him propitious toward himself, just as he himself made the Father propitious through these things.

This can be stated briefly as follows: He does not imitate him, and he will not give the price of the redemption of his soul—that is, the means by which he may redeem his soul.

Concerning this price the Lord says in the Gospel: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity.” *Mammon* in the Syriac language means money; and money is iniquitous, because blessed Jerome says: “Every rich person is either iniquitous or the heir of an iniquitous person. But this is the height of iniquity: if someone wishes to make private for himself what God made common.”

[Col. 0736D] Again, elsewhere the Lord says: “Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys.”

For the one truly gives the price of the redemption of his soul who gives alms worthily—that is, who gives both himself and his possessions. Hence it was said: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.”

He will not give a price for his soul, I say, and therefore he will labor forever. That is, to his temporal anxiety will be added the anxiety of eternal misery. And thus, although his life ends, his labor will not end. When he comes to the end of his life—the luxurious life he chose for himself—he will continue to live, not to be crowned but to be punished in hell.

He shall not see destruction. Therefore his labor will rightly be eternal, because he neither sees nor will see the true destruction, namely, the inward destruction, but only the outward destruction, when he sees wise people dying outwardly.

[Col. 0737A] For he says: “Look, this man was wise; he strove in every way to serve God, and yet he died. What, then, did his holiness profit him? Or what did his goodness help him? Certainly nothing. Therefore, while I live, I shall feast and rejoice; nor shall I labor in this kind of holiness.”

In saying this, the wretched man considers only the outward and not the true destruction of the mind. And because he does not consider the true destruction, therefore the foolish and the stupid alike will perish—that is, in body and soul.

The imprudent person is anyone who does not consider the extent of the misery in which he is here; the stupid person is one who does not provide for himself in the future.

And he shall leave his riches to strangers. The stupid and foolish will indeed perish; and, as they perish, they will leave their riches, in which they gloried, to those who will benefit them neither by alms nor by prayers.

For even if they leave them to grandchildren or children, they will nevertheless leave them to them as strangers—that is, as people who will contribute nothing to their welfare. Nothing will benefit anyone after death except what he carries away with him from here, or unless he has been such a person as to deserve to be helped by prayers and alms.

[Col. 0737B] They will indeed leave them to strangers and will derive no benefit from this, except that their tombs are of marble, and their houses are “forever”—that is, those strangers adorn their tombs as though they believed that the dead would remain there forever. They adorn the place where the body is to be placed, but do not consider where the spirit is tormented among the dead.

For this reason they also receive another useless thing from those same strangers: their tabernacles—that is, their palaces—from which they will depart, are called tabernacles existing in their lands, that is, in their estates. Those tabernacles, I say, through their inhabitants, they have called by their own names.

The strangers who inherit them—namely, the descendants—keep their memory at their anniversaries, invoking them by name and feasting abundantly. This is done not only among children and grandchildren, but among the departing generation and the succeeding generation—that is, among all later generations. This custom, it is said, both existed and still exists among the gentiles.

We, however, have transferred it to the service of religion, so that at the anniversaries of our fathers we do not invoke them by name, but invoke God for them through the celebration of Masses and through almsgiving.

[Col. 0737C] When man was in honor. It is as though he said: Such people, not giving God their propitiation or the price of the redemption of their souls, and leaving their riches to strangers, have perished because they will labor forever.

They are not excusable on this account, and the Creator is culpable—or rather, they themselves are culpable and the Creator is excusable—because he made them such that they could use reason; but through their fault it has come about that they are like horse and mule, which have no understanding.

This he says as follows: “When man was placed in honor,” because he was made in the image and likeness of God and could use reason, “he did not understand”—that is, he did not act intelligently, because he did not attend to reason. Hence he left his riches to strangers.

For if he had acted intelligently, he would rather have entrusted them to that human brother of whom it was said above, nourishing and clothing his members; and he would have restored them to him multiplied.

And because he did not act intelligently, therefore he was compared with foolish beasts—that is, he was bent toward earthly things like brute animals, which nature fashioned prone and obedient to the belly. As a result he truly became like them, namely, lacking the use of reason as they do.

Observe that the whole human race is signified here by one man, since in the first man it suffered the loss of reason.

[Col. 0737D] This way of theirs is a stumbling block to them. “Way” is understood as “life.” The meaning is as though he said: Let the life of those whom we mentioned above—their failure to act intelligently in this and that way, and their resemblance to foolish beasts—be a stumbling block to them alone, that is, to their eternal condemnation, and not to you, O Christian, to whom I speak.

That is, do not approve or follow such things as they follow, lest they become a stumbling block to you as they are to them.

Therefore I say that these things are a stumbling block to them, not to you, because afterward—that is, after they have persisted in this way and lived wickedly—they will please themselves, wishing to please others as well as themselves. And they do this not in the mouth of God but in their own mouth, that is, by persuading others of such things.

[Col. 0738A] This amounts to saying: They wish to please others for this purpose, namely, so that they may persuade them to follow what they themselves perversely pursue.

Or otherwise: “This way of theirs”—namely, acting unintelligently—is a stumbling block to them, that is, an offense and condemnation, because they did not consider that they had been made for the honor of God. Yet afterward, after they have been inwardly scandalized in this way and made like beasts, they will please themselves—that is, they will wish to please both God and themselves and those like themselves, as well as true preachers.

They wish to please God because they give thanks to him for the abundance of crops and for their lords, blessing him outwardly while cursing him in their hearts. They please themselves and those like themselves when they accuse their weakness and say: “We are naturally weak, and therefore we cannot help consenting to our frailty,” and similar things.

They also wish to please true preachers, saying: “Nothing is holier, nothing is more righteous for the Lord than to fast, give alms, and do everything you say”; yet they hate these very things in their hearts.

[Col. 0738B] The beginning of this verse may also be expressed in another way, as follows: Man has indeed been placed in honor because he was made in the image and likeness of God. Nevertheless, this way—the image and likeness of God, which ought to be their way, because they ought to attend to it whenever mention is made of it—is a stumbling block to them, because they refuse to hear it; or it is a stumbling block to them, that is, a road to eternal condemnation, because they neglect it.

And yet, after they have been corrupted in this way, they will please themselves, as was said above.

Like sheep in the underworld. It is as though he said: Because they have been scandalized and nevertheless wish to please themselves, they have been placed in the inner underworld, that is, in blindness of mind. They are there, I say, like sheep—that is, not fervent in spirit but weak like sheep—and they crop grass, that is, desire carnal pleasures.

And because they have been placed in the underworld like sheep, therefore death—that is, the devil—will feed upon them, that is, will be their shepherd.

[Col. 0738C] The devil is called death because he was the cause both of the death of the soul and of the death of the body, when he persuaded the first man to depart from his God into the region of unlikeness. There the death of the soul occurred, and the punishment of bodily death followed it.

And just as life—that is, Christ—is the shepherd of all those whose way of life is in heaven, for salvation, so the devil is the shepherd of all those who fix their mind upon earthly things, for condemnation.

Or it may be said in this way: “Death will feed upon them,” that is, will consume them, because it will delight in them. For it was said to the serpent—that is, to the devil—that he would eat earth, that is, the wicked.

And they shall rule over them. It is as though he said: Since death will feed upon those placed in the underworld, it will be necessary for them to persecute the godly. Nevertheless, there is no cause for concern. Even if now, while it is the time of winter and night, while the little plants are green and the trees are dry, the impious seem according to the flesh to oppress the righteous, yet when summer comes it will be otherwise.

For in the morning—that is, in that morning when the true sun of righteousness begins to appear, a morning without a succeeding night—the righteous will rule over them, namely, over the impious, according to the saying: “The saints will judge the nations and rule over peoples.”

[Col. 0738D] The righteous will therefore rule over them because they will perish, since their presumed support in this life, their glory—that is, riches, friends, and other such things—will grow old, that is, will be destroyed, while they are placed in the outer underworld, just as previously they had been placed here in the inner underworld.

Nevertheless God will redeem. The connection is as follows: Those such as we have described—those who do not give God their propitiation and so forth—will not be redeemed by a human brother; nevertheless, God will redeem my soul from the hand of the underworld, that is, from conformity with such underworld dwellers, and also from the power of the outer underworld, when he has already received me from it.

For by assuming me according to my nature from the Virgin’s womb and from the tomb, and by assuming me also through those like me after the victory over death, he has already received me from that outer underworld. Hence I am certain that in the end he will receive me also.

[Col. 0739A] This may be understood as the speech of someone from the later people. But if someone from the former people is speaking here, then “when he has received me” will refer to the future, as though he were foreseeing this through the Holy Spirit and announcing with certainty that it would happen.

It may likewise be said: Truly he will rescue me from the power of the underworld when he has already received me from the mass of those destined for destruction. For whoever is a participant in the first resurrection will also be a participant in the second.

Do not be afraid. It is as though he said: Since those whom death will feed upon will perish in the future, while the righteous will rule, therefore you, O Christian, who until now murmured against the Lord because you saw the good afflicted and the wicked prospering, should no longer fear that you have believed in God in vain whenever any impious person became rich, especially when the glory of his house—namely, money, friends, possessions, and similar things—was multiplied.

Rather, it is as though he said: If you see him flourishing, consider him finally dying and afterward withering.

[Col. 0739B] For when he dies. Therefore, when you see such things, you should not fear, because they will profit him nothing: when he dies, he will not take all those things with him. He will carry nothing with him except sins.

And truly he will not take everything with him, because his glory, which he chose for himself here, will not descend with him into the underworld. Rather, what he regarded as glory will be turned into disgrace.

Because his soul. His glory will rightly not descend with him, because, for the greater accumulation of his sins, he will not lack the encouragement of flatterers while he lives.

He says this as follows: “His soul,” that is, his animal life, will be blessed by the tongue of flatterers during his life—the life he himself chose, namely, a life flowing with pleasures.

For flatterers will say of him: “This man certainly lived well while he lived.” In fact, he lived badly while he lived, because he treated himself badly. Whatever he takes in here with pleasure, he will digest in hell with the greatest sorrow; and the one whose life is blessed here will have his spirit tormented in hell.

Therefore he will rightly have no glory, because this too is added to the accumulation of his misery: he will confess to you—that is, praise you—only when you have done him good, that is, when you have made something prosper for him; but he will curse you when he suffers some loss.

[Col. 0739C] He shall enter even to the generation of his fathers. Since his life will be blessed and he will confess to you only when he has been bribed, therefore he will enter deeply into the generation of his fathers—that is, he will become very much like his fathers, not Abraham, Jacob, and the other righteous, but his fathers Cain, Saul, and the other impious, so that even in the underworld he may share their miseries.

Therefore he will not see light—that is, he will not know God, who is the true light—blinded forever, that is, until they are carried from the darkness of dreams into the eternal darkness of torments, where he will be eternally deprived of the true light.

When man was in honor. It is as though he said: On this account the Creator is culpable and they are excusable—or rather, the reverse, because the Creator placed him in the honor of his image and likeness, but wretched man cast himself down from it. For “when he was in honor, he did not understand,” and so forth.

# ON PSALM XLIX

*Psalm of Asaph.*

[Col. 0739D]

## ARGUMENT

In the preceding psalm he addressed his speech to all people; now he speaks to the Jews, wishing to alarm and correct sinners who, neglecting the virtues, cared only about sacrifices. He carries the whole matter out with a more terrifying presentation, as though describing a judicial tribunal, so that the entire address of God may be full of dread. Likewise, it is to be read in relation to the Gospel of Matthew.

## EXPLANATION

Asaph was the son of Barachiah, from the family of Gershon, the son of Levi. In Chronicles he is recorded as having been chosen among the four leaders of the singers, so that he might cause psalms to resound to the Lord with musical instruments. He was not the author of this psalm, as has also been said concerning the others, but was an outstanding musician.

Nevertheless, in this title he deserved to be included because of the significance of his [Col. 0740A] name. For *Asaph* is interpreted as “synagogue” or “assembly”; but here that faithful synagogue is to be understood as speaking which both believed in the Christ who was to come and most gladly received him when he came.

It should be clearly understood that this psalm prophesies both advents of the Lord. In the first section the faithful synagogue speaks—the synagogue that now exists among Christian peoples—about the first and second advent of the Lord Christ. In the second, Christ himself admonishes the peoples that, having abandoned the sacrifices of cattle, they should offer a sacrifice of praise. In the third, the synagogue speaks again, charging sinners with their wickedness.

## COMMENTARY
“God of gods, the Lord has spoken.”

Such is the title: “A Psalm of Asaph.” Asaph was one of the precentors chosen by David. The psalm is not inscribed to Asaph because it was composed by him—for it is written, and it is true, that David composed all the psalms—but it is so entitled because the mystery of this name is rightly suited to it. For Asaph is interpreted as “gathering” or “assembly.” In this psalm the assembly of the former people speaks, because there were not lacking among that people those who, when the Holy Spirit revealed it, understood that the priesthood and sacrifice of Aaron, and the covenant, were to be changed. Such men speak here, warning their children not to think themselves excusable, since from ancient times they have clear and certain evidence from which they cannot pretend not to understand the time of visitation, the time of fulfillment and grace.

Nor should anyone be astonished on seeing the law given through a servant and the covenant changed, because the Lord of the Sabbath and of the law will be present—one who does not abolish the law but fulfills it. And he speaks as follows:

“The Lord”—not just anyone, but he who is “God of gods,” that is, God of the just, God of those who have been made gods. For if he justifies, he also deifies, since it is said of the just: “I said, You are gods.” There is indeed one God by nature, but many by grace. Thus one was born from the substance of the Father, while many were made by his grace. Hence the Apostle says: “See what sort of grace God has given us, that we are called and are the children of God.” And John says: “Beloved, we are children of God; what we shall be has not yet appeared. But when he appears in glory, we shall be like him.”

He alone is like by birth; we are like by living. We are merely like, not equal; he alone is like because he is consubstantial, coeternal, and coequal. And that one alone wished to have us as his coheirs because he loved us. That inheritance, however, is not diminished by the abundance of its possessors, nor does it become narrower through the multitude of coheirs, for it is as great in many as in few.

Let us now return to the literal sense. “The Lord God of gods, being, has spoken.” It is as though he said: He who formerly spoke through the prophets, through the patriarchs, and through the apostles now speaks through himself and through his apostles. He also speaks through us whenever we say anything true. He speaks through many vessels and through many instruments, himself sounding everywhere and himself inspiring everywhere. The Lord, I say, speaks, and by speaking he will summon the earth, both through himself and through his own people.

And how far will he summon it? [Col. 0740D]

“He will summon it from the rising of the sun to its setting.”

That is to say: He summoned as much of it as he created. He did not summon Africa alone, but he did not exclude Africa. And as much as he summoned, so much did he redeem. But he condemned the fathers who contradicted him.

And where did this summons begin? It began from Zion, that is, from the Jewish people. Zion is “the form of his beauty”; from there came forth the holy apostles, who are the form of his beauty. For his beauty—that is, God’s beauty—consists of all who believe in him. The holy apostles are the manifestation, that is, the ornament, of this beauty. On the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection they were the first to receive the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. Hence the Apostle says: “We ourselves have the firstfruits of the Spirit.”

Beginning from Jerusalem, they evangelized the kingdom of God, so that their sound went out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world.

“From the rising of the sun” may also be explained allegorically, so that the meaning is: By speaking he summoned the earth. And where did he begin? From the rising of the sun, that is, from the Jewish people, which alone was in the East through its legal institutions. Though these were in a certain sense shadowy, the true Sun of righteousness was to appear to it, and from there he began to summon. For he himself says that he was sent only to “the sheep that had perished, the house of Israel,” which must be referred to his bodily presence.

And by summoning through his apostles he reached as far as the setting, that is, as far as the Gentiles. They truly were at the setting, as it were, of the sun, because they did not even know the worship of God but adored idols. In accordance with what follows, this will be as though an explanation of the preceding: “From Zion will be the beauty of his appearance.”

“God will come manifestly.” I say that the Lord will speak because God will come manifestly—God, I say, our God, that is, having become a participant in our nature. In that nature he will give such evident signs that it will be clear that God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. Thus it may be said: “No one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.” God, I say, will come, and in coming he will not be silent concerning the commandment.

Truly he did not remain silent concerning the commandment who said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who tithe mint and rue and every herb, but pass over the weightier matters of the law, straining out a gnat and not swallowing a camel.” Again it is said of him: “He was speaking not as their scribes and Pharisees, but as one having authority.”

“Fire is in his presence.” It is as though he said: When God comes and gives commandments, the fire of love will blaze up—the fire of which it is said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” It will blaze up, I say, “in his presence,” that is, in those whom he himself will see standing near him: in the holy apostles and in the other members of the primitive Church.

“And around him”—that is, around his presence—there will be a violent storm: among those surrounding them, who will be a spectacle not for imitation but for persecution. In them, I say, there will be a violent storm, because just as a storm usually overturns things and sinks ships, so an evil conscience will lay them waste, so that “the one who is filthy may become still filthier.”

“He summoned heaven.” The Lord, I say, will come from above, that is, coming from the bosom of the Father, and he will first summon the heavens—those, namely, of whom it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” That is, he will choose the apostles; and through those heavens he will summon the earth, that is, the remaining faithful, who are signified by well-cultivated earth.

He will summon them “to discern his people,” that is, so that his people may be distinguished from the people who are not his: so that there may be a difference between one who believes and one who does not believe, between one who hopes in him and one who presumes upon himself.

“Gather his holy ones to him.” Behold, Asaph, foreseeing through the Spirit what would happen through the heavens, turns to those heavens. It is as though he said: When the Lord comes, you heavens will gather his holy ones to him. Gather his holy ones to him through faith, those who are now scattered among the ungodly.

And who are his holy ones? Those who live by faith and perform works of piety. [Col. 0741D] He subsequently defines them, as though he said: I mean those whom he calls his holy ones who “order his covenant above sacrifices,” that is, who place the new and heavenly promises before legal institutions and earthly promises, retaining the latter but postponing the former. This is understood from the word “order,” because in an arrangement one thing is always placed before another and another is postponed.

Or otherwise: Those who “order his covenant above sacrifices” are those who consider that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us,” who presume upon nothing in themselves but ascribe everything to the grace of God. Therefore they order his covenant—that is, God’s promises—above their sacrifices, that is, they prefer them to their good works, which are sacrifices offered upon the altar of faith. They do not think that they will attain the promised glory through their merits, but through grace.

“And the heavens will proclaim his righteousness.” The Lord will indeed summon the heavens, and those heavens will proclaim his righteousness to the whole earth, that is, his faith which justifies. For everywhere they proclaimed his death and resurrection.

And what should be understood by “upon the needy and the poor”? Those who attend to it rightly are justified; and this they will proclaim, so that his people may be distinguished from the people who are not his. The latter truly must be distinguished, because God, who searches even the marrow, will at last distinguish them, since he is the true judge.

Thus far concerns the Lord’s hidden coming. “God will come manifestly” has been inserted. Nevertheless, this same passage may also be read of his manifest and future coming, if the preceding words are understood in this way: “The Lord summoned as much earth as he created. From where, however, will this summons begin? From Zion, namely, the beauty of his appearance will come upon that earth.”

For from there the holy apostles were born and summoned. From there also, because—as has been said elsewhere—“salvation is from the Jews,” the hidden Lord came, because he came to suffer. Though he was strong in himself, he appeared weak and humble in our flesh. For it was necessary that he be seen and not recognized, and that he be despised, so that he might be crucified. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” Therefore he walked hidden among his enemies: hungry, thirsty, performing wonders, suffering evils, sorrowful, wearied, hidden in many ways, until he was crucified upon the wood.

And the Lord who came in this hidden manner will finally come manifestly. He who came secretly to be judged will come manifestly to judge; he who came secretly to stand before judges will come manifestly to judge those judges as well.

And this is what he says: “God will come manifestly for judgment,” because he will come in the majesty of the Father and of the holy angels—God himself, I say, our God, that is, of our nature. For he will come just as he ascended into heaven. And when he comes manifestly, he will not be silent concerning judgment, just as previously, when he came hidden, he was not silent concerning the commandment.

As for the fact that he now scourges some people, this is admonition, not condemnation, because he still intercedes for us. He has not yet exercised his wrath but is awaiting our repentance. [Col. 0742C]

“Fire is in his presence.” God, I say, will come manifestly, and before the presence of him who comes there will blaze—that is, it will burn outwardly—a fire. For just as an evil conscience now burns the wicked inwardly, so then fire will burn outwardly.

And what fire? The elemental fire, namely, which will encompass all the places that the waters of the Flood encompassed, and will rise as high as those waters rose. This fire will purify gold and reduce straw to ashes.

For the present, it is in your power what you become, lest, when what will come arrives against your will, you find yourself uncorrected. If, however, it were in our power that this fire should not come, and that judgment should not take place, and if we were always in complete abundance of every delight and free from sins, even then we ought always to grieve and always to lament, because we would be separated from him by whom we were created, namely, from the ineffable sweetness of the face of God.

But those who have not yet experienced sweetness should at least fear the fire. Let punishments terrify those whom rewards do not invite. And if what he promises seems worthless to someone, let him at least tremble at what he threatens.

“Fire will blaze before him, and around him there will be a violent storm.” By the surrounding storm he means the angels who will be around him—those, namely, of whom it is said: “He will send his angels, and they will gather all nations before him, and they will collect from his kingdom all scandals.”

Among these angels, when they gather those scandals—that is, the wicked—there will be a violent storm, that is, a great winnowing. It must be great, since it will winnow so vast a threshing floor. For now there is great mixture upon the threshing floor, because the good and the wicked are mixed together in the Church. Then that winnowing, carried out through the angels, will separate them, placing the good at the right hand and the wicked at the left.

“He summoned heaven.” Thus, I say, the Lord will come to judge, and then he will summon heaven, that is, the apostles, from below, where they naturally were because they were carnal, upward, so that they may sit with him and judge. He will summon not heaven alone but also the well-cultivated earth, that is, he will summon the faithful upward. But the uncultivated and marshy earth will be shaken downward.

He will summon the earth “to discern his people,” that is, so that his people may be distinguished from the people who are not his.

“Gather them to him.” Asaph, foreseeing through the Holy Spirit the future winnowing to be carried out through the angels, turns in an apostrophe to the angels themselves. It is as though he said: When the Lord comes for judgment, you heavenly armies will gather his holy ones.

And do this: gather to the Lord, that is, for his honor, his holy ones from faith—those who see and perform works of piety—so that he may deliver the kingdom to God and the Father. Then the holy ones who are now scattered among the wicked will truly be gathered, when they are called to eternal rewards, and they will no longer be separated from one another.

He determines whom he calls holy by saying: “Those who order his covenant above sacrifices.” This is not changed.

“And they will proclaim.” The Lord will indeed summon the heavens above, and then those heavens will proclaim his righteousness. That is, in the glorification of their dignity they will make manifest how greatly they labored here for righteousness. For because they labored here for righteousness more than others, they will be more worthy there. Thus their dignity will reveal the benefit of good works. This, I say, the heavens will proclaim—the heavens summoned above by the Lord—to discern his people.

His people will truly be distinguished, because God, who is the true judge, will distinguish it.

This verse may also be read in another way, so that what follows stands as an insertion. Asaph, speaking here, may admonish his descendants concerning God’s just judgment, saying: The Lord, in his manifest advent, will distinguish his people. And this distinction will not be hidden from you, descendants, because his righteousness—that is, this just judgment of God—will be proclaimed to you by the prophets and the angels. [Col. 0743C] The heavens also—that is, his apostles—will make known what must rightly be proclaimed, for it will truly come to pass, since God is judge.

“Hear, my people.” Here he returns to the principal subject. It is as though he said: The Lord God of gods first spoke through a created instrument, but he will speak through himself. He himself, I say, speaks as follows:

“My people hear.” It is as though he said: If you hear, you are my people; but if you do not hear, you are alien. Therefore hear attentively, and thus I will tell you what I want from you.

“Israel, hear, and I will testify”—that is, under the testimony of the prophets who attest the same thing, I will say to you this: “I am God, and I am your God.”

I am God because I am the one who is; I am your God because I am the God of your fathers—of Abraham, Jacob, and their like. And if I am God, I am God for your good; but if I am not your God, I am not your God for your harm.

“I will not reproach you for your sacrifices.” It is as though he said: I, who am your God, say this to you, Israel: I will no longer reproach you concerning your sacrifices, that is, concerning those instituted for you by the former fathers and offered to me with respect to their signs, though not with respect to what they signified.

For sacrifices as signs had a place as long as the Lord spoke through a created instrument. But after he spoke through himself, the signs that promised were removed, because the promised reality was presented. From then on, only the sacrifices that were signified have a place. He indicates this by saying:

“Your burnt offerings, namely, those signified, are always before me,” that is, they are pleasing to me.

It must be understood that God rejected certain burnt offerings. Hence it was said above, “Burnt offering and sin offering you did not desire,” and so forth. That must be understood of the signs. Here, however, speaking of what is signified, he says that burnt offerings please him.

Nor is this without reason. For ὅλον means “whole,” and καυστόν means “burnt” or “incense.” The whole burnt offering pleases God in this way: it is a certain fire of most ardent love. With this fire—that is, with this love—let our mind be kindled. Let this same love seize all our members for its own use, and not permit them to serve desire, so that the whole person may burn with the fire of divine love who wishes to offer God an acceptable sacrifice. For God is appeased by such a victim, namely, when everything is done in love.

“I will not take calves from your house.” Since I have said that burnt offerings are pleasing to him, lest that stiff-necked people return to the legal burnt offerings made from calves, goats, and other such creatures, he removes this possibility by saying: “I will not take calves from your house,” and so forth.

For he does not need them—as though he said: All the beasts of the forests are mine, not merely domestic animals but even wild creatures. He demonstrates this by parts. And because burnt offerings were also made from birds, he says:

“I know all the birds of heaven.” I know them not because I created them, but in order to create them; before I created them, I knew them. Therefore I have no need of them. Nor do I need sheaves of grain, because all the beauty of the field—that is, all the fertility of the field—is with me, that is, in my ordering.

For all the works of the Father that were to be displayed in time existed in the Word before all the ages, as was said above. Here he sends us back to the sacrifices of those earlier brothers, Abel and Cain. Cain offered a sheaf of grain, but his sacrifice was not acceptable to the Lord.

“If I were hungry, I would not tell you.” Truly I have no need of these things. For, to speak carnally according to you, since you are carnal: If I were hungry—that is, if it were possible for me to become hungry—I would not tell you to provide food for me.

For I—as though he said—am the Creator, while you are the possessor. All things are with me; with you there are few things. For the whole world and its fullness are mine, and everything contained in it.

“Will I eat the flesh of bulls?” For this reason I would not tell you if I were hungry: you think that I am fed with the flesh of bulls and drink the blood of goats. But this is literally false.

The same words may also be understood allegorically. It is as though he said: Israel, burnt offerings that are signified please me, but not burnt offerings that are accepted in the manner you suppose. For I will not take from your house—that is, from your stiff-necked people—calves, that is, I do not regard as acceptable those who revel in the liberty of the will, who grow proud of legal institutions, and who do not think that they need a physician, even though they wish to offer themselves to me.

Nor will I take from your stiff-necked flocks goats, that is, those who are always foul-smelling in their sins.

“For they are mine.” Therefore I will take them from your people, because I have chosen another people for myself. All the beasts of the forests are mine, that is, all those from the Gentiles who were formerly like wild creatures of the forest, because neither any law nor the prophets had tamed them.

He said “forests” in the plural because of the various teachings of the Gentiles. He explains the wild creatures by parts, saying:

“For the beasts of burden are mine,” that is, the simple and humble among the Gentiles are mine. And lest we understand foolish simplicity, he adds: “Beasts of burden existing only on the mountains,” that is, I receive such simple people as both feed and dwell by faith upon those mountains of which it was foretold that they would be transferred into the heart of the sea.

Those among the Gentiles who are oxen are also mine, that is, those who thresh, choosing what should be chosen and rejecting what should be rejected, and begetting others in faith.

Moreover, “I know all the birds of heaven,” that is, spiritual men from the Gentiles, who are birds of heaven, raising themselves from the earth and living in heavenly things. But I did not know the birds of the earth or of the water, that is, the high-minded among your people who uselessly exalt themselves.

Furthermore, “all the beauty of the field is with me,” that is, the fragrances and varied flowers of every kind of virtue that proceed from those same Gentiles who are now a well-cultivated field. They are with me, that is, they please me.

“If I were hungry, I would not tell you.” Because all these things are mine, therefore, if I were hungry—as indeed I am hungry—I would not tell you, the stiff-necked people.

For God hungers for faith and good works in us. I will not tell you, because you humbled my soul in fasting, as was said above. And for this reason I will not tell you, because the world—that is, the whole earth, which is round like a globe—all of it is mine. And its fullness, that is, those who are like its center and are more perfect among the perfect, is mine. [Col. 0745A]

“Will I eat?” For this reason also I will not tell you of my hunger, because you would feed me with the flesh of bulls, that is, you would return to the former sacrifices; or you would provide for me only bulls and goats, that is, the proud and those foul-smelling in sins, for whom I have no concern. The question has an equivalent force.

But when he says, “I will not tell you of my hunger”—this may seem strange, since he has proclaimed it to everyone. Yet it is not strange, because he says this with respect to affection: the stiff-necked people rejected the salvation sent to them.

“Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God.” Since I no longer accept the sacrifices mentioned above, you who are true Israel, sacrifice to me, God, a sacrifice of praise, that is, a praiseworthy sacrifice: calves not of the flock but of the lips.

That is, offer constant thanksgiving inwardly and outwardly to God, from whom comes whatever good you possess and by whom whatever evil is in you will be forgiven.

“And pay your vows to the Most High.” For you have vows from me, not just any vows but your own—that is, those which are in you, namely, yourself. Whoever considers what he may worthily cherish for God should offer his whole self and make a vow, because this is what is demanded and what is owed.

“And call upon me.” Pay your vows, I say, and then call upon me, presuming nothing upon yourself, “in the day of tribulation,” that is, in the day of pilgrimage. For there is no greater tribulation, since whoever does not attend to this does not seek his homeland from the heart.

Call upon me, I say, in the day of tribulation, because you are not afflicted without purpose. If you were not afflicted, you would not call upon me. But now, because you are afflicted, you will call upon me. And because you will call upon me, I will deliver you from tribulation. And once delivered, you will honor me, that is, praise me, never again departing from me:

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you.”

“But to the sinner God said.” The Lord God of gods said the preceding things to his own people; what follows he said to the sinner, that is, to the people who are not his. He said this:

“Why, since you are a sinner”—that is, a transgressor of my law—“do you recite my righteousnesses to others,” that is, my faith which justifies, or my just commandments? And why do you take up my covenant—that is, my promises—to recite them through your mouth?

For—as though he said—“praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.”

This seems to frighten sinful preachers away from preaching, and it is strange in view of what he says elsewhere: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Whatever they tell you, observe and do.” And Paul says: “By whatever occasion Christ is preached, let him be received.”

These statements seem contrary to what is said here, but they are not. Those statements are made so that hearers may not fear hearing something good, whatever the character of the person from whom they hear it. This statement, however, is made so that those who speak well and act badly may not have any security, but may always fear condemnation from their own speech. For to speak well and live badly is nothing other than to condemn oneself by one’s own voice.

“But you hated discipline and cast my words behind you.” You do indeed recite my righteousnesses and my covenant to others, but you ought not, because you are not among the sons to whom this pertains.

You hated my discipline, that is, my fatherly correction. It is as though he said: When I spare you, you sing and praise me; but when I reprove you, you grumble. It is as though I were God only when I spare you, and were not God when I reprove you.

But I reprove and chastise those whom I love. You hated this discipline because you are illegitimate, not a son. Hence the Apostle says: “If you are without discipline, then you are illegitimate, and not sons.”

You hated discipline, I say, and “cast my words behind you,” that is, behind yourself, though they were spoken through you. So that you would not see them, you cast them behind you, while nevertheless you wanted them to honor you.

[Col. 0746A] “When you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers.”

He shows by the effect what it means to have cast his words behind him: he consented to every wickedness. He says it this way: When you saw a thief, you ran with him, if not with your feet, at least in affection. And you placed your portion with adulterers by consenting to them. For not only those who act, but also those who consent, are worthy of death.

“Your mouth abounded in evil, and your tongue fashioned deceit.” You not only consented to thieves and adulterers, but your mouth also abounded in evil, because you not only failed to rebuke evil by keeping silent, but praised it so that it might increase. And you took pleasure in this.

He says it thus: “Your tongue fashioned,” that is, by taking delight it arranged, as though in something well-fashioned, “deceits,” that is, deceitful words with which you praised what ought to have been rebuked.

Moreover, you slandered your brother, and thus scandalized the son of your mother. Here “brother” means someone already perfect and spiritual; “son of your mother” means someone less perfect, who is still carnal and still needs milk rather than solid food.

Some people, pretending to be perfect, are accustomed to slander spiritual men in the Church, so that they may scandalize the lesser ones. Thus certain people at Corinth said of blessed Paul: “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible.” Through this they scandalized many of the lower members.

Hence he says: “You spoke in slander against your brother,” that is, against any spiritual and more perfect man who ought to be your brother. In this way you placed a stumbling block before “the son of your mother,” that is, by slandering one greater and more worthy, you scandalized the son of your mother, the Church—that is, any lesser and less worthy person who does not yet need solid food but milk.

All these evils, I say, you committed, and yet I was silent, that is, I refrained from vengeance, deferred my severity, prolonged my patience, and awaited your repentance. But you, according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of the revelation of God’s just judgment. [Col. 0746C]

“You wickedly thought that I would be like you; I will rebuke you and set you before your face.”

Because I was silent concerning vengeance, you wickedly thought that I was like you. Since you did not wish to be like me, you thought that I was like you. It seemed little enough to you that you were evil unless you also thought that I wished to be evil.

And because you did not regard me as one who refrained from vengeance in order to punish later, you thought me a partner in guilt and a corrupt judge. You thought this, I say. But at last I will rebuke you through a fitting vengeance and set you before your face.

That is, you who had placed yourself behind yourself so as not to see yourself, I will place before yourself so that you may see yourself. For if you saw yourself, you would displease yourself and please me. But now, because you do not see yourself and you please yourself, you will displease me and displease yourself.

You will displease me when you are judged; you will displease yourself when you burn. I will set you before yourself, I say, so that you may see your ugliness—not so that you may correct it, but so that you may be ashamed forever.

“Understand these things, you who forget God, lest he suddenly seize you and there be no one to rescue you.”

Thus far Asaph has spoken in the person of the Lord speaking to his own people and to the people who are not his. Here, however, he speaks in his own person, admonishing his descendants and other companions.

It is as though he said: Since the Lord says such things to his own people and such things to the people who are not his, therefore you who still forget God in deed, paying no attention to your former evil life and doing nothing good, understand both what the Lord says to his own people and what he says to the people who are not his.

Pay attention to these things, so that, considering our badly spent life in the bitterness of our soul, we may worthily say to God: “I will reflect upon all my deeds before you,” and so forth.

Understand them now, while there is time, lest, if you do not understand, he seize us at some future time as one who is powerful and whom no one can resist. Then there will be no one to rescue you from his hand, that is, no one who can rescue you.

“A sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God.”

It is as though he said: Understand these things, you who forget God—God, I say, who speaks these things for your instruction. “A sacrifice of praise,” that is, a praiseworthy sacrifice, “will honor me.”

Consider what a praiseworthy sacrifice is. For the person who persists in sins does not sacrifice praiseworthily. God does not want us to be either the thieves insulting him on the cross—that is, unconverted—or the Pharisee boasting of his merits in the temple. He does not want us to be arrogant and proud.

Rather, he wants us both to be converted and justified and to humble our souls, that is, to ascribe nothing to our merits. Then he does not want us to desire to be alone in possession of God’s riches, but, if there is any good in us, to wish it also for others.

Thus we shall sacrifice praiseworthily. For a praiseworthy sacrifice consists in being converted from injustice to justice, in being humble, and in possessing true affection of love not only toward God but also toward one’s neighbor—namely, that whoever loves God should also love his neighbor.

Hence he says: “A sacrifice of praise will honor me.” And this is because “in that sacrifice of praise there is a way,” that is, a path, by which way—that is, through which path—I will show him, namely, anyone who understands the things said above, that the salvation of God was necessary.

For whoever persists in a praiseworthy sacrifice attends to justice, humility, and love. These three were the reason for the Savior’s coming.

For someone to be made just from ungodliness, a physician was necessary. For someone to possess true humility, the one was necessary who became obedient to the Father even unto death. Likewise, for someone to possess love, this could happen only through him who, even in his Passion, prayed for his enemies, saying: “Father, forgive them,” and so forth.

INTO PSALM L

“To the end. A psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, when he went in to Bathsheba.”

ARGUMENT.

[Col. 0747C] Under the occasion of repentance, he shows how the people held captive in Babylon ought to repent. Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, where Paul is chosen, and the voice of Paul repenting.

EXPLANATION.

The story is well known: King David desired Bathsheba, seized her, and violated her; he sent her husband Uriah to his death by the sword of the Ammonites. But when his guilt was revealed through Nathan the prophet, he immediately washed away his sin with tears of repentance.

Here one must especially observe that even very holy men were sometimes permitted to fall into such things, and that both their sins and their repentance were included in Scripture, so that for us who are weak and lie far behind their footsteps, fear might commend caution to us in their fall, while their correction might offer an example of repentance and hope of pardon.

But since the deeds of the saints, even when they are dark, also bring about the mystery of our salvation, David signifies Christ. Bathsheba, whose name is interpreted as “well of fullness,” prefigures the Church. Uriah, whose name is interpreted as “my light of God,” represents the devil, who sought to usurp for himself the light of divinity but, struck down by the Lord, lost the kingdom of the world and left the Church of the faithful for the Lord to govern.

This psalm is divided into five parts. The first is satisfaction through the most perfect humility. The second is confidence in heavenly mercy. The third asks the Lord to turn his face away from sins. The fourth says that all sinners should be encouraged more and more to desire supplication, if such an enormous iniquity was forgiven him. In the fifth part the cause of the Church is recalled, for it was to be built through his offspring at the Lord’s coming.

There, now rejoicing, he promises calves to be offered upon the Lord’s altar; thus devout supplication is brought to its conclusion, and the joys of the salvation that is to come are announced.

COMMENTARY.

“Have mercy on me, O God, according to [your] great …”

This psalm, whose title is *A Psalm of David, when the prophet Nathan came to him, because he had gone in to Bathsheba*, makes those who have not yet fallen cautious, just as it does not wish those who have already fallen to be despairing. Therefore, whoever has sinned and hesitates to do penance for his sin, despairing of his salvation, look at David doing penance. The prophet Nathan has not been sent to you, but David himself has been sent. Look, then, at him crying out, and cry out together with him. Look at him groaning, and groan with him. Look at him weeping, and join your tears to his.

“Because he went in to Bathsheba.” Bathsheba was another man’s wife. I say this with grief and trembling. Yet God did not wish what he wished to be written to remain unspoken. I shall therefore speak, not encouraging imitation, but instructing toward fear.

The holy king and prophet David was captivated by her beauty when he was already at peace. As he stood on the roof, he saw her opposite him, shining and well adorned. He called her to him and went in to her. The woman was sanctified from all her uncleanness—that is, she conceived. The woman is understood to be cleansed from uncleanness through conception because after conception she suffers no flow of blood until she has given birth.

When David saw that the adultery could not be concealed, he recalled her husband Uriah from the army, so that Uriah might go in to her and the adultery might thus remain hidden. But when Uriah refused to go in to her, David wrote to Joab, the commander of his army, who was in charge of the troops, instructing him to place Uriah where the battle was fiercest, so that he might perish. This was done, and Uriah was killed. Thus holy David added murder to adultery.

Afterward the prophet Nathan was sent to him by the Lord, to rebuke him for so great a sin. What people ought to avoid has now been stated; we must now say what they should imitate if they have fallen. For many wish to fall with David, but do not wish to rise again with David. The example is not proposed as an example of falling, but, if you have fallen, of rising again.

Take care, therefore, lest you fall. Let the fall of the great not be a pleasure to the lesser, but rather let the fall of the great be a trembling for the lesser. For this purpose, for this reason, and for this the passage was written and often sung and read in the Church: those who have not fallen should hear it so that they may not fall; those who have fallen should hear it so that they may rise again.

Many hear of the fall of so great a man and seek for themselves defenses for sinning. But whoever does this because David did it acts worse than David would have acted. David fell through the lapse of desire, not under the protection of holiness. Many, however, hearing profitably of the fall of so great a man, measure their own weakness by it. Wishing to avoid what God condemns, they turn their eyes away from vanity and do not fix them on the beauty of another’s flesh, knowing that even if the woman is far away, lust is near.

“Do not let sin reign in your mortal body.” Sin is in the body when you take delight; it reigns when you consent. Whoever hears these things and has not fallen should rejoice with David in this and give thanks to the Lord his God. But whoever has already fallen and hears them should consider the greatness of his wound, yet not despair of the greatness of the physician. Groaning with David, let him cry out and say: “Have mercy on me, O God.”

The title given above is explained in this way: this psalm is attributed to David the prophet, namely, as sung when the prophet Nathan came to him—that is, to David himself—sent by the Lord to rebuke him because he had gone in to Bathsheba.

Let us now return to the literal meaning. It is the prophet’s voice after the adultery and murder had been committed, when Nathan had come to him, and David prayed in this manner:

“God, have mercy on me”—that is, apply to me your loving compassion, not a small compassion, but according to your great mercy. That is: apply great mercy to me; apply your loving compassion to me, because it is truly great. Whoever confesses great misery asks for great mercy. It is as though he were saying: “What I bear is exceedingly grave, but I flee to the Almighty. I would despair of my mortal wound unless I found so great a physician.”

“And according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity.”

It is as though he were saying: “My iniquity is that I did to another what I would not wish done to me: I committed adultery with another man’s wife and killed the man himself. You observed and recorded this iniquity. Now blot out that iniquity according to the multitude of your mercies,” that is, according to the many manifestations of your mercy. For from your abundant mercy proceed your many mercies. You look upon those who despise you in order to correct them, upon those who are ignorant in order to teach them, and upon those who confess in order to forgive them.

Those who sin unknowingly obtain your mercy; those who sin knowingly also obtain it—not merely some mercy, but great mercy and abundant mercies. I cannot say that I acted in ignorance. I did not fail to know the evil of touching another man’s wife or of killing a husband who neither knew nor was angry.

“Wash me more thoroughly.”

It is as though he were saying: “You wash those who sin unknowingly, but wash me more thoroughly from this iniquity of mine, and the others who sin knowingly. Or wash me more thoroughly than I know how to ask. Or wash me more thoroughly—that is, not only from my actual iniquity but also from original sin. Wash me in such a way that you cleanse me completely, both from this sin and from my other sins.”

He says more than before. For certain things can be washed and yet not be perfectly cleansed.

And as though someone were saying: “With what boldness are you crying out? With what confidence do you invoke the just God? If he is just, he hates sin; and if he is just, he has punished sin. Implore mercy, but consider justice. It belongs to mercy to forgive the sinner; it belongs to justice to punish sin. What, then, are you seeking? Will your sin remain unpunished?”

“No, Lord. I know the justice whose mercy I implore. But I do not wish you to punish my sin, because I am punishing it; and therefore I ask you to forgive, because I acknowledge it.” This is what he says:

“For I acknowledge my iniquity.”

This may be connected simply in the following way: “Truly you ought to cleanse and wash me, because, insofar as I am able, I make myself fit, since I acknowledge my iniquity, so that it may be forgiven by you.” Thus I understand that my sin is not behind my back, to be forgotten, but is always before me—that is, in my sight, for punishment.

His sin was behind his back when the prophet Nathan came to him. At that time, because he did not attend to his own iniquity, he judged another’s iniquity. When the prophet rebuked him by means of a parallel case, he said: “The man who did this shall surely die, and he shall restore the sheep fourfold.” Then God used his tongue as though it were a surgical instrument for cutting open his wound.

“Against you alone have I sinned.”

It is as though he were saying: “Because I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me, therefore, Lord, have mercy, blot out, wash, cleanse. I ask this of you because, although I am king, against you alone have I sinned.”

For when a king sins, he sins against God alone, because he will punish no other person for his sins. I sinned, I say, against you, and I committed the evil of adultery and murder—which I was able to conceal from others—in your presence; that is, it could not be hidden from you. Therefore have mercy, wash, cleanse.

And therefore I say, “Have mercy,” so that you may be justified—that is, appear just and true—in your words, that is, in your promises. For you promised: “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne.” Thus, in order that this promise may be fulfilled, have mercy on me and cleanse me. For you alone are true, while every human being is false.

I say, have mercy so that you may be justified and prevail, making me worthy when you are judged—namely, by those who say that it is unworthy for you to cause your Christ to be born from the seed of a man so condemned and wicked as I am.

This verse may also be understood in another way, as though he were saying: “For this reason I ask you alone to have mercy on me, because against you alone have I sinned. For you alone are without sin, and therefore you alone can heal and alone can forgive sins.” This is like a sick person saying to a good physician: “Against you alone am I sick”—that is, “I cannot be healed by anyone except you alone.”

I sinned, I say, against you alone, and I committed before you the evil that was hidden from others—that is, it could not be hidden from you. And I sinned against you alone to such an extent—that is, you alone are so entirely without sin—that you do not even sin with your tongue, but are justified in your words: that is, you are true in all your words, and you prevail over all who are judged, and even over the judges when you are judged, because you alone are judged without guilt.

It is difficult to determine to whom he is speaking, since it is clear that the Father, to whom he first seemed to speak, was not judged. But by the Spirit the prophet foresaw the true Judge who would be judged, and the just one who would be condemned by the wicked. He therefore speaks of one who prevails, because there would be nothing in him that could be judged.

He alone was true among human beings; he alone among human beings was without sin, according to what he himself says: “If you have seen sin in me, tell me.” And lest any fault that was hidden from human beings be hidden in him, as the time of his Passion approached he said: “For the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me”—that is, he found in me nothing deserving death or condemnation.

And as though someone were saying: “Why, then, do you die? Why do you suffer?” he adds: “I do not die or suffer because there is sin in me, but so that the world may know that I love the Father; and just as the Father commanded me, so I do. Rise, let us go from here.” Then he went to his Passion.

He suffered as the worthy one for the unworthy and the just one for the unjust. To this one, who had no sin, the prophet here speaks, saying: “You are so entirely without sin that you prevail when you are judged.” It is as though he were saying: “You surpass all human beings; you surpass all judges. In comparison with you, even those who appear just are unjust, because no one is clean in your sight—not even a child whose life has been but one day upon the earth. In comparison with you even the heavens are unclean. Thus you surpass all, because you alone are unjustly judged. You prevail, therefore, when you are judged.”

He calls those who have been judged the holy ones crucified, such as Peter and Andrew and others afflicted in various ways for the name of God. When the Lord was judged, he surpassed all of them, because even if something only slight was found in them, nevertheless something deserving death was found.

“For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins.”

It is as though he were saying: “See how you surpass all. You do not surpass only one such as I now am, after committing so great a crime; you also surpass me as I was at the beginning, and every human being, because you have something to impute to me and to all from our very origin.”

He says this by transferring the human race into himself, for “I was conceived in iniquities,” as every human being is. Was he, then, born from the righteous man Jesse and from a lawful wife, conceived in iniquities—that is, in adultery? Certainly not. This was a chaste act within marriage and does not in itself possess guilt, but it nevertheless draws the punishment that is due, namely, pleasure.

Because this pleasure proceeded from iniquity—that is, from the transgression of the first human being—and because it is itself in a certain sense iniquity, he says: “I was conceived in iniquities.” But he was victorious because he alone was conceived without pleasure; therefore he alone was born without pain. Thus he alone has what he may impute even to a child one day old.

“And in sins she conceived me.”

He proves what he has said as though from the greater case, through the more fragile sex. It is as though he were saying: “Truly I was conceived in iniquities. For if it can be said that I was conceived by my father in iniquities, it is necessary that my mother conceived me in the sin of pleasure.” The female sex is more easily and more greatly corrupted by pleasure.

This same verse may also be connected otherwise, as though he were saying: “Because I have sinned against you alone, therefore have mercy on me. It is necessary for you to have mercy, because I am oppressed not only by so grave an actual crime but also by original sin, since I was conceived in iniquities,” and so forth.

“For behold, you have loved truth.”

I say that I was conceived in iniquities, yet I do not say this in order to shift blame onto you as the author, but because it is true. And I speak the truth for this reason: you love truth—that is, those who speak truth.

The passage may also be connected in another way, as though he were saying: “Because I was conceived in iniquities, therefore, Lord, have mercy on me. I ask you to have mercy because, if you do not have mercy, you will punish. And behold why you will punish: namely, because you have loved truth”—that is, true judgment—to such an extent that, even when you forgive people’s sins, you do not leave them unpunished, because you have loved truth, that is, true judgment. Nevertheless, you have preferred mercy so that you might preserve truth as well. For you forgive the one who confesses but punishes himself. Thus both mercy and truth are preserved: mercy, because the human being is freed; truth, because the sin is punished.

“You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.”

The passage is connected in this way: “I say that if you do not have mercy, you will punish; but truly you will have mercy, because you have already promised this to me. For you made it known to me through the prophet Nathan—indeed, through the Spirit speaking to me through the prophet: ‘Your sin is forgiven.’”

You made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom—that is, of your design and of the new restoration of eternal blessedness. For he chose [us] in him before the foundation of the world.

What things were uncertain, and what things were hidden? Namely, that you forgive even such grave sins in people of this kind. This was previously uncertain to human beings, because they doubted whether God would forgive after so grave a fall; and so they did not know whether there would be any restoration of the human race.

But this was shown to David by experience, when the prophet said to him: “Your sin is forgiven.” Through this likeness he also observed restoration in others. Doubting this uncertainty—that is, restoration after so grave a fall—and whether they would ever be forgiven, the Ninevites did penance at Jonah’s preaching, humbling themselves in every contrition, from the least to the greatest.

That this was uncertain is shown by these words: “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and turn away from the fierceness of his anger, and we shall not perish?” The one who said this regarded the matter as uncertain. Yet the Ninevites, like him, did not wish to remain as they were, if it could be otherwise.

And because they did penance worthily, they learned in reality what they had previously held as uncertain. For, just as the prophet had threatened, their city was overthrown—overthrown for evil, yet rebuilt for good.

When he says “uncertain and hidden,” neither word is superfluous, because through “hidden” he defines “uncertain.” Some things are uncertain by their very nature. These things, however, were uncertain only because they were hidden from human beings.

The whole statement is equivalently this: “Through the prophet you made human restoration known to me.”

But how will this restoration take place? In this way: just as you commanded in the Law that lepers be cleansed by being sprinkled with hyssop dipped in the blood of a red heifer, so you will sprinkle me and others with hyssop and the blood of the calf—not with the sign, but with what was signified—and so we shall be cleansed.

These connections may also be made in part according to another interpretation. According to the way in which we connected the preceding verse—“I do not say this in order to shift blame onto the author, but because you, Lord, love truth”—the following repetition may be made so that what follows is connected:

“Because I was conceived in iniquities, therefore have mercy on me, O God, and cleanse me. And truly you will have mercy, because through the legal institutions you have already made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom”—that is, of your design, namely, the restoration of humanity.

And how did you make it known? In this way: you caused me to understand the things signified through the signs. For in the Law it was commanded that lepers be expelled outside the camp, and then, for their cleansing, be sprinkled with a bundle of hyssop dipped in the blood of a calf, and that, once cleansed, they be brought back. In this the restoration of humanity was prefigured.

Hyssop is a humble plant, useful for the disease of the lungs, from which breath proceeds; through that breath the swelling of pride is signified. By hyssop, however, the humility of Christ is understood, and this humility possessed the power of a medicine for suppressing in us the swelling of our former pride and passion.

The blood of the red heifer likewise signifies the Passion of Christ. The sprinkling of the hyssop dipped in blood, by which the lepers were cleansed, foretold that whoever conformed himself to the humble Christ and was sprinkled with his blood—that is, imitated his Passion—would truly be cleansed from every leprosy of sins. Holy David understood through the Holy Spirit that this would happen.

Therefore he says in this manner: “Through legal signs you made known to me the uncertain things of your wisdom, because you caused me to understand that, just as lepers were cleansed when sprinkled with hyssop and the blood of a calf, so you will sprinkle me and other imitators of Christ with hyssop dipped in the blood of the calf—not the sign but what was signified—and thus I shall be cleansed from sins.”

He explains how you will sprinkle: “You will wash me through that hyssop, and so thoroughly that I shall be made whiter than snow”—that is, I shall be cleansed inwardly beyond every bodily cleansing. This cleansing surpasses every outward cleansing. He uses snow for an outward and especially worthy cleansing because it is whiter than other outward things.

“You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the bones that have been humbled will rejoice.”

“I say, you will sprinkle me, and once sprinkled you will give me joy and gladness”—that is, you will give perfect and complete joy to my hearing, that is, to me who hear. This means: to me who humble myself and learn, not to me who speak—that is, defend my sin.

For hearing is far safer than speaking: the one who hears humbles himself and learns, whereas the one who speaks becomes proud. It is as though he were saying: “By hearing I shall rejoice, but by speaking I shall be sorrowful.”

He is ready to give forgiveness. Let us not therefore shut off forgiveness from ourselves by opening a voice of defense; let us rather open the bosom of confession.

Of this joy the one of whom it was said, “Among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist,” says: “The friend of the bridegroom does not speak and fall, but stands and hears.” Because he hears, he stands and rejoices with joy—not because he speaks, but because he hears the voice of the bridegroom; that is, because he learns.

“You will give me,” I say, “joy as I hear.” And this is because the bones—that is, the supports of my soul, namely the virtues that had previously been humbled—will rejoice by speaking, because they will recover their proper state by hearing.

This verse may also be understood of the future, as though he were saying: “Here you will praise me and make me white; but at last you will give complete joy to my hearing, namely, when I hear you say: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord.’ Then the bones—that is, the supports of my soul, humbled here through penance—will rejoice there, glorified through glory.”

“Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.”

It is as though he were saying: “I say that you will give me joy and that my bones will rejoice. And wherever this takes place, just as previously, when I turned my face away, you turned yours away, so now, when I turn mine away, turn your face away from my sins. Blot out all my iniquities, which previously, by turning away, you recorded; now, by turning away, erase them.”

“And so that you may erase them, O God, create in me a clean heart”—a heart made unclean through me—and make all my thoughts clean. “Renew a right spirit within me”: renew my understanding, now grown old and bent, so that you may make it upright in my inward parts, that is, in my soul.

This spirit was previously upright and aligned with the Spirit of God so long as it did not dissent from God’s will. But when it bent itself toward the desire of the flesh and earthly pleasure, then his spirit became distorted and old. Therefore he now asks that it be renewed and directed upward, so that it may again be aligned with the Spirit of God: that nothing pleasing to God may displease him, and that whatever he or another suffers, he may believe to be just.

His spirit was upright when he attributed all the persecution he suffered from his son Absalom to his own deserts. When Absalom’s soldier was heaping many insults upon him, and one of David’s men wished to kill him, David prevented it, saying: “Do not kill him; God has sent him to curse me because of my sins, which are many and beyond telling.”

“Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.”

“I say, renew my spirit, and henceforth do not cast me away from your face”—that is, do not allow me to fall back into sin, so that I may be cast away from your face, that is, become unworthy of your presence. And do not take your Holy Spirit from me, through whose gift I possess these things, so that I now confess and do penance for my sin.

No one possesses by himself the capacity to do penance and confess; rather, he possesses it through the Spirit of God, to whom crimes and uncleanness are displeasing, just as, conversely, they please an unclean spirit. It cannot therefore be denied that David, once he was already doing penance, possessed the Holy Spirit. He asks God not to take this Spirit from him—that is, lest he perhaps cease from confession and penance.

“Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a principal spirit.”

“I say, do not take your Spirit from me; and, by not taking it away, restore to me the joy of your salvation.” I lost this joy through sin, because I do not know that anyone can rejoice in his coming except one who has conformed himself to him.

Restore such joy to me through your Spirit; and once it has been restored, strengthen me so that I may not lose it again, with a principal spirit—that is, with the Holy Spirit, who is called “principal” because whatever good belongs to our spirit proceeds from him.

“I will teach transgressors your ways, and the ungodly will turn to you.”

“Strengthen me,” I say, “because once strengthened I shall not be ungrateful. For by word and example I shall teach all kinds of transgressors, through myself and through my successors, your ways—that is, your works. And I shall teach not only transgressors but also the ungodly, that is, idolaters, because I shall offer myself to them as an example, so that they may not despair. Thus the ungodly—that is, those other sheep—will turn to you.”

“Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, God of my salvation.”
