It is as though he were saying: “And so that I may teach transgressors and the ungodly, therefore, O God, deliver me from bloodguilt”—that is, from carnal desires. He had experienced these, because through them he had fallen; therefore he asks to be freed from them.

You, I say, who are God, the giver of my true salvation—that salvation into which no corruption will creep and to which no defect will approach, where we shall not be sustained by food or refreshed by nourishment, yet shall not then be without drink and food, because God himself will be our food and drink: food that refreshes and never fails.

“Deliver me,” I say. “And if you deliver me, then my tongue will rejoice”—that is, it will announce with exultation to others that all justice belongs to you and none to me.

It is as though he were saying: “I shall not belong to the number of those who presume upon their merits and, wishing to establish their own justice, refused to be subject to your justice. Therefore I shall proclaim not the justice of merits, but your justice alone, which freely justifies.”

“Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.”

Truly you will deliver me, because you, Lord, will open my lips—that is, the lips of my heart, which had previously been closed through sin. You will open them to understanding; therefore my outward mouth will proclaim your praise, not mine.

This is the praise: that I was created by you, that I was not abandoned when I sinned, that I was admonished so that I might confess, and that I was cleansed so that I might be secure.

It is as though he were saying: “I shall offer you a sacrifice of praise, and this alone, because you do not wish any other sacrifice to be offered to you. For if you had wished another, I would certainly have given it to you”—that is, I would long ago not have abstained from such things.

But it is as though he were saying: “You do not wish this because it will come to pass that you will take no delight not only in the lesser legal sacrifices, but also in holocausts, in which you seem especially to delight because nothing is withheld from you in them.”

It should be understood that in the time of holy David the legal sacrifices still had their place. Yet he perceived through the Spirit that they were signs and promises, and therefore that a time would come when they would become void and only the things signified and promised would have their place. After the truth was offered, the shadow ceased.

Nevertheless, the sacrifices signified always retained their place, because even while the shadow remained, the things signified were most pleasing to God.

“The sacrifice acceptable to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart.”

As though someone were saying: “Since the Lord does not want sacrifices, what shall we do? Shall we come to his altar empty-handed?”

Certainly not. For to you, God, the acceptable sacrifice will be a troubled spirit. He explains what a troubled spirit is: a heart contrite through the labor of penance and humbled by the fear of pride. This will be an acceptable sacrifice to you, because a time will come when you will despise the bull, the goat, and other such offerings, but you will never despise this.

“Deal graciously, Lord, with Zion according to your good will.”

So that such sacrifices may be offered to you, therefore, Lord, deal graciously with Zion—that is, send your Savior to your Church, whom you are going to send to her.

The Church is called Zion because by Zion all those who are in contemplation are signified: those who wish in the present to exist only in hope, and eventually in reality. Do this not according to her merits, but solely according to your good will. For grace is given freely.

“And let the walls of future Jerusalem be built”—that is, the fortifications of our immortality and incorruption. These walls are now built in Zion through faith, hope, and charity; then they will be firm when we reach Jerusalem, that is, true vision. For these walls are nothing other than unfailing immortality and impassibility.

This verse may also be referred by itself to any faithful soul, so that it may be said thus: “Deal graciously, Lord, with each Zion”—that is, with the faithful and contemplative soul—by sending it its Savior, not according to merits but according to your good will. “And let its walls be built”—that is, its fortifications, namely, its virtues. I mean the soul that is now Zion and will eventually be Jerusalem, when it reaches true vision.

“Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness.”

It is as though he were saying: “For now, in the meantime, you will accept for sin the sacrifice of a contrite and humbled heart. But then”—that is, once the walls of Jerusalem have been built—“you will accept,” that is, you will regard as acceptable, only “the sacrifice of righteousness,” namely, the calves of the lips that they will then offer to you:

“For blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you.”

This praise is called the sacrifice of righteousness because what is more just than that those established in eternal blessedness should praise the one through whom they will be there? Nothing indeed.

“And then you will accept offerings”—that is, sacrifice according to the soul—“and holocausts”—that is, sacrifice according to the whole human nature. For not only will the soul be consumed by charity as a sacrifice into its immortality and impassibility; the body also will be consumed into eternal incorruption and impassibility.

Therefore then they will place calves—that is, they will place themselves, renewed in the innocence of a new life—upon your altar, that is, in the innermost devotion of the mind, which is your altar, because there what is sacrificed to you is sacrificed. This means that with complete devotion they will present themselves to you in the innocence of a new life.

## ON PSALM 51

*For the end; for understanding; to David, when Doeg the Edomite came and reported to Saul and said: “David has come to the house of Abimelech.”*

## ARGUMENT

It may be understood as having been sung against the words of Rabshakeh. Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ directed toward Judas the traitor.

## EXPLANATION

[Col. 0754D]

Since the title is known according to the historical account, let us speak briefly about the allegory. Their “understanding” is inserted into the title so that you may not hesitate to seek a mystery, since David himself is also related to have understood from his own calamities what would happen concerning Christ.

Thus David is always Christ; Saul is the Jews who persecute him. Doeg the Edomite, whose name is interpreted as “blood-red movement,” is Judas the traitor. Abimelech the priest signifies the chosen disciples, among whom Judas both saw the Lord and betrayed him.

Some say that Doeg is the Antichrist, whose member Judas proved to be, because just as Doeg killed eighty priests, so the Antichrist will kill the martyrs who hold the faith of the resurrection.

In the first part of the psalm, the prophet attacks Judas or the Antichrist, warning him not to exalt himself in his crimes, since a most grievous end awaits him. In the second, he says that he will perish quickly and be deprived in every respect of the fellowship of the saints. In the third, he says that the saints will marvel when, at the end, they see the devil, now raging in the world, condemned. In the fourth, the prophet himself hopes to be blessed with the saints in the life to come.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0755A]

What do you boast of in wickedness, you who are powerful in iniquity?

The title is as follows: “For the end; an instruction for David, when Doeg the Edomite came and reported to Saul, saying to him: ‘David has come to the house of Abimelech.’”

It is read in the Book of Kings that Saul was established as king over Israel by the Lord, not to remain in that office, but because of the hardness of that people’s heart—not for their benefit, but for their correction. In accordance with this, Job says of him: “He makes a hypocritical man reign because of the sins of his people.” But when Saul transgressed and had been openly rejected, David, while still a boy, was chosen by the Lord for the kingship. Before he reached the kingship, however, Saul persecuted him severely. This happened for our instruction, namely, so that we might know that we would reach that kingdom only through tribulation. For our Lord himself carried the body he had taken from the earth into heaven by way of tribulation.

During the persecution just mentioned, David fled wherever he thought he could hide. As he fled in every direction, he reached the house of Abimelech the priest, where he received both the bread of the Presence and the sword of Goliath, which had previously been placed in the temple. This was done so that he might perfectly represent the one whose figure he bore in himself, who was destined to be the true Priest and King. He is to be understood as Priest through the bread of the Presence, and as King through the sword.

There Doeg the Edomite, Saul’s chief herdsman, was present and saw David. Later, when Saul became angry with his servants because they did not set an ambush for David or capture him, Doeg betrayed David and said: “David has come to the house of Abimelech.” Saul therefore sent to Abimelech and, through Doeg, killed him and the entire priestly order, because no one else was willing to lay a hand upon the Lord’s priests.

This psalm was written concerning that event, not historically but mystically. Saul signifies death and the earthly kingdom, since it is written concerning death: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living; but he created all things so that they might exist, and he made the nations of the earth healthy.” But the ungodly summoned death upon themselves by their hands and feet; and, judging it to be their friend, they slipped away.

David signifies life and the heavenly kingdom. Doeg is interpreted as “movement,” and Edomite as “earthly.” Therefore, through Doeg the Edomite are understood all those who are moved by earthly things and place their hope in them. Such people always betray and accuse the heavenly kingdom—that is, those in whom the true David dwells through faith and good works—before the earthly kingdom, because they are opposed to their works and because those works are burdensome for them to behold.

This psalm treats these two kinds of people: some are persecutors, others sufferers; some fix their hope on earthly things, others hope only for eternal things. By saying that Doeg, interpreted as “movement,” was the servant of Saul, who signifies the earthly kingdom, it is also indicated that this kingdom is in motion and quickly passing away. Therefore, those who belong to the heavenly kingdom, which is eternal, need not be concerned about its persecution.

The whole matter may also be referred to the Jewish people and Christ. When that Word which was in the beginning with God came into the house of Abimelech—whose name is interpreted as “my father’s kingdom”—that is, when he took flesh from the Jewish people, which was the Lord’s particular people, then Doeg, namely those who were moved from their place and nation—those, that is, who said to God that he had a demon and made similar accusations—betrayed and accused him before the earthly kingdom, that is, before Pilate, Annas, and Caiaphas.

Thus the earthly kingdom, namely those wicked rulers, sent Doeg; and through Doeg—that is, through those whose tongue was a sharp sword—they killed the priests, namely the Lord’s own human being, born from them, who was truly a priest because he sacrificed himself for us, as well as many others who adhered to him. But David escaped, because the immortal Word remained—the same reality prefigured by Isaac, for whom a ram was sacrificed.

The same may be understood if this is referred to all the faithful. When their bodies are killed, their souls freely fly away, until they receive those same bodies again, endowed with bodily immortality and glorified.

The title mentioned above is explained in this way: These words are referred to the end, not to history. They are an instruction proposed to David himself—that is, to the nobler members of Christ’s body—because they teach them to understand that they must suffer now and rejoice afterward, since there can be no rejoicing unless suffering has preceded it. This instruction was signified when the event occurred, namely, when Doeg the Edomite came and reported to Saul, and so forth.

Now let us approach the psalm. The prophet, foreseeing through the mystical Spirit that David would be persecuted by the mystical Doeg, rebukes in this psalm those persecutors who boast in iniquity. He shows, not through malice but through prophetic foreknowledge, what will happen to them, for the consolation of the good: they must not grow faint, but endure tribulations with complete patience. For even if those who persecute them flourish now, they will soon wither; whereas the flowers of those who now appear dry will never fail.

And he says:

You who are powerful—that is, you who reckon your power to consist in iniquity, where there is rather weakness—why do you boast in wickedness, in which there is no cause for boasting but rather for shame? Many destroy, but few build. Therefore one should not boast in wickedness; rather, “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.” In accordance with what is written: “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the rich man in his riches, nor the strong man in his strength; but let the one who boasts boast in knowing and understanding me, says the Lord.”

Your tongue devised injustice all day long; you acted deceitfully like a sharp razor.

He shows how the man boasts in wickedness: he pursues wickedness so diligently—although its glory is disgrace—as though true glory followed from it. He says this: Your tongue, that is, the tongue of your heart, devised righteousness all day long, that is, continually. You never cease from injustice, for even if it is not present in your actions, it is nevertheless present in your thoughts; and even if it is absent from your mouth, it is never absent from your heart.

But what concern is there? None, namely, because by this you have harmed none of the faithful. For you acted—that is, you completed your deceit. You, I say, being like a sharp razor, cut away only external and superfluous things; but you did not injure the interior, necessary, eternal things. A sharp razor cuts external things but does not cut into the bones.

It is as though he said: Let Doeg exercise his wickedness as much as he wishes; let him sharpen his razor. What will he finally do to David? He will shave off his hair, namely, and make him bald—that is, the sons of Korah. For hair signifies external and superfluous things.

Nevertheless, God did not make hair superfluous, since he created it as an ornament. But earthly superfluities are signified by hair because, just as hair is cut without sensation—that is, without pain—so these earthly superfluities, and even the bodies themselves, can be taken away without any pain from those who firmly cling to God in mind. For it is said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.”

Many good things can nevertheless be done with these superfluities: for example, if you break your bread for the hungry, clothe the naked, and do similar things. This was also signified by the woman who, after wetting the Lord’s feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair. The one who wets the Lord’s feet, as it were, with tears is the person who pities the Lord’s poor through devout affection. He wipes them with his hair, as it were, when, after compassion, he uses the abundance of these superfluities to relieve their poverty.

Or alternatively: Because you devised interrupting injustice, you therefore completed your deceit, being like a sharp razor—that is, with the greatest precision—so that you might take away as much as you could, leaving not even the bodies untouched. A sharp razor is made for this purpose: to shave the hair as closely as possible.

But if this is referred to Christ and the Jewish people, it will be said as follows: You completed your deceit as a sharp razor does its work. For just as a razor, which is sharpened so that the face may be beautified, disfigures it instead if it wounds it, so that particular Jewish people, chosen so that the Lord’s face might be represented and adorned in it, disfigured him instead, because it did not recognize the time of its visitation. It acted deceitfully in this, because it did one thing, whereas the Lord had chosen it for another.

You loved wickedness more than goodness.

It is as though he said: You continually devised iniquities because you loved wickedness more than goodness—that is, you preferred it to goodness—and thus perverted what was natural. Whatever each thing was made for is primary in it. Therefore goodness and righteousness, for which human beings were created, are prior in them; but wickedness, which entered through corruption, is later.

You loved wickedness more than goodness, I say, and therefore you preferred speaking iniquity to speaking righteousness. In this respect, it is as though he said: You do not observe the same rule in your speech as in other matters. You take care not to put sour food into your stomach, but do you not take care what you keep in your mouth? Just as you must choose what you eat, so must you choose what you say.

You loved every word.

It is as though he said: To bring your utter wickedness to its conclusion, I say that you loved every word of destruction; whatever leads to ruin and destruction, you loved—namely, a deceitful tongue. As some books read, you, Doeg, were a deceitful tongue, doing or saying nothing except deceit. Here understand “deceit” broadly as every form of iniquity.

But what benefit does that bring you? Every evil. Therefore God, who is able, will destroy you at the end, when it will no longer be possible to rise again. Or he will destroy you with an everlasting destruction, always tending toward its end—not for construction, but for destruction.

Meanwhile, he will uproot you from your tent, and he will do this by making you emigrate—that is, he will make you depart far from it. In the present life he will separate you morally from the communion of the faithful.

Some books, however, read “your tent” rather than “the tent,” which is quite appropriate, since every human being is naturally planted in this tent and has a root in heaven. Hence he says: He will uproot you here from your tent, that is, from what ought to be yours.

And because he will uproot you from the tent, he will finally uproot you also from the palace. He says this as follows: He will finally uproot your root—that is, what ought to be yours—from the land of the living.

Our root is charity; the fruits of this root are good works. Hence the Apostle says: “Let all that you do be done in charity”; and elsewhere: “Rooted and founded in charity.” This root, namely charity, he says is uprooted from the land of the living—that is, from heavenly rest—as far as the wicked are concerned, because they did not possess it, and therefore they will not be planted there through it. Charity, however, will always remain there, because “charity never fails.”

The righteous will see.

It is as though he said: The fact that God will condemn Doeg in this way will not be fruitless, but useful to his own people, because the righteous will see—that is, they will observe—both his present and his future condemnation. Therefore, now, while it is still the time of night, they will fear.

The Apostle speaks of this fear: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling”; and: “Let the one who stands beware lest he fall”; and again: “Keeping watch over yourself, lest you also be tempted.” For while we walk by the lamp, we must live in fear. Now we walk by the lamp, in accordance with what Peter says: “You possess the prophetic word, made more certain, and you do well to attend to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.”

Now we have, I say, the prophetic word made more certain—that is, certain promises—but we are in a dark place because we know only in part; and we shall know until that light comes of which it is said: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”

Now, I say, they will fear; but eventually they will laugh, having been placed above him, although now they are beneath him. Wisdom speaks of this laughter: “I spoke, and you did not attend to my words; but I will mock, and from above I will laugh at your destruction.”

Now is the time for grieving and compassion toward the wicked, while we can still benefit them, because then there will indeed be repentance, but it will be fruitless. Therefore let each of you repent now, and the one who will then judge you will be your advocate, because now you will have as helper the one whom you will then have as judge.

But after the sheep have been separated from the goats, then it will be time to laugh—that is, to rejoice in agreement with the divine judgment. They will eventually laugh, I say, and reproaching them will say: “Behold the man”—that is, behold what Doeg has been reduced to while he wished to exalt himself.

He did not make God his helper—that is, he did not place his confidence in God but in himself, because he trusted in the abundance of his riches. He does not say, “the one who was rich.” If someone has riches for his own needs and for the refreshment of others, that is not sin. But to hope in riches—that is, to possess them not for necessity but for pleasure—is sin.

If we read the books, we find that Abraham, Jacob, and the other ancient fathers were rich and yet happy. One must not consider whether you are needy in your possessions, but whether you burn with desire. God does not examine the chest but the conscience; it is not money that is condemned but greed. Conversely, it is not poverty that is praised but innocence.

Taking this into account, the holy apostles, when the Lord said to them, “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven,” said: “Then who can be saved?” For scarcely anyone does not desire to possess something.

Peter, however, spoke with considerable confidence when he said: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you.” He had left nothing except an old boat and a torn garment, and yet he said that he had left everything.

Blessed Gregory resolves this by saying: “He has left much who has kept nothing for himself. For as much has been left by those who follow as could have been desired before they followed.” And again: “He has left much who has postponed even the desire to possess.”

He hoped in riches, I say, and prevailed in his vanity—that is, he advanced more in vanity, in the things desired in the morning, than he advanced in truth; for he valued money more highly than God.

But I—

Here it is not just any single individual who speaks, but that olive tree, namely the Church, whose proud branches were broken off from the Jews and in whose place the humble wild olive of the Gentiles was grafted.

It is as though he said: Doeg, because he hoped in the abundance of his riches, will be condemned; but I, already placed in the house of God—that is, in heavenly rest—exist in hope, though not yet in reality, like a fruitful olive tree.

The fruit of the olive appears slowly, but it does appear. So too the fruits of the righteous come slowly, but they will appear. Therefore I am placed in the house of God because I have not hoped in money but in God’s mercy—his mercy, I say, leading me into eternity, that is, into the age following this age.

This is to say: I hoped in God’s mercy not for temporal advantage, as many do, but for the sake of eternity.

I, being such a person, will not be condemned, but I will give thanks to you—that is, I will offer you a laudatory confession—forever, that is, eternally. I will sacrifice to you eternally the calves of my lips. For: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you.”

And rightly will I give thanks to you, because you have done such a thing that you are worthy to be praised: you have condemned Doeg and crowned David. Or: You have made me such that I am worthy to be condemned by you eternally.

I will finally give thanks to you; meanwhile I will await your name—that is, I will not seize this name, “God,” in haste, as Adam did when he wished to be god for himself and to depend on his own will rather than yours. I will patiently wait until, through mercy and glory, I can attain it.

For we shall all be like immortal and impassible gods, in accordance with the saying: “I said, You are gods.”

And rightly will I await your name, because it is good—that is, it is sweet and pleasant. Since few have yet perceived that sweetness of which it is said, “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet,” they do not know that sweetness, just as someone who has not tasted honey does not know how sweet honey is.

Therefore he adds for whom it is sweet and when, saying: For your name is good, and it will appear in the presence—that is, in the fellowship—of your saints, to those, namely, who will be joined to them.

## ON PSALM 52

“For the end; concerning Abimelech; an instruction of David.”

### ARGUMENT

This psalm also strikes Rabsaces. Alternatively, it rebukes the unbelieving Jews who deny God by their deeds. It should be read in connection with the Gospel according to Matthew.

### EXPLANATION

The history of Kings relates that, while David was living in exile with Achish and went down with him into the camp to fight against Saul, Amalekite raiders devastated the city of Ziklag. After carrying away the wives, children, and possessions of David and his companions, they departed. When David learned this, he pursued them and, finding them amid their feasting, put them to the sword.

David therefore understood that Christ would be born from his descendants and that persecutions by the nations would rage against Christ’s Church, as Amalek had raged against David’s city, Ziklag. But he also understood that, once Christ had conquered, those same persecutors would soon be overthrown, either to faith or to condemnation, so that they could not kill the souls they had snatched from the Church.

Therefore the title rightly says: “For the end, concerning Amalek,” that is, “an instruction of David concerning Christ for the nations,” because David himself understood what mystery of salvation was contained in the things he had done.

Amalek is interpreted as “the licking people,” because those who desire earthly things excessively seem, in their coveting, to lick them. This psalm is therefore composed for the conversion or punishment of such people.

In the first section of the psalm the Church speaks, rebuking those who do not fear being corrupted either in heart or in deed. In the second it says that they will receive the evils they have inflicted on Christians. In the third it exhorts the faithful to bear the troubles of the world with equanimity until the judgment of majesty arrives, when all the blessed will be clothed and receive good things.

### COMMENTARY

The fool said in his heart: “There is no God.”

The title is as follows: “For the end, concerning Amalek—or concerning Melech—an instruction for David.”

Amalek was a persecuting people hostile to holy David and to the kingdom belonging to him, namely the Israelite nation. This Amalek burned the city of Ziklag and carried off David’s wife and household together with his possessions.

The Amalekites are interpreted as “those who lick the earth.” Through them the lovers of the world are understood, from whom the lovers of heaven—who are signified by David—must necessarily suffer persecution.

The title is explained as follows: These words are referred to the end of time, that is, to Christ born at the end of time, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “In these last days he has spoken to you in the Son.” Christ is the end toward whom we direct whatever good we do, and once he has been attained there is nothing further for us to seek.

These words are an instruction proposed to David himself, or to the nobler members of Christ’s body, concerning Amalek—that is, concerning persecution. In this psalm the prophet rebukes the persecutors of Christ’s body and exhorts that body, namely the Church, to endure tribulation and persecution with complete patience; finally, he inserts the consolation of that body.

Hence he says in the title that this psalm is an instruction proposed to the faithful concerning persecution, so that they may understand that persecution must be endured, because persecution will have an end, whereas the reward of persecution will have no end.

Or it may be “concerning Melech,” which Jerome says is interpreted as “a woman in labor” or “one who grieves.” Who, then, is this woman in labor or this grieving one? The body of Christ.

It grieves when it sees that, because iniquity will abound, the charity of many has grown cold. It gives birth to those for whom it grieves when it makes some of the impious pious. To give birth is to labor. Hence one member of this body, pregnant with charity, says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.”

Thus this psalm is an instruction proposed to David himself concerning Melech, that is, concerning the one giving birth or grieving. It teaches that the body of Christ is now giving birth and grieving, because these things will have an end, whereas their rewards will never end.

Here the prophet rebukes those on account of whom Christ’s body grieves and, as was said above, inserts its consolation.

Lest this psalm seem to have been repeated unnecessarily, it should be understood that here it has one purpose and above another. Who those are on account of whom Christ’s body grieves and gives birth, the psalm itself reveals when it says:

The foolish people, who make no provision for the future, said that there is no God. They said this in their heart, that is, in their thought.

Many also say with their mouth that there is no God. But so that this might be understood universally, he said, “in his heart.” For all those who think that their iniquity pleases God because he delays vengeance and does not punish it immediately openly say that there is no God.

If God exists, he is necessarily just; and if he is just, no iniquity pleases him. Those who think that iniquity pleases him destroy justice in him, and by destroying justice they destroy God as well.

They are corrupt.

The foolish people say that there is no God. But this is not the fault of nature; it is because they themselves have been corrupted away from the good nature in which they were created, in accordance with the saying: “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.”

Human nature was good as long as it remained in the fullness of virtue, because it lost its good nature through transgression.

They are corrupt, I say, and therefore they have become abominable to the Lord—that is, disinherited and accursed. As long as someone acts well, the Lord promises him an inheritance; but those who persist in iniquities—that is, who do not cease from iniquity—are abominable, because there is no one among them who does good.

God looked down from heaven.

The heart of the fool removes God; the heart of the wise person, that is, of the just person, establishes God. For God looked down from heaven—that is, from the heart of the just person, which is called heaven because it continually dwells in heaven and because God dwells there, since the soul of the just person is the seat of wisdom.

From that heaven, I say, God looked down. That is, God made that heaven—that is, he made the just—look down upon the children of men. He made them look from afar upon the children of men, that is, upon those who act wickedly; “from afar” not according to place but according to the dignity of their conduct, since the just are placed above them in moral dignity.

Sacred Scripture commonly attributes to God the things he works through us. Thus it says: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us,” meaning that he makes us intercede with ineffable groanings; and again: “The Spirit of God searches all things, even the depths of heaven,” meaning that he makes us search them; and: “God tests us, so that he may know,” meaning that he makes us know.

So here too it says: “God looked down from heaven,” meaning that he made heaven look down upon the children of men, so that it might see—that is, so that he might make that heaven see—and judge whether there is among those children of men anyone who understands God in his heart or seeks him in his works.

But there is no such person, because all have turned aside to evil—together, that is, both Jews and Gentiles. Therefore they have become useless, so completely that there is no one among them who does good; there is not one, I say, even up to a single person.

Or “up to the one who belongs to the One,” namely Christ, who is the one belonging to the many.

The children of men are called all human beings when they act wickedly. They are called children of God when they act well, because the one who made the Son of God the Son of Man made children of men into children of God through good works. He made him share in our misery so that we might share in his glory.

But once the Son of God—that is, those who act well—is removed from humanity, the children of men remain, namely those who act wickedly. Of these it is rightly said that there is not even one among them who does good.

Will all who work iniquity not know this—those who devour my people as though they were eating bread?

Since there is now no one who does good and all have turned aside, will not all those who now work iniquity eventually know—that is, recognize—that very iniquity?

It is as though he said: Those who now refuse to know iniquity, so that they may recognize themselves, will eventually know it so that they may mourn themselves.

They will know iniquity, I say, those who now devour—that is, strive to devour and naturally incorporate into themselves—my people, that is, my people belonging to God, of whom the prophet says, “I am a part.”

In this way they devour and despise that people, and they do so as though eating bread—that is, continually. For although we use other foods in various ways, we eat bread continually.

Here the consolation of the body mentioned above is inserted:

They did not call upon God; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear.

They will rightly know iniquity because they did not call upon the eternal things within themselves, but called upon temporal things—namely, the world—and not upon God.

God wishes to be worshiped freely; he wishes to be loved freely. Therefore whoever calls upon God for the sake of gold or anything worldly does not call upon God himself, but upon the thing he desires, and asks God to become the servant of his wickedness.

But the one who calls upon God within himself is the one who calls upon him solely in order to possess him as his possession and reward.

They did not call upon God, I say, because they did not fear losing eternal things but temporal things. Therefore they wished to retain temporal things, and by retaining them wickedly they lost both eternal things and temporal things.

This is what he says: They trembled with fear—that is, they were exceedingly afraid—there, namely, in the loss of temporal things, where there was no fear, that is, for things over which there should be no fear, since they are necessarily lost.

We should not fear for external things, since we should not even fear for the body, in accordance with what is said: “Do not fear those who kill the body.”

For God scattered the bones of those who please men; they were confounded, because God rejected them.

They did not call upon God, and they trembled where they ought not to have trembled, because God scattered—that is, in his just judgment allowed to be scattered—their bones, that is, the foundations of their souls, namely their virtues.

And this was deserved, because they strove to please not God but human beings. Therefore they were poured out, so that they did not attend to themselves. Hence it is said: “Return, transgressors, to your heart.”

Thus they are now confounded with an inward confusion, and eventually with an outward one, because God rejected and cast them away—them, namely, who please human beings.

Who will give salvation from Zion to Israel?

The unjust say that there is no God, but they lie, because someone—that is, someone who is God—will give salvation, namely eternal salvation, to Israel, made from Zion—that is, to those who advance so far in contemplation that eventually they rejoice in vision.

For now we are Zion, that is, “watchers”; eventually we shall be Israel, that is, “those who arrive” and “those who see.”

It is as though he said: Since no other giver can accomplish this, God himself will do it.

This salvation will be given when the Lord restores the captivity of his people—that is, when he removes captivity simultaneously from soul and body for those who preferred to be his people, the people of God, rather than the world. This will occur when the final death is destroyed and this mortal nature puts on immortality.

Then Israel will truly rejoice, because here Jacob will exult—that is, they will then rejoice in arriving, since now they rejoice in advancing.

This verse may also be read interrogatively from its beginning, as was explained sufficiently in the earlier interpretation of this psalm.

## ON PSALM 53

“For the end; with songs or hymns; an instruction of David, when the Ziphites came to Saul and reported to Saul: ‘Is not David hidden among us?’”

### ARGUMENT

It may be understood as spoken by Hezekiah when besieged. Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ addressing the Father, or of any faithful person imploring God’s help against vices.

### EXPLANATION

The “instruction of David” is to be understood as above, because David, beset by anguish but unexpectedly delivered, understood what would happen to Christ’s Church, of which he himself was also a member. He exalted this same understanding of his in songs—that is, in the greatest praises of joy.

For always, unless I am mistaken, psalms whose titles mention songs announce the exultation of the singer amid adversity.

The Ziphites are interpreted as “flourishing ones.” This is what is given to sinners in this world, where they are permitted for a time to prosper through faithless freedom, while the faithful are despised and confined by the obstinacy of the ungodly.

The prophet, delivered from Saul’s danger, gives thanks to the Lord throughout the entire psalm, because the betrayal of the Ziphites was unable to harm him.

In the first part he pleads that his powerful enemies may not prevail in oppressing him. In the second he asks, with spiritual piety, that his adversaries ought to be converted.

It is fitting for every Christian to make this request: that he may be delivered from the flourishing ones of this world in such a way that the grace of conversion is not denied to them.

God, in your name.

The title is as follows: “For the end, in songs, to David himself, when the Ziphites came to Saul and said: ‘Behold, David is hidden among us.’” [Col. 0762B] It has already been stated that Saul, who was chosen for kingship not to remain permanently but according to the saying of Scripture—“Who makes a hypocrite rule because of the perversity of his people”—represented the temporal kingdom destined for destruction. It has also been explained above that David represented Christ, both the Head and the Body. For the whole Christ is Head and Body. To this Head, set above, the Body is joined by hope, and the Head to the Body below by love.

Now Ziph was a village of Judea whose inhabitants were called Ziphites; while Saul was pursuing David, David hid among them. The Ziphites are interpreted as “those who flourish,” and by them are understood lovers of the world. Among these, however, David—that is, those whom that David represented—are hidden. Of these hidden ones the Apostle says: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your glory, appears, then you also will appear with Christ in glory.” Then those who are now hidden, because their good works do not [Col. 0762C] appear, will flourish. And the Ziphites, who now flourish, will then wither.

Through these two groups two kinds are understood, which must be clearly distinguished. Yet distinguishing them does no good if we are slow to choose. Now the power of choosing is given, while God delays the sentence of judgment; but after the sentence of judgment has come, there will no longer be power to choose. Let us therefore choose now, and prefer to be hidden rather than flourishing; to be humbled with David rather than exalted with the Ziphites; and let us understand what end the flower of the Ziphites will have. The Psalmist elsewhere reveals what that end is, saying: “The foolish man and the senseless will not understand these things,” and so on, until he says: “That they may perish forever and ever.” Their flower will end in eternal destruction, whereas the dryness of the good will have eternal joy.

This meaning is treated in the title when it says: “These words are referred to the end of time,” that is, to Christ. They are an understanding attributed to David himself, or to the more distinguished members of Christ’s Body, or to the prophet himself [Col. 0762D] acting in their place and exhorting us to understanding—namely, that we should attend to the end of the flower of the Ziphites.

This understanding must be held “in songs,” that is, in joy, not in sadness, because we should not grieve if we lack this flower and are afflicted; rather, we ought to rejoice in tribulation, knowing that “tribulation produces endurance,” and so forth. I say that this understanding is marked out in the history when the Ziphites came to Saul and said to him: “Behold, David is hidden among us.” For those who flourish always oppose the hidden and betray them, but they do them no harm. Thus the Ziphites betrayed David, but it did him no harm, because he escaped unharmed and entered the cave of Adullam.

When Saul the persecutor had also entered to relieve himself and thereby gave David an opportunity to kill him, David spared him and merely cut off the edge of his cloak. By this he signified to us that we should not persecute those who persecute us, nor hate them, but rather love them and pray for them.

Now let us approach the literal meaning. [Col. 0763A] It is the voice, as has been said, either of the perfect members of Christ’s Body, or of the prophet himself acting in their place and speaking as follows:

“God, save me by your name.”

It is as though he said: “I know that your name, which was preached to us in weakness—for you were announced to us as mortal and subject to suffering—has been exalted in power. You came to die in weakness, but you will come to judge in power. And those whom you now save through the name that preceded your coming, you will savingly deliver through your power that follows. Therefore, Lord, save me who believe and hope in your preceding name, not in myself.

“And rightly he says ‘save,’ because ‘the righteous lives by faith.’ Finally, deliver me perfectly through your subsequent power. And, O God, in order that you may deliver me, hear my prayer—not just any prayer, but mine, that is, the prayer of one who does not ask for the flower of the Ziphites. Hear the words of my mouth—not the words of the Ziphites, but mine, that is, the words of one asking you for eternal goods. They indeed hear those words, but do not perceive them, because they do not desire eternal things with me [Col. 0763B] if they desire earthly things. I say: perceive them—that is, show by their effect that you have perceived with your ears, that is, by the power of hearing which is in you.”

“For strangers have risen up against me; the strong have sought my soul, and they have not set God before their eyes.”

Therefore it is necessary that you save and deliver me, because strangers—that is, the Ziphites, strangers to me not by kinship but by affection, not by place but by their flower—have risen up to be against me, that is, to oppress me. They rose up in this way because they, who were strong not in reality but in their own estimation, sought my soul in order to make it conform to themselves. They did all this because they did not set God before their eyes, but the world; that is, they did not wish to love God, but rather wished to pile money upon money and increase every earthly advantage.

“For behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the protector of my soul.”

The strangers have indeed risen up against me, but what concern is that? None, certainly, because God helps me. God helps all his saints, and if not outwardly and openly, nevertheless inwardly and secretly, since it is truly a great help for them to be able to say: “Our glory is the testimony of our conscience.” This man too glories in that help when he says: “I will freely sacrifice to you,” and so forth.

God, I say, helps me. And behold how he helps: the Lord is the protector—that is, the defender—of my soul, even if he does not protect my body against the Ziphites, by giving me the glorious conscience that prevents me from consenting to them.

“Turn the evils away from my enemies, and in your truth destroy them.”

Here he inserts a prayer for those persecutors, giving us an example that we should not hate such people, but pray for them. It is as though he said: “They rise up against me, but you, Lord, turn away from them my interior and more serious evils. For no evil is more serious than loving earthly things and neglecting eternal things. And, having placed them in your truth—that is, in the love of eternal things—scatter them in their falsehood, [Col. 0763D] that is, in their affection for earthly things.”

“I will freely sacrifice to you, and I will confess your name, Lord, because it is good.”

This is connected with the principal statement. It is as though he said: “Truly, Lord, you help me and are my protector. This is evident from the effect, because I will sacrifice to you, that is, a sacrifice of praise. And I will do this not out of necessity but willingly. This means: I will praise you freely, and I will rejoice in your praise; once you are praised, I will never be ashamed.

“Let God be praised willingly, loved with charity, praised freely, loved freely. That is, let him be loved for his own sake, not from necessity—not for gold or silver or anything of that kind. I will sacrifice to you, I say, and I will do so in this way: I will confess you, that is, I will offer perfect praise to your name, Lord, with mouth, heart, and deed. And I will do this for no other reason than that he himself is good in himself.”

“For you have delivered me from every tribulation, and my eye has looked down upon my enemies.”

Rightly will I sacrifice [Col. 0764A] and confess to you, because you have already delivered me in hope from every tribulation, both inward and outward. And my eye—my inward eye, that is—having been brought about by this deliverance, has looked down upon my enemies; that is, it has regarded the flower of the Ziphites as contemptible, considering that “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell; but the word of the Lord,” that is, the Lord’s promises, “remains forever.”

Why? It is as though he said: “If I am humbled here, I will be exalted,” since the Lord says: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

## ON PSALM 54  
### For the end: an understanding of David’s song.

### ARGUMENT

This psalm is drawn from the person of the priest Onias, who voluntarily went to Egypt, when Jason, his kinsman but rival for his honor and life, bought the high priesthood from [Col. 0764B] Antiochus, son of Seleucus, on the condition that he would lead all the Jews over to the customs of the Gentiles. Onias himself, after constructing an altar in Egypt, devotedly restored the sacred rites which Jason had profaned at Jerusalem, together with such Jews as he had been able to find.

Alternatively, a faithful person may be understood to pray against the vices of the flesh and against the flesh itself.

### EXPLANATION

“For the end,” that is, to Christ; “in songs,” that is, in spiritual joys; “an understanding of David,” because David understood that Christ would become incarnate, through whom he knew that he would be delivered from tribulation.

Throughout the psalm, which is divided by two *diapsalmata*, the words are those of the Lord. In the first part he asks that his prayer, made while he is in tribulation, not be despised, and he pleads for the speedy deliverance which, because of the weakness of the flesh, he was shown to desire. In the second place he asks that the iniquities of the Jews be destroyed, because in their city there was contradiction of the truth. Third, he declares what he knew would happen to the obstinate Jews because of their crimes. After this, a [Col. 0764C] pious consolation is introduced, so that none of the faithful may be terrified on hearing of the judge’s severity.

### COMMENTARY

“Hear, God, my prayer,” and so forth. The title is as follows: “For the end, in hymns, an understanding to David himself.” This is explained as follows.

“These words are referred to the end,” that is, to Christ, who is the end for every believer in order to receive righteousness; “in hymns,” that is, in praises. This means that whether we exult and rejoice, or are afflicted and distressed, he must always be praised who instructs us in tribulations and consoles us in prosperity. The praise of God ought never to depart from the mouth and heart of a Christian—not so that he praises in prosperity but seizes hold of God in adversity, but so that, as the Psalmist says, “his praise is always in my mouth.”

Do you rejoice? Recognize the Father who corrects you, because whether he caresses or corrects, he instructs the one for whom he is preparing an inheritance. In this way the words “in hymns” are to be understood. And the understanding is attributed to David himself, from whose seed Christ proceeded according to the flesh, [Col. 0764D] because he was his Son according to humanity and his Lord according to divinity.

Here the whole Christ is signified, namely, the Head and the Body, because this psalm may be the voice either of the Head or of the more distinguished members of the Body. And it is an understanding. For we are admonished that, when we hear, we should understand, because it greatly concerns us to understand in what evil we are and from what evil we always desire to be delivered.

Amid the many tribulations of this world, this psalm laments something concerning understanding. Yet whoever lacks understanding does not lament with this psalm. Moreover, we ought to remember that according to understanding we were made in the image of God, and through understanding we differ from the other animals. Hence certain despisers of so great a good are rebuked in one psalm when it is said to them: “Do not become like a horse and a mule.” And again: “A man, when he was in honor, did not understand.”

Let us therefore recognize our honor and understand that this is not the homeland for rejoicing but for grieving, [Col. 0765A] not yet the time for exulting but still for groaning. For even if there is some exultation in us, it is not yet in reality but in hope. We rejoice because of the promise, knowing that the one who made the promise does not deceive us.

But as far as the present time is concerned, let us hear in what evil and in what distress we are, and let us recognize in ourselves what we hear. If we do not yet recognize it in ourselves, let us be incorporated into David and feel in this way, saying with him:

“God, hear my prayer,” that is, hear me praying. “And do not despise this,” that is, do not continue to despise my supplication.

The prayer of many is heard when they ask for temporal things, and they are granted what they request; yet afterward their supplication is despised, because they ask for earthly things, not eternal ones. Therefore this man places both things together: he asks that his prayer be heard and that his supplication not be despised—that is, that he not be permitted to pray for earthly things.

This is according to Cassiodorus, who does not distinguish between “prayer” and “supplication.” According to Augustine and Jerome, however, [Col. 0765B] it is distinguished in this way: “God, hear my prayer,” made for perseverance—that is, make me persevere among the wicked so that I may not fail, but rather advance. “And, in order that you may hear the prayer already mentioned for perseverance, do not despise the supplication made for sins.” First, each person must make supplication for sins; afterward, he must pray for perseverance.

“Attend to me,” I say, “in prayer; and, in order that you may attend, first hear me in my supplication.”

And as though he said to him, “Why do you groan? What do you suffer?” he adds:

“I am sorrowful in my exercise.”

It is as though he said: “You have placed me to be exercised among the wicked. But because they rise up against me beyond my strength, therefore you, Lord, calm their persecution.”

Placed among the wicked, this man wanted to extend his love even to his enemies. While, as a perfect man, he admonished and exhorted those among whom he lived, he accomplished nothing, because they reproached him with vices and insults beyond his strength, and also harassed him by their vices. He feared losing his love. He did not wish to overcome them with vices, because this is the rule of piety: [Col. 0765C] we must not overcome such people by insults, nor hate them, but rather pray for them, so that they may be converted and be exercised together with us.

For the wicked are not wicked without purpose: every wicked person either lives in order to be corrected, or through him the good person is exercised. Therefore this man did not wish to overcome the wicked with insults, but turned to prayer so that he would not lose his love—praying, that is, for perseverance among such people.

Above all, a good man must beware lest he lose his love in such tribulation, because we suffer two enemies: one visible and the other invisible. But if the one raging outwardly is loved, the one raging inwardly is easily overcome. Each of them strives to take away from us that in which he sees us to be superior. A man overcomes a man through earthly prosperity, but a man overcomes the devil through love of the enemy.

Hence blessed Gregory says: “Because the ancient enemy arouses the weaker brother against us, he does not care to take away our possessions, but to strike charity in us.”

Therefore this man, as we said, turned to prayer, [Col. 0765D] so that he would not lose his love. And he gives the reason why he prays, saying:

“I am sorrowful and troubled, fearing that I may lose my love in my exercise,” that is, while I am exercised among the wicked by admonishing them, and accomplish nothing, because they rise up against my strength.

Notice that he says “my.” For there are two exercises: one of the good and one of the wicked. The exercise of the wicked is useless, namely, when the wicked are oppressed by the wicked. The exercise of the good is an exercise toward piety, useful for everything; this is the exercise intended here.

And because he has stated two things, he adds two things, as though he said: “I am troubled by the voice of the enemy,” that is, because of the reproach and insults inflicted by the enemy. “And I am sorrowful because of the tribulation of the sinner,” who not only cursed but also acted against him by applying blows. For he is more sorrowful than troubled, because this disturbance lasts only for a time.

“For they have inclined.”

Therefore I am rightly sorrowful and troubled, because the enemies have inclined, [Col. 0766A] that is, as though they wished to turn aside and cast upon me—their iniquities, that is, they tried to make me conform to themselves, when rather they ought to have conformed to me.

“And they were troublesome to me,” that is, they harassed me by contradicting me and also by acting against me in their anger. They were angry with me because of my admonition and exhortation. Hence my heart—that is, my interior self—was troubled, yet in such a way that this disturbance remained within me alone, that is, it did not go outward into hatred of them. This qualifies the disturbance. It is therefore not superfluous, although the same thing was already said: “My heart was troubled,” I say.

And this happened to such an extent that “the fear of death fell upon me,” that is, fear not of outward death but of inward death. He did not fear outward death, against which the Lord had fortified him by saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” They feared inward death, which is more serious—that is, they feared hatred, because just as love is life, so hatred is the death of the soul.

[Col. 0766B] “Fear and trembling.”

In this way, I say, the fear of death fell upon me, because fear arising from anger and trembling arising from hatred came upon me. For anger is a brief madness, while hatred is anger grown old. Fear belongs to the soul, whereas trembling belongs to the body. Trembling appears to be the greater, since through the shaking of the body it outwardly reveals how great the inward fear is.

Therefore “fear” refers to anger, which is light, while “trembling” refers to hatred, which is serious. Here also the beam and the splinter may be signified, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye, and then the splinter from your brother’s eye.” The beam signifies hatred, while the splinter signifies anger. Many wicked teachers rebuke others for anger while inwardly harboring serious hatred themselves.

Fear, I say, and trembling came upon me, and this happened because the darkness of hatred “covered”—that is, oppressed—me. It did not truly cover him, but he was in such fear of losing love and falling into hatred that it seemed to him as though hatred itself were already in him. He calls hatred [Col. 0766C] “darkness” because, as the evangelist John says: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness.”

“And I said: Who will give me…”

Fear and trembling came upon me, I say; and, standing in that fear, I said out of weariness, because I saw that those whom I admonished were making no progress but rather falling away:

“Who will give me wings like a dove?”

When a holy man sees that the wicked among whom he lives are not progressing but rather, because they rise against him and trouble him, add sin to sin, it often happens through weariness that a desire for solitude seizes him. He wishes to depart from the body—not, of course, out of hatred, but so that those whom he could not benefit by exhorting he might at least benefit by praying for.

Yet many are not permitted to fly away in this manner, because they have wings bound not by birdlime but by duty. Therefore they seek another desert: they seek the desert of the heart, so that they may be alone in purity of mind, by which they may delight themselves with their God. Yet they are not alone in charity, because through charity they remain with those from whom they have withdrawn. [Col. 0766D]

Thus they seek rest in the mind while the body outwardly remains at work. This is the kind of withdrawal that this man desires when he says:

“Who will give me wings,” that is, withdrawal from these wicked people, who are failing through me rather than progressing? He says “wings” that are like the wings of a dove.

“And I will fly,” that is, I will withdraw from them into the solitude of the mind and thus rest.

It is as though he said: “Certainly you, Lord, will give me wings, since you hear my prayer and do not despise my supplication.”

Although ravens and hawks have wings just as doves do, he asks that only dove’s wings be given him, because the dove seeks flight from troubles but does not lose love; indeed, it is a sign of love in many ways. So this man seeks to fly away from wicked brothers whom he endures, so that he will not lose love but remain with them always through charity.

Here we are referred to that passage of Scripture where it is read that the dove sent out from the ark, because it found muddy places everywhere, returned to the [Col. 0767A] ark through love. So this man, who finds only the muddy places of the wicked, seeks to withdraw into the secret place of the heart while preserving love within himself.

“Behold, I have gone far away, fleeing.”

It is as though he said: “I asked that wings be given me, and behold, what I desired has happened, because wings have been given me. And I, fleeing, have gone far away,” that is, so that I might be alone in purity of mind, though not alone in charity; and in that solitude I remained.

Or: “I have gone far away,” directing myself bodily toward the desert but not in love. And I did this because I was waiting for him, namely God, until he strengthened me; for him, I say, who, just as he has already saved me in hope, will save me in reality from faintheartedness—that is, from weakness of spirit. He would confirm me so that I would no longer fear losing love among the wicked who troubled me.

Thus my spirit, previously weak through fear, would become strong by fearing nothing. He would save me from the storm, that is, from disturbance of mind. For if someone does not consider what the Lord suffered for him, in him [Col. 0767B] Christ is as though asleep, and therefore a storm of disturbance arises in his mind. But whoever considers what the Lord suffered and rejoices to be found in some likeness of Christ’s sufferings has Christ as though awake within him; he commands the sea and the winds, and thus the storm ceases.

Or it may also be said: “He would save me from the storm,” that is, from outward persecution—not because persecution would cease entirely, but because, once strengthened, I would no longer attend to it.

“Cast them down, Lord.”

The continuation is thus: “I was waiting for him who would save me.” I say, speaking in this way: “Cast them down, Lord,” and so forth.

Or, according to Augustine, it is understood thus: “The enemies have inclined their iniquities toward me; but you, Lord, cast them down from sin into sin. And divide their tongues from your truth,” so that they may always speak falsehood. I do not say this out of ill will, but because they are worthy of it, since “I saw iniquity,” and so forth.

This may also be understood in a good sense, so that it is said as follows: “Lord, cast them down from pride into humility,” that is, humble them. [Col. 0767C] “And divide their tongues,” which had previously conspired for evil, so that they may no longer agree with one another in evil but conspire together for good.

And it is necessary that you do this, because “in the city,” that is, in their multitude, “I saw iniquity in their deeds and contradiction in their words.” This means that their iniquity and contradiction are so manifest that they can be seen by everyone. Deliberately, he uses “iniquity” for evil works and “contradiction” for the fact that they always contradict the truth.

He calls their multitude a “city.” There is a certain city of confusion—namely Babylon—to which all the wicked belong, just as, conversely, all the good belong to Jerusalem.

Here we are referred to three different Scriptures. By “Cast them down” we are referred to the passage saying that certain proud men were cast down in the flood during the time of Noah, because their downfall signified the downfall of the just about whom he is speaking here. By “Divide their tongues” we are referred to those who, after the flood, wished to build a tower reaching [Col. 0767D] to heaven; through their pride their tongues were scattered, just as afterward, through the humility of the apostles, the tongues of the Church were joined together.

By “contradiction” we are referred to the beginning of the whole schism, namely, when Dathan and Abiram, usurping the priestly office for themselves contrary to divine command, came forward with many of their accomplices to burn incense. As a result, the earth swallowed the leaders Dathan and Abiram alive, while fire coming from heaven consumed all their followers.

“By day and by night.”

I saw iniquity, I say, in the city of the wicked, and to such an extent that iniquity itself surrounds that city day and night—that is, always. It envelops it on every side, insofar as the lesser members are concerned. And it envelops the lesser members so thoroughly that it also rises above its walls, that is, it envelops the greater members as well, such as Donatus, Arius, and others like them, who are its walls because they protect and surround it like walls.

Therefore iniquity surrounds it in this way because “labor,” that is, a commandment, is in its midst, [Col. 0768A] that is, in the heart of its multitude. For whoever speaks the truth does not labor; or, in its midst—that is, among its common people, who are surrounded by those greater men—there is oppression. And there is injustice among those greater men, since injustice properly concerns those who judge.

“And it did not fail.”

He shows in detail that the iniquity in the city mentioned above is truly manifest: “usury and deceit did not fail from its streets,” that is, from its public places. Usury and every kind of deceit are openly practiced in it, by which its iniquity is increased, since every evil becomes more detestable when it is conducted with public presumption.

Here he may mean the usury of which it was said elsewhere: “Who has not given his money at interest.” Or he may mean that most unjust usury by which, for a small offense, they exact an excessively severe punishment—when they kill someone for a mere word. This usury is followed by another, more serious usury, namely eternal condemnation.

[Col. 0768B] “For if an enemy…”

If earlier by “enemy” and “sinner” we understand only the one who has always been outside—that is, the unbeliever, as blessed Augustine says—then this verse continues as follows:

“You seek flight because of those who are outside. Rest, then, among those who are inside.”

He says: “I cannot, because even here false brothers persecute me, which is more grievous to endure. For if only an enemy who had always been outside had cursed me, I would certainly have endured it,” that is, I would have thought it necessary to endure it, because every evil should be accepted more patiently when it is found to come not unexpectedly than when it comes unexpectedly.

Any evil received from those who are outside comes not unexpectedly; what is received from a fellow citizen, from whom we expect no evil, comes unexpectedly. It is unexpected when it is received from a fellow citizen, from whom we expect no evil. Therefore it is more grievous, because no pest is more effective for harming than a familiar friend.

But if earlier by “enemy” and “sinner,” as some wish, we understand those who were previously inside but went out from us [Col. 0768C]—that is, false brothers—then the approach to this verse is clear in the following way:

“Cast down, Lord, and divide the tongues of those who were formerly with us and went out from us.” I do not say this out of ill will, but because it is deserved, since “I saw iniquity and contradiction even in the city,” that is, in the Church, where greater security seemed to exist.

And this was so much the case that “by day and by night,” that is, always—or in prosperity and adversity—it surrounds the city; and in the lesser and the greater, iniquity is found, as among other prelates. This is very grievous to bear, and rightly so, because if an enemy who had never been inside had cursed me, I would certainly have endured it—that is, I would have considered it necessary to endure.

But when a fellow citizen curses, it is intolerable, because of what has already been said. And if the one who hated me—that is, one whose hatred of me is evident because he prefers to serve the creature rather than the Creator—had spoken great things against me, [Col. 0768D] that is, had insulted me proudly and arrogantly, I might perhaps have hidden myself, that is, I might have been able to withdraw from him so that his insolence would cease when he no longer saw me as his adversary. But I cannot hide myself from one who is inside.

“But you, a man of one mind…”

The one who has always been outside is tolerable. But you are a man who came out from us, because you were not of us; you ought to have been of one mind with me. For at one time, while you were inside, you were my leader—that is, you often gave sound counsel, so that you took the lead in giving advice. As blessed Jerome says of Origen: “Where he is good, no one is better; where he is bad, no one is worse.”

You were also my acquaintance in the same institutions. He explains how you were an acquaintance: you partook together with many others of the sweet food of the divine words, being in this respect with me, because the teaching of truth was sweet to me as it was to you.

“For we walked together in the house of God,” that is, in ecclesiastical institutions, in agreement.

You, I say, who were formerly such a man and [Col. 0769A] then apostatized in this way—what do you force me to say? This:

“Let death come upon them!”

Here again we are referred to the beginning of the schism in Dathan and Abiram. It means: “Let death,” that is, blindness of mind, “come upon them,” namely, the lesser members, just as the fire of destruction came upon the fire of dissension among the supporters of Dathan and Abiram.

And just as the earth swallowed those leaders, Dathan and Abiram, alive, so let the leaders among these apostates, such as Donatus and Arius, descend alive—that is, knowingly and intelligently—into hell, that is, into the depths of vices. For someone who knows what ought not to be done and does it is like a person knowingly putting his hand into the fire.

Nor do I say this out of ill will, as though he said, but because they deserve it, since “wickedness is in their habitations,” that is, in their bodies, which they inhabit for a time because they will depart from them; and it is in their midst, that is, in their inward heart.

This means: They are unclean inwardly and outwardly.

“But I…”

In them there is wickedness inwardly and outwardly. But the Lord will save me from their wickedness, [Col. 0769B] so that I will not conform to them. This is because I cried out to God, that is, to the Lord himself.

Here he gives us an example of how we too can be delivered from such wickedness: namely, if we cry out to the Lord, that is, if we act well without ceasing.

“Evening and morning.”

The Lord will save me, I say, and once saved I will not be ungrateful, because I will recount for the edification of others what belongs to evening—that is, what has been proclaimed concerning the past. Or it may refer to the Lord’s birth, passion, resurrection, and similar events, which are signified by evening because when it is evening, the sun has passed.

“And I will proclaim” what belongs to morning—that is, what has been proclaimed concerning the future, such as his second coming. For proclamation properly concerns the future, which is signified by morning because when it is morning, the sun is still to come.

And because I will recount what belongs to evening and proclaim what belongs to morning, therefore the Lord heard my voice at midday, that is, by giving me eternal and abiding goods. These are signified by midday [Col. 0769C] because when the sun is in the southern circle there is greater brightness and heat, and it seems almost to stand still, since it is neither ascending nor descending.

Nothing is more worthy of standing or remaining than that to which nothing is added or taken away, as with eternity.

Or otherwise: “I will recount what happened in the evening,” that is, the wisdom of the one who died. For the Lord died in the evening. In this he exercised wondrous wisdom, although it appears foolish to the Gentiles, because by his temporal death he destroyed our eternal death.

“And I will recount what happened in the morning,” that is, the life of the one who rose. For the Lord rose in the morning, and by his resurrection he made known to us the ways of life.

“And I will proclaim what happened at midday,” that is, the glory of the one who ascended and sat at the right hand of God the Father, where he intercedes for us. This is shown by the effect, because the Lord the Father will hear my voice.

Or otherwise: “I will recount what ought to be recounted for edification in the evening and morning,” that is, in prosperity. These are signified by evening and morning because at [Col. 0769D] those two times the air is more temperate than in the heat; and because evening and morning, owing to the change in the breeze, are customarily favorable for sailors and others of that kind.

“And I will proclaim” also for the benefit of my neighbor “at midday,” that is, in the heat of adversity. This means: I will not be lifted up in prosperity so that I fail to recount, nor broken by adversity so that I fail to proclaim.

Therefore, when I cry out to him, the Lord will hear my voice. He will hear it in this way: he will redeem my soul, which was first placed in peace—that is, because it preserved peace among those who hated peace and did not lose love among persecutors—from those who approach me, that is, from the power and conformity of those who oppose me from nearby, because they are fellow citizens.

Therefore I say “those who approach,” because among many of them I was with them according to the orders of their institutions and sacraments. Another translation has: “For among the chaff they were with me,” which fits this interpretation better.

Or otherwise: It is necessary [Col. 0770A] that he redeem my soul from them because they were with me among many—that is, among chaff, not among grain. For there is more chaff on the threshing floor than grain. So too there are more pretended friends than true friends, concerning whom it was said: “The worst kind of friendship is to be enemies in heart while pretending devotion with the tongue.”

“God will hear.”

Truly God will redeem my soul from them, because God will hear me and exalt me. But those who have raised themselves up in dissension he will humble in condemnation—God, I say, who is before the ages.

It is as though he said: “A man who existed in time, such as Donatus or someone of that kind, raised them up; but God, who is before the ages,” that is, who is without time, “will humble them.”

Hence Cassiodorus says: “Let the Lord not be Lord to you who did not wish to be your fellow servant under the Lord.”

Non indeed is there for them. He will rightly humble them, because for them there is no change in the present, and therefore there will be none for them in the future. That is, they had no part in the first resurrection, nor will they have any in the second. There will nevertheless be a change for them in the future through resurrection, but not a change for the better, since they will rise for punishment, not for glory. There is no change for them, I say, and this is because they did not fear God—that is, they did not attend to the Judge who is to come, so as to keep his commandments. Therefore God stretches out his hand in retribution, that is, he will impose a full recompense for their wickedness. And rightly so, because they have defiled—that is, perverted—the testament, namely, his promises. For what was said to Abraham, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed,” they pervert—for example, those who say that this applies only to Africa. Therefore those who did not defile the testament have been separated from the defilers. This is through the anger of his countenance—that is, through the anger displayed in the severity of God’s countenance. They have already been separated from them through inner blindness, that is, morally. They will also then be separated locally, when it is said to them: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire.” And when those defilers have been separated and blinded, his heart—that is, God’s heart, namely, Holy Scripture—has drawn near to those who did not defile the testament. Scripture is called God’s heart because it contains his inner and hidden mysteries. It has drawn near to them, that is, it has been disclosed to those who did not defile the testament. Since those others had been rejected, it was necessary for them—that is, for the defilers—to seek out the truth of the Scriptures, so that they might be able to resist their falsehood. Thus the Scriptures drew near to them, because the more earnestly and frequently they sought them, the more they understood them. Hence the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest.”

Their words have been softened. He explains how God’s heart would draw near to them: namely, because his words—that is, God’s words—had been softened, made intelligible to them. These words sometimes contain certain hard sayings, as when the Lord said: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life.” This is a hard saying, and who can hear it? And nearly seventy-two, scandalized by it, went away backward. [Col. 0770D] But this saying became soft for Peter—not because Peter understood it, but because he believed that it had been spoken piously.

His words, I say, have been softened, and not a little, but beyond oil, that is, beyond every most fluid and delicate liquid. Oil is soft and thin to such a degree that it is said to penetrate the body; but these words are still softer, because they penetrate as far as the soul. Although they have thus become soft, they have not lost their strength, because they themselves are darts: they arm and fortify people against their enemies, and they shoot them like sharp arrows, piercing hearts and directing them toward charity.

Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself, and so forth. Here the greater ones, whose voice is heard in this psalm, exhort their inferiors. It is as though they said: In order that God’s words may also be softened for you who are inferior, let each of you cast your care upon him—that is, consider your own concern to be of no benefit to you, and let him himself take care of your salvation. As it is said elsewhere: “Casting all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you.” If you do this, he himself will nourish you, that is, he will advance you from virtue to virtue. And finally, when he has led you, a righteous person, into eternity, he will no longer allow you to waver, because eternity will be the harbor where you cast your anchor and thereafter remain steadfast. No one, however perfect, can attain this in the present life, since even Peter wavered at the voice of a maidservant.

But you, God.
