These people, Lord, you will nourish; but those previously mentioned—namely, those who defile the testament—you will lead, since you are God, into the pit of destruction, that is, into the pit of corruption, into the darkness of drowning. This is the depth of vices, which will become the pit of destruction, that is, eternal condemnation. You, I say, are the author of their guilt, but the condemner of their wickedness.

Men of blood and deceit. You will rightly lead them into the pit, because they are men of blood: they shed the blood of many, not physically but spiritually, because they kill souls. This is because they are deceitful, that is, they deceive others through their heresy. Such people will not halve their days, that is, they will not advance in wickedness as far as they thought, because they promise themselves a long life, but will not complete half of it, since they will often be consumed by a very swift death.

Or: they were not able—that is, they are not able—to serve God and Mammon. For they wish to halve their days, that is, their present life, which they ought to devote entirely to God’s service: they wish to divide it, so that they may serve partly themselves and partly Mammon. But they will not halve them, that is, they were not able to divide their days in this way for salvation. For “no one who puts his hand to the plow,” and so forth.

Or otherwise, as though someone were saying: “Will the good things they have done not benefit them?” Certainly not, because they will not halve their days—that is, their life. They will not be able to divide it in such a way that, through a few good deeds, they destroy the many evils they have done, since rather the few evils ought to be destroyed through many good deeds. This is to say: They will not be saved on account of their few good deeds; rather, they will be condemned on account of their many evils.

But I. Those people, I said, you will lead into the pit, but you will not lead me there, because I, Lord, will hope—that is, I will place all my hope in you.

Now, this psalm may be read as spoken by any perfect person who is attentive to the tribulation in which he finds himself and prays to be delivered from it. This is for our instruction, namely, so that, recognizing tribulation to be common to all, we may also make our prayer common. But if the same psalm is read as spoken by the Head, then the Head himself speaks as follows:

“God the Father, hear my prayer, made for the perseverance of my own; and, in order that you may hear the prayer, do not disregard the preceding supplication that I have made for them. Attend to me, I say, in my prayer, and hear me in the supplication made for my own.”

And it is necessary that you hear me on their behalf, because they will truly be distressed and troubled, since I myself was distressed in my exercise. It is as though he said: “If they have done this to me, the green wood, what will be done to the dry?” And: “If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more will they call his household servants,” and similar things.

Christ’s exercise was that of which he himself says: “For this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth.” This exercise was directed toward piety and was useful for everything, because in all that he did, whether by word or by example, he benefited us.

In this exercise he was distressed in two ways. First, he looked upon the Jewish people, which he had watered with the rain of his word, as though it were a dry fig tree, and found in it no fruit with which he might satisfy his hunger, but only leaves, that is, words. Second, he was distressed even by death itself, because he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” This was not because death itself was pleasant or agreeable to him, but because he transformed our weakness in himself.

This is what he says: “I was distressed in my exercise, in myself and in my own,” because they too were distressed, each in their own manner, in two ways. I was so distressed that I was troubled—that is, this distress was a trouble lasting only for a time, because it was quickly changed in him into the joy of the resurrection. It is also quickly changed into joy, in its own manner, in his own.

And because I was so distressed that I was only temporarily troubled, I was distressed in myself and in my people by the voice of the enemy, that is, on account of the enemy’s voice. And by the tribulation of the sinner, because I attended not to my own punishment but to his condemnation, and consequently grieved.

We may understand “the voice of the enemy” as referring to what they said to him: “You have a demon,” and similar things, as well as to the contradictions offered by his members. By “the tribulation of the sinner” we may understand his own passion and that of his people. Cassiodorus distinguishes this verse as we have just explained, and the distinction is quite effective under either reading.

For they have turned aside. It is as though he said: “I was distressed for this reason: they turned their iniquities against me, iniquities by which they deserved to destroy their place and nation, insofar as it lay within them. They regarded my life as a kind of pollution, and therefore believed that through my death they might, as though by a purification, cleanse both themselves and their city.” Hence one of them said: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish.”

And in their anger—that is, angry on account of their place and nation—they were troublesome to me, that is, they harassed me by their words and deeds. Therefore my heart, that is, my soul, was troubled. This did not happen through their coercion or lie within their power, but in me, that is, in my own will.

And the dread of death—that is, the condemnation consequent upon death, the thing on account of which death is feared—of death, I say, coming upon me, fell upon me; that is, it was destroyed. This is to say: Since death wished to claim me, over whom it had no right, it lost the right that it had possessed. For by his temporal death he destroyed our eternal death, and thus death was swallowed up in its own victory.

Fear and trembling. He also shows how death came upon him, saying: “Fear and trembling came upon me.” This describes our death through its effects. Since death—that is, the separation of soul and body—is feared, it causes fear in the mind and trembling in the body.

And darkness covered me. This too belongs to the preceding description, because here he touches upon the proximity of death. Darkness follows death, that is, the loss of this light.

Or otherwise: Fear and trembling came upon me because darkness—that is, those dark in understanding and lacking discernment—covered me, that is, surrounded me for condemnation. And because I perceived that these things were about to come upon me, I said: “Who will give me wings?” Surely you, God the Father? I mean wings that are like those of a dove. “And I shall fly away from these people, and thus I shall rest.”

Here we understand the wings as the power to lay down his soul and to take it up again. With these wings he flew away from his persecutors by dying and rising again—not with raven’s wings, but with dove’s wings: not in hatred, but in charity. For afterward he visited some of them, when three thousand believed in a single day, and many others afterward.

This was also charitable because he died for our sins and rose for our justification. After he had flown away in this manner, he rested in immortality and impassibility. True rest is that in which no further trouble intervenes.

Or he flew away from that people of which it was said: “I labored while enduring,” that is, from the Jews, and rested among that other people of which it was said: “A people whom I did not know served me at the hearing of the ear.”

Behold, it is as though he said: “What I desired has happened. Wings have been given to me, and I have withdrawn from them,” that is, from the Jews, by dying and rising again. He fled from them insofar as the greater part of them was concerned, but not insofar as his members were concerned, namely, the apostles. From these, who were his own members, he afterward permitted himself to be touched, so that they would not doubt. Nor did he flee from those whom he visited through the grace of faith.

And having withdrawn from them, I remained in solitude, that is, among the Gentiles, who were like a wilderness, deprived of the law and the prophets.

Or: I withdrew by fleeing, even with respect to everyone in bodily presence. And I remained in the solitude of the Father’s confession. This is rightly called solitude because, apart from him, no one had yet arrived there bodily.

And rightly so—as though he were saying—this was granted to me, namely, that I should fly away and rest, because I completed obedience with patience. For I patiently awaited him, that is, God the Father, who had first saved me in hope and will now save me in reality from faintness of spirit, that is, from that weakness of spirit on account of which he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” And from the storm, that is, from the assault of the raging people.

I speak as follows: “Hurl them down, Lord, and divide their tongues,” in the two ways mentioned in the first interpretation. I do not say this out of ill will, but because they are deserving of it. For in the city—that is, among the Jewish people, which was like a city because of the law and the prophets, so that it seemed less necessary to fear—I saw, that is, recognized and experienced more clearly, both contradiction and iniquity surrounding that city day and night, that is, always.

This was not only among the lesser people, but in such a way that it rose above its walls, that is, above its rulers, namely, Pilate, Annas, and Caiaphas. And this was because there was labor in its midst, as was said in the first interpretation.

For if an enemy had cursed me. I saw, I say, contradiction in the city, something most grievous and intolerable. For if an open enemy—that is, a Gentile people—had cursed me, I would certainly have endured it, that is, I would have regarded it as something to be endured.

This should not be understood as though God tolerates any iniquity, or spares someone’s iniquity, but rather as though he tolerates the iniquity of those who sin in ignorance, because he punishes it less severely than if they were sinning knowingly.

And if the one who openly hated me—because he preferred to worship a creature rather than God—had spoken great things against me, saying, “We have no king but Caesar,” perhaps he might have been such that I would hide myself from him, that is, I would not reveal myself to him through so severe a vengeance.

Perhaps he adds “perhaps” for this reason: among the Gentiles too there were some to whom God granted such great intelligence that they possessed the law written naturally in their hearts, such as Plato and the other philosophers. God does not hide himself from such people, since he will exact vengeance from them as severely as from those who received the written law.

But you, man. I would have endured that man and hidden myself from him. But you, whom I made human through the law that was given—that is, intelligent—and who ought to have been of one mind with me, my leader, whom I appointed as a guide to others so that in you they might see the face of God and understand what they should worship; and my acquaintance according to the flesh, who ate sweet foods with me, that is, the legal ordinances—which he calls sweet not with respect to their signs, but with respect to what they signified, although they did not attend to this.

And truly you were with me, for we walked together in agreement in the house of the Lord, that is, in the precepts of the law. He himself also fulfilled many of these physically, since he was circumcised and was presented in the temple [Col. 0773D] with offerings.

You, I say, a man so familiar to me—what do you induce me to say? This: “Let death come upon them,” and so forth. This is likewise said here, as in the earlier interpretation, with an evil meaning.

It may also be explained, according to Cassiodorus, with a good meaning, as follows: “Let death come upon them,” that is, let them die to their former life; and, while still living—that is, attending to the life they have lived wickedly—let them descend into hell, that is, let them anticipate hell in their minds and see what punishment is due to them, and thus be converted.

It is necessary that they do this because there is wickedness in their dwellings. This has the same meaning as above.

Or it may be said by way of mere comparison: They are so filthy in wickedness that they are like those whose dwellings are full of filth, not only in the corners but even in the middle.

But the Lord will save me from their wickedness, in myself and in my own. And once saved, I will recount it in myself and in my own in the evening, that is, by proclaiming what belongs to the past. And I will announce it in the morning, that is, by proclaiming what belongs to the future. And may he hear me and my own at midday, that is, by granting eternal things.

Other interpretations mentioned above may also be applied here, partly to him and partly to his people. And he will truly hear me, because he will redeem my soul, which exists in peace—that is, which preserves peace even among those who hate peace—from those who draw near to me, that is, from the power of the Jews, who oppose me because they are near me. This is necessary because they were with me among many, that is, only among chaff, as stated earlier.

They have defiled his testament. Here understand God’s testament as the promises concerning eternal things made under grace. The Jews did not order this testament above the legal sacrifices; rather, they placed earthly and ancient promises before it. Hence he says: They have defiled—that is, despised—his testament, confirmed by the blood of me, the testator. Therefore they have been separated, as before.

Men of blood. You will rightly lead them into the pit of destruction, because they are men of blood, desiring to shed my blood for the sake of their place and nation. And because they are deceitful—that is, they deal deceitfully with me—saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful,” and similar things.

Although by shedding my blood they intended to establish an eternal kingdom for themselves, they will not spend their days there as though eternally, because in the forty-second year they were overthrown and taken captive by Titus and Vespasian.

Or otherwise, as though someone were saying: “Will their legal observances not benefit them?” No, certainly not, because they cling only to the signs and not to what is signified. But they will not halve their days—that is, their life—in their carnal observances. They will not be able to divide them in such a way that those carnal observances, which are signs separated from what they signify, can save them.

For through the imperfect—that is, through signs alone—they will never attain the perfect, that is, true salvation. They, I say, will be condemned. But I and my own will not be condemned, Lord Father, because I and my own will hope in you alone.

## PSALM 55

For the end, concerning the people who have been made far from the holy ones; David, in the inscription of the title, when the Allophyli seized him in Gath.

[Col. 0774C]

### ARGUMENT

The supplication of the Maccabees, when, having conspired in defense of the law, they attempted to overcome both transgressing fellow citizens and enemies.

Alternatively, the voice of Christ to the Father.

Arnobius likewise says: “If the Allophyli have seized you, and have made you far from holy thoughts, cry out to the Lord, saying: ‘Have mercy on me, Lord, because man has trampled me down’”—the outward man, certainly. For through you he acts against you; through him your enemies fight against you all day long.

### EXPLANATION

In Hebrew it reads as follows: “For the silent dove of far-off places: David, humble and perfect, when the Philistines had seized him in Geth.”

The mute dove and David, humble and perfect, signify Christ in his passion. As for what our Translation says, “For the people who have been made far from the holy ones”—that is, for David’s companions who, exiled in Gath, were made far from Judea, where the Holy of Holies was—it signifies that the psalm was sung for Christ’s disciples, who were scandalized at the time of his passion. He himself bears witness that he prayed for their faith, so that it might not fail.

“David, in the inscription of the title,” signifies the Lord in his passion, when he was titled King of the Jews—that is, of all who believe and confess God.

“When the Allophyli seized him in Gath” signifies when the Jews, or Pilate’s soldiers, crucified him. Gath, which is interpreted as “winepress,” indicates the pressure of the cross.

In the mute dove, or in the people who have been made far from the holy ones, all the faithful may be understood: they are exiles from the eternal holy ones and, with the Apostle, say: “While we are in the body, we are pilgrims from the Lord.” For them David does not cease to sing psalms—namely, the one who sits at the right hand of God and now intercedes for us.

The psalm may also be understood as spoken in the person of the Church, which never ceases to suffer pressure in this world, burdened by various afflictions.

In the first section of the psalm, Mother Church prays, nevertheless confident that she will be delivered from her enemies. In the second section she enumerates her sufferings, giving thanks because she has been rescued from frequent dangers and does not fear evils that pass away very quickly. In the third place, in that future blessedness, she says that she will continually sing praises to the Lord, who has delivered her from the adversity of this world.

### COMMENTARY

Have mercy on me, God, because man has trampled me down. The title is as follows: “For the end, concerning the people who have been made far from the holy ones, in the inscription of the title, for David himself, when the Allophyli seized him in Gath.”

This is explained as follows. These words are referred to the end, that is, to Christ, who is the end of all our labor and intention. Thus the place toward which one tends is the end of the road, because just as he gave himself as an example of how to live here, so in the future he promised himself as the reward. And once we possess that reward, we shall find nothing further to seek.

The words, I say, were spoken by the Church concerning the people, so that she might be delivered from the oppression and conformity of that people who have been made far from the holy ones through the inscription of the title.

Who this people is, the title shows us. During the Lord’s passion a certain title was written in three languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, and was confirmed as though by three witnesses. When the Jews read this title, they became indignant and said to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but that he himself said, ‘I am King of the Jews.’” They were as though saying: “Write that he said it, not that he is it.”

But because it had been prophesied through the Holy Spirit, “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title,” Pilate, angered, said: “What I have written, I have written.” As though unknowingly he were saying: “I do not corrupt the truth if you love falsehood.”

And because they were offended by the title and had previously held it as a curse, when Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your king?” and they replied, “We have no king but Caesar,” they were made far from the holy ones.

Those, however, draw near to the holy ones who recognize Christ as king and desire to have him as king. This should not be referred only to them, namely, the Jews, but also to every people that takes pleasure in an earthly kingdom and rejects having God as king. Such a people has been made far from the holy ones. Nevertheless, primitive examples were given in that people, so that what every people ought to avoid might shine forth in it.

They openly despised Christ and chose Caesar as king. Their sin did not consist in choosing Caesar, but in despising Christ as king—Christ whom many even now, although he sits in heaven and reigns everywhere, refuse to have as king.

These too have been made far from the holy ones, not in body but in heart, and they persecute the holy ones. Against these people this psalm strengthens us, because we must endure such people, whom we would not endure unless this were beneficial. For temptation produces testing, testing produces hope, and so forth.

This is the meaning of “for the people who have been made far from the holy ones, in the inscription of the title.” The inscription, I say, was made for David himself, not historically, because we do not read that any title was written for the historical David, but mystically—namely, when the Allophyli seized him in Gath.

This too does not fit the historical David. It is indeed read that he came to the Allophyli in the city of Gath, but it is not read that he was seized by them. Therefore it must refer to the mystical David, that is, to Christ, whom the Allophyli truly seized.

The Allophyli are “foreigners,” or “those falling through drink”—that is, Jewish men who were foreigners, made far from the holy ones, and falling through drink, that is, enraged against him for the sake of their place and nation.

They seized him in Gath, which is interpreted as “winepress” or “pressure.” This means that they seized him in the pressure of his passion. In that passion the first cluster—that is, like a grape in the winepress—was trampled and expressed that exceedingly sweet wine of which it is said: “And how excellent is my cup, making me drunk!”

Christ is still held in his body as well, because “all who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus must suffer persecution.” No one who is outside suffering can be attached to this saying. Therefore we must fear being far from the passion and thus becoming far from the holy ones.

Tribulations and persecutions must therefore be attended to, indeed desired. We must also attend to the enemies who persecute us, because we suffer two enemies: one visible and one invisible. We see the human being but do not see the devil; we should love the human being and beware of the devil; we should pray for the human being and pray against the devil, and say: “Have mercy on me, Lord.”

This is the voice of Christ’s body, praying to be delivered from those who are far from the holy ones, so that it may not be conformed to them, but rather so that they may be converted and conformed to it. It speaks as follows:

“God the Father, have mercy on me by giving me steadfastness, so that I may not be overcome by the Allophyli or conformed to them.”

And it is necessary that you have mercy, because man has trampled me down. This means both the one who is figuratively called man, namely, the devil—as in the passage, “An enemy came and sowed weeds among it”—and the one who is naturally man, namely, the devil’s ministers.

He says rightly “trampled me,” because a grape hanging on the vine remains apparently barren, since its liquid is not visible within it; but when it is pressed in the winepress, it expresses sweet liquid. In the same way, the Church, placed in the winepress of persecution, has brought forth the outstanding merits of very many holy martyrs: the blind are enlightened at their tombs, the sick are healed, those possessed by demons are cured, and similar things occur.

Man has trampled me down, I say, in this way: by attacking me, he has afflicted me all day long, that is, continually, or throughout the entire time of the trampling.

He explains what he means by “man,” saying: “My enemies, both visible and invisible, have trampled me down all day long.”

Or he explains why he now speaks in the plural what he earlier expressed in the singular, saying: “Because those who fight against me inwardly and outwardly are many.”

But what concern is this? None, certainly, because I will fear from the height—that is, on account of some power or pride of the persecutors—although it belongs to the day, that is, to what is temporal and transitory? Certainly I will not fear. Rather, they will eventually fear and repent, but fruitlessly, because those who here hardened their hearts and ears against the Lord while he warned them will not there be able to harden themselves against him while he judges.

So great will be the terror of his sentence that it will crush all their pride. There the emperor will fear no less than the fisherman.

They, I say, will fear. I, however, ought to say, “I will not fear.” But lest this appear presumptuous, he gives the reason why he will not fear: namely, because I will hope in you, presuming nothing of myself.

And because I will hope in you, I will praise my words not in myself but in you, God, ascribing them to you and not to myself, if I say anything true.

Whoever recognizes that no one can speak anything true in God’s wisdom or in faith except what he has received from him who is the source and origin of all truth will praise his words in God. Those words belong both to him and to God: they belong to God because God gave them, and they belong to him because he received them. In asking God for them, he does not remain empty. By saying that they are his, but that he received them from God, he does not prove ungrateful.

In God I hoped. He repeats what he said earlier, as though saying: “I will not merely hope; I have already hoped in God, and therefore I will not fear what flesh can do to me.”

For what can flesh do to me? Let flesh rage as much as it wishes; it will do nothing to me except what flesh can do. I was a grape; flesh will trample me, and I shall become wine and be carried into the heavenly storehouse.

He uses “flesh” for man, a part for the whole, as in the passage: “The Word became flesh,” that is, “he became man.”

All day long they curse my words. He proceeds to describe the deeds of the flesh. It is as though he said: “Behold what flesh can do. For those who are understood by ‘flesh’ were cursing—that is, rejecting as abominable—my words all day long, that is, continually.”

And what wonder is it if they cursed my words, when they also cursed you, God, in those words, because they were praised in you? For “the disciple is not above his teacher, nor the servant above his lord.”

They cursed my words, I say, in such a way that all their thoughts, and not only their spoken words but also their deeds, were directed toward evil and against me, that is, toward my condemnation.

And yet, although they cursed me in this way and thought every evil against me, they will inhabit—that is, they will associate with me in the sacraments of faith. Thus they will hide themselves, that is, they will deal with me deceitfully and treacherously. For they came not to learn, but to obtain something with which they might accuse and reproach me.

Of such people the Apostle says: “Certain false brothers slipped in to spy out our freedom.” A person enters like Titus, so that he may not be avoided as a stranger.

They will hide themselves, I say, in order to lie in wait for me. And they will truly do this, because they will watch my heel, that is, they will lie in wait for my heel with great care—my heel meaning my fall—namely, to see whether I slip in speech, so that they may denounce me.

They will watch in this way, just as those did who endured my soul—that is, who considered my life hateful because I was burdensome to them even to look upon. For this reason they lay their snares more maliciously.

But you, Lord, will repay them, and you will make them safe—that is, you will finally save them from the corruption of the flesh by raising them for eternal punishment, not for glory. Such a salvation must be regarded as nothing.

And rightly as nothing, because in your anger you will break those peoples, as though they had been saved. Such will be the terror of the sentence that you will pronounce in anger: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire.” Their hope and pride will thereby be wholly broken and crushed.

Those people, I say, you will save for nothing; but you will save me not for nothing, but for something, namely, because I have proclaimed my life to you.

The preceding salvation may also be understood in a good sense, as follows: Although they are so wicked, you, God, will nevertheless make them safe, converted and made faithful. And this is nothing to you, that is, you regard it as nothing difficult, to save them, because you save them by a word alone. You do not labor in saving them, although we are astonished when we see it.

Or otherwise: You will make them safe for nothing, that is, without any preceding merit on their part. For what did Paul, when he was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent man, bring with him when he was cast down and saved by a word on the road? What did the thief bring to the judgment, from the judgment to the wood, and from the wood to paradise? Nothing at all, except the faith that was given to him by the one who hung beside him, namely, Christ.

In this way you will make them safe: by sending them certain tribulations, as though in anger, you will break—that is, humble—those peoples. For you are angry and break them, you rage and save them, you terrify and call them. Many, distressed by tribulation, have been filled with faith, because tribulation agitates them for this purpose: so that the vessel may be emptied of wickedness and filled with grace.

God, my life. Since you save even such people for nothing, therefore, God, I have proclaimed my life to you, not to myself, because every life must be ascribed to you, not to anyone’s merits.

When Paul said, “Although I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man, I received mercy,” and so forth, he proclaimed his life not to himself but to that one, namely, God, so that he might be believed. He was not seeking his own profit, but the profit of the one about whom he subsequently says: “Christ Jesus died so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for all.”

Therefore, if you live—and do not live from yourself, but because he enabled you to live—proclaim your life to him, not to yourself. Seek no longer your own profit, but his. For concerning some who seek their own profit rather than his, it is said: “They seek what is their own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ.”

And rightly I have proclaimed my life to you, because you have placed my tears in your sight, that is, you have heard me when I prayed, as had previously been foretold in your promise, when the prophet proclaimed this. For you promised that you would hear the one who weeps.

I believed, I wept, I was heard. This is the promise: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, I will turn to him.”

It is equivalently expressed as follows: “Therefore I rightly proclaim my life to you, because it is through you that I live.”

And because I received life from you, which I possess, therefore let my enemies be converted by my example. They were trying to go backward; let them not remain backward and fail to advance, but let them follow and not go ahead.

Here he prays for the visible enemy, as was indicated in the title. It is as though he said: “Truly my enemies will be converted, and in those who have been converted I will call upon you. And on whatever day—that is, with whatever purity of mind, or at whatever time—I call upon you in them, I shall know in those same people that you are both God and my God.”

And behold, it is as though he said: “Experience has given me confidence that, in those who are being converted, I shall truly come to know you. For already, in those who were previously converted, I learned that you are both God and my God.”

It is great knowledge to know one’s God. He is yours because he comes to your aid and does not make himself alien to you.

These are the great riches of the heart and the great light of the inner person: to know one’s God and to possess one’s God. This is to worship God freely, to love God freely, and to praise God freely. It is to call upon God truly.

But what I said—“I shall know in these people, because I knew in those people”—should not trouble you, because it is the voice of the Church, which called upon him in the preceding passages and will call upon him in those that follow.

In God I will praise. This repetition is on account of those who are to be converted, about whom this has been said. As though he were saying: Just as in those earlier ones I praise my words in you, God, presuming nothing upon myself, so in the case of those who are to be converted I will presume nothing upon myself, but in you, God the Father, I will praise my Word to you, not attributing it to myself; and in the Lord the Son, because he redeemed us from slavery. I will also praise my utterance, that is, the Word, and in the Lord the Holy Spirit—I ought to say—I will likewise praise; but he says only why, namely, because I hoped in God the Spirit, which is a common cause. For if he hopes in the Holy Spirit, he hopes in the Father and the Son, whose majesty and essence are one. I hoped, I say, in God, and therefore I will not fear what man may do to me. For what can man do to me? Let man rage as much as he wishes, let him take away gold and silver, let him take away everything earthly; nevertheless he will do nothing to me, because he will not take away my vows. For this treasure is enclosed in the heart, and man cannot take it away: from the altar of my heart I will bring forth the incense of praise; from the storeroom of a good conscience, the sacrament of faith. For God demands not a he-goat, not a calf, but he demands praise and confession, that is, faith, which no one will be able to take away if you do not despise it. And this is what he says: “Your vows, that is, those fitting and acceptable to you, are in me,” that is, they are closed within my heart, and therefore cannot be taken away. I speak of vows that I will always pay to you; and he says what those vows are, namely, praises.

For you have rescued my soul. Therefore I shall rightly praise you, because you have already, in hope, rescued my soul from death, that is, from the more serious actual sins; and likewise you have rescued my feet, that is, my affections, from falling—that is, even from lesser actual sins—so that I may not fall into them. And you rescued me for this purpose: that at last I might please you perfectly before you, God, namely, in the affection of the saints. I speak of myself as existing in the light of the living. The light of the living, the light of the saints, the light of the immortal, is freely to love, worship, and praise God. Or, “in the light of the living,” that is, in immortality and freedom from suffering, where I shall see face to face.

## PSALM LVI

To the end. Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title, when he fled from the face of Saul, king of Israel, into the cave.

### Argument

Here too, concerning the Maccabees. With victory already beginning to bring joy, a prayer is formed. Likewise, the voice of Paul after the resurrection. Likewise Arnobius:

“When you flee from the face of the prince of this world who persecutes you, just as Saul persecuted David, seek the cave—that is, so place yourself that you cannot be found by your enemy, while you indeed have your enemy in your hands, but he does not see you. For this will happen if with your whole heart you say to God: ‘In the shadow of your wings I will hope.’”

### Explanation

By “the end” he signifies the Lord, who remains for us the perfection of all good things, because when we have come to him, we shall have no need to seek anything further. “Do not destroy David”: Saul is forbidden to destroy him, since he had been prepared by the Lord for kingship. “In the inscription of the title”: this does not properly concern David, but the Lord, so that the title written at the Passion should not be altered. Yet because David bears the person of Christ, what was to be done in Christ’s Passion is now said about him: that David should not be destroyed from the kingdom assigned to him. Likewise, the inscription of the Lord’s title could not be changed when David fled from the face of Saul into the cave.

Just as David, fleeing from Saul, hid himself in a cave, so the divinity of Christ was hidden from the faithless Jews within the temple of his body. It may also be said that the Lord endured the Jews until he entered the cave of the tomb, especially since this psalm sings not only of his Passion but also of his resurrection. In the first part of the psalm the Lord prays, anxious according to his humanity, in which he suffered. In the second he recalls the glory of his resurrection. In the third he sings praises to the Father after the resurrection; these sections are also distinguished by the insertion of *diapsalms*.

### Commentary

Have mercy on me, God; have mercy on me, for my soul has trusted in you. This psalm, marked as concerning the Lord’s Passion, teaches how greatly we ought to love and what the perfect measure of love is that pleases God—the greatest measure, since he says of it: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.” The Lord himself did this; he taught this to his apostles; and through the apostles he taught it also to us. If anyone, considering his weakness, falls short in fulfilling the commandment, let him be strengthened by the example.

This is the voice of the Head, yet in such a way that we do not separate the voice of the Body, because he who did not wish to be separated from the Body did not wish to speak separately. In accordance with what he says: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.”

Its title is: “To the end. Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave.” What it says, “Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title,” cannot be adapted to the historical David, because no title is read as having been written for him that Saul or any of his persecutors corrupted. And because it is not found in the history, it must be found in allegory.

For a certain title is read as having been written at the Lord’s Passion, to reproach the foreheads of the Jews, who did not refrain their hands from the King. When the Jews read this title, they were offended and indignant that they should have such a king whom they could crucify. They said to Pilate, to whom they had also handed Christ over for crucifixion: “Do not write ‘King,’ but write that he himself said he was not.” But because it had been prophesied, “Do not destroy the inscription of the title,” Pilate, angered, answered them: “What I have written, I have written.” As though he were saying: “Why do you suggest falsehood? I do not corrupt the truth.”

Foreseeing their foolishness—or rather, their savagery and madness—the Holy Spirit warns them through the Prophet not to destroy David, that is, not to wish to drive the true David, namely Christ, from the kingdom assigned to him by withdrawing themselves from his rule, since he truly is their king—and is the king of all. They were offended at the inscription of the title made for David himself when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave.

This has both a historical and an allegorical meaning. The historical David fled from the savage and ungrateful persecutor Saul into the cave where he was hiding and was covered by the earth. Our David now likewise flees into a cave when the Word who was in the beginning with God assumed our weakness, in which he hid himself from those signified by Saul, namely, the Jews. He had to be seen in such a way that he could be understood; for if they had recognized him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

Why did they not recognize the Lord? Because he placed earth before their eyes and covered his majesty with earth; in that earth alone he could be held, scourged, and crucified. To those who sought earth wrongly he opposed earth; to those who sought rightly he preserved life.

It may also be said in another way that he fled, namely, because he allowed himself to be hidden from them to such an extent that he died on the cross and was placed in the tomb. From that tomb he rose incorrupt, just as David departed unharmed from the cave, hiding himself from his enemies and revealing himself to his members. For his apostles handled his limbs, because they believed that he had risen.

The title is constructed in this way: “These words are referred to the end and proposed for this purpose: that no one should corrupt David, being offended at the inscription of the title made when David fled.” Now let us approach the psalm.

It is the voice of the Head—as we have said—praying for himself and for his members. The pious Teacher prays in order to teach us to pray; he suffered in order to teach us to suffer; and he rose in order to give us hope of rising. And he speaks thus:

God the Father, have mercy on me by restoring me to immortality; and have mercy on me, that is, on my members, now through an inner resurrection, until it also comes through an outward one. And it is right for you to do this, because my soul and the soul of my members trusts in you alone, presuming nothing upon itself.

And I trust in you not only now, but also always, by hoping in my members, in the shadow of your wings; that is, just as the shadow of a mother’s wings protects her young, so you will protect me in my members by giving shade, lest I wither from the heat of iniquity. And I shall hope until iniquity passes away, that is, as long as the world endures.

Iniquity has already passed away with respect to the Head and certain saints, but iniquity has not yet perished. For now iniquity burns fiercely, and it will always burn as long as the world endures, because just as certain wicked people die and other wicked people succeed them, so when certain righteous people die, others are born. Thus in this life there will never be a lack of persecuting iniquity and justice giving birth.

I will cry to God Most High. Because I will hope in God, I will cry to God, to whom it is right to cry, because he is Most High, that is, he is above all things. Yet he is near to our misery, because just as he is God from afar, so also he is God from nearby. For just as he recognizes the lofty and proud from afar, so he regards the humble from near at hand, because the Lord is near to those who have crushed hearts.

I will cry, I say, to the Lord, and he himself will do good both to me and to my members. From this I have been given confidence by experience, because he has already done good to me in my members. For if he did good to my members before they knew him, sending me as their propitiator and consoler—one who would die for their sins and rise for their justification—will he not hear me when I cry, that is, when I act well without ceasing? Indeed, he will hear me.

He sent from heaven. He did good, I say, to my members in me; and in order to do good through me, he sent his divine power from heaven. He delivered me, a human being, taking me from the womb and making me free from sins; and he took me from the tomb by raising me. By this he has already, in his decree, and will in fact deliver those who trample upon me—that is, the Jews who afflict me—into reproach.

For it is a great reproach that in that city where they raged and acted proudly most of all, they lost every right, and, uprooted from there and scattered everywhere, became contemptible to all. It is also a reproach that they have become our book-carriers, that is, our copyists, because they carry their books for us, as servants customarily do after their masters. They themselves fail while carrying; Christians advance while reading.

They are like a blind man carrying a brilliantly shining mirror, in which his image shines for others but not for himself. For they carry books in which their own features—namely, what had been promised to them—shine for us, but do not appear to them. The greatest reproach, however, is that they hear everywhere that the one whom they thought they had utterly destroyed has been exalted.

God sent his mercy. God the Father sent his Word, I say, to free me; he also sent his mercy to free others through me—that is, he sent me, sympathizing with the miseries of others and showing mercy—and he sent me as his truth, that is, teaching true things.

Or it may be explained by analogy with an embassy in this way: God the Father sent the Word and assumed me as a human being. He also sent his mercy, because he dealt mercifully with me, and his truth, because he truly promised. In mercy he fulfilled what he had promised in truth, and he rescued my soul.

Above he said, “He delivered me.” Now he proceeds as though saying: He delivered me because he rescued my soul, raising me from the midst of lion cubs, that is, from the midst of the Jewish people, from lions, that is, from the rulers who had been led astray into killing me. By the cubs the lesser people are understood; by the lions, the greater, because all conspired in his death. The greater killed him, while the lesser consented.

And what need was there for rescue? Because I slept, that is, I underwent death—a death that ought rather to be called sleep than death, because I rose from it as easily as from sleep—I, I say, being troubled.

It seems contradictory that he both slept and was troubled, because one who is troubled is either awakened from sleep or prevented from falling asleep. But this is said with respect to those who thought him troubled by the death he underwent, though it was most joyful.

The sons of men. As though he were saying: Who troubled you? Answer: The sons of men troubled me. He specifies this in order to show that those who thought themselves excusable are not excusable when they said to Pilate: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone.” For the Prophet’s meaning is as though he were saying to them: If it is not lawful to kill, neither is it lawful to hand someone over for killing.

And as though he were saying: How did those who drew no sword against you trouble you? He says: Consider their tongue a sword, because their teeth—that is, their biting words—were weapons with respect to the plot they secretly devised. And they were arrows with respect to their flying words of accusation. And they were a sword with respect to the sentence of death, when they said: “Crucify him, crucify him.”

Be exalted above the heavens. They indeed thought to trouble me; but you, Lord the Word, human on the cross and God in heaven, exalt me, a human being who has been exalted, above the heavens—not only above the material heavens but above all the angelic orders. And may your glory, that is, your glorious one—namely, myself, glorified by you through immortality and incorruption—be exalted, not only above Judaea but above the whole earth. And this happened when he was preached through the apostles throughout the entire world.

They prepared a snare for my feet. It is necessary that you exalt me, because there are those who bring me down. For the sons of men prepared a snare, that is, an impediment, for my feet. Understand by “feet” either the threats or promises through which the teaching of truth advances, or the holy apostles through whom he himself advanced to the knowledge of the nations.

And they not only prepared a snare for me, but also bent down my soul and the soul of my members—that is, they wished to bend and oppress them. They bent down his own soul when they said: “You have a demon,” and “This man is not from God,” and similar things. They bent down the soul of his members when they wished to conform them to themselves.

They dug a pit before my face. In this way, I say, they prepared a snare for me, because they dug a pit, that is, they prepared deception and death for me, as though I were unaware of their intention. Nevertheless, it was before my face, that is, their heart was manifest to me, who knew it.

Or by “the pit” we may understand the manifest sentence of condemnation, because they despised him to such an extent that, before his face—that is, in his presence—they did not hesitate to condemn him, saying: “He is guilty of death.”

And they fell into the pit, because whoever prepares condemnation for another first condemns himself. For he sins against himself before he sins against another. And the sadness of the one who suffers is always happier than the wicked joy of the one who inflicts suffering.

Likewise, every unjustly delivered sentence condemns its author. This pertains to the later statement concerning the pit.

My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody to the Lord. They, I say, prepared a pit, but I prepared endurance; they prepared to bring me down, but I prepared to suffer.

For my heart is ready within me, and my heart is ready in my members. Therefore, O God the Father, I will sing to you in myself and in my members with heart and mouth, and I will make melody in my works.

And so that I may sing and make melody, he speaks as though saying: Let my disgrace—that is, my flesh—die, inasmuch as it is mortal and subject to suffering; and let it rise as my glory, that is, glorified in immortality and freedom from suffering.

Rise, I say, my flesh, being a psaltery and a lyre. It is one reality, and it contains two musical instruments, because in the one flesh of Christ two different kinds of actions have been displayed, signified by two different musical instruments.

The psaltery, which sounds from above, signifies the miracles divinely displayed for us. The lyre, which sounds from below, signifies the tribulations and weaknesses displayed in Christ’s body. The psaltery sounds when the blind see, the lame walk, and so forth; the lyre sounds when he suffers hunger, sleeps, is sorrowful, and so forth.

I say, “Rise.” And truly it will happen, because I shall rise. He says this in order to prove by it that the Word personally joined to him is coequal and consubstantial with the Father. For because the Father and the Word are one, the Father raised him, and he himself, according to the Word, raised himself.

He places “at dawn” either to indicate the time of the resurrection, which took place in the morning, or because just as dawn is named from the dispersal of darkness, so then, when the darkness of unbelief had been dispersed, the light of faith and truth began to shine.

I will confess to you among the peoples, Lord. Because I shall rise, therefore, Lord, I will confess you in the Jewish psalms. And I will make melody to you; I will praise you through good works also among the nations.

And rightly will I praise you, because I ought to be called not merely merciful, but your very mercy: although I was powerful, I became wretched in order to bring a remedy to the miseries of others. And I ought to be called your truth, because through me every truth has been shown to the world.

I have been magnified, that is, exalted, as far as the heavens are established and as far as the clouds are established. Understand “heaven” and “clouds” as preachers: heaven means the greater ones, such as the apostles; clouds, the lesser ones.

Or otherwise: It seems more appropriate for truth to be referred to the heavens and mercy to the clouds. For the heavens are the angels, who, the higher they are and the nearer to truth, behold and praise the hope of truth more perfectly, without the darkness of vision, saying: “Holy, Holy, Holy.”

The clouds are called preachers because of the darksome flesh with which they are covered, although through them the Lord thunders with threats and flashes with miracles. And because misery is present in them, they need mercy. Therefore mercy seems to belong to the clouds and truth to the heavens.

Nevertheless, truth certainly prevails in the angels, but the Lord gave it also to the clouds. And because the angels do not need mercy, the merciful Lord, having compassion on the miseries of human beings, gave them mercy; and through the clarification of resurrection and incorruption he made them equal to the angels.

Therefore it was rightly said: “For the mercy of God has been magnified as far as the heavens are established,” because through mercy human beings have been made heavens, that is, angels; and “truth as far as the clouds are established,” because the knowledge of truth has been given in its own manner to preachers.

Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth. So that peoples and nations may confess you. Or, so that mercy and truth may be magnified, therefore you, God the Word, human on the cross and God in heaven, exalt me, who have been exalted above all the heavens, and so forth.

This repetition arises not from the necessity of the narrator but from the affection of the one praying.

## PSALM LVII

To the end. Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title.

### Argument

As the fame and victory of the Maccabees increased day by day, certain deceitful enemies mingled themselves among them; by these Jonathan and Simon, together with their sons, were killed. This psalm therefore rebukes them. Alternatively, the Prophet speaks concerning the elders of the Jews.

### Explanation

The names “the end” and “David in the inscription of the title” designate Christ on the cross, and Pilate is warned not to destroy the written title that declared the Lord to be king.

In the first account the Lord reproaches the wickedness of the Jews. In the second he declares their punishments through highly appropriate comparisons. In the third, it is recalled what correction the righteous receive from the vengeance inflicted upon sinners.

### Commentary

If indeed you speak justice, judge rightly, sons of men.

The title is as follows: “To the end. Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title.” These words are referred to the end and proposed for this purpose: that no one should destroy David, that is, should dissipate, as far as lies within him, the kingdom of David by withdrawing himself from his rule—being offended, I say, at the inscription of the title.

For through the title David, that is, Christ, obtained a kingdom for himself among the Jews, that is, among those who confess. Those who say and do what is true are truly confessors. Whoever therefore acts otherwise than he speaks corrupts the title as far as lies within him, because he rejects from himself the kingdom of David, whom he does not wish to imitate.

For whoever says that he remains in Christ ought to walk just as he walked, that is, he ought to imitate him.

This psalm may be the voice of the Head or of the Church, or, more suitably, of the Prophet. The Prophet, living among the sins or dangers of those who curse and flatter, neither fears the reviler nor loves the flatterer. He hears everyone’s voice, attends to everyone’s lips, and observes lips and discordant hearts, because one thing resounds on the lips while another is concealed in the inner heart.

He urges them not to speak a false justice but a true justice, and to speak it as it ought to be spoken—that is, to prove by their works what they say with their mouths. And he speaks thus:

If you speak—that is, if you wish truly to speak justice, and if true justice ought to be spoken—you, I say, who are sons of men, that is, who possess reason and therefore ought to will what is good, judge rightly, that is, judge what ought to be judged. Let not only justice of the lips please you, but also justice of deeds; for if you act otherwise than you speak, you speak justice but do not judge justice.

For no one is so perverse and deviant that it is not easy for him to speak about justice, because truth has naturally implanted this in human beings: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.” Nor was anyone permitted to be ignorant of this even before the law was given, so that there would be a basis by which they might be judged and for which the law had not been given.

But lest human beings complain that anything was lacking to them, this was also written on tablets—what they had refused to read in their hearts—so that, through what was set before them externally, they might be compelled to return to their interior selves, as Scripture says: “Return, transgressors, to the heart.”

Who taught you not to wish anyone to approach your wife, or to seize anything from you by force or theft? Was it not your own heart? If, then, you do not live alone among human beings, but rather there is in the human race someone who was born together with you, whatever evil you do not wish to be done to you, do not wish to do to another; and whatever good you wish to be done to you, wish to bestow upon another.

It must be understood that someone can truly speak justice and yet not act according to it as he ought. For example, if someone is asked whether faith or money is more worthy, he can answer what is just and speak truly if he prefers faith, yet he may not do what is fitting. For if he speaks hastily, he will place faith after money. Therefore this explanation is certainly not superfluous.

It may also be understood as an inference, as though the Prophet were saying to those whom he admonishes: “I see that it is easy for all of you to speak about justice; therefore, if you wish truly to speak it, judge rightly.”

For in your heart. Therefore I say, “Judge rightly,” because you act otherwise. For you work iniquities in your heart, that is, you will every evil; and if you do not accomplish it, it does not remain undone because you do not wish to do it, but because you can no longer do it.

At this point blessed Augustine says: “Whatever you wish and cannot do, God counts as done. Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

You work iniquities, I say, in your heart. And is this only in the heart, and not also in frequent action? No: the hands serve their heart and follow it. Evil is conceived, and evil is done; or if it is not done, it is not because we do not wish to do it, but because we cannot.

And this is what he says: Your hands fashion, that is, weave together, sins, adding injustices—that is, evil works—because something similar is placed beneath something similar in a woven work. Concerning such people Isaiah says: “Woe to those who draw their sin like a long rope.”

And that such people weave together iniquities is not attributable to an author outside themselves; they themselves are blameworthy. For they either wholly despise being regenerated in the womb of Mother Church, or, if they are conceived there, they do not await birth but are miscarried.

The womb of the Church is the commandments of truth; her vulva is the perfected formation of these commandments. A child is born in and from the mother’s viscera: in the viscera when it is conceived, and from the viscera when it is brought forth through the vulva.

So a person is conceived in the womb of the Church when he begins to be formed by truth; but if he is perfectly formed, he is, as it were, born through the vulva. If, while he still needs milk, he wishes through pride to be a teacher, he exits from there by miscarriage; this is what heretics do.

There are many, however, who do not wish even to be conceived there. And this is what he says: Sinners—that is, transgressors of both written and natural law—are alienated from the womb, that is, from perfect regeneration.

Some never approached it at all; others, even if they approached it, are nevertheless alienated from perfection because, torn from the womb, they wandered: before they were perfectly formed in the womb, they violently shook the sides of Mother Church by their error and came forth like miscarried children.

And therefore they spoke false things, that is, false things please them. They do not wish even to hear what is true, because they are enraged—that is, they are angry against the preachers of truth—after the likeness of a serpent.

I speak of the serpent, like this serpent, the asp, which does not hear the voice of enchanters and does not hear the voice of the sorcerer who enchants. The Marsi skillfully draw asps from dark caves by chanting; from their venom they know how to make a certain antidote. But because that serpent naturally knows that it is being summoned to death, it places one ear against the earth and blocks the other with its tail, and thus often does not hear the enchanter.

The preachers are enchanters who enchant—that is, preach—for this purpose: to draw a human being out of the darkness of error or misery. They enchant skillfully because they urge people to strive from earthly things toward heavenly things.

Those who, through delight in present things—which is signified by the ear pressed against the earth—and through recollection of past pleasures—which is signified by the tail—harden their hearts so that they do not hear the proclamations of truth and remain in the darkness of their unbelief or error are signified by the asp.

The preachers are also signified by the sorcerer, because just as poison runs through the veins by its force, so their speech breaks through by its force into the inner parts.

God will crush their teeth in their own mouths. They indeed speak false things, but God will crush their teeth—that is, their biting words—in their own mouths, that is, by their own judgment and through their own words.

Hence it is said: “I will catch the wise in their craftiness.” This happened when certain people sought from the Lord a reason for accusing him, asking whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not. If he said that it was lawful, they would call him merciless, as one who made his people tributary; but if he denied it, they would say that it was lawful, because he would be guilty of treason against the emperor.

Yet the Lord caught them in their craftiness, because he refuted them by their own judgment, saying: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” He did the same with the woman caught in adultery and in many other instances.

Here, however, it should be understood in this way: “He will crush their teeth in their own mouths,” that is, through their own words he will make them recognize that their false contradictions are false. This refers to the lesser ones. What follows refers to the greater ones: he will break the molars of the lions, that is, the manifest contradictions of the rulers; that is, the Lord will make them ineffective.

For molars are the larger teeth, and therefore the more serious contradiction of the rulers is signified by molars. This is also understood with respect to their deeds.

They will come to nothing like water running away; he bends his bow until they are weakened.

In this way, I say, the Lord will crush the molars of the lions, because those lions, in their roaring, will come to nothing, that is, they will fail. And this will happen as swiftly as running water comes to nothing.

There is a kind of running water, namely a torrent, which is accustomed to swell with rainwater but soon hinders travelers and quickly subsides. So also the savagery of these people delays the preachers of truth, who are travelers journeying toward their homeland, but only briefly, because it is quickly emptied.

They will come to nothing, I say, and this is because the Lord bends his bow against them, that is, his threats of future condemnation, through the Scriptures and through his preachers. Nor will he cease to bend it until they are weakened in themselves, that is, until they recognize their weakness and confess it.

The one who fell on the road and said, “Lord, what do you wish me to do?” was truly weakened; for then he recognized himself as weak, whereas previously he had thought himself strong.

As wax that melts, they will be taken away. That is, those who have been weakened will be saved; but those who are now shaped in this way will be condemned, because they will be taken away like wax—that is, they will become comparable to wax, which melts when exposed to fire.

For fire, namely the fire of vices or incitements and of every depraved desire, destroys them inwardly. Thus their entire life is nothing other than a kind of flowing away from their Creator.

It must be understood that the fire of Gehenna is twofold: one is the fire of the underworld, which exists now; the other is the future fire into which the devil and his ministers will finally be cast.

A certain hidden fire precedes it, namely the fire of incitements, which is born with us through the transmission of sin. For naturally there is in us a tickling impulse toward sin. Whoever enters this fire will avoid the future one.

It is easily avoided if we always guard ourselves against it, because it is easy to overcome if we are willing to struggle against it. But if a person neglects his enemy and allows it to grow, after it has become stronger it will darken his understanding.

Then he will not see the sun, the one of whom it is said: “We have strayed from the way of truth, and the sun has not risen for us.”

And this is what he says: “Therefore I say that they will be taken away like wax,” because the fire mentioned above has fallen upon them—that is, it has fallen upon them in such a way that it has become superior to them. And when that fire has darkened their understanding, they did not see the sun, that is, they did not recognize the sun, namely, the sun of justice.

They suffered this blindness before your thorns understood the bramble—or, more properly, before the bramble understood your thorns. This means: They are secretly punished even here before they are brought to the manifest torments of wretched pleasures and delights.

The bramble is a plant that at first is quite soft and pleasant, but afterward hardens into the harshest thorns. By it either the flesh is signified, which now delights in sins, or sins themselves, which are presently sweet and pleasant but eventually produce the harshest thorns, that is, they produce eternal torments.

This is how we must understand what he says: “Before the bramble understands your thorns.” It does not mean that the bramble literally understands thorns, but that it will be the cause by which human beings understand them. Another translation renders this wording more appropriately: “Before the bramble produces thorns.”

As the living. The fire, I say, has fallen upon them, and that fire, I say, consumes them in the present; I speak of those who are not truly living but are like the living, because inwardly they are dead.

And it consumes them as in wrath. He says this because this wrath—that is, God’s vengeance against them—is a likeness of that grievous wrath which they will suffer in the future fire of Gehenna. Or it is because, although God seems angry with such people when he punishes them, wrath does not fall upon him, since it is said of him: “You, Lord Sabaoth, judge all things with tranquility.”

The righteous will rejoice. As though he were saying: God permits such people to be taken away like wax and consumed by fire, and this does not happen uselessly for his own people. For when the righteous person sees—that is, understands—vengeance being inflicted upon such people, he will rejoice, not over their condemnation but over his own liberation.

And rightly will he rejoice, because he will wash his hands, that is, cleanse his works, in the blood of the sinner, that is, in consideration of the sinner’s condemnation. Solomon says that when a fool is scourged, the wise person becomes wiser.

And then the human being, that is, the one truly using reason, says: Indeed—that is, truly—not only are eternal rewards reserved for the righteous in the future, but even in the present there is fruit for the righteous: namely, that the righteous person then becomes more righteous.

Indeed—that is, truly—the unjust will not only be condemned in the future, but God is also judging them, that is, condemning them, so that the unjust person becomes more unjust on earth, that is, in the present dwelling place.

## PSALM LVIII

To the end. Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title, when Saul sent and guarded his house in order to kill him.

### Argument

This psalm too is formed with reference to the person of the Maccabees. Likewise Arnobius:

“When the house of your body is ordered to be guarded by the prince of this world, so that you may be seized and killed by the sword of any sin, cry out with all your strength: ‘Deliver me from my enemies, my God.’”

### Explanation

The beginning of the title has often been explained, where Christ’s Passion and his inviolable kingdom are described.

“When Saul sent and guarded his house in order to kill him”: when the chief priests sent and guarded Christ’s tomb, so that they might keep him, as it were, in death, with the door to his resurrection closed.

At the psalm’s first entrance the Lord prays that his enemies may not prevail in harming him. In the second he explains how the Jews are to be converted at the end of the age, and a prayer is uttered for them with wondrous piety. In the third he states what they will do after their conversion and testifies that he rejoices in his saints. These sections are divided by the boundary of the *diapsalm*.

### Commentary
Rescue me from my enemies, my God.

The title is as follows: “For the end, do not corrupt David, in the inscription of the title, when Saul sent and guarded his house in order to kill him.” This psalm has a title derived from a title, like the two preceding psalms, because it is entitled, “Do not corrupt David in the inscription of the title.” There is a certain title written concerning the Lord’s Passion: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews,” in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. When the Jews read this, they were indignant and said to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘He is King,’ but write that he said he was.” [Col. 0786D] For the title—so to speak, it confirms that he himself is our King and that we are his kingdom. In this way, therefore, so far as it lay within them, they corrupted the title and contradicted the King.

But could they, by contradicting him, overthrow his dominion? Certainly not, because the title was not truly corrupted. By killing him, they rather made him King of the nations—the very one whom they killed—because he rose again, was preached to the nations, and thus became King not only of the Jews but also of the nations.

As for what is added, “When Saul sent and guarded his house in order to kill him,” it can be understood both historically of David and spiritually. Historically, Saul did send to David’s house to kill him. And the kingdom of the Jews, signified by Saul, after Christ had died and been placed in the tomb—which tomb was, so to speak, his house—sent men to guard him when it said to Pilate: “Lord, we remember that that deceiver said, ‘After three days I shall rise again.’ Command, therefore, that the tomb be guarded, lest his disciples [Col. 0787A] steal him and say to the people, ‘He has risen from the dead.’”

They therefore sent men to kill him—not insofar as this concerned the Head, who was already dead in that respect in which he could die, but insofar as it concerned his body, which is the Church—that is, so that he might not be raised, so that no one might believe in him, so that the lie of the sleeping guards might prevail, and so that the world might not follow him afterward.

But just as Saul could not bring about David’s death, so neither could the kingdom of the Jews, through its lie, make the lie of the sleeping guards prevail over the testimony of the vigilant apostles. The guards could rightly have been told: “If you slept, you did not know; but if you were awake, why did you not prevent the theft?”

This is the voice of the Head, praying to be freed from those guards through the resurrection and teaching us by his example to pray that we too may be freed. And he speaks in this way:

“God the Father”—God of all by nature, but my God and the God of my people by grace—“rescue me and mine from my visible and invisible enemies.” The enemies of Christ were, and still are, the devil, his angels, and his ministers, who attack his body. This is indicated shortly afterward when he says: “And deliver me from those who rise up against me,” especially against me and mine. For those enemies always rise up against us and seek to mock our weakness through suggestions, temptations, and various deceptions. But if our voice remains watchful and cries out to God, we shall undoubtedly be delivered.

“Rescue me,” I say, God the Father, “and mine, from those who work iniquity”—that is, either from the Jews who worked a particular iniquity, namely, the death of the physician, or rescue mine from all who work any kind of iniquity, lest they be conformed to them. “And save me and mine from men of blood.”

Men of blood were those who shed innocent blood and who cried, “Crucify him, crucify him,” while Pilate, a foreigner, wished to release him after washing his hands. They were also those who gave their descendants the blood of condemnation to drink, saying, “His blood be upon us and upon our children,” and those who raged against his body. For they stoned Stephen and killed many [Col. 0787C] others.

Such men of blood can also be understood among the nations, because the Gentiles too are persecutors of Christ according to the body. But Christ is delivered from all of them—from those of the present, those of the past, and those of the future: first from those of the past, future from those of the future, and present from those of the present.

“For behold, they have seized my soul.” For this reason I ask you, God the Father, to rescue me, because my enemies have seized my soul, in their own estimation, saying: “Pursue and seize him, for there is no one to rescue him”; or they seized my soul simply, that is, they killed me. And they seized my soul when they thought that they had conformed mine to themselves.

“Behold”—so to speak—“they thought they had seized what they seized, and they, the strong, rushed upon me and mine as though we were weak and infirm.” These strong ones may be understood as the devil and his angels, concerning whom it is said: “When a strong man guards his courtyard,” and so forth.

The strong may also be those swollen with earthly prosperity: some with their strength, some with glory, some with wealth. Of them it is said: “He who hoped in me, and so forth.” There is yet another kind of wrongly strong people who must be especially avoided: those who wished to establish their own righteousness and refused to submit to the righteousness of God.

The Lord did not come to call such strong people. He says: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” And again: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” These strong people insulted the apostles, saying: “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” They considered themselves righteous and the others unrighteous.

Likewise, when some whom they had sent to seize him said, “No one has ever spoken as this man speaks,” they replied: “Has any one of the scribes or Pharisees believed in him? Only this crowd, which does not know the law.” It was as if they said: “Only fools believe in him; we, however, are wise, and we shall not believe in him.”

These strong people rushed upon the stone of stumbling, because to them the Lamb appeared to be a kid; and because they killed the Lamb as though he were a kid, they did not deserve to be redeemed by the Lamb.

“Nor is there any iniquity of mine.” They did indeed rush upon me, but nevertheless found no sin in me, because there was neither my iniquity in actual deeds nor my sin in origin. Or: neither my iniquity in deed nor my sin in thought.

This is the reason: I ran, because no enticement of the flesh held me, since I was without iniquity. He became a participant in our weakness, not in our iniquity, so that, by sharing in what was ours, he might erase my iniquity. For this purpose I ran: to direct those who had been distorted toward evil back toward good. I directed them by word and example, insofar as it lay within me. But they could not follow me as I ran, because they did not recognize my footprints.

“Rise to meet me, and see; and you, Lord God of hosts, God of Israel.”

It is as though he said: “Because I ran, therefore, Lord Father, rise to meet me”—that is, come to my aid, so that you may follow me as I run—“and see,” that is, make them see my course. Make them understand that whatever I say or do is just. Let not what is straight in me appear crooked to them, nor what is directed according to the rule of truth distorted.

Or otherwise: above it was said, “His going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his meeting extends to its summit.” The Father is the summit of heaven, because he is higher than all spiritual things, namely, because he is light in himself, while the Son is light from the Father who is light. The Holy Spirit is light proceeding from lights.

Christ, who speaks here, was equal to this summit according to the Word, but this was not seen because of the weakness of the flesh and the affliction of the Passion. Therefore he says: “Lord Father, who seemed to lie prostrate in my Passion and weakness, rise to meet me”—that is, rise to my equality, or make it manifest through the glory of the resurrection and ascension that I am equal to you. “And see”—that is, make people see that, according to his humanity, he could be held, scourged, and killed, yet that he was not merely human but also [Col. 0788C] God and human.

“And you, Lord Father, also God of hosts”—that is, of the heavenly armies—“now regarded as God of Israel,” that is, as God of one nation only, because all the others worship idols, “attend”—that is, turn your attention—to visiting by your grace not only the Jews but all nations, so that what was spoken through the prophet may be fulfilled: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.” Another prophet likewise says: “Stretch out your stakes to the right and to the left, and your tents.” He continues:

“Do not have mercy on all.” I say, you will visit all the nations, but not all those among the Jews or all those among the nations who work iniquity and persist in it. Who would not be terrified by this sentence? Who, examining his conscience, would not tremble at it? For if every iniquity is sin, and none of us is without sin, then, if he will have mercy on none who works iniquity, he will have mercy on none of us.

But this was not said without reason. No iniquity, great or small, will remain unpunished. It will either be punished by a repentant person or by God the Judge. If you do not want him himself to punish you, go before his face in psalms and confession—that is, by confessing and doing good—as the psalmist says: “Let us go before his face,” and so forth. Then he will find you working iniquity and will have mercy on you in this way.

For, as far as the matter conceived by them is concerned, few will be converted.
