Or otherwise: there is a particular outstanding iniquity whose practitioners he will not pity—namely, when people defend their sin in such a way that even anyone who is misguided and perverse judges it to be abominable. For example, they attribute adultery to the highest good, that is, to God; and whatever good they possess they ascribe to themselves, while whatever evil they possess they attribute to God, saying: “If God did not want us to be such, we would not be so.” They also accuse fate, the stars, and similar things, proceeding by a circuitous route to accuse God, when they could take the direct route to appease God. Thus the sinner is excused and the Creator blamed.

“They will return toward evening.” This can be understood both of the Jews and of the nations. For now, however, let us first discuss the Jews and afterward, in order, the nations. The outstanding iniquity mentioned above pertains especially to the Jews who still defend themselves concerning the death of the physician.

The passage can be joined in this way: “I say, do not have mercy on the Jews who defend their iniquity and persist in it. But have mercy on some who neither persist nor defend themselves, so that they may be converted.” And so it will be, because “they will return toward evening,” that is, in a late conversion. They ought to have been converted in the morning, that is, while the physician was present. But because they were not converted, since they did not consider the physician necessary for themselves and crucified him, they will be converted toward evening, after his resurrection and ascension. And this is what happened.

For when they saw uneducated men—that is, the apostles—performing such great miracles [Col. 0789B] and speaking such marvelous things after the sending of the Holy Spirit, some of those who had crucified Christ, recognizing their sin, came to the apostles and said: “What shall we do, brothers?” Peter answered and said: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.”

It was as though he said to them: “Drink with confidence the blood you shed in your fury.” This should first be understood of those who were converted.

“Let them be converted,” I say, “and, once converted, let them hunger”—that is, let them be eager for the word and grace of God—“being like dogs,” that is, recognizing that they need a physician, like dogs, that is, like the unclean and idolatrous Gentiles. For they will recognize that they have not been justified either by their own righteousness or by the law, because in the law they did not understand Christ, who is the light of the law and the prophets.

And these converts, so that they too may convert others, “will go around the city,” that is, the correction of the faithful, or even the multitude of the entire human race, which is called a city because of the Jews scattered everywhere.

And behold—so to speak—why will they go around? For this reason: “They will speak,” that is, they will preach, “in their mouth,” in a hungry mouth, that is, with the steadfastness and boldness appropriate to those whose mouth hungers for the word of God. “And in their lips there will be a sword,” concerning which it is said: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of the Lord.”

I speak of those who say this, because, as far as their desire is concerned, few will be converted. “Lord, we labor in vain, for there is no one who believes our report. For who has heard us with an ear ready to hear?” No one, so to speak, has heard us.

“And you, Lord, will laugh at them.” It is as though he said: “They will speak in this way, considering it impossible for anyone to be converted; yet you, Lord, will laugh at them”—that is, you will make them worthy of ridicule, because you will easily accomplish what they considered impossible.

“For you will bring all nations to nothing,” that is, some from every nation, insofar as they were nations, that is, living like Gentiles. “Turn the ungodly, and they will be no more.” And this, so to speak, you will do through my strength—that is, through the strength of mine—because you will make mine steadfast in preaching. Their strength, because I am in them, is mine.

I speak of the strength that they will preserve for me, because they will not refer it to themselves, as the wrongly strong mentioned above did; rather, they will refer it to you, ascribing it to you, because whatever good they possess, whether in body or soul, they possess from you.

For even if the soul understands and distinguishes, it does not possess this from itself. Rather, it is a certain region of unchangeable truth; when it approaches that truth, it is strengthened and enlightened, but when it withdraws from it, it is darkened, obscured, and weakened.

He continues:

“For you are God, my upholder.” Rightly will I refer my strength to you, because you are God, my upholder and that of mine. You received me, a human being, through your Word, from the mass of those destined to perish; and you also received mine from the midst of evils.

For I know from where I came, from where you received me, and how much you have forgiven me. Therefore you are rightly my God and the God of mine: rightly do I love, worship, and praise you freely. And he turns to us so that we too may make him our God.

It is as though he said: “I say that you are my God because his mercy will now and always go before mine.” For neither I nor mine brought anything on account of which he would have mercy on us and justify us. His mercy alone, just as it went before me so that I might exist, will also go before me so that I might be good.

“God shows me.” I also say “my God” for this reason: God, having become mine in me and mine, shows me above my enemies—that is, me gathered while they were rejected and chosen while they were repulsed—so that I might recognize the riches of his grace through vessels of wrath in vessels of mercy.

It is as though he said: “Let the vessel of wrath compare itself with the vessels of mercy, the gathered with the rejected, the chosen with the reprobate, and let it recognize the riches of his grace, which he has displayed through vessels of wrath in vessels of mercy.” For the perfection of the good is recognized through the persecution of the wicked.

In this passage he understands the enemies as the Jews. And although, he says, I called them enemies, nevertheless, Lord, “do not kill them”—that is, do not permit them to be killed bodily in such a way that they pass over into the rites of the nations.

Although they were scattered by Titus and Vespasian, they did not lose their rite, because they are still circumcised, sacrifice the lamb, and perform many similar things. Therefore I say: “Do not kill them bodily, lest that people”—that is, the Jews, formerly one people but now, by the ordering of God, a people divided—“at some time”—that is, ever—“forget me,” that is, my law. Rather, let them always preserve its memory, even if not in their way of life.

And they are, so to speak, the book-carriers of my people, so that my people may have among them the means by which to convict their other enemies.

Or otherwise: “Do not kill them bodily, lest at some time those who are the grafted wild olive forget that people which was formerly mine.” Let them always pay attention to the fact that the natural branches were broken off, and thus not become proud, but fear, knowing that if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare the wild olive.

[Col. 0790C] “Scatter them.” Do not kill them, I say, but do to them what they deserve: “scatter them among all nations by your power, Lord,” because they presumed upon their own power; and “bring them down from the glory of their place and nation.”

You, I say, are “my protector,” that is, the protector of mine, in that you will take power away from those persecutors. And because you are a protector, therefore, Lord, “bring down the iniquity of their mouth, and bring down the word of their lips.”

Understand “the iniquity” as what they said: “We have no king but Caesar”; and “the words of their lips” as: “He is guilty of death,” and similar statements. God the Father brought all this down, that is, falsified it, when he raised Christ and made him King not only of the Jews but also of the nations.

He continues:

“And let them be seized in their pride.” As if he said: “I say that you should scatter them and bring them down, yet let some of them be seized in their pride”—that is, in the fact that they proudly rose up against the physician and killed him. Let them be seized, that is, recognize that no result will follow from this and that nothing remains for them except sin; and thus let them be humbled and confess their sin.

And let them be seized “because of the curse”—that is, because of the death of Christ, whom they themselves regarded as accursed and under a curse—and let them be seized because of the lie, that is, because through the lie of the guards they attempted to destroy the life of the one who had risen.

And truly they will be seized, because “in consummation,” that is, in perfection, they will be announced to others. For just as pride previously prevented them from being brought to completion, so humility will enable them to be perfected. “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more.”

Therefore their consummation will be announced to others, so that no one may despair concerning his own sin, since so great a sin was forgiven in these people.

Their consummation will be announced, I say, “in consummation and in consummation,” because “in the wrath of consummation”—that is, through wrath, namely, through the vengeance proceeding from God’s wrath—their consummation will consist in this: they will attend to their dispersion and the other things they suffer as consequences of their sin, and they will confess that sin.

They will be announced “in consummation,” which consummation will arise from the curse and the lie—that is, because they will attend to how great a sin that curse and lie were; and the more serious they recognize it to have been, the more grievously they will repent.

This consummation will also be “in wrath,” that is, through wrath, because they will attend to the wrath to come; and, in order to avoid it, they will be brought to completion. Once completed, they will no longer be what they previously were. “Turn the ungodly, and they will be no more.”

Then they will truly know—that is, recognize—“that God will rule over Jacob,” that is, over the Jews, “and over the ends of the earth,” that is, over the Gentiles. They will understand that Jacob cannot be saved through his own righteousness and that the physician is necessary both for him and for the nations.

And he gives the reason why he added the Gentiles: “And the nations will be converted toward evening,” and so forth.

Let us now return to the first occurrence of “They will return,” and let us read of the Gentiles what we have read up to this point concerning the Jews. The continuation will be as follows:

“Truly, the Lord Father will visit the nations, because the Gentiles will be converted toward evening,” that is, late. For just as Christ was principally sent to those of the house of Israel, so the apostles too were sent to them. But after they were rejected by them, the apostles turned to the conversion of the nations; therefore he says, “Toward evening they will be converted.”

For if the Jews were converted toward evening immediately at the first preaching of the apostles, much more can the Gentiles, who were converted much later, be said to have been converted toward evening.

“Let them be converted,” I say, “and, once converted, let them hunger,” that is, let them have the desire to convert others and incorporate them into themselves, as hungry dogs desire food. And because they will be so eager, they too, like those first converted from the Jews, will go around the city and speak the word of preaching in their mouth, that is, in a hungry and famished mouth.

“And in their lips there will be a sword,” that is, the word of God, by which some will be slain for faith and others for death: believers for life, unbelievers for death.

He then speaks at length about those who are slain for death, as if he said: “Truly, a deadly sword was in their lips, for who heard them with an ear ready to hear?” No one, that is, insofar as their desire was concerned.

“And you, Lord, will finally laugh at them,” that is, make them objects of ridicule, because they will not hear with an ear ready to hear, since you will bring all nations—that is, those living like Gentiles—to nothing.

For they will truly be brought to nothing, since their resurrection will not be unto glory but unto shame, and they will lack true being. And that you will bring all nations to nothing, you do through my strength and that of mine—that is, in comparison with mine, who will be strong, that is, steadfast in faith and virtues.

For the saints will judge the nations, not by words but by comparison, as it is said elsewhere.

I speak of the strength that I will preserve in myself and mine, referred not to you but to me.

The rest does not change up to “Do not kill them.” In this reading too the passage is joined in the same way as in the preceding one:

“Although they are my enemies, you, Lord, do not kill them.” He specifies what kind of killing he means: “Do not permit those people”—namely, the Gentiles—“at some time,” that is, when I am announced to them, “to forget my people,” that is, my law.

For the true killing of the soul is to forget one’s God. And he says “to forget” for this reason: every human being naturally possesses knowledge of God.

“Scatter them.” It is as though he said: “And so that they may not forget me, therefore, Lord, first scatter those who presume upon their own power in the thing in which they are to be scattered, namely, in evil, by your power; and bring down through humility those who were previously raised up through pride.”

You, I say, are in this “my protector,” that is, the protector of mine, so that they may not be conformed to such people. And because you are a protector, therefore, Lord, “bring down the iniquity of their mouth, the word of their lips”—that is, make their contradiction of the truth cease.

“And let those Gentiles be seized in their pride,” that is, let them recognize that they sinned because they presumed upon the power of their intellect and the freedom of their will.

“And let them be seized because of the curse,” namely, because they regarded the Christian name as accursed; “and because of the lie,” namely, because they placed the creature before the Creator, affirming that the creature was God, in which they lied.

And truly they will be seized, because “in consummation they will be announced.” The Gentiles too, as was previously said of the Jews, will be in “the wrath of consummation,” that is, in the consummation of the future judgment, through which they will be brought to completion and will no longer be what they previously were.

Then they will know—that is, understand—“that God will rule over Jacob,” namely, over the Jews, so many of whom were transgressors and whom they seemed entirely to have rejected, “as well as over the ends of the earth,” that is, over the Gentiles.

And truly he will rule over Jacob, because “a remnant from Jacob will be saved.” For the Jews will be converted toward evening, namely, in the time of Antichrist; and, once converted, they will hunger like dogs, that is, they will be so eager to convert others as hungry dogs are for food. Therefore they will go around the city.

It should be known that “They will return,” both this occurrence and the first, can be varied in three ways: first, so that the first “They will return” is understood of the Jews—those first converted and those to be converted at the end—and this one of the Gentiles; or that the first refers to the Jews converted earlier, and this one to those to be converted at the end; or that the first is understood of the Gentiles and this one of the Jews to be converted at the end.

“They will be scattered.” He shows for what purpose the Jews to be converted at the end—or, according to the preceding interpretation, the converted Gentiles—will go around the city, saying:

“For they will be scattered here and there to eat,” that is, to incorporate others into themselves. But if they are not satisfied by the multitude of believers, wearied by transgressors, they will murmur. In this interpretation, the Jews at the end will murmur, just as their fathers previously murmured in the desert. Or the Gentiles will murmur, just as the Jews first converted also murmured.

“But I will sing.” They will indeed murmur, but I will satisfy them, because I will sing of my strength in them—that is, I will make the steadfastness given by you praiseworthy in them. For they will be steadfast through God; all who see this will praise their steadfastness and strive to conform themselves to them.

“And when morning comes”—namely, at the future judgment, when the true sun will shine—“I will rejoice,” that is, I will joyfully proclaim your mercy to them. For their rewards will declare how great a mercy I have bestowed upon them.

Or, when morning has dawned in the present life among those who will be converted through them, I will exalt your mercy, because through this it will become apparent that you have dealt mercifully with them.

“For you have become my protector and my refuge on the day of my tribulation.” Therefore I shall rightly sing of your strength and exalt your mercy, because you have become my protector and that of mine, as was said above; and you are my refuge and that of mine against every trouble, “on the day of my tribulation,” that is, in the present life, where this is necessary, since tribulations and persecutions threaten.

And you are my helper in bringing mine to completion, namely, in accomplishing what I shall do. Therefore I will sing psalms to you by doing good, because you are my protecting God. And therefore you are my God, that is, therefore I make you my God. And rightly so, because you are my mercy, that is, whatever good I am, I am through you.

# PSALM LIX

“For the end, for those who will be changed, in the inscription of the title, to David himself, for instruction, when he set fire to Mesopotamia of Syria and Zobah, and Joab returned and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.”

## ARGUMENT

On the occasion of his victory he also foretells the triumphs of the Maccabees. Alternatively, it is the voice of the apostles when Christ suffered.

## EXPLANATION

“For the end” he speaks of Christ the Savior, for those who will be changed in the way in which the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord.” How they can be changed toward this end is explained in what follows.

“In the inscription of the title, David, for instruction.” The inscription of the title signifies Jesus Christ as King. Therefore let them be changed in such a way that, abandoning the devil, they submit their necks to Christ the King.

He added “for instruction,” namely, Christian instruction, because it is not enough to believe Christ to be King if his teaching is not also observed.

“When he set fire to Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah.” These victories indicate Christ’s triumph over the nations. By setting them aflame with the fire of his love, he rescued them from the kingdom of the ancient enemy, whom Hadadezer signifies, and made them tributary to his faith.

For Syria, which is called *Aram* in Hebrew and means “elevated,” signifies the pride of the Gentiles. He set fire to the two Syrian peoples, correcting alike the deeds and words of the Gentiles, so that they might pay the tribute of their faith and works to the one true King.

“And he returned Joab.” And he struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand. The Valley of Salt, which is called *Gemela* in Hebrew, signifies weak and earthly wisdom, with which both the philosophy of the Gentiles and the obstinacy of the Jews are armed against Christ. But both are struck when Joab, whose name is interpreted as “Father,” that is, a teacher of the faith who presses forward diligently, returns.

Thus *Gemela*, because it is the region of the Idumeans, can indicate the flavor of Gentile knowledge. But it is better understood of the Jews who will believe at the end of the world, either because of the twelve thousand, the number of Israel’s triumph, or because of the name Edom, which often signifies the Jews. Hence, under his person, it is said concerning them: “And the elder shall serve the younger.”

That people, therefore, changed from its ancient errors to the faith, first petitions that after the affliction it endured in making satisfaction it may be restored through the renewal of blessing. Second, after an intervening *diapsalm*, it asks that, following the tribulations it has suffered, it may be led by the Lord into a strongly fortified city, requesting that help be granted to it in its tribulation—a thing that is shown to be possible for the Lord alone.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0793C] “God, you have rejected and destroyed us; you have been angry, and you have had mercy on us.”

The title is: “For the end, for those who will be changed, in the inscription of the title, to David himself, for instruction, when he set fire to Mesopotamia of Syria and Zobah, and Joab returned and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.”

In this psalm, or in the title of this psalm, certain victories of David are recounted: victories that he achieved when, after the death of Saul, his persecutor, he came to the throne, defeating his enemies and making them tributary.

For he was king even before his persecution, because he had been anointed in his father’s house, but he was known only to God. Later, when his kingdom was manifest and visibly received, he defeated the nations of which the title speaks.

But just as the prophetic Spirit customarily departs somewhat in the titles of the psalms from the expression of events that occurred, and adds something different from what is found in the history, so that by this it may teach that the figure is to be pursued more than the allegory—as was said above in a certain title, where David is said to have changed his appearance before Abimelech, although the history says rather that he changed it before Achish, king of Gath—so in this title something is also added, by which we are warned of another matter.

For where David’s mighty deeds are recounted, nothing is recorded as having been set on fire; yet this is proposed most prominently in the present title. Let us therefore pursue the allegory here rather than the history.

These words refer “to the end,” that is, to Christ, through whom all our labor will come to an end. They are attributed to those whose voice this is: those who have partly been changed, are being changed, and from day to day will be changed—not by a change deserving blame but by one deserving praise.

For there are two changes, one praiseworthy and one blameworthy. Adam’s change was blameworthy: from life to death, from righteousness to unrighteousness, and from the delights of paradise to the labor of exile.

The change discussed here, however, is praiseworthy, and the Apostle also commends it when he says: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord.”

They are changed, I say, “in the inscription of the title,” that is, through this: a title is inscribed for them confirming both that they are his kingdom and that he himself is their King. For they have already passed from the kingdom of the devil into the kingdom of Christ, from the power of darkness into the kingdom of light.

And they are changed “to David himself, for instruction,” that is, so that they may be taught a new life—not to live any longer for themselves, but for him who died for all.

This change occurred when that David “set fire to Mesopotamia of Syria,” and so forth. This change was brought about by fire and by the sword, by that David who, as the Gospel testifies, brought fire and the sword into the world.

By fire, indeed, not visible fire, but the love of charity. This is the fire of which he himself says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?”

With this fire he set fire to Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah. Mesopotamia is a part of Syria, and its name means “elevated calling.” Syria means “sublime.” These signify those called from the Jews, who had previously been elevated by God through the worship of the one God and through the laws and prophets; but because they presumed upon themselves in these things, they were also proud, or “sublime.”

Zobah is interpreted as “vain antiquity.” Through it idolaters from the nations are signified, because nothing is more vain in antiquity than to place the creature before the Creator and to worship the creature in the place of the Creator.

Nevertheless, because some among them, especially on account of the nobility of their intellect and the freedom of their will, were proud—Plato and other philosophers, for example—they too were “Syria,” that is, sublime.

But the Lord usefully set fire to both groups with the fire of love for God and neighbor, and thus changed them.

Some say that by “Mesopotamia of Syria” those called both from the nations and from the Jews are understood: elevated through calling, and so elevated that they became sublime through hope. By “Syria of Zobah,” however, they understand those especially devoted to vain antiquity, who became sublime in hope only through their calling.

He continues:

“And he returned Joab.” Joab is interpreted as “father” or “enemy.” In this change the one of whom it is said, “You are of your father the devil,” was converted. He is also the ancient enemy of the human race, because the ruler of this world was cast out.

Or “the enemy was converted” when anyone who had been an enemy became a friend, anyone impious became pious, and anyone unbelieving became faithful.

“And he struck Edom.” Up to this point he has discussed the change brought about by fire. Now he discusses the change brought about by the sword—not by iron, but by the word of preaching.

Edom is interpreted as “earthly.” For this we must give great thanks to God: he has deemed the word of preaching worthy to strike the old man in us, so that we might put on the new. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, so let us bear the image of the heavenly.

In the Valley of Salt Pits. Salt pits are hollows in which seawater, when the tide ebbs, is retained for the production of salt. This may be understood in two ways: either, “He struck Edom,” which was previously placed in the Valley of Salt Pits, that is, [Col. 0794D] in the depression of bitterness. For a valley is a depressed place, and salt is understood to contain a certain bitterness. By both of these, the pilgrimage away from the true homeland is signified, a pilgrimage subject to the various bitterness of vices.

Or, “He struck Edom so that it might be in the Valley of Salt Pits,” that is, in a humbling that possesses savor. For a valley signifies humility, and salt has flavor. There is, however, a savory humility and an insipid humility. If someone is humbled for earthly things—that is, is afflicted and distressed, as merchants commonly are—that humility is insipid. But if someone labors and is afflicted for eternal things, he is wisely humbled.

“He struck Edom,” I say, “and those struck numbered twelve thousand.” The number one thousand is a perfect number and signifies perfection in those transformed by this striking. Twelve, however, which is composed of four multiplied three times by itself, signifies those soldiers—that is, the twelve apostles and their successors—through whom this striking was accomplished. Since three and four, joined simply together, constitute seven, this signifies the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, through which the sword—that is, the word of preaching—was wielded in this striking. By the four, it is shown that this took place in the four regions of the world; by the three, that it took place especially through knowledge of the Holy Trinity.

Now let us come to the psalm. It is the voice of those salutarily struck and profitably following David, praying that, whatever may happen concerning temporal salvation, they may obtain eternal salvation, and exhorting us to pray for the same thing, saying:

God the Father—or God the Word, or God the Trinity—you expelled us from the delight of paradise through the transgression of your law and placed us badly in the valley of error. By a certain force you drove us back from our error, and you destroyed us, badly constructed in our old hostility, with a good destruction, so that you might lead us forth into newness of life, that is, into new charity and humility. You were angry with our old age and, by showing us mercy, granted us newness.

[Col. 0795B] You have shaken the earth and troubled it; heal its fractures, for it has been shaken. In this way, I say, you destroyed us, because you shook the earth—that is, our earthliness—when the word of preaching was heard. You troubled it inwardly through the consciousness of sins, and outwardly even to bodily affliction through repentance. Therefore heal in reality, just as you have already healed in hope, its fractures—that is, the miseries and tribulations by which our earthliness is continually crushed within and without. Hence the Apostle says: “Although our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.”

And you ought to heal it because it has deserved this; that is what he says when he adds, “for it has been shaken.” The Gospel resounds, the word of preaching resounds; whoever is not shaken—that is, is not pierced by the goads of conscience and the goads of repentance; whoever does not beat his breast, shed tears, or pour forth prayers—is unworthy to be healed. For the first thing is that we cleanse our sins through the compunction of conscience and worthy satisfaction, [Col. 0795C] and then that we have patience against temptations. For Solomon says: “My son, when you approach discipline, stand in fear and trembling, and prepare your heart for temptations.” And Peter says: “It is necessary that judgment begin from the house of God. But if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who have not believed the Gospel? If the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” And this is what he says:

You have shown your people hard things; you have given us wine of compunction to drink. This follows in this way: I say, “Heal its fractures,” because this is necessary. For you yourself have shown your people—now your people, that is—who have been salutarily devastated by fire and sword, that hard things must be endured here. We ought to give great thanks to God, who wills that we suffer hard and harsh things in the present, so that in the future they may be soft and pleasant.

You have shown us hard things, I say, and you did this by giving us wine of compunction to drink—that is, by making the tribulation of compunction for us like a pleasant drink. Thus you gave your people, who fear you with chaste fear, a sign, that is, a lesson: [Col. 0795D] by this you correct every son whom you receive, so that through these tribulations they may flee from the face of the bow—that is, from the presence of the future judgment. And let them flee in such a way that your beloved may be completely freed from it—you, that is, who correct them here as an example of just judgment.

For whoever rejoices here in tribulations and says with the Apostle, “Not only do we suffer, but we also glory in those tribulations,” will escape that bow. But if someone prefers to take pleasure here rather than be afflicted, he will not escape the bow. For those to whom God postpones it now, he will not postpone it in the future, and the reverse is also true. Just as, in a bow, the farther the string is drawn backward, the more forcefully the front is struck, so the longer God postpones judgment for the wicked, the more grievously it will finally overtake them.

When he says, “from the face of the bow,” that is, from the presence of the bow, he says this because the time is short, and nothing that has an end should be considered long-lasting. By this he warns us to be more cautious.

You have given those who fear you a sign, I say, so that they may flee [Col. 0796A] from the face of the bow, so that your beloved may be delivered. Save me by your right hand. And therefore, Lord, cut, burn, scourge; do with me in the present whatever seems good to you, and save me by your right hand. It is as though he said: I do not ask you for any bodily or temporal salvation; concerning that, let what pleases you be done. Rather, I ask that in the future I not be found among the goats on the left, but among the lambs on the right. And in this hear me.

He says “Hear me” with such confidence because holy men often ask for bodily deliverance but are not heard. This is not to their folly, because they are not heard according to their will but according to their benefit. Whenever, however, they ask for eternal salvation, God cannot fail to hear them.

God has spoken in his holy one: “I will rejoice and divide Shechem, and I will measure out the Valley of Tents.” Truly I shall be saved by the right hand. For God the Father has spoken—that is, he has already promised me that salvation—in his holy one, that is, in the one in whom he could not deceive. [Col. 0796B] For “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.” I say that he promised it, if not in words, then in its effect: namely, because he raised him from the dead, caused us to rise in him, and made us sit at the right hand of his majesty in the heights.

What follows may be either the voice of Christ, in whom God the Father spoke, saying, “I will rejoice and divide,” and so forth; or the voice of the Church, as though it said: Since God the Father has spoken in this way, “Therefore I will rejoice and divide,” that is, I will joyfully divide Shechem.

Shechem properly denotes the place where, when Jacob was returning to his homeland, his wife Rachel hid the idols that she had stolen from her father Laban. By Shechem the Gentiles are signified, among whom idols were hidden, because they preserved and worshiped them. But since not all of them possess faith, either the Church or Christ divides them, taking some and leaving others.

Or otherwise: Shechem is interpreted as “shoulder,” and the Church divides this shoulder. It takes up those who willingly submit to the yoke of Christ, a yoke that does not depress but raises them; but those who prefer to burden themselves with earthly things—which, as blessed Gregory says, are a weight, not a support—it leaves behind.

And I will measure out—that is, divide—the Valley of Tents. When Jacob was returning from his father-in-law Laban, he placed his tents in the valley of Syria, where his sheep rested. Hence the place received its name, being called the Valley of Jacob’s Tents. By the tents, legal institutions are signified, established for a time; by the sheep, the Jews, who took delight and rested in them. The Church divides them, taking some and leaving others.

Or otherwise: By the valley, the humble are signified; by the tents, ecclesiastical precepts, in which some serve humbly, while others do not serve humbly, because they fulfill the precepts but then presume upon them and become proud. According to this interpretation, the text is explained as follows: “I will divide,” that is, I will take as my portion the Valley of Tents—that is, those who serve humbly in ecclesiastical precepts; but I will reject those who do not serve humbly.

[Col. 0796D] Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine, and Ephraim is the strength of my head. Truly I will divide Shechem and the Valley of Tents, because I will take some. For Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine.

Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” A heap grows from the lowest things upward into one. By this are signified those who grow from virtue to virtue until they arrive at unity—that is, until they see the God of gods in Zion—and who accumulate within themselves so great a testimony to Christ that they struggle even to the shedding of blood, that is, become martyrs. For “martyr” is interpreted as “witness.”

Manasseh, however, is interpreted as “forgetfulness.” By this are understood those who, with the Apostle, forget what lies behind and stretch forward toward what lies ahead—that is, toward future and eternal things. Or by Manasseh are understood those who disregard and forget whatever shameful and disgraceful things they have suffered for Christ. Hence through Isaiah it is said to the Church: “Forget the disgrace of your widowhood.” For the Church was like a widow [Col. 0797A] while the Christian name remained in disgrace.

It follows:

Ephraim is the strength of my head. Ephraim is interpreted as “fruitfulness.” By this are understood those who bear fruit in good works, whom the Church calls the strength of its head—that is, of Christ, by resemblance. For just as a good pillow for a sick head is a kind of strength, that is, a refreshment, so those who act well are Christ’s strength, because others, seeing their good works, glorify God.

But those in whom foxes have their dens and the birds of heaven their nests are not his strength but his weakness, because he has no place in them where he may rest his head.

Or otherwise: By Ephraim is understood that fruitfulness which came forth from the grain that died on the cross and was justified in the resurrection—that is, the harvest of believers throughout the world. Of it was said: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” This harvest is the strength of the head—that is, the increase and exaltation of Christ, who is the head of the Church. For that very weakness, namely the death of Christ, was the highest strength, because “what is weak in God is stronger than all human beings.”

And it should be understood that, insofar as this is the voice of Christ, it will be said: “Ephraim is the strength of my head,” since I am the head.

Judah is my king; Moab is the pot of my hope. Ephraim is indeed my strength, and Judah—that is, the one who descended from the tribe of Judah, to whom it was said figuratively, “Your brothers shall bless you”—is my king. He, I say, rules me, because he suffered first and was truly obedient.

And because I have such a king, Moab is the pot of my hope; that is, for this reason I also hope to be refreshed from those who abuse the law. For Moab was born from a grandfather and a sister contrary to the law, and therefore Moab is interpreted as “one who abuses the law.”

Or otherwise: Because I have such a king, I shall not fear iniquity boiling over. Rather, Moab, being the pot of iniquity, is for me a pot of hope, because through it I hope rather to advance than to decline. Just as the works of those who use the law well are good, so the works of those who use the law badly are evil. And these people persecute the Church of God. Hence it was said through Ezekiel: “I saw a pot boiling from the north.”

The boiling pot from the north is boiling iniquity, kindled by the north, which said: “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High.” It is as though he said: If that pot of iniquity boils, let the ardor of charity blaze in opposition to it. He will not be able to accomplish as much by persecuting as I shall be able to accomplish by loving and suffering.

And furthermore I will extend my sandal—that is, my Gospel, which shoes and protects the interior feet, namely the affections, just as a sandal protects the exterior feet—as far as Idumea, that is, as far as the most despairing.

Idumea is indeed interpreted as “earthly pleasure.” By it are signified those who pursue earthly things and cling to them most closely. And I will extend it so far that even foreigners—that is, the *allophyli*—will be subjected to me, namely so that they will at least fear me, although they do not wish to advance through me. For the wicked are often subject to the good not through love but through fear.

And it should be understood that, if the head is speaking here, we shall alter a few things from what was said above. It is as though he said: Judah is my king—that is, those who truly confess and govern themselves well are my kings, that is, kings over my people, governing them by word and example, like Peter, Paul, and others of this kind.

And therefore Moab is the pot of my hope: I hope also to be refreshed from those who abuse the law, that is, from converted transgressors. This is because I will extend my sandal—that is, I will make known the mystery of my incarnation—as far as Idumea, that is, as far as those most devoted to earthly things; and I will extend it so far that even foreigners, that is, the *allophyli*, will be subjected to me, not through love but through fear.

Who will lead me into the fortified city? Who will lead me as far as Idumea? Some wish this passage in both readings to be only the voice of the body. But nothing prevents it from also being the voice of the head, with respect to the body, to the very end. Thus it follows:

“I will extend my sandal,” I say, even into Idumea. But who will lead me—or the head, or the Church—into the fortified city, that is, into a nation so widespread and great? For the multitude of the people is the city’s fortification. Who, I say, will lead me as far as the Idumeans, devoted to earthly things and utterly despairing?

Or otherwise: Who in the future will lead me into the fortified city, that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem, which is a fortified city, to which no enemy approaches and from which no citizen departs? And who in the present will lead me as far as Idumea?

Is it not you, God, who have rejected us, and will you not go forth, O God, with our armies? Give us help in tribulation, for human salvation is vain. Through God we shall act valiantly, and he himself will bring those who trouble us to nothing.

That is, you appear to have rejected and outwardly despised us. And therefore I say, “You have rejected us,” because you are the God who went forth with the fathers, because you were present to them through manifest signs, so that they might understand that you were present. But you will not go forth in our strengths, [Col. 0798B] that is, outwardly in our armies, so that we may conquer bodily. Rather, you console and strengthen us inwardly and make the heavenly homeland lovable and the earthly homeland contemptible.

And because you are with us inwardly, although you have rejected us outwardly, therefore, Lord, give us inward help that comes from tribulation—that is, make the tribulation which we suffer outwardly become a cause of advancement, not decline, inwardly. I say this because human salvation outwardly is vain and useless. Truly he will grant what I ask, because through you, God, we shall act valiantly inwardly; that is, we shall be steadfast and victorious.

For blessed Laurence truly conquered when he said: “I am roasted; turn me over and eat.” And he turns toward us for our exhortation, as though saying: I have certainty of this matter because God himself will bring those who trouble us to nothing, both here and in the future.

Behold, by God’s grace they have been reduced to nothing, and the enemies of the Church are nowhere seen, unless perhaps drunkards persecute it with cups, just as formerly the furious persecuted it with stones. By “drunkards” understand either those intoxicated by this sweet life or those drunk with wine. They persecute the Church, as it were, with cups, because they often attack and oppose holy men.

## PSALM LX

**To the end. In hymns. Of David.**

### Argument

This psalm is composed in the person of the people situated in Babylon and imploring their freedom, while nevertheless nourishing hope of returning to their homeland.

### Explanation

“In hymns” is Greek and is interpreted as “in praises,” because the whole psalm will resound with proclamations of Christ. In the first part, the faithful people, from the ends of the earth, implore that their prayer be heard, so that, persevering in the holy Church, they may be protected under the shelter of its wings. In the second part, they give thanks because he has given his inheritance to the righteous and consecrated his name to eternal glory; for this reason they promise that they will continually render praises to the Lord.

### Commentary

Hear, O God, my supplication; attend to my prayer. The title is: “To the end. In hymns. A psalm of David himself.” What “to the end” means has often been explained. “In hymns” has been added so that, whether we exult and rejoice or are afflicted and distressed, he may be praised who instructs human beings in tribulations and consoles them in prosperity.

Here one person speaks, not in isolation, but through his members. He speaks as one, although he is not one individual; rather, unity speaks as one. For all of us are one human being in Christ. The head of this human being is in heaven, while the members labor on earth. And see what those who labor say.

It is the voice of the Church praying for steadfastness in tribulation and persecution, so that through these things it may be able to reach the same end to which its head has come. It speaks as follows:

God the Father, hear my supplication, made for my sins, and attend—that is, direct your attention—to my prayer for perseverance at the ends of the earth.

From the ends of the earth I cried to you when my heart was in distress; you exalted me upon a rock. I say this so that you may hear me, because I cried to you from the ends of the earth.

This may be understood simply, as though he said, “From every part of the earth.” Or it may be understood as a cause, as though he said: I cried not to gold, not to silver, but first to you from the ends of the earth—that is, through those who are the ends of the earth, because they have brought all earthliness to an end in themselves.

Who is this one who cries from the ends of the earth? It is because Christ is one, whose possession and inheritance is that of which it was said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth.” This is the body of Christ; this is Christ’s inheritance, which cries from the ends of the earth.

Why does it cry? He says: “When my heart was in distress.” While we are on pilgrimage, it is necessary that we suffer temptations and tribulations, but our temptation has a beneficial outcome. No one comes to know himself except by being tempted, and no one will be crowned unless he has conquered. He cannot conquer unless he has struggled, nor can he struggle if he has no enemy who tempts him.

I cried to you, I say, when my heart was in distress, but only so that it might not be overcome, because you exalted me upon a rock so that I would not be overcome. The rock, as the Apostle says, was Christ, who exalted us because he first chose, for our sake and from what was ours, to be seized, held, scourged, and struck, so that he might give us an example of living.

From me he took weakness for himself; from him I receive strength. From me he took disgrace for himself; from him I receive glory. From me he took death for himself; from him I receive life. From me he took humiliation for himself; from him I receive exaltation.

You have led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength in the presence of the enemy. You exalted me, I say, and led me from strength to strength. You led me, I say, because you are my leader; and through you, because you are the way to yourself, since you are my homeland.

And truly you have led me, because you have become my hope in Christ. Christ is our hope in this respect: he suffered, died, was buried, and rose again. In him we see both our labor and our reward—our labor in his passion, our reward in his resurrection—because we have two lives: one in which we are now, and another which we hope for.

If we patiently endure the life in which we now are, we shall reach the one we hope for. I did not know anything except that a human being is born and dies; I did not know that he could rise again and live eternally. He received what I knew and showed me what I did not know, namely the resurrection. Thus he became my hope and is for me a tower of strength from the presence of the enemy, that is, from the enemy’s presence, so that his weapons may not reach me.

Heretics lie in wait for me, pagans insult me, and all the wicked act as though there were no place of refuge for me. But Christ is a tower of strength for me. This tower is not visible outwardly, but it is always present inwardly.

Consider whatever you suffer: he suffered it first, and consider to what end. For he suffered in order to rise again, because you too hope for the same end; and thus you have entered the tower. You will no longer consent to the enemy, and the enemy’s weapons will not reach you. Rather, you will hurl your own weapons at the enemy—that is, good words with which you may pierce his heart and join him to yourself.

I will dwell in your tent forever; I will be sheltered under the covering of your wings. Because you have become my hope and tower of strength, I shall not be a worthless deserter. Rather, I will dwell—that is, I will be a permanent inhabitant—in your tent, that is, in your military dwelling, namely in ecclesiastical institutions.

“Forever” means for many ages. He says this because this Church will remain until it gathers all its children, and until there is so great a number of children as can restore the number of the condemned angels. Hence it was said: “Wait for a little while, until the number of your brothers is fulfilled.”

I will dwell, I say, not by my own power or by my own strength, but because I will be sheltered under the covering of your wings. Great is the heat of this age, because the tribulations of the righteous are many. But so great is the shadow of God’s wings—he means, “that it protects me from it.”

We may understand these wings either as love of God and neighbor, or as the Old and New Testament, or as mercy and truth: mercy in forgiving sins, truth in fulfilling promises; or also reproof and promise.

For you, my God, have heard my prayer; you have given an inheritance to those who fear your name. Truly you will protect me, because you have already heard my prayer, which was made for perseverance. You, I say, are my God—that is, the one whom I rightly love, worship, and praise freely for this reason.

It is evident that you have truly heard me because you have already given—and will give in its proper time, in reality—the eternal and true inheritance to those who fear your name with chaste fear, that is, this name “God” or [Col. 0800B] “Lord.” This name, “God,” is rightly to be feared by all, so that the creature may relate to him as a creature to its Creator. Likewise, this name, “Lord,” is justly to be feared by all, so that they may relate to him as a servant to his master and a subject to his superior.

You will add days upon the days of the king; his years will extend to the day of generation and generation. You will give the inheritance, I say, and you will give it in this way: you will add the days already given to our king Christ—immortal and eternal days—upon our just but mortal and transitory days. You will add his years upon our years until you bring them to the day, that is, to eternity.

That day is without end, because it is a day without night. I speak of the day of “generation and generation,” that is, where there will be an unfailing generation, in which they neither marry nor are given in marriage. It is signified not by the moon but by the sun, because then the righteous will shine like the sun.

The present generation is signified by the moon, because it receives increase and decrease. He placed the years of the king after the days in order to signify something greater. But because whatever one says about eternity is little in comparison with eternity itself, what he had first signified through days and years he then signified through one day without night and without end.

He remains forever in the presence of God; who will seek his mercy and truth? You will add, I say, the days of the king to us. But what king? He remains, namely, in the presence of God the Father forever. And since he remains forever with the Father, who then will seek his mercy and truth, so that where he is, there his servant may also be?

It is as though he said: It is difficult for anyone to do this.

Or otherwise: Truly you will give the inheritance to those who fear you. For you will add to the present days of the king other days of the king, namely eternal ones. And upon these years of the king you will add other years of his, until you bring that king and his kingdom to the day of generation and generation—that is, to eternity—where there will be generation and generation, namely an unfailing generation. [Col. 0800D] This is to say: You will make us such that Christ our king will reign in us not only in the present but eternally.

He remains forever. He determines what “generation and generation” is: that which remains forever in the presence of God. And for whom does it remain? For those who seek his mercy and truth, that is, for his honor. Who is the one who will seek this? The perfect person, certainly.

God’s mercy is that he does not consider our merits but his own goodness, so that he might forgive our sins and promise us eternal life. His truth is that he does not deceive in granting what he promised. Thus his mercy is shown in forgiving sins, and his truth in fulfilling promises.

Let us therefore attend to this mercy and truth, and let us practice them. Let us practice mercy toward the needy, the weak, and even our enemies. Let us practice truth by fulfilling what we promised in baptism, namely that we would keep the commandments, and thus not add sin to sin. We would add sin to sin if we did not keep the commandments, because the sin of transgression would be added to the sin of lying.

When he says, “Who will seek it for him?” this is not said without reason. Many seek mercy and truth in books, so that they may know in what ways he acted mercifully toward us and in which promises he did not deceive. They also teach others not chastely but for earthly profit. For some, as the Apostle says, preach Christ not chastely.

Such people do not seek mercy and truth for his sake. But those seek mercy and truth for him—that is, for his honor—who investigate them in order both to practice them and to teach them, not for earthly profit but for the benefit of their neighbors.

So I will sing the psalm to your name forever and ever, and I will fulfill my vows from day to day. It is as though he said: Whatever others may do, I will seek mercy and truth from you, Lord, because I will sing the psalm—that is, I will practice mercy and truth, both by doing and by teaching—not for myself but for your name, that is, for the honor of your name, extending into the age that follows this age, that is, persevering.

Thus I say: I will sing the psalm to your name, that is, for the honor of your name, forever, so that I may fulfill my vows to you—solely interior vows, that is, myself, going from this present day into the future day.

Cassiodorus dwells somewhat more clearly on the preceding verse and says: Since the generation mentioned above remains eternally in the presence of God, who will seek his mercy and his truth there? No one, certainly, because where there is no misery, mercy need not be sought. Likewise, where no falsehood ever enters, truth need not be sought, since it is always present.

And because no one will seek truth and mercy there, therefore here I will sing the psalm, and so forth—that is, I will seek mercy and truth here, so that there I may not need to seek them.

## PSALM LXI

**To the end. For Jeduthun. A psalm of David.**

[Col. 0801C]

### Argument

The words of the Maccabees when they were compelled by Antiochus to sacrifice and to be profaned. Alternatively, the voice of Christ concerning the Passion.

### Explanation

Jeduthun is interpreted as “one who leaps over,” that is, one who leaps over the lovers of this world. The person introduced is a soldier of Christ who has abandoned the desires of the world and remained steadfast in the Lord with the firmest hope.

This “leaper,” as we have called him, seeing the world full of errors and miseries, declares in the first part of the psalm that his soul is subject to God, because through the only-begotten Son he has received the saving gift. He reproves those who desire to be called Christians in name only.

In the second part, he again says that his soul is subject to the Lord the Father, because through his Word he has obtained saving patience. He strengthens the people through a faithful confession, so that they ought always to hope in the Lord with the devotion of their whole heart.

In the third part, he warns erring peoples to trust in the Lord more than in the fleeting prosperity of this world.

### Commentary

Will not my soul be subject to God? To the end. For Jeduthun. A psalm of David himself. What “to the end” means is known. Jeduthun, according to the Hebrew interpretation, means “one who leaps over them.” Whom does “them” mean? Those who remain in the lowest things and pursue earthly matters.

The psalm—that is, this praise—is attributed to David himself, that is, to the head or to some more worthy member, who is worthy to persevere and to leap over in the manner shown in this psalm. For this leaper who speaks here has already leapt over certain people, whom he looks down upon from above.

Let us see, therefore, how far he has leapt, whom he has leapt over, and where he has been placed—that is, beneath whom he still remains, although he has leapt over some. For from a certain spiritual and secure place he looks upon these lower things, not so as to fall, but so as to stir up the sluggish to follow him. And he commends the place to which he has already arrived by leaping over.

For he is above some people in such a way that he is also beneath someone. Therefore he first wished to make known beneath whom he is safe, so that what he has leapt over may be progress, not pride. Placed, then, in a certain secure place, he says:

Will not my soul be subject to God? This leaper had perhaps heard in the Gospel: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled,” and the reverse. Therefore, fearful lest he become proud by leaping over, he addresses certain citizens whom he endures.

For there are two cities, just as there are two rulers: Babylon and Jerusalem. Their citizens are always in conflict with one another: the former concerning vanity, the latter concerning truth; the former concerning injustice, the latter concerning justice.

Babylon was first in time, though not in dignity, because, as the Apostle says: “The spiritual was not first, but the animal.” Cain began it and built a city in a place where there had previously been no city. Jerusalem, however, was Jebus. Jebus was their destroyed city and was rebuilt, because no one is pious except from the impious, and no one is just except from the unjust.

These two contrary cities are at present mingled together, while the grains are pressed by the chaff. The leaper who speaks here, observing this, addresses the citizens of Babylon whom he endures. It is as though he said:

You prepare obstacles by insulting; you seek to cast me down by persecuting; you try to lead me astray by deceiving; you weave snares by flattering. Yet I have never remembered being above those over whom I am, in such a way that I forgot beneath whom I am.

Is not my soul subject to God? Certainly, however far I may rise, however far I may leap over, I shall never be against God but beneath God, attributing nothing to myself and everything to him. For I shall safely leap over other things if I keep myself beneath him who is above all.

And rightly my soul is subject to God, because my salvation comes from him—that is, my justification. For God himself is truly my salvation, because he is the one who creates and recreates me. He is my God because he made me, when I did not exist, so that I might exist; and he is my savior because he made me just.

He is my protector—that is, my defender against those who attack and persecute—and therefore I shall not be moved any longer. I was moved in Adam; I was moved in myself. But now, now, as though he said, I have been so strengthened by him that I shall not be moved any longer.

This is to be understood of a grave movement, such as that caused by mortal sins. It is the same as what is said elsewhere: “Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me.” When he said, “Will not the soul be subject to God?” he removed pride from himself. Here, however, when he says, “I shall not be moved any longer,” it is as though he said: “Let not the hand of the sinner move me.”

How long will you rush upon a human being, since he is my salvation and my protector? How long, then, will you, citizens of Babylon, rush upon me—a human being, that is, upon me who am weak and fragile—by insulting, persecuting, and flattering?

Certainly, you can rush upon a human being only as long as you are able, because you all kill. Here he addresses all the citizens of Babylon, scattered, dispersed, and mingled together—both those who are outside, like thorns in hedges, and those who are inside, like weeds among the grain.

It is as though he said: All of you, whether separated or mingled together, must now be endured, but at some point you will be separated, because all of you kill only the outward body, not the inward one.

You rush upon me, I say, and press upon me as upon a leaning wall—that is, one easily overcome in your estimation, just as a leaning wall is easy to overthrow—and as upon a displaced stone wall, that is, one not well founded in faith and firmly rooted in charity.

Or otherwise: All of you kill yourselves by rushing upon me, a human being. I say that you are comparable to a leaning wall and a displaced stone wall, because you rush upon an innocent person. For just as a leaning wall and a displaced stone wall are near to collapse, so you, because you oppress the innocent, bring yourselves near to falling.

Nevertheless, they thought of driving away my reward. I certainly admonished them in this way, but nevertheless they—even if they did not say it—at least some of them thought of driving away my reward from me, that is, they wished to provoke me to impatience; yet, as the Apostle says, patience is necessary for us to receive the promise, and thus they wished to deprive me of my reward and of the recompense of patience. Nevertheless, I ran through the divine commandments without any impediment, fulfilling them, and I did this in thirst, that is, thirsting to guide them by my example and to transfer them into my body. Blessed Augustine says that when we are thirsty, we transfer by the spirit into our body the liquid that is outside. Moses signified this when, angered, he cast the head of the molten calf into the fire, then crushed it, sprinkled it with water, and gave it to the people to drink. Through Moses, indeed, God the Father is understood: as though angered, he admonishes the people of evils—signified by the head of the calf—usually through the fire of tribulation and through fear of the future fire, and crushes the words of preaching. Through the water of baptism he gives the people something to drink, that is, he transfers it into the body of the faithful, and thus quenches its thirst. That woman, too, the Samaritan woman who first perceived the Lord as thirsty, signified this thirst, and the Lord drank her when she believed.

Now let us return to the literal sense. I was indeed thirsting for their salvation, but they blessed me with their mouths and cursed me in their hearts. For not only do those who bear the sacraments of faith while hating the divine commandments do this, but Jews and pagans as well bless the faithful with their mouths, though in their hearts they contradict them.

Nevertheless, be subject to God, my soul, for my patience comes from him. They indeed press upon me like a leaning wall, that is, one easily overcome; they wish to kill me, they think of driving away my reward, and while they bless with their mouths, they curse in their hearts. Nevertheless, you, my soul, be subject to God, so that you may not depart from true obedience and patience. And rightly you ought to be subject to him, since my patience comes from him, if I am able to remain patient amid tribulations and persecutions. This does not come from me, but from him. And truly it comes from him, because he is my God, creating me; my Savior, recreating me; and my helper against those who attack and persecute me, bringing me there, that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem, from which I shall no longer depart. And truly he is my Savior, because my salvation is in God, that is, all my justification and salvation now; and in the end he himself will be my glory, for I shall be glorified by him through resurrection, immortality, and impassibility. But meanwhile, what? Certainly, meanwhile he is the God of help, that is, he provides me assistance against the manifest attacks of those who are outside and against the deceitful speeches of false brothers. Therefore all my hope is rightly in him, who is God.

Hope in him. Here the one who speaks—leaping beyond himself—carries out what was stated in the title, namely, he admonishes others to follow him and, by his example, to leap beyond themselves, saying: Since I, Idithun, am a spirit in God, let the whole assembly of the people, that is, all of you who wish to be joined to the true people, hope in him, that is, imitate me, so that by my example you may hope in God; and pour out your hearts before him, that is, empty your hearts of what fills them, namely, wickedness, so that they may be filled with what they lack, namely, justice. Or, pour out before him—that is, confessing the sins hidden in your hearts, praying and hoping. And rightly you ought to hope in him and pour out your heart before him, because, since he is God, he is our helper against those who attack and afflict us, bringing us into eternity, that is, into eternal glory.

Nevertheless, the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are liars in the balances, so that they may deceive others, and from vanity they move together toward the same end. I admonished all concerning their salvation in this way, but, as though speaking to people who could receive nothing, I accomplished nothing, because they are vain, that is, devoted to earthly things, which are vanity; and they are liars, namely, promising themselves true blessedness in vanity, where no blessedness exists. This is because they are sons of men, that is, imitators of their ancient parents. He gives one example of their deceit in place of the rest, saying: “In the balances,” with “acting” understood, so that they may deceive others. But this profits them nothing; rather, it harms them, because they themselves are deceived, proceeding from this vanity toward the same end, that is, toward that vanity which is always itself, that is, remaining what it is. Through this vanity they are led to eternal punishments. These punishments are not called vanity because they truly punish the wicked, but with respect to the reward of the good; and because whatever is separated from true being is rightly regarded as almost nothing.

Or otherwise: The sons of men are vain because they cling to vain things, and they are liars in the balances, namely, because they place and weigh themselves with others on the scales and deceitfully prefer themselves to others, wishing to establish their own righteousness, as that Pharisee did who said, “I give you thanks, Lord, because I am not like the rest of men,” and so forth. They do this in order thereby to deceive others and thereby increase their own iniquity. Pretended equity is double iniquity. These people, I say, although they differ in the diversity of their opinions, nevertheless all proceed from vanity toward the same end. It is as though he said: Although their errors are manifold, they agree in this, that all direct themselves toward vanities.

Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire robberies; if riches abound, do not set your heart upon them. You sons of men, I say, have hitherto been vain and deceitful, but from now on do not hope in iniquity. This may also be referred to the good, whom he previously admonished, saying, “Hope in him,” and so forth. It is as though he said: The sons of men are indeed vain and deceitful, but you who wish to be the true people must not hope in iniquity.

Here we may understand “iniquity” either universally, as every kind of iniquity, or only as the pursuit of money. For it is said elsewhere: “Every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man.” He divides into two groups those whom he here takes together, namely, the poor and the rich. First he speaks of the poor, saying this: You poor, do not desire robberies, that is, unjust seizures of what belongs to others. Gain acquired at a loss is harmful: you acquire money and lose innocence. For you see what you seize, but you do not see from whom you are seized. Therefore do not rob on account of your poverty, because the one who made you will feed you. If he feeds you as a robber, he will feed you as an innocent person. If he feeds you while you are condemned, much more will he feed you when you are to be set free.

Therefore you poor, do not desire robberies; and if riches abound, that is, if you are rich, do not set your heart upon riches. This is what those do who prefer to store them away rather than distribute them to the poor; and while they guard them, they themselves inwardly flow away from true reason and understanding. Whatever they have retained beyond mere necessity, they have stolen entirely from the poor. Hence the Apostle says to Timothy: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to place their understanding in the uncertainty of riches,” and so forth.

God has spoken once. This is why I say that the poor should not rob and the rich should not set their hearts upon riches: because you, Lord, will both condemn the wicked and reward the good. This is what he says where he declares: “For you will repay each person according to his works”—rewards to some, punishments to others. The testing of both precedes this. It is as though he said: You will truly condemn the wicked, because you, Lord, possess the power to punish both great and small. And you will truly reward the good, because mercy belongs to you.

Let us therefore fear his power and love his mercy. Let us not presume upon mercy in such a way that we despise power; nor let us fear power in such a way that we despair of mercy, because both mercy and power are in God. By his power he humbles the proud; by his mercy he exalts the humble. That both are in God the Apostle indicates when he says: “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make his power known, endured with great patience the vessels of wrath destined for destruction”—there is power. Mercy follows, namely, “so that he might make known the riches of his grace in the vessels of mercy.”

Now let us return to the literal sense. To you, Lord, I say, belong power and mercy. And these two things I heard, that is, understood, because God has spoken once. Here Augustine raises a question, saying: It seems strange that he says God spoke once, while this person heard two things. It would not be so strange if he said that God spoke once and that he heard one thing. Yet even then the statement would not be entirely satisfactory, because God spoke both many times and in many ways. He spoke to Adam, saying to him, “Adam, where are you?” He also said to Cain, “Where is Abel your brother?” He spoke also to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to all the prophets; and finally he spoke in his Son.

Nevertheless, although he spoke in many ways through the subordinate creature, he spoke only once within himself, that is, he generated from himself only one Word, through whom all things were made and in whom all things exist together, in whom he foreknew what he was going to make in creation. He did not fail to know what he made, since in him he arranged once for all the things that he distributed at different times in different ways. He says here that he transcended himself to the point of understanding this Word, and there he heard many things, of which he presents these two as especially necessary for us: the wicked will be condemned, while the good will be rewarded.

This psalm may also be read as spoken by the Head, addressing his persecutors, the Jews, in this way: Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken truth to you? Surely my soul will remain subject to God in obedience rather than to you? Certainly it will. And rightly so, because my salvation, that is, my resurrection, comes from him. And truly it comes from him, because he is both my God, creating me, and my Savior, since through his Word he assumed me as a man and made me free from sin. He is also my supporter, either from the tomb or against those who attack and assail me. Therefore, once moved by death and raised again, I shall not be moved anymore. For Christ rose once, to live forever.

Or otherwise: He was moved in Adam with respect to the mass of humanity, but I shall not be moved anymore, that is, I shall not be moved with respect to the person. Naturally—that is, with respect to common human nature—Christ was moved in Adam; but he was not moved personally, because he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.

Why do you rush upon a man, when my Savior and supporter is God? Why then do you seek to kill me? You rush upon me, whom you regard as only a man; and how long do you rush upon me? Certainly, as long as you can, because all of you kill me outwardly, not inwardly. You, I say, rush upon me who am like a leaning wall and a displaced fence, that is, who am bent toward death and willingly coming to suffering, according to the saying, “I will sacrifice to you willingly.”

Or otherwise: You all kill me—you, I say, who rush upon me as upon a leaning wall and a displaced fence—because, just as someone who rushed against a wall already leaning and a displaced fence would be crushed, so what you do when you rush upon me, who have been placed in Israel for the fall of many, becomes your own oppression and condemnation.

Or otherwise: You all kill yourselves by rushing upon me for the sake of the place and the nation, because in this you are comparable to a wall that is leaning. Just as collapse threatens one who is near a leaning wall, so through my death, by which you think you will preserve the place and the nation, a fall from that same place and nation threatens you and is near at hand. You are also comparable to a displaced fence, that is, to a fragile wall without cement, because you do not possess the glue of charity and affection.

Nevertheless, they thought of driving away my reward; I ran in thirst; with their mouths they blessed, and with their hearts they cursed. I admonished them concerning their salvation in this way, but although they did not say it, at least they thought of driving away my reward, that is, of inciting me to disobedience, and thus taking from me the reward of that obedience, namely, the glory of the resurrection. But I ran, because no worldly attraction held me back; and I did this in thirst, that is, thirsting for their salvation, as before.

The remaining words do not change, except where it says, “For my patience comes from him.” This means: It is therefore right, my soul, that you should be subject to God, because my patience—that is, the tribulation I suffer—comes from him, that is, from his disposition, not from their assault. Moreover, what is said below, “Hope in the Lord, all the assembly of the people,” is to be referred in this reading to the Jews alone.

# ON PSALM LXII

*A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Idumaea.*

## ARGUMENT

It is sung in the person of those who lived in Babylon, distinguished by their merits.

## EXPLANATION

The Psalm and David frequently signify the Lord Christ and frequently the Church, because Christ is in his members and the members are contained in their Head. Therefore, the words that signify the Lord Savior are rightly prefixed to the Church that is going to speak in this psalm.

She dwells in the wilderness of Idumaea, that is, in the aridity of this world, where she thirsts and desires Christ. Hence Idumaea, in which David rejoiced, is interpreted as “earthly.” In the first part of the psalm the Church desires the Lord’s power, wishing to be filled with the abundance of every good thing, so that she may be found worthy of his praises. In the second she gives thanks because, under the shelter of the Lord’s wings, she has escaped the storms of the world; and she rejoices in proclaiming that, while her enemies are to be condemned in the lower regions of the earth, King Christ will rejoice in God the Father with the saints.

## COMMENTARY

“God, God, to you I keep vigil from dawn.” A psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Idumaea.

History records that when Saul was persecuting him, David came to the Idumaeans and hid there for a little while. The Idumaeans are a people whose region is Idumaea, which is interpreted as “earthly” or “bloody.” It signifies the present life, which in itself is a wilderness, because, insofar as it depends upon itself, it has no place of habitation; it is trackless, because in itself it is without the way of truth; and it is waterless, because in itself it lacks true refreshment.

In this life we necessarily suffer many temptations, tribulations, and persecutions. Therefore, while we are in it, we ought always to thirst and hunger, because if you perceive yourself thirsting here, eventually you will perceive yourself drinking. For blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, because they will truly be satisfied in the end.

Placed in this wilderness, our Lord Jesus Christ made habitable and passable whatever was in itself a wilderness and trackless, and he sprinkled with spiritual rain what was waterless. He teaches and admonishes us with what attentiveness, ardor, and desire we ought, amid our present failing state, to sigh to reach the place where there will be no misery and no deficiency. He says thus:

God the Father, although by nature you are the God of all, are specially my God and the God of my people by grace. I keep vigil, not for any earthly advantage, but so that I may come to you, where there is no deficiency. I have this not from myself, but “from dawn,” that is, from your illumination.

Notice that he says, “I keep vigil.” To keep vigil is nothing other than not to sleep. There are two kinds of sleep: the sleep of the body and the sleep of the soul. One is wholesome; the other deadly. Bodily sleep is wholesome and necessary, because unless the bodily members are restored by bodily sleep, they could not long sustain a vigilant mind devoted to its activities.

But the sleep of the soul is deadly, because the soul’s sleep is forgetfulness of God.
