The Apostle awakens us from this sleep, saying: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.” Our Lord Christ himself also admonishes us here by his example that our conduct and our life should keep vigil for God, so that other sleepers may be awakened by our vigils and keep vigil with us and say: “God, my God, to you I keep vigil from dawn.”

His addition of “from dawn” serves our instruction, namely, to teach by this that we should attribute nothing to ourselves, since the Lord Christ as man attributes his vigilance not to himself but to the Lord.

“My soul has thirsted for you.” Truly I keep vigil for you, both in soul and in body. For my soul, attending to the deficiency it suffers, thirsted, that is, it possessed thirst and great desire, so that through you, who are the way, it might be in you, because you are the homeland in which there is no deficiency. My flesh too thirsted in many ways, that is, because of its manifold deficiency it possessed a manifold desire.

For there are more deficiencies of the flesh than of the soul, and therefore he adds “in many ways” with reference to the flesh. He does not say that the flesh thirsted because the flesh itself thirsted, or because the soul thirsted by itself, but because his awareness of the deficiency of both was the cause of his thirsting.

My flesh thirsted, I say, and not for just anyone, but for you. It is as though he said: Others thirst for inheritance, property, or a wife, for money, and for similar things; but my flesh, or my soul, thirsted for nothing except you, in whom true refreshment exists. Eternal blessedness is promised to the soul, in which it perceives no deficiency, and therefore it always sighs for it. Resurrection, immortality, and impassibility are promised to the flesh, and therefore the flesh too rightly thirsts for these things.

“In a deserted, trackless, and waterless land, thus I appeared in the holy place, that I might see your power.” It is as though he said: Where was I placed when I thirsted so greatly? There, certainly, where thirsting is necessary: in the land, that is, in this earthly life, which in itself was deserted, that is, without any true habitation, until God the Father sent true inhabitants and companions into it, namely, holy men who would cultivate it. It was trackless until the way—that is, Christ—was sent down to it from above. It was waterless, that is, it lacked every true refreshment, but through ministers filled with the Holy Spirit it was drenched with the water of true refreshment, namely, spiritual teaching.

Placed in this land, I thirsted; and in this holy desire of mine, that is, in this thirst of mine, I appeared to you, so that I might see your power. That is, I prepared myself in such a way that I was worthy to appear before you because I saw—that is, understood—your power, namely, that I should thus thirst to be yours, not my own, and that the glory in it should be yours, not mine: that you, not I, should be glorified.

“For your mercy is better than lives; my lips will praise you.” Therefore I rightly thirsted for you, because although there are many ways of living, which different people choose for themselves in different ways—one for trading, another for soldiering, another for cultivating the land, and so forth—your mercy is better than that manner of life which you gave us, not on account of our merits but solely through your mercy. You found no merits in us to crown, but sins to forgive; if you punished those sins, you would be overcome, but this pertained to your mercy. You preferred to justify sinners rather than punish them, and to make the impious pious.

That manner of life, I say, is better—not merely a little better, but better “than lives,” that is, it far surpasses every other kind of life. Therefore my lips, that is, the lips of my people, will praise you in the future with true praise. It is as though he said: I have from you whatever enables me to praise you; my lips would not praise you unless your mercy preceded them.

“Thus I will bless you in my life, and in your name I will lift up my hands.” I will praise you in the future, I say, and even in the present I will bless you in my life, namely, the life that you gave me. I did not choose this myself: namely, always to attend to your mercy, not to my merits. And I will lift up—that is, exalt—my hands in prayer and good works, not for my own glory, but in your name, glorifying it, so that others, seeing my good works, may glorify your name.

But what will I pray for, or what will I receive? This, certainly: that my soul, that is, the soul of my people, may be filled as with fat and richness. Properly speaking, fat is the richness that surrounds the intestines; because it is interior, it signifies a good conscience. Richness, however, is that which lies outwardly in the limbs, and therefore by richness virtues and good works are signified.

He does not pray for bodily fatness, but for interior richness, namely, for an abundance of spiritual grace, without which the soul quickly fails in good works. Or perhaps he asks for that future richness, that is, future glory, in which all our need will pass away, because we shall possess whatever good we desire.

I ask, I say, that my soul be filled with richness, and thus my mouth, that is, the mouth of my people, will in the future praise you with lips of exultation, that is, with lips that exalt. For now exultation is not true, because we slip into sins and are saddened by our fall; we pour out groans and prayers. But after all our misery has passed away and prayer is no longer necessary, only the exultation of true praise will remain.

“Thus I remembered you upon my bed; at dawn I will meditate upon you, because you have been my helper.” Therefore I will finally praise you truly, because now I will meditate upon you, that is, all my attention will be directed toward you “at dawn,” that is, in good works. Dawn signifies works, because those who are diligent in working rise at dawn for their labor. Likewise, because light begins to appear at dawn, dawn signifies works of light, that is, good works. For the one who acts wickedly hates the light, while the one who walks in the light does not stumble, because he does not act wickedly. This is established by what precedes.

It is as though he said: If I always remembered you, even upon my bed, that is, at the time appointed for rest, when you seemed less necessary to me, then truly at dawn—that is, in labor, when I need you most—I will meditate upon you, that is, I will remember you. This proceeds from the lesser to the greater.

Dawn, which is a time of labor, may also signify adversity; the bed, on which one rests, prosperity. It is rightly necessary that if he remembered God in prosperity, he should remember him also in adversity.

It may also be explained otherwise, as an argument from equals. It is as though he said: My mouth will truly praise you in the end, because at dawn—that is, at the resurrection—whenever its dawn will be, I will meditate upon you. For the resurrection of the dead differs as star differs from star. Therefore he says “at dawn” in the plural.

Then, I say, I will meditate upon you, that is, all my attention will be directed toward your praise. This is because previously I remembered you in such a way that I was above my bed, that is, I did not acquiesce to flesh and blood, but compelled the weakness of my flesh to serve you.

And rightly I will then meditate—that is, my people will meditate—upon you, because without you we can do nothing. For you first were my helper, that is, the helper of my people, in meriting this; and you will always be my helper, because I will exult—that is, my people will exult—in the shelter of your wings, that is, in your protection, as a simple comparison.

Or by his wings we may understand the love of God and neighbor, or both Testaments, or mercy and truth, or threats and promises. And because I will exult in you, therefore my soul and the soul of my people rightly clung to you, that is, were glued to you by the bond of charity, yet in such a way as to be “after you,” that is, to wish to follow you and not precede you.

In this attachment it is necessary that I suffer many evils. But what concern is that? None, certainly, because your right hand has received me and my people in order to defend us against our enemies.

They, however, did not cease, but sought my soul and the soul of my people, not in order to imitate us but to destroy us. And this was in vain, because in it they harmed themselves more than they profited. This refers especially to the Head, whose soul the Jews sought in vain to destroy, because through his death, by which they thought they would preserve their kingdom, they rather destroyed it.

Therefore, as though he said, they sought my soul because “they will enter into the lower parts of the earth,” that is, they preferred the place and nation to themselves, and entered the earth out of desire. But it is far better to walk upon the earth and trample it, that is, to despise earthly things, than to move upon the earth out of desire. For whoever wickedly and to his own ruin desires earthly things places the earth above himself and enters into the inner parts of the earth as into a dark cavern.

They will enter the earth, I say, through desire for the place and nation. But what does this profit them? Nothing, certainly, because “they will be handed over to the hands of the sword,” that is, into the power of the Roman swordsmen, namely Titus and Vespasian, who will drive them from their place and nation. And this is because they will become portions, as it were, of foxes, since they associated themselves with those who acted deceitfully.

The fox signifies deceitfulness because it is an extremely crafty animal. Hence in the Gospel it is said of certain people: “Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven nests”; the Son of Man, that is, demons, have nests in you, and therefore the Son of Man has nowhere to recline his head.

Or otherwise: “They will be handed over to the hands of the sword,” that is, they will be killed; and those who are not killed will be portions of foxes, that is, they will be given over as a share and possession to foxes, that is, to rulers by whom they will be led into captivity. This is what happened. For eleven times one hundred thousand were led into captivity; as many perished from hunger, and as many were killed. The foxes signify earthly rulers, who chiefly enlarge their states by deceit. Hence the Lord also says of Herod in the Gospel: “Tell that fox that he will not grasp a prophecy outside Jerusalem.”

“But the king will rejoice in God; all who swear by him will rejoice, because the mouth of those who speak iniquity has been stopped.” The enemies, the Jews, will indeed be condemned, but the king will rejoice—that is, I, absolutely the king, whom they despised and in place of whom they chose a fox-king, namely Caesar, will rejoice in the Lord through the resurrection.

And not only will the king rejoice, but all who swear, that is, who affirm that they are in him and live in him, will finally be praised and will rejoice—or the order may be reversed. For great will be the praise when it is said to them: “Come, blessed of my Father.” And again: “Well done, good and faithful servant.”

Those who will be praised will not be few, because the mouth of all who speak iniquity, that is, who contradict the truth, will finally be stopped—and it is already stopped, because there are now few contradictors. For even the Jews, who cried out while the lamb was being killed, became silent after the strong lion rose again.

It should be known that this entire psalm may also be read in the voice of each more perfect member of the body. There is, however, a small difference, because what we have said concerning the Head applies in almost the same way to each more perfect member, who places himself as an example and speaks thus:

God the Father, God of all by nature, my God and specially the God of my people through participation by grace, I keep vigil for you from dawn, that is, diligently. For those who are diligent in their works rise from the beginning of dawn.

Or otherwise: I indeed keep vigil for you, and this does not come from myself, but from dawn, that is, from your illumination. It is as though he said: Just as many people sleep bodily after the sun has already risen and do not know that the sun is present because they are not illuminated by the sun, so many people still sleep even though Christ, the true sun, has already risen and is preached everywhere; they do not perceive that he is present because they have not yet received interior light.

But I, O God, keep vigil for you from dawn, that is, because I have received your light inwardly. He shows how he keeps vigil, as before, saying: “My soul has thirsted for you,” and so forth.

Nothing changes until he says, “Thus I appeared to you in the holy place.” This means: I thirsted for you, and in this holy desire of mine I appeared to you, that is, I became known, so that you too might become known to me; namely, so that in your Holy One, that is, in Christ, I might see—that is, understand—not merely a man but also your power, that is, the omnipotence of your Word, and your glory, that is, the salvation of the human race accomplished through him. This is your glory, because through him you made the impious pious, slaves free, and those condemned raised into the kingdom. For many think it a small matter that the Son of God appeared among human beings because they understand only a man in him, not divine power.

Likewise, where he says, “And in your name,” and so forth, there is only this slight change. It is as though he said: Just as you lifted your hands on the cross, so I will lift my hands in prayer and work for the glorification of your name.

Again, what is said in the penultimate verse, “They will enter into the lower parts of the earth,” is understood in this reading with respect to desire; and “they will be handed over to the hands of the sword” means that they will be killed, not outwardly but inwardly. This is because they will be portions of foxes, that is, deceitful agents.

But the king—that is, the one who governs himself in such a way that he does not conform to such people—will rejoice in God because of his deliverance. And all who swear that they live in this king, that is, his imitators, will rejoice and be praised. They will not be few but many, because the mouth has been stopped.

# ON PSALM LXIII

*To the end. A psalm of David.*

## ARGUMENT

David sang concerning himself when he was afflicted by Saul’s persecutions. Alternatively, it is the voice of the martyrs of Christ.

## EXPLANATION

The words of this title signify Christ, who is going to speak throughout the psalm about his passion. In the first section the Lord prays to be freed from fear of the Jewish people, teaching that they failed in their plots, while he rose again to glory. In the second he mocks the savagery of the Jews, because they themselves were more disturbed by their crimes when the Lord’s power was proclaimed after his resurrection. Then the joy of the righteous and the strength of right faith appeared.

## COMMENTARY

“Hear, O God, my prayer when I entreat you.” To the end. Of David himself—that is, these words are referred not to history but to the end, attributed to David himself, or to the Head, because in this psalm his passion is commended to us chiefly through the voice of the Head, as well as that of the holy martyrs. They could in no way have been strong unless they imitated him, that is, Christ, who first appeared strong and first suffered. Nor would they have endured such things in passion as he endured unless they hoped for such things in the resurrection as he demonstrated in himself.

Let us therefore hear his well-known voice, because here he speaks not only about himself but also about his members. His purpose in this psalm is to commend his passion to us, so that in him we may see both our labor and our reward: labor in passion, but reward in resurrection. Let us not fail in labor, so that we may reach the reward.

He speaks thus: God the Father, hear my prayer, made by me for my people, so that you may give them steadfastness and perseverance in tribulation, when I entreat you—that is, because I pray very earnestly for them. For this was the most powerful prayer, when he offered himself to God the Father for us; in it he truly excused our death and healed our wounds, and he caused himself to be heard on our behalf.

And because I entreat you, therefore deliver my soul from fear of the enemy. He does not pray that the souls of his people be delivered from their enemies so that they may not be killed, because many were killed. Rather, he prays that they be delivered from fear of their enemies, namely, from fear of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Let them fear lest they be turned away from him by their enemies; rather, let them fear the one who can cast both soul and body into Gehenna, that is, let them submit to his fear.

Let them not be free from fear altogether, but let them be delivered from fear of the enemy. For the holy martyrs were heard and were killed, yet they overcame their enemies. Many who feared consented and remained alive, but they were swallowed up by their enemies. Many were swallowed up while alive; many others, having died, were swallowed up.

Those who thought the Christian religion was vain were swallowed up dead. Those who believed the preaching of the Gospel to be true and Christ to be the Son of God, yet yielded to pains and sacrificed, were swallowed up alive. The former were swallowed up because they were dead; the latter, swallowed up, were dead. For although they were swallowed up alive, they could not remain alive.

You have protected me. Behold, he urges his faithful to be steadfast not only in word, that is, in name, but also by proposing his example—what he suffered and what he received—so that they too may endure the same things and receive such things. It is as though he said: “I pray that you may rescue me from the fear of the enemy,” and truly you do rescue me, because already, by your foreordination, you have protected me from the assembly of the wicked.

By “the assembly of the wicked” he calls the gathering of the Jews, who were truly acting wickedly: like madmen attacking a physician who had come to heal their sick, to give sight to their blind, and to cure their madness, they wanted to kill him. And you protected me not only from the assembly of those wicked Jews, but also from the multitude of all who worked that iniquity. He adds this on account of the Roman soldiers, who were Gentiles and who, in agreement with the Jews, carried out that iniquity.

What iniquity? This, namely: they sharpened their tongues like a sword—that is, both groups, but especially the Jews, uttered extremely sharp and poisonous words against me in order to kill me. The Jews cannot excuse themselves from having killed the Lord, for if they did not kill him with iron, they nevertheless did so with their poisoned mouths. Do not direct your attention to unarmed hands, but to an armed mouth, because their tongue was a sharp sword.

For when Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law,” they replied, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone.” And if it was not lawful to kill, was it lawful to hand someone over for killing? Certainly not. Nevertheless, they wished to shift their iniquity onto the human judge, but they could not deceive God, the judge. Pilate thus became more innocent by comparison with them, because he did many things to free him from their hands. For this reason he also brought him out after scourging him, hoping in this way to lessen their savagery.

But when he saw that they persisted in such madness, he washed his hands and said, “I am innocent of the blood of this just man.” He called himself innocent, but because he consented, he was nevertheless guilty. And if this man, who acted under compulsion, was guilty, how much more guilty were those who compelled him and who killed Christ with their poisonous mouths, shouting against him, “Crucify him, crucify him!”

Hence there is also that disagreement among the Evangelists: one says that the Lord was crucified at the third hour, while another says that it was at the sixth hour. For it truly was the third hour when they accused him before Pilate and chose Barabbas, while, raging, they demanded that Jesus himself be crucified. Therefore the Evangelist, looking to their intention, said that he was crucified at the third hour. The other said that it was the sixth hour, when Pilate sat on the tribunal, and then the officers of the authority crucified him whom the transgressors of the law had crucified at the third hour.

And then the hands of the former completed what the tongues of the latter had first done. They were more guilty because they shouted in fury, although the soldiers administered the act by obeying. “They sharpened,” I say, “their tongues, and they bent the bow,” that is, they prepared hidden ambushes, wishing to kill, as though unknowingly, one from whom nothing hidden in the human heart could escape. For he who made the human being knows what is in the human being.

The bow signifies hidden ambushes for this reason: whoever fights hand-to-hand with a sword fights openly; but whoever strikes with a bow in order to wound deceives. Hear of a bitter deed. Truly bitter was the deed that they wished to kill the one whom they saw raising the dead and doing such things. For this purpose, I say, they bent the bow, “to shoot the blameless,” that is, to kill him who had incurred no stain, because he committed no sin, and because he was so entirely free from stain that he even wiped away our stains. This was hidden insofar as it concerned them, but not insofar as it concerned him, from whom nothing could be hidden.

Suddenly they will shoot him. It is as though he said: “They will truly accomplish that for which they bent the bow, because they will shoot the blameless suddenly,” that is, unexpectedly, as far as their own judgment was concerned. “And they will not fear,” that is, they will not be astonished, although they shoot him. The judge was afraid; those who handed him over to the judge were not afraid. The authority trembled, but their savagery did not tremble.

This was because they confirmed their wicked speech when they repeatedly said, “Crucify him, crucify him,” for repetition is confirmation. They also confirmed it when they cried out unanimously against Pilate, “We have no king but Caesar.” Again, they confirmed their wicked speech when they said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” And they confirmed it for themselves, not for the Lord, because death did not kill him; he killed death. But their iniquity, which lived within them, killed them.

They have recounted. Because they confirmed their speech, therefore “they have recounted,” that is, they arranged and devised how they might hide snares—how, secretly and in their own estimation, they might prepare traps for the one who knows everything. They did this so secretly that they even said, “Who will see their snares?” Yet it could have been said to them: “He who made you sees you.”

They have searched out. They thought that no one would see the snares because they “searched out,” that is, with great diligence they fabricated iniquities—bitter and sharp counsels—namely these: “Let him not be handed over by us, but by a disciple; let him not be killed by us, but by the judge. Let us do everything in such a way that we seem to be doing nothing.”

But this simulated innocence was not innocence, because simulated equity is not equity but a double iniquity. What kind of innocence was it to refuse to put the money of blood into the treasury, while handing over innocent blood? For when the repentant betrayer, regretting his deed, threw the silver back to them, they said, “It is not lawful to put it into the treasury, because it is the price of blood.” The treasury, or *corbona*, was a certain chest into which contributions were placed for the use of the saints.

“They searched out,” I say, “iniquities.” But what happened to them as a result? This, namely: “while searching out the searches, they failed”—that is, the more sharply they thought they had discovered those sharp and bitter counsels, the more they failed to attain the light of truth and equity, and the more deeply they were submerged in the darkness of wicked counsels.

For justice has a certain law of its own, by which it floods and illumines the soul. But when the soul turns away from the light, the more it discovers what it can do against justice, the more it is driven from the light and sunk into darkness. Thus these men, the more sharply they plotted what they could do against the just man, the more they failed to reach the light of truth. They failed so completely that they did not even think that the God whom they themselves did not see saw their deceits, saying, “Who will see?”

A human being will approach. It is as though he said: “They were devising all these things as though against one unwilling and reluctant; nevertheless, a human being will approach,” that is, I shall willingly approach the Passion. The human being suffered himself to be seized, scourged, spat upon, and crucified, because he could not be seized, scourged, spat upon, and crucified except as a human being. The human being approached all these sufferings so that the human being might be freed.

“A human being will approach,” I say, “and a lofty heart”—that is, the eternal counsel within that human being will also approach. How did he approach? Because he presented the human being to their eyes alone, while concealing his divinity within. And thus the human being was killed, and the God-human was exalted. He was killed in weakness, but exalted in majesty.

And where did he go when exalted? To where, clearly, he had not departed when humbled: he returned to the bosom of God the Father, from which he had not departed through the humiliation of the flesh he had assumed.

Our translation has, “To a lofty heart,” which can be read quite suitably in this way: “They searched out their searches, and in completing this search a human being will approach from the lesser to the lofty heart,” that is, to the agreement of the rulers; the greater and the lesser will agree to carry out these bitter counsels. Or, simply, “a human being,” the persecutor, will approach the lofty heart, that is, Christ, in order to crucify him. In him there truly was a lofty heart, because in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself. And thus the human being will be killed, and the God-human will be exalted, as above.

The arrows of little ones. For this reason I say that the God-human will be exalted: they accomplished nothing. Their blows became “the arrows of little ones,” that is, they did him no harm, like arrows that children make from straw, which harm no one.

Or otherwise: children are accustomed to shoot arrows especially upward, where they harm no one, but often the arrows fall back upon the children themselves and kill them. So the Jews did not harm God by their blows, but rather killed themselves.

And truly they accomplished nothing, because their tongues were weakened, so that they were against them rather than for them. How so? After the Lord had been crucified and buried, they said to Pilate, “Sir, we remember that that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will rise again.’ Therefore command that the tomb be guarded until the third day, lest his disciples come and steal him and say to the people, ‘He has risen from the dead’; and the last error will be worse than the first.”

Then Pilate said to them, “You have guards; go, guard it as you know how.” Guards were set. The third day came. So many miracles occurred that even the guards, if they had wished to speak the truth, could have been witnesses. But the avarice that had captured the disciple, Christ’s companion, also captured the soldier guarding the tomb.

For the Jews said to them, “We will give you as much money as you want; say that his disciples came while you were sleeping and stole him.” In this way their tongues became opposed to them, because they confirmed the truth of the resurrection rather than destroying it, as they thought they would by means of such witnesses. For if they were asleep, they saw nothing; and if they saw and heard nothing, they could not be witnesses. The duty of a witness is to report what he has seen or heard.

Thus their tongues were weakened when the Lord rose and was everywhere preached and exalted in majesty—he who had previously been condemned in weakness. All those among the Jews who “saw them,” that is, who understood the hardness of their hearts, according to which they spoke such things rather than according to the truth, were first troubled in mind by the consciousness of sin. So were those who approached the apostles and said, “What shall we do, brothers?” Peter answered them in equivalent terms: “Drink in faith the blood that you poured out in your fury.”

They were troubled, I say, even more. Then every human being among them—every person truly using reason and understanding what they deserved for so great a crime—feared greatly the judgment to come. And the human being feared so greatly that the human being was no longer feared, that is, the Jews were no longer feared. After they heard Christ being preached everywhere and the world following him, they forbade anyone to speak in that name. Peter said or replied to them that it was more necessary to obey God than human beings.

They proclaimed the works of God. It is as though he said: “Christ had already been exalted in majesty, although previously he had been judged in humility.” Once they had been troubled and were afraid, the holy Apostles and their companions, rescued from the fear of their enemies after the certainty of the resurrection and the confirmation of the Holy Spirit sent upon them, proclaimed the works of God the Father—namely, that it was necessary for him who was to bring many sons into glory to perfect their author through death.

Therefore they proclaimed these things, because only then did they first understand his works—that is, God’s works. And what works? That Christ had to suffer in this way: with such gentleness that he was led like a sheep to slaughter, and with such humility that neither appearance nor beauty was visible in him; and that with such patience he endured those insulting him on the cross that he did not come down from the cross, on which he had to die for the sake of those destined to die and rise again for the sake of those destined to live eternally.

After those just men, who had previously been saddened when they doubted and thought that they had lost their hope, understood these things, they rejoiced. So did the first two just men whose eyes he restrained on the road, lest they recognize him. But after they recognized him in the breaking of the bread, they rejoiced.

These things were announced to another, more stubborn man, who had doubted and refused to believe until he touched his side. But after he placed his hand at his side, he rejoiced and said, “My God and my Lord.”

And not only did these just men rejoice; every just person will rejoice—not in the world, but in the Lord, because it was said, “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” And rightly he will hope in him, since the hope of resurrection has been given to him.

When every just person rejoices, all those who are upright in heart—that is, who justly judge whatever they suffer here as being suffered in imitation of him and do not murmur against or contradict his will—will also rejoice. These, I say, will rightly be praised both here and in the future, and thus they will rejoice.

And if these will be praised, it is therefore evident that those who are crooked in heart—namely, those who do not bring their heart into conformity with the heart of God, but rather seek to distort his heart according to their own—will truly be condemned.

## ON PSALM 64

**To the end. A psalm of David; a song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel for the people of the captivity, when they were beginning to set out.**

### ARGUMENT

He foretells the people’s return from Babylon, speaking in the person of those who are returning. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church before baptism.

### EXPLANATION

Since the opening elements of the title are already known, let us explain what follows briefly. When the people of Israel migrated to Chaldea, the prophets mentioned above foretold that after seventy years they would return to their homeland and rebuild Jerusalem, which had been overthrown by its enemies, in a better condition.

Therefore Jeremiah and Ezekiel did not compose the psalm. Rather, because the historical circumstances correspond to their time, it is entitled with their names. Many authors assert that Ezra did this, saying that he supplied titles to all the psalms and gathered into one volume those that until then had been unarranged and dispersed by differences of time and authority.

Spiritually, however, the people who, abandoning Babylon, hurried after their captivity toward Jerusalem represent those who, after their former sins have been condemned amid the confusion of this world, strive to come to the Church of Christ. According to the authority of the Fathers, this entire psalm must be applied to them.

That people, abandoning the sins of the world and returning to the Lord, recognizes its liberator at the first entrance of the psalm, asks that its prayer be heard, and declares blessed only the one who has deserved to reach his courts. In the second section it declares its hope that the Lord is the hope of all the ends of the earth, describing his power by an allegorical comparison and rejoicing in his saints through hymnic exultation in him.

### COMMENTARY

A hymn befits you, O God, in Zion. “To the end. A psalm of David, a song of Jeremiah, Haggai, and Ezekiel, concerning the word of pilgrimage, when they were beginning to set out.”

According to the historical account, the Israelite people were captured from their city Jerusalem and led into Babylonian servitude. The holy prophet Jeremiah had foretold that after the seventieth year the people would return from captivity, rebuild the temple of the Lord—which had been destroyed—and restore the city that he had mourned as conquered by its enemies.

This finally occurred according to the prophecy of the holy man. A large part of the people returned from captivity and restored the city and the temple that had been destroyed by the Chaldeans.

But since these things happened in figure for them and were written for our instruction, as the Apostle says, we too must first know our captivity and then our liberation. We must recognize Babylon, in which we are captives, and Jerusalem, toward which we sigh according to the literal sense. These two cities existed: Babylon, namely, and Jerusalem; and Jerusalem bore the figure of a certain eternal city.

But after the thing signified began to be preached more clearly, the city that signified it was neglected and the city that was its shadow was rejected. For this reason there is now no temple in it, although the temple had been built as a figure of that true temple of which it was said, “Destroy this temple,” and so forth. For when the truth came, the shadow departed.

Nevertheless, we are still in a certain captivity, because while we are in this body we are pilgrims away from the Lord. The names of these two cities should also be noted according to their interpretation. Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” while Babylon means “confusion.” Let us attend to the city of confusion so that we may understand the vision of peace.

The citizens of these two cities run together, mixed with one another, from the beginning of the human race; at the end, however, they will be separated. Hence even now the citizens of Babylon and the citizens of Jerusalem are distinguished. These two cities are made by two loves: Jerusalem is made by the love of God, while Babylon is made by the love of the world.

Let each person question himself concerning what he loves, and he will discover of which city he is a citizen. If he is a citizen of Babylon, let him uproot desire and plant charity. If he is a citizen of Jerusalem, let him endure captivity and hope for liberation.

Under this figure of captivity and liberation this psalm is sung. Its title contains the two prophets Jeremiah and Haggai, and they sing when they are beginning to depart. Someone begins to leave Babylon when he begins to love. Many leave secretly. One leaves it not with his feet but with his affections. A person leaves if those who were previously confused by desire are distinguished by charity. Once distinguished, they are not confused.

Although bodily they are still mixed together, they are nevertheless distinguished by holy desire. Even if, because of bodily presence, they have not yet departed, according to the inclination of their mind they have already begun to leave.

Let us therefore listen and sing, and desire the city whose citizens we are. Let us listen, I say, both to the joys sung to us and to the way in which the love of our city is restored within us—a city that we have forgotten during our long pilgrimage.

For our King sends us the sacred Scriptures like letters, in which the love of returning is formed within us. He urges us, and this psalm says briefly, to attend to the miseries and labor of pilgrimage, and thus always to sigh for our complete homeland, enjoying eternal happiness.

It should also be noted that Jeremiah is interpreted as “exalted” or “high.” Through him are signified people who despise what is low and seek what is high, that is, heavenly things. Haggai is interpreted as “solemn” or “festive,” and signifies people so advanced that they no longer seek rest except there where joys are without end and festivity without interruption.

Ezekiel is likewise interpreted as “memory of God.” This was added because some books have Ezekiel rather than Haggai.

The title is explained as follows: “These words are referred to the end. They are a psalm of David,” that is, of the faithful. The title determines both what a psalm is and whose it is, saying that it is a song—that is, an exultant hymn—of Jeremiah and Haggai, that is, of those two faithful people signified through the two prophets.

It is sung concerning the word, that is, concerning the knowledge of pilgrimage. Because they have known the bitterness of exile, they thirst for the sweetness of the homeland. Therefore they sing and urge others to attend to the same thing and thirst for the same thing.

I say that it was sung “when they were beginning to set out,” not by those prophets themselves but by those signified through them. As soon as someone begins to leave Babylon and senses the sweetness of the homeland, it is fitting for him to pray and sing thus:

“O God, a hymn does not befit you in Babylon”—that is, you are not fittingly hymned there by Babylonians, because praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner. “But a hymn befits you in Zion”—that is, you are fittingly hymned by those who are in Zion, that is, in present contemplation.

And finally the vow will be completely rendered to you by those same people in Jerusalem, because the one who now rejoices, Jacob, while setting out, will rejoice as Israel when he arrives.

Or, if we follow the Fathers, let us refer both Zion and Jerusalem to the same reality: “O God, in Babylon we hung up our instruments, and we did not hymn you, because Babylon’s hymn does not befit you. But in superheavenly Zion, where true contemplation is found, you are fittingly hymned, because there is no impediment there, and something great is promised us there: namely, that the author of that most beautiful city will be seen.”

Even if we are not there bodily, we are there in mind, because, as the Apostle says, “Our citizenship is in heaven.” And although we walk here bodily among Babylonians, we do not wage war according to the flesh. Just as we are already there in mind, so also we already hymn there in mind.

In Zion, I say, you are fittingly hymned, O God, and in Jerusalem—that is, in the same Zion, where we shall arrive at the vision—the vow will indeed now be made and then rendered to you completely. For then we shall be a perfect sacrifice to you, when the fire of the most ardent charity seizes us wholly for its own use.

Hear my prayer. And so that I may come and render my vow, therefore, O God, hear my prayer by giving me perseverance against the carnal desires that divide us, against which we struggle by refusing our consent for as long as we remain in this life.

Hear me, I say, so that I may come in order to render my vow, because it is necessary that I come. For “all flesh will come.” Christ assumed the firstfruits of flesh from the Virgin’s womb, and once the firstfruits have been assumed, it is necessary that the rest follow.

Therefore flesh of every kind—slaves, masters, learned and unlearned, old and young—will indeed come to judgment, because “we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ.” But not all will come to you, that is, to be incorporated into you, because some come to be condemned.

Therefore hear me, so that I may come and render my vow—that is, so that I may come to be saved, not to be condemned.

[Col. 0816B] The words of the wicked. It is necessary that you hear me because “the words of the wicked,” that is, of the Babylonians, “have prevailed over us.” It is necessary that, in whatever city someone is born, he learn both the language and the customs of that people.

So we too, living among Babylonians and amid their vanity—that is, having learned to love earthly things—have acquired their ways. Some have even learned their falsehood, because they have placed the creature before the Creator.

Thus their words—that is, the wicked doctrine of the Babylonians—prevailed over us because we consented; and they prevailed over us because they were the majority. Yet they did not crush us, because you, God the Father, will be propitious—that is, through your propitiator you will show mercy toward our sins, indeed even toward our impieties.

These words clearly show to whom this propitiation belongs. Such things are commonly said of priests, because through sacrifices and prayers they make God propitious toward us, so that we may find him acknowledging us and granting forgiveness.

So God the Father sent his Son, who offered on our behalf what he received from us. He himself is priest and victim, he himself is the one who offers and the offering, and through this propitiator he has mercy on us.

Blessed is the one whom you have chosen. “You will be propitious,” I say, “toward us through your propitiator,” who, chosen by your Word and specially assumed, is blessed.

And everyone whom you have already chosen by your foreordination, and through him have assumed in order to incorporate him, is also blessed, because he will finally dwell—that is, he will have his permanent home—in his superheavenly courts.

The courts are sometimes understood as the present Church. Here, however, the courts may also be understood as the heavenly dwelling, since courts are customarily adorned; and that dwelling is most beautifully adorned.

We shall be filled with good things. It is as though he said: “But meanwhile, what?” He should say, “We shall be filled with the good things of your house.” But because the one of whom he speaks is many, among whom he himself is included, he says, “We shall be filled with good things,” not with the goods of Babylon—gold, silver, gems, and other things belonging to vanity—but with the goods of your house.

Here he understands “house” and “temple” either as the superheavenly dwelling, which he also called the court, whose goods are things that “eye has not seen nor ear heard”; or he calls it “house” by analogy with the human being who belongs to the Lord. For “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself.”

He explains what the goods of that house are: holiness and equity. For your temple—or the heavenly dwelling, or that temple of which he said, “Destroy this temple,” and so forth—is holy, that is, full of holiness, and is wondrous not in gold, silver, or similar things, but in equity. Holiness pertains to religion, while equity pertains to justice.

Hear us. It is as though he said: “And there is a turning toward Christ.” And so that we may be filled, therefore you, God our Savior—that is, you who gave yourself in order to save us—hear us.

You, I say, who are the hope of all the ends of the earth, that is, in whom those placed throughout all the ends of the earth hope through faith, even if not everyone is everywhere, and those who are placed in the sea, that is, on islands of the sea, however far away.

Or otherwise: You are the hope of all the ends of the earth, that is, especially of all those who have made themselves the ends of the earth, and also of those who are in the sea—that is, who still cling to the world, signified by the sea, and therefore are far away.

For there is no class of wicked people so perverse that some among them do not turn and, believing, hope.

Preparing the mountains. It is as though he said: “By what means are you the hope of all these people?” By this, namely, that you prepare the mountains. You prepare certain mountains, some before others.

The mountains are those exalted in earthly affairs. The Lord prepares them for two reasons: either so that the good may be exercised through them, or so that the good may be supported by them.

In addition to these mountains, he also prepared certain more excellent mountains—namely those whom the rising sun first illuminated, and through whom it shone back into the valleys: the apostles. Through this it came about that all the ends of the earth hoped in him.

Therefore he says, “Preparing the mountains in your power,” not in their weakness. From you they are strong; from themselves they are weak. You were powerful enough to accomplish this, because you are girded with power.

One person is girded, and another is the one by whom he is girded. So here too the human being is girded and is girded by divine power—that is, by the Word personally joined to him.

You, I say, who through these mountains disturb the depth of the sea—that is, you disturb the sea so gravely that you shake it from its very bottom.

By “the sea” he calls earthly and worldly people: bitter through vanity, turbulent with storms, and devouring one another like fish through perverse and wicked desires. Their heart is the depth; and whatever is disturbed from within is disturbed more gravely.

Thus, while the apostles were proclaiming, the Lord disturbed the earthly among the Gentiles so deeply that he shook their heart, from which all the persecution they exercised against the saints proceeded through tongue and hand. He emptied it of what had filled it—that is, iniquity—and filled what had been empty—that is, equity.

This is what he says: “You who disturb the depth of the sea,” and by disturbing it, you also disturb “the sound of its waves,” that is, its roaring waves. This means that you make their forceful and threatening contradictions cease.

How do you do this? In this way: while the apostles were proclaiming, the Gentiles were first troubled by the consciousness of their sins, and then they feared—that is, they were greatly astonished—even those who inhabit the “ends,” that is, the boundaries of the earth, or those who, by inhabiting themselves, make themselves the ends of the earth, because of signs—that is, on account of the miracles they saw.

These signs were yours, that is, performed by you and not by others, in accordance with the saying, “The Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed.”

In this way you will make the morning departures and the evening departures pleasing—that is, make them pleasing rather than burdensome. The morning departure is contempt for worldly prosperity; the evening departure is contempt for worldly adversity.

Suppose that some powerful person, wishing to drive you into an injustice, offers you a great earthly profit. But you should instead attend to the Lord saying to you: “What exchange will a person give for his soul?” Or, “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?”

And again: “I am your good; I am your riches, not the world. I promise eternal things; the world promises transitory things.” Attend to these and similar sayings, and it will not be burdensome but pleasing for you to despise that profit.

If, however, seeing that promises have no force, he tries to overcome you by threats and punishments, attend to this in your heart: “My Lord commands me, ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.’” He also promises me safety concerning the body, saying, “Not a hair of your head will perish.”

Why, then, should I fear him? What can this person do to me that my Lord did not first suffer? Attend also to many similar things, and thus the adversity that he threatens will be pleasing to you to despise.

Prosperity is signified by the morning because of the joy of light; adversity is signified by the evening because of the sadness of night.

You visited the earth and intoxicated it. In this way, I say, you will make the contempt of prosperity pleasing to them in the morning and of adversity in the evening, because you have already visited the earth by your foreordination through grace—that is, the Gentiles who cling to the earth.

And you intoxicated it, that is, you drenched it with the word of doctrine, so that you intoxicated it with your splendid cup. Happy intoxication, salutary satiety: the more abundantly it is received, the more it deigns to grant sobriety of mind.

And you multiplied it to enrich it, that is, you enriched it abundantly with spiritual gifts, because to one is given knowledge of languages, to another the grace of healings, to another the discernment of spirits, and so forth.

The river of God is filled with waters. It is as though he said: “By what did you intoxicate it, and by what did you enrich it?” By the river, namely—that is, by the earlier believing people of the Jews, from whom, as from a river, streams of doctrine flowed over into others.

This river is filled with the waters of God—not waters that drown, but waters that refresh—that is, with spiritual doctrines given by God the Father.

Although I say that this was accomplished through the river, it was not the river but you who prepared food—that is, the refreshing doctrine of those who are signified by the earth.

You, I say, prepared it, because its preparation is of such a kind—that is, it is accomplished by you alone—for it is accomplished through grace, which no one can give except you alone.

Saturate its streams. It is as though he said: “Join good outcomes to good beginnings, O Lord; saturate the streams of its earth.”

Streams are properly furrows in the earth through which water flows. Here, however, by “streams” understand those capable of receiving powerful doctrine.

The meaning is: “Let the hardness of their hearts be split by the plowshare of your word, O Lord, so that streams may arise in them through which living waters may flow to others.”

And in this way multiply its offspring, that is, the generations of that earth: let believers produce other believers, and those others still more, so that the number of the faithful may increase.

And truly you will do this: you will saturate its streams, because even “the one who is sprouting,” that is, whoever is now beginning to believe, will rejoice in the raindrops of that river which saturates its streams.

By “raindrops” understand the milky doctrine, suitable for little ones—concerning which the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, and as infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not food.”

For just as someone watering his plantations introduces streams to some plants, namely those that already have roots, while infusing moisture into others only by dripping, so God nourishes lesser believers with milk, while feeding the more mature as though with bread or powerful doctrine.

This verse can also be read in such a way that “its” always refers to the river, and that “streams” and “the one who is sprouting” are understood as parts of the river. By “streams,” then, understand those more capable of receiving; by “the one who is sprouting,” those less capable, into whom doctrine is still being instilled by others.

Bless the crown of the year of your goodness. However this may be varied, you will bless it in the same way—that is, you will increase the crown, that is, the glory, of the year of your goodness, that is, of your fertility. When he says “crown,” understand the glory of victory. Victors were crowned for glory, and therefore “crown” is used for “glory”; while a good year is a fertile year. This fertile year of which he speaks began with the second [Col. 0818D] sowing. For there were two sowings. First the prophets sowed among the Jews alone, and the apostles reaped what they had sown, because the holy apostles were instructed through the teaching of the prophets. Hence it is said: “Others have labored, and others have reaped.” Then that same seed, purified and sown a second time, was sown among all the nations by the apostles; over it the enemy sowed weeds, because the devil introduced many heretical teachings. In this second sowing that year of fertility began, of which it is said: “Rejoice, barren woman, who do not bear,” and so forth; it continues until the end of the age.

“Bless,” I say, “and, when you bless, your fields,” that is, your humble ones, that is, believers, “will be filled” with the word, that is, with every fullness of virtues. This refers to the humble among the Jews. “The beautiful places of the desert,” that is, the hearts of the Gentiles, formerly barren with the thorns of sins but now made beautiful with the adornment of virtues, “will grow fat” in good works. Therefore “the hills,” that is, their prelates, “will gird themselves” [Col. 0819A] with exultation, that is, they will possess complete exultation. For the progress of their subjects is the great joy of prelates.

And not only the hills, that is, the lower prelates, but also “the rams,” leaders of the sheep, those who beget others in the faith and therefore strike with both horns—that is, the supreme leaders of the Church—will be clothed with exultation. Thus the holy apostles, their successors, and the evangelists have already had, and will have, complete exultation. This is because “the valleys,” that is, those humbler than these, will finally abound not in bristly barley, that is, carnal teaching, but in delightful wheat, that is, spiritual teaching. For the humbler someone is, the higher he is in spiritual things.

“And they will shout,” that is, both subjects and prelates will direct all their attention toward God. And truly they will shout, because they will sing a hymn, namely: “A hymn befits you, O God, in Zion.” For it is not shouting unless it is singing a hymn.

## PSALM LXV

*To the end; a song, a psalm of resurrection.*

[Col. 0819B]

### ARGUMENT

Here too he designates the return of the people, speaking in the person of those who, among them, are deservedly higher in rank, since the preceding song contains the prayers and wishes of the whole people. Alternatively, it is the voice of the apostles to the people.

### EXPLANATION

The title is clear: it announces the joy of the Lord’s resurrection not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles. Against the persuasion of the Jews, who claimed that they alone, above all others, belonged to the blessed life, Mother Church sings joyfully of the hope of the general resurrection, interposing three *diapsalmata*.

First, she exhorts the whole community to rejoice together over the Lord’s resurrection, which was to bestow eternal rewards upon all the faithful. Second, she invites everyone to come and contemplate God’s works, so that one faith may unite those [Col. 0819C] who await one reward. Third, she again admonishes the Gentiles to bless the Lord, who, although he tests us with various tribulations, nevertheless leads us to the repose of his mercy. Fourth, she again invites the whole community, so that, encouraged by the admonition and by the example of their deliverance, they may trust more fully in the Lord, blessing him because he has deigned to hear their prayer.

### COMMENTARY

**Shout joyfully to God, all the earth.** “To the end: a psalm of David, a song of resurrection.” These words are referred to “to the end,” namely, “a psalm of David,” that is, of Abraham, Moses, and the other faithful of the earlier people, who were awaiting, through evangelical grace and the hope of resurrection, the future incorporation of the Gentiles and Jews into one body. I say it is a psalm that is a song, that is, a song of joy—not of just any joy, but of the resurrection, which does not fail. For what joy is greater than that into which no sadness intrudes?

This psalm speaks of the resurrection, already accomplished in the head and still to come in the body, because whatever preceded [Col. 0819D] in the head also follows in the body, and this is our hope. For this we believe, for this we endure, and for this we persevere amid the great wickedness of this age, comforted by hope before hope becomes reality. Hope will become reality when we too rise and, changed into a heavenly condition, become equal to the angels.

The Jews held this hope as promised to themselves and greatly boasted of their good and supposedly just works, because they had received the law. They expected that, by living according to it, they would receive temporal goods and such things in the future, and they rejoiced here in whatever of them they possessed. For this reason they could not answer the Sadducees, who did not believe in the resurrection. If they did not hope for such things in the resurrection, they would not have been at a loss before the Sadducees’ question.

But the Lord, promising equality with the angels, not the corruption of human flesh, resolved the question and said: “You are mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God. In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, nor do they begin to die, but they will be equal to the angels of God.” Nor are [Col. 0820A] successors sought where there will be no predecessors.

And because the Jews held this hope as promised to themselves, they thought that they alone would rise to the blessed life, on account of the work of the law and the justification of the Scriptures, which they alone possessed, whereas the Gentiles did not possess them. Therefore this psalm acts against their presumption and pride, calling the Gentiles to the same hope of resurrection through faith.

And because this psalm speaks of immense and ineffable joy, it begins with a shout of joy: “All the earth,” that is, not only the Jews, but also you Gentiles, spread throughout the whole earth, “shout joyfully,” that is, burst forth in cries of gladness if your spoken words are not sufficient; and do this “to God,” that is, for the praise of God, who has also called us to the hope of resurrection.

Observe how he commends the universality of the Church when he says: “Let all the earth shout joyfully.” Whoever wishes to be only in a part, as the Africans wished, does not wish to shout joyfully but to howl. And it is as though he said: If you shout for joy inwardly, so that God may hear [Col. 0820B] a psalm, “sing a psalm,” that is, work well outwardly, so that your neighbor may see and receive an example. Do this not for your own praise, but for the glorification of his name, lest you be among those who wished for their own righteousness and refused to submit to the righteousness of God.

And by shouting for joy in this way, namely by singing psalms, give glory with both soul and body to his praise, that is, offer glorious praise not to ourselves but to him, that is, to God, from whom you have whatever good you possess.

**Say to God.** This is another division, and it means: Say this so that you may understand and thereby show it to God, that is, for the praise of God: “Lord, how fearful are your works,” that is, how greatly your works are to be feared. Why are they fearful? Because blindness has occurred in part in Israel, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter.

Rejoice, therefore, you Gentiles, in such a way that you tremble. Observe the branches broken because of pride, and the wild olive grafted in because of goodness; and, having become participants in the richness of the olive tree, do not become proud. The branches were broken because of unbelief, but you stand by faith. Do not be high-minded, but fear. For if he did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. God is able to graft them in again.

[Col. 0820C]

And this indeed happened. The Lord rose, and many believed in him. Those who previously had not known him while they were crucifying him believed and came to know him. The Lord’s blood was given to murderers—not to say “God-killers”—and the blood which they had shed in their cruelty they drank through grace.

Say to God also in such a way that you understand: “Lord, your enemies, the Jews, lie to you,” that is, for your glory. For “they will lie in the abundance of your power,” that is, so that your great power may appear. Their lie was different from other lies. Other lies ordinarily bring someone down, but the Jews’ lie against the Lord did not bring him down; it greatly exalted his power. For they lied so that he would be crucified. He was crucified, died, and rose again, and in this his power shone forth most brilliantly. For it was greater to rise after death than not to die.

The other signs that he performed he also worked [Col. 0820D] through his own servants; but this one he performed specially through himself alone, and therefore it is the greatest of all the others. The Lord himself also showed this when he said: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth.”

And when they asked him, “What sign will you give us, since you do these things?” he answered: “Destroy this temple,” and so forth. They also lied to him in this, because they charged him with having said: “Destroy this temple.” This was a lie on their part, because he had not said it in that sense; yet it was true, because Christ himself truly destroyed it. He handed himself over, and God the Father handed him over, and Judas handed him over. Judas betrayed his master out of greed, whereas Christ gave himself out of grace. Judas received the reward of wickedness, whereas Christ has the praise of grace.

They lied to him in the same way when they brought false witnesses [Col. 0821A] who denied that he had risen. The number of liars increased so that the reward of believers might increase. When the Lord rose, he appeared to his disciples, not to his enemies; when he was crucified, however, he appeared to everyone. After rising, the Lord appeared only to the faithful, so that those who wished might believe and have the hope of resurrection.

This verse can also be expounded differently, so that it means: Say to God, so that you may understand: “Lord, how fearful are your works,” that is, how greatly your works ought to be feared by all human beings, and especially by the ungrateful. What works? These, namely, that the King of angels became one of mortal human beings; that he who is invisible in his own nature became visible in ours; that the incomprehensible wished to be comprehended; and other such things. These works of yours, I say, are truly fearful.

Yet your enemies, the Jews, will lie “in the abundance of your power,” that is, in those signs through which your great power will be shown. For they said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons,” and many similar things. Yet this will be for you, that is, for your glory [Col. 0821B], because their falsehood will be recognized; and the more intense it has been, the more powerful your glory will be.

**All the earth.** Your enemies indeed lie about you and do not worship you. Therefore, Lord, let “all the earth,” that is, the earthly condition of the Gentiles converted, adore you, that is, venerate you in their minds; let it sing praise to you with its mouth and sing a psalm in its deeds—and let it do this not for its own praise but for the glorification of your name.

**Come and see.** He shows how they ought to adore the Lord and sing his praises. Come, you Gentiles who confess; leave those who lie, and see the works that ought to be seen, namely, the works of God, so that you may believe in the God whose purposes concerning the sons of men are fearful.

For the Son of Man is fearful in his purposes concerning the sons of men: they devised bitter and deceitful plans, namely, to crucify and kill him; but he devised plans to blind and save. The humble were to be saved, and the proud blinded. [Col. 0821C] He blinded them so that, having been blinded, they might be humbled; having been humbled, they might confess; and, confessing, they might be saved.

Or alternatively: “He is fearful in his purposes concerning the sons of men,” because the plan which they devised for the death of one person he turned toward the salvation of many.

**He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the river on foot; there we rejoiced in him.** Observe, I say, the works of God. What are those works? These, namely, that he turned the sea—that is, those who previously were bitter through falsehood, turbulent through wicked desires, and, through detraction, like fish devouring one another—into dry land, that is, he made them arable land, thirsty for sweet water, that is, sound teaching, so that they might say: “My soul thirsted for you, Lord, like a land without water.”

And those who previously were the sea, placed in the river, will pass through it on foot. The river is our mortal life, which possesses no stability but is always in motion. We entered this river riding, that is, through pride and transgression in our first parent. But we cannot pass through this river except by repenting, that is, unless we humble ourselves.

For the hope of a certain resurrection has been given to us, in which there will be nothing blameworthy in the soul and nothing changeable in the body. But we cannot reach it unless we humble our souls and imitate him who said: “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world.”

A person can both disturb and calm this river for himself. If the wretched soul is carried away by desires, the more violently it is carried away, the more it disturbs the river and plunges itself into it. Therefore let the wretched soul stand either on the bank or at least in the river, and not be carried away by the waves of wicked desire. Let it humble itself, so that at some time it may be able to swim out.

This is what he says: Those who previously were the sea, placed in the river through pride [Col. 0821D], will pass through the river on foot, that is, through humility; and there, that is, in the passage, we will rejoice not in ourselves but in him. Through ourselves we were saddened, because through our pride we fell; but in him we will rejoice, because through him we will truly rise again. [Col. 0822A]

He says “in him” because, although he was humbled for a time through our weakness, he nevertheless rules—not through something else, as many rule through their soldiers, but by his own power. He rules with a dominion that continues forever, because Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more.

Nor did he grant this grace, namely the passage mentioned above, only to the Jews, although he paid such a price, that is, although he offered himself; his eyes also look upon the Gentiles, that is, he looked mercifully upon the Gentiles, because he granted them the same grace, namely the hope of resurrection. [Col. 0822B]

Therefore let those who are “exasperated,” that is, the Jews who begrudge this grace to the Gentiles and thereby exasperate God, that is, make him angry, saying: “What benefit did the works of the law bring us? Or what value did the writings of the prophets have for us? Behold, the Gospel for us and the Gospel for the Gentiles; behold, the hope of resurrection for us and the hope of resurrection for the Gentiles,” and similar things—such people, I say, should no longer exalt themselves, that is, presume upon their righteousness or their merits. For the law is not their justification but their transgression.

Therefore let them humble themselves in themselves, recognizing that they are equal to the Gentiles, because Scripture enclosed everything under sin, so that they might be exalted in him who rules forever.

This can also be referred to the Gentiles, so that it means: He looked mercifully upon the Gentiles; but those Gentiles who exasperate him by remaining in their unbelief and failing to attend to the grace of their calling should no longer exalt themselves, that is, they should no longer presume upon the greatness of their intelligence or the freedom of their will. Rather, let them become weak in themselves so that they may be exalted in him.

**Bless our God, you nations, and make the voice of his praise heard.** Because the Lord’s eyes look upon the nations, therefore, nations, bless God. Or the passage may simply be continued in this way: Come, I say, you nations, and bless God, that is, do good works, so that those who see them may glorify your Father God who is in [Col. 0822C] heaven.

I say “your God,” that is, the God who is not only the God of the Jews but also of the nations. The earlier perfected ones who speak here say this in order to teach by it that, through the Holy Spirit, they foresaw the Gentiles being called to grace just as the Jews were.

“Bless,” I say, “and make the voice of his praise heard,” that is, humble yourselves in all things so that others may hear, that is, understand, with what voice you praise God. For this is the voice by which God is truly praised: that no one attributes anything to himself or presumes upon himself, but refers everything to God, saying: “By the grace of God I am what I am.”

**He set my soul toward life, and did not allow my feet to be shaken.** Bless, I say, you nations, God—the God who justified both us and the Jews, who could not be justified through the law by us, just as he justified you.

This is understood equivalently when he says: “The God who set my soul, rescued from death, toward life,” that is, who humbled it toward true life, and who also gave me perseverance, that is, made me stable. For he did not allow my inner feet, that is, [Col. 0822D] my affections, to be shaken, that is, to be moved by something that could truly be called a disturbance, so that I would be disturbed—that is, moved inwardly in such a way that I would also be moved outwardly, bringing that inward movement into action.

**For you tested us, O God; you examined us by fire, as silver is examined.** It is as though he said: How could there be disturbance in you? Because we suffer many temptations and tribulations. Why do you suffer? Because you, God, tested us, that is, led us into testing. He shows how he tested us: you examined us by fire, that is, by the most fervent tribulation, just as silver is examined.

It is as though he said: You set us on fire, but you did not reduce us to ashes. You set us on fire not to destroy us but to purify us. Silver is examined not to be destroyed but to be purified.

Another comparison, already given elsewhere, can also be drawn from examined silver. For just as examined silver, when beaten, does not fly apart but grows in length and breadth, so those who have been thoroughly refined by the fire of tribulation for the sake of faith, when beaten by enemies [Col. 0823A], do not fly apart, that is, they do not fail in charity. Rather, their charity extends in breadth and reaches even to their enemies, while in length it is carried forward through perseverance.

**You brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our back.** He shows the testing in its several parts. It is as though he said: You truly examined us, because in this and that way you brought us into a snare—that is, into chains, prison, and similar things, by which the flesh might indeed be overcome and the soul overwhelmed; yet through which we would not be entangled but freed.

And you placed tribulations upon our back, that is, you made us the anvil of every tribulation. We had been standing upright in a bad way, but you bent us, so that, once bent, we might be raised upright in a good way.

Moreover, you placed men over our heads, that is, you gave wicked men, namely tyrants, such power over us that they could even pronounce a capital sentence against us. For we endured those above us whom we knew to be worse than ourselves.

In this way we passed unharmed through the fire [Col. 0823B] of adversity and tribulation, because adversity did not break us. Thus we also passed unharmed through water, that is, through prosperity, because prosperity did not exalt us. For it is not safe to pass through water, since prosperity easily dissolves a person unless he has first been fully hardened in the furnace of tribulation. A clay vessel, unless it is first consolidated, dissolves from the heat when placed in water.

We passed, I say, through fire and water, and you led us unharmed out of fire and water. You led us into refreshment, that is, so that we might have a refreshed conscience. For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience.

And from this refreshment you will lead us into the most fervent fire, because “I will enter your heavenly house while being a burnt offering,” since I will be wholly kindled by the fire of the most ardent charity, so that I may be a burnt offering to God. For *holocaust* is interpreted as “wholly burned,” and he ought to say: “I will enter your house as a burnt offering.” But because the one who speaks here is one person in many, he says: “I will enter among burnt offerings,” because each person will be a burnt offering there. [Col. 0823C]

And there I will repay you, God, my vows, that is, the things which it is right for me to repay you, namely, a hymn of praise, in accordance with: “And with all the host of the heavenly army we sing the hymn of your glory, without end saying [s. f. d.].” My vows, I say, which my inner lips, that is, the lips of my heart, because I speak to you, distinguished from the outward vows as offerings to you.

And which my outer mouth also spoke in tribulation, because not even tribulation could tear these vows from me—that is, your praise. The person who praises God in tribulation is not broken by tribulation, but always says with blessed Job, that excellent singer to the lyre: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

For this reason he says: “In my tribulation,” because tribulation is useful and necessary, since it makes a person more devoted.

**I will offer you marrow-filled burnt offerings, with the incense of rams; I will offer you oxen with goats.** I will repay you, I say, my vows. And what vows? Namely, I will offer you marrow-filled burnt offerings, that is, pleasing offerings. For fat offerings were more acceptable. I will offer you complete praise and inward charity, which please you. [Col. 0823D]

And I will do this with the incense of rams, that is, through holy prayer offered for me by rams, that is, by the holy fathers who begot us in the faith, and through my prayer, which does not disagree with the tradition of those holy fathers. Such prayer is as pleasing to God as the scent of incense is sweet to someone.

For what is truly pleasing to God is proved by the authority of the holy fathers not to be discordant with their teaching.

I will offer burnt offerings, I say, and I will offer you oxen, that is, my teachers who thresh me. And I will offer you goats, that is, those who stink with sins, not goats by themselves only, but so that oxen may be with goats—that is, so that those who were previously goats may be threshed by the oxen and incorporated into them. For this sacrifice too pleases you: that sinners be converted here and incorporated with the good.

Nor should it trouble you that he says: “I will offer oxen and goats,” because in that earlier people who speak here, the converted were [Col. 0824A], as it were, both oxen and goats together.

This whole passage can also be read as referring to the present, so that it means: I will finally enter your heavenly house; and, in order that I may enter, I will meanwhile repay you my vows, namely those which my inner lips distinguished, that is, separated: that I accuse myself and praise you; that I call you Lord and myself servant; that you have no need of me, while I cannot exist without you; and similar things.

And what my outer mouth spoke especially in tribulation, where I ought to be more devoted. He says “my tribulation,” that is, tribulation useful and necessary for me.

“My burnt offerings,” I say, “my lips distinguished”: vows to be repaid to you. In making this distinction I will offer my burnt offerings to you, that is, offerings filled inwardly with charity, so that I may not love you only superficially but with inward love, and so that outwardly they may be made fat with faith, hope, and good works.

For an animal filled with marrow is full of marrow inwardly and fat outwardly. It is as though he said: What is to be offered to your majesty ought not to be empty and dry—empty of charity and dry of faith or hope. [Col. 0824B]

And I will do this either with the incense of rams, as we said above, or because some books have *cum incensu* (“with burning”), which signifies a conflagration. Thus we can say: I will offer you my burnt offerings with the burning of rams, that is, by setting fire to and destroying in myself wantonness, which is signified by the ram.

And I will offer you oxen with goats, that is, both oxen and goats likewise with burning: I will set fire in myself to stubbornness and pride, which are signified by the ox, and I will set fire in myself to the stench of sins, which is signified by the goat. I will offer these things, burned up, to you, because this will be a pleasing sacrifice to you.

**Come, hear, and I will tell all you who fear God what he has done for my soul.** This is another summons of the Gentiles. It is not excessive that they are called so many times, since some are still sluggish, although they have been called many times.

It is as though he said: Come, distant nations; bless God, you peoples. You also, all who fear God with chaste fear, come with the steps of faith, hear with the ear that hears, and I will tell you. There is no telling unless there has first been fear. [Col. 0824C]

What will I tell you? Namely, what great good God has done for my soul.
