The earlier ones among the Jews who speak in this psalm, not begrudging evangelical grace and the incorporation of the Gentiles, announce this to them so that they may come to the faith more attentively and receive the same grace as they themselves have received.

**To him I cried with my mouth, and I exalted him under my tongue.** I will tell you, I say, what great things God has done for my soul, because he did these two things for me above all: whereas previously I cried out with a mouth that was not truly my own, now I cried with my own mouth.

Previously I cried to Jupiter, Saturn, and the other demons; now I cry to the one true God. A person does not cry with his own mouth if, even when he acts attentively enough, he does not act with a devout intention. But someone cries with his own mouth, in harmony with his heart, when what he does or says outwardly proceeds from a devout intention.

In short, it means: God did these two chief good things for me, so that I might cry to him and cry with my own mouth, that is, cry most earnestly. [Col. 0824D]

And therefore I cried to him because I exalted him, that is, placed him above all things, “under my tongue,” that is, in my heart. Or rather, I rejoiced especially in him, since some books read *exsultavi* (“I rejoiced”).

The heart is said to be under the tongue because it is, as it were, a subject of the tongue. First comes thought, and then the tongue, that is, speech. Or it is called “under” because thought cannot reveal itself by itself but is opened through the tongue.

**If I had regarded iniquity…** Truly I rejoiced in him under my tongue, because there was no such iniquity in my heart as I would regard—that is, which would please me. For we cannot altogether deny that we have iniquity; if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.

Nor does the person in whose heart there is iniquity exalt God or rejoice in God. Where the neighbor is brought low, God is never exalted. Nor can we serve two masters. [Col. 0825A] Therefore he says: “I did not regard iniquity in my heart.” For, as though he were saying: If I had regarded it, I would not have exalted God, and therefore the Lord would not hear me.

But because I did not regard it, the Lord heard me when I cried to him. And truly he heard me, because he attended to the voice of my supplication, that is, to my earnest supplication made on account of sins.

Therefore blessed be the Lord—and he repeats the reason why: because he did not remove from himself my prayer made for perseverance, nor did he remove his mercy from me in either matter, namely, from my supplication and from my prayer. For he both forgave my sins and gave me steadfastness.

## PSALM LXVI

*To the end; in hymns, a psalm, a song of David.*

### ARGUMENT

This song too foretells the return of the people from Babylon. In it the eagerness of those who returned is expressed in the same words in which the law commands the priests to bless the people.

### EXPLANATION

[Col. 0825B]

“Hymn” and “song” signify praise. To show that this praise is given to the Lord Christ alone, “to the end” is placed first.

After the song of resurrection, the prophet entreats that, having been blessed, we may be led to divine knowledge, which our merits cannot reach. Therefore, in the first part, speaking to the faithful, he asks that he may deserve to be blessed by the Lord along with them, so that, enlightened in heart, they may recognize that the Lord Christ must be proclaimed among all the nations.

Then he says that, once converted to the Lord, the peoples are to confess to him the spirit of prophecy, because he judges the nations in equity. Third, he repeats the same verse which he spoke above, adding this as a mystery: the earth has now yielded its fruit, and therefore, by repeating the word, he asks that we ought to be blessed.

### COMMENTARY

**May God have mercy on us and bless us.** “To the end; [Col. 0825C] in hymns, a psalm, a song of David.” A prayer.

David—the holy men of the primitive people, patriarchs, prophets, and also the holy apostles—foreseeing through the Holy Spirit that the Jews and the Gentiles would in the future be incorporated into one body, that evangelical grace and the glory of resurrection would be shared by both, pray in this psalm that throughout the whole world those other sheep may be enlightened by God’s face shining upon them, a face that had been especially darkened in them by idolatry; that they may be gathered into one thing and become one flock, because there is one shepherd.

He exhorts us not to despair of those who are outside, but always to pray for them, that they may enter and be within with us, and to imitate those who pray in this way: “May God have mercy on us and bless us.”

The Lord and our Father is rightly called a farmer, in accordance with the Apostle’s testimony: “You are God’s agriculture; you are God’s building.” He cultivates us so that he may dwell in us as in his building, and thus have mercy on us. He also cultivates us as his field and as his vineyard, so that we may bring forth much fruit, and thus [Col. 0825D] he blesses us.

Let us therefore sing these words to him as to a farmer who waters us, saying them not with barren devotion or an empty voice, but with a truthful heart: “May God have mercy on us by dwelling in us, and bless us so that we may bring forth much fruit.”

When God blesses us, or when we bless God, we are the ones in need; he is neither increased by our blessing nor diminished by our cursing. But whoever curses him is diminished, and likewise whoever blesses him is increased. His blessing in us comes first; what follows is that we bless him. His blessing is like rain, while ours is like a flood.

People ask in many ways to be blessed by him, that is, to be multiplied. Some seek increase in money, others in power, others in glory, others in children, others in fields, and others in one thing or another. This blessing is also given to enemies.

There is another blessing, however, reserved for friends alone. That temporal blessing is a common advantage of the good and the wicked, because it is given both to [Col. 0826A] good and wicked people and taken away from both good and wicked people.

If such things were given only to the good, the wicked would think that God ought to be worshiped solely for those goods. If they were given only to the wicked, the weak would hesitate to believe, and those still less capable of the kingdom of God would be even less capable, because they would fear that these temporal goods would be lacking to them.

Likewise, if such things were taken away only from the good, there would be fear in the weak. If they were taken away only from the wicked, people would think that those things were true goods, since the wicked would be punished by their removal. Therefore God both gives and takes away these things alike from the good and the wicked.

He gives them to the good to comfort them on their journey; to the wicked he gives them so that, through the good, he may admonish them to seek other goods which they do not share with the wicked. When he gives these things to the good, let them not be lifted up by them; when he takes them away, let them not be broken. When he gives them, let them possess them not for condemnation but for consolation.

But with what blessing does the one who speaks here ask to be blessed by him? Certainly not with temporal blessing, which he does not regard as a great thing, but with that other blessing which he reserves for friends and gives only to the [Col. 0826B] just: namely, that his face may shine upon us.

For he makes this sun shine commonly upon the good and the wicked, and cattle also see this light together with the good and the wicked. But he asks for that other light which is given only to the just: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.”

The one who speaks here asks for this: that he may shine his face upon us, that is, show us his face, that is, his will—what he wishes us to do—so that what was hidden from us may be opened, namely, the truth of his commandments, and what existed but was hidden from us may be illuminated upon us, that is, revealed to us. This expresses the same thing as before, but more explicitly.

Or alternatively: “May he shine his face upon us,” that is, may he show us his image. It is as though he said: You impressed your face upon us, Lord; you made us according to your image; you made us your coin. But your image ought not to remain in darkness. Therefore send the rays of your wisdom, so that they may drive away our darkness [Col. 0826C] and your face may shine in us, that is, so that we may recognize your image in ourselves, in accordance with what is said in the Song of Songs: “If you know yourself, O beautiful among women,” that is, if you attend to the fact that you were made in the image of God.

It is as though he said: O beautiful one, that is, O precious soul redeemed by the blood of the spotless Lamb, consider how valuable you are; think about what was given for you.

Let us therefore say and desire that he may shine his face upon us. Truly, the face of God which we bear is sacred in his image. But the wicked do not wish to attend to the image of God in themselves, so that his face may shine upon them. Let them say: “Enlighten my darkness, Lord.” As though they were saying: I am in the darkness of sins; let the ray of your wisdom scatter my darkness, so that your face may appear; and, if it should appear through me, let what has been made deformed be restored by you, who formed it.

Let us therefore sing to the Lord our God as to a farmer, so that he may have mercy on us, bless us, and shine his face upon us—not with respect to himself, since he was never without light, but because his [Col. 0826D] face, obscured by the clouds of our sins, was, as it were, beneath us. Therefore let him illuminate it in us, so that it may be above us, that is, so that his excellence may appear, and thus he may have mercy on us.

This differs rightly from what was said above. In the earlier passage, “have mercy” is understood as the first mercy, which occurs at the beginning; here a greater mercy is understood, because it follows after blessing, that is, after abundant fruit. For the more good things or gifts God gives someone, the more he has mercy on that person.

That we may know on earth. To this end, I say, may your countenance shine upon us, and may you have mercy on us, so that in this land—that is, in this Idumea, a land pathless and without water, in which it is difficult to find the way—we may know your way, that is, the way leading to you, namely, that way which says: “I am the way.” And lest anyone fear going astray on this way, he adds: “And the truth.” Again, lest anyone fear failing, he continues: “And the life,” namely, [Col. 0827A] in which you will rest and not fail. And what that way is, he subsequently explains: namely, “that we may know your salvation,” that is, your Savior Christ, not only in Africa but among all the nations.

“Let the peoples confess to you, O God.” Because he said by way of desire, “May his countenance shine upon us,” so that we may know the way, therefore, in order to assure us that he has been heard, he urges us to confess, as though the way were already known, saying: O God, may the Jewish people confess their sin to you, and may they confess—that is, praise your glory—and may all the other peoples also, namely the Gentiles, confess their iniquity and your mercy. For, as the Apostle testifies, the nations honor God because of his mercy: let them accuse themselves, glorify you, condemn themselves, and praise you. Let a person find you to be his punisher, so that he may present himself to you as his salvation. Why are you afraid to confess? Do not fear confessing, because the one who confesses will be saved, while the one who remains silent will be condemned.

And because such confession [Col. 0827B] is not for punishment but for pardon, he therefore adds: “Let the nations rejoice,” any nations whatsoever, if they confess inwardly; and let them exult outwardly—that is, let them possess complete joy. It is as though he said: Thieves who have confessed weep before a human judge, but faithful people who have confessed rejoice before God. And from what should they rejoice, from what should they exult? From the confession itself, clearly, because you seek confession for this purpose: to free the humble. And also because of the dignity of the judge, since you—whom no one deceives and whom money does not corrupt—judge all peoples in equity, that is, so that you do not punish those who have punished themselves, but punish those who have not punished themselves.

And because the nations, crooked and perverse, could more properly find [Col. 0827C] in that equity of judgment a cause for sadness than for joy, he therefore sets forth beforehand the reason for it. It is as though he said: For this reason the nations ought to rejoice and exult in so equitable a judgment of yours: because on earth—that is, in this earthly life, which is full of errors—you so direct the nations that, although the judgment is equitable, they need not fear it.

And because the nations, now walking uprightly in faith and now doing good works in Christ, are navigating across this sea, and because seawater enters the ship through the tiniest cracks and crevices and creates a bilge, this bilge must be pumped out daily lest it fill or overwhelm the ship: by prayer, by giving alms, by fasting, and also by saying with a pure heart, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive,” and so forth. Therefore this outstanding orator, most excellent preacher and exhorter, repeats for this second confession—which pertains to the daily washing of the feet—the verse that he earlier set forth for the first and difficult confession, saying: “Let the peoples confess to you, O God,” the Jewish peoples; “let all the peoples also confess to you.”

And they ought to confess, because the earth—that is, our life—which was formerly full of thorns and produced thistles, has now yielded its fruit, that is, has performed good works by humbling itself and confessing. It would not have yielded this fruit unless it had been watered by those clouds of which it was said [Col. 0827D]: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon that harlot.” Through those clouds the Lord both thunders with threats, flashes with miracles, and waters with words. Let us therefore fear him when he thunders or flashes through those clouds. Let us receive him when he waters us; and, so that the earth may always produce fruit, therefore may he bless us—that is, may God the Father give us increase.

“May our God bless us.” That is, may the Son, made a participant in our weakness, bless us, so that we too might become participants in his glory. May God also bless us—that is, the Holy Spirit, one God with the Father and the Son.

This is also customarily understood in the following way: The earth—that is, our flesh, namely the virgin Mary—gave its fruit, because she bore the Savior, both ours and her own. Therefore may God the Father of that fruit bless us. “May our God bless us,” that is, the fruit itself. “May God bless us,” that is, the Holy Spirit. And in this blessing may all the ends of the earth fear him, fearing him chastely.

This was fulfilled when God the Father filled the whole world with the sons of his [Col. 0828A] Only-begotten as co-heirs and adopted them into the kingdom. He begot one, but did not wish him to remain alone, because he made many brothers for him—not by begetting them, but by adopting them.

## ON PSALM 67

**For the end. A psalm of a song. To David himself.**

### ARGUMENT

When David, after the Ark of the Covenant had undergone frequent removals, finally transferred it to himself amid great rejoicing, he sang this song. Remembering both that journey and its former transportation in the wilderness, he composed the psalm as though in the person of the leaders of that time, placing at its head the very verse that Moses also used to sing whenever the Ark was moved as a sign of departure. In another sense, the prophet announces the resurrection of Christ and the glories that followed.

### EXPLANATION

David signifies the Lord, as the ending itself declares. This is a long psalm, [Col. 0828B] marked beforehand by five diapsalms, through which we have indicated its sections. The whole psalm speaks through mystical comparisons; it is filled with evangelical mysteries and is shown to be especially important in its description of Christ’s ascension.

At the first entrance of the psalm, the prophet says what will happen to the Lord’s enemies, or what will befall the faithful at the future judgment. Secondly, he signifies the virtues that he bestowed upon the Jewish people, and then says how, from these, he perfected the Church. Thirdly, under the appearance of a mountain, he designates the Lord the Savior, recalling what benefits he bestowed upon the Church when he raised it up through the gift of his resurrection. Fourthly, he declares that the pride of the Lord’s enemies must be shattered, and says that conversions and martyrdoms will be brought about among both sexes, even from the worst people, when the Lord’s coming as Savior has shone upon the world. Fifthly, he says that the Lord must be blessed in the churches, where the Apostles and Christ himself preached, and he entreats him to preserve the gifts that he bestowed upon his faithful. He also urges those who dwell [Col. 0828C] in this world as in Egypt and Ethiopia to come swiftly to the Lord. Sixthly, he urges the whole human race to sing psalms to the Lord Christ, who has now revealed the miracles of his resurrection, and then concludes the psalm with praise of the Lord.

### COMMENTARY

**“Let God arise; let them be scattered.”** “For the end. A psalm of a song. To David himself.” These words refer to the end of time and are attributed to David himself; they truly constitute a psalm of a song. According to blessed Augustine, a song properly means that praise which is uttered by the mouth. A psalm, however, means that musical composition which is produced on a musical instrument called the psalterium, through the plucking of strings and the touch of the fingers.

“Song” is also understood as the intellect of the mind, because the soul acts well within itself by holy meditation and thought. For it is said: “And holy thought will preserve you.” This is known only to God, because he alone sees our thoughts. “Psalm” is likewise understood as exterior action, [Col. 0828D] which becomes known even to one’s neighbors.

Since these two are joined together, with “song” preceding, such action and such praise must be understood as pertaining to inward rejoicing, as here. For to sing such a hymn and to persist in this way with one’s God proceeds [Col. 0828D] from inward rejoicing: the saints of the earlier people, foreseeing through the holy prophetic Spirit that Christ would come in the flesh, die and rise again for us, ascend, and send the Holy Spirit, rejoice over the establishment of God’s holy place—that is, the Church—and over such an institution, and so they sing hymns. Thus they act with the Lord their God, and exhort us also to rejoice over it, because it pertains to our salvation that we sing a hymn, so that at last we may arrive at true rejoicing and praise without end.

Or, if, as some wish, this passage concerns the future resurrection, we shall say that the saints, contemplating that true glory of the resurrection, exhort us to sing and to play psalms now, so that we may be brought to it.

According to the earlier intention, [Col. 0829A] the meaning is as though he said: Let what is to come arrive; let what has been promised be accomplished. Let man die, and let God and man arise, and let his enemies be scattered. And so it happened: Christ arose, who is God blessed above all; and his enemies, the Jews, in the very place where they raised hatred against him and crucified their king, were conquered by the Romans, then taken captive and scattered throughout the whole world.

Nor indeed do they hate him whom they did not see—that is, Christ—yet they fear him whom they have present in his own people, in whom he appears. And so what follows came to pass: those who once hated him now flee from his face. For flight properly means fear of the soul. They flee from him spiritually, not bodily. How could they flee bodily from him who is present everywhere, and of whom it is said: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?”

They flee from him not in body but in mind [Col. 0829B]; they flee from him not by hiding but by fearing. Nor do they fear the face that they do not see, but the face that they have present—namely, the one of whom it was said: “From now on you will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven.” For he who once spoke through himself will speak through clouds, that is, through heralds. And the Jews fear this face of his—that is, the heralds in whom he appears and speaks—and they fear his whole Church, both because they are partly subject to it and because they abhor the whole Christian religion.

**“As smoke vanishes.”** Let the enemies, the Jews, be scattered, and let them vanish as smoke vanishes. Smoke rising from fire ascends on high and so vanishes. In the same way the Jews, lifted up in pride against Christ by the fire of their hatred, cried out: “Crucify him, crucify him!” After he had been seized, they insulted him and mocked him as he hung upon the cross. But those who had feared him as victors soon vanished as the vanquished, and so they perished, because they accomplished nothing. It follows:

**“As wax melts before the fire, so let sinners perish [Col. 0829C] before God’s face.”** Although this may be understood positively of the Jews, in the following sense—“Thus may the Jewish sinners perish before God’s face,” that is, through the heralds—it means: May the hardness of their hearts melt into tears of repentance through the fire of the steadfastness of the holy martyrs, or of any of those who are fervent in spirit and serve the Lord, just as wax placed near fire melts.

This is said with reference to certain Jews, namely those who approached the Apostles and said: “What shall we do, brothers?” and so forth. In accordance with this, the following verse will continue quite simply: “And having been made righteous, let them feast,” and so forth.

I admit that it can be understood in this way, yet here he seems chiefly to threaten them with eternal punishment: namely, that when the Lord comes in the majesty of the Father and of the holy angels, like fire to burn the wicked and illuminate the good—for in fire there are both heat and brightness—then the Jewish sinners who persist in their sins will be removed from God’s face. For “Let the ungodly be taken away, lest he see the glory of God”; let them perish, thrust into eternal darkness, as wax melts when brought near fire.

Then, by contrast, let the righteous [Col. 0829D] feast—that is, rejoice and exult in certain refreshment—in God’s presence, because they will behold God face to face and delight at that time, that is, in joy without sadness. For now the righteous rejoice, but not without sadness. It is said to them: “Serve the Lord with fear, and exult in him with trembling.” And elsewhere: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.” Therefore there is not yet true joy; true joy will come then, when sadness will never again arise.

The same verse may also be understood of the present, according to the earlier positive interpretation, in this way: Let sinners who have been made righteous feast—that is, let them be refreshed by the word of God as by a sweet banquet—and let them exult in God’s presence, that is, in their heart, where God sees them and is seen by them, and where they delight in this joy. For true joy is to know God.

What was said at the beginning [Col. 0830A] may also be referred not only to the Jews but to all enemies, so that it may be understood thus: Let man die; let God and man rise; let him ascend; and, after the Holy Spirit has been sent, let him arise into the knowledge of the nations. Let all his enemies be scattered with a good scattering, namely, so that from enemies they may become friends.

And let those who hate him—that is, those who hate the Christian name—flee from his face; let them flee from the face of the angry one to the face of the reconciled one. And just as smoke lifted high vanishes, so let them vanish and be caught in their pride. But those who do not wish this—namely, sinners persisting in their sins—let them perish, at last removed from God’s face, as wax melts before the fire. By contrast, let the righteous feast, as stated above.

This series may also be read in a third way from the beginning, with the whole passage referred to the final resurrection, so that it means: Let man indeed die, and let God still arise as man. At last, however, let him come to judgment in the majesty of the Father and of the holy angels; let him arise—that is, rise and appear manifestly to all—as the true God. Then let his enemies be scattered, as they truly will be gravely scattered, because they will be condemned. And let all who hate him, removed from his face, be scattered in such a way that they flee—that is, if they do not depart from him in the hope of returning.

For “to flee” properly applies [Col. 0830B] when return is despaired of. Therefore this says more than what was said earlier. They could be scattered for a time and then restored. For this reason he adds: “Let them flee and perish in their pride” at that time, as smoke vanishes. Truly the one who is separated from true being will perish. Let sinners, rejected from God’s face—“Let the ungodly be taken away, lest he see the glory of God”—perish when the fire of a strict sentence has been applied, as wax melts when fire is applied. By contrast, let the righteous feast, and so forth.

**“Sing to God.”** This continues in the same way according to the interpretations given above, namely as follows: So that you may rejoice and delight both here and in the future, therefore sing to God—that is, sing for the praise of God—and sing a psalm to his name, not glorifying your own.

He sings to God whose heart is always attentive to holy meditation and thought; but he sings a psalm who performs good works outwardly for the edification of his neighbor. It is as though he said: By singing and playing psalms, make a way for him in yourselves and in others—that is, prepare a way for the Lord—so that, through the beautiful feet of those who proclaim the Gospel, the hearts of believers may be made passable for him.

And I say, [Col. 0830C] “for him who ascended above the setting,” that is, who conquered the world, because by his death he destroyed our entire setting, that is, our death.

Or otherwise: all those who have received the faith and perform good works are called “risings”; all those for whom the true sun of righteousness has set are “settings.” Their understanding and reason have been darkened, and therefore their works are dead. The Lord has ascended above these in such a way that he overcomes the setting in them, because by his grace he also illuminates such people and brings about good works in them.

Matthew was such a person, whom the Lord took from the tax office, and Paul, whom he turned away from persecuting the Church and made its patron. And rightly did he ascend above the setting, because “Lord” is especially his name: he is the ruler of all and the redeemer of all.

He said [Col. 0830D]: “Make a way for him.” And because those who make a way endure many evils—for all who wish to live devoutly in Christ must suffer persecution, especially those who strive to live both devoutly and justly, devoutly with regard to God and justly with regard to their neighbor—he admonishes them by word and example, and therefore adds: “Exult in his presence.”

It is as though he said: Even if you are outwardly troubled, nevertheless exult in his presence, that is, within yourselves, where he sees you, rejoicing in hope and enduring tribulation. I say, exult nonetheless, because those who trouble you will not exult; rather, they will be troubled. For whoever he may be will bear judgment, removed from his face—that is, from the Lord’s face—of him who is the father of orphans, that is, who comforts orphans, and who is the judge, that is, the defender, of widows.

He calls “orphans” those whom the sword of God’s word has separated from the world as from a father and comforter, so that they are separated from the fellowship of worldly hope. By “widows,” understand something more: namely, those who, although formerly devoted to carnal things, have now been completely separated from every carnal delight, just as a widow is a woman who was formerly joined to a husband but is now widowed and separated from him.

And lest such people, whom he calls widows and orphans, seem to be desolate, he shows that they are not desolate, because he himself comforts them by making them his holy place and dwelling in them. He says this as follows:

**“God, being in his place.”** [Col. 0831A] That is, in his faithful, who are his holy place, established by him. And by what means was it established? By this, namely, that he makes them “of one manner,” that is, of one mind and consenting with one another, in accordance with the saying: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul.”

God, I say, being in his holy place, makes those whom he has made of one manner dwell in a house—that is, because they are of one manner, they cling firmly to ecclesiastical things.

**“He who led out the bound.”** He shows how he makes them dwell there: namely, because he led out the bound, that is, those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, since he loosed the bonds of their sins. He did this in strength, so that those who were formerly bound and powerless, once loosed, might be able to walk in the way of God’s commandments.

Likewise, he led out [Col. 0831B] those who provoked them, because they dwell in tombs. These are people who prefer to dwell in the body—that is, in carnal pleasures—and to yield to flesh and blood and to dead works, in which they rot and stink like corpses in tombs. They are those of whom it was said: “When a man is dead, as though he did not exist, confession perishes”; and: “The beasts have rotted in their dung.” And: “When the sinner has fallen into the depths of iniquity, he despises.”

The Lord will lead out both those people and these most abandoned ones, because it is one thing to desire righteousness, as the bound do; another to attack righteousness, which belongs to those who dwell in tombs; one thing to wish to be freed from evil, another to defend evil and refuse to confess it.

Yet the Lord, who wonderfully accomplished this in bodies [Col. 0831C]—since he freed a woman who had been ill for seventeen years from her infirmity, and raised Lazarus, who had been four days in the tomb—is able to accomplish it even more wonderfully in conduct. For he will make both the bound and the buried fit for the construction of his holy place.

**“O God, when you went forth.”** He turns to the Lord himself. It is as though he said: You will indeed lead out the bound and the buried, because when you went forth in the sight of your people—that is, so that you might be seen by your people, who had been released and raised up by you—then this occurred.

God’s going forth takes place when he appears in his works—not in just any works, but in those known by people who know how to contemplate his works, not the visible but the invisible: that is, the grace by which he both looses the bound and raises the buried.

When, I say, you went forth, and when you passed through either the desert [Col. 0831D] or, already being in the desert—that is, among the Gentiles, who were a desert because they had received neither the Law nor the prophets—when this occurs, then the earth—I do not say “was moved,” but “will be moved”—that is, earthly people will be stirred to faith.

He uses the past tense because what is future is as certain to the Holy Spirit as what is past. And the earth will be moved because the heavens, of which it was said, “The heavens declare the glory of God,” have distilled—or, rather, will distill—the evangelical grace. And this is not from themselves but from God’s face, that is, through him, because he will dwell in them so present among them that his face will appear in them.

And because those heavens are also mountains, what he first signified by the plural “heavens” he now signifies by the singular “mountain,” saying: “Sinai will distill before God’s face.”

Or by Sinai we may understand Paul, through whom the Law given to Moses on Mount Sinai was chiefly given to the Gentiles. Because Paul was also a zealous defender of the Law, he was better able to teach the agreement of the two laws. For this reason he singled him out from the others, saying: “Sinai,” that is, Paul, “will distill,” because he labored more.

Or, if we turn to the interpretation of the name, Sinai is interpreted as “commandment” or “measure.” Those heavens distilled Sinai—that is, the commandment—because they taught the precepts of the Law spiritually.

It may also be understood in this way: The heavens will distill evangelical grace. And this will not be from themselves but from the face of God, Sinai—that is, from the God of the Law: just as he was the giver of the Law, so also was he the giver of blessing, that is, of grace. He gave the Law in order to frighten the one presuming upon human strength; but he gave blessing in order to save the one who hoped and believed in him.

They will distill, I say, from the face of God [Col. 0832A]—not just any god, but the God of Israel, that is, the one who is God of the true Israelite people. The same will be said in each of the interpretations already given.

**“Rain willingly given.”** The heavens, I say, will distill this rain also, that is, evangelical grace, which they will distill as given not from our merits but from your goodness, in accordance with the saying: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth.”

That rain, I say, you will set apart, that is, give separately, to your inheritance, that is, only to those who believe in you, for faith does not belong to everyone. And because you will give it, that inheritance was weakened—or, rather, “will be weakened”—that is, it will recognize and confess its sin and weakness. But you will perfect it in spiritual gifts, because “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

These three verses mentioned above [Col. 0832B] may also be understood simply according to the historical sense. It is as though he said: You will lead out, Lord, the bound who dwell in tombs. And that you would lead out such people was prefigured when you led the children of Israel out of Egypt, for when you went forth—that is, when you appeared manifestly in the sight of your people, seen by your people—you went before them in a pillar of cloud by day and in a pillar of fire by night.

This prefigured that he would go before his own in the cloud of flesh and in the light of divinity, so that he would be understood by them as true God and true man. By the fact that he went before them in a cloud by day and in fire by night, it was signified that he would appear terrifying to sinners, who are represented by night; but to the righteous, who are understood by day, he would not appear terrifying but gentle. For fire is a more terrifying thing than a cloud.

When, I say, you went forth in this way, and when you passed here and there, leading your people through the desert of the Gentiles—by which it was signified that he would be preached everywhere through the desert of the Gentiles—then the earth was moved. There, it was Mount Sinai; here, it is the hearts of the Gentiles.

And indeed, if the earth, the lowest element, was moved [Col. 0832C], then the heavens too, the higher element, were in a certain way moved, because they distilled manna. And this was from the face of God, that is, through the presence and power of God—not of just any god, but of Sinai, that is, of the God who spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai and gave the Law. From the face, I say, of the God of Israel, that is, of the one who truly presided over the Israelite people.

**“Rain willingly given.”** The heavens, I say, distilled manna [Col. 0832D], and you, God, set apart this rain willingly given—that is, given from goodwill, not from their merits—for your inheritance, namely the manna, to your people, because he did not act in this way toward every nation.

And you will still set it apart, with regard to what it signifies—that is, with regard to evangelical grace—which you will give only to your inheritance. And that inheritance was weakened by that rain, because out of weariness they murmured against the heavenly food, desiring the foods they had been accustomed to eat in Egypt. But you perfected that inheritance.

It would seem that the text ought rather to say, “You struck it,” because, in truth, on account of their murmuring, of all those who had been led out of Egypt only two entered the Promised Land, since all the others first perished. Nevertheless, although it does not fit perfectly, this may be referred to their children, in whom he perfected that inheritance, just as in the Apostles and in others who were chosen from among them.

Here blessed Augustine says that, for the reason given above, this interpretation is not valid according to the literal sense. But because all these things happened to them as figures, he insists that only the allegory should be pursued here.

Nevertheless, within this same interpretation, the final verse may be read according to the letter as follows: “The heavens distilled manna from the face of God of Sinai,” that is, from the God who gave the Law on Mount Sinai. You both set apart and will set apart that willingly given rain—that is, the Law, which was rain because it softened the hardness of their hearts and caused some to bear fruit, and which was willingly given because it was granted not from their merits but from your kindness—for your inheritance: “set apart” with regard to the literal sense, and “will set apart” with regard to the spiritual understanding.

And that Law was weakened [Col. 0833A], because by threatening punishment it made the weak, rather than helping them by grace. But you perfected that Law, because what was impossible for the Law according to the flesh—that is, what could not be fulfilled according to carnal observance—you made easy to fulfill according to spiritual understanding.

Or it may be understood thus: Your inheritance was weakened through the Law because, when falsehood came, sin revived, and because through the Law they received not justification but transgression. But you perfected that inheritance because, when sin abounded and their weaknesses multiplied, they hastened to the physician, groaned, and prayed that, with his help, what was not fulfilled at his command might be fulfilled.

**“Your animals.”** [Col. 0833B] You perfected the inheritance, I say, and in that inheritance animals will dwell—that is, lesser believers who still need to be nourished. Animals, I say, that are yours, not their own; subject to you, not to themselves; free, needing you, not sufficient in themselves.

And for this reason they will dwell there: because you, God, prepared—or made ready—[it] for the poor, that is, for each person who inwardly makes himself poor and humbles himself in that inheritance. And this was not on account of their merits but in your sweetness, that is, in your goodness.

**“The Lord will give.”** [Col. 0833C] He shows what preparation he made and turns to us. It is as though he said: The Lord truly prepares a place for his animals, because he supplies them with food in this way: the Lord will give a word—that is, teaching with which his animals may be fed—to those who proclaim it with great power.

Or, he will give it in the strength by which he led out the bound, so that they may walk in the way of his commandments. Or, “with great power” means with a great display of miracles, according to the saying: “The Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed.”

The Lord, I say, will give the word. He is the King of the powers of the Beloved, that is, he rules those virtues—the heralds of the Beloved—who are already “virtues,” that is, strong in proclaiming, so that they may be such.

And understand that Beloved of whom it was said: “This is my beloved Son.” Beloved, I say, not of just anyone, but specially beloved and chosen, “to divide the spoils of the beautiful house”—or, as the text indicates, “for dividing the spoils of the beautiful house.”

Spoils are properly called [Col. 0833D] what is taken from an enemy. The beautiful house is the Church, as it is found in the Gospel: “When a strong man armed guards his courtyard, all that he possesses is in peace; but when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he will take away his armor and distribute his spoils.”

And so it happened. This Beloved came—that is, Christ came—into the house of the strong man, that is, into the human race, which was inhabited by the strong man, the devil, through the mystery of the Incarnation. He conquered that strong man through the sacrament of the Incarnation.

And the man, Christ in his humanity, captured him, because the devil, believing him to be merely human, laid his hand upon him, in whom he found no right belonging to himself. Therefore, by right, he lost those over whom he had possessed a right: the sons of unbelief, whose infidelity that strong man had formerly used to fulfill his will, and through whom he offered others the cup of death.

The Lord took these vessels away from him, cleansed them through the remission of sins, sanctified them with spiritual gifts, and then distributed them for the beauty of his house—that is, for the adornment of the Church—because he gave some as Apostles, some as evangelists, some as prophets, and some as teachers and pastors, and so forth.

If you sleep among the two lots. This verse is constructed in several ways, while its meaning nevertheless remains the same. In one way it is understood as follows: “The Lord will give the word to those evangelizing”—to you, I mean, who are divided as spoils through the manifestation of the Spirit, for the benefit of the beauty of the house—“if you sleep among the two lots, being wings of a silvered dove.” O you spoils who are divided through the manifestation of the Spirit for the benefit of the beauty of the house, if you sleep among the two lots, then the wings of the silvered dove will be made white in Salmon.

Or thus: O you who are divided, and so forth, if you, being the wings of the silvered dove, sleep among the two lots, while the heavenly one distinguishes kings over her, then those who have received the remission of sins through grace will be made white in Salmon.

Or thus: O you who are divided for the adornment of the house, if you sleep among the two lots, you will be the wings of the silvered dove. Of these constructions, the last and the first are the better, and Blessed Augustine and the other saints chiefly expound this verse according to them.

As for what he says, “among the two lots,” this is a Greek construction. For what Latin says “between me and you,” Greek says “between my middle and yours.” Some say that the two lots are the two Testaments, so that what produces something may be understood through the same thing that is produced. For inheritance is given through a testament, and *cleronomia* in Greek means “inheritance,” while *cleronomos* means “heir.” A *cleros*, however, is a lot, and “lot” is understood as a portion of an inheritance. Hence it was commanded that no lot—that is, no portion of an inheritance—be given to the Levites among their brothers, because they were to be supported by the tithes of the others.

The dove spoken of here is the Church, of whom it is said in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is one, my dove,” and so forth. The Church is called a dove because of her innocence, her frequent lamentation, and many similar qualities. This dove—that is, the Church—is silvered, that is, instructed by the splendor of divine speech.

Her wings are the holy preachers. They are called wings for two reasons: both because through their preaching the glory of the Church is raised up, and because they themselves are lifted to higher things. Hence one of them says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God,” and yet, however highly it may be exalted, they remain joined to the structure of the Church. Therefore he adds: “Whether we are sober, it is for you.”

Divine Scripture commonly takes “sleep” to mean death, as in: “I slept and took my sleep; I slept in confusion.” In this passage, however, “sleep” simply means rest: “to sleep among the two lots” means to rest between the two lots through the authority of the two Testaments, and thus to grant their teachings agreement—namely, so that whenever something is brought forward or proved from them, every dispute may be brought to a peaceful end through tranquil rest.

Thus those who evangelize with great power seem to be admonished that the word of truth is given to them, so that they may evangelize perfectly, if they do not abandon the authority of the two Testaments. And they will be the wings of the silvered dove, through whose preaching the glory of the Church will be exalted.

And the hind parts of her back will be in the pallor of gold. Take “the hind parts of her back” intransitively as that part of the back upon which a burden is borne between the shoulders—namely, as the Greek has it, where certain birds, such as eagles, are accustomed to carry their young. This is the region behind, around the heart, where the wings take root. Thus by “the hind parts of the back” only this is signified: that it bears a burden.

By the wings are signified the two commandments of charity; by gold, wisdom, that is, good conduct. This wisdom pertains to bearing the burden wisely—that is, bearing only the burden that ought to be borne, namely, Christ’s yoke, which does not weigh down but raises up.

The pallor of gold is the greenness of gold. For native gold has a redness, and therefore, if pallor is added to it, greenness is produced from the redness and pallor. This greenness signifies charity, which is always verdant, because it is said of it: “Charity never fails.” Through this charity it comes about that the two commandments of charity are easily fulfilled, and that the burden placed upon us is light. For what is difficult for one who is unwilling is easy for one who loves.

After charity has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, we freely do through love what previously we did servilely through fear, and we have become friends of what is right. For he is not a true friend of what is right who, if it could be done, would not wish what is right to be commanded.

There is another interpretation: by the two lots we may understand not the two Testaments but the two inheritances promised in them. The inheritance of the Old Testament is earthly happiness; that of the New is eternal immortality. Here “to sleep” will be understood as “to die,” as was said above. Thus to sleep among the two lots means to end one’s life between the two inheritances: neither to desire the earthly ardently, but patiently to await the eternal.

For those who serve God—or rather, who refuse to serve him—because they seek happiness in this life have been removed from these sleeps and do not sleep. Driven by inflamed desires, they are propelled into sins and crimes, and they do not rest at all, desiring to acquire and fearing to lose. But “the one who listens to me,” says Wisdom, “will dwell in hope and rest without fear.”

The best death is this: that a person, restraining his desires from earthly things and hoping for eternal blessedness, perseveres to the end and closes the final day of this life. Thus to sleep—that is, to end one’s life—between the two lots means to dwell, if not yet in possession, at least in hope of eternal blessedness, and to rest in the desire for eternal happiness.

For the dying are the wings of the silvered dove, because at the resurrection they will be snatched up to meet Christ in the air, and thus they will always be with the Lord. Or they are called wings for this reason: the more securely they are, the more sublimely the Church is proclaimed through them and raised up, as if by certain wings of exalted praise.

And truly, from the time when the distinction between the two Testaments was revealed, the holy apostles and all the elect up to the present have slept in this way: they have despised desire for an earthly kingdom and desired the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom. And because they have slept so well, the Church, the silvered dove, flies upon these wings and is raised up by praises. For through their fame those who come after them are invited to imitate them; while they sleep in this way, wings are added by which the Church is proclaimed and exalted.

What follows is also varied in this interpretation: “And the hind parts of her back will be in the pallor of gold.” By the back the labor of the present life is signified; by its hind parts, the life that follows and the reward of labor. These hind parts will be in the pallor of gold—that is, in such joy and glory as surpass every other glory, just as gold surpasses every metal. Thus the same thing will be signified by pallor and gold.

But if one wishes to distinguish the meanings, one may say: although their present life is in labor, its hind parts will nevertheless be in gold—that is, in royal splendor. For gold belongs to royal ornamentation, since crowns are made from it. Thus they will be in gold, which is in pallor—that is, in the greenness of gold, namely, in unfailing glory.

While the heavenly one distinguishes kings over her, with snow. “You will be,” I say, “the wings of the silvered dove” for as long as the heavenly one distinguishes kings over her. This belongs to the later interpretation. With respect to the earlier one, it is connected as follows: “The Lord will give the word to you who are divided through the manifestation of the Spirit for the adornment of the house, if you sleep among the two lots”—sleeping, I mean, for as long as that heavenly one, namely, the one who, coming from heaven, is above all things, or who ascended not only above the material heavens but also above all the orders of angels, that is, for as long as Christ distinguishes kings over the dove, the Church.

He calls preachers of the truth “kings,” since they rule both themselves and others in such a way that sin no longer reigns in them, to obey the desires of the flesh. Christ will distinguish these kings over the dove, the Church—that is, by giving some as apostles, others as evangelists, and others in other capacities.

And lest it be thought that these kings possess from themselves the power by which they rule themselves in this way, he shows from where they have it: namely, because they will be made white—that is, they will receive remission of sins, being made comparable to snow. Or “they will be made white with snow,” that is, according to snow. Or they are placed in snow through whiteness, according to the saying: “Though your sins are red like scarlet, they will be made white like snow.”

And this takes place in Salmon, that is, through the one who is understood by “Salmon.” Salmon is a mountain of the region of Palestine, and its interpretation is “shadow.” A shadow is made from two things: light and an intervening body. Therefore by Salmon, that is, by “shadow,” Christ is signified, united from two natures: the one which was in the beginning with God, and the one in human flesh.

Christ makes himself a shade—that is, a defense—through the grace of the Holy Spirit and the protection of his body, for all who believe in him, against the heat of incitements and carnal desires. In accordance with what was said to the glorious Virgin: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you”—that is, he will make you a shade against carnal desires.

This was most truly fulfilled, because she conceived the Lord not by carnal desire but by faithful belief.

He said that they would be made white in Salmon, and he explains what Salmon is by saying that it is the mountain of God. It is that mountain of which it was said: “And in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared.” This is also the stone cut from the mountain without the hands of those who embrace it—that is, Christ, born from the Jewish people without the hands of those who embrace it.

He is, I say, the fat mountain, strengthening the perfect; and he is the coagulated mountain, supplying curdled milk—that is, the milk of doctrine—to nourish the little ones. He is truly the fat mountain, that is, full of every spiritual gift.

And because, as we read in the Gospel, some called this mountain—that is, Christ—John the Baptist, others John, others Jeremiah, and others one of the prophets, the prophetic Spirit warns us not to compare other mountains with this mountain. For even if other mountains are coagulated, because they can nourish the little ones, this is not from themselves but from this mountain.

And he says: “Why do you suppose that coagulated mountains are comparable to this mountain?” Certainly you ought not to, because this mountain is such that in it God was especially well pleased, never displeased. The good pleasure consisted in dwelling in it in such a way that he was perfectly present in it.

For in him, as the Apostle says, “all the fullness of divinity will dwell bodily,” that is, wholly and fully. Therefore, when he says that he dwells specially in this mountain, I say that he does so because through it he dwelt in the others. For this Lord—that is, this mountain—principally dwelt in the other mountains, bringing them to himself as their end; and through this one, God the Father also dwelt in them.

## The chariot of God

For this reason also you ought not to compare the other mountains with this mountain: the others are the chariot of this one, who is God. They carry him as a chariot; he is carried through them to the knowledge of human beings. This chariot is ten-thousandfold in its multitude. A definite number is used for an indefinite one.

This chariot is understood as existing in all true preachers, from the time of grace to the end of the world. Therefore he adds that it is not only in ten thousand but also in a thousand thousands. And although they are sorrowful outwardly, because the just suffer many tribulations, inwardly they are joyful.

Why are they joyful? Because the Lord is in them. How is he in them? In Sinai—that is, in a commandment, not just any commandment but a holy commandment. Although he is sorrowful in bearing it, he rejoices in fulfilling the commandment. The one who gave them the will also grants them to accomplish it according to his good will.

He calls the law a holy commandment, concerning which the Apostle says: “The law indeed is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good.”

## You ascended on high

Therefore, I say, in that chariot there are thousands of joyful ones who previously were thousands of mourners: “because you took captivity”—either death, by which we were held captive, which you took captive by your death, that is, destroyed; or “you took captivity,” that is, us human beings, who previously had been taken captive through Adam’s transgression under the yoke of sin and death, and thus were the captivity of the devil.

You took us, I say, as your inheritance, because after defeating that prince you took us captive in a happy and liberating captivity: so that we, who were previously slaves of sin and free with respect to righteousness, might become slaves of righteousness, liberated from sin.

And thus you ascended on high, namely, to the right hand of the Father, where you made us sit with you; and from there you sent spiritual gifts to human beings. Because you were in them as if in your members, you received the same gifts that you gave.

There is another interpretation that agrees more fully with this one: “He gave gifts to human beings,” although this is found in no translation. But, as Blessed Augustine says, the Apostle inserted it on his own authority.

It can nevertheless be said simply: “You received gifts among human beings,” not gifts other than the human beings themselves, but the human beings themselves. Then the following verse will show whom he received—namely, unbelievers.

According to the earlier interpretation, the connection is as follows: Truly you took captivity, for you received those who did not believe that the true God dwells in human minds, that is, cares for human affairs. By these are understood the gentiles, who truly did not know that God cared for mortal things, because they placed the creature before the Creator.

Or, if the passage is understood of the Jews, it will be said thus: You also received the most despairing—the unbelievers in the Lord God, that is, in the Word of the Father, who is both God because he is Creator and Lord because he is Redeemer—dwelling, that is, dwelling in the man Christ.

This above all is what the Jews deny, both those who still exist and those who denied it in the past. Or you received even the Jews who justified themselves and were proud, who did not believe that God dwelt among the gentiles, whom they considered utterly impure, and therefore insisted that incorporation with them could not occur at all.

## Blessed be the Lord

The prophet, observing that God both brings the aforesaid chariot to its own end and has continually led our captivity forth happily into freedom through his grace, bursts into praise and says:

“Blessed be the Lord day by day”—that is, in such a way on this day that it is so every day. One translation has: “From day to day.” But Blessed Augustine says “day by day,” because it comes closer to the word found in Hebrew.

And so that it may be clearer from what cause he is blessed, he adds: because “he will make our journey prosperous.” That is, he will bring the chariot to its end and will always lead our captivity forth successfully—the one who is “the God of salvations,” that is, of our salvations both inwardly and outwardly.

Even if this is not yet so in reality, it is at least so in hope. He is, I say, our God—that is, he became a sharer in our mortality in order to make us sharers in his divinity. And because he is our God, he is therefore the God who makes us safe. For no other person could save us if he himself did not save us.

And lest someone say, “Why then do we suffer? Why do we die?” he adds: “And the exits of death belong to the Lord God.” As if he were saying: Why, miserable mortal condition, are you indignant? Why do you complain? You have no cause for indignation but for consolation.

To enable you to endure patiently not only tribulations but also death, you have this assurance: the exit from death belongs specially and absolutely to the Lord God. For he not only endured tribulations but also went out from the world through death.

## Nevertheless God will crush

As if he were saying: Although I say that the Lord died, human pride and carnal arrogance must not therefore presume upon impunity for sins. For although he is mortal, he is nevertheless omnipotent, because he is God. Therefore he will crush not only the lesser enemies of the Jews but also their heads, namely, the scribes and Pharisees.

Or by the heads of the enemies we may understand the aerial powers, which incite the enemies themselves. Or the raised-up heads may signify the stiff-neckedness of the Jews who exalt themselves.

He says “heads” in the plural because two heads raised themselves against the Lord. For they would not have shaken the external head by their insults unless they had first shaken the internal head against him. Therefore he says: “The Lord will crush the heads”—that is, the exaltation and stiff-neckedness of his enemies—both for good and for evil: some will be crushed so that, humbled, they may be saved; others will be hurled into eternal darkness and condemned.

He will also crush “the crown of the hair,” that is, the excessive pride of those who walk about—that is, who persevere and take delight in their sins, where they ought rather to mourn.

Understand here one group of enemies and another: earlier, those raging in the flesh; here, those tearing at divinity itself, namely, heretics. This is indicated by the fact that there he placed “heads,” but here he places “the crown of the hair,” which is above the head.

The crown of the hair is a height that people prepare by twisting their hair so that they may hold their head erect. So heretics, not through ignorance but through a certain arrogance, usurp a teaching authority over others.

Cassiodorus offers another interpretation: by the hair, which is gentile, we should understand their low and trifling opinions; by the crown, a certain cunning within those same opinions. For heretics commonly put forward worthless opinions and act within them with cunning and great ingenuity.

This entire verse may also be read of the aerial powers, so that “he will crush” is understood only in an evil sense, as follows: Although the Lord is mortal, nevertheless, because he is God, he will crush the heads of his enemies—that is, he will condemn not only the lesser demons but also their heads, that is, the greater ones.

“Of the enemies,” I say, “who walk about the crown of the hair, surrounding the top of the hair”—which is easily moved unless it is restrained by some perception of ours. This means that they deceive us imperceptibly. Therefore they must be guarded against most carefully. They do this in sins—that is, to persuade us toward sins. Since those sins occur through their incitement, they are not ours alone but also theirs.

## The Lord said: From Bashan I will turn back

According to the first interpretation, in which we understood human beings as the enemies, he now shows how the Lord crushes the enemies. Here he speaks of another kind of crushing, namely, a good one; at the end he will deal with the other, the evil one.

But according to the interpretation in which we understood only the aerial powers as the enemies, the verse is not connected in this way. Rather, it relates to what was said above: that he will make our journey prosperous.

As if he were saying: Truly the Lord will make our journey prosperous—that is, he will lead us out of captivity—because the Lord said, whether through the prophets or in his own determination: “I will turn back from Bashan,” or “I will be turned back from Bashan,” “and I will turn back in the depth,” or “into the depth of the sea.”

Bashan is interpreted as “confusion” or “dryness.” The Lord turns toward himself—or turns himself toward—those who are confused in their sins or greatly ashamed because of them, according to the saying: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you, says the Lord.”

That publican was truly confused about his sins: he did not dare even to lift his eyes toward heaven, and therefore he went down to his house justified.

Likewise, the Lord turns those who are dry—that is, those who do not justify themselves and attribute nothing to themselves but always thirst for grace. But he does not turn the fat ones, that is, the proud and arrogant; rather, he turns them away.

Confusion or dryness is therefore the reason why he turns them. Hence he says: “I will turn some from Bashan,” that is, because of Bashan. “I will also turn those who are in the depth of the sea,” or “turning toward the depth of the sea, I will turn those whom I find there.”

He understands the depth of the sea as the most despairing—the ones of whom it is said: “When the sinner has come into the depth of sin, he despises.”

## So that your foot may be dipped

Assign each statement to its corresponding subject. Truly the Lord will turn them from Bashan, for he will turn them so completely that they will become feet in his members—namely, the feet of which it is said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace!”

And let the evangelizers strive even to the shedding of blood. This is what he says: “So that your foot may be dipped in blood.”

Again, say: Truly, Lord, you will turn them in the depth of the sea, because you will turn them so completely that from those enemies of yours there will be the tongue of your dogs—that is, they will become articulate dogs.

Not those of whom the Apostle says, “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers,” but your dogs—dogs worthy of praise, not detestation; faithful dogs barking against the enemies for the house of the Lord. They will be loquacious dogs, not biting dogs, because these dogs are commended not for their teeth but for their tongue.

There are also other dogs, namely, mute dogs, unable to bark. And he turns toward us, as if saying: Let no one despair of the Lord’s mercy, because the fact that the most despairing enemies become such dogs comes from him—that is, through his grace and mercy.

## They saw your processions

As if he were saying: By what means will those turned from Bashan become your foot, and those turned from the depth of the sea become the tongue of your dogs? Because they saw your processions, O God—that is, they attended to the preachers, your other processions, and conformed themselves to them.

Or they saw, O God, your processions—that is, they learned your ways: with what humility you came into this world and what you accomplished. These were the processions, I say, of my God—that is, of my Creator—in that he is the Word, and of my King, in that he is human.

This God is “in the holy place,” either in that holy place which he established from those whom, through his grace and mercy, he led out from the bonds of sins and raised from the grave; or in the Holy of Holies, that is, in the Lord’s humanity, in which he was present in a special way.

Hence the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.”

## The princes went before

How did they see your processions? Through the princes—that is, through the apostles who went before, who preceded the others.

Or, according to the interpretation in which we understood the processions as preachers, it is said thus: “They saw your processions”—that is, your preachers—“among whom the princes went before, joined to those who sing,” that is, together with many others converted by them.

These are “those who sing,” praising God through good works as if with a visible instrument. I say that they were placed in an honorable office, in the midst of young women beating tambourines, like leaders of the song, foreseeing and arranging everything.

He calls the young women newly established Churches, adorned with new grace and constituted by the holy apostles. He calls these same Churches “those who beat tambourines.” For a tambourine is made from dry, stretched hide. Those Churches are tambourine players because they dry out—that is, mortify—the flesh, and praise God with the application of good meditation and holy action.

And lest anyone hearing this should turn his attention toward licentious dances, he shows what he calls the young women by adding: “In the assemblies bless.”

As if he were saying: You who have been turned from Bashan and you who have been turned from the depth of the sea, bless God, your Creator and Lord, your Redeemer, through good works in the assemblies—that is, in the fellowship of the Churches—having drawn your blessing from the fountains of Israel.

This means: with a blessing that does not disagree with the tradition of the holy apostles, who are the fountains of Israel, that is, from whom true Israelites have drawn the doctrine of truth.

## There is Benjamin

He invites them to fellowship with the Churches, commending the companions and leaders whom they will have there.

As if he were saying: You ought to bless in the Churches because Benjamin is there—that is, Paul, born from the most savage tribe of Benjamin; a young man, that is, newly taken up; and in this excess of mind, namely, at the time when, struck down on the road by the Lord, he was so beside himself that he neither saw nor heard anything.

Or he was “in an excess of mind” because he was of such perfection that in mind he surpassed himself for God, in accordance with what he himself says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God.”

Or also because he was carried away in ecstasy up to the third heaven with such rapture that he did not know whether this had happened in the body or outside the body.

Of this Benjamin it was said: “A ravenous wolf; in the morning he eats the prey, in the evening he divides the spoils.” This is to be understood as follows: In the morning, that is, in the first period of his life, Paul ate the prey, because he was a persecutor of the Church. In the evening, however—that is, after his conversion—he divided the spoils, because those whom he snatched from the devil by the word of his preaching he distributed among the various offices of the Church.

It may also be said that when morning came to him—that is, when he received the light of faith—he then, as it were, ate the prey, because he received into spiritual grace the one whom he had persecuted as an enemy.

According to the saying: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it,” he divided that spoil—that is, the same grace, as though captured by force from the enemy—in the evening, among the gentiles, who were like evening because they lacked the light of the true sun.

But if we attend to the interpretation of the name, the verse may be understood more broadly, so that it is said: “There is Benjamin”—that is, everyone seeking the better part, namely, the right hand. For Benjamin is interpreted as “son of the right hand.”

Benjamin, I say, is a young man—that is, renewed by grace—and placed in an excess of mind, namely, so that he surpasses himself as a human being in God, forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead.

Moreover, the best leaders are there. For the leaders of those existing in the Churches are princes from the tribe of Judah, from the tribe of Zebulun, and from the tribe of Naphtali, if we say that the holy apostles were taken only from these tribes. This cannot be either refuted or confirmed by any authority.

If, however, we attend to the interpretations of the names, we shall speak differently. Judah is interpreted as “confession.” The princes of confession are the holy martyrs, holding primacy in the Church, whose chief virtue is confession.

But because they must suffer much for this confession, it is necessary for them to enter a fortified place, namely, Zebulun. For Zebulun is interpreted as “dwelling of strength.” By Zebulun Christ is signified, who is for them a tower of strength, provided that they attend both to what he suffered and to what he received—namely, the glory of immortality and impassibility—and hope for the same reward.

Then they became steadfast for others, to whom they were examples. The princes of Zebulun are therefore the princes of strength.

And because praise of heavenly joys follows from this, there are also the princes of Naphtali. For Naphtali is interpreted as “my enlargement.”

We may also understand Judah as faith, Zebulun as hope, and Naphtali as charity. Rightly are they leaders of others who are princes in pure faith, who are strong in certain hope—which makes a person strong, so that he does not fail in tribulation—and who are strong in true charity, such as was shown by that prince who, in the very Passion, said on behalf of his enemies: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”

And because—he is as if saying—such subjects and such rulers exist in the Churches, therefore you who have been turned from Bashan and conquered, and you who have been brought from the depth of the sea, bless God in the heights.

And so that this may be done by many, O God, join good beginnings to good outcomes: “Command your power,” that is, make known to human beings the one who is your power and wisdom. For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

Or, as some books have it, “Command your power,” that is, commend and impose this upon your power, so that by making itself known it may cause you to be blessed.

Command, I say, by teaching, and strengthen by living—understand, among the gentiles—this grace which you have already worked in us, the first believers. I mean you who began from your temple, which is in Jerusalem—that is, from the people who believe in you and belong to Jerusalem.

For salvation proceeded from the Jews, since from them both the chosen apostles and Christ himself, according to the flesh, were born.

And truly you will command and strengthen, because kings will offer you gifts. A division may also be made at the end of the preceding verse, after which it may be said as before that you will truly command and strengthen, because kings coming from your temple in Jerusalem—that is, the holy apostles chosen from the Jews—will offer you gifts.

What gifts? Gifts full of grace and acceptable, namely, themselves and others converted together with them.

## Rebuke the beasts of the reeds

They will offer gifts, I say. But because many will oppose these gifts in a bestial manner—those who bear the Christian name but dissent from the faith, namely heretics—therefore, Lord, rebuke through those whom you have appointed to rebuke, namely, through your preachers, those beasts.

They are called “beasts of the reeds” because they exercise their savagery against the reed—that is, against sacred Scripture—which they destroy by interpreting it perversely.

Here the effect is given in place of what is effected: the reed stands for Scripture. Or, if we take the content for the container, the reed for the mud—for the reed loves muddy places—we shall say that those beasts are beasts of the reeds because they plunge and roll about in mud like swine.

For, despising true and sound meanings, they sink themselves into a false and erroneous interpretation.

Or those beasts are “of the reeds,” that is, comparable to reeds, because just as a reed is easily shaken by the wind, so they are easily carried about by every wind of doctrine.

## The assembly of bulls

Therefore I say that you should rebuke the beasts, because there will be many beasts. For there will be an assembly of bulls—that is, there will be many bulls, stiff-necked and having an untamed neck, namely, heretics, among the heifers of the peoples—that is, dwelling among the easily led souls of the peoples, who follow them as heifers follow bulls.

Or “among the heifers of the buffaloes,” that is, among heretical souls, dwelling like heifers of buffaloes, that is, like wild heifers.

For they do not attack those who are steadfast and strong in faith but the weak and easily led. Hence the Apostle says: “They enter houses and lead captive women weighed down with sins, led by various desires, always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth.”

And that such bulls will exist God will make useful for his own people, namely, so that they may bring forth—that is, make manifest—those who are skilled interpreters and have been tested in silver, that is, in divine speech.

Hence the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who have been tested may become manifest.”

In the art of working silver, “excluders” are called those who know how to bring forth the form of a vessel from the confused mass. Similarly, in divine Scripture, “excluders” are called those who have been given such intelligence that they can reduce what is obscure and ambiguous to a certain meaning.

It may also be said that he permits those bulls to exist for this purpose: so that those who have been tested in silver—that is, in divine speech—may exclude them, that is, drive those wicked ones out, and that this may be to their glory.

Or so that those bulls may exclude them from the heifers, those who have been tested in silver.

## Scatter the nations that desire wars

Thus I say: rebuke the beasts in such a way that you scatter those nations that desire wars—that is, those who devote themselves more to contention than to correction.

He calls the same people whom he called beasts “nations,” namely, heretics, not because of diversity of peoples but because of variety of sects. Some were Donatists, others Nicolaitans, others Arians, others Sabellians, and many others.

And truly he will scatter such nations, for you will do this through ambassadors of reconciliation and eternal peace, that is, through holy preachers.

They will come from Egypt and Ethiopia. Such an ambassador was the Apostle, who said: “We act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God.”

Egypt is interpreted as “darkness” or “affliction,” while Ethiopia is interpreted as “black.” By these two are signified the gentiles, who were both darkness—that is, they had an obscured understanding—and afflicted with blindness, because they placed the creature before the Creator. They were also blackened with the skin of the Ethiopian, that is, with the blackness of sins.

From these, then, the ambassadors truly came, so that they might scatter the nations mentioned above—such as Augustine, Jerome, and others like them.

He explains how ambassadors come from Ethiopia: because Ethiopia will anticipate God’s hand—that is, God’s future vengeance—by turning to the honor of God.

This means: Ethiopia will precede God’s vengeance by believing, and once it has believed, ambassadors will come from it.

This may also be understood differently, because Blessed Augustine says that in Hebrew the pronoun “his” here refers to the feminine, that is, to Ethiopia. Accordingly, it is said: “Ethiopia, by clinging to God through faith, will go before his hand”—that is, her own hands.

This means her works, because she will be justified through faith, since she cannot be justified through works. Hence the Apostle says: “We consider that a person is not justified by works of the law but by faith. For Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”

And before she is justified, ambassadors will come from her, as was said above.

## Kingdoms of the earth

Foreseeing the calling of both Jews and Gentiles, the prophet jointly exhorts them, saying: O you Jews or Gentiles, freely called and made into a kingdom from the earth, sing by holy meditation to God the Father; praise the Lord the Son by good works; praise also God the Holy Spirit—yes, praise the Lord who ascended, and so forth.

This entire passage can also be referred to the Son alone, so that we may say: Sing to God the Son as God, that is, as your Creator; praise him as Lord, that is, as your Redeemer; praise him also as God, that is, as your Resurrector, who raised you together with himself and made you sit at the Father’s right hand. This is suggested when he says, “Who ascended above the heaven of heaven.”
