Or this may be because he materially ascended into that heaven of which he himself, the Lamb, is the light—the heaven that is above our heaven, which is in the midst of the waters and formed from those waters themselves. Or he ascended above himself, since he is the heaven of the higher heavens. How? Because, I say, human flesh is also heaven, that is, the highest of those of which it is said, “The heavens declare the glory of God.” This flesh, I say, he exalted above itself, because although its nature tended downward, he made it tend upward—he himself, I say, tending toward the East, that is, toward the Father, who is his origin. In accordance with the words: “His going forth is from the end of heaven,” and so forth.

## Behold, he will give a voice to his own voice

For this reason I say: Sing and praise now, because if you do not sing now, you will eventually weep. For the one who, coming to be judged, gave to his voice the voice of weakness will, when he comes to judge, give to his voice the voice of power. He who came as a humble lamb will roar as a terrible lion when he says to his own: “Come, you blessed of my Father”; but to the others: “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire.”

And behold—as if he were saying: It is near at hand that you should do this. For the time is short, and it must not be thought long, since it has an end. And because this is both future and already imminent, therefore sing and praise; thus, in prosperity and adversity alike, give true glory and thanks to God. You ought rightly to glorify him, because his magnificence—that is, his magnificent glory—will be over Israel, that is, over all those who now labor in order to become Israel, namely, men who see God. He will glorify all these with immortality and freedom from suffering.

And his power, that is, his might, will appear clearly in the clouds, because those clouds—namely, the holy apostles—will be of such dignity that by comparison with themselves they will judge others. To show what clouds he means here, he adds:

“Wonderful is God.” As if he were saying: Truly his magnificence will be in Israel and his power in the clouds, because God will be wonderful in his saints, that is, in the rewarding of his saints. God, I say, the God of Israel, that is, of those who see God.

In what respect will he be wonderful? In this, namely, that he will finally give strength in the body to his people, now weak and feeble. For he will give them a body conformed to the body of his glory; and he will give them strength, that is, constancy of mind, so that they may suffer no further failure. For then death, the enemy, will be destroyed, and there will no longer be any place for sin.

And because, with God’s help, we have finally completed this difficult and lengthy psalm, blessed therefore be God.

# ON PSALM 68

*For the end, for those who will be changed. Of David.*

## Argument

A prayer suited to the persons and circumstances of the Maccabees is applied here. Alternatively, it is to be read in connection with the reading of the prophet Jonah and with the Gospel of John, as the voice of Christ while he suffered.

## Explanation

No one is unaware that “for the end” looks toward Christ; the Gospel itself also bears witness that in this psalm he is going to recount his passion, through which believers will be changed, putting off the old man and putting on the new.

Throughout the psalm Christ speaks in the form of a servant. In the first section he asks the Father to save him, since he was gratuitously hated by the Jews. In the second he petitions on behalf of the members, lest the hope of the faithful, which rested upon his resurrection, be deceived; he says that he endured with equanimity everything that the wicked inflicted. In the third he prays that his prayer may be heard, so that his blameless conduct may be freed from the clay of this world; he declares how greatly the Lord is attacked by the plots of his enemies, until he would reach the end of his passion through a danger deliberately devised against him.

In the fourth, by the power of his foreknowledge, he foretells the future events that could befall his enemies. In the fifth, in the form of a servant, he professes himself poor, and therefore says that he will render praises to the Father’s mercy. He exhorts the faithful to trust in the Lord, who has freed his Church from the adversity of this world and has provided his saints within it with everlasting happiness.

## Commentary

### “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered”

The present psalm is attributed to David himself; that is, it is a Song, because this psalm contains explicit words that were fulfilled in his passion, such as “They gave me gall for food,” and similar expressions.

It is said to be for those who will be changed. One change is for the worse, another for the better. Adam and Eve were changed for the worse; those, however, who through Adam and Eve clung to Christ were changed for the better. Iniquity brought about the change for the worse, whereas Christ’s mercy accomplished the change for the better.

The cause of this change for the better is also the passion itself, that is, Christ’s passage. For unless the one who descended had passed over, in order to free or raise us up, we who had fallen could in no way pass over. This passage is from the world to heaven, from earthly life to heavenly life, from mortality to immortality, from corruption to incorruption, and from labor to eternal rest.

Let us therefore hear, recognize, and lament in the sequence of this psalm the cause of our change—that is, Christ’s passion itself—and our voice amid tribulations. By hearing, recognizing, and lamenting, let us be changed; and, once changed, let us say together with our Head: “Save me, O God.”

In this psalm our Head exhorts us to attend, through his passion and reward, also to our own passion and reward, and so to suffer with him that we may also be glorified. For “if we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified.”

Thus he prays for himself and for his members:

“God the Father, save me by restoring me to immortality. Save my people also, for the present, by an inward resurrection, until there is also an outward resurrection. And it is necessary that you save us, because the waters have entered even to my soul.”

Here the waters are called the crowds of the Jewish people with respect to the Head himself; with respect to the members, the waters are likewise all those who persecute the Church.

When he says, “The waters have entered,” this is spoken by way of comparison. Just as water gradually enters until it submerges and overwhelms a ship, so the Jews gradually entered: first by enveloping themselves in concealed hatred, then by forming a plot with a disciple, and finally by attacking openly and shouting over him, “Crucify him!” Thus they entered—that is, prevailed—even to the soul, not to be imitated but to be drowned and destroyed according to their reputation. The same may be said of the members in their own way.

### “I am stuck fast in deep mire”

The waters prevailed over me for this reason: I am stuck fast in deep mire. Man was made by God from clay, but through transgression he became deep mire. He is deep because of the many punishments of sin.

Christ himself was stuck fast in this deep mire because he assumed human nature. Therefore he says: “I am stuck fast in deep mire.” And therefore I have no substance—that is, no subsistence—by which I could remain standing after being submerged by those waters, unless you raise me up.

### “I have come into the depth of the sea”

I am stuck fast, I say, in deep mire, and this did not happen from any necessity, because I came of my own will, not under compulsion, into the depth of the sea. That is, I assumed humanity, made bitter by the punishments of sin. The deep mire and the depth of the sea are the same thing in this passage.

These two verses may also appropriately be explained in another way. As if he were saying:

“I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep,” that is, the earth has been handed over to the hands of sinners. As we said earlier, man was made from clay, but through transgression he became deep mire. Whoever, besides original sins, plunges himself into actual sins makes this mire deeper the more sins he commits.

If someone despises this mire as it draws him toward some iniquity, he makes his mire gold, because in the end, having been changed into a heavenly condition, he becomes equal to the angels of God.

Christ was stuck fast in this deep mire because the corruption of nature—not only through original sins but also through actual sins—was the cause of his being stuck fast. Therefore he says: “I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep,” that is, I remained there because I was seized, beaten, scourged, and crucified.

And this was because there was no substance in me, that is, because I did not display to them the riches of my divinity, but the form of human poverty. “Substance” is often used for riches. His riches consist in this: he did not regard being equal with God as robbery, although according to the Word he is truly equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with God.

His poverty, however, consisted in this: he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and being found in appearance as a man. Through this poverty he became rich, because he filled us with many riches. Though he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty he might enrich us.

Or otherwise: “Substance” means whatever has been created by God. Man was created by God as substance, that is, as something worthy of him. If he had remained the substance that God brought forth, he would not have been stuck fast.

But man fell through iniquity. Iniquity is not a creature, because it is not the nature that God created; rather, it is the corruption of nature that man himself brought about in himself. Iniquity came from Adam, and it is not substance, because iniquity was not made by God. Indeed, it was not made, because all things were made through him, and every creature was made by God.

He praises him—not because he possesses a sense capable of praising, but because he provides material for praise. No defect is material for praising God; therefore iniquity is not a creature. For this reason he says: “I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep,” and this because there is no substance, that is, because I did not find in man the substance that I had made.

“I have come into the depth of the sea.” I am stuck fast, I say, but not from any necessity, because I came willingly into the depth of the sea, that is, into this life made bitter by the punishments of sin. Yet I was in the high sea, that is, in the place that was less disturbed: although I was shaken by the punishments of sin, I did not take sin upon myself to this extent. For the sea, and every body of water, is less disturbed in the part where it is deeper.

Or: “I have come into the depth of the sea,” that is, among those who were most bitter, namely, among the Jews. Therefore the storm—that is, the contradiction and fury of that people—not only submerged me when they shouted against me so that I might be crucified, but even overwhelmed me so completely that they buried me.

### “I have labored, crying out; my throat has become hoarse”

They indeed overwhelmed me, but I warned them about their salvation. Thus I labored, crying out to them, just as the one of whom it was said did not answer them a word. Isaiah says of him: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter,” and while he was treated in this way, “he did not open his mouth.”

Although he did not cry out during the passion, he had previously cried out at length, saying: “Woe to the world,” and “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who have the keys of knowledge; you do not enter yourselves, and you do not allow others to enter,” and many similar things.

Therefore he says: “I have labored, crying out.” Yet—as if he were saying—I accomplished nothing, because my throat, that is, my voice, became hoarse with respect to its effect. Just as the voice of someone hoarse is confused and cannot be heard, so my words were neither understood nor heard by them.

And surely, if my throat became hoarse for my adversaries, my eyes also failed—that is, those who clung to me and were eyes in my body, namely, the apostles. So too those two men who, while their eyes were held back on the road so that they would not recognize him, said: “We had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel.”

And my eyes failed while I hoped in you, God, because I performed no miracle and displayed none of my power; instead, I fixed all my hope in you, God, not by coming down from the cross but by awaiting you as my rewarder.

“My eyes failed” may also simply be a description of death. As if he were saying: Not only did my throat become hoarse, but my eyes also failed, that is, I was given over to death. In death the eyes fail. And they failed while I hoped in my God, as before.

### “Those who hate me without cause have multiplied”

Because my throat became hoarse, those who hated me without cause multiplied, both among their own people and among mine. One even came over to them from among the twelve, so that they became more numerous than the hairs of my head—that is, innumerable. The finite is taken here for the infinite.

Or, because the hairs cling to the head and we can understand by the hairs the adornment itself, we may understand friends clinging to him who is the Head. The meaning would then be equivalent to this: Those who resisted me became far more numerous than those who favored me.

Therefore my enemies were strengthened, that is, they prevailed and gained courage against me—enemies, I say, who persecuted me unjustly. And truly unjustly, because nothing is more unjust than wishing to kill the one who came to save them.

Then, when my enemies had been strengthened, I paid back what I had not stolen, that is, I endured punishment for sin although I had committed no sin. This is said by way of comparison, as though someone had stolen something and another person, who was without blame, paid for it.

Adam and Eve committed disobedience, for which Christ, who committed no sin, paid the penalty.

### “O God, you know”

As if he were saying: I did indeed pay what I had not stolen, but you, Lord, know why I did this, because you know my folly.

How can he call it his folly when true wisdom is in him? Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God; nevertheless, nothing is more like folly than this: that the one who could destroy all his enemies with a single word allowed himself to be seized, scourged, and killed by them.

But this folly was supreme wisdom, because “the foolishness of God is wiser than men.” For this reason he permitted the man who found nothing belonging to himself in Christ to lay hands upon him, so that he might destroy those in whom he truly had a claim.

Therefore he says: “You know my folly”—not a real folly, but what human beings regard as folly. You know it, that is, you approve it—you from whom all folly is absent—not merely by knowledge but by gracious regard. You know that it is not folly but true wisdom.

And my sins—not truly my sins, but according to the judgment of those of whom I am not the perpetrator but the bearer—are not hidden from you. I do not take the sins themselves upon me, but I suffer the penalties for them. Those sins, I say, are not hidden from you, from whom every sin is hidden by gracious regard.

Therefore let those who await you, the Resurrector, through me, the one resurrected, not be put to shame because I have not been raised. O Lord, Lord, I say, who are not only Lord of human beings but also of the heavenly powers.

Thus I say: Let them not be put to shame, so that they may not be confounded—that is, so that they may not understand themselves to be liable to confusion—when they attend to me, a man, and understand in me one who is needy and poor.

Or, if you understand “above” as referring to memory or action, let them not be confounded on my account—that is, because I have not been raised—those who seek you through me, O God of Israel.

To be confounded is more than to be ashamed; nevertheless, the one who is confounded is stung by conscience. The conscience of these people also would be stung if Christ were not raised, since he had said to them: “You believe in God; believe also in me,” and they believed.

For it could be said to them: “Where is the one in whom you believed? Where is the one on whom you relied?” and similar things.

### “For on your account”

Therefore I say: Do not permit those who await and seek you through me to be ashamed or confounded, because I endured reproach not on my own account but on yours.

Reproach is what an enemy throws against someone. Thus it was thrown against Christ: “You have a demon,” and similar accusations.

Every sinner suffers reproach on his own account, because he has the cause of reproach within himself; this is not a great thing. But if someone suffers reproach for God’s sake, he does something great, because a sure reward follows from it.

Christ patiently endured reproach not on his own account, because he committed no sin, but for God’s sake, namely, because he kept God’s commandments. He did this so that, by patiently suffering what was inflicted on him, in whom there was nothing blameworthy, he might teach us to suffer, in whom there are many faults.

Therefore he says: “I endured, Lord, reproach not on my own account but on yours.” And “confusion covered my face,” that is, I experienced complete confusion—not according to the truth of the matter but according to their opinion.

They said such things to him that they will rightly be confounded if those things were found in him, such as: “He saved others; he cannot save himself,” and similar sayings.

Confusion properly means the conscience’s remorse over guilt.

### “I have become a stranger”

Confusion covered me to such an extent that I became to my brothers—that is, to my kinsmen according to the flesh, from the same tribe—like a stranger; and to the sons of my mother—that is, to all those nourished by the milk of my mother, the Synagogue, from whatever tribe, that is, brought up under the same legal institutions—I became like a foreigner.

For they and the others alienated me from themselves like a stranger and foreigner.

If we wish, we may also understand “brothers” first as kinsmen in the faith, that is, the faithful; then, by “the sons of my mother,” understand generally all who belonged to the Synagogue.

### “For zeal for your house”

That is, the pious indignation that I felt for your house—a house dedicated to prayer, which they had made a house of commerce and a den of robbery—consumed me, that is, stirred me to do something by which I especially offended them, as is read in the Gospel.

Or otherwise: “The zeal of your house,” that is, indignation at the fact that, although they ought to prepare themselves as an adorned house for you, they instead prepared within themselves a house of commerce, that is, of greed, and a house of robbers, that is, of plots and frauds.

That indignation, I say, consumed me, that is, impelled me to rebuke them and not conceal their iniquity. Therefore the reproaches that their fathers once hurled in the desert—when they said, “Can God prepare a table in the desert?”—and likewise before the molten calf, “These are your gods, Israel,” and so forth, fell upon me.

Or both may be understood of the present in this way: The reproaches of those who reproach you through me—for whoever despises me despises you—fell upon me, that is, took effect upon me, because they saw me and found me.

It may also be said that the reproaches—namely, their calling him blasphemous and demon-possessed, and similar accusations—came upon him and fell upon him because, when he rose again, they were shown to be false.

### “And I covered myself in fasting”

“The zeal of your house,” I say, “consumed me.” And in that fasting, when I found nothing with which to refresh myself, I covered my soul, that is, I showed myself to them through some manifest judgment.

Or: In that fasting I covered my soul, although that fasting was like a cloak that veiled and pressed my soul on every side.

The fact that I did not consent to such people and fasted from such things became a reproach to me. For the wicked inflict reproaches upon the good precisely because the good do not consent to them.

### “And I made my garment”

I covered my soul, I say, and moreover I placed my garment, in which my divinity is clothed—namely, sackcloth; that is, I presented my human flesh to them as something against which they could rage.

Sackcloth is a rough garment made from the hair of goats and kids, and here it signifies Christ’s flesh. It pricked them through the punishments of sin and was, as it were, made from goat hair, because he came in the likeness of sinful flesh, though not in sinful flesh.

Or it may simply be said as follows: I presented my garment, that is, my flesh, to them as sackcloth, that is, as though I were some vile and despised person whom they might destroy.

Therefore I became to them a proverb, that is, a likeness, so that they might curse someone by saying: “May it happen to you as it happened to that man.”

Or otherwise: I put on sackcloth as my garment, that is, I incorporated into myself some of those who had previously been rough with sins, like sackcloth, and thus made them my garment.

In accordance with the words: “As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these things as with a garment.” Therefore I also became to them a proverb, so that “proverb” may have the same meaning as “reproach.”

They reproached him for taking such people to himself, saying that he ate with tax collectors and sinners.

### “Against me”

I became to them a proverb, I say, and this applied to both the greater and the lesser.

For those who sat at the gate—that is, the leading men who in ancient custom judged at the gate, that is, in public—who ought especially to have judged in my favor, spoke most vehemently against me. By the leading men, understand also the lesser ones.

Or otherwise: Those who sat at the gate were the scribes and Pharisees, who possessed the keys of knowledge and were content with themselves in the knowledge of the law and the prophets, which is the gate to truth; yet they themselves did not enter, nor did they permit others to enter.

Such, I say, were those who spoke against me.

Moreover, all who drank wine drank the wine of error, the wine of impiety—or the wine of earthly desire, being intoxicated by love of their place and nation. All these, I say, sang about me, that is, they made a psalm and song for themselves out of me.

Or otherwise: They spoke against me. But those who drank the wine of my cup—that is, those who attended to the sweetness that would come from my passion, such as the holy apostles and holy women—sang about me, that is, rejoiced in my power.

### “But as for me, my prayer [is] to you”

My enemies mocked me, but I, Lord Father, poured out my prayer for them to you, saying:

“O God, now is the time of your favor to be fulfilled, so that you may perfect for the world the grace of your visitation”—and this “in the abundance of your mercy,” that is, in your manifold mercy, because our misery is manifold.

And because the time has come, therefore, Lord, hear me “in the truth of your salvation,” that is, by granting to me and mine the true salvation promised by you.

“Truth” is to be understood in the promise, whereas “mercy” is to be understood in the remission of sins.

### “Deliver me from the mire”

I say: Hear me, so that you may deliver me—that is, my people—from the mire, that is, from association with those who are muddy, namely, sinners. Let it be so that, although they are joined to them in body, they are not fixed in them in mind, that is, they do not consent to them.

He explains how he asks that they be delivered, saying: “Free me,” that is, my people, “from those who hate me.”

And do this by freeing them from the depths of the waters, that is, from the deep iniquity of the peoples, so that they may not be conformed to them in the depth of their iniquity.

He continues this account of the deliverance. As if he were saying:

I ask that my people be delivered from the depths of the waters so that the storm—that is, the sedition and fury of the wicked people—may not drown me, that is, may not press down my people so that they consent to them.

Or, if it should drown them, may the deep not swallow me—that is, may my people meanwhile not be drowned and come into that depth of which it is said: “When the sinner comes into the depth of vices, he despises.”

Or, if they come into the depth, at least may that well not press its mouth shut over them.

This is said by way of comparison. The well, as it were, closes its mouth over the one whose mouth the depth of vices closes against confession, and in whom there is no hope of returning.

But if someone placed in the depth comes to his senses and cries out over his sins, saying, “I have sinned, Lord, have mercy,” the well does not close its mouth over him, because he belongs to those of whom it is said: “From the depths I have cried to you,” and so forth.

Therefore the Lord brings them out. But those who do not confess their sins and defend them he does not bring out. For there is no deliverer where you are your own defender. Therefore be your own accuser, so that he may deign to be your deliverer.

“Hear me, Lord, so that the well may not press its mouth over me.” Therefore, Lord, hear me and mine, because the time has come: tribulation has preceded, and therefore your mercy is now kind, that is, sweet and pleasant.

Just as rain is sweet in a drought, so mercy is sweet in tribulation.

As if he were saying: You delayed hearing me so that it would be sweet when you came to my aid. But now your mercy is sweet; therefore do not delay hearing me.

Tribulation has now reached a definite measure of calamity; therefore let your mercy be present, so that it may display the work of goodness.

Your mercy, I say, is kind to me and mine. Therefore you who previously looked away because of the multitude of iniquities now look upon me and mine according to the multitude of your mercies.

And you who previously turned away from the freedman and the proud, do not now turn your face away from your servant, that is, from me and my humble servants.

Hear me and mine quickly, that is, without delay, because I am afflicted, and mine are afflicted also.

This means: Do not delay hearing us, because tribulation has already preceded in me and mine, and it has made the hearing of us welcome.

He explains how he asks to be heard, saying:

“Attend to my soul,” that is, to the soul of my people, “and deliver it” by a hidden deliverance.

There are two tribulations of the righteous: one hidden and the other manifest. The hidden one occurs through the blinding of enemies; the manifest one occurs for the sake of conversion.

The three youths were manifestly delivered from the furnace of fire. This happened for the sake of Nebuchadnezzar, who afterward believed and confessed.

The seven Maccabees were secretly rescued, and this happened more for the sake of blinding the tyrant Antiochus.

Both kinds of deliverance are treated here.

Therefore, after saying, “Attend to my soul and deliver it,” which pertains to hidden deliverance, he adds concerning manifest deliverance, saying:

“Deliver me, the Head, manifestly by raising me from the dead.” That is, deliver me and mine manifestly, also for the sake of my enemies and the conversion of my enemies.

Therefore I say that you should deliver me and mine, and do so manifestly for the sake of the enemies, so that they may be converted. For you, who know all things by knowledge but not by gracious regard, know through gracious regard how much reproach, confusion, and shame I and mine suffer from our enemies.

I suffer reproaches for the great benefit of my people; my people also suffer reproaches, that is, for the exhortation of their neighbors.

Therefore you, who are ignorant of whatever is done wickedly—not by knowledge but by gracious regard—know this through indignation.

Reproach is what an enemy throws against someone. At the Head there was the reproach they hurled at him: “By Beelzebul, the prince of demons, he casts out demons,” and similar sayings.

Among the members, the reproach was that they believed in one who had been crucified and was dead, and similar things.

Therefore one of them, knowing that this was glory rather than disgrace, said: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth.

Confusion, however, is guilt that stings the conscience. In the Head it can in no way be understood as real, except according to their judgment. In some members, however, namely, those who believed from among the Jews, it was real, because their conscience was truly stung when it was said to them that they believed in the one whom they had crucified.

A sense of shame is what causes an honorable face to blush even at the accusation of a false crime. This likewise was not present in the Head. Nothing caused him to blush, since he came in order to suffer such things; nevertheless, they brought accusations against him which, if falsely brought against another, would still be shameful.

### “All those who afflict me are before your sight”

Therefore he says that you know my reproach, because all those who afflict me are before your sight, that is, all my tribulation proceeds from your disposition, and I did not evade it.

For my heart, that is, my soul, awaited reproach, because it both foresaw and foretold it; and, so that it might come, it endured it.

He foresaw it when he said to the disciples: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over,” and so forth.

He would not have wished to be born if he had not wished to suffer. For this reason he took upon himself the two things we knew—namely, birth and death—in order to show us the third thing we did not know, namely, resurrection and eternal life.

My heart awaited reproach, I say, and it awaited misery, so that those who inflicted reproach might recognize misery in themselves and find mercy in me.

I also awaited one who would grieve over this misery together with me, and there was no one who grieved.

The holy apostles were sad, and the holy women who followed him were also sad; but this was because of a carnal affection, namely, because they feared losing the hope and comfort they had in him.

The Lord alone grieved, as it were, over the commonwealth—that is, the common misery of human beings. He wished many to grieve with him, to advance through grieving, and thus to comfort him.

The progress of those under one’s authority and of those who are being healed is a great comfort to physicians and prelates. But there was no one who attended to these things.

Therefore he says: “I awaited one who would grieve together with me, and there was none; and I found none who would console me.”

And thus “they gave gall for my food.” What they gave was not food but rather gall; nevertheless, it was given as food.

The Lord had received food, because he ate the Passover with his disciples, in which he had commended the sacrament of his body.

Over this sweet food of unity—that is, of Christ’s body and Christ’s charity—which the Apostle also commends when he says, “Because we are all one bread, one body in Christ,” the Jews cast a drink of gall. This drink was themselves, since they tore themselves away from the unity of his body.

Even now, whoever destroys unity and charity, contradicts evangelical truth, or scandalizes the Church by living badly, offers a drink of gall over that food.

But what happens to such people? The same thing that the Lord did then: when he had tasted it, he did not wish to drink.

By this he signified the sacrament: such people are indeed to be tasted and endured, but not drunk, that is, they are not to be incorporated into us.

“They gave gall for my food,” I say, “and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink,” because while I thirsted for their renewal, they offered me the bitter oldness of their former state.

And let this table—that is, such a preparation of their table—become for them a snare, that is, an impediment rather than a means of escape, before them, that is, while they thirst for it and do not understand it.

Whatever is before someone is seen and understood. Many recognize their own malice and wickedness, yet persist in it obstinately. Such people act ruinously against themselves, because they descend alive into hell.

These were the sort of people of whom it is said here: “Let their table become a snare before them,” and let this happen not unjustly but in retribution, that is, justly, because they deserved it.

And let it become a scandal, that is, an offense, either to those same people, who are offended all the more the more knowingly they persist in evil, or to their descendants, for whom they asked this when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

This does not mean that the imprecation itself harmed them, but rather their imitation of it.

Or otherwise: Their table—that is, both Testaments, which were principally set before them so that they might be refreshed there as at a table—may become a snare for them, because they will be ensnared before what has been set before the Gentiles: namely, they will be provoked to jealousy when they see that the grace formerly offered to them has been made common to the Gentiles.

This happens to them for confusion, and not unjustly but in retribution, that is, justly. And let it also become a scandal for them, as was said above.

“Let their eyes also be darkened, so that they may not see,” and so forth.

The preceding verse may also be read in a good sense in this way:

“They gave me gall for food and gave me vinegar to drink. Let such a table of theirs—that is, one prepared by them—become a snare before them,” so that in their own sight they may recognize that this table has become for them a snare of confusion.

Let it become for them a retribution, so that they may understand that they suffer what they suffer because of it; and let it become for them a scandal, so that through it they may recognize that they have scandalized God, and thus be converted and repent.

But for those to whom this will not happen, let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see.

As if he were saying: Because they previously opened their eyes too widely to see what ought not to have been seen—namely, how they might twist everything said about Christ in the Law and the Prophets—therefore let their eyes not be darkened so that they may not see what ought to be seen, namely, so that they may not understand the new grace.

And so that they may not see, “bend down, Lord, their backs always,” that is, let them never be raised toward higher things. But because they bent themselves toward earthly things, since they placed their place and nation above innocence, therefore, Lord, bend them down more and more.

Bend them down—not by blinding them, but by not helping them; not by wounding them, but by not healing them. For God’s bending down consists not in doing evil but in failing to come to their aid.

Pour out your wrath upon them. As though he were saying: In addition to this hidden vengeance, increase your wrath against them, Lord, through outward vengeance as well. What, then, did it profit Caiaphas that he said, “If we let him go on like this, the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation”? Nothing, certainly. For they did not let him go; rather, they killed him, and yet the Romans came and destroyed both their place and their nation. And therefore he says—not from the hatred of one who curses, but from the foreknowledge of one who prophesies: “Pour out, Lord, your wrath upon them, and let the fury of your wrath”—[Col. 0850A] that is, your severe vengeance—“seize them,” however widely scattered they may be, so that they may everywhere be held in contempt.

Let their dwelling become desolate. As though he were saying: I say that you should pour out your wrath upon them so that their dwelling—that is, that city which they formerly inhabited and in which they raged most fiercely—may become desolate with regard to them, and that there may be no one who dwells—that is, who perseveres—in their tents, that is, in the institutions temporarily given to them. This happened in such a way because their city was emptied of them, and there is no one among them who observes the legal institutions.

For they persecuted the one whom you struck. As though he were saying: You will rightly pour out your wrath upon them, because they persecuted with tribulation, as far as they were able, the one whom you struck—that is, me. The Lord struck the whole human race in Adam and Eve with the wound of mortality and suffering when he said, “On whatever day you taste from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall die.” From this stricken condition Christ took flesh, and therefore he says: [Col. 0850B] “They persecuted the one whom you struck,” and upon the pain of my wounds”—and upon the sorrow which I experienced because of the wounds, that is, the sins, of my people—“they added,” because they hastened my death.

Alternatively: They added to the pain of the wounds of my servants, namely, the prophets previously sent to the vineyard, because they killed me, the Son.

Alternatively: They added to the pain of my wounds in myself, or the lie by which they wished to deny my resurrection.

Or “they added,” because they also laid hands upon the apostles and upon my household.

Add iniquity to their iniquity. As though he were saying: They themselves have now added evil to evil. And you, Lord, add—not by blinding them, but by withholding help—to their iniquity another iniquity. Their particular iniquity is that they neither consider a person’s righteousness nor how great a sin it is to kill a righteous person. Let another iniquity be added to this iniquity, so that they may not only kill a righteous person but also God.

Or, [Col. 0850C] “add iniquity to iniquity,” that is, add wicked children to wicked fathers.

Or, over the iniquity concerning my death, add another iniquity—namely, that they persevere in unbelief—and thus do not enter, that is, do not live, in this life, which is the entrance to the heavenly life, into your righteousness, that is, into the works justified by your faith.

Let them be blotted out of the book of the living. Let them, I say, not enter into righteousness, but rather be blotted out of the book of the living. He does not say “from the book” because there is literally some book there; the expression is drawn from human likeness. Among human beings, because their memory is unstable, it is necessary to keep books by which the human mind may be assisted in remembering. Here, however, the divine mind is understood as the book: nothing past slips away from it, nothing future becomes new, but it sees all things simultaneously as present. Thus he says: “Let them now be blotted out of the book of the living,” that is, let their manifest unbelief in the present show that they have fallen from the memory in which they especially suppose themselves to be placed—not by loss of knowledge, but by loss of favor. And in the future [Col. 0850D] let them not be written with the righteous, that is, let them not share blessedness with the righteous. For those who do not share in faith here will not share in blessedness there.

I am poor. There, I say, they will not be written; but I and my people will be written, because I am poor in myself and in my people—that is, attributing nothing to myself—and I am sorrowful, I indeed on behalf of my people. In accordance with this Isaiah says of him: “He was wounded for us in sorrow because of our iniquities.” My people, however, are sorrowful because of the misery of their mortality and suffering. And because I am poor and sorrowful, therefore, O God, your true salvation—namely, of eternity and freedom from suffering—has already received me and my people in its purpose, and will receive us into you.

Then I shall praise the name of God in myself and in my people with a song, that is, with joy without sorrow, and I shall magnify him in praise—that is, I shall praise God himself with magnificent praise, with true and unfailing praise. For “blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; throughout the ages they will praise you.”

A simple continuation and construction can also be made in these two [Col. 0851A] verses:

As though he were saying: Let them not be written, but I shall praise the name of God in myself and in my people with a song—and this because I am poor and sorrowful. Therefore, O God, your salvation has received me.

And it will please God. I shall praise, I say, in the future, truly and eternally, in myself and in my people. And that sacrifice of praise—namely, the calf of the lips—will please God more than a young calf producing horns and hooves, that is, it will be more pleasing to God than any present sacrifice. For in the Law such a calf was commanded to be offered, one that would produce horns—that is, would already have produced horns—and would have produced hooves.

Whoever is trained to endure and is rich in the praise of God ought to have horns, that is, reason and understanding, with which he may toss about any adversary, that is, any heretic, in combat. And he ought to have a calf, that is, solid arguments with which he may rouse the earth—that is, the sluggish—from praising God. For we know that calves, as they mature and grow into the boldness of bulls, do this. [Col. 0851B]

Someone is a young calf because he has been renewed by grace. A heretic contradicts him: let him have horns with which to toss him about. For someone contradicts him, but lives abjectly and has an earthly understanding. He has hooves with which to dig at him. And over such a calf God will be pleased—that is, that praise will be more acceptable and more pleasing to God than this calf—when I and my people offer it to him after his true salvation has received me and my people from poverty into riches, from sorrow into joy, into the fellowship of the angels, where there will be neither an adversary to toss about nor a sluggish person to rouse.

And let the poor see this—that is, let them attend to it—and rejoice, not be sorrowful over this poverty of theirs. He then turns to the poor themselves and says: Seek God.

As though he were saying: I see that you seek bread and other such things because of that which is less worthy, namely, because of the body. Seek the Lord, therefore, for the sake of that for which he is worthy, and my soul will truly live.

[Col. 0851C] For he has heard. The poor should rejoice because the Lord has both heard and will hear the poor; but he will not hear the rich. And he has not despised, nor will he despise, his bound ones, that is, those bound by his commandments.

Or alternatively: We are runaway slaves, and we offended God, and he fettered us with the chains of mortality and suffering. His bound ones, however, are those who recognize themselves to be bound and add to their chains not comforts but only what may lighten them—that is, those who seek only what is necessary for the relief of the journey while neglecting superfluities by which they would be burdened. The Lord has neither despised nor will despise such people.

And because the Lord has both heard the poor and not despised the bound, therefore let the heavens—that is, those who weep together—and the well-cultivated earth of the Jews praise him, and the sea—that is, the Gentiles, who previously were especially bitter—praise him. And let all the creeping things that are in them—not the flying things—namely, in the earth and in the sea, praise him; that is, let all who are truly humble and not arrogant, whether Jews or [Col. 0851D] Gentiles, praise him.

And for this reason they ought rightly to praise him, because God will save Zion, that is, because he will gather scattered Israel into one thing, namely, into faith. Hence it was said: “I will restore its leaders as before.” Thus he will save Zion—that is, the Church from the Jews—by calling and justifying it.

God will save Zion, I say, and the cities of Judah—that is, the assemblies of those from the Gentiles who see how to live truly, that is, who confess humbly. For “Judah” is interpreted as “confessor.” They will be built up in faith and good works. And once built, they will dwell there, that is, believers from Jews and Gentiles will be incorporated into Zion. And they will dwell there in such a way that they will acquire it—namely, Zion—as an inheritance (for “to the inheritance”), because it will be for them an inherited dwelling both here and in the future.

And I say that it will be an inheritance for them because they are the seed of his servants—that is, because they are all imitators of the faith of Abraham [Col. 0852A] and Jacob and the other former servants of God; God will save Zion. These, I say, will possess Zion both here and in the future.

And lest we understand “their seed” here as their children according to the flesh—for, as the Apostle says, “it is not those who are children according to the flesh who are counted as the seed, but those according to the spirit”—he therefore determines what seed he means here, saying:

And those who love his name in imitation of those former servants—that is, the name of God, namely, “Lord,” because they willingly subject themselves to him—those, I say, will dwell in Zion both here and in the future. And if those who love the name will dwell there, it is therefore evident that those who do not love it will be shaken out and condemned.

## PSALM LXIX

A Psalm of David, for the end, in remembrance that the Lord saved me.

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0852B] Having been brought by his son into danger concerning his kingdom and his salvation, he composed this psalm as a prayer. Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ or of the Church addressed to the Lord. Likewise, since the title is written “in remembrance that the Lord saved him,” it refers to the preceding psalm, where he says: “Save me, God.”

## EXPLANATION

“End” and “David,” as has often been said, signify the Lord the Savior, to whom these words of the faithful are directed, because this entire psalm is spoken in the person of the martyrs, in remembrance either of their deliverance or of their future reward. For it was fitting that, just as in the preceding psalm the Lord had set forth his passion and resurrection, afterward the members should speak after their head, proclaiming both their own sufferings and their subsequent glories.

The people of martyrs and confessors, who were suffering under a manifold but blessed defeat, first entreat the Lord to be delivered from the dangers of their persecutors [Col. 0852C] and to make their mockeries fruitless, so that, once converted, they may salutarily be ashamed of their words. In the second part, the faithful crowd begs that, while magnifying the Lord, it may rejoice, because he deigns to help and liberate his poor and needy.

## COMMENTARY

Attend, O God, to my help. “A psalm of David, for the end, in remembrance that the Lord saved him.” The voice in this psalm is that of the afflicted, that is, of the holy martyrs endangered amid their sufferings, yet presuming upon their head. Let us therefore hear them and speak with them, both with the affection of the heart and, even if not through a similar tribulation. They already rejoice, crowned; we are still afflicted, because our adversary has two forms: in attack he is a lion, in ambush a dragon. He does not cease to test; he does not cease to lie in wait. Let us therefore cry out and say with them:

“Attend, O God, to my help,” and so forth. These words are referred to “the end” because the psalm is attributed [Col. 0852D] to David—that is, to the holy martyrs—a psalm, I say, sung in remembrance, that is, in recollection. And because recollection may concern reward, punishment, condemnation, or salvation, he therefore specifies what kind of recollection this is: namely, that the Lord has already saved him—that is, each such David in his head, through hope—because in him he has already raised us together through hope and made us sit at the right hand of majesty.

The holy martyrs who speak here encourage us not to fail in tribulation by their example, so that we may attain the same reward. And they speak as follows:

Attend, O God, to my help. Divine assistance is always necessary for us, but it must especially be invoked in tribulation. Therefore the holy martyrs admonish us that each of us, placed in tribulation, should invoke God and say: “Attend, O God, to my help”; direct your attention toward helping me. And because he could help and yet not hasten [Col. 0853A] to do so, he therefore says: “Hasten to help me.”

Let them be confounded and put to shame. The holy man grieves that his soul is sought by evil people, not for imitation but for oppression; therefore he prays and says: “Let them be confounded and put to shame.”

Where, then, is that Gospel command: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you”? And again: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you.” Where also is the example of the merciful teacher, who taught us not only to love our enemies but also to pray for them, saying in his passion on behalf of his persecutors: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing”?

This person certainly does not disagree with that one, because he prays that those who formerly imprisoned, scourged, and killed his saints, and were thereby glorified, may be confounded—that is, recognize themselves as deserving of shame—and thus be put to shame, that is, be filled with fear, and beat their breasts with us.

The saints have already received such vengeance from their enemies. For Paul, who had received [Col. 0853B] letters from the chief priests so that he might go to Damascus and bring bound to Jerusalem any men he found belonging to the Christian religion, truly heard a divine voice on the road, confessed from his conscience, and was put to shame at such immodesty. He was struck down in order to obey, having previously been inflamed to persecute.

Let them be turned backward. Here he distinguishes the times of the Church’s tribulation and persecution. Formerly there was the assault of the persecutors; now there remains only the malevolence of those who plot. On behalf of these he asks that those who formerly wished to go ahead and be teachers may be turned away, so that they are behind, as happened to the one to whom it was said: “Go behind me, Satan.” That is, let them not go ahead to teach their wicked ways, but remain behind so that they may learn good ones.

Those, I say, who wish me evil—that is, who live wickedly in their minds and nourish their hearts in sensuality.

Let them be turned away at once. Because there is a twofold persecution of the Church—one violent, the other fraudulent—and the fraudulent [Col. 0853C] has two parts, namely malevolence and flattery, while the tongue of a flatterer often does more harm than the hand of a persecutor, he therefore says on behalf of these people: “Let them be turned away at once,” that is, without any delay, ashamed of their wickedness—those who say to me, “Good, good,” that is, those who praise me in order to deceive me.

For why do they praise me? Let them rather praise the one from whom I have whatever good I possess. Wisdom says that fire is the test of gold and silver, but the test of a person is the mouth of those who praise him. If he does not yield to flattery, if he does not consent to blandishments, he has been perfectly refined in the fire of tribulation. Thus both his entrance and his departure will be good.

As the Apostle says: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tested beyond what you can bear”—this is the entrance—“but with the testing he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure”—this is the departure. To be tested is the entrance; not to yield is the departure.

The heretics wish to fatten their heads with this oil of flattery, as did Donatus, who wished his disciples to hear him called “Good leader, [Col. 0853D] excellent leader,” and similar things. But the one who said, “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” did not desire this oil.

Let them exult and rejoice. Let those people and those people, I say, be turned away, and in opposition to those adversaries let them exult outwardly and rejoice inwardly—that is, let them possess complete joy—being founded in you and not presuming upon themselves, namely, all who seek you, who first sought them. For they would not seek you unless they had been preceded by your grace.

Or the same people may be understood in this way: Let all those who have been turned away and put to shame exult and rejoice in you, those who seek you as you seek them, attributing nothing to themselves but always saying, “Let the Lord be magnified,” never “the servant.”

He called the wanderer: “Let the Lord be magnified.”

He justified the sinner: “Let the Lord be magnified.”

He crowned the justified: “Let the Lord be magnified.”

Let those who love your salvation—that is, your Savior—say this, I say. And all who truly love the Savior love that they have been healed, [Col. 0854A] and they will recognize themselves as needy and that a physician was necessary for them.

But I am needy and poor. Let them say that concerning the Lord; but let each person say this concerning himself: “I am needy,” that is, in need of another’s help, because I see that the law in my members also fights against the law of my mind. And I am poor, that is, hungry and thirsty, and still insufficient for myself. Therefore you, God, who alone are able, help me.

And in saying “help me,” I mean: Be my helper against the contrary law in my members, which fights against the law of my mind, and my liberator from the entanglements of this world. And so that you may be my helper and liberator, therefore, Lord, do not delay—that is, do not make me feel that I am waiting too long for your promised reward. For if I do not have endurance, I shall be like those who failed in the desert and turned back in their minds to see what they had already left behind in body.

And I shall forget you, who said: “Remember Lot’s wife,” who, having gone out from Sodom, [Col. 0854B] failed on the way, but was changed into a pillar of salt to season you—that is, to teach you—so that you too may not fail on the way but may always direct your attention toward your homeland. And if he delays, wait for him, because “when he comes, he will come, and he will not delay.” For no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.

But if this psalm is read as spoken in the voice of the head, as some wish, then these two verses will be explained as follows:

As though he were saying: Let all who seek you exult and rejoice, I say, and let them say: “Let the Lord always be magnified.” But so that my people might say such things, I became truly needy and truly poor, so that I might be an example to my people. Therefore, O God, help me; and in helping me, be my helper in perfecting obedience and my liberator from enemies. Therefore, Lord, do not delay—that is, do not postpone my resurrection until the common resurrection of all.

## PSALM LXX

A Psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab and of the first captives.

[Col. 0854C]

## ARGUMENT

He foretells what the people were going to suffer in Babylon and that these things would come for their correction, while also promising their return. Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ addressed to the Father.

## EXPLANATION

The prophet Jeremiah reports that Jonadab was a priest of God who commanded his sons not to drink wine and not to live in houses but in tents. He found that they had great favor with the Lord because of this obedience; they are now presented as representing the faithful and devout.

Hence Jonadab is interpreted as “the spontaneous one of the Lord,” who can say: “I will sacrifice to you willingly.” With these, the former captives also pour out tears—those who first deserved to be taken captive and afterward to be redeemed. Having been made captives by sin but redeemed by repentance, they say: “And from the abyss of the earth you have brought me back [Col. 0854D] again.”

A general person is introduced, liberated from the captivity of sins and clinging to the divine commandments, proclaiming to us the extraordinary love of Christ the Lord, which is always freely bestowed without preceding merits.

In the first part of the psalm, this person continually asks to be liberated from human iniquities, so that he may deserve to give thanks to the Lord. In the second, he begs not to be deprived in old age of the benefits of the one whose help protected him in youth. In the third, listing his gifts, he promises that he will continually act.

## COMMENTARY

In you, Lord, I have hoped. Throughout all the divine Scriptures, God’s gratuitous grace is commended to us—the grace that freely liberates us. The Apostle commends it, and for this reason he deserved to have as enemies the Jews who presumed upon the letter of the Law and upon their own righteousness.

This grace is also especially commended to us in this psalm, so that all our hope may be in it, and so that we may presume upon nothing as though it came from our own [Col. 0855A] strength, lest, making our own what comes from him, we lose what we have received.

The title of the psalm is: “For the end, a psalm for David, of the sons of Jonadab and of those who were first led into captivity.”

This Jonadab is commended to us through the prophecy of Jeremiah because he was a priest of God. He commanded his sons not to drink wine and not to dwell in houses, but to live in tents. As though he were saying: They carefully kept that commandment, and therefore deserved to be blessed by God—not because the Lord had commanded that they should not drink wine, but because he had commanded that children should obey their fathers in the Lord.

They obeyed their father’s command as though it were the Lord’s, and therefore deserved to be blessed. Thus the prophet reproved through their obedience the disobedience of the Israelite people, arguing from the lesser: If these people obeyed their father’s command, how much more ought those others to obey the commands of the Creator?

Since it is beneficial for the soul to obey its God, for a son to obey his father, for a servant his master, and for a wife her husband, is it not much more beneficial for a human being [Col. 0855B] to obey God his Creator? Certainly it is.

Therefore, because those Israelites did not obey the Lord’s commands, they deserved to be taken captive into Babylon. The prophet foretold this to them, telling them to prepare themselves for captivity, since it could not be otherwise than that those who had been disobedient to the Lord their God should be taken captive. Thus the title says: “Of the sons of Jonadab and of those who were first led into captivity.”

Through the obedience of the former, the disobedience of the latter was condemned. And not only their disobedience, but every disobedience, including that of the first parents, is condemned through the obedience of these people. For captivity, signified in Adam and Eve, was brought about through the disobedience of these first captives. We are still held under that captivity, because even if we have already been liberated in hope, we have not yet been liberated in reality, since we still await the redemption of our body.

The Apostle recalls this captivity, saying: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law [Col. 0855C] in my members fighting against the law of my mind and leading me captive into the law of sin and death.” How, and by what means, anyone may be liberated from this captivity, the Apostle himself subsequently determines by saying: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, given through Jesus Christ.”

And because grace alone can liberate us from captivity, it is commended so strongly in this psalm, so that we presume upon nothing from ourselves and do not lose what we have received.

Jonadab is interpreted as “the spontaneous one of God.” He is the spontaneous one of God of whom it was said: “I will sacrifice to you willingly,” and similar things—that is, Christ.

His sons are his imitators, namely, all who serve God with a pure and free mind. He commanded them not to drink wine, that is, not to become drunk with the pleasure of earthly happiness. Hence one person shows that he was not drunk when he says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I always pursue the goal of the heavenly calling.”

[Col. 0855D] He also commanded them not to dwell in houses, that is, not to suppose that they have a permanent city here, but always to seek the city that is to come. He further commanded them to dwell in tents, that is, to understand that this life is nothing other than military service, and always to be ready to fight against extremely dangerous enemies.

The Apostle recalls their ferocity when he says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood,” that is, against visible enemies, “but against rulers and authorities, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.”

The title is explained as follows: These words are referred to the end of time. They are a psalm attributed to David—or to a prophet, or to anyone who is perfectly and truly obedient—who is the “psalm of the sons of Jonadab and of those who were first led into captivity,” because it commends the obedience of the former and reproves the disobedience of the latter.

For the holy person who speaks here, whether one person in himself or one person represented in many, embodies in himself the obedience of the sons of [Col. 0856A] Jonadab, praises it, and thus by contrast reproves the first captives and every disobedience.

Some authorities simply set out the title in this way: This psalm belongs to the sons of Jonadab, that is, it is attributed to all who are truly and perfectly obedient; and it belongs not only to them but also to all those who were first led into captivity, that is, to all who recognize themselves as captives in Adam. Thus, by “the sons of Jonadab” and “the first captives,” we understand the same people.

Otherwise this psalm could not be the psalm of captives, with the captives themselves acting in it. However it may be varied, this must remain certain: whoever speaks here commends, throughout nearly the entire psalm and almost syllable by syllable, the grace that freely liberates us.

Thus he begins:

As though he were saying: Adam hoped in himself, and therefore was eternally confounded. But I do not hope in myself; rather, I hope now and have always hoped in you—that is, in your grace, which freely liberates. Therefore, even if for a time I am confounded by Adam’s captivity, that is, by the punishments of sin, I will not nevertheless be confounded [Col. 0856B] with continuing eternal confusion; that is, I will not be eternally confounded.

And so that I may not be eternally confounded, therefore, Lord, free me now, lest I fail in tribulation, in your righteousness—that is, because I am not one of those who wish to establish their own righteousness and not be subject to your righteousness. Rather, I strive to carry out your righteousness and presume upon that alone, not upon my own.

And finally, rescue me perfectly. And so that you may finally rescue me, now bend your ear toward me, you who are high, toward me who am lowly, as a physician toward a sick person. And save me—that is, justify me by grace, since I could not be saved by my own righteousness.

And after you have justified me, be for me a protecting God—that is, be my God, my protector and shield, so that the arrows of the enemy may not reach me. And if they do reach me, so that they may not harm me, be my fortified place.

For if a high place on earth makes a person secure—as that man was secure who, stationed on a very high watchtower, despised a king passing by with his entire army—how much more does being placed in God, who made heaven [Col. 0856C] and earth, make a person secure.

Therefore, I say, be my protecting God and fortified place, so that at the end you may truly save me.

For you are my strength. Therefore I say that you should be my fortified place, because you are my strength. Through you and from you comes whatever strength I have against any temptations; from myself I am weak. And you are my refuge. I fled from the angry one; I shall flee to the gracious one. In fleeing I became weak; in taking refuge I shall be strengthened.

My God, rescue me. Up to this point he has been dealing with the inner war, namely, what we suffer from the inner enemy, the contrary law in our members. And because he fears that this inner enemy may be stirred up by the outer enemy and become more savage, he also prays concerning the outer enemy, saying:

“My God, rescue me from the hand of sinners,” that is, from the power of sin, the external enemy—so that it may not persuade me to iniquity by lying in wait, nor bring me to consent by raging.

Here he uses “sinner” for any transgressor of either the written law or the natural law. [Col. 0856D] Hence he subdivides the term, saying: “And rescue me from the hand of one who acts against the written law, and from the hand of every wicked person,” that is, one who acts wickedly without a written law; by this understand the transgressor of the natural law.

For you are my patience. Therefore I say that you should rescue me, because you, Lord, are my patience—that is, from you alone I have the fact that I am in some way patient toward the sinner or wicked person.

And I am patient through you because you, Lord, are my hope from my youth, that is, from the time when, having been renewed, I began to hope in you. And you armed me against the devil, so that, as one armed in the battle line of an army, I might fight against spiritual and invisible enemies with faith, hope, and the other gifts.

And you are not only my hope from my youth, but I have also been confirmed—that is, I received in you as much confirmation as could be possessed—from my mother’s womb, that is, from the time when I first began to be formed in the institutions of the Church. And from the time when I was coming forth from my mother’s womb—that is, from the time when I received perfect [Col. 0857A] regeneration in those same institutions—you have truly been my protector, my shield against the arrows of the enemy.

The womb here signifies the first beginnings of faith, such as exorcism and the sign made upon catechumens. Coming forth from the womb signifies true regeneration through baptism and instruction in the faith. Youth signifies something beyond these: full renewal, when a person, already perfectly armed with faith, hope, love, and the other gifts, is like a young man going to war.

My song is in you. Because you are my protector, therefore, Lord, let the song of others be in the world and in the things that belong to it; but my song—that is, all my glory and exultation—will always be in you, both in the time of hope, that is, in the present, and in the future, when we shall see you face to face.

And because my song is in you alone, therefore I have become to many—that is, to those who are scattered and do not strive toward one thing, namely, the wicked—like a portent, that is, like a monster. To those who do not believe that goods exist except present ones, [Col. 0857B] those who despise present goods and yet desire things that do not appear seem like monsters.

Hence the Apostle says: “If we are hoping in Christ only in this life, we are more pitiable than all human beings.”

I have become, I say, to many like a portent, that is, like a monster; yet I need not fear them, because you are my strong helper against those weak people, who are unable to kill anything except the body.

Let my mouth be filled. So that my song may always be in you, let my inner mouth—which was full of your praise as long as humanity remained in an abundance of virtues, but was emptied through transgression—be filled, that is, be perfectly filled, with your praise.

Let it be filled so that I may sing your glory by holy thought and action in myself—that is, your justification: that you have made the impious pious and have taken the condemned into the kingdom—and so that I may sing your greatness: that, when I did not exist, you made me exist; that you gave salvation [Col. 0857C] when I was sinning; that you forgave when I turned back; that you helped when I persevered; that you crowned.

And I shall do this not merely during a day without night, but throughout the whole day, both in day and in night. For the natural day contains both day and night, and here it is understood as prosperity and adversity.

A person sings as though only in the day if he praises God only in prosperity; but in the night, that is, in adversity, he does not praise but blames him, like the one of whom it was said elsewhere: “When you have done well for him, he will bless you.”

But the person who sings both in day and night praises God both in prosperity and in adversity, saying: “The Lord has given; the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.”

Both day and night are designated here by the superior part, that is, by day, because day ought not to serve night, but rather night ought to follow [Col. 0857D] day. Day serves night when God, who ought to be worshiped and praised, is worshiped for eternal goods alone and praised for temporal goods, which belong to night; this ought not to happen. Rather, night ought to follow day, that is, whatever temporal goods we have should be distributed in the praise of God.

Do not cast me away. And so that I may always sing your glory, do not cast me away—that is, do not make me appear to have been cast away by you in the time of old age. The present life is the time of old age, that is, the time of captivity and tribulation, because of the old age, that is, the antiquity, of the first parent.

He describes that time by saying: “When my strength fails,” that is, because I presume upon nothing of my own strength but hope solely in your grace.

And therefore, Lord, do not abandon me. The person who easily falls and cannot withstand certain tribulations appears to have been cast away and abandoned by God.

For they said. Therefore it is necessary that you not abandon me, because my enemies—for all the impious are enemies of the pious—said, that is, determined, not for their own benefit and power, as they supposed, but for me, that is, for my benefit.

And before he states what they said, [Col. 0858A] he determines which enemies he means, saying: “And those who guarded,” that is, watched for the capture of, “my soul,” that is, who acted not to imitate but to oppress me, “took counsel together,” namely, saying:

“God has abandoned him,” that is, God does not care about such people. “Pursue him, therefore, and seize him, because there is no one who can rescue him from our hands.”

Many pursue without seizing; but let those people pursue in such a way that they seize, since they bring down those whom they pursue.

These words, and certain others that follow, appear to pertain to the head, but they are more familiarly referred to us, because he spoke such things from our weakness, not from his majesty—from what he became for us, not from what he was by which he perfected us.

God, do not draw away. Indeed, the enemies say that God has abandoned me and that there is no one to rescue me; but you, God, do not draw away from me, just as in truth you will not draw away, [Col. 0858B] because the Lord is near to those who have been crushed in heart. My God, I say, who earlier despised me because of disobedience, now look upon me as I stretch myself toward your help—that is, by giving me patience; but to those who persecute me and refuse to be caught, give a true confession. He says this as follows:

“Let them be put to shame”—that is, let an evil conscience gnaw at their minds—and let them fail in their evil purpose, “those who slander my soul,” that is, who wish to drag down my soul and thus strip away its wings, namely, the virtues by which it ought to fly upward. The image is taken from birds: they are caught so that they cannot fly away when their wings are stripped from them. While I say, “Let them be put to shame,” I mean, “Let them be covered with confusion and disgrace”—that is, let complete confusion over their evil deeds and shame over the modesty they have lost come upon those who seek evil for me, that is, who seek to drag me down.

But I will not say, “I shall always hope,” as though I were wishing for something doubtful; rather, assured by your grace and not presuming upon my own strength, I will speak affirmatively: “I shall always hope in you.” And I shall hope for this reason: “I will add praise above all your praise.” What praise will he add, or to what praise will he add it? If this is read as spoken in the voice of the Head, as some wish for the whole of this psalm, it will be understood in this way:

God was praised for the ordering of the elements, the arrangement of the seasons, the composition of all creatures, and their governance; but he had not yet been praised for the resurrection of human flesh. Christ, the first to be raised from the dead, added this praise to his praise.

But if this is understood as spoken in the voice of the Body, as we have proceeded thus far, then we shall say that God is praised because he created humanity when it did not exist, made it rational, gave it free will, placed it in the delights of paradise, gave it a commandment, and foretold that certain death would come if it transgressed that commandment. He did nothing incompletely—that is, he did everything that ought to have been done for humanity. But wretched humanity fell through transgression and became in itself, as it were, a mass of perdition for the whole human race. If God had destroyed this entire mass, no one could have said that he was unjust, because he would have done so justly; and therefore he would also have been worthy of praise in this.

Behold, his praise is manifold. Yet above all this praise another praise is added when an impious person becomes pious and one condemned is taken up into the kingdom. This is the praise of which he says: “I will add praise upon all your praise.” He accomplishes and demonstrates this, as though he were saying:

“I will add praise to you above praise in this way: my mouth, inwardly and outwardly, will announce”—that is, will represent in words, deeds, and thoughts—that righteousness is yours, not mine; that is, that my justification comes from your grace, not from my merits. And “all day”—whether in adversity and prosperity, or “all day,” meaning continually—it will announce your saving help, that is, the salvation of your grace, whereas condemnation is mine.

According to the interpretation that this is the voice of the Head, what precedes will be said here: “My mouth,” that is, the mouth of my members. The meaning, however, will not change.

### For I have not known letters

That is, for this reason my mouth will announce that righteousness is yours and not mine: “because I have not known letters,” meaning that I do not presume to be justified by the letter of the law, as those do who cling only to the letter of the law and recoil from grace. They do not attend to the fact that the grace of the law is directed toward the sacrifice, nor to the fact that the grace of the one who assists is necessary for the command of the one who commands to be fulfilled. For if, presuming upon your own strength, you begin by your own power and then fail, the law will be for you a letter that punishes, not one that saves.

The law without grace is a letter that kills. It is useful only for convicting iniquity, not for granting salvation. “I have not known letters,” I say; and therefore “from now on I will not enter”—not into the power of the law, but “into the power of the Lord.” That is, from now on I will resolve to live not according to the letter of the law, which is powerless to justify, but according to the grace of the Lord, which is powerful to justify. And thus, O Lord, “I will remember your righteousness alone”: I will always keep in mind that the righteousness by which I am justified is yours. You did not repay me according to my merits with punishment, but bestowed grace, so that it might belong to you alone, and not to the servant who gave the law.

For, as the Apostle says, “If a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly have come from the law.” But this is not so, because “Scripture confined all things under sin.”

### God, you have taught me

He is saying, as it were: You, God, taught me to remember that righteousness belongs to you alone, from my youth—that is, from the time when I turned to you and was renewed by you, having been made by you. And how did you teach me? In this way: when I consider my former life, I see what was owed to me and what I received in place of what was owed.

Punishment was owed to me, but grace was given to me; Gehenna was owed to me, but the hope of eternal life was given to me. “You taught me,” I say, “from my youth,” and even until now you continue to teach me, because you still govern me—you who placed me on the way.

Therefore, until now I proclaim your wonders, and I shall always proclaim them by holy meditation and good works. “Until old age and gray hairs I bless your wonders.” For what wonders are greater than raising the dead? If we had not been dead, the Apostle would not say to us: “Rise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and God will enlighten you.” All sinners, even if they are outwardly alive, are nevertheless inwardly dead.

When the body is raised, it is restored to the world; but the soul is restored to itself. The raised body can live without its raiser, but the soul cannot, because there are two lives, one of the body and the other of the soul. Just as the body cannot live without grace, so the soul cannot live without the grace by which it is raised.

For this reason he says, “Until now you still teach me,” because a soul restored to itself could in no way live without the governance of grace. What is said here may be referred to every perfect person; thus, by “old age and gray hairs” we may understand either simply the end of life or, according to the Greeks, moral gravity by “old age” and complete perfection by “gray hairs.”

Among us, both terms are spoken by an old man and are taken as equivalent. Among the Greeks, however, “old age” is understood as that gravity of character which follows mature manhood, and they call such grave men *presbyters*. They understand “gray hairs” as decrepit age and call decrepit persons *gerontes*.

But if one person is speaking here who represents many—namely, the Church—we must distinguish these periods differently.
