By the youth of the Church we should understand only the time in which the holy Apostles lived and blood was poured out in many ways for the joy of the Church, that is, the blood of the holy martyrs. By mature manhood we should understand the present condition; by old age and gray hairs, the final period before the end of the world, the time of Antichrist.

“I will proclaim your wonders,” I say, “until old age and gray hairs.” And so that I may do this, O God, do not abandon me until I, the Church, proclaim through those who are present and those who persecute them—or I, the perfected one, proclaim through myself and my successors—your arm, namely that of which it is said: “To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” That is, your Son, through whom gratuitous deliverance has been given to us. Let me proclaim it “to every generation that is to come.” [Col. 0860A]

For the Holy Spirit foresaw that certain heretics would arise who would assert, and persuade their followers, that the Church would last only a short time. Through the prophet he refutes them equivalently, saying that the Church will not be absent as long as there is a generation. In this way he restrains the faithful, so that they may never believe such people.

### Your power

He explains what he understands by “arm.” He is saying, as it were: “Do not abandon me, I say, until I proclaim your arm”—that is, until I proclaim your power, meaning your grace, which makes us powerful to resist temptations—and “your righteousness,” that is, the same grace that justifies us. Thus power and righteousness are the same.

If we follow Cassiodorus, however, we may distinguish them: power may be understood as the manner of justifying, and righteousness as the final act of judgment.

“I will proclaim your power and your righteousness,” I say—“I,” extending even “to the highest great things,” that is, to the highest supercelestial creatures, exalted in dignity in relation to us, whom you nevertheless made what they are.

He adds these great things so that we might not think grace pertains only to human beings, since it also pertains to the supercelestial spirits. Both the fact that they are what they are and the fact that they live well—that is, that they persist in truth—come from grace.

It continues:

### God, who is like you?

He is saying, as it were: Since through your power not only earthly things but also supercelestial things persist, who, then, is like you? No one, certainly.

For their own ruin, the first apostate angel perversely wished to become like you—the one who did not rightly wish to be like you—and so did the second, the human being. Every day God calls us to a good likeness to himself, saying: “Be merciful, as I, your Father, am merciful.” He invites us to love our enemies and do good to them, because he makes his rain fall upon the just and the unjust. But that first one did not wish to be like him in this.

Since God is the good that is content with itself, and power that is subject to no power, that first one perversely wished to resemble him in this respect. He said: “I will set my throne toward the north,” so that power might stand against that power, not beneath it. Therefore he vanished in his own thought and fell from light into eternal darkness.

The wretched second one consented to this evil, wishing to be a god to himself and to depend upon his own will. He withdrew from the emperor and turned aside after the deserter. The emperor gave the law; the deserter suggested fraud. Wretched humanity believed what the devil persuaded it to believe and discovered what God had threatened, because it was condemned to death.

This is what he says: “How many things you have shown me.” The literal connection is as though he were saying: Since no one is like you, I, in Adam, perversely wished to become like you to my own ruin; therefore you showed me tribulations, and how many of them—great and evil ones.

Here he calls all the punishments of sin “tribulations,” although some of them seem pleasant to those who do not attend to them, such as eating, drinking, and similar things. But the one who does attend to them calls them evil.

The meaning is: Because I perversely wished to become like you, you punished me with great and innumerable tribulations. Yet you have given me life without revocation, because, turning from anger to mercy, you gave me life inwardly in reality and outwardly in hope.

Therefore I say, “You have given me life,” because you have brought my soul back again “from the depths of the earth.” This can be understood in two ways.

When the human being was made from the earth, the earth in its lowliness was brought forth into something worthy. But when the human being became a transgressor, the earth was reduced again to its lowliness. Then, when it was assumed by that Word who was in the beginning with God, it was brought back. It fell again in a certain manner when the assumed flesh died; it was brought back when that same flesh rose. Thus it was brought back again—that is, twice.

In this interpretation, understand “the abyss” as the lowliness of the earth.

Or otherwise: I say, “You have given me life,” because “in the earth,” that is, twice, you have brought me back “from the depths of the earth,” that is, from the depth of vices. First he brought us forth when our nature was assumed by the Word. There was another fall in death itself. From there he brought us back through his resurrection, in which the hope of our rising again was given to us. He will bring us back again when this hope is fulfilled, that is, when we are raised. Thus there will be this great restoration as a doubled restoration.

### You have multiplied your magnificence

How, I ask, have you given me life? In this way: You have multiplied your magnificence, that is, your magnificent power. For you not only bestow pardon; upon the sons whom you prepare for inheritance you also mercifully apply discipline. Just as, having turned from anger to mercy, you have consoled the mind inwardly, so you will also console it outwardly.

### For I also will confess to you

I say that you have consoled me because you have already granted this to me: even in the present I shall praise you in the vivification of the spirit and the mortification of the flesh. He says this as follows:

“For I also, like my Head, will confess to you, O God,” that is, I will praise your truth or the promises fulfilled in me.

Or: “I will confess your truth,” that is, I will praise your true commandments by fulfilling them for you, that is, for your honor; and I will do this “with the vessels of the psalm.”

As blessed Augustine says, the vessel of the psalm is the instrument of the psalm, namely, the psalter. Because it sounds from above, it signifies the vivification of the spirit, which comes from above.

The meaning is: “I will confess to you with the vessels of the psalm,” that is, in spiritual works, such as holy thought and prayer.

According to Cassiodorus, we may also take “with the vessels of the psalm” intransitively, as though he were saying: “I will confess to you in vessels”—what vessels?—that is, in such songs in which the praise of God is pure and incorporeal, just as uncorrupted liquid remains infused in a good vessel. This praise, however, pertains to the vivification of the spirit.

Or by “the vessels of the psalm” we may understand spiritual souls, in which the praise of God does not grow sour but remains wholesome, like liquid in a good vessel.

“I will confess to you,” I say, O God, “with the vessels of the psalm, and I will sing psalms to you on the lyre,” that is, in holy works pertaining to the mortification of the flesh, such as stretching out a hand to the poor, visiting the sick and those in prison, and similar deeds.

I will praise you, O Holy One—the Holy One, I say, of Israel—that is, you who sanctify every person who directs himself toward seeing you. For “Israel” is interpreted as “the man who sees God.” And the lyre, which sounds from below, appropriately signifies the mortification of the flesh.

### My lips will rejoice

Now, I say, I will confess to you with the vessels of the psalm and sing psalms on the lyre. But finally my inward lips will rejoice completely, namely, when I sing to you, that is, when I offer you a true and unfailing song.

“For blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you.”

And because inward lips are also mentioned, he adds, to explain which lips he has understood: “And my soul itself will then rejoice in your praise,” for this reason: You have redeemed it, and you will redeem it from every tribulation or mutability.

You will redeem not only the soul but also the body from corruption through incorruption, because “my tongue”—the tongue, that is, of the body—will meditate upon your righteousness. That is, in every intention it will agree with the soul in representing your justification, which will be your praise.

The meaning is: Then the flesh will not, through any corruption, hold the soul back from your praise; rather, it will agree with it, because I shall be wholly consumed as a holocaust in the most ardent fire of charity. This will be “all day,” that is, in the future, when there will be day without night.

Then, in contrast, those who now seek evil for me, wishing to drag me down, will become ashamed and disgraced—that is, they will have a conscience severely gnawed by remorse and will be exceedingly ashamed, saying: “We fools considered their life a disgrace,” and so forth.

## PSALM 71

### A psalm concerning Solomon

### ARGUMENT

This psalm is not sung simply concerning Solomon, but concerning Solomon on account of the common prosperity of the people, which was joined to the king’s prosperity. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church concerning Christ addressed to the Lord.

### EXPOSITION

Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful,” signifying the Lord Christ, of whom it is said: “Of his empire and peace there will be no end.”

Throughout the psalm the prophet foretells the coming of Christ. In the first part he speaks to the Father, asking that judgment be given to the Son for judging the peoples, although he knew that this had been predestined before the ages.

In the second part he says that, in the Lord’s judgment, the sons of the poor are to be saved and the pride of the devil humbled; he also explains the virgin birth itself through various comparisons.

In the third he relates the good things that occurred through the Holy Spirit, when the Lord Christ was born from the Virgin Mary.

In the fourth he says that Christ is to be worshiped by all kings, because he redeemed the human race from the power of the devil.

In the fifth he declares that, having been seen by human eyes, he was the support of believers and the unfailing progress of the righteous.

In the sixth he says that praises are to be offered to the eternal Lord by the unanimous consent of the whole world.

In the seventh he renders a hymn to the Lord Christ with the purest devotion.

### COMMENTARY

#### God, give your judgment to the king

These words refer to Solomon—not to Solomon, the son of the prophet David, but to the true peaceful one, that is, to Christ. For Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful.”

He is truly peaceful, through whom, having received the remission of sins as mediator, we have been reconciled to God. For the Apostle says: “While we were still sinners, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son.”

He is also truly peaceful who made both one, breaking down the middle wall, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace.

This may be understood of the two walls of the Church, which have been joined in the one cornerstone, that is, in Christ, after the middle obstacle by which they were separated—the carnal law—had been removed. Or it may be understood of the earthly and the heavenly Church, which Christ reconciled after removing the wall that sins had erected between them.

Christ the peaceful one can also be demonstrated in many other ways—not according to the peace that the world seeks and loves, but according to the peace of which the prophet says: “I will give you true consolation, peace upon peace,” namely, immortality upon the peace of reconciliation.

The prophet openly explains in this psalm his hidden and manifest coming in order to expose the hardness of that people which, through the prophetic Spirit, he foresaw would contradict all the things written about Christ in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms. He also does this to exhort them to recognize his hidden coming, lest in the end they experience his manifest coming.

He says, then:

“God, give your judgment to the king.”

The meaning is: Lord Father, send the one whom you are going to send, so that, having assumed human nature, you may give him your judgment as king—that is, a certain and provident judgment, which cannot be deceived as human judgment can.

“For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, because he is the Son of Man.”

Christ judges from the very humanity that he assumed, because the new man gave new commandments to the world. Those who keep them will be judged for good; those who despise them, for evil. It is entirely just that the one who became human for the sake of human beings should also judge human beings.

It continues:

#### And your righteousness to the king’s son

In other words, he repeats what he said before. The king and the king’s son are the same person. He is king according to his humanity, but the king’s son according to his divinity.

When he says, “Give your righteousness to the king’s son,” it is the same as saying, “Give him your just judgment.”

Such repetitions are not superfluous, for divine speech is greatly adorned by them; and they are necessary in the Psalms and in that kind of discourse by which the emotions of the mind are stirred.

#### To judge your people

“Give,” I say, “your judgment to the king,” namely, “to judge” your people—that is, to distinguish the sheep from the goats in righteousness.

He determines whom he calls the king’s people by saying:

#### And to judge your poor with judgment

The word “judgment,” standing by itself, is understood as “just judgment,” as blessed Augustine says.

When he says, “your poor,” he speaks by way of distinction, because there are some poor who are not his—those who, although outwardly poor, are inwardly rich through desire.

#### Let the mountains receive

He is saying, as it were: In order that that king may judge your people, let the mountains—that is, the holy Apostles, who are mountains, exalted in holiness and powerful in virtue—receive peace.

They are mountains because they speak in such a way that others may be faithfully instructed by them, and live in such a way that others may imitate them to their salvation.

Let those mountains, I say, receive the peace of which the Apostle says: “We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us; we beg you, on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.”

That is, let them receive the preaching of reconciliation to be announced to the people. Those who have ears for hearing and hear will be judged for good; those who do not hear, for evil.

And let the hills—that is, those inferior to the mountains and related to them as hills are to mountains, as Luke and Timothy were to Paul—receive righteousness. That is, let them obey the authority of the mountains, as is just. For he calls this very obedience righteousness.

Or otherwise: Let the mountains—that is, the rulers and superiors in the Church—receive peace and make harmony in the world or among the people. It pertains especially to rulers, through vigilant attention, to provide for peace, that is, harmony, so that schisms may not arise.

Therefore let the mountains receive peace, and let the hills receive it as well—that is, let inferiors, by obeying, follow the authority of the mountains, as is just.

#### He will judge the poor of the people

“Give,” I say, “judgment to the king,” and truly you will give it. That king will finally judge—that is, distinguish for salvation—the true poor from the primitive people.

And because he will also judge the wicked, he determines how he will judge these people, saying that he will not only save those earlier poor, but will also eternally save their sons—that is, all true poor imitators of those poor people.

Therefore he will humble the calumniator.

Here he calls the devil the “calumniator,” because through fraud and wickedness he always strives to crush those whom he accuses, whence elsewhere he is called “the accuser of the brethren.” He is especially grieved that our cause is before a judge so provident and kind.

He will truly then be humbled, because when death has been swallowed up and there is no longer any place for sin, his power will perish.

#### And he will remain with the sun

“And he will humble the calumniator.” And when, after the calumniator has been humbled, he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father, then he will remain eternally “with the sun,” that is, with the Father’s glory.

He will remain “before the moon,” that is, in the sight of the Church, so that the Church may be refreshed there from which he shone here.

He compares the Church to the moon because, just as the moon has no light of its own but receives it from the sun, so the Church has no light unless it receives it from the one who enlightens every human being coming into this world.

“Before the moon,” I say, “of generation after generation,” that is, before that generation which will be composed of all generations. According to another translation, however, you may say that he will truly remain before the moon because he will remain through generation and generation.

#### He will descend like rain upon a fleece

He is saying, as it were: The one who will come openly to judge in this manner will first come secretly to be judged, because “he will descend like rain upon a fleece.”

It should be known that what was said in the preceding two verses in the future tense can also be said in the present tense, as follows:

The Lord will finally judge the true poor of the people; even now he saves them by justifying both the poor themselves and the sons of the poor, that is, their imitators; and he humbles the calumniator.

For he will give his own such grace that the very thing by which the calumniator sought to accuse them—namely, that they would not worship God freely, as in the case of blessed Job, when he said, “Does Job worship God for nothing?”—will instead be the means by which he himself is humbled and defeated, because they worship God freely against his will.

Or otherwise: He will humble the calumniator through the sacrament of his incarnation. When the calumniator stretches out his hand against one in whom he finds nothing of his own, he loses the others over whom he had rights.

By saving his own and humbling the calumniator, he will remain with the sun—that is, as long as the sun rises and sets, at all times. And surely he will remain with the sun because he is before the moon, that is, before all times.

Similarly, one could say “before the sun,” but for variety of expression, since he had previously mentioned the sun, he now mentions the moon.

He will remain, I say, existing “through generation and generation,” that is, in the present generation, where one generation is passing away and another succeeding, and thus there are many generations.

#### He will descend like rain

“He will save,” I say, “the sons of the poor.” And in order to save them, “he will descend like rain upon a fleece,” that is, he will be born from an undefiled virgin.

For just as rain penetrates a fleece and falls from it without any tearing of its fibers, so the Lord entered and left the Virgin’s womb without any corruption of her integrity.

#### And like drops falling upon the earth

He says the same thing through another comparison. Just as drops of gentle rain fall secretly upon the earth, so the Lord was born from the Virgin without the noise of marital intercourse.

Alternatively, if we consider the historical sense: At the time when the Lord ruled the people through judges, he commanded Gideon to fight against the Midianites, promising him victory.

Gideon, however, wishing to make the promise certain for himself, spread a fleece upon the threshing floor at night and asked that this sign be given to him: that the fleece should be wet with dew while the threshing floor remained dry. And so it happened.

On the following night he again spread out the same fleece and asked that the fleece remain dry while the threshing floor became wet. This too was granted to him, and thus he became certain of victory.

The Jewish people are signified by the fleece. Just as a fleece is removed from a sheep, so this people was to be uprooted from the law and from the glory of its place and nation.

The Lord first descended like rain upon the fleece because he first drenched that people with spiritual grace. From there he chose his mother; from there he took the holy Apostles; from there he began the proclamation of evangelical truth.

Then he descended like drops falling upon the earth, because when the holy Apostles proclaimed, the Jews contradicted them and forbade anyone to speak in that name.

Thus the fleece remained dry, while the surrounding earth was drenched, because grace was withdrawn from the Jews and offered to the Gentiles. Then the holy Apostles went into the way of the Gentiles and entered the city of the Samaritans, which had previously been forbidden, saying:

“It was necessary to speak the word of God to you first; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.”

#### He will arise in his days

The Lord descended, I say, and “in his days righteousness,” previously hidden and not appearing in the law, “will arise,” that is, will be manifested.

“The righteous person lives by faith.” And an abundance of peace will arise, so that even enemies may be loved. This will last until the moon is removed—that is, until, through the death appointed to it, every defect of mortality is removed from the Church.

Or, according to another translation, we shall say: “Until the moon”—that is, the present Church, which is now compared to the moon because of its waning—“is lifted up” through the glory of immortality and impassibility.

Then it will no longer be necessary to love an enemy, because there will no longer be an enemy.

Moreover, this king will rule “from sea to sea,” that is, from the western ocean to the eastern ocean.

And where will he begin? He will begin “from the river,” that is, from the Jordan, which is a river of Judea and from which the proclamation of truth began.

And he will rule “to the ends of the inhabited world,” because “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

This plainly explained sense also shows that these things cannot, as the Jews think, be referred to the historical Solomon.

What he says may also be understood mystically: “He will rule from the eastern sea to the western sea.”

By the eastern sea the Jews are signified. Although they were bitter in their morals, they nevertheless worshiped the one God. By the western sea understand the Gentiles, for whom all knowledge of the truth had set.

By the river understand earthly rulers, who continually flow into worldly bitterness like a river flowing into the sea.

The meaning is: “He will rule from the eastern sea to the western sea,” that is, he will obtain dominion over both Jews and Gentiles.

And he will rule “from the river to the ends of the world,” because he will make those who were previously a river—continually flowing into worldly bitterness—into stable and well-cultivated earth; and not merely earth, but the whole world, perfected to such an extent that they become even the ends of the world.

That is, they will extinguish within themselves all earthly quality so completely that scarcely any of it will remain in any corner of them.

#### Before him the Ethiopians will fall

This king will rule, I say; and while he rules, the Ethiopians—that is, those blackened by sins and most despairing among the Gentiles—will fall before him. That is, they will humble their souls before him.

But his enemies, the Jews, will lick the earth—that is, they will love earthly things more than him, because they preferred to lose innocence rather than lose their place and nation.

Or otherwise: “His enemies,” that is, his opponents, “will lick the earth,” meaning that they will love earthly things. They will be wise in the sense of heretics, and will prefer to imitate their error rather than conform to his truth.

These are two interpretations in a negative sense. There are two others in a positive sense, so that you may say:

“The Ethiopians will fall before him,” I say, “and those who were formerly his enemies will lick the earth,” that is, they will not only humble themselves but will also desire that very humility as something exceedingly sweet.

Or otherwise: “His enemies,” that is, all who formerly opposed him, “will lick the earth,” meaning that they will love his humanity and even strive to imitate his humility.

#### The kings of Tarshish

The Ethiopians will fall before him for this reason: “The kings of Tarshish and of the islands will offer him gifts.” Literally, this can most appropriately be understood of the three kings.

Mystically, however, it is understood as follows. Tarshish is interpreted as “the exploration of joy.” Those who formerly sought joy in earthly things, where there is no joy but rather sorrow, will become kings—ruling their unlawful impulses well within themselves—and will offer pleasing gifts, namely, themselves and others converted through them.

Tarshish, as Jerome says, is also interpreted as “contemplation.” This too is sufficiently appropriate, because those kings who are truly in contemplation will offer him the gifts mentioned above.

“And the islands also will offer him gifts.” The islands are those who are so perfect that, placed in the salt sea of this world, although the waves of temptation assail them from every side, they nevertheless remain stable, like islands in the sea.

#### The kings of Arabia and Sheba will bring gifts to him

Arabia is interpreted as “level country.” It is a region in which every kind of spice is found.

By the kings of Arabia are understood such rulers among the Gentiles as, having been made level and fruitful from wild and thorny people, delight God with the fragrances of every virtue.

Sheba is interpreted as “burned,” and it is a frankincense-bearing region. Through it are understood those inflamed by the fire that the Lord came to cast upon the earth and wills to burn: those fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, and delighting God with good morals like incense.

This may also be said in a negative sense:

“The kings of Arabia,” that is, the kings of the Gentiles, are level and uncultivated; and “Sheba,” that is, those burned by the fire of incitements, will bring gifts to him—namely, by killing the holy martyrs, who will be like sweet sacrifices to the Lord.

#### And they will worship him

He is saying, as it were: Not only will the kings of Tarshish and other great kings offer gifts, but all kings also—that is, all who rule themselves and know that they rule themselves from him—will worship him.

They will worship, that is, they will venerate him greatly. And they will truly worship, because “all the nations”—that is, some people from every nation—will serve him with chaste fear. To serve him is itself to worship him.

#### For he will deliver the poor from the powerful

For this reason they will rightly worship him and serve him: because he has delivered and will deliver the poor—that is, the truly humble people—from the powerful, namely, the calumniator mentioned above.

The calumniator is not powerful over us by his own strength, but through our weakness. For by transgressing we were weakened and sold under sin, and we made him exceedingly powerful over us.

He will deliver the poor, I say; and it was necessary that he deliver the poor, “for whom there was no helper”—because neither philosopher nor angel nor archangel could aid him so that he might be delivered, except that one alone of whom it is said:

“While all things kept silence in the midst,” and so forth.

### He will spare the poor and needy

As if he were saying: How will he liberate the poor? Will he do so in such a way as to be pleased with his sin? No; rather, sin will be destroyed, because he will spare him by forgiving the sin of the poor—that is, of the one who humbles himself before him, as a poor man ordinarily does before a rich man—and of the needy, that is, of the one who is without help and considers grace necessary for himself. Finally, he will save the souls of the poor eternally.

And this for the following reason: [Col. 0866B] here he will redeem their souls from usury—that is, from the punishments of sins, which are ultimately owed to the wicked—and by this he will free them from punishments, because he will redeem them from iniquity, that is, because he removes the cause of punishments, namely, sin. Punishment itself is called “usury” for this reason: more evil is found in punishment than pleasure in sin. Here, the murderer kills only the body; but the one who does this is condemned there in both body and soul. Or, more generally, although someone’s sin is momentary, the punishment will be eternal.

He will redeem, I say, the souls of the poor from iniquity. And their name—that is, the name of the redeemed, namely, the name “Christian,” however despised it may be by the world—will nevertheless be very honorable before him, that is, in his sight, when he says to them: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

### And he will live, and it will be given to him

The Lord, I say, will descend and will rule from sea to sea. Though killed in weakness, he will live through majesty, because he will rise again, and death [Col. 0866C] will no longer rule over him. Or, he will live the true life, because he will be free from sin in himself, and also in his members, according to the saying: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me.” For every sin, whether small or great, is the death of the soul.

And because he will live, gold from Arabia will be given to him: that is, some of the foremost philosophers among the nations will be converted to him, such as Dionysius the Areopagite and many others. For the gold of Arabia is more precious than other gold. By gold wisdom is signified, and by Arabia the Gentile world.

And the fact that they will always worship—as in the petition “Your kingdom come,” which we pray daily—will be from him. For who would know what he ought chiefly to pray for, unless the one who first taught us to despise earthly things and desire heavenly things had come? No one, certainly.

Or otherwise: “They will always worship because of him,” with respect to the completion of the body. For holy men pray this most devotedly: that the body of Christ, that is, the number of the elect, may be completed. [Col. 0866D] Hence, in another Translation, one finds: “They will worship for his sake and bless him”; that is, they will increase in virtues and good works, which will be to bless him.

For whether he blesses us or we bless him, we will always increase; but he is not increased by our blessing, nor diminished by our cursing. And he will do this all day long, that is, in adversity and prosperity. For whoever praises God not only in prosperity but also in adversity has day even in the night, and thus praises God always in the day.

### He will be a foundation in the earth, on the summits of the mountains

They will rightly bless him, therefore, because, dwelling among them on earth for whose sake he assumed an earthly body, he will be a foundation—that is, a confirmation of truth—on the summits of the mountains, that is, in the prophets, who promised many things about him.

For however many promises there are, they are in him—that is, perfected in him—and he says of himself: “It was necessary that everything written about me in the Law, the Prophets, [Col. 0867A] and the Psalms be fulfilled.”

He calls the prophets the summits of the mountains, not because they are more worthy than the apostles, but because they came earlier in time. He will be, I say, a foundation, and his fruit will be lifted high above Lebanon.

Lebanon is a mountain where very tall and fragrant cedar trees grow, possessing imperishable wood. We can understand his fruit by analogy. For just as the fruits of the holy apostles are those whom they converted, to whom he said, “I appointed you to go and bear fruit,” and so forth, so the holy apostles whom he himself called are his fruits.

The meaning is: “His fruit will be lifted high above Lebanon,” that is, it will be greatly exalted above everything excessive, delightful, and precious in this world.

Or, because Lebanon is interpreted as “whitening,” the Jewish people are understood by Lebanon. They were like one made white among the nations because of the worship of the one God and the Law. Within that people, those were whiter who were more than others zealous for the traditions of their fathers, as Paul was. [Col. 0867B] Yet his fruit will be lifted high even above this Lebanon, because the holy apostles will be far more worthy than these, however zealous for the Law they may be.

### And they will blossom from the city like the grass of the earth

Because it is not stated from which city they will blossom, “city” can be understood either in a good or in a bad sense. If it is taken in the good sense, we shall explain it as follows:

Those who are from his city—that is, citizens of that king whose fruit will be so exalted—are all those who have been gathered into the Church for holy living. They will blossom like grass, not just any grass, but grass clinging to the earth, which is not quickly dried up but remains green for a long time. That is, they will blossom like fruitful grass, because they too will bear fruit.

Or they will blossom beneficially like the grass of the earth, that is, like wheat. For wheat is signified by “grass,” as in the book of Genesis, where it says: “Let the earth bring forth every kind of grass and every fruit-bearing tree,” and so forth.

But if we take “city” in the bad sense, we shall explain it thus:

Those who are from the city of Cain—who first built a city where previously no city had existed, because what is animal came before what is spiritual—will indeed blossom, because they will prosper in earthly things; but their blossom will be like the grass of the earth, which exists today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven.

### Let his name be blessed

Having seen and enumerated so many and such great goods that will exist in the days of this king, he blesses him, saying:

“Let his name”—namely, this name, which is “Christ” or “Lord”—“be blessed,” that is, multiplied in the veneration of many throughout the present ages, that is, through all times.

And rightly must it be blessed forever, because his name remains before the sun, that is, it is blessed before all times.

### And all the tribes of the earth will be blessed in him

I say that his name should be blessed, and I rightly say this, because not only Judea but all the tribes—that is, all the families of the earth—will be blessed in him, that is, they will be increased in virtues through him.

And I say “in him” for this reason: in him all the nations will be blessed, that is, some from every nation will magnify him, glorifying him through virtues [Col. 0867D] and good works. For in whatever consists his glorification, in that their blessing will consist.

Blessed, therefore, is the Lord Redeemer, God the Creator, Lord and God—I say, of true Israel—for he alone, through himself, does all wondrous things. Others, even if they perform wonders, do not possess this power from themselves, but through him.

Therefore, let the name of his majesty—that is, his majestic name, namely, “Lord”—be blessed forever, that is, let it be eternally exalted in his servants, so that they may present themselves as those worthy to have such a Lord.

And truly it will be blessed, because the whole earth will be filled with his majesty, that is, with his majestic gift, namely that of which it was said: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters will prophesy.”

For the apostles were principally filled with this gift, that is, with spiritual grace, and through them the whole earth received it, because “their sound went out into all the earth.”

And because the whole earth will be filled with his majesty, therefore [Col. 0868A] let blessing be given to him in the firstborn who have been filled; let it also be given to him in those born afterward.

## ON PSALM 72

### A Psalm of Asaph

### Argument

It is indicated how the people held captive in Babylon protested against providence, and how, as a testing of virtue in this life, the righteous are often tormented, while at other times they are raised up by unexpected successes. Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ to the Father concerning the Jews.

### Explanation

“Whereas in the preceding titles only David appears to have been inscribed, here he added ‘son of Jesse,’ so that we should understand this David as the father of Solomon.

Therefore the temporal praises that were rendered to the Lord in the Law after sacrifices of cattle and musical instruments have ceased and been changed, because now the Catholic Church [Col. 0868B] performs holy psalmody through the offering of the body and blood of Christ.

The Synagogue indeed worshiped the Lord, but, seeing the wicked flourish through their way of life, it had fallen into very evil thoughts. In its person Asaph himself speaks in this psalm; by his name he contains a symbol of the Synagogue. For he will say many things about the Gentile peoples and about those who received the Law, things that are usefully said for our correction, so that we may not be defiled by such thoughts.

Alternatively, the statement that the praises of David son of Jesse ceased pertains to the end of the fiftieth psalm; what follows, however, is the beginning of the next psalm.

Asaph, as we have said, speaks throughout the psalm in the figure of the Synagogue. In the first part he says that he envied worldly prosperity, observing the peace of sinners and wondering why such prosperity had come to the enemies of God and to pagans, so that they seemed to raise their mouths up to heaven.

In the second part he says that his people will return to sound counsel and will be ashamed of the perversity of their former thought, [Col. 0868C] until they deserve to understand and behold the final destiny of the ungodly.

In the third part he testifies that evils come upon the ungodly because of their deceits, since they seemed to scandalize holy men by their prosperity; nevertheless, he asserts that by the Lord’s favor he has been freed from these evils.

In the fourth part he says how, through the Lord’s mercy, he reached perfect understanding.”

### Commentary

#### How good God is to Israel, to those who are upright in heart

The title is: “The hymns of David, son of Jesse, have ceased; a psalm of Asaph.”

Asaph is interpreted as “gathering” or “congregation,” and here signifies the Synagogue—not the murderous Synagogue, but the imitative one.

The meaning is: This psalm belongs to Asaph, that is, to the Synagogue, because certain people from the Synagogue speak here. It is a psalm, I say, dealing with the fact that the hymns of David son of Jesse have ceased.

A hymn is praise of God accompanied by song. It is a very dangerous and tearful matter that those who not only praised God [Col. 0868D] but also sang his praise so quickly ceased to praise him. For whoever sings praise to someone not only praises him but praises him joyfully; and whoever sings someone’s praise not only sings but also loves the one whom he praises.

Nor does the name “David” seem to have been specified here in the title without reason by the words “son of Jesse.” This was done so that we might understand that the hymns ceased among the carnal people subject to the historical David, not among the spiritual people subject to the spiritual David.

At a certain time under the Old Testament, while the New Testament still lay hidden within it like fruit in a root, David himself, son of Jesse, was king of the Israelite people. At that same time, namely under the Old Testament, promises were made to that people as a carnal people—earthly and temporal promises—because a kingdom, subjection of enemies, the prosperity of children, the fertility of wives, the city of Jerusalem, and all that earthly happiness which they regarded as a great thing were promised to them, as though God had nothing greater or better that he could give them. [Col. 0869A]

For these things alone they praised and worshiped God. But after receiving them, when, deservedly because of their sins, they were attacked and overcome, and their city was destroyed and the land of promise taken from them—as was necessary, because it was a shadow—the hymns ceased among them. This happened because God is not praised in such hearts; rather, he is blasphemed.

They either think that he is unjust or that he does not care about mortal affairs, because he takes these temporal goods away from his friends and worshipers and gives them to his enemies, namely blasphemers and idolaters.

Some among them, however, were corrected—or, indeed, there were also people in that nation who understood the Holy Spirit and understood both what they had received, what God had promised them, and why he had taken these temporal things away from them and given them to their enemies.

Associating themselves with the others so that they might deal with them more freely, such people speak in this psalm, rebuke and correct them, and exhort them not [Col. 0869B] to envy the flourishing of the wicked any longer.

They teach them to understand that God had taken away these temporal things, which were not true goods, so that they might seek other true and eternal goods—not goods that were absent from those earthly things, but goods that were hidden within them.

And one of the corrected, or one of the perfect, says, associating himself with them:

“How good is the God of true Israel”—that is, how delightful he is—“to those who are upright in heart!”

But to those who are crooked in heart alone—those who either think that he is unjust or that he does not care about mortal affairs—he appears perverse. This does not mean that God is truly perverse; rather, when you are perverse, he appears perverse to you.

And he is not good to you, that is, he is not delightful to you but unpleasant, just as honey is not delightful to a feverish palate, nor the bright sun to a bleary eye. For the light that invigorates a healthy eye strikes an infirm one, and what illuminates one torments the other.

#### But my feet were almost moved

As if he were saying: God is indeed good to those who are upright in heart, but I previously had a crooked heart, and therefore he was not good to me.

[Col. 0869C] For my feet were almost moved, and my steps were almost poured out. Feet pertain to falling, because we fall with our feet; steps pertain to wandering.

Here he takes “feet” as the affections, and “steps” as conduct. For the feet were not entirely moved but almost moved, and the steps were not entirely poured out but almost poured out. He was indeed considering changing the pious affection that he had toward God for carnal things, and transferring the works of his service to the worship of demons; but he came to his senses. Therefore he says: “My feet were almost moved, and my steps were almost poured out.”

As if he were saying: I was falling, but I had not yet fallen; I was going, but I had not yet gone.

#### Because I was jealous

Therefore my steps were almost poured out, because I was jealous—that is, I felt indignation, making myself superior to the wicked, that is, justifying myself and preferring myself to the wicked.

And I was jealous for this reason: I saw the peace—that is, the prosperity—of sinners, namely, that everything was according to their desire.

#### For there is no regard for their death

[Col. 0869D] Therefore I was jealous, seeing the peace of sinners, because, although their merit is evil, there is no regard for their death, since it never looks upon them. And in their affliction—that is, if they are ever afflicted—there is no firmness, that is, no stability.

For if some sadness occasionally causes them to perish, pleasant things follow. Or “in their affliction there is firmness,” that is, their affliction is not loosened but strengthened, that is, made solid.

One may also read this entire verse in another way, so that it shows that prosperity is not given to sinners here for salvation but for condemnation.

The meaning is: I was jealous, seeing the peace of sinners. Why, however, is that peace given to them? Certainly for their destruction. For it is given to them because there is no regard for their death: the death owed to them never turns away from them so as to look upon them at some future time, but always looks upon them. That is, their sentence has already been pronounced.

And in their affliction there is no firmness, because their affliction—that is, their confusion—is continually loosened.

#### They are not in the labor of human beings

The continuation is the same according to either interpretation, as if he were saying:

[Col. 0870A] It is evident from this that there is no regard for their death, because no medicine is applied to them. For they do not of themselves engage in any labor of true human beings, namely, so that they might keep vigil, fast, or do anything of that kind.

Moreover, they are not scourged, nor will they ever be scourged with true human beings by him, because he scourges every son whom he receives.

And because they neither labor of themselves nor are scourged by God, pride has seized them, as though with certain hands, so that they would not escape. Therefore they are covered—that is, completely wrapped, as if in a cloak—with iniquity against their neighbor and impiety against God.

I say, with their own iniquity or impiety, that is, with what has arisen in them from their own fault. For they do not live soberly within themselves, because they are proud; nor justly toward their neighbor; nor piously toward God.

#### Iniquity came forth as from fatness

[Col. 0870B] They are covered, I say, with iniquity, and not because of any necessity, because their iniquity came forth not from dryness but as from fatness.

If a poor person, compelled by poverty, commits theft or robbery, his iniquity came forth as from dryness. But if someone who is prosperous and powerful seizes something, his iniquity does not proceed from dryness but as from fatness, that is, from arrogance and presumption.

They also passed beyond the bounds of humanity, or the rule of justice, stretching toward the desire of the heart, that is, wishing to fulfill every desire of their wicked heart.

For they conceived wickedness and also spoke it, so as to persuade others of it. And they did this not only among their own associates; they also spoke iniquity on high, that is, in public, so as to persuade everyone of it.

For this purpose they set their mouth in heaven—that is, against heaven—because they spoke blasphemies against God.

Or they set their mouth in heaven, that is, in a position of authority, so that their words might be regarded as authoritative, as though they were heavenly.

Or they set their mouth in heaven [Col. 0870C], that is, in disputation about future things, which pertains only to heaven, because they said: “We will do this and this, but we will abandon that.”

And though their tongue was on earth, that is, placed in a stable position, it crossed the earth by saying such things as had nothing to do with it.

Or it crossed beyond other earthly people by presuming beyond the common human capacity.

#### Therefore my people here will turn

As if he were saying:

I have marked their condemnation, granted to them through peace, so carefully for this reason: so that this people of mine, which wishes to be my companion and to be conformed to me, may turn—as it truly will turn.

Thus the people who previously thought that God was unjust or did not care about mortal affairs, because he took temporal goods away from his friends and gave them to his enemies, will now think the opposite.

And after they turn, then full days will be found in them, namely through their effect. For what was taught by the one who came in the fullness of time—that is, contempt for earthly things and love of heavenly things—will be in them.

Or they will turn here in the present, and finally full days [Col. 0870D]—that is, eternal days—will be found in them.

And it is necessary that they turn, because they had turned away. For they said either that God did not know everything, or that, if he did know, he was unjust or did not care about mortal affairs. This is what follows:

“They said: How can this be?” It is indeed commonly said that God knows everything, while he takes good things away from his friends and gives them to his enemies. Certainly, either that statement is not true, or, if there is knowledge on high, then—as they say—he is either unjust or does not care about mortal affairs.

#### Behold, these are sinners

As if he were saying: Here is why they speak such things: because, in their judgment, those sinners obtain the reward of their righteousness.

For those who are sinners and yet prosperous in this world have obtained riches, for which they worshiped God and justified themselves.

Behold the disgraceful transaction: to sell one’s righteousness for earthly money.

And I said: Those who had turned said this, and I too said: “Therefore, in vain,” and so forth.

This can be said from the beginning either by someone already corrected, with regard to his former state, or by someone perfect and understanding, though speaking in their person.

[Col. 0871A] The meaning is: Since another obtains the reward of my righteousness, therefore I justified my heart—that is, my thoughts—in vain, without benefit; and I washed my hands—that is, cleansed my works—in vain, so that I might be among the innocent.

And I was scourged in vain, that is, I endured scourges all day long, continually; yet my chastisement is in the mornings, that is, my chastisement is not delayed but is always, as it were, at the door, so that it may assail me each morning.

Their chastisement, however, is either late or nonexistent.

#### If I said

This, I say, I said. And finally I was saying:

“Lord, if I were to tell others that you are unjust, or that you do not care about mortal affairs because you take temporal goods away from your friends and give them to your enemies, behold, I would encounter a great absurdity: I would reject”—that is, separate from myself—“the nation” [Col. 0871B], that is, the entire generation of your sons, that is, of your preceding elect, namely Abraham and Jacob and others like them, because none of them agrees with me in this.

Placed in this difficulty, I was thinking in order to understand; that is, I was considering that it had to be understood. Or, as blessed Augustine says: “I resolved to understand.”

What was I to understand? Namely, that you are just and care about mortal affairs, and yet take earthly goods away from your friends and give them to your enemies.

But to understand this is a labor, that is, a certain difficulty placed before me as I wished to investigate it, until I should bring myself before you.

Or: “This understanding was a labor before me,” that is, greater than I, until I should enter either into the sanctuary of God—that is, into my own mind, by making it the sanctuary of God—or into the sanctuary of God, that is, into the secret disposition of God—or into the sanctuary of God, that is, into the Sacred Scriptures, where certain explanations of all these matters are given.

And it is a labor for me until I enter into their final destiny, that is, until in my mind I pass through to the future condemnation and punishments of the wicked.

And when I am in those final things, I will understand what I did not understand before: that God is just and cares about mortal affairs, and yet takes these goods away from his friends and gives them to his enemies, because he gives them to his enemies so that, if they have done any good, they may be rewarded through them, and so that they may be condemned more severely in the future. [Col. 0871C]

#### Yet because of this

He said, “And I will understand in their final destiny,” thereby indicating that they will be condemned in the future. But nevertheless—as if he were saying—they are also condemned here, because you, Lord, have set snares for them.

What snares? Namely, that, blinded inwardly, they abandon the eternal goods set before everyone and desire temporal things, which deceive them.

And this happened to them because of their snares, that is, because of their evil merit, namely because, insofar as it lies within them, they act deceitfully.

This same verse can also be connected somewhat earlier in another way.

The meaning is: Sinners, I say, obtained riches, in which they think that they are well treated; but nevertheless they are badly treated in this very matter [Col. 0871D], because you, Lord, set snares for them on account of their snares, as has been said.

And you set snares for them in this way: you cast them down while they were being raised up, that is, because their very elevation in earthly things is their downfall, namely their condemnation. For the prosperity of fools will destroy them.

#### How they were made desolate

In this way, I say, you cast them down, because they were made desolate, that is, because they were thrown headlong and already, by your disposition, destined for eternal condemnation.

And how—that is, how unexpectedly—this happened to them! Therefore I say that they were made desolate, because they suddenly failed and, already by disposition, perished; and this not through your justice but because of their iniquity.

Thus I say that they failed and perished like the dream of those who awake. Although they dreamed in sleep of many riches, when they arise they find nothing in their hands.

So these people are in this life as though in sleep. But when at last they are led out of this sleep and awaken, [Col. 0872A] they will find nothing in their hands, because when a man dies, his glory will not descend with him.

For, as the Apostle says, “We brought nothing into this world”; there is no doubt that we can take nothing away.

And truly they will perish, because you, Lord, will reduce their image to nothing in your city.

For just as they reduced your image—that is, their reason and understanding—to nothing in their city, becoming like foolish beasts, so you too will reduce their image—that is, the image of pride and of every kind of wickedness that they made within themselves—to nothing in your heavenly city, that is, in the fellowship of the saints.

This does not mean that they will be there, but that, although they ought to be there, they will be excluded from it and separated from true being, and thus reduced to nothing.

#### Because my heart was inflamed

You will rightly reduce them to nothing, because they also gave others an occasion for sinning.

For my heart was inflamed, after their example, with desire for earthly things; and my reins [Col. 0872B]—that is, my delights, which ought to have been spiritual—were changed into carnal ones.

Thus I, who ought to have been something, was reduced to nothing, that is, to desiring only earthly things, which are nothing. And I did not know, that is, I became ignorant.

And because I was ignorant, therefore, although I might have appeared sufficiently prudent and wise among them, before you I became like a beast, that is, irrational and foolish, while desiring things that are nothing.

And although I desired them, I was nevertheless always with you, because I do not ask these things from demons, as idolaters do, but from you alone.

Therefore you helped me, so that I would not fall completely, because you held my hand, making it right—that is, you made my works, which had previously been left-handed, that is, perverse, become right-handed, that is, good.

And having led me out of the darkness of error, you led me onward, that is, advanced me from virtue to virtue.

And you did this not because of my merits but according to your will. You have received me already in your disposition, and finally you will receive me with glory.

The two preceding verses may also be read in another way.

[Col. 0872C] The meaning is: You will indeed reduce their image to nothing, but you will not reduce mine to nothing, because my heart is inflamed with desire for you, and my reins—that is, my former carnal delights—have been changed into spiritual ones.

And I have been reduced to nothing, that is, I have considered myself as nothing with regard to those things which I formerly established for myself; and yet I sinned pardonably, because I did not know, that is, I was previously ignorant.

But now before you I have become like a beast, that is, like a tame and humble beast of burden, for whom your burden is always sweet and light.

Therefore from now on I will always be with you, because the flesh will never draw me away from your will. And rightly will I always be with you, because you held my hand, making it right, as was said above.

#### For what is there for me in heaven?

Truly you will finally receive me with glory. For what has been prepared for me in heaven? Certainly, something great: that glory which neither eye has seen nor ear heard and which has not entered the human heart.

And yet what did I, wretched man, desire on earth? [Col. 0872D] Certainly, something worthless.

This, as if he were saying, happened because of my deficiency in soul and body. For through Adam’s transgression my flesh and my heart—that is, my body and my soul—first became deficient in many ways.

But now you are the God of my heart, and so forth.

Or otherwise:

As if he were saying: Previously I desired something useful on earth, but now my flesh and my heart have failed in themselves so that they might advance in you.

And you are the God of my heart, that is, you are the one whom my heart loves as God, and you are my portion forever.

Let others choose whatever portion they wish in the world; I will choose you alone as my hereditary portion in heaven.

For behold, I rightly take you as God and Father, because all those who distance themselves from you—that is, who do not take you as their portion—will perish.

And truly they will perish, because you have already, by your disposition, destroyed everyone who commits fornication by departing from you.

Those fornicate with God who do not worship him chastely, because they worship him not for his own sake but for the sake of something else.

[Col. 0873A]

#### But it is good for me to cling to God

You have destroyed those who fornicate by departing from you, but you have not destroyed me, because I have not fornicated by departing from you.

For it is good for me—that is, it seems useful and pleasing to me—to cling at last to you, God.

And in order that I may cling to you then, I now meanwhile place my hope in you, Lord Redeemer and God Creator, so that I may announce all your proclamations, that is, all the praises by which you are to be proclaimed.

I announce them, I say, to the daughter of Zion, that is, to the Church, because outside the Church there is no place for true proclamation. The Church is compared to a daughter because of the adornment of its virtues and the fruitfulness of its children.

And I announce them in the gates, that is, in public, or in virtues.

## ON PSALM 73

### The Understanding of Asaph

### Argument

The Maccabees and their perils are recounted, and prayers are joined to them. [Col. 0873B]

### Explanation

“‘Understanding’ is placed beforehand in the title because a twofold captivity follows, bodily and spiritual. One captivity, after the temple was destroyed, led into Babylon; the other, after faith had been overturned, subjected people to the confusion of errors.

Jerome thinks that this psalm was sung against the Chaldeans; Cassiodorus, against the Romans; Arnobius, against the Philistines, when the priests Hophni and Phinehas had been killed and the ark of God was captured.

The Synagogue speaks throughout the psalm. In the first section it laments why they were handed over to the nations, so that the audacity of their enemies profaned the Lord’s sanctuary. It recalls that the impenitent heart of certain Jews provoked the Lord’s judgment, but prophesies that these people will nevertheless be converted at the end of the age.

In the second section it says that, at Christ’s coming, the superstitions and iniquities of human beings were destroyed. It enumerates the various great works he accomplished, among which it asks that help also be given to wandering Jews.

In the third section it asks that, mindful of his promises [Col. 0873C], he rescue the offspring of Abraham from destruction and let the pride of the enemies rise up to him—enemies who exalted themselves vainly.”

### Commentary

#### Why, O God, have you rejected us utterly?

Asaph, the understanding one, speaks in this psalm. For, as we have often said, the frenzied Jews, not recognizing the time of visitation and fearing to lose what they had received, killed the one who had given it.

But what happened to them? They lost even their earthly possessions; and where they killed him, there they themselves were killed.

And because, fearing to lose the land, they killed the giver of life, they lost that same land after being killed. And at the very time when they killed him, they were given a warning by that time itself as to why they suffered such things.

When the city of the Jews was destroyed, they were celebrating Passover, and the whole nation had come in many thousands to celebrate that festival.

There God—through those who were not good, yet himself good; through those who were not just, yet himself just—rightly took vengeance upon them, so that many thousands were killed and the city destroyed. [Col. 0873D]

The understanding Asaph laments this in the psalm. In the very act of lamenting, as understanding—that is, as one who understands—he distinguishes earthly things from heavenly things and new things from old, so that you may know what you should pass through, what you should await, what you should leave behind, and to what you should cling.

The prophet speaks in this psalm as Asaph, that is, as “one who gathers,” namely, so that he may gather others from that people to himself in this understanding: that they should distinguish earthly things from heavenly things, set earthly things aside, and cling to heavenly things.

He laments here their historical overthrow by the Romans, carried out by Titus and Vespasian, because they had not recognized the time of visitation. This was to overcome their hardness, so that those who had refused to recognize the physician while he was present might at least recognize him when admonished by such manifest evils in his absence.

Thus he begins:

“O God, why have you rejected us?” That is, why have you made us appear rejected from your protection? You rejected us with the rejection of finality, that is, with complete and irrecoverable rejection. [Col. 0874A]

For when they were so afflicted, when so many thousands were killed and so many led into captivity, they truly appeared to have been rejected by him.

Why, I ask, has your wrath grown angry against the sheep of your pasture, that is, against those whom you formerly chose and nourished with the legal and prophetic writings, as a devoted shepherd nourishes his sheep?

Certainly—as if he were saying—you rejected us and became angry because we clung to earthly things and did not recognize you as shepherd.

#### Remember your congregation

As if he were saying:

And so that you may not reject them forever, remember your congregation from the beginning. Even if these people are unworthy of your remembrance, at least remember Abraham, whom you formerly liberated by bringing him out of the city of the Chaldeans.

From him this people, whom you gathered and chose, physically descended, so that through him you might at some time liberate them.

Remember, I say, your congregation, which you possessed among the other nations by giving it the Law and commandments. For you did not act in this way toward every nation.

By saying “your congregation” and “which you possessed,” he draws the people who are listening toward himself—the very people to whom he speaks [Col. 0874B]—and here he enumerates many benefits of God previously granted to that people, so as thereby to lead them toward receiving further benefits.

## You Redeemed the Rod of Your Inheritance

Therefore you must also remember your congregation, because you redeemed the rod of your inheritance—that is, you liberated this inheritance of yours from Egyptian servitude by means of the rod, namely, through the many miracles performed by Moses with the rod. The historical account relates that, when Moses was staying with Jethro his father-in-law, the Lord appeared to him and commanded him to return to Egypt and lead his people out from there. When Moses doubted whether this could be accomplished through him, the Lord gave him this sign and commanded him to throw upon the ground the rod that he held in his hand. He threw it down, and it was changed into a serpent. When he was frightened, the Lord commanded him to seize the serpent by the tail. He seized it, and immediately the rod returned to its former state. Afterwards, through this rod, Moses performed all those signs by which the Israelite people were led out of Egyptian servitude [Col. 0874C].

The rod in the serpent signified Christ in death, which the Apostles feared: when they saw him dead, they doubted. But the Lord commanded them to seize the tail—that is, to consider not the death but what followed it, namely, the resurrection—and thus to be freed from fear. The serpent’s flowing movement may also signify the flow of our mortality. So that we might not fear it, the Lord commanded Moses to seize the tail; that is, he commanded us always to look toward that end when, changed into a heavenly condition, we shall be equal to God’s angels.

Or alternatively: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance” means that you liberated from servitude this inheritance comparable to a rod, because you performed many miracles through it, just as Moses did through the aforementioned rod. Or, you redeemed it so that it might be for you an inheritance measured by the rod—that is, originally a proper inheritance. Or, so that it might be for you “the rod of inheritance,” that is, a straight inheritance. For the rod is used to signify straightness. And because, according to these last two interpretations, “the rod of inheritance” seems to refer to the sheep from the nations, whom he chiefly received as an inheritance through the preaching of the Apostles, he determines in what follows which inheritance he means, as though he were saying: “But what is that inheritance?” Namely, Mount Zion—that is, the Jewish people, who historically dwelt on Mount Zion. “Mount Zion,” I say, in which you dwelt through legal institutions; you, I say, being present in it, since you dealt with them through signs so manifest that you were understood to be present there [Col. 0874D].

## Raise Your Hands

Here Asaph, understanding the matter, prays for the enemies, as though he were saying: “Remember us, Lord; remember also our enemies.” That is: raise your hands, meaning exercise your power against their pride, the pride of those through whom you rejected us and displayed your anger against us.

“Raise them,” I say, not for evil but for good—namely, by bringing them to the end, that is, to Christ, who is the end unto righteousness for everyone who believes. Or, “raise them toward the end,” meaning raise them as much as is necessary for you to raise them: namely, so far that they believe and become imitators and friends from persecutors and enemies. Where superstition held sway, let religion prevail [Col. 0875A].

But do not let it disturb you that no one from those Roman nations through whom that destruction was accomplished was converted. This does not hinder the matter, because the prayer was nevertheless fulfilled in their descendants. It is as though he were saying: “There is need for elevation, because that people truly acted as an enemy, preferring the creature whom it worshiped to the Creator. It acted wickedly”—that is, it behaved maliciously in many ways—“against the holy place,” by overthrowing the temple, destroying the priesthood, and doing other things against what had been made holy by you.

And how wickedly did it act? In the most unspeakable ways. I therefore say “how much,” because no repentance for their evil deeds followed; rather, they gloried in them—that is, they regarded the supreme sacrilege as their glory. They hated you “in the midst of your solemnity,” that is, during the common and greatest solemnity instituted for you. At Passover, the Jews, gathered from everywhere, raged against Christ; at Passover likewise they perished [Col. 0875B].

## They Set Up Their Standards

He shows the extent to which the enemies gloried as victors: they gloried to such an extent that they set up their standards—not yours—that is, eagles, dragons, and military ensigns, the signs of their victory. They set them upon the highest place of the city or temple, just as statues are usually set up at the exits of roads, that is, at crossroads or places where four roads meet, so that they may be seen by many. They did this because they did not understand.

What did they not understand? Namely, that the victory was not theirs by their own strength, but resulted from our iniquity. They did not consider that they were instruments of your anger, not the kingdom of one who was reconciled.

For God acts as a human being does: a man beats his son with any branch and then throws the branch into the fire, while preserving the inheritance for his son. So God chastises the good through the wicked, and through the temporal power of those who are to be condemned exercises discipline upon those who are to be liberated.

Or alternatively: “They set up their standards, and they did not understand that this was upon the highest place”—that is, by divine arrangement, not by their own strength—as became apparent at the outcome. For so few could never have overcome so many thousands in so fortified a place unless by divine disposition [Col. 0875C].

## As in a Forest of Trees

He expounds what the enemy did wickedly against the holy place. They cut down its doors—that is, those of the holy temple—with their axes, “as in a forest of trees”: that is, without any restraint, just as a tree is cut down in a forest, placed under no protection and assigned only for use as timber. They did this “with one accord,” that is, unanimously or persistently. And “they cut them down,” meaning the things hanging from the temple—or “it,” meaning the holy city—with axe and hatchet. He names these two implements for every kind of instrument.

Moreover, they set fire to your sanctuary—that is, the inner shrine of the temple, where the ark of the covenant and the other holy objects were kept. They defiled with the stalls of their horses, and in many other ways, the outer tabernacle dedicated to your name, which alone existed upon the earth.

And they said in their hearts—that is, they firmly resolved—not only those Romans, but also their kin, namely, others of the same kind, that is, Gentiles, such as Nebuchadnezzar, who had previously taken them captive, and other persecutors. All these, I say, agreed upon one thing: “Let us cause all the feast days to cease from the earth, which these people say belong to God’s resting”—that is, let us utterly remove them from the earth. Here “of God” is understood according to Asaph’s perspective, not according to theirs.

This verse may also be referred to the Jews themselves. It is as though he were saying: Asaph, understanding that the enemy had acted so wickedly against them, says that they were therefore blinded and said in their hearts—not merely a few of them, but all their kin together—that is, they all said one thing: “Let us cause all the feast days of God to cease from the earth.” Since God has rejected us and allows our enemies to rule over us, let us also withdraw his worship from him as far as lies within our power [Col. 0875D].

## We Do Not See Our Signs

Here is the just cause for the rejection. It is as though he were saying: “Why, God, did you reject us?” The answer is: deservedly, because we clung to earthly things and did not recognize you as our shepherd [Col. 0876A].

For we did not see—that is, we did not heed—“our signs,” meaning that the signs of the time of visitation given to us had already been fulfilled. Yet we could have seen them, because “there is no longer a prophet.” This is one of the signs, and he emphasizes it especially because in all the other captivities, apart from this final one, there were always some prophets who foretold their return from captivity and promised their liberation.

There were also other foretold signs of the time of visitation: namely, that there would be neither king nor priest, because there would be no anointing, according to the saying: “When the Holy of Holies comes, anointing will cease.” All these things ceased at that time because they were shadows. When the truth comes, the shadow must necessarily be removed.

“We did not heed,” I say, “our signs”; and because of our evil deserts, he will no longer know us—that is, he will no longer look upon us in order to defend us from our enemies. Blessed Augustine, according to the wording of his translation, says as follows: “And he will not yet know us,” and adds: “But if you do not know, does he himself know you?” Certainly he knows, because he has already come [Col. 0876B].

## How Long, O Lord?

Asaph, understanding this of the nations and foreseeing that other sheep would be brought to him, says this and turns to God. It is as though he were saying: “Indeed, O God, because of our deserts you will no longer know us; but how long will you delay those other sheep?”

This is what he says: “O God, how long will the enemy”—that is, the Gentile people—continue? That is, how long will it persecute and trample us? And how long will the adversary”—that is, the people—“provoke you,” meaning provoke you to anger, “through your name,” that is, through your praise and glory, which it contradicts? “Will this continue forever?” Certainly not, as though he were saying: “It will not continue forever, because those true other sheep will be brought in.”

And since you will do this with respect to the enemies, why, O Lord, do you turn away your hand—that is, us, who were formerly your hand, not your left but your right, because through us you performed many good works? Why, I ask, do you withdraw us from the midst of your bosom—that is, why do you withdraw your protection from us, making us appear as unclean as a hand removed from the bosom? “Will this continue forever?”

Here he sends us to the historical account. For the history relates that when the Lord showed Moses the sign in the rod that we have mentioned, he gave him another sign as well. He commanded him to take his hand out of his bosom. He did so, and behold, it appeared leprous. Again he commanded him to return it to his bosom. He did so, and behold, it was like the rest of his flesh.

This signified that whenever anyone goes out from the bosom of God—that is, from faith, hope, and charity—like heretics and schismatics, he is immediately filled with the leprosy of sin. But if he returns repentant, he immediately receives health [Col. 0876C].

## But God Is Our King

“We say,” I said, “that God has turned us away; but he himself has instead already come to us and called us.” God, having become our king through humility before the ages, and existing through majesty in the midst of the earth—that is, among our Jewish people, surrounded on every side by the nations—has worked salvation. What salvation? So that human beings might despise earthly things and desire heavenly things [Col. 0876D].

## You Established the Sea by Your Power

He explains how he worked salvation. It is as though he were saying: “Truly, Lord, you worked salvation, because just as, when you led your people out of Egypt, you established the divided sea on either side like a wall and dried up the waters in the midst, so you established the sea—that is, the bitter flow of vices—in us. You did not do this so that the vices would remain, but so that we would not continue to be swept away by vices as before. You did this not because of our merits, but by your power—that is, through your mighty grace.”

And just as in the waters of the sea you submerged Pharaoh’s soldiers, who had come to devour your people like dragons, and likewise their heads—that is, their leaders—so here, in the waters of baptism, you afflicted—that is, crushed and weakened—not only the dragons, meaning the lesser demons assigned individually to accuse us, who spiritually wish to devour us like dragons, but also their heads, meaning those who rule over the lesser demons [Col. 0877A].

You did even more, for in those same waters you crushed the heads of the dragon—that is, the highest demons who rule under Satan himself, who is the supreme head—and you gave Satan himself to the peoples of the Ethiopians, that is, to those who were formerly blackened by sins but have now been whitened by grace, like the holy Apostles and the other preachers of truth.

To them, I say, you gave Satan himself as food: namely, so that they might consume his body—that is, the wicked who cling to him as to their head—meaning that through the word of preaching they might conform them to themselves and transfer them into themselves. Hence it was said to one of them concerning this food: “Kill and eat.” Kill in them what they are, and transfer them into your body.

## You Split Open Springs and Torrents

You gave the dragons as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians, I say, because you split open springs and torrents. The rock in the desert, struck twice by the rod, was broken open, and from it flowed sweet and abundant waters [Col. 0877B].

The rock struck twice by the rod is Christ, crucified upon the twofold wood of the cross, from whom flowed abundant and copious water, the only sweet water in the desert of this life. Through it some became springs of living water leaping up into eternal life, while others became torrents.

Because water is continuous in springs, understand by “springs” the foremost teachers who instruct by word and example, since their teaching is stable.
