By “torrents,” understand those who, although they do not fulfill the word of truth in their works, nevertheless do not refrain from preaching; they quickly fail, like torrents.

Or, conversely, by “torrents” we may understand those in whom the force of teaching is present—that is, the greater teachers—and by “springs” the lesser teachers, from whom doctrine flows gradually.

When he says, “You split open springs and torrents,” this may be understood in two ways: either “you split them open,” meaning you caused the springs to flow; or, “you split open the springs themselves and the torrents,” meaning that you scattered them like separate channels and dried up the rivers of Ethan [Col. 0877C].

“Ethan” is interpreted as “strong” or “robust.” By him is understood that wickedly strong one who wished to be strong from himself and said: “I will set my throne in the north.” From this evil strength he offered the cup of death to our first parents, when he persuaded them to wish to be strong and gods for themselves by their own power.

From him also proceeded various rivers—namely, various heresies and errors—which God destroyed through his own rivers and torrents.

The entire verse may also be referred to Ethan, so that we may say: “Truly, you gave the dragon to the peoples as food, because you split open”—that is, destroyed—“the springs of Ethan.” These springs are springs of water leaping up into eternal condemnation, as are also the torrents and rivers. Understand them likewise in an evil sense, proceeding from the lesser to the greater.

## The Day Is Yours

It is as though he were saying: “When the rivers of Ethan had been dried up, some became day, some night, and so forth; and this was not accomplished by themselves but by you, because the day is yours and the night is yours.”

The days are spiritual people, those who preach spiritual things to spiritual people, such as the one who said: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth. The night, however, consists of those who announce only carnal things to carnal people.

Paul was night when he said: “I determined to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified”; but he was day when he said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” [Col. 0877D].

## You Fashioned the Dawn

That is, you caused each person who is beginning to shine in virtue. For the first light is dawn.

And you fashioned the sun—that is, anyone so perfect that he makes day for others.

You also made all the boundaries of the earth—that is, it is by your gift that all who make themselves the ends of the earth exist.

And you made summer—that is, all who burn with the Spirit and serve the Lord—and spring, those who blossom with virtues, or those who are newly beginning.

You, I say, fashioned these things, that is, all those mentioned above. From you alone they have what they are.

And because you fashioned them, therefore, Lord, preserve them. Remember this saying, because the enemy—that is, the Jewish people—reproached you, bringing many insults against you, Lord, and even against you, the green wood, calling you the son of a carpenter, a violator of the law, and the like. Thus that foolish people—that is, a people that did not look ahead to its future—incited your name [the wording is uncertain in the supplied text], provoking you to anger through your name, which it wished to remove entirely from the earth [Col. 0878A].

And if they did this to you, the green wood, what will they do to the dry? It is clear that they will spare the dry even less, since they did not spare you, the green wood.

Therefore, Lord, do not hand over to beasts—that is, to any persecutors possessing a bestial understanding—the souls that confess, meaning those who humble themselves and confess their sins to you.

“Do not forget the souls of your poor,” I say. It is as though he were saying: “Although the earth,” that is, their bodies, “are handed over into the hands of sinners, do not forget the souls of your poor,” that is, of your humble ones, so that they may not be devoured.

Or, if you do forget them, do not forget them forever—that is, do not forget them in such a way that they never recover their senses. For it is human to sin, but demonic to persevere in sin.

And do not forget your poor. Therefore, Lord, show mercy to all who attend to your covenant—that is, to all who desire the heavenly and eternal promises.

And therefore I say that you reject those others, because you despise those who attend to the covenant of the servant—that is, those who desire earthly things.

He intimates this when he says: “Because those who are darkened by the houses of the earth are filled with iniquities.” That is, their hearts have an earthly taste; they continually savor earthly things and continually desire earthly things, never raising themselves toward heavenly things. Hence, like foxes, they enter the lower parts of the earth [Col. 0878B].

## Let Not the Humble Be Turned Away

Thus, I say, you should look upon them so that the one who is truly humble may not be turned away—that is, devoured—when it is reproached that they believe in a dead man. Rather, let him grasp the serpent by the tail, meaning let him attend to the glory of the resurrection, and thus understand Christ not merely as a man but also as true God.

He may be turned away after becoming confused, or he may become confused through consciousness of sins.

He ought not therefore to be turned away, because he is poor—that is, one who is insufficient for himself and therefore conducts himself humbly toward you, as a poor man does toward a rich man—and needy, meaning one who considers grace necessary for himself.

These people, I say, by truly humbling themselves and doing good works, will praise your name.

And because they will praise you, therefore, O God who seemed to lie down, arise—whether here, in the knowledge of human beings, or finally, in order to reward them at the judgment—and judge, that is, discern your cause, meaning your faith: now by giving constancy in this mortal life to those who believe in you, and finally also in a local sense.

It is as though he were saying: “Let it not be in vain, Lord, that I believed in you. Let me not perish because I believed what I did not see. Let my hope not deceive me; let me receive what I believed.”

“Judge your cause,” I say, “and remember the reproaches of your servants,” namely, so that they may not prevail against them. I mean those reproaches that come “all day,” that is, continually, from the foolish persecuting people that does not look ahead to its future [Col. 0878C].

## Do Not Forget

It is as though he were saying: “I say, remember the reproaches, so that you do not forget the voices of your enemies,” that is, the reproaches brought against your people by their enemies. They are called “voices” because in these reproaches they openly contradict you.

But just as the pride of those who hate you among your own continually rises—that is, grows greater and greater—so, conversely, may your vengeance increase [Col. 0878D].

There is also another reading of this psalm from the beginning, if someone understands it not as referring to a historical but to a mortal destruction signified by it. He may say that Asaph, that is, the prophet, laments in this psalm the blindness of the Jews, who did not recognize the time of visitation. He does so to expose their hardness, so that if they did not wish to go before, at least afterwards, when the previously unknown people had become servants, they might be moved by emulation to follow the one who had gone before.

Thus he says: “O God, why did you reject us by blinding us, so that we would not recognize the time of visitation? Did you reject us forever”—that is, until that end when the remnant will be saved—or “with the end of rejection,” meaning with utter rejection?

Certainly not, because your fury, having been directed against the sheep of your pasture—that is, against us, whom you formerly fed with legal and prophetic writings, as a merciful shepherd feeds his sheep—is angered only briefly, as though it were to pass quickly. For anger is a brief fury [Col. 0879A].

“Remember your congregation,” so that God may not reject us forever. Rather, remember the congregation because it is yours: if not the straw, at least remember the grain. Remember the congregation, I say, which you possessed from the beginning, because there have never been lacking those who were to be reckoned among the seed.

You ought to remember them for this reason; you must also remember the congregation because you redeemed with the blood of your Son “the rod of your inheritance,” that is, an inheritance measured by the rod, meaning one proper to you; or an inheritance that would be “the rod of inheritance,” that is, a straight inheritance.

It is as though he were saying: “Did you pay so great a price for the nations alone?” But what is that inheritance? Namely, Mount Zion—that is, those exalted in virtues and contemplating only future things, both from the Jews and from the nations. “Mount Zion,” I say, in which you truly dwelt, being present in it through faith and action. In those earlier people you dwelt as if through a shadow [Col. 0879B].

## Raise Your Hands

Because you possessed the congregation and redeemed the inheritance, therefore, God, raise the hands of your power against their pride—against those upon whom your anger has been aroused, namely, those who spoke proudly against you, saying: “We have no king but Caesar,” and, “We do not know where this man is from,” and similar things.

Raise them, I say, bringing them to the end. Or raise them to the end of elevation, meaning as much elevation as is necessary for you to raise them.

And it is necessary for you to raise them, for how greatly—how proudly and cruelly—the enemy, that Jewish people, acted wickedly against your holy place, namely, the Holy of Holies! They seized him, bound him, spat upon him, crowned him with thorns, and did such things to him.

I therefore say “how greatly,” because those who hated you by hating the one who said, “Whoever loves me also loves the one who sent me,” gloried—that is, made for themselves a glory—out of what they had done wickedly against the Holy of Holies in the midst of your solemnity, when they ought rather to have been attending to the solemnity.

And they truly gloried, because they set up standards—standards, I say, of their own victory: soldiers, guards, and even the wood of the cross itself. They did not understand that this was “upon the highest place,” meaning not through their own strength but through your divine disposition, according to the saying: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above,” as became apparent in the very outcome, namely, in the resurrection [Col. 0879C].

## As in a Forest of Trees

They acted wickedly not only against the Holy of Holies but also against its members, because they cut down its doors—that is, those through whom entrance was made to it, namely, the holy Apostles—with axes, meaning the gravest tribulations. They did this “with one accord,” unanimously, as though they were cutting down something in a forest of trees—that is, one of the flock of the condemned and useless.

And they cut them down—that is, the things hanging from it, namely, the lesser members belonging to the Holy of Holies—with axe and hatchet.

By the axe understand hardships; by the hatchet, which hollows out more gently, understand flatteries, because often the tongue of a flatterer does more harm than the hand of a persecutor [Col. 0879D].

They set fire to your sanctuary—that is, to Christ himself—with fire, meaning the most ardent tribulation. And they defiled the tabernacle of your name, which alone existed upon the earth—that is, those dwelling with you from the former people—through their reputation, casting their bodies out to be devoured by beasts and birds.

Or they defiled it by throwing it upon the earth, with respect to certain people whom they devoured. And they said in their hearts: “All their kin together,” meaning that everyone agreed on this, to destroy the Christian name utterly, saying: “Let us cause all the feast days of God to cease from the earth.”

He takes “days” to mean those bright with the light of evangelical truth; by “feast days” he means those in whom God delights as human beings ordinarily delight in festivals, or those who rightly rest in God [Col. 0880A].

## We Do Not See Our Signs

“Why,” I ask, “God, did you reject us?” For this reason: because, as was said above, we did not see our signs. Yet we could have seen them, because “there is no prophet.”

And because the signs have been fulfilled, God will no longer know us within the discipline of Moses. After the truth has come, he will no longer know us within the shadow.

## How Long, God?

I say that, God, you will no longer know us in the shadow. But how long, God, will we remain in this blindness? That is, how long, God, will this Jewish people, the enemy, reproach you by calling you a dead robber and saying similar things?

How long will the adversary provoke you through your name, which it wishes to destroy from the earth? “Will this continue forever?”

Why, I say, do you turn away—that is, permit us to appear turned away—from your right hand, from the midst of your bosom, that is, from your faith and commandments? “Will this continue forever?”

## But God Is Our King

We did not heed the signs of the visitation; but God our king worked true salvation in the midst of the earth—that is, in the heart of the nations. In other words, those other sheep have already received grace.

Therefore, as though Asaph were saying: “Correct yourself. If you did not wish to go before, at least strive to follow the one who went before.” He then turns to God himself, showing how he worked salvation when he says:

## You Established the Sea by Your Power

This verse, together with the other verses that follow, is understood in the same way as in the first interpretation, because here “the sea” refers to the nations [Col. 0880B].

It should also be known that there were those who referred this psalm to the primitive Church. Following their interpretation, the Lord, because Asaph—that is, the prophet—laments in this psalm the persecution of the martyrs of the primitive Church, understands that persecution as having been suffered from both internal and external enemies, not so much on account of the martyrs’ tribulation as on account of the blindness of their persecutors.

He speaks as though associating himself with them: “O God, why did you reject us?” That is, why did you permit us to appear rejected and cast off by you while we were so afflicted by our enemies?

“And why was your anger aroused?” That is, why does your fury appear to have been aroused against the sheep of your pasture—that is, against us, whom you refresh in your Scriptures, as a merciful shepherd feeds his sheep?

“Do not reject us,” I say, O God, “and do not be angry against us, but remember your congregation,” gathering to us all those whom you foresaw would be gathered to us. “Your congregation,” I say, “which you possessed from the beginning,” according to the saying: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world.”

You also redeemed it with the precious blood of your Son, so that it might be for you “the rod of inheritance,” that is, a straight inheritance. This inheritance is Mount Zion, as was said above, in which you dwelt, being present in it through faith and action [Col. 0880C].

## Raise Your Hands

“This,” I say, “is how I speak: remember the congregation, so that you may raise your hands against their pride, the pride of those through whom you appear to have rejected us,” that is, against the pride of the persecutors, bringing them to the end.

Or raise them to the end of elevation, as much as is necessary for you to raise them: namely, so that those who were formerly leaders may become followers, and persecutors may become preachers.

I therefore say, “Raise them against their pride,” because how greatly—that is, how proudly and cruelly—the enemy, the persecuting people, acted wickedly in destroying your holy people [Col. 0880D]!

And they gloried—that is, considered themselves glorious—although those who hated you, meaning those who exercised hatred against you, were rather disgraceful. They did this “in the midst of your solemnity,” that is, among those men whose solemnity before all was commonly known.

For “midst” is understood as “common”: what is in the middle is approached equally by all and departed from equally by all.

The solemnity of God truly consists of those who not only condemn their past life but continually recognize that they have been sinners, and thus remain cautious regarding the future and rightly rest in God.

They also set up their standards, I say—standards, namely, various tortures—and devised unheard-of kinds of torment against the holy martyrs. In these they gloried as though they were prophets, and they did not understand that this was “upon the highest place,” meaning that it proceeded from the divine disposition, which willed that the blood of the holy martyrs be poured out so that the crop of the Church, enriched by it, might sprout and produce fruit a hundredfold, as became apparent in the outcome—that is, in the conversion and incorporation of the persecutors [Col. 0881A].

## As in a Forest of Trees

He expounds, as before, how greatly the enemy acted wickedly: they cut down the doors of his holy temple—that is, those through whom he had entered into that fellowship—as though they were cutting down something in a forest of trees, meaning as though they were cutting down useless and fruitless people.

And they cut them down—that is, the things hanging from it—or the city itself, with axe and hatchet.

They set fire to the sanctuary—that is, to the more perfect members. They defiled the entire tabernacle of your name upon the earth, as before.

The following verse likewise remains unchanged.

## We Do Not See Our Signs

It is as though he were saying: “Why, God, did you reject us?” For this reason: so that we might be made like our head.

Did we not see our signs, and the signs of our tribulation and persecution in our head? His tribulation was a sign of our tribulation. For whatever sufferings remain must be completed in the body of Christ [Col. 0881B].

And we see in him not only our tribulation but also our reward, because the unique and preeminent Prophet, Christ, is no longer as he was before: he has been made immortal and incapable of suffering.

Hence the Apostle says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer.”

And because in him we saw both what we ought to suffer and what we ought to hope for, he will no longer know us in the discipline of Moses. We should not cling to earthly things or live in carnal pleasures.

## How Long, God?

Here is how Asaph, understanding the matter, grieves more over the blindness of the persecutors than over the tribulation of the holy martyrs.

It is as though he were saying: “I say that you will no longer know us in pleasures. But how long, O God, will the enemy reproach you?” That is, how long will you tolerate the blindness of the enemies who persecute us?

And why do you turn away your hand—that is, how long will you permit us also to appear unclean and rejected while we are afflicted by them and they are not incorporated into us? “Will this continue forever?”

## But God

[Col. 0881C] We say that God has turned us away because we are afflicted. But through this he rather receives us, because he has already worked salvation through his holy martyrs in the midst of the earth—that is, in the heart of the nations.

For when the blood of the holy martyrs was poured out, the crop of the Church, enriched by it, sprouted and produced fruit a hundredfold.

And he shows how he worked salvation through them, saying: “You established the sea through them,” yet in such a way that this establishment did not come from them but from your power, you who said: “Without me you can do nothing.”

The remaining verses do not change.

# ON PSALM 74

**For the end: Do not destroy. A psalm of song, of Asaph.**

## ARGUMENT

After the victory over Sennacherib, duties and vows of thanksgiving are rendered on behalf of the entire people.

## EXPLANATION

[Col. 0881D] Asaph, as we have often said, is interpreted as “Synagogue”—that is, the Synagogue that believed, not the one that remained obstinate.

For after the Lord’s resurrection we read that many thousands of Jews confessed the faith. This Asaph now admonishes them not to corrupt their faith to the end—that is, in the Lord the Savior.

At the first entrance, the faithful Jews profess that they will declare all his wonders. In the second part, the King himself—Christ—speaks, promising that he will judge with justice when the time of the general resurrection arrives.

He also warns that no one should dare presume anything against the divine commandments, since he is able to inflict eternal punishment.

## COMMENTARY
We will confess to you, O God; we will confess. This psalm brings the remedy of humility against the swelling of pride, working so that no one presumptuously relies on himself, while no humble person despairs of the Lord. Rather, whatever his condition in this life, a person should have no refuge except God and no joy except in his promises. Its title is: “For the end, do not corrupt; a psalm, a song, or of a song, of Asaph.” This psalm is referred to the end of time, which is a song because it pursues an activity belonging to spiritual joy—namely, true confession, invocation, and narration. I say that the song is attributed to Asaph, that is, to one who truly gathers, namely to him who gathered scattered Israel through faith. It has this purpose and exhortation: “Do not corrupt.” What does “do not corrupt” mean? It means that each of you should fulfill what you promised. For in baptism you promised God that you would renounce the devil and all his pomp; “do not corrupt” this promise by going onward to the end, as blessed Augustine understands it—that is, by attending to his promise. The mind is directed there, and whatever occurs in the present is entirely passed over so that the end may be reached. Nor need one fear that some powerful person will corrupt his promises, provided that you do not corrupt yours. He does not corrupt them, for he is truthful; no more powerful person will corrupt them, for no one is more powerful. Confident, then, in his promises, let us sing the words with which the psalm begins.

For our sake our Head speaks these words: “O God, we will confess to you”—that is, we will humble ourselves and confess our sins to you completely, because we will do this many times, and thus invoke your name. It is as though he said: “Do not invoke unless you confess; first confess, and then invoke.” Confession cleanses the temple, so that the one invoked may come. But he repeats “we will confess” so that you will not regret having confessed. For confessing repeatedly to a human judge prepares death, whereas confessing repeatedly to God the Judge prepares salvation. Confess confidently, therefore, because the one to whom you confess is good, as the Psalmist says: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good.” He is good because he forgives the one who confesses. By confessing, therefore, make favorable the one whom, by remaining silent, you do not make ignorant. But he does not wish to come when called if you are proud. If you are proud, you cannot confess. Humble yourself, then, and confess, and thus truly invoke his name, because by making you his servant the Lord will display this name in you. But whoever is proud does not display the name “Lord” in himself; indeed, he wishes to appear equal or superior.

We will recount your wonders. “We will confess,” I say, “and invoke, and then recount your wonders.” What wonders? The ancient ordering, the new restoration, and eternal blessedness. What is more wondrous than the raising of the dead? For all the wicked, although alive in body, have nevertheless been stripped of their minds. Otherwise the Apostle would not say to them: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will illumine you”; and the order of the words should be observed. The one who confesses has emptied himself of evils; the one who invokes has filled himself with good things; the one who recounts pours forth what has filled him.

“We will recount,” I say, “your wonders.” And after the narration I, as the chief among those who confess, invoke, and recount, though unjustly judged, will judge acts of righteousness, giving thanks for his mercy, since he first wished to narrate before judging. For if he judged first, he would find no one to set free. [Col. 0882D] Let us therefore hear him as he narrates, because, as we shall have tempted him as narrator [Latin *tempserimus*, perhaps corrupt], so shall we experience him as judge. Now, in the time of mercy, he gives commandments to the one who confesses; but in the time of judgment he will spare no one who despises them. Whoever, then, wishes not to fear him as punisher then should love him now as giver.

It follows:

“When I receive the appointed time.” It was not the one by whom we were created who received the appointed time, but the one through whom we were restored. The one by whom man was assumed and changed for the better received the appointed time; he received it as Son of Man, while he governs the appointed times as Son of God. And just as he received the appointed time for being born, dying, and rising again, so he has now received, by the divine ordering, and will finally receive the appointed time for judging. Let us therefore also now receive the time for practicing righteousness, so that we may not fear at the time of judgment.

What he says, “I will judge righteous acts,” may be understood in three ways: either, “I will judge righteous acts,” that is, “I will judge justly”; or, “I will judge those who, emphatically, are to be called righteousness itself,” that is, “I will judge them worthily and separate them,” as the holy apostles; or, “I will separate righteousness from unrighteousness.”

“The earth melted.” I must judge righteous acts because there is something mixed together that needs to be separated. For when “the earth melted”—that is, when those devoted to the earthly desires of the flesh were dissolved—they became dissolute. What else is the life of such people than a kind of flowing away from their Creator? For just as the mind is strengthened by love of higher things, so it is dissolved by desire for earthly things, together with all who dwell in it.

If we understand “earth” as “earthliness,” then we shall say that those who dwell in it—that is, those who take greater delight in it—have melted most of all. But if you understand “earth” as the container standing for what it contains, then the statement simply shows why he says that the earth melted: because of the people who dwell in it.

It follows:

“And I strengthened its pillars.” He calls the pillars of the earth those upon whom the earth, dissolved within itself, is rebuilt and made firm—namely, the holy apostles, upon whom that building was founded, of which it is said: “You are God’s building; you are God’s cultivation.” These pillars wavered in a kind of earthquake because they doubted and despaired at the Lord’s death, saying: “We thought that he was going to redeem Israel.” But when he rose again, he strengthened them, showing those who feared that death need not be feared, and that even the body itself need not be feared in those who die.

“I said to the wicked.” “I strengthened the pillars,” I say, “and through those pillars I said to the wicked: ‘Do not act wickedly any longer.’” He says “wicked” because he found no one righteous; for all have sinned and lack the glory of God. And he spoke this also to those who transgressed afterward. To abandon means to pass beyond a command that has been given. To them, I say, he said: “Do not exalt your horn.”

It is as though he said: “If you have committed wickedness through desire, do not defend it through pride.” For whoever commits wickedness is wicked; but whoever defends it is both wicked and proud. He subsequently explains what “horn” means, as though saying: “Do not, I say, raise your horn on high, [Col. 0883C] and bring down God’s horn to the depths; rather, let our horn be broken, so that God’s horn may be exalted in us.”

Our horn comes from presumption and pride; God’s horn consists of the virtues that reach upward like a horn, and through them the enemy is scattered.

“And do not speak wickedness against God.” He does this who takes away God’s kingdom, saying: “How is God thought to govern mortal affairs? How can he be believed to care for what is on earth? Surely, if he cared for them, so many wicked people would not abound in prosperity, nor would so many good people be oppressed by troubles.” He also speaks wickedness against God who, whenever he suffers something, says that he suffers it unjustly. Thus he declares unjust the one by whose judgment he suffers it: he justifies himself and condemns God.

“For neither from the east, nor from the…” It is as though he said: “You ought neither to do nor to speak wickedness, because a judge is to come against your wickedness. But that judge will come neither only from the east, nor only from the west, nor only from the deserted mountains, because [Col. 0883D] he is God—that is, he is present everywhere, manifest everywhere, hidden everywhere. He will not come from different places; rather, he is in your hearts. And there he will be as you too will be: if you are good, a helper; if evil, a punisher. No escape, therefore, remains except to flee from the angry one to the one who has been appeased.”

He calls the southern and northern regions “deserted mountains”: one is deserted because of the cold, the other because of the heat. They are called mountains because they are elevated regions. This is the literal meaning.

Allegorically, the aforementioned regions may also be understood, so that the meaning is: “You ought not speak wickedness because judgment concerning your wickedness is to come. But it will not be human judgment, which could be deceived. Your judge will be neither from the east—that is, from those people who are ‘east’—nor from those who are ‘west,’ nor from the deserted mountains, because only God will be your judge, and his judgment cannot be deceived.”

Those people are called “east” who have received the light of righteousness. Those, however, upon whom the sun of righteousness has not yet shone are called “west.” The deserted mountains are heretics, who make themselves mountains by usurping the office of teacher, but are deserted because they are useless and fruitless.

“He humbles one and exalts another.” “God,” I say, “is your judge.” What does that judge do? He humbles the one boasting of his merits, like the man who said: “Lord, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity,” and the rest. Through him that people is represented which wished to establish its own righteousness and not be subject to God’s righteousness.

But the other—the one who cries out and humbles himself—he wounds and exalts, as with the one who did not dare even to raise his eyes toward heaven. Through him the Gentile people are represented, since they do not presume upon their merits. Therefore he exalts one and humbles another, because he is, so to speak, like the powerful cupbearer who has authority in the emperor’s house to give this one and that one to drink. For “the cup is in the hand of the Lord,” by which he gives drink to whomever he wishes.

He calls the sentence of the strict judge a “cup.” This cup is full of mixed wine because it contains both the reward of the good and the condemnation of the wicked. Yet it is pure wine, because on neither side is anything done except what is pure—that is, just. He first inclined this cup toward one vessel, namely, toward those who are to be rewarded, and from that vessel toward another, namely, toward those who are to be condemned—or conversely, according to your preference.

Although he inclined it, what happened with this cup was not as with other cups. However much it might be inclined, its dregs were not emptied, that is, they were not poured out, because there were no dregs there, but only pure wine, as we have said. Nevertheless, all the sinners of the earth—that is, all earthly transgressors, who, so to speak, seemed worthy only of a dreggy drink—will drink from that cup as is fitting.

Or otherwise: the cup is the whole Scripture of the Old Testament, in which the spiritual understanding lies hidden as if in the dregs of the carnal sacraments. From it the pure wine is strained out—that is, the spiritual understanding. Hence the one of whom it is said: “The one who humbles himself” is given to drink, or rather, is made drunk. In accordance with the saying: “The Lord’s cup, how brilliant it is, making drunk!”

The dregs, however, remained there for the one who is given to drink of whom it is said: “The one who exalts himself.” This is to say: He humbles one and exalts another because he is powerful. For the aforesaid cup is in the hand—that is, in the power—of the Lord. I say it is a cup of pure wine, containing spiritual understanding as pure wine. Yet it is full of mixed wine—that is, of carnal understanding, which is like mixed, turbid wine. He first inclined this cup toward one vessel, namely, toward the proud Jewish people, and poured the mixed wine into it. From this vessel he inclined it toward another vessel, namely, toward the humble among the Gentiles, and poured the pure wine into it.

Although he inclined it even toward these, its dregs were not emptied; rather, the dregs settled, because the Jews retained both the letter and the carnal observances. In this way all the sinners of the earth will drink from that cup: the humble, confessing their sins, will drink the pure wine; the proud, who justify themselves, will drink the mixed wine. And just as those who drink the mixed wine will vanish, so those who drink the pure wine will advance.

Or otherwise: the cup—that is, the Scripture of the Old Testament—is in the hand of the Lord. In this cup there is pure wine, that is, the simple letter or understanding, insofar as it concerns the Jews, who devote themselves only to carnal things. But it is full of mixed wine insofar as it concerns us, who ascend through carnal things to spiritual things.

He inclined this cup toward one vessel, namely, toward the primitive people of the Church, and poured the mixed wine into it. From this vessel he inclined it toward another vessel, because through the holy apostles and the other early believers he poured the mixed wine into those who came later from the Gentiles. But although he inclined it toward these also, its dregs were not emptied, because some very lowly carnal things still remained, such as those practiced by the Jews when they circumcise boys and do other things of that sort. They neglect the greater matters of the Law, and all the sinners who cling to earthly things will drink of these dregs. This does not mean that everyone observes carnal practices, but just as those who delight in those observances drink, as it were, from the dregs, so whoever delights in any carnal things shares, as it were, in a certain dreg.

“But I and mine”—as though he said—“will not drink from those dregs.” Or, according to the earlier interpretations, he says: “But I and mine will drink separately, because through words and deeds I will announce, in myself and in mine, what must be announced in this present age. And finally I will truly sing to the God of Jacob,” that is, to the God of the later people. For “blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you.”

“And then I will break all the horns of sinners,” that is, I will crush and annihilate all the pride and power of sinners, through myself and through mine. For “the saints will judge nations and rule peoples.” And the horns of the righteous—that is, the virtues and spiritual gifts of the righteous—will be exalted, because they will be crowned with eternal glory.

## ON PSALM LXXV

“For the end, with praises, a psalm of Asaph, a song for the Assyrians.”

[Col. 0885B]

### ARGUMENT

As above. Alternatively, the voice of the Church to Christ.

### EXPLANATION

“Assyrians” is interpreted as “those who direct,” namely, those who, already instructed in the rules of faith, strive to walk along straight paths. Asaph addresses them, singing the praises of the Lord with wondrous variety.

Some books read: “A song against the Assyrian,” in which case this psalm is understood to have been sung against the devil under the person of Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians. Against him God became known in Judea in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. In the first part Asaph addresses the “those who direct,” that is, the faithful Jews, indicating where the name of the Lord became most widely known through the manifestation of his powers. The second part speaks of the wondrous things he accomplished. The third admonishes all the devoted not to cease offering gifts to the fearsome God—gifts that purify the spirit of rulers through salutary correction. These sections are divided by the insertion of diapsalmata.

### COMMENTARY

“God is known in Judea.” The title is as follows: “For the end, with praises, a psalm of Asaph, a song for the Assyrians.” These words are referred to the end, and the psalm is attributed to Asaph—that is, to the earlier faithful who wished to gather others from their own people to themselves, foreseeing that they would be proud and stiff-necked.

This psalm is to be understood as being “with praises,” because it is truly a great praise of God that he regards the humble and despises the proud. This is marked in the psalm. It is also a song because Asaph sings it to the Assyrians with great exultation and joy.

“Assyrians” is interpreted as “those who direct.” Those think that they direct themselves who wished to establish their own righteousness and not be subject to God’s righteousness, and who did not glory in the reality but in the name. Therefore these things are sung so that they may be Assyrian men—that is, so that they may truly direct themselves rather than do so crookedly: they should not presume upon their own righteousness but subject themselves to God’s righteousness. They should attend to what true Judea and the true Israel are, and show themselves to be people who glory not falsely in a name but truly in the reality.

For the Jews, who are known to be the Lord’s enemies by all, commonly glory especially in this psalm and insult the Gentiles, as though God were known only to them and to no others, since the Prophet said so long beforehand: “God is known in Judea,” and so forth. But if they attend to what true Judea and the true Jew are, we grant them that God truly is known in Judea alone.

For true Judea is the Church of Christ, believing in him as the king who came from the tribe of Judah through the Virgin Mary. Concerning him the Apostle, writing to Timothy, says: “Remember that the Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead, from the seed of David according to the flesh.” From Judah came David, and from David came Christ—the one whom they denied as king and chose Caesar as king. Therefore they ceased to be true Judea, [Col. 0886A] and so let them no longer boast that God is known among them.

Likewise, the true Jew is one who is a Jew not outwardly but inwardly, not in the circumcision of the flesh but of the heart, not in the letter but in the spirit. For many holy fathers possessed circumcision of the flesh because of that very faith, but these people, degenerating from them, remained Jews in the flesh but pagans in the heart. Therefore let them not boast that God is known to them.

It follows:

“In Israel his name is great.” For in true Israel the name of God is magnified through good works. But who the true Israel is, he himself reveals in the Gospel when he says: “Behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” But if they themselves are deceitful and lying, how is the name of God great among them?

“Judea” is interpreted as “confession,” while “Israel” means “a man seeing God.” And you, whoever you are, as long as you do not confess your sins through humility, are in a certain way contending with God. For as long as you praise what displeases God, are you not quarreling with him? Humble yourself before him, therefore, and confess your sins, and then you will be Israel—that is, “a man seeing God”—if not yet by sight, nevertheless by faith. And just as previously you displeased him through dissimilarity, so now you will please him through likeness.

Then at last what Scripture testifies will come to pass in you: “His place has been made in peace.” For warfare will be left to you—not warfare against yourself within yourself, but also against spiritual wickedness. Thus, if anger or some illicit impulse rises within you, your members will not be instruments of wickedness for wickedness. This is true peace. For true peace is to be at war with vices and in harmony with the best moral qualities.

In such peace his place is established, because God dwells in such people. His dwelling—that is, his fixed place, which is indicated by “to dwell,” a frequentative verb—is in Zion, in accordance with the saying: “We will come and make our dwelling with him.” God comes to many through faith and confession, but does not make his dwelling there, because they believe for a time and withdraw at the time of temptation. But in Zion—that is, in those who place present things after future things and contemplate what is to come—he truly makes his dwelling, because he remains in them. Make yourself, therefore, a Zion, whoever you are, and you will be his dwelling.

“There he broke.” Behold the signs of his dwelling. It is as though he said: “He truly dwells in Zion.” For there he broke—that is, humbled—the powers. He explains those powers: there he broke the bow, that is, hidden opposition; and the shield, that is, the protection of empty presumption; and the sword, that is, open assault; and thus every form of warfare.

“You are illuminating wondrously.” He turns in direct address to God himself, and “You” is to be pronounced with emphasis. It is as though he said: “You, God, who are known in Judea and great in Israel; you who alone exist through yourself, without whom no other exists—you ought to say, ‘You will be fearsome,’ which follows later. But first he places his humility, saying: ‘You are the one who illuminates from the eternal mountains.’”

He calls the apostles “eternal mountains,” whom the sun of righteousness first illumined, raising them to eternity. Through them he illumined the valleys, that is, other lower places, and did so wondrously—that is, by bearing witness to their teaching through wondrous signs, in accordance with the saying: “While the Lord worked together with them,” and so forth.

Or he did so wondrously because it was sufficiently wondrous that, after so great a fall, God had mercy on humanity. “You,” I say, “illuminated from the eternal mountains, and while you were illuminating, all the foolish in heart were troubled.” Eternal life to come was preached, and the wise became blind because they despised the present life and loved the one that followed.

But the foolish were troubled in heart: at first they were astonished, but they were not awakened, because they fell back into their sleep. Their sleep is blindness of heart and love of earthly things. They slept their sleep—that is, they rested and delighted in the love of earthly things—because they preferred temporal things to eternal ones.

And what did this bring them? This, namely: they themselves—the men of riches—found nothing in their hands, for whatever strength they possess is devoted only to acquiring earthly riches. That is, they became like men who dream of heaps of wealth but, when they awaken, find nothing in their hands. So they too, when at last they rise from the sleep in which they now lie, will find nothing in their hands.

“At your rebuke, O God.” It is as though he said: “Why did they sleep their sleep?” Because of your just judgment, O God of Jacob, who make the one who is filthy become filthier still. God blesses Jacob because Jacob gave present things for future ones—lentil stew, namely, in exchange for the birthright. Therefore those who prefer present things and despise future things are rightly rebuked by God.

In a remarkable way he seems to place “rebuke.” For rebuke contains a loud sound, and a loud sound awakens. But God’s rebuke is of such weight that it does not awaken; rather, it makes one fall asleep. And not only did those mentioned above sleep, he says, but all who mount the horses of apostasy—that is, the first parents and all others who apostatized from the Lord through pride—slept badly.

“You are fearsome.” After making this insertion, he sets down the point toward which, as we said, the prayer is directed. It is as though he said: “You, I say, O God known in Judea, who first appeared in humility, will be fearsome when you come in judgment. And who will then resist you?” No one, certainly: an emperor no more than a shepherd. This is because from that time—that is, from that moment—your anger will appear. Now, while you do not yet exercise vengeance, your anger is as if hidden. Therefore it seems that someone might resist you, but then this will not be so.

“You made judgment heard from heaven.” “You will be fearsome,” I say, “and you made your judgment”—that is, you will make it—heard when you come from heaven in the majesty of a judge. It will be made known through the evangelical trumpet, which says: “Rise, you who lie in the tombs; come to judgment.”

Then the earth will tremble—that is, those who now prefer to be earth rather than become heaven will tremble then. And then they will rest, not from punishments but from sins, since now they do not wish to rest. I say “then,” when God will rise for judgment—that is, for the purpose of judging and condemning the wicked. This is drawn from the conduct of severe and angry judges, who, whenever they wish to judge someone more severely and harshly, rise up so as to show it even by their posture.

Nor will he rise in judgment only against the wicked; he will also save all the meek of the earth—that is, all those who do not mount the neighing horses of apostasy but have made themselves meek earth. In prophetic fashion he put the past for the future, because to the Holy Spirit future things are as known as past things.

Or otherwise: “From that time, your anger.” It is as though he said: “Since no one will be able to resist you in judgment, the Jews resisted you to their own harm, saying: ‘We have no king but Caesar,’ and ‘We do not want this man to reign over us,’ and similar things. For from that time—from the moment they presumed to do this—your anger appeared against them. For a partial blindness came upon Israel so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter.

“And you made this judgment of yours”—that is, this vengeance of yours against them—“heard,” that is, made known, from each heaven—that is, through each apostle. Then the whole well-cultivated earth, both among Jews and among Gentiles, feared and ceased from evil works when God rose in judgment—that is, when it became manifest to them that God would finally rise to judge the wicked and save the good.

Again, otherwise: “From that time, your anger.” It is as though he said: “Since you are so great that no one will be able to resist you in judgment, the wretched first parent resisted you to his own harm, wishing to depend upon his own will. From that time your anger appeared in him and in all his descendants, because you punished them with countless penalties for sin.

“And you made this judgment of yours heard”—that is, you made it known—“especially from the principal heaven,” that is, through your Son, who is the heaven of heavens, and then also through the other heavens. Hence the whole well-cultivated earth, both among Jews and among Gentiles, feared and ceased from evil works.

The following verse, as was just said, remains unchanged.

[Col. 0888A] “For the thought of man.” “Therefore,” I say, “you will save the meek of the earth, because the thought of man will confess to you,” and so forth. This may be understood in two ways.

When a person reflects upon his badly conducted life and condemns it, he makes a confession that is praiseworthy before the Lord. But when he brings what he has thought into action—namely, when he punishes himself for past sins by praying, fasting, and doing similar things—then the remnants of his thought keep festival for the Lord, because, attending to the severity of satisfaction, he is restrained from sins.

Or otherwise: when a person reflects that he was a sinner and gives thanks to God, his giver of life and redeemer, then he confesses to him, because this is confession—that is, his praise. And the remnants of his thought—that is, the recognition of the destruction caused by his past crimes, after tears have been shed and continual contrition of heart—keep festival for the Lord, because such remembrance makes a person cautious in other matters, and thus he is restrained from sins.

[Col. 0888B] “Vow and fulfill your vows to the Lord.” It is as though he said: “And so that he may save you, vow to the Lord and to our God”—that is, to your redeemer and creator—“what ought to be vowed,” namely, yourselves. For whoever considers what good thing he should vow should vow himself and offer himself. This is what is required; this is what is owed.

“Vow,” I say, “and fulfill what you have vowed.” For it is evil to vow and not fulfill. Yet this does not mean that one should not vow; rather, one must both vow and fulfill. In a certain sense the act of vowing comes from us, while fulfillment comes from him.

And it is as though he said: “You ought to vow and fulfill, because all who surround him”—that is, all who approach and cling to him—“will not come empty-handed but will bring gifts,” that is, they will vow and give themselves.

“They will bring,” I say, “to the one to whom they ought to bring them,” namely, to the fearsome one—that is, to him who, though now humble, will be fearsome in the future—and to the one who takes away the spirit of princes—that is, the proud spirit—and gives a meek spirit.

To the fearsome one, I say, not only among the poor but also among kings—that is, among the most powerful people of the earth.

Or, he is fearsome, if not among the perverse, nevertheless among the kings of the earth—that is, among those who rule their own earth well.

## ON PSALM LXXVI

“For the end, for Jeduthun, a psalm of Asaph.”

### ARGUMENT

He foretells what the people were to suffer in Babylon and how, because of these very things, they would freely make complaint, as in Psalm 72. Alternatively, the voice of Christ to the Father.

### EXPLANATION

Asaph is understood as “the congregation of the good”; Jeduthun as “the one who leaps over worldly things”; and the end of those who make progress is understood to be Christ. Thus this entire psalm is sung by the faithful congregation, which, leaping over the vices of this age with glorious steps, reaches that end to which nothing can be found comparable.

But it should be known that in Hebrew the reading is “through Jeduthun,” not “for Jeduthun,” so that it signifies that the psalm was sung not for him but through him. The words that follow, “a psalm of Asaph,” are not found in the reliable copies.

This Asaph, whom we have said is one who leaps over vices, testifies in the psalm’s first section that he cries out to the Lord and that he has been instructed through his tribulations. In the second he lists the thoughts that ordinarily assail the hearts of those who labor in this world. In the third he declares that, through divine favor, he has been changed to a better understanding, so that with a steadfast mind he might contemplate God’s work and power; through these things he is known to have progressed by continual practice. In the fourth he explains how divine miracles have been accomplished among the peoples through the Lord the Savior.

### COMMENTARY

“With my voice I cried to the Lord.” These words are referred to the end, and the psalm is Asaph’s, sung through Jeduthun. “Jeduthun” is interpreted as “one who leaps over.” In this psalm the congregation that leaps over speaks, because “Asaph” is interpreted as “congregation,” and “through Jeduthun” means that it exhorts us to be those who leap over as well: that is, to despise all these lowly things and direct our attention to the highest.

The context of the psalm shows what must be leapt over until we reach that end where there will be nothing left for us to leap over. For we must leap over whatever impedes, entangles, binds, or burdens the mind, until we reach that which is sufficient, beyond which there is nothing, beneath which all things are, and from which all things come.

Whoever therefore wishes to experience, imitate, and retain the soul of this psalm should leap over all carnal desires, trample underfoot the pomp and allurements of this age, and choose nowhere else to stand except in the one in whom all things exist. In all these matters he himself labors by leaping over them until he reaches the true end.

Because Asaph intends in this psalm to urge us to leap over such things, he immediately indicates how this must be done: namely, that we cry out to the Lord not for anything else but for the Lord himself. For many cry out to the Lord to obtain advantages, avoid disadvantages, secure the safety of their relatives, and for many other things. Finally, they cry out even for bodily health, which is the patrimony of the poor. But such people do not leap over anything.

There is scarcely anyone who cries out to the Lord for the Lord’s sake. Great indeed is this passage across; therefore he teaches us to leap over in this way and says: “I cried out to the Lord.” And because many say, “Lord, Lord,” but do not do what is commanded, he adds: “With my voice.”

He cries out to the Lord with his own voice whose voice is in harmony with his heart—namely, when he desires in his heart what ought to be desired, that is, God, and asks for him with his voice. But if he desires and requests something else in his heart, he does not cry out with his own voice, because his voice is not in harmony with his heart; such a person is not sound in mind.

This may also be understood simply: “With my voice I cried out,” that is, with the voice of one who leaps over. And lest it seem that he cried out to the Lord for any reason other than for the Lord himself, he repeats the point, as though saying: “I cried out, I say, with my own voice to the Lord, for God himself alone, and for nothing else.” And not without reason, because he directed himself—that is, made himself intent—toward me. Whoever cries out to the Lord for the Lord’s sake directs himself toward him; whoever cries out for something else does not direct himself toward him.

“In the day of my tribulation.” He shows how one must cry out to the Lord. It is as though he said: “In this way I cried out to the Lord: I sought God with my hands,” that is, through good works, “in the day of tribulation”—that is, in this life, which is tribulation because it is nothing but temptation.

It is called a “day” with regard to the life of the good, which is called day in comparison with the life of the wicked, which is night alone. Yet because this same life of the good, which should be called day because of the good works they perform, is night in relation to the future life, in which we shall be equal to the angels, what he called day he calls night.

It is as though he said: “I said that I sought God in the day; rather, I shall say that I sought him in the night”—that is, in this present ignorance—with hands made or possessed against him, that is, through works done not for human sight but for his sight. And I was not deceived, because in firm hope I already hold what I sought.

“He refused to be comforted.” Because I was not deceived—or because I sought God alone—my soul refused to be comforted by earthly things. This was because I remembered God—that is, eternal things—and delighted only in them. And this was not for an hour; rather, I practiced them, that is, I maintained continual exercise in them. For exercise is the continuation of an undertaking once begun.

I was so exercised in them that “my spirit,” in the sense of what was mine—that is, the will to please myself in earthly things—“failed within me,” while “my spirit,” in the sense of what is yours—that is, the will to please myself in eternal things—“made progress within me.”

My eyes anticipated the watches. Therefore my spirit failed, because my eyes anticipated the watches—that is, I became like one who anticipates the watches. For just as someone who anticipates the watches has become diligent in his work, so I became diligent in that exercise. Yet I was troubled by human weakness, because I thought myself incapable of that exercise. I did not express that trouble, however, so as to throw the blame back upon the Maker, saying that he had made me so weak; rather, I patiently endured it by keeping silent and recognizing that I was suffering it by a just judgment.

This may also be understood differently in part, if “My spirit failed” is taken in its proper sense. It is as though he said: “I delighted, I say, and exercised myself in eternal things, and in that exercise my spirit failed, because it was not sufficient for it. And this was because my eyes anticipated the watches”—that is, they became like those of one who anticipates the watches. For just as someone who continually anticipates the watches becomes bleary-eyed, so my inner eyes, namely reason and understanding, became bleary and dimmed through the sin of our first parent. Therefore I was troubled—that is, I experienced trouble and fear because of this weakness. Yet I did not speak of that trouble as before.

I considered the ancient days. I did not speak, I say, but rather contemplated both my deserved condition and the dignity which you had granted me in my first parent. This is what he says: “I considered,” that is, I kept in memory, “the ancient days”—namely, the fall of our first parent, through which the ancient and old age became useless. For if Adam had not sinned, the day would always have been new and one. I also kept in mind “the eternal years,” that is, the dignity in which our first parents were created, by which, had they persevered in the commandment, they would have reached true eternity.

I not only kept it in memory, but also meditated upon it with my heart—that is, with the greatest attention—and this “in the night,” that is, even when rest was interrupted; or “in the night,” meaning in this present ignorance, I meditated upon it, so that I might see how I could recover that lost dignity. Yet I did not meditate upon it merely for a time; I exercised myself in that meditation, and thus I swept my spirit clean. For my spirit seemed to have been irritated by its love of earthly things; but by sighing for the lost dignity and desiring heavenly things, I swept it clean—that is, I smoothed and leveled my spirit.

*Scobs* is the iron filing with which bakers’ vessels are cleaned; hence the verb *scobere*, “to scrape clean.” This passage may also quite reasonably be read, if it is found in some books, as *Scropebam* or *scrobebam*.

Will he cast off forever? “I was scraping clean,” I say, my spirit, saying: “God, who has already cast man away—that is, driven him far from his face—once because of transgression, has he cast him away forever,” that is, irrecoverably? Certainly not.

Or, will God, being angry, not add anything further, so that he might become more favorably disposed? It is as though he said: “He has already made himself reconciled with respect to certain persons, whom he received both before the Law and under the Law; will he not also add further, so that he may be more favorably disposed toward us, by receiving us as well?” He certainly will.

Or, will he who has already cut off his mercy through the first sin cut it off forever—that is, eternally? That is, will he cut it off from the present generation, extending into the generation to come, so that, just as he cuts it off from this carnal generation, he may also cut it off from that spiritual generation? Certainly not.

Or, will God, whose characteristic is to show mercy, forget to show mercy—that is, so that he may never again have mercy? Certainly not; rather, after he has been angry, he will remember mercy.

Or, will he restrain his mercies in anger—that is, will his anger shut off his mercy? Certainly not. Rather, as he seems to say, his mercy will shut off his anger.

And I said. It is as though he said: “By meditating so much upon the dignity lost in Adam, and by exercising myself in that meditation, I have now passed over to understanding that mercy is not shut off by anger.” Yet I said: “Now I have begun,” that is, I, a wretched man, must be regarded as one who is beginning. For when a human being has completed his course, then he will begin, since nothing in human affairs is perfect.

And it is as though he said: “I said this while contemplating the first fall. And this change”—namely, that from such great perfection, which I possessed in my first parent when he was placed in an abundance of virtues, I fell into this imperfection, so that, although completed, I must be regarded, in human estimation, as one who is beginning—“is the right hand of the Most High,” that is, the change brought upon me because of the sin of my first parent, by the right hand of him who could sufficiently cast me down and punish me, because he is absolutely Most High.

I remembered the works of the Lord. It is as though he said: “I certainly came to know that I had now begun for the first time, when I seemed to be complete; yet I did not cease,” and this because I remembered the works of the Lord—that is, because I considered how great a dignity God had wrought in our first parents, and I did not wish to cease striving toward it.

And I remembered those works because I will remember your wonders—that is, because I must always, O Lord, remember your wonders performed from the beginning. Here “wonders” means the same as “works,” namely, the dignity of our first parents. For what is more wondrous than that God made heaven—that is, human beings equal to heavenly creatures, namely angels—from such lowly material as earth? Nothing indeed.

And I will meditate upon all your works. Because I remembered, and must always remember, your wonders, therefore, O Lord, I will meditate upon the completion of all your works—that is, upon the things you command to be done. And this not merely for a time, but I will exercise myself not in my inventions—which are drunkenness, fornication, and similar things—but in yours.

Understand his “inventions” in the same sense as his “works,” concerning which it was said that he “devised every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his chosen one.” Yet, as if he were to say: “However much I meditate or exercise myself by my own efforts, it will amount to nothing, because no one reaches you by himself. For, O God, your way—that is, the way leading to you—is only in the Holy of Holies, namely, in Christ.”

The foregoing may also be expounded in part as follows, beginning again with “And I said”: “I was scraping clean,” he says, “my spirit, saying: ‘Will God cast off forever?’” and so forth. Finally I said: “Now I have begun,” that is, “Now for the first time I have found what I sought,” namely, that this change—the fact that mercy will not be shut off by anger, but rather anger by mercy—will be “the right hand of the Most High,” that is, it will take place through Christ, who is the right hand of God the Father. Concerning him it is said elsewhere: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” Through him alone it happened that anger was turned into mercy.

And therefore I say: “Now I have begun,” because only now have I remembered the works of the Lord—that is, those works which the Lord the Father wrought through that right hand of his. And I remembered the works because I remembered from the beginning your wonders, performed from the beginning, whose memory I will retain—that is, I must always remember them. This means: “I considered the signs preceding from the beginning, and the things signified through those signs.” For here he takes “wonders” as signs, but “works” as the things signified.

And because, as if he were saying, “I have thus remembered the works which you are going to accomplish through him,” nevertheless, Lord, so that I may conform myself to him, I will meditate upon the completion of all works—not my works, but yours, that is, the things you command to be fulfilled. And I will exercise myself in inventions—not mine, but yours—as before.

God, your way is in the sanctuary. It is as though he said: “What are those works, and what are those inventions? Your way, namely, exhibited to us in the Holy of Holies.” Whatever must be said, whatever must be done, and even whatever must be thought, has been set before us in him. We may call him “the way,” or we may call him the one who, as has been said elsewhere, was sent to us as a book, according to whose model we were to be written. Or we may understand as the works and commandments exhibited to us in him.

Having seen all these things that God the Father has wrought in his Holy One, the Psalmist adds with a certain astonishment and admiration: “Who is a great God?” and so forth. It is as though he said: “Since your whole way will be set before us in that Holy One, what God is so great as our God”—that is, Emmanuel, a sharer in our nature?

And he turns toward him, saying: “You are the God who works wonders.” For what is more wondrous than to give life to the dead—that is, to make the godless godly, and to take the condemned into the kingdom? He then shows what wonders he works, saying: “You have made your power known among the peoples,” that is, you have made known to the peoples what you were able to do.

You manifested this in the following way: You redeemed your people by raising them from inward death through your arm—that is, through your strength. And he specifies which people: “You redeemed the sons of Jacob and Joseph.” By the sons of Jacob, who was one of the three patriarchs, he means the Jews. “Joseph,” however, is placed here with reference to its interpretation. For it is interpreted as “increase,” and here signifies the Gentile people, by whom the Church has been increased. For concerning the Gentiles it was said: “I have other sheep, which are not of this fold,” and so forth.

The foregoing may also be referred to the Father without changing the sense of “in the sanctuary,” as though he said: “Since God the Father sets his way before us in his Holy One, what God is great like our God”—that is, who is favorable toward us by sending his Savior? And he turns toward him, saying: “You are the God who works wonders,” as above.

And truly you work wonders, because “you have made your power known among the peoples,” that is, you have made your salvation known. For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. And “in your arm”—that is, in that power which is your arm—you redeemed your people, namely, the sons of Jacob and Joseph, as before.

The waters saw you, O God. He shows how he redeemed them, namely, by making himself known to them. He takes as “the waters” the same people whom he previously took as the sons of Jacob, namely, the Jewish people. His meaning is: “O God, the waters”—that is, the Jewish people—“saw you,” that is, they came to know you; and when they saw you, they feared, that is, they almost stood still in their flowing.

He refers us to the historical event in which the waters were divided in the sea. For just as, when Moses struck the sea with his rod, those waters, as though sensing the divine power present, stood divided, so these waters, recognizing the power of God, stood still, because they restrained themselves from the flow of vices and carnal desires.

The waters, I say, saw and feared, and the abysses also were troubled. An abyss is a depth of waters. Here he takes “the abysses” as the Gentiles, either because of the depth of their vices or because of the profound understanding found in some of them.

And lest we understand the abysses as troubled only in part, he says that they should rather be understood universally, because “the multitude of the sound of the waters” was troubled. By the multitude of the sound of the waters understand the multitude of the Gentiles who contradicted the truth fiercely at first, both by their deeds and by their words.

And therefore, as if he said, “the waters feared and the abysses were troubled,” because your clouds—that is, your preachers, covering the earth with their words—gave forth a voice. And therefore also the abysses were troubled. For your arrows—that is, your angelic judgments, spoken by the clouds—pass back and forth throughout the whole world. “Their sound has gone out into all the earth.”

And therefore they were also troubled because “the voice of your thunder”—that is, of your threatening, uttered by the clouds—passes in the wheel, that is, through the wheel, namely, through the world, which is revolving like a wheel. For those clouds promised not only eternal rewards but also threatened eternal punishments, saying: “Woe to the world because of scandals,” and similar things.

Your lightnings flashed. By “lightnings” he either means the same thing as he called “the voice of thunder,” or the miracles displayed through the preachers, according to the saying: “The Lord working with them,” and so forth.

Whereas earlier he called it “the wheel,” he now calls it “the world.” And because, as if he said, “your lightnings also flashed,” and because this happened, the Jewish land was shaken and trembled—that is, along with it the other land, the Gentile land, also trembled. And while it trembled, your way—that is, Christ, who is the way to you—was known in the sea, namely, among the Gentiles, who had previously been made bitter by vices.

And your paths—that is, your commandments—were known in the waters, that is, among many peoples. Here “paths” means any commandments. But if earlier “the way” was taken as the commandments, then by “paths” understand only the stricter commandments.

In the sea, I say, your way was known, yet your footprints will not be known upon the earth. For footprints appear on land, but not in the sea. By cultivated land Judea is signified, because it had received the Law; by the sea, however, the Gentiles are signified, toward whom no cultivation had been directed.

In Judea there were indeed footprints, because Christ appeared bodily there and preached. But the Jews did not recognize the footprints, because they did not worship Christ, who was truly the footprint of God the Father.

You led your people like sheep. Your footprints, I say, will not be recognized on the earth; nevertheless, they ought to have been recognized there; they ought to have been mindful of your benefits. For you led—that is, you brought from Egypt into the promised land, through the desert—that people of yours “by the hand,” that is, under the leadership of Moses and Aaron, just as any pious shepherd leads his sheep.

This verse may also be connected with the beginning of the preceding verse in the following way: “In the sea, I say, your way was known, and your paths in the waters, because you led”—that is, you fed like a pious shepherd feeds his sheep—“your truly own people,” that is, the people of grace, “by the hand,” that is, by the power, of Moses and Aaron—not the historical Moses and Aaron, but the true Moses and Aaron.

For Moses is interpreted as “aquatic,” while Aaron is interpreted as “mountainous.” The true Moses and the true Aaron, therefore, is the one who has given us drink for salvation from the water of teaching and has raised our hearts toward the heights: Christ, the Son of God.

# ON PSALM 77: “THE UNDERSTANDING OF ASAPH”

## ARGUMENT

The prophet composed this psalm while commending to the people the pursuit of virtue and the observance of the Law. In it he urges them reverently to fear God, who had anticipated the sanctions of his Law by the abundance of his benefits, so that those who were already liable to punishment might more readily submit. Finally, he exhorts them to preserve harmony with attentive minds. Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ concerning the Jews.

## EXPLANATION

We said that Asaph is interpreted as “the Synagogue,” that is, “the assembly.” But because he placed “understanding” first, he showed that the faithful Synagogue can speak here.

In the first part of the psalm, only two verses are assigned to the person of the Lord, so that reverence might grow among the teachers, for whom the king himself had established the beginning. In the second part, Asaph speaks at greater length, charging the Jews with having contemptuously disregarded the Lord’s commands with a perverse heart, ungrateful for his benefits. In the third, he recounts how many gifts he bestowed upon Israel, yet Israel did not cease murmuring. In the fourth, he declares what sort of vengeance came upon them and how the sentence was softened by the Lord’s compassion. In the fifth, vengeance was taken upon them because of their murmuring, but again, recognizing his greatness, they returned to supplication before the Lord. In the sixth, they again spoke deceitfully to him and followed their customary errors, yet God’s mercy did not destroy them as they deserved. In the seventh, he says how they provoked the Lord in the desert, although Egypt had been afflicted on their account. In the eighth, after the Lord’s benefits have been recounted, the guilt of Jewish obstinacy is appended. In the ninth, the gravest vengeance follows, so that, after the people had been taken captive, he rejected the tabernacle at Shiloh; afterward he chose Mount Zion and David the king, from whose seed Christ, the saving physician, would come.

## COMMENTARY

Give ear, my people, to my law. This psalm contains the events narrated as having taken place among the ancient people. But the more recent and later people are warned to take care lest they be ungrateful for God’s benefits and provoke his anger against themselves, whose mercy they ought obediently and faithfully to receive. Otherwise, he says, “they will become like their fathers, a perverse generation,” and so forth.

This is the purpose of the psalm, its usefulness, and its most abundant fruit. Although the things said in the psalm may seem clear and obvious, because its title is “The Understanding of Asaph,” they nevertheless seem to seek a reader who does not attend merely to the surface but understands inwardly.

Moreover, they appear to seek such a reader for another reason: the psalm says, “I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak propositions.” For parables are likenesses of things, in which something is compared with the matters under discussion. Here the manna is being discussed, and the living bread that descended from heaven is compared with the manna; the same applies to the other matters.

“Propositions,” which in Greek are called *problemata*, are questions containing something in themselves worthy of resolution. Thus the understanding Asaph speaks in this psalm, because among that people there were those who understood and possessed faith—faith that was afterward revealed as belonging not to the letter of the Law but to the grace of the Spirit.

For they were not without faith who were able both to foresee and to proclaim to others the revelation of the Law in Christ. Let us therefore hear the psalm, not as though it were sung to the Jews, but as though it were sung to us. For it is sung more particularly to us, since the Apostle says that “all these things happened to them in figure, but were written for our correction.” If those punishments were to be avoided, then the things signified by them must be avoided with much greater diligence.

For just as, among good things, the things signified are often far more worthy than the signs that signify them, so among evil things the things signified are necessarily more serious than the signs. What the Apostle calls “figures,” the Psalmist calls “parables”—not because faith is placed in the events as mere events, but because faith is placed in the things to which they are rationally compared.

Let us therefore hear the psalm and attend to the Law of God, not according to what it sounds like on the surface, but according to what it signifies through mystical action. To this the understanding Asaph invites us in the following way:

“My people”—that is, all of you who wish to be my companions and belong to my people. I am part of it—that is, of the understanding people. It is as though he said: “Let the one who is Christ be joined to me.”

“You, I say, attend”—that is, consider inwardly—“the law which I make my own by understanding and fulfilling it spiritually, so that you too may make it your own.” Take “law” to mean the Scripture of the Old Testament.

He says how one ought to attend to it: “Incline,” that is, humble, “your ear to the words of my mouth,” that is, in order to understand the words of the Law which my mouth—the mouth of one who understands—will speak to you. For the person truly attends to the Law who humbles himself so as both to understand and to fulfill it.

I will open my mouth in parables. Therefore, as if he said, you ought to incline your ear to my words, because I will not speak to you without substance. For I will open my mouth in parables, saying one thing and signifying another inwardly; and I will speak to you propositions. These propositions and parables are “from the beginning,” that is, they are taken from the Old Testament, which is the beginning of these parables and propositions; their end, however, is the New Testament.

The Old Testament is the beginning because it contains the signs; the New Testament is the end because it contains the things signified.

Or, alternatively: “I will speak parables and propositions existing from the beginning”—not from that beginning when heaven and earth were made, but, as if he said, from the beginning of this assembly, from the time when Abraham was led out of Ur of the Chaldeans. For this assembly began there, and from that time propositions and parables existed.

What parables and propositions are has already been said above. It should also be understood that the same thing can be both a parable and a proposition, with respect to different aspects. For it is a parable insofar as it is a comparison; but insofar as it contains within itself something worthy of resolution, it is a proposition. The term “parable” can refer both to the thing that is compared with another through a certain likeness and to the speech that compares the things themselves.
