All that we have heard and known. I will speak parables and propositions because we have heard many things prophesied in parables and propositions by those who came before us, and we have known them fulfilled by those who came afterward—indeed, countless things.

And therefore I say “we have heard,” because our fathers—that is, our predecessors—related them to us by deeds, words, and writings. By deeds, as Abraham in the offering of his son, Abel in his death, and many others likewise. By words and writings, as Isaiah and the other prophets. Some also announced many things to us through their own condemnation.

They were not hidden from their children. It is as though he said: “Because they related them to us, they are not hidden but known; for they were also fulfilled by us, their children”—that is, their descendants existing in another generation.

What is this other generation except the one to which regeneration has been given? For “another” is said with reference to two. And with respect to the carnal generation that preceded it, this one is rightly called “another.”

Note that the understanding Asaph says that he belongs to the other generation. For all who, from the earlier people, understood and fulfilled the Law spiritually belonged to this other generation, which now exists through faith.

Recounting the praises of the Lord. The fathers, I say, related them to us, and they related the praises of the Lord—that is, those things in which the Lord is rightly to be praised—and his powers, that is, those things in which his power appears—and his wonders, that is, those things worthy of admiration.

I say “wonders” that he himself made, that is, that he himself performed. He takes the same matter in these three expressions: the examination of the testimony, the attainment of the Law, or its establishment, as the following verse indicates.

The Law is wondrous if it is understood not according to the signs but according to the things signified. It is also wondrous because it makes those who fulfill it wondrous.

And he raised up a testimony in Jacob. I say that he performed wonders, and I say this because of the examination of the testimony in Jacob and the establishment of the Law in Israel.

The Law was given naturally to the first human being when he was told: “Eat from this; do not eat from that.” But that Law lay dormant in him through disobedience. It was afterward raised up—that is, confirmed—through Scripture.

The Scripture itself may also in a certain sense be called “raised up.” For just as death is called pale because it makes someone pale, so Scripture may be called “raised up” because it raised up sin. The Apostle testifies to this when he says: “When the commandment came, sin revived.” For I did not know that desire was sin unless the Law said: “You shall not covet.”

The wording seems to demand this, because it says, “He raised up a testimony.” Scripture itself is called “testimony” insofar as it proves something; for those who use it legitimately, it is a testimony of condemnation. Although it is also a testimony of liberation for those who use it legitimately, nevertheless, with respect to the wicked, it is rather called “testimony,” because testimony against the wicked is especially necessary.

The same Scripture is called “law” insofar as it prohibits or commands something.

This verse may also be read so that we understand less by “Jacob” than by “Israel.” By Jacob, let us understand those who are progressing, who understand carnally and do not yet see; by Israel, which is interpreted as “the man seeing God,” let us understand those who have arrived—that is, those who are closer to salvation and understand spiritually.

Likewise, let us understand less by “testimony” than by “law,” because the same Scripture is more worthy insofar as it is law than insofar as it is testimony. “He raised up” also signifies less than “he established.”

Thus it may be said: “The Lord raised up the Scripture of the Law so that it might be a testimony of condemnation”—namely, in Jacob, that is, only among those who are progressing, not among those who have arrived—and “he established the same Scripture as law in Israel,” that is, so that it might be law, namely, prohibition.

Observe that here he says “established,” whereas there he says “raised up.” It was established because it is firm in these people; but there it was only raised up—that is, barely stirred—because it did not adhere firmly to them.

And for these people the Law is rightly a prohibition, because they abstain from sins not merely out of fear of punishment but out of love of justice. For both the person who abstains from theft through fear of punishment and the person who abstains from it through love of justice have a similar hand, but not a similar heart. They are alike in their deed but unlike in their will.

This same verse may also be explained simply, so that we understand the same thing by Jacob and Israel, and by law and testimony, in the following manner: “The Lord raised up testimony so that it might be in Jacob,” that is, in the Jewish people. And what he calls “testimony” he explains by saying: “And he established the Law in Israel.” Take “Israel” here simply, without interpretation.

Yet here too [lacuna], namely, because he imposed the Law—a heavy yoke—upon sinners. For, as the Apostle says, the Law was not established for the righteous but for the unrighteous, because the righteous person is not under the Law but in the Law.

All that he commanded our fathers. He raised up testimony, I say, and established the Law; and in the Law he commanded our fathers—that is, our predecessors—to make known countless things, so that they might make them known to their children, that is, to their descendants.

Some made them known, and some did not. Those who understood and fulfilled them spiritually made them known properly; the others neither understood them nor made them known.

They were to make them known so that the other generation—that is, the spiritual generation—might learn what the earlier, carnal generation did not know.

And so that we may know what he calls the other generation, he says that “the generation to come” will be the children who will be born—not now bodily, but spiritually—and in such a way that it may rise up, that is, raise hearts upward toward eternal things, rather than depress them toward earthly things as those earlier people did.

These people will also recount them to their true children—that is, to those who imitate their faith—namely, so that these children, like the others, may place their hope in God. This means that they should not wish to establish their own righteousness and refuse to be subject to the righteousness of God, but should hope only in the righteousness of God, because no one will be saved through the righteousness of works, but only through the righteousness of faith.

They will also recount to them that they should not forget the works of God—that is, that they should not be ungrateful for God’s benefits and magnify their own works. Rather, they should forget their own works and magnify the works of God, so that they do not provoke his anger but win his mercy.

And they should seek his gifts, given through mercy, not merely in order to know but in order to do.

Let them do all these things, I say, lest they become abominable to God like their carnal fathers. These fathers were a perverse generation, one that provoked God; and he says in what respect they were a perverse generation: in that they were a twisted generation that did not direct its heart.

For the person who does not direct his heart is the one who does not correct what he understands wrongly and does not put into practice what he understands correctly.

That generation was also one that provoked God because its spirit was not believed with God—that is, because it did not possess faith, and faith commands what the Law commands. For when the Spirit of God cooperates with our spirit, what the Law commands is fulfilled; and this cannot happen except by believing in the one who justifies the ungodly.

To have one’s spirit believed with God means to believe that one is not sufficient for a good work without the Spirit of God cooperating. And this is to believe in God, to have faith: namely, by believing God, to cling to him, cooperating rightly with the one who works good.

They, however, did not have their spirit believed—that is, entrusted—with God. For whoever clings to him becomes one spirit with him. They thought themselves sufficient for righteousness without the cooperation of God’s Spirit.

The sons of Ephraim. It is as though he said: “Not only were the lesser among them a perverse generation, but also the sons of Ephraim”—that is, those from whom good was especially hoped and who were preferred to others, just as Ephraim was preferred to his elder brother in the blessing of his grandfather Jacob.

What else did Jacob’s action seem to promise concerning Ephraim in that preference except virtue and every good thing? Nothing indeed.

Therefore “the sons of Ephraim” is placed here to designate those from whom better things were hoped, yet who became a perverse generation. This is to be understood both of the later people and of the earlier people.

He shows in what respect these too were a perverse generation: because, as though bending a bow and shooting—not a bow, but the things shot by a bow—they turned back on the day of battle. That is, although they seemed to be preparing for war with weapons, at the time of conflict they gave themselves over to flight.

This means: “They outwardly imitated the work of the Law, which they did not inwardly love.” For they said: “Whatever the Lord commands us, we will do.” Yet they did nothing of the kind, and thus, as though in the time of battle, they retreated.

Likewise, whoever now says, “Lord, Lord,” but withdraws in the time of temptation and does not do what is commanded, yields as on the day of battle. For a promise of obedience is not tested by hearing but by temptation.

They did not keep the covenant of God. This is the reason why they turned back on the day of battle: namely, because they did not keep the covenant of God. They did not attend to the true and eternal promises of God, nor observe them, but chose something cheaper—that is, earthly things.

And because they were unwilling to walk in his Law, even if at some time they observed something from the Law, they did not do so from a good will but under the compulsion of fear.

Moreover, they forgot his benefits, that is, they proved ungrateful for the benefits God had bestowed upon them; and they forgot his wonders, which he showed them—that is, which he performed before their eyes.

Here he takes “wonders” as the evils which he displayed against their enemies. I say that they forgot the wonders because he performed certain wonders before their fathers.

Here he takes “fathers” not as those who were the perverse and provoking generation, as before, but as Moses and Aaron, who are called fathers both as an honorific and because of the similarity of their care.

Although the Lord said in the Gospel, “Do not call anyone your father on earth,” he did not wish to remove this name from ordinary human speech. Rather, he wished us not to attribute the grace of spiritual regeneration to any holiness or power, but to him alone through whose mercy it takes place. Thus Moses and Aaron are appropriately called fathers here.

Before these fathers—that is, while they stood by, and while they themselves acted and bore witness—he performed wonders in the land of Egypt, the subject of this passage, and he specifies the place: in the plain of Tanis.

Tanis is a city of Egypt, near which those ten plagues were inflicted by the Lord upon Pharaoh through Moses.

Likewise, before our spiritual fathers—that is, while they see and also act—the Lord performs wonders spiritually in us, both for good and for evil, in Egypt, that is, in this life, which is ignorance and temptation.

Egypt is therefore rightly used as a symbol, because Egypt is interpreted as “darkness” or “tribulation,” while we still remain in the plain of Tanis, that is, in the level place of the humble commandment.

For “plain” signifies a level place, while Tanis is interpreted as “humble commandment.” In this life the humble commandment is given to us plainly—that is, openly—namely, that we should learn to be humbled here, so that at last we may deserve to be exalted with the one who, for us and through us, wished to be humbled in this Egypt.

He divided the sea. It should be understood that he now postpones the wonders about which he has spoken most particularly and first recounts the benefits afterward bestowed upon the people. He does this in order to aggravate their ingratitude: although they ought to have been sufficiently grateful merely for the wonders he performed against their enemies, they nevertheless received so many additional benefits and remained ungrateful.

And if these things are parables, as the psalm testified above, we must attend not only to what they sound like on the surface but also to what they signify through mystical action. For whatever good or evil happened historically to them or to their enemies happens spiritually in us: good through grace, evil through justice.

Let us therefore attend to these things, lest we be ungrateful for God’s benefits. Let us place our hope not in ourselves but in him, and fear him with chaste love, not servile fear, lest what happened in them also happen in us—namely, that we become a perverse and provoking generation.

You may connect the literal text as follows: “Behold, wonders in Egypt.” Afterward he bestowed these benefits upon them: when they had come to the Red Sea and, because of the pursuing enemies, were afraid, he divided the sea for them and brought them safely to the opposite shore, secure from their enemies. As they crossed, he established—that is, made firm—the waters of the sea, as though they had been gathered together by force. This is what happened to them historically.

The same thing also happens to us spiritually. The water of baptism, reddened—that is, made like the Red Sea—by the blood of Christ, which is mingled with it through the signs of the cross, is separated from ordinary waters, because it is now water suited not only to washing bodies but also to cleansing minds.

Through this water, in which we renounce Satan and his pomp and receive the faith, the Lord leads us into the security of our heavenly homeland—if not in reality, then at least in hope. And all the enemies pursuing us—that is, all vices, both former actual sins and original sin—are extinguished there.

Through the same renunciation and faith he makes firm the waters of desires and vices, which are fluid and slipping away, so that they may no longer, as before, pour themselves out within us.

And he led them on. He brought them, I say, to another shore, and from that place led them through the wilderness by a cloud during the day and throughout the night by the illumination of fire—that is, going before them by day in a pillar of cloud, which protected them from the heat, and by night in a pillar of fire, which showed them the way.

Similarly, after the passage mentioned above, he leads us into this wilderness, and in this wilderness—that is, in this life—under the protection of the cloud, meaning Christ’s humanity. For what else was accomplished for us through it than a kind of shelter from the heat of temptations? He himself first suffered, so that we would not have to suffer; and he rose again so that we might have the same hope. Thus he became for us a shade and a strong tower, as has been said elsewhere. Christ’s flesh is called a cloud because in it the divinity was hidden from the wicked but shone forth upon the good. It was also a cloud belonging to the day—that is, it was itself day—because it was bright and without the mist of sins. Hence it is said: “The Lord ascended upon a light cloud; he will enter Egypt and shatter all the idols of Egypt.” And throughout the night—that is, in the midst of such great ignorance—he leads us by the illumination of fire, enlightening us with his spiritual gifts. By fire, in which there are both brightness and heat, this is signified: he will enlighten the good both here and in the future, and at last burn the wicked.

He split the rock. Another benefit was this: in the waterless wilderness the Lord split the rock, struck twice with the rod by Moses, and such an abundance of water flowed forth—as though from a vast abyss—that they could be watered. In this way he watered them, for he brought water out of the rock, and not a little water: he brought forth waters like rivers, that is, waters in the greatest abundance.

This relates to us as follows. The rock in the wilderness, struck twice by the rod, is Christ crucified upon the double wood of the cross. In his Passion the veil of the Temple was torn, because everything that had previously been hidden was revealed; and the rocks were split, because hearts of stone received faith, and immensely abundant waters followed that faith. These are the waters of which he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, rivers will flow from his belly,” and so forth. That is, exceedingly abundant spiritual gifts followed.

And they added still more sin against him; they provoked the Most High to anger in the waterless place. So many benefits had been bestowed upon them by the Lord, and yet they continued to add sin against him. And therefore—he means, as it were—I say that “they added sin,” because they had sinned before. For earlier they had provoked the Most High, that is, the Lord, to anger by doubting his power in the waterless place, meaning in the arid region, and more particularly in the dryness of the mind than of the belly. Their bellies were full, but their minds were empty.

He then explains in what they added sin: namely, in this, that when they had come to a place where nothing could be planted or sown, they tested God in their hearts. They asked not by believing but by testing, having one thing on their lips and another in their hearts. Thus, I say, they tested him by asking for food for their souls—that is, for their own advantage, not for their spirituality.

We likewise add sin in the waterless place if, after receiving spiritual gifts through God’s mercy, we become so dry that we completely neglect the good works we could perform; in this dryness we provoke him to anger. We add still more sin when we test him, seeking from him not true goods but false ones, as though he did not know what ought to be requested, although he says concerning true goods alone: “Ask, and you will receive,” and so forth.

And they spoke wickedly against God; they said: Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? He explains how they tested God: they spoke wickedly against him, reviling him, because they said: “Can God prepare a table,” that is, some kind of refreshment, “in this wilderness?”

And as though someone were to say to them, “He can, because he has done what was equally impossible by bringing waters from the rock,” they reply, in order to destroy that argument: “For he struck the rock and brought out waters.” But can he also give bread in this wilderness, or prepare a table—that is, some refreshment—for the people, although they call them his own? Certainly he cannot, as though they were saying: “That was possible in some way; this, however, is impossible.”

Allegorically, this applies to those who, after recognizing and understanding that Christ truly died for our salvation and that baptism also serves for our salvation, nevertheless doubt whether in this wilderness—that is, in this life—he can refresh us with his blood and body. They speak as though saying: “Since God struck the rock—that is, since the Lord died for us—and waters flowed from it, as was said above, can he also give bread? Can he refresh us in the wilderness of this life with his body and blood?” As though they were saying: “This is impossible.”

By “bread,” in the mystery, understand one sacrament alone, namely, the body; by “table,” understand both. Such were those of whom it is written that, when the Lord said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,” nearly seventy-two were scandalized and went away, saying: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” “Will he cut off pieces of his flesh and give them to us to eat?” and so forth.

Therefore the Lord heard. Those people, testing him, doubted, and therefore the Lord heard them. He also hears us when we doubt him, yet he delayed the punishment in order first to satisfy their unbelieving desire and to display his power. If someone carefully considers what follows, it can most appropriately be applied to us.

He states what he delayed: namely, that a fire was kindled—that is, a blinding of the mind occurred—in Jacob, meaning among the lesser ones, the doubters. Historically, this also happened among them, because fire came into their camps. And God’s anger rose against Israel, meaning against the greater ones.

For the greater often descend so far to the level of the lesser through human compassion that they do not impose a correction proportionate to their vices, attributing their sins instead to human weakness. Therefore God’s anger—that is, blindness of mind—enveloped them all alike, because they ought not to have shown compassion in that manner, as blessed Gregory testifies when he says: “We owe compassion to nature, but strictness to vices.”

Historically, this too occurred among them, because Aaron was excessively compassionate toward them when, satisfying their perverse desire, he allowed a molten calf to be made. For this he deserved God’s anger, namely, that he should not lead that people of his into the promised land.

Because he did not believe. Therefore, I say, fire was kindled in Jacob because they did not believe in God—that is, they doubted God—and consequently did not hope in his salvation, that is, they despaired of his salvation.

[Col. 0899D]

And he commanded the clouds. Behold why he delayed the punishment: namely, so that he might first fulfill their unbelieving desire, because he commanded the clouds coming from above to rain and opened, as it were, the doors of heaven.

And he rained manna upon them for food. By saying “manna,” he identifies what he gave them: he gave them the bread of heaven, that is, bread sent from heaven. “Man ate the bread of angels.” History truly records that God rained manna upon that murmuring people.

Manna was of such a kind that it tasted to them like every food. The word manna is interpreted as “What is this?” He does not call it the bread of angels because angels use it, but because it descended, as it were, from their region—that is, from above. Or he also called manna the bread of angels because it signified that true bread which descended from heaven, by which the angels are refreshed.

History also records that, because manna had a confused or mixed flavor, it began to become distasteful to them. They began to desire more savory foods, and then God sent them other provisions besides manna in abundance. He sent them in this way: he transferred the south wind, that warm wind, from heaven to the earth, and also brought in the African wind beside it—not by the south wind’s power, but by his own power, he who makes it what it is.

In the force of those winds he rained flesh upon them like dust, that is, abundantly. He explains this by saying that he rained winged creatures upon them like the sand of the sea, that is, in the greatest abundance. For there are also certain flying creatures without wings, such as butterflies. Those winged creatures—namely, quail—fell in the middle of their camp and around their tents up to a cubit’s height, as the history relates. They did not eat moderately, but some were excessively filled, even to vomiting.

In this way the Lord brought them what they desired: he filled their unbelieving appetite. And he truly brought it, because they were not deprived of their desire. But because they were excessively filled, while the food was still in their mouths, God’s anger immediately rose against them—that is, divine vengeance overwhelmed them.

Similarly, the Lord commands the clouds—that is, his preachers—and opens the doors of heaven, opening their hearts to an understanding of the truth. Through them he rains upon us that true manna by which the angels are refreshed, which descended from heaven so that man might eat the bread of angels. He does this by making known to us the history of the Incarnation of his Christ, the mystery of that Incarnation, and, in addition, by making him known to us in the sacraments of the altar.

After we have received all this through his mercy, if we continue to seek higher things, as though seeking more savory food—such as knowledge of his divinity and of still higher mysteries—then the Lord transfers from heaven, not the North Wind, which is cold, but the South Wind and the African Wind, southern and warm winds: namely, the shining and fervent spirits of preachers. In heaven they heard secrets that it is not permitted for a human being to speak, but he makes them descend to us so that we too may ascend with them.

Through them he rains upon us flesh and winged creatures—that is, he makes known to us things more savory and more exalted—like dust and like sand. By dust, which is extremely fine, understand the subtlety of meanings; by sand, their abundance; by the sea, which is salty, their savor, because although they are not the savor of life unto life for everyone, they are so for some. We may also understand dust as their lowliness and sand as their barrenness, insofar as they concern the wicked.

Those winged creatures fall both in the middle of our tents and around our tents. Those in the middle are the things we learn from our own prelates; those around are the things we learn from outsiders. But if we are refreshed by them not to sobriety but to drunkenness—that is, if we wish to investigate them too deeply and to know more than is fitting to know, so that we become proud and turn into teachers of error—behold, while the food is still, as it were, in our mouths, God’s anger immediately rises against us, because we are punished with blindness of mind.

Blessed Augustine pursues this allegory very elegantly and appropriately, saying:

“He rained manna upon them, and he who gave it to the tempting synagogue will not deny it to the believing Church. For he who was able to refresh the bodies of those who tested him can also feed the little faith of those who do not test him—that is, of believers—with signs of words uttered in the flesh and passing through the air like winged creatures. Yet they do not come from the North, where cold and darkness prevail—that is, from eloquence pleasing to this world—but from the South and the African Wind, which are warm winds, transferred from heaven.

“Where? To the earth, namely, so that the little ones in the faith, hearing earthly things, may be nourished to receive heavenly things. For if they do not believe earthly things, they will not believe heavenly things either, according to the Lord’s saying: ‘If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?’

“That South Wind from heaven, where it heard secrets that it is not permitted for a human being to speak, was truly transferred to the earth when he said: ‘I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food.’

“By the South Wind and the African Wind understand the fervent and shining spirits of preachers who come to us from above and bring words sent by God, so that each person may gather them, both in his tent and around his tent, and worship God in his own place.”

And he killed their fat ones. It is as though he says: His anger rose against them in this way, because he killed those among them who had become fat—that is, those who had been excessively filled—historically in body. His doctrine killed those who had become excessively fat in mind, and hindered the chosen of Israel, so that they could not benefit those whom they wished to assist with paternal affection.

For what does human mercy accomplish where divine vengeance is present? Or he hindered them in this way: by showing too much compassion, they did not turn their vices into an occasion for strict correction, and so they themselves suffered together with them. Thus the prophets were often led into captivity with the others, not only as an example of justice but also of patience.

They were an example of justice so that the others might know that if God does not spare his children, he will not spare his fugitive servants. They were an example of patience so that, following their example, the others might learn to endure evils patiently.

In all the evils mentioned above the Lord afflicted them, and in all these things, although corrected by the Lord, they still sinned. They sinned because they did not believe in God, failing to attend to his miracles, which ought to have admonished them. He calls “miracles” the benefits and punishments inflicted upon them, insofar as they signified something else.

And they came to an end. It is as though he says: Because they did not believe in his miracles, they devoted themselves to vanity, that is, to earthly things. In that vanity their days and years came to an end hastily, because twenty-three thousand fell in one day, and others perished from serpents and various diseases.

When he says “hastily,” he does not mean that their years hastened toward death, but that, because they were not corrected and were always driven toward worse things, they seemed to be hastening toward destruction. Similarly, although the days of us all were created for eternity, if we devote ourselves to vanity, those days certainly fall away from eternity; and when we sin day after day without correcting ourselves, our minds, created for eternity, hasten as though toward destruction or nothingness.

When he killed them, they sought him. Their years came to an end, I say, because God was killing them. And when he killed them, they sought him—as though not the slain themselves, but others who feared being killed sought him.

They sought him in this manner: they returned to God, from whom they had previously departed, not with the heart but with the mouth; and at dawn—that is, as though zealously—they returned to him. Then they remembered him, though not truly, because they did this only to obtain some advantage or avoid some misfortune.

They remembered, I say, that God was their helper—that is, that without God they could accomplish nothing—and that he was their Redeemer, because he had redeemed them from Egyptian slavery. Therefore they loved him only in word, not in heart. They honored with their mouths the one whom they despised in their hearts. And they lied to him with their tongues, saying: “Whatever the Lord commands, we shall do.” But they quickly did otherwise and forgot.

But their heart. They loved him, I say, only with the mouth, but their heart was not right with him. The heart of one who seeks God only for God’s sake is right with God. These, however, sought God not for his own sake but for the sake of other things.

And because their heart was not right with God, they were not considered faithful, but rather faithless, in the covenant—that is, in his promises—because they did not faithfully attend to what the Lord promised, namely eternal and heavenly things, but chose earthly and transitory things instead.

But he is merciful. They were such people that they lied to him and did not possess a right heart with him; therefore they deserved to be utterly destroyed. Yet he was merciful toward them, because he did not completely destroy that people, for the sake of the succession of their offspring: some of their descendants were going to believe and become perfect, such as the holy apostles and many others, and Christ was going to be born from their seed.

And he will be gracious toward their sins—not toward the sins of those who were sinning and persisting in unbelief, but toward those who would be converted from among them, as we have said previously. For this reason he would not utterly destroy them.

It should be understood that from this passage some sinners have presumed to assert the impunity of sins, saying that they too were like those people, and yet God had mercy on them, because it is said here: “He is merciful, and he will be gracious toward their sins.” They fail to observe that God’s patience now leads to repentance, whereas in the future he will have mercy on no evil.

And he abounded. He was merciful to them in this respect: he did not utterly destroy them. And he abounded in mercy—that is, he showed them still greater mercy—namely, so that he might turn away his anger, even granting them the blood of his only-begotten Son, as he did to those who came to the apostles and said: “What shall we do, brothers?” In response Peter said to them: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord.”

Therefore he will not kindle all his anger, so as to destroy that people completely, for the sake of the succession of their offspring, as we said above. He will not kindle it also because he remembered that they were flesh. This does not mean that forgetfulness occurs in God, in whom no defect occurs, but that earlier, when he struck them down, he seemed to have forgotten their weakness.

Now, when he spares them, he seems to have remembered that they are flesh—that is, that they are made from weak material. Consequently, what they do wrong arises from weakness. He also remembered that they are a passing spirit, inclined to sin and unable to return by itself, but only through God’s mercy. For a human being can destroy himself, but cannot save himself.

Hence Solomon says concerning the way of iniquity: “Everyone who walks in it will not return.” And it should be understood that, just as some took from the preceding passage an occasion for presumption of impunity, so others took from this saying an occasion for despair.

How often they provoked him. He repeats the same unbelief of theirs that he mentioned above. He repeats it for this reason: he wishes to add the plagues that the Lord inflicted upon the Egyptians on their account, so that they may appear all the more ungrateful, since they ought to have remembered both their own benefits and the evils inflicted upon their enemies for their sake.

The connection is therefore as follows: They truly are flesh and a passing spirit, because, if they were not such, they would not provoke the Lord so often. For how often—indeed, indefinitely often—they provoked him in the wilderness; that is, they stirred him to anger in the waterless place, not so much through dryness of the belly as through dryness of the mind.

They provoked him in this manner: they turned to him, saying, “Whatever the Lord commands us, we shall do,” and yet immediately tested him. From this it is clear that they had not truly turned. For Christ’s soldiers are not mere petitioners. In this way they provoked him—that is, made the Holy One of Israel angry with themselves—meaning the one who sanctifies all Israel, that is, every person who sees God. Or “the Holy One of Israel” means the one whom they themselves ought to sanctify within themselves, if they were true Israel.

Similarly, we too turn to God, saying, “Lord,” and immediately test him, because at the time of temptation we withdraw. Thus we provoke the God whom we ought rather to appease.

Therefore, I say, they provoked the Holy One of Israel because they did not remember his hand—that is, his power—displayed on the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the one who afflicted them, Pharaoh. Cassiodorus says that tribulation, and the things that cause pain, are especially apt to remain in the memory. Yet these people did not remember even their tribulation; how much less, then, did they remember their benefits? Thus they were exceedingly ungrateful.

As he placed them in Egypt. He redeemed them, I say, just as he truly redeemed them then, when he placed his signs in Egypt. Or they did not remember his hand displayed in that manner, just as it had been displayed when he placed—that is, firmly and clearly established—his signs in Egypt.

He calls the plagues inflicted upon the Egyptians “signs” because they signified something else. Therefore he immediately calls those signs “wonders” and identifies the place, saying: “And his wonders in the field of Zoan.” Wonders are so called as things that act far onward. Those plagues acted far onward, that is, they signified things that would occur spiritually in us.

He begins to enumerate those signs, saying: “And he turned their rivers into blood,” and their rainwaters as well, so that they might not drink from either the rivers or the rainwaters. Historically this truly happened: the rivers became bloody, the fish died, and the Egyptians dug cisterns, where they also found blood.

Similarly, even now the Lord turns the rivers into blood for those who follow that people and wish to remain in Egypt, that is, in darkness. He makes the doctrine of Sacred Scripture insipid and undrinkable to them, so that they understand the causes of things not spiritually but carnally, and understand spiritually accomplished things in a carnal manner.

This is what it means to turn what was savory into insipidity. Conversely, water, which is without flavor, is changed into wine, that is, into flavor, when the letter of the Law is understood spiritually. By the rain, which is water coming from above, are signified the higher matters within that teaching, which ought to be understood most spiritually.

He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them. The dog-fly is a canine fly, greatly troublesome to dogs. By it—as I may put it—canine behavior is signified: through such behavior the wicked are consumed inwardly while wishing to devour the people of God, so that they show no honor even to their parents. Yet the Lord commands in the Gospel: “Honor your father and mother, so that you may live long upon the earth.”

The Lord also sent a frog into Egypt, and it destroyed them. The frog signifies loquacity, because the Lord destroyed persecutors and wicked people: by devoting themselves to utterly empty talk, they lose their authority.

And he gave their fruits—that is, the fruits of the Egyptians—to blight. Blight is a moth or rust that harms secretly; its effect is especially evident in ears of grain. By blight is signified hidden pride among the wicked, namely when they become prouder than they ought and consider themselves to be something when they are nothing. Through this their fruit is destroyed, although by understanding and reason they ought to produce it.

For every human being naturally possesses this through understanding and reason: to render fruit to God, that is, to perform good works.

And their labors to the locusts. The locust harms with its mouth, because it gnaws. By it is signified that wickedness in the evil by which they disparage the good works of their neighbors, or even give false testimony against their neighbor.

Their labors are given to this locust because, while principally destroying the good works of others, they erase whatever good they themselves may have done. No one sins first against himself before sinning against another.

According to another comparison, the instability of the wicked may also be understood by the locust: they believe for a time, but at the time of temptation they withdraw.

And he killed their vines with hail. By the vine is signified compunction—that is, compassion toward one’s neighbor—which ought to be as delightful to us as wine and through which we ought also to forget our own concerns. For elsewhere it is said: “You gave us to drink the wine of compunction.”

This vine is struck by hail among the wicked when they devastate the goods of others through rapacity, plunder, or any other means. They devastate themselves inwardly far more than they devastate others outwardly.

And he killed their mulberry trees with frost. The mulberry is a tree easily damaged by frost. Frost is a certain cold nocturnal dew, and it signifies hidden hatred: when, through the darkness of folly—as through the cold of night—the love of one’s neighbor freezes within us, the mulberry, that is, whatever fruit of love for one’s neighbor ought to exist, perishes in us.

The mulberry is rightly taken as signifying love of one’s neighbor, because its fruit is red, and this love ought to be so effective in us that we lay down our life for our brothers and shed our blood.

The darkness of folly mentioned above consists in refusing to imitate the one who wished to lay down his life for all. Conversely, to imitate him is like the light of wisdom.

Or alternatively: frost strikes fruit prematurely, even before it has produced leaves or blossoms. This signifies the wickedness of the evil, which anticipates every work of their good neighbors by discouraging and diverting them, so that no good is accomplished in them. According to this interpretation, understand the mulberry as any kind of fruit.

And he delivered their beasts to hail. Historically, this happened: hail struck the Egyptians’ animals. By the loss of the animals, the loss of chastity is understood. Beasts are prepared only for producing offspring, and therefore chastity is suitably signified by beasts.

Or alternatively: because animals are called *jumenta* from *juvare*, “to help,” wives may be signified by animals, since they are a help—not in virginal chastity, but in marital chastity. These animals are, as it were, struck by hail when wives become contemptible to their husbands, just as husbands often become contemptible to their wives.

For God delivered them, as the Apostle says, to a reprobate mind, so that men, abandoning the natural use of women, and women, abandoning the natural use of men, might do things that are improper, and so forth.

Their possessions to fire. Our possession is the inner human being, according to the saying: “In your patience you will possess your souls.” This possession is delivered to fire when our mind is devastated by the fury of savage anger. For just as it is preserved through patience, so it is devastated through impatience.

It should be noted that, just as ten plagues of Egypt are enumerated in Exodus, so they are enumerated here. Three of those listed there are not found here; three others are set here in their place, not for historical reasons but for allegorical ones.

One of these is this: that the possession was delivered to fire. Another is: “He killed their mulberry trees with frost.” The third is: “He gave their fruits to blight.” It is customary in this Scripture often to place one thing in place of another for the sake of allegory. Thus earlier he placed Abimelech in place of Achish.

[Col. 0904C]

He sent among them. It is as though he says: The Lord inflicted all the things mentioned above upon the Egyptians, and he did so in this way: first he sent indignation among them, then anger, and finally tribulation. This is what is meant by: “He sent among them the anger of his indignation.”

He specifies the order: first indignation, then anger, and then tribulation. He carried out this sending through evil angels, ministers of his anger. He sent indignation immediately, when they did not comply with the first warning to release his people. But when they began to grow more proud, their obstinacy deserved anger. Hardening followed, and tribulation followed as well.

Understand indignation in the first plague, anger in the second, which was more severe, and tribulation in all the others.

Similarly, when we sin, the Lord sends indignation—that is, blindness of mind—then anger, meaning a more severe blindness; and finally tribulation, when we are hurled into the depths of iniquity.

There is no doubt that evil angels are those for whom eternal fire is prepared. Through them God not only condemns the wicked but also tests the godly, as he tested blessed Job. Nevertheless, they possess one kind of power over the wicked and another over the good.

They can accomplish nothing in the good unless they are permitted to do so. In the wicked, however, because the wicked have already come under their right and authority, they can do whatever they wish, even without permission. It is like a peasant who does not work another person’s ox unless he receives permission from its owner, but works his own according to his pleasure.

Good angels also have the power to inflict bodily harm upon wicked people. The three angels whom Lot received as guests were good angels, yet through them the destruction of Sodom took place. But it is not recorded that good angels inflicted any bodily injury upon good human beings.

He made a path for the way of his anger. He shows how he carried out the sending mentioned above through evil angels: namely, he made a path for his anger. For as long as God’s hidden justice punished their iniquity, it was, as it were, only a path of God’s anger.

But after he permitted them to be led by evil angels from hidden matters into manifest ones, so that he might punish evident sinners with evident punishment, then the narrow path became a broad road.

And he truly made a road, because he did not spare their souls from death. Or alternatively: what I called a path of God’s anger was the punishment by which he struck them in their external goods. But when he struck those same people themselves by drowning them in the sea, behold, he made the path a road.

According to this interpretation, what follows explains how he made the path a road: namely, because after he had first struck them in their external goods, he finally did not spare their souls from death—that is, he killed them with the most grievous death. By saying less, he signifies more.

And he shut up their beasts in death, because he drowned them, together with their horses and chariots, in the sea.

Similarly, in us he makes a road from what was, as it were, a path of his anger when he continually permits us to be hurled from grave sins into worse ones. He does not spare us from the death of our souls when he finally gives us over to the depths of iniquity and to the eternal darkness of the mind. And with us he shuts our beasts up in death, because he permits all chastity in us to perish.

And he struck every firstborn, from human being to beast, as the history relates, in the land of Egypt. Moreover, he struck the firstfruits of all their labor, that is, all the first growth of agricultural work, such as hay, barley, flax, and similar things—not in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, but in the tents of Ham, that is, in the land of the enemies.

Understand “the tents of Ham” as referring to the land of Egypt. Augustine and Cassiodorus say that Ham was also the father of Canaan, whose descendants are known to have possessed that land.

The firstborn of animals may signify either faith, without which every good work is useless and fruitless; or the love of God and neighbor, upon which the whole Law and the Prophets depend; or justice, which is the principal and social virtue, because through it the entire human race is united, at least in its natural condition.

The firstfruits of labor signify what is most important in our actions, just as the things mentioned above are the chief elements among the virtues. The Lord strikes all these—that is, reduces them to nothing—not in the land of Israel but in the land of Egypt, that is, among those who persecute his people, love darkness more than light, and constitute the tents of Ham, in whom the devil reigns.

For Ham is interpreted as “cunning.” And who is more cunning than that ancient, many-turning serpent? Certainly no one.

And he led them out like sheep. It is as though he says: After striking and destroying the sheep, the Lord took his people from their midst—the people whom he had specially chosen for himself from among all the nations. As a good shepherd leads his sheep out of dangers, so he led them through the wilderness, that is, brought them to safety, like a shepherd leading his flock.

The Lord also takes us away, if we are his people—that is, obedient to his commandments—from the power of our spiritual and bodily enemies, feeding us with spiritual sacraments, just as a kindly shepherd feeds his sheep. In the wilderness—that is, in this life, which is a wilderness in comparison with the future life—he leads us to safety by sight, having made us into a flock, that is, gathering us into one heart and one soul.

And he led them in the hope of the promised land; he also leads us in hope. For we have been saved in hope. They did not fear their enemies, and neither do we fear our enemies, because if God is for us, who can be against us?

Therefore those enemies, attacking or confronting them from the side, did not frighten them, because the sea covered all their pursuers. In the same way, after all our pursuing enemies—that is, all original and actual sins—have been destroyed in the sea, meaning in baptism, we will fear our enemies no longer, if we are careful.

And he brought them out of Egypt, after leading them to the mountain of his sanctification, that is, to Jerusalem, situated in the mountains, where they were sanctified through sacrifices and the other instruments given to them. Historically, Egypt lies in a valley, while Jerusalem lies in the mountains.

Therefore he says: “He brought them to the mountain”—the mountain, I say, which not their sword but his right hand, that is, his power, acquired for them, because he dealt with them through such manifest signs that his presence could be understood.

Similarly, after bringing us out of the valley of error and darkness through faith and the grace of baptism, he has already led us in hope—even if not yet in reality—to the mountain of his sanctification, that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem, where we are truly sanctified through true confession, meaning the praise of God, because then the final death will be destroyed.

Our merits did not acquire this mountain, but his right hand—that is, his Son—acquired it for us through his blood.

And he cast out. He led them in, I say, and cast out from before them the nations that had occupied that land—namely, the Hittites, the Hivites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, and others. Then he divided the land among the tribes by the cord of distribution [Col. 0906B], that is, by a measured and equal distribution. An inheritance is customarily distributed by a cord, and this by lot, that is, through the casting of lots.

In the same way, after he has led us through hope into the heavenly Jerusalem, he has cast out the nations—that is, the errors of the gentiles, namely, the unclean spirits that ruled over us—from before our inner face, that is, from the soul. And he divides for us, as by the cord of distribution, that is, according to measure, the land equally among us: the heavenly homeland. For, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places.” Or, he divides among us that land from which we are nourished, that is, spiritual gifts, because each person has his own gift from God according to his measure.

And he made the tribes of Israel dwell there. Historically, this means in their tabernacles, that is, in those of the nations cast out from before them. In the same way, he has already made the tribes of Israel—that is, all who strive for this, to see by faith and hope the God whom they do not see—dwell through hope in their tabernacles, that is, in the places of heaven from which the transgressing angels were cast out. These places may in a certain sense be called tabernacles, insofar as those angels themselves were there for a time [Col. 0906C].

And they tempted and provoked him. I have said that he led them into the mountain and cast out the nations from before them; yet they still tempted him by asking, not by believing. They tempted God, although he is exalted. This was because they did not keep his testimonies, that is, his commandments. They turned away from him and did not keep the covenant, that is, the promises they had made to him when they said, “Whatever the Lord commands us, we shall do.” Their fathers did the same—not Moses and Aaron and the other good men, but those of whom it was foretold: “A perverse and provoking generation.”

Thus I say that they did not keep the covenant because they turned into a crooked bow. A crooked bow is one that, when it is drawn so that something may be shot through it at the enemy, slackens, so that nothing is shot through it. Such were they: they were as though drawn taut when they promised that they would do everything commanded, but immediately became slack because they did nothing.

Or it may be understood in this way: If a bow could be so crooked that, when it ought to act on behalf of someone by shooting an arrow at the enemy, it instead acted against him by turning the arrow back upon him [Col. 0906D], those people would be comparable to such a bow. They ought to act for God by fulfilling his covenant, but instead acted against him by accepting another covenant opposed to him.

And they stirred him to anger by sacrificing, each one, on his hills, and provoked him to jealousy with their carved images. Each of them carved an idol for himself and chose some shady and pleasant hill where he might worship it and sacrifice to it.

In the same way, after we have already arrived through hope in the promised land—that is, in the heavenly homeland—we still tempt God by asking him for things that ought not to be asked. We provoke him because we do not keep his testimonies, that is, his commandments. We turn away from him by turning ourselves toward another. We do not keep the covenant, that is, the promise we made to him in baptism, where we established a kind of covenant with him, promising that we would believe in him and renounce the world with all its pomp [Col. 0907A]. Therefore I say that we do not keep the covenant because we turn into a crooked bow. For when we ought to act for God, we instead act against him. Or, although we are drawn taut like a bow by making many promises, we become slack in such a way that we do nothing.

And on the hills—that is, in the fear and exaltation of the mind—we stir him to anger because we are disobedient. Then each of us carves for himself something like an idol to worship: one chooses to serve Venus, another avarice, another this thing, another that. In this above all we provoke him to anger.

God heard and rejected them. They had indeed stirred God to anger on the hills and with their carved images, and had done one thing and another. God heard—that is, he recognized it—and rejected Israel, not the Israel that then existed, but the Israel that ought to have existed, because he delivered them into the power of their enemies. He reduced them greatly—that is, excessively—to nothing, so that they could resist no enemy.

Similarly, when we stir God to anger on the hills, that is, in the exaltation of the mind, because the soul speaks to God, God hears it and rejects us, though we ought to be Israel. He gives us into the power of our inner enemies and reduces us greatly to nothing, so that we are unable to resist any vices [Col. 0907B].

And he rejected the tabernacle. This was the tabernacle that was at Shiloh, when he permitted it to be captured by the foreigners and the ark that was in it to be carried away. I say “his tabernacle,” where he himself dwelt—not truly, since God does not dwell in temples made by human hands—but where he dwelt there in a certain figurative manner. He did this so that he might be among human beings, that is, for the sake of human beings.

He did this so that they might pay attention to the purpose for which the tabernacle had been made and to what the things in it signified spiritually, and so that they might prepare themselves to be the holy tabernacle of God. For God dwells worthily in holy people; hence the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are.” But because the people did not attend to this and did not make themselves a tabernacle for God, the Lord rightly rejected both the tabernacle and them.

That tabernacle signifies ecclesiastical institutions. Shiloh is interpreted as “shaking” or “removal.” And in Shiloh—that is, in those who tear themselves away and break themselves off from him—he rejects that tabernacle, that is, ecclesiastical institutions, insofar as he makes them useless to such people. I say “his tabernacle,” where he does not truly dwell, but dwells for the sake of human beings, as in the preceding sentence.

And he delivered up. He explains the rejection of the tabernacle, saying: The Lord delivered their strength—that is, that in which they trusted and by which they were victorious, namely, the ark of the covenant—into captivity, so that it might be carried away captive by the Philistines. And their beauty—that is, the same ark in which they took pride—he delivered into the hands, that is, into the power, of the hostile people.

Therefore the Lord immediately enclosed them, that is, permitted his people to be shut in and afflicted on every side by the sword of their enemies. And he seemed to reject the inheritance that ought to have been his when he permitted it to be trampled by everyone. For fire—that is, hostile fury—consumed the young men, that is, destroyed and carried away their warriors. Their maidens, led into captivity, were not lamented because of fear of the enemy; each person was afraid for himself.

Their priests also, Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, fell by the sword of the Philistines, for they were killed by them. When their father heard this, he fell from his seat upon the threshold and died with his neck broken. Such a great disaster overwhelmed them that their widows were not mourned according to funeral custom, because of fear of the enemies.

In the same way, if we do not attend to the ecclesiastical sacraments so as to prepare a worthy tabernacle for God, but instead break ourselves away from him, provoking him to anger on the hills and with carved images, he delivers our strength into captivity. That strength is faith and the other ecclesiastical institutions through which we ought to be strong and victorious over our enemies. He permits them to be taken captive—that is, taken away from us—by the devil and his ministers, through whom some are often led astray [Col. 0908A].

And he delivers our beauty—that is, those same things in which we ought to take delight—into the hands, that is, into the power, of the enemy, the devil. After his grace has thus abandoned us, he encloses us on every side, because temptations arise everywhere and various deceptions arise everywhere; and this occurs through the sword, that is, through the victorious devastation wrought by the enemy. He rejects us, who ought to have been his inheritance, because he permits us to be overcome by every kind of vice.

For the young men—that is, the licentious and irreligious—are consumed by the fire of incitements, or by the fury of God’s anger. Such were those of whom the Apostle says: “I see that some are walking disorderly among you.” And the maidens—that is, those barren in good works—are not lamented. For the priests, that is, the prelates, who ought to have compassion on them and mourn for them, have fallen by the inner sword, because inwardly they have been deprived of every virtue. And the widows—that is, the churches widowed by them—were not mourned, because no good person was left to mourn them. For “every head is sick, and every heart is sorrowful, from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, and there is no soundness in it.”

And he was awakened. No one would dare to say this about our Lord unless the Holy Spirit had announced such things about him. Nevertheless, it may be said of him by a certain comparison. He seems to sleep when he does not come to the aid of one who suffers as quickly as seems necessary to that person, just as at that time, when that people was being taken captive and enclosed in the manner described above, he did not come to their aid.

But he seemed to be awakened with a kind of fury and force when he delivered them with such power and majesty and struck their enemies so heavily. Therefore it says: “The Lord, previously as though sleeping, was awakened by wine, like a powerful man overcome with drink,” that is, he was awakened as if in fury, like one who is roused from the sleep caused by wine—not an ordinary person, but a powerful man overcome with wine, that is, well fed, of whom it is evident that he has drunk much and therefore rises with greater fury.

Similarly, the Lord seems to sleep with regard to us when he permits us to fall from vice into vice. But when, after we have nearly fallen into the depth of wickedness, he recalls us, he seems to be awakened.

And he struck. Truly the Lord was awakened in fury, because he struck the enemies of his people—and therefore his own enemies—the Philistines, with a shameful plague in their hinder parts, for mice gnawed their anuses. By this he gave them everlasting disgrace, because he never again exacted such vengeance upon any nation.

In the same way he strikes the persecutors and corrupters of his true people, that is, of the people of grace, in their hinder parts, because he gives them over to a reprobate mind, so that they place what is behind—things that ought rather to be regarded as refuse—before what is ahead, contrary to the Apostle who says: “Forgetting the things that are behind and reaching forward to the things that are before.” Thus he gives them over to everlasting disgrace, that is, to the eternal punishments of hell, which will be everlasting dishonor for them.

It should be known that when the Philistines had carried away the Lord’s ark captive from Shiloh, they placed it in their temple beside their idol Dagon. In the morning Dagon was found with his neck broken and his hands and feet cut off, lying upon the threshold of the temple. Those who, having received newness, still retain the old are compared with him. They do not yet wish to lay it aside completely; nevertheless, this benefits them nothing, because the oldness will be destroyed. “All things will pass away, but the word of the Lord remains forever.”

And he rejected—that is, he struck the enemies and, for the liberation of the people, rejected the tabernacle. He did not choose the tribe of Joseph, nor did he choose the tribe of Ephraim, which, according to human judgment, seemed to possess something of distinction, both because of the nobility of its lineage and because of the interpretation of its name. Joseph means “increase,” while Ephraim means “fruitfulness.” Yet there was no true increase or true fruitfulness in them. Rather, he chose the tribe of Judah, which nevertheless seemed to possess something in his sight because it was humble and lowly: Judah was the son of Zelpha, Leah’s handmaid. His name also signified this, since Judah is interpreted as “confession,” and confession pertains to humility.

The mystery, however, is this: God chose the weak and foolish things of the world in order to confound the strong and destroy the wise. It should also be known that God chose the tribe of Judah because of David, through whom he delivered his people from their enemies; and he chose David because of the true David.

God chose, I say, the tribe of Judah, that is, those who confess humbly. He then specifies what he understands by the tribe of Judah: he chose Mount Zion, that is, he chose those who are a mountain—firm in faith and exalted in virtues—and who are Zion, that is, despising present things and contemplating future things. He loves these people uniquely.

Here he seems to transfer himself entirely to allegory, thereby indicating that the preceding matters too should be understood allegorically. Nevertheless, we may also speak historically, since he chose Mount Zion, that is, Jerusalem, in which there was a hill called Zion.

And he built his sanctuary like that of the unicorn [Col. 0909B]. Historically, you may say that he built his temple as pure as the dwelling place of unicorns. The unicorn is an exceptionally chaste animal. Indeed, it is captured only by genuine virgins, because it comes to them, places its head in their lap, and falls asleep. It is said to have an exceedingly pure dwelling place.

Allegorically, however, you may say that he built his sanctuary—that is, his holy Church—like the sanctuary of unicorns: a sanctuary in which there are only unicorns, that is, those who in the present wish to be singular in hope, not multiple in actuality. The unicorn has one horn; and through that one horn what else is signified but the one thing mentioned above: “One thing I have asked from the Lord,” namely, one hope.

He built his sanctuary, I say, on a land that he founded forever, that is, only in those who have been well cultivated by the teaching of the commandments and founded eternally in his faith. Historically, this cannot be said of that land except insofar as it is understood according to what it signifies, or unless we take “forever,” as is often done, in a temporal sense [Col. 0909C].

And he chose David. He chose, I say, the tribe of Judah, and from that tribe he chose David his servant. He took him from the flocks of sheep, because he was transferred from the care of sheep to rule over human beings. The same thing is expressed in other words: he took him from the place that is “behind the ewes,” that is, he took him from the pastoral office.

He also chose the true David, his servant, with regard to his humanity, not with regard to his equality with the divinity. For it was truly said of him: “I have found David, the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart.”

And he took him—that is, he exalted him—transferring him from sheep to other sheep, that is, from the Jews to the gentiles. As it is written: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the gentiles.”

I say that he took him from that place which was “behind the ewes.” It is as though he were saying: He was not first transferred from sheep to sheep until he had produced many offspring among those earlier sheep—namely, others who would generate in faith and nourish with milk—which he had led before him like a shepherd.

For he had first chosen there the twelve Apostles, the other seventy-two, and many others, both directly and through them. Of these offspring it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep ascending from the washing, all of which bear twins, and none among them is barren.” We have already expounded this elsewhere.

To feed Jacob. For this purpose, I say, he chose David historically: to feed Jacob, that is, the new people who are truly his servant. Just as Esau signifies the earlier and old people, so Jacob signifies the later and new people. And because Israel comes from Jacob, so that just as he now sees by faith, he may then see by sight—and then he will truly be God’s inheritance—he adds: “And to feed Israel, his inheritance.”

For then he will truly feed them, when he is all in all. And he fed them in the innocence of his heart. That feeding was nothing other than that sweet and most health-giving teaching by which he taught them true innocence. True innocence is that which harms neither oneself nor another.

It can happen that someone harms no one externally and yet is not innocent in heart, because he often thinks evil even though he does not carry it out. And he led them from virtue to virtue, through the restoration of the understanding of his hands, that is, so that he might restore in them the understanding that his hand—that is, his power—had placed in the first parent when it set him amid an abundance of virtues.

Or, he led them from virtue to virtue through the understanding of his hands, that is, through his intelligible works. Those works are truly intelligible that are taught not only in words but also in deeds. He himself did this, because it was said of him: “The first account I composed concerning all that Jesus began to do and teach.” He did first, before he taught, and therefore his teaching was truly intelligible.

## ON PSALM LXXVIII

**A Psalm of Asaph**

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0910B] It is sung in the person of the Maccabees, who, under Antiochus Epiphanes, compelled by the greatest afflictions and with Matathias as their leader, undertook to defend their ancestral laws and walls. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Apostles concerning the passion of Christ. Alternatively, the penitent soul supplicates God against its most wicked neighbors, that is, the demons.

### EXPLANATION

This psalm, like Psalm seventy-three, is full of lamentation. It mourns future times as though they were past and, moved by devotion, asks Christ the Lord to come to the aid of the people destined to be grievously afflicted because of the hardness of their hearts. Asaph speaks throughout the psalm under the figure of believing peoples.

In the first part, he recounts how much the Jewish people suffered in the time of Antiochus, as the Book of the Maccabees indicates. In the second, he asks the Lord to pour out his anger upon the powerful enemies mentioned above and to deign to be merciful toward the sins of his servants. In the third, in the spirit of prophecy, he asks that the people be avenged—not from a desire for destruction, but from a zeal for correction.

Arnobius composed the following argument for this psalm: “Psalm seventy-eight, following the summit of its predecessor, Psalm seventy-seven, pours forth David’s lament together with prayer. While its historical account explains the slaughter of the Philistines in the past, its prophecy recalls that of Nebuchadnezzar in the future” [Col. 0910C].

### COMMENTARY

“God, the nations have come into your inheritance.” A psalm of Asaph. In this psalm Asaph—whether the prophet or some perfect person from the earlier people—laments the destruction of the city and temple by the nations, transferring to himself those who would exist when these events took place.

In prayers, people customarily say to God what he does when he takes vengeance, and then add a petition that he may now have mercy and spare. The same thing is done here: things are spoken by the one who foretells them as though they were being foretold by those to whom they happened. The prayer itself is also prophecy. What appeared in the spirit as future is spoken of as though it were past.

It begins in this way: “O God, the nations have come”—that is, they will come—“into your inheritance.”

If, in this prophecy, that earlier people is understood, it seems surprising that it should be called God’s inheritance, since, by killing the cornerstone, they rejected him who rose, ascended, and sat at the right hand of God the Father; and, despite seeing so many signs and miracles, they did not wish to believe in him.

Yet this is not surprising, because, as the Apostle says, “God has not rejected his people.” If he rejected the chaff, he did not reject the grain. From that people came the virgin Mary, blessed Joseph her guardian, Joseph of Arimathea, the holy Apostles, and many others. With respect to these grains he says: “The nations have come into your inheritance.”

This inheritance was not left to him by a father who died; rather, the Son himself wonderfully acquired it through his death. The nations came into this inheritance not by believing but by persecuting, intending to destroy it and to eradicate its name entirely from the earth.

It follows:

“They polluted your holy temple.” This is not a temple constructed of marble or built of wood, but your holy temple of which it is said: “The holy temple of God, which you are.” They polluted this temple when they were able to lead some people astray through torments or flatteries.

Observe that he always adds “your,” both to “inheritance” and to “temple,” so that he may contrast the enemies’ assault with the benevolence of the one speaking and of those on whose behalf he speaks.

“And they made Jerusalem”—not the earthly Jerusalem, but the one above, that is, the Church, which is our mother—“a place for guarding apples,” that is, they made it like a place for guarding apples.

A place for guarding apples is the hut in a garden where the peasant lies at night, or where, lying down, he guards his apples until they ripen. Once the apples have been gathered, he leaves it deserted. Similarly, once the spirits of the holy Apostles and the other holy martyrs have been gathered from the Lord’s garden into the heavenly Jerusalem, the Lord’s garden itself—the Church—remained like a deserted and desolate place, as though it had been a table laden with many pleasant and sweet apples [Col. 0911B].

“They placed the corpses.” It is as though he were saying: Once the spirits had been gathered above, what did they do with the bodies? They placed the corpses—that is, the slain bodies of your servants—outside, to become food for the birds of heaven.

He says the same thing in other words: “They gave the flesh of your saints as food to the beasts of the earth.” This may be understood literally.

It may also be understood allegorically in this way: “They placed the corpses”—that is, they gave the bodies of your saints, through many tortures, as food for the birds of heaven. This does not mean that the persecutors intended it, but that by divine providence it happened that the birds of heaven—that is, those whose minds are in heaven—were refreshed by them, observing their patience and courage. Thus they were not so much terrified by their punishment as stirred by their glory to imitate them.

But they simply gave the flesh of your saints as food to the beasts of the earth, because both the persecutors and the other earthly, beast-like people noticed nothing beyond the slain bodies themselves and obtained a kind of nourishment from them, as though wiping away filth.

[Col. 0911C] “They poured out their blood.” I have said that they gave the flesh of the saints to the beasts of the earth; and they did this not in one place only, but in many, because they poured out their blood like water, abundantly and without restraint, around Jerusalem—that is, throughout the whole gentile world that surrounded them on every side.

“And there was no one to bury them.” The fear of the persecutors was so great that no one dared to bury the bodies of the saints except secretly.

Or, there was no one to bury such great patience in the saints, that is, to store it in the heart.

Or otherwise: “They poured out the blood of the saints like water,” that is, for the washing of many, as water is customarily poured out for washing. The persecutors did not intend this, but by divine providence it happened that the outpouring of the saints’ blood served for the cleansing of many, namely, of those who imitated them. Yet none of those who poured it out buried it—that is, none stored in his heart such patience in the saints [Col. 0911D].

And therefore, as if he were saying, “We have become a reproach”: we have become so worthless that they now held us up to our neighbors as a reproach. By “neighbors” understand either others of the same people or any persecutors from neighboring nations. They are called bad neighbors because they tortured them. Indeed, someone is sufficiently a neighbor to another if he takes out his eye.

“Mockery and derision to those who are around us.” This may refer to distant nations if by “neighbors” you previously understood nearby nations. But if you understood “neighbors” to mean only those of the same people, then here understand every nation surrounding them.

“Mockery” refers specifically to the contempt expressed by wrinkling the nose; “derision” refers to words of ridicule.

“How long, O Lord?” It is as though he were saying: You seem, O Lord, to be angry with us because we are tortured and despised in this way. But how long will you be angry—that is, how long will you exercise this anger against us? Will it be forever?

“And will your jealousy,” that is, your indignation, which you now display against us, “burn like fire”—the kind of fire that normally burns, namely, fire that incinerates—or like fire that purifies? Certainly, he means, like purifying fire, not incinerating fire.

Your anger and jealousy will remain as long as is necessary for the punishment of our wickedness and the exacting of purity. That is, you permit us to be tortured and mocked by persecutors until the iniquities we have committed are fully punished and purity is perfected in us, so that our soul no longer despises the law of its God and does not perish by committing fornication with him.

“Pour out your anger upon the nations.” This may be understood either in a good or in a bad sense.

If it is understood in a bad sense, we shall say that it is spoken not as a wish but as a prophecy, just as things are often said not by way of command but by way of announcement, as in, “Gird yourself with your sword,” and similar expressions.

It is as though he were saying: “Do not be angry with us forever, O Lord; but pour out your anger,” that is, send your complete anger, both here and in the future, upon the nations that have deserved it, that is, upon those that did not wish to know your name. And not only upon the lesser peoples, but also upon the kingdoms, that is, upon the rulers of those nations who did not invoke your name.

This seems contrary to the Gospel saying: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows; but the servant who does not know his master’s will and does things deserving of blows shall be beaten with few.” Here, however, it seems that God’s anger will be greater against the nations that do not know him.

But there is no contradiction. The Gospel speaks only of servants, and there is a great difference between servants who do not know their master’s will yet live in his household and family, and enemies who refuse to know his will, do not invoke him, and even oppose him in his servants [Col. 0912B].

“For they have devoured Jacob.” You ought to pour out your anger upon the nations for this reason: they have devoured Jacob, that is, they took great pleasure in leading astray and persecuting the one whom you esteem so highly—namely, Jacob, that is, the new and first people.

“And they have desolated his place,” whether Jerusalem, because they killed all who were there, or his place, that is, they desolated the stability of faith [Col. 0912C]. His place was truly desolated when some people were led astray.

Observe that, although he could have used many other names that might perhaps offend the hearer, he chose the name of so great a patriarch, loved by God and increased by God the Lord, with considerable rhetorical skill, so as thereby to arouse greater hatred against the persecutors and goodwill in the hearer.

“Do not remember our iniquities.” It is as though he were saying: Pour out your anger upon the enemies, but show mercy to us; do not remember our iniquities, and so forth.
