As we said above, the preceding verse, “Pour out your anger,” may be understood in a good sense, so that it reads: “Pour out your anger, O Lord, upon the nations,” that is, make known to the nations that do not know you the complete anger of the future judgment, and upon the kingdoms that have not invoked your name, so that at least they may be converted through fear of that anger.

You need to do this for them because they have devoured Jacob, and so forth. In this way: “Do not remember our iniquities.” For if you did not convert them by displaying your anger to them, on seeing their persecution and corruption, [we would fear] that you remembered our iniquities.

I mean our ancient iniquities, that is, those long past, although we do not cease from them even for a single hour; or our iniquities, that is, those we inherited from our fathers. For these, correction is no longer owed to us, but condemnation, unless the mercy of your grace is present.

For it is written: “The soul that sins, it shall die.” And: “I will visit the sins of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation.” It is therefore clear that if any son imitates his father’s iniquity, the sins of the fathers will also rebound upon him. Some people say that certain original sins remain even after baptism.

They say that both original and preceding actual sins are forgiven in baptism, provided that the promises made there are kept. But if someone there merely gave words and then returns to his vomit, he will be guilty of the things that had been forgiven [Col. 0913A].

“Do not remember,” I say, “our iniquities, but let your ancient mercies quickly anticipate us,” that is, come before our fall—before we are led astray—or before the future judgment.

Therefore I say that your mercies should come to our aid, because we despair of our merits. For we have become poor, that is, exceedingly insufficient in ourselves, both in soul and in body, because “we are flesh, and a spirit that goes and does not return,” as was said above.

Therefore, O God, help us to accomplish the good. You, I say, are our savior, that is, we are saved by your grace alone, not by our merits. When he says “Help,” he is not ungrateful for grace, nor does he remove free will. For he possesses something to receive from free will, and therefore asks to be helped.

“Help us,” I say, “and deliver us, O Lord, from our past sins,” for the glory of your name; and be propitious toward our future sins, not because of our merits, but for the glorification of your name.

[Col. 0913B] “Lest they should say among the nations.” I ask you to be propitious toward our sins so that this may not happen: that some among the nations, that is, among our persecutors, should insult us by saying, “Where is their God?”

For if you were not propitious toward our sins and we were led astray because of them, then surely the persecutors would say either that our God, in whom we hope, does not exist or that he does not care for us.

But lest this happen, may the vengeance for the blood—that is, vengeance taken on account of the blood of your servants that was poured out—carried out among the nations, that is, among the persecuting peoples, become known before our eyes. This may refer either to vengeance already accomplished in reality, with respect to their inner blindness, or to vengeance accomplished only in the divine plan, with respect to future condemnation.

That vengeance, I say, which is not visible to their eyes, according to the saying: “The wicked man does not know that he is being punished until he openly pays the penalty unwillingly, though he committed the deed willingly,” may become known before our inner eyes, that is, may be revealed to us, so that we may be all the stronger and more steadfast.

Here it is spoken not as a wish but as a prophecy.

It may also be spoken as a good wish in this way: “Let the vengeance for the blood of your servants that was poured out, carried out among the nations, become known to us”—so that we may quickly see that judgment has been carried out upon our persecutors in such a way that those who were enemies become friends and blasphemers become praisers.

“And let the groaning of the prisoners enter,” that is, let it appear to have entered and to have been received, “into your sight.” The prisoners are those who recognize that they have been placed in the fetters of mortality.

Or the groaning of the prisoners means those who have been entangled in and cling to the fetters of your commandments. For God’s commandments are called fetters. Hence Solomon says: “Put your foot into the fetter,” that is, apply your affection to God’s commandments, so that you may fulfill them not under compulsion but from the affection of the heart.

“According to the greatness of your arm.” It is as though he were saying: I say that the groaning of the prisoners should enter before you, so that you may also do this: possess not only those who have been put to death but also their sons, that is, their imitators [Col. 0913D].

These are the holy martyrs, who are truly said to have been put to death because they not only mortified themselves inwardly but were also put to death outwardly by their enemies.

And you, O Lord, possess those sons according to the greatness of your arm, that is, according to the greatness of your power. Let the punishments suffered by the martyrs not frighten them so much as their crowns encourage them to imitate them.

“And repay our neighbors”—that is, our persecutors—“with the reproach with which they reproached you, O Lord, through us.” Just as they wished to destroy your name in us, so may they themselves be destroyed, both here and in the future.

“Repay them,” I say, “with reproach in their bosom,” or secretly, because they are unaware both that they are being blinded here and that they will finally be condemned forever; or “in their bosom,” that is, firmly, as something possessed firmly is said to be held in one’s bosom.

“And sevenfold,” that is, both in body and in soul. The number seven consists of three and four. Three pertains to the soul because of the soul’s three principal powers: irascibility, concupiscibility, and rationality. Four pertains to the body because of the four elements of which it is composed.

It may also be understood in a good sense as follows: “Repay our neighbors with the reproach with which they reproached you,” that is, with the thing by which they wished to erase your name in us. Repay it to our persecutors in their bosom, that is, in their soul, and sevenfold, that is, through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

Repay it to them in such a way that, once their hearts have been enlightened by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, they themselves may suffer from others the same reproach with which they reproached you in us.

“But we are your people.” Repay that reproach to them, while we are the people whom they reproached and led astray, the people subject to you, and the sheep of your pasture, that is, those whom you have nourished with spiritual teachings and sacred institutions.

We, I say, do not merely say that we will confess, as though this were uncertain; rather, I say with certainty that we will confess to you. We will not cease from your praise throughout this present age, and finally we shall truly and eternally proclaim your praise from generation to generation—that is, in the future generation, which will be an unfailing generation.

## ON PSALM LXXIX

**For the end; for those who will be changed; a testimony of Asaph; a psalm.**

### ARGUMENT
And here the prayers of the Maccabees resound, asking that the Lord not withdraw his customary benefits. Alternatively, it is the voice of the apostles speaking from the Church to the Lord.

## EXPLANATION

Since the first words of the title are already familiar, it remains for us to inquire what “a testimony of Asaph” signifies. This Asaph, formerly fearful and formerly anxious, who in the preceding psalms pleaded for the sins of the Synagogue, is now filled with such confidence that, with things changed for the better, he offers a testimony of conduct. For he speaks of the Savior’s first coming, by which he brought corrupted humanity to the gifts of salvation and made firm by its root the vine of his power that had been transferred from Egypt. This is what is meant by “a testimony for those who will be changed”: this Asaph, whom the title announced, changed. In the first section he implores the Lord’s coming. In the second he testifies how the vine, which is the Church, has been spread throughout the whole world. In the third, by the benefit of the Lord’s Incarnation, he implores that the Church be visited through the likeness of a vine, and asks that he himself may cling to the Lord.

## COMMENTARY

“Pay attention, you who rule Israel.” This psalm is sung concerning the coming of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and concerning his vine; Asaph sings it after being enlightened and corrected. Its title is: “For the end, for those who will be changed: a testimony of Asaph, a psalm.” How will they be changed? Certainly, for the better. And it says: “A testimony to Asaph himself,” with “attributed” understood. A testimony, certainly, of truth, a good testimony. This testimony, finally, confesses Christ and the vine—that is, the head and the body, the king and the people, the shepherd and the flock—and the entire mystery of all the Scriptures, namely, Christ and the Church; and it concludes, “for the Assyrians.” The Assyrians are interpreted as “those who direct.”

For Asaph sings this psalm—that is, this testimony of Jesus—for all those who will be changed for the better, but especially for those who direct themselves badly, who wish to establish their own righteousness and not be subject to the righteousness of God. This is so that they may no longer be a “perverse and provoking generation,” because they have not directed themselves, but may direct themselves onto the way of eternal salvation. Let us therefore hear what the spirit of prophecy conveys in this passage, speaking thus through Asaph:

“Pay attention, you who rule Israel.” It is as though he says: You by whose will all things are created and governed, but especially you who rule Israel—that is, those who are men who now see you, God, by faith and will finally see you in appearance—you, I say, who were previously withdrawn when you lay hidden beneath the cloud of flesh, pay attention; that is, make yourself attentive to us by revealing to us your divine power and the light of your grace.

You, I say, who lead Joseph through the desert of this life—that is, the people signified by Joseph—feeding them with spiritual ordinances and mysteries as though they were sheep, pay attention. He is invoked to come, awaited to come, desired to come; therefore, may he find those who direct themselves. Joseph himself, however, is the sheep.

Understand by Joseph the faithful from the Gentiles, according to the interpretation of the name; by Israel, however, understand the faithful from the Jews. Joseph, when the interpretation of his name is considered, signifies “increase.” That grain indeed fell into the earth and was put to death so that it might rise multiplied—that is, so that the people of God might increase. Yet we must observe what happened in Joseph himself. He was sold by his brothers, dishonored by his own people, and exalted among foreigners. Let us understand in whose flock we ought to be, together with those who now direct themselves, so that the stone rejected by the builders may become the cornerstone, holding together two walls coming from opposite directions yet meeting in the corner. It follows:

“You who sit above the cherubim.” “Cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” But the one who has charity has the fullness of knowledge, because charity is the fullness of the law. Therefore, lest we be scattered among many things, lest we wander among many things, if we wish to have the fullness of knowledge, let us have charity. For what does the one who knows charity not know? Certainly, he knows everything, because he knows God. For it is written: “God is charity.”

It is also to say: You who sit above the cherubim—that is, you who sit in those who are cherubim, as above; for the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom—manifest yourself. It is as though he says: We have gone astray because we did not recognize you as shepherd; therefore, manifest yourself to us, so that we may no longer go astray. “Manifest yourself,” I say, so that you may be present—that is, so that you may appear to Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh.

These names seem to signify something greater, one than another, yet they signify the same people, namely, those who have been enlightened and corrected. They are interpreted as follows: Ephraim means “fruitfulness,” Benjamin “son of the right hand,” and Manasseh “forgetfulness.” And truly, the Lord is manifested to those who bear fruit in good works, who are sons of the right hand—that is, who devote themselves to better things—and who forget what lies behind while stretching forward toward what lies ahead, because they are known by him more and more.

“Rouse your power, Lord, and come.” It is as though he says: And in order that you may be manifested, Lord, rouse your power, which previously seemed asleep when you were betrayed by a disciple, scourged, crucified, and, while hanging on the cross, were told: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.”

For then you seemed to have no power, because your persecutor prevailed over you, as you had prefigured in Jacob’s struggle with the angel. The angel was overcome by Jacob, but because he wished it; so you too were overcome by the Jewish people, because you were killed, but because you wished it. Hence you also said: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above.”

Thus Jacob held the defeated angel and asked to be blessed by him, and the angel blessed him; yet in a certain manner he also cursed him, because he touched the breadth of his thigh and made him limp. So too the Jewish people held you defeated in part and received blessing among the faithful as a whole, but lameness among the unbelieving as a whole. Let us now return to the literal sense.

“Rouse your power.” It is as though he says: You died through weakness; rise again in power. This must be referred to knowledge: come into our awareness in such a way that you may make us believers saved in you. For everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.

“God, turn us.” It is as though he says: And in order that you may save us, O God—not only of human beings but also of the heavenly powers—turn toward us, who were previously turned away, and turn us toward yourself. And in order that you may turn us, show us your face, which you concealed beneath the cloud of flesh, because you yourself were not seen when you went before us on the cross, as has now been accomplished.

Asaph did not recognize the Lord present on earth, performing miracles and dying. But after the Lord rose from the dead and ascended, he then recognized him, and, pierced in heart, spoke this testimony concerning him. How, then, will those to whom he speaks this testimony—that is, the Assyrians—recognize him? Because he will show them his face, and they will be saved. It is as though he says: You concealed your face, and we fell ill; show your face, and we shall be saved.

“Lord, God of the powers.” “Show your face,” I say. For you seem almost angry so long as you delay showing it. But, O Lord God even of the heavenly powers, how long will you be angry over prayer—that is, how long will this anger of yours remain over prayer, since it causes the prayer of your servant to have no effect?

It is as though he says: If you were angry with your enemies, are you still angry with your servants? You have turned us, and we have recognized you, and are you still angry? Certainly you are angry, but not as a judge ruling; rather, as a father correcting.

Certainly you are angry, because it is written: “My son, when you approach the service of your father, stand in fear and trembling, and prepare your mind for temptation.” Let us not think that God’s anger has passed because he has turned toward us. It has passed in the sense that he will not punish us forever. Yet he scourges and does not spare, because he corrects every son whom he receives. If, therefore, you shrink from being scourged, how do you wish to be received? For he scourges everyone whom he receives, since he did not spare even his own Son—and in this consists his anger.

As for the prayer of which he speaks, understand it as the prayer immediately preceding this, namely, “Show your face,” and similar prayers in the psalm. Anger seems to prevail over this prayer so long as we are scourged and afflicted by our enemies. When he says, “How long will you be angry over the prayer of your servant?” understand it as though he says: Certainly, how long will it be necessary for us?

“You will feed us with the bread of tears.” It is as though he says: Truly you are angry with us, for you will feed us with the bread of tears—that is, with tears that restore us. He expresses the same thing through another comparison: “And you will give us drink in tears.”

He calls the bread of tears and the drink of tears the tribulations and scourges that the saints endure in this life, which is full of sorrows. In these the Lord gives them bread and drink—that is, complete refreshment—so that they are not merely afflicted but also glory in their tribulations, knowing that “tribulation produces perseverance, perseverance produces proven character,” and so forth.

And he gives these things to them in measure—that is, according to what their weakness can bear—so that they may be instructed, not crushed. He does this so that they may not fail but advance, because, as the Apostle says: “God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure.”

“You have made us a reproach.” In this way, I say, you will feed and give us drink with tears, because you have made us a reproach to our neighbors—that is, you have made us people whom our neighbors from the same people would contradict.

“And our enemies”—that is, persecutors from the Gentiles—“mocked us,” saying: “Who are these people who worship a dead man and believe in one who was crucified?” This truly happened. For after the Lord rose and ascended, a new life and a true resurrection were preached—a credible reality, if miracles gave faith in what seemed incredible.

Many contradicted it, but the one who contradicted was overcome, and from being a contradictor was made faithful. Nevertheless, there was much flame—that is, much tribulation. The holy martyrs were fed with the bread of tears and given drink in tears, but in measure: according to what each person could bear, so that the crown of joys might follow in proportion to the tribulations.

“God of the powers, turn us.” You have made us, I say, a reproach and an object of mockery. But lest we be turned away from you because of this, O God of the powers, turn toward us and turn us, and so forth. This repetition arises not from the necessity of the narrator but from the affection of one who prays.

“You transferred a vine from Egypt.” Until now he has dealt with the coming of the Savior, namely, with the way in which he comes daily into human knowledge. Now, however, he deals with his vine, and he begins from the beginning. “For the first people,” as Augustine says, “are the Jews, the beginning of this vine.”

It is as though he says: Turn us, I say, O God, and join better outcomes to good beginnings. For you began well, because you transferred your vine. Through physical fathers and also through certain spiritual fathers, you transferred it from Egypt, where it was oppressed by servitude. You drove out from before it the nations that had occupied the land of promise, and you planted it there.

“You were its guide on the journey.” The preceding verse takes the matter only literally, whereas this one applies to both senses, including the mystery. Just as he provided that physical people with guidance by the light at night and the shelter of a cloud by day, so too he provides spiritual guidance to this vine, illuminating it with his spiritual gifts in the ignorance of this life and overshadowing it from the incitements of vices through his protection within us—that is, through the mystery of his Incarnation.

He himself became the way, of whom he said: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” For unless he himself were its way, what follows could not occur: namely, that he should fill the whole earth. Here he passes entirely to the mystery when he says:

“And you planted its roots.” He calls the patriarchs the roots of this vine. He planted them through faith in their spiritual descendants and, in some cases, in their physical descendants as well. In this way he filled the earth, not through physical offspring but through spiritual offspring.

“And its shade”—that is, the figurative utterances made concerning this vine—“covered the mountains.” Here he calls the prophets, eminent in virtues, mountains. They were covered—that is, they became obscure and clouded—because they spoke many things concerning this vine figuratively, that is, mystically.

“And its branches the cedars.” He calls the lesser prophets “branches,” but “cedars” the exalted and powerful people of the world. This means that not only the greater prophets presided over this vine, but also the branches—that is, the lesser prophets—covered the cedars. They grew so far over the shadows of the cedars—that is, the exalted things of the world—that they covered them, meaning humbled and enveloped them, and made the cedars of the world into God’s cedars, as happened also in Paul and Dionysius.

Moreover, this same vine extended its shoots to the sea. He calls those people shoots to whom the Lord himself said: “I am the vine; you are the shoots”—that is, the holy apostles, who proceeded principally from the vine itself, because they were chosen by the Lord. These shoots extended to the sea—that is, to the bitterness of the Gentiles—because their sound went out into the whole earth.

“And its branches to the river.” He calls those regenerated in faith through the shoots “branches.” A branch grows from a shoot, and these branches extended to the river, because through their example and admonition even those who were a river—those who flowed in the most bitter and swelling waves of this age—became branches.

And in this way, through the prophets, through the shoots, and through the branches, what happened was that this vine filled the whole earth.

“Why have you destroyed its hedge?” Here Asaph laments the bodily destruction of that people whom we said was the beginning of the vine, but he does so without abandoning hope, because he speaks, as was stated in the title, about direction. If such treatment was appropriate for the straw, it should not have been applied in the same way to the grain.

It is as though he says: Since, O Lord, you brought that vine out of Egypt and planted it, why then did you destroy its hedge? The enlightened and corrected Asaph does not say this as one who is ignorant. He knew that the hedge had to be destroyed, because the Lord had threatened it through Isaiah, saying: “I will destroy its hedge.” And he adds the reason: “For I expected it to produce grapes, and it produced sour grapes. I expected it to produce justice, and it produced iniquity.”

But he says this for the sake of the Assyrians, so that they may consider both this destruction and its cause, and thus beware lest they suffer anything similar. The cause of the destruction was that the vine became proud against its cultivator: it killed the servants sent to it to collect the tenants’ due, and it cast out and killed the heir himself. Yet, though he was cast out, he possessed more, because a partial blindness happened to Israel so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter.

Understand the hedge of the vine as its fortification, namely, the kingdom and the priesthood, and especially the Lord’s protection, by which they were safer than by anything else. “Why,” I say, “did you destroy its hedge, and why do all who pass along the road gather its grapes?” This is said by way of comparison. Just as, if a vineyard were situated beside a road and its hedge had been thrown down, it would be harvested by any passersby, so they harvested that vine after its fortification had been destroyed—that is, Antiochus and many others divided it into various parts, and finally the Roman rulers did so.

“Those who pass along the road” can be understood in two ways: either as those who do not recognize the true way, namely Christ, or as those who deviate from the true way of ruling, namely those who rule temporally.

“The boar from the forest ravaged it.” It is as though he says: It was not harvested by just any passersby, but by those whom they themselves considered especially unclean, because the boar ravaged it. Nothing was more unclean or contrary to the Jews than a pig; the boar, moreover, is a pig.

Understand by the boar the Gentile Vespasian, because there is no greater uncleanness than that of the Gentiles, who placed the creature before the Creator. This means: The boar, coming from the forest—that is, from the Gentile world, which was uncultivated because it had received neither the law nor the prophets—ravaged it, meaning that he drove that vine outside its boundaries. Those who were not killed either perished from hunger or were led away captive.

“And the solitary one, the wild beast, grazed upon it.” Understand this as Titus, the son of Vespasian; “solitary one” denotes Titus as the individual, while “wild beast” means cruel and proud. He grazed upon it, meaning that he had that vine consumed, because he especially stripped and devastated it. For when his father Vespasian returned to Rome, Titus remained at the siege, and finally captured the city and utterly destroyed it.

“God of the powers.” It is as though he says: If such treatment was appropriate for the straw, let it not, Lord, be applied in the same way to the grain. But, O God of the powers, turn toward us, so that you may turn us.

You who previously seemed to have despised this vine in those physical fathers, look upon it with merciful affection from the heaven of heavens—that is, through the Lord’s human being—by sending to it the one whom you are going to send. And see it—that is, hold it before your eyes—so that you may have full mercy on it.

And thus visit this vine through your grace, as though it were weak and unable to rise by itself. Perfect it in merit and number; do not establish another, because, as it were, he says: The true seed of Abraham is there. There is that seed in which all nations will be blessed, that is, the root into which the wild olive is grafted. Perfect it, I say, since it does not have its existence from itself but from you, because your right hand planted it.

And thus, I say, perfect it so that it may be founded upon the Son of Man, that is, Christ. For the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation apart from the one that has been laid, which is Christ.” I speak of the Son of Man whom you especially confirmed for yourself, that is, for your honor, among all others. You placed Adam in an abundance of virtues, but you did not confirm him, because he could fall.

“Burned with fire.” Truly you will perfect it, because those burned with fire and dug under will perish in it at the rebuke of your face. The face of God the Father is Christ himself, “the radiance and figure of his substance,” as the Apostle says. The holy preachers also display his face.

But what does this face of God rebuke except sins? Through its rebuke our sins will perish. All sins that we willingly commit arise either from an evil love or from an evil fear; conversely, every good work is done either from a good love or from a good fear.

Suppose that someone wants to induce us to give false testimony against our neighbor, or to do something similar, and promises us many things. If we take pleasure in them and consent, behold, we sin through evil love—that is, inflamed by perverse desire.

But if the grace of God then inspires us and we consider what he proposed for us to imitate, namely: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?”—behold, through this Lord’s rebuke, the effect of evil love, that is, sin, perishes in us.

Then, seeing his promises despised, that person may perhaps turn to threats and threaten us not merely with expulsion but with death itself. If, terrified at that point, we consent to him, behold, humbled by evil fear, we sin.

But if divine grace then strengthens us inwardly and we hold in mind what he proposed for us to imitate, namely: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul,” and we resist and do not sin, then it is better for another person’s iniquity to destroy our flesh than for our injustice to destroy our soul.

However much the world promises us when we are unjust, God will give the just far more when he says: “Come, you blessed of my Father,” and so forth. However much the world threatens us who are just, God threatens the unjust far more, because he will say: “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire.”

This is what he means by “burned with fire”: sins committed in the burning heat of perverse desire; and “dug under”: those sins committed through the humiliation of evil fear. They are called “dug under” because a wall that is dug under is humbled. Both kinds of sin, I say, will perish through the rebuke made by your face, O God. This is the opinion of blessed Augustine and many others.

Cassiodorus, however, understands “burned with fire” in the same way, namely, as those sins committed through the burning heat of evil love; but he calls “dug under” all those sins that are committed through ambush or deceit, as though they had been dug in.

“Let your hand be upon it.” Since your rebuke is so beneficial, let your hand therefore be upon it, O Lord—that is, let your correction always remain upon the man who is to be established, so that one perfect man may be established, namely, Christ, the head and the body.

“Upon the man,” I say, “of your right hand,” that is, in whom your right hand—that is, your power—will appear. He determines which man he means by adding: “And upon the Son of Man.” For all who bear the image of the Son of Man are, together with him, as one Son of Man.

You confirmed this Son of Man principally in the head and secondarily in the members, for yourself—that is, for your honor.

Or it may be understood otherwise, as though he says: In order that the vine planted by your right hand may be perfected, and in order that those burned with fire and dug under may perish in it, let your hand, O Lord, be upon the man of your right hand—that is, upon everyone who exercises whatever strength he possesses on the right hand and not on the left.

And especially let your hand be upon the Son of Man, who is their head. For the Lord did not give him the Spirit by measure. I speak of the Son of Man whom you confirmed for yourself, as stated above.

“And we shall not depart from you.” Let your hand, I say, be upon the man of your right hand and upon the Son of Man. And thus may we, who previously departed from you when we worshiped you for the sake of something else, no longer depart from you, worshiping for your sake; for you will give life through spiritual gifts to us who were inwardly dead in sins.

Therefore, from now on we shall invoke your name alone and no other. In order that this may happen, Lord God of the powers, turn toward us and turn us, and so forth.

# ON PSALM LXXX

“For the end, for the winepresses, a psalm of Asaph himself, for the fifth day of the week.”

## ARGUMENT

Foretelling the people’s return from Babylon, he summons everyone to give thanks. He has prefixed “winepresses” in the title because either the afflicted people themselves or their enemies have been crushed by them. Alternatively, it is the voice of the apostles concerning Pentecost.

Arnobius likewise says concerning Psalm Seventy-Nine: “The vine is restored”; and concerning Psalm Eighty, “the winepresses are treated”: “Rejoice in God, because his vine has risen again.” For the one whom the unbelieving people destroyed has risen; they destroyed the very one who said: “I am the true vine.”

## EXPLANATION

“The fifth day of the week” is the fifth day from the Sabbath, which the Gentiles call Thursday and we call the fifth feria. On that day God said: “Let the waters bring forth reptiles with living souls, and winged creatures flying beneath the firmament of heaven,” mystically signifying that men of diverse virtue would be born from the waters of baptism.

The intention of this title, therefore, is as follows: “For the end” designates the Lord Christ; “for the winepresses,” the Church tested by persecutions; “Asaph,” the congregation; “the fifth day of the week,” baptism. From this it follows that the psalm will speak in the Lord’s Church about the congregation reborn.

Here Asaph certainly speaks historically to the Jews, but he is better understood spiritually by the Christian people. In the first part of the psalm Asaph speaks to the faithful, so that through various musical instruments they may sound praises to the Lord for benefits often received. In the second, the words are those of the Lord threatening that they should not worship idols but adore him alone, since he is accustomed to reward. In the third, Asaph speaks again, reproving the faithless for having proved deceitful, although the Lord’s gifts had been abundantly bestowed upon them.

## COMMENTARY

“Rejoice in God our helper.” The title is as follows: “For the end, for the winepresses, on the fifth day of the week, a psalm of Asaph himself.” It is expounded in this way.

These words refer to the end. They constitute a psalm sung to Asaph himself—that is, to the Lord’s congregation—for the winepresses, on the fifth day of the week.

There are two things in a winepress: weight and pressure. From the pressure two things proceed: oil and dregs. The oil is stored in the storeroom, while the dregs are trampled in the streets.

On the fifth day of the week God created all the reptiles of the waters, because on the fifth day he said: “Let the waters bring forth every reptile with living souls.” Through the reptiles created in the waters are signified all those regenerated through the water of baptism.

Some of these live worthily according to the sacrament of baptism; these are signified by the oil. Others live unworthily according to the sacrament of baptism; these are understood through the dregs.

Together these constitute the Lord’s congregation, to which the prophet sings this psalm concerning the winepresses on the fifth day of the week—that is, concerning pressure that must be intended and desired, because all who wish to live devoutly in Christ must suffer persecution.

I speak of pressure that separates the things signified by the things created on the fifth day of the week, namely, the very people to whom these words are sung. Those who live worthily according to the sacrament of baptism do not evade being afflicted here. They are not only inwardly afflicted, denying themselves, but are also tested “at the water of contradiction,” as the psalm says—that is, they are afflicted outwardly.

Those who live unworthily according to the sacrament of baptism, however, prefer to enjoy themselves here rather than suffer tribulation. Thus they are separated by pressure in the present; in the future they will be completely separated, when the oil will be drained into the Lord’s storeroom, while the dregs will be cast out to be trampled eternally.

Behold, we have heard the light of the psalm. Let us enter, hear, rejoice, fear, flee, and desire, because these things are found in the psalm.

The prophet first addresses the oil, saying:

“Rejoice in God.” It is as though he says: Around you are those who rejoice in the world, their deceiver and deserter; some even rejoice in their belly as their god. But you, O truly Lord’s congregation, rejoice in God—that is, give thanks to God with every joy, not to the world. I speak of God as “our helper.”

When he says “our helper,” he neither shows ingratitude toward grace nor removes freedom of choice. “Sing for joy also to God,” who is truly the God of Jacob, the later-born—that is, the God of the people of grace.

It is as though he says: What you can express, proclaim aloud; what you cannot express, sing for joy. For jubilus is such great joy of mind that words are insufficient to express it.

See how clearly he invites them to the pressure about which the title speaks when he says: “Rejoice in God; sing for joy to God.” For whoever truly rejoices in God does not shrink from tribulation; rather, he desires it, so that he may reach the one in whom he rejoices.

“Take up the psalm.” It is as though he says: And in order that you may truly rejoice and sing for joy to God, take up the psalm and give the tambourine.

The Apostle, speaking somewhere as though reproving and grieving, says that no one shared with him in the matter of giving and receiving. What it means to share in giving and receiving, however, he explains clearly elsewhere when he says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your physical things?” Certainly not.

Thus it is also said here: “Take up the psalm and give the tambourine”—that is, receive spiritual things and give physical things. For the psalm, since it comes from above, pertains to spiritual things; the tambourine, because it is made from dried hide, signifies physical things.

This means: If you are eager to receive spiritual things, be devoted in distributing physical things. It is as though he says: Receive our voice and our exhortation; accept our holy teaching, and give your hands—that is, perform good works.

You ought to do this because “the psaltery joined with the lyre is pleasant.” These are two different instruments: the psaltery sounds from above, while the lyre sounds from below. The teaching of God’s word comes from above because it is heavenly.

Thus the meaning is as though he says: If you expect such things from us, do not be sluggish in performing our physical works; answer the word of God through your deeds. For the psaltery joined with the lyre is pleasant—that is, it produces a sweet melody for God.

“Blow the trumpet at the new moon.” The Israelite people were accustomed to celebrate a festival and blow trumpets at the new moon. *Neon* means “new,” while *mene* means “moon.”

Our mortal and failing life, renewed by grace, is signified by the renewed moon. This means: In order that you may rejoice in God worthily, blow the trumpet at the new moon—that is, preach the new life more openly, clearly, and confidently, without fearing the noise of the old life.

He determines which new moon he means by adding: “Blow the trumpet on the notable day of your solemnity.” The notable day is the entire time of grace, which is also the solemnity of supreme joy: the old order’s arrangement, the new restoration, and eternal happiness.

“For it is a commandment in Israel.” Therefore you ought to blow the trumpet at the new moon, because this is the commandment of Israel. Just as the commandment was given carnally to physical Israel, so it was given spiritually to spiritual Israel; and if it was given to the former, much more to the latter.

That commandment must not be neglected, because when it is neglected, judgment is assigned to the God of Jacob. For if anyone neglects it, it follows that the God of Jacob judges him—that is, condemns him.

Since physical Jacob was condemned for neglecting a physical commandment, much more will the spiritual person be condemned if he neglects a spiritual commandment. Therefore this commandment is a judgment belonging to the God of Jacob, as are all the others, because “all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law.” Truly judgment belongs to him, because he says of himself: “I came into the world for judgment.”

“He established it as a testimony in Joseph.” He adds this in order to specify that he is not dealing here with the physical commandment given to that people, but saying: The same commandment that was given to Israel, the Lord established as a testimony in Joseph.

It is a testimony of condemnation when neglected, but a testimony of liberation when observed. By Joseph, whose name is interpreted as “increase,” understand all those who were earlier increased through faith, whoever they may be, whether Jews or Gentiles.

When this Joseph went out from the land of Egypt, he heard a language that he did not know. Just as that Apostle, who was descended from Joseph and his other brothers, after he went out from the land of Egypt and crossed the Red Sea heard a language that he did not know because he received the law, so this spiritual Joseph, after passing out from the land of Egypt—that is, from the darkness of sins—through the water of baptism reddened by Christ’s blood, heard a language that he did not know.

That language was the commandments of newness, so that he might know where he ought now to have his heart: not in earthly things but in heavenly things.

Through that language, the one who established the testimony turned Joseph’s back away from burdens; that is, he raised him up, bent beneath sin as though beneath many burdens. After showing from what burdens he had turned away, he says: “For his hands served at the basket.”

A basket is a vessel for dung. Therefore, by the basket are understood carnal desires. This means: “His hands served at the basket”—that is, his deeds were devoted to the fulfillment of carnal desires and carnal longings.

This truly was servitude, because “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.” From these burdens—that is, from these dead works—the one who says, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you,” delivered him.

He himself, I say, spoke to him in this way:

In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you. Let each person examine his conscience, whether he has devoutly crossed the Red Sea, whether with faith he has heard the tongue that he did not know. Let him consider his tribulation, because it is truly a great tribulation to be weighed down by the burden of sins, since the relieved conscience rejoices. Behold, you have been baptized, and your conscience, which yesterday was weighed down, rejoices today, and you have been delivered in tribulation. Remember your tribulation before you approached baptism: what anxieties you carried in your heart, what fasts you promised, what tears and inward, devout, dedicated prayers you offered. Behold, all your enemies have been slain—that is, all your sins have been wiped away. And so, because in tribulation you called upon me, I delivered you. And after delivering you, I heard you in the hidden place of the storm—that is, not in a storm at sea, but in the storm of the heart.

Yet it is necessary that, after someone has been heard in the hidden place of the storm, he be tested at the water of contradiction. Therefore he adds: “I tested you at the water of contradiction.” For after you have believed, crossed the Red Sea, and been heard in the hidden place of the storm, and after you have begun to take the path of God, behold, the water of contradiction still remains. For then many rise up to harass you, many to call you away—now with threats, now with flatteries. But do not be ashamed to proclaim what you can defend. Do not be ashamed even among blasphemers to proclaim what you have believed. For if you have been heard in the hidden place of the storm, “with the heart one believes unto righteousness.” But if you are tested at the water of contradiction, “with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.”

This water, however, has been almost dried up in our time. In the time of the holy apostles and of the other founders of the Church, it flowed most abundantly. When Samson was asking the Philistines for a wife—that is, when Christ, the Sun of them—for this is what Samson means—through his preachers sought for himself a bride, the Church, from the nations, then a roaring lion met him. But it became in his hands like a young goat—that is, like a weak sinner—and afterward honey was found in the mouth of the dead lion, because the prince of the nations, after first contradicting and roaring, once converted, brought forth laws and institutions for the Christian name, which he had previously attacked.

[Col. 0922D]

Israel. What has been said from the beginning of the psalm up to this point has concerned the oil. What follows, however, is more to be feared and avoided, because it concerns the lees; nevertheless, it must be heard. Thus, let the one who seems to be oil rejoice, while the one who is still in danger should beware lest he become lees. And so the passage is connected. To the oil he said: “In tribulation you called upon me,” and so forth. But to the lees he says the following: “My people, hear.”

He calls them his people, not because they obeyed his commands, but because they had been initiated into his sacrament of baptism and into the other sacraments. He determines which people he means by saying: “Israel”—seeing God by faith, even if not yet by hope—“hear me, and I will testify against you,” that is, I bring or have others as witnesses to this matter: namely, that if you hear me—that is, if you obey my commands and attend to them diligently—“there will be no newly made god in you,” that is, in your heart, because you will recognize me, the Word coeternal and consubstantial with the Father. For man is recent, whereas the Word was in the beginning with God, coeternal with him. Therefore you will not imagine a false god. For if you imagine a false god, you will never worship a fabricated god. This is what follows: “Nor shall you worship a foreign god.”

This must be understood both of inward and outward idols. Different people fashioned different gods for themselves, both outwardly and inwardly. But although there was variety in their error, there was nevertheless identity in their vanity. Samson signified this when he tied many little foxes together by their tails and fastened burning torches to their tails, so that they might burn the crops of the Philistines.

[Col. 0923B]

Foxes are heretics, as though lurking in caves and lying in wait like foxes. Concerning these foxes it is said in the Song of Songs: “Catch for us the little foxes.” For the little fox—that is, the heretic—is caught when he is convicted of error.

Samson, whose name means “their sun”—that is, Christ—tied these little foxes together at the tail, because they disagree in their opinions but agree at the end, that is, in vanity. Although there is variety in error, there is identity in vanity. He also applied fire—that is, he added the error by which they could deceive others—so that they might burn the crops; that is, their works might be destroyed—not the crops of friends, but of the Philistines, that is, of enemies, whom he permitted them to lead away and associate with themselves.

“For I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” Therefore, if you hear me, there will be no strange god in you, because I am—that is, because “I am” properly belongs to me. “Will be” or “will become” does not apply, but “I am” expresses an eternal and unchangeable state. Why, then—as if he were saying—do you wish to worship what does not exist? For concerning every god who departs it can be said that he does not exist, because he existed when he did not exist, and will exist when he will not exist.

Therefore you shall not worship a foreign god, because I am the Lord your God by redemption, your God by creation. And—as if he were saying—because I am above all things. Yet what have I bestowed upon you temporally? Much indeed: “For I brought you out of the land of Egypt.” All of us who believe have been brought out of the land of Egypt—that is, from the darkness of ignorance—and have crossed the Red Sea and heard the tongue that we did not know. Let us therefore not be ungrateful to God, nor forget the abiding God in order to fabricate a recent one. The text continues:

“Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it.” It is as if he were saying: Your heart suffers narrowness because of the false god; but because I am your Lord and God, open wide your mouth, by believing, loving, preaching, and confessing, and I will fill it. Inwardly I will fill the mouth with faith and love; outwardly, with confession and preaching.

[Col. 0923D]

“And my people did not hear.” It is as if he were saying: I called them in this way and admonished them in this way, yet my people, who ought to have been mine, did not hear my voice—that is, they did not obey my holy commands. Behold how the lees flow. And therefore I say that they did not hear, because they did not attend. Who? To whom? Israel, to me.

O unhappy soul, why do you not attend to him by whom you were created, recalled, cleansed from sins, and brought into form?

“And I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart.” Behold the fitting punishment, behold the divine vengeance. They, I say, did not hear me, and I repaid them what was just: namely, I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart. That is, they were handed over to a reprobate mind, so that they might do what is not fitting. Therefore they will go—that is, they will fall and drift—in their own inventions; they will not stand in mine.

“If my people had heard me.” Now, because they did not hear me, I dismissed them. But if my people, who ought to have been mine, had heard me—what it means to hear him he explains, saying:

“If Israel had walked in my ways”—that is, if he had delighted in my commands—“I would have humbled their enemies,” both inwardly and outwardly, perhaps to be regarded as nothing.

This “perhaps” is not used doubtfully but threateningly, with reference to those who showed that they doubted his power. This is demonstrated by the result, because they did not hear his voice. In the same way, when threatening a rebellious servant, we say: “Perhaps it will yet appear that I am your lord.”

And what he had said, “I would have humbled their enemies,” he repeats equivalently, making it clearer: “And I would have laid my hand upon those who troubled them.” He calls those who troubled them the same people whom he had previously called their enemies. To lay his hand upon them means the same as to humble them.

“The enemies of the Lord.” Behold, he returns to prophecy, as if saying: The Lord indeed spoke in this way and in that way to that people, but his speech did not take hold in them. For although they ought to have been friends, they became enemies; they proved worse than all other enemies. Other enemies promised nothing, but these lied, because they promised and deceived in everything. It is better not to promise than to deceive.

And because they did this, “their time will be forever.” There is an ellipsis when he says, “their time.” He wishes it to be understood that the time of their condemnation and destruction will be forever—that is, they will be condemned eternally.

Some books read, “in the age,” according to which the passage is understood as follows: “Because the enemies of the Lord lied to him, therefore their time”—what they themselves desire, that is, their delight—“will be for me in this present age.” Hence it follows that they will soon be condemned forever. And deservedly, because the one whom they deceived bestowed upon them every human kindness and mercy.

“And he fed them with the fat of wheat,” that is, with the innermost marrow of wheat, because he refreshed them with the mystery of his Incarnation and with the other inward mysteries of holy teaching. “And he filled them with honey flowing from the rock.” The rock, however, was Christ. By the honey, which holds the chief place in sweetness, understand the knowledge of the eternal Word.

The meaning is: He instructed them to satiety—that is, fully—with knowledge even of the Word, which surpasses all knowledge.

# ON PSALM LXXXI

A Psalm of Asaph.

## ARGUMENT

Those who turn aside into wickedness are censured, as are those who pretend to be impartial judges while disputes are in progress. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church concerning the Jews.

## EXPLANATION

Asaph signifies the Synagogue, which was deemed worthy to behold the Lord and Savior even in his bodily presence. Throughout the psalm, Asaph speaks against the Jews concerning the coming of Christ.

In the first part he admonishes them that God has stood in their midst and that therefore they ought not to enter into partnership with sinners. In the second, he warns them to understand that he himself is Christ, who in the assumption of flesh seemed to be poor and needy. In the third, he says that they were honored so that they might become sons of God, but that they themselves through their own fault fell into the snares of death.

## COMMENTARY

“God stood in the synagogue. A Psalm of Asaph.”

The faithful from the former people, foreseeing through the Spirit the time of visitation and of the Lord’s Incarnation, exhort their descendants in this psalm not to judge unjustly and to pervert the heir’s case, as they did to the servants sent beforehand to the vineyard.

They clearly show them in this psalm, in its first verse, the time of visitation and of the Lord’s Incarnation, because standing, sitting, going, and such things are positions only of bodily beings, not of incorporeal ones.

The meaning is: “The God of gods”—that is, through whom all those who become gods not by nature but by God’s grace are deified—“stood.” He himself, invisible in his own nature, became visible in what is ours. “He stood”—for “he will stand”—“in the synagogue.”

He mentions the synagogue because he was born from that people. From that people came David; from David, Mary; from Mary, Christ.

And he rightly says, “He stood,” because he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. Yet he will not stand idly—as if he were saying—for he himself, standing in the midst, that is, openly, fulfills the saying: “After this he was seen on earth and lived among human beings.”

Or “in the midst” means in public, because he came not only for the salvation of the Jews—although they alone presumed upon grace—but also for the salvation of everyone.

God, I say, being in the midst, “judges among the gods,” that is, distinguishes those who made themselves gods, accepting some and rejecting others.

He himself, I say, speaks to them in this way:

“How long will you judge unjustly?” It is as if he were saying: If you have judged unjustly up to the coming of him who is the light of the heart, will you continue to judge even now?

And again: I gave the law, but you resisted fiercely. I sent servants to the vineyard; you treated some with insults, expelled others, and killed others. Will you also kill the heir?

He said this to the leaders: You who are subject to them, how long, by remaining silent and not resisting, will you take on the faces of sinners? That is, do you wish to imitate those sinful leaders as though they were innocent?

For whoever wishes to resemble someone seeks, as it were, to put on that person’s face. Therefore he says this to the people, because in the Gospel it is said that the leaders held the people in their power. Hence it is clear that the people could have prevented Christ’s death. And whoever does not prevent what he can prevent truly gives consent.

“Judge for the needy and the orphan.”

You leaders ought not to judge wickedly against Christ, nor should you, the lesser members, consent. For did he not hunger for us and thirst for us as one needy? And he who was in heaven without a mother—did he not wish for us on earth to be without a father, as an orphan?

And did he not call and continue to call to you: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart”? And did not he who was rich in himself become poor so that he might enrich us by his poverty?

Therefore judge, you leaders, for the needy and the orphan—that is, honor him because for your sake he became needy and orphaned, and justify him because for your sake he became humble and poor: that is, believe him righteous and proclaim him righteous.

Do not instead act for yourselves alone, because you are rich and proud. Do this, I say, you leaders. But you, the lesser members, rescue what belongs to him who became poor for your sake, and free him who became needy for your sake from the hand of the sinful ruler.

For, as has been said, they feared the people. Thus those who consented by remaining silent and not resisting deserve such severe condemnation that the same fate will come upon those who perpetrated the wicked deed itself.

“They did not know, nor did they understand.”

This is Asaph’s voice. It is as if he were saying: The Lord spoke in this way both to the leaders and to the lesser members, but his speech did not take hold in them, because they did not know—that is, they were ignorant. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

“Nor did they understand,” that is, they did not proceed intelligently into his works. For if they had understood, they would not have asked that Barabbas be released and Christ crucified.

Therefore they did not understand because “they walk in darkness,” that is, because they delight in their place, their nation, and other earthly things, which are the reason they are dark—that is, ignorant.

They did not understand, I say, but nevertheless they could have understood, because such manifest signs were given at his Passion that it was sufficiently clear that he was God.

Since this was future when these words were spoken, he also expresses it in the future tense: “All the foundations of the earth will be shaken.”

When the whole earth was shaken by an earthquake, its foundations too were moved.

Or otherwise: They indeed will not understand, but they could have done so, because others farther away will understand. For “all the foundations of the earth”—that is, everything upon which earthly people are founded, such as dignities, riches, powers, and the like—“will be shaken,” that is, many will despise them. When the new life and resurrection were preached, earthly happiness too was despised.

Or otherwise: They walk in darkness because they prefer to lose innocence rather than their nation and homeland. Yet this will profit them nothing, because all the foundations of that land will be shaken—that is, taken away from them by the Roman rulers.

“I said: You are gods.”

Again this is the voice of the Lord addressing them. The passage is connected as follows: God, I say, in the midst judges among the gods, saying to them:

I alone, as one powerful and suitable for this, said to you that you are gods—that is, you can be gods if you do what I command you. And all of you, without exception, can be sons of the Most High: sons by adoption and gods by grace.

“But you will die like human beings, and like one of the princes you will fall.”

It is as if he were saying: I promised you heavenly things and called you to the heights, but you descend to the lowest places. You, the lesser members, will die in your soul through the deception of the leaders, just as human beings—that is, the first parents—died through the deception of the devil. And you, the leaders, will fall through your first exaltation, as one of the princes—that is, of the angels who are princes over human beings and rule them—fell through his own exaltation when he said: “I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High.”

“Rise, God.”

Behold, Asaph speaks in his own person. It is as if he were saying: They prefer to be brought down to the depths rather than called to the heights; but you, God, do what belongs to you. Die, namely, among the hands of those who judge unjustly, and rise as God to judge.

Die in weakness, indeed, and rise in power; “judge the earth,” that is, condemn those earthly people, not merely by scattering them outwardly, but by blinding them inwardly.

And truly you will do this when, after rejecting them, you will inherit—that is, obtain an inheritance—among all the nations. “A partial hardening has happened to Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter.”

Or otherwise: “Rise, God, and judge that land which swelled up against you when it condemned and crucified you.” That is, humble it in part, so that the one who previously wished to go before may follow.

And truly this will happen, because through those people, humbled and scattered throughout the whole world for preaching, you will inherit among all the nations. For “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

# ON PSALM LXXXII

A Song of the Psalm of Asaph.

## ARGUMENT

He prays against the faithlessness of the nations, which, envying the glory of the Maccabees, attempted to destroy their devout undertaking together with the annihilation of the whole people. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church to the Lord concerning the Jews and concerning human vices.

## EXPLANATION

A “song of the psalm” occurs when, while the organ leads the melody, the voice of the mouth is heard following it and answering it, imitating the modes of the psalter with vocal melodies.

Since a song mystically demonstrates contemplation of divine wisdom, whereas a psalm, made with the hands, signifies the perfection of works, it is rightly called a “song of the psalm” when knowledge and teaching are joined to the accomplishment of good works. This agrees with what was said: “You desired wisdom; keep the commandments, and God will grant it to you.”

The example of this was wonderfully evident in the centurion Cornelius. What the “psalm of a song” is and what it signifies has already been stated in the thirty-ninth psalm.

Asaph, who had already foretold much above concerning the Lord’s Incarnation, will now speak in the first section about his second coming. He asks that, just as at the end of the age his enemies are to be raised up exceedingly through the Antichrist, so his judgment may come quickly, lest the prolonged license of that most grievous enemy be able to devastate the whole Church.

In the second section he asks that vengeance be taken upon those who are indicated through certain likenesses of their names, with the desire for correction, not through an impulse of cursing.

## COMMENTARY

“God, who will be like you? Do not be silent, nor be restrained, God.”

The “song”—that is, this rejoicing—is Asaph’s song of the psalm, that is, of praise, because in this psalm, in this praise—which is truly praise of God—the destruction of the wicked army accomplished through him is commemorated.

He sings—that is, he rejoices. For there were not lacking among that people those who understood, possessing the faith that was afterward revealed. Foreseeing through the Spirit that the one who had first come secretly in weakness—because he wished to be likened to many while being judged, so much so that he was even counted among the wicked—and who endured many insults and left us an example of patience, would finally come so openly that no one, even among the devout, would be likened to him, they rejoiced in anticipation.

They foresaw that he would then judge us and free us from all insults. Foreseeing these things, I say, they rejoiced, exhorted us toward the same hope, and sang, saying:

O God who came secretly, you were even counted among the wicked. But when you come openly, who, even among the devout, will be like you? Certainly no one, because then even the angels will tremble.

Therefore, do not then be silent, nor be restrained—you who will truly appear as God, just as you acted earlier when you seemed weak. For as long as he was placed in weakness, he indeed gave commands but remained silent concerning vengeance. He also restrained the power of his divinity when he placed before his enemies the flesh against which they might rage.

For unless he restrains himself, how could he be seized, held, and crucified? When he answered them, “I am he,” those who were seeking him went backward and fell. But when he comes openly, then certainly he will not be silent regarding vengeance, nor will his power be restrained.

“For behold, your enemies have sounded forth, and those who hate you have raised their head. They have plotted wickedly against your people and have devised plans against your holy ones.”

Because he had prefaced two things, he also repeats two things. It is as if he were saying: Do not then be silent, because your enemies earlier did not remain silent, but sounded forth against you and yours. Therefore he says “sounded forth” rather than “remained silent,” because one is not said to be silent except after speaking. But what is uttered irrationally should not be called speech, but sound.

And do not then be restrained, because those who hate you have raised their head—that is, they have lifted themselves up with excessive pride against you and yours. Here “head” means the mind.

But if we wish to refer this to the final times, we can understand the Antichrist by the head. Concerning him the Apostle says: “Who is exalted above everything that is called God or worshiped.”

And behold—as if he were saying—how they sounded forth and how they raised their head: namely, because they “plotted wickedly,” that is, they devised a wicked plan against your people. And they took counsel for this reason: because they had first devised plans against your holy ones.

But what could they accomplish against those who knew how to say: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” Nothing, certainly.

“They said, ‘Come.’”

They plotted wickedly, I say, and after their plot they said to one another: “Come, let us destroy them as a nation through contempt.” It is as if he were saying: Let us make them vile and abominable, and let us destroy them so completely that the name Israel, according to faith and not according to the flesh—that is, the Christian name—will no longer be remembered.

“For they devised unanimously.”

Therefore they all said this, because they had first devised it unanimously—that is, all of them had thought this. And because they had all thought it, they all together established a covenant—that is, an agreement—the one already mentioned: “Come, let us destroy him,” and so forth.

A covenant is not called only that which has force when its witnesses are dead; it can also mean any agreement that people make with one another.

They established a covenant, I say, against you and yours. But who did this? The camp—that is, the forces—of the Edomites, and the Ishmaelites with those who follow.

Behold the gathering of the wicked army that persecutes God’s people. Let us therefore examine, through the interpretations of their names, how great is the wickedness of each.

The Edomites are interpreted as “blood-red” or “earthly.” By the Edomites, therefore, are understood those who are born not from God but from blood and the will of the flesh; that is, those who are born not spiritually but carnally and are given over to the desires of the flesh and to earthly longing.

The Ishmaelites are interpreted as “obedient to themselves.” And who can more rightly be called obedient to themselves than those who hasten to fulfill whatever the carnal mind suggests?

The text continues:

“Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, and foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre.”

Moab is interpreted as “from the father,” because, through an abuse of the law, he was born from a grandfather and a sister. He is also said to mean “one who abuses the law.” Therefore, through him are understood those who abuse the law, both natural and written. It is clear that they are truly opposed to those who use the law properly.

The Hagarenes are interpreted as “proselytes” or “strangers.” Proselytes were those who converted from paganism to the rites of the Jews. By these are understood those who, under the pretext of doing harm and with a foreign and alien mind, live among God’s people.

Gebal is interpreted as “vain valley.” A valley is proud humility. For some outwardly pretend humility while carrying pride in their hearts. In them wickedness is manifold, because simulated wickedness is double wickedness.

Ammon is interpreted as “a people of sorrow” or “a turbulent people.” Therefore by Ammon are understood those who grieve excessively over the loss of temporal things or are excessively inflated by their acquisition.

Amalek is interpreted as “licking the earth.” Therefore Amalek signifies those who desire and love earthly things.

He used “foreigners” for Philistines or allophyles, who are interpreted as “those falling through drink.” By these are understood those whom the drunkenness of carnal pleasure has completely stupefied and caused to exceed themselves.

Tyre is called *Sor* in Hebrew, and *Sor* is interpreted as “tribulation” or “anguish.” Tyre can therefore signify those of whom the Apostle says: “Tribulation and anguish upon every soul of the human being who works evil.”

The inhabitants of Tyre are those who are diligent and persevering in works of tribulation and anguish.

“For Assur also came with them.”

Therefore all these established a covenant against you, Lord, because they had an evil prince. For Assur came with them as their leader.

By Assur we can understand the people who persecuted the Israelite people, according to the saying: “Assur, the rod of my fury.” But he himself did not understand.

The devil is understood here, the one who works in the sons of distrust, as in his own vessels, to attack the people of God.

Some say that Assur is interpreted as “afflicting” or “exalted.” We have not heard the authority for this interpretation. The text continues:

“And all those whom Assur brought became an aid to the sons of Lot.”

For they are the instruments of the sons of Lot, that is, of the sons of decline. Lot is interpreted as “declining.” And a decline from the truth generated, as it were, apostate angels, who use wicked human beings like weapons to trouble God’s people bodily, while they themselves persecute them spiritually.

“Do to them as to Midian.”

Asaph says this not by wishing but by prophesying, not by praying but by foretelling. It is as if he were saying: All those mentioned have come against you and your people; but you, Lord, do to them as you did to Midian: just as Midian was destroyed by carnal Israel, so may they be destroyed and perish by spiritual Israel, that is, by your people, as Jabin and Sisera perished.

Midian is interpreted as “declining judgment.” Those who decline judgment are those who do not attend to the force of reason. Therefore they act irrationally, as do those who place the creature before the Creator and earthly things before eternal things. Such people are deservedly destroyed.

Sisera was a certain prince of the Midianites. While fleeing and hiding in the shelter of a certain woman, he fell asleep. She secretly approached him with a tent peg and a hammer, fastened him to the ground, and killed him.

Sisera is interpreted as “exclusion of joy.” By him are understood those who seek joy in earthly things and exclude true joy from themselves.

Jabin too, a prince of the Midianites, was killed in the torrent of Kishon. Jabin is interpreted as “wise.” But who is wise? The one of whom the Apostle says: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe?” That is, the one who is wise in his own generation, who should rather be called foolish, because “the wisdom of the flesh is death.”

By the torrent, dryness is understood, because a torrent properly means a place where water once flowed but is now dry. Kishon is interpreted as “their hardness”; hardness follows dryness.

Those who are carnally wise—that is, dry, because they are not watered by the teaching of God—and therefore hard, that is, without mercy, perish in this dryness and hardness.

The text continues:

“They perished at Endor.”

Historically, Endor is a certain spring where many of Midian perished; it is interpreted as “the spring of generation.” By Endor, therefore, those are signified who remain in the spring of generation—that is, in their carnal birth—and do not approach the grace of rebirth. All such people deservedly perish.

The text continues:

“They became”—that is, those perishing at Endor, along with the others mentioned above—“like dung of the earth,” that is, like dung that rots in the earth.

For they rotted like beasts in their own dung. Or they became like dung of the earth—that is, like the earth’s decay—because nothing but carnal fecundity proceeded from them. They raised buildings, gathered great riches, and strove to do similar things that belong only to the flesh.

Or otherwise: “They became like dung of good soil,” that is, they made good soil fertile, because for their condemnation the good became more diligent and more cautious. According to the saying: “The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner.”

“Set their princes like Oreb and Zeb, and Zebee and Salmana.”

Because they became dung of the earth, therefore, Lord, set—that is, depose—their princes as you deposed Oreb, Zeb, Zebee, and Salmana.

Oreb is interpreted as “dryness.” Therefore by Oreb are understood the dry: those barren in good works, without the sprinkling of affection and charity.

Zeb is interpreted as “wolf.” By the wolf are understood the rapacious, who, as the Apostle says, will not possess the kingdom of God.

Zebee is interpreted as “the wolf’s victim.” These are those in whom the devil takes the greatest delight and who are food for the serpent. For it was said to the serpent: “You shall eat earth.”

Salmana is interpreted as “the shadow of commotion.” These are those who sometimes seem to be under a certain shelter and to cease from vices, but immediately fall back into them, because they are as unstable as a shadow moved by the wind. For they believe for a time, and in the time of temptation they withdraw.

“All their princes who said: ‘Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.’”

I say this so that you may depose their princes, and also set them all like a wheel. This is what he says:

“All their princes”—namely, those of the groups mentioned above—“who said,” that is, who dared to say: “Let us possess the sanctuary of God”—that is, let us take as an inheritance the people of God, whom God makes holy for his inheritance; let us draw that very people away and associate it with ourselves, so that we may cultivate it as though it were ours through our teachings.

All of them, I say, my God, “set like a wheel and like stubble before the face of the wind.”

A wheel rises from behind and is pressed down toward the front. So here too he says: “Set them like a wheel,” that is, let them grow in earthly things, which are called what is behind, so that the very growth may be their downfall and their failure in what is ahead, that is, in eternal things. For “the prosperity of fools will destroy them.”

Stubble, too, because it is light and dry, is easily lifted by the wind. Thus here too he speaks not by wishing but by prophesying: let them be “like stubble before the face of the wind,” that is, let them easily be carried about by every wind of doctrine and be unstable in every temptation.

“Like a fire that burns the forest, and like a flame that burns the mountains, so you will pursue them in your storm, and in your anger you will trouble them.”

It is as if he were saying: Do these things to them in the present; but in the future you will pursue them in your storm and trouble them in your anger.

By “storm” he means that great force of judgment which in that great threshing will separate grain from chaff and sheep from goats.

“Anger” is the reason for vengeance. Although it may appear as anger to those who suffer, he himself will not become angry, because it is said of him: “You, Lord of hosts, judge all things with tranquility.”

You will pursue and trouble them in this way, that is, with such powerful force as belongs to the mighty fire that burns the forest and to the flame that burns the mountains.

Where fire has greater material, as in a forest, it is more powerful. Likewise, a flame has greater force in elevated places where the wind prevails.

Or otherwise: You will pursue them and trouble them as powerfully as the fire—that is, your fury—deservedly ought to trouble them, burning—that is, punishing—the forest in them, meaning barrenness, for wooded places are barren; and as the flame—that is, your anger—burns in them the mountains of pride.

The meaning is: You will punish them as severely as those deserve to be punished who are empty of every righteousness, signified by the forest, and filled with every pride, signified by the mountains.

“Fill their faces with disgrace, and they will seek your name, Lord.”

I say that in the future you will pursue and trouble them. But for some who wish to turn back, fill their faces with disgrace—that is, infamy. Make them recognize how infamous their sins have made them before you, so that they may repent.

And truly you will do this, because, converted to you, those who previously sought their own name will seek your name, for their own sake and not for anything else.

But those who—as if he were saying—do not wish this, let them finally be ashamed, truly saying: “We foolishly considered their life madness,” and so forth.

“And let them be troubled with an everlasting disturbance,” by a strict sentence, with a disturbance continuing forever—that is, eternally. In that disturbance let them be confounded, that is, recognize themselves as deserving of confusion, and yet perish in that same confusion.

They will repent, but fruitlessly. Therefore—as if he were saying—let these things happen to them, so that those who now refuse to know may at least then recognize that this name, “Lord,” properly belongs to you alone.

For in you alone is true lordship, because you do not need a servant, as the Psalmist testifies, saying: “You have no need of my goods.”

And let them also recognize that you alone are the Most High, that is, the Most Powerful, throughout the whole earth, both in condemning and in saving. For you are no less powerful in the condemnation of the wicked than in the rewarding of the good.

# ON PSALM LXXXIII

“For the end, for the winepresses, for the sons of Korah: a psalm.”

## ARGUMENT

He foretells that those who returned from Babylon would go around all the places, recall the ancient solemnity, and scarcely at last be satisfied by contemplating the places desired for so many years. Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ concerning the Church.

## EXPLANATION
Three psalms are entitled “For the winepresses,” that is, for the sufferings of the holy Church: the eighth, the eightieth, and the eighty-third. In these, the number eight and the number eighty [Col. 0930D] signify the hope of the future resurrection together with the ten of eternal life, which will receive the Church after its pressures, as a wine cellar receives it after the winepress.
