This is that most blessed end which is inserted into all the headings “for the winepresses.” The fact that the eighty-third is the last psalm designated “for the winepresses” shows that, in the vision of the Holy Trinity, the resurrection of the Church is consecrated, when “the God of gods was seen in Zion.”

The sons of Korah are the sons of the cross, as was said above; or, as Arnobius explains, when in the preceding psalm they have been confounded and have experienced what those were like who, wishing to occupy the sanctuary of God, caused weariness of charity and generated obstacles to the other virtues, then, while the Lord reigns in us, we who were sons of Korah the transgressor—this evil father having been swallowed up by the earth—are made sons of God. And those who formerly thought to bear a fire alien to God, the fire of lust and avarice, now kindled with the fire of divine love, say: “How lovely are your tabernacles [Col. 0931A], O Lord of hosts!” Arnobius’s interpretation seems to be supported by the fact that, in the first, second, and third places where the sons of Korah are mentioned, the interpretation is attached at the same time. At the third place, moreover, as though the sons of Korah had been corrected by a more careful examination, it is written: “For those who will be changed, for the sons of Korah, for understanding.”

At the beginning of the psalm, the sons of Korah show their own immeasurable longing for the Church. In the second manner, they declare blessed the one to whom the Lord grants assistance and enables to attain the grace of confession. In the third, they say that it is far better to dwell as an outcast in the house of the Lord than to enter the tabernacles of sinners together with whatever honors of the world.

## Commentary

“How beloved are your tabernacles.” A psalm “for the winepresses, for the sons of Korah.”

This psalm is entitled “for the winepresses”; but since nothing follows in the psalm concerning a winepress, a vat, or any of the other visible instruments of [Col. 0931B] winepresses, the Spirit of God wishes us to seek and understand other winepresses. Let us therefore recall what happens in visible winepresses, so that we may recognize how the same thing occurs in spiritual winepresses, that is, in the churches of God.

The grape hangs on the vine, and the olive on the tree; winepresses are usually prepared for these two fruits. While the grape hangs on the vine and the olive on the tree, they enjoy the free air. Before the pressing, the grape is not wine, nor the olive oil. So it is with human beings whom God predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, who was supremely a great cluster pressed out in his passion.

These people, therefore, before they approach the service of God, enjoy in this age a pleasurable freedom, like a grape in the free air while it hangs on the vine. But since it is written, “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and trembling and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation,” whoever approaches the service of God should recognize that he has come to the winepresses. For he is afflicted, crushed, compressed, and stripped of the coverings of carnal desires, like wine separated from the [Col. 0931C] grape-skins.

But since this happens only through pressure, the Church of the present age is called a winepress. “For the sons of Korah” is added in the title because those who are in the winepresses are sons of Korah. For Korah is interpreted as “bald.” Christ is called bald because he was crucified at the place of Calvary; and the sons of Christ are called imitators of his passion. Therefore the winepresses are those of Christians.

In the winepresses, that is, established amid pressures, we are afflicted and crushed for this purpose: that we may forget the love of worldly things, lay aside the love of earthly possessions, and attend to our pilgrimage, tribulation, temptation, and manifold labor. We then begin to seek the rest that does not belong to this life, that is, rest without end and without labor.

Established amid pressures, therefore, let us utter this voice and send our longing ahead, saying:

“How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord. My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.”

“Tabernacle” [Col. 0931D] sometimes means the present Church, and properly so, because in it one serves for a time; sometimes it is also used for the heavenly court, where one serves and dwells without end, as here. The meaning is: O Lord, even of the heavenly powers—or of the powers, that is, of the armies acting by force—how beloved are your heavenly tabernacles! That is: how sweet and how delightful they are!

The one speaking here was already in certain tabernacles of the Lord, where there were tribulation, distress, and pressure. He desired and sighed for those tabernacles where there is no pressure, and in a certain way, through carnal longing, he was dissolving into them. Therefore it follows: “My soul longs, and in longing languishes away from itself,” so that it may advance into you and reach the courts of the Lord, the courts where there is no pressure.

For the grape also languishes away from itself in the winepress, becoming wine; from the winepress it goes to the vat, and from the vat to the storeroom, where it is preserved in great quiet. Here it is desired, there it is received; here it is sighed for, there it rejoices; here there is groaning, there joy.

[Col. 0932A] And just as, while the grape is in the winepress, one must fear that it may be eaten by wild beasts or birds, so the one speaking here was in sadness and great fear, saying: “My soul longs and languishes.” He did not yet possess what he desired, but nevertheless he was not without joy. He rejoiced in hope, although not yet in reality. As the Apostle says: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, awaiting with all patience.” What is delayed can indeed be endured, because when it comes, it is not taken away.

He next shows what kind of joy he possessed, saying: “My heart”—that is, my soul, since I no longer receive it in vanity—and “my flesh,” since it no longer desires against Christ: considering their manifold languishing, they “rejoiced,” that is, by rejoicing through hope they went into the living God. This means that they went into that divine condition of immortality and impassibility where there is no misery, no defect, and where he truly lives. For here he does not truly live, where there is only one hour of birth and all the rest are hours of dying.

[Col. 0932B] For the sparrow finds a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest in which to place its young.

After the two things already mentioned, he gives two others by means of comparisons with birds. He calls the soul a sparrow because the sparrow is a plaintive bird, cautious of snares, and exercises itself in its wings. The soul that groans here, attending to the sadness and labor of pilgrimage, guards itself against the devil’s deceptions by not yielding to the desires of the flesh, and exercises itself in wings by which it may be lifted on high—that is, in the virtues of this life, namely faith, hope, and charity.

Such a soul, therefore, flying away from the earth and dwelling among heavenly things, finds a house for itself there, in which it may always remain and bring all its misery to an end.

He compares the flesh to the turtledove because, just as the turtledove has a groan for its song, so it belongs to the flesh, because of its manifold and endless defect, always to groan. He gives young to this turtledove because it belongs to the flesh to perform works of mercy: to clothe the naked, [Col. 0932C] feed the hungry, visit the sick, and do other such things.

These young, however, are not to be placed just anywhere, lest they be trampled and perish, but in a nest, that is, in the faith and fellowship of the Catholic Church. Outside it there is no place for a true sacrifice, for pagans too often perform works of mercy; but because they do not have a nest, their works are trampled and perish.

The Apostle places a certain woman in the person of this productive flesh when he says: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived by the serpent; afterward Adam consented to her and was deceived.” So also our woman, that is, our flesh, is deceived by the serpent when, through the devil as instigator, stirred by the titillation that is in us, carnal desires and illicit impulses arise.

If the mind and reason consent to these, behold, the man too is deceived. But if reason restrains carnal desires, properly governs illicit impulses, and keeps its wife under its authority—for “the head of the woman is the man, and the head of the man is Christ,” as the Apostle says [Col. 0932D]—behold, the woman, that is, the flesh, begins to have young, that is, to perform works of mercy, and so is saved.

The Apostle shows this afterward when he says: “She will be saved through the generation of children.” That these young are not to be placed just anywhere, but in the faith and fellowship of the Catholic Church, he shows when he says: “If she perseveres in faith and love with sobriety.”

In order that we might have from which to gather a nest for our young, our Lord, clothed in the hay of the flesh, deigned to descend to us, because this is the true faith: the Word incarnate, suffering, dead, and resurrected, and other such things. In this faith our young do not perish, but advance.

It should be noted that he gives the souls a house because of their enduring dwelling in heaven, but gives the flesh a nest, which is inhabited only for a time and then abandoned, because both faith and the works of mercy performed by the flesh are temporary. When the manifestation comes, faith will pass away, and there will be no need of mercy where there is no misery.

[Col. 0933A] The text is read as follows: “My soul and my flesh have truly rejoiced in the living God, because my soul, being a sparrow, found a house for itself, and my flesh, being a turtledove, found a nest in which to place its young.” And, as though he were saying, “Whatever flesh is such,” it passed joyfully into the living God. He continues to explain what that nest is of which he speaks:

“Your altars, O Lord.”

An altar is the place where our vows are placed so that they may be acceptable to God. Therefore “altars” are used for faith, which ought to precede in us; afterward good works are to be built upon it. Otherwise they are unacceptable and useless.

The text is read as follows: “The turtledove, I say, found a nest,” namely, it found “your altars,” that is, your faith and the other ecclesiastical institutions. O Lord, even of hosts, my King and my God—that is, you who rule me and bring me to find these altars, just as you also created me.

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house.”

[Col. 0933B] The one speaking here, placed amid pressures and sighing for those tabernacles where there will be no pressure, says with a certain astonishment and wonder: Truly and ineffably blessed, O Lord, are those who reach your courts, where there is no pressure and no misery.

He marks a twofold blessedness in them: in possessing and in acting. He indicates their blessedness in possessing when he says: “Those who dwell in your heavenly house,” in which there are both an eternal dwelling and joy without sadness. For there is no poor person there, no miserable person, no sick person, no needy person—in short, no one except one filled with supreme happiness.

He indicates their blessedness in acting when he says: “They will praise you for ages of ages,” that is, eternally. Do not doubt that you will be able to praise the one whom you cannot fail to love. Beauty is insatiable, and therefore love is without weariness.

“Blessed is the man.”

As though he were saying: Not only are those in the homeland blessed, but those on the way and in the service are blessed as well. For everyone is blessed—and truly a man, that is, acting manfully—who receives his help from you, that is, whom you assist.

For by your help he has arranged ascents, [Col. 0933C] not bodily steps but steps in his heart, that is, spiritual ones, and this in the valley of tears, that is, in the present life, which is tearful and miserable. For one weeps where one sows; one rejoices where one gathers.

I speak of ascents that lead to that place which God himself established and set before all as something to be sought—the place which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart.”

Or otherwise: He arranged ascents in the valley of tears, in that place which the miserable human being himself established for himself through transgression, that is, made. Or again, in the place which God set before all like a racecourse, so that in it we might fight against vices and spiritual enemies. For “the life of man upon earth is a warfare.”

He calls the necessary virtues of an active life “ascents,” namely faith, hope, and charity, as well as the four principal virtues—prudence, justice, temperance, and fortitude—and those subordinate to them.

Prudence is that by which we distinguish between good and evil. Justice is that by which we give each person what we owe, as the Apostle says: “Owe no one anything except to love one another.” Temperance is that by which we restrain lust and all carnal desires. Fortitude is that by which adversity is endured.

These virtues belong only to the present life, not to the future. We will not need prudence where no evils occur, nor justice where nothing unjust is done, nor temperance or fortitude where there is no desire and no adversity.

“For indeed [Col. 0933D] the lawgiver will give a blessing.”

He shows how the one whose help is from the Lord was able to arrange ascents, namely because he was assisted by uplifting grace. For indeed the lawgiver will give a blessing—that is, the Lord who gave the depressing law will also give uplifting grace.

The law is called depressing because it could not save, but only reveal sins. Hence the Apostle says: “For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would truly have come from the law.” [Col. 0934A] The law could also show sin, but it could not remove it, as the same Apostle shows when he says: “For, taking occasion through the commandment, sin worked in me every kind of desire,” and so forth.

Thus the law produced the sick, but did not heal them. So too those five porticoes around the sheep-pool produced sick people but healed none. The water surrounded by five porticoes is the Jewish people enclosed by the five books of the law.

Into this water the angel of the Lord descended from heaven and stirred it. Whoever first descended into the troubled water was healed. Similarly, when the Angel of Great Counsel descended from heaven, the water—that is, the people—was so troubled that even madmen killed the physician.

That troubled water is understood as the passion of Christ, which came about through that disturbance. If anyone descends in faith into the humility of this passion, and is “one,” not divided—for the Church has no schism—that person will truly be healed through faith, that is, [Col. 0934B] through grace, because he cannot be healed through the portico, that is, through the law.

Therefore grace is called uplifting; he calls this grace “blessing” because it has conferred many virtues. “To one is given the word of knowledge, to another prophecy, to another kinds of tongues,” and so forth.

And as though he were asking, “What does that blessing give them?” he answers: Very much indeed. Through it they will go from the virtue of action—which is not one but manifold, as was said above—to the virtue of contemplation, that is, as far as contemplating Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God.

Through this one virtue—for they will have other virtues of contemplation as well—they will possess the most perfect charity, so that they may praise God eternally, together with immortality, impassibility, and similar gifts. He determines into what virtue they will go by saying: “For God of gods will be seen in heavenly Zion,” that is, Christ, the God of Christians, “who gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name.”

[Col. 0934C] “O Lord God of hosts.”

The one speaking here, returning from the recollection of joys to his former condition, namely to the winepresses, saw that he had already gone ahead in hope but was still in the present reality. He saw that it was still time for prayer, not yet for praise, and time for groaning, not yet for rejoicing. Therefore he prays and says:

“O Lord, God even of hosts, hear my prayer. I say, receive it even with your ears—that is, hear it in such a way that you show most clearly through its fulfillment that you have received it—you who are the God of Jacob, making those who set out into those who arrive.”

As though he were saying: You, Lord, who made Jacob into Israel, make me, as one who is setting out, see the God of gods in Zion.

“Our protector.”

“Hear my prayer,” I say, “O God of Jacob, you who are our protecting God,” that is, you who protect us on the way, not so much with nocturnal light as with daytime shade.

“Look upon us” through mercy; and you who previously despised us in our own face, “look upon the face of your anointed,” that is, look upon us, in whom the face of your anointed already appears, so that you may make us from Jacob into Israel, that is, so that we may see the God of gods in Zion.

[Col. 0934D] “For one day is better.”

Therefore I pray that you may make Jacob into Israel, because the day that is always one in your heavenly courts—the day without end, without rising or setting, which is not preceded by yesterday or pressed upon by tomorrow—is better than thousands, that is, far better than many thousands of our days.

Miserable human beings desire thousands of days; let them despise thousands of days and desire one day, because one day is better than many thousands of days.

“I have chosen to be an outcast.”

Because one day is better, therefore, in order to reach that one day, I have chosen to be an outcast, that is, humble and despised, in the house of my God, that is, in the present Church, which is also called a tabernacle by analogy, rather than to dwell—that is, to abound in riches and reign—in the tabernacles, that is, in the abundance of sins, even if I could dwell there, that is, remain there forever.

[Col. 0935A] The one speaking here understood what is read in the Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” He saw humility as the chief and highest step by which to ascend to the divine heights, because things are different in divine matters than in human ones.

Among human beings, whoever wishes to ascend to high places must not lower but exalt himself as much as possible. In divine matters, however, the more humble a person makes himself, the more he advances toward the heights.

Because he saw this, he chose to be humbled and rejected rather than to pursue anything worldly. Humble yourself, and the one who invited you will say: “Friend, come up higher.”

[Col. 0935B] “Because mercy and truth.”

I chose to be an outcast because God loves to give mercy and truth to the outcast and the humble. First he gives mercy by forgiving sins; he will give truth in reward, when he returns to believers what he promised.

That mercy and truth are to be understood in this order the Apostle shows in his own case when he says: “I, who was formerly a blasphemer and persecutor and insolent, received mercy, so that in me, first of all, Jesus Christ might show all patience toward those who would believe in him for eternal life.”

Who, then, would doubt that whatever sins can be forgiven, when he sees such great crimes forgiven to the Apostle?

Later, when he was already near his passion, he said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day.”

As though he were saying: He has already given mercy, and he will also give the crown, because he is the giver of forgiveness but the debtor of the crown—not because he owes anything, but because by promising he made himself a debtor.

And truly, as though he were saying, God loves finally to give truth, because after giving mercy he will give grace, that is, perseverance; and at last he will give glory, the crown, immortality, and impassibility.

[Col. 0935C] “He will not deprive those of good things.”

He will truly give glory, because God will not deprive those who walk—that is, those who now delight in innocence and are willingly innocent—of true good things; rather, he will enrich them in many ways.

True innocence is that which harms neither itself nor another. And because those good things are inexplicable and indescribable, he cries out with astonishment and wonder:

“O Lord of hosts, truly and inexplicably blessed is the person who hopes in you,” that is, who rejects and humbles himself, placing all his hope and all his labor in you.

# Psalm LXXXIV

A psalm of David, “For the end, for the sons of Korah.”

## Argument

Here too there is a return, as though from the person of the people themselves, asking that the royal edicts concerning the return of the captives be confirmed through the kindling of divine grace. Alternatively, it is the apostolic voice addressed to the new people.

## Explanation

[Col. 0935D] This psalm, speaking of the first coming of the Savior, corresponds to the persons of those who sincerely believed in him. In the first part of the psalm, the prophet briefly gives thanks to the Lord because from the ancient condition of the Jewish nation the people came to the worship of the Lord the Savior.

In the second part, he reports how the Lord deigned to mitigate his anger against the Jewish people, seeking the coming of Christ, in whom human blindness received the light of faith.

In the third part, he turns his words toward himself and, in the spirit of prophecy, proclaims the coming of the incarnate Word.

## Commentary

“You have blessed your land, O Lord.”

“For the end, for the sons of Korah.”

These words are referred “to the end,” that is, to Christ. If we strive toward him, we will not go astray, because he is the truth toward which we hasten; he is the way along which we run.

They are presented “for the sons of Korah,” that is, for the sons of Cain—not so that we may mock him, but so that we may weep before him. Certain senseless children mocked a bald man and were devoured by beasts; the [Col. 0936A] mad Jews also mocked that bald man who was crucified at the place of Calvary.

But if we believe in him, we are his sons. This psalm is sung for us, since it is inserted among the psalms for the sons of Korah. For we are sons of the bridegroom, that is, of the bald man.

That bridegroom has already given his bride her pledge: his blood, by which he redeemed us, and the Holy Spirit, by which he enriched us, while for the present, during this pilgrimage, reserving his hidden riches for us.

The Prophet sings as though the future were past because, through the Holy Spirit, he foresaw what was to come; for what is future has already been accomplished in God’s disposition.

He sings of the first coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, commending him to us so that we may consider how innumerable are the benefits and gifts, and how great the glory, that God the Father has bestowed upon us by sending him and offering him as a sacrifice for us. Thus we may not be ungrateful, but prepare ourselves as worthy recipients of such great benefits. He says:

“Lord, you cursed the land,” that is, human nature, “at first; but in the second instance you blessed it,” when it was made yours, that is, [Col. 0936B] assumed by your Word.

“And by blessing it you turned away the captivity of Jacob.”

Although Jacob signifies that people who was led into the promised land, and who had often previously been taken captive and liberated because of its sins, in the end, because the madmen killed their physician, they were taken captive and scattered throughout the whole world.

Nevertheless, the true later people, that is, the people of grace, is also frequently designated by Jacob, because Jacob gave present things for future ones. It was said: “The elder shall serve the younger,” and again: “It is not the children of the flesh who are counted as descendants, but the children of the promise.”

All these things properly pertain to the later people. In its designation, therefore, Jacob is placed here, and captivity is understood here.

That people alone was not held captive, but the whole human race, through the transgression of the first parent, was held captive under the prince of the devil, sold under sin. From this captivity the Lord has already in some manner liberated Jacob by forgiving sins, and at last he will truly liberate him.

[Col. 0936C] That we are still in captivity the Apostle shows when he says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin and death.”

And he cries out to show who the liberator from this captivity is: “Wretched man that I am, who will liberate me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ.”

Through this Mediator this turning away of captivity, of which the psalm speaks, has taken place. Let us therefore acknowledge our captivity, confess our captivity, and we will be liberated. Whoever does not understand the enemy does not call upon freedom, and so will not be liberated.

“You forgave iniquity.”

“You turned away captivity,” I say, in this way: because you forgave the iniquity, that is, the sin, of your people, which was the cause of captivity.

Sin was, as it were, intensified when we were oppressed both by sin itself and by the punishments of sin. [Col. 0936D] It was remitted when the sin itself was both forgiven through faith and the punishment of sin alone remained.

Thus I say that you forgave, because you covered through faith all their sins, both actual and original. This does not mean that you did not see them—for you see all things—but that you did not punish them.

Therefore I say that you covered their sins because you mitigated all your anger: anger against actual sins and anger against original sins. You did this because you will not punish them eternally.

Anger nevertheless remains, because you scourge every son whom you receive. Thus I say that you mitigated it because you turned yourself away from the anger resulting from your indignation.

God’s indignation was, as it were, present when Adam stretched out his hand toward unlawful things. Anger followed that indignation, that is, the infliction of punishment.

And just as Adam’s former life was eternal conditionally—namely, if he did not sin—so, after he sinned, God’s anger against him was eternal conditionally—namely, if he did not repent. From this anger, therefore, the Lord turned himself away eternally, provided that he repented.

[Col. 0937A] “Turn us, O God.”

How can the one who previously said, “You turned away,” now say, “Turn us, O God, and turn away your anger”? No one will regard this as inconsistent. Because he saw the future through the Spirit, he foretold what was to come; but because it had not yet happened, he now prays that it may happen, saying:

“O God, you who have turned toward us, turn us, because you are our Savior, by whose grace alone we are saved, not by our merits; and by turning us, turn your anger away from us.”

“Will you be angry forever?”

You will truly turn your anger away. For you will not be angry with us forever, and will you remain angry? Certainly not.

By God’s anger we are mortal, and by God’s anger we eat our bread on earth in poverty and labor. This is what Adam heard when he sinned: “In Adam all will die.”

We were that Adam, and what he heard followed us also. For we did not yet exist as ourselves, but we were in him. Therefore whatever happened to him followed us, so that we would die; for in him we were all present.

The sins of parents do not pertain to children when the [Col. 0937B] parents commit them after the children have already been born. The children then belong to themselves, and the parents to themselves. Therefore, if children who have been born follow the evil ways of their parents, they must bear their parents’ merits as well.

But if they change themselves and do not imitate their evil parents, they begin to possess their own merit and not their parents’ merit. Indeed, if you change yourself, your father’s iniquity does not harm you; nor does it harm him if you change yourself.

Because we were all in Adam, and whatever happened to him followed us so that we would die, whatever our flesh received for this mortality it derived from him: the frailty of the flesh, the torment of labor, the bond of death, and the snares of temptation. We carry all these things in our flesh.

This is God’s anger, because it is God’s vengeance. But because it was going to happen that we would be made new by believing, that our immortality would be assumed in the resurrection, and that the newness of the whole human being would be restored through Christ, the prophet, who foresaw this through the Spirit, says:

“Will you be angry forever?” Certainly not. “Or will you extend [Col. 0937C] your anger,” that is, so that you do not punish eternally, “from a carnal generation into a spiritual generation?” Certainly not.

The carnal generation was mortal because of anger. But this generation, that is, the spiritual one, is immortal in hope through mercy.

And because we had nothing by which we could bring about our own conversion, when he himself would call us back—us who had turned away, us who were fugitives—the prophet, showing that not only our vivification but also the benefit of conversion must be attributed to him, says: “God, you who have turned.”

The thought is connected as follows: Truly, you will not extend your anger into this generation, because you, God, having turned toward us—not we toward you—will turn us, and thus you will vivify us inwardly and outwardly through hope.

Therefore the people, now no longer yours but its own, will rejoice in you by merit and will rejoice in its own good, whereas previously it rejoiced in itself to its own harm. For by seeking joys in itself, it found every sorrow arising from itself.

Therefore, whoever wishes to rejoice securely, do not rejoice in gold or silver, or in estates, or even in the brightness of this light. Rejoice instead in that light which says of itself: “I am the light of the world.” In saying this, it calls you; having called you, it turns you; having turned you, it heals you; and having healed you, it shows you your Liberator.

[Col. 0937D] “Show us, O Lord.”

And so that they may rejoice in you, show us—that is, make known to us—O Lord, the one who is to be called not merely merciful but Mercy itself, emphatically, because through him great mercy has been displayed to the world.

Blessed is the one to whom the Lord shows his mercy. Such a person can no longer be proud, because when mercy is shown to him, he is taught to understand that he possesses no good except from the one who is all our good—that good, certainly, which no one can take away unless you take it away from yourself.

Whatever you possess bodily, someone can take from you; but God, whom you possess bodily, no one can take from you.

“Show us,” I say, “your mercy now; and finally grant us to see [Col. 0938A] your salvation,” that is, your Savior.

As though he were saying: We know your Christ; we see your Christ—not as those who crucified him saw him, but as the angels see him and rejoice. Therefore grant us your salvation.

You have already given a human being to human beings; give God to gods. It might sound arrogant to say that we are gods if the prophet had not said: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.”

For we are sons of God, and although not yet in reality, nevertheless in hope. For “we have been saved in hope.” But hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience.

What do we await? That by remaining in faith we may see what we believe. Accordingly, the evangelist John says: “Beloved, we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. When it appears, we shall be like him, and we shall see him as he is.”

The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and I will love him, and I will reveal myself to him.”

[Col. 0938B] He has already revealed the flesh to flesh, but not the divinity. Therefore he revealed the flesh to flesh so that the heart might be cleansed by faith and this might be fulfilled: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

“I will hear what he will speak.”

“Show us,” I say, “your mercy, and I, insofar as I am able, will present myself as worthy,” that is, by restraining myself from every worldly disturbance, “so that I may hear,” that is, understand, what the Lord will speak within me through truth, that is, through the reason presiding within me.

Therefore I say that I may hear what he speaks within me, because he will truly speak to me through that very reason: peace now, and peace finally coming upon peace through his mercy upon his people.

The merciful one came for this purpose: so that those who believe in him might have peace here in their conscience—conflict with vices and harmony with excellent moral conduct—and finally might have peace upon peace, that is, perfect peace, against which no opposite force will prevail.

Of this peace Isaiah says: “I will give you true consolation, peace upon peace.” [Col. 0938C] The prophet, enlightened by the Holy Spirit through reason, saw this future, and therefore says for our exhortation:

“I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me,” so that we too may restrain ourselves from worldly disturbance and hear the same thing.

“And upon his holy ones.”

Here he divides the people mentioned above into Jews and Gentiles. He calls the Jews holy, that is, justified, as though on account of the law, the prophetic writings, and the worship of the true God.

The meaning is: I said that peace would come upon his people. This peace will come upon his holy ones, that is, the Jews, if they turn back to the heart; and, moreover, upon all who turn back to the heart, that is, upon the Gentiles.

[Col. 0938D] Although the Jews were turned away from the heart, because they worshiped the Lord not for his own sake but for earthly things, the Gentiles were even more turned away from the heart, because they worshiped the creature in place of the Creator. Therefore it was, as it were, more necessary for the Gentiles than for the Jews to turn back to the heart.

For the Jews, turning the heart means recognizing that God is to be worshiped for his own sake and not for anything else. For the Gentiles, turning back to the heart means recognizing, as though by re-sculpting their own heart, that the creature is inferior to the Creator and must not be worshiped in his place.

And through these visible things they may ascend to contemplate his invisible things, as the Apostle says: “[lacuna].”

Nevertheless, near those who fear him. As if he were saying: Peace was indeed common to Jews and Gentiles, but the one through whom it would be given would nevertheless be nearer to the Jews—not because grace was nearer to them, but because he received flesh from them. This is what he says: “Nevertheless, his salvation,” that is, his Savior, namely the Lord, through whom peace would be given, “will be near those who fear him.” He calls the Jews those who fear the Lord, because, even though they feared him not for his own sake but for the sake of earthly things, they nevertheless sought these things not from demons, as the Gentiles did, but from him alone. He was near them because from them came the patriarchs [Col. 0939A] and prophets; from them came the holy one in whom all the Gentiles were to be blessed; from them came the virgin Mary; there Christ was born and brought up; there he preached and performed miracles. Of this people also he said: “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel.” The prophet explains in what sense he says “near.” As if he were saying: I say that he will be near in such a way that glory—that is, that glorious one through whom every glorious person will be glorified—may dwell in our land, that is, may receive flesh from our people and dwell there, according to the saying: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

“Mercy and truth.” He will dwell, I say, in glory, among us; and in this glory—that is, in this glorious head—“mercy and truth met one another” (for “will meet”), that is, in him, as in the cornerstone, the two walls of the Church, coming from opposite directions, came together at one angle. By “truth” he understands those to whom the utterances of God were entrusted, namely, the Jews, and those to whom the promises had been made through carnal things—that is, the Jews. By “mercy” he understands those in whom grace worked through mercy alone, without any merits—that is, the Gentiles. This does not mean that grace was given to some on account of merits, but that in the Jews, because of their observance of the law, certain merits seemed in some way to have preceded, whereas in the Gentiles nothing worthy of salvation seemed to exist. Concerning them the Apostle says: “But the Gentiles glorify God on account of mercy.” Yet these two walls met one another in that cornerstone, as though the head were saying: “Recall to me those who have turned away; bring back to me those who have fled. Let those who refused to seek me find me seeking them.” But how was this accomplished? Through this, namely, that justice and peace—these two virtues—“kissed one another,” that is, came together in Jews and Gentiles.

Many hate justice and wish to have peace; but if anyone attacks justice, it is necessary that he not have peace. These two virtues are like two sisters, because neither wishes to come without the other. Therefore, if anyone offends justice, he will not have peace, because peace will not come unless justice precedes it.

“Truth from the earth.” For this reason, I say, justice and peace came together in them: because from the earth from which falsehood had previously arisen—that is, from those very human beings—truth has now arisen, namely, true confession of sins. That truth pertains to confession the Apostle John demonstrates when he says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess, he is faithful and just, and he will forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all our iniquity.” And because, as though he were saying, truth has arisen from the earth, therefore justice has looked upon us from heaven, that is, from God. This means that heavenly justification was given to us, as though the Lord were saying: “Let us spare this man, because he does not spare himself. Let us forgive him, because he does not forgive himself. He has turned toward punishing himself; I will turn toward freeing him.”

“For the Lord will give.” I say that justice has looked upon us from heaven because all evil is from us. From him, however, [Col. 0939D] comes every good, for the Lord will give kindness. When you confess and punish your sins to others, you in a certain way become like him, because you begin to hate what he hates and love what he loves. Then he himself will give you kindness—that is, this sweetness and gentleness—so that you who formerly delighted in injustice may delight in justice; you who formerly rejoiced in thefts may now rejoice in almsgiving; you who formerly rejoiced in committing robberies may now rejoice in giving what is yours; you who formerly delighted in games may now delight in hymns; and so forth.

The Lord will give kindness, I say, and thus the earth—that is, our flesh—will give its fruit, that is, will perform good works, namely works of mercy. I say that he will give this because justice—that is, this confession and punishment of our sins, which is the first justice of a human being—will walk before him, that is, before the Lord, preparing a way for him. And on the way—that is, after such a way has been prepared for him—he will set his footsteps in us, that is, he will conform us [Col. 0940A] to his tracks. For, with respect to this perfection, the justice mentioned above precedes him. In another sense he himself precedes us, because he is the beginning of every good action and thought of ours.

The words above, beginning with “Show us your mercy,” can also be read in another way, as though the prophet were saying: “And so that your people may rejoice in you, therefore, Lord, show us your mercy and give us your salvation,” that is, send us the Savior whom you are going to send. “And I, insofar as I can, will make myself fit for such great benefits, withdrawing from all external tumult, so that I may hear what the Lord God speaks within me through the truth that possesses me inwardly”—that is, what he requires of me in return for such great benefits. I say that he speaks, because he truly speaks—that is, he requires from me true peace: conflict with vices and harmony with the best moral dispositions. I speak of peace that is to come upon the people, that is, what he will require also from all his people. And he says what that people is: it will come through assistance upon his saints, those sanctified by him, and especially upon those who [Col. 0940B] turn back to the heart.

“Nevertheless, near those who fear him.” I say that peace will be among all who turn back to the heart; but his salvation—that is, true salvation belonging to him—will nevertheless be near those who fear him perfectly, with chaste fear. Those who fear him perfectly are people who, even if the Creator himself were to say to them, “Behold, possess these good things of yours eternally,” would nevertheless not prefer them to him, because they would fear him for his own sake rather than for the sake of those things. But not all who have turned back to the heart are such. Therefore he rightly said separately: “His salvation is near those who fear him.”

And he is there for this purpose: that the glory of immortality and impassibility—which did not dwell in Adam because he did not persevere—may at last dwell also on earth, that is, in our flesh. In this glory, mercy and truth met one another—that is, will meet one another—because then God will truly fulfill what he previously promised mercifully. This will happen because justice and peace have here already kissed one another—that is, will kiss one another in human beings. And they will kiss one another for this reason: because truth—that is, the one who must be called not merely true but, emphatically, truth itself—has arisen from the earth, that is, from the virgin Mary. Through him heavenly justification will be given to human beings, and true peace will accompany it.

And truly justice will be given through him, because the Lord the Father will give through him kindness—that is, forgiveness of sins and the abundance of spiritual grace—and thus he will give its fruit from our earth. These two verses may also be read in this interpretation, just as in the preceding one. And truly our earth will give its fruit, because justice—that is, the one who must be called not merely just but justice itself—will walk before him, that is, before God the Father, conforming us to himself and thus making a way in us. And by approaching us along this way, he will set his footsteps in us, that is, he will perfectly conform us to his affections and his will.

# ON PSALM 85. A Prayer of David.

[Col. 0940D]

## ARGUMENT

David himself, placed in distress, prays. It can also apply to Hezekiah, besieged by the Assyrians. Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ to the Father.

## EXPLANATION

David signifies the Lord Savior, either because his interpretation is understood as “strong of hand” and “desirable,” or because the one who is God over all, blessed forever, took flesh from his stock. Throughout the psalm the Lord Jesus Christ prays. In the first section he says things that appear to apply to him alone. In the second he supplicates more humbly on behalf of his members, of whom he is the head. In the third he speaks again in his own person, saying what pertains especially to him.

## COMMENTARY

“Incline your ear, O Lord.” A prayer of David. The Lord, the son of David according to his humanity, but Lord and creator of David according to his divinity, prays in this psalm in the person of David the servant and from the person of the servant. Since Christ is one, head and body, whoever prays in the body of Christ prays because he is one with him, and prays in his person.

The David mentioned above prays for his outward resurrection and for the inward resurrection of his members in the present time, and finally for their outward resurrection—not because he himself needs to pray, but so that he may give us a pattern for praying, just as he gives us an example of living. He says:

“O Lord, incline your ear to me,” as to one who is humble, as to one in need of mercy. As if he were saying: “I do not lift up my neck; you incline your ear. For I understand you as above and myself as below, you in exaltation and myself in humility.”

“Incline your ear,” I say, “and hear me,” that is, show by the result that you have heard me. And you ought to hear me because I am needy in myself and in my members—that is, I consider myself insufficient and in need of mercy—and I am poor, that is, humble. God does not hear the rich and proud.

Yet no one should think that God does not hear those who possess gold and silver. Abraham, Jacob, and David possessed many things, but God heard them because they were his poor. Whoever rejects what could make him proud and despises within himself what could inflate him is truly poor. Concerning such poor people the Apostle says, writing to Timothy: “Command the rich of this age not to be high-minded, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living and true God, who abundantly provides us with all things for enjoyment.”

“Guard my soul.” As if he were saying: “I say, hear me in such a way that you guard my soul, so that it may not depart from obedience.” You did not guard Adam’s soul, and therefore it did not remain in obedience. Therefore I say that you should guard my soul, because I am holy.

Perhaps this seems to someone to apply only to him who committed no sin, who alone among all is not the perpetrator but the forgiver of sins. But certainly it also applies to his members. It would be unworthy for members not to be joined to so worthy a head as holy members. He is holy in one way, and we in another. He is holy as the one who sanctifies; we are holy as those who have been sanctified, as the Apostle says: “And such were some of you, but you were washed, but you were sanctified.” If one of the members says of himself, “I am holy,” this will not be the arrogance of one puffed up, but the confession of one who is not ungrateful.

“Guard my soul,” I say, “and, in order that you may guard it, save me,” because of my perseverance, me your servant who hopes in you and does not presume upon himself. You ought to do this because you are my God. I am not my own god—that is, I wish to depend upon your command, not my own, as wretched Adam wished.

“Therefore have mercy on me,” that is, on my members, “O Lord,” raising them inwardly now and outwardly at the end. You ought to have mercy because I cried out—that is, I worked unceasingly in them, striving toward you and not toward any other reward—and did so “all day,” that is, continually.

And that you may have mercy, “gladden the soul of your servant,” which appears to have been saddened by enemies, by raising me outwardly. Therefore I say, “gladden,” because, O Lord, I have not pressed my soul down toward earthly things, but have lifted it—not against you, as Adam did, but toward you—because I directed all my intention toward you.

And rightly toward you, because you, Lord, are sweet: with you there is joy without sorrow and every sweetness, whereas on earth there is every bitterness. You are gentle because you bear with us while perfecting us, namely until we find our heart and learn to pray. Various illusions and phantasms rise up against us and obstruct our heart, so that we may neither think of you nor pray to you worthily. But your patience sustains us until we recover our senses, return to the heart, and thus pray to you.

You are of great mercy because, where our iniquity abounds, your grace abounds all the more. And because you also reward your gifts in us—for you give us the will and enable us to accomplish what we rightly will, and thus to rejoice eternally—you do this for all who call upon you, that is, for those who call upon you, and not upon something else, within themselves.

“Give ear.” And because you are of great mercy, therefore, Lord, “give ear,” that is, show by the effect that you have heard my prayer, made for the perseverance of my members, and attend to the voice of my supplication, made for the sins of my members. Here the great fervor of the one praying is indicated. When he says, “Give ear,” it is as though he were saying: “Fix my prayer in your ears, so that it may not depart from them.” And truly he fixes our prayer in his ears if we fix his law in our hearts.

“In the day of tribulation.” Therefore you ought to hear my prayer and attend to my supplication for my members, because I cried out to you in them “in the day of tribulation,” that is, throughout the whole time of pilgrimage. For as long as we are in this body, we are exiles from the Lord.

Therefore no Christian should think that he is without tribulation. Even if all temporal goods overflow for him, he is still grievously troubled, because pilgrimage itself is a great tribulation. And for anyone to whom tribulation is not grievous, the homeland is not sweet. If we consider how wretched our pilgrimage is, the whole day will be tribulation; and this will continue until there is exultation in the homeland.

“I cried out to you,” I say, “O Lord, in the time of tribulation.” This is evident from the fact that you heard me; the effect itself plainly shows that I cried out to you.

“There is none like you.” And rightly I cried out to you, because not only among the images of demons, which foolish human beings make and worship as gods, but not even among the gods—deified by your grace—is there anyone like you in power. Nor is there any angel or human being comparable to you in works, because you alone, aided by no one, do whatever you do; all others do whatever they do through you.

And because you are such, all the nations that you have made—that is, created—will come to you by the steps of faith. Those who formerly came to Jerusalem to pray will now worship before you, each in his own conscience, where he possesses you as present. For God is present to every good conscience. Those who formerly glorified their own name will now glorify your name through good works.

And rightly so, because you alone are great, filling every place, since you are present everywhere, whereas all others are small. You alone perform wonders, that is, the inward resurrection of the dead and the restoration of the human race. Therefore you alone can do these things, because you alone are truly God.

“Lead me, O Lord.” And because you alone are the true God who performs wonders, therefore, Lord, “lead me,” that is, lead me from virtue to virtue—lead my members who have been placed in your way, that is, placed in my body, which is your way, because it leads to you.

“And I will enter,” that is, let my members live in this life, which is an entrance into the future life, “in your truth,” that is, in the truth of your commandments. We can also understand “way” as the commandments, so that what follows—“I will enter in your truth”—is an explanation of the way.

“I will enter in your truth,” I say, “and my heart will rejoice through hope,” yet in such a way “that it may fear your name.” For there is not yet joy without sorrow. When this mortal nature puts on immortality and the final death is destroyed, only then will there be joy. Full security does not yet exist, because complete delight does not yet exist. If there were no delight at all, we would fail; but if there were full security, we would rejoice wrongly.

Therefore, when he says, “Let my heart rejoice, so that it may fear,” he asks the Lord both to grant joy and to inspire fear. Elsewhere also it is said: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling.” And the Apostle says: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.”

“I will confess.” And truly you will lead my members, because even in the present I will confess to you in my members, “with all my heart,” that is, without excluding any corner of my heart; and “forever,” that is, in the eternal life that is to come, I will glorify your name. “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you.”

“For your mercy is great toward me.” Therefore rightly I will confess to you now and glorify your name [Col. 0943A] forever in the future, because your mercy will be great toward me and toward my members. He shows what that mercy is: namely, that you have already rescued my soul by determination and will rescue it in reality from the lower hell.

There is a certain heavenly region of the angels, in which there is the life of the angels’ ineffable joys, where immortality and incorruption flourish, and where everything remains unchangeably through God’s gift and grace. This is called the heavenly region.

There is another region where flesh and blood, and every mortality, prevail—where hope is fragile and everything is perishable and fleeting. In comparison with the former, this is called the lower region or hell. And rightly so, because it is full of the place of the dead. The body is dead because of sin, as the Apostle says. It is not dead in the sense that it exists apart from the soul; but although our body is animated, it is afflicted by so many penalties of sin that it is as though dead in comparison with the body that will exist in us when it is changed into a heavenly condition.

In comparison with this hell, the lower hell can commonly be understood as the place to which souls descend after this life, whether they are to be condemned eternally or punished temporarily. To both these hells the Lord the Father sent his Son, freeing us from all sides: to the upper one by being born, to the lower one by dying. For that most holy soul, separated from the divinity, descended there so that he might lead out his own who were being held in darkness. He did not remain there, but returned from it in triumph, according to the saying: “For you will not abandon my soul in hell,” and so forth.

Therefore he says: “You have rescued my soul from the lower hell.”

This can also be understood with respect to the members in the following way: in the places of punishment we may understand an upper and a lower place as an upper and lower hell. We may take the upper place as that where holy men—Abraham, Lazarus in his bosom, and others—were kept in a certain repose before the Lord’s coming. The lower place, however, may be understood as that where the rich man’s pride was condemned along with those who were to be punished eternally.

That the former place was above and the latter below the Evangelist testifies when he says: “But the rich man, being in torments, lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham from afar, and Lazarus in his bosom.” For he would not have lifted up his eyes unless he had looked upon something that was above.

According to this second interpretation, the meaning is: “You have rescued my soul,” that is, the soul of my members. If you freed them for a time from the upper hell, where they were awaiting purification—[the source reads *vacatis illis*; the syntax is uncertain]—then you also rescued them from it. Unless they were freed, they would truly have been cast down there.

It is like someone saying to a physician, “You have saved me from death,” not because he had died and the physician had raised him, but because the physician gave him a potion without which he would have died.

Another interpretation is also commonly offered here: that we understand both hells in this life, the upper hell as actual sins and the lower as mortal sins. But it is not necessary to distinguish them separately, because they are included within the upper category in a certain way.

At this point blessed Augustine says that, whichever of the interpretations mentioned above is or is not correct, no one should regard him as a rash assertor, but as a faithful interpreter of the word of God.

“O God, the wicked have risen up against me.” I say that you will rescue my soul and the souls of my members from the lower hell, because I and my members will be compelled to descend there. For this reason, O God, the wicked Jews have risen up—that is, will rise up—against me, to crush me.

The wicked will also rise up, that is, all unjust persecutors against their own members, because it is necessary that he complete in his body what remains of Christ’s sufferings. And not only, as though he were saying, have wicked men from among the lesser Jews risen up against me, but “the synagogue of the powerful,” that is, the assembly of proud rulers, has sought my soul—not in order to imitate me, but to destroy me.

“And they have not set you before their eyes,” that is, they have not considered you in me, but only me as a human being. Or, “they have not set you before their eyes” so that they might spare me, though innocent. They would then have had God before the eyes [Col. 0944A] of their heart if they had recognized that he was an innocent human being—or not merely human, but also God—and thus had spared him.

“And you, O Lord.” They, I say, have risen up against me; therefore you, Lord, are “a merciful God” in your manifestation and compassionate in your affection, “patient,” because your patience leads us to repentance, and “of great mercy,” because you not only forgive sins but also reward your gifts in us, and “true” in your promises.

You, being such, “look upon me,” whom they think you have despised, “and have mercy on me,” raising me from the dead. “Give your power,” that is, your judicial authority, “to your servant,” that is, to me your servant. For “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,” because he is the Son of Man.

The meaning is: “I who formerly appeared contemptible will appear terrible; I who came to be judged will come to judge; I who displayed patience in my passion will display power in judgment.”

“Give power,” I say, “to your servant,” and, in order that you may give it, “save me through perseverance,” me who am not the Son of you, your servant, but the Son of your sole handmaid—namely, the one who answered the angel: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

And after you have perfected me through perseverance, “make with me,” that is, make in me, the sign shown in Jonah, according to the saying: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was,” and so forth. This means: Raise me from the dead.

That sign is for good, or will be for the good of many, that is, for salvation. He says “my sign” because God the Father also raised him, as he testified when he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

“Make,” I say, “the sign with me, so that those who hate me may see and be confounded”—now beneficially and profitably, whereas they were destined to be confounded disastrously and uselessly.

“What,” I ask, “may they see?” This: “That you, Lord, have helped me so that I would not fail in tribulation, and have comforted me through the resurrection.”

# ON PSALM 86. A Psalm of Song for the Sons of Korah.

[Col. 0944C]

## ARGUMENT

After the Assyrians had captured the ten tribes, although they besieged Jerusalem, they nevertheless could not conquer it. Alternatively, it is the apostolic voice concerning the Church.

## EXPLANATION

The “sons of Korah” signify the faithful Christians, to whom the prophet proclaims the city of God, so that their affection for such great glory may be the greater. Alternatively, nearly all the psalms entitled “for the sons of Korah” are full of joy. For they did not follow their father’s iniquity and lustfully take up fire alien to God; rather, loving what the Lord loves, they speak of the glorious city of God.

In the first part the prophet speaks to the faithful, proclaiming the heavenly city. In the second the Lord Savior declares, through an allusion to various names, that she will believe, rebuking the synagogue for not recognizing the God in whom the devoted faith of the Gentiles would believe. In the third part the prophet touches in one verse upon the blessedness of the future age. These sections are also distinguished by the insertion of *diapsalmata*.

## COMMENTARY

“His foundations are in the holy mountains.” The psalm—that is, this work, namely the establishment of the city discussed here—is a work of song, that is, it pertains to spiritual joy. All who direct themselves toward being in that building should therefore rejoice spiritually on its account.

It is presented to the sons of Korah, that is, to the sons of Christ, so that, if they are true sons, they may strive to be placed within the structure of that building.

A certain city is sung and commended to us in this psalm. We are its citizens insofar as we are Christians, and from it we are exiles as long as we are mortal; toward it we journey along its way. It was as though obstructed by thickets and thorns and could not be found, until the king of that city made himself our way so that we might reach it.

Therefore, as we walk in Christ, still journeying as exiles and sighing with desire for the ineffable joy of that city, let us sing in such a way that we desire it. Let us see how ardent were the lovers of that city from whom these things were declared and sung to us, and with what affection they commended them to us. Fear of the city produced this affection in them, while the Holy Spirit poured love into them.

Filled and inflamed by this Spirit, a certain citizen who was turning many things over inwardly concerning his desire and love for that city breaks into this utterance, as though he had previously said something about it that could be referred to it. Yet when did he not speak about it, since from the moment he came to know it he never kept silent about it in his heart? Indeed, he always spoke about it.

It is as though he were saying: “Wondrous and ineffable things must be said about that city, but I say only this about it: its foundations are in the holy mountains.” That is, the holy mountains on which this city is built are also its foundations.

And as though someone asked, “Whose foundations are they?” he says: “Of Sion.” That is, the heavenly Jerusalem is a certain city whose gates the Lord loves above all the tents of Jacob.

He calls patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and other eminent teachers “holy mountains,” because they are called mountains on account of the constancy of their faith and the excellence of their virtues. They are the foundations of this city because our weakness rests upon them and is strengthened through their authority.

This spiritual building differs from every dead and earthly building. In earthly buildings the foundations are one thing, the stones from which the building is constructed another, the gates another, and the inhabitants another. In this spiritual building, however, the holy mountains whom we have said to be its foundations are also its citizens. They spoke about it in order to exhort other citizens. The living and squared stones from which the building is assembled are also its gates.

They are called squared stones because, just as what is truly square is stable whichever way it falls—as with a die—so all who are in this building are such that, whatever tribulations or pressures threaten them, through which they might seem likely to fall, they nevertheless do not fall under any temptations.

The aforementioned mountains are also gates, because through their teaching we gain access to knowledge of the truth.

It should be understood, however, that although we have said that this building has several foundations, it nevertheless has one principal foundation, the foundation of foundations, of which the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ.”

This same one is the cornerstone of the building, holding together two peoples like two walls coming from opposite directions and meeting at one angle. This cornerstone is both at the top and at the bottom: at the top in those who are already above, and at the bottom in those who are still below on earth—not with respect to his humanity, but with respect to his divinity, which is present everywhere. Everything here is in likenesses, not in proper realities.

This must be considered especially in this building: it does not rise from below to above, as other buildings do, but extends from above to below. Christ, who is the foundation, is truly the highest. Those built upon him are lower.

This building is said to have twelve gates and one gate. It is one gate because of Christ, who calls himself the gate, saying: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me,” and so forth. They are twelve because the number twelve consists of four and three. Those called to its construction come not from one part of the building alone but from all four parts of the world, through knowledge of the Holy Trinity.

The Lord loves these gates of Sion above all the tents of Jacob, that is, more than all the legal institutions of the ancient people, which signified the things mentioned above and those that now exist in the Church. “Jacob” here signifies the carnal people, while the “tents” signify the legal institutions that were added for a time.

“Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God.” As if he were saying: The Lord rightly loves your gates because, O city of God, glorious things have been spoken of you by the prophets, and even by the Lord himself, when he said to the Jews: “Amen, I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God.”

He calls the city of God the heavenly Jerusalem, distinguished from the earthly city on account of its dignity.

“I will remember Rahab.” Truly, glorious things have been spoken of you. For the Lord also spoke this glorious thing about you, O Sion, to those who know me—that is, who recognize my power and my will—and therefore build you: “I will remember Rahab and Babylon,” so that people like Rahab and Babylon, converted, may be placed in your building.

Rahab was a prostitute in Jericho. She received the messengers of the Israelite people who had been sent to spy out the land, welcomed them as guests, and allowed them to depart. She made them promise under oath that, just as she had preserved them, so they would protect her and her household when they captured the city. They agreed and instructed her to hang a scarlet cord from her window when the city was overthrown. She did so and was delivered.

Rahab is interpreted as “proud,” while Jericho means “moon.” Through the moon the decline of mortality is signified. Rahab is understood as the universal prostitute, that is, the Gentile world, which was in Jericho because it clung only to the decline of earthly existence. It was proud because it placed the creature before the Creator.

Whoever from that people receives the messengers of the Israelite people—that is, preachers of the truth—and hangs the passion of Christ, signified by the scarlet, that is, red cord, from the window of reason—that is, believes it rationally—will be saved when Jericho is handed over to the fire of eternal destruction.

Babylon is likewise interpreted as “confusion.” By it those who are confused above all by earthly desire are signified. When converted and cleansed, they too are placed in the city of God. This is the glorious thing the Lord said about it. For it is the same as saying: “This city cleanses all unclean things and sets right all that is confused.”

“Behold, foreigners.” He speaks as though it were past, although through the Spirit he foresaw what was to come. As if he were saying: “Behold, the glorious things spoken of the city of God have been fulfilled—not in the same people, but in people who have been changed.”

By “foreigners” understand all who are alien in mind from the people of God, that is, persecutors. By Tyre—which in Hebrew is called *Sor*, interpreted as “tribulation” or “distress”—those are signified whose souls, on account of their evil desert, were destined to experience every tribulation and distress unless they repent. By the people of Ethiopia are signified those who are deeply blackened by sins and utterly despairing.

“Will Sion say, ‘A man’?” Not only that glorious thing we mentioned, but also this other glorious thing has been said about the city of God: namely, that someone was born in it as a human being for our sake, and that he himself, the Most High—that is, [the source reads *eus ante nos quia Deus*, perhaps corrupt; literally, “he is before us, because he is God”]—founded it.

It is not surprising that the one who created the mother from whom he was to be born also founded the city in which he was to be born.

And, O Sion, will a human being alone say—that is, presume to explain or understand—this? As if he were saying: Certainly no human being by himself, without the illumination of the Holy Spirit, can aspire to this.

He understands Sion as the same one mentioned previously. Nor should it trouble you that in the city of God, which we have said is the heavenly Jerusalem, a human being is said to be born. For not only the heavenly Church above but also the present Church is called the heavenly Jerusalem, because that one and this one are the same.

As the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in the heavens.” Christ was born in this citizenship—that is, in the present Church—even though he was born from the Jews, because the blessed virgin Mary, on account of the faith she possessed, was already a member of the Church that was still to be revealed.

The Lord will recount it in the Scriptures. As if he were saying: Although it is not for man to say or understand that—that both a man was born in it and that he founded it—nevertheless it is certain and true, because the Lord, who neither deceives nor is deceived, both has recounted and will recount it in the Scriptures, not Aristotelian or Platonic writings, but those of peoples, that is, in Scriptures directed toward correcting and teaching peoples. And in the Scriptures of princes, that is, those which princes both wrote and taught—princes, I say, not just any princes, but these great princes [Col. 0947A] who were involved in building that city. By “princes” here he means the holy apostles and the other founders of the Church, who, although they were poor and fishermen, nevertheless hold primacy over all the princes of this age, as the matter itself demonstrates.

For whoever goes to Rome, the city of the Christians, is happier to possess a memorial of Peter the fisherman than to take care to visit the palace of the emperor Nero. It should be known that blessed Augustine above gives this wording: “Mother Zion will say, ‘A man.’” There is another way of connecting the passage, as though it were said: How will this happen, that foreigners, Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians are in that city? In this way, namely, because someone of such a kind will be born who will both be powerful and fit to introduce them. For someone will say, “O mother Zion,” like any other man. And this is one who was both born in it—a man for our sake—and who himself, before us, founded it. The meaning is not changed. It is as if he were saying: By this it is known and held certain that the Lord both has recounted and will recount this in the Scriptures of the peoples, and so forth.

Like those who rejoice. Since, O city of God, so many and such glorious things have been said about you, and the holy mountains are your foundations, and the Lord loves your gates, therefore the dwelling of all who dwell in you is like that of those who rejoice. As if he were saying: The dwelling of the earthly city is like that of those who weep and grieve; but your dwelling is that of those who rejoice, that is, those who enjoy gladness. For when necessity perishes, all the works of necessity will perish, and joy alone will follow. Therefore he says that it will be the dwelling of those who rejoice. And lest we hasten toward some earthly joy, supposing that this is that joy, he added “like,” so that we might know that this has no relation to that except by mere resemblance.

## ON PSALM 87

A song of the psalm for the sons of Korah, to the end, for Maheleth, for responding; an understanding of Heman the Ezrahite.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0947C] Alternatively, the voice of Christ to the Father concerning his Passion.

### EXPLANATION

Melech is interpreted as “choir,” singing divine words, and what is added, “for responding,” signifies that musical instruments went before and that the choir responded solemnly. Mystically, this indicates that the Lord’s Passion, which is sung in this psalm, ought to be imitated concordantly by the Church. For Heman the Israelite, who is interpreted as “his brother” and “a man seeing God,” likewise signifies the same people of the faithful. Of them it is said: “Go, announce to my brothers.” Heman was the son of Joel, son of Samuel, of the family of Kohath, son of Levi, one of the singers whom David appointed over the others to sing when the ark was placed in position.

Jerome explains this title as follows: “This psalm refers to faith, and while the sons of Korah lead the singing, the entire choir, composed in prudence and understanding, responded with the same voice to Heman the Israelite.” Arnobius writes as follows concerning the title of this psalm: “The sons of Korah are indeed named, but the psalm directs its song for Melech and gives an understanding of Heman the Israelite. The Hebrews call Melech ‘destitute,’ and Heman ‘needy.’ Therefore the speech is addressed to the destitute and poor man, whom I believe to be the one whom the disciples abandoned and fled, the one who, although he was rich, became poor for us. The Lord speaks throughout the entire psalm.

“In the first part he implores help through various comparisons, referring to the contempt he was to suffer from the Jews. In the second he enumerates what he is going to suffer, asserting that the dead cannot be raised by physicians so that they may confess to the Lord. In the third he denies that those buried can proclaim the Lord’s mercy or that the lost can resound with the Lord’s praises; therefore he implores that resurrection may come to him most swiftly. Persevering in this prayer, he speaks, recalling various sufferings on behalf of the members, which both he himself and his devoted people endured.”

### COMMENTARY

“Lord, God of my salvation.” A song of the psalm for the sons of Korah, for Maheleth, for responding, to the end; an understanding [Col. 0948A] of Heman the Israelite, or the Jezrahite, or nevertheless the Ezrahite. In this psalm our Head treats of his Passion and resurrection, accumulating the tribulations and miseries that he suffered for us, so that he may make us all the more attentive and ready to respond worthily to him. And since this action pertains to our spiritual gladness and joy—because his death is our life and his condemnation our justification—this psalm is therefore called “a song of the psalm,” and this song is proposed to the sons of Korah, that is, to the sons of Christ, “for Maheleth, for responding.”

In Hebrew, Maheleth is called a choir in Greek, and a choir is a multitude singing concordantly; it is used to signify concord. The meaning is: This song alone is proposed to the sons of Korah, “for Korah,” for responding, so that there may be a choir responding concordantly to its leader in singing. The manner in which they should respond is indicated by the apostle Peter, who says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow in his footsteps.” John likewise shows this when he says: “As he himself laid down his life for us, so we too ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.” And this is to be done only in charity, because the Apostle says: “And if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.”

The holy martyrs responded to this leader in singing principally and worthily. Yet it must not be denied that the others also respond to him, because, although they do not suffer persecution externally, they nevertheless mortify themselves inwardly and are always disposed so that, if necessary, they do not hesitate to lay down their lives for their brothers. Thus this is proposed to the sons of Korah for responding—I mean to those who through this response are striving toward the end of eternal crowns, that is, toward the glory of immortality and freedom from suffering.

And this is “a song of the understanding of Heman the Ezrahite.” Heman is interpreted as “his brother.” Those are his brothers who understand the mystery of his cross in such a way that they not only are not ashamed of it, but glory in it, like the one who said: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Hence this song is rightly called “the understanding of Heman”—Heman, I say, the Israelite. For everyone who understands in this way is such a person of whom it can be said: “Behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.”

“Jezrahite,” or “Ezrahite,” is interpreted as “an eastern immigrant.” For the Lord placed us in the East when he established Adam in an abundance of virtues; but through transgression we fell from the East into the West, that is, into this ignorance and mortality. If we wish to return to our homeland, it is necessary for us to attend to our exile and strive to respond concordantly to our leader in singing, which everyone who is truly a brother does.

It should be known, however, that blessed Augustine says that this psalm was written among the others concerning the Passion, and that he specially entitled it “for Maheleth, for responding” for no other reason than to reveal variation and prevent weariness. Or, if there is another reason why the title of one psalm cannot apply to another, he says that, although he labored much, he was unable to discover it. He also says that if some before him spoke or wrote about this matter, either they did not help his slowness, because he was unable to understand them, or they did not satisfy his expectation, because what they said was weak.
