Let us therefore listen in this psalm to our leader in singing, the Lord, and let us hear how his choir responds to him by imitation or thanksgiving. To him, I say, who speaks as follows: “Lord, God, author of my salvation and of the salvation of my people.” And rightly so, because “I cried out,” that is, I acted earnestly before you, not for the sight of human beings. And this was “by day and by night,” that is, both in prosperity and in adversity. For the one who truly cries out by day and by night is the person whom prosperity does not exalt and adversity does not break.

“Lord God, let my prayer enter before you,” a prayer made not merely on the lips externally, but in your sight, that is, in the heart, where you see. Or, if “in your sight” is not taken in that way, it may simply be understood as: “Let my prayer enter into your presence,” that is, may my prayer be acceptable to you. This is drawn from the practice whereby envoys who bring a ruler an acceptable embassy are immediately admitted before him.

Incline your ear to my prayer. He appears to say the same thing in other words. For the inclination of the ear is nothing other than merciful hearing. And certainly he inclines his ear to us if we do not stiffen our neck.

For my soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to hell. Therefore I ask you to incline your ear to me, because I am suffering necessity. For my soul is filled with evils. With what evils? Certainly not with vices, because he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth, but with human evils, namely sadness, tribulation, and pain. For the soul sympathizes with its flesh when pain inevitably threatens the flesh itself. Of these evils he said: “My soul is sorrowful.”

He assumed these things—that is, these emotions of human weakness—not under the compulsion of necessity, but by the will of compassion, just as he assumed flesh and even death itself. [Col. 0949B] For he transferred his members into himself, so that if perhaps one of his members were saddened or touched by pain amid bodily tribulations and afflictions, it would not therefore consider itself alien to his mercy. And he did this to show that these things are not vices but signs of human weakness.

And therefore—as if he were saying—I say that my soul is filled with evils because my life has drawn near hell, that is, death. We may also understand “evils” here as the sadness and pain of compassion that he himself had, because he saw those whom he had come to refresh instead falling away from the truth and defiling themselves in such a great crime. In accordance with what the Apostle says: “Great sadness and continual pain are in my heart for my brothers according to the flesh, who are Israelites.”

I am counted among those who descend into the pit; I have become like a man without help, free among the dead. Therefore my soul is filled with evils and my life has drawn near hell, because I was considered by those whom I had come to raise from the dead, heal from their infirmities, and free from sins, to be among those who descend into the pit—that is, equal to those who descend into the pit, namely, into the deep misery of the vices of this life. Or “into the pit,” that is, into the lower hell.

And I also became, in their estimation, like a man without help, that is, as though deprived of every assistance, because they said: “Pursue and seize him, for there is no one to deliver him.” Such, I say, was I considered by them, although I was alone free among the dead. For his death was truly free, not compelled, because he had power to lay down his life and to take it up again. He was also free among the dead because he had neither a preceding cause of death, namely sin, nor feared a punishment that would follow.

Like the wounded, sleeping in the tombs, whom you remember no longer. This means: I, wounded by the spear, was considered dead under compulsion, like others who were wounded—not just any wounded, but those who have died [Col. 0949D] and sleep in tombs awaiting the resurrection, and who slept in such a way that you no longer remember them with regard to their transformation for the better.

Or alternatively: I was considered by them like the wounded, that is, pierced by the arrows of divine opposition—that is, like those who are completely blinded inwardly, sleeping in tombs, namely, resting content in dead works, whom you no longer remember by restoring them.

And they have been driven away from your hand. As if he were saying: They thought me, O Lord, deprived of your help, and therefore they themselves were driven away, both inwardly and outwardly, from your hand, that is, from the protection of your mercy.

They placed me. They were rightly driven away from your hand, because in their perverse estimation they placed me in the lower pit. Above, by “pit” we understood the deep misery of this life and the lower hell; here, however, we understand something more: the deepest condemnation of the wicked, and here finally the matter is made clear. Therefore—as if he were saying—they placed me in the lower pit because they received me among the darkness, that is, among those given over to darkness and deprived of the light of truth. And also in the shadow of death, that is, among those who are so utterly lost that they already display in themselves the shadow, or likeness, of death.

Your fury has been confirmed against me. As if he were saying: In their evil estimation they also said this about me: that your anger, O Lord, would not be against me for a time only, but that your fury had been confirmed, so that it would remain against me both here and in the future. They also said that in your ordering you had brought all your waves upon me, that is, both present tribulation and eternal damnation.

You have put my acquaintances far from me. As if he were saying: To increase the heap of my misery, this too was added: You caused—or permitted it to happen—that my acquaintances were far from me, if not in place, then in affection; namely, those who had both seen the miracles performed by me and understood my works. [Col. 0950B] And truly they were made far away, because they placed me before themselves as an abomination. For the one who began to detest him and swear that he did not know the man judged him sufficiently to be an abomination.

I was betrayed by one of them, and yet I did not go out, that is, I did not display the power of divinity. And therefore my eyes grew weak, that is, I was handed over to death, so that this may simply be a description of death. Or “eyes,” that is, even the more excellent members of my body through which I looked upon others, grew weak, that is, failed me through deprivation, because I displayed only the form of poverty, not the riches of divinity.

I cried out to you, O Lord. As if he were saying: Although I was surrounded by so many afflictions, I nevertheless did not therefore depart from my purpose, because, O Lord, I cried out, that is, I acted earnestly toward you to win your favor; and this not for an hour, but all day, that is, throughout the entire time of my service. I stretched out my hands, that is, I displayed my good works, to give an example to others, looking not toward human opinion, but toward you.

Will you work wonders for the dead? As if he were saying: Because I cried out to you, Lord, because I stretched out my hands all day, therefore repay me and raise me up, so that through me, once raised, you may work wonders, that is, restoration, for the living; for through me, dead—that is, not raised—you will not work wonders for the dead.

From this a syllogism by disjunction seems capable of being formed: Since it is certain that you will accomplish restoration through my death, either you will work wonders for the dead through me who am dead, that is, not raised, or for the living through me who am raised and living. But you will not work wonders for the dead through me who am dead; therefore, you will work them for the living through me who am alive.

In the book he places the assumption in the form of a question when he says: “Will you work wonders for the dead through me who am merely dead?” As if he were saying: This is impossible. Here he calls “dead” those who are dead both inwardly and outwardly, who are already descending to punishments suited to themselves; and therefore it is impossible for them to be restored any further, because there is no redemption in hell. Understand “the living,” however, as those who, although they are dead inwardly, nevertheless live outwardly, and therefore there is hope of restoration in them.

It is clear from this that restoration must take place through him, because he himself says in the Gospel: “For this I came, to bear witness to the truth.” Let us now return to the literal wording. “Will you work wonders for the dead through me who am dead?” Certainly not. “Or will physicians, future physicians”—namely, physicians of souls, true physicians, that is, holy teachers—raise the dead, that is, will they be able to raise those dead through restoration? Certainly not. Will those dead confess you any more in a salvific way? Certainly not, because hell will not confess the Lord.

Will anyone recount it? Truly physicians will not raise the dead, because they will be unable to recount your mercy to them, nor will anyone else. He says this in the form of a question: “Will anyone now recount your mercy, that is, your restoration, to the dead and to those placed in the tomb, and will anyone recount your truth to those placed in perdition, that is, in eternal damnation”—your truth, that is, either your true commands or the fulfillment of your promises? No one indeed.

Will your wonders be known in darkness? He says more than before. For he says that even if someone could recount these things to them, they nevertheless would not understand them, asking as follows: “Will your wonders, that is, your restoration, be able to be known by those who are in darkness, that is, in the dark places of hell? And will your justice, that is, your justifying grace, be known in the land of forgetfulness, that is, in that land of which you have completely forgotten through the visitation of your mercy?” As if he were saying: Certainly not; and even if there were someone who could recount these things to them, there would be no one who could understand them.

And I cried out to you, O Lord. As if he were saying: Since you do not work wonders for the dead through me who am dead, therefore, O Lord, raise me up, so that through me who am alive you may work wonders for the dead. Or repay me in kind, because I cried out to you. And truly you will do so, because my prayer will precede you, that is, it will appear to have gone before you and to have obtained its effect with you through my resurrection, which took place in the morning.

Why, O Lord, do you reject my prayer? Do you turn your face away from me? As if he were saying: Since you are going to hear me, why then, Lord, do you reject—that is, make my prayer appear to be rejected by you? And why do you seem to turn your face away from me, while you permit me to be so despised and so afflicted by my enemies? As if he were saying: Certainly you know, and I know, why this is so.

I am poor and in labors from my youth. Therefore, I said, you turn your face from me—as it appears—because I alone am suitable for your anger to pass through, and thus for restoration to take place. For I am truly poor, attributing absolutely nothing to myself. And I am in labors, bearing the weight of your commands from my youth, that is, from even that age which is more prone to falling.

But that I am poor and laboring does not arise from my incapacity, because I have been exalted through freedom from sins and the fullness of virtues. And yet I have been humbled by persecutors, and this not eternally but only for a time, because I was troubled. Why was I humbled, and why was I troubled? Namely, so that your anger, coming upon me, might pass through me, just as it truly did pass through me.

And so that your terrors, arranged by you, might pass through me—in accordance with the saying: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above”—I say, your terrors troubled me. And therefore I say “they troubled me,” because those torrents surrounded me like water, that is, so as to envelop and drown me, all day, that is, throughout the entire time of the Passion. I say that they surrounded me similarly, namely both the Jews and the Roman soldiers.

And to increase the heap of my misery you distanced—or permitted to be distanced—from me, if not in place, then in affection, a friend dear to me in heart and near in the flesh, such as James. You also distanced all my acquaintances, namely those to whom your signs and works had become known, from me—not as a poor man, but as one regarded as misery itself, that is, as leprosy.

[Col. 0951D] Will you work wonders for the dead, or will physicians raise them and will they confess to you? The passage can also be connected and read in this way. As if he were saying: I indeed cried out to you, O Lord, and stretched out my hands all day; why then do my enemies rage against me? Namely because they are dead inwardly, that is, blinded, and do not attend to my works.

And therefore there will be no restoration, which he says in the form of a question: “Will you work wonders, that is, restoration, for the dead whom your grace does not inwardly enlighten, so that the works of truth displayed by me may move them?” Certainly not. “Or will future physicians raise such people from their inward death so that they may confess to you?” Certainly not, because they will not even recount your wonders to them, in accordance with the saying: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.”

And this is what he says: “Will any of the physicians recount the mercy of your restoration to those placed in the tomb,” that is, persisting in and delighting in dead works, “and your truth to those placed in perdition,” that is, in eternal damnation? No one indeed. And rightly so, because even if it were recounted to them, they would not recognize it. For will your wonders be known in darkness, that is, among those whose reason is darkened because it has been deprived of the light of truth? And will your justice be known in the land of forgetfulness, that is, among those irrecoverably condemned? Certainly not.

And I. As if he were saying: I say that your wonders will not be known in darkness and that you will not work wonders for the dead; nevertheless, for some of them I cried out to you, Lord, as when he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” For this prayer benefited many, such as the centurion who said during the Passion: “Truly this was the Son of God,” and those who approached the apostles and said: “What shall we do, men and brothers?”—and many others.

And this is what follows: “And in the morning my prayer will precede you.” As if he were saying: I cried out to you for them. And not in vain, because my prayer will precede you, that is, it will appear that what I asked obtained its effect with you, as those who precede are accustomed to obtain something when the morning has come—that is, when the illumination of some of them had taken place, as in those whom we mentioned.

And because the scourges were increasing, since God chastises every son whom he receives, in accordance with the saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in fear and trembling, and prepare your soul for temptations,” he therefore adds: “Why, O Lord, do you reject?”—that is, make it appear that you reject, as so many evils increase upon them—“the prayer of my people,” which I call my own because of my excessive affection. And why do you appear to turn your face from me, that is, from my people?

As if he were saying: You certainly do this because you know them to be suitable people for whom, through such scourges, you prepare an eternal inheritance. For I am poor in them, because they presume nothing concerning themselves and attribute nothing to themselves. And I am in labors in them, because they bear the weight of your commands from a youth that is not theirs but mine, that is, from the renewal which not they but I effected in them through grace.

At times I have also been exalted in them, namely when the scourge is withdrawn and they are spared. For, as has already been said, if there were no delight, we would fail. And again I have been humbled in them when the scourges return and increase, because if there were complete security, we would rejoice wrongly. Yet I have been humbled in such a way that I was troubled, that is, humbled only for a time. He says this for our consolation, so that we may not fail in tribulation: tribulation will last only for a time, but rejoicing will be eternal.

And therefore—as if he were saying—I have been humbled in them so that your anger might pass into me, that is, into those who are mine, just as it truly did pass into them. Yet this was not done through them but through me. For so that your anger might pass into them, your terrors—that is, those arranged by you—troubled me. What follows does not change.

## ON PSALM 88

An understanding of Ethan the Ezrahite.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0952D] He foretells the captives in Babylon, relying not at all on their own merits but on the promises made by the Lord to David, so that he who had promised to preserve the whole race of the Jews, or its kings, may deign to fulfill the pledge by his deeds, protecting the peoples in honor of the kings. Or it is the voice of Christ to the Father concerning the Jews. Alternatively, the history is sung concerning the time when the people were counted.

### EXPLANATION

Ethan is interpreted as “strong.” Since this psalm was going to recount the Lord’s praises and promises, the unchangeable firmness of faithful words is indicated beforehand by the name “strong.” An “understanding” is necessarily prescribed here, since an eternal throne of David is promised, which meanwhile, according to the historical account, is seen formerly to have been destroyed.

This Ethan, like Heman, is either one of King David’s singers, whom the Books of Chronicles mention—namely, the son of Kishi, son of Abdi, of the clan of Merari, son of Levi—or he is one of those wise men to whom Solomon’s wisdom is preferred in the Book of Kings. “Wiser,” it says, “than Ethan the Ezrahite and Heman.” This song therefore possesses such great knowledge that it deserves to be attributed to the name of that exceedingly wise man.

This Ethan, the strong man, was filled with such illumination of mind that he is most truly called an Israelite. At the beginning of the psalm he says that he will sing of the Lord’s mercies, because the Lord promised many things that would benefit the faithful people. In the second part he describes the Lord’s praises and power in various ways. In the third he enumerates the paternal promises concerning Christ. In the fourth the Lord himself is declared to have been handed over to enemies because of the Passion he endured. In the fifth he asks that help be given to human weakness, since he formed the children of human beings in vain. In the sixth he asks the Lord to fulfill his promises, which he is declared to have made to David his servant, and to remember the reproaches that his servants endured from the wicked.

### COMMENTARY

I will sing the mercies of the Lord forever. An understanding of Ethan the Israelite. This psalm treats of the hope of God’s promise that we have in our Lord Jesus Christ, because he who promised will complete the rest as well, just as he has already completed much. It gives us confidence in him, not our merit but his mercy. This is the understanding of Ethan, from which the psalm received its title.

I say, Ethan the Israelite, because no one can attain this understanding unless he is such a person of whom it can be said: “Behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” For Solomon says that the Spirit of holy discipline will flee deceit and will not dwell in a body subject to sins.

Ethan is interpreted as “strong,” and no one in this age is strong except in the hope of God’s promise. As far as our merit is concerned, we are weak; but as far as his mercy is concerned, we are strong. Therefore this man, weak in himself but strong in the hope of divine mercy, begins in this way:

“I will sing,” that is, I will frequently praise, both in myself and in others, the mercies of the Lord—that is, the restoration accomplished not by our merits but by the Lord’s mercy alone. In myself I will praise them by doing good; in others I will praise them by showing that whatever they are is due solely to mercy.

Or: I will sing the Lord’s mercies in myself and make them singable to others—mercies, I say, that will remain forever. He uses the plural “mercies” because as many as have received mercy, that is, have been restored through mercy, so many are the mercies. He adds “forever” to show by this that the anger through Adam was temporal, whereas the mercy granted through Christ is eternal.

From generation to generation. I will sing, I say, the mercies, and I will announce your truth, not my falsehood, with my mouth now speaking, that is, with a harmonious heart, because I announce what belongs to you. As if he were saying: Let my members serve my Lord; I will speak, but I will speak your words, because I will announce your truth with my mouth.

For if I do not serve, I am not a servant; and if I speak my own words, I am a liar. Therefore, so that I may both speak and speak what is yours, there are two things here, one mine and the other yours: your truth and my mouth. Therefore I will announce your truth with my mouth, truth, I say, extending from generation to generation, that is, forever, just as mercy does.

Or, according to another wording, we shall say: truth existing from generation to generation, that is, in every generation. Blessed Augustine says that one generation cannot be repeated as often as one generation dies and another succeeds. Therefore the phrase “from generation to generation” is expressed with repetition so that the whole matter may be understood.

Understand “mercy” throughout the psalm as the remission of sins, and “truth” as the fulfillment of promises. Yet sometimes “truth” may also be understood as the fulfillment of commands. Let us hear, then, what mercies he sings and what truth he announces.

For you have said. Therefore I will confidently sing your mercies, and therefore I will announce your truth, because you, who neither deceive nor are deceived, have said, that is, promised mercy and truth, saying in your ordering as follows:

“Mercy,” that is, future restoration, “will be built up through grace,” that is, it will be perfected and extend forever. This means: I build in such a way that I will not destroy. And it truly will be so, because in those restored through mercy and made heavens your truth, that is, the completion of your promises, will be prepared—that is, displayed to others—so that they may not despair but hope, and so that through their constancy it may clearly appear in them: in one there will be knowledge of languages, in another the grace of healings, in another the discernment of spirits, and the other spiritual gifts, just as you promised when you said: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh.” When others see this, they will not despair of the fulfillment of the promises.

Or alternatively: You said, I say, that mercy will be built up forever. And truly it will be so, because truth, that is, your true commands, will be prepared—more worthily than in others—in certain heavens, of which it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God,” and so forth. And thus they will be in them, that is, they will clearly appear in them, because they will do what he says. Through whom? As if he were saying: That mercy will be built up in others. (So much for this.)

I have established a covenant. As if he were saying: You said that, and you also said this: “To my rejected ones I gave a certain old covenant, but for my chosen ones I established my covenant,” that is, the new covenant, through which they would be restored to eternal glory.

And not only did I establish it, but I also swore, that is, firmly promised it, to David my servant. What did I promise? This, namely: “I will prepare your seed, which will remain forever.” God’s oath is nothing other than confirmation of a promise. And he can safely swear, lest he incur perjury through a habit of swearing.

If above he made this man confident in announcing mercy and truth because he said, “I have spoken; I have established,” he now makes him much more confident because he says, “I have sworn.” It is as if he were saying: “I have spoken; I have established.” If that is not enough, “I have sworn.”

Although this prayer was historically made to David, it was nevertheless done in such a way that the promise was to be fulfilled not in David himself but in his seed. David’s seed is the same as Abraham’s seed. Abraham’s seed is the one of whom it was said: “And to your seed, who is Christ.” Understand Christ not only as the one who was born according to the flesh from the Virgin Mary, but also as all those who believe in him. For the whole Christ is Head and body, because no one can behead this body, nor can this Head exist without the body. Therefore Christ and his body are the seed of David. And concerning this seed it was said: “I will prepare your seed forever.”

And I will build. I have sworn, I say, to David: “I will prepare your seed.” And I also swore this to him: “I will build your throne,” that is, those in whom you sit, not through yourself but through your seed, from generation to generation.

There are two generations: one by which we are generated here, and the other by which we will be regenerated in the resurrection. Christ is proclaimed in both: in this one so that he may be believed, and in the other so that he may be seen. A throne is prepared for him in this generation, because if he did not sit in us, he would not rule us. If we were not ruled by him, we would fall through our own agency.

Therefore he sits in us in this generation, reigning; he will also sit in us in regeneration, because he will reign forever in his saints.

The heavens will confess. Ethan spoke the preceding words in the voice of the Lord; here he speaks in his own voice. The connection is therefore as follows: Since through your mercy the heavens were made, and your truth, not theirs, will be prepared in them, therefore, Lord, the heavens will confess, that is, praise your wonders, not their own.

What wonders? Namely, that the lost have been redeemed and the dead have risen. For it is a great wonder that those whom yesterday we saw as a whirlpool of drunkenness, today we behold as an adornment of sobriety; those who were formerly filth of lust are now the glory of self-control; and those who were formerly blasphemers today adore the Creator.

And truly they will confess your wonders, for—in place of “because”—they will confess your truth, that is, the completion of your promises, or your true commands. Yet they will not do so in such a way as to scatter pearls before swine; rather, they will do this especially in the Church of the saints, where it ought truly to be done.

Because who among the clouds can be compared with the Lord? Therefore, deservedly, the heavens will confess your wonders, not their own, because none of them can be compared with you. For who among the clouds can be compared with the Lord of the clouds? Certainly no one. The Apostles and the other holy preachers are called “heavens” because of the flashing forth of truth; they are also called “clouds,” for many other reasons, and especially because of the hiddenness of the flesh, that is, hidden thoughts. For we see what comes forth from a cloud, but we do not see what lies hidden within the cloud. Likewise, we can judge what a person says or does, but what he thinks is seen only by him who searches the heart and the kidneys. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not judge before the time,” and so forth. Christ himself also had a cloud, because he concealed the majesty of his divinity beneath the cloud of flesh. [Col. 0955B] But this cloud differs from those clouds: this one is from an undefiled virgin, whereas those are from a corrupt mother; this one is without sin, while those were cleansed from sin through it. And therefore he says: “Who among the clouds can be compared with the Lord of the clouds?” Or, “Who among the sons of God will be like the Lord, the Son of God?” Certainly no one. For he is one by nature, whereas they are many by grace. He is from eternity, they are from time—and there are many other differences.

**The God who is glorified.** Truly, no one is like him. For this is the God who is glorified in the counsel of the saints, that is, whose glory increases through the counsel that the saints have concerning him: namely, that they should believe in him and no longer seek what is theirs, but what is God’s. Thus, “let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.” Solomon says: “In the multitude of the people is the glory of the king; but in the diminution of the people is the ruin of the prince.” And deservedly (as if he were saying): He is glorified in the counsel of the saints, because he alone is great, while all the others are small. For he is great who fills every place according to his divinity, and he is terrifying not merely in one nation, but likewise over all who are around him. [Col. 0955C] For he willed to be born, crucified, die, rise again, and ascend for our sake in that one nation alone, which was surrounded on every side by the other nations as land is surrounded by the sea. That nation alone was cultivated because of the Law and the prophetic writings; all the others were the sea, that is, remaining in the bitterness of their barrenness. Yet he did not make his truth known only in that one nation; nevertheless, there he thundered forth especially, from the cloud of his flesh, among those nations through other clouds, just as he himself promised, saying: “From now on you will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven.” And what is said here came to pass. For the sound of the holy Apostles went out into all the earth, threatening tribulation and distress to every soul that works evil. Thus he became terrifying over all who were around him. Understand “himself” together with those who believe in him as the body of Jesus from that people; for it is with reference to this that the prophet says that the nations are around him.

**Lord God of hosts, who is like you?** As if he were saying: [Col. 0955D] Therefore, no one is like you. And truly no one is, because you alone, Lord, are powerful. Great indeed is the power of him who made heaven and earth and all that is in them.

**And your truth is around you.** As if he were saying: Your power, Lord, is indeed great, but your mercy is far greater, through which your truth—that is, your true commandments—has been spread around you. For if his truth had been spread only in that nation in which he willed to be born, crucified, and die for us, then only what the Apostle says would have been fulfilled: “I say that Christ Jesus was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers.” But what follows would not have been fulfilled, namely: “But the Gentiles are to glorify God for his mercy,” and so forth.

This spreading could not take place without great contradiction and persecution. For then the roaring lion met Samson as he was going to take, or seeking to take, a wife from the foreigners, and became like a young goat in his hands. That is, the raging Gentile world firmly contradicted and resisted the [Col. 0956A] holy preachers at first; but after it recognized its sins, it became like a languishing sinner in their hands, because it humbled itself and repented. And this is what follows:

**You rule the power of the sea, its movement.** As if he were saying: When your truth, Lord, was being spread around you, the sea of the Gentiles was troubled. But what did the sea do? It killed the martyrs, certainly; it poured out the seed of blood, through which the crop of the Church sprang up. Let the sea therefore rage; let the sea be troubled as much as it wishes. Nevertheless, it will be able to do nothing except insofar as it is permitted. This is evident from the fact that you rule the power of the sea, that is, those who, when they were the sea, were so powerful in contradicting and persecuting, have now passed into your dominion. The sea has indeed been moved, but you calm the movement of its waves without removing it altogether. For contradiction and persecution still remain, even among false brothers.

**You humbled.** Truly you rule the power of the sea, because the prince of this world has been cast out; for you, [Col. 0956B] having been humbled, humbled that proud one. For that proud one possessed the proud. But when human beings were given so great an example of humility in Christ, they learned to condemn pride and desire humility. Thus that proud one was humbled, because one stronger than he entered his house, plundered his goods, and transferred them into the adornments of the Church. You, I say, being humbled, humbled the proud one; and you, being wounded, wounded him as one wounded—not with flesh pierced, but with heart transfixed, as though his spirit and power had been diminished. In this way you scattered your enemies, so that those who had previously been enemies might become friends. And you did this by the arm of your power, through him who is your arm and your power. For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

**The heavens are yours.** And because you rescued them from the yoke of the proud one who had been humbled, therefore, Lord, the heavens—that is, those who pour down rain—are yours. For what they are and what they pour down is yours, and the earth, once rained upon, which had previously been alienated, is yours. And rightly yours, because you founded—that is, established—in the [Col. 0956C] knowledge of your truth the circle of the earth, that is, that earth, making it a circle, that is, perfect. And you did this not sparingly, but abundantly, because you founded its fullness.

And truly you founded it, because you created in good works the North, that is, those in whom charity had grown cold through iniquity, because they were members of that North of which he said: “I will set my throne in the North, and I will be like the Most High.” You also created in good works the sea, that is, those who were bitter in their barrenness.

Or otherwise: as if he were saying: Since you founded the circle of the earth and its fullness, therefore the North is no longer to be feared by them. Or the sea is the North, the ancient enemy. And the sea—that is, those in whom he works as in his vessels to attack the people of God—are not to be feared, because you created the North and you created the sea. And since they are your creation, they can do nothing against you except by permission. As if he were saying: What you have done in them for your condemnation is stronger than their will toward their [Col. 0956D] own wickedness.

**Tabor and Hermon.** You founded the earth, I say, and you began from Jerusalem. This is indicated by the very order of the words, when he says: “Tabor and Hermon will rejoice,” no longer in their own name, but in the glorification of your name.

*Tabor* is interpreted as “the coming light.” The coming light is the Jewish people, who were principally illuminated and came like a light to others, because through those illuminated from that people, others from the Gentiles were illuminated. Whence, then, did this light come? From him, certainly, who illuminates every person coming into this world: the light that is kindled by no other and will never be extinguished.

*Hermon*, however, is interpreted as “his anathema.” By this the Gentiles are understood, now anathematizing and rejecting him—that is, the devil—who previously they loved and worshiped. And deservedly (as if he were saying): These will rejoice in your name, because your arm, which made the former people illuminators and the latter people those who anathematize the [Col. 0957A] one whom they had previously loved, is with power—that is, it is truly powerful—whereas all the others are powerless.

**Let your hand be strengthened.** As if he were saying: And so that they may always rejoice in your name, therefore, Lord, let your hand—that is, your protection—be strengthened, that is, let it be firm and sustaining in them, so that they may not fail but progress. And let your hand now be strengthened in such a way that at last your right hand may be exalted, that is, that those destined to stand at your right hand may be exalted.

And truly this will happen: your right hand will be exalted, and it will be the preparation of your throne, that is, it will prepare for you a judicial throne in them through righteousness and judgment—that is, through action and discernment. Judgment properly consists in distinguishing between good and evil; righteousness consists in adhering to the good and rejecting evil.

Or otherwise: Let your hand be strengthened in them, as above. But in those in whom your hand is not now strengthened, let your right hand—that is, your power—be exalted at last. Such is the meaning of: “Your right hand will find all those who hate you.” And this will truly happen, because the preparation of your throne will be that which you judge. [Col. 0957B] And what will be judged by you? Righteousness, certainly, and judgment. Relate righteousness to the good, but judgment—which is used here for condemnation—to the wicked. For then there will be righteousness, when the good rejoice as they see what they believed without seeing it. There will be judgment, however, when the wicked tremble as they see what they refused to believe while mocking it.

**Mercy and truth.** As if he were saying: At last your right hand will be exalted; meanwhile, however, mercy and truth will go before your face, that is, your manifest coming. Mercy consists in the acquittal of sinners, while truth consists in the fulfillment of promises. Or mercy consists in promising mercifully, and truth in faithfully fulfilling what was promised. Whoever pays attention to this will ultimately be among those for whom there is righteousness; whoever does not pay attention will be among those for whom there is judgment.

In the earlier reading, the passage will be connected in this way: Righteousness and judgment will indeed prepare a throne for you in them, but they will not have this from themselves; rather, they will have it from you, because mercy and truth will go before your face—that is, your presence [Col. 0957C] in them—and will accomplish this.

And since the preparation of your throne will take place through mercy and truth, both here and at the end, therefore that people is truly blessed which knows how to rejoice worthily—that is, which understands the reason why it ought to praise you so greatly that it cannot express it in words, and therefore begins to rejoice with inarticulate jubilation.

**Lord, they will walk in the light of your countenance.** For this reason I call that people blessed: it knows worthily the reason for rejoicing, because it certainly understands that all that it is comes from your mercy, Lord, as is truly the case. For they will walk in good works in the light of your countenance, not their own—that is, in the illumination of your will, not of their own merits. And they will rejoice in your name, glorifying it, not in their own; and they will rejoice in yours all day long, that is, continually, both here and in the future. For if they rejoiced in their own name, they would quickly cease rejoicing. And they will be exalted in your righteousness, because previously they were humbled in their own.

**For you are the glory of their power.** Or for this reason they will deservedly [Col. 0957D] rejoice in your name: because you are the glory of their power, while they themselves are the disgrace of their weakness. Whatever power there is in them of which they can boast comes from you, not from themselves. Therefore our horn—that is, our spiritual exaltation—will be lifted up in your good pleasure, not in our merit. And truly in your good pleasure, because our assumption belongs to the Lord—that is, to you.

This means that it is solely from your mercy that you assumed human nature for the sake of redeeming us, or that you assumed us from the mass of those who were perishing. And he specifies whose assumption it is: that of the Holy One of Israel, that is, of him who sanctifies everyone who is a true Israel. And he is our King, that is, he governs us in the virtues so that we may attain to the true vision, where we shall see face to face.

**Then you spoke.** As if he were saying: And concerning this assumption just mentioned, you then spoke to your saints, that is, to the prophets, in vision—that is, through revelation in words and deeds. Visions properly belong to the prophets; hence [Col. 0958A] in former times the prophets themselves were also called “seers.”

And then, I say, you spoke to your saints, namely when you said that which was mentioned above: “Mercy will be built up forever.” And in speaking you promised—that is, you said this: I, who previously placed my help in a certain powerless one who did not persevere and was not an example of obedience, will now place my help in one who is truly powerful. And because you cast down that rejected one, I will exalt this chosen one from my people.

And deservedly will I exalt him, because in this David I found truly my servant, who will not apostatize even in thought. In accordance with the saying: “I have found David, the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart.” Therefore I will anoint him with my holy oil—that is, with the oil of which it is said elsewhere: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.” This means: I will fill him with spiritual gifts.

**For my hand.** Truly I will anoint him, because I will act toward him in this way: my hand—that is, my mercy and protection—will help him with regard to the humanity he has assumed. And my arm—that is, my Word personally united to him—will strengthen him against [Col. 0958B] every fall. Therefore the enemy, the devil, will accomplish nothing in him.

As if he were saying: In Adam the enemy did and completed his work; in this one he will indeed do what is his—that is, he will tempt him—but he will accomplish nothing, either in him or in those who belong to him. He will exercise him, but he will not harm him. By raging, the enemy will be of benefit, in that these others will be crowned through conquering; and the son of iniquity—that is, the apostate angel, whom iniquity begot—will not add to harming him.

He will indeed attempt to harm him when he causes him to be crucified and killed; but after he sees him rising and ascending, he will no longer add to harming him. Indeed, he [Christ] will rejoice eternally that the enemy had previously attempted to harm him.

**And I will crush.** The enemy, I say, will accomplish nothing in him; and therefore, just as Moses crushed the head of the molten calf and gave it to the people to drink, so I will crush—that is, gradually grind down—his enemies and transfer them into his body. And I will do this from his face, that is, from his presence. For his very presence and knowledge will be the cause of this.

And thus I say that I will crush them: I will turn those who previously hated him [Col. 0958C] to flight, so that they flee from the angry one to the reconciled one.

Or otherwise: In the future I will crush his enemies from his face, that is, I will drive them from his presence into eternal darkness. For it is said: “Let the ungodly be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God.” And meanwhile I will turn those who hate him to flight, so that they flee from the angry one to the reconciled one.

**And my truth and my mercy will be with him.** This seems impossible to say with reference to the head itself. For he did not need mercy, since he had nothing that could be forgiven. Nevertheless, even in him we can call the assumption of humanity itself mercy, and truth the fulfillment of that promise, because God gave him the name that is above every name. And because he did not give him the Spirit by measure.

Or, if this interpretation pleases no one, let him say that the statement refers to the members, in whom there truly are both truth in the fulfillment of promises and mercy in the remission of sins. Throughout the whole of divine Scripture these two things in particular are set before us—mercy and truth—so that we too may practice them: mercy [Col. 0958D] by showing mercy to the miserable, and truth by judging what is just. Thus neither mercy may exclude truth in us, nor truth exclude mercy. For many, through a perverted compassion, often prefer the unjust cause of a poor person to the just cause of a rich person.

My truth, I say, and my mercy will be with him; and in my name—that is, because he and those who belong to him are glorifying my name, not their own—his horn will be exalted, that is, his spiritual exaltation and that of his own. For my glorification itself will be their exaltation.

And I will place his hand—that is, his power—in the sea, that is, among the Gentiles who are becoming bitter in their barrenness. And I will place his right hand also in the rivers, that is, among those who, through desire, flow more and more into the bitter waves of this sea, just as rivers flow into the sea. This means: We shall subject even the most desperate to him.

**He will call upon me.** I will therefore do for him the things I have said, because he alone will worthily call upon me, saying: “You are my Father, my God according to your divinity, and my God according to my humanity, [Col. 0959A] and the protector of my salvation,” because you assumed me with regard to the humanity assumed and with regard to salvation.

**And I will make him the firstborn.** He will indeed worthily call upon me, and I will repay him in kind, because I will make him firstborn. This means either honored above all, just as firstborn sons were honored above all in the household, or firstborn in the sense of being free among the dead. And I will make him exalted not only above tyrants, but also above the kings of the earth, that is, above all who rule illicit movements within themselves.

And I will preserve for him, in those who belong to him, my mercy forever, because I will always be merciful toward them. And this because my covenant—that is, the New Covenant—is faithful, not unfaithful; that is, it is firm and certain for him and his own.

It is so for him because this covenant was also contemplated in him, and he is the mediator, the signer, the witness, and the guarantor of the covenant, as well as the inheritance of the covenant and its co-heir.

[Col. 0959B] **And I will establish his seed forever and ever.** Because my covenant will be faithful to him, therefore I will establish his spiritual seed, not carnal seed, lasting forever and ever—that is, eternally—and his throne, that is, those in whom he will sit as in his judicial power. For the soul of the righteous is the seat of God.

Those, I say, I will establish like the days of heaven, that is, they will be so illuminated that, like the days of heaven, which no night interrupts and which are without darkness, they will guard themselves from all sins that can truly be called sins. For no one is so perfect that he does not occasionally fall into some venial sins. We do not yet possess these days of heaven; but in the future, when we are crowned with immortality and impassibility, we shall possess them.

For there will not be many days, but only one day without end, because it will be without night; nevertheless, because of its great duration, he calls that one day “days” in the plural.

**But if his children forsake.** As if someone were to say to him: You promise that his seed will remain forever; but what if his children sin? He shows that even for this reason [Col. 0959C] his promise will not be removed, saying:

If his children forsake my law—and they will therefore forsake it because they have not walked in my judgments, that is, they have not done what my law judges ought to be done, but rather the opposite, because they will profane—that is, pollute—my righteous ordinances, introducing injustices in their place; and if they do not keep, indeed neglect, my commandments—if, I say, they do this and that, I will not therefore despise them, nor will I leave them in destruction. Rather, like a physician, I will visit their iniquities with a rod, that is, with a father’s chastisement, so that I may correct, not destroy.

And he specifies what he understands by the rod and by iniquities, saying: “And I will visit their sins with blows.” Behold the mercy of God, not only when he calls, but also when he chastises. For it is better to be corrected and instructed under a father’s punishment than to perish under a robber’s flattery.

**But my mercy.** I will indeed visit them with the rod, but in doing this I will not withdraw it from that David, that is, from that seed. Rather, I will preserve [Col. 0959D] my mercy in him. Let him therefore impose discipline, so that he may not remove mercy from him. Let him strike the obstinate, so that he may restore the inheritance.

I say that I will not scatter my mercy from him, nor will I ultimately harm him in my truth, that is, in my judgment, when my truth is revealed. For mercy, which delivers, is not scattered for this purpose.

**Nor will I profane my covenant.** As if he were saying: I will not scatter my mercy from him, I say; and in this way I will not profane my covenant, that is, my pact made with him.

We may understand “covenant” either as that saying found elsewhere: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you, says the Lord”; or as what has been said here, namely: If his children sin, I will not allow them to perish, but I will visit them with the rod.

I will not profane the covenant, I say, and I will not make void—that is, render empty—but will make firm and stable the things that proceed from my lips, namely, that his seed will remain forever. For even if his children sin incorrigibly and [Col. 0960A] perish without being corrected by the father’s chastisement, nevertheless the grain will not be rejected because of the chaff, nor will the good fish be cast out because of certain evil fish. For I have already foreseen other children in whom the things that proceed from my lips will be fulfilled.

**Once I swore by my holiness.** Truly I will not make void the things proceeding from my lips, because I swore—that is, I firmly promised—to David by my holiness, that is, in my holiness, that his seed would remain forever. And once I swore to him; do not expect me to swear a second time, as though I would deceive him after the first. If, then (as if he were saying), I lie to David, I will no longer tell the truth to anyone.

**And his throne.** Truly his seed will remain forever, because it will be restored to eternity both according to the inner person and according to the outer person. He says this equivalently: His throne—that is, those who are his seat—will ultimately be placed in my sight, that is, restored to eternity. In soul they will be like the sun, that is, as unfailing as the light of the sun; and in body [Col. 0960B] they will be like the moon.

And because sacred Scripture commonly signifies the defect of mortality by the moon, he therefore adds: “Perfect forever.” As if he were saying: If there were a moon that were perfect forever, understand this statement with reference to it, because they will be like the moon.

Behold, a useful restoration is promised to us in both respects, in soul and in body. Many doubted this restoration, not with regard to the soul—for philosophers had said much about its eternity—but with regard to the body. In this matter all the Jews except the Pharisees also erred. Hence, when Paul was being beaten by other Jews because he preached the resurrection, he cried out: “I am a Pharisee; I am being judged concerning the resurrection,” so that he might be rescued by the Pharisees themselves.

And because there would be manifold doubt about the restoration just mentioned, the Prophet adds a testimony of truth to confirm what he has said. As if he were saying: I have spoken of the future restoration of soul and body, and there is a faithful witness of this matter in heaven: namely, the one who rose from the dead, ascended, and sits at the right hand of Majesty. [Col. 0960C] And when he rose, he retained the scars in his flesh, so that he might heal the wound of doubt in our heart.

**But you have rejected.** Blessed Augustine says that what seem to be said here concerning the overthrow of the promises are to be understood of David in the historical sense. According to the letter, ignorant people seemed to think that the promise had been made in such a way that it would be fulfilled in his carnal seed. The Prophet gives voice to such a literal approach:

You promised this to David your servant, Lord. But, on the contrary, you acted otherwise. Where, then, are your promises, about which shortly before we rejoiced, over which we clapped our hands eagerly, with which, as though secure, we congratulated ourselves—as though one person had promised and another had overturned them? You yourself truly promised; indeed, because of human doubt, you swore as well. Yet you have done this. Where, then, is your promise? Show what you swore; give back what you promised.

It has been taken away in this David, so that what the Spirit himself saw when he said, “But you have rejected,” and so forth, should not be expected in this David. After this, however, in explaining the [Col. 0960D] meaning, he says:

The promise was truly made so that it might be certain. And David was appointed as the one to whom all these things were promised as things to be fulfilled in his seed, which is Christ. But because ignorant people thought that, on account of the promise, these things were to be fulfilled in David, God therefore destroyed in David the things that nevertheless had to be fulfilled. Thus, when they seemed not to have been fulfilled in him, another would be sought in whom they would be recognized as completed.

So it was prophesied concerning those two brothers, Esau and Jacob, that “the elder will serve the younger.” But because this was not fulfilled in those two themselves, the two peoples signified by those two had to be awaited, in whom what God, who cannot lie, had deigned to promise would be fulfilled.

So also it was promised to David that his seed would remain forever. A son was born to him of such wisdom and such power that the promises of God seemed to have been fulfilled in him. But Solomon fell, and gave place to hope in Christ. Since God could not be deceived, and since he would not place his promise in one whom he knew would fall, after Solomon’s fall [Col. 0961A] we sought another to whom the promise belonged.

In this interpretation, the text is explained as follows:

You, God, who promised David that his seed would remain forever, and the other things mentioned above, acted contrariwise, because you rejected him from the kingdom through the persecution of his son Absalom, your Christ—that is, your anointed one—and in rejecting him you despised him, that is, made him contemptible. And therefore I say that you rejected and despised him, because you delayed him from the integrity of the kingdom through that persecution. For it is said that before the death of Absalom he was king over Israel, and that he had likewise been anointed in the person of Adam.

**You have turned away.** What follows is said concerning David himself with regard to his body. For just as the multitude of believers is understood as the body of Christ, so that carnal people are understood as the body of David.

The meaning is: You rejected him in himself, and you also turned away the covenant—that is, the pact made with that servant of yours—in those who belong to him. For where, as if he were saying, is the kingdom? Where is the priesthood? Where is the sacrifice? Where is the legal institution? They have certainly [Col. 0961B] perished.

And you profaned his sanctuary—that is, the place where holy things were kept, namely, the Temple, which alone existed on earth—by allowing it to become profane and polluted.

You destroyed all his hedges, that is, the prophets and kings who stood around and defended him in those who belonged to him. And you made the stronghold fear, that is, the tribulation of those defenders was so great that anyone would fear to strengthen—that is, defend—him.

Therefore all who passed along the way plundered him in those who belonged to him, whether these were those who ruled temporally or those who did not know the truth, as has already been said elsewhere. And he became a reproach to his neighbors, that is, to all the nations around him.

And therefore he became a reproach, because you exalted the right hand—that is, the power—of those who oppressed him to such an extent that you made all his enemies rejoice through the victory granted over him.

And in order to exalt the right hand of those who oppressed him, you turned away the help of his sword, that is, you withdrew yourself from him. With your help, two had previously put ten thousand to flight. [Col. 0961C] You, who previously went out with him to battle, because you acted with him through such manifest signs that you were understood to be present, have now not helped him in war.

You destroyed him from outward cleansing, because you made him appear unclean to all, and from inward cleansing, concerning which it is said: “Cleansing hearts by faith.” And you shattered his seat—that is, the city in which he had previously rested and greatly delighted—which was reduced to the earth, that is, utterly destroyed.

And deservedly he was defeated and destroyed; deservedly he lost that land for which he killed his Lord.

**You shortened the days of time.** Because, while they promised themselves a divine and eternal status in their legal institutions, you quickly brought them to an end. And you covered him with confusion, that is, you gave him complete confusion: inwardly, blindness of mind; outwardly, tribulation of the flesh.

**How long, O Lord?** [Col. 0961D] All the things mentioned above happened in David, in whom foolish and ignorant people thought that God would fulfill his commandments, so that the promises of God might be fulfilled more firmly in Christ and in his kingdom. Therefore he adds: “How long, O Lord, will you turn away?”

As if he were saying: If this had to be done with the chaff, it must not be done in the same way with the grain. How long, then, Lord, will you turn yourself away from that people, permitting it to remain turned away? Perhaps not forever, because even if blindness has come upon Israel in part, so that the fullness of the Gentiles may enter, from this the remnant will be saved.

Meanwhile, however (as if he were saying), let your anger burn like fire—that is, in such a way that it may purify some, namely those who are converted, and reduce others to ashes, namely those who will not be converted, just as material fire reduces some things to ashes and purifies others.

**Remember what my substance is.** As if he were saying: Do not turn away altogether from that people, Lord, but remember what my substance is—that is, who it is through whom I and the others who believe in you subsist—so that you may spare that people.

For the root has not perished completely; rather, the seed to which the promise was made will come. For from that people came [Col. 0962A] the Virgin Mary, and from Mary came Christ, who is the substance of all believers.

Remember this substance, therefore, because unless you remember it, you seem to have established the children of human beings in vain. But did you establish them in vain? Certainly not. Rather, they went away of themselves into vanity, from which they must necessarily be recalled.

What cleanser, what restorer will they have, unless you preserve for them someone through whom they may be recalled? And who is he? That man, certainly, who, having died, will live and will no longer see death. For Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies; death will no longer rule over him.

And because this could also apply to every holy man, since a dead person will live in the resurrection and afterward will not see death, he therefore adds: He himself will rescue his soul by his own power from the hand of the underworld, that is, from the power of death. For this applies to no one else except the Lord Jesus Christ alone. And this is our catholic faith.

Because this faith was long resisted and the holy preachers were opposed with many troubles and tribulations, the Prophet, [Col. 0962B] praying for the incorporation of those who resisted and for the cessation of persecution, says: 

**Lord, where are your ancient mercies?** That is, those promised from of old, just as you swore—those which you swore to David in your truth.

As if he were saying: We have now recognized Christ the cleanser; we now hold the one in whom you fulfill your promises, because he is the one who will live and will not see death, and who himself will rescue his soul from the hand of the underworld. Yet we are still afflicted and suffer persecutions, because for your sake we are put to death all day long.

**Remember, Lord.** As if he were saying: Even though Christ has come and taken his seat in heaven, we still suffer reproach in him, because it is thrown in our face that we worship one who died, that we believe in one crucified as a thief, and similar things. Therefore, Lord, remember the reproach of your servants—the reproach, namely, of many nations. Of the nations as those who inflict it, and of the servants as those who endure it.

I have contained this reproach in my bosom, and I have already foreseen it, hidden, as something destined to occur [Col. 0962C] in those who will be born from my bosom.

Or “which I have contained” [*continui*, in place of *contenturus*, “about to contain”], that is, which I will suffer in those who will not depart from my bosom, so that the hand brought forth from the bosom may be unclean; but the hand will be clean when brought back into the bosom, that is, they will remain with me in the same faith.

Or “which I have contained” [*continui*, in place of “which I will contain”] in my descendants through faith, in my bosom—that is, with me—because I will not dare to repel that reproach by contradicting it; rather, by remaining silent, I will conceal it within myself.

For as long as the Church remained in persecution and tribulation, and it was a crime to be a Christian, just as it is now a crime to be a pagan, the wicked freely insulted and reproached the faithful, because they could find nothing with which to contradict them.

Thanks be to God, however, that now no one insults the Church—or, if anyone does insult it, does not do so publicly. The evil things he says he is more afraid will be heard than eager to have believed.

“Remember” is understood in two ways: either remember in such a way that those who inflict the reproach, once converted, may themselves suffer from others the same reproach that they [Col. 0962D] now inflict upon the servants of God; or remember in such a way that, because of this temporal reproach, they may be given over to the reproach of eternal punishments.

What they reproached. He shows how they said that reproach belonged to many nations—namely, to those who reproached, not to those reproached. For your enemies among the nations, Lord, reproached this reproach; I mean those who reproached the exchange involving your servants, the exchange involving your Christ. What—that is, the matter—which they reproached most of all. He calls Christ’s death by the honorable name “exchange,” and rightly, because there truly was an exchange there, that is, a change for the better: from mortality to eternity, corruption to incorruption, disgrace to glory, and death to life. For this exchange, I say, such great hope has been given to us. Blessed forever be the Lord, who by his blood freely made us safe: he sought out the wandering, found them, redeemed them; he freed us from the dominion and power of the devil and transferred us from the kingdom of darkness into the kingdom [Col. 0963A] of light. Let blessing be given to him in those people; let it also be given in these.

From the place where we made the digression to the historical David, nearly everything that follows can be read differently, so that we remain above with the true David alone. According to this, the preceding lengthy continuation may be abbreviated as follows: “You indeed promised these things, Lord, but you acted otherwise, because you rejected”—that is, permitted him to appear rejected by you—“when your Christ was scourged and crucified. And you despised him”—that is, made him appear despicable—“when he was spat upon and crowned with thorns. And you delayed him”—that is, as regards the body, you permitted him to remain delayed for a long time. For the Church from the nations, as though a barren and widowed bride of Christ, remained after his death; afterward his brothers, namely the apostles, approached her and raised up seed for the dead brother. Thus at last Christ, who had previously been delayed as regards his members, was perfected … [lacuna].”

You overturned the covenant. You delayed Christ, I say, and in this way you seemed to have overturned the covenant of your servant, that is, the promise you had made to that servant of yours—namely, that his seed would remain forever. You profaned—that is, permitted to appear polluted—those who were his sanctuary, that is, his secondary dwelling place on earth, such as the holy apostles and the other earlier believers, who became the refuse of all and a spectacle to angels and human beings. You also destroyed—that is, permitted to be destroyed—all his hedges. By “hedges” understand lesser persons, yet such persons as would serve as protection for others who were lesser. And the tribulation was so great that you made his stronghold fear, as above.

All who passed along the road tore him apart externally, as above. And he became a reproach to his neighbors, that is, to his persecutors, because you exalted the right hand of those who oppressed him, permitting him to be overcome externally in his members, to such an extent that you gladdened all his enemies. You turned away the assistance of his preaching, so that what ought to have been his assistance instead became his harm. [Col. 0963C] And you did not assist him in battle, that is, in proclaiming. You destroyed him from external cleansing, so that in his members he might appear unclean to everyone. And you struck down his seat—that is, certain people in whom he himself sat—permitting it to be broken and cast down, so that they were humbled to the earth, that is, completely relapsed into earthly things.

You also shortened his days of time in certain persons—not that the days were truly shortened, for it is said: “You established his boundaries, which they will not be able to pass”; but because, when they were taken away through tribulations, they appeared to their subjects, for whose instruction—or even for whose needs—they were necessary, to have been removed before the proper time. And so you drenched him with confusion: inwardly, through the grief of brotherly devotion; outwardly, through the toil of tribulation.

How long, Lord? You delayed your Christ, I say. But how long, Lord, will you turn away from him by delaying him, because you do not accomplish the incorporation of the other sheep? Will you turn away forever? Perhaps not forever. And will this anger of yours—by which you destroy him and drench him with confusion—burn like a fire that reduces to ashes, or like a fire that purifies? Certainly, like one that purifies.

Observe, however, that “how long,” both here and in all other similar passages, is not the word of indignant impatience but of prayerful justice.

Remember what my substance is. Do not turn away, Lord, but remember what my substance is—that is, how worthy he is through whom I subsist. For it is not fitting that so great a head should have a small body. I say, remember, because if you do not remember, you established all the children of human beings in vain, as above.

But so that you may not establish the children of human beings in vain, remember who the human being is—that is, what is fitting for that human being who, though dead, will live and will not see death, as was said above. In whom—that is, in which human being—are your mercies to be completed, Lord, as you swore to David in your truth. What follows remains unchanged.

## ON PSALM LXXXIX. The Prayer of Moses, the Man of God

[Col. 0964A]

### Argument

Deliverance from captivity is requested from the Lord. Such an effective supplication is poured out that it seems to belong to Moses. The voice of the apostles to the Father.

### Explanation

There is no doubt that such names are applied to titles as may clarify the text of the psalms by their interpretation. Therefore, rightly, to display the effectiveness of this supplication, the name of Moses is attached. By praying frequently, he appeased the anger of the Lord; he was also the minister of the old covenant and became a prophet of the new. Since this psalm joins both covenants, it is titled with his name.

The name itself also shines forth with a twofold sacramental meaning. Moses is interpreted as “taken up,” because he was lifted from the waters by Pharaoh’s daughter; this signifies the Israelites through the Red Sea and Christians through baptism. Alternatively, since the Psalmist was about to speak of God, eternal before the ages, the maker and ruler of the world, and of the human race, which on account of sins was liable to death—matters he had learned through Moses’s narration—it was not inappropriate for him to consecrate to Moses’s name what he had learned from Moses himself.

In the first section Moses begins with praise of the judge, briefly recalling his benefits and power. Then he asks that help be given to our weakness, which he himself also demonstrates in many ways. Third, he asks that the Savior’s coming appear more swiftly, for he knew that the Savior would provide what would benefit the human race.

### Commentary

Lord, refuge. This psalm is titled “The Prayer of Moses, the Man of God,” not because it was written by Moses, but because, for the sake of a certain signification, the name of a servant of God of such great merit was attached, so that the reader’s or hearer’s attention might be directed.

Through this man of his the Lord gave the law to his people; through this man he freed his people from Egypt and led them through the desert. Thus Moses became the minister of the old covenant and the prophet of the new. In accordance with this dispensation, therefore, which was accomplished through Moses, this psalm must be examined, since it received its title from his prayer.

Because this psalm contains the old life and the new life, mortal life and vital life, years that are to be counted as nothing and years full of mercy, the sin and punishment of the first covenant, and the kingdom and grace of the second, the name “man of God” was applied. Through that old covenant, which Moses administered, earthly promises were given under a veil, coverings, and certain figures; through them the highest and eternal goods of the new life were promised.

Therefore, when one comes to Christ, the veil Moses had over his face is removed, because, when the shadow has withdrawn, the truth must appear. It is titled “The Prayer of Moses” because it was very familiar to that man to pray and by his prayer to make God favorable toward that people. Through this he admonishes us also to make God favorable toward us by constant entreaties and prayers—not through fear of punishment, but through love of justice. This is indicated by the fact that he did not say “servant of God,” but “man of God.”

It may be the voice either of the prophet or of Moses himself, exhorting us to forget what is behind and to reach forward to what lies ahead. Thus he says: “Lord, although you are the maker of all things, you were made for us. For the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. And you became our refuge,” that is, a tower of strength, as was said above. “And this was from the former generation into this generation.” He adds this because even in that generation there were people who possessed the faith that was later revealed.

Before the mountains. It is as though he says: “I say that you were made, but nevertheless you existed before every created thing, because before the mountains were made or the earth formed”—that is, you existed before every rational creature; and if before the rational creature, it is certain that you existed much more before the irrational creature.

By the mountains is signified the height of the supercelestial rational creature; by the world, the lower rational creature, the earth. The meaning is: You existed before the mountains—that is, before the heavenly rational creatures were made—and before the earth was formed, that is, advanced into something worthy. I say “formed” so that it might be a world, that is, perfect: before the human being was made from the earth, the ornament of the earth, so that there might be on earth one who recognized and praised you.

And truly you existed before these things, because you are from age to age—that is, from eternity to eternity, because you are before the world and after the world. Because the Greek word is ambiguous, certain interpreters, as blessed Augustine says, used “age” for “eternity.” “You are” is said to mark the unchangeability of the divine essence: it neither “was” nor “will be,” but only “is.” And he gives the reason why he says “are”: namely, because you are God.

[Col. 0965B]

Do not turn the human being toward humiliation. This holy man, fearing lest amid so many tribulations, temptations, and bodily troubles of this age, which he had learned by experience, the wretched human being should fall away from that refuge of his, prays in this way and says:

“Lord, our refuge, do not turn”—that is, do not permit—“the human being to be turned away from the highest and eternal goods toward humiliation,” that is, toward desiring and coveting these low, base, and carnal things. I say, therefore, “Do not turn,” because you said this, that is, commanded it, saying: “Turn back to me, children of human beings.”

It is as though he says: “Give, Lord, what you commanded, by hearing the prayer of the one who asks and assisting the faith of the one who wills, because without your help we cannot overcome the temptations of this life by the will of free choice.”

For a thousand years. Rightly we ought to turn away from these fleeting and transitory things and turn toward eternal and stable things, as you, Lord, commanded, because however long these present things may be, they are not even a moment when compared with those things. He expresses this equivalently when he says: “For a thousand years”—that is, however great the length of our life may be—is to be considered, for us who exist before your eyes, as one day; not as the present day or a future day, but as yesterday’s day, which has passed—that is, which no longer exists. Whatever is enclosed within the limits of time must be counted among things that do not exist.

And as a watch in the night. A watch in the night is much shorter than a day, because there are four watches of the night, each of which consists of only three hours. He does not add this without reason. A watch of the night signifies ignorance and fear. So too our life is both in ignorance of the truth and in fear—namely, so that whoever stands may watch lest he fall. It continues:

They are counted as nothing. He explains the misery of our mortality while also displaying the condition of the happiness of the old covenant, which is temporal, so that we may turn away from these low things with more ardent zeal and turn toward those that are high.

It is as though he says: “Therefore, Lord, I pray that you do not turn the human being toward humiliation, because their years”—that is, the years of those who have turned away—“will be counted as nothing,” that is, they will be comparable to things that are valued as completely worthless; their years will be considered as though they did not exist.

This is also true, because before they have come, they do not yet exist, and after they have come, they no longer exist. For they do not come in order to exist, but in order not to exist.

In the morning, like grass—in the morning. Having explained the misery of our mortality, because he recognized that this had happened to us through God’s just anger, he rejoices in the divine judgment. It is as though he says: “Let it be so, Lord, for we have deserved it.”

“Let our morning”—that is, our childhood—“pass away like grass, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven. Let our morning also flower”—that is, let the flower of youth arise in us—and immediately pass away. “Let it fall in the evening,” that is, into that age where it begins to decline. Then let it harden into burdensome old age and finally wither into decrepitude.

Alternatively, let it fall in the evening—that is, let death harden it in the corpse and let it wither in the dust. For after the human being comes the corpse, after the corpse the worm, and after the worm the ash.

And rightly do I say this, because we have deserved it. For in your anger, Lord, which our first parent deserved, we have failed—and not only have we failed, but we have also been troubled. We failed through weakness, but we were troubled through fear of death. We are weak, yet we tremble at bringing our weakness to an end. He takes “anger” and “wrath” as equivalent.

You have set our iniquities. Since you have punished us so severely, it is evident that you have set our iniquities before your sight—that is, you did not neglect them but thoroughly noticed the evil we committed. And when he said “iniquities,” he calls it “age,” saying:

“You have set our age”—that is, our evil deed, which we committed in Adam—“in the illumination of your face,” that is, before your facial appearance; in other words, your face did not keep our sin hidden but clearly perceived it, the sin we committed in Adam.

For all our days. Truly you have set our iniquities before your sight, because all our days have failed—[Col. 0966B] days that we made our own, or because, by directing our attention toward vain and transitory things, we have failed, or because the days themselves have been reduced to fewness. Hence elsewhere: “Behold, you have made my days measurable.” And “in your anger we have failed,” as before.

Our years. Truly we have failed in anger, because our years will meditate—not that the years meditate, but that we meditate in those years.
