Or, in this way: we have failed, yet we wretched people do not notice this failure, because we meditate like a spider: we labor at corruptible things and weave vain and useless things like a spider. And the days of our years—that is, in each of our individual days—we meditate like a spider.

In those seventy years. He seems to explain the brevity of this life and human misery, because those who reach seventy years at this time are called long-lived. But if they are spent “in strength”—that is, if we look to vigor—there will be eighty years, for a human being remains in his strength until eighty years.

“More than this”—that is, whatever is beyond eighty years—is nothing for human life except labor and sorrow: bent and trembling old age, always tending toward destruction.

This does not contradict the statement found in Macrobius, in his account of the generation of the human being, that a person grows in strength up to sixty years. In the sixtieth year his strength begins to diminish, and so he continually decreases in strength until the end of life. I say that this is not contradictory, although it may appear so.

For here he seems to say that in the eightieth year the human being becomes stronger and possesses the greatest strength. The other author, however, plainly says that in the sixtieth year a human being possesses his greatest strength, and that afterward it diminishes and declines. Yet his strength does not decline during those twenty years to such a degree that it can appear diminished. Thus, to anyone who considers the matter carefully, the prophet and that author do not seem to disagree literally.

But since we have seen many people worn out and afflicted by miserable old age before seventy, and many others retaining youthful strength beyond eighty, it is better to refer this to the allegorical meaning, in which we never go astray.

Seventy and eighty years, as they are commonly reckoned, amount to one hundred fifty. It must be understood that there are three units. The first unit is the unit itself; ten is the second unit; one hundred is the third unit. Since one hundred fifty contains fifteen tens, there are fifteen second units in it.

What one hundred fifty signifies mystically is signified by fifteen in this passage, because fifteen consists of seven and eight; and seven here has the same mystical value as seventy and seven, while eight has the same value as eighty.

Let us therefore consider how seven and eight relate to the old covenant and the new. Seven pertains to the old covenant, either because of the observance of the Sabbath, which he commanded to be kept on the seventh day, or because it promised earthly and temporal goods, which revolve according to the sevenfold number of days, or because that carnal people to whom such things were promised was held in captivity for seventy years.

Eight refers to the new covenant, either because the Lord’s resurrection took place in the morning of the eighth day, through which we were restored to eternity, or because there are six ages of this world: the seventh belongs to those who sleep, that is, those who still await the common resurrection; the eighth belongs to those who rise, when the last death will be destroyed and we will be clothed in a double garment, in soul and body.

Eighty also pertains to us, because just as that carnal people returned from captivity to its homeland in the eightieth year, in the first year of the eighth decade, so we, after the six ages of the world and the seventh age of those who sleep, will return to our homeland in the eighth age of those who rise. That is, from the captivity of this life, in which we are held for seventy years because this life revolves according to the sevenfold number of days, we will return to the homeland where we will remain forever.

The literal explanation is as follows. It is as though he says: “Therefore, I say, our years will meditate like a spider, because in our years, if they are not spent in strength”—that is, if they are not conducted by the power of reason and true understanding—“there will be seventy years,” that is, there will be only the pursuit of temporal matters, which is empty, brief, and hollow in comparison with the pursuit of the heavenly homeland.

These temporal matters were promised in the old covenant, to which we said that seven and seventy refer, to those who understood perversely and corrupted Scripture. As long as we pursue them with all the desire of our soul, we will be in the captivity to which we said above that seventy refers. The Israelite people were likewise held captive in Babylon for seventy years.

And just as that people returned to its homeland in the eighth decade, so we, if we do not desire earthly things but remain continually occupied in the labor of heavenly study, will return to our homeland in the eighth age.

This is what he says: “But if our years are spent in strength,” that is, if they are conducted with the power of reason, so that, abandoning earthly promises, we desire heavenly things, “then there will be eighty years in our years,” that is, the pursuit of restored eternity and immortality, which has been given to us in hope through the Lord’s resurrection; the pursuit of the restored inheritance and the restored homeland—that is, the pursuit of returning to the homeland—and truly of keeping Sabbath on the eighth day.

And beyond this, their labor and sorrow. It is as though he says: “If anyone wishes to add something beyond this pursuit, it will be labor and sorrow for him.” For many, after receiving the faith, promising in baptism to renounce earthly things and to strive for restored eternity, relapse into the pursuit of earthly things. For such people there is labor here in acquiring them, and there will nevertheless be sorrow when they are cast into the outer darkness.

For gentleness comes upon. He shows how there will be sorrow: namely, because gentleness—that is, he who earlier appeared so gentle that he could even be called gentleness itself—comes upon us in a terrifying manner. Then we will be corrected, not for benefit but for harm; for then there will be repentance, but fruitless repentance.

Note that he says “has come upon us,” as though to overwhelm and crush us. Hence elsewhere: “But upon whomever the stone falls, it will crush him.”

Or alternatively: “And beyond this, their labor and sorrow” may be understood positively. No man is so holy or so bound to heavenly study that he is never moved by concern for the necessities of food and clothing. For these things he experiences labor and sorrow. The labor of seeking them seems burdensome to him, and he is especially sorrowful because he is compelled to seek them.

Hence the Apostle also says: “And not only this, but we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption of sons, the redemption of our body.”

And as though someone might say: “Since this is labor and sorrow, why does God permit holy men to suffer such things?” He answers: “For this reason: if we are corrected, we will be reformed, so that gentleness may come upon us”—that is, so that we may be gentle creatures and obedient to the Lord.

“For whom the Lord loves, he corrects. He scourges every son whom he receives,” because he also gives certain great men a stimulus of the flesh by which they may be struck, lest they be lifted up by the greatness of revelations. This is what he says: “Gentleness has come upon us.” The order is inverted.

Who knows your power? The statement is connected in the same way to both alternatives: truly we will be corrected, whether the wicked toward evil or the good toward good. For you, Lord, are more powerful to correct us than anyone can know.

“For who knows the power of your anger?”—that is, who knows your powerful anger, by which you will ultimately avenge the wicked and now correct the good? It is as though he says: Very few know the power of your anger, because when you spare many wicked people, you are angry with them, so that it appears to pertain not to anger but rather to your gentleness. The labor and sorrow by which you correct and instruct those whom you love are intended to prevent them from being tormented by eternal punishments.

“And who knows how to number”—that is, discern—“your anger among the good and among the wicked, in accordance with your fear,” that is, so that he may place your fear before himself and always fear you?

It is as though he says: It is very difficult to find one who knows how to number your anger through fear, so that he also adds this and understands it as belonging to your anger: that you seem to spare certain people with whom you are more angry, so that the sinner prospers in his life and receives greater things in the future.

Only a few who have been instructed understand that the prosperity of the wicked is God’s greater anger, empty and deceptive happiness. Few learn, through fear of God, to number his anger and to assign prosperity to the number of punishments.

The meaning is: Few know how to discern God’s anger in this way, so that they understand that the more the wicked person prospers, the more God is angry with him; and the more severely God chastises and punishes the righteous in this life, the more he spares him.

Your right hand. It is as though he says: “Few indeed, Lord, know either the power of your anger or how to number your anger. But you, Lord, make your right hand known to us,” in such a way that we know how to number your anger through fear of you.

“Make your right hand known,” that is, send the one whom you are going to send, and make your Christ known to us—your right hand and your arm—so that through him people may learn not to seek or receive as something great those goods displayed in the Old Testament, but rather those revealed in the New.

And indeed this occurred in accordance with the prayer of this man of God: in the passion of his Son and in the contempt for this world which Christ both had and taught, God the Father showed his faithful that these earthly things are not to be desired, but rather heavenly ones.

Alternatively, let “right hand” be understood as God’s power, so that the meaning is: “In order that we may know how to spend our days and years in strength, make your right hand known to us,” that is, your power, so that we may pass through temporal goods without losing eternal goods.

Or rather, let it be said this way: “Make your right hand known,” that is, your power, so that we may understand that, by scourging and not sparing us, you place the corrected at your right hand; and that, by sparing them while the wicked prosper in his way, you appoint the condemned to the left.

“Make it known,” I say, in such a way that we may number your anger. It continues:

And those instructed in heart in your wisdom. This means: Do not merely make your right hand known to us; also, so that we may imitate them, make known to us those instructed in heart—not in the prudence of the flesh, which is death, but in true wisdom.

Those are called instructed in heart in wisdom to whom it was said: “Put your foot into his fetters.” He means the foot of the heart, not the foot of the body. For those bound by his golden fetters did nothing other than despise earthly promises and, through their sufferings, bear witness to their desire for eternal things.

Hence they are also called “witnesses,” because *martyr* in Greek means “witness” in Latin.

Alternatively, let no one consider people instructed in heart or wise except those whom the misery of their condition continually touches before the eyes of the heart as a consequence of your just judgment, so that from this they may perceive how great your right hand is in helping, toward which no one ought to be ungrateful.

Hence the Apostle says: “To know also the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge,” who showed mercy to those upon whom such great anger is directed. Make your Christ known to them in such a way that in him they may learn not to fear those who kill the body.

Turn, Lord. He said: “Make your right hand known, and those instructed in heart.” For whoever truly knows Christ’s imitators and pays attention to God’s right hand must suffer many tribulations and persecutions. For all who wish to live piously in Christ must suffer persecutions. Again: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.”

This man of God, who speaks here, observed this and feared that amid so many tribulations and bodily troubles we might fail, overcome by the various temptations brought upon us, and be turned away from him who is our refuge. Having compassion on our weakness, as he has often done, he prays and says:

“Lord, you who previously turned away from us, turn”—that is, turn toward us by making yourself known to us. Or: “So that you may no longer permit us to be turned away, turn,” I say, “as far as is necessary,” that is, to the degree of conversion necessary for us: namely, do not permit us to be afflicted beyond what we are able to endure; give us tribulation in proportion to our capacity and strength.

For God does not permit anyone to be afflicted more than he can bear. As the Apostle says: “God is faithful, who will not permit …, but with the temptation he will also provide a way of escape, so that you may be able to endure.”

“Turn,” I say, Lord, and you who were previously inexorable toward those who made themselves your freedmen, become entreatable—that is, able to be entreated—toward those who make themselves your servants, obedient to you in all things and presuming nothing of themselves.

We have been filled in the morning. Truly you will turn and become entreatable, because we will certainly be filled in such a way that we can say: “We have already been filled in the morning,” that is, in the resurrection, when the last death will be destroyed and there will be only morning—that is, a day without night, because it will be without end.

Then, I say, we will be filled with your mercy—that is, we will receive the double garment, which will not be given to us because of our merits, although we suffer much in this age. For the sufferings of this time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us; only your mercy will give it to us.

Or “in the morning”: when the night of unbelief has passed, we will be filled in this life with your mercy, by which you call, forgive sins, and justify. Or “in the morning”: when the night of persecution has passed, we will be filled with your mercy both here and finally.

Then, namely when we are filled with your mercy, we will rejoice outwardly and delight inwardly, placed in our days—that is, in eternity, where all our days will be ours, because we will always progress and never fail. For in this life not all days can be ours, since we fail more often than we progress.

We have rejoiced. Truly we will be filled with your mercy, because “we have rejoiced”—that is, we will rejoice in the future—for the days in which you humbled us, that is, permitted us to be humbled and scourged, and for the years in which we saw—that is, suffered—evil.

We will rejoice forever, as though he says: “For this temporal sadness, eternal joy will be recompensed to us.”

And so that we may rejoice in our days, you, Lord, who previously despised us as your freedmen, now look upon us who have become your servants. Or: “Look upon the servants,” so that they may be conformed to your Son.

And to gain greater favor, he says: “Look upon your works,” not their works—that is, look upon those who are what they are as your work, because you created and recreated them.

And so I say: “Look upon them; direct the children,” that is, direct their works. The works of that person are directed because he makes his will level with the will of God, presumes nothing of himself, and whose spirit is believed to be with God, because he thinks that he can do no good without the cooperation of God’s Spirit.

Or: “Direct the children,” that is, always direct their imitators toward better things, so that they may not be crooked in heart.

[Col. 0970A]

And let splendor. And so that the children may be directed—that is, our works—let the splendor of the Lord be upon us, that is, let the face of the Lord, which was previously obscured from us, be illuminated in our higher part; let the image of God appear in us.

Or: let the splendor of God—that is, the manifold grace of the Holy Spirit—illuminate our mind.

And so that splendor may be upon us, Lord, direct the works of our hands, our good works, so that they may not be distorted beneath us but directed above us. The works of those people are distorted beneath them when they do good for the reward of earthly things, like that carnal people to whom earthly promises were made. Our works, however, are directed above us when we do good for the reward of heavenly things.

And the work of our hands. Blessed Augustine and Jerome say that this is not found in certain translations and that, if it is found, it should be marked with an asterisk or obelus.

Nevertheless, it can be connected in this way. It is as though he says: “I say that you should direct the works, so that all of them may become one work,” that is, so that they may be done with charity and tend toward charity as their one end.

For works done without charity are of no benefit, as the Apostle says: “If I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, I am nothing.” If they are done in charity, then, although they are many in their activity, they are nevertheless one in their end. For the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfaltering but true faith.

## ON PSALM XC. A Song of Praise of David

### Argument

It is sung for Hezekiah’s victory over the Assyrians. Alternatively, it should be read in relation to the Gospel of Mark, where Christ is tempted. The voice of the Church to the Lord.

### Explanation

“A song of praise” is divine praise; David himself should be understood as the prophet. We continually set this hymn against the demons with devout confidence, so that they may be defeated by us precisely through the means by which they deceitfully attempted certain things against their Creator.

In the first part the Psalmist professes that every person who is most faithful is surrounded by divine protection. In the second he sings praise to Christ. In the third, the words are those of the Father to every faithful person whom he knows to hope most devoutly in him, promising that he will defend that person in this world and grant him rewards in the world to come.

### Commentary
He who dwells in the help. Praise of a song of David.

This is the psalm concerning which the devil dared to tempt our Lord, that is, Christ. Let us therefore dare, so that, instructed, we may be able to resist the tempter—not trusting in ourselves, but in him who was tempted first, lest we should be overcome in temptation. Let us note that he wished us to imitate him in his humility, not in his majesty. For he said: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart.” And if at some time the tempter himself, either secretly by himself or through the sons of distrust, in whom he works [Col. 0970D] as in his vessels, brings upon us various temptations, tribulations, and bodily troubles, let us endure them patiently and bear them with all gentleness and humility, just as he wished to be tempted and scourged for us, and so forth.

For whoever imitates Christ in such a way that he patiently bears the temptations, tribulations, and bodily troubles of this life, and places all his hope in him, so that he is neither caught by enticement nor broken by fear—this is the one who, following the example of his Lord, dwells in the help of the Most High and abides in the protection of the God of heaven. The Prophet, foreseeing through the Holy Spirit that someone would come from the human race who would be our help and example, so that we would not be overcome in temptations, yield to the tempter, or be broken by troubles or injuries inflicted upon us, just as that one first became an example of falling and conquering—that is, so that we might be conquered—the Prophet, I say, foreseeing this, praises him out of devotion.

And it does not pertain only to devotion, that is, to a pious and attentive affection [Col. 0971A] toward God; the song pertains to exultation. Therefore this psalm is rightly called “a song of praise,” that is, praise full of exultation, or exultant praise, because in it he praises the one from whom our help and example come, and in praising him exults, saying as follows: “He who dwells in the help,” and so forth.

It is as though he were saying: Someone was placed in the help of the Most High, but did not dwell there, because he did not persevere; rather, he withdrew from obedience when he extended his hand toward what was forbidden. He wished to be in his own help when he trusted in himself, wished to be a god, and wished everything to depend upon his own will. When he listened to the serpent’s suggestion, he believed what the devil promised and found what God had threatened.

But someone is to come from the human race—namely, Christ—as help and example to all who will not trust in their own help but will trust in the help of the Most High, that is, of God the Father. Since he is the Most High, he could rightly be helped by him both in himself and in his own. He will not withdraw from that help but will dwell there, that is, he will remain there; and he will also abide there, that is, he will remain there entirely, because he will not apostatize either in deed or even [Col. 0971B] in thought.

He will dwell, I say, not in protection of his own according to human nature, but in the protection of God—and not of just any god, but of the God of heaven, that is, of the one who makes human beings heavenly. Although he could resist the devilish tempter both in himself and in his own, he preferred to endure patiently. He did not trust in himself but bore everything with patience, so that he might be an example to us of trusting not in ourselves but in God, and of enduring everything patiently. For by patiently enduring tribulations and temptations, not trusting in our own strength but placing our hope in the protection and help of God, we shall be able to resist the tempter and his followers.

“He will say to the Lord.” Truly he will abide in the protection of God, not in his own, because he will say to the Lord, that is, to God the Father, whose servant he will truly make himself: “Lord, you are my protector; I am not.” That is: my cause exists through you, not through me, because you, like a merciful protector, receive [Col. 0971C] and defend it; and you, not I, are my refuge.

And rightly so, because refuge is found with you alone, since you are God, that is, you are above all things. “My God,” I say—that is, the one whom I make my God, rather than making myself god, as Adam wished to set himself up as his own god. These things, I say, he will say to the Lord, that is, to the Lord’s honor.

But what follows he will say for the exhortation of his neighbor, saying as follows: “I will hope”—not trusting in myself, but placing my hope in him. And rightly so, because not I, but he, delivered me: he delivered me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word.

So you also, he says, place your hope not in your own strength but in the Lord. And rightly so, because he, and no other, will deliver you from the snare of hunters and from the ambushes and deceptions of the devil and his followers.

The devils are hunters or hunters’ agents, because they possess a thousand harmful arts by which they deceive the wretched souls of those who trust in themselves and do not place their hope in the Lord. Such people are quickly caught by enticement and [Col. 0971D] broken by fear. These hunters—that is, the devils—stretch out their snares and traps not in the road but beside the road, so that if anyone strays from the road, he may be caught.

But if you wish to be secure, be on the road and walk in the road, that is, in Christ and in his commandments. He says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” Let him be your way who for your sake became the way, so that through himself he might lead you to himself. For he is the way by which we go, and he is the end toward which we strive.

Whoever walks in Christ and in his commandments will be delivered from the snare of hunters, that is, from the deceptions of the devil, and from the harsh word. A harsh word is called a word of evil persuasion. Whoever yields and consents to such evil persuasion throws himself into the devil’s snares.

Or a harsh word is called a word of detraction, as when someone disparages his neighbor by saying: “You alone wish to appear righteous among us. You act and present yourself as though no one were good except you.” Whoever yields to this detraction, either by ceasing from good work or by becoming proud of what is thus charged against him, throws himself into the hunters’ snares. [Col. 0972A]

“By his shoulders.” It is as though he were saying: You will not merely deliver yourself from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word because you will hope in him; I say that he will deliver you and your own. He will also overshadow you—that is, he will make a shade for you, and for your own if they hope in him—from the heat of incitements, that is, by his shoulders, or through his shoulders.

Wings rest upon shoulders, and feathers are in wings; therefore by shoulders wings and feathers are understood. Here we take wings to mean love of God and neighbor, by which, like wings, we fly toward the kingdom of heaven and are lifted from these lowest things to the highest.

The phrase “he will overshadow you” is spoken by way of comparison: he will make a shade for your own, so that the heat of incitements may not harm them; and this will be in his wings, that is, if they rest upon love of God and neighbor, just as a hen makes shade for her chicks beneath her wings.

If a hen’s chicks are safe beneath her wings from the kite and the hawk, how much more shall we be safe beneath God’s wings from the aerial powers that fly around like kites and [Col. 0972B] hawks. And God’s wisdom is rightly compared with a hen, because no bird shows such compassion toward its young. Out of excessive compassion for her chicks she becomes hoarse in voice, appears rough in her feathers, and seems altogether weak.

So too God’s Wisdom, that is, the Son of God, taking pity on our weakness, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. In that form he humbled himself so greatly for us, becoming obedient to the Father even unto death, that neither appearance nor beauty was evident in him.

Let us now return to the literal meaning. It was said above: “She says this to the Lord; she will say that for her neighbor.” But what follows she will say while rejoicing with herself: “The Lord the Father will overshadow you,” that is, he will make an inner shelter for you from the incitements of vices, protecting you with his shoulders, that is, with his wings. This occurs through love of God and neighbor.

And you, placed beneath his feathers, that is, in the protection of his wings, will rightly hope in him for yourself and for your own, trusting in nothing of your own strength but in his protection, and attributing whatever good there is in you [Col. 0972C] to his grace.

“He will surround you with a shield.” You will rightly hope beneath his feathers—that is, your own will hope—because if you are beneath his feathers, that is, if you possess love of God and neighbor, the truth, that is, the fulfillment of his commandments, will be in you. For the whole law and the prophets depend upon these two commandments.

And this truth will surround you—that is, it will fortify you and your own like a shield. Another truth may also be understood here: the truth of which it is said elsewhere, “Truth has sprung up from the earth,” that is, true confession and discernment of sins.

Whoever truly loves God distinguishes himself, although a sinner, from other sinners: he distinguishes himself as one who confesses sins from those who defend themselves, as humble from the proud, and as one who trusts in God from those who trust in themselves. Thus that tax collector who cried out in the temple distinguished his wounds from the Pharisee’s boastful merits.

The wording may be continued in the same way as before: You will rightly hope, because if you have hoped beneath his feathers—that is, if you have possessed true love of God and neighbor—you will be true, [Col. 0972D] that is, confessing sins rather than concealing them, and thus distinguishing yourself from those who do not confess but defend themselves. This truth will surround you, that is, your own, like a shield.

And thus you will not fear—that is, your own will not fear—the fear of night. Four things are mentioned here: the fear of night, the arrow flying by day, the business wandering in darkness, and the attack and noonday demon.

It should be understood that whoever sins unknowingly sins as though at night, while whoever sins knowingly sins as though by day. By the fear of night, therefore, a light temptation is understood, one that occurs in ignorance: night signifies ignorance, while fear signifies lightness, because as long as some evil is feared, a person does not suffer as much as when it is inflicted.

By the arrow flying by day, a light temptation that occurs among those who know is signified. Day signifies those who know, while the arrow signifies a light temptation, because a person is not wounded as much by an arrow in flight as when struck at close quarters [Col. 0973A] by a sword.

A light temptation is one that does not press very hard and is quickly avoided. But let the tribulation be made heavier, and let the two things that follow correspond to the two already mentioned: let the wandering business in darkness correspond to the fear of night, and the attack and noonday demon to the arrow flying by day.

Behold, the temptation has been made heavy for both the ignorant and the uninformed. That grave temptation which presses so sharply upon the ignorant is rightly called “business,” that is, “the removal of leisure,” because it takes away all rest. It is called “wandering,” that is, enduring in darkness, that is, among darkened people, namely, the ignorant.

The grave tribulation that falls upon those who know is called an attack because it presses sharply, and it is called a noonday demon. It is called a demon because it occurs through the instigation of the devil who suggests it; it is called noonday because the sun burns more fiercely and shines more brightly at noon.

By the heat that is fiercest at noon, persecution is understood; by the brightness, because it occurs among those who are not ignorant. There are some who do not know the reason for their Christianity—that is, they are not yet so perfect [Col. 0973B] that they understand that all who wish to live piously in Christ must suffer persecution.

There is also the saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice, fear, and trembling, and prepare your soul for temptation.” When grave, pressing, and enduring tribulation comes upon such people, it finds and seizes them, and thus they are overcome.

There are others who know the reason for their Christianity well. They understand that God’s promises do not concern this earth or this life, that all earthly things are to be despised and heavenly things desired. But the torturer presses upon them: he presses heavily, burns, and torments. The attack and the noonday demon press upon them, and thus they are overcome.

What constitutes light and what constitutes grave tribulation can be recognized from the time when the Christian name began to increase. At that time the enemies of the Christian name—kings and emperors, namely—wishing to destroy it, issued an edict of this sort: “Whoever confesses Christ shall be struck with the sword.” Many were killed, [Col. 0973C] because they considered it a light thing to be struck with the sword for Christ’s name.

But when those enemies saw people hastening in this way toward death, and the whole world going after Christ, they said: “Shall we alone remain? Shall we kill the entire human race?” Therefore they issued another edict: “Whoever confesses Christ shall be tortured until Christ is denied.”

If one compares being struck with the sword and being tortured for so long, the former may be seen as the flying arrow, and the latter as the attack and the noonday demon. When such a great and gravely pressing persecution arose, many, both those who knew and those who did not know the reason for their Christianity, fell.

This happened because they relied upon their own strength, not upon God. They did not dwell in the help of the Most High and did not say: “You are my protector, Lord, and my refuge.” The Lord allowed them to fall for this reason: to show his faithful that he alone protects, moderates temptations, and permits only as much to come as can be endured when it comes. [Col. 0973D]

Let us now return to the literal meaning. He said: “His truth will surround you,” and it will surround you in such a way that you will not fear—that is, your own will not fear—the fear of night, and so forth. That is, they will fear neither the light nor the grave tribulation that occurs among the ignorant, nor that which occurs among those who are not ignorant.

“A thousand shall fall at your side.” Although I say that your own will not fear, nevertheless many of those who appeared to be your own will fall at your side and at your right hand.

By “at your side” are understood those who thought that they would be at the Lord’s side and judge with him, because they followed what the Lord said to his disciples: “You who have left everything and followed me shall sit upon thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

But many of these, overcome by severe persecution and tribulation, fell, and thus they fell at his side, that is, from the hope of receiving the reward of a tribunal seat.

By “at your right hand” are designated those who thought that they would be placed at the right hand and hear, at the judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father,” because of the works of mercy they had done, [Col. 0974A] and because, like devoted provincials in the Lord’s commonwealth, they had supplied provisions and pay to his soldiers, that is, to the holy monks, hermits, and other defenders of the homeland.

But because many even of these were overcome by pressing necessity or tribulation, they fell at the right hand, that is, from the hope of being placed at the right hand and receiving recompense for their services.

And because there are far more who will be judged than those who will judge, the Prophet assigned the lesser number to those at the side and the greater number to those to be judged, saying: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.”

But what concern is that? None, because however many may appear to fall at the side or at the right hand, that noonday demon—that is, the burning and pressing tribulation—will not approach you, that is, those who are truly your own: those who trust in nothing of themselves, but dwell in the help of the Most High, abide in the protection of the God of heaven, and say to the Lord: “You are my protector,” and so forth.

To these, I say, it will not approach the flesh; it does not approach merit. For the error of those who torture is far [Col. 0974B] from the faith of those who believe. Faith is in the soul, to which the torturers do not attend; even if they kill the body, they cannot kill the soul.

“Nevertheless.” I say that tribulation will not approach you, that is, your own will not fall through tribulation; nevertheless they are not troubled without cause, because they are troubled both for their own instruction and for the condemnation of the wicked. You will consider this with your eyes.

That is, only your eyes and those of your own who have been enlightened by you will attend to this, and not the eyes of others. For it is no small matter to observe the wicked flourishing for a time and to keep one’s eyes upon him, so that one may see what he will suffer at the end.

You, I say, will consider and understand that the tribulation of your own is the recompense of sins, that is, of evil, because what will be repaid to them is not the good that they did unknowingly—that is, the perfection of your own—but the evil that they knowingly did, namely, either to turn your own away or completely destroy them.

Or, if we understand “sinners” not as people but as sins, we can refer this recompense to both groups: [Col. 0974C] to the good who endure and to the wicked who inflict suffering. For the same tribulation belongs both to the light sins of the good, by which they are purified, and to the grave sins of the wicked—not so that the wicked may be purified through it, but so that they may be condemned more gravely.

Or, alternatively, I say that many will fall at your side and at your right hand, but you will nevertheless see with your eyes that no one of those who are your own will fall. You will see the recompense of sinners—that is, you will see that fall to be just in those who fall, because their sins had deserved it.

It should be known that some have understood the temptations mentioned above in another way, and say as follows: Because the truth will surround you like a shield, you will not fear—that is, your own will not fear—the fear of night, that is, the fear inflicted by those of the night, namely, heretics who walk in darkness and strive to drag others along with them in the night.

They will not fear the arrow flying by day, that is, arrogance and vainglory, which proceed from the day, that is, from prosperity. Nor will they fear the business—that is, the error of certain heretics [Col. 0974D]—wandering, that is, persisting in darkness, that is, in the flesh of Christ, which is called darkness in relation to his divinity.

There were heretics who said that our Lord Jesus Christ had a phantom body; others said that he was not born from a virgin but from a woman. There were many other heresies of this kind concerning his humanity.

Nor will your own fear the attack and noonday demon, that is, the demonic and vehement zeal of those who labor to deceive at noon, that is, in a matter as clear and bright as the sun at noon—namely, in matters concerning his divinity. They say that the Son is less than the Father, although it is manifest that he is equal and consubstantial with the Father, both from his many statements—he said, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also,” and, “I and the Father are one,” and many similar things—and from his works, concerning which it was said: “No one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.”

“Thousands shall fall at your side.” For this reason your own will not fear the fear of night [Col. 0975A] or any of the things mentioned above: a thousand of this temptation will fall.

He should have said “at your left,” since in the other part he says “at your right”; but because there is nothing left-handed in God, he simply says “at your side,” indicating those who will be at his side, that is, those who will surround him. Those who fall at the right hand he understands to be the most perfect.

Therefore he says that ten thousand such heretical temptations will fall without affecting those at your right hand, that is, those who belong to your right hand, namely, to your more excellent goods.

But, as though he were saying: Although they fall at the side and at the right hand, they do so without any injury to those people, because the attack and the noonday demon, or any of the things mentioned above, will not approach you, as stated earlier.

“Nevertheless.” Such temptation will indeed not approach your own, but they are not tempted without cause, because this happens for their testing and for the condemnation of temptations.

“For you are.” The same meaning is contained in both clauses, [Col. 0975B] as follows: It will not approach you—that is, your own—because you, Lord the Father, are my hope, that is, the hope of my own.

And by saying that you are the hope of my own, I mean that you have made me their refuge and set me as the Most High, that is, as the most strongly fortified place, to which no enemy, nor any harmful heaven, can reach.

Consider how our Lord, that is, Christ, is the hope and resurrection of his own. The human race knew that a human being could die, but did not know that he could rise again. It had something to fear, but had nothing from which to hope.

Therefore, so that the one who through fear had brought about death might, for the reward of future life, give the hope of resurrection, the Lord Jesus Christ died first and rose again. He died after many, but rose before all. By dying he did what many had done before him; by rising he did what no one had done before him, so that I might have the hope of resurrection that I had not possessed.

It is as though he were saying: “You have risen and ascended so that I might hope to follow where you have gone before.”

**[Col. 0975C] “No evil shall approach you.”**

I rightly said that your refuge is the Most High, because no evil shall approach your tabernacle any longer. He calls Christ’s flesh the tabernacle, concerning which it was said: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” and so forth.

This same flesh of Christ is that bride whom he brought to himself. Her bridal chamber is the virgin’s womb. Hence the Apostle says: “The two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery, but I speak of Christ and the Church.”

In this tabernacle, therefore, our emperor fought for us. And lest we should be overcome, he permitted himself to be tempted. Nor should we pass over the fact that he says this for our instruction: “No evil shall approach you, and no scourge shall come near your tabernacle,” namely, so that we too may suffer what he suffered, and for the purpose for which he suffered, and may attain the same security.

**[Col. 0975D] “For he will command his angels concerning you.”**

This was prophesied concerning the ascension of our Lord, that is, Christ. But the devil abused the truth in tempting him and thereby had the greatest opportunity to tempt him. He thought that it had to happen because it had been prophesied.

The Lord truly ascended into heaven, carried by angels—not because he would have fallen if they had not carried him, but so that honor and service might be shown to him, and so that the dignity of the human nature he had assumed might thereby be demonstrated.

And just as the law, which was intended to instill fear, was given fifty days after the sacrifice of the paschal lamb, so, after the Lord had ascended, he gave the Holy Spirit to the apostles fifty days after the true Lamb, that is, after his resurrection. The Spirit would turn fear into love, so that what fear could not accomplish, love might accomplish.

Thus he freed his own from the guilt of the law, so that they might now preserve it and act rightly, not through fear of punishment but through love of justice.

The text may be continued as follows: I say, therefore, that no scourge will approach your tabernacle, because angels will carry you there, to a place where nothing evil approaches eternally.

This is the whole meaning intended when he says: The Lord the Father commanded—that is, gave this command to his angels concerning you—that they guard you and your own in all your ways, that is, in all your works and those of your own.

We must know that Christ was not without angelic guardianship; hence it was also said: “An angel of the Lord appeared to him, strengthening him.” And again: “Angels came and ministered to him.” This was not because he in any way needed to be guarded, but for the sake of honor and service.

**“They will carry you in their hands.”**

It is as though he were saying: Because the Lord commanded his angels to guard you, they will therefore carry you in their hands into heaven—not because you would have fallen if they had not carried you, but because they are offering you honor.

They will carry you, I say, into heaven, so that from there you may send the Holy Spirit, who will turn the hearts of your own from fear to love.

This is so that you may not perhaps strike your foot, which is still on earth, against a stone. That is, it is so that those who are your foot may not stumble over the hardness of the law, doing good works out of fear of punishment rather than out of love of justice.

The feet of Christ are called those through whom he traversed the whole world, because “their sound has gone out into all the earth.” These feet are distinguished from their head, which is already above, by place but not by pious affection. That they are united in affection the Lord himself showed when he said to the persecutor Paul: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

**“Upon the asp and the basilisk.”**

And because your foot will not strike against a stone, you will walk—that is, your own will walk—upon the asp and the basilisk. This means that they will simply despise and trample underfoot everything harmful.

By the basilisk, which is the king of serpents, understand the very head of the demons; by the asp, understand those subject to that head.

**“And you will trample upon the lion and the dragon.”**

The lion and the dragon are the same, namely, the devil himself. When he rages openly against us, he is a lion; when he lies in wait, he is a dragon. But the lion will not conquer you, and the dragon will not deceive you. Conquer the lion, therefore, and you will not fear the dragon.

The same may also be understood through the first two creatures as through these latter two. If we attend to the fact that the basilisk harms even by its breath when it is not seen, the basilisk signifies hidden persecution; the asp, which harms only through its venom, signifies persecution that is manifest.

**“Because he has hoped in me.”**

Continue it in this way: The Lord indeed commanded his angels to guard you; he commends you to them in this way because this one, both in himself and in his own, did not trust in himself but hoped in me, God. I shall deliver him in his own, calling them to him and forgiving their sins. After delivering them, I shall also protect them in his own from the incitements of vices.

And rightly so, because he, both in himself and in his own, recognized my name, namely, the name “God.” Everyone truly recognizes this name who distinguishes himself as a creature and God himself as the Creator. Therefore he does not wish to be god for himself or to depend upon his own will, as wretched Adam did.

**“He cried out to me.”**

Because he and his own recognized my name, he cried out to me alone, not to anything else. His own also cried out, and therefore I shall hear him both in himself and in his own.

I shall be with him and with his own in tribulation, so that they may not fail. For if faith is with you, he too will be with you.

I shall deliver him in the present from tribulation, and I shall also deliver his own. And truly I shall glorify him, because when he was full of the shortness of days in his own and also in himself, insofar as human nature is concerned, I shall fill him with length of days, that is, I shall give him eternity.

Then I shall show him my salvation, that is, my Savior, my Word. I shall show him to his own, because then we shall see him as he is, and also show him in himself. For although God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, nevertheless it must be believed that his most holy soul possessed, after the resurrection, a far purer understanding of divinity than it had possessed before.

# IN PSALM CXI. A song of praise on the Sabbath day.

## ARGUMENT.

After the Assyrians were defeated under Hezekiah, many give thanks. Alternatively, the voice of the Church.

## EXPLANATION.

**[Col. 0977A]**

The psalm signifies spiritual works that tend upward toward the Lord. In these we ought always to sing, that is, to give thanks to God our helper.

The Sabbath day is interpreted as rest. Through it we are reminded to cease from every evil action and likewise to hope with the greatest certainty and devotion for the rest that is to come.

Arnobius says as follows: “On the Sabbath day the enemies of the Lord perish, so that on the Lord’s Day the friends of the Lord may rejoice. For on the Sabbath the Lord lies dead in the tomb, and on the Lord’s Day he is worshiped alive among the angels.”

“In this matter his thoughts have become exceedingly deep, which the foolish man does not understand.”

At the first entrance the Church speaks, recalling that it is good to proclaim the praises of the Lord, and professing that the foolish and irreligious person does not understand this.

Second, it asserts that sinners will perish quickly like grass.

Third, it says that the righteous will flourish like a palm tree and grow like the cedars of Lebanon, so that [Col. 0977B] the promise of happiness may correct the obstinate in fear and lift up the devoted.

## COMMENTARY.

**“It is good to confess to the Lord.”**

A song of praise on the Sabbath day. The Jews celebrate the Sabbath in a certain languid and luxurious leisure. They refrain from good work, but not from idle work.

Our Lord, however, enjoins a Sabbath upon us. What kind? To be free, namely, from evil works; whereas they are free from good works.

Our Sabbath, that is, our delightful Sabbath, is within the heart. Many rest outwardly in darkness but are in turmoil in their consciences, because no evil person keeps the Sabbath. His conscience never rests anywhere, but he lives continually in disturbances.

But whoever has a pure conscience is tranquil, and tranquility itself is his Sabbath. The Sabbath is of the heart. Although a person labors in the present, he is nevertheless extended through hope of the future, and every cloud of sadness is made bright.

Our Sabbath is itself the object of our hope. This, therefore, is sung [Col. 0977C] and taught in this psalm: how every Christian ought to be in the Sabbath of his heart, that is, undisturbed by imitation, tranquility, and purity of conscience. This psalm teaches how each person ought to keep the Sabbath in his heart.

First, if you have made any progress, confess it to the one from whom you have made progress. His are the gifts, not your merits.

Second, do not excuse yourself for what you have done wrongly, but rather accuse yourself. For whatever evil you have comes from yourself; whatever good you have comes from God.

But the perverse, who do not possess the Sabbath, attribute the good they do to themselves; while for the evil they do, they look for someone whom they may accuse. Some say: “Satan persuaded me to do this,” as though he had the power to compel. He does indeed possess cunning for causing harm, but he does not possess the power to compel.

Satan does not cease persuading toward evil; Christ does not cease admonishing toward good. You, therefore, placed between the one who admonishes and the one who persuades, why do you incline your ear to Satan, who persuades and deceives [Col. 0977D], rather than to Christ, who admonishes and does not deceive?

Satan can compel you to nothing against your will. Therefore do not accuse the one who has no forgiveness, but accuse yourself, who will receive pardon.

Others, in order to excuse themselves, accuse fate, the stars, and other such things. They wish to come to God by the long way of accusing him, because they do not wish to come by the short way of appeasing him.

There are also others who come directly and openly to the Lord himself, saying: “If God did not wish it, I would not be such a person.”

But what does the psalm say? It teaches and admonishes this: not only that one should hear the warning not to sin, but also that, if one sins, one should accuse oneself.

It is the voice of the Prophet saying: “It is good”—that is, exceedingly pleasant and useful—“to confess to the Lord,” that is, for us to praise the Lord, confessing to him in both circumstances: in the good, because he has done it; in the evil, because we have done it.

Therefore it is good to sing praise to the Most High, that is, to do good works for your name, that is, for the glorifying and preserving of your name, so that our name may not perish.

For if we glorified our own name, [Col. 0978A] then our name would be destroyed. But if, insofar as it lies within us, we preserve his name, then our name—that is, our glory—is preserved by him.

Thus, when the Lord had sent his disciples to preach, and they returned saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name,” he saw that they were aiming at his name and preserved their name, because they had first preserved his. He corrected them, saying: “Do not rejoice in this, but rather rejoice because your names are written in the book of life.”

The psalterium is our good work. Whoever acts well sings the psalterium; whoever praises God with his voice sings. Let us therefore sing with our voice and sing the psalterium through our works.

**“To proclaim your mercy in the morning.”**

It is good, I say, to sing praise to you, Most High—to sing praise, I say, in order to proclaim, that is, so that through us it may be proclaimed to others, that your mercy is in the morning and your truth is through the night.

It is morning when things go well for us outwardly; [Col. 0978B] it is night when things go badly. When things go well, praise God, because it comes from his mercy. When things go badly, likewise praise him, because it comes from his truth, that is, from his justice.

For he is just, because he scourges you on account of your sins. Therefore, when you suffer something, do not judge God unjust, but attribute it to your sins and to his correction.

Or alternatively: I say that it is good to sing praise for this purpose, namely, so that through our good works we may proclaim to our neighbors that the morning—that is, our illumination—is your mercy. This means that, when the darkness of unbelief has been driven away, illumination through faith and knowledge of the truth exists in us because of your mercy, which first calls us and forgives our sins.

And let us proclaim through the night—that is, through the tribulation that we endure patiently—the truth, that is, your recompense. Not that the night itself is the recompense, but because in a certain way it is the beginning of recompense, namely, because it makes us fit for recompense.

Or alternatively: It is good to sing praise. I say that one should sing praise in order to proclaim to one’s neighbor that the morning [Col. 0978C]—that is, the perfection of virtues in us, namely, our ascent from virtue to virtue—is from your mercy.

And we should proclaim through the night—that is, through a fall—that your truth is present: if at some time we fall, this is from your truth, that is, from your justice. For if someone is worthy to be saved, you permit him to fall so that he may rise stronger, as Peter rose stronger through his fall. But if someone is worthy to be condemned, you permit him to fall so that, being filthy, he may become filthier.

### On the Ten-Stringed Instrument

He said that it is good to sing psalms; now he shows how we ought to sing, namely, on a ten-stringed psaltery—that is, in the fulfillment of the ten commandments of the Law. By the psaltery, which sounds from above, a spiritual work is understood; by the ten strings, the ten commandments of the Law. There are many who carry a psaltery but touch not even one string: thus the Jews do indeed carry a psaltery, because they possess the ten commandments, but they touch not even one string, because they fulfill none of them. He truly touches the strings who puts those commandments into practice. Some touch only one string, others several. It belongs to the perfect, however, to touch all ten strings. And to make this noteworthy he added “ten-stringed,” although every psaltery is ten-stringed. It follows:

### With a Song on the Lyre

For we ought not devote ourselves only to spiritual things, which are understood by the psaltery; we must also sing with the lyre, that is, perform works of mercy. The lyre is the mortification of the flesh. To mortify the flesh is for you to withhold from your own flesh what will enable you to refresh the flesh of the poor; and this must be done with a song, that is, with joy, not with sadness. “God loves a cheerful giver.” Or, “with a song,” that is, with a word of admonition, because we must not only provide the poor with necessities, but also offer them the word of sound doctrine and counsel for salvation.

### For You Have Gladdened Me

I said that it is good to sing to your name, and this for the following reason (as though he were saying): I afflicted myself because of my making, but you have gladdened me—that is, you have bestowed great joy upon me—in your making, because you restored me and made me fruitful in good works. Hence the Apostle says: “For we are his workmanship, created in good works.” And because you gladdened me in your work, I shall rightly rejoice in the works of your hands—that is, in the restoration which you have accomplished in me.

And I shall rightly rejoice in the works of your hands, because your works, Lord, which you have accomplished in me and in others—that is, in those restored by your grace—how greatly have they been magnified! That is, how astonishing and delightful they are! For you have made sons from slaves, and taken those condemned into the kingdom.

And truly your works have been magnified, because your thoughts—that is, the dispositions inspired in us by you—have become exceedingly profound, namely because we consider that these earthly things, however lofty they may be, will nevertheless soon come to an end. It is as though he were saying: An ignorant and foolish man does not perceive these thoughts, as he clearly demonstrates by his conduct: he desires these earthly things, but does not understand that they will soon come to an end.

Or otherwise: Above he said that it is good to sing on a ten-stringed psaltery, and that there are many who neither possess a psaltery nor touch a single string; but they do everything contrary to these strings, for some commit adultery and others steal possessions. They are plainly caught taking delight in every evil work, and yet they prosper in every worldly success. From this there arose a wicked thought in certain weak people who had formerly sung on the psaltery and then on the lyre, as they thought to themselves: “We labor, we suffer, we hunger, and endure every misery; but these people have joy and every abundance.” This wicked thought rose so high that they said that God truly loved the wicked and hated the good. Thus the Sabbath is excluded from them by the strings, and they imitate the wicked in their flourishing.

The prophet, therefore, observing this, bursts forth with a kind of astonishment into these words: “Lord, these are your works”—namely, that by permitting the wicked to prosper you condemn them, and that you associate with condemnation certain people who sing to you because they imitate the wicked in their flourishing, while by permitting your own people to be afflicted you save them. “These, I say, are your works, Lord—how greatly have they been magnified,” that is, how astonishing, extraordinary, and incomprehensible they are! It is as though he were saying: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!”

And rightly do I say that they have been magnified, because your thoughts—that is, your dispositions from which these works proceed—have become exceedingly profound. Truly they are exceedingly profound, because no sea is higher and no sea is deeper. In this depth all the wicked are shipwrecked. But if you wish to swim out, hold fast to the wood of God—that is, to the voice of Christ and to his passion—for he labored first, and let it not grieve you, his servant, to labor. On the third day he raised his flesh, so that you should not despair.

Therefore do not envy the flourishing of the wicked, and do not let their prosperity disturb you. Look to his eternity, because from eternity he sees what he will spare in the wicked and what he will reserve for the godly. Do not look to the shortness of your days, within which all things cannot be completed—namely, so that the good may be rewarded and the wicked condemned. Rather say to the Lord your God: “Lord, how greatly have your works been magnified! You reserve everything for your judgment. The godly are scourged because they are corrected as sons; the wicked prosper because they will be condemned as runaway slaves.”

But this the ignorant and foolish man, who envies their flourishing, does not consider. And this is what he says: “The ignorant man will not know this, and the foolish will not understand.” He calls the one who envies the flourishing of the wicked ignorant and foolish: ignorant because he does not look ahead for his own future; foolish because he does not consider how fragile and liable to fall are the things he desires.

And to show what he does not understand, he adds: “When sinners have sprung up like grass”—which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven. It is as though he were saying: Let not their flourishing delight you; rather, let their swift withering terrify you, because they are like grass. And as soon as they all appear—I do not mean those who have committed evil, but those who persistently commit iniquity—when this has happened, the ignorant and foolish man does not understand what immediately follows. That is, he does not understand how the sinners and workers of iniquity will perish forever and ever—that is, how they will be handed over to the destruction of their eternal punishments. For eternal sorrow will be repaid to them in exchange for this temporal joy. And when they are thus condemned, it is clear that those who envy their flourishing will truly be condemned.

It follows:

### But You Are the Most High

They will be condemned, but your people will be saved, because you, Lord, will be their Savior forever. You, I say, who are the Most High—that is, who already see from your height both that the time of the wicked’s prosperity will soon end and that the time of the good’s reward will soon arrive.

### For Behold, Your Enemies

Truly the sinners will perish, because they will perish; and they will perish because they are your enemies. “Behold, your enemies.” For the time is short. The repetition confirms the statement.

The Lord’s enemies are called not only those who blaspheme against him, but also those of whom James says: “Whoever is a friend of the world is constituted an enemy of God.” Such people are understood here as enemies. It follows:

### And All Who Work Iniquity Will Be Scattered

I say that your enemies, Lord, will perish. And this is true, because all who work iniquity—that is, who persist in the work of iniquity—will be scattered, that is, separated from the good at the future judgment.

Or they will be scattered among themselves, because they will quarrel violently against one another and will displease one another, saying: “We fools considered their life madness,” and so forth.

Or they will also be scattered from the present prosperity in which they trusted. For it was said of them: “When he dies, he will take nothing with him; nor will his glory descend with him.”

### And My Horn Will Be Exalted

The wicked will indeed be scattered and the righteous saved. This is what he ought to have said; but because the prophet himself was one of them, he speaks of himself on behalf of all, saying:

“And then my horn,” that is, my exaltation, “will be exalted”—that is, I shall be crowned as he deserves to be exalted who is a unicorn: one who prefers to be singularly in hope in the present rather than possess many things in reality.

The unicorn is also customarily understood as signifying the unity of the Church, because it has only one horn. In accordance with this, the passage may also be understood as follows: “My horn will be exalted,” like the horn of one who rightly deserves to be exalted, who is not separated but is a unicorn—that is, who remains in unity. For then unity alone will be crowned, while schism will be condemned.

“And my old age”—that is, my later condition—“will be in abundant mercy.” This does not mean that mercy will exist there, where there will be truth alone; nevertheless, because what is promised here mercifully will be fulfilled there, he therefore says that mercy will be there. And because what is now in hope will then be in reality, he adds “abundant.”

He calls it old age by comparison, because however much he may be despised here in his abundance, there he will be revered and honored like an old man. Understand the whole of the present labor after faith has been received as youth, because it is a kind of renewal leading to that blessedness.

### And My Eye Has Looked Down

It is as though he were saying: Since I am certain of that future blessedness, therefore my eye—that is, my reason—has looked down upon my enemies, that is, the flourishing wicked, because neither their persecution nor their flourishing moved me.

And I shall always look down upon them, because when those who do evil rise up against me—that is, when they rise against me by persuading me to evil, so that they may lead me astray—then my ear, the ear of my heart, will hear this from the truth presiding within it: “Do not assent to these people so as to desire their flourishing.”

For it is not yours to flourish according to time, because “the righteous will flourish like the palm tree.” That is, the flourishing of the righteous will come late, like the flower of the palm, which does not bear fruit before its thirtieth year.

Or for this reason “like the palm”: just as the palm is rough on its trunk but exceedingly beautiful at its summit, so the life of the good is, at the beginning, as it were ugly and rough, but at the end it will be most delightful.

And therefore “the righteous will multiply like the cedar of Lebanon,” because he will also be filled with every fragrance of virtue. And just as the cedar spreads its branches only at the top, so the merits of the righteous are extended—that is, they will appear—at the end.

And just as these trees are not dried up by the sun when it rises in summer, whereas grasses rather put forth their flowers, so when the sun rises in summer—that is, when it comes for judgment—the righteous will not wither but will flourish. The wicked, however, who are compared with grass that is green in winter and withers in summer, will wither.

### Planted in the House of the Lord

Truly the righteous will at last flourish, because he has been planted in the house of the Lord—that is, in the present Church, which is called the house of the Lord. He has been firmly planted in faith and also rooted in charity.

And all who have been planted in this way in the house of the Lord will truly flourish in the courts of the house of our God—that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem. It is called the house of God because of the abiding dwelling that is in it, and a court because of its adornment and delight.

He uses “courts” in the plural because “in my Father’s house are many dwelling places.”

### They Will Still Multiply in Old Age

Truly those planted in the house of the Lord will finally flourish in the court, because they will multiply—that is, they will be glorified in many ways—because they will be clothed in the double garment in abundant old age, as was said above.

This is still to be awaited, as though he were saying: “Wait a little while, until the number of your brothers is fulfilled.” Meanwhile they will be good sufferers—that is, without murmuring—and will await it with complete patience, so that by this very patience they may announce to others:

“For”—in place of “because”—“the Lord our God is upright,” that is, just in the rewarding of the righteous, who suffer so much for his name. And by contrast they may announce that “there is no iniquity in him”—that is, in God—in the condemnation of the wicked, because they did not heed the patience he displayed toward them and therefore neglected to be corrected.

## PSALM XCII

A Song of Praise to David, on the Day before the Sabbath, When the Earth Was Founded

### Argument

Foretelling the return from Babylon, he adorns the song with the customary pattern of narrative, by which divine matters are more fully commended and assistance is unfolded. What he says in the title, “Because the earth was inhabited,” signifies that captivity had been loosened. It should truly be noted that this psalm, as well as the preceding one, is without a title among the Hebrews, that is, lacking an inscription.

### Explanation

This song, to the praise of the divinity, attributed to David, is suitably applied to Christ. It is asked how the earth was founded on the day before the Sabbath—that is, on the sixth day—when Genesis records that dry land appeared on the third day.

Here, however, we must understand the earth as the human being, to whom it is said: “You are earth, and into earth you will go.” Just as he was made by God the Creator on the sixth day, so also, in the sixth age of the world, he was restored by that same God and by the Creator who was of David’s seed. The earth was then founded when faith in him was firmly established in the human race.

Therefore the praise of his holy Incarnation is sung throughout this psalm. The first section proceeds from his beauty; the second from his strength; the third from his works; the fourth from his power; the fifth from the praises of the whole universe; the sixth from the truth of the teachers; and the last from praise of his house, which ought to rejoice in eternal exultation.

Some manuscripts read: “On the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was inhabited.” This seems more consonant with the historical sense, because the earth was founded first, but on the sixth day before the Sabbath its completion came through the herds of animals and the habitation of the human being himself.

On that same day the Lord restored to paradise, through the wood of the cross, the human being whom he had established there from the beginning: “Today,” he said, “you will be with me in paradise.”

### Commentary

### The Lord Reigned

In this psalm the prophet joyfully and devoutly praises a certain victorious king, whose praise ought to make everyone rejoice, because everyone ought to share in the joy of his victory. Therefore it is entitled: “A song of praise to David.” Devotion belongs to praise, while exultation belongs to song.

This praise is sung on the day—that is, in contemplation of the day before the Sabbath. For the earth was founded on the fifth day, as it is read in the book of Genesis: “God made all the irrational animals.” On the day before the Sabbath, that is, on the sixth day, he made the human being. On the seventh day he saw that everything he had made was very good, and he rested from all his work that he had prepared.

These days were arranged in this way not without cause, but because such things were also to take place in the second course of time, before we should rest in God. If we do good works, we shall truly rest in him. For this reason the example was given that he saw all the things he had made to be good and rested on the seventh day.

He did not rest because he became tired or weary, in accordance with the saying: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” Yet he is never wearied, because he does everything with tranquility. In accordance with this Solomon says: “You, Lord of Sabaoth, judge all things with tranquility.”

We, however, do not perform the good works we do without labor, as long as we remain in the promised rest—not yet possessing it in reality, but nevertheless possessing it in hope. If we were not in hope, we would fail in our labor. But when we are in rest, we shall rejoice without end. Hence the Sabbath day is not said to have an evening, because our rest will have no end.

The second course of time follows the arrangement of the days. The first age extends from Adam to Noah, like the first day. The second extends from Noah to Abraham, like the second day. The third age extends from Abraham to David, like the third day. The fourth age extends from David to the Babylonian captivity, like the fourth day. The fifth age extends from the Babylonian captivity to the preaching of John the Baptist, up to the end of the world, like the sixth day.

In this sixth age the Lord came in the flesh and restored the human being whom he had first made on the sixth day. On the sixth day and at the sixth hour of that same sixth age, by pouring out his blood on the cross—the true day—he redeemed him from the power of the devil.

And this is what the title says: “On the day before the Sabbath, because the Lord founded the earth.” He founded it upon that foundation of which the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, namely Christ.”

The prophet’s purpose in this psalm is to exhort us not to be ungrateful to our Lord and King, who became victorious for our sake, and to prepare a worthy seat for him within us. And he speaks in this way:

“The Lord reigned,” that is, he secured the kingdom for himself; or because, coming in the flesh, he bound the ruler of the world and cast him out; or when, rising from the dead, he conquered death.

And truly he reigned, because he was clothed with beauty—that is, he clothed and incorporated into himself those who had previously been made ugly, making them beautiful. Those who had previously been a gulf of drunkenness became an ornament of sobriety; those who had been filth of lust became the adornment of temperance. Thus they became his clothing, in accordance with the saying: “As I live, says the Lord, you will be clothed with all these things as with a garment.”

And “the Lord was clothed with strength,” that is, he clothed with strength those who had previously been weak and impatient, making them strong and patient.

### And He Girded Himself

To gird and to gird oneself are different. To gird oneself is to gird something to oneself, as in the saying, “Gird yourself with your sword”; but to gird something before oneself is to place it in front of oneself.

The meaning is therefore this: The Lord clothed those people with strength in such a way that he girded himself with them—that is, they were his girding, and they recognized that all their strength consisted in humility, remembering that when the Lord displayed humility by bending before the feet of his disciples, he was girded with a linen cloth. In this he taught them always to place humility first, because through it they would be strong against every pride and hostile power.

Or otherwise: “He girded himself with strength,” that is, he girded strength before himself, meaning patience. For we endure detractors both behind our backs and before our faces. Therefore we ought to have patience girded before us—that is, placed especially before our eyes—in regard to those who insult us to our faces, so that we may not return evil for evil but, on the contrary, bless them. Patience is necessary for us to receive the promise.

The passage may also be understood in another way: “He was clothed with beauty and strength.” He put on beauty when, taking three disciples, he went up the mountain and was transfigured before them. He put on strength when, in response to his enemies who were seeking him, he said, “I am he,” and by that one word cast them to the ground. Again, he put on strength when he made a whip from cords and drove the sellers and buyers from the temple.

Or, as the Gospel relates, some said of him, “He is good,” while others said, “No, but he deceives the crowds.” Between these he put on beauty and strength, because for our instruction he assumed such a bearing that he was neither delighted by the tongue of those praising him nor broken by the tongue of those reviling him. This was truly both beautiful and a sign of great strength.

You can plainly apply to both interpretations the statement that follows: “He girded himself with strength.”

### For He Established the World

Truly the Lord was clothed with beauty and strength—that is, he made people beautiful and strong—because he established the world, that is, those who had previously been changeable and unstable in earthly things like the world, he made stable and immovable in faith.

Or he established the world, that is, he made people such that they would neither soften beneath the tongue of flatterers nor be broken by the tongue of detractors. This is the world, I say, which will not be moved.

There is indeed a certain world which will not be moved, namely the heretics, whose movement the Apostle explains to us in part when he says: “Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have strayed from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they overthrow the faith of some.”

He subsequently makes clear what the world is that will not be moved, saying: “The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his’; and, ‘Let everyone who invokes the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.’”

### Your Throne Is Prepared

This is an apostrophe to the Lord. It is as though he were saying: You have indeed established the world, and in this way your throne has been prepared—from that time, namely, either from the time when the Lord reigned or from the time when the earth was founded.

And although, as he were saying, your throne has been prepared for you in time, it is nevertheless an eternal throne, because you are from eternity and you are eternal. The Greek word αἰών (*aiōn*) is ambiguous, because it is used both for “age” and for “eternal”; and for this reason Latin translators are often found to have used it for “eternal.”

The thrones of God are those in whom God dwells. Of them it is said through the prophet: “Upon whom will my spirit rest, if not upon the quiet and humble person who trembles at my words?” Be quiet, therefore, not quarrelsome; humble, not proud; and thus you will be a throne of God.

Nor does he fear the one holding a throne in you [F. *time tenentem*: “fear [the one] holding”], because he himself established it.

### The Rivers Have Raised Their Waves

It is as though he were saying: In order to prepare this throne of yours, the rivers, which previously feared, have raised their voices.

By “rivers” he understands those from whose womb—that is, from whose memory—spiritual gifts flowed abundantly into the nations, namely the holy apostles. The head, that is, the fountain, of these rivers is the one who said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his womb.”

One of these rivers, which had previously been very timid when it denied the Lord three times at the voice of a servant girl—namely Peter—then boldly raised its voice. After the rulers and priests had released them, having imprisoned and scourged them and commanded them no longer to speak in the name of Christ, he answered boldly: “Judge whether it is right in God’s sight to obey you rather than God. For we cannot not speak of what we have heard and seen.”
