He also truly raised his voice when, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, “standing in the midst, he opened his mouth and said: ‘Men, brothers,’” and so forth. Likewise, the others also acted with the greatest boldness on their own behalf.

And this is what he says: The rivers that had previously been afraid, when they despaired as though during the Lord’s death and passion, after the confirmation of the Holy Spirit—which turned their fear into love—raised their voices. They raised their voices, that is, they confidently preached Christ. I rightly repeat that the rivers raised their voices.

The repetition confirms the statement. And they not only raised their voices in gentle admonition, but also raised their waves—that is, their threats—saying: “Woe to the world because of scandals”; and, “Woe to you unless you repent.”

The waves, I say, were increased by the voices of many waters, that is, of many peoples. For when the holy apostles preached, many immediately believed and also received the Holy Spirit; and thus many of them raised their voices, that is, began to preach Christ. For this reason the holy apostles were able to raise their voices with even greater confidence.

Or otherwise: When the holy apostles were released by the priests and rulers, as we said above, they came to their own people and recounted everything that the rulers and priests had said or done to them. When the others heard this, they raised their voices together, saying: “Lord, you made heaven and earth,” and so forth.

Strengthened by the joy of these people, the apostles were encouraged to raise not only a voice of admonition but also waves of threat.

And behold, what follows came to pass: the wondrous surges of the sea—that is, of the Gentiles embittered in their barrenness—rose up against them. Then the roaring lion met Samson as he went to take a wife from the foreigners, as was said above.

But what concern was this? None, certainly, because the Lord was wondrous in suppressing those lofty surges. For he who had previously trampled the sea beneath his feet himself subdued the pride of the Gentiles.

### Your Testimonies Are Trustworthy

And because the sea stirred up such great surges, therefore your testimonies—that is, what you had testified to them, Lord—became exceedingly, that is, very, trustworthy through the apostles. You had said to them: “In the world you will have tribulation, but in me you will have peace.”

The experience of one thing—the tribulation they endured in the world—was for them the certainty of the other, namely that they would truly possess eternal peace in you.

And this holiness—that is, this kind of instruction through scourges, which truly is holiness, meaning sanctification and testing—befits your house, that is, those who are your holy temple, in whom you dwell. It is a house, I say, destined to endure for length of days—that is, eternally.

Or otherwise: “The rivers have raised their waves.” It is as though he were saying: In order to hinder the throne that was being prepared for you, Lord, the rivers—that is, the philosophers of the world—raised their voices, namely their reasons and arguments, against your truth.

And not only did the rivers raise their voices; the rivers—that is, the rulers who embitter the age and send in their waves—also raised their waves, that is, their threatening contradictions. The waves, I say, were stirred up by the voices of many waters, that is, of many peoples, because, as another psalm says: “The peoples have meditated on empty things,” and so forth, “against the Lord and against his Christ.”

In this way the surges of the sea became wondrous, as before; but the Lord was wondrous in suppressing those lofty surges. And he was wondrous in this way because your testimonies—that is, the things they themselves testified about you—which seemed unbelievable, nevertheless became exceedingly, that is, very, trustworthy through the display of miracles.

What they said they proved by their deeds, with the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed. And because this holiness and sanctification—namely, the confirmation of words by deeds—befits your house, Lord, destined to endure forever and ever, the passage may be read as above.

It can also be read in accordance with the preceding interpretation: “The wondrous surges of the sea.” It is as though he were saying: Because the rivers—that is, the apostles—raised their voices or waves by threatening human beings with eternal punishments if they did not convert, therefore the sea—that is, the bitterness of paganism, which previously lay immersed in desires for earthly things—made wondrous surges. That is, it swelled wondrously, because what had been below was made high: it converted the love of earthly things into love of heavenly things.

This happened because the Lord was wondrous in the depths—that is, in the deep waters—of that sea. For just as he once sweetened the waters through Moses his servant by casting wood into the sea, so, by casting the wood of his cross into the sea of paganism—that is, by making known to the Gentiles the faith in his passion and resurrection—he changed their bitterness into sweetness. Those who had previously been lovers of the world became lovers of heaven and despisers of the world.

And in this way, Lord, your testimonies—that is, the things you had testified concerning the incorporation of Jews and Gentiles—were spoken:

“I have other sheep, which are not from this fold, and I must bring them also,” and so forth.

Such things became exceedingly trustworthy. And this holiness—that other sheep also would be converted and incorporated—befits your house, that is, your Church, which ought not to be confined within narrow spaces. It is a house, I say, destined to endure for length of days—that is, forever.

## PSALM XCIII

A Psalm to David, on the Fourth Day of the Week

### Argument

After the evils inflicted by the victorious Chaldean have been enumerated, there is added the prayer of the defeated, captured, and deported people. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church concerning the Jews addressed to the Lord.

### Explanation

The fourth day of the week is the fourth day from the Sabbath, on which day the Lord created the lights of heaven. This is to be applied to holy men whose heavenly manner of life shines upon earth; it is of them that this psalm is about to speak.

The prophet, observing the hearts of the foolish disturbed—as though God did not care about mortal affairs—when they saw the wicked prospering and the righteous afflicted, first asks the Lord to repay the proud, through whom he had learned that the world was corrupted by such an estimation.

Second, he reproves those who, in foolish blasphemy, think that God does not see human affairs, although he grants understanding and perception to his creatures. He calls blessed the one who, despising the world’s prosperity, perseveres in reverence for God.

Third, in order to encourage their hearts, he says that the Lord has been his refuge and will be the avenger of sinners.

### Commentary

### God, the Lord of Vengeance

Many customarily murmur against God’s patience and grieve that the wicked live, possess great power, and—what is more serious—oppress the good. In this way impatient and weak souls are perverted, as though it were useless to be good because God has turned his eyes away from them and increased the wicked in the things they love.

Thus, thinking that they live well without cause, they are invited to imitate the wickedness of those whom they see flourishing. If, however, because of weakness of person or spirit, they fear doing evil lest they themselves suffer evil, they indeed abstain from evil deeds but do not abstain from wicked thoughts.

Among their evil thoughts this is the height of impiety: they think that God neglects and does not care about human affairs, or that he regards good and evil people alike; or, what is more destructive, that he favors the wicked and hates the good.

This psalm addresses such silent thoughts of human beings, and also those that break out in words or deeds, if they are willing to attend to it. For it teaches patience amid the labor of the good and against the prosperity of the wicked. Its title is: “A psalm to David, on the fourth day of the Sabbath.”

On the fourth day of the Sabbath, as it is read in Genesis, God made the lights—that is, the sun, moon, and all the stars—and placed them in the firmament of heaven.

What, then, does it mean that the psalm received its title from the fourth day of the Sabbath? In this psalm we are taught patience amid the labor of the good and against the prosperity of the wicked. You have the Apostle saying to the faithful strengthened in Christ:

“Do all things without murmuring and disputing, so that you may be blameless, sincere, and spotless children of God in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life.”

The lights fixed in the firmament, however much people may speak falsely about them, however many reproaches they may utter against them—calling one star Venus and another Jupiter—and however much the lower regions may be disturbed by every kind of disorder, nevertheless do not abandon their courses. They maintain their paths through the heavenly regions as their Creator appointed for them.

So too people whose hearts are fixed in the firmament of heaven and in the book of God’s law, and who do not hear “Lift up your hearts” in vain, whose treasure and manner of life are in heavenly things: however much evil people, persuaders, and detractors may lie about them and curse them, however much they may disparage them, they nevertheless complete their course—that is, they do not depart from their good purpose.

The voice of such people is in this psalm. They exhort the weak and murmuring to patience amid the labor of the good and against the prosperity of the wicked, and they rebuke the wicked who flourish without knowing the truth.

The title is explained as follows: “A psalm,” that is, this praise, is attributed to David himself—not to just anyone, but to the one signified by the created things of the fourth day of the Sabbath. That is, it is attributed to all the faithful saints strengthened in Christ, whom the Apostle calls the lights of the world. Their voice, as we said above, is in this psalm, correcting those who murmur against God’s patience in the following manner.

It is as though he were saying: You murmur that God does not immediately punish the wicked. You ought not to murmur; rather, you must take care lest you yourself be among them, because he will indeed punish them.

For God exists, and if God exists, he is not unjust. Therefore he will leave nothing unpunished that you do not punish. And because he is God, he will therefore be the Lord of vengeance.

God, I say, will truly be the Lord of vengeance, that is, he will finally exercise power and lordship in taking vengeance. For, as though he were saying: He will act freely.

And truly he will then act freely because he acted freely before, since he spared no one in his word. The Lord was in the humility of the flesh, but in the word of truth he respected no person. He spared no one in his word, so that there might be those whom he could spare in judgment.

For it was said of him: “He was speaking as one having authority, and not like their scribes and Pharisees.” And he who spared no one in his word—when he comes to be judged—will he spare anyone in his sentence when he comes to judge? And he who feared no one in humility, will he fear anyone in majesty? Certainly no one. Therefore, he who previously acted freely will at last act freely.

Exalt yourself, you who judge the earth. He said that he acted freely, but wicked men—namely, the Jews—did not tolerate this freedom of his, because he was opposed to their deeds. Yet they seized him, scourged him, crowned him with thorns, raised him upon the cross, and finally killed him. Therefore the prophetic spirit, foreseeing this, said: “Exalt yourself, you who judge the earth.” As though he were saying: “Die, Lord, so that you may be exalted; and exalt yourself, so that, judged by the earth, you may judge the earth”—you, I say, who truly judge, that is, who will judge the whole earth, both cultivated and uncultivated. “Therefore repay the proud according to their deserts.” The proud are those for whom it is not enough to sin, but who even dare to defend their sins. And the Lord will repay such people according to their deserts. What repayment? Certainly, eternal damnation. But he will not repay the humble. For example, certain people among those who crucified the Lord, after seeing so many miracles and hearing such great proclamations from the apostles, humbled themselves: they recognized their sin, and, believing, drank the price of their redemption, which they had poured out in their fury, when they approached the apostles and said: “What shall we do, men and brothers?” and so forth. Such people will not be repaid. But the proud, for whom it is not enough to have done wrong, and who strive even to defend it, will be repaid. This is said for their correction, so that they may be converted at least through fear of punishment. It should be understood that when he says, “Exalt yourself and repay,” this is the prophecy of one who foreknows, not the audacity of one who commands. The Lord did not act because the Prophet foretold it; rather, the Prophet foretold it because the Lord was going to act.

[Col. 0986D]

How long, sinners? Behold, the prophetic spirit assumes the role of some eloquent comforter. For he associates himself with those who murmur, whom he consoles in their ignorance—not because he did not know what he asks as though ignorant, but so that his consolation might be more acceptable to those with whom he sympathizes. It is as though he were saying: “For this reason I say that you should repay the proud, because how long, Lord, will sinners glory?” Certainly, as though he were saying, sinners will glory as long as you are pleased that they should—“how long” meaning “for as long as it pleases you.” He shows how they glory: they will speak forth, that is, they will speak outwardly. This means that they will persuade others to wickedness. And they will speak it forth because they first speak it in their hearts. For they think to themselves: “Certainly, if the things I do displeased God, he would not allow me to live, but would have killed me long ago.” And because they think this to themselves, they later give it eloquent expression, so as to persuade others of the same thing. This is what he says: “They will speak forth,” and first “they will speak wickedness within themselves.”

[Col. 0987A]

They will speak because they act unjustly. I say this confidently, because they also carry their injustice into effect: that is, they bring to completion the wickedness they have conceived. This is what he says: “All who act unjustly will speak.” And because you, Lord, do not correct them, they will also extend their wickedness over others, because they have humbled your people.

The passage may also be connected in this straightforward manner: What injustice do they commit? This, namely, that they have humbled your people by calling them away from the Lord and incorporating them into themselves. Which people, and what humiliation, he specifies when he says: “And they have harassed your inheritance.” And truly, as though he were saying, they have harassed them—either inwardly, by denying them, or, if not inwardly, at least outwardly: the widow, that is, someone lacking consolation in the world as though lacking a husband; and the stranger, who believes that he has no abiding city here but seeks one in the future. They have also killed some physically and others spiritually: orphans, that is, those who had been deprived of a father in the world.

[Col. 0987B]

While doing these things they said: “The Lord will not see them, nor will the God of Jacob understand them”—that is, the supplanting God; the following phrase is corrupt, but appears to refer to the presence of those who despise him, whom these people make their end—as though they were saying: “Because you, Lord, prolong your forbearance excessively, they themselves add wickedness upon wickedness.” First they judged you unjust when they said that their wickedness pleased you. Now they add another wickedness to it, asserting that you do not care for human affairs when they say: “The Lord will not see,” and so forth.

Understand, you foolish ones. He turns to those who murmur and are weak, teaching them not to imitate the wicked, seduced by their prosperity. It is as though he were saying: “They persuade others to wickedness and even diminish the Lord’s power, saying that he will not see the evils they commit. But you, the weak among God’s people, foolish because you do not provide for yourselves in the future, do not cling to such people by envying their prosperity. Rather, understand what must be understood.”

[Col. 0987C]

And you fools do not consider how vain and fragile is what you desire. If you have previously gone astray, come to your senses at least now, because those who say, “He will not see or understand,” are lying. For truly the Lord understands and sees. He who planted the ear—that is, who made this organ of hearing, which is the ear—will he not hear? And he who fashioned the eye, the organ by which we see, will he not observe? And he who everywhere rebukes the nations, sending his heralds throughout the world to proclaim the truth and rebuke falsehood—will he not finally rebuke those who receive grace in vain?

[Col. 0987D]

And as though someone might say, “He would rebuke them, certainly, if he knew,” he adds: “Fool, he who teaches human beings knowledge does not himself lack knowledge.” Certainly not. For the Lord is absolute, that is, he has all things in his power. And if all things, then knowledge as well. Since he possesses knowledge, it is evident that he knows not only human deeds but also human thoughts—not in order to approve them, but rather to condemn them, because he knows that they are vain.

[Col. 0988A]

But human beings, as though he were saying, do not know God’s just and true thoughts; that is, they do not know why he spares the wicked. Let us therefore abandon the vain thoughts of human beings, so that we may know the true thoughts of God. Who, then, knows the Lord’s true thoughts? No one, certainly, except the one whom the Lord has instructed—that is, the one whose heart is fixed in the firmament of heaven, namely, in the book of God’s law. Therefore truly blessed is everyone whom you instruct.

And for this reason I say “blessed,” because you teach him from your law—that is, making your law his instruction, namely, your paternal scourges. They are understood as a law because the law inflicts punishments. You will make them an instruction for him in order to temper him: that is, to make him tempered and restrained, so that he may not be led astray by evil days.

The evil days are those in which the wicked flourish and the good suffer. But the suffering of the good is a paternal scourge, while the prosperity of the wicked is their pit. For this reason he says, “Temper him away from the evil days,” because the evil days will last until the pit is dug—that is, until eternal damnation has been fully prepared for the sinner.

And it is as though he were saying to anyone who murmurs against God’s forbearance: “You indeed wish to bury the wicked now, but the time has not yet come, because the pit has not yet been prepared. Wait, therefore, until the pit is dug for the sinner.”

Here he calls “the sinner” the person who does not wish to practice penance in the confession of sins, so as to be saved through humility. For it is necessary that in everyone, whether man or woman, humble confession should come first, followed by salutary repentance capable of correcting the person rather than mocking God. And if he does good works, let him give thanks to God for them, and not despise another, as though God’s mercy—which is abundant toward all—had been shut off from that person.

[Col. 0988B]

The Pharisee, however, was not condemned because he gave thanks for his good works, saying, “I give you thanks, Lord,” but because he despised the publican, saying, “Because I am not like the rest of humanity: robbers, or even like this publican.” He was proud of his good works. For, he says, “This man went down to his house justified”; he does not drive him away from that way.

He said that the evil days would last until the pit was dug for the sinner. And it is as though he were saying: “Until the exercise of discipline has been prepared for his people.” For the Lord will indeed exercise his people through eternal scourges, but he will not drive them away. Rather, through this discipline he will draw his inheritance to himself. This is his people, which is his inheritance.

And he will not abandon them for so long as—“until” meaning “up to that time”—justice is converted into judgment: that is, until that Just One who is emphatically called “justice” is changed from humility into judgment, so that he who first came humble to be judged may come in terror to judge.

And who will then be beside that justice? That is, who will then stand alongside that Just One coming to judgment, so that they may judge with him? All who are upright in heart.

Or the passage may be understood differently: “Until our justice is converted into judgment,” that is, so that those in whom it formerly went before may become judges. As though he were saying: “Now possess justice; now hold fast to justice, while you are not yet able to possess judgment.” For the holy apostles first possessed justice—that is, they endured wicked people—and afterward they will judge. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself first wished to be judged before judging. First came the time of his Passion, then the time of judgment; first the time of humiliation, then the time of exaltation. Therefore now hold fast to justice, if you wish eventually to possess judgment.

And who, as though he were saying, are beside that justice? Who are those who, even if they do not now possess it fully, nevertheless approach it as far as is possible for a human being? This is what “beside” indicates: we can approach justice, but we cannot possess it fully. Who, I ask, is beside it? All who are upright in heart.

Those are upright in heart who are pleased by what pleases God, and who do not twist God’s upright heart toward their own. But if some desire arises in them that displeases God, they immediately align it with his will, as with a straight rule.

That there are two wills in us, the Lord Jesus Christ graciously prefigured in himself. By the drops of blood that came forth from his body like sweat, [Col. 0989A] that good and steadfast will was signified which is immediately aligned with God’s will. By the words through which he transferred our weakness to himself—“Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”—he prefigured in us the weaker will. But that such a will must immediately be directed and made straight toward God’s will, he showed when he added: “Nevertheless, not as I will, Father, but as you will.”

Who will rise? Again, that perfect one who speaks here—whether the sun, the moon, or any one of the luminaries—teaches the foolish among God’s people to invoke divine help, so that they may possess the justice that will eventually be converted into judgment. It is as though he were saying: “No one can possess judgment unless justice has preceded it; and no one can possess justice unless he is upright in heart. Therefore you who murmur among God’s people and are foolish, invoke divine help, so that through it you may attain these things, and say:

[Col. 0989B]

Who will rise for me—that is, to help me—against those who act maliciously, that is, who persuade others to evil? By “those who act maliciously” he means the devil and his angels, and also the children of distrust, in whom he works as in his vessels.

Or who will stand with me, bringing me assistance against those who practice wickedness? That is, against those same malicious beings who also work within us the evils that they persuade us to commit.

Who, I ask, will rise, or who will stand? The Lord, certainly, who both formerly and truly stood with me before, because my soul dwelt in hell. This means: “I wished, deceived by their prosperity, to imitate their malice, and so I nearly perished, so that my soul might dwell—that is, cling firmly—in that hell of which it was said above: ‘Until the pit is dug for the sinner.’ Yet it was a lesser thing that I did not dwell there; and this ‘less’ was only a little—indeed, the very smallest—because, although I was close to a true imitation of them in my will, I had not yet imitated them in reality. Nevertheless,” as though he were saying, “although I was so near, I did not dwell there, because the Lord helped me so that I would not fall completely. If he had not done so, I truly would have dwelt there.”

And, as though he were saying, “Because he helped me then, he will also help me now.”

If I said, “My foot has been moved.” Here the perfect one, speaking in his own person, says this, continuing to teach those who murmur and are foolish. It is as though he were saying: “You say that the Lord helped you before, and certainly he will still help you if you say to him: ‘My foot has been moved’; for when I once said this to him, he helped me.”

Here the humility of confession is commended. It is so pleasing to God that even after our foot—that is, our affection—has moved, if we confess immediately after the movement, we do not have to mourn our fall. This is what he says: “I did not say ‘I said,’ but ‘I was saying’”—that is, even if I was beginning to say, “Lord, my inner foot has been moved,” your mercy immediately helped me, so that I did not have to mourn my fall.

As though he were saying: “If I was moved as a human being, you were present to me as God.”

[Col. 0989D]

According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart. I rightly say: “Your mercy was helping me.” For your consolations have gladdened my soul. Above all, they gladdened me in this respect: that I know that through these consolations I will eventually cling to you.

But they—the malicious and those who practice wickedness—will not [lacuna]

## ON PSALM XCIV

### ARGUMENT

Foretelling the events that either happened to those leaving Babylon or to those dwelling in Babylon, at the beginning of the psalm he calls everyone to give thanks; then, by the example of past events, he introduces the usefulness of entreaty. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church urging repentance.

### A SONG OF PRAISE; FOR DAVID HIMSELF

### EXPLANATION

“Praise” signifies devotion of voice, and “song” gladness of mind; “for David himself” designates Christ our salvation, so that we may [Col. 0990A] rejoice together not in vain pleasures but in the Lord.

The prophet, foreseeing that the Jews might resist Christ, first invites their peoples to psalmody, describing the praises of the Lord in the sweetest variety. Second, the Lord himself speaks, warning that this people should not harden its heart, lest what happened to their fathers befall them—those who did not deserve to enter the promised land.

## ON PSALM XCV

A song for David himself, when the house was being built after the captivity.

### ARGUMENT

Thanksgiving is celebrated for the return from Babylon. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church calling. Likewise, the house whose destruction we lamented in the preceding psalm—that is, the rule of discipline—we now celebrate as restored.

### EXPLANATION

[Col. 0990B]

In its literal sense, it signifies the time when, after the Babylonian captivity had been released, the temple at Jerusalem was restored. Spiritually, however, the destroyed house is built when, after captivity to sin, the soul recovers the way of truth.

For this house—that is, the universal Church in which Christ dwells—is continually built of living stones, until the number of the predestined is completed at the end of the age.

In the first part of the psalm the prophet urges all people to sing to the Lord and to proclaim throughout the whole world the advent of the Lord’s Incarnation, because the true Lord is above all gods. In the second, he admonishes the nations in various ways first to offer themselves and afterward to present the offerings of their preaching, commemorating both aspects of the Lord’s advent: either his coming when judged by the world, or his coming when he will judge the world.

## ON PSALM XCVI

For David himself, when his land was restored to him.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0990C]

A triumph over the Babylonians and thanksgiving for the people’s return are celebrated, where the majesty of the reigning God is described according to the customary pattern. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church concerning the Lord’s advent.

### EXPLANATION

Refer “for David himself” to Christ. Understand “his land restored” either as the resurrection of the flesh that he assumed from the Virgin, or as sinners of every kind returning to him after their sins, as happened among the Jews who washed away through repentance the crime of the Lord’s crucifixion.

In the first section of the psalm, the prophet describes the Lord’s powers after the Resurrection through varied preaching and rebukes the worshipers of idols with a deserved reprimand. In the second, he turns his words toward the Lord, rejoicing that the Church has believed in its creator and urging the faithful to rejoice in the Lord because he is accustomed to free them from the pressures of the wicked.

## ON PSALM XCVII

A psalm for David himself.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0990D]

When the captivity has been released, an exhortation to devoted observance in the Lord is joined to it; according to the customary pattern, the pageantry of the victory prepared over the Babylonians is described. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church addressed to the Lord and the apostles.

### EXPLANATION

This title refers to the Lord Christ, concerning whose twofold advent the psalm which it precedes is about to speak. Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks.

In the first part he urges the Christian people to rejoice with the exultation of a new song, when Christ’s wondrous advent has been granted. In the second, he says more fully and in various ways that rejoicing is necessary, because at the end the longed-for judge will come for the righteous.

## ON PSALM XCVIII

A psalm for David himself.

### ARGUMENT

As above. Alternatively, it is the voice of the apostles addressed to the people.

### EXPLANATION

[Col. 0991A]

Understand David as Christ, whose honor and power are sung in this psalm.

In the first section the prophet urges all peoples to confess Christ the Lord, because he has executed judgment and justice in Jacob. In the second he urges the people to adore the Lord the Savior, who showed mercy to Moses, Aaron, and Samuel because they kept his commandments. Hence the Lord, who graciously listened to his faithful, must be exalted and adored.

## ON PSALM XCIX

A psalm for confession.

### ARGUMENT

As though already brought back from Babylon and dwelling on their own soil, they are urged to enter God’s temple in order to give thanks. Through frequent preaching and exhortation, the prophet diligently strives to rescue them from both despair of returning and negligence in giving thanks, and confidently delivers this message.

Alternatively, it is the voice of the apostles addressed to the people.

### EXPLANATION

Although confession is frequently placed in the psalms according to the appropriateness of the circumstances, here it is singularly assigned in the title because this entire psalm pertains to both kinds of confession: namely, confession of repentance and confession of praise.

In the first part of the psalm the prophet urges the whole community to praise the Lord with rejoicing. In the second, lest one think that this same kind of confession must always be used, he promises us that those who repent of their sins can enter through the gates of his indulgence.

## ON PSALM C

A psalm for David himself.

### ARGUMENT

It is sung in the person of the righteous in Babylon, [Col. 0991C] and things are foretold that would be appropriate to each person during the time of tribulation according to his conscience. Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ addressed to the Father concerning the remnants of the saints.

### EXPLANATION

The title is familiar, and the psalm itself is enclosed within the form of perfect holiness; it ought to await the hundredfold fruit of rewards.

In the first part of the psalm the Church says that it will sing mercy and judgment to the Lord and avoid companionship with the worst people. In the second it asserts that it loves the faithful and rejoices in their fellowship, while driving demons and their assaults from its heart, knowing that they have no share with God’s servants.

## ON PSALM CI

The prayer of the poor man when he is anxious and pours out his prayer before the Lord.

### ARGUMENT

To the sad sufferings foretold for the Babylonian captivity he adds joyful things, namely, the hope of return.

[Col. 0991D]

Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ and the Church when Christ had ascended to the Father.

### EXPLANATION

Although some have thought that the present psalm should be applied to the Lord the Savior, it seems more fitting that the person introduced should be that of an afflicted and groaning poor man, just as the title itself contains.

When he says that the one praying directs his attention before the Lord, he shows that, after the tumult of thoughts has been driven from his mind, he remembers nothing except himself and the one to whom he pleads.

And note that, although names are placed in the titles everywhere, here a poor man is introduced speaking without a name, so that, when one person is given to us, all the poor of Christ may recognize that person as assigned to themselves.

This poor man, lacking worldly goods but rich in virtues, at the beginning of the psalm repeatedly asks the Lord to attend to his prayers, because, crushed by continual affliction, he has borne bones as though they had been broken. Then follows a mournful disclosure of his needs, lest after so many calamities he should appear ungrateful for his chastisement.

In the third part he continues the Lord’s praises. [Col. 0992A] He says that at the Lord’s advent the Church will be built; and although all things will be changed, he himself will nevertheless remain forever. There is also an exceedingly desirable conclusion: the seed of the saints is to be directed to the place where the Lord dwells in everlasting glory. Thus the poor man’s prayer, which began with tears, is brought to completion in joy.

## COMMENTARY

Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you. The prayer of the poor man when he is anxious and pours out his prayers before the Lord.

That poor man speaks in this psalm who, although he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that we might be enriched by his poverty. From him come all riches, both true and false.

His riches are: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.” His poverty is: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” There he made himself poor where he enriched us.

Let us therefore hear the poor man by choice, praying for us who are poor by necessity—[Col. 0992B] namely, Christ poor in us, poor with us, and poor for our sake. Let us hear his prayer, recognize his person, and whatever we see that does not suit his majesty, let us attribute to our weakness.

He is anxious and prays not for himself but for us, teaching us not to be anxious for our own sake, so that we may escape both voice and groaning, recover the eternal days that we have lost, and pray not only for ourselves but also for our brothers.

And he says this: “Lord Father, hear my prayer, made for the perseverance of my people, and let my cry come”—that is, let it enter—to you. This is repetition, as blessed Augustine says, so that the feeling of the one praying may be shown.

It may also be understood as something greater, namely, as referring to that intense prayer which the Apostle shows to have been truly heard when he says: “In the days of his flesh he offered prayers to God with a strong cry, and he was heard because of his reverence.”

Do not turn your face away. Therefore, I say, hear my prayer; do not turn your face away from me—that is, [Col. 0992C] from my people. He does not say this with reference to himself. For when did God turn away from him of whom it is said, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself”? Or when did the Father turn away from the Son?

He says this with reference to his own people, from whom God would truly turn his face if he allowed them to be led astray. “Do not turn your face away,” I say, but rather turn it toward me on whatever day I am afflicted—that is, at whatever time my people are afflicted.

For Christ is always afflicted, and will be afflicted, in his members who pass away and those who succeed them, until the end of the age. Therefore he rightly says: “On whatever day I am afflicted,” that is, on whatever day my people are afflicted—namely, when they recognize that this pilgrimage is a time of affliction, something they cannot do without humbling themselves.

Then you, who turn your ear away from the upright, bend your ear toward me in my people, as the exalted bends toward the humble, and the physician toward the sick.

Or otherwise:

[Col. 0992D]

On whatever day. On whatever enlightened day—that is, whenever my people, enlightened by your grace, recognize that the present life is a time of affliction and humble themselves—then bend your ear toward them, because then, as though he were saying, they will invoke you.

And on whatever day—that is, at whatever time, or whenever my people, enlightened, invoke you within themselves, no longer as earthly people but as the redeemed, no longer bearing the image of the earthly but of the heavenly—hear me, that is, hear my people, and hear them quickly.

For you did not say “Behold, I am present” except with such a desire, while you were still speaking. And as though someone were to say to him: “Why do you invoke him? For what poverty do you cry out? For what want do you knock?” The answer is:

I rightly cry out; I rightly invoke, because the days that should have been mine and my people’s, and would have been ours if Adam had not transgressed—that is, the eternal days—have failed, that is, vanished like smoke.

O days—if only they were days! Wherever “days” is heard, light is understood. But my days have failed like smoke. Why like smoke? Because of exaltation. See smoke swelling like pride, rising [Col. 0993A] and vanishing; certainly, failing and not enduring.

Such days the proud Adam deserved to receive; from him Christ took flesh and freed us from the days of smoke. For our sake he graciously used the language of the days of smoke, and he adds the reason why the days failed:

They failed because those things that should have been all my bones—that is, the supports of the soul in my people, namely reason and understanding—withered. That is, having lost their contemplation of the truth, they became defective and weak, like *cremium*.

* Cremium* is what remains after fat has been melted out, once it has been burned so thoroughly that it becomes entirely without moisture. It is something very worthless and weak.

Struck. I have not been weakened only outwardly in this way; I have also been struck outwardly, and in me and in my people I have become like grass, because I have fallen from my former greenness into this misery.

This is that stricken one of whom it is said through Isaiah: “I will not be angry forever. For the spirit proceeds from me. I made every breath; but because of [Col. 0993B] sin I saddened him a little, and I struck him. And I turned my face away from him, and he went away sorrowful in his ways.”

This striking in outward things also applies to the Head himself, on account of the punishments of sin that he shared with us. He repeats what he said earlier in order to show that this is its cause.

As though he were saying: “The fact that I was struck outwardly happened because my heart—that is, the soul of my people—withered,” that is, became worthless, after losing the powers of understanding and reason.

And it rightly withered, because in my people I forgot to eat my bread—that is, to observe the Lord’s commandment. When the serpent suggested and Eve transgressed, wretched Adam forgot the Lord’s commandment, which ought to have been his delight like bread, the food of the body. He stretched out his hand toward what was forbidden and did not find what the devil promised, but what God threatened.

From the voice of my groaning. He said, “My heart withered.” Now he shows how he says, “My mouth has clung to my flesh”: that is, my stronger part in my people clung to my weaker part. Adam’s mind consented to his Eve—that is, reason [Col. 0993C] consented to sensuality.

This proceeded from the voice of my groaning, namely, from the voice of the serpent, who said: “You will be like gods.” This voice is the voice of my groaning because on its account I must always grieve for my people, always groan within them.

Because of this voice, over which I must grieve in my people, I became like a pelican of solitude by being born, like a night-raven by dying, and like a solitary sparrow on the roof by rising again.

The pelican is a certain bird that seeks deserted places and especially inhabits the deserted banks of the Nile River. This bird kills its young, then mourns over them, and again beats itself with its wings and beak, so that on the third day it sheds blood. As soon as the young are sprinkled with it, they come back to life.

This is not inconsistent with our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the bird of solitude: born alone from a virgin, conceived alone without pleasure, and born without pain. He killed his young—that is, human beings made by him—by his just judgment. And he mourned over them because he wished to become weak for their sake.

Hence, as we have said elsewhere, the Wisdom of God is also compared to a hen.

[Col. 0993D]

After the law—that is, in the time of grace, which is as though the third day—by pouring out his blood on the cross he gave life to those whom he had killed before the law and under the law.

That killing may also be understood here as the conversion of the wicked, concerning which he himself says: “I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal.” For the wicked persecutor Saul would never have been killed and Paul, the excellent preacher, brought to life unless he had been redeemed by his blood, poured out on the third day—that is, after the law.

The same applies to the others killed in this way, both before the law and under the law, and after the law.

This is what he says: “I have become like a pelican of solitude.”

I have become like a night-raven dwelling in a ruin. The night-raven is a bird that flies in darkness. Christ is compared to it because he came into darkness, that is, into the ignorance of the Jews. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

A ruin is a destroyed building in which only the walls remain. Hence another translation has, “among the walls.”

The destroyed building was the Jewish [Col. 0994A] people because of their transgression. And because they were transgressors, they chose a human king and utterly despised the law; they asked that a robber be released to them, but crucified Christ.

I kept vigil. As though he were saying: “I slept and awoke,” because I rose from the dead. And I became like a sparrow—that is, one flying away—being solitary on the roof, that is, in heaven, because that one High Priest alone has entered into the inner parts of the tabernacle, where, seated at the right hand of the Father, he continually intercedes for us.

And because, as though he were saying, I humbled myself so greatly that I became like a pelican and like a night-raven, therefore my enemies reproach me all day long—that is, continually—and so forth.

This likeness of the birds can also be applied to the body. But certain things said above must be changed, namely: “My bones have withered like *cremium,” and “from the voice of my groaning.” Yet the following verse is not changed.

The bones in the body of Christ are the stronger members of the Lord; their *frying* by analogy signifies the weak, who often fall into danger by slipping and sometimes yield to persecution.

[Col. 0994B]

The stronger are fried by these weak members because of the compassion and love they will have for them. Each bone is fried all the more in proportion to how much it loves. For if love is absent, no bone is fried.

Therefore he says: “My bones”—that is, the stronger members of my people—“have withered like *cremium*,” through compassion for the weak.

The following verse is not changed.

From the sound of my groaning. He said, “I have been struck down like grass.” And from this (as if he were saying) comes the fact that “my bone has cleaved to my flesh,” that is, that the stronger members in my body have been joined to the weak through compassion. And this comes from “the sound of my groaning” in those weak members—namely, those who groan over what should not be mourned, or do not groan over what should be mourned. Someone groans because he has lost money, but does not groan because he has lost innocence. In this way they make themselves objects of lamentation, and the stronger members cannot abandon such people, because, as the Apostle says, the stronger ought to bear the infirmity of the weak, since they ought to correct and instruct them.

From this follows what he adds: “I have become like the pelican of the wilderness among my own” [Col. 0994C], and so forth. He sets forth three kinds of birds and three places, and by this indicates three kinds of people. Some of those who are bones in the body of Christ, fearing that dominical sentence, “Wicked and lazy servant, why did you not put my money on the table, so that when I came I might have collected it with interest,” and wishing to seek Christ’s profits and faithfully distribute the treasure entrusted to them, become like the pelican, that bird which seeks deserted places. They go into the desert—that is, to those who have not yet received the faith—and there, by preaching and teaching, whether they make progress or not, they nevertheless complete what is theirs to do.

Others, likewise among Christ’s bones, or even belong to the same body at another time, are like the night-raven [nycticorax] in dwelling places, because they come to those who are a dwelling place—that is, a ruined building—who have fallen away from the faith. Of such the Apostle says: “Hymenaeus and Philetus, who, having gone astray concerning the truth, overthrow the faith of many.” In this they are night-ravens: just as that bird loves [Col. 0994D] darkness, so they frequent and love the darkness of their errors—not so that they may remain in it, but so that they may make light shine forth from the darkness.

There are also others among Christ’s bones who come to those who, although they stand in the faith, are nevertheless under a roof, because they live carnally. Among these, as though sleeping, they keep watch—that is, they have been given over to quiet. In accordance with the saying: “The righteous entrusted his heart to keeping watch at dawn.” And they are like the sparrow—that is, cautious and sorrowful, because they grieve for those people. I say “a solitary sparrow on the roof,” because they are not with him under the roof, but are alone on the roof; for although they walk in the flesh, they do not live or wage war according to the flesh, and they strive to draw even those who are under the same roof with them toward themselves.

Or alternatively: let the three kinds of birds that he sets forth signify three kinds of people and three places, but in another way. The continuation then connects with the first interpretation, concerning the head. For, because of the voice of groaning that must be removed, some who are in the body of Christ are like “the pelican of solitude,” because they desire the eremitical life. Others are like the night-raven, because they flee the common sight of human beings as that bird flees the light—or as holy monks do—and they are not in a building but in a dwelling, that is, in a ruined building, because the world has been ruined for them.

These sleep away from secular care. There are others, however, who keep watch because they have children, a wife, and many possessions, as Job and Abraham did, and yet they are like the sparrow, that is, cautious. Therefore I say that they are like the sparrow, because they are solitary on the roof—that is, in human society—insofar as they possess all things as though they did not possess them and use the world as though they did not use it.

This is what he says: “Among some of my own I have become like the pelican of solitude,” in this way or that. “Among others I have become like the night-raven dwelling in the desert. And among others I kept watch and became like the sparrow, solitary on the roof.” Hence—for I myself was such, and so were those who belonged to me—my enemies reproached me, saying: “Why does your teacher eat with sinners and tax collectors?” and many similar things.

They also reproached my followers, because in the earliest times the impious reproached the holy preachers, saying that they corrupted human laws and customs and secretly induced people to sin by promising forgiveness. But blessed Augustine says that they would sin more because of despair concerning forgiveness. If you expected nothing except torments to remain for you, you would wish to fulfill all carnal desires here. And he rightly corrects you who promises pardon and says: “Return, transgressors, to your heart.” Nor should you despise God, as though by promising forgiveness he made sinners secure. Indeed, lest we live worse because of despair concerning forgiveness, he promised the harbor of pardon. Again, lest we live worse because of hope of forgiveness, he made the day of death utterly uncertain. In his providence he established both: namely, that there should be a place where those returning might be received, and that there should be something by which those delaying would be terrified.

Now let us return to the literal sense. “My enemies reproached me,” and those who praised me and my followers swore against me. For with their mouths they praised us, but in their hearts they prepared ambushes. This was because “I ate ashes,” that is, because I received and incorporated into myself sterile and utterly despairing people, such as Paul the worst persecutor and Matthew the tax collector, as though they were bread—that is, like Peter, a simple man and fisherman. I also received others who lived simply, because they were like suitable bread, whom I and my followers would eat and incorporate into ourselves.

“And I mixed my drink with weeping.” This means: Whenever some temporal pleasure came to me or to my followers, I mixed weeping with it—that is, the bitterness of sorrow. Or alternatively, let this be a hypallage, as if he were saying: “I ate bread, in myself and in my followers, as ashes, and I mixed my cup with weeping; it was a great sorrow to me that food and drink necessary for me were present.”

From the face of wrath. I say that “I ate ashes as bread.” And this was “from the face of your wrath and indignation,” that is, from the anger that followed your indignation, whose face—that is, whose presence—still remains in us through the punishments of sin. I speak of the wrath of the one who, “lifting me up, dashed me down.” For that very lifting up was a dashing down: insofar as he exalted human beings above the other animals, he punished the transgressor with a proportionately heavier penalty.

My days have declined like a shadow. I say that you dashed me down, and this is how: my days declined—that is, they became inclined to decline and unstable, as a shadow is unstable. Blessed Augustine inserts this remark: “Certainly your days would not decline if you had not declined from the true way. For what is surprising if your days have become like you?”

Or alternatively: “My days declined, becoming like a shadow,” because they are not days but only the shadow of true days. And my days declined because “I withered like grass,” that is, I fell from my former greenness into this misery. Let the grass, therefore, watered by the blood of its Savior, grow green again.

[Col. 0996A] But you, Lord. I indeed withered, fell, and grew old by your just judgment; but you, Lord, did not fall or grow old, because you remain forever. Therefore, you who are eternal, preserve me who am temporal. Be strong to free me, just as you were strong to condemn me.

You, I say, remain forever, and “your memorial”—that is, your deed worthy of remembrance—will remain through the departing generation and the succeeding generation. What, then, is that memorial? This, namely: You, who lay in the servants sent to the vineyard, rising in me, your heir, by raising me from the dead, will have mercy on me and through me make others rise also; you will have mercy on Zion, showing mercy to the Jewish people by calling them, justifying them, and forgiving their sins.

And truly you will have mercy, because the time for having mercy on her has come—the time, namely, of fullness, concerning which the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law,” that is, Zion. I say that the time has come because the time truly has come, as a certain man who was foremost among the builders testifies, saying: “Behold, the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation,” and so forth.

For they have been pleased. I say that you will have mercy on Zion in this way: “For her stones have been pleasing”—that is, they will please—“to your servants,” who are especially familiar with you, namely, your Apostles. These stones are the prophets, so that they may carry them—that is, explain what those prophets foretold concerning the building of the true Zion—and make them its foundation, upon which Zion may be built.

And thus they will have mercy on its earth—that is, on those who were earth in the carnal Zion—by receiving them, so that they may be living stones in the new building. They were earth, however, in relation to the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense—namely, the stone that became the cornerstone, which the builders themselves rejected. Therefore they fell back into the earth from which they had previously been made.

But that voice of petition could not have been ineffective: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And therefore—that is, the three thousand and the five thousand, that is, all those who placed the price of their sold possessions at the feet of the Apostles—were made from this earth by the one who first made Adam from the earth.

Or alternatively: “In this way, I say, you will have mercy on Zion, because her stones”—that is, all the believers from that people who became living stones in the primitive Church—“will please her servants,” that is, the Apostles. And thus they will have mercy on her earth, that is, on that people.

Then the nations will fear your name, Lord, because your servants, driven out from there, will preach to everyone, in accordance with the saying: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the nations.”

And not only the lesser people, but also all the kings of the whole earth—or all those among the nations who rule their earth well—will fear, that is, revere, your glory. Here he takes “name” and “glory” as referring to the same thing, namely, his praise.

For the Lord will build. Therefore the servants, beginning from Jerusalem, turn to the nations, because the Lord will build Zion in this way: from those two peoples, as from two walls coming from opposite directions but not holding different beliefs. And in this Zion he will be seen—that is, recognized—and at last in his glory, namely, in his resurrection, ascension, and sitting at the right hand. Previously he was seen in his humiliation.

He has looked upon the prayer of the humble. I say that the Lord will build Zion in that carnal Zion in this manner: he has looked—that is, he will look—upon the prayer of the humble, that is, of believers from both this people and that, who pray concerning this. And he has not despised—that is, he will not despise—their prayer; that is, he will receive it for confirmation.

Let these things be written. Namely, that the Lord will first have mercy on Zion and afterward on the nations, and that he will build Zion from these not through their merits but through his mercy alone. Let these things, I say, be written—that is, announced by those who came before as though written and established—to another generation, that is, to the succeeding spiritual generation, and from that generation to another, so that they may recognize that they were freed not by merits but by glory alone. In this way every succeeding people that is created will praise the Lord in good works.

For he has looked forth from on high. And rightly will they praise the Lord, because they did not look upward from their weakness toward the Lord; rather, the Lord looked forth—that is, looked from afar—from his holy height, that is, through me, his holy of holies and his exalted one, in order to descend to the humble and exalt the humble.

The Lord, I say, looked upon the earth from heaven—that is, through me, his heaven—in order to make earth and heaven.

To hear the groaning of those in chains. This shows why the Lord looked forth: namely, to hear the groaning of those in chains. He calls the Apostles and holy martyrs “those in chains,” because they bore those chains concerning which it is said: “Put your foot into his chains,” that is, into the discipline of the Lord, who chastises every son whom he receives, and into his fear and commandments.

These chains had the effect that they did not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, they feared the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. These chains should not be avoided by anyone, lest dangerous security and the sweetness of this temporal life be sought—sweetness that is followed by everlasting bitterness.

The Lord hears the groaning of the holy martyrs in their pressures and humiliation, so that in our times the Church might exist in as great a glory as we see today: namely, that the kingdoms which formerly persecuted her should now serve the Lord.

This is what he says: “To hear the groaning of those in chains, and thus to release from fear of death the sons of the slain,” that is, the imitators of the holy martyrs who were slain. I say that he released them in such a way that they now freely proclaim the name of the Lord in Zion, that is, in the Church.

For the Church was in distress when those who were bound were being killed. After their death, however, the Church came to possess such peace that everyone dared freely to proclaim the Lord’s name within her.

[Col. 0997C] In this way release from the fear of death was granted to the sons of the slain. There was also release in them through the remission of sins. For whenever they were compelled to die, they did not fear death because, through the remission of sins, they were secure concerning what follows death.

And his praise in Jerusalem. This is a repetition for confirmation. He takes Zion and Jerusalem to mean the same thing, namely, the Church. Likewise, he takes “the name of the Lord” and “his praise” as referring to the same thing.

When they assemble. I say, so that they may proclaim it. And they do so in this manner: “when they assemble,” that is, when they address the peoples and also the kings who formerly persecuted them, exhorting them toward one thing, namely, the catholic faith, so that they may no longer serve the world but the Lord.

And from where did this happen, unless because, as we said above, “the groaning of those in chains” was heard in their pressures and humiliation?

He answered him. Blessed Augustine asks what the expression “he answered him” refers to, since it is singular while only the plural “peoples” and “kings” precedes it. But he says that it refers to what was mentioned earlier: either to “praise” or to “Jerusalem.”

The meaning is this: In that proclamation, “he answered him”—that is, the praise of the Lord, which is Jerusalem; his praise, being his, answers him when they give him thanks because they were called by him. He calls; we answer.

If we live so well that he is praised through us, then his praise in us answers him. According to this, he says that his praise answered him.

Jerusalem also answered him—not that Jerusalem which did not hear when it was called, concerning which it was said: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate,” but that Jerusalem concerning which it was said: “Rejoice, barren one who does not bear, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.”

For this Jerusalem, when called, did not despise the call. He rained; she produced fruit. But where did she answer him? Certainly not in herself, because she had no answer in herself except an answer of death or iniquity. Rather, she answered him in [Col. 0998A] the way of his strength.

The way of strength is Christ, because before the resurrection he was not recognized; rather, crucified in weakness, he remained hidden, so that in the resurrection he might appear strong. On this way of strength she answered him, because after the resurrection he would call the Church from the whole world—not weak upon the cross, but already strong in heaven.

This is the chief strength of our faith: that we believe not only that he died, but also that he was raised, and that we hope that we too will be raised through him. Hence the Apostle says: “If you believe in your heart that Christ is Lord and confess with your mouth that God raised him, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto God,” or unto salvation.

Now let us return to the literal sense. Jerusalem answered him in the way of his strength, saying: “Lord, make known to me the fewness of my days,” that is, make me attend to how tightly I am confined by the small number of my days, lest my few days hold me back from your many days.

This is what he adds: “Do not recall me,” that is, “Do not permit me, Lord, to be recalled from your eternal days halfway through,” through the imperfection of my days. For everything that is half is imperfect.

Therefore (as if he were saying): I say that my days are imperfect, because your years are perfect and eternal only in “generation upon generation.” This generation of mine does not share in your years, but only that generation which will be “the generation of generations,” that is, composed of all generations.

It should be understood that God’s years are eternity. Eternity is his unchangeable substance, to which “was” or “will be” does not belong, but only “is.” As he himself said to Moses: “I am who I am,” and so forth: “He who is has sent me to you.”

Yet, lest you despair, he says—as though addressing human weakness: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” You have heard what I am in myself; you have also heard what I am for your sake. This is something very great.

Yet this eternity called us, and from eternity the Word came forth. Eternity already exists, and the Word already exists, but time does not yet exist—for time too was made. “All things were made through him.” Behold the Word before time, because he made time; yet he was born in time, although he is eternal life. And he called us temporal beings so that he might make us eternal.

This is that generation which, as was said above, shares in the years of God.

Or alternatively: Jerusalem answered him when gathering peoples together, that is, she answered him in unity. For whoever is not in unity does not answer him; only unity answers the One, because he is one and the Church is unity.

There were some who wished to tear this unity apart, saying that the Church would not last until the end of the age but would soon cease. Foreseeing by the Spirit that this would happen, the prophet introduces the Church saying: “Lord, make known to me the fewness of my days.”

As if she were saying: “Some utterly ruined people will arise, saying that I will soon be destroyed and will not last until the end of the age. Therefore, Lord, make known to me, as a testimony against such people, the fewness of my days”—that is, make known to me how long my temporal days will last, since they are few in comparison with your eternal days.

The Lord gave her this testimony when he said: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age.” But because there were some, such as the Donatists, who through ignorance claimed that this had been said about themselves, saying that the catholic Church had already been destroyed, blessed Augustine says that the Lord gives testimony against them: “And this Gospel,” he says, “will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come”—that is, after some from every nation have believed, then the end of the age will come.

Let heretics, therefore, not flatter themselves against me, as though I were soon to cease and would not remain until the end of the age. And so that they cannot flatter themselves: “Do not recall me, Lord, halfway through,” that is, in the imperfection of these days. Perfect my brief days, so that at last you may give me your eternal days.

And truly you will give them, because your years will be through generation upon generation, as before.

In the beginning, you, Lord. It is as though he were saying: The fact that the generation of generations will share in your years will not come from itself but from you, because you, Lord, founded that cultivated earth in faith and good works, “in the beginning”—that is, through me, whom you willed to be the beginning of all creatures.

And you not only founded the earth but also its cultivators, because “the heavens are the works of your hands.” It should be understood that although it is said elsewhere, “He spoke and they were made,” this does not mean that he makes one thing by word and another by hand, since he does everything by power alone. But because of the excellence of the holy Apostles and the other holy preachers, it says that the heavens are the works of his hands.

They will perish. It is as though he were saying: Although the heavens are a very worthy work, they cannot be compared with you, because they have become changeable, while you are unchangeable. They will perish with regard to the body, but you remain unchangeable.

And truly they will perish, because they will grow old insofar as they are “like a garment,” that is, in the body, which is the garment of the soul. And you will change them—that is, renew them—as some covering is changed which, after being worn on the outside, is turned inside out so that it may appear new.

Then they will be changed with a worthy change, because “what is sown is a natural body; it will rise a spiritual body. What is sown is corruptible; it will rise incorruptible,” and so forth.

But you yourself remain the same in substance and also in will, that is, remaining unchangeable in every respect. Therefore your years will not fail, because neither will they come nor go.

And lest we despair of being able to reach those years, he adds: “The sons of your servants, Lord, will always dwell in these years.” And he directs us to that fact that none of those who were led out of Egypt entered the promised land except Caleb and Joshua—that is, except unity and unity.

But just as only the sons entered that land, and the fathers entered through them, so only sons—that is, those regenerated through faith—will reach the eternity of God, and this through sons, that is, through the good works that precede them.

Therefore he did not simply say, “Your servants,” but “the sons of your servants,” that is, your servants, being made sons through their sons, will dwell in your years.

And not only they, but also “all their seed”—that is, all who follow them—will be directed into that age, that is, into that eternity.

## Psalm 102. For David

### Argument

The blessedness of return is proclaimed, and thanksgiving to God is commanded after captivity has been released. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church addressing her own people.

### Explanation

After the most humble prayers of that blessed poor man and the groanings of penitence that have been unfolded, this entire psalm overflows with the praise of the Lord, and the joys of praise follow the preceding tears.

For David himself, as always, discloses Christ, to whom praise is given. Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks. In the first part he commands his soul to bless the Lord and to remember his benefits. In the second he says what benefits the Lord bestowed on Moses and on his other faithful servants, so that he may be understood to have been generous from all ages. In the third he turns his words toward the angels and invites the heavenly powers and the other rational creatures to devote themselves continually to the praises of the Lord.

### Commentary

Bless the Lord, my soul. For David. In this psalm the prophet exhorts us, observing in all God’s works the mercy he shows toward us, not to be ungrateful for his benefit but always to return fitting thanks to him.

The meaning is as though he were saying: In every gift of God, in every correction, in every consolation, and in his grace by which he has deigned to grant pardon and has not repaid what was deserved: “Bless the Lord, my soul.”

Let each one of us also arouse and exhort his soul and say: “Bless the Lord, my soul.” Let the soul listen, consider all the things by which it is aroused, and see whether it ought to bless anyone but the Lord.

And all that is within me, his holy name. He takes “soul” as animality, that is, as sensibility; but what is within it is reason and understanding.

The meaning is as though he were saying: Let the sound of external voices vary according to circumstances, but let the voice of what is within be perpetual. Let your inner faculties always bless the Lord.

You are conducting some business: conduct it justly, and you bless the Lord. You are sleeping: if the thought of theft or some crime does not awaken you, you bless the Lord. Innocence even in the sleeper is the voice of praise belonging to your soul.

You eat and drink: do so for refreshment, not drunkenness, and you bless the Lord. In short, our inner faculties—that is, prayer and the mind—always praise the Lord if, in making judgments, we continually attend to this: that we do only what is good; and if we understand higher things in order to burn with desire for them and despise earthly things.

Bless. This is repetition arising from the affection of the one praying, as if he were saying: “Bless the Lord without ceasing, my soul.”

And in order that you may bless him always, do not forget all his recompenses. For if you forget them, you do not bless him. But we cannot keep all his recompenses before our eyes unless we also keep our sins before our eyes.

Let not the pleasure of past sin be before your eyes, but its condemnation. For if condemnation comes from you, salvation will come from him.

He gave you this, since in Adam he placed you in an abundance of virtues and made you according to his image and likeness. But in return for giving thanks, submission, service, and religious worship, you repaid him with pride, disobedience, and every wickedness.

Although he could justly have repaid you, along with the wicked, with every evil, he repaid you good for evil. He called you, justified you, forgave your sins, and promised eternal rewards.

Therefore do not forget his recompenses. Confess, and he forgives. And do not forget, because God is pleased by such a sacrifice. He wishes to be praised by you so that you may progress, not so that he himself may be exalted.

Who is propitious. Do not, I say, forget him who bestows so many good things upon you—namely, him who is propitious toward all your iniquities, both actual and original, and so forth.

The meaning is as though he were saying: Behold the recompenses of God. For what was owed to you as a sinner except punishment, and to you as a blasphemer except Gehenna?

Therefore do not forget his recompenses, but imitate him, lest you experience recompenses—not, I do not say, evil ones, since if they are just they are not evil, but nevertheless evil for you who suffer them.

He who heals—that is, he will at last heal all your infirmities. After the remission of sins it is necessary for the soul to be shaken by disturbances and to move amid the dangers of temptations, and often to be captured, because death has not yet been swallowed up in victory, nor has this corruptible nature yet put on incorruption.

The Lord will heal all these sicknesses and infirmities in you. He made you such that you would never become sick if you kept his commandments. You did not then listen in order to retain salvation; listen now in order to recover salvation. For now our pardon is supported by daily medicines, and help is given to every weary person, although another weariness is immediately indicated.

Who redeems. In this way he will heal your infirmities, because he redeems your life—that is, your soul—from destruction, that is, from the necessity of corruption, because the body that is corrupted burdens the soul.

He has already shown in an example what he promised as a reward: just as he died because of our sins, so also he rose because of our justification.

Who crowns you. Let no one who hears this applaud himself; let no one attribute his crowning to himself. For no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully. And the one who helps you while you compete will crown you—not with your merits, but with his gifts.

Therefore he adds: “With mercy and compassion.” Understand mercy as the loving disposition, and compassion as its manifestation.

Who fills in us. He said, “He will crown you,” and he will crown you in this way: he fills your desire with good things, leading you to that good which is the highest of all goods—not to those goods in which, wherever you turn, what has kindled desire becomes worthless once possessed.

When I do not have something, I desire it; but after I have it, I despise it. And through those goods your youth will be renewed, like that of the eagle.

Because of old age, the eagle’s upper beak grows over the lower to such an extent that it can neither open its mouth nor nourish itself, and so it fails from lack of food. In such distress it seeks a sharp stone and repeatedly beats the growth of its beak against it until it can nourish itself. Then it recovers both the brightness of its feathers and the vigor of its strength.

So our soul was not fit to be refreshed by that bread on which the angels feed, because our mouth was held closed by the truth. But a rock was given to us, namely Christ; by being worn against it through old age, our mouth was opened by renewal and made fit to eat that bread of angels. Concerning himself this bread said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.”

This bread is now eaten by the soul of each person who has been renewed. Then we will be fully refreshed by it, when we are changed into the evangelical condition, and he himself will be all in all.

And as though someone might ask: In the meantime, during this pilgrimage, what happens? Certainly we are not abandoned, because the Lord is one who performs acts of mercy—but only for those who perform acts of mercy. For “blessed are the merciful, because they will obtain mercy.”

What measure of mercy does he require? This: “Love your enemy,” and “Give to everyone who asks you.”

But what is said seems to conflict with this: “Do not look upon the wicked,” and: “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may give it.”

The Lord nevertheless wants you to show mercy even to the wicked, but not as wicked. An unrighteous person comes before you. The unrighteous person is God’s work, but the unrighteous deed is the work of a human being. Give to God’s work without attending to the person’s deed—that is, do not let his wickedness please you.

For if you receive the wicked person in the name of the wicked person, you will receive the reward of the wicked person; just as whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive the reward of the righteous person.

But someone, taking mercy perversely and excessively, says: “Should I not correct a lustful son or a wicked servant?” Let him know that the Lord’s rule does not condemn these actions when they are done; rather, it condemns their omission.

For you ought to correct all who belong to your sphere of correction. But if people who have no relation to you inflict an injury upon you, you should bear it patiently. For just as you will be merciful if you show mercy, so he will also be merciful, ensuring that whatever you suffer for the sake of justice does not remain unavenged.

Therefore he adds: “For he will execute judgment for all who suffer injury for the sake of justice.”

Reverse the order of the next two verses, and say: Truly the Lord performs acts of mercy, because he is compassionate and merciful. He is merciful in disposition and compassionate in manifestation, because from every side he calls us to conversion and from every side to repentance.

As the Apostle says: “Do you not know the riches of God’s grace? Do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance?”

He calls us through the benefits of creation; he calls us through spiritual gifts. Therefore he is compassionate and merciful. But he is to be understood as merciful in such a way that he is also seen to be just.

For just as he is now merciful, so at last he will be truthful. Therefore we must fear lest at last we experience as just the one whom we now despise as kind.

Long-suffering, greatly merciful. He is long-suffering who does not immediately punish our sins, but in his long-suffering seeks good works.

For if he punished the sinner, whom would he have as a praiser? Yet he does not want delay in a raven’s voice, but confession in a dove’s groaning.

He is greatly merciful because he rewards in us not our merits but his gifts.

Take up the whole verse again and say: The Lord, compassionate and merciful, long-suffering and greatly merciful, made known his previously mentioned ways—namely, mercy and judgment—through which he himself comes to us and we come to him.

[Col. 1002A] To Moses. By Moses all the perfect are to be understood, but he names Moses above all because through him he gave the law.
