There is a great mystery in the giving of that law. The law was given so that, as sin increased, the proud might be humbled; once humbled, they might confess; and once they had confessed, they might be healed.

He made these hidden ways of his known to Moses, through whom the law was given, by which “the offense increased, so that grace might also abound.”

Nor was this done with such cruelty, but for the sake of healing. Many are sick but do not perceive it and do not seek a physician. The illness grows, the distress increases, the physician is sought, and the sick person is healed.

Behold how mercy pertains to the law. Understand judgment in the opposite way, insofar as it pertains to those who do not attend to this.

And he made his ways known not only to Moses and the others, but also to the sons of Israel—that is, to all the lesser people who do not yet see God by faith but will eventually see him in appearance.

He made his wills known. This, however, is his will: that we attend to our manifold misery and seek medicine.

And in this way he will not be angry forever. He adds this for our consolation. For we should not strive merely to escape future wrath, but to lay aside present wrath.

Concerning this the Apostle says: “For we too were once by nature children of wrath.” And therefore, to console us, he says: “He will not be angry forever.”

Already in hope we have escaped the wrath in which we still are—that is, the punishments of sin—and eventually we will escape it completely. And just as he will not be angry forever, so neither will he threaten forever; for this present wrath is a threat of eternal wrath.

Not according to our sins. The meaning is as though he were saying: I say that he will not be angry forever or threaten forever. And we already possess the pledge of this salvation, because when nothing but punishment was owed to us sinners, “he did not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities.”

He takes “iniquities” and “sins” as referring to the same thing. Or you may refer “sins” to original sins and “iniquities” to actual sins.

## Because According to

Truly, he did not [Col. 1002C] deal with us according to our sins, because he acted mercifully toward us; for he strengthened—that is, confirmed—his mercy over those who fear him, according to the height of heaven above the earth. Heaven, that is, the firmament, is equally high above the earth on every side, and protects the earth everywhere. And all the earth’s temperate condition, that is, all its beneficial climate, comes from heaven. And it is to say: The Lord so confirmed his mercy over those who fear him that, just as heaven cannot separate itself from protecting the earth, so his mercy does not separate itself from protecting those who fear him.

Or otherwise: He confirmed his mercy according to the height of heaven above the earth, that is, to the extent that those who have been made heaven from earth now differ from another earth, or from themselves as they previously were when they were earth. He demonstrates the same thing through another comparison, saying: For he has made our iniquities far from us as far as the rising is from the setting; these natural opposites are distant from one another.

Or otherwise: Grace has risen, while sins have set; therefore “rising” signifies [Col. 1002D] grace, and “setting” the punishment of sinners, which has been taken away through the removal of sins. It is to say: As far as the rising is from the setting, that is, grace from punishment, so far has he removed our iniquities.

He shows how he did this, saying: The Lord has had mercy on those who fear him in the manner in which a father has mercy on his children. Therefore, beneath the Father who strikes, let us weep; beneath his correction, let us groan, because his scourge is medicine, not punishment, and his chastisement is not condemnation. And therefore he had mercy, because he himself knew our formation. For he knows what he made, how it fell, and how it ought to be restored.

## He Remembered

For this reason also he had mercy on us: because he remembered that we are dust. And truly dust, because we are human beings—that is, from the earth. Therefore let wretched humanity consider what a human being is, so that a human being may not grow proud. For why does a human being grow proud? Certainly in vain, because his days are like hay: now blooming, and immediately withering; and a human being will flourish like a flower of the field. [Col. 1003A] No flower of the field endures forever; so every human dignity, both in itself and in external things, lasts only briefly and quickly dissolves.

## Because the Spirit

Truly, a human being does not remain, because what appears more stable in him is changeable. For the spirit that is in him will not remain, but will pass away. It is separated from the body at death; and even while it is in the body it does not remain fixed, because it is inconstant. It understands, fails to understand, rejoices, grieves, and so forth. Whether it passes away or slips away, it will no longer know its place by itself, because after death it does not return by itself to the body in order to raise it up, nor after its fall does it recover by itself; for it is said concerning the way of iniquity: “Everyone who walks in it will not return.”

## But Mercy

By itself it will indeed not recognize, but through God’s mercy it will recognize again. Behold the exceedingly abundant mercy of God: he made that Word which remains forever into a brother for our transient hay—namely, the only Son begotten from the Father’s heart—and made him, for us adopted children, [Col. 1003B] a brother of the same family, so that by sharing in our hay he might make us share in his gold.

For he became a participant in our mortality so that he might make us participants in his divinity. This mercy—that is, this loving affection of God the Father toward us—is understood and expressed here when he says: “The mercy of the Lord is from eternity,” because he chose us in it before the foundation of the world; “and it will endure forever,” because he will make us share in his gold. I say that it will be, not over just anyone, but only over those who fear him.

Therefore let those who fear him rejoice, because the mercy of the Lord will be over them forever. But let those who do not fear him grieve rather than rejoice, because they will be hay, and with hay they will be in torments: for their flesh will be raised for punishment, not for glory.

## And His Justice

Our children are our good works; the children of these children are the recompense of good works. It is to say: The mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity, and through this mercy his justice—that is, the Lord’s just [Col. 1003C] judgment—will be upon the children of children, that is, upon the recompense of good works.

And this will not be upon just anyone, but upon those who, by acting well, keep for themselves his covenant, that is, the inheritance promised by him. He explains who they are, saying: “And they remember his commandments,” which are the way to the covenant—not merely for knowing, but for doing, in the recompense of good works.

For the Lord who descended from heaven, who died and rose again, who raised upward the human being he had assumed, and who stood mocked before the judge, has already prepared his seat, that is, his judicial seat, in heaven—that is, in holy men whom he inhabits and through whom he distributes judgments to others.

Let people therefore do on earth whatever they wish—for no justice will go without reward, nor wickedness without punishment. For the Lord has prepared his judicial seat in heaven.

And truly, he is still powerful, for his kingdom—that is, those in whom he reigns—will rule over all good and evil things. For the saints will judge the nations, placing some at his right hand by comparison with themselves and others at the left. Among those at the right hand, justice will not go without reward; nor among those at the left hand will wickedness go without punishment.

## Bless

Here he understands “angels” as holy preachers. It is to say: Since no justice will go without reward, therefore, all his angels, bless the Lord—that is, exalt the Lord both in yourselves and in others. I mean you who rightly ought to do so, because through him you are so exalted that you are powerful in virtue, that is, in miracles, and are [not] only announcing his word in speech, but also carrying it out in action, so that his words may be heard from you in the voice of his discourses—that is, so that his sermons may be heard from you aloud and openly.

Indeed, those who proclaim God’s words openly truly announce them, because what they cry out with their voice they demonstrate in their works. Conversely, those who praise with their mouths but deny him by their deeds announce him in darkness.

[Col. 1004A]

## Bless the Lord, All His Powers

The “powers” are those who dispense well the talent entrusted to them and what belongs to him, that is, to the Lord, because, as he himself says: “Without me you can do nothing.” He specifies which powers he means.

It is as if he said: I call you lesser powers, who are his ministers—and ministers in this respect, that you do his will, distributing provisions to his servants as he wishes.

You also, all his works, bless the Lord here—that is, all whom he gathers as inferior beings. He says “his works” for this reason: what we do in blessing him, he himself works in us. For we are his creation in good works; or “all his works” may be understood broadly of every creature.

It is as if he said: All works, bless him—that is, offer yourselves as material for blessing the Lord. For everything made by him will bless him, not because it possesses the understanding necessary to bless, but because it is material for blessing him.

And this is not only in one place, but in every place of his dominion. The places of his dominion include both the good and the evil. He will be blessed not only in the rewarding of the [Col. 1004B] just, but also in the just condemnation of the wicked.

But whatever may be the case with others, you, my soul, for all his benefits, always bless the Lord, rendering him worthy thanks.

# Psalm 103

## To David Himself

## Argument

The present psalm, as well as Psalm 148, is sung in praise of God through consideration of his creatures. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church praising God.

## Explanation

“David” indicates the person speaking, while everything else is sung to the Lord Christ, who is the creator, governor, and redeemer of the world.

The prophet, wishing to show that the ordering of things signifies divine mysteries, first celebrates, through the construction of heaven and earth, the mysteries of Christ and the Church. Second, he enumerates the works of the Lord, concealed under various figures. Third, he professes that in that eternal age he will continually declare the praises of the Lord—praises that he had also sung during the brief span of this life.

## Commentary

### Bless the Lord, My Soul

The psalm is “to David himself.” In this psalm we are going to hear great, joyful, beautiful, desirable gifts of him, full of gladness and joy—gifts which the one who conceived this psalm was already seeing with the mind and was pouring forth in exultation at that vision.

It is as if he said: For such great benefits and such great and numerous gifts of his grace, bless the Lord justly, my soul. It is as if he said: I exhort my soul to bless you, because you, Lord my God, have been greatly magnified.

The Lord is always great and magnificent in himself, even when hidden; but he is magnified for me, because the more his works are understood by us, the more he is magnified for us.

And see those magnificent works for which the author of all magnificent things alone should be praised, namely this:

[Col. 1004D]

### You Have Put On Confession and Beauty

If anyone wishes to be God’s garment, let him be displeased with his own ugliness and confess it, and thus he will become a beautiful garment for God. For confession comes first, and then beauty. Confession concerns sins, while beauty concerns right actions.

This is what he says: “You have put on confession and beauty,” that is, you have made for yourself a garment consisting of those who confess their ugliness and have been made beautiful. Hence it is said through Isaiah: “The Lord lives, because you will be clothed with all these things as with a garment.”

I say that you are clothed with light, that is, with luminous people as with a garment. He calls “light” those of whom the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”

By the phrase “clothed with”—which refers to what is placed upon the head—he indicates that these people are greater than the preceding ones. For among those who are Christ’s garment, some are at the edge of the garment and others around the head because of their excellence; some hang down like fringes, while others occupy this or that part according to their various dignities.

### Stretching Out Heaven Like a Skin

If you wish to read this literally, understand it as though he were saying: It is no wonder that you, Lord, have made beauty from ugliness and caused light to shine from darkness, because what is incredible to us is easy for you.

For you stretch out heaven—that is, the firmament, which is such a great thing—as easily as someone stretches out a skin. This was said to remove the foolish opinion of those who thought that there was labor in divine works just as there is in human works.

I say that you stretch out heaven, you who cover its upper regions with waters. For there are waters above heaven—that is, above the firmament—because it is said that God placed the firmament in the midst of the waters and joined it to those waters.

You, I say, accomplish this because you possess such great power: you who make the cloud your ascent. For the cloud received him from their eyes.

### Who Walks Upon the Wings of the Winds

[Col. 1005A]

[Col. 1005B]

The winds are said to have wings because of their speed. But he walks upon those wings, he who made all things together, because his Word surpasses every speed of the winds and at once penetrates all things.

And you make heavenly spirits assume bodies and become angels, that is, your messengers. And you make not only lesser spirits but also consuming fire—that is, the seraphim, those who are higher—your ministers. For “seraphim” is interpreted as “burning ones” or “those who walk.”

And you founded the earth upon stability, that is, you made stability the foundation of the earth. What that stability is upon which it rests, we do not know.

And because you founded the earth, therefore it will not be moved forever and ever, that is, it will remain eternally. For although it is said, “Heaven and earth will pass away,” the earth will not pass away so as not to exist, but only insofar as it serves our weakness.

### The Abyss

I say that the earth will not be moved, yet it appears to be moved because it is shaken on every side. For the abyss—that is, the depth of the waters—is its garment, surrounding it everywhere like clothing.

The Ocean divides it into four parts: two below and two above, as is read in Macrobius.

[Col. 1005C]

### The Waters Will Stand Above the Mountains

Here the literal sense fails. The future cannot be taken for the past, as though this were referring to the time of the Flood. Yet it has not been placed here without reason, because the prophetic spirit often wishes us to dwell on a point where the literal sense, rather than the allegory, offers something of this sort, thereby warning us to return to the mystery.

Therefore let us turn what we have said literally up to this point toward the mystery and say: How did it happen that the ugly became beautiful and that light shone from darkness? It happened because you, Lord, stretch out heaven like a skin.

He calls “heaven” the immortal Word and also other heavenly secrets. By “skin,” however, mortality is signified, because a thing is properly called skin only after it has been stripped from an animal.

The Lord chooses certain mortals and, using mortal language, mortal sound, and other mortal instruments, makes heaven for us through them—that is, he opens his immortal Word to us. [Col. 1005D] And to the extent that their authority and renown are extended, to that extent the heavenly secrets explained by them are spread abroad.

This is what he says: “Stretching out heaven like a skin.”

I say that you cover—that is, protect—the upper regions of this heaven with waters, that is, with spiritual gifts. In that mortal Word, the “upper regions” are the things spoken about his divinity, such as “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth, in contrast to the things spoken about his humanity.

Those upper regions are protected from ignorance and uncertainty by spiritual gifts. For unless those men were filled with spiritual gifts, they could not establish either themselves or us so firmly in those matters.

That waters are understood as spiritual grace is confirmed by the Lord in the Gospel, when he says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

Or otherwise: Heaven is the sacred Scriptures, because they conceal—that is, contain within themselves—secret mysteries. And just as a skin stretched after an animal has died is extended into a certain durability, so the sacred Scriptures, through their deceased authors, were extended into enduring authority.

While Paul was still alive, his Epistles were valued by only a few; but after he was no longer alive, they were regarded throughout the whole world as most sacred, and are still so regarded. [Col. 1006A]

This is what he says: “Stretching out heaven like a skin.”

I say that you cover—that is, obscure—the upper commandments of this heaven, that is, of the Scriptures, such as “Honor your father and mother.” What commandment is more excellent than the commandment that orders you to extend your hand to the poor? And there are many similar examples.

You cover these, I say—that is, overshadow them—with waters, that is, with the two most excellent commandments: love of God and love of neighbor. For just as gold placed beside silver obscures the silver, so these two most excellent commandments, when compared with any other higher commandments, make those others seem almost worthless.

Consider also that it is said: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts.” And pouring belongs properly to water. Therefore the love of God and of neighbor is rightly signified by waters, because nothing softens the human heart more, or softens it away from sins.

Or otherwise: Heaven is the holy Fathers, who by their example, words, and deeds are an overshadowing for us against the incitements and excesses of vices. Just as skins, when tabernacles were first made from them, served as protection against the harshness of the air, so the holy Fathers protect us.

This is what he says: “Stretching out heaven like a skin,” you who cover—that is, protect—the upper regions of this heaven with the waters of spiritual grace.

He calls the upper regions of those holy Fathers the things which they established with greater force of reason, such as those about which the Apostle says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God.”

He protected these upper regions in them through spiritual gifts in two ways: against error, so that they would not err, and against exaltation, so that they would nevertheless not grow proud.

### Who Makes the Cloud His Ascent

[Col. 1006B]

There are various ways of construing this and the similar expressions that follow. It is to say: You make the cloud your ascent—that is, you make holy preachers, who are called clouds because they rain down words, thunder threats, and flash with miracles, into steps for us toward you, that is, toward the vision of you.

Another translation has “its,” referring it to heaven, so that it reads: You make its cloud the ascent of heaven, that is, you make preachers a step for us toward heaven—that is, toward understanding the Scriptures—or even toward the other holy Fathers, whose words and deeds they make known to us.

The text continues:

### Who Walks Upon the Wings of the Winds

[Col. 1006C]

The soul is called a wind. For just as that incorporeal thing, whatever it may be called, moves corporeal things, so the soul, though incorporeal, nevertheless moves bodies.

The wings of the soul are virtues. And although the soul is endowed with virtues, including those two distinguished wings, namely love of God and love of neighbor, nevertheless the Lord walks upon all these wings, because his love for us is much greater than our love for him. For he loved us first, and whatever we love has proceeded from him.

### Who Makes Angels

He calls “angels” preachers whom the Lord makes spiritual from carnal people, so that, although the spirit is held in the flesh, it does not serve the flesh. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is judged by no one.”

And you make your ministers—that is, your lesser preachers—a consuming fire, fervent in spirit and serving the Lord. For the one who preaches sets others on fire all the more easily if he himself burns first.

[Col. 1006D]

### Who Founded

He calls the Church “earth” because of its cultivation. It is to say: You founded the earth upon its stability, that is, upon the one who is its foundation, concerning whom the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, namely Christ.”

And therefore it will not be moved, that is, it will not be shaken forever and ever.

Yet many wish to move it, because the abyss is its garment like a covering. The abyss is the depth of the sea waters. Through it the bitterness of persecutions is signified. At a certain time this bitterness grew so greatly in the Church that it overwhelmed even mountains—that is, those eminent in virtues; it killed some, drove others into flight, and forced others to hide.

Foreseeing this, the prophet said through the Spirit that the abyss would prevail so greatly over the earth—that is, over the Church—that even the waters would stand above the mountains.

But what concern is there? None at all, because the waters will flee—that is, persecutions will cease—at your rebuke, that is, through the rebuke you will deliver through your servants.

And truly they will flee, because they will fear the voice of your thunder, that is, on account of the manifest threat of your servants, who say: “Woe to the world because of scandals!” Again: “Unless you repent, you will perish,” and similar things.

When the persecution has ceased, the mountains that had been oppressed will ascend, that is, the eminence of the holy apostles and other prelates will then appear. And the humble plains, the subjects, will descend. For the more those men rise in authority, the more these will advance in submission.

Yet neither will those ascend nor these descend except into the place you founded, that is, firmly established. For each person has his own dwelling from the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1007A]

### You Set a Boundary

I say that you set a place for them because you established a boundary, that is, a fixed limit for all—the mountains, the plains, and the waters—which they will not cross. [Col. 1007B]

Therefore, after the waters have fled at your command, they will never again return to cover the earth.

It is as if he said: The sea will be moved and the waves will beat upon the shore, because persecution will not be entirely eradicated; nevertheless the waters will never again return to that condition in which they cover the earth and oppress the Church as before.

For even if a severe persecution is to come in the time of Antichrist, it will nevertheless be lighter, because it will not be everywhere.

### Who Sends Forth

You have set a boundary for them, I say—you who send forth springs in the valleys.

The valleys are depressed and narrow places between mountains. Through them the humble are signified, concerning whom it is said through the prophet: “Upon whom will my spirit rest, except upon the quiet and humble person who fears my words?”

For the more humble they are, the more fertile they are in spiritual grace. Therefore he says: “Who sends forth springs,” that is, who prepares inexhaustible and refreshing doctrine in the valleys.

They will pass through the midst of the mountains, that is, they will not dissent from the common doctrine of the mountains, that is, of the apostles. For this concord must truly be observed in the Church.

Hence the Apostle Paul, who had learned neither from a human being nor through a human being, nevertheless, so that he would not appear to dissent from the others, brought what he had received before them, and thus removed every wrongful suspicion concerning himself.

Or otherwise: The waters proceeding from the valleys will pass through the midst of the mountains, that is, they will flow through the valley, because they will reach human beings alone; but they will not reach the mountains—that is, the proud.

And notice that he says “they will pass through” because, as the Apostle says: “Whether prophecies or knowledge, they will be abolished; for when what is perfect has come, what is partial will be abolished.”

[Col. 1007C]

### They Will Give Drink

It is as if he said: From the waters of the valleys all the beasts of the field will drink—that is, some from among all the beasts of the field.

He calls the Jews “beasts of the field,” and calls them beasts because, although they worshiped the true God, they did so only for carnal reasons. By “field” is signified the cultivation of the law and the prophets bestowed upon them.

And not only the beasts of the field, but also the wild asses—that is, the Gentiles, who were like forest asses, foolish and untamed—will await being given drink from those waters.

They will do this in their thirst, that is, in the thirst given to them by God. Some will receive more, others less, because these waters are measured out so that great and small, learned and unlearned, old and young may drink from them, each according to his capacity.

Here the elephant swims, while the lamb walks; here the wild ass is refreshed, and the hare is not frightened.

[Col. 1007D]

### Above Them

It has been said: “The mountains ascend, the plains descend, and springs arise in the valleys.”

And above these—that is, above the mountains, plains, and valleys—will be the birds of heaven, that is, spiritual men whose citizenship is in heaven, because they will rely upon the authority of those others.

And they will dwell—that is, adhere to them in heart—in such a way that they will think nothing apart from them. This is shown when he says: “For they will utter a voice from the midst of the rocks,” that is, from the common doctrine of the mountains.

Or otherwise: The birds of heaven, who were previously unstable, will dwell above them—that is, they will be made stable, founded in the faith of the mountains and valleys—and they will give a voice from the midst of the rocks, as before.

[Col. 1008A]

### Watering the Mountains

It has been said: You send forth springs in the valleys. You, I say, also water the mountains from their upper regions, that is, you imbue the mountains with spiritual gifts which proceed from you, who are truly above, because you are the creator.

For “every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights.”

And because they have these things from you, not from themselves, therefore the earth associated with them will be satisfied through them from the fruit of works—not their works, but yours. For neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth.

### Producing Hay

The earth will be satisfied, I say; the earth, I mean, producing hay for beasts.

Or it may be referred to the Lord, so that it reads: You send forth springs, watering the mountains and, by satisfying the earth, producing hay—that is, necessary carnal provisions—for beasts, that is, for holy preachers who thresh, separating grain from chaff, that is, the good from the evil.

Concerning them it is said: “You shall not muzzle the ox that threshes.”

Devout provincials ought to distribute provisions to the soldiers of Christ, as the Apostle commands, saying: “Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him.” And elsewhere: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?”

For holy preachers give gold and receive hay; that is, they give eternal things and receive transitory things.

Therefore, to express more fully what they receive, he adds: “And producing grass for the service of human beings.”

By “the service of human beings” he means human beings, whom he also calls beasts, because the Apostle says: “We are your servants through Jesus Christ.” And elsewhere: “Although I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all.”

[Col. 1008B]

### That You May Bring Forth Bread

For this purpose, I say, you produce hay from the lower earth for the beasts, so that from the higher earth—that is, from the preachers—you may bring forth bread, that is, spiritual nourishment, for those below.

And wine—that is, the splendid cup of the Lord, which does not stupefy the [Col. 1008C] body but gladdens the human heart.

It is as if he said: Let no one prepare his mouth for drunkenness, but his heart, because this wine does not stupefy the body but the heart.

For truly it had stupefied the heart—that is, alienated it from reason—of the man who, half-roasted, did not fear the torments but insulted the tyrant, saying: “I am roasted; now turn me over and eat.”

### That It May Gladden

Some books read: “That he may bring forth bread,” which agrees well with this passage, so that it reads: Therefore the Lord produces hay for the beasts, so that he may bring forth bread and wine. And after these things, “that he may gladden,” that is, make the inner face joyful with oil, that is, with spiritual grace.

After someone has been nourished with that bread and given drink from that wine, it follows that he should be filled with spiritual grace.

Therefore, he will gladden the face with oil, because bread preceded it, and bread strengthens the human heart. He adds this because he had simply mentioned bread.

It is as if he said: Hunger inwardly and thirst inwardly, because inwardly you will be refreshed.

[Col. 1008D]

### They Will Be Satisfied

The trees will be satisfied with this bread—not now wild trees, but trees of the field, that is, already levelled and suitable for placement in a building.

Understand by “trees” the lesser peoples of the nations. And not only they, but also cedars—that is, the powerful and noble—will be satisfied with that bread.

I say that these are cedars of Lebanon, that is, whitened ones; but they are not whitened by themselves, if he himself planted them. For every planting that my Father did not plant will be uprooted.

And there, in the cedars, there the sparrows will build their nests.

He calls “sparrows” those who have renounced this age and, transferring themselves to the common life, dwell in monasteries which the cedars have built. They are cautious and continually complain about their sins.

And although they have hope in those cedars because of temporal necessity, their principal hope is in the house of the heron. For the house of the heron is their leader.

The heron is a bird that nests in the low rocks of the sea, which are struck by waves on every side but are not broken; rather, they break the waves. So too Christ was struck in himself and is struck in his members by the waves of temptations and tribulations; he breaks them all and is not broken.

And this house of the heron—that is, Christ—is the leader of the sparrows.

The lofty mountains too—that is, the apostles—are leaders for the deer. Those are called deer who already have agile feet, that is, dispositions ready for leaping across. These heavenly things too are full of thorns and briars and difficult to climb.

And for such people the lofty mountains—that is, the apostles—are leaders through their doctrine and example. Nevertheless the rock, that is, Christ, is their principal leader and principal refuge.

He proves this from the greater, saying: For it is a refuge even for hedgehogs—that is, for those enveloped in the thorns of sins and in utter despair, who hope to be freed only through it.

Or otherwise: The mountains—that is, the higher commandments—are leaders for the deer; but this is not attributed to them, rather to the Lord, because the rock is their refuge. For even for hedgehogs it is a refuge, as before.

[Col. 1009A]

### He Made the Moon

It is as if he said: By satisfying the trees of the field and doing the other things mentioned above, he made the moon—that is, the present Church, which is compared to the moon because of its increase and decrease.

I say that he made the moon for seasons, that is, destined to last only for a temporal period.

And he also made the sun, by which the moon would be illuminated, because he made his Word become incarnate.

To distinguish this from our sun, he says: “The sun, which knew”—that is, foresaw—“its setting.” For just as he took human flesh by his will, so by his will he laid it down; yet he took it by his power, as he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life and to take it up again.”

[Col. 1009B]

### You Set Darkness

It is as if he said: Why is he killed? For this reason: because you set darkness—that is, because blindness occurred in Israel.

For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

Darkness was set when they did not understand the things said about him in the Scriptures. Night—that is, the thickest darkness—was made in them when, despite the teaching and miracles he performed before them, they did not understand or recognize him, although one of them, seeing the miracles, said: “No one can do these signs that you [Col. 1009C] do unless God is with him.”

And in that night all the beasts of the forest—that is, the Jews, no longer beasts of the field but beasts of the forest, untamed and incorrigible, as though entirely deprived of both the yoke of the prophets and the law—will pass through.

They will pass from knowledge to persuasion, from persuasion to action, and thus into perseverance.

He shows whom he understands as the beasts of the forest, saying: “The young lions”—that is, not only the greater but also the lesser among the Jews—“will pass through, roaring together: Crucify him, crucify him!”

They do this in order to seize and seek food for themselves, that is, to satisfy their carnal heart concerning him.

They could not have done this unless it had been permitted by God. Hence, when the corrupt judge said: “Do you not know that I have the power to release you and the power to crucify you?” the Lord pierced the swollen bladder and expelled all its air, saying: “You would have no power over me,” and so forth.

[Col. 1009D]

### The Sun Has Risen

They will indeed roar in order to seize and seek food. But what concern is there? The sun has risen—that is, by rising again and ascending, it will rise—and they, fearing, will gather together so as to command that no one speak in his name.

And they will be placed in their dens, that is, in their wicked consciences.

But the one who will be a human being—that is, one who uses reason—will go out from his wicked conscience to his work, that is, to the work useful for him: they will confess their sins, as those who came to the apostles said: “What shall we do, brothers?”

And afterward they will go out to their work, that is, they will work in the vineyard until evening, that is, until the end of their life.

Or otherwise: He said that the sun sets, and at that setting you set—or will set—darkness, that is, doubt, in the hearts of the apostles and other believers.

Night will also come, that is, despair in some of them, because they will say: “We thought that he was going to redeem Israel.”

Concerning this night the Lord said to Peter: “Simon, Simon, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail, and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers.”

Night will come, I say, and in that night all the beasts of the forest—that is, the [Col. 1010A] head of the demons and all his forces, who are called beasts of the forest because they have been condemned without hope of returning home—will pass through, that is, pass from one person to another.

And not only the greater demons, but also the young lions, will pass through roaring like the greater ones, in order to seize and seek food for themselves, that is, to find someone from whom they can refresh themselves.

They will not have that food except as it is given to them by God. For they have the will to harm, but they have no power except insofar as they are permitted.

But that passage will quickly end, as if he said, because the sun will rise. Then those beasts, driven out from the hearts of the faithful, will be gathered as though into a corner and placed as though in their dens, that is, in the hearts of unbelievers.

And thus the human being—that is, the one truly using reason—will go forth in peace to his work.

He explains what he calls “work”: he will go forth in peace to his work in the Lord’s vineyard until evening, that is, until the time of Antichrist, who will come in the evening of the world.

Then night will come again, because, as the Apostle says: “Such a time will come as has not been since the nations began to exist.”

[Col. 1010B]

### How Magnified They Are

Seeing these beautiful things ordered and arranged by God, proceeding in their appointed times, and considering the glorious Craftsman in his works of art, the prophet bursts into this admiration, saying: “Lord, how magnified are your works!” Nor is it surprising that the works are magnificent, since they are made by the Magnificent One. For “you made all things in wisdom,” that is, through your Son, of whom the Apostle says: “We preach Christ Jesus crucified, a stumbling-block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles; but to the Gentiles who are called, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

And he briefly repeats those works, saying: “The land of Judea has been filled with your possession,” that is, with a new possession: many of the Jews believed in you and became your possession, in accordance with the saying: “Behold, old things have become new.” And the Apostle says: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” And not only the land, but also “this great sea,” that is, the Gentile world placed in the bitterness of vices, has been filled with your possession.

And this sea is “spacious in its hands,” that is, in its works; for “the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few.” There, that is, in the sea, are reptiles whose number is beyond counting: there are many thousands of suggestions and temptations. They are called reptiles because they steal in gently; or because they make us crawl, that is, cast us down to the earth. There are there small animals with great ones, that is, heretics stirring up heresy among the great and among the small: among the great, in the divinity of the Word; among the small, in his humanity. But although, as he says, they are animals and reptiles, nevertheless the ships, that is, the Churches adhering to the cross, will not suffer shipwreck there, that is, in that sea, but will pass through it safely.

### This Dragon

Not only the small and great reptiles and animals, but this notable dragon also is there, namely, the head of all evil. He whom you formed in dignity deformed himself beforehand, and thus was formed for mockery, that is, in such a way that the faithful might mock him. For he loses many whom he pierces through the throat, because you pierced his jaw with a bracelet.

By the bracelet, which is round and solid, grace is signified; for just as a bracelet surrounds the neck or arm, so grace surrounds certain people in such a way that, through repentance, it causes them to escape from the jaws of the devil, in which they were already held shut through their fall.

And all these things, namely the dragon and the animals, await this from you: that you give them food at the time appointed by you. And therefore I say that they await it from you, because they will gather food with you giving it to them—that is, not what they wanted, but what you will give. For the dragon wants to devour everyone, but he does not devour everyone he wishes.

If someone is good, he will be Christ’s food, and he will have Christ as his food. But if someone is evil, he will be the serpent’s food, because it was said to the serpent: “You shall eat earth.” If, then, you do not wish to be the serpent’s food, be good, and, with the Apostle, set your mind on the things above, not on the things upon the earth.

It follows:

### When You Open Your Hand

“When you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness.”

This means: Those creatures will indeed gather food wherever you permit them; nevertheless, all things that may properly be called “all”—that is, all those who are to be numbered among created beings—will be filled with goodness, that is, with freely given grace, when you open your hand, that is, when you reveal your word, through which you made all things.

### But When You Turn Away

I say that they will be filled with goodness, and yet they will be troubled, that is, they will sometimes undergo the disturbance of a fall when you turn your face away from them because of some presumption.

So it happened to Peter when he did not attend to whom he had beside him, but presumptuously said of himself: “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to death and to prison.” Therefore he was troubled, since at the voice of a maidservant he denied him.

But nevertheless, as he says, “we know that all things work together for good for those who love God.” And therefore their disturbance will benefit them, because in this way you will remove their proud spirit, and they will fail in their own spirit and advance in yours; they will return to their own dust, that is, they will recognize their weakness.

And thus you will send them your Holy Spirit, and they will be created in good works. By removing their spirit and sending yours, you will renew the face of the earth, that is, the interior face of those earthly people.

When he had seen all these things, he says, rejoicing in divine mercy:

“May the glory of the Lord be forever,” that is, may the Lord be glorified eternally in this way: by permitting his own people to be troubled, may he remove their spirit and send them his own Spirit.

And truly this will happen, because “the Lord will rejoice in his works.” For those renewed by him will act well, and on this account the Lord will rejoice. I mean the Lord who makes them such that he may rightly rejoice in them.

For he looks mercifully upon the earth and makes it tremble, as the Apostle says: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.” I mean that he looks upon it who touches the mountains—that is, the proud—with an outward scourge and a hidden inspiration; and “they smoke,” that is, they pour forth tearful prayers to the Lord.

### I Will Sing to the Lord

Because the Lord looks upon the earth and does the other things mentioned above, therefore “I will sing to the Lord in my life,” that is, I will live in such a way that my life will be a song to the Lord. And so that this may happen, “I will sing psalms to my God,” that is, I will act well for the honor of my God for as long as I exist, as long as I ought to sing his praises.

I will always desire this: that “my speech,” that is, my disputation—namely, that I accuse myself and praise him—may be pleasing to him.

And truly it will be pleasing to him, because I will delight not in the world but in the Lord. And I will delight in this truly, that is, in true delight: now in hope, but finally in reality.

Therefore, so that sinners too may delight in him, let them, following my example, withdraw from the earth, that is, from earthly desire. I mean the sinners who are the Jews, transgressors of the law they received; and likewise all other wicked people, following my example, so that they may no longer be as they formerly were. For “turn the wicked away, and they will be no more.”

And so that these and those may imitate me, therefore, my soul, for such great benefits and so many gifts of his graces, bless the Lord.

Blessing at the beginning, blessing at the end: we began with blessing; let us return to blessing, so that we may reign in blessing.

## ON PSALM 104. ALLELUIA

### Argument

This psalm is formed altogether appropriately and skillfully through remembrance of ancient holy people and ancient times, for the benefit of those now living. Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ to the Apostles concerning the Jews.

### Explanation

“Alleluia” is a Hebrew name, to be declined in the neuter gender, as Jerome shows; it is interpreted as “Praise the Lord.” Wherever it is placed in headings, it teaches that the power of the Creator must always be praised.

What we say once must be observed in all cases. In whichever psalm “Alleluia” is written first, that psalm also has “Alleluia” placed after it at the end. Many people, not knowing this, suppose that it is the beginning of the following psalm. Indeed, you will often find two “Alleluia”s placed before one psalm. This signifies that one belongs to the end of the preceding psalm, while the other belongs to the beginning of the following one.

The prophet knows that the people of Israel are accustomed to place their hope in temporal benefits. In the first part he admonishes them always to seek him spiritually. In the second he strengthens them through the examples of the patriarchs, because they were not abandoned by the Lord, since they served under his command. In the third he enumerates how much he bestowed upon their fathers, recalling Joseph’s dangers and honors and the entry of the Hebrews into Egypt. In the fourth he relates how Israel was delivered from its enemies through the various plagues of Egypt. In the fifth he describes how much he bestowed upon them in the wilderness, so that they might not rejoice in temporal goods, but, softened by his benefits, might observe his justifications and his law.

### Commentary

#### Confess to the Lord and Call upon His Name

There were not lacking in that former people those who were to be reckoned among the seed, as the Apostle shows when he says: “For God was not well pleased with all of them.” When he says “not with all,” this is understood to mean “with some,” and the psalm deals with those people.

The seed of Abraham is here admonished—the children of promise who belong to the inheritance of the eternal covenant—to choose God himself as their inheritance and to worship him freely, that is, for his own sake, not for some profit or reward outside him.

They are to do this by praising him, calling upon him, and proclaiming him; by working well through faith, not for their own glory but for his; by rejoicing in hope; and by burning with charity.

Because the psalm commends such people, it does not deal here with the iniquities, provocations, and bitterness of those in whom God was not well pleased. The following psalm deals with them, although they belonged to the same people.

This psalm is entitled “Alleluia,” which is Hebrew and is interpreted in Latin as “Praise the Lord.” Therefore it begins with the confession of one who praises: “Confess to the Lord,” and thus “call upon his name.”

Here confession must be understood not as the confession of one who groans, but of one who praises, because invocation follows. For we cannot call upon him unless we are such in our life that we praise God.

The Lord hears the one who calls upon him whom he sees praising; and he sees as praising the one whom he approves as loving. Therefore it follows: “Declare his works,” that is, the rejection accomplished through him among the nations—namely, that whoever loves God should love his neighbor.

He explains how this should be proclaimed, saying: “Sing to him with your mouth, and sing psalms to him through your works.” And so “tell him all his wonders,” both those he visibly performs outwardly and those he invisibly performs inwardly.

And so that you may recount them, “be praised,” that is, be worthy of praise by living well. Do this “in his holy name,” namely, so that you do not seek your own glory, but that “the one who glories may glory in the Lord,” so that the heart of those who seek the Lord may rejoice through your example by imitating you.

#### Seek the Lord

So that others may seek the Lord through your example, “and be strengthened while seeking him,” that is, approach him and be enlightened, so that you may not be hindered by blindness from seeing what must be seen, nor by weakness from doing what must be done.

Do not seek his face for a time only, but always seek his face. For he must always be sought here and finally found.

But perhaps, even when found here, he must still be sought. Our faith finds him; our hope seeks him. Charity finds him through faith and seeks him through hope. But after it has found him, he is no longer to be sought.

Perhaps, however, even there he must be sought without end, because he must be loved without end. For discovery does not bring an end to that seeking which signifies love; rather, love always grows, and so does seeking.

#### Remember His Wonders

It is as though he says: I have said, “Seek the Lord.” And if it is too great for you to see or seek him himself, at least see him in his works. That is: if you have not been able to see the sun in its sphere, at least behold him on earth, so that the hearts of the little ones may be nourished and strengthened in faith.

An example is here proposed from the patriarchs and from their faith and promise, so that, by imitating them and prospering, we may not despair concerning the seed. For all who throughout the whole earth receive this grace are to be reckoned among the seed.

“You are the true seed of Abraham, his servants; and you are not carnal but spiritual children of Jacob, his chosen ones,” because, he says, “the elder shall serve the younger.”

I say, all of you: if you cannot see him as he is, at least remember his wonders that he performed. And he explains what those wonders are: namely, remember his signs that he performed at the exodus from Egypt—not with regard to the signs themselves, but to what they signified. And “remember the judgments,” not of the mouth of the servant, that is, of the old law, but “the judgments of his mouth,” namely, both what he himself commanded to be observed in the newness and what he indicated would be received in return for them.

#### He Himself Is My Lord

I say that they are the judgments of his mouth because he himself, our Lord—that is, the Lord and God of all—is not God of the Jews alone. And truly he is God of all, because his judgments are throughout the whole earth, so that whoever keeps the commandment may receive the promise.

He, I say, “remembered his covenant to be extended forever,” and “remembered the word that he commanded for a thousand generations.”

Although the following words are stated below—“I will give you the land of Canaan”—this must not here be understood of the old covenant. For how could those promises, since they were temporal, be “forever,” that is, eternal?

The old covenant is also called old because it is abolished by the new. How could there be a thousand generations from the time when the old covenant was given until the new, since there cannot be that many from Abraham, nor even from Adam, to the end of the world?

Blessed Augustine says that if they count a thousand generations, according to those who interpret the passage in that way, they amount to fifteen thousand years, which exceeds the duration of the world according to the law.

Therefore the old covenant is not to be understood here, but the covenant of justification and eternal inheritance.

The word also that he commanded—that is, faith—does not belong to the covenant but to faith. A commandment is what we ought to do; a promise is what we ought to receive. Therefore the commandment is faith, so that “the righteous may live by faith.” Eternal inheritance is promised to this faith.

“A thousand generations” is used for all generations because of the perfection of the number. This means that as long as generation follows generation in succession, so long it has been commanded that we live by faith.

The people of God rightly preserve this: the children of promise coming into being by birth and departing by death until the common generation comes to an end, which is signified by a thousand because of the solid square of ten, which reaches a thousand.

He says that God remembered because he seemed to have forgotten this covenant when he made earthly promises, and seemed forgetful of the word when he gave carnal commandments. But he remembered both when he gave commandments concerning faith and promised eternity.

#### Which He Ordained

It has been said that he remembered the word which he ordained for Abraham, that is, which he ordered and promised to Abraham, saying to him: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed.”

And he remembered his oath made to Isaac, that is, the same word which he firmly promised to Isaac. Isaac was the son of promise and signifies the one in whom the promise was fulfilled; therefore he attributes the oath to Isaac.

And he established that word—“Jacob, as a commandment, and Israel, as a covenant.” There is labor in the commandment, but reward in the promise. Therefore he says “established,” so that the word might be a commandment for Jacob, that is, for those making progress, and an eternal covenant for Israel, that is, for those who attain the goal. For when the commandment has been observed and fulfilled, he will finally give something eternal, namely eternal life.

#### Saying, “To You I Will Give”

He ordained his word for Abraham, I say, saying this: “To you, Abraham, and to your true seed, I will give the land of Canaan.”

After Abraham had been led out of Ur of the Chaldeans, while he was dwelling as a stranger in the land of promise, which Canaan, the firstborn of Ham, possessed, the Lord said to him: “The land in which you dwell I will give to you and to your seed after you.”

But if it is the land of Canaan, how can it be something eternal except in relation to what it signifies? The land of Canaan is a land flowing with milk and honey, by which grace is signified, in which one tastes how sweet the Lord is.

But because grace is not given to everyone—for “faith is not of all”—he therefore adds: “The measuring cord of your inheritance,” that is, the inheritance specially divided for you, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and for those who imitate your faith. Hence elsewhere: “The measuring cords have fallen to me in pleasant places.”

It should be known, moreover, that Canaan is interpreted as “humble” and signifies servile fear because of the sentence pronounced by Noah, who said: “Canaan shall be the servant of his brothers.”

But because “a servant does not remain in the house forever,” therefore, after the Canaanite was expelled, that land was given to Abraham’s seed as a possession, because perfect charity casts out fear.

#### When They Were Few in Number

This is introduced for the consolation of weak souls, to show that although God must be worshiped freely, he nevertheless does not abandon his worshipers in temporal necessity.

According to blessed Augustine, the passage is connected as follows. It is as though he says: How could Abraham and his descendants inhabit that land? Quite well, certainly, because although they were few in number and strangers in it—although the farmers of the Lord were very few—they nevertheless lived securely in that land. And they passed securely many times from one nation to another and from that kingdom to another people.

He calls that land a kingdom, not because it was then a kingdom, but because it was destined to become one.

Some, however, connect the passage simply in this way: The Lord said to Abraham, “To you I will give the land of Canaan.” Although they were few in number in that land, they nevertheless lived there securely and previously passed from nation to nation.

This was because he did not allow anyone to harm them, either in that land or outside it. He also often rebuked kings for their sake, such as Pharaoh, king of Egypt, for Abraham’s sake, and Abimelech, king of Gerar, for Isaac’s sake, as the history relates.

He did this, I say, saying to those kings: “Do not touch my christs, and do not harm my prophets.”

There is no doubt that they were prophets, because prophecy was present in their words and deeds. But how they were christs, that is, anointed ones, is questioned, since anointing in that people began only with Saul, whom David succeeded.

They were anointed, however, if not bodily, then spiritually, because they foresaw the one who was to come and believed in him. In Hebrew he is called *Messiah*, in Greek *Christos* (Χριστός), and in Latin *unctus*, “anointed.”

Blessed Augustine says in this passage:

> “For no one can be reconciled to God the Father except by that faith which is in Christ Jesus, whether before his Incarnation or afterward, as the Apostle says: ‘There is one Lord, one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus.’”

#### And He Called Famine

He said above that they passed from nation to nation, which involved descending into Egypt many times. First he gives the reason for this, saying: “For the Lord called famine upon the land.”

But it is asked how he called famine upon the land as though it were some person, since famine is nothing other than a destructive condition brought about by lack of food, which is driven away by nourishment just as disease is healed by medicine.

It must be understood, however, that individual devils are appointed over the administration of individual plagues. Hence elsewhere it is said: “He sent an invasion through evil angels.”

Therefore he says: “He called famine,” that is, he called the one appointed over famine upon the land; that is, he commanded that the famine which had been in his disposition before the foundation of the world should be upon the land.

“And he destroyed every support of bread,” that is, he took bread away from that land, by which human beings are strengthened.

Before he did this, however, so that they might have a refuge to which they could flee, he who also uses wrongly performed things for good sent a certain man ahead of them into Egypt.

For Joseph “was sold,” that is, God permitted him to be sold by his brothers to the Egyptians for service, or as a slave.

And if Joseph, sold by his brothers, humbled and exalted, made a place for God’s people among temporal goods so that they might not be established over their enemies, how much more did the mystical Joseph, sold by his brothers, humbled according to the flesh and exalted in heaven, make a place among eternal goods for God’s people triumphing over the devil and his angels.

#### They Humbled Him with Fetters

Joseph was indeed sold to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians humbled his feet with fetters.

For Potiphar, Pharaoh’s official, put him in prison because of the command of his wife, to whom he refused to consent, as the history relates.

Then iron—that is, the harsh tribulation of necessity—passed through his soul. This lasted until his word came, that is, while he interpreted the dreams of the chief cupbearer and the baker who were with him in prison.

He did not possess this interpretation from himself, but because “the word of the Lord,” that is, the Holy Spirit through whom the Lord spoke to him, inwardly inflamed him—that is, enlightened and kindled him—to interpret.

Afterward, when the king had seen a dream and could find no suitable interpreter, having been informed about Joseph by the chief cupbearer, he sent to the prison. The ruler of the peoples, that is, Pharaoh, released him and let him go.

And he appointed him lord of his house, and so forth.

#### And Israel Entered Egypt

Here is the passage mentioned above. He calls Egypt the land of Ham because the descendants of Ham possessed it.

#### And He Increased the People

Israel entered Egypt, I say, and there the Lord greatly increased his people and strengthened them over their enemies.

This was not the case at the time when their males were being killed and they themselves were being oppressed by brickwork. Rather, this strengthening occurred when all their enemies were found dead beside the shore.

#### He Turned

It is as though he says: Their enemies were worthy for the Lord to strengthen his people over them in this way, because “he turned their heart to hate his people.”

This is not to be understood as meaning that God is the author of any evil. Rather, he permits the heart that is evil by itself to decline into worse by his just judgment, so that “the one who is filthy may become filthier still.”

So it is here. The heart of the Egyptians was evil because they envied Israel’s happiness. And the Lord “turned,” that is, completely turned, their heart—not by inciting them to evil, but by doing good to his own people—“into hatred of his servants,” that is, into envy. For envy is hatred of another’s happiness.

And they did this “to deceive his servants.” Those who did this outwardly pretended to be friends, yet secretly suggested to Pharaoh that he oppress them.

Because of this hatred and grief, the Lord sent Moses, his servant, into Egypt from Midian, where he was staying with his father-in-law Jethro, saying to him: “Return to Egypt, so that you may free my people. Seeing their affliction, I have seen it, and I have heard their groaning.”

But because Moses replied: “Lord, from yesterday and the day before, from the time you spoke to me, I am uncircumcised in lips and heart,” the Lord said to him: “Take your brother Aaron with you.”

Therefore the prophet adds: “He also sent Aaron,” whom he chose for the very task for which he had chosen Moses.

And in those two he placed—that is, firmly established—them in such a way that “the words of his signs and his wonders would not fail,” that is, his lesser signs and greater wonders, which were like words, because just as words signified something else, so too did those signs signify something else.

I mean his signs and wonders performed “in the land of Ham,” that is, in Egypt.

And he explains those signs, that is, those wonders, saying: “He sent darkness, and it became dark in Egypt.”

And thus “he embittered the Egyptians with his words,” because they attacked the Lord’s words with their stubborn replies and contradictions; therefore these words were embittered for them.

Blessed Augustine sets out the text in this way and says that he found very few books in which it did not read “he did not embitter.”

Nevertheless, it can be understood in this way: He did not embitter his words to Moses and Aaron, because whatever he said to them he displayed in his work. For if he promised something that he did not fulfill, then his words would have seemed bitter to them.

The things that follow concerning the plagues are to be understood only historically, and therefore we need not linger over them. “He said”—whether Moses or the Lord, who ordained once for all in his Word everything that is done temporally before all times.

#### And the Dog-Fly and the Mosquito Came

Contrary to what some think, these are not one plague but two. But the locust and the caterpillar, as blessed Augustine testifies, are one plague. One is the parent; the other is the old one.

#### And It Devoured All the Grass in Their Land

“Grass” also signifies wheat. “And it devoured all the fruit of their trees in their land.”

“And the Lord struck every firstborn in their land,” and “the firstfruits of all their labor.” Understand “firstborn” among human beings, but “firstfruits of labor” among the other animals.

#### And He Led Them Out

The Lord did those things to the enemies; but this he did for his own people: he led them out with gold and silver, which they had received as loans from the Egyptians.

Blessed Augustine says that the Lord did this because they were carnal and were not such people as could or would despise their labor—even though it was temporal, it was nevertheless their due and just reward.

Nor, because they deceived the Egyptians by trickery, should one think that the Lord commanded or approved such trickery among that people, whose heart was directed upward. Rather, through those words of God, who saw their carnal heart and examined their desire, they were permitted to do those things rather than commanded to do them.

Nevertheless, what they did was not without benefit to their carnal soul, since they took these things from people who justly deserved to suffer such treatment. Although they took them through trickery from wicked people, they took away what was justly owed to them.

Just as he used the Egyptians’ iniquity, so he used the weakness of these people to reveal what was signified in those deeds: namely, that we should take gold and silver from the Egyptians—that is, take the rhetorical ornaments of sentences from the books of unbelievers and transfer them as adornment to the Holy Scriptures.

#### Egypt Rejoiced

Not at first, but after they heard that their own people had been destroyed in the sea while the Israelites had departed unharmed. For they were greatly afraid that Israel might return and occupy the whole of Egypt.

“In that perfection he spread the cloud,” and so forth—that is, he protected them by the pillar of cloud during the day and by the pillar of fire during the night.

#### They Asked

“And with the bread of heaven,” that is, manna—which is called the bread of heaven because of what it signifies, or because it descended from a higher region—he satisfied them.

He did not satisfy them only in a barren place; he also gave them drink in a dry place, because “he split the rock, and waters flowed.” They were not small streams; rivers themselves flowed through the dry place, that is, where there had previously been dryness.

He displayed this to the carnal people because he remembered his holy word, that is, the eternal promise signified through those temporal goods. He had given this word to Abraham, his servant, that is, to one who worshiped him in simplicity.

And so “he led out his people with rejoicing”—some only in outward rejoicing, but others also in inward rejoicing, namely those in whom God is well pleased. The psalm speaks of them: “And his chosen ones in gladness.”

This is repetition for confirmation.

Blessed Augustine says in this passage:

> “It is to be understood that the servants of God in this passage, and the chosen children of promise, the seed imitating Abraham’s faith, do not receive these temporal goods from God so that they may flow away in luxury among them or grow lukewarm through perverse security. Rather, all these things have been prepared by divine mercy so that they may contribute to that eternal good.”

#### And He Gave

After he led them out into the wilderness, he gave them the regions of the nations. They possessed the labors of many peoples, not so that they might worship him on account of this, but so that they might also refer these things to the good nature.

For whatever other goods God gives are to be referred to his free worship; but free worship itself is not to be referred to anything else.

This is what he says: He gave those things to them so that they might keep his justifications. And he explains what it means to keep the justifications, saying: “And that they might seek his law.”

Here too blessed Augustine adds words of this kind:

> “Hear, therefore, seed of Abraham—not boasting in the flesh, but imitating faith. Hear, servants and chosen ones of God, possessing the glory of the life that now is and of the life to come. And if temptations are hard for you in this world, think of Joseph in prison and Christ on the cross. But if prosperity in temporal things is present, use those things not for their own sake, but for God’s sake; and do not think that God is necessary to his worshipers on account of these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”

## ON PSALM 105. ALLELUIA, ALLELUIA

### Argument

This psalm is sung as though from the person of the people already situated in Babylon, confessing their sins and lamenting that they had always proved ungrateful for God’s benefits. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church to the Apostles. It should be read in connection with Exodus.

### Explanation

The title briefly gives this preliminary instruction: it is to be sung to the Lord with the jubilation of the whole psalm.

A confessing people of the Hebrews is introduced, a people who, having abandoned the faithlessness of their fathers, was led to the devotion of the Lord by his own mercy. We are thus to understand that, when they have been converted, they too rightly sing “Alleluia” for their redemption.

In the first narrative, therefore, it prays that it may be joined to the people in whom God is well pleased, because that people was destined to be gathered from the nations through the coming of the Lord Savior.

In the second, it diminishes the sins of their fathers, which they committed in Egypt, when they paid no attention to the Lord’s wonders, although the merciful Lord delivered them from their enemies.

In the third, it relates that they returned to their eagerness for sinning, but that the Lord was softened by Moses’ prayers.

In the fourth, it asserts that their iniquities were repeated, and that the Lord’s impending wrath was appeased by Phinehas’ supplication.

In the fifth, it recalls that they embittered Moses at the waters of contradiction and afterward sacrificed their own children to idols. Therefore, being exceedingly angry, the Lord handed them over to the servitude of the nations. Then, taking pity on them, he restored glory to them in the sight of their enemies.

In the sixth, it prays concerning what it knew would come to pass: that the Catholic Church would be gathered from all nations and would celebrate praises to the Lord in eternal rejoicing.

### Commentary

#### Confess to the Lord, For—

This is the second of the alleluiatic psalms, and it is inscribed twice with “Alleluia.” Some say that one of these belongs to the preceding psalm. But blessed Augustine says that if this were so, the word “psalm” would have been placed between the two “Alleluia”s.

He also says that it is not necessary for it to be added twice, since once is sufficient.

This psalm is joined to the preceding one through the following connection: just as the former deals with those in the earlier people in whom God was well pleased, so this one deals with those who embittered the Lord for themselves, although divine mercy was by no means lacking for them.

These words are spoken in the person of all those who, if they beg forgiveness, recall examples of those toward whom the mercy of God also appeared abundantly even when they were sinners.

Like the preceding psalm, this one begins with confession. But the confession of one who groans must be understood, since the psalm says: “We have sinned with our fathers.”

Nevertheless, the confession of one who praises is also implied, since it adds: “For he is good, for his mercy is forever.” For no confession of sins is worthless when God is not praised in heart and mouth.

And because the Lord is praised in both confessions, the psalm is entitled twice “Alleluia.” Thus it begins: “Confess,” that is, make confession to the Lord, first accusing yourselves, then praising him.

And you ought to confess to him because he is good, that is, gracious and sweet to all who worthily taste him, and because his mercy is forever.

The Greek word for “age,” **αἰῶν** (*aiōn*), is understood equivocally, both as “eternity” and as “time.” If it is understood as time, then we understand mercy as that by which he both consoles us in this misery and frees us from this misery.

But if it is understood as eternity, then we understand that mercy without which no one can be blessed in that life—namely, the mercy by which he rewards our temporal labor with eternal rest.

#### Who Will Speak of the Mighty Deeds?

Filled with consideration of the divine works, the one who seeks mercy adds: “Who will speak of the mighty deeds of the Lord?” and so forth.

Considering the commandments of God, whose works are his praises when he works in his people, he says: “Who, having confessed, will speak of the mighty deeds of the Lord?” That is: who will be able to explain to anyone the Lord’s commandments, by which he powerfully heals and justifies us?

And because God performs certain things invisibly, and those things are unspeakable, he adds: “Or who, having heard them, will perform,” that is, if he hears them, will he also be able to perform all his praises?

His works are the praises of his commandments. But he used “praises” rather than “works” or “commandments” because, insofar as this occurs, they are his praise, since he is the one who works in us both willing and accomplishing according to his good pleasure.

Or alternatively: “Who, having confessed, will speak,” that is, will worthily represent in himself the mighty deeds of the Lord—how powerfully he formed the human being and how powerfully he reformed him?

Who, I ask, will speak in such a way as to perform all these praises of his once they have been heard—that is, so that he may not only say them with his voice but also display them in his works?

Certainly no one.

Blessed are those who keep. The continuation is the same, but the sentence has two parts. As if he were saying: No one, indeed, will be able to perform all his praises; nevertheless, there are some who are blessed without performing them—namely, those who keep judgment and practice righteousness, that is, those who judge rightly and do what is right, not for a time but always. For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved. This means that those who keep judgment in faith and practice righteousness in action are blessed, because the time will come when the judgment now kept in faith will be exercised in action—namely, when righteousness will be turned into judgment, that is, when the righteous receive the power to judge rightly those by whom they are now judged wrongly. [Col. 1018C] And because no one can keep judgment and practice righteousness unless healed from iniquity by him who justifies the ungodly, he adds the reason. As if he were saying: In order that we may keep judgment and practice righteousness, therefore, Lord, remember us, who were forgetful of you, in the good pleasure of your people—that is, by associating us with those in whom you take pleasure. And visit us with your salvation, that is, make your Savior known to us. In him sins are not only forgiven, but the soul is also healed, so that it may keep judgment and practice righteousness.

To see in the goodness. Remember us, I say, and visit us so that we may see—that is, so that we may not remain blind, but see what ought to be seen—and this not through our merit, but in the goodness of your chosen ones, that is, through that grace which you bestow upon your chosen. Or otherwise: Remember us, in the good pleasure of your people, so that we may see in the goodness of your chosen ones—that is, so that at last we may see you in that sweetness in which your chosen will see you. [Col. 1018D] And so that we may rejoice in the joy of your nation: so that we may rejoice in that joy in which your people will rejoice, that is, in you, when you will be all things. And I do not say only, “that we may see” and “that we may rejoice,” but also, “that you may be praised with your inheritance”—that is, that your inheritance may be praiseworthy and you may be praised in it.

We have sinned with our fathers. As if he were saying: It is necessary, Lord, that you remember that we sinned with our fathers—that is, while we were still in the loins of our fathers, as it is said elsewhere that Levi was tithed, that is, paid tithes, while in Abraham’s loins. Or, “We have sinned with our fathers” means: We sinned in the same way as our fathers. For we acted unjustly toward our neighbor, and he pursues the matter of iniquity—that is, of impiety toward God—by saying how the fathers sinned: Our fathers did not understand your wonders, Lord, performed in Egypt. That is, they did not consider what you wished to grant them through those wonders: namely, eternal life rather than temporal life, [Col. 1019A] an unchangeable good that ought patiently to be awaited. But they murmured impatiently and thought themselves blessed by temporal goods, which do not confer true blessedness, because they do not extinguish insatiable desire. He continues:

They did not remember the multitude of your mercy. Here he reproves both memory and understanding. Understanding was needed so that they might understand what God wished to lead them toward through those events; memory was needed so that, at the very least, they would not forget the wonders performed in time, but would trust faithfully that by the same power with which he had freed them from the power of Egypt, he would free them from the persecution of their pursuing enemies. In particular, he refers to his statement that they did not remember the wonders when, shut in by mountains on one side, by the Red Sea on another, and by the pursuing Egyptians on the third, they despaired of being able to be delivered by the Lord. This is what he says: Because they did not remember, therefore they provoked him—that is, [Col. 1019B] they provoked God to anger by despairing of his power—when they were going up. He says this with reference to the position of the place: for the descent is from Judaea into Egypt, while the ascent is from Egypt into Judaea. “They provoked him,” I say, “going into the Red Sea,” which they feared so greatly. Or it may simply be said with reference to the position of the place: they were going up into the Red Sea.

Although they provoked him, the Lord nevertheless saved them—not because of their merit, but for the sake of his name, namely, to make his power known to others. And he saved them wondrously, because he rebuked—that is, admonished—the Red Sea as a master rebukes a servant, and it was dried up. And he led them through the depths—that is, through the place where the depths had previously been—with as much security as they later had in the wilderness. And in the sea itself he saved them from the hand—that is, from the power—of the Egyptians. Thus he saved them and wholly redeemed them from the hand of their supreme enemy, Pharaoh. He does not say “redeemed” because he gave some price there, but the Prophet anticipates what had already been foreshadowed: [Col. 1019C] the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he saw would be poured out for our redemption.
