And truly he saved them from the hand of those who hated them in the sea, because the water covered them, so that not one of them remained. Then our fathers believed his word—that is, the Lord’s promises, made through Moses, concerning their deliverance—and in his praise—that is, praising him, they sang his hymn, saying: “Let us sing gloriously to the Lord.” But they did this quickly—that is, those praises soon came to an end—because they forgot his works. And they did not endure—that is, they did not lift themselves upward in contemplation of his purpose, so as to recognize that those benefits bestowed upon them were not empty, but that through them the Lord wished to lead them to something great, namely, eternal life. And because they did not endure the Lord’s purpose, therefore they craved cravings in the wilderness and tempted the Lord in the waterless place. Yet divine mercy did not fail them, because he gave them what they requested—that is, a carnal request with regard to drink. And he sent fullness, raining manna [Col. 1019D] into their understanding and rational considerations into their souls, that is, into their animal nature.

And they provoked him. As if he were saying: In addition to the things already mentioned, some of them also did this: they provoked Moses in the camp—and not Moses alone, but also Aaron, the holy one of the Lord, that is, the one whom the Lord commanded to be sanctified. For Moses consecrated Aaron as priest at the Lord’s command. Two of the people, Dathan and Abiram, dissented from him, saying that he was overly intent on advancing those of his own lineage; and, despising the Lord’s command, they wished to make themselves priests. Taking fifty men with them to burn incense, they came forward.

But what happened to them? The earth opened and swallowed Dathan and Abiram. It also covered—that is, closed itself over—their assembly, that is, over those fifty men who imitated them. The remaining accomplices of theirs were consumed by fire from heaven. This is what he says: “And fire blazed in their assembly, and flame consumed [Col. 1020A] the sinners.”

Yet after this divine correction they made a calf on Mount Horeb—not even merely something created, but a carved image. And they exchanged their glory—that is, God, in whom they ought to have gloried—not for a calf, which is at least an animate creature, but for the likeness, that is, the image, of a calf eating grass, just as it did them, because they were grass—that is, earthly—and the devil consumed them. They did this because they forgot God who saved them, who performed great deeds in Egypt, who performed great wonders in the land of Ham—that is, in Egypt—and who performed not only great but also terrifying wonders in the Red Sea, that is, wonders greatly to be feared.

And because they forgot God, therefore he said—that is, God determined—to destroy them. Yet this does not mean that he had actually determined to do so; for if he had determined it, they would have been destroyed. Rather, their iniquity was so great that it could appear that God had determined to destroy them utterly. And he truly would have destroyed them if Moses, his chosen one, had not stood before him on their behalf in opposition—that is, in humility [Col. 1020B] of spirit—in his presence, that is, in his heart, where he sees, saying: “Lord, if you forgive this people, forgive them; but if not, erase me from the book that you have written.” He said this confident in his own righteousness, in order to turn away his anger so that he would not destroy them.

Yet they were worthy of being destroyed, because when their scouts had been sent into the promised land and had brought back from there, in praise of the land’s greatness, such a cluster of grapes that two men could scarcely carry it, they considered that desirable land worthless. Yet do not understand that they were condemned because of their contempt for that land; rather, they were condemned because they neglected what it signified. That cluster, which the envoys brought from the promised land, signified Christ. The one who carried it in front, with the cluster behind him, signifies the Jewish people, who did not recognize Christ. The one who followed, looking upon the cluster before him, signifies the gentile people, who recognize Christ and always set him before the eyes of their mind, not behind them.

[Col. 1020C] They did not believe. Therefore, I say, they considered the desirable land worthless because they did not believe his word—that is, the Lord’s promise. And therefore they murmured in their tents, but they did not listen to the Lord’s voice. Therefore the Lord raised his hand over them—that is, he postponed the punishment which they then deserved, so that he might punish them more severely afterward. Or, “He raised his hand over them” means that he raised it to strike them more severely, namely, so that he might then overthrow them especially in the wilderness, and afterward cast down their offspring—that is, their children—among the nations, that is, throughout the nations, as he did with the Philistines, and through Assyria, and through many others. And so that he might scatter them throughout the regions, as they are scattered today.

And this was deserved, because they dedicated themselves—or consecrated themselves—to Beel; or, “they were initiated,” that is, they sacrificed to Beel, who was worshiped at Peor. For Belus was the father of Ninus, and his son made an idol in his honor called Beel, which was worshiped in the region of Peor; to this idol they sacrificed in the wilderness. It may also be said that they were so mingled with the nations that some of them [Col. 1020D] worshiped Beel at Peor and ate sacrifices offered to the dead—that is, sacrifices offered to Bel, who was already dead.

Thus they provoked God by their inventions—not because they themselves then invented those rites, which the nations had previously invented, but because they devoted themselves to them there as though they themselves had newly devised them. Therefore their ruin multiplied, because they perished both from serpents and in many other ways. While others were provoking God, Phinehas the priest stood firm, for he did not fall with them. He appeased God by thrusting through a certain Hebrew who was having intercourse with a Midianite virgin. And because he did this not from a desire for vengeance but from love, the others were corrected, and so the shaking ceased, because God no longer inflicted tribulation upon that people for this offense, as he had previously been accustomed to do.

Moreover, in addition to the things already mentioned, they provoked the Lord at the waters of contradiction, when they quarreled against Moses, saying: “Give us water to drink.” Then Moses was vexed—that is, [Col. 1021A] agitated—because of them, since they embittered—that is, provoked to anger—his spirit. Therefore he made a distinction, that is, he made a distinction with his lips. For whereas in all the other miracles he had been certain and had spoken confidently, here he spoke doubtfully, saying: “Can we draw water for you from this rock?” Therefore he did not lead the people into the promised land.

They provoked the Lord not only at the waters of contradiction, but also in this: after they had been brought into the promised land, they did not destroy all those nations which the Lord had told—that is, commanded—them to destroy. For they did not destroy certain nations, but made them tributary to themselves. Thus they were mingled among the nations and learned their works. He explains what works he means, saying: “And they served their carved images.” This became a scandal to them, that is, a ruin.

And deservedly so, because they sacrificed not only sheep and oxen, but also their sons and daughters to demons. This is not found in the historical account, [Col. 1021B] but it is no less to be believed on that account by the prophetic spirit, which says it, and by the other prophets who often reproach them with the same thing. He continues by explaining how they sacrificed them: “And they poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan.” In this way the land was slain in blood, with the container standing for what it contained. That is, those earthly people were inwardly slain because of the innocent blood poured out to demons.

And the land was defiled by their works. He explains how: because they fornicated in their inventions, that is, in their pursuits, since they abandoned their own God and clung to false gods. Therefore the Lord was angry with that people, or against that people, in fury—that is, in severe anger—and therefore he abhorred them, that is, made his inheritance vile. By calling it “inheritance,” however, he shows that this abhorrence was not entirely for destruction but for [Col. 1021C] correction.

And truly he says that he abhorred his inheritance, because he delivered them into the hands of the nations. This happened in such a way that those who hated them ruled over them. This is the most grievous form of servitude: to suffer as master one whom you have as an enemy. And because they ruled over them, their enemies afflicted them, and thus they were grievously humbled under their hands. Yet the Lord often delivered them.

They, however, did not attend to this, but provoked him by their counsel—that is, because they did not attend to his counsel, but to their own. For God’s counsel was to lead them through temporal goods to eternal goods. They did not attend to this, but preferred to follow their own counsel, namely, to seek what was theirs rather than what was God’s. Therefore deservedly they were humbled by their iniquities, that is, in such a way that their iniquities became the cause of their humiliation.

Again, divine mercy did not fail them, because the Lord saw them when they were afflicted. He does not say this because he ever fails to see; nevertheless, he is said to see our tribulation most especially when [Col. 1021D] he has mercy. Therefore he adds: “And he heard their prayer.” He did all this not for the sake of a shadow but for the sake of the figure, because he remembered the covenant—not the old covenant, which is being abolished, but the new covenant, which was signified through it.

Therefore he repented according to the multitude of his mercy—not because repentance ever existed in him, in whom no evil deed preceded it, but because he dealt with them so mercifully that he could appear to repent of the affliction he had previously inflicted. And truly he showed them great mercy, because he gave them into the mercies of all who had captured them—that is, he caused even the enemies who held them captive to deal mercifully with them.

Or otherwise: “He gave them into mercies” means that he dealt with them so mercifully, by sending his Son and freeing them from their inward enemies, [Col. 1022A] that those enemies could be called not merely merciful but, because of the excellence of that mercy, mercies themselves. He did this in the sight of all who had captured them—that is, while those who still held them captive observed and took note. They held them captive through the captivity brought about by the transgression of the first man. To say this equivalently is: He casts demons out from them.

And because it is said in the Gospel: “Behold, I cast out demons, and today and tomorrow I complete healings, and on the third day I am perfected,” therefore, after saying that he casts out demons, he adds a prayer for the completion of healing, saying: “Lord our God, save us by perfecting healing in us.”

“Today” may be understood as the time under the Law, and “tomorrow” as the time of grace, during both of which he worked healing. Or “today” may be understood as the time of his presence in the flesh, and “tomorrow” as the time of the apostolic mission and extending to the end of the age, during which he also completes healings through his preachers. The third day, on which he is perfected, will be when we all meet him together as one perfect man, according to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.

And so that you may save us, gather us, the true seed of Abraham, from all the nations [Col. 1022B] through the unity of faith, so that we may confess your holy name and at last glory in your praise—that is, in the praise of those who praise perfectly, because they love perfectly. They love perfectly because they contemplate face to face. I speak of us saying: “Blessed be the Lord from age to age,” that is, eternally, “the God of Israel,” that is, the one who makes those who see him through faith see him through sight. And all the people will say this.

But so that he may then be able to say it, let there now be blessing for him among the Jewish people, and let there also be blessing in the uncircumcision.

## ON PSALM CVI. Alleluia.

### ARGUMENT

The return of the people from Babylon is foretold. First, they are commanded to exalt with devoted voices of thanksgiving the benefits that have been bestowed upon them; then the evils that they suffered in captivity [Col. 1022C] are described in varied narrative. Alternatively, this is the voice of Christ concerning the Jews; it is to be read alongside the readings from Numbers and Judges.

### EXPLANATION

In the first alleluia the Jewish people are commended; there is no complaint against them. In the second, he recalls those who, within the same nation, went astray through very frequent offenses and returned to the Lord’s grace through his own mercy. Here, however, the Christian people [Col. 1022D] are admonished to render praise to the Lord for the benefits bestowed upon them.

Alternatively, the first alleluia was concerned with the baptism of believers; the second with reconciling penitents—there, “he received his people with rejoicing, and his chosen ones with gladness.” Here he hears penitents and gives them into mercies in the sight of all who had captured them. In the third, our daily practice is recapitulated, and the Novatian heresy is condemned.

After the confession of the Hebrew people, of whom the preceding psalms have spoken, the Prophet comes to the Christian people, who wandered errantly throughout the expanses of the whole world in the solitude of superstitions. In the first section he admonishes them to confess the praises of the Lord, by whose blood he received the redeemed churches, which had been carried away in foolish error through the altars of demons and the sacred groves.

In the second, he declares that thanks must be rendered to the Lord, who satisfied the souls of the gentiles, famished for the nourishment of truth, with the abundance of his religion, and who broke their bonds of sin by unconquerable power. In the third, he commands thanks to be rendered to the Father, because, when Christ came, he broke the gates and bars of the devil. In the fourth, he admonishes the priests to offer to the Lord a sacrifice of praise—the priests who preside over the governance of the churches amid the waves of the world—and he describes how God also deigns to assist them in their temptations. In the fifth, he again says that the Lord is to be praised by priests and elders, who by a heavenly gift transformed the world, parched by the dryness of sin, into the most delightful joy. Seeing this, the upright in heart rejoiced. [Col. 1023A] These sections begin with similar verses, which are called refrains.

### COMMENTARY

“Confess to the Lord, for he is good.” This psalm commends God’s mercies, repeatedly proven in us, and is therefore sweet to those who have experienced them. It is plainly sung concerning the universal Church, spread throughout the whole world: that is, concerning the two walls meeting in one cornerstone and crying “Abba, Father” elsewhere; hence it bears the title “Alleluia” twice.

And because it commends God’s mercies, let us therefore consider what we are admonished about, what we should rejoice over, what we should lament, from where we should ask for help, from where we are abandoned, from where assistance is given to us, and what we are through ourselves. As if he were saying: By his mercy we exist; let us see how our pride is crushed and how his grace is glorified, so that what the psalm commends may meet each person in himself. Those who have experienced it should approve it, while those who have not experienced it should desire it.

And it begins in this way: “Those who have been redeemed by the Lord”—[Col. 1023B] not redeemed from the hand of Egyptian servitude, not from useless labors and works of clay, not redeemed from that narrow Egypt, since all were redeemed together and their enemies all perished together; but redeemed from the broad Egypt of this world. They are redeemed daily, both collectively and individually, and their enemies are daily drowned in the sea. The Lord did not redeem them from the hand of Pharaoh, but from the hand of the ancient enemy. He redeemed them in such a way that he gathered them not from one place alone but from many regions.

And truly, from the regions, because they came from the rising and the setting of the sun. At the rising of the sun were the Jews, who had received the sun’s light from there through the Law and the Prophets. The gentiles were at its setting, because, having set aside the Creator, they worshiped the creature. He explains “the setting” by saying: “From the north and from the sea.” By the north understand that charity had grown cold in them; by the sea, that the bitterness of persecution was also present in them.

Let such people, I say, who have been redeemed, say to one another: “If you have tasted, confess to the Lord.” For if you have not tasted, you cannot confess. If you have tasted with eagerness, [Col. 1023C] belch forth your confession. And rightly you ought to confess to the Lord, because he is good to all who taste him worthily, and because his mercy is forever, as we said in the preceding psalm.

He says “those who have been redeemed,” because this redemption is not simple but manifold. Therefore the psalm sets forth four temptations, four cries, four deliverances, and four confessions of God’s mercies.

The first redemption is from ignorance, error, and hunger for the word of God. Let us suppose someone seeking nothing good, living his former life in a deceptive security, thinking that nothing exists after this life, which will eventually end, and devoted to the enticements and deadly pleasures of this age. At some point the grace of God inwardly raises such a person as though from sleep; he discovers himself in error and becomes deeply concerned for his salvation. This is the first tribulation and temptation.

Then, as best he can, he knocks and cries out to the Lord, and the Lord delivers him from the darkness of error. He places him on the road leading to [Col. 1023D] the city of habitation—that is, in faith and in reflection upon, or knowledge of, himself—and refreshes him with instruction in the word of God. He rightly owes confession to the Lord.

But once he has been placed on the road and knows what must be done and what must be avoided, he begins to fight against his former habits. Yet because he does not consider from where he ought to take his weapons or whom he ought to have as his helper—for if he presumes upon himself, divine assistance having abandoned him—he may labor greatly but accomplish nothing. This is the second temptation, called the difficulty of doing good.

Then condemnation, deliverance, and confession follow. For when that person recognizes his ineffectiveness, he cries out to the Lord, and the Lord delivers him by breaking the bonds of difficulty and placing him in the practice of righteousness. What was difficult for him becomes easy, and for this he ought to confess to the Lord. The Lord could grant this to us without difficulty, but if we had no difficulty, we would not recognize the author of so great a good.

Likewise, once he has been placed in the ease of doing good, [Col. 1024A] after overcoming the difficulties of his former habits, he is not brought back from that ease into some depraved habit. Rather, he encounters a third temptation: weariness of the divine word—that is, weariness of praying, reading, fasting, keeping vigil, and the other practices by which he might advance toward what is better—and thus he is endangered.

The former fellowship should not make him secure; rather, because of this weariness he should fear that he will die. For just as the body is destroyed by distaste for bodily food, so the soul is endangered by distaste for spiritual food. But again he cries out to the Lord and is delivered; nevertheless, it follows that he must confess.

Behold: the darkness has been illumined, the difficulties of former habits have been overcome, and weariness of the word of God has been driven away. Such people are now fit to be advanced to the governance of the churches, and they are advanced. But the more they are exalted, the more they are endangered, because then a storm arises in the sea, shaking the Church and troubling its governor. Thus they are endangered, at one moment ascending to the heavens by hoping, at another descending [Col. 1024B] to the depths by despairing. Yet they cry out to the Lord and are delivered; therefore they rightly confess.

This is the fourth temptation, called danger in the governance of public affairs. No one should think that this temptation concerns only prelates, because everyone is carried in the ship, both those who work and those who are governed; together they are endangered at sea, and together they will be saved in the harbor.

As we have said, the psalm sets forth these four temptations. The first is where it says: “They wandered in the wilderness.” The connection is as follows: It was necessary that they be gathered from the regions because previously they wandered in the wilderness—not just any wilderness, but a waterless one. He calls the wilderness the desert of ignorance and error; by “waterless” he signifies the uncultivated condition, because they were without water, that is, without the refreshment of instruction.

They could not find by themselves the road to the city of habitation—that is, the road leading to the city in which one truly ought to dwell. For there is a certain city in which one ought not to dwell, but which ought rather to be destroyed, [Col. 1024C] namely Babylon.

They wandered, I say, naturally hungry and thirsty, because every soul naturally hungers for the good. Behold the grave tribulation: while they were in the wilderness and ignorant of the road by which they might come to habitation, they were also hungry and thirsty. Therefore their soul, existing only in them, failed.

But when it extended itself toward the Lord, it made progress. This is what he says: “And they cried out to the Lord when they were in tribulation,” that is, when they had begun to attend to the tribulation of pilgrimage, which no one attends to unless his homeland is dear to him. And because they cried out, therefore the Lord delivered them from their necessities—that is, from the darkness of error and the famine of the word of God.

He did this in the following way: he led them out of their necessities and brought them onto a straight road—that is, into knowledge of himself and the catholic faith—in order that they might go to the city of habitation. Therefore let them worthily confess to the Lord his mercy, not his poverty. And let them confess his wonders displayed to the children of human beings—that is, to the children [Col. 1024D] of the old age. This means: Let those confess to the Lord who, although dead in old age, were made alive by him through newness. This is a great wonder.

And because he had not previously stated the other part of the deliverance, he adds: “Therefore I say that they should confess to the Lord, because he satisfied the empty soul with regard to thirst, and he satisfied the hungry soul with eternal goods.” That is, he removed the famine of the word of God from them.

And—as if he were saying—it was necessary that they be led out and satisfied, because they were sitting in darkness, and not just any darkness, but in the shadow of death: that is, in such darkness as would overshadow them unto death. They were bound in poverty and iron—that is, in harsh poverty. For it is a grievous poverty to hunger and thirst in the wilderness.

Because they embittered. It was not the author’s fault that they were in darkness and poverty, but theirs, because they themselves embittered—that is, made bitter and harsh—the words of God for themselves, at the time when it was said to them: “Eat from every tree of paradise, but do not eat from the tree of the [Col. 1025A] knowledge of good and evil.” In this they provoked him—that is, made void—the counsel of the Most High. His counsel was to raise them through obedience and command to something more worthy; but by transgressing and disobeying, they made that counsel void.

And their heart was humbled. Here he begins the second temptation. As if he were saying: The Lord led them out of the darkness of error and placed them on the road of truth, so that they would know what must be done and what must be avoided. But they presumed upon themselves. Therefore, when they wished to attack their former habits by their own strength, their heart was humbled by labors, because they labored greatly; and they became weak—that is, they proved ineffective in their labors—because there was no one to help them as long as they presumed upon themselves.

And they cried out to the Lord when they were in tribulation. He presents the two deliverances together, because he repeats the earlier one, saying: “And he led them out of the darkness and shadow [Col. 1025B] of death,” as before. Now he also broke their bonds—that is, he broke the bonds of difficulty—and placed them in the practice of righteousness, as was said above. Therefore let them confess to the Lord his mercy and his wonders to the children of human beings, as before.

They ought to confess to him because, while they were so held back that they could not go out to do good—just as elsewhere they were confined behind bronze gates and iron bars so that they could not go out to do anything—the Lord shattered the bronze gates and broke the iron bars. That is, he freed them from every difficulty.

He did this in the following way: he took them from the way of their iniquity, that is, he freed them from presumption, which made them unjust, that is, irreligious. Their iniquity was not the author’s doing, because they were humbled on account of their injustices: they acted unjustly by ascribing to their own strength what belonged to God.

Every food was abhorred. Here is the third temptation. As if he were saying: Although the darkness has now been illumined and the difficulties of former habits overcome, another danger still remains: their soul [Col. 1025C] abhorred every food—not bodily but spiritual food. That is, as was said above, they experienced weariness of the word of the Lord.

Therefore they drew near to the gates of death—that is, to destruction—because just as it is dangerous for the body to loathe bodily food, so it is deadly for the soul to loathe spiritual food. Again they cried out to the Lord when they were in tribulation, and he delivered them from their necessities. That is, in this way he sent the word: he commanded and willed the same thing, namely, that they be healed, and thus he healed them.

The same may be seen in the Gospel: “Lord, say only the word, and my boy will be healed.” And truly he saved them, because he rescued them from their destructions. Therefore let them also confess to the Lord his mercy and his wonders to the children of human beings.

They ought to confess in such a way that they sacrifice a sacrifice of praise—that is, attributing nothing to themselves but everything to God—and announce his works, that is, his manifold labors, not in remembrance alone but in rejoicing.

[Col. 1025D] Those who go down to the sea in ships. Here is the fourth temptation. As if he were saying: Not only those whose souls have fallen into weariness of the word, and the others mentioned above, have experienced God’s mercies; so also have those who, placed in ships—that is, perfected for the governance of the churches—go down upon the sea, that is, are humbled on account of bitter tribulation from without, inner contradiction, and grief for their subjects. They go down, I say, carrying out their work—that is, their governance—in many waters, that is, among many peoples.

They saw the works of the Lord and his wonders: that is, in the deep they came wondrously to know his mercy toward them—in the depth, that is, in the danger of the sea, or into the deep, that is, into the hidden places of the hearts of their subjects. One person secretly harbors adultery, another murder, another one thing, another another. All these matters are reported to those prelates. And if they are then able to govern and to give counsel to each person so that they do not perish, they recognize in this the greatest mercy of God.

[Col. 1026A] “He spoke, and it stood still.” Truly they saw the works of the Lord and his wonders. For they saw them in this way: the Lord spoke, that is, commanded at some time, and the storm-wind stood still, that is, grew fierce; a great tempest arose, and its waves were exceedingly exalted. Before this happens, however, those prelates ascend to the heavens by hoping well concerning their subjects; when the storm stands still, they descend to the depths by despairing. They descend because their soul—that is, the soul of the prelates—was wasting away, that is, failing, amid their evils, namely, amid the pressures caused by their subjects.

Or otherwise: “The Lord spoke,” that is, the Lord commanded, “and it stood still,” that is, the storm became calm; and afterward its waves were again exalted. When the storm stood still, the prelates themselves ascended to the heavens by hoping well; but when the waves were exalted, they descended to the depths by despairing. This happened because their soul was wasting away amid evils, as before.

And he shows how he says, “They were troubled within themselves”: inwardly they were disturbed and moved in order to free themselves, but [Col. 1026B] only “like a drunk man,” that is, they moved uselessly while relying upon themselves, because they were indeed moved but did not advance. This was because all their wisdom—namely, their wisdom for preaching, praying, and reading—was swallowed up, that is, reduced to nothing. Hence the Apostle says:

“We do not want you, brothers, to be unaware of the affliction that came upon us in Asia, because we were weighed down beyond our strength and beyond measure, and we had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we might not be confident in ourselves but in him who raises the dead.”

When he says, “We had within ourselves the sentence of death,” he shows that his wisdom had been swallowed up.

And again these men cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he brought them out of their necessities. Truly he brought them out. For in this way he made their storm—or the depth of the sea—into a gentle breeze, that is, into calm and peacefulness. Again, this is shown by the words, “All its waves were silent.” Then the prelates rejoiced, because the waves were silent; and rightly so, because he led them into the harbor of their desire, that is, into all the tranquility and security [Col. 1026C] they themselves had wished for.

Therefore let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men. And let them confess in such a way that they exalt him alone in the assembly of the people, that is, in the Church of those who are well governed. And let them praise him in the seat of the elders who rule well. This is to say: Let the subjects, because they are well governed, and the prelates, because they govern well, attribute this not to themselves but to the Lord alone, and offer praises to him alone.

“He made rivers into a desert.” As if he said: They ought rightly to praise him, because he resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. First he shows how he resists the proud, saying: “He made rivers”—that is, those among whom flowed the streams of doctrine through the prophetic writings and the institutions of the Law, namely, the Jews—“into a desert.” For although they preserved the writings, they nevertheless lost true understanding. He proves this by adding:

“And the sources of waters”—that is, those same people from whom doctrine went forth to others through the prophetic writings and through the primitive Church taken from them—“he made into thirst,” that is, he left them in their natural thirst. [Col. 1026D]

“A fruitful land.” He repeats the same point through another comparison, meaning: He reduced those who had previously been a fruitful land, at least with regard to certain people, since there were some in that earlier people who ought to be regarded as seed. These, I say, he reduced to saltiness, that is, to bitterness and barrenness, because they did not recognize the time of visitation and did not heed the righteousness of God, but wanted to establish their own righteousness. Although they had earlier believed something concerning him, now none of them believes in him.

Saltiness properly means the earth’s bitter sap, which is accompanied by barrenness. And he says that this did not proceed from the land’s own injustice, but from the wickedness of those dwelling in it. This is to say: By his just judgment the Lord turned that land into saltiness, because the wickedness of those who cling too closely to earthly things brings this about.

“He made a desert into pools.” He shows how he resists the proud and how he gives grace to the humble, [Col. 1027A] saying: He made those who had previously been a desert, deprived of the Law and the Prophets—that is, the Gentiles—into pools of water. For from them, through certain men such as Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, and many others, teachings of truth flowed forth to others.

And there, that is, in that land, he placed hungry and eager farmers. And they established a city for habitation, that is, they built the Catholic Church, which is truly a city of habitation. And they sowed the fields with the seed of God’s word, that is, they made many people fruitful in good works. And they planted vineyards, that is, they established various churches, and they produced the fruit of birth.

The founders and those founded by them did not differ from the apostles in the fruit of birth—that is, in their works and doctrine—for through the apostles’ teaching they were born into good works. And the Lord blessed them and gave them increase. They multiplied to such an extent that certain people were even excessively multiplied, namely, those who, having become heretics through pride, went out from us. Of them the Apostle says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would not have gone out from us.”

And although some were excessively multiplied, nevertheless [Col. 1027B] “he did not diminish their cattle,” because none of those who were cattle—that is, not greatly learned but nevertheless full of faith, namely, the simple—went out.

“And they became few.” Some, I say, were excessively multiplied, and therefore they became few, whether with respect to the earlier number, as those who remained; or with respect to those who went out, since not as many went out as remained. And this was because nothing contributes more to the diminution of gifts than what is owed to destruction.

“And others were afflicted,” that is, those who remained were afflicted by the trouble caused by the wicked: tribulations were inflicted by the evil who went out through their malicious questions. They were also afflicted “by sorrow,” that is, because of the compassion they had for the other person who was suffering with them.

“Contention was poured out.” He shows how they were afflicted by sorrow: namely, because through the perverse doctrine of those who went out, contention was poured out upon their rulers who remained. [Col. 1027C] This means that even their truthful teachers were despised, or were regarded as contemptible, because of those false teachers who had gone out.

And therefore the Lord made them—that is, those who went out—wander in a trackless place. Those of whom we heard above were led into the way and directed to the city of habitation; but these were not led, rather they were led astray, that is, abandoned to themselves, because God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, so that they might do what is unfitting. Thus they wandered in a trackless place, and some of them never again returned to the way.

And the Lord helped the poor man, that is, his humble people remaining within, out of poverty, that is, out of the smallness of that number which some of those who went out had caused. For those who went out, through their perverse questions and contradictions, became for the others an occasion for exercising inquiry and an example of fear. The more one answers heretics, the greater the correction made among Catholics. Hence the Apostle also says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest.” [Col. 1027D]

Or otherwise: “Contention was poured out.” As if he said: They became few in this way, because there were certain people who wanted to make themselves rulers, that is, teachers of error. Among them that contention was poured out of which the Apostle says: “If anyone proclaims to you something other than what you received, even if it is an angel from heaven, let him be accursed.” This means: You who remain within became few because the proud were excluded.

And them—that is, the proud—he made to wander in a trackless place, and not in the way, as before. But he helped the poor man, that is, his humble people, out of poverty, that is, out of simplicity of understanding. For the fact that they understood not in many ways but simply was a help to them, so that they would not go out but remain within.

And he placed his families—one from circumcision and the other from uncircumcision—in such subjection to him as sheep are to a shepherd. As he himself says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them.”

“The upright will see.” I say that he placed the families like sheep. [Col. 1028A] In this way he placed them, and will place them, in such great subjection that all those who have now gone out will close, that is, shut, their mouths. For that man is truly wise, since they will dare to contradict nothing further. And every wise person ought to heed all these things that have been foretold.

Who, then, is truly wise? I say “who” because the one who is truly wise will keep, that is, observe, all these things foretold through humility. And he will understand that the Lord’s mercies are present in all these events: that he led the one who was wandering and hungry into the way and fed him; that he released and freed the one fighting against the difficulty of his sins and bound by the chains of habit; that he restored the one who was disgusted with the Word of God and almost dying from weariness by sending the medicine of his Word; that he led the one in danger amid shipwreck and perilous crises to the harbor after calming the sea; that in that people, where he resists the proud but gives grace to the humble, he caused this to be so; and that he willed one who remained to multiply, not one who went outside to be diminished.

# ON PSALM 107

*A Song, a Psalm of David.*

## Argument

It is sung under the persona of the Maccabees, and contains prayers of rejoicing over victory against enemies. It may also be understood of David himself, since he ruled over many nations. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church concerning elevation.

## Explanation

A song refers to the contemplation of divine things; a psalm refers to active works, provided that they accord with the divine commandments. He himself attests this in the first verse: “I will sing and make a psalm to the Lord.”

David signifies the King Christ, who will speak in this psalm. Throughout the psalm the Lord speaks. First, he gives thanks to the Father because, after the triumph of his Passion, he rose perpetually into glory. [Col. 1028C] Second, he humbles himself through his humanity, while nevertheless also displaying the power of his own majesty, so that you may recognize that the two natures truly exist in the one person of the Lord Christ.

It should be noted that Psalm 107 is composed from the concluding portions of two psalms. In it the Lord, through his Passion and Resurrection, joined two peoples to himself in one faith, made them fruitful by the one grace of the Spirit, and exalted them by the same gift of eternal life. The number one hundred signifies the life that is at the right hand; the number seven signifies the Holy Spirit. These are fittingly joined together in this psalm after being made one from two, because only spiritual people are deemed worthy to receive eternal life.

## Commentary

“My heart is ready, O God.” The song of the psalm—that is, this exultation of action, or this exultant action—is attributed to David, that is, to the Head, because our Head speaks in this psalm about the glory of his Resurrection and Ascension. Hence all who have been called to hope for that same glory ought rightly to rejoice.

He sets before us an example of obedience, exhorting us to practice the same obedience that he himself practiced, and thus to attain the same glory. It is as if he said: O God the Father, foolish people think that I sacrifice to you unwillingly and as though compelled; but I will sacrifice to you willingly, because my heart is ready in me, and my heart is ready to fulfill obedience in my members.

Or, if we choose the better interpretation, let us refer both meanings to him, and understand it thus: “My heart is ready to fulfill obedience in action. My heart is also ready in every intention.” This is because I, who earlier seemed to weep in my weakness, once placed in my glory—that is, in the glory of Resurrection and Ascension—will sing with my mouth and make melody through my work. For I will give others hope in me of that same glory, and thus I will make them sing with their mouths and make melody through their works.

It should be known that almost this entire psalm is gathered from certain preceding psalms. Blessed Augustine says that he finds no other reason why it has been repeated except that it pleased the Holy Spirit to do so. Therefore no one should wonder if the individual points are not investigated here with equal care, since they have already been fully explained above in their proper places. [Col. 1029A]

“Awake, psaltery and lyre; I will rise at dawn.” The flesh of Christ is called a lyre because of its experience of weakness and death; the psaltery is so called because of heavenly works. It is as if he said: In order that I may sing and make melody in glory—that is, in order that my flesh may do so—die and rise, so that you may be a psaltery. I therefore say, “Rise,” because you are a lyre.

Although the flesh of Christ was previously also a psaltery, it became a psaltery especially through the glory of the Resurrection and Ascension. And truly, he says as if, “you will rise,” because I will rise at dawn, when the Resurrection has taken place. Thus, Lord Father, I will confess you among the Jewish peoples, and I will make melody to you among the nations of the Gentiles.

I will confess you among the former and make melody among the latter because I, who am to be called not only your merciful one, will be great above [Col. 1029B] the heavens—that is, I will be magnified above all those who are heavens—because none of them had the power to lay down his soul and take it up again. And the truth of your commandments, given through me, will be magnified even to the establishment of the clouds.

And because I will thus be magnified, therefore, O God the Word personally united to me, exalt yourself above the heavens, with me the man exalted. And let your glory—that is, the flesh taken by you, which was previously your disgrace but through the Resurrection and Ascension became your glory—be exalted above the whole earth, that is, let it now be glorified throughout the earth, so that your beloved may be delivered from the fear of death through hope of the Resurrection.

And in order that this may happen, save me, Lord Father, by your right hand, that is, through your confession; and in this hear me.

Then he turns toward us. It is as if he said: You truly save by your right hand, because God the Father spoke in his holy one, that is, promised this in his holiness. And therefore I will truly be exalted through Resurrection and Ascension.

“And I will divide Shechem.” Or otherwise: God, who previously spoke in his servants, appeared to the world and spoke in me, his holy one; and therefore I will truly rejoice, as before.

Or otherwise: God the Father spoke in his holy ones, that is, he promised through me, his holy one, this very thing: that I would rejoice in the glory of Resurrection and Ascension, “and I will divide Shechem,” and so forth. What follows from there—“O God, who have rejected us”—you will find explained fully above. [Col. 1029C]

# ON PSALM 108

*To the end. A Psalm of David.*

## Argument

It is sung under the persona of the Maccabees, who lamented the adversities they suffered from outsiders and from their own people and sought vengeance against those who, through false accusation, inflamed the kings Antiochus or Demetrius against them, and who made the dignity of the priesthood a matter of sale. This was done not only after Onias had been excluded, but throughout the entire subsequent period during which Judaea was liberated by the Maccabees’ warfare.

Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ [Col. 1029D] to the Father concerning the Jews.

## Explanation

This familiar title refers the psalm to the Lord Christ. In the first part the Lord rebukes the Jews, who preferred to repay evil for good to their Creator. In the second, the wickedness of Judas the betrayer and of the faithless people is recounted, together with what was to come upon them for so great a crime. In the third, he prays that, having been delivered from the danger of the Passion, he may quickly attain the glory of the Resurrection.

## Commentary

“God, do not be silent about my praise, because the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful man have been opened against me.” These words refer “to the end,” that is, to Christ; the psalm is attributed to David himself. In this psalm our Head commends to us his Passion, so that he may also commend the Resurrection—that is, the reward and glory of the Passion—because “if we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him.”

[Col. 1030A]

It is as if he said: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready.” Therefore, God the Father, do not be silent about my praise; rather, make me glorious and worthy of praise through the Resurrection and Ascension. You, I say, must not be silent about my praise, because, as if he said, my enemies do not keep silent about my dishonor.

For “the mouth of the sinner has been opened against me,” that is, against me to condemn and devour me. That transgressing people was the sinner, concerning whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “If they believed Moses, they would certainly believe me also, because he wrote about me.” And the mouth of the deceitful people was opened because not only the Jews but also the Roman soldiers, who were Gentiles, consented to his death.

But why does he call it deceitful? He supplies the reason, saying:

“They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue,” that is, with a deceitful tongue for my condemnation, calling me “Teacher” and using similar expressions. And truly it was a deceitful tongue, because afterward they surrounded me with words of hatred, crying: “Crucify him, crucify him.”

“And attacking me, they overcame me by their opinion,” or with regard to my outward appearance; yet they hated me without cause. Truly without cause, because they slandered me for what I had deserved to have them love me. I had raised their dead, healed their sick, and given sight to their blind. Although they ought to have loved me for these things, they instead slandered me, saying: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath,” and similar things.

But I, on the contrary, prayed for them, saying: “Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing.” And as the most significant kind of repayment, they “placed”—that is, firmly established—evil against me in return for good, in their action, and hatred for my love in their affection.

“But you, Lord, repay them what they deserve.” This he says correspondingly, not by cursing but by prophesying and rejoicing in the divine judgment, as follows:

“Since that people refused to be subjected to me, therefore, Lord, appoint a sinner”—that is, the father of all sin, the devil—“over it.” And do this to such an extent that the devil stands at its right hand, that is, that the devil’s works have greater power over it than yours, so that it may be judged both here and thereafter.

This is what he says: “When he is judged here through inward blindness, let him also go forth condemned at last,” that is, let his end be eternal condemnation. “And let his prayer become sin.” For every prayer that is not made through our Mediator, the Lord Jesus Christ, does not cleanse sin but increases it. Therefore he says: “Let his prayer become sin.”

“And let his days”—that is, the days of his kingdom and priesthood, which he promises himself will be prolonged through my death—“become few” through that same death. This truly happened, because in the forty-second year they were utterly destroyed by the Roman rulers.

“And let another receive his bishopric”—that is, his priesthood, namely, the order of Melchizedek, which had been promised to him through the priest Aaron. Let another, namely a Gentile, receive it instead.

“And let his sons”—that is, his successors—“become orphans.” Truly he is an orphan who, deprived of God the Father, submits himself to the devil as father.

“And let his wife become a widow.” You may understand the wife of that people as the subjected populace or the city itself, in which they delighted as in a wife. The populace indeed became widowed, because it was left without any government; and so did the city, because it was deserted by them. Therefore he says: “Let his wife be a widow.”

“And let his sons be transferred from place to place,” wavering throughout the whole world, that is, having no fixed dwelling. “And let them beg everywhere,” that is, let them need the help of others. “And let them be driven from their dwellings,” that is, from their own places; or let them be driven from the stability of their hearts through the smoke of an evil conscience.

“And let the moneylender”—that is, the devil, who makes a person fall into some serious sin so that afterward he may hurl him into another and then another, and for this reason is called a moneylender—“search out all his substance,” that is, every sin of that people by which it believes it can sustain itself. Let him search it out so that he leaves none unpunished.

For when they said, “If we let him go on like this, the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation,” their sin is therefore called their substance. “And let foreigners plunder his labors.” For they are still circumcised and observe the other legal practices. But evil spirits [Col. 1031A] plunder these things, because they render them ineffective and useless; and since they are rightly enemies, they are called foreigners.

Or the entire verse may be understood only as a comparison. Thus, let the moneylender—that is, Titus or Vespasian, comparable to a moneylender who searches out and takes away all the debtor’s household goods when he is unable to repay the loan—search out all the substance of that people. Let foreigners—that is, their soldiers—plunder his labors, so that nothing remains to him.

And because they did not want me as their helper, let there be no helper for him, neither king nor priest; and let there be no one who pities his orphans, that is, his descendants deprived by you, the true God.

“Let his descendants be made for destruction,” that is, let all his posterity be such as seem to have been born not in order to live but in order to perish eternally. “And let his name”—that is, his memory—“be erased in one generation,” that is, only in the carnal generation, and never let it come to the spiritual generation.

“And let the iniquity”—that is, the murmuring and stubbornness—“of his fathers return to memory,” that is, let it not be handed over to oblivion [Col. 1031B] but remain before the Lord. “And let the sin of his mother”—that is, of the Synagogue—“not be erased from the Lord’s memory.”

This means: Let not only their own sins be repaid to them, but also the evil merits of their parents, whose wickedness they imitate. For it was truly said through the prophet: “I will visit the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation.”

And in order that this may happen, “let the iniquity of his fathers and of his mother be against the Lord,” so that it is not forgotten but always seen by him, “and let their memory perish utterly from the land of the living.”

I rightly say this on account of the fact that he did not remember to show mercy to himself, according to Solomon’s saying: “Have mercy on your soul, and you will be pleasing to God.”

He shows in what respect he did not remember this, saying: “And he pursued me, a man made poor and a beggar on his account.” And he pursued not only me but also my people, wishing to put to death every person who was contrite in heart, such as the holy apostles and also all those who came to the apostles and said: “What shall we do, men and brothers?” and so forth.

In this too he did not remember to show mercy to himself: he loved the curse, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” And because he loved it, it will come upon him. He did not desire blessing, because he scorned being blessed in the one in whom all nations will be blessed. Therefore blessing will be removed far from him—and deservedly so—because he put on the curse like a garment outwardly when he said, “His blood be upon us,” and so forth.

It also entered his inward parts like water and was like oil in his bones. Water drenches, and oil makes the face joyful. In the same way that curse somehow softened them, because it pleased them and made their heart, as it were, joyful. He rightly says “like oil in the bones,” because the more someone delights in sin, the stronger he becomes in sinning.

“Let it be to him like a garment.” As if he said: Since he devoted himself so greatly to the curse, let the curse therefore be to him like a garment, covering him completely, both outwardly and inwardly. There is a kind of garment that does not cover the whole body but only part of it; therefore it is not superfluous that he adds, “with which he is covered.”

“And let it be to him like a belt with which he is always girded,” that is, let this sin be for him like equipment for committing further sins, so that “the filthy may become filthier still.”

This, he says, is not a wish of ill will but a just repayment of them, because this is their work: their wicked action deserves this. They slander me before the Lord, that is, insofar as it lies within them, by their lies they strip me of the divinity by which I am equal to the Lord Father, saying: “This man is not from God,” and similar things.

Moreover, they speak many evil things against my soul, saying: “This man said, ‘I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days,’” and: “We found this man subverting our nation and forbidding the payment of tribute to Caesar,” and many such things.

And because they intend my condemnation, therefore, Lord Father—I call you Lord, as if to say, “you who alone are truly Lord”—[Col. 1032A] “act with me,” that is, cooperate with me in my Resurrection, not on account of my merit but on account of your name, which is to be glorified through me.

He himself raised himself according to the Word, and the Father raised him. Therefore, as if he said: I ask you to act with me, because your mercy—that is, the Resurrection accomplished through your mercy—is sweet to me according to my humanity.

Or otherwise: “You, Lord, act with me,” that is, help me to complete obedience for the sake of your name, not on account of my merit. This is because your mercy, that is, your help, is sweet to me.

Therefore deliver me by raising me, or by giving me steadfastness, because I am needy and poor in myself, that is, I regard myself as needy and poor. And since my heart has been troubled by the sadness of the Passion, this is within me, that is, of my own will and not by compulsion. Hence elsewhere: “I will sacrifice to you willingly,” and so forth.

Or otherwise: “My heart has been troubled,” not on my own account but because I take upon myself the weakness of those who are within me, that is, who are only in my body. [Col. 1032B]

This may also be referred to the members, as follows: “Deliver me”—that is, my people—from those who devour them, which you ought to do because I am needy and poor in my members. And if at any time my heart has been troubled in my members, whether by fear of death or through the natural movement of anger, that disturbance is only within me, that is, in the heart of my members; it does not also break out into any action. Hence elsewhere: “Be angry, and do not sin.”

“Like a shadow when it declines, I have been taken away.” I say, “Deliver me,” and it is necessary that you deliver me, because I have already been taken away from this life, as far as the will of my enemies is concerned; and in myself and in my members I have been taken away as a shadow is when it declines.

For when the sun is setting and the shadow declines, night comes; and when life declines, death comes. Therefore he says, “I have been taken away,” as a day is taken away when the shadow declines.

“And I have been shaken out,” either from this life or from the hearts of my members, “becoming like a locust,” that is, unstable.

“My knees have become weak from fasting, and my flesh has been changed because of the oil.” Truly I have been shaken out of the hearts of my members, because my knees—that is, those who were like a knot and joint, the firm support in my body, namely the apostles—became weak from fasting, that is, because of my absence. I was taken away from them through death, though previously they had refreshed themselves in me.

Or those became weak who said: “We had thought that he was the one who would redeem Israel.” But what of this? Those knees will be changed from sadness into joy because of the oil, that is, because of the gladness of the Resurrection.

And truly the knees will be changed, because the flesh also—that is, the weaker members of my body—will be changed on account of that oil.

The oil may also be understood as the gladness of the Holy Spirit, who was sent upon the apostles on the fiftieth day after the Resurrection; the rest of the meaning remains unchanged.

Or otherwise, by way of comparison, it may be understood as follows: “My knees have become weak from fasting,” that is, I and my people have become comparable to those whose knees fail because of fasting, since we could not find anything in which to refresh ourselves. For he scarcely found the thief hanging beside him, in whom he might refresh himself, [Col. 1032D] and that centurion who, seeing the earthquake and the signs he performed, exclaimed: “Truly this was the Son of God.”

“My knees, I say, have become weak from fasting, and my flesh has been changed,” that is, given over to death because the oil was withdrawn, that is, because I did not find others who might gladden me.

“And I have become.” Continue this in either interpretation: Since my knees have become weak, I have therefore become a reproach to them. They saw me only outwardly, that is, they considered in me only weakness and not divinity. Therefore they shook their heads in contempt of me, saying: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God,” and similar things.

Therefore, Lord God the Father—that is, the one whom I make my God, and I am not God to myself, as Adam wanted to be god to himself—help me in completing obedience, and save me by raising me, not on account of merit but according to your mercy.

And therefore I say, “Save me,” [Col. 1033A] so that the enemies may know that this event, namely my Passion, is your hand and not their hand, that is, that it proceeds from your power and disposition and not from their power.

And truly it is your hand, because you, Lord, made it, that is, permitted it—namely, my Passion and tribulation. Hence elsewhere: “You would have no power against me at all unless it had been given you from above.”

Or otherwise: “Let them know,” that is, let the enemies at last experience what they now refuse to recognize: that this hand—that is, that I—am your hand, through whom you have worked all things from the beginning and before the ages. Yet you, Lord, made this hand, that is, made me according to my humanity.

Or otherwise: “Let the enemies know,” that is, recognize, “that this event,” namely my Passion, “is your hand,” that is, your great power, because you, Lord, made it by your permission for my great glorification.

“They will curse him.” Truly you made it, not they, because they will curse me by casting me down, while you, on the contrary, will bless me by exalting me. And because they will curse, let those who rise up against me be put to shame, whether with a good or an evil shame.

But “your servant”—that is, I—will not merely, as a wish, rejoice; rather, with complete certainty I say that he will rejoice through the Resurrection. [Col. 1033B]

“Let them put on.” As if he said: Let them be so put to shame that they put on shame, that is, that they experience the greatest humiliation from it, whether for good or for evil—those who slander me, not only outwardly but also inwardly; or not only before human beings but before God as well.

This is what he says: “Let them be covered with their own shame as with a double cloak.” *Diplois* is a double garment, and therefore by the double cloak both kinds of shame are rightly signified.

But I do not merely say, “I confess”; rather, it is certain that “I will confess to the Lord with my mouth,” offering him calves, namely the calves of my lips. And I will confess to him greatly, that is, exceedingly—not only with my voice but also through my work.

“And I will praise him in the midst of many,” that is, among many, namely in the Catholic Church; or “in the midst,” that is, in the hearts of many.

And rightly I will confess to him, as if he said, because he stood at the right hand of the poor man, that is, of me. This means that he made me choose what is better, namely himself, so that, by delivering my soul and the souls of my people from their persecutors, he might save them, lest either I or my people be overcome by them.

# ON PSALM 109

*A Psalm of David.*

## Argument

It is sung concerning the Lord Christ, as he himself explains to the Pharisees. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church concerning the Father and the Son.

## Explanation

This psalm sings briefly and most fully of the Lord’s Incarnation and of his divinity. In the first verse the prophet reports what the Father said to the Son, displaying at once the nature of his divinity and humanity. In the second division the Father indicates something of his divine nature according to the measure of our capacity. In the third the prophet speaks again, to the end, once more displaying the form of his humanity.

## Commentary

[Col. 1033D]

The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand.” A psalm attributed to David himself, that is, to the prophet. The prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit, foresees in a certain secret chamber of God’s mysteries—by the Spirit presiding within and illuminating him inwardly—the hidden plan of God the Father concerning the incarnation of his Word, his kingdom, and his priesthood. What he foresees secretly, he foretells openly; what was hidden, he prophesies with great confidence. He did this for the correction and instruction of that people whom he foresaw would be of such hardened heart and stubborn neck that it would oppose his kingdom and contradict his priesthood.

And he begins thus: The Lord God the Father said to the Lord, his Son, according to his divinity; but to my Son and Lord according to his humanity—for to him was given the name that is above every name. Therefore he is truly Lord of all also according to his humanity. To this Lord, I say, thus acting, “my heart is prepared,” and “do not withhold my praise.”

The Lord the Father said this: “I am the beginning”—the whole, that is, “you and I are the beginning,” though not because there are two beginnings, just as there are not two gods; for those whose power is the same have the same essence. It is as though he said: “I am the beginning with you, not in the obscurity of your weakness, but in the day, that is, in the brightness of your power”—that is, of your divinity—for according to his divinity he is one with the Father.

It is as though he himself testified, saying: “He who sent me is with me, and he has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him.” And again: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” and many similar statements. “I am also the beginning in the splendors of the saints,” that is, in the Holy Spirit, who is therefore called the splendor of the saints because he makes the saints radiant. He ought to have said, “in the splendor of the saints,” but, because of the various gifts of the Holy Spirit, he uses the plural, “in the splendors.” Hence it is also said elsewhere: “All these things are effected by one and the same Spirit.”

And since there was no doubt concerning the Spirit’s quality, but because of the humanity assumed by the Son there could be doubt concerning him, he proves this only of the Son. It is as though he said: “Truly I am the beginning with you: for I begot you from the womb,” that is, from my innermost substance, in which I am hidden and am whatever I am—not that God has a womb, but this is said only by way of likeness. “And I begot you before the morning star,” that is, so that you would be more excellent than every creature, indeed more excellent than that chief angel. When I had made him a morning star, he made himself a deadly star through his pride.

Or, “I begot you before the morning star,” that is, before all time, so that by the more excellent part, namely, the morning star, we may understand all the stars; and by the stars, time—for, as pagan and Catholic authors say, they were created to serve as signs and for seasons, days, and years. And if he begot him before time, then he must have begotten him eternally.

Therefore that begetting is rightly ineffable, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “Who shall declare his generation?”

It is as though he said: “And because I begot you from the womb, therefore, in return for your proven warfare and humbly completed obedience, sit at my right hand”—that is, receive me from labor into equality with me.

Observe, however, that he also says “sit” by way of command. We do not command anyone except an inferior; and sitting, standing, and similar positions belong only to bodily things. Therefore, with respect to his humanity alone, he says: “Sit at my right hand.” He sits both in what is exalted and in what is hidden. He is exalted so that he may rule; he is hidden so that he may be believed in, and so that the justice may be accomplished of which it is said: “The righteous person lives by faith.” Elsewhere it is said of this justice: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning justice, and concerning judgment”: concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning justice, because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me.

For this is true justice: that now we believe in the one whom we do not see. The reward of this justice, once our hearts have been cleansed by faith, is that at last we shall see the one in whom, though now unseen, we believe.

### Until I place

“Sit,” I say, “at my right hand,” hidden and immovable, until you come openly—not to be judged, but to judge; and until I place your enemies as the footstool of your feet,” that is, until I subject your enemies to you.

He calls all sinners whom he finds “enemies,” whether they later become friends from being enemies or remain in enmity, because all, even if secretly, are always subject to him. When he comes to judge, they will then be openly placed beneath his feet.

Some will have there a place of punishment, while others will have a place of mercy: those who humbly fulfill obedience in imitation of him; and those who oppose his kingdom and contradict his priesthood will occupy the place of punishment.

### The rod of your strength

He turns to the Son himself, as though saying: “This, I say, God the Father promised you, and he will truly fulfill it, because the Lord will send forth among all nations the rod of your strength”—that is, the rule of your power—so that you may rule them with an iron rod, that is, with the flexible authority of justice. Hence the Apostle Peter says: “Whom heaven must receive until the times of the nations are fulfilled.”

This was said in correspondence with the words, “Until I place your enemies as the footstool of your feet.” Elsewhere it is said: “Beginning from Zion,” that is, from the Jewish people, as the Apostle says: “For repentance and the forgiveness of sins must be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.”

To this end, I say, the Father will send forth the rod of your strength, so that he may rule in the midst of your enemies. Let it therefore be done—that is, let him rule; let dominion be yours, or obtain dominion in the midst of your enemies, that is, among your enemies, or in their hearts.

### The Lord has sworn and will not repent

It is as though he said: “The Lord God the Father spoke the foregoing concerning your kingdom. But what did he say concerning your priesthood? He certainly swore, and he will not repent: ‘You are a priest forever,’ and so forth.”

The preceding sequence may indeed be read in this order: The Lord God the Father said to his Son, according to his divinity—and to my Son and Lord, according to his humanity, in return for this proven justice and humbly completed obedience: “Sit at my right hand, hidden and immovable, until I place your enemies as the footstool of your feet,” as above. And truly he will fulfill what he said, because the Lord will send forth the rod of your strength, beginning from Zion, as stated earlier.

### With you is the beginning

The passage continues thus: “I rightly say to you, ‘Sit at my right hand,’ because I am the beginning with you,” as above. And this is as though he said: “Although you did not appear in the night of your weakness”—that is, when he was handed over for us, suffered, and was buried—“you will appear in that day when your power is revealed,” namely, when he comes in the majesty of the Father and of the holy angels, and in the splendors of the saints”—that is, when the saints will shine like the sun.

Hence it is said elsewhere: “The righteous will shine like the sun,” and so forth.

The prophet’s voice follows: “I, David, begot you, but solely from the Virgin’s womb, without any marital union”—something that applies to no one else. Others beget from the womb, but not without conjugal union. “And I begot you before the morning star,” that is, before every creature, as above; or “before the morning star,” that is, before the day. For Christ was born at night, and he came to remove the night.

He rightly said, “I begot you.” For if David begot Jesse, Jesse begot Mary, and Mary Christ, then David too begot Christ.

### The Lord has sworn

It is as though he said: “I begot you, I say, so that you might be a priest forever, as indeed you will be, because the Lord God the Father swore”—that is, firmly established—and in such a way that he will not repent, that is, will not alter this.

What, I ask, did he swear? This, namely: “You are a priest, not according to the order of Aaron,” whose priesthood was temporary, “but according to the order of Melchizedek,” which is eternal.

Melchizedek was the first to offer bread and wine to the Lord. Christ exercised this priesthood when he offered himself to God the Father on the altar of the cross for us, becoming both the true priest and the true sacrifice. His life is the bread by which we are refreshed. Hence it is said elsewhere: “For my flesh is truly food.” His passion is that cup of which it is said: “How splendid is the Lord’s inebriating cup!”

The Church offers this bread and this wine daily, imitating the humility of his life and his passion. Therefore he is a priest forever.

It must be understood, however, that when God is said to repent, this is said only by way of likeness. There is no repentance in God, since wrongdoing cannot befall him, and repentance follows wrongdoing. But when we sin grievously, God appears to have determined that we should die eternally. In fact, he would do so if we persisted. But if we repent of our guilt, God repents of the punishment—not because he had determined that we should die, for if he had determined it, it would be so, but because this seemed to follow from our sin.

### The Lord is at your right hand

The prophet turns to the Lord God the Father. It is as though he said: “Truly, Lord, you will accomplish what you have determined, because the Lord your Son according to his divinity, but my Son and God according to his humanity, to whom you said, ‘Sit at my right hand,’ and so forth, is ‘the beginning with you in the day of your power.’ And concerning his priesthood you have sworn.”

That Lord, I say, being at your right hand, “has broken kings”—that is, he will break all the proud—if not in the night of his wrath, when he secretly blinds them inwardly, at least he will crush them in the day of his wrath, that is, at last, when his anger has been revealed. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.”

Meanwhile, what does he do? He will judge—that is, he will exercise hidden judgment among all nations—because he will fill the ruins, that is, those who attend to their own ruin and fulfill humility. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Every valley shall be exalted.”

Or otherwise: “He will fill the ruins of sinners,” namely by making the one who is filthy become filthier still.

“And he will crush”—that is, break—“the heads,” that is, the stubbornnesses, of many in this land, some for evil and others for good.

And therefore, as though he said: “At last they will judge, and now he will exalt his head”—that is, the Father has given all judgment to the Son, because he is the Son of Man. And he exalted his head because he became obedient to the Father.

This is what he says: “Because he drank from the torrent on the way.” The torrent is the flow of our mortality. The Word of God the Father drank from this torrent when, by being born, dying, and suffering, he came into this life. But he drank from it only “on the way,” that is, in passing through it, because he was free from every sin. We, however, drink from it while lingering here, because we take pleasure in the desire of the flesh.

## PSALM CX. Alleluia

### Argument

David gives thanks for the benefits conferred upon the people, especially for the release from Babylonian captivity. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church concerning Christ, with praise.

### Explanation

His people praise the Lord, having been liberated from the ruin of the world and no longer knowing how to endure slavery to vices.

This psalm is the first among the Hebrews to proceed through the alphabet in its entirety, although many think that others too were composed according to the order of the letters. In those psalms, however, some letters are missing or additional letters occur; and sometimes one verse is short while another is extended to infinite length. I therefore think that this resulted from the practice of the readers rather than from the care of the writer. Finally, the Seventy translators, because some difficulty arose for them in these matters, did not wish to place the Hebrew letters in the transmitted text.

The people of the blessed are gathered from the various regions of the world. At the beginning of the psalm, he says that he will confess to God in the assembly of the righteous, where there is eternal praise and proclamation without end. Secondly, he says that the faithful, satisfied with an abundant gift, await the coming of the Lord, so that they may seek the promised inheritance with the greatest eagerness. Thirdly, he asserts that Christians have been redeemed and that the new covenant has been consecrated by eternal grace.

The first part contains six letters, the second ten, and the third six. Just as children are instructed through letters so that they may advance toward wisdom, so psalms of this kind are given to the unlearned and beginners, so that their beginnings may be instructed, as it were, by certain elementary principles.

### Commentary

### I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart. Alleluia

Those days that we spend in sorrow and affliction of the flesh, counted as four times ten, before the joy of the resurrection, signify the present life. In it we ought to restrain our carnal pleasure, as it were with the reins of fasting and of every good action, weighed down and groaning, and desiring to put on over ourselves our dwelling that is from above.

Those days, however, during which the song of joy, that is, “Alleluia,” is repeated until the fiftieth day, on which we received the spirit of freedom rather than of fear, in which we cry, “Abba, Father,” signify the jubilee year—that is, the year of true remission and freedom. We already possess it in hope, though not yet in reality, through the hope of the Lord’s resurrection. For we have been saved in hope, awaiting the redemption of our body.

With this period in view, the people of Christ, whose breast is full of joy, pour forth praise to God, because here the body of Christ speaks, already liberated in hope of his resurrection from all evils and separated from wicked people—not yet locally, but morally—saying:

“O Lord, I will confess to you with my whole heart,” that is, “I will praise you here in hope, and at last in reality, in every corner of my heart.”

“I have been placed in the counsel of the righteous,” that is, of the apostles and other saints, so that I may not seek what is mine but what belongs to Jesus Christ. This is the counsel of the righteous. And because I am here in their counsel, I shall therefore be in their assembly, that is, at last I shall be gathered together with them. Whoever is not here in their counsel will not at last be in their fellowship.

### Great are the works of the Lord
