It is as though he said: “That I will confess to the Lord I do not have from myself, but from him, because the works of the Lord in me are great.” I call them “exquisite,” that is, perfect. For refined gold is called perfect gold.

And they are perfect because they proceed toward all his wills, that is, because they oppose him in nothing. And if someone were to ask what those works are, lest anyone presume upon his own works: “The confession of sins is his work in me,” that is, the fact that I confess my sins is not one of my merits; rather, he himself works it in me.

And “magnificence” is also his work in me. Confession is the condemnation of sin; magnificence is the justification of the sinner. For what is more magnificent than to make the just from the sinner, the chosen from the condemned?

And here, as though he said, magnificence is not temporary but everlasting, because “his justice”—that is, his justification—“endures forever and ever.” [The following sentence is textually defective:] That justice itself is eternal, because it ends with the human being; but the reward of justice—because, as though he said, through this he works justice in me—...

For he is the Lord who is merciful in effecting, compassionate in displaying. He “has made a memorial of his wonders,” that is, of the signs performed in the wilderness. In the wilderness he rained manna from heaven, brought water forth from the rock, and did many other such things. He made a memorial of these signs through their signified meanings, because every signified reality is a memorial of its sign.

And he shows how he says this: “He gave food to those who fear him.” For he sent the living bread from heaven, which is the true nourishment of all who fear him with chaste fear; the manna signified this bread.

Alternatively, the preceding verse may be read in this way:

### Great are the works of the Lord

It is as though he said: “I will rightly confess to the Lord, because the works of the Lord are great”—namely, because mercy abandons no one who confesses, and no one’s iniquity will remain unpunished, since he does not even spare the sons whom he receives.

Let a person therefore choose what he wishes. For the works of the Lord have not been established in such a way that a creature, established in the free will of the Creator, can overcome his will by acting contrary to it. God does not will that you sin; indeed, he forbids it.

But if a person sins, do not suppose that the person has done what he wished and that what God did not wish has happened to God. For just as God wills that you not sin, so he wills to spare the one who confesses, so that he may be converted and live. Finally, he wills to punish the one who persists in sins, lest the rebellious person escape the power of justice.

Whatever, therefore, you choose, the Almighty will not lack the means by which to fulfill his will concerning you. And therefore he says: “The works of the Lord are great.” If they are “exquisite,” that is, carefully considered, they will be seen to tend toward the fulfillment of all his wills, whether of sparing or of punishing.

### Confession and magnificence

It is as though he said: “The works of the Lord are truly great because confession and magnificence”—that is, the condemnation of sin and the justification of the sinner—“are his work in those whom he rewards.”

And his justice—that is, the fact that he is just—is displayed in those whom he condemns, so that punishment does not now abandon anyone who confesses. This justice, I say, endures forever and ever, because it never spares iniquity unless you yourself spare it. For whatever you punish, that alone he does not punish.

### He has made a memorial

According to this interpretation, the passage is joined to the first verse in the following manner: “Therefore I will rightly confess to the Lord, because the Lord, merciful and compassionate, has made a memorial of his wonders,” as stated above.

### He will remember

“He gave food,” I say, “to those who fear him”; and through this memorial “he will remember his covenant,” that is, he confirmed his promises—not promises that were temporary, but those that are eternal; not carnal promises, but spiritual ones.

He uses *saeculum* for “eternity” because of the Greek word αἰών (*aiōn*), as stated above.

And he will truly remember, that is, he will announce or reveal to his people—the primordial people of grace—what he caused the holy apostles to understand: “the power of his works,” that is, the force and meaning of his sacraments.

For a sacrament is the sign of a sacred reality. The manna was a sacrament because it was a sign of the true bread that descended from heaven. The Lord will make known the force of such sacraments to the apostles and their other companions, so that he may give them “the inheritance of the nations,” that is, give the nations to them as an inheritance.

This is like the one who said: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded,” and so forth. By such things and others like them, they cultivate the nations as an inheritance.

The text continues:

### The works of his hands

It is as though he said: “Although I say that they cultivate the nations as an inheritance, the Lord himself is nevertheless the principal actor in this, because the works of his hands”—that is, of his power—“are truth and judgment.”

This is his power: he works truth in them, that is, the fulfillment of his commandments, and judgment, that is, discernment between good and evil; and thus he cultivates them.

These two things—truth and judgment—are, as though he said, “his commandments.” Therefore they are faithful, because all his commandments are faithful, that is, not deceptive but certain, and for that reason they must be observed. They are not temporary but confirmed forever and ever.

This is because they were made not in shadow but in truth; and they were made in equity, not in iniquity, as in “an eye for an eye,” “a tooth for a tooth,” and similar commands, which, I say, were not rightly understood.

### He sent redemption to his people

It is as though he said: “Therefore these commandments have been confirmed eternally”—confirmed because they were not made through a servant, as those earlier commandments were, but through the Lord. For the Lord God the Father sent him to his people—that is, to the people who were to be established.

[lacuna]

## PSALM CXI. Alleluia of the return of Haggai and Zechariah

### Argument

He instructs all collectively in the pursuit of virtue, showing what fruit good works will also obtain. Among other things, he adds riches and recalls the contempt of enemies, which was bestowed upon those returning from Babylon. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church concerning Christ.

### Explanation

The prophets Haggai and Zechariah, who lived under King Darius long after these songs had been sung, returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian deportation. When they saw the Temple being restored, they poured forth praises to the Lord with great exultation.

In imitation of this, the present psalm too is composed from the letters of a complete alphabet; after the absolution of sins, a Christian ought to sing it with the greatest possible joy.

Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks. In the first admonition he shows what the blessed man does and what good things he deserves. Secondly, he signifies the coming of the Lord, through whom human beings, from sinners and impious persons, merit becoming blessed forever. Thirdly, he testifies that contrary things befall the impious.

The first division contains six letters, the second thirteen, and the third three. The length of the verse woven into Psalm CXVIII is completed here by two little verses, so that what one letter accomplishes there is accomplished here by two different letters following one another in order.

### Commentary

[lacuna] to himself. In accordance with what Solomon says: “Have mercy on your own soul, and you will be pleasing to God.” And in this he commends himself, that is, he proposes himself as an example to others.

And rightly—as though he said: “Such a person is pleasing to the righteous, because he will arrange your words by which he may be defended at the judgment.”

“Words” means good works. This is drawn from the likeness of advocates: just as they, before coming to court, arrange among themselves how each person should speak in defense of the case, and through this are safe against their adversaries, so good works will be a safe refuge for each righteous person at the future judgment.

And truly he will arrange his words, because he will not be moved by them until he brings him into eternity.

Or otherwise: He will rightly arrange them because, through that arrangement, he will obtain this: that forever—that is, in eternity—he will not be moved from the right to the left. Thus he will be in eternal memory, because he is righteous.

And truly he is righteous because in this life he will not fear an evil report, that is, detraction or evil persuasion.

Or otherwise: He will rightly not be moved here from his words because, having thus been made righteous, he will be in eternal memory. And therefore at last he will not fear an evil report, namely, when it is said to the reprobate: “Depart from me, you accursed,” and so forth.

And rightly he will not fear, because “his heart is prepared,” and so forth.

Or otherwise: “He will not fear,” I say, “in the present an evil report,” but rather his heart is prepared to hope—not in the world, but in the Lord—and his heart is confirmed in that hope. He will never be moved from it until he despises—that is, until he recognizes as contemptible—his enemies.

For those who love the things that are seen are enemies of those who prefer the things that are unseen to the things that are seen.

### He scattered; he gave to the poor

Because his heart is confirmed in hope of eternal things, he scattered whatever he possessed of earthly goods—not to prostitutes, but he gave them to the poor.

Therefore “his justice,” that is, the reward of his justice, “remains”—that is, will remain—“forever and ever.”

And truly it will remain, because the one whose humility was despised by the proud on earth will have his “horn,” that is, his humility, exalted in glory as strength.

The sinner will see this exaltation—the sinner who preferred the things that are seen—and then he will be angry. With whom more justly than with himself? He will say: “What profit did pride bring us? What did the boasting of riches bring us?” For all these things have passed away.

And he will gnash his teeth, because there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there. And he will waste away, that is, he will completely fail through grief—but fruitlessly, because then repentance will be fruitless.

And therefore he wastes away, because then the desire for sins will perish.

## PSALM CXII. Alleluia

### Argument

He instructs his hearers in the duties of singing psalms, teaching them that they ought to praise God with greater care because he is great by nature and beneficent by will. Alternatively, it is the voice of the Church concerning its faithful.

### Explanation

The following psalm explains the words of the title. Since “Alleluia” means “Praise the Lord,” it begins in the same way.

In the first part, the prophet exhorts the devout continually to offer praises to the Lord and to proclaim them throughout the whole world. In the second, he himself does what he urges others to do.

### Commentary

### Praise the Lord, children. Alleluia

Some connect this psalm to the preceding one in the following way: “Since the horn of the one whose heart is prepared and confirmed to hope in the Lord will be exalted in glory, be children in malice so that you may be perfect in understanding, and thus praise the Lord.”

And explaining how he is to praise, he says: “Praise the name of the Lord.”

Whoever makes himself a suitable servant praises the name of the Lord. And let the name of the Lord always be blessed—that is, increased—in you. For the more our servitude is multiplied in us, the more his name is increased in us.

Let this blessing of his name begin from the present time, so that it begins now, that is, without delay, because the one who promised forgiveness to the penitent did not promise tomorrow to the one who delays.

And let it continue forever, that is, eternally. Let it take place not only in one people but in both. This is what he says: “Let his name be praised from the rising of the sun to its setting,” that is, among the Jewish and gentile peoples.

By the rising of the sun the Jews are signified, for whom the knowledge of truth and the sun of justice had shone through the commandments of the Law. By the setting, the gentiles are understood, who were in the setting of the true sun because they placed the Creator after the creature.

### The Lord is exalted above all nations

Therefore the name of the Lord is rightly praised among both Jews and gentiles, because the Lord is exalted not only above the Jews but above all nations.

And because it would be little to say that he is merely above the nations, he adds: “And his glory is above the heavens,” that is, he is glorious not only above the nations but also above the heavenly creature, that is, above the angelic spirits.

And rightly—as though he said—his glory is above both nations and heavens, because he alone is truly Lord. For who else rules as the Lord does, as our God?

And he shows how our God rules, saying: “He dwells in the heights,” that is, by dwelling in them he makes them lofty. For the fact that the heavenly spirits persisted in truth, they did not have from themselves but from his indwelling.

And he not only dwells in the heights but also regards the lowly, that is, his regard makes them humble. For his regard is in heaven and on earth—that is, in the lower rational creature—and among those set over others who water them, that is, in heaven and among the subjects who are signified by the watered earth.

This occurs both among Jews and among gentiles. This is what he says: “Raising up the needy,” that is, the Jewish people, who could be saved neither through free will nor through carnal institutions and were therefore needy.

The Lord raises that needy person from the earth, that is, from the earthly desires to which he clung, making him a good needy person—that is, humble, presuming nothing upon free will or established laws.

“And he raises the poor,” that is, the gentile people, impoverished in virtues, “from the dung,” that is, from the unbelief of idolatry in which they lay foully.

He raises them, I say, to such dignity that he places them with princes, that is, incorporates them with princes—not with just any princes, but with the princes of the people, that is, with those princes who are supreme among the people of grace, which is especially his own: the holy apostles.

He incorporated Augustine and Jerome with Peter and Paul.

He is the one who, through this incorporation, makes the barren one—that is, the Church from the gentiles, of whom it was formerly said, “Rejoice, barren one; burst forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail”—this barren woman, I say, dwell joyfully in the house, that is, in the Church, made the mother of many children.

For as the Apostle says: “The children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband.”

This was said by way of likeness, because wives who do not bear children do not possess the whole dowry, while those who bear children both possess the whole dowry and remain in the house.

## PSALM CXIII. Alleluia

### Argument

By recalling ancient deeds, he instructs his hearers in knowledge of the deity, and, through the support of divine benefits, brings about hatred of idols. He speaks in the person of the people and introduces them conversing with one another, showing by what beginnings the recognition and worship of the divine grew among them.

### Explanation

Just as divine praise is gathered from various actions, so “Alleluia” is applied to varied narratives and appropriate matters.

The purpose of this psalm is that, through the great miracles granted to the Hebrew people, the fullness of the Law—who is the Lord Christ—might be announced to the world; and that, through these likenesses drawn from events, he might prove that even today each Christian is liberated.

Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks. First, he recalls that the Lord granted miracles to the Hebrews and to the Christian people. Secondly, in the form of a question, he asks why the sea fled and why the Jordan held back its course, joining to this the most welcome answer: that the earth was moved at the presence of the Lord. Thirdly, he demonstrates to their worshipers the uselessness of the nations’ images, and then explains how life-giving and salutary the worship of the Lord is for its own worshipers.

### Commentary
## On the Departure of Israel from Egypt. Alleluia.

### Commentary

“On the departure of Israel from Egypt.” Alleluia. We read that the Israelite people were liberated from Egyptian slavery and led across the Red Sea and the Jordan after these had been dried up. The prophet appears here to repeat this, not as one narrating history, but as one inviting an allegorical interpretation. For in that historical account the Jordan is not said to have flowed backward, but to have stood still; nor is it said there that the mountains leaped like rams or the hills like lambs of sheep.

Let us therefore consider what we are being admonished about, because those events too are figures of our own realities, and these words exhort us to recognize ourselves. If we retain with steadfast heart the grace of God that has been given to us and the mercy shown to us, we are Israel, because we imitate the traces of the faith of our father Abraham, and we are Jacob. But that people, rejected on account of its faithlessness, belongs to Esau.

Egypt, which is interpreted as “darkness” or “affliction,” is placed figuratively for this world. We must depart from it in particular, lest we become yoked together with unbelievers. Thus each person becomes a worthy citizen of Jerusalem if he renounces this age. Just as that people could not be brought into the promised land until it had been led out of Egypt, and just as that people could not leave Egypt unless it had been liberated by divine assistance, so no one will be able to renounce this world unless aided by divine mercy.

What was once figuratively represented there is fulfilled in the daily offspring of the Church in this final age of the world, because “all these things happened to them as a figure.” What was then prefigured as future is now read as past and recognized as present.

A person begins to leave Egypt when he begins to apply his heart to God and submit his devoted spirit to his gentle yoke, departing from the former desires of his ignorance as from muddy works in which he labored in vain; for, as it is said elsewhere, “His hands served in the basket.” He leaves the barbarian people when he separates himself from the society of blasphemers and from conformity with the wicked, and thus Judea becomes his sanctification.

Let each person therefore ask himself whether faith circumcises his heart and confession cleanses his heart, for one is not a Jew who is so outwardly, but one who is so inwardly. Nor is circumcision in the flesh, but that which is in the spirit. If he finds this in himself, he has been sanctified, and Judea has become his sanctification. Israel—that is, the vision and knowledge of God—becomes his power. For those who were formerly powerless in Egypt become powerful: authority is given them to become children of God.

While these things are happening, many worldly obstacles arise. The sea makes a din—that is, many tongues of carnal friends who dissuade him, and of other earthly people. But after it is recognized that the heart of the one leaving Egypt is prepared to hope in the Lord and has been established in that appearance, the sea flees, because he withdraws from the obstacles. Thus the way to spiritual freedom is opened for the one who leaves.

Or the sea flees beneficially because often many of those who had become bitter, following the example of the one who leaves, are changed from bitterness into sweetness.

The Jordan also turns backward. By the Jordan, which is interpreted as “descent” or “a descending,” those are signified who have already received the grace of faith but have fallen back into the bitter waves of this age, so that they had the fountain—that is, their Creator—behind them, while they had the sea—that is, the world into which they were truly rushing—before their face.

Such people, seeing that departure so steadfast, are also shaken and flow backward, so that they have the Creator before their face. They have the sea—that is, the world—behind their back, forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead.

In brief, the prophet intends to teach and exhort us in this psalm to hasten, after setting aside every obstacle, to leave this Egypt, lest, as was said above, we become yoked together with unbelievers. He says accordingly:

“At the departure of Israel from Egypt”—that is, when someone wishing to become Israel, wishing to come to the knowledge of God, departs from Egypt. “And at the departure of the house of Jacob from a barbarian people”—that is, when that same person, now belonging spiritually to Jacob, departs from the barbarian people, as was said above.

“Judea became his sanctification.” For faith circumcised his heart, and confession cleansed it. “And Israel”—that is, the Israelite land—“became his power,” because, although he had previously been powerless in Egypt, through the knowledge of God he became powerful, as was said above.

The sea saw this departure—that is, others who were becoming bitter in sins recognized that the one who was leaving had a heart prepared and established to hope in the Lord. Therefore they fled in the two ways we mentioned above. The Jordan too, seeing that departure, turned backward, as we said above.

Because of this flight of the sea toward the good, and because of the Jordan’s turning, the mountains—that is, the leaders in the Church, eminent in various virtues and steadfast in faith—leaped for joy, as those who were rams ought rightly to have leaped for joy. They were rams—that is, leaders of the sheep—through whose imitation and teaching this occurred.

The hills too—that is, the lesser members—leaped for joy at that flight and turning, as those rightly ought who were lambs of the sheep, that is, the subjects of those leaders.

### “What is the matter with you, O sea?”

He asks this question not because he does not know or wishes to make the matter doubtful, but to place us in greater certainty. It is as though he were saying:

“O sea, which until now were barking, what is the matter with you that you have now fled from bitterness to sweetness? And you, Jordan, which previously had the fountain behind you and flowed into the sea, what is the matter with you now that you have turned backward? And you mountains and hills, what is the matter with you that you mountains leaped for joy like rams and you hills like lambs of sheep?”

The one who did this is certainly he who is truly powerful and Lord. For the earth—that is, earthly nature—was shaken at the face of the Lord, because certain people who had previously been in Egypt and among the barbarian people received knowledge of the Lord. Following their example, the sea fled, the Jordan flowed backward, and therefore the mountains and hills leaped for joy.

I say that the earth was shaken at the face of God—not of just anyone, but of the God of Jacob, that is, the man of your people. Although God is naturally the God of all, he is nevertheless the God of this people by grace.

Therefore he says, “God of Jacob”—God, I say, who turns the rock into pools of water. This means that he softened himself by making himself known: as long as he had been unknown, he was like an unbearable rock; by revealing himself he became in the hearts of believers a spring of water welling up into eternal life.

And he turns the crag—that is, Paul, who truly had previously been a harsh and unyielding crag—and other holy preachers, through knowledge of himself, into springs of water, so that they might show others living waters, that is, heavenly teaching and spiritual gifts.

### “Not to us, O Lord”

It is as though he were saying: “Yes, Lord, do this; grant this glory, namely, that you turn the rock into pools of water and the crag into springs of water—not to us the greater, not to us the lesser, that is, not because of our merits, but for the glory of your name alone.”

It is as though he were saying: “Let no one suppose that our merits accomplished this. We did not earn it; only the grace of the one who makes sinners righteous, servants into sons, and the condemned into the elect accomplished this.”

### “Because of your mercy”

“Grant,” I say, “glory to your name,” and do so in this manner: through your mercy and truth, which have been shown from above. Mercy, by which you call and forgive sins; truth, by which you reward those who have been called and come. But those who have been called and refuse to come, you condemn.

Therefore, he says—as though he were saying, “I ask that through these things having been shown you grant glory to your name”—lest the nations, at some time, say—that is, lest they be able universally to say in opposition to the rule of your people, “Where is their God?”

Such a thing usually happens when we see the servant of some well-nourished master conducting himself poorly. For it is said, “Where is this man’s master?” But this is not said of one who conducts himself well and honorably; rather, the servant is praised, and the master is praised as well.

### “But our Lord”

It is as though he were saying: “For this reason I say that the reproach should never be spoken or said universally: for although it is spoken among the straw, it has not yet been spoken among the grain; although on earth, not yet in heaven.”

For our Lord made everything that he wished among those who are heaven—that is, his dwelling places. For the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.

### “The images of the nations”

It is as though he were saying: “Our God, I say, made whatever he wished, but the gods of the nations do nothing, because they are not gods; indeed, they are not even human beings.”

And truly they are not human beings, because they are works of human hands, made of gold and silver. He does not say this because all the gentiles possess golden and silver gods—for some have wooden and earthen ones as well—but if they are ashamed of gods made from more precious materials, they should be even more ashamed of those made from cheaper ones.

And it is as though he were saying: “They are not just any kind of works, but images,” that is, imitated and fabricated works. He proves that they are truly not merely images of human beings but not human beings, because although they possess the outline of a human body, they do none of the things that belong to a human body. This is what he says:

“They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes, but they will not see; they have nostrils, but they will not smell; they have hands, but they will not feel,” and so on.

Therefore, he is as though saying: “They are not human beings.” Indeed, they are not only not human beings, but not even bodies, because they will not cry out with their throat—that is, they emit from themselves neither a roar nor the sound of any kind of animal.

### “Let those who make them become like them”

It is as though he were saying: “From what has been said above it is evident that the images of the nations are not to be worshiped as gods, although certain people do this and venerate them.”

But let all who make them—and not only those who make them, but also those who consent to them, that is, all who in any way place their trust in them—become like them: although they have eyes, let them not see the truth; although they have ears, let them not hear what ought to be heard; and so forth.

He says this not as a curse uttered by one who wishes evil, but as the foreknowledge of one who prophesies.

### “House of Israel”

It is as though he were saying: “Let those who trust in images receive the fate we have described. But the house of Israel”—that is, the gathering of the multitude of the faithful—“will not fear such things, because it has not hoped in them, but only in the Lord,” in whom it has already hoped.

And rightly has it hoped in him, because he is their helper in what is good, and their protector from evil.

The house of Aaron also—that is, the greater members—will not fear, because they will hope in the Lord alone, as before. And because there are greater and lesser members, let all who fear the Lord hope, since they too have hoped in the Lord.

And rightly so, because he is their helper and protector, as before.

It should be understood that whenever Israel and Aaron are found in this way, the greater members are understood by Aaron, who was a priest and leader, and the lesser by Israel. What is said here, however, is to be understood only of the earlier people, because below he will add the other sheep as well.

### “The Lord has remembered us”

He said that he is their helper. And it is as though he were saying: “That he is our helper is not due to our merits, but solely to his grace. We did not remember him; he remembered us, because he sent us a Savior and blessed us,” that is, he gave us an increase of virtues.

“I say that he blessed the house of Israel and the house of Aaron,” that is, both the greater and the lesser. Thus he blessed all who fear the Lord with chaste fear in the primitive people.

He proves this by repetition: he blessed all, both the little ones and the greater.

### “May the Lord increase you”

Here he introduces the other sheep, as though he were saying: “May the Lord who blessed you, the primitive people, add others to you, bringing those other sheep. And may he add them in such a way that over you lesser members he places other greater members, and over your sons—that is, over your subjects—other lesser members.”

And may both of you—that is, the greater and the lesser, whether from the primitive people or from the secondary one—be blessed, that is, may you always receive increase from the Lord. He made you, the greater, heaven, still so that you might sow spiritual things; and you, the lesser, earth, still so that you might return carnal things.

He did not merely make you leaders heaven, but also made heaven of heaven—that is, the Lord’s man—so that he might be the heaven of other heavens. “Heaven of heaven,” I say, to be worshiped by the Lord. For in him all the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily.

But the earth—that is, the lesser members—he gave to be cultivated by the sons of men, that is, by you leaders who imitate the patriarchs and prophets, who are not heaven but the heaven of earth.

“Heaven of heaven” can also be referred to the members, such as Paul, who is rightly called “heaven of heaven,” because he learned neither from a human being nor through a human being, but, struck down on the road, heard and learned everything at once from the Holy Spirit.

### “The dead will not praise you”

It is as though he were saying: “For all these things mentioned above, O Lord, the dead will not praise you”—that is, they will not offer fitting thanks—those who still remain in the first death, because a dead person cannot praise the living.

Nor will all those who, having been brought to life by grace, have fallen back into death praise you, because they descend into hell—that is, into the depth of vices.

But we alone, who have been raised by your grace and live, bless you—that is, we will always give thanks to you, Lord, for the mercy bestowed upon us—beginning from this time and now, that is, persevering without delay until you bring us into the age, that is, into eternity.

## On Psalm 114. Alleluia.

### Argument

The thanksgiving of the people brought back from Babylon. Alternatively, the voice of Christ or of any faithful person rescued from temptations.

### Explanation

The solemn and true admonition of the prophet, who has been liberated from the deep pit of sins and established upon that rock of mercy, awakens us from the sleep of this age.

In the first section he gives thanks because he knows that he has been heard, and he declares that, amid all the dangers of death, he effectively called upon the Lord, so that, once liberated, he might reach that everlasting rest which the Lord promises to grant to the faithful as a gift.

### Commentary

### “I loved, because the Lord will hear”

Alleluia. The faithful soul sings this song—that is, this praise—while it is still wandering away from the Lord. It is that sheep which wandered away, that son who had been dead and came to life again, who had been lost and was found.

Therefore let our soul sing this with all the saints who desire that rest, and let it say: “I loved, because…” and so forth.

Here he sets forth three things: faith, hope, and charity, but in reversed order. The greatest of these, as the Apostle says, is charity, which he places first when he says, “I loved.”

Then he indicates hope through its effect when he says, “Because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer.” For he hopes for this reason: that the Lord will hear him.

Faith, however, is gathered from his saying, “Because he inclined his ear to me,” that is, because he first loved us. He did not spare his only Son, and thus he wished to commend his love toward us by sending Christ to be sacrificed for us sinners.

It is as though he were saying: “He inclined his ear to me”—that is, he sent the one through whom he caused me to believe. And because I believed, I hoped; therefore I loved, because I loved.

Therefore, O Lord, I will call upon you in my days—that is, in days of tribulation and imprisonment, in days of cloud and every misery—which I made my own by departing from you, my Father, into a distant land of unlikeness, where I fed pigs and worshiped demons.

He then gives the reason why he must necessarily call upon the Lord in his days, saying:

### “The pains of death surrounded me”

That is, pains leading to death. By this he understands sins of every kind, even simple ones.

“And the dangers of hell found me”—that is, dangers leading to hell, that is, into the depth of vices.

It is as though he were saying: “They would not have found me if I had not wandered away.” For previously I had been placed in a place of riches, but by apostatizing I came into a place of serpents. Therefore the serpents rightly prevailed against me, and every evil and danger came upon me.

Placed amid these dangers, in my ignorance I thought that I ought to rejoice in such prosperity and take pleasure in earthly happiness. But at last I discovered that human salvation is vain, and therefore I said, “Give us help, O Lord, from tribulation.”

I found tribulation—not something that did not exist, but something hidden from me. I found not torment by adversities here, but bondage through prosperity. I found not pleasure but tribulation, not joy but sorrow, not a homeland but a wretched exile.

This is what he says: “I found tribulation and sorrow.” And therefore I said, “I will arise and go to my Father,” and so forth.

This means: I called upon the name of the Lord, saying, “O Lord, deliver my soul.” Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ.

Let those who have not yet heard and do not yet know hear this, and let them seek misery and call upon the name of the Lord, and they will be saved.

I do not mean that they should seek misery which they do not have, but that they should discover the misery which, without knowing it, they do have. Nor do I mean that they should abandon the earthly necessities they need while living morally, but that they should mourn and grieve because they have lost heavenly fullness and have deserved to depend upon earthly necessities for sustenance.

Let them recognize and mourn this misery. Thus the one who wished always to be merciful will make those who mourn blessed. For “blessed are those who mourn, because they will be comforted.”

The text continues:

### “The Lord is merciful”

It is as though he were saying: “While calling upon him I said, ‘O Lord, deliver my soul.’ The Lord will deliver me—the Lord, I say, who is merciful, because he calls and forgives sins; and just, because after calling, he scourges those who sin; and he is our God, because after the scourging he has mercy on those whom he scourged by receiving them.”

Nevertheless, it should not seem bitter that he scourges the humble, but rather sweet that after the scourging he receives them.

### “The Lord preserves the little ones”

Truly the Lord has mercy, because he guards the little ones—that is, the humble—with paternal love, so that he may make them great heirs.

And I—as though he were saying—have been humbled; that is, I have made myself little. Therefore the Lord has already delivered me, in appearance, from every evil.

### “Return”

Because the Lord is of such great goodness that he guards the little ones, therefore, my soul, return to your rest—that is, turn back to your Lord—and you will have rest. Previously turned away, you found nothing but unrest.

And truly, if you turn back, you will have rest. That is, the Lord will do good to you, because he has already done good to you in this respect: he has already delivered your soul from death, both actual and original.

Therefore I am certain that in the end he will deliver my eyes from every tear, because God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. For there is no weeping where there is no falling; and there will be no falling there where there is an incorruptible body.

He will also deliver my feet—that is, all my affections—from every fall. For there will be no falling of the feet there where weak flesh will have no slipperiness.

### “I will please”

And because my feet will be delivered from falling, I will please the Lord, placed in the land of the living, whereas now I displease him in the land of the dead.

For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. Whoever falls, even in thought, necessarily displeases the Lord.

## On Psalm 115. Alleluia.

### Argument

It is sung in the person of the sick Hezekiah. Alternatively, the voice of the Apostle Paul. The Fifth and Sixth Editions join this psalm to the preceding ones; Symmachus and the Seventy Interpreters divide them.

### Explanation

Throughout the psalm the words of unconquered martyrs are recounted. In the first section they recall the Lord’s benefits. While they were wondering what worthy return could be made to him, there came to mind the glorious cup of the martyrs, which nevertheless is granted through the Lord’s generosity.

In the second section the chorus itself declares that it is the Lord’s servant and a son of the Catholic Church, lest you suppose that even the martyrdom of heretics is pleasing to the Lord.

### Commentary

### “I believed; therefore I spoke”

Alleluia. The Apostle says that there are certain people who do not preach Christ purely—that is, not with a simple and pure heart, nor with sincere faith that works through love. While attending to earthly desires, they announce the heavenly kingdom, having falsehood in their breast but truth on their tongue.

Such people do not believe what they say, and therefore they have been rejected. Concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whatever they tell you, do; but do not act according to their works, for they say and do not do.”

There are also others who believe rightly but do not speak, either through laziness or through fear.

Through laziness, like that servant who did not put out at interest the talent he had received but hid it. Hence he heard from the judging Lord: “Wicked and lazy servant.”

Through fear, like those of whom it is said in the Gospel: “Many of the rulers of the priests believed in him, but because of fear they did not speak.” For they feared being put out of the synagogue.

And because they loved human glory more than the glory of God, these too were rejected.

Since both these groups have been rejected, that servant alone is rightly faithful who does not speak before he believes, and when he believes does not remain silent. That is, he neither withholds what he possesses nor fails to distribute what he has, but immediately distributes it when he possesses it.

Such a servant speaks in this psalm, destined to hear from his Lord: “Enter into the joy of your Lord.”

And he says: “I believed; therefore I spoke”—that is, I believed that he exists in himself. For those who refuse to speak what they believe do not believe perfectly, since the faithful servant is not praised because he received, but because he faithfully distributed.

Therefore he says: “I believed; therefore I spoke.” For at the same time he believed what reward he ought to hope for by speaking and what punishment he ought to fear by remaining silent.

The text continues:

### “But I was humbled exceedingly”

This means: “I spoke what I believed, but by speaking I was exceedingly humbled”—that is, I was greatly humbled.

For he suffered many tribulations and many persecutions because of the word of truth, which he both faithfully held and faithfully distributed.

It can happen that the one who announces the truth is humbled by those who oppose the truth, while the truth itself is not humbled. Hence the Apostle, speaking of his chains, says: “They were able to bind me, but the word of the Lord has not been bound.”

Therefore this servant says: “I, not the truth, have been humbled.” Pursue the thought and say: “I said in my excess, ‘I have been humbled.’”

“I”—he insists upon the pronoun. By “I” he indicates that he considered human weakness, because previously he had in some way presumed upon himself by speaking what he believed. But when threats and pressures approached, he was afraid and almost kept silent about what he believed.

Therefore he says: “I,” that is, understanding my weakness, “in my excess,” when in my fear I said, “Every human being is a liar.”

This means: A human being must not presume upon himself or place confidence in himself, because every human being, insofar as he is human, is a liar if he makes any promise on his own behalf. God, however, is truthful.

By his grace he makes the one who is a liar of himself truthful, insofar as he submits himself to the truth of the one who raises the dead, makes the tongues of infants eloquent, and consoles the humble, filling them not only with faith to believe the truth but also with confidence to announce the truth.

Alternatively, because “excess” is sometimes understood also as divine revelation, this may be said in the following way: “In my excess”—that is, by passing beyond myself as a human being into myself as God, in accordance with what the Lord promised when he said, “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High”—“I understood in that brightness and said that every human being is a liar on his own.”

### “What shall I repay the Lord?”

Considering that of himself he is only a liar, but through the Lord’s grace truthful, he says:

“What worthy return shall I make to the Lord, not only for this truth but for all that he has repaid me?”

For he first gave me good things, while I repaid him with evil; but he repaid my evil with good. What praises, then, what thanksgivings shall I repay him?

Certainly, I will take the cup of salvation—that is, I will imitate his passion.

Someone might object to him: “O human being, a liar in your sin but made truthful by God’s gift, and therefore no longer merely human, what do you possess from yourself that you can repay to the Lord? For what do you have that you have not received? Is it not from him that you have the ability to receive the cup of salvation? Is it not from him who said, ‘You will be able to drink the cup that I am about to drink’? Is it not from him that you have the ability to imitate his passion? He suffered first.”

In answer to such an objection he adds:

### “And I will call upon the name of the Lord”

This means: “I say that I will receive the cup, but I do not possess the ability to receive it from myself. I will call upon the name of the Lord”—that is, I will call it into myself. By this I make myself a worthy servant.

He then shows how he will receive the cup, saying:

### “I will fulfill my vows to the Lord”

Not external vows, but my own vows, which are within me. This means: I will offer myself to the Lord.

Whoever considers what he ought worthily to vow to God should vow himself to God and offer himself to God. This is what is required; this is what is owed.

And I will offer myself before all his people—that is, in the faith commonly held by all his people. This is in Catholic communion, outside of which there is no place for true sacrifice.

The text continues:

### “Precious in the sight of the Lord”

It is as though he were saying: “I shall rightly receive the cup of salvation, because the Lord purchased this cup from me.”

For my death and the death of his other saints, once accomplished, is precious not in human sight but in the Lord’s sight; that is, it was purchased at a great price by the Lord himself.

He first poured out his own blood for the salvation of his servants, so that the servants would not hesitate to pour out their blood for his name.

And because—as though he were saying—“by your death you purchased my death,” therefore, O Lord, I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise—that is, I will offer myself to you as a praiseworthy sacrifice.

And rightly do I call you Lord, because I am your purchased servant.

I am also your natural servant, because I am the son of your handmaid. He adds this because many are his servants who are not sons of the handmaid—that is, sons of the Church—such as all schismatics and all heretics.

### “You have broken my bonds”

I am truly your purchased servant because you have broken my bonds, by which I was held bound under the yoke of another power, namely, the devil’s.

For, as the Apostle says, we were sold under sin.

And because—as though he were saying—“you led me out of my bonds,” therefore I shall rightly sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise, as was said above.

And in order to sacrifice worthily, I will call upon the name of the Lord within me, making myself a worthy servant.

Just as above he explained how he would receive the cup of salvation, so now he explains how he will sacrifice the sacrifice of praise, saying:

“I will fulfill my vows to the Lord,” as was said above, “in the sight of all his people,” that is, in the faith common to all his people.

He specifies whom he understands by “his people,” saying:

### “In the courts of the house of the Lord”

That is, in the present Church, which is like a forecourt before the heavenly Church. Because of its enduring habitation, the heavenly Church is rightly called the house of the Lord.

He again specifies which courts he means, saying:

### “O Jerusalem”

“I will fulfill my vows in your midst,” that is, in the communion that exists in you, namely, in the Catholic faith.

He calls the present Church Jerusalem. And lest Jerusalem be understood as belonging only to the earlier people, he subsequently determines how it is to be understood.

It is as though he were saying: “Jerusalem consists not only of the Jewish people, but also of all nations and all peoples”—that is, all who from any nation or people have been chosen through faith.

## On Psalm 116. Alleluia.

### Argument

Hezekiah, recovering from illness, summons not only the Jews but also all nations to praise the Lord, so that those who were astonished at the new portent of the sun’s return might worship the Lord as the author of so great a miracle. Alternatively, the voice of the apostles.

### Explanation

The honor of the title is expressed in two words, but with complete fullness, so that we may understand that although few words are used in the Lord’s praises, they are always entirely full.

This psalm too must be applied to the persons of the martyrs, who, as though they had already undergone their glorious passion, stir up all nations to the praises of the Lord. He bestowed such things upon his servants that they might rather be imbued with his own examples.

### Commentary

### “Praise the Lord”

Through good works, all nations and all peoples.

And it is right—as though he were saying—that you praise him, because his mercy, weakened in that former people by its pride, was strengthened over us by grace: by calling us, justifying us, and forgiving sins.

Alternatively, his mercy, weakened through the first human being, was strengthened over us through the second.

Therefore the Lord must be praised, because the Lord’s truth remains forever, both in rewarding the righteous and in condemning the wicked.

## On Psalm 117. Alleluia.

### Argument

He testifies that the people brought back from Babylon could not be oppressed by the neighboring nations, and a pattern is composed of those mutually exhorting one another to praise God. Alternatively, the voice of Christ speaking about himself.

### Explanation

This psalm, the first, concluded four verses with the same ending, so that the faithful people, freed from the bonds of sins, might be admonished through a fourfold exhortation that the whole world owes its praises to the one Lord, in accordance with the Gospel number.

In the first section he generally exhorts everyone to confess to the Lord, because, having been heard in tribulations, he discovered that no human being should be feared.

In the second he says that one must trust in the Lord alone, through whom, having been tested, he escaped the hostility of the nations and reached the remedies of the truest life.

In the third he says that the gates of righteousness must be opened to him, and he then adds the cornerstone, that is, the Lord the Savior.

In the fourth he persuades the other Christians to frequent the courts of the Lord, rejoicing with sweet delight at the coming of the holy incarnation.

### Commentary

### “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, because forever”

Alleluia. Confession may be either confession of praise or confession of sins. Here, however, confession is not to be understood as showing wounds to a physician, but as giving thanks for received health; this is not confession of sins but of praise.

It is the voice of the primitive Church, with reference, however, to certain more distinguished people, exhorting the greater and lesser members of that former people to confess to the Lord with a voice of praise, while setting forth many reasons. Finally it admonishes those other sheep also to confess to the Lord by attending to these same reasons in their own case.

It is as though he were saying: “You, my fellow members of the people, confess to the Lord with a praiseworthy confession, to whom you rightly ought to confess, because he is good”—that is, because he is God. For, as the Gospel testifies, no one is good except God.

Or, “because he is good”—that is, because he is sweet and pleasant to all who worthily taste him.

Or you ought to confess to him because his mercy is not only for the present, but will endure forever—that is, into eternity.

And because he is such, let Israel now—that is, the lesser members, one exhorting another—say to one another without delay, exhorting each other: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is everlasting.”

Let the house of Aaron also—that is, the greater members, one to another—say: “Confess to the Lord,” and so forth.

Thus, through the greater and lesser members, let all who fear the Lord among the people say the same thing.

### “From tribulation I called upon him”

I said that the Lord is good, and let someone among the holy apostles believe me as one who has experienced this, since they especially suffered tribulations and persecutions in the primitive Church.

For when I was placed in tribulation, I called upon the Lord, and I called from within tribulation so that my tribulation would not be fruitless. The Lord heard me by placing me in a broad space.

Or in this sense: I was not merely troubled, but also gloried in tribulations.

Or in this sense: I even came to love the enemies who persecuted me.

### “The Lord is my helper”

Truly the Lord heard me. For the Lord was my helper, so that I would not fail but rather progress in tribulation.

Therefore I will not fear what a human being—that is, one clinging to flesh and blood—can do to me.

And because not only such people oppose us, but also those rulers of whom the Apostle says, “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places,” he says a second time, “The Lord is my helper.”

Therefore I will despise my enemies, whatever kind they may be: whether they arise from the race of wicked human beings or from the most wicked race of evil spirits.

### “It is good to trust”

It is as though he were saying: “I will despise my enemies, but I will look to the Lord,” and rightly so, because it is good to trust in the Lord. It is so good that it is better than trusting in any human being.

This is said because, in certain human beings too—such as holy men—one should trust according to the measure appropriate to them.

And it is good not only to trust but also to hope, that is, to place one’s hope in the Lord for a long time. It is so good that it is better than hoping—not merely in human beings, but even in superheavenly rulers, that is, in angels.

Angels are called “rulers” because it is written in Daniel that each religious community has been granted some angel or archangel for its defense.

Hence the statement: “Nevertheless Michael, your archangel-prince, will be my helper.”

All nations. Truly it is good to trust in the Lord. For all nations surrounded me, as I trusted and hoped in him, afflicting and persecuting me; and yet this surrounding was accomplished in the name of the Lord, to his glory, because they did not conquer but were conquered. This is what he says: For I have taken vengeance upon them with a good vengeance—that is, because I slew the wickedness of some of them with the sword of the Spirit, whereas they did not slay me.

And not only foreign nations, but those surrounding me also surrounded me—that is, those living together with me, namely, people from my own nation; or “those surrounding me,” that is, false brothers. And again, this surrounding was accomplished in the name of the Lord, to his glory, because I took vengeance upon some of them by putting them to death in evil and giving them life in goodness.

I say that both—the nations and those surrounding me—surrounded me like bees, killing not me but themselves when they wounded and afflicted me. For bees are said by nature to have this characteristic: that they lay down their life in the wound.

Or otherwise: “They surrounded me like bees,” that is, like bees easily overcome. Whenever they go out in an army, they are easily—by the casting of a little dust—driven back and recalled to their camp.

Or otherwise: “They surrounded me like bees.” For just as bees, with great zeal and diligence, skilfully construct a honeycomb, so the more diligence they expended in tormenting and surrounding me, the more they made me, as it were, skilfully formed—that is, more exemplary and venerable. For the more punishments Laurence endured, the more he became worthy of veneration and imitation by the good.

“And they blazed against me like fire among thorns,” that is, they were comparable to the fire that blazes among thorns. For just as that fire burns the thorns’ spines, which are slender, but does not harm the trunk covered by grass, so they shook out the spines of iniquity in sinful flesh by their tortures inflicted upon me, but did not injure the strength of my soul.

And all this surrounding was accomplished in the name of the Lord, to his glory, because I took vengeance upon them, as stated above.

This verse may also be understood in a good sense: “Some of the nations and those surrounding me surrounded me like bees.” For just as bees at a certain time pack a honeycomb very densely, in order to gather from it what is sweet, so they, crowding closely around me, drew forth from me, as from a honeycomb, the honey of the sweetness of God’s word. “And they blazed like fire among thorns,” that is, so vehement was the love kindled in them as was the force of the heat in that fire which blazes among thorns. And so that surrounding was accomplished in the name of the Lord, as above.

I was thrust and overthrown. The sense continues thus: Truly the nations surrounded me. For they thrust me toward falling, and thrust me so violently that I was overthrown—that is, I gave, as it were, certain signs of falling. For in so great a tribulation it cannot happen that weak flesh is not changed in some way. Yet I did not fall, because the Lord supported me so that I would not fall.

And God supported me because of this confidence: I am not strong in myself—that is, I am not praiseworthy in myself—but the Lord is my strength and my praise, because I considered myself strong and praiseworthy only in him. Therefore he became my salvation, because I had become death to myself.

The voice of rejoicing and salvation. Truly he became my salvation. For in this manner—namely, because the Lord is in the tents, that is, in the hearts of the righteous—there is not the voice of sorrow and the answer of death, as you suppose while raging outwardly against me; rather, there is the voice of rejoicing, that is, manifest rejoicing, the answer of true salvation.

[Col. 1050C]

The right hand of the Lord. The sense continues thus: Truly the Lord supported me. For the right hand of the Lord—that is, his power—performed a mighty deed: it worked in me a victory arising from suffering, and truly a mighty deed. For the right hand of the Lord exalted me.

Great indeed is the power that exalts the humble, makes the mortal divine, brings perfection out of weakness, and glory out of subjection. I say that the right hand of the Lord performed a mighty deed—that is, salvation from tribulation—so that the true salvation of God might be evident to those afflicted, while only the weak salvation of man remained for those inflicting affliction.

Therefore, as though he said: I shall not die, as you suppose while putting my body to death; rather, though outwardly still in the flesh, I shall live through veneration and eternal remembrance, and thus I shall recount the works of the Lord. For even now the primitive Church daily recounts the works of the Lord: how it conquered those striking it by being beaten, its assailants by suffering, and those raging against it by loving them.

Chastening, the Lord chastened me. Therefore I say, “I shall not die,” because what I suffer is not death but the Lord’s chastening. Therefore you persecutors should claim nothing for yourselves, because it is not you who do this, but the Lord, who chastens me.

And because he chastens me, he will not hand me over to death—that is, he will not permit me, even if he puts me to death outwardly, to be put to death inwardly.

Open to me. As though he said: Therefore you persecutors, do what you have begun: imprison me in every way and torture me, because this will not harm me but benefit me. For in this way you will open for me the gates of righteousness—that is, I shall enter into eternity and blessedness, which is the gate of righteousness, because only the righteous will enter there.

Therefore open these gates for me—that is, do not desist from what you have begun. And for this reason, as though he said, I ask you to open them: because, once I have entered them, I shall at last worthily confess to the Lord, with that confession of which it is said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord,” and so forth.

For this reason also I say, “Open,” because this is the gate of the Lord—that is, because after such tribulations the Lord entered into eternity. For it was necessary for Christ to suffer and thus to enter into his glory. And into this gate—that is, into eternity—only the righteous, that is, those who imitate the Lord, will enter.

I shall confess to you. He turns toward the Lord, as though he said: I say that, having entered the gates of righteousness, I shall confess to the Lord—and this I shall truly do. For then, O Lord, I shall confess to you; and rightly to you, because you previously heard me here in tribulation, lest I should fail, and thus became my salvation, when I had become death to myself.

The stone that the builders rejected. Truly he became my salvation. For in this manner: the stone which the builders—that is, the Jews, wishing to establish their own righteousness and not to be subject to the righteousness of God—rejected, choosing a human king: this stone, I say, you made my head—that is, you subjected me to its rule, as a limb is subject to the head.

And it was made not only my head, but also the head of many others, because it became the head of the corner—that is, it became the cornerstone, joining two walls coming from different directions but not holding different opinions.

And this fact—namely, that it became the head of the corner—although the Jewish enemies in some sense brought it about, because they crucified him, they did not intend this; rather, they wanted to destroy his name. Therefore it was not made by them but by the Lord, who permitted this so that Christ might die, rise again, ascend, and send the promised Spirit to the apostles. Through their preaching the whole world would follow after him, and thus he would become the head of the corner.

And because it was done by the Lord, it is therefore wondrous—that is, desirable—in our eyes, namely, in the inward eyes of believers, those who hope and love. For we ought greatly to desire to be under such a head.

Or otherwise: He said that the stone was rejected by the builders, and that this rejection was done by the Lord—that is, by the arrangement of the Lord the Father, who willed that blindness should occur in part in Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter, and thus all Israel might be saved.

Therefore this is wondrous—that is, fearful—in our eyes: namely, that someone should have lofty understanding, yet remain afraid. For if God did not spare the natural branches up to this point, neither will he spare the wild olive grafted into him.

This is the day. We ought rightly to marvel at this, because this day—that is, this time of the ancient dispensation, the new restoration, and eternal blessedness, of which the Apostle says, “Behold, now is the acceptable time,” and so forth—is the time in which the stone rejected by the builders became the head of the corner.

This day, I say, is the one day that the Lord made in an exceptional way. Therefore we must rejoice in it bodily and be glad in mind.

Therefore, O companions from my people, let us rejoice on this day, doing good—or doing well—outwardly, and let us be glad by thinking good thoughts inwardly. I say that we should say: O Lord, save us—that is, complete in us the salvation whose work you have begun.

O Lord, prosper us—that is, make our journey prosperous as we return to you from a distant land.

Or otherwise: “Prosper us,” that is, make prosperous and successful that salvation which you are working in us and in those other sheep, so that you may bring them also, and there may be one flock, just as there is one shepherd.

And for this reason, as though he said, you ought to prosper us: because the one who is to come comes not in his own name but in the name of the Lord. This means that someone will come in his own name, namely, the son of perdition, and he will be accursed. But someone will come in your name, namely, the one who says: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me, the Father.” And he will be blessed—that is, worthy of a great increase of members. For so great a head must have a large body.

We have blessed you. “Let us rejoice,” I say, “and let us be glad,” saying this and also saying to those other sheep:

We who are from the house of the Lord—that is, we who are members of the Lord’s household through the legal and prophetic writings—have blessed you other sheep in our fathers, who prophesied this; and we shall bless you, that is, we bring you good news in our own persons.

This is it: The Lord is God—that is, our Redeemer is the true God. Conversely, God has become our Lord—that is, our Redeemer—and this has already shone upon us from the house of the Lord, that is, it has been made known to us.

And so that it may also shine upon you, establish in yourselves a solemn day—that is, sincerity of mind—and advance in dense gatherings, not of peoples but in the frequent practice of virtues, up to the horn of the altar—that is, up to the solemnity of divinity.

He calls the altar by analogy with that heavenly sanctuary where Christ, the true priest and victim, offers himself daily to God the Father for us. For he does not wish them to stop at his humanity alone, but to contemplate his divinity also.

My God. “Establish,” I say, “a solemn day, advancing up to the horn of the altar.” I say that you should say: Lord, you are my God. This means:

Lord, truly our fathers worshiped falsehood and vanity, which profited them nothing, saying to a stone, “You created me,” and to wood, “You gave me birth.” But I say to you: You are my God, because you created me, you who gave me birth. Therefore I shall confess to you—that is, rightly praise you with my heart.

I say: You truly are my God; therefore I shall exalt you as my God with my mouth, and I shall confess you by my works. And rightly so, because you heard me, bringing me back from the shadow of death and the darkness of unbelief; and you became my salvation, although those things had previously been salvation to me.

Confess to the Lord. As though he said: Say this also to one another, exhorting one another: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good,” and so forth.

# ON PSALM 118. Alleluia

## ARGUMENT

This entire psalm, which is full of exhortations and instructions, is sung in the person of the righteous living in Babylonian captivity. They sometimes mingle in voices suitable to the people, both humbly ranking themselves with the guilty in the confession of sins and teaching that these things happened to the people on account of their deserts. Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ to the Father concerning the Jews and concerning his own passion.

### Aleph, doctrine

## EXPLANATION

[Col. 1052C]

A desirable alleluia is prefixed to this festive psalm, which is filled with the power of divine things, so that the merit of the divine song may be recognized from the honor of its title.

It is composed in Hebrew letters, arranged to instruct the inexperienced and teachable peoples in the school of Christ, in such a way that eight verses begin with each letter. Here, I think, the mystery of the resurrection and of true circumcision is revealed.

Josephus, however, reports in the books of the *Ἀρχαιολογίαι* [*Antiquities*] that this psalm, Psalm 144, and the Song of Deuteronomy were composed in elegiac meter: namely, that the first verse consists of six feet, while the following one ends in a pentameter with one foot fewer.

Throughout the psalm the universal choir of the saints speaks—those who have existed, now exist, or are believed to be destined to exist from the beginning of the world. Among them are found apostles, prophets, martyrs, confessors, and ecclesiastical orders who serve the Lord with holy integrity.

Therefore, since in each of the individual letters what follows must be understood according to the interpretation of that letter, it is fitting that the first letter, *aleph*, be interpreted as “doctrine.” In this doctrine eternal blessedness is promised to those who are blameless in the way of the Lord.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 1052D]

Blessed are the blameless. Alleluia. Aleph—that is, this praise concerns doctrine. For *aleph* is interpreted as “doctrine,” and it concerns doctrine because this psalm exhorts us to blessedness, which no one fails to desire. For all wish to be blessed.

But what need is there of exhortation concerning something that the human mind desires of its own accord? Perhaps this is because everyone desires blessedness, but most do not know by what order it is attained.

Therefore this psalm teaches the matter when it says: “Blessed are the blameless,” and so forth. As though it said: I know what you want; you seek blessedness. Therefore, if you wish to be blessed, be blameless.

Everyone wants the former—that is, blessedness—but few want the latter, without which one does not attain what everyone wants. That is, few desire blamelessness, without which blessedness cannot be attained.

This exhortation is necessary for our minds. For what good that thing is—toward which many are sluggish—is shown when those who do it are called blessed. The purpose is that, for the sake of what everyone wants, what most do not want may also be done: that, for the sake of the reward of blessedness, the work of blamelessness may not be avoided.

To be blessed is indeed so great a thing that both the good and the wicked desire it. Nor is it surprising that the good are good in order to be blessed. It is very surprising, however, that the wicked are also wicked in order to be blessed.

For whoever commits adultery, or theft, or murder, or anything similar, pursues such things for this reason: because through them he seeks blessedness. But these are certain byways leading toward a likeness of blessedness. The psalm recalls such people from them.

As though it said: What are you doing? Where are you heading? Upon what way are you proceeding? One does not go rightly by this route; these are certain deviations from the way to blessedness. By this route you will not reach where you are heading. You seek blessedness, but by these roads you will fall into misery.

Therefore abandon wickedness, since you cannot abandon your desire for blessedness. In vain you grow weary by striving toward that place where, upon arrival, you will be defiled. For it is not the defiled who are blessed, but the blameless.

And he shows who the blameless are when he says: “Those who are in the way”—not those who, by sinning, do things outside the way. The way, as though he said, is the law of the Lord. Those who walk in that law—that is, take delight in it as in a good path—those who fulfill the law of the Lord not from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness, are blameless already through hope, and because they are blameless, they are blessed.

Blessed are those who search out his testimonies. He does not seem here to be taking up another kind of blessed people than before. For those who walk in the law of the Lord and those who search out his testimonies are the same, unless perhaps more is understood when he says, “Those who search out his testimonies”: that is, those who strive to fulfill the Lord’s commandments even to the shedding of blood.

And the meaning is: Blessed, I say, are the blameless in the way, and blessed are those who search out his testimonies—that is, the Lord’s—in such a way that they seek him with their whole heart.

This addition is not pointless. For the Holy Spirit saw that many search out the testimonies not in order to be righteous but to be learned; not in order to do what should be done but to know what should be done, so that they might gain from it either human praise or some worldly reward.

Therefore he adds, “with their whole heart.” This is to be understood as follows: Blessed are those who search out the Lord’s testimonies for the purpose for which they were given—namely, that in them they may seek him alone with their whole heart, that is, with their entire intention, and find him once they have sought him.

For those who seek him are not blessed, but those who find him—though not yet in possession, but only in hope.

For those who work iniquity. The sense continues from what precedes: Truly those who search out his testimonies as they ought to be searched out are blessed. For those who do not search them out as they ought to be searched out—which is equivalently expressed when he says, “Those who work iniquity”—are not blessed.

He states the same equivalently when he says: “They have not walked in his ways.”

The connection with the first verse may also be made as follows: Truly the blameless walk in the law, that is, in the ways of the Lord. For those who are defiled—which is equivalently expressed by “those who work iniquity,” that is, sin—do not walk in his ways.

In both these connections there is force by contrast.

But why every iniquity is sin, as John testifies when he says, “Whoever commits iniquity commits sin,” seems to follow from this verse: that no one who commits sin walks in his ways. Therefore we must see to it that what has been rightly said does not disturb the reader when it is wrongly understood.

For that same John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” And his fellow apostle Paul also confesses that he commits sin when he says: “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want—that I do.”

Therefore either such people must be thought not to walk in his ways, or they must be without sin. But the latter contradicts their own statements. It is likewise contradictory to say that they do not walk in his ways. For if one is such as this man—for example, a beautiful virgin—and another is one who labored more than all, if they do not walk in the way, who else does walk in it?

Let the apostle Paul himself be questioned, and let him say how they both commit sin and walk in the way of the Lord.

Concerning sin he says: “It is not I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.” He also shows that he walks in the way when he says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I continually pursue the prize of the heavenly calling, which is in Christ Jesus.”

Behold, the question is solved. But again another question arises. It is asked how the same person both commits and does not commit sin.

The answer is as follows: Whenever unlawful impulses arise in us, if only the inclination arises and no action follows—if we do not yield our will to their desires, and if we restrain ourselves so that we do not offer our members as weapons of iniquity for iniquity—behold, we do not commit sin.

The Apostle likewise commands: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body,” and: “Do not offer your members to iniquity as servants for iniquity.”

Nevertheless, since that from which unlawful desires arise in us is not the strength of another nature but the weakness of our own infirmity, the Apostle says: “But sin dwelling in me.” Therefore we also commit sin, and thus we both commit and do not commit sin.

And so it is asked again whether, in the Lord’s Prayer, we say daily, “Forgive us our debts,” either for those things which we do with our consent, or for the desires produced not by us but by the sin dwelling in us.

Blessed Augustine resolves this question as follows:

> “As far as I am presently able to understand, I say that the whole guilt of our weakness and infirmity, together with all those things which we have said, done, or thought with our consent, has been removed by the sacrament of baptism. Therefore, although weakness remains in us, it does not harm us if we do not consent to it by doing, speaking, or silently approving. But because human life is warfare upon the earth, we do indeed keep watch against greater crimes, yet certain things often creep upon us when we are unguarded. Although each of them does not crush us by its own weight, many accumulated together nevertheless overwhelm us with their heap. Therefore we must pray, fast, and give alms daily for these things.”

Now let us return to the text, which is explained as follows: Those who work iniquity—that is, those who, by consenting to the tinder of sin through speaking, doing, or thinking, work iniquity, that is, any sin—do not walk in his ways, because they are not blameless but defiled.

That outstanding iniquity by which one departs from the faith and does not approach the faith may also be intended. The Lord singularly calls this “sin” in the Gospel when he says: “Concerning sin, because they do not believe in me”; and elsewhere: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin,” that is, unbelief.

Thus the meaning would be: Those who work iniquity—that is, unbelief—do not walk in the ways of the Lord, because they do not believe in him.

And therefore they do not experience his ways, namely those ways of which it is said: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” Mercy consists in forgiving sins, while truth consists in fulfilling promises.

You have commanded. The sense continues: Truly those who search out the testimonies are blessed. For you, O Lord, who command nothing except what contributes to blessedness, have commanded that the commandments—that is, your precepts—be kept, and this exceedingly.

The word “exceedingly” may be referred either to “you have commanded that they be kept,” and it should not be understood otherwise, as in the saying, “so that there may be nothing excessive.” Or it may mean “very greatly,” as in: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly delight in his commandments.”

Behold, the law has been established, since it was said: “You have commanded your commandments.” But because many have said that the mere knowledge of the law is sufficient for the assistance of free will, this person subsequently asks for the assistance of grace, thereby teaching how necessary grace is.

He introduces a word of desire in order to remove the pride of presumption, saying:

[Col. 1055A]

Would that my ways were directed. As though he said: I see, O Lord, that I cannot direct my ways either through the commandments or through free will, because it is not for man to direct his own ways.

Therefore I desire that, through your grace—which alone can accomplish this—my ways may be directed: that is, that my works may be directed toward keeping your justifications, that is, toward truly fulfilling your precepts, which justify.

Then I shall not be put to shame. For this reason I desire that my ways be directed so that I may keep your commandments. For when I have examined myself—that is, when I have perfectly come to know myself as though in a mirror—trained in all your commandments, then I shall no longer be put to shame.

I shall not be put to shame either by that shame in which I merely know and do not act, or by the saying: “This man began to build and was unable to finish.”

He rightly says, “When I have examined,” because the divine commandments, whether they are read or turned over in memory, must be regarded as a mirror, so that a person may come to know himself in them, as in a mirror.

The apostle James bears witness to this when he says: “If anyone is merely a hearer of the word and not a doer, he will be compared to a man looking at the face of his birth in a mirror.
