For he looked at himself, went away, and immediately forgot what he was like. But whoever looks into the law of perfect liberty and perseveres, not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, will be blessed in his deed.”

The Spirit seeks such a person here when he says, “When I have examined,” namely, one who is not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work.

I shall confess to you. When, I say, I have examined myself, then I shall not be put to shame, but I shall confess to you through good works, with a directed heart—that is, with a straight heart.

I say that my heart is directed in this, namely, by what I have learned concerning the judgments of your righteousness—that is, those things which you, not men, justly judge ought to be done—not merely to know them but to do them.

For it is as though he said: If I merely know and do not act, I shall have nothing in which to rejoice, but something for which I shall be condemned.

It should be noted that this verb, “I have learned,” contains this implication. He would not otherwise speak truly unless he also acted. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who has heard from my Father and learned comes to me.”

I shall keep your justifications. “I shall confess to you,” I say, “and I shall keep your justifications,” that is, your precepts that justify, not so much in memory as in life. For it is useless if they are kept only in memory and not practiced.

And in order that I may keep them, O Lord, do not abandon me by withdrawing the presence of your help, until I am abandoned by every kind of abandonment—that is, by complete abandonment.

Who is abandoned by complete abandonment? Whoever glories only in himself and not in the Lord, or whoever falls and does not rise again but perishes forever.

### Beth, house

## EXPLANATION

The faithful people explain the pleasures they enjoy in the words of the Lord, showing themselves to be the house of the Lord and the receptacle of his commandments. The mystery of this is contained in the second letter.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 1055D]

By what does a young man correct his way? As though he said: I shall rightly keep your justifications. For by keeping these—which is equivalently expressed as “by keeping your words”—a younger person corrects his way, that is, his life.

“By a younger person” means everyone belonging to the younger people, represented by the younger Son, who, rising, said in himself: “I will arise and go to my father,” and so forth.

A person is called “younger” if he bears the image of the new man, just as a person is called “older” if he bears the image of the old man.

And truly, as though he said: In these he corrects himself. For in what else is he corrected? Therefore, if not in anything else, he must truly be corrected in these.

And therefore, as though he said: O Lord, I have rightly sought you in these justifications with my whole heart—that is, with my entire intention and soul.

And because I have sought you, O Lord, do not drive me away from your commandments—that is, let your grace help me to fulfill your commandments. For the one who is not aided by grace is rightly considered rejected.

In my heart. As though he said: Truly I have sought you. For I have hidden your words in my heart.

Note that the Lord’s precepts must both be hidden in the heart and not hidden. They must be hidden and firmly retained in our heart for our edification. Hence it is said here: “I have hidden them” for this purpose, so that I may not sin against you—that is, so that through forgetfulness I may not transgress your commandments.

But they must not be hidden; rather, they must be proclaimed, lest we deny nourishment to our fellow servants. For the Apostle commands both, saying: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.”

Blessed are you, O Lord. As though he said: Because I have valued your words so greatly, O Lord, teach me further, and teach me further to attend to your justifications—that is, your precepts that justify.

Therefore I ask you to teach, because you are blessed—that is, because manifold blessing proceeds from you, namely, manifold mercy. For you make the sinner righteous, the servant a son, and the condemned one an heir of the kingdom.

With my lips. As though he said: You ought to teach me for this reason: I have not merely hidden them for my own edification, but I have also declared with my lips, lest I deny nourishment to my fellow servants, all the judgments of your mouth.

How does he say that he will proclaim all his judgments, when the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments”? And elsewhere it is said: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.”

But how can this be possible? The same prophetic Spirit determines this by adding: “of your mouth.” As though he said: I did not conceal all those judgments of yours, but proclaimed to others those which your mouth—that is, your grace—revealed to me.

For the grace of God is called his mouth because, just as a person opens the secrets of his heart with his mouth, so God opens his secrets to us through grace.

In the way of your testimonies. As though he said: I both hid and announced them for this reason: because I took delight in the way of your testimonies.

That is, I did not take delight in the glory of the world, but all my delight was in Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. He is called the way of testimonies because he testified how great a love God the Father commended to us—namely, that he did not spare his own Son, and that Christ died for the ungodly.

I took delight in Christ, I say, as much as a miser delights in all riches, because, through excessive desire for riches, he completely departs from himself.

This is the voice of Paul and of the other perfected members of Christ, speaking together with him: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth.

I shall exercise myself in your commandments. As though he said: Because I have taken such delight in Christ, I shall therefore exercise myself in your commandments, given through him—that is, I shall prattle not only in words but also in deeds.

Another translation has, “I shall prattle.” And therefore I shall consider your ways—that is, I shall always keep your works before my eyes.

But I shall set aside my own ways—that is, my own works. And I shall not only exercise myself outwardly, as though he said, but I shall also meditate inwardly upon your ways. That is, all my thought will be upon your precepts and justifications.

Therefore I shall forget my own words, but I shall not forget your words—that is, your justifications.

### Gimel, retribution or fullness

## EXPLANATION

He asks that grace be repaid to the saints who are resident aliens on earth, which they had lost in their first parent; but he also says that what they accomplish must be restored to them through their persecutions.

Thus this retribution of merits, this fullness of just judgment, is prefigured by the name of the third letter.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 1057A]

Repay your servant. The sense continues: Since I shall exercise myself and meditate in your justifications, setting aside my own ways and words and preferring your ways and words, therefore repay me, your servant.

He shows what he asks to have repaid when he adds: “Give me life, and I shall keep your words.”

As though he said: Repay me, your freedman, with death. But being dead I cannot keep your words. Therefore repay me, now made your servant, with the giving of life, and thus I shall keep your words, not so much in memory as in life.

He asks for a repayment that proceeds from undeserved grace. For there are four kinds of repayment: one is good for good, another evil for evil, another good for evil, and another evil for good.

The first two belong to justice; the third to undeserved grace; the fourth is unknown to God and belongs only to the wicked. God knows the third, because if he did not repay good for evil, there would be no one to whom he could repay good for good.

It should also be noted that this man was not entirely dead. For he already possessed the beginning of a good desire, since he was asking for the life of obedience.

What he says, “Give me life, and I shall keep your words,” belongs to the life of obedience.

But because he sees that the words cannot be fulfilled through obedience unless they are perceived through understanding, he prays and says:

Reveal my eyes, O Lord—that is, illuminate my inward eyes through the illumination of grace. Then, with my eyes revealed, I shall consider the fulfilled wonders proceeding from your law: namely, that sinners are made righteous, servants sons, and so forth.

Or: “the wonders proceeding from your law” means the wonders commanded by your law, such as loving enemies, repaying good for evil, and similar things.

For I am a resident alien. As though he said: You ought rightly to reveal my eyes, because I am your fellow citizen. For I am not native to this land but a resident alien—that is, a foreigner.

All who belong to the people of God, although they dwell bodily on earth, dwell in the heavens in mind, because, as the Apostle says, “Our citizenship is in heaven.” Therefore they are not citizens here but sojourners, because they do not consider themselves to possess here a lasting city but seek one that is to come.

And because, as though he said, I am not a citizen but a resident alien on earth, therefore, O Lord, do not hide your commandments from me.

But how can he ask that commandments be not hidden from him when they are known to everyone, even to unbelievers? For what is better known among the faithful than “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself”? This is equivalent to: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.”

It therefore stands that this is also known among unbelievers. Would that the commandments were as dear to as many as they are clear to! Perhaps he asks that they not be hidden because it is difficult to know God, whom one must consequently love and find within those very commandments—God far more difficult to know than one’s plainly visible neighbor.

But since it is difficult for anyone to know himself as he ought, how will one who does not know himself love his neighbor as himself?

Therefore he asks that the commandments which are known to some extent not be hidden, so that they may be known more and more, enabling him to know himself and thus love his neighbor as himself, and through love of neighbor ascend to the love of God.

My soul has desired. As though he said: You ought not to hide your commandments from me for this reason: my soul has desired to desire—that is, to desire eagerly—your justifications, that is, your truly justifying precepts, more than it desired anything else.

And this has been so at all times—that is, in adversity and in prosperity.

Rebuked. As if he were saying: For this reason my soul rightly desired your ordinances eagerly: because you rebuked harshly those who, not desiring them eagerly but neglecting them through pride, deserved rebuke. He calls the first parents proud, because they neglected God’s commandments not through weakness or ignorance, but through pride. For they presumed upon this, because the serpent had said, “You shall be like gods”; and while they desired what was above them, that is, what they had rightly received they lost, because they were condemned to death. This is what he says: “[Col. 1058A] You rebuked the proud.” And you rebuked not only those first proud ones, but all those who, following their example, turn aside from your commandments are also accursed—that is, condemned to death.

Take reproach and contempt away from me. As if he were saying: So that I may not turn aside, therefore, Lord, take reproach and contempt away from me—that is, remove from me every deed deserving reproach and contempt. You ought to do this because I have sought your testimonies—that is, I have devoted myself wholeheartedly to your commandments, even to the shedding of blood. And I did not presume this of myself, but sought it from outside myself—that is, I asked grace for help.

Or otherwise: Those who turn aside from the commandments are accustomed to reproach God’s servants for believing in one who was crucified and worshiping a dead man, and for similar things. Therefore this man asks that reproach be removed, not because he considers the punishment from which he will receive a crown something to be avoided, but, out of compassion for such people, he desires that the reproachers be converted and suffer the same reproach from others. Thus he says: “Take away from me that reproach and contempt [Col. 1058B] which I suffer because I have sought your testimonies”—that is, because I have loved your martyrdoms and your commandments, by which you have testified how great a love God the Father commends in us.

For princes sat. Truly I have sought your testimonies, because I did not deny them in spirit on account of kings or governors, from whom I suffered many evils. For princes sat—that is, in the tribunal seat—and, after a delay and under the moon, acted against me; and they spoke against me not merely with words, but with the gravest tortures. But your servant—that is, I—did not therefore fail; rather, I was always exercising myself in doing and proclaiming your ordinances. And truly I shall exercise myself in them. For both by meditating and by giving counsel—this is what he says—“For my meditation is your testimonies, and your ordinances are my counsel.” The counsel, namely, of those who endure, against the counsel of those who persecute. For the persecutors’ counsel was to destroy the assembled holy martyrs; but the counsel of those who endured was to pray for the persecutors themselves, that they might be converted, and to love them.

**Daleh**, poor, or tablet, or door.

## EXPLANATION

He says that he is constrained by bodily necessity, but that he is to be saved solely by the Lord’s compassion. He asks that the Lord remove from him the ways of iniquity, because he has chosen the way of truth. Thus, through worldly poverty, he opens a door to severe riches; and through frequent meditation, he offers the inmost parts of his heart to God’s commandments as though they were tablets. Smoothed like soft wax, they would most readily receive the command of the one giving orders, as soft wax receives a writer’s stylus: “I have clung,” he says, “to your testimonies, Lord.”

## COMMENTARY

My soul clung to the pavement. As if he were saying: I say that your testimonies are my meditation and my counsel. Yet I still fear failing, because my soul clings to the pavement. The whole world is understood as a kind of great house, whose chamber, so to speak, is heaven; [Col. 1058D] but the earth that is trampled is the pavement, and our body is from the earth. Hence our body itself may also be called pavement.

Since our flesh is earth, therefore, while we are on this pilgrimage, earthly thoughts often creep upon us, because the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and earthly thought depresses the soul as it considers many things. Hence, in this life, we must always fear that we may fail. Considering this, the one who speaks here says: “I fear, O Lord, that I may fail, however much I exercise myself in your ordinances, because my soul still clings to the pavement”—that is, to carnal desires, from which, as if he were saying, death threatens it. Therefore, Lord, give me life by making me cling to spiritual affections; and do this not on account of my merit, but on account of your word—that is, according to your promise—so that I may not be a son of presumption but a son of promise.

My ways. As if he were saying: You ought therefore to give me life because I have declared to you my ways, foul and not beautiful; and you heard me by placing me in your beautiful ways. Therefore, Lord, teach me to persist more and more in your ordinances—that is, in your commandments, which truly justify. And he explains how he asks to be taught, saying: “Instruct me to frequent more and more the way of your ordinances”—that is, your ordinance, which is the way—and thus I shall exercise myself in your wonders, that is, in your commandments, which make those who examine them wondrous: namely, they make heaven from earth, a lamb from a wolf, a free man from a slave, and similar things.

My soul slumbered. As if he were saying: It is necessary, Lord, that you instruct me, because my soul slumbered—that is, it acted more sluggishly and negligently than it ought—and this because of weariness, that is, because I suffer weariness of God’s word. Hence elsewhere: “Their soul abhorred every kind of food,” and so forth.

Or otherwise: “My soul slumbered,” that is, it suffered a certain restlessness and movement, just as one who is drowsy is restless, because he is neither wholly asleep nor wholly awake. And this was because of weariness—that is, because the wicked among whom I live are wearisome to me, drawing me away through so many bad examples. Therefore, Lord, strengthen me in your words—that is, in your commandments—and, in order that I may be strengthened, remove my iniquity from me and place me in the way of equity. This is what he says, adding equivalently: “And have mercy on me according to your law,” supplying: by placing me there.

And, as if he were saying, you ought to have mercy on me because, insofar as it was within me, through free choice I chose the way of truth—that is, I chose your true commandments as the way in which I should run—and I have not forgotten your judgments, so that I might run. I have clung to your testimonies, so that I might run, presuming nothing on my own but attributing everything to your grace. Therefore, Lord, do not put me to shame—that is, make me such that it cannot be said to my shame: “This man began to build and was unable to finish.”

The way of your commandments. As if he were saying: For this reason you ought not to put me to shame, because I ran—that is, with every effort and desire I devoted myself to the way of your commandments [Col. 1059C]—and this is not from myself, but because you enlarged my heart—that is, you gave expansion to my heart, acting so that I might run through it with love.

**He**, she herself, or receiving.

## EXPLANATION

In many ways the blessed people ask that they ought to be guarded by the gift of the law of their Lord; and she is rightly called “receiving,” who says: “Give me understanding.” Nor is she improperly so called, since, remaining always in the same intention, she turns her eyes away from the vanity of the world.

## COMMENTARY

Establish the law for me. He says the same as before: “I ran the way of your commandments.” Now he asks that the law be established for him, which seems contrary to the Apostle, who says: “The law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the unrighteous.” For the man who previously said that he had run cannot be understood as unrighteous; rather, his heart has been enlarged on the way of the commandments, which belongs only to the righteous.

Yet he does not ask for the law to be established for him according to the former people, to whom the law was given on tablets of stone. Rather, he asks that the law be given to him on tablets of the heart, because it is written: “I will take away from you your heart of stone, and I will give you a heart of flesh”; and: “I will give my law in your minds, and I will write it in your hearts.” He asks for the law not merely so that he may know it by understanding, but so that, by loving it, he may fulfill it—not in the narrowness of fear, but in the breadth of love.

But the people who received the law on tablets of stone had those stones inscribed with letters not so that they might be honored, but so that they might be burdened—not a title of honor, but the weight of a burden. For one who fulfills the law under compulsion is not the law’s friend but its enemy.

The wording is connected and explained in this way. As if he were saying: So that I may run with an enlarged heart along the way of your commandments, therefore, Lord, establish for me the way of your ordinances—that is, your ordinances, which are the way—as a law: make the law stable for me, namely, so that what I previously understood according to the letter I may fulfill spiritually. Therefore you ought to establish the law for me, because I shall seek it, so that I may progress in it more and more; and this always—that is, for as long as I am in this life. For here it is always sought in order that it may be held, and it is held lest it be abandoned.

But since even that law of which it is said, “The law entered in so that the offense might abound,” cannot be understood unless understanding is requested from him, therefore this man asks for understanding for this spiritual law, which is far more excellent, when he says: “Lord, give me understanding”—that is, make me possess an enlightened understanding. Once understanding has been given, I shall examine your law, not in order to know it, but in order to do it. And truly I shall examine it, because I shall keep it with my whole heart—that is, I shall keep it in such a way that I love God with my whole heart and with my whole soul, and my neighbor as myself.

Again, because it cannot be kept unless the one who commands gives help, he adds: “Lead me, Lord,” because by myself I cannot advance along the path of your commandments—that is, make me fulfill your commandments, which are the path. And he rightly says “path,” because it is the narrow way that leads to the courts of life. Yet one does not run along it without God’s help; therefore he adds: “Because I desired it.” And since it is not the willer’s or the runner’s achievement, but God’s, who has mercy and gives us both the will and the ability to complete what is good, he therefore adds:

Incline my heart toward your testimonies. That is, give me a willing and devoted mind toward your commandments, because you have testified that God demands of us that we struggle even to the shedding of blood. Incline it in such a way that it is not directed toward greed—that is, so that I may worship you freely, not for some profit outside yourself. For all greed is cut away if God is worshiped freely.

And because greed concerns not only money but also human praise, he adds: “Turn my inner eyes away”—those, namely, of which it is said: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light.” Turn these eyes away, I say, lest, in observing his law, they see—that is, set before themselves—vanity. For our actions are judged not by their outward function but by their intention and end: namely, when we do something good, whether we do it for human praise or for some such motive. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Take care not to practice your righteousness before people; otherwise you have no reward with your Father.”

He said, “lest they see vanity,” because death follows vanity; therefore he adds: “Give me life, Lord, in your way, dead as I am in my vanity.” He calls Christ “the way,” since Christ said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” And he rightly asks to be given life in truth, for truth is opposed to vanity. Therefore, just as vanity brought death, so truth will bestow life.

Establish your word for your servant. As if he were saying: In order that you may give me life, therefore, Lord, you who made your word unstable for your free man, make your word stable for your servant—that is, make me not merely know what you speak, but do it. And let this be in your fear—not servile fear, but filial fear, which perfect love [Col. 1060D] does not cast out.

Cut away my reproach. As if he were saying: In order that your word may be stable for me, cut away my reproach—namely, that which I suspected in others, that they did not worship you freely. Thus the accuser of the brothers said of blessed Job: “Does Job worship God for nothing?” For many, through ill will or rivalry, accuse others from mere suspicion in this way, because what they see in themselves they easily suspect in another.

But this man, considering what is commanded—namely, “Do not judge before the time,” and similar things—desires to be given a love that removes every wicked suspicion concerning his neighbor. Therefore, as if he were saying, you ought to cut away my reproach, because my judgment, which arises from suspicion, is bitter and tasteless to me; but your judgments—since you command that nothing concerning one’s neighbor be judged except what is good and true—are pleasing to me, that is, pleasant and sweet.

These judgments may also be understood as those that are true and certain, which will finally appear when the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts.

Behold, I have desired your commandments. As if he were saying: Behold why I ask that you take away my reproach: namely, because I have desired your commandments—that is, the love by which I may love my neighbor as myself and no longer, through ill will or envy, suspect any evil concerning him, but judge everything good that you commanded when you said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.” For the new man gave new commandments to the world.

And because I have desired your commandments, therefore, Lord, give me life in your equity—that is, in Christ, who has been made for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.

**Vau**, and he himself.

## EXPLANATION

The holy congregation asks that the Lord who saves be granted to it, so that it may put its enemies to shame concerning eternal reward and make progress in the law of the Lord through constant meditation. Therefore the Lord himself and Savior is designated by the name of the letter Vau. Notice how beautifully the fifth letter itself is now called the sixth, and he himself is the one of whom it is said: “But you are the same”—that is, eternal. Through faith in him, the Church itself has merited to exist and, with one and the same devotion, to reign with him here and in the future.

## COMMENTARY

And let it come upon me. As if he were saying: I say that you should give me life in equity, so that, having been given life, I may desire your commandments. Therefore, O Lord, let the one who ought to be called not merely merciful but your very mercy—because through him you will show and bestow all mercy upon the world—come upon me to conform me to himself. Let this happen not through my merit, but through your word—that is, according to your promise—namely, so that, according to faith, the promise may be firm for all the seed.

And I shall answer. As if he were saying: When he comes upon me, I shall answer confidently—that is, I shall set forth the word of faith to those who reproach me for that very word of faith. This is the word of faith: “If you believe in your heart that Jesus is Lord, and confess with your mouth that God the Father raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” For one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation.

In answering, I say, I shall not presume upon myself, but because I have hoped in your words. That is, I shall place my hope in this alone, because you said: “It is not you who speak; for I will give you a mouth and wisdom,” and so forth.

But because many, unable to endure reproaches, fell by denying, yet afterward came back to life through repentance—as Peter, terrified by fear, sinned for a moment, but afterward was restored by weeping and even crowned by confessing—while many others fell completely through denial because afterward they did not progress by weeping, this man, fearing human weakness, implores divine mercy, lest he ever fall by denying under some terror without at least coming back to life through repentance.

Therefore he says: “And do not take away.” This is connected as follows: He said, “I have hoped in your words”; and because I have hoped in you, therefore, Lord, “do not take away the word of truth”—that is, do not allow the word of faith to be taken from my mouth through any terror of reproach. Let it not be taken away altogether—that is, do not let it be removed to such an extent that it could be said to have been taken away in every manner. For it is taken away altogether from those who deny in such a way that they make no further progress through repentance.

It follows:

For I have hoped exceedingly in your judgments. This means: I ask that you not take it away altogether, not absolutely, because if I should ever fall, this will not be for my despair but for my salvation, since “all things work together for good for those who love God.”

As if he were saying: The saints and elect, presuming upon you, did not fall; others, presuming upon themselves, fell away from you. Yet they belonged to your body, because, recognizing themselves, they wept and found grace much more firmly, since they lost their pride. Therefore I do not despair, but rather hope in your judgments—that is, if you judge me to be such that I should at some time fall in order to rise stronger. And I do not hope a little, but beyond what we ask or understand.

And I shall keep your law. I say, do not take the word from my mouth; and if you do not take it away, then I shall keep your law—that is, love, which is called law because the whole law and the prophets depend upon the two commandments of love.

And I shall keep it always, truly always, both in this age and in the age to come after this age. Hence the Apostle says: “Whether prophecies will be abolished, or knowledge destroyed, love will never fail.” For here its commandments are kept, but not without fear; then, without any fear, falls will be guarded against, because the nearer we see God, the more ardently we love him. And then one’s neighbor will be loved without any suspicion, since he himself will be all in all.

And I walked in spaciousness. The preceding verses of this psalm contain prayer and supplication; those that follow contain, as it were, an account of the effect of that supplication. The connection is therefore as follows.

As if he were saying: I was praying for the things just mentioned, and you heard me by placing me in spaciousness; in that spaciousness I walked—that is, I took delight. He calls the Spirit “spaciousness,” of which it is said: “The love of God has been poured out in your hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” He made us ask for what we desire to receive, seek what we wish to find, and knock at what we strive to reach.

And truly so, because he says: “I walked in spaciousness,” since I sought your commandments by asking, seeking, and knocking—not in order to know them, but to do them.

And I spoke of your testimonies. Truly I sought the commandments. For I did so by speaking, meditating, and practicing. He sets down these three in order, beginning with speech: Thus I spoke of your testimonies, or announced and commended your commandments, even in the presence of kings; and I was not put to shame by silence, nor was I led astray.

And truly I was not put to shame, because I meditated on your commandments, always thinking about them, for I loved them. And I not only spoke and meditated, but also lifted up my hands toward them, because I loved them. The hands are works; and the one who lifts up his hands toward the commandments is the one who does them not for earthly remuneration but for eternal reward. But one who acts for human praise or for some earthly thing does not lift up his hands but lowers them.

And, as if he were saying, in these three ways—speaking, meditating, and lifting up my hands—I was always exercising myself in your ordinances, that is, in your commandments, which truly justify.

**Zain**, olive, or fornication.

## EXPLANATION

That chorus of saints commends the hope of the Lord’s promises wholly to our understanding, so that what glorious truth promises may remain firm in our minds. It declares that for this reason the faithful endure the world’s adversities most willingly. For who would fear temporal death when eternal life is promised to him?

That very life, which is received here in hope and there in reality, is expressed under the name of the olive, which the letter Zain designates. For even in this pilgrimage the faces of the saints are gladdened by oil; and in that homeland the saints grow rich through the eternal vision and indwelling of the Holy Spirit. Since the grace of that same Spirit is sevenfold, the seventh letter is rightly called “olive.” The name “fornication,” however, suits sinners who abandon the law of the Lord.

## COMMENTARY

Remember. As if he were saying: Because I was exercising myself in your ordinances, therefore, Lord, you who were forgetful of your freedman, remember your word—that is, the promise made to your servant. Fulfill your promise to your servant, which you made to him when you said: “In your patience you will possess your souls. Not a hair of your head will perish. God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able,” and so forth.

Remember the word in which you gave me hope—that is, caused me to hope—and this hope comforted me in my humiliation, that is, in the most severe tribulation, persecution, and abasement by which my persecutors thought to humble me—that is, to lead me astray. And therefore it comforted me because your word, the aforementioned word of promise, gave me life—that is, gave me the assurance of true life—as in: “In your patience you will possess your souls.”

The proud acted wickedly. As if he were saying: Why do you say that you have been humbled, and whence has humiliation come upon you? The answer is: I have been humbled because the proud—that is, persecutors unwilling to obey God’s law—wanted to make me so. But while they acted wickedly and led me astray, I persisted, because I did not turn aside by transgressing your law.

And I did not turn aside because, O Lord, I remembered your judgments made from of old—that is, I kept in mind the just condemnation and abasement made from the beginning, in the first parents, because they turned aside from your law. And I was comforted in them by contrast, considering that if their neglect of your commandments brought death, then, conversely, their observance by me would bring life.

Weariness seized me. Refer this verse to the first part of the preceding verse in this way: Because I remembered your judgments, therefore weariness seized me—that is, I was troubled, fearing that I might fail. And this was on account of sinners who abandoned your law—that is, on account of the persecutors who transgressed and tried to lead me astray and associate me with themselves.

Refer the following verse likewise to the final part of that same verse: Because I was comforted by your commandments, therefore your ordinances were songs for me—that is, sweet and delightful—even in the place of my pilgrimage, that is, in this present life, where there is every misery and scarcely anything delightful.

The preceding verse, in which he said, “Remember the word,” may also be understood otherwise; and, according to this interpretation, what has been said from that point to here must be partly changed. The continuation would then be as before.

As if he were saying: Because I shall exercise myself in your ordinances, therefore, Lord, remember the Word who is to be incarnate, whom you promised to your servant. That is, send the one whom you are going to send, so that through him I may learn how I ought to exercise myself in your ordinances.

Remember, I say, the Word in whom you gave me hope—namely, that through him blessing would come to all the nations. And this hope comforted me in my humiliation—that is, in the humiliation of mortality and suffering, which I contracted from the first parents. And therefore, as if he were saying, the hope given to me in him comforted me, because your word ministered through him gave me life—that is, your teaching, presented to the world through him, restored the life of the soul within me.

[Col. 1063D] The proud acted wickedly. As if someone were saying: “Have you really been humbled?” Indeed I have, through the transmission of sin from the first parents. For the proud—that is, the first parents, who transgressed God’s command not through weakness or ignorance but through pride—they, I say, acted wickedly, and not a little wickedly, but altogether, that is, in every way. For through their sin they not only deserved death themselves, but also handed the cup of death to their descendants.

But I did not turn aside from your law. As if he were saying: I shall not follow them, because insofar as I could, I did not turn aside from your law. And I did not turn aside because I remembered your judgments made from of old, as was said above.

And because I remembered your judgments made from of old, therefore weariness seized me—that is, I feared falling and failing on account of sinners who abandoned your law. This was because of the mortal and suffering weakness that I contracted from those first transgressors. The following verse is understood in this sense as in the earlier one.

I remembered your name in the night. As if he were saying: Truly your ordinances were songs for me in the place of my pilgrimage, because, O Lord, I remembered your name. That is, I did not claim it for myself, nor regard your name as something to be seized, as though I wished to be God for myself and have everything depend on my nod. Rather, I always kept this name—which is “Lord”—in my memory, considering you Lord and myself servant, you omnipotent and myself powerless and stone-like. And this was in the night—that is, in adversity, not only in prosperity—or in the night of mortality and suffering, that is, in this present life, in which the very ignorance of truth is a dark night.

And because I remembered your name, therefore I kept your law—that is, I did not apostatize as the first proud ones did. I remembered your name, I say, in the night—that is, in tribulation. And this night—that is, this tribulation and persecution—was made for me by persecutors who abandoned your law, because I sought the ordinances that they neglected, namely, your commandments that justify, not in order to know them but to do them.

Or otherwise, according to another interpretation of “night”: this night—that is, the cloud of mortality and suffering—was made useful to me because, considering that they had fallen into this misery through neglect of your commandments, I sought your ordinances all the more earnestly—that is, your commandments that justify—so that what had been neglected unto death might, when observed, be for me unto salvation.

Or otherwise: I remembered your name, I say, and this memory was made effective for me because I sought the ordinances mentioned above—that is, I loved your ordinances with my whole heart.

**Heth**, life.

## EXPLANATION

The blessed host has come to the eighth letter, in which it is known to have obeyed the commandments while desiring to see the face of the Lord. [Col. 1064C] And because this desire will be fulfilled in the glory of the resurrection, the eighth letter rejoices in the name “life.”

## COMMENTARY

My portion. Notice that this is at the end of this group of eight, because the continuation looks back to that point. As if he were saying: Because I have sought your ordinances, therefore, Lord, teach me those very ordinances, so that I may progress in them more fully. You ought to do this because you are my portion—“portion” meaning participation. That is, because I participate in you as Lord. For while a human being remains human, he cannot be God; yet by participating in God, not by nature but by grace, he is joined to those gods of whom it is said: “I said, You are gods,” and so forth.

Or otherwise: “You are my portion,” that is, my share. As if he were saying: Let others choose whatever share they wish from worldly things; I shall choose you alone as my portion in the whole company of the guilty. Therefore teach me your ordinances.

I said that I would keep. He proves what he said previously, namely, that you truly are my portion, because you are the portion of all who keep your law, and so forth, which follows concerning those who act. And, as if he were saying, I am one of them, because I said—that is, firmly resolved—to keep your law. Therefore you are my portion; therefore teach me your ordinances.

But since his law cannot be kept unless he is continually invoked, he must be invoked, because faith obtains what the law does not obtain. Therefore he adds: “I have entreated your face”—that is, so that your face, not mine, might appear in me through its effect; that is, so that your will, not mine, might appear, and I might be fit to keep your law.

And this was with my whole heart—that is, with every affection and all my strength. Therefore have mercy on me, not because of my merit, but according to your word—that is, according to your promise—so that I may be a son of promise, not of presumption.

And, as though certain that he would be heard, he adds: “I considered my ways.” As if he were saying: Because I entreated your face, therefore I considered—that is, attended to—my foul ways, and turned my feet—that is, my affections [Col. 1065A]—toward your testimonies, that is, toward your beautiful ways.

I am ready. As if he were saying: I turned my feet so completely that I am ready to keep your commandments as they ought to be kept. And I am so ready that I have not been disturbed in keeping them by any fear.

And as if someone were asking, “From where did you get this fear of disturbance?” he adds: “The ropes of sinners.”

As if he were saying: I have not been disturbed, although I suffer many impediments. For the ropes of sinners—that is, the many entanglements and impediments of those sinners of whom it is said, “Woe to those who drag their sins as a long rope”—surrounded me, that is, encompassed me on every side, now with threats and tortures, now with blandishments. Yet they did not destroy me, because I did not forget your law.

At midnight. Truly I was not disturbed in keeping your commandments, because at midnight—that is, in the fiercest tribulation—I rose. For tribulation did not press upon him in such a way as to cast him down, but exercised him so that he might rise.

I rose, I say, to give thanks to you—that is, to praise you with heart and also mouth. And I did this because I was above your judgments—that is, I was made not inferior but superior through your righteous judgments, through your just correction, which did not depress but justified.

He calls tribulations and paternal scourges “judgments,” with which he scourges every son whom he receives. Concerning these the Apostle Peter says: “It is necessary that judgment begin from the house of God; but if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who have not believed the Gospel? If the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?”

I am a participant. I rose, I say, to confess to you, and by confessing to you I thus became a participant with all who fear you with a chaste fear. Why is “to be humbled” placed here rather than “to be exalted”—of those who fear you and keep your commandments? As if he were saying: In this I became a participant with those who fear you, that I keep your commandments, which they themselves keep.

And their number, as if he were saying, is not small, because “the earth everywhere is full of the mercy of the Lord”—that is, full of those restored and renewed by the Lord’s mercy, namely, by him who should be called not merely merciful but the very mercy of the Lord, because through him the Lord showed and bestowed all mercy upon the world.

And because I have become a participant with those who fear you, therefore, Lord, teach me your ordinances.

**Teth**, good.

## EXPLANATION

The blessed people enter to sing the ninth letter. In it they give thanks that they were humbled, so that they might reach the Lord’s ordinances with the greatest devotion. They assert that his testimonies are greater than all riches for them, and, explaining the name of the present letter as well, they say that their good is to meditate humbly on the word of God.

## COMMENTARY

You have dealt well. This is connected with what precedes as follows: Therefore I ask that you teach me your ordinances, so that I may progress in them more fully, because they are sweet and delightful to me. And this is not from myself, but because you have dealt well with your servant—that is, you have made the good itself delightful to me. And this is a great gift of God: that good should delight anyone.

But when the work of the law, which is good, is performed out of fear of punishment and not out of love of righteousness, God is feared, not loved; it is done servilely, not freely. “The servant does not remain in the house forever, but the son remains.” Therefore you have dealt well with your servant by making him who previously was a servant a son, so that what he previously did servilely he may do freely. And you did this not because of my merit, but according to your word—that is, according to your promise—namely, so that I may be not a son of presumption but a son of promise; or, I speak of a servant who is now acting according to your word.

Goodness and discipline. As if he were saying: Because you have shown goodness to me, your servant, therefore teach me goodness and [Col. 1066A] discipline and knowledge. He asks that these be increased and perfected in him. For how can one who earlier said, “You have shown goodness to your servant,” now say, “Teach me, Lord, goodness,” unless it is so that divine grace may become more manifest through the sweetness of goodness? Those too had faith who said, “Increase our faith, Lord.” And this is the prayer, or song, of those making progress, for as long as one lives here. In this life one must always pray to the Lord that every good thing may be increased: “Teach me discipline.” By discipline he means the Lord’s fatherly correction, concerning which Solomon says: “For whom the Lord loves, he corrects; but he chastises every son whom he receives.” Concerning this the Apostle Peter says: “Every discipline at present seems to be not of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have struggled through it.” Whoever, then, is shown goodness by the Lord—that is, whoever is inspired by him with delight in the good—must earnestly pray that this good may be so greatly increased in him that he not only despise bodily pleasures for its sake, but also patiently endure every kind of suffering for it. Thus salutary discipline is joined to goodness—not to just any small goodness, but to so great a goodness, that is, holy charity, which under its pressure cannot be extinguished but is rather kindled more and more.

Therefore, because it was insufficient simply to have said “goodness”—meaning, naturally, goodness strong enough to endure discipline—a third statement is added: When charity in goodness becomes so great that it cannot be extinguished by the tribulations and temptations imposed by discipline, then this statement becomes necessary: that a person know himself and understand what he has deserved and what he has received from the Lord, lest he prove ungrateful. Thus he says: “Teach me, Lord, goodness,” by inspiring charity; “teach me discipline,” by granting patience; “teach me knowledge,” by enlightening understanding.

It follows: “For I have believed your commandments.” It seems more fitting if he had said, “For I have obeyed your commandments.” One believes promises, therefore, and obeys commandments; but here he receives “commandments” in another sense. His meaning is: Therefore you should teach me goodness, [Col. 1066C] and so forth, because I have believed your commandments—that is, I have believed your commandments to be the justifications mentioned above. Therefore, as if he were saying: “Your faith”—that is, “I have believed in the grace of the rock, by which I shall fulfill what you have commanded.”

Before I was humbled, I went astray. The Lord said, “Teach me discipline,” and someone might say: “Why must you be chastised?” The answer is: Because I transgress, just as I must be chastised; as before, because I transgressed, I was chastised. For [it is] as if he were saying: I was humbled in the first parent by the punishment of death. “Before I was humbled, I went astray”: this is the transgression that preceded and caused the humiliation. This humiliation must rightly be referred to Adam, in whom the whole of human nature was corrupted as in its root, because he refused to be subject to the truth. It benefits the vessels of mercy to undergo this humiliation, so that, condemned for their pride, they may love obedience. It follows:

Therefore I have kept your word. This means: Because you humbled me so severely on account of the first transgression, therefore, lest I be humbled again in the same way, I have kept, as far as I could, your word—that is, your commandments. 

You are good. As if he were saying: Because I have kept your word, therefore, Lord, teach me more and more to attend to your justifications; and let this be in goodness—that is, not in sadness but in joy. For God loves a cheerful giver. I say, in your goodness, and therefore “your,” because you are naturally good, that is, holy and joyful. Nothing is more equitable than that the goodness of the one who is truly good should be preserved.

The iniquity of the proud has multiplied against me. This continues the earlier statement, “Teach me discipline.” As if he were saying: It is necessary that you teach me discipline by giving knowledge, because I fear that I may fail. For the iniquity of the proud—that is, the unjust tribulation and seduction of persecutors—has multiplied against me. But, as if he were saying: However fiercely iniquity may rage, charity will not grow cold in me, because with my whole heart—that is, with my entire mind and all my strength—I will search out your commandments. “I give you a new commandment,” he says, “that you love one another.”

Or alternatively: “The iniquity of the proud”—that is, the sin of the first parents, who through pride, not through weakness or ignorance, neglected God’s commandments—“has multiplied against me” with respect to punishment, because through it I have become weak in many ways, inwardly and outwardly. But, as if he were saying: In order that I may escape, whatever others may do, I will not imitate their pride; rather, with my whole heart I will search out your commandments—not in order to know them, but in order to do them. “Commandments” is taken here in a general sense as divine precepts; in the earlier statement it refers specifically to the commandment of love.

Their heart is congealed. This continues as if he were saying: Certainly the heart of the proud—whether persecutors or the first parents—which by nature had been softened through grace, just as milk is naturally soft, was congealed, that is, hardened, by their own wickedness. But my heart, as if he were saying, has been softened, because God gives grace to the humble: namely, so that now they may love obedience and eventually receive exaltation.

It is good for me that. Earlier he said, “The iniquity of the proud has multiplied against me,” meaning the persecutors. And this, as if he were saying, is good—that is, useful—to me, because it serves for my correction. For through those tribulations you humbled me, so that I might learn your justifications—that is, so that I might attend more closely to and love your commandments. For, as Solomon says, “The prosperity of fools will destroy them.”

Or alternatively: “The iniquity of the proud of the first parents has multiplied against me”; and this is good for me, that is, useful, because you humbled me in this way so that I might learn to attend to and observe your justifications, from which I had earlier withdrawn through pride, by means of obedience. But because these justifications cannot be learned except by one to whom they are sweet and delightful, he therefore adds: “The law of your mouth is good for me.” As if he were saying: I say that I may learn your justifications; and you ought to teach them to me because the law of your mouth is good for me—that is, because your commandments are joyful and pleasant to me—and not a little so, but more than thousands of gold and silver. Charity loves the law of the Lord more than the avaricious person’s greed loves many thousands of gold and silver.

Ioth, knowledge or beginning.

## Explanation

The glorious host advances to the tenth letter. In it, the people ask that understanding of the commandments be granted to them, so that they may enjoy the gift of true life; and they ask that, through the Lord’s mercy, they may become blameless, lest they be confounded in that judgment. The letter is therefore rightly called “knowledge” or “beginning,” since in it the faithful people seek understanding from the one from whom they received the beginning of life. “Your hands,” it says, “made me and fashioned me; give me understanding,” and so forth.

“Knowledge” or “beginning” may also be interpreted in relation to the statement: “I have known, Lord, that your judgments are righteous,” which is read in the Hebrew truth as: “I know, Lord, that your judgment is just.” This is the beginning of a more perfect knowledge, which is to be revealed in the future, because now we know in part and prophesy in part.

## Commentary

Your hands made me. Since the law of your mouth is so delightful to me, therefore, Lord, give me understanding—that is, restore in me the rational and intellectual nature that you placed in me before the transgression, when I existed in an abundance of virtues. And rightly, as if he were saying, I ask to be restored by you, because you created me. For your hands made me inwardly in my soul and fashioned me outwardly in my body—as though one might add, “and by the Spirit presiding within.”

For what [benefit?] do you ask to be restored? The reason is so that others may be conformed to me. This is what he says: “Those who fear Christ”—that is, all who fear you with chaste fear—“will strive to be conformed to me and to imitate me.” And they will rejoice in you, not on my account, but because I have hoped in the word—that is, in your promise—beyond what we ask or understand. [Col. 1068A] For the good that awaits us will be greater than either our reason asks or our measure understands. Such is what the Apostle says: “Be imitators of me, beloved children”—that is, not insofar as I am from myself, but insofar as I imitate Christ.

I have known, Lord, that. As if he were saying: Therefore I have hoped not in myself but in your word, because I have truly known that your judgments—that is, your commandments, which you judge ought to be observed—are not merely equitable but are equity itself, because those who observe them are made equitable and just. Therefore they must be held fast and loved. But I neglected them, and therefore you humbled me with mortal humiliation in the root; and this was in truth, that is, according to your true judgment.

Let your mercy come. As if he were saying: Since your anger came upon the one who had earlier withdrawn from your commandments, therefore, Lord, grant your mercy to your returning servant. For to one who acts according to your word—that is, according to your commandments—let your mercy come; that is, let your merciful affection be applied, so that in this stormy life of temptation it may console me. For now there are the consolations of the miserable; eventually there will be the joys of the blessed.

Let your mercies come to me. As if he were saying: I ask not only that your mercy be shown to me, but also that your acts of mercy come to me—namely, that you call me, forgive my sins, and justify me, so that I may live with true life. I say “live,” because your law is my meditation; that is, because I meditate continually on your law. This meditation is the thought of one who strives. For the one who meditates on God’s law in such a way that he loves God possesses true life. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Observe the commandments, if you wish to attain life.”

Let the proud be confounded. As if he were saying: Let your mercies come to me, whereas the proud—that is, the persecutors—should be confounded; that is, let them recognize themselves as deserving of shame, whether by a good or by an evil shame. I say, therefore, “Let them be confounded,” because they acted unjustly; and truly unjustly, because they practiced iniquity against me. For what is more unjust than for a person to be evil in himself and also to labor to draw others into evil? They, I say, wanted to lead me astray; but I, rather than yield to them, will exercise myself in your commandments—not to know them, but to do them.

Let those who fear you turn to me. As if he were saying: Since I will exercise myself in your commandments, therefore let those who fear you turn to me—that is, let them conform themselves to me. And, as if he were saying: By “those who fear you” I mean those who have understood inwardly your testimonies—that is, your commandments—not merely to know them but to do them.

Let my heart be blameless. As if he were saying: So that others may be converted by my example and imitate me, therefore, Lord, let my heart become blameless—that is, without blemish—and irreproachable in your justifications, so that I may not be confounded; that is, so that those who follow me may not be able to say, “This man began to build but was unable to finish.”

Caph, hand.

## Explanation

[Col. 1068D]

The pilgrim people sing the eleventh letter in this land, in which they joyfully confess their immense desire for the Lord’s coming. They also enumerate how many insults from the proud they have endured. Finally, they ask to persevere in the Lord’s commandments by his gift. This devotion of the mind is signified by the letter Caph, which is interpreted as “hand” in such a way that it signifies the palm or hollow of that same hand: that is, not contracted but open, with the fingers spread wide. The hand therefore signifies the works either of the heart, of the body, or of love itself within. Its opening is what the Psalmist commends when he says: “Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him,” and so forth.

## Commentary

My soul has languished for your salvation. As if he were saying: Therefore, Lord, you ought to make my heart blameless in your justifications, and my soul has languished in itself so that it might make progress in me.

It must be understood that not every languishing is a punishment or a fault; there is also a laudable and desirable languishing. Since progress and decline are opposites, progress is properly understood in the good and decline in the evil. Yet, in order to indicate that one may progress in evil or decline in good, the meaning is specified: progress may also be understood in evil, and decline from good into evil is bad, whereas decline from evil into good is good.

That progress may be understood in evil is testified by the Apostle when he instructs Timothy: “Avoid profane and vain babblings, for they will advance greatly toward impiety”; and elsewhere: “They will progress toward worse things.” Decline from good into evil is bad, but decline from evil into good is good. Such is the languishing understood here. It signifies a certain desire arising from love.

This desire was not absent from the creation of the world until the birth of the Virgin in the body of Christ. There were always some who awaited the one desired by all nations to be revealed, as Simeon did, who said: “Do you think I shall endure? Do you think I shall see?” and so forth. After the Virgin’s birth this desire in a certain way came to rest until the Lord’s ascension. After the ascension, however, there have not ceased—and until the end of the world there will not cease to be—those who await the revelation of that one desired by the world.

The Apostle shows this when he says: “As for the rest, there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord will render to me on that day; and not only to me, but also to all who love his manifestation”—that is, who desire his coming and his kingdom. Concerning this affection, namely, the fact that such desire is signified, the speaker says: “My soul has languished in itself, reaching toward your salvation,” presuming nothing from itself but everything from your salvation. And therefore my soul has languished, because I have hoped not in merits but in the word—that is, in your promise—so that I might be a son of promise, not a son of pride. And I have not hoped for little, but for more than we ask or understand; for the future reward will be greater than the labor in the vineyard. This hope causes what believers do not see to be awaited through patience.

[Col. 1069C] My eyes have languished. He seems to say the same thing by another comparison drawn from servants. Servants turn away from looking upon themselves and look toward the gaze of their masters, so that they may always be ready to do what their masters indicate. Similarly he says: My eyes—and the inward eyes, reason and understanding—have withdrawn from their own gaze and are directed toward your word, that is, toward your promise. My eyes, I say, presuming nothing on my part but everything from your promise, say: “When will you console me?” For speaking belongs to the mouth, whereas seeing belongs to the eyes.

He rightly says this, because he means not outward eyes but inward eyes, whose speaking is the very desire of prayer. When he says, “When will you console me?” he shows that he is suffering delay. This may be so that the deferred joy may come more sweetly, or because the experience of those who desire is being expressed: within the passage of time that is brief to the one who comes to help, it is slow to the one who loves him. Thus “When will you console me?” means, “How long will you delay true consolation from me?” Here there is only the consolation of the miserable, not yet the consolation of the blessed, which he desires. As spiritual desires burn, carnal desires undoubtedly grow numb.

This is what he says: “For I have become like a wineskin in frost.” By the wineskin is understood mortal flesh; by the frost, which is the hard dew of heaven, is understood the heavenly gift, by which, as though restrained by cold, carnal desires become numb. His meaning is: Therefore you ought to console me, because you have made me fit for this. For I have become like a wineskin placed in frost. A wineskin is soft by itself, but if it is placed in frost it becomes hard. So our flesh, which by nature is soft because of its desires, becomes hard and rigid through heavenly grace, lest it dissolve amid the flowing desires of the flesh. Hence it comes about that God’s justifications do not slip from the memory, because the mind is occupied with nothing else. Therefore he says next: “I have not forgotten your justifications,” for the fervor of desire had made a clamour [the syntax is uncertain], so that the love of charity might burn. [Col. 1070A]

Or alternatively, as if he were saying: I rightly desire consolation, because, just as a soft wineskin, if placed in frost, becomes useless for receiving liquids unless it is first softened by heat, so, because charity has grown cold in me through the abundance of iniquity, I have become useless for receiving liquids—that is, for fulfilling your commandments and teaching—unless I am first dissolved by the ardor of your Spirit, that is, by charity. And it is as if he were saying: However useless I may be, I have nevertheless not forgotten, insofar as I could, your justifications.

How many are the days of your servant, when will you execute judgment on those who persecute me? He said, “When will you console me?” And rightly, as if he were saying: I desire consolation because I am in my days—that is, in days of calamity and complete misery—which I made my own by transgressing. For the days you had given me were full of joys and eternal; but I made for myself days full of hardship and misery.

And how many are such days of your servant—that is, how long will you delay bringing me out of the days of prison and tribulation? And when will you execute judgment—that is, make a distinction—so as to bring me out from those who persecute me? That is, how long will you delay separating locally those whom you have already divided morally?

The wicked have recounted fables to me, but not like your law. As if he were saying: I did not speak idly when I said “those who persecute me,” because the wicked have recounted their fables to me—that is, their trifles—to deceive me and lead me astray. But those fables are not to be heard as your law is. And rightly I say “as your law,” because all your commandments are truth, whereas theirs are fables. Your law is such that it does not depend so much on the ornament of elegant words as on the force of its meanings. It was on account of this truth that the wicked persecuted me. Therefore, Lord, help me, so that I may not decline into evil and may progress in the good.

They nearly finished me on earth, but I did not abandon your commandments. As if he were saying: It is necessary that you help me, because the wicked finished me—that is, afflicted and put me to death—and this is my completion, that is, my perfection. They were raging, I say, on earth, that is, in my flesh. And “nearly” means that it was very nearly the case that they fulfilled their entire will against me. For I seemed to have received a sentence of death in myself; yet, however fiercely they raged against me, I did not abandon your commandments.

Or alternatively: “They finished me by dragging me down to earth,” that is, into earthly and carnal desires—not because true completion consists in clinging to earthly things, but in their judgment. For just as spiritual men proclaim that completion consists in clinging to heavenly desires, so carnal men announce that true completion consists in clinging to earthly things. Therefore he says: They finished me according to their judgment, turning me toward the earth. Nevertheless, I did not abandon your commandments.

And therefore, Lord, give me inward life; and if I am put to death inwardly, do so according to your mercy—that is, let me not love life in such a way that, by denying life, I lose life. Thus, since I do not wish to abandon truth for the sake of life, I shall live by dying for truth. And therefore, as if he were saying, I ask you to give me life, so that I may keep all your testimonies—not by knowing but by doing them—that is, your commandments, which you have attested not only by deed but also by word.

Lamed, discipline.

## Explanation

The heavenly people arrive at the twelfth letter. In it, describing the Lord’s power and deeds, they say that all temporal things can come to an end, whereas his commandments can never find an end. They gladly proclaim themselves subject to their discipline: “I will never forget your justifications,” and therefore Lamed signifies discipline.

## Commentary

Forever, Lord. The one who speaks here, wearied, as it were, by the instability with which this life of temptation is filled, and inflamed in his tribulation by desire for the heavenly homeland, that is, the Jerusalem above, looks upward, as it were, and says: “Forever, Lord,” and so forth.

As if he were saying: I say, Lord, that you should give me life; but those who are in heaven—that is, the angelic spirits—do not need to be given life, because your word remains in them forever, that is, the commandment of truth.

Throughout one generation and another. As if he were saying: Your word remains not only in heaven but also on earth, because your truth is from generation to generation—that is, in every generation that succeeds and passes away—in the generation belonging to the Law and the Prophets, since even then there did not fail to be those who possessed the faith that was afterward revealed in Christ, and in the generation belonging to evangelical grace.

As if he were saying: Whether in this generation or in that one, your truth remains—not from itself, but because you established the cultivated earth, that is, firmly fixed the Church upon the foundation of which the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid,” namely, Christ. And because you established it, your truth remains.

By your ordinance. As if he were saying: Your truth remains on earth not only because of your foundation but also in heaven, because the “days”—that is, the heavenly spirits belonging to the true day, to true brightness—did not cling to the apostate angel but persevered in the truth. They do not possess this from themselves but from your ordinance, that is, from your disposition and will. And truly they possess it from you, since they serve you—that is, are subject to you—and obey you in all things, not only earthly but heavenly.

Alternatively, as if he were saying: I ask you to give me life; but those whom your grace has made heaven—that is, those who rain upon others—do not need to be given life, because in heaven, that is, in such persons, your word remains forever. And it remains not only in heaven—that is, in preachers who rain upon others through the words of their teaching—but also in those upon whom the rain falls, both in the earlier generation belonging to the patriarchs and prophets and in the later generation belonging to evangelical grace. This is not from themselves, but because you established the earth, and it remains, as was said above. You established not only the cultivated earth but also its cultivators, because the “days”—that is, all who belong to the light of faith, including knowledge of your commandments—and both cultivators and cultivated persevere in the truth, not through themselves but through your ordinance; for all things serve you, as was said above.

Unless your law had been my meditation. As if he were saying: Since all things serve you, therefore, Lord, give me life according to your mercy, so that I may not perish in my humiliation—that is, in mortal humiliation. This is taken from the end of the verse, where he says: “I would have perished in my humiliation.” He means: So that I may not perish, as I might perhaps have perished when the wicked nearly finished me on earth, unless this had helped me: that your law was my meditation. It was certainly the law of faith, not empty, but one that works through love, and through which grace makes people strong in temporal suffering, so that they do not perish in mortal humiliation.

I will never forget your justifications. As if he were saying: Since your law helped me so that I would not perish, therefore I will not forget your justifications—that is, the commandments of your law that justify. He repeats the equivalent reason, saying: Because you gave me life in them, lest I perish in mortal humiliation.

I am yours. As if he were saying: Since, insofar as it depends on me, I will not forget your justifications, therefore, Lord, save me—that is, make me persevere in them. You ought to do this because I am yours. I wished to be my own, and you lost me; but now I have become yours—that is, I attend to your will and set mine aside. Therefore you ought to save me. And truly I am yours, because I have sought your justifications—not to know them but to do them—setting my own aside.

The wicked have waited for me. Truly I have sought your justifications, because when sinners—that is, persecutors—were waiting for me, that is, dealing with me through delay and “luna” (“moon”; the sense is uncertain), as it says elsewhere, “Princes sat and spoke against me,” when, I say, they waited for me, as they truly did wait, in order to destroy me—that is, to lead me astray and conform me to themselves; and if they had done so, they would truly have destroyed me. Nevertheless, they did not lead me astray, because I understood your testimonies: I had true understanding of your commandments, namely, that they were not merely to be known but to be done, and that one must die before withdrawing from your commandments.

All perfection. As if he were saying: I understood your testimonies for this reason: I saw—that is, set before myself—the end of all perfection. All perfection consists in struggling for truth to the shedding of blood and in enduring every hardship for the supreme good. Its end—that is, its reward—is in life, acquired through the tribulations and many reproaches of this life and through death.

But since neither of these forms of perfection is beneficial unless charity is present in the one who suffers and confesses, as the Apostle testifies when he says, “If I deliver my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing,” he therefore adds: I saw—that is, I set before myself—not only the end of perfection but also your commandment. “I give you a new commandment,” he says, “that you love one another”—that is, the commandment of charity, which is exceedingly broad. For what is broader than that upon which the whole Law and the Prophets depend?

Or alternatively: I truly understood your testimonies because I considered that they are fulfilled in charity. This is what he says equivalently: “I saw”—that is, I attended to—“your commandment,” which is exceedingly broad: namely, that charity is the end of all perfection, as the Apostle says: “The end of the whole commandment is charity,” and so forth.

Mem, from which, or from the commandments themselves.

## Explanation

The blessed people, having advanced through much meditation on the Prophets and the Gospel, declare that they have understood the divine commandments beyond their teachers and elders, and therefore testify that the sweetness of the divine Scriptures has come to their mouths, surpassing honey and the honeycomb.

Thus Mem is interpreted as “from which,” as in the statement: “How I have loved your law, Lord!” and again: “How sweet are your words to my palate!” That is, from the affection of sweetness and love, signifying “from the inmost heart.” But when it is interpreted as “from the commandments themselves,” it means that love of them is to be conceived from the Lord’s commandments themselves; hence he says: “From your commandments I have gained understanding,” and so forth.

## Commentary

How I have loved your law. As if he were saying: I truly understood your testimonies, for I understood your law—that is, the law of faith. How? That is, in the manner in which it ought to be loved. He explains what that manner is by saying: “It is my meditation all day long”—that is, without interruption, with my whole heart and all my strength I meditate on it—not in order to know it but to do it. This is how the law of the Lord must be loved. Hence it says elsewhere: “His will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night.”

More than my enemies. As if he were saying: Rightly, Lord, I have loved your law, because through your commandment—that is, through your law—you made me wiser than my enemies. All who understand the law carnally are enemies of those who understand it spiritually. For, wishing to establish their own righteousness and refusing to be subject to God’s righteousness, they think they are saved by the righteousness of their works; therefore they are hostile to those who attribute salvation to no merits but to grace alone—that is, to those who understand the law spiritually.

Accordingly, understanding the law spiritually, he says: “You have made me wiser than my enemies through your commandment,” because I understood what they could not understand: namely, that people cannot be justified by the works of the law but by the law of faith alone. This is what the Apostle says: “The Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, attained righteousness; but Israel, pursuing the law, did not attain the law of faith, because it was not from faith but as though from works; for they stumbled over the stone of stumbling.” It follows:

Because it is mine forever. As if he were saying: Therefore I say that you have made me wiser than my enemies: your commandment, which is for them as though temporary, is for me eternal. As if he were saying: I expect eternal things from it, whereas they expect temporal things.

More than all my teachers. He said, “You have made me wiser than my enemies,” and, as if he were saying, not merely wiser than any enemies but even wiser than the foremost of them: I understood more than all who taught me—that is, I understood better than all the scribes and Pharisees who wanted to teach me and considered themselves alone to know the law perfectly. To them it is said in the Gospel: “Woe to you, who possess the keys of knowledge; you yourselves do not enter, and you prevent others from entering.”

And truly I understood more than they did, because while their thought is earthly vanity, your testimonies—that is, your commandments—are my meditation, as I testify to them even to the shedding of blood.

[Col. 1073B] I have understood more than the elders. He said, “I understood more than all who taught me,” and repeats the equivalent statement for another reason, which he adds, saying: “I understood more than the elders”—that is, more than those solemn and morose men who wished to be teachers, who merely enlarged their phylacteries and magnified their tassels, carrying the written law on their foreheads while they were transgressors in their hearts. And truly I understood more than they did, because I sought your commandments not in order to know them but to do them, which they did not do.

From every evil way. Truly I sought your commandments, because I restrained not only my hands but also my feet—that is, my affections—from every evil way, that is, from every evil work. Therefore I restrained not only my hand but my soul, so that I might keep your words—that is, your commandments—which must be kept in holiness.

From your judgments. He said, “I restrained my feet,” and [now explains] in this way, as if he were saying: I restrained them because I did not turn aside from your judgments—that is, from those works that you judge ought to be done. And rightly so, because you, who command nothing useless, have established nothing that contributes to your life. You have set before me a law that I did not fear as a servant but loved as a son.

How sweet are your words to my palate! As if he were saying: Since you have set your law before me, therefore your words—that is, your commandments—are sweet, for they are to my palate sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, that is, sweeter to me than every earthly sweetness.

Or alternatively: By clarified honey is understood the manifest teaching of wisdom; by the honeycomb, the hidden wisdom of teaching, enclosed in more obscure mysteries as honey is enclosed in the honeycomb. The image is drawn as though from earthly cells and from the mouth of one chewing. Thus he says: Your words—that is, the commandments which you yourself specially gave—are to my palate sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; that is, they are sweeter to me than every teaching of wisdom taught by teachers, whether it is manifest or conceals things.
