To me they are sweet.

From your commandments. As if he were saying: I rightly gained understanding through your words, because I gained understanding from your commandments—that is, I gained true understanding of your commandments, because I learned them not merely by hearing, as the scribes and Pharisees did, but by doing them. For the one who learns a thing by doing it knows it more perfectly.

And because your words are so sweet to me, this is equivalent to saying: Because I have loved the way of equity, therefore I have hated every way of iniquity. For no one perfectly loves equity who does not perfectly hate iniquity.

Nun, everlasting, or fish.

## Explanation

The blessed host reaches the fourteenth letter. In it, it rejoices that the light of the Lord’s word shines upon its feet; it commends its soul with the humblest act of satisfaction, seeking the Lord’s everlasting rewards, on account of which this letter received the name “everlasting.”

Moreover, that it is also interpreted as “fish” is shown by the one who, covered by the waves of the world, seeks the light of the word, saying: “I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord,” and so forth.

## Commentary

[Col. 1074A]

A lamp for my feet. As if he were saying: Rightly your words are a lamp for my feet—that is, for my works. And they are a light for my paths—that is, they are illumination for those narrower ways to which I must attend.

Notice that he says they are both a lamp and a light. A lamp receives its light from the Light, as do those mountains concerning which it is said: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help may come to me.” These are the apostles: they were illuminated from the Light, because the Sun of righteousness, rising, first illuminated them and through them led light down into the valleys. Therefore, in these and in other teachers, the divine word is a lamp. In Christ, however, who had illumination from himself because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, it is not a lamp but the Light itself—that is, the divine Word.

Juravi et statui. As though he were saying: Since your word is for me both a lamp and a light, therefore I swore and resolved, etc. Whatever the faithful soul resolves, this oath ought to arise from faith itself. And therefore he says: “I swore,” that is, I firmly confirmed it; and I say that I swore because I resolved to keep the judgments of your justice, that is, your commandments, which you judge to be just. For keeping them I have been humbled exceedingly, having suffered every kind of tribulation. For all who wish to live piously in Christ must suffer persecution. And because I am mortified outwardly, therefore enliven me, Lord, inwardly. This is the prayer of one who is making progress, as long as life is lived here. He had already been enlivened, but he asks to be enlivened more and more. “Enliven me,” I say, and this not according to my merit, but according to your word, that is, according to your promise—namely, that I may not be a son of presumption, but a son of promise.

Make acceptable the free offerings of my mouth, Lord, and teach me your judgments. As though he were saying: In order that you may enliven me, Lord, make me such that the free offerings of my mouth may be acceptable to you—that is, sacrifices of praise offered in a confession of love, not from the compulsion of fear—and teach me further to attend to your judgments, that is, your just commandments. This too is the voice of one making progress, as long as life is lived here.

My soul is always in my hands. As though he were saying: I therefore ask you to teach me your judgments, so that my soul may always be in my hands—that is, so that I may always offer my soul to you to be enlivened and sanctified. In this sense the expression is used only by way of comparison. Or, if “hands” is understood as works, we shall say: “May my soul always be in my hands,” that is, make me such that in all my actions I attend to the fruit of my soul. And you ought to do this, because, insofar as I could, I have made myself fit for it. For I have not forgotten your law—that is, the law of faith, which works through love.

Many, however (as though he were saying), have labored so that I might forget it, because sinners—that is, transgressors of that very law—set a snare for me, that is, prepared many obstacles for me. Yet I have not strayed from your commandments.

You acquired them as an inheritance. Truly I have not strayed; rather, I acquired your testimonies—that is, martyrdoms and commandments—to possess as an inheritance. Or, I acquired them by inheritance, that is, for an inheritance—namely, so that I might be your witness and your martyr. I speak of your testimonies as advancing into eternity. He says “into eternity” because they do not contain the temporal glory of people seeking a vain glory, but the eternal glory of people who suffer briefly and reign without end. Therefore he adds: For they are the rejoicing of my heart. As though he were saying: I rightly made them hereditary, because although they are an affliction of the body, nevertheless, because of the eternal glory that I hope to obtain through them, they are the rejoicing of my heart.

I inclined my heart to perform your justifications forever, because of tribulation. As though he were saying: Since your testimonies are the joy of my heart, therefore I inclined my heart—that is, I devoted my mind—to perform your justifications forever. Earlier he said: “Incline my heart, Lord.” Now he says: “I inclined my heart,” to show that what we do rightly is both a divine gift and an act of our own will.

But why does he say that the justifications are eternal, when the justifications themselves—that is, works of mercy performed for the needs of others—are temporal? Perhaps he says this because those works, if performed without love, are not justifications. If they are performed through love, however, love itself is eternal, and an eternal reward is prepared for it. Accordingly he says: “Forever, because of recompense,” that is, so that the one who loves forever may find in eternity what he loves.

### Samech, assistance

### Explanation

The Catholic company reaches the fifteenth letter, in which it says that the wicked—that is, the adversaries of the law—were hateful to it, while it loved the law of the Lord. It asks to be received by him so that it may escape the evils of the world; and it desires that its flesh be subjected to the fear of the Lord, lest it be judged for its transgression. It also explains the name of the letter, saying: “Help me, and I shall be saved.”

### Commentary

I have hated the wicked. This continues the same thought as the preceding verse. As though he were saying: Since your testimonies are the rejoicing of my heart, therefore I hated the wicked who wished to draw me away from them, and I loved your law.

It might seem more fitting for him to have said: “I hated the wicked and loved the just,” or: “I hated iniquity and loved righteousness.” For “just” and “wicked,” “righteousness” and “iniquity,” are opposites. But he placed “law” after “wicked” in order to show that he did not hate wicked people according to the nature by which they were made human, but hated their iniquity, because they had become enemies of God’s law.

But since no one can hate iniquity perfectly and love righteousness perfectly unless divinely assisted, he adds: “My helper and my protector.” As though he were saying: I say that I loved your law, but this was not from myself; it was because you are my helper, Lord, in bringing good to completion, and my protector in avoiding evil. Therefore I rightly hoped in your words—that is, in your promise, upon which we base our request or understanding, as we have often said already.

Depart from me, evildoers. He said that he loved the law, and therefore he turned to the wicked who wished to draw him away and said: “Depart from me,” that is, cease from your attempt to draw me away and from your harassment, you evildoers; then I shall scrutinize the commandments of my God.

He did not say, “I shall perform,” but “I shall scrutinize.” In order to know the law carefully and perfectly, he even urges the evildoers to withdraw from him. For the wicked do indeed drive people toward performing the commandments, but they draw them away from scrutinizing them—not only when they quarrel and persecute, but also when they honor and serve them, distracting them through their wicked counsels and deceitful dealings.

Receive me according to your word, and I shall live, and do not put me to shame in my expectation. Having brushed the evildoers away from the eyes of his heart like flies, he continues his prayer to the one of whom he spoke above. As though he were saying: Evildoers, away from my eyes! But you, Lord, receive me to protect me from evil and strengthen me in good, according to your word—that is, according to your promise, not according to my merit—and thus I shall live in the body, although dead because of sin. And because I shall live, therefore do not put me to shame in my expectation. His expectation was life; if they do not obtain life through this expectation, they are put to shame, because they would say: “This man began to build, but was unable to finish.”

Help me, and I shall be saved, and I shall always meditate on your justifications. It is as though someone were saying: Do you wish not to be put to shame in your expectation? Then meditate continually on the path of reading. But this man, fearing that such constant meditation might be interrupted by weariness of spirit, prays and says: “Help me.” This means: In order that I may not be put to shame in my expectation, therefore, Lord, help me to bring to completion the good that I began through the freedom of my will; and with your help I shall be saved—that is, I shall attain true salvation. And I shall be saved for this reason: because I shall always meditate on your justifications.

You have despised all who depart from your judgments, because their thought is unjust. Truly you will save me, who am always meditating on your justifications. For you will not condemn those who meditate continually. This is what he says: You have despised—that is, already condemned through inner darkness—all who depart from your righteousness, that is, all who are *orarii* [meaning uncertain] and do not meditate continually on your commandments. These are not only just, but justice itself, because when observed they make people just. And rightly you have despised them, because their thought is unjust.

It would seem stronger if he had said: “Because their works are unjust.” But he speaks of thought because all works, whether good or evil, proceed from thought. A person is first innocent or guilty in thought. It is said: “Holy thought will save you.” Of evil thought it is also said: “There will be inquiry into the thought of the wicked”; and the Apostle says: “Their thoughts accusing or defending one another.”

I have regarded all the sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I loved your testimonies. As though he were saying: Truly their thought is unjust, because they are transgressors. But since the Apostle says, “Where there is no law, there is no transgression,” and Gentiles who received no written law might therefore applaud themselves, he establishes a universal judgment and says: “All the sinners of the earth,” that is, all who cling to earthly things. In clinging to earthly things they are sinners—that is, transgressors of the law, even if not of a written law, nevertheless of the law given naturally.

All these, I say, I regard as transgressors, and the thought of all of them is unjust; therefore they will be condemned. But I, in order not to be one of them, therefore loved your testimonies—that is, your commandments—not merely to know them, but to perform them.

Nail me to the fear. As though he were saying: Since I loved your testimonies, therefore, Lord, nail my flesh—that is, restrain my carnal desires—with your fear, with a chaste fear, not a servile one but a filial one, which perfect love does not cast out. Hence the Apostle says: “I am crucified with Christ.” And elsewhere: “They crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.”

For the Lord did not, without reason, although he could have suffered and died on a simple piece of wood, stretch himself out upon a threefold wood so that both his feet and his hands were immovable. By this it was prefigured that we ought to imitate his passion and be conformed to him in such a way that all our members, as though nailed in place, may be immovable from works of iniquity.

What he adds about fear has this meaning, as though he were saying: With your fear, I say—with a chaste fear—restrain my flesh. For that law which threatens punishment but does not give righteousness does not nail my flesh. It restrains the hand, but does not restrain the mind, because the will to sin remains; this becomes apparent in the deed if impunity is expected.

But if your chaste fear nails my flesh, I shall not sin even if impunity is expected. For through love of righteousness, sin itself is a grievous punishment to me. He continues:

For I feared your judgments. As though he were saying: I therefore ask you to nail my flesh because I fear your judgments. I do not fear human judgments, however, but ultimately fear your future judgments; therefore I strive to avoid them.

### Ain, fountain or eye

### Explanation

The sixteenth letter is reached by the living members of the Lord, in which they ask for the advent of the sacred Incarnation, saying that the time has come for divine power to be displayed in destroying the proud. This, then, is the living fountain that is sought; this is the pure eye that seeks: “My eyes,” he says, “have failed in longing for your salvation.”

### Commentary

[Col. 1077A]

I have done judgment. Earlier he said, “I loved your testimonies,” and truly—as though he were saying—I loved them because I did judgment, distinguishing what ought to be approved from what ought to be rejected; and I did righteousness, bringing into action what ought to be approved. Therefore, Lord, do not hand me over to those who slander me.

Those who slander are persecutors: they bring false charges and draw one away. A person is handed over to them when, by God’s just judgment, he is permitted to consent and conform to them.

Receive your servant. Do not hand me over, I say, to those who slander me; rather, receive me as your servant when they drive me toward evil, so that I may be strengthened in good. And so that the proud—that is, those persecutors—may not slander me, that is, may not deceive me through their slander. This is the Greek construction. In our language it would be more suitably expressed: “Let them not slander me.” He calls “slander” the false charges, such as believing in a crucified thief, worshiping a dead man, and similar accusations.

The meaning is: Let the poisonous slanders of the proud not harm me, Lord, because my eyes have failed in longing for your salvation—that is, because I look toward the bronze serpent. It is known to all that the children of Israel perished in the desert because they transgressed and were destroyed by serpents. After many had perished, the Lord commanded Moses to make a bronze serpent and suspend it high in the middle of the camp. Whoever had been bitten by serpents and looked at that serpent was not harmed by the poison.

The bronze serpent is Christ, who came in the likeness of flesh, but not in sinful flesh, just as that serpent had the form of a serpent but was not a real serpent. It was rightly bronze, because bronze is solid and firm. “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.” Therefore, whoever looks upon Christ with the most diligent and intense devotion, attending to the fact that the innocent died for sinners and the merciful for the ungodly, will not be harmed by the poisonous objections mentioned above.

Therefore he says next: My eyes—that is, my inward eyes—have failed by going out toward your salvation, that is, by looking toward Christ, from whom all salvation comes. And they have been intent upon the word of your justice—that is, either upon your commandments, which justify, or upon your just promise.

Therefore, Lord, deal with me, your servant, not according to my merit but according to your mercy. And in this I ask for your mercy: teach me further to attend to your justifications. This is the song of one making progress, as long as life is lived here.

I am your servant. I rightly say, “Deal with your servant,” because I truly am your servant. Therefore give me understanding, so that I may know your testimonies. This too is the song of one making progress.

And you ought (as though he were saying) to show mercy to your servant because, O Lord, it is time to show mercy—that is, it is time to reveal grace and send the one whom you are going to send. Truly it is time to show mercy to your servant, because servants did not destroy your law by transgressing it.

Therefore grace must be revealed, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound even more. Hence the Apostle says: “The law entered in so that transgression might abound; and where transgression abounded, grace abounded even more.” Through this grace sins are forgiven and the works of the law are fulfilled.

Therefore I loved your commandments more than gold and topaz, that is, more than every precious thing of this world. And truly I loved your commandments because I hated every way of iniquity. For whoever perfectly loves righteousness must perfectly hate every iniquity. Hatred of iniquity itself is for that person a kind of direction toward righteousness. He indicates this when he says: “Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments.”

### Phe, mouth—from *ore*, not from *bone*

### Explanation

The prayer of the holy people enters the seventeenth letter, asserting that it opened its mouth and drew in the Spirit so that its prayer might be heard, and that its eyes poured out streams of water—pious tears—because the law of the Lord was not kept by the Jews. Rightly, then, this letter receives the name of “mouth,” in which a small and humble person opens the entrance of the heart and drinks in the Spirit of divine love.

### Commentary

Wonderful are your testimonies. As though he were saying: I rightly loved your commandments, because your testimonies—that is, your commandments—are wonderful. When observed, they accomplish something wonderful: earth becomes heaven, a wolf becomes a lamb, and similar things occur. Or they are wonderful in this respect also: they cause enemies to be loved and good to be returned for evil.

Therefore my soul scrutinized them, not merely to know them. And rightly so, because the exposition of your word—that is, of your testimonies—enlightens the simple. It truly enlightens them because it gives true understanding, namely, what the simple—that is, the humble—must avoid. For God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.

Therefore I made myself simple, because I opened my mouth in humility and confession. What could be more astonishing than this: although the good God gave good commandments, he nevertheless gave the law to people whom that same law could not enliven, and from the law itself there was no righteousness for them?

Hence the Apostle says: “For if a law had been given that could enliven, righteousness would truly have come from the law. But Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ.”

Why, then, was a law given that could not enliven, and from which there was no righteousness? Surely this is astonishing, surely astounding. And this man’s soul scrutinizes these wonders.

But what does it discover by scrutinizing? This, namely: that the exposition of your words enlightens and gives understanding to the simple. To which simple people? To the humble and the weak.

Do not therefore become proud or presume upon yourself, and you will understand why the good law was given by the good God, even though it could not enliven and from it there was no righteousness. For it was given in order to make you, who were great, small, and to show that you did not possess the strength from yourself to fulfill the commandments. Thus, in need of help, you would flee to grace and cry out: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak.”

For who can perform the Lord’s commandments as they ought to be performed except through faith, which works through love, and unless love is poured into his heart through the Holy Spirit?

This is what the simple man, understanding it, says: “I opened my mouth in humility and confession,” that is, I asked for or received and drew in the Spirit, through whom he works what I could not do by myself.

Hence it is said in the Gospel: “If you, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him.”

“I drew in the Spirit,” he says, because I desired to fulfill your commandments. But how could the weak do strong things, the small great things, except through the Spirit, through whom love has been poured into our hearts?

Look upon me. He said, “I drew in the Spirit,” and the more sweetly he drank, the more ardently he thirsted. Therefore he says next: Look upon me in my humility, you who despised me when I was growing proud, and have mercy on me by pouring love into my heart through the Spirit.

Have mercy, I say, according to the judgment of those who love your name—that is, according to the judgment you have made concerning all who love your name: namely, that you loved them first so that they might love you, as the Apostle John says: “We love him, but for this reason, because he first loved us.”

Or: according to the judgment of those who love your name, that is, according to the way in which you judge concerning all who love your name, saying: “I shall love those who love me.”

Direct my steps according to your word. What else was he asking than that, by God’s gift, he might love God, and by loving God love himself, and thus rightly love his neighbor as himself? And again, what else was he asking than that the commandments God imposes by commanding might be fulfilled by him through God’s help?

Direct my steps, I say, so that no iniquity may rule over me—that is, so that none may rule over me. For the more love rules in us, the less iniquity reigns in us.

So that no iniquity may rule over me: when an unlawful impulse comes, let it not be carried through to consent or to an act of injustice. Rather, redeem me by your Holy Spirit from the slanders of men—that is, make me unafraid of the slanders of men, lest they overcome me and lead me into evil works.

Slander is a false charge, and it does not make a person guilty except before a human judge. But where God is judge, no one is condemned by a false charge.

Why does he ask to be redeemed from slanders? He adds: So that I may keep your commandments. And in order that I may be able to keep them, make your face shine upon your servant; or make your face—that is, your will—appear in me through its effect.

For those who hear divine commandments and do not perform them, even if they retain them in memory, should not nevertheless be said to have learned them, since the Lord himself says: “Everyone who has heard from my Father and learned comes to me.”

Because my eyes have poured out streams of water. Recalling the time of sorrow for his former transgression and fearing to experience it again, he says: Teach me, Lord, your justifications, so that I may not fall into transgression again.

For my inward eyes have poured out streams, shedding broad channels of water; this is said hyperbolically. And why did his eyes pour out streams of water? He adds: Because they did not keep your law.

Why, then, is the failure to keep the law mourned, except so that grace may fulfill what ought to be fulfilled by those who ask, and assist the will of the believer?

### Sade, righteousness

### Explanation

The company of the saints, triumphant over its flesh, reaches the eighteenth letter. In accordance with the name of the letter, it confesses the Lord’s righteousness and says that it continually venerates his fiery words with uninterrupted love. Finally, it asks for understanding of the testimonies by which it may be enlivened forever.

### Commentary

[Col. 1079C]

You are righteous, Lord. As though he were saying: My eyes rightly wept because the law was not kept, since you, Lord, are the just author of that law. Therefore whatever you command is just, and your judgment will be right in the future, in which nothing is left unpunished.

In order to avoid this judgment, you commanded us earnestly—“to observe” is understood—to keep your testimonies, which are justice and truth. The Lord’s commandments are justice because they permit or prohibit nothing except what ought to be permitted or prohibited. They are also truth because whatever they threaten to the wicked or promise to the righteous is true. They are testimonies of salvation when fulfilled, but of condemnation when neglected.

My zeal has made me waste away. As though he were saying: Since you, Lord, are righteous and your judgment is right, therefore zeal—that is, devout indignation—made me waste away out of compassion, which I felt not only for friends but also for enemies. They had forgotten your words, through which they will incur your judgment.

And this did not arise from myself, but from the fact that your fiery word burned intensely within me, kindled by the fire of truth. Concerning this fire it is said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?”

This man was more truly kindled by that fire because he strove to lead his neighbors toward what he himself loved most ardently. He says: “Your word is exceedingly fiery, and your servant loved it.”

Because of this love I was regarded as a younger son by my older brother, that is, by the Jewish people: a youth, that is, foolish and small, and also despised, that is, contemptible to all.

Or it may be understood this way: Through this love I am a youth, that is, renewed in faith, and therefore despised by all. Yet I did not do what my older brother did. For he wished to establish his own righteousness and not be subject to the righteousness of God; therefore he forgot your justifications.

But I have not forgotten your justifications. And rightly so, because your righteousness is a righteousness producing eternity, whereas their righteousness consists in washing vessels and other such things. Your law is not a shadow, as their law is, but truth.

For the sake of keeping this law, outward tribulation and inward distress found me—that is, overwhelmed me. Yet your commandments are my meditation, namely, so that I might love those by whom I was being oppressed.

Let them rage, therefore, as much as they wish, and persecute me, provided that your commandments are not abandoned; rather, for the sake of those very commandments, let those who rage be loved.

Your commandments, I say, are my meditation. And rightly so, because your testimonies are commandments that endure forever. They are not only equitable but equity itself, and they make people equitable. I speak of them as leading into eternity.

Therefore give me true understanding in them, namely, so that I may understand how contemptible is whatever can be taken away by enemies, and that one must even die for those enemies; and thus, by dying, I may live in the land of the living.

Or: may I live by bringing life to an end amid tribulations, so that I may live forever. For one always lives from him through whom life is ended amid tribulations.

### Coph, calling

### Explanation

The most reverend chorus enters the nineteenth letter. In accordance with its name, it cries to the Lord with its whole heart, diligently seeking his justifications, rejoicing in the anticipation of confession in his word, and adding that it has learned that the testimonies of the Lord are founded forever.

### Commentary

I cried with my whole heart. As though he were saying: You ought rightly to give me understanding, because I sought you as one who ought to be sought, for I cried with my whole heart.

Many cry with their mouths but not with their hearts, and their cry is empty. Many, even though they are silent with their mouths, cry out in their hearts. Their cry may be hidden from human beings, but it cannot be hidden from God.

The cry of the heart is a strong intention of thought. In prayer it expresses the great affection of the one who desires, so that the result may not be despaired of. They truly cry with their whole heart when they think of nothing else.

These thoughts occur in many, but are frequent in few, because only the faithful cry in this way, so that they think of nothing else. This is what he confesses when he says: “I cried with my whole heart.” Therefore, Lord, hear me, so that, having been heard, I may seek your justifications more and more—not merely to know them, but to perform them.

I cried, I say, to you; therefore save me by giving perseverance, lest through weakness I deny you. For there is no salvation where weakness succumbs and truth is abandoned.

Save me, I say, so that I may keep your commandments. And you ought to save me because I anticipated your face in confession at the proper time, that is, with continual diligence.

This is drawn from neighbors who possess common fruit, each of whom is diligent to gather the fruit before the others. Or, if *in* is not taken as an added word, this may be the voice of those faithful people who were under the law but nevertheless foresaw through the Spirit that the Lord would come in the flesh, and conformed themselves to him.

The time was unripe because they were still oppressed by the law and had not yet been assisted by grace. For the holy patriarchs and prophets were still awaiting the Lord as though in darkness, through whom grace would be administered so that they might be saved.

In this unripe time many anticipated his face in confession, not believing that they would be justified through the law, but through the grace of the Lord. Thus they cried to him because they placed their hope beyond hope in his words and promises.

Or “unripe time” may be understood as this time of tribulation, labor, and complete misery, in comparison with the time when God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints. Here joy exists only in hope; there it will be received in reality. Therefore here one must give, and place hope beyond hope in the Lord’s words.

It may also be understood in another way, so that there is an apposition rather than a composition, as was said in the first interpretation. The present time, which is unripe, may also be called ripe in another respect, namely, because now weeping is profitable and repentance fruitful.

The unripe time, however, will be the time of the final judgment, because even then there will be repentance, but fruitless repentance, when the wicked will say: “We fools regarded their life as madness and their end as without honor. See how they have been counted among us, how they are numbered among the children of God,” and so forth.

Therefore in this ripeness of time one must confess and cry out to the Lord, and place hope beyond hope in his words. Hence whoever comes and knocks in this ripeness of time will immediately have the door opened to him.

My eyes anticipated you. Therefore he expresses it in clearer words: My eyes, with “toward you” understood, anticipated you at dawn, that is, with continual diligence. Hence elsewhere: “My eyes anticipated the watches.”

Or: my eyes, intent upon you, anticipated through tears the coming dawn of heartfelt contrition, when the hidden things of the darkness of hearts will be revealed and the purposes of hearts made manifest.

Or, if that portion of the faithful speaks which was under the law, we may understand the dawn as the day of the Lord’s Incarnation. For he, the only-begotten Son of God, like the true sun, dispelled every error of truth by the ray of his light. Many anticipated this day by hoping and by acting well in faith.

Such people can say: My eyes, intent upon you, anticipated the dawn, so that I might still meditate upon your words—not merely to know them, but to perform them. Therefore, Lord, hear my voice—that is, the voice of my heart—not according to my merit but according to your mercy, that is, so that you may grant me mercy; and then enliven me through judgment.

Mercy must be asked first, lest we be burdened by judgment, because God first takes away those from sinners without mercy to whom he will first give judgment and then life. This man, attending to this, says: “According to your judgment enliven me.”

And it is necessary that you enliven me inwardly, because there are those who put me to death outwardly. For persecutors have drawn near to me. They have drawn near enough, since they tear your flesh. And by drawing near to me, they have drawn near to iniquity. For the more someone persecutes the righteous, the more wicked he is reckoned. Thus they have become far from your law, which commands that even enemies be loved; or they have become far from me, who keep your law, although they might seem to draw near.

You are near. As though he were saying: The persecutors draw near outwardly, but you, Lord, are near inwardly. And all your ways—that is, all your scourges—are truth, because you scourge no one without cause.

It is said elsewhere: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” Here, however, he says that all God’s ways are truth, which seems contrary but is not. In good things, both are found in the ways of the Lord, namely mercy and truth, because by judging he comes to the aid of people, and by showing mercy he supplies what he promised.

In evil things and in all who are scourged, the Lord’s ways are truth alone, because, as we have said above, he scourges no one without cause.

And this, as though he were saying, that all your ways are truth I learned from your testimonies, or through your commandments, in the beginning—that is, in the earliest righteous people. Otherwise you would not scourge Abel and Job and the other early righteous people, unless your scourges were truth.

And let no one think that what happened to Abel was unjust. When a sin is expiated temporally, it is done so that the person may not be punished eternally.

### Res, head

### Explanation

Behold, the people victorious over vices now enter the twentieth letter. In it they ask to be enlivened because they sought the Lord’s commandments with the greatest devotion. They recall that salvation is far from sinners because they did not do similar things. They also testify that the beginning of the Lord’s words is truth. This is the “head” that the present letter reveals.

### Commentary
See my humiliation and rescue me. “Humiliation” may be understood here in three ways: either as the humility that every believer ought to display by acknowledging his weakness, yet nevertheless presuming concerning himself; or as the tribulation and degradation inflicted by persecutors; or as the humiliation brought about in our first parent. It is as though he said: “Be near, I say, O Lord, and see my humiliation; keep before your eyes the fact that I humble myself, and rescue me from exaltation, so that I may be able to be humbled; for I have not forgotten your law.” He means that law which is immutably established with you: that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Therefore, O Lord, judge this judgment by which I judge that I must be humbled, making my state—that is, my being—useful and lasting for me; redeem me from exaltation, and then revive me because of your word. This word pertains to that law which he has not forgotten, so that, in order to be exalted, he might humble himself; justification itself, however, is exaltation. For what else is the exaltation of the righteous than eternal life?

Because sinners do not attain it, he therefore adds: “Salvation is far from sinners.” And rightly so, because they have not sought your justifications. And it is as though someone asked him: “Who has distinguished you in such a way that salvation belongs especially to you, while it is far from sinners?” He answers: “Is it not because I sought God’s justifications, which they neglected?” But, recognizing that this seeking proceeds solely from God’s mercy, he adds: “Your mercies are many, O Lord.” It is as though he said: “Salvation is indeed far from sinners because they have not sought your justifications. But your mercies, O Lord, are many toward those who seek, because you call, forgive sins, and justify.” Therefore, O Lord, revive me according to your judgment—the judgment by which you act, namely, that the one who shows mercy is not without mercy, or according to your declaration: “I love those who love me.”

And it is necessary, he says, that you justify me, because those who press me toward death are not lacking. Many indeed persecute me outwardly and afflict me inwardly. Yet I have not turned aside from your testimonies. Nor was it enough for me merely to be good myself; rather, I wanted others to be good. I saw transgressors and was wasting away with a good zeal, arising not from envy but from love, because they did not keep your words. Therefore, O Lord, look upon me—that is, show me mercy—because I have fulfilled your commandments, O Lord, as far as I could, not from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness. Therefore, O Lord, justify me with true life, not on account of my merit but on account of your mercy.

This is the song of one making progress while living in this present life. And rightly have I loved your commandments, because “the beginning of your words is truth”—that is, your words proceed from truth, because they proceed from you, who are truth. Therefore they are true, that is, they deceive no one, announcing life to the devout and punishment to the guilty. And this is immutable, because all the judgments of your righteousness endure forever. Hence elsewhere: “The word of the Lord endures forever.”

Alternatively: “Look, O Lord, upon my humiliation”—that is, pay attention to my tribulation and degradation, to how I suffer at the hands of persecutors—and rescue me from this humiliation, not so that I may be free from tribulation, but so that I may not fail within it; for I have not forgotten your law, namely, the law that commands us also to love our enemies and to lay down our life for our brothers. And because I have not forgotten the law, therefore, O Lord, judge this judgment of mine—that is, this chastisement of mine—so that it may serve my progress. Redeem me, lest I fail under pressing afflictions; and though I have been put to death outwardly, revive me inwardly because of your word, which I have kept. For others are put to death because they have not kept it. He expresses the equivalent thought when he says: “Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought your justifications.” But toward those who seek, your mercies are many, as above.

Alternatively: “Look, O Lord, upon my humiliation”—that is, pay attention to my mortality and susceptibility to suffering, into which I was humbled through our first parent—and rescue me, lest I fail in this humiliation. You ought to do so because I have not forgotten your law, that is, your commandments, as those first parents did. And you, O Lord, who judged the sentence against those proud ones in death, judge the judgment of me, the humble one, in salvation. Redeem me from mortality and susceptibility to suffering; revive me with true life, not because of my merit but because of your word—that is, your promise—or because I have kept your commandments.

It is necessary that you revive me, because I was put to death in the first parents. For salvation—that is, true life—was made far from sinners and from those who imitate them, because they did not seek your justifications. But, so that all might not perish in Adam, you sent your merciful one, and through him many mercies were displayed: calling, justification, and the forgiveness of sins. Therefore revive me.

“I saw transgressors”—that is, pay attention to the punishment inflicted on the first transgressors—and I wasted away from fear, because they did not keep your words. And you, O Lord, who turned yourself away from them, look upon me with the regard of mercy, because I have loved your commandments. Just as you put them to death in anger, so revive me in your mercy. The following verse is unchanged.

**Sin, teeth.**

**EXPLANATION.**

The twenty-first letter is now entered by the assembly of the saints. In it, the persecutions of those who rage against them are said to be exceedingly welcome to them because of the Lord’s love. He also says that he has praised the Lord seven times a day, and professes that his ways are known to him. The “teeth” expressed by the name of this letter may be understood either as the saints, who praise the Lord, or as the persecutors. Of the latter it is said: “The sons of men—their teeth are weapons and arrows.”

**COMMENTARY.**

“Princes persecuted me.” It is as though he said: “Revive me in your mercy, because princes persecuted me in their wickedness.” Or in this way: “I loved your commandments. For this reason princes persecuted me, in order to hand me over to death, and they did so without cause.”

The saints nowhere prohibited the payment of what was owed to princes. For the Lord himself, the complete example of humility and righteousness, paid the royal tax on Peter’s behalf—the drachma taken from the fish’s mouth—and in the Gospel he commands: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” John, his herald, was also asked by soldiers what they ought to do for eternal life. He did not say to them, “Untie your belts, lay down your weapons, and abandon your commander,” but said: “Extort from no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your pay.” Paul, that outstanding soldier, also said: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities.” And again: “Pay everyone what is owed: tax to whom tax is due, revenue to whom revenue is due, fear to whom fear is due, honor to whom honor is due. Owe no one anything, except to love one another.”

It is therefore clear that princes and wicked teachers persecuted the saints without cause—that is, for no reason. This is what is said here: “Princes persecuted me without cause.” Yet my heart did not fear their words, but feared your words. Their words were: “I kill, I proscribe, I tear limbs apart,” and similar threats. His words, however, are: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna,” and similar sayings. It was such words alone that this man’s heart feared; or he feared them because he despised the raging persecutor and conquered the deceiving devil.

“I will rejoice over them.” It is as though he said: “I feared your words; therefore I will rejoice over your words”—that is, having been made superior through your words, I will rejoice because I will fulfill them out of love. For when commandments are fulfilled from fear of punishment, not from love of righteousness, a person is not above them but beneath them. “I will rejoice,” he says, as greatly as someone greedy rejoices when he finds abundant spoils.

“I hated iniquity.” He said: “They persecuted me without cause,” and truly without cause, because I had done them no wrong.

**Tau, sign or consummation.**

**EXPLANATION.**

With the Lord’s help we have reached the twenty-second letter. In it, the choir of the saints, being as near to the end of the psalm as it is, longs to draw equally near to Christ. The whole passage concerns the coming of the Lord and Savior, whose faithful devotion awaited him with unspeakable longing, so that he might deign, through the gift of his compassion, to recall the lost sheep. He himself, therefore, is the consummation of all virtues for us, because whoever is found worthy to see him will have no need to seek anything further. He is the one whose sign we, the redeemed, sing: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord.” [lacuna]

## ON PSALM 119. A Song of Ascents

### ARGUMENT

This is sung in the person of David when he rejoiced amid Saul’s persecutions. Alternatively, it is Christ’s voice to the Father concerning the Jews.

### EXPLANATION

“Singing of ascents” means songs of ascent, which is why the Greek says more expressively: *ᾨδὴ τῶν ἀναβαθμῶν*—“Song of the Ascents”—because they strive only toward heavenly things. It is as if someone had fallen into a pit and a ladder were placed there, giving him the means to climb out.

When the Israelite people had fallen into the pit of captivity and were being afflicted, they cried out to the Lord and were heard; they were brought back to their homeland, so that, after the city and temple had been restored, they could say: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord.”

By this example, the one who has fallen into the pit of sin needs the steps of humility by which to return to heavenly things. These are rightly said to be fifteen steps, whether those described in the Psalter or those constructed in Solomon’s temple. They signify that through the week of the Law and the octave of the Lord’s resurrection we can rise to heavenly things; nor can anyone otherwise escape the ruler of this world, unless the soul’s rest after the flesh is created as though in the seventh age, and the resurrection of the flesh at the end as though in the eighth.

Because of these fifteen steps—that is, the knowledge of both Testaments—it is said that the water of the Flood, which had risen immeasurably above the hollows of the valleys and the level ground of the fields, surpassed the highest mountains by fifteen cubits. For the faith of the Church, consecrated by the wave of baptism, easily surpasses pagan customs and overcomes the highest philosophical intellects by the summit of virtue. It knows how rightly to see in this age and how to believe, hope for, and love the perpetual life of the soul together with the resurrection of the body in the age to come.

Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks. In the first part he cries out to the Lord to be delivered from unjust lips and a deceitful tongue. In the second he is severely afflicted: because he remains longer in this life, he is weighed down by having to endure the vices of others and by his mingling with the wicked.

### COMMENTARY

“To the Lord, when I was afflicted. A Song of Ascents.”

It is written that the temple Solomon built in the Lord’s honor was approached by ascending fifteen steps, and this is not without a mystery. That temple prefigured the temple that the Lord builds in the heavenly Jerusalem from living stones, to which one ascends as though by fifteen steps.

Fifteen is a number composed of seven and eight. As we have often said, the number seven signifies earthly things, which revolve in a cycle of seven. When these are despised and rejected, one ascends to the Lord’s temple through the number eight, that is, through heavenly things, which are acquired through the eight beatitudes.

Alternatively, because there are seven deadly vices, they may be understood by the number seven—vices that anyone who wishes to ascend to the Lord’s temple must despise. How, then, should one ascend? Through the eight beatitudes, which are understood by the number eight.

And because the fifteen psalms that follow invite us to ascent, they are all marked with the same title, namely, “A Song of Ascents,” which in Greek is called *Ἀναβαθμῶν*, meaning “of ascent,” just as *καταβαθμῶν* means “of descent.” Steps belong both to those descending and to those ascending. The steps marked in these psalms signify ascent.

Let us therefore understand this psalm as an ascent, and let us not seek to climb by bodily steps but by spiritual affections. Hence another psalm says: “He arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of weeping, to the place he appointed.” It says that he placed ascents in his heart and indicated from where one must ascend: from the valley of weeping.

One must ascend to something else, to an ineffable and incomprehensible good, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart.” Therefore, since the prophet cannot explain it, he leaves it undefined and says: “To the place he appointed.”

The valley of weeping signifies humility, just as a mountain signifies exaltation. There is a spiritual height, a mountain to which we may ascend. And what is this mountain of exaltation except our Lord Jesus Christ, who through suffering made himself a valley of weeping, while remaining in himself the mountain of exaltation?

Let us hear how he is a valley of weeping: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” And how was he a valley of weeping? He was filled with reproaches, seized, bound, struck on the face, spat upon, crowned with thorns, crucified, given vinegar to drink, and pierced with a lance. Thus he became a valley of weeping.

Yet he is the mountain of exaltation, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” He descended to you in such a way as to remain in himself. He descended to us to be the valley of weeping; he remained in himself to be the mountain of exaltation.

From here, then, we must ascend, following his example, to his divinity. For he made himself our example by humbling himself. Those who did not wish to ascend from the valley of weeping were brought low by him, because they wanted ascent in the wrong order. They imagined lofty honors but paid no attention to the way of humility.

Therefore, when the mother of two disciples asked that one of her sons sit at his right hand and the other at his left, the answer was given: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” They were seeking exaltation and did not wish to imitate humility in the valley of weeping. Thus the answer concerned humility: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” They were recalled from error so that they might understand that one must first be humbled and afterward exalted.

Let us therefore sing the psalm as we ascend in our hearts, because, in order that we might ascend, he descended to us. Adam fell, and therefore Christ descended. Adam fell through pride; Christ descended through mercy.

He did not descend alone. He alone descended from heaven, but many holy people descended to us by imitating him. Paul descended to us from a hidden state and spiritual understanding, where he heard secrets that it is not permitted a human being to speak. In condescension to human weakness, he said: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food.”

But when a Christian begins to wish to make progress, he suffers the tongues of opponents and slanderers. For as long as someone has not suffered, he does not progress; and whoever does not yet suffer has not yet begun to strive for progress.

He therefore begins to wish to advance and ascend: to despise earthly things, to regard fragile and temporal things and worldly happiness as nothing, to think of his God, not to rejoice in profits, not to waste away over losses, to sell all that he has, distribute it to the poor, and follow Christ.

But when someone wishes to make progress in this way, he begins to suffer the tongues of slanderers, many who contradict him, and how burdensome are those who, as though confidently giving advice, draw him back from salvation. For one who gives advice claims to be concerned for salvation. Since such a person has the cloak of an adviser but the poison of a destroyer, his tongue is called deceitful. Against this tongue the speaker entreats the Lord, saying: “To the Lord, when I was afflicted.”

A person is afflicted when he longs for heavenly things and considers earthly thoughts or pleasures contemptible. Whoever takes pleasure in these things is not afflicted. Thus he says: “When I was afflicted”—that is, while I was considering my miseries, I cried out to the Lord, and he heard me, placing me among the steps, so that I might already have the will to make progress.

And because one who wishes to progress suffers many tongues that discourage him, he asks to be delivered from such people, saying: “O Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and a deceitful tongue.”

Unjust lips are the lips of people who turn the faithful away from the best life. There are many who, when they see others wishing to make progress, discourage them from doing so. They say that such a life is difficult, one in which hardly anyone can persevere. They also point to many who began this life but did not persevere.

When the soul would not accept such arguments, because it no longer dared openly to blaspheme that way of life—since the authority of the Gospel is everywhere respected and received—they attack him deceitfully. They say that there is no need to lead another kind of life, because it is safe to live as one is. Thus the tongue that was previously unjust becomes deceitful: it has beneath it the cloak of advice and the poison of harm, the appearance of an adviser and the destruction caused by a destroyer.

The speaker asks to be delivered from such a tongue, as though questioning himself: “O soul, what can be given to you”—that is, what do you think is necessary, or what can be added to you—“against a deceitful tongue?” He adds: “To overcome it and escape it.”

“See what will be given to you: sharp arrows of the mighty one, and burning coals of desolation.”

The sharp arrows are evangelical words, piercing human hearts, killing the old nature, and generating love of renewal. These are the arrows of the mighty archer, the Lord, who sends his arrows far, because “their sound has gone out through all the earth.”

The Lord knows how to shoot beautifully with these arrows: he kills what was badly built and restores the new temple.

But because the things commanded by the evangelical words are difficult—for they say, “Go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor”—the arrows must be given together with burning coals of desolation, that is, with the examples of the holy Fathers who fulfilled these commands. These Fathers too were formerly burning coals of desolation, extinguished in the old condition but brought back to life by putting on newness.

In this way anyone can appropriately be drawn to the good life: after the evangelical commandments, the life of the saints is introduced as an example. For everyone more readily strives to imitate what he sees another person doing.

Alternatively: “The sharp arrows of the mighty one, together with burning coals of desolation”—that is, coals that lay waste to us so that we may not take pleasure in these earthly things. Hence another translation says: “With coals of devastation,” because the holy Fathers devastate in us the desire for earthly things; that is, they awaken in us love of heavenly things.

“Woe is me, for my sojourn.” Now that consolation has been given to overcome the deceitful tongue, we must still groan, because as long as we groan in the body, we are away from the Lord, since we live among the children of Babylon. Thus he says: “Woe is me, because my sojourn has been prolonged”—that is, my exile has lasted far too long.

An inhabitant who dwells in another’s land is like an exile. So too are all who have no abiding city here but seek the one that is to come. “Woe is me, because my sojourn has been prolonged,” and this because “I dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar”—that is, with those whose understanding is darkened in darkness.

Cedar is the place where Hagar, expelled with her son Ishmael, pitched her tent. Cedar is interpreted as “darkness,” because all who imitate Ishmael—that is, lovers of the world—live in darkness. Thus the speaker says: “I dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar.”

And lest we understand this exile as belonging only to the body and not also to the soul, he adds: “My soul was a long-time inhabitant,” because I was peaceful with those who hated peace—that is, I brought peace, while they spoke of war and I spoke of true peace.

“And they attacked me without cause,” because while I loved them, they hated me.

Alternatively, the earlier passage may be read as though the Lord answered when he asked to be delivered from unjust lips and a deceitful tongue: “What do you wish to be given to you? Or what do you wish to be added to you against a deceitful tongue? See what will be given: sharp arrows of the mighty one together with burning coals of desolation.” The rest remains unchanged.

## ON PSALM 120. A Song of Ascents

### ARGUMENT

A preaching or instruction in supplication suitable for the people living in Babylon. Alternatively, these are called songs of ascents because the individual psalms were sung on the ascent of the temple, one psalm at each step. Alternatively, the Church’s voice to the apostles.

### EXPLANATION

At first, while placed in tribulation, the prophet, following the example of that tax collector who, striking his breast, did not dare to raise his eyes toward heaven, asks to be delivered from unjust lips and a deceitful tongue.

Now, breathing more freely as he reaches the second step, he raises his eyes toward the mountains, namely, toward the holy intercessors, through whose aid he might merit gifts. The prophet speaks this in his own person, although he himself was also a mountain and a remarkable patriarch. He therefore reports that he has ascended appropriately through these steps so that he might show us, who are ignorant, the distinct kinds of heavenly virtues through an ordered account.

As we have said, the prophet ascending toward the heavenly Jerusalem says in the first part that he raised his eyes toward the merits of the saints, so that he might be helped by their prayers and his mind might not succumb to hostile assault. In the second section he confidently promises himself what he knew he had fully requested, teaching that whenever we ask for good things with a steadfast heart, we should believe without doubt that they will be granted to us.

### COMMENTARY

“I raised my eyes. A Song of Ascents.”

Again this spirit admonishes us to ascend, because the title is “A Song of Ascents.” Whoever begins to wish to advance by ascending ought to set before himself the example of the holy Fathers, so that he may make greater progress by ascending according to their example.

Or let us understand the speaker who says: “I raised my eyes toward the mountains”—that is, toward the holy prophets and patriarchs—by considering the excellence of their life. “From where,” that is, “from whom, will help come to me?” From them, because I will be moved by their example to ascend.

Yet although help is to be received from them, help must principally be obtained from the Lord, who made heaven in the higher things and the others the earth. Hence the saying: “Neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth.”

“Let him not give [your foot] to agitation.” It is as though he said: “Since my principal help must be sought from the Lord, therefore, O soul, let him not give your feet”—that is, your affections—“to that agitation by which the first man, placed in paradise, was moved and fell, and by which the angel was moved, fell from heaven, and became the devil.”

“Let him not give your foot to agitation, nor let him who guards you slumber.” This is in the likeness of a negligent guard who, by sleeping, neglects those whom he ought to guard. And as though the soul were asking where it could find such a guardian who would not slumber, he adds:

“Behold, he will neither slumber nor sleep, who guards Israel.” It is as though he said: “Seek the guardian of Israel. He will neither slumber nor sleep.”

Everyone slumbers because he bears mortal nature; he sleeps when he dies. But the righteous Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps, because Christ, having risen, dies no more, and death will no longer rule over him.

Note that Israel means “the man who sees God”: now in hope, and one day seeing him in reality. Therefore be Israel, and the Lord will guard you. The Lord is your protection over your right hand, because he protects your faith, through which you will come to the Lord’s right hand; and that right hand is yours, because it has been promised to you.

The hand signifies faith, because faith is power, according to the saying: “He gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name.” Thus the speaker says: “The Lord is your protection over your right hand.”

Being protected by him, the sun will not burn you by day. The sun signifies divinity, by whose ray the mind of each person is illuminated as by the sun. And because day signifies wisdom, through which one ascends to divinity—hence the saying, “Day unto day pours forth the word”—it is especially necessary for everyone to be protected, lest the sun burn him by day; that is, lest this divinity permit him to stumble in wisdom.

A person stumbles in wisdom when he doubts that the Son, whom he ought to understand through wisdom as equal to the Father, is lesser. This is what is meant by: “The sun will not burn you by day.”

“Nor the moon by night.” By the moon either Christ’s flesh is signified, because of the weakness of mortality and susceptibility to suffering, or the Church, which is his body. By night knowledge is understood, through which one understands matters concerning Christ’s flesh or concerning the body that is the Church.

The moon burns someone by night when, through knowledge, he understands concerning Christ’s flesh or his body things that ought not to be understood. Therefore the Lord must protect everyone. If he is the protector, the sun will not burn you by day, nor the moon by night.

So that this may happen, may the Lord guard you from every evil; may the Lord guard your soul—that is, your animal nature—lest reason, overcome by animality, succumb.

So that this may happen, may the Lord guard your entrance—that is, lest you fail in tribulations, which are the entrance of every believer—and your exit, lest you grow proud after overcoming tribulations. He will do this from now and forever.

## ON PSALM 121. A Song of Ascents

### ARGUMENT

Because in the preceding psalm he had heard: “May the Lord guard your entrance and your exit,” he now says that he has rejoiced because entrance into the house of God has been promised to him. Alternatively, the Church’s voice to the apostles.

### EXPLANATION

We hear of a step; let us understand an ascent to higher things. But this ascent is firm, preserved by the Lord’s guardianship. Behold, the prophet is now lifted by the third step, made higher than before, and it is declared that he has begun the psalm from that very joy.

In the first part the prophet rejoices that he has been reminded that he will come to the heavenly Jerusalem, where the saints already dwell in secure prosperity and, through the Lord’s merciful generosity, will judge with the Lord. In the second part he speaks to the citizens of Jerusalem, wishing them an abundance of peace, which he says he has proclaimed out of love for his brothers and love for the Lord.

### COMMENTARY

“I rejoiced in the things that were said to me.”

Just as love inflames the soul toward desire for earthly things and, as it were, plunges it into the depths, so holy love raises it toward heavenly things and inflames it to desire eternal things—namely, things that do not pass away but always remain. This spirit, whose title is “A Song of Ascents,” urges us toward love of them.

The steps belong to those ascending, not to those descending. Therefore let everyone who sings this psalm ascend. And where should he ascend except into heaven, where the angels, our fellow citizens, dwell, while he is an exile from those citizens on earth?

In exile we sigh; in the city we will rejoice. Yet we find companions in this exile, because they have already come to know that city and invite us to run toward it. The speaker rejoices to come to them when he says: “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me by those mountains.”

The holy patriarchs, apostles, and prophets said to us: “Let us run. Let us run, because we will go into the house of God. Let us run, and we will not grow weary, because we will come to the place where we will not grow tired.” This is what he says: “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me by those mountains. Let us run, let us run, and so forth.”

That house of the Lord was not made by human hands but is eternal in the heavens. And as though he were asking which house it is, he says: “Jerusalem,” where the Lord, who founded that city, is the delight of all who dwell in it.

Here there is hope; there, reality. We ought to sigh toward it with such affection that, while we are making our way toward it, we may think that we are already there because of the intensity of our desire.

It is not surprising that those running toward this city on the road should act as though they were already there, since those who are traveling toward a temporal festival often speak on the way as though they had already arrived. The speaker observes this when he says here: “We will go into the house of the Lord.”

And I am not merely certain that we will go, but, after hearing these things, I am certain that we will be “in Jerusalem, in your courts”—that is, in contemplation of your adornment, which is signified by the court, because a court is the place before a house and is customarily decorated so that the sight of one who comes there may rejoice in a certain delight.

In that delight [lacuna]

## TO THE READER

When Bede wrote the history that he calls Ecclesiastical, he was already sixty years old. Later, although his disciples repeatedly urged him, he was unwilling to undertake an exposition of that book, considering the depths of its mysteries and its sacred prophecies in the Psalms. Nevertheless, in order to satisfy his followers in some fashion, he briefly composed an argument for each psalm.

When his hearers pressed him again with their importunity, he finally illustrated the psalm titles for them with very brief explanations. After these were completed, they indulged their own desires more than they respected the old age of their teacher and compelled the Venerable man to write complete commentaries on the psalms as well.

He was overtaken by death before he could complete all of them, having explained 120 psalms, but he left behind this inimitable work. Moreover, certain passages are missing here and there in our copy, wherever dots have been placed. Whether they perished through an interruption in the old man’s writing, through the disciples’ failure to collect them, or through the carelessness of copyists is uncertain to us.

## ON PSALM 122. A Song of Ascents

### ARGUMENT

This is sung in the common person of all who were led into captivity, asking the Lord for the freedom of return. Alternatively, Christ’s voice to the Father.

### EXPLANATION

The one who previously raised his eyes toward the mountains now lifts the eyes of his heart toward the Lord himself. The prophet, fearing that he might lose what he possessed and cautious precisely in the direction in which he had grown, devotedly carries out the perseverance of his prayers in the first part, so that the gifts he had received might be preserved by divine reward.

In the second part he asks the Lord to grant him mercy, because, through the devil’s instigation, he suffered many adversities from those who attacked him—so that, although they could not stain him by association, they might at least stain him through proud contempt.

## ON PSALM 123. A Song of Ascents of David

### ARGUMENT

This too is sung in the person of the people already liberated, giving thanks while recounting the evils they had endured from Babylon. Alternatively, the apostles’ voice.

### EXPLANATION

Because these steps are climbed both by the one Church and by its countless members individually, the psalmist sometimes speaks in the singular and sometimes in the plural. The holy confessors remember how many dangers, through the Lord’s mercy, they escaped like the force of a torrent.

In the first section they confess that they were delivered from so many afflictions solely by God’s mercy. In the second they give thanks because they were not deceived by their persecutors but were rescued when the persecutors’ plots were overturned.

## ON PSALM 124. A Song of Ascents

### ARGUMENT

This is sung in the person of those returning from captivity who, with God’s help, overcame their attackers—that is, the neighboring nations. Alternatively, the Church’s voice.

### EXPLANATION

At the sixth step the prophet cries out that we must confess in the Lord, lest we labor in vain. In the first admonition, concerning the faithful people, he strengthens them by saying that those who trust in the Lord cannot be moved in any way. He gives the reason why he does not permit sinners to increase beyond the lot of the righteous. In the second part he prays that prosperity may come to the upright and punishment to the wicked.

## ON PSALM 125. A Song of Ascents

### ARGUMENT

This is sung in the person of the captives, who supplicate for freedom and say how many good things and how great a clear praise will follow such liberation.

Alternatively, when the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion—that is, of Jerusalem, which had first returned home—we became like those who were desolate; it does not say, “like those who were comforted.” For the joy of the others who remain in captivity is not yet complete.

Alternatively, the apostles’ voice concerning the ungodly Jews.

### EXPLANATION

After the captivity of all sinners, how sweetly the voices of the blessed ascending to the heavenly Jerusalem are offered, so that, placed on a difficult journey, they may console themselves with a holy song.

In the first part of the psalm, the holiest men, liberated by divine compassion, give thanks that they were delivered from the most savage obstinacy of sinners and received into such great grace that among the nations they were found worthy of praise.

In the second they pray that their captivity may be changed into joy, adding a marvelous and true statement: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy.”

## ON PSALM 126. A Song of Ascents of Solomon

### ARGUMENT

Although this song appropriately accords with Solomon as the one who established the house of the Lord, it must nevertheless be applied to prophecy and to the second building, which those who returned from Babylon were striving to accomplish, because both efforts are futile unless they rely upon God as guardian and protector.

Alternatively, Christ’s voice to the future Church.

### EXPLANATION
Therefore this psalm is prefaced with Solomon’s name as its title, so that the builder of the temple himself may teach that he is powerless to build it without the Lord’s assistance. In the mystical sense, however, Solomon, whose name is interpreted as “peaceful,” signifies Christ. Concerning him the Apostle says: “For he himself is our peace, who made both one,” that is, he joined circumcision and uncircumcision in one faith. Hence, most appropriately, in order to distinguish the Testaments, Solomon’s name is recorded here after the seven Gradual Psalms, at the head of the remaining eight, and above, after the seventy Psalms, at the head of the following eighty. [Col. 1090D] The prophet, rejoicing that he had foreseen by the Spirit the grace of the New Testament, and lest harmful presumption should steal in because of so great a gift, teaches at the outset that no good should be attributed to one’s own powers, since everything rests in God’s power, and that no one should wish to anticipate the time arranged by the Lord’s ordinance. In the second manner he speaks of the Lord himself and of his apostles, or of anyone who fulfills his commandments.

## ON PSALM 127. A Song of Ascents.

### ARGUMENT.

He teaches those who returned from Babylon that they must strive after virtues, since such devotion cannot remain unrewarded. Alternatively, the prophet speaks of Christ to the Church.

### EXPOSITION.

[Col. 1091A] How magnificent the ninth degree is, the number itself declares: extended through a threefold multiplication, it displays to us the holy summit of the Trinity. Rightly, therefore, both in such a degree and everywhere, the fear of the Lord is commended to us, since it is shown to be a necessary guardian. In the first section the prophet, by various allusions, enumerates the blessings of those who fear God, so that he may kindle devout souls with the warmth of heavenly reward. In the second he blesses them, so that they may receive eternal joys and that no one may fear this most gracious fear.

## ON PSALM 128. A Song of Ascents.

### ARGUMENT.

He teaches those who will return from Babylon to remember former blessings and to give thanks for their present happiness; thus the prayer is formed in the person of those returning. Alternatively, the voice of the Church.

### EXPOSITION.

[Col. 1091B] Because those who labor in the Lord’s vineyard are rewarded with the denarius of the eternal kingdom, endurance of suffering is urged in the tenth degree, since the affliction of the Church is frequently recalled. In the first section he instructs the people of Israel to say that they have endured struggles and ambushes from their own enemies, so that none of the faithful might despair of his own troubles. In the second he calls down, through parables, what he knew would befall the Church’s enemies at the future judgment.

## ON PSALM 129. A Song of Ascents.

### ARGUMENT.

It is sung in the person of those from Babylon, namely, those who had distinguished themselves there by their merits. Alternatively, it is to be read in relation to the reading of the prophet Jonah.

### EXPOSITION.

[Col. 1091C] Placed in the eleventh degree, the prophet prostrates himself in penitential satisfaction, since no one, however holy, while established in the flesh, can avoid sins completely; but this too must be said: every sin is, as it were, an “eleven,” because it transgresses the perfection of the Decalogue. The prophet cries to the Lord to be freed from the depth of sins, by the goodwill of the good judge, from the calamities he has described. Without delay he comes to the joys of thanksgiving, so that penitents may recognize with what great grace they are received, since swift healing is nevertheless granted them.

## ON PSALM 130. A Song of Ascents of David.

### ARGUMENT.

This psalm too is sung in the person of the saints dwelling in captivity. Alternatively, the voice of the reigning Church.

### EXPOSITION.

[Col. 1091D] After the labors of repentance, the prophet sends us the sweet nourishment of songs, singing this entire psalm about gentleness and humility, so that those whom the labor of the preceding confession had afflicted may be refreshed by the sweetness of glorious devotion. First, teaching humility and gentleness by his own example, the prophet imposes a most severe penalty upon the Christian people if they should not receive the Lord’s commandments with the greatest humility. Second, turning to Israel, he urges it to hope continually in the Lord, so that, strengthened by such hope, it may prevail in enduring all the adversities of the world.

## ON PSALM 131. A Song of Ascents.

### ARGUMENT.

The argument of this psalm is the same as that of Psalm 88: for, foretelling what happened to the people in Babylon, the prophet introduces that people as reminding God how great a concern blessed David had for religion and divine worship, how great an eagerness he had undertaken for the building of the temple, and how God in turn had said [Col. 1092A] that he would reward him, through promises directed either to his nation or to those who were to reign from his line. Since these promises were aimed at ensuring that that people’s rule served the common good, the prophet therefore composed psalms of this kind, by which he might nourish the people’s hope; and they might believe that, at least because of faith, their captivity would be relaxed, so that the people might return to their ancestral land and David’s descendants might be established in a victorious rule. Alternatively, the prophet speaks to the Father concerning Christ.

### EXPOSITION.

This degree describes the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation. For it was fitting that, after the number of the twelve apostles, he himself should come as the thirteenth, as the head of them all. For that humble one, who had hitherto cried from the depths, could not suddenly have raised himself to such great praise. But David is to be understood as Christ in this passage. In the first part the prophet reports Christ’s words, in which he promised the Father that he would not take rest [Col. 1092B] by any other means unless he had poured the devotion of true religion into human hearts. In the second he says that what Christ had truly promised had become known, adding his prayers that he might come to save the whole world. In the third he declares that the promise made to him by the Father was to be fulfilled: that the fruit of the virginal womb should sit upon the throne of the kingdom forever, so that he might bless his Church, feed the poor, glorify the priests, and extend his power; that he might clothe his enemies with shame, while the sanctification of eternal justice flourished over him.

## ON PSALM 132. A Song of Ascents.

### ARGUMENT.

The prophet foretells that the twelve tribes, which had previously always been at odds, would after the captivity be joined in a single harmony. Alternatively, the voice of the Church.

### EXPOSITION.

[Col. 1092C] After the most holy preaching of the preceding psalm, the prophet, now placed in the fourteenth degree, proclaims blessed unity to the peoples, so that those who bind themselves together in the Christian religion may persevere in one agreement of charity. Like Psalm 116, this psalm does not admit division—and rightly so, because the former urges all nations and peoples to the praise of one Lord, while this one urges them to the unity of brotherly love.

## ON PSALM 133. A Song of Ascents.

### ARGUMENT.

As though, after the return, the house had already been built, the devotion of freedom. Alternatively, the voice of the Church in the future.

### EXPOSITION.

After the exhortations to mutual love, he now accordingly urges that the happy union should be stirred to the praises of the Lord by the most ardent zeal of charity. In the first part [Col. 1092D] the prophet invites the people to bless the Lord, and therefore addresses the people mentioned above in the plural number. Then he blesses the people individually, because holy unity is the Church’s glory and virtue.

It is pleasing to recount [Col. 1092D] how these degrees reached the heavenly Jerusalem. In the first degree he signifies the horror of the world, after which one hastens toward the pursuit of every virtue. In the second the divine virtue of protection is explained, and it is shown that nothing can oppose it. In the third it is said to be a great joy to dwell in the Church of the Lord with a pure mind.
