In the fourth he teaches that, amid every kind of distress, one must confidently rely upon the Lord until, in his mercy, he hears. In the fifth he warns that, once freed from dangers, we should attribute nothing to ourselves, but everything to the virtues of the Lord. In the sixth the confidence of the most faithful Christian is compared with the firmest mountains. In the seventh it is said how abundant are the fruits reaped by those who sow in tears. In the eighth it is said that nothing endures which each person has accomplished by his own will, but that only those things are most firmly established which are built with the Lord as their author. [Col. 1093A] In the ninth it is declared that a person becomes blessed through the fear of the Lord, and that everything beneficial is granted to him. In the tenth he instills patience in the devout, commending it to the Lord through the words of the Church, so that the extent of divine power may be perceived in the liberation of human beings. In the twelfth the virtue of gentleness and humility is displayed. In the thirteenth the promise of the holy Incarnation and the truth of the declarations are confirmed. In the fourteenth the union of spiritual brothers is proclaimed, over whom the Lord’s blessing and eternal life are shown to come. In the fifteenth that perfect charity is awakened in the praises of the Lord, than which nothing greater can be said or anything more glorious found, as the Apostle testifies: “For God is love.”

This number also contains the following mystery: when the five bodily senses, through which frail humanity contracts every sin, have been overcome by the power of the blessed and undivided Trinity, it leads us upward to the summit of the fifteen Gradual Psalms.

## ON PSALM 134. Alleluia.

[Col. 1093B]

### ARGUMENT.

Those who returned from Babylon are instructed to give thanks to the Redeemer both for the vengeance taken upon their enemies and for their own protection; he had always strengthened them with many kinds of consolation. Alternatively, the voice of the Church speaking to those who are at work, since it rebukes idols.

### EXPOSITION.

After the beautiful construction of the Gradual Psalms, which raised us all the way to the summit of perpetual happiness, an alleluia is most appropriately placed, so that the holy Church may rejoice in the Lord’s praises, since such a gift is known to have been prepared for it. Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks. At the outset he says that praises are owed to the Lord because of the power of his name, since he has done whatever great things he wished, recalling his various works. Second, since the perfect praise of truth is the destruction of falsehood, he rebukes idol-worshipers with ridicule. Third, he admonishes the various orders [Col. 1093C] not to cease praising the Lord.

## ON PSALM 135. Alleluia.

### ARGUMENT.

As above. The voice of the apostles to the synagogues.

### EXPOSITION.

Again we must say alleluia—a grace indeed ever new, yet the last in this continuous exposition. Hence the following psalm has been placed here; through its unbroken verses it repeatedly impresses upon us the Lord’s mercy, and not without reason. For it is by his clemency that we live, and by his mercy that we have strength. Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks. In the first part he declares the Lord’s magnificence and the creation of the whole world. In the second he recounts the miracles he performed in Egypt and among the Jewish people. In the third he descends to Christians, enumerating in due order the Lord’s benefits. [Col. 1093D]

## ON PSALM 136. A Psalm of David concerning Jeremiah.

[Col. 1093D]

### ARGUMENT.

The Babylonian captivity is prophesied. Alternatively, the voice of the Church.

### EXPOSITION.

This psalm can be understood in three ways: as concerning the captivity that befell the Jewish people when they were transferred to Babylon and there mocked in various ways; as concerning sinners who, cast out from the Church, are handed over to the devil’s power; and as concerning the earlier captivity by which, in the first parents of our race, we were cast down from the joys of paradise into the valley of tears. In the first section the Hebrew people enumerate the calamities they were to suffer in Babylon, adding that amid every distress of this world they would never in any way forget Jerusalem, although it was certain that she would be overthrown. [Col. 1094A] In the second he turns his words toward the Lord, asking him to remember those who insult the Church, and declaring blessed those who, beginning in their own hearts, hurl evil thoughts away.

## ON PSALM 137. For David himself.

### ARGUMENT.

The preceding psalm contains the complaints of captivity in Babylon; this one contains the returning people’s vow and explains how great the thanksgiving they wished to render to God in their own land would be. Alternatively, the voice of Christ to the Father.

### EXPOSITION.

“For David himself” signifies “for the Lord Christ himself,” to whom the whole confession of this psalm refers. Throughout the psalm the universal Church speaks. In the first narrative it praises the Lord’s benefits bestowed upon it, asking for patience in the future, so that by his gift it may endure the world’s adversities. In the second it asks [Col. 1094B] that the kings of the earth confess the Lord as exalted, since he deigns to display the wonders of his majesty in all things, praying that he not despise converted sinners whom he deigned to create.

## ON PSALM 138. A Psalm of David, “To the End.”

### ARGUMENT.

This psalm is composed in the person of the faithful people who understand the Lord’s power and that not even hidden things can escape his majesty. Alternatively, the voice of the penitent apostle Peter.

### EXPOSITION.

“To the End” refers to Christ, in whose person this entire psalm is sung. In the first part the Lord speaks of his rest and resurrection, saying that all his thoughts are known to the Father. In the second he explains the power of the Father’s divinity: insofar as he is human, he cannot hide from his knowledge in any place or at any distance. [Col. 1094C] He adds that, with the Father protecting him, he was preserved from his mother’s womb, and that he overcame the vices of the world through glorious holiness. In the third he declares that he will praise the Lord from the position in which he is subject to the Father, whose works, power, and wonders are now known. In the fourth he asserts that the dominion of all the blessed has been confirmed, ordering the impious and obstinate to depart from him—those who nevertheless were not to be saved by any humility of repentance.

## ON PSALM 139. A Psalm of David, “To the End.”

### ARGUMENT.

Hezekiah prays against the Assyrians, so that he may not be overcome by the force or deceit of foreigners. Alternatively, it is the voice of Christ.

### EXPOSITION.

Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes. [Col. 1094D] In this psalm he is proclaimed as coming to us, as though with the voice of a herald along the road: terrible, almighty, and greatly desired. Throughout the psalm the holy Church speaks. In the first section it beseeches the Lord to deign to free it from the wicked devil, who attempts by many deceits to overthrow the devotion of the faithful people. In the second it asks not to be handed over to the most wicked tempter, since it is already clear that, with the Lord protecting it, it has been freed from heaps of dangers. In the third it says that vengeance will come upon them in the future judgment who persecute his poor with mad assaults.

## ON PSALM 140. A Psalm of David.

### ARGUMENT.

It is sung in the person of Hezekiah, practicing repentance so that he might not be swept into anger in opposition to the Assyrians’ anger. Alternatively, the voice of the Church against heretics, as above.

### EXPOSITION.

[Col. 1095A] The prophet begs to be freed from various errors amid these worldly activities. In the first section he asks the Lord that his prayer be heard, adding from which errors he especially wishes to be freed. In the second he chooses to be rebuked by the righteous rather than praised by the sinner, begging to be guarded from sinners’ snares, since he testifies that he has no fellowship with them.

## ON PSALM 141. “Understanding of David, when he was in the cave: a prayer.”

### ARGUMENT.

The title plainly concerns David. It may also be understood as having been spoken by Hezekiah when besieged.

### EXPOSITION.

David, a fugitive because of Saul’s plots, prayed while hiding in a cave, because he signified that the Lord Christ, in the body, would do this before his Passion. For when “understanding” is prefixed to this prayer, [Col. 1095B] it signifies that David understood, amid his distress and the hiding places of his flight, what the Lord would suffer from the Jews and how he would ask the Father. In the first part the Lord cries out to the Father, setting forth the wicked deceits of the consummation of judgment. In the second he begs to be freed from the prison of hell, since the faith of all the saints depended upon his resurrection.

## ON PSALM 142.

“A Psalm of David, when Absalom his son was persecuting him.”

### ARGUMENT.

The title plainly indicates that this is spoken by David against Absalom. It may also be understood as having been spoken by Hezekiah against Sennacherib.

### EXPOSITION.

This history is well known from the reading of the books of the Kings: David was persecuted by his son. As some [Col. 1095C] maintain, the likeness extends to every Christian who, amid the harshness of this world, is tormented by raging sins as though by his own children; but against these things the healing remedy of repentance contained in this psalm is applied. Although the prophet wrote many psalms of repentance, nevertheless he is so deeply affected by contrition of heart that, salutarily examined, he might appear cleaner in the divine sight. Therefore, in the first prayer, he asks the Lord Christ not to enter into judgment with his servant, but begs his mercy to come to the aid of his distress. In the second he asks to arrive swiftly at pardon, so that, led onto the way of truth, he may be freed from the enemies’ ambushes.

## ON PSALM 143. A Psalm of David, against Goliath.

### ARGUMENT.

The title itself explains this psalm; it also presents a thanksgiving by Hezekiah, [Col. 1095D] saved from siege and illness. Alternatively, the voice of the Church against the devil and his satellites.

### EXPOSITION.

This Davidic battle was permitted as a sign of the Lord Christ’s struggle, so that just as David struck down the glory of Goliath—whose name is interpreted as “revealed” or “migrating”—by combat with a stone missile, so the devil’s strength might be conquered through the rock, which is the Lord Christ. After Goliath’s death, in the first part the prophet gives thanks to the Lord for having been freed from the danger of the completed battle, begging that the Lord’s coming be declared quickly, through which the devil was conquered and spiritual Israel freed. In the second, in the New and Old Testaments, the prophet promises to sing to the Lord, freed from the worst enemies who placed their blessedness in the happiness of this world; he defines as blessed only those whose God is the Lord.

It should also be noted that, with Goliath’s death mentioned, a kind of boundary has been placed upon worldly affairs. For after this [Col. 1096A], nothing is narrated either about the Church’s labors, the bitterness of the world, the tribulation of penitents, or the abominations of Antichrist. Rather, the remaining seven, adapted to a great mystery through divine proclamations, appear to be filled with heavenly joy.

## ON PSALM 144. Praise for David himself.

### ARGUMENT.

It is sung in the person of the people freed from captivity, marveling at God’s power and giving thanks for his benefits, since he habitually comes to the aid of all who are placed in tribulation. Alternatively, the voice of the Church to Christ.

### EXPOSITION.

It may be asked why this title contains the singular expression “Praise for David himself,” when the glory of David himself—that is, of the Lord Christ—is proclaimed in all the psalms. But here it has been placed more strictly and forcefully because, once everything by which human ignorance was to be instructed has been completed [Col. 1096B], the command is now given to invoke the Lord’s praises alone. These praises, because of the Sabbath of the future age, as I believe, are contained in the number seven among the psalms. For it says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you.”

This psalm also preserves the order of the Hebrew alphabet at the beginnings of its verses. It should nevertheless be noted that the letter Nun is not found in the Hebrew volumes; but the Septuagint translators added this verse: “Faithful is the Lord in all his words, and holy in all his works.” The praise of Christ proposed by the prophet is explained in three narratives. The first is the infinite promise of his praise. The second says that the Lord’s praise is to be performed in nine ways. In the third part he explains somewhat more broadly and clearly what he briefly proposed in the second concerning Christ’s proclamation, concluding by reminding us that the Lord must be praised by every flesh. The first division therefore contains three letters of the aforementioned alphabet, the second four, and the third fourteen.

## ON PSALM 145. Alleluia of Haggai and Zechariah.

[Col. 1096C]

### ARGUMENT.

The people saved from Babylon recall God’s benefits toward them from the beginning. Alternatively, the voice of Christ to the people.

### EXPOSITION.

The remembrance of the Lord’s praise, which he had previously set down in Latin under the preceding title, the prophet now wished to augment with the Hebrew word alleluia, as a culmination of the same praise, desiring that the Lord’s praises be sung with the whole heart. At the outset he says that no trust at all is to be placed in human beings, lest one seek anything from him half-heartedly if someone else were believed capable of providing it. [Col. 1096D] Second, he declares that all hope must be placed in the almighty Lord; and since he is the Lord, he is most beautifully defined by his deeds, so that the Gentiles, convicted by such frequent reasoning, may abandon their errors through faithful devotion.

## ON PSALM 146. Alleluia.

### ARGUMENT.

The liberated people are urged to praise God. Alternatively, the voice of the Church and of the apostles to the newly formed people.

### EXPOSITION.

The following text explains the words of the title: alleluia means “praise the Lord.” Indeed, the Fifth Edition placed the beginning of this psalm as follows: “Praise now,” that is, “the Lord,” because *Ia* is understood as one of the ten names of God, which Jerome, writing to Marcella, recalls in this way.

The first name is *Heli*, that is, “strong.” Then *Elohim* and *Elohe*, both of which mean “God.” Hence the name is often doubled, as in: “God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” and “God, God, I watch for you at dawn,” and similar passages. The fourth [Col. 1097A] is *Sabaoth*, which means “of hosts.” The fifth is *Ielon*, which we call “the exalted one.” The sixth is *Eser Eiae*, which is read in Exodus: “the one who sent me.” The seventh is *Adonai*, which we generally call “Lord.” The eighth is *Ia*, which is applied only to God and sounds as the final syllable in *alleluia*. The ninth is the tetragrammaton, which is called “ineffable.” The tenth is *Sadai*, that is, “strong and sufficient to accomplish all things.”

In the first manner the prophet urges the devout people to praise the Lord, who raises up the humble and cuts down the necks of the proud. In the second he says that the Lord, who grants beneficial gifts to those who beseech him, is to be sung to with alacrity; for those who presume upon their own strength could not please him.

## ON PSALM 147. Alleluia.

### ARGUMENT.

He turns from special thanksgiving for the return to the general praise of God. Alternatively, the voice of Christ to the Church.

### EXPOSITION.

[Col. 1097B] We return to the customary alleluia, but we are in no way wearied of repeating it, since this word possesses such honor that, although it is hidden in the Hebrew language, it is nevertheless not translated into any foreign language. Rather, whatever is devoted to the Divinity venerates the dignity of this name with pious devotion.

In the first section the prophet addresses Jerusalem, that is, the heavenly city, so that, now restored to security in her citizens, she may praise the Lord with continual rejoicing. In the second, through mystical addresses, he enumerates at greater length how much the merciful Lord has granted to his people.

These psalms of David’s praise are arranged so that first there is discussion of the commands of divine proclamation, then of fleeing the world’s perversity, and third of the gathering of the Church. Fourth, the psalm now brought to completion commands the assembled Jerusalem to celebrate the Lord’s praises; she is known to have been established in eternal rest after being freed from the various dangers of this world. Therefore that most holy choir, gathered from the regions of the world, will add a threefold rejoicing, so that the grace of the Trinity may shine everywhere in the most holy work. [Col. 1097C]

## ON PSALM 148. Alleluia.

### ARGUMENT.

Every creature of the world is summoned to praise God. Alternatively, the voice of the apostles to the people.

### EXPOSITION.

By mentioning a few, the prophet urges all creatures to praise the Lord: rational and intellectual creatures by themselves, but those lacking intellect or sensation through those creatures that praise the Lord’s works with the wisest consideration. In the first part he urges the heavenly beings to praise. In the second, through allegorical allusions, he reminds earthly things to celebrate the Lord with devout minds, adding one probable cause applicable to both: it is fitting that the creature praise its creator.

## ON PSALM 149. Alleluia.

[Col. 1098A]

### ARGUMENT.

Those who returned from Babylon are commanded to give thanks because, with God’s help, they defeated the neighboring nations that opposed them. Alternatively, the voice of Christ to the faithful concerning the future and the resurrection.

### EXPOSITION.

We are likewise reminded to keep this name in use, since the New Testament is suitably fitted to the Old and the Old to the New: the former where the miracles of Egypt and the benefits of the Red Sea are described, the latter in the present psalm, in which we are commanded to sing a new song to the Lord. In the first section, because of the new song, he says that Christ the Lord must be sung in various ways, since by his mercy he built a universal Church from the whole world. In the second, describing the joys and virtues of the saints, he says that the punishment of sinners is the glory of the righteous. In the preceding [Col. 1098B] psalm he had urged all creatures to the Lord’s proclamations; here he signifies more distinctly and specifically that Israel must sing a new song and rejoice in its own Lord, who caused it to be gathered from the multitude of the nations. The power granted to the saints in that judgment is also recalled, so that the Lord’s virtue may be recognized in their glory.

## ON PSALM 150. Alleluia.

### ARGUMENT.

The prophet urges both future generations and those now living to persist in the duties of singing psalms. Alternatively, the voice of Christ rejoicing in his kingdom after the world has been conquered. Amen.

### EXPOSITION.

[Col. 1098C] The city of God is admonished, gathered from the circuit of the world, to praise the Lord and sing both with mouth and with mind. This psalm, raised to the harmonious unity of all the saints, ought not to have a division, because it has brought the whole work to the power of the inseparable Trinity. Its final purpose is that the Lord be praised by the congregation of the saints. Amen. Praises be to God.

## ARGUMENT OF THE PSALM

This psalm was properly written by David outside the numbered sequence, when he fought with Goliath. The fiftieth is about repentance, the hundredth about mercy and judgment, and the one hundred fiftieth about the praise of God in his saints. For in this way we move toward eternal and blessed life: first by condemning our sins, then by living well, so that after a condemned evil life and a good life rightly lived we may deserve eternity. For, once called, we renounce the devil through repentance, so that we may not remain under his yoke; justified, we are healed through mercy, so that we may not fear judgment; glorified, we pass into eternal life, where we may praise the Lord without end.

[Col. 1097]

# OF THE PRESBYTER BEDE: AN EXPOSITION OF THE PSALTER AND OF ITS TERMS, AND A COLLECTION CONCERNING THE DIAPSALMS

## Catalogue of the Diapsalms

# INTERPRETATION OF THE PSALTER: THE ART OF SINGING, THE VARIOUS INSTRUMENTS, AND THE NAMES MENTIONED IN THE PSALMS

[Col. 1099] As Jerome says, the psalter is a resonant hollow instrument formed in the shape of the letter delta, having a broad belly in its upper part, where the strings, fastened in an orderly manner, are said to produce a most pleasing melody when struck by the plectrum. Its arrangement seems contrary to that of the cithara: what the former contains below, the latter, turned in the opposite direction, bears at its top. This kind of melodious and distinctive instrument is applied to the body of the Lord Savior, since, just as the former sounds from higher places, so the latter celebrates the heavenly things of a glorious institution. Among the Hebrews this is called *nablum*. The word *psalm* itself is evidently Greek; some wish it to derive from **ἀπὸ τοῦ ψάλλειν**, that is, “from touching.” For we also call women who play the psaltery or cithara *psaltriae*, since they express musical melodies with a trained thumb. A psalm is a certain sweet and melodious modulation poured forth from that second musical instrument, namely, the psalter.

A song is produced when someone uses the freedom of his own voice and is not joined in harmonious modulation to any resounding musical instrument.

A psalm is a hymn composed according to the law of a certain meter, which, in the likeness of the instrument mentioned above, is understood to indicate to us heavenly virtue.

[Col. 1101B] *Framea* sometimes signifies a spear, sometimes a cuirass, sometimes a sword sharpened on both sides. Arnobius gives another explanation: “Human writings,” he says, “specifically call a *framea* the king’s lance. We, however, generally understand *framea* in the Holy Scriptures as a sword.” The *cinyra* is fitted with ten strings and is struck by a plectrum; the *nabla*, having twelve tones, is played with the fingers.

The cedar is useful only after it has been cut down. For, while remaining in its own root, it produces no profitable fruits, just as arrogance does not.

Hermon is a small mountain situated near the Jordan, as is known from the reading of Deuteronomy: “We took the land at that time from the hands of the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, from the torrent of Arnon as far as Mount Hermon.”

Myrrh signifies the death that the Mediator undertook for the salvation of human beings.

The drop called ammoniacum cures hardenings contracted through some necessity; it is fittingly compared with the Incarnation [Col. 1101C] of the Lord, because through holy preaching it dissolves the hardness of the human heart.

Cassia, which our people call “fistula,” signifies the redemption of the human race through the water of baptism, since this kind of herb is said to be found in watery places. These substances also possess a sweet fragrance, so that both the power of the herbs and the sweetness of their scent may rightly be compared with the holy Incarnation. Let us not understand ivory as pertaining only to riches, but also because the elephant, whose bones these are, is said to possess extraordinary chastity: among quadrupeds it is highly intelligent, mates temperately with its female, and does not take a second mate. This is fittingly applied to chaste women.

Hyssop, although it is a very small herb, is said to penetrate with its roots into the entrails of rocks. It is also shown to be suitable for wounded interiors of human beings; and in Leviticus, dipped in the blood of a sacrificed victim, it used to be sprinkled seven times over the body of a leper, signifying that the stains of sins are [Col. 1101D] effectively washed away by the precious blood of the Lord our Savior. Buckthorn is a very troublesome kind of thorn, which first grows as a very soft herb; but when it has hardened in maturity, it produces pointed little branches, and afterward its spines become rigid with the solidity of a tree.

A dry-stone wall is a construction of stones, built upward without any binding material and fitted together without mortar.

A tympanum is an instrument which, when struck, usually resounds with stretched hide joined, so to speak, above two points connected from the sharp end, just as the human body, when shaken by tribulation for the Lord’s sake, is more sweetly attuned to the heavenly commandments.

**[Col. 1102A]** The asp is a monstrous kind of serpent which, through natural obstinacy, is said not to admit the words of enchanters. So that it may not hear their words and abandon its hiding places, it is said to stop one ear by bending its tail over it, while pressing the other into the ground.

The pelican is an Egyptian bird, similar to storks in the largeness of its body, and always afflicted by natural emaciation. For, as the natural philosophers hold, with its intestine stretched through its entrails it passes through whatever food it takes without any digestion. It does not fly in a flock like the other birds, but takes comfort in solitary wandering; one kind of these birds inhabits marshes, while another, as has been said, lives in desert and secluded places. *Nycticorax* in Greek means “night raven”; some have said that it is an owl, others a screech owl. Still others testify that it is more similar to a raven in size and color and is found especially in the regions of Asia. Just as the brightness of day hides it, so the coming of night brings it forth; and contrary to the habits of birds, it begins to keep watch and seek food when all living creatures are settling into sleep.

**[Col. 1102B]** The sparrow is a small bird, but watchful with no small cleverness. It is neither easily entangled in snares nor deceived through gluttony by the lure of food. Because of its weakness, lest it itself be caught by a predator or its offspring be devoured by the ambushes of serpents, it hastens to the high roofs of houses. The turtledove is said to be the most chaste of birds, content with a single mating.

A fire-bundle is a bundle of dry twigs, suitable for nothing except burning. The coot is a tame and black bird, indeed smaller than a duck but similar in bodily form; it dwells delightfully in marshes. The hedgehog, which we call *ericius*, is an altogether timid animal, yet by nature always equipped for defense. Its skin is densely covered with very sharp bristles, whose spines press closely together, and it always has refuge among rocks. Topaz is a kind of precious stone said to possess two colors, one of the purest gold and the other [Col. 1102C] shining with an ethereal brightness. Its luster is rosy and modest, and in size or color it is close to the chrysoprase, shining most brightly when struck by the sun’s radiance. If one wishes to polish it, one makes it dark; if one leaves it to its own nature, it gives off light. It is said to originate on the island of Topaz, which belongs to the province of Thebaid; hence it receives its name. Crystal is ice hardened like glass through many winters: a fluid substance brought to the hardness of stone.

An organ is a kind of tower constructed with various pipes, in which the sound produced by the blowing of bellows is greatly amplified. To shape that sound into a graceful melody, it is constructed on the inside with certain wooden tongues, which the fingers of trained masters press down skillfully, producing a loud and very sweet song.

Cymbals are small bowls made of mixed metals, struck against one another with artful modulation; they produce a very sharp sound through a pleasing combination.

**[Col. 1102D]** The word *Selah* the translators known as the Seventy, Symmachus, and Theodotion rendered as *diapsalma*, while Aquila rendered it as *always*. I think that it is either a sign of some musical sound or certainly indicates the permanence of what has been said. Wherever *Selah*, that is, *diapsalma*, or *always* is added, let us understand that the matter concerns not only the present time but also eternity—either what follows or what has preceded. Thus Jerome. Augustine, however, thinks that wherever *diapsalma* is inserted, a change of persons or meanings takes place: just as *sympsalma* in Greek means a joining together of voices, so *diapsalma* is a broken continuation of voices.

## ITEM: INTERPRETATION OF THE NAMES OF THE HEBREWS. (C, S)*

**[Col. 1101D]** Abessalon: Father of peace. Asaph: gathering. Abraham: Father seeing the people, or Father of many—that is, of nations. Allophyli: foreigners. Egypt: constricting tribulation. Ethiopia: darkness, or fire. **[Col. 1102D]** Arabs, Hagarenes: newcomers. Ammon: people of sorrow. Assur: directing. Abaron: Father raising up sorrow. Aaron: mountain of strength. Amorites: bitter ones. Aleph: thousand, or teaching. Benjamin: son of the right hand. **[Col. 1103A]** Bashan: fatness, or a locust; for what is usually interpreted as “shame” is called *busa*. Babylon: confusion. Belphegor: having a skin-covered mouth. Kadesh: changed, or holy. Chesion: their hardness, or joy. Koph: calling, or bird, but better, shaking off. Kedar: darkness, or sorrow. Cush: Ethiopian, or notable—this refers to Saul, because he towered above others from the shoulder upward. Yr: the whole people. Ham: hot; but it should be understood that in Hebrew it is written *chi*, although it is written with *heth*, which is pronounced with a double aspiration. Canaan: their movement, or merchant, or humble. Cherubim: multitude of knowledge, or understanding of knowledge. Horeb: written *Oreb* in Hebrew; in one sense, heat or dryness, and in another, raven or solitude. David: strong of hand, or desirable. Dathan: their house, or sufficient gift. Ezrahites: seed of God. Hermon: his anathema. Endor: eye, or fountain of generation. Ephraim: fruitful, or increasing. Ephrathah: abundance. Gilead: heap of testimony. Gebal: ancient valley. Idumea: **[Col. 1103B]** earthly, or bloody. Israel: man, or mind seeing God, but better, “prince with God.” Isaac: **[Col. 1104A]** laughter, or joy. Ishmael: hearing of God. Jabin: wise, or understanding. Jacob: supplanter. Jonadab: spontaneous of the Lord. Jordan: their descent. Joseph: increase. Judah: praise, or confession. Judea: confessing, or praising. Lot: declining. Manasseh: forgotten. Moab: from the father. Moses: taken up. Manna: what is this? Madia: from judgment. Melchizedek: king of righteousness. Naphtali: breadth, or comparison. Nun: offspring or fish, or everlasting. Phinehas: feeding at the mouth, or resting at the mouth. Pharaoh: destroying, or uncovering him. Oreb: dryness. Og: heaping up, or hidden. Zion: citadel, or watchtower. Shechem: shoulder. Sinai: commandment, or measure. Salmon: shadow of a stumbling block, or image of strength. Sheba: captivity. Selom: tearing away, or release, or “where he is.” Sisera: exclusion of joy. Samuel: his name is God. Sihon: useless shoot, or vexing temptation. Tyre, which in Hebrew is called “lot”: tribulation, or distress. Tanis: commanding humble things. Tabor: coming light, or “let light come.” **[Col. 1104B]** Zeb: wolf. Zebaee: victim. Zebulun: dwelling place of strength.

# SERMON OF THE VENERABLE PRESBYTER BEDE ON THE PASSAGE READ IN THE PSALMS: “THE LORD LOOKED DOWN FROM HEAVEN UPON THE CHILDREN OF MEN, TO SEE WHETHER THERE WAS ANYONE WHO UNDERSTOOD OR SOUGHT GOD.” (G, S)*

## PROLOGUE TO THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK

**[Col. 1103B]**

When I observed that several clerics placed in the school were devoting themselves above all to acquiring knowledge of secular letters—letters that teach their hearers with the greatest diligence to desire carnal things, to strive for worldly glory, and to learn the subtleties of syllogisms and arguments so that they may mock any simple people whom they can entrap with such verbosity—I too undertook to read those writings by which I might urge some toward the rule of sacred faith, [Col. 1103C] toward care for the fear and love of God, toward purity of spiritual life, toward devotion to humility and charity, toward repentance for wrongdoing and correction of morals.

For I understood that what is written is true: “For those who love God, all things work together for good,” because both evil and good can benefit those who love God in truth. I pass over the good, since it is sufficiently clear how it benefits. I wish to speak about evil, because it produces progress in three ways, but only for those who fear the Lord.

One way is this: when God sees some people dissolute and negligent in every pursuit of good works, he permits them to fall into some crime or great danger, so that, humbled and afflicted by this, they are compelled to call upon him for their needs. In this way, therefore, and by such evil, many have been compelled to turn to the Lord. Concerning this compulsion we also read in the Gospel: when a certain man had prepared a great dinner and invited many who did not wish to come, he finally commanded his servant, saying, “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter.”

This compulsion [Col. 1103D] is of the following kind. When our Lord, who is signified by that man, had called many from both the Jews and the Gentiles and from all the wise people of this world, they, wishing to establish their own righteousness and not submitting to the righteousness of God, he turned to the weak and ignoble—that is, to various sinners—to call them. Because they were weighed down by excessive sins and had no confidence in their own merits, they hastened, as though compelled, to the grace of God. The servant who called such people to the dinner is understood to be any preacher, saying to them: “Unless you are converted, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

The second way is when, having been tested in tribulation or temptation like gold in a furnace, some people thereby become worthy of obtaining a heavenly reward, according to the saying: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation,” and so forth. In this way every persecutor, whether he wishes it or not, serves the progress of the good. This is clearly demonstrated in blessed Job. For the more the wicked enemy tried to overthrow him by tempting him, the more, although unwillingly, he made him better.

The third way is when, [Col. 1104B] turning the efforts of the wicked toward the opposite, we do good through the same striving and rivalry with which they seek to do evil. We read that the Lord used this argument in the Gospel when he gave the parable of a man who had a steward. Recognizing that he was to be removed from his stewardship, the steward fraudulently arranged what would benefit him after his dismissal.

The Lord did not relate this parable in order to incite anyone to commit fraud, but to teach us to be as prudent in good things as that steward was in evil things—namely, by wisely administering [Col. 1104C] everything that God grants us in this world. It is clear that the cause of this argument is so great that it can be drawn not only from wicked human beings but even from the author of wickedness himself, if, turning what is written about him—“The devil goes about seeking whom he may devour”—to the opposite, we say: “Just as the devil goes about seeking someone to devour, so we too ought to go about seeking someone whom we may rescue from his wickedness.”

Imitating this kind of argument in the present little sermon, I have endeavored that, just as many scholars train themselves in secular letters for the love of secular life, so I too might train myself in the sacred Scriptures, in the rudiments, and in all the moral matters that came to mind, selecting and writing from them whatever seemed profitable for readers and suitable for the edification of souls.

# COMMENTARY ON PSALM 52

The grace of almighty God, desiring to save all human beings, indicates to us, dearly beloved brothers, through the Psalmist [Col. 1104D] how continually he observes us, saying: “God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there was anyone who understood or sought God.”

Although these words are few, they nevertheless offer an especially important and salutary teaching to all who seek God in truth. For they teach that God continually looks upon us in order to discover whether there is anyone among you who understands or seeks God.

In these words we must first note that God, who knows everything before it happens, is not said to inspect us so that, as though ignorant, he may learn from our condition or movement what is within us. Rather, he is said to do so so that we may learn and be admonished to consider how mercifully and subtly God continually examines within us what we are planning concerning our salvation, and how much concern we have—not only to obtain the supports of the present life but also to attain eternal life.

As I have said, this intention must first of all be retained in the Psalmist’s words just quoted. Then we must consider more deeply **[Col. 1105A]** how we can in some measure fulfill that for which God looks upon us: namely, that we may understand and seek God.

Whatever must be understood and sought concerning God must be accomplished through the labor of the inner person, because both are invisible—God, of course, and our inner person, who was made in the likeness of God. Each also invisibly perceives what must be perceived and sought concerning the other, although God surpasses the human being incomparably. God knows everything through himself; the human being, however, can know nothing either from himself or without some addition.

By “addition” I mean all visible things through which we are instructed to understand invisible things. As it is written: “The invisible things of God are perceived through understanding from the things that have been made.” I also call an addition those gifts of understanding that, by God’s grace, we continually retain within ourselves. Such is the saying: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.”

For if we ought to do none of those things to another that we do not wish done to ourselves, and if we altogether wish no evil to be done to [Col. 1105B] us, then we plainly know that no evil ought to be done to another either. By this judgment we are convicted of knowing everything that we ought to show to others. We shall later offer some examples of these things.

For now, let us do what is immediately required, speaking of a third kind of addition through which we are instructed to understand and seek God. This kind is found in all the books of sacred Scripture. In these three additions, therefore, the whole human race that has reached at least the age of understanding is tested as to what it understands concerning God and how it seeks him.

Through the two things mentioned above all who are ignorant of books are tested; those who know books are tested in every respect. Now, since it is very well known how one reads visibly in books and what sort of knowledge is acquired from them, we must say only how we may read spiritually in those two additions, as though in books.

A book may be called both spiritual and bodily, as is found in [Col. 1105C] sacred Scripture, especially in the Apocalypse. Hence the passage: “I saw a book in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne.” That book must certainly be understood as spiritual, and whenever we deal with spiritual matters, we read in a spiritual book.

We can read in it all the more easily because we have it readily available, and neither night nor any darkness can prevent us from such reading. Since, then, we know the nature of that book in which both laity and clergy can read, let us also ask where we ought to read in it and where God, who continually looks upon us to see which of us understands and seeks God, is to be sought.

Both of these activities must take place in our heart, because God commonly comes there and, carefully weighing the intention and concern of each reader, addresses him through inspiration according to how he sees himself loved. Hence the Psalmist says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me.”

You have heard what the spiritual book is and where one must [Col. 1105D] read in it; hear also how one must read in it. But before we read anything, let us state the example from which we have derived this manner of reading.

When our Lord and Savior wished to disclose certain secrets of the heavenly kingdom, he brought forward comparisons of a kind that suited everyone’s understanding. Paul likewise testifies that heavenly things can be contemplated by means of comparison, saying: “Now we see through a mirror and in a riddle.”

Therefore, just as our Lord opened many secrets to all the faithful through comparisons, so I too, insofar as divine grace grants it, wishing to do the same in this sermon, have decided to call “a book” a form of speech that is very easy to understand and is found in the conscience of every wise person. In it, anyone who reads spiritually may recognize the secrets of his own heart.

Since, then, we hold the book, let us first read that from which it may also be recognized that every contemplation of heavenly life is revealed only through the instrument of some [Col. 1106A] comparison.

We all know that whenever an outstanding structure is to be built, it cannot first be raised high until steps have been made by inserting poles and stakes everywhere into the work itself. Upon these the workers can stand, and by them a passage is provided downward and upward.

Through these visible instruments, which are known to everyone, we are instructed to do the same in invisible matters, gathering various comparisons by which we may be able to build higher the arduous work of the heavenly kingdom that we have begun through faith.

Taught by these things, we can establish a firm step, so that, for the completion of the work begun, we may descend or ascend. To descend from such a work is to provide occasionally for the care of the flesh and whatever active life requires; to ascend is again to exercise with all one’s strength the pursuit of the contemplative life.

For the perfection of the contemplative life is not obtained without the support of the active life, because what must be possessed in higher [Col. 1106B] things must be gathered from lower things. Behold one sufficiently clear comparison, in which, as though by reading, it can be recognized how we ought to work in spiritual building.

Having said these things about the manner and nature of building, let us now lay such a foundation that neither rivers nor winds can move it, and that can firmly support every building to be placed upon it.

Believing such a foundation to be faith in the supreme Trinity and unity, we wish first to speak of a comparison whose meaning no one will be able to evade and through which everyone who wishes to seek God may understand him.

We know that there are three persons in one element of water, in one substance, when we say: “That is a spring, that is a stream, that is a pool.” We also know that these three contain such equality that, if you pour any one of them into another, you find no difference in them, provided that no external impurity enters.

Who, then, seeing these things in visible creation, cannot believe in the Trinity and unity of the invisible Creator? Who, I ask, knowing [Col. 1106C] that the spring, the stream, and the pool have one and the same substance—that is, water—cannot understand what our Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever sees me sees the Father,” and, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”?

Does anyone possessing any reason fail to know that the spring is in the stream and the stream in the spring? Therefore he labors in vain who thinks he can flee from his own conscience.

For unless God knew that he could be sought and understood by us to some extent, he would not permit the words I have already quoted to be spoken: “God looked down from heaven,” and so forth; nor those that the Psalmist elsewhere speaks in the person of the Lord: “Be still and see that I am God.”

These words clearly demonstrate that unless we withdraw from worldly tumult, we cannot behold with a pure gaze of mind even that God exists.

Let us speak of another comparison from water, in which the immensity of divine mercy and the extent of our negligence can be weighed. All water, except what has been corrupted [Col. 1106D] by some impurity or filth, is suitable for everyone who approaches it in order to wash; it drives away no one, whether very or slightly dirty.

By this comparison we are all equally admonished that none of us should despair of obtaining purification from his sins, provided only that, wishing to wash away the filth of those sins, he hastens to the fountain of living water—that is, to God—and there washes himself with tears of repentance.

For, as it is written, nothing takes place on earth without a cause. Every creature and every instrument that is useful, and reason itself given to us, cries out through some comparison that we should seek God.

But, to speak further about the comparison of washing that we have begun: unless there were a spiritual washing as well as a bodily one, the Psalmist would never say: “Wash me more thoroughly from my iniquity,” and, “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.”

Hence the prophet also admonishes us in the person of the Lord, saying: “Wash yourselves; be clean.” And to make more explicit that these words signify a spiritual rather than a bodily washing, [Col. 1107A] he immediately added: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes; cease to act perversely,” and so forth.

Amid these things, I also think that we must consider very carefully why the Lord commands the bodies of those who are to be baptized to be visibly washed: namely, so that through this we may be admonished to believe that their souls are likewise purified there by an invisible baptism.

Therefore, while we have time, let us wash ourselves in the bath of divine grace, which flows around us everywhere.

I also think that a third comparison can be found in water. We know that when it is divided by an inserted hand or some other object, after the hand is withdrawn it returns to its former state without retaining any trace of the division.

I do not think this happens without a reason. Rather, I believe that it signifies that every creature is so penetrable by divine power that nothing entering or departing bears signs of corruption, just as happened when our Lord entered to the disciples while the doors were closed.

There the flesh was truly present, but by the deity that possessed the same flesh he penetrated the barriers in such a way that [Col. 1107B] he left no trace of himself.

Having spoken of these three sacraments of water, let us next say what comparison is to be considered in the sun.

For just as its immense splendor is diffused everywhere throughout the world, so the immensity of divine power and presence is contained above all things. The truth of this comparison can be recognized especially from the fact that, wherever you go in any part of the earth, one and the same radiance of the sun appears to you in the same proximity.

Since, then, the presence of the sun—which is certainly a creature—is so extensive, no one may doubt the power of God almighty, the Creator of all. God is also proved to be present everywhere by the fact that he is immediately perceived to hear many who call upon him.

I could say more about the sun that would accord with the holy faith, but, out of consideration for weary hearers, I pass over it.

Let us also say what God teaches us through the various kinds of offices that are usually found in the court of certain [Col. 1107C] rulers.

There are men and women there, some continually walking about in more splendid clothing and maintaining greater familiarity with the lord and lady. It is also carefully guarded by many that none of the women who are assigned to remain there continually be stained by any mark of fornication, so that if one of them should happen to turn her eyes toward a man with a lustful gaze, she immediately hears words of severe correction.

There are also some assigned to inner offices and others to outer offices. All of them observe whatever has been entrusted to them so carefully that they claim nothing beyond what has been assigned to them.

Although the basis of this comparison has been corrupted by many worldly rulers, it can nevertheless be recognized in the few who remain in the love and fear of God and live religiously, so that its meaning may be understood.

It signifies that, just as any religious ruler placed in secular life rightly governs himself and his people under various arrangements in his household, so one must act in the holy Church, [Col. 1107D] which is the household of the supreme ruler.

There, pastors, established in both canonical and monastic habit, ought to be such that they can fittingly and familiarly cleave to and speak with their prince about everything that must be done in the holy Church; they must also warn lest any of those entrusted to them go about in attire more lowly than is fitting—that is, be negligent in good works—and in every way guard against anyone who has professed the obligations of chastity and continence transgressing such vows.

Monks and nuns living chastely are represented by attendants. The rest, who are unable to observe the innermost and spiritual offices, are like farmers or those placed over secular concerns.

Yet all of these—both farmers and attendants—if they faithfully carry out what has been entrusted to them and what belongs to their care, attain the heavenly kingdoms.

This seems to be expressed by the words that the Lord says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places.” As though [Col. 1108A] he said: “Just as there is a great diversity of merits on earth, so there are many dwelling places in the heavenly kingdom.”

Let us proceed still further, speaking of another comparison by which we may be able to ascend toward contemplating the excellence of divine work.

Just as a skilled and wealthy goldsmith, wishing to make some marvelous work, gathers from every source distinguished and precious stones to set among gold or silver, both to display his skill and to enhance the splendor of the marvelous work, so almighty God, wishing to display the riches of his wisdom, has expressed such skill and such excellence of artistry in the structure of human beings and the world that all wise craftsmen always have something to admire and venerate.

Hence the Psalmist says: “How magnificent are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom.”

But since we have mentioned gold and silver and precious stones, by which every work of craftsmanship is especially adorned, it is fitting that we explain in a few words how these three apply to the spiritual adornment of the holy [Col. 1108B] Church.

By the name of silver, therefore, the order of holy preachers is represented, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire.” Solomon also says: “The chosen silver is the tongue of the righteous.”

Gold signifies those who, tested by various and prolonged labors in the monastic life or in another suitable place, shine with such holiness that they are a wonder and an example to all who desire holy conduct.

By the name of precious stones—especially those that are red or sky-blue in color—are signified those who either redden with the purple blood of martyrdom or shine from their earliest age to the end in chastity and in every splendor of perfection.

With such metals our Lord usually adorns the structure of his Church. To this agrees what is read in the Song of Songs: “King Solomon made himself a litter of the woods of Lebanon; he made its columns of silver, its reclining-place of gold, its ascent of purple, and its middle [Col. 1108C] he paved with love for the daughters of Jerusalem.”

These words differ little from what we have said. What we called a structure is there called a litter. That litter is believed to have been made from the woods of Lebanon because the holy Church, invited to eternal banquets, has been built from incorruptible woods—that is, from the elect.

Its silver columns signify teachers shining with the splendor of holy eloquence. The golden reclining-place signifies the hope of perpetual rest, in which the souls of the elect, still laboring in the prison of this world, recline as though resting.

The purple ascent made on the aforementioned litter signifies the passion of all the holy martyrs, because through that passion, reddened with the color of purple blood, they were found worthy to ascend to the joys above.

But what follows in the description of the litter—“he paved its middle with love for the daughters of Jerusalem”—designates the rest of the faithful people, who are suited neither to the word of holy preaching nor to [Col. 1108D] offering their blood for Christ, but who can be saved solely through the virtue of perfect love.

Therefore let us, who are sufficient for neither of these, love God and our neighbor with our whole mind.

Let no one, I ask, find displeasing what has been said about the structure of the holy Church and Solomon’s litter. Every work becomes more splendid the more varied its adornment. Let us therefore insert still more poles and stakes of comparisons, by which we may ascend upward as we build.

Just as any great building can be constructed only at great expense, so the highest virtues can be obtained only through great labor.

Hence our Lord presents the same comparison in the Gospel by asking: “Which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the expenses necessary to complete it?” All who heard this comparison could easily understand it and answer that certainly no one who wishes to build a tower fails first to calculate [Col. 1109A] the expenses necessary for its completion.

Then he would immediately add: “So anyone who desires to obtain any virtue ought first to consider carefully that it cannot be obtained without the expense of great labor.”

This question may also be understood in another way. Since visible things have been created by God in such a way that all who understand and seek God can easily be instructed through them to recognize invisible things, “God’s questioning” means that he tests each person carefully through those same visible things, to see whether he loves and fears God by obeying his commandments or serves his own pleasure by consenting to diabolical illusions.

Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord questions the righteous and the wicked; but the one who loves iniquity hates his own soul.”

As though he said: “The Lord permits both the righteous and the wicked to be tempted, but the righteous resists the tempter and his persuasions. The wicked or unbelieving person, however, either remains unbelieving or, believing for a time and then departing at the time of temptation, desires carnal and transitory things more than attaining heavenly and eternal [Col. 1109B] joys.”

Therefore, whoever loves such great iniquity hates his own soul, reckoning it as nothing that it will be tormented forever, provided that he may enjoy good things for a time.

Just as the children of Israel, once murmuring against the Lord, were permitted to be tortured by fiery serpents, so it happens daily to those who detract from divine mercy or surrender themselves to crimes of many kinds.

They are permitted to be tortured not only bodily but also spiritually by wicked spirits, who may rightly be called fiery serpents: they are handed over to a depraved mind so that they may do what is unfitting.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Many are the scourges of the sinner.”

Likewise, just as the children of Israel, tortured by fiery serpents, were healed when they looked upon the bronze serpent, so all who look upon our Lord, made mortal in the likeness of sinful flesh—that is, believing that he is the Savior of all who believe in him, for they cannot look upon him in any other way—are rescued from all the temptations of the deadly [Col. 1109C] serpent.

Hence it is often read in the Gospel that those who looked upon the Lord through believing—such as the woman suffering from a flow of blood, the Canaanite woman, Mary Magdalene, Zacchaeus, the centurion, and the thief—though they were weighed down by whatever infirmity of themselves or their loved ones, or by the burden of sins, were all found worthy to be healed.

Among these things we must consider most carefully that, just as the aforementioned bronze serpent was not like other serpents in possessing a poisonous nature but only had outwardly the likeness of a serpent, so our Lord in the outward appearance of a human being was like other human beings, but inwardly he was far different.

Other people exist as though filled with the poison of sins, both by nature and by action; but he was free from every sin, as it is written concerning him: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.”

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, considering these things, look upon the Lord with your whole mind through faith, so that he may also deem fit to rescue you from the bites of the fiery serpents—[Col. 1109D] that is, of demons.

As fire is very easily extinguished if all the fuel by which it is produced is entirely removed, so the incitements of the flesh are more easily extinguished if the material and occasions from which they arise are completely taken away. But for this to be properly accomplished, God must be invoked with the whole mind; without him nothing is effective. May he himself, like water poured down from above by his grace, extinguish within us every sinful blaze.

Thus, just as this vice is committed by two faculties—namely, the mind and the flesh—for the pleasure belongs to the mind, while the actual deed belongs to the flesh, so it can be overcome only through the labor of both. And this is accomplished all the more easily when action is taken before the same vice begins to rule through habit. For who does not know that a fire which is sometimes extinguished but later burns so fiercely that it seems to consume everything nearby with its flames is eventually overcome with much greater labor than one which is immediately extinguished at its beginning, so that not even a spark of it remains? [Col. 1110A] Hence the Psalmist says: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash his little ones against the rock.” As though he were saying: Blessed is he who, as soon as evil thoughts begin to arise in him and are still small, confesses them to Christ, who is called the rock, asking him to drive them away from him before they reach the accomplishment of greater wickedness.

As a skilled harpist, stretching many strings upon a harp, tunes them by sharpness and flatness in such a way that the higher strings correspond melodically with the lower—some producing the interval of a semitone, some of one tone, some of two tones, others the consonance of a fourth, others of a fifth, and still others of an octave—so almighty God, holding in his hand all those predestined for the harmony of heavenly life as though they were a harp arranged with corresponding strings, tunes some to the high sound of the contemplative life, while relaxing others toward the gravity of the active life.

When he has arranged them in this way in both kinds of life, he places his finger upon them—that is, the Holy Spirit—and [Col. 1110B] strikes them in various modes. He chooses from among them those whom he will fill with such an abundance of virtues that, compared with the others, they produce something like the consonance of the octave, which consists of eight strings, retaining those eight beatitudes which the Lord enumerates in the Gospel, saying: “Blessed are the poor,” and so forth.

Those whom he chooses for the consonance of the fifth, which consists of five strings, may be understood as those who have already attained such perfection that they restrain themselves from quickly falling through the five bodily senses—namely, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Likewise, those who are chosen by God’s finger for the fourth, which consists of four strings, may be understood as those who strive above others to love prudence, temperance, sobriety, and justice.

By the smaller intervals of sound, which produce two tones, one tone, or a semitone, we may understand those who, through the impulse of divine inspiration, are chosen above others for the twofold love of God and neighbor, or for some particular virtue, or even for the state of married life. [Col. 1110C] Although, in comparison with others, this may seem like a semitone, because such a person is usually more attached to the world than the others, it is nevertheless necessary to all the higher degrees, just as the semitone is necessary to the consonances.

But because a semitone is found both among the high-sounding and the full-sounding strings, let us place among the high-sounding strings—that is, in the contemplative life—as a semitone, those married people who are indeed spouses in outward form but followers of the spiritual life in reality, fulfilling the Apostle’s words: “Let those who have wives be as though they had none.” Such people rightly belong to the number of the high-sounding strings. God delights in such a melody, and in such an instrument he places those whom he deigns to draw to himself.

As wise physicians commonly bring the bodily sick to the gift of health through certain inexpensive kinds of medicine, so almighty God restores the human race, which through the transgression of our first parent fell into the greatest weakness of both parts of the human being through [Col. 1110D] many preparations of a lowly antidote. For what can be imagined cheaper than this: that we are born in sins and then, like irrational animals, are provided for and fed by the very meager assistance of parents or nurses?

What, I ask, is cheaper than the fact that we cannot remain even one day without sin, and that sometimes we cannot be bent toward the good except by being permitted to fall into the worst things, so that, compelled even in this way, we may flee to the true physician and anticipate his face in confession? Yet when we refuse to be healed even through so great a medicine of divine compassion—for it is a great act of mercy both to endure the sinner and, by the excessive practice of sin, to show him who he is and where he is heading, so that, recognizing his condition, he may shudder and return to the Lord—God does not for that reason cease to heal us. Rather, he applies to us another kind of medicine, like cauterization, which everyone acknowledges to be bitter but beneficial to bodily health. Spiritually, he imposes it upon us by allowing us to be afflicted bodily in various ways, “so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.”

[Col. 1111A] The Psalmist testifies that such cauterization benefited some, saying: “When he slew them, then they sought him and returned.” But concerning others who had become hardened and sunk deeply into sins, we read that it did not benefit them, in the Prophet’s words: “You struck them, Lord, and they felt no pain”; and: “With cruel punishment I struck you, daughter of Zion, but your fracture is incurable.”

There are also many other forms of humiliation in which we become entangled daily, both spiritually and bodily, so that in this way, humbled, we may be compelled to seek the gift of true soundness.

As a poor person, or anyone unjustly stripped of his own possessions, makes a complaint before the judges and rulers of this world, accuses the robber, and asks that his property be restored to him, so all the saints continually cry out to God over the destruction of their monasteries, beseeching him either to restore to the monasteries the goods handed over to them and acquired justly, or to pass a just judgment upon those who have dared to rob them. [Col. 1111B]

If anyone doubts that it is a sin to rob monasteries or anyone else of what belongs to them, let him carefully consider what is read about the rich man in the Gospel. He is said to have been led to hell not because he took away another’s property, but because he did not distribute his own to others. Yet we all know that it is a lesser sin not to give one’s own than to steal what belongs to another. Therefore, if that rich man was punished for the lesser sin, those who commit greater sins—namely, those who seize what belongs to others—will be punished all the more.

By “what belongs to others” we mean what has been given not for our use but for the use of others, such as the estates of monasteries, given to the monks so that they and their servants, as well as the poor and passing pilgrims, may be nourished from them. Such care concerns all Christians.

But because, both among certain clergy and among laypeople, alas, nothing is more difficult to believe than that it is a sin to seize and alienate monastic estates, I wish to offer another example that particularly suits the argument at hand. [Col. 1111C] For what we have said about the rich man can be applied to all who unjustly seize anything from anyone.

It is therefore read in Saint Gregory’s book that a certain monk, the superior of a monastery which he himself had built in the city of Rome, was devoted to many vices. Among other things, he took away documents deposited in the monastery as confirmation of a certain estate and handed them over to outsiders. When the death of this monk was approaching, he was carried in spirit before God. All his offenses were brought forward, with the devil accusing him; but through the assistance of Saint Andrew the Apostle and Saint Gregory, all were forgiven except the one he had committed in handing over the documents.

If that man did not deserve to obtain forgiveness for carelessly handing over the monastery’s documents, then those who, by handing over or seizing the estates of monasteries that have been retained by right, scatter and destroy them must be greatly afraid lest they fall under the same judgment.

I beg you, rulers, to attend to these matters. Remembering what is written—“A most severe judgment will be upon those who rule” [Col. 1111D]—exhort one another to restore the monasteries that have been destroyed. First, let the estates taken from them be returned to the monks; then let those who fear the Lord and walk in his ways be placed above the others.

For God has been offended above all by the fact that those places dedicated and consecrated to him and to his saints have been destroyed through the negligence of rulers. If those serving God in monasteries had the necessities of life, they could certainly perform divine service more eagerly; they could pray more devotedly for the welfare of their king, bishops, and princes, as well as for the condition of the entire Church; and if they exceeded anything in the rule of their profession, they could be corrected more freely by their pastors.

But, alas, all these matters are treated with such negligence by many bishops that, if anyone needs either pure prayer or suitable correction and admonition, they disdain to attend to it, concerning themselves only with having services pleasing to themselves and performed continually. [Col. 1112A] This too is deeply grievous: since the estates once given to monasteries by religious princes have now been taken away by kings or bishops, no due almsgiving can be carried out there, no guest or pilgrim can be refreshed. It is as though such care did not belong to Christians, and as though we ought not at all to believe what the canons especially command bishops: that they establish many hospices for the care of the poor.

How great a reward those deserve who strive in this way to refresh the poor can be inferred from the Lord’s prediction in the Gospel, when he says that at the judgment he will declare: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.” Therefore I admonish bishops: when, while reading, they seek in the canons where they ought to demand tithes, let them also seek what has been established concerning the refreshment of the poor and guests, and concerning provision for monasteries, lest that terrible sentence of our Lord be spoken to them: “Woe to you who tithe mint and dill and have left the weightier matters”—that is, mercy [Col. 1112B] and judgment.

I wish to offer another comparison for the admonition of bishops. Just as many people do not hesitate, if they find some long-standing negligence in their fields and estates, to convert them to better use, so they may certainly know that if they find destruction in the monasteries entrusted to them, they are even more permitted to correct it for the use of the spiritual life than to follow or increase the destruction they have found.

Let those who have been appointed in any way to the governance of souls and monasteries attend to this comparison. If they find monasteries destroyed through neglect of both spiritual and bodily resources, they not only take no care to improve them but destroy them still further, saying: “We wish to retain in every respect the custom which we know our predecessors had here, in services of every kind obtained by whatever means, because we are in no way inferior to them in dignity or lineage.”

We answer them that [Col. 1112C] if they do not know how to provide for the losses affecting their estates, but allow them to remain in the negligence they found, it is pardonable for them to do the same concerning the souls or monasteries entrusted to them. But if they know how to care for the usefulness of earthly property while neglecting what is divine, they may indeed pretend ignorance before human beings, but God knows every secret of the heart. He allowed them to be placed over others so that, once their own wickedness had been revealed to them, they might correct themselves with all the greater diligence, the more they had discovered themselves to be rulers of the kind they ought to have been—and perhaps had resolved in their hearts to be before receiving the office of rule.

Let us also offer a comparison concerning what is written: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.” It is evident that all people wish good things to be bestowed upon themselves by others and that they ought likewise to bestow similar things upon others; and this kind of exchange is fulfilled among some people, [Col. 1112D] for many customarily bestow such things upon their friends. Let us say, then, how they ought to be bestowed upon God.

Just as we do not wish any fraud, disobedience, or wickedness to be practiced against us by our subjects and servants, so we, who know that God is the Lord of all lords and the most powerful above all, ought to practice no fraud, no disobedience, and no wickedness against him in any matters entrusted to us.

For God has entrusted to us such great things, both in ourselves and in others, that they cannot in any way be described in a brief account. Let us mention at least a few, so that the rest may more easily be understood.

First of all, our soul, made in the image and likeness of God, has been entrusted to us, so that, nourishing it toward that same likeness of God, we may fulfill within ourselves with the greatest care everything we know to be pleasing to God. Next, we have been entrusted with the task of drawing everyone, by words and deeds, toward better things.

If, then, we are faithful to God in such entrusted matters, we fulfill what is written: [Col. 1113A] “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.” For we do not wish any unfaithfulness to be practiced against us.

Let us say more. Just as we wish our servants or subjects, if they have offended us in any way, to seek our reconciliation with complete humility, so we ought to do whenever we offend the Lord by our sins. Likewise, just as we wish our friends and faithful companions, if they hear of any slander or injury committed against us, immediately to restrain it by faithful reasoning—or, if they cannot do so, to flee lest they seem willingly to listen to our injury—so we ought to act toward our Lord if we see someone dishonoring him by words or deeds and are unable to prevent such dishonor.

We ought to be faithful to him, both in working with him and in suffering with him, because he is faithful to us, as the Psalmist says of him: “The Lord is faithful in all his words.”

By this comparison, written and understood in the heart of every wise person, God is sought and recognized; and no one of sound mind [Col. 1113B] will be able to excuse himself from this understanding. Let these things, then, be said as an addition to our understanding of what has been bestowed within us by divine grace. Now let us return to the additions of comparisons concerning what lies outside us.

As the substance of winds cannot in any way be seen, yet their existence is understood in some manner through their immense blasts and movements, so the divine substance, although invisible, can nevertheless be recognized with the firmest faith through the immense power and authority which it exercises over every creature, and especially over those who try to resist it.

For the more someone has wavered in this faith, the more he will be subjected to all the enemy’s temptations. This can plainly be demonstrated from the Gentiles, who, having no knowledge of divine power and saying in their hearts, “There is no God,” are read to have devoted themselves to every kind of crime. Some of them even decreed that the highest good consisted entirely in serving pleasure.

Likewise, those who [Col. 1113C] firmly confess that God exists but deny him by their deeds—whether entangled in some heresy or devoted to capital vices—can resist no temptations. Therefore, only through faithful invocation of the divine name shall we be rescued from the dangers of temptation. Hence the Psalmist says: “In you, Lord, I shall be delivered from temptation.” And again: “You are my refuge from tribulation, which has surrounded me.”

As a faithful envoy or servant, when some good entrusted by his master for distribution is committed to him, is not accustomed to claim for himself any favor or reward from its distribution, so anyone to whom, through divine goodness, the gifts of some outstanding virtue have been granted ought not to acquire for himself any favor on the grounds that he deserved such gifts.

The holy Fathers, having learned through much experience that this is how one must act, did not dare to attribute to their own merits anything they accomplished either through miracles or through other remarkable works. They continually considered what the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” [Col. 1113D]

Blessed Peter paid close attention to this when, to the Jews who marveled at the miracle performed upon the lame man, he said: “Why do you look at us as though by our own power or piety we had made this man walk? God has glorified his Son,” and so forth. The Psalmist also, firmly believing that God works good things in us, asks him to confirm those same things, saying: “Confirm, O God, what you have worked in us.”

As in the fortification of a city, if even a small place of entry is left open, enemies can enter there and devastate the entire city, so it happens to those who think it sufficient to practice some virtues without the others. Wherever care for any virtue is lacking, there the host of spiritual wickedness enters, sometimes dispersing the defenses of many virtues.

Thus we read in the Gospel about the Pharisee, who, having fortified the citadel of his heart with many virtues, neglected to maintain the guard of humility, saying: “Because I am not like the rest of humanity—robbers, unjust,” and so forth. [Col. 1114A] Through this negligence he plainly allowed spiritual enemies to enter him; they even stripped away the virtues he possessed and left him naked.

The Apostle James says something similar: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it.” Hence Holy Scripture, admonishing each person, says: “With all vigilance guard your heart.”

As no rich person clothed in costly garments can rightly blame some peasant or poor person wrapped in a cheap garment for walking about so dressed when he has no better clothing, or perhaps does not wish to use more expensive clothing for the love of God, so no one who overflows with the pompous learning of secular letters and knows various refinements of polished speech ought to criticize the simple words sometimes found in Holy Scripture, which teaches them differently from dialectic and grammar—provided that those words are found uniformly in old and corrected books.

[Col. 1114B] If the books differ, they must be corrected according to both the rule of grammar and the sense of the reading. Such disagreement arises through the ignorance or carelessness of scribes and must therefore be corrected through the expertise of teachers.

Nor should those be criticized who, out of humility, choose to follow the simplicity of Holy Scripture rather than the distinguished eloquence of secular learning, desiring to be numbered among those little ones of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones.”

They likewise fear what the Apostle says: “The wisdom of the flesh is death.” For carnal wisdom, since it strives for nothing except to be proud, to please human beings, and to embrace the glory of the world in every way, tends toward that death which has no end.

As a pregnant woman needs extraordinary care so that, conducting herself cautiously everywhere, she may preserve the child she has conceived, so all who retain the authority of ecclesiastical governance ought to be watchful lest, by some evil example, they corrupt the subjects whom they have taken under their care for instruction, as though to bring forth children of God.

[Col. 1114C] Hence the Apostle Paul says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” How he would labor to give birth to them so that Christ might be formed in them, he states elsewhere: “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected.”
