For if, while preaching to others about observing the divine commandments, he himself did not observe them, he would certainly corrupt those whom he had undertaken spiritually to beget. Through this comparison, those already placed in positions of governance are admonished to consider why they have been set over others.

Through the comparison which follows, those who desire to be placed over others without election and contrary to the regulations of the canons may be admonished. Just as it is improper and dishonorable for a woman to go about seeking a husband, and it is more fitting for a man to seek the woman who is to be joined to him, so it is wholly unsuitable for any teacher to seek pastoral care; rather, he should be sought out to undertake it.

In that matter, Christ, choosing each person [Col. 1114D] for ecclesiastical governance as though for the undertaking of marriage, is represented by the person of the man; but the one who undertakes governance, because he ought by words and deeds to beget children of God, is represented by the person of the woman.

But lest anyone be able to reject this interpretation, by which we said that the spiritual shepherd is to be understood in the person of a woman, let us strengthen it with the testimony of our Lord himself. For he says in the Gospel: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.”

From these words it is gathered that if a faithful person, doing the will of the heavenly Father, is called a spiritual sister and mother, while sister and mother belong to the person of a woman, then anyone chosen to beget spiritual children may also be called a woman.

As our Lord, seeing the city of Jerusalem, wept over it because its inhabitants would suffer innumerable punishments, both in this world and in the future, for their unbelief, so he daily grieves over all who refuse to be turned from their wickedness [Col. 1115A] to repentance by any correction or admonition.

Hence, through the Prophets, he often cries out: “Turn to me, and you shall be saved.” Through the Psalmist he also admonishes us, saying: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.” And again: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened.”

Whoever in this life despises either believing or following these admonitions of divine compassion, although alive in body, is dead in soul and assigned to eternal damnation.

As a mother does not become angry over the various troubles and uncleanness of her little nursing child, which she continually endures, but bears them as her duty requires, so our Lord both mercifully endures all the negligences of our weakness, by which we are continually made filthy, and, if we produce worthy fruits of repentance, forgives them as though they were a debt and cleanses us in the bath of his mercy.

Hence he himself says through the Prophet: “Hear me, house of Jacob, you who have been carried from my womb to old age. I made you, and I shall bear you; I shall carry you and save you.” And [Col. 1115B] elsewhere: “Can a woman forget, so as not to have compassion on the child of her womb? And even if she should forget, I will nevertheless not forget you.”

From these words it is gathered that divine compassion surpasses every expression of human tenderness. Another point may also be gathered from the words, “And even if she should forget, I will nevertheless not forget you.” For although in human compassion no devotion is greater than that shown in nurturing children, nevertheless it fails in those mothers who either carelessly raise their children or kill them immediately after birth. Foreseeing this impiety in women, God immediately added after the words just mentioned: “Even if she should forget, I will nevertheless not forget you.”

As any master is stirred to anger if his servant, when water for washing is nearby and an ample supply of fine clothing is available, approaches him in a filthy and disgraceful appearance, so almighty God is provoked when someone, doing no penance for his sins and negligences, neglects to seek [Col. 1115C] forgiveness from him who is always ready to forgive.

The nearness of the water signifies the certainty of divine grace, while the abundance of clothing signifies the opportunity for good works. For the soul is clothed with good works just as the body is clothed with fine garments. Hence the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Put on, as God’s elect, compassion, kindness, modesty, patience.” The Psalmist also, praying for such clothing, says to the Lord: “Let your priests, Lord, be clothed with righteousness.”

As tiles properly fitted together on the roof of a single house, however numerous or varied they may be, come together as one, and there both the smaller and the larger tiles are necessary, so all the virtues distributed to each person through the grace of the Holy Spirit become one in the perfection of the spiritual building.

Although martyrdom and virginity, along with many other virtues, are especially eminent there, nevertheless those which are lesser are also necessary. Therefore, the person who refreshes anyone with spiritual or bodily food [Col. 1115D] and performs other works belonging to the active life is placed under the same roof as the one who, abandoning all his possessions for Christ’s name, binds himself by the strictest rule according to the perfection of the contemplative life.

The Apostle shows who is the craftsman and director of such tiles when, after enumerating the heavenly gifts, he says: “But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills.”

As those who engage in single combat are sometimes defeated by one opponent and sometimes overcome him, but soon the person who had been defeated for a time, recovering his breath and restoring his strength, throws down his victor, and so they fight by turns until one completely overcomes the other and brings the contest to an end, so a daily struggle takes place between us and the invisible enemies who fight against us.

They sometimes defeat us by enticing us into some sin. But if, immediately observing the character of the contest—namely, that the one who wins now is often defeated later—we invoke divine assistance, our strength is restored [Col. 1116A] so that we may overcome those same enemies. For God knows both our weakness and the strength of our enemies, and he does not despise us when we have been defeated, provided that we take care to recover ourselves.

The Psalmist knew that he was engaged in such a war when he so often invoked the Lord: “Judge, Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight me”; and: “Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me from those who rise up against me”; and: “O God, attend to my help; O God, hasten to help me. Let those who seek my life be put to shame and turned back.”

The Apostle also speaks of this same warfare: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of darkness.” If, therefore, mindful of so great a contest, while we still can, we anticipate the end of our life with repentance and confession of sins, then the wicked enemies, although they may previously have defeated us very often, will at last themselves be thrown down by us as the defeated.

As the children of Israel, once departing from Egypt, stripped [Col. 1116B] the Egyptians of their gold, silver, and precious garments and, carrying these things with them, devoted them to the honor of God, so everyone who turns from the vanity of the world to the purity of the spiritual life ought to act.

If he has acquired any knowledge of secular literature, let him choose from it whatever is precious—namely, words that are honorable and suitable for the spiritual life—and carry these away with him, both for the praise of God and for the edification of the faithful. For many venerable and holy fathers are read to have acted in this way, placing in their writings many teachings which, like gold set in mud, are found in the books of the pagans.

Let him do the same with the other arts employed by secular wisdom, choosing from them whatever can in some way appropriately be applied to the use of the spiritual life. But whoever, after being converted, makes no distinction between what is precious and what is worthless, weighing mud as though it were gold, seems still to wish to dwell with the Egyptians rather than to depart from them and strip them.

Hence the Lord says through the Prophet: “If you separate what is precious from what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth.” As though he were saying: [Col. 1116C] If someone converted from secular life wholly avoids what is not permitted after conversion, while carefully considering and doing what is suitable and necessary, he bears witness to my commandments by separating what is lawful from what is unlawful.

The apostles followed such commandments when one of them, who before his conversion had presided over the tax office, did not return to that business after his conversion, while the others, who had been fishermen, continued to practice fishing even after their conversion.

Likewise, just as many nations were once subjected to the Israelites by God, while a few were not subjected for the purpose that, by continually fighting against them, the Israelites might not grow slack through an unprofitable peace, so our Lord deals daily with his elect. He subjects to them a great multitude of spiritual wickednesses, but does not subject certain others, so that, trained and humbled by spiritual warfare against them, they may learn that they ought never to place confidence in themselves but in the Lord.

Hence the Apostle says: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond [Col. 1116D] what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it.” By “a way out” he means that, wearied by various temptations but crying out to God, they are delivered.

Through this we learn how great is the wickedness of the devil who attacks us and how great is the grace of God that delivers us from it. Once we have thus become more certain of divine grace, we shall more easily endure all the temptations of diabolical deceit. A great “way out” may also be called the fact that whenever we resist temptation, we shall deserve to obtain as many crowns in the heavenly kingdom.

As it is improper, when counting, to say two or three or any other number before saying one, so it is inappropriate for the order of anything to be confused by putting first what ought to be postponed or postponing what ought to be put first.

For just as unity must be placed before every number, so that, beginning to count from it, we may proceed [Col. 1117A] to the number we designate, so all divine things must be placed before human affairs, so that afterward we may proceed in due order to consider or love human things.

Hence our Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me.” He did not say simply, “Whoever loves son or daughter,” but added, “above me,” so that we may learn that God is to be loved before all things, and human beings afterward.

As many princes grant their servants certain small benefits on the condition that, if they remain faithful and render prompt service, greater benefits may at some time be bestowed upon them, but if they act otherwise they are not even permitted to retain the small benefits, so almighty God acts with those to whom he grants temporal goods.

If they remain faithful in the temporal goods bestowed upon them—whether possessions, secular power, spiritual knowledge, or bodily health—refreshing the poor with food and drink, rescuing the oppressed from persecutors [Col. 1117B] or unjust judges, bringing the erring back to the way of righteousness, and occupying themselves with various necessary works, then, if they faithfully practice such endeavors, they will receive eternal goods, which are the greatest.

Many people, both young and old, living religiously, already taste in this life the rewards of divine recompense. For when they strive to fear and love God while abstaining from unlawful things, they are exalted by him through such miracles and virtues that they seem to command heaven, earth, and every creature.

Of these the Lord says: “To everyone who has, it shall be given.” That is, to the one who has fear and love of God, it shall be given that everything be subjected to him in his name. Immediately he adds concerning the reprobate: “From the one who does not have, even what he seems to have shall be taken away from him.” As though he were saying: Whoever refuses to be subject to God alone will neither obtain what truly exists—namely, eternal joys—nor be permitted to possess what merely seems to be something, namely, temporal goods.

As children are forbidden [Col. 1117C] to touch knives and swords, lest they injure themselves by handling them carelessly, so childish and wanton senses must be forbidden from both spiritual and secular concerns, lest, handling them foolishly, they spiritually wound both themselves and those entrusted to them and deliver them to everlasting death.

Hence it is written: “Woe to the city whose king is a child.” As though it were said: Woe to those people whose ruler is wanton, negligent, and irreligious, because, as Holy Scripture testifies, “there will be a downfall of people when the wicked rule.” A great ruin must indeed be said to occur when a multitude of subjects falls into the same vices which it sees its ruler committing.

As wise pupils of a goldsmith or of other craftsmen do not seek to praise their work, even if it is excellent, in the presence of their teachers, but leave to their teachers’ judgment whatever deserves praise, so all the disciples of Christ ought to seek praise from no one except him.

Hence our Lord, telling his disciples how the scribes and Pharisees openly performed good deeds so that they might be praised by everyone, [Col. 1117D] added: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward.” By these words it is made clear that if we desire to be praised by human beings for our good deeds, we shall receive no reward from God.

As a painter uses various colors when he strives to paint an elegant picture, so almighty God painted the appearance of the world and of humanity with innumerable ornaments and colors of the finest quality. Hence it is written: “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good.” Iron is not bad because gold is made at much greater expense; rather, because both will be necessary, both are good. For all things that are equally necessary likewise exist and are equally good. Just as the color white is made known only through a color opposed to it, so every good is adequately recognized only through its opposition to evil. Darkness shows how great a good light is; similarly, sickness shows how great a good health is. For if there were no sickness, health would be reckoned as nothing. [Col. 1118A] Likewise, if there were no wickedness, neither would God, from whom all good things proceed, have anything by which he could be distinguished from the creature, nor would human beings have anything by which they might advance or be tested.

Just as in every school rods are customarily kept, not for anyone’s destruction but for salutary fear, so almighty God displays in the present age all the judgments of his severity, whether they are read about or experienced in some way, in order that, restraining people from vices, he may save them in the future. Hence the Lord himself says: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise.” Solomon likewise says: “Do not reject the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when you are rebuked by him. For the Lord reproves the one whom he loves, and, like a father with a son, he takes pleasure in him.”

Just as it is not in the power of rods when or how severely someone is beaten with them, but in the power of the one who holds those rods in his hand, so it is not in the power of the devil or of any wicked people who persecute others to chastise them according to their own desire, but in the permission of God, who holds everything in his hand [Col. 1118B] and permits some to be chastised for testing, others for correction, and still others for condemnation. The devil and all the wicked, through whom others are scourged, are called the scourge or rod of God. Hence he himself says through the prophet Isaiah: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my fury!” From these words we also gather that, since “woe” is pronounced not against those who are scourged but against those who scourge, those who scourge are sometimes subjected to greater punishments than those who are scourged. Such were Nebuchadnezzar, Antiochus, Herod, and many others, who, after crushing others with various blows, were themselves crushed with a double crushing.

Just as many works can be carried out in summer that cannot be carried out in winter, so also in youth what cannot be done in old age, and in this life what cannot be done in the future life. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “See that your flight does not take place in winter or on the Sabbath.” By “winter,” of course, he signifies the time of the future judgment, in which no flight through fruitful repentance will be found. Solomon also warns us to escape such a winter, saying: “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth,” and so forth. [Col. 1118C]

Just as a poor man goes about clothed in torn pieces of cloth of varied color and quality, so the human race, expelled from its homeland in paradise through the guilt of the first man and cast into the exile of this world, is clothed in varied misery, as though in pieces of cloth of different quality, and thus, like a beggar, turns in various directions for the support of its present life. The Psalmist had perceived this poverty when he said: “Let your mercies, O Lord, quickly come to meet us, for we have been made exceedingly poor.”

Just as a servant, having been deprived by his master of one foot because of some serious transgression, is afterward unable to perform any work with a sound step, so the entire human race, cast down from the dignity of its condition through the transgression of the first man and weakened like a mutilated body, limps in all its works and cannot do anything good without the guidance of divine grace.

Just as on a public and frequently traveled road that has many muddy and dangerous pits, travelers easily become filthy, so those who walk along the common road of worldly concerns are stained by various crimes. Hence Saint Gregory says: “There are many occupations that can scarcely, or not at all, be carried out without sins.” Therefore, since very many people considered and recognized that this was so, they abandoned worldly occupations and fled to monasteries, where they might serve God with a freer spirit. [Col. 1118D]

Just as all who are bodily ill seek and desire bodily medicine from every quarter, so those who are sick in mind ought in every way to seek the spiritual physician, that is, almighty God, asking from him the grace of the Holy Spirit, through which the mind’s sight is enlightened and through which both the ability and the will to perform every good work are supplied together. In this petition they ought to be all the more frequent and steadfast the more severely they feel themselves weighed down by spiritual sickness, attending to the faith of the Canaanite woman and of many others of whom we read in Holy Scripture; [Col. 1119A] and continually recalling inwardly that great argument for importunate prayer which the Lord, speaking to his disciples, said: “Who among you will have a friend?” and so forth, up to: “If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him?”

Just as those sailing on the sea or on any stormy expanse promise themselves no security before reaching the shore, so all who struggle for the love of Christ amid the most dangerous storm of this world ought to place no confidence in their security before, stripped of the bodily prison, they reach the shore of eternal rest. Hence Solomon says: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful.” Scripture says again: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin.”

Just as any faithful person sitting at table customarily tastes none of the food set before him until it has been blessed, so our Lord, whose food is the salvation of all the faithful, determines to taste nothing of anyone until he has been blessed by the sanctification of baptism. [Col. 1119B]

Likewise, just as it is customary for meat to be eaten only when cooked or roasted, so almighty God does not choose us as his food unless all that is raw in us—that is, all that is vicious—has been cooked by the fire of the Holy Spirit.

Just as any master or teacher, when his subjects have done wrong, corrects them as he wishes, either strictly or mercifully, or simply leaves them alone, so almighty God exercises whatever vengeance he wishes upon sinners. Yet he scourges differently in this respect: his will is always just, whereas ours very often turns either toward unjust anger or toward unjust favor.

Just as someone who continually fears being surrounded by enemies, carrying a sword with him everywhere, watches himself carefully, so the person who is continually harassed by carnal desires through the devil’s snares must always fortify himself with spiritual weapons, that is, vigils, prayers, fasts, sacred reading, and the other virtues. Hence the Apostle warns us, saying: “Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil.” [Col. 1119C]

Just as a seed cast into the earth produces no fruit unless it first dies, so a human being cannot produce spiritual fruits unless he first dies to vices and carnal desires. Hence the Apostle warns us, saying: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth,” that is, “fornication, uncleanness, lust.” To some others he said: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”

Just as sailors, when they labor at rowing, first lift their hands with the oars upward and then plunge them into the water, so all the faithful, before undertaking any earthly work, ought to entrust themselves to heavenly grace. For lifting the oars on high and then putting them into the water signifies that spiritual and heavenly things must first be sought, and afterward provision must be made for the work of earthly concerns. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”

[Col. 1119D] Just as immense cold corrupts all the fruits of the earth, so human wickedness and unbelief close off all recognition of divine mercy, from which spiritual fruits arise. Hence it is read in the Gospel concerning our Lord that he could perform no miracles because of the unbelief of certain people. Elsewhere it is written: “Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins.”

Just as a beast caught in a net becomes entangled so that it cannot escape, so a person captured by the riches and pleasures of the present life scarcely, or not at all, escapes from them. He scarcely escapes because he overcomes his accustomed pleasures only with great labor. Hence the Lord says: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.” For those are especially violent who can break through and escape the countless snares of the devil placed both in adversity and in prosperity.

Just as an animal that falls through carelessness into a pit or mud makes no effort at all to get out, so the person acts who, having fallen through the devil’s suggestion into some capital crime or into any negligence, no longer cares how he might rise from such a fall through repentance and amendment. Hence the Psalmist prays, saying: “Deliver me from the mud, so that I may not become fixed in it.” Then, reporting that his prayers concerning this matter had been heard by the Lord, and as though urging other fallen people to offer the same prayers, he says: “He heard my prayers and brought me out of the pit of misery and from the mud of filth.” [Col. 1120A]

Just as a farmer carrying the foulest manure to his field uses it for the good of multiplying the crop, so almighty God does not disdain to bring any good works out of our filthy and evil deeds. These works should be attributed to us all the less, the less our intention was directed toward performing them out of fear or love of God. We must believe that this happens by divine arrangement, lest anyone, presuming upon his own merits, strive to glory in himself, but rather glory in the Lord, as it is written: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord.” [Col. 1120B]

Just as the quality of an engraving impressed in a seal can be adequately recognized only through its impression in wax, so the secrets of invisible and heavenly things cannot be perceived except through the impressions of visible examples. Hence our Lord, speaking of the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom, frequently added some likeness drawn from the present life, thereby making the unknown known, as in: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder,” and many similar passages.

Just as tender and small shoots can be bent for whatever is needed more readily than large and ancient trees, so people in childhood or youth can be converted more easily to the proper discipline of the Christian religion than those in old age, because old age is reluctant to bend toward anything unfamiliar. Hence it is written: “What you do not gather in youth, how will you be able to possess it in old age?”

Just as those sailing on the sea can travel so far from the shore that they no longer see it, so those who serve worldly concerns or carnal desires [Col. 1120C] can come to such a depth of negligence that they neither remember the divine judgment nor believe in any vengeance of eternal punishment. Hence it is written: “When the wicked comes into the depths of sins, he despises.”

Just as a lion and a wolf visibly lie in wait for herds of animals, so the devil, continually seeking someone to devour and drag to destruction, lies invisibly in wait for all the faithful. Hence it is written: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about, seeking someone to devour.”

Just as the queen of Sheba, hearing from rumor of Solomon’s wisdom, came to him and, after remaining with him for some time, saw there a glory of wisdom far greater than what she had previously apprehended from the report she had heard, so every faithful soul, when it begins to correct its disordered affections and flees with all its strength to the true Solomon, that is, Christ, will there experience far greater wisdom and grace than it has heard of him through any indications in writings or sayings. [Col. 1124C] [Col. 1120D]

Just as no one can build a dwelling for himself unless he first has some place on which to build, so no one can do anything good unless he has first obtained a good will. Hence we must pray continually and say: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.” And: “O Lord, grant me the will to do good and the strength to accomplish it.”

Just as fish are never dragged from the waters of their own accord, but only after being deceived by some skill of the fisherman and caught, so all those predestined to eternal life are freed from the worldly waves by the grace of God alone, as though by a certain net cast over their heads. No one enters such a net of his own accord; rather, summoned by some dispensation of divine mercy—sometimes through prosperity, sometimes through adversity—he is drawn there. Hence our Lord says in the Gospel: “No one can come to me unless my Father, who sent me, draws him.”

Just as the vastness and depth of the sea cannot be drained [Col. 1121A] or fully explored, so the divine judgments cannot be investigated completely. Hence the Psalmist says: “Your judgments, O Lord, are a great abyss.” The Apostle Paul likewise says: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” and so forth.

Just as in time of war a much larger number of soldiers is needed to resist enemies than in time of peace, so one must strive with greater efforts in the virtues when either the holy Church as a whole is more severely harassed by spiritual wickedness, or someone in particular is attacked by sharper incentives to vice.

Just as roofs that are extremely badly constructed gradually collapse altogether through the dripping of the eaves unless they are repaired, so it happens to the negligent soul. At first, small drops, as it were, of negligence corrupt it; then, as its character increasingly deteriorates through carelessness, very heavy rains of vices pour in. Hence it is written: “The one who despises small things will gradually fall.”

Just as every grain is beaten out from the chaff by threshing, so the faithful soul, which is enclosed within the body as grain within chaff, must be beaten free from the chaff of vices through various tribulations. Hence it is written: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” [Col. 1121B]

Just as clay is in the potter’s hand, so that he may make from it whatever kind of vessel he wishes, so all human beings are in the hand of God. Whomever he wishes he chooses for grace; whomever he wishes he leaves to wrath. Hence he himself says to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will be gracious to whom it pleases me.”

Just as all eyes are situated in the head, so all the intention of the faithful ought to be fixed in Christ, who is the head of the body, the Church. Hence Solomon says: “The eyes of the wise are in his head.” As though he were saying: The intention of every faithful person ought to be in his head, that is, in Christ. Through such likenesses, therefore, everyone who understands and seeks God can be instructed, so that while he is bodily on earth, he may contemplate heavenly things in spirit and mind. To make him more readily instructed in this, I wish to add still more likenesses of shorter meaning than those given above, because the order of building itself also requires that smaller stones be placed higher than those at the base. [Col. 1121C]

Just as both small and large stones are placed in the construction of a wall, so people of both lesser and greater merit are gathered by the Lord into the building of the holy Church.

Just as a ladder, assembled from two pieces of wood lengthwise and from many pieces across, is climbed upward, so by the twofold love of God and neighbor, into which the other virtues must be inserted, we can ascend to heaven.

Just as the sun’s radiance does not repel anyone who comes into its rays but illumines him, so our Savior mercifully receives all who come to him, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.”

Just as horses running without a driver fall into precipices, so the bodily senses, without reason and the command of the soul, rush toward their own destruction. Hence the Psalmist warns us, saying: “Do not become like a horse or a mule.”

[Col. 1121D] Likewise, just as horses are restrained by a bridle so that they do not run headlong according to the impulse of their will, so many people are curbed by God’s scourge, lest they be able to fulfill the desires of their folly and wickedness. Hence the Psalmist invokes God, saying: “Bind their jaws with bit and bridle.”

Just as the moon’s splendor is nothing in comparison with the sun’s, so all the holiness of the Church vanishes when compared with divine holiness. Hence the Lord says: “No one is good except God alone.” As though he were saying: Turn to God with all your heart, so that you may be able to discover how merciful he is toward all who turn to him.

Just as a little wormwood thrown into a large quantity of honey gives it a swift bitterness, while even if twice as much honey were added to wormwood, its sweetness could not be obtained, so a small spark of wickedness greatly corrupts the good. Hence it is written: “The one who offends in one thing loses many good things.”

Just as every wise ruler, because he orders his manifest [Col. 1122A] judgments wisely and justly, is believed to exercise that same justice in his secret judgments, so almighty God must be believed to judge most justly all the things he judges secretly, on the basis of the evident equity of his judgments.

Just as the sweetness of honey is not known unless something of it is tasted, so the immeasurable sweetness of divine mercy cannot be known or believed unless it is tasted through some experience. Hence the Psalmist says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.”

Just as no full vessel can receive anything else unless what it contained has first been poured out, so the grace of the Holy Spirit will not enter a soul full of vices unless it has expelled those vices through confession and repentance.

Just as innumerable particles are seen in a sunbeam admitted through a window, although they cannot otherwise be seen, so a person enlightened by God’s grace recognizes in himself innumerable sins that had previously remained hidden. For although he abstains from capital sins—which all the faithful must also strive to do—he cannot be without innumerable lesser sins. Hence it is written: “We all offend in many things.” [Col. 1122B]

Just as food must be prepared according to the condition of the sick, so the customs of the faithful must be established with such discretion that those among them who are held by spiritual weakness may neither grow sluggish because of leniency nor collapse because of severity. Severity is needed for the proud and negligent, but leniency for the fainthearted and simple.

Just as many foods are of no benefit without salt, so all virtues are of no benefit without charity. Hence the Apostle says: “If I distribute all my possessions as food to the poor, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.”

Just as the body is nourished by bodily food, so the spirit must be nourished by spiritual food, that is, by fasts, vigils, and the other virtues. Hence our Lord says in the Gospel: “Human beings do not live by bread alone, but by every word that [Col. 1122C] proceeds from the mouth of God.”

Just as a woman, when she gives birth, experiences sorrow but afterward rejoices over the child born, so all who labor to obtain eternal happiness are sorrowful and groan in this life, but afterward will rejoice forever. Hence the Lord says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.”

Just as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings to protect them, so the grace of God covers and protects all who flee to him. Hence the Psalmist, beseeching God, says: “Under the shadow of your wings, O Lord, protect us from the face of the wicked.”

Just as a branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains on the vine, so we cannot bear any fruit of good work unless we remain in Christ.

Just as a tree planted beside running waters will give its fruit in its season, so the blessed man who meditates day and night on the law of the Lord produces various fruits of the soul.

[Col. 1122D] Just as the deer longs for springs of water, so the faithful soul ought to long to reach God.

Just as wax melts before the face of fire, so sinners perish before the face of God.

Just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.

Just as a person cannot hide fire in his bosom without his garments’ burning, or walk on burning coals without his feet’s being scorched, so the one who goes in to his neighbor’s wife is not clean when he has touched her.

Just as silver and gold are tested in fire in the furnace, so God tests human hearts.

Just as a honeycomb is exceedingly sweet to the throat, so is the teaching of wisdom to those who love it.

Just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.

[Col. 1123A] Just as a dog returns to its vomit, so the foolish person repeats his folly.

Just as it is not good for someone who eats much honey, so the one who is a scrutinizer of majesty is overwhelmed by glory.

Just as an open city without a surrounding wall is like a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking.

Just as a horse needs a whip, so a rod is needed for the backs of the imprudent.

Just as fire is extinguished when wood fails, so, when the whisperer is removed, quarrels subside.

Just as the faces of those who look into water are reflected in the water, so human hearts are manifest to the prudent.

Just as fish are caught with a hook and birds are captured in a snare, so perverse people are caught by their own wickedness.

Just as you do not know what the way of the spirits is, or how the members are joined together in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the works of God, who is the maker of all things.

Just as smoke is scattered by the wind, so the hope of the wicked vanishes. [Col. 1123B]

Just as domestic animals are altogether subject to their owners, so we too ought to be subject to God. Hence the Psalmist says: “I became like a beast before you.”

Just as dry land yields no fruit, so the human heart hardened in wickedness cannot receive anything good.

Just as it is a more serious danger for pestilence to spread among many than for one person to be consumed by disease, so it is a more serious sin for many subjects to be corrupted by the fault of one shepherd than for that shepherd alone to die in his injustice.

Just as a viper is killed when it is torn apart by its offspring situated in its womb, so evil thoughts, if nourished within us until they reach the effect of sin, kill our soul by tearing it apart.

Just as it is foolish if a blind man promises to guide someone, so it is irrational if an unlearned person takes up the unfamiliar responsibility of governance. Hence the Lord says: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into a pit.”

Just as a blind person walking easily stumbles, so the inexperienced easily falls into the pit of error. [Col. 1123C]

Just as no one can cross the stormy waves of the sea except rowers laboring with great effort, so no one can escape the dangers of worldly concerns except with the greatest vigilance.

Just as smoke never arises except from the vapor of fire, so no storm, pestilence, famine, or other scourge occurs except because of some merits of human wickedness.

Likewise, just as smoke disappears when the fire is extinguished, so, when the fuel of vices—that is, the desire to sin—has been calmed through tears of repentance and the effort of amendment, the scourges will cease. Hence it is written: “When the ways of a man please the Lord, he makes even his enemies turn to peace.”

Just as someone stripped naked in public is put to shame in this world, so the one who is not covered in the future by any garment of virtues will suffer shame before all the angels and the elect.

Just as the foundation of any building is laid below, and afterward the entire building is raised upward, so every human being, created from the lowest material and formed, as it were, upon a foundation of clay, ought, when he has reached the age of understanding, immediately to be raised upward, that is, to the pursuit of spiritual life. [Col. 1123D]

Just as honey is gathered from various flowers, so every virtue ought to be gathered from various people. Concerning such gathering it is written: “The wise man seeks out the wisdom of all the ancients.”

Just as the running of any horse is tested in an open space, so a person’s will is tested in the freedom of choice granted to him and in the things permitted to him. There each person runs farther ahead of another to the extent that he acts better. Hence the Apostle warns us, saying: “Run in such a way that you may obtain.” Understand: the rewards of heavenly life.

Just as a pipe produces no sound without someone blowing into it, so the human heart receives no good without divine inspiration. Hence our Lord says in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing.”

Just as a useless horse, unfit for carrying any loads, quickly grows tired on the road, so an impatient sick person placed in a community is weak in bearing all that he ought to endure for Christ’s name or for love of his brothers, disregarding what the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens.” [Col. 1124A]

Just as, during a terrible storm, shelters beneath trees or houses are sought, so in a time of tribulation and temptation the protections of divine grace and of spiritual men must be sought.

Just as deadly poisons are given not openly but secretly under some appearance of goodness, so many vices conceal themselves under the appearance of virtues in order to deceive some people.

Just as a pig lying in a filthy wallow is befouled, so is the one who is entangled in adultery and other impurities of fornication.

Just as a dead body is without a soul, so a soul is dead without God.

To gather many things into a single likeness: just as someone who knows letters, when he sees or hears them, immediately understands what they signify, so everyone who understands or seeks God, whenever he sees any creature or [Col. 1124B] rightly considers it, immediately grasps in it, as though reading, some understanding of spiritual life. For example, when he has looked upon or remembered the immense splendor of the sun, he immediately infers from it the immensity of the divine presence, knowing for certain that if a creature possesses such power of radiance, the Creator must rightly be believed to possess a far greater power, though invisible.

In the same way, when he is refreshed by bodily and perishable bread, he immediately infers that the spiritual and eternal bread—that is, Christ, who said, “I am the living bread”—can provide a greater refreshment; and he learns to believe in him and entrust himself to him.

In the same way, when he notices the simplicity or purity of a child, who is called a child because he is purer than others, he immediately considers how he may be built up from this example. In accordance with the saying, “Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” he desires that God grant him some virtue of this kind.

Likewise, when he sees or remembers the beauty of the many things possessed in this world, he immediately considers that, if transient things have been created so beautifully by God, the eternal joys that he has prepared for his elect in the heavenly kingdom are far more beautiful. Therefore, stirred by these thoughts, he strives in every way to become worthy of reaching them.

Likewise, when he hears or remembers the sweet melody of strings or organs, he immediately infers that, if the momentary melody of the present life possesses such sweetness, the sweetness of perpetual heavenly harmony must be believed to be far greater, in accordance with the saying: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard,” and so forth. Therefore, moved by this thought, he often desires to reach that place.

But when he sees or remembers the weak and needy, the poor in either aspect of the human person, he is immediately moved as though by sacred reading and considers how many thanks he ought to give God because he has not permitted him, though perhaps devoted to many crimes, to be tormented by such miseries.

He can also [Col. 1124D] be built up in another way when he observes or remembers those who are miserable in this life. For he considers that if those who are weak or poor in this life suffer such misery, those who are found miserable and poor in the future life—that is, empty of virtues—will be tormented by a far greater misery. Thus he strives in every way not to be carried away to the torment of eternal misery.

When he has considered that it is just for obedience and devoted service to be offered by sons, servants, and disciples to their earthly parents, masters, and teachers, he immediately learns, as though reading in these examples, that the Lord of lords, the Father of all, and the heavenly Teacher must be obeyed and served much more.

In this way, then, everyone who understands or seeks God knows how to read: the more he understands and seeks him, the more ardently he thirsts for knowledge of him. Thus, wherever his sight or hearing, or even his memory, is drawn by any element, there he immediately meditates, as though reading, upon something spiritual.

For when he observes turtledoves, pigeons, or [Col. 1125A] serpents, he immediately considers how he may be built up through them, namely, by imitating their nature in chastity, simplicity, and prudence. The turtledove naturally observes chastity, the pigeon simplicity, and the serpent prudence.

When he also notices the watchful guard kept by certain dogs, he immediately strives to read in them that pastors and rulers of the Church ought spiritually to exercise the same guardianship, watching and barking against diabolical and human wickedness, lest they seize or scatter anyone entrusted to them.

Likewise, when he sees or remembers steps made in any building, or wax or stones, he immediately considers how he may be built up through them. In the steps, he learns that just as one reaches higher places only from lower ones, so no one can reach greater virtues unless he has been diligent in observing lesser ones, in accordance with our Lord’s saying: “The one who is unfaithful in the least is also unfaithful in the greater.”

In wax, he learns that, in accordance with its own malleability, he should become pliable and humble, softened by the fire of the Holy Spirit so that he may learn every good thing, as it is written: “Learn to do good, seek justice, and humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God.” [Col. 1125B]

In stones, he learns to be hard and steadfast against every evil, and also cautious, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Be steadfast and immovable, and do not believe every spirit.”

In these things, therefore, which we have now mentioned, and in countless others, everyone who understands or seeks God learns, as though reading, what he ought to believe or think about God. This includes the nature of all the elements, as in what we have said about the sun, water, stone, wax, turtledove, pigeon, serpents, and other creatures; and the rational instrument, as in what we have said about methods of building, steps, and the harmonious melody of strings and organs. There is also moral instruction, as in what we have said about the obedience owed to parents, masters, and teachers; and likewise every scourge that admonishes a person to submit and show reverence to his Creator. [Col. 1125C] Hence those three young men once enclosed in the furnace of fire, exhorting all things to praise God, say: “Bless the Lord, all works of the Lord; praise and exalt him above all forever.”

For from whatever creature a person is moved to praise God, he blesses God in a certain mode of speech, because that creature makes him a praiser. Since enough has now been said about how you may read in visible things, I ask you to read in them before our Lord, the teacher of all, with as much care as you would wish to see those whom you knew to be instructed by you read before you with all wisdom. For if they did not read wisely before you, they would receive harsh scourges. Believe that the same will happen to you if you do not read before him with pure intention—before him who gave you life and instructed you in every way.

[Col. 1125D] Since we are now approaching the end of the building constructed through likenesses, I wish, following the custom of certain people who build observation towers in lofty buildings so that from them they may look far and wide, that we too should attempt something similar here, explaining how God looks out over the sons of men. Let the likeness of divine contemplation be the watchtower of this building; from it one can to some extent observe both the free will given by God and the fact that this same free will can grasp no good without God’s grace.

Just as some powerful person, remaining in a lofty building, looks down from above upon everything that is done around that same building, imposing no necessity to act upon anyone by his observation, but merely directing his attention carefully to everything done there, so almighty God invisibly observes everything that is done in this world. By observing, he compels no one to any action, but leaves all people to their own free choice and grants them members suited both to doing evil and to doing good, so that through this everyone’s inclination may be tested and the merit of each may be revealed.

Nevertheless, lest every human being, loosened by such freedom of choice, should fall like a wanton beast into the pit of destruction [Col. 1126A], he converts and draws to himself those whom he wishes, both through his inspiration and through various teachings, and also through some cause of sickness or scourging.

Behold, dearest brothers, as best I could, with God’s help, I have constructed a spiritual building upward by means of comparisons, so that through them I might explain, in some fashion, how God is to be sought and understood by us. Now, since the time seems to have come for a roof to be built upon it, I am pleased to construct the roof also from the same kind of stone that I placed in the foundation. The kind of stone placed in the foundation was a particularly apt comparison for the Holy Trinity. Therefore, so that I may continue building in the same manner in which I began and complete the building, I wish to set forth some comparisons appropriate to the Holy Trinity, by which I endeavor to explain that all the persons of the Holy Trinity are to be invoked by us, but especially the Holy Spirit—not because we ought to believe that this person, who is third in the Holy Trinity, is greater or earlier, but because by his activity we are instructed in the recognition not only of himself but also of the Father and the Son. [Col. 1126B]

We gather this, evidently, in the following way. Since, then, it is one thing merely to subsist, and another to be made alive as a rational animal capable of understanding the creator of the whole substance, we who already subsist through the activity of the Father and the Son—for all things were made through them—thereafter especially need to recognize from whom we subsist, how much more excellent we are than the other creatures, and what thanks we ought to render to divine mercy for this. This pertains to the activity of the Holy Spirit, because through him we are kindled to the recognition and love of all goodness, although the operation of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is undivided in all things.

But because these matters are obscure, it is necessary to explain them by means of some comparison. Thus, just as in a lighted candle there is an undivided operation of three elements—that is, wick, wax, and flame—and all work together, yet illumination of those who dwell nearby belongs in a special way to the flame of the light—for those situated in darkness [Col. 1126C] cannot see even the things from which the light itself proceeds without the light, whereas by the effect of the light they see everything—so also, although the operation of the Holy Trinity is undivided, divine inspiration belongs in a special way to the person of the Holy Spirit, who is signified by the light. Through this inspiration we are instructed not only to recognize the gifts of that same Holy Spirit, but also the mysteries of the whole Trinity, just as our Lord promised when he said: “The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things.”

When he says “all things,” he excluded none of the good things in which we are to be instructed. Yet it must not be believed that this instruction takes place without the cooperation of the Father and the Son, just as the light of a candle does not operate without the cooperation of the wick and the wax.

It is also possible to signify by a candle, which is accustomed to shine not always but at appointed hours, that the light of the Holy Spirit does not always remain in the hearts of the faithful. Rather, arranging all things according to the progress or condition of each person, he now illuminates them as though setting them on fire, and now, as though extinguishing that same light, abandons them for a time, [Col. 1126D] so that through this those who have been tested may learn that they possess nothing in themselves, but have all things in God. Hence it is written that the spirit of prophecy was sometimes lacking to the holy prophets.

But as great as the difference is between the usefulness of a lighted and an unlighted candle, so great also is the difference between the condition of one who has already been illuminated by the Holy Spirit and that of one who has not yet been illuminated. And just as a lighted candle provides light not only for itself but also for all who approach it, so the person who has been illuminated by the grace of the Holy Spirit desires to benefit not only himself but also all who come to him, through the wisdom given to him.

But the one who has not yet been illuminated desires to benefit neither himself nor anyone spiritually. Rather, subsisting merely like an irrational animal, he seeks nothing by which he might subsist or what he owes to God in view of the excellence of human nature.

Many testimonies of Sacred Scripture can be found which indicate that all the gifts of divine mercy are bestowed upon the faithful through the grace of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1127A] For example, the Lord himself says through the Prophet: “Upon whom my Spirit rests,” and so forth—signifying, namely, by the agent and giver the efficacy of spiritual gifts.

A similar statement is read in the Gospel, spoken by the Lord to the disciples: “If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts, ... the good Spirit to those who ask him.” By saying that he would give the good Spirit to those who ask him, he signified the gifts of the virtues, which are bestowed through the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

Elisha likewise said to Elijah: “I beg you, let your spirit be doubled in me.” By the person of the Spirit he signified, evidently, all the gifts of the virtues that Elijah had received from God. For he possessed nothing of himself that was worthy of desire.

The passage also in which it is read that, when the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles, he bestowed upon them knowledge of all languages and confidence to speak against all their adversaries sufficiently indicates to all the faithful [Col. 1127B] what that same Spirit is able to do and how great are the gifts bestowed through his grace. Concerning all these things the Apostle gives the clearest testimony when he says: “One and the same Spirit works all things,” and so forth.

These statements, then, as I believe, are sufficient for what I said: that the grace of the Holy Spirit is to be specially invoked by us. Now I also wish to explain how he seems to be near us—not spatially, but by consoling us; hence he is called *paraclesis*, that is, “consolation.” In the same way, the Samaritan in the Gospel is said to have been near the man who fell among robbers because he showed him mercy. For every merciful person is proved to be near the miserable.

Although this meaning is sufficient to establish the testimony of the promised explanation, I am nevertheless pleased to clarify the same meaning by another comparison. It is known to all who know how to count that, when three units are stated for the three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the third unit is nearest to plurality, that is, to four and the numbers that follow. And to anyone who, by counting through these numbers, wishes to approach the persons of the Holy Trinity, [Col. 1127C] the third person is encountered first.

From this it is made intelligible that, just as the unit and the third person are nearest to plurality, by which human beings are signified, and just as one cannot pass from that plurality to the second unit except through the third, so the grace of the Holy Spirit—which is established as near to us and is signified by the third unit—must always be invoked first and entreated from the Father and the Son, so that by his inspiration he may direct us into the way of righteousness.

For, as the Apostle says: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” If, then, no one can utter the name of such great power except in the Holy Spirit, it is plainly evident that no good action can be performed without him, and that through him we are to be introduced into the way of complete salvation, that is, to Christ, the Son of God.

And when we have been led to him by this faith, he, like a doorkeeper, will lead us to the first Unity, that is, to the Father. Thus the promise of the same Lord is fulfilled when he says: “I am the door,” and, “Whatever you ask the Father,” [Col. 1127D] and so forth. For whoever believes that he cannot be saved except in the name of the Son of God finds that he himself becomes the door of salvation. But whoever believes otherwise should attend to what he says elsewhere: “No one comes to the Father,” and so forth.

Therefore the eucharistic prayers in which the person of our Lord Jesus Christ is not mentioned are to be concluded in this way: “Through Christ our Lord,” or “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son,” and so forth, if you wish to commemorate the whole Trinity. But if, in the concluding division of the prayer, the person of the Son has been mentioned, there is no need to repeat the same person at the end; it is enough to say: “Who lives with you,” or “Who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit,” and so forth. Thus it comes about that we ask all things either in the name of the Lord or of the whole Trinity.

Let these statements, then, stand against those who believe that the invocation of God the almighty Father alone is sufficient for them, without the person of the Son and the Holy Spirit. To them I say again what I said above: just as, from plurality—by which all human beings are signified—before they attain that unity of divine grace [Col. 1128A] for which our Lord Jesus Christ also prays when he says to the Father, “I ask that they may be one, as we are”—just as no one can reach the first unity by counting except through the proper order of the third and second units, so no one can come to the Father unless he believes that the grace of both—the Son of God, that is, and the Holy Spirit—must equally be invoked.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let all these things that I have said to you about the Holy Trinity serve as the roof and protection of our building, which I constructed by means of comparisons. And, so that it may stand more pleasantly, I am pleased to place upon the roof the trophy of the holy cross, expressed by an appropriate comparison.

For just as any powerful person, striving to grasp and draw many things to himself, stretches out his arms in order to draw them, so our Lord Christ, stretched out upon the cross by his hands, mystically drew to himself all that he wished. Hence he said: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.” Among all these things [Col. 1128B] may he also deign to draw us to himself, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## ON PSALM XC

Because the devil does not cease tempting the members of Christ at night and likewise during the day, the Psalmist bears witness when he says: “His truth will surround you with a shield; you will not fear the terror by night, the arrow flying by day, the business that walks about in darkness, or the assault and the demon of noonday.” The character of the temptations is expressed according to the diversity of the hours.

What else is the shield of truth than love of righteousness? For every lover of righteousness is proved to be an advocate of truth. By embracing righteousness, he strives to defend the truth. The faithful mind is rescued from five swift attacks, described below, if it is fortified beforehand with the shield of truth.

First, it escapes free from the terror by night. The terror by night is the present life, whose darkness surrounds us as we make our way toward our homeland. Meanwhile, as we journey without interruption, we endure the secret and open warfare administered by the ancient enemy. Nevertheless, although we are surrounded as if by the blind darkness of night, we are often quite unable to discern clearly from which direction the blows are aimed against us.

If, at any time, an arrow shot from the bow of deceit attacks you yourself, then, because you have devoted yourself to serving under the commands of the supreme King, you have from that moment taken up his shield. Fulfill your promise; beware of lying, lest, I beg you, you become one who turns backward. In this way you will surely see the arrow of wickedness turning aside from you, its wound having been rendered ineffectual.

What, then, is signified by the arrow except iniquity that attacks unexpectedly? And what is represented by the name of “day” except discernment? The arrow therefore flies by day when, once the cloud of lack of discernment has been removed, the person who is tempted perceives that what seeks to conquer the virtues of the soul is unquestionably sin.

The enemy sometimes appears to negotiate with a person, when he so instills in him the pleasure of committing wickedness that he remains suspended between rejecting what the enemy persuades him to do and carrying it out. Here the name “business” (*negotium*) plainly seems to resound. For *negotium* is said as though it meant “denial of leisure” (*negans otium*). Therefore everyone who suffers a diabolical attack, wavering between either alternative, experiences the power of this “business.” No rest is granted him until the choice between perseverance and ruin has been settled.

And since he is often found ineffective in this matter, having been overcome, he exerts all his strength against such a combatant. But when he sees the person wavering, as though conducting business, he immediately strikes him with the greatest force and drags him, with whatever strength he can, into the abyss of pleasure. This is what is expressed by the term “assault.”

What more is there to say? There follows the violent fury of the demon of noonday, which attracts the person’s consent to foul pleasure. For just as, when the sun has risen to the zenith of the noonday region, it has no higher place to which it can rise, so the evil spirit, after enticing the soul into consenting to it, finds no higher place into which it may creep.

[Col. 1129]

## VENERABLE BEDE’S EXPOSITION OF THIS VERSE OF GENESIS:

“Rise, go out from this place, because the Lord will destroy this city.” And he seemed to them to be speaking as though in jest (Gen. XIV, 19).

*(From Sirmond [Note: [Col. 1129A]*

Sirmond, reporting that exposition of Bede, says: “Bede, intensely learned in the divine Scriptures, while expounding that passage of Genesis, asserted without hesitation that the good and the wicked are predestined.”

The author of the book *On Three Epistles*, chapter 7, likewise quotes this testimony in full and attributes it to the holy doctor of the Church, the priest Bede, who was expounding the passage in Genesis, chapter XIX, concerning Lot’s rescue from the destruction of the Sodomites. It is not, however, found in Bede’s exposition or commentary on that chapter of Genesis that is extant today.]

, vol. II, p. 970.)

[Col. 1129A] The fact that the angels shut the door on Lot, so that the Sodomites could not seize either him himself or anyone from his household and carry them away to destruction, plainly indicates that no one of God’s elect will be destroyed by the ungodliness and persecution of the reprobate, since the Lord says concerning his sheep: “And I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them from my hand” (John X, 23).

Likewise, the fact that Lot, although the angels had given him the opportunity, could not bring any of the treacherous citizens back to salvation—not even his own relatives or friends, though he tried very hard—signifies that no human labor can add even one soul to the number of the predestined, who were chosen by the Lord before the foundation of the world. “God knows those who are his” (II Tim. II, 19).

Nevertheless, although the weakness of those who belong to the lot of the elect is hidden from us, we must not therefore cease to take care for our salvation, nor must our tongue be restrained from instructing our neighbors. Rather, following the example of blessed Lot, we must live chastely and also extend the duty of piety toward the correction of those who err. For it is certain that, although we cannot save those predestined to destruction, we nevertheless do not lose the reward of our kindness, which we have expended for their salvation.
